## Volume Front Matter

### Series Title Page

**The Complete Course of Patrology, or Universal Library, Complete, Uniform, Convenient, Economical, of All the Holy Fathers, Doctors, and Ecclesiastical Writers Who Flourished from the Apostolic Age to the Time of Innocent III; a Chronological Reprinting of All Extant Monuments of Catholic Tradition Through the First Twelve Centuries of the Church, According to the Most Accurate Editions, Collated with One Another and with Certain Manuscripts, and Most Carefully Corrected; Continually Elucidated by Dissertations, Commentaries, and Variant Readings; Enlarged by All Works Discovered after the Most Extensive Editions completed during the last three centuries; Furnished with Particular Analytical Indexes Following Either Individual Volumes or Authors of Some Importance; Arranged with Chapters Properly Disposed within the Text Itself, and with Titles at the Upper Margin of Each Page Indicating the Subject Matter Treated; Expanded by Works Both Doubtful and Apocryphal but Possessing Some Authority in Relation to Ecclesiastical Tradition; Enriched with Two General Indexes: One, namely, of Subjects, by consulting which whatever each Father wrote on any theme may be perceived at a glance; the other, of Sacred Scripture, from which the reader may readily discover which Fathers commented upon each scriptural text of each book, and in what passages of their works.**

A most accurate edition, easily to be preferred to all others if one considers: the clarity of its type, the quality of its paper, the completeness of its text, the perfection of its correction, the variety and number of works reprinted, the highly convenient form of its volumes, consistently alike throughout the course of the whole work, the modesty of its price, and especially this single methodical and chronological collection of six hundred fragments and minor works hitherto scattered here and there, but now for the first time gathered in our library from works belonging to every age, place, language, and form.

**Second Series, in Which Are Published the Fathers, Doctors, and Writers of the Latin Church from Gregory the Great to Innocent III.** Edited by J.-P. Migne, editor of the *Library for the Entire Clergy*, or of complete courses in the individual branches of ecclesiastical science. Patrology has been issued from the press in two editions: one Latin, the other Greek-Latin. — The twelve hundred volumes of the Latin edition are sold for one thousand francs; the thirteen hundred Greek-Latin volumes for one thousand eight hundred francs. — The purely Latin edition embraces all authors, Western as well as Eastern; the latter, however, are given in it only in Latin translation.

# A.D. 1118: Paschal II, Roman Pontiff

[Col. 0009]

## Notice from the Bullarium

(Vol. II, p. 111.)

[Col. 0009A] Paschal II, a Tuscan by nation and a native of Bleda, formerly Rainerius or Ragingerius, was a monk of Cluny and abbot of the monastery of Saints Lawrence and Stephen outside the walls, then cardinal-priest of the title of St Clement. He was elected Roman pontiff on 13 August 1099 and consecrated on the following day. He sat in the pontificate for eighteen years, five months, and seven days.

> [Note: Col. 0009B] Thus it is read in the fourth of the catalogues prefixed to Baronius’s *Critics*. In the sixth, nine days are read, both endpoints being included; in the seventh, eight days, with the day of death included; in the eighth, six months, through the copyist’s carelessness, and seven days.

The emperors were Alexius Comnenus in the East and the two Henrys, III and IV, in the West. He died on 21 January, A.D. 1118, and was buried in the Lateran patriarchal palace.

> [Note: Col. 0009B] Baronius places the death of Pope Paschal on the eighteenth of this month, and adds only four days to his pontificate of eighteen years and five months, relying upon the authority of Pandulf of Pisa, who writes that Paschal paid the debt of the flesh on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of February. But since, according to the same author Pandulf, the see was vacant for three days, while Gelasius, his successor, was elected on 25 January, as we shall show, the reading should apparently be the twelfth day before the Kalends of February.

The see was vacant for three days.

> [Note: Col. 0010B] As is stated by the eighth of the catalogues mentioned above.

## The Twenty-Fourth Schism in the Church, Threefold

In the first or second year after the election of Pope Paschal, Guibert, the antipope whom we have said was called Clement III, fled from place to place and at last, unhappy man, ended his final day in flight. Yet the Church’s tranquillity was not thereby restored. For, through the agency of Henry [III], says Baronius, three false pontiffs, succeeding one another, were set up after Guibert: Albert, Theodoric, and Maginulf, unhappy branches of the curse withering away from their own root.

[Col. 0009B] “After Guibert’s death,” says Pandulf of Pisa, “two popes were immediately chosen, one after the other. One was captured by the faithful on the very day of his election; the other on the 105th day after his election. Albert was confined at St Lawrence; Theodoric was assigned, by the judgment of the Fathers, to learn the eremitical life at Holy Trinity in Cava. A third was also chosen, named Maginulf, formerly an archpriest, who assumed the name Silvester IV. Because by tales of necromancy he had enticed the simple populace—especially those who had taken refuge with him because of consciousness of crimes or ambition for future advancement—he set a heavy foot upon the Church. But while, trusting in auguries, he strove to obtain the pontificate, which could not be given by the devil, he deservedly lost it, being deprived of divine assistance; and the unhappy man was not permitted to retain the priesthood which he had seized without God. He also lost the city, and, an exile afflicted by severe poverty and miseries, ended his life along with his crime, his tongue, as they say, having been gnawed away.”

[Col. 0009]

## Notice from the Councils

(Mansi, vol. XX, p. 977.)

[Col. 0009C] Paschal was born in Tuscany, son of Crescentius and Alsatia, and was formerly called Rainerius. From being abbot of the monastery of Saints Stephen and Lawrence, through the counsel and exhortation of his predecessor Urban, and amid the common applause of all clergy and people, he reluctantly attained the pontificate in A.D. 1099, on the Ides of August, while Henry IV and Henry V were emperors. He held it, as had been revealed to a certain religious man, according to Dodechin, on a slip partly clean and partly rough, for eighteen years, five months, and nine days.

Under Hugh, abbot of Cluny, he cultivated monastic life, and Gregory VII made him cardinal-priest of the title of St Clement. At the beginning of his pontificate, Guibert the antipope, called Clement III, died at Rome in the Castle of St Angelo. For twenty-one years, through a most ruinous schism, he had troubled the Church under the three preceding pontiffs. He was buried at Ravenna, where, five years later, his corpse was exhumed and reduced to ashes by authority of the Council of Mainz. That council had decreed that bishops who defended the Henrician heresy should be deposed from their sees if alive, but drawn from their tombs and burned if dead.

[Col. 0011B] After the death of the false pontiff Clement III, three antipopes and false pontiffs were in rapid succession forced upon the Apostolic See by schismatic cardinals in opposition to Paschal: Albert of Alatri, Theodoric the Roman, and Silvester IV. The first, while imprudently approaching to harass Rome, was intercepted by Paschal’s soldiers; after four months of his see, he was compelled to renounce the pontificate and was banished to the monastery of St Lawrence. The second, wandering incautiously through Campania, was captured by a pontifical force; he abjured the Guibertine schism and entered the monastery of the Holy Trinity, where he led a solitary life, after violently and tyrannically invading the Apostolic See for three months. God, who is supremely good, swiftly removed the third from the world, stripped as he was of all resources and therefore languishing in great distress of mind; thus He afterward granted peace and concord to the holy Church, which had been troubled by a long schism.

Paschal ordered Philip, king of the Franks, excommunicated by decree of the Council of Poitiers because he refused to dismiss the concubine he had introduced; in this way he brought him to seek repentance and absolution. He fought most vigorously against investitures of churches usurped by kings of various realms in England, France, and Germany, through St Anselm—banished for this reason for three years—Ivo, and other resolute defenders of ecclesiastical liberty and immunity; and against both Henry IV and Henry V, father and son, the latter heir to sacrilege, even until his own imprisonment.

[Col. 0011D] For he excommunicated Emperor Henry III and his father, Henry IV, king of Germany, on account of the stain of simony and other crimes mentioned below at the Lateran Council; he deprived them of the insignia and ornaments of kingdom and empire. Henry’s son was substituted for his father by the common agreement of the magnates: Henry V, king of Germany, equally hostile to the Roman pontiff and the Church of God.

For, by God’s just judgment, after he had captured his excommunicated father at Bingen, thrown him into prison, and compelled him to resign the empire and all its ornaments; after he had driven him thence to Cologne and, when Cologne was besieged, to Liège, where, after writing letters concerning the injury done to him and lodging an appeal to the Apostolic See, he died suddenly; and finally, at the pope’s urging, had left the dead and excommunicated man’s exhumed body unburied for five years—then, in A.D. 1110, he made for Rome, both to receive from Paschal the imperial crown according to ancestral custom and to reclaim his rights, which he complained had been diminished at the Council of Troyes.

[Col. 0012A] When he had reached Sutri, says John of Tusculum, bishop of that time, in a letter to Richard, pontiff of Albano, preserved in Papirius Masson: “He sent certain envoys to Rome, who confirmed by oath that they would conduct the envoys of Lord Pope Paschal safely to him and back; that they would bind the king himself by oath utterly to renounce every investiture of churches, even to give hostages lest he return to this enormity, and entirely to leave ecclesiastical property, royal rights, and the patrimonies of Blessed Peter free and undisturbed; and that he would give hostages for security when the pope went out to the basilica of Blessed Peter to crown him.

“Afterward, on the Church’s side, secular men confirmed that, if the aforesaid king observed what had been promised, our lord would receive him kindly and place the royal diadem upon him; and that, once crowned, he might enter the city if he wished. He also received hostages for the crossing of the bridge, in return for whom he gave an oath that, if the king crossed the bridge on that Sunday, he would restore them on that very day to the free custody of our party.

[Col. 0012C] “When, therefore, all these oaths had been partly performed and hostages had been given, as the pope went out to St Peter’s church to crown him, the king disregarded both oaths and hostages, violently seized the pope in that very church along with the bishops, cardinals, and many Romans, and held him in the strictest captivity. On the following day, however, the Romans gathered together and attacked the enemies of the Church, compelling them to flee from the portico, after many of their men had been killed and horses, tents, money, and countless furnishings lost. After this all the Romans unanimously swore, with one mind and one will, to fight against him.”

Later writers, on the authority of I know not whom, assert that the emperor committed that treachery only when the pontiff, having been asked, refused to confirm the election of those bishops whom the emperor had formerly elected. How much credit should be given to Abbot of Ursperg and the writers who follow him in relating these events, I have explained above.

While the pope had been captured and detained for some time in the city of Viterbo, the emperor was recalled by the citizens; receiving from the pope the investitures of bishops—that is, ring and staff—he took care to reconcile the pope and the Roman citizens by gifts. Crowned by the pope, he received imperial favour and title in the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1111, the sixth year of his reign from the time when his father had resigned the royal rights to him.

[Col. 0013A] Sigebert, partisan of the schismatic emperors, adds that during the celebration of Mass the pontiff gave the emperor the body of the Lord to confirm peace, saying:

> “Lord Emperor, we give you this body of the Lord, born of the Virgin Mary and suffering on the cross for us, as the holy and apostolic Church maintains, as confirmation of true peace between me and you.”

So Sigebert.

After these things had been transacted, the emperor, having obtained what he desired, returned to Germany. Paschal, however, afterward held a synod of bishops at the Lateran and rejected the privilege concerning the granting of investitures, recounted above, which had been extorted from him by imperial threats and terrors, “as a privilege”—these are the words of Godfrey of Viterbo.

[Col. 0014A] Paschal’s letter from the synod to the emperor is preserved by Dodechin in the appendix to Marianus Scotus; you will find it printed below, together with several other pieces on this subject. He granted a dispensation for the impediment of consanguinity in the marriage contracted between Bolesław, duke of Poland, and Sbislava, daughter of the king of Rus’, who was related to him in the fourth degree of consanguinity.

Pope Paschal died in A.D. 1118, on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of February, after sitting for eighteen years, five months, and four days. He was buried in the Lateran basilica.

[Col. 0013]

# Life of Pope Paschal II, by Peter of Pisa

(Bollandists, in the *Propyleum to the Acts of the Saints for May*, p. 314.)

## Editorial Notice

The continuator of Hermann the Lame, ending with the first year of this pontiff and writing thus concerning the preceding year in which he was created, says:

> “At Rome the venerable Pope Urban, second of that name, after governing the Roman See for eleven years and five months, departed this life at last, after many tribulations, on the fourth day before the Kalends of August. After his death Lord Paschal, also called Regingerus, was ordained the 162nd pope in succession; and it was everywhere proclaimed that this had taken place through divine revelation. He was ordained by clergy and people on the sixteenth day after the death of his predecessor, and celebrated the Nativity of the Lord at Rome in great peace.”

This pontiff is said to have belonged to the province of Flaminia, insofar as Suburbicarian Tuscany—where Bleda, undoubtedly ancient Blera, lies twenty-four Roman miles from Rome, on the left of the Flaminian Way—is concerned. Although his history is lengthy, it should please the reader to find it written by a contemporary author, P., and preserved in our manuscript. Orderic Vitalis says “that he was a monk from the Valley of the Bruttians.” That he was a monk will soon be evident from the *Life*. I know the Bruttians as an ancient people of Calabria; but I have as yet found no Valley of the Bruttians in Tuscany. That this denotes a monastery is more clearly indicated by the same writer when he says in Book X:

> “When Pope Urban died, Rainerius, monk of the Valley of the Bruttians, was elected Pope Paschal and was canonically consecrated on the sixteenth day after the passing of his predecessor,”

that is, after 29 July. This agrees excellently with what has been said and will be said, and Vitalis later confirms the same thing, before the middle of that book.

Baronius calls the author of the *Life*, whose name we find written only as the initial P., Peter; and it is probable that he was Peter of Pisa, whom Ciacconius calls the pope’s secretary. St Bernard had to labour for his reconciliation because, as a schismatic, he had adhered to the antipope Anacletus against Pope Innocent. This Pisan had proposed, as I have said, to write of the deeds of the Pisans; afterward he was a priest, but at that time a cardinal-deacon. Pandulf, whose style is otherwise very different, may perhaps not yet have been a cleric; from him we shall have the Lives of the two following pontiffs. This author also differs in birthplace from the Peter of Pisa already mentioned—although they share the initial P.—for he had the same native place as his uncle Hugh of Alatri.

As to this pontiff’s bulls, Doublet, in his *History of Saint-Denis*, p. 475, says that Paschal was the first to have the heads of Saints Peter and Paul, with a cross between them, impressed upon the reverse side of leaden bulls, which had formerly been marked only with the pope’s name. They may be seen in their original form in Mabillon, p. 447. His successors did not immediately follow this practice, however. Dominic Raynaldus, keeper of the Vatican Library, who carefully investigated similar matters in Du Cange’s *Glossary*, declares that he had seen no older bulls thus marked than those of Adrian IV, who first began to sit in 1154. Leo Allatius discusses at greater length, in Book I, chapter 6, of *On the Agreement of the Two Churches*, why in these same bulls Peter’s image occupies the left side and Paul’s the right.

## The Life Begins

[Col. 0013B] **1.** This man, made a monk as a boy [at Cluny], was instructed in the arts of philosophy. In the twentieth year of his age he came to Rome on business entrusted to him by his abbot on behalf of his monastery. The gravity of his monastic order, the uprightness of his character, and the prudence of his resourceful mind in matters committed to him made him known to Lord Gregory, who at that time ruled the monarchy of the supreme pontificate with Catholic firmness. Gregory saw him, tested him, approved him, retained him for a time, and ordained him priest in the church of St Clement in the City. How great were the good things that afterward came to him you shall hear in what follows.

**2.** When the magnanimous Lord Pope Urban died, the Church in the City sought to have a shepherd given to it. Therefore the cardinal-fathers, bishops, deacons, leading men of the City, *primiscrinii*, and regional scribes assembled in the church of St Clement. While many persons were discussed, it suddenly seemed best that this man should be chosen. When the good man learned this, it displeased him; wishing to avoid it, he fled and hid himself. But one whom the grace of divine majesty had resolved to reveal for the salvation of many could not long remain hidden from human counsel.

He was found, brought to the assembly, and confronted; the Fathers reproved him for fleeing. “It was more fitting for me,” he said, “Fathers, to flee than, through the excessive presumption of my mind, to undertake the weight of a burden unequal to me. Nor did it become me, a priest, to gird myself with the belt of that honour under whose binding burden I should collapse.”

The Fathers said: “You must not do so, not so; rather, your purpose ought to be held fast where you have recognized that the wisdom of the divine regard has fixed itself. Behold, the people of the City have chosen you to be given to them as shepherd; the clergy choose you; the Fathers acclaim you; indeed, the examination of the whole Church has found rest in you alone. These things come from God; gathered here in the Lord’s name by divine providence, we both elect and confirm you to the summit of the supreme pontificate.”

[Col. 0015C] **3.** Thus, while he resisted for a long time, the *primiscrinii* and regional scribes changed his name and acclaimed him three times; the response was: “St Peter has chosen Paschal as pope.” When these and other acclamations had been solemnly completed, the Fathers clothed him in a scarlet cloak.

> [Note: Col. 0015D] That is, the violet or blue colour was still then seen only in the dress of cardinals, as Angelus de Nuce teaches from ancient paintings of his monastery of Monte Cassino, in the notes to Leo’s *Chronicle*, Book III, chapter 66, where Desiderius, elected pontiff, consented to put on a red cope. This is the garment called here a scarlet cloak.

A tiara was placed upon his head, and, accompanied by a singing throng, he was carried to the Lateran. He was brought before the gate on the southern side of the basilica of the Saviour, called the Constantinian Gate. He descended from his horse and was seated in the chair located there. Then they ascended to the patriarchal palace, and he proceeded to the two curule seats. There he was girded with a belt from which hung seven keys and seven seals, so that he might know that, according to the sevenfold grace of the Holy Spirit, he must exercise over the governance of the holy Churches entrusted to him by God such care in closing and opening as the solemnity with which the act is performed requires.

After he had been seated in each of the curule seats—

> [Note: Col. 0015D] The Vatican manuscript adds, by way of explanation, that these are ivory seats. To understand their use better, it will help to read Valerius Chimentelli’s learned commentary, *On the Honour of the Bisellium Used by the Romans*.

—with a rod placed in his hand, he completed the rite of election, now sole lord, whether seated or passing through the other parts of the palace assigned solely to Roman pontiffs. On the following day, the fourteenth day of the sixth month, he was to be consecrated pontiff.

> [Note: Col. 0016D] That is, Sunday.

**4.** The bishops who were to consecrate the pontiff came with a multitude of people and common folk to the basilica of Blessed Peter. Their names were Odo of Ostia, Maurice of Porto, Walter of Albano, Bozo of Labicum, Milo of Palestrina, and Otto of Nepi. During the solemnities of Mass, in the proper place and at the proper time, they laid their hands upon him. Odo of Ostia was first in the consecration; using the pallium for this purpose, he blessed and anointed him with chrism.

Therefore, canonically consecrated pontiff by Catholic and orthodox bishops, with the pallium transferred to him and the remaining Mass solemnities completed, Lord Pope Paschal II, crowned amid full praises, immense applause of people and commoners, and the gladness and devotion of the Fathers, returned to the City.

> [Note: Col. 0016D] That is, from the Vatican basilica of St Peter. Since it lies, together with the whole Leonine City, beyond the Tiber in Etruria, it is not even now counted as part of the City; rather, those going there from the borough of St Peter say that they are going to Rome, as I myself have often heard.

**5.** While these things were happening at Rome, Albert, bishop of Alatri, saw through an oracle what was to come. A person of religious appearance appeared to him, and, when asked who would succeed Lord Urban, replied: “Rainerius.” “For what reason?” he asked. “Because of his faith and constancy,” said the other, “the Lord has chosen him.” Again he said: “Do you think that he will live?” “He will live,” came the answer, “and will sit”—and he showed this written—“four times four and three.”

The bishop, wishing to learn the matter, came to Rome. When he saw him enthroned and pope, he said: “What I saw, thank God, I see; and may you see for as long as you shall live.” He said: “Four times four and three. By this number a period of nineteen years is expressed; for, since so many days, weeks, and months have already passed while he has remained alive, we expect through God’s grace that his life will be extended to the same number of years.”

His strength and success in the things of God and of human beings increased and grew through solemn devotion, better hope, and assured grace. Everything in the City was prosperous and wholesome: rest instead of tumult, peace instead of war; in place of seditions, welcome and inseparable concords were joined together. All rejoiced, cried that he had come from heaven, and rightly said that he ought to rule, since he understood the condition of the City, the manners of people, their resources and wants. He began to provide, publicly and privately, for the welfare of many people. He was lovable to all and loved by all, so that each person rejoiced in his pontificate with as much affection as he had formerly been united with him in priestly fellowship.

**6.** Matters now pressed upon him, counsels multiplied, and people and commoners began to flow to him from every side in increasingly dense crowds. They spoke in his ear, brought news, and reported everywhere things now certain, now more certain. Each person began to think that his own interests ought now to be provided for more advantageously. They said that it ought rightly to seem shameful that the heresiarch Guibert—so often condemned in his head by the Church, and for long a fierce adversary of his predecessors, the pontiffs of marvellous virtue Lord Gregory of glorious memory, magnanimous Urban, and devout Victor—should continue his plotting; all cried that they could not endure him.

The Fathers said: “If money is lacking, we shall supply gold and silver.” While his deposition was being vigorously pressed on both sides, envoys of Count Roger came into the City, entered the curia, and in their lord’s manner most dutifully greeted the pope on the count’s behalf. Bowing at his feet, they laid down one thousand ounces of gold. This was received as devoutly as it had been seasonably sent.

[Col. 0017B] With these resources gathered from above to overthrow the aforesaid heresiarch, the lord pontiff took courage. “Now,” he said, “thanks be to God, we can act rather than deliberate. Guibert was at Alba; he made an effort, and Alba expelled him. Alba’s defection drove him from the City. The man held out while he could; God prevailed when He willed. Wretched Guibert—now no pope, indeed never a pope—having left the City and still not secure, rushed into a castle.

> [Note: Col. 0017D] I think the author may deliberately have concealed the name, rather than that it dropped out through the negligence of a copyist. Although various castles of the suburban district are named, including the castle of Gandulf not far from Alba, long ago assigned to pontifical retreat and lately restored and adorned with remarkable beauty by Alexander VII, conjecture nevertheless inclines to the Roman castle situated between Alba and Ostia, since from there escape toward the sea was more readily open. Yet wherever it was situated, here he was “less safe.”

“And here he was less safe—and deservedly so. For, while he proudly tried to flee God, whom he had offended in His servants, the unhappy man was overtaken by sudden death and encountered the devil whom he had stubbornly served. I judge that mortals ought not to know the day of his departure—or rather, of his death—nor should his memory be written on earth, since God has erased his name from the book of life in heaven. He was a heresiarch: let that be his title.”

**7.** Therefore, when Guibert had been removed by divine judgment, Ravennate arrogance fell and the Roman Church breathed again. Yet the devil, instigator of evils, did not lack material with which to divide unity and trouble the Church. Two popes were immediately chosen, one after another. One was captured by the faithful on the very day of his election, the other on the 105th day after his election. Albert was confined at St Lawrence; Theodoric was assigned, by the judgment of the Fathers, to learn the eremitical life at Holy Trinity in Cava. Thus the Lord cast them down while they were being lifted up (Psalm 72:18).

A third also was elected, named Maginulf. Because by tales of necromancy he had enticed the simple populace—especially those who had sought refuge with him from consciousness of crimes or ambition for future advancement—he set a heavy foot upon the Church. But, while he strove through reliance on auguries to obtain the pontificate, which could not be given by the devil, he deservedly lost it, deprived of divine assistance. The unhappy man was not permitted to retain the priesthood which he had seized without God. He also lost the City, and, as an exile afflicted by severe poverty and miseries, ended his life with his flesh—or perhaps, “with his crime” (*crimine* is uncertain in the printed reading)—his tongue, as they say, having been gnawed away.

Thus, when the first, second, and third yielded to and fell away from the impious see, confessing their heresy, the Church—which piously presided over all—was strengthened and came to rest in the one man who was Lord Pope Paschal.

**8.** At that time the lord pope, through his men, attacked the city of Civita Castellana, a place sufficiently fortified by nature, and, by God’s nod and help, gained possession of it through force. Shortly afterward he also obtained Benevento. In those days Peter de Colonna had invaded Cava, a town belonging by right to Blessed Peter; but while he strove obstinately to retain what belonged to another, he shamefully lost even his own possessions.

The lord pope left the City and recovered Cava. Colonna and Zagarolo, towns subject to his jurisdiction, were wisely besieged and prudently taken. They say that in these years there were also prodigies: that in some places the sea occupied the shore twenty paces farther than usual, while elsewhere it swelled nearly a hundred paces upward; that the sky appeared, in the manner of a tent, marked with red and reddish bands from above downward; and that a rainbow almost wholly enclosed it.

9. For twenty-nine days a comet appeared at noon, of astonishing power and length, so that its remaining extent occupied a fourth part of the sky; and before the sun’s setting it appeared together with the sun. Yet even now the Aetna of the wicked smokes, having been overcome by Paschal’s strength; and the more firmly it is stripped on the outside, [Col. 0018C] the more violently it boils within, because the Corsican [villages], namely those of Stephen and of his sons and brothers, had all already been destroyed by Pope Paschal. This Stephen, blazing excessively with anger, seized the church of St. Paul together with all its possessions, gathered all criminals into alliance with himself, and thus threw the city into confusion: nothing was safe in the City, nothing secure outside it; right and wrong alike prevailed together. Incited by these provocations, the leading men of the curia cautiously attacked the church of St. Paul and the stronghold occupied by Stephen. Keys were impressed, Ulysses-like, in wax and iron keys made from their pattern; ambushes were laid by night. While the others within neglected what they feared from without, our men without feigned what they were plotting within; the tower was taken, the gates thrown open, and troops brought in, and they suddenly discovered what they had not suspected. [Col. 0018D] Both sides fought fiercely: the inner tower and steep portico preserved the strength of one side; easy entry and assured reinforcements increased the boldness of the other. In the morning the lord pope, with the full body of citizens, attacked and also took the stronghold, and expelled the sacrilegious Stephen. Since he appeared to be a monk, he allowed him to depart unharmed.

10. The enemies of the Church having thus been terrified, and the City partly pacified, [Col. 0019A] in that year the lord pope held a council in Tuscany, at Florence. There he disputed at length with the bishop of the place concerning Antichrist, because the latter said that he had been born. But because of the crowd of people, who, out of curiosity concerning the novelty of the matter, had flocked together densely and tumultuously from every direction to hear it, neither the council nor the debate reached a conclusion.

He also held a council in Lombardy at Guastalla, at which definite chapters were enacted concerning investitures, homages, and oaths rendered or to be rendered by bishops to laymen. Thus he proceeded into France and held a council at Troyes. There he ordained many matters that needed ordering, and in good faith abolished those that needed abolition.

11. [Col. 0019B] When the lord pope returned, he found the City disturbed—as usually happens in the absence of rulers. The coastal region above [Rome], through Stephen whom he had released, had rebelled and was being occupied after being drawn under Stephen’s control. Indulgence caused the wicked man to grow worse, because one who never ceases to be wicked cannot be softened by an affection of piety into becoming good. He proudly fortified on the outside what he had disgracefully lost within: he garrisoned and armed Ponteclem and Montalto, towns belonging by right to St. Peter. The lord pope attacked these places, captured one of them, and, because of the oppressive autumn in those regions, after devastating what lay outside, left the other.

These alarms made simple people fear that new seditions were arising and old wars reviving, each man feeding upon another’s death; [Col. 0019C] although they had nothing to fear, since thefts and factions would cease with him. The lord pope bore this calmly, partly because the unfavourable season then prevented him and partly because he had decided to cross into Apulia. Therefore, summoning his faithful supporters, he entrusted the care of the churches to the bishop of Labico; the City and its urban affairs to Peter Leo and Leo Frangipane; and the remaining patrimonies of St. Peter outside the City, together with his nephew Geoffrey, commander of the army, to Ptolemy for defence. He himself made the crossing at the appropriate point in his plans; after staying as he ought, he did what was fitting, and returned when he ought.

12. While on the journey, he heard that innumerable and terrible seditions were being plotted in the City; that outside it [Col. 0019D] Anagni, Palestrina, Tusculum, and even the Sabine country had rebelled; that Ptolemy would be the head and strength of this rebellion; that he had enlisted Peter de Colonna, abbot of Farfa; that the forces of the Romans, and Alba and the coastal country that remained loyal, had been ravaged by hostile incursions; and that Ptolemy himself had muttered that Alba should be occupied, lest it furnish the returning pope with an approach to the City. But the Lord, who is accustomed to protect the Church through the faith of St. Peter, granted him a prosperous return.

He summoned Richard of Aquila, duke of Gaeta, and charged him to be his guide on this journey. Three days later he overtook us in the coastal districts, and thus, with the aid of God and St. Peter, reached Alba. At Alba the lord pope was received with as much devotion as he had been awaited with longing; and, after paying the donative owed to the hereditary soldiers, [Col. 0020A] he came to Rome. Whom he found there as enemies, and whom as faithful friends and allies, could not at first be fully determined. But when he began to take counsel with his followers, he recovered all the possessions of St. Peter, among which, with great effort and much loss of life, he recovered Tivoli. Shortly afterward he ascended the Capitol.

“Here,” he said, “Montalto and the other patrimonies of St. Peter must be torn from the hands of Abbot Stephen; and, because of his obstinate pride, punishment without mercy ought deservedly to be inflicted upon his own person.” Therefore, after a small but quite dreadful battle, houses were taken and towers overthrown. They were so terrified that they restored both the patrimonies of St. Peter and those of the other churches which they had unjustly usurped; and, touching the most holy Gospels, gave hostages [Col. 0020B] that they would neither take vengeance for what they had endured nor henceforth injure the Church through disgraceful conditions. Thus victorious everywhere, the lord pope gave the people of the province a peace sufficiently trustworthy and firm; and each person was content with what was his own.

13. This peace flourished until the wrath of divine vengeance drew Henry, destroyer of the land, son of Henry, into Italy. It would be a long matter to recount in detail all that this aforesaid enemy of the Church did on his journey; nevertheless, as briefly as possible, we seek to make it known to posterity. On the journey, by deceptively holding out peace, he overthrew many cities and castles; he did not cease to destroy churches; he seized religious and Catholic men whom he could find; and those whom he could not seize, he did not cease to drive from their own [Col. 0020C] homes. Acting thus impiously, he came through Lombardy and Tuscany.

When he came to Rome, the thing itself clearly demonstrates what evil he did in her who is the head of the whole world. First he swore, then he did not hesitate to perjure himself. What he could do, he did not refuse to do; what he could not do, he left undone not for God’s sake but from fear of men. As has been said, when he began to approach the city, the chief men of Rome had been warned. According to custom, clergy wearing chasubles, copes, and dalmatics received him in procession from the city gate near the castle of St. Angelo to the church of St. Peter. The chief men—namely the cardinals, bishops, and priests—[Col. 0020D] together with the deacons, subdeacons, other orders, and the lord Pope Paschal, awaited him within the church of St. Peter. The magnates—namely judges, advocates, and notaries—all came in his retinue, rendering him the same praise as the others and saying: “St. Peter has chosen King Henry.”

14. Having been received by the supreme pontiff, he would not enter the church until he saw that it was held in his own right and under his own lordship by his faithful followers. The church and all the fortifications around it were therefore surrendered to him. In this surrender he gave hostages—his nephew and other barons—showing that he would keep faith, though he kept it utterly badly. By deceit and fraud he seized Pope Paschal, together with the bishops, [Col. 0021A] cardinals, other orders, and a great many magnates. Of others he made a very great slaughter. He stripped clerics, archpriests, and priests, taking their chasubles and incense; nor did he leave them even their own garments in which they were clothed, nor allow them to retain even undergarments and breeches.

These things were done in February, on 12 February, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1111, indiction IV. For it was the Sunday on which the Gospel was read: “Jesus took the twelve, etc., and said to them: Behold, we go up to Jerusalem, and all things that are written by the prophets concerning the Son of Man shall be fulfilled; for he shall be delivered to the Gentiles, and shall be mocked, scourged, and spat upon.” This ascent was a descent: for as the Lord suffered injury from evil men, so this man was maliciously captured by barbarians. The things were fulfilled in Christ because it had been foretold by the prophets that he would suffer at Jerusalem; in this man, because it had already many times been said that he would not go, or, if he went, that he would not return before doing everything that he wished. [Col. 0021B] He was delivered up by his own people and not by strangers; he suffered scourges and many reproaches from them for a long time. From the aforesaid day—namely, 12 February—until the fifth day before the Kalends of May, the devout pontiff of God was afflicted with many torments. Yet at last, for the release of the Church and of many captives detained with him, he made a certain peace with the aforesaid destroyer; but it did not last long.

15. [Col. 0021C] When Henry departed, peace returned to Rome—not the peace they had merely pretended to arrange, since it contained too little good, but peace was restored to the land because all the possessions of St. Peter which he had taken away were restored to St. Peter. Peace flourished for approximately nine years, scarcely believable to posterity. I myself saw it so great that even a timid ploughman desired it, while a bold robber feared it: every place protected a deposit entrusted to it.

What the outstanding enterprise and admirable perseverance of the Pisans, under the same lord Pope Paschal, achieved in the Balearic islands of Ibiza and Majorca; what equipment, forces, reinforcements, and legate they had; under which consul and emperor [Col. 0021D] they fought; beneath what ensign they served; which of them acted bravely; with how many ships and in what manner they went; what shipwreck and what labour they endured in repairing their vessels; likewise that glorious and admirable relief, in which they did not despair; and how, after tearing captives away, seizing spoils, and overthrowing cities, they returned victorious—because I have resolved to set this forth in a work worthy of the subject, I have deferred it to its proper place and time.

16. Portents of this period. At Mamistra an earthquake overthrew all the walls and houses and buried the greater part of the people in the ruins. While a certain soldier, hastening toward Antioch, sought to flee it, he was suddenly swallowed with his horse by a fissure of the earth and was buried before he was dead. In the same place another man was caught by another fissure [Col. 0022A] of the earth: his lower body slipped downward, while his upper body remained hanging by the horns. At Rome, in the Lateran basilica, lightning struck the sacred tower and cast down part of the roof, the bronze weathercock, and the bells; it shattered a corner of the same basilica and utterly destroyed the pope’s tomb below it. It struck the church of St. Paul from the apse with fire from heaven, so that the lead of the roof melted and the beams visibly burned. Indeed, the whole church would have burned unless the water and the people of the City, flocking together with the apostles’ aid, had prevented it; the beams bear witness to this.

At Benevento I heard of a two-headed being born without feet. At Rome, in the Portico of Galla, I saw this marvel as well: a woman named Gloriosa, glorious in name and virtue, seized a good son, a most daring young man then carrying a sword and spear, by his right shoulder; and, taking hold of him, said, “Are you that villain who killed my husband?” Then, drawing the knife that he held from his over-garment, she disembowelled him. When others wished to take vengeance, [Col. 0022B] she said, “Why did he kill my husband?” Thus, gloriously exacting punishment, Gloriosa remained glorious.

17. In the seventeenth year of the pontificate of the said lord pope, in the tenth year of peace, in the first month—that is, March—on the twenty-sixth day of the month, on the day of the Lord’s Passing, God’s wrath rose from the earth out of the hand of his cup. After the prefect of the City had died, wicked and seditious men, prone to evil, managing private affairs badly and public affairs most badly, elected a young boy as prefect of the City without consulting the Fathers and leading men. The measure—or rather, the excess—of this act was as follows. While the father, the prefect, died at home in a hair-shirt, outside, upon the steps, the son was elected prefect. The father’s corpse was borne to church, while the son’s arrogance was directed toward the prefectural offices. Funeral rites in church attended the father; prefectural acclamations in the atrium applauded the son. They laid the father in the tomb, to render account to God; they placed and raised the son upon the ambo to swear an oath to the people. A wretched event for both. You, father, lost your funeral rites for your son’s election assembly; and you, son, lost the applause of your election assembly for your father’s funeral rites. Let whoever wishes draw the conclusion and say that the father met a bad end, [Col. 0022D] whose wife rejoiced at his death, whose son was glad, and whose whole household exulted because the son had begun his wicked rule; and that the son began wickedly, at whose election his mother mourned with torn hair, his son groaned in rent garments, and the entire household was sad.

18. Both the father’s death and the son’s excess disturbed the lord pope and the whole curia together. Having taken counsel, he said: “Because they seize what is ours before its time, they deservedly lose what is not theirs in its time. Go, Peter, and you, Constantine, and, from all matters pertaining to the prefecture, invest yourselves, for the advantage of the curia, in the presence of this our venerable deacon.” I obeyed the commands. On my return I endured a riot and plots against the life of the lord pope. Having arranged supports ready for assistance, I promised that I would act excellently in the proper place and time, and then announced that I would be at hand for him.

Already that man, amid a riot of people and commoners, had set foot upon the threshold of the Constantinian basilica, when suddenly the oil to be consecrated as chrism—already scented with balsam and prepared—was spilled when the vessel was drawn. [Col. 0023A] The Fathers were disturbed and the lord pope astonished; they did not believe it a portent, because, being in prosperity, they feared no approaching calamity. Again, after other oil had been prepared, the lord pontiff ascended the altar to perform the mystery of so great a solemnity. He had already begun, from his seat in the apse, the prayer, “O God, from whom both Judas received the punishment of his guilt and the thief the reward of his confession,” when they set the boy before him, between the altar and the apse, and demanded that he be confirmed as prefect of the City. Since, according to his lordship’s custom, he deferred his answer because of the office he had begun, they became angry, shouted loudly, invoked God as their witness, and swore their vows that, unless he answered—and if he should think otherwise—he would see the miseries of a cruel fate that day.

At last the lord said: “Why do you ask that he be confirmed as prefect, when neither can we properly grant it nor can you honourably request it today? The funeral rites of this day rightly exclude you from election assemblies, and the chrism of this solemn day justly removes us from such matters. When these have been performed, an answer will properly be given.” They replied: “We shall use the arrangements according to our wish.” Then they departed in tumult; and they would have opened a way for their plans, had not fear of our forces weakened the boldness which anger had swollen.

19. On the following day, the day of Preparation, while all the citizens of this City, especially in the sacred devotion of ancient custom, were spreading in dense crowds with bare feet through the holy places, the cemeteries of the martyrs, and the votive solemnities in the City and suburbs, [Col. 0023C] those men compelled the simple people and commoners, under arms, to swear into the Charybdis of their faction; and they did so more severely on Holy Saturday and on Easter Day. On Monday, as the lord pope went to the basilica of St. Peter, the boy confronted him in tumult near the foot of Trajan’s bridge and sought confirmation. Since he did not obtain it, he began to mistreat some members of the papal household and inflicted injuries on others.

On the return journey, after the lord pope had been crowned according to the custom of that day, while the Fathers were proceeding solemnly to the curia and the Capitol, they pursued them with uproar, shouting, and stones. Nor was this yet enough: they sent delegates after him, and he could not even take off his sacred vestments before he was compelled to answer that deliberation on the confirmation would take place by common counsel on the following Friday. But he was not content with this delay; on that day he caused all the remaining prefectural rights that he could obtain to be carried out for himself. On Friday he blazed into such boldness that he overthrew the houses of those whose religious loyalty would not permit them to act treacherously against the lord pope. Seeing that this ruin could not be resisted without much bloodshed, the lord pope withdrew to Alba. The fury of the boy and his supporters was wholly directed against the church and house of Peter Leo, which appeared to protect it; and he could not endure it unless, on returning, he were supported by his own allies. On his return, he bestowed gifts upon the leaders of the curia in proportion to the arduousness with which he had learned that they would have to be won over by their military exertions: Aricia to Ptolemy, and gold, silver, and an abundance of other furnishings to the rest.

20. [Col. 0024A] Secure in the hope of this good assistance, our party deployed troops along the Tiber to fight them. Battle was immediately joined. Although it seemed as though nearly all the soldiers of the City had to test the fortune of war against our few hereditary troops, our men, with great daring, suddenly won. They bound some of the enemy, by the sacred obligation of an oath, to return to obedience under the lord; others, together with the boy himself, they carried off as captives.

Our men had already crossed Alba, hurrying toward Fumone; they had already entered Ptolemy’s territory carelessly, at ease, unprepared, and unarmed; they had already reached Algido—when Ptolemy came upon them, released the captives, and captured their captors. He did not fear the lord pope, despite the threefold sacred obligation of the oath he had newly undertaken in return for a benefice. This treachery of Ptolemy, once accepted as an example, infected almost everyone with the contagion of perjury, so that because they shared in the crime with their associates, in the City and elsewhere on every side, perjury was held to be neither disgraceful nor criminal.

[Col. 0024B] Abominable to tell! Horrible to hear! By this audacity and this indulgence toward crime, the monstrous rebellion engulfed Sarmineto, Nymphae, Tiberia, and the whole coastal district, together with the entire City. Among many people scarcely one could be found whom probable indications in word or deed did not show guilty of faction. The whole place boiled with engines and weapons in the quarter where the cliff of the Capitol overhangs the adjoining buildings of Peter Leo; they were preparing every possible assault by arms, fire, and hand. Envy, rather than reason, softened them; and it came about that he alone, on one side, endured throughout the whole what all men everywhere could bring together against one person.

[Col. 0024C] Yet the swelling wave of this attack finally began to subside, whether through divine works or rustic labours, since nearly everyone was occupied with the season’s harvest; and the curia itself withdrew into Campania and the coastal district because of the oppressive summer in those places.

21. In the following year King Henry returned to Italy, an open enemy of the Church, and as much more hostile to the good and religious as he was kinder to the wicked and seditious. His counsellors and intimates were the abbot of Farfa, condemned twice and three times in person by the Church for sacrilege and faction; John the Accursed; Ptolemy; and their supporters. As soon as he entered Latium, he made war upon the faithful of St. Peter. He attempted great things, did famous things, but achieved little. For the glory of this victory [Col. 0024D] which he had won—namely, because he had seized certain castles—the Roman people and populace devised a triumph for him. With the City crowned, the king and queen passed through the midst: great display, small glory. No Father, no bishop, no Catholic priest met him. A procession was made for him, purchased rather than proclaimed. Intending to go to the basilica of St. Peter, he crossed by ship, not by bridge. Having crossed, he sought to be crowned. The answer was given: “He who is to be crowned in that basilica must be crowned by the pope or the Fathers; otherwise it cannot be done. If you wish it, it must be requested from them.” A consultation was held, and he sent an embassy in the following terms.

22. “If it had been divinely granted, Conscript Fathers, that the condition of public affairs were governed with worthy moderation, and that their rulers should honourably defer to one another, there would be peace. The emperor of the world would not harm the pontifical office, but each would sustain the other’s glory; the glory of one would be the glory of both; the strength of both, their mutual love, and the fear of all would turn the whole city. We Fathers, we consuls, we leaders, we all would be regarded by the good of City and world; Goths, Gauls, Spaniards, Africans, Greeks and Latins, Parthians, Indians, and Arabs would either fear us or love us. But now, since affairs are conducted otherwise, the outcome is otherwise: leaving other matters aside, we harass one another and are harassed by one another; deservedly we suffer this from all men, are cursed, and are driven out.

“Therefore turn, and receive the request and reform proposed by me, though I am a sinner; lest, while justice hardens against me through you, [Col. 0025B] it may have no means, by multiplying crimes in others, to harden without me as well. Behold: I have come from Gaul to the City to be crowned by the father of the Roman Church, the lord pope. I count his absence among my misfortunes; but now I request this from you. It will be all the more pleasing to him when he receives it, because I have worked all the harder to have it done for me. Men are accustomed to cultivate more carefully what is discovered after long dangers in seeking it. Let there be peace. Indeed, there will be, if you wish. I speak without offence. Surely, once the winds are calmed, the seas will be still.” Thus the king.

23. To this the Church which was in the City replied: “We judge it quite dishonourable and unworthy, king, that you should sometimes address us with sweet words while you do not cease day after day to entrap us with deceitful deeds. Do you think, king, that we should believe you have come to repent and make satisfaction—you through whom we see bitter wrath, continual barbarian incursions, sacrilegious plunderings, execrable ordinations, impious disorders, and incessant seditions being stirred up and carried out? As soon as you entered Latium, king, you made war upon the faithful of St. Peter. If your wish did not succeed, we owe that to God, not to the king.

“Come then: for whom is this action being taken? The abbot of Farfa and Ptolemy, both anathematized. Against whom is it taken? The blessed Peter and Paul. In what places is it taken? In their patrimonies, in their own house. Forgetting these things, king, with those men as leaders you boldly and brazenly entered the church of St. Peter. Accompanied by what clerics? By what Fathers? With which bishops? How can silence be kept? How ought action to be taken? Add also: who are those now keeping watch before its doors? Are they not seditious men? Are they not heretics? Alas, alas! Having expelled Catholics, through you heretics occupy the church of St. Peter, revered by all peoples. Is this, king, the way by which you may deserve forgiveness as a penitent? The satisfaction by which you may be reconciled to the Church? The peace through which wars may cease, seditions end, winds be stilled, and the sea subside? Surely, unless, converted and forgetful of evil, you think differently with God, king; and God, the King of kings, will think differently with the king. We know that we neither ought nor can hold an assembly with excommunicated persons, king—especially since whoever of us attended your first assembly trembles to be present at your second.”

24. Distrusting this response, the king summoned Maurice, archbishop of Braga. Because of his proud frivolity he had become a courtier and, for two years, outside his own Church, had wandered softly and dissolutely here and there in sumptuous and royal display. Before the body of St. Gregory he had himself crowned, and then departed from the City accompanied by a retinue. [Col. 0026A] He was on the road, equally distant from Rome and Sutri, when he heard that the prince of Apulia had entered Campania with picked cavalry and that Pillo was being ravaged by them because of its rebellion. A council was held: they might be driven away if aid were brought before daylight, while the royal army was off guard. Without delay he directed the entire strength of the army there with speed. And indeed the undertaking would have succeeded as desired, if a certain noblewoman from Plumbinaria, seeing the army hurrying in this manner, had not sent a courier to warn the prince of the danger she feared was coming. Thus, while she took precautions for one side, she provided for both, so that the two very fierce armies, now almost in contact, withdrew unharmed, one to Maurice’s village and the other to the fortress of Acuto.

25. After holding the council which he had assembled in Apulia, the lord pope returned to Campania and brought Pillo and Pillano in the coastal district, and the stronghold of St. Silvester, under his control. Autumn was already approaching; oppressed outwardly by its heat and swelter, inwardly weakened, being an old man and frailer in camp, he went to Anagni. There illness so overwhelmed him that the physicians present judged him more destined for death than life. But God, the author of life, prolonged his life. When he restored firmness to the inwardly loosened members of his frame and gave the strength of fomentations to his outwardly exhausted body, it came about that the man who formerly could scarcely sit up in bed even with another’s help [Col. 0026C] later stood upright by himself before the altar and celebrated the solemnities of Mass.

In this state of health he came to Palestrina and dedicated there the church of St. Agapitus. At Rome he celebrated most devoutly the vigils of the Lord’s Nativity, the Masses of Ordination and the matins after Mass, then again Mass and procession, with every devotion and solemnity due to that day; likewise the Octave and Epiphany. Having granted leave to the envoys of the emperor of Constantinople whom he had received there, he came to Rome in a covered litter, intending to free the basilica of St. Peter amid so many enemies. At his unexpected and sudden arrival, such terror seized Ptolemy and the prefect that, before the lord pope should be unwilling to grant peace, it was evident that, despairing of favour, they were preparing to abandon their households and hide in the City.

26. [Col. 0026D] The good pontiff had already caused engines, weapons, and every necessity for war to be prepared by his followers with incredible speed over two days, to complete what he had begun. You would have said that he had conquered rather than that he was about to conquer. But while he did what he wished, the Lord ended the life which he had deferred for mercy’s sake, because it was owed. Two days after his return, illness grew proportionately more severe because of the strain of the journey and the crowd of people, as it had earlier weakened through rest, continual care, and the pleasantness of attendance. The holy man was dying and working. Summoning the Fathers, he charged them to follow him in steadfastness of faith and sincerity of truth; to beware of the deceit of those within and without; to pursue the followers of Guibert and the monstrous German evil; to love one another, say the same thing to one another, and in all things hold fast to that true God whom they loved.

After this, anointed with sacred oil, having made confession, and after everything fitting for a saint had been performed for him, singing with those who sang, at midnight—as one hastening from darkness to light—the honourable old man, indeed honour itself, paid the debt of the flesh on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of February.

27. His body, anointed with balsam and vested in sacred garments according to custom, was carried with due rites and fitting honour, amid a multitude of clergy and people. It was not laid upon an ordinary bier for so great a burden to be borne, but was honourably carried by the Fathers themselves to the basilica of the Saviour. [Col. 0027B] It was placed in its proper seat in the patriarchal palace, on the right side of the church, in a mausoleum of purest marble, marvellously carved, on the eleventh day before the Kalends of February [Col. 0028A].

This most blessed man made very many ordinations in various months: he ordained fifty priests, thirty deacons, and one hundred bishops; he consecrated twenty churches. At Rome, in the second year of his pontificate, he dedicated the church of St. Adrian at the Three Fates; and he likewise consecrated the church of St. Mary in the district of Areola, in the place called Monticelli. He also rebuilt from its foundations and consecrated the church of the Holy Four Crowned Martyrs, which had been destroyed in the time of Robert Guiscard, prince of Salerno, on the twentieth day of January in the seventeenth year of his pontificate. He held a council at Guastalla in Lombardy and another at the city of Troyes in France.

> [Note: The Chronicle of Malleac mentions two of the aforesaid councils. First: “In the year 1107 there was a council at Troyes in France, held by Pope Paschal, in which he decreed that no houses should be burned in any war, nor sheep or lambs taken.” A useful decree, worthy of the laws of Christian warfare—but alas, how far removed from the practice and usage of our most calamitous age! And again: “In the year 1116 there was a council at Rome, last held by Paschal.” And: “In the year 1118, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of February, Pope Paschal died, and Gelasius succeeded him.” Caesar Rasponi mentions his tomb in the Lateran and assigns it a position toward the oratory of St. Thomas. [Col. 0027B–0028B]]

After his death, the episcopal see was vacant for three days.

[Col. 0027]

## Metrical Praise of Pope Paschal II, by Milo, Cardinal of St. Albinus, Monk of the Monastery of Angers

(Dom Martène, *Voyage littéraire de deux religieux Bénédictins*, vol. II, p. 24.)

[Col. 0027C]

Worthy to be magnified, revered by all, feared everywhere,  
You who uphold the temple of Peter in faithfulness to justice;  
By name Paschal, a venerable man of singular excellence,  
Light, glory of the Church, head of the world, image of Wisdom,  
Touchstone of law, pious model to be followed by those to come,  
At whose arrival Benevento’s terror was broken.  
Through him may He be saved whom the Virgin’s womb brought forth.

Though dialectic renewed every genus and species,  
Though great Aristotle recovered all his knowledge,  
Though Cicero and Plato rose again from a reborn spring;  
[Col. 0028C]  
Though Naso brought songs down from Parnassus,  
They would scarcely utter praise worthy of you, so worthy of praise.  
In the nobility of your race you are supremely distinguished;  
In character and life you are more than pontifical.  
Had Rome, head of the world, been duly fortified,  
Long ago she would have entrusted to you the rights of the Apostolic See;  
Your voice would have set nothing before the law of justice.  
May life thus be governed at the supreme Samian crossroads.  
Let not the left hand raise up what is slight; let the right follow lightness.

[Col. 0027]

## EPISTLES AND PRIVILEGES OF PASCHAL II, ROMAN PONTIFF

### I. To Hugh, Abbot of Cluny.—He announces the death of Urban and his own election. (10 September 1099.)

[MABILLON, *Annals of the Benedictine Order*, V, 407.]

[Col. 0031A]

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his most reverend brother HUGH, abbot of Cluny: greeting and apostolic blessing.

How holy and pleasing to God were the teaching and life of our lord and father Pope Urban is certainly attested by his still happier end and by the very grief of the whole Church. Therefore it is fitting that both we and you should give thanks to almighty God in common prayers. Know, moreover, that his death occurred on the fourth day before the Kalends of August [29 July], and was marked by the mourning and sorrow of the whole city of Rome. [Col. 0031B] On the sixteenth day after his passing, we—though unworthy—were chosen to fill his place with the consent of the entire clergy and Catholic people.

### II. Rescript to Pibo, Bishop of Toul.—He confirms for the monks of Chaumousey the altar of a parish church, given by Pibo. (19 November 1099.)

[MARTÈNE, *Thesaurus Anecdotorum*, III, 1171.]

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother PIBO, bishop of Toul: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Just as we must restrain evil when we can, so, when the opportunity exists and God is its author, we ought to confirm good. Therefore we have graciously received your petition, dearest brother [Col. 0031C] Pibo, bishop of Toul, and by the authority of this present letter we confirm the gift which your generosity has bestowed upon the brethren of Chaumousey. For we decree that the altar of that parish church, which you have granted for the use of those brethren, shall always remain under their control in firm and unshaken security; and that, just as hitherto the priest who held the church received the altar from the bishop’s hand, so henceforth whoever wishes to hold the church shall receive the altar from the hand of the abbot of Chaumousey. Whoever, moreover, attempts to withdraw or remove this same gift from the possession of the monastery of Chaumousey shall be struck by the sword of apostolic vengeance.

Given at Rome, on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of December [19 November].

### III. To Bertrand, Archbishop of Narbonne.—He confirms to him, inviolate, the primacy over the metropolitan see of Aix and every dignity or honour which the Church of Narbonne has possessed. (1099.)

[Dom BOUQUET, *Recueil*, XV, 17.]

[Col. 0031D]

[Col. 0032A] PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved brother in Christ BERTRAND, archbishop of Narbonne: everlasting salvation in the Lord.

What Peter merited in the Church by his most true confession, when the Master and Lord said to him, “You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church”; and what Paul, the teacher of the nations, professed—that he bore in himself the care of all the churches—this, we believe and confess, was granted to us, although unworthy, who hold their office in the Church of God, by blessed Peter himself through the one who cried out **[perhaps Clement; the Latin is corrupt]**. [Col. 0032B] Since, therefore, the care of all the churches has been entrusted to us, we earnestly admonish your charity, dearest brother in Christ, that, in the Church over which by the Lord’s gift you preside, you show yourself in all things a teacher of truth and a ruler of justice; that you do not despise the person of the poor in judgment nor regard the face of the powerful. Let judgment always be tempered for you with mercy, so that the severity of justice may be restrained by the bridle of mercy, and the gentleness of mercy strengthened by the vigour of justice. Watch continuously and diligently over the flock entrusted to you, lest the wolf seize or the thief destroy. Gather together what has been scattered, preserve what has been gathered without its being mingled or confused, and show yourself in every respect such among God’s flock that you appear a shepherd, [Col. 0032C] not a hireling.

We also fortify by the authority of the apostolic see the venerable Church of Narbonne, over which God has graciously willed you to preside. We decree that the following cities shall always render due obedience to that Church and to your brotherhood: namely Toulouse, Carcassonne, Elne, Béziers, Agde, Maguelone, Nîmes, Uzès, and Lodève. Furthermore, we decree that the primacy of the metropolitan see of Aix, which is second to Narbonne, and whatever dignity or honour it may be established that the Church of Narbonne itself anciently possessed by right, shall remain forever unshaken and inviolate by the text of this present decree. In all places canonically subject to your Church, whether monasteries or churches, we confirm to you the exercise of canonical right, [Col. 0032D] without prejudice to the canonical right of other churches.

Consider, moreover, what a burden this imposes upon you. [Col. 0033A] For you ought to be chaste, sober, merciful, devoted to prayer, generous in almsgiving, not silent in preaching, outstanding in hospitality, and compassionate toward the needs of your brethren. These things and many others like them, which you yourself know, dearest brother, it is fitting for you to observe with the greatest diligence. Acting thus, you will be seen to be what you are called. If anyone should perhaps, by rash presumption, attempt to violate the rights of this privilege, and, having been admonished twice or three times, should disdain to make amendment, whether cleric or layman, we declare that he is to be excluded from the body and blood of the Lord. Amen, amen, amen.

Given at Rome by the hand of Docibilis, cardinal deacon of the Holy Roman Church, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1099, indiction VIII, in the first year of Pope Paschal II.

### IV. To Alfonso, King of the Spains.—That Didacus (Peláez) has been canonically removed from the Church of St James of Compostela. (29 December 1099.)

[FLÓREZ, *España sagrada*, XX, 25.]

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his dearest son ALFONSO, king of the Spains: greeting and apostolic blessing.

We have graciously received your petition concerning the Church of blessed James, both because we too deeply lament its affliction and because we regard you as so great a son of the Catholic Church that, in matters which are just and ought to be granted to any mortal, we should admit you especially. Therefore, after reviewing the letters of our lord and predecessor Urban of holy memory, and after consulting the brethren who had assisted that same lord Urban in the legal examination, it was plainly established that our fellow-brother Didacus, formerly bishop of the Church of Iria, had been justly and canonically removed from the episcopate, although our lord Urban had permitted him to exercise episcopal office if he were called by a vacant church. [Col. 0033C] It therefore pleased all the brethren assembled with us to put a definite end to such extensive uncertainty, lest the Church of blessed James be further left destitute on his account. Setting aside every ambiguity, we direct that a person suited both in religious character and episcopal governance be chosen, by the Lord’s favour, for the Church of blessed James at Compostela and sent back to us for consecration.

As for the above-named former bishop Didacus, we ask your kindness to confer upon him, within the divinely granted extent of your kingdom, so much honour as may suffice honourably for his support. You will learn our situation more fully from the report of the legates, and you will know in what manner and condition the apostolic see is being conducted. But you, since you love the members of the Church, do not cease to love, assist, and honour her as the head. May almighty God kindle you with his love, make you victorious over your enemies, and absolve you from all sins.

Given at the Lateran, on the fourth day before the Kalends of January [29 December].

### V. To the clergy and people of the Church of Compostela, concerning the same matter. (29 December 1099.)

[FLÓREZ, *ibid.*, p. 26.]

[Col. 0034A]

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the clergy and people of Compostela and to the bishops of the same province: greeting and apostolic blessing.

No corner of the Spains now fails to know by how great calamities the Church of blessed James has long been afflicted through the absence of a shepherd. Therefore the Roman Church, mother of all Catholics, does not allow the sufferings of so great a member, which she bears most gloriously in her body, to be endured any longer. Accordingly, after a careful examination of the enactments both of the commands of the apostolic see and of the synodal assembly held in your province through its vicar for this same affair, [Col. 0034B] we have decreed, by the fuller judgment of our brethren and, as we believe, at the prompting of the Holy Spirit, that the Church of St James must be freed from such calamities. Therefore, setting aside every ambiguity, and every hope or ambition which our brother Didacus continued to entertain, through the mercy shown by the apostolic see, after the synodal judgment of his deposition, hasten to elect for the Church of Compostela a person suitable in religious character and episcopal governance, and send him to us without delay for consecration.

Given at the Lateran, on the fourth day before the Kalends of January [29 December].

### VI. He forbids Godinus of Oria, under penalty of excommunication, to claim for himself the goods of the bishopric of Brindisi. (1099.)

[UGHELLI, *Italia sacra*, IX, 31.]

[Col. 0034C]

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to GODINUS of Oria: greeting and apostolic blessing.

We are greatly astonished that you have broken out into, and persist in, such madness as to claim the goods of the bishopric of Brindisi as your private property. We therefore command that, if you love us and desire to enjoy the favour of blessed Peter, you desist from this madness; otherwise, know that you will be deprived of communion. For the Church of Oria is subject to that of Brindisi. Therefore no separation ought to exist between them, etc.

### VII. To Gebhard, Bishop of Constance. (18 January 1100.)

[JAFFÉ, *Regesta of the Roman Pontiffs*, 479, from Pertz’s papers.]

[Col. 0034D]

He exhorts G[ebhard], bishop of Constance, to rebuke, in season and out of season, those who turn their hearing from the truth. He then replies: first, that clergy who do not willingly admit excommunicated laypersons to divine offices are not, on account of infants to be baptized, to be thought obliged to withhold participation in chrism, unless the sponsors of the baptized are found to be wholly excommunicated; second, that a man who, being alone with his wife, was compelled, at the moment of death, to baptize their miscarried child, is on no account to be separated from that wife for this reason; third, that monks holding no ecclesiastical office may not carry sacred vessels to the altar, [Col. 0035A] nor may those guilty of crimes be ordained to any ministry whatsoever; fourth, that what urban priests may not do, and what is not presumed even in the churches of monks or canons, village priests may not do: namely, say the angelic hymn on the feasts of martyrs. It begins: “In the words of the letter.”

### VIII. Bull to Ivo, Bishop of Chartres.—No one, on his death or that of any successor, may presume to despoil the episcopal residence. (14 February 1100.)

[*Gallia Christiana*, new ed., VIII, 307, from the authentic copy of the chapter of Chartres.]

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother IVO, bishop of Chartres: greeting and apostolic blessing.

[Col. 0035B] It is fitting readily to grant consent to devout desires, so that the devotion of the faithful may obtain a swift result. Therefore, dearest brother and fellow bishop Ivo, we give a favourable hearing, in apostolic kindness, to your petition, so that we may confer upon your brotherhood by the singular confirmation of this document what we know is justly due to all brethren of the priestly order. Provision has indeed been made for the goods of all bishops and clerics, since at the Council of Clermont, where twelve archbishops and eighty-two bishops sat, our lord and predecessor Urban of blessed memory salutarily decreed: “If anyone seizes the goods of bishops, priests, or other clerics who have died, let him be excommunicated until he makes satisfaction.” [Col. 0035C]

Confirming this synodal decree by our own authority, we make this special ordinance concerning your episcopal residence, which your diligence has built at great cost: that no one, when you die, or when any of your successors departs this life or leaves office for any reason, may presume to destroy or despoil that house; nor may any furnishing of iron, lead, glass, wood, or stone be carried away from it or be buried beneath ruins. All structures belonging to the episcopal dwelling—namely kitchens, granaries, cellars, presses, ovens, and the houses of the ovens—shall remain intact and be kept wholly free from plundering. Moreover, woods and whatever pertains to the bishop’s maintenance, whether outside or within the city, shall neither be given away, sold, nor alienated under any other pretext; rather, with every plundering and act of violence removed, they shall be preserved for the successor whom, by God’s grace, is to govern the church. [Col. 0035D]

If in future any archbishop or anyone holding any clerical office or dignity, or any king, prince, duke, count, viscount, judge, advocate, defender, or any secular person whatever, knowing this text of our constitution, should rashly attempt to act against it, and, having been warned a second or third time, does not correct the matter by appropriate satisfaction, let him be subject to excommunication. But upon all who observe the decrees of this apostolic constitution may the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ rest, so that they may receive here the fruit of good conduct and find, before the strict Judge, the rewards of eternal peace. Amen, amen.

[Col. 0036A] Written by the hand of Peter, regional notary and scriniary of the Sacred Palace.

Given at Rome by the hand of John, cardinal deacon of the Holy Roman Church, on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of March [14 February], indiction VIII, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1100, and in the first year of the pontificate of Pope Paschal II.

### IX. He directs Ivo, Bishop of Chartres, and Ranulf, Bishop of Saintes, not to disregard the decree of the Council of Clermont concerning monastic altars. (14 March 1100.)

[SIRMOND, *Works*, III, p. 492.]

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the venerable bishops IVO of Chartres and RANULF of Saintes: greeting and apostolic blessing.

[Col. 0036B] We believe that you are not unaware, according to the enactments of the holy canons, what punishment awaits men of ecclesiastical rank who disdain the decrees of the apostolic see. You yourselves were present at the Council of Clermont, at which our predecessor Pope Urban of good memory presided while the bishops of Gaul sat with him; there it was decreed that altars which monasteries are known to have possessed for thirty years, even under payment for vicars, should henceforth remain securely with those monasteries, peacefully and without any molestation. But you attach incompatibly double dealing to this straightforward rule, and endeavour, under altered names, to extort a payment for persons. Yet it is necessary for us to meet such evasions with the sincerity of apostolic truth.
