[Col. 0036C] We therefore command that that decree be observed wholly and intact, and that you demand nothing further concerning these same altars. What we say to you, moreover, we command all other bishops of Gaul likewise to observe with regard to the monasteries of their dioceses.

Given at Rome, on the second Ides of March [14 March].

### X. Paschal confirms the privilege of the monastery of Vendôme that its abbot need not make a profession. (14 March 1100.)

[It does not survive.—See Sirmond, *Works*, III, p. 468, note e.]

### XI. He informs the assembly of the Church of St James of Compostela that Didacus, a canon and *vicedominus* of their church, has been ordained subdeacon by him. (18 March 1100.)

[FLÓREZ, *España sagrada*, XX, 27.]

[Col. 0036D]

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the whole assembly of the Church of St James: greeting and apostolic blessing.

We have received with fatherly kindness Didacus, canon and *vicedominus* of your Church, when he came to us. Having ordained him subdeacon in the bosom of the apostolic see, we send him back to your charity. We judge that no complaint of **[“genii,” perhaps a corrupt reading]** ought to impede him; nor do we wish him to be troubled by causes preceding that time, so that henceforth, by the Lord’s favour, he may in due course be promoted to holy orders.

Given at Rome by the hand of John, cardinal deacon and librarian, on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of April [18 March].

### XII. He confirms to the monastery of Reinhardsborn the church of Titteborn. (1100.)

[Col. 0037A] [It does not survive.—See *Thuringia Sacra*, p. 207.]

### XIII. To Hermann, Bishop of Augsburg. (7 April 1100.)

[JAFFÉ, *Regesta of the Roman Pontiffs*, from Pertz’s papers.]

To HERMANN, bishop of Augsburg: greeting and apostolic blessing.

The reason why we have so far made no reply to the repeated letters of your brotherhood was that we believed you to be outside Catholic unity. But now, since, as we have learned from the letters of our vicar G[ebhard], bishop of Constance, [Col. 0037B] you have by God’s grace returned to Catholic communion, we greatly rejoice in your conversion. For we desire to recall not only you but all those regions to obedience to the apostolic see. Therefore by this present letter we send you the grace of fatherly greeting and apostolic blessing, asking you to persevere in obedience to that apostolic see, as we believe has been enjoined upon your beloved self by our said vicar. (There follows a formula anathematizing Wibert, the antipope.)

### XIV.

He takes the monastery of Der into protection, or that of St Bercharius; confirms its possessions and privileges; and furthermore decrees that no secular or ecclesiastical person shall draw the abbot or his successors before a secular court, nor shall any bishop compel them to attend a synod—“unless because of a matter of faith”—or finally compel them to leave the solemn observances of their own monastery in order to attend those of a city.

After Paschal, the letter is subscribed by Albert, cardinal of Santa Sabina, and Augustine, cardinal of Saints Four Crowned Martyrs, both of whom call themselves “unworthy” cardinals. “Given at the Lateran, on the third Ides of April [11 April], indiction VIII, by the hand of Lanfranc, writer of the palace, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1100, and in the first year of the pontificate of Pope Paschal II.”

[Note: [Col. 0037D] This privilege was occasioned by Philip, bishop of Châlons, who wished to compel the abbot of Der to attend both the synod and the solemnities of his city. On this matter the pontiff wrote the following letter to Philip.] (11 April 1100.)

### XV. Letter of Pope Paschal to Philip, Bishop of Châlons. (1100.)

[MABILLON, *Annals of the Benedictine Order*, V, 420.]

[Col. 0037C]

[Col. 0037D] PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother and fellow bishop PHILIP of Châlons: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Since no bishop may be ignorant of the canons, we are greatly astonished that you do not hesitate, by compelling the abbot of St Bercharius, to summon him to the festivals of your city. How absurd this is, and how contrary to your office, no one doubts who knows that the sacred canons forbid abbots even to be compelled to attend a synod. [Col. 0038A] Nor do we believe that it is unknown to your brotherhood how the ordinances of the holy Fathers forbid anyone to receive the cleric or monk of another. We have heard, not without astonishment, that you are doing this with monks of the aforesaid abbot. By the authority of this present letter, therefore, we command your charity not to compel the aforesaid abbot to attend your festivals, nor to receive his monks against him.

[Note: [Col. 0037D] This rescript, which we extracted from a parchment manuscript of Der, lacks chronological indications; yet it is understood to have been given in this year, both from the preceding diploma and because Bishop Philip died in that same year, as we learn from Hugh of Flavigny and from the Chronicle of St Peter of Châlons.]

### XVI. Bull of Paschal II on the union of the Church of Orange with that of Tricastin. (1100.)

[*Gallia Christiana*, I, Documents, 120.]

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother and fellow bishop GIBELIN of Arles: greeting [Col. 0038B] and apostolic blessing.

Your brotherhood is not unaware what our predecessor Lord Urban decreed concerning the union of the Churches of Orange and Tricastin. Therefore, in the letters received from your charity, we were unable to write you anything certain, because the bishop of Tricastin had not yet come to us. But now that our fellow brother and bishop William has been raised, as we believe, from mortality to immortality and from earthly things to heavenly, the time has come for the Church of Orange to be restored to the bishop of Tricastin. Since disputes concerning this matter have long been debated, by the authority of this present letter we command your brotherhood to restore that church to the aforesaid bishop, and to ensure that both clergy and people obey him.

Given at the Lateran.

### XVII. Bull of the same pope concerning the aforesaid union. (1100.)

[*Gallia Christiana*, *ibid.*]

[Col. 0038C]

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons, the clergy and people of the Church of Orange: greeting and apostolic blessing.

The unity of the whole Church, entrusted by God’s authorship to blessed Peter and, after him, to his successors, must be preserved by us with such charity that, in pious concern, we provide for the salvation of the souls entrusted to us and do not depart from the decrees and constitutions of the holy Fathers. For it is right and authoritative that whatever is prescribed by the ordinances of our predecessors [Col. 0038D] Gregory, Victor, Alexander, and Urban **[Note: Some material is missing.]** [lacuna] should be void; it is established that the Church of Orange is united to the Church of Tricastin. Since the question concerning this matter has long been debated, we have decreed, in accordance with their ordinances and by the counsel of our fellow bishops, to impose an end upon it. By apostolic authority we command you henceforth, laying aside all opposition, to obey the bishop of Tricastin as your own bishop and, with tranquillity and peace, to remain reverently in obedience to your bishop, so that the fullness of the entire [Col. 0039A] Church may remain in the firmness of unity and all further dispute on this subject may be so silenced that nothing at all is reopened after matters have been well settled. Whoever after lawful and divinely inspired constitutions wishes to break them must plainly be recognized not as one at peace with the Church but as a rebel.

Therefore, charity prompting us, we admonish your brotherhood not to disdain subjection to the bishop of Tricastin, who will render an account to God for you; and recognize yourselves to be Christ’s sheep in such a way that you do not hesitate to obey him who presides in Christ’s place. May you who obey attain eternal life through the prayers of the apostles Peter and Paul.

Given at the Lateran, on the third Ides of April 1100 [11 April].

### XVIII. To Norigaud, Bishop of Autun.—He confirms his election, all the possessions of his church, and makes certain other decrees. (14 April 1100.)

[MANSI, *Councils*, XX, 1017.]

[Col. 0039B]

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved brother NORIGAUD, bishop of Autun, and to his successors canonically appointed for ever.

Since, by the dispensation of divine judgment, we have been raised, though unworthy, to the rank of this office in order to hold in the governance of the Church the place of the prince of the apostles, we must labour and make every effort that, in ordering ecclesiastical affairs, we emulate with most faithful devotion and devoted faith the counsels and ordinances of him whose faith and love were so especially approved by the Lord [Col. 0039C] that the Son of God willed to establish and confirm, upon the immovable stability of his faith in particular, the Church redeemed by his precious blood, saying: “You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church” (Matthew 16). He also granted him such a prerogative of power that what he chose to bind in heaven and on earth should be bound, and what he chose to loose should be loosed. He granted this succession of his authority to blessed Clement and, through him, to all who have striven to preside rightly over his see and to order the Church of God by canonical ordinance.

Strengthened by the authority of that faith, we confirm to you, beloved brother Norigaud, and to all who canonically succeed you, everything which appears to pertain to the Church of Autun, in which we believe you have been canonically ordained: both churches, parishes, cemeteries, presbyteries, and all ecclesiastical orders, and estates and every other possession, movable and immovable, which has been acquired or may justly be acquired. [Col. 0039D] You and your successors shall be permitted to possess all these as freely as your predecessor is shown to have possessed them peacefully and lawfully on the day before his death.

Moreover, by apostolic authority we decree that no priest—whether living, dying, passing to another religious order, or retiring to a life of repose—may remove or diminish the goods which, from the day of his ordination, he has acquired or may acquire in the Church in which he was ordained. Rather, he shall permit them to remain untouched and unimpaired in the Church in which they were acquired. By the same authority we also forbid anyone to presume to receive into communion, or restore to office, those whom we have excommunicated or removed from divine offices because of their offences. We further decree that absolutely no payment shall be exacted by anyone for a place or space of burial. As for redemption from sins, we establish and wholly confirm, according to apostolic decrees, that persons at death shall give alms in the Church in which they received the sacraments of faith. If anyone, living or dying, wishes to transfer himself to another church, he shall leave to the mother Church, in accordance with apostolic decrees, a portion of what he has decided to give for the salvation of his soul. [Col. 0040A]

If any ecclesiastical or secular person should rashly attempt to act against this text of our constitution, we judge and confirm that such a person, as guilty of sacrilege, must be excluded from the thresholds of God’s holy Church. But upon all who preserve what is just for that Church may the peace of the Lord Jesus Christ rest, so that they may receive here the fruit of good conduct and find the rewards of eternal peace with the rewards of the rewarders of good things [text corrupt]. Amen, amen.

Written by the hand of John, scriniary of the Sacred Lateran Palace.

I, Paschal, bishop of the Catholic Church, have subscribed. I, Walter, unworthy bishop of the Church of Albano, have subscribed. I, Albert, cardinal of the title of St Sabina, have subscribed. [Col. 0040C] I, Bernard, unworthy cardinal of the title of St Chrysogonus, have subscribed. I, Alberic, by God’s grace humble priest of the title of the Apostles at the Chains, have subscribed in confirmation. I, Augustine, unworthy cardinal of the title of Saints Four Crowned Martyrs, have subscribed.

Given at the Lateran by the hand of Leo, writer, on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of May [14 April], indiction VIII, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1100, and in the first year of the pontificate of Pope Paschal II.

### XIX. Privilege for the Church of Mâcon. (14 April 1100.)

[SEVERTIUS, *Historical Chronology of the Succession of the Hierarchy of the Archbishops of the Archbishopric of Lyons*.—Lyons, 1628, folio, vol. II, p. 121.]

[Col. 0040D]

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to brother BERARD, bishop of Mâcon, and to his successors canonically appointed for ever.

Because by the dispensation of the divine judgment we have been raised, though unworthy, to the rank of this office, to hold the place of the prince of the apostles in governing the Church, we must labour and strive altogether to imitate, in the ordering of ecclesiastical affairs, with most faithful devotion and devoted faith, the admonitions and institutions of him whose faith was pre-eminent and whose devotion was approved by the Lord; so that, upon the immovable stability of his faith, the Son of God willed to establish and confirm his Church, redeemed by precious blood [Col. 0041A], saying: “You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church” (Matt. 16:18). To him he also granted such a prerogative of power that whatever was to be bound or loosed in heaven and on earth should be bound or loosed at his discretion. He himself transmitted this succession of his power to blessed Clement and, through him, to all who should lawfully preside over his see and endeavour to order the Church of God by canonical ordinance.

Strengthened by the authority of this faith, we confirm to you, beloved brother Berard, and to all who shall canonically succeed you, just as our predecessor Urban confirmed to your predecessor Landric, all things which appear to belong to the Church of Mâcon, in which we believe that you have been canonically ordained [Col. 0041B]: churches, parishes, cemeteries, priests, and every ecclesiastical order, as well as estates and all other movable and immovable possessions that have been acquired or may lawfully be acquired. We further decree by apostolic authority that you and your successors may possess all these things as freely as your predecessor is shown to have possessed them on the day before his death; and that no priest, whether living or dying, or moving to another religious state and a life of repose, may remove or diminish property which, from the day of his ordination, he has acquired or may acquire in the Church in which he was ordained; rather, it shall remain untouched and unimpaired in the Church in which it was acquired.

We likewise prohibit by the same authority that those whom we have excommunicated [Col. 0041C] and removed from divine offices for their offences should be received by anyone into communion or presumed to be restored to those offices. We also decree that no payment whatsoever shall be demanded from anyone for a place or space of burial. But, for the redemption of sins, we wholly decree and confirm, in accordance with apostolic decrees, that those dying in the Church in which they received the sacraments of faith may give alms.

If any person should presumptuously attempt to act against this document of our constitution, we judge and confirm that such a person, as guilty of sacrilege, is to be excluded from the thresholds of the holy Church of God. But may the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ be upon all who preserve the rights of that Church [Col. 0041D], so that they may receive here the fruit of good works and find with the rewarder of good people the rewards of eternal peace. Amen.

Written by the hand of Peter, regional notary and servant of the sacred palace. I, Paschal, bishop of the catholic Church. I, Albert, unworthy cardinal of the title of St. San… I, Bernard, unworthy cardinal of the title of St. Chrysogonus. I, Walter, unworthy bishop of the Church of Albano, have signed.

Given at the Lateran through the hand of Leo, scribe, on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of May, in the eighth indiction, in the year 1100 of the Lord’s Incarnation [Col. 0042A], and in the first year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Paschal II.

## XX. Letter to the Archbishop of Auch  
*(A.D. 1100, April 20)*

[D. Bouquet, *Recueil*, vol. XIV, p. 188.]

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother R[aymond], archbishop of Auch, greeting and apostolic blessing.

Our brother, the bishop of Dax, a suffragan of your Church, has long complained that portions of his diocese have been cut away by his fellow bishops of Bazas and Oloron. He asserts, indeed, that those parts of his diocese which the bishop of Bazas had taken were restored to his predecessor B[ernard] [Col. 0042B], but were then violently taken from him again. Therefore we command your charity, after convening an assembly of the brethren, diligently to investigate this matter; and that the portions of the parishes concerning which the case is being heard be awarded to whichever party justice permits.

Given at Rome, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of May.

## XXI. To the Army Fighting in Palestine  
*He congratulates it upon its victory and at the same time urges it to advance. (A.D. 1100, May 4.)*

[Mansi, *Concilia*, XX, 979.]

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the venerable brethren and sons—bishops, clerics [Col. 0042C], nobles, soldiers, and all the people of the Christian host triumphant in Asia—greeting and apostolic blessing.

We recognize fulfilled in you what the Lord promises his people through the prophet: “I will dwell in them,” he says, “and walk among them” (2 Cor. 6); for through faith he dwells in your breasts, and through your deeds walks among you in such a manner that he is plainly seen to have overcome his enemies in you. For the Lord has renewed the ancient miracles, so that one might pursue a thousand and two pursue ten thousand, and, with these arms of the Church—the trumpets of priestly prayers—open the walls of hostile cities.

How great, in your judgment, is the joy and how mighty the miracle that he revealed to your eyes the lance stained with the blood of his most holy side and offered you a portion of the life-giving Cross for your hands to touch! Neither the human mind can conceive nor the tongue adequately recount how great thanks we owe our Redeemer for these things. For we see the enemies of the Christian faith and oppressors of the Christian people, by divine mercy, partly crushed by your hand and partly driven from lands long possessed; we see the Eastern Church, after long periods of captivity, restored in great measure to its ancient glory of freedom. Therefore we must say with the mouth and say with the heart: “Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to people of good will” (Luke 2). We must also persevere in prayer and vigils, that he may bring to fulfilment what he has begun and preserve unspotted until the end your hands, which he consecrated with the blood of his enemies [Col. 0043A], abounding in steadfast devotion.

Therefore act, most dearly beloved children in Christ. Recall how much you have left behind for love of the Lord and how many dangers you have undergone for the salvation and deliverance of your brethren: you set aside homeland, homes, and parents; you consigned yourselves to exile and exposed yourselves to death. Take care now always to strive toward better things; preserve peace with all, that by the Lord’s mercy you may attain eternal peace.

We refrain from communicating many things to you by parchment and ink, since from the bosom of the apostolic see we are sending our most beloved brother Maurice, bishop of Porto, so that you who undertook the pilgrimage of so great a journey through the vicar of blessed Peter, our predecessor Urban of holy memory in Christ [Col. 0043B], may always abound in the consolations of blessed Peter; and that, having had him as the foundation of so great a work, you may also hold him as its head unto the end, in faith and obedience.

We have also entrusted our authority to that brother Maurice, the bishop, so that you must reverently receive and hear him in all things, and through him obey us—indeed, blessed Peter. We have instructed him to attend vigilantly to the ordering of the Church which the Lord has liberated through you and is yet to liberate. If he finds anything not suited to canonical rules, he is to correct it; and, with your aid, to plant what must be planted and build what must be built. We therefore exhort you, and in exhorting command you, to take care to obey him in all things, as one who represents our person. May almighty God grant you both the will and the power, so that what you know must be done by his authority you may accomplish with his aid. May he absolve you from all sins and grant you, in exchange for your exile, your eternal homeland.

Given at Rome, on the fourth day before the Nones of May, in the eighth indiction, through the hand of John, deacon.

## XXII. Letter to the Archbishops and Bishops of Gaul  
*He decrees infamous those who, bound by a vow to undertake the journey to Jerusalem, withdrew themselves, or who disgracefully departed from the siege of Antioch; but he orders the restoration of their property to those who return after the victory. (A.D. 1100.)*

[Dom Bouquet, *Recueil*, XV, 20.]

[Col. 0043D] PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to all archbishops, bishops, and abbots throughout Gaul, greeting and apostolic blessing.

We owe innumerable thanks to the mercies of almighty God, since in our times he has deigned to rescue the Church of Asia from the hands of the Turks and to open to the Christian host the very city of the Lord’s Passion and burial. We must pursue divine grace with whatever resources it has given us and effectively assist our brethren who have remained in those regions formerly belonging to the Palestinians or Canaanites. Therefore exhort all the soldiers of your regions, for the remission or pardon of their sins, to hasten to that mother of ours, the Eastern Church. Especially compel those who have taken the signs of the Cross under a vow of this military service to hasten there, unless they are held back by the obstacle of poverty; otherwise we decree that they are to be regarded as infamous.

> **Note:** [Col. 0043D] That this letter was written in the year 1100 is inferred from the fact that in the following year the French, stirred by these letters, undertook a second expedition. Orderic Vitalis expressly testifies this concerning Stephen, count palatine of Blois, in book X of his *Ecclesiastical History*, p. 789: “Stephen also, count palatine of Blois,” he says, “was censured by almost everyone and continually ashamed because he had shamefully fled from the siege of Antioch and abandoned his glorious companions struggling in Christ’s martyrdom. He was often rebuked by many persons, and was compelled by both fear and shame to resume Christ’s military service. His wife Adela also frequently admonished him, and amid the endearments of friendly marriage said: ‘Far be it from you, my lord, to consent long to endure the reproaches of so many people [Col. 0044D]! Recall the renowned valour of your youth, and take up the arms of praiseworthy warfare, so that from this there may arise throughout the whole world great rejoicing among Christ’s faithful, terror among the heathen, and the public overthrow of their wicked law.’ The wise and spirited woman said these and many other similar things to her husband; but he, knowing the perils and difficulties, feared to undergo harsh labours again. At last he recovered courage and strength, set out with many thousands of Franks, and reached Christ’s tomb, though very serious obstacles had opposed him. Then Harpin sold the city of Bourges to Philip, king of the Franks, and set out for Jerusalem with Goscelin of Courtenay and Milo of Bray,” etc.

[Col. 0044B] But those who withdrew from the siege of Antioch weak and wavering in faith are to remain under excommunication unless they confirm by reliable assurances that they will return. Moreover, we command that all their possessions be restored to the brethren who return after the victory wrought by God, as you remember was established by the synodal decree of our predecessor Urban of blessed memory. Act thus in all things; labour according to your office, so that, by the Lord’s gift and through common efforts, that mother of ours, the Eastern Church, may be restored to her proper condition.

## XXIII. *To the Consuls of Pisa*  
*He praises them because “in the preceding year” they devoted themselves to the conquest of Jerusalem. He promises that Daibert, their archbishop, “now patriarch of the city of Jerusalem,” will be defended by him against Arnulf, usurper of the same see, and will be commended to “the noble and valiant man Godfrey, and the other Christian princes still remaining in Syria and the lands beyond the sea.” He commends his legates, “who are first to depart for Genoa and then for Sardinia.”*

*(A.D. 1100.—See Dal Borgo, *Raccolta di diplomi Pisani*, 1765, quarto, collection 83.)*

[Col. 0044C]

## XXIV. *To Godfrey, Bishop of Maguelonne*  
*He commands him to consecrate Didacus, bishop-elect of the Church of Compostela.*

*(See letters 25 and 41.)*

## XXV. On the Destruction of the Church of Compostela  
*He forbids the clergy of Compostela to abandon their province under pretext of the journey to Jerusalem. (A.D. 1100, October 14.)*

[Flórez, *España sagrada*, XX, 28.]

[Col. 0044D]

[Col. 0045A] P., bishop, servant of the servants of God, to P., bishop of Lugo, Al. and G., bishops, and all the clergy of St. James, greeting and apostolic blessing.

We have long grieved over the destruction of the Church of Compostela. But now, when through your letters the captivity of Christians has been reported to us, greater grief has affected us. Therefore we grant your petition without difficulty, so that we may spare the bishop-elect of that Church from coming to us at this time. Accordingly, by the authority of our letters, we command our brother, the bishop of Maguelonne, to go to consecrate him [Col. 0045B]. If he should perhaps be unable to do so, the bishop of Burgos, who is subject to our jurisdiction, is to be summoned. By the authority of these present letters we also command the bishop-elect himself to accept, trusting in the Lord’s mercy, the burden imposed upon him by the common consent of the Church.

Moreover, as we forbid soldiers, so we also forbid clerics of your region to presume, under pretext of beholding Jerusalem, to abandon their Church and province, which the ferocity of the Moabites so frequently attacks.

Given at Melfi, on the second day before the Ides of October.

## XXVI. To Adefonsus, King of the Spains  
*He grieves over his troubles. (A.D. 1100, October 14.)*

[Flórez, *España sagrada*, XX, 29.]

[Col. 0045C] P., bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his most beloved son A., king of the Spains, greeting and apostolic blessing.

As we rejoice, as you know, in your prosperity, so indeed we are afflicted by your adversity. Therefore, taking thought for the borders of your kingdom and those of your neighbours, we forbade your soldiers whom we saw going to Jerusalem to go. We have furthermore dispatched into your kingdoms and counties letters containing this same prohibition and the pardon of sins for the combatants. We were especially affected by what you reported concerning the captivity of Christians, and we have decided not to deny what you requested concerning the bishop-elect of Compostela. For by letters we have commanded the bishop of Maguelonne to go and consecrate him bishop [Col. 0045D]; should he fail, the bishop of Burgos, who is subject to our jurisdiction, is to be summoned. May almighty God grant to the Church and to you victory over his enemies.

Given at Melfi, on the second day before the Ides of October.

## XXVII. He Confirms, at the Request of Bishop Stephen, the Boundaries of the Diocese of Mazara in Sicily  
*(A.D. 1100, October 15.)*

[Mansi, *Concilia*, XX, 1131.]

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved brother STEPHEN, bishop of Mazara, and to his successors to be canonically installed in perpetuity.

By the will of almighty God times change and kingdoms are transferred [Col. 0046A]. Thus we read that nations once great and renowned have been cast down and humbled, while mean and small ones have sometimes been exalted. Thus, in certain regions, the power of the Christian name has occupied pagan lands; and in others the dignity of Christian power has trampled down pagan tyranny. So in our own times the merciful favour of heaven, through the valour of the most glorious princes Duke Robert and Count Roger, has overcome all Saracen violence on the island of Sicily and restored the ancient condition of the holy Church according to the good pleasure of its will.

For this we give thanks to that ineffable mercy; and upon those distinguished brethren—one now dead, the other surviving in his presence—we invoke its favour. According to the duty of our office, we are eager to order and confirm the churches on that island. Therefore, just as the dioceses of Mazara and of the others were ordered, God consenting, through our predecessor Urban of happy memory, so we confirm by the authority of this present decree the diocese of the Church of Mazara, over which, by God’s will, you preside. We decree, honourable brother and fellow bishop Stephen, that all which is contained within the boundaries written below shall remain forever under your episcopal right, and that of your lawful successors, to govern and administer: namely, from the place where the river Belich enters the sea to the Cava, thence to Corleone; this Cava extends to the rock of Zineth [Col. 0046C]; from Zineth this diocese extends to the boundary of Jatina and Cephala, namely to the great ridge; from the ridge it extends to Sagana; from Sagana to Carini; from Carini to the sandy district where the boundary between Palermo and Carini lies; and thence to the sea.

Within these boundaries lie Mazara with all its appurtenances; Marsala with its appurtenances; Trapani with its appurtenances; Calathameth with its appurtenances; Calathabubi with its appurtenances; Parthenith with its appurtenances; Cinos with its appurtenances; Carini with its appurtenances; Jath with its appurtenances; Calathaczaruch with its appurtenances; Belich with all its appurtenances; and all other castles, hamlets, or cities which now exist or shall subsequently be established. The hamlet of Buxei, with one hundred villeins, is to be preserved in the personal right both of yourself and your successors, as it was granted by our aforesaid son Count Roger [Col. 0046D].

Moreover, whatever the same Church of Mazara may hereafter lawfully and canonically acquire by the generosity of princes or the offerings of the faithful shall remain secure and inviolate for you and your successors. We therefore decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb that Church, take away its possessions, retain what has been taken, diminish them, or harass it by reckless vexations; but that all shall be preserved whole and intact, to be of every possible benefit for the use of you, the clergy, and the poor.

If, therefore, any ecclesiastical or secular person in the future, knowingly acting against this document of our constitution, should rashly attempt to violate it, then, after a second or third warning, unless he makes suitable amends, let him lose the dignity of his power and honour; let him know himself guilty before the divine judgment for the wrong committed; let him be separated from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Redeemer; and at the last judgment let him be subject to severe punishment [Col. 0047A]. But may the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ be upon all who preserve the rights of that Church, so that they may receive here the fruit of good works and find with the strict Judge the rewards of eternal peace. Amen, amen, amen.

I, Paschal, bishop of the catholic Church, have subscribed. I, Alberic, cardinal priest of the title of St. Peter in Chains, have subscribed. I, Odo, bishop of Ostia, have subscribed to this privilege [Col. 0047B]. I, Milo, bishop of Palestrina, have subscribed. I, John, bishop of Tusculum, have subscribed. I, Albert, archbishop of Siponto, have subscribed. I, Robert, cardinal priest of the title of St. Eusebius, have subscribed. I, Robert, bishop of Messina, have subscribed. I, Roger, bishop of Syracuse, have subscribed.

On the seal: “By the word of the Lord the heavens were established.” St. Peter; St. Paul; Pope St. Paschal II.

Given at Melfi through the hand of John, cardinal deacon of the Holy Roman Church, on the Ides of October, in the eighth indiction, in the year 1100 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the second year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Paschal II.

## XXVIII. To Alberic, Abbot of the New Monastery of Chalon  
*Concerning the privilege granted there. (A.D. 1100, October 19.)*

[Mansi, *Concilia*, XX, 980.]

[Col. 0047C]

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable son ALBERIC, abbot of the New Monastery situated in the diocese of Chalon, and to his successors to be regularly appointed in perpetuity.

A desire shown to concern a religious purpose and the salvation of souls must, with God’s help, be fulfilled without delay. Therefore, most beloved sons in the Lord, without any difficulty we grant the request of your prayers [Col. 0047D], because we rejoice in your religious life with paternal affection. We decree that the place which you have chosen to inhabit for monastic quiet shall be secure and free from the molestations of all mortals; that an abbey shall be maintained there forever; and that it shall be especially protected under the guardianship of the apostolic see, so long as you and your successors remain in the observance of the discipline and frugality which you observe today, without prejudice to the canonical reverence due to the Church of Chalon.

Accordingly, by this document of the present decree, we forbid any person whatsoever to alter the condition of your way of life, receive monks of your monastery, called the New Monastery, without regular recommendation [Col. 0048A], or disturb your community by any trickery or violence. We confirm as reasonable and praiseworthy the settlement of the dispute which our brother, the bishop of Lyon, then vicar of the apostolic see, made between you and the monks of the Church of Molesme, together with the bishops of his province and other religious men, by command of our predecessor Urban II of apostolic memory.

You therefore, most beloved and dearly desired sons in Christ, ought to remember that some of you have left behind the broad freedoms of secular life, and others even the less severe restrictions of a more relaxed monastery. Therefore, that you may always be judged more worthy of this grace, strive to keep the fear and love of God always in your hearts; and, the freer you are from secular tumults and pleasures, strive all the more with the powers of your whole mind and soul to please God.

> **Note:** [Col. 0047D] These words occur henceforth word for word in the privilege of Urban II for the Church of Arles. HARD.

If in the future any archbishop or bishop, emperor or king, count or viscount, judge, or any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowingly acting against this document of our constitution, should rashly attempt to violate it, then, after a second or third warning, unless he makes suitable amends, let him lose the dignity of his power and honour; let him know himself guilty before the divine judgment for the wrong committed; let him be separated from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ; and at the last judgment let him be subject to severe punishment. But may the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ be upon all who preserve the rights of that place [Col. 0048C], so that they may receive here the fruit of good works and find with the strict Judge the rewards of eternal peace.

I, Paschal, bishop of the catholic Church, have subscribed.

Given at Troia through the hand of John, cardinal deacon of the Holy Roman Church, on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of May, in the eighth indiction [Note: [Col. 0048D] It appears that XIV Kalends of November should be read. Jaffé.], in the year 1100 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the second [first] year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Paschal II.

## XXIX. At the Request of Bishop Hubert, He Takes the Church of Troia under Protection and Confirms Its Goods and Privileges  
*(A.D. 1100, November 10.)*

[Ughelli, *Italia sacra*, I, 1345.]

[Col. 0048D]

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved brother HUBERT, bishop of Troia, and to his successors to be canonically appointed in perpetuity.

It is fitting that we grant assent to just vows and lend an ear to just petitions, since, though unworthy, by the Lord’s dispensation we are seen to be stationed as guardians and heralds of justice upon the lofty watchtower of the princes of the apostles, Peter and Paul. Therefore, most beloved brother Hubert in Christ, assenting to your just petitions, we strengthen the holy Church of Troia, over which by God’s will you preside, by the authority of the apostolic see.

We decree that the bishops of that Church of Troia shall forever be consecrated by the pontiff of the apostolic see. We confirm to that Church, and to you and your lawful successors, to possess by proper right: Mount Majurum; the estate called St. Lawrence; and whatever you may hereafter, by the Lord’s gift, lawfully and canonically acquire as the property of the Church’s possessions. We also decree that the following are to be governed forever by episcopal right: the city of Troia itself; within it, the monastery of St. Nicholas with its dependent churches; Holy Cross of Portula; Felice; Castellione; the new castle of Biccari with the abbey of St. Peter in Burgo and its dependent churches; the church of St. Vitus; the fabric of St. Mary of Foci; St. Peter of Montella [Col. 0049B]; St. Justa; and all estates contained in the authentic privileges of our predecessors granted to your Church.

We therefore decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb that Church, take away its possessions, retain what has been taken, claim for personal use things unjustly given, diminish them, or harass it by reckless vexations; but that all shall be preserved whole and intact, to benefit in every way those for whose support and governance they were granted. If any archbishop, bishop, emperor, king, prince, duke, count, viscount, judge, or any ecclesiastical or secular person in the future knowingly attempts rashly to violate this document of our constitution, then, after a second or third warning, unless he makes suitable amends, let that person lose the dignity of power and honour; let that person know himself or herself guilty before the divine judgment for the wrong committed; let that person be separated from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Redeemer; and at the last judgment let that person be subject to severe punishment [Col. 0049C]. But may the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ be upon all who preserve the rights of that Church, so that they may receive here the fruit of good works and find with the strict Judge the rewards of eternal peace.

I, Paschal, bishop of the holy catholic Church, have subscribed. I, Odo, bishop of Ostia, have subscribed. [Col. 0049D] + I, Odorisius, cardinal and abbot, have subscribed. + I, Albic[us], cardinal deacon of St. Peter, have subscribed. + I, Milo, bishop of Palestrina, have subscribed. + I, Bruno, bishop of Segni, have subscribed. + I, Teuzo, cardinal of Saints John and Paul, have subscribed. + I, Paganus, cardinal deacon of the Roman Church, have subscribed.

Given at Cassino through the hand of John, cardinal deacon of the Holy Roman Church, on the fourth day before the Ides of November, in the eighth indiction, in the year 1100 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the second year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Paschal II.

## XXX. Privilege by Which He Receives the Monastery of Souvigny, as a Member of the Abbey of Cluny, under the Protection of the Apostolic See, in the Same Manner as Pope Urban II  
*(A.D. 1100, November 14.)*

[*Bullarium Cluniacense*, p. 31.]

[Col. 0050A]

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the most beloved sons in the Lord, the monks of the monastery of Souvigny, greeting and apostolic blessing.

We recognize that by the Lord’s disposition we have been advanced to the service of the apostolic see so that we ought effectively to assist his children when they seek aid, and, insofar as the Lord grants, defend and protect those obedient to him. Therefore, in accordance with the enactments of our lord and predecessor Urban II, we receive you and your place as a member of the monastery of Cluny, to be fostered forever under the protection of the apostolic see [Col. 0050B]. We decree that your monastic site shall never at any time suffer the loss of any interdict; and that no living person may, within the bounds long ago established for the monastery or the adjacent village, make an attack or seize or plunder any person.

We also judge that the agreement which the knight Archimbald made in the hand of that same predecessor of ours, as contained in his privilege, is to remain perpetually valid: namely, that all which his father and grandfather had conferred upon your place, both in property and in immunities and customs, shall at all times be preserved unimpaired. We further decree that the burial-place of that site is to remain entirely free, so that no one, except the excommunicated, may obstruct the final wish of those who choose to be buried there.

Moreover, by this document of the present decree, we decree by apostolic authority that whatever your monastery possesses today, or may hereafter acquire by grants of pontiffs, the generosity of princes, or the offerings of the faithful, shall remain secure and inviolate for you and your successors. Among these we have considered it necessary to specify the following by name: the monastery of Campovold; the chapel of Curtiliis; the chapel of Lonver; the chapel of Villar; the church of Cantaneto; and the church of Cyriliac. These churches, therefore, together with the other churches which you possess by privilege of the apostolic see, we grant to you on the following terms: preserving the right of bishops, which they are known hitherto to have retained there in procurations and synods [Col. 0050D], you shall possess in full whatever you may hereafter acquire in them, both within and without, from offerings, burials, and tithes, whether major or minor; and no ecclesiastical or secular person shall ever dare to interfere against you in any matters pertaining to them.

You may also choose priests in your churches, provided that they receive the cure of souls from bishops or episcopal vicars without payment. But if those should, God forbid, wickedly refuse to grant it, then the priests, by the favour of the apostolic see, shall obtain permission to celebrate there. Nor may anyone disturb you concerning alms for the living or dead which are given for salvation; rather, you may receive, for the benefit of God’s servants and the poor, the offerings brought to you by men and women, clerics and laypeople alike [Col. 0051A].

We therefore decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb this monastery, take away its possessions, retain what has been taken, diminish them, or harass it by reckless vexations; but that all shall be preserved whole and intact, to benefit in every way those for whose support and governance they were granted, while preserving in all things obedience to the abbots of Cluny. If any ecclesiastical or secular person in the future, knowingly acting against this document of our privilege, should rashly attempt to violate it, then, after a second or third warning, unless that person makes suitable amends, let that person lose the dignity of power and honour; let that person know himself or herself guilty before the divine judgment for the wrong committed; let that person be separated from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ; and at the last judgment let that person be subject to severe punishment [Col. 0051B]. But may the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ be upon all who preserve the rights of the aforesaid place, so that they may receive here the fruit of good works and find with the strict Judge the rewards of eternal peace. Amen, amen, amen.

I, Paschal, bishop of the holy catholic Church. I, Odilo, bishop of Palestrina. I, John, bishop of Tusculum. I, Teuzo, cardinal of Saints John and Paul. [Col. 0051C] I, Alberic, by God’s grace cardinal of the title of St. Peter in Chains. I, Paganus, deacon of the holy Roman Church, of the deaconry of St. Mary Nova.

Given at Anagni through the hand of John, cardinal deacon of the Holy Roman Church, on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of December, in the eighth indiction, in the year 1100 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the second year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Paschal II.

## XXXI. Privilege Confirming All Goods and Rights of the Monastery of Cluny  
*(A.D. 1100, November 15.)*

[Cocquelines, *Amplissima Collectio Bullarum, Privilegiorum ac Diplomatum Romanorum Pontificum*—Rome, 1739, folio, vol. II, p. 114.]

[Col. 0051D]

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother HUGH, abbot of Cluny, and to his successors to be regularly appointed hereafter.

The zeal for the Lord and the prerogative of religious observance by which, through God’s grace, your community has shone forth in our times throughout almost all the West, together with the unshaken unity by which, amid every storm, you have adhered to the Apostolic See, strongly exhort—indeed urge and compel—our mildness to grant assent to your petitions and to provide more carefully hereafter for your peace. Therefore, whatever liberty and authority the Roman [Col. 0052A] pontiffs, our predecessors, especially Gregory VII and Urban II of apostolic memory, conferred upon your monastery and the places belonging to it, we also, by this present decree, God being its author, confirm. Moreover, we add that in all priories and cells which are now subject to your governance without an abbot of their own, no one shall ever presume in future times to appoint an abbot; but both those priories and cells, and likewise all other properties in whatsoever places with which your fraternity was invested at the time of the Council of Clermont, celebrated by the aforesaid Pope Urban, concerning which no question was then raised—at which council indeed you yourself were present—shall always be preserved to you and your successors in peace and tranquillity. Among these, the following seemed proper to be recorded by their own names:

[Col. 0052B] St Mary of Charity at Martignac (*Mar.*: of Marciniac); St Peter of Munsiac (*Mar.*: of Cusiniac); St Peter of Leniciis (*Mar.*: of Leuntii); St Paul of Bergamo; St Isidore of Spain; St Odilo (*Mar.*: Orylius) of Scarrione; St Marcellus of Salsimoniac; St Marcellus of Chalon; Dear Place; Paredus, the Roman monastery; St Victor of Geneva; Paterniac; St Saturninus of Provence; St Eutropius; St Martin of Auch; the monastery of Cacerris; St Mary of Toulouse; Boort (*Mar.*: St Mary of Tobosa Boarum); Tiernus; St Martin of the Fields; Sylviniac; Virgenus; Ginniac; Nantuac; St Pancras of England; St Lecerius of Nazara; St James

[Col. 0052C] of Potino; St Gabriel of Cremona; St Saviour and St Stephen of Nevers.

We also command that all your churches or chapels and cemeteries be free and exempt from every exaction, apart from the customary episcopal *parata* and jurisdiction over priests if they show themselves to have acted contrary to the dignity of their order; excepting, of course, those churches which remain under the abbot’s authority without such subjection. It shall also be lawful for you, together with your rights (*Mar.*: or “your brethren”), to choose priests, provided that they receive the care of souls from bishops or the bishops’ vicars without simony. But if those men should refuse, God forbid, through perversity to confer it, the priests shall, through the benevolence of the Apostolic See, obtain permission to celebrate the offices. Nor shall anyone have authority ever to disturb the bounds either of your cloister

[Col. 0052D] or of your places on account of alms given for the salvation of the living or the dead; but it shall be lawful to receive, for the use of the servants of God and Christ’s poor, the offerings of both men and women which are offered to God.

We likewise entrust to you the abbeys which our predecessor Pope Gregory VII committed to your disposition and that of your successors: namely Virhelva, St Giles, St John of Angély, St Peter of Moissac, Moliac, St Martial of Limoges, the new monastery of St Cyprian of Poitiers at St Sacco; adding also that St German of Auxerre, St Astrimonius of Maurienne, and St Bertin of Tarvannes shall be subject to the same disposition, saving of course the right of the holy Roman Church.

No less do we confirm the aforesaid chapter of Pope Urban II,

[Col. 0053A] that the brethren of your cells situated anywhere shall not suffer suspension from the divine offices on account of any interdict or excommunication; but that both the monks themselves and their servants, and those who have devoted themselves to the monastic profession, with the church doors closed and diocesan clergy excluded, shall celebrate the offices of divine worship and perform the rites due to burial. We also grant you leave to receive through your places laypeople or secular clerics for conversion or burial, except those excommunicated for specified crimes. We grant to your religious body the right to receive regular clerics who flee to your monastery out of necessity and to admit them to your way of life.

Moreover, we decree that absolutely no person may rashly disturb your venerable monastery and its dependent places; rather, their churches, possessions, and other goods which have been given for the salvation of souls, or which may hereafter, through God’s mercy, be given, shall remain secure and inviolate to you and your successors—whom indeed we know to keep themselves, with due discernment, apart from excommunicated and rapacious persons.

[Col. 0053B] If, therefore, any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowing this charter of our constitution, should rashly attempt to act against it, after a second and third warning, unless he makes amendment by fitting satisfaction, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and honour; let him know himself guilty before the divine judgment for the wrong committed; and let him be excluded from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Redeemer

[Col. 0053C] of us all, and be subject at the last judgment to severe vengeance. But upon all who preserve what is right for that place, may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that they may receive here the fruit of good action and find, before the strict Judge, the rewards of eternal peace. Amen.

I, Paschal, bishop of the holy Catholic Church. I, Odo, bishop of Ostia, have subscribed. I, Milo . . . bishop of Palestrina. I, Alberic, cardinal of St Peter in Chains. I, Walter [otherwise Gualter], bishop of the Church of Albano, have subscribed. I, Teuto, cardinal of SS John and Paul. I, John, bishop of Tusculum. [Col. 0053D] I, Paganus, cardinal of the holy Roman Church, have subscribed.

Given at Anagni through the hand of John, cardinal-deacon of the holy Roman Church, on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of December, in the eighth indiction, in the year 1100 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the second year of the pontificate of Lord Paschal II, pope.

### XXXII. Letter of Paschal to the bishops of Gaul.—He commends the monastery of Cluny. (1100, 19 November)

[Mansi, *Concilia*, XX, 1037.]

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the venerable

[Col. 0054A] brethren, archbishops and bishops throughout Gaul: greeting and apostolic blessing.

We believe that your brotherhood does not fail to know how great a reverence is owed to the constitutions of the Apostolic See. But if anything appears either to have been stated insufficiently or to have been understood otherwise, let those who are accustomed to complain against the holy Roman Church recall what Pope Gelasius of holy memory answered the Eastern bishops concerning the writings of Pope Felix issued against Acacius.

Therefore we bring to your brotherhood’s remembrance that the monastery of Cluny, from the very beginning of its foundation, was offered to the holy Roman Church. Religious bishops and distinguished princes have indeed enriched it, because of its exceptional religious observance, with their gifts and possessions. The Roman pontiffs,

[Col. 0054B] guarding it as the pupil of their own eye, entrusted to the governance of those brethren many places belonging to them and fortified both the monastery itself and the other places connected with it by the protections of their privileges. For you know how many new institutions have been founded through them in the regions of Gaul, and how ancient monasteries have been found restored to religious life [perhaps “restored”]. Therefore we warn, beseech, and command your charity not to attempt to oppose the privileges of so many and such great pontiffs, lest by violating them you incur, God forbid, the indignation of the Apostolic See. Be imitators of your fathers, who cultivated that venerable congregation with fuller devotion; and join helping hands to the salvation which the Lord works through them in the case of many sinners.

[Col. 0054C] Love them, protect them, and cherish them in such a way that through you they may serve the Almighty more peaceably, while you, who stand amid the whirlwinds of a changing world, may obtain through them the grace both of the Apostolic See and of almighty God.

Given at the Lateran, 13 December.

### XXXIII. He receives the Greater Monastery under protection and confirms its possessions and privileges, imposing upon the monks an annual payment of one gold denarius. (1100, 19 November)

[Works of Guibert, abbot of St Mary of Nogent, ed. Achery, Notes, p. 588.]

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the venerable brother HILGOT, abbot of the Greater Monastery,

[Col. 0054D] and to his successors regularly appointed in perpetuity.

Although, by the authority and benevolence of the Apostolic See, we are bound to all the children of the holy Church, it is nevertheless fitting that we apply ourselves with a more earnest devotion of charity to those places and persons distinguished by a fuller grace of religious observance. Accordingly, most beloved son in Christ Hilgot, granting the just petitions of you and your brethren, both out of devotion and reverence for the blessed confessor of Christ Martin and on account of the prerogative of your religious observance, we have specially received under the guardianship and protection of the Apostolic See your monastery, called the Greater Monastery, formerly built by blessed Martin.

[Col. 0055A] Therefore, by this present charter of our privilege, we command by apostolic authority that whatever the same monastery now justly possesses, and whatever it may hereafter be able justly and canonically to acquire by grants of princes, offerings of the faithful, or concessions of pontiffs, shall remain secure and inviolate to you and your successors. We decree, therefore, that absolutely no person may rashly disturb that monastery, take away or diminish the possessions subject to it, or harass them by reckless vexations; rather, everything shall be preserved whole for the use of those for whose support and governance it was granted.

We utterly prohibit public Masses being celebrated in the aforesaid monastery by any archbishop or bishop,

[Col. 0055B] or stations being held there, lest any occasion be afforded for popular gatherings in the retreats of God’s servants. We also forbid anyone to compel the monks of that place, against their own will and that of their abbot, to attend any church for a station or for celebrating funerals.

Adding and commanding further that no archbishop or bishop henceforth presume, for any reason and in any place, to excommunicate the Greater Monastery of Blessed Martin or the monks of that Greater Monastery; rather, every more serious case concerning them shall depend upon the judgment of the Apostolic See.

Nor shall the brethren of your cells suffer suspension of the divine

[Col. 0055C] offices on account of any interdict or excommunication; but both the monks themselves, their servants, and those who have devoted themselves to the monastic profession shall, with the church doors closed and diocesan clergy excluded, celebrate the offices of divine worship and perform the rites due to burial.

When you, the present abbot of that place, or any of your successors, dies, no one shall be put over it by any crafty deception or violence, except one whom the brethren, by common consent—or the sounder part of the brethren’s counsel—have elected.

Furthermore, because the bishop and clergy of the Church of Tours, though warned by repeated letters of our predecessor Urban II of apostolic memory and also by ourselves,

[Col. 0055D] have in no way consented to desist from assailing you; indeed, while communicating more familiarly with the Apostolic See, they have not feared to excommunicate you and proclaim you excommunicated, to the point of withdrawing the monks of St Julian, other religious brethren, and abbots from your abbot’s burial and from communion in your profession. With the Lord’s aid, we have withdrawn your religious body from their excommunication. For, on the testimony of blessed Ambrose, we have learned that whoever dissents from the Roman Church is plainly a heretic; and Samuel says that it is a crime like idolatry to refuse obedience. But we embrace you, as sons of our household, with the bond of communion, charity, and grace.

[Col. 0056A] Therefore, as justice requires, we establish that an abbot regularly elected shall be consecrated either by the Roman pontiff or by whatever Catholic bishop, sharing our communion and household, they may prefer to summon; and, supported by your authority, he shall provide what is requested. Let the brethren of your places receive from the bishops in whose dioceses they are situated chrism, holy oil, consecrations of altars or churches, and ordinations of monks who are to be promoted to holy orders.

Moreover, we add that the monastery of Blessed Martin, free from the jurisdiction of every mortal, shall, God granting, remain subject to the Roman Church alone and shall always rejoice in so great liberty and authority.

[Col. 0056B] As a token of this liberty received from the Roman Church, it shall pay to the Lateran palace one gold denarius every year.

If, therefore, in future any archbishop or bishop, emperor or king, prince or duke, count, viscount, judge, or any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowing this charter of our constitution, should rashly attempt to act against it, after warning, unless he makes amendment by fitting satisfaction, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and honour; let him know himself guilty before the divine judgment for the wrong committed; and let him be excluded from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, our Redeemer,

[Col. 0056C] and be subject at the last judgment to severe vengeance. But upon all who preserve what is right for that place, may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that they may receive here the fruit of good action and find, before the strict Judge, the rewards of eternal peace. Amen, amen, amen.

I, Paschal, bishop of the Catholic Church. I, Odo, bishop of Ostia. I, Miro [Milo], bishop of Palestrina. I, Paganus, cardinal-deacon of the Roman Church. I, Alberic, cardinal by God’s grace.

Given at the Lateran through the hand of John, cardinal-deacon of the holy Roman Church, on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of December, in the eighth indiction, in the one thousand one hundredth year of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the second year of the pontificate

[Col. 0056D] of Lord Paschal II.

### XXXIV. Letter of Pope Paschal to Hugh, abbot of Cluny.—Privilege for Cluny. (1100, 20 November)

[Mansi, *Concilia*, vol. XX, 1038.]

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to HUGH, abbot of Cluny, and his successors regularly appointed in perpetuity.

Both the prerogative of religious observance, by which, through God’s grace, your congregation excels in your time throughout all Gaul, and the unshaken unity of charity by which, amid every storm, you have adhered to the Apostolic See, strongly exhort—indeed urge and compel—our mildness to grant assent to your petitions

[Col. 0057A] and provide more carefully hereafter for your peace. Therefore, whatever liberty, protection, and authority the Roman pontiffs, our predecessors—especially Gregory VII and Urban II of apostolic memory—conferred upon your monastery and the places belonging to it, we also, by this present decree, God being its author, confirm.

Moreover, we add that both the priories and cells, and all other properties in whatsoever places with which your fraternity was invested at the time of the Council of Clermont, celebrated by the aforesaid Pope Urban, concerning which no question was then raised—at which council you yourself were present—shall always be preserved to you and your successors in peace and tranquillity.

[Col. 0057B] We also command that all your churches or chapels and cemeteries be free and exempt from every exaction, apart from the customary episcopal *parata* and jurisdiction over priests if they offend against the dignity of their order; excepting, of course, those churches which remain under the abbot’s authority without such subjection. It shall also be lawful for you or your brethren to choose priests in your churches, provided that they receive the care of souls from bishops or the bishops’ vicars without simony. But if those persons should perversely refuse to confer it, then the priests shall, through the benevolence of the Apostolic See, obtain permission to celebrate the offices. Let the brethren of your places receive the consecration of churches or altars from the bishops in whose dioceses they are situated, provided those bishops are willing to provide it freely and without perversity.

[Col. 0057C] Otherwise, they shall receive the sacraments of consecration for those churches from whichever Catholic bishop you prefer.

Nor shall anyone have authority to disturb either the brethren of your cloister or of your places because of alms given for the salvation of the living or the dead; rather, it shall be lawful to receive the offerings of men and women brought to them, for the benefit of God’s servants and the poor. No less do we confirm the aforesaid chapter of Pope Urban II, that the brethren of your cells situated anywhere shall not suffer suspension of the divine offices because of any interdict or excommunication; but both the monks themselves and their servants,

[Col. 0057D] and those who have devoted themselves to the monastic profession, with the church doors closed and diocesan clergy excluded, shall celebrate the offices of divine worship and perform the rites due to burial. We also grant you leave to receive through your places laypeople or secular clerics for conversion or burial, except those excommunicated for specified crimes. We grant to your religious body the right to receive and admit to your way of life regular clerics who either cannot be saved in their own places or flee to your monastery out of necessity.

Moreover, we decree that absolutely no person may rashly disturb your venerable monastery and the places subject to it; but its churches, possessions, and other goods that have already been given for the salvation of souls, or may hereafter, through God’s mercy, be given, shall remain secure and inviolate to you and your successors. We know indeed that they keep themselves more vigilantly apart from excommunicated persons with devout discernment.

[Col. 0058A] If, therefore, any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowing this charter of our constitution, should rashly attempt to act against it, after a second or third warning, unless he makes amendment by fitting satisfaction, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and honour; let him know himself guilty before the divine judgment for the wrong committed; let him be excluded from the most holy body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, our Redeemer; and let him be subject at the last judgment to severe vengeance. But upon all who preserve what is right for that monastery may there be the peace of our Lord

[Col. 0058B] Jesus Christ, so that they may receive here the fruit of good action and find, before the strict Judge, the rewards of eternal peace. Amen, amen, amen.

I, Paschal, bishop of the Catholic Church, have subscribed. I, Odo, bishop of Ostia, have subscribed. I, Milo, bishop of Palestrina, have subscribed. I, Alberic, archbishop and cardinal of St Peter in Chains by God’s grace, have subscribed. I, Walter, bishop of the Church of Albano, have subscribed. I, Paganus, cardinal of the holy Roman Church, have subscribed.

Given at the Lateran, through the hand of John, cardinal of the holy

[Col. 0058C] Roman Church, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of December, in the eighth indiction, in the year 1100 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the second year of the pontificate of Lord Paschal II, pope.

### XXXV. Bull of Paschal II for the union of the Church of Orange with that of Tricastin. (1100, 10 December)

[Gallia Christiana, new edition, I, Documents, 120.]

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the clergy and people of Orange: greeting and apostolic blessing.

We are astonished that you oppose the decrees of the Apostolic See with such obstinacy. For when our predecessor had determined something for authoritative confirmation, you have likewise so despised [Col. 0058D] whatever we commanded in accordance with that determination that you have deigned to offer no subjection or obedience to the bishop of Tricastin. At length, tolerating such obstinacy with the mildness of apostolic affection, we commanded in a repeated threatening letter that you should not strive to violate the union of churches established by our predecessors, but should finally obey the aforesaid brother, your bishop, with humility.

Given at the Lateran, 10 December.

### XXXVI. Privilege for the monastery of St Saviour at Pavia. (1100)

[Margarini, *Bullarium Casinense*, II, 119, from the archive of the monastery of St Saviour at Pavia.]

[Col. 0059A]

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the beloved son in Christ JOHN, abbot of the venerable monastery called that of the Lord Saviour, situated near Pavia, and to his successors regularly appointed in perpetuity.

A devout petition ought to be fulfilled with the effect sought by its purpose, so that both the sincerity of devotion may shine forth commendably and the requested benefit may undoubtedly acquire force. Since, therefore, your belovedness, fleeing to the harbour of the Apostolic See, has duly sought its protection, we graciously assent to your petition. We receive under the guardianship of the Apostolic See the monastery of St Saviour, over which, God being the author, you preside, together with all that belongs to it. This is the monastery which the august empress Adelheid is known to have restored at her own expense and likewise enriched by her liberality.

[Col. 0059B] Following in the footsteps of our holy predecessors, the pontiffs of the Apostolic See, we establish by the authority of this present decree that whatever goods, whatever urban or rural estates, cultivated or uncultivated lands, whatever possessions, furnishings, and ornaments have been conferred upon that monastery from her own right either by the aforesaid Augusta or by other faithful persons, or whatever it may hereafter be able justly and canonically to acquire through concessions of pontiffs, the liberality of princes,

[Col. 0059C] or offerings of the faithful, shall remain secure and inviolate to you and your successors. We decree, therefore, that absolutely no person may rashly disturb that monastery, take away or retain its possessions, property, furnishings, or ornaments, diminish them, or harass them with reckless vexations; rather, everything shall be preserved whole, for the use of those for whose support and governance it was granted, and for their manifold benefit.

Nor shall the tithes of the revenues of the aforesaid monastery of the Lord Saviour be demanded by the prelate or ministers of any church. When you, the present abbot of that place, or any of your successors, dies, no one shall be placed over it by any craft of fraudulent encroachment or violence, except one whom the brethren, by common consent—or the sounder part of the brethren’s counsel—have elected according to the fear of God and the Rule of blessed Benedict.

[Col. 0059D] Once an abbot has been elected, there shall always be freedom to choose whatever bishop they wish, who, for the abbot and the other brethren, with fear of God and the consent of the entire community, shall confer the insignia of consecration wherever they wish, by the privilege of our authority and without any payment of a price. You shall receive chrism, holy oil, consecrations of altars or churches, and the ordinations of your monks or canons who are to be promoted to holy orders, from whatever Catholic bishops you prefer. Moreover, we permit baptism to be celebrated in those churches of the monastery where it has hitherto customarily been celebrated.

[Col. 0060A] We forbid public Masses to be celebrated in that monastery, or any station or ordination to be held there, without the abbot’s consent or by any bishop. Furthermore, in accordance with the enactments of our predecessors, we grant to you and your successors the use of dalmatic, sandals, and gloves. Thus we decree that the monastery itself shall remain free from every yoke or jurisdiction of any person, being subject only to the holy Roman and Apostolic Church.

If any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowing this charter of our constitution, should rashly attempt to act against it, after a second or third warning, unless he makes amendment by fitting satisfaction, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and honour;

[Col. 0060B] let him acknowledge himself guilty before the divine judgment for the wrong committed; let him be excluded from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, our Redeemer; and let him be subject at the last judgment to severe vengeance. But upon all who preserve what is right for that place may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that they may receive here the fruit of good action and find, before the strict Judge, the rewards of eternal peace. Amen, amen.

Given in the year of the Lord 1100.

### XXXVII. He grants “the pallium and a privilege” to Gerald, archbishop of Braga.

(There is only a mention in Gerald’s *Life*. See Baluze, *Miscellanea*, Luc. ed., I, 132.)

### XXXVIII. Rescript of Pope Paschal to the Church of Strasbourg. (About 1100)

[Mansi, *Concilia*, XX, 1092.]

[Col. 0060C]

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the clergy and people of Strasbourg: greeting and apostolic blessing.

[Note: [Col. 0059] See below the letter of the Church of Strasbourg to Paschal.] Having examined your letter, we have felt paternal sorrow over your oppression and the destruction of your Church; but because you suffer for justice, for which you shall be blessed, we rejoice with you. Therefore, that you may attain that blessedness, persevere steadfastly in your good purpose, and resist manfully that intruder into the Church of God; for by God’s grace we have neither given nor shall give our consent to his election or consecration. For our part,

[Col. 0060D] in all that you do for justice, our counsel and help shall never fail you, through the Lord who lives and reigns for ages of ages. Amen.

### XXXIX. Letter of Paschal to Bernard, archbishop of Toledo.—He confirms the primacy of the Church of Toledo. (1101, 6 March)

[Mansi, *Concilia*, XX, 982.]

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the most reverend [perhaps “most reverent,” Hardouin] brother BERNARD, archbishop of Toledo, and to his successors canonically appointed in perpetuity.

On examining the decrees of synodal acts, it is clear how great the dignity of the Church of Toledo was in antiquity, and how great were the benefits that accrued through it in ecclesiastical affairs.

[Col. 0061A] Therefore we too desire, so far as our ability permits and with the Lord’s help, to establish the status of that city in the glory of ecclesiastical dignity [variant: “to establish it in the glory of ecclesiastical dignity”]. Accordingly, both because of the benevolence owed by the holy Roman Church, because of the due reverence for the Church of Toledo, and also at the request of our most reverend [perhaps “most reverent,” H.] son, the most excellent King Alfonso—by whose valour and prudence the Church [variant: city] of Toledo was freed from the yoke of the Moors and Moabites—we establish, by authority of the present privilege, that you, dearest brother, shall be primate throughout all the kingdoms of Spain, in accordance with the enactment of our predecessor Pope Urban II of holy memory, just as the bishops of that city are known to have been in ancient times.

[Col. 0061B] You shall, however, use the pallium only in the celebration of Masses, at the times of the following principal feasts: on the three days of the Nativity of the Lord; Epiphany; Hypapante; the Lord’s Supper; Holy Saturday; the three days of Easter; Ascension; Pentecost; the three feasts of St Mary; St Michael; St John the Baptist; all feasts of the Apostles; the martyrs whose relics rest in your church; St Martin and St Ildefonsus, confessors; the Commemoration of All Saints; at the consecration of churches, bishops, and clerics; on the annual anniversary of your consecration; and on the feast-days also of St Isidore and Leander.

All the bishops of Spain shall look to you as primate; and they shall refer to you whatever may arise among them worthy of a more serious question, while preserving, nevertheless, the authority of the Roman Church and the privileges of each metropolitan. Therefore, by the tenor of this privilege, we confirm to you and to your canonical successors, should divine grace grant it, the Church of Toledo in perpetual right, together with all the churches and dioceses which it is known to have possessed from antiquity by its own right.

[Col. 0061C] Concerning those now subject to Saracen rule, we command that, when it pleases the Lord to restore them to the power of the Christian people, they shall be returned to the due obedience of your Church. We subject to your jurisdiction, upon this condition, the dioceses of those cities which, through Saracen invasion, have lost their own metropolitans: so long as they remain without their own metropolitans, they shall be subject to you as to their proper metropolitan. But if any metropolitan see is restored to its former condition, its diocese too shall be restored to its own metropolitan. Yet your brotherhood should not for that reason strive less diligently that the glory of its dignity may be restored to each metropolitan see.

All these things, and everything else that can be proved to belong to the ancient apostolic grant of the see of Toledo, we convey and confirm to you and your successors for perpetual possession. We exhort you, most reverend brother, with deep affection, always to show yourself worthy of so great an honour of pontifical office,

[Col. 0062A] taking care always to be without offence to Christians and Saracens, and, as the Lord grants, striving to convert unbelievers to the faith by word and example. Thus may you excel in human eyes through the dignity of your pallium and the prerogative of primacy, while inwardly you are strong in excellence of virtues before the eyes of the heavenly Majesty.

If, therefore, any ecclesiastical or secular person in future, knowing this charter of our constitution, should rashly attempt to act against it, after a second or third warning, unless he makes amendment by fitting satisfaction, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power or honour; let him know himself guilty before the divine judgment for the wrong committed; let him be excluded from the most holy body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Redeemer; and let him be subject

[Col. 0062B] at the last judgment to severe vengeance. But upon all who preserve what is right for that Church may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that they may receive here the fruit of good action and find, before the strict Judge, the rewards of eternal peace. Amen, amen.

Written through the hand of Peter, notary, regional official, and scrivener of the sacred palace.

I, Paschal, bishop of the Catholic Church, subscribe.

Given at the Lateran through the hand of John, cardinal-deacon of the holy Roman Church, on the second day before the Nones of March, in the eighth indiction, in the year 1101 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the second year of the pontificate of Lord Paschal II, pope.

### XL. Papal privilege for the monastery of St Sabinus at Piacenza. (1101, 7 March)

[Campi, *Dell’ historia ecclesiastica di Piacenza*, vol. I, p. 525.]

[Col. 0062C]

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the beloved son ALBERIC, abbot of the monastery of St Sabinus, situated near Piacenza, and to his successors regularly appointed in perpetuity.

We acknowledge that, by the Lord’s ordering, we have been advanced to the service of the Apostolic See so that we ought effectively to assist its children when they seek help and, insofar as the Lord grants, defend and protect those obedient to it. Therefore, dearest son, we have judged it fitting by the charter of this present decree to oppose your persecutors

[Col. 0062D] and to provide more carefully, with the Lord’s help, for your peace and welfare. We establish that whatever estates and goods in cells, churches, villages, or other properties your monastery lawfully possesses at present, or may hereafter justly and canonically acquire through the concessions of pontiffs, the liberality of princes, or the offerings of the faithful, shall remain secure and inviolate to you and your successors.
