We decree, therefore, that absolutely no person may rashly disturb that monastery, take away its possessions, retain what has been taken, diminish them, or harass them with reckless vexations; rather, everything shall be preserved entire for the use of those for whose support and governance it was granted, and for every kind of benefit.

[Col. 0063A] Moreover, following the example of our predecessors Sylvester and Alexander, Roman pontiffs of happy memory, we decree that the use of the mitre and other pontifical insignia shall be entirely free to you; and we add that, while celebrating the sacred mysteries, you may strengthen the people with the sign of the holy cross. If any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowing this charter of our constitution, should rashly attempt to act against it, after a second or third warning, unless he makes amendment by fitting satisfaction, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and honour; let him know himself guilty before the divine judgment for the wrong committed; let him be excluded from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, our Redeemer; and let him be subject at the last judgment to severe vengeance. Upon all,

[Col. 0063B] however, who preserve what is right for that place, may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that they may receive here the fruit of good action and find, before the strict Judge, the rewards of eternal peace. Amen, amen.

Written through the hand of Peter, notary, regional official, and scrivener of the sacred palace.

I, Paschal, bishop of the Catholic Church.

Given at the Lateran through the hand of John, cardinal-deacon of the Holy Roman Church, on the Nones of March, in the ninth indiction, in the year 1101 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the second year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Paschal II.

XLI. Letter to Godfrey, bishop of Maguelone.—He expresses surprise that his letters, sent “in the preceding autumn,” concerning the consecration of the elect of Compostela had not arrived. He orders him to carry out the consecration. (1101, 25 March.)

[Flórez, *España sagrada*, XX, 29.]

[Col. 0063C]

P., bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother G., bishop of Maguelone: greeting and apostolic blessing.

We believe that your brotherhood knows that the Church of Compostela obtained a privilege from our predecessor: namely, that it should be subject to no metropolitan see, and that its bishop ought to be consecrated by the Roman bishop. But its elect, hindered by many obstacles, is certainly unable to come to the Apostolic See. Therefore, in the preceding autumn we sent letters to your brotherhood, which, we are surprised to learn, did not reach you. We therefore again command that you go there and, in our stead, bless the said elect as bishop.

Given at the Lateran, 25 March.

XLII. To the clergy of St James at Compostela.—He repeats what he had already directed by letter concerning the consecration of Didacus. (1101, 25 March.)

[FLÓREZ, *España sagrada*, p. 30.]

P., bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons, the clergy of St James: greeting and apostolic blessing.

For some time now we have grieved over the deprivation of your Church of Compostela. Therefore, in the preceding autumn we assented to your petition, so that we might spare the elect of that Church the necessity of coming to us at that time. We are surprised that the letters which, as we learned from your messengers who bore them, were sent to you, did not reach you. Accordingly, by the full authority of our letters we command our venerable brother, the bishop of Maguelone, to go and consecrate him. But if he should perhaps be unable to do so, let the bishop of Burgos or another Catholic bishop be summoned.

By the authority of the present letters we likewise command the elect himself to accept, trusting in the mercy of the Lord, the burden imposed upon him by the common consent of the Church. Moreover, we forbid both the soldiers and clergy of your regions to presume, on the occasion of the journey to Jerusalem, to abandon their Church and province, which the savagery of the Moabites attacks so frequently.

Given at the Lateran, 25 March.

XLIII. To King A[lfonso].—He announces what he has already ordered concerning the consecration of Didacus. (1101, 25 March.)

[FLÓREZ, *España sagrada*, XX, 29.]

P., bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son A[lfonso]: greeting and apostolic blessing.

In the preceding autumn we consented to your request concerning the consecration of the bishop of Compostela. We were therefore surprised that you asked us again. Since we have heard that those letters were intercepted, we again command, by the authority of our letters, our venerable brother the bishop of Maguelone to go and consecrate him. But if he should perhaps be unable to do so, let the bishop of Burgos or another Catholic bishop be summoned.

Given at the Lateran, 25 March.

XLIV. To the clergy and laity dwelling in the kingdom of A[lfonso].—The Western Church is not to be laid waste on the pretext of a journey to Jerusalem. (1101, 25 March.)

[FLÓREZ, *ut supra*, p. 88.]

P., bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the clergy and laity dwelling in the kingdom of A[lfonso]. [Note: [Col. 0063D] Alfonso, namely Alfonso VI.] Greeting and apostolic blessing.

It greatly endangers your salvation that you despise obedience to the commands of the Apostolic See. For some time ago we wrote to you that you should not abandon your regions on the occasion of the expedition to Jerusalem, since they are attacked by the daily incursions of Moors and Moabites; for in your departure we greatly fear their tyranny for the western regions.

Therefore, we command all those of your regions, both clergy and laity, whom we have been able to see, to desist from setting out for Jerusalem and to return to their homeland. Know also that we have compelled the bearers of this letter—Munio, Didacus, and Nuno, together with their followers—to return. We therefore command your charity that no one presume to defame them for this return or assail them with any accusations.

Accordingly, by a repeated command we order you all to remain in your regions and attack the Moabites and Moors with all your strength. There, by God’s grant, perform your penances; there receive the remission and grace of the holy apostles Peter and Paul and of their Apostolic Church.

Given at the Lateran, 25 March.

XLV. Privilege for the monastery of Monte Cassino. (1101, 31 March.)

[MANSI, *Concilia*, XX, 1133.]

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother and fellow-priest ODERISIUS, abbot of Monte Cassino, greeting and apostolic blessing.

The authority of our office exhorts us to be solicitous for the condition of churches and to establish firmly what has rightly been established. Therefore we have judged that the case of your monastery concerning the cell of Cingla should in no way be moved from the settlement instituted by the written decision of our lord and predecessor, Urban of holy memory.

At the synod of Melfi, which, by the Lord’s grant, we solemnly celebrated in the second year of our ordination, the abbess who had formerly held the cell of Cingla protested most vehemently, asserting that she had been wrongly treated and had suffered an injury. When she had filled the whole assembly with her complaints, John, our common son and a deacon of our Church, at last rose, troubled by your absence, and explained that the matter had been canonically decided.

Our fellow brother Odo, bishop of Ostia, immediately added testimony to his report, saying that the abbess had indeed been restored to that cell by the judgment of Lord Pope Urban; that after three months she had indeed been summoned to the council at Bari; and that, when she had not gone, she had sent a messenger. That messenger, evading the conclusion of the case, maintained that the abbess had not been fully restored, because she had by no means received certain charters of the cell or documents necessary for its defence. It was therefore arranged that the charters themselves, not previously demanded, should be returned in the presence of the council through the hand of Lord Roffrid, bishop of Benevento.

After the pope had returned to Benevento, the abbess was again summoned by letter to come to Sinuessa. Since she neither came to Sinuessa nor stated what burden she justly complained of suffering, she was granted a postponement for coming to the town of St Germanus, adjacent to Mount Cassino. At last she came, but refused to take up the case, still complaining that she had not received all the documents of the cell of Cingla. The brethren of Cassino, however, were ready to prove on oath that they had found in that place neither more nor other charters than those they had returned. She showed certain of our men, secretly, documents concerning the charters, but would not produce them before the pontiff.

At last, disregarding the exhortations of Lord Pope Urban, who urged concord, and our own admonitions, she departed secretly and thereby yielded her place to judgment. Thus our lord Pope Urban, of holy memory in Christ, having carefully reread the decrees of the Roman pontiffs, the enactments of emperors, and the founder’s written instruments for the place, restored that cell to the monastery of Cassino, to be possessed in perpetuity. For the abbess’s contrived absence was judged, according to the sanctions of the canons, to be equivalent to a confession by all the bishops and cardinals then present.

Albert, now bishop of Siponto, but at the time of the action in question a cardinal-priest of the Roman Church, added the support of his testimony to these words of our fellow brother the bishop of Ostia, since he too had been present. The Roman judges Peter and Raimbald likewise declared that the matter had been tried in their presence, and that they too had given their judgment from the books of Roman law.

Having heard these matters, we declared that it seemed grave to us for decisions made by our predecessors to be reconsidered. But when that abbess pressed our brethren most vehemently, we commanded certain bishops to withdraw and deliberate whether this case seemed to require further reconsideration. Upon their return, Bruno, bishop of Segni, speaking for them, said that the judgment of Lord Pope Urban appeared reasonable and just to them, and that it ought to be held valid, as having been conducted in canonical order.

We therefore judged that it should always remain in the same condition; and, as then by word, so now by writing, we decree that the cell of Cingla is always to be administered under the discipline of monastic religious life and belongs forever to the right and possession of the monastery of Cassino. Should anyone, having learned the tenor of this definition and confirmation, presume to oppose it and separate that cell from the monastery of Cassino, let that person likewise be separated from the body of the Church by the judgment of the Church.

Written through the hand of Peter, regional notary and archivist of the sacred palace.

I, Paschal, bishop of the Catholic Church, have subscribed.

Given at the Lateran through the hand of John, cardinal-deacon of the Holy Roman Church, on 31 March, in the ninth indiction, in the year 1102 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the second year of the pontificate of Lord Paschal II.

[Col. 0066D] (A pendant lead seal is present.)

XLVI. To the people of Velletri.—He revokes the unlawful measures instituted among them by Guibert. He defines their boundaries. (1101, 6 April.)

[MANSI, *Concilia*, XX, 1048.]

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the citizens of the city of Velletri, faithful of the Apostolic See: greeting and apostolic blessing.

We are admonished, by the duty of our entrusted office, both to correct what is wrong and to confirm what is right. Therefore, in accordance with your petition, by the authority of this present document we decree the utter abolition from your city of all wrongful customs or exactions imposed by the heresiarch Guibert, formerly bishop of Ravenna and then invader of the Apostolic See.

Moreover, we decree that the favour which your city obtained from our predecessor Gregory VII, of holy memory, shall remain firm both for you and for your descendants who remain faithful to the Apostolic See: namely, that the more powerful persons in your locality, whose right you yourselves do not deny, may not dare to impose heavier burdens upon you. Not only the inhabitants of your city, but also its ancient boundaries, are to be preserved from every invasion of secular power and kept safe from molestation.

By the boundaries of the city we mean those which encompass its appurtenances far and wide. (He specifies those boundaries and enumerates many places.) We absolutely forbid, by apostolic prohibition, that these boundaries be altered to your detriment. We establish that whatever they contain is to be peacefully possessed in perpetuity, according to each person’s right, by you, your heirs, and those to whom you lawfully grant it.

If any person, great or small, should attempt with rash boldness to contravene this apostolic decree and command, and, after being admonished once, twice, and a third time within suitable intervals, should not repent and suitably correct what has been unjustly done, let that person know that he must pay one hundred pounds of Pavia denarii: one half to our treasury and one half to those suffering injustice.

Written through the hand of Peter, regional notary and secretary of the sacred palace.

[Col. 0067C] I, Paschal, bishop, have subscribed.

Given at the Lateran, through the hand of John, cardinal of the Holy Roman Church, on 6 April, in the ninth indiction, in the year 1102 [1101] of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the second year of the pontificate of Lord Paschal II.

XLVII. Confirmation of the endowment of the monastery of St Benedict at Alpirsbach. (1101, 12 April.)

[PETRUS, *Suevia ecclesiastica*, Augsburg, 1699, folio.]

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son CONO, abbot of the monastery of Alpirsbach, and to his successors regularly promoted in perpetuity.

It is fitting readily to grant assent to religious desires, so that faithful devotion may obtain a prompt fulfilment. Therefore, considering the devotion of the religious nobles Rotmann of Husin, Adelbert of Zolro, and Count Alwic of Sulzo, we assent to their desires. By the protection of this present decree, under God’s authority, we establish that the monastery of St Benedict, which they founded on their own estate—that is, in their hereditary place called Alpirsbach—together with the adjoining forest and its boundaries; likewise the other estates and serfs which they jointly transferred through the hand of the free man Bernard of Flurin to St Benedict in the villages called Dornheim, Homesingen, Hevingdorff, Garta, Hasela, and Veringen; and those which Adelbert of Zolro individually transferred at the time of his conversion in the other places named below, namely Unzin, Geroldisdorf, Sulzo, Bollo, Norwilo, and Bosingin; and whatever the aforesaid nobles or any other faithful persons may in future offer from their own right to the same monastery—shall remain forever secure and unimpaired.

We therefore decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb that monastery, remove its possessions, retain what has been removed, diminish them, or harass it with reckless vexations; rather, let all things be preserved whole, for the complete benefit of the uses for which they were granted, namely the support and governance of those concerned.

The abbots, together with the brethren, shall appoint for themselves as advocate whomever they consider more useful. If he should later become unprofitable to the monastery and burdensome to the brethren, they shall remove him and appoint another. Nor may anyone else receive the ban of advocacy from a Catholic king unless he has been chosen by the abbot and brethren.

Upon the death of you, the present abbot of that place, or of any of your successors, no one may be set over it by any trick of stealth, cunning, or force, except one whom the brethren by common consent, or the sounder part of the brethren, shall elect in the fear of God and according to the Rule of St Benedict.

As a sign of the liberty commanded by the Roman Church, you shall pay annually to the Lateran palace one gold coin called a Byzantine. If in the future any archbishop or bishop, emperor or king, prince or duke, count, viscount, judge, or any ecclesiastical or secular person should violate the text of this our constitution, or knowingly attempt to contravene it, and, after a second or third admonition, should fail to make suitable amends by appropriate satisfaction, let that person be deprived of the dignity of power and honour; let him acknowledge himself guilty before the divine judgment for the iniquity committed; let him be cut off from the most sacred Body and Blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Redeemer; and let him be subject to strict vengeance at the last judgment.

But upon all who preserve what is right for the same place, may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that they may receive here the fruit of good action and, before the strict Judge, find the rewards of eternal peace. Amen, amen.

Written through the hand of Peter, regional notary of the sacred palace.

I, Paschal, bishop of the Catholic Church, have subscribed.

[Col. 0068D] Witnesses present when the estate of Vischenboch was granted: Frederick and Arnold, brothers of Wolva, grantors of that estate; Count Barthold of Nuinburch; Wernher of Hophu; Dictersius of Nuinburch; Cuono of Horn; Rudolf of Wildorff; Sigeboto of Noviwiler; Egilolt of Berndec; Eigiswart of Lappil; Adelbert of Westirhein—at Offenburg.

Given at the Lateran through the hand of John, cardinal-deacon of the Holy Roman Church, on the day before the Ides of April, in the ninth indiction, in the year 1101 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the second year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Paschal II.

XLVIII. Paschal’s letter to Lambert, bishop of Arras.—He confirms the bishopric of Arras and establishes its boundaries with Cambrai. (1101, 15 April.)

[MANSI, *Concilia*, XX, 1014.]

[Col. 0069A]

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother LAMBERT, bishop of Arras, and to his successors to be canonically appointed in perpetuity.

What the Fathers have established ought indeed to be maintained under reverence and with inviolable authority. It is fitting that such things be neglected through no sloth, violated through no dissension, and disturbed through no contention. Therefore, considering that what our predecessor Urban, of pious memory, established concerning the restoration of the Church of Arras is wholly just and consonant with the sacred canons, we too enact it by the authority of our decree: namely, that the same Church, as it formerly shone in episcopal dignity, may also henceforth obtain, through God’s grace, a principal bishop.

We too ought to follow and support with fitting aid the purpose of divine mercy that operates in the restoration of churches and their peoples. Therefore, most beloved and reverend brother, whom our predecessor established in the Church of Arras when the Lord restored it, we likewise confirm, with the assistance of divine favour, in the exercise of episcopal dignity.

[Note: [Col. 0069] From this point onward, the text is identical, word for word, with the privilege of Urban II to the same Lambert. HARD.]

Whatever St Remigius granted to the said Church, and whatever it is established to have possessed in ancient times while it flourished in episcopal dignity, we decree shall remain entirely yours and your successors’, saving lawful enactments and the privileges of the Roman Church. Among these, we expressly confirm for the said Church two archdeaconries, one called that of Arras and the other that of Ostrevant. We command that the boundaries between the Churches of Arras and Cambrai shall be precisely those which can be proved to have existed in antiquity by written records, the division of territories, or other certain indications, so that, by God’s favour, the peace of the Churches may be troubled on no pretext and what has been established for the salvation of the faithful may endure with unshaken stability for all time.

If any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowing the text of this our constitution, should rashly attempt to contravene it, and, after a second or third admonition, should fail to make suitable amends by appropriate satisfaction, let that person be deprived of the dignity of power and honour; let him acknowledge himself guilty before the divine judgment for the iniquity committed; let him be cut off from the most sacred Body and Blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ; and let him be subject to strict vengeance at the last judgment.

But upon all who preserve what is right for the same place, may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that they may receive here the fruit of good action and, before the strict Judge, find the rewards of eternal peace. Amen, amen.

[Col. 0070A] Written through the hand of Peter, regional notary and archivist of the sacred palace.

Paschal, bishop of the Catholic Church.

Given at the Lateran through the hand of John, cardinal-deacon of the Holy Roman Church, on 15 April, in the ninth indiction, in the year 1101 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the second year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Paschal II.

XLIX. To Henry, king of the English.—Against ecclesiastical investitures. (1101.)

[MANSI, *Concilia*, XX, 1058.]

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son HENRY, king of the English: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Most beloved son, we gratefully received the words of your embassy; but we would have preferred the obedience of the one making the promise. In them you promised the Holy Roman Church in your kingdom those things which it had possessed in your father’s time, demanding the honours which your father had possessed in the time of our predecessors. All these things, certainly, would seem welcome on the surface; but when examined more deeply and explained by your envoy’s words, they proved weighty and most serious.

For you demanded that the Roman Church should grant you the right and power to appoint bishops and abbots by investiture; and that what the omnipotent Lord declares can be done by himself alone should be done by royal power. For the Lord says: “I am the door. If anyone enters through me, he shall be saved” (John 10). But when kings arrogate to themselves the role of the Church’s door, it follows that those who enter the Church through them are regarded not as shepherds but as thieves and robbers, as the same Lord says: “He who does not enter the sheepfold through the door, but climbs in by another way, is a thief and a robber” (*ibid.*).

Indeed, if your belovedness were asking something great of us that could be granted consistently with God, justice, and the safety of our order, we would certainly grant it reluctantly [variant: gladly]. But this is so grave and so unworthy that no Catholic Church can admit it on any ground. Blessed Ambrose could more easily have been compelled to suffer any extremity than to permit an emperor authority over the Church. For he replied (*Book II, Letter 14, to Marcellina*):

> “Do not burden yourself, Emperor, by thinking that you have any imperial right in matters that are divine. Do not exalt yourself; rather, if you wish to reign longer, be subject to God. It is written: ‘Render to God the things that are God’s, and to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s’ [Matthew 22]. Palaces belong to the emperor; churches belong to the priest. The right over public walls has been entrusted to you, not over sacred things. What have you to do with an adulteress? For she is an adulteress who is not joined in the lawful marriage of Christ.”

You hear, O king, that a Church not lawfully wed is called adulterous. For every bishop is regarded as the Church’s spouse, according to that Scripture which commands a brother to raise up children in his brother’s name by his brother’s wife, and commands the despiser of the bride to be stripped of his shoe by the future bridegroom. You see, therefore, O king, how dishonourable and dangerous it is for a mother to be defiled by adultery through her own sons.

If, then, you are a son of the Church—as every Catholic Christian certainly is—allow your mother to obtain a lawful spouse, so that the Church may be joined not through a human being but through God and man, Christ, her lawful spouse. For the Apostle Paul testifies that bishops are chosen by God when they are canonically elected, saying: “No one takes the honour to himself, but he who is called by God, as Aaron was” (Hebrews 5). And Blessed Ambrose says: “He is rightly believed to have been chosen by divine judgment when all have sought him.” And shortly afterward: “Where the petition of all agrees, we ought not doubt that there the Lord Jesus will be both author of the will, arbiter of the petition, presider over the ordination, and giver of grace.”

Furthermore, the prophet David, speaking to the Church, says: “In place of your fathers sons have been born to you; you shall appoint them rulers over all the earth” (Psalm 44). The Church has borne sons; the Church appoints rulers. We could offer other testimonies and examples from Holy Scripture establishing that bishops, the Church’s spouses and shepherds, are to be set over it not at the nod of secular powers, but by Christ’s dispensation and the Church’s judgment.

Accordingly, Emperor Justinian also enacted in his laws:

> “It must first be examined whether the bishop’s life is good or blameworthy, and whether he is supported by good testimony or not.”

And later:

> “Let everyone have the opportunity, if he wishes, to object; and if an objection is made before consecration, the bishop must not be consecrated until the objection has been examined and the person called to the episcopate has been shown innocent in every respect.”

Behold: what the emperor declares belongs to the whole people, royal power has attacked as its own alone. By a law of the same emperor it is also provided that no bishop may have either access to or departure from the emperor without letters from his metropolitan. The man whom you ought not admit into your court without letters from his metropolitan, do you wish, O king, to appoint as a ruler in the Church? It is surely monstrous that a son should beget his father, that a human being should create God. For it is manifest that priests are called gods in Holy Scripture as God’s vicars.

Accordingly, the emperor Constantine, of holy memory, is recorded not to have dared to adjudicate the cases of bishops. For this reason the holy and apostolic Roman Church, through our predecessors, took care vigorously to oppose royal usurpation and the abominable practice of investiture; and, though subjected to the gravest persecutions by tyrants, it has not desisted down to our own time.

Yet we trust in the Lord that Peter, prince of the Church and first of bishops, will not fail to preserve the strength of his confidence in us as well. Moreover, the Apostle Paul explains what the office of secular powers and kings is in the Church, saying: “For he is God’s minister for your good. For he does not bear the sword without cause. For he is God’s minister, an avenger in wrath upon the one who does evil” (Romans 13). The Apostle Peter agrees in the same terms: “Whether to the king,” he says, “as supreme, or to governors as sent by him for the punishment of evildoers and the praise of the good” (1 Peter 2).

Amid these considerations, O king, let no profane persuasion steal in upon you, as though we wished either to diminish anything of your power or to claim something more for ourselves in the advancement of bishops. Rather, if for God’s sake you desist from what is manifestly against God—what neither you can practise nor we grant consistently with God or with our salvation or yours—then whatever you subsequently ask that we can grant consistently with God, we shall grant more willingly, and we shall apply ourselves more eagerly to your honour and exaltation.

Do not think that the support of your power will be weakened if you desist from this profane usurpation. On the contrary, you will reign more strongly, more robustly, and more honourably when divine authority reigns in your kingdom. Then you will obtain our friendship and familiar association more firmly, and rejoice in having the blessed apostles as protectors of your kingdom. Nor shall we now be unable to assist you in your requests, when we perceive that the Lord is present as the supporter of our own requests.

May Almighty God, in whose hand are the hearts of kings, be present to our exhortation and to your hearing, so that, when you order your actions in accordance with his commands, he may order your kingdom with the stability and exaltation of his peace and honour. Amen.

L. Privilege for the Church of Chaumousey. (1101, 5 May.)

[Dom CALMET, *History of Lorraine*, II, *Proofs*, p. 109.]

[Col. 0072C] PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons SEHER, abbot, and his brethren professing the canonical life in the Church of Chaumousey, and to their successors who shall remain in the same religious life, in perpetuity.

It is fitting readily to grant assent to religious desires, so that faithful devotion may obtain a prompt fulfilment. Therefore, sons, assenting to the prayers of you all, we receive both you and all that is yours under the protection of the Apostolic See. We establish that you and your successors shall serve forever under the yoke of canonical discipline. By the present decree we also enact that your Church of Chaumousey shall remain free from every yoke of living persons, and that no one shall exercise dominion over it or its resources except the bishop of the Roman See, saving the canonical right of the bishop of Toul.

We further add that whatever goods and estates faithful persons have hitherto bestowed from their own right upon the place, and whatever you may in future be able justly and canonically to acquire, by the Lord’s grant, through the concession of pontiffs, the generosity of princes, or the offerings of the faithful, shall remain secure and unimpaired for you and your successors.

Upon the death of you, the present abbot of that place, or of any of your successors, no one may be set over it through stealth, cunning, or force, except one whom the brethren by common consent, or the sounder part of the brethren, shall judge fit to elect according to the fear of God. Nor may any ecclesiastic intrude himself there, except such spiritual men as your community invites to the election of an abbot.

The elect himself shall be confirmed by the bishop of Toul, according to the custom of your place or province. You shall likewise receive from that bishop the ordinations of clerics and the consecrations of altars and churches, provided that he has the grace and communion of the Apostolic See and is willing to provide them freely and without misconduct. Otherwise, you may approach whatever Catholic bishop you prefer and receive from him the blessing or the consecration of the brethren; supported by the authority of the Apostolic See, he shall grant what is requested and, when invited, shall come also for the consecration of altars.

Furthermore, we prohibit and forbid anyone to presume, under any pretext, to make an assault within the precinct of your monastery. But if, God forbid, violence should occur in your court, whether through the shedding of blood, the infliction of blows, or anything of that sort, your church is in no way to be forbidden divine offices because of this.

As a sign of the liberty received from the Roman Church, you shall pay to the Lateran palace a priestly stole every second year. If any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowing the text of this our constitution, should rashly attempt to contravene it and, after a second or third admonition, should not make suitable amends by appropriate satisfaction, let that person be deprived of the dignity of power and honour; let him acknowledge himself guilty before the divine judgment for the iniquity committed; let him be cut off from the most holy Body and Blood of God, our Lord Jesus Christ; and let him be subject to strict vengeance at the last judgment.

But upon all who preserve the rights of the same place, may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that they may receive here the fruit of good action and, before the strict Judge, find the rewards of eternal peace. Amen, amen.

Written through the hand of Peter, regional notary and archivist of the sacred palace.

Given at Rome, in the portico of Blessed Peter, through the hand of John, deacon of the Holy Roman Church, on 5 May, in the ninth indiction, in the year 1102 [1101] of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the second year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Paschal II.

I, Paschal, bishop of the Catholic Church.

LI. Privilege for the Church of St Vincent at Bergamo. (1101, 15 May.)

[See LUPI, *Codex diplomaticus Bergomatis*. Bergamo, 1784, fols. 1–2, vol. II, p. 829.]

LII. To William, bishop of Melfi.—He abolishes the bishopric of Lavello; confirms the possessions and rights of Melfi. (1101, 29 September.)

[MANSI, *Concilia*, XX, 1049.]

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother WILLIAM, bishop of Melfi, and to his successors to be canonically promoted in perpetuity.

[Col. 0074A] Through Anacletus, disciple and successor of the Apostle Peter, we have received the Apostle Peter’s command that bishops are not to be ordained in villages, towns, or small cities. For it is a great loss to the Church when the name and dignity of bishops are made cheap by their frequency and poverty.

Admonished by the justice of this provision, by the authority of this present decree and in accordance with the enactments of the holy Fathers, we decree that no episcopal see shall in future be established at any time in the town of Lavello, which is a town of Melfi. We confirm that town itself, with its appurtenances and boundaries, shall be governed, held, and administered in perpetuity by episcopal right by you, venerable brother William, bishop of Melfi, and your lawful successors.

Moreover, we decree that the village of Salsuga, Gaudianum, and the possessions of St John of Iliceto shall remain forever in the proper possession of the Church of Melfi, just as they were granted and confirmed by written instrument in his time by our son Duke Roger. By this document of privilege we establish the same concerning the tax paid by the Jews, the revenues of the baths, the dues of the villagers, mills, vineyards, fields, and all other things, whether within or outside the city of Melfi, which the same duke granted to your Church.

Furthermore, whatever your Church now possesses by proprietary or baronial right, or may hereafter, by the Lord’s grant, be able justly and canonically to acquire, shall remain secure and unimpaired for you and your successors. Moreover, with respect to the legation [lacuna], that whoever shall thereafter succeed, by God’s appointment, in the episcopal Church of Melfi shall receive the grace of consecration from the pontiffs of our Apostolic See.

If, therefore, in the future any ecclesiastical or secular person, etc., as in certain other letters.

I, Paschal, bishop of the Catholic Church, have subscribed.

Given at Benevento through the hands of John, deacon of the Holy Roman Church, on 29 September, in the tenth indiction, in the year 1102 [1101] of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the third year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Paschal II.

LIII. To Constantine, bishop of the Church of Ravello.—He confirms the privileges and possessions of the Church of Ravello. (1101, 29 September.)

[MANSI, *Concilia*, XX, 1050.]

[Col. 0074D]

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother CONSTANTINE, bishop of the Church of Ravello, and to his successors to be canonically promoted in perpetuity.

The pious request of a will ought to be fulfilled by effectual execution, so that both the sincerity of devotion may shine forth commendably and the benefit sought may undoubtedly acquire force. Therefore, venerable brother Constantine, bishop in Christ, we graciously assent to your petitions, because long-standing affection has demonstrated the sincerity of your devotion toward the common mother, the Roman Church. In consideration of that disposition, with the Lord as author, we have readily granted that the condition of the Church entrusted to you may always endure in unshaken stability. By the authority of this present decree, therefore, we ordain that the Church of Ravello, over which, by God’s grace and through the ministry and laying on of hands of our predecessor, you preside, shall always be preserved with special benevolence under the protection of the apostolic see; and that whatever bishops shall thereafter, by God’s ordering, succeed to the Church of Ravello shall receive the grace of consecration from the pontiff of that same apostolic see, as is known to have been established by our predecessors of holy memory, Victor III and Urban II. We also confirm to you and to your successors forever the entire extent of the parish of Ravello, as it was possessed by your predecessor Urso, of reverend memory in Christ. Moreover, whatever the aforesaid Church now possesses by right either of ownership or of parish jurisdiction, or may in future, by the Lord’s gift, justly and canonically acquire, shall remain free and unimpaired to you and your successors.

[Col. 0075B] Therefore we decree that no person whatever may rashly disturb that same Church, or take away its possessions, retain things taken away, diminish them, or harass it with reckless vexations; but that all things shall be preserved intact, for the benefit of both yourselves and the clergy and poor. But if any ecclesiastical or secular person, etc., as in certain other letters.

I, Paschal, bishop of the Catholic Church, have subscribed.

Given at Benevento, through the hand of John, cardinal-deacon of the holy Roman Church, on the third day before the Kalends of October, indiction 10, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1102 [1101], in the third year of the pontificate of Lord Paschal II, pope.

### LIII bis. To Madelmus, abbot of Saint Sophia.—Privilege for the monastery of Saint Sophia. (1101, October 27.)

[MANSI, *Concilia*, XX, 1024.]

In the name of the Lord God, our Savior Jesus Christ, the eternal Lord: PASCHAL, pope and bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son in Christ, MADELMUS, abbot of the venerable monastery of Saint Sophia situated within Benevento, and to his successors to be regularly promoted forever.

[Col. 0075D] The pious request of a will ought to be fulfilled by effectual execution, so that both the sincerity of devotion may shine forth commendably and the benefit sought may undoubtedly acquire force. Therefore, most gracious son Madelmus, assenting to your pious requests, we decree by the authority of this present document that the monastery of Saint Sophia, over which, by the Lord’s disposition, you are known to preside, shall remain forever under the protection and jurisdiction of the apostolic see, as it has hitherto remained; so that it shall be held subject to the Roman Church alone and free from the yoke of all Churches and persons. We likewise grant to you and to your successors to be regularly promoted, by this present privilege, all things which have been assigned by the privileges of our predecessors to your predecessors or to you, for the immunity or possession of that same monastery.

[Col. 0076A] Accordingly, we confirm for perpetual possession the dependent houses, churches, and estates which, through the exertions of your predecessors or of yourself, appear to have been justly and reasonably acquired for the aforesaid monastery: namely, the church of Saint Benedict, etc.

(Here the possessions of that monastery are enumerated.) Together with all their appurtenances, movable and immovable. By the authority of this present and our privilege, we ordain that whatever that same monastery justly possesses, and whatever it may hereafter be able justly and canonically to acquire through the grant of pontiffs, the generosity of princes,

[Col. 0076B] or the offerings of the faithful, shall remain firm and unimpaired to you and your successors. Therefore we decree that no person whatever may rashly disturb or destroy that same monastery, or take from it any possessions, retain things taken away, diminish them, harass it with reckless vexations, or molest it in any manner; but that all things shall remain and be preserved intact, for the fitting benefit of those for whose support, maintenance, or government they were granted. Upon the death of you, the present abbot of that place, or of any of your successors, no one shall be placed over it through any craft of usurpation or by violence, except one whom the brothers by common consent, or the part of the brothers of sounder counsel, shall have elected. The person elected

[Col. 0076C] shall be consecrated by the Roman pontiff. You shall receive chrism, holy oil, consecrations of altars or churches, and the ordinations of monks who are to be promoted to sacred orders, from the bishops in whose dioceses you are situated, provided that they possess the grace and communion of the apostolic see and confer these things freely and without abuse. But if any obstacle should arise in these matters, you may receive the sacraments named above from whatever Catholic bishop you choose. If any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowingly, should rashly attempt to act against this document of our constitution, and, having been warned a second or third time, should fail to make suitable amendment by satisfaction, let that person be deprived of the dignity of office and honor, and recognize himself or herself as answerable to divine judgment for the wrong committed, and be cut off from the most sacred body and blood of God and of the Lord, our Redeemer Jesus Christ, and at the last judgment be subject to severe vengeance.

[Col. 0076D] But upon all who preserve the rights of that place may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that they may receive here the fruit of good action and find, before the eternal judge, the rewards of eternal peace and recompense. Amen. Fare well.

I, Paschal, bishop of the holy Catholic Church, have subscribed.

Given at Capua, through the hand of John, cardinal-deacon of the Holy Roman Church, on the sixth day before the Kalends of November, indiction 11. [Note: At [Col. 0075D], indiction 10 should be written. HARD.] In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1111,

[Col. 0077A] in the third year of the pontificate of Lord Paschal II, pope.

### LIV. Privilege for the monastery of Monte Cassino. (1101, November 17.)

[GATTULA, *Historia Casinensis*, I, 411.]

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the venerable brother ODERISIUS, abbot of Monte Cassino and cardinal-priest of the holy Roman Church, greetings.

Both because of reverence for our blessed father Benedict and because of the many merits of both yourselves and your predecessors, we acknowledge that we owe a very great debt to your house. We therefore judge it right to apply diligent charity to the enlargement of your monastery. Accordingly, in the city of Benevento, which is clearly subject to our Roman jurisdiction, we grant to your monastery for perpetual possession the church of Saint Nicholas, situated at a corner of the city beside the pagan tower, and we confirm that grant by the document of this present decree. We decree that this church shall remain forever whole and unimpaired to you and your successors, together with all that presently belongs to it. These things are believed to have been acquired or purchased for the most part from property belonging to our curia, namely:

[Col. 0077B] two mills under one roof; another called the *centimolum*; gardens with various trees; an estate at Roseto, with one piece of land; an estate on the Tasi stream; the estate of Homodei; the estate of Martin Alberic with Silvola; two estates of Rocco; the estate of the deacon Musus; an estate on Mount Rostari; an estate at Sajano; the estate of Valentinus; lands in the place called Mediana, within their boundaries and limits; the church of Saint Nicholas at Urbiliano near Petra Pelicina, with its appurtenances; the property opposite, before the gate of the church, within its boundaries; the house to the left of the church, within its boundaries, beside the city wall. To these possessions of that church we also add the church of Saint Nicholas called “of Rodenandi,” with its appurtenances; the church of Saint Mary called “the Round,” with its appurtenances; and the new bath beside the church of Saint Polittus.

[Col. 0077D] Whatever else that cell of Blessed Nicholas may in future acquire through the grant of pontiffs, the generosity of princes, or the offerings of any faithful persons, shall be preserved forever under the direction and authority of you and your successors. No person may ever separate the aforesaid cell from the unity of your monastery or, on any pretext, transfer it to a possession other than that established by us. If anyone should presume otherwise, let him be punished by the judgment of the apostolic see and remain under excommunication until making suitable satisfaction. But upon all who preserve the rights of that place may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that they may receive here the fruit of good action and find before the strict Judge the rewards of eternal peace. Amen, amen, amen.

[Col. 0078A] I, Paschal, bishop of the Catholic Church, have subscribed.

Given at the Lateran, through the hand of John, cardinal-deacon of the holy Roman Church, on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of December, indiction 10, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1102 [1101], in the third year of the pontificate of Lord Paschal II, pope.

### LV. To Lanuin, prior of the Tower: he writes that through Richard, bishop of Albano, he has learned that “the peace and concord of the hermitage have been restored and that he has succeeded Bruno.” He exhorts him to emulate Bruno’s virtues. (1101, November 26.)

[MABILL., *Annales Benedictini*, V, 445.]

When brother R. [Richard], bishop of Albano, returned, we learned that peace and concord had been restored to the hermitage and that you had succeeded to the place of Bruno, that great man of holy memory.

[Col. 0078B] Therefore may the spirit of that same man be in you; may there be in you the same vigor of eremitical discipline and the same steadfastness of character and gravity. For, with the Lord’s help, whatever authority and power the sound wisdom and religion of that worthy master personally obtained from the apostolic see, we grant to you, as you are accompanied by that same spirit. We desire, moreover, that you should visit us during the coming Lent, so that we may speak more fully face to face concerning the secrets of the heart, etc.

Given at Rome, on the sixth day before the Kalends of December.

### LVI. He confirms the privileges and possessions of the Church of Saint James of Compostela. (1101, December 31.)

[FLOREZ, *España sagrada*, XX, 32.]

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the venerable brother DIDACUS, second bishop of Compostela, and to his successors to be canonically promoted forever.

The order of justice and reason advises that one who wishes his own commands to be approved by successors should beyond doubt observe the will and enactments of his predecessor. Therefore, observing the enactments of our predecessor Urban II, of holy memory, we establish by legitimate and perpetual authority, out of reverence for Blessed James, that, just as your predecessor, Bishop Dalmatius of good memory, obtained through the grant of the apostolic see the episcopal see in the city of Compostela,

[Col. 0078D] where the body of Blessed James is believed to rest, so you and your successors ought henceforth, with the Lord’s help, to possess it for all time. We therefore decree that all things belonging by ancient right to the diocese of the city of Iria shall remain forever whole and unimpaired to you and to your lawful successors residing at Compostela. Moreover, because of special devotion to Blessed James, we grant that neither you nor your successors shall be subject to anyone except the Roman metropolitan, and that all who succeed you in that see shall be consecrated by the hand of the Roman pontiff as special suffragans of the Roman see.

Furthermore, by a decree to remain perpetually in force,

[Col. 0079A] we have ordained that whatever has hitherto been justly offered to the church of Blessed James by kings or by any of the faithful; whatever is contained in lawful inventories; and whatever the see of Iria is known justly to have possessed in parishes, shall always be preserved firm and whole to you and to your lawful successors residing at Compostela. We absolutely prohibit any person ever from having the power, on any pretext, to withhold from the church of Blessed James that payment which certain kings of Spain, of noble memory, predecessors of the present A[lfonso], established for the salvation of the whole province: namely, a payment to be made annually from each pair of oxen, from the river Pisuerga to the shore of the Ocean, as is contained in the writings of that same church. Henceforth it befits your holiness

[Col. 0079B] to observe in all things the decrees of the holy Roman Church and so to shine inwardly and outwardly with the light of virtues that all may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven.

But if in future any archbishop or bishop, emperor or king, prince or duke, margrave, count, judge, or any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowingly, should rashly attempt to act against this document of the decree, and, having been warned a second or third time, should fail to make suitable amendment by satisfaction, let that person be deprived of the dignity of office and honor, recognize himself or herself as answerable to divine judgment for the wrong committed, be cut off from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, and at the last judgment be subject to severe

[Col. 0079C] vengeance. But upon all who observe these things and venerate the oft-mentioned church of Blessed James may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that they may receive here the fruit of good action and find before the strict Judge the rewards of eternal peace. Amen.

Written through the hand of Peter, notary of the region, keeper of the archives of the sacred palace.

I, Paschal, bishop of the holy Catholic Church.

Given at the Lateran, through the hand of John, cardinal-deacon of the holy Roman Church, on the second day before the Kalends of January, indiction 10, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1102 [1101], in the third year of the pontificate of Lord Paschal, pope.

[Col. 0079D]

### LVII. To Didacus, bishop of Compostela.—Concerning the reform of the corrupt morals of that Church, which had entered into it through wars. (1101.)

[MANSI, *Concilia*, XX, 1001.]

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the venerable DIDACUS, bishop of Compostela, greetings and apostolic blessing.

The Church which, by the Lord’s ordering, you have undertaken to govern has for a long time lacked the consolations of a shepherd, even when it appeared to have a shepherd. Therefore your diligence must apply itself more watchfully,

[Col. 0080A] so that all things in it may be rightly ordered according to the rule of the apostolic see. Appoint as priests or deacons in your Church such cardinal clergy as are able worthily to bear the burdens of ecclesiastical government entrusted to them. Further, matters belonging to priests shall be entrusted to priests, and matters belonging to deacons to deacons, so that no one may intrude to the detriment of another’s office. If any persons contracted marriages according to the common custom of their country before they accepted Roman law, we do not exclude the sons born from them from either secular rank or ecclesiastical dignity. It is altogether improper, however, that, as we hear, monks live with nuns throughout your region. Your experience must undertake to remove this practice, so that those who are now together shall be separated into dwellings far apart, as shall seem best according to your judgment and the counsel of religious men; nor shall such a custom be presumed in the future.

[Col. 0080B] Given at the Lateran, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1103 [1101], in the fourth [second] year of our pontificate.

### LVIII. To Bernard of Toledo, Giraldus of Braga, etc.—He commands them to come to a synod to be held at Rome. (1101.)

[FLOREZ, *España Sagrada*, XX, 89.]

P. [Paschal], bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the venerable brothers and fellow bishops B. of Toledo, G.

[Note: At [Col. 0079D], Giraldus of Braga died on 5 December 1109. In that year, however, the invitation was issued to the council held at Rome in 1110, on the third day before the Nones of March.]

of Braga,

[Col. 0080C] and their suffragans, and D. of Compostela, greetings and apostolic blessing.

Your belovedness knows how much terror the battle-array of a synodal council brings to the enemies of truth and how much strength to the Church. Therefore both we and you must make vigorous provision, with God as author, that we may gather in a plenary synod, which, by the favor of the same our God and with the assistance of the merits of the holy apostles, we have decreed to celebrate at the beginning of the coming Lent. We therefore exhort your diligence that, laying aside every excuse and having summoned the abbots of your dioceses, you take care to come to the City at the stated time. We likewise invite the abbot of Saint Facundus.

### LIX. To Anselm, archbishop of Canterbury.—He is to labor for the restoration of the English Church and reconcile the king of England with the count of Normandy. (1101.)

[MANSI, *Concilia*, XX, 1019.]

[Col. 0080D]

Paschal, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the most reverend brother and fellow bishop ANSELM, archbishop of Canterbury, greetings and apostolic blessing.

As we sympathized with your injuries and exiles, so, by the Lord’s gift, we rejoice in your restoration and honor. And you, most reverend brother in Christ, since you have seen in person the injuries and storms suffered by the Roman Church,

[Col. 0081A] now that you are in harbor, do not cease to labor the more effectively for us on its behalf. First, ensure that the condition of the Churches in the kingdom of England is corrected and ordered according to the enactments of the Roman Church. Then strive more effectively concerning the king’s love and due fidelity toward us, and concerning the restoration of Saint Peter’s payment. For you know how severely we are besieged by the straits of poverty. Since the Roman Church labors on behalf of all Churches, whoever takes what belongs to it is recognized as guilty of sacrilege not against it alone, but against all Churches. We further inform your belovedness that the count of the Normans, Robert, has complained to us against the king of England that, after swearing an oath to him concerning the acquisition of that same kingdom, the king violated the oath and invaded the kingdom. And you know that we owe aid to that count because of the labors which he undertook in the liberation of the Asiatic Church. Therefore we desire that, if peace has not yet been made between them,

[Col. 0081B] it be made through your exertions, with our envoys intervening. For all these matters we send to you John, whom you know, whom you once educated as a son and who is now your brother and fellow bishop, and our familiar Tiberius. We ask that, in all matters to be conducted among you, they may be instructed by your counsel and aided by your help, so that through them the most holy Roman Church may more effectively experience the ability of your religious devotion and wisdom.

### LX. He commands P[eter], bishop of Poitiers, to make satisfaction to the monastery of Cluny concerning the abbot of Saint Cyprian whom he consecrated; and orders the abbot of Maillezais likewise to make satisfaction to that monastery. (1101.)

[MABILL., *Annales Benedictini*, V, 460.]

[Col. 0081C]

P. [Paschal], bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved brother P. [Peter], bishop of Poitiers, greetings and apostolic blessing.

Since you are members of the Roman Church, we are astonished that you knowingly act against your head. For you are not unaware that the monastery of Saint Cyprian has been entrusted to the monastery of Cluny by the disposition of the apostolic see. Yet you, as we have heard, consecrated there an abbot who had been suddenly elected, contrary to the privileges of the Roman Church. Therefore we command that that brother abbot

[Col. 0081D] be deprived of office until he makes satisfaction to the abbot of Cluny, and that the Church itself remain, in accordance with Roman constitutions, under the ordering of the abbot of Cluny. We also command concerning the abbot of Maillezais that, in accordance with the command of Lord Urban, he make satisfaction to the abbot of Cluny. Otherwise take care lest you experience the indignation of the apostolic see on their account, and they do not escape their fitting sentence.

### LXI. To the bishops of Scotland, suffragans of the Church of York, on behalf of the archbishop of York. (1101.)

[Monasticon Anglicanum, III, 146.]

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the venerable brothers, suffragans in Scotland of the metropolitan see of York, greetings and apostolic blessing.

[Col. 0082A] Let your belovedness know that, by the grace of almighty God, we have promoted our venerable brother Gerard, formerly bishop of Hereford, to be metropolitan of York. From the generosity of the apostolic see we have granted him the pallium and a privilege. Therefore, commanding you, we order that henceforth you render him due obedience as your archbishop.

### LXII. He grants the pallium to Gerard, archbishop of York. (1101.—Fragment.)

[STUBBS, *Acta pontificum Eboracensium*, in Twysden, *Historiae Anglicanae Scriptores*, I, 1710.]

[Col. 0082B] PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the venerable brother GIRARD, archbishop of York, greetings and apostolic blessing.

Among the other kingdoms of the earth subject to the apostolic see, etc.

### LXIII. Privilege for the monastery of Jesus of Nazareth. (1102, January 11.—Fragment.)

[AYNSA, *Fundación, excelencias, grandezas y cosas memorables de Huesca*. Huesca, 1619, folio, p. 455.]

… I, Paschal, bishop of the Catholic Church, consented to and subscribed this agreement.

Given at the Lateran, through the hand of John, cardinal-deacon of the holy Roman Church, on the tenth day before the Kalends of April, indiction 12, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation

[Col. 0082C] 1105 [1102], and in the fifth [third] year of the pontificate of Lord Paschal II, pope.

### LXIV. Privilege for the monastery of Saint Ambrose at Milan. (1102, February 14.)

[PURICELLI, *Ambrosianae Mediolanensis basilicae Monumenta*, p. 509.]

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son in Christ, JOHN, venerable abbot, greetings in Christ, and to his successors.

Although, by reason of the universality of the see which we unworthily serve, we embrace and exercise with loving concern the care of all Churches, yet we are moved with greater vigilance and held by special affection toward those Churches which the devotion of the faithful is known to have entrusted to the protection of this holy universal see by a salutary arrangement; and if they desire to be elevated through our decree or consent in any matter, it seems to us that such requests should be granted with the greatest goodwill. Therefore, at your request that we should fortify by an act of apostolic authority the monastery of Saint Ambrose, where his holy body rests together with those of the holy martyrs Gervasius and Protasius, and over which divine providence has willed you to preside, and that we should confirm all its appurtenances to remain inviolable by perpetual right, we, moved by your prayers and following the authority of our predecessors, decree by the privilege of this our enactment, and, for love of Saint Ambrose and of the holy martyrs Gervasius and Protasius, in whose honor

[Col. 0083A] the place is dedicated, grant to you and to your successors whatever, by apostolic authority of our predecessors, you have deserved to possess concerning the use of the dalmatic, sandals, and gloves, and the permission to carry the bell of the chapel. We grant you lordship over the whole church after the archbishop; likewise we grant lordship over the hospital, with the church founded there in honor of Saint Michael; the church of Saint Augustine with its dependent parish; the church of Saint Satyrus with its dependent parish; and the church of Saint Peter called “at the Hall,” with its parish, tithes, and first fruits. We confirm the monastery within the city of Milan itself, called Aurona, with all its honors; the estate of Pasiliano with all appurtenances, including the churches built there; the estate of Feliciano; the estate of Monte, with the churches built there;

[Col. 0083B] Capiate with its churches, tithes, and first fruits; Civenna; holdings at Clavero, Badello, and Colonia; at Baraza, one church called Saint Damian, with tithes and first fruits; Antizago with the churches founded there; Casterno with two churches; Balaradeglo; Vite Alba; Saint Syrus at Bevra; in the diocese of Lodi, one church of Saint Savior and another church near Codogno, founded in honor of Saint Ambrose; in the diocese of Pavia, an estate called Villa Regia; and a monastery called Saint Quentin,

[Col. 0083C] to be under the power and governance of the abbot of Saint Ambrose himself; the church of the Holy Sepulchre with tithes and first fruits; Dubini with one church; and, in the diocese of Piacenza, an estate called Ceresola. Furthermore, you and your successors shall possess forever, in all security and peace, every urban or rural place, cultivated or uncultivated, together with tithes and first fruits, tenants, male and female slaves, and *aldiones* [a class of dependent persons], which most faithful Christians have granted to that monastery or which appear to belong to that religious place by other lawful titles. Thus no successor of ours among the pontiffs, no emperor, king, duke, or any person may ever presume to strip, molest, or disturb that monastery in respect of any of the aforesaid

[Col. 0083D] things which appear to belong to it. We decree this under the pronouncement of divine judgment, confirmation, and the prohibition of anathema. So that this may remain firm and inviolable now and in times to come, we confirm it by our privilege, for the honor of God, Saint Ambrose the confessor, and the holy martyrs Gervasius and Protasius, whose bodies lie in your monastery. But if anyone, with rash boldness—which we do not believe will occur—should attempt to act against the tenor of this our apostolic authority and confirmation, let that person know that he is excommunicated by blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, and by our apostolic authority. But whoever shall be guardian and observer of this our privilege may deserve to obtain from the Lord the grace of blessing

[Col. 0084A] and eternal life.

I, Paschal, bishop of the Catholic Church, have subscribed.

I, Coyro, bishop of Palestrina, have subscribed.

I, Richard, bishop of Albano, have subscribed.

Given at the Lateran, through the hand of John, cardinal-deacon of the holy Roman Church, on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of March, indiction 10, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1103 [1102], in the third year of the pontificate of Lord Paschal II, pope.

### LXV. He confirms the privileges of the monastery of Saint Peter in the Golden Heaven at Pavia. (1102, February 14.)

[Only a mention of this privilege survives in ROBOLINI, *Notizie*, III, 223. The chronological indicators are faulty.]

[Col. 0084B]

### LXVI. At the request of Abbot William, he confirms the privileges of the monastery of Montmajour near Arles. The diploma enumerates those things which had been bestowed through grants of pontiffs, the generosity of princes, or offerings of the faithful, including the castle of Biduini with its appurtenances, said to belong to the jurisdiction of the holy Roman Church, “on the condition that from this possession three pounds of incense should be paid to the Lateran Church every five years, and from the head monastery itself four solidi of Merguel currency annually.” Moreover, the monastery of Saint Martin of Alamonte, and, in the county of Riez, the castle of Crisellum and the monastery of Stabloni, are confirmed to that abbey. “Written through the hand of Peter, notary of the region of the sacred palace”; and after the pope’s subscription: “Given through the hand of John, cardinal-deacon of the Holy Roman Church, on the fifth day before the Kalends of March, indiction 10, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1102, in the third year of the pontificate of Lord Paschal, pope.”

[MABILL., *Annales Benedictini*, V, 454. Fragment.]

[Col. 0084C]

### LXVII. At the request of Bishop John, he confirms the property of the Church of Fiesole. (1102, March 11.)

[UGHELLI, *Italia sacra*, III, 237.]

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved brother JOHN, bishop of Fiesole, and to his successors to be canonically promoted forever.

It is fitting for us to grant assent to just vows and lend our ears to just petitions, since, although unworthy, we are seen by the Lord’s ordering to have been placed as guardians and heralds of justice upon the watchtower of the Church of the chief apostles Peter and Paul. Therefore, beloved brother John in Christ, assenting to your just petitions, we strengthen by the authority of the apostolic see the holy Church of Fiesole over which, by God’s agency, you preside. We confirm to you and your lawful successors, to be possessed by episcopal and seignorial right, the fortress and city of Fiesole, with the churches, estates, and adjoining lands. Likewise, the castle of Monte Lauro; Monte Regis; Bojana; the estate of Sala; Festiliano; Prato del Re; the church of Saint Mary at Urbana with its estate; Libiano and Bivigliano; and the castle built in the aforesaid bishopric

[Col. 0085A] beside the river Faltona, with the estates of Riviferioli and Pulcanti; the castle of Cisilo; the estate on Monte Acuto; and, in the Ampiniana district, the church of Saint Gaudentius with the Alps and their appurtenances, as they were granted to your Church by royal concession; the castle of Agne; the estate of Turricha; Castiglione; a share of Monte Bontilli; a share of the castle of Rufiano; the monastery of Saint Savior situated in the diocese of Pistoia, with the churches and estates belonging to it; the monastery of Saint Bartholomew; the monastery of Saint Martin; the monastery of Saint Gaudentius, with their appurtenances; the patrimony of the sons of Benno; the castle called Flumen; and whatever, by right of the aforesaid Church, is held in the territory of Mugello by the sons of Ugo, the sons of Rumbert and Azzo son of Albizo, the sons

[Col. 0085B] of Azzo of Castanicula, Longobard of Molezzano, the sons of Ugo of Casola, Longobard of Ferliano, and Longobard of San Giovanni Maggiore; or whatever right of your Church any person appears to hold in the aforesaid territory; and whatever Ugo son of Raynerius gave to the aforesaid Church in Ampiniana, on Monte Acuto, at Reu Mangana, and at Politiano; and half of the church and estate at the place called Quaracla; and the estate of Marina.

Furthermore: the parish church of Saint Crisci situated at Albino; the parish church of Saint Gervasius with its estate, situated at Alpiniano; the church of Saint Minias with its estate; the parish church of Saint John situated on Monte Lauro; the parish churches of Saint Babillus and Saint Ditalis; the parish church of Saint Leoninus; the parish churches of Saint Mary and Saint Stephen; the parish church of Saint Jerusalem situated at

[Col. 0085C] Pomino; the parish church of Saint Jerusalem situated at Glaceto; the parish church of Saint Gervasius situated at Soriano with its estate; the parish church of Saint Peter situated at Casua, with its estate and a share of the castle called Novum; the parish church of Saint Mary situated at Sco with its estate; the parish church of Saint John situated at Ca…plia [uncertain due to lacuna]; the parish church of Saint Pancras; the parish church of Saint Romulus with its estate; the church of Saint Minias with its appurtenances; the church of Saint Mary situated at Carpinione, with a small estate; the parish church of Saint Vitus; the parish church of Saint Leoninus situated at Retiano; the parish church of Saint Lawrence with castle and estate; the parish church of Saint Minias situated at Rubiano; the parish church of Peter with its estate, situated at Cintoria; the church of Saint Justus situated on Mount Rantuli; the parish church of Saint Peter situated at Sillano; the parish church of Saint Crescius situated at Novole; the parish church of Saint Leoninus situated at Panzano with its estate; the church of Saint Euphrosyne

[Col. 0085D] with its estate; the church of Saint Paul with its estate, located beside the castle of Corbuli; the parish church of Saints Mary and Peter situated at Avanano; the parish church of Saint Justus with its estate; the parish church of Saint Paul with its estate; the parish church of Saint Leoninus at Collina; the parish church of Saint Mary on Monte Migliaio; the parish church of Saint Martin at Tertinulo with its estate; the church of Saint Mammilianus with its estate; the parish church of Saint Peter at Ormena with its estate; and the parish church of Saint Mark at Stilliana. Whatever else your aforesaid predecessors appear hitherto to have possessed, either in the parish of the Church of Fiesole or in the parishes of other Churches, we decree shall remain unimpaired to you and to your lawful successors. Therefore we decree that no person whatever may rashly disturb that same Church, take away its possessions, retain things taken away,

[Col. 0086A] diminish them, or harass it with reckless vexations, but shall preserve everything wholly intact for the benefit both of yourselves and of the clergy. But if any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowingly, should rashly attempt to act against this document of our constitution, and, having been warned a second or third time, should fail to make suitable amendment by satisfaction, let that person be deprived of the dignity of office or honor, recognize himself or herself as answerable to divine judgment for the wrong committed, be cut off from the most sacred body and blood of God and of the Lord, our Redeemer Jesus Christ, and at the last judgment be subject to severe vengeance. But upon all who preserve the rights of that place may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that they may receive here the fruit of good action and find before the strict Judge the rewards of eternal

[Col. 0086B] peace. Amen, amen.

Written through the hand of Peter, regional notary and scribe of the sacred palace.

I, Paschal, pope of the Catholic Church, have subscribed.

I, bishop of Palestrina, have subscribed.

I, Crescentius, bishop of Salona, have subscribed.

I, Richard, bishop of Albano, have subscribed.

I, Anastasius, cardinal of Saint Clement, have subscribed.

Given at the Lateran, through the hand of John, deacon of the holy Roman Church, on the fifth day before the Ides of March, indiction 12, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1103, in the third year of the pontificate of Lord Paschal II, pope, etc.

LXVIII. He confirms the exchange made between Gerenton, abbot of Saint Benignus of Dijon, and Gilbert, abbot of Caen, and the possessions of the monastery of Dijon. (1102, 14 March.)

[PÉRARD, *Collection of Several Curious Documents Serving the History of Burgundy*. Paris, 1664, folio, p. 205.]

[Col. 0086C]

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son GERENTON, abbot of the monastery of Dijon: greeting and apostolic blessing.

The authority of our office urges us to be solicitous for the condition of the Churches and to establish firmly those things which have rightly been ordained. Therefore, by the present decree we confirm that exchange which was made between you and Gilbert, abbot of the monastery of Caen: namely, that those possessions which the monastery of Dijon had held in the lands of the Normans—namely, the church of Saint Albert with its appurtenances, and the church of Longchamp with its lands and tithes—shall henceforth remain in the possession of the monastery of Caen; and likewise that those possessions which the Church of Caen had held in the region of the Burgundians—namely, the monastery of Saint Hippolytus, the estate of Becalt [lacuna], with all its appurtenances—shall henceforth remain under the right of the monastery of Dijon.

We also confirm to you and to your successors the monastery of Saint Vigor, with all that belongs to it, in persons as well as in possessions and tithes: specifically, the full tithe of the whole village in which the monastery is situated, of all things belonging to that same village; the full tithe of Tor, Crissoto, Olferes, Colgrino, and the whole village of Chricha, together with the priests’ lands, as these were delivered to you by Odo, bishop of Bayeux, of blessed memory, and confirmed with the assent of the prince and of others.

Likewise we confirm this gift which Robert, duke of the Normans, made to the aforesaid monastery: from his own demesne revenues, both from passage-dues and tolls and from other proceeds, throughout all his land, according to free customs; and also four asses, to be loaded daily at Vernet with green wood.

Whatever else your monastery now peacefully possesses, or may hereafter be able justly and canonically to acquire by grant of popes, generosity of princes, or offerings of the faithful, shall remain firm and inviolate for you and your successors. If any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowing the contents of this page of our constitution, should rashly attempt to act against it, and, having been warned a second or third time, should fail to make fitting satisfaction, let that person be deprived of the dignity of his power and honour; let him know himself answerable before the divine judgment for the iniquity committed; let him be cut off from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, our Redeemer; and let him be subject, at the final judgment, to strict vengeance. But upon all who preserve the rights of that place may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that here they may receive the fruit of good action and before the strict Judge may find the rewards of eternal peace. Amen, amen, amen.

Written through the hand of Peter, regional notary and scriniary of the sacred palace.

I, Paschal, bishop of the Catholic Church, have subscribed.

[Col. 0087C] Given at the Lateran through the hand of John, cardinal deacon of the Holy Roman Church, on the second Ides of March, in the tenth indiction, in the year 1102 from the Incarnation of the Lord, and in the third year of the pontificate of lord Pope Paschal II.

LXIX. (1102, 15 March.)

[LOREZ, *España Sagrada*, XX, 90.] To Giraldus, archbishop of Braga, Didacus, bishop of Compostela, and Adefonsus, bishop of Tui.—Pelagius’s marriage is not to be dissolved.

P., bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brethren and fellow bishops G., of Braga, Didacus, of Compostela, and A., of Tui: greeting and apostolic blessing.

[Col. 0087D] In the presence of many of our brethren, we investigated carefully the case of Pelagius. In that investigation, in accordance with the tenor of your letters, it became clear from P.’s own confession that the woman, out of fear of abduction, had taken the veil of religion; and many who were present likewise confessed this with their own mouths. Yet, in accordance with the prescription of the Council of Carthage, she neither vowed herself to God nor, having laid aside secular dress, appeared in religious habit under the witness of a bishop or of the Church. Therefore, because the sacraments of this kind were lacking from that temporary veiling, the sacrament of marriage which P. contracted with her does not appear to be dissolvable in any way.

But because, according to the decree of blessed Innocent, she feigned a religious purpose, she is to be enjoined to perform penance for some time; for, according to the Apostle, she is not bound by the breach of a promised faith. Accordingly, having considered this reasoning, we absolve the same P., while remaining in marriage, from the bond of excommunication.

Given at the Lateran, on the Ides of March.

LXX. He confirms the privileges of the monastery of Saint Denis. (1102, 21 March.)

[MABILLON, *De re diplomatica*, I, 463.]

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son ADA, abbot of the venerable monastery which is in honour of Saint Denis, etc.

[lacuna] and let him be subject, at the final judgment, to strict vengeance; but upon all who preserve the rights of that place may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that here they may receive the fruit of good action and before the strict Judge may find the rewards of eternal peace.

Written through the hand of Peter, regional notary and scriniary of the sacred palace.

I, Paschal, bishop of the Catholic Church, have subscribed.

I, Richard, bishop of Albano, have subscribed.

Given at Rome through the hand of John, cardinal deacon of the Holy Roman Church, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of April, in the tenth indiction, in the year 1103 from the Incarnation of the Lord, and in the third year of the pontificate of lord Pope Paschal II.

LXXI. He receives the monastery of Saint Mary of Rosenfeld under protection and endows it with privileges, imposing upon the monks an annual census of one Byzantine. (1102, 11 April.)

[LAPPENBERG, *Hamburgisches Urkundenbuch*. Hamburg, 1842, quarto, p. 118.]

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son WERNER, abbot of the venerable monastery of the holy Virgin Mary, Mother of God, situated in the place called Rosenfeld, and to his successors canonically appointed in perpetuity.

It is fitting that we, who, though unworthy, are by the Lord’s ordering placed as guardians and heralds of justice upon the lofty watchtower of the chief apostles Peter and Paul, should grant assent to just vows and lend our ears to just petitions.
