Therefore, venerable and most dear son in Christ, assenting to your just petitions, we have undertaken to cherish and protect under the special guardianship of the Apostolic See the monastery of Rosenfeld, over which by God’s favour you preside, in honour of the holy Virgin Mary, Mother of God, to whose name it is dedicated.

The noble margrave Udo, together with his brother Rudolph and their venerable mother Oda, rebuilt this monastery at their own expense and enriched it by grants from their own possessions. For the salvation of his own soul, of the souls of his parents, and of those who rest there, he is known to have offered it to the blessed Apostles Peter and Paul and to have entrusted it in perpetuity to the protection of the Roman pontiff.

[Note: [Col. 0087D] Udo, margrave of Stade, and his mother Oda, his brother Rodolf, and Frederick, count palatine of Pütelendorf, the husband of their sister, with the counsel of Herrand, bishop of Halberstadt, and of other religious men, expelled the clerics from the place of their foundation, Herseveld, and placed monks there. Thus what had been a provostship became thereafter [Col. 0090D] an abbey. *Saxon Annals*, year 1087.]

[Col. 0089A] Confirming their vow by the bond of our assent, we decree by apostolic authority, through the present page of our privilege, that whatever belongs by lawful right of ancient possession to that same place; whatever the aforesaid princes have justly offered to the same monastery from their resources; and whatever it now justly possesses, in serfs, fields, woods, meadows, waters and watercourses, mills, holdings, and other revenues; or may hereafter be able justly and canonically to acquire by consent of popes, generosity of princes, or offerings of the faithful—shall remain firm and inviolate for you and your successors.

We therefore decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb that monastery, take away the aforesaid possessions, retain what has been taken, diminish them, [Col. 0089B] or harass it by rash vexations. Rather, may they be kept wholly intact and be of every benefit for the use of those for whose support and governance they were granted, saving the canonical right of bishops.

Upon the death of you, W., now abbot of that place, or of any of your successors, no one shall be set over it by any craft of deceit or violence, except one whom the brethren by common consent, or the sounder part of the brethren, shall elect according to the fear of God and the Rule of blessed Benedict. If they cannot find within their own community one judged suitable for this governance, they may choose a man of their order and profession from whatever place they prefer.

You shall receive chrism, holy oil, consecrations of altars [Col. 0089C] or churches, and ordinations of monks to be promoted to sacred orders from the bishop in whose diocese you are, provided that he enjoys the favour and communion of the Apostolic See and is willing to supply these things freely and without misconduct. Otherwise, you may approach whatever Catholic bishop you prefer and receive from him the consecration of the sacraments, provided that, supported by the authority of the Apostolic See, he grants what is requested.

Furthermore, we establish that the aforesaid margrave, advocate of your monastery, as chosen by you, shall remain so while he lives, and likewise his descendants if they are suitable. Hereafter, we decree that no one may presume to be advocate of your monastery unless the brethren by common consent judge him worthy of election. As a token of the freedom received from the Roman Church, in accordance with the ordinance of that margrave already mentioned, you shall pay annually one Byzantine to the Lateran palace.

If in future any archbishop or bishop, emperor or king, prince or duke, count or viscount, judge or other person, powerful or powerless, knowingly attempts rashly to contravene this page of our privilege, and, having been warned a second or third time, fails to make worthy satisfaction, we decree that he shall incur the peril of losing his honour, and we separate him by the authority of apostolic power from the body of Christ’s Church. But upon those who observe these provisions may peace and mercy from God be preserved in the present and future ages. Amen, amen.

Written through the hand of Pyderius, regional official and referendary of the sacred palace.

Given at the Lateran through the hand of John, cardinal deacon of the Holy Roman Church, on the third Ides of April, in the tenth indiction, in the year 1102 from the Incarnation of the Lord, and in the third year of the pontificate of Pope Paschal II.

LXXII. To the abbot and monks of the monastery of Bec.—He affirms to the monastery of Bec the churches “granted as a stipend” by William, archbishop of Rouen, and by Ivo, bishop of Chartres, and Geoffrey, bishop of Paris. (1102, 12 April.)

[MANSI, *Councils*, XX, 1068.]

[Col. 0090B]

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons WILLIAM, abbot, and the whole community of the monastery of Bec: greeting and apostolic blessing.

The dignity of the Apostolic See requires that right order be established throughout all God’s Churches and that things rightly ordered by others be confirmed. You have informed us, venerable brethren, that William, bishop of Rouen, Ivo, bishop of Chartres, and Geoffrey, bishop of Paris, each granted to your monastery, as a stipend, churches in their respective dioceses: namely, in the diocese of Rouen, [Col. 0090C] the church of Saint Peter of Pont-Isara; in the diocese of Chartres, the church of Saint Nicasus of Mellent; and in the diocese of Paris, the church of Saint Honorina of Conflans. Therefore, providing for your peace in the future, we confirm these churches to you and to your successors, so that, as ordained by those bishops, they may always remain in the possession of your monastery. If anyone, in rash presumption, should presume to detach and separate these churches from the body of your monastery, let him be punished by the sword of blessed Peter and the vengeance of his Apostolic Church.

Given at the Lateran, on the second Ides of April, in the year 1104 from the Incarnation of the Lord [Note: [Col. 0090D] That 1102, rather than 1104, must be read is shown by the tenth indiction. JAFFÉ.], in the tenth indiction.

LXXIII. To Anselm, archbishop of Canterbury.—That he should act steadfastly in defending the liberty of the English Church. (1102, 15 April.)

[MANSI, *Councils*, XX, 1019.]

[Col. 0090D]

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother and fellow bishop ANSELM of Canterbury: greeting and apostolic blessing.

You do not fail to know the counsel of the divine will: that your religious devotion should preside in the realm of England. For [Col. 0091A] when, avoiding the hatred of the wicked king, William Rufus, you had chosen exile and, dwelling with God far from the disturbances of the English, lived for God, the omnipotent Lord terribly executed His judgments upon that wicked king.

[Note: [Col. 0091D] While hunting, he was killed by one of his own men.]

But by the vehement petition of the whole people and the remarkable devotion of the new king, Henry I, brother of William Rufus, He recalled you to the see which you had left for God’s sake. Thanks be to God, because episcopal authority always endures in you, and, though placed among barbarians, you do not desist from proclaiming the truth, whether through the violence of tyrants, the favour of the powerful, the kindling of fire, or the shedding of blood.

We therefore ask that you do what you do and say what you say. For He who was the Word in the beginning will not fail to be the beginning of our words and deeds; [Col. 0091B] nor shall we fail in Him, who is the power of God and the wisdom of God. Possessing the same spirit as our fathers, we believe, and therefore we speak. The word of God is not bound, though we are greatly humbled. Yet in this humiliation, when in mind we are raised beyond ourselves with God, we behold human falsehoods in His truth.

For this reason, in the synod lately held at the Lateran court, we renewed the decrees of our fathers, decreeing and forbidding that any cleric whatsoever should do homage to a layman or receive churches or ecclesiastical goods from the hand of a layman. For this is the root of simoniacal depravity: foolish men desire to please secular persons in order to obtain ecclesiastical honours. Therefore the venerable authority of holy councils decreed that the power of secular princes should be excluded from ecclesiastical elections, so that, just as through Christ alone the first gate, in baptism, and the last gate, in death, of eternal life is opened, [alternative reading: “is opened”]; so through Christ alone the doorkeeper of Christ’s sheepfold may be appointed, through whom entrance and departure unto eternal life may be provided for Christ’s sheep—not for the reward of the sheep, but for Christ.

These matters, dearest brother, could be treated at greater length both in discourse and in argument; but it is sufficient to have suggested these few things to your wisdom, which abounds both in eloquence and in acquaintance with ecclesiastical reasoning. Teach this as you know to be expedient for your primacy. We confirm that primacy to your fraternity full and entire, [Col. 0091D] as it is established that your predecessors possessed it, adding this personal provision: so long as divine mercy preserves your religious devotion for that kingdom, you shall be subject to the judgment of no legate whatsoever, but only to ours.

Given on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of May.

LXXIV. To the same.—He answers many matters concerning which Anselm had consulted him. (1102, April.)

[MANSI, *Councils*, XX, 1020.]

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the venerable father and fellow bishop ANSELM: greeting and apostolic blessing.

[Col. 0092A] Those questions which you transmitted to the Apostolic See through your venerable messengers, Baldem and Alexander, your fraternity could indeed have examined in conference with the brethren around you, using the consideration of the wisdom and understanding divinely given to you. But, as you have been accustomed to do in other matters, in this too you have taken care to preserve reverence for the common mother of Catholics. Therefore, adhering to the footsteps of the holy Fathers who, by the Lord’s ordering, preceded us in the Apostolic See, we have determined that these answers should be given to your consultation.

**Anselm:** May a bishop or abbot receive from the hand of a layman churches which the layman holds in his own lordship, when he gives them not to the individual but to the bishopric or abbey?

[Col. 0092B] **Paschal:** A bishop already consecrated ought not to receive from the hand of a layman churches situated in another diocese; but if they are in his own diocese, he may receive them lawfully. For this does not appear to be a gift but a restoration, since all churches in their respective dioceses ought to be under the power of the bishops, while abbots receive through the hands of bishops.

**Anselm:** What is to be done concerning sons of priests or concubines who formerly received certain orders and wholly wish to return to the impurities of the world unless promoted to higher ranks, though they promise a religious life [perhaps, “promise”]?

**Paschal:** Concerning what manner of life is to be maintained by sons of priests or concubines, we believe you know what the pontiffs of the Apostolic See, our predecessors, established. Nor do we wish to depart from their footsteps. You will therefore be able to determine, by comparison with that decree itself, what is to be arranged concerning these matters in barbarian regions.

**Anselm:** May one receive penance and the body of the Lord in danger of death from priests who keep women, when no continent priest is present? And if this is permitted, but they refuse to administer them because their masses are despised, what is to be done?

[Col. 0092C] **Paschal:** We judge that one in danger of death should rather receive the Lord’s body from the hand of any cleric than depart from the body without viaticum while awaiting a devout priest. But if any priests, because their past life has been held in contempt, deny viaticum to persons at the point of death, they are to be punished more strictly as murderers of souls.

**Anselm:** If a king possesses lands belonging to a bishopric or abbey which he is unwilling in any way to restore, and wishes in exchange to give some church which he holds in his own hand and which is no less useful, may it be received, lest it be judged a purchase?

[Col. 0092D] **Paschal:** It is scarcely permissible to receive churches from the king’s hand in exchange for the lands of churches, lest consent to sacrilege [perhaps, “by sacrilege”] seem to be given. For things dedicated to God belong among no person’s property, and what has once been offered to God ought not to be appropriated for other uses. Indeed, under exchanges of this kind, greater licence is safely granted to secular power.

**Anselm:** If no cleric ought to become the man of a layman, yet must hold from a layman certain benefices or non-ecclesiastical possessions, and the layman will not give them to him unless he becomes his man, what is he to do?

[Col. 0093A] **Paschal:** Paul says that the Church is free. It is therefore unworthy that a cleric, who has already been taken into God’s portion and has already risen above the status of laypeople, should do homage to a layman for earthly profit—lest, because he is found subject to a secular lord, the Church be left unattended or burdened. For it is written: “No one serving God entangles himself in secular affairs” (2 Tim. 2).

**Anselm:** It is often necessary to relax something of the apostolic and canonical decrees for the sake of compensations, especially in a kingdom where almost everything is so corrupt and perverted that scarcely anything at all [the text is defective: “or anything similar”] can be done there in accordance with ecclesiastical enactments. I ask that, by your permission, I may moderate certain matters as God gives me discretion. I asked this of lord Pope Urban, and he left it to my judgment.

[Col. 0093B] **Paschal:** The method of dispensation, as blessed Cyril says in the letter to the Ephesian Synod, has never displeased any of the wise. For we know that our holy Fathers, and the Apostles themselves, employed dispensations suited to circumstances and to the conditions of persons. Therefore, having no doubt whatever about your long-tested and widely proven religious devotion and wisdom, we entrust to your judgment that, according to the understanding divinely given you, when the great necessity of the Church over which you preside requires it, you may suitably and reasonably [perhaps a word is missing: “by compensation”] moderate the strictness of the holy canons and decrees.

**Anselm:** Ranulf, concerning whom I formerly sought your counsel, has been restored to his bishopric by the king. Therefore, if it please you, inquire concerning his life from our bishops who have now come to you, and deliberate with respect to him, his archbishop, and me, his primate.

[Col. 0093C] **Paschal:** Since Bishop Ranulf has been restored to his own see in accordance with our command, we do not permit his case to pass without investigation. For exceedingly grave charges against him have been brought to the Apostolic See by the reports of many. We therefore desire that, before you, in an assembly of bishops, you investigate more fully the matters written to us concerning him. After an inquiry has been held, unless he can clear himself with the seventh hand of men of his order, [Col. 0094A] let him immediately be sent to us with testimony in your letters. But if, trembling on account of his conscience, he is unwilling to come to our examination, let him be expelled, by your proven judgment, from the Church which he occupies, and let a bishop be appointed there in accordance with canonical enactments.

[Note: [Col. 0093D] A person clears himself “with the seventh hand” when he himself swears that he has committed no crime, and brings seven others who confirm by oath that they believe the person seeking clearance is speaking the truth. The accused swears to the truth of the matter; the compurgators, as teachers of canon law say, swear to their belief. Some were required to clear themselves with the fifth hand, others with the twelfth or fourteenth hand, according to the gravity of the ill repute, scandal, or suspicion. Nor were these oath-helpers or fellow-swearers—terms likewise used for them in the law of the Alemanni—always all of the same rank. Thus the bishop of Trent, in 2, question 5, and in *Extra*, *On Purging*, canon 5, is ordered to clear himself with the third hand of men of his own order and the fourth hand of abbots and religious priests. Indeed, sometimes all were of an inferior rank, as at the Council of Chalon in 1063: Drogo, bishop of Mâcon, was ordered to clear himself with seven clerics; Peter Damian, who presided at the synod, remitted two of that number. See Gratian, 2, question 5, and the whole title of the Decretals, *On Canonical Purging*. It will also be useful to read the law of the Alemanni, especially title 6.]

LXXV. To Henry, king of the English.—Against ecclesiastical investitures. (1102.)

[MANSI, *Councils*, XX, 1060.]

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his dearest son HENRY, king of the English: greeting and apostolic blessing.

[Col. 0094B] We give thanks to the Lord, King of kings, who raised you to the kingdom by the good pleasure of His will and, in ineffable mercy, has preserved you as a Christian king by the good pleasure of His will. We pray, therefore, that He may increase the good beginnings of your reign for the better and preserve His gifts in you to the end. For you have rejected the impiety of your brother the king, which you see terribly avenged by divine judgment. You restored the churches to freedom, began to honour the clergy, and to venerate the bishops, the leaders of the clergy—indeed, Christ the Lord in them.

We therefore trust that you will continue to hold the same views to the end and will persevere in the same uprightness, unless there are men of perverse mind who try, through the investitures of bishops and abbots, to make the hearts of kings fit for divine indignation [the text has *dignationi*, “favour,” apparently in error]. Their counsels in this matter must be avoided by you as poison, lest you offend Him through whom kings reign and rulers decree what is just (Prov. 8). If you have Him favourable, you will reign happily and possess undiminished power and riches; but if—may it not be so!—you offend Him, then neither the counsels of nobles, nor the aid of soldiers, nor weapons, nor riches will be able to help when He begins to overthrow you.

Moreover, in honouring the Lord and preserving the Church’s freedom, you will have us as friends and helpers. Do not suppose that anyone will sever us from friendship with you if you abstain from investitures and preserve for the Church the honour due to it and the freedom instituted by the Lord. For by the judgment of the Holy Spirit we forbid the investitures of churches to kings and princes—indeed, to all laypeople. [Col. 0094D] It is not fitting that the mother should be consigned to servitude by her son, or that she should receive a husband whom she did not choose. She has her own spouse, our King and Lord, who by His mercy may preserve you in power and uprightness and lead you from earthly things to heavenly. Amen.

LXXVI. To Bishop Osbern.—That monks should not be prohibited from having in their monastery a cemetery in which to bury their own. (1102, April.)

[MANSI, *Councils*, XX, 1061.]

[Col. 0095A]

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother Bishop Osbern and to the clerics of the church of Exeter: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Both the authority of the Fathers has ordained, and the settled custom of the Church requires, that just as religious monks live within their cloisters, so the bodies of the dead should rest within the precinct of their monasteries, so that they may be able to sing with the heart’s exultation through divine gift: [Col. 0095B] “This is my resting-place for ever and ever; here will I dwell, for I have chosen it” (Psalm 131).

But you, as we have heard, forbid the monks of Saint Martin of Battle, living in your city, to be buried within the precinct of their monastery. It is grievous that anyone should live in a place for the sake of devotion from which he foresees that his corpse will in every way be expelled. Therefore, by the present letter we command and forbid your beloved persons henceforth to prohibit the aforesaid monks from having a cemetery in which to bury their own. Rather, as was commanded to you by the letters of our predecessor, lord Urban, of blessed memory, you shall allow it.

It also concerns you, brother Bishop Osbern, to bless a cemetery for those brethren and to foster their religious life in the service of almighty [Col. 0095C] God. If anyone should attempt to oppose this ordinance, we have enjoined upon our venerable brother and fellow bishop Anselm that he exercise against him the vengeance of apostolic severity, as against a contemner of the Apostolic See.

LXXVII. Robert, bishop of Coventry.—He decrees that Bishop Robert and his successors shall have their see at Coventry, not at Lichfield or Chester, and confirms the possessions of the Church of Coventry. (1102, 18 April.)

[MANSI, *Councils*, XX, 1069.]

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother ROBERT, bishop of Coventry: greeting and apostolic blessing.

[Col. 0095D] Through Anacletus, a successor of the disciple of the Apostle Peter, we have the command of the Apostle Peter that bishops are not to be ordained in villages, castles, or small cities. It has also been established by the same pontiff and by later Fathers that priests appointed to any Church ought to remain in it for the days of their lives. Moved by the reasoning of this justice, dearest brother and fellow bishop Robert, we have judged it necessary to provide that the see of you or of your successors shall not fluctuate in future; for the place of Lichfield and the town of Chester, in which your predecessors or you have hitherto had their sees, do not deserve the throne of episcopal dignity on account of their smallness and poverty.

We therefore decree that at Coventry an episcopal see shall be maintained in perpetuity for you and your successors. Moreover, the monks living at that place in the monastery of blessed Mary shall always remain under the obedience of you or your successors and shall perform the due divine offices in that episcopal church, according to the institution which we know was established in the Church of Canterbury by blessed Augustine of former times and ratified by the teaching of our most holy father and predecessor Gregory, doctor of the Catholic Church. Nor may any of your successors whatsoever remove the men of monastic discipline from that Church, or take from them the possessions or other goods which have been offered and acquired for the monks’ maintenance by Leofric, count of distinguished memory and founder of that monastery, or by other faithful persons, or which may hereafter, by the Lord’s ordering, be offered. [Col. 0096B]

Furthermore, we decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb that Church, take away its possessions, retain what has been taken, diminish them, or harass it by rash vexations. Rather, may all things be preserved whole and be of every benefit for the use of those for whose support and governance they were converted. If any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowing the contents of this page of our constitution, should rashly attempt to act against it, and, having been warned a second or third time, fails to make fitting satisfaction, let that person be deprived of the dignity of his power and honour; let him know himself answerable before the divine judgment for the iniquity committed; let him be cut off from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, our Redeemer; and let him be subject, at the final [Col. 0096C] judgment, to strict vengeance. But upon all who preserve the rights of that place may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that here they may receive the fruit of good action and before the strict Judge may find the rewards of eternal peace.

Written through the hand of Raynerius, scriniary of the sacred palace.

I, Paschal, bishop of the Catholic Church.

Given at the Lateran through the hand of John, cardinal deacon of the Holy Roman Church, on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of May, in the tenth indiction, in the year 1104 [read 1102] from the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the third year of the pontificate of lord Pope Paschal II.

LXXVIII. To Crescentius, archbishop of Salona.—He confirms his metropolitan rights and grants him the pallium. (1102, 9 April.)

[FARLATI, *Illyricum sacrum*, III, 162; FEJER, *Codex diplomaticus Hungariae*, II, 36.]

[Col. 0096D]

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother CRESCENTIUS, archbishop of Salona: greeting and apostolic blessing.

The kindness of the Apostolic See is accustomed to preserve each person’s rights, and so to guard the privilege of honour bestowed by the Lord that it does not deny fellowship in dignity to worthy brethren. Therefore, venerable brother Crescentius, archbishop of Salona, by the present page of our decree we confirm to your fraternity and to your successors [Col. 0097A] the diocese of the city of Salona with all its appurtenances, the parish of Maronia, and whatever is known to belong to the Church of Salona by episcopal or metropolitan right.

Furthermore, in apostolic generosity we grant to your fraternity the pallium—that is, the fullness of the pontifical office—which you are to know may be worn only within the church, at the solemn celebration of Mass, on the following specified days: the Lord’s Supper; the Resurrection; the Ascension; Pentecost; the Nativity of the Lord; Epiphany; the three feasts of Saint Mary; all feasts of the Apostles; the Nativity of John the Baptist; the feast of Saint Domnius; consecrations of churches, bishops, priests, and deacons; the anniversary of the Church of Salona; and the day of your consecration.

We desire you in all things to vindicate the character proper to this pallium. The honour of this garment consists in humility and justice. Therefore let your fraternity hasten to show itself with all its heart humble in prosperity; upright in justice amid adversity, should it occur; a friend to the good and opposed to the wicked; never accepting anyone’s person against the truth, never oppressing a person who speaks for truth; devoted to works of mercy according to the measure of its resources and yet desiring to act beyond that measure; compassionate toward the weak; rejoicing with the well-disposed; reckoning others’ losses as its own; rejoicing in others’ joys as in its own; mercifully severe in correcting vices; soothing the minds of hearers in fostering virtues; retaining judgment without anger in wrath; [Col. 0097C] and, in tranquillity, not abandoning the restraint of just severity.

This, dearest brother, is the dignity of the pallium you have received. If you preserve it diligently, you will possess inwardly what you show that you have received outwardly. May divine mercy deign to preserve your fraternity unharmed through many times. Amen, amen, amen.

I, Paschal, bishop of the Catholic Church.

Given at the Lateran through the hand of John, cardinal deacon of the Holy Roman Church, on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of May, in the tenth indiction, in the year 1103 [1102] from the Incarnation of the Lord.

LXXIX. He confirms the rights and privileges of the abbey of Saints Philip and James and Walburga in the Haguenau Forest, founded by Frederick, duke of Alsace and Swabia, and by Peter, count of Luxembourg. (1102, 26 April.)

[WURTWEIN, *Nova Subsidia diplomatica*. Heidelberg, 1781, octavo, vol. VI, p. 274, from an inspected copy of the record of the court judge of Strasbourg for the year 1487, in the archive of the bishop of Speyer at Bruchsal.]

[Col. 0097D]

PASCHALIS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son BERTULF, abbot of the monastery constructed in honour of the holy apostles Philip and James and of Saint Walburga, virgin, in the diocese of Strasbourg, namely at the place called the Holy Wood, and to his successors regularly appointed for ever.

A desire shown to pertain to a religious purpose and the salvation of souls ought, with God as its author, to be fulfilled without any delay. For the religious princes Frederick [Note: [Col. 0097D] Namely Frederick I, duke of Alsace and Swabia, whose death Otto of Freising places in the year 1105, *Chronicle*, book VII, chapter 9.] and Peter [Note: [Col. 0097D] That Peter, count of Luxembourg, son of Frederick, count of Monçon, and Agnes, daughter of Peter, count of Savoy. Frederick, brother of Theodoric of Moncouz, begot Peter of Luxemburg. Thus says the author of the Genealogy of St Arnulf in Duchesne, *Scriptores rerum Francicarum*, vol. II, p. 643.] built, upon their freehold within the diocese of Strasbourg, namely in the place called the Holy Wood, a monastery which they offered to blessed Peter and his holy Roman Church under an annual payment of one gold coin; they petitioned that it be dedicated in honour of the blessed apostles Philip and James and Saint Walburga, virgin, and fortified by the protection of the Apostolic See. [Note: [Col. 0098D] From this the error of Wimpheling, *On the Bishops of Strasbourg*, p. 45, and of others who attribute the foundation of the abbey of St Walpurga to Theodoric, count of Montbéliard, is evident.]

[Col. 0098B] Therefore, rejoicing in their devotion, we grant that the monastery itself be dedicated, and by the page of this present privilege fortify it with the protection of the Apostolic See. We decree that everything granted to the same monastery from their own right by the aforesaid founders or by other faithful persons, and whatever may hereafter, by God’s favour, be given, offered, or acquired by other lawful means, shall remain undisturbed and inviolate to you and your successors. Let absolutely no person, therefore, presume rashly to disturb that place, diminish it, or harass it by reckless vexations; but let all things be preserved entire, to be of every benefit for the use of those for whose support and governance they were granted.

Moreover, we decree that the tithes of your produce and livestock shall be rendered to and possessed by your hospice without objection from bishops or episcopal [Col. 0098C] officials; nor may any advocate be attached to that monastery except one chosen by the abbot with the brethren. We further decree that the burial-place of that site shall be wholly free, so that no one may oppose the devotion and last will of those who have decided to be buried there, unless they are excommunicated.

You shall receive the consecration of altars and the ordination of monks to be promoted to holy orders from the bishop in whose diocese you are, provided that he enjoys the favour and communion of the Apostolic See and is willing to provide these things freely and without misconduct. Otherwise, you may approach whichever Catholic bishop you prefer [Col. 0098D] and receive the same sacraments from him, he being supported by the authority of the Apostolic See and granting what is requested.

If in the future any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowing this page of our constitution, should rashly attempt to act against it, and, having been warned a second or third time, should fail to make suitable amendment by due satisfaction, let that person be deprived of the dignity of office and honour, know himself or herself guilty before divine judgment of the iniquity committed, and be separated from the most sacred [Col. 0099A] body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ the Redeemer; and at the final judgment let that person be subject to strict vengeance. But upon all who preserve what is right for the aforesaid monastery, may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that here they may receive the fruit of good deeds and before the strict Judge may find the rewards of eternal peace. Amen, amen, amen.

I, Paschal, bishop of the Catholic Church.

Given at the Lateran through the hand of John, cardinal-deacon and librarian of the holy Roman Church, on the sixth day before the Kalends of May, in the tenth indiction, in the year 1102 of the Lord’s Incarnation; in the fourth year of the pontificate of Lord Paschal II, pope.

LXXX. Bull concerning the foundation of the monastery of Cheminon. (A.D. 1102, September 23.)

[*Gallia Christiana*, X, 158.]

[Col. 0099B]

PASCHALIS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons ALARD, provost, and his brethren: greeting and apostolic blessing.

To those inhabiting the land of the south, the Lord commands through the prophet that they should meet the fugitive with bread. Therefore, dearest sons, we gladly receive you as fugitives from the world and cherish you through the grace of the Holy Spirit under the protection of the Apostolic See. We confirm by the authority of this present privilege the order of canonical life which you have professed according to the Rule of blessed Augustine; and we forbid anyone, after making profession, to possess private property or, without the permission of the provost or the congregation, to leave the enclosure of the cloister.

Accordingly, beside that cloister, namely in the wood of Luyz, we decree that all that freehold shall remain quiet and free for ever to you and to your successors who will live in the same religious order; this is the freehold which Countess Alaidis granted you, with the consent of her sons Philip, bishop of Châlons, and Count Hugh. Therefore, let the whole land surrounding your church, extending to half a league, with waters, woods, and all other appurtenances, be preserved always in your right, so that no one whatsoever may carry out any work there without your consent; nor may bishops or any ministers of churches impose tithes, land-dues, or burdens from the fruits of that land cultivated by the labours of [Col. 0099D] your house, so that you may be able to render freer service to almighty God.

Furthermore, whatever estates and goods you may in future lawfully and canonically acquire by grants of pontiffs, generosity of princes, or offerings of the faithful shall remain firm and inviolate to you and your successors. We decree, therefore, that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb that church, take away its possessions, retain what has been taken, diminish it, or harass it by reckless vexations; but that all things shall be preserved entire, to be beneficial in every way for the use of those to whose support and governance they have been entrusted. If, indeed, any ecclesiastical or secular person knowingly attempts rashly to act against this page of our constitution and, after a second or third warning, does not make suitable amendment by due satisfaction, let that person lose the dignity of office and honour, know himself or herself guilty before divine judgment of the iniquity committed, and be separated from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ the Redeemer, etc.

I, Paschal, bishop of the Catholic Church.

Given at Benevento through the hand of John, cardinal-deacon of the holy Roman Church, on the ninth day before the Kalends of October, in the eleventh indiction, in the year 1103 [1102] of the Lord’s Incarnation; in the fourth year of the pontificate of Lord Paschal II, pope.

LXXXI. To Ivo, bishop, and the canons of Chartres.—He forbids payment to be taken for ecclesiastical benefices and ecclesiastical business to be brought before secular authorities, etc. He then confirms the excommunication pronounced by Ivo concerning houses adjoining the church. (A.D. 1102, November 11.)

[Dom BOUQUET, *Recueil*, XV, 24.]

[Col. 0100B]

PASCHALIS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the venerable brother I. [IVO], bishop of Chartres, and the brethren of the whole chapter: greeting and apostolic blessing.

We have heard that certain corrupt customs have arisen in the churches of your regions and especially prevail in your church; moreover, that certain things contrary to the decrees of the canons are presumed. Following the decrees of the holy Fathers and desiring that they be observed inviolate by all, we wholly reject these customs and, by the authority of the Holy Spirit, forbid any payment to be demanded for prebends or ecclesiastical benefices. [Note: [Col. 0099D] Ivo clears himself of this accusation of simony in Epistle 133 to Richard, bishop of Albano, legate of the Apostolic See.—See *Patrologia*, vol. CLXII.]

We also command that clerics who burden the Church by bringing ecclesiastical matters before secular powers shall be held infamous until they make fitting satisfaction; that the decree issued by our predecessors concerning the sons of concubines shall be observed inviolate; and that those who, without a prior canonical excuse, do not permit themselves to be promoted shall be made inferior to their own juniors.

According to the second canon of Carthage and the ordinance of Pope Gelasius, a [Col. 0100D] priest shall receive more than a deacon, a deacon more than a subdeacon, and one who serves more zealously than those who are slower shall receive greater stipends. No one shall sell or alienate the ornaments of the Church except in the necessity which the canons permit; and whoever does otherwise shall be held guilty of sacrilege and contempt of the canons. With regard to those matters among you called *precariae* [revocable grants], whatever your brotherhood decides, we ratify.

We likewise confirm, by the authority of our own affirmation, that excommunication which you have pronounced, for the good of the same church, concerning the houses adjoining your church.

Given at Benevento, on the third day before the Ides of November.

LXXXII. Privilege for the monastery of Vichpach. (A.D. 1102, November 21.)

[*Monumenta Boica*, X, p. 437.]

[Col. 0101A]

PASCHALIS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son in Christ HENCHINRULD, abbot of the venerable monastery of Saint Martin, situated in the place called Vispach, and to his successors regularly appointed for ever.

A petition arising from pious intention ought to be fulfilled by its effect, so that the sincerity of devotion may shine forth commendably and the benefit sought may unquestionably gain strength. Therefore, since your belovedness, fleeing to the refuge of the Apostolic See, has sought its protection with due devotion, we graciously assent to your petition, receive under the guardianship of the Apostolic See the monastery of Saint Martin, over which, by God’s ordering, you preside, and fortify it by the page of this present privilege. That monastery was offered to blessed Peter by its founders themselves, Countess Hazica and her sons, Counts Hecard, Bernard, and Otto.

Therefore, by the page of this present privilege, we establish by apostolic authority that whatever now belongs to the same monastery by the lawful gifts of its founders, and whatever it may hereafter lawfully and canonically acquire by grants of pontiffs, generosity of princes, or offerings of the faithful, shall remain firm and inviolate to you and your successors. We decree, therefore, that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb that monastery, take away or diminish its possessions, or harass it with reckless vexations; but that all things shall be preserved entire, to be beneficial in every way for the use of those for whose support and governance they were granted.

When the present abbot of the place, or any one of your successors, dies, let no one be placed over it through any deceitful contrivance or violence, except the one whom the brethren by common consent, or the sounder part of the brethren, elect according to the Rule of blessed Benedict. You shall receive chrism, holy oil, the consecration of altars or churches, and the ordination of monks who are to be promoted to holy orders from the bishop in whose diocese you are, provided that he enjoys the favour and communion of the Apostolic See and is willing to provide these freely and without misconduct. Otherwise, you may approach whichever Catholic bishop you prefer and receive from him the sacraments of consecration, he being supported by the authority of the Apostolic See and granting what is requested.

Furthermore, we appoint as advocate of the same monastery Count Otto, a man of outstanding valour, and after him his eldest son, provided that he remains in his father’s integrity. But if not, it shall be within your discretion to choose whom you please as a suitable protector of your monastery, one who will zealously and reverently render this service to God without demanding secular profit.

Therefore, dearest sons in Christ, you ought to labour more diligently and devotedly in the observance of regular discipline, so that, the freer you are from secular tumults, the more earnestly you may strive to please God with all the powers of mind and body. As a token of the liberty received from the Roman Church, you shall pay each year one gold bezant to the Lateran palace.

If any ecclesiastical or secular person knowingly attempts rashly to act against this page of our constitution and, after a second or third warning, fails to make suitable amendment by due satisfaction, let that person lose the dignity of office and honour, know himself or herself guilty before divine judgment of the iniquity committed, and be separated from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ the Redeemer; and at the final judgment let that person be subject to strict vengeance. But upon all who preserve what is right for that place, may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that here they may receive the fruit of good deeds [Col. 0102B] and before the strict Judge may find the rewards of eternal peace. Amen, amen, amen.

I, Paschal, bishop of the Catholic Church.

Given at Benevento through the hand of Equitius, acting in place of the chancellor, on the eleventh day before the Kalends of December, in the eleventh indiction, in the year 1102 of the Lord’s Incarnation; in the fourth year of the pontificate of Lord Paschal II, pope.

LXXXIII. To Altard, abbot of Vézelay.—Privilege of Vézelay. (A.D. 1102, November.)

[MANSI, *Councils*, XX, 1028.]

PASCHALIS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved brother ALTARD, abbot of the monastery of Vézelay, and to his lawful successors for ever.

Since ecclesiastical order must be governed by apostolic teachings, the Lord’s flock ought to be guarded and governed with eager spirit and continual vigilance. But lest any night or hour of darkness oppress or confuse the vigilance of prelates, charity—which is God, and which knows no “one” and “another”—must be loved and maintained with all one’s strength and whole mind.

Since, not by any preceding merits but by the grace of almighty God alone, we hold Peter’s place in the Church, it is necessary that we devote ourselves to all churches, especially those known to belong to the jurisdiction of blessed Peter and those which, with filial affection, invoke the counsel and help of their mother. Therefore, since the love of your brotherhood has requested that a privilege be made for the monastery of Vézelay, whose government has by God’s ordering been entrusted to you, and since its founders, the most noble Count Gerard and his wife Bertha, offered it by pious devotion and confirmation of testament to blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, we assent to your prayers and, by apostolic authority through this present privilege, confirm and decree that no emperor, no king, no count, no bishop, nor anyone else whatsoever may, under any pretext, diminish, take away, or retain what has been taken from the goods already offered or granted to the said monastery by the aforesaid founders or other God-fearing persons, or from goods to be granted thereafter.

Among these we expressly confirm to the same monastery, [Col. 0103A] in the diocese of Autun, the church of Saint Peter, etc.

(Here all the possessions are enumerated.)

Furthermore, we decree that the consecration of that monastery and of the churches in the surrounding town, as well as the ordination of monks and clerics, shall take place there or wherever the abbots of Cluny prefer, with the counsel of those abbots of Cluny to whom our predecessors and we have granted in perpetuity our authority in the aforesaid monastery. Let them also receive chrism and holy oil from whichever Catholic bishop they prefer. But the churches of that monastery situated in various provinces, and their altars, shall be consecrated by the bishops in whose dioceses they lie. Priests and clerics likewise shall be ordained, and shall receive chrism and holy oil from those bishops, if they enjoy the favour of the Roman See and are willing to give these freely and without any misconduct; otherwise, they shall receive them from whichever Catholic bishop they prefer.

When the abbot of that place, or any of your successors, dies, no one shall be elected there through violence or any deceitful contrivance; rather, the brethren by common consent, or the sounder part of the brethren, shall elect according to the Rule of blessed Benedict and at the command of the aforesaid abbots of Cluny. The one elected shall be consecrated either by the Roman pontiff or on the counsel of those same abbots.

Unless invited by the abbot of that monastery, the bishop of the diocese himself shall not be permitted to conduct public processions or celebrate private masses in the same monastery. Nor shall he have any right of donation, subjection, or authority to impose prohibitions in that monastery and the surrounding town.

We have also decreed that no person whatsoever may disturb or trouble that monastery, harass the servants of God with vexations, take away or diminish its possessions; but that all things shall be kept intact for the use of those for whose support and governance they have been granted to the same monastery. As a token of this liberty, it shall pay yearly one pound of silver to the Apostolic See, to whose jurisdiction it is known to belong.

If anyone knowingly attempts to act against the page of this our decree and, having been admonished a second or third time, does not repent, let that person be separated from the most sacred body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ. [Col. 0103D] But whoever observes it shall receive the blessing of the holy apostles Peter and Paul and deserve to enjoy their fellowship in the life to come.

May almighty God, who is true salvation and true protection, protect and defend you and the congregation entrusted to you; and through the intercession of blessed Mary Magdalene, who came with a fountain of tears to Christ, the fountain of mercy, may he grant you to attain the end which has no end.

I, Paschal, bishop of the Catholic Church, have subscribed.

Given at Benevento through the hands of Walter, cardinal-deacon of the Roman Church, in the year 1103 [1102] of the Lord’s Incarnation, in November, in the [Col. 0104A] eleventh indiction, in the fourth year of the pontificate of the same Paschal II, pope.

LXXXIV. Bull for the abbey of Saint John at Vallée. (A.D. 1102.)

[*Gallia Christiana*, VIII, 307, from the domestic cartulary of M. de Gagnières in the Royal Library.]

PASCHALIS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved brother in Christ ALBERT, abbot of the canonical church of Saint John the Baptist in the suburb of Chartres, and to his brethren who shall live under the rule for ever.

Just as no result should be granted to those requesting what is unjust, so the petition of those desiring what is lawful should not be delayed. Accordingly, assenting both to your petition, dearest son Albert, and to those of our brother Ivo, bishop of Chartres, [Col. 0104B] we protect you and all that is yours under the protection of the Apostolic See.

For, as that same brother informed us in his letters, by his effort the church of blessed John the Baptist, over which you preside by God’s ordering, has been transferred from a secular mode of life to the regular life of canons, by the Lord’s favour. The clerics of the chapter of Chartres consented that the following rights, which they had lately held by his grant, should be transferred to that church: namely, the prebend of Saint Mary, to be held in perpetuity; the church of Saint Stephen with its appurtenances; half the church of Ferni; the church of Saint Faith in the suburb of Chartres; the tithe of Osanivilla, with the land held there by the canons, the customary due held there by the provost, and half a mill.

Therefore, we confirm by the authority of this present privilege the order of canonical life which you have professed, and we forbid anyone, after making profession, to possess private property or, without the permission of the abbot or congregation, to leave the cloister. Furthermore, by the page of this present privilege, we apostolically confirm to you the land-dues and parish which our same brother Ivo held at Luceium. In addition, we decree that whatever has been granted to your church by the same bishop of Chartres with the consent of the clerics for the common support of the brethren, whatever it now lawfully possesses, and whatever it may hereafter lawfully and canonically acquire by grants of pontiffs, generosity of princes, or offerings of the faithful, shall remain firm and inviolate to you and your successors.

We decree, therefore, that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb that church, take away its possessions, retain what has been taken, diminish it, or harass it with reckless vexations; but that all things shall be kept entire, for the benefit alike of you, the canons, and the poor, saving the canonical reverence due to the bishop of Chartres. Moreover, providing for your peace, we decree that, when you, the present abbot of that place, die, no one shall be appointed abbot there except one whom all the brethren by common consent, or the sounder part of the brethren, with the counsel of the bishop of Chartres—provided that he is Catholic—and of the same chapter, shall regularly choose according to the fear of God.

If any ecclesiastical or secular [Col. 0105A] person knowingly attempts rashly to act against this page of our constitution and, after a second or third warning, fails to make suitable amendment by due satisfaction, let that person lose the dignity of office and honour, know himself or herself guilty before divine judgment of the iniquity committed, and be separated from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ the Redeemer; and at the final judgment let that person be subject to strict vengeance. But upon all who preserve what is right for that place, may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that here they may receive the fruit of good deeds and before the strict Judge may find the rewards of eternal peace. Amen, amen.

Paschal, bishop of the Catholic Church.

Given at Benevento through the hand of Equitius, acting in place of the [Col. 0105B] chancellor, on the fourth day before the Nones of December, in the eleventh indiction, in the year 1103 of the Lord’s Incarnation; in the fourth year of the pontificate of Lord Paschal II, pope.

LXXXIV bis. He confirms the privileges of the monastery of Saint Martin on the mountain of Pannonia.

(A.D. 1102, December 8.—See FEJÉR, *Codex diplomaticus Hungariae ecclesiasticus et civilis*, Buda, 1829, octavo, vol. II, p. 40.)

LXXXV. To Anselm of Canterbury.—Investitures are not to be granted to kings or other lay magistrates. (A.D. 1102, December 12.)

[MANSI, *Councils*, XX, 981.]

PASCHALIS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to ANSELM, [Col. 0105C] the venerable brother and fellow-bishop of Canterbury: greeting and apostolic blessing.

We have received the most gracious letter of your love, written with the pen of charity. For the pen wrote upon the parchment nothing other than that with which it was dipped from the fountain of charity. In it we embrace the reverence of your devotion; and, considering the firmness of your faith and the earnestness of your pious concern, we rejoice that, through the help which God’s grace affords you, neither threats shake you nor promises exalt you.

We are grieved, however, because, although we had kindly received our brother bishops, envoys of the king of England, on their return home they reported things which we neither said nor thought. For we heard that they said that, if the king acted well in other matters, we would neither prohibit investitures of churches nor excommunicate investitures already made; and that we were unwilling to commit this to writing lest, under this pretext, other princes too should protest against us.

Therefore we call Jesus, who searches hearts and inward parts, as witness upon our soul that, since we began to bear the care of this holy See, this monstrous crime has never even entered our mind. May God avert this from us, lest it infect us, whether openly or by stealth, so that we have one thing ready upon our lips and another hidden in our heart; since through the Prophet he pronounces a curse against liars, saying: “May the Lord destroy all deceitful lips” (Ps. I [Psalm 12:3]).

But if by our silence we allowed the Church to be polluted by the gall of bitterness and the root of impiety, by what reasoning could we excuse ourselves before the eternal Judge, when the Lord says to the prophet under the figure of a priest: “I have appointed you a watchman for the house of Israel” (Ezek. V [Ezekiel 3:17])? He does not guard a city well who, positioned in a cave, by failing to resist exposes it to be plundered by its enemies.

If, therefore, a lay hand gives the staff, the sign of pastoral office, and the ring, the seal of faith, what are bishops doing in the Church? The Church’s honour is crushed, the vigour of discipline is dissolved, and all Christian religion is trampled underfoot, if we permit lay rashness to presume what we know is owed to priests alone. It does not belong to laymen to confer the Church, nor to sons to defile their mother by adultery. Rightly, therefore, is one deprived of an inheritance who pollutes his mother by adultery; nor does he deserve fellowship in the Church’s blessing who persecutes her by impious assault. For it belongs to laymen [Col. 0106B] to protect the Church, not to confer her.

Indeed, Uzziah, when he claimed for himself an unlawful priesthood, was struck with leprosy (2 Chronicles XXVI). Likewise the sons of Aaron, because they offered strange fire, were consumed by divine fire (Leviticus X). For it is alien to the Church and prohibited by the sacred canons that princes and secular men should not only fail to give investitures but should not even dare violently to intrude themselves into the election of bishops. For, as you know, it is written in the seventh [otherwise eighth] synod: “The holy and universal synod has decreed that none of the lay princes or powerful persons is to intrude himself into the election or promotion of bishops.” Therefore, if Aaron’s sons were bodily punished because they introduced strange fire, these persons, who received the Church from laymen—by whom such action is alien—are struck by the spiritual sword.

We exclude from the favour of blessed Peter and from our communion those bishops who have provoked truth by falsehood, truth itself—which is God—being brought into their midst, until they satisfy the Roman Church and acknowledge the weight of their guilt. Whoever within the aforesaid period of truce has received investiture or consecration, we hold both those ordained and their ordainers to be excluded from the fellowship of the brethren. Nor is deception sufficient for their excuse, since even the prophet deceived by another prophet did not thereby escape death.

Meanwhile, we ask your charity to commend us in your holy prayers, so that, the more swiftly you hasten toward God by the steps of virtues, the more you may extend to us the hands of your prayers. May almighty God, who called you to run in this course, bring you by a happy completion to the prize.

LXXXVI. To Anselm, archbishop of Canterbury.—Concerning ecclesiastical investitures; the sons of clerics; and the case of the Welsh bishop. (A.D. 1102, December 12.)

[MANSI, *Councils*, XX, 1061.]

PASCHALIS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the venerable brother ANSELM, archbishop of Canterbury: greeting and apostolic blessing.

How vigorously, severely, and firmly our fathers resisted in past times that poisonous root of simoniacal wickedness—namely, the investiture of churches—is sufficiently known to your wisdom. In the time of our predecessor of revered memory in Christ, Pope Urban, when a council of venerable bishops and abbots gathered from various regions at Bari, at which your religiousness and we ourselves were present, as those who attended with us recall, a sentence of excommunication was pronounced against the same pest. And we, having the same spirit as our fathers, hold the same judgment and bear the same witness.

You remember that we wrote to you some time ago concerning the sons of priests and Levites. But if such persons have been found already promoted, and, after hope of further promotion has been removed, wish to remain in the order in which they were found, because that stain attached to them not through the fault of any guilt of their own, it does not seem that a sentence of deposition should be pronounced against them, if they are otherwise worthy, so as to involve them again in secular affairs, since at the time of their ordination the choice of their own will no longer remained to them.

The Welsh bishop is not unaware that his case is wholly contrary to the sacred canons. Yet because he was promoted barbarously and foolishly among barbarians, we leave the matter to the judgment of your brotherhood; provided, however, that in future no such irregularity is presumed in that region. What we send through trustworthy messengers concerning the affair of that bishop and other matters, hear as though from our own mouth. We have received with thanksgiving the gifts which you sent to blessed Peter; may you receive your reward for them from him who is the rewarder of all good things.

Given at Benevento, on the second day before the Ides of December.

LXXXVII. To Gerard, archbishop of York.—He is admonished to make his profession to Anselm of Canterbury, according to the custom of his predecessors. (A.D. 1002 [1102], December 12.)

[MANSI, *Councils*, XX, 1004.]

PASCHALIS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the venerable brother GERARD, archbishop of York: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Although we are not unaware that you have acted wrongly against us—or rather, against your mother, the holy Roman Church—nevertheless by this present letter we command you not to neglect making your profession to our venerable brother Anselm, archbishop of Canterbury. For we have heard that Thomas, once your predecessor, raised a dispute over this very matter; and when it was debated in the presence of Lord Pope Alexander II, after a determination had been obtained by his command and various inquiries conducted, Thomas made the same profession to his predecessor Lanfranc and to Lanfranc’s successors. Therefore, what was decided at that time, we desire, by God’s authority, to be maintained firm and inviolate.

Given at Benevento, on the day before the Ides of December.

LXXXVIII. To Robert, count of Flanders.—That he should expel from the Church the schismatic men of Liège adhering to Emperor Henry. (A.D. 1103, January 21.)

[MANSI, *Councils*, XX, 986.]

[Col. 0108A]

PASCHALIS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to ROBERT, count of Flanders: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Blessed be the Lord God of Israel, who works in you the efficacy of valour, who, having returned from the Jerusalem of Syria, strive by deeds of righteous warfare to go to the heavenly Jerusalem. It is the part of a lawful soldier to pursue more earnestly the enemies of his king. We therefore give thanks to your prudence because you carried out our command in the parish of Cambrai; we command the same concerning the excommunicated pseudo-clerics of Liège. For it is just that those who have separated themselves from the Catholic Church should through Catholics be separated from the Church’s benefices.

And not in this matter only, but everywhere, when you are able, pursue with all your strength Henry, the head of heretics, and his supporters. Certainly you can offer no sacrifice more pleasing to God than by attacking him who has raised himself against God, who strives to seize the kingdom of God’s Church, who has set up Simon’s idol in the holy place, and who has been expelled from the house of the Church by the judgment of the Holy Spirit through God’s holy princes, the apostles and their vicars. We command this to you and your soldiers for the remission of sins and for familiarity with the Apostolic See, so that by these labours and triumphs, with the Lord granting it, [Col. 0108C] you may attain the heavenly Jerusalem.

Given at Albano, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of February.

LXXXIX. He grants to Peter, archbishop of Aix, the use of the pallium. (A.D. 1103, March 28.)

[*Gallia Christiana*, I, 66.]

PASCHALIS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the venerable brother PETER, archbishop of Aix: greeting and apostolic blessing.

The benevolence of the Apostolic See requires that each person’s rights be preserved, and that the privilege of honour established by the Lord be so safeguarded that worthy brethren are not denied a share in that honour. Therefore, venerable brother Peter, Archbishop of Aix, we confirm to you and to your successors whatever is known by right to belong to the Church of Aix in respect of parish, metropolis, or bishopric. Moreover, from the generosity of the Apostolic See we grant to your brotherhood the pallium, that is, the fullness of the pontifical office. You are to know that you may wear it only within the church, at the solemnities of Mass on the days specified below: the Nativity of our Lord Jesus Christ, Epiphany, the Presentation in the Temple (*Ypapante*), the Lord’s Supper, the Resurrection, Ascension, Pentecost, the three solemnities of the Blessed Virgin Mary, the feasts of the holy Apostles, the commemoration of All Saints, Saint Mary Magdalene [Note: [Col. 0107] The feast of Saint Mary Magdalene was then solemnly celebrated in Provence.], Maximinus, confessor and bishop, and those martyrs who rest in the Church of Aix; at the consecrations of churches, bishops, priests, and deacons; and on the anniversary of your consecration [Note: [Col. 0109D] These words are taken from Epistle 125 of Pope Saint Gregory, Book IX, second indiction, to Maximus, bishop of Salona, in the latest edition which we prepared.]. We desire you in every respect to maintain the proper character of this pallium.

For the honour of this garment is humility and justice. Therefore let your brotherhood strive with all its heart to show itself humble in prosperity; upright with justice in adversity, should it ever occur; a friend to the good and opposed to the wicked; never accepting any person against the truth, nor ever suppressing any person speaking for the truth; desiring works of mercy according to its means; compassionate toward the weak; rejoicing with those who prosper; regarding another’s losses as its own, and [rejoicing] in the joys of others, etc. . . . May divine mercy deign to preserve your brotherhood unharmed through many years. Amen.

Given at the Lateran through the hand of John, cardinal-deacon of the Holy Roman Church, on the fifth day before the Kalends of April, in the tenth indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1104, and in the sixth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Paschal II [Note: [Col. 0109D] The chronological indications are corrupt.].

XC. He confirms the gifts made to the abbey of Saint Aubert, of Regular Canons following the Order of Saint Augustine, at Cambrai. (A.D. 1103, April 1.)

[Miraeus, *Opera diplomatica*, III, 24.]

PASCHAL, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son ADAM, abbot of the Church of Saint Aubert, and to his brethren, canons in the same Church [Col. 0109C], greeting and apostolic blessing.

It has come to the hearing of our apostolate that the nobleman Gerard of Saint Aubert, knight, with the consent of his brothers Hugh of Beaumont and Anselm of Lieven, likewise knights, out of reverence for the decree promulgated concerning tithes held by laymen, peacefully surrendered to you, through the hand of the diocesan bishop, a certain tithe belonging to your church from Iwry. Considering this surrender pleasing and acceptable to us, we decree that it shall stand confirmed, etc.

Written through the hand of John, regional secretary and notary of the sacred palace.

[Col. 0109D] Given at the Lateran through the hand of John, cardinal-deacon of the Holy Roman Church, on the Kalends of April, in the eleventh indiction, in the year 1104 [1103] of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the fourth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Paschal II.

+ I, Paschal, bishop of the Catholic Church.

XCI. He confirms the possessions and privileges of the Church of Saint Aubert at Cambrai. (A.D. 1103, April 1.)

[LEGLAY, *Glossaire topographique de l’ancien Cambrésis*, Cambrai, 1849, p. 27.]

[Col. 0110A]

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son ADAM, abbot of the Church of Saint Aubert, and to his brethren who profess the canonical life in the same church, and to their successors who shall remain in the same observance for ever.

The promises of our Saviour are these: “Whoever has left brothers or sisters or fields or houses for my sake shall receive a hundredfold and shall possess eternal life.” And if, therefore, compelled by persecutions, you have left fields or houses for God’s sake [Col. 0110B], you nevertheless possess no less what belongs to the Church, because you seek a better and abiding substance. We therefore confirm to your beloved community, by the present charter of privilege, the Church of Saint Aubert at Cambrai itself, with all its goods, both given and yet to be given; and we grant due assent in kindness to your petition. For we strengthen by the authority of this decree the order of canonical life which you have professed there. We forbid anyone, after making profession, to possess anything as private property, or to leave the cloister without the permission of the abbot or the community; and we fortify both you and all that is yours by the protection of the Apostolic See.

Accordingly, we decree that you and your successors who remain in the same religious life shall possess for ever [Col. 0110C] all those things which appear to belong to the aforesaid monastery of blessed Aubert through lawful gifts of the bishops of Cambrai or of other faithful persons: namely, the Church of Saint Vedast, situated in the aforesaid city of Cambrai, with sixty-five *mansi*, three breweries, and two ovens [Note: [Col. 0109D] “And three breweries and two ovens.” The word *camba*, apparently peculiar to the idiom of the North, means a brewery. It derives from the Teutonic language, which, if Ducange is to be believed in his *Glossarium Mediae Graecitatis*, col. 564, received it from the Goths. Our old local customs still employ the words *cambage* and *cambier*. As for banal ovens, [Col. 0110D] everyone knows that they still existed toward the end of the last century, and that each lordship had its own. In volume V of the *Ordonnances des rois de France*, pp. 508 ff., there is a very curious regulation for the bakers of Arras, which also applies to banal ovens. The most minute precautions are taken there to prevent fraud and ensure that bread is properly made. See, among other curious provisions, article 19: “Whoever trims his nails at his own stall or at another’s stall owes four deniers to the mayor.”]; one mill; land; and the tract beyond the river called the Scheldt, from the gate as far as the road of Saint Remigius; likewise the whole village called Tiletum, and whatever belongs to it; the altar-right of Vinciacum, with all its dependencies; the altar-right of Vilers-Remaldi; and the land which the three brothers Hugh, Wibald, and Elbert granted to the same church in that village from Haistald’s meadow, together with whatever right they possessed in the village called Berilgias and at Dehereias, entirely freely and without any exaction; the altar-right of [Col. 0110D] Goegium; the altar-right of Otvilers; the Church of Saint Aubert in the village called Andra, with fifty-four *mansi* and arable land; the altar-right of the village called Saint Vedast, and the fourth part of the allod at Alberciis; the allod [Col. 0111A] given by Robert of Pulchro Manso at Fentanas; the Church of Siccis-Avesnis, with fifty-four *mansi*, arable land, and woodland; likewise the altar-rights of Thiens, Maten, and Sausoio, half the altar-right of Ruva, and likewise half that of Ivirium; the altar-right of the village called Strada; the altar-right of Ghaun; the altar-right of Gualhuncourt; the altar-right of Maalvilla; the altar-rights of Barastra and Silviniacum; at Scalduvrium, two *mansi* and land with the entire tithe of that land; at Navia, the ten *mansi* which Geoffrey delivered. We decree that these altar-rights themselves shall be possessed for ever by the same church without a personal redemption-payment, saving the bishops’ rights and those dues which among us are called *obsonia*. You shall receive, free from obstruction, the oil for the sick and for catechumens from the episcopal see [Col. 0111B], for anointing the brethren and other faithful persons who have recourse to you.

Upon the death of you, the present abbot of the same place, or of any one of your successors, no one shall be set over it by any cunning of fraud or violence, except one whom the brethren by common consent, or the sounder part of the brethren’s counsel, shall foresee, according to the fear of God, as fit to preside over them, from their own community or, if necessary, from another. If any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowingly, should rashly attempt to act contrary to this charter of our constitution, then, after a second or third warning, unless he makes amends by suitable satisfaction, let him lose the dignity of his power and honour; let him know that he stands guilty before divine judgment [Col. 0111C] for the iniquity committed; and let him be separated from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, our Redeemer. But upon all who preserve what is just for the same place, may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that they may receive here the fruit of good action and find, before the strict Judge, the rewards of eternal peace. Amen.

Written through the hand of John, regional secretary and notary of the sacred palace.

Given at the Lateran through the hand of John, cardinal-deacon of the Holy Roman Church, on the Kalends of April, in the ninth indiction, in the year 1104 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the fourth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Paschal II.

I, Paschal, bishop of the Catholic Church.

XCII. He confirms the privileges and exemption of the Abbey of Saint Peter on Mount Blandin, of the Order of Saint Benedict, near Ghent. (A.D. 1103, April 3.)

[MIRAEUS, *Opera diplomatica*, IV, 7, from the archives of the Abbey of Saint Peter.]

[Col. 0111D]

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son SIGER, abbot of the monastery of Blandin, and to his successors to be regularly appointed for ever.

A devout request ought to be fulfilled by the ensuing result of its wish, so that the sincerity of devotion may shine forth praiseworthily and the benefit sought may assuredly gain strength. Your belovedness has indeed asked us to confer the safeguards of the Apostolic See upon the monastery of Saint Peter of Blandin, over which, by God’s ordering, you preside [Col. 0112A], and through them to assign it, by special prerogative, to the Roman Church. Therefore, by the charter of the present privilege, we specially receive the aforesaid monastery under the sole lordship and protection of blessed Peter and of ourselves, and decree that it shall remain so for ever.

By apostolic authority we establish that henceforth no bishop shall presume, in any manner or by any demand, to diminish anything from the revenues, property, estates, or villages of the same monastery; to make any impositions there; to dare to establish a cathedra there; to build a common [building]; or to hold pleas or exercise any power of command, unless requested by the abbot of that place.

We also establish that whatever goods and whatever possessions [Col. 0112B] are known to belong to the same monastery of the holy Apostles Peter and Paul through the lawful donations of the faithful, and whatever it may hereafter be able rightly and canonically to acquire by the grant of pontiffs, the generosity of princes, or the offerings of the faithful, shall remain secure and unimpaired to you and your successors. We utterly prohibit public Masses or stations from being held in the same monastery by a bishop contrary to the will of the abbot and brethren, lest any occasion for popular gatherings be afforded in the retreats of God’s servants.

We decree that the altars which the same monastery now possesses canonically, or shall possess in the future, shall be possessed peacefully and without any molestation by you and your successors who keep the institutions of regular discipline [Col. 0112C], without personal succession-payment; that no exaction shall be demanded from them by bishops or their ministers on any pretext; and that they shall not be deprived except by canonical judgment—while in all things preserving the authority of the Apostolic See and the canonical right of the diocesan bishop. We further establish that, according to the decree of Pope Urban II of blessed memory, you shall install priests in the parish churches which you hold, with the bishops’ consent. The bishops shall, in the customary manner, entrust them with care of the parish, so that those priests may render account to the bishop for the care of the people, but shall show to you due subjection in matters belonging to the monastery.

Upon the death of you, the present abbot of the same place, or of any of your successors [Col. 0112D], no one shall be set over it by any cunning of fraud or violence, except one whom the brethren by common consent, or the sounder part of the brethren’s counsel, shall elect according to the fear of God and the Rule of blessed Benedict. If in future any archbishop or bishop, emperor or king, prince or duke, count, viscount, judge, or any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowingly, should rashly attempt to contravene this charter of our constitution, then, after a second or third warning, unless he makes suitable amends, let him lose the dignity of his power and honour; let him acknowledge himself guilty before divine judgment for the iniquity committed; let him be separated from the most sacred body of God and of Jesus Christ our Redeemer; and [Col. 0113A] let him be subject at the last judgment to strict vengeance. But upon all who preserve what is just for that place, may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that they may receive here the fruit of good action and find, before the strict Judge, the rewards of eternal peace. Amen.

Written through the hand of John, regional secretary of the sacred palace.

Given at the Lateran through the hand of John, cardinal-deacon of the Holy Roman Church, on the third day before the Nones of April, in the second indiction, in the year one thousand one hundred and four [three] of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the fourth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Paschal II.

XCIII. He confirms the possessions of the Church of Compostela. (A.D. 1103, May 1.)

[FLOREZ, *España sagrada*, XX, 34.]

[Col. 0113B]

P[ASCHAL], bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother D[IDACUS], bishop of Compostela, greeting and apostolic blessing.

Just as no effect ought to be granted to those who ask unjustly, so the petition of those who desire what is lawful ought not to be delayed. Therefore, dearest brother in Christ, assenting to your petitions, we establish by the assurance of this present charter that, just as the Church of Compostela rejoices, because of its singular devotion to blessed James, in being fortified by the protection of the Apostolic See, so also the other churches subject to its jurisdiction, situated in various parishes and appearing to belong to the aforesaid church through the donations of the faithful, may deserve to be cherished by the same protection. Receiving these churches under the guardianship of the Roman Church [Col. 0113C], we decree by apostolic authority that whatever goods and whatever possessions are known to belong lawfully and canonically to those churches shall be kept secure and unimpaired for you and your Church. We decree, therefore, that no person may rashly invade the same churches, take away their goods, or retain goods taken away; rather, let all be kept whole, for the benefit both of you and of the clergy and poor. We further add that neither bishops nor the bishops’ ministers may impose any new customs in the same churches, nor excommunicate or place under interdict their clerics or the churches themselves without your examination and certain knowledge of the offence; but let them remain entire and undisturbed [Col. 0113D] under your lordship and that of the Church of Compostela. If any ecclesiastical or secular person knowingly [acts] against this charter of our constitution, etc. (as above). Amen, amen, amen.

Given at the Lateran on the Kalends of May, in the eleventh indiction, in the year 1103 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the fourth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Paschal II.

XCIV. He commands G[undisalvus], bishop of Mondoñedo, either to restore to D[idacus], bishop of Compostela, the two archpresbyterates unjustly retained, or to state his case before Bernard, Archbishop of Toledo and legate of the Apostolic See. (A.D. 1103, May 1.)

[FLOREZ, *España sagrada*, XX, p. 76.]

P., servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother G., bishop of Mondoñedo [Col. 0114A], greeting and apostolic blessing.

We have received the complaint of our venerable brother Didacus, bishop of Compostela, and of his clerics concerning the archpresbyterates of the Church of Saint James, which we have heard that you are unjustly retaining, and because you have disregarded the judgment of our legate, the Archbishop of Toledo, which he recently pronounced in council at Carrión.
