## CXXX. He advises Gisela, abbess of Remiremont, to accept an exchange from the canons of Chaumousey for her share in the parish church of St. Mary. (Between A.D. 1101 and 1105, February 6.)

[Martène, *Thesaurus Anecdotorum*, III, 1175.]

[Col. 0139D]

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved daughter GISLA, abbess of Remiremont: greeting and apostolic blessing.

We have carefully heard the case being litigated between you and the canons of Chaumousey, both from your envoys and from theirs. Therefore, concerning the parish church of St. Mary, in which both your monastery and theirs [Col. 0140A] possess a share, we give the following counsel: since the church is less necessary to you, through the grace of God, in your abundance, you should accept from the canons of Chaumousey—although they are poor—in another place, on the advice of good men, such an exchange for your share that you cannot justly complain that your monastery has suffered loss thereby.

But concerning the place on which their new monastery has been built, we deliver this judgment in canonical equity: if they demonstrate, through proof given by qualified persons under oath, that the foundation of the monastery was made lawfully and has remained for ten years without a lawful claim by the people of Remiremont; and if it is established that the donor of the place or his predecessors possessed the estate itself for thirty years without a lawful claim, and that there appears to have been no interruption in the forty-year period, then they shall suffer no further molestation from you concerning the same matter. For we cannot permit these men, who serve the Lord religiously under the protection of the Apostolic See, to be oppressed by unjust vexations either by you or by others.

[Col. 0140B] Given at the Lateran, on the eighth day before the Ides of February.

## CXXXI. He commands Gisela, abbess of Remiremont, to desist from injuries against the monks of Chaumousey. (The same year, October 27.)

[Martène, as above, vol. III, p. 1175.]

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved daughter GISLA, abbess of Remiremont, and her community: [Col. 0140C] greeting and apostolic blessing.

Because great peace belongs to those who love the name of the Lord, and rest is always necessary to those who serve him, the discord carried on between you and the brethren of Chaumousey on account of temporal property is grievous to us. We therefore wrote to your affection that you should leave that portion of the church undisturbed or accept an exchange from land due to you; but you have thus far neglected to do either. Therefore, repeating that command, we order you altogether to desist from injuries against them; otherwise, with St. Peter’s help, we shall pronounce his vengeance against you more sternly.

Given at the Lateran, on the sixth day before the Kalends of November.

## CXXXII. He admonishes Count Eustace to allow Bishop Lambert of Arles to remain in possession of certain altars. (A.D. 1104–1105, February 27.)

[Baluze, *Miscellanea*, Luc edition, II, 148.]

[Col. 0140D]

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the illustrious Count EUSTACE: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Things begun with good principles, unless they are concluded with a good end, deserve not praise but blame. Therefore we admonish and, in admonishing, entreat your valour that you repent of none of the good things you have begun, but remain steadfast in them; that you permit, henceforth, [Col. 0141A] Bishop Lambert of Arras, our brother, and his church to possess quietly and without any molestation forever the altars which you are said to have restored to him under a certain condition; and that you establish complete peace and concord with him. For it is very dangerous to offend those whom God called the apple of his own eye. Therefore we admonish your nobility again and again to permit the Church of Arras to possess those altars peacefully for all time, and to take care to revere and love the bishop of that church as a spiritual father and to maintain full peace with him. May almighty God, by the merits of the holy apostles, protect and defend you from every evil, grant you perseverance in good things, absolve you from sins, and lead you to eternal life.

[Col. 0141B] Given at Terracina, on the third day before the Kalends of March.

## CXXXIII. To Manasses, archbishop of Reims—Concerning the restoration to Lambert of ten churches. (A.D. 1104–1105, February 28.)

[Baluze, as above.]

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother MANASSES, bishop of Reims: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Our brother, the bishop of Arras, complains concerning Guarinfrid, archpriest, that he violently takes away and has long obstinately retained ten churches belonging to his jurisdiction, situated, it is said, in the territory of Arras, [Col. 0141C] and that he has been excommunicated by that same brother of ours. Therefore we command your affection to summon Guarinfrid; and if he refuses to make satisfaction to our brother, then, because of his contumacy toward him, you shall pronounce not only excommunication but also anathema.

Given at Terracina, on the eleventh day before the Kalends of March.

## CXXXIV. To Lambert, bishop of Arras—Concerning certain clerics absolved from excommunication. (A.D. 1104–1105, December 5.)

[Baluze, as above, p. 149.]

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother LAMBERT, bishop of Arras: greeting and blessing.

[Col. 0141D] Several clerics of your church appeared before us, bringing various complaints. Having heard these in order and considered them in consultation with our brethren, we absolved them all from the bond of excommunication, on their promise, of course, of due satisfaction. For all of them promised, according to the tenor we prescribed, the obedience due to you as their own bishop. With regard to those who complained that they had suffered plundering of their goods by your retainers, we ask your kindness to administer justice concerning the plundering of those same goods; we send you through your archdeacon the description of those matters presented to us.

Moreover, the two deacons Algisus and Robert renounced upon the most holy Gospels the wives whom they had hitherto had; we urge and request your dispensation for them, that you should provide in future for their life and welfare. [Col. 0142A] But Hugh, son of Baldwin, bound himself by sworn assurance that, within forty days after he has returned to his country by God’s ordering, he will render you justice concerning the complaint brought against him—unless as much is remitted to him by your mercy. In Robert’s case, moreover, the judgment of blessed Siricius, stated before us and carried into effect, was as follows. Writing to Himerius, bishop of Tarragona, he said: “Any cleric who takes a widow, or indeed a second wife, shall at once be stripped of every privilege of ecclesiastical rank, with lay communion alone granted to him.” We then gave him orders that henceforth he should strive humbly to obey you as his own bishop. He too, when released from the bond of excommunication, had sworn upon the holy Gospels that in the present matter he would do whatever we commanded. Therefore receive him also as a son now obedient, and extend to him whatever paternal mercy you can rightly give. But whatever good you mercifully grant, we shall tolerate for the peace of the Church.

[Col. 0142B] Given at the Lateran, on the Nones of December.

## CXXXV. To B[ernard, archbishop of Toledo], D[idacus] of Compostela, D. (?) of Mondoñedo, and P[eter] of Lugo, bishops—Concerning the abbot of Cinis. (A.D. 1104–1105.)

[Flórez, *España sagrada*, XX, 91.]

[Col. 0142C]

P., bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brethren and fellow bishops: B., legate of the Apostolic See; D. of Compostela; D. of Mondoñedo; and P. of Lugo, greeting and apostolic blessing.

Count P. Froylaz violently expelled from his place the abbot of the monastery of Cinis, restored by the judgment of an episcopal assembly. Yet you burn with such zeal for your great office that you endure in silent outcry so great an injury to the Church, and you do not fear the reproach of the prophet, in which it is said from divine indignation: “By night I caused your mother to be silent.” Therefore awaken and cry out; summon the same count by every suitable means so that he may allow Abbot Nuno himself to return to his place and to hold the property of the monastery peacefully according to [Col. 0142D] the bishops’ judgment. If he scorns to do this until the middle of the coming Lent, take care to restrain him by authority both ours and yours.

## CXXXVI. *He strengthens the immunity of the Church of Affligem.

(See Sigebert’s *Affligem Continuation* under the year 1105, in Pertz, *Monumenta Germaniae Historica*, *Scriptores*, vol. VI, p. 400 [*Patrologia*, vol. CLX].)

CXXXVII. To Stephen, Abbot of Bèze.—Confirms the possessions and rights of the monastery of Bèze. (1 January 1105.)

[MANSI, *Councils*, XX, 1033.]

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son Stephen, abbot of Bèze, and to his successors to be regularly appointed for ever.

It is fitting readily to grant assent to religious desires, so that faithful devotion may attain a prompt result. Therefore, fostering the desires of your religious community, we bestow upon your monastery of Bèze, built in honour of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul, the protection of those same apostles through the benevolence of the apostolic see. We ordain and establish by the text of this present decree that the church of Albignac, the church of Saint Benignus, and the chapel of Saint Mary situated in the castle of Mont-Salvion and belonging to the aforesaid church of Albignac; likewise the church of Champlitte, the church of Mâis with its appurtenances, and the chapel of Foncevaux, shall remain for ever so firmly, freely, and peacefully attached to your monastery [Col. 0143A–B] as they were granted by our brother Robert, bishop of Langres, with the assent of the entire clergy of Langres.

We likewise decree concerning the two prebends which Hardouin and Hugh, bishops of Langres of blessed memory, granted to the brethren serving the Lord in the church of Saint Gengulf at Langres.

We likewise decree concerning the church of Sivoje with its dependencies; the chapel of Saint Maurice or Saint Denis; the chapel of Saint Valerian; the church of Rayol; and the fourth part of the church of Saint Martin of the monastery, together with the other properties which Hugh, bishop of Besançon of blessed memory, granted to your monastery [Col. 0143B–C]. Furthermore, we decree that the church of Saint Remigius in the borough of Bèze, and the church of Bellenave with its appurtenances, shall always remain in your possession as free and exempt from all customary dues as they were endowed with liberty and immunity by Alberic, formerly bishop of Langres of blessed memory, and by his successor Rainard, venerable bishop of the same church.

Moreover, we confirm to you the church of the Saviour at Vieilles-Vignes; the church of Saint Martin of Luc; the church of Saint Lawrence of Bèria; the church of Saint Benignus of Boënsville; the parish church of Saint Seine; the church of Saint Valery of Talmay; the church of Saint Leodegar of Gensivac; the church of Saint Martin of Belmont; and also the chapel of Saint Marcellinus [Col. 0143C–D], which Geilo, bishop of Langres of blessed memory, is known to have granted for the lights of the altar of your church, when he placed beneath that same altar the relics of the blessed martyr Prudentius, with its appurtenances and male and female dependants, just as the aforesaid bishop exchanged them with the bishop of Verdun. We also confirm the church of Saint Hippolytus of Pontiliac with its appurtenances; the church of Saint Symphorian at Casor; the church of Saint Mary of Foncevaux, granted with its dependencies by Lambert, bishop of Langres; and the church of Saint Gengulf named above.

Furthermore, we establish for you in perpetuity that the village of Bèze adjoining the monastery of the holy apostles Peter and Paul, with all its appurtenances, shall remain free from the molestation of all persons, as it is today [Col. 0144A]. We likewise establish that the fishery from Fontis-locus as far as Pincianum shall always remain freely and peacefully in your right and possession.

Moreover, whatever the said monastery now justly possesses, or may in the future be able justly and canonically to acquire through the grant of pontiffs, the liberality of princes, or the offerings of the faithful, shall remain firm and unimpaired for you and your successors.

We therefore decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the said monastery, take away its possessions, retain what has been taken, diminish them, or harass it with reckless vexations; but that all things shall be preserved intact for the benefit in every way of those for whose support and governance they were granted [Col. 0144A–B], saving the canonical rights of the bishop of Langres. Nevertheless, neither the bishop nor the bishop’s officers may in any respect burden the monastery or its places, plunder the ornaments of the church under any pretext, or impose exactions or customs harmful to the peace of the brethren. We also forbid anyone to dare reduce the monastery of Bèze to the status of a cell so long as the observance of the monastic order shall, by God’s favour, flourish there.

If in future any archbishop or bishop, emperor or king, prince or duke, count, viscount, judge, or any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowingly attempts to contravene this text of our constitution, and, having been warned a second or third time, does not make suitable amends, let that person be deprived of the dignity of power and honour; let that person know that he or she is liable before the divine judgment for the iniquity committed; let that person be separated from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, our Redeemer; and let that person be subject to strict vengeance at the final judgment [Col. 0144B–C].

But upon all who preserve what is right for that place may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that here they may receive the fruit of good action and before the strict Judge may find the rewards of eternal peace. Amen.

Written by the hand of Raynerius, scriniary and notary of the sacred palace.

Given at the Lateran by the hand of John, cardinal deacon of the Holy Roman Church, on the Kalends of January, in the thirteenth indiction, in the year 1105 of the Lord’s Incarnation [Col. 0144C–D], and in the sixth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Paschal II.

I, Paschal, bishop of the Catholic Church, have subscribed.

CXXXVIII. *Urges King Henry concerning “the joint reconciliation of Saxony and the Roman Church.”

(See EKKEHARD, *Universal Chronicle*, under the year 1105 [*Patrology*, vol. CLIV].)

CXXXIX. Confirms the possessions and privileges of the monastery of Monte Cassino. (17 March 1105.)

[COCQUELINES, *Enlarged Collection of Bulls and Privileges of the Roman Pontiffs*, Rome, 1739, folio, vol. II, p. 126.]

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the most reverend and dearest brother ODERISIUS, consecrated by the hands of our predecessor Urban as priest-cardinal of the holy Roman Church and abbot of the monastery of Monte Cassino, and to his successors to be regularly appointed for ever [Col. 0145A].

It is established that the monastery of Monte Cassino, under Saint Benedict, both legislator of monks and lawgiver, was instituted by the Lord as the head of all monasteries throughout the West. This place indeed has remained, and remains, a refuge of the sons of the apostolic see in times of need. Accordingly, responding both to this divine institution and to the sweetness of fraternal goodwill, we decree that the place itself and all things belonging to it shall always remain peaceful, free from the yoke of every mortal, and held under the perpetual right and protection of the holy Roman Church alone [Col. 0145A–B]. Among these we have judged the following worthy of recording by their proper names:

First, the monastery of the Lord Saviour situated at the foot of that mountain; the monastery of Saint Mary, Virgin Mother of God, called Plumbarola; likewise the monastery of Saint Mary at Cingla; the cell of Saint Benedict at Capua with its cells and appurtenances; Saint Sophia at Benevento; Saint Mary at Canneto beside the river Trivium; Saints Benedict and Lawrence at Salerno; Saint Mary at Tremiti with the islands themselves; Saint Liberator in the March with all its appurtenances; Saint Benedict in the Marsi; Saint Mary at Luco; Saint Cosmas at Civitella; Saint Angelus at Barregio with all its appurtenances; Saint Mary, Handmaid of God, in the city of Cosenza; Saint Mary at Banse; and Saint John of the girls at Capua [Col. 0145B–C]; Saint Angelus ad Formam; Saint Agatha at Aversa; likewise Saint Rufus and Saint Benedict of Pizzuli at Capua; Saint Peter of the Lake; Saint Peter of Avellana; Saints Erasmus, Benedict, and Scholastica at Gaeta; Saint Magnus at Fondi; Saints Stephen and Benedict at Terracina; Saint Peter in Foresta; Saint Paul in the same place; Saint Mary at Pontecorvo; Saint Dionysius at the Bridge; Saints Anastasia and Benedict at Benevento by the gate of Rufinus; Saint Benedict in Pantano; Saints Angelus and Nicander at Troia; Saint Cecilia at Naples; Saint Eustasius of Pantesia; Saint Benedict at Larino; Saint Benedict at Pectinari; Saint Mary at Casale Piano; Holy Trinity at Termoli; Saint Focas at Lesina with its mouth and fishery; Saint Benedict [Col. 0145C–D] at Ascoli; Saint Eustasius at Pietrabbondante; likewise Saint Eustasius of Vipera; Saint Mary at Barventano; Saint Scholastica at Penne; the Saviour at Tave; and Saint Nicholas beside the river Trustino.

In Abruzzo: Saint Benedict at Tronto; Saint Benedict on the river Tisino; Saint Apollinaris at Fermo, called Aplanus; Saint Mary at Arbascla; Saint Martin in Sabina; Saint Angelus at Marano; Saints Seven Brothers, Lawrence, and Benedict at Ripa Ursa.

In the county of Aquino: the cell of Saint Gregory; Saint Maurice; Saint Paul; Saint Constantius; Saint Christopher; Saint Nicholas; Saint Mary at Albaneta; Saint Nicholas at Ciconia; Saint Benedict at Clia; Saint Nazarius at Comino; and Saints Valentine, Martin, Urban, Angelus, Paul, Felix, the Saviour, and Angelus at Vallelucce [Col. 0145D–0146A]; Saint Michael at Oliveto; Saint Nicholas at Pica; Saint Angelus at Cannutio; Saint Mary at Veroli; Saint Peter at Ascleta; Saints Lucy and Peter at Curulis; Saints Sylvester, Martin, and Lucy at Arpino; Saint Mary of the Castle of Zupponi; Saint Benedict on the hill of the island; Saint Mary at Banco; Saint Nicholas at Turice; Saint Germanus at Sora; Saint Benedict at Paschesano; Saint Peter at Morino; Saint Angelus at Pesco Canale; Saint Patris in Formis; Saint Angelus at Albe; Saint Erasmus at Pompeano; and Saint Mary in the Cells.

At Venafro: Saints Benedict and Nazarius; Saint Martin at Furca itself; the estate of Saint Mary at Sala; Saint Benedict at Pizzuli; likewise Saint Benedict at Cesama; Saint Benedict at Svessa; the estate called Lauriana; Saint Benedict at Teano; Saint Mary at Calvi; Saint Nazarius at Anglena; Saints Adjutor and Benedict at Alife; Saint Domnus at Telese; and Saint Martin at Volturno [Col. 0146A–B].

At Amalfi: Holy Cross and Saint Nicholas; Holy Cross at Isernia; Saint Mark at Carpinone; Saint Valentine at Ferentino; Saint Angelus at Algido; Saint Mark at Ceccano; Saint Agatha at Tusculum; and Holy Jerusalem and Saint Benedict at Albano. At Rome: the monastery of Saint Sebastian called Pallaria. At Lucca: the cell of Saint George and the Saviour at Civitella. In the duchy of Spoleto: Saint Mary at Calena; Saint Benedict at Trani; Saint Benedict at Bari; and Saint Peter Imperialis at Taranto. In Calabria: the cell of Saint Anastasia; Saint Nicholas at Salectano; Saint Mary at Tropea; and Saint Euphemia in the March [Col. 0146B–C].

Likewise, the town called Saint Germanus, situated at the foot of that mountain; the castle of Saint Peter, which from ancient times has been called the castle of Cassino; the castle of Saint Angelus; Pignataro; Plumbariola; Piedimonte; Giuntura; Saint Ambrose; Saint Apollinaris; Saint George; Vallefredda; Saint Andrew; the monastic *vautra* [uncertain place-name]; the comital *vautra* [uncertain place-name]; Saint Stephen of Teramo; Tracte; Mortula, with the estate itself called Casafortini; Saint Saviour called Cocuruzzo; Torre at the sea beside the river Garigliano; Saint Peter in Colia; Saint Victor; Torraclo; Cervaria; Saint Elias; Valle Rotonda; Sarra-Cenesca; and the castle of Pontecorvo, which has been acquired in our own times [Col. 0146C–D].

In the March of Chieti: the castle called Lastiniano; Monte d’Alberici; Mucella; Saint Quiricus with the port of Frisa; and Saint Justa. In the county of Ascoli: the castle called Octavus, and the places beyond Mount Cimiano, Trivillano, and Cavino. In the principality: the castle called Ripa Ursa, Montebello, and Pietrafracida. In Comino: the castle called Vicalico. In the territory of the Marsi, in Carseolano: the castle called Auricula, Pireto, the fortress called Camarata, and Fossaceca. In Calabria: Cetraro; at Amalfi [Col. 0147A], Fundicum; in the territory of Troia, Castellione de Baroncello; in the territory of Capua, Gualdo di Liburia and the estate of Saint Felix of Miniano, with the church of Saint Hippolytus.

Moreover, by the text of this present privilege, we establish by apostolic authority that whatever your monastery now justly possesses, or may in the future be able justly and canonically to acquire through grants of pontiffs, the liberality of princes, or offerings of the faithful, shall remain firm and unimpaired for you and your successors. We therefore decree that no person whatsoever may disturb the said monastery, take away its possessions, retain what has been taken, claim for personal use things unjustly given, diminish them, or harass it with reckless vexations; but that all things shall be preserved intact for the benefit in every way of those for whose support and governance they were granted [Col. 0147A–B].

Furthermore, we do not wish any prejudice to arise for your house from the privileges which, while unaware of your charters of protection, we are known to have granted to the monastery of Saint Sophia within Benevento or to the monastery of Bandusino; rather, the protections granted to the monastery of Monte Cassino by our predecessors shall retain their proper force. Following in their footsteps, we declare that the monastery of Monte Cassino is to be preferred to all other monasteries throughout the West, and establish that both you and your successors shall sit above all abbots in every assembly of bishops or princes, and shall pronounce judgment before all other men of your order in judicial proceedings [Col. 0147B–C].

We also grant to you and your successors the use, on principal feasts, of sandals, gloves, dalmatic, and mitre, apart from the right of the cardinalate which you exercise at the apostolic see. We forbid any bishop or priest of any church, except the Roman pontiff, to presume within the venerable monastery itself or its cells to exercise any jurisdiction of excommunication, interdict, or summons to a synod. Unless invited by the abbot or prior of the place, no one may dare celebrate the solemnities of Mass there. The brethren of the monastery itself and its cells may receive, without opposition from bishops, clerics of any order and from any bishopric who come for conversion [Col. 0147C–D]. They may judge, without prohibition by any secular or ecclesiastical authority, both monks and religious women subject to their monasteries. The brethren in cells established in towns may ring the bells for celebrating divine offices whenever they wish. You may receive chrism, holy oil, and the consecration of altars or churches from whatever Catholic bishop you choose. You shall administer baptism through your clergy in your towns and villages. We remit for your ship, should one arrive there, the duty customarily exacted by our officials at Ostia or Porto from ships.

We also grant to you and your successors the cell of Palladio as a perpetual lodging, so that you may appoint there whomsoever you choose from your congregation; and if it should please the Roman pontiff to promote him to the abbacy [Col. 0148A], we nevertheless decree that, as a monk of your congregation, he shall remain wholly under your direction. Upon the death of yourself, now abbot of that place, or of any of your successors, no one may be set over it by any stratagem of usurpation or by violence, except one whom the brethren, by common consent or by the judgment of the sounder part of the brethren, have elected according to the fear of God and the Rule of Saint Benedict.

Moreover, opposing the greed and malice both of present and future persons, we forbid by apostolic authority all riots, called *laevae*, or plunderings that are committed upon the death or election of any abbot. If in future any archbishop or bishop, emperor or king, prince or duke [Col. 0148A–B], count, viscount, judge, or any ecclesiastical or secular person knowingly attempts rashly to contravene this text of our constitution, and, having been warned a second or third time, does not make suitable amends, let that person be deprived of the dignity of power and honour; let that person know that he or she is liable before the divine judgment for the iniquity committed; let that person be separated from the most sacred body and blood of God and of Jesus Christ our Redeemer; and let that person be subject to strict vengeance at the final judgment. But upon all who preserve what is right for that place may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that here they may receive the fruit of good action and before the strict Judge may find the rewards of eternal peace. Amen.

Written by the hand of Raynerius, regional scriniary [registrar], and notary of the sacred palace [Col. 0148B–C].

I, Paschal, bishop of the Catholic Church.

Given at the Lateran by the hand of John, cardinal deacon of the holy Roman Church, in the thirteenth indiction, on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of April, in the year 1105 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the sixth year of the pontificate of Lord Paschal the Second.

CXL. *Confirms the privileges of the monastery of Saint Peter of the Golden Heaven at Pavia. (18 March 1105.)

[PENNOTI, *Tripartite History of the Order of Canons Regular*, p. 202, on the testimony of ROBOLINI, *Notizie*, III, 227.]

CXLI. Confirms the possessions and privileges of the monastery of Saint Benedict of Polirone, imposing upon the monks an annual payment of two ounces of gold. (20 March 1105.)

[COCQUELINES, *Collection of Bulls, etc., enlarged*, II, 128.]

[Col. 0148D]

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son in Christ ALBERIC, abbot of the venerable monastery of Saint Benedict upon the Po, and to his successors to be regularly appointed for ever.

It befits us to grant assent to just requests and to lend our ears to just petitions, since, although unworthy, we are seen by God’s disposition to stand as guardians and heralds of justice in the Church of the chief apostles Peter and Paul. Therefore, dearest son Alberic, assenting to your petitions, we receive your monastery under the protection of the apostolic see [Col. 0149A], as it was received by our predecessor Urban II of holy memory.

Accordingly, by apostolic authority we confirm for you and your successors to be regularly appointed all things now belonging to it: namely, half the island called Saint Benedict upon the Po, with all its tithes, islands, woods, and fisheries; the church of Saint Blaise with the whole island called Gurgo, its wood and adjoining marshes; the castle called Castellus with its village and church of Saint Bartholomew, all tithes, and the other things belonging to it; the village called Caput-vici; the village of Sabiana with the church of Saint Andrew, its tithes and appurtenances; the church of Saint Venere of Marceneto with half of that castle; the bearded hamlet (*casale barbatum*) with the baptismal church of Saint Michael, with the river-toll upon the passage of ships and the land belonging to that bank [Col. 0149A–B]; the chapel at Labiola; the chapel of Saint John at Burbatio with its appurtenances; the chapel of Saint Matthew at Nucetulo with the village itself; and the chapel of Saint Valentine of Marengo with its appurtenances.

In the diocese of Brescia: the church of Saint Justus within the castle of Medula, and outside it the church of Saint Vitus, with lands belonging to those cells. In the diocese of Ferrara: the church of Saint Benedict with its appurtenances near the town of Ficarolo. In the diocese of Bologna: the church of Saint Mary in the place called Lambriano, with the church of Saint John called Dalmanzaticum. In the diocese of Parma [Col. 0149B–C]: the church of Saint Leonard situated near the city; likewise the church of Saint Michael within that same city; likewise the church of Saint Michael in the place called Teliore; and the chapel of Saint Michael of Coturlione. In the diocese of Metamoco: the monastery of Saint Cyprian. In the diocese of Treviso: the church of Saint Helena in the place called Tassaria. At Mantua: the hospital house newly built by Countess Matilda and entrusted to you, with its chapel and all appurtenances.

Likewise, in the borough of Saint Benedict: the baptismal church of Saint Florian; the church of Saint Syrus situated on the island of Saint Benedict; and the baptismal church of Saint Mark in the place called Villula, with its tithes and lands. Likewise, in the borough of Saint Benedict near Gonzaga, with the chapel of Saint Mary within the castle, the lands and tithes of that village which the said monastery is seen to possess to this day, saving the right and obedience due to the bishop of Reggio [Col. 0149C–D]; the chapel of Saint Sixtus in the place called Lectum Paludanum; at the castle of Ariano, the church of Saint Prosper; likewise the baptismal church of Saint Vitalis with half the tithes and other things belonging to it; likewise the church of Saint Domnus, the church of Saint Prosper, and the church of Saint Gregory.

In the diocese of Lucca: the monastery of Saint Martin on the hill, with its two dependent churches, namely Saint Mary in the place called Turrilum and the Saviour beside the castle of Vivenarium; likewise the church of Saint Bartholomew near the city of Lucca [Col. 0150A].

These and the other places or estates already granted to your monastery, or which may hereafter, by God’s mercy, be justly and reasonably granted, shall remain firm and unimpaired for you and your successors. Moreover, we add that in all priories and cells now subject to your rule, no one shall ever in future presume to appoint an abbot. All churches, chapels, and cemeteries within your authority shall be free and exempt from every exaction. Nor shall the brethren of your cells, wherever located, suffer suspension of divine offices in the parish through interdict or excommunication; but the monks themselves, their servants, and those who have devoted themselves to monastic profession shall, with the church doors closed and diocesan officials excluded, celebrate the offices of divine service and perform the rites due for burial [Col. 0150A–B].

We also grant you the right to receive laypersons or secular clerics for conversion at your places, and to obtain the tithes of your demesne lands. If, moreover, the venerable Countess Matilda gives your monastery anything from those properties which she possesses through blessed Peter, we grant this, saving the ownership of the Roman Church. We entirely forbid the public celebration of Masses by a bishop in your monastery, lest any occasion for popular gatherings be afforded in the retreats of the servants of God.

Upon your death, now abbot of that place, an abbot shall be regularly elected by the brethren with the consent and authority of the abbot of Cluny [Col. 0150B–C]. The elected man shall be blessed by the bishop of Mantua, if he is canonical and Catholic, without exaction of burden, payment, service, or an asserted condition; otherwise, he shall await consecration from the Roman pontiff. When invited by the abbot, the bishop shall willingly and freely ordain the clerics of the monastery without exacting any profession or condition. He shall freely consecrate oratories built by them in places where evident necessity requires it. He shall willingly supply chrism and holy oil to the monastery or its baptismal churches. Without the permission of ourselves or our successors, he shall not presume to excommunicate the abbot or monks or impose upon them or upon the monastery a sentence of interdict.

But if he is not canonical and Catholic, or if he wishes unlawfully to exact anything further on these grounds [Col. 0150C–D], the abbot may approach whatever Catholic bishop he chooses and receive from him whatever necessity requires. If, after becoming acquainted with the text of this our privilege, either the bishop of Mantua or others in whose dioceses your possessions lie presume with rash boldness to disturb you, diminish the property of the monastery, or henceforth appropriate it for their own uses, let them know that they will lose all authority which they have hitherto possessed. But you, brethren, take care to apply yourselves more diligently to divine service and to observe regular discipline more strictly.

In acknowledgement of this liberty received from the apostolic see, you shall pay annually two ounces of gold to the Lateran palace. Therefore, if in future any archbishop or bishop, king, prince, duke, margrave, prefect, judge, count, viscount, or any person great or small, knowingly presumes to infringe or violate this privilege of our enactment and rashly attempts to burden or disturb that monastery [Col. 0151A], and, having been warned a second or third time, does not make suitable amends, let that person be separated from the body of Christ and of the Church by the authority of apostolic power. But for those who preserve it, may peace and mercy from God be preserved in the present and future ages. Amen.

Written by the hand of Raynerius, regional scriniary and notary of the sacred palace.

I, Paschal, bishop of the Catholic Church, have subscribed.

I, John, bishop of Tusculum, have subscribed.

[Col. 0151B] John, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Eusebius, has subscribed.

Richard, bishop of Albano, has subscribed.

Risus, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Damasus, has subscribed.

Given at the Lateran by the hand of John, cardinal deacon and librarian of the holy Roman Church, on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of April, in the thirteenth indiction, in the year 1105 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the sixth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Paschal II.

CXLII. To Guy, bishop of Pavia.—Confirms the privileges, possessions, and rights of the bishopric of Pavia. (22 March 1105.)

[MANSI, *Councils*, XX, 1049.]

[Col. 0151C] PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the venerable GUY, bishop of the people of Pavia, and to his successors for ever.

Just as no effect should be granted to those asking for unjust things, so the petition of those desiring lawful things ought not to be delayed. Therefore, assenting to your prayers, dearest brother in Christ, we also confirm by the authority of this present privilege the whole dignity of your Church granted through the privileges or authentic documents of our predecessors. Indeed, we have adorned your fraternity with the pallium during the solemnities of Mass; and we grant both to you and your successors the right, in the procession on Palm Sunday and on the Monday after Easter, to ride a white horse covered with a *udone* [a cloth or covering], and to have the cross carried before you as you proceed [Col. 0151C–D].

The monastery of Saint Donatus, founded at Seovilla by a former bishop of Ticino, and the monastery of Saint Mary at Cairate, although they seem to be situated outside your diocese, shall, with all things belonging to them, remain always under your jurisdiction and administration as they have hitherto been held. Moreover, the canonical administration of the monasteries within the bounds of your diocese, and the examination, election, and consecration of the abbots and abbesses in them, shall always be reserved to your discretion, saving in all respects the privilege of the apostolic see; and it is proper that they, or their priests, should come to your council when required.

We forbid general baptism to be sought at monasteries or any chapels other than the mother church [Col. 0151D–0152A]. If any prescriptions issued contrary to the sacred canons happen to be found therein, they shall not prejudice our canonical enactments. No one may presume, without your knowledge, to bring the clergy, religious women, or widows of your city to judgment or to inflict violence upon their property. No person may presume to remove from you the care or authority of cemeteries within or outside the city. Nor may any person of whatever rank or power presume, under the pretext of hospitality, to reside in your venerable episcopal residence, or in the houses of your priests or of all your clergy, without the consent of yourself and your successors. Nor do we permit, against your will and without legal cause, invasion or violence to be committed against movable or immovable property, or persons of whatever condition, belonging to your Church [Col. 0152A–B].

We therefore decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb that same Church, take away its possessions, retain what has been taken, diminish them, or harass it with reckless vexations. Rather, all things shall be preserved wholly intact for the benefit in every way of those for whose support and governance they were granted. If any ecclesiastical or secular person, etc., as in the preceding letters.

Written by the hand of John, regional scriniary and notary of the sacred palace.

I, Paschal, bishop of the Catholic Church, have subscribed.

Given at the Lateran by the hand of John, cardinal deacon and librarian of the holy Roman Church [Col. 0152B–C], on the eleventh day before the Kalends of April, in the thirteenth indiction, in the year 1105 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the sixth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Paschal II.

CXLIII. To Martin, prior of Camaldoli.—Receives under protection the monasteries subject to the hermitage of Camaldoli. (23 March 1105.)

[MITTARELLI, *Annals of Camaldoli*, vol. III, appendix, p. 191.]

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son in Christ MARTIN, prior of the venerable hermitage of Camaldoli, and to his successors to be regularly appointed [Col. 0152D] for ever.

We acknowledge that, by the Lord’s disposition, we have been raised to the service of the apostolic see in order that we ought effectively to assist his children who implore aid and, insofar as the Lord grants, defend and protect those obedient to him. Therefore, we ought to extend the hand of protection to venerable places and provide more attentively for the peace of the servants of God.

Accordingly, assenting to your prayers, venerable son Martin in Christ, and those of your brethren, we strengthen you and your place by the authority of this present decree, and grant and confirm to you and your successors to be regularly appointed the hermitage itself called Campo Amabile, with all cells adjoining it. We also confirm by the text of this privilege whatever has been bestowed upon your place by the lawful gifts of the faithful [Col. 0153A]. Among these, the following seemed worthy of being specified by their proper names:

The monastery of Saint Donatus, called Fontebuono, with its hospice and estates: namely, the estates of Monte, Partina, Soci, Condolere, Arcena, Ormena, Pumina, Fogiano, and Campi; the monastery of Saint Mary situated at Poppi, with its churches and dependent properties; the church of the Saviour situated at Florence, with its appurtenances; Saint Peter’s at Arezzo, with its appurtenances; Saint Peter’s at Fontiano, with its churches and appurtenances; the monastery of Saint Fridianus at Pisa, with its churches and appurtenances; Saint Peter’s at Puteoli, with its churches and appurtenances [Col. 0153A–B]; the monastery of Saint Peter situated at Lucca, with its castles, churches, and appurtenances; the church of Saint Sabinus situated at Chio, with its appurtenances; the monastery of Saint Bartholomew at Anghiari, with its monasteries, churches, castles, estates, and appurtenances in their entirety, as held by Bernard, son of Sidonia; the church of Saint Peter of the Hermitage, which is at Faioli, with its appurtenances; Saint Quiricus of Fogiano, with its appurtenances; and Saint George’s situated at Murro, with its appurtenances.

Moreover, whatever you justly possess today, or may in the future be able justly and canonically to acquire through grants of pontiffs, the liberality of princes, or offerings of the faithful, shall remain firm and unimpaired for you and your successors. We therefore decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the said monastery [Col. 0153B–C], take away its possessions, retain what has been taken, diminish them, or harass it with reckless vexations; but that all things shall be preserved intact for the benefit in every way of those for whose support and governance they were granted.

Chrism, holy oil, confirmations, consecrations of altars or basilicas, and the ordinations of monks who are to be promoted to holy orders, you shall receive from the bishop in whose diocese you are, provided that he enjoys the favour and communion of the Apostolic See and is willing to confer these things freely and without impropriety. Otherwise, you may approach whichever Catholic prelate you prefer and receive from him the sacraments of consecration; supported by the authority of the Apostolic See, he shall grant what you have requested. [Col. 0153D] Moreover, we add that no bishop shall have power to subject you or the brothers of your congregation to excommunication without canonical judgment. If any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowingly, should attempt rashly to contravene this page of our constitution, then, having been warned a second or third time, unless he makes suitable amendment by satisfaction, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and honour; let him know that he stands guilty before the divine judgment for the iniquity he has committed; let him be cut off from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, our Redeemer; and let him be subject to strict vengeance at the final judgment. But upon all who preserve what is right for that same place may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that here they may receive the fruit of good [Col. 0154A] works, and before the strict Judge may find the rewards of eternal life and peace. Amen.

Written by the hand of Raynerius, regional scrivener and notary of the sacred palace.

I, Paschal, bishop of the Catholic Church, have subscribed.

Given at the Lateran, on the tenth day before the Kalends of April, through the hand of Equitius, acting in place of the chancellor, in the thirteenth indiction, in the year 1105 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and the sixth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Paschal II.

### CXLIV. To Anselm, Archbishop of Canterbury.—The supporters in England of investitures were excommunicated at the Lateran Council.  
*(A.D. 1105, March 26.)*

[MANSI, *Concilia*, XX, 1062.]

[Col. 0154B] PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother ANSELM, Archbishop of Canterbury: greeting and apostolic blessing.

The members of the Church suffer no little from the injury inflicted upon you. For, as the Apostle says, “if one member suffers” [corrected from: “if anything suffers”], “all the other members suffer with it” (1 Cor. 12:26). Although we are separated in bodily presence, nevertheless we are one in the Head. We bear your injuries and rebuffs as though they were our own. This too grievously afflicts us: that your religious presence has been removed from the kingdom of England. For sheep without a shepherd are seized and scattered by the wolf. Therefore, by every means we can, we labour for your return to them.

Accordingly, in the council recently held, it was determined by the common judgment of our brothers and fellow bishops [Col. 0154C] that the king’s counsellors who urge him toward the disgrace of investiture, and those who have received investiture from him, should be driven from the thresholds of the Church, because they seek to make a free woman into a slave. We have indeed pronounced this sentence, by the judgment of the Holy Spirit, against the Count of Meulan and his accomplices; and, by the judgment of that same Holy Spirit, we confirm it against those who have received investiture from the king. Judgment upon the king himself has been deferred for this reason: he was obliged to send his envoys to us at the time of the past Easter.

Given at the Lateran, on the seventh day before the Kalends of April.

### CXLV. [Col. 0154D] To Robert, Count of Meulan.—He threatens him with God’s wrath if he persists in persuading the King of England “to oppose the Roman Church in the matter of investitures.”  
*(A.D. 1105.)*

[*Works of Anselm of Canterbury*, Letters, book IV, epistle 62.—Cf. the same author, Letters, book IV, 73.]

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son ROBERT, Count of Meulan: greeting and apostolic blessing.

We admitted you into our familiarity and believe that we have you as a companion in the affairs of God and in the service of blessed Peter. You have now promised us this very thing in a second letter. But those who know you report quite otherwise. For they say that you, almost alone, or alone before all others, persuade the King of England to oppose the Roman Church in the matter of investitures. [Col. 0155A] If this is true, we are deeply grieved concerning you, since your very age urges conversion to God upon you. Therefore, just as we offered forgiveness of sins and the Lord’s favour to you in obedience, so, to you if you refuse obedience and consent to such great wickedness, we threaten the wrath of the Lord. We also declare that we ourselves shall not endure this any longer without this disgrace being avenged especially upon you.

### CXLVI. He rebukes Gerard, Archbishop of York, because he “has neither sworn to help Anselm nor opposed the king’s injustice.”  
*(A.D. 1105.)*

[*Works of Anselm*, Letters, book IV, epistle 38.]

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to GERARD, [Col. 0155B] Bishop of York.

The kindness of the Apostolic See knows how to tolerate offending sons for a long time, so that their transgressions may be cured by fitting correction. The Roman Church long ago did this in your case, but you have still scorned to correct your offences. You yourself also know that we consented to your promotion in the hope that you would stand as a helper and fellow-worker with our brother Anselm, Archbishop of Canterbury, in cutting away the infections of the kingdom of England. Yet, forgetful of our gentleness, you have neither sworn to help that brother nor, as your office requires, opposed the king’s injustice; indeed, you are said to lend it support.

Nevertheless, we still bear with you in the gentleness of the Apostolic See, on this condition: that you correct your offences, amend your former life, and make satisfaction to us as is fitting. Know, moreover, that the king’s counsellors—namely the Count of Meulan and those who urge the king toward the disgrace of investiture—were driven, by the judgment of the Holy Spirit, from the thresholds of the churches in the council which we celebrated during the past Lent; and that the same sentence has been confirmed against those who have received investitures. [Col. 0155C] We command you to announce this to everyone. Judgment upon the king himself has been deferred for this reason: he was obliged to send his envoys to us at the time of the past Easter.

### CXLVII. He confirms the possessions and privileges of the monastery of Altorf, imposing upon the monks an annual payment of one Byzantine.  
*(A.D. 1105, April 5.)*

[See *Wirtembergisches Urkundenbuch*. Stuttgart, 1849, 4to, vol. I, p. 336.]

[Col. 0155D]

### CXLVIII. He confirms the privileges of Pontius, Bishop of Le Puy.  
*(A.D. 1105, April 6.)*

[CHENU, *Chronological History of the Archbishops and Bishops of Gaul*. Paris, 1621, 4to, p. 407.]

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to PONTIUS, Bishop of Le Puy: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Among the other churches of the kingdom of the Franks, the church of Blessed Mary at Le Puy is known to adhere in a special manner to the Apostolic See, as a member to its head. Hence [Col. 0156A] it deservedly merited from the liberality of that See, under our predecessors, to be distinguished by the honour of the pallium. This very reason most strongly impels our concern to cherish that church more intimately and to preserve firm and stable the dignity granted to it.

Therefore, reverend brother Bishop Pontius, by the page of this present decree we confirm to you and to your successors whatever is known to belong by special parochial right to the church of Le Puy; and by a decree intended to endure forever we establish that you and your successors henceforth shall be subject to no metropolitan but the Roman one, and that all who are to succeed you in that see shall be consecrated by the hand of the Roman pontiff as special suffragans of the Roman See.

Know also that the pallium, granted to your brotherhood by the liberality and concession of the Apostolic See as the fullness of the pontifical office, is to be worn only within the church, at the solemnities of Mass, on the days listed below: at the Nativity of the Lord, Saint Stephen’s Day, Epiphany, Hypapante, the Lord’s Supper, the Resurrection, Ascension, Pentecost, the three solemnities of Holy Mary, the Nativity of blessed John, the feast of the Apostles Peter and Paul, the commemoration of All Saints, and the feasts of those martyrs or confessors who rest in the church of Le Puy; at consecrations of churches, priests, and deacons; and on the anniversary of your consecration. [Col. 0156B] We wish you in every respect to uphold the character of this pallium, for the honour of this garment is humility and justice.

Therefore, let your brotherhood hasten to show itself with all its heart humble in prosperity and, in adversity, should such arise, upright with justice; friendly to the good and opposed to the perverse; never suppressing one who speaks truth because of anyone’s person; devoted, according to the ability of its resources, to works of mercy, yet rightly desiring to go beyond its ability; compassionate toward the weak, rejoicing with the kindly disposed, counting others’ losses as its own, and exulting in others’ joys as if they were its own; mercifully vehement in correcting vices; most reverently soothing the hearer’s mind in fostering virtues; maintaining judgment without anger, yet in tranquillity not abandoning the censure of just severity. [Col. 0156C] This, brother, is the dignity of the pallium you have received: if you preserve it carefully, you will possess inwardly what you show yourself to have received outwardly. May the Holy Trinity surround your fatherhood with the protection of its glory and grant you to attain the end that has no end. Amen, amen.

Written by the hand of John, regional scrivener and notary of the sacred palace.

I, Paschal, bishop of the Catholic Church.

Given at the Lateran, 8 April [Note: [Col. 0155] Read either “the eighth day before the Kalends of April” or “the eighth day before the Ides of April.” JAFFÉ], through the hand of Equitius, acting in place of the chancellor, in the fourteenth indiction, in the year 1105 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and the sixth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Paschal II.

A lead seal was appended on silken cords of saffron and red colour. On its obverse are [Col. 0157A] images of Saints Peter and Paul; on the reverse is written: PASCHAL, POPE THE SECOND. [Note: [Col. 0157C] Notwithstanding this privilege, Lord Anthony of Senecterre, summoned to the provincial council held at Bourges in September of the year of the Lord 1584, [Col. 0157D] testified by letter that he could not attend that council because of occupations and disturbances of war; nevertheless, he would approve whatever might be determined or decreed, and would ensure its observance by the diocesan subjects under him, as is read at the end of that same council.]

### CXLIX. To the clergy of the Church of Paris.—He commends to them Galo, made Bishop of Paris, as he departs from him, and sends him with the fullest authority. He forbids senior prebendaries to receive homages from junior ones. He entrusts to Galo’s judgment the monastery of Saint Eligius, notorious for the disorder of its nuns.  
*(A.D. 1105, April 6.)*

[MANSI, *Concilia*, XX, 1044, from the lesser *Pastoral* of the Church of Paris.]

PASCHAL, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons, the clergy of the Church of Paris: greeting and apostolic blessing.

[Col. 0157B] Both we and you ought to rejoice that, after the many adversities that befell your church, God’s mercy has looked upon you. For by his goodness he has granted you, for the governance of your Church, a person worthy and suited to the sacred canons. Therefore we accompany him as he returns to you with this letter of recommendation, asking you to love him with full affection and venerate him with full humility. For we trust that he will be a guardian of ecclesiastical discipline and a diligent provider for your salvation. Obey him in devoted service; through him gain for yourselves heavenly favour. Assist him with common support in recovering the goods of the church which, it is said, were dispersed in the time of his predecessor, both in persons and in landed estates.

For vigorously pursuing this matter, with the Lord’s help, [Col. 0157C] we have granted him the exercise of our authority, so that, if the bishops whose parishioners plunder these goods, or the bishops in whose parishes the same goods are situated, either refuse or are negligent in rendering justice to your Church, he may have power to place them under interdict or excommunicate them if they do not make satisfaction.

Furthermore, we have heard that among certain clerics it is done that senior prebendaries receive homages from junior ones. We command that this be restrained and, by these present letters, forbid it to be done further. [Col. 0158A] For in such a compact ambition is evident, and a more serious scandal appears to arise in the Church. What should be done concerning the monastery of Saint Eligius we have entrusted to his provision. For it is said both to be situated in a most unsuitable place and, through the negligence of its inhabitants, to be as notorious as it is gravely exposed to misery.

Given at the Lateran, on the eighth day before the Ides of April.

[Note: [Col. 0157D] This Galo was first Bishop of Beauvais and afterwards Bishop of Paris. Addressed to him already as Bishop of Paris, you have below a notable letter of Pope Paschal. We owe both letters to the most distinguished Vion of Hérouval, a most sagacious and fortunate investigator of ancient monuments. The authority which the Bishop of Paris here receives from Paschal II—to excommunicate anyone of another diocese who retains goods of the Church of Paris, if that person’s bishop either refuses or delays to compel him to make satisfaction—the same authority, or one not greatly different, was later granted by Honorius IV to the dean and chapter of the same church. “By the authority of these presents,” he says, “we grant you that, in regard to laypersons inflicting injury in the aforesaid matters”—that is, goods situated outside the [Col. 0158C] diocese of Paris—“if their bishops refuse to compel them to provide the satisfaction due to you, after more than a month from the time when [Col. 0158D] they have been requested by you with proper humility, you may exercise ecclesiastical censure, after canonical warning has been given.” This letter of Honorius occurs in both manuscript *Pastorals* of the Church of Paris under the title: “On excommunicating wrongdoers.”

Galo carried out the charge given him by Paschal concerning the monastery of Saint Eligius. In the same lesser *Pastoral* there survives his order by which he expelled the disorderly nuns and granted the monastery to the abbey of Saint Peter of Fossat to possess as a cell, in which at least twelve monks with their prior should live according to the Rule of Saint Benedict; while retaining for himself in that place the same authority which his predecessors had possessed over the monastery of nuns. King Philip confirmed Galo’s letters, issued in 1107, by his own letters in the same year. But after many changes, in the present century that same place was at last granted by the Bishop of Paris to the most devout clerics of Saint Paul. GABRIEL COSSART.]

### CL. To Daimbert, Archbishop of Sens.—He commends the Bishop of Paris, consecrated by himself.  
*(A.D. 1105.)*

[MANSI, *Concilia*, XX, 1013.]

Paschal, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable [Col. 0158B] brother Daimbert, Archbishop of Sens: greeting and apostolic blessing.

The elect of the Church of Paris came to us, bearing the testimony of you and of your suffragans, together with, through envoys and letters, the prayers of that church that he might by God’s grace be consecrated bishop by us. Seeing the gravity of the person, observing the maturity of his character, and having compassion on his protracted illness, we judged that the Church’s prayers should be heard. Therefore, without prejudice in any respect to the right of the Church of Sens and with due reverence for your person, we consecrated him, by the Lord’s gift, with our hands as with the hands of blessed Peter. Thus we send him back to your affection with the grace of blessed Peter and earnestly commend him by this present letter, praying Almighty God that he may restore him to you [Col. 0158C] unharmed and grant that he may be more useful to his church.

### CLI. The establishment of the collegiate church of Saint Mary at Bruges is confirmed.  
*(A.D. 1105, April 8.)*

[*Gallia Christiana*, V, 354.]

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son GUMMARUS, greetings and apostolic blessing.

The authority of our office urges us to be concerned for the condition of churches and to establish what has been rightly ordained. Therefore, acceding to your requests, we too confirm by the authority of this present decree the grant of our brother Baldwin, Bishop of Tournai, who, at your request, granted the parochial church of Saint Mary in the town of Bruges. [Col. 0159A] We establish that that altar of Blessed Mary shall be kept free from every secular exaction; that the canons established there shall have the power to elect their superior, to whom the bishop shall entrust the spiritual care of the canons and the oversight of their temporal substance; and that this superior himself shall receive both offices of leadership from the bishop and shall render to the bishop canonical and due submission in each.

The superior, elected by the canons and canonically installed by the bishop, shall likewise retain the canonical authority to dispose of prebends; and every year, on the feast of the holy Apostles Simon and Jude, he shall pay five solidi in acknowledgment of the Church. Further, the brethren themselves shall exercise the power canonically to excommunicate and absolve malefactors against that church. Whatever that church now possesses, or may hereafter lawfully acquire by the Lord’s gift, shall always be preserved undisturbed and intact for those serving the Lord there. That all these things may endure in perpetual stability, we decree them by the judgment of the Holy Spirit and by the sanction of apostolic authority.

Given at the Lateran, on the sixth day before the Ides of April, in the thirteenth indiction.

### CLII. Confirmation of the goods belonging to the Church of Ferrara, whose boundaries are assigned; eleven lesser estates from the patrimony of the Roman Church are granted to it.  
*(A.D. 1105, April 8.)*

[COCQUELINES, *Expanded Collection of the Bullarium of the Roman Pontiffs*, II, 131.]

[Col. 0159C]

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother LANDULPH, Bishop of Ferrara; to WILLIAM, son of Bulgarus; PETER, son of Arimundus; HUBERT, consul; and through them to both the Church and city of Ferrara: in perpetuity.

The authority of our office urges us to be concerned for the state of churches and to establish what has been duly ordained. Therefore, as was determined by the decisions of our holy predecessors Adrian and Benedict, we confirm to the holy Church of Ferrara, [Col. 0159D] as a special daughter of the Apostolic See, the estates and patrimonies of its mother: namely, the estate called Ferrara, or the Babylonian estate, with its twelve holdings. To it we subject eleven other, smaller estates of ours, with every obligation and service: that is, the estate and riverbank of Palatiulus with its twelve holdings; the estate of Constantiacus with its twelve holdings; likewise the estate of Quartisiana with its twelve holdings; the whole and undivided estate of Donoro with its twelve holdings; similarly the estate of Popularem with its twelve holdings; and Castellone likewise with its holdings; and, in the same way, the estate called Formignana with all its holdings.

These aforesaid [Col. 0160A] estates, with everything pertaining to their rights, we give and convey from the lordship, right, and power of the holy Roman Church to the holy Church of Ferrara by this page of donation and conveyance. From this hour onward, you, dearest brother Bishop Landulph, and your successors may ordain and consecrate churches, with clerics, priests, and deacons, in each of these estates. We establish in every respect that the Church of Ferrara, together with its whole parish, shall forever remain in the right, lordship, and privilege of our holy Roman Church of blessed Peter, whose patrimony it is: so that it shall always be subject to our election, ordination, and consecration; and whoever is there elected, ordained, and consecrated by us shall enjoy the full integrity of this honour and authority.

The boundaries and limits of the county of Ferrara are as follows. On the east, on one side of the River Po, lie our fiscal and Veteran estates; from Veteran it crosses the River Sandali as far as Buccilletum; through Buccilletum it crosses the River Gabiana by Ludurium; it encircles Villamagna and Madraria, arriving at Maletum; from Maletum it proceeds beside Argile Anxianum, through marshes and fisheries as far as Vitrica; crossing Vitrica, it comes to the Burana ditch; through the Burana ditch it enters the Po and descends westward as far as the fair elm, which is the established boundary between Romagna and Lombardy. [Col. 0160B] On the other side of the river, the limits likewise begin in the east at the boundary road, which is the boundary of our county of Comacchio; they extend through marshes and fisheries to the ditch of Filule, encompass the estate of Corneto and Languavanum, which belong to our county of Ferrara, and thence descend westward through marshes and fisheries to the River Tartaro, and by that River Tartaro issue into the River Po.

For the inhabitants of the principal estate of Ferrara, we abolish evil and perverse customs. Except only as an aid to the holy Roman Church, every free person shall annually give one Venetian denarius through their representative. Of the rents, tribute, and toll from the riverbank and river, we grant one half, as a blessing, to the common benefit, improvement, and restoration of the aforesaid principal estate; [Col. 0160D] we reserve the other half to ourselves. Similarly, we retain one half of the market toll for ourselves, and remit the other half to your aforesaid bishop. We likewise retain the general court under the lordship and authority of our holy Roman Church, provided that, when our representative administers justice once each year, it shall be attended by all for three days. We exact no levy or fodrum, nor any evil or unjust service, payment, or custom; but, for the fear and love of God, we receive all these things for our aforesaid Church of Saint George from all inhabitants of that principal estate, and likewise subject the other smaller estates with all their services, as has been stated above.

If any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowingly, should attempt to contravene this page of our constitution, or presume either to diminish the Church of Ferrara in the matters written above or to take away from the holy Apostolic See the rights indicated above, he shall pay, by way of penalty and composition, one hundred pounds of the finest gold to that same holy Apostolic See. Unless he corrects by suitable satisfaction what he has wrongly undertaken, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and honour; let him know that he is guilty before the divine judgment for the iniquity he has committed; let him be cut off from the most sacred body and blood of God and our Redeemer Jesus Christ; and let him be subject to strict vengeance at the final judgment. But upon all who preserve what is right for these same churches may there be the peace [Col. 0161B] of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that here they may receive the fruit of good works and before the strict Judge may find the rewards of eternal peace. Amen.

Written by the hand of Raynerius, regional scrivener and notary of the sacred palace.

I, Paschal, bishop of the Catholic Church.

Given at the Lateran, through the hand of John, deacon cardinal and librarian of the holy Roman Church, on the sixth day before the Ides of April, in the fourteenth indiction, in the year 1106 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and the seventh year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Paschal II. [Note: [Col. 0161D] The chronological data are corrupt. JAFFÉ.]

### CLIII. To Bernard, Archbishop of Toledo, and Didacus, Bishop of Compostela (see above, letter 135).  
*(A.D. 1105, April 11.)*

[FLOREZ, *España sagrada*, XX, 91.]

[Col. 0161C]

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brothers and fellow bishops BERNARD of Toledo, vicar of the Apostolic See, and DIDACUS of Compostela: greeting and apostolic blessing.

After we had written the judgment which you know concerning the case of the monastery of Cine, our son Count P. came to us and presented many documents of that monastery. In them we clearly recognized that the place itself had been established for the religious life of nuns. Moreover, we were informed that the place does not possess resources sufficient to provide the support of two communities. Therefore it seemed more fitting that, if possible, the former state of nuns should be restored there; but if this cannot at all be done, then, lest the monastic religious life there should utterly perish, a community of monks should be admitted.

Given at the Lateran, on the third day before the Ides of April.

### CLIV. Privilege for the monastery of Tournus.  
*(A.D. 1005, April 24.)*

[JUENIN, *New History of the Royal Abbey of Saint-Philibert and of the Town of Tournus*. Dijon, 1733, 4to, proofs, p. 147.]

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved in Christ PETER, abbot of Tournus, and to his successors [Col. 0162A] canonically to be promoted, in perpetuity.

It is fitting for us to grant assent to just vows and lend our ears to just petitions, although unworthy heralds of justice, since by the Lord’s ordering we are seen to have been placed on the lofty watchtower of the Apostles Peter and Paul. Therefore, graciously acceding to your petitions, we extend the safeguard of apostolic protection to the monastery of Tournus, over which, with God as author, you preside. And by the page of this present decree we confirm to you and to your successors those places which the industry either of your predecessors or of your own diligence has reasonably acquired or lawfully recovered, or which have been granted to that monastery by the liberality of ancient princes or bishops.

Namely, in the diocese of Clermont: the monastery of Saint [Col. 0162B] Pourçain, with the churches of Besson, Quintiniacum, Polines, Celsiacum, Travallium, Fellinia, Montaureum, Sustres, Charel, Liriniacum, Martiliacum, Monfanc, Boiacum, Barbariacum, Vernei, Villena, Lupiacum, Paredo, Briasis, Varinnas, Voroz, and Saint Lupus; the churches of Bisiacum, Nuilliacum, Capelz, Branciacum, and Floriacum with the chapel of Cava Roua; the church of Salviliis, of Libiacum; the church of Saint Nicholas and the church of Vernolium.

In the diocese of Chalon: Pristiacum, Aguliacum, the church of Baldreas, the church of Saint Andrew, Lambras, Manciacum; the church in the village of Ginniacum, and that of Ver; the church of Saint Martin of Griviliacum and that of Cusiriacum.

In the diocese of Lyons: the church of Saint Andrew of Belgiacum, [Col. 0162C] Vesliacum, Brienna, Juvenciacum; the church of Saint James of Grassiacum and Saint Benignus; the church of Cabrosium, the church of Cavannis, Bisiacum, the church of Saint Mary of Soliniacum, and Saint Martin of Butella; the church of Saint Andrew, popularly called Pannos; the church of Mont-Raculphus, the church of Sasixiacum, and the church of Peroniacum; the chapel of the castle of Corgenon; the church of Saint Leodegar, popularly called Olives; Lovincum and Silviniacum.

In the diocese of Mâcon: Ulchisiriacum, Villare, Plotas, Belniacum, the church of Saint Donziacum, the cell of Saint Romanus, Saint Maurice, Saint Symphorian, Saint Mary of the chapel of Reverias, Saint Peter of Romaniscas; the church of Aziacum, of Fisiacum, Saint Julian of Lonciacum, [Col. 0162D] and Saint Vitalis of Lenna.

In the diocese of Bourges: the church of Saciacum.

In the diocese of Autun: the church of Pariniacum with its chapel, and the church of Petraficta with the chapel of Saint Justus.

In the diocese of Nantes: the monastery of Saint Philibert; the church of Saint Vitalis of Raas; the church of Machicol; Saint Martin of Paciacum; Saint Liminus; the church of Limoziveria; Saint Columban; the churches of Corcoiacum; the churches of Mores Mansiones, Legiacum, Tolvei, and Monasteriis.

In the diocese of Poitiers: the island of Herum; the churches of Bellovidere with its cemetery; the cell of Saint Mary of Laudun; the church of Saint Nicholas, Saint Peter, the churches of Basilicis and of Holy Cross; the churches of Berniziacum and Aziacum; Maciacum, [Col. 0163A] Taziacum; the church of Madernas; the churches of Bernazai, Mont-Saint-Leodegar, and Estivalibus.

In the diocese of Tours: Pontiacum, Verniacum, Corcoriacum.

In the diocese of Angers: the cell of Cunaldus with its appurtenances; the churches of the castle of Doadi, Saint Denis, Saint Peter, Saint John, Saint Leodegar, and Saint Lawrence; the village of Landrum, Trenciacum, the churches of Varinas, and Saint Mary of Tanoys with its chapel.

In the diocese of Geneva: the church of Perois.

In the diocese of Le Puy: the monastery of Saint Philibert; the church of Saint Peter of Solitas; Saint Felix of Laudons; Saint Mary of Pratalias; Saint Martin of Cocornensis; the chapel of Saint Philibert; Saint Cyricus; Saint Maurice of Amblavensis; Saint Vincent; the chapel in the castle of Syroi; Saint Mary of Bozac; the chapel of the castle of Rocos; Saint Julian of Caspiniacum; [Col. 0163B] the chapel of the castle of Mercolium; and the church of Saint Quintin.

In the diocese of Die: the church of the castle of Grainan, Saint Vincent, Saint Romanus, and the church of Torrites.

In the diocese of Tricastin: the church of Valle-Nymphis, Saint Martin, Saint Mary, Saint Peter, Saint Romanus, the chapel of Saint Michael of Gaba, the church of Eleemosyna, and Saint Mary of Grainan.

In the diocese of Orange: the church of Dosera, Saint Mary, Saint Benedict, Saint Christopher, and Saint Saturnin.

In the diocese of Vaison: the church of Saint Germanus, Saint Peter of Falco, and Saint Mary of Purpureas.

In the diocese of Vienne: the cell of Saint Agnes of Mota; Saint Martin of Aziacum with its cemetery; Saint Veranus of Rivas; the church of Fai; Saint John of the castle of Miron; the church of Villanova; the chapel of Saint [Col. 0163C] Michael of Albon; the church of Saint Saturnin with its parish; the cell of Saint Philibert of Minniacum; the church of Saint Romanus, Saint Andrew, and the church of Saint Ferreolus.

In the diocese of Besançon: Saint Cornelius, Saint Desiderius, and the church of Arzon.

Whatever else, by God’s gift, you may hereafter be able justly to acquire, shall remain firm and inviolate for you and your successors. We decree, therefore, that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb that same monastery, take away its possessions, retain what has been taken, diminish them, or harass it with reckless vexations; but let all things be preserved whole, for the benefit in every way of those for whose support and governance they were granted.

Moreover, we add that the place in which rest the bodies of blessed Valerian the martyr and Saint [Col. 0163D] Philibert the confessor shall forever be kept free from every yoke of secular power. No bishop, of whatever diocese, may disturb that place on grounds of excommunication, absolution, or any other arrangement, or impose crosses or any new exactions upon the borough and the other possessions of the monastery. We also forbid public Masses to be celebrated in that monastery, or a station to be held there by a bishop, against the will of the abbot and brethren. We likewise confirm all other things confirmed for the monastery of Tournus by the privilege of Pope John of revered memory.

Furthermore, in reverence for the Blessed Mary ever Virgin, whose name makes your place illustrious, we grant that, at the Annunciation [Col. 0164A] of our Lord and Saviour, the abbot or brethren may pronounce the angelic hymn during the solemnities of Mass. Upon the death of you, the present abbot of that place, or of any of your successors, no one shall be placed over it by any device of deception or violence, except one whom the brethren by common consent, or the sounder part of the brethren, shall elect according to the fear of God and the Rule of Saint Benedict, to be consecrated by the bishop of the Apostolic See, or by his legate because of the difficulty of the journey.

If, therefore, any ecclesiastical or secular person hereafter knowingly attempts rashly to contravene this page of our constitution, then, having been warned a second or third time, unless he makes suitable amendment by satisfaction, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and honour; let him know that he is guilty before the divine judgment for the iniquity he has committed; let him be cut off from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, our Redeemer; and let him be subject to strict vengeance at the final judgment. But upon all who preserve what is right for that same place may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that here they may receive the fruit of good works and before the strict Judge may find the rewards of eternal peace. Amen.

I, Paschal, bishop of the Catholic Church.

Given at the Lateran, through the hand of John, deacon cardinal of the holy Roman Church, on the eighth day before the Kalends of May, in the thirteenth indiction, in the year 1105 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and the sixth year also of the pontificate of Lord Pope Paschal II.

### CLV. Privilege for the nunnery of the Fountain of Evrard.  
*(A.D. 1106, April 25.)*

[*Gallia Christiana*, old edition, IV, 410.]

[Col. 0164C]

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to all the faithful throughout Aquitaine: greeting and apostolic blessing.

It is fitting that ready assent be given to religious desires, so that faithful devotion may attain a swift result. For our venerable brother Peter, bishop of Poitiers, represented to our hearing that the priest Robert, a man of great religious devotion, among the other pursuits of religion to which he unceasingly applies himself, had gathered no small community of nuns for divine service in the place called [Col. 0164D] Fons Evrardi. He also asked our charity to fortify that same community of nuns and the place itself by the privilege of apostolic authority. Therefore, by the present decree, we establish that this place and the community remaining in it shall always be preserved under the protection of the Apostolic See. Accordingly, we confirm to the nuns themselves and to their successors living in the same religious life all that we have learned has been bestowed by the nobles of your regions for their governance: namely, the estate of Raireigium, Fons Buldarius, Logiae, the Wood of St. Hermetis, and Podia. Moreover, whatever goods or possessions they now hold, or may hereafter acquire, whether by grant of pontiffs, liberality of princes, offering of the faithful, [Col. 0165A] shall remain forever firm and unimpaired both for them and for their successors.

Let no one, moreover, be permitted rashly to disturb this church, or under any pretext to take away or diminish what belongs or has belonged to it, or harass it with reckless vexations; but let all things be kept whole, to serve in every way the benefit of those for whose support and governance they were granted, without prejudice to the due reverence owed to the bishop of Poitiers. We also admonish and entreat all of you, for the salvation of your souls, to take care both effectively to protect this place, already distinguished by the name of the blessed Mary, Mother of God, and to enrich it from your resources. Whoever shall take care to foster this house and those serving the Lord in it, and to honour it with his resources, shall obtain the grace of almighty God, of the Lord Jesus [Col. 0165B] Christ, and of His Mother, and forgiveness of sins. But if anyone—which God forbid—should attempt to oppose this our decree, let him be punished by the judgment of the Holy Spirit and the censure of the Apostolic See, unless he corrects his presumption by fitting satisfaction.

Given at the Lateran, through the hand of John, cardinal deacon and librarian of the holy Roman Church, on the seventh day before the Kalends of May, in the thirteenth indiction, in the year 1106 from the Incarnation of the Lord, and in the sixth year also of the pontificate of Lord Pope Paschal II.

CLVI. He receives the monastery of St. Michael (diocese of Verdun) under protection and confirms its possessions. (A.D. 1105, April 30.)

[DOM CALMET, *History of Lorraine*, I, Documents, p. 521.]

[Col. 0165C]
