PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to ODELRIC, abbot of the venerable monastery of St. Michael, situated above the river Marsupia in the district of Verdun, and to his successors regularly appointed for ever.

The blessed Apostle Paul says that those who are companions of sufferings also hope to be companions of consolation. Since, therefore, we have learned that you have suffered much for the Catholic faith amid the sufferings of the Roman Church, we desire that you should also share in that consolation. By the present privilege we grant to you and your successors the safeguard of apostolic [Col. 0165D] protection, and confirm everything belonging to your monastery through the gifts of Duke Wolfaud, other princes or kings, grants of bishops, offerings of other faithful persons, or other just means: namely, the village of St. Michael itself; the village of Widinis; the village of Vodonis; Marsupia; the village of Mononis; the court of Calvo; a share in the village called Ervia; the village called Cula; the court of Rofrid; a share in the village called Bannonis curtis, with its church; the village of Fraxinum, with its church; the village called Trunio, with church and altar; the village called Buxerias, with its church; the village called Crux, with its church; Domnus Remigius, with its church. In the suburb of Verdun, a church with altar and an allod of [Col. 0166A] seven holdings. The village called Lederna. One share in the court of Eppo.

The village called Ulmus, which among the people is called Coria. The village of Villonis. The village of Cussiriacum. The village of Condatum, with church and tithes. At Vicus and Marsal, an *inio* for making salt, with a holding, a serf, and a house. The village called Bethelani mons. A fourth part of the village [lacuna], with church and tithes, both greater and lesser. The village of Ansold; the village of Thiegisil. Longum Mons; the court of Moricus, with church and tithes, both greater and lesser. The village of Saponaria. The church of Vetus Villa, with both greater and lesser tithes. The church of Acciaca Villa, with both greater and lesser tithes. Two churches in Thyriacum, [Col. 0166B] with both greater and lesser tithes and with the customary freedom proper to them. The church of St. Balsamus, with both greater and lesser tithes. The court of Vermarus, with church and both greater and lesser tithes. The village of Viletta; Baldricus’s Mount, with church and tithes. The court of Lusanus; the village of Friscus; Nova Villa; the village of Martio and Boveia, with churches and tithes. The village of Corridum. The stream of St. Hilary, with church and tithes. The court of Robald, with church and tithes. The court of Hermar. The church of Dagon’s village, with tithes. The church of the village, with seven holdings. Half of the village of Sechanis. At Nanceyacum, a certain share. At Salemannia, an allod. At Sarnacum, a certain [Col. 0166C] share. At Ruviene [lacuna], a certain share.

At Saponaria, a church with mill, cultivated and uncultivated lands. A church with altar and tithes at Barri Villa; the cultivated land given for Count Hugh; and a hospice, with church and appurtenances. The court of Waher, with church and tithes. The village of Vedanus, with church and tithes. The village of Maurus, with church and appurtenances. A share of Mariacum, with church and tithes. The village of Toralia. The court of Bodelinus. Longa Aqua. The village of Vodelina. Vallis Village, with church. The church of Alier. The church at Mannes, with appurtenances. A share in the village of Gyro. A share in Verthisiacum. An allod in Framea Villa, with male and female serfs, cultivated and uncultivated lands. A share [Col. 0166D] in Mererinia. A share in Gereya. A share in Ponto; the cell called Harei Villa, with the possessions belonging to it, namely Periacus and the court of Holtrannus. A share of Lifagium. A share of the court of Vreher. Frisvilla. At Cussiacum, an allod with male and female serfs. At Parniacum, an allod with appurtenances. Braco’s Court Village. At Balneolum, an allod with male and female serfs.

Likewise, we confirm to you the cell called Rooldi curtis, with its appurtenances; the cell called Merodorum, with its appurtenances; and the cell called Asmingia, with its appurtenances. This last is so free that it owes no subjection either to bishop or archdeacon. Likewise, the cell called Vetus Monasterium. Its possessions are these: Bucconis [Col. 0167A] Villa, with appurtenances; Curezele, with church and appurtenances; Morlensis curtis, with church; the church of Floriacum; at the court of Vertyhernei, a church with both greater and lesser tithes; Bruno’s Maslinus, with appurtenances; the church of Maslinus; the church at Ligmers, with appurtenances; at Toul, an allod of vineyards, meadows, and holdings; an allod at Palladius’s holding; three parts in the church at Helesin; half the church at Roseria; Lusanivilers, with appurtenances; an allod with a spring at Domnus Peter; Warner’s village, with appurtenances; an allod at Bannonis curtis; Mononis curtis, with appurtenances; a fourth part of the church at Berlei Villa, with appurtenances; the church at Acuti curtis, with holdings, male and female serfs, and appurtenances; the church at Juniolas, [Col. 0167B] with appurtenances; two mills at Ramberti curtis, with seven holdings; the church of Thail, with appurtenances; the church at Rambert; Masniolus, with ten holdings; a mill at the ford of Verdun, with holdings and meadows; one holding at Tiliacum.

At Hunonis Villa, one holding. At Maferez, male and female serfs, with cultivated and uncultivated lands and a mill. At the neighbouring holding of Amarus, one and a half holdings. At St. Balsamus, seven holdings, with the ban-right and a mill. At one neighbouring holding, three holdings. Beneath Prisneium, one vineyard. At Asmantia, two holdings with a vineyard. At Pompanium, two holdings with a vineyard. At Pompanium, two holdings with vineyards. At Venderia, a vineyard with lands. At St. Raguerinda, one vineyard. At Grossum [Col. 0167C] Robur, a meadow and mill. At Theoldi curtis, one meadow. At Samboldi Mons, male and female serfs with cultivated and uncultivated lands. At Parva Coria, male and female serfs with cultivated and uncultivated lands. At Pischunmes, male and female serfs with appurtenances. At Haum, whatever belongs there.

Likewise, we confirm to you the cell of Salona, whose possessions are these: the village called Letrau; Fezzonis curtis; Eligesindis Villa; Abonis curtis; Romans; Almeri curtis; Vunzonis curtis; Vivi curtis; seven holdings of Malodis curtis; Mori curtis, with church; Curcellae, with appurtenances and church; the market of Diosmis; thirty holdings between Aliacy and Malesei Villa; an allod in the settlement, with pans, plots, and *iniones*, and the remaining appurtenances. We grant that [Col. 0167D] said cell of Salona shall remain in its customary liberty, free from every exaction; and that neither the bishop nor the bishop’s officials may exercise there, without the abbot’s consent, a synod, judicial jurisdiction, or any coercive authority.

If, beyond these estates, any goods are now lawfully possessed by the said monastery of St. Michael, or shall hereafter, by the Lord’s bounty, come to be justly and canonically acquired and possessed, let them always be preserved peaceably and intact for you and your successors living in the same religious life. We therefore decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb that monastery, take away its possessions, retain possessions taken away, or harass it with reckless [Col. 0168A] vexations; but let all things be kept whole, to serve in every way the benefit of those for whose support and governance they were granted. Upon your death, now abbot of that place, or that of any of your successors, no one may be set over it by any artifice of intrusion or by force, except one whom the brethren by common consent, or the sounder part of the brethren’s counsel, shall elect from their own community or, if necessary, from another, according to the fear of God and the Rule of blessed Benedict.

If, therefore, any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowing this charter of our enactment, should rashly attempt to act against it, and, after second or third admonition, fails to make suitable satisfaction, let that person forfeit the dignity of his power and honour; let him know himself guilty before the divine judgment for the iniquity committed; let him be separated from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ the Redeemer; and let him be subject to strict vengeance at the last judgment. But upon all who preserve what is right for that place, may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that they may receive here the fruit of good works and find, before the strict Judge, the rewards of eternal peace.

Written through the hand of Raynerius, regional scrivener and notary of the sacred palace.

I, Paschal, bishop of the Catholic Church, have subscribed.

Given at the Lateran, through the hand of John, cardinal deacon and librarian of the holy Roman Church, [Col. 0168C] on the second day before the Kalends of May, in the thirteenth indiction, in the year 1106 [1105] from the Incarnation of the Lord, and in the sixth year also of the pontificate of Lord Pope Paschal II.

CLVII. He confirms the ancient exemption of the see of Oviedo. (A.D. 1105, September 30.)

[FLOREZ, *España sagrada*, XXXVIII, 340.]

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother PELAGIUS, bishop of Oviedo, and to his successors canonically appointed for ever.

Ecclesiastical authority has established that in weightier affairs recourse must be had to the Apostolic See, as to the head and mother of all; for she knows, from the bowels of maternal charity, how to assist the oppressed, and so to defend her own rights as to take care that the rights due to others also be maintained. Therefore, dearest brother Pelagius, bishop of Oviedo, we receive with due kindness the prayers of you and your Church, so that we preserve for the Church of Oviedo the right of liberty held through the long continuance of ancient times. For although it has flourished among the other cities of Spain, illustrious and wealthy, it is nowhere recorded ever to have been subject to a metropolitan. We therefore decree by the authority of this present enactment that this freedom of the church shall remain valid, whole, and so firm, in accordance with your petitions, that if any surreptitious procurement [*subrectio*, perhaps *subreptio*] during the occupations of the Apostolic See has perhaps extorted an enactment contrary to this liberty, it shall inflict no prejudice upon that liberty. [Col. 0169A] For the good of liberty is protected by every provision of the laws, so that it may not be exposed to destruction by any pretexts.

We therefore establish that, in accordance with the enactments of your predecessors and of yourself, your successors also shall never be subject to any metropolitan other than the Roman one; and that all who are to succeed you in that see shall be consecrated through the hand of the Roman pontiff as special suffragans of the Roman See. Furthermore, by a decree to remain in force for ever, we ordain that whatever has hitherto been justly offered to the aforesaid Church of Oviedo by royal charters, and whatever it is known to possess by lawful possession of parishes, shall always be kept firm and whole for you and your lawful successors.

If any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowingly acting against this charter of our enactment, [Col. 0169B] should rashly attempt to oppose it, and, after second or third admonition, fails to make suitable satisfaction, let that person forfeit the dignity of his power and honour; let him know himself guilty before the divine judgment for the iniquity committed; let him be separated from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ the Redeemer; and let him be subject to strict vengeance at the last judgment. But upon all who preserve what is right for that Church, may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that they may receive here the fruit of good works and find, before the strict Judge, the rewards of eternal peace. Amen.

I, Paschal, bishop of the Catholic Church.

Given through the hand of John, cardinal deacon and librarian of the holy Roman Church, at the city [Col. 0169C] of Castellana, on the second day before the Kalends of October, in the year 1102 from the Incarnation of the Lord, and in the seventh year of the pontificate of Lord Paschal II.

[Note: [Col. 0169D] The chronological indications are corrupt. JAFFÉ.]

CLVIII. To the bishop of Beauvais, concerning a certain land of St. Bertin called Hubertuisin. (A.D. 1105, October 11.)

*Collection des cartulaires de France*, Paris, 1840, quarto, vol. III, p. 251.]

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the venerable WALON, bishop of Beauvais, greeting and apostolic blessing.

By many proofs we have already learned that justice is dear to you; therefore we confidently entrust to your zeal what belongs to justice. In your presence, indeed, and in that of other fellow bishops, our son Lambert, abbot of St. Bertin, stated that he had rightfully vindicated for his monastery a possession called Hubertuisin, in the village of Bury, which a certain Hugh of Bury holds by force with the assistance of Fulco, son of Ebalus. For this reason he is said to have been excommunicated by our legate Celestine, bishop of Palestrina, at the council of Reims. We therefore admonish and command your prudence to administer justice to the monastery, as it is known to you. And you are not only to maintain the excommunication pronounced against that Hugh and his supporters, but also to prohibit divine offices throughout the whole village of Bury and throughout all [Col. 0170A] Fulco’s land, until they make satisfaction to the monastery.

Given at Ferentino, on the fifth day before the Ides of October.

CLIX. To Didacus, bishop of Compostela—Concerning the wearing of mitres. (A.D. 1105, October 24.)

[FLOREZ, *España sagrada*, XX, 93.]

P., bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother D., bishop of Compostela, and to the beloved sons, the canons of the Church of Compostela, greeting and apostolic blessing.

We have received with paternal kindness your petition, which you presented to us through our son G., archdeacon of your Church. For the Roman Church has always held it as especially proper to herself, as a mother to her children, to impart to other churches the favours of her dignities. Therefore, by the authority of these present letters, we grant that on solemn days the chief persons of your Church may cover their heads within the church with jewelled mitres, in the likeness, that is, of the cardinal priests or deacons of the Apostolic See. It will therefore be your concern always to show yourselves grateful toward the holy Apostolic See, so that the Roman Church, as a mother rejoicing in good children, may always rightly rejoice that she has bestowed grace upon grace on the Church of Compostela, whether in its head or in its members.

Given at the Lateran, on the ninth day before the Kalends of November.

CLX. To G[undisalvus], bishop of Mondoñedo—He states that he has learned that the archpresbyterates of Bisancos, Trasancos, and Salagia belong by right to the Church of Compostela, and commands him not to claim them further. (A.D. 1105, October 25.)

[FLORES, *España sagrada*, XX, 78.]

[Col. 0170C]

P., bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother G., bishop of Mondoñedo, greeting and apostolic blessing.

As we have learned from the representation of our fellow bishop of Burgos, to whom we had entrusted the matter, and as we have understood from the testimony of the venerable bishops Peter of Lugo and Alfonso of Tui, who, together with another man of episcopal office whose letters we have not received, bore witness from their recollection concerning the same affair, it was established in common deliberation that those archpresbyterates regarding which a dispute had been brought before us—Bisancos, Trasancos, and Salagia—belong by right to the Church of Compostela. For they had been assigned by the bishop of Iria or Compostela to the bishop of Mondoñedo for assistance. Therefore we command your belovedness henceforth to permit those archpresbyterates, which are known indeed to belong by right in this way to the Church of Compostela, to remain peaceably and wholly in the right of that Church; otherwise, by resisting justice, you shall feel the sword of justice more effectually.

Given at the Lateran, on the eighth day before the Kalends of November.

CLXI. He confirms the goods and privileges of the monastery of Tulle. (A.D. 1105, October 31.)

[BALUZE, *Historia Tutelensis*, p. 449.]

[Col. 0171A]

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son GUILLELMUS, abbot of Tulle, and to his successors regularly appointed for ever.

A pious petition ought to be fulfilled by a result corresponding to its will, so that the sincerity of devotion may shine forth commendably and the requested benefit may undoubtedly acquire force. Your belovedness has asked us to confirm the enactments of our predecessor Urban II of holy memory and, through them, to confer upon the monastery of Tulle, over which you preside by God’s authorisation, the safeguards of our confirmation. Therefore, by the present privilege, [Col. 0171B] we establish by apostolic authority that whatever goods and possessions are shown to belong to the same monastery through the lawful grants of the faithful, and whatever it may hereafter be able justly and canonically to acquire through concession of pontiffs, liberality of princes, or offerings of the faithful, shall remain firm and unimpaired for you and your successors. Among these, the following are deemed to require expression by their proper names: in the adjacent borough, the church of St. Peter and the church of St. Julian; the church of Altoire; of Monedeira; of Gransania; of la Mazeyra; of Espinaciis; of Marceliacum; of Clergor; of Braguisa; of Spaniacum; of Acuto Monte; the chapel of Roca; the chapel of Marco; the chapel [Col. 0171C] of la Garda; the church of St. Bonitus; the church of Aquina; of Madrangas; of Olonziacum; the chapel of la Valeta; the church of Reliacum; of Aureliacum; of Planis; of la Capella Genesta; of Auriolum; of Bellopodium; in the district of Cahors, the church of St. Michael; the church of Banieyras; in the borough of Vairac, the churches of St. Martin, St. Stephen, and St. Germanus; the church of Mairona; of Vogairo, with the chapel of Bellocastellum; of Rocamadour; and St. John’s church of Furtin.

We therefore forbid injuries to be inflicted upon that monastery by any persons on account of offences committed by the knights of Tulle. We likewise decree that the burial-place of that place shall be entirely free, so that no one may obstruct the devotion and last will of those who decide to be buried there, unless they happen to be excommunicated. Upon your death, now abbot of that place, or that of any of your successors, no one may be set over it by any artifice of intrusion or by force, except one whom the brethren by common counsel, or the sounder part of the brethren’s counsel, shall elect according to the fear of God and the Rule of blessed Benedict. Moreover, we forbid in every way that any gift be exacted from any living person upon the entry of an abbot.

Furthermore, we decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the monastery, take away, retain after seizure, diminish, or harass its possessions with reckless vexations; but let all things be [Col. 0172A] preserved whole, to serve in every way the benefit of those for whose support and governance they were granted. Therefore, most beloved sons in Christ, in order that you may become worthier of this present grace, strive always to have the fear and love of God in your hearts, so that, the freer you are from secular tumults, the more earnestly you may long with all the powers of mind and soul to please God.

If, therefore, in the future any archbishop or bishop, emperor or king, prince or duke, count, viscount, judge, or any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowingly acting against this charter of our enactment, should rashly attempt to oppose it, and, after second or third admonition, fails to make suitable satisfaction, let that person forfeit the dignity of his power and honour; let him know himself guilty before the divine judgment for the iniquity committed; let him be separated from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ the Redeemer; and let him be subject to strict vengeance at the last judgment. But upon all who preserve what is right for that place, may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that they may receive here the fruit of good works and find, before the strict Judge, the rewards of eternal peace. Amen, amen.

Written through the hand of John, regional scrivener of the sacred palace. Fare well.

I, Paschal, bishop of the Catholic Church.

Given at the Lateran, on the day before the Kalends of November, through the hand of Julian, cardinal deacon and librarian of the holy Roman Church, in the thirteenth indiction, in the year 1105 from the Incarnation of the Lord, [Col. 0172C] and in the seventh year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Paschal II.

CLXII. He receives the monastery of St. George in the Black Forest into the special protection of the Apostolic See. (A.D. 1105, November 2.)

[SCHOEPFLIN, *Alsatia diplomatica*, Mannheim, 1772, folio, p. 185.]

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son DICKER, abbot of the monastery of St. George in the Black Forest, beside the river Brigach, and to his successors regularly appointed for ever.

It is fitting that ready assent be given to religious desires, so that faithful devotion may attain a swift result. Accordingly, following in the footsteps of our predecessor Urban II of holy memory in response to the devotion of your desire, we have received the monastery of your place under the special fostering protection of the Apostolic See; and, by the present privilege, we establish by apostolic authority that whatever estates or possessions the noble men Hetzilo and Hesso, founders of that place, or any others have offered from their own right to the aforesaid monastery, and whatever you may hereafter justly and canonically acquire through concessions of pontiffs, liberality of princes, or offerings of the faithful, shall remain firm and unimpaired for you and your successors. Nor may any priest, king, duke, count, or any other person [Col. 0173A] claim in that place for himself any proprietary claim—whether hereditary right, advocacy, or any exercise of authority—that harms the monastery’s freedom. The abbot, with his brethren, shall have free power to appoint whatever advocate they choose; and if he later proves useless to the monastery, they shall remove him and appoint another. Upon your death, now abbot of that place, or that of any of your successors, no one may be set over it by any artifice of intrusion or by force, except one whom the brethren by common consent, or the sounder part of the brethren’s counsel, shall elect according to the fear of God and the Rule of blessed Benedict.

And so that the brethren assembled in that place may be freer to devote themselves to the service of almighty God, we decree that no person whatsoever may [Col. 0173B] rashly disturb that monastery, take away or diminish its dependent possessions, or harass it with reckless vexations; but let all things be preserved whole, to serve in every way the benefit of those for whose support and governance they were granted.

But you, sons redeemed in Christ, ought diligently to apply yourselves to the observances of regular discipline and to strive with all the powers of soul and mind, so that, walking by the narrow way, you may please almighty God and attain the heavenly breadth. In acknowledgment of this liberty received from the Roman Church, you shall pay every year one gold Byzantine to the Lateran palace. If any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowingly acting against this charter of our enactment, should rashly attempt to oppose it and, after second or third admonition, fails to make suitable satisfaction, let that person forfeit the dignity of his power and honour; let him know himself guilty before the divine judgment for the iniquity committed; let him be separated from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ the Redeemer; and let him be subject to strict vengeance at the last judgment. But upon all who preserve what is right for that place, may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that they may receive here the fruit of good works and find, before the strict Judge, the rewards of eternal peace. Amen.

Written through the hand of Raynerius, regional scrivener and notary of the sacred palace.

I, Paschal, bishop of the Catholic Church.

[Col. 0173D] Given at the Lateran, on the fourth day before the Nones of November, through the hand of John, cardinal deacon and librarian of the holy Roman Church, in the thirteenth indiction, in the year 1105 from the Incarnation of the Lord, and in the seventh year of the pontificate of Lord Paschal II.

CLXIII. To Hugh, abbot of Cluny. (A.D. 1105, November 7.)

[Gall. Christ., XIII, 13.]

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother HUGH, abbot of Cluny, greeting and apostolic blessing.

From the letters of our predecessor Urban II of holy memory, we have learned that a cemetery was granted to the monastery of St. Mary situated near the city of Toulouse and subject to the jurisdiction of your monastery of Cluny [Col. 0174A], and that by those same letters he directed the bishop of that city to consecrate it. Therefore we too, in accordance with the petition of your religious devotion and preserving the enactments of that predecessor of ours, confirm to the aforesaid monastery of Blessed Mary the perpetual possession of a cemetery. And, to repel the injuries of rivals, we establish by this present decree that, if any secular persons should desire burial at that monastery, they shall be prevented by no obstacle, unless they are bound by the bond of excommunication. We order that the possessions belonging to the same monastery which are now held by certain clerics living in secular fashion shall, after their deaths, be restored to the use of monks living according to the rule. [Col. 0174B] Furthermore, whatever the aforesaid monastery lawfully possesses, or may hereafter justly and canonically acquire by the Lord’s bounty, shall always be preserved firm and unimpaired. No one may rashly disturb the place itself, take away or diminish its possessions, or harass it with reckless vexations; but let all things be preserved whole, to serve in every way the benefit of those for whose support and governance they were granted. If anyone, having learned the tenor of this decree, should attempt to oppose it, unless, after canonical admonition, he has made satisfaction to God and to the brethren of the Church, let him know that he is to be punished by the indignation of almighty God and of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, and struck by the sword of the Holy Spirit. But whoever takes care to honour that monastery and those serving the Lord in it with favour [Col. 0174C] and with his resources shall obtain the grace of almighty God and His apostles.

Given at the Lateran, on the seventh day before the Ides of November, through the hand of John, cardinal deacon and librarian of the holy Roman Church, in the thirteenth indiction, in the year 1105 from the Incarnation of the Lord, and in the seventh year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Paschal II.

CLXIV. To Rothard, archbishop of Mainz—Concerning bishops invested by kings; likewise concerning those consecrated during the time of schism. (A.D. 1105, November 11.)

[MANSI, *Councils*, XX, 1027.]

[Col. 0174D]

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother ROTHARD, bishop of Mainz, greeting and apostolic blessing.

For a long time there has been a grave scandal between priesthood and kingship, because, while kings usurp what is not theirs, the Church has lost what belongs to her liberty. Simon Magus surely found this path, this doorway, for his wickedness. For when an ambitious mind believes that ecclesiastical offices can be obtained only through a deceptive investiture, it subjects itself to courtly service and prepares to bend the royal heart by ampler gifts. This avarice, indeed, as is read in the books of Kings, overthrew the religious order of ancient times as well. But how divine indignation raged against kings who presumed such things is not passed over in silence in those same writings.

And [Col. 0175A] truly, it is a great crime for a son to consign his mother to servitude, so that against her will she enters marriage-chambers which she rejects. We must be stirred to new concern over this matter, since divine providence has provided an opportunity in the new reign. For we desire that kings should preserve whole whatever is theirs by right, nor do we diminish it in any respect, provided that they permit whole the liberty of the bride of their Lord, which the Redeemer earned by His own blood. If they act thus, they shall obtain our aid, our counsel, our concord, and our goodwill; otherwise, we cannot endure so great an indignity to our mistress and mother. For what has the episcopal staff to do with a soldier, or the priestly ring with him? Let kings have their primacy in the Church, that they may be defenders of the Church and enjoy the Church’s aid. [Col. 0175B] Let kings have what belongs to kings; let priests have what belongs to priests. Thus let them keep peace with one another and honour each other in the one body of Christ.

Concerning the ordinations of clerics ordained during the schism of our times, we have judged that nothing else should be written than what was determined at the Synod of Piacenza by our predecessor Urban of holy memory. But we consider that bishops who received the laying-on of hands while under excommunication in that schism ought to be referred to the judgment of a council. For the evil involving so many and such great persons must be either healed or cut away by a general deliberation. It is for you, after taking counsel with your brethren, to inform us promptly whether a council is to be held in your regions, and concerning its place and time. [Col. 0175C] For we desire—and it is most expedient—that, either among you through our legates or in Italy through ourselves, God granting it, it should be held, so that by common deliberation, through God’s grace, we may deal with removing the scandal between priesthood and kingship and with establishing peace.

Moreover, concerning the churches of schismatics, we transmit the words of Pope John of holy memory. For he says to the bishops established throughout Italy: “Wherever you find the churches of the Arians, consecrate them Catholic by divine prayers and rites without any delay.” And farther on, he recalls that he had done the same thing in the regions of Constantinople, saying: “Whatever churches of theirs we were able to find in those regions, we consecrated them Catholic, with the Lord bringing help.”

[Col. 0175D] May almighty God, whom we believe to be our peace and salvation, through your diligence bring about the peace and salvation of His Church by the abundance of His mercies.

Given at the Lateran, on the third day before the Ides of November.

CLXV. At the request of Gertrude, countess of Flanders, he confirms certain possessions of the Church of St. Walburga at Veurne. (A.D. 1105.)

[MIRAEUS, *Opera diplomatica*, III, 24.]

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son HERIBERT, provost of the church of St. Walburga situated in the town of Veurne, and to his successors for ever.

[Col. 0176A] When requests are made by secular persons for matters to which they ought to be encouraged by our exhortations, we ought to grant them with a more gracious readiness.

Accordingly, we have kindly received the petition of the illustrious lady Gertrude, Countess of Flanders, and, God granting, have more readily approved it. By the text of this present decree we strengthen your whole church by the authority of the Apostolic See, and we confirm in perpetuity to that Church the gifts of her devotion which, with the consent of her illustrious son Count Robert, she has bestowed: namely, for the prebends of the said brethren, eighty measures of land, from which twenty pounds are paid every year.

For the restoration of the church and the support of the schools, moreover, two sheepfolds. Further, whatever [Col. 0176B] goods, whether in landed lordship or in the revenue of tithes in the three parishes—namely Binaburgh, Butanburgh, and Wulpam—which the aforesaid Church of St Walburga is known to hold by lawful possession; and if hereafter the parishes of that same Church should happen to be enlarged by an increase of land, may the tithes arising from them remain secure and unimpaired for you.

If, indeed, any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowing this document of our ordinance, should rashly attempt to act against it, let that person be deprived of the dignity of his power and honour; let him know himself to be liable before the divine judgment for the iniquity he has committed; let him be excluded from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord, Redeemer Jesus Christ; and let him be subject to strict vengeance at the final judgment.

But upon all who uphold what is just for that same Church, may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that they may receive here the fruit of good action and find, before the strict Judge, the rewards of eternal peace.

I, Paschal, bishop of the Catholic Church.

Given at the Lateran through the hand of John, cardinal-deacon and librarian of the Holy Roman Church, in the year 1106 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and the sixth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Paschal II.  
[Note: [Col. 0175D] The chronological indications are corrupt. JAFFÉ.]

CLXVI. Privilege for the bishopric of Pistoia. (14 November 1105.)

[ZACHARIA, *Anecdota medii aevi*. Turin, 1755, folio, p. 225.]

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother ILDIPRAND, bishop of Pistoia, and to his successors canonically promoted for ever.

Just as no effect is to be granted to those who ask what is unjust, so the petition of those who desire what is lawful is not to be delayed. Therefore, brother Ildiprand, beloved in Christ, assenting to your just petitions, we strengthen by the authority of the Apostolic See the holy Church of Pistoia over which, by God’s authority, you preside. We decree that the diocese of the bishopric of Pistoia, just as its boundaries were defined by the privilege of our predecessor of holy memory, Urban, shall remain in the right and jurisdiction of the bishop of Pistoia without anyone’s molestation or disturbance.

Within these boundaries are established the following chapels and churches: the chapel of Capraria; the chapel of the Hospital of Rosaria; the parish church of Massa; the chapel of Vincio; of Bucuniano; of Castelnuovo; of St Martin on Mount Culli; the chapel of Vacazano; the chapel at Verruca; the chapel of St Mary Magdalene at Colle; the chapel of Galciano; of Venua, concerning which the judgment of our aforesaid predecessor Urban was pronounced after a third and fourth hearing; the chapel of the Hospital of Fanano; the chapel of Prato del Vescovo; of Rotie; of Certaria; of Monte Acuto; of Insula; and the chapel of St Saviour situated at Prato, with its parish churches. We also confirm to the holy Church of Pistoia the estate called Pavana within the county of Pistoia, together with the castle of Sambuce built within the estate’s boundaries, [Col. 0177B] just as it is known to have been restored, after a claim long examined by many judges and legal experts, through the judgment of Bernard, our vicar and priest of the Apostolic See, from the venerable Countess Matilda, daughter of blessed Peter, into your hands and those of your fellow brethren.

Furthermore, no one shall ever presume to alienate from the right of the Church and the use of the clergy the tithes of Monte Murto, Prato, St Paul, Cholonica, Monte Magno, the estate of Lamporecchio, Creti, and Spanarecchio, which the diligence of your religious community has recovered from lay hands. We command the same concerning the other estates and properties which now remain in the possession of the Church of Pistoia: namely, the estates of Lizzano, Mammiano, Cavinana, Batoni, [Col. 0177C] Saturnana, Brandellio, Gropula, Piscia, Vinacciano, Tobiana, Publica, Silva Mortua, Vizule, Pezzanese, Celeri, and the land situated within the bishopric of Bologna which the men of the valley of Biderla held; and the estate of Spallioro.

Moreover, whatever the Church of Pistoia now justly possesses, or may hereafter be able justly and canonically to acquire through the generosity of princes or the offerings of the faithful, shall remain secure and unimpaired for you and your successors. Therefore we decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb that Church, take away its possessions, retain what has been taken away, diminish them, or harass it with reckless vexations; rather, let all be preserved intact for the benefit of you and the clergy. We also forbid that, when you or any of your successors have been summoned to the Lord, anyone whatsoever, against the will of the clergy of your church, should dare to take away, plunder, or alienate the property either of bishops or of the church. If, therefore, hereafter any archbishop, etc. Amen.

Written through the hand of Raynerius, regional scrivener and notary of the sacred palace.

I, Paschal, bishop of the Catholic Church, have subscribed.

Given at the Portico of Blessed Peter through the hand of John, cardinal-deacon and librarian of the Holy Roman Church, on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of December, in the thirteenth indiction, in the year 1105 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and the seventh year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Paschal II.

CLXVII. To Eustace, abbot of St Nicholas.—Privilege of that abbey. (18 November 1105.)

[MANSI, *Concilia*, XX, 1051.]

[Col. 0178A]

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son in Christ EUSTACE, abbot of the church of St Nicholas, greeting and apostolic blessing.

Almost the whole world knows that, in the time of our predecessor of holy memory Victor III, the body of Blessed Nicholas was brought from the lands across the sea of the Greeks to the city of Bari. Our predecessor Urban II reverently laid that body in the lower crypt where it is now kept with fitting reverence, and consecrated an altar above it in honour [Col. 0178B] of the Lord. It was requested and is said to have been granted that the basilica of Blessed Nicholas to be built in that place should thereafter be held especially under the protection of the Apostolic See.

Since, therefore, by the Lord’s gift, that basilica has now been completed with suitable construction, on ground belonging to the public right, granted by a charter of Duke Roger, we receive under the protection of the Apostolic See that house, soon by God’s authority to become a church, at the request of our son Bohemond, brother of that same duke and now lord of the city of Bari. By the text of this present privilege, therefore, we establish by apostolic authority that whatever lands or goods have already been given from their own right to the aforesaid church of St Nicholas, or may hereafter be given or offered to it, whether by our aforesaid son Roger, duke of Apulia, Calabria, and Sicily by the grace of Blessed Peter and ourselves, or by his aforementioned brother Bohemond, now prince [Col. 0178C] of Antioch, or by other faithful of Christ, shall always remain secure, undisturbed, and unimpaired.

Therefore we decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb that church, take away its goods, retain what has been taken away, diminish them, or harass it with reckless vexations; rather, let all be preserved intact for the use of the clergy and the poor. We grant you and your successors authority to correct the faults of the clergy, with due charity and severity, without opposition from the bishop. But if any graver complaint arises against you, it shall be reserved for the hearing of ourselves or our successors.

Nor do we permit any archbishop or bishop to restrain that church or its abbot, without the knowledge of the Roman pontiff, either by excommunication or interdict, so that this venerable place, distinguished by the body of so great a confessor, may continue under the guardianship and protection of the Roman pontiff, just as through the Roman pontiff it first received the beginnings of its consecration.

If, indeed, hereafter any archbishop or bishop, emperor or king, prince or duke, count, viscount, captain, *stratigos* [Greek στρατηγός, “military commander”], judge, castald, or any ecclesiastical or secular person, etc., as in certain other letters.

Written through the hand of Raynerius, regional scrivener and notary of the sacred palace.

[Col. 0179A] I, Paschal, bishop of the Catholic Church.

Given at the Portico of Blessed Peter, Rome, on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of December, through the hand of John, cardinal-deacon and librarian of the Holy Roman Church, in the fourteenth indiction, in the year 1106 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and the sixth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Paschal II.

CLXVIII. To the whole clergy of Gaul.—He recounts Werner’s invasion of the Apostolic See. (26 November 1105.)

[MANSI, *Concilia*, XX, 1085.]

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the bishops, abbots, princes, knights, and all [Col. 0179B] the faithful throughout all Gaul, greeting and apostolic blessing.

We do not wish what has occurred among us in these times to remain unknown to your brotherhood. A certain Werner, servant of the German kingdom, came into the neighbourhood of the city of Rome, summoned by certain men of treacherous mind. Some of these outside the city had seized, through the hand of the former king, the right or revenues of the Apostolic See; others within the city, because they could not obtain the offices or familiar favour of our court, had resolved to disregard God and faith in God.

A certain newcomer priest of the city of Rome joined himself to companions of this kind—a man concerning whom we do not know either who he is, where he is from, or by whom he has hitherto been ordained.  
[Note: [Col. 0179D] Therefore not the abbot of Farfa, as Urspergensis has it.]

This eminent person, said to be full of necromantic deceits, they introduced into the Lateran Church when our faithful people, on account of the Truce of God, were wholly abstaining from arms; and, gathering the remnants of the Wibertine dregs, they most perniciously imposed upon him the name of bishop. At that time we remained in the portico of Blessed Peter, on account of the dedication of the Apostolic basilica, which by God’s grace we had solemnly performed the preceding day in a most celebrated assembly. When, however, we returned into the city on the next day, [Col. 0179D] that monster fled shamefully from the city; where he went we do not know.  
[Note: [Col. 0179D] Urspergensis is shown false, since he places this masked pontiff’s assumption at the time when Paschal was staying at Benevento. [Col. 0180D]]

We now briefly inform your brotherhood of everything, lest you should in any way be deceived by hearing of such impostures, or be moved from your steadfastness. Through God’s grace we remain honourably and safely within the city, and in this crowd we have lost none of our companions. Nor did the sedition of Korah, Dathan, and Abiram take the people away from Moses; nor did the pride of the exalted angel who wished to be equal to God diminish God’s majesty. May that same majesty protect you in all things and grant you happily to tread underfoot the lion and the dragon.

Given at the Lateran, on the sixth day before the Kalends of October [December].

CLXIX. Paschal’s reply to the letter of Otto, bishop-elect of Bamberg, in which he stated that he had received the bishopric from the emperor but did not wish to remain in it unless he were invested and consecrated by the pope. (1105.)

[MANSI, *Concilia*, XX, 1044.]

[Col. 0180A]

PASCHAL, servant of the servants of God, to OTTO, beloved brother and bishop-elect of the Church of Bamberg, greeting and apostolic blessing.

“A wise son makes his mother glad” (Proverbs 10). Your actions and your counsel show you to be a prudent man. We have therefore judged it fitting to honour you and aid your advancement. Accordingly, doubting nothing of our goodwill, come to us as soon as you can. For we are certain that divine wisdom knows how to make good use even of evil men.  
[Note: [Col. 0180D] Otto afterwards went to the pontiff and was consecrated by him. See Letter 184.]

CLXX. He commits the case of Odo, abbot of St Quentin, to the bishops of Chartres and Paris. (1105.)

[*Gallia Christiana*, X, Instrumenta, 249.]

[Col. 0180B]

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother, the bishop of Beauvais, greeting and apostolic blessing.

It is the office of the priesthood to love and cherish religious men and, according to the power granted to it, defend them from the attacks of the wicked. But you not only do not love the brethren of Blessed Quentin dwelling at Beauvais [read perhaps: “not” is to be added], but, as I have now heard, you willingly permit them to be vexed and troubled by the unlawful presumption of certain persons. Do not doubt that this certainly concerns the peril of your soul, unless you strive promptly to correct it by amendment [Col. 0180C] and to provide more carefully for their peace.

Therefore we command you wholly to restrain the clergy of the Church of Beauvais from molesting those brethren, both in spiritual and temporal matters; otherwise, the sword of Blessed Peter will be drawn both against their audacity and against your negligence. We also command that the same church of Blessed Quentin, while preserving the reverence due to you, be administered and ordered according to the counsel of our brethren and fellow bishops Ivo of Chartres and G. of Paris. Furthermore, whatever has been done by that same brother G. throughout the bishopric of Beauvais, where by God’s grace he canonically presided, whether in that church or in the others, we decree shall remain valid and unshaken. As for the man who is said to preside over the aforesaid church of St Quentin, we wish his case to be considered by the counsel of the aforementioned brethren and [Col. 0180D] brought to its proper conclusion.

CLXXI. He forbids Abbot A[damo] and the monks of St Denis “to approach bishops other than Galo, bishop of Paris, without his permission, in order to receive the sacraments.” (1152.)

[DUCHESNE, *Hist. Franc. Scrip.*, IV, 763.]

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother A., abbot, and to the monks of St Denis, greeting and apostolic blessing.

[Col. 0181A] From the report of our fellow brother Galo, bishop of Paris, we have learned that, without his permission, you approach various bishops to receive holy oil and chrism, and for the ordinations of your monks or clergy; or summon them to your monastery for the celebration of those sacraments; and that you impose penances for crimes upon laymen. These practices are indeed greatly contrary to the sacred canons. Privileges, moreover, are granted for no wicked or evil purpose; they are granted to anyone for edification, not for the destruction of the canons.

Since, therefore, the aforesaid brother Bishop Galo, your bishop, is held by God’s grace to be good and Catholic, and grants the aforesaid sacraments freely and without wrongdoing, we forbid you, without his permission, to approach other bishops to receive those same sacraments; and we prohibit all archbishops and bishops from administering them to you.

CLXXII. Charter confirming the churches held by the canons of Langres. (Circa 1105.)

[*Gallia Christiana*, IV, 153.]

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother ROBERT, bishop of Langres, and his successors canonically promoted for ever.

It is fitting for us to grant assent to just vows and give ear to just petitions, since, although unworthy, by the Lord’s ordering we are seen to have been placed as guardians and heralds of justice upon the lofty watchtower [Col. 0181C] of the princes of the apostles, Peter and Paul. Therefore, brother Robert, most beloved in Christ, assenting to your just petitions, we strengthen by the authority of the Apostolic See the holy Church of Langres, over which by God’s authority you preside; and we decree that the city of Langres, with all things belonging to it both outside and within, whether in church, county, or all its appurtenances, shall be possessed in perpetuity by you and your lawful successors.

We also confirm to the right and jurisdiction of your church the two abbeys in the castle of Dijon: that of St Benignus, which belongs to monks; and that of St Stephen, which belongs to canons. Likewise the abbeys of Bèze, Molesme, Melun, St Michael, St Seine, [Col. 0181D] and St John of the Meadow. Also the abbeys of canons: one in the castle of Châtillon, and the other called that of the Holy Twins. Likewise, the abbeys of St Peter at Polungio and St Mary of Red Mount.

Furthermore, we confirm in the perpetual possession of that same church the castle of Gurgeium with all its appurtenances; the castle of Châtillon; Tylecastrum; the castle of Mount Salgion; the castle of Confluens; the castle of Fons-Vennae; the castle of Choscolum; the castle of Graneyum; the castle of Sala; Barrum on the Aube; likewise Barrum on the Seine; the castle of Chacennaium; the castle of Saxonis-Fontem; the castle of Tonnerre; the castle of Blaseium; in the bishopric of Besançon, the castle of Acrimont and the castle of Bourbon; [Col. 0182A] in the bishopric of Autun, the castle of Duisme and the castle of Grinon; and, near Grinon, the castle of the duke of Burgundy.

Whatever further towns, possessions, and estates your church presently possesses, and whatever it may also acquire in the future through the lawful gifts of the faithful, shall remain secure and unimpaired for you and your successors. Therefore we decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb that church, take from it its possessions, retain what has been taken away, diminish them, or harass it with reckless vexations; rather, let all things be kept whole for the benefit of the clergy and the poor.

If, indeed, hereafter any archbishop or bishop, emperor or king, prince or duke, count, viscount, judge, or any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowing this text of our ordinance, should rashly attempt to act against it, then, after a second or third warning, unless he makes proper amends by suitable satisfaction, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and honour; let him know himself liable before divine judgment for the iniquity committed; let him be excluded from the most sacred body and blood of God and our Redeemer Jesus Christ; and let him be strictly subject at the final judgment. But on all who uphold what is just for that Church, may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that they may receive here the fruit of good action and find, before the strict Judge, the rewards of eternal peace. Amen.

CLXXIII. He commands Gisla, abbess of Remiremont, under penalty of excommunication, to cease harassing the monks of Chaumousey. (Between 1102 and 1106.)

[MARTENE, *Thesaurus Anecdotorum*, III, 1178.]

[Col. 0182C]

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved daughter GISLA, abbess of Remiremont, and her sisters, greeting and apostolic blessing.

For the brethren of Chaumousey, behold, we have now sent letters to you for the second time. Since they are prepared, according to the judgment we have pronounced, to prove by oath through suitable persons that the foundation of their new monastery on the site where it was built was made peacefully; that it remained for ten years without a lawful claim from the people of Remiremont; [Col. 0182D] and that the giver of the site or his predecessors possessed the land for thirty years without legal claim, we command your affection by the authority of this letter henceforth to bring no claim against those brethren concerning the aforesaid land. We command the same concerning the portion of the parish church of St Mary—a portion which, in the presence of your messengers, we have learned that those brethren possessed there. Otherwise, if their outcry concerning this complaint again reaches us, we shall exclude you from the thresholds of the Church.

Given on the day before the Ides of April.

CLXXIV. Bull for the monastery of St Peter of Chartres. (6 January 1106.)

[*Gallia Christiana*, VIII, 311.]

[Col. 0183A]

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son WILLIAM, abbot of the venerable monastery of the holy apostles Peter and Paul, situated near Chartres, and to his successors regularly promoted for ever.

A devout request ought to be fulfilled by the accomplishment of the will that follows it, so that the sincerity of devotion may shine forth commendably and the requested advantage may undoubtedly gain force. Since, therefore, your belovedness has fled to the haven of the Apostolic See and with due devotion sought its protection, we mercifully assent to your petition and receive under the protection of the Apostolic See the monastery of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul of Chartres, over which, by the Lord’s authority, you preside, together with all its appurtenances.

Therefore, by the text of this present privilege, we establish by apostolic authority that whatever estates and goods now belong to that monastery through the grant of pontiffs, the generosity of kings and princes, or the lawful offerings of other faithful people, or may belong to it in the future, shall remain secure and unimpaired for you and your successors. Among them, the following have been thought fit to be recorded by their proper names: the churches of St Hilary, St Leobinus, Campifauni, Manuvillaris, Mitanvillaris, Verni, Alona, Boasvilla, Reclainvillaris, Imonisvilla, [Col. 0183C] Germenonisvilla, Ursivilla, Alpedani, and the royal chapel—while, in those matters which pertain to the bishop’s own order alone, his right is preserved according to custom.

Likewise, six altars: the altar of Bruerolles, Armentières, Roheria, Buxet, Cruciaco, and Castellariis, as established by our venerable brother Ivo, bishop, to be held freely and peacefully, without any further redemption payment, free from synod and *circada*, from every customary due and disturbance, and from every exaction of jurisdiction by the priests serving in the aforesaid places. Excepted are those matters which pertain to their own order, concerning which those priests shall answer to the bishop or archdeacon.

We also confirm to you the church of Giziaco and the church of Fontanet in the district of Vexin, [Col. 0183D] in the diocese of Rouen, just as they have hitherto been freely held by your monastery. And we confirm the six prebends in the Church of Blessed Mary at Chartres, to be possessed as freely and wholly as they were granted to your monastery by Rainfred, bishop of Chartres, of good memory.

Therefore we decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the same monastery, etc. We further add that the same monastery with its appurtenances, and its monks, shall be secure from every harassment of secular service and removed from every burden of worldly oppression, so that, diligent in the observance of holy religion, they may remain at peace by the Lord’s gift. If, therefore, any ecclesiastical or secular person should knowingly act against this text of our ordinance, etc.

[Col. 0184A] This privilege was read and approved in the chapter of Blessed Mary at Chartres, in the presence of Bishop Ivo, Dean Ernald, and others.

Written through the hand of Raynerius, regional secretary and notary of the sacred palace.

I, Paschal, bishop of the Catholic Church.

Given at the Lateran through the hand of John, cardinal-deacon and librarian of the Holy Roman Church, on the eighth day before the Ides of January, in the fourteenth indiction, in the year 1106 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and the seventh year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Paschal II.

CLXXV. Bull for the monastery of St Valery. (12 March 1106.)

[MABILLON, *Annales Benedictini*, V, appendix, 679.]

[Col. 0184B] PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son in Christ LAMBERT, abbot of the venerable monastery of St Valery, situated in the county of Ponthieu, and to his successors regularly promoted for ever.

Just as no effect is to be granted to those who ask what is unjust, so the petition of those who desire what is lawful is not to be delayed. Therefore, son Lambert, most beloved in Christ, assenting to your just petitions, we receive under the protection of the Apostolic See the monastery of Blessed Valery, over which by God’s authority you preside, and everything belonging to it. That monastery is known to have been built by the late Count Hugh in the place called Leuconaus.

Therefore, by the text of this present privilege, we establish by apostolic authority that whatever estates and goods that same Count Hugh or other faithful people are known to have bestowed upon the monastery from their own right, and whatever may hereafter lawfully be given or offered through the grants of pontiffs, the generosity of princes, or the offerings of the faithful, shall remain secure and unimpaired for you and your successors. The monastery itself also, according to the enactments of our predecessors, shall always remain under the jurisdiction of the holy Roman Church.

No priest may exercise authority in that monastery or harass its goods under any pretext. We wholly forbid public masses to be celebrated in the monastery or processions to be held there without the will of the abbot and brethren, lest [Col. 0184D] any occasion for popular assemblies be given in the retreats of the servants of God.

Therefore we decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the same monastery, take away or diminish its possessions, or harass it with reckless vexations; rather, let all be preserved intact for the benefit in every way of those for whose maintenance and governance they were granted.

You shall receive chrism, holy oil, consecrations of altars and basilicas, and the ordinations of monks to be promoted to sacred orders from the bishop in whose diocese you are, provided that he enjoys the favour and communion of the Apostolic See and is willing to administer these things freely and without wrongdoing. Otherwise, you may approach whatever Catholic bishop you wish and receive from him [Col. 0185A] the sacraments of consecration, provided that, supported by the authority of the Apostolic See, he grants what is requested.

The adjacent parish, together with the church of Blessed Martin and its priest, shall remain in the liberty which it has hitherto possessed. If, indeed, any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowing this text of our ordinance, should rashly attempt to act against it, then, after a second or third warning, unless he makes proper amends by suitable satisfaction, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and honour; let him know himself liable before divine judgment for the iniquity committed; let him be excluded from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord, Redeemer Jesus Christ; and let him be subject to strict vengeance at the final judgment.

But upon all who uphold what is just for that place, may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus [Col. 0185B] Christ, so that they may receive here the fruit of good action and find, before the strict Judge, the rewards of eternal peace. Amen, amen, amen.

I, Paschal, bishop of the Catholic Church, have subscribed. Fare well.

Given at Benevento through the hand of John, cardinal-deacon and librarian of the Holy Roman Church, on the fourth day before the Ides of March, in the fourteenth indiction, in the year 1106 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and the seventh year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Paschal II.

CLXXVI. To Bertramnus, prior of St Faith at Sélestat.—He confirms the goods and privileges of that monastery. (12 March 1106.)

[WURTWEIN, *Nova Subsidia diplomatica*, Heidelberg, 1781, octavo, vol. VII, p. 5.]

[Col. 0185C]

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons BERTRAMNUS, prior of the cell of St Faith situated in Alsace in the town of Sélestat, and his brethren, greeting and apostolic blessing.

It is fitting readily to grant consent to religious desires, so that faithful devotion may obtain a swift result. Therefore, in accordance with your petition, attending to the religious desire of the illustrious Duke Frederick and his brothers, we grant effect to their devotion. We decree that the offering which, by the Lord’s inspiration, they presented to the blessed martyr Faith and her monastery of Conques shall always remain valid and unshaken.

Accordingly, the cell in the town of Sélestat, distinguished by the name of the Holy Sepulchre, where the commemoration of the blessed martyr Faith is also solemnly observed, shall always remain under the right and direction of the monastery of Conques, just as it was entrusted by the aforesaid Duke Frederick of good memory and his brothers, with a specification of fixed boundaries, as a grant of possessions or possessors. Indeed, no advocate for that cell shall be appointed other than the person whom the abbot of Conques, by his free discretion, shall set over it for the provision of the brethren.

Moreover, the church of that place, together with its churchyard, shall be free from every enemy attack and exempt from the oppression of bishops or episcopal officers. We also decree that its burial ground shall be wholly free, so that no one may obstruct the devotion and final wish of those who have decided to be buried there, unless they are excommunicated.

Furthermore, whatever estates and goods have already been offered or granted from their own right by the aforementioned prince or his brothers, or may hereafter, by the Lord’s gift, be offered or granted, shall always remain peaceful and free, immune from every yoke of secular lords just as they are known to have remained during the lifetime of those princes. Therefore we decree that no person may rashly disturb that Church, take away or diminish its possessions, or harass it with reckless vexations; rather, let all be preserved intact for the benefit in every way [Col. 0186B] of those for whose maintenance and governance they were granted.

If, indeed, any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowing this document of our ordinance, should rashly attempt to act against it, then, after a second or third warning, unless he makes proper amends by suitable satisfaction, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and honour; let him know himself liable before divine judgment for the iniquity committed; let him be excluded from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord, Redeemer Jesus Christ; and let him be subject to strict vengeance at the final judgment. But upon all who uphold what is just for that place, may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that they may receive here the fruit of good action and find, before the strict Judge, the rewards of eternal peace. Amen, amen, amen.

[Col. 0186C] Given at Viterbo [Note: [Col. 0185D] It should read “Benevento.” JAFFÉ.] through the hand of John, cardinal-deacon and librarian of the Holy Roman Church, on the fourth day before the Ides of March, in the fourteenth indiction, in the year 1106 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and the seventh year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Paschal II.

CLXXVII. To Anselm, archbishop of Canterbury.—He congratulates him on the peace made with the king. (23 March 1106.)

[MANSI, *Concilia*, XX, 1003.]

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother ANSELM, archbishop of Canterbury, greeting and blessing.

We give thanks to the Lord of mercies, in whose hand the hearts of kings are turned, that the gracious condescension of almighty God has inclined the king of England to obedience to the Apostolic See. We believe that this was brought about through the merit of your charity and the persistence of your prayers, so that heavenly mercy might look upon, in this matter, that people over whom your solicitude presides. And know that our yielding so far, both to the king and to those who appear liable, was done with such affection and compassion that we might be able to raise up those who had fallen. For one who stands and does not extend a hand to raise one who has fallen will never lift him up unless he too bends down. Yet, although bending seems to approach a fall, it nevertheless does not lose the uprightness of its stance.

But you, venerable and most dear brother in Christ, we absolve from that prohibition—or, as you believe, excommunication—which you understand to have been issued by our predecessor Pope Urban of holy memory against investitures or homages. [Note: Col. 0187D: At the councils of Clermont and Rome.] You, moreover, shall receive, with the satisfaction which, through the common envoys William and Baldwin—[Note: Monks of Canterbury, envoys of St Anselm.]—men faithful and truthful, we communicate to you, and, with the Lord’s help, shall absolve by the authority delegated from us those who have either received investitures, blessed persons invested, or performed homages. You shall either bless them yourself or order them to be blessed by whomsoever you wish, unless perhaps you find in them some other matter for which they should be excluded from sacred offices.

You shall, however, withdraw from the abbot of Ely participation in your commission so long as he presumes to retain the abbey which, despite the prohibition pronounced by our own mouth and heard by him in person, he presumed through a repeated investiture to seize [reading uncertain: *per ... repetitam investituram*]. If, moreover, any persons hereafter assume ecclesiastical prelacies apart from investitures, even if they have rendered homage to the king, they are by no means to be barred from the grace of blessing on that account, until, through the grace of almighty God, the royal heart may be softened by the rains of your preaching to abandon this practice.

Furthermore, regarding the bishops who, as you know, brought us a false report, our heart has been moved more vehemently [variant: “is more grievously burdened”], because they not only injured us, but deceived the souls of many simple people and stirred the king against charity toward the Apostolic See. Therefore, with the Lord’s help, we shall not allow their offence to go unpunished. But because the entreaty of our son the king presses us more earnestly on their behalf, you shall not deny even to them participation in your communion. Certainly, you shall absolve from sins and penances, according to our promise, the king and his wife, and those nobles who, by our command, have laboured and will endeavour to labour with the king [variant: “around the king”] in this affair; you will learn their names from the recommendation of the aforesaid William.

Therefore, since almighty God has granted you to make progress in this reform within the kingdom of England, for His honour and that of His Church, let your brotherhood henceforth strive, with such gentleness, prudent dispensation, and foresight toward the king and princes, that what has not yet been sufficiently corrected may, with the help of the Lord our God, be corrected through the diligence of your solicitude. In this matter, understand our support to be so present to your charity that what you loose we shall loose, and what you bind we shall bind. We have committed to your judgment the case of the bishop [William] of Rouen and the interdict pronounced as justice required. What you remit, we remit. May heavenly graciousness preserve your brotherhood unharmed for many years.

Given on the tenth day before the Kalends of April [23 March].

## CLXXVIII. To William, bishop of Rouen.—William had been suspended: the pope writes to him that, out of regard for Anselm, who intercedes for him, he will remit whatever Anselm remits. (1106, 28 March.)

[MANSI, *Concilia*, XX, 1062.]

[Col. 0188A]

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother WILLIAM, bishop of Rouen, greeting and apostolic blessing.

Although the character of your case greatly burdens our patience, nevertheless, out of reverence for our brother the bishop of Canterbury and affection for our son William, bearer of the present letter, who have interceded most earnestly with us for you, we are moved toward you by paternal kindness. We have therefore committed your case to that same brother, the bishop of Canterbury, so that we may remit whatever he remits. This is, indeed, with the intention and condition that you dismiss from your household the evil counsellors at whose instigation you incurred many wrongful acts.

Given at Benevento, on the fifth day before the Kalends of April [28 March].

## CLXXIX. To William, archbishop of Rouen. (1106, 30 March.)

[MANSI, *Concilia*, XX, 1070.]

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother WILLIAM, archbishop of Rouen, greeting and apostolic blessing.

We have ordered Turold, bishop of Bayeux, to appear before our fellow-brother, the bishop of Lyons, on the coming Kalends of October, for the determination of his case. But because we have heard that he has not yet been reinstated, we have extended his reprieve until the coming Easter. Then let the same case be entirely concluded before our fellow-brother Anselm, archbishop of Canterbury, acting in our stead, with a full report to be made to us; or let the bishop himself appear before us together with his adversaries.

Given at Salerno, on the third day before the Kalends of April [30 March].

## CLXXX. To R[uthard], bishop of Mainz. (1106, 31 March.)

[MANSI, *Concilia*, XX, 1091.]

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the venerable R., bishop of Mainz, greeting and apostolic blessing.

Your brotherhood’s prudence knows how to provide for the peace of Church and kingdom, for the ordering of the churches, for the concerns of our party, and for the general deliberation that must be held. Therefore we have judged it fitting, and after much consultation have determined, that we ought to hold a synodal assembly with you on the coming Ides of October. Accordingly, by the present letters we admonish both you, most dear brother, and all the suffragans of the Church of Mainz that, having summoned the abbots of your dioceses who seem most worthy, and having also summoned such clerical persons as are needed for the deliberations of the council, you should take care, setting aside every excuse, to meet with us south of the Alps at the aforesaid time, so that, with the Lord’s aid, the causes of schisms having been removed from the midst, the wholeness of peace may be restored to Church and kingdom.

Given on the eleventh day before the Kalends of April [22 March].

## CLXXXI. To Guy, bishop of Pavia, and the clergy of Pavia. (1106, 29 April.)

[ROBOLINI, *Notizie appartenenti alla storia della sua patria*, Pavia, 1823, 8vo, vol. III, p. 225.]

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother GUY, bishop, and to the clergy of the church of Pavia, greeting and apostolic blessing.

Both episcopal solicitude and clerical charity require that scandals arising in the Church be dealt with peacefully and that quarrels be removed with every effort. Yet you have kindled—or through negligence permitted to be kindled—by the devil’s envy, from a very small spark, such great masses of fire that, over the offering of blessed water, three men have been killed and blood shed; and, even over the sacrament of baptism, the corpses of two baptized persons have been laid low. We consider it tedious to recount more concerning the robberies; but by repeated command we order that they be fully repaired.

Your own prudence recognizes with us how contrary all this is to the Church and how unworthy of you; nor can it readily be thought right that these matters should pass unexamined and unpunished. For the monks of St Peter have presumed upon nothing new. By ancient tradition and by the more ancient privileges of the Holy Apostolic See, they have the right to receive from any Catholic bishop the consecrations of churches, the ordinations of monks or clerics, oil and chrism; to celebrate baptism at the Paschal solemnity through clerics subject to the monastery; and, despite episcopal opposition, to retain the obedience of clerics subject to the monastery. We will that the monastery retain its liberty together with its other immunities, which were conferred through the provision of the Roman Church because of the misconduct of bishops. Those who henceforth presume in such matters shall, as despisers of the Apostolic See, certainly be punished by its indignation.

Given at Cassino, on the third day before the Kalends of May [29 April].

## CLXXXII. Privilege for the monastery of St Saviour and St Julia of Brescia. (1107, 11 May.)

[MARGARINI, *Bullarium Casinense*, II, 124.]

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his most dear daughter in the Lord ERMINGARD, abbess of the monastery of the Lord Saviour and of St Julia, virgin and martyr, called the New [Monastery], founded by the most devout Queen Ansa within the city of Brescia; to you and your successors in perpetuity.

By the Lord’s ordering, we are seen to have been raised to the governance of the Apostolic See so that, by His grant, we ought to increase religion and provide protection to its servants. Therefore, beloved daughter in the Lord, Abbess Ermengard, assenting to your petitions, we receive the monastery of the Blessed Saviour, over which you preside by God’s gift, just as we know it was received by our predecessors into the guardianship and protection of the Apostolic See.

We decree that no ecclesiastical or secular person may, without the abbess’s permission, exercise any jurisdiction or hold any court in any places belonging to that monastery; or exact fodder-dues, lodging-dues, river-dues, requisitions, or any public services. Wherever the abbess wishes within those places, she may establish or build a market without anyone’s opposition, and may exercise jurisdiction over servants or free persons. Nor do we permit any bishop to exercise any authority in the aforesaid monastery, and we forbid public masses to be celebrated there against the abbess’s will.

We therefore confirm to the same venerable monastery the possessions of earlier times: namely, Sirmione, with the churches of the Lord Saviour, St Martin, and St Vitus the martyr; Cessianico, with the church of St Julia the martyr; Nuvolaria, with the church of St Lawrence; Berciago, with the churches of St Zeno and St Stephen; Barbada, with the churches of St Mary and St Blaise; Calvatone, with the churches of St Mary and St Julia; Liconia, with the church of St Mary; the village of Maione, with the church of St Alexander; Gaseliago, with the church of St Martin the confessor; Miliarina, with the church of St Julia; and Sermida.

Furthermore, whatever estates or possessions now belong, through the lawful offerings of Catholic kings or other faithful persons, or may hereafter come to belong, by the Lord’s grant, shall remain secure and inviolate to you and your successors. We decree, therefore, that it shall be lawful for no person at all rashly to disturb this monastery, take away its possessions, retain what has been taken, diminish them, or harass it with reckless vexations; but that all things shall be preserved intact for the use and benefit in every respect of those for whose support and governance they were granted. We do not permit tithes and first-fruits granted to your monastery by the authority of our predecessors henceforth to be usurped by bishops or their officers.

You shall receive chrism, holy oil, consecrations of altars or churches, and ordinations of an abbess, monks, or clerics to be promoted to sacred orders, from whichever Catholic bishop you prefer. Upon the death of you, the present abbess of that place, or of any of your successors, no person shall be set over it by any craft of deception or violence except one whom the sisters, by common consent, or the sounder part of the sisters’ counsel, elect in the fear of God and according to the Rule of St Benedict. She shall certainly have authority to establish chapels and churches wherever she wishes on lands belonging to the aforesaid monastery.

Moreover, we confirm in every respect for the sisters’ use the fisheries belonging to that monastery, so that no one may have power to invade or alienate them on any pretext. Therefore, beloved daughters in Christ, in order that you may always be judged more worthy of this favour, strive always to have the fear of God in your hearts, so that, the freer you are from secular persons, the more earnestly you may strive to please God with all the powers of mind and soul.

If any archbishop or bishop, emperor or king, prince or duke, count, viscount, judge, or any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowing this charter of our constitution, should rashly attempt to act against it, then, having been admonished a second or third time, if he does not make fitting satisfaction, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and honour; let him know himself guilty before divine judgment for the wrong he has committed; let him be cut off from the most sacred Body and Blood of God and of our Redeemer Jesus Christ; and let him be subject to strict vengeance at the last judgment. But upon all who preserve what is right for that place may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that they may here receive the fruit of good action and, before the strict Judge, find the rewards of eternal peace. Amen, amen, amen.

Written by the hand of Raynerius, regional scrivener and notary of the sacred palace.

I, Paschal, bishop of the Catholic Church, have subscribed.

Given at the Lateran, through the hand of John, deacon-cardinal and librarian of the Holy Roman Church, on the fifth Ides of May [11 May], in the fourteenth indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1107 [1106], in the seventh year of the pontificate of Lord Paschal II, pope.

## CLXXXIII. To R[uthard], archbishop of Mainz.—He commends Otto, bishop of Bamberg, whom he himself consecrated. (Year given as 1006.)

[MANSI, *Concilia*, XX, 1091.]

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to R., archbishop of Mainz, greeting and apostolic blessing.

We judge that your prudence knows well how familiar the Church of Bamberg has been to the Apostolic See from the beginning of its foundation.
