We therefore thought it fitting that we should receive with the favour due to that earlier intimacy our venerable brother O., elect of that church, when he came to us. Furthermore, because that same Church has now for a long time lacked the care of episcopal office, and because, as a consequence of the former schism, very few in the German lands exercise episcopal office, we conferred upon that brother, at the petition of the Church itself—when he had come to us through many dangers—and with the consent and unanimous decision of all the brothers present with us, by the Lord’s gift, the hand of episcopal blessing, while preserving, of course, the reverence due to your metropolitan see.

Accordingly, as we send him back to you with the gracious favour of our goodwill, we commend him to your brotherhood by the present letter, so that, as he is judged more closely attached to the Apostolic See, so he may be held dearer among you.

Given at the Lateran, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of June [21 May].

## CLXXXIV. To the clergy and people of Bamberg.—He commends Otto to them as bishop. (1106, May.)

[MANSI, *Concilia*, XX, 999.]

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the clergy and people of Bamberg, greeting and apostolic blessing.

Although we might not otherwise know how greatly the Church of Bamberg has been bound, from the very beginning of its establishment, by a debt of affection to the Apostolic See, the statement in your letters makes this clear. The venerable brother Otto, elect of your church, is known to have steadfastly maintained and still to maintain this debt of affection, since he has hastened through so many and such great dangers to visit the Apostolic See. We have therefore received him with the affection of due kindness and, in accordance with your beloved wish, have, as though by the hands of St Peter and without prejudice to metropolitan right, ordained him by God’s grace as your bishop.

Accordingly, as we send him to govern your church under cover of the present letter, we exhort you with full affection to love him and with full humility to venerate him. For we trust that he will be a guardian of ecclesiastical discipline and a watchful provider for your salvation. Therefore obey him with diligent service, and through him win heavenly favour for yourselves. Always preserve inviolate in all things the integrity of the Catholic faith; always cleave with more devoted loyalty to the Apostolic See, so that through communion with it, freed from every contagion, we may deserve, by the Lord’s grant, happily to reach the harbour of eternal salvation.

## CLXXXV. He praises the parishioners of the church of St Frigdian of Lucca because they obey the canons. (1106, 23 May.)

[BALUZE, *Miscellanea*, ed. Lucca, I, vol. IV, p. 584.]

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the parishioners of St Frigdian, greeting and apostolic blessing.

We rejoice greatly at your devotion because, as we have learned from the report of our venerable son Rotho, you diligently love the church of Blessed Frigdian and the brothers serving God there; you enrich that place by contributions from your goods; and you more willingly obey their admonitions for the salvation of your souls. Since this grace of the Lord has likewise been bestowed upon you through mercy, we give thanks both to Him and to you, asking that He may perfect this grace in you and render you the rewards of eternal recompense for it.

Therefore, most dear children in the Lord, we exhort you always to remain more steadfast in the purpose of this devotion, turning over in your heart that saying of the Lord when He spoke to His disciples: “He who honours you honours me; and he who touches you touches the pupil of my eye.” For His mercy will accompany your good vow and good purpose to its fulfilment. May He Himself teach you by His anointing what we say; may He Himself bless you; and, through the merits of Blessed Frigdian, may He mercifully absolve from sins and bring to eternal life both you and others who, through the grace of divine charity, give their help to those same brothers.

Given at the Lateran, on the tenth day before the Kalends of June [23 May].

## CLXXXVI. He confirms the privileges of the church of St Frigdian of Lucca. (1106, 24 May.)

[BALUZE, *Miscellanea*, vol. IV, p. 584.]

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons in Christ, Rotho the provost and his brothers professing the regular life in the church of Blessed Frigdian, and to their successors remaining in the same religious observance, forever.

[Col. 0193B] “The desire which,” etc., as in the privilege of the year 1104, no. 119, down to “have held from the Apostolic See.” Then follows:

From him, indeed, you shall receive chrism, holy oil, the consecration of altars or churches, and the ordination of clerics, if he is willing to provide them freely and without improper dealing; otherwise, you may receive those sacraments from whichever Catholic bishop you prefer, one supported by the authority of the Apostolic See and willing to grant what is requested. Nor may that bishop in any way excommunicate or place under interdict the place itself or the brothers dwelling there on account of hostility toward our enactments, except for definite offences which those brothers, having been canonically admonished, have refused to amend.

We confirm forever the use of baptism on the holy Saturday of Pentecost, held from former times, so that it may not be forbidden by any hostilities or plots. Nor may any secular authority lodge within the enclosure of your monastery, lest any of the regular brothers be disturbed by such presumptions. We further decree, etc., as in the said privilege.

Written by the hand of Raynerius, scrivener, etc.

I, Paschal, etc.

Given at the Lateran through the hand of John, deacon-cardinal and librarian of the Holy Roman Church, on the ninth day before the Kalends of June [24 May], fourteenth indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1106, in the seventh year of the pontificate of Lord Paschal, pope.

## CLXXXVII. To B[ernard], archbishop of Toledo. (1106.)

[FLOREZ, *España sagrada*, XX, 79.]

[Col. 0193D]

P., bishop II, to B., archbishop of Toledo, greeting and apostolic blessing.

We have received a very brief letter from your charity, in which, apart from the case being litigated between the church of St James and that of Mondoñedo, you were unwilling to tell us anything else concerning the condition of the Spanish lands. And although you say in that letter that you held a council, you took no care to inform us, apart from the aforesaid case, about the matters conducted in that council. You should know that we are greatly surprised at this, because we should gladly wish to see you and to learn the condition of your land.

But as for that case which, as we said, is being litigated between the clerics of Mondoñedo and the clerics of St James: if the men of Mondoñedo, as you reported, have failed in proving possession, let your brotherhood summon both parties at a suitable place and time and see that the matter is decided peacefully, lawfully, and without delay. Do not delay to pronounce a canonical sentence against those who fail to appear at the place and time appointed by you.

## CLXXXVIII. To Peter, archbishop of Acerenza.—He confirms his election and the rights of the metropolitan see of Acerenza; he sends the pallium. (1106, 16 June.)

[MANSI, *Concilia*, XX, 1055.]

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to our venerable brother PETER, archbishop of Acerenza, and to his successors to be canonically promoted, forever.

The Church acknowledges that authority to bind and loose in heaven and on earth was principally entrusted by God to Blessed Peter and his successors in the words by which the Lord addressed Peter: “Whatever you bind upon earth shall be bound also in heaven; and whatever you loose upon earth shall be loosed also in heaven” (Matthew XLVI). Likewise, by God’s authorship, he is proclaimed the confirmation of his own faith and that of others, when it is said to him: “I have prayed for you, Peter, that your faith may not fail; and you, once converted, strengthen your brethren” (Luke XXIII).

It is therefore fitting that we, who, though unworthy, seem to sit in Peter’s place, should correct what is wrong, confirm what is right, and order matters throughout the whole Church according to the judgment of the inward Judge, so that our judgment may proceed from His countenance and our eyes may behold equity. Assenting, therefore, to the just petitions of your brotherhood, we fortify the holy Church of Acerenza by the authority of the present decree, confirming to you and your successors everything known to have belonged to it in earlier times by metropolitan right: namely, Venosa, Gravina, Tricarico, Tarsus, and Potenza. You and your lawful successors shall have authority to ordain and consecrate bishops therein canonically and by decree, while preserving in all things the authority of the Holy Roman Church.

Further, we decree that whatever towns, villages, or parish churches are possessed by right by the same Church of Acerenza, and whatever goods it now justly possesses or may hereafter justly and canonically acquire, shall remain secure and inviolate to you and your successors—excepting, of course, those protected by special privileges of the Apostolic See.

Moreover, from the liberality of the Apostolic See we grant your brotherhood the pallium, that is, the fullness of the pontifical office. You are to wear it in church only at the solemnities of Mass on the following days: the Nativity of the Lord, Epiphany, Hypapante, the three feasts of Blessed Mary, the Lord’s Supper, Holy Saturday, the Resurrection, Ascension, Pentecost, the Nativity of St John the Baptist, the feast of all the apostles [the word *all* is perhaps superfluous, H.], St Michael the Archangel, the commemoration of all saints, and the martyrs or confessors who rest in the church of Acerenza; and at the consecration of churches, bishops, priests, and deacons. In every respect we wish you to vindicate the character of this office.

The honour of this garment is humility and justice. Therefore let your brotherhood hasten with all its mind to show itself humble in prosperity and, in adversities, should they occur, upright with justice; friendly to the good and opposed to the perverse. Never respect anyone’s person against truth; never oppress anyone’s person. Persist in works of mercy according to your ability, and yet desire to persist even beyond your ability. Have compassion on the weak; rejoice with those of good will; count others’ losses as your own; rejoice over others’ goods as though exulting over your own. In correcting vices, be mercifully severe; in fostering virtues, soothe the souls of your hearers. In anger, maintain judgment free of anger; in tranquillity, do not abandon the discipline of just severity.

This, dearest brother, is the worthiness of the pallium you have received. If you observe it diligently, you will possess inwardly what you show that you have received outwardly. May heavenly mercy deign to preserve your brotherhood unharmed for many years. Amen, amen, amen.

I, Paschal, bishop of the Catholic Church.

Given at Albano through the hand of John, deacon-cardinal of the Holy Roman Church, on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of July [16 June], in the fourteenth indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1106, in the eighth year of the pontificate of Lord Paschal II, pope.

## CLXXXIX. Bull for Benedict, abbot of the monastery of St Saviour at Moxi. (1106, 19 September.)

[MURATORI, *Antiquitates Italicae*, III, 1105.]

[Col. 0195C]

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son BENEDICT, abbot of the monastery of St Saviour situated in the place called Moxi, and to his successors regularly promoted, forever.

A devout petition should be brought to fulfillment by an effective result, so that the sincerity of devotion may shine forth worthily and the requested benefit may undoubtedly acquire force. Therefore, since your belovedness, fleeing to the harbour of the Apostolic See, has with due devotion sought its protection, we graciously assent to your petition and receive under the protection of the Apostolic See the monastery of the Blessed Saviour over which you preside by God’s gift.

By the text of the present privilege, we decree by apostolic authority that whatever estates or goods are now seen to belong by lawful possession to that monastery, or may hereafter, by the Lord’s grant, come to be justly and canonically acquired through the grants of pontiffs, the generosity of princes, or the offerings of the faithful, shall remain secure and inviolate to you and your successors. Among these, the following seem proper to specify by name: the church of St Mary with a share of the estate of Dolia; the church of St Lawrence with a share of the estate of Rasiniana; the church of St Frigdian and St Nicholas with a share of the smallholding of Instuli; at Bodio, the church of St Mary; and at Paterno, the church of St Michael.

We decree, therefore, that it shall be lawful for no person at all rashly to disturb this monastery, take away its possessions, retain what has been taken, diminish them, or harass it with reckless vexations; but that all things shall be preserved intact for the use and benefit in every respect of those for whose support and governance they were granted. Upon the death of you, the present abbot of that place, or of any of your successors, no one shall be set over it by any craft of deception or violence except one whom the brothers, by common consent, or the sounder part of the brothers’ counsel, may provide to be elected, whether from their own community or, if necessary, from another.

We further decree that the burial-place of that location shall be altogether free, so that no one may oppose the devotion and final will of those who decide to be buried there, unless they are perhaps excommunicated. Nor may a bishop place under interdict either the monastery itself or its churches except for an offence, or burden it with new exactions. Moreover, we grant you possession, without opposition from any persons, of the tithes of your own labours.

If any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowing this charter of our constitution, should attempt to act against it, then, having been admonished a second or third time, if he does not make fitting satisfaction, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and honour; let him know himself guilty before divine judgment for the wrong he has committed; let him be cut off from the most sacred Body and Blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, our Redeemer; and let him be subject to strict vengeance at the last judgment. But upon all who preserve what is right for that place may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that they may here receive the fruit of good action and, before the strict Judge, find the rewards of eternal peace. Amen, amen, amen.

I, Paschal, bishop of the Catholic Church, have subscribed.

Given at Florence through the hand of John, deacon-cardinal and librarian of the Holy Roman Church, on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of October [19 September], in the fifteenth indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1106.

## CXC. To the bishops of Gaul.—Against the murderers of the abbot of Vézelay. (1106, 25 October.)

[MANSI, *Concilia*, XX, 1031.]

[Col. 0196D]

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brothers, the bishops of Gaul, greeting and apostolic blessing.

It seems utterly unworthy of the charity of the priestly order that you are said to foster criminal persons whom you ought to pursue for their crimes. For the murderers of the abbot of Vézelay are said to live freely in the parishes of some among you. Therefore, reproving your brotherhood with fitting rebuke, we command by the authority of the present letter that you drive into exile, according to a fitting measure of penance, those who so wickedly killed their lord, priest, and abbot. If they refuse to obey, subject them to excommunication. Nor may the abbot of Vézelay, or any provost, ever have authority to leave to those murderers or their heirs anything belonging to the Church. But those shown to have been instigators of this homicide, unless they perform fitting penance, make strangers to the Church.

Given at Guastalla, on the eighth day before the Kalends of November [25 October].

## CXCI. To Gisela, abbess of Remiremont: if she has refused to carry out his command concerning the monks of Chaumousey “by the beginning of the coming Lent, he forbids her entrance into the church from that time.” (1106, 27 October.)

[MARTÈNE, *Thesaurus Anecdotorum*, III, 1180.]

[Col. 0197B]

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved daughter GISELA, abbess of Remiremont, greeting and apostolic blessing.

Concerning the injury done to the religious brothers of Chaumousey, we have sent you letters three times, asking and commanding that you either accept an exchange, from an estate suitable for you, for your share in the parish church of Blessed Mary, which is common to you and them; or leave them undisturbed in their share—namely, the tithes of their allodial estate which lies within their parish. Yet you have disdained to heed us.

Although repeatedly disregarded, therefore, we nevertheless send you repeated letters, commanding you to carry out whichever of these alternatives you prefer, as has been ordered. If you refuse to fulfill this by the beginning of the coming Lent, from that time we forbid you entrance into the church.

Given at Guastalla, on the sixth day before the Kalends of November [27 October].

## CXCII. To Gebehard, bishop of Constance, and Oderic, bishop of Passau.—Not all excommunicated persons are to be avoided. (1106.)

[MANSI, *Concilia*, XX, 1002.]

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brothers GEBEHARD, bishop of Constance, and ODERIC, bishop of Passau, and to all Catholic clergy and laity in the German lands, greeting and apostolic blessing.

We rejoice at the fervour of your religious life, and give thanks to almighty [Col. 0197D] God, who confirms you in the love of his name. Yet we have heard that some among you have a zeal for God not according to knowledge: so that, while avoiding association with the wicked, they contemplate even leaving your regions. Such persons are assuredly in no way worthy of apostolic praise, since they cannot persevere in the midst of a crooked and perverse nation, among whom they ought to shine as lights in the world, holding fast the word of life. For they weigh human sins with a single measure, judging equally guilty both those excommunicated through their own voluntary fault and those who communicate with the excommunicated; whereas different intentions entail different guilt.

For if anyone is called criminal, according to the Apostle, [Col. 0198A] such a person must altogether be avoided. The same caution must be observed toward those who knowingly associate themselves with such named persons by deed when able to do so, or by will when unable. But those who are joined to such excommunicated persons wholly against their will, whether through service or cohabitation, if they are touched with grief at such a state of affairs, are not to be entirely avoided; nevertheless, neither are they to be admitted to communion without the remedy of correction. Hence our predecessor of holy memory, Pope Gregory VII, decreed that the wives, sons, servants, and peasants of excommunicated persons—whose counsel or will had not brought about the offence deserving excommunication—as also travellers who against their will communicated with the excommunicated through necessity of travel, were not bound by the bond of excommunication; as blessed Augustine, writing [Col. 0198B] to Auxilius, plainly shows. “Let the brethren,” he says, “learn in all things to keep the way, and let them strive to shine as lights in the midst of a crooked and perverse nation, so that they may deserve to receive from God the reward not only of their own salvation but also of another’s.” He examines each person’s intentions and investigates causes, because all things are naked and open to his eyes. We trust in his mercy, since the gloom of darkness shall not overwhelm the body whose eye is single, for charity covers a multitude of sins. May divine mercy, as you obey our admonitions, keep you and absolve you from all sins.

### CXCIII. To Hugh, Abbot of Saint-Gilles: he confirms the Abbey of Somogy, founded by Ladislaus, King of the Hungarians. (1106, 2 November.)

*[Gallia Christiana, VI, 189.]*

[Col. 0198C]

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son in Christ HUGH, abbot of the monastery of Saint-Gilles, situated in the valley of Flaviana, and to his successors to be regularly appointed in perpetuity.

It is fitting readily to grant consent to religious desires, so that faithful devotion may attain a swift result. Ladislaus, king of the Hungarians of good memory, founded the church of Somogy in honour of God and of the holy apostles Peter and Paul, in memory of Saint Giles the Confessor; and through the hand of Odilo, your predecessor of happy memory, he offered it to the monastery of Blessed Giles, over which, by God’s authorisation, you preside, where also the saint’s venerable body rests. [Col. 0198D] We therefore, by God’s grant, confirm by the authority of the apostolic see this offering made for the salvation of souls, to which your monastery in the valley of Flaviana is acknowledged to have been given by the same Saint Giles as an endowment.

Accordingly, by this present decree we ratify the disposition of the aforesaid king: whoever is abbot of Somogy shall profess obedience to, and steadfastly observe it toward, the abbot of your monastery, which, as we have said, was founded in the valley of Flaviana by Saint Giles. Matters arising in the monastery shall be settled by the king’s counsel, and no one other than the king shall presume to judge concerning the property of the church. Moreover, the monastic church, together with its precinct, shall always enjoy such liberty that those taking refuge there suffer no prejudice in their persons or property. [Col. 0199A]

Therefore we decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb that monastery, or take away, diminish, or harass by reckless vexations its possessions; but that all things granted there from their own lawful property by the same King Ladislaus or by other faithful persons, or which may hereafter, by the Lord’s gift, come to be granted there, shall always be preserved firm and whole, saving the canonical reverence due to the diocesan bishop, and shall in every respect benefit the uses for whose support and governance they were granted.

If anyone, therefore, after learning the tenor of this decree, attempts either to withdraw the cell of Somogy from subjection to your monastery or rashly to deprive that same cell of its goods, and, having been warned a second or third time, does not take care to amend this unlawful presumption by suitable satisfaction, [Col. 0199B] let him be excluded from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ the Redeemer, and be liable at the final judgment to severe vengeance. But upon all who observe these ordinances, may the peace of the Lord Jesus Christ rest, so that they may receive here the fruit of good action and find before the strict Judge the rewards of eternal peace. Amen, amen, amen.

I, Paschal, bishop of the Catholic Church, have signed.

I, Bruno, . . . . . bishop, have signed.

I, Landulf, cardinal priest, have signed.

Given at Parma through the hand of John, cardinal-deacon and librarian of the Holy Roman Church, on the fourth day before the Nones of November [2 November], in the fifteenth indiction, in the year 1106 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the eighth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Paschal II. [Col. 0199C]

### CXCIV. To Guido, Abbot of Saint Stephen of Lodi.—Privilege of the Monastery of Saint Stephen. (1106, 15 November.)

*[Mansi, Councils, XX, 1054.]*

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son GUIDO, abbot of the venerable monastery of Saint Stephen, situated in the county of Lodi beside the Po, and to his successors to be regularly appointed in perpetuity.

We are instructed by divine precepts and apostolic admonitions to watch with untiring zeal over the state of churches. Your belovedness has asked us to confirm certain enactments of our predecessors and, through them, by God’s authorisation, to strengthen the condition of your monastery. That . . . . . monastery is known to have been built and endowed from her own resources by the venerable Countess Anselda together with her sons Lanfranc, Arduin, and Manfred. Therefore, by the text of this present privilege, we establish by apostolic authority that whatever estates or goods have been given from their own lawful property by the aforesaid countess, her sons, or other faithful persons, and whatever may hereafter be granted to that monastery through the concession of pontiffs, the generosity of princes, or the offerings of the faithful, shall remain firm and unimpaired for you and your successors. [Col. 0199D]

We accordingly confirm to the aforesaid monastery of Saint Stephen the adjoining village, the castle within which that monastery was built, and the other things contained in the charter of Bishop Nokenus. [Col. 0200A] When you, the present abbot of that place, or any of your successors, die, no one shall be placed over it through any trickery of usurpation or by force, except one whom the brethren, or the sounder part of the brethren’s counsel, shall decide ought to be elected from their own community or, if necessary, from another, in accordance with the fear of God and the Rule of Blessed Benedict. The person elected shall go to the Roman pontiff for consecration.

Furthermore, we decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb that monastery or harass its possessions with reckless vexations; but that everything shall be preserved whole for the benefit in every respect of those uses for whose support and governance it was granted. If therefore any ecclesiastical or secular person, etc., as in certain other letters.

[Col. 0200B]

I, Paschal, bishop of the Catholic Church.

Given at Piacenza, through the hand of John, cardinal-deacon and librarian of the Holy Roman Church, on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of December [15 November], in the fifteenth indiction, in the year 1106 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the eighth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Paschal II.

### CXCV. To the monks of Saint Peter and Saint Saviour at Pavia. (1106, 19 November.)

*[Robolini, Notizie, III, p. 226.]*

When the venerable Bishop G. [Guido] of Pavia and your abbots A. and . . . . . . . had appeared before us, after many complaints had been set forth . . . It therefore pleased our brethren to have recourse to the decision which, in the preceding summer, had been made in the letters that we had sent from Monte Cassino to the aforesaid bishop concerning these same complaints . . . . .

Given on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of December [19 November].

### CXCVI. To the Canons of Augsburg. (1106, 22 November.)

*[Mansi, Councils, XX, 1214.]*

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the canons of the Church of Augsburg and the other parishioners, greeting and apostolic blessing.

Our brother Herimann, bishop of your city, came to us unbidden, asking that his case be settled by a more definite decision. Remembering your complaints, however, because the brethren who had presented charges against [Col. 0200D] him before us in council were not then present with him before us, and lest either party should be able to complain of prejudice against us, we deferred, by the deliberation of our brethren, consideration of his case until the next Kalends of November. By this letter we have summoned to our hearing, at that stated time, all who bring a case against him. In the meantime we grant our aforesaid brother authority to excommunicate, in accordance with canonical sanctions, those who seize and invade the goods of the church. For we desire that both he and the church under him may, by the Lord’s gift, enjoy peace and tranquillity until the appointed time.

Given on the tenth day before the Kalends of December [22 November].

### CXCVII. *He directs Didacus, Bishop of Compostela, together with “the bishops of the provincial sees, Peter of León, Pelagius of Asturias, and others, to determine by the most exact inquiry the dispute concerning the boundaries of the common parish between the clergy of the Churches of Osma and Burgos.”

[Col. 0201A]

(See the *Historia Compostellana*, in Flórez, *España sagrada*, XX, 63.)

### CXCVIII. Privilege for the Church of Coimbra. (Between 1099 and 1107.)

*[Brandão, Monarchia Lusitana, III, p. 283.]*

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother [MAURICE], bishop of Coimbra, greeting and apostolic blessing.

[Col. 0201B] The authority of the apostolic see, which by God’s authorisation we serve, and our duty compel us both to provide for churches laid waste and to cherish with ready solicitude those not laid waste—especially those which lie near the ferocity of barbarians and which we find enclosed by habitations. Therefore we establish that whatever goods and whatever diocese that church now justly possesses, or may hereafter justly and canonically acquire, shall remain firm and unimpaired for you and your successors; so that if anyone should hereafter, with God’s help, be able to recover any part of the ancient boundaries of the parish which the Moors and Moabites now possess, those territories shall be incorporated whole into the same church. In the meantime, from Coimbra to the old castle, the division made for the Church of Coimbra by bishops in the time of King Theodemir shall remain in force. [Col. 0201C]

Secondly, we entrust to your provision and care, and to that of your successors, the former cathedral churches of Lamego and Viseu, until the Lord shall ordain either that the diocese of Coimbra be restored or that those churches, restored to their own parishes, may be able to have cardinal bishops. Thirdly, we have confirmed Vacariça, together with its churches, settlements, and estates, under the bishops of Coimbra, as it was offered by the distinguished count in written testimonies, etc.

### CXCIX. To Hugh, Abbot of Cluny.—He forbids anyone to exact a road-toll or anything else from those going to or leaving Cluny within the designated boundaries. (1107, 2 February.)

*[Bouquet, Recueil, XV, 34.]*

[Col. 0201D]

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother HUGH, abbot of Cluny, and to all the brethren of the same congregation, greeting and apostolic blessing.

Just as our predecessors, the pontiffs of the apostolic see, took care to provide for your peace and freedom by decrees as well as writings, so also, by God’s grace, we both wish and ought to do. Therefore, among the other enactments concerning your peace and immunity, we decree, command, and determine by precept that from Mâcon to Cluny, from Saint Mary of the Wood to Cluny, from Corella to Cluny, from Mont-Saint-Vincent to Cluny, from [Col. 0202A] Jullié to Cluny, from Beaujeu to Cluny, and from Brancion or Trinorchi to Cluny—that is, not even from the intermediate points of these boundaries, by the roads extending in equal directions to Cluny—no person may presume to levy a road-toll or impose any new exaction upon persons going to Cluny or returning from it, or to molest their persons, take away their goods, or seize them. We decree that whoever knowingly violates this law shall be barred from entrance into the church until he makes satisfaction for the offence to the abbot of Cluny or to the community itself.

Given at Chalon, on the fourth day before the Nones of February [2 February], in the fifteenth indiction, in the year 1106 of the Lord’s Incarnation.

### CC. He confirms the rights and possessions of the Monastery of La Chaise-Dieu. (1107, 4 February.)

*[Mabillon, Benedictine Annals, V, 499.]*

[Col. 0202B]

After Paschal had celebrated the Nativity of the Lord at Cluny, he remained there until February of the following year. At that time he granted a charter to Aimeric, abbot of La Chaise-Dieu, by which, following the example of Gregory VII and Urban II, he confirmed all the monastery’s rights and possessions, as well as the monasteries and cells subject to it: namely, the monastery of Saint Andrew at Vienne, granted by Archbishop Guy; the church of Saint Trivier, recently conferred by Archbishop Hugh of Lyon, of venerable memory; and the cell of Veriano, granted by Bernard, bishop of Agde.

Given at Cluny through the hand of John, [Col. 0202C] deacon and librarian of the Holy Roman Church, on the second day before the Nones of February [4 February], in the fifteenth indiction, in the year 1106 of the Lord’s Incarnation according to the old computation, and in the eighth year of the pontificate of Lord Paschal II.

### CCI. To William of Sabran and the other associates of Count Bertrand of Toulouse.—He summons them to make satisfaction, under penalty of excommunication, for injuries inflicted upon the Monastery of Saint-Gilles. (1107, 4 February.)

*[Bouquet, Recueil, XV, 34.]*

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the noblemen WILLIAM OF SABRAN, EMENON his brother, RAINARD OF MÉDANES, ARBERT OF MONTCLAR, RICHARD OF CLARET, DALMATIUS OF ROQUEMAURE, and RAIMUND PETER OF GORRE.

We have no doubt that you were privy to and counsellors of Raymond, count of illustrious memory, when he utterly renounced the town of Blessed Giles through the hand of our predecessor of holy memory, Pope Urban, and caused both himself and his heirs to be excommunicated if at any time they should presume to usurp anything in that town against the will of the abbot. We know that it is very well known to you how often your Count Bertrand has sworn the same thing. But recently, invading not only the town but even the monastery itself by force, seizing some men and wounding others, he thus drove out the monks; he seized the monastery’s goods and the offerings of the altar, destroyed its buildings, and brought prostitutes into the dwellings of God’s servants. Moreover, [Col. 0203A] he built, and is building, new towers upon the very church of Blessed Giles. The brethren of Saint-Gilles complain that you were both privy to and active agents in these crimes.

For all these matters, by the present letter we summon you to make due satisfaction before our brother the archbishop of Narbonne by the beginning of the coming Lent, and to do justice by his judgment and that of the other brethren. Otherwise, from that time we place both you and your land under interdict from divine offices, except for the baptism of infants and the penance of the dying; and we declare you bound by the bonds of that excommunication into which you voluntarily entered, since you are guilty of sacrilege, and Bertrand, whose associates you have made yourselves, is bound by the bond of excommunication not only because of his invasion of the monastery and the aforesaid town, but also because of his rejection of his wife and his repeated [Col. 0203B] adulteries.

Given on the second day before the Nones of February [4 February].

### CCII. To Richard, Archbishop of Narbonne, and the bishops of the province.—He recounts the adulteries of Bertrand, Count of Toulouse, and the injuries inflicted upon the Monastery of Saint-Gilles, and urges them to restrain others from assisting and communicating with him and his associates. (1107, 4 February.)

*[D. Bouquet, Recueil, XV, 35.]*

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brethren and fellow bishops RICHARD of Narbonne, RAYMOND of Maguelonne, RAYMOND of Nîmes, and the other bishops of the province, greeting and apostolic blessing.

[Col. 0203C] It is most widely known, not only to you who are nearby but also to those far away, how Count Bertrand has long been subject to excommunication because of the wife he rejected and his many adulteries. He is also fettered by the bonds of that anathema by which Raymond, count of illustrious memory, at the Council of Nîmes, caused himself and his heirs to be excommunicated by Pope Urban II of holy memory if at any time they should presume to usurp anything in the town of Blessed Giles and its monastery against the will of the abbot. We believe that you know how often Count Bertrand has likewise sworn this. Recently, however, by violently invading not only the town but even the monastery itself, seizing some and wounding others, he thus drove out the monks; [Col. 0203D] he seized the monastery’s goods and offerings, destroyed its buildings, and brought prostitutes into the dwellings of God’s servants. Moreover, he built, and is building, new towers over the very church of Blessed Giles.

We condemn the structure of this construction by the anathema of Jericho, so that those who shall hereafter attempt either to build it or to retain what has been built may be punished with perpetual malediction. By the present letter, under obedience to the apostolic see, we earnestly exhort your prudence to apply yourselves more diligently to correcting and restraining these acts. For these crimes we have summoned, by our letters, William of Sabran, Hemenon his brother, Rainard of Médanes, Harbert of Montclar, Richard of Claret, and Dalmatius of Roquemaure, as Bertrand’s counsellors and authors of this sacrilege, to make satisfaction before your brotherhood. Unless they do so by the beginning of the coming Lent, we shall from that time place their land under interdict from divine offices and declare them bound by the bonds both of sacrilege and of the aforesaid excommunication, into which they voluntarily entered. [Col. 0204A]

Restrain others also from aiding or communicating with this same Bertrand, unless he restrains himself from such great evils and from maintaining that new construction. Meanwhile, we place the land under his lordship under interdict from divine offices, except for the baptism of infants and the penances of the dying; and wherever he may reside, no divine offices shall be celebrated there for as long as he remains in that place.

Given on the second day before the Nones of February [4 February].

### CCIII. To the clergy of Augsburg.—He rejoices that they have been reconciled with Bishop Herimann. (1107, 6 February.)

*[Mansi, Councils, XX, 1215.]*

[Col. 0204B]

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons, the clergy of the Church of Augsburg, greeting and apostolic blessing.

After the accusation which you brought against your bishop, we received a letter from your belovedness in which you informed us that you had peace and concord with the same bishop. We rejoiced, if it shall prove that this concord was made freely. Nevertheless, we await the appointed date, [Col. 0204C] so that, with the Lord’s help, we may carry out whatever equity shall dictate.

Given on the eighth day before the Ides of February [6 February].

### CCIV. To Hugh, Abbot of Cluny.—He confirms the rights and possessions of Cluny. (1107, 8 February.)

*[Mansi, Councils, XX, 1039.]*

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his most reverend brother HUGH, abbot of Cluny, greeting and apostolic blessing.

The benevolence of the apostolic see rejoices, through the grace of almighty God, in your religious life. For in many places, through the zeal of your care, by the Lord’s gift, religious observance has been established where none existed, [Col. 0204D] and restored throughout the regions of Gaul where it had failed. Therefore, as from the very beginnings of your monastery, so, by the Lord’s gift, until the end the authority of the apostolic see protects you as its dearest sons. Accordingly, we strengthen by the authority of the apostolic see all things belonging to your monastery, as they were strengthened by our predecessors. Among them we have thought fit to specify in their own names those things which, acquired in our time through God’s grace, are known to be subject to the direction of your government.

(The items are enumerated. Then:)

By the authority of this present document we decree that all these things shall remain forever under the right and governance both of you and of your successors, as limbs joined to the head, [Col. 0205A] for your monastery. Nor may anyone whatsoever withdraw them from your subjection or alienate them by any pretext from the right of the monastery of Cluny. If, therefore, any ecclesiastical or secular person hereafter knowingly violates the text of this constitution, etc., as in certain other letters.

I, Paschal, bishop of the Catholic Church, have subscribed.

Given at the estate of Saint-Hippolyte, through the hand of John, cardinal-deacon and librarian of the Holy Roman Church, on the sixth day before the Ides of February [8 February], in the fifteenth indiction, in the year 1106 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the eighth year of the pontificate of Lord Paschal II.

### CCV. Confirmation, made for Abbot Gauceran, of the churches and possessions of the Athanacensian Monastery. (1107, 12 February.)

*[Gallia Christiana, IV, 13.]*

[Col. 0205B]

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son GAUCERAN, abbot of the Athanacensian monastery, and to his successors to be regularly appointed in perpetuity.

We are seen to have been raised, by the Lord’s disposition, to the government of the apostolic see for this purpose: that, with his assistance, we ought to increase religious observance and provide protection for its servants. Therefore, assenting to your just petitions, beloved son Gauceran, abbot in the Lord, we strengthen by the authority of the apostolic see, against the wickedness of evil men, the Athanacensian monastery of Blessed Martin, over which, by God’s authorisation, you preside. We establish that the church of Saint John, given to you in his diocese by Guy, bishop of Gévaudan; also the church of Saint Romanus of Agenta in the diocese of Sion; likewise the church of Issiniac in the diocese of Le Puy, given to you by Bishops Adhémar and Pons, together with their appurtenances; and all other things which, in the present fifteenth indiction, whether through the concession of pontiffs, the generosity of princes, or the offerings of the faithful, your monastery lawfully and peacefully possesses—namely, at the time when, by the Lord’s disposition, we consecrated your church—and whatever it may hereafter, by the Lord’s gift, justly and canonically acquire, [Col. 0205C–D] shall remain firm and unimpaired for you and your successors.

We therefore decree that no person may take away the possessions of that monastery, retain possessions taken away, unjustly claim for his own use things given to it, diminish them, or harass them with reckless vexations; but that everything shall be preserved whole and serve in every respect the uses for whose support and governance it was granted, saving the canonical reverence due to the archbishop of Lyon. If any ecclesiastical or secular person hereafter, knowingly violating this text of our constitution, attempts rashly to act against it, and, after a second or third warning, does not make amends by suitable satisfaction, let that person be deprived of the dignity of office and honour, and know himself or herself guilty before divine judgment of the iniquity committed; let that person be excluded from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ the Redeemer, and be liable at the final judgment to severe vengeance. [Col. 0206A] But upon all who preserve what is right for that place, may the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ rest, so that they may receive here the fruit of good action and find before the strict Judge the rewards of eternal peace. Amen, amen, amen.

I, Paschal, bishop of the Catholic Church.

Given at Belna, through the hand of John, cardinal-deacon and librarian of the Holy Roman Church, on the second day before the Ides of February [12 February], in the fifteenth indiction, in the year 1107 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the eighth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Paschal II.

### CCVI. He adjudicates the dispute between the Abbey of Remiremont and the chapter of Chaumousey. (1107, 24 February.)

*[Martène, Thesaurus Anecdotorum, III, 1182.]*

[Col. 0206B]

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God.

A dispute had long been carried on between the monastery of Remiremont and the chapter of Chaumousey concerning the portion of the estate on which that chapter stands, and also concerning the portion of the parish church of Saint Mary, which had hitherto appeared to be common. It had often come to our attention; accordingly, it seemed fitting that both parties should appear before us. Gisela, abbess of Remiremont, renounced into our hands the disputed portion of the estate on which the chapter stands. Since she had recognized that the whole estate belonged to the same [Col. 0206C] canons by ancient possession derived from donors, she promised, in the presence both of ourselves, our brethren, and many bystanders, that neither she nor her sisters would ever thereafter bring against them any complaint or dispute concerning that portion of the estate on behalf of the monastery’s right. Thus, receiving a staff from the hand of the abbess and sisters, we confirmed that entire portion of the estate, free from claim, to the brethren of Chaumousey.

As regards the share of the tithes, it seemed right to us and to our brethren, and was determined by the judgment of pontifical decrees, that since a lay knight could not lawfully give church property unjustly held, especially as these brethren had received the said gift after the council of Pope Gregory VII of apostolic memory—at which council that pontiff, renewing the enactments of his predecessors, forbade the receiving of tithes or other ecclesiastical property from laymen, while allowing what had been received before that time—the brethren of Chaumousey relinquished this portion to the judgment of the church. To that judgment was also added, and by the ruling of Blessed Gregory determined, that no tithes or first-fruits were to be exacted from their plough-teams, labours, or beasts of burden either for that parish church or for any others whatsoever. [Col. 0206D]

Done at Langres, on the sixth day before the Kalends of March [24 February], in the sixteenth indiction, in the year 1106 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the presence of the venerable bishops Richard of Albano, Aldo of Piacenza, and Odard of Cambrai; and of the cardinal priests of the Roman Church, Riso of the title of Damasus, Landulf of the title of Saint Lawrence, and Division of the title of Saint Martin; and of the deacons John of the title of Cosmidis, and Berard of the title of Saint Angelo; also in the presence, among the venerable clergy, of Ralph, provost of Reims, Richin, primicerius of Toul, and Rembald, archdeacon of Toul; and among the laity, Duke Theoderic of Lorraine, Albert of Brienne, Garin of Monson, Olderic of Acromont, and Henry of Saint-Vaast. [Col. 0207A]

### CCVII. To the monks and burgesses of Saint-Gilles.—He declares that Count Bertrand of Toulouse has been excommunicated by him, and orders them, under penalty of excommunication, to abstain from him. (1107, 14 March.)

*[D. Bouquet, Recueil, XV, 37.]*

[Col. 0207B]

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons, the monks and burgesses of Saint-Gilles, greeting and apostolic blessing.

Know that Bertrand, invader of the altar of Blessed Giles and obstinately resisting our commands, has been excommunicated by the judgment of the Holy Spirit. Whoever henceforth shall be his helper or counsellor in connection with this invasion, we declare to be a participant in the same excommunication until he has rendered due satisfaction. We therefore command all of you wholly to abstain from the same Bertrand as long as he chooses to persist in this obstinacy.

Given on the second day before the Ides of March [14 March].

### CCVIII. Privilege for the Monastery of Saint-Germain-des-Prés. (1107, 4 April.)

*[Bouillard, History of Saint-Germain-des-Prés, Documents, p. 39.]*

[Col. 0207C]

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son RAINALD, abbot of the monastery of Saint Germanus, bishop of the city of Paris, and to his successors to be regularly appointed in perpetuity.

It is fitting readily to grant consent to religious desires, so that faithful devotion may attain a swift result. Since, therefore, your belovedness has fled to the haven of the apostolic see and devoutly sought its protection, we graciously assent to your petition and receive under the guardianship and protection of Blessed Peter the monastery of Blessed Germanus, over which, by God’s authorisation, you preside, together with all things belonging to it. [Col. 0207D] By the text of this present privilege, therefore, we confirm to you and your successors in perpetuity that whatever liberty or dignity has been bestowed upon your monastery by the privilege of Blessed Germanus and by the written grants of Childebert, Clothar, and other kings of the Franks; whatever goods or possessions are known to belong to that monastery through the concession of pontiffs, the generosity of princes, or the offerings of the faithful; and whatever it may hereafter justly and canonically acquire or obtain, shall remain firm and unimpaired for you and your successors.

We decree, therefore, that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb your church, take away, retain after seizure, diminish, or harass with reckless vexations its possessions; but that all things shall be preserved whole and serve in every respect the uses for whose support and governance they were granted. Every abbot after you who is elected by the congregation of that monastery according to the Rule of Blessed Benedict shall be consecrated by the Roman pontiff, or by whatever Catholic bishop they prefer. [Col. 0208A] By apostolic authority we also command that none of the bishops may deny them, or their successors, oil, chrism, blessings, consecrations, ordinations, or any other things required from episcopal ministry.

Accordingly, we forbid masses, ordinations, and stations to be held in that monastery by any bishop or cleric of the Church of Paris without the consent of the abbot or congregation. Nor do we grant them there any power of command: nor power to place them under interdict or excommunicate them, nor to summon to synod the abbot or monks, priests or clerics of the churches of that place. If any ecclesiastical or secular person hereafter, knowingly violating this text of our constitution, attempts rashly to act against it, and, after being warned a second or third time, does not make amends by suitable satisfaction, let that person be deprived of the dignity of office and honour, and know himself or herself guilty before divine judgment of the iniquity committed; let that person be excluded from the most holy body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ the Redeemer, and be liable at the final judgment to severe vengeance. But upon all who preserve what is right for that place, may the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ rest, [Col. 0208B–C] so that they may receive here the fruit of good action and find before the strict Judge the rewards of eternal peace. Amen, amen, amen.

I, Paschal, bishop of the Catholic Church, have signed, etc.

Given at the Lateran through the hand of John, cardinal-deacon and librarian of the Holy Roman Church, on the Kalends of April [1 April], in the fifteenth indiction, in the year 1107 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the seventh year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Paschal II.

### CCIX. He confirms the privileges of the Monastery of Saint Laumer of Blois. (1107, 2 April.)

*[Mabillon, Annals, V, 500.]*

[Col. 0208D]

The pontiff celebrated at Tours, at Saint Martin’s, the Sunday *Laetare Jerusalem*—that is, the fourth Sunday of Lent—which in that year fell on the ninth day before the Kalends of April [24 March], wearing the *phrygium*, that is, the tiara, as is the Roman custom. Shortly afterward he went to Marmoutier, where he granted a diploma to Maurice, abbot of Saint Laumer, confirming his monastery, “situated near the town of Blois and enriched with many possessions and goods by the former King Rudolph, as well as by Charles and Louis, kings of the Franks.”

Given at Marmoutier, on the fourth day before the Nones of April [2 April], through the hand of Equitius, acting in place of the chancellor, in the fifteenth indiction, in the eighth year of Paschal.

### CCX. *He confirms the privileges of the Monastery of Saint John of Chartres. (1107, 19 April.)

[Col. 0209A]

[Only a notice of this privilege survives: *Gallia Christiana*, new edition, vol. VIII, *Instruments*, 308.]

### CCXI. Privilege for the Abbey of Saint Martin of the Fields. (1107, 30 April.)

*[Dom Marrier, History of Saint Martin of the Fields, p. 153.]*

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son in Christ THEOBALD, prior of Saint Martin called “of the Fields,” greeting and apostolic blessing.

[Col. 0209B] It is fitting to grant ready assent to religious desires, so that faithful devotion may attain a swift result. Therefore, most dear son, acceding to the petitions of your desire, we strengthen by the authority of this present decree the monastery of St Martin, over which you preside by appointment of our venerable brother Hugh, abbot of Cluny, so that, like the other members of the Cluniac monastery, it may always remain under the protection of the Apostolic See. We also decree that all things which in the present fifteenth indiction appear to belong to it shall always remain peaceably and wholly yours: namely, the church of St Pantaleon within Beauvais, with the holding of the two brothers Hugh and Garnerius, their own house and the other adjoining buildings, and with the vacant land outside the wall, situated beside the aforesaid church; [Col. 0209C] and the vineyard on Mount Ruber and the meadow at Guhincurt; together with the tenants before the gate of the city, as these things were offered by the aforesaid brothers for the salvation of themselves and their parents, granted with the favour of Geoffrey, bishop of Beauvais, and confirmed in our presence. Likewise, in the district of Paris, the churches of Duniacum, Ermenonville, and Eriniacum, granted to you by our venerable brother Gaulo, bishop. In the district of Senlis, the church of St Nicholas with its appurtenances. In the district of Amiens, the church of Liniacum with its appurtenances. In the district of Noyon, the altar-right of Curcellis and the altar-right of Ruveron. In the district of Soissons, the altar-right of Gozencurt, and the other things contained in the privilege of our predecessor of holy memory, Urban II.

[Col. 0209D] Moreover, whatever has been bestowed upon the same place out of anyone’s rightful property, or may hereafter be bestowed upon it, shall remain forever firm and unimpaired, to be possessed, governed, and administered in perpetuity by you and by the others who shall have been placed over that place through the abbots of Cluny. We therefore decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb this monastery, take away its possessions, retain those taken away, diminish them, or harass it with reckless vexations; but that all things be preserved whole for the use and benefit, in every respect, of those for whose support and governance they were granted.

If, therefore, any ecclesiastical or secular person in time to come, knowing this page of our constitution, should rashly attempt to act against it, and, having been warned a second or third time, does not make due amends by suitable satisfaction, let that person be deprived of the dignity of his power and honour; let him know himself guilty before the divine judgment of the iniquity committed; let him be cut off from the most sacred Body and Blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, our Redeemer; and let him be subject to severe vengeance at the last judgment. But upon all who preserve what is right for the same place, may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that here they may receive the fruit of good works and before the strict Judge may find the rewards of eternal peace. Amen.

Given at the monastery of St Denis, through the hand of John, cardinal-deacon and librarian of the Holy Roman Church, on the second day before the Kalends of May [30 April], in the fifteenth indiction, in the year 1108 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the eighth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Paschal II. [Col. 0210B]

CCXII. Privilege for the monastery of St Arnulf. (1107, 3 May.)

[CARLIER, *History of the Duchy of Valois*, vol. III, p. X.]

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son STEPHEN, prior of the monastery of Crépy, and to his brethren: greeting and apostolic blessing.

It is fitting to grant ready assent to religious desires, so that faithful devotion may attain a swift result. Therefore, most dear Stephen, acceding to the petitions of your desire, we strengthen by the authority of this present [Col. 0210C] decree the monastery of the blessed martyr Arnulf, over which you preside by appointment of our venerable brother Hugh, abbot of Cluny. We confirm to you and to your successors, to remain in the same freedom in which they were granted, all things known to have been given to St Arnulf of old and to your community by the founders of your house, Walter of blessed memory, count of Amiens, and his wife Adela.

We decree that all things which in the present fifteenth indiction appear to belong to your house shall always remain peaceably and wholly yours: namely, the church of St German, situated beside the castle of Pontoise, with its appurtenances; [lacuna] which is called the monastery of Morannum; the holding in the village of Bileti, near Mont-Désiré; the village altar-right; the altar-right of Garminacum, which you possess through the charter of Bishop Fulk; [Col. 0210D] the church at Lacelles; the church at Bonoculum; and the church of Restolium, with all their appurtenances; the allod of the knight Guy at Mairomont; the allod of Leocaldus at Dilucium, offered by those persons themselves; Vallis-villa, Villanova, and the vineyard of the knight Gualier; the allod of Frasneta.

Moreover, whatever has been bestowed upon the same place out of anyone’s rightful property, or may hereafter be bestowed, shall remain forever firm and unimpaired, to be possessed, governed, and administered in perpetuity by you and by the others who shall have been placed over the same place through the abbots of Cluny. We therefore decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb this monastery, take away its possessions, retain those taken away, diminish them, or harass it with reckless vexations; but that all things be preserved whole [Col. 0211A] for the use and benefit, in every respect, of those for whose support and governance they were granted.

If, therefore, any ecclesiastical or secular person in time to come, knowing this page of our constitution, should rashly attempt to act against it, and, having been warned a second or third time, does not make due amends by suitable satisfaction, let that person be deprived of the dignity of his power and honour; let him know himself guilty before the divine judgment of the iniquity committed; let him be cut off from the most sacred Body and Blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, our Redeemer; and let him be subject to severe vengeance at the last judgment. But upon all who preserve what is right for the same place, may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that here they may receive the fruit of good works and before the strict Judge may find the rewards of eternal [Col. 0211B] peace. Amen, amen.

It is subscribed:

I, Paschal, bishop of the Catholic Church.

Given at Latiniacum, through the hands of John, deacon, chaplain, and librarian of the Holy Roman Church, on the fifth day before the Nones of May [3 May], in the fifteenth indiction, in the year 1108 [1107] of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the eighth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Paschal II.

CCXIII. He confirms the possessions of the abbey of Elnone, or St Amand, of the Order of St Benedict, and safeguards them with apostolic privileges. (1107, 24 May.)

[MIRAEUS, *Diplomatic Works*, vol. II, p. 1151.]

[Col. 0211C] PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son in Christ HUGH, abbot of the venerable monastery of St Amand, called Elnone, and to his successors to be appointed in Christ for ever.

We acknowledge that, by the Lord’s ordering, we have been advanced to the service of the Apostolic See in order that we should effectively assist its children when they seek help, and defend and protect the obedient. Therefore we ought to extend the hand of protection to venerable places and provide with closer care for the peace of God’s servants. Accordingly, out of reverence for the most precious protomartyr Stephen, we receive into the bosom of the Holy Roman Church, entirely free under the protection of the Apostolic See, the monastery of Elnone, over which by God’s authority you preside and where the most sacred body of St Amand also rests, [Col. 0211D] in accordance with the privilege of liberty granted by our predecessor Pope Martin of holy memory to the same blessed Amand at his request.

Therefore, by the confirmation of this present decree, we establish for you and your successors, by the Lord’s gift, all that lawfully belongs to that monastery: namely, the village of Elnone adjoining the monastery, with all its appurtenances, free from every lordship of secular persons, as it was established by the religious emperors Dagobert, Pippin, Charles, Louis, Lothair, and Charles the Bald.

In the district of Laon: the cell of Barisiacum, with its dependent families and appurtenances.

[Col. 0212A] In the district of Cambrai: Braceolum, Villanova, and Halciacum, with their appurtenances.

In the district of Hainaut: Guariniacum and Scalpus, with their appurtenances.

In the district of Ostrevant: Diptiacum, Ferinum, Scaldinium, Lurcium, and Ruoth, with their dependent family and appurtenances.

In the district of Tournai: Guillelme, Frigidus Mons, Hertinium, Bovinas, Ruma, Spiare, and Holten, with their appurtenances.

In the district of Brogbatensis: Herinias, Sein, Alenium, Warcinium, Arminium, Securiacum, Vilare, Novae-Donnes, Herlegona, the lands of Germino, Milla, and Roda, with their appurtenances.

In the district of Menpiscus: the lands of Bonarda, Roslare, [Col. 0212B] Ledda, Hardoia, Guniguiniis, Marchegen, Lapiscura, and Berneham, with their dependent family and appurtenances.

On the River Meuse: the village of Haryngas, with its dependent family, church, and appurtenances.

On the River Rhine: the lands of Sula and Bobarga.

In Frisia: tribute-paying lands at Dechenchas and Stouras. Further, we decree that the altar-rights which you lawfully possess in various parishes shall be kept for ever free of every *personatus* [parochial incumbent’s right] for you and your successors, while nevertheless preserving the customary provisions due to bishops or episcopal officials.

In the bishopric of Noyon: the altar-rights of St Martin, Cella, Ruma, [Col. 0212C] Guillelme, Frigidus Mons, Hertinium, Macnengen, Guniguiniis, Berneham, Sedelengen, Bichengen, and Ledda.

In the bishopric of Laon: the cell of Borisiacum with the altar-right of St Remigius.

In the bishopric of Cambrai: the altar-right of Novavilla with its appurtenances; the altar-rights of Guariniacum, Scalpus, Guariniacum with its appurtenances, Vilari, Anurnio, and Herlengona.

In the bishopric of Arras: the altar-rights of Lurcium; Scaldinium with its appurtenances, Drueth; Bulciniolum; and Ditiacum with its appurtenances.

Whatever estates and whatever goods your monastery possesses today, and whatever it may hereafter acquire [Col. 0212D] by the grant of pontiffs, the generosity of princes, or the offerings of the faithful in hope of eternal salvation, shall remain forever firm and unimpaired to you and your successors.

We therefore decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb this monastery, take away its possessions, retain those taken away, diminish them, or harass it with reckless vexations; but that all things be preserved whole for the use and benefit, in every respect, of those for whose support and governance they were granted.

Upon the death of you, the abbot of that place, or of any of your successors, no one shall be set over it by any craft of intrigue or by force, except the person whom the brothers by common consent, or the sounder part of the brothers’ counsel, choose, whether from their own body or from another, according to the fear of God and the Rule of Blessed Benedict. [Col. 0213A]

We further add that no person may invade the same monastery, exercise any power of command there, demand banquets or provisions from that church in any fashion, or make any regulation, however slight, without the will of the abbot and brethren, so that the monks may always remain undisturbed under their abbot’s authority.

If in the future any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowing this page of our constitution, should rashly attempt to act against it, and, having been warned a second or third time, does not make due amends by suitable satisfaction, [Col. 0213B] let that person be deprived of the dignity of power and honour; let him know himself guilty before the divine judgment of the iniquity committed; let him be cut off from the most sacred Body and Blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, our Redeemer; and let him be subject to severe vengeance at the last judgment.

But upon all who preserve what is right for the same place, may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that here they may receive the fruit of good works and before the strict Judge may find the rewards of eternal peace.

+ I, Paschal, bishop of the Catholic Church.

Given at Troyes, through the hand of John, cardinal-deacon and librarian of the Holy Roman Church, on the ninth day before the Kalends of June [24 May], in the fifteenth indiction, in the year 1107 of the Lord’s [Col. 0213C] Incarnation, and in the eighth year of the pontificate of Lord Paschal II, pope.

CCXIV. To Gebhard, bishop of Constance.—He reproves him because he attended the consecration of the investee (Henry, archbishop of Magdeburg), and did not come when summoned to the council. (1107.)

[NEUGART, *Codex Diplomaticus Alemannicus*, II, 42.]

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother G., bishop of Constance: greeting and apostolic blessing.

In consideration of your many labours, we spared you for the fault you had committed. Yet again, although forbidden by our letters, you attended the consecration of him who had been invested. [Note: [Col. 0213D] The reference is to Henry of Magdeburg, whom Gebhard consecrated bishop. Labbe, *Collection of Councils*, vol. X, col. 755; *Gallia Christiana*, vol. V, col. 911.] [Col. 0213D] Summoned to the council, you did not come. [Note: [Col. 0213D] The council intended is that of Guastalla, 22 October 1106, convened by Paschal II. Labbe, cited work, col. 718.] On these grounds the sword of justice would have raged even to the point of forbidding you the exercise of your office; but the remembrance of your previous good conduct and the entreaty of our brethren restrained us. Therefore even now we spare you on the understanding that henceforth you entirely desist from presumption of this kind and do not involve yourself in such offences. For we do not wish you, God forbid, to omit in old age the contests of youth.

Know further that our brother [Col. 0214A] of Mainz—[Note: [Col. 0214D] That is, Ruthard. See the *Saxon Annals* under 1107.]—together with all his suffragans except the bishop of Bamberg—[Note: [Col. 0214D] St Otto was then head of the Church of Bamberg.]—and the bishop of Chur—[Note: [Col. 0214D] This was Ulrich III.]—who attended the Lombard synod, have been forbidden the exercise of their offices for absence from the council. Nor should you be unaware of that conciliar decree: whoever among clerics henceforth receives investiture of any church or its dignities from the hand of a layman, and the person who lays his hand upon him, shall jeopardize his rank and be deprived of communion. [Note: [Col. 0214D] This sentence was enacted at the Council of Troyes, in May 1107.]

Given . . .

CCXV. He does not grant the petition of Reinhard, bishop of Halberstadt, because “he received the governance of the Church through investiture from a lay hand.” He reports what was decreed at the Council of Troyes. (1107.)

[MANSI, *Councils*, XX, 1091.]

[Col. 0214B]

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to R., bishop of Halberstadt: greeting and apostolic blessing.

We have been established in God’s Church in order that we may preserve the order of the Church and the commands of the Fathers. You, however, have departed so far from the order of the Church that, contrary to the decrees of the Fathers, you received the governance of the Church through investiture from a lay hand. This is why we have been unable to grant your petition. We urge one thing upon your charity: hasten to amend so grave an offence. It was indeed decreed at the Council of Troyes that if anyone receives the investiture of a church from a lay hand, both he and his ordainer shall be deposed and removed from the communion of the Church. [Col. 0214C] We certainly wish and desire to have you as a brother and close associate. Farewell.

CCXVI. To Rothard, archbishop of Mainz.—He rebukes him for certain offences committed by him; lest he err in future through ignorance, he sends him extracts from the sacred canons, and, at the request of certain prelates, graciously grants him indulgence. (1107.)

[MANSI, *Councils*, XX, 1220.]

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother ROTHARD, archbishop of Mainz: greeting and apostolic blessing.

The more you assert that hitherto you have been obedient to the Roman Church [Col. 0214D] and have endured much for it, the more gravely you are proved now to have sinned against it. For after the Holy Roman Church had opened upon you the bowels of a mother and mercifully received you into her bosom, you were summoned to the council but did not come, nor did you offer canonical excuses. After synodical prohibition, you restored to office the publicly criminal bishop of Hildesheim; in these matters you feared to offend men more than God, since, despising both the canons of the Apostles and the ordinances of very many saints, you turned yourself to disobedience—the disobedience which expelled the first man from Paradise and irrevocably deprived Saul of his kingdom. Therefore, lest in the laying-on of hands you may hereafter have room to excuse yourself on the ground of ignorance, . . . and in view of the Apostle’s saying, “Do not lay hands hastily on anyone, lest you share in the sins of others,” we have judged it necessary to write to you certain extracts from the ordinances of many holy Fathers.

From the canons of the Apostles: “If any bishop employs secular powers in order to obtain through them a church, let him be deposed and separated, together with all who communicate with him.”

Likewise, from the Council of Antioch: “If any presbyter or deacon obtains a church of the Lord through secular rank, both he and his ordainer shall in every way be separated from communion and placed under anathema, as Simon Magus was by the Apostle Peter.”

Likewise, Stephen, martyred pontiff: “Nowhere is any authority found to have been granted to laypersons, however religious, to dispose of anything belonging to ecclesiastical resources.”

Likewise, Symmachus: “It is fitting that an improvident decision be rendered without force and brought to nothing, lest it remain as a precedent for presumption, and lest any laypersons, however religious or powerful, be allowed, in any city and in any manner, to decree anything concerning ecclesiastical resources, the care of disposing of which God teaches has been entrusted to priests alone.”

We too, following the ordinances of the holy canons, decreed with our brethren at the Council of Troyes [Col. 0215C] that any cleric who from this time receives from the hand of a layman the investiture of a church or ecclesiastical dignity, and the one who lays his hand upon him, shall jeopardize his rank and be deprived of communion. Yet you, venerable brother, although until now you have been a transgressor of these commands, have nevertheless, at the prayers of our venerable brethren the bishops of Trier, Constance, and Bamberg, and the abbot of Hirsau, been mercifully granted permission by us to perform the offices of my person, if, correcting the past, you prove a guardian and observer of these commands. Otherwise, we shall neither share offices with you nor give ear to prayers offered for you.

CCXVII. To Nicholas, abbot, and the monks of Corbie.—For the benefit of the schools of Corbie, he confirms King Philip’s grant that merchants may have free passage to the fair of Corbie. (1107, 29 May.)

[Dom BOUQUET, *Collection*, XV, 37.]

[Col. 0215D]

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons NICHOLAS, abbot, and the monks of the monastery of Corbie: greeting and apostolic blessing.

We ought not merely to favour the worthy pursuits of schools, but also to encourage their minds toward them, since by our office we provide for their welfare. Therefore, by the Lord’s gift, we confirm by these present letters the grant which our son Philip, king of the Franks, restored to your monastery of Corbie for the remission of his sins: namely, that any merchants wishing to come to the fair of Corbie may travel freely, by water or by land, with no one hindering them. By the letters of this present decree, therefore, we forbid any person henceforth to inflict any injury on the church of Corbie in this matter, lest it lose through anyone’s rash presumption what it has held by long possession. [Col. 0216B] But if anyone, knowing the tenor of this decree, should attempt to act against it, let him be punished by the correction of canonical severity.

Given at Auxerre, on the fourth day before the Kalends of July [28 June]. [Note: [Col. 0215D] Correct to June.]

CCXVIII. He confirms certain privileges of the monastery of St Remigius at Reims. (1107.)

[VARIN, *Administrative Archives of the City of Reims*, vol. I, part I, p. 255.]

[Note: [Col. 0215D] Cartulary B of Saint-Remi, p. 6, and cartulary A, p. 46, contain a second bull of the same pontiff, dated 3 January 1110, which repeats word for word that of 1107, except for four variants which we shall indicate.]

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son in Christ AZENARIUS, abbot of the venerable monastery of St Remigius, situated beside the city of Reims, and to his successors to be regularly [Col. 0216C] promoted, for perpetual remembrance.

Just as no effect should be granted to those seeking what is unjust, so the petition of those desiring what is lawful should not be delayed. Therefore, most dear son Azenarius, acceding to your just petitions, we strengthen by the authority of this present decree the monastery of Blessed Remigius, over which by God’s authority you preside. [Note: [Col. 0215D] From this point, the bull of 1110, omitting everything concerning Guy, continues as follows: “But we strictly forbid that at the market . . .”]

For we decree that the grant of Guy, bishop of Reims, of blessed memory, which he conferred upon your monastery through the intervention of Blessed Leo IX, shall remain forever firm and inviolable: namely, that at the market customarily held on the twelfth day before the Kalends of November [21 October] beside the borough of Blessed Remigius, no one save the abbot or the abbot’s officers shall forcibly take anything, and no one shall presume to harm those attending or despoil them of their goods. We also remove from your monastery, in accordance with the determination of the aforesaid bishops, the meal which the bishops of Reims customarily exact without measure from it on the two feasts of Blessed [Col. 0216D] Remigius. [Note: [Col. 0216D] The bull of 1110 reads: “. . . which they customarily receive, together with all their expenses, we remove from that same monastery. For these things our venerable brother Rudolf, bishop of the Church of Reims, granted in our presence and caused to be confirmed by the authority of a privilege of both parties. Further . . .”] We likewise forbid other expenses to be exacted from it or its officers, as they were remitted by the aforementioned Guy through the hand of Blessed Leo.

Furthermore, we grant to you and your successors the right to appeal to the Roman [Col. 0217A] Church in more serious cases; nor may the bishops of Reims prevent you from visiting the Apostolic See. Moreover, whatever estates and whatever goods the monastery of Blessed Remigius lawfully possesses today, and whatever it may hereafter lawfully acquire by the grant of pontiffs, the generosity of princes, or the offerings of the faithful, shall remain firm and unimpaired to you and your successors. We therefore decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb this monastery, take away its possessions, retain those taken away, or harass it with reckless vexations; but that all things be preserved whole for the use and benefit, in every respect, of those for whose support and governance they were granted.

If, therefore, any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowing this page of our constitution, should rashly attempt to act against it, and, having been warned a second or third time, does not make due amends by suitable satisfaction, let that person be deprived of the dignity of power and honour; let him know himself guilty before the divine judgment of the iniquity committed; let him be cut off from the most sacred Body and Blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, our Redeemer; and let him be subject to severe vengeance at the last judgment. [Col. 0217B] But upon all who preserve what is right for the same monastery, may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that here they may receive the fruit of good works and before the strict Judge may find the reward of eternal peace. Amen, amen.

I, Paschal, bishop of the Catholic Church, have signed. [Note: [Col. 0217D] From this point the bull of 1110 reads: “Written through the hand of John, scriniary and notary of the sacred palace. Given at the Lateran, through the hand of John, cardinal-deacon and librarian of the Holy [Col. 0218D] Roman Church, on the third day before the Nones of January [3 January], in the third indiction, in the year 1110 of the Incarnation, and in the eleventh year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Paschal II.”]

[Col. 0217C] Given at Auxerre through the hand of John, cardinal-deacon and librarian, in the fifteenth indiction, in the year 1107, and in the eighth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Paschal II.
