CCXIX. At the request of Bishop Humbald, he confirms the possessions of the Church of Auxerre. (1107.)

[*Deeds of the Bishops of Auxerre*, in LABBE, *New Library of Manuscripts*, vol. I, p. 458.]

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother HUMBALD, bishop of Auxerre, and to his successors to be canonically appointed for ever.

[Col. 0217D] It befits us to grant assent to just wishes and to give ear to just petitions, since, though unworthy, we are by the Lord’s ordering set as guardians and heralds of justice upon the lofty watchtower of the chief Apostles Peter and Paul. Therefore, most dear brother Humbald in Christ, acceding to your just petitions, we strengthen by the authority of the Apostolic See the holy Church of Auxerre, over which by God’s authority you preside. We decree that all things which your Church of Auxerre is known to possess in the present [Col. 0218A] fifteenth indiction from the times in which they were possessed by our ancient predecessors shall always be kept free and unimpaired for you and your successors. No one whatsoever, of whatever dignity or order, may dare, against your will or that of your church, to invade, take away, or in any manner withdraw the dependencies of your church or the property in your possession; but all shall remain under the obedience and administration of you and of your successors living in canonical integrity. For this is believed to have been established by our predecessors, the pontiffs of the Holy Roman Church, at the petition of Blessed Germanus, whose patrimony the diocese of Auxerre had been.

If, therefore, any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowing this page of our constitution, should rashly attempt to act against it, and, having been warned a second or third time, does not make due amends by suitable satisfaction, [Col. 0218B] let that person be deprived of the dignity of power and honour; let him know himself guilty before the divine judgment of the iniquity committed; let him be cut off from the most sacred Body and Blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, our Redeemer; and let him be subject to severe vengeance at the last judgment. But upon all who preserve what is right for the same place, may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that here they may receive the fruit of good works and before the strict Judge may find the rewards of eternal peace. Amen, amen.

CCXX. Privilege for the monastery on the island of Agensis. (1107, 30 May.)

[ARCERE, *History of La Rochelle*, Proofs, vol. II, p. 637.]

[Col. 0218C]

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son WILLIAM, prior of the monastery of Blessed Martin on the island of Aya, in the diocese of Saintes, and to his successors regularly appointed: perpetual peace.

It is fitting to grant ready assent to religious desires, so that faithful devotion may attain a swift result. Therefore, most dear son in Christ, considering the reasonable object of your desire, we have graciously received your petitions and decree that the cell of Blessed Martin, over which you preside by the appointment of our brother Hugh, abbot of Cluny, shall always adhere, together with the whole island itself, to the monastery of Cluny as a member to its head, as it is known to have been offered by William, count of Poitou, of blessed memory, and the knight Isembert. [Col. 0218D] We also decree that all things belonging today to that cell through the above-mentioned offering of these men and of other faithful persons, through the grant of pontiffs, the generosity of princes, or other lawful means, and whatever may hereafter be bestowed there by the Lord’s gift, shall always remain firm and unimpaired.

We further decree that the burial-place of the same house shall be entirely free, and that no one shall obstruct the devotion and final will of those who choose to be buried there, unless they are excommunicated. We therefore decree [Col. 0219A] that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb this monastery, take away its possessions, retain those taken away, unjustly claim for his own use things granted to it, diminish them, or harass it with reckless vexations; but that all things be preserved whole for the use and benefit, in every respect, of those for whose support they were granted.

If, therefore, any ecclesiastical or secular person in the future, knowing this page of our constitution, should rashly attempt to act against it, and, having been warned a second or third time, does not make due amends by suitable satisfaction, let that person be deprived of the dignity of power and honour; let him know himself guilty before the divine judgment of the iniquity committed; let him be cut off from the most sacred Body and Blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, our Redeemer; and let him be subject at the last judgment to severe [Col. 0219B] vengeance. But upon all who preserve what is right for the same place, may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that here they may receive the fruit of good works and before the strict Judge may find the rewards of eternal peace.

I, Paschal, bishop of the Catholic Church.

Given at Clamitiacum, through the hand of John, secretary of the Roman Church, cardinal-deacon and librarian, on the third day before the Kalends of June [30 May], in the fourteenth indiction, in the year 1107 of the Lord’s Incarnation.

CCXXI. To Anselm, bishop of Canterbury.—He permits Anselm to promote sons of priests to holy orders and to receive Abbot Richard into communion; he entrusts other dispensations to him as circumstances require. (1107, 30 May.)

[MANSI, *Councils*, XX, 1063.]

[Col. 0219C]

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother ANSELM, bishop of Canterbury: greeting and apostolic blessing.

We do not believe that your brotherhood is unaware what has been established in the Roman Church concerning the sons of priests. But since in the kingdom of the English there is so great a multitude of such persons that almost the larger and better part of the clergy is counted in this category, we entrust this dispensation to your care. We permit those whom learning and [Col. 0219D] life commend among you to be promoted to sacred offices, according to the necessity of the time and the benefit of the Church, provided that prejudice to the ecclesiastical constitution be avoided in the future.

Concerning the person of Richard, abbot of Ely, at the request of our sons King Henry and William of Warelwast, we permit you, after satisfaction has first been made, to receive him into your communion; and, if his person appears suitable for the government of the monastery, we entrust this to your dispensation. Likewise, let the care of your wisdom and religious devotion dispense whatever else in that kingdom must be dispensed because of the necessity of the time, according to the barbarism of the people and according to the needs of the Church.

Given on the third day before the Kalends of June [30 May].

CCXXII. Bull confirming the exemption, already granted by a bull of Pope Nicholas II, of the monastery of Corbiniacum from subjection to Flavigny. (1107, 31 May.)

[*Gallia Christiana*, IV, Documents, 85.]

[Col. 0220A]

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son HUGH, abbot, and the brethren of the monastery of Corbiniacum: greeting and apostolic blessing.

The authority of our office urges us to be concerned for the condition of churches and to make firm what has been rightly established. Therefore we have graciously received your petition, in order to free your monastery from the attacks of the monks of Flavigny. For we have seen [Col. 0220B] the determination of our venerable brothers Bishops Hugh and Amatus, who were then exercising the legation of the Apostolic See in the regions of Gaul, which they issued concerning this matter at the Council of Exoldunum. Having heard the allegations of both sides and inspected the letters and evidentiary documents produced by each party, they decreed by sentence of the council that the monks of Flavigny, who were attempting to reduce your monastery to a cell, must altogether desist henceforth from this harassment. Having received the abbot of Flavigny’s renunciation into their hands, they fortified that determination with their own subscriptions and with the names of many bishops who had been present.

Therefore we too, as the evidence of letters shows that our predecessor Pope Nicholas of holy memory decreed, remove entirely from your monastery by the confirmation of this present decree this claim of the monks of Flavigny, and command that, once suppressed, it shall cease for ever. Further, if the bishop of Autun, to whose jurisdiction your place belongs by parochial right, persists in inflicting any burdens upon you, we grant you free right of recourse to the Apostolic See. If anyone should stubbornly presume to act against these provisions, let him be punished by the vengeance of apostolic indignation. You therefore, beloved sons in Christ, strive always to keep the fear and love of God in your hearts, so that, the freer you are from secular disturbances, the more earnestly you may strive to please God with the powers of your whole mind and soul.

[Col. 0220D] I, Paschal, bishop of the Catholic Church, have subscribed.

Given at Lupertiacum, through the hand of John, cardinal-deacon and librarian of the Holy Roman Church, on the second day before the Kalends of June [31 May], in the fifteenth indiction, in the year 1107 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the eighth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Paschal II.

CCXXIII. To Hugh, Abbot of Cluny.—He adjudges to the Cluniacs the cell of Saint-Denis of Nogent, against William, Abbot of Saint-Pierre of Chartres. (6 June 1107.)

[MANSI, *Councils*, XX, 1040.]

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother HUGH, Abbot of Cluny, greeting and apostolic blessing.

[Col. 0221A] Matters once justly and reasonably decided are often reopened in renewed lawsuits through negligent forgetfulness. Therefore, by the present letter we record how the dispute between the monks of your monastery and William, Abbot of Saint Peter of Chartres, concerning Saint-Denis of Nogent, was resolved upon its renewed presentation. For the same Abbot of Chartres, after the decree of Pope Lord Urban, was assailing your brethren with legal claims concerning that same cell, while we presided at the council of Troyes. Therefore, lest any spark of contention remain, we judged that everything brought forward by either side should be examined.

Certain letters were accordingly produced by the Abbot of Chartres, by which that place had been entrusted to the monks of Chartres by Count Retroccus [corrected: Joffridus] under a certain condition. [Col. 0221B] These contained no date and no assent either of a bishop or of clerics. In response, Count Retroccus, son of Joffridus himself—the man who, together with his wife Beatrice, had offered that place to your monastery—asserted that those letters must be considered forged. For one of the subscribing witnesses, the brother of the aforesaid Joffridus, still living, utterly denied that he had been present at all; and he reported that those same letters had at another time been forged in the chapter of Chartres, producing in public, under oath, a witness of that forgery.

On the other hand, Count Joffridus’s grant to your monastery more clearly specified the place, the time, the consent of the bishop and metropolitan, and the favour of Count Theobald and his son Stephen, from whose fief the same place was held. [Col. 0221C] It was thus agreed by all that the decree of Pope Lord Urban rested upon the full weight of apostolic authority. Accordingly, by judicial decision the complaint of the Abbot of Chartres was silenced, and perpetual possession of the aforesaid cell was established for your monastery.

The venerable bishops Leodegar of Bourges, Aldo of Piacenza, Gerard of Angoulême, Hildebert of Le Mans, and Landulf, cardinal of our holy Roman Church, of the title of Saint Lawrence called “in Lucina,” were present with us at this judgment. Therefore we also add the force of our own sanction to the sanction of our predecessor, commanding and strictly forbidding anyone henceforth to presume to disturb your Cluniac monastery [Col. 0221D] concerning this matter. Whoever presumes to do so shall be punished by the censure of canonical discipline.

I, Paschal, bishop of the Catholic Church, have subscribed.

Given at Silviniacum through the hand of John, deacon of the holy Roman Church, on the eighth day before the Kalends of June [25 May], indiction XV, in the year 1107 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and the eighth year of the pontificate of Pope Lord Paschal II.

CCXXIV. He grants a bull to Hugh, Abbot of Saint-Germain of Auxerre. (9 June 1107.)

[Mention only survives in MABILLON, *Annals of the Benedictine Order*, V, 501.]

CCXXV. To Richard, Archbishop of Narbonne.—He confirms the possessions and rights of the Church of Narbonne. (13 July 1107.)

[MANSI, *Councils*, XX, 1025.]

[Col. 0222A]

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother RICHARD, bishop of the first see of Narbonne, and to his successors to be canonically installed in perpetuity.

It is a proper gift of charity to provide for the advancement of others. For charity “does not seek its own” (1 Cor. 13). Hence also the Apostle says: “Now we live, if you stand firm in the Lord” (1 Thess. 3); and again: “For what is our hope, or joy, or crown of glory? Is it not you before our Lord [Col. 0222B] Jesus Christ?” (1 Thess. 2). We are therefore moved by this debt of charity, and compelled by the authority of the Apostolic See, to render due honour to our brethren and to impart to the other Churches, each according to its condition, the dignity of the holy Roman Church.

Therefore, venerable brother Richard, Archbishop of Narbonne, by the page of this decree we confirm to you and your successors whatever parishes are known by ancient right to belong to the Church of Narbonne, the first see. Furthermore, within those parishes we decree that you and your successors shall hold, govern, and administer by right of ownership: the church of Saint Paul with all its appurtenances; the town of Caput Stagni; Salas; Aruscadas; Argens; Fontem Iocosum; Auriac; Villam Rubeam; Segionum; [Col. 0222C] and all other estates, cells, and possessions which have been offered, whether by kings or by other faithful persons, to the church of the holy martyrs Justus and Pastor, both in the county of Narbonne and in those of Béziers, Rhedae, Substantion, and Nîmes.

Within the city of Narbonne itself, we confirm one half of the county, one half of the toll, port-dues, *rasica*, saltworks, and the other revenues exacted by the count of the city from both maritime and land merchants. In monasteries and other churches throughout the Church of Narbonne, saving the authority of the Apostolic See, we permit you to exercise canonical jurisdiction.

We further decree that the episcopal sees belonging to your metropolitan jurisdiction—namely Béziers, Carcassonne, Toulouse, [Col. 0222D] Elne, Agde, Lodève, Maguelonne, Nîmes, and Uzès—shall remain subject to you and your successors in perpetuity and shall preserve their due obedience. We also confirm to you the primacy over Second Narbonensis, that is, the metropolitan see of Aix, as established by our predecessors; and we decree that whatever belongs by ancient right to the oft-mentioned Church of Narbonne shall remain forever ratified and inviolate.

We therefore decree that no one may rashly disturb that Church, take away its possessions, retain possessions taken away, diminish them, or harass it by reckless vexations; but that all things shall be preserved whole, for the benefit in every respect of those for whose support and governance they were granted. If, therefore, any ecclesiastical or secular person hereafter, knowing this page [Col. 0223A] of our constitution, rashly attempts to act against it, and, after a second or third admonition, fails to make fitting amends, let that person lose the dignity of authority and honour; let that person know himself or herself liable before divine judgment for the iniquity committed; let that person be cut off from the most sacred Body and Blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ the Redeemer; and let that person be subject at the last judgment to strict vengeance. But upon all who preserve the rights of that same Church may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that they may receive here the fruit of good action and find before the strict Judge the rewards of eternal peace. Amen.

I, Paschal, bishop of the Catholic Church, have subscribed.

[Col. 0223B] Given at Privas, through the hand of John, cardinal-deacon and librarian of the holy Roman Church, on the third day before the Ides of July [13 July], in the year 1107 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and the eighth year of the pontificate of Pope Lord Paschal II.

CCXXVI. To the Abbot of Saint-Pons and the Abbot of Elne.—That they are not to receive persons excommunicated by the Archbishop of Narbonne. (1107.)

[MANSI, *Councils*, XX, 1026.]

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to P. . . . . . , Abbot of Saint-Pons, to R., Abbot of Elne, and to the other monks, greeting and apostolic blessing.

Our brother Richard, metropolitan of Narbonne, [Col. 0223C] complains against your beloved community that you receive into communion and participation, before their absolution, persons whom he has excommunicated or placed under interdict. Yet not only you but even laymen know that it is wicked and contrary to the canons to communicate with those under interdict or excommunication and thereby become entangled in their sins. At the council which we celebrated at Troyes, following the decrees of the holy Fathers, we forbade bishops, abbots, and all other clerics henceforth to receive in their own dioceses persons excommunicated or interdicted by another. Therefore, lest you appear contemptuous of our command, we order you to cease altogether from such conduct, lest you be bound by the bond of excommunication.

CCXXVII. To the Monks of Saint-Gilles.—He announces that he has absolved Count Bertrand after he repaired the damages inflicted upon the monastery of Saint-Gilles. (25 July 1107.)

[D. BOUQUET, *Recueil*, XV, 38.]

[Col. 0223D]

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons, the monks of Saint-Gilles, greeting and apostolic blessing.

Because of the oppressions inflicted upon your monastery and town, we long restrained Count Bertrand by the severity of anathema. At length, when he came to us, in the presence of your abbot Hugh, the brethren, and the burgesses who had come with him, we caused the charter of Count Raymond to be read in his hearing. [Col. 0224A] In that charter, his father, Count Raymond, is said to have relinquished all the rights of Saint-Gilles which he appeared to hold, whether justly or unjustly, both in your town called Flaviana and outside it—namely, all lawful or unlawful customary exactions which he or his predecessors had held there—and to have granted full jurisdiction to Abbot Odilo of blessed memory and the brethren then with him, through the hand of our predecessor Pope Urban at the Council of Nîmes.

In the same terms, he too relinquished into our hand all rights over Blessed Giles and the customs of your borough; and he completely remitted to your abbot, to the burgesses, and to all their helpers through whom those injuries were inflicted, whatever damages or other wrongs had befallen him in the war which he had waged against you and your burgesses. Thus we absolved him from the bond of excommunication.

Done at the cell of Saint Marcellus [Note: [Col. 0223D] The cell of Saint Marcellus was in the diocese of Valence; Paschal was staying there in July 1107.], on the eighth day before the Kalends of August [25 July], indiction XV, in the presence of Bishops Eustace of Valence, Berengar of Béziers, and Leodegar of Viviers; Cardinals Landulf, priest, and John and Berard, deacons, of the Roman Church; and Bertrand’s nobles, William Hugh of Montilius, William of Sabrano, Bermund Pelet, Pons of Medenas, Rostagnus of the Port, and the burgesses Pagan, Causitus, and Count Bertrand, knight, of Poscheriis.

CCXXVIII. Decree for the district of Salmoriacum. (2 August 1107.)

[D. BOUQUET, *Recueil*, vol. XIV, p. 957.]

[Col. 0224C]

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, etc.

For many years, and in many councils, a dispute concerning the district of Salmoriacum was debated between our venerable brethren Guy, Archbishop of Vienne, and Hugh, Bishop of Grenoble. Most recently, before our presence at Lyons, they reached the following agreement through the provision of our judgment: they were to make an equal division of the said district, and the portion of the division nearer to each was to be assigned respectively to the Churches of Vienne and Grenoble.

Whatever the Archbishop of Vienne claimed in the territory lying between the Bourne and the Isère toward Grenoble [Col. 0224D] was henceforth to pass to the Church of Grenoble free from every claim. Moreover, the Bishop of Grenoble was to possess by right of ownership the church of Blessed Donatus, situated within the diocese of Vienne, with all movable and immovable property belonging to it; he was to administer both the canonries of that church and everything belonging to it. The bishop of Vienne, however, was to exercise only parochial right in the consecration of clerics and altars.

By equal and common consent, therefore, the district of Salmoriacum was divided as follows: eleven castles, with their churches, parishes, and all their jurisdictions, were assigned to the Church of Vienne; and eleven castles, with their churches, parishes, and all their jurisdictions, to the Church of Grenoble. The castles set apart as the portion of the Church of Vienne are: the castle of Saint-Georges, Brissiacum, the castle of Vetus Villa, the castle of Orniciacum, the castle of Bonocellum, the castle of Leemps, the castle of Planilla, the castle of Clermont, the castle of Saint-Lorius, the castle of Paladrudum, and the castle of Vireu. The following fell to the portion of the Church of Grenoble: the castle of Vinniacum, the castle of Nerpoicum, the New Castle, the castle of Tullinum, the castle of Ruens, the castle of Moirencum, the castle of Vorione, the castle of Tuluwis, the castle of Miribellum, the castle of Minuetum, Scalis, the castle of Vorapium; and, in addition, the church belonging to the chancellor, with its whole parish. [Col. 0225B]

Thus, by the Lord’s bounty, the long duration of the aforesaid dispute was brought to an end, and the stability of peace and concord between the Churches of Vienne and Grenoble and their bishops—both agreeing to this—was established. By the Lord’s bounty we confirm that stability to endure forever, commanding and decreeing in every way that the part which, as written above, has passed to the Church of Vienne or Grenoble shall always belong to its diocese; and that absolutely no person may ever withdraw from Vienne its designated portion or from Grenoble its designated portion.

If either party, without due consideration, brings a dispute or violence against the other, then, according to the condition by which each bound himself in the judgment, let that party lose possession of the portion received and henceforth lose absolutely every right of action in the same matter. Furthermore, it has been commanded, and we confirm the command by repeated injunction, that the bishop of Vienne may no longer demand peace-money, *communitas*, or any exaction in that portion belonging to the Church of Grenoble, otherwise than in the dioceses of Riez or Viviers belonging to the metropolitan see of Vienne. Present at the judgment and agreement made at Lyons on the fourth day before the Kalends of February [29 January] were the venerable bishops Richard of Albano, Aldo of Piacenza, Potius of Le Puy, Leodegar of Viviers, Guy of Geneva, Eustace of Valence, Cono of Maurienne, and Count Guigo of Albon.

[Col. 0225D] Given through the hand of John, cardinal-deacon and librarian of the holy Roman Church, at the church of Saint Peter of Alaverdus, on the fourth day before the Nones of August [2 August], indiction XV, in the year 1107 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and the eighth year of the pontificate of Pope Lord Paschal II.

CCXXIX. To Hugh, Abbot of Cluny.—He subjects to him for reform the abbey of Saint-Wulmar; its abbots are forever to be appointed by the abbots of Cluny. Any monk may transfer to the monastery of Cluny. (4 August 1107.)

[MANSI, *Councils*, XX, 1040.]

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable [Col. 0226A] brother HUGH, Abbot of Cluny, greeting and apostolic blessing.

A desire shown to concern religious purpose and the salvation of souls ought, by God’s agency, to be fulfilled without delay. Our venerable brother John, Bishop of the Morini, at the request of Count Eustace of Boulogne, entrusted the abbey of Saint-Wulmar to your care, dearest brother Hugh, for reform. Therefore, in accordance with his wish and decision, we decree by the force of this present act that the monastery of Blessed Wulmar shall always remain under the governance of you and your successors, and that no other abbot shall be installed there except one chosen by your decision.

We establish the same concerning the monastery of Menat, which has now long remained under your governance. Furthermore, because almighty God has deigned, both before our time and in our days, to preserve in your monastery an outstanding discipline of monastic religion, we grant you this privilege: whenever a monk of another monastery transfers to you for the improvement of his life, let him be received freely, all complaints of his former house set aside, so that, by the Lord’s bounty, he may attain among you the result of the salvation he appears to seek. If anyone presumptuously attempts to oppose these saving ordinances, let that person be punished by the vengeance of apostolic indignation and suffer exclusion from ecclesiastical communion.

I, Paschal, bishop of the Catholic Church, have subscribed.

[Col. 0226C] Given at Aquambella through the hand of John, cardinal-deacon and librarian of the holy Roman Church, on the second day before the Nones of August [4 August], indiction XV, in the year 1107 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and the ninth year of the pontificate of Pope Lord Paschal II.

CCXXX. *He grants certain privileges to the monastery of Saint Benedict of Polirone. (1 September 1107.)

[See BACCHINI, *On the History of the Monastery of Saint Benedict of Polirone*, Modena, 1696, quarto, collection, p. 68.]

CCXXXI. At the request of Bishop Rangerius, he confirms the privileges of the Church of Lucca. (18 September 1107.)

[BALUZE, *Miscellanea*, Lucca edition, IV, 187.]

[Col. 0226D]

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother RANGERIO, Bishop of Lucca, and to his successors to be canonically promoted in perpetuity.

It is fitting that we grant assent to just wishes and lend an ear to just petitions, since, though unworthy, we are, by the Lord’s disposition, set as guardians and heralds of justice in the lofty apostolic watchtower of the blessed Peter and Paul. Therefore, venerable brother and most dear fellow bishop Rangerius in Christ, acceding to your just requests, we strengthen by the authority of the Apostolic See the holy Church of Lucca, over which by God’s agency you preside.

We decree that all parish churches throughout the diocese of Lucca shall always remain in the obedience and governance of you and your successors who remain in communion with the Apostolic See. Nor shall any person have the power to remove churches situated within or outside the city of Lucca from their customary service to you, or to withdraw chapels of parish churches from their unity and subjection. We strictly forbid anyone hereafter, whether cleric or monk, to receive a chapel or church from the hand of a layman, since the property of a church or churches must, in accordance with canonical sanctions, be kept under episcopal supervision.

Moreover, because, according to the Apostle’s saying, “the labouring husbandman must first partake of the fruits,” we confirm to you and your successors labouring in pastoral care the shares of altar and sacristy, so that, free from the opposition or harassment of any persons, you may possess forever for the support of yourselves and of guests the shares of offerings made at the altars of the mother church, at the shrine of the Holy Face (*Vultus Sacrarium*), or in parish churches, just as your predecessors, the bishops of many generations, are known to have possessed those shares quietly and peacefully. [Col. 0227B]

If, therefore, hereafter any bishop or abbot, emperor or king, prince or duke, count, viscount, castald, or any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowing this page of our grant, rashly attempts to act against it, and, after a second or third admonition, fails to make fitting amends, let that person lose the dignity of authority and honour; let that person know himself or herself liable before divine judgment for the iniquity committed; let that person be cut off from the most sacred Body and Blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ the Redeemer; and let that person be subject at the last judgment to strict vengeance. But upon all who preserve the rights of the aforesaid Church of Lucca may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that they may receive here the fruit of good action and find before the strict Judge the rewards of eternal peace. Amen.

I, Paschal, bishop of the Catholic Church.

Given at Fiesole through the hand of John, cardinal-deacon and librarian of the holy Roman Church, on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of October [18 September], indiction I, in the year 1107 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and the ninth year of the pontificate [Col. 0227D] of Pope Lord Paschal II.

CCXXXII. *He confirms certain privileges of Gregory the archdeacon, Hubert the archpriest, Raynerius the primicerius, Guy the cantor, and the brethren of the Church of Lucca. (18 September 1107.)

[See *Memoirs and Documents Serving the History of the Principality of Lucca*, Lucca, 1813, quarto, V, I, 378.]

CCXXXIII. To John, Abbot of Florence.—Privilege of the Florentine monastery. (24 September 1107.)

[MANSI, *Councils*, XX, 1052.]

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son JOHN, Abbot of the Florentine monastery called Saint [Col. 0228A] Mary, and to his successors to be regularly promoted in perpetuity.

A devout petition should be brought to the effect of its wish, etc. Moreover, whatever that monastery today possesses through the grant of pontiffs, the liberality of princes, the offerings of the faithful, or other just means, or may hereafter justly and canonically acquire, shall remain firm and unimpaired for you and your successors. We also grant you and your successors who remain in monastic religion the tithes of your labours, to be held free from any opposition.

You shall receive the consecration of altars and churches, and the ordination of monks or clerics belonging to the monastery, from the Bishop of Florence, provided that he remains in the favour of the Apostolic See [Col. 0228B] and is willing to provide these things freely and without burdensome exaction. Otherwise, you may approach whichever Catholic bishop you choose and receive from him the sacraments of consecration, provided that, supported by the authority of the Apostolic See, he grants what you request.

Moreover, we remove all jurisdiction of bishops and episcopal officers from the churches and clerics of that monastery. We also decree that the burial-place of the same house shall be altogether free, so that no one may obstruct the devotion and final wish of those desiring burial there, unless they are excommunicated. If, therefore, any ecclesiastical or secular person, etc.

I, Paschal, bishop of the Catholic Church.

Given at Florence through the hand of John, cardinal-deacon and librarian of the holy Roman Church, in the year [Col. 0228C] 1108 of the Lord’s Incarnation, on the eighth day before the Kalends of October [24 September], indiction I, in the ninth year of the pontificate of Pope Lord Paschal II.

CCXXXIV. Bull of Pope Paschal II.—Privilege for the nunnery of Saint Peter of Luco. (3 October 1107.)

[MITTABELLI, *Annals of Camaldoli*, III, appendix, 204.]

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved daughter BEATRICE, abbess of the monastery of Saint Peter, situated near the town of Luco in the diocese of Florence, and to her successors to be regularly installed in perpetuity.

The Lord commands through the prophet that those dwelling in the land of the south meet the fugitive with bread. [Col. 0228D] Therefore, dearest daughters, we gladly receive you as you flee from the world and cherish you through the grace of the Holy Spirit under the protection of the Apostolic See. We decree that whatever estates and goods that monastery now possesses through the offering of Gothidius, a man of blessed memory, and the grant of Rudolph, Prior of Camaldoli, or may hereafter, by the grant of pontiffs, the liberality of princes, or the offerings of the faithful, by the Lord’s bounty justly and canonically acquire, shall remain firm and unimpaired for you and those who succeed you.

Among these, the following seemed fit to be stated by their proper names: a portion of the town of Luco with its appurtenances; a portion of the estate of Larciano with its appurtenances; a portion of Contanceruto; of Rivo Frigido with its appurtenances; [Col. 0229A] and of Rivo Cornoclaria with its appurtenances; a portion of the estate of Castro; and of the estates of Silva and Frena with their appurtenances. Within the city of Florence: one house beside the church of Saint P. . . . . ., another beside the church of Saint Donatus, and other properties which you acquired at your monastery’s expense in the territory of that city.

We also grant you forever the tithes of your labours, free from opposition by the bishop or episcopal officers. We decree that no one whatever may rashly disturb the same monastery, take away its possessions, retain possessions taken away, diminish them, or harass it by reckless vexations; but that all things shall be preserved whole, for the benefit in every respect of those for whose support and governance they were granted.

Moreover, [Col. 0229B] the place itself shall always remain under the supervision of the Prior of Camaldoli. Neither the bishop nor his officers may excommunicate, place under interdict, or harass in any matter the community of that place or its priests, unless they have first sought out the Prior of Camaldoli in a spirit of charity. If, therefore, any ecclesiastical or secular person hereafter, knowing this page of ours, rashly attempts to act against it, and, after a first, second, and third admonition, does not make fitting amends, let that person incur excommunication, lose the dignity of authority and honour, know himself or herself liable before divine judgment for the iniquity committed, be cut off from the most sacred Body and Blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, and be subject at the last judgment to strict vengeance. But upon all who preserve what is just for that community may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that they may receive here the fruit of good action and find before the strict Judge the rewards of eternal peace. Amen, amen, amen.

I, Paschal, bishop of the Catholic Church.

Given at Bibbiena through the hands of John, cardinal-deacon and librarian of the holy Roman Church, on the fifth day before the Nones of October [3 October], indiction I, in the year 1107 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and the ninth year of the pontificate of Pope Lord Paschal II.

CCXXXV. To Daimbert, Archbishop of Sens.—He entrusts to him for judgment the case of two abbots. (23 October 1107.)

[MANSI, *Councils*, XX, 1016.]

[Col. 0229D]

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother DAIMBERT, Archbishop of the Church of Sens, greeting and apostolic blessing.

The greater the care of souls entrusted to you, the more attentive you must be in all things. Watch therefore, dearest brother, like a good shepherd over the Lord’s flock, so that you may present it to the Lord in such a condition as both pleases him and shows you worthy of a good reward. Your end approaches daily; and although this is certain to all, the last day is nevertheless uncertain. Therefore be always vigilant; and if perhaps you have at some time conducted yourself negligently, [Col. 0230A] now strive through God’s grace to amend everything, so that when the Lord comes he may find you watchful and so prepared that you may deserve to be received into the glory of eternal life.

Render due justice in the complaint which the Abbot of Virziliacum brings against the Abbot of Fleury concerning a certain church. For we do not wish any Church to suffer prejudice under the pretext of privileges [probably: “so that any Church may suffer prejudice under the pretext of privileges,” II].

Given at Tifernum, on the tenth day before the Kalends of November [23 October].

CCXXXVI. To the clergy, King [Baldwin], and people of the Church of Jerusalem. (4 December 1107.)

[Eugène DE ROZIÈRE, *Cartulary of the Holy Sepulchre*, Paris, Imprimerie nationale, 1849, p. 8.]

[Col. 0230B] PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the clergy of the Church of Jerusalem, to King B[ALDWIN], and to the people, greeting and apostolic blessing.

We are grieved all the more vehemently by the scandals in your Church because, owing to the great distances between places, we are less able to attend to their remedy—especially since the city of Jerusalem is distinguished by the reverence due to the Lord’s Sepulchre and is situated among many nations, some of which endeavour to mock the Christian faith and others the customs of Latin purity. Your Church was first thrown into disorder over Daibert and afterwards over Evremar.

For it is known that a most bitter conspiracy was formed against Daibert of blessed memory, our brother and fellow bishop; to decide that matter we sent the legate of our See, Robert, cardinal-priest. Then indeed a sentence of deposition was pronounced against the same bishop because he seemed to have defaulted in the judgment. But that brother, coming to the Apostolic See, confessed that he had not defaulted but had been driven away by fear of the king; therefore he pursued judgment before us. Meanwhile, we learned that Evremar had been chosen, with the favour of our legate, to govern the bishopric among you.

Having received Daibert’s satisfaction in the Lateran Church, we restored him by synodal judgment to his office and to the see of Jerusalem; but we removed Evremar from the see of Jerusalem, while reserving to him episcopal office, because he seemed to have succeeded, with the assent of our legate, to what was a vacant place. Nevertheless, this concession was reserved for Evremar: if he should be called by some vacant Church, or if after Daibert’s death he should be requested by the Church of Jerusalem, he was to exercise episcopal office there. [Col. 0230D]

But before this judgment of our authority could be notified to you by letters, our fellow brother Daibert was taken from this light at the Lord’s summons. Recently, moreover, the aforesaid brother Evremar and Arnulf, archdeacon of your Church, with some others, came into our presence, bringing many varied and highly discordant letters. Evremar brought letters from the chapter, bishops, and king, asking and requesting that, by granting him the pallium and a privilege, we should confirm him by authority of the Apostolic See as bishop of the see of Jerusalem. The letters of Archdeacon Arnulf, which he presented as sent by the chapter, bishops, and king, on the contrary requested unequivocally that we should remove Evremar entirely from the Church of Jerusalem as useless and as a contemner of the synodal judgment.

No less disagreement and contention appeared in the statements of either party. Evremar made complaint against the archdeacon and those with him that they were disobedient to him, although after Daibert’s death and after the council’s judgment had become known they had accepted him as father and bishop. There was also great disagreement between them about the date of the letters. Evremar asserted, in support of his claim, that the letters which he had brought had been given to him after Daibert’s death and after the council’s judgment was known, by the king, the chapter, and the others whose names were written in them. His opponents, on the other hand, maintained that the letters had been given before the synodal judgment was certainly known; they declared that, after certain knowledge of that judgment, neither they nor the other brethren of the chapter had rendered him any subjection or obedience as their bishop, but rather that both they and the king had pressed him to depart from the Jerusalem cathedra, as appeared in the letters of the king and others which they had brought. [Col. 0231B]

After this prolonged contention, by the Lord’s inspiration and with the counsel of the brethren present with us, the following judgment was pronounced: Evremar was to produce witnesses who would swear upon holy things that, after certain knowledge of the synodal judgment, the Church of Jerusalem had elected him bishop and had given him the letters which he brought. For according to the terms of the judgment, they were free either to retain him, if they wished, or not to retain him, if they did not wish. But because neither Evremar’s party seemed able sufficiently to establish this nor the opposing party to disprove it, it seemed good to us that the final determination of this matter should be deferred until all of you were present, where, by God’s grace, what was actually done and what rests upon truth cannot remain hidden.

For knowledge of the case and its certain resolution, we are sending our legate to your Church. Thus the following judgment has been established by us and our brethren: if among you it is certainly established that, after certain knowledge of our synodal judgment, you elected him together in chapter [Col. 0231C]—that is, at the Church’s request and in response to the request contained in the letters which you sent us through him—then henceforth you ought wholly to obey him as your bishop. But if it is established that matters proceeded otherwise, he shall henceforth withdraw from the Church of Jerusalem. For then you were free either to retain him if you wished or not to retain him if you did not wish; now, however, for the sake of scandal to the Church, if he was rejected then, he is permitted to preside over you; but by God’s grace and with a common vote and common counsel, choose in accordance with the canons a canonical pastor.

If, however, there is contrary disagreement among the parties on this point, our brother Evremar, in accordance with the tenor of the judgment set forth above, shall establish the certainty of his assertion by oath with seven suitable witnesses.

[Col. 0232A] Given at the Lateran, on the second day before the Nones of December [4 December], indiction I, through the hand of John, deacon.

CCXXXVII. *He subjects certain monasteries to the monastery of La Chaise-Dieu. (5 December 1107.)

[Mention only of this privilege survives in MABILLON, *Annals of the Benedictine Order*, V, 453 and 501.]

CCXXXVIII. He commands Anselm, Archbishop of Canterbury, to judge the marriage of Count Robert, held captive by the King of England. (1107.)

[Anselm of Canterbury, *Works*, Letters, book IV, letter 83.]

PASCHAL, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother Anselm, Archbishop of Canterbury, greeting and [Col. 0232B] apostolic blessing.

We give thanks to almighty God because, through your many labours, the darkness having been driven from the English Church, its ancient light has shone forth again. Yet care must be taken lest, in the Lord’s field, the enemy cast tares upon the good seed, and lest an evil root produce an evil shoot. We have learned, moreover, that a certain Count Robert, who is held captive by the king of England, married a wife under the prohibition of consanguinity, whom her relatives sent back to the aforesaid count. We therefore command your belovedness to summon that count; and, if you find these things to be true, having employed suitable witnesses, to arrange the matter so wisely that, freed from their sins, both may be able freely to serve God. [Col. 0232C] May your belovedness pray for us.

CCXXXIX. Privilege for the Church of Saint Martin. (Year 1107.)

[MEICHELBECK, *Historia Frisingensis*, Augsburg and Vienna, 1729, folio, I, I, 293.]

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son DICTERAMUS and his brethren, professing the canonical life in the monastery of Blessed Martin: for ever.

It is fitting for us to grant assent to just desires and to lend an ear to just petitions—we who, although unworthy, are seen, by the Lord’s ordering, to have been placed as guardians and heralds of justice upon the lofty watchtower of the chief apostles Peter and Paul. For Udascalchus, [Col. 0232D] abbot of Tegernsee, for the increase of religious life, resolved, through the Lord’s bounty, to maintain from the possessions of his monastery a community of regular brethren, called canons, in the place named the cell of Saint Martin. Therefore, recognizing the just vow and pious desire of that abbot and his monks, we confirm by the favour of this present decree what has been established by them.

For we protect, under the safeguard of the Apostolic See, that cell itself and the community of canons there assembled or yet to be assembled, decreeing that whatever lands and whatever goods have been granted by right to that place itself, whether by the aforesaid abbot of the monastery of Tegernsee or by other faithful persons, and likewise whatever may hereafter happen justly to be given or offered there through the grant of pontiffs, the liberality of princes, [Col. 0233A] or the offerings of the faithful, shall remain secure and unimpaired for you and your successors. We decree, therefore, that absolutely no person may rashly disturb that church, carry off its possessions, retain what has been carried off, diminish them, or harass it with reckless vexations; but let all be preserved whole, for the benefit in every way of the uses of those for whose support and governance they have been granted, saving the canonical reverence due to the bishop of Freising.

We also grant to you and your successors, notwithstanding any opposition from episcopal officers, that you may possess the tithes of your newly cleared lands. Certainly, after the profession has been made, none of you may possess anything as his own, nor leave the cloister without permission of the provost of the community, so that, by the Lord’s bounty, you may remain steadfast for ever in the purpose which you have undertaken. If, therefore, any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowing this charter of our constitution, should rashly attempt to act against it, then, after a second or third warning, unless he makes suitable amends by satisfaction, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and honour; let him know himself to be guilty before the divine judgment for the iniquity committed; let him be cut off from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord, Redeemer Jesus Christ; and at the final judgment let him be subject to strict vengeance. But upon all who preserve what is just for that place may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that here they may receive the fruit of good action and, before the strict Judge, find the rewards of eternal [Col. 0233C] peace. Amen.

These things were enacted in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1107, in the eighth year of Pope Paschal II.

CCXL. To Adelgot, Archbishop of Magdeburg.—He summons him to the Apostolic See to render an account of an offence committed. (Year 1107.)

[MANSI, *Concilia*, XX, 1223.]

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to ADELGOT, [Note: [Col. 0233D] The Paderborn annals report that he was by birth Count of Loe: a man of great generosity toward the poor and of devotion toward God; by his steadfastness toward the Apostolic See, an ornament of Saxony. He died in 1119. MARTENE.] Archbishop of Magdeburg: greeting and apostolic blessing.

The more abundantly we love you, the more vehemently are we astonished at your offence: namely, that after the promulgation of a synodal injunction you are seen to have been the first to incur transgression. We believe that correction of this transgression cannot otherwise be made unless you yourself come into the presence of the Apostolic See. Therefore, by the present letter, we admonish your belovedness to present yourself before us [Col. 0234A] at such fitting time as seems good to you, so that what has been wounded in you may, through the mercy of almighty God, be healed by the remedy of the Apostolic See.

CCXLI. To Bruno, Archbishop of Trier.—He entrusts to him the absolution of the Bishop of Liège from excommunication. (Year 1107, November 11.)

[HONTHEIM, *Historia Trevirensis*, I, 488.]

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable fellow-brother BRUNO, Archbishop of Trier: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Our brother, the Bishop of Liège, [Note: [Col. 0233D] This was Obertus, of whom the author of the *History of the Monastery of Andage*, in Martène’s *Collectio Amplissima*, vol. IV, p. 974, writes: “Hardly had the death of Henry, bishop of Liège, been heard when Obertus, without an ecclesiastical election, extorted the episcopate from the hand of King Henry IV [Col. 0234D], by the greatest promised rewards, and moreover gave him fealty under oath.” For these crimes Obertus had incurred excommunication.] having sent an embassy to us, humbly sought fellowship in our communion. Knowing the will of the Lord, [Col. 0234B] who wills all human beings to be saved and no one to perish, we entrust our authority in this matter to you: after receiving the written profession set out below, absolve him and the clergy and people of Liège from the bond of excommunication, and reconcile them to the Catholic Church.

For what our brother, the bishop of Magdeburg, is said to do indiscriminately in reconciliations of this sort [Note: [Col. 0234D] Doubtless relying upon the title of his primacy.], we cannot hold valid, as having been done without the command of the Roman Church.

> “I, N., anathematize every heresy, and especially that which disturbs the order of the present Church, which teaches and asserts that anathema is to be despised and the bonds of the Church disregarded. This heresy, with its supporters and authors, I condemn and anathematize. Moreover, under the witness of Christ and the Church, I promise obedience to P., bishop of the Roman See [Col. 0234C], and to his successors, affirming what the holy and universal Church affirms and condemning what it condemns. If I should attempt to depart in any respect from this my profession, I judge that I myself have pronounced upon myself the sentence of condemnation.”

Given on the third day before the Ides of November [11 November].

CCXLII. To Conrad, Archbishop of Salzburg.—He consoles him because he had suffered much from his own people; likewise, concerning certain persons interdicted by him, and concerning the Guibertines. (Year 1107.)

[MANSI, *Concilia*, XXI, 417.]

INNOCENT [PASCHAL. [Note: [Col. 0234D] Jaffé notes, on the authority of the Vienna manuscript, that *Paschalis* should be read in place of *Innocentius*: Wattenbach, in Pertz, *Archiv*, X, 491.]] bishop, servant of the servants [Col. 0234D] of God, to his venerable brother CONRAD, Bishop of Salzburg: greeting and apostolic blessing.

The distress of the suffering which, dearest brother, you have reported yourself to endure from your sons whom you undertook to nurture in the Lord, indeed appears grave. But we are instructed concerning the reward of suffering by the voice of our Shepherd, [Col. 0235A] who says that if you suffer for righteousness, you shall be blessed (1 Peter 3). Therefore do not give up; do not withdraw timely help from Christ’s sheep, lest an entrance into the Lord’s sheepfold be left open to the ravaging wolf. You are sufficiently instructed by the words of divine Scripture as to how you ought to fight. Through God’s grace you will always find the aid of our resources ready.

Henry, Duke of Carinthia, has petitioned us concerning certain churches interdicted by you; but we entrust the whole matter to your judgment. For your belovedness will be able, by deliberation with wiser brethren, to determine what should be done about it. Concerning Hugh of Brixen, we order that what has been decreed in councils concerning the other Guibertines be observed: that they are neither to be promoted nor received in their orders.

CCXLIII. He assigns the monastery of Saint Germanus at Auxerre to Hugh, Abbot of Cluny. (Between 1099 and 1108.—Fragment.)

[BALUZE, *Miscellanea*, Lucchesi edition, II, 177.]

[Col. 0235B]

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God [lacuna]

[lacuna] Moreover, when, through the merits of Blessed Germanus, the mercy of almighty God looked upon that place, it was humbly proposed to our predecessor Urban II, of holy memory, at the present request of our venerable brother Humbald, bishop of Auxerre, and at the supplicatory representation of noble persons—namely Stephen, Count of Blois, and his wife Adela, and William, Count of Nevers—that the same monastery [Col. 0235C] be entrusted to the care of our most reverend brother Hugh, abbot of Cluny, in order that it might be restored to the discipline of the regular order.

Accordingly, compelled both by the desire of these principal petitions and by the authority of a pontifical command, he undertook the care of the place; and he appointed you, dearest son Hugh, more worthily trained in the cloister of Cluny, as abbot there, and, by the Lord’s bounty, restored the discipline of the regular order. We therefore also confirm, through God’s grace, the lawful establishment of our predecessor by the charter of the present decree: namely, that the aforesaid monastery of Blessed Germanus shall remain for ever under the administration of the aforesaid Hugh, abbot of Cluny, and of his successors, etc.

CCXLIV. To R[angerius], Bishop of Lucca: he commends to him the canons of Saint Frigdianus. (Between 1099 and 1108.)

[BALUZE, *Miscellanea*, Lucchesi edition, IV, 586.]

[Col. 0235D]

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the venerable brother R., bishop of the Church of Lucca: greeting and apostolic blessing.

We have no doubt whatever of your uprightness and charity: that you love religious men and strive to support them according to the measure of your means. Yet for the common sons, the canons of Blessed Frigdianus, we ask and command you with greater earnestness to take care to love and honour them. Do not allow troubles to be inflicted upon them either by clerics subject to your jurisdiction or by any others; and punish those already inflicted with the suitable severity [Col. 0236A] of your office. May the almighty Lord preserve your fraternity amid every adversity.

CCXLV. He reproves R[angerius], Bishop of Lucca, because he allows the canons of Saint Frigdianus to suffer injuries. (Between 1099 and 1108.)

[BALUZE, *Miscellanea*, Lucchesi edition, IV, 585.]

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to R., Bishop of Lucca: greeting and apostolic blessing.

It is the duty of shepherds, as your prudence knows, to provide for their sheep, to protect them from assaults and the snares of oppressors, and to defend and support religious men—which we believe you do. We are therefore astonished that you permit the religious men, the canons of Saint Frigdianus, whom we have received under apostolic protection, to be disturbed, although they are ready to obey you. We love you as a most dear brother, and do not regard it as a small matter that we have now long borne with you in this matter.

For we have heard that the chapel of Saint Michael has been destroyed by one of your parish priests and taken from the aforesaid brethren without judicial process. We therefore command your fraternity to order the aforesaid church rebuilt, and to cause it to be restored, consecrated, by the next Kalends of August [1 August]. But if the parish priest believes that he has any case against the canons, let him pursue justice before you, so that henceforth no ground of complaint may remain and the religious life of the brethren may not be hindered in the least. Otherwise, through God’s grace, we shall no longer [Col. 0236C] refrain from drawing the sword of Blessed Peter against those who have presumptuously inflicted injury upon the authority of the Apostolic See, and from issuing an appropriate sentence.

CCXLVI. To R[otho], Provost of Saint Frigdianus. (Between 1099 and 1108.)

[BALUZE, *Miscellanea*, Lucchesi edition, IV, 584.]

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son R.: greeting and apostolic blessing.

It seems that what Wisdom says to her children has happened to you and your brethren: “My son, when you come to the service of God, prepare your soul for temptation.” But the Apostle consoles us: “All who wish to live devoutly [Col. 0236D] in Christ must suffer persecution.” We have written to our brother, the Bishop of Lucca, and through our brother Bishop Reginus have requested that he conduct himself toward you more kindly and gently, both in matters of orders and in other things. But if they are unwilling to listen to us on your behalf, the consolation of Blessed Peter will not fail you and your brethren. We ask, moreover, that you, either personally or through your brethren, visit the canonical community of Blessed Floridus, so that what has been well begun may, with the Lord’s cooperation, be brought to a better conclusion.

CCXLVII. To R[angerius], Bishop, and the canons of the Church of Lucca.—Concerning the canons of Saint Frigdianus. (Between 1099 and 1108.)

[BALUZE, *Miscellanea*, IV, 585.]

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved [Col. 0237A] brethren R., bishop, and the canons of the Church of Lucca: greeting and apostolic blessing.

We have heard that you have turned your disposition toward the canons of Saint Frigdianus, so as to be well-disposed toward them and show them kindness. This is so pleasing to us that we give thanks to your belovedness on their behalf. We also ask that, if you have done them good, you may do better things for them in the future; for what you bestow upon them, you grant to yourselves. For they are your sons and brethren; their good is your good, if they are cherished by your charity. May the Lord increase his grace in you, so that through the concord of temporal peace you may arrive at eternal peace.

CCXLVIII. *He confirms the possessions and privileges of the monastery of Saint Michael of Siegburg.* (Year 1108, 7 January.)

[Notice of this privilege survives only in JAFFÉ, *Regesta Romanorum pontificum*, p. 496, “from Pertz’s notes.” Its opening is: “Just as unjust …”]

[Col. 0237B]

CCXLIX. He commands Lambert of Arras and John of Thérouanne to judge between the canons of Tournai and the monks of Saint Martin. (Year 1198.)

BALUZE, *Miscellanea*, Lucchesi edition, II, 156.

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brethren and fellow-bishops LAMBERT of Arras and JOHN of Morinia [Thérouanne]: greeting and apostolic blessing.

The complaint of the canons of Tournai, long pursued [Col. 0237C] against the monks of Saint Martin, is still being prosecuted more vigorously. We therefore command your belovedness to appoint a place suitable for both parties and, after diligently examining the aforesaid complaint, to endeavour to decide it wholly and impose its due conclusion, appeal being set aside, so that through God’s grace no occasion for complaint may thereafter remain.

CCL. Privilege for the Church of Saint Evasius. (Year 1108, 25 February.)

[DE CONTI, *Notizie storiche della cita di Cazale*, Casale, 1838, octavo, I, 328.]

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son GIRARD, provost, and his brethren living canonically in the Church of [Col. 0237D] Saint Evasius, and to their successors for ever.

It is fitting readily to grant assent to religious desires, so that faithful devotion may attain a swift effect. Therefore, assenting to your prayers, we establish by the present decree that whatever goods your Church now lawfully possesses, or may hereafter, through the Lord’s favour, justly and canonically acquire, shall remain secure and unimpaired for you and your successors. We decree, therefore, that absolutely no person may invade that church or the houses of your cloister, take away its possessions, retain what has been taken away, diminish them, or harass them by reckless vexations; but let all be preserved whole for the benefit in every way of the uses of those for whose [Col. 0238A] support and governance they have been granted.

Moreover, we strictly forbid anyone among the military or any secular persons whatever to presume to take tithes from the aforesaid properties of the same Church or from peasants belonging to the parishes of that Church; rather, in accordance with canonical enactments, they shall be assigned to your use or to that of your Church. We further grant to you and to your successors remaining in the unity of Catholic truth that, whenever the Church of Vercelli lacks a Catholic bishop, you may receive chrism, holy oil, and the ordinations of clerics from whichever Catholic bishop you prefer, while preserving for the future the due reverence owed to a Catholic bishop.

If, therefore, in the future any ecclesiastical or secular person, [Col. 0238B] knowing this charter of our constitution, should rashly attempt to act against it, then, after a second or third warning, unless he makes suitable amends by satisfaction, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and honour; let him know himself guilty before the divine judgment for the iniquity committed; let him be cut off from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord, Redeemer Jesus Christ; and at the final judgment let him be subject to strict vengeance. But upon all who preserve what is just for that place may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that here they may receive the fruit of good action and, before the strict Judge, find the rewards of eternal peace. Amen, amen.

I, Paschal, bishop of the Catholic Church.

Given at the Lateran through the hand of John, cardinal-deacon and librarian of the Holy Roman [Col. 0238C] Church, on the fifth day before the Kalends of March [25 February], in the first indiction, in the year 1108 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the ninth year of the pontificate of Lord Paschal II, pope.

CCLI. *He confirms for Otto, Bishop of Bamberg, the town of Albeguinstein, granted by King Henry.* (Year 1108, 4 March.)

[A notice survives in LANG, *Regesta, sive Rerum Boicarum autographa e regni scriniis*, Munich, 1822, quarto, vol. I, p. 111.]

CCLII. To P[eter] of León, D[idacus] of Compostela, R. of Palencia, P. of Nájera, and P[elagius] of Asturias, bishops: he writes that the boundaries of the Church of Burgos are not to be diminished. (Year 1108, 11 April.)

[FLOREZ, *España sagrada*, XXVI, 471.]

[Col. 0238D]

PASCHASIUS [Paschal], bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brethren and fellow-bishops P. of León, D. of Compostela, R. of Palencia, P. of Nájera, and P. of Asturias: greeting and apostolic blessing.

It had indeed been our wish that our brother G., Bishop of Burgos, should grant to the Church of Osma something from a part of his diocese, because it appears poorer. But your fraternity, to whom we ordered an investigation of the boundaries then in dispute, wrote back to us that Gomizo, Bishop of Burgos of good memory, had held those boundaries for three years immediately after the division [Col. 0239A] had been made. But when the Archbishop of Toledo, holding Osma, had seized those boundaries and the whole remaining diocese as far as the stream of Aslanza and Saint Peter of Barilangas, Garcia, Bishop of Burgos, recovered all this by letters of the Roman Church.

Furthermore, that ancient writing which the Bishop of Osma says he possesses is held authentic neither by you nor by us. Certainly, what and how our predecessor Urban determined concerning all these matters is more surely proved by his own records. It is therefore established that our brother, the Bishop of Burgos, cannot be compelled by judgment to cede a portion of his diocese. Therefore, lest the peace of the Church be disturbed further, let the Church of Burgos now and in the future possess with perpetual stability those boundaries that have hitherto been disputed, and the rest, [Col. 0239B] as they have been defined in Roman privileges.

Given on the third day before the Ides of April [11 April], in the first indiction.

CCLIII. At the request of Bishop Garcia, he confirms the boundaries of the diocese of Burgos. (Year 1108.)

[FLOREZ, *España sagrada*, XXVI, 469.]

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved brother GARCIA, Bishop of Burgos, and to his successors to be canonically promoted: for ever.

It is not uncertain that the Churches of Spain have been so disturbed partly by the tyranny of the Saracens and partly by the incursions of various kings that some have been wholly destroyed, [Col. 0239C] some devastated, and the dioceses of others have been usurped by both. This, indeed, was the cause why a prolonged controversy concerning parishes existed between the Churches of Burgos and Osma.

Our predecessor Urban, of holy memory, settled this controversy by the decision recorded in his documents, after frequently hearing the matter in his presence with both parties present and consenting: namely, Bernard, Archbishop of Toledo, to whom the Church of Osma belongs by metropolitan right; Gomizo, the first Bishop of Burgos; and you personally attending at the time following Gomizo. We enact that the boundaries of the aforesaid Churches shall remain for ever as they had been found to be divided, in the time of Gomizo your predecessor, at a council of bishops, with the illustrious King Alfonso and the magnates of his kingdom approving, at the monastery of Fusellis:

Namely, from the boundary of Canatanazor, Murello, and Arganza; from the castle called Mesella and the castle called Speia; and from the villages called Congosto and Buezo; and as the water itself runs and flows into the water of Aranda, and runs through Clunia as far as the rock of Aranda, until it flows into the River Douro; and all the villages on the northern side of the River Aranda in which the Saio of Clunia runs, that is, belonging to the lordship of Clunia; likewise, beyond the River Douro, the castle of Maderolum and Bozichellas, and as far as the city of Septipublica, and whatever lies beyond, shall fall [Col. 0240A] within the diocese of the Church of Osma. But the lands lying on this side of the boundaries noted above, toward the northern quarter, shall be possessed in perpetual right by the Church of Burgos, which is the vicariate of the Church of Oca.

We too, following in the footsteps of this same predecessor of ours, uphold by the authority of the present decree his settlement concerning the diocese of Burgos. We decree that the other boundaries of your diocese shall remain undisturbed, as they had remained before that time under the bishops Muño, Simeon under Muño himself, and Gomizo. In addition, we establish that the village of Fenicularis; the cell of Saint Mary of Ravenaria; the monastery of Saint Euphemia of Cuzolo, with its villages, dependencies, and other appurtenances, which have been assigned as property to the Church of Oca or Burgos by royal enactments; and any other possessions in other dioceses which have been conferred upon the Church of Burgos by the testamentary grants of Catholic rulers, shall always remain, dearest brother Garcia, in the disposal, by proper right and possession, [Col. 0240B] of you and your successors—saving whatever parochial right the diocesan bishops customarily possessed.

Likewise, we confirm to your Church, and to you and your successors, by proper right, the monastery of Valeranica, which is known to have been founded in the diocese of Burgos, with all its appurtenances. The same we decree concerning all the villages and dependencies of that Church. Whatever the same Church of Burgos may hereafter be able justly and canonically to acquire, whether through the liberality of princes or the offerings of the faithful, we command by the authority of the present decree that it be possessed for ever.

Certainly, if hereafter any archbishop or bishop, emperor or king, prince or duke, count or viscount, judge, or any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowing this charter of our constitution, should rashly attempt to act against it, then, after a second or third warning, unless he makes suitable amends by satisfaction, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and honour; let him know himself guilty before the divine judgment for the iniquity committed; let him be cut off from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord, Redeemer Jesus Christ; and at the final judgment let him be subject to strict vengeance. But upon all who preserve what is just for that Church may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, [Col. 0240D] so that here they may receive the fruit of good action and, before the strict Judge, find the rewards of eternal peace. Amen.

Written through the hand of Rainerius, regional chancery clerk and notary of the Sacred Palace.

I, Paschal, bishop of the Catholic Church, have subscribed.

CCLIV. To certain bishops and abbots of Gaul.—Concerning the legation of the Apostolic See entrusted to Girard, [Note: [Col. 0239] Concerning this Girard, the anonymous author of the *Deeds of the Bishops and Counts of Angoulême* says: “Besides the other things which he performed outstandingly in his legation, he held eight councils.” What these were, however, is uncertain.] Bishop of Angoulême. (Year 1108, 14 April.)

[MANSI, *Concilia*, XX, 1016.]

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable [Col. 0241A] brethren the archbishops, bishops, abbots, and princes established throughout the provinces of Bourges, Bordeaux, Auch, Tours, and Brittany, and to all others, clerical as well as lay: greeting and apostolic blessing.

By the authority of the Apostolic See, over which, though unworthy, we preside by the Lord’s ordering, we are obliged to provide, not only for faithful persons nearby, but also for those far away, those things which concern the salvation of the soul. So far as lies in us, with the Lord’s help, we strive to fulfil this. Therefore, brethren and sons all, we bestow upon you the blessing of the apostles Peter and Paul, and exhort you with paternal affection in the Lord to hold fast until the end to a firm purpose of justice, [Col. 0241B] being about to receive the greatest reward of your labour in eternal glory.

And so that you may have among yourselves one to whom, when appropriate, you may bring your complaints and affairs, and by whose counsel and exhortation you may perform those things that pertain to salvation, we have entrusted our authority to our dearest brother Girard, Bishop of Angoulême, associating him with our pastoral responsibility. Obey him faithfully in our stead, as our and the apostles’ vicar in your regions, for God’s honour and for the salvation of your souls, so that, through God’s grace and your cooperation, he may be able to root out what must be uprooted and strengthen what must be strengthened. Nor, dearest brethren, should you begrudge the effort, whenever the need of ecclesiastical utility requires it, of holding synodal assemblies with him. [Col. 0241C] For in our stead we have granted him authority to summon them.

Given at the Lateran, on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of May [14 April].

CCLV. Privilege for the Church of Saint Mary of Vasatensis. (Year 1108, 27 April.)

[BOUCHE, *History of Provence*, II, 64.]

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother ROSTAGNO, Bishop of the Church of Vaison, and to his successors for ever.

“To grant assent to just desires,” etc. Therefore, venerable brother Rostagno in Christ, assenting to your just petitions, etc. We establish that the half of the city of Vaison which the church of Blessed Mary, ever Virgin and Mother, had possessed by ancient right, and [Col. 0241D] the other half which Geoffrey, count of Provence, together with his brother Bertrand, delivered to the same church through the hands of Peter, bishop of good memory, with every right reserved, and in the fields and boundaries contained in the charter of the aforesaid counts, etc.; and all things which appear justly to belong to the same church, shall always be preserved free and unimpaired under the administration and governance of you and your successors, etc.

Written through the hand of Rainerius, etc.

Given at the Lateran through the hand of John, cardinal-deacon and librarian of the Holy Roman [Col. 0242A] Church, on the fifth day before the Kalends of May [27 April], first indiction, in the year 1108 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the ninth year of the pontificate of Lord Paschal II, pope.

CCLVI. He informs Lawrence, Abbot of Saint Vitonus, that Richard, Bishop of Verdun, has not been received by him into communion. (Year 1108.)

[Dom CALMET, *History of Lorraine*, I, Preface, p. 129.]

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son LAWRENCE, Abbot of Saint Vitonus: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Richard of Verdun, having come to us, gave the Church no satisfaction for his offence; hence he has neither been received by us into communion nor absolved from the bond of excommunication. [Col. 0242B] We therefore command your belovedness to avoid fellowship with him altogether and to declare that he, all his supporters, and all who knowingly communicate with him, are excommunicated by us.

CCLVII. To Eustace, Bishop of Valence, and Leodegarius of Viviers.—That they restrain Count Bertrand of Toulouse, absolved from the bond of excommunication at their prayers, from again despoiling the monastery of Saint-Gilles. (Year 1108, 14 May.)

[Dom BOUQUET, *Recueil*, XV, 41.]

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved brethren and fellow-bishops EUSTACE of Valence and [Col. 0242C] LEODEGARIUS of Viviers: greeting and apostolic blessing.

We believe that your belovedness has by no means forgotten with what urgency of prayers Bertrand sought to be absolved from the bond of anathema, and how earnestly your fraternity also pleaded with us for him. Accordingly, yielding both to his prayers and yours, and having received from his hand a renunciation of all the possessions of Saint-Gilles for which he had been excommunicated, we absolved the man. But after our departure he returned, like a dog, to his vomit; and, as we have heard, he began to commit deeds much worse and more shameful than he had done before. For he shamefully dishonoured captured brethren of the monastery, attacked the town, and carried off its inhabitants as captives, whom he still holds.

Since we can no longer endure any of this [Col. 0242D] for any reason, we command your belovedness, if you truly love Blessed Peter, to take every care to avenge his injury. Therefore summon and admonish that man, and by the authority of the Church command him wholly to desist from this course, restore what he has taken, and permit the monastery with all its appurtenances to remain free and undisturbed. If he does not do so, we repel both him and all his supporters from the thresholds of the Church by apostolic authority. [Note: [Col. 0242D] Bertrand appears to have complied, for in the following year he set out on the journey to Jerusalem.]

Given at Sutri, on the second day before the Ides of May [14 May].

CCLVIII. To Berengar, Bishop of Fréjus, and Leodegarius, Bishop of Apt.—That they cease attacking the monastery of Saint-Gilles with the Count of Toulouse. (Year 1108, 14 May.)

[Dom BOUQUET, *Recueil*, XV, 42.]

[Col. 0243A]

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved brethren and fellow-bishops in Christ BERENGAR of Fréjus and LEODEGARIUS of Apt: greeting and apostolic blessing.

We have heard, contrary to the priestly office which you hold, that you are attacking the monastery of Saint-Gilles with Bertrand, although it is the property of Blessed Peter. If this is true, you yourselves recognize how contrary it is to your office. Therefore, by the present [Col. 0243B] letters, we command your belovedness both to desist from this madness and to restrain your knights from aiding Bertrand, knowing beyond doubt that, if you do not cease from this wicked deed, we remove you by apostolic authority from all divine offices. We also separate Bertrand himself from the fellowship of the faithful if he does not desist from this wrongdoing and restore what has been taken.

Given at Sutri, on the second day before the Ides of May [14 May].

CCLIX. He confirms the liberty, privileges, and possessions of the monastery of Saint Bertin at Sithiu. (Year 1108, 25 May.)

[Collection of Cartularies, III, 217.]

[Col. 0243C] PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son LAMBERT, abbot of the venerable monastery of Saint Bertin at Sithiu, and to his successors to be regularly appointed: for ever.

We acknowledge that, by the Lord’s disposition, we have been advanced to the service of the Apostolic See in order that we may effectively assist its children when they implore aid, and, as the Lord grants, defend and protect those obedient to it. Therefore we ought to extend the hand of protection to the venerable and to provide more diligently for the peace of God’s servants.

Accordingly, out of reverence for the blessed confessor Bertin, we receive under the protection of the Apostolic See the monastery of Sithiu, over which, by God’s ordering, you preside—namely, the monastery which the same blessed Bertin is known to have founded in honour of the apostles Peter and Paul—and all that pertains to it. Concerning the charge of that monastery, which the Cluniac monks claim was granted to them through our brother John, bishop of Thérouanne, or through Robert, count of Flanders, or through you, without consultation of your chapter and that of Thérouanne—something which ought by no means to have been done—we, after taking counsel with our brother bishops and cardinals, annul, as justice requires, the privileges which those claiming this right assert that they possess. By apostolic authority we release them from that charge, in accordance with what was judged before us; and we decree that the aforesaid monastery and its local abbot shall continue permanently in the former condition of their liberty and immunity.
