By the authority of this present privilege, therefore, we decree that whatever lands or goods have already been offered to your monastery, have been acquired by other lawful means, or may hereafter, with God’s help, happen to be given or offered, shall remain forever firm and inviolate both for you and for those who succeed you in that place and religious observance. We decree, therefore, that no one at all may rashly disturb the same monastery, take away its possessions, retain possessions taken away, diminish them, or harass it with reckless vexations; but that all things be preserved intact for the use and benefit in every way of those for whose support and governance they were granted.

[Col. 0296C] The canonical reverence due to the bishop of Poitiers is, of course, reserved; yet he may by no means bring burdens upon that monastery, impose exactions, or enforce customs harmful to monastic peace.

Moreover, we decree that the burial-place of that house shall be wholly free, so that no one may oppose the devotion and final will of those who decide to be buried there, unless they are excommunicated. As a token of the protection and freedom received from the Roman Church, you shall pay annually two solidi in the coinage of Poitiers to the Lateran Palace. If any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowing this charter of our constitution, attempts to act against it, then, after a second or third admonition, unless he makes suitable satisfaction and amendment, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and honor; let him know himself guilty before divine judgment for the iniquity committed; let him be separated from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ the Redeemer; and let him be subject to strict vengeance at the last judgment. But upon all who preserve what is right for that monastery may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that they may receive here the fruit of good [Col. 0297A] action and, before the strict Judge, find the rewards of eternal peace. Amen.

Given at the Lateran through the hand of John, cardinal-deacon and librarian of the holy Roman Church, on the Nones of April, in the fifth indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1113, and in the thirteenth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Paschal II.

### CCCXL. To Ralph, Archbishop of Reims.—He confirms privileges granted to the bishop of Arras. (A.D. 1112, April 6.)

[MANSI, *Councils*, XX, 1031.]

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the venerable RADULPH, archbishop of Reims, greetings and the apostolic blessing.

[Col. 0297B] Know that what was done concerning the restoration of the bishopric of Arras by our predecessor Urban of holy memory remains firm and inviolable with us; nor shall we ever permit it to be subjected to the Church of Cambrai. Moreover, by the authority of these letters we require both you and your successors diligently to supervise the election of a bishop there after the death of the bishop of Arras, and to take care to consecrate the person elected without the obstacle of a prolonged delay. If anyone attempts to act against these provisions, let him be bound by the bond of excommunication.

Given at the Lateran, on the eighth day before the Ides of April.

### CCCXLI. To the clergy and people of Arras.—He forbids the Church of Arras to be subjected to that of Cambrai. (A.D. 1112, April 6.)

[MANSI, *Councils*, XX, 1032.]

[Col. 0297C]

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the clergy and people of Arras, greetings and the apostolic blessing.

We have heard that certain perverse persons, wishing to nullify the authority of the apostolic see, are directing the contrivance of their efforts to this end: that the Church of Arras, endowed with an episcopal see, may be overthrown and made subject to the Church of Cambrai. We therefore send these letters to all of you and decree, by the authority of almighty God—the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit—that the restoration of the bishopric of Arras made by our predecessor Urban, and confirmed by us [Col. 0297D] through God’s grace, shall remain firm and inviolable. Whatever possessions that bishopric has possessed since its restoration, it shall always possess peacefully and intact.

We also prohibit under an anathema that the status of the Church of Arras [Col. 0298A] ever be subjected to the Church of Cambrai. Those who, with rash presumption, dare to act against these provisions, let the judgment of Dathan and Abiram follow them, who attempted to suppress the authority divinely given to Moses and Aaron. Therefore, after the death of our venerable brother Lambert, who now presides over the Church of Arras, we command that you by all means elect a bishop. If canonical statutes do not prohibit him, he may by no means evade an election imposed by the consent either of the whole body or of the better part.

Given at the Lateran, on the eighth day before the Ides of April, in the fifth indiction.

### CCCXLII. He exhorts Baldwin, count of Flanders, and his mother Clementia to favor the liberty of the Church of Arras and protect its possessions. (A.D. 1112, April 6.)

[BALUZE, *Miscellanies*, Lucchesi edition, II, 136.]

[Col. 0298B]

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son BALDWIN, count of the Flemings, and to the distinguished countess CLEMENTIA, his mother, greetings and the apostolic blessing.

Know that what was done concerning the restoration of the bishopric of Arras by our predecessor Urban of holy memory remains firm and inviolable with us; nor shall we ever permit it to be subjected to the Church of Cambrai. If anyone attempts to act against these provisions, let him be bound by the bond of excommunication. We therefore admonish, request, and command you, as sons of the Church, not to allow the possessions [Col. 0298C] which the bishopric of Arras has held since its restoration to be taken away or diminished by anyone. But if anyone should presume to do so, provide defense for that Church for the remission of your sins.

Given at the Lateran, on the eighth day before the Ides of April.

### CCCXLIII. He specifies the churches and enumerates the privileges of the monastery of Saint Martin of the Valley, to which he grants the protection of apostolic guardianship. [Note: [Col. 0297D] This abbey of Saint Martin of the Valley, formerly subject to the Benedictine order, had already, in the year 1453, by command of Nicholas V—whose diploma we shall give in its proper place—been transferred to the revenues of our Vatican basilica. It is therefore appropriate that, in treating matters pertaining to that abbey, we present the papal constitutions, beginning with Paschal II, since earlier documents either do not exist or, if any exist, are unknown to us. Much remains to be said here concerning the abbey’s origin, rights, privileges, and jurisdiction, which was troubled for so long; these matters will someday fill many pages of a dissertation. Nor do we touch upon the very beginnings of the abbey, since a more fitting discussion will recur below in the notes to the bull of Honorius III. Our sole purpose here is to elucidate the churches named by the present constitution; although we do not conceal that two matters above all cause us no slight concern: first, the extremely great obscurity of the earliest events with which we are dealing; secondly, the text of the bull available to us, which is insufficiently accurate and which we have been unable to correct by a reliable judgment derived from elsewhere.] (A.D. 1112, April 14.)

[*Vatican Bullarium*, I, 44.]

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son UBERT, abbot of the Church of Saint Martin of the Valley, [Col. 0298D] and to his brethren, both present and future, in perpetuity.

The Lord commanded through the prophet those dwelling in the land of the south to meet the fugitive with bread. Therefore, since you, dearest sons, fleeing from the world, have withdrawn to the mountain of the Lord, we receive your brotherhood with favour and cherish it by the grace of the Holy Spirit under the protection of the apostolic see. For we decree that the monastery of your dwelling-place shall remain free from the right and power of all persons, so that you may enjoy every tranquillity in the service of the Lord. Therefore, all things which are given by the faithful for the expenses of your life, or offered to your church, which is called that of Saint Martin [Note: [Col. 0299A] The church of Saint Martin, from which the monastery [Col. 0299B] and abbey took their name, is situated in the valley of Magellana between two Alps—that is, between two mountains, Majellanus and the Apennines—although there are no Alps in the province of Aprutium. The church bears two additional names: Saint Martin of Fara, from the neighbouring castle; and Saint Martin of the Valley, from the level character of the place. The greater part of this church, together with the whole mass of the monastery buildings, has long since fallen down. Yet a certain part of the ancient church remains, confined within a smaller circuit, in which worship is performed and in which, as we learn from the Acts of the Visitation of 1598, fol. 7, candles and olive branches are distributed annually.], or acquired by other lawful means, or which may hereafter be offered or acquired, we decree shall remain peacefully and unimpaired in your possession. Among these, the following have seemed fit to be stated by their proper names: namely, the church of Saint Maurus of B . . . ja [Note: [Col. 0299B] These three churches, which the bull first mentions—the one of Saint Maurus, the other of Saint Comitius, and the third of Saint Lucy—remain inaccessible to us; and, what is more surprising, even the locality assigned to these churches is unknown to us. Thus far we have obtained nothing from inventories, nothing from visitations, though we have examined a great many of them.], the church of Saint Comitius of Saint Comitius, the church of Saint Lucy of C . . . io, [Col. 0300A] the church of Saint Lucy of Mount Moriscus [Note: [Col. 0299C] Mount Moriscus is described as a fief near the territory of Gipsi; but in such a fief no church bearing the name of Saint Lucy occurs. Consult the codex of the Visitation of 1594, fol. 16.]; at Saint Vitus, the monastery of Saint Angelus [Note: [Col. 0299C] It is described as ruined in the Visitation of 1583, fol. 97, where the location of the monastery near Saint Vitus is defined as a certain wood, called from the title of the monastery the Valley of Saint Angelus.], the church of Saint Mary of Penna [Note: [Col. 0299C] It occurs nowhere except in an inventory of churches drawn up in 1583, where, at fol. 72, the church of Saint Mary of Penna is located near Mount Saint Martin in the territory of Spoleto. Whether the church named by the bull and that described in the inventory are one and the same, we leave to another’s judgment.], the church of Saint Nicholas of P . . . [Note: [Col. 0299C] The obscure indication of the place prevents us from identifying the church of Saint Nicholas with certainty. The reading of the word is uncertain because of the difficulty of the handwriting; the meaning of the place-name is uncertain. If we examine the formation of the letters, the place from which the church of Saint Nicholas takes its name seems to be read as “of Picho,” or “of Righo.” But what do we infer from this for our purpose? Absolutely nothing. We therefore preferred to omit the place-name and to substitute dots for the letters. There is indeed a church of Saint Nicholas of Myra, subject to this abbey of Saint Martin, situated outside the castle of Fara beside the River Viride; not only ancient but also more recent records—namely, the Acts of Visitations recorded in 1716 and 1733—mention it. The proximity supports the identification; the church’s name agrees; the antiquity of the building accords with it. But the designation of the place furnished by the copy of the bull is against it—unless perhaps we say that an error has entered the copy of the bull itself.], near Civitella, the church of Saint Mary and the church of Saint Justin [Note: [Col. 0299D] Both these churches, built outside the castle of Civitella, suffered the same destruction, though with differing outcomes. [Col. 0300A] The one bearing the title of Saint Mary was rebuilt with new and solid [Col. 0300B] walls and rose from its ruins; but that dedicated to Saint Justin lies overwhelmed by ruins and will lie so forever. Hence, in 1598, the prudent visitor caused the title of the ruined chapel to be transferred to the nearby church of Saint Mary of Laude. Consult the Acts of the same Visitation, fol. 16. From the revenues of both churches there arose one ecclesiastical benefice, the right of presentation to which belongs to the Vatican chapter.], with lands and vineyards, and there a village and possessions of lands and vineyards; near the Hill of the Millstones, the church of Saint Peter, the church of Saint Angelus, the church of Saint Sylvester, the church of Saint Quiricus [read: Saint Clericus], the church of Saint Paul [Note: [Col. 0300B] The five churches named in one sequence as situated on the Hill of the Millstones all still exist and annually pay a fixed due to the Chapter of the Vatican Basilica. Consult the inventory of 1593, fol. 116.], and there possessions of lands; at Pr . . . a [Note: [Col. 0300B] The very incomplete reading of the word removes knowledge of the place. The unknown place is the reason why the churches subsequently listed near it remain inaccessible to us. Among so great a multitude of churches presenting themselves under the same titles, to determine one fixed and certain identification, unless the neighbourhood of places offers guidance, is a matter full of danger. The epithet *dello casale*, added to the church of Saint Mary, has not yet occurred. Should better evidence emerge, we shall provide it someday.], the church of Saint Mary *dello Casale*, the church of Saint Peter; at Laroma [Note: [Col. 0300C] We learn from the Acts of the Visitation of 1598 that the castle of Larome, or Larona, had long since been destroyed by the violence of wars. Such a castle is everywhere located in the district of Camlarum; hence the expressions “the fief of Laroma” and “the territory of Casulara” are likewise used. Five churches subject to the jurisdiction of the abbey of Saint Martin lay adjacent to that fief, according to the testimony of the bull. The destruction which afflicted the castle also afflicted all the churches.] the church of Saint Mary, the church of Saint Peter [Note: [Col. 0300C] We treat the two churches of Saint Mary and Saint Peter in a single note, because not only did both undergo the same ruin, but they moreover eventually came together into one ecclesiastical benefice reserved to the presentation of our chapter. The Acts of the Visitation compiled in [Col. 0300D] that same year, 1604, fol. 211, show that this union was earlier than 1604.]; the church of Saint Mary of the Plain [Note: [Col. 0300D] Lest similarity of name mislead anyone, we observe that two entirely distinct churches of Saint Mary of the Plain, bearing the same title, must be distinguished: one in the fief of Laroma and the other in the territory of Comino. The former belonged to the abbey of Saint Martin; the latter was subject to the abbot of Majella. Consult the index compiled in 1383 by Giovanni Battista Corrado, commissioner of the chapter, and the matter will become plain at a glance.]—Saint Mary of the Plain [Note: [Col. 0300D] Lest the memory of both churches should finally perish amid their ruins, the title of each chapel was transferred to the parish church of Saint Remigius in the town of Fara. To prevent the goods from being dispersed, provision was made that an ecclesiastical benefice, to be administered by the Chapter of Saint Peter, should be established from their collected revenues. We drew this from fol. 182 of the Visitation of 1604.]—the church of Saint [Col. 0301A] Lucy, the church of Saint Sylvester [Note: [Col. 0301D] Inventories of 1583 and 1593, fol. 16, and also the Visitation of 1594, fol. 8, mention both churches as situated in the territory of Palumbianum. In these [Col. 0302D] records, however, the name of Saint Flavian is always read, and never that of Fabian. Hence we not without reason suspect that the copy of the bull is corrupt in this part.], and there Villani and possessions of lands; at Pallunianum, the church of Saint Fabian [read: Saint Flavian], the church of Saint Angelinus Cam, with villagers, lands, and vineyards.

You shall receive chrism, holy oil, the consecration of altars or churches, and the ordination of clerics to be promoted to holy orders, from the diocesan bishop, provided that he is catholic and has the favour and communion of the apostolic see, and is willing to provide these to you freely and without any impropriety. Otherwise, you may approach whichever bishop you prefer, who, supported by our authority, shall grant what you request.

Upon the death of yourself, the present abbot of that place, or of any of your successors, no one shall be set over it by any craft of intrigue or violence, save one whom the brothers by common consent, or the sounder part of the brothers’ counsel, in the fear of God and according to the Rule of blessed Benedict, shall provide to be elected, and who shall come to the apostolic see to be blessed.

We therefore decree that absolutely no person may rashly disturb the aforesaid monastery, take away its possessions, retain those taken away, diminish them, or harass it with reckless vexations; but that all things shall be preserved whole, for the complete benefit of those for whose maintenance and governance they were granted. Moreover, as a memorial and token of this liberty received from the Roman Church, you shall pay two solidi annually to the Lateran palace.

If, therefore, in future any archbishop or bishop, emperor [Col. 0301C] or king, prince or duke, count, viscount, judge, or any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowing this page of our constitution, shall attempt to act against it, and, having been warned a second or third time, shall fail to make amendment by suitable satisfaction, let that person be deprived of the dignity of office and honour; let that person know that he or she is liable before divine judgment for the iniquity committed, be separated from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Redeemer, and be subject to severe vengeance at the final judgment. But upon all who observe what is right toward this place may the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ rest, so that they may receive here the fruit of good works and find, before the strict Judge, the rewards of eternal peace. Amen, amen.

Written by the hand of John, scriniarius and notary of the [Col. 0301D] sacred palace.

Given at the Lateran, through the hand of John, cardinal chancellor and librarian of the holy Roman Church, on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of May, in the fifth indiction, in the year 1112 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the thirteenth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Paschal II.

### CCCXLIV. He takes the monastery of Saint Bertin of Sithiu under protection and confirms its possessions.  
*(A.D. 1112, June 19.)*  

*Collection des Cartulaires*, III, 250.

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son LAMBERT, abbot of the monastery of Sithiu, and to his successors regularly appointed in perpetuity.

We are seen, by the Lord’s ordering, to have been raised to the governance of the apostolic see in order that, with him providing the means, we may promote religious life and ought to extend protection to its servants. Therefore, most beloved son in the Lord, Abbot Lambert, granting your just petitions, we receive under the guardianship and protection of the apostolic see the monastery of Saint Bertin of Sithiu, situated in the parish of Thérouanne, over which, by God’s authority, you preside; and we fortify it against the malice of wicked people by the privilege of that see’s authority.

We decree that all things lawfully belonging to that monastery shall always remain peaceful and inviolate for you and your successors; and that the monastery itself, in accordance with the enactments of our predecessors Victor and Urban, shall be preserved forever in its full liberty and immunity, so long as the vigour and discipline of the regular order endure there.

Furthermore, we determine that no abbot shall preside in that monastery save one whom the brothers, by common consent or by the sounder part of their counsel, shall elect according to the fear of God and the Rule of blessed Benedict.

We therefore decree that absolutely no person may rashly disturb that monastery, take away its possessions, retain things taken away, diminish them, or harass it with reckless vexations; but that all things shall be preserved whole, for the complete benefit of those for whose maintenance and [Col. 0302C] governance they were granted, saving the canonical reverence due to the bishop of Thérouanne.

If, therefore, any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowing this page of our constitution, shall rashly attempt to act against it, and, having been warned a second or third time, shall fail to amend by appropriate satisfaction, let that person be deprived of the dignity of office and honour; let that person know that he or she is liable before divine judgment for the iniquity committed, be separated from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Redeemer, and be subject to severe vengeance at the final judgment. But upon all who observe what is right toward this place may the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ rest, so that they may receive here the fruit of good works and find, before the strict Judge, the rewards of eternal peace. [Col. 0302D] Amen.

Written by the hand of Rainerius, regional scriniarius and notary of the sacred palace.

Given at the Lateran, through the hand of John, cardinal deacon and librarian of the holy Roman Church, on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of July, in the fifth indiction, in the year 1112 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the thirteenth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Paschal II.

### CCCXLV. He confirms for the monastery of Anchin the church of Saint George near Hesdin, granted by John, bishop of Thérouanne.  
*(A.D. 1112, June 19.)*

[MIRAEUS, *Opp. diplom.*, I, 170.]

[Col. 0303A]

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son ALWIS [Note: [Col. 0303D] Alwis. Formerly a monk of Saint Bertin and prior of Saint-Vaast, he was elected abbot of Anchin and was finally made bishop of Arras in 1131. He died in Palestine in 1143.], abbot of the monastery of Anchin, and to his successors regularly appointed.

The authority of our office urges us to be solicitous for the condition of churches and to establish what has been rightly ordained. Accordingly, by this present letter we confirm the cession made to you and your monastery by our venerable brother John, bishop of Thérouanne. For he granted the church of the blessed martyr George, situated beside the castle of Hesdin, to you and your successors, to possess forever as a cell, [Col. 0303B] and confirmed the grant by a charter, together with all lands, meadows, woods, waters, mills, and whatever other revenues were bestowed upon that church by Count Ingelram [Note: [Col. 0303D] Ingelram (called Ingelran by others), count of Hesdin, who restored the church of Auchy in 1072 and was buried there. Thus the Chronicle of Auchy.], Ernulf of Hesdin, and Nicholas the knight, as well as by other faithful people. Indeed, his predecessor Gerard of blessed memory had granted the same thing with the counsel and consent of the canons of his church.

Therefore we too establish the same by the authority of this present decree, saving, of course, the right of the Church of Thérouanne, as is shown to have been set forth in the charter of the aforesaid bishop. We also grant and confirm by the authority of this present decree the two altars, namely those of Fraisnoith and Huby, just as they were granted by that bishop to the aforesaid church of Saint George [Note: [Col. 0304D] The cell or priory of Saint George, founded and endowed in 1072 by Count Ingelram, Ernulf of Hesdin, and Nicholas the knight, still flourishes today. It lies not far from the ruins or remains of old Hesdin, destroyed in 1553 by order of Emperor Charles V, when a new Hesdin was built from the foundations in a more convenient location against the French.].

[Col. 0303C] Moreover, we decree that the burial-place of that site shall be free from every exaction, so that no one may obstruct the devotion and last will of those who decide to be buried there, unless they are excommunicated.

Given at the Lateran, on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of July, in the fifth indiction, in the year 1112 of the Lord’s Incarnation.

### CCCXLVI. To Bernard, Patriarch of Antioch.  
—He announces that, by granting the aforesaid privilege, he did not intend to diminish the dignity of the patriarchal Church of Antioch.  
*(A.D. 1112, August 8.)*

[MANSI, *Concil.*, XX, 1006.]

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother BERNARD, patriarch of Antioch: greeting [Col. 0303D] and apostolic blessing.

Although, among the other sees, that apostolic see is preeminent which the supreme divine favour glorified through the bodily death of the apostle Peter, nevertheless such great charity is recorded formerly to have existed between the bishops of Rome and Antioch that no difference between them seemed visible. The same person of Peter made both churches illustrious.

Many ages afterward passed during which the dominion of unbelievers impeded this unity in the persons presiding over them. But thanks be to God, who in our time restored Christian rule in the city of Antioch. It is fitting, therefore, dearest brother, that the unity of this same charity should remain firm; nor should any opinion enter your mind that we wish to abase or dishonour the Church of Antioch.

If, then, concerning the boundaries of parishes, we have written anything regarding either the Church of Antioch or that of Jerusalem perhaps otherwise than was proper, this must be attributed neither to frivolity nor to malice, nor on that account should scandal be stirred up against us. For both the great remoteness of the places and the alteration of ancient names that has occurred to cities and provinces have brought us much uncertainty or [Col. 0304B] ignorance. Besides, we have desired and do desire to furnish our brothers not occasion for scandal but for peace, preserving to every church its own right and honour.

Given at the Lateran, on the sixth day before the Ides of August.

### CCCXLVII. He confirms the liberty of the Church of Orange, separated from that of Tricastin.  
*(A.D. 1112, October 18.)*

[Gall. Christ. I, 132.]

. . . . . . The people of the city of Orange were at one time so exalted that the name of that city was celebrated everywhere in popular songs; at another time so reduced that its church was either subject or united to the church of another city. Again, through the disposition of heavenly [Col. 0304C] wisdom, in our times or those of our predecessors so great a population was restored to that city and church that, at the instance of the archbishop of Arles, that church received its own cardinal priest, in accordance with what was determined in the African council concerning a diocese which had once had a bishop: namely, that if the population has increased and wishes to have its own ruler, it may have its own bishop with the consent of the person in whose power the diocese has been established.

Therefore, since two bishops [William and Berengar] have in our memory been appointed to the episcopal chair of the city of Orange, we assent to your petition and to the devotion of the numerous people, dearest brother; and, following the canon of the Council of Chalcedon, [Col. 0304D] we establish by the authority of this present decree that the ecclesiastical parishes shall follow the civil arrangements and public order of the city of Orange.

Accordingly, we confirm to you and to your lawful successors the integrity of the parish of Orange exactly as it is known anciently to have remained to the Church of Orange. Nor may the bishop of Tricastin, or any bishop henceforth, invade the boundaries of that parish [Col. 0305A] or the other things belonging to the aforesaid church, or withdraw them by any contrivance; but all things shall remain peaceful and unimpaired for you and the clerics serving in that church.

If, therefore, any ecclesiastical or secular person in future, knowing this page of our constitution, shall rashly attempt to act against it, and, having been warned a second or third time, shall fail to amend by appropriate satisfaction, let that person be deprived of the dignity of office and honour; let that person know that he or she is liable before divine judgment for the iniquity committed, be separated from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Redeemer, and be subject to severe vengeance at the final judgment. But upon all who observe what is right toward this church may the peace of our Lord Jesus [Col. 0305B] Christ rest, so that they may receive here the fruit of good works and find, before the strict Judge, the rewards of eternal peace. Amen, amen, amen.

+ I, Paschal, bishop of the catholic Church.

Given at the Lateran, through the hand of John, cardinal deacon and librarian of the holy Church, on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of November, in the fifth [sixth] indiction, in the year 1113 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the fourteenth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Paschal II. With the seal of the lord pope.

### CCCXLVIII. He confirms the decrees of the council held at Vienne by Guy of Vienne and other archbishops, bishops, and abbots.  
*(A.D. 1112, October 20.)*

[MANSI, *Concil.* XXI, 76.]

[Col. 0305C]

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brothers GUY, archbishop of Vienne and vicar of the apostolic see, and the other archbishops, bishops, and abbots, or priests of the Lord, assembled at Vienne: greeting and apostolic blessing.

When the head is affected by the onset of some illness, all the members must labour together and with the utmost diligence to expel it completely. We have learned from the report of our brothers that you have assembled and, through God’s grace, celebrated a council at Vienne. There you deliberated concerning the increase of religious life, the ordering of the Church and of ecclesiastical affairs, and the correction of wicked people rising up against the [Col. 0305D] holy Church. We therefore give thanks to God; we receive and confirm as valid the things established there; and, with the Lord God cooperating, determine that they shall remain inviolate. We exhort the aforesaid bishop, our beloved brother, diligently to fulfil before God the legation entrusted to him.

Given at the Lateran, on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of November.

### CCCXLIX. *He summons the bishops of Spain to a synod to be held “on the next feast of Blessed Mary” (2 February 1113, at Benevento), “that they may discuss in his presence the affair of the king of Aragon and Queen Urraca, and the question of peace and concord.”*

(See the *Historia Compostellana* in FLOREZ, *España sagrada*, XX, 139, 140.)

### CCCL. He confirms the possessions and privileges of the monastery of Nonantola.  
*(A.D. 1112, November 10.)*

[MURATORI, *Antiq. Ital.*, V, 343.]

[Col. 0306A]

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son in Christ JOHN, consecrated by our hands through God’s grace as abbot of the monastery of Nonantola, and to his successors regularly appointed in perpetuity.

. . . . . . By authority and duty we are compelled to labour for the condition of all churches, and especially, with the Lord’s help, to provide for the peace of those which adhere more particularly to the apostolic see and are subject to it as by their own proper right. Therefore, dearest son in Christ, we have thought it right to grant your petitions, so that we might fortify by the privilege of our predecessors and of that same apostolic see . . . the monastery of Nonantola, over which, by God’s authority, you preside, and which was offered to the apostolic see by its founder himself, namely Aistulf, king of the Lombards.

By the text of this present privilege, therefore, we establish by apostolic authority that whatever now belongs, in this sixth indiction, justly and lawfully to the aforesaid monastery of Nonantola, or may hereafter be justly and canonically acquired through the grant of popes, the generosity of princes, or the offering of the faithful, shall remain secure and inviolate for you and your successors. Among these, the following have seemed fit to be recorded by their proper names: namely, [Col. 0306C] the castle of Nonantola itself; Castelvecchio; Galliano; Catiniano; Fainano; Lizano; Scoppano; Sanono; Campiglio; Marano; Monte Oliveto; the meadow of Albino; the monastery of Saint Lucy of Roffeno with its churches and appurtenances; the church of the Holy Trinity of Savino; Manzolino; Taivalo; Rastellino; Saint Mary in Grumolo; Spina Lamberti; Solara; Roncaglia; Camurana; Sorbara; Curtiule Secco; the castle of Pile; Trecentola; Bondeno; Staggi; the castle of Cella; and Marzaglia, with their appurtenances. Furthermore, we confirm in perpetuity to your monastery the castle of Cellula, the court of Ragusa, and the castle of Tedaldo, with all the allods which Margrave Boniface acquired and possessed in that county of Ferrara; likewise the things which Countess Matilda, from the offering that she had made to Saint Peter and the Roman Church, is known recently to have given to you, under an annual rent of one gold piece.

Indeed, neither the bishop of Modena nor any bishop, prince, ecclesiastical or secular person may impose any burden or exaction upon the aforesaid monastery, its cells, churches, or other possessions, nor convene or hold a court or conference without the consent of the abbot and brothers.

Upon the death of yourself, the present abbot of that place, or of any of your successors, no one shall be placed over it by any craft of intrigue or violence, save one whom the brothers by common consent, or the sounder part of the brothers’ counsel, according to the fear of God and the Rule of blessed [Col. 0307A] Benedict, shall elect to be consecrated by the bishop of the apostolic see.

You shall receive chrism, holy oil, the consecration of altars or churches, and the ordination of monks to be promoted to holy orders, or of clerics belonging to the monastery, its cells, or churches, from whichever catholic bishop you prefer, provided that he has the favour and communion of the apostolic see and is willing to provide these freely and without impropriety. For we do not permit any bishop, against the abbot’s will, to perform ordinations in the monastery, its cells, or churches; to celebrate public masses there; or to claim their tithes. Nor may any person obtain by stealth a rescript concerning the monastery itself or its property, or procure one in any manner. [Col. 0307B] If this should perhaps be presumed, it shall be held wholly invalid.

Adding these provisions, we decree that absolutely no person may rashly disturb that monastery, take away its possessions, retain things taken away, claim for personal use things unjustly granted, diminish them, or harass it with reckless vexations; but that all things shall be preserved whole, for the complete benefit of those for whose maintenance and governance they were granted, so that in all things it may always rejoice in the defence and protection of the apostolic see, to which it properly belongs.

If, therefore, in future any archbishop or bishop, emperor or king, prince or duke, count, viscount, judge, castellan, or any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowing this page of our constitution, [Col. 0307C] shall rashly attempt to act against it, and, having been warned a second or third time, shall fail to amend by appropriate satisfaction, let that person be deprived of the dignity of office and honour; let that person know that he or she is liable before divine judgment for the iniquity committed, be separated from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Redeemer, and be subject to severe vengeance at the final judgment. But upon all who observe what is right toward this [Col. 0308A] place may the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ rest, so that they may receive here the fruit of good works and find, before the strict Judge, the rewards of eternal peace.

Written by the hand of Chrysogonus, notary of the sacred palace.

I, Paschal, bishop of the catholic Church, have subscribed.

Given at Tibur, through the hand of John, cardinal deacon and librarian of the holy Roman Church, on the fourth day before the Ides of November, in the sixth indiction, in the year 1113 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the fourteenth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Paschal II. [Note: [Col. 0307C] Here you have the fourteenth year of Pope Paschal II joined with the year 1113 of the Lord’s Incarnation and the sixth indiction. You may think that you have immediately discovered an obvious error here when, from Donizo, Baronius, Pagi, and others, you learn that Paschal himself ascended the Roman see on 14 August 1099. [Col. 0307D] But be patient. There are other bulls proceeding according to this reckoning, so that one is almost brought to believe that Paschal was proclaimed supreme pontiff in the following year, 1100. See the *Bullarium Casinense*, part II; Ughelli; the *Bullarium Cluniacense*; Baluze in the *Miscellanea*; and, to omit the rest, Mabillon, book V, table 51 of the *De re diplomatica*, where he reports an autograph bull of this pope: “Given at Rome through the hand of John, cardinal deacon of the holy Roman Church, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of April, in the tenth indiction, in the year 1103 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the third year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Paschal II.” These dates plainly disagree with the calculations of Pagi and others.

Since the year and month in which Paschal II entered the pontifical office are fixed—namely, 14 August 1099—we must understand, and this must be observed with the greatest care in resolving other problems of this sort, that he sometimes used the Pisan era, which begins the new year not from the Nativity or Circumcision [Col. 0308C] of the Lord but from his Incarnation, that is, from 25 March, and therefore precedes our ordinary year by nine months. Consequently, although the bull just produced gives the year 1113, it indicates no other year than 1112. The sixth indiction used there began in September [Col. 0308D] of that same year 1112.

The aforementioned Mabillon produced another bull of Paschal II in the appendix to volume V of the *Annales Benedictinorum*, p. 693: “It was given on the second day before the Ides of April, in the sixth indiction, in the year 1114 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the fourteenth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Paschal II.” The distinguished man judges that “seventh indiction” should there be written, for this is indeed required by the ordinary year 1114. But the matter concerns the Pisan year, and consequently the bull was given in the preceding year according to our reckoning, when in fact the sixth indiction was current on the second day before the Ides of April.

Thus in Father Pez’s *Thesaurus Anecdotorum*, vol. III, part II, p. 659, another bull of the same pope is reported: “Given on the eighth day before the Kalends of November, in the twelfth indiction, in the year 1105 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the sixth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Paschal II.” There also understand the ordinary year 1104, in which the sixth year of Paschal was running in October, as was the twelfth indiction, continuing to the end of the year.]

### CCCLI. Privilege for the monastery of Arouaise.  
*(A.D. 1112, November 15.)*

[Gall. Christ., old ed., vol. IV, p. 113.]

[Col. 0308B]

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son GISLEBERT, abbot of Saint Peter of Arouaise, and to his brothers, professing the canonical life in that church, both present and future, in perpetuity.

A desire shown to concern a religious purpose and the salvation of souls ought, with God as its author, to be fulfilled without any delay.

For since you, O dearest sons in Christ, inspired by divine grace, have resolved to restrain your conduct under the discipline of the regular life and to serve the Almighty in common according to the institution of the holy Fathers, we rejoice in your vows with paternal affection. [Col. 0308C] Therefore we grant due assent, in our kindness, to your petition. By the authority of the present privilege we confirm the order of canonical life which you have professed; we forbid anyone, after making profession, to possess anything as private property or to leave the cloister without permission of the provost or of the community; and we place both you and all that is yours under the protection of the Apostolic See.

[Col. 0309A] Accordingly, for you and your successors who shall remain in the same religious observance, we decree that you shall possess in perpetuity all those things which you are now seen lawfully to possess: namely, in the district of Poitou, the church of St Paul of Hydriac, St Martin of Alhaic, St Hilary of Borno, St Martin of Gemellis, St Peter of Solobria, St Mary of Toxoneries, St Martin of Loon, St Michael of Crum, St Mary of Mosronia, St Eparchius of Germund, St Mary Magdalene of Pristiniac, St Benedict of Boxemia, the church of St Veranus, St Mary Magdalene of Thouarn, St Paul of Bosco, St Stephen of Amaillo, the churches of St Lupus and St Pancras, St Martin of Salis, and the church of Bocaic. These our brother Peter, bishop of Poitiers, the founder of your religious community, [Col. 0309B] granted you for the common support of your livelihood, or they had been given to the same monastery by his predecessors.

Likewise, in the district of Anjou, the church of St Peter of Dampierre and St Alfinus of Torcam, which our brother Rainald, bishop of [Studegava], and Geoffrey, his predecessor, granted to your church. If, moreover, any estates or possessions have been offered to your monastery by the foundress of the church, the viscountess Aldcarda, and her successors, or by other successors from their own right; or if, by the Lord’s bounty, they should hereafter be offered, or have been or shall be acquired by other lawful means, may they remain firm and unimpaired for you and your successors.

[Col. 0309C] We therefore decree that absolutely no person may rashly disturb this church, take away its possessions, retain those taken away, diminish them, or harass it with wanton vexations; but let all be preserved intact, for the benefit of the uses of those for whose support and governance they were granted, saving the due reverence owed to the bishop of Poitiers. And we decree that this place itself shall remain for ever, by the Lord’s gift, peacefully and freely in the observance of canonical discipline, as was established by our aforementioned brother Peter, bishop of the Church of Poitiers.

If, therefore, in the future any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowing this page of our enactment, should rashly attempt to act against it, then, after a second or third warning, unless he makes suitable amends, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and honour; let him know himself guilty before the divine [Col. 0309D] judgment for the iniquity perpetrated; let him be excluded from the sacrament, body, and blood of God and of our Redeemer Jesus Christ; and at the final judgment let him be subject to severe vengeance. But upon all who preserve what is right for that place may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that here they may receive the fruit of good action and before the strict Judge may find the rewards of eternal peace. Amen, amen, amen.

Written by the hand of Glisogonus, notary of the sacred palace.

Given at Princerno, through the hand of John, cardinal-deacon and librarian of the holy Roman Church, on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of December [15 November], in the sixth indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1113 [1112], in the fourteenth year of the pontificate of lord Pope Paschal II.

I, Paschal, bishop of the Catholic Church.

### CCCLII. To the bishops established throughout Dacia, among other matters: concerning the tribute

“We wish your brotherhood, together with our brother the archbishop of Lund, to be diligent concerning the tribute which your predecessors established to be paid annually to Blessed Peter, so that the Roman Church may no longer suffer fraud in this matter, but that your prudence may wisely undertake in full this obligation of charity.”

(Between 1100 and 1113. Fragment.—See the list of Cencius Camerarius, “On Rents,” in Muratori, *Antiquities of Italy*, V, 891.)

### CCCLIII. To Baldric, bishop of Noyon and Tournai.—That he not allow the brethren of the monastery of St Martin to be harassed by the clerics of Tournai.  
(About 29 October 1113.)

[D’Achery, *Spicilegium*, Labarre edition, II, 915.]

[Col. 0310B]

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother BALDRIC, bishop of Noyon and Tournai, greeting and apostolic blessing.

We have already sent a second letter to your brotherhood, instructing you to do justice to the monks of St Martin concerning the injuries which they suffer from the clerics of Tournai. Yet your brotherhood long and repeatedly neglected to administer that justice. We therefore judged it expedient to entrust this same affair to Lambert of Arras and John of Thérouanne, our brother bishops of the same province; these men, indeed, being religious men and applying themselves too strongly to peace, handled the affair less canonically.

For this reason we summoned both parties before us. We showed those clerics themselves, on the authority of the holy Fathers, how improperly they burdened the monks by demanding tithes and forbidding burials. For Blessed Gregory, writing to Augustine, bishop of the English, says: “For those who live the common life, what need is there for us to speak any longer of making distributions, requiring hospitality, and performing mercy, when everything that remains must be expended upon pious and religious causes?”

Leo IV, moreover, decreed in a synodal constitution that tithes and first fruits, and whatever offerings of living persons and of the dead, are to be faithfully rendered to the churches of God by laypeople. Here it should be noted [Col. 0310D] that tithes are ordered to be rendered not by monks but by laypeople. For monks—since most of them are either Levites or priests, or enjoy other ecclesiastical orders, and by God’s grace continually serve in divine ministries—must certainly be considered exempt from such exactions.

The same Leo, writing to the bishops of Britain, indicates that tithes are due only to those churches called *plebes*, where the most holy baptisms are administered. These words plainly show that tithes are rendered by the people on account of baptism, the Eucharist, penance, and the other offices which clerics provide for the people; in all these matters no service is furnished by clerics to communities of monks.

Further, there is a clear judgment of Blessed Gregory concerning the permitting of burial in monasteries. He restrained John, bishop of the Old City, who forbade the burial of the dead in a monastery, with these words: “If this is so, I exhort you to depart from such inhumanity, and henceforth to permit the dead to be buried there and masses to be celebrated, with no opposition whatsoever; lest Agapitus, a venerable man, be compelled again to bring before me a complaint about what has been done.”

Having ascertained the authority of the holy Fathers and recognized the reason of truth, the aforementioned clerics of Tournai who had come before us yielded with due humility and promised that henceforth they would bring no further vexatious complaints against the monks in these matters. Therefore, dearest brother, we admonish your diligence not to permit the brethren of the aforesaid monastery [Col. 0311B] to be further assailed by such molestations; neither establish a cathedra there nor introduce anything else by which the regular order may be disturbed.

As to those portions of alms which dying persons ought to leave to churches, it concerns you to instruct the parishioners of your diocese, so that, through the diligence of your vigilance and by the Lord’s bounty, what is just may be preserved both for clerics and monks and firm peace may remain among the churches.

Given at the Lateran, through the hand of Cardinal John, on the fourth day before the Kalends of November [29 October].

### CCCLIV. To Galon, bishop of Paris, and the chapter of the Church of Paris.—That the dependants of the Church of Paris be admitted to give testimony in legal cases.  
(24 January 1113.)

[Mansi, *Councils*, XX, 1036, from the great Pastoral Register of the Church of Paris.]

[Col. 0311C]

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother GALON and to the chapter of the Church of Paris, greeting and apostolic blessing.

As we have learned from your report and from the king’s letters, the Church of Paris has hitherto suffered great detriment to its affairs because the dependants of that church, whom among you are improperly called *servi* (“serfs”) in common speech, were not admitted as witnesses against free persons in judicial and civil cases or pleas.

For the benefit of the Church, our beloved son Louis, king of the Franks, judged that provision should be made as follows: with the counsel and assent of bishops and magnates, he decreed that the dependants of the Church of Paris should have, in all cases, pleas, and business matters, full and unrestricted liberty to give testimony and to wage judicial combat against all persons, free as well as unfree; and that no one should impugn their testimony on account of their ecclesiastical servile status.

We, therefore, considering your petition reasonable, confirm the same by the authority of our decree, for the sake of ecclesiastical advantage and justice. For it is not equitable that the household of the Church should be bound by the same conditions by which the slaves of secular persons are bound. Accordingly, as the aforementioned king of the Franks has established by royal favour, so by this grant of our authority we endow the household of your church, which is under the jurisdiction of the bishop or canons, so that in judicial and civil cases or pleas it may be effectively admitted as testimony against any secular persons, and that its testimony may not be rejected because of the obligation of ecclesiastical clientship, provided that no other impediment exists.

Given at Benevento, through the hand of John, cardinal-deacon and librarian of the holy Roman Church, on the ninth day before the Kalends of February [24 January].  
[Note: Col. 0311D: False dating. Hardouin.]

In the sixth indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1114, in the fourteenth year of the pontificate of lord Pope Paschal II.

### CCCLV. To Emperor Henry.  
(25 January 1113.)

[Mansi, *Councils*, XX, 1095.]

[Col. 0312B]

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son in Christ HENRY, august emperor, greeting and apostolic blessing.

Although the affection of friends is great, paternal love is greater indeed among human beings. Whatever others may say to you, whatever flattery they may employ, it is ours to show you the truth more plainly and truly to provide for your honour and welfare. We have heard that A. [Albert, archbishop of Mainz], your chancellor, has been captured by you. So far as we know him and have experienced him, we bear testimony that he loved you above all things. On this account, many indeed, both friends and enemies, speak against you.

Therefore, as a father admonishes a son, we urge you to adopt such counsel in this matter, consistent with the safety of the realm, that neither your person nor your kingdom incurs any infamy, and that he may obtain the grace of release.

Given at Benevento, on the eighth day before the Kalends of February [25 January].

### CCCLVI. Judgment concerning the dispute between the abbots of Monte Cassino and of the monastery of Terra Maggiore over the church of St Mary of Casale Piano, which is adjudged to Monte Cassino.  
(13 February 1113.)

[Cocquelines, *Collection of Bulls*, II, 147.]

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to all the faithful throughout Campania, Apulia, Capitanata, and Samnium, greeting and apostolic blessing.

Accounts of deeds performed are committed to the trust of letters so that the truth of those deeds may not be withdrawn from the memory of posterity. Therefore we command that the decision of the long-standing lawsuit carried on between the abbots of Monte Cassino and of the monastery of Terra Maggiore over the church of St Mary of Casale Piano and its possessions be set down in writing, lest any occasion for disturbance between them remain in the future.

Having received the complaint of Oderisius, abbot of Monte Cassino, of revered memory, against the abbot of the monastery of Terra Maggiore, that he had seized the aforesaid church of Casale Piano, we repeatedly sent letters and even imposed an interdict of place or order. Thus we compelled the abbot of Terra Maggiore, although he neglected to come to us, to invest the aforesaid Abbot Oderisius with the said church of Casale Piano.

After the death of Abbot Oderisius, we imposed upon both parties a fixed time for litigation, ordering them to meet, fully prepared to conduct the case, at the appointed term. At the designated time, Gerard, abbot of Monte Cassino, and Benedict, abbot of Terra Maggiore, appeared before us. The legal experts were given two days’ leave to argue. At last the representatives of the monastery of Terra Maggiore asserted proof of forty years’ possession. Yet their witnesses, declaring testimony not from sight and hearing but from report, could be admitted neither by laws nor by canons.

The men of Monte Cassino, however, established in the following ways interruption of forty- or thirty-year possession. They produced two monks of known religious standing as witnesses, one a bishop and the other a deacon. They asserted that, in their presence and in the presence also of Benedict, abbot of Terra Maggiore of good memory, the aforesaid church of St Mary of Casale Piano had been leased by Abbot Desiderius of happy memory to the priest Rudolph, as the written lease showed, at a rent of six Byzantine coins, in the year 1071 of the Lord’s Incarnation.

They also produced three lay witnesses, who professed that for forty years, before the monastery of Terra Maggiore had invaded that church, they had seen monks of Monte Cassino appointed there; and that they had seen the priest Rudolph, who had received the lease mentioned above from Abbot Desiderius of happy memory, paying the said rent of six Byzantine coins to the monastery of Monte Cassino.

Having considered the authority of the laws, this judgment was pronounced by our brethren and, by God’s grace, confirmed by us. Since the representatives of the monastery of Terra Maggiore failed in the proof which they had asserted of forty years’ possession over St Mary of Casale Piano, we impose perpetual silence upon them in this matter, and decree that dominion over the same church of Casale Piano, together with its possessions, shall remain peacefully and perpetually with the monastery of Monte Cassino.

After this very full examination, by the tenor of this judgment we restore the aforesaid church of Blessed Mary of Casale Piano with its possessions to our venerable son Gerard, abbot of Monte Cassino, to the right and perpetual possession of the monastery of Monte Cassino; and by the authority of the Apostolic See we decree that it shall remain unshaken and secure.

Written by the hand of Crisogonus, notary of the sacred palace.

I, Paschal, bishop of the Catholic Church, in our presence confirmed and subscribed this judgment which was rendered. I, Sennes, by God’s grace archbishop of Capua, appointed judge, was present and subscribed. [Col. 0314A] I, Cono Richard, bishop of Albano, subscribed. I, Landulf, archbishop of Benevento, appointed judge, was present and subscribed. I, Gregory, bishop of Terracina, appointed judge, was present and subscribed. I, Gualo, bishop of Paris, appointed judge, was present and subscribed. I, Ascherus, bishop of Centumcellae, appointed judge, was present and subscribed. I, Raymond, archbishop of Auch, was present and subscribed. I, Almericus, bishop of Clermont, was present and subscribed. I, William, by God’s grace bishop of Troyes, [Col. 0314B] was present and subscribed. I, Anastasius, cardinal-priest of the title of Blessed Clement, subscribed. I, Romuald, cardinal-deacon, appointed judge, was present and subscribed. I, Boso, cardinal, appointed judge, was present and subscribed. I, Gervasius, abbot of the monastery of Telese, was present and subscribed. I, Roland, legate of the Church of Antioch, was present and subscribed. I, Pontius, legate of the Church of Antioch, was present and subscribed.

Done at Benevento, in the principal palace, on the second Ides of February [12 February]. Besides those subscribed above, many others were present also, both bishops and abbots: namely Riso of Bari, Leo of Ostia, and Fulco of Venosa.

Given at Benevento, through the hand of John, cardinal-deacon and librarian of the holy Roman Church, on the Ides of February [13 February], in the sixth indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1113, in the fourteenth year of the pontificate of lord Pope Paschal II.

### CCCLVII. Bull granting the protection of the Apostolic See to the hospice of St John of Jerusalem.  
(15 February 1113.)

[Mansi, *Councils*, XXI, 87.]

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable son GERAUD, founder and provost of the hospice of Jerusalem, and to his lawful successors in perpetuity.

A pious request ought to be brought to effect by its fulfilment. Your belovedness has requested that the hospice which you founded in the city of Jerusalem beside the church of Blessed John the Baptist be strengthened by the authority of the Apostolic See and fostered by the patronage of Blessed Peter the Apostle.

Delighted by the pious labours of your hospitality, we receive your petition with paternal benevolence; and by the authority of the present decree we establish that that house of God, that hospice, shall remain under the guardianship of the Apostolic See and the protection of Blessed Peter.

Therefore we command that all things acquired for that same hospice, through the exertion of your solicitude, for the support of pilgrims and the needs of the poor—whether within the parishes of the Church of Jerusalem or of other churches and in the territories of cities—or offered by any faithful persons, or which, by God’s bounty, may hereafter be offered or acquired by other lawful means; and whatever has been granted by the venerable brother bishops of the Church of Jerusalem, shall always be preserved untroubled and entire for you, your successors, and the brethren who there care for pilgrims.

We decree that the tithes of your crops, which you gather anywhere at your own expense and labour and which have been assigned to the hospice without objection from bishops or episcopal officials, shall be held valid. Upon your death, now being the guardian and provost of that place, no one shall be placed over it by any deceitful device or violence except the person whom the brethren professed there, according to God, shall judge should be elected.

Furthermore, whatever dignities or possessions that same hospice possesses beyond or on this side of the sea, namely in Asia or Europe, or may hereafter obtain by the Lord’s bounty, we confirm in perpetuity, both for you and your successors engaged in the pious work of hospitality, and through you for the same hospice.

Moreover, we decree that absolutely no person may rashly disturb that hospice, take away its possessions, retain those taken away, diminish them, or harass it with wanton vexations; but let all be preserved intact, wholly useful for the purposes of those for whose support and governance they were granted.

We establish that the hospices, or poorhouses (*ptochia*), in the western regions at the borough of St Giles, Asti, Pisa, Bari, Otranto, Taranto, and Messina, known under the title of Jerusalem, shall remain for ever under your and your successors’ authority and administration, as they are today.

If, therefore, in the future any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowing this page of our constitution, should rashly attempt [lacuna], then, after a second or third warning, unless he makes suitable amends, let him lose the dignity of his power and honour; let him know himself guilty before divine judgment for the iniquity perpetrated; let him be excluded from the most sacred body and blood of God and of the Lord our Redeemer Jesus Christ; and at the final judgment let him be subject to severe vengeance. But upon all who preserve what is right for that place may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that here they may receive the fruit of good action and before the strict Judge may find the rewards of eternal peace. Amen, amen.

I, Paschal, bishop of the Catholic Church, subscribed. I, Richard, bishop of Albano, subscribed. I, Landulf, archbishop of Benevento, read and subscribed. I, Cono, bishop of the Church of Palestrina, read and subscribed. I, Anastasius, cardinal-priest of the title of Blessed Clement, subscribed. I, Gregory, bishop of Terracina, read and subscribed. I, John, bishop of Malta, read and subscribed. I, Romuald, cardinal-deacon of the Roman Church, subscribed. I, Gregory, cardinal-priest of the title of St Chrysogonus, read and subscribed.

[Col. 0316A]

Given at Benevento, through the hand of John, cardinal and librarian of the holy Roman Church, on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of March [15 February], in the sixth indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1113, in the fourteenth year of the pontificate of lord Pope Paschal II.

### CCCLVIII. To Lanuin, prior of the Tower, he grants permission “to instruct and bless anchorites.”

(20 February 1113.—See *Life of St Bruno*, p. 409. Brussels, 1639, octavo.)

### CCCLIX. To Bernard, patriarch of Antioch.—States that he did not grant a privilege to the Church of Jerusalem to the prejudice of Antioch.  
(18 March 1113.)

[Mansi, *Councils*, XX, 1010.]

[Col. 0316B]

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his fellow bishop BERNARD, patriarch of Antioch, greeting and apostolic blessing.

As we wrote to your brotherhood in other letters, we love with full affection both your person and the church entrusted to you. In no way do we wish the honour of your dignity to be diminished; rather, we wish the primacy of the patriarchate of Antioch to be preserved whole in the future, by the Lord’s favour, just as it has been preserved in former times.

That which we granted to our son Baldwin, king of the people of Jerusalem, at the intercession of his messengers, ought not at all to disturb your charity, if you examine more deeply the meaning of our letters. For thus it is written in them: “The boundaries and possessions of churches which were or are in those regions have been thrown into confusion by the long possession and tyranny of unbelievers. Since, therefore, we cannot by the present deliberation assign them definite boundaries, we have judged it right to assent to your prayers: because you have devoted your person to the utmost dangers for the exaltation of the Church of Jerusalem, whatever cities of unbelievers you have taken or may take shall be subject to the governance and dignity of that church.”

The words which we wrote to Gibelin, patriarch of Jerusalem of happy memory, concerning cities and provinces acquired by God’s grace through the wisdom of the aforesaid King Baldwin and the blood of the armies following him must be interpreted in the same sense. For we wish those churches to be subject to that church to which they are known to belong by ancient right, if definite boundaries can be assigned to them and if their boundaries and possessions have not been confused by long possession and tyranny.

For we do not wish either ecclesiastical dignity to be diminished because of the power of princes, or the power of princes to be impaired because of ecclesiastical dignity.

Given at Benevento, on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of April [18 March].

### CCCLX. To Baldwin, king of Jerusalem.—On the same subject.  
(18 March 1113.)

[Same source, col. 1011.]

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his dearest son BALDWIN, illustrious king of the people of Jerusalem, greeting and apostolic blessing.

The concession which we granted at your petition—that whatever cities of unbelievers you have taken or may take should be subject to the governance and dignity of the Church of Jerusalem—has greatly disturbed both our brother Bernard the patriarch and the whole Church of Antioch.

For since we granted that concession concerning those churches whose boundaries and possessions have been confused by the prolonged possession and tyranny of unbelievers, they complain that, with your connivance, churches have been seized by the patriarch of Jerusalem concerning which there is no doubt that the see of Antioch possessed them even in the times of the Turks or Saracens, because their bishops, even though oppressed by the tyranny of unbelievers, rendered obedience to the patriarch of Antioch.

In letters sent to the aforesaid patriarch, we decreed that the primacy of the patriarchate of Antioch should be preserved whole in the future, just as it was distributed by the ancient Fathers and preserved in former times. We therefore admonish your valour, and in admonishing command you, not to allow such seizures to be made by you where the truth is manifest; but let every church enjoy the limits of its own right.

For we cannot openly oppose the ordinances of our holy Fathers. Nor do we in any way wish either ecclesiastical dignity to be diminished for the power of princes or the power of princes to be impaired for ecclesiastical dignity, lest peace in the Church—God forbid!—be disturbed among you upon either pretext.

We also command the clerics of Jerusalem by these present letters, since they have left their ancestral possessions and native land, as is believed, for the exaltation of the Church and for the observance of religion, that they be content with the right of the Church of Jerusalem and not seek unjustly or arrogantly to usurp things certainly known to belong by right to the Church of Antioch.

May the Almighty Lord protect you in all things by His right hand and grant you triumph over the enemies of the Church.

Given at the Lateran, on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of April [18 March].

### CCCLXI. Privilege for the monastery of St Nicasius of Rheims.  
(10 April 1113.)

[Marlot, *Metropolis of Rheims*, II, 253.]

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son JORAN, abbot of St Nicasius, greeting and apostolic blessing.

[Col. 0317D] Set in the watchtower of shepherds [lacuna]. Therefore, in accordance with the petition of our venerable brother Rodolph, archbishop of Rheims, we confirm for you and your successors the church of St Peter of Rumigny, with the altar of St Sulpicius, which have been taken from lay hands; likewise the altar of Luneio and the altar of Clerum, etc.

Given at the Lateran, on the fourth Ides of April [10 April], in the year 1114, in the fourteenth year of the pontificate of lord Paschal.

### CCCLXII. General privilege of the monastery of St Nicasius.  
(10 April 1113.)

[Varin, *Administrative Archives of Rheims*, I, I, 261.]

[Col. 0318A]

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son JORAN, abbot of St Nicasius, and to his successors to be regularly appointed in perpetuity.

Set as shepherd over the Church, we must oppose thieves and robbers and, by the enactment of our decree, check the presumption of secular persons who claim and stubbornly usurp churches and church property as though they were their own. Therefore, dearest son, assenting to your petitions, we strengthen the monastery of Blessed Nicasius [lacuna] by the authority of the Apostolic See, confirming to it [lacuna] the estate of St Hilary, which Gervasius, archbishop of Rheims, purchased from certain knights [lacuna] out of his own resources; and, having wholly freed it from the service of all persons, handed it over to God and St Nicasius, to be possessed in full liberty for the remedy of his soul, together with its *ban* and jurisdiction, its demesne holding, adjoining lands and pastures, and the free outlets of the same village; with mill-sites exempt from every exaction of freemen, both in the village and outside it; likewise the watercourse and the whole fishery, from the meadow from which the inhabitants of St Martin owe pasture-dues to Blessed Nicasius as far as the division of the territory of Mont-Saint-Remi; the church of St Hilary and three parts of the entire tithe, and the whole tithe of the produce of the monks’ estate.

At Sarnac, land sufficient for one plough-team and six mowings of meadow; half of the mill and of the entire fishery; half of the whole allod of Haideric’s court and all its appurtenances; the church of Vilterzet, with the whole tithe and one holding of arable land; the church of Betenacourt, with the two chapels of St Simeon and St Nicholas, to be maintained; and all the easements of the land of the whole aforesaid lordship, for the use of the monks serving God and Blessed Mary of Betenacourt; and the whole tithe of their cultivation and produce.

The monks, moreover, while retaining according to custom and usage the alms left to themselves, divide all the alms of parishioners granted to the parish priest and likewise the offerings brought to the hand of that priest or chaplain; they claim half thereof for themselves, except confessions, the two coins from marriages and blessings, and one coin from reconciliations, [Col. 0318D] which specifically belong to the priest’s portion.

The church and village of Sennicourt with its three appurtenances, Calmontana, Senuifa, and Raravilla, with the whole tithe, watercourse, meadows, lands, woods, and vineyards belonging to Sennicourt; and the *ban* and jurisdiction of all these things [lacuna]; the whole tithe of Vertiti; the whole tithe of Mello Fonte; the whole tithe of Lisunii as far as the ditch reaching beside Berlize, and belonging to the church of Sennicourt; the palace of Muncey, with all lands lying within the circuit of its walls, in full liberty; likewise the allod in the adjoining village, in fields and woods; the oak-grove below the hill, the wood of Arsuris, and a house in the middle of the village; half of the mill in the valley of Cierge; John Asinus and Alard Luseus with all their possessions; the land of Vivers before Ralph’s gate; the mill, vineyard, and meadow of Warne; a quarter-holding of land and the meadow of Reomela; the house belonging to the church of Maceries; land at Campilium yielding four solidi and eight denarii, with the wood of the same village, its sluice and watercourse, its *ban* and jurisdiction; likewise the wood above Cierge; the church of St Mary Magdalene of Cimac, with the hospital and the house before the gate, and gardens lying behind the church; the church and village of St Genevieve with their appurtenances; the allod of St Genevieve, in fields extending nearly two leagues, woods, meadows, waters, and mills, with male and female serfs, *ban* and jurisdiction, and the full liberty of all these things; one ninth of the entire cultivation of the lord of Cimac throughout all Sarto, which Lord Alard of Cimac gave to be possessed in perpetuity; the church of St Peter of Rumigny, with the full liberty of its endowment called Mont Baie and Ailimpre; the altar of St Sulpicius, with two chapels at Evernis and Livinis; a free market and toll, with stall-dues, at St Peter’s Chains, together with schools, male and female serfs, and one ninth of the meadow and of the three cultivated fields of the lord of Rumigny; half of Augusta, the mill, oven, woods, and lands, with *ban* and jurisdiction and a third of the tithes; the village of Pree, with the house of the church of St Albinus, woods, lands, mill, male and female serfs, *ban* and jurisdiction; the altar of Antinno with the chapels [lacuna] of Fouzis and Ogias.

[Note: Col. 0319D: A bull of 1136 reads: “Anteniacum with the chapels of Oggeium and Fulseium.” Two bulls of Paschal II, both of which seem to us to belong to the year 1112, and which occur again in the Cartulary of St Nicasius, fol. 12, no. 4, and fol. 20, no. 26, add: “At Murigny, Richard’s land; at Châtillon, vineyards and lands of the authors or painters [lacuna]. The altar of St Sixtus, with the rent of the surrounding borough, its investitures and sales, and the parish of Uriliac [lacuna]; and the cloister of the monastery with the suburb belonging to it [lacuna].”]

The altar of Attovillari, with its endowment and a third of the tithe; the altar of Bunut; the altar of Hanape; Alavio; the mill, lands and meadow, and one fourth of Flengni; the estate of Wlfereio. We confirm to you [lacuna] three parts of the two villages of Sincelia and Subnaym, with all revenue and customary exaction, together with two churches, male and female serfs, woods, meadows, and fields; these three parts being redeemable from the church of St Nicasius for thirty marks; the altar with the church of Morlines; half the allod of Florines, which after the death of Alpaïs and of her second generation shall pass, with all its appurtenances, freely and without claim to the church of St Nicasius by right of possession; together with half of Anolvit and the church with its appurtenances [lacuna]. Therefore let no person, etc., etc.

Given at the Lateran, through the hand of John [lacuna], cardinal-deacon [Col. 0320A] and librarian, on the fourth Ides of April [10 April], in the sixth indiction [lacuna], in the year [lacuna] 1114.

[Note: Col. 0320D: This date appears suspect. The sixth indiction and the fourteenth year of Paschal’s pontificate, combined with the given date in April, correspond to the year 1113. The same observation applies to the preceding bull and to the following bull addressed to the two abbeys of Saint-Remi and Saint-Nicasius. It was made before us by Mabillon (*De re diplomatica*, book II, chapter 25, no. 9), and *The Art of Verifying Dates*, I, 18, seeks to resolve the difficulty which it raises.]

In the fourteenth year of the pontificate of lord Pope Paschal II.

### CCCLXIII. He assigns the cell of Gordanicum to the monastery of Aniane. (12 April 1113.)

[Mabillon, *Annals of the Benedictines*, V, appendix, 695.]

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son PETER, abbot of the monastery of Aniane: greeting and apostolic blessing.

By the authority and duty of the Apostolic See, we are bound, while taking thought for the condition of all Churches, to provide, with the Lord’s help, for their peace. Therefore, while we were staying in the regions of Gaul, we judged it fitting to entrust for examination and determination to our venerable brothers Arbert, bishop of Avignon, Eustace, bishop of Valence, and Hismion, bishop of Die, that controversy which was being litigated between the monastery of Chaise-Dieu and the coenobium of Aniane concerning the cell of Gordanicum [Col. 0320B]. Having carefully discussed and canonically examined the arguments of both parties, as we have learned from their written allegation and deed, and having inspected the pontifical and royal documents and the evidence of other charters, they judged it just, and decreed by writings and subscriptions, that the monastery of Aniane ought to govern and hold in perpetuity for God’s service the aforesaid cell of Gordanicum. For, to use their own words, between the first lawful acquisition and the final lawful reinvestiture which they had received through us, they were unable to discover any lawful interruption of that possession [Col. 0320C].

We therefore confirm by the decree of this present letter the judgment of the aforesaid brethren, whom in this matter we appointed judges in our stead; and we decree that the aforesaid cell of Gordanicum shall remain secure and undisturbed for ever to you, most beloved Peter, abbot of the aforesaid monastery of Aniane, and to your successors. We command and prohibit that the brethren of Chaise-Dieu should presume any longer to harass the coenobium of Aniane with a complaint concerning this matter; rather, it shall be preserved peacefully and freely in perpetuity under the right and possession of the coenobium of Aniane, with all its appurtenances and possessions [Col. 0320D], as the record of the royal instrument declares that it was granted and conveyed to the coenobium of Aniane by Emperor Louis, son of Emperor Charlemagne.

If, therefore, in the future any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowing this page of our confirmation, should rashly attempt to act against it [Col. 0321A], let that person be deprived of the dignity of office and honour; let him know himself to stand guilty before divine judgment for the iniquity committed; let him be cut off from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, our Redeemer; and at the final judgment let him be subject to stern vengeance, unless, having been warned a second or third time, he correct his presumption by suitable satisfaction. But upon all who preserve what is just for that same coenobium may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that they may receive here the fruit of good action and find before the strict Judge the rewards of eternal peace. Amen, amen, amen.

I, Paschal, bishop of the Catholic Church, have subscribed.

Given at the Lateran, through the hand of John, cardinal and librarian of the Holy Roman Church [Col. 0321B], on the second Ides of April [12 April], in the sixth indiction [read: seventh], in the year 1114 from the Incarnation of the Lord, and in the fourteenth year of the pontificate of lord Paschal, the second pope.

### CCCLXIV. He exhorts the bishops and princes of Spain to put an end to the destruction of churches, killings, robberies, and burnings. (14 April 1113.)

[Mansi, *Councils*, XXI, 118.]

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brothers BERNARD, primate, and the other bishops and princes of Spain: greeting and apostolic blessing.

We grieve that in your regions calamities, the overthrow of churches [Col. 0321C–0322A], killings, robberies, and burnings occur in greater number than can be recounted by us. Accordingly, by this present letter we admonish your wisdom to seek remedies for such great evils through shared deliberation.
