We have indeed resolved, God assisting us, to send to you a legate of the Apostolic See as soon as we can. Meanwhile, by the capacity providentially granted you by God, take care in an assembly of bishops to provide for the public peace; and let whatever is canonically done therein obtain its effect hereafter by apostolic authority.

Moreover, those nobles or knights who have invaded and occupy offices of honour, obediences, villages, and other ecclesiastical goods, unless they desist from that invasion, we remove from communion with the Church. We also subject to excommunication the instigators of every faction [Col. 0322B], through whom wars and other crimes are committed among you, unless they desist from this wickedness. May our peace and our salvation, the Lord, mercifully bring about your peace and your salvation.

Given at the Lateran, on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of May [14 April].

### CCCLXV. Privilege concerning the borough of Saint-Remigius and the agreement between the aforesaid abbey of Saint-Remigius and the abbey of Saint-Nicaise. (15 April 1113.)

[Varin, *Administrative Archives of Reims*, I, I, 264. Archives of Saint-Remi, bundle 17, no. 1. — Cartulary B of Saint-Remi, p. 7. — Cartulary A, ibid., p. 47.]

[Note: [Col. 0321C] By this bull Paschal put an end to a serious quarrel which had arisen between the abbeys of Saint-Remi and Saint-Nicaise. This quarrel, whose history belongs to that of the internal government of our city, was recorded in a contemporary *factum* found at the end of the manuscript of Saint-Nicaise. We have been unable to recover either the manuscript entitled *Liber passionum sanctorum* (“Book of the Passions of the Saints”) or the text of the *factum* itself, but only an analysis given by Father Égée in his *History of Saint-Remi*. From it we borrow the following extract, collected by Lacourt, *Marl. Ann.* II, note at the beginning, fol. 29 verso.

However well established the rights of the abbey of Saint-Remi were over the whole borough, or ban, of Saint-Remi, Joran, abbot of Saint-Nicaise, nevertheless began about this time to dispute them in part and to bring against it litigation which lasted several years and could be ended only through the mediation of Pope Paschal II. Its subject and occasion were as follows.

When Archbishop Gervais placed religious at Saint-Nicaise in 1065 or 1066, Erlebaud, a canon of the church of Reims, still held by title the church of Saint-Xiste and received the tithes and quit-rents dependent upon it. But, having incurred the displeasure of that prelate, he was obliged to leave Reims and his benefices. Since the abbey of Saint-Nicaise was only newly founded and was not yet wealthy, Gervais gave it the church of Saint-Xiste with all its revenues. It enjoyed these peacefully during Gervais’s pontificate, and no one thought of troubling it in its possession. But Manasses I, who succeeded him in his see, having other purposes, recalled Erlebaud, had his prebend restored to him, and reinstated him in possession of the church of Saint-Xiste [Col. 0321D–0322C].

Furthermore, when Erlebaud fell ill some time later, he surrendered, at the persuasion of the same prelate, the altar and rights of Saint-Xiste into the hands of the abbot of Saint-Remi, to unite them to the chapter of Saint-Timothy. They were in fact united, and the canons enjoyed them until the deposition of Manasses and until Raynaud du Bellay had been substituted for him. Then Alberic, abbot of Saint-Nicaise, so won the prelate’s goodwill that he changed the arrangement and awarded the benefice of Saint-Xiste to the abbey of Saint-Nicaise, to the prejudice of the canons of Saint-Timothy, who had held it. An ancient author who relates this event, and who lived in or nearly in the same century, adds that Abbot Alberic employed every most illicit means to achieve his ends, and that only by force of money did he regain this benefice [Col. 0322C–D].

Be that as it may, when he was later accused and convicted by his own religious of having entirely dissipated the temporal goods of his monastery, he was canonically deposed for his poor administration, sent to the monastery of Saint-Remi to do penance there, and the abbey of Saint-Nicaise was committed for a time to Henry, abbot of Saint-Remi, by Archbishop Raynaud. The latter, however, passed through Chaise-Dieu while on his way to the Council of Clermont; and, since regular observance was then in full vigour, he gave the abbey of Saint-Nicaise to Seguin, abbot of Chaise-Dieu, that he might establish regular discipline there and appoint an abbot of his own choosing. Abbot Seguin, full of gratitude, came himself to Reims and established as abbot of Saint-Nicaise one of his religious, named John. Seguin even remained for some time at the monastery of Saint-Nicaise and subscribed several charters as abbot of Saint-Nicaise. But after his departure Abbot John yielded to the piety of the age and, having taken the cross after the example of so many other abbots, went to Jerusalem, where he died [Col. 0322D–0323A].

Joran was elected abbot of Saint-Nicaise in 1103. Not content with enjoying the altar and revenues of Saint-Xiste as his predecessors had done, he also undertook to add the right of jurisdiction there, rejecting the jurisdiction of Saint-Remi, to which alone recourse had previously been had in all contested matters for more than two hundred years. Nor did he confine his claims to this. Feeling himself supported by the authority of Archbishop Manasses II, whose favour he had cultivated with great care, and by the favour of his principal officers—namely Provost Raoul-le-Vert and Scholaster Odalric—he brought a second suit against Dudon, dean of Saint-Timothy, and his chapter, concerning a portion of the tithes of Vrilly which they had long possessed. By dishonest legal quibbles he had it awarded to himself, although Azenaire, abbot of Saint-Remi, had taken their side in this matter and intervened in the suit [Col. 0323A–B].

But the first affair must be resumed. When Archbishop Manasses II died in 1106, Raoul-le-Vert was elected by one part of the clergy and people, but his election was opposed by the other. The scholaster Odalric, among others, could not accept it; the reason is unknown. He deliberately journeyed to Rome to bring his complaints to Pope Paschal II, who had nevertheless consecrated Raoul himself at Troyes [lacuna]. The pope detained him at Rome and created him cardinal.

Joran, who had counted them all as friends, omitted nothing to secure the continuance of their favour, particularly that of Cardinal Odalric [Col. 0323B–C]. He soon made very useful use of it and obtained from Rome, through that cardinal, a brief of Pope Paschal II confirming the abbey of Saint-Nicaise in possession of the altar of Saint-Xiste and awarding it the jurisdiction, pleas, customs, and other rights which the abbot of Saint-Remi claimed had belonged to him originally and before any other person.

Joran nevertheless kept the affair secret and took great care not to publish his brief. But when the time of the synod arrived, he appeared there with the abbots of the diocese and, by virtue of the brief delivered to him by the sister of Cardinal Odalric, named V[—], in return for four marks of silver which he gave her, he sought justice from Archbishop Raoul against Abbot Azenaire, who was present at the synod. The prelate replied to Abbot Joran that he must produce his brief. When Abbot Azenaire heard it read, he was extremely surprised, protested against this surreptitiously obtained brief, and summoned the abbot of Saint-Nicaise before the pope, whom he chose as judge in the matter [Col. 0323C–D].

But Archbishop Raoul, seeing how deeply Abbot Azenaire took the matter to heart and how firmly he maintained his rights, represented to him that it was not yet time to bring the case to Rome, since no judgment had yet been rendered against him as a consequence of the brief. He added that he would convene bishops before whom he would submit the affair. Trusting these promises, Abbot Azenaire halted his proceedings and no longer considered going to Rome. But he had the vexation of finding himself deceived: several assemblies of bishops were held at Reims without any discussion of resolving the dispute in question.

Meanwhile, the abbot of Saint-Nicaise remained in correspondence with Cardinal Odalric. He communicated to Archbishop Raoul a letter from the cardinal informing him, on the pope’s behalf, that he should choose the most capable member of the community and send him to Rome, because the Holy Father intended to create him cardinal [Col. 0323D–0324A]. Bishop Raoul agreed, and the religious departed with his approval, but found the place apparently filled without having been admitted to the Sacred College. The pope merely charged him with a rescript for Archbishop Raoul, ordering him to restore peace and good understanding between the two abbots, with authority to excommunicate anyone who opposed it.

The prelate at once made his orders known to the parties and set about executing them. The abbot appeared so disposed to comply that, when the archbishop suggested that he give one hundred marks of silver to Saint-Nicaise, in return for which all litigation would be ended, he was willing to consent [Col. 0324A–B]. But when his religious learned of this, they joined with the burgesses of the ban of Saint-Remi in vigorous opposition; they even threatened to depose Abbot Azenaire if he thus betrayed the interests of the monastery. More than that, they urged and persuaded him to go without delay to Rome and bring his complaints to the pope. This so alarmed Raoul that, to prevent the journey, he again promised to give him complete satisfaction and be more favourable to him.

But as soon as he learned of the detention of Pope Paschal II, whom King Henry V had caused to be arrested at Rome, he pressed Azenaire hard to pay the one hundred marks upon which they had agreed. When the latter refused, Raoul pronounced judgment in the affair, refusing to grant the six-month delay sought by Abbot Azenaire. He gave the abbot of Saint-Nicaise jurisdiction in the ban of Saint-Remi and threatened Azenaire with censures if he did not accept the sentence [Col. 0324B–C]. Far from submitting to it, however, the religious of Saint-Remi and the burgesses of the ban protested that they would never do so. Learning that, under this sentence, the abbot of Saint-Nicaise had caused certain dues to be levied by officers accompanied by one of his religious, they immediately sent men to recover them. As soon as they learned that the abbot of Saint-Nicaise had shown only contempt for their delegates, they assembled in a crowd numbering as many as ten thousand and went tumultuously to carry off, up to the gates of the abbey, the flocks of the religious of Saint-Nicaise and all that belonged to them.

They intended to force the monastery in order to set it on fire; but the wiser restrained this popular fury, and perhaps still more did the vigorous resistance they encountered. For the religious of Saint-Nicaise, together with their men, climbed the bell tower and rained down upon the assailants a hail of stones and arrows, by which several burgesses were wounded [Col. 0324C–D]. The author describing this military action makes particular mention of one Bacherius, parish priest of Faverolles, who was then at Saint-Nicaise and was given command of the war engines. He operated them with remarkable skill, which contributed most to dispersing the mutinous crowd.

When Raoul learned what had occurred, believing the religious of Saint-Remi to be the authors, or at least the instigators, of these acts of violence, he summoned before the ecclesiastical court the burgesses of the ban of Saint-Remi. They refused to appear; and he placed under interdict all the churches of the borough except that of Saint-Nicaise. In vain did the religious of Saint-Remi point out to him that their church had been consecrated by Pope Leo IX, who had granted it great privileges, and that Pope Paschal II, still living, had granted it a privilege forbidding, under penalty of anathema, the troubling of the religious who served it [Col. 0324D–0325A]. No regard was paid to this, nor to their statement that the time had not yet arrived when the bishops and abbots of the province were to settle the dispute.

All they could obtain was permission to celebrate the divine office in their church behind closed doors, admitting no lay person and with no ringing of bells [Col. 0325A–B]. This did not satisfy the religious of Saint-Remi, and their servants were so indignant that all withdrew and abandoned them, one hundred in number, rather than submit to the interdict. The religious were thereby unable to celebrate the divine office.

In this extremity, they sent two of their number, Lambert and Geoffrey, to Rome to inform Pope Paschal II of everything that was occurring; they also brought their complaints to the court. Raoul took occasion from this to urge Azenaire to accept a settlement. He consented and appeared with Joran before five bishops who were to decide their dispute. The abbot of Saint-Nicaise frankly acknowledged that the borough of Saint-Remi belonged to Azenaire. “But since the pope has given me a part of it,” he said, “it is not just that I should be deprived of it or stripped of a privilege which permits me to enjoy it.” The abbot of Saint-Remi replied at once that the alleged privilege ought to be put into his hands and that this must be the first step [Col. 0325B–C].

The bishops then proposed another expedient: Joran would absolutely surrender all claims to jurisdiction in the ban of Saint-Remi, acknowledge that it belonged solely to the abbot of Saint-Remi, and receive in return an additional annual rent of one hundred sous. In order that Joran’s successor abbots might later avail themselves of this privilege, it would be placed in the hands of Archbishop Raoul, who would issue a charter of this agreement sealed with his seal. This proposal was read in the chapter of Saint-Remi in the bishops’ presence, and Azenaire was not opposed to it. But the religious of Saint-Remi, fearing that someone wished to deceive them, refused to accept it. They preferred to send two of their number, Odo and Roger, to Rome to make known the state of affairs to the pope and implore his protection.

He had already given it to them with wholly paternal kindness, as appears from the letter which Lambert and Godfrey had brought to Archbishop Raoul. It is dated from Anagni, on the fourth Ides of October [12 October], and states in substance that he was surprised that, on the occasion of a privilege granted to the abbot of Saint-Nicaise, Raoul troubled and ill-treated the religious of Saint-Remi; for he knew Raoul’s prudence and believed that, as common father, he ought to have equal affection for both parties. Moreover, it was not his intention that this privilege, which may have been obtained by surprise, should inflict any prejudice upon the religious of Saint-Remi [Col. 0325C–D]. “Therefore,” he added, “settle this dispute with the advice of the bishops and abbots of the province, or send the two abbots to Rome; and meanwhile let the monastery of Saint-Remi remain in its customary peace and quiet.”

The refusal of the religious of Saint-Remi to subscribe to the settlement proposed by the bishops did not prevent Azenaire from conferring with the prelates on the same subject and labouring with Raoul to remove obstacles to a good agreement. With this purpose, the abbot of Saint-Remi, who had escorted the bishops to the archiepiscopal residence, said on his return that the office could be celebrated. When the religious asked whether the archbishop had ordered this, he said that he had not forbidden it, but only ordered them carefully to avoid the excommunicated [Col. 0326A–B].

Meanwhile the delegates of Saint-Remi, Odo and Roger, returned to Reims bearing a papal letter for Raoul. It appears from this letter that the prelate had informed the pope that peace had been completely restored and had even set forth all its conditions in detail. “Your letters,” the pope said to him, “contain very different things. You first inform us that you have settled the dispute in question without derogating from the privilege which we granted to the abbot of Saint-Nicaise, and that you have preserved the rights of both claimants without impairing either; then you ask us to issue new letters to prevent this privilege from giving rise to fresh disputes. Since we desire nothing more than peace for our brethren, we must not scandalize them by such a course.

“We judge it more fitting that the abbots of Saint-Remi and Saint-Nicaise come to Rome for the coming feast of Christmas, bringing the draft of their agreement and the privilege granted to Saint-Nicaise, so that, if anything needs correction, we may correct it ourselves; and, after seriously examining the right of the parties, may, by the Lord’s grace, give peace to the monasteries. We nevertheless desire that the privilege granted by us to the religious of Saint-Remi at Auxerre in 1107, in your presence and with your consent, remain in full force; and you must ensure that those of your officers who have boldly violated it make satisfaction to the monastery. As for the other complaints of the religious of Saint-Remi, you will render them justice. It is wholly fitting that, as son and successor of so celebrated a father, you show your zeal for him by protecting his interests” [Col. 0326B–C].

There is no knowledge that the abbots of Saint-Remi and Saint-Nicaise went to Rome. But there is every reason to believe that they sent the proposed settlement, prepared and drafted by the bishops of the province—Lisiard, bishop of Soissons; Galderic or Valderic of Laon; Humbert of Senlis; and Odo of Cambrai—and accepted by the parties. For the pope, to confirm it, sent a brief to Abbot Azenaire declaring that, in accordance with this agreement, the abbot of Saint-Remi would alone have jurisdiction over the borough and could hold pleas there three times a year; that the right of stallage, the wine toll, and the apprehension of thieves together with cognizance of offences would belong jointly and undividedly to him and the archbishop; that the abbot of Saint-Nicaise would enjoy the parish and church of Saint-Xiste and the tithes of Vrilly; and that the church of Saint-Timothy would have the parish of the borough. This brief, which ended all proceedings, was issued at Saint John Lateran on 14 April 1114 [Col. 0326C–D].]

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his lord son AZENAIRE, abbot of the venerable monastery of Saint-Remigius [Col. 0323A], and to his successors to be regularly promoted for ever.

Of Jesus Christ, God and man, namely our head, it is written: “For he himself is our peace, who made both one.” Likewise it is written concerning him: “Who was made for us wisdom from God and righteousness” [Col. 0324A; 0325A]. It is therefore fitting that we who are members of that head should, according to his grace, provide peace for the lower members, who indeed are members from a member, and wisely determine justice. Hence it was expedient to remove the causes of dissension and disputes between the monasteries of Saint-Remigius and Saint-Nicaise [Col. 0325A–0326A], which had arisen between those monasteries concerning the intervening borough.

Therefore, just as in the presence of our fellow brother Raoul, archbishop of Reims, and certain bishops of the same province, the rights of that borough were distinguished between you, venerable son Azenaire, [lacuna] and Joran, venerable abbot of Saint-Nicaise, so we confirm that distinction by the declaration of our authority: the abbot of Blessed Remigius shall hold sole jurisdiction in that borough and shall hold pleas three times each year; but jointly with the archbishop of Reims he shall hold the grain-measure, the wine toll (*roaticium*), and a thief, if he be captured there [lacuna] [Col. 0326A–0327A]. The abbot of blessed Nicaise shall hold the rest, as is contained in the records of our privilege. But the church of Blessed Timothy shall hold the parish of that borough peacefully and quietly, so that no occasion for dissension concerning these matters may henceforth remain between the same monasteries [lacuna].

Given at the Lateran, through the hand of John, cardinal and librarian of the Holy Roman Church, on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of May [15 April], in the sixth indiction, in the year [lacuna] 1114 from the Incarnation, and in the fourteenth year of the pontificate of lord Paschal II, pope [Col. 0327B].

### CCCLXVI. He confirms the possessions of the monastery of Saint Victor of Marseilles. (23 April 1113.)

[*Gallia Christiana*, I, 115.]

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son in Christ, OTTO, abbot of the monastery of Marseilles, and to his successors to be regularly appointed for ever.

By the authority and duty of the Apostolic See, we are bound to take thought for the condition of all churches and, with the Lord’s aid, to provide for their peace. Therefore we have judged that your petitions, most beloved son Otto in Christ, should rightly be granted, so that we might fortify the monastery of Marseilles [Col. 0327C], over which by God’s authority you preside, with the privilege of the Apostolic See, following the example of our predecessors Gregory VII and Urban II. By the page of this present privilege, therefore, we confirm for you and your successors those things which were confirmed by the aforesaid pontiffs:

In the diocese of Arles: the monastery of Saints Genesius and Honoratus; the church of St Peter and Holy Trinity of Fanobriculum; that of Saints Sergius and Bacchus in the Camargue; the church of St Caesarius of Villanova; St Caesarius of Bodenenc; the cell of St Michael of Barzaneges, with its chapels; St Victor of Marmana; and St Heymetis.

In the diocese of Avignon: the cell of St Saturninus; St Mary of Roccamartina; and St Mary of Mirano.

In the diocese of Chalon [Cabillon]: the monastery [Col. 0327D] of St Mary; St Veranus of Vaucluse; the church of St Julian; the cell of St Michael of Balina; the parish of St Agoldus; and the church of St Faith.

In the diocese of Carpentras: the parish church of Rocca; the cell of St Romanus; St Mary of Vellaloue; and the monastery of St Felix of Vennesta.

In the diocese of Valence: the monastery of St Mary; St Victor; St Peter of Grausello; the parish church of the castle of Malancena; St Michael; St Peter with its chapels; St Desiderius; St Martin; St Mary; the Holy Sepulchre; the chapels of Albaruscum; the church of St Mary of Vellis; of Mirabel; St Blaise; St Mary of Villanova; and one half of all the parish churches of the Valley of Pladianus.

[Col. 0328A] In the diocese of Marseilles: the church of St Peter of Paradis; St Ferreolus; St Mary; St Margaret; the cell of St Genesius; St Justus; St Mitrius; St Mary of Evola; St Michael of Plano; St Pontius of Geminas; the church of St John of Roccafort; St Paul of Carnot; St Mary of Cezeresca; St Damian; the parish church of Cadeira with its chapels; the cell of St Peter of Auriol, with the parish of that castle and its chapel; the cell of Zachariah; the church of St Victor of Savard; the parish church of Castelli nautis, with its chapels; the cell of St Victor of Causalo; St James of Alniis, with the whole village; the church of St Victor; St Mary of Balma; St Cassian; the cell of St Saturninus in the castle of St Cannat; and the church of St Andrew.

In the diocese of Toulon [Col. 0328B]: the church of St Mary of Sexfurnis; St John of Crota; St Nazarius; the cell of St Victor of the Island; St John of Ferleda; the church of the Holy Trinity; the parish church of Solariis; St Michael of Eiras; the cell of St Benedict; St Bartholomew of Belgensier; St Martin of Corias; St John of Petrafoco; the parish church of that same castle, with its chapels; St Martin; St Mary of Colobreira; the parish church of St Pontius of that same castle; St Cedomius; St Mary of Dexesa; St Lawrence of Pinet; St Victor of Carnola; and St Michael.

In the diocese of Aix: the church of St Peter; the cell of St Peter of Gardana; the church of St Valentine with its chapels; St Andrew of Bac; the cell of St Hippolytus; the church of Vellana; the cell of St Mary of Nicar; St John of [Col. 0328C] Segia; the parish church of St Peter of Caudalonga; St Germanus; the church of Venel; St Michael of Fuel with its parish church; the cell of St Peter of Favarico; the church of St Julian of Podionigro; St Peter and St Victor in the castle of Trets; the cell of the Holy Trinity; the parish church of St Mary; the chapels of St Andrew, St Cecilia, and St Michael of Castellar; the parish church of Roccafolio; St Audertus; the parish church of Porcils; St Antoninus of Barda; St Servus; St Pematus of Rosceto with its parish church; St Pontius of Podium Luparium with its parish church; St Pancras; St Mary of Sale; the parish church of Porreiras with its chapels; the monastery of St Maximinus; St Mitrius; the church of St Stephen of Fur; St Simeon of Auriac; the cell of St [Col. 0328D] Mary of Brusa; St Mary of Sporrone; and the parish church of St Faith of Artiga; the cell of St Stephen of Tresde; St Victor of Gontarelle; St Victor of Adonia; the parish church of Laberbent; St Martin of Toulant; St Leodegar; St Raphael; the parish church of Roger of Caudalonga; the cell of St Stephen of Torreves; the church of Graleu; St Julian of Gaisola; St Mary; the cell of St Perpetua; St Peter; the parish church of Braquola; the church of St John; St Mary of Campis; St Mary of Garelle; St Medard; St Eucherius of Brar; St Victor of Curcurim; St Peter of Arara with its parish church; St Mary of Belmont; St Maurice of Reliana; the Holy Sepulchre [Col. 0329A] of the Cross; the parish church of St John; St Maurice of Torreves with its chapels; and St Peter of Sillone.

In the diocese of Fréjus: the parish church of St Mary of Cabaza; St Pontius; St Peter; the cell of St Mary of Luc; St Peter of Archs; the parish church of that castle with its chapels; the church of St Julian of Ailla; the cell of St Cassian of Salelaudimia; St Victor of Mota; St Romanus of Escaus; St Mary of Palione; St Victor of Roccataliada; St Saviour of Burnis; the parish church of Celians; the church of St Mary; the cell of St Mary of Bariemone; St Ausilius; the parish church of Colar; the cell of St Torpetis; St Pontius; St Mary of Questa; the parish church of Gival; St Antoninus of Nistra Castle; [Col. 0329B] the monastery of St Mary of Villacrosa; St Peter of Salernas, with its parish church; St Dominus of Tortorium; St Mary of Villa-alta; and St Martin of Rocabenna.

In the diocese of Riez: the cell of St Julian of Lauguias; St Mary of Aiguvia; St Maurice of Merresta; St John of Castromonasterii; St Guiricus; St Stephen of Recena; St Peter of Archinzosch; St Martin of Bromede; St Trophimus; the Holy Cross; and St Cassian of Tavernas.

In the diocese of Apt: the cell of St Paul; St John of Campanias; St Symphorian; the parish church of Bouils with its chapel; and the church of Cezarista.

In the diocese of Sisteron: the cell of St Mary of Mannasca; St Martin; St Marcellinus of Moazaellis; St Provianus of the Lime Kiln; and St [Col. 0329C] Mary of Petramordi.

In the diocese of Gap: the cell of St Mary of Mandamaes; St Christopher of Estradis; the parish church of Scola; St Martin of Cornilhon; St Dominus in Valletrari; St Genesius of Dromon; the parish church of that castle with its chapels; the cell of Fistal; St Eregius of Valerna with the parish church of St Mary; the church of Almebel; St Peter of Valadoira; St Clement of Tresclens with the other churches of that castle; St Peter of Roma; and St Eregius of Medulone.

In the diocese of Embrun: the church of Carde; St Mary; St Victor; St Christopher; St Ballus; St Mary of Bredula with the parish church of St Mary; St Peter of [Col. 0329D] Bigernis; the parish church of Bellefaire; the church of St Mary; and St Genesius of Curies; St Mary; and St Pontius of Falcone.

In the diocese of Glandèves: the cell of St Peter of Bonovillari; the cell of Penna; St Pontius of Adaunot; St Cassian; the Holy Sepulchre at Mugillos; and St Mary of Toraminas.

In the diocese of Narbonne: the cell of St Mary at Bargo; St Crescentius in the viscounty of Minervois; the cell of St Mary of Soea; and St Marcellinus with its chapels.

In the diocese of Maguelone: St Nazarius of Medullium; and the cell of Burgeries.

In the diocese of Nîmes: St Victor of Armareis; St Martin [Col. 0330B] of Airas; the parish church of St Peter of Mauroix; St Peter of Ariges; St Mary of Sauviana; St Martin of Alzone; and St Peter of Vicavo.

In Uzès: St Mammetus; St Amantius of Tezeno; and St Peter of Vulpereries.

In Toulouse: the cell of Castillione of Maderies.

In the diocese of Albi: the cell of St Sigolena of Gana; St Mary of Ambilet; St Peter of Ammone; and St John of Helvas.

In Rouergue: the cell of Petra; St Mary of Melias; the monastery of St Stephen; St Peter; St Lawrence; the cell of Cambolas; St Genesius of Valcenga; the cell of Mistoliol of Clara Fara; St Michael; St Mary of Castronovo; the monastery of Vabres; and St Amantius.

In Gévaudan: the monastery of Cirac with its parish church; St Martin of Canonica; St Martin of Salmonte with its chapels [Col. 0330C]; St Martin of Colomeo; and St Mary of Nabinals.

In Auvergne: the cell of Ruina.

In the diocese of Pisa: the cell of St Andrew; and the monastery of the Holy Apostles.

In the diocese of Vic: the monastery of St John of Ripoll, as it was entrusted to you, by the counsel of Pope Urban, through Bernard, count of Besalú; etc. We decree, therefore, that no person whatsoever may, etc.

Written by the hand of Crysogonus, notary of the Sacred Palace.

Given at the Lateran, through the hand of John, deacon cardinal of the Holy Roman Church and librarian, on the ninth day before the Kalends of May, in the sixth indiction, in the year 1114 of the Incarnation, in the fourteenth year of the pontificate of Paschal II.

CCCLXVII. Bull enumerating and receiving under Apostolic protection the Camaldolese monasteries. (A.D. 1113, November 4.)

[MITTARELLI, *Annals of Camaldoli*, III, Appendix, 1243.]

[Col. 0330D]

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable son GUIDO, prior of the Camaldolese, and to his successors for ever.

Thanks be to God for His inexpressible gift. For in our times the religious life of the Camaldolese hermitage or monastery has so increased and so flourished that diverse communities have, by the grace of God, come together into one congregation, and very many places have maintained one discipline, one order, and one government, as though of one heart and one soul. Desiring that this unity should always be preserved in the Lord, [Col. 0331A] we command and, by the authority of this decree, enact that no person whatsoever—cleric, monk, or layman, of whatever order or rank, now or in time to come—may in any way divide from its subjection and unity the communities and places which have accepted the discipline and order of the Camaldolese hermitage or monastery and which are today under its rule.

For the sake of preserving this unity, these places and communities have seemed fit to be recorded by their individual names. In the diocese of Arezzo: the monastery of St Saviour of Borardingorum; St Peter in Rota; St Mary in Agnano; St Quiricus in Rosa; the hermitage of Fleri; the monastery of St Virianus; St Bartholomew in Anglare near the baths; and the monastery of St Mary [Col. 0331B] in Trivio.

At Galeata: the monastery of St Mary on the island, and the hermitage of Fajoli.

In the diocese of Bologna: the monastery of the Holy Archangel near the castle of Britti, and that of St Felix.

In the diocese of Florence: the monastery of St Petrinus of Luco, and St Saviour near the city.

In the diocese of Fiesole: the monastery of St Mary in Poplena.

In the diocese of Volterra: the monastery of St Peter in Fontiano; St Mary in Puliciano; St Peter in Cerroto; St Justus near the city; and St Mary in Morona.

In the diocese of Pisa: the monastery of St Stephen in Cintoria, and that of St Sabinus in Cerosolo. In the city itself: the monastery of St Michael and St Frigdianus.

In the diocese of Lucca: the monastery of St Saviour in Cantiniano and St Peter in Puteoli. Likewise, [Col. 0331C] in Sardinia, in the diocese of Torres: the monastery of the Holy Trinity of Sacaria and the church of St Peter of Scanno. Likewise, in Tuscany, in the diocese of Chiusi: the hermitage on Mount Amiata.

We therefore decree and, by the authority of the Apostolic See, enact that all these places, together with everything belonging to those monasteries, shall remain for ever as one body under one head—that is, under the prior of the Camaldolese hermitage—and shall persevere in the observance of that discipline, under that prior, namely, who, by the Lord’s favour, shall be canonically elected from among the abbots or priors of that congregation and the hermits themselves.

Moreover, we decree that the congregation itself shall perpetually be fostered under the protection of the Apostolic See, so that no bishop may have authority, without the consent of the prior [Col. 0331D] or the permission of the Apostolic See, to excommunicate anything belonging to these monasteries or to prohibit them from divine offices. The brethren, however, shall be free to receive the sacraments of consecration and ordination from whatever Catholic bishop they prefer.

Furthermore, we decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb these monasteries, take away their possessions, retain what has been taken away, diminish them, or harass them by reckless vexations; but that all things shall be kept intact for the benefit, in every respect, of those for whose support and governance they were granted [Col. 0332A].

If, therefore, in the future any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowing this page of our constitution, should rashly attempt to act against it, and, having been admonished a second or third time, should not make amends by suitable satisfaction, let that person be deprived of the dignity of office and honour, recognize himself or herself as liable before the divine judgment for the iniquity committed, be separated from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ the Redeemer, and at the last judgment be subject to severe vengeance. But upon all who observe what is just in relation to these same monasteries may the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ rest, so that they may receive here the fruit of good works and find, before the strict Judge, the rewards of eternal [Col. 0332B] peace. Amen, amen, amen.

Written by the hand of Crisogonus, notary of the Sacred Palace.

I, Paschal, bishop of the Catholic Church, have subscribed.

Given at Anagni through the hand of John, deacon cardinal of the Holy Roman Church and librarian, on the second Nones of November, in the seventh indiction, in the year 1114 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the fifteenth year of the pontificate of lord Pope Paschal II.

CCCLXVIII. To the clergy of the Church of Tournai.—He grants them leave to have a bishop of their own, the yoke of the Church of Noyon having been cast off. (A.D. 1114, November 6.)

[Dom BOUQUET, *Recueil*, XV, 55.]

[Col. 0332C] POPE PASCHAL to GOTER, dean of the Church of Tournai [Note: [Col. 0331D] Lambert, who then held jointly the bishoprics of Noyon and Tournai.], LAMBERT, archdeacon, and the chapter, the abbots, and the other provosts of churches.

We are not unaware that your church has been greatly impaired by many losses, because for so long a time it has lacked the assistance of a pastor of its own. We have also learned from the report of worthy men that so great a multitude of people has now grown up there that it necessarily requires a bishop of its own, even if it had not possessed one in ancient times.

Accordingly, compelled both by the enactments of the sacred canons and by the earnest purpose of our predecessor Pope Urban, of holy memory—who had considered this very matter [Note: [Col. 0331D] See among Urban’s letters under the year 1098.]—we are obliged to restore a cardinal priest to your church. Therefore, by these present letters, we admonish your whole community and command by Apostolic authority [Col. 0332D] that, after consultation with the bishops of the province, namely of Thérouanne (John) and Arras (Lambert), you shall, without delay, make an election of a pastor in accordance with the canons, so that your church may be wholly severed from the Church of Noyon [Note: [Col. 0331D] By force of these letters the people of Tournai elected Herbert as their bishop; but he was rejected by King Louis and compelled to yield to the aforesaid Lambert [Col. 0332D].]. We lay upon him whom the consent of the brethren elects the obligation of obedience, that he accept the election, unless he knows himself to be prohibited by the sacred canons.

Given at Anagni, on the eighth Ides of November. [Note: [Col. 0332D] In the year 1114, as is inferred from Paschal’s sealed diplomas issued at Anagni in that year and month, which may be seen in the deeds of his reign set out above by us. Hence the need to correct the chronology of the bishops of Noyon in the latest *Gallia Christiana*.]

CCCLXIX. To Lambert, bishop, and the canons of Arras. (A.D. 1113, November 9.)

[BALUZE, *Miscellanies*, Lucca edition, II, 156.]

[Col. 0333A]

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved brethren LAMBERT, bishop, and the canons of the Church of Arras: greeting and Apostolic blessing.

The dispute that has long been conducted between you and the monks of St Vedast grieves us deeply. For we love both you and them, and desire concord and charity to prevail among you. Recently, however, we have heard that a frivolous question has arisen between you concerning the people of the chapel of St Maurice: namely, that on the principal [Col. 0333B] feasts they ought not to receive the sacraments of the Lord’s body and blood in that chapel itself. This certainly appears wholly frivolous and irrational: that a people admitted throughout the whole year to divine offices in that place should be excluded from communion in the Lord’s body and blood on solemn days, unless perhaps they are under interdict or are liable for some crime.

We therefore admonish your charity by these present letters to desist from such a contention and not further harass on this account either the aforesaid brethren or their priest who is stationed in the chapel. If any should wish to approach the mother church on the principal solemnities for the joy of more celebrated days, we by no means prohibit it. But if you should wish further to burden them in this matter, then, God granting, we shall extend a helping hand to those suffering injury.

Given at Anagni, on the fifth Ides of November.

CCCLXX. To Lambert, bishop of Arras. (A.D. 1113, December 13.)

[BALUZE, ibid.]

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother LAMBERT, bishop of Arras: greeting and Apostolic blessing.

The length of your illness has caused the canons of your church great alarm lest the affairs of the church be squandered by certain intruders. Hence, at their request, we have thought it fitting, with the Lord’s help, to provide for the condition of that church. We grant to the monks of St Vedast, as was determined in the judgment of ourselves and our brethren, the continued possession of those things designated by the letters of our authority. But we do not permit them, or any others hereafter, to invade or, without the will of the bishop and clergy, to usurp what belongs to the right of your Church of Arras.

Moreover, let all parishioners of the mother church of Blessed Mary, both within and outside Arras, render to that mother church first-fruits, tithes, solemn offerings, and the other parochial dues—namely, those parishioners who receive baptism, instruction, and burial from that mother church. For it is fitting that temporal things be reaped from those in whom spiritual things are sown. If they refuse to render them, let them be compelled by the bishop, at the instance of the canons and the canons’ priests who exercise pastoral care over them. Let those parishioners be admitted to communion by the priests who receive their confession and have charge of them.

We nevertheless grant free-will offerings both to the mother church and to the other churches to which they are given through the devotion of the faithful. But if anyone, knowing the tenor of this decree, should rashly attempt to oppose it, let that person be punished by the vengeance of Apostolic displeasure.

Given at the Lateran, on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of January, in the seventh indiction.

CCCLXXI. He protects the liberty of the monastery of St Bertin at Sithiu against Pons, abbot of Cluny. (A.D. 1113.)

See Iperius, *Chronicle of St Bertin*, in MARTÈNE, *Thesaurus Anecdotorum*, III, 609.

[Col. 0334B]

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, etc.

To this end, the Lord so disposing, etc.

Given in the year of the Lord 1113.

CCCLXXII. To William, archbishop of Besançon. (A.D. 1100–1114.)

[MANSI, *Councils*, XXI, 141.]

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother GUIDO, archbishop of Vienne and legate of the Apostolic See: greeting and Apostolic blessing.

You are to know that the controversy between the canons of St John and St Stephen at Besançon, so long [Col. 0334C] turned over and reconsidered, has at last been decided before us by canonical judgment. For the former, namely the canons of St John, asserted that the episcopal seat had remained in their church for many years; while the latter, namely the canons of St Stephen, maintained through certain privileges and precepts that their church was the mother church, but complained that, on the occasion of its destruction, the cathedra had been removed from it.

Accordingly, by the decrees of the Council of Chalcedon and with the common consent of our brethren, it has been adjudged that, if the canons of Blessed Stephen can prove by suitable witnesses that, after the restoration of their church, they brought proceedings within thirty years regarding this complaint, such that their possession may be seen to have been interrupted—whether before their bishop or before our legate in a public hearing—then, once this proof has been completed, their privileges shall retain their proper force and the episcopal seat shall henceforth be held at the church of Blessed Stephen. Otherwise, the canons of Blessed John shall remain free from this claim and shall hold the episcopal seat as they have held it.

Certainly, in carrying out this business, that prolonged excommunication which they suffered from your brotherhood on account of this matter shall not hinder them in any way. Furthermore, the canons of Blessed Stephen have complained that the muniments of their church are being withheld by the canons of St John. Likewise, the canons of St John complained that certain customary provisions had been taken from them by the others. It has therefore been adjudged that the muniments of the church be returned altogether to the former, [Col. 0335A] together with wine and the mansionary’s prebend; and that the latter receive restitution of their material goods, namely wine, meat, and wax.

We therefore command your diligence, in order to carry out this matter and to quiet the dispute of so great a scandal, to meet, having with you wise and religious brethren, either at Dijon or at another more suitable place, to which they can bring without burden the persons necessary to them. Setting aside every partisan animosity, receive the completion of this judgment so sincerely and so clearly that no further litigation or complaint concerning this matter may remain between them. The witnesses who establish this case must be five, whether clerics or laymen, since a graver cause concerning the head church of the parish is at issue; and, in accordance with canonical enactments, they must give testimony from sight and hearing.

We expressly command that the execution of this judgment be completed and concluded by the coming Assumption of Blessed Mary. Meanwhile, the processions and celebrations of offices customarily performed by either church shall be reciprocally rendered according to custom.

Given at the Lateran, on the tenth day before the Kalends of May. [Note: [Col. 0335D] Guido obeyed the pontiff’s command and convened the Council of Trénorcy in 1115, as will shortly be proved, to decide this dispute. What was done there Guido himself recounts in the constitution which he issued on this matter after becoming supreme pontiff and changing his name to Callistus II [Col. 0336D].]

CCCLXXIII. To the twelve arbitrators of Arras.—That they decide the dispute between the clerics of the Church of Arras and the monks of St Vedast without partiality toward either party. (A.D. 1113–1114, November 6.)

[MANSI, *Councils*, XX, 1033.]

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the worthy men HUGH the elder, DODO of HASTIS, the brothers GUAZELIN [Col. 0335C] and GONZELIN, FULCO son of Anselm, HILVIN son of Adelfrid, GUASELIN the knight, GIRARD the Saracen, GERBOD father of Baldwin, THEOBALD son of Bonevita, HERIBERT, and AGANO, citizens of the municipality of Arras: greeting and Apostolic blessing.

We have heard that you are worthy men and therefore, as good sons of the Church, we confidently command you what must be commanded. For the dispute conducted between the clerics of your church and the monks of Blessed Vedast is exceedingly troublesome and burdensome to us. Most recently, in order to settle that litigation concerning the boundaries of the old and new borough, they chose you as more truthful arbitrators.

Therefore, by the authority of God and Blessed Peter, we command you and impose upon you, for the remission of sins, that, laying aside every friendship and enmity, you declare whatever you know more truly and certainly concerning the boundaries of the old and new borough. And so that no party may doubt the truthfulness of your testimony, we command, for the salvation of your souls, that each of you take this oath: that he will state, to the best of his knowledge, the truth about these boundaries, and that he will not speak falsely for friendship, enmity, or money. If, however, two, three, or four of you disagree or are absent, the assertion of eight witnesses shall have force.

Given at Anagni, on the eighth Ides of November.

CCCLXXIV. To Lambert, bishop of Arras.—He writes concerning the arbitrators selected by himself to settle the dispute between the canons and monks of Arras. (A.D. 1113, November 6.)

[MANSI, *Councils*, XX, 1032.]

[Col. 0336A]

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother LAMBERT, bishop of Arras: greeting and Apostolic blessing.

Concerning the long-standing dispute between your canons and the monks of St Vedast, we have often written to you and you have sent us letters. Yet, to our considerable grief, the same dispute continues. For we could not justly compel the monks, who were absent, to accept the division that you settled. But when messengers of both parties recently came to us, we compelled both parties by our authority to choose these arbitrators. We therefore ask your charity not to take it ill that we have in no way confirmed the division of the old and new borough communicated in your letters, because, as we have said, the monks could not justly be compelled to accept it. Yet we wish you to exert yourself wholly to have this settlement carried out within forty days, as we have determined, since neither party can oppose the arbitrators selected.

CCCLXXV. Privilege for the monastery of St Rufus of Avignon. (A.D. 1114, January 10.)

[*Gallia Christiana*, old edition, IV, 802.]

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved [Col. 0336C] son ADELGERIUS, abbot of the canons of St Rufus in the diocese of Avignon, and to his successors canonically appointed for ever.

It is fitting to grant ready assent to the desires of religious devotion, so that faithful devotion may attain a swifter result. Therefore, assenting to the petitions of your devotion, we receive under the protection of the Apostolic See the church of Blessed Rufus, over which by God’s authority you preside, with all its appurtenances. By the page of this present privilege, therefore, we establish by Apostolic authority that whatever goods and possessions seem to belong to the monastery of Blessed Rufus by the lawful gifts of the faithful or by other just means, and whatever it may hereafter be able justly and canonically to acquire through grants of pontiffs, the liberality [Col. 0336D] of princes, or offerings of the faithful, shall remain firm and inviolate for you and your successors. Among these we have thought fit to record the following by their proper names: the church of Tauliniacum, with all its appurtenances; the tithe of Buxa, as it was granted to you by Gibelin, archbishop of Arles, of good memory; the church of St Mary of Turre; St Victor; St Eulalia; St Lawrence of Barbana; the church of Mondolio in Besalú; the church of St Mary with its dignities and possessions and the churches subject to it, saving the right of the Lateran Palace; the churches of St Peter and [Col. 0337A] St Mary of Egara; and St Julian of Terrassa, with the subject possessions and churches established through them, which Raymond, bishop of Barcelona, granted you together with his former patrimony and the other possessions bestowed upon you and the clerics living with you, together with the estates and churches of St Adrian, excepting the demesne of the bishop of Barcelona.

We also confirm for you the possession which Raymond, count of noble memory, gave you in the region of Tripoli, together with the church of St Rufus which he built within that possession. We decree, therefore, that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the aforesaid monastery, take away its possessions, retain what has been taken away, diminish them, or harass it by reckless vexations; but that all things shall be kept intact for the benefit in every respect of those [Col. 0337B] for whose support and governance they were granted.

Let no opposition from any bishop or provost prevent you from receiving laymen or clerics who come for conversion and from admitting them to divine offices, unless they are perhaps excommunicated. Furthermore, we add that no bishop may, without a hearing before the Roman pontiff and his legate, subject you or your places to interdict or excommunication, or oppress you by judicial sentence. We decree that the burial grounds of your places shall be wholly free, so that no one may oppose the devotion and final wish of those who resolve to be buried there, unless they are perhaps excommunicated. We likewise grant and confirm by privileges all the other things that were granted to you and confirmed by privileges by our predecessor Pope Urban, of happy memory, etc.

I, Paschal, bishop of the Catholic Church.

Given at the Lateran through the hand of John, deacon cardinal of the Holy Roman Church and librarian, on the fourth Ides of January, in the seventh indiction, in the year 1115 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the sixteenth year of the pontificate of lord Pope Paschal II.

CCCLXXVI. Privilege for the Church of Apt under Bishop Langerius. (A.D. 1114, January 13.)

[*Gallia Christiana*, I, 77.]

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the beloved [Col. 0337D] sons, the canons of the Church of Apt, present and future, for ever.

The authority of our office urges us to be solicitous for the condition of churches and to establish what has been rightly ordained. Therefore, by the authority of the Apostolic See, we confirm your vow and your purpose: that henceforth, in the mother church of Apt, of the Blessed Mother of God and ever-virgin Mary and of Blessed Castor, they shall live clerically and according to rule for all time, and that whatever estates or goods have been assigned for their maintenance shall always be preserved to them peacefully and intact.

Moreover, we confirm for that church and its bishops the castle of St Martin and the castle of Saignon, which, though they belonged to the Church of Apt by ancient right, have been restored to that church through the endeavours of our fellow brother [Col. 0338A] Bishop Langerius. We also establish by the authority of this present decree the other gifts which that bishop made and confirmed by the assurance of his writing, both for you and for your successors, provided you remain in the observance of the regular life.

When he or any of his successors is called to the Lord, whatever belongs to the bishop shall remain under the care of the canons; nor shall another bishop be appointed in the Church of Apt unless he has been canonically advanced by their counsel and election. Let no layman whatsoever presume to invade or plunder the goods of a deceased bishop. We decree, therefore, that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb that church, take away its possessions, retain what has been taken away, diminish them, [Col. 0338B] or harass it by reckless vexations; but that all things shall be kept intact for the benefit of those for whose support and governance they were granted.

But if anyone—God forbid!—knowing the tenor of this decree, should rashly attempt to act against it, let that person suffer the loss of office and rank, or be punished by the coercion of excommunication, unless he corrects his presumption by worthy satisfaction. But upon those who observe it may the grace of almighty God and the blessing of the blessed Apostles Peter and Paul be bestowed.

Given at the Lateran through the hand of John, deacon cardinal of the Holy Roman Church and librarian, on the Ides of January, in the seventh indiction, in the year 1115 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the fifteenth year of the pontificate of lord Pope Paschal II.

CCCLXXVII. At the request of Bishop Berard, he confirms the possessions of the Church of the Marsi. (A.D. 1114, February 25.)

[UGHELLI, *Italia Sacra*, I, 892.]

[Col. 0338C]

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son BERARD, bishop of the Church of the Marsi, and to his successors canonically appointed for ever.

As unjust petitioners are to be granted no effect, so the petition of those who desire lawfully ought not to be delayed. Therefore, dearest brother in Christ, assenting to your prayers, for the perpetual peace and stability of holy Mother Church we enact by the firmness of this present decree that all the boundaries of the parish, as they have been possessed by your predecessors down to the present day, [Col. 0338D] shall in every respect be preserved forever both for you and for [your] successors. These boundaries run from the Tower of Ferraria to the head of Corritus; thence by the road from Merso to Postella of the Putrid Valley; through the land of Feresca, through Argato, through the land of Camno, through the land of Formella; thence to the Old Mill; thence to the Fork of Aura through the land of Vivo; through the land of Troja; thence to the Pasture of the Canal; thence to the Emperor’s Rock through the land of Cervara; thence to Saint Britius through the Fork of Auricula; thence to the Arch of Saint George; by the river Risana; through the Towers of Ofrano; through Scalellas; through Tufum of the river Remandi; through Trepont; thence to the Dead Fox by the Mouth of Teba; through the Field [Col. 0339A] of Pezza; through the Stream of Gambarara; through the land of Candida; through Venetrinum; and return to the Fork of Ferratus.

Within these boundaries, whatever towns, whatever villages, whatever parishes, whatever churches are situated, or shall hereafter be situated, shall remain under the episcopal care and governance of you and your Catholic successors. From all of these, episcopal dues shall be rendered to you, both in the ordination of clerics and consecration of churches, and in the payment of tithes and offerings, as well as in the correction of offenders.

Moreover, we wholly forbid within the boundaries of the Marsi that perverse presumption of monks which has arisen partly through bishops’ absence and partly through their obstinacy: namely, that they should no longer perform baptisms in monasteries; that they should not dare to leave their cloisters for [Col. 0339B] anointings of the sick; that they should not admit lay persons for the imposition of penance; and that they should not receive into communion persons excommunicated by the bishop, nor receive those under interdict for sacred offices.

Further, we decree that the church of Blessed Savina the martyr shall always be regarded as the mother church, as it has hitherto been regarded, and that the episcopal see shall remain there. The churches with their estates, which have been possessed in past times, shall remain in its possession and jurisdiction, peacefully, freely, and intact for all future time; namely: Saint Paul at Pesculum Serulae; Saint Mary in Campo Mitio; Saint Nicholas at the Fountain of the Queen; Saint Quintinus in Vico; Saint Martin in Agne; Saint Martin in Betorrita; the Holy Archangel above [Col. 0339C] Mesula; Saint Mary in Ortucula; Saint Mary and Saint Peter in Veneri; Saint Felix in Ferrati; Saints Valentinus and Peter in Apiniacis; Saint Mark in Geno; Saint Martin in Filincino; Saint Peter in Cerverano; Saint John in Pentoma; Saints Marcellus and Angel in Arca; Saint Mary in Palute; Saint Anatolia of Lione; Saint Felicitas in Cerferro; Saint Lawrence in Praetorio; Saint Felicianus in Villa Magna; Saint Mary in Avando; Saint Vitus in Ozano; Saint Christina in Suppezzano; Saint George in Besola; Saint John at the Head of the Water, with its dependent chapels; Saint Patitus at the Castle; Saint Felix in Porciano; Saint Lawrence in Curia; Saint Caesidius with its dependent chapels; Saint Vincent in Forma with its dependent chapels; Saint Vincent in Forma with its dependent chapels; Saint Vincent in Forma with its dependent chapels; Saint Andrew in Ancezzano; Saint Mary [Col. 0339D] in Vico; Saint Peter in Capistrello; Saints Peter and Mary in Albe; Saint Mark in Massa; Saint Martin in Valle with its dependent chapels; Saint Joanna in Marano; Saint Felix in Montecelle; Saint Mary in Elireto with its dependent chapels; Saint Nicholas in Erse; Saint Mary in Furca; Saint Erasmus with its dependent chapels; Saint Andrew in Casellaco; Saint Maximus in Cerro; Saint Victoria in Cellis; Saint Mary in Carseo with its dependent chapels.

Moreover, we decree that whatever possessions and estates are known lawfully to belong to the same church, or which it may hereafter, by the Lord’s gift, acquire through any just means or contracts, shall remain inviolate for you and your successors. Therefore let no person whatsoever be permitted rashly to disturb the aforesaid Church, remove its possessions, retain what has been removed, or [Col. 0340A] claim for his own use things unjustly given, diminish them, or harass them with reckless vexations; rather, let all be preserved intact for the benefit of both you and the clerics.

If, therefore, henceforth any archbishop or bishop, emperor or king, prince or duke, count, viscount, judge, castaldus, or any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowing this page of our constitution, should rashly attempt to act against it, then, after a second or third warning, unless he makes satisfaction and duly corrects the matter, let him be deprived of the privilege of authority, honor, or rank; let him know himself to stand guilty before the divine judgment for the iniquity committed; let him be excluded from the most sacred body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ, our Redeemer; and at the last judgment let him be subject to strict vengeance. But upon all [Col. 0340B] who preserve the rights of the Church, may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that they may receive here the fruit of good action and that, before the strict Judge, the rewards of the eternal Father may remain [or: be found]. Amen, amen.

Written by the hand of Gervasius, regional writer and notary of the sacred palace.

I, Paschal, bishop of the Catholic Church, have subscribed.

I, Richard, bishop of Albano, have subscribed.

I, Leo, bishop of Ostia, have subscribed.

I, Cono, bishop of the Church of Palestrina, have subscribed.

I, Romanus, cardinal of Saint Prisca, have subscribed.

I, Benedict, cardinal of the title of Eudoxia, have subscribed.

I, Cardinal Raynerius of Saints Marcellinus and Peter, have subscribed.

I, Conradus, cardinal of Saint Pudentiana, have subscribed.

Given at the Lateran through the hand of John, cardinal and librarian of the Holy Roman Church, [Col. 0340C] on the fifth day before the Kalends of March, in the seventh indiction, in the year 1115 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the fifteenth year of the pontificate of Lord Paschal II, pope.

### CCCLXXVIII. To John, Bishop of Thérouanne.—On preserving the liberty of the monastery of Saint Bertin at Sithiu. (A.D. 1114, March 20.)

[Collection des Cartulaires, III, 253.]

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the venerable JOHN, bishop of the Morini, greeting and apostolic blessing.

Both from the letters of your brotherhood and from the privileges of my predecessors Victor and Urban, of holy memory, we have learned and clearly seen [Col. 0340D] that the monastery of Blessed Bertin remained continuously in the enjoyment of its liberty until the time of your advancement, saving only the right of the Church of Thérouanne. Therefore, justice has seemed to us and to our brethren to require that, if anything has been conducted with insufficient foresight or insufficient reason by you, by the count of Flanders, or by the abbot of that place, no loss shall on that account be inflicted upon the monastery. We therefore decree that the place itself, so long as it is manifestly flourishing in monastic observance, and the abbot of the place, shall remain in its liberty and immunity.

Given at the Lateran, on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of April.

### CCCLXXIX. He secures to the monastery of Saint Bertin at Sithiu the land of Berquaria, [Col. 0341A] given by Baldwin, Count of Flanders, in exchange for the estate of Ostresala. (A.D. 1114, March 25.)

[Collection des Cartulaires, III, 258.]

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons LAMBERT, abbot, and the brethren of Saint Bertin, greeting and apostolic blessing.

The authority of our office urges us to be concerned for the condition of the Churches and, with the Lord’s assistance, to provide for their peace. Accordingly, we assent to your petitions and, because we believe it useful to the monastery, confirm by the assurance of this present writing the exchange made between you and Baldwin, Count of the Flemings.

For in exchange for the estate called Ostresela, which is recognized as belonging by right to Saint Bertin, the count gave [Col. 0341B] your monastery a certain tract of land at Veurne, namely Berquaria, in the parish of Wlepem. From this Erembold Musolf, as a *berquarius*—that is, the holder of a sheepfold or sheep-pasture—formerly paid rent. This land, measured by fixed dimensions according to the custom of that country, yields an annual revenue of twenty-eight pounds. We decree that this *berquaria*, with the same income, shall remain forever wholly exempt and free from every exaction, just as the count himself possessed it and conveyed it to your monastery by hereditary right in the presence of his leading men.

We also decree that two sheaves of tithe from the newly cultivated land called Dipesele, two sheaves from the newly cultivated land called Hucmareserce, and a certain parcel of land in the estate called Atrike, as they were granted by the same count [Col. 0341C] to your monastery, shall remain to you free and intact. Further, we confirm to you in perpetual possession two altars: one of the chapel of Eggafrid and the other of Warnestum, which our beloved and venerable fellow-brother John, bishop of Thérouanne, conveyed in perpetual possession to Blessed Bertin, saving the annual payment owed from those altars to that bishop.

Let no one therefore hereafter be permitted to sever from the unity and possession of your monastery the things noted above; rather, as stated, let all of them remain peaceably and intact under its right and lordship. If anyone, having knowledge of the tenor of this decree, should rashly—God forbid!—attempt to oppose it, let him incur the peril of his office and rank and be punished by the penalty of excommunication [Col. 0341D], unless he correct his presumption by worthy satisfaction.

Given at the Lateran, on the eighth day before the Kalends of April, through the hand of John, deacon cardinal and librarian of the Holy Roman Church, in the year 1115 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the seventh indiction [Note: [Col. 0341D] Read: “eighth.”], and likewise in the fifteenth year of the pontificate of Lord Paschal II, pope.

### CCCLXXX. Privilege for the monastery of Tulle. (A.D. 1114, March 31.)

[Baluze, *Historia Tutelensis*, 463.]

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved [Col. 0342A] son EBALUS, abbot of Tulle, and to his successors canonically appointed in perpetuity.

By the authority and duty of the Apostolic See, we are constrained to concern ourselves for the state of all Churches and, with the Lord’s assistance, to provide for their peace. Therefore, dearest son in Christ, we have rightly judged that your petitions should be granted, so that we might fortify the monastery of Tulle, over which by God’s authority you preside, by the privilege of the Apostolic See.

Accordingly, by the page of this present privilege, with apostolic authority we decree that whatever estates and possessions are lawfully seen to belong to the same monastery shall be preserved for you and your successors. Among these, we have judged that the following should be recorded by their proper names: in the adjacent borough, the church of Saint Peter and Saint Julian; the church of Aquina; the church of Acuto [Col. 0342B] Monte; the chapel of Roca; the chapel of Marco; the chapel of Aureliac; the chapel of Bosquet; the chapel of Lagarda; the church of Spaniac with its chapel; the church of Saint Mary of Clergor; the church of Saint Mary of Spinaciis; the church of Saint James of Altoire; the church of Saint James of Monedeira; the church of Madranges; the chapel of La Valeta; the church of Planis; the chapel of La Genesta; the church of Auriol; the chapel of Bellopodium; the church of Brancelles; the chapel of Capiac; the church of Saint Bonitus of Avalosa; the churches of Vairiac, namely those of Saint Stephen, Saint Martin, and Saint Germanus; the church of Saint Michael and the chapel of that castle; the church of Saint Peter of Bagneriis; the church of Saint Mary of Matheria; the church [Col. 0342C] of Mairona; the church of Saint Peter of Vogairo; the chapel of Bellocastellum; the church of Saint George of Mairac; the church of Saint Mary of Rocamadour; the church of Gransania; the church of Saint Mary of Seillac; the church of Olonzac; the church of Marciliac; the church of Saint Aredius; the church of Saint Julian of Porcaria; the church of Saint Maurilius; the church of Bragusa; the church of Lagarda; the church of Saint Fortunata with the chapel of Saint Faith of Castaneo; the church of Albuciac; the church of Novavilla; the church of Molseon; the church of Saint Amantius; the church of Saint Martial of Faorzes; the church of Saint Bonitus of Vern; the church of Saint Pardulphus of La Crozilla; the church of Saint Martin [Col. 0342D] situated between Dostra and the Dordogne; the church of Saint Peter of Sadran; the church of Saint Maxentius; the church of Saint Lawrence of Gorra; the church of Mairignac; the church of Peirac; the church of Caleis; the church of Saint Medard; the church of Mordelgue; the church of Matheria; the church of Traignac with the chapel of its castle; the church of Saint Julian of Garriga; the church of Saint James situated at Cahors; and whatever may hereafter, by God’s providence, be offered, given, or come to the same monastery by other just means. Let all these always be preserved for you and your successors peaceably and intact.

We order that churches with their appurtenances and estates alienated from the same monastery be restored and preserved forever [Col. 0343A]. By the authority of the Apostolic See, we forbid any ecclesiastical or secular person to presume to resist or impede this just restoration. We forbid anyone to take away from you or interrupt the burial rights of the knights of Gimel, Bar, and Corrèze; of Boltzac, Seillac, Saint Clement, and Saint Germanus; of Saint Ferreolus and Favars; of Cornil, Saint Fortunata, Lagarda, and Saint Amantius; of Navis, Roca, Marciliac, and Saint Aredius; of Campaniac, Clergor, Latigniac, and the castle of Tulle; and of all the viscounts of Turenne, Comborn, and Ventadour.

We therefore decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the same monastery, take away its possessions, claim for personal use things unjustly [Col. 0343B] given, diminish them, or harass them by reckless vexations. Rather, let all be preserved intact for the benefit in every way of those for whose support and governance they were granted. If any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowing this page of our constitution, should rashly attempt to act against it, then, after a second or third warning, unless he makes amends by suitable satisfaction, let him be deprived of the dignity of his authority and honor; let him know that he stands guilty before the divine judgment for the wrong committed; let him be excluded from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, Redeemer; and at the last judgment let him be subject to strict vengeance. But may the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ be upon all who preserve what is right for that place, so that they may receive here [Col. 0343C] the fruit of good action and find, before the strict Judge, the rewards of eternal peace. Amen, amen, amen.

Written by the hand of Gervasius, registrar, regional official, and notary of the sacred palace.

I, Paschal, bishop of the Catholic Church, have subscribed.

Given at the Lateran through the hand of John, deacon cardinal and librarian of the Holy Roman Church, on the second day before the Kalends of April, in the seventh indiction, in the year 1115 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and likewise in the fifteenth year of the pontificate of Lord Paschal II, pope. Fare well.

### CCCLXXXI. Bull for the monastery of Ébreuil, Esbreville or Ebrevil. (A.D. 1114, April 4.)

[*Gallia Christiana*, II, 121.]

[Col. 0343D]

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son TEOTARD, abbot of the monastery of Ébreuil, and to his successors regularly appointed in Christ.

A devout request ought to obtain its effect, so that the sincerity of devotion may shine forth praiseworthily and the requested benefit may undoubtedly acquire force. Therefore, because your belovedness, fleeing to the harbor of the Apostolic See, has with due devotion sought its protection, we mercifully assent to your request and receive under the protection of the Apostolic See the monastery of Blessed Leodegarius at Ébreuil, over which by God’s authority you preside.

Accordingly, by the page of this present privilege, we confirm in perpetuity to you and your successors [Col. 0344A] Nurgum, with the church of Saint Gereon and its chapels in the district of Auvergne; the church of the Holy Cross of Velcia, with the chapel of Saint Maurice of Vico; Saint Mary of Caliniac; Saint Mary of Salas; Saint Bonitus of Cambra; Saint Mary of Ecclesiola; Saint Bonitus of Cervant; Saint Genesius of Buissirolas; Saint Victor of Pozols; Saint Pardulphus; Saint Mary of Marcillac; Saint Peter of Campis; the church of Saint Paul; Saint Genesius of Ret; Saint Anianus of Betgue; Saint Quintinus; Saint Leodegarius of Laiac; Saint Leodegarius of Monte Frumino; Saint Peter of Chapde; Saint Peter of Nerdugna; Saint Pardulphus of Vilorzangas; Saint Peter of Valle; Saint Pardulphus of Carro; Saint Praejectus; Saint Julian of Muroile; Saint [Col. 0344B] Martin of Garriga; Saint Bravius of Puntiac; Saint Hilary; Saint Peter of Cella; Saint Magnerius; Saint Mary of Virgiac; Saint Gall; and Saint Saturninus of Ventac.

In the bishopric of Bourges: the church of Saint Marcellus of Scaceras; Saint Hilary of Dorminnac; Saint Bonitus of Balanava; Saint Andrew of Valiniac; Saint Portianus of Navas.

In the district of Rodez: the church of Saint Mary of Logangnac; Saint Mary of Jeveirac; Saint Martin of Cromeras; Saint Mary of Lelna; Saint Martin; Saint Maurice of Marnac; and Saint Agangus.

In the bishopric of Sens: the church of Saint Leodegarius with its chapels; Saint Mary; Saint Martin of Cunniac; Saint Sulpicius; Saint Mary Magdalene of Crong; Saint Mary of Salas; the church of Botsac; Saint Bibianus of Charues; the church of Genten; the church of [Col. 0344C] Gaverda; the church of Saint Leodegarius of Ariazo; Saint Peter of Liriorta; and all other things which that monastery lawfully possesses in the present seventh indiction or may hereafter lawfully and canonically acquire by grants of pontiffs, generosity of princes, or offerings of the faithful.

We decree, therefore, that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the same monastery, take away its possessions, retain what has been taken away, diminish them, or harass them with reckless vexations; rather, let all be preserved whole for the benefit in every way of those for whose support and governance they were granted, so that, by the Lord’s authority, the place may always flourish in the observance of regular order and remain forever in its liberty.

Further, we decree that the burial ground [Col. 0344D] of the same place shall be wholly free, so that no one may obstruct the devotion and final wish of those who have decided to be buried there, unless they are excommunicated. Upon the death of you, the present abbot of that place, or of any of your successors, no one shall be set over it by any deceitful contrivance or force, except one whom the brethren by common consent, or the sounder party of the brethren, shall elect—whether from their own community or, if necessary, from another community—according to the fear of the Lord and the Rule of Blessed Benedict, to be consecrated by the bishop of Auvergne.

If any ecclesiastical or secular person in the future, knowing this page of our constitution, should rashly attempt to act against it, then, after a second or third warning, unless he makes amends by suitable satisfaction, let him be deprived of the dignity of his authority [Col. 0345A] and honor; let him know that he stands guilty before the divine judgment for the wrong committed; let him be excluded from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, Redeemer; and at the last judgment let him be subject to strict vengeance. But may the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ be upon all who preserve what is right for that place, so that they may receive here the fruit of good action and find, before the strict Judge, the rewards of eternal peace. Amen, amen, amen.

Written by the hand of Chrysogonus, notary of the sacred palace.

I, Paschal, bishop of the Catholic Church.

Given at the Lateran through the hand of John, deacon cardinal and librarian of the Holy Roman Church, on the second [Col. 0345B] day before the Nones of April, in the seventh indiction, in the year 1115 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the same fifteenth year of the pontificate of Lord Paschal II, pope.

### CCCLXXXII. He confirms all possessions and privileges of the monastery of Subiaco. (A.D. 1114, April 11.)

[Muratori, *Antiquitates Italicae*, IV, 1058.]

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son JOHN, abbot of the monastery of Subiaco, and to his successors regularly appointed in perpetuity.

[Col. 0345C]

“I will glorify those who glorify me,” says the Lord, who does not lie. The blessed God, keeping this promise of his truth through the ages to his faithful servant Benedict, has deigned wonderfully to glorify him not only in heaven but also on earth, so that the places themselves in which this servant of God dwelt may be held glorious among men. We too follow this gracious act of God the Creator by striving to glorify in God this same our Father. Therefore we hold glorious and venerable, and fortify with the authority of the Apostolic See, that place where he is known, by God’s ordinance, first to have lived, to have built a monastery for the glorification of God, and to have gathered many people for God’s glory—the place, namely, called Subiaco.

Accordingly, dearest son, we confirm to you and through you to the aforesaid monastery of Saint Benedict [Col. 0345D] the cave in which that most holy man dwelt at the beginning of his religious life, with the adjacent forest and mountain all around it, and with all boundaries and appurtenances established from ancient times. Under that same cave we also confirm the lake, or the river issuing from those same lakes. In those waters no one, without the consent of the abbot and brethren, may fish or build a mill as far as the arch called Ferrata. Likewise, from the ancient channel which carries water from the river to the parish church of Saint Lawrence, and from the water called Augusta, no one may divert water without your consent, except so much as is sufficient for watering gardens and filling the baptismal font in that church. Nor may anyone presume to build any watermill there without your consent as far as the aforesaid Arch of Ferrata. If anyone acts otherwise, [Col. 0346A] let him be bound by the ban of the Roman curia; half of the fine imposed by that ban shall be paid to the sacred palace and half to the same monastery.

We also confirm to you and your monastery the castle called Subiaco, with all its appurtenances, as is known to have been granted by our predecessors: with mountains and hills, estates and hamlets, with all churches and all things belonging to them generally and in their entirety; the estate of Canali and the estate of Gennae entire with their appurtenances; the estate of Frassinum with all its appurtenances; and the place called Fundi, as it extends to the Emperor’s Rock and goes to the mountain called [Col. 0346B] Pionica; thence through Serra to Monte Romano; and comes out at Campo Longo; thence to Campo Catino; then returns to the aforesaid Emperor’s Rock; and the place called Geminarium with its boundaries, as is contained in the privileges of our predecessors; the castle of Augusta with its estates and hamlets; and the hamlet of Saint Felicitas, with that church, its estates and hamlets, and all its appurtenances, as is contained in those same privileges; Rocca Cervaria with its estates, hamlets, and all appurtenances; the castle of Marano, Rocca Martini, and Rocca de Nesso with all their appurtenances; the castle of Canterano with its fortress, estates, and hamlets; Monte de Grosso, Valle Frigida, [Col. 0346C] Monte de Mesu, and Funsstellae with all their appurtenances;
