the castle of Cerreto with all its appurtenances; the castle of Giranum, with mountains and hills, estates and hamlets, as appears fitting for the monastery, with holdings and all its appurtenances, together with the monastery’s ancient inheritance; the castle of Apolloni with mountains and hamlets, and half the castle of Saint Angelo, with their churches, estates, holdings, and appurtenances; Rocca Santo Stefano with its appurtenances; the Valley of Annito and the Hill of Occia, with their mountains and hills, estates and hamlets; Tovanellum, the estate of Ottanum, the estate of Maciomanum, the estate of Camanum, the estate of Acquaviva, and half of Monte [Col. 0346D] Afilano, with all their appurtenances; the castle of Affile with mountains and hills and all its appurtenances; and the castle of Ponza with mountains and hills and all its appurtenances.

Moreover, by ancient right and by the grants and privileges both of Roman pontiffs and emperors, the following are known to belong to the same monastery of Saint Benedict: the town of Sala, called Carseoli, with its holdings, estates, and hamlets; Auricula; Rocca di Botte; Rocca in Camerata; Rocca Rosunum; Arsulae; Rubianum; another Rubianum upon the river; Anticulum; Garracinescum; Rocca Demasii; Rocca de Surici Siciliani; half of Deilica; the holding of Saint Valerius; Siscanum; Mons Casalis; Civitella; Olivanum, with all their estates and hamlets; the town of Tusculana with its fortress and all its appurtenances; and the castle of Gallicano with churches, estates, hamlets, and all its appurtenances.

[Col. 0347A]

We also confirm the cells belonging to the same monastery. Likewise: the church of Saint Angelo located at Effide; the church of Saint George, with all their appurtenances and with the ancient inheritance of Father Saint Benedict; the church of Saint Angelo at Petralata; Saint Sebastian at Paliano; the church of Saint Quintinus; Saint Blaise at Antido; Saint Leucius at Babuto, situated in the territory of Campanino, with all their appurtenances; at Carsoli, the church of Saint Peter; at Camerata, the church of Saint Martin of Egellis and Saint Peter of Castruino; [Col. 0347B] in the territory of the Marsi, Saint Peter at Verse, Saint Benedict at the Stream of Meruli, Saint Thomas of Transacque, with the church of Saint Nicholas in the Valley; in the territory of [lacuna], the church of Saint Paul in Villa, with all their appurtenances; Saint Angelo in Albe; Saint Saviour in Avelano; Saint Mary of Tuffo, with all its appurtenances; in the Valley of Sora, the church of Saint Paul, with three other churches, and with the estate situated beside it, and with all its appurtenances; in the city of Tivoli, the churches of Saint Antoninus, the Holy Cross, and Saint Barbara, with all their possessions; another cell in honor of the Holy Cross at Quintiliolo, with its olive grove and other appurtenances; and six ounces of the church of Saint [Col. 0347C] Mary situated on the same mountain; the estate of Calicianum with the church of Saint Peter, lands, and vineyards, as appears from the ancient boundary markers; the estate called Papicum; the church of Saint Mary, with lands, vineyards, and the mountain called Monicula; the church of Saint Mary located at the Gate; the church of Saint Sebastian with all its appurtenances; three watermills, one at Castrum Vetus, another outside the Greater Gate, and another in Vesta beside the castle of Gallicano; the churches of Saint Pastor, Saint Angelo, Saint Mary, and Saint Lawrence in Aqua Alta, with all their possessions; and, at Rome, the monastery of Saint Erasmus with houses, gardens, and other possessions.

[Col. 0347D]

We therefore decree that all the aforesaid things, together with the possessions which the same venerable monastery holds in the present seventh indiction, shall be preserved for you peaceably and intact. And whatever lawfully belongs to its right, whether through the grant of pontiffs, the generosity of emperors and princes, the offering of any faithful persons, or other just and legal means, shall always remain in its right and possession. Let no person whatsoever be permitted rashly to disturb the same monasteries of Saint Benedict, take away their possessions, retain what has been taken away, claim for personal use things unjustly given, diminish them, or harass them with reckless vexations; rather, let all be preserved intact for the benefit in every way of those for whose support and governance they were granted.

[Col. 0348A]

Further, because of the frequent injuries inflicted upon monasteries by bishops or the agents of bishops, we decree that the authority granted to your monastery by our predecessors shall remain valid for you also: whenever churches must be dedicated, or clerics ordained, whether in the monastery, its cells, castles, or estates, you may receive consecration from us if you can reach us in time, or you may approach whichever Catholic bishop you prefer, who, supported by the authority of the Apostolic See, shall provide what is requested. You shall suffer no opposition or complaint on this account from the bishop of that Church. We also forbid [Col. 0348B] any priest of any Church to exercise any jurisdiction over the aforesaid monastery of Saint Benedict except the Apostolic See.

Upon the death of the abbot of that place or any of his successors, no one shall be set over it by any deceitful contrivance or force, except one whom the brethren by common consent, or the sounder party of the brethren, shall elect according to the fear of God and the Rule of Saint Benedict. The person elected shall be consecrated by the pontiff of the Roman See.

If any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowing this page of our constitution, should rashly attempt to act against it, then, after a second or third conviction, unless he makes amends by suitable satisfaction, let him be deprived of the dignity of his authority and honor; let him know that he now stands guilty before the divine judgment for the wrong committed; let him be excluded from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, [Col. 0348C] Redeemer; and at the last judgment let him be subject to strict vengeance. But upon all who rightly preserve that place may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ; likewise, may they receive here the fruit of good action and find before the strict Judge the reward of eternal peace. Amen.

Written by the hand of the notary of the sacred palace.

I, Paschal, bishop of the Catholic Church.

Given at the Lateran through the hand of John, deacon and librarian of the Roman Church, on the third day before the Ides of April, in the seventh indiction, in the year 1115 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the pontificate of Lord Paschal . . . . . . .

### CCCLXXXIII.

[Col. 0348D]

*He orders that Landulf, archbishop of Benevento, having been deprived of episcopal office, be “summoned” to the synod to be held on the Ides of October. (See Falco of Benevento, under 1114, p. 88: “When you ordered me to be summoned by your letters”; and: “I have beyond doubt granted a date for coming, namely from the Ides of April, with an interval of six months.”)

### CCCLXXXIV.

*He invites Landulf de Graeca, constable of the Beneventans, to the synod to be held on the Ides of October. (See Falco of Benevento, under 1114, p. 87.)

### CCCLXXXV. *He confirms the possessions of the church of Farinata, founded by the counts of Bergamo and bestowed upon Blessed Peter, on condition that twelve coins of Milanese [Col. 0349A] currency be paid annually to the Lateran palace. (A.D. 1114, April 14.)

[See Lupi, *Codex diplomaticus Bergomatis*, II, 885.]

### CCCLXXXVI. Privilege for the church of Blessed Lawrence at Florence. (A.D. 1114, April 15.)

[Lami, *Ecclesiae Florentinae Monumenta*, III, 1772.]

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons JOHN, prior, and the brethren living under rule in the church of Blessed Lawrence near Florence, both present and future, in perpetuity.

The pious petition of a willing purpose ought to be brought to fulfillment, so that the sincerity of devotion may shine forth commendably [Col. 0349B] and the benefit sought may assuredly gain force. Since, therefore, your belovedness, fleeing to the haven of the Apostolic See, has with due devotion requested its protection, we graciously assent to your supplication and receive under the protection of the Apostolic See the church of Blessed Lawrence, over which, by God’s agency, you preside, together with all that pertains to it.

By the present document of privilege, therefore, we establish by apostolic authority that whatever goods and possessions the same Church is known to possess in the present seventh indiction, whether by grants of pontiffs, the generosity of princes, offerings of the faithful, or other just means, or may hereafter, by God’s bounty, lawfully acquire, shall remain secure and unimpaired for you and your successors, [Col. 0349C] without prejudice to the right of the bishop of Florence. Yet he may not burden that church, take away its goods, grant them in fief to any persons, or alienate them by any means whatsoever. We therefore decree that no person at all may rashly disturb the same church, take away its possessions, retain what has been taken, diminish them, or harass it with reckless vexations; but that all things be preserved intact, to benefit in every way the use of those for whose support they were granted.

Moreover, let no one’s opposition prevent you, on solemn days, from holding processions in the cloister or churchyard, or from chanting Masses at terce; rather, strive in every way to glorify almighty God and, through His assistance, diligently attend to the salvation of your souls. If, therefore, in the future any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowing this document of our constitution, should rashly attempt to act against it, then, having been warned a second and third time, unless he makes suitable amends, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and office; let him know himself guilty before divine judgment of the wrongdoing committed; let him be cut off from the most holy body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Redeemer; and let him be subject at the last judgment to severe punishment. But upon all who preserve what is just for that place, may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that here they may receive the fruit of good action and before the strict Judge may find the rewards of eternal peace. Amen.

[Col. 0350A] I, Paschal, bishop of the Catholic Church, have subscribed.

Given at the Lateran through the hand of John, cardinal-deacon and librarian of the Holy Roman Church, on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of May [15 April], in the seventh indiction, in the year 1115 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the fifteenth year of the pontificate of Lord Paschal, the second pope.

CCCLXXXVII. To Maurice, Archbishop of Braga. (Year 1114, 18 April.)

[MANSI, *Councils*, XX, 117.]

Among the other complaints brought to the Apostolic See against you, the invasion and [Col. 0350B] destruction of the Church of León has grieved us more severely. Warned about these matters by our letters, and summoned to a council by our vicar Bernard of Toledo, you scorned both to come and to make satisfaction. Moreover, because of this wickedness and disobedience, having been forbidden by him both priestly and episcopal functions, you have stubbornly presumed to perform those same offices. Therefore we, by God’s authority, avenging so great a crime of wickedness and pride, forbid you both those offices and obedience to the Church of Braga, until, coming to your senses, you obey and make fuller satisfaction.

Given at the Lateran, 14 May, seventh indiction.

CCCLXXXVIII. Privilege for the Church of St. Evasius at Casale. (Year 1114, 27 April.)

[De Conti, *Historical Notices of the City of Casale*. Casale, 1838, octavo, I, 332.]

[Col. 0350C]

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons GIRARD, provost, and his brethren living under rule in the church of St. Evasius at Casale, present and future, forever.

It is fitting readily to grant assent to religious desires, so that faithful devotion may obtain a swift effect. Therefore we grant your petition our due and kindly assent. By the authority of this present privilege, we confirm the order of canonical life which you have professed; and we forbid anyone, after making his profession, to possess anything as his own or to leave the cloister without the permission of the provost [Col. 0350D] or the community.

We decree that all those things which we see you now lawfully possess for the maintenance of the common livelihood shall be held in perpetuity by you and your successors who remain in the same religious life. Whatever you may hereafter acquire through grants of pontiffs, the generosity of princes, offerings of the faithful, or other just means, shall remain secure and unimpaired for you and your successors. No provost may have authority to give the Church’s estates in fief to secular persons or to alienate them through any contrivance whatsoever.

We therefore decree that no person at all may rashly disturb the same church of Blessed Evasius, take away its possessions, [Col. 0351A] retain possessions taken away, diminish them, or harass it with reckless vexations; but that all things be preserved intact, to benefit in every way the use of those for whose support and governance they were granted. Moreover, no opposition by any bishop or provost shall prevent you from receiving secular clerics for conversion by your provost.

If, therefore, in the future any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowing this document of our constitution, should rashly attempt to act against it, then, having been warned a second and third time, unless he makes suitable amends, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and office; let him know himself guilty before divine judgment of the wrongdoing committed; let him be cut off from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Redeemer; [Col. 0351B] and let him be subject at the last judgment to severe punishment. But upon all who preserve what is just for that place, may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that here they may receive the fruit of good action and before the strict Judge may find the rewards of eternal peace.

I, Paschal, bishop of the Catholic Church.

Given at the Lateran through the hand of John, cardinal-deacon and librarian of the Holy Roman Church, on the fifth day before the Kalends of May [27 April], seventh indiction, in the year 1115 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the fifteenth year of the pontificate of Lord Paschal the Second.

CCCLXXXIX. Privilege for the episcopal see of the Church of Bologna. (Year 1114, 2 March.)

[SAVIOLI, *Annals of Bologna*, vol. II, appendix, p. 152.] From the archive of the archbishopric of Bologna.

[Col. 0351C]

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved brother in Christ VICTOR, bishop of Bologna, and his successors canonically appointed forever.

Just as no assent ought to be granted to those seeking unjust things, so the petition of those who desire what is lawful ought not to be delayed. Accordingly, beloved brother, assenting to your prayers, for the perpetual peace and stability of the holy Church of Bologna we establish by the firmness of this present decree that the entire boundaries of the diocese shall be preserved in perpetuity as they were by your predecessors.

These boundaries run from the river Gaibana to the stream Sablosulum; then to the road called [Col. 0351D] Ungarista; then to the station Gallam and to the place called Curte; then to the river called Leo; then to the river called Muzza. Within these boundaries, whatever parish churches and other churches or monasteries, villages or towns are or have been situated shall remain under the episcopal care and authority of you and your Catholic successors. All persons, of whatever condition, living on the land of the Church of Bologna shall be kept under our power and protection.

We grant you the estate (*massa*) of Vulpini and Mozolarii, and the estate of Nerpulini. We likewise confirm to your brotherhood everything granted to the Church of Bologna by our predecessors—namely Agapetus, Pelagius, Gregory Dialogus, and Gregory VII: the monastery of St. Stephen [Col. 0352A] called Jerusalem, founded by St. Petronius, bishop; those of St. Proculus the martyr; of Saints Nabor and Felix; of Saints Gervasius and Protasius; of St. Columbanus the confessor; of St. Mary Major; of Saints Vitalis and Agricola in the Arena; of St. Barbazian; of St. Margaret; of St. Michael the Archangel on the paternal estate, with its appurtenances; St. Mary’s, situated on Mount Palense, with the court there held and called Aurelia, together with the mountains lying around the aforesaid monastery; St. Lucy of Roffeno; the monastery of St. Helena; St. Prosper at Paniosate; St. Martin at Poio, with its court and all its appurtenances; St. Peter in Strada; St. Mary in Strada, with all its appurtenances; St. Peter, with the court called Nucifatico [Col. 0352B] and all its possessions; and St. Martin at Casalecchio, with all its appurtenances.

Further, in response to your petition, we grant the gate of the city of Bologna called St. Peter’s, and the Salt Road (*strata Salaria*) with its road-toll (*strataticum*) and every payment which those travelling upon it are accustomed to render; also the churches of St. Andrew the Apostle before St. Peter’s Gate, St. Thomas the Apostle, and St. John the Evangelist on Mount Olivet, with all their appurtenances.

We also confirm to you the court called Abillonis, with its port, bank-toll (*ripaticum*), toll (*teloneum*), and market; with woods, hunting-rights, marshes, fisheries, male and female slaves, tenants, and all its appurtenances. Likewise, the court of Brento; the court called Bombiano with all its appurtenances; Mount Cavallorum; and the port called Galliano, with bank-toll, toll, marshes, fisheries, woods, and everything belonging to that port. Also, two courts: one called *Prata Major* and the other *Prata Minor*, situated within the parish called Boida. Likewise, the court called Marsumaticum, with all its appurtenances.

We subject to your authority and that of your Catholic successors abbots, monks, priests, deacons, learned and unlearned clerics, male and female servants of God, and all persons of both sexes dwelling within the above-mentioned boundaries of the Church of Bologna. Furthermore, whatever estates or possessions have been granted to the Church of Bologna by our predecessors, bishops of the Apostolic See, or by any Catholic kings—Charles and Otto—we also confirm by the authority of this present decree. [Col. 0352D] In addition, we establish that, according to the ancient custom of the Church of Bologna, those elected shall always receive from the Roman pontiff the grace of episcopal consecration, just as you yourself, by the help of almighty God’s grace, have received it.

If hereafter any archbishop or bishop, emperor or king, prince or duke, count, viscount, judge, or ecclesiastical or secular person, knowing this document of our constitution, should rashly attempt to act against it, then, having been warned a second and third time, unless he makes suitable amends, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and office; let him know himself guilty before divine judgment of the wrongdoing committed; let him be cut off from the most sacred [Col. 0353A] body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Redeemer; and let him be subject at the last judgment to severe punishment. But upon all who preserve what is just for that Church, may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that here they may receive the fruit of good action and before the strict Judge may find the rewards of eternal peace. Amen, amen.

Written by the hand of Raynerius, regional scriniary and notary of the sacred palace.

I, Paschal, bishop of the Catholic Church.

Given at Alba through the hand of John, cardinal-deacon and librarian of the Holy Roman Church, on the second day of March, in the seventh indiction, in the year 1114 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the fifteenth year of the pontificate of Lord Paschal II.

CCCXC. Confirms the possessions of Oggerius, bishop of Riez, and describes the boundaries of the diocese. (Year 1114, 28 May.)

[Sim. BARTEL, *Historical Nomenclature of the Prelates of the Holy Church of the Realm*, p. 175.]

[Col. 0353B]

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother OGGERIUS, bishop of the Church of Riez, and to his successors canonically appointed: greeting and apostolic blessing.

It is fitting that we give assent to just wishes and lend our ears to just petitions, since, though unworthy, we are, by Christ’s ordering, set on high as guardians and proclaimers of justice. Accordingly, beloved brother in Christ Oggerius, assenting to your just petitions, [Col. 0353C] we fortify by the authority of the Apostolic See the holy Church of Riez, also called Ricomagensis, over which, by God’s agency, you preside.

We establish that everything which your diligence has recovered from the hands of occupiers and restored to the right of the Church of Riez shall always be preserved free and unimpaired for that Church: namely, the castle called the Royal Castle, in which are the episcopal see and the Church of Blessed Maximus. Upon this castle we establish a perpetual prohibition: no secular person whatsoever may seize it through any fraudulent device or claim it as his own dominion by any contrivance. Nor may any bishop, provost, cleric, or any person whatsoever transfer the same castle into a secular person’s power or withdraw it from the dominion and possession of the Church and bishop.

We confirm in perpetuity for you, your successors, and the clerics of your Church the tithes and churches which have been or shall be taken from secular hands either by you or by your predecessors. Moreover, we decree that the church of St. Mary of the Marsh shall always remain under the bishop’s right and authority in the canonical observance which you have established. This church William, now provost of Riez, his brother Stephen, and William the younger had wickedly claimed as hereditary possession; they restored it to your jurisdiction and to the mother church and, having professed the regular life, submitted themselves to canonical ordering and observance.

We decree that the boundaries of the diocese of Riez [Col. 0354A] shall remain entire as they were possessed by your predecessors and are more peacefully possessed by your brotherhood: namely, from the boundaries of St. Julian of Montanarius to the boundaries of the town of Ragonis; likewise, from the boundaries of Mosiacum to the boundaries of the town of Cornert. Furthermore, whatever estates and possessions that Church lawfully possesses in the present seventh indiction, and whatever it may hereafter, by the Lord’s bounty, justly and canonically acquire, shall remain secure and unimpaired for you and your successors.

We therefore decree that no person at all may rashly disturb that Church, take away its possessions, retain those taken away, diminish them, or harass it with reckless vexations; but that all things be preserved intact for the benefit both of you and of the clerics and poor. Further, we forbid anyone, when you or any one of your successors has been called to the Lord, to dare, against the will of the clerics of your Church, to take away, plunder, or dispose of the property of bishops or of the Church. [Col. 0354B]

If, therefore, in the future any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowing this document of our constitution, should rashly attempt to act against it, then, having been warned a second and third time, unless he makes suitable amends, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and office; let him know himself guilty before divine judgment of the wrongdoing committed; let him be cut off from the most holy body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Redeemer; and let him be subject at the last judgment to severe punishment. But upon all who preserve what is just for that place, [Col. 0354C] may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that here they may receive the fruit of good action and before the strict Judge may find the rewards of eternal peace. Amen.

I, Paschal, bishop of the Catholic Church.

Given at Tiberias through the hand of John, cardinal-deacon and librarian of the Holy Roman Church, on the fifth day before the Kalends of June [28 May], in the seventh indiction, in the year 1115 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the fifteenth year of the pontificate of Lord Paschal II, pope.

CCCXCI. Privilege for the Church of Lescar. (Year 1114, 5 June.)

[MARCA, *History of Béarn*, 383.]

[Col. 0354D] PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother GUIDO, bishop of Lescar: greeting and apostolic blessing.

It is fitting that we give assent to just wishes and lend our ears to just petitions, since, though unworthy, we are, by the Lord’s ordering, set as guardians and proclaimers of justice upon the lofty watchtower of the apostles Peter and Paul. Therefore, beloved brother in Christ Guido, assenting to your just petitions, we fortify by the protection of the Apostolic See the holy Church of Lescar, over which, by God’s agency, you preside.

We confirm by the firm authority of this decree the order of canonical life established in that church by your holy predecessor of good memory. And we forbid any canon, after making his profession, to possess anything as his own [Col. 0355A] or to leave the cloister without your or the chapter’s permission. Moreover, besides that general care belonging to the episcopal office, we grant to you and your lawful successors special authority to correct the canons of the aforesaid church, assign them through obediences, or canonically remove them from those obediences.

Further, for you and through you for the Church of Lescar, we confirm the gift of the bridge of Gavar and of other properties which Gaston, viscount of good memory, and his wife Talesia gave for the support of the brethren living in common. We also confirm whatever is known to belong to that Church by parochial right or ownership: namely, the church of St. Stephen of Carrena with its tithe; Marlanensis; St. Faith’s and St. Andrew’s; the monastery of St. Peter of Regula; the monastery of St. Peter of Generensis; one fourth of the tithe and of the daily offering of the Church of St. Peter of Servimac; Pausam with its appurtenances; and the castle of Morelli with its appurtenances.

Likewise, all things given to that Church from their own right by faithful persons, or acquired by other just means, or which may hereafter, by God’s bounty, be acquired justly and canonically through grants of pontiffs or the generosity of princes, shall remain secure and unimpaired for you and your successors. We therefore decree that no person at all may rashly disturb the aforesaid Church, take away, diminish, or harass with reckless vexations anything which is or shall be its own, for any pretext whatsoever; [Col. 0355C] but that all things be preserved intact for the benefit both of you and of the clerics and poor.

If anyone, knowing the tenor of this decree, should rashly attempt to oppose it, unless he corrects his presumption by worthy satisfaction, let him suffer loss of his honors and office or be punished by the penalty of excommunication. But upon all who preserve what is just for that place may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that here they may receive the fruit of good action and find the rewards of eternal peace. Amen.

Given at Tiberias through the hand of Chrysogonus, acting in the place of Lord John, chancellor, on the Nones of June [5 June], in the seventh indiction, in the year 1115 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the fifteenth year of the pontificate of Lord Paschal the Second, pope.

CCCXCII. To Lawrence, abbot of St. Viton.—That he shall extend neither obedience nor communion to the clerics of Verdun. (Year 1114, 10 June.)

[MARTENE, *Anecdota*, I, 338.]

[Col. 0355D]

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons L., abbot, and the brethren of the monastery of St. Viton: greeting and apostolic blessing.

We have heard that the clerics of Verdun have broken out into such obstinacy that they endeavor to claim for themselves the subjection [Col. 0356A] and obedience of your Church, although they themselves are outside the unity of the Catholic Church. For a long time, because of the wickedness of their obstinacy, they have been excommunicated by the Apostolic See, which was established by almighty God Himself as the head and mistress of all churches. Certainly, he who does not agree with it is beyond doubt, as Blessed Ambrose writes, a heretic.

They are alien from the fellowship of the Church; how then do they seek preeminence in the Church? As blessed Cyprian testifies, a branch broken from a tree cannot put forth shoots, and a stream cut off from its source dries up. Since, therefore, they have cut themselves off from the Roman Church, we command by the injunction of these present letters, and order both you and your successors to observe, that you ought to extend to those clerics neither subjection, [Col. 0356B] obedience, nor communion until they return to the unity of the Catholic Church. For one divided from his lord cannot rule over his fellow servants. And the Psalmist says: “Do I not hate those who hate you, O God?” Therefore, until they return to communion and favor with the Apostolic See, let no subjection, obedience, or communion be granted to them by you.

Given at Tiberias, 10 June, seventh indiction.

CCCXCIII. Urges D[idacus], bishop of Compostela, to labor for the restoration of peace. (Year 1114, 24 June.)

[FLOREZ, *España sagrada*, XX, 193.]

P., bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother D., bishop of Compostela, [Col. 0356C] [Note: [Col. 0355D] The bishop of Compostela was seriously and most eagerly considering the transfer of the metropolitan see of Mérida to his own church. This was his chief concern; the pope’s reply relates to this matter, although it says nothing expressly of the petition.] greeting and apostolic blessing.

Although we are far from you, we have nevertheless learned of your tribulations; and what you suffer in body, we feel in heart. If we possess any ability to help, we willingly render aid to your brotherhood. But you, beloved brother, as you have begun, act manfully and labor in every way to restore peace. For the war in your regions is more dangerous to the Church, both because of the ferocity of the peoples and because of the proximity of unbelievers, to whom the Christian faith is made a mockery on account of deeds of this sort.

Because of these disturbances in your kingdom and Church, we cannot at present answer your request in accordance with your wishes, since new arrangements of churches can less suitably be made in such tumults, as they seem more likely to bring disturbance to the Church than peace. [Col. 0356D] But if divine mercy restores peace to your territories, we shall take care more willingly to deal with this matter in whatever way may be expedient.

Given at the Lateran, on the eighth day before the Kalends of July [24 June].

CCCXCIV. Confirms the possessions and rights of the Church of Blessed Mary in the Port of Ravenna. (Year 1114, 5 July.)

[See the *Lateran Bullarium*, Rome, 1727, folio, p. 5.]

CCCXCV. Takes under protection the monastery of St. Mary of Charity, once consecrated by himself, and confirms its possessions “in the present seventh indiction,” at the request of Odo, prior, through Pons, abbot of Cluny. (Year 1114.)

[Col. 0357A]

[This privilege exists in the Hamburg Library. Jaffé gave the title in *Regesta of the Roman Pontiffs*, 507, with this notice: “From Pertz’s papers.”]

CCCXCVI. To the canons of the Church of Chartres.—Confirms the decree of Bishop Ivo by which he restored to common uses the provostships and other benefices called *precariae*. (Year 1114, 2 November.)

[Dom BOUQUET, *Collection*, XV, 54.]

[Col. 0357B] PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons, the canons of the Church of Chartres: greeting and apostolic blessing.

From the letters of our venerable brother Ivo, bishop by God’s grace, we learned that he had issued a decree concerning certain complaints. We also examined that decree [Note: [Col. 0357D] See Ivo’s decree among the documents in vol. VIII of *Gallia Christiana*, col. 314.] with our own eyes. It stated that the canons of your Church had raised outcry and complaint before him concerning their provosts, who, seeking private advantage, diminished wherever possible every benefit of the brethren and wrongfully kept for themselves certain things owed to them by right; they subjected the poor of the Church placed under their protection to various hardships. The bishop enumerates these hardships in the written text of that decree, and, after enumerating them, continues:

> “By the counsel of our leading men, we have decreed that the canons have a just cause, and we order that henceforth the provosts shall not impose these exactions upon the Church’s peasants, nor further diminish the common benefit in the matters mentioned above.”

This decree and injunction, established for your Church by our aforesaid fellow-brother, its bishop, since it seems just and reasonable and conducive to the Church’s peace, we approve through God’s inspiration and confirm by the authority of the Apostolic See. [Note: [Col. 0357D] King Louis took this very ill, and the provosts carried their complaints to him. “They,” says Ivo in Letter 271 to Pope Paschal, “led the king astray in whatever way they could and wished, so that he sent me threatening letters against the clergy, containing threats that he would take the clergy’s goods for himself wherever he could, unless your privilege were destroyed and the rapacity of the provosts permitted in peace.”]

Likewise, later on, the same bishop writes that he had granted that the Church’s benefices called *precariae* [Note: [Col. 0358D] A freehold or estate received from a church under stated conditions, for use during life or for a specified term.]—and [or] had been made *precariae* (because four men were selling what belonged to all)—[Col. 0357D] should be brought into common uses; he enumerates those same benefices by their proper names. We likewise declare this grant valid and confirm it by the authority of the Apostolic See. We also strengthen by the assertion of the present decree the grant concerning the canons’ houses made by the same bishop, as it had been established by his predecessor, Bishop Frobold.

If anyone, knowing the tenor of this decree, should rashly—which God forbid—attempt to oppose it, [Col. 0358A] let him suffer loss of his honor and office or be punished by the penalty of excommunication, unless he corrects his presumption by worthy satisfaction. Amen.

Given at Anagni through the hand of John, cardinal-deacon and librarian of the Holy Roman Church, on the fifth day before the Nones of November [1 November], eighth indiction, in the year 1114 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the sixteenth year of the pontificate of Lord Paschal II, pope.

CCCXCVII. To Pons, abbot of Cluny.—Confirms possessions acquired by him. (Year 1114, 7 November.)

[MANSI, *Councils*, XX, 1042.]

[Col. 0358B] PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his most beloved son PONS, abbot of Cluny, and his successors regularly appointed forever.

By the authority and duty of the Apostolic See, we are compelled to provide for the condition of all churches, and, with the Lord’s aid, especially for the peace of those which adhere more particularly to that See, are subject to it as by a proper right, and are distinguished by a more eminent grace of religious life. Accordingly, beloved son in Christ Pons, we have rightly judged that your petitions should be granted, so that we might fortify the monastery of Cluny, over which, by God’s agency, you preside, by a privilege of the Apostolic See.

We therefore confirm to you and your successors, and through you to the monastery of Cluny itself, those things acquired during your prelacy and given by bishops or confirmed through bishops: namely, in Normandy, etc. (They are enumerated.) [Col. 0358C] Furthermore, whatever estates or possessions you may hereafter justly and canonically acquire through grants of pontiffs, the generosity of princes, or offerings of the faithful, shall remain secure and unimpaired for you and your successors.

We therefore decree that no person at all may rashly disturb that monastery, take away its possessions, retain what has been taken, diminish them, or harass it with reckless vexations; but that all things be preserved intact for the benefit in every way of those for whose support and governance they were granted. If, therefore, in the future any ecclesiastical or secular [Col. 0358D] person, knowing this document of our constitution, etc., as in Letter 34.

I, Paschal, bishop of the Catholic Church, have subscribed.

Given at Anagni through the hand of John, cardinal-deacon and librarian of the Holy Roman Church, on the sixth day before the Ides of November [8 November], eighth indiction, in the year 1114 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the sixteenth year of the pontificate of Lord Paschal the Second, pope.

CCCXCVIII. To Pons, abbot of Cluny.—Grants pontifical ornaments. (Year 1114, 7 November.)

[MANSI, *Councils*, XX, 1043.]

[Col. 0359A]

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his most beloved son PONS, abbot of Cluny: greeting and apostolic blessing.

When the Apostle was enumerating the different gifts which, by God’s grace, are given to the faithful, he added, saying: “Love without hypocrisy; hating evil, clinging to good; loving one another with brotherly affection, outdoing one another in honor” (Rom. XII). Preserving through God’s grace this love without hypocrisy toward your person, beloved son, [Col. 0359B] and cherishing the brotherly love of the brethren over whom, by God’s ordering, you have been set, we have decreed to outdo you in the privilege of honor. For, hating evil, we rejoice that you cling to good. We love God in you, from whom every good proceeds. The Psalmist also exhorts, saying: “You who love God, hate evil” (Ps. XCVI).

Accordingly, we confirm for you and your successors the grant of our predecessor Urban II, of blessed memory, which he conferred upon your predecessor, Abbot Hugh of venerable memory, concerning the use of the mitre, dalmatic, gloves, and sandals on eight principal feasts. Moreover, we grant you personally the use of the same insignia on every feast on which you chant the angelic hymn during the solemnities of Mass. To express also love without hypocrisy and an outdoing in honor, we have given to your belovedness the dalmatic with which we were accustomed to be clothed, so that, mindful of our affection, you may strive always to hate evil, to cling unceasingly to good, always to love in the Lord the brethren entrusted to you, and more effectively to urge them toward unity in the assembly of the Lord’s congregation.

[Col. 0359C] Given at Anagni through the hand of John, cardinal-deacon of the Holy Roman Church, on the seventh day before the Ides of November [7 November], eighth indiction.

CCCXCIX. Privilege for the monastery of St. Victor at Paris.—Confirms to the canons of St. Victor the grants made by royal diploma. (Year 1114, 1 December.)

[MARTENE, *Most Ample Collection*, VI, 219.]

[Col. 0359D]

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons GILDUIN, prior, and his brethren in the church of St. Victor near Paris, professing the canonical life, present and future, forever.

It is fitting readily to grant assent to religious desires, so that faithful devotion may obtain a swift effect. Our most beloved son Louis, illustrious king of the Franks, having endowed your church with his benefactions for the sake of his own soul and that of his father, requested that these be confirmed by our authority. We therefore establish that the discipline of canonical observance shall, by the Lord’s gift, always be maintained in your [Col. 0360A] church. Upon the death, however, of the abbot of your community, the free power of electing an abbot shall remain with you, all opposition by secular authority being set aside. Moreover, the villages, estates, and other benefices which the aforesaid king has assigned from his own right to your use, we decree shall be held by you and your successors in perpetuity, etc.

I, Paschal, bishop of the Catholic Church, have subscribed.

Given at the Lateran through the hand of John, cardinal-deacon and librarian of the Holy Roman Church, on the Kalends of December [1 December], eighth indiction, in the year 1114 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the sixteenth year of the pontificate of Lord Paschal, pope.

CD. To John, prior of the church of Blessed Peter of Valeriis in Septimania. (Year 1114, 2 December.)

[BALUZ., *Miscellanies*, Luc. ed., III, 12.]

[Col. 0360B]

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son JOHN, prior of the church of Blessed Peter of Valeriis, and to his successors canonically appointed forever.

By authority of the Apostolic See and as our duty requires, we are constrained to take thought for the condition of all the Churches, and, with the Lord’s help, to provide especially for the peace of those which are subject to that See as by its own right. Therefore, dearest son John, we have rightly judged that your petitions should be granted, so that we might strengthen by the privilege of the Apostolic See the church of Saint Peter of Valeriis, over which, by our appointment, you preside by God’s authority [Col. 0360C]. For although that place was uncultivated and solitary, since by ancient tradition it was distinguished by the name of blessed Peter, it was handed over by the possessors of the place—namely, Lords Rainard Amatus and his sons Bernard and Ermengaud—through the hands of Framald, priest of the Apostolic Church, into the right and possession of the Apostolic See; and thereafter it was enlarged by the gifts of many faithful persons.

We therefore decree that the place itself shall always remain free from the power, invasion, oppression, and burden of all mortals, as it is enclosed within its boundaries in the present eighth indiction: namely, from the hill above Guaida, thence above Mount Rotundus, and above the beginning of the Valley of Leporaria; thence to the allod of Bochet and as far as Portellus itself; thence to Pertusatae and to Guaita, above Embriciatae, above the field of Ardo, and above Mala Celata, as far as the sea. Whatever therefore is contained within these boundaries—cultivated or uncultivated land, pastures, fisheries, ponds, saltworks, together with tithes and first-fruits and their other appurtenances—shall be preserved wholly, entire, and unimpaired for the use of the aforesaid church of Blessed Peter and of the servants of God dwelling there.

Moreover, whatever the same church lawfully possesses in the present eighth indiction, or may hereafter, by God’s bounty, be able justly and canonically to acquire through the grant of pontiffs, the liberality of princes, or the offering of the faithful, shall remain firm and unimpaired to you and your successors. Let no opposition of any bishop or provost prevent you from receiving laymen or clerics living in the secular manner for conversion [Col. 0361A]. We further decree that the burial-place of the same house shall be wholly free, so that no one may oppose the devotion and final wish of those who determine to be buried there, unless they are excommunicated.

Furthermore, we add that no bishop shall have authority to subject that place to an interdict or excommunication, or to prohibit anyone from its offices and offerings, so that the brethren, enjoying the favour of Roman liberty, may more freely devote themselves to the service of Almighty God. You shall receive chrism, holy oil, consecrations of altars, and the ordinations of clerics who are to be promoted to sacred orders from the bishop in whose diocese you are, provided that he has the favour and communion of the Apostolic See and is willing to supply these things freely and without improper dealing [Col. 0361B]. Otherwise, you may approach whichever Catholic bishop you prefer and receive from him the sacraments of consecration; supported by the authority of the Apostolic See, he shall grant what is requested.

We therefore decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the same church, take away its possessions, retain possessions taken away, diminish them, or harass it with reckless vexations; but that all things shall be preserved intact, wholly serving the needs of those for whose support and governance they have been granted. As a sign of the liberty received from the Roman Church, you shall pay annually to the Lateran palace five solidi in Luccan denarii.

If, therefore, any ecclesiastical or secular person in the future, knowing this page of our decree, shall rashly attempt to act against it, and, having been warned a second or third time, does not make suitable amends, let that person be deprived of the dignity of his power and honour; let him know himself to be guilty before the divine judgment for the iniquity committed; let him be cut off from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, our Redeemer; and let him be subject to severe vengeance at the final judgment [Col. 0361C]. But upon all who preserve what is just for this place may the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ rest, so that they may receive here the fruit of good action and find, before the strict Judge, the rewards of eternal peace. Amen.

I, Paschal, bishop of the Catholic Church.

[Col. 0361D] Given at the Lateran through the hand of John, cardinal-deacon and librarian of the Holy Roman Church, on the fourth day before the Nones of December, in the eighth indiction, in the year 1114 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the sixteenth year of the pontificate of Lord Paschal II, pope.

CDI. He confirms the boundaries of the diocese of Braga at the request of Archbishop Maurice. (A.D. 1114, December 4.)

[RISCO, *España sagrada*, XL, 351.]

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother MAURICE, archbishop of the Church of Braga, and to his successors canonically appointed in perpetuity.

[Col. 0362A] Just as no effect is to be granted to those who ask unjust things, so the petition of those who seek what is lawful is not to be delayed. Therefore, assenting to your prayers, brother Maurice in Christ, for the perpetual peace and stability of the holy Church of Braga, we establish by the authority of this decree that the boundaries of the entire diocese, as they are recorded to have been marked out in the time of King Miro by a council of bishops, and as they have been possessed by your predecessors down to the present day, shall be preserved wholly and unimpaired for you and your successors in perpetuity.

Their description is as follows: from the mouth of the river Limia, along that river itself as far as Lindosum; thence to Portella de Homine, to Portella de Lavanca, and to Carragium as far as Petra Fita; thence to Mount Miserus, to Colinaria [Col. 0362B], and to the foot of the Alp of Cespiacius; thence by the mountain summits to Bouca de Vaccis as far as the harbour of Mirleus; and from that harbour by the river Estola into the river Douro; and by that river itself to the mouth of Corrego; thence to Mount Maraon and to the castle called Villa Plana, as far as the ancient bridge of the river Tamica; and along that river itself as far as the useful river now called de Utribus; thence to Lumba as far as the harbour of Burganum; and from that harbour along the bed of the river Avia as far as the sea.

Whatever the Church of Braga possesses within these boundaries, or in parts of other dioceses, by right of proprietary lordship, we establish for it as quiet and entire possession—indeed, we establish for it quiet and entire possession. Whatever else it may justly and canonically acquire through the liberality of princes [Col. 0362C] or the offering of any of the faithful shall remain firm and unimpaired for you and your successors.

We therefore decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the same Church, take away its possessions, retain gifts that have been taken away, diminish them, or harass it with reckless vexations; but that all things shall be kept wholly intact for the benefit of your uses and those of the clergy and the poor. If, therefore, any ecclesiastical or secular person in the future, knowing this page of our decree, shall rashly attempt to act against it, and, having been warned a second or third time, does not make suitable amends, let that person be deprived of the dignity of his power and honour; let him know himself to be guilty before the divine judgment for the iniquity committed [Col. 0362D]; let him be cut off from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, our Redeemer; and let him be subject to severe vengeance at the final judgment. But upon all who preserve what is just for this place may the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ rest, so that they may receive here the fruit of good action and find, before the strict Judge, the rewards of eternal peace. Amen, amen, amen.

I, Paschal, bishop of the Catholic Church.

Given at the Lateran, through the hand of John, cardinal-deacon and librarian of the Holy Roman Church, on the second day before the Nones of December, in the eighth indiction, in the year 1114 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the sixteenth year of the pontificate of Pope Paschal II.

CDII. First confirmation of the foundation of the monastery of Saint Margaret of Baumburg, offered by its founder, Blessed Peter. About A.D. 1114, April 7.

[*Monumenta Boica*, II, 179.]

[Col. 0363A]

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son EBERWIN, provost of the church of Saint Margaret, situated at Baumburg in the diocese of Salzburg, and to his brethren who profess the canonical life there, both present and future, in perpetuity.

Just as no effect is to be granted to those who ask unjust things, so the petition of those who seek what is lawful is not to be delayed. For Count Berengar of Sulzbach offered his allod in the district of Salzburg [Col. 0363B] to blessed Peter and his holy Roman Church, under an annual payment of one gold piece; and, building there a church of Blessed Margaret, he assigned that place to the order of regular canons. We therefore, in accordance with the founder’s devotion, take the place itself under the patronage of Blessed Peter and strengthen it by the authority of this decree. We establish that everything granted to the same place from rightful property, whether by the aforesaid count or by other faithful persons, and whatever may hereafter be granted or offered there through the concession of pontiffs, the liberality of princes, the offering of the faithful, or other lawful means, shall remain firm and unimpaired to you and your successors.

We therefore decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the same church [Col. 0363C], take away its possessions, retain possessions taken away, diminish them, or harass it with reckless vexations; but that all things shall be preserved intact, wholly serving the needs of those for whose support and governance they have been granted. On the death of you, now provost of that place, or of any of your successors, no one shall be put in charge there by any stratagem of deceit or violence, except one whom the brethren, by common consent or by the counsel of the sounder part of the brethren, in the fear of God, shall have duly chosen.

Moreover, after making profession, none of you may possess anything as private property, nor may anyone leave the cloister without the permission of the provost or the community. We grant to you and your successors the tithes of your newly cleared lands, free from the opposition of episcopal officials [Col. 0363D], so that, by God’s bounty, you may remain in perpetual peace in the purpose you have undertaken.

If, therefore, any ecclesiastical or secular person in the future, knowing this page of our decree, shall rashly attempt to act against it, and, having been warned a second or third time, does not make suitable amends, let that person be deprived of the dignity of his power and honour; let him know himself to be guilty before the divine judgment for the iniquity committed; let him be cut off from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, our Redeemer; and let him be subject to severe vengeance at the final judgment. But upon all who preserve what is just for this place may the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ rest, so that they may receive here the fruit of good action [Col. 0364A] and find, before the strict Judge, the rewards of eternal peace. Amen.

Given at the Lateran, on the seventh day before the Ides of April.

CDIII. To the clerics of the Church of Chartres. (Between A.D. 1099 and 1115.)

[*Works of Ivo*, II, 233.]

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the clerics of the Church of Chartres: greeting and apostolic blessing.

We have learned from the unquestionable report of truthful brethren that great seeds of hatred have arisen among you, because, over those oaths which were made among you to repel the *conditionarii*, you have hurled insults, reproaches, and injuries at one another [Col. 0364B]. Moreover, you have devised certain bonds and agreements to injure brotherhood, contrary to the Lord’s covenant. On this account, we ask your charity and, as the Lord commands through us, order you to forgive whatever you hold against one another in this matter. For we too have become sober, and we too bear apostolic weakness for your sake, so that we may win you for God and the Church in the peace of the Church.

If therefore you love God, if you reverence the Apostolic See, forgive me—rather, I should say, forgive yourselves—this injury. But if anyone is still contentious, he is not of our body, because we have no such custom, nor has the Church of God. Further, we forbid the mutual acts of homage (*hominia*) which clerics among you perform, that they may not be done in future; and we hold those already done void, since they appear to be performed contrary to ecclesiastical propriety [Col. 0364C]. For that Jerusalem which is above is free and is the mother of all the faithful, with the freedom by which Christ made her free.

Given at the Lateran, on the ninth day before the Kalends of December.

CDIV. To Bego, abbot of Conques.—He grants to the people of Conques that they may celebrate the vigil of Saint Faith with a solemn fast; that, in the order of Mass, the name of the same martyr may be included among the other virgins; and that, in reverence for the same saint, the abbot of Conques shall always be summoned to the election of the bishop of Rodez. (Between A.D. 1099 and 1115, December 24.)

[MARTÈNE, *Thesaurus Anecdotorum*, I, 337, from Colbert manuscripts.]

[Col. 0364D] PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son in Christ BEGO, abbot of the monastery of Blessed Faith of Conques, and to all the brethren of the same place: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Although the order of ecclesiastical offices is rightly established in ecclesiastical books in its lawful arrangement, we nevertheless believe that it does no harm to religion—indeed [read: *imo*], is of very great benefit—if anyone reasonably adds something of observance and devotion to those same offices. For our Samaritan, when he produced two denarii for the innkeeper to care for the sick man, said: “Whatever you spend beyond this, I will repay you when I return.”

Therefore, in the district of Rodez, especially at your monastery of Conques, where the body of Blessed Faith is believed to rest [Col. 0365A], we permit and confirm by the authority of this decree that, before the second day before the Nones of October, on which that virgin is recorded to have completed her martyrdom, vigils and a solemn fast be celebrated, as we have heard that you most devoutly do according to custom. For where blessed martyrs rest in bodily presence, it is certainly fitting, and confirmed by ecclesiastical custom, that they be honoured with more solemn offices.

Accordingly, we also grant that, in the order of Mass, the commemoration by name of that holy virgin and martyr be celebrated among the other virgins.

> **Note:** [Col. 0365D] That is, in the Canon, in which the ancients inserted the names of more eminent saints together with the names of apostles and martyrs, especially Saints Martin, Hilary, Ambrose, Jerome, Augustine, Gregory, and [Col. 0366D] Benedict, as I have shown more fully in vol. I of *On the Ancient Rites of the Church*. From this passage, however, it may be inferred that this was not done without the consent of the supreme pontiff.

We also approve, for the reverence of the same virgin, that the Passion and miracles concerning the same holy virgin, which are believed to have been written by Catholic men, be read in the Church. For we desire that the feast-days of that glorious virgin and martyr be celebrated with great devotion and reverence, both in [Col. 0365B] our most holy Roman Church and in other parts of the world, to the honour of God and the common salvation.

For the devotion to the aforesaid martyr and the honour of the monastery of Conques, we further decree that the abbot of Conques must always be called to the election of the bishop of Rodez, because in that city the election is often presumed upon without due order, because the place of Conques is considered so near the city, and because the person of its abbot is held in such esteem that he ought especially and deservedly to be present in so great a matter of the Church. We command our legates—those now in Gaul and those who shall be there in the future—to settle more diligently the other affairs of your monastery as matters more especially belonging to us [Col. 0365C]. For we desire your monastery and all that belongs to it always to remain peaceful, free, and entire, with its privileges. May Almighty God bless you by his grace and, through perseverance in holy conduct, bring you to eternal life. Amen.

Given at the Lateran, on the ninth day before the Kalends of January.

CDV. To Lambert, bishop of Arras. (Between A.D. 1099 and 1115.)

[BALUZE, *Miscellanea*, Luc. ed., II, 155.]

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother LAMBERT, bishop of Arras: greeting [Col. 0365D] and apostolic blessing.

There is uncertainty and dispute between your clerics and the monks of Saint Vaast concerning the extent of the old borough and the new borough. We therefore entrust to your brotherhood the examination of this matter, so that you may carefully seek certainty through older and more truthful persons, who are suspected by neither side, and so that, once all uncertainty has been removed by God’s grace, they may thereafter preserve peace and mutual affection.

CDVI. He forbids Husger, a canon of Auxerre, to be deprived of the provostship granted by Bishop Humbald. (Between A.D. 1099 and 1115.)

[LABBE, *Nova Bibliotheca manuscriptorum*, I, 459.]

[Col. 0366A]

PASCHAL, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons, the canons of the Church of Auxerre: greeting and apostolic blessing.

We thank both you and our brother Humbald, bishop of your Church, because he has treated kindly our son Husger, your canon, and with your consent has given him the dignity of the provostship. We wish you to know, moreover, that we will that both he himself and all that belongs to him remain under the protection of the guardianship of the Apostolic See [Col. 0366B]. By the authority of these present letters, therefore, we forbid any ecclesiastical or secular person to presume to trouble our same son concerning the benefit of the aforesaid provostship.

CDVII. To the knights of San Gimignano. (Between A.D. 1099 and 1115.)

[MANSI, *Councils*, XX, 1097.]

PASCHAL, pope, servant of the servants of God, to the knights of San Gimignano and the other neighbouring towns: greeting and apostolic blessing.

The one Catholic Church of God confesses that there is one faith. Hence the Apostle says: “One Lord, one faith” (Ephesians 4:5). Therefore, one who is compelled to renounce the faith which he owes to his father and lord, and who, when able, does not return to amendment, is proved no longer faithful but faithless [Col. 0366C]. Accordingly, by these present letters we warn you, and in warning command you, to return with due humility to fidelity toward your father and lord, W., our brother Roger, bishop of Volterra; and, for the honour of God and your salvation, to continue, as reason requires, in obedience and service to the Church.

If any of you, in defence of justice, has struck down some sacrilegious person or robber, he is not regarded as liable for homicide. For you may lawfully bear arms to protect justice, and all laws and every legal system permit force to be repelled by force. Nevertheless, if anything has been done through rashness, let it be corrected at the discretion of our aforesaid brother and fellow bishop. May Almighty God, through the prayers of the blessed apostles, absolve from all sins and bring to eternal life those who obediently persevere faithfully [Col. 0366D] in the service of God and the Church.

CDVIII. To Countess Matilda.—One who demands a due payment must state its basis. (Between A.D. 1099 and 1115.)

[MANSI, *Councils*, XX, 1074.]

It has come to our attention that the abbot of Frassinoro has plundered the church of Carpi [Col. 0367A], on the pretext of a certain due payment, though it is unknown for what purpose this payment ought to be made. When our archpriest questioned us about this, we gave the answer that seemed reasonable. A payment whose purpose is unknown is found in neither divine nor human laws. Every payment must, indeed, be known beforehand: for what purpose and in what manner it should be paid. We therefore command your belovedness to cause that spoil to be restored to the church of Carpi, and not henceforth permit the abbot of Frassinoro or anyone else to trouble it.

> **Note:** [Col. 0367] This is also found, in a shorter form and with some variation in the readings, in the *Extravagantes*, *On Dues*, ch. 5.

CDIX. To Lambert, bishop of Arras. (Between A.D. 1100 and 1115, March 21.)

[BALUZE, *Miscellanea*, Luc. ed., II, 149.]

[Col. 0367B] PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother LAMBERT of Arras: greeting and apostolic blessing.

The bearers of the present letter, Robert and A., came to us with a complaint; by the grace of Blessed Peter we send them back without a complaint, because peace has been reconciled between them and their adversaries without dispute. Since they say that they came without your permission, we ask you to forgive this offence against us. Henceforth treat Robert more kindly, as your predecessor Bishop Gerard is known to have treated him. For he is prepared in all things to obey you, because from now on he desires to be a son of the Roman Church.

Given at the Lateran, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of April.

CDX. To the canons of the Church of Chartres. (Between A.D. 1100 and 1115.)

[MANSI, *Councils*, XX, 1070.]

[Col. 0367C]

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the clerics of the chapter of Chartres: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Your memory recognizes that the counts of Chartres formerly exercised improper customs over the houses and property of the deceased or deposed bishop of Chartres. Through the labour and diligence of our brother Ivo, bishop of Chartres, as you know, it was obtained from the distinguished Count Stephen that he should renounce those customs. We, moreover, have forbidden by the page of our decree that anyone should presume to do the same in future [Col. 0367D].

We now forewarn your vigilance and, in forewarning, command that if perhaps any of the counts of Chartres, or any of their officials, should at any time, with greedy rashness and rash greed, violate the liberty granted by the count and confirmed by us, they shall be excommunicated by you or your successors as invaders of ecclesiastical right; and both the city churches and the suburban churches shall be closed to them until they make satisfaction. We add also that if a bishop, through fear of losing his bishopric, or a bishop-elect, through ambition to obtain it, absolves or supports without satisfaction the perpetrators of that sacrilege, he shall be deprived of office as a participant in sacrilege and a purchaser of the episcopate [Col. 0368A]. For a new remedy must be applied to new practices, and the safety of the Church must be preserved by every means.

Given at the Lateran, on the seventh day before the Kalends of April.

CDXI. Privilege confirming the donations to the Church of Berchtesgaden. (Between A.D. 1100 and 1115, April 7.)

[HUND, *Metropolis Salisburgensis*, ed. Gewald, Munich, 1620, folio, II, p. 155.]

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons Counts BERENGAR and CHUNO: greeting and apostolic blessing.

A petition of pious intention ought to be brought to fulfilment, so that the sincerity of devotion may shine forth commendably and the requested benefit may undoubtedly acquire force [Col. 0368B]. Therefore, dearest sons in Christ, assenting to your just requests, we have received under the protection of the Apostolic See your allods—namely, the estate of Berthersgodmen and Nidernhaim with all their appurtenances—which you offered to God and Blessed Peter under an annual payment, for the remedy of your souls and that of your mother.

We establish, therefore, that no person whatsoever may withdraw from Blessed Peter the aforesaid allods, diminish them, or harass them with reckless vexations; but that all things shall be preserved intact for the benefit and support of the monastery which, by the Lord’s bounty, you have wished to build upon those same allods. But if anyone, knowing this page of our decree, rashly attempts to act against it, and, having been warned a second or third time, does not make suitable amends [Col. 0368C], let him know that he is to be struck by the indignation of Almighty God and by the terrible judgment of the Holy Spirit.

Given at the Lateran, on the seventh day before the Ides of April.

CDXII. To John, bishop, and the canons of Castello. (Between A.D. 1100 and 1115, April 10.)

[BALUZE, *Miscellanea*, Luc. ed., IV, 584.]

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother JOHN, bishop of Castello, and to his canons: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Know that we have entrusted the administration of your canonry to our venerable brother Rothon, prior of Saint Fridianus; therefore we remind you of your promise or undertaking which you made in our hand [Col. 0368D]. For we will—and, as we have commanded, so we command—that you take care to render him obedience in the administration of your canonry as to ourselves. If anyone presumes to oppose him in this matter, he shall be struck by the drawn sword of Blessed Peter.

Given at the Lateran, on the fourth day before the Ides of April.

CDXIII. He exhorts G., bishop of Pavia, to settle the disputes with the monks of Saint Peter in Ciel d’Oro. (Between A.D. 1100 and 1115, April 17.)

[Only a notice of this letter survives in ROBOLIN, *Notizie appartenenti alla storia della sua patria*, Pavia, 1823, octavo, III, 224–225.]

CDXIV. To Bono the Elder, bishop of Reggio.

1. Those born of a godfather or godmother after they have received spiritual sons from the font cannot be joined in marriage. (Between A.D. 1100 and 1115.)

[MANSI, *Councils*, XX, 1079.]

[Col. 0369A]

After a spiritual son or daughter has been received from the font, those born of that godfather (*compater*) or godmother (*commater*) cannot be joined in marriage, because the laws of the secular world forbid unemancipated children to be united with adoptive parents.

2. A man may marry the wife of his godfather, if she herself was not his godmother.

After the death of his wife, no authority or reason appears to forbid a surviving man from being joined in marriage with his wife’s godmother. For spiritual kinship is not equated with kinship of the flesh [Col. 0369B], nor does one pass from union of the flesh to union of the spirit.

3. The wives of two first cousins cannot marry one and the same man.

Further, the wives of two first cousins, even at different times, cannot marry one man, one after the other’s death: public decency itself, apart from canonical authority, forbids it. And your prudence knows that abstention is required from the blood relatives of a wife just as from those of a husband.

CDXV. To the clerics of Thérouanne.—Those unwilling to leave their wives are to be deprived of offices and benefices. (Between A.D. 1100 and 1115, November 24.)

[MANSI, *Councils*, XX, 1024.]

[Col. 0369C] PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the clerics of the diocese of Thérouanne: greeting and apostolic blessing.

We have heard a very grave matter from your regions: that after so many decrees of holy pontiffs, after the prohibitions of councils, men of clerical rank—those who dare, openly; those who do not dare, secretly—associate with women. Concerning them, among others, our predecessor Pope Urban of pious memory decreed that they should be deprived both of offices and of the benefices of the Church. We likewise, agreeing with the judgment of that same predecessor, command by these present letters that whatever clerics among you, having been canonically admonished by their bishop, refuse to desist from such wickedness, shall be punished by deprivation both of offices and benefices [Col. 0369D].

Given at the Lateran, on the eighth day before the Kalends of December.

CDXVI. To R[aymond], bishop of Uzès. (Between A.D. 1100 and 1115.)

[*Gallia Christiana*, VI, 655.]

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved brother R., bishop of Uzès: greeting and apostolic blessing.

We have learned from the representation of the brethren of Aniane that you have absolved Pons William of Barjac, who was excommunicated on account of the property of the monastery of Cordanica, which he sacrilegiously holds and from which he endowed his daughter, without the remedy of satisfaction having first been provided. By what right, and how seriously, you have transgressed against our order in this matter [Col. 0370A], it is surprising if you do not yourself see. We therefore command that, setting every excuse aside, you render due satisfaction to the aforesaid brethren concerning that man, lest the punishment for so great an offence in this matter be remitted.

Given at the Lateran, on the fifth day before the Kalends of December.

CDXVII. He charges Bernard, archbishop of Toledo, not to undertake anything against the bishop of Burgos. (Between A.D. 1100 and 1115.)

[FLÓREZ, *España sagrada*, XXVI, 470.]

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother B., primate of Toledo: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Our predecessor Pope Urban, of happy memory, and we ourselves have loved your person abundantly and honoured you with especial favour [Col. 0370B]. But you do not respond correspondingly to the merits of the Roman Church: you do not allow one place and one person, whom she decreed should be fostered under her protection throughout the extent of your regions, to remain at peace. For you have long afflicted the Church of Burgos and its bishop with many injuries, and though often asked and often warned, you do not consent to desist.

Moreover, you presumed, in the queen’s court, to suspend from office and excommunicate him whom we had withdrawn from your jurisdiction. We hold this act of vengeance by your charity invalid, and command that you henceforth undertake nothing against him or his Church; and that you wholly restrain the bishop of Osma from invading and harassing the diocese of Burgos.

[Col. 0370C] Given at the Lateran, on the eleventh day before the Kalends of January.

CDXVIII. Letter of Pope Paschal II to the canons of Lyons.—He rescinds the sentence of interdict imposed by Hugh, archbishop of Lyons, upon the churches of the monastery of Savigny, and commands that the settlement made by the bishop of Mâcon concerning the castle of Varennes be observed. (Between A.D. 1113 and 1115, December 9.)

[Dom BOUQUET, *Recueil*, XV, p. 24.]

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons, the canons of the chapter of Lyons: greeting and apostolic blessing.

We have received the complaint of the brethren of Savigny concerning the castle of Varennes and concerning hostages extorted from the abbot on account of the castle [Col. 0370D]. We judge that the hostages were extorted wrongly and contrary to the ecclesiastical manner of judicial proceedings; but that the castle above the monastery was rightly destroyed, because neither it nor any other was permitted to be built to the injury of the monastery, nor ought one to be built thereafter. We therefore command that the hostages be restored to the abbot, and we absolve the churches which were unjustly put under interdict. We decree that the cemetery of Bulliacum (Bully) shall remain free and whole to the monastery, as it had been granted by the Church of Lyons.

Moreover, we command that the settlement made between the abbot and Stephen of Varennes through the agency of the bishop of Mâcon, Wicard of Beaujeu, Vigo of Igny, and Berard, archdeacon of Mâcon, be observed [Col. 0371A], provided that Stephen himself is willing to observe it.

> **Note:** [Col. 0371D] Mabillon explains the substance of these disputes as follows in vol. V of the *Annals of the Benedictines*, p. 462: “Formerly the monks of Savigny had a certain parishioner called Iterius of Bully, who had unjustly taken from them a certain cemetery but, repentant of his deed, finally restored it. After this Stephen of Varennes, his son-in-law, not only invaded that cemetery anew but also built a fortification not far from the monastery, and from it began to harass its tenants; indeed, he even drove out six monks living in a neighbouring cell. When the quarrel went further, Hugh, archbishop of Lyons, intervened as mediator and judged that the fortification should be surrendered to Abbot Pons. Stephen seemed to submit to the archbishop’s judgment, but deceitfully; for he remained in the fortification with armed men and never ceased to provoke the men of the monastery, afflicted by threats and injuries, into battle. Since matters stood thus, the abbot, on the advice of friends, decided to repel force by force and finally demolished the fortification. Moved by this, the archbishop excommunicated the abbot and monks, placed their churches under interdict, and further received hostages from them, on the condition that he would restore the fortification. When complaints about this were brought to Paschal, the pope, suppressing the archbishop’s name—for he had gone to Jerusalem, on which journey he was from the year 1101 until the end of 1103—rebuked the canons of the chapter of Lyons, approved the destruction of the castle, ordered the hostages restored to the monks, and so forth, as is contained in his letter.”

Henceforth let Stephen altogether desist from harassing the monastery; otherwise, as a contemner, let him be subject to canonical punishment.

Given at the Lateran, on the fifth day before the Ides of December.

CDXIX. To Berengar, bishop of Girona.—Concerning the privileges of the Church of Girona. (A.D. 1115, January 22.)

[MANSI, *Councils*, XX, 1071.]

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother BERENGAR, bishop of Girona, and to his successors canonically appointed in perpetuity.

As no effect is to be granted to those who ask for unjust things, so the petition of those who desire lawful things ought not to be delayed. Therefore, acceding to your prayers, dearest brother in Christ Berengar, we decree by the authority of this present enactment, for the perpetual peace and stability of the holy Church of Girona, that all the boundaries of your diocese, as they have been possessed by your predecessors down to the present day, shall be preserved wholly intact in perpetuity for you and your successors: namely, those boundaries which on the south touch the limits of the dioceses of Barcelona, on the east of Vic, on the north of Urgell and Elne, and on the west extend to the sea. We also confirm to the same Church of Girona all that is seen lawfully to belong to it in the present eighth indiction, and whatever it may hereafter be able justly and canonically to acquire.

We therefore decree that it shall be lawful for no person whatsoever [Col. 0371C] rashly to disturb the same Church, or to take away its possessions, or retain those taken away, diminish them, or harass it with reckless vexations; but that all things shall be preserved entire, for the benefit of your use and that of the clergy and the poor. Moreover, we altogether forbid the clerics of the same Church to retain or appropriate for their own use its prebends or possessions after they happen to be transferred to a bishopric, abbacy, or other offices of other churches. If, therefore, in future any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowing this charter of our constitution, shall rashly attempt to act against it, then, having been warned a second and third time, unless he makes fitting amends by satisfaction, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power [Col. 0371D] and honour; let him know himself guilty before the divine judgment for the iniquity committed; let him be separated from the most holy body and blood of God and Lord [Col. 0372A] Jesus Christ our Redeemer; and at the last judgment let him be subject to severe punishment. But upon all who preserve what is just for that place, may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that here they may receive the fruit of good action and before the strict Judge may find the rewards of eternal peace. Amen, amen.

I, Paschal, bishop of the Catholic Church, have subscribed.

Given at the Lateran through the hand of John, cardinal-deacon and librarian of the holy Roman Church, on the eleventh day before the Kalends of February, in the eighth indiction, in the year 1115 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and the sixteenth year of the pontificate of Lord Paschal II, pope.

## CDXX. Privilege for the Monastery of Vallombrosa. (1114, February 8.)

[LAMI, *Monuments of the Florentine Church*, 559.]

[Col. 0372B]

Paschal, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons Adhemar, abbot, and the other brothers of the Vallombrosan congregation, both present and future, in perpetuity.

A desire shown to pertain to a religious purpose and the salvation of souls ought, with the Lord as author, to be fulfilled without delay.
