Since, therefore, your purpose—through the prevenient and accompanying mercy of God—your community’s simplicity of religious life, and the fragrance of your good repute have inspired even those far away, we, wishing by the Lord’s assent to add assistance to your advancement, receive your monastery, which is dedicated in reverence for the Blessed Mary ever Virgin, [Col. 0372C] into the ownership, guardianship, and protection of the Roman Church. Strengthening it with the privilege of apostolic authority, we decree that it shall remain free from every yoke of secular persons.

Therefore, by the present charter of our privilege, we establish by apostolic authority that whatever your monastery now rightfully possesses, or may hereafter be able to acquire justly and canonically through the grant of pontiffs, the generosity of princes, or the offering of the faithful, shall remain secure and inviolate for you and your successors. By “successors” I mean those who shall strive to preserve the same rule of religious life and constancy of faith, and zealously serve almighty God with a steadfast purpose. You may receive chrism, [Col. 0372D] holy oil, the consecration of altars and basilicas, and the ordination of clerics from whatever Catholic bishop you choose, provided that he enjoys the favour and communion of the Roman [Col. 0373A] Church; supported by our authority, he shall grant what is requested.

Furthermore, we enact and establish that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the monastery, take away or diminish the possessions subject to it, or harass it with reckless vexations; rather, they shall altogether be kept whole, fully benefiting the uses of those for whose support and governance they were granted. Nor shall any bishop have power to impose excommunication or an interdict upon you, so that you, having been received as special sons of the apostolic see, may not rashly be subjected to another’s judgment.

And since, by the Lord’s inspiration, several of your monasteries have agreed with you in the same form of religious life, namely:

[Col. 0373B]

The Congregation of Saint Salvius near Florence; Saint Fidelis of Strumi; Saint Saviour of Sophena; Saint Mary of Nerana; Saint Cassian of Montescalario; Saint Angel near Pistoia; Saint Saviour of Fontana Thaonis; Saint Mary of Pacciano; Saint Mary of Caprimvenio; Saint Peter of Musceto; Saint Paul of Razzolo; Saint Reparata in the diocese of Faenza; the Congregation of Rivo-Cesare; and the Congregation of Monte Armato. [Col. 0373C] Saint Paul of Pisa; Saint Bartholomew of Cappiano; Holy Trinity of Florence; Saint Lawrence of Cuttu Buono; Saint Mark of Piacenza; Saint Basilides in the diocese of Parma; and Saint Gervasius in the diocese of Brescia.

To you and to all who may hereafter wish wholly to associate themselves with the observance of the same religious life, we grant by apostolic authority the liberty of this present privilege, so long as they strive to remain in the same unity of religious life and observance. Nor shall any person have authority to uproot and remove any monastery of your congregation from the stability of its own place without the consent of the abbot and congregation.

[Col. 0373D] We establish, moreover, that the monastery situated in Vallombrosa shall be regarded as the head of them all. When, by divine disposition, the end of life comes to your pastor, the person to be appointed in his place—because he must preside both over you and over all the others—shall be elected by the consent and judgment of all who preside over the other monasteries. If, perhaps, any one of those abbots is, by the Lord’s disposition, elected to this general government, he shall transfer in chief fashion to your principal monastery; and thereafter, at his judgment, all the other monasteries united to you shall be governed, as is known to have been done in the days of John, your first abbot, of venerable memory.

As a token of this liberty received from the Roman Church, each year you shall pay to the Lateran palace twelve arm-lengths of Cilician cloth. [Col. 0374A] If in future any archbishop or bishop, emperor or king, prince or duke, count, viscount, judge, *castaldus*, or any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowing this charter of our constitution, should attempt to act against it, then, having been warned a second and third time, unless he makes fitting amends by satisfaction, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and honour; let him know himself guilty before the divine judgment for the iniquity committed; let him be separated from the most holy body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, our Redeemer; and at the last judgment let him be subject to severe punishment. But upon all who preserve what is just for that place, may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that here they may receive the fruit of good action and before the strict Judge may find the rewards [Col. 0374B] of eternal peace. Amen, amen.

Written through the hand of Gervasius, *scriniarius regionarius* and notary of the sacred palace.

I, Paschal, bishop of the Catholic Church, have subscribed.

Given at the Lateran through the hand of John, cardinal-deacon and librarian of the holy Roman Church, on the sixth day before the Ides of February, in the eighth indiction, in the year 1115 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and the sixteenth year of the pontificate of Lord Paschal II, pope.

## CDXXI. He confirms the possessions and privileges of the Monastery of Saint Peter at Perugia. (1115, February 8.)

[MARGARINI, *Casinensian Bullary*, II, 132.]

[Col. 0374C] Paschal, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son John, abbot of the venerable monastery of Saint Peter situated near the city of Perugia, and to his successors to be regularly appointed in perpetuity.

By the authority and duty of the apostolic see, we are compelled to take pains for the state of all churches and, with the Lord’s help, to provide for their peace, especially that of those which adhere more particularly to the same see. Accordingly, dearest son in Christ John, abbot, we have rightly judged that your petitions should be granted, so that, following the example of our predecessors, we might strengthen the monastery of Saint Peter, over which you preside by God’s agency, with the privilege of the apostolic see.

Therefore, through this charter [Col. 0374D] of the present privilege, we confirm churches and cells, their estates, parish churches, landed properties, and hamlets: namely, the parish churches of Saint Constantius, Saint Rufinus, Saint Martin, and Saint John; the parish church of Saint Martyrius; the church of Saint Benedict at Agellione, with its appurtenances; the church of Saint Justine with its estate; the churches of Saint Andrew and Saint Angel of Alliano, with their appurtenances; the church of Saint Mary at Petiniano; the church of Saint Clement; the estate of Casale; the estate of Petroniano; what belongs to you from the estate and church of Saint Donatus at Civitella; and also the land of Hugh, nephew of Berno of Montenigro.

By apostolic authority we also confirm to you the churches of Saints Apollinaris, [Col. 0375A] Blasius, and Montanus, with all their appurtenances, the annual due to the Church of Farfa being reserved. Moreover, we confirm three *massae*—landed estates—in the county of Perugia: one called Pusulo, another Filoncio, and another called Casalina, with churches, houses, vineyards, fields, gardens, mountains, cultivated and uncultivated land, and all their appurtenances. We likewise confirm the monastery of Saint Angel in the county of Assisi, at the place called Limisano, with its cells and chapels and all that belongs to it; the church of Saint Archangel, situated near Lake Perugia, with all that belongs to it; the church of Saint Sylvester at Murculle; the church of Saint Donatus and whatever belongs to you at Agello; the church of Saint Mary at Poggio, with all its appurtenances; [Col. 0375B] the church of Saint Paul at Monticello; and the church of Saint Peter of Petroniano, with its estate.

Whatever else your monastery now lawfully possesses in the present eighth indiction, or may hereafter, with the Lord’s bounty, be able justly and canonically to acquire, shall remain firm and inviolate for you and your successors. You shall receive chrism, holy oil, the consecrations of altars and basilicas, the ordinations of monks to be promoted to holy orders, and of clerics belonging to the monastery itself, from the bishop in whose diocese you are situated, provided that he enjoys the favour and communion of the apostolic see and is willing to provide these freely and without improper conduct. Otherwise, you may approach whatever Catholic bishop you choose [Col. 0375C] and receive from him the sacraments of consecration; supported by the authority of the apostolic see, he shall grant what you have requested.

Upon the death of you, the present abbot of that place, or of any of your successors, no one shall be placed over it by any trickery of usurpation or by force, except the person whom the brothers, by common consent—or the sounder part of the brothers’ counsel—shall elect according to the fear of God and the Rule of Saint Benedict, to be consecrated by the Roman pontiff. We altogether forbid public masses to be celebrated in the same monastery by the bishop, or stations or any ordinations to be held, apart from the will of the abbot and brothers, lest any opportunity for popular gatherings be afforded in the retreats of God’s servants.

Nor shall any [Col. 0375D] bishop, apart from authorization by the Roman pontiff, have leave to burden, place under interdict, or excommunicate that monastery or its cells, or impose new exactions. Nor may any secular magnate extort from the same monastery or its appurtenances a *fodrum* or any other service. Adding to this, we decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the same Church, take away its possessions, retain those taken away, appropriate for personal use possessions unjustly held, diminish them, or harass it with reckless vexations; rather, all things shall be kept whole, fully benefiting the uses of those for whose support and governance they were granted.

If, therefore, in future any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowing this charter [Col. 0376A] of our constitution, shall rashly attempt to act against it, then, having been warned a second and third time, unless he makes amends by satisfaction, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and honour; let him know himself guilty before the divine judgment for the iniquity committed; let him be separated from the most holy body and blood of God and Lord Jesus Christ our Redeemer; and at the last judgment let him be subject to severe punishment. But upon all who preserve what is just for that place, may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that they may receive the fruit of good action and before the strict Judge may find the rewards of eternal peace. Amen, amen, amen.

Written through the hand of Gervasius, *scriniarius regionarius* and notary of the sacred palace.

I, Paschal, bishop of the Catholic Church, have subscribed.

[Col. 0376B] Given at the Lateran through the hand of John, cardinal-deacon and librarian of the holy Roman Church, on the sixth day before the Ides of February, in the eighth indiction, in the year 1115 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and the sixteenth year of the pontificate of Lord Paschal II, pope.

## CDXXII. To the Church of Canterbury.—Concerning the transfer of Ralph from the see of Rochester to Canterbury. (1115, February 18.)

[MANSI, *Councils*, XX, 1066.]

Paschal, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the sons of the Church of Canterbury: greeting and apostolic blessing.

We kindly received the envoys of your Church as religious and prudent men; but the embassy [Col. 0376C] which they brought us together with your letters was not merely unwelcome to us, but grievous. For it was reported that the bishop of Rochester had been transferred to your metropolitan see—an action which ought in no way to have been undertaken without our knowledge and approval, since it is plainly recognized to be prohibited by the decrees of the holy Fathers. Nevertheless, because of the religious character and integrity of the person said to have been transferred, we tolerate this presumption on your part; but, God willing, we shall soon send our legate to you, who shall determine what must be arranged in this affair.

Given at the Lateran, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of March.

## CDXXIII. To Henry, king of the English.—He permits the transfer of Ralph from the see of Rochester to Canterbury, but rebukes its having been undertaken without authorization from the apostolic see. (1115, March 30.)

[MANSI, ibid.]

[Col. 0376D]

Paschal, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son Henry, illustrious king of the English: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Since you have received in abundance from the hand of the Lord honour, riches, and peace, we are greatly astonished and distressed that in your kingdom and jurisdiction Blessed Peter—and in Blessed Peter, the Lord—has lost his honour and justice. For envoys or letters of the apostolic see receive no welcome or access within your jurisdiction without the command of royal majesty. [Col. 0377A] No complaint from there, no judgment from there, is sent to the apostolic see. Therefore many unlawful ordinations are presumptuously undertaken among you, and those who ought to restrain license in wrongdoing sin with impunity.

Yet in all these matters we have hitherto exercised exceptional patience, hoping that all would be corrected through the diligence of your integrity. For what honour, wealth, or dignity is diminished for you when the reverence due to Blessed Peter is preserved in your realm? These things are indeed all the more offensive to us because we know that your kingdom, in the time of ancient kings, adhered most closely to the apostolic see. We read, indeed, that the kings themselves visited the thresholds of the apostles and remained there until death. We read that certain governors and teachers of churches were voluntarily sent there by Roman pontiffs.

Therefore, to deal with and correct these matters among you, we have sent to your excellency our dearest son Anselm, your intimate, now abbot of Saint Sabas. Through him, moreover, we have complied with the petition of you and the bishops in the matter of the bishop of Canterbury, although it was contrary to the authority of the apostolic see; we hope that you in turn will henceforth satisfy the apostolic see with respect to the justice of its dignity. Otherwise, if you withdraw from Blessed Peter his rightful due, he too will henceforth withdraw from you the benefits of his dignity. What is expressed less fully in letters will be supplied by the living voice of the legate. May almighty God protect you with his right hand and perfect you in his love.

The alms of Blessed Peter, as we have heard, [Col. 0377C] have been collected so wrongly and deceitfully that the Roman Church has hitherto received not even half of them. All this, like the other matters, is imputed to you, because nothing is undertaken in your kingdom without your will. We therefore desire that you cause them henceforth to be collected more fully and send them through the present envoy.

Given at the Lateran, on the third day before the Kalends of April.

## CDXXIV. To Arnald, bishop of Carcassonne. (1115, March 31.)

[Gallia Christiana, VI, Instrumenta, 433.]

Paschal, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother Arnald and his successors canonically appointed as bishops of Carcassonne [Col. 0377D] in perpetuity.

To the just requests of petitioners, etc. We therefore establish that the church of Saint Mary in the borough of Carcassonne shall remain under your lordship with all its appurtenances, excepting the revenue which the canons of Saint Nazarius have customarily received; in the estate of Caparais, the church of Saint Stephen with its appurtenances; the church of Saint Mary of Varnasona; the church of the Holy Sepulchre, also called Saint Fulk’s; the church of Saint Clement; the church of Saint Peter of Leuc; the church of Saint Felix of Prexan; and the church of Saint Germanus of Allairac, with all their appurtenances.

Furthermore, we decree that all things bestowed by you or your predecessors for the common use of the canons [Col. 0378A] living regularly in the church of Blessed Nazarius shall stand ratified and shall remain whole and undisturbed for them in perpetuity; from these, those whom the bishop elects shall jointly celebrate the divine offices in the aforesaid church of Blessed Mary. We also forbid that, when you or any of your successors is called to the Lord, anyone whatsoever should dare, against the will of your church’s clerics, to take away, plunder, or alienate the property either of bishops or of the church. We likewise decree that the cloister of the clerics itself and the houses of the cloister shall always remain so free that no one may inflict violence there. We further decree that no person whatsoever, etc.

I, Paschal, bishop of the Catholic Church, have subscribed.

Given at the Lateran through the hand of Brother John, cardinal-deacon [Col. 0378B] and librarian, on the day before the Kalends of April, in the eighth indiction, in the year 1115 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and the sixteenth year of the pontificate of Lord Paschal II, pope.

## CDXXV. To King Henry and the Bishops of England.—He rebukes them for improperly doing many things without consulting the pope. (1105, April 1.)

[MANSI, *Councils*, XX, 1067.]

Paschal, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son Henry, illustrious king, and to the bishops of the English realm: greeting and apostolic blessing.

How the Church of God was founded need not now be discussed by us. For the text of the Gospel and the letters of the apostles declare this more fully. But how the Church’s condition may endure through the Lord’s favour is both a matter for us to report and to act upon. For it was said to the Church by the Holy Spirit: “In place of your fathers, sons have been born to you; you shall appoint them princes over all the earth” (Psalm XL). Concerning this appointment the apostle Paul commands, saying: “Do not lay hands hastily upon anyone, nor share in the sins of others” (1 Timothy V). Explaining this saying of the same apostle, Saint Leo the teacher says: “What is it to lay hands hastily, except to confer priestly honour upon men not tested—before the age of maturity, before the time of examination, before the merit of labour, before experience of discipline?”

By what reasoning, then, can we confer confirmation of priestly honour [Col. 0378D] upon bishops of the English kingdom whose life and learning we know by no examination? When the Lord Jesus Christ himself, head of the Church, entrusted the Church to Peter, the first apostle and shepherd, he said: “Feed my sheep; feed my lambs” (John XXI). For the sheep in the Church are the governors of churches, who, by God’s gift, are accustomed to beget children for God. How, then, can we feed either lambs or sheep whom we neither know nor have seen, whom we neither hear nor are heard by? How shall we fulfill concerning them the Lord’s command by which he instructs Peter, saying: “Strengthen your brethren” (Luke XXII)?

Our Lord and Master indeed allotted the whole world to his disciples, but he committed the regions of Europe in a special manner to Peter and [Col. 0379A] Paul. And Europe as a whole was converted and confirmed not only through their disciples, but through the disciples and legates of their successors. Hence, down to us, their unworthy vicars, the practice has come that the more serious affairs of churches in the provinces should be conducted or reconsidered through the vicars of our see.

But you decide even bishops’ affairs without consulting us, although Victor the martyr, pontiff of the Roman Church, says: “Although it is permitted for bishops of the same province to investigate the case of an accused bishop, they are nevertheless not permitted to decide it without consulting the Roman pontiff.” Zephyrinus likewise, martyr and pontiff, says: “Judgments concerning bishops and major cases are to be decided by the apostolic see, and not by another.” You withhold from those under oppression the right of appeal to the apostolic see, although the councils and decrees of the holy Fathers have enacted that all who suffer oppression must appeal to the Roman Church. You celebrate synodal decrees without informing us, though Athanasius writes to the Church of Alexandria: “We know that at the great Council of Nicaea, of three hundred and eighteen bishops, it was unanimously confirmed by all that councils ought not to be held without the knowledge of the Roman pontiff.” The holy pontiffs themselves confirmed this in their writings and declared councils conducted otherwise null.

You see, then, that you too have transgressed greatly against the authority of the apostolic see and gravely impaired its dignity, and that the obligation of our office presses upon us to ensure that those upon whom we confer [Col. 0379C] priestly dignity have been tested, lest, contrary to the apostle, by laying hands hastily upon anyone we share in others’ sins; for, as Saint Leo says, “He inflicts grievous harm upon himself who raises an unworthy man to the fellowship of his own dignity.” You also presume, without our authority, to make transfers of bishops, though we know that this is altogether forbidden without the authority and permission of the most holy Roman see.

If, then, you agree in all these things to preserve the dignity and reverence of the apostolic see, we shall preserve toward you, as brothers and sons, the charity due to you, and, with the Lord’s favour, shall graciously and gladly grant what ought to be granted to you by the apostolic Church. But if you decide still to persist in your obstinacy, [Col. 0379D] then, in accordance with the Gospel saying and apostolic example, we shall shake the dust of our feet against you and hand you over to divine judgment as persons withdrawing from the Catholic Church; for the Lord says: “He who does not gather with me scatters; and he who is not with me is against me” (Luke XI). May almighty God grant that you may be with us in him and be gathered with us in him, so that he may grant you to attain to his eternal unity, which remains one and the same.

Given at the Lateran, on the Kalends of April, in the eighth indiction.

## CDXXVI. To Bernard, primate of Toledo and vicar of the apostolic see.—Concerning the election of the bishop of Burgos. (1115, April 10.)

[MANSI, *Councils*, XX, 1036, from the Primacy of Toledo, Castejón.]

[Col. 0380A]

After we had replied to your letters, granting leave to consent to the bishop-elect P. of the Church of Burgos, we unexpectedly received other letters from the clergy and people of Burgos. In these it was reported that the same Paschal, archdeacon, had been elected on your advice indeed, but without the king’s knowledge and without the people’s awareness. But after that election, while the people waited, with all the clergy consenting and the king likewise willing, the king’s own brother was said to have been designated for the episcopate [Col. 0380B] of the Church of Burgos.

Certainly, amid these varying disagreements, it is ours both to preserve the justice of the canons and to provide for the Church’s welfare. Therefore we send these present letters to your care, commanding that, after summoning the bishops of the province, you order both parties to appear before you at a suitable place and time. There, with every favouritism, all deceit, and the perversity of partisan hostility set aside, we command that the case of the two elections be decided wholly according to canon law.

Given at the Lateran, on the fourth day before the Ides of April.

## CDXXVII. To Guy, archbishop of Vienne and legate of the apostolic see.—That he bring to an end the dispute between the canons of Besançon and Saint Stephen. (1115, April 22.)

[MANSI, *Councils*, XX, 1047, from manuscripts.]

[Col. 0380C]

You are to know that the controversy which has for so long been turned over and reconsidered between the canons of Besançon and Saint Stephen has now at last been decided before us by canonical judgment. We therefore command your care that, in carrying out this business and quieting the litigation of so great a scandal, you meet, accompanied by wise and religious brethren, either at Dijon or another more suitable place, where they may bring without burden the persons necessary to them. With all party hostility set aside, receive the execution of this judgment so honestly and so clearly that no further dispute or complaint regarding this matter may remain between them. The witnesses who establish this question [Col. 0380D] shall be five, clerics or laypersons, who, according to canonical enactments, give testimony from sight and hearing; for a more serious case is at issue concerning the head of a parish.

## CDXXVIII. He effects peace between the brothers of Molesme and the monks of Saint Aper disputing over the cell of Castiniac. (1115, May 24.)

[Dom CALMET, *History of Lorraine*, documents, p. 537.]

Paschal, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the faithful throughout the diocese of Toul: greeting and apostolic blessing.

For some time a dispute between the religious men of Molesme and the monks of Saint Aper concerning the cell of Castiniac had been debated and examined before us and our brethren. In the course of this proceeding it was established that the monks of Saint Aper had formerly possessed the same cell, but that through their neglect the men of Molesme were subsequently introduced into that place. When the decision of the affair appeared then to be approaching the conclusion of an oath, it pleased the brethren to end the matter by charity rather than contention.

Accordingly, Guy, abbot of Molesme, together with the brethren present with him, in our presence and that of our brethren, restored the cell of Castiniac to the abbot of Saint Aper and to his brethren then present, with its entire integrity and appurtenances, in all movable property and land. They also promised that, in the assembly of the brethren at Molesme, they would have this restoration approved by the brethren themselves, confirm it in writing and under the seal [Col. 0381B] both of their own monastery and of the bishop of Langres, and hand it over to the monks of Saint Aper.

In return, Guiric, abbot of Saint Aper, together with his monks then present, took care out of charity that the men of Molesme should not suffer loss of the expenses which they had incurred in constructing that cell and acquiring immovable and movable goods. Accordingly, in our presence and that of our brethren, they gave the abbot of Molesme and his brethren an estate called Ixei and a village free of an advocate, in complete integrity, with cultivated and uncultivated lands, meadows, waters, mills, woods, male and female serfs. They likewise promised that they would have this donation approved in their cloister by the remaining brethren in the presence of those brethren, strengthen it by writing and seal both of their monastery and of the bishop of Toul, and hand it over to the monks of Molesme.

Therefore, providing through God’s favour for the future peace of religious men, we have approved this agreement and concord, and commanded that all things promised and determined before us be fulfilled by both sides. Furthermore, through the written text of this present charter, we establish by the authority of the apostolic see that this restoration and donation between the monks of Molesme and Saint Aper shall remain firm and inviolate for ever; nor shall it be lawful in any way for the present or future abbots or monks of the same monasteries to transgress or violate these provisions. If anyone, having learned the tenor of this our decree, should presume by rash daring [Col. 0381D] to oppose them, let him be subject to the censure of canonical severity.

Done at Benevento, in the principal palace, before many witnesses, on the ninth day before the Kalends of June.

I, Paschal, bishop of the Catholic Church, approved and subscribed.

I, Sennes, by the grace of God archbishop of Capua, was present and subscribed.

I, Rainald, by the grace of God bishop of Angers, was present and subscribed.

I, William, by the grace of God bishop of Troy, was present and subscribed.

I, P. P., bishop of Terracina, was present and subscribed.

[Col. 0382A] I, Risa, bishop of Bari, was present and subscribed.

I, Anastasius, cardinal-priest of the title of Blessed Clement, was present and subscribed.

I, Romuald, deacon, was present and subscribed.

I, Adelbero, archbishop of Metz, was present and subscribed.

I, Garland, master of the schools of Metz, was present and subscribed.

I, Unald, canon of Toul, was present and subscribed.

Given at Benevento through the hand of John, deacon and librarian of the holy Roman Church, on the ninth day before the Kalends of June, in the year 1115 of the Lord’s Incarnation and the sixteenth year of the pontificate of Lord Paschal, pope.

## CDXXIX. To Archembald, abbot of Saint Albinus at Angers.—He confirms Urban II’s judgment concerning the agreement made between the monks of Saint Albinus and those of Vendôme. (1115, May 25.)

[BALUZE, *Miscellanies*, Lucae edition, III, 53.]

[Col. 0382B]

Paschal, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son Archembald, abbot of the monastery of Saint Albinus situated at Angers: greeting and apostolic blessing.

From the letters of our predecessor Urban II, pope of holy memory, we learned that before him the monks of Saint Albinus had raised a dispute against the men of Vendôme regarding the church of Saint Clement at Credon. Then, by the decision [Col. 0382C] of the same pontiff, it was determined that, in compensation for the aforesaid church, the brethren of Vendôme should hand over another church to the monks of Saint Albinus. Thus the men of Vendôme gave those monks the church of Saint John on the Loire; this was confirmed by the favour and consent of both communities.

In our time, however, Geoffrey, abbot of Vendôme, sought to trouble Archembald, abbot of Saint Albinus, concerning that same church of Saint John. At his request, we summoned Archembald himself to the case by our letters. But after the term fixed by us, when they had set for themselves a second or third date at another time, as was reported to us in their letters, Archembald was ready to set out, as we learned from his embassy; the abbot of Vendôme not only did not come but did not even offer reasonable excuses. Therefore, considering such evasions and delays, and at the request of our venerable brother Rainald, bishop of Angers, we judged it necessary to provide henceforth for your peace in this matter.

Accordingly, by the charter of this present decree, we decree that the agreement established through the decision of our aforesaid predecessor shall remain firm in perpetuity, altogether forbidding the abbot of Vendôme henceforth to presume to harass the monastery of Saint Albinus concerning that church of Saint John. If he should presume to do so, the harassment itself shall have no force.

[Col. 0383A] I, Paschal, bishop of the Catholic Church, have subscribed.

Given at Benevento through the hand of John, deacon and librarian, on the eighth day before the Kalends of June, in the eighth indiction, in the year 1115 of the Lord’s Incarnation.

## CDXXX. Bull for Maurice, archbishop of Braga. (1115, July 23.)

[ARGOTE, *Memoirs for the History of Braga*, Lisbon, 1732, III, 451.]

Paschal, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother Maurice, archbishop of Braga: greeting and apostolic blessing.

The transfer of the cathedral of Mondoñedo, as you know, was effected by deliberation of a provincial council, although you hold the position of metropolitan of that same Church for the time being. If, therefore, anything in this matter needs correction, our legate, when he comes to you, will, by God’s grace, make provision. Nevertheless, we do not wish any injuries to be inflicted upon the clerics of that place; and we command that any benefices which have been taken away be restored to the bearer of this letter and to the others.

Given at Benevento, on the fifth day before the Nones of June.

### CDXXXI. At the request of Bishop William, he confirms certain possessions of the Church of Chieti.  
*(A.D. 1115, 18 July.)*

[UGHELLI, *Italia sacra*, VI, 702.]

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to all the faithful throughout the diocese or county of Chieti, greeting and apostolic blessing.

From a document of our predecessor, Pope Urban II of holy memory, we have learned that the counts of noble memory Robert—whose surname was “of Loreto”—and his brother Tassio bestowed or restored certain possessions or churches upon the bishop of Chieti, and by their own documents confirmed them to be possessed forever in full right or lordship.

[Note: [Col. 0383D] Platina mentions Count Robert of Loreto in his *Life of Pope Calixtus II*. William, however, died in the year 1117, on the eighth day before the Ides of June.]

Robert’s donation indeed contained the following: in Aterno, the parish church of Saints Leontianus and Domitianus; at the foot of that city and at the gate facing the sea, the church of St Thomas the Apostle; outside it, the church of St Nicholas; lands, vineyards, houses, persons within and without, tithes, and offerings of the living and the dead; beyond the fishery, lands in the dependency of Sculcula; the castle of Genestrale; the castle of St Caesidius with its appurtenances; and a church in Buclanico, dedicated in honour of the Holy Saviour and St Michael, with the count’s tithes and the tithes of the castles in the bishopric of Chieti which were under Robert’s lordship, together with what the Church of Chieti held in the castle of Setti.

Tassio’s restoration and confirmation recorded the following: namely, the city of Chieti, Trevelliano, Villamagna, Mount Filardo, the church of St Mary at Bari, of St Blaise at Lanciano, of St Leucius at Atessa, the churches of St Mary and St George at Ortona, and Monte Acuto with the church of St Nicholas.

Besides these, the document of our aforesaid predecessor relates that Rainulf, bishop of Chieti of good memory, by his own efforts and with ecclesiastical money, recovered for the lordship of the Church the following: on Mount Oderisius, the churches of the Holy Saviour, St Nicholas, and St Peter, with their benefices; the monastery of St Maurus with its benefice; in the town of Luparello, the parish church of St Peter with its appurtenances; the monastery of St Mary of Letto with its hamlet and the other things belonging to it; at Abatico, the parish church of St Martin with its appurtenances; at Caramanico, the parish church of St Mary with its estate; and at Torre, the parish church of St John.

We have also learned, from the report of our brother William, bishop and present holder of the Church of Chieti, that after that time Bishop Rainulf acquired from the aforesaid Count Robert, for the bishop’s lordship, at Aterno the churches of the Holy Saviour and of Holy Jerusalem; beyond Pescara, at Monte Silvano, St Mary at Rivolo and the castle of Lattiniano; in the county of Chieti, the castle of St Paul and the castle called Furca; in Buclanico, the parish church of St Silvester; and in Gissi, the parish church of St Mary with its appurtenances. The same Bishop Rainulf, after an exchange with Hugh, abbot of St John of Ardano, received Mucela, which lies near Ortona. Robert, son of the aforesaid Count Robert, restored to the same bishop the castle of Sculcula. Further, his successor, the above-named Bishop William, son of Tassio, reported that he had acquired the castle of Montipolo, Giuliano, and Orno with all their appurtenances.

Therefore, moved by the prayers of our aforesaid brother Bishop William, we confirm, without prejudice to the authority of the Apostolic See, the aforesaid donation of the aforesaid counts and of William Tassio. Under the attestation of the divine judgment, we decree that no person whatsoever may take away, retain after taking away, diminish, or harass with rash vexations either what has been granted by the aforesaid persons, or whatever the Church of Chieti now justly possesses or may, with the Lord’s help, justly acquire in future; but that these things shall remain forever firm and unimpaired for the present bishop and his successors.

If, therefore, in future any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowing this charter of our constitution, should rashly attempt to act against it, then, after a second or third warning, unless he makes suitable satisfaction, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and honour; let him know himself guilty before the divine judgment for the iniquity he has committed; let him be excluded from the most sacred Body and Blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ the Redeemer; and at the final judgment let him be subject to severe vengeance. But upon all who preserve the rights of that same Church of Chieti may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that they may receive here the fruit of good action and find, before the strict Judge, the rewards of eternal peace. Amen.

Given at Benevento through the hand of John, deacon, on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of August, in the eighth indiction, in the year 1115 of the Lord’s Incarnation.

### CDXXXII. To the archbishops, bishops, and others throughout Spain—concerning the holding of a general council at Rome.  
*(A.D. 1115, 15 August.)*

[FLOREZ, *España sagrada*, XX, 203.]

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved brothers the archbishops, bishops, abbots, and clerics throughout Spain, greeting and apostolic blessing.

From the Fathers of the Church, whom Christ our Lord and Master established as the salt of the earth and light of the world, we have received examples and precepts that, whenever more serious questions arise in the Church, a larger gathering of the brethren should be summoned. Indeed, concerning the investitures of bishoprics and abbeys—which laymen have for a long time arrogated to themselves—such scandal has arisen in the Church that it has proceeded to schism. Therefore we have judged it fitting and most necessary to summon your fraternity to a general council, both concerning these investitures themselves and concerning the occupation of churches.

We ask and command that, from each province, those bishops who are known by God’s grace to be wiser or more devout, and from the dioceses abbots or clerics learned in the Holy Scriptures and in ecclesiastical institutions, make every effort to assemble with us in the city of Rome on the fourth day before the Nones of the coming March. Thus, by God’s aid, being prepared for questions of this kind, may the unity of our assembly bring strength to the unity of the universal Church.

Given at Benevento, on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of September.

[Note: [Col. 0385] In the year 1115 a council was proclaimed, which was held at Rome in March of the immediately following year.]

### CDXXXIII. He exempts the Church of Portugal from metropolitan jurisdiction and establishes and confirms the boundaries of its diocese.  
*(A.D. 1115, 15 August.)*

[FLOREZ, *España sagrada*, XXI, 297.]

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother HUGH, bishop of the Church of Portugal, and to his successors canonically appointed in perpetuity.

The writings and monuments of eminent bishops and martyrs who shone in them testify that, in former times, cities of outstanding episcopal rank flourished in Spain. Afterwards, however, the destruction of cities and churches shows—and the memory of our own times does not fail to know—that for many years the greater part of Spain was invaded and occupied by the Moors or Ishmaelites. Since indeed in our times it has pleased almighty God to free certain cities from the tyranny of the Moors and to recall those lying desolate to the support of restoration, we have judged it altogether fitting to restore episcopal sees in those cities.

Since, therefore, your brotherhood has been appointed by the common counsel of the brethren to reform the condition of the Church of Portugal, we warmly support its reform and its execution through your devotion, venerable brother and fellow bishop Hugh. We have decreed that your person, and the Church itself restored by God’s grace, shall be specially cherished under our protection, granting you the liberty that you shall be subject to no metropolitan except the Roman pontiff or a legate sent from his side; and that, free from disturbances, you may devote yourself peacefully to the Church entrusted to you.

We decree, therefore, that whatever estates and whatever diocese that Church now justly possesses in the present eighth indiction, or may in future justly and canonically acquire, shall remain firm and unimpaired to you and your successors; and that whatever, from the ancient boundaries of its diocese, has been occupied by other churches while the Church of Portugal lay overthrown, shall, with God’s help, be restored to that Church. The delimitation of these boundaries is said to extend along the following limits: from the mouth of the River Ave, where it falls into the Ocean Sea, upstream along that river to the Avicella stream; along the Avicella to the arch of Palumbarius; thence to the Anta of Temone; thence to Mount Ferrati; thence to Mount Marannis; thence to the Campeana stream; and along that stream, as it flows into the Bandugium; along the Bandugium as it runs into the Corga; along the Corga into the River Douro; thence across the Douro to Piscarium; by the great mountain to the Antoana stream; and along that stream as it descends to the Ocean Sea.

We command that whatever churches or monasteries lie within these boundaries shall render due obedience and justice to the aforesaid Church of Portugal. Furthermore, we decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb that Church, take away its possessions, retain what has been taken away, diminish them, or trouble it by reckless vexations; but that all things shall be preserved whole, for the benefit both of you and of the clerics and poor people. If, therefore, in future any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowing this charter of our constitution, should rashly attempt to act against it, then, after a second or third warning, unless he makes suitable satisfaction, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and honour; let him know himself guilty before the divine judgment for the iniquity he has committed; let him be excluded from the most sacred Body and Blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ the Redeemer; and at the final judgment let him be subject to severe vengeance. But upon all who preserve what is just for that same place may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that they may receive here the fruit of good action and find, before the strict Judge, the rewards of eternal peace. Amen.

I, Paschal, bishop of the Catholic Church.

Given at Benevento through the hand of John, cardinal-deacon and librarian of the Holy Roman Church, on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of September, in the eighth indiction, in the year 1115 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the seventeenth year of the pontificate of Lord Paschal II, pope.

### CDXXXIV. He commands Gonsalvo, bishop of Coimbra, to restore to Bishop Hugh the occupied portion of the diocese of Portugal.  
*(A.D. 1115, 19 August—see RIBEIRO, *Dissertações chronologicas e criticas sobre a historia de Portugal*, Lisbon, 1810, octavo, V, 6.)*

### CDXXXV. To Didacus, bishop of Compostela.  
*(A.D. 1115, 20 August.)*

[FLOREZ, *España sagrada*, XX, 202.]

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother DIDACUS, bishop of Compostela, greeting and apostolic blessing.

We have learned that the disturbance of your kingdom bears down no little upon your person, partly because of the greatness of the church of Blessed James, over which by God’s disposal you preside, and partly because of the shrewdness of your mind, which is seen as formidable to certain persons. For this reason those who strive to disturb the state of the kingdom are said to pursue you with no small hatred; and you must certainly guard more carefully against their plots, lest injury—may God avert it—come either to your person or to the Church.

For this reason, our brother Hugh, bishop of Portugal, and Laurence, a cleric of your Church, bringing and faithfully executing the embassy of your fraternity, earnestly requested that we release your person from attendance at the councils held throughout the provinces. Therefore we desire, by God’s grace, to provide for your safety as for our own, and that your person may be rescued and kept away from every danger. Accordingly, with due kindness we assent to your petition; and, so long as war and disturbance in the kingdom continue, we grant that your person shall remain free from attendance at councils.

Moreover, for the honour of your fraternity, we grant that in your daily conduct you may go clothed in tunic and stole. This attire is indeed a mark of priestly dignity. For we desire that you may obtain temporal safety and strive in all things to please almighty God.

Given at Benevento, on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of September, eighth indiction.

### CDXXXVI. To Guido, legate of the Apostolic See—concerning a dispute between the canons of Bizantini and of St Stephen.  
*(A.D. 1115, 27 August.)*

[MANSI, *Concilia*, XX, 1047.]

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother GUIDO, archbishop of Vienne and legate of the Apostolic See, greeting and apostolic blessing.

We are greatly surprised at your prudence, because in the case of the Church of St Stephen you have not been willing to accept the testimony of the clerics themselves [variant: “their own clerics”]; whereas Blessed Gregory, in cases of this kind involving churches, places the burden of proof upon the claimants [variant: “the parties bringing the action”]. For there are different classes of claimants in legal causes, and criminal accusations are not pursued in every kind of case. In criminal cases, to be sure, the strict rule concerning witnesses for the accusers must be observed, as contained in the canons, so that members of one’s own household are not admitted as proof. But in disputes concerning possessions and other matters of this kind, those especially ought to be admitted who handled the transactions in question, concerning whose sight or hearing [variant: “or hearing”] there can be no hesitation.

If, therefore, those clerics are competent witnesses, they must not in any way be excluded from asserting that case. Rather, as has been determined in other letters, let that dispute between the canons of St John and of St Stephen be fully decided. Let the zeal of malice and the quibbling of deceit now cease, and let the case of the aforesaid churches be carried through in every respect according to the tenor of the letters. Otherwise, fully prepared and instructed, let them return to our presence at the time of the next Lenten council.

Given at Troia, on the sixth day before the Kalends of September, in the eighth indiction.

### CDXXXVII. To Alexius, emperor of Constantinople.  
*(A.D. 1115.)*

*Register of Pope Paschal*, book XIV (XVII?), chapter 6.—Extracted from Vatican Ottobonian codex no. 3057 by W. Giesebrecht; published by Philipp Jaffé, *Regesta Romanorum pontificum*, p. 510.

To ALEXIUS, emperor of Constantinople.

We give thanks to the condescension and mercy of almighty God, because He has deigned to encourage and strengthen your heart for the restoration of the unity of the Catholic Church. We pray for the power of the Holy Spirit, the Paraclete, that, as He deigned in His apostles to unite the diversities of all nations, so He may bring about in us the effect of this unity.

In this matter, indeed, there is great difficulty for us, because the diversity of our peoples cannot easily come together into a single agreement. But for you, by the grace of almighty God, the means are open, because the clergy and laity, superiors and subjects [lacuna], depend upon your decision, since benevolence of will is present in you. Both your letters have informed us of this devout and holy purpose, and the report of your most faithful and most prudent envoy, B. Mesimeri, has fully assured us. For he strives with all his desires to press forward your embassy, as one who burns wholly both with zeal for your loyalty and with longing for Catholic unity.

The experience of your wisdom knows how great, in former times, was the devotion and reverence of the patriarchs of Constantinople toward the Roman bishop. But for a long succession of years, the prelates of the imperial city, together with their clergy, have withdrawn themselves from the affection and obedience of the Roman Church, beyond all hearing, to such a degree that they have not deigned either to receive letters sent from the Apostolic See or to communicate with its representatives. Unless the wisdom of your empire showed sweetness of love toward us and our envoys, division between us would remain altogether, so that neither we would have knowledge of you nor you of us, and no remembrance of reconciliation between us would exist today.

The first path to this unity, therefore, appears to be that our brother, the patriarch of Constantinople, recognizing the primacy and reverence due to the Apostolic See—as established in the enactments of the devout Prince Constantine and confirmed by the agreement of holy councils—should correct his former obstinacy, as you will learn from the communication of our legates. Let those metropolitan sees and provinces which formerly were subject to the direction of the Apostolic See return to the obedience and direction of that See, so that the condition maintained between Old and New Rome in the times of our predecessors and yours may now, with God’s cooperation, be restored through the efforts of your highness.

For those matters which create [diversity] of faith or customs between Latins and Greeks do not seem capable of being settled otherwise than if the members first adhere to the head. How, indeed, amid the conflicts of those who disagree and oppose one another, can the diversity of disputed questions be examined, while neither side deigns either to obey or to agree with the other? Then, by God’s grace, the prelates of the apostolic sees, with both our effort and yours cooperating, must assemble at a place and time which we shall appoint, so that, after consultation, the scandals of the disputed questions may be cut away according to the right rule of the Holy Scriptures.

It falls to your prudence to determine what place for this meeting will be healthier and more convenient for our brethren travelling to you. By the Lord’s cooperation, we have foreseen the month of October in the following year as the suitable time. Therefore, to discuss all these things with the moderation of your wisdom, we send to your presence our venerable brother M[aurus], bishop of Amalfi; our dearest sons N., abbot, and Hugh, priests of our see; and our dearest B., subdeacon of our see. We ask that they be sent back to us more speedily, so that, having learned the certainty of your response, we may, with God as author, appropriately arrange what must thereafter be prepared for carrying this matter out.

At Troia.

### CDXXXVIII. To T[heoderic], cardinal-priest and legate of the Apostolic See.  
*(A.D. 1115.)*

[MANSI, *Concilia*, XX, 1096.]

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to T., cardinal-priest and legate of the Apostolic See, holy and apostolic blessing.

From ancient report we have learned that the Saxons, from the beginning of their conversion to God, have been faithful and obedient to the blessed pontiff and the Apostolic See. Since, therefore, you have gone into those regions, as we have heard, and disturbances have arisen concerning my churches and certain other affairs, whatever you may be able to do justly and canonically there or elsewhere, do it with the support of our authority and the Lord’s cooperation. If you are able to provide any aid or consolation to our bishop of Halberstadt, provide it, so that he may rejoice in the visitation of the Apostolic See.

Given at Ferentino, on the sixth day before the Ides of October.

### CDXXXIX. He takes under protection the oratory of St Mary near Nieuwburg by Oudenaarde, a dependency of the Church of Ename.  
*(A.D. 1115, 18 October.)*

[*Historia Mechliniensis*, II, 253, according to Brequigny, *Table chronologique*, II, 455.]

### CDXL. He confirms the possessions of the monastery of St Sixtus at Piacenza and grants the monks the right to elect an abbot.  
*(A.D. 1115, 30 October.)*

[MABILLON, *Annales Benedictini*, VI, 607.]

After peace had been restored in the City, Paschal returned to Rome in the autumn. There he resided on the third day before the Kalends of April in this year 1115, when he granted a pontifical charter to Abbot Odo of the monastery of St Sixtus, situated at Piacenza. Monks had recently been installed there in place of nuns of disreputable life, chiefly through the agency of Countess Matilda of illustrious memory, so that the religious observance of the monastic order might be maintained there and that the possessions of the monastery, long devastated, might be restored through their efforts. The pope also confirms all the estates and possessions which the Empress Angilberga, founder of that monastery, had bestowed there, and all other things granted or to be granted to the same place by the faithful. He grants the monks free power to elect an abbot according to the Rule of St Benedict.

Written through the hand of Gervasius, regional scriniary and notary of the sacred palace. Given at the Lateran through the hand of John, cardinal-deacon and librarian of the Holy Roman Church, on the third day before the Kalends of November, in the ninth indiction, in the year 1115 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the seventeenth year of the pontificate of Lord Paschal II, pope.

### CDXLI. He commands Bishop G[onsalvo] of Coimbra to return to obedience to Mauricius of Braga.  
*(A.D. 1115, 3 November.)*

[BALUZE, *Miscellanea*, Lucan edition, I, 139.]

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother GONSALVO, bishop of Coimbra, greeting and apostolic blessing.

How grave a crime contempt of ecclesiastical authority is held to be may be understood from the prophetic words where it is written: “To refuse obedience is like the sin of idolatry” (1 Kings 15). By letters sent and resent, we have warned your brotherhood to render reverence and obedience to our brother Mauricius, archbishop of Braga, as to your metropolitan. But you have both despised our letters and, in such contempt, trampled underfoot the privileges which we granted to the Church of Braga by authority of the Apostolic See.

Yet, still showing patience toward you, we command that henceforth you must obey that archbishop as your metropolitan. But unless within forty days after receiving this letter you render him the obedience due, from that time we suspend you from the episcopal office.

Given at Anagni, on the third day before the Nones of November.

### CDXLII. To Bernard, archbishop of Toledo and legate of the Apostolic See.  
*(A.D. 1115, 3 November.)*

[BALUZE, *ibid.*]

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother BERNARD, archbishop of Toledo and legate of the Apostolic See, greeting and apostolic blessing.

We have often warned your brotherhood concerning the injuries suffered by our brother Mauricius, archbishop of Braga; but he still complains that he is grievously burdened by you. You have withdrawn from him the obedience of the bishop of Coimbra, contrary to the privileges granted by Roman authority. Likewise, in the Church of Lugo, which belongs to his metropolitan jurisdiction, after its bishop had been expelled without judgment, you proposed to install another over it. He complains that the same has been done in the monastery of Blessed Peter of Monte. You consented to the dispersal of the goods of the Church of Braga by others, and you yourself have consumed a long stay there with your household. Throughout the whole province also, without his consent or knowledge, you exercise the power of your own will. To enlarge Salamanca, you diminished the diocese of the Church of Astorga without his consent.

But in these matters we take serious account of the disturbance of the kingdom, your age, and your infirmity. Therefore we release you from the charge of legation imposed upon you with respect to the archbishop and province of Braga, so that he himself may more freely exercise justice in his province.

Given at Anagni, on the third day before the Nones of November.

### CDXLIII. Between Anastasius, abbot of SS Andrew and Gregory on the Clivus Scauri at Rome, and the “Guild of the Fishers of the Pond,” he settles in favour of the abbot a dispute concerning part of that pond.  
*(A.D. 1115, 24 November—see the charter in MITTARELLI, *Annales Camaldulenses*, III, 166–167.)*

### CDXLIV. He confirms the privileges of the monastery of Sinsheim.  
*(A.D. 1115—see the *Chronicle of Sinsheim* in MONE, *Quellensammlung*, I, 206.)*

### CDXLV. To the canons and lay parishioners of the church of St Fridianus at Lucca.  
*(Between A.D. 1100 and 1116, 5 January.)*

[BALUZE, *Miscellanea*, Lucan edition, IV, 586.]

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons, the canons and lay parishioners of the church of St Fridianus, greeting and apostolic blessing.

The usefulness of charity is immeasurable and incomprehensible, because almighty God Himself is immeasurable and incomprehensible charity. From the root of charity proceeds the strength of all virtues, and the constancy of every good work is generated. Because of His boundless charity, the Lord of all descended from the heights to the depths, so that we might be able to ascend from the depths to the heights. And so that charity might remain in us, He gave this commandment: that we should love one another.

Therefore we have judged it fitting to visit your love by apostolic letters, giving thanks to God and to you because we enjoy, in the person from among you—namely, your prior—the good grace of God, useful also to us. We ask, then, that no indignation enter your hearts. For although, in the interest of maintaining canonical order, we retain him in our church, he is nevertheless with you in spirit and, by the Lord’s gift, will at some time not be absent from you in body. Do not therefore be at all indignant; but, as one body in the Lord, offer one another the support due to charity, so that almighty God, who is true charity and true glory, may take glory in the bond of your love. As you pray, may divine mercy preserve you.

Given at the Lateran, on the Ides of January.

### CDXLVI. To the canons of St Fridianus at Lucca.  
*(Between A.D. 1100 and 1116, 27 January.)*

[BALUZE, *ibid.*]

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons, the canons of St Fridianus, greeting and apostolic blessing.

We rejoice in your religious observance, and we desire that, by God’s grace, you may always remain in the things belonging to religion. In the matter in which you sent two canon-brothers from among yourselves to your prior, we understand your charity, since charity does not exist between fewer than two persons. Yet we learn that those brethren did not undertake an embassy of charity, but went either to bring back the prior or to obtain permission to elect another. We therefore admonish your love to desist altogether from these things, imitating Him who, leaving all things, followed the Lord.

For it is quite unworthy of your religious profession that you cannot endure even a small hardship. If, therefore—God forbid—any tares spring up, strive to uproot them completely, so that the Lord’s crop may rise more freely to its height and, by the Lord’s bounty, bear abundant fruit. For although your prior is with us, he has not departed from you.

Given at the Lateran, on the sixth day before the Kalends of February.

### CDXLVII. He exhorts the parishioners of the church of St Fridianus at Lucca to restore to the church tithes and offerings that have been withheld.  
*(Between A.D. 1100 and 1116, 29 January.)*

[BALUZE, *ibid.*, p. 587.]

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons, the parishioners of the church of St Fridianus, greeting and apostolic blessing.

Both we and you ought to give thanks to almighty God, because through your church that divine light of the common and apostolic life has been diffused even to the summit of the First See. For although the Roman Church is mother and teacher of all churches, it has pleased her to adopt for herself the order of regular life from the church of Blessed Fridianus and to establish it through Lord R., the prior, and your other brethren.

We have heard that some of you have been so scandalized by this that they have withheld their tithes and offerings from the church of Blessed Fridianus. Yet it would have been fitting for them to remember the benefits which almighty God has bestowed upon that place, not to withhold its due or resent the grace of divine generosity. The illumination of the divine light is sufficient both for us and for you. Nothing is taken away from you through our sharing, nor from us through yours.

Therefore, greeting your love by this address of apostolic visitation, we admonish you to recall God’s kindness and to remain effectively and unanimously in those things that please Him. But to those who are said to have withheld tithes and offerings from the church, we command that they restore what has been taken away and make satisfaction with due humility. Otherwise, whatever sentence the lord prior himself or his brethren may pronounce against them, we shall, with God’s help, hold valid.

Given at the Lateran, on the fourth day before the Kalends of February.

### CDXLVIII. Privilege for the canons of St Fidelis.  
*(Between A.D. 1100 and 1116, 30 January.)*

[TATTI, *Annali della città di Como*, II, 866.]

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother, the bishop of Como, greeting and apostolic blessing.

It is the duty of the episcopal office to watch carefully over the flock entrusted to it and, by God’s grace, to provide what concerns its salvation. Even though an evil shepherd may appear diligent, if he neglects concern for his flock he does not escape the punishment of a graver guilt. Hence the Apostle writes: “If anyone does not provide for his own, and especially for those of his household, he has denied the faith and is worse than an unbeliever.”

The brethren of St Fidelis complain that, against their wishes and contrary to the resources of their church, certain clerics are forced into their church. We entrust to your care that you render due justice to these brethren. Do not allow them to suffer so great an injury, nor their church to be so heavily burdened; nor, on that account, exclude them from your communion. For it is yours, by the Lord’s aid, so to provide for persons and churches that you may deserve, at the judgment of God our rewarder of all good things, the reward of a good shepherd.

Given at the Lateran, on the third day before the Kalends of February.

### CDXLIX. To Bernard, primate of Toledo and vicar of the Apostolic See—he assigns to his person the city of Segovia and grants the monastery of St Servandus.  
*(Between A.D. 1100 and 1116.)*

[MANSI, *Concilia*, XX, 1037.]

We have graciously accepted your fraternity’s petition. For we desire that you may honourably enjoy the legation of the Apostolic See entrusted to you. We assign the city of Segovia to your person because of the necessity caused by your greater poverty, unless that city itself should desire its own bishop. We know that the monastery of St Servandus, which belongs to our jurisdiction, was entrusted by our predecessors to the monastery of Marseille long ago. But because we have learned that, owing to Saracen violence, the monks withdrew from that place, we entrust the monastery itself to your care for restoration and administration. If, by the mercy of almighty God, it should be restored, you shall pay each year the due rent to the Lateran palace.

Given at the Lateran, on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of April.

### CDL. He confirms the excommunication pronounced against the priest Ubertus by R[otho], provost, and the brethren of St Fridianus.  
*(Between A.D. 1101 and 1116, 6 March.)*

[BALUZE, *Miscellanea*, Lucan edition, IV, 585.]

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons R., provost, and the other brethren of St Fridianus, greeting and apostolic blessing.

The form of regular life is known to have been instituted by the apostles in the primitive Church. For none of them possessed anything as his own, but all things were common among them. Their soul was one and their heart one. Blessed Augustine embraced this form so gladly that he shaped it in his rules; and you too, by the Lord’s gift, have received it. Whoever has once received it together with the profession of a vow can in no way abandon it without the guilt of transgression and after the example of Lot’s wife.

We have heard, however, that a certain priest among you, named Ubertus, after making his profession, broke out into such madness that, setting aside the life he had undertaken and the observance of your cloister, he looked back toward Sodom and Gomorrah and turned himself again to the mire of the broader way. Since, after admonition, he scorned to return, we have heard that you pronounced a sentence of excommunication against him. We wish it to be known among you and those in your regions that we confirm that same sentence by the judgment of the Holy Spirit. For no one who puts his hand to the plough and looks back is fit for the kingdom of God.

Given at the Lateran, on the second day before the Nones of March.

### CDLI. To the Florentine clerics—that on Sundays and principal feasts they should attend the office of the principal Mass, as they had formerly been accustomed.  
*(Between A.D. 1101 and 1116, 13 March.)*

[MANSI, *Concilia*, XX, 1052.]

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons, the Florentine clerics, greeting and apostolic blessing.

We have heard that it was an ancient custom of your mother church that the clerics of the canonries and chapels were accustomed to assemble, both on Sundays and on the principal feasts, for processions and for the office of the principal Mass until the Gospel had been read. But now, for what reason we do not know, you have withdrawn yourselves from this due obedience and honorable custom of that church; and this seems to us to be schism and division of the Church. We therefore command and enjoin you [Col. 0395A] to return to the Church’s former custom, lest you incur the canonical sentence of the Church.

Given at the Lateran, on the third day before the Ides of March.

CDLII. To Lanuin, prior of Torre. (Between 1102 and 1116, January 27.)

[MABILLON, *Annals of the Benedictines*, V, 456.]

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son LANUIN, greetings and apostolic blessing.

Whenever our brethren request something consonant with the rules of the holy Fathers, it is fitting that their petitions be heard the more willingly. Therefore, by the present authority, establish a monastery in that church having the right of a hermitage, which is situated near Squillace, [Col. 0395B] so that brothers unable to endure the austerity of the hermitage may there serve almighty God according to the Rule of blessed Benedict. We further command that this dwelling be governed and administered by a provost and a dean, provided nevertheless that the provost of the hermitage shall always take precedence and be accounted the superior; and, just as the monastery itself is subject to the direction of the hermitage, so the provost and dean of that place shall be subject to the master of the hermitage.

Given at the Lateran, 27 January.

CDLIII. To O[tbert], bishop of Liège.—Concerning the complaint of Ralph, archbishop of Reims. (Between 1107 and 1116, December 27.)

[MARTÈNE, *Amplissima Collectio*, II, 624.]

[Col. 0395C] PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother O., [Note: [Col. 0395D] Otbert, formerly provost of Holy Cross at Liège; for more concerning him, see the *Cantatorium*, or history, of the monastery of Andage.] bishop of Liège, greetings and apostolic blessing.

We have received the complaint of our fellow-brother Ralph, [Note: [Col. 0395D] Ralph, called the Green, friend of Saint Bruno, founder of the Carthusians, made archbishop in 1108.] archbishop of Reims, that in the castle of [Note: [Col. 0396D] Otbert had, indeed, purchased the castle of Bouillon from Duke Godfrey, as Alberic attests in his chronicle.] Bouillon you have usurped a part of the parish of Reims and, against his will, have ordained a priest in the church of Saint John. We therefore command your brotherhood either wholly to relinquish that part of the parish, or to render justice concerning it to the Church of Reims by the judgment of our fellow-brethren, the bishops of Châlons and Toul, at such place and time as they shall determine. Otherwise, concerning that priest who is said already to have been intruded into the church of Saint John, we confirm the judgment of our fellow-brother, the archbishop of Reims.

[Col. 0395D] Given at Rome, 27 December.

CDLIV. To Reinhard, bishop of Halberstadt.—He commends him for reforming certain nunneries. (Between 1108 and 1116, March 20.)

[MARTÈNE, *Collection*, I, 637.]

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother REINHARD, bishop of Halberstadt, greetings and apostolic blessing.

[Col. 0396A] We have heard that certain monasteries of nuns have been corrected through your diligence, so that, once the vain displays of the secular world have been removed, they may devote themselves to regular discipline. We consider this concern of yours worthy of praise and confirm it by the strength of our approval. We therefore decree that monastic religious life shall always be maintained in those places, and that no one may remove regular discipline from those monasteries, so that the grace of your reform may be preserved there for all time.

Given at the Lateran, 20 March.

CDLV. To A[delgot], archbishop of Magdeburg, etc. (Between 1109 and 1116, October 27.)

[ECCARD, *Corpus historicum*, vol. II, p. 278.]

[Col. 0396B] PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brethren A[DELGOT], metropolitan of Magdeburg, and his suffragans, greetings and apostolic blessing.

Our fellow-brother, the elect of Magdeburg, coming to the thresholds of the apostles, set forth before us his complaint: namely, that he was elected by the clergy and people of the Church of Merseburg, with you present and approving, and received in that church the office of priest by your ordination. Thereafter, without any preceding judicial proceeding, not only was the grace of episcopal consecration denied him, but he was violently expelled from that Church as though by our command. Therefore, as we send him before us to the presence of your brotherhood with this letter, we command that the same brother be [Col. 0396C] fully restored to this election and Church, and that his cause be decided by the judgment of your assembly according to the canonical sanctions. But if a difficulty in judgment should arise among you, let the same cause be referred for examination to the Apostolic See with a joint letter and envoys from your brotherhood.

Given at Rome, 27 January.

CDLVI. He informs the clergy and people of Merseburg concerning the preceding letter to Adelgot. (Between 1109 and 1116, October 27.)

[ECCARD, *Corpus historicum*, vol. II, p. 277.]

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the clergy and people of Merseburg, greetings and apostolic blessing.

[Col. 0396D] Gregory, our fellow-brother and bearer of the present letter, came into our presence with two clerics and an equal number of laymen from your Church. He maintained that he had been elected by you with common consent, while the metropolitan of Magdeburg and his suffragans were present and approving. Yet he complained that, before this, without any judicial proceeding and as though by our command, he had been violently expelled from his election and his Church by that same archbishop. We have therefore sent letters to that archbishop and to the bishops of his province, so that [Col. 0397A] whatever has been done unjustly in this matter may be corrected. It is not, moreover, our will that the cause of this brother should suffer any prejudice.

Given at Rome, 27 October.

CDLVII. To Vitalis, abbot of Savigny.—He permits the brethren of Savigny to celebrate the divine offices during an interdict. (Between 1112 and 1116.)

[MARTÈNE, *Thesaurus anecdotorum*, I, 336.]

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son VITALIS, abbot of Holy Trinity of Savigny, greetings and apostolic blessing.

We have heard that, by your diligence, a church has been built in a certain deserted and inaccessible wood, and that brothers have been gathered there in religious service to God. [Col. 0397B] We therefore give thanks to almighty God, from whose grace proceeds every good thing that we do; and we have taken care, as our office requires, to provide for your peace. By the authority of the present letter we grant this concession to your religious community: that, on account of a general interdict of the parish in which you reside, your church shall in no way be deprived of the divine offices. Therefore, venerable one in Christ, remember to pray more earnestly for the mercy of almighty God, both for us and for the universal Church, that through his grace he may always preserve us in his love.

Given at the Lateran, 23 March.

CDLVIII. He frees the monastery of Faverney from the authority of the bishop of Basel and confirms its possessions.

[Col. 0397C]

(1116, January 29.—See EICHHORN, *The Bishopric of Chur in Raetia*, 1797, quarto, preface, p. 46.)

CDLIX. To the clergy and people of Florence.—He declares their bishop innocent; he deprives his slanderers of offices and benefices. (1116.)

[MANSI, *Councils*, XX, 1053.]

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons, the clergy and people of Florence, greetings and apostolic blessing.

Some time ago our fellow-brother G. [Godfrey], your bishop, laid before us his complaint against the archdeacon of your Church and his [Col. 0397D] associates—namely, John, prior of the church of Saint Lawrence; Peter of Saint Peter of Scaradio; and Rambald, prior of Saint Stephen—that they accused him among the people of the depravity of simony. We therefore sent letters and fixed a date for each party to conduct the case. When the bishop came on the appointed date, they did not come at all into our presence, alleging fear of capture on the journey. But, so that we might accommodate them in this pretext, we took care to provide them, through the same bishop and the bishop of Volterra, with a journey entirely safe. The archdeacon indeed, and the prior of Blessed Lawrence, appeared before us; the other men neither came nor sent representatives for themselves. Then, in their presence, the bishop complained against them [Col. 0398A] that they had withdrawn themselves from obedience and communion with him; that they had accused him among the people of the crime of simony; that they had cursed his consecrations; and that they had formed a conspiracy against him in secret assemblies. They, however, after an interval allowed for deliberation, wholly denied that they were the bishop’s accusers or the provers of that charge. They asserted that they had held gatherings of clergy or laity in churches, but for the purpose of investigating the truth of the report that had spread against the bishop; and in these gatherings we understood there to have been conspiratorial assemblies. They also confessed that they had offended in the other matters.

Accordingly, various chapters of the holy Fathers appropriate to these cases were produced: namely, the fifth of the Synod of Antioch, “Concerning those who withdraw from [Col. 0398B] ecclesiastical ministry and gather separately”; likewise the eighteenth of the Synod of Chalcedon, “Concerning conspiracy or confederacy”; and that of Pope Calixtus to the bishops established throughout Gaul, beginning: “We have heard that the crimes of conspiracies flourish in your regions.” Likewise that of Pope Alexander: “Concerning those who persecute the saints, or strive to remove or rend them.” Likewise that of Pope Stephen: “Concerning those who take arms against the Fathers and slander the brethren.”

Therefore, instructed by the authorities of so many Fathers, we remove the aforesaid men, convicted by their own confession, from their offices and dignities by judicial sentence, unless the Church shall hereafter extend mercy to them. We impose the same judgment also upon the others [Col. 0398C] who, having been summoned, neglected to come into our presence, because they seem to be implicated in the same chapters. For it is equitable that they should not gain a postponement of sentence by their absence, since each person confesses all things if he thinks he can evade [perhaps, “if anyone thinks he can evade.” HARD.] judgment through delays.

Therefore, by the authority of the present letter, we command all of you to love and respect your bishop in unanimous concord as catholic through God’s grace. But if any clerics or laymen shall henceforth, with rash presumption, attack such a bishop, let them know that by their obstinacy the clerics shall be punished by deposition, and the laymen subjected to excommunication.

[Col. 0398D] Given at the Lateran, 3 March, indiction 9.

CDLX. Brief to Stephen of Autun. (1116, March 14.)

[*Gallia Christiana*, IV, 88.]

PASCHAL, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother STEPHEN, bishop of Autun, etc.

It is fitting for us to grant assent to just wishes and lend ear to just petitions, since, although unworthy, we are seen, by the Lord’s ordering, to have been placed as guardians and proclaimers of justice upon the lofty watchtower of the princes of the apostles, Peter and Paul. Therefore, dearest brother Stephen in Christ, assenting to your just petitions, we fortify the holy Church of Autun, over which you preside by God’s authority, by the authority of the Apostolic [Col. 0399A] See. We decree that the towns, villages, churches, and possessions which the Church of Autun possessed in the time of your predecessor Agano shall be preserved to you and to your successors secure, firm, and whole.
