Moreover, all else that has been recovered or acquired for the same Church of Autun through your diligence—namely, the churches of Saint Mary and Saint Lazarus of Avalon, and the castle of Toilon with their appurtenances—or that may in future by God’s grace be justly and lawfully recovered or acquired, shall always remain peaceful and intact in the right and possession of that Church. We therefore decree that no one may rashly disturb that Church, take away its possessions, retain what has been taken away, diminish them, or harass it with reckless vexations; rather, let all be preserved intact for your use and that of the clerics and poor.

[Col. 0399B] If, therefore, any ecclesiastical or secular person in future, knowing this text of our constitution, should rashly attempt to act against it, then, after a second or third admonition, unless he makes amendment by fitting satisfaction, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and honor; let him know himself guilty before divine judgment for the iniquity perpetrated; let him be separated from the most sacred body and blood of God and of Christ Jesus, our Lord and Redeemer; and let him be subject to strict punishment at the final judgment. But upon all who preserve what is just for that Church, let there be peace, etc.

I, Paschal, bishop of the catholic Church, have subscribed.

[Col. 0399C] Given at the Lateran, through the hand of John, cardinal-deacon and librarian of the Holy Roman Church, 14 March, indiction 9, in the year 1116 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the seventeenth year of the pontificate of lord Paschal II.

CDLXI. To Gozeran, archbishop of Lyons.—He confirms his primacy over the provinces of Lyons. (1116, March 14.)

[MANSI, *Councils*, XX, 1079.]

Therefore, venerable brother Gozeran, archbishop of Lyons, by this text of the present decree we confirm to your brotherhood and your successors, and through you to the Church of Lyons itself, the primacy over the four primatial sees of Gaul: Lyons, [Col. 0399D] Rouen, Tours, and Sens, as is known to have been established by our predecessors.

CDLXII. Privilege for the church of Saint Pancras at Hamersleben. (1116, March 20.)

[LEUCKFELD, *Antiquities of Halberstadt*, Wolfenbüttel, 1714, quarto, p. 704.]

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons THIETMAR, provost, and his brethren in the church of Blessed Pancras near the village of Hamersleben, who profess the regular life, both present and future, for ever: greeting.

Whatever is shown to pertain to a religious purpose and to the salvation of souls ought, with God as author, to be carried out without any [Col. 0400A] delay. Thus our venerable brother Reinhard, bishop of Halberstadt, diligently devoting himself, as his office requires, to religious life, established in his aforesaid village a community of clerics living according to the Rule of blessed Augustine; and he desires that both their order and their peace be fortified by our authority. Therefore, assenting to his wishes, we receive you, dearest sons dwelling together in the aforesaid church of Blessed Pancras, under the protection of the Apostolic See and fortify you by the authority of the present decree. We confirm by this charter of privilege the order of canonical life which you have professed. And we forbid anyone, after making his profession, to possess anything as his own or to leave the cloister without permission of the provost or the community.

[Col. 0400B] Further, providing more carefully for your peace, we decree that everything granted by the aforesaid bishop for the support of your brotherhood, and whatever has been given already by other faithful persons from their own right, or may in future be given, offered, or acquired by other just means, shall remain firm and inviolate for you and your successors. We decree, therefore, that absolutely no person may rashly disturb the same church, take away its possessions, retain what has been taken away, diminish them, or harass it with reckless vexations; rather, let all be preserved intact and serve in every way the use of those for whose support and governance they were granted, saving, however, the canonical reverence due to the bishop of Halberstadt.

[Col. 0400C] If any ecclesiastical or secular person in future, knowing this text of our constitution, should rashly attempt to act against it, then, after a second or third admonition, unless he makes amendment by fitting satisfaction, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and honor; let him know himself guilty before divine judgment for the iniquity perpetrated; let him be separated from the most sacred body and blood of God and of Christ Jesus, our Lord and Redeemer; and let him be subject to strict punishment at the final judgment. But upon all who preserve what is just for that place, let there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that here they may receive the fruit of good action and find, before the strict Judge, the rewards of eternal peace. Amen.

I, Paschal, bishop of the catholic Church.

Given at the Lateran, through the hand of John, cardinal-deacon and librarian of the Holy Roman Church, [Col. 0400D] 20 March, indiction 9, in the year 1116 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the seventeenth year of the pontificate of lord Pope Paschal II.

CDLXIII. He grants Dominic, abbot of the monastery of Saint Facundus at Sahagún, “the power of binding and loosing over the burgesses of Saint Facundus,” who, “when a violent and prolonged war had arisen between King Alfonso, son of King Sancho, and Queen Urraca, daughter of King Alfonso,” had inflicted various injuries upon the abbot and monastery.

(1116, March 21.—See ESCALONA, *History of the Royal Monastery of Sahagún*, Madrid, 1782, folio, p. 514.)

CDLXIV. Bull for the monastery of Saint Thibéry. (1116, March 22.)

[*Gallia Christiana*, VI, 316.]

[Col. 0401A]

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son ARNALD, abbot of the monastery of Saint Thibéry, situated at Cessero in the territory of Agde, and to his successors canonically appointed for ever.

It is fitting for us to grant assent to just wishes and direct our attention to just petitions, since, although unworthy, we are seen, by the Lord’s ordering, to have been placed as guardians and proclaimers of justice upon the lofty watchtower of the princes of the apostles, Peter and Paul. Therefore, dearest brother in Christ, assenting to your just petitions, [Col. 0401B] we fortify the monastery of Blessed Thibéry, over which you preside by God’s authority, by the authority of the Apostolic See.

We decree that no ecclesiastical or secular person shall ever dare, in the adjacent village or its boundaries, to build any castle or fortification; extort any exactions from the people of that village apart from the abbot and his officials; exercise the office of vicary; or claim the field pertaining to that vicary, which lies beyond the River Thongue beneath Ceyrac, whether by permission of the abbot or of any other person.

We confirm to you and your successors, in the territory of Agde, the church of Saint Mary of Grau, the church of Saint Martin of Vallevrages, the church of Saint Sulpicius of [Col. 0401C] Castelnau, the church of Saint John of Florensac, the church of Saint Martin of Grenolheriis, and the church of Saint Andrew of Romignac, with their appurtenances. Likewise, in the bishopric of Béziers, the church of Saint Mary of Sérignan with its appurtenances. Likewise, in the territory of Toulouse, the church of Saint Peter and of the Holy Virgins with its appurtenances. Likewise, in Gascony, in the county of Armagnac, the church of Saint Julian of Galian, with its churches, villages, and all else belonging to it. Likewise, in the parish of Comminges, the church of Saint Mary of Aurignac; and all other things which your monastery lawfully possesses in the present ninth indiction, or may hereafter, through God’s bounty, reasonably and lawfully acquire.

We decree, therefore, that absolutely no person [Col. 0401D] may rashly disturb that monastery, take away its possessions, retain what has been taken away, diminish them, or harass it with reckless vexations; rather, let all be preserved intact and serve in every way the use of those for whose support and governance they were granted. Upon the death of you, the present abbot of that place, or of any of your successors, no one shall be set over it by any craft of deception or force, except one whom the brothers, by common consent or by the judgment of the sounder part of the brothers, shall provide to be elected from their own community—or, if necessary, from another community—in accordance with the fear of God and the Rule of blessed Benedict.

Moreover, as was established by our predecessor of happy memory, Pope Sergius, that place shall always remain under the right and protection of the Apostolic See, subject to an annual payment of one gold piece to the Lateran palace.

[Col. 0402A] If any ecclesiastical or secular person in future, knowing this text of our constitution, should attempt to act against it, then, after a second or third admonition, unless he makes amendment by fitting satisfaction, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and honor; let him know himself guilty before divine judgment for the iniquity perpetrated; let him be separated from the most sacred body and blood of God and of Christ Jesus, our Lord and Redeemer; and let him be subject to strict punishment at the final judgment. But upon all who preserve what is just for that monastery, let there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that here they may receive the fruit of good action and find, before the strict Judge, the rewards of eternal peace. Amen, amen, amen.

[Col. 0402B] I, Paschal II, pope of the catholic Church.

Given at the Lateran, through the hand of John, cardinal-deacon and librarian of the Holy Roman Church, 22 March, indiction 9, in the year 1116 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the sixteenth year of the pontificate of lord Pope Paschal II.

CDLXV. He confirms certain possessions and privileges of the monastery of Saint Facundus at Sahagún, imposing upon the monks an annual payment of two solidi.

(1116, March 22.—See ESCALONA, *History of Sahagún*, p. 513.)

CDLXVI. By judgment of a synod, he commands that the episcopal see of Besançon remain in the church of Blessed Stephen. (1116, March 24.)

[MANSI, *Councils*, XXI, 149.]

[Col. 0402C]

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved brethren and sons, the suffragans, clergy, and people of the Church of Besançon, greetings and apostolic blessing.

We believe that you have heard more fully and know more certainly how great and prolonged was the dispute between the canons of Saint Stephen and Saint John concerning the episcopal cathedra. The canons of Blessed Stephen defended themselves by privileges of the Roman pontiffs and by royal documents, maintaining that the bishops had departed from there because their church had been destroyed, with the result that the sacraments of episcopal ministry were celebrated in the church of Saint John. In response, the canons of Blessed John cried out that for many years, without any dispute, the episcopal cathedra had remained with them and that their church was the mother church. To this the brethren of Blessed Stephen alleged that their predecessors had often made complaint concerning the matter either before the vicar of the Apostolic See or before the bishops of Besançon.

Therefore, after long conflicts of argument, it was determined by the common judgment of our brother bishops, who had then assembled at a synodal summons, and of the cardinals, that if the canons of Blessed Stephen could prove through suitable witnesses that, within thirty years after the restoration of their church, they had litigated this complaint, so that the prescription asserted by the others might appear interrupted—namely, either [Col. 0403A] before their bishop or before our legate in a public hearing—then, once this proof had been made, their privileges should obtain perpetual force and the episcopal see should thereafter be held at the church of Blessed Stephen. Otherwise, the canons of Blessed John should remain free from this complaint and should hold the episcopal see as they had held it.

Accordingly, four clerics of the same church—Peter and Hugh, cardinal-priests; Bonifilius, sub-chanter; Guarinus, priest; and Alofricus, archpriest of Saint Gorgonius—were produced before the clerics of Saint John to give testimony. After they had immediately been examined by episcopal judgment and found suitable, they gave the following testimony in our presence, having touched the most sacred Gospels:

[Col. 0403B] “I saw and heard that Hugh, dean of Saint Stephen; Hugh of Palma; and Ebrard, canons of Saint Stephen, brought a case against the canons of Saint John—Mainerius, dean; Bernard, master; and Stephen, cantor—concerning the episcopal see, before Hugh III, archbishop of Besançon and brother of Guy, archbishop of Vienne, in the cloister of Saint John, within thirty years after the restoration of the church of Saint Stephen.”

Once this restoration had thus been established, we have decreed, by the common judgment of our brother bishops, many of whom had then gathered at a synodal summons, and of the cardinals, that the privilege of Blessed Stephen should have perpetual force; that the primary episcopal see shall henceforth remain in that same church of Blessed Stephen; and that all offices of episcopal ministry customarily performed at mother churches shall be celebrated there. We decree that documents which, before certainty had been obtained in this inquiry, were either procured from us or less prudently extracted from our vicars, shall henceforth have no effect or force whatever.

[Col. 0403C] As these things have been determined in our presence by the present judgment and confirmed by the letters of this decree, so by apostolic authority we command that they be preserved for ever whole and inviolate. If anyone, having learned the tenor of this decree, should rashly attempt—God forbid!—to oppose it, let him suffer loss of his honor and office or be punished by the penalty of excommunication, unless he correct his presumption by fitting satisfaction.

I, Paschal, bishop of the catholic Church, holding this judgment valid, have subscribed. I, Crescentius, bishop of Sabina, have subscribed. I, Peter, bishop of Porto, have subscribed. I, Cono, bishop of Palestrina, have subscribed. I, Anastasius, cardinal-priest of the title of Blessed Clement, was present and have subscribed. I, Dinizo, cardinal of the title of Equitius, have subscribed. I, Boso, priest of the title of Saint Anastasia, have subscribed. I, Beltrannus, bishop of Bazas, have subscribed. [Col. 0404A] I, Arnald, archbishop of Bordeaux, have subscribed. I, Hugh, bishop of Portugal, have subscribed. I, John, bishop of Saint-Brieuc, have subscribed. I, Baldric, archbishop of Dol, have subscribed. I, Leo, cardinal-deacon of the church of Saint Vitus, have subscribed. I, Romuald, cardinal-deacon of Saint Mary, have subscribed. I, Aldo, cardinal-deacon of the venerable diaconia of Saints Sergius and Bacchus, have subscribed. I, Peter, cardinal-deacon of the church of Saints Cosmas and Damian, have subscribed. I, John, cardinal-deacon of Saint Lucy, [Col. 0404B] have subscribed.

Given at the Lateran, through the hand of John, cardinal-deacon and librarian of the Holy Roman Church, 24 March, indiction 9, in the year 1116 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the seventeenth year of the pontificate of lord Pope Paschal II.

CDLXVII. At the request of Archbishop Gregory, he receives the Neapolitan monastery of the Holy Archangel of Morfisa into protection and confirms its possessions and privileges. (1116, April 11.)

[UGHELLI, *Italia sacra*, VI, 94.]

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son GREGORY, abbot of the monastery of the Holy Archangel, called “of Morfisa,” within the city of Naples, [Col. 0404C] and to his successors canonically appointed for ever.

A devout request ought to be followed through to its desired effect, so that both the sincerity of devotion may shine forth notably and the requested benefit may assuredly acquire force. Therefore, since your belovedness, fleeing to the haven of the Apostolic See, has duly sought its protection with devotion, we, through the intervention of our venerable brother Gregory, bishop of Naples, mercifully assent to your petition and receive under the protection of the Apostolic See the monastery of the Blessed Archangel, over which you preside by God’s authority.

Therefore, by the text of the present privilege, we decree by apostolic authority that whatever estates and possessions the same monastery lawfully possesses in the present ninth indiction, [Col. 0404D] and whatever it may in future acquire by concession of pontiffs, liberality of princes, offerings of the faithful, or other just means, shall remain firm and inviolate for you and your successors. We decree, therefore, that absolutely no person may rashly disturb that monastery, take away its possessions, retain offerings made to it, claim for his own use gifts justly made, diminish its goods, or harass it with reckless vexations; rather, let all be preserved intact and serve in every way the use of those for whose support and governance they were granted, saving the canonical reverence due to the bishop of Naples. Yet he may in no way burden the monastery itself, impose exactions upon it, or enforce customs [Col. 0405A] injurious to the brothers’ peace.

If any archbishop or bishop, emperor or king, duke or prince, commander of soldiers, count, viscount, judge, *castaldus*, or any ecclesiastical or secular person in future, knowing this text of our constitution, should rashly attempt to act against it, then, after a second or third admonition, unless he makes amendment by fitting satisfaction, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and honor; let him know himself guilty before divine judgment for the iniquity perpetrated; let him be separated from the most sacred body and blood of God, our Lord and Redeemer Jesus Christ; and let him be subject to strict punishment at the final judgment. But upon all who preserve what is just for that monastery, let there be the peace of our Lord [Col. 0405B] Jesus Christ, so that here they may receive the fruit of good action and find, before the strict Judge, the rewards of eternal peace. Amen, amen, amen.

+ I, Paschal, bishop of the catholic Church.

Given at Albano, through the hand of John, cardinal-deacon and librarian of the Holy Roman Church, 11 April, indiction 9, in the year 1118 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the seventeenth year of the pontificate of lord Pope Paschal II.

CDLXVIII. To R. William, provost of Nantes, concerning the subjection of the monastery of Nantes to that of Vabres. (1116, April 13.)

[*Gallia Christiana*, I, 61.]

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved [Col. 0405C] son R. WILLIAM, provost of Nantes, greetings and apostolic blessing.

From the records of that good man Bernard we have learned that the church of Nantes was established as a monastery in fulfillment of the vow and offering of the same Bernard, and was committed to the administration and direction of the monastery of Vabres. Therefore, by the common counsel of our brethren, it has been adjudged that the church of Nantes ought to be subject to the direction of the abbot of Vabres, so that the vow and offering of the aforesaid good man Bernard may remain intact, and that the monastic order may, through God’s grace, endure there through his care. The monks of that monastery must likewise obey their own abbot. Therefore, by repeated letters, we have commanded you to obey [Col. 0405D] and be subject to the abbot of Vabres; otherwise, as has been established in other letters, we command that you remain forbidden the divine offices until satisfaction is made.

Given at Albano, on the Ides of April.

CDLXIX. He releases Oldegarius, abbot of Saint Rufus and bishop-elect of Barcelona, from the governance of the monastery and commands him to accept the episcopate. He sends Boso, cardinal-priest, as legate into Spain. (1116, May 23.)

[FLÓREZ (Risco), *España sagrada*, XXIX, 468.]

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved brother OLDEGARIUS, abbot of Saint Rufus and bishop-elect of Barcelona, greetings and apostolic blessing.

Since the care of pastoral office demands it, and the vigor [Col. 0406A] of equity and order of reason require that matters requested of us, if they are just and honorable, be brought to their due effect, you should therefore know that from the letter of our dearest son Raymond, count of the Barcelonans, and from the representations of their Church and people, we have learned this concerning you. You did not, like the useless servant, bury in the earth the gift of knowledge entrusted to you by the householder like a talent to be traded with; rather, when assumed to pastoral care, you so strove, in accordance with the Apostle, to fulfill the work of a ruler, to honor your ministry, and to preside in abbatial care, that, as we believe, you may truly say with the prophet: “I stand continually by day upon the Lord’s watchtower, and I stand throughout the nights at my post of watch” (Isaiah 21:8). Thus you showed yourself faithful in small things so as to deserve to be set over greater things.

[Col. 0406B] The beloved sons, the canons of the Church of Barcelona, wisely observing this, after their bishop of good memory had been removed from this light and they had long deliberated concerning the appointment of a bishop, at last—through the working of him who makes both one, as the wishes of clergy and people coincided—elected you, with unanimous consent, as their bishop and pastor. When this became known to you, you fled back to your abbey and disappointed everyone’s expectations, so that you seem to resist the Holy Spirit and refuse to put your hand to the plough. Therefore they caused humble and urgent supplication to be made to us that we might deem it fitting, by apostolic exhortation, to compel you to undertake the burden of such an office, since they believe that many benefits will accrue to their Church through your prudent care and carefully exercised solicitude.

We therefore, having learned that they are now united and agreed in the aforesaid election and petition, have, yielding to their prayers, judged their election to be accepted and approved; and, releasing you from the governance of the monastery of Saint-Ruf, we approve their election. Therefore, by these apostolic letters we command and enjoin your brotherhood that, accepting the summons made concerning you, and lest you appear to resist the divine ordering, you proceed to the aforesaid Church of Barcelona and devote yourself so diligently to its pastoral care that, through the foresight of your solicitude [Col. 0406D], its condition may be increased both temporally and spiritually, according to its own expectation and ours; so that, as you appear to advance from rank to rank, you may likewise appear to advance from virtue to virtue. But if—God forbid!—you refuse to render obedience to this page of our command, we command and enjoin by apostolic letters our venerable brother Boso, cardinal-priest of the Holy Roman Church, whom we are sending as apostolic legate into the regions of Spain, that he shall not cease to compel you by ecclesiastical censure, until you obey, to assume the helm of the aforesaid Church of Barcelona, to which we know you have been elected, after prior admonition, without appeal, and notwithstanding any letters obtained from the Apostolic See prejudicial to truth and right; according to the form enclosed under our mandate and given to him, commanding the chapter, clergy, and people of Barcelona [Col. 0407A] that they humbly attend upon you as their bishop and show you obedience and reverence, both due and devoted.

Given at Trastevere, through the hand of John, cardinal-deacon and librarian of the Holy Roman Church, on the tenth day before the Kalends of June, in the ninth indiction, in the year 1117 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the seventeenth year of the pontificate of Lord Paschal II.

I, Paschal, bishop of the Catholic Church.

### CDLXX. To Raymond, Marquis of Barcelona

—He congratulates him on the victory won over his enemies and receives him and his family under his protection. (A.D. 1116, May 23.)

[MARTÈNE, *Amplissima Collectio*, I, 636.]

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son RAYMOND, marquis of the Barcelonans, of Besalú, and count of Provence, greeting and apostolic blessing.

We congratulate your devotion, dearest son, because amid the concerns of war you desire above all to be strengthened by the protection of blessed Peter. We willingly grant this petition of your devotion, because we know that you labour effectively in God’s service. For that labour which you sustained throughout the year in the Balearic Islands has won no little merit for your nobility; and to your glorious campaign, in which you and your followers took part, almighty God has deigned to grant a glorious victory over the enemy. Moreover, you are preparing the noble industry of your spirit to attack the Moors and Moabites in the regions of Spain and to besiege Tortosa, their stronghold [Col. 0407C]. Therefore we grant a more ample assent to the petitions of your graciousness.

Accordingly, by the decree of this present document, we receive under the protection of blessed Peter and of his Apostolic See your person, that of your wife, and those of your children, together with your honour and all that you hold in the present new indiction or shall, by God’s favour, hold in the future, subject to an annual payment of thirty morabatins. We command and firmly establish that no person whatsoever may presume to inflict injury upon you or your honour. But if anyone—God forbid!—should attempt to inflict harm or injury upon you or your honour, the protection of the Apostolic See shall be effectively afforded and duly exercised on your behalf [Col. 0407D].

Given at Trastevere, through the hand of John, cardinal and librarian of the Holy Roman Church, on the tenth day before the Kalends of June, in the ninth indiction. [Note: [Col. 0407] Here there is an error in the indiction, which, for the year 1116 of the Incarnation and the seventeenth year of the pontificate of Pope Paschal II, ought to be the ninth.] In the year 1116 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and the seventeenth year of the pontificate of Lord Paschal II, pope.

### CDLXXI. To the archbishops, bishops, and clergy of England

—He announces that he is sending Anselm, abbot of Saint Sabas, as legate to England, to hold synodal assemblies. (A.D. 1116, May 24.)

[WILKINS, *Concilia Britanniae et Hiberniae*, I, 377.]

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the venerable [Col. 0408A] brothers, archbishops, bishops, and abbots throughout England, greeting and apostolic blessing.

Although we know you to be devout and prudent, we nevertheless are not unaware that many things worthy of correction are done among you. For the Church of God abounds not only in fruitful branches but also in fruitless ones; hence farmers must often apply the pruning-hook to cut away what is useless. This concern has, from the Apostles themselves, established the custom in the most holy Roman Church of sending its envoys through the various provinces, who ought diligently to urge the Lord’s labourers to care for the Lord’s vineyard.

Therefore we send to you with these present letters our beloved son Anselm, abbot of Saint Sabas, a man indeed devout and wise, so that he may hold synodal assemblies with your brotherhood and, by God’s grace, endeavour to uproot what ought to be uprooted and plant what ought to be planted [Col. 0408B]. We therefore command that, receiving him reverently as the representative of our person, you labour with united efforts, with due zeal and diligence, to cultivate the Lord’s vineyard. We have learned that hitherto you have acted too sluggishly in collecting the alms of blessed Peter; therefore we admonish and command your brotherhood henceforth to send it more diligently and without deceit by anyone to the Roman Church.

Given at Trastevere, on the ninth day before the Kalends of June.

### CDLXXII. To Henry, King of the English

—He announces that he has granted Anselm, abbot of Saint Sabas, “the exercise of apostolic authority in England.”

[Col. 0408C]

(A.D. 1116, May.—See EADMER, *Historia nova*, book V, p. 91.)

### CDLXXIII. To B[ernard], Archbishop of Toledo, and M[Maurice], Archbishop of Braga; to Al[fonso], bishop of Tuy; Ie[ronymus], bishop of Salamanca; Queen T.; and her barons P. Guncalviz, E. Muniz, and E. Gusendiz

—He announces that he has assigned the church of Lamego, adjudged away from Gonzalo, bishop of Coimbra, to Hugh, bishop of Portugal.

(A.D. 1116, June 18.—See Ribeiro, *Dissertações cronológicas sobre a história de Portugal*, IV, I, 157.)

### CDLXXIV. To the bishops, abbots, priors, clergy, king, and people of the Church of Jerusalem

—He announces that Patriarch Arnulf, to whom his legate had forbidden the exercise of pontifical office, has been restored by him. (A.D. 1116, July 19.)

[ROZIÈRE, *Cartulaire du Saint-Sépulcre*, 11.]

[Col. 0408D]

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved brothers and sons, the suffragan bishops, abbots, priors, clergy, king, princes, and people of the Church of Jerusalem, greeting and apostolic blessing.

To quiet the disturbances of your Church and investigate certain charges which, by widespread report and the testimony of good men, had reached our hearing against our brother Ar[nulf], your patriarch, we recently sent you an envoy of our authority. For it was alleged that he had been born of an illicit union, defiled by intercourse with women, and thrust into ecclesiastical pre-eminence by the king’s violence. Yet, contrary to our opinion and expectation, the disturbance among you increased so greatly that the same patriarch, with certain brethren, was compelled to come into our presence.

They brought us letters in the names of your brotherhood from the king, bishops, abbots, priors, and clergy, setting before us the Church’s manifold necessities and earnestly imploring the mercy of the Apostolic See that what they had done concerning their prelate might be confirmed by the grace of apostolic dispensation [Col. 0409B]. We therefore detained them with us for a considerable time, awaiting the return of our legate. They complained very strongly against him: that, after hearing one side, he had hastily pronounced sentence against the patriarch himself, disregarding an appeal to the Apostolic See.

But since we could obtain neither the same legate nor more certain information concerning him, after finally holding deliberation and counsel with our brethren, we investigated the charges with all the care we could. The venerable brethren Aschetinus, bishop of Bethlehem; Hugh, abbot of the monastery in the Valley of Jehoshaphat; Arnald, prior of the church on Mount Sion; and Peter and William, canons of the Lord’s Sepulchre, having touched the most holy Gospels, swore in these words [Col. 0409C]:

> “For the peace and necessity of the Church of Jerusalem, by common wish and consent we chose for ourselves as patriarch Lord Arnulf, with the king’s violence excluded.”

Our brother Patriarch Ar[nulf] himself, having touched the Gospels, likewise asserted that he was wholly innocent of the crimes alleged against him. Moreover, nearly everyone recognizes, not only we, how great his usefulness has been and is among you since the beginning of the Jerusalem expedition.

Having judicially dealt with these two charges, we judged that the third, which had been circulated concerning his birth, should be tolerated under the provision of apostolic dispensation: because of the many and various benefits of his person, too numerous to recount, and for the peace and necessity of the Church of Jerusalem, whose danger had indeed been grave in the past and seemed likely to be far graver in the future [Col. 0409D]. We know from the teaching of the Apostle that charity covers a multitude of sins. Observing this principle, we restored the aforesaid brother to the pontifical office which had been forbidden him by the legate; confirmed him as bishop or patriarch of the Church of Jerusalem; and, what was still lacking to his dignity, granted him from the kindness of the Apostolic See the vestment of the pallium.

Now, therefore, sending him back to you with the full integrity of patriarchal dignity and the fullness of our favour, we ask and command that you love him with due affection and truly honour him with due obedience [Col. 0410A], as a father, teacher, and God’s vicar. May almighty God grant that in his sight he may deserve glory from you and you from him!

We also wish it to be manifest to you all that the women by reason of whom, as stated above, the same patriarch was defamed were said to be, one the wife of Gerard, the other a Saracen woman by whom he had begotten a son. Moreover, Ebremar and his accomplices were wholly excluded from the common wish and consent of the election set forth above in the oath.

Given at Priverno, on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of August, in the ninth indiction, in the year 1117 of the Lord’s Incarnation.

### CDLXXV. To Robert, Abbot of Vézelay

—He declares that Robert is under the protection of the Apostolic See. (A.D. 1116, October 25.)

[MANSI, *Concilia*, XX, 1030.]

[Col. 0410B]

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son ROBERT, abbot of Vézelay, greeting and apostolic blessing.

Both the enactments of divine and human laws teach us, and natural reason itself exhorts us, that we ought to love not only our familiars and household members but also all those who love us. Therefore, dearest son in Christ, Abbot Robert, since you have long proved to be a familiar and member of the household of the Roman Church, and since you are established in the very estate of blessed Peter, we embrace you with special affection and sustain you with the protection of blessed Peter.

We forbid anyone whatever to presume to disturb or harass either your person or the office entrusted to you; rather, remain in peace, that you may freely render to almighty God the service due to him [Col. 0410C]. But whoever presumes to act against these provisions shall know that he will incur the indignation of almighty God and of the Apostolic See. Whoever proves obedient and observant, however, shall obtain the grace of the Lord our God and of his Apostles.

Given at Trastevere, on the eighth day before the Kalends of November.

### CDLXXVI. Decree confirming to the Abbot of Alet the monastery of Saint-Polycarp against the Abbot of Lagrasse

(A.D. 1116, November 23.)

[*Gallia Christiana*, VI, Instr. I, p. 107.]

[Col. 0410D]

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son RAYMOND, abbot of the monastery of Alet, greeting and apostolic blessing.

Your frequent complaint, and that of your brethren, has been brought to the Apostolic See against the brethren of the monastery of Lagrasse concerning the church of Saint-Polycarp. When the matter was heard last year at Saint-Gilles in the presence of our legate at a council, that legate fixed for each party a date for appearing before us. At the appointed time, therefore, the brethren of your monastery came before us and into the presence of the Apostolic See. But the monks of Lagrasse, though awaited long beyond the date, neither came nor sent any excuses [Col. 0411A].

We then received from your brethren sworn testimony that our predecessor, Pope Urban of reverend memory, after hearing the abbot of Alet’s complaint once and again, had ordered that the abbot himself and the monastery of Alet be reinvested with the church of blessed Polycarp. Having received this allegation, we ordered the brethren of Alet to be reinvested with the church of blessed Polycarp, while reserving whatever right the monastery of Lagrasse might have. We also immediately set a date for both parties to pursue their rights before us. Then the envoys of your monastery appeared, bringing suitable proofs for their case; but from the monastery of Lagrasse one brother appeared, producing neither witnesses nor proofs. When we had waited many days beyond the appointed date, no one besides him arrived.

Accordingly, in the hearing and investigation of the dispute, it became evident from the opponent’s own account that the aforesaid church of Saint-Polycarp had in ancient times belonged to the monastery of Alet, and that it had been removed from the possession of the monastery of Alet not by the truth of an ecclesiastical judgment but by the violence of secular powers. The proofs of your monastery were laid before us, containing written evidence of the donation made by Count Guillelmundus to that monastery of Alet, in the time of Emperor Charles, concerning the aforesaid church of Saint-Polycarp; and likewise of the restoration or donation made by Count Raymond during the reign of Philip, king of the Franks [Col. 0411C].

The brother from Lagrasse, however, relied only upon bare assertions. It was agreed by both parties that Countess Ermengarde had both confirmed the church of blessed Polycarp to the monastery of Alet and contested it on behalf of the monastery of Lagrasse. Thus, once the truth of justice had been made plain, by the judgment of our brethren we restore the aforesaid church of blessed Polycarp to your brethren and the monastery of Alet, and by the authority of this present document confirm it to be possessed in perpetuity. We command and decree with perpetual stability that the same church of blessed Polycarp shall always remain under the obedience and direction of you and your successors, the abbots of Alet; and that no ecclesiastical or secular person may have authority to remove that cell, with all its appurtenances and dependencies [Col. 0411D], from the unity and possession of the monastery of Alet.

I, Paschal, bishop of the Catholic Church, have confirmed and subscribed.

I, Peter, bishop of Porto, have subscribed.

I, Cono, bishop of Palestrina, have subscribed.

I, Peter, cardinal-deacon of the Roman Church, was present at this determination and have subscribed.

I, Peter, cardinal of Saints Cosmas and Damian, have subscribed.

I, G[regory], cardinal-deacon of Saint Angelo, was present and subscribed.

I, Amiso, cardinal-priest of the title of Equitius, approved and subscribed.

I, Desiderius, cardinal-priest of the title of Saint Praxedes, approved and subscribed.

[Col. 0412A] I, G[regory], cardinal-priest of the title of Lucina, approved and subscribed.

I, John, cardinal-priest of the title of Saint Eusebius, approved and subscribed.

Given at Trastevere through the hand of John, deacon and librarian of the Holy Roman Church, on the ninth day before the Kalends of December, in the tenth indiction, in the year 1116 of the Lord’s Incarnation and the eighteenth year of the pontificate of Lord Paschal II, pope.

### CDLXXVII. To the clergy of the Church of Augsburg

—Their bishop, accused of adultery, has not yet been absolved by him. (A.D. 1116, November 23.)

[MANSI, *Concilia*, XX, 1009.]

[Col. 0412B]

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons the clerics of the church of Augsburg, greeting and apostolic blessing.

Concerning certain complaints which reached our hearing regarding your bishop five years ago, we remember that at that time we forbade him the episcopal office. For, as your letters report, although summoned by our legate of good memory Richard, bishop of Albano, and forewarned by our command, he took no care whatever to appear before us on the appointed date or to provide the required purgation. Since that time we do not remember ever having remitted the prohibition.

### CDLXXVIII. To Arnold, Archbishop of Mainz

—He entrusts to him the hearing and decision of the case of the bishop of Augsburg. (A.D. 1116.)

[MANSI, *Concilia*, XX, 1009.]

[Col. 0412C]

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to ARNOLD, venerable brother and archbishop of Mainz, greeting and apostolic blessing.

Beyond the other dreadful matters and disgrace which have long been reported to the hearing of the Apostolic See concerning the person of the bishop of Augsburg, we recently received, in a tearful petition, the complaint of Adalbert, a citizen of Augsburg. It is indeed shameful for ecclesiastical persons both to utter and to hear that complaint, but you may learn it from Adalbert’s own account [Col. 0412D].

Therefore, by the injunction of these present letters, we charge you—since this inquiry pertains to you by reason of the obligation of metropolitan dignity—to investigate diligently the truth of this matter, having summoned the brethren, and to decree what justice requires. For whatever shall be justly and reasonably established by you, with God as author, we shall hold ratified.

### CDLXXIX. Privilege granted to John, Abbot of Saint Bartholomew, confirming all the goods of the monastery

(A.D. 1116, December 2.)

[*Anecdota Ughelliana*, 390.]

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son JOHN, abbot of the monastery of Saint Bartholomew, which is situated [Col. 0413A] in the district of Penne, and to his successors canonically appointed in perpetuity.

By the Lord’s ordering we are seen to have been raised to the governance of the Apostolic See so that, by his grace, we ought to promote religious life and extend protection to its servants. Accordingly, granting your just petitions, beloved son in the Lord John, abbot, we receive under the protection and guardianship of blessed Peter the monastery of Saint Bartholomew, over which by God’s authority you preside, and strengthen it by the privilege of his authority against the wickedness of evil men.

Therefore, by this present decree, we establish that whatever goods and possessions the same monastery possesses by lawful means in the present tenth indiction—through the grant of pontiffs, the generosity of princes, or the offerings of the faithful, wherever situated—or may hereafter obtain by God’s favour, shall remain secure and inviolate for you and your successors. Among these, the following have seemed fit to be expressly named: the castle of Carpineto; the castle of Fara; the churches of Saint Vitalis, Saint Tegrinus, and Saint Nicholas of Vico; the church of Saint Mary at Serane; the church of Saint Mary and Saint Felix at Latumano, with its appurtenances; the churches of Saint Nicholas and Saint Mary, and Saint Justa of the castle of Deretani; the churches of Saints John and Paul, of the Holy Sepulchre, and of Saint Angelo; the churches of Saint Mary of Brittoli, Saint Herarmus, Saint Mary at Pisciano, Saint John at Bagno, Saint Lawrence of Unciano, Saint Mary in Piano, Saint Mary in the Cells, and Saint Lucy at the Old Altar [Col. 0413B].

We decree, therefore, that no person at all may rashly disturb the same monastery, take away its possessions, retain what has been taken, diminish them, or harass them by reckless vexations; rather, let all be preserved whole for the use and benefit in every way of those for whose sustenance and governance they were granted. We likewise decree that the burials of the same monastery shall be entirely free, so that no one may hinder the devotion and final wish of those who decide to be buried there, unless they happen to be excommunicated.

If, therefore, any ecclesiastical or secular person hereafter, knowing this document of our constitution, should attempt to act against it, then, after a second or third warning, unless he makes amends by suitable satisfaction, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and office; let him know that he stands guilty before divine judgment for the iniquity he has committed [Col. 0413D]; let him be cut off from the most sacred body and blood of God and of the Lord, our Redeemer Jesus Christ; and let him be subject at the last judgment to strict vengeance. But for all who preserve what is right for the same monastery, may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that here they may receive the fruit of good action and before the strict Judge find the rewards of eternal peace. Amen, amen, amen.

I, Paschal, bishop of the Catholic Church.

Given at Trastevere, through the hand of John, cardinal-deacon and librarian of the Holy Roman Church, on the Nones of December, in the tenth indiction, in the year 1116 of the Lord’s Incarnation and the eighteenth year of the pontificate of Lord Paschal II, pope.

### CDLXXX. To the canons of Saint Mary in Porto in the Ravennate exarchate

—That they are to observe the rule composed by Canon Peter. (A.D. 1116, December 21.)

[RUBEI, *Historia Ravennatis*, p. 321.]

[Col. 0414A]

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons dwelling regularly at the church of Saint Mary in Porto of the Ravennate exarchate, greeting and apostolic blessing.

This rule of canonical observance—conceived both by the authoritative teaching of the holy Fathers and formed by the examples and upright conduct of devout men—we have examined and, by God’s authority, accepted. Confirming it by the authority of the Apostolic See, we enjoin upon you its effective observance through God’s grace [Col. 0414B], so that you may attain in heaven the fellowship of those whose footsteps you have vowed to follow on earth.

Given at Trastevere, on the Kalends of January, in the tenth indiction.

The following cardinals subscribed to these pontifical letters: Crescentius, bishop of Sabina; Peter, bishop of Porto; Cono, bishop of Palestrina; Vitalis, bishop of Albano; Boniface of the title of Saint Mark; Deusdedit of Saint Lawrence; Desiderius of Saint Praxedes; Guido of Saint Balbina, priests; Peter of Saints Cosmas and Damian; Peter of Saint Adrian; Rosemanus of Saint George at the Golden Veil; Comes of Saint Mary in Aquiro; Gregory of Saint Angelo; and John of Saint Lucy, deacons.

### CDLXXXI. Privilege for the Church of Blessed Mary in Porto

(A.D. 1116, December 22.)

[FANTUZZI, *Monumenti Ravennati*, Venice, 1801, quarto, IV, 237.]

[Col. 0414C]

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son PETER, prior of the church of Blessed Mary in Porto, and to his successors canonically appointed in perpetuity.

By the Lord’s ordering we are seen to have been raised to the governance of the Apostolic See so that, by his grace, we ought to promote religious life and extend protection to its servants. Therefore, dearest son in Christ, Prior Peter, we grant paternal assent to your petitions, so that the peace of your house may, through God’s grace, remain tranquil and secure.

Whatever estates belonging to the right of our holy Roman Church have henceforth been given to your house by any tenants, together with the other things which you are known to possess in the present tenth indiction, we grant and confirm by this present decree to you and your successors who advance in the same observance of regular life [Col. 0414D]. We likewise decree that the burial-place of your house shall be entirely free, so that none may hinder the devotion and final wish of those who decide to be buried there, unless they happen to be excommunicated.

We permit the brethren of your house to receive the ordinations of clerics from whichever Catholic bishop they prefer, whether the Church of Ravenna has no bishop or its bishop is known not to be Catholic. Moreover, we permit no bishop to prevent you from receiving laypersons from any parishes for conversion to the discipline of regular life, unless they happen to be bound by legal obligations; likewise, no bishop may prevent the tonsure of clerics who decide by profession to live regularly in your house [Col. 0415A]. We also grant you possession, without objection from a bishop or episcopal ministers, of the tithes of your fruits which you gather anywhere at your own expense and labour.

If anyone, having learned the tenor of this decree, should rashly—God forbid!—attempt to oppose it, let him suffer the loss of his honour and office or be punished by final excommunication, unless through [lacuna] he corrects the matter by worthy satisfaction.

I, Paschal, bishop of the Catholic Church, have subscribed.  
I, Peter, bishop of Porto, have subscribed.  
I, Cono, bishop of Palestrina, have subscribed.  
I, Boniface, cardinal of Saint Mark, have subscribed.  
I, John, cardinal of Saint Cecilia, have subscribed.  
I, Desiderius, cardinal of Saint Praxedes, have subscribed.  
I, Deusdedit, cardinal of Saint Lawrence in Damaso, have subscribed.  
I, Peter, cardinal-deacon of Saints Cosmas and Damian, have subscribed.  
I, Bonsemannus, cardinal-deacon of Saint George, have subscribed.  
I, Comes, cardinal-deacon of Saint Mary in Aquiro, have subscribed.  
I, Peter, cardinal-deacon of Saint Adrian, have subscribed.  
I, Gregory, cardinal-deacon of Saint Angelo, have subscribed.  
I, John, cardinal-deacon of Saint Lucy, have subscribed.  

Given at Trastevere through the hand of John, cardinal-deacon and librarian of the Holy Roman Church, on the eleventh day before the Kalends of January, in the tenth indiction, in the year 1116 [Col. 0415C] of the Lord’s Incarnation and the eighteenth year of the pontificate of Lord Paschal II, pope.

### CDLXXXII

—At the request of Margrave Herman, he receives the church of Saint Pancras of Backnang under his protection and confirms its possessions, on condition that one gold coin be paid annually to the Lateran Palace.

(A.D. 1116.—See *Württembergisches Urkundenbuch*, Stuttgart, 1849, I, 343.)

### CDLXXXIII. Privilege for the monastery of Saint-Bertin of Saint-Omer

(A.D. 1116? October 8.)

[*Collection des Cartulaires*, III, 251.]

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved [Col. 0415D] son Lambert, abbot of the monastery of Saint Bertin, greeting and apostolic blessing.

What has been established with a view to religious life ought to be preserved with enduring firmness. Therefore we will that the religious observance and discipline which you have received from the monastery of Cluny be maintained among you in perpetual observance. Furthermore, what was adjudged concerning the liberty of your monastery in the Lateran Palace before us by our brethren, the bishops and cardinals, and confirmed by our privilege, we establish by renewed sanction. By the disposition of apostolic authority we decree that it shall remain so ratified and unshaken that henceforth no one shall ever be permitted to infringe it, nor anyone to reconsider it with rash presumption.

Given at Viterbo, on the eighth day before the Ides of October.

### CDLXXXIV. To the brethren of Saint Fridianus

(A.D. 1116? October 15.)

[BALUZE, *Miscellanea*, Lucchesi edition, IV, 586.]

[Col. 0416A]

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons A., prior of Saint Fridianus, and his brethren, greeting and apostolic blessing.

“Many are the afflictions of the righteous, and from them all the Lord will deliver them.” The enemy attacks us in many ways, and divine mercy consoles us in still more. Therefore, dearest sons in Christ, if all persecutors rise against you, do not be astonished; but run to the true and highest refuge, seeking his mercy [Col. 0416B] and fixing all your hope and trust in him. For he is able to deliver you and will not permit you to be tempted beyond your strength.

We too shall willingly give you whatever consolation we can, as sons most dear in Christ. We do not see how one who is sacrilegious, a plunderer of churches, an oppressor of the poor, and an agent of the worst possible deeds can be in communion with God’s servants. For how can a servant receive one whom the Lord rejects? Behold, the Psalmist says: “Did I not hate those whom the Lord hates?” Ought the children of the Church to have communion with those who, by the judgment of our God and because of their iniquities, are cast out from the bosom of Mother Church? Whoever is not with the Lord is against the Lord. Therefore, if we wish to be with the Lord, we must not be with him who is [Col. 0416C] against the Lord.

Given at Trastevere, on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of November.

### CDLXXXV. To the monks of Saint-Gilles

(Between A.D. 1100 and 1117.)

[MANSI, *Concilia*, XX, 1070.]

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons, the monks of the monastery of Saint-Gilles, greeting and apostolic blessing.

The monastic state is wholly separated from the world so that it may cleave to God. Others may both serve God and not abandon the world. But monks are permitted to have neither their bodies nor their will in their own power [Col. 0416D], so that the Lord’s saying may be fulfilled in them: “I came not to do my own will, but the will of him who sent me” (John 6:38).

Therefore, by these present letters we admonish your beloved community to bind yourselves more closely to divine love with every effort and all diligence; and, putting aside the vanities of the world, always seek God’s face with the whole desire of your minds. For this reason it is fitting that you maintain more effectively, as your predecessors arranged, the strict observance of the Cluniac order. If you act otherwise, you will both expose yourselves to men’s detractions and incur more gravely the indignation of the Apostolic See. For the order of the monastery of Cluny has, by God’s grace, shed the light of fuller religious observance in many places.

Given at Benevento, on the third day before the Kalends of July.

### CDLXXXVI. To Hermann, Bishop of Augsburg

(Between A.D. 1101 and 1117.)

[Published by Philipp JAFFÉ, *Regesta pontificum Romanorum*, p. 515, “from Pertz’s papers.”]

[Col. 0417A]

To H[ERMANN], bishop of Augsburg, greeting and apostolic blessing.

The case of the bearer of this letter has been investigated more carefully before us. Our brother H., the venerable abbot, has also represented that he diligently examined the same case in the very congregation of your church, with devout monks and prudent men. Thus we learned, both from the cleric’s own confession and from the said abbot’s representation, that, when this cleric was despaired of during an illness and had already lost consciousness, he was clothed in the monastic habit neither voluntarily nor knowingly [Col. 0417B]. But when he soon returned to himself, he opposed that habit and, upon being summoned by letters from your predecessor and the congregation of the church of Augsburg, received the benefice and prebend of the same church.

Since, therefore, the sequence of this case stands thus, it seemed both to our brethren and to us that the same cleric should not be compelled, by any obligation of justice on these grounds, to return to the monastery. Your brotherhood, therefore, is not to harass him further. We waited for your envoys for five days after this man’s arrival; but as no one came to us, we dismissed him in peace.

Given on the third day before the Ides of March.

### CDLXXXVII. Privilege for the canons of Saint Fidelis

(A.D. 1117, January 1.)

[TATTI, *Annali della città di Como*, II, 266.]

[Col. 0417C]

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the venerable brother, bishop of Como, greeting and apostolic blessing.

Although you know that authority over the ordering of churches has been granted to you, you must nevertheless take diligent care to use it for building up and not for destruction. Therefore, as we command others, so by these present letters we ask and command you not to inflict any injuries or burdens upon the clerics of Saint Fidelis, nor introduce clerics into their church against their will. If any have been intruded, let them be restrained by due justice [Col. 0417D], and do not permit the others to be hindered any longer; rather, let them receive clerics into the assembly of their congregation according to their own judgment.

Given at Trastevere, on the Kalends of January.

### CDLXXXVIII

—He confirms the possessions of the monastery of Micy.

(A.D. 1117, March 12.—See *Annales Benedictini*, VI, 2.)

### CDLXXXIX. To the bishops and king of England: concerning the dignity of the Church of Canterbury

(A.D. 1117, March 24.)

[MANSI, *Concilia*, XX, 1011.]

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the venerable [Col. 0418A] brethren, the bishops of England, and to his dearest son HENRY, illustrious king, greeting and apostolic blessing.

When our most dear and most reverend brother Ralph, the archbishop, came to us, we learned of the embassy which you had sent to us through the venerable Herbert, bishop of Norwich. Those same brethren and fellow bishops, indeed, being prevented by the severe discomforts of illness, were wholly unable to come into our presence. But when the envoys—persons honorable and venerable—arrived, we received their writings, in which we discerned both their requests and the wishes of your embassy. For this was desired and requested: that in our time the Church of Canterbury should not be deprived of its dignity; that we should neither diminish that same dignity nor permit it to be diminished—the dignity which it has possessed since it was founded by St. Gregory through St. Augustine. Besides the evidence of the letters, the envoys sent to us, as wise and energetic men, advanced their arguments prudently, persistently, and effectively. We have certainly received kindly and gladly the persons of the envoys, their arguments, and the embassy of you all, as of most dear brethren; and we desire that this may please you in the Lord, for the Lord’s sake.

We therefore wish to make known to your charity that we neither diminish, nor desire to diminish, the dignity of the Church of Canterbury. For we venerate blessed Gregory, pontiff of the Apostolic See, in every respect—as a foremost member of Christ the Lord, as shepherd and teacher of the Christian people, and as minister of eternal salvation—and we wish those things which proceeded from his ordinances to remain valid. Therefore, the dignity which the Church of Canterbury received from him through St. Augustine, and which our brother Anselm, of holy memory, is known to have held by right and lawful possession, we by no means diminish; rather, we wish the Church of Canterbury to remain in that state in which its authentic privileges, in accordance with the enactments of the canons, suffer no disturbance.

Given at Benevento, on the ninth day before the Kalends of April.

CDXC. To the canons of the Church of Augsburg.—Concerning the case of their bishop.  
(1117, April 1.)

[MANSI, *Councils*, XX, 1009.]

[Col. 0418D]

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons D., dean, and the other canons of the Church of Augsburg, greeting and apostolic blessing.

For a long time our brother Herimann, your bishop, has been accused before us on three counts: namely, of an improper approach to election and consecration, of depraved conduct, and of alienating ecclesiastical property. On these grounds, after he had been suspended from episcopal office, a date was fixed by which each party ought to appear before us. Within that period, however, your fellow brother and fellow canon Conrad came to us and, as he himself maintains, received from us the ruling that the bishop would be free if they did not appear by the appointed date. Since, therefore, that bishop was recently denounced before us also on certain other serious charges, those former matters likewise returned to our recollection. We consequently judged it expedient to bring his case to an end, lest it continue longer to cause harm to the Church.

But since, owing to the difficulties of travel and bodily infirmity, he cannot present himself before us, we have provided that this matter be entrusted to our fellow brother Wido, bishop of Chur. We therefore command that he hear the entire case with greater care. And if your bishop makes amends concerning ecclesiastical property and his life of depraved conduct, and clears himself of the other accusations by the hands of three bishops or five priests, he shall obtain restoration to the office from which he has been barred.

Given at Benevento, on the Kalends of April.

CDXCI. He confirms to Abbot Albin and the canons of St. Mary of the Wood (de Rota) the chapel of St. Nicholas at Credon.  
(1117, April 4.)

[BALUZE, *Miscellanea*, Luc. ed., III, 18.]

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons ALBIN, abbot, and the canons of St. Mary of the Wood, greeting and apostolic blessing.

Because we know that you are free to devote yourselves to the vision of God, we make more gracious provision for your peace in accordance with your request. Therefore, by the present page of decree we confirm to you that chapel of blessed Nicholas which, in the castle of Credon, you received through the hand of Rainald, bishop of Angers; namely, the chapel which that same Bishop Rainald had received from the control of Hugh of Credon. Accordingly, just as it was granted and delivered to you by him, so we decree that it shall remain yours forever, peaceful and whole, with all its appurtenances.

Saving, however, the annual payment of ten solidi, which must be paid to the mother church of St. Maurice. Further, we decree that all estates and gifts which Rainald, the grandfather of the aforesaid Hugh, offered to the same chapel out of his own right and assigned by a written instrument, as well as those bestowed by Maurice, son of that Rainald, shall remain yours forever, peaceful and whole.

[Col. 0419D] Given at Benevento, on the second day before the Nones of April, in the tenth indiction.

CDXCII. Privilege for the abbey of Fontevraud.  
(1117, April 5.)

[PAVILLON, *Life of Robert of Arbrissel*, Proofs, p. 623.]

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the religious handmaids of God, the nuns of St. Mary of Fontevraud, greeting and apostolic blessing.

From his own writings we have plainly learned how Peter, bishop of Poitiers, of blessed memory, entrusted the place of Tucion to Lord Robert of Arbrissel, a religious man and founder of your monastery, and gave it into the possession of your monastery. For when the monks of Nanteuil laid claim to that place because of a certain church whose foundations appeared there, he went with his clergy and with Fulcard Frenicard, under whose right that place had been, to the monastery of Nanteuil; and concerning this wrongful claim he made an agreement, in the common chapter, with the abbot and monks of that place.

For this agreement Fulcard Frenicard gave the monks of Nanteuil four measures of grain annually from the tithe of St. Médard of Vertou. Accordingly, Walter, abbot of Nanteuil, in the chapter of the Church of Nanteuil, with the bishop and clergy present and with the assent of his monks, entirely released and abandoned that claim; and he renounced the church of the place of Tucion and the place itself in its entirety to the aforesaid Lord Robert, to your congregation, and to the men serving him, to be administered and possessed in perpetuity.

We therefore judge the grant of the aforesaid bishop, made on such reasonable grounds, to be valid, and confirm it by the authority of this present document. We enact and altogether forbid that either the archbishop of Bordeaux, the abbot of Nanteuil, or any ecclesiastical or secular person may withdraw it from the possession and unity of your monastery. But if anyone should rashly attempt to act contrary to this, let him be punished by the authority of canonical vengeance.

Given at Benevento, on the Nones of April, tenth indiction.

CDXCIII. To Henry, king of England.—Concerning Thurstan, archbishop-elect of York, expelled from his Church without judgment.  
(1117, April 5.)

[MANSI, *Councils*, XX, 1012.]

[Col. 0420C]

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to HENRY, illustrious king of the English, greeting and apostolic blessing.

By God’s authorship, we have confidence in your integrity—not merely good confidence, but better. We therefore exhort your eminence always to remain mindful of divine grace, which has bestowed on you both peace in your kingdom and knowledge of justice. Carefully preserve, then, the honor of God and of His churches in your realm, and execute justice effectively; for through the honor of God your own honor will surely increase.

We have heard that the archbishop-elect of York, a wise and vigorous man, has been removed from the Church of York without a judgment; and this plainly conflicts with divine justice and the ordinances of the holy Fathers. We wish neither that the Church of Canterbury be diminished nor that the Church of York suffer prejudice; rather, we decree that the arrangement established between those churches by St. Gregory, apostle of the English people, be preserved firm and inviolate. Therefore the same elect is, as justice requires, to be restored to his church in every respect. But if any dispute arises between those churches, it shall be examined in our presence, with both parties present.

CDXCIV. To Ralph, bishop of Canterbury, concerning the primacy over the Church of York.  
(1117.)

[*Monasticon Anglicanum*, III, 143.]

[Col. 0421A]

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother RANULPH, archbishop of the Church of Canterbury, greeting and apostolic blessing.

The more confidence we have in the sincerity of your charity, the more we wonder that you seem to demand matters which appear to belong to the Roman Church alone. For you know, dearest brother, the words of blessed Gregory to Augustine: in his letter it is so ordained concerning the bishop of York that, after your death, he shall preside over the bishops whom he has ordained, so that he may in no way be subject to the jurisdiction of the bishop of London. But if thereafter the distinction of honor between the bishops of the cities of London and York is to be that he who was ordained first be considered first, then in what manner and on what grounds do you require a profession from the elect of the Church of York? And why, on that account, do you refuse to lay hands on him, when under the aforesaid constitution of blessed Gregory he ought in no way to be subject to your jurisdiction?

We therefore command that, according to the custom of your churches and in accordance with the ordinances of the holy canons, you are to consecrate him, setting aside every demand of subjection; otherwise, we command that he be consecrated, according to the common custom of the churches, by the suffragans of the Church of York. And since he holds the place of priority, he is neither a suffragan of your Church nor does he owe you obedience.

CDXCV. Confirmation of King Louis’s privilege for the Church of Chartres.  
(1117, April 13.)

[*Collection des Cartulaires*, II, 270.]

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother GEOFFREY, bishop of Chartres, greeting and apostolic blessing.

Things justly and lawfully established by secular princes are worthy to be confirmed also by the authority of our favor. We therefore confirm by the authority of this present decree the ordinance issued by our illustrious son Louis, king of the Franks, for the peace of the Church of Chartres. The words of this ordinance are specifically as follows:

> “Out of reverence for blessed Mary and blessed Peter the Apostle, in the estates of the Church of Chartres, both episcopal and canonical, and in the estates of the monastery of St. Peter the Apostle—which had long been oppressed by the lords of Puteaux—we utterly abolish the aforesaid oppressions, so that no forced labor or violence may be inflicted, whether in the name of our royal majesty or in the name of any other authority; no exactions and no burdens may be imposed. Rather, all their revenue shall benefit only the uses of those for whose support those estates were granted to the aforesaid sacred places by the offerings of the faithful and secured by the confirmation of our predecessors.”

We therefore decree that the aforesaid king’s just and lawful ordinance be preserved valid and inviolate in succeeding times, so that, if anyone should rashly violate it, he shall be excluded from the thresholds of the Church as sacrilegious until he makes satisfaction.

Given at Benevento, on the Ides of April, in the tenth indiction.

CDXCVI. He grants privileges to Anthony, provost of St. Peter’s at the oratory of Capistrano, cardinal priest.  
(Fragment. 1117, April 20.)

[UGHELLI, *Italia sacra*, IX, 506.]

. . . . . Therefore to you, beloved son in Christ, Anthony, provost, whom by God’s favor we have consecrated cardinal priest in our holy Roman Church, and to your successors . . . . .

Given at Benevento through the hand of John, cardinal deacon and librarian of the Holy Roman Church, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of May, tenth indiction, in the year 1117 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the eighteenth year of the pontificate.

CDXCVII. To the king of the Danes.  
(1117, April 23.)

[“From the Register of Paschal II, book XVIII, chapter 21”—extracted from Vatican MS Ottobon. no. 3057 by W. Giesebrecht; edited by Philipp JAFFÉ, *Regesta Romanorum Pontificum*, 515.]

To the king of the Danes.

We read in the Apostle Paul: “There is no authority except from God.” But authority is rightly exercised when it looks to God, from whom it is given. Therefore, son, always direct your attention to God, so that, as you have received authority from God, you may likewise always be able, by His grace, to please Him. Venerate gladly and humbly the churches and priests of the Lord; extend the aid of your protection to orphans and widows. Exercise justice effectively, and restrain by your authority those who resist justice. Do not allow the goods of churches to be plundered by any wicked persons, because it is the crime of sacrilege, and their fault concerns you as well. For things granted for the salvation of many ought not to be seized by the violence of a few.

In restraining these and other wickednesses, you ought to be a helper and collaborator to the bishops of your realm. For the world is rightly governed when royal power accompanies priestly authority; for priests are the eyes in Christ’s Church. It is fitting that the people follow them, because by the Lord’s power His body too is illumined. It belongs to them, indeed, to proclaim the Lord’s truth, so that they may preserve the Lord’s bride chaste and undefiled.

Therefore we wish you to know that neither they nor we can alter our teaching concerning the chastity of priests and deacons. For the Lord’s saying is: “Let your loins be girded and lamps burning in your hands,” so that we may be chaste in body and shine with the brightness of our deeds. But if any are softened into resisting the truth, they are to be admonished by the priestly ministry and restrained by royal power.

We therefore commend to your authority our fellow brethren, the metropolitan of Lund and the other bishops of the kingdom of the Danes, so that you may show them obedience with reverence and provide them effective assistance, that by God’s grace you may both obtain temporal glory peacefully and merit happily to attain eternal salvation.

Given at Benevento, on the eighth day before the Kalends of May.

CDXCVIII. To Frederick, archbishop of Cologne.—He approves his excommunication of the king and exhorts him to aid the Church of Rome.  
(1117.)

[MANSI, *Councils*, XX, 1084.]

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother F., bishop of Cologne, greeting and apostolic blessing.

Your fraternity has informed us that, on account of sacrileges, robberies, arsons, and other wicked deeds, you have pronounced a sentence of excommunication against the king. We, taking heed of the passage of the Doctor of the Gentiles where among other things it is read, “If anyone called a brother is sexually immoral or greedy, with such a one do not even eat” [1 Cor. 5]; and fearing likewise another saying of blessed John the Apostle, which states concerning similar persons that whoever says “greeting” to him shares in his evil works; and considering also the decree of the Council of Nicaea that one excommunicated by one person is not to be received by another—we, exhorting you to act in the same way, have entirely withdrawn ourselves from communion with that king.

Whether for this reason or for another, we do not know, but he came to Rome, stirred up sedition among the people, received into communion persons excommunicated by the Church, attacked the faithful of St. Peter and does not cease to attack them; he occupied as much as he could of the patrimony of St. Peter and exposed other parts to devastation. For these acts, excommunication has already long been pronounced by our predecessors—by Lord Pope John in a council of forty bishops, and by certain others. Those coming to the thresholds of the Apostles and into our presence are seized by guards placed on the roads, stripped of their possessions, and are not allowed free passage. Why he ought to do these things against us and against blessed Peter, we do not know.

Making these matters known to your charity, we exhort you for the sake of your mother, the Roman Church, and invite you as brethren and most beloved sons in Christ to come to her aid. For it is most shameful for sons to see their mother worn down before their eyes and not bring aid when they are able. Therefore help your mother, and strive, with God’s aid, to supply her needs. For what you have done concerning him, we have upheld and, God granting, will uphold.

CDXCIX. Privilege for the churches of St. Peter of Nurki, St. Nicholas of Nugubii, and St. Elias of Setin.  
(1117, April 20.)

[GATTULA, *History of Cassino*, 425.]

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the illustrious man GUNNAR, lordling, greeting and apostolic blessing.

[Col. 0424A] We have observed your devotion, because you request that the churches of St. Peter of Nurki, St. Nicholas of Nugubii, and St. Elias of Setin—which you have built within the parishes of Turritana and Empuritana, namely on your own patrimony—be fortified by the protection of the Apostolic See. Assenting, therefore, to your requests, we establish that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb these churches, remove their possessions, retain things removed, diminish them, or harass them by reckless vexations. Rather, all things which have already been bestowed upon them by you, or which hereafter, by God’s generosity, may be given, offered, or acquired by other just means either by you or by other faithful men, shall always be preserved peaceful and whole, for the benefit of the clergy serving there, saving the canonical reverence due to our fellow brethren and fellow bishops.

If, therefore, in the future any judge, lordling, official, or ecclesiastical or secular person, knowing this document of our constitution, should rashly attempt to act against it, let him incur the peril of his rank and office or be punished by the penalty of excommunication, unless he corrects his presumption through worthy satisfaction. But whoever endeavors to foster these churches and those serving the Lord in them, and to honor them from his own resources, may he obtain the grace of almighty God and His Apostles and forgiveness of his sins. Amen, amen, amen.

I, Paschal, bishop of the Catholic Church, have subscribed.

Given at Anagni through the hand of Chrysogonus, cardinal deacon of the Holy Roman Church, acting in place of Lord John the chancellor, on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of September, in the tenth indiction, in the year 1113 of the Lord’s Incarnation [Note: [Col. 0423] That the year should be read as 1117 is evident from the tenth indiction and the eighteenth year of the pontificate. JAFFÉ.], in the fourteenth year of the pontificate of Lord Paschal II, pope.

D. He confirms certain possessions of the monastery of Subiaco.  
(1117.)

[MARGARINI, *Bullarium Casinense*, II, 131.]

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son in Christ JOHN, abbot of Subiaco, and to his successors canonically appointed and remaining forever in the fidelity of St. Peter.

Although by the authority and benevolence of the Apostolic See we are debtors to all the children of the holy Roman Church, it is nevertheless fitting that we devote a more earnest care of affection, and, with the Lord’s help, provide more attentively for the peace of those places and persons that adhere more especially and intimately to the same Roman Church. The monastery of blessed Benedict at Subiaco, over which, John, beloved abbot in Christ, you are known, by God’s authorship, to preside, was long enlarged by many offerings of the faithful and expanded with many possessions, both because of reverence for our most blessed father Benedict himself and because of the constancy of its religious brethren.

But although it had long flourished both spiritually and temporally, when the power of those who fear God at last failed and the violence of tyrants increased, that place was severely oppressed and greatly diminished in its possessions. Our predecessor Pope Gregory, of happy memory, taking this grievously, labored in his days for the restoration of that monastery. We too, following in his footsteps, have devoted our efforts to the same end; and, through the favor of divine mercy, have recovered in the territory of Campagna certain things that had been taken away and restored them to that monastery. Because of the malice of wicked men, your charity requested their confirmation from the Apostolic See.

Accordingly, assenting to your request, most beloved son in Christ, we confirm them by this document of privilege to you and your successors, and through us to the aforesaid monastery of St. Benedict: namely, Affile and Pontia, with their churches, lands, hamlets, woods, and appurtenances, as contained in the offering of Benedict, duke and consul of noble memory, and in the charters of our predecessors Benedict VI and John X, Roman pontiffs.

We therefore decree that no person whatsoever shall have power to withdraw these things from the monastery’s possession, diminish them, or disturb them by reckless vexations; rather, all things, as set down above, shall be preserved for that place always peaceful and whole, for the use of the brethren there serving the Lord under the Rule of blessed Benedict. If, in the future, any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowing this document of our constitution, should rashly attempt to act against it, then, having been warned a second or third time, if he does not make correction by fitting satisfaction, let him be deprived of the dignity of his authority and rank; let him know himself guilty before divine judgment of the iniquity he has committed; let him be cut off from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Redeemer; and at the last judgment let him be subject to strict vengeance.

But upon all who preserve justice toward the aforesaid monastery may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that they may receive here the fruit of good action and find, before the strict Judge, the rewards of eternal peace. Amen, amen, amen.
