I, Paschal, bishop of the Catholic Church.

Given at Anagni through the hand of Chrysogonus, cardinal deacon of the Holy Roman Church, acting in place of Lord John the chancellor, on the ninth day before the Kalends of . . . . .

DI. To Roger, count of Sicily.  
(1117, October 1.)

[“From the Register of Paschal II, book XVIII, chapter 3.”—Extracted from Vatican MS Ottobon. no. 3057 by W. Giesebrecht; edited by Philipp JAFFÉ, *Regesta Romanorum Pontificum*, 516.]

To ROGER, count of Sicily.

Before the Saracen invasion, the island of Sicily was so closely connected with the Roman Church that the Roman pontiffs always had there both administrators of their patrimonies and representatives acting in their place. Divine grace, however, conferred upon your father the prerogative that, through his and his men’s labor and blood, the Saracens should be driven from that island and the churches of God restored within it. Therefore, as you stated in your letters, my predecessor graciously granted to your father the office of legate. We likewise granted it to you, his successor, after him, on this condition: that whenever a legate is sent there from our side—whom we certainly understand to be a vicar—the matters to be carried out by him shall be brought to effect through your diligence.

For we read that secular powers are ordered in the Church so that what ecclesiastical humility is less able to accomplish, secular power may carry out through the force of its authority. Yet nowhere do we read that judgments concerning ecclesiastical persons or dignities were entrusted to laymen, even religious laymen. Moreover, when has a legate or vicar ever arrogated to himself the summons of bishops to a synod? Such summonses are customarily made, sometimes by individual letters and sometimes by collective letters, through whatever messengers may be available.

Know, dearest son, your proper measure and the authority given you by the Lord; do not raise authority against the Lord. For the power of the Roman Church has been bestowed by the Lord in such a way that it cannot be taken away by human beings. Learn, within your county, from the examples of good emperors: strive not to attack churches but to assist them; do not judge or oppress bishops, but venerate them as vicars of God. Let what was given to the Church by your father, Count R[oger] of noble memory, in no way be diminished through you; rather, let it be increased.

Do not go before God, but follow Him; for with Him as your guide you will not stumble, but will possess the light of life. These things I command and urge upon you as a most beloved son. If, as you promise, you obey and comply, you will surely be complying for your own salvation. May almighty God guide, preserve, and guard you according to His good pleasure.

Given at Anagni, on the Kalends of October.

DII. To Gerard, bishop of Angoulême.—He consoles him in affliction and confirms the interdict imposed upon the abbot of Redon.  
(1117, November 30.)

[MABILLON, *Benedictine Annals*, VI, 634.]

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother GERARD, bishop of Angoulême, vicar of the Apostolic See, and to the brethren with him, greeting and apostolic blessing.

The affection of our charity sympathizes with your brotherhood because we know that you are distressed by many troubles. Yet we too endure no lighter burden of tribulations. We ask your brotherhood, therefore, to pour out prayers and groans to almighty God, and to command that the same be done throughout all your parishes, so that almighty God may look upon His Church with manifold compassion and command the heat of persecutions to cease.

We consider valid the sentence of interdict which you pronounced against the abbot of Redon and his abbey, until he makes satisfaction to your judgment. We also admonish the count by our letters not to lend his assent to that man’s obstinacy, but rather to compel him to obey you. If he acts otherwise, whatever more severe decree you make against him by common counsel, we confirm by the assent of our favor.

Given at Trevana, on the second day before the Kalends of December.

DIII. He exhorts Conan, count of the Bretons, to compel the monks of Redon to restore Belle-Île to the monks of Quimperlé.  
(1117, November 30.)

[MABILLON, as above.]

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son CONAN, illustrious count of the Bretons, greeting and apostolic blessing.

You ought to know, dearest son, that there is no authority except from God. Therefore, having received authority through Him, do not raise the neck of your heart against Him, nor attack His Church. Rather, consider His omnipotence and humbly keep the commands of the Church, so that you who have received great things may merit to receive greater ones.

We have heard that the abbot of Redon, disregarding the reverence due to our vicar, the bishop of Angoulême, invaded Belle-Île by the force of your power and expelled from it the monks of Quimperlé. Since he refused to obey the judgment of the vicar in this matter, he was forbidden by that vicar from the office of abbot and priest, and the whole abbey was deprived of divine offices. Yet they despise that interdict with obstinate presumption.

We therefore admonish your natural disposition and command you, as a son of the Church, not to associate yourself with their arrogance, but yourself to compel them to submit to the Church’s judgment. Otherwise, whatever sentence proceeds against you for this offense, we shall, with God as author, hold it valid.

Given at Trevana, on the second day before the Kalends of December.

DIV. To William, count of Nevers.—That he should allow the monastery of Vézelay to remain undisturbed and free.  
(1117, December 21.)

[MANSI, *Councils*, XX, 1030.]

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to WILLIAM, illustrious man, count of the people of Nevers, greeting and apostolic blessing.

Your reputation among us is not slight, and we believe and have believed that you have fear and love of God, that you love justice, and that in other matters, as is fitting for so great a man, you conduct yourself honorably by God’s grace. We therefore exhort you to free the churches near you from oppression and to inflict no troubles upon them—especially those which belong to the protection or patronage of St. Peter. Such is the monastery of Vézelay: we wholly forbid and prohibit any exactions or usurpations to be established there by you or through the presumption of any persons whatsoever.

Indeed, as has been decreed by our predecessors, the pontiffs of the Apostolic See, and as we decree, leave that monastery peaceful and free by the right of St. Peter, according to the provisions of the testament of Count Gerard of noble memory. Otherwise St. Peter will exercise against you the vengeance of his lordship, and we shall defend his place by apostolic authority.

Given at Palestrina, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of January.

DV. To Daimbert of Sens and other bishops.—That they should protect the monastery of Vézelay.  
(1117, December 21.)

[MANSI, *Councils*, XX, 1031.]

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brethren and fellow bishops DAIMBERT of Sens, HUGH of Nevers, STEPHEN of Autun, JOCERAN of Langres, and HUGH of Auxerre, greeting and apostolic blessing.

[Col. 0428B] Your knowledge, we believe, is not unaware that, by the offering of its founder Count Gerard of illustrious memory, the monastery of Vézelay belongs by right to St. Peter. But certain persons, as we have learned, are attempting to impose exactions upon that place and inflict grave injuries. We therefore ask and exhort your brotherhood that, in fulfillment of your office, you strive to protect that place; and, if anyone causes it trouble, when requested by the abbot or brethren, administer justice in the matter in such a way that you may receive thanks from St. Peter and from us.

Given at Palestrina, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of January.

DVI. [Note: [Col. 0427D] The letter is wrongly entitled elsewhere: “to the archbishop of Poland”; elsewhere, “to the archbishop of Palermo”; [Col. 0428D] elsewhere, “to N., archbishop of the Poles,” etc. JAFFÉ.] To the archbishop (of Split): he explains why his legates, bearing the pallium, required an oath from him. He proposes the example of the Saxons and Danes for imitation.  
(Between 1099 and 1118.)

[MANSI, *Councils*, XX, 984.]

[Col. 0428C]

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to N., archbishop of the Poles.

You have reported, dearest brother, that the king and the great men of the realm were moved to astonishment because the pallium was offered to you by our envoys on the condition that you swear the oath which they had brought from us in writing. Brother, in the pallium the fullness of pontifical office is granted, because, according to the custom of the Apostolic See and of the whole Church, before receiving the pallium metropolitans are by no means permitted either to consecrate bishops or to hold a synod.

Let them be astonished in this matter also at the Lord Jesus Christ. For when the Lord Jesus Christ was about to entrust to Simon Peter the care of all His sheep, He set a condition, saying: “Do you love me, Simon Peter? Feed my sheep” [John 21]. If the maker and creator of consciences employed this condition—not only once, but a second time and even until grief—then with what care, with what forethought, ought we to impose upon brethren so great a preeminence in the Church and so great a care of Christ’s sheep, especially upon men whose consciences we do not see, with whom we have no familiarity, and whose affection we wholly do not know?

They say that every oath was prohibited by Christ God in the Gospel, and that no ordinance can be found concerning it either from the Apostles after the Lord or in councils. What then is the meaning of what the same Lord goes on to say: “What is more than this is from evil” [Matt. 5]? For the evil that compels us, by His permission, to require this additional thing is this: is it not evil to withdraw from the unity of the Church and from obedience to the Apostolic See? Is it not evil to break out against the ordinances of the sacred canons? How many have presumed to do this even after taking an oath! Did not your predecessor condemn a bishop without the knowledge of the Roman pontiff? Under what canons, under what councils, is this read to have been permitted? What should I say concerning translations of bishops, which among you are undertaken not by apostolic authority but at the king’s nod? To avoid these and other evils, such an oath is required.

Moreover, the Apostle James plainly teaches, adding why the Lord prohibited swearing: “that you may not fall under judgment” [James VI]; lest anyone, as St. Augustine explains, through the habit of frequent swearing slide by custom into perjury. Therefore no one should use an oath except from necessity, when he sees that people are slow to believe what it is useful for them to believe unless it is confirmed by an oath. We are plainly compelled by this evil and necessity [perhaps: “by this necessity”; H.] to require an oath for faith, obedience, and unity. Moreover, Paul’s Epistles testify that the Apostle swore because of the distrust of his hearers.

They say that no such statute is found in the councils—as though [Col. 0429C] any councils had prescribed a law for the Roman Church; whereas all councils have both been held by the authority of the Roman Church and received their force from it, and in their decrees Roman authority is expressly excepted. Was it not decreed in the sixteenth session of the Council of Chalcedon that, before all else, the chief honor of primacy should, according to the canons, be preserved for the most reverend archbishop of ancient Rome? Therefore, when the king and magnates judged that you should be released from the aforesaid condition of the oath, does this seem to you an evangelical judgment? Does it seem to you that our chief honor of primacy is preserved? Has that saying of the Lord slipped from your mind: “The disciple is not above the master” (Matt. 10)? Was it to the Hungarian prince that it was said: “And when you have turned, strengthen your brethren” (ibid.)? [Col. 0429D] Do we demand these things for the advancement of our own advantage, rather than establish a support for Catholic unity? They may despise the Apostolic See; they may raise their heel against us; they cannot overthrow or take away the privilege given by God, by which it was said to Peter: “You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church” (Matt. 16); and: “To you I will give the keys of the kingdom of heaven” (ibid.). Yet in four decrees of councils the manner of granting the pallium has been prescribed, and the form of profession or obedience has been established.

Since, therefore, you seek from the Apostolic See the insignia of your dignity, which are received only from the body of blessed Peter, it is just that you too should render to the Apostolic See [Col. 0430A] the due signs of submission, declaring that you adhere to blessed Peter as a member to a member and preserve the unity of the Catholic head. In these matters our predecessors have employed such moderation that nothing injurious, nothing difficult, has been imposed which all bishops ought not to observe even apart from our demand—those bishops who have decreed to remain in obedience and unity under the princes of the apostles, Peter and Paul. Are not the Saxons and Danes farther away than you? Yet their metropolitans both affirm the same oath, treat the legates of the Apostolic See honorably, assist them in their necessities, and visit the thresholds of the apostles through their envoys, not merely once every three years but every year. Thus, dearest brother, may we rejoice in you in the Lord, so that through you there may arise no occasion of withdrawal and dissension in the churches—far be it!

### DVII. To R[otho], prior of St. Frigidian at Lucca.  
*(Between 1099 and 1118.)*

[BALUZE, *Miscellanea*, Lucca edition, IV, p. 587.]

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable son R., prior of St. Frigidian, greeting and apostolic blessing.

We give thanks for your charity because you persevere more firmly in the unity of the Church, concerning which we had not the least doubt. For we have hoped, and do hope, good things from your wisdom; and in the Lord’s vineyard you have labored [Col. 0430C] and will labor as a good cultivator, and by God’s bounty you will receive from your labors an everlasting fruit. We have desired, and desire, peace and unity in the Church with the Lord; we have wished, and wish, scandals to be cut away. We ask, however, that if you should perhaps see any arise, you take care to inform us, since we cannot be everywhere in person or see everything with our own eyes. May your blessedness pray for us.

### DVIII. To the canons of St. Frigidian at Lucca.  
*(Between 1099 and 1118.)*

[BALUZE, *Miscellanea*, IV, p. 585.]

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons, the canons of St. Frigidian, greeting and apostolic [Col. 0430D] blessing.

Blessed be the Lord and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of mercies, who has deigned to multiply his grace in you. For a good report concerning you has spread not only in Tuscany but also in regions farther away; and the Lord himself also provides temporal goods more abundantly for your service. Therefore you ought to be more humble and serve him more fully. We therefore admonish you, sons, and beseech you in the Lord always to strive toward better things. For no one is so good that, through God’s grace, while life is lived in this world, he cannot advance to better things. Conduct yourselves, then, so that you may always be found more worthy of God’s grace.

### DIX. To the canons of Blessed Martin at Lucca.  
*(Between 1099 and 1118.)*

[BALUZE, ibid.]

[Col. 0431A]

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons, the canons of Blessed Martin, greeting and apostolic blessing.

In your common and individual affairs which came before us, we have always shown you our kindness. But certain of you, returning evil for good, broke out in injury against us, when you inflicted especially serious injuries and insults upon our sons, the canons of St. Frigidian. Although this appeared grave and intolerable to us, nevertheless, because the aforesaid brethren entreated us for you [Col. 0431B] and said that they kept peace with you, we forgive you all this. We ask that you love them with brotherly charity and endeavor to support one another, so that by God’s grace you may quietly devote yourselves to God’s service and always retain our good will.

### DX. To Rotho, prior of St. Frigidian at Lucca.  
*(Between 1099 and 1118.)*

[BALUZE, ibid.]

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son ROTHO, prior of St. Frigidian, greeting and apostolic blessing.

We entrusted the church of Blessed Floridus to your care, hoping that through your diligence it would be restored to a state [Col. 0431C] of regular discipline. But, for reasons unknown to me, you both ceased to provide for that church, and the community itself has fallen into decline. We therefore direct your charity to come to us by the next feast of blessed Martin, because we shall cause both the clergy of that church and the bishop to come to us at the same time, so that, God granting, we may order that church as is fitting.

### DXI. To Rotho, prior, and the canons of St. Frigidian at Lucca.  
*(Between 1099 and 1118.)*

[BALUZE, ibid., p. 584.]

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons ROTHO, prior, and his canons, greeting and [Col. 0431D] apostolic blessing.

Those who persecute you because of the protection of blessed Peter persecute not you but the Roman Church; concerning them it must be said to us: “Beware of your sons, and be watchful against those of your household” (Ecclus. 32). But do not fail in temptations; rather, stand courageously, according to that saying of the wise man: “My son, when you come to the service of God, stand in trembling and fear, and prepare your soul for temptation” (Ecclus. 2); and: “Take up the armor of God, that you may be able to resist on the evil day, and to stand perfect in all things” (Eph. 6). For we, with the Lord as author, shall persist, as we have begun, in protecting you. Blessed Peter does not know how to fail, for whose faith Christ himself, the author of faith, [Col. 0432A] prayed. May he protect you in all things with the shield of good will and grant that you may please him.

### DXII. He confirms the privileges of the monastery of Göttweig, at the request of Abbot Hartmann.

*(Between 1099 and 1118—Life of Altmann, bishop of Passau, in* Acta Sanctorum, *August II, p. 376.)*

### DXIII. He sends Abbot Hartmann of Göttweig “letters in which he forbids him and those subject to him communion with the excommunicated.”  
*(Between 1099 and 1118.)*

[BOLLANDISTS, August II, p. 376.]

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his dearest brethren HARTMANN, abbot of Göttweig, and his community, greeting and apostolic blessing.

[Col. 0432B] “Heaven and earth shall pass away, but the words of God shall not pass away” (Matt. 24). For he himself foretold what we see, what we experience daily: “Because iniquity has abounded, the charity of many shall grow cold”

(ibid.), etc.

### DXIV. Privilege for the church of Holy Trinity at Norwich.  
*(Between 1099 and 1118.)*

[*Monasticon Anglicanum*, I, p. 410.]

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother HERBERT, bishop of Norwich, greeting and apostolic blessing.

The authority of our office urges us to be solicitous for the condition of churches and to establish what has been rightly ordained. Therefore, dearest brother, by the authority of this present decree we confirm [Col. 0432C] your foundation: namely, that a community of monks living according to the rule shall always be maintained in the church of Norwich, which your energy has established from its deepest foundations in the name of the Holy Trinity. We further decree that, as hitherto it was at the town of Thetford, so henceforth the episcopal see shall be maintained for you and for your successors at the church of Norwich. None whatsoever of your successors may remove men of monastic discipline from the church, or take away its possessions and other goods provided by you, or those things which through your diligence, or through King Henry of England or other faithful persons, have been offered and allotted for the monks’ support, or which may hereafter, God disposing, be offered. [Col. 0432D] Moreover, these monks shall always remain in obedience to the bishop of Norwich and shall duly perform the offices of divine worship in that episcopal church, as we know was instituted in the Church of Canterbury by blessed Augustine and confirmed by the declaration of the most holy father Gelasius, doctor of the Catholic Church.

Adding these provisions, we decree that no person whatsoever may disturb that church, take away its possessions, retain what has been taken, diminish them, or harass it with rash vexations; but let all things be preserved whole for the benefit in every way of those for whose maintenance and governance they were granted. If any ecclesiastical or secular person in the future, knowing this page of our constitution, should rashly attempt to act against [Col. 0433A] it, and, after a second or third warning, does not make amendment by suitable satisfaction, let that person be deprived of the dignity of his power and honor; let him know that he stands guilty before the divine judgment for the iniquity committed; let him be cut off from the most holy body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Redeemer; and let him be subject to strict vengeance at the final judgment. But upon all who preserve what is right for that place, may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that they may receive here the fruit of good action and find before the strict Judge the reward of eternal peace. Amen.

### DXV. He takes the monastery of Andres under protection and confirms its goods and privileges, at the request of John, bishop of Thérouanne.  
*(Between 1099 and 1118.)*

[D’ACHERY, *Spicilegium*, II, p. 794.]

[Col. 0433B]

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son in Christ RAINALD, abbot of the monastery of Andres, situated in the diocese of Thérouanne, and to his successors to be regularly appointed forever.

A request of devout will ought to be brought to fulfillment with a corresponding result, so that the sincerity of devotion may shine forth laudably and the utility sought may assuredly acquire strength. Since, therefore, your belovedness, fleeing to the harbor of the Apostolic See, has duly and devoutly requested its protection, we, at the intercession of our venerable brother John, bishop of Thérouanne, graciously grant your petition and receive under the protection of the Apostolic See the monastery of Andres, situated in [Col. 0433C] the diocese of Thérouanne, over which, God being the author, you preside. This monastery, in the place called Andres outside the town of Guînes, Baldwin, count of Guînes of noble memory, with his wife Adela, is known to have built, through the grace of that same Savior, by the counsel of his sons and barons, for the salvation of their souls, in honor of the Lord and Savior and in the name of St. Rotrude the Virgin.

We therefore confirm to you and your successors, to possess forever, all things granted to your house through the aforesaid bishop of the Church of Thérouanne: namely, the chapel of St. Mary within the town of Guînes; the altar of Bredenarde; the altar of Lullinghem; the altar of Fercnes; and the altar of Eilinghem. [Col. 0433D] We also confirm to you all things which the aforesaid counts Baldwin and his wife, and his son Manasses, or their barons, have conveyed from their own right to this monastery of the Lord and Savior and St. Rotrude the Virgin: namely, all pasture around the place of Andres itself; rights of use in marsh, water, and turf; the land of Anteghem, with its villagers, all its revenues, and woodland; in the village of Guînes, a fishpond and the site of a mill; the land of Suanacas with its villagers and water-rights; the land of Campanies; the land of Bicedenarde; the land, villagers, woodland, and mill given by Garin of Fielnes and his mother; and other things which, because of their number, we refrain from listing. Whatever has also been given to the same monastery by other faithful persons, or may in the future be given or offered by the aforesaid counts and their barons, or by other faithful persons, or acquired by other just means, [Col. 0434A] shall remain secure and undiminished for you and your successors.

We decree, therefore, that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb that monastery, take away its possessions, retain what has been taken, diminish them, or harass it with reckless vexations; but let all things be kept whole for the benefit in every way of those for whose maintenance and governance they were granted, without prejudice to the canonical reverence due to the bishop of Thérouanne. We decree that the burial-place of that house shall be altogether free, so that both the descendants of the aforesaid counts [Col. 0434B] and all the barons called peers of the castle may be buried there according to their intention and determination. Nor may anyone oppose the devotion and last will of other persons who decide to be buried there, unless they are excommunicated.

If, therefore, any ecclesiastical or secular person in the future, knowing this page of our constitution, should rashly attempt to act against it, and, after a second or third warning, does not amend by suitable satisfaction, let that person lose the dignity of his power or honor; let him know that he stands guilty before divine judgment for the iniquity committed; let him be cut off from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Redeemer; and let him be subject to strict vengeance at the final judgment. But upon all who preserve what is right for that place [Col. 0434C] may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that they may receive here the fruit of good action and find before the strict Judge the rewards of eternal peace. Amen.

### DXVI. To Guy, archbishop of Vienne.—He confirms for him the bishopric and metropolitan rights, and sends the pallium.  
*(Between 1099 and 1118.)*

[MANSI, *Councils*, XX, p. 1046.]

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved brother GUY, archbishop of Vienne, and to his successors canonically appointed forever.

The Church recognizes that the power of binding and loosing in heaven and on [Col. 0434D] earth was principally entrusted by God to blessed Peter and his successors in the words by which the Lord addressed Peter: “Whatever you bind on earth shall be bound also in heaven” (Matt. 18). By the same divine author, both his own steadfastness and the strengthening of another’s faith are also granted to him when it is said: “I have prayed for you, Peter, that your faith may not fail; and when you have once turned, strengthen your brethren” (Luke 21). It is fitting, therefore, that we, who, though unworthy, seem to sit in Peter’s place, should correct what is wrong, establish what is right, and order throughout the whole Church those things which must be ordered according to the judgment of the inward Judge, so that our judgment may proceed from his countenance and our eyes may behold equity.

Accordingly, granting your just petitions, dearest brother [Col. 0435A] Guy, we fortify by the authority of the Apostolic See the holy Church of Vienne over which, God being the author, you preside. Therefore, by a decree to remain forever, Grenoble, Valence, Die, Alba—also called Viviers—Geneva, and Maurienne ought by perpetual right to be subject to the holy Church of Vienne as metropolitan. Moreover, we decree that Tarentaise shall always remain under the primacy of the Church of Vienne, as is known to have been established by our holy predecessors Leo, Nicholas, and Urban. We entrust to your brotherhood the governance and ordering of abbeys situated both within and outside the walls of the city of Vienne. Furthermore, we decree that whatever estates and gifts were granted or restored to your church by Roman emperors or kings of Burgundy, whatever it possesses today, and whatever it may in the future acquire lawfully and canonically, shall remain secure and undiminished for you and your successors. In addition, the privileges issued concerning the right or possessions of the Church of Vienne by the above-named predecessors of ours and by other Catholic pontiffs of the Apostolic See, we likewise decree shall remain forever firm and entire by authority of this present decree.

Your brotherhood is to remember to use the pallium only at the solemnities of Mass, and only on those days granted to your predecessors by the authority of the Roman Church; and we wish you in every respect to preserve its proper character. For the honor of this vestment is humility and justice. [Col. 0435C] Therefore your brotherhood should hasten to show itself with all its mind humble in prosperity; and in adversity, should it ever come, may it be found upright with justice: friendly to the good, opposed to the perverse, never showing partiality when truth speaks. Persist in works of mercy according to the means of your substance, yet desire to go beyond your means; sympathize with the infirm, rejoice with those in good health, exult in others’ joys as though they were your own; rage piously in correcting vices, and in fostering virtues soothe the souls of your hearers. In anger, preserve judgment free from anger; in tranquility, do not abandon the censure of just severity. This, dearest brother, is the dignity of the pallium. If you preserve it diligently, you will have inwardly what you show that you have received outwardly. May the condescension of heavenly mercy preserve your brotherhood safe for a long time.

Written by the hand of Peter, notary and regional official of the sacred palace.

### DXVII. Privilege for the Church of Beaulieu.  
*(Between 1099 and 1118.)*

[*Gallia Christiana*, old edition, IV, p. 152.]

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved brother in Christ B., abbot of the church of Beaulieu, and to his successors canonically appointed forever.

[Col. 0436A] It is fitting that we grant assent to just vows and lend our ears to just petitions, since, though unworthy, we seem, by the Lord’s ordering, to be placed as guardians and heralds of justice upon the lofty watchtower of the princes of the apostles Peter and Paul. Your brotherhood therefore requested that, following the example of our predecessors, the bishops of the Apostolic See, we should also fortify by a page of our privilege the church founded in honor of the Holy Sepulchre, over which, with the Lord as author, you preside. Therefore, from the benevolence of the Apostolic See, which is accustomed to assist all who ask for what is just, graciously granting your petition, venerable and beloved brother B. in Christ, because of the love and reverence of the Holy Sepulchre in which Christ deigned to be laid for us, we confirm by the page of this present decree the devout constitution of the holy [Col. 0436B] Church, as it was founded in ancient times and confirmed by the authority of our predecessors’ privileges—yet without prejudice to the rights of the Church of Tours.

Moreover, with the approval and consent of R., your metropolitan, we add and command under anathema that the consecrated cemetery of your church shall be the exclusive burial-place, all others being set aside, for every person, cleric or layman, of the castle of Loches. But the cemetery which the canons of St. Mary have usurped in that same castle contrary to Roman authority shall be considered invalid and abandoned by them, so that henceforth neither cleric nor layman shall be buried there.

### DXVIII. To the canons of St. Martin.—Whatever a faithful person offers to the Church is included under the name “offering” and ought not to be possessed by secular persons.  
*(Year uncertain.)*

[MANSI, *Councils*, XX, p. 1074.]

[Col. 0436C]

Moreover, first-fruits, tithes, and offerings are numbered chiefly among the goods of churches. Offerings are whatever things faithful persons offer to the Church from their own lawful possessions. Whoever, therefore, obtains them through secular power unquestionably strives against God and the decrees of the holy Fathers. Indeed, both the person who receives and the person who gives them is judged a robber and a sacrilegious person.

> **Note:** [Col. 0435] This also appears in Collection I, under the same title and chapter, differing in a few words from the Gregorian edition.

### DXIX. It teaches this: Where correction is undertaken in order to prevent sin, the principal person is admitted as a witness.  
*(Year uncertain.)*

[MANSI, *Councils*, XX, p. 1074.]

[Col. 0436D]

In every matter, the principal person, declaring the truth about a matter known to himself, is most properly to be accepted as a witness. When one such person is joined, two witnesses are made; when two are joined, three are made. The Lord plainly shows this when he says: “If your brother sins against you, rebuke him between yourself and him alone. But if he does not hear you, take with you one or two, that every word may stand in the mouth of two or three witnesses” (Matt. 18). And elsewhere he affirms, saying: “Let not one stand against another, [Col. 0437A] but let every word stand in the mouth of two or three witnesses” (John 8). Again elsewhere: “I am he who bears witness concerning myself, and the Father bears witness concerning me. For it is written in your law that the testimony of two men is true” (Deut. 19).

### DXX. Whether clerics owe tithes to clerics.  
*(Year uncertain.)*

[MANSI, as above.]

It is a new kind of exaction for clerics to demand from clerics tithes of crops or animals. Nowhere do we read that this is commanded or permitted in the law of the Lord. For Levites are not recorded as having received or extorted tithes from Levites. Those clerics who receive from clerics the labors of spiritual ministries owe tithes [Col. 0437B] to them.

> **Note:** [Col. 0437] See chapter 9, “On Tithes,” of the Gregorian Collection, where there is variation in several readings.

### DXXI. Those who do not permit the Church of God to be regularly ordered are to be judged sacrilegious.

[MANSI, ibid.]

There are some who, either by violence or by favor, do not allow churches to be regularly ordered. We have decreed that these too are to be judged sacrilegious.

### DXXII. He sells the Holy Spirit who grants tithes for money.

*(Ibid.)*

No believer is ignorant that to give an altar and tithes for money, and to sell the Holy Spirit, is the Simoniacal heresy.

### DXXIII. No bishop shall confer episcopal functions upon abbots who refuse to be subject to any bishop.

*(Ibid.)*

[Col. 0437C]

No bishop whatsoever shall administer any episcopal functions to abbots who are subject neither to a bishop, nor to a metropolitan, nor to a primate, nor to a patriarch. For since they profess themselves subject to no bishop whatsoever, it follows that no bishop should grant to them, as outsiders, those things which are his own.

### DXXIV. Monks and canons must by no means be compelled to pay tithes from their own labors.

*(Ibid.)*

[Col. 0437D] Divine law has ordained that tithes be rendered by the people to priests and Levites. But no principle permits soldiers, bishops, or any persons whatsoever to extort from monks or clerics living in community tithes from their labors, maintenance, or property. Hence blessed Gregory says: “For those who live the common life, what need is there for us to speak of making distributions, offering hospitality, and fulfilling works of mercy, when all that remains ought to be spent on pious and religious purposes, as the Lord says: ‘Give what remains as alms, and behold, all things are clean for you’” (Luke 11).

### DXXV. 1. Let one who obtains churches through laymen be excommunicated.

*(Ibid.)*

[Col. 0438A]

If any cleric, abbot, or monk obtains churches through laymen, let him be subject to excommunication according to the canons of the holy apostles and the chapter of the Council of Antioch.

#### 2. Let one who obtains churches through laymen, and the person who lays hands upon him, be deprived of communion.

Following the constitutions of the holy canons, we decree that any cleric who from this hour onward receives investiture of a church or ecclesiastical dignity from a lay hand, both he and the person who lays hands upon him shall be liable to the loss of his rank and shall be deprived of communion.

### DXXVI. On the same matter.

*(Ibid.)*

[Col. 0438B]

No layperson shall occupy or dispose of churches or the goods of churches. Whoever acts otherwise shall, according to the chapter of blessed Alexander, be excluded from the thresholds of the Church.

### DXXVII. On the same matter.

*(Ibid.)*

Just as the Lord’s garment was not torn, but lots were cast for it, so the Church must not be divided, because she exists wholly in unity. Therefore churches are to be restored to the authority of their own bishop and ordered by him, as the sacred canons provide. Otherwise [Col. 0438C] both the churches themselves and their clerics shall be deprived of divine offices.

### DXXVII *bis*. It establishes these provisions concerning burials and the wills of the dead.

[MANSI, *Councils*, XXII, p. 404.]

We wish—and this seems to us probable according to the judgment [variant: ordinances] of the canons—that, just as a dying person is permitted to make disposition of his possessions in whatever place he pleases, so it is likewise just that a person choosing burial should have freedom concerning his own body, in whatever place his wish may be, whether in monasteries or in other places [variant: religious places].

### DXXVIII. To Lanuin, prior of La Torre.  
*(Between 1101 and 1118.)*

[CAPIALBI, *Memorie della Chiesa Miletese*, p. 145.]

[Col. 0438D]

PASCHAL, bishop, etc., to his beloved son LANUIN, etc.

The sincerity of your religious life and the diligence of your ministry, which you exercise in restoring monasteries and churches, strongly move us to love you and cause us to give great thanks to Almighty God. Therefore, rejoicing in your religious life and placing great confidence in your zeal, dearest son, we exhort and command you diligently to inquire into the monasteries of our jurisdiction around you, and to endeavor, with [Col. 0439A] every discernment and moderation, to correct what has there fallen away from the discipline of the monastic rule; nor are you to neglect to restrain those who have hitherto lived in corrupt habits. For we command you to approach our brother the bishop of Miletus and confer with him fraternally concerning the complaint which he brings against the monks of St. Angelo. If you cannot establish peace and concord between them, at a suitable time let each party be sent to our judgment. For we do not fail to know that, at the instigation of his clerics, he has broken out so far as to tear the goods of blessed Peter with so many attacks; but against such instigators, unless they desist, we shall indeed wield the sword of blessed Peter and take vengeance ourselves.

> **Note:** [Col. 0439D] Father Mabillon, *Annales Benedictini*, book LXX, §55, reports this epistle down to the words *destinetur examen* (“be sent to our judgment”). I give it entire, having taken it from Tromby’s *Historia Cartusiana*.

### DXXIX. To Lanuin, prior of La Torre.  
*Fragment—Between 1101 and 1118.*

[In MABILLON, *Annals of the Order of St. Benedict*, V, p. 446.]

[Col. 0439B]

“Our mouth has been filled with joy, and our tongue with exultation” (Ps. 125:2), because we have heard that what had been broken has been made firm, and what had been dissolved has been bound together. Take care, therefore, lest Satan again deceive you and you return to the same thing—may God avert it. Do not presume upon fasts and prayers; embrace God, who is charity, etc. Pray for us.

### DXXX. To Victor of Bologna.—Monks must not usurp episcopal rights without the consent of bishops.  
*(Between 1104 and 1118.)*

[MANSI, *Councils*, XX, p. 1073.]

[Col. 0439C]

It has come to us, at which we greatly marvel, that certain monks and abbots in your diocese arrogantly claim for themselves episcopal rights and offices, contrary to the decrees of the holy Fathers: namely, penance, remission of sins, reconciliation, tithes, and churches. Yet without the permission of their own bishop or the authority of the Apostolic See, they ought by no means presume to do this, as the holy Fathers provided concerning such matters in the Council of Chalcedon and forbade it to all monks under the bond of anathema. We therefore direct your belovedness to summon them and altogether forbid them to presume henceforth to do such things.

### DXXXI. He confirms the monastery of Odense and its possessions, at the written request of King Nicholas and Bishop Hubald.  
*(Between 1105 and 1118.)*

[THORKELIN, *Diplomatarium Arna-Magnaeanum*. The Hague and Leipzig, 1786, quarto, I, p. 244.]

[Col. 0439D]

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother HUBALD, bishop of Odense, greeting and apostolic blessing.

[Col. 0440A] We have received the letters of our illustrious son King Nicholas, in which he stated that, by your counsel and consent, he had brought it about that, in this place, a community should be assembled according to this established form of religious monks. He asks that it be fortified by the authority of the Apostolic See, lest after his death or ours it be troubled by human assaults. In your letter likewise we learned that this was your desire and petition. Therefore, assenting to your wishes and petition, we fortify that community, by the Lord’s favor, by the page of this present privilege and the authority of the Apostolic See. We decree, therefore, that all estates and possessions which that same king, from royal right or generosity, has bestowed from the appurtenances of the Church of Odense for that community’s food and support shall always be preserved for it peacefully [Col. 0440B] and intact. Whatever may further be given or offered to that monastery by you yourselves or by other faithful persons, or acquired by other just means, with the Lord’s gift, shall remain established for it in perpetual stability. No bishop, king, or ecclesiastical or secular person whatsoever shall have authority to remove the monks from that place or to expel by force or stratagem the regular order of life there established; rather, let them always persevere peacefully in the observance of monastic life and in the service of almighty God.

We decree, therefore, that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb that monastery, take away its possessions, retain what has been taken, diminish them, or harass it with reckless vexations; but let all things be preserved whole for the benefit in every way of those for whose support and governance they were granted. If any ecclesiastical or secular person in the future, knowing this page of our constitution, should attempt to act against [Col. 0440C] it, and, after a second or third warning, does not amend by suitable satisfaction, let that person lose the dignity of his power and honor; let him know that he stands guilty before divine judgment for the iniquity committed; let him be cut off from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord, our Redeemer; and let him be subject to strict vengeance at the final judgment. But upon all who preserve what is right for that monastery, may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that they may receive here the fruit of good action and find before the strict Judge the rewards of eternal peace. Amen, amen, amen.

### DXXXII.  
> **Note:** [Col. 0439D] In this and the following two letters [Col. 0440D], the Vienna manuscript is reported to read P[aschal] instead of Innocent, and Ar[twic], bishop of Regensburg, instead of Henry, bishop of Regensburg; Wattenbach notes this in *Pertz Archiv*, X, p. 491. JAFFÉ.

To Conrad, archbishop of Salzburg.—That he should investigate the case of the abbot of St. Emmeram, accused of simony.  
*(Between 1107 and 1118.)*

[MANSI, *Councils*, XXI, p. 418.]

[Col. 0440D]

INNOCENT [PASCHAL], bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother CONRAD, archbishop of Salzburg, greeting and apostolic blessing.

[Col. 0441A] After we had sent letters to your brotherhood concerning the case of Pavo, abbot of St. Emmeram, our venerable brother the bishop of Regensburg wrote to us that the same abbot had been accused in a judicial proceeding, convicted of the crime of simony, and thus deposed. We therefore entrust the examination of this matter to your diligence in our stead, so that, going in person to the Church of Regensburg, you may carefully investigate whether the trial was regularly held; whether the accusers and witnesses were different persons; whether testimony was given against him in his presence and under oath; whether proceedings were conducted against him in writing; whether he had permission to answer and defend himself; and whether the status of the accusers or witnesses seems sufficiently consistent with the canons. If you find that these things were fully carried out, [Col. 0441B] let the judgment, as rendered, stand. Otherwise, let the abbot himself be restored to the aforesaid monastery according to the tenor of our letters, and, at a suitable date without delay, be canonically judged in the presence of you and our brethren.

### DXXXIII. To the same.—Concerning the bishop of Regensburg, who denies obedience to the Roman Church.  
*(Between 1107 and 1118.)*

[MANSI, ibid.]

INNOCENT [PASCHAL], bishop, servant of the servants of God, to CONRAD, archbishop of Salzburg, greeting and apostolic blessing.

As we recently learned of your adversities, so we would also desire to learn of your prosperity. For if you share in suffering, so do we; if you share in joy, we too share in joy. Moreover, concerning our brother, the bishop of Regensburg, we wish you to know how he has observed the obedience promised to the Roman Church. For the letters which we sent to him through the abbot of St Emmeram he at first treated lightly; on the second occasion he would not even receive them, and he subjected their bearer to grave insults. Therefore we forbid him, until he makes satisfaction, from every episcopal function, as he will be able to read in the letters which we have sent to him. We particularly wish these to be presented to him through you, lest they either be slighted or their judgment be kept secret.

### DXXXIV. To Henry [Artwic], Bishop of Regensburg—That he restore the Abbot of St Emmeram, or know himself to be under interdict. (Between 1107 and 1118.)

[MANSI, ibid.]

[Col. 0441D]

INNOCENT [PASCHAL], bishop, servant of the servants of God, to HENRY [ARTWIC], bishop of Regensburg, venerable brother: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Hoping that some benefit to the Church would come from you, we tolerated the less commendable beginnings of your advancement. But, contrary to our expectation, you are said to be bringing injury upon the Roman Church and to be scorning the obligation of the obedience you promised. You are attempting to remove from our jurisdiction the monastery of St Emmeram, which is known to belong to the Roman Church; and you so despised the letters of our authority, sent to you through the abbot of that monastery, that you subjected the bearer of the second letters to grave insults. Nor should you regard as a lesser offence the fact that, having been summoned by general letters to a synodal assembly, you wholly scorned to come.

[Col. 0442B] We cannot pass over in complete silence so great a contempt for the Apostolic See. Accordingly, sending repeated letters to you, we set before you this binding command: within twenty days after receiving this letter, you are to make full amendment for your former transgression—namely, restore Abbot Pavo completely to the aforesaid monastery and thereafter cease molesting him. Otherwise, know that you are forbidden from every episcopal function until you effectively fulfil this command and render us justice for your contempt of us.

### DXXXV. To Pontius, Abbot of Cluny—On not administering communion by intinction.

> **Note [Col. 0441D].** To understand properly what the pope here decrees concerning the prohibition of administering communion by intinction, and its administration separately under the form of bread and separately under the form of wine, consult the *Micrologus*, whose author flourished under Gregory VII. In chapter 26, on avoiding intinction, he wrote as follows: “It is not authorized that certain persons dip the Lord’s body [the consecrated bread] and distribute it, dipped, to the people as the completion of communion. For the Roman order is opposed to it,” etc. Since this improper practice, introduced into communion, did not cease even after this rebuke, Paschal prohibited this manner of distribution by apostolic authority and restored the former practice by this decretal letter. But because the introduced practice of intinction did not cease even then, the Church afterwards began to communicate frequently under the single form of bread only, and thereafter rightly commanded this practice to be frequent. SEV. BIN. See the note of Peter de Marca on canon XXVIII of the Council of Clermont. P. COSSART.

(Between 1109 and 1118.)

[MANSI, *Concilia*, XX, 1013.]

[Col. 0442C]

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his dearest son PONTIUS, abbot of Cluny: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Writing to Caecilius, Blessed Cyprian says: “When anything is commanded by God’s inspiration and ordinance, it is necessary that the faithful servant obey the Lord. He is excused before all, because he presumptuously assumes nothing for himself, lest anything be done by us other than what the Lord first did for us.”

Therefore, in receiving the body and blood of the Lord, the Lord’s tradition is to be observed, according to Cyprian himself; nor is departure to be made, through a human and novel institution, from what Christ the master both commanded and performed. For we know that bread separately and wine separately were delivered by the Lord himself. We teach and command that this custom is always to be maintained in the holy Church, except for little children and persons wholly infirm, who cannot swallow bread.

### DXXXVI. Bull for Gerard of Ham, dean of the church of St Quentin. (Fragment; between 1115 and 1118.)

[COLLIETTE, *Mémoires du Vermandois*, II, 157.]

[Col. 0443A]

We have learned that our fellow brother Lambert, bishop of the Church of Noyon, granted certain altars, which your church possessed partly through concessions of former bishops and which had partly been restored by the brethren who possessed them, to be established as free; so that, once the difficulty of the *personatus* [personal benefice] has been removed, they may henceforth remain peacefully in the possession of St Quentin—namely, the altar of the Cross of Hamel, Aintencourt, Roupi, Alisia, Lulliaco, and Burencourt. Therefore, by the authority of this present document, we confirm this arrangement of those altars.

## DOUBTFUL DOCUMENTS

[Col. 0443]

### DXXXVII. He grants various privileges to the Church of Christ at Colchester and confirms its possessions.

[Monastic. Angl., II, 45.]

[Col. 0443A]

[Col. 0443B] PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son in Christ ERNULPH, provost, and to the other beloved sons and brethren of the Church of Christ at Colchester: greeting and apostolic blessing.

It has always been the distinctive privilege of the Apostolic See that, through us, though unworthy, the condition of the churches subject to us throughout the world may be directed, established, and increased. Moreover, although by the authority and goodwill of the Apostolic See we owe this to all the children of holy Church, it is especially fitting that we apply ourselves with more earnest care to those places and persons distinguished by a fuller measure of religious devotion, so that, to those upon whom God, the universal Creator, has bestowed a more abundant bounty of his mercy, we too, following his example, may confer a more eminent dignity.

[Col. 0443C] Therefore we judge, not without reason, that your place or canonical community should be honoured with more ample gifts of our favour, since almighty God has planted there, as a model of the primitive Church, a certain outstanding prerogative of the primitive Church itself—showing what the potter can do with clay, the moulder with a formed thing, God with a human being. For, as we have learned from religious persons, you were the first in your land to flourish as professors of canonical religious life, freely offering to God your Creator the firstfruits of your bodies and souls.

And therefore, by the authority of this our second privilege, we decree that, just as you were the first in England to serve in this order, so you are always to be held first also in its dignity; so that, wherever weakness is perceived among canonical communities in England through the negligence of the brethren, your strong authority, through us, may bring assistance. And if perchance, at the instigation of the devil, any brother should fall away from this order, whether for a worldly cause or in imitation of another order, he is to be recalled by the authority of the aforesaid community of Colchester, wherever he may be found, and punished as an apostate and deserter from his former service.

[Col. 0443D] All other communities are therefore to be governed according to the pattern of your canonical life or institution. From you, wise persons are to be chosen; once chosen, they are to be distributed among the canonical communities; and, if necessary, once distributed, they are to be placed over individual houses. Thus, in every place where the integrity of canonical religious life flourishes, your regular authority shall, through us, prevail above all. We command that the Church of Holy Trinity in London, entrusted to you by Queen Matilda, together with the Church of St Leonard and all the other obediences which you possess, shall be subject to your jurisdiction; and in accordance with this command we promulgate the present decree.

[Col. 0444A] If any of the brethren dwelling there, through pride, deceit, secretly or openly, and as though introducing the authority of secular power, should attempt to withdraw them from your hand, may he whose bodily sword deprived Malchus of his ear destroy that man’s soul with his spiritual sword. Concerning all else granted to you—whether tithes or other possessions—which you have justly acquired, or may acquire, through the compassion of kings or the generosity of princes, let the same judgment stand by the judgment of the Holy Spirit.

That we may provide for your peace in every respect, we will that you be free from every yoke, whether of secular or ecclesiastical persons. In the name of the Lord and by apostolic censure, we forbid and establish, by the authority of St Peter,

[Col. 0444C] that no archbishop or bishop, no king or prince, and no person at all, great or small, may rashly presume, under penalty, in any manner or upon any occasion, to take away or diminish anything belonging to the monastery of Colchester, to inflict violence, harass it, or disturb God’s servants; so that, defended solely by the protection of the Holy Roman Church, they may remain secure forever.

Upon the death of you, Ernulph, the present provost of that place, or of any of your successors, no one is to be placed over it by any crafty device, except one whom the brethren, by common consent or by the sounder part of their counsel, elect. The person elected is to be presented to the bishop of London for consecration, and from him they are to receive chrism and holy oil, consecrations of altars and churches, and ordinations of canons—provided that he possesses the favour and communion of the Apostolic See, and is willing to furnish all these things freely and without burden to the brethren, every exaction set aside.

[Col. 0444D] But if anything should prevent this, it shall be lawful for the aforesaid provost or the brethren to approach whichever bishop they wish and receive from him the aforesaid sacraments, so that the same canonical community may appear subject solely to the Roman Church and to none other except in this respect.

Since from the time of our fathers the ministry of the word of God, the office of preaching, baptism, and reconciliation of penitents have always been entrusted to this order—as may be seen in the treatises of St Augustine addressed to Pope Aurelius—we, following their examples and considering more carefully the high dignity of the order,

[Col. 0445A] confirm the enactments of the Fathers and sanctify what we confirm by the authority of this present document. Whoever shall rashly presume to transgress them in any respect shall, by the judgment of the Holy Spirit and of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, be bound by the bond of anathema and assigned to eternal punishments with the transgressing angels and Judas the betrayer, unless he promptly repents with fitting satisfaction. But upon those who preserve these provisions may blessing with mercy remain, so that here they may receive the fruit of their good action and, before the strict Judge, find the rewards of eternal recompense.

You know, brethren, that, as a further measure of our love, we twice sent you an altar, upon which relics of saints had been placed, through the hands of our son, your brother Zeno, entreating

[Col. 0445B] you to walk worthily of the calling to which you have been called.

Written by the hand of Grisogonus, registrar and notary of the sacred palace.

Given at the Lateran through the hand of Gaietanus, chancellor and librarian of the Holy Apostolic See, in the month of August, in the year 1116 of the Lord’s Incarnation, the ninth indiction, the twentieth year of the pontificate of Lord Paschal II, pope; in the reign of our Lord Jesus Christ, whose praise and dominion endure unto ages of ages. Amen.

### DXXXVIII. He confirms the privileges of the Church of the Holy Saviour at the Lateran.

[COCQUELINES, *Ampl. Collect.*, II, 134.]

PASCHAL, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons ROCIO, prior of the venerable basilica of the Holy Saviour, and his brethren, present and future, professing the regular life: perpetual greeting and apostolic blessing.

[Col. 0445C] The greater the dignity which the Lateran Church is known to possess by ancient institution, the more fitting it is that this same venerable place should be held in greater reverence and that efforts should be made by us and by other faithful people of God toward its increase, both spiritual and temporal. Nor is there any doubt that, if we grant the petitions of religious men with paternal kindness, we find the merciful Lord favourable in our own necessities.

Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, out of reverence for

[Col. 0445D] the Saviour and blessed John the Baptist, we grant and confirm to you and your successors forever the whole and undivided parish, so that during our lifetime and after our death special prayer may continually be offered to the Lord for us: namely, from the church of St Nicholas of Forna, along the road which comes from Stephen on the Caelian Hill and reaches the aforesaid basilica of our Saviour; and from the gate of the monastery of the Holy Four Crowned Ones, descending by the slope onto the Via Maggiore, and thence along the street on both sides as far as the Lateran field; then turning above the church of Saints Marcellinus and Peter as far as the church of St Bartholomew at the head of the Merulone; then from St Daniel, descending to the gate of the church of the City, and turning before the church

[Col. 0446A] of St Nicholas of the Hospital to the aforesaid basilica of the Saviour.

We further establish, and by the authority of the Apostolic See confirm, that this parish shall henceforth be under no obligation whatsoever to render spiritual or divine services to any other church, monastery, or pious establishment; but shall remain forever, peacefully and freely, under the jurisdiction of the aforesaid basilica of the Saviour, in the capacity of a parish. The hereditary right, however, which within the aforesaid boundaries is recognized as belonging to the aforesaid churches, monasteries, or pious establishments, is reserved.

We therefore command that no person may lawfully build churches, erect an altar, or establish any religious institution within the aforesaid parish, apart from the aforesaid basilica of the Saviour.

[Col. 0446B] Establishing by apostolic censure, under the adjuration of divine judgment and the prohibition of anathema, that none of our successors ever, nor any other person, great or small, may presume to violate or disturb the gift of this our privilege. Moreover, if anyone—which we do not believe—should attempt to oppose or act against this our apostolic command, let him be bound by the bond of anathema and be estranged from the kingdom of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ.

But whoever, with devout intent, shall prove the guardian and observer of this our privilege, may he deserve to obtain from our most merciful Lord the grace of blessing unto ages of ages. Amen, amen, amen.

I, Paschal, bishop of the Catholic Church. I, Lambert, bishop of Ostia, was present and subscribed. [Col. 0446C] I, Vincentius, bishop of Porto, subscribed. I, Cinthius, bishop of Sabina, was present and subscribed. I, Denigo, bishop of Tusculum, was present and subscribed. I, Conrad, bishop of Palestrina, subscribed. I, Leo, bishop of Albano, was present and subscribed. I, Benedict, cardinal priest of the title of Eudoxia, was present and subscribed. I, Theobald, cardinal priest of the title of Pammachius, subscribed. I, Raynerius, cardinal priest of the title of St Eusebius, subscribed. [Col. 0446D] I, Arnaldus, cardinal priest of the title of St Clement, was present and subscribed. I, Raynerius, cardinal priest of the title of Saints Marcellinus and Peter, subscribed. I, Otto, cardinal priest of the title of St Pastor, subscribed. I, Peter, cardinal priest of the title of Equitius, subscribed. I, Amicus, cardinal priest … was present and subscribed. I, Paul, cardinal priest of St Sixtus, subscribed. I, Jonatas, cardinal deacon of Saints Cosmas and Damian, subscribed. I, Theoninus, cardinal deacon of St Mary in Portico, was present and subscribed. I, Gregory, cardinal deacon of St Angel, subscribed. I, John, cardinal deacon of St Lucy, was present and subscribed. [Col. 0447A] I, Gregory, cardinal deacon of St Lucy, was present and subscribed.

Given at the Lateran through the hand of John, cardinal deacon and librarian of the Holy Roman Church, on the sixth day before the Kalends of January, in the fifteenth indiction, in the year 1116 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and the seventh year of the pontificate of Lord Paschal, pope.

[Col. 0447]

## LETTERS OF VARIOUS PERSONS TO POPE PASCHAL

### I. Letter of Pibo, Bishop of Toul, to Paschal on behalf of the canons of Calmosiacum. (1099.)

[MARTENE, *Thesaurus Anecdotorum*, III, 1171.]

[Col. 0447B]

To PASCHAL, supreme pontiff of the holy and apostolic see, PIBO, by the gift and grace of God bishop of Toul: the unwearied rendering of due obedience.

Although an immense desire and pressing necessity to approach your presence have always been mine, I feel the desire and necessity increase daily within me, while the possibility of attaining them retreats ever further. For the failing of my body, now through old age no longer governing itself—indeed, no longer even sustaining itself—denies this to me, and the heavy burden of pastoral care weighs me down. Since I do not presume that I have exercised the direction of this care as I ought, I, being most negligent, dread to come without intercessors for pardon before the judgment-seat of the Shepherd of all shepherds.

[Col. 0447C] This was especially my reason for wishing to come to you: to receive from you absolution for my innumerable faults. But because I fail in this, and do not in the least doubt that you care for me, since you care for all, I implore with tearful prayers another favour from your most generous mercy.

There are in my diocese regular canons, observing, according to their capacity, the Rule of blessed Augustine, who live in a place called Calmosiacum. Desiring to enjoy their acquaintance and fellowship, most pleasing to me, I visited their place; and, being admitted into their community, I conferred upon that place the altar of the parish church, concerning which there is a dispute between them and the people of Remiremont, upon this condition: that, just as until now the priest who held the church received the altar from my hand, so henceforth the person wishing to hold the church should receive the altar from the hand of the abbot of that place.

[Col. 0447D] Since I do not fail to recognize that the greater part of their peace and tranquillity depends upon that church, and since I have no hope of being left in peace if I do not establish them in peace, therefore, Holy Father, I and our clergy, prostrate at your feet, ask that you confirm by your authority, as enduring forever, the gift which you have heard was made by me. And so that all our successors, both bishops and the other persons of the Church of Toul, may know

[Col. 0448A] that I first performed this on my own part, which I ask to be confirmed by apostolic authority, I have left my seal attached to this charter as a memorial of the act. I beseech all my successors in Christ to apply their zeal to its observance as they themselves desire that their good deeds be kept inviolate by those who come after them.

### II. Letter of Walter, Bishop of Chalon, to Pope Paschal, on behalf of the monastery of Cîteaux. (1100.)

[Gall. Christ., Nov. IV, 234.]

To the venerable Father Pope PASCHAL, WALTER, servant of the Church of Chalon: greeting and due submission.

As your holiness ardently desires that the faithful may advance in true religion, so it is not fitting that they should lack the shelter of your protection and the support of your consolation.

[Col. 0448C] We therefore humbly request that you approve what was done concerning those brethren who, desiring a stricter life, withdrew from the church of Molesme at the counsel of holy men, and whom divine mercy has placed in our episcopal jurisdiction. The bearers of this letter, sent by them, are present before you. We ask that, in accordance with the command of your predecessor and of the archbishop of Lyons, then legate of the Apostolic See, and with the decision and written instrument of the fellow bishops and abbots—in this matter we too were present and, with others, its authors—you may deign to approve what was done and to strengthen by the privilege of your authority that that place remain forever a free abbey, while preserving the canonical reverence due to our person and to our successors. The abbot whom we ordained in that place, together with the other brethren, likewise most urgently seeks this confirmation from your mercy as a safeguard for their peace.

### III. Circular letter of Daimbert, Archbishop of Pisa, Godfrey of Bouillon, and Raymond, Count of Saint-Gilles—On the victories won by the Christian army in the Holy Land. (1100.)

> **Note [Col. 0447D–0450D].** Caesar Baronius had before him a copy of these letters full of errors. With the assistance of William of Tyre, he published them in some measure corrected in his *Ecclesiastical Annals* under the year 1100; nevertheless, even so corrected, they still fail in many respects. Here we present a much improved text from a manuscript codex of the monastery of Signi.

[MARTENE, *Thesaurus Anecdotorum*, I, 281.]

To the lord pope of the Roman Church, to all bishops, and to all worshippers of the universal Christian faith: I, the archbishop of Pisa, and the other bishops; GODFREY, by the grace of God now advocate of the Church of the Holy Sepulchre; RAYMOND, count of Saint-Gilles; and the entire army of God which is in the land of Israel: greeting, and the multiplying of prayers and supplications with joy and exultation in the sight of the Lord.

[Col. 0449A] For God has magnified his mercy by fulfilling in us the things which he promised in ancient times. When the army departed after the capture of the city of Nicaea, there were more than three hundred thousand there. Although this enormous multitude could have occupied the whole of Romania, drained all its rivers, and consumed all its crops in a single day, yet the Lord led them with such abundance that a ram could scarcely be bought for one coin and an ox for twelve. Moreover, if Saracen princes and kings rose against us, by God’s will they were easily defeated and trampled down.

On account of these successes, because some had become puffed up, God set Antioch before us—a city impregnable by human power. There he detained us for nine months, and so humbled us in the siege outside it that all the swelling of our pride gave way to humility. Thus, when we had been humbled to the point that scarcely one hundred good horses could be found in the entire army, God opened to us the abundance of his blessing and mercy,

[Col. 0449B] led us into the city, and delivered the Turks and all their possessions into our power. When we held these things as though gained by our own strength and did not worthily magnify God who had bestowed them, we were besieged by so great a multitude of Saracens that no one dared go out from such a great city. Moreover, famine grew so severe in the city that some scarcely restrained themselves from human food.

It would take long to recount the miseries within the city. But the Lord, looking upon the people whom he had scourged for so long, graciously consoled them. Thus, as though in recompense for their affliction, he offered us his lance—an unseen gift, a pledge of victory from the time of the apostles. He then so strengthened human hearts that he infused the power to take up arms and fight manfully against the enemy into those whom illness or hunger had deprived of strength to walk.

Then, after the enemy had been overcome, when the army was wasting away at Antioch from famine and weariness, especially because of the dissensions of the princes,

[Col. 0449C] we set out for Syria, captured the Saracen cities of Barra and Marra, and gained possession of the fortresses of the region. When we had resolved to remain there, the famine in the army became so great that the Christian people ate the bodies of Saracens already putrefying. Then, as we advanced by divine direction into the interior of Hispania [probably a corrupt reading; contextually, Syria], we had with us the most generous, merciful, and victorious hand of the almighty Father. For the citizens and castellans of the region through which we advanced sent envoys ahead to us with many gifts, ready to serve and surrender their towns; but since our army was not numerous and they hastened unanimously to reach Jerusalem, we accepted guarantees and made them tributary, although a single one of the many cities along that coast had more inhabitants than there were men in our army.

[Col. 0450A] When it was heard at Antioch, Laodicea, and Edessa that the hand of the Lord was with us, many from the army who had remained there joined us at Tyre. Thus, with God travelling and working with us, we reached Jerusalem. During its siege the army endured great hardship, chiefly because of the shortage of water. After taking counsel, the bishops and princes proclaimed that the city was to be encircled barefoot, so that he who entered it for our sake in humility might, through our humility, open it to us for his own sake, in order to execute judgment upon his enemies.

Accordingly, appeased by this humility, the Lord on the eighth day after the act of humiliation gave us the city together with its enemies—on the very day when the primitive Church was driven from it, when many faithful celebrate the feast of the Division of the Apostles. And if you wish to know what was done to the enemies found there, know that in Solomon’s portico and in his temple our men rode in Saracen blood up to their horses’ knees.

[Col. 0450B] Then, after arrangements had been made for those who were to retain the city, while others wished to return out of love for their homeland and devotion to their relatives, it was reported to us that the king of Babylon had come to Ascalon with an innumerable multitude of pagans, intending to lead the Franks who were at Jerusalem into captivity and to capture Antioch. So he said; but the Lord had determined otherwise concerning us.

When we had ascertained for certain that the army of Babylon was at Ascalon, we hurried to meet them, leaving our baggage and sick people in Jerusalem with a guard. When our army and that of the enemy came into view of one another, we bent our knees and called upon God our helper: since he had confirmed the law of the Christians in our other necessities, may he now, by breaking the strength of the Saracens and the devil, extend everywhere the kingdom of Christ and the Church from sea to sea.

[Col. 0450C] Without delay God came to those crying to him and supplied us with such strength of courage that anyone who saw us charge the enemy would have judged a thirsty stag sluggish beside a spring of living water. This was extraordinary, since our army had no more than five thousand knights and fifteen thousand infantry, while that of the enemy may have had one hundred thousand cavalry and four hundred thousand infantry.

Then the Lord appeared wonderful in his servants, when, before we fought, by our charge alone he turned that multitude to flight and stripped them of all their weapons, so that, should they afterwards wish to resist us, they would have no weapons in which to place hope. There is no need to inquire how great the booty was, when the treasures of the king of Babylon were seized. More than one hundred thousand Moors fell there by the sword.

[Col. 0450D] Their terror was so great that up to two thousand were suffocated at the city gate. There is no count of those who perished in the sea. Thickets also trapped many of them. Indeed the whole world fought for us; and had the plunder of the camp not detained many of our men, few from so great a multitude of enemies would have remained able to report the battle.

Although the matter is lengthy, this must not be passed over: on the day before the battle, the army captured many thousands of camels, oxen, and sheep. When, by command of the princes, the people released these and advanced to battle, marvellous to relate, the camels formed many and varied squadrons; the oxen and sheep did likewise. These animals accompanied us: when we stood, they stood; when we advanced, they advanced; when we ran, they ran. Clouds also defended us from the sun’s heat and refreshed us.

[Col. 0451A] When the victory had been celebrated, the army returned to Jerusalem. Leaving Duke Godfrey there, Count Raymond of Saint-Gilles, Count Robert of Normandy, and Count Robert of Flanders returned to Laodicea. There they found the Pisan fleet and Bohemond. After the archbishop of Pisa had reconciled Bohemond with our lords, Count Raymond resolved to return to Jerusalem for God and for the brethren.

Therefore, we invite you to the devotion displayed in the wondrous courage of your brethren, to so glorious and desirable a reward from almighty God, to the remission through God’s grace, so earnestly to be desired, of all your sins, and to the rejoicing of Christ’s Catholic Church and of the whole Latin people; and we invite all bishops, clerics and monks of good life, and all laypeople. May he who lives and reigns with the Father, God in the unity of the Holy Spirit through all ages of ages, make you sit at God’s right hand. Amen.

[Col. 0451C] We ask and implore you through the Lord Jesus, who has always been with us, laboured with us, and delivered us from every tribulation, that you remember your brethren who are returning to you: do good to them and pay their debts, so that God may do good to you and absolve you from all sins, and that God may grant you a share in every good which either we or they have deserved before God.

### IV. First letter of Lambert, Bishop of Arras, to Paschal. (1101.)

[BALUZE, *Miscellanea*, ed. Luc., II, 155.]

To the reverend Father and lord, Pope PASCHAL, LAMBERT, unprofitable servant of the holy Church of Arras: due reverence with prayers.

[Col. 0451D] Your highness, reverend Father, was pleased to entrust to my weakness the division of the old and new borough between the canons and monks of Arras. Desiring to satisfy your command, and with both parties absent so that contention might not arise between them or the arbiters be corrupted in any way, we carefully investigated the matter through the oldest and most truthful persons, whom we believed suspect to neither side, as you commanded. We reported the division, once determined, to the canons and monks. But the abbot, because he had not been present at this division, refused to accept it.

Since a meeting of fellow bishops was soon to take place at Reims, we sent both parties there with their assent, so that on the appointed day we might carry out, with their counsel, what should be done in this matter. When we met on the appointed day and wished, as the abbot had requested, to complete the division through the counsel of bishops in the presence of religious men, both abbots and prelates, we admonished those arbiters, in the name of obedience and on the part of almighty God, blessed Peter, yourself, and ourselves, to divide the old and new borough truthfully.

[Col. 0452B] When, to prevent the truth from being silenced, we placed a stole around our neck under pain of excommunication, the monk William—subjected to no oppression and burdened by no prejudice on the abbot’s part—summoned our canons before you, for the coming Kalends of October, to your and our injury, not concerning the case then being heard but concerning nine denarii. By thus creating disturbance, he caused the abbot to withdraw from our presence and from the case.

The canons, perceiving that this had been done in order to delay and take away their cause, compelled by this oppression and other pressures, appealed to the Roman hearing, summoning the abbot himself to appear before you at the approaching feast of St Andrew. Thus, reverend Father, the canons of Arras, compelled like wards,

[Col. 0452C] flee humbly to the mercy of your consolation, to be cherished as though in a mother’s bosom. They ask—and we ask for and with them—that you defend the Church of Arras from the hands of those stronger than it, establish it in peace, and by your authority restore the parochial rights which canonically belong to it.
