For in our days the Church of Arras, as though brought out from a prison-house and released from bonds, has through your privileges and writings, and those of your predecessor of worthy memory, Pope Urban, been restored to freedom and to its ancient condition; it has already begun somewhat to recover its breath and strength. Sustain it in such a manner that you may deserve to receive a good reward from the Lord Jesus Christ.

But now, since the hand of the Lord weighs heavily upon me by day and night, gracious Father, and since, labouring upon the sea, I have made little progress and continue to make little progress,

[Col. 0452D] pray to God, the Father of mercies and of all consolation, that through your holy prayers he may deign, by his only-begotten and beloved Son, our Saviour, to save me a sinner from being overwhelmed in the sea and mercifully lead me out of the darkness of this life.

### V. Second letter of the same to Paschal—Concerning the clerics of Ypres. (1101.)

[*Actes de la province ecclésiastique de Reims*, II, 153.—The following letters of Lambert are drawn from the same collection.]

To the most reverend lord and Father of fathers, PASCHAL, [Col. 0453A] LAMBERT, by God’s mercy bishop of Arras: due submission with prayers.

We have decided the case of the bishop of Thérouanne and the clerics of Ypres in the following manner, as Your Fatherhood commanded us. When both parties appeared before us on the day appointed for them, we gave them the option of choosing judges against whom no suspicion could be raised, so that nothing contentious might be done in this case. The bishop agreed; the clerics refused. Finally, the bishop said that he was prepared to prove that they had obtained the Church of Ypres by simony; that they had received it from Lord Gerard after the Council of Nîmes; and that this same Gerard had at that time been suspended by Pope Urban of blessed memory from every episcopal function. The clerics, however, were wholly unwilling to give any answer to this objection of his [Col. 0453B], asking only that we grant them a postponement because one of their companions was absent, whom they said was ill. Therefore, when we directed them to undergo judgment on these matters, they said that they had not come to submit to any judgment, but would withdraw unless the postponement they requested were granted. Acting by your apostolic authority—that is, exercising your office in this matter—we forbade them to depart from our presence, or rather yours, except in judicial and canonical order. But they made light of all this; disobedient to God, to you, and to us, and without any judgment having been rendered against them or any prejudice done to them, they declared that they regarded us and all our brethren as suspect, and appealed again to your hearing. Yet Your Holiness knows [Col. 0453C] that such an act, not an appeal but mockery, must be invalidated for two reasons: first, because it is not lawful to appeal from the Apostolic See to another; secondly, because we gave them the option of chosen judges, from whom it is likewise not lawful to appeal. Accordingly, our brethren judged that the bishop of Thérouanne had established his case, and that they ought to be bound by the bond of anathema if, from that day forward, they should wrong the bishop concerning that church. We therefore entreat Your Holiness that what, obeying your command and acting in your stead, we have decided truly and without respect of persons may be strengthened by your authority. We also seek the counsel of your Apostolic See on this matter of God and ours. In our presence, a certain cleric accused an abbot [Col. 0453D] of having bought a church by simony, which he promises to prove. Let Your Fatherhood therefore write back to us with how many witnesses and by what persons he may prove this—whether laymen, clerics, subdeacons, deacons, or priests—and what the abbot is to do if the cleric fails.

VI. The same writer’s third letter to Paschal.—On behalf of the Archbishop of Reims. (Year 1101.)

To the most reverend lord and Father of fathers, Pope PASCHAL, LAMBERT, by God’s mercy bishop of Arras, due submission together with prayers.

On behalf of our venerable metropolitan, Lord Manasses, Archbishop of Reims, concerning whom Lord John, bishop of Thérouanne, is being sent to the discretion of Your Holiness, that you may deign to hear him, our humility most humbly entreats Your Excellency. For we know by experience that the aforesaid metropolitan reveres the decrees of the Apostolic See, loves truth, fears God, honours religious men and men of good repute, and, especially, shows himself diligent in the care of the poor. May favourable Divinity long preserve safely among us the holiness of your fatherhood, which bears the care of all the churches.

VII. The same writer’s fourth letter to Paschal.—On the Synod of Paris. (Year 1103.)

To the most reverend lord and Father of fathers, Pope PASCHAL, LAMBERT, by God’s mercy bishop of Arras, due submission together with prayers.

The archbishops assembled at Paris by your authority—Lord Daimbert of Sens and Rodulf of Tours—and likewise the bishops Ivo of Chartres, John of Orléans, Humbald of Auxerre, Gualo of Paris, Manasses of Meaux, Baldric of Noyon, and Hubert of Senlis, caused to be read the letters sent from your see concerning the king’s satisfaction and absolution. When the letters had been read and understood, they sent the bishops John of Orléans and Gualo of Paris to ask the king whether he would make satisfaction according to the tenor of your letters and had resolved to renounce the sin of carnal and unlawful union. [Col. 0454C]

He replied graciously that he willingly wished to make satisfaction to God and to the Holy Roman Church, and to comply with the command of the Apostolic See and with the counsel of the archbishops and bishops present. Accordingly, in the presence of the aforesaid bishops and also of the abbots Adam of Paris, of the title of Saint-Denis; Renald, of the title of Saint-Germain of Paris; Ulric of Paris, of the title of Saint-Magloire; likewise Rainold of Étampes, of the title of the Holy Trinity; of very many archdeacons; and of the honourable clerics and laypeople standing about, the king came most devoutly and very humbly, barefoot, renouncing the sin and making amends for the excommunication; and thus, by your authority, he deserved to receive absolution.

When this had been done, touching the most holy Gospels, he renounced the union and the offence of the unlawful relationship in these words:

> “Hear, Lambert, bishop of Arras, who here acts in the Apostolic stead; hear, archbishops and bishops present, that I, Philip, king of the Franks, will no longer practise the sin and custom of carnal and unlawful union which until now I have practised with Bertrada. Rather, I utterly and without any reservation renounce this sin and offence. Nor shall I hold private conversation or cohabitation with the same woman, except under the testimony of persons wholly beyond suspicion. All these things, as the pope’s letters state and as you understand them, I shall observe without any evil intent. So help me God, and these most holy Gospels of Jesus [Col. 0455A] Christ.”

Likewise Bertrada, when she was released from the bond of excommunication, touching the most holy Gospels, swore this same oath in her own person. May the Holy Trinity, our God, long preserve safely Your Holiness, labouring and praying for the Catholic Church; and because you have stood with us, together with the holy Roman Church, in judgment and justice, may recompense be rendered to you in the resurrection of the righteous.

Done at Paris in the year of Christ our God 1104, on the fourth day before the Nones of December [2 December], in the fifth year of the pontificate of Pope Paschal II.

VIII. The same writer’s fifth letter to Paschal.—On the dispute that arose between the canons of Arras and the monks of Saint-Vaast. (Year 1107.)

To the reverend Father and lord, Pope PASCHAL, LAMBERT, unworthy minister of the holy Church of Arras, due reverence together with prayers.

We have received, lord Father, the letters of Your Highness concerning the inquiry into and division of the old and new borough between the canons of Arras and the abbot and monks of Saint-Vaast. Having investigated and examined it, as truthfully as we could, in accordance with your command, through the oldest and most truthful parishioners, we wished to give it in writing to the abbot; but he would neither receive nor even hear it, and instead summoned our canons again, although by your letters [Col. 0455C] you had commanded the same abbot wholly to accept the division examined by us.

Considering the abbot’s presumption, and since the canons protested and requested the portion of the division belonging to them, we handed over the inquiry, made with the counsel of the lord archbishop of Reims and of the bishops of Soissons, Châlons, Laon, and Amiens. Since, because of our grave and continual illness, we are unable to compel the abbot to do justice, we beseech you as though prostrate at the feet of your apostolic office to confirm the inquiry and division given by us to the canons, lest we be held in derision and the command of your Sublimity be annulled.

A case concerning our parishioners living around the chapel of Saint Maurice was heard at the Council of Troyes, by your command, before cardinals and the bishops of Thérouanne, Amiens, and Paris, and other religious and synodal persons. There it was judged that the priest of Saint Maurice, because he exercises no pastoral care over the people by authority of the bishop, should by no means presume to administer to the aforesaid parishioners the sacraments of the Lord’s body and blood on the holy days of Easter, Pentecost, and the Nativity of the Lord, nor receive their offering. [Col. 0455D] On the other days of the year, however, if anyone wishes to make voluntary offerings to him, we do not forbid it, provided that he is not excommunicated.

It was also judged that the priest of Saint Mary, the mother church, who by authority of the bishop has their pastoral care, receives confession, and discharges every parochial duty, should administer the sacraments of the Lord’s body and blood to these same parishioners on the aforesaid days. [Col. 0456A] Following the footsteps of the holy Fathers, because this judgment has been determined by canonical, synodal, and your authority, we wish firmly to maintain it. We leave to your judgment the wrong done both to you and to us by the abbot through his irregular summons and contempt. May Your Holiness, reverend Father and lord, remain well for a long time and always in the only Son of God; and remember me, a sinner, before God.

IX. Letter of Odo, abbot of Lézat, to Paschal.—He reports how the small abbey of Saint Peter of Courte, as it is called, which “as justice required” was subject to the rule of the monks of Lézat, passed into the right and jurisdiction of Moissac. (Year 1104.)

[MABILL., *Annals of the Benedictines*, V, 470.]

[Col. 0456B]

To the universal Father, Lord Pope PASCHAL, brother O. [ODO], abbot of Lézat, his servant.

May it be known to your majesty, most universal Father, that Gerald, abbot of Lézat, our predecessor, endeavoured to set in proper orthodox order the little abbey of Courte, which, as justice required, was under our rule, so that filth might be removed from it, worship due to God rendered, and brought to full perfection—had not invading Cluniac monks opposed this with their left hand and prevented the brethren of that place from embracing discipline.

When the community of Lézat learned this, it grieved deeply; and, complaining repeatedly about it and fearing that the everlasting loss of the brethren would be demanded by the strict Judge from him to whom the pastoral care of that place had been entrusted, it finally found this course: that it should entrust the cause and care of that little abbey, commended to it, to its mother church of Moissac, so that the most renowned Church of Moissac might supply what the Church of Lézat itself was altogether unable to accomplish through its weakness. [Col. 0456C]

When our brethren had found this counsel of higher wisdom, they came into chapter; and there, once the affair had been disclosed as is customary, Abbot Gerald of Lézat, with the common assent of all the brethren, brought our privilege concerning Courte to Moissac and ceded in perpetuity to Lord Abbot Asquilin and his successors our right and jurisdiction over the little abbey of Courte. I, named above, like the other members of the community, was a grateful approver of this act and was in all things its constant helper and co-worker. If perhaps this is doubted, it may be learned briefly by reading: what I then praised as a monk in my spiritual Father, I now praise far more highly and, placed in the honour of government, confirm it by every means, giving it my full support. But since that same fatherhood commanded that this testimony of mine be presented to you for confirmation, I would gladly and joyfully have done so, had bodily illness not prevented me.

X. First letter of Seher, abbot of Chaumousey, to Paschal. (Before 1105.)

[Dom CALMET, *History of Lorraine*, Proofs, p. CII.]

To PASCHAL, most blessed Father and, by God, appointed in the first see as a refuge of the afflicted, SEHER, an unworthy abbot, together with the whole community joined to him, offers what alone they can: obedience and prayer.

Since you hold in the holy Church the place of Him who loves the importunities of all who rightly petition him, we trust that you are not without this mercy. Therefore we dare often to have recourse to you, because we hope that you do not disdain our importunities. Whether we wish it or not, we imitate the habit of nursing infants: the more they are frightened by the troubling of some matter, the more closely they cling to their mother and embrace her.

Now therefore, reverend Father, that we may briefly disclose to you how greatly we are afflicted, we confess, setting shame aside, that we are truly near despairing of our peace. For that abbess—Gisela, abbess of Remiremont—about whom you have received so many of our complaints, and to whom you have already sent your letters a second time, has shown herself obstinately disobedient to everything that you commanded her both by precept and by counsel. [Col. 0457B]

For in your first letters you advised her to accept a suitable exchange for the church’s portion, and you judged that, concerning the accusation over the foundation of a new monastery, she ought to admit our proof through truthful witnesses. In the second letters, because she regarded what you had said not as a command but as mere advice, you commanded her, under a certain alternative, either to accept an exchange in suitable land for the church’s portion, or to leave us our portion free and in peace, and to cease in every way from wronging us; otherwise, she should know that the vengeance of blessed Peter would fall upon her.

Although, if Your Holiness deigns to remember, you commanded all these things to her, she has in no respect whatsoever obeyed them. Recently, in the presence of Lord Richard the cardinal, Duke Theoderic, the bishop of Metz, and many other worthy men, clerics as well as laymen, and under the authority of the king’s letters—for she had already said that she dared not do it unless he consented—we offered an exchange worth fully, and much more than, that portion of the church. [Col. 0457C] She neither granted it unconditionally nor rejected it outright, but in the presence of so great an assembly appointed a day on which the matter should be settled.

But when we met from both sides on the appointed day, she refused the exchange, denied that we possessed the portion which we have in the church, and, so far as lay in her power, has already taken it from us; and, although we were ready there with witnesses, she refused to receive our proof. If you ask concerning the injuries that she inflicts upon us, what greater injury, holy Father, can be done to us than that there should be taken away what nearly all our fellow provincials know that we and our predecessor possessed for many years without challenge, and that, once this is taken away, our house should be destroyed?

Having briefly recapitulated these matters, because perhaps what both we and she possess in that church has slipped from your memory, let Lord Ascelin and Lord Arnulf be questioned about them, if it please you, since they know it and you have heard it from them. Once these matters have been diligently examined, and once it is remembered that the altar of that church, given to us by the bishop of Toul, has already been confirmed by your authority to remain ours, it will be yours to decide how you ought to end so hostile a contest and establish in peace your little flock, devotedly subject to you.

XI. The same writer’s second letter to Paschal.

[Dom CALMET, *ibid.*]

To PASCHAL, supreme pontiff of the holy and apostolic see, SEHER, unworthy abbot of Chaumousey, with his brethren, the devoted performance of due obedience.

[Col. 0458B] Now, holy Father, we are weary: we of writing letters, and you of hearing them; yet we have made no progress, and nothing remains except that we have now despaired of our peace. Indeed, it is harsh and irreligious that we confess ourselves to have despaired. But we are compelled thus to express our straits to you. For who could keep his hope unshaken when he plainly perceives that what he had hoped would surely remedy his injustice turns to the contrary?

For, lord, with your leave, we find that your letters to the abbess—which we have always believed would mitigate our disturbance—have become most cruel incentives to the same abbess and her supporters. Up to the point at which, in your third letter, you threatened them with your sentence if they did not cease troubling us, they frightened us with threats alone. But afterwards they attacked us with sudden assaults by their armed men, so that all who wish to observe can clearly see that their sudden fury against us arises not so much from hatred of us as from regard for you. [Col. 0458C]

For already three times since then they have violently carried off the goods of the church over which the dispute exists; having taken away what they could, they devastated the rest, and by tyranny invaded everything indiscriminately, both what was ours and what was theirs. Though we endured these and other injuries, we resisted them in no way. Yet, by the authority of God and yours, we opposed them in every matter as far as we were able. Nor have we yet made any formal complaint concerning these things, because we did not judge that a matter already discussed and settled in the presence of your majesty should be reopened elsewhere.

Therefore, holy Father, as though all present, we lie prostrate at your feet and implore you with tearful prayers: if you have purposed to extend to us any mercy, any compassion, any peace, do not, for the Lord’s sake, delay longer.

XII. Letter of Matilda, marchioness, to Pope Paschal. (Before 1106.)

[*Works of St Anselm*, p. 442.]

To the most holy and venerable Father and lord in Christ, PASCHAL, bishop of the first see, MATHILDA, marchioness by God’s grace, whatever she may be, offers the service of total submission, both due and faithful.

[Col. 0459A] Among the other matters concerning which we presume to petition your fatherhood, we especially entreat your clemency concerning the exile of our Father and lord Anselm, the venerable Archbishop of Canterbury: that, according to the judgment due from your see, you may faithfully consider, as a gracious Father and lord, the tribulations and miseries which so holy and reverend a Father suffers for the Catholic faith and the holy Roman Church; that you may sympathize with his sorrowful complaint; and that you may more mercifully extend the hand of counsel and aid to holy undertakings.

For it is unseemly that so eminent a member of the holy Roman Church should lie in exile for so long, almost as something putrefying among other things, and should not promptly perform the office entrusted to him. We grieve, therefore, that the Church’s body is deprived in the greatest measure of the ministry of one whose governance, we know, is in every respect and for all purposes necessary to it. Therefore, with bended knees, we petition your clemency concerning him, since after the Lord we undoubtedly believe you to be his singular refuge; and we desire that this confidence in him be increased, not diminished, even by our merits.

XIII. Letter of Reinhard, bishop of Halberstadt, to Pope Paschal II.—He asks the pope to confirm the tithes lawfully granted to his Church, and requests instruction about what ought to be done concerning clerics ordained and churches dedicated by Frederick, imposed upon his see and deprived of authority by the Apostolic See. (Year 1107.)

[Martène, *Amplissima Collectio*, I, 618, from the manuscript of Saint-Germain-des-Prés.]

[Col. 0459C]

To PASCHAL, supreme pontiff, REINHARD, by God’s grace and yours bishop of Halberstadt, prayers and service, and both willing and due obedience in all things.

Although I cannot adequately repay the benefits of your mercy, by which you exalted me, unworthy and undeserving, I shall nevertheless hope always to retain through you, my Father and lord, that which I received from you. Therefore, because I place great trust in you, as a servant in his lord and a son in his father, I humbly petition Your Holiness to confirm by privileges of your authority the boundaries and tithes of our Church, which it received from your predecessors, the Roman pontiffs, and from Catholic emperors, at the beginning of its foundation and dedication. Thus we may be able to resist with the sword of your authority the enemies of God and the Church, who attack us daily. [Col. 0459D]

I, miserable man, received a miserable church under compulsion; unless it is defended through you, it will become most miserable. I await your judgment concerning what must be done about the clerics ordained and the churches dedicated by Frederick, imposed over us and lawfully deposed by you. In these matters and in all that you deign to write back to me, I shall always obey you, as I ought, to the extent of my knowledge and ability. What the letter lacks of my petitions, the messenger will faithfully convey. I shall receive the blessing of Your Holiness as the greatest gift.

XIV. The same bishop to Paschal.—Suspended from office, he humbly asks absolution from the supreme pontiff because, unaware of his decree, he unlawfully received investiture from a layman; he excuses himself for being unable to come to him because of the disorder of the times. (Year 1107.)

[MARTÈNE, as above, p. 619, from the same manuscript.]

To PASCHAL, pope by God’s grace, REINHARD, bishop of the Church of Halberstadt, whatever he may be, offers both willing and due obedience in all things.

Receiving with gratitude and blessing the letters sent to us by Your Holiness, we rejoiced greatly that you wished to call me, not by my merits, your brother [Col. 0460B] and familiar. In them I also recognized the exceeding affection of your fatherhood toward me, because you made known to me the offence of my ignorance and did not conceal my wrongs. For it belongs to a good father to rebuke the son whom he loves and to scourge everyone whom he receives.

A cloud of sadness, however, has been spread over the serenity of so great a joy by certain persons, who say that the ordinations of clerics have been forbidden to me by your blessedness. When, because of these words, we sent brethren to your desired presence and, upon their return, heard that I had not been deprived, I yielded the hand of obedience, because obedience is better than sacrifice and because the shepherd’s sentence must be feared by the flock. Thus I submit myself at your feet as though I had been summoned to a council and had not come, and for that reason had been suspended from office—although, as your letters testify, I was not summoned, and I am wholly ignorant when or where I was suspended. [Col. 0460C]

It is clear that our ordination was performed by the metropolitan in his own see, with our Church itself present as witness and petitioner. Yet innocence often does not free a person when ignorance, delay, or some suggestion has compelled the judge’s sentence to err. Moreover, concerning the investiture which, before the decree of your sentence and in ignorance, I unlawfully received: since I have now asked pardon twice and have not received it, have sought and not found, I shall now knock a third time, that I may obtain by my persistence at least what I need. For I am certain that He who learns in blessed Peter how he ought to forgive others will never forget to show mercy. [Col. 0460D]

For nowhere, as blessed Augustine says, ought the bowels of mercy to be more active than in the Catholic Church, so that, like a true mother, she may neither proudly insult her sinful children nor find it difficult to forgive those who have been corrected, since she received blessed Peter himself into her maternal bosom after his denial and wicked dissimulation, once he had been rebuked. The reason why we cannot now present ourselves to your sight as we wished and intended is the pressing wickedness and disturbance of the times, which is raging especially in our regions.

XV. Letter of Gervasius, Hugh count of Rethel, and Melesinda’s son, archdeacon of Reims, to Pope Paschal, written on the occasion of the schism between Hodulf and Gervasius over the archbishopric of Reims. (Year 1107.)

[MARLOT, *Metropolis of Reims*, II, 242.]

To the most excellent Father of fathers and bishop of bishops, PASCHAL, GERVASIUS, called bishop, faithful service together with the prayers of my lowliness . . . [lacuna]

Let my opponents say as much as they please that I am unfaithful and rebellious against your authority: I profess my submission to you, and whoever, of whatever rank, denies it to you cannot remain in communion with me. Without regard for anyone, we observe [perhaps: “I observe”] your suspension and interdict, not without great injury to our churches and to ourselves. That suspension also hindered my service toward you. [Col. 0461B]

[Note: [Col. 0461D] He speaks here of the interdict by which the pontiff had severely and forcefully bound the Church of Reims, mentioned by Ivo in Letter 189, because Gervasius himself, though an intruder, was putting himself forward as though canonically elected. [Col. 0462D]] etc.

XVI. Letter of Suavius, abbot of Saint-Sever, Duke William, and Gaston to Pope Paschal. (Year 1107.)

[MABILL., *Annals of the Benedictines*, V, appendix, p. 676.]

To PASCHAL, by God’s grace bishop of the holy Roman Church, SUAVIUS, abbot of Blessed Severus of Gascony, and the whole community entrusted to him, together with WILLIAM, duke of Aquitaine, and GASTON, proconsul of Béarn, having held a council of the ecclesiastical order and the barons of all Gascony, offer what is due to their most dear lord and shepherd before God.

All of us alike are scandalized by certain arguments which some of your representatives, under the appearance of judicial procedure, advanced in the lawsuit between the abbot of Saint-Sever and the abbot of Holy Cross. Had they wished to investigate any path of justice, they would by no means have set aside, for their own inventions, the decree of Lords Alexander and Gregory VII, supreme pontiffs of the holy Roman Church. Yet we rejoice greatly that your holy discernment kept itself apart from their judgment, because when the abbot of Saint-Sever sought counsel from you, you advised him, saying:

> “If you can produce sealed letters of our Fathers Alexander and Gregory VII, which you say you possess, send them to me. When I have seen them, I shall summon you and the abbot of Holy Cross, that you may return for judgment on an appointed date.”

Therefore, since by God’s grace the letters have been found, we your little servants petition Your Holiness that, after the example of the prophet Daniel, who brought the deficient judgment concerning holy Susanna back to complete justice, you may deign by your letters to summon both abbots before your reverend presence. Thus may your most exalted discernment, with the Paraclete Spirit going before, restore to the justice of the canons the wrong which we believe your representatives inflict upon the abbot of Saint-Sever. May your life flourish for the increase of justice.

XVII. Letter of Peter the Sinner, cleric of Ravenna, to Paschal, pontiff of the supreme see, in which he also sends the Rule of Clerics for correction.

(*Works of St Peter Damian*, II, 268.)

To PASCHAL, by God’s will bishop of the supreme and apostolic see, P. [PETER] the sinner, cleric, together with his fellow brethren, greeting in Christ and every obedience.

Since divine grace has granted Your Blessedness to hold Peter’s place in the Church, we reasonably believe that whatever is established anywhere to be done in the churches ought, by the judgments of your authority, either to be rejected as unjust or confirmed as just. Therefore we have directed that this Rule of canonical institution, compiled from many sources, as will appear below, and prudently framed in view of the frailty of our times, be presented to Your Majesty. After examining it and correcting it where necessary, may you return it to us, confirmed and accepted by the authority of this Apostolic See, to be observed henceforth at your command. Farewell.

XVIII. The community of the Church of Canterbury to Pope Paschal. (After 1109.)

[EADMER, *Historia novorum*, book V, p. 87.]

To PASCHAL, lord and supreme shepherd of the holy universal Church, the community of Christ Church, Canterbury, faithful prayers and the service of all holy devotion.

We do not doubt, gracious lord, that it is known to your glorious fatherhood that our mother, the Church of Canterbury, the special daughter of the holy Roman Church, has, through our sins, been deprived of pastoral governance for five years since the death of our Father Anselm, archbishop of blessed memory. [Col. 0462C] Recently, however, through God’s merciful regard, when an assembly of the whole English realm had been gathered in the presence of our glorious king Henry, Ralph, bishop of Rochester, was elected by us, the clergy, and the people to govern that Church. He is most fully known to us and is greatly acceptable to the whole realm both for the merit of his life and for the fruit of his holy manner of life.

Bishops, abbots, and magnates of the realm were present at this election, along with a vast multitude of the people; our lord the king consented, praised the same election, and confirmed it by his authority. Therefore, since this is the situation, we send to you, entreating by every means in our power that the man whom God has chosen, insofar as we are given to understand, for the relief and consolation of his Church, may be confirmed by your holy authority in that to which he has been elected; and that you may deign to send him the pallium which all his predecessors received from the most sacred see of blessed Peter. [Col. 0462D] Otherwise, should Your Holiness—God forbid—not incline ears of mercy to our prayers, our Church, your daughter, may by some event relapse into her former miseries.

For he himself is burdened by such bodily weakness that at this time he cannot present himself at your feet without grave danger to himself and loss to us all. May almighty God deign to preserve your holy apostolic office safe for many years to the honour of his holy Church, most worthy Father. Amen.

XIX. Letter of Saint Bruno, bishop of Segni, to Paschal. (Year 1111.)

[*Works of St Bruno*, II, 626.)

To PASCHAL, supreme pontiff, BRUNO, sinner, bishop, servant of Blessed Benedict, offers what is due to so great a lord and Father.

My enemies tell you that I do not love you and that I speak ill of you; but they lie. For I love you as I ought to love a father and lord; and while you live, I wish to have no other pontiff, as I promised you along with many others. [Col. 0463B] Yet I hear my Saviour saying to me: “Whoever loves father or mother more than me is not worthy of me” (Matt. 10). And the Apostle says: “If anyone does not love the Lord Jesus, let him be anathema—*maranatha*, ‘the Lord comes’” (1 Cor. 16). Therefore I ought to love you, but I ought to love more highly him who made both you and me. Nothing must ever be preferred to so great a love.

But I do not approve that agreement—so foul, so violent, concluded with such great betrayal, and so contrary to every piety and religious principle. Indeed, as I have heard from many who report it, neither do you. For who could approve an agreement in which faith is violated, the Church loses liberty, the priesthood is abolished, the one and singular door of the Church is closed, and many other doors are opened through which everyone who enters is a thief and a robber? [Col. 0463C]

We have the canons; we have the ordinances of the holy Fathers from the times of the apostles down to you. We must walk on the royal road and not turn from it to either side. Your constitution and the constitution of the apostles are one and the same; and it is highly praiseworthy. For the apostles condemn and separate from the communion of the faithful all who obtain the Church through secular power. Laypeople, even though religious, have no power to dispose of the Church. Likewise your constitution, which has flowed from the apostolic source, condemns and separates from the communion of the faithful all clerics who receive investitures from a layman’s hand and all who lay hands upon them.

For this constitution of the apostles and yours is holy; it is Catholic; whoever contradicts it is not Catholic. For only those are Catholics who do not contradict the faith and teaching of the Catholic Church. Conversely, those are heretics who stubbornly contradict the faith and teaching of the Catholic Church. [Col. 0463D] Therefore, venerable Father, confirm again this constitution of yours and of the apostles; proclaim it publicly and for all to hear in your Church, which is the head of all churches; condemn by apostolic authority this heresy which you yourself have called heresy. Then you will immediately see the whole Church reconciled to you; immediately you will see all streaming to your feet and, with great joy, obeying you as Father and lord.

Have mercy on the Church of God; have mercy on the bride of Christ. Through your prudence may she recover the liberty which she now seems to have lost through you. As for me, I make little of that obligation and oath of which we have spoken above; nor shall I ever be less obedient because of that obligation.

XX. Letter of the Church of Strasbourg to Paschal.

[MANSI, *Councils*, XX, 1092.]

To PASCHAL, universal pontiff of the Romans, the brethren of the Church of Strasbourg offer faith and obedience.

All your concern being for the Churches, venerable Father, you have come as a refuge for the wretched—indeed, as the longed-for protection of the world; therefore God does not yet disdain to provide for humankind through these new events [Col. 0464B], since light has shone in darkness. Blessed, then, are you, at whose coming God has blessed us, and may He bless us. Look upon a people marked by miseries and oppressions: come and behold the daughter of Zion mourning and captive, expecting neither relief nor consolation except from you alone. Go forth, beloved one, into the field: the time of pruning has now come; with the apostolic sickle, therefore, whatever is defective must be cut away, lest what is sound be drawn away with it. Come, then, and visit our vineyard, demolished by little foxes and grazed over by the solitary wild beast. For, to come to the matter itself, for about thirty years now we have always wandered like bleating sheep; we have rarely carried the streams of the word knowingly, and now we no longer know the shepherd’s voice. What remains, therefore, except that the flock follow the tracks of its companions? [Col. 0464C] But if, shepherd, you do not strictly judge such watchfulness, and if room is granted in the Church to a wolf lying in wait for Christ’s sheep, there will be no room for them. As for what must henceforth be done concerning our own, as he is called, bishop—who for so many years has indeed possessed the name of dignity but by no means its office, and whose life and lofty entrance are now answered by the heights of the mountains and the low valleys—we desire to hear the counsel and command of your holiness. You, therefore, foundation of Catholic peace, sign of the inviolable rock, cause the rashness of Roman counsels to yield to authority.

## XXI. Letter of Otto, Bishop of Bamberg, to Pope Paschal II

—He states that he received the bishopric from the emperor, but does not wish to remain in it unless he is invested [Col. 0464D] and consecrated by the pope.

[MANSI, *Councils*, XX, 1044.]

To his lord and father PASCHAL, universal bishop of the holy and apostolic see, OTTO of the Church of Bamberg sends prayers and service of devotion as well as of due submission.

Because the foundation of all ecclesiastical dignity and religion is Christ the rock, and Peter His disciple and Peter’s successors, I have judged it madness to depart from this line, from this rod of rectitude—the rod of kingdoms, pontificates, and every power in the Church. Therefore, most holy Father, devoutly submitting my neck to you and to our holy mother the Roman Church, I ask assistance and counsel concerning my affairs. For, while I remained for several years in the service of my lord the emperor [Col. 0465A], and found favour in his eyes, I regarded investiture at a prince’s hand with suspicion; and once and again, when he wished to give it, I refused the bishopric. But now, for the third time, he has ordained me to the bishopric of Bamberg. Yet I shall by no means remain in it unless it pleases your holiness that I be invested and consecrated by you. Whatever may please your judgment concerning me, make it known through messengers to me, your servant, lest perhaps I run in vain if I begin to run to you. May the Almighty preserve your gracious welfare.

## XXII. Letter of Baldwin I, King of Jerusalem, to Pope Paschal

(Before 1112.)

[WILLIAM OF TYRE, book XI, ch. 28.]

[Col. 0465B]

Meanwhile, says William of Tyre, it occurred to the lord king that he should send envoys to the Roman Church and present petitions to the lord pope. Their tenor was that whatever cities and whatever province, by the labour of war and royal exertion, with the Lord as author, he might be able to claim for himself and violently snatch from the enemies’ power, should all be subject to the jurisdiction and governance of the Church of Jerusalem.

Concerning this he obtained a rescript from the apostolic see, the tenor of which, etc. See above, under the year 1112.

## XXIII. Synodal Letter of the Fathers of the Council of Vienne in Germany, at Which Emperor Henry V Was Excommunicated [Col. 0465C] for Extorted Investitures

(1112.)

[LABBE, *Councils*, XI, 785.]

To the holy and most beloved lord and father PASCHAL: GUIDO, Archbishop of Vienne and legate of the apostolic see [Note: [Col. 0465D] Later Pope Calixtus II.], and all the other bishops and abbots who were present at the Council of Vienne, due submission and obedience.

Following the commands of your holy fatherhood, we assembled at Vienne. There, through the cooperating grace of the Holy Spirit, we took care to deliberate diligently concerning investitures, your capture and that of your people, royal perjuries, and that most evil compact and privilege which he violently extorted from your majesty. The king’s legates were present, boldly producing sealed letters as though sent by you [Col. 0465D] to him. In them your favourable disposition towards him, of peace, concord, and complete friendship, was signified. The king himself testified that he had received these letters and that they had been sent to him after the council which you held at Rome during the past Lent. Though this occasioned great astonishment among us, yet, mindful of the letters which you had sent to our humility, and of those which you had sent to Gerard, bishop of Angoulême and legate of your see, concerning steadfast perseverance in good justice, and wishing to avert the ruin of the whole holy Church and of our faith, encouraged by God’s honour and yours, we entered upon the canonical course.

[Col. 0466A] Therefore, at the prompting of the Holy Spirit, we judged every investiture of an ecclesiastical thing from a lay hand to be heresy.

We condemned that writing which the king extorted from your simplicity.

Upon the king himself, by name, solemnly and unanimously, we also pronounced the sentence of anathema. And now, lord Father, we humbly beseech your majesty, as is fitting, that you solemnly confirm by apostolic authority what we have done for the strengthening of the holy Church’s faith and for the honour of God and of yourself. Deign to communicate to us, through open letters, evidence of this confirmation, so that we may send them to one another and our joy may be complete. And since the greater part of the princes of the earth [Col. 0466B], and the multitude of almost all peoples, agree with us in this matter, impose upon all, for the remission of their sins, the obligation that, should need arise, they render unanimous assistance to us and to our country.

We also suggest to your mercy, with due reverence, that if you stand with us in these matters, if you confirm this as we request, and if henceforth you abstain from letters, speech, and gifts from that most cruel tyrant and his messengers, you shall unanimously have us, as is fitting, for sons and faithful subjects. But if, which we least believe, you begin to take another course and are unwilling to strengthen the foregoing declarations of your fatherhood, may God be merciful to us, for you will drive us away from your submission and obedience. Farewell.

## XXIV. Letter of Matilda, Queen of the English, to Pope Paschal

—She gives thanks for exhortatory letters sent to her husband.

(*Works of St Anselm*, p. 403.)

To PASCHAL, supreme pontiff and universal pope, MATILDA, by God’s grace queen of the English, wishes that he may administer in time the rights of apostolic dignity in such a way that, with sheaves of justice, he may deserve to be enrolled forever in the joys of everlasting peace in the apostolic senate.

To the sublimity of your holiness, O apostolic man, I offer such thanks and praises as I can for those things which your paternal charity has already frequently deigned, by the living voices of legates, to command my lord the king and me by way of admonition, and [Col. 0466D] to send in writing under your own hand. I do not cease, nor shall I cease, with all my heart, all my soul, and all my mind—prostrate at the paternal knees—to urge, by importunate and opportune petition, the frequent visiting of the apostolic thresholds of the most holy Roman see and the embracing of the footsteps of my holy father, the apostolic pope, insofar as I may and can; until I perceive that either my humble submission, or rather the persevering importunity of my knocking, has been heard by you. Yet let not your excellence be angered at this boldness of mine, because I presume to speak thus; nor let the prudent senate of the Roman clergy and people wonder. For there was—there was, I say—among us [Col. 0467A] and among the English people, then indeed fortunate, under your apostolic dignity, Anselm our archbishop, foster-child of the Holy Spirit: ours, and the most prudent comforter and most loving father of the aforesaid people. What he drew abundantly from the exceedingly rich treasures of his Lord, of which we knew him to be the keeper of the keys, he dispensed to us yet more abundantly—especially since that faithful minister of the Lord and prudent steward both seasoned all that was to be distributed with abundant savour of wisdom, softened it with sweetness of eloquence, and spiced it with a certain marvellous charm of speech. Thus it came about that neither was a very great abundance of milk lacking to the Lord’s tender lambs, nor the richest abundance of pasture to the sheep, nor the fullest plenty of food to the shepherds. [Col. 0467B] Since all these things have now turned out otherwise, nothing remains but that the shepherd, seeking food, the flock, pasture, and the offspring, udders, should cry out with many groans. For while, through the absence of the greater shepherd, especially Anselm, each of those aforesaid is deprived of its own proper thing—or rather all are deprived of everything—in the sorrowfulness of so great a grief, in the disgrace of so great a pain, in the mockery of so great a disfigurement of our kingdom and so great a loss, nothing remains to me in my astonishment except, having cast off stupefaction, to flee to blessed Peter the apostle and to his vicar, the apostolic man. Therefore I flee to your kindness, lord, lest we and the people of the English kingdom fall through such a failure, through such a lapse. For what profit is there in our blood, when we descend into corruption? [Col. 0467C] Therefore may your fatherhood take good counsel, so far as concerns us, and, within the period concerning which my lord the king asks your goodness, deign so to open your paternal compassion over us that we may rejoice at the return of our dearest father, Archbishop Anselm, and preserve unimpaired our due submission to the holy apostolic see. And I, instructed by your most health-giving and most beloved admonitions, so far as womanly strength may suffice, and having also the assistance of worthy men, shall strive with all my power that what your sublimity has advised may, insofar as it can, be fulfilled by my humility. May your fatherhood prosper happily.

## XXV. Rescript of Emperor Augustus Henry V to Pope Paschal

—That churchmen should surrender their royal rights and fiefs to the empire and Caesar, and live in the Church content with tithes.

(GOLDAST, *Imperial Constitutions*, vol. I, p. 252.)

Caesar most recently wrote to Pope Paschal:

> “Although he may retain by right and arms the ancient custom and rite observed by so many most holy Fathers for so many years, nevertheless it matters nothing to him if he loses the pontifical counties, provided that bishops, the initiated ministers (*mystae*), monks (*monarchi*), their stipendiary estates, fiscal domains, the resources of the commonwealth, fortresses, cities, towns, boroughs, royal villages, castles, restore to the commonwealth and to Caesar, and live content with tithes; that they pursue the cause of God, the poor, and the people by interpreting divine philosophy, expounding vows, and bearing before them the Cross of Christ [Col. 0468A]; and that, by emulating the poverty and simplicity of our Saviour and of His companions—that is, His apostles—they shine before all Christians.”

Accordingly it was agreed between the supreme pontiff and Caesar that priests, flamines, and pontiffs, great, lesser, and intermediate, setting aside thorns of this kind belonging to the commonwealth—as Christ our master calls them—should be content with readily obtainable and modest sustenance, pursue, so far as possible, the moderation and poverty of Christ our teacher, and devote themselves to the study of letters.

## XXVI. Letter of Duke Theodoric of Lorraine to Paschal

—Concerning the cell of Castiniacum. (1115.)

[Dom CALMET, *History of Lorraine*, Documents, p. 537.]

[Col. 0468B]

To PASCHAL, universal pontiff of the Catholic Church, THEODORIC, by God’s mercy duke and margrave of the Lorrainers, perpetual service of everlasting obedience.

That your fatherhood has frequently deigned to comfort my littleness by letters of its blessing, I hope always to deserve, if not by service, at least by love; nor indeed would the service of my resources fail if an opportunity should ever appear. I make known to you, Father and lord, that my mother vowed to God the parish church which she possessed on her own estate and in her castle, and gave it to the church of St Aper, the abbey at Toul. Accordingly, at her request, the abbot of that time, by command of the bishop, was to build a monastery there at his own expense, procure its dedication when built, and make the remaining arrangements as time required. But after the abbot had died, and my mother also had been removed from the scene [perhaps “carried off”], contention concerning the appointment of an abbot continued for a long time because of the conflict between kingdom and Church which then raged most fiercely. Hence the place whose construction had begun was insufficiently provided for. Since I too, still a young man, paid little attention to such matters, especially in circumstances of this kind, the advocate of the aforesaid castle—who also belonged to our family—without consulting me insincerely introduced monks from Molesme into the monastery vowed by my mother, and protected them in his time. But when I had come to use more mature counsel and more fully understood the matter, amid the many petitions [Col. 0468D] and complaints of the monks of St Aper, I nevertheless allowed the aforesaid monks, by a dispensatory arrangement, to remain in another’s possessions outside the law and against order, in case the place might perhaps grow through them. But now, unable to endure that my mother’s vow and gift should remain void any longer, and finding in many ways loss through the monks’ neglect of the place, I went there once and twice, that they might return to their own house and that the place might be restored to its former order. Since, therefore, by an imprudent contrivance they attempt resistance and cloak their invasion of property under a name, I beseech you, most holy Father, to restrain them from such imprudence by letters of your authority; and if anyone should perhaps attempt to suggest something else to you, do not listen in the least, since many honourable persons still survive among us who were present at this gift of my mother, and since I myself can and wish to prove this by the testimony of all those [Col. 0469A] who enjoy the best reputation in the bishopric of Toul. Farewell.

[Col. 0469]

## Letters to Paschal of St Anselm, Archbishop of Canterbury; Geoffrey, Abbot of Vendôme; and St Ivo of Chartres

They are extant among their writings, in volumes CLVII, CLIX, and CLXII of the *Patrology*.

[Col. 0469]

# Councils Concerning the Investiture of Prelates

(PERTZ, *Monumenta Germaniae*, *Leges*, vol. II, p. 180.)

Although it lies outside the purpose of this work to dwell upon general councils, it will nevertheless not seem irrelevant if, especially in this place, we add some matters bearing upon the councils concerning investitures at the beginning of the twelfth century, which we found in codices of that very period at Vienna, Rome, and Munich: the canons of Wastall and Troyes from the Royal Munich codex, folio 7; and the Lateran council, at which Paschal’s privilege concerning investitures was annulled, from Vatican codex no. 1984, folios 193–194. From this source there now proceeds a text better and more authentic than those already published.

## Council of Paschal II at Wastall

(1106, October 22.) Chapters of Blessed Pope Paschal at Wastall.

[Col. 0469]

[Col. 0469B] For many years now the broad extent of the German kingdom has been separated from the unity of the Church; in this schism, indeed, such danger has arisen [Note: [Col. 0469] *tantum periculum factum est* (“such danger has arisen”) is lacking in the codex.] that, to say it with grief, scarcely a few bishops or Catholic clerics can be found in so great an extent of lands. Since so many sons lie fallen in this slaughter, the necessity of Christian peace requires that, concerning this matter, the bowels of mercy of mother Church [Note: [Col. 0469] The codex lacks *christianae pacis necessitas exigit ut super hoc matris ecclesiae* (“the necessity of Christian peace requires that, concerning this matter, [those] of mother Church”); it reads *matris* (“of the mother”) for *materna* (“maternal”).] be opened [Note: [Col. 0469] *misericordiae* (“of mercy”) is absent from the printed editions.]. Instructed by the writings of the holy Fathers [Col. 0470B], who received Novatians [Note: [Col. 0469] *novitianos* in the codex.] and Donatists in their orders [Note: [Col. 0469] The remainder is lacking in the codex.], we receive into episcopal office bishops of the aforesaid kingdom ordained in schism, unless they are proved to be either intruders, simoniacs, or criminals. We establish the same concerning clerics of every order whom life and learning commend.

## Council of Paschal II at Troyes

(1107, May.) Decrees of Pope Paschal at Troyes.

[Col. 0469]

[Col. 0469C] 1. Chapter. If anyone has received investiture of a church or ecclesiastical dignity from any lay person, both he and the person who laid hands on him shall be deposed and deprived of communion.

2. Concerning married and concubinous priests, we decree that they be entirely removed from service at the altar and deprived of ecclesiastical goods.

3. Let no one usurp for himself another title, as many customarily do in calling archpriests those who are not priests, archdeacons those who are not deacons, and deans those who are not priests. We absolutely forbid this.

4. If anyone demands a payment for the offerings of the faithful, for the prebends of canons or monks, or for any ecclesiastical order, let him be expelled from the Church and deprived of communion.

## Council of Paschal II at the Lateran

(1112, March 18.) Proceedings of the Council against the Heresy of Investitures.

[Col. 0471]

[Col. 0471A] In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1112, in the fifth indiction, in the thirteenth year of the pontificate of the aforesaid pontiff, in the month of March, on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of April [18 March], a council was held at Rome, in the Lateran, in the Constantinian basilica. When Lord Pope Paschal [Note: [Col. 0471] “Pope Paschal” in the codex.] sat with archbishops, bishops, cardinals, abbots, and a varied multitude of clerics and laypeople, on the final day of the council, after making before all a profession of Catholic faith so that no one might doubt his faith, he said:

> “I embrace all divine Scripture, namely that of the Old and New Testaments: the law written by Moses and by the holy prophets. I embrace the four Gospels, the seven canonical epistles, the epistles of the glorious teacher blessed Paul the apostle, the holy canons of the holy apostles, the four universal councils, as the four Gospels: the Council of Nicaea, of Ephesus, of Constantinople, of Chalcedon, and the Council of Antioch; and the decrees of the holy Fathers, of the Roman pontiffs, and especially of my lord Pope Gregory VII and Pope Urban II of blessed memory [Note: [Col. 0471] “Urban” in the codex.]. What they praised, I praise; what they held, I hold; what they confirmed, I confirm; what they condemned, I condemn; what they rejected, I reject; what they forbade, I forbid; what they prohibited, I prohibit—in all things and through all things; and in these matters I shall always persevere.”

When this had been completed, Gerard, bishop of Angoulême, legate in Aquitaine, rose on behalf of all; and, by the common assent of Lord Pope Paschal and of the whole council, read before all this writing:

> “That privilege which is not a privilege, but ought truly to be called a *pravilege* [a corrupt or perverse privilege], [Col. 0471C] extorted from the lord pope through the violence of King Henry [Note: [Col. 0471] “King Henry” in the codex.] for the liberation of captives and of the Church: all of us assembled in this holy council with Lord Pope Paschal condemn it by canonical censure and ecclesiastical authority, by the judgment of the Holy Spirit; judge it void; and utterly annul it. And lest it have any authority or efficacy, we entirely excommunicate it. It has been condemned for this reason: because that *pravilege* contains the provision that a person canonically elected by clergy and people shall be consecrated by no one unless he has first been invested by the king. This is contrary to the Holy Spirit [Col. 0472A] and canonical institution.”

When this charter had been read, the whole council cried out: “Amen! Amen! *fyad! fiad!*” (“Let it be done! Let it be done!”)

The archbishops who attended with their suffragans were these: John, Patriarch of Venice; Landulf of Benevento; Sennes [Note: [Col. 0471] *Senne* in the codex.] of Capua; the archbishops of Amalfi, Reggio, Otranto, Brindisi, Conza, Girgenti, Rossano, and Santa Severina; and the Roman bishops Cencius of Sabina, Peter of Porto, Leo of Ostia, Cono of Palestrina; Gerard of Angoulême; Galo of Lyon; the archbishop of Vienne; Roger of Volturno; Walfred of Siena; Rodland [Note: [Col. 0471] *Rodlandus* in the codex.] of Populonia; Gregory of Terracina; William of Syracuse, legate for all Sicily; William of Troia; [Col. 0472B] and nearly one hundred other bishops, including Bruno of Segni and John of Tusculum.

The bishops who were in Rome but were not present at the council on that day, and who afterwards, when the condemnation of the wicked *pravilege* had been read, consented to and praised it, were the cardinal priests of the city of Rome: Boniface of the title of St Mark; Robert of the title of St Eusebius; Romanus of the title of St Prisca; Gregory of the title of the Apostles; Benedict of the title of St Eudoxia; Anastasius of the title of St Clement; Riso of the title of St Damasus; Romanus of the title of St Praxedes; John of the title of St Cecilia; Diviczo of the title of Equitius; Theobald of the title of Pammachius; Augustine of the title of St Chrysogonus; Rainerius of the title of Saints Marcellinus and Peter; Vitalis of the title of St Balbina; Peter of St Sixtus; and [Col. 0472C] Alberic of St Sabina, cardinals.

Those who were in Rome but were not present at the council on that day, and who afterwards, when the condemnation of the wicked *pravilege* had been read, consented to and praised it, were the deacons: John, abbot of Subiaco; John Gaetanus, abbot of St Andrew; Leo; Gregory; Aldo; Theobald; Hugh; and Ruscimannus. All these consented to the condemnation of the aforesaid *pravilege*, together with the abbots and an innumerable multitude of clerics and laypeople.

# In the Year of the Lord 1119: Gelasius II, Roman Pontiff

[Col. 0473]

## Life of Gelasius II, by Pandulf of Alatri, a Member of His Household

(BOLLANDISTS, in the *Chronico-Historical Essay* appended to the *Propylaeum* for May, p. 328.)

[Col. 0473]

## Notice

1. Orderic Vitalis describes the pontificate of Gelasius II thus at the beginning of book X of his *Ecclesiastical History*: “In the year from the Lord’s Incarnation 1118, in the eleventh indiction, after Pope Paschal had died, John Cajetanus, the longtime chancellor and master of the Roman pontiffs, was elected Pope Gelasius; and, despite the emperor’s opposition, was canonically consecrated by the Roman clergy.” And below: “Pope Gelasius was exceptionally learned in letters and became experienced through long practice—for he had served as *apocrisiarius* [papal representative] of the pontiffs for almost forty years—but he presided over the Roman Church for not quite two years.” Indeed, not even one full year; for below he again says: “In the year from the Lord’s Incarnation 1119, in the twelfth indiction, Pope Gelasius II died and was buried at Cluny on the fourth day before the Kalends of February [29 January].” We have the day of death from the Beneventan Chronicle by a contemporary author, namely the fourth day before the Kalends of February. Since the epitaph to be given presently says that only two days were lacking to complete the full year of his pontificate, it follows that he was elected at the end of January in the preceding year. Finally, because the author of the *Life*, who was present and saw these things, says below that he was ordained before the Kalends of March, which in that year fell on Thursday, I understand that the ceremony occurred on the preceding Sunday, namely 24 February, the feast of St Matthias the Apostle.

2. From the Cluniac Chronicle we have that Pope Gelasius was buried at Cluny, between the cross and the altar which stands beyond the cross of the great basilica. Our Oldoinus recites this epitaph, as though taken from that same chronicle, in these words: “To God, Best and Greatest. Gelasius II, supreme pontiff, fearing the fury of Emperor Henry IV, who brought many disasters upon Italy and maintained that Maurice of Braga was pope, fled into Gaul with the better part of the cardinals of the Holy Roman Church, to Louis VI. When he reached Plagonia, he became ill of pleurisy; while Louis hastened to meet him, he died at Cluny and is buried there in this place, about the year of Christ 1119 and the first year of his pontificate. Guido, archbishop of Vienne, son of the duke of Burgundy, was immediately thereafter appointed Roman pontiff by the sacred college of cardinals under the name Calixtus II.”

3. But no one can fail to see that this epitaph is an entirely new composition and no older than the present century. Therefore we should attach more weight to that which perhaps was anciently read in that place, and is still found under the name of its author Peter of Poitiers, monk, as follows:

> John, a man weighty and wise in deed and word,  
> Having first been a monk and then, because of his great ability,  
> Archdeacon and chancellor of the city,  
> After Bishop Paschal had been carried by his merits to the stars,  
> At last deserved to ascend the sacred seat,  
> Worthy to be Gelasius the Second after the First.  
>   
> But because he had been raised without the king’s command,  
> The prince raged terribly; and sweet daughter Gaul,  
> In her own fashion, received the fugitive father.  
> Had it been permitted him, I firmly believe, under his rule  
> Virtue, piety, and every honourable quality would have increased,  
> And the peace of the Church would have flourished throughout the world.  
>   
> Now black death has seized the man, when the venerable shepherd  
> Had scarcely completed the first year of his pontificate;  
> Only two days remained when, in the Cluniac  
> Asylum belonging to Roman jurisdiction, he slept [Col. 0475].  
>   
> Here, therefore, laid among beloved foster-children,  
> He rests with the holy Fathers and desires that the Creator  
> And Judge of the world may someday come in power  
> And restore the fallen ashes beneath their former limbs.  
>   
> Therefore, most happy Cluny, you shall always remain,  
> Because the apostolic Father of the world and supreme priest,  
> Special son of the Church and of your mother,  
> Passed to the heights from among you and rests buried in you.  
>   
> Nor do we judge him less happy for this,  
> To whom gracious Christ gave, as a great gift,  
> That monks might continually behold, as dear pledges,  
> A monk who was also their father, and, watering his tomb with tears,  
> Might always hold him especially in their holy prayers.

4. Moreover, I wonder how Martin of Poland and Werner Rollevink assigned Gelasius eleven years and five days; Godfrey of Viterbo, one year and six days; and Stella, one year and five months. His life was accurately written by the aforementioned Pandulf, nephew of Hugh of Alatri, cardinal priest of the Holy Apostles, then living with the pontiff and present at everything. Baronius inserted it into his *Annals* almost entire, but had often to interrupt it, as the plan of the *Annals* required. Therefore I judged it worthwhile to give it here complete in continuous sequence from our manuscript.

## The Life Begins

[Col. 0475]

[Col. 0475A] 1. Gelasius, also called John, a native of Gaeta, sat for one year. Happily brought up by noble parents according to the rank of the age, he was entrusted to the study of letters with a pure intention of mind. In a sufficiently short time he learned all the things belonging to boys and committed everything to memory beyond his contemporaries. Then, at the request of the lord abbot Oderisius of holy memory, he was assigned to serve there—at the head and source, as it were, of all monasteries—and was devoutly received by the aforesaid abbot and lived according to the rule with many others. There, joined to men highly skilled in every discipline, of whom the monastery had no small abundance, he learned the liberal arts and, beyond almost all other boys of notable ability from different regions [Col. 0475B], quickly mastered those arts and the monastic rule completely. For some time he took care to live blamelessly in the monastery of the most holy Father Benedict.

At that time the Roman Church, wearied no little by its customary evasions, was troubled by many tempests. For one Guibert, once called archbishop of Ravenna, a learned and noble man who might perhaps have pleased God had this crime not taken place, was placed by Emperor Henry the Elder of Germany, in opposition to Pope Gregory, upon the very chair of Peter by violent intrusion; and he tyrannically occupied it for no short time. Besides innumerable evils which he committed, he left behind a shoot of his own dregs, so rash and, as it were, concealed under a fox, that the whole world is today compelled to eat its deadly fruit. May the Almighty destroy it. Something, however, has already been said concerning that intruder in the acts of Pope Paschal.

[Col. 0476A] 2. In those days, not, I believe, without the oracle of the consoling Spirit, Brother John Cajetanus, now a young man and a monk of Monte Cassino, was summoned by the whole Catholic Church together with Pope Urban, who presided, to give help, counsel, and a share in the concern arising from such great disturbances; so that he might at last be raised, with divine mercy assisting, to the fullness of supreme power, as what follows will show. Thanks be to blessed Peter, apostle of Jesus Christ, who first adopted so worthy a young man as his son and afterwards as his worthy vicar.

Behold, Lord Urban, first bishop of Ostia and then pope of Rome—who, as has just been said [Col. 0476B], summoned John Cajetanus—was so pressed by the German persecution through Guibert into such misery that, leaving aside other matters, on the island of Lycaonia, between the two distinguished bridges of the Tiber, he was scarcely sustained against the enemies’ snares by a most famous and illustrious man, Peter Leo, and lived upon alms from Roman matrons and at times poor women. Then that pope, most learned and eloquent, recognizing Brother John as indeed a wise and provident man, ordained him, brought him into the curia, and, after deep deliberation, made him his chancellor, so that John, by the eloquence bestowed on him by the Lord, might, at the prompting of the Holy Spirit, restore to the apostolic see the style of ancient charm and eloquence, by then almost wholly lost, [Col. 0476C] and might bring back the Leonine cursus in radiant swiftness.

3. When that pope departed this life, Paschal succeeded him. [Col. 0477A] The chancellor himself always adhered to Paschal with inseparable affection amid countless adversities, and in all things and through all things remained the staff of his old age. From this pontiff he obtained, among other holy acts, the promotion at various times of Gregory of Ciccano, Aldo of Ferentino, Peter of Pisa, Chrysogonus and Hugh of Pisa, Hugh of Alatri, Crescentius, Lord Saxo of Anagni, Gregory Cajetanus, all his scribes and chaplains, as priests, deacons, and cardinals, along with not a few others in these and lesser orders. He refreshed all Roman clergy, greater and lesser, abbots and abbesses, nuns and monks, and all the poor together, with gracious words; and he strove to supply them and many others with bodily necessities from what he could acquire honourably. What he endured in German captivity under his wicked kinsman, the tyrant Henry, and how, though bound in chains, he stood before him as a father of widows and orphans—let every diligent reader observe from his other good deeds, and call him a second Peter against a new Simon.

How brilliantly he raised above all others the Roman diaconia commonly called St Mary in Cosmedin, entrusted to him by Lord Paschal as cardinal deacon—in gold and silver, books and vestments, innumerable houses, estates and farmsteads, and especially in religious observance, so far as Rome permits—will shine more clearly than daylight to one who carefully investigates it. For the monastery of Monte Cassino, both on account of the church and deserved reverence of blessed Father Benedict and because he had taken the habit of monastic religion there, he recalled the beginnings of his conversion and carefully reflected upon the holy life of the Fathers serving the Lord there. He strove with all effort and strength not only to govern it more diligently in matters belonging to God, [Col. 0477C] but also, outside these matters, to set himself against the hostile snares of the wicked as an unconquerable tower.

4. Meanwhile, Pope Paschal having died, the venerable lord Peter, bishop of Porto, who for a long time had held the primacy next after the pope, together with all the priests, deacons, and cardinals, began both collectively and individually to deliberate concerning the election of a pontiff, and concerning the lord chancellor, who was residing in the monastery of Cassino. While these matters were taking place, entirely without his knowledge, a messenger appeared who, as he had received orders, caused the chancellor himself to return with all speed to the cardinals at Rome. Why delay? Brother John, sorrowful and recalling aloud the death of so great a father, obeyed as a son of obedience: he mounted a mule, hastened his journey, entered the City, and exhorted and adjured his brothers and sons.

On the following day, as they had arranged, there assembled the honorable father C., bishop of Porto; Centius, bishop of Sabina; Vitalis, bishop of Albano; Lambert, bishop of Ostia; Divizo [Baronius: Domnizo] of St. Martin; Boniface of St. Mark; Desiderius of St. Praxedes; Peter of Pisa of St. Susanna; John of Crema [Baronius: of Cervia] of St. Chrysogonus; Saxo of Anagni of St. Stephen on the Caelian Hill; Amicus of Holy Cross; Sigizo of St. Sixtus; Amicus of Saints Nereus and Achilleus; John of St. Cecilia; Deusdedit of St. Lawrence in Damaso; Anastasius of St. Clement; Ranerius of Saints Marcellinus and Peter; Benedict of St. Peter in Chains; Chunrad of St. Pudentiana; N. of Saints John and Paul; Theobald of St. Anastasia; Guirard [B.: Gerard] of St. Prisca; Guido of St. Balbina; Gregory of St. Lawrence in Lucina; and six other cardinal priests. (For Hugh of Alatri, the twenty-eighth [indeed, the twenty-seventh, unless someone has dropped out] cardinal priest, had held the fortress of Circeii for Pope Paschal and returned shortly afterward.) Likewise there assembled Gregory of St. Eustachius, who was also abbot of St. Andrew; Oderisius of Sangro [Ciaconio: “of Sangro”; B.: “the Sacristan”] of St. Agatha, who was afterward made abbot of Cassino; Roscemannus of St. George; Henry of St. Theodore, also dean of Mazara; Aldo of Saints George and Bacchus; Peter Leonis of Saints Cosmas and Damian; the Count of St. Mary in Aquiro; Chrysogonus of St. Nicholas in the Tullian Prison; Stephen of St. Lucy in Silice; Gregory of St. Angelo; and eight other cardinal deacons. Nicholas the primicerius came with the school of singers; all the subdeacons of the palace, many archbishops, and many other clerics of lower rank; some Romans from among the senators and consuls, besides our household.

5. All these men, wishing to avoid the scandal which, through our sins, is wont to occur in elections of this kind—though, as the outcome afterward showed, the contrary happened, as all have acknowledged—believed a certain monastery called the Palladium, within the houses of Leo and Centius Frangipane, to be the safest place, as one scarcely yielding to the curia. They assembled there in order to deliberate concerning the election according to the provisions of the canons. In that place, after prolonged debate and diverse inclinations, with some seeking now this, now that, they at last, after taking counsel together, unanimously agreed in one resolve, one vote, and one desire—through the mediation also of Him who made both one—that they should elect and have as pope the lord John, the chancellor.

Without delay, he was seized by all, acclaimed by all, and approved also by the bishops. Their sole authority in the election of the Roman pontiff is to approve or oppose, and, upon the common petition first of all the cardinals and afterward of the others, simply to lay hands upon the person elected. Thus, unwilling and resisting, the lord John of Gaeta was today elected pope as Gelasius, through the grace of the Holy Spirit, and was placed by common consent in the highest see, while all praised the mighty works of God.

6. Hearing this, Centius Frangipane, the aforesaid enemy of peace and disturber, hissed like a most savage dragon and drew long sighs from the depths of his breast. Girding himself with a grim sword, he ran at once, broke down the gates and doors, and furiously entered the church. There, having removed the guard, he seized the pope by the throat, dragged him about, struck him with fists and kicks, and cruelly bloodied him with spurs within the threshold of the church, as though he were a brute animal. The robber dragged the lord himself by hair and arms, while good Jesus meanwhile slept, led him away to his house, chained him there, and shut him up.

Then the aforesaid bishops, all the cardinals and clerics, and many of the people who had assembled, were similarly bound by Centius’s officers; they were thrown headlong, with their heads down, from horses and mules, stripped, and afflicted everywhere with unheard-of miseries, until some at last returned half alive to their own homes. He came to his own harm who was unable to flee.

When this report spread, a Roman multitude assembled: Peter, prefect of the City, Peter Leonis with his men, Stephen the Norman with his men, Stephen de Petro with his men, Stephen de Theobald with his men, Stephen de Berizone with his men, Stephen Quatrale with his men, Bucca Pecorini [otherwise Bucca Porcina] with his men, Bonesci with his men, and Berizasi with his men. The twenty-two districts of the Roman city, the people of Trastevere and of the Island, took up arms, mounted the Capitol with great uproar, and again sent messengers to the Frangipani. They demanded back the captive pope. Without delay, the terrified Frangipani—especially Lord Leo, pious amid his treacherous impiety—immediately restored the pope. Embracing his feet, he cried repeatedly, “Lord, have mercy.” And thus, because his excessive sins required it, he escaped, so that once again he might toss the Church with uplifted horns.

7. Then the holy pope was raised up, mounted a white horse, was crowned, and the whole city was crowned. Proceeding along the Sacred Way, he went up to the Lateran, with heraldic proclamations and other insignia preceding and following him, according to Roman rite and custom. The pope therefore sat, as it seemed, in peace. Counts and barons frequented him; those who came for answers to particular matters were graciously received; and, until they had completed the business for which all had assembled and departed with his blessing, they were treated in every respect kindly, like sons by a father. Thus the whole curia possessed in peace all that it held through God’s grace.

All who had remained outside the City on one side and the other returned. Among them returned Hugh the Great, greatly honored, from the fortress of Circeii, which the ever-provident Pope Paschal had recently entrusted to that noble and illustrious man in order to guard again against German fury. Nevertheless, the new pope ordered by messengers and letters that it be restored to the people of Terracina—would that he had not done so, for he soon repented beyond measure.

8. When all had assembled from every direction, all deliberated as to the certain dates on which the pope should be promoted and consecrated; for he was a deacon, not a priest. But the ancient enemy, as he had once done in heaven, would by no means allow so great a peace to endure long. For while these matters were being carried on, during the silence of the untimely night, someone was sent to the said Lord Hugh the cardinal by a certain man who thereafter had no small abundance of friends, and told him that Henry, called emperor of the Romans, had arrived armed against the pope in the portico of St. Peter’s.

Why say more? It is unnecessary. The pope learned of it through the cardinal; and, because, being now nearly worn out by old age and illness, he could not flee so suddenly, he was led by the hands of his servants. Thus carried on horseback, he fled that very night to Lord Bulgaminus and lay hidden.

9. We all fled with him. At dawn we were all troubled and astounded, since we could neither safely remain in the City nor flee by land, the road being hedged about everywhere with thorns. The decision was therefore made to take flight by sea, and this was done. We quickly entered the River Tiber and descended in two galleys as far as the harbor.

Heaven, earth, sea, and almost everything in them had conspired everywhere against us. The sky poured forth heavy rain, hail, and thunder, continual flashes and lightning; the sea and the Tiber rebelled against Peter’s vicar with such violent storms that we could scarcely remain alive in the harbor, much less enter the sea. Moreover, the savage German barbarians along the bank were hurling poisoned missiles at us. They also threatened to burn us as we floated in the water with fire from a pinnace [perhaps *picco*], unless we surrendered the pope and ourselves into their hands. And, I believe, we should have been captured had night and the fury of the thunderbolt not hindered them.

What could the wretched men do in these circumstances? Lord Hugh, cardinal and priest, took—indeed, carried—our pope upon his shoulders and thus bore him by night to the castle of St. Paul at Ardea. At dawn on the following day the Germans returned, eager to make us their prey. At last they were sworn to that the pope had fled, and, thanks be to God, they departed from us.

10. Meanwhile we tried again to see whether we could yet enter the sea. We brought back the pope by night; with him, not without danger, we reached the sea-waves; on the third day we scarcely arrived alive at the shore of Terracina; and on the fourth we entered the harbor of Gaeta, where we were received with the greatest honor and treated kindly by those people.

The report spread throughout the land and neighboring regions. There assembled the archbishops Sennes of Capua, Landulf of Benevento, Alfanus of Salerno, Maximus of Naples, Riso of Bari, Hubald of Trani, Bajalard of Brindisi, and very many others from Apulia and Calabria, together with William of Troia and bishops from various regions; Gibald, abbot of Cassino, and Sigenulf of Cava with other abbots.
