In their presence the same lord pope, through the hands of Lambert, bishop of Ostia, Peter, bishop of Porto, and Vitalis, bishop of Albano, with the cooperation of many archbishops and bishops, other religious men attending, and Duke William of Apulia, Prince Robert of Capua, Robert of Aquila, and many other barons being present with them—all of whom then swore him fealty—while clergy and people were innumerable, under the prompting of the Holy Spirit, was made a priest and consecrated Pope Gelasius before the Kalends of March. There he promoted Peter Rufus, a cardinal deacon, Baron, a subdeacon, and me, Pandulf the doorkeeper, who wrote these things, to be reader and exorcist; and he ordained many others in the lesser orders. He restored to his rank Laetus by name, bishop of Veroli, who had been appointed and deposed by Pope Paschal. He made Chrysogonus deacon and chancellor. Remaining there throughout the whole of Lent, we solemnly celebrated the Easter feast at Capua.

11. When we had now in some measure caught our breath, men arrived to say what we had first learned at Gaeta by rumor: that Henry the barbarian had set up a certain Maurice, bishop of Braga, as a kind of new idol in the pope’s place, and had thus named that intruded man his Pope Gregory. Behold, through a recurrent wound we relapse into the ancient pattern.

The messenger further reported that this same barbarian was besieging the castle near the little tower, held by the brothers of St. Andrew. The pope recovered his strength and gave firm orders to Duke William, Prince Robert of Capua, and the other barons that all should quickly prepare arms against the barbarian. He spoke, and it was done. The pope prepared to return, and the barons returned with him. From there we reached St. Germain, that is, the monastery of Cassino, where we waited several days for Duke William.

Meanwhile Lord Laudo of the little tower, Oddo, Coctus, and Gisolphus, his brothers, were fiercely fighting the king with him. They made screens, wickerwork, crossbows, and bows against the engines. There, for the first time, a contrivance was devised and invented against stone-throwers: a net for covering towers against that crafty tyrant’s engines, to the harm of very many and the benefit of many.

There too, marvelous to say, a dog—a faithful animal—carried letters suspended from its neck to a certain Armicus, a minor castellan of those lords [the reading is uncertain; perhaps “Arnico … Castellano”]. Now entering the little tower, now hastening back from it to Runcum, it faithfully brought daily, in turn, to those lords whatever urgent messages they had repeatedly dictated, employing, as it were, a kind of intelligence.

12. Meanwhile the duke came to the pope, and then they began to hasten their return. When Henry learned this, he withdrew from the castle with his undertaking unfinished and returned to Germany by the same road on which he had come, God being angry with him; he left in the City the idol he had fashioned.

Then the pope greatly wished to possess the fortress of Circeii, which he had most unwisely ordered restored. Therefore the duke and prince returned with the barons. As the pope came into his own territory, namely Campania, his followers received him, not without a price; and so, step by step, more as pilgrims than as masters, we entered Rome, as God knows.

The lord pope lay hidden—rather than lodged—in a little church called St. Mary at the Second Candle, between the houses of the distinguished men Stephen the Norman, Pandulf his brother, and Peter Latro Corsorum. There he diligently conferred with the whole Church concerning imminent dangers, especially the intrusion of Bardinus. A certain cardinal, Desiderius of St. Praxedes—because a feast was near, would that he had not thought of it!—invited him one evening to sing Mass in that very church. The pope granted this far too simply. On the following day, although many disapproved because the church lay within the strongholds of the Frangipani, they went and sang, trusting in the long-proved bravery of Stephen the Norman and of Crescentius of Gaeta, the pope’s nephew.

13. The offices had not yet been celebrated when, behold, the impious Frangipani appeared with no small force of cavalry, infantry, and other insolent men. They rushed upon us, hurled stones and arrows, afflicted our men, and crushed many of the few. Stephen the Norman and the glorious Crescentius resisted with him; our men resisted everywhere. The missiles sent were returned in kind; sword was battered by sword, and a blunted lance was blunted [by a lance]:

> Here the foot-soldier, there the knight, falls everywhere amid the slain;  
> Everywhere the battle is fierce. One man seeks to seize the pope,  
> Another protects him; on either side the knight falls.

The crowds rushed in, foot-soldiers leapt over the walls, and some of our men—though not men of distinction—were captured. Oh, what grief for all! What lamentations especially from the matrons, who saw the pope alone, restored in part to his sacred vestments, fleeing across the fields as though he were a buffoon, as fast as his horse could go. His cross-bearer followed him, but fell. A little woman whom he then encountered hid him, concealed his steed and cross, and brought him back at evening.

14. For how great a part of the day the battle was fiercely fought on both sides! Then Stephen the Norman, believing that the pope had escaped to safety, addressed the Frangipani thus: “What are you doing? Where are you rushing? The pope whom you seek has already departed; he has already escaped by flight. Do you wish to destroy us also? We are Romans, indeed, like yourselves, and, if it may be said, your kinsmen. Withdraw, I beg you, withdraw, so that we too may withdraw together, exhausted as we are.”

At these words his nephew Leo Frangipane, groaning when he heard that the pope had been freed, withdrew with his mad brother Centius and the others. Our men also returned, though not all. Meanwhile the pope, pursued on both sides, was at last found weary, sad, and lamenting in the fields adjoining the church of St. Paul, and was brought back. That day dinner and supper became one meal; the hearts of all swayed painfully between hope and fear. So far as that day was concerned, memorable for a long time, they took counsel; night broke off the deliberation.

15. On the following day, while each man according to his inclination ventured this or that proposal, the pope, after hearing the opinions of all, said:

> “Brothers and sons, just as the evil is not far away, so no long or novel speech is needed. Follow our fathers, for it is very good to follow our ancient parents. Let us likewise follow the Gospel: since we cannot live in this city, let us flee into another; let us flee Sodom, let us flee Egypt. Believe me: a time will come—come it will—when we shall return, either all together or those whom God permits, with the south wind blowing, and better times will return. Before God and the Church I say: if it could ever be possible, I should prefer one emperor to so many. Where one man is wicked, at least he would destroy men more wicked than himself, until the Emperor of all emperors should also exact manifest justice from him.”

To this all cried out together with one voice: “Let it be so, let it be so, let it be so.” Accordingly, with all delay set aside, offices of the Church were assigned and granted to individuals, each according to the capacity and measure of all.

The venerable Lord Peter, bishop of Porto, was appointed the pope’s vicar in his place, and certain cardinals were associated with him as helpers. The defense of the city of Benevento was entrusted—not, as we shall see, without an oracle of the Holy Spirit—to my most reverend and prudent lord and uncle, Hugh, cardinal of the Apostles. For shortly afterward, when the pope was gone, unless he himself had resisted and shrewdly countered them in a thousand ways, the Normans, rather than the pope, would today possess that city.

To Nicholas, the elder, was granted the school of singers. To Peter, called prefect—through whom many evils had come upon our lord Pope Paschal of holy memory—the prefecture of the City was, on this occasion (for otherwise it could scarcely have happened), established for a wicked and utterly unworthy man. Stephen the Norman, the leader and shield of all the curial men together, was, with the praise of all, appointed protector and standard-bearer in the name of God the Father, with great effectiveness, and was assigned, together with those already named, to the defense of the City.

16. Meanwhile several other ships were prepared as the occasion required. Since he could not travel by land, the pope entered the sea, while we made for Benevento, and after several days he safely reached Pisa (on 2 September, according to the Chronicle of Benevento). With him went Lord John of Crema, Guido of St. Balbina, and, among the cardinal deacons, Lord Peter Leonis, Gregory of St. Angelo, Roscemannus, and Chrysogonus. Among Roman nobles there also went Peter Latro and John Bellus, brother of Peter the prefect, as well as certain other lesser clerics and laymen, apart from their own households and guards.

All these men, together with the pope, were received and treated at Pisa with considerable honor and solemnity by an innumerable multitude of clergy and people. There the same pope, among many other things, delivered such a discourse on the Psalmist’s words, “I said, ‘I will declare against myself my injustices to the Lord, and you forgave the impiety of my heart’” (Psalm 31:5), as Origen himself could scarcely have delivered while in the flesh.

Remaining there for some time and administering every matter of his office with complete freedom, he again entered the sea. Thus, with the Lord guiding him, he reached the harbor of St. Giles sound and safe with all his companions. There he was received with the highest praise and honor by the venerable Abbot Hugh and the brothers of that monastery, who were gathering from all sides. How well and generously they treated him there for a considerable time is sufficiently clear.

All bishops and monks, nobles and commoners of every rank, assembled there alike, ready to serve according to their means. The Lord Pons, abbot of Cluny, arrived and supplied thirty mounts together with other small gifts; the abbot of St. Giles supplied ten, with other presents. With these and others the lord pope rode through that country. In those neighboring districts, with the assistance of many bishops from nearby cities, he dedicated the church of St. Cecilia of Stagello, the church of St. Silvester of Fillavo, and that of St. Stephen of Tornaco. He set up boundary stones which no one might ever cross to the injury of either the place or any property without incurring perpetual curse.

17. From there the pope proceeded without delay and hastened through Le Puy into France. Among other towns where he was received in the place of blessed Peter, he visited the monastery of Cluny. There he was received in a manner befitting the greatness of that place and an apostolic man. All the archbishops and bishops of the country entered with him well and joyfully; kings and princes too, as though they were visiting Peter himself, assiduously attended him both in person and through messengers, with no small gifts.

All were embraced in fuller arms of charity by so great a father and lord. They came joyful and departed more joyful, at length nourished to the marrow by heavenly feasts. The most holy man considered how he might provide in every way and in all things both for those whom he had brought with him and for those whom he had left in the City.

And indeed, with the Lord’s help, he had already accomplished much as he wished, when, rejoicing as though he had almost been brought into harbor, he was suddenly seized by the illness which the Greeks from the coast call *pleuresis*, “pleurisy.” Having summoned his own people and many brothers from every direction, made confession, and received the body with the blood of the Redeemer, and having laid his little body upon the ground according to the monastic form, that holy soul, released from the flesh, ascended hence to heaven, Peter being its guide.

His body rests honorably in peace within the threshold of the monastery of Cluny. Amen. The Romans who were present and those who had remained at Rome, all the clergy and people, then mourned him and mourned him as a father of justice, refusing consolation. The see was vacant for fifteen days.

> **Note [Col. 0483D].** That is, until the creation of his successor; for his successor’s ordination did not take place until those who had carried the election there for approval had returned to Rome.
>
> Moreover, from two letters of this pope preserved by Baronius—one dated at Rome, through the hand of Chrysogonus, cardinal deacon of the Holy Roman Church, on the Kalends of September, in the twelfth indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1119, in the first year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Gelasius II, on the day before he left the City intending to sail to Pisa and thence to Gaul; and the other at St. Giles on the seventh day before the Ides of November, in the same indiction and year—it is understood that the curial style then in use began the indiction on the Kalends of September and, in Pisan fashion, anticipated the Kalends of January by nine months.
>
> But his letter, given at Gaeta to the bishops of Gaul after the elevation of the antipope, is incorrectly subscribed “the seventeenth day before the Kalends of February,” when his predecessor Paschal was still alive. It is therefore rightly corrected by Baronius, who substitutes the month of April.
>
> Alphonsus Ciacconius, the first to undertake the collection of the names of as many cardinals as possible under each pontificate, begins with this Gelasius distinctly to enumerate those present at each pope’s election in the order in which they had been created by a predecessor: first bishops, then priests, thirdly deacons. But this author must be understood proleptically to grant bishops the right of election and to count them among the cardinals, since neither belonged to them at this period. This is understood, first, from the Life of this very pope, which testifies to the matter very explicitly; and second, from the letter of Peter, bishop of Porto, to the four bishops of the Innocentian party against Anacletus. There he explains in almost the same words as this Peter what office belongs to the suffragan bishops of the Roman see in relation to the pope, saying: “It was not yours, any more than mine, to elect, but rather to approve the person elected by the brothers”—that is, the cardinals.
>
> Thus too, in the letter which the brethren who were at Rome sent to Lothair, king of the Romans, in their own justification, the cardinal priests and deacons write their names first, twenty-five in all; then Peter the Elder, bishop of Porto, … together with the other suffragans of the Roman Church; all the subdeacons; the primicerius with the whole school of singers; Peter, archpriest of the basilica of the Savior called the Constantinian [basilica], … with the other archpriests of the Roman Church and with all the Roman clergy; Anastasius, abbot of St. Paul, … with the other abbots. There one sees the order of each rank carefully preserved with respect to elections. In synodal subscriptions and the subscriptions of papal privileges, however, one always finds the names of bishops in the first place, as men placed in a higher rank, and then those of cardinals. Peter also observes this order when listing those who attended this election.
>
> I would add here, from Mabillon’s *Italian Journey*, p. 147, that the aforesaid suffragans of the Roman pontiff—or at least two of them—were called “bishops of the City” in the Middle Ages, since they scarcely ever resided in the city of their own title but always resided at Rome, like bishops whom people now call vicars. Mabillon deduces this from the following inscription at Rome in the church of St. Mary of the Chapel, formerly called *ad Pineam*: “In the year of the Lord 1090, indiction XIII, on 25 March, this church of St. Mary called *ad Pineam* was dedicated by the bishops of the City, namely V. [Ughelli: Ubald], bishop of Sabina, and John, bishop of Tusculum, in the time of Lord Pope Urban II, and it contains relics,” etc.
>
> Mabillon likewise notes from the Farfa cartulary that Dodo, bishop of the holy Roman Church, gave five pounds for posthumous matters in October during the time of Benedict VIII—that is, between 1011 and 1004. He thinks that Dodo was also the Sabine bishop omitted by Ughelli and was therefore the successor of Rainerius in 1003 according to the Chronicle of Farfa. Finally, he says that he saw another diploma in which the same men are called Roman bishops.

[Col. 0485]

## Diplomatic Notice on the Letters of Gelasius II

(Philipp Jaffé, *Regesta Pontificum Romanorum*, p. 522.)

+ In the bulls of Gelasius the following words are customarily added:

> I, GELASIUS, BISHOP OF THE CATHOLIC CHURCH, [MAKE] THE SIGN OF MY HAND: GOD [elsewhere: THE LORD] IS IN HIS HOLY PLACE

(5, 8, 10, 13, 15, 16, 17, 19, 20, 23, 26, 27, 28).

Those subscribing were:

Lambert, bishop of Ostia, from 21 March 1118 onward.  
Peter, bishop of Porto.  
Crescentius, bishop of Sabina.  
Hugh, cardinal priest of the title of the Apostles, from 21 March 1118 onward.  
Guido, cardinal priest of the title of St. Balbina.  
Deusdedit, cardinal priest of the title of St. Lawrence in Damaso.  
Peter, cardinal priest of the title of St. Susanna, from 21 March 1118 onward.  
Peter, cardinal deacon of St. Adrian.  
Peter, cardinal deacon of Saints Cosmas and Damian.  
Peter, cardinal deacon of St. George.  
Rossemannus, cardinal deacon of St. Mary [in Via Lata].  
Romuald, cardinal deacon of St. Mary in Aquiro.  
Comes, cardinal subdeacon and abbot of St. Lawrence Outside the Walls.  
Amicho, on 26 September 1118.

The bulls were issued through the hand of Chrysogonus, cardinal deacon of the Holy Roman Church.

[Col. 0487]

# Letters and Privileges of Gelasius II, Roman Pontiff

## I. To A., prior of the church of St. Frigdianus at Lucca, and his brothers, under the personal name John by which he was called before assuming the pontificate.  
(21 February 1118.)

[Muratori, *Rerum Italicarum Scriptores*, III.1, p. 384.]

R. [perhaps “most reverend”] J[OHN], deacon of the Roman Church, now, by the Lord’s disposition, elected pope, to his dearest sons in Christ, A., prior of the church of St. Frigdianus, and his brothers: greeting and apostolic blessing.

As you yourselves know, our lord pope brought your prior into the Lateran church in order that he might remain with it always in one bond of charity. For one charity in Christ makes diverse souls one, as the course of Holy Scripture makes clear. Therefore, by this present letter, we commend to your affection our son V., prior of the Lateran Church, who is coming to you, so that in matters which are necessary, and especially with respect to clerics, you may give him your assistance. Thus may your house, with God’s cooperation, remain with the Lateran in the perpetual unity of love and charity. For whatever you bestow upon him, we account as bestowed upon us. We commend our lowliness, our labors, and those of the whole Church to your prayers.

Given at the Lateran, the ninth day before the Kalends of March.

## II. To the clergy and people of Rome.—He commends their steadfastness against the intruded false pope.  
(1118.)

[Mansi, *Concilia*, XXI, 168.]

GELASIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons in Christ, the clergy and people of Rome: greeting and apostolic blessing.

We give thanks to the Lord for your love, because you have stood firm with one mind and have refused fellowship with the works of darkness. We have also heard that that friend of ours, the lord emperor, has forced his intimate associate Maurice, archbishop of Braga—formerly his legate for negotiating peace—into our Church. Concerning him, know that it is said that formerly, according to custom, he received the pallium from us by confirmation and consecration, and that we received from him, according to canonical enactments, an oath of fidelity and obedience, etc.

We therefore ask your love and command you by precept to abstain from him as from one excommunicated, perjured, an invader, and a violator of holy mother Church and of the Catholic faith, etc.

Given at Gaeta, etc.

> **Note [Col. 0488C].** The passage is corrupt.

## III. To Jordan, archbishop of Milan.—Concerning the restoration of Landulf.  
(15 March 1118.)

[Muratori, *Rerum Italicarum Scriptores*, V, p. 505.]

G., bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother JORDAN, archbishop of Milan: greeting and apostolic blessing.

This brother Landulf complains that he has been driven from his Church. The demand that he provide proof of his title according to Blessed Gregory is shown to be absurd. For he must prove what he asserts in accordance with the sayings of that same blessed Gregory and the statutes of the laws; otherwise such a calumny is not to be brought against him on grounds of this kind. Unless some other cause hinders it, he is to be restored to his Church.

Given at Gaeta, on the Ides of March.

## IV. To the Gauls.—He commands them to arm themselves against Maurice, bishop of Braga, the false pope intruded into the see by Emperor Henry.  
(16 March 1118.)

[Mansi, *Concilia*, XXI, 166.]

GELASIUS, servant of the servants of God, to the archbishops, bishops, abbots, clerics, princes, and other faithful throughout Gaul: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Because you are members of the Roman Church, we take care to report to your love what has recently happened in it. After our election, the lord emperor came secretly and with unexpected speed to Rome and compelled us to leave. He afterward demanded peace with threats and terrors, saying that he would do whatever he could unless we gave him assurance of peace by oath.

To this we replied as follows:

> “Concerning the controversy between Church and kingdom, we willingly submit either to agreement or to justice, at a fitting place and time—namely, at Milan or Cremona, at the forthcoming feast of blessed Luke—under the judgment of our brothers, because they have been appointed judges in the Church by God, and without them this cause cannot be dealt with. And because the lord emperor seeks security from us, we promise it in word and writing, unless he himself should meanwhile impede it. For otherwise neither the honor of the Church nor custom permits us to give such security.”

Immediately—namely on the forty-fourth day after our election—he forced into the bosom [elsewhere: “invasion”] of mother Church Maurice, bishop of Braga, whom our lord predecessor Pope Paschal had excommunicated in the council of Benevento in the preceding year. Although Maurice had formerly received the pallium through our hands, he had sworn fidelity to that same lord of ours and to his Catholic successors, of whom I am the first.

Yet in this great crime the lord emperor had, thanks be to God, no Roman [elsewhere: “member of the Roman clergy”] as an accomplice. The Guibertines alone—Romanus of St. Marcellus, Cencius who was called “of St. Chrysogonus,” and Teuto [elsewhere: “and Euzo”], who raged for a long time through Dacia—celebrated so shameful a glory.

Therefore, by the receipt of this present letter, we command your experience that, considering these matters in common deliberation through God’s grace, you gird yourselves, with common aid and God’s assistance, for the vindication of mother Church, as you recognize to be fitting.

Given at Gaeta, the seventeenth day before the Kalends of February.

> **Note [Col. 0489].** Elsewhere, “Roman clergy.” On this word Binius offers the following scholion: “By ‘Romans,’ understand Catholics; by ‘Guibertines,’ schismatics.”

## V. He appoints Oldegarius, bishop of Barcelona, over the Church of Tarragona and grants him the pallium.  
(21 March 1118.)

[Flórez, *España sagrada*, XXV, p. 221.]

GELASIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother OLDEGARIUS, bishop of Barcelona: greeting and apostolic blessing.

The records of ancient writings and of provincial divisions declare that the Church of the city of Tarragona was formerly a distinguished metropolis. Our predecessors, moreover, are known to have laboured greatly for its restoration; hence, in our own times, our predecessor Pope Urban of holy memory bestowed the pallium upon Berengar, bishop of Osona. We therefore, applying ourselves wholly to the restoration of that same city, appoint you, dearest brother Oldegarius, bishop of Barcelona, as pontiff of that Church, and from the generosity of the Apostolic See grant you the pallium itself, with the provision and confidence that, according to the power given you by the Lord, you will strive by every means to restore that city and Church to the honour and glory of the Lord our God.

Moreover, if divine clemency restores Tortosa to the Christian people, we grant it as a suburban diocese to the metropolitan see of Tarragona, until, by God’s favour, the Church of Tarragona recovers the strength of its former standing; thereafter Tortosa itself is to have its own pastor. Further, by this document of the present decree we confirm to you and to your successors, metropolitan bishops of that see, for ever, the city of Tarragona with its boundaries, as it was handed over through your hands to the Church of Tarragona by Raymond, the illustrious count of the Barcelonans, and secured by the legal force of his written charter. To you, therefore, and to your lawful successors to be established in the same see—and, through you, to the Church of Tarragona—we reaffirm that province of Tarragona, so that henceforth within it you may ordain suffragan bishops, celebrate councils according to canonical form, and, by the Lord’s grant, make every provision in accordance with metropolitan jurisdiction, the authority and reverence due to the Apostolic See being preserved in all things.

Your brotherhood is to understand that it may use the pallium only within the church and only at the solemn celebrations of Mass, namely on the following days: the Nativity of the Lord, the Circumcision, Epiphany, the Lord’s Supper, Holy Saturday, the Resurrection of the Lord, the Ascension, Pentecost; on the feasts of the Blessed Virgin Mary, Mother of God; on the nativities of Blessed John the Baptist and of all the apostles; on the feast of Blessed Thecla and of Blessed Fructuosus the martyr; at the consecrations of churches and bishops, and at the ordinations of clergy; and on the anniversary of your own consecration.

We desire you in every respect to uphold the character of this pallium; for the honour of this vestment is humility and justice. Therefore let your brotherhood hasten, with all its heart, to show itself humble toward its neighbours; upright with justice in adversities, should they occur; never accepting anyone’s person against the truth; never suppressing the person of one speaking the truth; compassionate toward the weak; rejoicing with the well-disposed; reckoning others’ losses as its own; mercifully severe against vices; soothing the souls of hearers in fostering virtues; maintaining judgment without anger in anger; and, in tranquillity, not abandoning the censure of just severity. This, dearest brother, is the dignity of the pallium you have received: if you preserve it diligently, you will possess inwardly what you show yourself to have received outwardly. May the Holy Trinity preserve your brotherhood unharmed through long ages.

I, Gelasius, bishop of the Catholic Church.

The sign of my hand: **GOD IS IN HIS HOLY PLACE.**

I, Crescentius, bishop of Sabina, etc.

Given at Gaeta, through the hand of Chrysogonus, cardinal of the Roman Church, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of April [21 March], in the eleventh indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1118, and in the first year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Gelasius II.

## VI. To Bernard, Bishop of Toledo, Primate of Spain.—Concerning Maurice, intruded into the see. (1118, 25 March.)

[MANSI, *Concilia*, XXI, 167.]

GELASIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother BERNARD, archbishop of Toledo and primate of the Spains, greeting and apostolic blessing.

We believe that it has not escaped your brotherhood how our former brother Maurice, bishop of Braga, has long conducted himself: how he abandoned his Church, how he attached himself to an excommunicated king, and how, contrary to canonical enactments, he forced himself into the bed of the Roman Church [Col. 0491C]. Nor are we surprised that he has entirely denied you the obedience due to you and the ancient honour of primacy belonging to your Church: he who attempts not merely to deny but in some manner to destroy the Roman Church, which is mother and teacher of all Churches, etc. We therefore admonish and command you, in accordance with the instruction of our predecessor, to give, with due charitable concern, effective aid and assistance toward holding an election in the Church of Braga. And make known to the other prelates of the Spains that Maurice himself is excommunicated, perjured, and a public violator of the mother Church, etc.

Given at Gaeta, etc.

## VII. To Bernard of Toledo and the Other Bishops of the Spains. (1118, 25 March.)

[BALUZE, *Miscellanea*, ed. Luc., I, 144.]

[Col. 0491D]

GELASIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother BERNARD, primate of Toledo, and to the other bishops of the Spains.

We believe that it has not escaped your brotherhood how our brother Maurice, bishop of Braga, has long conducted himself, how he abandoned his Church, and how he attached himself to an excommunicated king. You also know, as we suppose, that he was excommunicated in a council by our predecessor Pope Paschal of holy memory, and that the Church of Braga [Col. 0492A] was instructed to provide itself with another pastor. Now, at last, through the tyranny of the king, after a long interval following my election, he has forced himself into the bed of the holy mother Church. We therefore command your brotherhood to give, with due charitable concern, assistance toward holding an election in the Church of Braga. Make known to the other children of the Church that Maurice himself is excommunicated, perjured, and a violator of the mother Church.

Given at Gaeta, on the eighth day before the Kalends of April [25 March].

## VIII. To Pontius, Abbot of Cluny.—Privilege for Cluny. (1118, 12 April.)

[MANSI, *Concilia*, XXI, 171.]

[Col. 0492B] GELASIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his dearest brother PONTIUS, abbot of Cluny, greeting and apostolic blessing.

The wise religious devotion and devout wisdom of the monastery of Cluny, both before our time and in our time, have made the Roman Church especially indebted to it. But beyond that common debt of affection, the sincerity of your person—ever pleasing and ever desired by me—has, as you know, enlarged the depths of our affection to their fullest bounds. Therefore we have not thought fit to oppose your petitions, especially those concerning the peace and welfare of your monastery.

Accordingly, by the document of this present decree, in accordance with your brotherhood’s request, we command and establish that whatever possessions belonging to the monastery of Cluny your predecessor Hugh of most reverend memory possessed peacefully and without challenge on the day of his death by the authoritative grant of the Roman pontiffs, you likewise, and your successors, shall possess peacefully and without challenge. We also decree that those things lawfully acquired for the monastery of Cluny after your advancement, through your brethren’s diligence, shall be preserved firm, peaceful, and entire. For we desire the monastery of Cluny, by God’s authorisation, to remain in perpetual peace and tranquillity, so that, free from secular tumults, you may more peacefully devote yourselves to the service of almighty God.

I, Gelasius, bishop of the Catholic Church, have subscribed.

[Col. 0492D] Given at Capua, on the second day before the Ides of April [12 April], through the hand of Grisogonus, deacon-cardinal of the Holy Roman Church, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1118, the eleventh indiction, and in the first year of the pontificate of Pope Gelasius II.

## IX. The Pope informs C[onon], Bishop of Palestrina and Legate of the Apostolic See, concerning the Archbishop of Braga installed by the emperor. (1118, 13 April.)

[MANSI, *Concilia*, XXI, 173.]

GELASIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother C. [CONON], bishop of Palestrina and legate of the Apostolic See, greeting and apostolic blessing.

[Col. 0493A] Some time ago we sent you letters, but we do not know whether they reached you. Their contents were these: after our election, the emperor’s deacon came secretly to Rome with unexpected speed and compelled us to leave. Afterwards he demanded peace through threats and intimidations, saying that he would do what he could unless we assured him of peace by oath. On the counsel of our brethren we offered him peace. Immediately—namely, on the fourth day after our election—he thrust the bishop of “Baracensem” [Bracarensem]—that is, Braga—called Burdinus by the Normans, into an invasion of the mother Church. As you know, in the preceding year this man had been excommunicated in the Council of Benevento by our lord and predecessor Pope Paschal. You also know that, when he had formerly received the pallium through our hands [Col. 0493B], he swore fidelity to our aforesaid lord and to his Catholic successors, of whom I am the first.

In so great a crime the emperor had, thanks be to God, no accomplice from the Roman clergy. But certain Wibertines—Romanus of San Marcello, Centius, called of Saint Chrysogonus, and Teuto, who raged throughout Italy for so long a time—celebrated so infamous a triumph. Indeed, on the previous Palm Sunday at Capua, we, together with our brethren and the college of bishops, excommunicated the king himself together with his idol. We therefore command your prudence to endeavour to make all these matters known, throughout the territories entrusted to your legation, to the brethren established there; and, as you know to be fitting, to arm yourself, God granting, for the vindication of the mother Church.

[Col. 0493C] Given at Capua, on the Ides of April [13 April].

## X. To Bernard, Abbot of the Monastery of Saint Sophia at Benevento: a privilege concerning the conveyance of water from the River Calore. (1118, 18 April.)

[MURATORI, *Rerum Italicarum Scriptores*, III, I, 390.]

In the name of the Lord. GELASIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of the Lord, to his beloved son BERNARD, abbot of the venerable monastery of Saint Sophia, greeting and apostolic blessing.

We see that religious places in our times, because of common sins, are tossed about and oppressed by many hardships and tribulations. Therefore we have judged it fitting and necessary, according to the power divinely given, to assist the necessities of such places more graciously and gently by the favour of the Apostolic See. Accordingly, assenting to your petitions, beloved son in Christ, Abbot Bernard, we grant that henceforth you and your successors may take water from the River Calore through the construction which we have begun, and convey it through your land as far as that same River Calore for two mills or other uses of the monastery.

If need arises, you are to have permission to take the same water above or below the aforesaid construction, insofar, that is, as your land and the water extend. But if, under the pressure of necessity, for that same aqueduct you take land from the adjacent inner road, you shall possess and appropriate it to yourselves for ever according to your will and free judgment, without dispute from any person, great or small; and you shall take an equal amount of your own land and restore the other part. We also hold ratified and acknowledged the exchange which you have made, and caused to be made, there from the intervening land.

I, Gelasius, servant of the servants of the Lord and bishop of the Catholic Church, have written.

The sign of my own hand: **THE LORD IS IN HIS HOLY PLACE.**

I, Peter, bishop of Porto, have consented and likewise subscribed with my own hand.

[Col. 0494B] I, Hugh, cardinal-priest of the title of the Apostles, have consented of free will and judgment and have subscribed.

I, Peter, cardinal-priest of the title of the most holy Virgin Susanna, protector of the monastery, have subscribed and given my consent and will.

Given at Capua, through the hand of Constantine Chrysogonus, deacon and cardinal of the Holy Roman Church, on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of May [18 April], in the eleventh indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1118, and in the first year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Gelasius II.

## XI. To D[idacus], Bishop of Compostela. (1118, 16 June.)

[FLOREZ, *España sagrada*, XX, 259.]

GELASIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable [Col. 0494C] brother D., bishop of Compostela, greeting and apostolic blessing.

Although occupied with weightier affairs, we cannot forget our former affection and friendship. We therefore visit your brotherhood by these present letters, asking and admonishing you to remember the Roman Church, burdened by many afflictions and wearied by many disturbances, and to assist both its needs and ours with due charity. We commend to your goodwill our common sons, Cardinal P. and Peter the treasurer, that for love of us you may hold them dearer than your dear ones.

Given at Ferentino, on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of July [16 June].

## XII. To the Abbots and Monks of Terra Maggiore.—He orders them to cease neglecting the arrangements made by Pope Paschal between them and the Bishop of Civitate (province of Benevento). (1118, 7 August.)

[MURATORI, *Rerum Italicarum Scriptores*, III, I, 396.]

[Col. 0494D]

J[OHN  
[Note: [Col. 0493D] He writes under his own name, by which he was called before he assumed the pontificate.]] of Gaeta, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons, the abbot and monks of Terra Maggiore, greeting and apostolic blessing.

Since, concerning the dispute long ago conducted between you and our venerable brother, the bishop of Civitate, an amicable settlement was reached by the agreement of both parties through the authority of our predecessor Pope Lucius of blessed memory [Note: [Col. 0494D] Read: Paschal II.], as we recall, we have learned, from the report of the aforesaid bishop, that you neglect to observe that settlement and do not hesitate, contrary to its terms, to withhold from him his due right. Since therefore we neither wish nor ought to allow matters settled by apostolic favour or judgment to be reopened through anyone’s renewed malice, or anything to be attempted to their prejudice, we command you by apostolic letters to observe that same settlement inviolably, all contradiction and appeal ceasing, and henceforth not presume to act against it.

And if you have withheld anything from the aforesaid bishop contrary to the terms of that settlement, do not delay to restore it to him without any delay, contradiction, or appeal; or render suitable satisfaction concerning it, and take care more cautiously to abstain from exercising the episcopal office at San Severo, in accordance with the said settlement. Otherwise, on the coming feast of Saint Luke, you are to present yourselves before us, to make a full answer on these matters to the said bishop. No letters obtained from the Apostolic See, should any appear, are to prejudice truth and justice.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, on the tenth day before the Kalends of August [23 July], in the first year of our pontificate.

## XIII. To Gualter, Archbishop of Ravenna.—He confirms his election after the renunciation of schism and grants him the pallium with other rights. (1118, 7 August.)

[MANSI, *Concilia*, XXI, 168.]

[Col. 0495C]

GELASIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother GUALTER, archbishop of the people of Ravenna, greeting and apostolic blessing.

Thanks must be given to the grace of the divine Trinity, which by the spirit of its charity joins what has been divided and makes many minds one in itself. For the Church of Ravenna, severed for many years from unity with the Apostolic See, inflicted many persecutions upon that Apostolic See and supplied many Churches with fuel for perverse schism. Therefore, in order to restrain its wickedness, the Apostolic See took to itself certain Churches subject to it [Col. 0495D], that by this means it might recall it to the path of humility and unity.

But when at last it pleased the divine majesty to recall the Church of Ravenna itself, by the grace of its mercy, to unity and obedience to its mother, the Roman Church, its sons, acknowledging their own iniquity, proved willing to correct their fathers’ offences. Thus those who in former times received, through royal tyranny, bishops pleasing to kings, might now at last elect a bishop pleasing to God according to canonical enactments, and, having renounced schism, return to the bosom of the Catholic congregation.

For they set you, most reverend brother Gualter, forcibly removed from the discipline of regular brethren, upon the chair of Saint Apollinaris [Col. 0496A] by common vote and desire, on account of your pre-eminence in religion and wisdom; and they returned unanimously to obedience to the Apostolic See. Therefore, giving thanks for the unity of the divine Trinity, we consecrate your person to the episcopal ministry, by the Lord’s aid and by the right of our Church; and we restore to you—and through you to the Church of Ravenna—all the dignity which it had possessed through the Roman Church before the time of that division.

By this document of privilege, while preserving in all things the right and authority of the Apostolic See, we grant to you and to your successors who remain in the faith and obedience of that Apostolic See the bishoprics of the province of Aemilia: namely, Piacenza, Parma, Reggio, Modena, Bologna, Ferrara, Adria, Comacchio, Imola, Faenza, Forlì, Forlimpopoli, Bobbio, Cesena, and Ficocle. We also confirm to you the duchy of Ravenna and the monasteries of Saint Adalbert and Saint Hilary of Galliata, together with the other monasteries and possessions conveyed by authentic privileges from our predecessors and from Catholic kings. We entrust to your religious care the monastery of Pomposa, preserving the right of our Church, so that regular discipline may be reformed by your diligence, the Lord granting it.

Moreover, we freely grant your brotherhood the pallium, that is, the fullness of the pontifical office. Your brotherhood is to understand that it may wear it according to the custom of your Church, permitted by a grant of the Apostolic See; and we desire you in every respect to uphold the character of this pallium—perhaps “the enemy” in the printed text should read *nimirum*, “namely.” For the honour of this vestment [Col. 0496C] is humility and justice. Therefore let your brotherhood hasten, with all its heart, to show itself humble in prosperity and upright with justice in adversities, should they occur; friendly to the good and opposed to the perverse; never suppressing the person of one speaking the truth; both persisting in works according to the virtue of constancy and desiring to persist even beyond virtue; compassionate toward the weak; rejoicing with those in good health; exulting in others’ joys as though they were its own; mercifully severe in correcting vices; soothing hearers’ minds in fostering virtues; maintaining judgment without anger in anger; and, in tranquillity, not abandoning the censure of just severity. This, dearest brother, is the dignity of the pallium you have received: if you preserve it diligently, you will possess inwardly what you show yourself to have received outwardly.

I, Gelasius, bishop of the Catholic Church.

The sign of my hand, Gelasius: **GOD IS IN HIS HOLY PLACE.**

Given at Rome, through the hand of Chrysogonus, deacon-cardinal of the Holy Roman Church, on the Kalends of September [1 September], in the twelfth indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1119, and in the first year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Gelasius II.

## XIV. To R., Provost of the Church of Springiersbach, and His Brethren. (1118, 11 August.)

[Published by Ph. JAFFÉ, *Regesta pontificum Romanorum*, with this notice: “Wattenbach supplied it from a copy by Quix.”]

To R., provost of the church of Springiersbach, and his [Col. 0497A] brethren, greeting and apostolic blessing.

We have heard that a question has arisen among you concerning the Rule of Blessed Augustine, because certain matters are written in it—namely, concerning the offices, manual labour, and fasting—which cannot be fulfilled in our provinces. In these matters appropriate moderation must be applied. For those things which concern good morals are to be observed, by the cooperation of divine grace. But those things written by that Doctor concerning the offices cannot be observed, since they differ from the custom both of the Roman Church and of the other Churches. Likewise, certain prescriptions about such observances are written in the Rule of Blessed Benedict which are observed quite differently in monasteries in our time; yet monastic profession is not for that reason thought impaired.

We therefore command that the celebration of the offices among you be observed according to the common custom of the Catholic Church. Manual labour and fasting, however, are to be practised according to the character of the place and the capacities of persons; but the common custom of regular brethren is also to be preserved inwardly. The enactments of the holy Fathers instruct us how participation with excommunicated persons must be avoided. Yet if any, through some frailty or through the violence of the wicked, have defiled themselves by communion with them, they are to be absolved by the judgment of the prior after a suitable penance has been imposed. For our tribulation and that of the Roman Church, let your brotherhood intercede without ceasing with almighty God.

[Col. 0497C] Given at Rome, on the third day before the Ides of August [11 August].

## XV. To the Canons of Lucca.—He approves and renews their customs. (1118, 13 September.)

[MANSI, *Concilia*, XXI, 173.]

GELASIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons BENEDICT, archdeacon; UBERT, archpriest; RAINER, primicerius; MAURO, cantor of the Church of Lucca; and to their brethren, present and future, for ever.

It is characteristic of the good of charity to reckon others’ losses as one’s own and to rejoice in others’ progress as in one’s own. Therefore we graciously admit your petitions and confirm to you the ancient customs of the mother church: namely, that the anointing of the sick and the burials belonging to the mother church of the city, and the office and share in funeral benefices belonging to other churches, shall not be withheld from you by any clerical cunning or by any laypersons whatsoever.

Elections of priors and the appointment of clergy in another church within the city or outside it in the suburbs are not to take place without the consent of the bishop and of the priors established in office and named by the mother church. Nor is any election of priors or clergy in any of the churches to occur through lay violence. No church of your bishopric is to be subjected to another church without their consent. Nor may the bishop, against their will, arrogate to himself any public and major business of the churches [Col. 0498A], or impose public penances. Nor may he attempt to infringe the judgments and interdict of the mother church. No person of your bishopric is to be excommunicated without the consent of the bishop or of the priors established in office and named by the mother church; and what has been bound by the bishop is not to be treated as void by anyone.

Moreover, the clergy of your city and those in the suburbs shall render their customary obediences to that church, so as to be present with you at litanies, common processions, feasts, and stations of the greater church. Further, on the night of Thursday before Easter, no church shall ring bells according to the custom of your church, nor bless the paschal candle on Holy Saturday; rather, the aforesaid clergy shall come for baptism, as is customary. No church, moreover, shall celebrate solemn Masses on the feasts of Blessed Martin and Saint Regulus, on Easter Monday, or during the processions of Lent, until the assemblies for the station have been dismissed. Nor may any cleric presume to perform or celebrate the office of the living or the dead belonging to the mother church.

In addition to these matters, we establish that the tithes of the mother church shall not be withheld by those who pay them, and that no clerical person shall steal or diminish them. Nor may any bishop deprive a canon of the mother church of office or benefice without canonical judgment. Further, we command that those charitable food-benefices which you have been accustomed to receive from your bishops, whether present or absent, at the more solemn feasts, be preserved valid and unimpaired for you and your successors.

In all these matters we confirm and strengthen with perpetual stability the privilege of our predecessor Pope Paschal of holy memory. If, therefore, any ecclesiastical or secular person in the future knowingly attempts rashly to contravene this document of our enactment, and, after a second or third admonition, fails to make amendment by suitable satisfaction, let that person be deprived of the dignity of office and honour; let that person know himself or herself answerable before divine judgment for the iniquity committed; let that person be excluded from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ; and let that person be subject to strict vengeance at the last judgment. But upon all who preserve what is right for this assembly, may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that they may receive here the fruit of good conduct and find before the strict Judge the rewards of eternal peace. Amen.

+ I, Gelasius, bishop of the Catholic Church, have subscribed.

The sign of my hand: **GOD IS IN HIS HOLY PLACE.**

+ I, Deusdedit, cardinal-priest of the title of Saint Lawrence in Damaso, have subscribed.  
+ I, Peter, cardinal of the title of Saint Susanna, have subscribed.  
+ I, Guido, cardinal-priest of the title of Saint Balbina, have subscribed.  
+ I, Peter, cardinal-deacon of Saints Cosmas and Damian, have subscribed.  
+ I, Peter, cardinal-deacon of Saint Adrian, have subscribed.

[Col. 0499A] Given at Pisa, through the hand of Crisogonus, cardinal-deacon of the Holy Roman Church, on the Ides of September [13 September], in the twelfth indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1118, and in the first year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Gelasius II.

## XVI. To the Regular Canons of Saint Frigidian at Lucca.—He confirms their rights and liberties. (1118, 26 September.)

[MANSI, *Concilia*, XXI, 175.]

GELASIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his chosen sons in Christ, ATTO, provost, and his brethren in the church of Blessed Frigidian, who profess the regular life, and to their successors who remain in that same religious profession for ever.

Taught by the Apostle Paul, we know that [Col. 0499B] “where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is freedom.” Since, therefore, we believe that the Spirit of the Lord dwells in you, and are confident of this from the evidence of your very works, we confirm, with the Lord’s help, the freedom bestowed upon you by our predecessor Pope Paschal of holy memory. What he granted you by the document of a privilege, we likewise grant by the authority of the present decree and decree that they shall remain valid and stable, the reverence due to the bishop of Lucca being preserved, as was established by him.

Moreover, for the increase of the religious profession you have undertaken, we grant you authority to observe canonical customs. Nor do we permit any burden to be imposed upon you through the privilege which the canons of Saint Martin obtained from us for the ancient customs of their church; for those provisions do not prejudice regular congregations. Let no summons to processions or litanies disturb your peace, except those which are publicly held before the Ascension of the Lord with the whole city gathering together. No one may, against your will, excommunicate your parishioners or presume to admit them to penance, unless perhaps they are implicated in a public crime, as is contained in the letter of the above-mentioned predecessor of ours. Nor may any chaplain, without your consent, bury the dead of your parish. Rather, you are to anoint them when sick, as you have been accustomed to do, and bury them when dead without anyone’s interference.

The clergy of the greater church are not to take away, under this pretext of the city, the chrism and oil of the sick which your church receives by ancient custom. Nor may they prevent your clergy from being ordained, so that, living quietly and peacefully by God’s grace, you may observe more fully the purpose of your profession. If, indeed, any ecclesiastical or secular person knowingly attempts rashly to act against this document of our enactment, and, after a second or third admonition, fails to correct the matter by suitable satisfaction, let that person be deprived of the dignity of office and honour; let that person know himself or herself answerable before divine judgment for the iniquity committed; let that person be excluded from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, our Redeemer; and let that person be subject to strict vengeance at the last judgment. But upon all who preserve what is right for that place, may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that they may receive here the fruit of good conduct [Col. 0500A] and find before the strict Judge the rewards of eternal peace. Amen.

+ I, Gelasius, bishop of the Catholic Church.

The sign of my hand: **GOD IS IN HIS HOLY PLACE.**

+ I, Lambert, bishop of Ostia.  
+ I, Deusdedit, cardinal-priest of Saint Lawrence in Damaso.  
+ I, Guido, cardinal-priest of the title of Saint Balbina.  
+ I, Peter, cardinal-deacon of Saints Cosmas and Damian.  
+ I, Peter, cardinal-deacon of Saint Adrian.  
+ I, Amicus, cardinal-subdeacon and abbot of Saint Lawrence Outside the Walls.

Given at Pisa, through the hands of Chrysogonus, cardinal-deacon of the Holy Roman Church, on the sixth day before the Kalends of October [26 September], in the twelfth indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1119, and in the first year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Gelasius [Col. 0500B] II.

## XVII. He takes under protection the monastery of Saint Mamilian, situated on the island of Montecristo, and confirms its possessions and rights. (1118, 1 October.)

[UGHELLI, *Italia sacra*, III, 379.]

GELASIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son HENRY, abbot of the monastery of Saint Mamilian, which is on Montecristo, and to his successors regularly appointed for ever.

We acknowledge that we have been advanced, by the Lord’s disposition, to the service of the Holy See, so that, as God grants, we ought to defend and protect its children who seek help. Therefore, beloved son in Christ, Abbot Henry, acceding to your petitions, we fortify with the protection of the Apostolic See the monastery of Blessed Mamilian on Montecristo, over which, with God as guide, you preside.

We establish that no one shall disturb your island, whether with beasts or with any device, and that all things which your monastery possesses, in the forthcoming twelfth indiction, in Corsica or Sardinia, at Piombino or Elba, or elsewhere, shall be preserved for you peaceful and entire. Among these we have thought fit to record by their own names: in Sardinia, the church of Saint Mary of Scala Heliae, Saint Gregory . . . and Saint Mamilian of Simassi with their appurtenances; in Corsica, the monastery of Saint Stephen of Venaco, the monastery of Saint Mary [Col. 0500D] of Majaja, the church of Saint Peregrine, and the church of Saint Paul of Conca with their appurtenances.

Whatever you may hereafter be able to acquire justly with God’s consent shall remain firm and unimpaired for you and your successors. We therefore decree that no person may rashly disturb the same monastery, take away its possessions, retain what has been taken away, diminish them, or harass it with reckless vexations; rather, all things are to be preserved entire for the benefit in every way of those for whose support and governance they were granted.

When you, the abbot of that place, or any of your successors, dies, no one is to be placed over it through any cunning of usurpation or by force, except the person whom the brethren by common consent, or the sounder part of the brethren’s counsel, in the fear of God and according to the Rule of Saint Benedict, determine should be elected. We also decree that burial in the same monastery and its dependent cells shall be free, so that no one may oppose the devotion and last will of those who resolve to be buried there, unless they are excommunicated. We grant that the tithes of your lands, wherever you possess them, shall remain peacefully yours without any claim by bishops or episcopal officials. Nor may anyone’s opposition prevent you from receiving laypersons or secular clergy into conversion.

If, therefore, any ecclesiastical or secular person in the future knowingly attempts to act against this document of our enactment, and, after a second or third admonition, fails to correct the matter by suitable satisfaction, let that person be deprived of the dignity of office and honour; let that person know himself or herself answerable before divine judgment for the iniquity committed; let that person be excluded from the most sacred body and blood of the Lord Jesus Christ, our Redeemer; and let that person be subject to strict vengeance at the last judgment. But upon all who preserve what is right for the same monastery, may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that they may receive here the fruit of good conduct and find before the strict Judge the rewards of eternal peace. Amen.

I, Gelasius, bishop of the Catholic Church, have subscribed.

The sign of my hand: **GOD IS IN HIS HOLY PLACE.**

Given at Pisa, through the hand of Chrysogonus, cardinal-deacon of the Holy Roman Church, on the Kalends of October [1 October], [Col. 0501C] in the twelfth indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1118, and in the first year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Gelasius II.

## XVIII. He assures the Canons of Lucca that, in confirming the privileges of the canons of Saint Frigidian, he has not diminished their rights. (1118, 2 October.)

[MURATORI, *Rerum Italicarum Scriptores*, III, I, 406.]

GELASIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons B., archdeacon; V., archpriest; R., primicerius; P., cantor; and to the other canons of the Church of Lucca, greeting and apostolic blessing.

We heard that your fraternity has been greatly disturbed, as though we had done something against you deserving of disturbance. But we want you to know entirely that we love you as our brothers in the charity of Christ. For although we wish the church of Blessed Frigdian to remain at peace, we have nevertheless neither done anything to you, nor taken anything from you, nor impaired anything belonging to you.

Given at Pisa, the sixth day before the Nones of October.

## XIX. Bull listing the possessions at Nouaillé.  
*(Year 1118, October 23.)*

*[Gallia Christiana nova, II, documents, 347.]*

[Col. 0502A]

GELASIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son RADULPH, abbot of the monastery of Saint Junian at Nouaillé, and to his successors canonically appointed in perpetuity, etc.

For we decree that the church of Saint Luke in the city of Poitiers, together with the churches of Saint Peter of Pranzay [Note: [Col. 0501] Pranzay-lez-Lusignan.], Saint Aquilinus of Lusignan, Saint Peter of Mazerolles [Note: [Col. 0501] Mazeroles.], Saint Mary of Boueresse [Note: [Col. 0501] Boueresse, together with the castle of Moncontour.], together with the castle of Moncontour; with the church of Auvrilly [Note: [Col. 0501] Auvrilly.], with two mills near that same city, with gardens and its other appurtenances; the church of Saint Mary of Lusignan [Note: [Col. 0501] Notre-Dame de Lusignan.], [Col. 0502B] Saint Martin of Anjambes [Note: [Col. 0501] Anjambes-lez-Lusignan.], Saint Florence of Condat [Note: [Col. 0501] Comblé.], with their appurtenances; the church of Marsay [Note: [Col. 0501] Saint-Médard de Marsay.] with the chapel of Saint Amand of Colombiers; of Faduntiis, with its appurtenances; the church of Saint Martin of Fleuré [Note: [Col. 0501] Fleuré.] with its appurtenances; Saint Mary of Availles [Note: [Col. 0501] Availles.] with the woods of Bourneau [Note: [Col. 0501] Bois de Bourneau.], Pinier [Note: [Col. 0501] Pinier.], and Bornet; Saint Mary of Allone [Note: [Col. 0501] Allone.]; Saint Hilary of Jugo Arenae [Note: [Col. 0501] Jouaràne.], with the land of Vintray [Note: [Col. 0501] Vintray.], with mills, meadows, and all else belonging to it; the church of Saint Jurian of Mairé [Note: [Col. 0501] Mairé-l’Évescaut.] with the churches of Pliboux [Note: [Col. 0501] Saint-Martin de Pliboux.], Limalonges [Note: [Col. 0501] Saint Jean-Baptiste de Limalonges.], Conay [Note: [Col. 0501] Conay.], Clussey [Note: [Col. 0501] Notre-Dame de Clussey.], and La Chapelle [Note: [Col. 0501] La Chapelle de Saint-Junien Poulioux.], together with the lands of Libardon [Note: [Col. 0501] Libardon.] and Farlan [Note: [Col. 0501] Farlan.], and with their villages, lands, and appurtenances; the church of Saint Peter of Exoudun [Note: [Col. 0501] Exodun.], Saint Nicholas of Sivray [Note: [Col. 0501] Sivray.] with the parish of that same castle, Saint Martin of Couhé [Note: [Col. 0501] Couhé.] with the parish [Col. 0502C] of that same castle; Saint Martin of Brutz [Note: [Col. 0501] de Brutz.] with the land of Premilban [Note: [Col. 0501] Premilban.]; the church of Rom, of Ardilleux [Note: [Col. 0501] Saint-Junien d’Ardilleux.] with its appurtenances; the church of Saint Genard [Note: [Col. 0501] Saint-Genard.] of Notiac, with the church of Paizay [Note: [Col. 0501] Paizay-le-Tort.] and all its other appurtenances; Saint Peter of Frontenay-l’Abattu [Note: [Col. 0501] Frontenay-l’Abattu.] with its appurtenances; Saint Saviour in Aunis [Note: [Col. 0501] Saint-Sauveur-en-Aunis.] with its village and with the church of Rioux [Note: [Col. 0501] Rioux.], with mills, saltworks, meadows, lands, and all its other appurtenances; Saint Maurice of La Chanelle-Soudan [Note: [Col. 0501] La Chanelle-Soudan.]; the church of Colombiers [Note: [Col. 0501] Notre-Dame de Colombiers] in the castellany of Château-Airaud; Saint Peter of Pugny [Note: [Col. 0501] Pugny.] with its appurtenances; Saint Gaudent [Note: [Col. 0501] Saint-Gaudent.] near Frontenay; Saint Brice of Cundagia [Note: [Col. 0501] Saint-Bris de Dine.]; the land of Ferrières; the land of Ferrabeuf [Note: [Col. 0501] Ferrabeuf.]; and likewise everything which that monastery either possesses at present or may in future acquire by the grant of princes, the offerings of the faithful, or other just means: may all these things remain secure and unimpaired for you and your successors.

We therefore decree that no one, etc. Moreover, concerning priests who are installed in churches throughout parishes belonging to monasteries, we confirm the ruling of our predecessor of holy memory, Pope Urban II: namely, that abbots, with the counsel of bishops, shall appoint priests in the parish churches which [Col. 0503A] they hold; and bishops, with the abbot’s consent, shall entrust the care of the parish to the priest, so that such priests shall render account to the bishop for the care of the people, but shall show the abbot due subjection in temporal matters belonging to the monastery; and thus each person’s rights shall be preserved.

Indeed, by the prohibition of this present decree, we abolish that wicked custom whereby, on the feast of Blessed Junian, the clerics of Saint Hilary attack or disturb the choir, refectory, and cloister of the monastery. Rather, the monks shall peacefully and privately perform their solemn observances according to regular custom, without the disturbance of secular clerics. If therefore in future any ecclesiastical or secular person, etc., may they find the rewards of eternal peace. [Col. 0503B] Amen.

I, Gelasius, bishop of the Catholic Church.

The sign of my hand: GOD IS IN HIS HOLY PLACE.

Given at Marseilles through the hand of Gregory, cardinal-deacon of the Holy Roman Church, the tenth day before the Kalends of November, indiction XII, in the year 1119 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the first year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Gelasius II.

## XX. He confirms the privileges of Bernard, primate of Toledo.  
*(Year 1118, November 7.)*

*[MURATORI, Rerum Italicarum Scriptores, III, I, 411.]*

GELASIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his most reverend brother BERNARD, primate of Toledo, and to his successors canonically appointed in perpetuity.

[Col. 0503C] It is charity’s own good to rejoice together in the progress of others, etc. Therefore, following in the footsteps of our predecessors of holy memory, Urban II and likewise Paschal II, we confirm, by the Lord’s grant, both to you and to your successors who adorn the chair of the Church of Toledo, the primacy of all Spain, while preserving, nevertheless, the authority of the Roman Church and the privileges of each metropolitan, etc.

I, Gelasius, bishop of the Catholic Church, subscribe.+

The sign of my hand: GOD IS IN HIS HOLY PLACE.

Given at Saint-Gilles, through the hands of Chrysogonus, cardinal-deacon of the Holy Roman Church, the seventh day before the Ides of November, indiction XII, in the year 1119 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the first year [Col. 0503D] of the pontificate of Pope Gelasius II.

## XXI. To Diego, bishop of Compostela.—He commends his envoys.  
*(Year 1118, November 17.)*

*[FLÓREZ, España sagrada, XX, 267.]*

GELASIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother D., bishop of Compostela, greeting and apostolic blessing.

[Col. 0504A] We do not wish to forget the love of our former friendship; you yourself will read more clearly upon the tablet of your heart what it has long been toward you. Therefore, as we are about to summon our brother bishops of Spain to the council which, with God’s help, we have resolved to hold in Auvergne on the Kalends of March, we address you alone apart from them, because the affairs of that kingdom depend in your hands. We commend to your goodwill our envoys whom we are sending for this summons. Remember: the villager, friend, and physician are tested in time of need.

Given at Maguelone, the fifteenth day before the Kalends of December.

## XXII. Prohibition against abbots or priors of other monasteries receiving those professed in the church of Saint Mary of Fontevraud.

*[COCQUELINES, vol. II, 160, from the Vatican archives.]*

GELASIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons, the abbots and priors of monasteries, greeting and apostolic blessing.

You ought to remember that the Lord says in the Gospel: “Whatever you wish people to do to you, do likewise to them.” For we have heard that some of you receive persons professed in the church of Saint Mary of Fontevraud, where, by the Lord’s grace, the strictest observance of religious life has now been maintained for a long time. By such misplaced kindness, the bonds of religious life and profession are plainly dissolved. Therefore, by these present letters we command all of you not henceforth to receive persons professed in that church, but that they keep, in that very place, for God’s honour and the salvation of their souls, the pledge of their profession.

Given at Maguelone, the twelfth day before the Kalends of December. [Note: [Col. 0503D] In this year Gelasius came to Maguelone. He withdrew from there after remaining at Pisa for several days, embarking again upon the sea and reaching the harbour of Saint-Gilles, as Pandulf of Pisa—an intimate of Gelasius and his biographer—relates. That Gelasius was at that harbour on 7 November of this year is evident from the privilege issued there, by which he confirmed to Archbishop Bernard of Toledo [Col. 0504D] and his successors the primacy of all Spain. For at its end (the fragment is quoted by Baronius in the additions and corrections to the year 1118) one reads: “Given at Saint-Gilles through the hand of Chrysogonus, etc., the seventh day before the Ides of November, indiction XII, in the year 1119 of the Lord’s Incarnation,” according to the Pisan reckoning, which corresponds to the year 1118.]

## XXIII. Bull for the abbey of Lagrasse.  
*(Year 1118, November 30.)*

*[Gallia Christiana, VI, documents, 434.]*

GELASIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son BERENGARIUS, abbot of the monastery of Blessed Mary of Lagrasse, situated in the diocese of Carcassonne, and to his successors canonically appointed in perpetuity.

In the registers of the Lateran palace we find that Emperor Charles, when founding the monastery of Blessed Mary of Lagrasse in the diocese of Carcassonne, offered it to Blessed Peter together with all that he had bestowed upon that place. We too, therefore, accepting that offering of the Catholic king, have decreed to foster that monastery under the protection of Blessed Peter, determining that everything conferred upon it by that same king or by other Catholic princes, or acquired by other just means, shall remain forever secure and unimpaired. Among these we have judged the following worthy of being recorded by their proper names.

[Col. 0505A] In the diocese of Narbonne: the church of Saint Lawrence (Saint-Laurent-de-Cabreresse); Saint Stephen of Camplong; Saint Paul of Rivo Putido [Note: [Col. 0505D] It is now destroyed.]; Saint Felix of Capestang; Saint Peter of Licis; Saint Eulalia of Roubian; Saint Peter of Najoaras; Saints Felix and Nazarius of Lézignan; Saint Julian of Fonte Cooperto; Saint Saturninus of Villarubea; Saint Eulalia of Tezano; Saint Adrian of Tornezarno; Saint Sebastian of Ripa Alta; Saint Peter of Pratis; Saint Acisclus of the village of Berziano; Saint Martin of Triviac; Saint Romanus of Furca; Saint Mary Magdalene of Quintiano [otherwise, Quintiliano]; Saints Adrian and Mary of Mairolas; Saint Julian of Calzcastel; Saint John of Perron [otherwise, Berron]; Saint John of Palma; Saint Martin of Novellis; [Col. 0505B] Saint John of Tusciano; Saint Mary of Fausta; Saint Peter of Paderno; Saint Mary of Vigrado [otherwise, Vinogrando]; Saint Martin of Molleta; Saint Andrew of Mansionibus; Saint Saturninus of Palairac; Saint Fructuosus of Casa Cooperta; Saint Martin of Puteo; Saint Stephen of Romaneto; Saint Romanus of Laurera [otherwise, of Leyreiria]; Saint Cyprian of Cuciis; Saint Peter of Planeda; Saint Felix of Malverzo [otherwise, Malverio]; Saint Stephen of Cepiano; Saint Martin of Palazol; Saint Andrew of Azillano; and Saint Peter of Capraspina, with their appurtenances.

Also in that same diocese: the castle of Leco with its appurtenances; the castle of Laco with its appurtenances; and the coastal districts of Lézignan, Roubian, Caputmortis, Luc, Rivo Putido, Camplong, Villarubea, [Col. 0505C] Calzcastel, and Novellis, with their villages and appurtenances; the village of Palma, Tezano, Castoga, Ferrals, Fonte Cooperto, Ripa Alta, Tornisarno, Prati, the village of Borciano, Triviac, Quartilianis, Tuxsani, Fausta, Molleta, Paderno, Taxi, Mansionis, Palairac, Buxenac, Lairere, Buxa, Aurciole, Caprespine, Malverii, Sipiani, Cuxani, and Planede, with their churches and appurtenances; and the allod of Capestang, Cuxiac, Saint Jorio, Narbonne, Harpadeux, Faberzan, Palasolel, Bernet, and Agantan.

In the diocese of Carcassonne: the church of Saint Michael of Nahusa; Saint Martin of Podiolato; Saint Julian of Rabendosa; Saint Peter of Alaric; Saint Cucuphas of Lausa; Saint Martin of Curtis; Saint Mary of Cominiano; [Col. 0505D] Saint Peter of Millanello; Saint Andrew of Milhano; Saint Paul of Coloniaco [otherwise, Bolhonaco]; Saint Fulk; Saint Hilary of Casilaco; Saint Mary of Veziliano [otherwise, Verzellano]; Saint Cyricus of Agrifolio; Saint John of Upper Agrifolio; Saints Stephen and Cyprian of Faveriis; Saint Mary of Tautirano; Saint Martin of Cosano; Saint Mary of Cerviano; Saint Stephen of Caunas; Saint Peter of Bagnuls; Saint Mary of Petramala; Saint Cyprian of the village of Alzenaria [otherwise, Asinaria]; Saint Genesius of Septembisano; Saint Felix of Mirallas; and Saint Mary of Casillars, with their appurtenances; and the castle of Alaric, and the village of Saint Cucuphas of Lauza, and Flexi, Curtes, Cuminian, Milani, Bolonaci, Cazilaci, Virziliani, Upper and Lower Agrifolium; [Col. 0506A] and the allod of Badenx and of Beriac, with its appurtenances.

In the diocese of Toulouse: the monastery of Blessed Mary of Camon, with its appurtenances; the church of Saint Peter of Marenx; Saint Vincent of Ax; Saint Peter of Prades; Saint Saturninus of Arsat; Saint Peter of Sorsat; Saint Peter of Podio; Saint Peter of Agenat; Saint Mary of Ravat; Saint Felix of Faulinges; Saints Mary and Paul of Alta Ripa; Saint Martin of Petrafitta; Saint Mary of Porcelligrisei; Saint Stephen of Soplesenx; Saints Lupus and John of Tortorag [otherwise, Tourriac]; Saint Mary of Beced, with their villages and appurtenances; and Saint Mary of Solario.

In the diocese of Elne: the churches of Saints Stephen and Vincent of Stagello; Saint Martin of Corneliano; [Col. 0506B] Saint Mary of Fonte; Saint Felix of Peziliano; Saint Saturninus; Saint Stephen; Saint Mamet; Saints Mary and Andrew of Ripa Alta; Saint Columba; Saint Mary of Toluges [otherwise, Coluges]; Saint Mark [otherwise, Saint Cyricus] of Canoas; Saint Martin of Canoas; and Saint Peter of Prata; the monastery of Saint Martin of Canigou; and Saint Andrew of Subereta, with their villages and specified appurtenances.

In the diocese of Girona: the monastery of Saint Mary of Riudazer [otherwise, Rividario]; Saint Sepulchre of Paleira; Saint Stephen of Catnellas; Saint Felix of Lagostera; Saint Peter of Gallicantu; and Saint Felix of Geisal [otherwise, Gersan], with their villages and appurtenances.

In the diocese of Saragossa: the monastery of Jassaria, with its appurtenances.

In the diocese of Urgell: the church of Saint Peter of Burgal [Col. 0506C] [otherwise, Burgaliis]; Saint Peter of Linars; and the villages of Cinzors and Roret, with their appurtenances.

In the diocese of Albi: the church of Saint Peter of Rosen [otherwise, Rosieux], with its appurtenances. Moreover, whatever you may in future be able justly and canonically to acquire through grants of pontiffs, the generosity of princes, or the offerings of the faithful, shall always be preserved for you and your successors undisturbed and intact.

We therefore decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the aforesaid monastery, take away its possessions, retain what has been taken, diminish them, or harass it with reckless vexations; rather, all these things shall be preserved intact for the benefit in every way of those for whose support and governance they were granted. [Col. 0506D]

Moreover, in order that the same monastery of Lagrasse, established under the protection and jurisdiction of our holy Roman Church, which by God’s authorship we serve, may not be subjected to the dominion of any church of another jurisdiction, we forbid every priest of any church to exercise any jurisdiction there, save the rector of this Apostolic See; so strictly that, unless invited by the abbot, he may not presume even to celebrate the solemnities of Mass there.

Upon the death of you, abbot of that place, or of any one of your successors, no one shall be put in charge there by any trickery of deceit or by force, except one whom the brethren, by common consent, or the sounder part of the brethren, shall elect in the fear of God and according to the Rule of Blessed Benedict, [Col. 0507A] to be consecrated by the Roman pontiff or by one to whom he has entrusted this office. You shall receive chrism, holy oil, consecrations of altars and churches, and the ordinations of monks who are to be promoted to sacred orders, from the diocesan bishops—provided that they have the grace and communion of the Apostolic See and are willing to provide these freely and without impropriety. Otherwise, you may approach whatever Catholic bishops you prefer and receive from them the sacraments of consecration; upheld by the authority of the Apostolic See, they shall grant what is requested.

Nor, because of interdicts imposed upon neighbouring parishes, shall your brethren who reside in your churches be suspended from divine offices or prohibited from conducting the funerals of their dead. Rather, they alone, together with their [Col. 0507B] dependants, shall perform the offices of divine worship behind closed church doors and render the rites due for burial. We also judge that the burial of those who have resolved to be buried at your places shall be free, and no one shall oppose their devotion and last will, unless they happen to be excommunicated.

Moreover, concerning priests installed in churches throughout parishes belonging to monasteries, we confirm the ruling of our predecessor of holy memory, Pope Urban II: namely, that abbots, with the counsel of bishops, shall appoint priests in parish churches which they hold; but bishops, with the abbots’ consent, shall entrust the parish to a priest, so that such priests shall render an account to the bishop for the care of the people, but shall show the abbot due subjection in temporal matters belonging to the monastery, [Col. 0507C] and thus each person’s rights shall be preserved. As an acknowledgment of the liberty received from the Roman Church, you shall pay five gold coins each year to the Lateran palace. If therefore in future any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowing the text of this our constitution, should rashly attempt to violate it, etc.

I, Gelasius, bishop of the Catholic Church.

The sign of my hand: GOD IS IN HIS HOLY PLACE.

Given at Maguelone through the hand of Grysogonus, cardinal-deacon of the Holy Roman Church, the second day before the Kalends of December, indiction XII, in the year 1119 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the first year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Gelasius II.

## XXIV. To Bernard, Archbishop of Auch.  
*(Year 1118, December 8.)*

*[D. BOUQUET, Recueil, XIV, 322.]*

[Col. 0507D]

GELASIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable [Col. 0508A] brother BERNARD, Archbishop of Auch, greeting and apostolic blessing.
