Concerning the cemetery of Saint Orientius, many complaints have often been made in our presence before the tribunal of the Roman pontiffs. Yet it has altogether pleased them that that cemetery should be preserved in the future as it was established in antiquity. We therefore command you not to trouble the brothers of the monastery of Saint Orientius over this matter; but let the cemetery remain henceforth peaceful and intact, as it has remained until now, and let no new one be constructed contrary to ancient custom.

Given at Tornac, the sixth day before the Ides of December. [Note: [Col. 0507D] Tornac, in the diocese of Alès, where Gelasius stayed in 1118 while travelling to Cluny.]

## XXV. To the army of Christians besieging the city of Saragossa.—He grants indulgence to all who contribute something to it.  
*(Year 1118, December 10.)*

*[MANSI, Councils, XXI, 1169.]*

[Col. 0508B]

GELASIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the army of Christians besieging the city of Saragossa and to all adherents of the Catholic faith, greeting and apostolic blessing.

We have examined the letter of your devotion and have willingly lent our favour to the request which you presented to the Apostolic See on behalf of the elect of Saragossa. Therefore, sending back to you that same elect, consecrated by the Lord’s gift through our hands, as though through those of Blessed Peter, we bestow upon you the blessing of apostolic visitation, imploring the equitable mercy of almighty God that, through the prayers and merits of the saints, he may cause you to accomplish his work for his honour and the enlargement of his Church. [Col. 0508C]

And because you have resolved to expose both yourselves and your possessions to the utmost dangers: if any of you, having received penance for his sins, dies on this expedition, we absolve him from the bonds of his sins through the merits of the saints and the prayers of the whole Catholic Church. Furthermore, those who labour or shall labour in the same service of the Lord, and those who give or shall give something for the rebuilding of the church of the aforesaid city, destroyed by Saracens and Moabites, and for the maintenance of the clerics serving God there, shall, according to the extent of their labours and of the benefits bestowed by them upon the Church, obtain, at the judgment of the bishops [Col. 0508D] in whose parishes they reside, remission and indulgence of their penances.

Given at Alès, the fourth day before the Ides of December. [Note: [Col. 0507D] (10) Upon receiving these, the same Peter, having been ordained bishop of Saragossa, took care to publish throughout the whole Christian world, with letters of his own appended, this diploma of indulgences, writing as follows:

“To all faithful of the Church throughout the world—to archbishops, bishops, abbots, priests, and all adherents of the Catholic faith—PETER, though unworthy bishop of Saragossa, greeting and blessing. Through the favour of divine mercy, your prayers, and the courage of valiant men, you have heard sufficiently that the city of Saragossa has been brought under Christian control and that the church of the blessed and glorious Virgin Mary, which for a long time—alas!—[Col. 0508D] lay under Saracen domination, has been liberated; you know that it flourishes under the blessed and ancient name of holiness and dignity. Yet you know that, exhausted by the sorrow of its former captivity, it lacks nearly everything: both because it has no means by which the ruined walls and ornaments of the aforesaid church can be restored, and because the clerics there, occupied day and night in divine service, possess no means of livelihood.

“We therefore beseech your mercy: if you cannot visit it in bodily presence, at least visit it mercifully through the offering of your alms, remembering the Psalmist’s words: ‘Blessed is he who considers the needy and poor; on the day of evil the Lord will deliver him’ (Psalm XL). But for those who grieve with the aforesaid church, destitute of necessary relief, over the sufferings of its poverty, and send one denarius—or as much as they can—for its restoration, we, trusting in divine mercy and in the authority of Lord [Col. 0509C] Pope Gelasius (you will find written on the above-mentioned page a copy of the letters of the cross which we have signed in our church), and in that of Lord Bernard, archbishop of Toledo and legate of the Holy Roman Church, and of all the bishops of Spain, … [Col. 0509D] remit their penance. Others, indeed, shall obtain remission of their sins according to the amount of their benefactions and the merit of their works. May those who receive kindly this our archdeacon named Miorrandus and his companions, bearers of the present letters, or assist them, obtain eternal life from the Lord. Farewell.”

Thus Peter, bishop of Saragossa, who, as you have heard, sent the apostolic letters along with these, all strengthened by the subscriptions of Archbishop Bernard of Toledo and of the other bishops of Spain, in this form:

“I, Bernard, archbishop of the Church of Toledo, make and confirm this absolution.”

“I, bishop of Huesca, make [Col. 0510C] and confirm this absolution.”

“I, Sancho, bishop of Calahorra, make [Col. 0510D] and confirm this absolution.”

“I, Guido, bishop of Lescar, make and confirm this absolution.”

The legate of the Apostolic See, who was then residing in Spain, also appears subscribed twice in this manner: “I, Boso, cardinal of the Holy Roman Church, make and confirm this absolution.”

Thus far the monuments of venerable antiquity, brought to light through the industry of Jerónimo Blancas in his *Commentaries on Aragonese Affairs* from the Saragossa archive. They reveal the ancient practice of promulgating indulgences and, at the same time, the ancient cult of the most devout church of the Blessed Virgin, called “of the Pillar,” which even now is frequented not only by the peoples of Spain but also by foreign visitors and is renowned throughout the Christian world for its illustrious fame. SEV. BIN.]

## XXVI. To Pontius, Abbot of Cluny.—He confirms the privileges of the monastery of Cluny.  
*(Year 1118, December 16.)*

*[MANSI, Councils, XXI, 171.]*

[Col. 0509A]

GELASIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his dearest son in Christ, PONTIUS, abbot of Cluny, and to his successors canonically appointed in perpetuity.

It is a legal command that fire should always burn upon the altar. The priest who succeeded his father by right was to sustain it, placing a pile of wood beneath it so that it should not fail. The true priest, the Son of the eternal Father, has long preserved this in our hearts; for even before he raised you to the office of abbot and me to the ministry of the pontificate, he kindled our hearts with the fire of love, preserved mutual charity in us, and enlarged it after we received our offices. [Col. 0509B]

Therefore, in the matters which you request for the welfare and tranquillity of the monastery of Cluny, we have judged it unworthy to refuse your beloved person. The venerable religious life of that place itself and the venerable life of your predecessors also compel us to do these things. Accordingly, at your request and that of your brethren, we decree that everything which your predecessor, Abbot Hugh of blessed memory, possessed on the day of his death in such peaceful and unchallenged possession that he declined no canonical judgment concerning it, shall be held and possessed by you and the monastery of Cluny hereafter peacefully and without disturbance.

We also remove, by the protection of the Apostolic See, that grievance which you suffer: namely, that bishops, in controversies which frequently arise between you and them, grievously afflict with their interdicts innocent persons in your parishes who have no part in the dispute. We also entrust to your diligence, and to that of your successors who remain in the same observance of religious life and love of the Apostolic See, the administration of the abbeys which our predecessors, pontiffs of the Apostolic See, prudently committed by their privileges to your predecessors, [Col. 0510A] so that through your industry, with the Lord’s help, the state of religious observance may be preserved in them: namely, in the diocese of Limoges, the abbey of Saint Martial; in that of Angoulême, the abbey of Saint Cybard; in that of Saintes, the abbey of Saint John of Angély; in the city of Poitiers, the abbey called the New Monastery; in the diocese of Toulouse, the abbey of Lézat; in that of Cahors, the abbeys of Moissac and Figeac; in that of Nîmes, the abbey of Saint-Gilles; in the district of Auvergne, the abbeys of Mozac, Thiers, and Menat; in the diocese of Autun, the abbey of Vézelay; in the city of Auxerre, the abbey of Saint Germanus; in the diocese of Cambrai, the abbey of Anchin; in that of Rouen, the abbey called Pontoise; [Col. 0510B] in that of Thérouanne, the abbeys of Saint-Bertin and Saint-Winoc; and in Italy, the abbey of Saint Benedict above the Po.

May those things which have been lawfully acquired in our time through the diligence of you or your brethren remain undisturbed and unimpaired for you and your successors. Further, concerning the use of the dalmatic and sandals, which our predecessor of holy memory, Pope Paschal, granted chiefly at our intercession to your person, we grant you this special token of more abundant affection: whenever you celebrate solemn Masses or celebrate before the people, you may use those same insignia.

Furthermore, whatever liberty and whatever protection has been granted by our predecessors, we also strengthen for you and your successors by the text of this present decree. If anyone, knowing the tenor of this decree, should rashly attempt—God forbid!—to oppose it, let him be punished by the vengeance of apostolic indignation unless he corrects his presumption by fitting satisfaction.

I, Gelasius, bishop of the Catholic Church, have subscribed.

Given at Avignon through the hand of Chrysogonus, cardinal-deacon of the Holy Roman Church, the seventeenth day before the Kalends of January, indiction XII, in the year 1119 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the first year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Gelasius II.

## XXVII. Bull for the monastery of Caunes, in the diocese of Narbonne.  
*(Year 1118, December 20.)*

*[BALUZE, Capitularies, II, 1557.]*

[Col. 0511A]

GELASIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son ARNALD, abbot of the monastery of Caunes, and to his successors canonically appointed in perpetuity.

We are instructed by the precepts of the Gospel to grant what is asked of us by every petitioner. Accordingly, at the request of our venerable brothers, the archbishops of Narbonne and Arles, we receive under the protection of the Apostolic See, following the example of our predecessor of holy memory Pope Urban, the monastery of Caunes, over which by God’s authorship you preside, together with all that belongs to it. This monastery was built by Count Milo under the authority of Emperor Charles of good memory [Col. 0511B] and fortified by royal charters, both by him and by his son Louis and his grandson Charles, likewise emperors, in honour of the holy Apostles Peter and Paul.

Therefore, by the authority of this present decree we establish that the liberty granted to that place by the aforesaid emperors shall be permanently preserved. That is: no public judge and no official of the court shall constrain the tenants of that church without the consent of the abbot and brethren, nor presume to exact from the property of the monastery any census payment or tax whatsoever. And whatever the monastery of Caunes possesses in the districts of Narbonne, Minervois, Carcassonne, Razès, or Albi shall remain free from every person’s molestation or disturbance.

[Col. 0511C] Namely, in the district of Narbonne, from the very times of the aforesaid emperors: the church of Saint Paul; saltworks in the place called Cagacanes; and the island called Dumanas. In Minervois: the village called Libras with its church; the village of Bajani with its church; Vitesia with its church; a part of the village of Trenciani; a part of Villare; a part of the village of Abrensis; a part of the village of Campolong; the village of Cros with its church. In the mountain district of Spinacia, with its villages: a part of the village of Raberti. In the district of Carcassonne: the village or church of Saint Fructuosus; the church of Saint Lawrence; the village of Baniolas with its church; the village of Palazol with its church; Orris with its church; and a part of the village of Glujani. In Razès: the village of Recemiro [Col. 0511D] with its church. In the district of Albi: the church of Saint Amantius. Likewise in the district of Carcassonne: part of the village of Fonte Cooperta.

Furthermore, we decree that whatever this monastery rightfully possesses today, or may in future be able justly and canonically to acquire through grants of pontiffs, the generosity of princes, or the offerings of the faithful, shall remain secure and unimpaired for you and your successors. Therefore no person whatsoever may rashly disturb this monastery, take away its possessions, retain what has been taken, diminish them, or harass it with reckless vexations. Rather, all things shall be preserved intact for the benefit in every way of those for whose support and governance they were granted.

Nor shall that monastery be subjected by force to another authority so long as, by the Lord’s gift, the strength of regular discipline endures in it, while preserving the canonical reverence due to the archbishop of Narbonne. Upon the death of you, the present abbot of that place, or of any of your successors, no one shall be set over it through any artifice of deceit or force, except one whom the brethren, by common consent or the sounder part of the brethren, in the fear of God and according to the Rule of Blessed Benedict, shall provide to be elected from their own congregation or, if necessary, from another. [Col. 0512A]

We also decree that the burial-ground of that place shall be wholly free, so that no one may oppose the devotion and final will of those who resolve to be buried there, unless they happen to be excommunicated. If therefore in future any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowing the text of this our constitution, should rashly attempt to violate it, then, after a second or third warning, if he does not make amendment by suitable satisfaction, let him lose the rank of his power and honour; let him know that he stands guilty before divine judgment of the iniquity he has committed; let him be separated from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Redeemer; and let him be liable to severe vengeance at the final judgment. [Col. 0512B]

But upon all who preserve justice toward that same place may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that they may receive here the fruit of good action and find, before the strict Judge, the rewards of eternal peace. Amen.

I, Gelasius, bishop of the Catholic Church, have subscribed.

The sign of my hand: GOD IS IN HIS HOLY PLACE.

Given at Orange through the hand of Grysogonus, cardinal-deacon of the Holy Roman Church, the thirteenth day before the Kalends of January, indiction [Col. 0512C] XII, in the year 1119 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the first year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Gelasius II.

## XXVIII. Privilege for the monastery of Saint Andrew of Avignon.  
*(Year 1118, December 20.)*

*[History of Languedoc, vol. II, Proofs, p. 407, from the archives of the abbey of Saint Andrew of Avignon.]*
GELASIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son PETER, abbot of the monastery of Saint Andrew, situated on the summit of Mount Andaon above the river Rhône, and to his successors to be regularly appointed for ever.

The authority of our office exhorts us to be solicitous for the condition of churches [Col. 0512D] and to strengthen whatever has been rightly established. Although we owe this to the other churches, we are bound to show it with a more gracious familiarity to your church, which, while we were in the regions of Gaul, divine providence granted should be consecrated by our own hands. Therefore, all things which have been granted and confirmed to your monastery by the authority either of our ordainer and predecessor, Pope Urban of holy memory, or of the other Roman pontiffs Gregory, Victor, and John, we likewise grant and confirm by the present page of privilege, etc. But as a token of the liberty received from the Apostolic See, you shall annually pay to us and to our successors three pounds of wax from the monastery of Blessed Andrew itself, and two from the aforesaid church of Blessed Peter of Todona, which you hold by right from [Col. 0513A] the holy Roman Church, etc.

I, Gelasius, bishop of the Catholic Church.

The sign of my hand: GOD IS IN HIS HOLY PLACE.

I, Lambert, bishop of Ostia.

I, Boso, cardinal.

[Col. 0514A] I, Peter, cardinal-deacon of Saint Nicholas in the Tullian Prison.

Given at Orange, through the hand of Grysogonus, cardinal-deacon of the Holy Roman Church, on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of January, in the twelfth indiction, in the year 1119 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the first year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Gelasius II.

IN THE YEAR OF THE LORD 1119: LAURENTIUS OF VERONA, PISAN DEACON

[Col. 0513]

[Col. 0513]

## HISTORICAL NOTICE ON LAURENTIUS

(Fabricius, *Bibliotheca medii et infimae Latinitatis*, IV, 251)

Laurentius of Verona, a Pisan deacon, in the time of Peter II, archbishop of Pisa from 1103 to 1120, wrote in heroic verse seven books *On the Balearic War*, or *On the Pisan Affairs in Majorca and Their Triumph Celebrated at Pisa in the Year 1115*:

> When the one thousand one hundred and fifteenth year had come,  
> Since Christ was veiled in the covering of flesh.

Ughellus published it in the new edition of *Italia Sacra*, vol. X, p. 127.

[Col. 0513]

# THE SEVEN BOOKS OF LAURENTIUS OF VERONA, PISAN DEACON, ON THE BALEARIC WAR, OR ON THE PISAN AFFAIRS IN MAJORCA AND THEIR TRIUMPH CELEBRATED AT PISA IN THE YEAR OF SALVATION 1115

(Edited by Ughelli, *Italia Sacra*, vol. X, p. 127, from the parchment manuscript of Viviano de Vivianis, bishop of Insula.)

## BOOK ONE BEGINS

[Col. 0513A]

We write of arms, ships, a people, vengeance wrought from heaven,  
and the harsh toils of land and sea;  
of men spreading through the fields of Geryon,  
the slaughter of Moors, and kingdoms despoiled and subdued.  
For these beginnings, Christ, deign to grant your favour.

He had terrorized Hesperia, returning to the Latin cities,  
and was well known in many places throughout the countryside to the Goths;  
[Col. 0514A] he had appeared also to the Gauls, driven through every land.

For evil Majorca had taken up deadly weapons,  
waging bloody wars against faithful peoples.  
Her madness and violent fleet had reached and ravaged  
the Italian, Sicilian, and Greek regions.  
After burning fortresses, ships, and villages,  
and violating the holy objects upon the altars of burned temples,  
[Col. 0515A] it urged captives to deny Christ’s commands  
and embrace the empty precepts of its own “resulla” [reading uncertain].  
Those who believed such things it loved with excessive reverence;  
those who resisted it subjected to various tortures.

Fetters, heavy manacles, and prison subdued some;  
hateful hunger, dense crowds, and excessive labours subdued others.  
And, as those whom they say report truth testify,  
there were more than thirty thousand captives,  
whom the cruel tyrant of the Balearics bound and held,  
apart from those whom he transferred by trade  
upon ships to unknown places, or whom a harsh death released from the flesh.

The report of so great an evil, known through many lands,  
at once stirred Pisa, eager for gain.  
Anger roused the elders—men able to conquer Punic kingdoms  
and subject a people to their tribute.

[Col. 0515B]

Here, while they recount their noble deeds and the wars of Palermo—  
how Africa was captured and made tributary,  
and how very many battles were won amid changing fortunes—  
they kindle the spirits of young men, to whom dreadful exploits,  
toil, sweat, and the glory of harsh Mars  
were preferable to riches and pleasures.

Then the pious bishop Peter, radiant in virtue,  
recalling these things to his citizens, took up  
the renowned signs of the cross; and the bands, moved in turn by piety,  
were likewise numerous in taking up the signs of the cross,  
as they hurried at the solemn season of Easter,  
when they partake of Christ’s body and holy blood.

Then they appointed twenty-two men of the highest nobility,  
to whom the power of consul and commander was entrusted,  
[Col. 0515C] so that they might govern all gravely;  
and their unsullied judgment, arranging each matter  
suitable for warfare, might prepare what could aid the men  
and equip the fleet.

And lest their names pass you by, reader,  
search the following letters with attentive mind.

Among them was Gerard, son of Gerard, eminent,  
a praiseworthy and eloquent speaker;  
and Gerard, son of Hugh, named after his uncle,  
now worthy of his uncle’s celebrated honour;  
and Peter, born of Sicherius, adorned with the same distinctions;  
and Azo: these likewise are named in that number.

Join to these Hildebrand, son of Roland,  
distinguished in strength, deeds, and nobility;  
then one born of Heritho, bearing his father’s name;  
[Col. 0515D] also Henry, deriving his lineage from Gniriton;  
and Letharius, together with Dodo, both young man and elder.

Rudolf, son of Stephen, graced these men;  
and Lambert, illustrious son of Hubert, in the lower city;  
and Robertinus, splendid offspring of Francard.

By their counsel, envoys went to Rome with the renowned and worthy bishop.  
The venerable pope, named Paschal, received them with great honour,  
granting the cross and Roman standards to the bishop,  
and to the commanders of the expedition—standards which Azo received in person.  
After he had instructed the bands in the doctrine of piety  
and in how greatly Scripture urges suffering for brethren,  
and exhorted all to persevere in their holy undertaking,  
he remitted all sins for so great a deed,  
[Col. 0516A] and conferred this lofty authority upon the Pisan bishop.  
The latter hastened back to his own city.

Received at once by the people with fitting ceremony,  
he filled the assembled crowds with the pope’s admonitions.  
And as iron, when it has gained control, hardens  
while Vulcan tempers the heated axe in water,  
so, by the consecrated voice of the Pisan bishop,  
the brave Alphean ranks burned equally for war.

Soon afterward, within the passing of very few days,  
a third embassy, dispatched at the gentle bishop’s request, invited Genoa  
and promised aid in the war,  
but deceitfully sought excessive and prolonged delay  
until the yearly season should pass.

The Pisan fathers learned of the fraud and trickery;  
at last the deception became apparent. Loosing his moorings,  
[Col. 0516B] the sailor turned his sails back toward the Pisan city.

Then Pisa rang with such grief  
that not even mighty thunder could have been heard.

Whatever timber wooded Corsica then possessed,  
or pitch, was brought for the countless requirements of ships;  
and the forests of Luna were stripped of their strength.  
Curvaria remained sparse after its trees were cut;  
lofty Mugello supplied timber  
to bear the masts that carry sails.  
Every wood is cut down; what is cut descends to the waves.

From this, ships of varied construction are made:  
gatti, drumanes, garabi, swift galleys,  
barques, currabii, skiffs, great fishing-boats,  
and many other vessels bearing various names.  
Horses are carried in these; some are fitted for provisions;  
[Col. 0516C] other enormous vessels can carry crowds.  
Smaller vessels know how to serve and attend upon them.  
These never fear to touch neighbouring lands;  
they bring water and convey men to the shores.

The lower decks of galleys suit the arms of young men;  
a hundred oars usually drive each of them,  
arranged in double order and pressing upon the smooth water.  
Ploughing the straits, they flee and pursue in such fashion  
that in swift course over the wave-tossed sea  
they can surpass swift goats and flying birds.

Nor is timber useful only for the fleet.  
From it are carried towers, bridges, and ladders  
by which the ranks may assault lofty walls.  
From it also engines are prepared which may hurl great masses against walls,  
[Col. 0516D] batter and break houses.  
From it are procured the threatening ballista, ram, and tortoise.  
Thus wood is distributed among innumerable uses.

The craftsmen do not cease; iron is consumed on Elba.  
From it come the fittings that join ships, and gleaming arms—  
breastplates, rigid swords, and swift arrows.  
Because it serves diverse things and functions,  
its varied working is divided among a thousand craftsmen.

No craft is idle: colours paint the arms;  
helmets shine, shields and saddles gleam,  
and gold set above them glitters with gems.

Some arrive from a distant people;  
Rome and Lucca send aid for the war.  
Genoa alone refuses aid to the war  
and hinders the Pisans in every way it can.

[Col. 0517A]

O Antonia, happy enough in your most distinguished father!  
Indeed, the care of your country’s city as a whole  
is entrusted to the hero of your region, who may drive away and repel enemies.

At last the completed ships are sent into the waves.  
The river Sarnus—called Alpheus after the Greek river—receives them:  
ancient Pisa, now fallen, adjoins it,  
and from it the Pisan who founded this Pisa  
gave his name to an Italian river and city.

Thereupon each ship is moored in its assigned station  
and filled with provisions, horses, arms, and men.  
The surest signals are assigned to every vessel,  
and standard-bearers to the troops and companies.

Their valour, well known among Latin peoples,  
believes that it can lead the ranks easily to war.  
But anxieties deceive mortal hearts;  
[Col. 0517B] what each man supposes, he will scarcely accomplish himself,  
because fortune opposes human plans,  
and the divine will does not wish  
to put an end to anyone’s evil deeds before their time.

What is sown flourishes in its season and grows white  
at its proper moment; each thing has its appointed time.  
The order of time teaches, nature’s law requires,  
that fruits be gathered from the tree only when ripe.

But all things are subject to the Lord, who can do all things,  
and every good is ordered by his will.  
For love of him, the Pisans left  
their kinsfolk and parents, wealth, and homeland.

And now the most celebrated day of Saint Sixtus was at hand,  
on which the Pisan annals recall with votive praise  
[Col. 0517C] their triumphs after the Carthaginians had been subdued in war.

Then the populous fleet floated along the waters of the Alpheus  
and the ships assembled at the narrow mouths of the muddy river.  
But, being unable to pass, they began,  
while attempting an outlet, to adorn their hulls, white with the stream,  
with provisions and arms.

After this, the sailors directed their course over the broad sea,  
leaving the lands behind them. With fixed gaze upon their peaceful city,  
they entrusted their walls, fields, homes, wives, homeland,  
and the pledges of their children to divine care.

As the ships depart, mothers weep upon the shore;  
the thirsty sands are sated with the tears of those weeping.  
A parent goes breast-deep down into the clear waves  
and gently blesses his son upon the sea.  
[Col. 0517D] The father prays thus for his sons, brothers, and husbands.  
Others pour out immeasurable laments upon the shore.

So, it is said, the Achaeans mourned the Greeks  
when the violent Danaan ships sought Pergamum;  
nor did they cease to mingle lament with prayer,  
until a wind issuing from Aeolus’ hall  
bore those snatched from sight across the broad sea.

The stagnant plain was left on the left, and Livorno;  
Gorgona remained on the right.  
The shoals, the land of Populonia, and its black mountain  
escaped their sight as the wind blew over the sea.  
Corsica lay behind their sails, with Capraia,  
and Planasia left on the left-hand side.

While the winds favoured them, leaving Taurus behind,  
the ships reached Languedoc and touched at the shore,  
[Col. 0518A] and held the harbour named for the saint  
whom they call Reparata; its walls, ancient temple, standing stones,  
and rocky shore bear witness.

Preparing to leave these bays, they likewise regained  
the approaches to Torres, where Constantine had his seat.  
That famous king is greatly celebrated by all  
the people of Sardinia. The Pisan people delay there  
for twice six days, equipping themselves.

Then they return to the bay commonly called Capo Bianco,  
because its shore is troubled by no wind.  
There Dutibinus joins the Pisans,  
who formerly ruled the kingdom of Cagliari,  
together with Saltarus, son of Judge Constantine.  
The former is strong with the javelin; the latter with eminent intelligence.

[Col. 0518B]

In like manner Hecate received the Danaans in her halls  
when Menelaus was about to march against the Phrygian enemy.

Here the bishop spoke much to the citizens concerning peace;  
through a few he scattered many seeds in vain,  
yet from many of them he received fruit.

Then all the leaders together entrust the advance signals at sea  
to Passarinus and Alpherolus;  
the sailors are ordered to follow and observe them.  
The fathers’ commands lie disregarded; order is overturned.  
For whoever could outstrip the others in a swift vessel  
displayed his ship to his companions by sail and oar.

After two days and two nights had passed,  
the third daylight had gone, and the third night of September  
had already begun—the one nearest the Kalends,  
only the next day being expected as its second by lot.  
[Col. 0518C] No night was darker: everywhere it thundered,  
and frequent lightning flashed on every side.  
You could see sailors and the rest in turmoil,  
especially those not yet well acquainted with the use of the raging sea.

No stars were visible to the eyes;  
the sailors saw only the shining fires lit on the ships.  
Not even Laertes’ son would have been fearless amid such terrors,  
though he overcame Circe’s arts,  
had fortune led the commander into these waves.

It was a miserable time, when each man’s lot  
was to pass through the cruel dangers of the storm.  
But the Lord, accustomed to aid his own servants,  
who always saves and increases those who love righteousness,  
[Col. 0518D] strengthened Boreas’ gentle breaths over the sea.  
They carried the ships through the whole night upon a calm surface.  
Soon, when darkness had been driven away, the shining stars appeared;  
night departed, and the brightness of splendid day followed.  
With swift lightness the fleet ran on,  
and as the day increased they began to see Spanish lands,  
but thought them the Balearics, until the anchor was cast  
at the shore of Blanes.

Having made fast there, the men brought from the Latin shore  
raised battle-threatening standards upon their spears,  
covered their brave limbs with shining shields,  
and drew their rigid swords with all their strength.  
The whole shore resounds with the hoarse voice of trumpets.  
Whomever natives they saw, they seized or put to flight;  
these declared themselves Christians and Catalans.

[Col. 0519A]

The Pisans turned troubled thoughts over in their hearts;  
laying down their arms, they sat sadly on the shore.  
When they then recognized the Pyrenean coast,  
they changed their plan, fearing diverse dangers:  
there was no shelter there from every wind,  
and summer, bounded by heat, had also passed.

Then one of the consuls, Roland’s son—  
to whom birth, intelligence, a distinguished civic name,  
public esteem, and wealth had given renown—  
is sent to the count whose power embraces Barcelona and Girona  
and who rules many cities according to his strength.  
His name was Raymond; he had performed  
innumerable fruits of knightly glory and famous deeds.  
Fear of him had shaken the Spanish enemies.

When Roland’s son came to him  
[Col. 0519B] and greeted him, he said: “Most illustrious of counts,  
the Pisan people, strengthened by Christ’s power,  
has come, behold, by God’s favour to these regions.

“Perhaps you have already heard from another’s words  
that, if duty calls—or if you desire to see wealthy strongholds—  
you should hasten to visit the Pisan fleet  
and join yourself to it in war. Our ranks desire you  
as ally and commander, and the fierce enemy challenges you.

“For who is not warned by the fame of the cruel Balearic tyrant,  
which shakes the bounds of the resounding world  
and presses hard upon the Latin peoples and all the Achaeans?”

The consul had not yet finished, and was preparing to say more,  
when Raymond gave thanks in reply: “May God,” he said,  
“make all your affairs prosperous for you, be present in all things,  
and deliver the common enemies of the world into your hands,  
[Col. 0519C] and join us in the service of the holy lot,  
that we may always do what is most pleasing to him.

“Against no men shall I move arms more justly.  
They drive away Christ’s servants with many tortures  
and make my coast devoid of inhabitants.

“For the walls and temples you see built upon the shore of Blanes  
once shone with wondrous images; now ivy covers their tops,  
or a leafy vine conceals them, or fig-trees or any tree occupies them.  
In many temples monks and priests were slain by these people,  
their throats staining the altars;  
the remaining men, whether distinguished by age or skill,  
they forced to serve in harsh chains.  
Fetters, labour, and hunger often killed them,  
or forced them sorrowfully to place Mohammed’s law  
[Col. 0519D] as a yoke upon their necks. Who is not stirred by this grief?

“If God should perhaps grant you power  
to bring an end to so great an affliction,  
we shall furnish every assistance for the Lord’s expedition,  
and, joining forces, overcome the fierce enemy.”

A letter, soon to bear the message of these words, is written,  
in which he promises himself a friend to Christ’s soldiers  
and grants everything in the Pyrenean land.  
Then he gives Hildebrand, and earnestly asks  
that he join himself to the Latins in allied affection.

When the next daylight had brought the citizens together,  
Azo addressed his companions in these words—  
Azo whose people celebrated him for the gift of pleasing speech:

“What is ordered by the Lord’s will  
[Col. 0520A] is recognized as wholly remote from human calculation.

“We saw huge waves and flashing thunder;  
we believed the lightning threatened sudden winds.  
Soon the Lord’s mercy restored to us calm sea-waters:  
such indeed is the power of the Thunderer.  
For according to his will he directs worldly events,  
and by his pious judgment rules every cause.

“He granted that our feet should reach this land,  
so that divine forgiveness might relieve the allied bands.  
Therefore, learned men, while we stand upon this shore,  
we ought to increase our ranks,  
so that the forces may truly be called fortunate, and not in an empty name.

“Now, with God’s help, no small assistance  
can be prepared for you by the Pyrenean count.  
He asks you to carry two hundred of his knights;  
[Col. 0520B] he promises to convey one hundred in his own ships.  
He has also sent this letter.” He presented the letter and added:

“The Lord led us here, not our own will.  
Let him who serves him hope well and be assured  
that he will never be defrauded of true benefit.

“The bishop is absent and is in a harbour six thousand paces from here.  
I think we should be sent to him;  
and, if these proposals please him, then let us proceed to action.”

When he had finished, his words pleased everyone.  
The count’s letter is requested and, its seal broken,  
Lodovicus examined it and read it properly.  
When it had been read, it pleased all; the ranks praise the count.

That people called the harbour in which the bishop was staying  
the harbour of Saint Felix. The envoy hastened to him,  
and the bishop received and confirmed the proposals.

[Col. 0520C]

After this they leave Blanes with a wind  
and seek the harbour in which the holy bishop was staying;  
at its entrance an adverse wind fought against them.

When the ships had taken the harbour, and an assembly began to be held,  
and the gathering was already standing in a grassy field,  
the excellent bishop, a lover of holy piety,  
admonished the Alpheans with these memorable words:

“You whom Christ redeemed from the enemy with his own blood,  
flee true thorns—the ancient ruins.

“Behold, there are three falls by which Adam was overcome:  
the man who wickedly desires and is proud loses God;  
and he to whom vain glory is prepared rejoices wickedly.  
From this arise hatred, discord, envy, and anger.

[Col. 0520D]

“These grim things can move the inmost hearts of men.  
He who is subject to these vices cannot be good;  
no one can conquer who is himself conquered by them.  
For they tear hearts apart and drag away the mind; like enemies,  
they plunder and capture. Close your gates against them.

“Men ought to remember that the Lord’s Only-Begotten bore torments,  
not for himself, but for humankind.  
He diminishes our weakness and guilt;  
he removes punishments and puts all sufferings to flight.

“They must seek God in peace and simplicity of heart,  
not human beings through hatred or harshness.  
Those who bring peace can dwell in heaven.

“You must, brethren, with your whole heart,  
[Col. 0521A] if you do not love those whom you now perhaps see,  
never give me hope concerning those not yet seen.  
For whoever despises the present love of these people,  
how can he relieve the sorrows of those others?

“The possession of a lover of peace is no small thing:  
blessed, he possesses the stars, the sea, and the fields.  
After the Lord made Saul his friend,  
let none of us count his brother an enemy.

“Let concord among us be true, not false,  
if you wish to cross safely through the salt waters,  
so that God’s great power may terrify our enemies  
and his peace may hold our gates within their boundary.”

Meanwhile, the common people, freed from fear of the sea,  
murmur and shamefully long for their native shores;  
trying to stir foolish complaints against their leaders,  
[Col. 0521B] they threaten together to return, abandoning the enemy.

Moved by this, Fralmus of Lucca spoke as follows:

“Everyone rejoices in God whose affairs are all prosperous,  
and he is glad for whom all suitable things are provided.  
Now I think it suitable both to multiply our allies  
and to find men as support for our own undertaking.  
He who can increase his allies strikes well at his enemies—  
enemies against whom divine grace has prepared  
men sufficiently excellent for us. Let no disturbance possess any of us.

“Since no one has yet conquered an enemy in war  
since we began this undertaking, nor has anyone been conquered by the enemy,  
why does such great disturbance possess your minds?

“Perhaps the cowardly repent of the honour of the enterprise begun,  
when the voice of these men pollutes noble ears.  
[Col. 0521C] These regret having come: men accustomed  
to turn the soil and always bend over curved ploughs,  
spending all their time turning clods of earth.  
Now, since they cannot entrust their seed to furrows  
or press down the must, crushed beneath their feet,  
they complain night and day of these delays and mishaps  
and perhaps threaten to return to their homes.

“Let these base men, whose wretched life  
brings no advantage to the present people,  
keep acting thus, groaning and stirring up complaints.  
It is no disgrace for them to retain their own habits.

“Let goodness and bright honour separate us from them,  
and let concord always remain in our undertaking.  
[Col. 0522A] Let him who wishes to serve the Thunderer be free of hatred.

“If the journey is prevented ten times, let it be attempted ten times;  
let the way be tried repeatedly until it is accomplished.  
Let reverence, as it always has, govern our concerns,  
because the whole world watches what we do.  
If what we desire does not quickly arrive,  
let no one remain touched by fear on this account:  
what the months withhold, the Kalends give back to you.  
What perhaps is denied by God for no short time,  
he quickly bestows in a single day when he is prayed to.”

When the people had lent eager ears to these words,  
joy followed; disturbance and anxiety departed.

On the following day Lord Raymond Berengar arrived there  
with a few of his men, joined in friendship, and the Pisans rejoiced in the alliance  
and gave the new ally an outstanding gift.

While they delayed, a pestilent disease spread;  
many among the people were overcome by untimely deaths.  
Here Caim died, leaving the citizens mournful with the bishop,  
not destined to return whole to his native shores.

While they restrained their tears, William, native of the mountain of Puy,  
entered the camp with a hundred companions,  
conveyed in armed ships and with a troop of foot soldiers,  
whom about twenty ships had brought over the sea.

But Aimeric, born of noble stock,  
whom Narbonne honours as lord, father, and commander,  
is said to have led twenty ships over the glassy waves  
and arrived across the sea in swift course.

[Col. 0522C]

Raymond also followed, whose origin was from Baux,  
to whom Arles strives to pay its customary honours,  
and who is found rich in camps and fields beside the Rhône.  
He led seven ships full of praised soldiers over the wave-tossed sea.  
Raymond the powerful sacristan, vigorous in martial deeds,  
and he who shone at Arles, came over the glassy waters  
with the same number of his own ships.

Such leaders were followed by Roussillon, broad Béziers,  
and the whole province together with Nîmes.  
As great were the forces said to have come into the fields of Girona  
as those which once passed through the Antonian lands  
when Caesar, coming to Rome to terrify the senate,  
compelled the conquered Gauls to bear the yoke.

## BOOK ONE ENDS

## BOOK TWO BEGINS

[Col. 0521]

[Col. 0521D]

Now, when the fleets were preparing to plough the sea, grievous to the peoples,  
Albert returned from the ship and entered the camp.  
He reported that Pirene, their commander, had come,  
and that his ship had remained unharmed;  
but that their horses, oppressed by thirst, had drunk wine,  
then, lifeless, had sunk beneath the wet waves of the sea  
before the prow reached Lesser Balearica.

He also reported that Moors had come to him asking  
what country they were from and to what shores they were proceeding.

“We seek Bougie,” said the Genoese sailor,  
“because we especially retain affection for you.  
Fearing to touch this shore was our concern;  
for your sake we fled enemies made against us.

[Col. 0522D]

“For they cannot match our strength in battle;  
without any fault of ours they attack whomever they can.  
All seas lie open to the treacherous Saracens,  
and every realm of the sea is disturbed by their rage.

“We saw them ploughing the strait, and, as we think,  
they pitch tents on any shore of yours.  
Whether they intend to kill us or carry off our goods,  
we ask you to give us swift assistance.  
We know they have come, and we are greatly afraid.”

Then they say: “Perhaps you brought horses that were neighing.”  
The rustic crowd replies: “When angry, it often acts thus by nature,  
making neighing and causing tumult.”

Then the hostile troop swiftly enters in burning fury upon its ships  
[Col. 0523A] and plans to trouble us with aimed arrows,  
rebuking us with wholly false speech.

Our band, sufficiently confident, took up arms no less promptly  
and kindled its anger to barren fury.  
For when a swift wind stretched the sails,  
it enabled us to reach the shore of Greater Balearica.

Having disembarked, we saw a man wandering through the countryside  
and asked how far that place was from the city. He said: twenty miles.

We drew water; abundant water was given us.  
After taking men and vessels aboard the ship,  
Zephyr ruffled the sea, and favouring Zephyr  
we turned our sails toward the Sardinian shore.

As we ploughed the sea, we saw sails approaching.  
At first there was uncertainty; then you could see  
[Col. 0523B] the troops of young men hastening swiftly to arms.

Just as men whom a rain-bearing south wind terrifies  
hurry to cover their homes, lest their poorly sheltered household goods  
perish in their houses beneath the force of descending rain,  
so every man strove to take up his sword and shield  
and diligently prepare his curved bow.

Thus the ships come, ploughing the sea,  
as dolphins move together through the waters  
when they swim over the sea without leaping.

We recognize one another; they receive and return our greetings.  
With sudden joy we laid aside our anger.

After they learned the route we ourselves had taken  
and the burden of toil we had undergone everywhere,  
they finally reported that they had left Sardinia.  
Boreas prevailed over Zephyr for twice five days;  
he carried us over the sea, and we ran with that wind.

[Col. 0523C]

Yet no one learned in what direction the island then lay,  
or in what place of the sea Majorca stood behind us.

Meanwhile, a wind issuing from the Libyan shores  
seized the waters, holding the sails above the leaping waves,  
and brought us back to the Pyrenean river.

As he said these things, the people gathered around him, all asking  
whether their friends were well or suffering, and whether they were safe.  
After the named man made his report, all the bands returned  
to camp with joyful murmur.

When a day twice twelve hours had doubled,  
ten ships from the mountain of Puy arrived,  
sent from Pisa in the month of August  
to all the broad borders held by Provence.

In them came the renowned Guido with Consul Dodo,  
a Levite, skilled in the discipline of the trivium,  
[Col. 0523D] in order to draw the people of that country into the war.

Phoebus was rising in his accustomed course,  
and the splendour of the sun had not yet thinned the shadows,  
when the signal sounded for the commanded departure.

The bishop ordered the fleet to strike the sea  
and the ships to cross swiftly to where Barcelona  
shines aloft with its lofty walls.

All approved the command; nor did those whom their vows did not delay  
begin to board the ships with sluggish pace.  
But as a swarm flies through the open air  
when it desires to change its homeland, place, and dwelling,  
so the Pisan host, using swift north winds,  
hastened to the renowned city with rapid oar.

[Col. 0524A]

Mount Judaeus (Montjuïc), stretching a little way from sunset over the sea  
and breaking and receiving the waves worn out by their accustomed motion,  
lies there separated from the city by a plain;  
it does not shelter ships from east winds or hot south winds.  
Every ship made land on its Spanish side.

When the Latin and remaining ships drew near shore,  
the naval force occupied your slippery waters all the way to the coast.  
So great was the pressure of the great fleet upon the banks  
that they are said to have collapsed.

Here, when concord changed disputes into peace,  
the most celebrated feast of Saint Matthew arrived.  
All bells sounded throughout the night;  
all make vows and importune the Thunderer with prayers and vows.  
Each honours the saint whose feast he observes  
and sets his candles upon a summit  
[Col. 0524B] or wherever their light might be clearly seen by all the people.

The third day had come, when a wind occupied the level sea  
which one could call neither north wind nor east wind,  
but was intermediate between them. The sailors beat their breasts  
and complain that so many days and nights are passing idly.

Therefore, at midday, when Titan high in heaven  
looked down upon lands and waters from the middle of his course,  
the fleet departed from the Catalan shore.

The Pisan host, urging on its men, preparing its white sails,  
and loosing its ships, raised no lesser cry than the noise  
which Thracian birds make with whirring wings  
and high-resounding songs when, flying in formation,  
they return to other regions.

Then four notable ships went ahead.  
[Col. 0524C] Francard and the Pyrenean commander were standard-bearers;  
the rest of the fleet followed in renewed order.

Day departed and black night came. When at last it had passed—  
whether half-passed or more than half—contrary winds  
drove the sails backward; for that reason the leader  
turned his canvas toward the shore of Tamarit.

From there he seeks Tarragona and deserted Salou.  
Here Zephyr breaks the waters and the south wind makes them surge.  
Yet, on three sides, winding rocks lie more open to Zephyr;  
the sea surrounds the rock,  
while a small tree-covered plain faces east,  
raised on the side of the high rock.

Here, it is said, were the camps of King Charles  
when once in harsh conflict he struck down the Iberians.  
[Col. 0524D] Here the Franks are said to have endured winters and summers  
when by their exceptional strength they took the land.

After the interval of the past night and the ensuing day had been spent,  
the first among them to arrive gave knowing signals—  
the watch-fires he had borne—so that the place  
might not be uncertain or doubtful to the ships.

After daylight had been restored to all the lands  
and the men had drawn water, they began to embark.  
The fleet, set in motion, cuts the glassy storms with sails and oars.  
Land, now left behind, could no longer be clearly seen,  
hidden as it was by high mountains;  
and as the day declined, the twilight of night came on.

A wind, not straight, had turned the sails from their direct course.  
The struggling sailors are thrown into turmoil upon the sea  
and shout to one another that they are unwillingly going to Denia.

[Col. 0525A]

Meanwhile dawn, having dispelled the night’s darkness,  
was shining bright when the winds began to draw turbulent clouds  
from the quarter where the public light of the world declines.  
They strive lamenting to turn their sails toward Salou;  
so great a force carries them there.

As the ships arrived, with night already near,  
the men leapt forth to draw fresh water.  
Behold, Moabites ride up on horseback,  
as an arrow released from the string comes,  
when the Parthian bends his powerful bow more violently.

Having captured men who were likewise taking water from the stream,  
they led them by a long path to their own homes.  
But fear of the Alphean people delivered them from bondage,  
for that people shook the fierce Iberians.

Therefore, because this had happened badly to them,  
[Col. 0525B] an order is given to the rest not to proceed unarmed.

While they delay and the troops wander through empty fields, there was murmuring.  
For the Lucchese bands, being less able to endure the sea and its waves,  
and greatly wishing to use their attendant allies,  
filled the people each day with complaint.

Hugh of Pisa, venerable archpriest, then raised his lofty right hand  
and, with the people silent, spoke thus:

“God’s goodness alone, who governs and possesses all things,  
has inspired the Pisan citizens to such great deeds;  
and, having tested themselves, they summoned no one to war.

“No one was compelled to come to endure these things.  
You came to us of your own will, and freely we gave  
[Col. 0525C] no trifling gifts—the ships you sought from us.  
You were allies transported in ships and became so by coming.

“Tell me, Lucchese: did anyone perhaps compel you?  
Indeed, you did not wish to come here unwillingly;  
therefore no one will be able to hold you here unwillingly.

“We forbid only the Pisans to depart.  
For others neither horses, provisions, nor arms are prohibited.  
Let them take these whenever they wish and depart unharmed;  
let them seek safe guides, and such guides shall be given,  
with whom they may reach the borders of Italy.”

After these words, the aforementioned lord sat down.

Then the aforementioned Guido began in this manner:

“Since God ought to be placed before all actions,  
neither piety nor love of piety is possessed by anyone  
[Col. 0525D] who contends only for worldly honour.

“Let worldly honour contend; let wisdom contend—whichever…”

He imitated love for the Lord in worldly affairs,

and preferred and bestowed honours that must always perish;

therefore, since God’s power sees our minds,

against whom there was a vast murmur from the whole host,

he grants you this opportunity.

Among the Hebrew people there was a murmur like this,

when they recalled pots filled with meat,

and preserved foods together with the beloved and greatly pleasing

dishes which they enjoyed upon the shores of the Nile.

For they preferred to bear the yoke of a cruel tyrant,

and rather to remain under a servile condition,

than to restrain the vice of the belly or to lack rich fare.

That ancient people resides within your breast;

[Col. 0526A] you possess its customs, its dispositions, and its ways.

Whoever longs to receive healing from so great a wound

must repent of having hastily willed an evil and unjust thing.

Whoever he was acted foolishly and fell backward;

indeed, in our age he committed a great crime.

Perhaps someone will complain that we detain him:

whoever besides the Pisans wishes to depart,

let him go whenever he pleases; he is not forbidden to take his belongings;

certainly no violence shall be done to one departing.

Therefore, when he has come to his ancestral home

and, amid a crowd, has recounted notable deeds,

he will be able truly to report this account of himself:

that he has never seen those enemies from whom he fled so far.

We shall endure the sea, the winds, and the weight of the waters,

and in the Lord’s works we shall not have inferior comrades in arms,

[Col. 0526B] comrades whom all Gaul shall follow;

indeed, with God’s favour, much better men shall come,

together with us, to overcome the burdens of war.

Then William, lord of the mountain of Pesulano, said:

“Never grieve at the departure of these men.

For every man who perhaps departs now,

we shall furnish four no worse for battle,

who will be able to bear the labour of six of these.”

Henry, made—or appointed—by Guinitho, rose

and urged the citizens to strengthen the war, before

he confessed that he himself would swear together with the fathers.

The pledged faith followed: all swore alike.

Now, near Phoebus’ setting, the most radiant lamp

was touching the shining flames upon the glassy sea.

That night was given to deliberations; when it had wholly passed

[Col. 0526C] and the bright day now shone forth with Phoebus’ radiance,

behold, squadrons of horsemen and foot-soldiers departing,

having left the ships, hastened in rivalry toward their own homes.

The Italians returned and, leaving Salodon,

heaped many insults upon the undeserving sailors.

Moreover, the rustic crowd mocked the songs composed for the sails,

and whatever speeches a sailor customarily recounts

to his comrades on the stern.

Meanwhile, because winter frequently changed the weather,

and the harbour afforded protection to very few ships,

and there was no confidence in an unknown people,

alas, Barcelona was sought; they resolved to bring back the entire fleet

and to winter there together, making their plans in that place.

The feast-day derived from the Lord’s name had arrived,

and the gentlest breeze gave light breaths of air,

[Col. 0526D] by means of which the Latin vessels, their rowers aided by winds,

reached the city of Pisa in swift sailing.

When the Pisans now had an abundance of shore,

they hastened to unload the ships; the greater part of the fleet

was set upon land and likewise hauled up in that daylight.

The following night found whatever ships had remained upon the clear waters;

the unbearable wrath of the wild sea made them loose,

and no rest could come to the storms of the sea

until the sea’s force had shattered sixty ships.

Then the companies wept, and the bishop and fathers grieved,

and according to their power gave help to the shattered

ships, until they were dragged onto the dry sand.

The widowed Sabine women did not groan with any lesser sorrow

when Rome carried off their beloved girls.

[Col. 0527A] Yet amid the griefs and unexpected pains

which the Pisan people happened to endure,

they had forgotten nothing of what had to be done,

nor could they set aside the counsels of their clear mind.

They ordered timbers suitable for ships to be gathered,

and planks which the cruel wave of the sea had cast ashore.

The ingenuity of the learned people quickly prepared covered structures and ships,

working night and day, striving, that is,

by every means to complete those which the sea’s wrath had broken;

and, in equal manner, they set up towers and engines throughout the whole

field, destined to bring ruin upon the Balearic Islands.

Thirty biremes were appointed to go to Pisa,

by which the naval strength for the begun war might be restored,

so that with all their efforts they might fill the fleet and the renowned

ranks of soldiery of Pisa, famous through the ages.

[Col. 0527B] Then, because Pyrenean provisions were exceedingly dear,

the companies dispersed through many lands.

One part remained in the camp; another came to those

whom Provence is said above to have possessed within its borders.

Mighty Gerard, lord and count of Livanti, reached

your renowned citadels, Mount Pesulano.

There too Gualandidus, illustrious in the works of war,

Peter, son of Hugh, and Roland’s offspring,

the vigour of Barvius, and likewise Vivian and the abbot,

taught the Goths unfamiliar doctrines of warfare.

Many came to Nîmes, more to Arles,

and found a pious people, pleasing in every respect,

which cherished the Pisan ranks with great love.

Here Holebrand wished to cross the Rhône in a little boat,

[Col. 0527C] but while he happened to sit on horseback,

he was pleased to watch boys at their games;

and when he threw a stone sought by them among them,

his spur struck the horse, which, leaping into the river,

drowned a young man of Lucca in the rushing waters.

Neither tears nor prayers poured forth availed the falling man.

When his dead horse had been dragged from the river,

the Pisan youths drew out the drowned rider.

After they had mourned their companion with abundant lamentations,

the bishop, clergy, and powerful people of Arles

saw to the man’s burial with the highest honour.

But Hugh, who governed the Pisan city in the count’s stead,

whom every branch of military service praised,

who preserved an honourable life amid the whole army

through spear-games and contests on horseback,

[Col. 0527D] and, assigning prizes to the winner of the race,

trained Pisan horsemen in the Roman manner—

all Catalonia, thronging around that distinguished man,

and the count of Sardinia celebrated him with lofty honour.

The goodness of the consul Henry, and of the others,

leaving neither quarrels nor crimes unpunished,

maintained the rule of justice throughout the entire army.

For, while the comrades known to them happened to support them,

they gave all men the calm restraints of equal law,

and appointed men to keep watch throughout the host,

so that they might guard the ships during the night.

Twice ten vessels guarded the Balearic realms,

pressing pagan frenzy with mighty force

and causing the wild hearts of the savage tyrant to falter,

if the new age rightly weighs the warlike Pisans,

[Col. 0528A] extending their double power by sea and land.

The Pisans do for Rome what pleases both alike;

when the fierce Iberian people behold their standards,

they groan and are consumed by fear of the enemy they have seen,

while the lover of Mount Pesulano guards the camp.

He refuses to return first to his ancestral home

until he knows whether he has taken arms for a cause or in vain.

This shook the lands of central Catalonia:

the Pisans, using no more restrictive customary expenditures,

carried provisions found from every quarter

and purchased various merchandise for silver;

thus they favoured the Pyrenean regions with generous kindness

and relieved their impoverished borders by trade.

But the bishop, guardian of sincere religion,

acted vigilantly lest those committed to him conceal matters.

[Col. 0528B] Therefore, having found a welcome day and a time for speaking,

he said, after he had taken the fruit of the tree,

the food of death, when that ancient father received its taste from the enemy:

God ordered him to depart from the walls of Paradise;

by condemning the proud man, the sentence of Him whose will

abhors this crime drove him out.

Every kind of vice proceeded from this vice,

invading posterity in this order:

the origin of the worldly race entered these shadows.

Jealousy drove the first man’s sons, those borne to him by Eve;

an impious right hand struck brother against brother.

He fell; his blood’s voice cries before God.

A solitary wanderer roams through dense woods and fields.

But most righteous Enoch ascended to the star-bearing dwellings.

After him righteous Noah made the ark;

[Col. 0528C] the weight of excessive waters washed over all the earth.

The waters ceased on the eighth day; then the sole righteous man came forth

from the ark, and peoples multiplied.

Afterward came the succession of patriarchs, then prophets;

yet no one had escaped the infernal dwellings.

Therefore God’s mercy, seeing the cruel deaths of humankind,

sent forth his Son from heaven in order to save them;

and that the things which the sacred mouths of the prophets sang might [not] be vain:

[The supplied text reads *Et vana forent*, “and might be vain”; “not” is supplied conjecturally to repair the apparent loss of a negative.]

the King of Heaven became man.

Thus the Maker of humankind, taking flesh from the Virgin,

bore the servile condition of men for their benefit;

and through his own death, having slain death together with sin,

he drew captive souls from the gulf of hell.

In this sequence the Lord’s grace saved the nations,

[Col. 0528D] and blessing came upon all posterity.

While Peter presided over his apostolic host,

for his confessed belief in the sacred faith

he deserved to become the pious key-bearer of the heavenly court.

He holds the keys, he who ruled ships upon the sea.

May he carry you unharmed in his ship across the worldly waters,

and may he beseech the Almighty that you may be worthy ministers

of his vessel’s rowing,

so that you can lead safely over the sea those

whom holy baptism purified from the sacred flood.

Therefore, beloved brothers, teach men pious doctrines,

and by holy admonitions restrain them from crimes,

so that you may be able to lead them to the heavenly kingdoms;

and may the heavenly reward never fail you,

which the Lord granted only to the blessed to possess.

[Col. 0529A] After the example of Christ, whose power rules all things,

may pious concern for their brothers free captive brethren,

whom the barbarian enemy oppresses, from the cruel tyrant.

Peter instructed you how much love you owe

to your brethren and to the Lord, together with the Master who went before.

Christ was fixed upon the cross for Peter and for all believers;

Peter was stretched upon the cross for him.

Therefore let no one refuse to help his brethren.

[Col. 0530A] For Judas [rescued] his brothers; the patriarch

Abraham rescued his beloved nephew from the bonds of an enemy.

Let those to whom it is permitted strike the enemy with swords;

may the Maker of humankind defend them from the cruel enemy,

and may the noble and much-loved Levite defend them.

What has just been written is episcopal speech.

This is enough; let Ubertis recount it better to one who seeks fuller knowledge.

**HERE ENDS THE SECOND BOOK.**

**THE THIRD BOOK BEGINS.**

[Col. 0529]

[Col. 0529A] Meanwhile Haerare Declus Burabe, the king whom the Balearic land worships,

terrified by these events and shattered into a hundred [lacuna], summoned all

the chief counsellors with whom he was accustomed to deliberate;

he sought their counsel in plain speech,

whether they preferred to hand over the land to the Moabites

or to form some alliance with the Pisans.

The men accustomed to offer greater counsels replied,

men known to surpass others in judgement:

“We are a crowd and your servants. Whatever appears

to you more steadfast and excellent in your deliberation,

know that we are ready to follow immediately without dispute.

Consider, no less, the people desiring war: let your nation earnestly wish to remain in peace.

For this grievous fault has brought horrible disasters upon us.

All subject to the Balearic kingdom would rejoice

if it were granted us to have an alliance with the Pisans.

But our clear trust in the Moabites

expects no good: they provide only insults,

which the joys of the Spanish land groan to endure.

[Col. 0529C] Consider what the men of Tortosa do, and with how great

destruction they oppress Denia. Taking pity in your mind upon our complaints,

undertake to seek out every captive slave and treat them better,

because through them peace and life,

and likewise a kingdom and honour, shall be granted to you.

The enemy will never be appeased by deeds not performed;

for to the worshippers of Christ, who labour for piety,

the bodies of their captive brethren are dearer

than the wealth of a hundred kingdoms appears to them.”

When these words had been spoken, the heart of the cruel king

trembled with fear. At once he ordered every captive—

old and new—sought out in all directions.

Those whom chance, wind, and wave had unwillingly afflicted

after the ship’s good fortune, he took care to treat decently.

[Col. 0529D] He also wrote a letter to the Pisans at that time,

in which he greeted the bishop, fathers, and people.

Though in his mind he devised something wholly different,

the enemy nevertheless sent rich words, making no supplication;

he declared that he stood firm without treachery.

He added the count of Empúries as a witness to his statements, saying:

“When the count of Empúries, undertaking a pilgrimage from Jerusalem,

was moved by conspicuous renown, I preserved his land unharmed

under treaty with him.

For I have deceived no man either in war or peace.

If the Pisan force wishes to have a treaty of peace with me,

I shall immediately restore the captives and am ready

to give my wealth; let it leave my realms, and I shall likewise repay

its expenses and the price of its labour.

But if it perhaps prefers to contend by arms

[Col. 0530A] and believes that it can conquer my people by fighting,

let it defend itself there together with the common city;

in that city its labours render its kingdom nothing.”

When these things had been understood, Pisa received the letter,

and the following brief reply was returned:

[Col. 0530B] “You who have brought such letters and writings,

the law of messengers bearing no evil is that they suffer nothing.

We must employ common customs toward men.

Treaties cannot be made with your king,

nor is it right for us to grant him any peace,

unless he first leads his forces into your lands.

May the King who sees all things, known as a just judge,

there openly determine the matter—that pious judge

who judges all the inward acts of men.”

He is said to have sent other writings besides these,

which bore very mild words in their markings;

in them he also made many promises in private.

He commended Albicio’s son in friendly words,

and urged him to remember the treaty made,

which his father and grandfather had maintained with Mugetus,

[Col. 0530C] and which Peter had held already for a long time.

Mugetus had been king of the Balearics and king of Denia;

in swift wrath he invaded the Sardinians.

When these had quickly been subdued in violent war,

and the tyrant held all the mountains with a full force,

the Pisan people, immediately stirred by these deeds,

boarded swift ships ploughing the sea.

Then no one was ashamed, however noble he might be,

to drive the oars through the watery waves with strength;

if the breeze was light or had wholly failed,

their shared strength fulfilled the desired course.

As hawks pursue frightened doves,

and as Libyan lions seek herds

when long hunger creeps through their bellies,

so they hasten, so roaring they demand war—

[Col. 0530D] those whom the Pisan force led against savage enemies.

When the remarkable squadrons bearing sails upon their ships

could be seen from the shore of Sardinia,

the king fled with his people and abandoned the land.

The heroes therefore, having won praise in their enterprise,

returned victorious and entered their ancestral borders.

But in the following year Mugetus, violently stirred,

led Moors into the kingdom of Cagliari;

the latter forces exceeded the former in number.

While he was building, Sardinians’ bodies were made to support the walls;

the man placed upon the wall, who all day brought water and crops,

filled the wall in place of a stone.

Many Sardinians, whom the tyrant’s wrath oppressed,

[Col. 0531A] are thought to have suffered the penalties of so cruel a death.

Thereupon Pisan honour, recovering strength and spirit,

did not hesitate to cross the glassy waters again.

After the warriors occupied the lands and fields,

and many had now been slain in war, the barbarian is said to have fled;

he withdrew, with his son captured together with his wife.

The Sardinians were freed from the yoke and were safe;

from that time all the realms of Sardinia remained subject to Pisa.

The elders taught the things which I recount.

The Sardinians whom you seek will not deny these things to be true:

the king’s boy, who is said to have been captured,

the victorious Pisans sent to King Leman.

The noble prince loved this boy’s grandfather Peter,

who gave Alanta, a desired gift, to Alphaeus.

He returned the most beloved gift, the son, to his father;

[Col. 0531B] for this reason Albicio and his successors are called

the brothers and successors of Mugetus and his descendants.

Therefore whoever holds the Balearic sceptres of kings

asserts on this account that he is brother to this stock.

Peter, born of Albicione, thrives as its descendant,

adorning the Pisan citizens with the image of uprightness.

Why do I recall such things? Peter and the Balearic ruler

were the cause; but now let us return to our purpose.

The season of returning March pressed on,

when dispatched ships entered the territory of Ebusus.

Soon men of the common people, greedy for plunder and food,

entered the houses carrying neither shields nor weapons.

While they filled their bodies with Saracen must,

while they rejoiced to eat raisins and figs,

Ebusitan horsemen came moving through the fields of that place.

[Col. 0531C] They cut down with swords the unwary men wandering through outlying fields,

and destroyed them also with varied wounds.

Peter Ascensus, bearing the standards entrusted to him,

roused his bold companions against the dreadful enemy.

Battle began before the ships; the Ebusitans fought

and pressed the unconquered men with all their efforts,

not allowing them to touch the shore with their feet.

There lies a small island, not far from the sunrise,

which looks toward the city of Ebusus from its low rocks;

it receives the galleys returning from battle.

But after rest had little refreshed their youthful limbs,

the men returned without hesitation to the windings of the harbour;

they found the ships, captured, drove off, and hauled them away,

and, before the Ebusitan people’s eyes, carried captive men

[Col. 0531D] to their comrades, their hands bound behind their backs.

An island stands in the sea, looking southward

toward Libya, named Frumentaria.

Latin men made for it and there began hastily

to find the consolations of gentle plunder: provisions,

and very fat oxen, which they could have eaten,

had pious seasons not forbidden meat to Christians.

Searching the place where the hostile people hid,

they led men dragged from caves to Ebusus in chains.

Then, by the order of Lambert and Noritho,

Peter Ascensus divided among twelve men previously mentioned

the ships and weapons.

From the west he began to join battle;

with Senagenes accompanying him,

the standard-bearer Ascensus hastened to leave his vessel

[Col. 0532A] and with great strength assailed the enemy ranks.

Then noble Arduin of Lucca,

encouraging his comrades, made resistance in the foremost line.

But an Ebusitan standard-bearer, having hurled his spear,

turned his back on the enemy and fled, leaving his companions.

The javelin, left upon the ground, wounded no one;

the man of Lucca pursued him through stony fields

and immediately cut his throat with a Bavarian sword.

Horsemen approached again, and another infantry line,

which had secretly lain hidden behind huge rocks.

Then the consul Eritho, aided by his comrades, rushed upon the enemy

and drove back those opposing him with spear and sword.

One part of the harbour lacks [ships]; the other part of the fleet moves toward it

and, with inflamed spirits, begins to invade the land

and to seek the Moors with burning energy.

[Col. 0532B] They repulse the Pisan companies with sharp and savage weapons;

soon the Latin multitude seeks the enemy line,

presses the combatants, and bravely constrains them.

Thus all the Ebusitans, disordered, fled—

men whom you, Lambert, victor in fierce wars, put to flight—

as doves flee eagles with swift lightness,

and as frightened fish flee spears.

And when you bent your bow with mighty strength,

an arrow shot through a Moor’s breast;

he fell face-down in the fields, blood flowing.

A hill stretches long from the shore,

where Peter Ascensus pressed the Moors from behind.

The barbarian people gained this hill with no slow steps,

although the long road to the city seemed longer than was fitting.

But when it felt the Pisan bands and their wounds,

[Col. 0532C] wounded, it ran across the ridges of the crested mountain.

While the Pisan columns pressed forward with all their force,

they laid countless Moors low in diverse death.

Now the pursuing crowd had reached the gate of the fortress,

which that steep place shows from the warm south.

[lacuna] “I shall speak,” whom the son of Lucca

had struck down standing nearby, piercing him with a bare sword.

This armour-bearer of Eritho, bravely pressing the enemy,

fell dying, struck down by a stone’s blow.

Thereafter the Saracens, once they mounted the walls with high towers

and hurled down great stones,

sought the protected bands, whose dwellings lay beneath the city

on the western side, where the unarmed populace remained.

From there they dragged men and boys, mothers and daughters-in-law,

[Col. 0532D] cloths and garments stripped from captured houses,

and rustic women remaining at home in a safe station,

who thought little or nothing of captivity;

like a herd of cattle they led the captives to the shore.

March had wholly completed its course, and

April had already passed its middle,

when, with warm west winds rolling the savage sea,

the sailors turned their sails wherever their vows carried them.

As the rushing force of the glassy wave bore them onward,

panting winds brought them to the Balearic shores;

they hung their light ships over the waters by their oars.

Meanwhile two galleys were sent to the Balearics,

and Consul Lambert, son of Uberto, was aboard them.

Swiftly they reached the harbour called Picci

and saw the half-marine king guarding the shore,

[Col. 0533A] asking in a woman’s voice why they had come.

But the horsemen and foot-soldiers remained on the shore,

vainly bending their bows with all their strength.

He ordered his own men to stop and harm no one,

and asked the Pisans to bring their ships out safely.

The consul replied: “Faith that is too ready to believe is evil for us;

therefore we can place little trust in bare words.

Behold, we offer a pledge that we shall not vainly keep:

the king, if he wishes, may enter our ship upon this pledge,

speak his words, and return unharmed.”

He more justly replied: “It is fitting for the conquered to trust their king.

If he orders anyone to come merely by word,

that man can go more safely, since every word of kings

is wholly steadfast. Your faith, by contrast, is seen to be incredulous

toward words, you whose strongholds we have tested.

[Col. 0533B] Yet if you wish to take anything from our resources,

remain in safe station in this harbour,

and accept whatever the royal care shall soon order given you.”

The consul said: “This island calls you its king;

but many of ours stand under the rule of law,

and whichever of the Balearics is better stands under it.

Your faith is nothing: drunken Machomet proclaimed it,

but Christ, glory of the saints, proclaimed ours.

Therefore he might trust far better in our simple words,

for ours are men of most holy mind,

than we can trust in your oaths.”

The ruler of the Balearics replied: “You seem to doubt too much

and tremble, shaken by empty fear.

But lest the good matters which seem fit for negotiation be disturbed,

and so that fear may cease, let us at least speak by letters,

[Col. 0533C] so that, after what you yourselves seek has become known,

I may fulfil what our will desires,

in order that we may always be able to remain good friends.”

The consul said: “Let no companion or scribe remain farther away;

we shall go, and both of us, weighing our thoughts in our hearts,

shall set down in writing whatever each shall declare.”

At once he ordered the sailors to launch the ships,

arrange the oars in order, and strike the mighty waves.

As birds, which a light feather is accustomed to bear through the air

by grace of its granted swiftness, hasten onward,

so the two galleys raced back to the remaining ships.

After the sea’s customary labour had brought these together,

they entered your safe harbours, Capraria,

and the next day brought the Latin heroes into the territory of Polentia.

The valley’s inhabitants learned of them;

[Col. 0533D] fleeing, they abandoned their houses stripped of provisions,

leaving the field empty for grazing herds.

Although invincible Minorca received the Latin youths,

they carried plunder scattered through the fields;

against us came companies of horsemen and foot-soldiers,

[The supplied text has *Nos*, “us”; the following lines refer to the Latin youths in the third person.]

turned them to flight as far as their ships,

and hurled stones and thick arrows at them,

not allowing them to remain at peace in the harbour.

Food failed the Latin men, and the land gave them for sustenance

herbs torn out by the roots.

The seafaring heroes could bear [it] no further—Camoena (“Muse”). [The supplied line, *Usque Camoena nequeunt hereos ferre marini*, has corrupt syntax; this rendering of the endurance clause is tentative, and the function of *Camoena* remains unclear.]

They abandoned the straw and resolved to return to the Pyrenees.

For the tyrant was suspected of treachery;
