therefore no intention remained of returning to him.

[Col. 0534A] Meanwhile Aeolus released from his dreadful prison a wind

whose name was the pitiless Africus;

it made white the waters which it had ruffled,

the strait swelled, the blast troubled the deep,

and the storm itself separated the two galleys.

The forces throughout the entire field wept, shaken.

Peter embarked; the son of Aldert served him as *Nuclerius* [probably “shipmaster,” a form of *nauclerus*];

Hugh had that which was commonly called “Sea-Eater,”

whose prow bore the carved figure of a dragon.

But the island received the other ships in its harbours.

When the time admonished them and the wind’s rage had subsided,

they attempted again to furrow the glassy billows;

their common desire now was to cross the strait.

When dawn brought them to the shore,

[Col. 0534B] messengers sent to victorious Pisa the happy news,

recounting their adventures and the perils of so great a labour.

Two galleys carried it in swift course,

and the joyful companies began to dance for them.

One, if I am not mistaken, you commanded, Marcellinus;

Guido, who is called a priest, was your companion.

The other was governed under the care of the praised baron.

After each vessel had reached the Catalan shores,

and preparations for war had been reported on both sides,

the letters said that allies would soon come.

A legate came, sent from the city of Rome:

Father Boso, reverend in holy religion

and dear to the lord pope for his height of virtue.

Then, after the apostolic blessing had been pronounced

upon all the people, they raised their hands toward the stars

[Col. 0534C] and praised the Lord of Heaven with full hearts,

that he might deign to preserve for them so great a master

of warfare, through whom heavenly blessing is conveyed

and companions in holy service are joined to them.

With no different prayers had the fathers and people of Rome

beheld their own men bearing the civil laws,

when the beginnings of law were promulgated upon ten tablets.

When the cold had passed, they returned to the cheerful season of warmth;

the gentle strait was smoothed by a calm breeze,

and part of the mighty fleet, led through the waters of the Arno,

arrived, a storm passing swiftly toward the south

and overcoming opposing winds together with the waves.

The city of Genoa, marvelling at their swift preparations,

watched the sails with a jealous and downcast face.

At last, attended by gentle winds,

[Col. 0534D] forty twice ships, leaving Lérins behind them,

entered the bays of Marseilles, their prows furrowing the sea.

Now the fleet hastened with great strength to ascend

the waters whose rushing force carries them to the Rhône.

Rich Arles supplied it with resources as far as Maguelone,

which the swift Eurus brought forth.

At last Boreas came forth from Aeolus’ caverns,

and all the air, together with its clouds, served him.

The wave seized the ships, and under the favouring wind

the vessels came to rest upon the Catalan shore.

Brother placed his arms about his brother’s neck,

and, after exchanging embraces and mutual kisses,

asked how the dear consolations of life fared.

The Sabine people had not felt joys so great

[Col. 0535A] when in former times children born from the Roman race

went before their parents.

With what affection the fathers embraced their hoped-for children,

how closely the children embraced their gentle parents,

and how tightly brothers’ arms held one another’s necks!

Made joyful by the sight of their beloved Pisans,

they began to express their joy in vigorous movement.

When May or June was proceeding in its course,

behold, Consul Dodo and Atho came to the camp.

All the cohorts beheld them with rejoicing;

they brought greetings sent by the father of the Apostolic See

and in a firm voice recounted the course of their labours,

giving in order the reasons why they had come late.

Then a hundred fathers held the papal commands.

Father Boso, acting on behalf of the omnipotent

[Col. 0535B] and unconquered God, who created all things,

and on behalf of the holy service of pious Peter

and of Lord Pope Paschal II in the City, commanded

that the servants of Christ who had borne pious standards,

whom the Lord’s baptism makes his own, and whom the rule makes brothers,

should rescue their brethren from cruel chains by pious concern.

All the bands and companies approving these things

entered ships ready to furrow the sea;

the writings then counted those vessels as five hundred.

The Pisan bishop, whose greatest concern was

to lead aid to the captive brethren,

first gave sails to the sea and crossed Salodon.

From there he reached the Iberus, the river of Tortosa.

Because he first raised the standards of this expedition

and animated the Pisan leaders in so great a deed,

[Col. 0535C] the whole fleet followed the father as he went,

bearing nine hundred horsemen over the wavy sea.

The Iberus filled the fleet with water and provisions; the nobles

made agreements with the leaders and swore to those agreements.

Only a few days’ interval had passed,

when they prepared to give their sails to the rising north winds.

But after they struck the lofty sweating waves,

a gentler breeze bore the vessels that had entered the sea,

giving them favourable sailing throughout the night.

The sun was beginning to climb the path of heaven

when the companies saw Mount Colubrarem,

which, full of snakes, gave them their name.

They hastened; soon there appeared a rocky island,

hidden amid the Tyrrhenian waters,

[Col. 0535D] looking with its stony summit toward the western shore.

They call it Ebusus; the city takes its name from the island.

A great harbour is in it, called Great by its neighbourhood,

able to preserve innumerable ships within its spaces;

it is seen to belong to the Spanish region of Denia.

From here it extends its head to where Boötes drives his wagons.

[Col. 0536A] The island spreads its right side toward the setting sun,

and its other side from the quarter of the rising sun;

it looks neither toward the sunset nor wholly toward the south,

and does not properly bear its end toward western regions.

Rocky mountains surround all its plains;

the field produces countless herbs and sufficient fruits,

and sweet draughts flow from springs.

It bears abundant barley, vines, and fertile soil.

Its boundary, which does not properly look toward western regions,

lies four thousand paces from the city of Ebusus.

Excellent hills, level views of the plain,

bold citadels, and secure walls were there.

A wave forms a great bay facing the cold North,

and the double island lying above it creates a harbour.

Everywhere sweet waters, springing from fountains, flow;

[Col. 0536B] grass is green, and reeds and marsh-rushes grow.

A hill rising higher from the middle into the air

held remarkable citadels with lofty towers;

but three steep walls surrounded it on the seaward side.

Ditches dug from the mountain rested beneath the walls.

The broad walls possessed twelve towers.

As far as an archer can carry an arrow from them,

tower-bearing walls stood with mountain strength;

pathless rocks gave difficult approaches.

At twice the distance that a missile is cast from a strong bow,

the circuit of the described outer city can be seen,

its walls encircled with towers and a strong rampart;

a triple ditch washed its inviolable defences.

The ditch overflowed with waters supplied by marshes.

The citadel stood at the city’s summit, on the southern side.

[Col. 0536C] Outside, a mountain was struck by the sea wave’s force,

beside which the bends of the shore made long harbours.

The other side of the mountain, which seems cut away

toward the sunset, descends into the deepest ditches;

descending from there, it looks upon suburban houses.

But on the cold northern side the triple ditch does not extend wholly

as far as the bridge; the sea also guards the wall on the east,

where an upright wall separates from the city

a great rock placed above the waters.

It begins at the harbour and stretches to the place

where the steep mountain looks down upon the waters below.

From there a towered double wall ascends to the highest citadels,

protected by the triple defence of the ditch.

The flowers of Bougie and the flower of the Iberian people

defend the city of Ebusus with strong forces.

[Col. 0536D] Second in command of this force after the king

was said to be Abulmunzor, to whom the land had been entrusted.

He was a savage man, a captive from the city of Girona,

who had apostasized by denying Christ’s baptism;

he was Satan’s native-born slave, more cruel than any other.

**HERE ENDS THE THIRD BOOK.**

**THE FOURTH BOOK BEGINS.**

[Col. 0535]

[Col. 0535D] Night was beginning; Hesperus had preceded the stars.

The Pisan ships arrived; the youth of Ebusus

stood in great density between the enclosed walls.

The trumpet is filled with breath, as are the clarions and horns;

the whole fleet resounds, citizen and stranger shout together,

but the cry raised by the Latin people prevails.

They shoot frequent missiles and fires cast from the walls.

[Col. 0536D] After Phoebus had risen from the watery wave

and the day had become bright, fit for the peoples in battle,

the ranks gathered round and the camp was put in order.

The valley held many tents, the hill many more;

swift Pisan youth ran across the fields

and with no sluggish step attacked their enemies.

Stones fly like rain from the high towers;

[Col. 0537A] weapons and stakes wear down the enemies nearest the walls.

Through difficult approaches and the hard perils of the ditch,

the Pisan ranks advance, even beneath the gates themselves.

They do not shrink from cutting down the hard walls with swords.

Their spirits blaze; the fighters press closely forward.

Shields and helmets are worn away by continual blows.

No breastplate can prevent the penetrating weapons;

wounds and death are everywhere, and blood flows freely.

When night came and broke off the raging warfare,

the weary Pisans returned to their tents.

But when day returned and the companies sought their weapons,

a machine was constructed by the power of skilled

craftsmen, striking and dispersing the lofty towers.

Then a battering-ram and hurdles were added against the walls;

a vinea, full of men, also enclosed the ditch,

[Col. 0537B] men striving with varied exertion to break down the defences.

A sea-bank stands covered with protected wickerwork,

and the armed cohorts hastening to war draw strength of spirit from it.

Mars rages amid the waters; the wave does not hold the men back;

companies stand in the midst of the flood,

exposed to countless dangers from human weapons.

The struggle is waged with swords; the anxious ardour of battle rages;

the ships attack the wall’s tower-bearing defences.

Bartolot and Anfossus together are swept into the waters;

they do not escape the blows, but upon the level sea

they harshly overthrow the resisting walls with hurled spears.

Then mighty Opitho turns his reins this way

and pierces a Moorish foot-soldier in mid-water.

Tall Peter of Parlasius and noble Bono,

son of Guido, hurl spears with their points; then

[Col. 0537C] the Moors fall, while arrows thicken from the city.

The skilful bowman strikes by sight; and the men from the fleet

attack the wall set over the waters

and the companies assault the lofty towers.

Others leap across the ditches, hastening to set ladders

for climbing the steep height of the wall.

The Moors hurl stones, weapons, and stakes from the walls

and drive back the Pisan strength;

the ranks press on until the burning sun

compels them, scorched by its heat, to return to their camp.

Meanwhile they build a tower and, by their accustomed arts,

break the walls and ramparts each day.

A violent desire for war seizes the Pisans.

And fighting men enter the broad ditches from every side.

[Col. 0537D] At last five young men, advancing toward the walls, press the Moorish wedges with violent strength. They, in return, hurl stones and swift missiles. Four of them, taking a leap, do not hesitate to cross the approaches; the fifth, Pipin’s son, remains among them, abandoned by his companions. What was he to do, or whose aid could he seek in battle? From the high towers they cast stones upon him. With the wall at his back, against which a great mass of enemy troops is arrayed, he is struck by countless missiles and varied arrows. Though only fifteen years old, he fights like a man and manfully lays low the enemies turned against him. Yet when their excessive force bears down upon him, he falls and together with his blood pours out his life. Countless swords assail a boyish body.

[Col. 0538A] The Moors rejoice; his comrades stand grieving at the slaughter. While the Pisan people were carrying out their tasks, Oriciades constructed a remarkable engine, which from a long distance might strike the wall’s defences, and likewise the contrivance of a tortoise-shelter. In this, a battering ram gladly strives to overthrow the wall’s courses and, driven with swift impact, breaks through the walls.

But the Ebusitans’ ingenuity was not unequal to war: they devote all their strength to the struggle and, employing devices with unequal resources, endeavour wholly to frustrate the Pisans’ designs. While the Pisans compete to bring immense stones, carried by a high engine, against the walls so as to cause vast ruin, the wall is protected with cloths and broad tapestries, and garments furnish the towers with their defensive covering.

[Col. 0538B] Supports often neutralize the blows of the mass, and screens placed against them cover the rest. As birds repair nests which a storm destroys, when the force of the wind shakes the trembling branches in the air, so the anxious Ebusitans strive to restore their walls and every fortification; their wakeful and continuous care weakens their own strength.

The tortoise had made several openings in the wall; Astus had constructed its design for Oriciades. Now the troops believed that the tower also was about to fall, when the leaders order the tortoise’s operations to cease until chosen young men may be sent into it, men who, with all their strength, may hold the city once it has been taken.

By chance the world was celebrating your greatly praiseworthy feast, holy Victor, when the martyr and fair virgin Pianes was raised above the stars.

[Col. 0538C] On this day Phoebus was already halfway through his course; the heat was great. The heavenly host is thought to have asked God together with you. The Pisan bishop and all the clergy prayed steadfastly with the holy bishop that he might help his combatants. It is believed that, when appealed to, the divine [being—lacuna] heard such prayers and brought the poured-out tears to the Thunderer’s notice. Whoever denies that such are God’s acts goes astray, and whoever, to the measure of his ability, does not praise the Almighty.

Immediately, while Titan was traversing the middle of heaven, the tower was shaken and visibly fell heavily. The place trembled, and dust filled the neighbourhood. Banquets, still untouched, lie upon the tables. It is reported that Latin or French guests entered straightway:

[Col. 0538D] Hugh, who held the rank of count at Pisa; Dodo, born of Tepertus and renowned in battle; Cunithon’s son, distinguished in courage and deeds; and a certain Catalan, well prepared in arms. Entering from the harbour through the gates together, they storm Ebusus, strike down and wound its fierce defenders by force, and kill the enemy with joyful success.

As tigers pursue a herd through the walls when long hunger powerfully constrains them, so, no differently, the pagan ranks are put to flight by the heroes’ swords. Then troops come to aid from every side. Sparing none, they cut down both sex and age alike. At one entrance the Ishmaelites held their ground; there a fierce Moor, terrible in arms, fought, believing that he could prevent every delayed approach.

[Col. 0539A] Ildeprandus Enfraxius raises his sword against him and, in a marvellous blow, cuts down the man as he strikes. Those who finally entered through breaches in the wall cut down with steel the barbarian bodies of the fugitives. Then Ebusitan youth falls, struck by swords: here are heads and hands, there legs and feet; wherever one set foot, limbs torn from the bodies of the dying lay cast about. Warlike companies trample thousands; but those who survive the slaughter climb up between the two enclosing walls.

Another rushing multitude flees to the lofty rocks which, as we said above, look out upon the sea. Some plunge down from them; others are cut to pieces; and others are thrown from the highest cliffs into the salty water.

[Col. 0539B] This was the grievous leap which the Moors then learned—those who did not flee, and did not hold their hands back from the rocky blows, hurled from the walls and broken in every part, lay in the middle of the street.

While Titan declined midway through his course over the sea, and burning heat drove the fighting men on, the first city had been conquered by divine power. The victors come to the gates and walls of the second city and labour in war to force the upper approaches. Many-sounding machines resound in varied rumblings; stones fly, and arrows launched from either side rain down. The nobles urge on the wings of fighting men. Both crowds roar, their voices rise to the stars, as the troops fight their way up the twin towers and believe they will more swiftly overcome the remaining city.

[Col. 0539C] The Ebusitan force runs up and attacks the enemy more violently, repelling them with stones, missiles, and stakes, and forces them down the joined ladders. When warfare brings the men no advantage, they quickly move their camp and enter the barbarian dwellings. But lest they be corrupted by the smell of the dead, the slain enemy is consigned to crackling flames.

The following dawn arises; the roused companies press on with burning zeal toward the remaining city. Night and day they vigorously employ their devices. The eighth day returns: the engine, battering the towers, makes them lean, and the tireless tortoise breaks through the walls. When night had passed into the dawn close beside it, Aurora’s gates lay open and Phoebus returned. At once the troops climb the high towers.

[Col. 0539D] The barbarian crowd is terrified and retreats to the lofty citadels. The Alphean people, treading on the corpses of the dead, lay the hostile wedges low with sword and spear. And while they hasten sufficiently to draw the fortress-walls up over the steep heights—the work that Dominic’s skilful care had prepared—clouds of missiles are sent from the summit of the citadel, and huge [stones—lacuna] fly above the Sarnicolae.

But how greatly Christ’s mercy and divine grace always sustain and strengthen those who hope in him, no human tongue can fully say. For by Christ’s deed—he who is known to be able to do all things—the Pisan people, always trusting in him, deserved, on Victor’s feast, he who had conquered the first city, to overcome the second on its eighth day.

[Col. 0540A] At last the victors strive to keep their captives and hold the place; they order detachments of the army to be posted all around. They obey, and all add a closer siege against the walls enclosing the city. No rest was granted to anyone by darkness or daylight. They attacked the high towers and walls with engines; the machine which sends out heavy masses far away carried rocks even to the windows of the lofty walls, often overthrowing the interior buildings. The neighbouring [siege-engine?], unmatched by any army, was repeatedly hauled into the lofty court. Now it carried stones beyond the towers and below them, and often wrought ruin among the sacrilegious.

[Col. 0540B] By these and other devices the Pisan people acted and tried to overcome hard fortune. Then Guidorubeus and the Catalan hero did not direct their arrows in vain. Conversely, the Moors often attacked the fighting ranks, though they did not wage battle with equal right hands.

At last cruel Abulmunzor, standing upon the steep walls, sadly looked with fixed gaze upon the broken tower. A man of low birth bent his bow by chance and, shooting an arrow in return, struck the watching Moor in the middle of the throat. He had formerly sworn by the ordinances of Mahomet that he would never surrender intact to anyone the land subject to him. Then his citizens urged him with such arguments: that he was bound by no obligation of the oath, and pointed to the blood recently shed.

[Col. 0540C] “For he is not sound in mind whose throat arrows have pierced. Therefore, while you still possess yourself, make surrender quickly, and save yourself with us alike from death.”

The prince was moved by the words and prayers of his people. A man is sent to the Alphean leaders to announce this. The terms of the agreement please the Pisans. At once those men, doubting nothing, surrendered everything without condition, themselves as well, with fear of death removed.

Then, merciful Lawrence, the world was observing your feast. The people of the Church suppose, and the faithful believe, that by your gentle prayer, venerable one, you moved God. When the troops set their standards upon the towers, the entire army had sung praises to the Lord three times; horn-blowers, clarions, and trumpets gave forth their notes, and resounding bells raised devout peals.

[Col. 0540D] The nobles hasten to climb the highest citadels, but order the common booty to be gathered quickly in one place. Eagerly competing, they demolish the towers and every wall and level the towers. Twice six months had passed in swift revolution, and a year had been spent in varied labours. It was the season when you bear grape-clusters, Augustus, when the troops carried must sooner than usual; and factions reveal the angers begun by disputes, which the swelling fury of plunderers had provoked.

From their entry into the captured territory, even before the warlike people had conquered anything of the city, the common crowd had been hauling together plunder from the countryside in every direction; and while brave men prepared siege engines against the walls,

[Col. 0541A] the ignorant crowd pursued the business of the furnace. O with what exertions bread is sold, and that by which coined money fills purses! After this, from the spoils which the Alphean people had brought together in one place, the anxious crowd raises murmurs and demands shares; it refuses to divide the seized property. Those whom Majorca inwardly torments in their minds, lest the shares retained in the booty should delay them, place the plunder aboard safe ships. The fleets cast off; the seas, torn by oars, foam; sails swell in the west winds, and the breeze sweeps over the liquid storms. They arrive at Balea: Latium’s following, and those who had borne heavenly standards on Balea’s account, arrive with them.

There is a bay of no small size on Balea’s southern side, like a harbour, where two headlands may be seen, separated by twice ten hundred paces.

[Col. 0541B] The sea, sweeping in from the Libyan shore, fills either side and stretches its boundary to the northern coasts. Where the bay ends, on its left side, there was an ancient city inhabited by few colonists. From there savage peoples, driven from the Iberian regions, came by swift ship under the leadership of Moalfac; having expelled the worshippers of Christ, they established many homes here, where Majorca stood broad within its high walls.

A small island lies five miles from it, enclosed by the curve of the bay and nearest the land on the left. Neighbouring Rhodus calls its side a harbour. From this city’s position its lofty walls can be seen—the city over which the Pisans endured such great labours.

[Col. 0541C] That eighth day shone upon the joyful peoples, on which the virginal offspring received his blessed mother above the stars—the mother of whom God was made man. The small island gathers the arriving ships; and the day following was that on which Christ, rising from death, gave life and salvation to those born into the world.

Men of this people, wishing to draw water, disembark from the ships and walk unarmed through the countryside. But horsemen of the region lay hidden in the valley. Attacking many unsuspecting foot-soldiers, they cut them down with the sword, seized some, bound them harshly with their halters, and led them away. Thereupon the nobles grieve with the consuls, and all alike.

[Col. 0541D] Then Bishop Peter exhorts the people as follows:

“Your will has hastened toward the gates of Tartarus,” he said, and pointed with his right hand to the Balearic walls. “There, I confess, your pious Creator is taken captive in his members. Who will not fight to rescue him, even though war itself threatens death? Yet do not fear death in war: for the author of life is sought only on behalf of war, he who gives life and prepares its use for all, who for us was fixed to the wood of the cross. Now taken captive with the captives and bound, he remains that he may give aid to those in bonds and draw them out of their chains. Whoever abandons the captive Lord, or him engaged in battle, is justly [lacuna] condemned and deservedly deprived of honour,

[Col. 0542A] and remains infamous, excluded from city and forum.”

Father Boso and the bishop of Cagliari add the same in comparable words and with flowing tears. After these words, eager youth sit upon the rowing-benches and stir the calm waters. The wind blows into the sails, and with the ships set in motion the sea is furrowed. Birds are not borne with such lightness of wing as the lightness with which the ships are carried across the peaceful water.

The people of Balea marvel at the white sails; the tyrant, holding his grim eyes fixed on the fleet, sheds tears under the compulsion of great grief. Then, repressing fear, he leads out from the city crowds of every sex whom he is thought to govern, so that their broad appearance may terrify the approaching enemy. Yet although they saw so many scattered bands across the fields,

[Col. 0542B] those whose bold minds the island had stirred could not tremble, sustained by splendid hope.

There was a pine forest where a broad sandy expanse opened, six miles from the walls of Balea, on the side toward which Titan drives his chariot into heaven. Its marsh and sea show by their waters a double retreat, east and west. For one making for the wooded countryside, Sivum provides an entrance; the places are called Ramora. Or indeed Forenna; many call them Catinos.

Here, where the swift prows had reached the flat shore, they quickly bring out horses; still more quickly the warrior people take up arms and survey the unfamiliar ground, driven by a more righteous anger. Those to whom certain companies had been entrusted order them, drawn up in formation, to follow their standards.

[Col. 0542C] After this, a small body of the king’s horsemen advanced from the city and saw from the hills the army already encamped. A swift Pisan cavalry force pursued them and drove them to the sands beside Sweet Water, the stream commonly called Luidis in that region.

Night returns; the watchful camp keeps guard. The stars, shining exceedingly bright, make the night clear, and under that night the sky displays its signs. A falling star seems to divide its tresses into a thousand parts; its division signifies the divided kingdom of Balea. “To Balea!” cries the people. “That hairy star bids us hasten there—hasten mightily. It is granted us to overcome the Balearic kingdoms; you see the star’s rays have fallen upon Balea.”

[Col. 0542D] The returning dawn was the day on which the devotion of the wide world celebrated Saint Bartholomew’s feast. Red Titan shone with rays; there was no wind, and the wave of the calm sea lay like milk. The Alphean leader and Pyrenes’ ruler, having drawn up the ranks, advises them to move camp a little. He instructs each man to follow his own standards: “Let him be ready in arms,” he said, “who desires to win another’s territory.”

The people, most eager for war, obeyed these commands. The fleet crossed the bank of the stream just mentioned, and companies disembarking in full force pitched camp on the plains near the city’s walls.

**Here ends Book Four.**

**Book Five begins.**

[Col. 0543]

The eager battle-lines watched Mars’s contests, each fighter considering from where he might rush against his enemy. The barbarian field was crowded with Moors and dreadful black Africans. Some carried round shields; part were covered with captured Latin arms, seized when a pirate band had once taken Pisan ships. The grim people display their strength.

Then Hugh, Bellonius’ son, and the Moor advance together, swept into a cavalry circuit, and first challenge the Moorish wedges to battle. Then heroes of Pisan stock, born of Bisocton, following Count Levannus’s standards, charge into the midst of the enemy and do not cease to lay low the dense crowds, like Libyan lions. The Balearic squadrons immediately give them an opening,

[Col. 0543B] then swiftly encircle and shut them in with their surrounding force, believing that they can hold men whom a sufficiently reckless hope deceives. Perils themselves create courage and furnish strength to those whose hearts are tormented by inward anxiety. Each man lays low and skilfully kills his enemy; wherever they rush, the field opens wider before them.

And as Rhodian men strike down and kill birds when, splitting the air with shining wing, they attack the birds and tear them apart in open fields, so the Pisan soldier, with bloodied spear, fiercely crushes Balea’s broken host by force, and returns unharmed, while all marvel at the deed.

After this the Balearic cavalry and infantry are divided into two parts.

[Col. 0543C] Some occupy the fields; others come near the sea-waves and fiercely attack the opposing Pisan force, pressing upon its thinned-out wings with standards raised. The Alphean squadrons yield, but with slow steps, and never turn away from the enemy placed against them.

William of the Arles contingent strikes down in this battle Bernardus, son of Daneta of Milda, and, planting his spear in the fallen man’s belly, attacks. The Moors carry their companion away from the slaughter. Then Valandus, standard-bearer of the Pisan city, leads his wedges into the open field. Here Ildebrandus, the consul bearing the standards of Holy Mary, charges the savage enemies with his right hand. Atho bears the standard of the Apostolic See

[Col. 0543D] and assails the dreadful troops with violent soldiery. As the Pisans pursue them in the heat of war, they are immediately swept among the dense enemy ranks.

Then the noble power of the Pyrenean people followed, whose standards a troop of helmeted soldiers carries across the dusty fields. Gerard of Le Mans bears this leader’s standards, and the forces advance toward the left-hand gate, which opens toward the bright lamp of the rising sun and is known as nearer the salt water. The old Count of Empúries follows this line, he to whom the Balearic ruler had been a close friend; surrounded by brave soldiers, he enters the battle.

[Col. 0544A] The battle-lines advance, and both sides struggle by force. The Ishmaelites fight their opponents from afar: some hurl stones, while another part assails the enemy with missiles. The sky is covered with dark clouds of weapons; dreadful arrows come down upon horses and men. Mars rages, and heaven resounds with great cries.

Then the Latin companies, fear of death set aside, charge the Moors and press the fight hand-to-hand. The sword does its work, and the flying weapon ceases. The earth, soaked in blood, supports heaps of the dying; groans mixed with combat resound over the whole field.

Hugh of Parlasio, reared and born under covered roofs, shaking the golden javelins which he wielded in his right hand, sent them through the breast of the fighting Alantis. He swiftly falls from his horse and, his blood poured out,

[Col. 0544B] quickly sends his breath to the Tartarean shades.

Cytharon, coming up and moved by his friend’s fall, pierces Hugh’s hardened shield with his spear. Because his short spear cannot reach the enemy, Hugh repays him with the sword and leaves him deprived of a fist. You, Dodo son of Percius, and Bernardus, following him, strike the iron gates with threatening spears. As they prepare to withdraw, two men who oppose their retreat—Bachimas the Spaniard and Ander—fall together. After Dodo had driven his spear into one man’s throat, he drew back its blood-soaked shaft with the spearhead. But, Ander, Bernard’s right hand is able to bear its weapon into your side: the shades carried to Tartarus receive you, and the Stygian halls open for those hastening there.

[Col. 0544C] The king of Balea had seen that he could not prevent their return as they battered the thresholds of the city gate. “I used to think that Balearic strength defended mere troops,” he says, “but now I believe these men are lions.”

The Catalan leader, challenging savage Moldonea, says: “Since you offer yourself first against our strength, you shall not escape our gaze whole.” Immediately he urges on his horse, not turning its gentle reins; piercing the man’s breastplate, shield, and left breast with his missile, he passes it out through the right shoulder. The man falls backward from his horse, and the spear breaks in the blow; but another golden spear is given to the count’s right hand, which, when brandished, lays low fierce Ishmaelites.

Gerard strikes Porion down with a huge spear, and sends both standard and lance into the man’s breast.

[Col. 0544D] Daridis’ lance pierces Umbertus’s ribs; Danius is run through by Ildeprandinus’s spear; Garsias, son of Rodulphus, is laid low by Roland’s sword; savage Recuccus falls before Dareta. And as he was knocked from the horse’s back by a spear, Count Gerard, leader and lord of Levannus, while the battle-proved soldier rages against the Moors, strikes the fighting Lelaphus of Frascina with a spear and penetrates the man’s shoulders with the same blow. Both the struck man and the violent warhorse fall in that mighty blow; the horse, driven more violently, crushes the dusty field with its master’s body and, falling, breaks the arm of the master who guided it.

[Col. 0545A] Rainerius, Raineria’s offspring, with Tegrinus, most eagerly rushed into the heaped-up enemy. Tegrimus here lays low Lephaton, child of Alance; there Gerard of Gaeta, with a spear-thrust, sends Rachius transfixed to the Cerberean shores. Guiscardus lays Hilion low with a deadly wound.

Then Albertinus, famous son of Bellonimus, fixes the huge Anetes through the middle of the throat. Guido of Buti receives the fierce Lavis as he advances and adds him, conquered, to the Stygian shades, though he himself, grievously wounded, withdraws from the battle. Ildebrandinus, son of Julista, brings down Gairus of Ilerda, noble by birth, with his spear.

Gualandus, Gualandus’s offspring, wielding a huge spear, which both his strong arms brandished,

[Col. 0545B] throws a monstrous Libyan backward upon the hard ground. Albertus, Gualandus’s brother, pierces Rachis’s back with the blow of his spear, the iron sent through his breast. The spear of Molfena, consul Dodo’s man, lays the brave warrior low, its swift arrow having pierced his horse. Hugh, son of Gausmarus, renowned in cavalry fame, pierces Dianensis with a sharp missile and makes a mortal wound by piercing his throat. Sicherius, Gualandus’s brother, strikes down Idas.

Then Mucharellus, Ildebrandus’s offspring, rushes forward and slays Gurion, whom Cordoba had sent to war. Albertus, Hugh’s offspring, strikes Ermon; Lanfredus’s right hand kills Anticus the Libyan; Hugh, Mathilda’s son, lays low the man of Ilerda.

[Col. 0545C] Then Sapibonides casts Aristes down upon the field, and Sofredutius runs Maula through with his spear. A rustic of Popiliensis, urging on a swift horse, drives a cruel spear through Tanes’s loins. Nelops hurls a javelin at him with great effort, and the deadly lance passes through the man’s body. The latter, more fierce, transfixes the Moor with the same missile and, killing three others, sends them in horror to Orcus. But when the man’s limbs have been emptied of blood, dying he sends his blessed spirit to heaven.

Garathas falls by the spear of red-haired Guido, and Cliton needs his lord’s affection. The abbot’s lance pierced his right side, cut the man’s neck with its point, and cast him upon the dust of the field beneath horses’ feet.

[Col. 0545D] Galindus, violently roused by burning wrath over his slain companion, attacks you, Vivian, because of your violent deeds, and gladly desires to cut your throat in vengeance for his friend’s death. You do not flee the bold blow of the approaching soldier; you lay the man coming swiftly low upon your spear and join him in death to his companion.

Lanfrancus, Albicione’s son, very famous for arms, killed Dedo as he confronted him. Then, driving his spear at the fleeing Arab’s loins, he forced him to slip down from the left side of the saddle. Sparse cavalry and dense infantry by the sea constrain the barbarian wedges amid the shriek of battle and with utmost efforts wear down the fighting enemy. The Alphean foot-soldiers, the Lord granting strength, here deal many blows with sword and spear.

[Col. 0546A] Their ranks battered by the blows and now unable to endure battle, the barbarian phalanxes return to their homes and fasten the iron-clad gates with a hard barrier. Within the walls, their anxious ruler runs everywhere and commands them to remain, lest, when the hinge is shut, they return to the field and renew the harsh battle, seeking again the hard enemy for their ancestral laws; lest they fail or allow themselves to be conquered. He sets forth how much glory victory gives, how much advantage it grants the victors, and how great the shameful reproaches are that disgrace the defeated: from them all honour flees, all worth abandons them; slavery, grief, and every sorrow thereafter follow.

Weeping, he adjures them by the shrines of the kingdom not to fear peoples hated by Mahomet’s law,

[Col. 0546B] but to fight so as to conquer and retain them in perpetual chains—they who do not wish to destroy themselves and their kingdom. Thus he speaks and restores courage and strength to all.

The nobles encourage the king, forbid him to fear, and promise rather to die than to yield in war. Burabe takes up the standards; the right-hand gate is opened; companies leap forth, and battalions hurry to battle. With standards drawn up, Burabe already stood in the field; fierce Alas bore the standards of the right-hand cohort, while grim Corace had charge of the left wing. Bugles filled with human breath sounded forth; no war-stirring trumpet or horn was lacking. When they saw the holy companies thus deployed, they hasten into battle with standards set in order

[Col. 0546C] and strive together to attack the right-hand gate.

The barbarian enemy was dense and innumerable—the enemy that also beheld, Phoebus, your bright rising. Now William, lord of Montpellerin, arrives, giving firm signals amid a famous accompanying band, and swiftly offers himself to such great conflicts. The duke called Herbonensis after his ancestral name orders bright battle-lines, adorned with brave soldiery, to halt rapidly before his eyes. He calls his men by name and promises lavish honours; he strengthens those whom he sees bold with doubled courage and warns the standard-bearer not to tremble with any fear, but to press eagerly forward before the allied companies.

Beside him Raymond hastens to battle, whose seat was Arles, whose native land Balcia.

[Col. 0546D] He encourages the Arlesians, eager for battle, not to be among the last. Peter Grossus came no less eagerly to this contest and exhorts his knights, after spear-strokes, not to forget to strike their enemies with the sword.

The sides meet; battalions mingle on both sides. Stones rush down; thickest javelins fly through the air; martial standards sound; voices rise to the stars. Anger and fury drive the mingled enemies against one another. Shields and helmets are worn down by clouds of weapons; arms clang against arms; the dreadful sword flashes in blows. The ground is satiated with blood shed from wounds, and the corpses of the fallen cover the fields.

Milgdas and Nerius attack Henry, but his very tough shield repels both their missiles.

[Col. 0547A] Gui, born of Thone, son of Sigonundus, from the territory of Dertosa, runs both these powerful knights through and throws them from their horses’ backs. Fierce Perithon, sent as a reinforcement to Balea by Cordoba, might have shared their death, had he not turned his reins more swiftly in flight, carried over the Spanish seas with a hundred companions.

Then the consul born of Erithon lays low Danaen, and Gerard lays low Aronta; each is remarkable in strength. Then the Balearic hero cuts apart the opposing wedges, throws down an Arab, and kills Cosellus by crushing him. Beltraminus lays low Nilgdona, Corace’s brother; Hugh of Landa pierces Tagus with a spear and takes his head with the sword. After this, driven by youthful strength, Imon Alcimionius falls.

[Col. 0547B] But the right hand of Peter’s brother strikes down Nicales. Mighty Raymond the Sacristan urges on his horse, strikes Neliobe with a powerful thrust of his spear, seizes the warhorse—one of no small value—and gives its doubled reins to his armour-bearer.

Then Consul Ildeprandus, transfixing dreadful Niceronta through the breast with steel, directs his spear and carries away the Moor’s standard soaked in blood. Balager attacks Petuma of Parlasio, whom war had sent from the shore, but, struck by the great blow of the Alphean warrior Acula’s spear, he is driven backward and turns his reins toward his comrades in flight.

A spear hurled by Dodo’s arms transfixes Pusius. Hocius falls by the sword; Oddo, son of Gellius, with gathered strength, pierces him through with a deep blow.

[Col. 0547C] The distinguished knights of Montpellerin come to these blows, following William’s standards. There Dalmatius of Castrum sends Molfena’s son to death with the thrust of a sharp spear; and [lacuna] old Sichardus [casts down] Emon. Peter attacks Amunta; Bernardus, born of Amunte, and the offspring of Froccardus cast down and kill together [lacuna]. The huge spear of William of the town of Balea pierces Machumata. Then Berengar, knight of Oran of Verona, kills Raymundus Midan, born of Eradius, and joins him to Gehenna. William of Dertosa, whose home was the land of Dinianus, makes [him] enter the hollow pits with his spear.

[Col. 0547D] Duke Aimelricus, famed for splendid arms, attacks the opposing troops with burning force. Fierce Alcimio meets him, hastening toward his evil fate and wishing to avenge his son’s death. The leader of Atax forestalls him, and the blow does not miss: the firm spear flies through his breast, piercing the boss of the shield; he dies and, dying, bites the grass with his teeth.

Atilas, Henry’s ash-wood spear, fixed you in the middle of the breast; the iron drew out all your vital parts. Lambertus, brother of Pusius, kills Agranta. Rainutius, called from the coast of Esculea, terribly impales Carben Ricapecora of Minolon. Poarutius sends his spear through the shoulders of Valentinus Glego, striking his left breast, and casts the transfixed man down in the middle of the field.

[Col. 0548A] Pharion the Spaniard is laid low by Guinacellus’s blow. As he falls, [lacuna] he rushes among the places of flight, where Saltarus’s staff had pierced him when, throwing his javelin, he fixed two black Africans at once.

Opizo, Gerard’s offspring, with the youth of his own men, attacks the battle-line and strives to lay low the Moors. Gaufredus crushes Parthus, Rainerius the African; the two brothers make them companions in death. Here Bernardus Marinialnus gives Ilonea to death, driving his slaughtering spear through his ribs. Olphes, enriched by Silletus’s spear, is thrown down; Gruirnius [throws down] Alcheon; Mauretus lays low Edon. Running everywhere, the Catalan leader scatters the enemy and heartens his comrades with rich exhortation. The brave knights of Empúries and Dusilientes,

[Col. 0548B] aiding their leader, inflict many deaths upon the Moors.

But Peter Grossus’s spear had struck down Corace, whose ready horseman had performed many deeds. Yet when he was now preparing to cut the man’s throat with his sword, running Moors carried their companion away from the slaughter. The Alphean standard-bearer rushes fiercely into the midst of the enemy and sharpens his stout comrades for war. As the queen of birds lays low the remaining birds, so he, pressing on, crushes the hostile phalanxes.

All the barbarians are immediately thrown into confusion and then turn in flight. The Pisans follow behind and drive the troops between the city gates. Countless horses and weapons are captured; lakes of blood poured over the fields lie there. Phoebus, rising higher, had shortened the shadows.

[Col. 0548C] The victorious troops return to their tents. The military deeds in Balea’s fields were now evident; both the barbarian people and the Pisan troops wished to look upon the slain men strewn across the grass. Envoys came and went. Hawks, clothing, and private gifts were bestowed. To those to whom the Count of Empúries judged these things should be awarded, mercy was sold. Then the greatly erring hero sends letters to the king and secretly receives the king’s writings in reply.

Meanwhile, while the pestilential enemy sought treaties, those whom divine love—not plunder nor any quarrel, but Christ’s mercy—had summoned to just warfare wished for all captives under a condition.

[Col. 0548D] Nazacedeolus was not prepared to surrender without a settled agreement; those worn down by fetters and hunger and stretched out in prisons were killed by wasting away. Keeping Pharaoh’s fury in mind, he denied tomorrow what he had promised yesterday. When the leaders see the king’s deceitful deceits, they comfort the people, and the people rejoice in the consolation.

While they strive in their hearts to weigh new thoughts—and soon recall the days, for one and another pass—the camp gradually changes position and lies nearer the walls, while frequent tumult proceeds from the city.

Excellent Dalmatius, you did not approach him slowly: for you are seen to be quick to appear in battles often fought, so great was your ardour for battle. Therefore, one day, seeking the enemy willingly with few companions,

[Col. 0549A] and ordering his comrades to stand aside, you alone contend with two Moors. One falls, overthrown by your strength; soon the right hand of the other pierces your penetrable shield, and his spear also penetrates straight through your middle. Thereupon you are exposed; an unarmoured soldier, thrown from your horse, you prepare to fight. But weakened by the wound, you fall while facing innumerable horsemen rushing lawlessly upon you. A barbarian sword strikes and beheads you; your blessed breath passes to heaven.

When battle-mighty William hears such things, he sheds tears and pours out sorrowful complaints for the man’s death. Yet he does not linger over these matters, but cries to arms and hastens to avenge his slaughtered friend. A hundred heroes, brilliant in arms, follow him,

[Col. 0549B] men accustomed to show ready courage in war. He spurs them on and seeks the field; the Moors, meditating these things, enter their walls with hurried steps. Since he cannot now be the avenger, he seeks the Gothic people’s head. At last, after the Moor had changed [his course—uncertain], the day before the Lord’s day, the dawn that always shines nearest to it returned; the weather was clear without storm, and Phoebus had already completed the ninth hour of his course when the strong Moors returned to battle. They think that the worshippers of Christ seek the camp only with a strong number of faithful cavalry and infantry. But the watchful Pisan foot-soldiers joyfully run to arms and energetically attack the enemy in sight. One could see spears, missiles, and stones coming across the fields, and arrows like rain.

[Col. 0549C] The passion of battle rages; strength abounds among the Pisans. As they deal blows and press with all their force, they drive the Ishmaelite wedges into the walls and strive to overthrow the summit of the rampart. They transfix horsemen trampled underfoot as they approach the threshold of the gate, and their horses too, with unyielding spears. They cast them down from the tops of the walls; likewise they shake the gates themselves and manfully pour forth the enemy. At last they behold the foundations of the double ditch, marvel at the walls and defences around the city—whatever reaches the ears differs from what sight reveals—and terror enters the hearts of many.

[Col. 0550A] Many therefore lose confidence and, in silent speech, shake their trembling heads; though themselves brave in such great strength, they despair of overcoming the mighty city.

There were three cities which bore one name. Yet, if you seek their distinct names, you may designate each by a different name. The wall called Arabathalgid, constructed by that city itself and enclosing the city’s body from its beginning, reaches the waters of the sea; beside it the sea rolls onward, where the city Elmodenia thickens its lofty towers. A wall divides these; one city is enclosed by the other two, which a circuit of ten thousand cubits surrounds.

When three times three and two are subtracted from this number, there are, by exact reckoning, four and ten times seven hundred towers to be noted. [Col. 0550B] These three together may be called the most famous single city. Majorca is the name common to the three. Between them also ran a very gentle torrent; when the rush of its liquid water flowed more fully, five bridges could cross its channel. They call it Ezechin; the water which flows more abundantly into the stream is called Enelamur, led through channels. It gives sweet draughts for the men to drink, for all the native peoples. And, because of their greatly increased resources, the walls would have been secure, had God wished to love the contemptible hosts of such wicked men.

No one should trust in a multitude of people who raises lofty fortresses against the Lord. Thus the Balearic ruler had hired for war Boabites, Getulian Arabs, Parthians, Libyans, Medes, [Col. 0550C] and also Spaniards, for much gold; and he offered immense rewards, leaving nothing unattempted through which every possible support might be furnished to his whole country.

Accordingly, the number of those able to handle the weapons of battle manfully was sixty thousand or more; he is said to have had three thousand cavalrymen. A hundred enormous engines were supplied; the number of bowmen amounted to four thousand, men able to strike designated places with their discharged arrows. Because of their multitude, the number of slingers was not certain, nor likewise that of those who hurled stones.

**Here ends Book Five.**

**Book Six begins.**

[Col. 0549]

[Col. 0549D] The leaders soon recognize that such great strength cannot be overcome. They urge on their allies and prepare to hasten strength against strength. First they decide that the ships must be hauled up, and all the companies willingly carry out these orders: only the drawn-up keels held the ground.

Then the Latin commanders order that the camp be moved nearer in haste, and their commands are obeyed. On the seaward side stood the lodging of Bishop Peter, a house neither humble nor excessively lofty, from which he could often watch the beginning of the battle. The priest Signoretus entered and occupied it, possessing ready generosity; here, Gratian, were your men powerful in arms, O Vicedonne, and here whoever was more ready with hand or foot. With you Oberto watched the repeated blows.

[Col. 0550D] Beside the pontiff’s dwelling stood the tents of the leaders, so that they might come to him more quickly when often summoned. Not far away, the dense flower of nobility had its quarters. In front stood the brave companies of the Pisan people, a people who had spent all their life under arms and were accustomed to enduring unceasing hardships. Neither cold nor dreadful heat troubled them; neither fierce hail nor snow nor rain deterred them as they attacked the enemy and the walls more violently.

This was a youth remarkable for resourcefulness and arms, hating gluttony and excessive rest, and knowing how to submit its eyes to brief sleep. But the strong troop of horsemen, not dispersed through the army, pitched its tents beside the left-hand gate.

[Col. 0551A] Thus the heroic Catalan people, stretched out from the seaward side, watched both gates. In their midst stood a most secure wall; for Latin strength was stationed on right and left, fortifying the commander’s lodging behind and before it. Behind the Pisans stood Carduma’s ruler; and beyond him were the companies sent by the Gothic land of Phorima, who pursued booty rather than waged war.

Before the other commanders Guidelmus made his camp, nearer than the rest to the gate on the right; beside him the hero Balcius likewise began his own. After these stood the glittering ranks of the lord of Herbon, joined with those whom the ruler of Roussillon had brought; the ruler of Ampurias held camp beyond all the rest, enclosed solely by his own people.

[Col. 0551B] They make for woods and fields, herds in abundance, plundered flocks, and whatever the cultivated land produces; by a changed route they bring them to the allied ranks. They drag in wooden roofs wherever they find them, straw, and branches torn from trees together with their trunks. Gothic foot-soldiers, or those sent by Provence, race through the whole army with goods seized, and make saleable whatever the island had commonly provided.

The Pisans repel the enemy with utmost efforts, and, following the commands of the venerable leaders, build two towers surpassing all else—wooden walls, commonly called castles. The work rises high; their lofty summits mount into the airy sky among the highest clouds and withstand fully two hundred cold winds. [Col. 0551C] Not even crafty Daedalus made anything more ingenious by his art.

Wicker screens, brought from the nearby countryside, and many oxhides covered their sides. Then, when the prepared supports had been set beneath them, they move forward under a powerful impetus and with swift motion—like clouds swollen with rain, which a violent south wind drives heavenward in a storm, clouds whose heads seem often to stir the sky as they advance over the fields.

Many bystanders marvel at their movement, since they had never been able by their own strength to bring such towers into position. Soon the two covered engines approach the walls; and while the tumult of Mars was frequent and varied, the violent Moabites often sallied from the city walls. Impulse draws out those who sally, and chance, rather than military order, directs them.

[Col. 0551D] When Robert saw them stirred by bold courage, he said: “God is the author for those who fight on His behalf, and He increases the strength of those who battle for Him.” He had spoken, and alone hurried against many enemies. He divided them and, pressing upon the fugitives, opened a way through the walls by fighting.

His horse fell into a pit—alas, cruel chance! Immediately, leaving its rider’s saddle, it compelled him to go on foot. First with shield and javelin, then with sword, the consul fought, contending with Hector’s strength. He endured innumerable destructive blows directed against him and also fought bravely with bare sword; alone he felt the strength of many men.

[Col. 0552A] While stones rained down and missiles fell upon him, behold, a swift spear was fixed above his left breast. Neither shield nor breastplate had prevented the rushing spear from easily piercing the man. His companions hasten up and carry him off from battle.

Now the strength of the ditch, dug out beneath the castles, filled the broad trenches under the two covered engines. Balearic ingenuity raised a mast on a tree, visible also from two castles; at its summit a warrior had a high and secure station, protected by many small coverings and seven raised hides. As lofty ships often travel across the broad sea in fear of pirate warfare, he wore secure mail and a round shield; [Col. 0552B] his head was protected by a crested helmet. With skillful use of three ropes, the mast extended the empty rigging of ships into the air; from it he could cast rocks down upon the towers below, stone the men, and send missiles.

The combatants’ ingenuity fiercely attacks the mast and cuts two ropes with a sharp sickle. A third rope held the mast in the air. The Moor feared that, should the sickle cut it, he would unwillingly fall or be dragged by the hook. Therefore, like a mass torn from the top of cliffs, he slid down the rope and leapt within the walls. The palms felt the great weight of his descent. The Christians rejoice; the cheerful ranks applaud, astonished to see the man run through the empty air.

[Col. 0552C] The Balearic towers shook and the walls fell, which the rejoicing digger undermined with all his effort; for each day he was given a gold coin. A double ram, operated from the covered engines and castles, struck them with heavier blows. From these the engineers throw bridges upon the high walls; whenever they wish, they can assault the towers.

The entrance was open and broad for forty paces; a hundred cohorts made it. Boso, one of the foremost leaders, spoke thus and gave this exhortation; his counsel and words are recorded:

“You who have left your native lands, parents, wives, children, and all that seems sweet to human senses, have done so for piety’s sake. [Col. 0552D] If the love of piety called you with its reward, why does the honor of piety not make you strong against the entrails of impiety? Look upon the Lion of the Balearics, who cruelly treats the sheep and scatters Christ’s lambs. He watches our labors from the lofty walls; he thinks the towers and strongholds constructed in vain, and he mocks both us and the Almighty, the author who has set Himself at the head of this host.

“That he may instruct you, despoil Egypt. Behold your brothers serving in Pharaoh’s chains; let avenging right hands break these impious bonds of Tartarus, and let their brothers be drawn from punishment. Blessed be the man who dies in these combats, that he may not suffer the punishments of Gehenna. Let no demon dare to bring a conflict against him before God on account of sin or guilt.

[Col. 0553A] “Let joys without end be given him—those which the splendor of the saints, the loving light, and the glory of Jesus customarily preserve or bestow upon the blessed. Let not those doubt for whom the Queen of the heavens, together with her Son, has fought: for God, whose is the pious cause for which you have borne arms, will be your helper, will terrify the enemy, and divine power will trample down your foes.

“Let this hope invite you as you go to battle. Let Michael the standard-bearer go before you; John the Baptist, with his companions, will wage these wars, as will the lofty choir of patriarchs and prophets. Do not tremble: Peter, the secure pillar of the Church, with Paul, will become your commanders in battle.

[Col. 0553B] “Matthew also, Luke, Mark, and John, and the rest, will bring help to your battle. Stephen the protomartyr, with his companions, Silvester with Nicholas, will assuredly give you aid. The virgin choir will help you, and holy hosts will grant assistance. Hold this faithful hope.”

He had spoken, and tears flowed down the speaker’s face from his eyes. The companies weep because they see him weeping, and together promise battle with all their prayers. At last they return to camp when Titan is already descending beneath the waters. Night departs; Phoebus rises from the quarter of dawn. The signs of war sound, and with all their force the Pisan strength and all the Gothic peoples, or those sent by Provence, hasten toward the city entrance.

[Col. 0553C] Within, the Hagarenes stand firm and remain upon the rampart. Dense engines hurl ruined masses from every side. The Pisan ranks fight and hold back the entrance. With utmost strength, amid the city’s buildings, they bravely drive back the enemy wings. Footmen are followed by horsemen, who press more fiercely. The encounter is difficult for horses, and return is exceedingly hard when they wish to retreat. Everywhere the Balearic soldier summons his own men to arms, brings up strength, and revives those fighting Alphaeus’s contest with missiles and swords. The enemy, opposing them with united force, hold them back.

Clouds of missiles and falling stones come upon them, wearing down those drawn up at the rampart’s edge. They prepare to turn their backs; reins are turned backward, [Col. 0553D] driven to excessive haste by Balearic strength. But the Pisan cohort, wounded in many places, returns to its camp, abandoning the wall’s defenses.

The Balearic phalanxes then eagerly make for the towers, applauding joyfully, and begin to beat drums with glad blows for their supreme joy; in them Fury and Bacchus might have been discerned. They raise the stars into daylight. Anger and grief do not pass away. When the next light returns, the Pisan battalions contend for the walls, for these conflicts are their concern. A broad way is made twice over and tried; the strength of all prepares to enter. When Phoebus, rising from the sea, drove his light aloft, the foot-soldier enters the open city through the made entrances and, driven fiercely against the resisting crowd,

[Col. 0554A] inflicts terror of death upon the barbarian companies. But the path along the edge was too narrow for the horseman. The foot-soldiers invite the cavalry to enter; they turn back toward the tents, with reins withdrawn, whom a wound or the death of horses makes afraid.

Then the inner troop of cavalry, seeing the fear caused by the broken walls and their collapsed strength, ceases. The Moabites see this and, their courage restored, horse and foot come through every street. The Pisan force turns its back; although it had been granted to invade the walls, many immediately scatter, abandoning their shields. Raynerus remains there, called by the byname “the Ill-Advised.” After his fleeing companions had abandoned him, he ran among the Hagarenes with naked sword.

[Col. 0554B] Yet whenever they made room, he could have escaped, if flight had been safe; he stood with threatening sword, and whoever fell under his violence sought Cerberus’s jaws and black Tartarus—or, while that man lived, would not be without deadly pain. Therefore, only at Coracis’s command, the cohorts attacked him and, surrounding him, pierced him with javelins. He fell after receiving a thousand wounds; after so many wounds the lifeless man lies there. His head was carried off; pious lament sought the stars.

Anger grips the leaders and the people; with great compassion they seek their slain and their sick companions. For, after the ranks drank water rather than wine, they collapsed from illness: the change of food brought loosened bowels into many dangers.

[Col. 0554C] Hence no small force, oppressed by evils, was falling. Many noble men fell in countless numbers, men who bore their heads high with illustrious titles, and many others whose renown stood equal to their death. Now tombs covered the road and the countryside alike; one could see the coffins of nobles set upon the shore and in the remaining places.

Amid so many tears of children or parents, though the illustrious multitude endured so many and such great sorrows, it nevertheless did not cease from battle and its remaining labor. The leaders decide to fight and, courageously restoring their strength, encourage the ranks to war.

While all ages celebrated the Lord’s day, Bertraminus, illustrious in battle, attacked the Moors. His wealth shines at Arles, and the origin of his parents [Col. 0554D] flourishes there in the bright titles of his noble family. He was girded with a sword and, master of the sling, attacked the hostile ranks by casting stones.

Because he had often performed distinguished deeds—for he had voluntarily offered himself in every conflict—he feared the opposing enemy battalions little or not at all, though they stood high upon the walls. Often, like a bird avoiding a hailstone’s blow by swiftly hiding its head behind a branch or leaf, he avoided the hurled stones beneath whatever cover there was. Then a Balearic, protected by sevenfold hide, came more swiftly against this fearless young man.

[Col. 0555A] Taking the shield of a foot-soldier who followed behind him and pursuing the enemy, he challenges the savage Moors to battle from the wall’s edge. Then a Parthian—whose mind was ready enough, but whose bow and arrow were readier—after drawing his bow, pierced his throat; the missile penetrated his windpipe. Black death takes away the bold and noble man, whom his companions mourn and heaven crowns.

The ground lacked dew, as Phoebus gave warmth and the morning chill had now abated. Having taken food and Bacchus’s liquor, the troops went with ready, unhesitating steps against the Balearic walls. Trumpets filled the neighboring space with their sounds; the ranks of cavalry and infantry stood in their formations, and standards gleamed upon their spears. Standard-bearers lead the ranks, but shouting spurs them on as they go, and the companies assault the open walls.

[Col. 0555B] The enemies run together against them with all their force and attack the Alphaeans, pressing with all their strength. Rocks fall, missiles rain, and darts, like driving hail, completely shake down, strike, crush, and press the peoples attacked on both sides; they seem to tear the wicker screens to pieces. Others fall wounded; many die on both sides, and blood is seen poured out everywhere.

Now the exhausted companies prepare to withdraw from battle and cannot bear such difficult labor any longer. Alphaean standard-bearer runs eagerly through the conflict and restores his cohorts with exhortations. A stone comes upon him with a great rush,

[Col. 0555C] tearing the standard and shattering the spear and his left arm. Swift companions snatch him from death’s dangers; he receives the care of healers. Peter Gerard, son of Bonus, and Hugh immediately treated him with Paeonian herbs.

Here, through varied fortunes, the hazards of Mars are waged. Many die; no one returns unwounded. Such was the Achaean people returning from the walls of Ida, and such were the Trojans in battle, while noble Hector and Priam remained unharmed.

They return at once from battle; but the barbarian host is believed to have had more causes for mourning in its various funerals, and to have suffered far more grief.

[Col. 0555D] No small anxiety and grief oppressed the Latin leaders because fighting well had brought them no advantage: victory had not been accomplished by their hands. The enemy pursued war more than concern for peace; and the count of Ampurias, as well as the Catalan hero, urgently sought to return to their native homes.

A letter sent from Balearic Diana announced what the reason and manner of their withdrawal was. It reported that the Moabite king was preparing war and that the finest territory had been greatly laid waste; throughout every place it reported Moors and fire ravaging fields, houses, crops, fruits, and peoples alike. After much damage had been inflicted by the mad people, the writing said that Tramarica had been captured.

[Col. 0556A] The man who had brought this letter was loyal to the count. But the matter was otherwise than rumor had reported: the enemy had reached the Pyrenean city and pitched camp upon a Jewish hill. They say that the count of Urgell, the count of Sardinia, and other chosen horsemen of the region from Giumda, gathering an army, had—by God’s action—marvelously repelled the cruel Ishmaelites, for whom battle brought grief. A few men, fighting, routed innumerable ranks; many, turned to flight, fell, until they came to the deserted places of the aforesaid Salodi.

They say that Pyrenean horsemen and foot-soldiers captured many horses and seized rich booty, and that Tramarica had not been captured, as that man had said. There had indeed been losses, but the gains were greater.

[Col. 0556B] We have stated the count’s reason for seeking departure; the order of events calls us to the remaining deeds. The leaders gently advised the count to desist from this; they asked that the common agreements and his oaths remain unbroken. Although he knew that the reason stated by the leaders was true, he did not withdraw himself from gain; and soon the agreements were renewed. They decreed in final words that the loss to the Pyrenean land should be repaired.

The leaders order dwellings suitable for the heavy winter season to be built, and the castles to be drawn back. They prepare an increase of war. The enemy demands new agreements; he does not dare place much trust in agreements when he seeks to subdue such savage enemies by force.

[Col. 0556C] Guard duty should not be entrusted to unguarded men. The age of young men is praiseworthy, but not every judgment of flourishing youth is to be praised in every respect: wine, feasts, and sleep often deceive them, and all things cannot be present to youth, which loves these things too much.

Therefore the young Pisans, their bodies satiated with sleep-inducing wine, rest beneath the covered engine at night—men from whom sleep had been driven by the enemy through countless nights. The Balearic therefore instructs [his men] to seek the Pisan camp at night: “Hurry, I pray you. Those whom I can hold are in the covered engine; I keep them by wine and rest.”

The Balearic host followed one who spoke such things in the silent night, after whose first watch [Col. 0556D] had passed. A thousand armed men come seeking the camp, carrying flames of pitch mixed with sulphur. Someone detected the smell of pitch and warned them to wake, but those whom easy sleep covered with its wavering wing could no longer wake.

They listen; from the covered engine these men throw down and introduce fire. There is nothing in them but sleep. As flames spread through the planks, the roofs burn. The youth, deceived by sleep, perceives the noise; dreams are quickly dissolved by the crackling flame. At once the men seize arms and begin to shout loudly; the enemy likewise raises one cry, and the whole host thunders round about with the loudest voices. Tumults conceived from every side stir the camp.

[Col. 0557A] The surrounding people went toward the Balearic walls. After the pyre had consumed everything, the strength of the flames had destroyed the timbers. The Moors call upon their gods and frequently blaspheme the saints and Mary, Queen of Heaven.

When, darkness having fallen away, Phoebus brought forth light-bearing rays from the sea, amid the people’s fervent complaint the leaders gave immediate signs for a council. The whole host comes together from every side. Azo begins to complain; the entire assembly attends to the complainant as he recounts each matter in brief words, calling certain men cowardly or contemptible, and men who defrauded the oath of piety. The remaining leaders, people, and counts all demand these things with repeated voices, not merely once or twice.

Immediately they draw back two castles and at the same time quickly prepare to build two others. [Col. 0557B] Soon they pledge to provide all the wood and rafts. Without delay, mule, horse, and man bring wood and oxen; from the enemy’s realms they bring countless twigs, vines, apple trees, nut trees, and gray willows—whatever you could recognize in any countryside; you were the bonds of these things.

Long ago we could have seen four castles rise through the airy sky from the Pisan stronghold—when Marseille, once Rome’s violent power, to which sea, land, and many kingdoms looked, sought to overcome it. Certainly no higher work had the Balearic ruler built. Day and night he cannot turn his eyes away from these towers; and Latin craftsmen swiftly made, by sudden skill, as many like them.

They prepare, with swift effort, to build walls where the double ram had often laid them low with its blows.

[Col. 0557C] Then the king of Balea sends a sealed letter to the city of Diana. He begins to cut the short sea with ships; when land and shore have been reached in a brief time, Diana and aid for the allies were present. The people had begun to hear writing of this sort:

“Nazaredolus, ruler and founder of the Balearic kingdom, sends a thousand prosperous gifts to his Buthalian subject, and no small joys of safety to the people of Diana. Once I should have earned from you the right to ask securely for your support; yet now I request from you that support which I know may by no right be refused to a king.

[Col. 0557D] “All enemies together oppose him who worships the Machamatic divinity that must be honored [reading uncertain; *eum cunctos communiter hostes*]. They forbid us to retain these laws and ancestral customs; they urge us to observe whatever stands against their doctrines, and teach that our commands of Rafulla are to be avoided. They demand the captives whom the broad sea, from the Ocean onward, has caused to serve me and Balea. They demand all possessions without distinction, once the captives have been secured; indeed, without condition they demand that, with no part of my kingdom left to me, content with life, I alone enter whatever regions and cities they please, leaving behind friends and allies.

“You who now give Machamata’s laws through us—[Col. 0558A] by my welfare, which I beg and which should be granted, believe that this distinguished rule, which redounds to your honor, must never be given to the Christians for Balea to be ravaged; for its many goods fill your lands.

“But if you do not wish to hear our complaints, and your minds are not moved by piety alone, behold: I hand over to you the Balearic kingdom. Descend, lest enemies enter the hearts of your land. They have laid Ebusus low; Balea sees what threatens her. Having now endured every danger for two months, fighting men, strong in battle, have laid her low. Few remain to me who are able to prevail. I desire strength and men powerful in war. Behold, I abandon the walls which the vast enemy has overthrown.

[Col. 0558B] “The towers and fortresses of warlike Balea are repaired; the most savage enemy repairs the shattered towers and strives with utmost efforts to add others. Remind the king beneath whose wing I do not doubt that you enjoy the secure repose of peace. Convey these complaints, which I make unwillingly, on my behalf. Let him accept the not-to-be-despised service of Balea, and I ask him for tribute by which I may retain my crown. I desire our rule to bear witness to Machamata, and I invoke the laws granted, which we have received from him, or the oaths which I can add more surely. I shall make all things known to your envoys when they come.

“Only give aid to your Balearic region, so that she who compels it may quickly be saved from the enemy.”

After the matters told in the king’s letter had become known, writings were sent through envoys to the king from Buthali:

[Col. 0558C] “To the ruler of Balea and to the peoples defending her: noble Diana, secure under her own commander, sends greeting. It grieves us that the Latins have invaded your regions, and we certainly regard these as common injuries if Balearic prosperity is removed from our honor. That they perhaps wish you to abandon your ancestral laws, we know must never be done with our consent. Christians are always opposed to our doctrines; if they could, they would wish to subject us to their own law and to make all things serve their tribute. For they strive to subject the gentile peoples to themselves—both us and you alike, slaves under equal danger. Who could doubt that, if violence conquered you,

[Col. 0558D] we possess resources and defend our honors and the rule of Balea? We approve that every writing you have sent to Morocco be carried to our Moabite lord. Moved by the beloved entreaties of his people, he will send a company of horsemen. As quickly as possible we prepare a fleet and men, that we may set them safely upon your shore. When they arrive, you will see signal fires made on your mountains; watch your mountains.”

The boat returns to Balea. The tyrant believes true whatever the letter reports and places great hope in the promises of men which dead hides declare. Cymbals and drums are beaten throughout the city; neither trumpet nor clarion ceases from these devout observances, for such things are the Balearics’ sport of rejoicing.

[Col. 0559A] Meanwhile the great Catalan hero learns why the barbarian people displayed such joy. He calls the nobles and all the cohorts into assembly, and frightens them with words, if they could be frightened. He says that the Moabites are of supreme strength; he explains openly that they fight by fleeing, that they are not to be fed unless drawn into a narrow place, and that, in Parthian fashion, they strike the pursuer while fleeing. He says that they fight hand to hand only with the sword; when the sword is available, they deal heavy blows. Whoever does not know them may therefore fear them enough; but we, who have known them in varied wars, shall, if they come, with God as author, safely seek them again.”

So speaks the count. But the leaders together hasten to send twenty ships running toward Ebusus; [Col. 0559B] six of these, which had gone before over the deep, crossed the strait in swift course, arriving where an island remains in the sea, hard and safe. The deserted city of Buthali had furnished harbors. He hears that Latin ships have arrived and captured two vessels which he himself had led.

But, turning doubtful thoughts at last toward better counsel, he considers how the Alphaeans may go safely, never perceive his arrival, and, scattered through the countryside, proceed for plunder or remain safely at rest. His true reflections are not deceived by a vain opinion. Therefore, ordering the remaining ten ships to remain where the harbor was safe and nearer the city, he commands [the others] with swift rowing to attack the deceptive waves and seeks out and circles around the harbors and entrances.

[Col. 0559C] He anticipates the Latin bays where he knew they were. These men rise from sleep and prepare to fight. Marinianus, having thirty men among those whom he had brought with him, prepared to go more quickly and thought himself both about to fight and about to flee. With ten ships he commits the youthful force to battle upon the waves, but Marinianus is wounded. They prepare to set sail, so that he might escape; but the sail which he had then spread for departure hinders him.

The Moors then hasten tumultuously upon him and capture the man, his companions, and the ship, first disabling all with varied wounds. They finally conquer three other ships, protected by only a few men, and take them away over the waves.
