[Col. 0559D] Those who had been in remote places come to the castle which King Norguenius had once given to flames when he ploughed the sea with a hundred Spanish ships and, victorious after plundering the enemy, hastened toward Jerusalem’s holy fortresses.

The Pisans hold this place, making excursions to the villages. They live on meat, carob-pods, and wild herbs; many also subsist on roots and modest provisions, enduring many dangers there. Often fat asses were food for them; Saracens, fighting, frequently attacked them. The castle was a defense and lodging for the Latins.

Meanwhile two of the six ships return, the rest having been lost; they bring back booty and a ship which Balea’s ruler is said to have sent to Diana.

[Col. 0560A] A burden of letters which a man could scarcely lift from the ground is delivered to the leaders, and envoys are present. Among them writings of like import are found:

“Nazaredolus, retaining his standards under unfavorable omens, bids his dear Buthali prosper in all things. I do not doubt that you received the writings sent to yourself and your people and desired to read their forms. When ships could cleave favorable waves, my ready trust believed that you would use the sea; nor did my hope, well acquainted with your mind, deceive me.

“The journey had begun; the island first subjected by me to sudden ruin furnished us a harbor. I rejoice at hearing of your triumph over the enemy, as though the victory had been accomplished by my own hand. Yet my mind has not thereby attained its fullest joy; for rumor frequently reports your withdrawals to me, and I desire to see from the lofty height the promised fires. But when I wish to behold them, clouds with darkness prevent me, should they be made.

[Col. 0560B] “Angry with them, I say: ‘Depart quickly. Because of you I cannot see my great desires.’ They depart, and the summit of the whole mountain lies open. I look: nowhere upon it does the said fire flourish. Yet that fire of mine, which burns through so many, so many nights, sends forth great lights with its flame into the height.

“I cannot believe that your ships remain behind rather than come. The hour will afford an opportunity in which you may come fearlessly, bringing support to Balea. If any concern for me enters your heart, beloved faithful one, do not scorn my rule, my harbors, or my gifts.

[Col. 0560C] “Therefore, smiling, when the enemy has been put to flight and conquered, you may steadfastly possess kingdoms in common with me and a common good.”

After these have been read, many more writings are read, telling of those sent to death and their names. They also designate by what blows they died, and how the people, compelled by sickness, hunger, and sword, would soon suffer the losses of swift ruin.

Meanwhile the remaining ships, keeping the sea but despising the leaders’ command and pursuing booty, roam through neighboring villages and strongholds by sea. Here battalions borne by Moorish ships rejoice to check in swift tumult men scattered through the countryside and likewise to deny victory to the defeated.

[Col. 0560D] Among them was Salomon, born of fair-haired stock, joined to the Pisan forces with two ships: huge in strength and limbs and handsome in appearance. Within the fields of a certain strong castle, he was hastening toward his ship with collected spoils. Many horsemen and many foot-soldiers rush against him and attack the man who resists with united strength. After pagan ranks had laid him low, they cut off the head of the man abandoned by his companions, and took away his standard and his life together.

These new events fly abroad, terrifying all things in many ways; and the days approach of the advent of the Almighty and unconquered God born of the Virgin, when Christ our salvation, being born, received flesh from His parents. Severe illness and dear famine had greatly weakened the barbarian people in the Balearic city.

[Col. 0561A] Hence, besides meat, all provisions of warfare were dear in winter, and none was dearer than wine. The island of Balea is ravaged; the king seeks an agreement. Rumor reports that the counts spoke with the king about peace, had been bought, and requested private gifts; and that, because of their return, they would have Balearic ships by which they could return to their native ports—if only the Pisans were unwilling to join themselves to him by treaty.

Therefore, before the Alphaean leaders, they make speeches as though about religion. They say that fraternal concerns are in their hearts, that captives must be sought, and, after hostages have been taken, request a swift return. Before everyone, they speak as follows:

“What we ask, the king does in full. You seek the honor of praise and wage war only for praise [Col. 0561B] or wealth; and uninjured Majorca values your great labors very little. You believe the clergy, who, ordering you to fight, watch your troops already surging over so much of the field. They wish to see war; they rejoice in our blood—those who reject the teaching, counsels, and commands of men who wish to return victorious from battle. Therefore no priest should command these men to fight. He does not know what sword cuts or what spear pierces. Let him begin and do what he loves to command. Deeds indeed seem far removed from words.

“We who feel and repay repeated blows ought to fight by our own judgment, not by these men’s commands. No one can justly undertake battle against justice. Recognize the just cause of the righteous.

[Col. 0561C] “They profess that they came for captives, but they contend excessively for worldly honor. Once the captives have been secured, let everything else be left aside; beyond this, let neither fame in the world nor honor nor empty display be sought. Let six common standards be displayed upon the towers. Whoever seeks greater things after these looks upon the Balearic walls with an unjust gaze.

“Add the Moabites, whom they are said to await: military experience has taught you how much they can do with swords and spears, men indeed of Mars.”

If they come, therefore, you will carry off plunder from the countryside.

Indeed, you will be exceedingly fortunate if you are also able promptly to hold the camp and protect yourselves from them. There will be no hope of plunder; by what law will the people be able to live when the use of horses will certainly fail you, and provisions are lacking to us? Nor should there be any further delay by such a long circumlocution. Say, therefore, whether you desire royal treaties; if you do, let us together make for our native homes; if you refuse, we shall depart without delay.”

Henry and Azo came forward in reply:

“Whoever may perhaps seek some other object in these regions, we confess that we have come here for the captives—not only for those whom the island holds captive, but also for those whom it had defended [or: had been defended; *sic*]. By God’s working, we think to root out the evil. Nor do we wish so great an abyss to remain behind us. Not because more Pisans are held in its pestilential chains than men of your nation are slaughtered by the hostile multitude in everlasting punishments.

Your faith, pledging an alliance and compact with us, bound itself by oath; and beyond what is just we cannot entreat that just men be recalled. This oath will not be recalled by its tenor [perhaps *timor*, “fear”], nor shall we ever wish to withdraw from our purpose. Things once justly done are often shameful to undo. We obey the clergy, because the command to fight came from the sacred order: the pope of the Apostolic See commanded the battles, and, following his precepts, we can nowhere alter so great a purpose. Unless you depart, we have not acted—and shall not act. Nor should departure seem honourable to you. If clothing is lacking, if provisions are lacking to you, we shall provide everything suitable for you and yours.”

When the count’s words had been heard, those fell silent who had often sought lavish support from the fathers and diverted every common resource to their private use.

After the fury of the Gothic nobles had fallen silent, the public guard-ships returned from the sea, bringing writings which a boat had carried to Majorca. Among them was a letter of the aforesaid Buthalis. Recalling the many expenses incurred by his friend’s behalf, it reported that the king should take care to repay whatever he had requested his friend to provide for him. If that man ordered any remaining aid to be prepared, he should quickly see to sending the immense expenses. He gave warning beforehand that he himself would come before the moon could double its paired horns.

[Col. 0562C] But the Pisan force did not abandon its accustomed arts, hastening to construct what might benefit it. Narolus, the prudent envoy, advanced to the besieged city and addressed the king in equal terms:

“O king, the command of Pisa, intimidated by no deeds, ordered me to come to you with a single voice. Sent here by the fathers and their favourable allies, I am present, and they have placed public affairs in my judgment. Consider what learned men ought to foresee in every matter, and strive to retain your rule in peace. Not because the Pisans greatly care for your treaties, or wish to return from Majorca without completed triumphs; these are words most firmly fixed in your mind, nor will you remember each one with a dull understanding. Mark what I say, and now weigh what threatens you. You are accounted wise: therefore take counsel for your own kingdom, so that you may be able to preserve your faithful subjects safe for yourself.”

He had spoken, and received the king’s most gentle words. The king promised all treasures and the spoil of the city, and openly declared that he wished to hold his kingdom for holy Peter and for the Pisans. He further promised swiftly to give his answer.

Nanolus [Narus?; the source reads *Nanolus* here] then returned. The Pisan companies received his words; they loved, praised, and desired peace. But afterward, when hostages were demanded in accordance with the agreement—the sons of nobles—the tyrant changed his words. He said that it was not his law to pay tribute to Christians, or to retain his government from them. He affirmed that these also had been the counsels of his ancestors.

[Col. 0563A] Sated with desire for riches, he marvelled at the old man’s affection and asked that the man whom he knew to have been removed from him without his own fault or wrongdoing might eagerly be seen. This man, being summoned, approached the king and brought his nephew with him. Won over by the king’s reciprocal affection, he urged him to fulfil the whole will of the Pisan people; the king promised, yet not without deceit.

Meanwhile the ruler who holds the stars, turning his merciful eyes upon Pisa, looked down from heaven upon the camp; and the companies that had languished soon grew strong. Yet there was no rest for the men: labours by day, the camp boiling at night with sudden tumult; the shrieking Ishmaelites repeatedly troubled them. And when a certain hour of the ninth day was succeeding and Titan was seeking the bounds of the Ocean sea,

[Col. 0563B] the illustrious Hugh, acting in the count’s place, sought the field. Tempexedes and Recuccus were his companions. Amid dense battalions, the memorable hero attacked a standard-bearer and drove the penetrable iron of his spear, braced against the breast, into the man as he fell to the earth. Then a certain Libyan rushed upon him and fell struck by his blow [*sic*]; the earth held the iron point, and the outstretched spear broke. But on foot a Moor sought the hero with javelins and pierced the bowels of his snorting horse with steel.

Angered, warlike Hugh prepared to cut down the barbarian youth and ran into the midst of the enemy; but his wounded horse sank down upon the tender grass. He roared, and, gazing upon the Moors with blazing eyes, fought and struck with his sword those attacking him on every side.

[Col. 0563C] Alone he received the clash of many men at once. When Perlasius, Hugh, and Dodo came to his aid, Recuccus, well prepared, quickly gave him a horse and arms. The fathers renewed their commands and added this for the raiders: that they should not cease to burn the districts outright and slaughter whatever men they could find. They promised five solidi for the head of a mounted man and decreed that two be given for the throat of a foot-soldier.

Thus sword and fire laid waste the kingdom of Majorca. Hence money came to the men, and Majorca’s ruin. The Pisans resolved both to slaughter all the enemy’s horsemen and to surround the force continually throughout the nights. They divided the three watches of the night excellently among three noble men, so that they might alternate their unbroken labours and restore themselves by rest.

Thus Gualandus son of Gualandus held charge of the first watch; the charge of the second was entrusted to you, Ildebrand, most fair offspring of Otto; Leo, noble descendant of illustrious Leo, presided over the last. Armed in mail, these men went with accompanying companions, repeatedly seeking the approaches to the walls amid terror. Delaying by day in making fortresses, they hastened to order timber drawn, hurdles made.

The Catalan leader, who possessed very great cunning, stood with many soldiers intent upon the places and routes by which there was a way to the city, intent upon plunder and upon killing Saracens.

[Col. 0564A] He zealously dealt frequent deadly destruction to them. Balcius, that heroic and famous warrior among commanders in war, pursued this same effort beyond all others. Whoever he could overcome by prompt strength, he beheaded, sparing him not even for gold.

In the accustomed course of things, when cold December stood midway, the winds brought much frost and white rime; then Majorca’s mountains were white with snow and hail. Cares born of the cold distressed the Moors: indeed, they were observed to utter laments in song, such as sentries customarily utter upon walls under grievous anxiety. The Pisans and the other peoples endured the cold and freezing rimes with joyful hearts.

But the fathers, recalling every detail with great energy, ordered the war to be hastened by frequent conferences.

[Col. 0564B] Having left Ibiza, they sent armed ships, and light vessels began to furrow the sea. But first a not-large ship departed from Majorca and, arriving at Ibiza, sought the Iberian shores. On the aforesaid ship was a certain distinguished woman returning to her homeland with her small son. Those who were encamped saw it furrowing the sea and first concealed themselves so that they might not be seen by anyone. Soon the ship approached bays near the fortress, and men hurried to disembark from the vessel.

While they went exploring the place with even steps, a very ready Pisan phalanx sprang out and first killed the resisting Moors with javelins and swords; but the woman with her small son was preserved by them. They therefore prepared to enter the ship and sail over the deep, fitting the sails to all the oars,

[Col. 0564C] when suddenly they saw two ships cutting the straits. Not quickly with their course, though using oars and waves, had they reached the shore nearest the neighbouring fortress.

Meanwhile the king summoned Peter. Summoned, he hastened to the king, greeted him calmly, and said to the crafty man in cautious words:

“As I have well learned, dearest ruler, the truth is that Pisa will make treaties with you on the first terms. I believe that you remember the earlier words; with them make haste, while you can, to establish firm peace, and do more quickly whatever they demand. For I am a Pisan; yet do not despise believing me on that account. If you avoid trusting my counsels,

[Col. 0564D] a time will come when you will wish to believe me and would be able to obey my words.”

But the ruler of Majorca answered Peter thus:

“Peter, they wish to take every treasure from us and leave absolutely nothing to your citizens. A few men in our city become rich from our wealth. Such a great sum of money cannot be given even by a few. Why do your companies demand from me what exceeds my power to give? Let them seek what I can bestow. If I return the captives, that is sufficient for the army, and let them leave my kingdom under a perpetual treaty. If your men are not persuaded toward these terms, then between us and them it shall occur according to the will of the Thunderer.”

Thus he spoke. When these things had been heard, each departed; and as days passed, the Latin host hastened its preparations, manfully compelling the enemy. Some attacked villages and countryside; others besieged the city. Everywhere the kingdom was ravaged by slaughter and flames.

[Col. 0565A] Then the ruler of Arles, surveying every place, refused to see camps made without bloodshed. He repeatedly caused many Saracens, headless trunks, to be seen; no sword returned without having shed blood, nor the spear with its sharp point. Thus he compelled many seeking the underworld to proceed through the empty spaces of black Tartarus. Cerberus, gatekeeper of the shadowy hall, was astonished; he barked, and his chattering voice returned the frightened king of the realm of shades to him who held the black kingdom.

The king said to his servant: “Why do you bark, Cerberus? Come, reveal at once what this is; why do you thus disturb my laws with your pestilent clamour and grim barking? Unhappy one, restrain all voices and sounds—or tell me swiftly what nation is entering my realm, who gives such hope to so many peoples seeking lightless darkness. Reveal the cause as well, Cerberus.”

[Col. 0565B] He spoke thus to his king with triple mouth:

“O dark Father, the forces of the Pisan people are said to have made war upon the shore of your Majorca. If Majorca is a part of our realm, Rome has indeed admonished them, and the pope has remitted guilt to the people wishing to fight for captives. They inflict very many losses. No power of Tartarus frightens those dying under his admonitions, and we suffer these things. But the Pisan cohort and the hero Balcius have sent their work, and them, into the realms of Tartarus.

[Col. 0565C] Many now come; believe me, many more will come when the Latin bands enter our city with swords laying it waste. Order chains to be made at once, as I advise; your crowd deserves to be bound, lest it escape the punishments it is already thought to have earned. It will follow the king of Majorca as he comes far and wide, and will indeed bring many companies with it into your realm.”

He spoke, and the furious ruler of Avernus roared; the tyrant terrified the shades with plaintive clamour. Souls miserably released from flesh howled; at the roaring voice of their leader, they soon fled back to the depths of the valley. Weariness then seized the king under the influence of fear. He complained that his head hurt and his breast was oppressed. Preparing to enter his chamber, he is said to have lost blood,

[Col. 0565D] and thereafter lived only a few days. Yet before this he is thought to have yielded rule to Buraba. Buraba then anointed his father’s body with balm, buried it, and wept greatly as he placed it in the tomb.

After Cerberus had departed to the caves of Gehenna and led Machamatus through the dark city, the shades approached him with staffs and crowded together from every side.

[Col. 0566A] “Perhaps the rider of Avernus himself calls me!” [*sic*] Aeacus stood at the right hand, Rhadamanthus at the left, and amid the flames they spoke as follows:

“Father, in the whole host there is none equal in fierceness to the king of Majorca, who made many men die by the sword and compelled many to abandon Christ’s law. Since he brought us companions whom we love, grant that he may stand forever in your flame-bearing hall, and quickly inflict punishments worthy of his merits. Command his people to remain in eternal flames and to bear perpetual chains as companions.”

The multitude convicted the savage king of Majorca and was suddenly assigned to various torments. He stirred up burning fires with his trident

[Col. 0566B] and made the scorched roof admit ashes; and, preparing banquets of poisonous flesh, he said: “You, my faithful ones, recline at table with me.” They obeyed the commands; the shades came to the feast. Burnt stones were served at their feet; a consuming flame wholly devoured those seated. Their first hot courses were serpents, which while alive twist the fiery entrails of those who taste them. The drinkers’ thirst was dry; dragon’s blood, black with much gall, furnished a draught. A scorched buffoon pursued these dishes in the first course; they were innumerable, and the poisons of Lerna together poured a strong liquid over them. Cups mingled with various poisons followed. After they twisted the burning entrails of those tasting them,

[Col. 0566C] the ruler of black spirits spoke thus:

“O my band, lead the king of Majorca to my dwelling; and because the entrails of all are burning, let him go with you to the waters of Tantalus. But first I require you to see your sport in this matter.”

You might have seen the king of Majorca stand mute as stone; forgetfulness had carried away his senses. He was stupefied because terror had taken his mind. At last, after the tyrant’s commands, the diners sprang up and dragged the seized king through the walls. They tear him in Tartarus and put him into icy waters: thirst is relieved by cold. He is cast into flames: there is pain, cold, and heat. After, with his entrails dried out, they had felt the pestilential thirst removed,

[Col. 0566D] he hurried to the stream, but could not remove the burning heats by the water. For after he wished to touch the waters with his lips, they fled from the shadow standing there. Then, upon the riverbank, wholly stunned, he clung motionless like a stone. A shape of various beasts devours the wretch; thus dark Orcus destroys the savage king.

**Here ends Book Six.**

**Here begins Book Seven.**

[Col. 0565D] After these things Buraba, raised to the royal throne, soon mounted honours that would not endure; for he enjoyed the kingship for no long time. When the band of Pisans demanded captives from him, it received unsuitable words from the cruel leader.

[Col. 0566D] It was now the Nativity, on which Christ, born of a Virgin, filled the dark world with divine light. While the high honours of the holy feast were celebrated, and after the light had shone twice four times upon the pious people, the new king ordered Maimo and the companions given him to go to Dian[a]. The ship entered the sea-waves.

[Col. 0567A] The Pisans quickly saw the vessel hastening. Then they prepared to board their ships in haste; the fathers increased their resources, providing every necessity. While perhaps food and weapons were being given to the men, Maimo continued his course; but, drawn where his impulse led him, he unfurled his sails thither without keeping to the route. There was hope that he could quickly be captured if the ship should show any signs whatsoever; but the wind blowing through the sails swiftly removed the vessel from their sight. Maimo made his way; the Latins returned, wishing to give diligent attention to the kingdom of Majorca.

As they strove to overcome the tasks begun, many said in turn that, whether through strength or skill, they could not win triumph over the enemy; they denied that they could return to their own homes or remain any longer because of sickness or heat. They recalled that many—alas!—had died of disease or by the sword, and said that few companions survived; that Pisa likewise was being destroyed for Majorca; and that it was sufficiently foolish to appear without a city, without resources, without sense.

[Col. 0567B] Therefore they worked to repair all the ships with swift help, and did not abandon their efforts on behalf of the captives.

Meanwhile the Catalan hero burned with zeal for war. Accompanied by a great band, he stationed himself in a valley at a place suited to ambush. The sun had made all things radiant with its first light; the gate stood open, and Moors came forth from the walls and passed through safe places in their customary bearing.

But the count boldly sprang upon the savage enemy and joined battle near the city gate which looks toward the harbour called Pineus. After he had laid a Moabite low upon the green grass, a spear hurled from the walls passed through the man’s right arm. The Moors rejoiced, thinking this mortal for the count; thereafter they hastened through the city spreading false reports invented about the count’s death.

Thus the remaining bands guarding the walls rejoiced; they sang that the count was slain, threatened to kill the Alphaeans or wear them away in perpetual chains, and loudly declared varied punishments. Likewise they cried that the Alphaeans were left without their leader, urging them, if they cared to live, to hasten and surrender themselves.

[Col. 0567C] But the Pisans answered: “Your insults and threats compel us to fear nothing under the king of heaven. We came from our homeland under the supreme prince Christ. Through the aid of the cross we shall overcome the city of Majorca; he himself will bind Satan’s servants in heavy chains and give them wholly to be slain by our swords. Know, dogs, that Count Pyrenus is unharmed, and that the time of your destruction is near.”

After this they hastened to lead towers to the walls. The people were divided among locations, the fathers divided, and the warfare divided. Soon timber, stone, green sods, and heaps thrown down quickly levelled the ditches of solid earth. The Moors remained upon the walls and did not advance from the city. Then Alphaean strength led towers against the walls; battle-lines stood by, and the companies broke through the walls.

[Col. 0568A] Meanwhile at Pisa matrons and maidens laid aside their finery and clung continually to the churches. They made vows and brought most celebrated incense to the saints; often, going barefoot to the holy churches, they shed tears, kissed the hard earth, prayed to the Thunderer full of mercy for their loved ones, and asked to see their husbands victorious and safe.

Bishop Roger, worthy prelate of lofty Volsci, terrified those wishing to strip laurel-bearing Pisa of its companions; he checked threats and prohibited plunder. Throughout Latium the pope ordered holy fasts and prayers, and a letter likewise admonished the Gauls. Divine power assented to the praying crowd, and the groan of those weeping moved the divine ears.

The fortieth day, to be celebrated in every age, after the Virgin’s childbirth, was returning as a festival for the peoples—the day on which the holy Virgin went with her son to the sacred temple and Simeon held the holy infant in his arms.

[Col. 0568B] Before the next day of the famous feast had come, the Latin forces set fire by night and swiftly burned one fortress from the camps. This fortress had recently been devised by skilful Greeks, a marvel not hidden anywhere from men once it had been commanded. Towers then flew everywhere, and easily kindled ashes; a spark driven from one fortress entered another’s hurdles, which burned more swiftly as flames grew. As a candle, when placed close to dry wood, turns dry material into slender flames, and as a great heap gradually but quickly grows white-hot, so you might have seen the remaining fortress suddenly glow,

[Col. 0568C] while the Virgin Mother, ruling with the holy child, who alone fills all ages with his own light, was present. That night was filled with joy; with the coming of daylight, no small joys anticipated the holy peoples.

When the annual solemnities of Saint Agatha returned, the Pisan force entered the city of warlike Majorca with strong strength through three entrances beneath the fortress which stood by the sea-gate. But few Latin battalions entered the walls. Within, many horsemen came to the aid of the frightened wing, powerfully on right and left, and pursued the Latin force through the fairly broad streets. Two of the Latin people fell; the rest held their entrance and endured the attacks

[Col. 0568D] of hurled stones and flying missiles. But after they overcame the dense barrage of missiles, and there was no place for swords, they swiftly fled outside. Barbarian fire spread over the bridge laid upon the ditch; but the fearful Alphaeans pressed on despite their success and strove at close quarters to extinguish the fire with water.

At the first entrances, into which Provence had sent forces, they prepared to engage in the contest of harsh fighting and disdained to prefer their Latin allies to themselves. The Balearic crowd saw them protected by short shields and struck head or legs with countless arrows; they fled and were shamefully driven from the whole city.

On this day the parish priest Henry learned all the omens of coming joy. A voice addressed the man: “Hear with your ears,” it said,

[Col. 0569A] “the stars decree that the Pisans will today be driven back from the city; tomorrow, in the evening hours, the force that has suffered much will enter the city, conquering by the will of the Thunderer.”

The same spirit of the dead Narolus said to his brother: “Do not fear: the saints will come to battle, and innumerable men will be present, mounting the walls with you. Nor will missiles be able to strike you while I accompany you.”

The army had now despaired of being able to take the city. Therefore the fathers and leaders ordered, with one voice, that battle be joined three times in the morning. The time was neither fully bright nor free from storm when the battalions of infantry uncertainly entered battle. Ten times they attempted to enter the open approaches, and ten times they were driven out and repelled from the walls.

As the day passed, those who held the recently captured tower of Majorca began to join battle seven times. The tower had been entered first by brave Bruno, repaying the deeds of the holy men. He had advanced, braced against the wall’s rocks, and while he was already attempting to overthrow the muddy work, a Moorish band attacked. Missiles, sent in swift flight, fixed themselves in his tough shield as he resisted. When a Moor saw his great strength, he immediately attacked and drove a stout spear through his sevenfold covering; but the Moor, immediately pinned more firmly by Bruno’s missile, fell from the high walls; another fell, struck by Hugh’s sword.

[Col. 0569C] The Moorish battalions advanced more fully upon the high strength of the wall, believing they would overcome the seven men and deprive those already defeated of present life. Then the divine spirit, coming from above, kindled the companions; their threefold voice, trusting in the resounding Maker of things, prayed to the Lord.

After they had covered their bodies with heavy shields, they sought the opposing enemies with hard swords. They dealt many blows by joined strength, and many more were dealt them by the savage foe. Then God granted prosperity to the Alphaeans, disclosed joyful success and their desired vows, and changed the omen of the barbarian people with misfortunes. A little band, made fierce by heavenly strength, assailed the savage Moors with dreadful cry and sword.

Bruno cut off the great head of Peranseus with his sword and received in the breast the missile of savage Beroens. Peter struck Eugubius down with a javelin; Hugh, son of Sebald,

[Col. 0569D] rounded off Alphaena’s head with a sharp sword. Pathus, offspring of Ildebrand, crushed Arphipon; then Herricus hurled a javelin and pierced Luba’s groin. Uguiccio the German [the syntax is uncertain]; Marutia, the true offspring of Uguiccio Verardus, struck Machion down with the sword, taking away his feet.

And as tigers and savage lionesses attack a herd when most fierce hunger drives them, tearing the pestilential entrails of cattle with their teeth, so, pounding them with javelins and swords alike, the barbarian crowd fled. With a Latin shout raised, they begged their companions to enter through the open approaches.

Raynerius, offspring of Sicheria, outstripped all the others, and the hero Terpeteius; with them were the companions of Guiscard and Grunnius. They pursued the barbarian backs and slaughtered the retreating crowd by striking them with javelins.

[Col. 0570A] Until old Elmodenia, opening her strong gates, gave entry to the fleeing foster-sons. From the seaward side the warlike Eufraxius entered the city with his son. A Moorish band stood in the street and rushed in haste upon the men with clashing arms; rolling stones could have frightened them sufficiently.

Bernard remained fearless with his father and laid Alcen, who stood against him, low with a hardened spear. Then Ildebrand said: “Strike, I pray, excellent son, and spare no one with the sword if your spear fails. It is fitting to fight for one’s homeland, venerable antiquity; our ancestors once shone through arms.”

[Col. 0570B] He spoke, laid Agilion low with a javelin, and, striking Brusaeus, severed his head from his neck with the sword. The rest immediately scattered; the men pressed upon the fleeing, and the son, born with his father, struck through the barbarian backs.

Horsemen and infantrymen, bold in spirit, came running from every direction and entered in compact steps, just as swarms enter their accustomed dwellings. Thus Alphaean strength, advancing into the broad city, scattered the dispersed bands with javelins and swords. Here one lay with head cut off, another with breast transfixed, another with entrails spilled upon the ground. You would think that the earth was drenched too deeply with human blood and that streams, stirred by blood, flowed—just as rivers, released in their first course, spread over fields when they are recalled into their channel,

[Col. 0570C] producing many streams and thick pools.

But after the sword had destroyed the raging enemies, the Christians, whom long labour had now worn thin, held the walls with their roofs and the city churches. They guarded the city itself with watchful zeal and were never removed from their accustomed practice of war. They applied their skills, performed and overcame their labours. With buildings destroyed, a way was made and siege-machines drawn forward. For two gates were hidden at Bebolgedit, and as many at the walls of Emodenum. Finally a Latin engine brought down the towered wall; the ditches were swiftly levelled with fortification, and were filled with many corpses and timbers.

The barbarian people, violently shaken by great fear, entered Count Pyrenus’ camp trembling,

[Col. 0570D] wishing to join whatever treaty he might choose, provided that the warriors were allowed to depart safe, unbound, uninjured, and free. As they reported these things, they were hastened together into one assembly. The summoned people discussed a treaty of peace.

The day was shining on which the Shepherd of the Church, full of holy learning, assumed the rights of the chair. Clergy and nobles alike were present. Great contention arose; divided minds disclosed opposing struggles. One party inclined toward agreement, the other loved war. The clergy praised the party wishing to fight; the holy bishop, together with the chapter, judged for battle, and the battle-lines supported them. Against this, the Catalan hero, the old man of Ampurias, and Guidelmus strove,

[Col. 0571A] labouring with lavish gifts, prayers, and payment, to turn the firm minds of the holy clergy. When the pious order rejected this, it endured insults.

Then Gratianus with Bernard replied in honourable words, suitable to the eager words of the Goths. The sorrowful bishop with his chapter poured forth deep tears and prayed thus, kneeling, to the heavenly power:

“Almighty Creator of heaven and Maker of earth, by whose everlasting command the ages and everything that flourishes or is seen within them were created: heed the mournful prayers of us who cry out. Preserve those who trust in you, best Father; come with pious aid to your Church, willing to fight for you. Grant victory over the sacrilegious people drenched in the blood of many saints.

[Col. 0571B] And in your mercy look upon your servants who entreat you and always worship you as Maker of all things. And you, holy Mother of God, queen of the heavens, together with the saints, fulfil our prayers.”

Meanwhile the Pisan youth burned in the camp. Oliverius, offspring of Brunicard, promptly began the fight—the Oliverius whom you sent into arms at the ford—and mighty Roland, begotten by father Rodulphus. The Latins sought arms; Count Pyrenus directed the war. They approached the walls and attacked the Ishmaelites; they forestalled the entrances and pressed close upon the gates.

Against them the pagan phalanxes mingled fierce warfare, guarding the broken walls with unconquered strength. The Alphaeans pressed on more fiercely and, compelled by courage, burst through the hard approaches with flashing arms.

[Col. 0571C] Stones, weapons, discharged arrows, and the masses hurled by engines within assailed them. They protected their limbs, covered by shields and breastplates; with hurled javelins and swords they attacked the enemy, held their ground immovably, renewed and endured battle.

After these, a dense mixed force, having suffered frequent missiles, burned to run swiftly upon the opposing crowd, from which heavy millstones were hurled onto shields. Here men of the common people were seen to turn their backs and fall in shameful ruin from the broken walls. But those who could endure war by strength of spirit repelled the opposing bands with unbroken force, although three allies had been repelled from the battle.

Then Hugh, acting in the count’s place and powerful in strength,

[Col. 0571D] entered the city with few accompanying soldiers. He attacked the Moors and scattered them with a sharp spear, as a leopard pursues swift deer through trackless fields. While the huge and powerful Alchas, his groin grievously pierced by the hero’s efforts, was hastening to the shades, the remaining forces came running and searched the city with flashing steel. Yet the earth received much blood before they were forced to turn their backs and abandon the street where they had then stood fighting.

Francardus, offspring of Ansualdus, carrying the infantry standard, attacked the enemy from another side. But he was accompanied by the forces of Hugh and Uguiccio, powerful workers in gold, and by the son of Sibylla with a great band. These vigorous men eagerly desiring battle

[Col. 0572A] attacked Dartana in fighting and gave Majorca’s forces over to death. They swiftly sought the citadel, and wherever they rushed you might see deadly battle. Corpses lay slain throughout all the temples; wounds dripped from bodies, and streams of blood poured everywhere through the Latin streets. Some fell struck by the sword; some were held captive; but old Elmodenia preserved the remaining people.

The count Pyrenus, hurrying from another side, received all the Jews here under his protection. The holy people hurried through the captured city, releasing the iron chains of their captive brothers. Their spoils were purple-dyed cloth, fine linen, and purple garments, gold with jewels, and Spanish cloaks.

Part of the labour still remained; part had been completed.

[Col. 0572B] The city of Elmodenia was surrounded by peoples; the prudent nation besieged it and constantly maintained its walls. In order to draw up siege-machines, the Pisans overthrew walls and levelled every obstacle in the captured city. Those in charge of the walls sought altered terms of treaty, and harmony could not exist for men defeated in various ways.

A corner tower held them; the forces broke it and entered the approaches made by the strength of combatants. The tower was taken by force; labour there was immense and swiftly became greater through the engineers’ effort. They set up standards and cried that the walls were taken. Men ran together from every side; everywhere there was haste to arms. The Moors defended themselves with javelins and swords from a window made by the Latins. One of them, very eager in the fierce fight, held his head out of the window;

[Col. 0572C] drawn by his hair by an Alphaean, he was hauled outside and beheaded, Rasullas being unable to help him.

The entrance now lay open; the joyful Alphaean youth entered. The phalanx was dying and, forced back, returned to the city which fairly narrowly encircled the king’s citadel. Nevertheless, many fell by the sword, as the widely shed blood outside made evident. The surrounding Pisan force broke down the wall-strengths with roofs and swiftly drew two towers toward the walls. The barbarian crowd was shaken with fear; a few sought safeguards for their lives. The Alphaeans neither granted nor rejected terms.

Some, supported on ladders, mounted; others, driven to the extremities, climbed the lofty towers with no sluggish strength. The barbarian people fled and climbed into the citadel.

[Col. 0572D] The citadel, unconquered, remained to be overcome by bloody wars. It extended seven towers high into the air, much higher than the lofty theatres of the Romans. Broad Pontic water beneath steep rocks washed one side of the castle, safely situated; on the remaining sides it was enclosed by a deep ditch. A thousand warriors defended it in battle, and two strong towers positioned above Dartana strove boldly likewise to hold out and displayed their vigorous rage for war.

While they made repeated assaults, inflicted wounds, killed many, and shed much blood, the Alphaean youth, pressing upon the two towers, terrified the hard Iberians defending the walls.

[Col. 0573A] By the throw of an engine the walls and the enemies were brought down; the dense mass battered and shook the fortresses it struck. The Moorish force quickly forced into collapse the wall obstructing the tower, toward which the tortoise-siege engine was being drawn by the strength of the young men. The struck corner of the tower fell; the wicked crowd immediately fled. Raymond climbed the ladder into it and, fighting, drove out thirty Moors.

Then, bold, he laid one man low with his huge spear and, pressing on with the sword, killed many by striking. With these successes he pursued the remaining enemies. The barbarian companies fled from another abandoned tower in a precipitous leap, but five remained above. They struck the man fighting most strongly with a beam; he endured, until he was broken by the blow of a heavy stone.

[Col. 0573B] The thrown mass smashed his face and mouth amid his jaws. Then the warrior fell from the high wall and died; heaven received his soul released from the flesh. His companions mourned him lovingly. Known and unknown alike gave tears, laments, and shared loud groans.

The forces came up, fire was set beneath the tower, and Hugh climbed the upper stages of the ladder. The five remaining enemies, with opposing strength and much clamour, hemmed in the striving youth. At last no one could come to his aid. Bearing a thousand blows upon shield and helmet, he endured long and excessive dangers. From the first light of the sun he had entered battle, which is said to have lasted until the ninth hour.

[Col. 0573C] At last, with spirits kindled, one of his companions cautiously entered the tower and climbed to the top. While the five attacked him with bare swords, Hugh entered the tower, and two men followed immediately. First he quickly deprived a Moor of his head with his sword; then, placing a wheel [or shield-like device], he swiftly received that man’s shield and cut down two with drawn sword. Two companions struck down the other two.

The citadel, never to be overcome without the shedding of blood, remained; but the Pisan power surrounded it.

They watch at once, like a hunting band,  
the dreadful bears which the cavern keeps confined.

Meanwhile the new king, terrified by these exploits,  
after he saw the comet overcome by Pisan strength,  
[Col. 0573D] turned in fear toward the citadels, that he might escape alive.  
He fulfilled with promises his sufficiently tested friends,  
and departed by ship, seven men accompanying him,  
who had formerly ruled the Balearic land.

Dodo, who had guarded the sea with wakeful care,  
brought him back as he ploughed the deep, desiring to return to the camp.  
To wear down Christians in harsh chains recently.  
The king, held in fetters, underwent iron bonds.

Thereupon the Balearic people made Alant,  
a Spaniard, their king; but his reign was not to last.  
Terrified by Dalmatius’s death,  
he who had seized the head trusted himself to no one ever again.  
Recalling these things in fear, he found for himself two skins;  
inflating the empty hides with much breath,  
he closed their openings with cords fastened within.

[Col. 0574A] Thus the Spaniard, using skins as wings in place of a ship,  
made his way across the long straits—you would think him a dolphin swimming—  
and here made his escape over the sea, leaving his companions behind.

The Pisan forces break through the city’s walls and houses;  
through openings made, siege-engines are drawn forward.  
By devices and contrivances—so the text reads—  
the machines rise through the air through the craftsmen’s zeal;  
each man labours, even the stranger,  
to inflict excessive damage by the ruin of the opposite side.

Stones, rock, and turf, the foundations of a broad ditch,  
thrown within, fill it; the nearby siege-engines  
stand against the walls; the hard wall of Berbece is pierced;  
towers are constructed upon the citadel by alternating labour.  
They lay supporting beams above and costly cloths,  
such as a merchant would not make even for much gold.

But those posted beneath the fortress send fires from the walls,  
[Col. 0574B] sulphurous flames through the open apertures.  
Waters drawn from wells and springs, which they called for,  
they thought had extinguished the Latin flames and brands.  
The guards were in secret; but then there was a lofty mass of palace [sense uncertain].  
They bring up engines and contend with the towers by hooked ropes,  
and the towers, dragged down, are drawn to the ground below.

After several days the strength of the hidden fire  
grew beneath; smoke too issued forth such as comes from Etna  
when Vulcan in his grim cavern  
stirs up fire-bearing clouds full of darkness.

Then water is swiftly demanded and more water added,  
but what is thrown cannot extinguish the concealed flames.  
They at once draw the siege-engine back, until the fire should cease,  
after the flame had subsided from its own heat;  
the ingenious troop brings the siege-engines again against the citadel.

[Col. 0574C] A battering ram, striking with a swift blow,  
shakes the lofty timbers of the tower; rocks fall to the depths below.

Meanwhile Sachi withdrew from the citadel with two  
soldiers, boys accompanying them, and girls,  
and offered Alphaeus a great, uncounted ransom;  
but the rest threaten to give themselves to the flames.  
Unless they win their freedom, whatever valuables they possess,  
they are permitted to depart for whatever places they please.

Alphaeus replies in turn: “May the Almighty destroy both you  
and your gold, since you think such perverse thoughts.  
It is dearer to us to be released by such a death  
than Balearic treasures or anything else of greatest value.”

The Geryonean host does not receive such words in its ears.  
The troop of Alphaeus surrounds the citadel with engines  
and establishes two bridges of remarkable strength.

[Col. 0574D] One timber structure, built and laid upon the walls,  
at once rises; while the other is being slowly set in place,  
the Moors fight and attend to such great labours.  
The men of Alphaeus hasten forward; Grunius proceeds first  
and crushes the violent enemy set against him.  
Beside him the others soon advance into the citadel.

Some of the Moors at once begin to descend the ladders;  
many do not hesitate to expose themselves to the perils  
of death, lest they be stabbed without vengeance.  
But just as hawks are wont to hurry in swift flight  
with the lightness of their feathers, when a great flock of geese,  
suspended in the air, leaves the riverine fields,  
and, pursued, lies torn by ready talons,  
scattered with its feathers pulled apart, so one might see

[Col. 0575A] the Pisans hastening, and barbarian limbs lying strewn.

Then the ruler of the Pyrenean region,  
ascending joyfully into the citadel, reproaches the conquered enemy.  
Many fall by the sword; many fell from the windows.  
One strives here to cut down the men; another drags away the girls;  
when plunder has been taken, the wall and houses are destroyed.  
Then fire consumes the slain amid the wooden roofs;  
the stranger, laying waste the fields, ranges through the places of the land.

Then men come, and at last mothers with their children;  
[Col. 0576A] then oxen, herds of cattle, and much household equipment.

Easter is celebrated; Batales is released from his bonds;  
the Pisan power grants the kingdom to his son.  
At last the victors, with their fortunate fleet prepared,  
each make for his own home; those on shore watch them,  
and the peoples sing the wondrous mighty deeds of Christ.

Burabe, finally led into the city of Pisa,  
offered himself to Italy as a spectacle, a monster.

Here ends the book of Lawrence of Verona concerning the Majorcan war.

Then there was, from Christ’s taking on the covering of flesh,  
the year one thousand one hundred and fifteen.

# In the Year of the Lord 1119: The Anonymous Deeds of the Bishops of Metz

(Edited by Georg Waitz, public professor at Göttingen, in Pertz, *Monumenta Germaniae Historica*, *Scriptores*, vol. X, p. 531)

[Col. 0575]

# Preliminary Observations

The bishopric of Metz was the first on this side of the Alps to have the deeds performed by its bishops described by Paul the Deacon, while he was staying at the court of Charlemagne. Angelramnus induced him to illuminate with a narrative, though brief, this see, made illustrious by bishops descended from Charlemagne’s line. [Note: [Col. 0575B] *SS.* II, p. 261.]

We are surprised that for nearly four centuries no one followed him, since neither the Church of Metz nor the monasteries situated around it lacked an abundance of learned men and persons skilled in writing. [Note: [Col. 0575B] At the monastery of Saint Arnulf certain writings concerning the foundation of the monastery and the deeds performed by its abbots exist; Calmet edited them in I, *Probb.*, p. 545 ff. These appear to have been compiled at a later date, but from old charters. A codex written in the fourteenth or fifteenth century is now kept in the library of the city of Metz, N. G. 76; see *Archiv* VIII, p. 457.]

At the beginning of the eleventh century Constantine wrote the deeds of Adalbero; [Note: [Col. 0575B] *SS.* IV, p. 659.] in the middle of that century Sigebert composed the Life of the first Theodoric; [Note: [Col. 0575B] Ibid., p. 462.] but only in the middle of the twelfth century was a continuous history of the bishops undertaken. The writer’s name is concealed—and this is no cause for regret. For he produced a dry and meagre work, in which he assembled scarcely anything of true history, a few fragments of ecclesiastical tradition, but an ample crop of fables and errors.

He wished to add something to Paul’s very brief book, and therefore took years from a catalogue of bishops, such as you see printed in *Mon. SS.* II, p. 268 (*Patrologia*, vol. XCV, col. 673), [Note: [Col. 0575B] The readings of the Chronicle almost always agree with the codex published by Freher.] and compared them with a certain sequence of emperors and supreme pontiffs; yet in connecting these he committed almost laughable errors. [Note: [Col. 0575B] For example, in chapter 48 he reports that Theodoric II (1006–1046) held office under the apostolic bishops Marinus, Agapitus, and Octavian—that is, in 942–964. But these statements are almost everywhere utterly false, although he appears to have devoted at least some effort to indicating the years correctly; cf. chapter 1. [Col. 0576B] A fourteenth-century writer already noted these errors; see below, no. 29.]

Nor did he use popular tradition more successfully on occasion. What he recounts concerning Charlemagne’s expedition to Jerusalem [Note: [Col. 0576B] Chapter 29.] and Saint Ulrich’s vision [Note: [Col. 0576B] Chapter 46.] is extremely slight; nor will those matters which ought to illuminate the final period of Bishop Herimann (+1090) commend themselves to the reader. [Note: [Col. 0576B] Chapter 50.] These perhaps were drawn from the *Miracles of Saint Clement*; and the writer himself declares that he composed this saint’s Life, [Note: [Col. 0576B] Chapter 17: “they were conveyed to blessed Clement, as we noted in the second little book of his Life.” Calmet, *Hist. de Lorraine* I, p. XIV, and (Tabouillot), *Histoire de Metz* I, p. 203, discuss the unpublished Lives of Saint Clement. Cf. *Hist. littér.* XI, p. 127. They have not yet been published in the Bollandist *Acta Sanctorum*.] which, unless I am mistaken, has remained unpublished to this day.

He saw the poems of Fortunatus, [Note: [Col. 0576B] Preface.] the Lives of Bishops Arnulf, [Note: [Col. 0576B] Chapter 29.] Theodoric [Note: [Col. 0576B] Chapter 46; cf. preface.] and Adalbero, [Note: [Col. 0576B] Chapter 47.] but did not choose to copy them. He sometimes followed Paul closely, [Note: [Col. 0576B] E.g. chapters 11 and 37.] and sometimes, though changing the language, seems nevertheless to have derived matters from Paul’s book; [Col. 0577] [Note: [Col. 0577A] Cf. chapters 13 ff. and 29.] furthermore, he seems to have used certain brief annals of the Church of Metz [Note: [Col. 0577A] See chapter 37 on Pope Stephen; chapter 38 on Leo; chapter 42 on the battle fought against the Northmen; chapter 44 on the Hungarian invasion. It is evident that these must be referred to ancient annals; nevertheless, I have not found the copy that our author used. Cf. *Annales sancti Vincentii Metensis*, under the year 926, *SS.* III, p. 157. He did not possess the Annals of Metz compiled in the tenth century, *SS.* I, p. 314 ff.] and also a Carolingian genealogy [Note: [Col. 0577A] Chapter 26.] and the book called Charlemagne’s *Itinerary*, which he himself cites, [Note: [Col. 0577A] Chapter 29. This book seems hitherto to have been unknown to everyone. Cf. *Histoire de l’académie des inscriptions* XXI, p. 138 ff.] adapting them to his own purposes. Finally, he accepted certain individual matters from the report of contemporaries. [Note: [Col. 0577A] Chapter 48: “the succession of modern writers relates.”]

But even for the more recent period these materials are not of great importance. For he omitted not only Bishop Theoger, whom he may perhaps have seen himself (+1120), but also related less accurately other matters which preceded the election of Bishop Stephen. Nevertheless, it is plainly indicated that the book was written under this Bishop Stephen, who held the see of Metz from 1120 to 1163. [Note: [Col. 0577A] Chapter 51: “Since he is still flourishing in life and vigorous in age,” etc.] It is already likely from what has been said that Stephen’s first years are not intended. Certainly our author knows that Adalbero, primicerius of Metz, was made Archbishop of Trier [Note: [Col. 0577A] Chapter 51. Newly discovered verses written about Metz are mentioned [Col. 0578A] in the preface; this may belong to the time of Sigebert, from whom he appears to have taken them.]—which occurred in 1132. On the other hand, he says nothing about the translation of Saint Legontius in 1142, [Note: [Col. 0578A] See the old notice of this event in Calmet II, p. CCCXLVII.] so that perhaps it may be determined that he wrote between these years.

It is therefore evident that those who tried to attribute either the entire book or part of it to Sigebert of Gembloux—a most learned man and weighty writer, who died in 1112—have strayed far from the truth. [Note: [Col. 0578A] Cf. Hirsch, *De Sigeberto Gemblacensi*, p. 348 ff., who has sufficiently refuted this. Neither the computation of years nor the events related agree with Sigebert’s Chronicle.] Nor do those require refutation who have held that one author of the book lived in 1095 and another in the twelfth century. [Note: [Col. 0578A] *Hist. liter.* VI, p. 437; more correctly, however, ibid., XI, p. 126; Tabouillot, II, p. 257.] There is one author of the booklet down to Stephen’s time, and he was certainly a cleric of Metz; the matters we have presented forbid us to count him among the outstanding writers of the Middle Ages.

Yet his labour was not wholly fruitless. For at a later time continuators appeared, who committed to memory the succeeding bishops of the Church of Metz with greater historical benefit. They too are brief in expounding events, but they consider them established, refrain from fables and empty traditions, and strive only to present a trustworthy survey of Metz history. The first undertook the work shortly after 1180 and, while Bishop Bertram was still alive, reviewed the acts of five bishops over sixty years down to that year. He too sometimes departed from the truth, whether through carelessness or excessive devotion to the Church of Metz, [Note: [Col. 0578A] Cf. what I noted in the annotations to chapters 1 and 3.] and was not sufficiently accurate in indicating dates; otherwise he appears well acquainted with events and especially engaged in elucidating the bishops’ public affairs.

The second continuation passes Bertram’s later years over in silence, but from 1212 to 1260—more briefly at first and more fully later—it deals with three bishops of this period, pursuing them with the highest praise. Its style is fuller than in the preceding portions of the Chronicle, at points inflated and entangled in empty words. Yet we should with difficulty dispense with this account, since it contains events described so faithfully by no one else. For even in these periods the history of Metz suffers from a great scarcity of sources.

For this reason the third continuation too, although very brief, is by no means to be neglected. In it the writer of a certain codex carried the succession of bishops down to 1296, adding a few words about the preceding four and explaining somewhat more fully the deeds of the fifth, namely Burchard. Our edition proceeds thus far; we judged that matters written by others in more recent times should now be set aside, since they scarcely—even scarcely at all—cohere with the work begun in the twelfth century.

The materials available for publishing these works were as follows.

1. Paris, Royal Manuscript no. 5357, parchment folio. Its final fourteen folios, written in the fourteenth century, contain the *Deeds of the Bishops of Metz* enlarged by the first continuation. The words indicating the age of the first writer have been omitted, and much is rendered carelessly and less accurately.

2. Paris, Saint-Germain Manuscript no. 1396, formerly marked “from the library of Claude Sauraa, senator in the upper court of the realm,” then “from the books of Raymond Formentin,” and subsequently “Saint-Maur-des-Fossés 122.” It is a paper manuscript of the fifteenth century, comprising thirty-three folios, in which the *Deeds* with two continuations are copied. The script is inelegant and not free from errors. A later hand corrected some things and added others, [Note: [Col. 0578A] Cf. below, no. 32.] which are easily seen to be alien to the genuine text.

3. Paris, Royal Manuscript no. 5532, formerly de Faure; parchment, fourteenth century, quarto. In one hand, over twenty-one folios, the *Deeds*, the first continuation, the second, and also the third were written. In another fifteenth-century hand, shorter additions were made here and there; and at the end five new paper folios were filled with a history of the bishops down to 1376. To this are appended another, very brief continuation to 1466 and another to 1530. This book too does not excel the others. It usually agrees with manuscript 1, but also has its own errors.

These codices appear especially to have distorted the first part of the Chronicle. In writing words they follow fourteenth- and fifteenth-century usage and here and there show traces of French speech. Thus *c* (or *t*) and *s* are frequently interchanged: *metencium* (2), *metentium* (3), *treverencem* (3), *gorzience* (3), *obcessi* (2); *Dyoclesiano* (3), *advocasiam* (2), *Fransi* and *Fransia* (2), *composisio* (2), *sisternae* (2), *resepiscet* (for *recepisset*, 3). The letter *n* is used for *m*, and *on* for *um*: *novenbris* (2), *membrana* (1, 2), *ponpose* (1, 2), *circundatus* and *circonseptus* (2), *colonbina* (2). Very frequently *y* appears for *i*, *th* for *t*, *ph* for *f*, and similar forms; letters are sometimes doubled: *defendit* (2), *Phillippus* (2), *parentilla* (3), *civille* (3), *committante* (2); sometimes omitted: *comunis* (1, 2), *aplausus* (1). I did not wish to report these individually in the notes. I nevertheless recorded the remaining variation of readings, although it is scarcely worth much attention. There are, moreover, errors which seem already to have entered an older exemplar of the book and which must be removed not with the aid of manuscripts but by mere conjecture.

In the Middle Ages this Chronicle scarcely passed beyond the boundaries of the bishopric of Metz. A brief account concerning the founding of the church of Saint John, published by Calmet (I, *Probb.*, p. 71), copied certain things either from this book or from a common source. [Note: [Col. 0578A] Cf. chapter 13. This narrative cannot be considered a source of the Chronicle; for it adds several matters entirely foreign to the account of Paul the Deacon, from which these items flowed—matters which the author of the Chronicle would not have omitted had he possessed them.]

Furthermore, at the end of the fourteenth century a new history of the bishops of Metz was composed and continued to 1376; I saw its copy at Paris among the Baluze collections (Armoire II, p. 5, no. 2). [Col. 0579] You may readily recognize the old *Deeds* as the foundation of this work, but many things were either added or changed. [Note: [Col. 0579C] When the second continuation of the *Deeds* is finished, the author proceeds thus: “Note that from the beginning of the book down to Bishop Stephen, who was made bishop of Metz in A.D. 1120, there appears to be a deficiency in the years; I do not know whether the see was vacant for so long a time, because it is written that after Bishop Hermann’s death it was vacant for some time. Likewise, in year 42, the supreme pontiffs are cited less well alongside the emperors under the holy Bishop Walon. I have taken care to note this, wishing to complete the chronicles, exclusive of Bishop James, down to Theodoric the Fifth inclusive, so that an error may not be imputed to the later writing.” After Theodoric, the names of bishops are added in this copy down to: “Eighty-sixth: the illustrious prince Henry of Bourbon.”] This work, together with another and different continuation down to the same year 1376 (manuscript 3), must be edited on another occasion.

Andrew Duchesne first made part of the *Deeds* public. In the proofs to the history of the counts of Bar, he inserted chapters 1 and 2 of the first continuation and other fragments in other works. [Note: [Col. 0579C] *Histoire généalogique de la maison de Bar-le-Duc . . . par André Duchesne* (Paris, 1531, folio), *Preuves*, pp. 15, 16.] He followed manuscript 1 or one similar to it. Later D’Achery (*Spicilegium* VI, p. 643) produced an edition of the *Deeds* from manuscript 2, [Note: [Col. 0580C] He himself identifies it: “We acknowledge receiving the manuscript Chronicle of the Bishops of Metz from the very learned Raymond Formentin, fellow of the Sorbonne.”] but increased its false readings with new errors. Matters there corrected or added at a later time [Note: [Col. 0580C] D’Achery notes that these are owed to the hand of H. Valesius: “The corrections made by the distinguished man Adrian Valesius, who had already read that Chronicle before it came into my hands, were also of assistance to me.”] he had printed as genuine; but he rashly omitted what seemed to him fabulous and excessively false. Nor did the second edition of the *Spicilegium*, edited by Barré (II, p. 224), improve anything.

Later Calmet (*Hist. Lotharing.* I, *Probb.* 1, p. 59; 2nd ed., I, p. LXXII) included the greater part of the book, from Bishop Angeramnus onward, where Paul’s book ends, in his large collection of materials for the history of Lorraine, removing more serious errors here and there. The continuators of Bouquet likewise provide some fragments (XI, p. 198; XIII, p. 642; XVIII, p. 677). To these the present edition is now added; benevolent readers will recognize that its genuine text has been restored and illustrated with necessary annotations.

Written at Göttingen after my return from the first court at Frankfurt.

GEORG WAITZ.

[Col. 0579]

# Deeds of the Bishops of Metz

[Col. 0579A] Metz [Note: [Col. 0579] Thus manuscript 1 almost throughout this part of the book; *metis* in 2 and 3.] is an ancient city situated in the province of First Belgica in Gaul, [Note: [Col. 0579] Omitted in 3.] sufficiently pleasant for the charm of its rivers, most fertile in vineyards and groves, conspicuous for its hills, [Note: [Col. 0579] *comspicabilis* in 1; *Opiscalibus* in 2.] more distinguished than other cities by nearby veins of salt, healthy in air, and established on the very shore of the Moselle. Of it Fortunatus [Note: [Col. 0580C] III, poem 14, to Villicus, bishop of Metz; V, 15.] says: “A city exceedingly well fortified, which wall and river surround.” [Note: [Col. 0579] “A city … river” omitted in 3.]

For its position and for various reasons, it is called by many names. [Note: [Col. 0579] *vocabilis* in 7.] Thus it was called Divodunum, as if “the hill”—*dunum*, that is, “mountain” [Note: [Col. 0579] Omitted in 2.]—of the gods, [Note: [Col. 0580C] Cf. Sigebert, *Life of Theodoric*, ch. 17, *SS.* IV, p. 477.] because to those approaching from the opposite direction it is seen rising high with its tower and buildings. It is also called Mediomatricum [Note: [Col. 0579] *mediomatricum* in 3.] from its situation among the surrounding cities. For it has Trier, the metropolis, to the north; Toul to the south; Verdun to the west; and between them flourishes like a mother in the middle.

Metz is also called after a certain conqueror of its own, named Metius, [Note: [Col. 0579] *v. s.* in 2; “also, as if from a certain conqueror, Metius,” in 3.] according to the following verse: [Note: [Col. 0580C] Sigebert also adduces these verses, book I.]

[Col. 0580A] “Metius, appointed in the city, had given it a name.” [Note: [Col. 0579] *urbem* in 3.]

And according to the following distich, recently found carved on stones unearthed from the ground: [Note: [Col. 0579] *scultum* in 1 and 3.] [Note: [Col. 0580C] Marmoutier.]

> At the time when Caesar brought his arms against the Gauls,  
> Metius then conquered the city of the Mediomatrici.

For Roman victory used to impose upon cities it had subjected to itself the names of its great men, [Note: [Col. 0579] *imponebant* in 2.] so that by this means it might establish for them a memory as though enduring. Thus Rheims is named from Remus, brother of Romulus; Toul from Tullus Hostilius; and the city of Cologne was called Agrippina from Agrippa. [Note: [Col. 0579] *fr. rom. remo* in 1; *egyppa* or *agippa* in 2; *argyppa* in 3. The phrase “the city … Agrippina” is omitted in 1.]

To the aforesaid city of Metz the blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, sent the venerable man Clement—formerly consul and patrician of the Romans, [Col. 0580B] [Note: [Col. 0579] *ac* in 2 and 3.] adorned with every virtue [Note: [Col. 0579] “adorned with all the beauty of virtues” in 2; “adorned with all beauty” in 3.]—from the city of Rome, and ordained that he should preside in pontifical rank over those whom he would subject to Christ.

[Note: [Col. 0579] “In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity” in 3; the red rubric is absent in 2, where “First bishop” is read.]

# In the Name of the Holy Trinity Begin the Deeds of the Pontiffs of Metz

[Col. 0579]

[Col. 0579B] **1.** [Note: [Col. 0579] At the head of each chapter the number of the bishop is written in red.] Blessed Clement therefore came to Metz [Note: [Col. 0579] *metim* in 2 and 3.] in the fifth year of Claudius. He occupied the bishopric for twenty-five years, [Note: [Col. 0579] “and four months,” added afterwards in 2.] namely, eleven under Claudius [Note: [Col. 0579] Nine in 1 and 2.] and fourteen under Nero. He died in the time of Vespasian, [Note: [Col. 0579] *vaspasiani* in 3.] after the passion of blessed Peter and Nero’s death, [Col. 0581A] while the blessed Clement, Peter’s cousin, was presiding after the apostle Peter over the Roman faithful. [Note: [Col. 0581] *presidendi* in 2.]

I have noted this calculation [Note: [Col. 0581] *supput.* in 1; *supplicacionem* in 3.] because, unless you include the periods of the pontificates of Linus and Cletus within the duration of the episcopate of blessed Peter, the years of the Roman pontiffs will not correspond consistently with the years of the emperors. For it is known with certainty that the blessed apostle devoted the office of his ministry chiefly not to baptizing but to converting people, as the book of the *Acts of the Apostles* testifies: after the coming of the Holy Spirit upon Cornelius and his household, he commanded them to be baptized; and this was to avoid schism, lest those baptized by the apostle should think themselves superior to the rest (Acts 10:48).

Accordingly Paul too writes to the Corinthians in his first epistle: “I give thanks to God that I baptized none [Col. 0581B] of you except Crispus and Gaius, lest perhaps you should say that you were baptized in Paul’s name” (1 Cor. 1:14). [Note: [Col. 0581] “I give thanks” added afterwards in 1; “I give thanks” in 3.] For those ordained presbyters by the apostles ranked above the others as bishops. But uncertainty in the reckoning [Note: [Col. 0581] *supp.* in 3.] of years grew up in the Church partly through writers’ negligence and partly, I suppose, through the pressure of persecutions.

**2.** When blessed Clement departed to heaven, Saint Celestis succeeded him in the episcopal office and held it for fifteen years: seven under Vespasian, [Note: [Col. 0581] *vespesiano* in 1; *vaspasyano* and subsequently *thyto* in 3.] two under Titus, and the remainder under Domitian. [Note: [Col. 0581] *reliquis* in 2 and 3.] He died in the time of that persecutor, under Pope Anacletus. He was buried before the doors of the crypt [Note: [Col. 0581] *cripe*, corrected to *cripte*, in 1.] of Saint Clement; [Note: [Col. 0581] “on the day before the Ides of October,” added in 3.] but after the passage of time he was translated by Drogo, Archbishop of Metz, into Alsace [Note: [Col. 0581] *alsaciam* in 3.] to the monastery of Maurus, [Col. 0581C] [Note: [Col. 0580] Marmoutier.] where he is worthily venerated.

There too the following notable event is related of him. [Note: [Col. 0581] *insignum* in 2.] When his relics were at one time being carried for a common necessity together with the relics of Saint Auctor, Saint Auctor, who was being carried before because he was reputed more famous, [Note: [Col. 0581] *preferabatur* in 3.] is said to have resisted until Saint Celestis went first. Although his other deeds are believed to have been great, no writings of earlier generations have transmitted anything concerning them to us.

**3.** After blessed Celestis, Saint Felix presided over the people of Metz for forty-two years, under the apostolic bishops [Note: [Col. 0581] *aplis* in 1 and 2.] Evaristus, Alexander, and Sixtus, in the times of Domitian, Nerva, and Trajan. He died in Hadrian’s time, under Pope Telesphorus. [Note: [Col. 0581] *thelesphoro*, with “on the ninth day before the Kalends of March,” in 3.] Felix is buried beside Saint Celestis; but long afterwards he was translated into Saxony by Emperor Henry of Bamberg. [Note: [Col. 0581] *babenbergense* in 2; *bavebergensi* in 3.]

[Col. 0582A] **4.** Saint Patiens, fourth bishop of Metz, [Note: [Col. 0581] *metensis* in 2 and 3.] succeeded Felix. He was Greek by birth and a disciple of John the Evangelist. He is said to have been sent to Metz by divine revelation, so that, just as John the Evangelist was associated with Peter in every work of power according to the *Acts of the Apostles* (Acts 3:4), so too the Church of Metz might be distinguished by his instruction, as also by the disciples of blessed Peter.

He built on the southern side of the city itself a church dedicated to Saint John the Evangelist, [Note: [Col. 0581] *uerbis* in 1.] supported by marble columns; it was later burned by the Huns. [Note: [Col. 0581] *unis*, corrected to *hunis*, in 1; *Hinniis* in 3.] In this church he placed a tooth of his own master together with twelve other relics of the apostles; there he himself later rested in burial, as we shall say in its proper place. [Note: [Col. 0581] “On the sixth day before the Ides of January,” added in 3.]

He held the episcopate for fourteen years, partly [Col. 0582B] under Hadrian and the rest [Note: [Col. 0581] *reliquis* in 3.] under Antoninus Pius. [Note: [Col. 0581] *antonio* in 2.] He died in the latter’s time, while Pius was presiding as pope after Hyginus over the Roman Church. [Note: [Col. 0581] “Pope Hyginus,” later corrected in 2; “after Pope Hyginus or Eugenius,” in 3.]

**5.** Victor succeeded Saint Patiens [Note: [Col. 0581] *pacienti* in 2 and 3.] as fifth bishop of Metz. [Note: [Col. 0581C] He is thought to have subscribed to the Council of Sardica in 347, but this is very doubtful; cf. Rettberg, [Col. 0582C] *Kirchengeschichte Deutschlands* I, p. 197.] He held office for nine years. [Note: [Col. 0581] “Nine years” in 3.] He died on the tenth day before the Kalends of October, under the already mentioned Pope Pius and Antoninus Pius, [Note: [Col. 0581] *antonio* in 2.] and was buried [Note: [Col. 0581] Omitted in 2.] in the church of blessed Clement (about 250?).

**6.** After him another Victor, the sixth, attained the episcopal chair, [Note: [Col. 0581] Omitted in 3.] occupying it for three years under Antoninus Pius [Note: [Col. 0581] *anthonio* in 2.] and Pope Anicetus. He died in the time of the same rulers. Concerning the translation of these two bishops, as also the account of their deeds, silence is maintained, except that they too were buried in the church of blessed Clement.

[Col. 0582C] **7.** Next [Note: [Col. 0581] *Huic* in 1; *Hunc* in 2.] Saint Symeon was consecrated the seventh bishop. [Note: [Col. 0581] Omitted in 3; “consecrated bishop” in 3.] He presided over the people of Metz [Note: [Col. 0581] *metensibus* here and often afterwards also in 1; “thirty years” in 3.] for thirty years, during the final period of Antoninus Pius, and in the times of the emperors Marcus, Verus, [Note: [Col. 0581] *Nerei* in 3.] and Lucius Commodus, and of Popes Anicetus, Soter, and Eleutherius. [Note: [Col. 0581] *eleutherii* in 3, where is added: “He died on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of March.”] He died under Eleutherius [Note: [Col. 0581] *eleutherio* in 2 and 3; omitted in 2.] and the Emperor Commodus. [Note: [Col. 0581] *comodo* in 1; “emperor” in 3.] He likewise was buried in the church of blessed Clement, [Note: [Col. 0581] *sancti* in 2 and 3.] but later was translated to the monastery of Senones. [Note: [Col. 0582C] Under Bishop Angelramnus; cf. Richer, *Chronicle of Saint-Savin* II.2, in D’Achery, 2nd ed., vol. II, p. 612.]

**8.** After him Sambatius, eighth bishop, presided over the Church of Metz. He held office for eighteen years, under the apostolic bishops Eleutherius, [Note: [Col. 0581] *eleutherio* in 2; *eleucterio* in 3.] Victor, and Zephyrinus, in the times of Lucius Commodus, Helvius [Note: [Col. 0581] *Nelii* in 3.] Pertinax, and Severus. He died in Severus’s time and under Pope Zephyrinus. He was buried [Col. 0583A] in the church of blessed Clement [Note: [Col. 0583] *sancti* in 2 and 3.] and was translated to Othrenheim. [Note: [Col. 0583] *othrentheim* in 1; *othrenhim* in 2; *orthrenheum* in 3. [Col. 0583C] Othernheim in the diocese of Worms. But others report this about Rufus, Sambatius’s successor; see *Hist. de Metz* I, p. 223.]

**9.** Rufus was the ninth bishop of Metz after Sambatius. [Note: [Col. 0583] *sabatium* in 2; *sanhatium* in 3.] He held the episcopate for twenty-nine years [Note: [Col. 0583C] The catalogue of the bishops of Metz, *SS.* II, p. 268, has twenty-eight years, later corrected to twenty-nine.] from the time of Severus and Antoninus Caracalla, Macrinus, Aurelius Antoninus, and Aurelius Alexander, under the apostolic bishops Callixtus, Urban, and Zephyrinus. [Note: [Col. 0583] “Macrinus, Aurelius Antoninus” omitted in 3; “Zephyrinus” omitted in 1; *zefirini* in 2; *zeph[yrinus], sixth day before the Kalends of September* in 3.] He was buried in the church of Saint Clement.

**10.** The tenth bishop of Metz [Note: [Col. 0583] *ep. m . . .* in 1.] was Adelfus. [Note: [Col. 0583] “presided” in 2.] He held office for seventeen years, under Aurelius Alexander, Maximinus, Gordian, and the Christian Philip together with his son Philip, and under the Roman bishops Pontianus, Anterus, and Fabian. [Note: [Col. 0583] *ab* in 1 and 3.] He too was buried in the church of Saint Clement.

[Col. 0583B] **11.** Firminus succeeded him as the eleventh bishop of Metz. [Note: [Col. 0583] *ep. meten.* in 3.] He held office for forty-five years, namely under Decius, Gallus and Volusian, Valerian, [Note: [Col. 0583] *velariano* in 2.] Gallienus, [Note: [Col. 0583] *galieno* in 1; *galliano* in 2.] Claudius, [Note: [Col. 0583] *claudiano*, corrected to *claudio*, in 2.] Aurelian, Tacitus, Florian, Probus, Carinus, Numerian, and Diocletian; [Note: [Col. 0583] *dyoclesiano* in 2; *dyocleciano* in 3.] and under the Roman bishops Cornelius, Lucius, Stephen, Sixtus III, Dionysius, Felix, Eutychian, Gaius, Marcellinus, and Marcellus. He died in the final period of those named.

The bodies of Saints Rufus and Adelfus and of others had been buried near the crypt of Saint Clement, toward the north. A certain devout man frequented the basilicas of the saints at night, as Paul the Italian recorded in his series of these bishops. [PAUL THE DEACON, *Patrologia*, vol. XCV, col. 673.] When he came to the basilica of blessed Clement, because permission was not granted to enter inside, [Col. 0583C] he approached the place opposite where the aforesaid bodies of the saints rested, [Note: [Col. 0583] “their holy bodies” in 3.] and devoutly prostrated himself in prayer. When he had finished the prescribed measure of prayer, he rose and, in memory of the saints at whose tombs [Note: [Col. 0583] *sepulchra* in 3.] he had prayed, pronounced the verse of the psalmist: “The saints shall exult in glory.” [Note: [Col. 0583] *qui* in 3.] Immediately he heard from within a voice adding: “They shall rejoice in their resting places.”
