**12.** Legontius [Note: [Col. 0583] *Leguncius* in 2; *Legoncius* in 3.] succeeded Firminus as the twelfth bishop of Metz and presided for thirty-four years, under Bishops Eusebius, Miltiades, [Note: [Col. 0583] *melchaide* in 1.] Sylvester, and Mark, while the most Christian Constantine was emperor. He died [Note: [Col. 0583] “on the twelfth day before the Kalends of March,” added in 3.] [Col. 0584A] in Constantine’s final period and was buried in the church of blessed Clement. In this same period the glorious confessor Nicholas flourished, from Constantine, son of Helena, down to Justin.

13. Saint Auctor succeeded him and presided for forty-nine years, under the bishops Julius, Liberius, Felix, and Damasus, while Constantius, Julian, Jovian, Valentinian, and Valens were emperors. [Note: “emperors” 2, 3.] In the same period Martin of Tours and Maximinus of Trier are said to have lived; together with them he condemned at the city of Cologne the heretic Ephraem. [Note: “at the city of Cologne he condemned” 2.] [Note: “Euphrates” 3.] [Note: “heretic” 2.] [Note: Cf. *Gesta Treverorum*, ch. 19. This council is placed in the year 346 [Col. 0584C], but it is fictitious; cf. Bettberg I, p. 123 ff. These Acts present not Auctor, but Bishop Victor.] [PAUL. D., same place.]

This blessed Auctor was called to the government of the Church during that same stormy time (450?), when not only Gaul but almost the whole West suffered the savagery of the barbarians. [Note: “called” 2.] The account of the ancients has handed down to the memory of posterity these two memorable deeds concerning this bishop. [Note: “distinguished” 2, written over two lines.] [Note: He seems to follow Paul, though in altered language.]

Therefore, as we have said, while the Lord’s harvest was being beaten down by the hailstorm of barbarians, Attila, king of the Hungarians, [Note: “Hungarians” 2.] taking up the Lord’s sword to cut back the overflowing wantonness of the Gauls, [Note: “to cut back” 3.] and having crushed King Gondegarius of the Allobroges, [Note: “Allobroges” 3.] loosened the reins of his cruelty throughout all Gaul. During this tempest Saint Servatius, bishop of the Tungri, [Note: omitted in 3.] set out for Rome [Note: “set out” 2.] to the thresholds of the apostles, [Note: “to the thresholds of the apostles” 3.] intending to implore the Lord’s remedy through their exalted merits. [Note: “through their merits” 3.] There, as he offered himself to God like a victim, in order that the Lord’s wrath might be held back from the people, [Note: “for indeed, as a victim” 1; *cum* corrected from *enim* in 2.] the blessed prince of the apostles said to him in a vision: [Note: “the blessed prince” 2.] [Note: “to him” 3.] “Know, dearest one, that it has been determined by divine judgment that nearly all Gaul shall be handed over to the fire of the barbarians, [Col. 0584C] except the oratory of the proto-martyr Stephen, [Note: “of Stephen” 3.] which was built at Metz.”

Having received this oracle, holy Servatius [Note: “Saint Servatius” 3.] returned with swift step; [Note: “returned with swift step” 3.] but the Hungarians [Note: “Hungarians” 3.] had already filled Gaul and had surrounded the city of Metz with siege. [Note: 3 reads: “but when they surrounded the city of Metz, being frustrated for the time being in their attempt to take it by force, they withdrew.”] Yet, frustrated for the moment in their assault because of the strength of the walls, [Note: “strength” 2.] they withdrew. When they had departed, [Note: “departure” 3.] Saint Servatius came to Metz and revealed the aforesaid revelation [Note: “account” 1.] to blessed Auctor, [Note: 3 reads: “revealed … and returned.”] then returned to his see at Tongeren. [Note: “Tongeren” 1.] When he had gone, the walls of the people of Metz fell down. [Note: 3 reads: “the walls of Metz fell.”]

Seeing this, blessed Auctor [Note: “Saint” 3.] summoned the citizens, urged them to confess their sins, [Note: 3 reads: “he exhorted them to confess their sins.”] imposed penance, [Col. 0585A] and ordered infants to be baptized. For it was the Saturday of Easter. The barbarians, quickly recalled by report, invaded the city, slaughtered everyone, [Note: 2 reads: “they slaughter and plunder.”] and plundered everything. Why say more? They filled the churches with the blood of innocents, [Note: “innocent persons” 3.] and cut down the priests. Only those were spared who were to be reserved for mockery.

In fury they surrounded the oratory of the holy proto-martyr, [Note: “of Saint Stephen” 3.] tried its entrance, [Note: “entrance” 3.] but the raging attack could not break into that which heavenly aid protected. [Note: 3 reads: “which heavenly aid protected.”] At last, like the Sodomites long ago at Lot’s house, deceived in their own attempt, [Note: 3 reads: “At last, like the Sodomites once …”] they set the city on fire and carried off the bishop himself with the rest. They had already gone far from the city, to a place called Decempagi (“Ten Villages”); [Note: 3 reads: “which is called Pagos.”] and behold, the barbarians were afflicted with blindness, like the Egyptians of old, and could not go anywhere.

In this distress [Col. 0585B] they asked [Note: “ask” 2.] the Christians whom they were carrying away [Note: “bringing” 1.] by what magic this had happened to them. [Note: “to them this” 2, 3.] The Christians replied: “Do not suppose that this is sorcery, [Note: “sorcery; but believe that God’s wrath …” 3.] but believe that the wrath of God hangs over you, because you are wickedly carrying off Saint Auctor, bishop of Metz.” [Note: “bishop of Metz” 3.] [Note: “carrying off,” corrected from *ab* in 1.]

At once Saint Auctor was sought, found, and entreated. He was offered whatever he wished to take, [Note: “that he himself might [take]” 3.] provided only that he would not withdraw from them the benefit of light. He said that he wanted none of the spoils, [Note: 3 reads: “he says that he wishes …”] but asked only that the captives be restored to him as a favor. [Note: 3 reads: “that the benefit of light be restored to them.”] It was granted; they restored the captives, and so escaped the darkness. Thus it came about that, when the shepherd had been taken captive, the flock of captives was set at liberty. [Note: 2: “obtained freedom”; 3: “came into possession of freedom.”]

Another deed of this blessed Auctor is also reported. [Note: 2, 3 read: “Another deed is reported.”] [Note: 3 reads: “another deed of blessed Auctor.”] By chance, when a beam, weakened by age, [Note: “by old age” 1.] suddenly [Note: omitted in 3.] fell upon the altar of blessed [Note: “saint” 3.] Stephen, [Col. 0585C] it broke the consecrated marble of that altar into a thousand pieces. [Note: Paul says “into two pieces.”] [Note: “broke into pieces” 3.] Blessed Auctor came; and—marvellous to tell—gathering and fitting together every tiny fragment of the broken marble, he poured out prayer, [Note: “prayers” 3.] made the sign of the cross over it, and immediately, by divine power, that shattered marble became solid, so that, although the scars of the fragments were visible, [Note: “scars of the fragments” 2.] nothing appeared more solid. [Note: “appeared” 3.]

Blessed Auctor died on the fourth day before the Ides of August, under Pope Siricius, while Gratian and Valentinian were emperors. [Note: “Cyricius” 1.] [Note: “emperors” 2.] [Note: 3: “Valentinian”; where a later hand wrote in a subsequently added leaf: “That his holy election was wondrous is evident, etc.; and a prayer concerning this saint, etc.”]

14. Epletius [Note: “Eplecius” 2, 3.] succeeded Saint Auctor as fourteenth bishop of Metz. [Note: “of the people of Metz” 2; “of Metz” 3.] He sat for sixteen years, under Emperor Theodosius and Bishops Siricius [Note: “Syritius; Anastasius” 1.] and Anastasius. [Col. 0586A] He died under the same rulers [Note: “and died” 3.] and was buried at Saint Clement’s.

15. Urbitius succeeded Epletius as fifteenth in the bishopric of Metz. [Note: “after Epletius” is lacking in 1.] [Note: “bishop of Metz” 3.] He is called the first archbishop of that city. [Note: Thus in the catalogue of bishops, *SS.* II, p. 269.] He presided for twenty-nine years, under the emperors Arcadius and Honorius and the Roman bishops Innocent and Zosimus. [Note: “Zosimus” 3.] He was buried [Note: “was buried” 3.] in the church of Saint Maximin [Note: “Maximian” 2; “Maxinin” 3.] beyond the Seille. [Note: Seille. Cf. Meurisse, *Hist. episcop. Met.*, [Col. 0586C] p. 61.]

16. Bonolius [Note: “Bonolus,” corrected to “Bonolius,” 2.] succeeded Urbitius as sixteenth bishop of Metz. [Note: “bishop of Metz” 3.] He sat for three years. He died on the eighth day before the Ides of October, under Pope Boniface, [Note: “Bonifacius” 2.] while Honorius and Theodosius were emperors. [Note: “emperors” 2, 3.]

17. Therentius succeeded him as seventeenth. He sat for twenty years. He died on the fourth day before the Kalends of November, under Popes Celestine [Col. 0586B] and Sixtus, while Honorius and the younger Theodosius reigned. In their time the body of the blessed proto-martyr Stephen was found with Gamaliel, Abibon, and Nicodemus. [Note: “and” 3.] Hence it is proved that the relics of blessed Stephen, through whose aid the church of Metz escaped the incursion of the Huns, were sent by the apostles to Saint Clement, as we noted in the second little book of his life. [Note: As far as I know, this Life of Saint Clement has not yet been published; cf. preface, no. 10.]

18. Gonsolinus succeeded Therentius as eighteenth in the priestly office. [Note: 3 reads: “and succeeded him as eighteenth, and sat”; 2: “and sat.”] He sat for eighteen years. [Note: “for eighteen years; years” 2.] He died on the second day before the Kalends of August, under Pope Leo I, while Marcian, Valentinian, and Leo were emperors.

19. Romanus succeeded Gonsolinus as nineteenth bishop of Metz. [Note: omitted in 3.] He sat for thirty-six years, under Popes Hilary, [Note: “Ylarius; Simplicius” 1.] Simplicius, and Felix, while the emperors Zeno and Anastasius reigned. [Col. 0586C] He died on the Ides of April.

20. Fronimius [Note: “Pronimius” 1, 2.] succeeded Romanus as twentieth bishop of Metz. He sat for eight years, under Felix, Gelasius, and Anastasius, while Anastasius was emperor. [Note: “Anathasius” 1; after “Augusti,” 2 supplies “Emperor Anastasius.”] He died on the sixth day before the Kalends of August.

21. Gramatius [Note: “Grammatius” 2.] succeeded in the bishopric of Metz as twenty-first. He sat for twenty-five years, under the Roman bishops John, Symmachus, [Note: 3: “and Symmachus and Hormisdas.”] and Hormisdas, under the rule of Anastasius [Note: “Anasthasius” 1.] and Justin the Elder. He died on the sixth day before the Kalends of May.

22. Agatimber [Note: 1, 2 read: “Grammatius Agatimber.”] succeeded Gramatius as twenty-second. [Col. 0587A] He sat for twelve years, under the apostolic bishops Felix, Boniface, Mercurius, Agapetus, and Silverius, while Justinian was emperor. He died on the fourth day before the Ides of May. [PAUL. DIAC. II, same place.] The preceding three bishops of Metz [Note: “three bishops of Metz,” 1; corrected in 2.] are believed to have been of Greek origin because of the etymology of their names.

23. Sperus succeeded them as twenty-third. [Note: Hesperius, bishop of the church of Metz, subscribed to the Council of Clermont in 535.] He presided over the church of Metz for seventeen years, under Pope Vigilius and the emperor Justinian (c. 535). He died on the tenth day before the Kalends of September. [Note: “December” 2.]

24. Vilicus [Note: “Vilieus” 1; “Willicus” 3.] succeeded as twenty-fourth bishop of Metz. He sat [Note: 1 lacks from “He sat” through “Peter, bishop of Metz”; therefore the number twenty-five was deleted and the following was written in the margin: “Here the scribe has made an error.”] for twenty-five years, under the apostolic bishops Pelagius I, John III, and Benedict I, while Justin and Tiberius Constantine were emperors (c. 550–570). He died on the tenth [Note: omitted in 3.] day before the Kalends of May.

[Col. 0587B] 25. Peter, bishop of Metz, succeeded Vilicus [Note: “Pilicus” 2; “Vuilicus succeeded” 3.] as twenty-fifth. He sat for ten years. He died on the fifth day before the Kalends of October, under Pope Pelagius II, while Tiberius Constantine reigned [Note: thus 1, 2, 3 at this place] (c. 570–580).

26. Aigulfus succeeded Peter as twenty-sixth bishop. He sat for twelve years. [Note: 1: “twenty”; 3: “twelve years.”] He died on the tenth day before the Kalends of December, under Pope Gregory I, while Maurice was emperor (c. 580–600). [Note: 3: “these were later corrected: ‘died in 598’; and again written: ‘he died on the tenth day before the Kalends of December.’”] This Aigulfus was descended from a daughter of Clovis, [Note: “Clodoveus” 3.] king of the Franks. [Note: 2: “born in,” with “is” written above; “bishop of Metz.”] [Note: Cf. Paul the Deacon II, p. 264. Here, however, he says: “who is said … to have been begotten.”] He enlarged the bishopric of Metz with estates both his own and those of his household. [*Carol. gen.*, *SS.* II, p. 310.]

For, receiving the village of Arisidium from his brother Deotharius, [Note: “Dotharius” 3.] he conveyed it by the hand of King Theudebert [Note: “Teodebert” 1.] into the possession of Saint Stephen the proto-martyr, and consecrated his aforesaid brother, Lord Deotharius, as bishop there. [Col. 0587C] The great teacher Gregory also addressed letters to this Aigulfus. [Note: XI, 58; Gregory the Great, *Works*, Benedictine ed., II, p. 1144.]

27. Arnoaldus succeeded this Aigulfus in the bishopric of Metz as twenty-seventh, [Note: “twenty-seven years” 1.] [PAUL. D., same place.] his nephew. He sat for eight years, under the bishops Sabinian, [Note: “Sabianian” 1.] and Boniface III, while Phocas reigned; under him he died on the seventh day before the Ides of October (c. 600).

28. Papolus succeeded Arnoaldus as twenty-eighth. He sat for twenty-four years [Note: “twenty-four years” 3.] [Note: On the date of Pappolus, see Tabouillot I, p. 344.], under the apostolic bishops Deusdedit, [Note: “Deodatus” 3.] Boniface V, Honorius, and Severinus, under the empire of Heraclius. He died on the eleventh day before the Kalends of October. This Papolus built a church in honor of Saint Symphorian the martyr [Col. 0588A] [Note: “of Metz” 3.] on the southern side of the city of Metz, and rests there. [Note: Thus it was called in the tenth century after Saint Symphorian’s relics had been translated there by Adalbero II.]

29. Blessed Arnulf succeeded him in the episcopate as twenty-ninth bishop of Metz (c. 610–625); [Note: “followed” 1.] [Note: “in the episcopate” 2.] [Note: “bishop of Metz” lacking in 1 and 3.] [PAUL. D., same place.] a man illustrious in every way, both through the light of holiness and through the splendor of his lineage. [Note: 2 reads “and through”; “and through” is omitted in 3.] He governed the Church so wisely by his teaching that he also directed the royal court by his counsel. [Note: omitted in 3.] His deeds survive, teaching that he shone with great miracles both after death and during life.

Charlemagne was his great-great-great-grandson, [Note: “was” 1.] whom the Roman Church chose as her defender and whom the emperor of Constantinople honored as lord. When he met him as he returned from Jerusalem, [Note: “returned” 1.] he devoutly bestowed upon him [Note: 1 and 3: “not devoutly”; 2: “and not undevoutly.”] a substantial portion of the thorny crown of Jesus Christ together with other relics of the apostles. [Col. 0588B] Whoever desires to know these things should read the itinerary of Charlemagne. [Note: “itinerary” 2.] [Note: To my knowledge, the book bearing this title has not been published. Compare the account of this fabulous expedition of Charles in the *Chronicle of Saint-Denis*, Bouquet V, p. 273 ff.; it is of almost the same subject, though different in many details.]

There too one reads that the emperor of Constantinople [Note: “Constantinopolitan” 3.] tested him by greed, offering exceedingly great gifts two miles from the city of Byzantium; [Note: “Bizantheos” 2, 3.] but Charles restrained his men by such discipline that they took none of the treasures offered. Accordingly, he was honored with the highest reverence among the Greeks, and very great gifts were bestowed upon him: silk, precious stones, and a great abundance of ecclesiastical ornament. [Note: 1 reads: “and gifts were bestowed upon him in silk …”] Departing from Constantinople, Charles received from the emperor a treaty of friendship [Note: “amicinarum” 2, 3; “anneuiarum” 1.] and returned safely to Francia.

When they reached Paris, he assembled a multitude of bishops and religious men from his realm, [Note: “religion” 1, 2, 3.] and by their authority decreed [Note: “stood firm” 1, 3; “that” omitted in 1.] that the day called the Day of Indulgences should be observed every year in worthy commemoration of the aforesaid relics. [Col. 0588C] [Note: “worthy remembrance” 2.] By their counsel it was also enacted [Note: “for it was enacted” 3.] that every sinful person who came there [Note: “come” 3.] should receive the remission of one third of his penance, [Note: “remission” 2; “of remission” 3.] provided he did not yield to continual delight in sins. [Note: “yield” 3.]

Charles also enlarged beyond all Frankish kings the religious endowments of churches. He consecrated to the worship of Christ the gold and silver with which the ancient kings had adorned idols. [Note: omitted in 1.] He also investigated the life of Saint Arnulf, his ancestor, [Note: 1 lacks “Saint”; 2 reads: “also [investigated] Arnulf, acts, miracles”; 3 adds after “ancestor,” “in an account.”] and was astonished not to find written in it the miracle concerning Arnulf’s ring, which fresh report still celebrated. [Col. 0589A] [Note: Cf. Paul, *SS.* II, p. 264.]

Therefore he summoned a notary named Paul and ordered the deeds of the bishops of Metz to be investigated. [Note: “and ordered” 2; 3: “he ordered that the deeds of the bishops of Metz be investigated.”] But, finding virtually none—for when the barbarians had invaded long ago [Note: “long ago” 3.] they had been burned with the city itself [Note: “itself” 2; “burned” 2.]—he ordered that at least those matters which had come down from the ancients to posterity by report should be written down, beginning with Saint Clement, the bishop himself. Among these, the very miracle is found recorded. Its substance is as follows.

The same blessed Arnulf had been count palatine under Chlothar, [Note: “Dotarius” 3.] son of King Guntram, [Note: “Gontranius” 2; “Goncianus” 3.] governing six provinces at his own discretion. He had fought many battles and had even exercised justice upon his own relatives. [Note: “increased” 3.] [PAUL. D.] [Note: These matters derive from Paul, though the language is altered and certain details have been added, perhaps already by another writer.] Therefore, because it is characteristic of good men to fear penance even in matters that are permitted, he acted, like David, in contrition of heart before God. [Col. 0589B] [Note: 1 lacks from “in the sight” through “contrition of mind.”]

While in this contrition of mind he was crossing the bridge of the river Moselle at Trier, he threw into the waters the ring which he had with him, saying: “Then shall I know that I am released from the bonds of sins, when I receive again this ring which I cast away.” Afterwards, [Note: “after these things” 3.] when he had been elevated to the bishopric of Metz by the force of the people, just as David, by God’s command, withdrew himself from building the Temple because of the shedding of blood, [Note: “commanded” 2.] so this man of God, after receiving the ring from a fisherman in the Vosges—the ring having been found in the entrails [Note: “excis” 1, 2; “picis” 2.] of a fish—left the episcopate and all worldly glory [Note: “his glory” 3.] and sought the wilderness, [Note: Cf. *Life of St Arnulf*, ch. 21; Mabillon, *Acta ordinis S. Benedicti* II, p. 155.] where he rested in peace. [Note: 1: “where also”; 3: “where.”] [Note: “rested” 3.]

He presided over the church of Metz for fifteen years, under the apostolic bishops John, Theodore, Martin, and Eugene, while Heraclius ruled with his mother Heraclona and his son Constantine. [Col. 0589C] [Note: “emperors” 2; 3: “and another and Constantine.”] He died on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of September, [Note: “December” 2.] under Constantine, son of Heraclius. [Note: “Heraclius” 2.]

30. Saint Goericus, who was also called Abbo, [Note: 3 lacks “who was also called.”] succeeded this saint as thirtieth bishop of Metz. [Note: “bishop of Metz” 3.] He had first been king of the Aquitanians, [Note: Thus the later-written *Life of St Goericus*, *Acta SS.*, September VI, p. 28; cf. Tabouillot I, p. 384.] and afterwards, having become bishop, enriched the church of Metz with very many possessions. [Note: “church of Metz” 3.] He built a basilica for Saint Peter, [Col. 0590A] [Note: The Martyrology of Metz, 16 November, says: “Dedication of Greater Saint Peter within the house which Saint Goericus the bishop built” (Tabouillot I, p. 387); it was later called Saint-Pierre-aux-Images and was destroyed in 1755.] brought back his predecessor’s body [Note: omitted in 1; supplied after the fact in 2.] from the wilderness, and honorably buried it in the basilica of the apostles. [Note: “in the basilica of the apostles” 2.]

He presided over the Church for seventeen years, [Note: “eighteen” 1.] under the apostolic bishops Vitalian and Adeodatus, while Constantine, son [Note: “born” 3.] of the earlier King Constantine, [Note: “Constanni?” 2; “earlier” 1, 2.] reigned (c. 625–640). He died on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of October and was buried in the church of Saint Symphorian the martyr of Metz. [Note: 3 adds this marginal gloss in a fifteenth-century hand: “Outside the walls of the same city, which in the year of the Lord 1444 was also destroyed by the citizens of Metz, together with many others, because of the war of the people of the king of France, etc.”] Later his bones were translated to the castle called Spinal. [Note: Épinal. Under Bishop Theoderic I, tenth century; see *Life of Adalbero*, ch. 14, *SS.* IV, p. 662; Sigebert’s *Life of Theoderic*, ch. 12, ibid., p. 469.]

31. Godo [Note: “Dodo” 3.] came [Note: “succeeded” 2.] after him as thirty-first among the people of Metz and assumed the charge of the episcopal office. He sat for ten years [Note: 2 omits “and”; 1 adds “and ten years.”] and two months, [Note: “with” 3.] under the apostolic bishops Donus, [Note: “Domnus” 3.] Agatho, Leo, Benedict, John, Conon, [Note: “Gunnon” 1; “Conon” 3.] and Sergius, under the aforesaid Emperor Constantine [Note: omitted in 1; 3: “Constantine, aforesaid emperor.”] (c. 640–650). He died on the eighth day before the Ides of May. [Col. 0590B] [Note: 2 adds: “Buried in the church of Saint Symphorian.”]

32. Saint Glodulf, [Note: “Clodulf” 2.] the illustrious offspring of blessed Arnulf, was consecrated thirty-second bishop of Metz, in keeping with the glory of his father’s holiness. [Note: “bishop of Metz” 3.] He enriched the church of Saint Stephen with possessions. [Note: Especially through the gift of Saint Trudo; cf. *Life of Trudo*, ch. 9, in Mabillon, *Acta* II, p. 1077.] He sat for forty years [Note: 2: “forty,” corrected to “forty-two”; apparently 3 likewise.] and twenty-five days, [Note: “five,” corrected, appears to have been added in 3.] under the Roman pontiffs Sergius, John V, John VI, Sisinnius, Constantine, Gregory II, [Note: 1 lacks from “Gregory” through “Constantine.”] and under the emperors the aforesaid Constantine, Justinian the Younger, [Note: 3 lacks “Justinian the Younger, Leontius, Tiberius, likewise Justinian.”] Leontius, Tiberius, the same Justinian mentioned above, Philippicus, and Anastasius II [Note: erased in 2.] (c. 650–690). He died on the sixth day before the Ides of June; [Note: “July” 1, 3.] he was buried in the church of the apostles, where his father had been buried. [Note: “was buried there” 3.]

33. After him Abbo was called as thirty-third to govern the faithful people of Metz. [Note: “govern” 1.] He sat for ten years, under Pope Gregory III, while Theodosius and Leo were emperors (c. 690–700). [Col. 0590C] [Note: “while [one] emperor ruled” 1.] He died on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of May. [Note: omitted in 1.]

34. Aptadius succeeded as thirty-fourth. He sat for thirteen years, [Note: The catalogue of bishops, *SS.* II, p. 268, has seven years.] under Pope Zacharias, while Constantine V was emperor (c. 700 ff.). He died on the twelfth day before the Kalends of February. [Note: “Fabruary” 3.] [Note: 2 adds: “Buried in the church of Saint Symphorian.”]

35. Felix, the thirty-fifth bishop, presided over the people of Metz [Col. 0591A] for nine months, [Note: 2 puts “bishop of Metz” before “Felix”; 3: “presides over the people of Metz.”] under the aforesaid Pope Zacharias. He died on the eleventh day before the Kalends of January, while the aforesaid Constantine was emperor. [Note: 2 adds: “Buried at Saint Symphorian.”]

36. Sigibald [Note: He is named in a charter of Wulfoald assigned to 708; Bréquigny, *Chartae* I, p. 381.] presided over the church of Metz as thirty-sixth for twenty-five years, under the apostolic bishops Stephen and Paul, and under the empire of the aforesaid Constantine and Leo IV (c. 708–740). [PAUL. D., same place.]

This blessed Sigibald was born of noble lineage, [Note: “born noble” 3.] enlarged the religious life of the faithful, and was wholly devoted to the welfare of God’s holy Church. He built two monasteries, Elariacum [Note: 1, in another hand above the text: “i. sce. nofor,” uncertain.] and Novum-vilare. [Note: “Villare” 1.] A cruel pain of gout afflicted him; yet, although the outward man suffered, the inward man nevertheless advanced from strength to strength, restoring the ruins of churches. And—what is greater than the powers of bodily miracles—he healed souls [Col. 0591B] troubled by diverse vices [Note: “conversant” 1.] with the medicine of preaching and example, [Note: 3 reads: “by examples he raised [them] from spiritual death through the medicine …”] and raised them from spiritual death. And if such gifts are granted to a man, do you suppose that, if the faith of those present had required it, healing from bodily diseases would have been lacking? He died on the seventh day before the Kalends of November. He was buried in the church of blessed Symphorian the martyr in the suburb of Metz. [Note: 3: “in the church of Saint Symphorian near Metz.”] [Note: His relics were found there in 1107; Tabouillot I, p. 448.]

37. After him the distinguished man Grodegang, worthy to be extolled with every praise, [Note: 1: “distinguished … worthy of praise”; “Grodegandus” 2; “Chrodegangus” 3.] was chosen bishop. He was from the district of Hasbania, [Note: “Hasdenia” 3.] born of the foremost nobility of the Franks, his father being Sigramnus and his mother Landrada. [Note: “Ludrada” 1; “Laudrada?” 2, 3.] He was reared in the court of Charles the Mayor and served as that ruler’s referendary. [Note: “Refredarius” 1.] At length, in the time of Pippin (741), whom the above-mentioned Pope Zacharias [Note: omitted in 3.] consecrated king of the Franks [Note: “Fransis” 2.] after Childeric had been deposed, he attained the pontifical dignity of the church of Metz as its thirty-seventh bishop.

He was altogether most illustrious and resplendent with every kind of nobility, [Note: “choruscus” 2; “choruscens” 3.] handsome in appearance, most eloquent in speech, trained both in his native tongue and in Latin; [Note: “also” omitted in 2; “is trained” 1, 2.] a nourisher of God’s servants [Note: 1: “of nourishers, orphans.”] and not merely a provider for orphans and widows [Note: “widows” 2.] but also their most merciful protector. [Note: “more lofty” 1; “also” omitted in 3.]

Since he was richly endowed in every respect, [Note: “locuplex” 1, 2.] he was singled out by King Pippin and the entire body of the Franks and sent to Rome; and he summoned the venerable Pope Stephen to Gaul, as everyone fervently desired. [Note: “hanhelabant” 1; “annelabant” 2.] [Cf. *Annales Laurissenses minores.*] This Stephen, the third of that name in the papal succession, [Col. 0592A] blessed Pippin’s two sons, Charlemagne and his brother Carloman, as kings of the Franks. [Note: 3: “his brother.”]

This same Grodegang [Note: “Grodegandus” 2.] assembled the clergy [Note: 2: “the clergy [from] clergy.”] and caused them to live within the enclosure of the cloisters after the model of a monastic community. He established for them a rule governing how [Note: “as if” 3.] they ought to serve in the Church. [Note: “to serve” 3.] He generously supplied them with provisions and the necessities of life [Note: *subsidia* is omitted in 1, 2, 3.] so that, free from want and not occupied with perishable concerns, [Note: “not” 1.] they might keep watch solely for divine services. He also instructed this clergy, abundantly trained in divine law and Roman chant, to preserve the custom and order of the Roman Church—something never done in the church of Metz up to that time. [Note: 1: “was done at Metz”; 3: “was done at Metz.”]

With the aid of King Pippin he ordered the fabric of the church of Saint Stephen the proto-martyr to be built, together with its altar, [Col. 0592B] screens, presbytery, [Note: “prbm.” 2; 1 adds “he ordered [it] to be made”; 3 omits “and arches.”] and surrounding arches. Likewise, [Note: omitted in 3.] he ordered a presbytery to be made in the greater church of Saint Peter. [Note: “greater” 1; “larger” 3.] He also constructed an ambo adorned with gold and silver [Note: “and silver” 3.] and arches around the throne before that altar.

Moreover, in the parish of Saint Stephen, in the district of the Moselle, [Note: “perrochia” 2; “Mosolensis” 3.] he built a monastery in honor of the most blessed [Note: “saint” 3.] Apostle Peter. He endowed it with great wealth, established monks there, and united them in one love under the Rule of Saint Benedict the Father. [Note: 3 reads: “united [them] in the way.”] He also built another monastery called Gorze, [Note: “Gorgia” 1, and so below.] where in like manner he assembled a considerable multitude of monks. [Note: “a multitude” 3.]

Finally, he requested from Paul, bishop of Rome, three bodies of holy martyrs: namely, [Note: “that is, martyrs” 3.] Gorgonius, who rests at Gorze; [Col. 0592C] Nabor, [Note: 3 omits “and … where Saint Nabor.”] whose body was deposited in the monastery of Hilariacum; [Note: “Hyliriacum” 1; “Hylariacum” 2.] and blessed Nazarius, whom he placed beyond the river Rhine in the monastery called Lorsch, in a basilica of wonderful beauty built in honor of that martyr. [Note: “and of blessed” omitted in 2; “of the martyr” omitted in 3; 1, 2 have “basilica,” and 2 adds “placed.”]

The estate was formerly handed over to the said Bishop Grodegang, for Saint Stephen’s portion, by the religious woman Chilliswindis [Note: “Chillisrundis” 2; “Chiliscundis” 3.] and her son Cangro. [Note: “Sangro” 1.] This blessed man was lavish in almsgiving, most pure in charity, [Note: “most pious” 1, 3.] and a receiver of guests and pilgrims. [Note: “and” 3.] But because it would be lengthy to recount in order the good deeds which he performed, [Note: “whatever” 2; 3: “to recount in order.”] let it suffice to have sampled these few out of the many.

He consecrated very many bishops in diverse cities, and likewise priests, [Col. 0593A] deacons, [Note: omitted in 3.] and the remaining ecclesiastical orders, according to the custom [Note: “custom” 3.] of the Roman Church, on the Ember Saturdays of the four seasons of the year. He governed the church of Metz for twenty-three years, while the Romans Irene, [Note: “Hyrini” 1; “Hyrin” 2.] after the death of her son Constantine, Nicephorus, Stauracius, and Michael were emperors. He died on the day before the Nones of March, in the days of Pippin, [Note: “Pippin at this point” 1.] father of Charlemagne, [Note: “the Great” 2.] and Carloman, his brother. [Note: “his own” 3.] He rests at Gorze, in the monastery which, after Bishop Saint Clement of Metz, he built up from small beginnings into greatness from its foundations (766). [Note: “rested” 1.] [Note: Cf. *Account of the Foundation of the Monastery of Gorze*, Calmet, *Proofs* I, p. 293.]

Source preparation: Exact canonical local source; no recovery placeholders.

38. [Compare the Catalogue of Bishops.] This distinguished man was succeeded by Lord Angerannus, thirty-eighth in order (768). [Variant: *augerannus* in witnesses 1 and 3.] He was archchaplain of the palace of Charlemagne. [Variants: *archipellanus* in witnesses 1, 2, and 3.] In his time the imperial authority was transferred from the Greeks to the Frankish kings, reportedly in the following manner. [Editorial note: I have been unable to discover which author the writer followed here. The events are remarkably confused.]

Leo III, an emperor by name, among his other crimes caused the sacred images to be abolished and broken, failing to consider that an image is the memorial of the one whose worship belongs to religion. For just as the idols of the pagans are detestable as memorials of abominable beings, so the images of the saints are venerable because of their memory. [Variants: *atendens* for *attendens*; *cui* for *cujus*; *ab eorum* and *ab eorum memoria* for *ob eorum memoriam*.]

Hence, condemned by a general council [some witnesses omit “by a general council”; one has “by a deliberation”], made hateful to the faithful, and disfigured in the beauty of his countenance, he was thrust into a monastery after he had reigned for three years. [Variant: *i. a.*—apparently “three years”—in witness 1.]

The Romans, filled with the zeal of fury, seized Pope Leo and wished to deprive him of his eyes, but they could not wholly extinguish his sight. [Variant: *extingere* for *extinguere*.] Fleeing to Charles, he was honourably received by him and, brought back to Rome with the power of an army, was restored to his see. Therefore Charlemagne was anointed emperor by that same pope in the church of Saint Peter on the day of the Lord’s Nativity, in the year 801 from the Lord’s Incarnation, in the ninth indiction. [Variant: *inventus* for *unctus*; one witness gives “the ninth indiction, where after it has been added: June.”]

[Compare the Catalogue of Bishops.] Among his other good deeds, the aforesaid Angerannus built the monastery of Novae Cellae, in which he also rests. He governed the bishopric for twenty-three years, under the apostolic lords Adrian, the aforesaid Leo, and Stephen III. He died on the eighth day before the Kalends of November—that is, 25 October (791). [One witness reads December.]

39. After him Gundulfus was raised up as the thirty-ninth bishop of Metz, venerable in manner of life and faith. [Variants: *gondulphus* in witnesses 2 and 3.] He sat for six years, in the time of Charlemagne, under the apostolic lords Paschal and Eugenius (818–824). [Editorial note: This is false. The writer seems not to have noticed that the bishopric remained vacant for twenty-seven years; see *Catalogue of Bishops* II, p. 269.] He died on the seventh day before the Ides of September—that is, 7 September. [One witness omits “seventh.”]

40. After him Drogo, son of the emperor Charlemagne, ascended as the fortieth to the summit of the priesthood of the church of Metz. [One witness reads “he ascended the fortieth”; another has “to the fortieth.”] He sat for thirty-two years, under the apostolic lords Valentine, Gregory IV, and Sergius (824–855). He was elevated to the dignity of an archbishopric and served as administrator of the sacred palace. [Variant: “to the honour of an archbishopric.”] He raised from the earth the body of the virgin Saint Glodesindis (830).

[Marginal addition in a fifteenth-century hand: “Here also he transferred the body of the blessed Celestius II, the second bishop after the blessed Clement, to Alsace, to the monastery of Maurus, where it too is worthily venerated.”]

He performed many magnificent deeds, as one who exercised apostolic authority throughout all Gaul on this side of the Alps. [One witness reads *cysapes*.] He died in Burgundy on the sixth day before the Ides of November—that is, 8 November. His body, brought back from there, is buried in the church of Saint John the Evangelist at Metz [variants: *metis*, *metis*], that is, in the monastery of Saint Arnulf, where his brother, the emperor Louis the Pious, also rests happily with his mother, Queen Hildegard. [One witness omits “happily.”]

41. Adventius, forty-first, succeeded him in the bishopric (855), born at Metz from a family of rather free or distinguished rank. [Variant: *liberiore* for *liberiori*; *ortus* for *natus*.] He enlarged the church of Saint Stephen with ornaments and treasures.

In his time Hincmar was archbishop of Rheims; he and Adventius crowned Charles at Metz after Charles’s brother Lothar had been slain by divine judgement (869). [Variants: *hincimiarus*; *Mettim* and *meti*; *Lotario*.] Adventius sat for seventeen years, under the apostolic lords Leo IV, Benedict, and Nicholas. Nicholas condemned Theutgaud, archbishop of Trier, and Gunther, archbishop of Cologne, supporters of King Lothar’s adultery, and annulled the council which they had held at Metz. [Variants: *tieg.* for *Thiegaudum*; “archbishop of Cologne” appears in witness 2; *consiliumque* for *conciliumque*; *tenuerat* for *tenuerant*; *cessavit* for *cassavit*.]

The aforesaid Adventius was buried at Metz in the chapel of Saint Gall; he died on the second day before the Kalends of October—that is, 30 September (875), at the estate called Sault [editorial identification: Sault], under Pope Adrian II. [One witness reads: “He died on the third day”; another adds that he was buried on 30 September.]

42. After him Walo was elected as the forty-second bishop (876). [Variants: *valo*; one manuscript adds, after “after him,” *Wallo*.] He sat for six years and fifteen days, under the apostolic lords Gregory V and John VII, from whom he also obtained the pallium. [Compare the diploma of John in Hontheim, *Historia Trevirensis* I, p. 217; compare also *Gesta Treverorum*, chapter 27, *Monumenta Germaniae Historica*, *Scriptores* VIII, p. 165.]

While Walo, with his men and unequal forces, was fighting against the Northmen, who were then ravaging Gaul, he was cut down on the third day before the Nones of April—that is, 3 April (882). [Variant: *normamnos* for *Normannos*; *pugnabat* for *pugnat*. Compare Regino’s *Chronicle* for the year 882.] Brought back to Metz, he was buried in the church of the Saviour, which he himself had built. [One witness reads “the church of Saint Saviour”; another omits “which he himself had built.”]

[Col. 0595A]

43. Lord Robert, reformer of monasteries and of the city walls, succeeded him as the forty-third. [One witness omits “and of the city walls.”] He sat for thirty-four years [one witness reads thirty-three], under the apostolic lords Leo V and John VII, in the times of the younger kings Carloman, Louis, and Charles (883–916). Robert was of distinguished Alemannic lineage [one variant reads “was distinguished in lineage”]; he obtained the pallium from the Roman pope. He either altered or renewed many of the ornaments of the monasteries [one witness omits “or”], together with the walls that had collapsed through age. [One witness reads “he arranged” for “he renewed.”] He died on the fourth day before the Nones of January—that is, 2 January—and was buried in the church of Saint Gall. [One witness reads “and is buried.”]

44. Wigericus, forty-fourth, succeeded Robert. He sat for ten years and thirty days. He died at Metz on the Kalends of March (916–927). [One witness reads “the eleventh day before the Kalends.”]

In his time Leo VII, Benedict IV, and Gregory VI successively governed the Roman Church. In their time the Hungarians, ravaging Gaul for the second time, reduced many cities and churches to ashes, and the relics of many saints were transferred from place to place. [Variant: *plurimorum* for *plurium*. Compare the *Annals of Saint Vincent of Metz*, *SS.* III, p. 157.] In their time Arnulf was reigning.

45. The forty-fifth, Lord Adelbero of blessed memory, succeeded Wigericus. [Editorial note: The author has omitted Benno.] Among many other things, he rebuilt the almost ruined monastery of Gorze with estates and buildings and enclosed it with a wall. [Variant: *calapsum* for *collapsum*. See Adelbero’s charter in Calmet I, *Preuves*, p. 338.] In like manner he provided many benefits for the church of Saint Arnulf at Metz. [Variants: *metim*, *Meten*; *comoda*, *commodo*. See the same work, pp. 346, 349.]

He sat for thirty-five years, nine months, and twenty-five days, under the apostolic lords John VII, John VIII, and Leo VII (929–964), while Zentebodo and [lacuna] were reigning. [The supplied text has a lacuna after “and”; witnesses variously omit or alter the following words.] He died on the sixth day before the Kalends of May—that is, 26 April. At Gorze he awaits the day of resurrection. [One witness reads “and at Gorze”; another adds “he died.”]

[Col. 0595C]

46. Theodericus, forty-sixth, succeeded to the episcopal mitre. He honourably built the monastery of Saint Vincent the Martyr in the suburb of Metz and adorned it with many pledges—relics—of saints, which he had brought with him from Italy. His deeds are recorded. [Editorial note: They were written by Sigebert; see *SS.* IV, p. 462 ff.]

He flourished under the first Emperor Otto, son of Henry, king of the Lotharingians, under the apostolic lords Leo VIII and Stephen V (964–984). [Variants: *octone*, *Othone*; *lotaringiorum*, *lothor.*; *sr*, an abbreviation for *super*, “under.”]

While the aforesaid Otto [editorial note: Otto II] was ruling, a famous battle took place in Calabria between him and the Saracens (982), in which an innumerable multitude of Christians conquered by dying, on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of August—that is, 16 July. [Variants: *kalabria*; *sarazenos*; *multitudo innumerabilis*. See Giesebrecht, *Jahrbücher* II.1, p. 77.]

A vision of this kind was divinely revealed to the blessed bishop Odelricus of Bavaria. [Editorial note: These matters are plainly very confused. Udalricus died in 973. What is reported concerning a victory gained on Saint Lawrence’s Day pertains to the battle against the Hungarians fought at Augsburg in 955.]

He seemed to see God, the just Judge, in the form of Jesus Christ, seated upon a lofty throne, with all the order of heaven standing around. A weighing in the balance was prepared; the question was debated to whom victory would yield, to the heathen or to one who professes Christ. The iniquity and sin of the Christians had grown to such a point that they were judged deserving of subjection to the sword of the Saracens.

Awakening, the holy priest made the vision known to the whole army. They therefore devoted themselves alike to prayers and fasts, placing the hope of their salvation in pure confession. Meanwhile a multitude of common people, crushed by hunger and want, withdrew themselves from the army and resolved to fight the Saracens, preferring to perish by the sword rather than by hunger. Divine mercy, ever providing for the salvation of souls, permitted them to be killed at that time, foreseeing that the glory of eternal rest would be granted them.

When this lamentable slaughter of the common people had taken place, unknown to the royal army, the blessed bishop Odelricus was again caught up in vision. Once more, as at first, he saw our Redeemer and Judge upon the throne. His glorious mother Mary, together with the whole order of heavenly beings, was beseeching him not to allow those who confessed their offences to be punished by a heathen triumph.

The balance was set up a second time, and the equality of both parties, faithful and unbelieving, was considered. The repentance of the faithful, proceeding from the groaning of the heart, outweighed the justice of the natural law.

Behold, Saint Lawrence the martyr was also present, whose feast day was imminent. Representing the cruelty of the torments consummated in himself and the compassion of his faithful peoples, he obtained victory for the faithful people together with the heavenly company.

The priest therefore swiftly sent a messenger to the emperor and ordered him to engage the enemy. When battle had been joined under the invocation of Christ and his martyr Lawrence, the enemies turned their backs; faith was strengthened and impiety weakened. From that time the feast of Saint Lawrence has been celebrated more solemnly.

47. His kinsman Adelbero succeeded him as the forty-seventh bishop of Metz; much honourable material is read concerning him. [Editorial note: His *Life*, written by Constantine, was published in *SS.* IV, p. 659 ff.] Above all, he renewed the monastery of Saint Symphorian the martyr, and he himself brought other monasteries, merely begun by his predecessors, to completion. [Variants: *S. m.*; *suisa* and *a predecessoribus*.]

Whoever wishes to know his deeds should deign to read what has been written concerning him. He sat for twenty-eight years. [Editorial note: He governed the Church for only twenty-one years.] He served under the apostolic lords John, Leo, and Stephen V (984–1005). He died on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of January—that is, 15 December—while Henry I was reigning. [Editorial note: He seems to mean Henry II as king and Henry I as emperor; compare chapter 49. Variants: *hinrico*, *hyncrico*.]

He was buried in the church of Saint Symphorian, where the bishops Saint Epletius, Papolus, Godo, Aptatus or Optatus, and Felix—distinguished in merit—also rest. [Variant: *eplitius* or *eplicius* for *Epletius*; one witness adds Goericus after Papolus; *requiescunt* for *quiescunt*.]

48. Theodericus, forty-eighth, ascended to the bishopric after him (1006). He built the principal monastery of the city for Saint Stephen the Protomartyr (1014), having acquired the saint’s arm from the city of Besançon.

During the considerable discord between himself and Emperor Henry, he distributed many ecclesiastical estates as assistance over ten years (1007–1017), as the succession of modern writers reports. [Variant: *dissensio* for *dissensione*.] He ruled the see with power for thirty years, under the apostolic lords Marinus, Agapitus, and Octavian. [Variant: *Octavianus* for *Octovianus*.]

He died on the second day before the Kalends of May—that is, 30 April (1046). He was buried at Metz. [A later hand supplies: “He was buried in the church of Saint Stephen.”] In his time Abbot Guarinus built a basilica for Saint Arnulf, which Saint Leo IX dedicated (1049) and elevated by his privilege. [Variants: *Garinus*; *sancto Arnulfo*; *Alnulpho*.]

[A fifteenth-century note adds: “Namely, in honour of Saint John the Evangelist and all the Apostles and Saint Arnulf, bishop and confessor, in the year 1049 from the Lord’s Incarnation, in the presence of three metropolitans and six bishops, as well as the princes of the whole realm and an innumerable multitude, as is recorded for that day, namely 2 October, in the martyrology of the said church.”]

[Editorial note: On Leo’s charter, see Tabouillot II, p. 138.]

49. Adelbero, forty-ninth, distinguished by holiness and venerable religious devotion, succeeded him (1046). He was a lover of peace and a restorer of monasteries.

In his time the Roman Church was governed by Saint Leo IX, formerly bishop of Toul; by Stephen, also called Frederick, brother of Duke Gocelo; and by Alexander, whom Hildebrand succeeded, he who is called Gregory VII. [Variants: *leuchorum*; *Fredericus*; *Gocelonis*.]

Adelbero enlarged with his own estates the church of Saint Saviour within the city (1070), in which he rests. [Compare Tabouillot II, p. 169.] He died on the Ides of November (1072), while Henry was reigning after Conrad. [Editorial note: Henry III as king and Henry II as emperor is meant. One witness omits “second.”]

[Col. 0598A]

50. Thereupon Lord Herimannus was summoned from the church of Liège and ordained the fiftieth bishop of Metz. At this time a very great schism arose between royal power and the priesthood. Thus king was set against king, pope against pope. This persisted for a long time, after which it declined from its former vitality. [The Latin is uncertain at this point: *ex quo discubuit a sua vivacitate*.]

Bishop Herimannus, admonished by a vision, raised Saint Clement, the first teacher of Metz, from the earth (1090), and died on the third day. [Editorial note: Compare Hugh of Flavigny, *SS.* VIII, p. 472.]

When the blessed Clement had been brought to the mother church, he delighted the peoples with great miracles for three days. After the bishop’s death, he displayed no signs for two days. Therefore the astonished citizens became sad; but joy soon returned, and the reason was disclosed.

For it was revealed to a certain religious man named Lubricus, founder of the church of Saint Peter of Mont Briancy [editorial identification: Pierremont, said to have been founded in 1096], that during that delay in the miracles Saint Clement had fought most fiercely before Christ’s tribunal with the devil for the soul of the aforesaid deceased bishop.

The enemy alleged against him that, through fear of death, he had acted inconstantly amid the dissension between royal power and the priesthood, fleeing persecutions and invasions of his own church, and had violated the oath which by imperial custom is required to be sworn beforehand. [The transmitted wording is corrupt: one edition places *fuga* before *persecutiones*; witnesses give forms meaning “persecution,” “provision,” or “violation of the oath.”]

But the blessed shepherd Clement, taking up the cause of his vicar, on bended knee poured forth most devout prayers to the Most Merciful One for each matter of the judgement. What more need be said? The divine sentence, moved by the supplication of its priest, granted pardon and, with a curse, commanded silence to the accuser. [Variants concern whether *maledicto* modifies the command or the accuser; witnesses read forms meaning “cursed,” “to the accuser,” or “a curse.”]

Yet although there is no delay in the efficacy of divine power, nevertheless, because the essence of the Trinity judges all things in the person of Christ’s humanity, delays are said to take place according to the order of the dispensation. [One witness reads “indicates” for “judges.”]

This Bishop Herimannus, taken from the church of Liège, was buried in the church of Saint Peter at Metz, while Gregory VII presided over the universal Church and the empire was tottering. [One witness adds “or wavering.”] He died on the fourth day before the Nones of May—that is, 4 May—and the bishopric of Metz remained vacant for many years.

51. [A rubric in manuscript 3 adds: “After the translation of blessed Clement, the first bishop after the aforesaid bishop.”]

Therefore, while the sea of the age was tossing, as it were, under the south-west wind and the north wind [variants describe it as “tossing,” “blowing,” or “fluctuating”], the Catholic people of Metz, setting imperial terror aside, chose as bishop Lord Popo, a noble person from the church of Trier and one in agreement with the Catholics (1090). His consecration was performed by the legate of the Apostolic See. [Compare Bernold’s *Chronicle* for 1093, *SS.* V, p. 456.]

When the imperial power sought to introduce another—namely Adelbero [marginal addition in a later hand]—the people of Metz resisted with steadfast faith. As they had formerly expelled the two intruders Bruno and Gualo, so too they deposed the third, Adelbero, who had been excommunicated, not without much labour and danger to their possessions. [Editorial note: Adalbero was deposed by the pope at the Council of Rheims in 1115.]

In this struggle Lord Adelbero was like an undaunted standard-bearer and fearless in every conflict. Later the glorious archbishop of Trier [editorial note: elected in 1131 and confirmed in 1132], promoted step by step, had served in the armies of the Church from his very childhood for the Catholic faith, until he won for the Church from schism the trophy of peace. [One witness omits “glorious.” Another identifies him as Adelbero, archbishop of Trier.]

After Lord Popo’s death (1103), who had been a kindly provider for the clergy of his time, they received as bishop, for the course of his life and without prejudice to the privilege of the church of Trier, the magnificent and noble Lord Stephen, summoned from the archbishopric of Vienne, consecrated with apostolic blessing in Rome and honoured with the dignity of the pallium (1120). [Editorial note: This was not after Popo’s death in 1103. Stephen became bishop after Adelbero’s deposition in 1116 and the death in 1120 of Theotger, Adelbero’s successor. Compare the continuation of the *Gesta Treverorum*, chapter 23, *SS.* VIII, p. 196.]

Since he still flourishes in life and vigour of age, let the temptation of pride arising from the pest of flattery be silent, and let prayers be offered to God for the unceasing course of his labours. [One witness omits the entire sentence beginning “Who, since…”.]

## First Continuation

[Col. 0599]

1. [Note: “Fifty-second,” namely bishop; manuscript 1 adds “bishop,” and manuscript 3 adds “the eleventh,” referring to chapter 51.]

Lord Stephen succeeded Lord Popo in the year of the Lord 1120, namely in the second year of Pope Calixtus. Popo was illustrious by descent both from Burgundians and Lotharingians, but more illustrious in virtue and nobility of spirit. Stephen was Calixtus’s nephew through his sister. [Editorial note: Thus the continuation of the *Gesta Treverorum*. Stephen was the son of Count Theoderic of Bar and Ermentrude.]

Although he had not yet received the regalia from Henry V, who then held the citadel of imperial power, while the schism between royal power and the priesthood still continued, he was consecrated in Rome by that same supreme pontiff and honoured both with the dignity of the pallium and with the title of cardinal. [The manuscript wording is uncertain around *nondum* and *recepisset*.]

Excluded from the city of Metz for two years and more because he did not yet possess the favour of the aforesaid prince, he celebrated his first ordinations in the place called Saint-Quentin-Mount [editorial identification: St-Quentin]. By the aid of his brother, Count Reinald of Bar, and of his other kinsmen and friends, he recovered with remarkable speed all the estates of the bishopric which tyrants had occupied, except Rumilly. [Variants: *Rumiliaco*, *ruiuiliaco*, *rumuliaco*; editorial identification: Rumilly.]

In the first freshness of his advancement, he destroyed and levelled with strong hand the castle of Terli [variants: *cerli*, *terli*; editorial identification uncertain], which was very harmful to travellers passing through those regions; the duke’s castle near Vic; the fortress situated in the marshy place between Vic and Marsal; and the castle of the count of Hoembure, adjoining Marsal, which had long been burdensome and damaging to the whole town. [Variants: *tran­s­euntibus*, *trans­eantibus*; *partes*, *pertes*; *Hoembure*, *Hoemborc*, *Homborc*. Editorial identification: Moyen-Vic; compare Tabouillot II, p. 212, which treats these places more precisely.]

Later, having gained imperial favour and continually ascending from strength to strength, he fortified the castle called Ramberti-villare [editorial identification: Remberviller]. He granted to Saint Stephen the noble castle of Lucelnburch [variants: *lucelborc*, *lucemborc*], which had descended to him by hereditary right. [Editorial note: This seems not to be the well-known castle of Luxembourg, but Lutzelburg near Pfalzburg.] With the aid of the emperor Frederick, he acquired for himself and his successors, to hold freely for ever, the castle of Hoembure, which had descended from him by feudal right but had been occupied by the duke of Lorraine after the death of Count Hugh. [One witness reads “with the aid of his father.”]

He also acquired in perpetuity for himself and his church the castle of Viviers, the duke of Lemburc’s share in the castle of Rucei [variants: *rucey*, *ruceij*; editorial identification: Roucy], with all its appurtenances, and the dependencies of Asperimont [editorial identification: Deneuvre and Apremont]. He likewise acquired the castles of Mirabel and Falconismont [editorial identifications: Mirebaux and Fauquemont].

He bravely subdued the rebellions of Danubrium [variants: *Danubii*; one witness omits the name], after strengthening fortifications in front of those castles. At Épinal he regained by powerful force from the duke the tower called Moronis [variant: *Morronis*]. Much later, because of the advocate’s insolence and unrestrained excesses, with Duke Matthew’s help he besieged and captured the upper castle.

Then the duke, in recompense for this service, received from him by feudal right the advocacy of Épinal. Conversely, the duke freely granted to Saint Stephen of Metz, to hold peacefully for ever, the allod which he possessed at Vic. [One witness reads “and every allod.”]

This venerable bishop also besieged the castle called Petra-pertusata [editorial identification: Pierre-Percée] for a full year and more, after strengthening three forts around it, traces of which remain visible to this day, and finally compelled it to surrender. When grave injuries had repeatedly been inflicted through the castle of Deulewart [variants: *deuluuart*, *deulouwart*], he at length took it by assault and reduced it to ashes and cinders.

Likewise, he destroyed and overthrew the fortified tower at Tihecurt [variants: *tyhecurt*, *thiecurt*, *tiheycort*; editorial identification: Thiaucourt] and the castle situated at the place called Walter’s Mount [editorial identification: Watimont], because they grievously harassed the bishopric. [One witness omits “situated in the place.”]

Nor should it be omitted among his outstanding deeds that, at a certain time when the duke was making war upon him, he courageously besieged the duke’s castle of Prinei [variant: *Priney*; editorial identification: Preney according to Bouquillon, but Perny according to Tabouillot II, p. 269]. He would undoubtedly have captured it when its walls had already been breached, had his brother, the count of Bar, not impeded the victory already prepared and imminent. If I wished to enumerate and set forth in writing his illustrious deeds, worthy of annals, parchment would fail before material did. [One witness reads *membrana*; the reading is secure.]

After sitting for forty-three years, under the apostolic lords Calixtus, Honorius, Innocent, Celestine, Lucius, Eugenius, Anastasius, and Adrian, and under the Roman rulers Henry V, Lothar, Conrad, and Frederick, he departed to the Lord on the third day before the Kalends of January—that is, 30 December—full of years and merits, as a Catholic during the schism of Alexander and Victor, which had already begun (1163). [One witness reads four days; another gives “Victor of Alexandria.” Editorial note: He had earlier been a follower of Pope Victor; see Alexander’s letter 165 in Martène, *Collectio* II, p. 780.]

He deserved to be buried beside the entrance to the choir, on its right-hand side.

2. [Note: “Fifty-third” in one witness; another reads “third.”]

In the year of the Lord 1164 Lord Theodericus succeeded him, son of his brother the count of Bar, truly close to him both in character and blood. His greatest concern and special care was that, under him, the audacity both of robbers and thieves should be restrained by fear of justice; that innocence should be safe among the wicked; and that, where malice had been accustomed to rule, the power to do evil should be curbed. [One witness omits the clause from “the audacity” through “had been accustomed.”]

He provided with such diligence for the peace and tranquillity of the churches and for the interests of all his creditors that soldiers, clergy, and people revered him as a lord and loved him as a father. Prudently and skilfully forestalling the evils and injuries which might daily have been inflicted upon the bishopric through the castle of Habundanges, should any other powerful man have obtained it, he acquired it for himself and his successors and built there a splendid residence. [Editorial identification: Habondange, between Morhange and Château-Salins.]

He also acquired for himself and his descendants Werinesperc [variants: *Winiperch*, *Winispere*, *Wermnesperc*; editorial identification: Varnesberg] and Radonis-villa [editorial note: perhaps Raville]. He made the castle of Conflans [editorial identification: Conflans-en-Jarnisy] secure by a firm settlement and adorned it with a noble palace. [One witness reads “he restored it more securely.”]

When the cardinals of Octavian the heresiarch entered the city of Metz with the emperor’s messenger in great pomp and wished to compel the entire clergy to swear an oath of obedience to their idol, he bravely resisted them to their face. Their business—the purpose for which they had come—was completely undone, and he made them depart with shame and utter confusion. As a result, very many cities of the empire took from his deed an example of emulable virtue and the courage likewise to despise them. [Variants concern *imperatoris*, “of the emperor,” and *pompose*, “with pomp.”]

He sat for nine years and seven months. [Editorial note: He sat for only seven years.] He served under the supreme pontiff Alexander III, while Frederick was emperor. Because of the dangers threatened by the still-continuing schism, he feared to ascend to priestly rank and episcopal consecration. Thus, only elected and a deacon, armed with the shield of faith amid all the storms and tempests of that great schism, he died as a Catholic on the third day before the Ides of August—that is, 11 August (1171).

Only the entrance of the choir separates his sarcophagus from the burial-place of Lord Stephen, his predecessor and uncle, so that those whom affection and blood had joined in life might be separated in death only by the small distance between their places.
