### First Continuation, 1–2

**1. Stephen.** The heading reads “Fifty-second,” namely bishop; witness 1 adds `episcopus`, and 3 adds `11us (v. c. 51 n. I.)`, “eleventh (see chapter 51, note I).” `burgundiorum` (2), Burgundians; `lothoringiorum` (3), Lotharingians. Editorial note: “Thus the continuation of the *Gesta Treverorum*. Stephen was son of Count Theoderic of Bar and Ermentrude.” *nondum*, “not yet,” is omitted in 3, while 2 reads `nundum`; `resepiscet` (3), a corrupt form for “had received”; `h. est` (3), “was honoured.” Editorial note on the text: “I judged that `a civitate Metensi` should be written thus in this place with all the codices.” `ruiuiliaco` (3), `rumuliaco` (2), Rumilly; editorial identification: Rumilly; `accepto` (3), “received,” for “excepted”; editorial note: Count Reinald [of Bar].

`cerli` (1, 2, 3, Chesn.), the Terli castle-name, corrected by a recent hand in 2 to `terli`; `transeantibus` (2), “passing”; `pertes` (3), “parts”; `marcellum` (2), Marsal; editorial identification: Moyen-Vic, with “compare Tabouillot II, p. 212, which discusses these places more exactly.” `hoemborc` (2), `homborc` (3), Hoembure; `marsello` (2), Marsal; `honerosum` (2), burdensome. Editorial note: Ramberviller. `lucelborc` (2), `lucemborc` (3), Lucelnburch; editorial note: “Apparently not the famous castle of Luxembourg, but Lutzelburg near Pfalzburg.” `patris` (2), “of his father”; 1 and Chesn. transpose *adquisivit omni aevo libere tenendum*, “acquired [it] to be held freely for all time” (apparatus `acq. o. e l. t.`) `lamburc` (1), `lamborc` (3), Lemburc; `rucey` (2), `ruceij` (Chesn.), Rucei; editorial identification: Roucy; `omnibus suis` (1), “all his [appurtenances],” and Chesn. `omnibus ap. s.`, “all appurtenances”; editorial note: Deneuvre and Apremont. Editorial identifications: Mirebaux and Fauquemont.

`danubii` (1), “of the Danube/Danubrium,” and 3 omits the name; `morronis` (Chesn.), Moronis; `occessus` (3), excesses; `et omni` (2), “and for all time.” `q. d. petra percusata` (3), “which is called pierced rock”; editorial identification: Pierre-Percée; `depulit` (1), “drove [it] out,” for “compelled [it]”; `de deuluuart` (1), `deulouwart` (3), Deulewart; `tyhecurt` (1), `thiecurt` (2), `tiheycort` (3), Tihecurt; editorial identification: Thiaucourt; 3 omits `in loco`, “in the place”; editorial identification: Watimont; 2 has `q; (que)`, the “and” form, against *quia*, “because”; 2 transposes *eximia gesta ejus*, “the outstanding deeds of his” (apparatus `eximia g. ei.`); `guerram` (1), `guerwerram` (3), war; `priney` (3), Prinei; editorial note: “Preney, Bouquillon; but Tabouillot II, p. 269, calls it Perny.” 3 omits `muris`, “with walls”; `peforans` (3), “piercing”; `trater`, a corrupt form, “brother”; `membrana` (1, 2), parchment; `adriane` (3), Adrian; `loario` (1), Lothar; `IV` (2), four, for “three days before the Kalends”; `vitoris` (2), Victor; 3 has disrupted `alexandrie victor` against “of Alexander and Victor”; it retains the two papal names in altered forms, with the conjunction lost Editorial note: “But formerly he was a follower of Pope Victor; see Alexander’s letter 165 in Martène, *Collectio* II, p. 780.”

**2. Theodericus.** The heading has `LIII.` (1), “fifty-third,” and `III.` (2), “third.” Witness 1 gives the erroneous year `MCXLIII`, 1143; `thedericus` (2), `theodoricus` (3), Theodericus; `pinquus` (3), “close/related.” Witness 3 omits the long clause from “the audacity” through “had been accustomed”; `facl'atas` (3), a corrupt *facultas*, “power.” `tranquillati` (3), tranquillity; `comod.` (2, 3), “advantages”; 2 has `et populus`, “and people.”

`habodanges` (1, 3), Habundanges; editorial identification: “Habondange, between Morhange and Château-Salins.” Witness 1 has the transposed wording `s. ac suis ipsum castrum posteris`, “for himself and his successors, that castle”; `winiperch` (1), `winispere` (Chesn.), `w'iuuesperc` (3), `wermnesperc` (2), Werinesperc; editorial identification: Varnesberg; editorial note: “Perhaps Raville, Calmet.” `conflanz` (1), Conflans; editorial identification: Conflans-en-Jarnisy; `redidit` (2), “gave back/made.” `octaviani` (2), Octavian; 2 has `impatris`, a malformed reading at *imperatoris*, “of the emperor”; 3 reads `impiis`, “impious [men],” in an anomalous dative/ablative plural here; `pomp.` (1, 3), `pomposo` (2), “pompously/with pomp”; 1 omits *in facie*, “to their face” (apparatus `in f. des.`); the note marks an omission of these words, not the end of the witness; 2 omits “the business for which they had come”; `commod[a]` (3), “advantages,” for *confusione*, “confusion”; `sumpserant` (2), “had taken.”

`cismate` (3), schism; `imminebat` (1), “threatened”; `levitha` (3), Levite/deacon; `sarchofagum` (3), sarcophagus; the edition adds `predecessoris sui et patrui`, “his predecessor and uncle”; `indica` (3), “Indian,” a corrupt reading for the small distance (*modica*).

3 [Note: [Col. 0601] Fifty-fourth, MS 1.]. By the common election of the clergy [Note: [Col. 0601] omitted in MS 1.] and the applause both of knights and citizens, he had as successor [Col. 0603A] a noble man, worthy of perpetual remembrance, Lord Frederick [Note: [Col. 0603] freder, MS 3.] of Pluviosa [Note: [Col. 0603] pluyiosa, MS 2; pluyosa, MS 3.]. He acquired Ennery [Anerei] for blessed Stephen [Note: [Col. 0603] anerey, MS 2.] [Note: [Col. 0603] Ennery.]. Though he suffered both from decrepit old age and from an incurable illness, he never laid aside his manly spirit, his liberality, or his courtliness, to which he had devoted himself from the cradle [Note: [Col. 0603] never, MS 1; “never his courtliness,” MS 2.] [Note: [Col. 0603] omitted in MS 1.]. Divine mercy most fittingly provided in this matter: he preserved intact both his own possessions and those of the churches entrusted to him, so that under his rule they experienced no diminution and absolutely no loss [Note: [Col. 0603] powers, MS 2.] [Note: [Col. 0603] rule, MS 3.]. Under the aforesaid supreme pontiff Alexander, while Frederick was emperor, he sat for only two years and the same number of months as bishop-elect and deacon, because of the aforementioned dangers of the schism [Note: [Col. 0603] omitted in MS 1.]; then, on the fifth day before the Kalends of October, he departed as a Catholic to the Lord [Note: [Col. 0603] Frederick was expelled in 1173, but restored in 1179.] (1173). He was buried in the oratory called Saint Gall’s, before the altar of Saint John the Evangelist, as he himself had requested while at the point of death.

4 [Note: [Col. 0603] Fifty-fifth, MS 1.]. He was succeeded by Theoderic [Note: [Col. 0603] theodoricus, MS 3.], son of the duke of Lorraine (1173–1179). Immediately after his son’s enthronement, his father, Duke Matthew, granted to blessed Stephen of Metz, by a solemn donation made upon the altar, his castle of Sierck [Note: [Col. 0603] surkes, MS 2.] [Note: [Col. 0603] Sierck.], which he held by allodial right [Note: [Col. 0603] alodii, MS 3.]. He also surrendered into the hands of that same son and wholly renounced the advocacy of Épinal [Spinal], which Lord Stephen had granted him [Note: [Col. 0603] “donation upon the altar,” MS 1.] [Note: [Col. 0603] omitted in MS 2.] [Note: [Col. 0603] wirpuit, MS 1; w'ipiuit, MS 2; w'irpiuit, MS 3.].

He recovered for himself and his successors the tower situated in the middle of the castle of Luxembourg [Note: [Col. 0603] lucenburch, MS 1; lucemborc, MS 3.] [Note: [Col. 0603] (116) Compare above, no. 97; Luzebourg between Phalsbourg and Saverne in this place, Calmet.], which at that time the count [Col. 0603C] of Sarwerden [Note: [Col. 0604] Sarwerden.] held, after capturing that count. He sat for six years and a little more, under Pope Alexander and his maternal uncle, Emperor Frederick [Note: [Col. 0603] “while his uncle was emperor,” MS 2.]. He might perhaps have performed other deeds worthy of annals [Note: [Col. 0603] omitted in MS 2.] [Note: [Col. 0603] years, MS 1; arms, MS 2.], had he not felt the heavy hand of that same Alexander III, by whom his election was annulled [Note: [Col. 0603] shaken, MS 3.] because it had been celebrated while he was still in minor orders [Note: [Col. 0604] Compare Tabouillot II, p. 298.].

5 [Note: [Col. 0603] Fifty-sixth, MS 1.]. After the bishopric had been vacant for almost a year after him [Note: [Col. 0603] for a year, MS 3.] [Note: [Col. 0603] was vacant, MS 1.], in the year of the Lord 1181 [Note: [Col. 0603] MCLXXXI corrected from MCLXXX, MS 2.], it had as successor Lord Bertram, a native of the regions of Saxony [Note: [Col. 0603] saxoe, MS 2.], distinguished indeed by birth, altogether commendable for the honourableness of his life and character, and exceptionally learned in both divine and human law. He too had experienced the severity of Alexander III when he had been elected bishop of Bremen [Note: [Col. 0603] breuiensis, MS 3.] [Note: [Col. 0604] In 1178. Albert of Stade calls him Berthold.]: that pope also annulled his election under the pretext of this ground [Note: [Col. 0603] cause, MS 3.], namely, that it had been celebrated while he was in minor orders. Public report declared that this was done more from hatred of Emperor Frederick, to whom he was very dear [Note: [Col. 0603] catus, MS 2.] and familiar, than from love of justice.

But happy is the fall that is repaired for the better. He fell there in order that he might rise here stronger [Note: [Col. 0603] omitted in MS 2.]. Divine providence plainly wished him to be transferred here, so that here he might advance further and bear more abundant fruit. Such, then, were his beginnings and first works among us. He recalled to his own hand and table almost all his vineyards, which his predecessor had exposed to creditors, more quickly and easily than could have been believed or hoped. He prudently and courageously recovered, by imperial justice and the judgment of princes, the estate of Argancy [Arkentiacum; Note: [Col. 0603] arkentacum, MS 1; archansiacum, MS 2.] [Note: [Col. 0604] Argancy.], which that predecessor had pledged to the count of Dabo [Dasburg] [Note: [Col. 0603] dasburch, MS 1; dasbore, MS 3.] for 700 pounds. Subsequently he built a noble residence at Vic, and acquired for himself and his successors the castle of Bascourt [Note: [Col. 0603] bascort, MS 3.].

Nor should it be passed over in silence that, in the course of time, he destroyed by force of a strong hand a certain castle built by Waltrann, a man of the count of Dabo [Note: [Col. 0603] bascurt, MS 2, corrected to dasburch, MS 1; dasbor, MS 3.], not far from Saarburg [Saleburc; Note: [Col. 0603] salcburc, MS 2; saleborg, MS 3.] [Note: [Col. 0604] Saarburg.], a castle very harmful to the bishopric in those regions [Note: [Col. 0603] nocuum, MSS 1 and 3.].

These things being so, and while he was applying diligent care to the concerns of peace, religion [Note: [Col. 0603] “the concerns of religion, of peace—which are hateful [with *and* written above]—and of justice,” MS 2.], and justice, behold: as though the Lord wished to test him in a furnace [Col. 0604C] and make his virtue shine amid the storms and tempests of this world, He permitted him to be scourged for a time by an unexpected persecution. For when, at the command of Pope Urban III (1186), he received Lord Folmar, the bishop-elect of Trier [Note: [Col. 0603] formarum treuer., MS 1.], whom the supreme pontiff had consecrated against the will of Emperor Frederick [Note: [Col. 0603] fred., MS 1; fedrici, MS 3.], since he neither ought nor dared to oppose that command; and when, wishing to render to Caesar what was Caesar’s and to God what was God’s [Note: [Col. 0603] and what, MS 2.] [Note: [Col. 0603] “are God’s,” MS 2.], he showed him due reverence [Note: [Col. 0603] exibuit, MS 2.], the prince, stirred to wrath and indignation [Note: [Col. 0603] incit., corrected from another reading, MS 2.], caused all his goods to be confiscated [Note: [Col. 0603] cepit, MS 1.] and the entire bishopric of Metz to be seized by his ministeriales in vengeance for this deed (1187), as though it were an enormous and detestable crime [Col. 0605A] to obey the supreme pontiff and fear God more than man.

On hearing this, he took counsel for the safety of his person by the protection of flight, like another Athanasius [Note: [Col. 0605] Iliis, MSS 2 and 3.] [Note: [Col. 0605] presiduo, perhaps MS 2.] [Note: [Col. 0605] athaniasius, MS 3.], and went [Note: [Col. 0605] miganis, MS 3.] to Cologne. In the church of Saint Gereon, where he had formerly been a canon, he cast the anchor of his hope and there found an asylum, there a homeland in place of exile. There, not only his brethren and fellow-canons but the entire clergy of Cologne [Note: [Col. 0605] cl. col., MS 1.], and especially its illustrious metropolitan Philip [Note: [Col. 0605] phillippo, MS 2.], paid such reverence to his person and merits [Note: [Col. 0605] omitted in MS 3.] [Note: [Col. 0605] “reverence,” MSS 1 and 3.], showed such compassion for his humiliation, and supplied so much assistance for his needs out of their liberality, that they almost made him forget his homeland and revenues while in exile [Note: [Col. 0605] “and him,” MS 2; “so that when,” MS 3.].

When, after two full years, imperial serenity had been restored to him through divine assistance and the petitions of many princes and others, our long-desired Job at last returned to his church (1189) [Note: [Col. 0605] tandere, MS 3.], though by no means restored twofold [cf. Job 42:10]. On leaving, he had left wine in the cellars, grain in the granaries, and other goods in abundance; but on his return he found everything emptied [Note: [Col. 0605] “all emptied,” MS 1.] and utterly exhausted [Note: [Col. 0605] exhusta, corrected after exhausta, MS 1.], so that he again had to devote himself to renewed cares and labours, and, as if from the beginning, set about acquiring everything necessary for human use [Note: [Col. 0605] denuo, MS 1.]. May blessed divine mercy deign to grant increase to his years and merits; and may there not be lacking one who, in the proper place and time [Note: [Col. 0605] “at the time,” MS 2.], records his subsequent deeds in annals and makes them known [Note: [Col. 0605] agn., MS 1.] to posterity. [Note: [Col. 0605] “may make it known to posterity,” MS 2. At this point MS 1 ends.]

## Second Continuation

[Col. 0605B] 1 [Note: [Col. 0605] Fifty-seventh, MS 2; seventh, MS 3.]. After Lord Bertram of happy memory, Lord Conrad was elevated to the bishopric of Metz (1212): a vigorous man [Note: [Col. 0605] “a certain,” MS 2.], descended from the German people, illustrious in blood but nobler in character and virtue, and among the princes of the Empire adorned by personal charm and elegance of body. He was also bishop of Speyer and chancellor of the imperial court. As a prudent and faithful steward, with fidelity accompanying his discretion of mind, he managed the affairs of the Empire in such a fashion that, not slumbering idly over the talent entrusted to him but keeping watch diligently, he was able to render his lord a full account of it and would enter with joy into his lord’s rest.

Loving the beauty of the house of the Lord and the place of His dwelling, he adorned the church of Metz with exquisite [Col. 0605C] ornaments. At the town of Vic, which at that time was not enclosed by any defensive work [Note: [Col. 0605] “which,” MS 1; “fortified by some defensive work,” MS 2.], he strengthened a noble castle with lofty walls and towers [Note: [Col. 0605] tower, MS 2.]. Although he was occupied for the greater part of his time with the affairs of the Empire entrusted to him and could only rarely and briefly be present in the diocese of Metz, still, while he was absent [Note: [Col. 0605] obsentia, MS 2.], the reputation of his probity, prudence, and valour stood in his stead: he protected and defended the land of the bishopric of Metz manfully against the strong and powerful as though he were present, and restrained the violence of rebels shrewdly, both by arms and by prudence. In the twelfth year of his pontificate he happily ended his life (1224) and was buried in the choir of the church of Speyer [Note: [Col. 0605] spirensi, MS 2.] [Note: [Col. 0605] sepelitus, MS 2.].

2 [Note: [Col. 0605] Fifty-eighth, MS 2; eighth, MS 3.]. He was succeeded by Lord John, brother of the lord of Apremont [Note: [Col. 0605] Gobert.], whose noble birth [Col. 0606B] adorned him outwardly and whose gravity of character made him illustrious inwardly. While he was in the flower of his youth, below the age required in episcopal elections, the stainlessness of his life more than fully supplying in him the deficiency of age [Note: [Col. 0605] subpl., MS 2.], with the concord of the clergy and joy of the people alike concurring, he was made bishop of Verdun [Note: [Col. 0605] in 1219.]. There, advancing day by day from good to better, he so sustained and increased the fame of his goodness that, because of the merit of his goodness [Note: [Col. 0605] “goodness and” are omitted in MS 3.] and conduct, he was unanimously transferred to the bishopric of Metz.

O inexpressible man! Clothed in the breastplate of righteousness, armed with the shield of self-restraint, protected by the helmet of patience, and surrounded with the weapons of virtues, he nourished those who saw him by the grace of his countenance, refreshed his hearers by the honeyed moderation of his words, stood by the humble with dove-like simplicity [Note: [Col. 0605] colonbina, MS 2.], aided the great with serpent-like cunning, and resisted tyrants with lion-like ferocity [Note: [Col. 0605] leoninia, MS 3.].

While he was constantly vigilant in the affairs of the church of Metz, the illustrious count of Dabo [Daubore; Note: [Col. 0605] dabore, MS 3.] [Note: [Col. 0605] Dasburg; compare Richer, *Chronicle of Sens*, III.21.] entered upon the way of all flesh (c. 1214). His daughter [Note: [Col. 0606] Gertrude.], who had succeeded as sole heir to her paternal inheritance, urgently requested the bishop to restore to her the fief which her father had held from the bishop of Metz. The bishop restored it to her, not without the supplication and request of many nobles, but with this condition added: if she should die without an heir of her own body, that fief should return in full right to the church of Metz. This same condition was secured by authentic seals and confirmed alike by the testimony of witnesses [Note: [Col. 0605] “the same condition,” MS 2.] [Note: [Col. 0605] and, MS 3.].

But when the countess died without an heir of her own body, by a hidden [Col. 0607A] judgment of God (1225), Duke Walter of Limburg [Lembore; Note: [Col. 0607] lamborc, MS 3.], count of Luxembourg, and many other more powerful nobles of the Empire—her kinsmen and supporters—wickedly seized [Note: [Col. 0607] susierunt, MS 3.] the castles belonging to the said fief with their appurtenances. They sought to usurp them for their own dominion and hold them forever [Note: [Col. 0607] imperp., MS 3.] contrary to the obligation of the aforesaid condition.

The bishop, however, a man of manly and resolute spirit, neither lifted up by prosperity nor cast down by adversity, with prudence accompanying his power [Note: [Col. 0607] prudenti, MS 2.] [Note: [Col. 0607] potentia, MS 2.], resisted them powerfully and openly. Amid the long hazards of wars, the clash of arms, and the labyrinth [Note: [Col. 0607] “abundance,” MS 3.] of expenses, he laboured tirelessly for so long that divine providence, which does not fail in its ordering, brought the affair to a successful issue. Thus the bishop acquired the county of Metz and four noble castles—namely Saarburg [Saraborc; Note: [Col. 0607] sareborc, MS 3.], Salm [Albam; Note: [Col. 0607] Saralbe.], Turquestein [Truquestein; Note: [Col. 0607] truquestem and arestem, MS 2.], and Herrenstein [Herrestein; Note: [Col. 0607] Turquestein and Hernestein.]—which belonged to the aforesaid fief, with their appendages, and granted them to the church of Metz for perpetual possession (c. 1227). In acquiring them, to say nothing of the strength of the castles and the pleasantness of the sites, he doubled the revenues of his bishopric.

Moreover, he exchanged the advocacy of Marsal [Note: [Col. 0607] advocasiam, MS 2.], in which the advocate had much more than the lord, for certain vineyards of modest value by comparison; thereby he made the condition of his church much better. But when these things had prospered for him and a time of tranquillity [Note: [Col. 0607] transq., MSS 2 and 3.] and peace had now arrived, the enemy sowed tares and stirred up the plague of discord between him and his citizens of Metz [Col. 0607C] (1231). Those citizens, whose iniquity issued from their abundance, swollen with pride, burned the bishop’s manor called Châtel [Castel; Note: [Col. 0607] chates, MS 2.] [Note: [Col. 0607] Châtel.] before Metz, blinded one cleric, and inflicted many other injuries, too numerous to entrust to the record of letters.

Since the bishop could not overlook this [Note: [Col. 0607] “when previously,” added after *bishop*, MS 2.], after issuing an appropriate warning he excommunicated the citizens and, increasing his severity against them, placed the city under ecclesiastical interdict. Finally he left the city and withdrew to the hill of the castle called Saint-Germain, which he had fortified before Metz [Note: [Col. 0607] “in the castle which is on the hill of Saint-Germain,” MS 3.] [Note: [Col. 0607] formaverat, MS 2.] [Note: [Col. 0608] Compare the *Annals of St Vincent of Metz*, year 1231, *MGH SS* III, p. 159.]. After him, too, the estimable and powerful kindred of Porte-Sailly [Porta-salis; Note: [Col. 0607] porsallis, MS 3.] were expelled from the city, because of the civil hatred hidden among the citizens, and especially because that kindred faithfully supported the bishop in his right and commendably adhered to him. Thus not even one person of that family and its adherents remained in the city; all left it and [Col. 0608A] took refuge in the said castle, their houses being utterly destroyed [Note: [Col. 0607] diruptis, MS 3.] and all the goods which they had left in the city confiscated [Note: [Col. 0607] “their goods,” MS 3.] (1232).

When the bishop could not restrain the malice of those citizens by the spiritual sword [Note: [Col. 0607] gradium, MS 2.], he invoked the aid of the secular arm, namely the duke of Lorraine and the count of Bar [Note: [Col. 0607] “count of Bar,” MS 2.], his vassals. By the bond of alliance and the giving of an oath, he bound them to his assistance against the citizens of Metz through the obligation of fealty by which they were held to him, for a threefold cord [Note: [Col. 0607] “alliance,” MS 2.] [Note: [Col. 0607] omitted in MS 2.] is not easily broken [Ecclesiastes 4:12; Note: [Col. 0608] Compare the *Annals of St Vincent of Metz*, at this year.].

But because faith is secure nowhere and the favour even of brothers is rare, these nobles, corrupted also by money, which often blinds those who see, not only abandoned—not without the stain of treachery—the bishop whom they ought to have supported [Col. 0608B], but even presumed to oppose him. During the hazards of war between them for three years [Note: [Col. 0607] “favours,” MS 2.], these nobles and the commune of Metz, together with them, unexpectedly besieged the aforesaid family [Note: [Col. 0607] parentelem, MS 2; first letters corrected, MS 3.] in the aforesaid castle (1234).

Hearing this, the bishop—more steadfast amid adversity [Note: [Col. 0607] “with all steadfast constancy,” MS 3.], firm in faith with Abraham, not unlearned in the wisdom of Solomon [Note: [Col. 0607] intectus, MS 2.], not lacking Job’s patience [Note: [Col. 0607] pacientia, MS 2.], supported by Simeon’s hope [Note: [Col. 0607] sepe corrected to spe, MS 2; aff., MS 3.]—was abandoned by certain of his faithful clergy and laity [Note: [Col. 0607] quidem, MS 2.]. His brother was not with him, having gone into France in order to return with an armed force and aid his brother; nor could the bishop of Verdun, his kinsman, who would gladly have assisted him with a strong hand, reach him [Note: [Col. 0607] “the same bishop,” added in MS 2.] [Note: [Col. 0607] fransiam, MS 2.]. Although fortune was so hostile to him that another man might have fallen into the eclipse of despair, so that no hope of his recovery remained, this man recovered his strength of spirit. He turned to Germany [Teuthonia; Note: [Col. 0607] theuthoniam, MS 2; theutoniam, MS 3.] and foreign peoples, where he sought the aid of the illustrious counts of Eberstein and Dabo [Note: [Col. 0607] vicorum, MS 3.] and of many other nobles powerful in military resources.

United with him both by entreaty and [Note: [Col. 0607] “with,” MS 3, corrected to *then*, MS 2.] payment, they gathered a great army, followed him, and advanced so far that they took up position on the Moselle. Some of his men advised that they should not cross the river that night, and that the bishop should not allow men exhausted by a long journey to toil further by crossing that night, but should defer the crossing and give rest to men and beasts. Yet he, guided more by his own judgment and intelligence than by that of others, and trusting himself more than others [Col. 0608D] [Note: [Col. 0607] sibi, MS 3.], although his adversaries firmly believed that he would not thereafter cross the Moselle, forded the Moselle with his numerous army [Col. 0609A], though its channels were then full [Note: [Col. 0609] plenus, MS 3.], to the amazement of many. Not even one remained who did not cross the river.

A marvellous thing! For had they not crossed that night, the river rose so much during that very night that in the morning they could by no means have crossed. Thus those besieged in the castle—whose blood their fellow citizens cruelly thirsted for [Note: [Col. 0609] cumcives, MS 2.] [Note: [Col. 0609D] thus the edition; “civilly,” MSS 2 and 3.]—would have been exposed to the danger of death, since they could not expect relief for more than eight days. But the Saviour, who wills all men to be saved and wills no one to perish, gave the bishop the will to cross, and he crossed [Note: [Col. 0609] transivit, MS 3.]. Entering the lands of the said nobles and setting the anchor of his hope in the Lord, he chose rather to commit himself and his men to the hazard of Mars [Col. 0609B] than to leave the right of his church undefended and let his besieged friends lie under peril of death.

When, in the midst of the territories of the duke and count, aided also by the commune of the citizens of Metz, he stood ready to fight them, and the battle-lines of the camps were already drawn up in terrible order on either side [Note: [Col. 0609] omitted in MS 3.], the venerable bishop of Toul came forward between them. Kneeling, he begged, entreated, and urged the bishop of Metz to accept words of peace. Therefore the bishop, moved by compassion for that family, neither forgetful nor ungrateful for the loyalty which they had long exercised toward their lords in devoted zeal, and led by pity [Note: [Col. 0609] that is, compassion; French *pitié*. Calmet.], chose, in order that he might free them without danger to life or property—for their ransom or deliverance [Col. 0609C] could not be attained except through him—and because the outcomes of wars are uncertain, the certainty of settlement and peace for their liberation.

Thus he, moved by pity for his own people, and his adversaries, upon whom sudden fear and trembling had fallen, ended the most grievous plague of war [Note: [Col. 0609] gerre, MS 2.] [Note: [Col. 0609] gravissima, MS 2.] in glad peace and laudable [Note: [Col. 0609] “with peace,” MS 3.] concord, through the mediation of the bishop of Toul, amid the shedding of many tears and the confusion of the enemy of the human race. The bishop and the faithful, strong, and steadfast family of Porte-Sailly [Note: [Col. 0609] “faithful and robust,” MS 2.] returned joyfully to their homes [Note: [Col. 0609] redierunt, MS 2.].

In the fifteenth year of his episcopate, 1238, while Pope Innocent IV [Note: [Col. 0609] eighth, MS 2; third, MS 3.] presided as supreme pontiff and Lord Frederick, son of Lord Henry the emperor, reigned, he happily completed his life. [Col. 0609D] He was buried in the choir of the greater church of Metz [Note: [Col. 0609] Verses added in MS 2.].

[Note: [Col. 0609] His epitaph, inscribed on the tomb: see Meurisse, p. 456.] For he possessed what these times rarely possess [Note: [Col. 0609] “at this time,” MS 2.]:

> A gentle life, a clean hand, a chaste body.

[Col. 0610A] 3. After him, in the Lord’s vineyard of the church of Metz, a fruitful planting flourished in harmonious growth: the native-born and reverend father James, bishop of Metz (1239), descended from royal stock. He was brother of the noble Lord Matthew, formerly duke of Lorraine [Note: [Col. 0609] maheu, MS 2.], born to Ferri, formerly duke of Lorraine, by the sister of the count of Bar. This bishop, noble by birth, shone still more brightly in virtues and character. In him was gathered whatever virtues require: friendship with peace, desire for chastity, vigour in power, distinction in vigour, kindness, wisdom tempered with prudence; and in him, free from envy, the form of the good bound together the elements [and [Note: [Col. 0609] “the elements bound, and” omitted in MS 2, but supplied in the margin by the same hand after *eadem*] joined the elements], and the implanted virtue of holiness [Note: [Col. 0609] justice, MS 2.] [Note: [Col. 0609] omitted in MS 2.] shone forth, stifling discords by the strength of peace. He stood undisturbed amid prosperity and adversity, surrounded on every side by the adornments of character [Note: [Col. 0609] circonseptus, MS 2.].

The sun and moon marvelled at the beauty [Note: [Col. 0609] “the beauty of,” MS 3.] of his virtues. The harmony of his entire homeland applauded his rule [Note: [Col. 0609] “of the whole homeland,” MS 3.], a harmony which, now that he has been removed, the scourge of pestilence has not left to the present age, since no one heals the wounds of the troubled homeland or extends the hand of the Compassionate One to it as it lies fallen and shaken [Note: [Col. 0609] “to compassionate Metz, which is the diocese,” MS 3.]. The diocese of Metz, which beneath his shadow had been the stronghold of the homeland’s strength [Note: [Col. 0609] “was formerly,” MS 3.], has through his eclipse become weak in resources [Note: [Col. 0609] imbetal, MS 3.] and is grievously shaken by swelling storms [Note: [Col. 0609] “is then shaken,” MS 3.]. The Lord’s flock now seems almost deprived of pastoral government. In his own time, holding the reins of surrounding affairs [Note: [Col. 0609] abenas, MS 3.], he regulated everything according to the rule of law [Col. 0610C], checked the efforts of greed, and restrained its unlawful bites.

He appeared everywhere to restore at marvellous expense the buildings of his diocese, ruined by age; to strengthen weak towns, castles, and fortresses; to construct new ones; and to adorn the same diocese with very many newly acquired possessions. At the town of Saarburg [Saleborc; Note: [Col. 0609] sarborg, MS 3.], which had been begun in his predecessor’s time with ardent desire [Note: [Col. 0609] incoatum minutionibus, MS 3.], he completed notable fortifications, towers, ditches [Note: [Col. 0609] “buildings, perhaps walls, perhaps completed,” MS 3.], and very strong wall-battlements. At Salm [Alba], Herrenstein [Herrestein; Note: [Col. 0609] herresteyn, MS 2; herreste, MS 3.] and Drukestem [Note: [Col. 0609] druchesteyn, MS 2; drukesten, MS 3.] [Note: [Col. 0610D] The same place as what above, ch. 2, is written Truquestein.], he improved the repair of towers and walls, digging new cisterns [Note: [Col. 0609] sisternas, MS 2.]. He fortified the towns of Vic and Marsal [Marsello; Note: [Col. 0609] marcello, MS 2; marsual, MS 3.] so thoroughly [Note: [Col. 0609] “in . . . . . .,” a blank space left in MS 3.] that they could not be stormed by hostile assaults. Around the town of Remberviller [Reimberviler; Note: [Col. 0609] reymbervilleir, MS 2.] [Note: [Col. 0610D] Remberviller.], which had been surrounded by hedges, he set the splendid enclosure of very strong walls and twenty-four high towers. He repaired the castle and town of Épinal [Spinalense] with great fortifications [Col. 0611A], and fortified with deep ditches the castle of Conflans, almost collapsed and consumed by age, adorning it with defences of towers and walls.

Moreover, beside old Homburg [Homborc; Note: [Col. 0611] homborch, MS 3.], the watchtower of the whole world, he built anew at enormous cost and incalculable expense [Note: [Col. 0611] imp., MS 3.] a castle on the summit of a certain deserted mountain [Note: [Col. 0611] monti, MS 3.], still called Homburg [Note: [Col. 0611] homborch added in MS 3.], for the protection of the entire bishopric. There the quarters of knights, citizens, inhabitants, and the bishop stand forth separately from one another, distinguished by the height of their walls, the strength of their towers, and the beauty of their buildings [Note: [Col. 0611] insignata, MS 3.]. There he established secular canons from the revenues of the episcopal table (1254), assigning them adequate revenues for divine worship [Col. 0611B] [Note: [Col. 0611D] See the bishop’s charter in Calmet II, p. CCCCLXXIV.]; and he adorned the oratory itself [Note: [Col. 0611] omitted in MS 2.] by the construction of ponds [Note: [Col. 0611] stannorum, MS 3.] and mills.

Likewise, in the abbeys of Beaupré and Salival [Saline-vallis; Note: [Col. 0611] sallivaliis, MS 2.] [Note: [Col. 0611D] Beaupré and Salival.] and in other places, he raised innumerable buildings at great expense. Moreover, he acquired for the perpetual possession of the bishop of Metz the profitable fief of Blâmont [Albo-monte; Note: [Col. 0611] albo monto, MS 2.] [Note: [Col. 0611D] Blamont.], with all its appurtenances [Note: [Col. 0611] “with its …,” omitted after it in MS 3.].

Furthermore, when the Church had directed its attack against Lord Conrad [Note: [Col. 0611] conraldum, MS 2.], son [Note: [Col. 0611] “brother, emperor’s son,” MS 3.] of Emperor Frederick, after a sentence of deposition had been issued against him, Lord James came with a strong hand and uplifted arm [Note: [Col. 0611] omitted in MS 3.] to aid [Note: [Col. 0611] adjurium, MS 2.] the Church. By the strength and skill of his valour and soldiery, he wonderfully put the said Conrad [Note: [Col. 0611] conraldum, MS 2.] to flight and defeated him (1251), sparing no expense.

[Col. 0611C] Likewise, he acquired in perpetuity for the bishopric the profitable fief of Morimont [Maurimont; Note: [Col. 0611] marrimont with its appurtenances, MS 3.] with its appurtenances; the profitable fief of Ruxanges [Rukesinges; Note: [Col. 0611] ruckesingnes, MS 2.]; and the fief of Habondanges [Note: [Col. 0611] gabondanges, MS 2; honbondonges, MS 3.] with its appurtenances, yielding revenue to the bishopric, from the illustrious Count Th. [Note: [Col. 0611] so in the manuscripts; “count Th.,” MS 3.] called Sabert [Note: [Col. 0611] soiberto, MS 2.].

Likewise, from the illustrious Lord Henry of Salm he acquired the profitable fief of Pierre-Percée [Pierepercie; Note: [Col. 0611] piere persie, MS 2.] [Note: [Col. 0611D] Pierre-Percée; compare Richer, *Chronicle of Sens*, V.6.] with its appurtenances; and [Note: [Col. 0611] “and … profitable” omitted in MS 2.] the profitable fief of Salm with its appurtenances and homages. Likewise, from Lord Th. of Craincourt [Creincort; Note: [Col. 0611] Orioncourt, MS 3.] he acquired Delmes [Demes; Note: [Col. 0611] defaies, MS 3.] [Note: [Col. 0611D] Delmes.] with its appurtenances; and from Lord Werric [Note: [Col. 0611] werico, MS 2.] called *le Vogien*, part of his advocacy of the Valley of Faulx. Likewise [Note: [Col. 0611] and, MS 3.], from Lord Peter, son of Lord Peter, formerly knight of Neufchâteau, he acquired the advocacy of Châtel before Metz [Castris ante Metim; Note: [Col. 0611D] Châtel-sous-Saint-Germain.]. Likewise, he acquired from the advocate [Note: [Col. 0611] advocatio, MS 2.] of Metz [Note: [Col. 0611] omitted in MS 2.] the advocacy of Metz.

Likewise, when there was a dispute [Note: [Col. 0611] omitted in MS 2.] between him and Duke Ferri [Note: [Col. 0612D] Ferricum.] of Lorraine, his nephew [Col. 0612B], because he claimed from the duke a part of his inheritance descending to him through his father and mother, he finally obtained, retained, and possessed by a settlement everything which the duke held at Marsal [Note: [Col. 0611] marcellum, MS 2; letter *a* written above in MS 3.], Vic, Remberviller [Remereiville; Note: [Col. 0611] remereville, MS 2.], Courbesaul [Corbesal; Note: [Col. 0612D] Courbesaul, Gelacourt, Remberviller, Sornonville, Velaine, Bussoncourt. Calmet.], Gelacourt [Gellancort; Note: [Col. 0611] sellacort, MS 2; gelleracourt in James’s charter, no. 41.], Remberviller [Note: [Col. 0611] rembervilleir, MS 2; areubeviller in James’s charter.], Sornonville [Sorneville; Note: [Col. 0611] sorneiuille, MS 3; sornonville in James’s charter.], Velaine [Villeinnes; Note: [Col. 0611] villanes in James’s charter.], and Bussoncourt [Bissoncort] (1259), as is set out more fully in the documents drawn up concerning this [Note: [Col. 0611] “concerning which they,” MS 3.] [Note: [Col. 0612D] See these in Calmet II, *Proofs*, p. CCCCLXXXIII, though not all these estates are named there.]. The bishop granted all these possessions, acquired by the aforesaid settlement [Note: [Col. 0611] “acquired. Likewise, bishop …,” MS 2.], to the bishopric of Metz (1260), as is stated more fully in his charters [Note: [Col. 0612D] Dumont, *Corps diplomatique*, I, p. 402.].

Having governed the diocese prudently in temporal as well as spiritual affairs over the course of twenty-two years, he then triumphed happily in the Lord and fell asleep with the fathers [Col. 0612C]. Done in the year of the Lord 1260 [Note: [Col. 0611] omitted in MS 2.], in the month of September [Note: [Col. 0611] septembris, MS 2; October, MS 3.], while Pope Alexander IV [Note: [Col. 0611] omitted in MS 2.] presided in the supreme pontificate [Note: [Col. 0611] At this point MS 2 ends.].

## Third Continuation

[Col. 0611]

[Col. 0611C] 1 [Note: [Col. 0611] Tenth, MS 3.]. He was succeeded in the bishopric of Metz by the venerable Philip of Flörchingen [Florehenges], sprung from an illustrious family and of the same blood, commendable for gentleness and humility of heart and bearing (1261–1264).

2 [Note: [Col. 0611] Eleventh, MS 3.]. After him, William of Trainel [Triegnel; Note: [Col. 0612D] Trainel.], a man noble in birth and character, faithful and prudent, was honourably elevated to the same episcopal seat [Col. 0612C]. When his soul departed from this world, his body [Note: [Col. 0611] corus, MS 3.] was most devoutly committed to burial in the church of the Friars Preachers at Châlons [Cathalaunensium; Note: [Col. 0611] cathanlen., MS 3.] (1264–1269).

[Col. 0613A] 3 [Note: [Col. 0613] Twelfth, MS 3.]. He was succeeded in the cathedra by Lawrence, a spirited, capable, and highly learned man, since he had previously been notary to the supreme pontiff; he was also trained as an outstanding preacher (1269–1279).

4 [Note: [Col. 0613] Thirteenth, MS 3.]. After him, Lord John, son of the count of Flanders, was raised to the same office from a distinguished family [Note: [Col. 0613] utpete, MS 3.]. Handsome in appearance, pleasant in speech, and recently licensed at Paris in decretals, he was subsequently transferred to the church of Liège (1280–1282).

5. [Note: [Col. 0613] XIV. 3.] For that same desolate church of Metz, provision was thereafter mercifully made by the Apostolic See in the person of a man of illustrious birth, brother of the Count of Hainaut, Lord Burchard [Note: [Col. 0613] “Bochard” in 3.], a man, I say, renowned, prudent, capable, and sufficiently learned [Note: [Col. 0613] “sufficit” in 3.] (1283). How many and how great were the hardships which both he himself and the four venerable men just mentioned immediately endured in defending the interests of that church, and what advantages they acquired for it—though at some burden to themselves and to their own followers—is made clear by the circumstances of the present day, and these deeds deserve to be commended to perpetual memory. In due course, according to the deserts of each, they may be recorded more fully with the others [Col. 0614A], when an appropriate occasion for praise reaches its fitting harbor. He sat for thirteen years, winning valiant triumphs over many enemies. He also appears to have incorporated the monastery of Gorze into the bishopric of Metz through the Apostolic See.

In the eleventh and twelfth years of his time, namely 1294–1295, there was an unheard-of dearth; and in the latter year such an abundance of wine occurred that a modius could be had for three and a half solidi, whereas previously—when the vineyards had frozen in winter—it had sold for 26, so that within one month one modius of wine could be had for three solidi; so that [the text is corrupt] it could be had for one quarter of grain and one modius of wine. [Note: [Col. 0613] “for three solidi” added again in 3.] [Note: [Col. 0613] “wine” added in 3, where this passage is corrupt.]

In the same thirteenth year there was such an inundation of rain that many hills and houses collapsed, and even the mountains themselves were horribly split apart. He died in the year of the Lord 1296, on the day before the Kalends of December [30 November], and was buried at the entrance of the greater choir of the church of Metz. By order of the supreme pontiff, as was said above, he had been transferred to that same church as bishop in the year of the Lord 1283. May his soul, through God’s mercy, rest in peace. Amen.

## In the Year of the Lord 1119: Placidus, Prior of the Monastery of Nonantola of the Order of St Benedict, Afterwards Bishop of an Unknown See

[Col. 0613]

[Col. 0613]

# Book on the Honour of the Church

(Extracted by Fr Bernard Pez, Benedictine and librarian of Melk, from a manuscript codex of the illustrious Benedictine monastery of Göttweig in Austria, and published in *Thesaurus Anecdotorum Novissimus*, vol. II, part II, pp. 73–180.)

## Notice

(Introductory dissertation to the same volume, p. XXIII.)

[Col. 0613] Of Placidus of Nonantola none of the ancient authors who treated ecclesiastical writers makes mention, except the Anonymous of Melk alone, first published by us in the Appendix to the Benedictine-Maurist Library. In chapter 115, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, he has these words:

> Placidus, prior of the monastery of Nonantola, writes against investitures and the unjust power of Henry IV.

By these words he undoubtedly indicates and points out this very work of Placidus—indeed a distinguished and excellent one—which we here bring to light from a six-hundred-year-old manuscript codex of the illustrious monastery of Göttweig. For Placidus does nothing else in it than keep secular rulers as far as possible from the conferring and ordering of sacred dignities and offices, and persuade readers that secular princes have no authority in the sanctuary of the Lord—a moderation and integrity always dear and customary to all the holiest princes.

Yet it is pleasing to hear Placidus himself in his prologue, from whose discourse we shall learn both the occasion for writing the book and, at the same time, the subject of the whole work. The work itself is divided in the Göttweig codex into 168 chapters, whereas the prefixed table or index promises 171. Nor do the chapter headings set out in the index everywhere agree with the headings in the body and sequence of the book, as is evident from chapters 2, 29, 30, 31, 32, 33, 34, through 42, where they again agree word for word. This discrepancy in chapters and headings perhaps arose from a copyist who divided the text of the book without sufficient care and did not diligently consult the index prefixed to the work.

The matter would be easy to investigate if Placidus’s book still existed in the library of St Peter, where we learn that it formerly existed from a catalogue of books of the monastery of St Peter written five hundred years ago. In it certain volumes are listed thus:

> Josephus, *On the Destruction of Jerusalem*. Hilary on the Psalter. Conferences of the Fathers in two volumes. Canons of Mainz. Honorius, *On the Image of the World*. Origen, *On the Singularity of Clerics*. Song of Songs. Passion of St Paul the Apostle. Life of Giles; Passion of St Antoninus the Martyr, in one volume. Laws of the Lombards. Bede on the Acts of the Apostles. Cosmography. Chapters of the Greek canons. Rule of St Benedict. Placidus, *On the Honour of the Church*, etc.

But this latter codex, though the entire library was searched by us, appeared nowhere. Therefore another handwritten copy must be awaited from elsewhere, in order that the origin of this confusion of chapters and headings in Placidus’s work may be discovered.

Now, to return to Placidus himself: he was not only prior of the monastery of Nonantola, as the Anonymous of Melk observed, but also a bishop, as we learn from chapters 82 and 83; although neither from Ferdinando Ughelli’s *Italia Sacra* nor from elsewhere have we been able to discover what see he adorned by his by-no-means ordinary virtue and learning. More certain evidence concerning the period in which he flourished is supplied by this very book, *On the Honour of the Church*. For in chapter 53 Placidus speaks thus explicitly:

> Therefore the holy Fathers knew that, if something new should arise, God, who was in the hearts of His elect, would Himself give counsel. That this is true is testified by the council of the holy Fathers, reverently celebrated in modern times, namely in the year of the Incarnation of the Lord 1078, in the city of Rome under Gregory VII of holy memory, universal pope, according to ancient and ecclesiastical custom, etc.

And in chapter 117, after recounting that Pope Paschal II is said, compelled by force and out of compassion for his brethren and sons, whom he saw cruelly treated, to have given his consent, allowing by a granted privilege that a bishop should not be consecrated unless invested with ring and staff by kings, and that the pope should not elect a pastor without the king’s permission, etc., he adds, addressing Paschal as though present:

> Therefore the holy pope ought not to observe this, but should instead most zealously correct it, imitating the faith of his most blessed father, the Apostle Peter, whose place, through the grace of God, he holds in the holy Church—Peter who diligently sought, with great love of heart, to correct what he had fearfully denied.

From this it is clear that Placidus wrote under the pontificates of Gregory VII, Urban II, and likewise Paschal II, the last of whom presided over the Church from 1099 until 1118. These facts—and no more concerning Placidus of Nonantola—are owed henceforth by learned men to the most reverend and most illustrious Lord Godfrey Bessel, the most eminent and learned abbot of Göttweig. Moved by our repeated requests and letters, he at length graciously sent the codex to Melk, from which, in the haste of our work, we transcribed it in approximately eight or ten days.

# Here Begins the Prologue to the Book on the Honour of the Church

[Col. 0615]

[Col. 0615A] The Word and Wisdom of God the Father, our Lord Jesus Christ, who deigned to descend from heaven for the salvation of His Church, deigns to strengthen her by the grace of His Spirit and always to illumine her against all heresies by the light of true wisdom. Hence it is that even in our own days He has deigned to arm and fortify her against defenders of perverse doctrine, not only by the grace of that same Holy Spirit, but also by the teachings both of the Old and New Testaments and by the sayings of the holy Catholics.

For certain persons said: “The Church is spiritual; therefore nothing of earthly things belongs to it except the place alone that is customarily called a church. If those who serve it require any earthly things, they cannot hold them by right of the Church. For unless we give them, bishops or clerics [Col. 0615B] can possess nothing, except what is offered at the altar, tithes, and first-fruits; for all other possessions are ours. Therefore, let those who seek bishoprics and abbeys obtain them through us, or otherwise let them not possess what is ours [Col. 0616A]. But if they are willing to be content solely with tithes, first-fruits, and offerings brought to their altar, that may rest in their own choice; but if they desire to hold what was formerly given to the Church, let them obtain it through us.”

All Catholics abhorred this reasoning, as contrary to the gifts of the Holy Spirit, who deigns to give not only spiritual but also bodily things to His Church and wills that bishops should themselves possess these, so that one who has been consecrated may have in his power both small and great possessions that have been consecrated to God. They therefore took care to arm themselves against so great an impiety with divine words.

Then I also, the least of all Christians, striving to collect the opinions of the holy Fathers, produced a small book for the honour and defence of holy mother Catholic Church [Col. 0616B]. In it, speaking first of the primacy of St Peter over the whole Church, I subsequently explained what the Church is and how great is its value before God. Next I took care to add that holy Church must be honoured not only with spiritual [Col. 0617A] but also with bodily gifts, and consequently that those act rightly who, in giving something of their own right to her, honour her in Christ’s stead.

In confirming this, we prove that what is bestowed upon the Church is certainly given to Christ; and, proving by sayings of the holy Fathers that what belongs to the Church ought to remain in the power of its prelates, we have taught that its pastors are to be appointed not by any earthly power, but by the common election of clergy and laity. We have shown that this election ought to be confirmed by the judgment of bishops, and that holy Church owes kings nothing except the payment of tribute. There also, adding a discussion of church property not to be taken away, we prove that those who do not fear to take from the Church what has been given to it are sacrilegious.

There likewise, demonstrating by whom investiture of churches ought to be performed, we endeavour to show more clearly than light that no bishop ought to subject churches to a man outside his own order. And as for the claim that St Adrian or other holy pontiffs gave assent to this practice, if it is true, we teach how it must be understood, and show that this occasion must not be used to act against divine law. Proving all these things by testimonies from the Old and New Testaments, we have taken care also to establish them by the authority of the canons and by sayings of the holy Fathers.

To these words [Col. 0618A] we add examples of saints who preferred to die for justice rather than yield, and seek briefly to admonish that, despising the present life for the love of God and His Church, we should not fear death; for we are certain that one who dies for love of holy Church is proved to die for Christ, who laid down His own life for her. Whoever has died for Him shall live eternally.

Proving all these things, as we have said, by testimonies both of the Old and the New Testament and by sayings of the holy Fathers, wherever it seemed right we have also endeavoured to add something of our own, only in wording and not in meaning, to these most sacred words—as though giving voice from the midst of rocks. Wherever we have cited the words of a teacher, we have noted in the margin both his name and his book. But we have marked with *ex ratione* [“from reasoning”] what has been bestowed upon us by divine grace [Col. 0618B].

For all this, expecting mercy not from human beings but from Christ the Lord—who promised that He would grant a reward for a cup of cold water—we implore the charity of the Holy Spirit in the heavenly kingdom, that our labour in defence and honour of holy mother Catholic Church may not be fruitless for the holy prelates of the present age, in imitation of the ancient Fathers, or for all the orthodox; but that, strengthened by the grace of the Holy Spirit, we may reject evil and hold most firmly to what is good. Amen.

# Chapters of the Book

[Col. 0617C]

I. That our Lord Jesus Christ entrusted holy Church in a special manner to blessed Peter.  
II. What the Church is.  
III. That holy Church is the bride of Christ.  
IV. That Christ is the head of the Church and holy Church is the body of Christ.  
V. That the honour of holy Church is the honour of Christ.  
VI. That holy Church is to be understood not only in spiritual but also in bodily things.  
VII. On the possessions of the Church.  
VIII. On the same subject.  
IX. Again, on the same subject.  
X. That a vow to God must in every respect be fulfilled.  
XI. That laypeople must not administer ecclesiastical matters.  
[Col. 0617D] XII. What punishment awaits those who seize ecclesiastical property.  
XIII. That one who seizes ecclesiastical property must be excommunicated.  
XIV. What belongs properly to priests and to peoples.  
XV. That earthly powers must not invade bishops.  
XVI. That princes are held under the discipline of faith.  
XVII. On imperial law.  
XVIII. How the saying is to be understood: “Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s, and to God the things that are God’s.”  
[Col. 0618C] XIX. An admonition from the words of St Ambrose.  
XX. A further confirmation of the same point.  
XXI. By whom bishops must be ordained.  
XXII. To whom the election of priests properly belongs.  
XXIII. That those ordained contrary to the canons are not to be regarded as bishops.  
XXIV. That the election of a pontiff does not at all belong to the emperor.  
XXV. That the agreement of all is required in an election.  
XXVI. On the same subject.  
XXVII. That the sacred canons do not assign to emperors the elections of bishops.  
[Col. 0618D] XXVIII. What governance an elected pastor undertakes.  
XXIX. That the care of all Church property properly belongs to the bishop.  
XXX. That the bishop is to have care of ecclesiastical property.  
XXXI. That a bishop has authority over Church property for the provision of the poor.  
XXXII. That bishops ought to hold ecclesiastical property in their power.  
XXXIII. That the Church ought also to possess earthly things.  
[Col. 0619A] XXXIV. That ecclesiastical property does not concern laypeople to administer.  
XXXV. On the same subject.  
XXXVI. An admonition that these opinions be properly understood.  
XXXVII. A synodal decree of Pope St Symmachus concerning laypeople who desire to administer the Church on their own authority.  
XXXVIII. That princes are not excluded from the election of pontiffs, but from domination.  
XXXIX. What constitutes a canonical election of bishops.  
XL. On the same subject.  
XLI. That emperors may not introduce bishops into the Church.  
XLII. That ecclesiastical offices must not be obtained with money.  
[Col. 0619B] XLIII. That the grace of God also gives us earthly things.  
XLIV. On the possessions of the Church.  
XLV. On parish offerings.  
XLVI. That shares should be assigned from the revenues of the Church.  
XLVII. That what has once been given to the Church must never be taken from it.  
XLVIII. On earthly things to be given to Christ.  
XLIX. On those who take away what has been given to the Church.  
L. That all churches, with all that they possess, should be in the bishop’s power.  
[Col. 0619C] LI. That what belongs to clerics belongs to the churches in which they hold title.  
LII. That everything offered to God is called an offering.  
LIII. How great an evil it is to take away Church property.  
LIV. That ecclesiastical property is a gift of God.  
LV. Why the ancient Fathers did not expressly oppose lay investiture of churches.  
LVI. That laypeople must in no way dare to invest churches.  
LVII. That it is a grave crime for laypeople to invest churches with staff or ring.  
LVIII. Against those who say that we teach this in order to diminish the honour of the kingdom.  
LIX. That the true emperors of our time should deign to follow the example of the great Emperor Constantine.  
[Col. 0619D] LX. An example of the great humility of Emperor Constantine.  
LXI. An example of the true humility of Emperor Valentinian, and concerning the election of St Ambrose.  
LXII. That St Ambrose excommunicated Emperor Theodosius.  
LXIII. On Emperor Marcian.  
LXIV. An example of the obedience of Emperor Charles.  
LXV. Where Emperor Charles promises to correct that concerning which he had been admonished by the Apostolic See.  
LXVI. On the same subject.  
LXVII. On the same subject.

# The Book of Placidus the Monk on the Honour of the Church

[Col. 0623]

## Chapter I. That Our Lord Jesus Christ Entrusted Holy Church in a Special Manner to Blessed Peter

[Col. 0623B]

It is clear to all the faithful that the Lord Himself entrusted the care of the Lord’s sheepfold to the blessed Apostle Peter. For, having risen from the dead and shown His disciples the truth of His resurrection not only by being seen but also by eating with them, He said among other things to blessed Peter: “Simon, son of John, do you love me more than these?” When Peter answered, “Lord, you know that I love you,” the Lord said to him: “Feed my sheep.” He enjoined this once, twice, and even a third time: namely, that Peter should show in feeding His sheep the love by which he confessed that he loved Him.

When going to His Passion, He had also said to him: “Simon, behold, Satan has sought you, that he might sift you like [Col. 0623C] wheat; but I have prayed for you, that your faith may not fail; and when you have turned again, strengthen your brethren” (Luke 22). And earlier He had said to him: “You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church” (Matthew 16). In these words, as all the holy doctors most truly judged, a certain special prerogative in guarding holy Church is imposed upon blessed Peter.

Although all the apostles are shepherds—especially those who heard from the Lord Himself, “You are the light of the world” (Matthew 5); and again, “I chose you out of the world, that you may go and bear fruit, and that your fruit may remain” (John 15); and again, “Go, teach all nations” (Matthew 28); and again, appearing to them on the day of the resurrection, He said, “Whose sins you forgive are forgiven them” (John 20)—nevertheless, in order that the bond of unity might be more earnestly commended, the care of the Church is entrusted in a special manner [Col. 0623D] to blessed Peter.

## Chapter II. What the Church Is

The Church is well known to be the congregation—or rather, the convocation—of the faithful. Hence Blessed Augustine says (*On Psalm* 126):

> The Lord Jesus Christ builds His house. Now the house of God is the people of God, that is, the Church of God. What is the house of God? The temple of God. And what does the Apostle say? “The temple of God is holy, which you are” (1 Corinthians 3). But all the faithful, who are the house of God—not only those who now exist, but also those who were before us and have already fallen asleep, and those who will come after us, still to be known in human affairs until the end—when gathered together into one, innumerable faithful, yet numbered by God, of whom the Apostle says, “The Lord knows those who are his” (2 Timothy 2), those grains which now groan among the chaff and will form one mass when the threshing floor has been winnowed at the end (Matthew [Col. 0624C] 3): therefore the entire number of holy faithful who will be transformed from human beings so as to become equal to the angels of God, joined also with those angels themselves, who are not now on pilgrimage but await us until we return from pilgrimage—all together make one house of God and one city. This is Jerusalem, that is, the holy Church of God.

## Chapter III. That Holy Church Is the Bride of Christ

The Lord promises holy Church through the prophet, saying: “I will betroth you to myself in justice and judgment, in mercy and compassions; I will betroth you to myself in faith, and you shall know that I am the Lord” (Hosea 2). Hence also the blessed Apostle, speaking to the Church, says: “I have betrothed you to one husband, to present you as a chaste virgin to Christ” (2 Corinthians 11). And the Psalmist says: “Your wife is like [Col. 0624D] a fruitful vine” (Psalm 127).

Explaining this, St Augustine says, on this Psalm 137: “Your wife is spoken of in relation to Christ; therefore His wife is the Church. Not without reason was Eve herself made from the side of the man while he slept (Genesis 2), because the Church was made while Christ was dying. The one was taken from the side of the man when a rib was removed; the other from the side of the man when His side was pierced by the lance (John 19), and the sacraments from which the Church was formed flowed forth.”

## Chapter IV. That Christ Is the Head of the Church and Holy Church the Body of Christ

The blessed Apostle Paul, speaking of the Lord, says: “God the Father subjected all things beneath Christ’s feet and gave Him as head over all the Church, which is His body, the fullness of Him who fills all things in all” (1 Corinthians 15). Again he says of Christ: “All things hold together in Him, and He is the head of the body, the Church” (Colossians 1). Hence the Lord Himself says through the prophet [Col. 0625B]: “The Lord has clothed me with the garment of salvation and surrounded me with the robe of joy, like a bridegroom adorned with a crown, and like a bride adorned with her jewels” (Isaiah 61).

## Chapter V. That the Honour of Holy Church Is the Honour of Christ

It is plainly apparent that, since Christ is the head of the Church and holy Church the body of its Redeemer, it is proved by these sacred testimonies that one who honours her also honours Christ, and one who despises her also despises Christ. This is shown by the reasoning of truth not only in divine matters, where the source of true charity is found, but we can also consider it in a human way. For whoever treats the bride of another with honour or contempt, the bridegroom most truly declares that this is done to himself.

Yet let us show that divine testimony supports this evident reasoning. For the Lord Himself says to His saints: “Whoever honours you honours me, and whoever despises you despises me” (Luke 10).

## Chapter VI. That Holy Church Is Understood Not Only in Spiritual but Also in Bodily Things

It is evident that holy Church is spiritual and enriched with spiritual gifts. Thus she is always illumined by the sevenfold grace of the Spirit and daily gives birth to spiritual children for God. Yet the most sacred institution of the holy Fathers plainly testifies that they earnestly decreed that she should also be honoured and reverenced with bodily things.

For, so that the honour of God might thereby increase more abundantly, they taught us not merely to revere God in the heart but also to build churches in His honour, where the assembled people might hear the Lord’s commandments and worship God in invisible mysteries; where we might continually praise God; where His body and blood might be received daily through the ministry of priests by the sanctification of the ineffable Spirit; where sacred chrism might be prepared; and where we might be made children of God by adoption in baptism. This place was also instituted to be called a church, precisely because it was decreed that the faithful people should gather there in God’s honour.

The most blessed and illustrious teacher Ambrose, archbishop of the Church of Milan, bears witness to this in the hymn which he composed for the dedication of a church, speaking thus to the Lord:

> This house is known to have been duly dedicated to you, in which the people receive the sacred body and drink the blessed draught of blood. Here the most holy waters wash away age-old sins and destroy offences; here, through chrism, the race of Christ-worshippers is created. This place is indeed called the hall of the boundless King and the snow-white gate of heaven, which receives all who seek the homeland of life.

Hence many of the faithful, wishing to entrust themselves and their possessions to God, gave these things with great humility of heart to the Church—that is, the bride of Christ—in God’s stead. Others also, establishing churches and monasteries on their own property, faithfully transferred all their goods to the servants of God serving God there, believing that they were truly fulfilling what the Lord said: “Sell all that you have, give to the poor, and come, follow me” (Luke 18).

All the most devout emperors—namely Constantine, the first Roman emperor to believe in Christ, as well as Theodosius and Justinian, together with many other Christian emperors—bestowing imperial strength and confirmation upon this matter, took care to confirm and establish it for Christ’s honour.

## Chapter VII. On the Possessions of the Church
What has once been given to the Church belongs to Christ forever, and can in no way be alienated from the Church’s possession; so much so that even the very founder of a church, after dedicating it to God and having it consecrated, can thereafter retain no right in it. It can no longer be appointed through him, nor can it be invested by him. These things are attested not only by the most sacred Scriptures of the New, but also of the Old, Testament.

Therefore, as is known to all [Col. 0626C], things are given to the Church so that Christ’s poor may be fed from them, and so that those serving God in the sanctuary may have the means of sustenance: namely, that, most devoutly and always intent upon divine contemplation and his continual praise, free from the cares of this world, they may constantly cleave to God. To those who furnish resources for his Church—that is, who minister in this world to the holy poor—the Lord says: “Make for yourselves friends from the mammon of unrighteousness, so that when you fail, they may receive you into eternal dwellings” (Luke 16). “Lay up for yourselves treasures in heaven, where neither rust nor moth destroys” (Matt. 6).

How great an evil it is to wish, by any contrivance, to take away again what has once been given to God, he himself shows in saying: “No one who puts his hand to the plough and looks back is fit for the kingdom of God” [Col. 0626D] (Luke 9). Thus also in the Acts of the Apostles, Ananias and Sapphira, who attempted secretly to withhold what they had vowed to God, were delivered to death by the rebuke of the blessed apostle Peter (Acts 5). Here one must also weigh with grave fear what punishment awaits those who not only do not give their own goods to God, but do not fear to take away things offered by others; if those who attempted, contrary to God’s sacred ordinance, to withhold not another’s property but their own, already vowed to God, deserved sentence of death.

## CHAPTER VIII.—On the same matter

Since, then, we have adduced the judgment of the New Testament, let us also bring forward that of the Old. For on this matter the holy lawgiver Moses pronounced judgment as follows:

> [Col. 0627A] “When you make a vow to the Lord your God, you shall not delay to fulfil it, because the Lord your God will require it of you. And if you delay, he will reckon it to you as sin. If you are unwilling to promise, you will be without sin; but what has once gone forth from your lips you shall observe and do, as you promised the Lord your God and spoke of your own free will from your mouth” (Deut. 23).

## CHAPTER IX.—Again, on the same matter

When he commanded tithes, firstfruits, and freewill vows to be offered to God, he further commanded that whoever had once offered something to God should no longer have the power to withdraw or alter it. If he did so, Moses most plainly decreed that both what he first vowed and what he later substituted should come under the Lord’s claim. It is well known that the things given to the Lord belonged to the priests, to whom cities and their surrounding lands were also granted. They lawfully possessed all these things without any dispute (Exod. 22; Num. 30).

## CHAPTER X.—That a vow made to God must be fulfilled in every respect

The Psalmist also exhorts us to make vows to the Lord and fulfil them, saying: “Make vows and fulfil them to the Lord your God, all you who offer gifts round about him” (Ps. 75). Explaining this, St Augustine says, in his exposition of this psalm:

> My brothers, let each person vow and fulfil what he can. Do not make vows and fail to fulfil them. What, then, ought we to vow? To believe in him, to hope in him, to live well, not to do evil. These things are common to all. Then some vow chastity; others that their house shall be hospitable to all holy visitors: they make a great vow. Another vows to leave all that he has, distribute it to the poor, and enter the common life and fellowship of the saints: he makes a great vow. Let him only take care, with God’s help, earnestly to fulfil what he has vowed.

Again, on this matter St Augustine says to Christian rulers and peoples (*Sermon to the People*):

> We exhort your Christianity that, in accordance with the ordinances of the holy canons, no priest coming from elsewhere be received in churches founded by you unless he has been consecrated by the bishop of your Church, or is received from him by letters of recommendation.

## CHAPTER XI.—That laymen should not dispose of ecclesiastical matters

[Col. 0627D]  
(From the Register of St Gregory, Pope Gregory I.)

The order of reason does not permit a lay person to claim at his own discretion the property of monasteries or other churches.

## CHAPTER XII.—What punishment awaits those who seize ecclesiastical property

(From the Rule of St Gregory, Pope Gregory I.)

If any king, priest, judge, or secular person presumes unjustly to alienate the property of churches from the churches, let him lose the dignity of his authority and honour, and know himself guilty before the divine judgment. Unless he restores what he has taken away, or mourns it in fitting repentance, he shall be cut off from the most sacred body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ, and in the eternal judgment shall lie under strict vengeance. But let peace be upon those who observe these things, [Col. 0628A] and may the blessing of the Lord Jesus preserve them for ever.

## CHAPTER XIII.—That one who seizes ecclesiastical property must be excommunicated

(From a Roman council in the time of Pope Gregory VII.)

Whoever among soldiers, or any person of whatever rank or profession, has received, shall receive, or has seized ecclesiastical estates from any king or secular prince, or from bishops, abbots, or other rulers of churches against their will; or has held them even with the corrupt or vicious consent of those same rulers—unless he restores those estates to the churches—shall be subject to excommunication.

## CHAPTER XIV.—What properly belongs to priests and peoples

[Col. 0628B]  
(From an epistle of St Clement, Pope.)

It is yours, O priests who perform the Lord’s embassy, to teach the peoples; and it is theirs to obey you as they obey God.

## CHAPTER XV.—That earthly authorities should not hinder bishops

(From an epistle of Pope Alexander.)

Let no count, no judge, and absolutely no person in clerical or secular dress hinder or presume to disturb the mission of bishops.

## CHAPTER XVI.—That rulers are held under the discipline of faith

(From the sayings of St Isidore, bishop.)

The powers of the world are subject to the discipline of government; and although they are endowed with the summit of royal power, they are nonetheless bound by the bond of faith, so that they may preach the things of Christ and show in works what they preach [Col. 0628C].

## CHAPTER XVII.—On imperial law

(From the decrees of Pope Pius.)

The law of emperors is not above the law of God, but beneath it.

## CHAPTER XVIII.—How the saying is to be understood: “Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s, and to God the things that are God’s”

Many bring an accusation against us, saying that we act unjustly because we proclaim that the emperor ought to seek no right in the Church, and that he ought not only not to invest it, but ought not in any way to exercise lordship over it. For they say that Christ himself paid tribute, and, when a denarius was shown to him, said: “Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s, and to God the things that are God’s” (Matt. 22).

That this must not be understood as meaning that the Church is subject to the emperor is attested by St Ambrose, who says in his letter on the handing over of the basilica:

> “We render to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s, and to God the things that are God’s. Caesar’s tribute is not denied; the Church belongs to God and certainly ought not to be assigned to Caesar, because the temple of God cannot be Caesar’s right. No one can deny that this was said with honour for the emperor. For what is more honourable than for the emperor to be called a son of the Church? When this is said, it is said without sin; it is said with grace. For the emperor is within the Church, not above the Church. A good emperor seeks the Church’s aid; he does not reject it.”

We state these things humbly, but we expound them firmly.

## CHAPTER XIX.—An admonition drawn from these words of St Ambrose

Let those, therefore, who maintain that pastors of the Church are to be given by [Col. 0629A] emperors see how seriously they resist the words of the Holy Spirit, spoken through the mouth of blessed Ambrose. For in what way can the Church ever be more gravely subjected to the emperor than if it cannot have a pastor unless the emperor himself has sent and invested him? In what further way can the emperor possess right or lordship in the Church?

The emperor ought not to rule the Church, but rather to guard and save it, as the most dutiful son of his most holy mother.

## CHAPTER XX.—A further confirmation of the same matter

Although we believe that no one can doubt the words of the most holy Ambrose, let us nevertheless adduce the words of our Lord Jesus Christ himself, who says: “I am the door.” Explaining this, St Augustine says in his tractates on John:

> Whoever wishes to enter the sheepfold must enter through the door; that is, he must seek Christ’s glory, not his own. For many, in seeking their own glory, have scattered Christ’s sheep rather than gathered them. The door is low; one must humble oneself in order to enter with an uninjured head. But one who does not humble himself, but exalts himself, wishes to climb over the wall. Whoever climbs over the wall is raised up in order to fall. By the wall is rightly understood the empty glory of this world. For just as a wall surrounds a place, but because it quickly collapses does not long protect what it encloses, so too the empty glory of this world, although it may seem for a time to protect one who trusts in it, will quickly fall together with the one who trusts in it. Therefore the prophet also says: “They were building a wall without mortar. Say to those who build without plaster that it shall fall; for there will be a flooding rain and a violent wind” (Ezek. 13). A wall without mortar is plastered when human power is strengthened by human favour, not by the grace of the Holy Spirit. Therefore let one who climbs over the wall and desires to obtain Christ’s sheep know that he will fall, and that he is not a shepherd but a thief, because he does not enter Christ through the lowly door.

## CHAPTER XXI.—By whom bishops are to be ordained

(From the Council of Laodicea, canon 5.)

Let bishops be advanced to ecclesiastical rank by the judgment of the metropolitans and of the bishops in the surrounding region—those, namely, who have been tested for a long time both in the word of faith and by the example of upright conduct.

## CHAPTER XXII.—What kind of man ought to be chosen bishop

[Col. 0629D]

The Apostle, speaking to Titus about how a pastor of the Church should be chosen, shows this when he says:

> “For this reason I left you in Crete: that you might set right what remains to be set right and appoint presbyters in every city, as I directed you. If any man is without reproach, the husband of one wife, having children not accused of debauchery or insubordination. For a bishop must be without reproach as God’s steward: not arrogant, not quick-tempered, not violent, not greedy for shameful gain; but hospitable, kind, sober, just, holy, self-controlled, holding fast the faithful word which accords with the teaching, so that he may be able both to exhort in sound doctrine and to refute those who contradict it” (Titus 1).

## CHAPTER XXIII.—That those ordained contrary to the canons are not to be regarded as bishops

[Col. 0630A]

(Pope Leo, canon 15.)

No principle permits those to be counted among bishops who have neither been elected by the clergy, nor sought by the people, nor consecrated by the bishops of the province with the judgment of the metropolitan.

## CHAPTER XXIV.—That the election of a pontiff does not belong to the emperor

The blessed apostolic Leo lived, as is known, in the time of the most Christian Emperor Marcian. Yet in the election of a pontiff, it is evident that not only was the emperor’s lordship not introduced, but even his name was not mentioned.

## CHAPTER XXV.—That the agreement of all is required in an election

[Col. 0630B]  
(Pope Celestine, canon 18.)

Let no bishop be imposed upon unwilling persons. The agreement and desire of clergy, people, and order are to be required.

## CHAPTER XXVI.—On the same matter

(From the Council of Orléans, canon 2.)

No one is to be ordained bishop unless the clergy and parishioners have been summoned and agree together.

## CHAPTER XXVII.—That the sacred canons do not assign episcopal elections to emperors

It should be noted and committed to memory that in no canon of the holy Fathers is the election of the pastor of the holy Church assigned to earthly rulers.

## CHAPTER XXVIII.—What government the elected pastor undertakes

It is clear that the elected and consecrated pastor undertakes the care both of souls and of bodies. Therefore the Lord says to blessed Peter: “I have prayed for you, that your faith may not fail; and when you have turned again, strengthen your brothers” (Luke 22). And again: “If you love me, feed my sheep” (John 21).

The same blessed Peter says in his Epistle to the pastors of the holy Church concerning care for the bodies of those subject to them:

> “I exhort the elders among you, as a fellow elder and a witness of Christ’s sufferings, and a sharer in the glory that is to be revealed: feed the flock of God which is among you” (1 Pet. 5).

Explaining this, St Gregory says:
