> In this passage he made plain what suffering, of heart or of body, he recommended when he added: “Overseeing it, not under compulsion, but willingly according to God; not for the sake of shameful gain [Col. 0630D], but voluntarily.” By these words pastors are surely warned with pious concern not, by creating the want of those subject to them, to kill themselves with the sword of ambition; lest, while their neighbours are sustained through them with the helps of the flesh, they themselves remain hungry for the bread of righteousness.

Here it must be considered that, unless the blessed apostle Peter and his disciple St Gregory had decided that the pastors of the Church should hold under their authority the things belonging to the Church, they would never have taught these things to pastors. But in the present time the pastors of many churches do not have under their authority what belongs to the Church; namely, because the rulers of this world, subjecting to themselves what belongs to the Church, do not fear to claim the Church itself for their jurisdiction. Consequently, oppressed by many hardships, the poor of those churches cannot serve almighty God as they ought [Col. 0631A].

## CHAPTER XXIX.—That preachers ought to live from the Gospel

Ordaining that all preachers should live from the Gospel, the Lord said: “The labourer is worthy of his wage” (Luke 10). Therefore the Apostle also says: “Those who serve at the altar share in what is offered on the altar” (1 Cor. 9).

The same blessed Apostle not only showed that preachers rightly live from the Gospel, but also permitted believers who had secular disputes to have them judged only before the saints, saying:

> “Does any one of you, having a dispute with another, dare to be judged before the unrighteous rather than before the saints? Do you not know that the saints will judge this world? And if this world is to be judged by you, are you unworthy to judge the smallest matters? Do you not know that we shall judge angels? How much more, then, secular matters? Therefore, if you have secular judgments, appoint as judges those who are held in contempt in the Church” (1 Cor. 6).

## CHAPTER XXX.—That ecclesiastical men are to be honoured with double honour

The holy Apostle, writing to Timothy that ecclesiastical men are to be honoured with both spiritual and temporal honour, commands:

> “Let the presbyters who govern well be considered worthy of double honour, especially those who labour in word and teaching. For Scripture says: ‘You shall not muzzle an ox while it treads out the grain’; and: ‘The labourer is worthy of his wage’” (1 Tim. 5).

## CHAPTER XXXI.—That bishops ought to have ecclesiastical property in their authority

[Col. 0631C]  
(From the Council of Antioch, canon 25.)

Let the bishop have authority over ecclesiastical property, in order to distribute it to all who are in need, with the greatest reverence and fear of God.

## CHAPTER XXXII.—That the Church ought also to possess temporal goods

(From the same canon.)

That the Church ought to possess lands is shown by the holy Fathers when they say concerning a bishop: “Let not the bishop administer badly those things that belong to the Church from lands or from any other ecclesiastical resource.”

## CHAPTER XXXIII.—That the disposal of Church property does not concern laymen

[Col. 0631D]  
(From the Council of Compiègne, canon 10.)

It has been decreed by synodal ordinance that laymen or secular persons should not suppose or presume that anything concerning men dedicated to God or the resources of the Church pertains to them, except reverence; for it is taught that God has indisputably entrusted the charge of administering all such things to their priests. Whoever presumes to act against this shall be struck with anathema.

## CHAPTER XXXIV.—On the same matter

(From the same council, canon 3.)

No power to dispose of men dedicated to God or ecclesiastical resources has ever been found to have been granted to laymen, however religious.

## CHAPTER XXXV.—An admonition that these rulings be rightly understood

One must consider with the utmost seriousness what presumption it is to wish to dispose of the Church’s ruler himself, when, under so great a threat, every power whatsoever to dispose in any way of the things belonging to the Church is utterly taken away [Col. 0632A].

## CHAPTER XXXVI.—Synodal decree of St Symmachus, Pope, concerning laymen who desire to regulate the Church on their own authority

(From the decrees of Pope Symmachus.)

In the time of St Symmachus, bishop of the Roman Church, a certain agreement was made by secular men, namely powerful men and magnates, among whom was present the patrician or prefect, at the shrine of the blessed apostle Peter. There the aforesaid men, as though led by zeal for Christianity and love of the holy Church, dared to decree that thereafter no Roman pontiff ought to be elected without them.

When Pope Symmachus learned of this, [Col. 0632B] he summoned a synod, and this written agreement was read in their hearing. In it they had decreed that no election of anyone ought to be held without their consultation. In the same way, concerning the disposition of ecclesiastical property—which canonically belongs to bishops, not laymen—they had affirmed that no bishop should do anything without them.

Hearing this, the venerable archbishops Laurence of Milan, Peter of Ravenna, and Eulalius of Syracuse, together with the whole holy synod, said:

> Laymen, nor any rulers whatever, however religious, may have any power to enact ordinances in the Church; nor can they possess any right to dispose of ecclesiastical resources. Therefore we decree this document to be of no force. And although certain bishops participated in it [Col. 0632C], it has no validity, because it is most manifestly contrary to the holy canons. For this is why a bishop is ordained: that he may have under his care the things belonging to the Church. This document had to be invalidated and reduced to nothing in the synodal assembly by every means, even if it could have had some basis for standing, lest it remain as a precedent for any laymen—however religious or powerful—to presume, in any city and in any way, to decree anything concerning ecclesiastical resources. For it is taught that God has indisputably entrusted the charge of administering these things to priests alone.

And Pope Symmachus, three archbishops, and sixty-five other bishops subscribed.

## CHAPTER XXXVII.—That rulers are not excluded from the election of pontiffs, but from lordship

Now consider these things, dearest brothers, you who are accustomed to rebuke us by saying: “How is it that all churches, because of the temporal possessions which they hold, do not belong to him to whom all the earth is subject? For if the people ought to be present and consent in the election of a pastor, how much more should the emperor or rulers?”

We greatly marvel at these words. For we do not exclude rulers from the election of pontiffs; rather, we say that they ought not by their own power to place pastors in the Church, whether through investiture or by any exercise of lordship. Instead, by the common election of the clergy and the consent of the people, both greater and lesser—among whom kings and rulers are counted—a pontiff ought to be elected in those churches of which they are counted more particularly as sons. There the emperor or his ruler ought to be present, not as a lord but as a son [Col. 0633A].

When an election is thus conducted, it is canonical and is attributed to the grace of the Holy Spirit. But when it comes about through human power, it is contrary to spiritual grace. Therefore a religious and pious emperor ought to uphold a canonical election so firmly that, if anyone attempts anything against it, he should judge that person to be pursued even with the material sword. In doing this he will properly fulfil his office. For his sword has been permitted to exist in the Church in order that those who do not fear the spiritual sword may be recalled to justice by fear of the material sword. Thus, when the apostles said that they had two swords, the Lord said: “It is enough” (Luke 22); that is, it is sufficient for you to uphold justice with the spiritual and material sword [Col. 0633B].

## CHAPTER XXXVIII.—What the canonical election of bishops is

Although we have already shown very fully what a canonical election is, let us nevertheless set forth the decree of the holy Council of Nicaea, which was made through the activity of Emperor Constantine and with his presence among them. The Council of Nicaea stands above all others, and all Christians ought in every respect to obey it as they obey the holy Gospel.

## CHAPTER XXXIX.—On the same matter

(From the Council of Nicaea, canon 3.)

A bishop ought above all to be ordained by all the bishops of the province. But if this is difficult either because of urgent necessity [Col. 0633C] or because of the length of the journey, at least three must by all means assemble for this purpose; and the absent bishops must likewise determine the matter and consent in writing. Then the ordination may be performed. But confirmation of the acts in each province is to be given by the metropolitan bishop.

## CHAPTER XL.—In what manner ecclesiastical office ought to be received and retained

(From the *Moralia* of St Gregory, Pope.)

Authority is rightly exercised only when it is retained not through love of it but through fear. In order that it may be rightly administered, it is first necessary that it be imposed not by desire but by necessity. Once received, it ought neither to be abandoned through fear nor embraced out of pleasure; lest one arrogantly grow proud under a show of humility by scorning, through flight, the order of divine dispensation, or cast off the yoke of the heavenly Ruler precisely because private rule over others delights him.

## CHAPTER XLI.—That emperors may not introduce bishops into the Church

The great Constantine was present at the Council of Nicaea, and yet the holy Fathers said that nothing in the ordination of a bishop belonged to him. But some say: ordination—that is, consecration—truly belongs to bishops alone; whereas the grant of temporal goods belongs to the emperor. Since the Church possesses many things belonging to the realm, they say, it must therefore be invested and endowed by the emperor.

Let such persons recognize that they do not speak rightly or peaceably [Col. 0634A]. For if a bishop must obtain the temporal things that the Church possesses through secular persons, and spiritual things through spiritual persons, then the Church is in some manner divided. But just as one who separates the body from the soul destroys a human being, so one who separates the Church’s material goods from its spiritual things destroys the Church. For just as the human soul [or: a human being; the text reads *anima homo*, perhaps for *anima hominis*] cannot subsist in this life without the body, so the holy Church cannot subsist in this world without material goods. For not only other gifts of God, but even baptism itself is not completed without the use of material things.

Therefore one who teaches that spiritual things ought to be obtained through spiritual persons, but material things through secular rulers, wishes as it were to establish two doors for Christ’s sheep; which is openly contrary to him who said that he himself was the one door (John 10) [Col. 0634B]. Hence the sacred canons command that rulers of the world, even very religious ones, are not to administer ecclesiastical matters; and that, if kings of the world wish to give any Church property to anyone, it is to be held invalid.

## CHAPTER XLII.—That the grace of God grants us temporal things as well

Therefore, dearest ones, attend to this, cast away empty disputes, and, giving to God alone what belongs to God, believe with full certainty that by his grace not only spiritual but also temporal things will be granted to you.

## CHAPTER XLIII.—On the Church’s possession

There are, however, some who say that churches are entitled only to tithes, firstfruits, and offerings, that is, only movable goods. But immovable property—namely castles, [Col. 0634C] villages, or fields—does not belong to the Church unless its pastor has received it from the emperor’s hand. Above we have shown in many ways, and by the various judgments of the saints, that they speak wrongly. Yet let us now add that everything once offered to God is permanently subjected to his right.

For holy Moses likewise says in Leviticus: “Everything consecrated to the Lord, whether a human being, an animal, or a field, may neither be sold nor redeemed. Whatever has once been consecrated shall be most holy to the Lord. All tithes of the land, whether from crops or the fruit of trees, belong to the Lord and are sanctified to him” (Lev. 27). And again: “Possession consecrated to the Lord belongs by right to the priests” (*ibid.*).

## CHAPTER XLIV.—How many portions ought to be made from the revenues of the Church

[Col. 0634D]  
(From an epistle of Pope Gelasius.)

It is fitting, as was reasonably decreed long ago, that four portions be made both from revenues and from the offerings of the faithful, according as the resources of each Church permit.

## CHAPTER XLV.—That what has once been given to the Church must never be taken away

(From the Council at Valence.)

Clergy also, or laymen, who persist in retaining offerings of their parents, whether donated or left by wills, or who think that what they themselves have given to God ought to be taken away from churches or monasteries, are, as the holy synod decreed, to be excluded from the churches as murderers of the poor until they make restitution.

## CHAPTER XLVI.—On temporal goods to be given to Christ

[Col. 0635A]  
(Augustine, in the book *On Heirs*.)

St Augustine says to a man possessing many of this world’s goods and unwilling to give to Christ:

> With what face do you seek an inheritance from Christ when you have defrauded Christ of your inheritance? He admonishes us, saying: “Lay up for yourselves treasures in heaven” (Matt. 6). And again: “For what does it profit a man if he gain the whole world but lose himself and suffer the loss of himself?” (Luke 9). And again: “Make for yourselves friends from the mammon of unrighteousness, so that when you fail, they may receive you into eternal dwellings” (Luke 16).

## CHAPTER XLVII.—On those who take away things given to the Church

(From the Rule of St Benedict.)

Whoever unjustly takes away Church property should fear, as St Benedict says, lest he perhaps suffer in his soul the death which Ananias and Sapphira suffered in their bodies. For Church property is consecrated to almighty God. Therefore one who seizes it, or gives it to someone else as though it were his own, and does not allow persons consecrated to God peacefully to possess it in accordance with God’s ordinance, commits sacrilege [Col. 0635B].

## CHAPTER XLVIII.—That all churches, with everything they possess, are under the bishop’s authority

(From the Canons of the Apostles.)

It is decreed in the holy canons that all churches, with their endowments, tithes, and all their property, are to remain under the authority of their own bishop and are always to pertain to his ordering or administration.

## CHAPTER XLIX.—That clerics’ possessions belong to those churches to which they are attached

(From the Council of Africa.)

It was resolved that bishops, presbyters, deacons, and any other clerics, once consecrated, should have all that they possess belong to the churches to which they are attached.

## CHAPTER L.—That all things offered to God are called offerings

The possessions of the faithful are rightly called offerings, because they are offered to the Lord. They ought not therefore to be diverted to uses other than those of the Church and of the aforesaid Christian brethren or persons in need, because they are the vows of the faithful and the price of sinners, entrusted to the Lord for accomplishing the aforesaid work.

(From the Decrees [Col. 0635D] of Pope Urban.)

But if anyone—God forbid!—acts otherwise, let him beware lest he incur the condemnation of Ananias and Sapphira and become guilty of sacrilege, as were those who withheld the proceeds of the aforesaid goods, of whom it is written in the Acts of the Apostles (Acts 5).

## CHAPTER LI.—How great an evil it is to take away Church property

Consider this, dearest sons, kings and rulers; consider it also, their counsellors. See what punishment those deserve who dare to take away what others have given to the Church. Those who wished to withdraw not another’s goods but their own, which they had promised, were punished with death.

## CHAPTER LII.—That ecclesiastical goods are gifts of God

(From an epistle of Pope Urban II.)

Teaching that no one ought to appropriate to his own right, either by force or by any payment, the external goods of the Church which derive from consecration, St Urban says:

> Whoever sells or buys Church property—which is the gift of God, since it is offered by God to the faithful and by the faithful to God; which is received freely from him and therefore ought to be given freely—for his own profit, thinks with Simon that “the gift of God may be possessed with money” (Acts 8) [Col. 0636A].

## CHAPTER LIII.—Why the ancient Fathers did not expressly oppose lay investitures of churches

Many wonder why the canons of the ancient holy Fathers do not expressly prohibit the investitures of churches being performed by laymen. But there is no cause for wonder in this matter. How could they prohibit something that had never been done or even heard of? It must also be understood that this seemed to them so absurd that they never believed so great a wickedness could arise in the holy Church.

What they recognized as possible, however, not modern people alone but even the Apostles themselves, as we said above, prohibited, wholly forbidding anyone to obtain the Church through secular powers. Whoever does this is commanded to be deposed and separated.

There is also another plausible reason why the holy Fathers were silent on this matter: they firmly believed that the promise of our Lord Jesus Christ, which he made to all his own, would remain until the end of the age: “Behold, I am with you all days, until the consummation of the age” (Matt. 28). He also says to the holy martyrs: “When you stand before kings and governors, do not consider how or what you are to speak. For in that hour what you are to speak will be given you. For it is not you who speak, but the Holy Spirit” (Mark 13). And again through the prophet: “I will not forsake you or abandon you” (Josh. 1; Heb. 3).

The holy Fathers knew, therefore, that if anything new arose, God himself, who dwelt in the hearts of his elect, would give counsel. That this was true is testified by the council of the holy Fathers, reverently held in the modern age, namely in the year 1078 from the Incarnation of the Lord, in the city of Rome under Gregory VII, pope of holy memory, in accordance with ancient ecclesiastical custom. In that synod the holy Fathers openly testified [Col. 0636D] that investitures of churches ought by no means to be performed. Since the practice had already taken deep root, they endeavoured to forbid it under a grave threat, saying:

## CHAPTER LIV.—That laymen must in no way dare to invest churches

Since we have learned that in many regions investitures of churches are being performed by lay persons contrary to the ordinances of the holy Fathers, and that from this many disturbances arise in the Church through which the Christian religion is trampled down, we decree that no layman shall receive investiture of a bishopric, abbey, or church from the hand of an emperor, king, or any lay person, male or female. If he presumes to do so, let him recognize that such investiture is void by apostolic authority, and that he is subject to excommunication [Col. 0637A] until he has made fitting satisfaction.

## CHAPTER LV.—That it is a grave crime for laymen to invest churches with staff or ring

Let us see, even from a lesser case, by way of example, how great a wickedness this is. Who would ever tolerate it if someone wished, before becoming a presbyter or afterward, to be invested by another with a chasuble or stole in respect of Church property which he ought to administer by virtue of the presbyteral order? Who would not pronounce him mad—or, if he sought to defend the act, a heretic? And how can this be tolerated in the case of a bishop or abbot, if it would be punished in the case of a presbyter as a crime previously unheard of?

[Col. 0637B] But perhaps some may say that these cases are not comparable, because the chasuble and stole are consecrated, whereas the staff and ring are not. Let them recognize that they do not speak rightly. For when a presbyter is ordained, he receives the chasuble and stole from the bishop’s hand and signifies by those outward signs that he has received the blessing of the presbyterate. Likewise, when a bishop is blessed, he receives the staff and ring from the archbishop’s hand: the staff indeed, that he may govern the people well; the ring, that he may know he has received the sign of the eternal mystery.

We know that both are derived from the Gospel. For the Lord commanded preachers to carry a staff, by which, as the blessed Father Augustine understands it, he showed that temporal support was owed to them from their preaching itself. Therefore we too ought to understand that bishops or abbots were instituted to receive the staff from a bishop’s hand when they are consecrated, so that they may know that they have then truly received from the Lord dominion over the temporal things which the Church possesses [Col. 0637C]. In the ring, moreover, the mystery of the most sacred union—namely, of Christ and his Church—is most certainly signified. These rites are performed in the bishop because he is joined to the holy Church in Christ’s stead.

Consider, therefore, how wrong and perverse it is to wish to receive these things from the hand of an emperor or any human power, whether before consecration or afterward; and desist from committing so great an iniquity.

## CHAPTER LVI.—Against those who say that we speak thus in order that the honour of the kingdom may be diminished
We therefore do not say this in order that the honour of the kingdom may thereby be diminished, but rather that it may be increased. [Col. 0637D] For, as we have taught above from the words of St Ambrose, we wish to render to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s, and to God the things that are God’s. For not only consecration belongs to God: things offered to God are also truly known to be God’s. We have proved above by many and varied evidences that the possessions of certain persons, once they have been devoted to God, belong to no emperor, king, or prince of this world whatever, but to God alone and to His Church. Yet we truly grant the Christian Caesar what is his, because we preach in every way that the Christian people should support him in justice. We even add from our own resources, because, when necessary, we render him the aid of charity. But what belongs to God we wish to render to God alone, because we desire that the elections of bishops [Col. 0638A] and abbots should be made by each Church, as has been established by the most holy Fathers. The person elected, moreover, ought to govern the Church’s property and administer it for the benefit both of souls and of bodies.

## CHAPTER LVII.—That the emperors of our time should deign to follow the example of the great Emperor Constantine.

But because examples often accomplish more than words, let the most Christian emperors consider the example of admirable humility set by the venerable and God-beloved Constantine, the first of the Roman emperors to embrace the faith of Christ. For, having believed in Christ, and declaring it utterly unworthy that an earthly emperor should have the seat of his kingdom where [Col. 0638B] almighty God had established the prince of holiness, the vicar of the blessed apostle Peter, he left all the western regions to the most blessed Pope Sylvester. Building a most noble city bearing his own name, he transferred his kingdom there, desiring, that is, that every earthly kingdom should be wholly subject to the true heavenly King, our Lord Jesus Christ. Therefore both he and all the peoples of the Roman Empire, who, through his example, holy exhortation, and zeal, had now begun to abandon idols and worship the living and true God, wished the holy Church to be held pre-eminent and illustrious in every respect, not only in spiritual but also in temporal matters.

For the time had now come when, according to the prophet, the holy Church was to be set in everlasting exaltation. Thus St Isaiah prophesied: “O afflicted one, tossed by the tempest” (Isa. LIV)—that is, oppressed by great tribulations—“because you were forsaken and hated, I shall set you in the exaltation of the ages; and you shall suck the milk of nations, and shall be nursed at the breast of kings” (Isa. LX). [Col. 0638C] Then, as is known, all these things began to be fulfilled; and St Augustine affirms this, nor is it doubted that they will be fulfilled through the Lord’s grace until the end of the age.

Meanwhile, compelled by charity, we who are weak and sinners desire to admonish the Lord’s holy priests that, although kings of the age have exalted them, they should nevertheless show in themselves the example of the Lord Christ, who, “though he was rich, became poor for our sake” (II Cor. VIII), and should by no means themselves administer temporal affairs. For these things were not bestowed upon them so that they might neglect spiritual matters and apply themselves to temporal ones, but so that they might strive ever more diligently to save the souls of sinners. For when secular judges seize criminals in an offence, serving not their salvation but their own greed, they despoil them of everything or even condemn them to death. As St Augustine plainly declares concerning such a sentence, those who are killed do not escape everlasting death.

Therefore the Church’s authority was given so that, when sinners for whom Christ died are apprehended in an offence, pastors might keep themselves from all greed and cruelty and endeavour to deal with them according to the canons of the holy Fathers in such a way that souls are saved; and so that, the more the holy Church [Col. 0639A] prevails in the world, the more earnestly it may labour for human salvation on behalf of the Creator of the world. But since we have touched briefly upon these matters, let us now bring forward further examples of Constantine’s holiness, in order, through Christ’s grace, to urge our God-fearing emperors of the present age to imitate the example of his venerable memory.

## CHAPTER LVIII.—An example of the great humility of Emperor Constantine.

When that venerable emperor grieved that the faith of Christ was being disturbed by the attacks of the Arians, he sent leading men from his court, gathered bishops from the whole world, and convened an ecumenical council. There the faith of Christ, preached by the apostles and prophets, was firmly confirmed by the voice of the saints, the grace of the Holy Spirit enlightening [Col. 0639B] them. There he displayed such humility that he sat in that council upon a lower seat than all the bishops. And when some of them accused others, he said: “You are gods; I am a man. It is therefore not fitting that a man should judge gods. Hear the case among yourselves and make peace. For if I saw a priest of God sinning, I would cover him with my cloak.”

This most religious man, the first of the Roman emperors openly to attain the faith of truth, granted those living throughout his empire permission not only to become Christians, but also decreed that churches might be built and estates bestowed. Finally, this same aforementioned prince established immense gifts and the construction of a shrine at the principal see of Peter, chief of the apostles, so that he abandoned the imperial seat over which Roman rulers had presided and granted it, as we have said, for the benefit of blessed Peter and his bishops. [Col. 0639C]

From that time onward religious persons consecrated not only the possessions and estates which they held, but even themselves, building basilicas on their own lands in honour of saints throughout the cities, and countless monasteries in which assemblies of those serving the Lord might gather. Finally, kings, governors, and magistrates not only granted this freedom from tribute [the text appears to read *a tributi*; perhaps *attribuerunt*, “assigned/granted”], but themselves also bestowed their own property throughout all the kingdoms of the earth upon God and His Church. The Council of Nicaea ordained that ecclesiastical persons should guard and administer all these things. That same [Col. 0639D] council also forbade secular business to clerics. Here it is plainly evident that ecclesiastical property, though it may appear worldly, truly belongs not to the world but to God. It ought therefore to be disposed and ordered not by the judgement and administration of an emperor, a king, or any secular person, but by those who have been consecrated to God.

## CHAPTER LIX.—An example of the true humility of Emperor Valentinian, and of the election of St Ambrose.

Since we have put forward the example of the most glorious Emperor Constantine, let us also set forth that of the most Christian Valentinian. As the Ecclesiastical History called the Tripartite relates, this religious emperor came from the East to the western regions after the death of Auxentius, teacher of Arian perfidy, who had ravaged the Church of Milan like a wolf. When, by God’s ordering, he wished a Catholic bishop to be consecrated there, he summoned the bishops and spoke to them as follows:

“You who are instructed in the divine words know plainly what sort of pontiff a bishop ought to be, and that he ought to govern those subject to him not by word alone but also by his manner of life; he must show himself an imitator of every virtue and possess good conduct as a witness to his teaching. Establish, therefore, in the episcopal see such a man that we also, who govern the Empire, may sincerely submit our heads to him, and, whenever we sin as men, may necessarily receive his admonitions as remedies from one who heals us.”

When the emperor had said this, the synod asked him rather to make the decision himself, since he was wise and pious. But he replied: “Such an election rests with you. [Col. 0640B] For you, possessing divine grace and shining with that splendour, will be able to choose better.”

Then the priests withdrew and deliberated concerning the episcopal see. When Ambrose—who had undertaken the administration of the consular provinces of Aemilia and Liguria—was elected by divine appointment, the emperor exclaimed: “I give thanks to you, Lord God Almighty and our Saviour, because I had entrusted bodies to this man, but you have entrusted souls to him; and you have shown that my judgement accords with justice.” When St Ambrose was distressed at what had occurred, as he himself wrote in his letters, the emperor encouraged him and said: “Do not fear, because God, who has chosen you, will always help you; and I too shall always be your helper and defender, as befits my rank.”

St Ambrose, therefore, as is known to those who have read his life or his own letters, preserving the dignity of his office intact, never flattered emperors or judges, but always, with God’s help, secured by priestly authority those things that were necessary. [Col. 0640C]

## CHAPTER LX.—How St Ambrose excommunicated Emperor Theodosius.

Accordingly, he publicly excommunicated the religious ruler Theodosius and separated him from the Church because of the destruction of the city of Thessalonica. This most devout emperor, greatly fearing God in His priest, performed public penance and washed away with tears the evil he had done. Because of this humility, therefore, the Lord granted him victory over the tyrant Eugenius.

He always feared the sentence of excommunication so greatly that, on one occasion, when a monk had dared to excommunicate him over a complaint which he had not promptly settled, he feared the excommunication made in the monk’s name and by his authority. Although it was already the hour of the meal, he would not eat until the monk was found and absolved him. The monk had written out the sentence of excommunication on a little paper (*pyttacium*) and had thrown it down where it might be found by the emperor, then gone away. Although many bishops were present and gave him permission, together with the bishop of the aforesaid monk, he did not consent before the monk was found. Therefore, from this let magnates, [Col. 0641A] princes, and all peoples see how greatly the excommunication of bishops should be feared, if a most Christian emperor feared so much the excommunication of a single member of the monastic order.

## CHAPTER LXI.—On Emperor Marcian.

Marcian also, a Catholic emperor in the time of Pope St Leo, convened an ecumenical council. Humbly submitting himself to the holy bishops, he and his wife set forth their faith in that council with great devotion.

## CHAPTER LXII.—An example of the obedience of Emperor Charles.

Charles also, king of the Franks, as is known, met blessed Pope Adrian at Rome with great humility; and after kissing all the steps of St Peter’s, [Col. 0641B] he threw himself at the holy pope’s knees. Having wrested with a strong arm from the Lombards the cities and fortresses which they held, he restored them to the same apostle of God for perpetual possession. The holy pope made him Roman patrician; and afterward, as is said, when successes followed, he was also raised to be emperor of the Romans.

## CHAPTER LXIII.—Where Emperor Charles promises to correct the matter concerning which he had been admonished by the Apostolic See.

When, as often happens, bishops later flattered him excessively and attended his retinue beyond measure, he was reproved for this; correcting himself, he spoke as follows:

“On a second occasion, instructed by apostolic authority and the admonition of many bishops because of a more abundant excess, and taught by the rules of the holy canons, and indeed with the counsel of all our nobles, we correct ourselves and give an example to our successors. We wish that no priest should proceed on campaign, except only two or three bishops chosen by the rest, for blessing, preaching, and reconciliation of the people; and with them priests chosen to give penance to the people, celebrate Masses, care for the sick, administer the anointing of sacred oil with holy prayers, and above all ensure that no one departs from this world without viaticum.”

## CHAPTER LXIV.—On the same matter.

See how Charles of venerable memory, reproved by the Apostolic See and other holy bishops [Col. 0641D] because he exercised too much domination over bishops, did not take it arrogantly, but, showing himself corrected, also set forth an authoritative ruling.

## CHAPTER LXV.—An admonition to emperors that they should follow the examples of the preceding emperors.

Therefore let the emperors, kings, and princes of our time follow him; and concerning matters for which they are reproved by the Apostolic See and other saints, let them not resist in pride, but rather correct themselves by humbling themselves, so that they may deserve to find Christ’s grace.

## CHAPTER LXVI.—On the same matter.

Let them follow the example of Constantine, to whom God granted the whole Roman world in its entirety because he subjected himself to the holy Church. Let them imitate Theodosius, Justinian, and the other faithful emperors, [Col. 0642A] who, by serving the holy Church, merited not only an earthly kingdom but also a heavenly one.

## CHAPTER LXVII.—Why St Adrian could permit emperors to invest churches.

Let not religious emperors therefore say: “The Apostolic See injures our established right, since it does not observe toward us what the most holy Pope Adrian gave to Charles.” For it is not credible that St Adrian could ever have granted that the Church of God should be invested by laymen, except perhaps solely as a sign of guardianship. For he not only did not grant that any prince should exercise lordship over the Church of God, but expressly forbade it with a grave threat, saying:

“It is not lawful for an emperor, or for anyone who preserves piety, to presume anything contrary to the commands of the Godhead, nor to do anything [Col. 0642B] opposed to evangelical, prophetic, or apostolic rules. An unjust judgement or unjust decree, carried out through royal fear or command, shall have no force; nor shall anything stand which is contrary to divine authority and the canons of the holy Fathers; and whatever has been done by heretics shall be wholly annulled.”

## CHAPTER LXVIII.—What investiture signifies, and how grave a crime it is to seek to invest God’s sanctuary.

We must investigate what investiture signifies and why it is so called. It is called investiture because, by a sign that belongs to our legal right, we show that we have given something to someone. When we wish to grant to someone, for possession on our behalf, something that is ours, we take care to invest him with it, signifying by that sign both that what we give belongs to us by right and that the recipient possesses through us what is ours. By the very term, therefore, it is most plainly demonstrated how great an impiety it is to desire to invest God’s sanctuary.

The prophet, with a grave threat, declares that it is a great sacrilege for any person to wish to possess God’s sanctuary, saying: “Make their princes like Oreb and Zeb, Zebee and Salmana, all their princes, who said: ‘Let us possess God’s sanctuary as an inheritance’” (Ps. LXXXII). He adds that what should justly happen to them for this iniquity: “My God, make them like a wheel,” and so forth until the end of the psalm. [Col. 0642C] In this passage one may also perceive that, just as Gehazi and Simon were cursed by the prophet Elisha and the apostle Peter—one of whom wished to sell the grace of God (Acts VIII), the other to earn it (IV Kings V)—so too those who seek to claim God’s sanctuary as their inheritance were punished with an eternal curse by holy David, filled with the same Spirit. One should further consider that even if this could by some argument be defended as not simoniacal, it would nevertheless have to be avoided in every way and forbidden to all Christians, because it is deserving of eternal curse.

## CHAPTER LXIX.—Why the investiture of churches ought not to take place.

It must also be considered that, even if these things had truly been granted to emperors by saints and could at that time have been done very usefully and rightly, nevertheless, since so great a presumption has arisen from it that the Church of God is sold like a secular commodity, or granted to someone on account of human favour—and especially since this is done by laymen, for which clerics, if they dared to do it, ought to be deposed from every ecclesiastical rank—it ought in every respect to be corrected. For not only would what St Adrian had done, if he had done it, have to be corrected in every way; even if one found an apostle or prophet saying something by which the Church of God would be destroyed (which God forbid), it would have to be utterly rejected.

Accordingly, the blessed Apostle Paul, providing for the Church of God in rejecting Jewish baptism [the text corrects *Judaismo* to *Judaico*], did not spare even the most blessed Peter (Gal. II). King Hezekiah, also of holy memory, did this: seeing that the Jewish people, contrary to divine law, venerated the bronze serpent, he did not fear to break the work of Moses, the man of God, and commanded the people to worship God alone (IV Kings XVIII). [Col. 0643B] On this point the holy Fathers understand what we have said above, declaring:

“For this is the greatest proof that can advance the edification of the Church, if there is one able to observe why Hezekiah, with great praise for himself and for the salvation of souls, destroyed what Moses, by God’s command, had made for the salvation of this people. For who does not know that Moses was of greater merit than King Hezekiah? For in the Book of Numbers the Lord said to Aaron and Miriam concerning Moses: ‘Hear my words: if there be a prophet among you, the Lord shall make himself known to him in a vision, and shall speak to him in a dream. But not so my servant Moses in all my house: mouth to mouth shall I speak to him. He sees the Lord in visible form and not through riddles’” (Num. XII).

For because Moses, as has already been said, had made the serpent at God’s command so that the people might not perish by serpentine death when they looked upon it, the people began to venerate and worship that serpent because God had commanded it to be made. Thus, whereas their fathers had escaped death only for a time, yet were to die again, they secured for themselves death anew, dying in soul forever. Therefore one man destroyed what the other had made by God’s command. Hence this principle must have great authority in the Church: if some of our predecessors or elders have done things which in their time could be without blame and superstition, but later begin to engender [an evil consequence is unspecified], they must be destroyed by successors without delay and with great authority.

## CHAPTER LXX.—The Roman pontiff must strive with the utmost zeal to ensure that the institutions of the saints are preserved.

There are some who say that it has always been lawful for the Roman pontiff to establish new laws. We not only do not deny this; we strongly affirm it. But it must be understood above all that he can establish new laws in matters on which the holy Fathers, and especially the apostles and evangelists, have said nothing. But where the Lord, or His apostles, and the holy Fathers who followed them, have expressly determined something by a definitive judgement, there the Roman pontiff must not enact a new law, but rather must confirm, unto life and blood, what has been preached. For if he strove to destroy what the apostles and prophets taught (which God forbid), he would be proved not to render a judgement but rather to err. But let this be far from those who have always guarded the Church of the Lord most excellently against the snares of wolves.

## CHAPTER LXXI.—Why, because of the earthly possessions held by the Church, it should not be subjected to the emperors’ jurisdiction.

Let us therefore consider further whether the proposition is true which some have propounded: that because of the temporal possessions which the Church holds, bishops and abbots ought to receive investiture from the emperor, that is, the prince of earthly things. That this ought not to be so is sufficiently clear from what has been said above. Let us add further that, as holy Pope Urban, blessed Melchiades, and his successor the most holy Sylvester say, the practice by which the Church holds earthly possessions was instituted by the holy apostles at the time when each of the faithful sold his possessions and laid their price at the apostles’ feet (Acts IV). [Col. 0644B]

The holy apostles did this only in Judaea, because they knew that they would not remain there long. But among the Gentiles, where they knew the Church would remain until the end of the age, both they and their apostolic successors received the offerings of the faithful as they stood, so that the poor might more suitably be fed from their fruits. Therefore, just as the apostles received what was brought to them without the command or any investiture of an earthly prince, so they taught their disciples—the holy bishops—to do likewise, while observing, as the Apostle says, that they should render “tribute to whom tribute is due, tax to whom tax is due, honour to whom honour is due” (Rom. XIII).

The Lord Himself did this, paying the tax for Himself and Peter (Matt. XVII), though He had first answered that He owed them nothing. As blessed Jerome says, Christ pays the tax for us just as He bore the cross. Shall we not pay tax in honour of Him? Yet what we owe Christian princes is this: that we should not cease to assist them by prayer and preaching. But we ought neither to give the goods of the poor—that is, the possessions of churches—to them, nor even convert them to our own private uses, except only so far as we may, having food and clothing from the Church, be able to serve it. [Col. 0644D] For, as the same St Jerome says, the Lord paid the tax not from the money-bag which Judas carried, but from another source by a miracle, because He considered it wicked to convert the goods of the poor to His own use or that of His followers; and He provided us with the same example.

## CHAPTER LXXII.—That pastors ought to have care not only for souls but also for bodies.

It should also be known that not only ought this wrong not to be inflicted upon God and His Church—that a bishop or abbot, chosen by it as pastor without the investiture of secular persons, should not possess what belongs to it—but it would not be just to forbid even an orphan or widow to administer their own goods, lawfully inherited, through one of their servants and determine that they should serve him from them. [Col. 0645A] What just judge would ever commend that? Yet the holy Church commands this of one of its servants when it chooses a pastor for the very purpose that he may care for its weak members, both souls and bodies.

What servant of God would praise a condition in which a man can do nothing in the Church without the command or investiture of a human power, when the Apostle himself says: “A bishop must be blameless, as God’s steward” (Tit. I)? Blessed Apostle Peter commands bishops to care not only for souls but also for bodies, saying: “Feed the flock of God which is among you, providing with all solicitude willingly, not for the sake of shameful gain” (I Pet. V). From what then will they feed it if they do not possess what belongs to the Church? Therefore let all earthly rulers incline their ear to these holy admonitions, and let them strive not merely not to take away anything of their own from the holy Church [the text evidently requires *non*, “not”], but also to give it their own property, so that they may receive eternal reward from Him who promised His faithful: “You shall receive a hundredfold and possess eternal life” (Matt. XIX). [Col. 0645B]

## CHAPTER LXXIII.—That no bishop should subject any church to laymen.

It is evident that the gifts of the Holy Spirit shine forth especially in ecclesiastical offices. Above them all episcopal grace is pre-eminent. It ought to arise not by appointment of kings or princes, but through the election of the clergy and the petition of all the people. The judgement concerning this election belongs so properly to the lord apostolic [the pope] and his vicars or archbishops [Col. 0645C] that they should on no account grant it to any man outside their order.

For the salvation of their souls, princes ought to choose a watchman who is able to see and announce the sword coming upon themselves and their people. Likewise, no people ought by its own power or authority to bring anyone into the Church. For the Holy Spirit cannot be subjected to anyone so as to grant a spiritual gift to one to whom a prince, serving greed and desiring to possess God’s sanctuary as an inheritance, has presumed, for his own honour rather than God’s, to give an investiture in an ecclesiastical prelacy. Whoever thinks this believes that the Holy Spirit, Creator of all things, can be subjected to a human being; and, as Pope St Urban teaches, it is manifest that even to imagine this is an unheard-of crime and exceeds Arian impiety. Therefore hands should not be laid upon such a person; rather, unless he repents from the heart, it must be preached that eternal condemnation hangs over him.

The holy Fathers of Chalcedon also show that ecclesiastical matters must be handled holily and purely, when they say:

“If any bishop performs an ordination for money and reduces to a price the grace which cannot be sold, and ordains for money a bishop, priest, deacon, or anyone else numbered among the clergy; or if, for the profit of his most shameful gain, he promotes for money a steward, advocate, or any person subject to the rule: the person proved guilty of attempting this shall incur peril to his own rank; and the person ordained shall gain nothing from this ordination or promotion conducted by commerce, but shall be excluded from the dignity or office which he sought with money. If anyone has acted as intermediary in such shameful and impious giving or receiving, if he is a cleric, let him fall from his own rank; if a layman or monk, let him be anathematized.”

If, then, according to the decree, a lay intermediary who is appointed steward—that is, the Church’s *oeconomus* or administrator—for money must be anathematized, should one consent to a lay coercer in order that he may subject the whole Church to his own jurisdiction? Is someone who receives a bishopric from him to be consecrated? For even if he sought this solely for God’s honour, he ought by no means to obtain it, because, as we have already said, it does not belong at all to his office.

What some say—that this belongs to the emperor because he has been anointed with sacred oil to kingship—wholly fails to accord with the truth. He is not anointed to dispose of bishoprics or abbeys, but so that, strengthened by the grace of the Holy Spirit signified through that anointing, he may most rightly uphold God’s justice. But when even to a very religious emperor, who does not seek this for the honour of his kingdom, it is granted that clergy or people may not dare make an election of prelates without his permission; that, if they do, he may alter it at his pleasure; and that no bishop may dare consecrate the person elected before he has been invested by the emperor with staff and ring—is this canonical? [Col. 0646C] Where are such canons found? Since the sacred canons anathematize secular persons who subject churches to their own jurisdiction, do they not subject the keys of the kingdom of heaven to his dominion if they grant him this? And if under no appearance of religion this prerogative can be granted to him, ought anyone in any way consent to one who seeks it for the honour of his kingdom and attempts to obtain it by force?

## CHAPTER LXXIV.—Examples proving that the holy Roman Church has always ordered the greater Churches of God.

As we have taught above, the holy Roman and Apostolic Church has always endeavoured to order and invest all the greater Churches of God by itself, and not through any laymen—even very religious ones. This was unheard of among the ancient Fathers and has, in modern times, crept in rather than been introduced in an orderly fashion. Hence the apostle Peter, when founding the Church of Alexandria, sent the evangelist Mark there; he gave the pastoral staff with his own hands to Hermagoras, patriarch of Aquileia; he sent Apollinaris as archbishop to Ravenna; and commissioned Martial to Limoges. His successor Clement sent Dionysius to the Church of Paris. Gregory I [Note: [Col. 0645D], read II.] taught the people of Milan to choose as worthy successor St Ambrose.

And why say more? The day would fail before examples could be exhausted in which [Col. 0647A] it is plainly shown that the holy Roman Church, either by itself or through its vicars or metropolitans appointed by it, has always established pastors for every holy Church of God. Therefore let what has been established until now be maintained with God’s help to the end, so that apostolic teaching may always receive increase through the grace of the Holy Spirit.

## CHAPTER LXXV.—On excommunication and the tares.

It must meanwhile be noted that some contend that we act contrary to the Gospel parable in which the Lord commanded that the tares should not be uprooted (Matt. XIII), when we subject persons worthy of excommunication to excommunication. They also say that St Augustine contradicts this in the place where he says that unity must not be cut off: “The wicked are to be struck, not cut off.” To them the first answer must be this: if heretics and wicked persons are not to be excommunicated, why did Father Augustine himself, together with the legates of the holy Roman Church and all his fellow-bishops, excommunicate Pelagius and Celestius, who were introducing a new heresy into the holy Church of God, and separate them from the Church of God? Why did he hold the Donatists themselves—against whom he says these and many similar things—to be excommunicated with the whole Church of God, and refuse them communion unless they first repented of their impious schism and were reconciled by the laying on of hands? [Col. 0647B]

## CHAPTER LXXVI.—That the Lord Himself commanded excommunication, and the difference between excommunicating and uprooting.

[Col. 0647C] Since we have prolonged our discourse, let us state briefly the judgement on this matter, lest we seem to linger over what is evident. The same Lord who here expounds this parabolically elsewhere expressly commands excommunication: “A brother who is corrected by the Church and does not obey, let him be to you as a heathen and a tax collector” (Matt. XVIII). Hence it is plainly apparent that excommunication is one thing and uprooting another. For the person excommunicated, as the Apostle says, is excommunicated so that his spirit may be saved on the day of the Lord (I Cor. V). Excommunication is discipline, not uprooting—unless perhaps it results from contempt and pride.

The Donatists, however, so far as lay in their power, had uprooted from God’s field the whole Church spread throughout the world, believing themselves alone to be truly Christians. This evil had grown so great that they dared even to rebaptize Catholics; and no wise person can fail to know that this truly is uprooting. This schism arose because they accused Caecilian of having unjustly assumed the bishopric of Carthage, an accusation which they could not prove before an ecumenical council held at Rome. Therefore Caecilian was confirmed in the episcopate by the judgement of bishops. Angered by this, they created a schism and separated themselves from all the Christian people on account of a false accusation against one man.

Hence blessed Augustine says very often: “Even if these charges were true, you ought not for that reason to separate yourselves from all Christians. The wicked are to be borne; they may be in the field with you, but by no means in the granary.” Seeing this evil, the holy Catholic Church of God convened councils and excommunicated them. They did not fear, but began to persecute the Church of God spiritually and bodily. When emperors who worshipped Christ saw this, they enacted by law that heretics should lose all that they possessed and should never remain settled in any fixed place. Consequently many of them were converted; and through the severity of the laws and the clemency of the priests, who, to invite them to concord, decreed that bishops and clerics should be received in their own rank provided only that, repenting of the past, they should amend their conduct in the future. [Col. 0648A]

## CHAPTER LXXVII.—The purpose for which excommunication ought to be imposed.

[Col. 0648B] Therefore, contrary to what they say, we do not uproot them when we subject them to excommunication; rather, we impose discipline upon them so that, abandoning the evil they commit, they may most rightly uphold God’s justice with us. Some of them, however, uprooted and condemned themselves by appointing other bishops for themselves—some already condemned, others entangled in crimes.

Although we too are sinners, we show ourselves in this matter to be true Catholics, obedient to Christ and following the example of the saints, who said: “If anyone called a brother among you is a fornicator, adulterer, or drunkard, do not even take food with such a person” (I Cor. V). And again: “If anyone comes to you and does not bring this teaching, do not even say ‘Hail’ to him; for whoever says ‘Hail’ to him shares in his evil works” (II John). [Col. 0648C] Therefore we excommunicate them so that, abandoning the evils which they commit, their spirit may be saved on the day of the Lord (I Cor. V).

For we do not do this in order to profess falsely that we are without sin—for the holy apostles themselves confessed this, saying, “For we all stumble in many things” (Jas. III). We do it solely because the Church’s discipline cannot be maintained without severity: we subject them temporarily to excommunication so that, compelled by the fear of excommunication, all may return to justice. And we do not communicate with them so that by this they may know how grave it is, through the deserts of sins, to be separated eternally from the communion of the saints.

## CHAPTER LXXVIII.—A bishop cannot delegate his authority in ecclesiastical matters to laymen.

But, to return to the point from which we have wandered a little, it must be known that there are some who say that the Roman pontiff can delegate to the emperor his own role in the prerogative of investing bishops. Let them consider what the holy Fathers have pronounced on this matter, and endeavor to correct what they rashly assert. For they established it thus, saying:

> By a new proceeding we have learned that certain persons of our body have, contrary to ecclesiastical custom, appointed stewards in divine matters. Therefore, after deliberating together, we have chosen that each of us, in accordance with the decrees of the Fathers of Chalcedon, appoint for himself a steward from his own clergy. For it is improper that a layman should be the vicar of a bishop [Col. 0649A], or that secular persons should judge in the Church. In one and the same office there ought not to be a divergent profession. This is also prohibited in the divine law, Moses saying: “You shall not plough with an ox and an ass together” (Deut. XXII); that is, you shall not associate persons of differing profession in one office. Hence we must obey both the divine books and the commands of the holy Fathers, establishing that those who are joined to pontiffs in the administrations of the Church must differ neither in profession nor in dress. For those whose pursuits and vows are different cannot be restrained and joined together. If any bishop, after these things, entrusts an ecclesiastical matter to lay administration, or believes that it may be governed without the attestation of a steward, he shall truly be judged, as a despiser of the canons and a defrauder of ecclesiastical [Col. 0649B] goods, guilty before Christ concerning the goods of the poor; and he shall also remain liable to the council.

## CHAPTER LXXIX.—Against flatterers who strive to give authority contrary to the canons.

Therefore let those who maintain what we have set forth above—namely, that the lord Apostolic may grant to the emperor bishoprics or abbeys to be appointed or invested—consider what these holy Fathers have pronounced on the matter. They did not even grant a bishop authority to appoint a layman as steward of the Church. Let them cease to speak against apostolic ordinances and to destroy the souls of the unlearned. For concerning them the prophet Ezekiel says: “Woe to those who sew cushions beneath every elbow” (Ezek. XIII).

## CHAPTER LXXX.—Whether anyone ought to be permitted to appoint to a church for the sake of earthly honor.

[Col. 0649C]

Let the most blessed Fathers, Apostolics of the supreme see, also deign to consider how great an execration their predecessor Urban of venerable memory judged the selling or buying of ecclesiastical offices to deserve, when greed rules through the price of a gift from hand, tongue, or service. For he openly testified that this is simony, saying:

> Whoever bestows or acquires ecclesiastical things, not for the purpose for which they were instituted but for his own profit, by a gift of speech, undue service, or money, is a Simonist; since Simon’s principal intention was mere greed for money—that is, idolatry—as the Apostle says: “And covetousness, which is the service of idols” [Col. 0649D] (Col. III).

And now, when someone does not indeed buy a church for a price, but—what is even abominable to say—obtains it by the sword, and through the greed of his own ambition invests and rules, does he not imitate, or even surpass, Simon’s wickedness? For Simon, although he wished to buy with money, nevertheless did not extort by force.

But if someone, free from the evil of invasion and not coveting monetary wealth, nevertheless, through an excessive ambition for the loftiness of earthly honor—which the blessed Father Gregory most openly defines as greed—presumes to invest a church for the sake of his earthly honor, he does not escape the vice of the Simoniacal heresy. For Simon was condemned because through greed he thought that he could possess God’s gift. Therefore that person too is held fast in the same snare of earthly ambition [Col. 0650A] who, through greed for his own honor and not God’s, thinks that ecclesiastical offices can be given or received.

Moreover, the recipient, even if he were distinguished by good morals and otherwise canonically elected, must by no means be consecrated because of the giver’s secular ambition and his own faithless supposition—that through greed for elevation and domination he can receive God’s gift. For if such a man is consecrated, the example of blessed Peter is not observed. For when someone wishes to choose a bishop, not for the salvation of his soul, but by investing—that is, by exercising dominion—to give someone the insignia of episcopal office, and seeks his consecration, what else does he wish except that the one upon whom he himself has laid hands—that is, to whom he has given power over the Church’s earthly goods—should receive the Holy Spirit?

The example of the blessed Apostle testifies that this must not be granted him, when Peter said to Simon, who wished this: “May your money be with you unto destruction, because you thought that God’s gift could be possessed by money” (Acts VIII). For what else does this man suppose except that God’s gift is possessed through greed, when he supposes that one can become bishop to whom he himself, excessively desiring eminence and earthly honor, has given investiture of the episcopal office—thus claiming for himself what belongs to God? But we have already taught above sufficiently and abundantly that not only spiritual things, but also bodily things possessed by the Church, belong to God. For we have demonstrated from the sayings of both the Old and New Testaments and of the holy Fathers that everything offered to God is sacred.

## CHAPTER LXXXI.—Against those who think that the emperor invests churches justly because some of the ancients who were invested were saints.

Certain persons produce some privileges of holy Apostolics, under whose protection they think they can overthrow the canonical reasoning which we defend and rightly reduce it to nothing. To them the first thing to be said is that “a disciple is not above his master” (Luke VI). No disciple can destroy what the holy Apostles ordained. If anyone attempts it, Christian reason declares that he acts unjustly.

If, therefore, it is true that saints enacted these privileges, it must first be understood that they did this for no other reason than that discord, which often tends to arise in an election, might be expelled by royal authority. Their own writings [Col. 0650D] declare this to be true: they acknowledge that they acted thus so that great discord, which often arose in an election, might be calmed by royal provision, and so that the Simoniacal heresy, which sometimes defiled holy order, might in no respect steal in.

But when what they had thought would be a remedy began to break out into a deadly wound and to seize almost the whole body of the Church, it is manifest that it was justly forbidden. For, as we have already said, they had granted this so that charity might endure more firmly and Simoniacal ambition might have no place at all. But when death began to enter by the very means through which it was thought to be expelled, other holy Apostolics worthily and justly prohibited it, because they saw that it harmed Christ’s bride.

Therefore, just as those earlier men granted this for God’s honor and not for human honor, so these later men, seeing it injure the Church, prohibited it for God’s honor. The holy intention of both parties was one and the same: the salvation of the Church and the honor of God. As what the former did could then be preserved because it caused no harm, so it must now be abolished because it most certainly does harm. For this purpose pastors possess the keys of the Church: that they may remove what harms and introduce what helps. What is known to furnish support to most evil trafficking must be removed from the holy Church, as the Lord himself commanded, saying: “Take these things away; do not make my Father’s house a house of trade” (John II).

It must not, therefore, be thought that the former granted this so that someone, using secular powers, might obtain a church through them, and that the latter corrected something which those earlier men had done wrongly. Rather, both sought, as we have said, that peace might be maintained more firmly and the Simoniacal heresy confounded. For both knew and observed the decrees of the ancient Fathers Clement and Alexander, who command in their Decrees:

> If any bishop, using secular powers, obtains a church through them, let him be deposed and separated, together with all who communicate with him.

And rightly so. For episcopal office ought to arise not from human will but from divine calling, as the Apostle says of Aaron (Heb. V). For he is truly called by God whom the clergy and Christian people—in whose hearts God dwells—have chosen purely and simply for the salvation of their souls.

But there are those who say: “Then are not some of the ancients, who received investitures of churches from kings, saints?” We answer: we do not deny that they are saints, but believe that they are. Yet because they did this simply, it was forgiven them, through the cooperation of divine grace with their other holy works, according to the Psalmist’s proclamation: “Blessed are those whose iniquities have been forgiven and whose sins have been covered” (Ps. XXXI).

So too, as we know on the testimony of Saint Augustine, it happened to blessed Cyprian in regard to baptism; nevertheless, he remained in holiness through the bond of charity and good works. For the investiture of churches was not a heresy in its first stages, because it was done simply and contention had not yet grown. For new opinions, as blessed Augustine says of the Pelagians, who defend free will too greatly, are not heresies when rejected by the Church unless they grow through contention. When those defending them have been reproved, if they withdraw they are Catholics; if they persist and defend them, they become heretics.

We know that the same has happened in the present matter. In its first stages, when this began, it was a vice; but after it was forbidden in general synods held under the Apostolics Gregory VII and Urban II, and now is defended not only in words but even striven for by arms, how grave a crime it is becomes plainly apparent. For is not one ambitious who desires to make investitures of churches in order to seek greater worldly honor, to have more righteous people subjected to himself, and to acquire this world’s riches? And what is the vice of the Simoniacal heresy except ambition for spiritual honor for the advantage or glory of this world?

Spiritual honor, however, is understood not only in the laying on of hands, but also in the external ecclesiastical things which, according to Saint Paschal I, bishop of the apostolic see, ought to result from consecration. And rightly so. For as the body is enlivened and governed by the soul, so the Church’s material things are sanctified by the gifts of the Holy Spirit; and to the person to whom spiritual holiness is granted, material things are rightly granted as well. For just as the soul in this life does not govern without the body, so the holy Church does not in the present use spiritual things without material gifts.

Thus, one who buys a human being, although he seems to have bought the body and not the soul, is truly convicted of having bought the soul also, because he does not delight in possessing the body without the soul but hastens to bury it. In the same way, one who strives to obtain the Church’s material things by force, or to possess God’s gift with money—or, what is worse, by violence—is thereby shown to will such possession.

Therefore, when the emperor or some prince, striving to obtain the investiture of churches—the sign by which possession and dominion are displayed—grants it for his own glory and not God’s, he bestows consecration too for his own glory. For the one who is invested is consecrated, and is consecrated because he has been invested. It is therefore plain that his consecration also is bestowed for worldly glory—that is, for “the lust of the eyes” and “the pride of life,” which are not from the Father but from the world.

It is certain, however, that the Holy Spirit is not given to the person who, invested, has dared to seek consecration by the Holy Spirit while pursuing worldly pride and greed, which plainly are not from the Father. For “the Holy Spirit of discipline will flee deceit” (Wis. II). For this is truly a counterfeit of discipline: when anyone thinks that he ought to be consecrated because he has been elected by the people and invested by the king. But the discipline of the Holy Spirit is that every pastor be chosen, purely and simply for the salvation of souls, by all the clergy of each individual church; and all the children of that church which is to be provided with a pastor ought most devoutly to assent and obey for the salvation of their souls.

The discernment of this election has been granted by God not to any human power but to the metropolitan bishop. Once the election has been proved canonical, the person chosen should be invested and consecrated not by the emperor but by the archbishop, who blesses him in Christ’s stead. Once ordained and consecrated, he should take care fully to render to the emperor whatever the Church entrusted to him has from ancient times canonically owed, unless perhaps the emperor has remitted it for the remedy of his own soul.

But the most devout emperor should strive most earnestly not to burden the Church but rather to serve it as his spiritual mother. For he is not anointed with holy oil in order to dominate the Church, but so that, serving Christ the true King, he may protect Christ’s bride from the snares of the wicked by human power. The election of abbots, moreover, belongs only to monks, as the Rule of the most holy Father Benedict bears witness.

[Col. 0653A] Behold, this is the discipline of the Holy Spirit: that a pastor of the Church ought to be elected. But whoever fights against this authority, introduces a pastor into the Church by his own novel authority, is himself introduced in that way, or—assenting to such persons—presumes to consecrate the introduced person, plainly acts against the discipline of the Holy Spirit.

## CHAPTER LXXXII.—A true and certain demonstration that, just as one ordained through greed for money is a Simonist, so too one ordained through greed for eminence is most certainly proved a Simonist.

It is manifest that the ancient holy doctors of the Church left us their teaching most fully concerning the matters that were disputed in their own days. Thus, in the days of the holy Gregory II [Note: [Col. 0653D] Thus the manuscript; but I seems to be the correction.] and Ambrose, kings defended the Church against heresies; but the clerical order had already declined into the greed of ambition to such a degree that, after a price had been received, the laying on of hands was sold by some. Others, though not selling so openly, nevertheless did not hesitate to confer holy orders or honors for human favor.

For this reason, in their teachings, or even in those of other doctors whom the holy Church now holds in special esteem, one scarcely finds the new and most wicked head of the hydra of the present time refuted. Yet one who, more subtly instructed by divine inspiration, desires to discover in their teaching how abominable this is, is plainly granted, by divine grace, to see it.

For blessed Father Gregory says, when speaking in his exposition of the Gospel concerning the Lord’s temptation:

> The ancient enemy rose against the first human being, our parent, in three temptations; for he tempted him by vainglory, gluttony, and greed, and in tempting conquered him, because through consent he subjected him to himself. He tempted him by gluttony when he showed him the food of the forbidden tree and urged him to eat, saying: “Taste” (Gen. III). He tempted him by vainglory when he said: “You shall be like gods” (ibid.). And he tempted him by greed for advancement when he said: “Knowing good and evil” (ibid.); for greed is not only for money but also for exaltation. For greed is rightly so called when eminence is sought beyond measure. If rapacity did not belong to greed for honor, Paul would never have said of the only-begotten Son of God: “He did not deem equality with God a thing to be seized” [Col. 0653D] (Phil. II). Therefore the devil drew our parent into pride by inciting him to greed for exaltation. But by the same means through which he laid low the first human being, he was overcome when tempting the second human being. He tempts by gluttony when he says: “Command these stones to become bread” (Matt. IV). He tempts by vainglory when he says: “If you are the Son of God, throw yourself down” (ibid.). He tempts by greed for exaltation when he shows all the kingdoms of the world, saying: “All these I will give you, if you fall down and worship me” (ibid.). But by the same means through which he boasted that he had conquered the first human being, he is conquered by the second, so that, captured at the very entrance through which he had entered, he may depart from our hearts.

If, therefore, according to this teaching of the holy doctor, greed is not only for money but also for exaltation, it is plain that just as the person who, through greed for money, by a price given or received, buys ecclesiastical offices, whether spiritual or material, is a Simonist, so likewise is the person who, through greed for eminence and desire for honor not of God but of himself, presumes to give or receive the same ecclesiastical offices, spiritual or material.

But Simonists, according to the authority of the Fathers of Chalcedon—that is, six hundred and thirty bishops—are to be degraded if clergy, and anathematized if monks or laypersons. And rightly. For Saint Father Ambrose plainly indicates in his book *On Priests* (chapter 5) that they are judged worthy of great execration in God’s sight, that the grace of the Holy Spirit in no way belongs to them, and that through them the whole body is corrupted. He says:

> There are those who are lamented as having prodigiously produced in this age a new rule, and who, following the judgment of Gehazi and the sect of Simon, have bought up the grace of the holy episcopate with money. They do not at all fear that, when they buy priestly honor with money, they have been condemned with Simon by blessed Peter the Apostle, as he says: “May your money,” he says, “be with you unto destruction, because you believed that you could purchase the gift of the Holy Spirit with money” (Acts VIII). Let them believe that they have received leprosy with Gehazi from holy Elisha, who think that they can purchase the rank of priesthood with money. For such men, once we have said these things, it ought to suffice that in purchasing they possess their own leprosy.

> For just as, when the head has been diseased by more violent illnesses, the rest of the body must necessarily be fatally drenched by the overflowing higher disease, so those who seem to be the head of the Church corrupt the brotherly body with their pestilential disease, so that nothing in the frame of the whole body can escape unwounded from the deadly poison of negligent priests’ depravity. Thus you may see throughout the Church those whom not merits but money has advanced to the rank of bishop, and a frivolous and ignorant people who have taken such a priest to themselves. If you carefully ask them who made them priests, they immediately answer and say: “I was lately ordained bishop by the archbishop [Col. 0654D], and I gave him a hundred solidi, that I might deserve to obtain episcopal grace. Had I not given it, I would not today be bishop. Therefore it is better for me to bring gold out of my treasury than to lose so great a priesthood. I gave gold and bought the episcopate. Yet, if I live, I do not doubt that I shall immediately recover those solidi. I ordain priests, consecrate deacons, and receive gold. Likewise, from the other orders I expect to exact profit in money. Behold: I have recovered in my own treasury the gold that I gave, and have received the episcopate for nothing.”

> Surely this is what I grieve over: the archbishop has made a bishop carnally. For on account of money he has specifically ordained a leper: “May your money,” he says, “be with you unto destruction,” because you purchased the grace of the Holy Spirit for a price and conducted a pitiable commerce unto the ruin of souls. And ignorant and unlearned people cry out and say at their ordinations: “You are worthy and just”; while wretched conscience says: “You are unworthy and unjust.” Such a bishop addresses the people, saying: “Peace be with you.” To bodily eyes he appears a great bishop; to divine sight he is seen as a great leper. Through money he acquired an unlawful order, and before God lost the inward person. The flesh received dignity, and the soul lost honor; the flesh, a servant, became mistress of the soul, and the soul, which was mistress, became servant of the flesh. The flesh rules peoples, and the soul serves [Col. 0655B] the devil; it purchased priesthood for the flesh and prepared loss for the soul.

> “What does it profit such a man if he gains the whole world and suffers loss to his soul?” Or: “What will a man give in exchange for his soul?” (Matt. XVI). What he gave when he was ordained bishop was gold, and what he lost was his soul. When he ordained another, what he received was money, and what he gave was leprosy. These are the wares of the wicked, unto their ruin.

> Nevertheless I ask my brother and fellow bishop—for I too am a bishop, and I speak with a bishop. Tell me, then, brother bishop, briefly: when you gave money, what did you receive? “I received episcopal grace.” Therefore I ask you this: why is grace called by such a name? You answer: “Why do you ask?” As I suppose, because it is given freely, it is called grace. Therefore, if grace is so called because it is free and is not valued in gold, why is grace purchased by you with money?
