You answer: “It would not have been given me if it had not been bought with money; I would not have been ordained bishop if I had not given money.” Therefore, as is apparent from your replies, you did not receive grace when you were ordained, because you did not obtain it freely. And so, brother, if you did not receive grace, how could you become bishop? For the Lord also says to his disciples: “Freely you received; freely give” (Matt. X). Why, then, did you think that you possessed freely given grace by means of a price? For, as I see, in giving gold you lost it, and you did not acquire holy grace.

> Yet, adding one more question, I inquire of my brother bishop, lest we seem to have omitted anything from the proofs of true judgment. Who gives episcopal grace, brother: God or man? You answer: “Without doubt God; yet God gives through man. The man lays on hands; God bestows grace. The priest lays on his supplicating right hand, and God blesses with his mighty right hand. The bishop initiates the order, and God grants dignity.” O justice! O equity! If money is given to the human being who performs nothing more in the order than the service entrusted to him, why is everything withheld from God, who bestows it upon you through that order? Does it seem just to you that the servant should be honored while the Lord suffers injury, that the priest should unjustly receive money while God suffers insult from man?

> But because God expects nothing from you for the order granted, why does the priest foolishly expect money from you? God wished freely to grant to a human being, and does the rapacious bishop demand money from a human being for nothing? God, being certainly beneficent, bestowed it freely upon the human being, while the wicked priest despoiled him without cause! “For what do you have that you did not receive? But if you received it, why do you boast as though you had not received it?” (I Cor. IV).

> Behold to what evils the divine order is reduced! Behold to what disgraces priests have fallen—those who deserved to hear from the Judge of the world: “You are the light of this world” (Matt. V). Behold to whom the nations are subjected, to whom the Lord said: “You are the salt of the earth” (ibid.). Therefore, if a bishop duly ordained by the Lord is the Church’s light, so that by the radiant utterance of his preaching he illumines the darkness of ignorance and the darkness of consciences, why is he himself held fast in palpable darkness? Nor is it only that, in acting wickedly, he deservedly perishes himself; beyond that, he undeservedly destroys others with himself. For if you have deserved to possess the savor of salt, so that you may season the fields of the foolish, why, rendered tasteless by such a vice, have you offered yourself to be trampled beneath the filthy feet of swine, so that you can season neither others nor yourself?

> You also sought the office of eyes in the body—that is, in the Church—of your own will, so that through you the rest of the body might have the guidance of light. And now, darkened by a certain blearedness and gloom of vices, do you neither present yourself as fit for light nor give light to others? Of these eyes the Gospel says: “If your eye is single, your whole body will be full of light” [Col. 0656C] (Matt. VI); that is: if the bishop, who has merited to preside as light in the body, is adorned with holy simplicity and innocence, the whole Church is made radiant by the splendor of light. “But if your eye is evil, your whole body will be dark” (ibid.); that is: if the bishop, who seemed to provide light to the body subject to him, is clouded by the blindness of wickedness, what are the other members to do, when the light of the eyes has been taken from them? That is: what will the secular multitude do when a bishop has bred a multitude of people into a similar abyss of crimes by unlawful pleasures and actions? Then nothing at all will seem unlawful which a bishop commits as though lawful; rather, people think praiseworthy whatever the bishop has found pleasing, and no one will say that he does doubtfully what [Col. 0656D] the pontiff does without hesitation.

> For you are unquestionably called bishop by all, especially when you bear the very name—provided, however, that your action accords with the name and the name is joined to the action. For what else does *episcopus* mean except “overseer”? Especially since he sits upon a higher throne in the Church and so looks upon all that the eyes of all look upon him. Therefore, since this is so, why do you show yourself as a foul mirror to every eye, so that they cannot adorn themselves more fittingly because of your darkness?

> Let it suffice thus far that we have somewhat extended our discourse to our fellow priests, in which we have shown both their excellence and their fall, lest, trusting in the height of their honors, they should not seek perfection of morals and should think that they ought to glory in being priests in name alone more than in deed. And although I know that because of this little book many priests who refuse to do what we say will speak against me faithlessly, I nevertheless believe that many who do these things or endeavor to do them will faithfully pray for us. But as we are not weighed down by the attacks of detractors, so we are aided by the prayers of approved and holy men.

> Come now, Holy Spirit, who have aided us in this work by divine inspirations: aid all priests, and grant that they may do what you yourself inspired us to set forth in this little work, so that with me you may grant them the kingdoms of heaven which you promised to give to the saints in the kingdom of heaven. Amen.

## CHAPTER LXXXIII.—How great the glory and honor deserved by holy priests are.

Since, therefore, we have shown how great is the wretchedness in which evil priests are held in God’s sight [Col. 0657B], let us also show how great the glory is of which good bishops are judged worthy before God and human beings. For Saint Ambrose says of them in the same book, *On Priests* (chapter 2):

> Brothers, the honor and loftiness of the episcopal office can be equaled by no comparisons. If you compare it with the splendor of kings and the diadem of princes, it will be far inferior—just as lead is inferior when compared with the brightness of gold. For you see the necks of kings and princes bowed at the knees of priests; having kissed their right hands, they believe themselves fortified by their prayers. What need I say even of the common multitude of the people? The Lord has not only granted that priests should be set over it, but has commanded by evangelical precepts that they should protect it as by a paternal right.

Certainly the Lord thus says to blessed Peter: “Peter, do you love me?” And he: “Lord, you know that I love you” (John XXI). And when he had been questioned a third time and had followed with a threefold answer, the Lord repeated for the third time: “Feed my sheep” (ibid.). The Apostle Peter received those sheep and that flock not only then; he received them with us, and with him all of us received them. Hence, because they are entrusted to priests to be governed, they are rightly said to be subject to their rulers. For the Lord himself says: “A disciple is not above his master” (Luke VI). From these preceding statements it is plainly shown that nothing in this world is more excellent than priests, nothing more exalted than bishops. Therefore the greatest care must be taken that a holy life befit a holy order.

## CHAPTER LXXXIV.—A true proof that one who receives ecclesiastical offices from laypersons is a Simonist.

[Col. 0657D]

Illumined by the grace of the Holy Spirit, which rests in all the faithful and especially in ecclesiastical persons, let us see whether receiving ecclesiastical offices from the emperor or other princes of the world is merely a vice, or whether it is most truly proved to be the Simoniacal heresy.

Blessed Gregory accordingly says:

> There are some who do not indeed receive the rewards of gifts from an ordination, yet nevertheless confer holy orders for human favor and seek from that same generosity only the reward of praise. These certainly do not give freely what has been received freely, because from a bestowed office of holiness they seek the coin of favor. Hence the prophet, when describing the just man, rightly said: “Who shakes his hands free from every gift” [Col. 0658A] (Isa. XXXIII). For he did not say, “Who shakes his hands free from a gift,” but added, “from every.” For one kind of gift is from service, another from the hand, another from the tongue. A gift from service is improperly rendered subjection; a gift from the hand is money; a gift from the tongue is favor. Therefore the person who confers holy orders shakes his hands free from every gift when, in divine matters, he seeks not only no money but also no human glory.

Therefore, just as the person who sells or buys ecclesiastical offices through a gift from the hand is a Simonist, so, according to the example of the holy doctor which we have set forth, the person who obtained this through human favor rather than love of the Lord is likewise proved in every respect to be a Simonist.

But if one who, by using human favor, unjustly seeks to obtain ecclesiastical offices even from ecclesiastical persons is condemned, then without any contradiction that person must be condemned far more gravely who, favoring iniquity, praising it, and “blessing the sinner in the desires of his soul” (Ps. X), affirms that a temporal prince has a rightful claim to invest and rule churches, and endeavors to receive from him a bishopric or any ecclesiastical office.

That this may become still more clearly manifest as truly Simoniacal, let us set forth the example of two bishops. One, canonically elected by clergy and people, refuses in every way to consent to be invested by the emperor and thereby to receive the bishopric from him, avoiding sacrilege. The other, likewise canonically elected by clergy and people, not only does not refuse to be invested by the emperor, but greatly desires it, professes that the emperor possesses this right, and asserts that no one can hold ecclesiastical pre-eminence or the Church’s earthly goods without investiture.

Therefore, when the emperor grants the prerogative of episcopal office to the one who says that this right belongs to him, but does not allow the other, who contradicts him, to possess the bishopric, is it not plain that he honors the former because, supporting such great wickedness, he presumes to praise injustice? Even if he has not given a coin of money, can it in any way be proved that he has not given a coin of favor? Or is it worse to give money, which God created, than to give wickedness, which the devil devised?

It is therefore plain that such persons too are truly Simonists and that the grace of the Holy Spirit in no way pertains to them. For anyone who thinks that the grace of the Holy Spirit is given to Simonists may learn from the words of the holy Fathers how grievously he errs: some of them declare such people not bishops, others lepers, while others define them as worse than Arians.

## CHAPTER LXXXV.—That it is grave sacrilege to take from the Church what has been given to it.

How great a wickedness it is not only to desire to possess the sanctuary of God as an inheritance—for it is manifest that he wills this who objects that the prelates of the Churches, which are sanctuaries, should hold them without his investiture, a desire which the Prophet also punishes with a curse—but also in any way to take away or alienate those things which have been offered to God and to His sanctuary, St Urban, apostolic martyr, shows [Col. 0659A], saying:

> The property of the Churches is not to be invaded by anyone, lest those who remove it from the place to which it was entrusted incur the guilt of sacrilege; and, what is worse, let them become *anathema maranatha* [accursed until the Lord comes], and—even if they do not fall dead in body, as Ananias and Sapphira did—let their soul, which is more excellent than the body, fall dead and estranged from the fellowship of the faithful, and sink into the depths of hell. Therefore all the faithful must take heed, faithfully preserve these things, and repel the outrage of that usurpation, lest estates dedicated to the uses of the heavenly mysteries be harassed by certain assailants. But if anyone does this, after the severity of the due punishment which ought rightly to be imposed upon sacrilegious persons, let him be condemned to perpetual infamy and committed to prison, or held in exile by perpetual deportation [Col. 0659B]; because, according to the Apostle, such a man must be delivered to Satan, that the spirit may be saved on the day of the Lord (1 Cor. V).

In agreement with this, St Lucius, likewise bishop of the Apostolic See, says in his Decrees (appendix VI):

> It is undoubtedly a most grievous sin for the property of churches and the offerings of the faithful to be harassed by anyone and taken from ecclesiastical persons, as Scripture testifies when it says: “Whoever takes anything from his father and says, ‘This is not a sin,’ is a partner of a murderer” (Prov. XXVIII). Our Father, therefore, is without doubt God, who created us; and our mother is the Church, which gave us spiritual birth in baptism. Accordingly, whoever takes away, defrauds, or plunders Christ’s money and that of the Church shall be reckoned a murderer in the sight of the just Judge.

Therefore it is written: “He who [Col. 0659C] plunders his neighbour’s money commits iniquity; but he who takes away the money or property of the Church commits sacrilege.” Hence Judas also, who defrauded the money which, by the Saviour’s command, was distributed for the Church’s uses—that is, for the poor whom the Church ought to feed, and whose office bishops hold—not only became a thief, but a sacrilegious thief.

For concerning such persons—that is, those who seize, defraud, or take away their own resources from the Church—the Lord speaks threateningly through the prophet:

> O God, do not keep silence; do not be silent and do not rest, O God. For behold, your enemies are in tumult, and those who hate you have raised their heads. They have devised wickedly against your people and taken counsel against your hidden ones. They have said: “Come, let us destroy them from being a nation, and let the memory of their name be remembered no more.” For they have plotted [Col. 0659D] together with one heart; they have made a covenant against the covenant: the tents of Edom and the Ishmaelites, Moab and the Hagarenes, Gebal, Ammon, and Amalek, Philistia with the inhabitants of Tyre; Assyria also has joined with them; they have become an arm to the children of Lot. Deal with them as with Midian, and Sisera, as with Jabin at the torrent of Kishon. They were destroyed at Endor; they became like dung upon the earth. Make their princes like Oreb and Zeeb, and Zebah and Zalmunna, all their princes, who said: “Let us possess for ourselves the beauty of God.” My God, make them like a wheel, and like stubble before the face of the wind. As fire burns the forest, and as flame devours the mountains, so shall you pursue them in your tempest, and trouble them in your whirlwind. Fill their faces with shame. And they shall seek [Col. 0660A] your name, O Lord. Let them be confounded and troubled for ever and ever; let them be ashamed and perish; and let them know that your name is the Lord: you are Most High over all the earth (Ps. LXXXII).

The decrees of prophets, apostles, their successors, and all the Catholic Fathers forbid these acts and judge such presumptions to be sacrileges. Following their examples, we, together with you, by apostolic authority drive away and condemn from the thresholds of holy Mother Church all such presumptuous persons, plunderers of the Church, and alienators of her resources; we judge them sacrilegious, and not them alone but also all who consent to them. For not only those who do such things are judged guilty, but also those who consent to those who do them (Rom. I). For equal punishment embraces both the perpetrators and those who consent [Col. 0660B].

It is most certain that this rule applies to things offered to God, whether great or small. But if a faithful emperor or any prince wishes to give to the shepherd of the Church that which is his by right, he should grant an investiture customary for other men, not by the pastoral staff or episcopal ring, by which the mysteries of the Lord Christ are signified and therefore are most truly proved sacred. For it is not fitting that investiture in temporal things should be bestowed by temporal princes through episcopal insignia, because, as we have said, through these the gift of the Holy Spirit is signified.

## CHAPTER LXXXVI.—That bishops hold the place of the apostles in the Church

[Col. 0660C] St Augustine shows whose place bishops hold in the Church and who ought to confer this dignity upon them, saying (on Ps. XLIV):

> “In place of your fathers, sons have been born to you” (Ps. XLIV). The fathers sent forth were the apostles; in place of the apostles sons have been born, that is, bishops have been appointed. For from where have the bishops who are throughout the world today been born? The Church herself calls them fathers; she herself bore them and herself placed them in their fathers’ sees. Therefore, O Church, do not think yourself forsaken because you do not see Peter, because you do not see Paul, because you do not see the sons through whom you were born. From your offspring fatherhood has grown for you. “In place of your fathers, sons have been born to you.” “You shall appoint them princes over all the earth.” The Church bore sons and appointed them, in place of her fathers, princes over all the earth.

## CHAPTER LXXXVII.—On the temporal power of holy Mother Church

[Col. 0660D]

The same Father Augustine, showing that the Church possesses great authority even for temporal preservation and can save all who flee to her, says (on Ps. XLVI):

> Many who are not yet Christians now run to the Church, asking for the Church’s aid. They wish to be aided in temporal matters, even though they do not yet wish to reign with us eternally. When both Christians and those not yet Christians seek the Church’s aid, has He not “subjected peoples to us and nations beneath our feet”? (Ps. XLVI.)

## CHAPTER LXXXVIII.—On ecclesiastical offices not being sold

Who are those who sell oxen and doves? They are those [Col. 0661A] who seek their own interests, not those of Jesus Christ. They have everything for sale because they do not wish to be redeemed. They do not wish to be bought, yet they wish to sell. For it is good for them to be redeemed by Christ’s blood, so that they may attain Christ’s peace.

For what profit is there in acquiring any temporal and passing thing in this age—whether money, pleasure of belly and throat, or honour in human praise? Are not all things smoke and wind? Do not all things pass and run on? Woe to those who have clung to passing things, who pass away with them! Do not all things, like a rushing river, run into the sea? And woe to him who falls, for he is drawn into the sea! Therefore, my brothers, we must restrain every affection from such desires, since those who seek such things are sellers.

For Simon too wished to buy the Holy Spirit because [Col. 0661B] he wished to sell the Holy Spirit; and he thought the apostles were merchants such as the Lord drove from the Temple with a whip. He himself was such a merchant, and wished to buy what he might sell; he was among those who sold doves. For the Holy Spirit appeared in the form of a dove (Matt. III).

But who, brothers, are those who sell doves? Those who say, “We give the Holy Spirit.” Why do they say this, and for what price do they sell the price of their own honour? They accept temporal seats as the price, so that they may seem themselves to sell doves. Let them beware the whip of cords. The dove is not for sale; it is given freely, because it is called grace (*gratia*). Therefore let those also beware who say that the outward Church, so to speak, is a good thing, and hand it over to those who wish to dominate it in every respect according to their own will [Col. 0661C]. For although God dwells in the minds of the faithful, the Apostle nevertheless calls their bodies temples of the Holy Spirit. But when the ordering of the Church is granted to persons who ought to be ruled and ought not to have the guidance of souls, it is undoubtedly a most grievous error.

## CHAPTER LXXXIX.—On the honour which emperors have shown to priests

St Gregory shows how great the honour is which emperors ought to show priests, saying to the Emperor Maurice (book V, epistle 40):

> May our Lord not be more quickly offended with priests because of earthly power; rather, with exalted consideration for Him whose servants they are, let him so exercise rule over them as also to render them their due reverence [Col. 0661D]. For in the divine utterances priests are sometimes called gods, sometimes angels. Through Moses it is said of one who must be brought to an oath: “Bring him to the gods” (Exod. XXII), namely, to the priests. And again it is written: “You shall not speak evil of the gods” (*ibid.*), namely, of priests. And the prophet says: “The lips of the priest keep knowledge, and they seek the law from his mouth, because he is the angel of the Lord of hosts” (Mal. II). What wonder, then, if your Piety deigns to honour those to whom God Himself, conferring honour upon them in His own word, gives the name either of angels or of gods?

Ecclesiastical history likewise bears witness that, when written accusations against bishops had been presented to Constantine of pious memory, he received the documents of accusation; and, summoning the bishops who had been accused [Col. 0662A], he burned in their presence the documents he had received, saying:

> “You are gods, appointed by the true God. Go and judge your own cases among yourselves, because it is not fitting that we should judge gods.”

In this decision, pious Lord, he benefited himself more through humility than he conferred anything on them by the reverence he rendered. For earlier, pagan rulers in the commonwealth, ignorant of the true God, worshipped gods of wood and stone, yet nevertheless paid the greatest honour to their priests. What wonder, then, if a Christian emperor deigns to honour the priests of the true God, when pagan rulers, as I have said, knew how to render honour to priests who served gods of wood and stone? I submit these matters to the piety of my lords not for myself, but for all priests [Col. 0662B].

## CHAPTER XC.—That the earthly kingdom has grown through honouring holy Church

We said earlier in this little book that the honour of the earthly kingdom has grown more and more in this world through the honour and possessions of holy Church. That this is true is attested by the example of Constantine the Great, to whom God deigned to grant victory over his enemies through the power of the holy Cross. After he had later been baptized by Blessed Sylvester, and had resolved in true humility of heart that it seemed unjust for him to maintain an imperial seat where God had appointed the vicar of Blessed Peter, he built the city of Constantinople and there reigned gloriously.

Because he honoured the blessed apostle and left the western kingdom to his vicar, God granted him possession of the entire Roman empire in its fullness [Col. 0662C]. For although he gave it, blessed Pope Sylvester, following the example of the Lord Christ, did not permit a royal crown to be placed upon his most holy head; rather, he urged him to hold the kingdom and devoutly serve holy Church.

Thus those appear not to hold the truth who maintain that duchies, marches, and other exalted possessions of the Church ought not, under the name of possessions, to be subject to her. Would the most holy Sylvester, being most prudent and wise, have permitted this to be given to holy Church unless he knew with absolute certainty that it accorded with the divine will and had long before been foretold by the holy prophets?

Therefore the holy prophet says concerning this [Col. 0662D], speaking to holy Church:

> The kings of the nations shall minister to you. In my indignation I struck you, and in my reconciliation I had mercy on you. The strength of the nations shall be brought to you, and their kings shall be led to you. For the nation and kingdom which will not serve you shall perish (Isa. LX).

And again:

> The glory of Lebanon shall come to you: fir, boxwood, and pine together, to adorn the place of my sanctification; and I shall glorify the place of my feet. The bent-down sons of those who humbled you shall come to you, and all who spoke evil of you shall worship the footprints of your feet (*ibid.*).

And again:

> Because you were forsaken and hated, and there was none who passed through, I shall make you the pride of ages, a joy from generation to generation. You shall suck the milk of nations, and you shall nurse at the breasts of kings; and [Col. 0663A] you shall know that I am the Lord saving you (Isa. LX).

The Life of St John Chrysostom also shows how much the wisdom and power of priests benefit the kingdom, when it relates that he visited a certain tyrant, Godolias, to whom the emperor could send none of the princes, and calmed his fury by his wisdom. Blessed Leo, bishop of the Apostolic See, likewise compelled that most famous Attila, called the scourge of God, by his prudence to withdraw from the borders of Italy.

It is evident, however, that they could not have accomplished this unless, supported by the revenues of the Churches, they had the Church’s military service with them. Since it is known that they did not accomplish such things while supported solely by tithes and offerings, let those who have dared to say that nothing belongs to Churches except tithes, first-fruits, and offerings presented at the altar assent to the truth; and let them know that it is true that the earthly kingdom is fortified and defended by the support of the Church [Col. 0663B].

## CHAPTER XCI.—Against those who say: So much is given to the Church that scarcely anything will remain for the kingdom

There are some simple people who say: “If these things continue in this way, the Church will be able to possess all earthly things.” What answer should be given them except what the Lord said concerning virgins: “Not all receive this saying” (Matt. XIX)? For when will all give their own possessions to the Church, when they are trying to take away the very things she has possessed from ancient times?

## CHAPTER XCII.—In what order priesthood and kingdom may be reconciled without contravening the holy canons

Since the Lord says, “My peace I give to you; my peace I leave to you” [Col. 0663C] (John XIV), every effort must be made that peace may exist between priesthood and kingdom and, by God’s help, endure firmly. As we understand under divine inspiration, this can come about if, when the shepherd of a Church has been canonically elected, invested, and consecrated, he then approaches the emperor in person or through his faithful representatives and requests an imperial charter concerning the property of the Church entrusted to him.

The most pious emperor, willingly granting and confirming this according to the custom of his spiritual mother, ought to grant what his predecessors are manifestly known to have conceded to that Church, promising that Church and its shepherd his most pious protection in all things. We have said that holy shepherds may accomplish this not only in person but also through their envoys, because it often happens that holy Church seeks to choose for herself as holy shepherd an elderly man, or one infirm in body—as holy Roman Church chose Gregory of venerable memory, the outstanding teacher, and as the Milanese sought to choose Simplicianus, a good old man, successor to Blessed Ambrose [Col. 0663D]. It is therefore not fitting that such men should be wearied by a long distance of travel.

If, therefore, both holy bishops and venerable emperors hold this arrangement ratified, suppress the insolence of the proud, and rest in peace, then the Church herself can, with God’s help, be reconciled and united in the peace of Christ. Bishops or clerics who have departed from holy Roman Church and wish to return to her with sincere repentance should be received [Col. 0664A] with the counsel of holy bishops. Although justice may rightly require that many of them be rejected, yet, because mercy exalts itself above judgment, if they turn with their whole heart, it is good for the unity and concord of holy Mother Church that they be restored to their ranks.

In places where there were Catholic bishops and schismatics, Catholics should occupy the episcopal see, while schismatics should exercise the honour of presbyter. This was done in the time of St Augustine with the Donatists, and holy Church was united. If the same is done in this time, we believe in the mercy of Him who deigned to unite in Himself, the cornerstone, two divergent corners: holy Church will be free from its present discord and will rest in peace.

## CHAPTER XCIII.—On the severity of kings against the Simoniacal heresy

[Col. 0664B]

In the time of St Gregory, pope and outstanding teacher, such force of religion existed in earthly rulers that they not only restrained laymen from evil, but also compelled clerics to serve justice. Thus, writing to Theodoric and Theodebert, kings of the Franks, he says:

> It is reported that the Simoniacal heresy—which first crept against the Church through a diabolical planting, and was struck down and condemned in its very birth by the zeal of apostolic vengeance—rules within the borders of your kingdom; whereas in priests both faith and life must be chosen, and ambition must be entirely avoided. Therefore, with fatherly affection, we ask, dearest sons, that you endeavour to prohibit so detestable an evil from the borders of your kingdom.  
> *(From the Register of St Gregory [Col. 0664C] the Pope.)*

## CHAPTER XCIV.—That a private law cannot establish a common law

Thus also, wishing to free from the perversity of evil men a certain monastery or hospice situated in the same kingdom of the Franks, because it was not administered canonically owing to the ambitions and disputes of certain persons, he ordered that no abbot should ever be introduced there by any surreptitious contrivance without royal provision and the election of the monks. He also ordered that the abbot of that monastery should never be elected to an episcopate, lest the abbey perhaps suffer any loss on account of the episcopate.

But this privilege belongs to that particular Church in such a way that it cannot at all establish a common law for kings or abbots [Col. 0664D]. For what is specially granted to one does not immediately suit all.

## CHAPTER XCV.—That “grace, unless received freely, is not grace”

Grace, unless it is received freely, is not grace. But Simoniacs do not receive freely what they receive. If they do not receive it, they do not possess it. If they do not possess it, they can give it to no one, whether freely or not freely. What, then, do they give? Certainly, what they possess. But what do they possess? Assuredly, the spirit of falsehood.

How do we prove this? Because, if the Spirit of truth, as Truth itself from whom He proceeds bears witness, is received freely, then that which is received not freely is beyond doubt proved to be the spirit of falsehood.

## CHAPTER XCVI.—That Simoniacs are worse than Arians

[Col. 0665A]

He who defends another’s error is far more condemnable than those who err, because he not only errs himself but also prepares and confirms for others stumbling-blocks of error. Therefore, since he is a teacher of error, he must be called not merely a heretic but also a heresiarch. Let defenders of Simoniacs therefore consider by what name they ought to be designated.

For Arians, although they err especially in asserting that the Son is less than the Father and is a creature, and likewise that the Holy Spirit is less than the Father and Son and is a creature, nevertheless call both God and strive to subject neither of them to any creature whatsoever, but only to God the Father, Creator of all things visible and invisible [Col. 0665B].

But Simoniacs, not at all content with so great an Arian sacrilege, believe the almighty Holy Spirit not merely inferior to the Father and Son, or subject only to the Father and Son, but even inferior and subject to themselves, as though He were some saleable and contemptible slave. They suppose that, whether willing or unwilling, He obeys their wishes and, drawn by the cords of money or bound as it were in their golden chains, administers the fullness of His sanctification and grace to their sacrilegious offices and accursed consecrations, and cooperates with their venality or activity.

Even to entertain such a thought for a moment is an intolerable, and perhaps unforgivable, blasphemy, because it is to sin against the Holy Spirit, or at least to speak a word against Him. By this judgment alone Simon, the first author and standard-bearer of their sect, after whom they themselves are named, was condemned beyond recovery [Col. 0665C].

## CHAPTER XCVII.—That the earthly kingdom ought to serve holy Church

A king ought not to rule the Church for the honour of the kingdom; rather, for the honour of the heavenly kingdom, the earthly kingdom ought to serve the Church. The Holy Spirit testifies that this is true through the mouth of St Gregory, saying in the *Morals* (book XXXI, ch. 6):

> The Lord speaks to Blessed Job concerning earthly rulers who were to serve holy Church, saying: “Will you not have confidence in the great strength of the rhinoceros, and will you leave your labours to him?” (Job XXXIX). The Lord declares that He has confidence in the rhinoceros’s strength because He has bent toward the worship of His own veneration the strength which He gave to the earthly ruler, so that, from the power received by which he formerly swelled against God, he may now render religious service more extensively. For the more power he has in the world, the more he prevails on behalf of the world’s Creator. Hence it is added: “And will you leave your labours to him?” The Lord entrusted His labours to this rhinoceros, because to the converted earthly ruler He committed the Church which He had purchased by His death, entrusting to his hand the duty of guarding the peace of faith with the greatest care. Thus he who formerly raged against the Church by varied torments now promulgates laws for the Church.

Behold: by these words which the Holy Spirit spoke through the mouth of St Gregory, it is plainly taught that holy Church has been entrusted to earthly rulers only for the protection of the peace of faith [Col. 0666A]. This, moreover, is the true peace of faith: that heretics be resisted and that it be truthfully proclaimed that God’s gift cannot be bestowed by human beings. Therefore let most sacred emperors and princes strive to confirm and strengthen this preaching in all ways, so that by devoutly serving holy Church in their kingdom, they may deserve to be companions of her blessedness in the heavenly kingdom.

## CHAPTER XCVIII.—In what matter earthly rulers ought to exercise power within the Church

St Gregory’s words show in what matter earthly powers ought to have a place within the Church, and whether by their own authority or at her summons [Col. 0666B] (Morals, book XXX):

> In order to break the hardness of wicked persons who oppress the humble, holy Church sometimes seeks the aid of an earthly ruler, because she is insufficient by her own strength. When earthly rulers do this, they serve not themselves but God.

Therefore, in the election of shepherds of holy Church, earthly rulers ought to exercise their power in God’s service only when, as often occurs, discord arises between parties concerning the election and cannot be restrained by the authority of priests. Then they ought to support the judgment of priests and pursue wicked persons in every way.

We read that this also occurred in the Apostolic See: when dissenting peoples had ordained two men, Eulalius and Boniface, Placidius Augustus and his son Valentinian Augustus, asked by the Catholic priests and peoples, established Boniface [Col. 0666C] and expelled Eulalius from the City. Yet on this account they did not subject the Church to their own jurisdiction; rather, they rendered their service to her, because afterwards they sought no right in the election of the Roman pontiff.

Catholic emperors ought to act similarly in bishoprics and abbeys if they are called upon by the Church. But if the Roman emperor is not Catholic, the Church ought not merely to refrain from seeking his aid, but rather oppose him in all things. If he becomes so proud as to cause another to be ordained bishop of Rome, as though by his own power or authority, that man is not to be regarded as bishop; rather, the true bishop is he whom the Catholic Church has chosen for herself.

All Catholics who fear God ought not only to refuse service to an emperor doing this, but also, insofar as they are able, resist him, knowing that for this they will receive an eternal reward from the Lord, if they do it chastely and with zeal for God; and knowing, conversely, that it is sin if they neglect it [Col. 0666D].

## CHAPTER XCIX.—On Pope Gregory VII

We have an example of this matter in modern times. When the Roman emperor, resisting the Catholic faith, had placed his own bishop there, all Catholics rejected and anathematized him, while they loved Gregory VII, canonically ordained, and confessed him as the vicar of Blessed Peter. Even after Gregory’s death, God confirmed his teaching by not allowing the gates of hell to prevail against His Church.

## CHAPTER C.—How purely holy ecclesiastical offices ought to be administered

[Col. 0667A]

St Urban, bishop of the Apostolic See, bears witness that he is a Simoniac who buys or sells for a price—the gift of the hand, tongue, or service, as Blessed Gregory testified—the Church’s property which comes from consecration, even if he does not buy or sell the laying on of hands itself. He says (from the Council of Urban):

> Why does the Council of Chalcedon, of 620 bishops, prohibit the procurator or defender of a Church, or anyone subject to a rule, from being appointed through money, and anathematize even the agents of so great a crime, unless it judges them Simoniacs? If the aforesaid soldiers of the Church are struck down for such a crime, no wise person will deny that those not serving in the Church should be struck down far more condemnably for the same cause—that is, selling or buying [Col. 0667B].

But our blessed predecessor Paschal affirms, concerning consecration and things which proceed from consecration, that whoever sells either of two things without which he cannot possess the other leaves neither unsold.

## CHAPTER CI.—How Pope Adrian anathematized rulers who insert themselves into the election of prelates

Holy Pope Adrian VIII, presiding over a synod, says that emperors or princes ought not to insert themselves into the election of pontiffs (from the Council of Pope Adrian):

> In agreement with the earlier councils, this universal synod has defined, established, and lawfully decreed that the promotions and consecrations of bishops are to be carried out by the election and decree [Col. 0667C] of bishops. No layman—whether prince or powerful person—may insert himself into the election or promotion of a patriarch, metropolitan, or any bishop, lest disorderly and improper confusion or contention arise from this. Above all, none of those who hold power, nor any other layperson, ought to have any authority in such matters. Rather, he should remain silent and attend to himself until the election of the pontiff receives its regular conclusion from the college of the Church.

> But if any layman is invited by the Church to contend and cooperate, it is permitted for such a person, if he wishes, respectfully to comply with those who summon him. In this way they regularly promote a worthy shepherd for the salvation of their Church. But whoever among secular princes, powerful men, or laymen of any other rank [Col. 0667D] attempts to act against the common and harmonious canonical election of the ecclesiastical order, let him be anathema until he obeys and consents to whatever the Church shows that she wishes concerning the ordination and election of her own prelate.

## CHAPTER CII.—Why emperors were permitted to invest Churches

Since, then, it is certain that most blessed Adrian taught concerning the election of a pontiff, it is remarkable that, as some say, he is found to have granted Emperor Charles permission to invest Churches. What, then, ought be considered and judged in these matters, except that—even if it is true that this was granted to him—it was not done in order that he might hold the Church of God subject to his own jurisdiction in temporal matters, but rather that, by this sign, he might in some fashion be permitted ever more fully to serve her and defend her against enemies [Col. 0668A]?

## CHAPTER CIII.—How the election of a shepherd ought canonically to be made

Therefore admonish the people that they must not in any way disagree in choosing a priest, but with one consent choose for themselves as priest or bishop to be consecrated one whose conduct is praiseworthy and whose person may be pleasing to God and men, lest, if it should be done otherwise, God forbid, in diverse … [lacuna]

## CHAPTER CIV.—That an archbishop ought not to be elected without the command or knowledge of the vicars of the Lord Pope

(From the decree of Pope Calixtus.) When a metropolitan has died [Col. 0668B] and another must be appointed in his place, the provincial bishops ought to assemble in the metropolitan city, so that, after the will of all the clergy and all the citizens has been examined, the best man may be chosen from the presbyters or deacons of that Church. The provincial bishops shall present his name to your knowledge, fulfilling the wishes of those who ask, once they know that what has pleased them has also pleased you. For as we do not wish just elections to be delayed by any postponements, so we permit nothing to be undertaken without your knowledge.

## CHAPTER CV.—That the desire for primacy arises from boastfulness of heart

To desire a good work is indeed good; but to covet the primacy of honour is vanity. For performing a good work belongs to our will, our action, and our labour. Therefore I do not know whether anyone deserves any reward from a primacy of honour. For the desire of primacy is born from boastfulness of heart. But he who is humble in heart considers himself more unworthy than others, according to that apostolic precept which says: “Each esteeming the other superior to himself”; and he never desires to appear superior [Col. 0668C] [Cod.: *superiore*]. For primacy seeks one who flees it and hates one who seeks it.

## CHAPTER CVI.—That clergy and people ought to choose a priest for themselves

(From the decree of Pope Anastasius.) Therefore, when the election of the supreme priest is being considered [Col. 0668D], let him be placed before all whom the united agreement of clergy and people has requested. But if the votes of a few have perhaps divided themselves in favour of another person, by the metropolitan’s judgment let him be preferred to the altar who has been superior both in merits and in support.

## CHAPTER CVII.—That there should be no partiality in conferring holy orders

St Augustine, explaining the saying of St James the Apostle (Jas. II), “My brothers, do not hold the faith of our Lord Jesus Christ with respect of persons,” says:

> It must not be supposed to be a slight sin to hold the faith of our Lord Jesus Christ with respect of persons, if we refer that distinction between sitting and standing to ecclesiastical honours. For who could bear it if [Col. 0669A] a rich man were chosen for the Church’s seat of honour while a poorer man, better instructed and holier, were despised? For God has chosen the poor, rich in faith.

## CHAPTER CVIII.—That money should have no place in ecclesiastical offices

(From the decree of Pope Gregory.) If money has any place in ecclesiastical offices, what is sacred becomes secular. Whoever seeks to obtain this by the giving of a price desires not to be a priest, but merely vainly to be called one.

## CHAPTER CIX.—That those ordained through ambition are not true bishops

(From the Register of Pope Gregory.) If the matter is weighed by the examination of a proper balance, when someone wickedly seizes a position of usefulness for vain glory, he is thereby all the more unworthy the more he seeks honour [Col. 0669B]. Just as one who resists when invited and flees when sought ought to be brought to the sacred altars, so he who voluntarily canvasses and importunately thrusts himself forward must without doubt be rejected.

## CHAPTER CX.—How grave it is to profane holy order through any deceit

(From the Register of Pope Gregory.) If any man, neither distinguished by holy conduct nor called by God and the people or compelled by insistence, already defiled by any crime, should shamelessly receive Christ’s priesthood—whether episcopal or priestly dignity—through an unjust desire of the heart, filthy prayers of the heart, a retinue, manual service, or a fraudulent little gift; if he receives it, supported not by concern for souls but by covetousness for vain glory, and does not voluntarily relinquish it during his life, and harsh death does not find him in repentance, he shall without doubt perish eternally [Col. 0669C].

## CHAPTER CXI.—That things badly begun are difficult to bring to a good conclusion

(POPE LEO.) But a ruler whom either sedition has forced upon others or ambition has seized, even if he gives no offence in his character and actions, is nevertheless harmful by the example of his very beginning; and it is difficult for things begun under a bad principle to be brought to a good conclusion.

## CHAPTER CXII.—That many testimonies make clear that sacred dignities ought not to be sought through ambition

Behold, these holy testimonies make utterly clear [Col. 0669D] how great an evil it is to seek sacred dignity through ambition, and that earthly rulers ought to claim nothing in the election of pontiffs or abbots. Nevertheless, let us still bring forward the words of Saints Gregory Nazianzen and Augustine.

## CHAPTER CXIII.—How grave it is to seek the prerogative of priesthood through ambition, and by what penance such a person may be aided
(GREGORY NAZIANZEN.) For concerning one who strives to purchase God’s gift with money: it is beyond doubt that he can by no means thereafter remain in, or be restored to, sacred order, and that he must in every way be cut off from communion. Yet the remedy of his penance must be considered very carefully. For one who presumes to buy the gift of the Holy Spirit with a price—what else is that but a capital crime and the Simoniac heresy? Clearly we can find no other judgment, but only that contained in canonical and apostolic censure. A presbyter or deacon who takes a wife, commits adultery, or commits a capital crime is to be publicly deposed, shut up in a monastery, and there do penance all the days of his life. But concerning this destructive heresy, the canons prescribe that he be cut off from communion by every means; nevertheless, at the point of death, out of mercy, we judge that he may receive communion twice.

### CHAPTER CXIV.—Concerning the princes of the holy Catholic Church.

Blessed Augustine, moreover, testified thus concerning the primacy of the holy Church in his exposition of the Psalms, saying (on Psalm XXX):

> In the holy Church, those who were the despised things of the world became princes. Was a fisherman then a prince? Was a tax collector a prince? Certainly they were princes—but they became so in her. What kind of princes came from Babylon? Believing princes came from the world; princes came from the city of Rome, as though from the head of Babylon. They did not go to the emperor’s temple, but to the memorial of a fisherman. Whence came these princes? “God chose the weak things of the world to confound the strong; and God chose the base things of the world, and things which are not, as though they were, that the things which are might be brought to nothing” [1 Cor. II].

From these sacred testimonies and the words of the holy Doctor, it is clearly evident that the princes of this world ought not to rule over the princes of the holy Church—that is, the holy pastors [Col. 0670C]—but to serve them, since they have become their sons in the holy Church. Accordingly, the same holy Father Augustine says elsewhere: “It is better, when the emperor comes to Rome, that he should weep at the memorial of the fisherman, than that the fisherman should weep at the memorial of the emperor; because ‘God chose the weak things of the world to confound the strong.’”

### CHAPTER CXV.—An example from the Life of St Martin, showing how much reverence earthly rulers ought to show priests even in temporal matters.

The Life of St Martin also shows how much reverence earthly rulers ought to have for priests. For Sulpicius Severus says of him:

> [Col. 0670D] When many persons from different parts of the world had gathered before the Emperor Maximus—a man of fierce disposition, puffed up by victory in civil wars—and when the shameful flattery of all about the prince was conspicuous, and priestly dignity had submitted itself to the unworthy instability of the royal court, apostolic dignity remained intact in Martin alone. For even if a petition had to be made to the emperor on behalf of anyone, he commanded rather than begged. Though frequently invited to Maximus’s banquet, he abstained, saying that he could not share the table of one who had expelled two emperors, one from his kingdom and the other from life.
>
> At last Maximus declared that he had not seized imperial power of his own will, but that it had been imposed upon him by the soldiers through divine direction; that he had defended by arms the necessity of his rule; that God’s will could not seem alien to him [Col. 0671A] in whose hands victory had been placed by so incredible an outcome; and that none of his opponents had died except on the battlefield. Then Martin, overcome either by the reasoning or by the entreaties, came at last to the banquet. The king rejoiced wonderfully that he had obtained this.
>
> The guests were present as if for a feast day: the highest advocates and distinguished men, Evodius the prefect and consul, a man than whom none was ever more just; two counts invested with the highest authority; the king’s brother and uncle; and, between them, Martin’s presbyter reclined. Martin himself sat on a small seat placed beside the king. About the middle of the meal, as customary, a servant offered the cup to the king. He ordered it instead to be given to the most holy bishop, waiting and hoping to receive the cup from his hand. But Martin, when he had drunk, handed the cup [Col. 0671B] to his own presbyter, judging no one worthier to drink before anyone else after him. Nor would he have thought it proper had he preferred either the king himself or those nearest the king. The emperor and all who were present were so astonished by this act that the very thing in which they had been passed over pleased them.

Therefore let devout emperors, considering this example too, not be angry at those who preach that they ought to claim no right in the Church, but rather, acknowledging the truth, honor them.

### CHAPTER CXVI.—How great evils have arisen from the authority of laymen in the Church.

As we have shown above from the sayings of St Adrian, pope, and of other saints, by many and varied examples, an emperor or other princes ought to have no right or dominion in the election of any pastor of the holy Church, whether by investiture or by intruding themselves in any other manner. Therefore what certain persons assert to have been granted to them contrary to the canons and decrees of the holy Fathers must be corrected.

Although many say that it is better to observe what certain holy Apostolic men granted to the emperor and to remain at peace with him, because no mortal can equal those who made this concession either in holiness or knowledge, reason itself cries out that they must nevertheless not be heeded. For it is evident that this peace is not the peace which the Lord gives. For he himself said to the apostles: “Freely you have received; freely give” [Matt. X]. It is evident, however, that the holy apostles gave this power [Col. 0671D] only to their successors. Therefore anyone who grants this power to secular persons acts plainly against God’s will. It must therefore be corrected.

But if, as is reported, St Adrian did this, and if it is true, he did not do it with the intention claimed by these men; or else it was foisted upon him as upon a man. What wonder, moreover, if something could be foisted upon Blessed Adrian, when we read that this happened even to most blessed Peter after he had been strengthened by the Holy Spirit? For, as Blessed Paul testifies, fearing the Jews, he compelled even the Gentiles by his example to Judaize. St Paul did not yield to him even for an hour [Gal. II], so that the truth of the Gospel might remain among us.

Thus the priests of the present time ought to act in this matter. For so many and such great evils have sprung from it that, if we examine the heart of Blessed [Col. 0672A] Adrian or of other holy pontiffs, we clearly see that they would have chosen death rather than have given any assent to this thing, had they foreseen it.

For from this matter the princes of the world, badly deceived, imagined that they could rule the Church according to their own will or advantage, and that the consent given to them was not merely for its defense. They therefore did not fear to grant it according to their own pleasure, not only to clerics but also to laymen. Indeed, after accepting a price, they did not shrink from introducing bishops or abbots into the Church. Thus it came about that they not only openly served the Simoniac heresy, but also greed, which the Apostle declares to be the service of idols [Col. III].

From this presumption many diverse evils arose in God’s holy Church, so that in many churches two bishops and two abbots were found. Hence it came about that, as Blessed Gregory says of Simon, “he wished to buy in order to sell more wickedly,” all the lesser churches were everywhere sold—not only, as we have said, to clerics, but even to laymen; and further still, horrible to say, in some places even to women. When they were told, “You ought not to sell churches to us,” not knowing what they said or whereof they affirmed, they replied that they sold land, not churches. Yet the holy Fathers, speaking through the Holy Spirit, as we have demonstrated above by many and diverse proofs, affirm most plainly that one who sells the Church—because he presumes in any way to sell or invest ecclesiastical offices for his own advantage or glory—and one who does this, sells the Holy Spirit, so far as lies in him [Col. 0672C].

Because of this injustice churches were troubled and despoiled, and Christ’s poor became the prey of wicked men. Many murders were committed; severe famine, almost unheard of in all preceding ages, grievously devastated humankind when wars and seditions were stirred up by this cause. Monasteries were nearly destroyed, and many churches were violated and laid waste. Moreover, some churches remained without a pastor for many years, which is plainly contrary to the canons. For the sacred canons allow no church to be without a pastor for more than three months.

In many places, too, certain laymen or women so dominated churches, claiming that they had received them from emperors, that, taking away everything from which monks or clerics ought to live, they assigned it to their own use and that of their dependants. And why say more? Days would fail us if we wished to recount in order all the evils committed on this occasion. Therefore, if the most holy Fathers and Apostolic men had foreknown these perversions, as we have said, they would have chosen death rather than give assent to this matter.

What wonder, moreover, if modern Fathers did not foresee this, when even St Moses, with whom God spoke face to face, left in the tabernacle the bronze serpent which he had raised in the wilderness. Later the people adored it and worshipped it as God. Wishing to destroy this error, King Hezekiah was not deterred because Moses, the servant of the Lord, had made it. Rather, considering that the people venerated it contrary to God’s will, [Col. 0673A] he broke it in pieces and commanded the people to worship God, who by his own power had given salvation to their fathers.

The same course, therefore, must be followed in the present matter. Since the pastors of the holy Church know that such great evils are committed on this occasion, they ought in every way to uproot this evil completely. But they cannot eradicate it at all if they permit churches to be invested by secular persons, even very religious ones. Therefore let them not permit it. Rather, let them strive most faithfully to conform God’s Church to the mind of the apostles, saints, and ancient Fathers, and, aided by the grace of the Holy Spirit, to order it accordingly.

### CHAPTER CXVII.—An exhortation to persevere in the good that has been begun, to correct evil by every means, and concerning the stater found in the fish’s mouth.

[Col. 0673B]

The supreme and universal pontiffs Gregory VII, Urban II, and Paschal II, seeing so many and such great evils as we have briefly enumerated springing up like shoots from a poisoned root through the investiture of churches, so that now almost the whole body of the Church was being overspread by the leprosy of iniquity, most justly decreed in synodal councils that investitures of churches were not to take place. By God’s grace this had begun to be observed and kept most devoutly in the holy Church.

But now certain persons, in the manner of Gehazi or Simon—one of whom wished to purchase God’s grace, the other to draw it to his own uses—desiring to destroy what was well done, assert that kings have the right to invest churches, namely because they are anointed with holy oil. They do not remember that St David was anointed with holy oil, and yet, despite that anointing, he was permitted neither to appoint priests nor even to build the Temple.

Solomon, however, who built the Temple, did not merit this because he was anointed with holy oil to kingship, but because by his very name he prefigured Christ, who, being truly Peaceful, builds the holy Church. Therefore, if this lesser thing was not granted to holy David, full of prophetic grace, because he was a man of war, much less ought it to be granted to the emperors of our time—that, by investing priests, they should claim the Church as their own right.

For what the Church possesses [Col. 0763D] belongs to Christ and not to the emperor, because not only the Church’s spiritual possessions but also its temporal possessions are dedicated to Christ. Therefore we ought to receive what belongs to Christ from Christ, not from earthly princes. If one of the people outside the Church is recognized as possessing without any investiture what belongs to him by right and has been lawfully left to him, how much more ought the Lord Christ to possess what has been justly bequeathed to him, and to grant it, without anyone’s dispute, to whom he wills?

There are, however, certain churches which receive possessions in such a way that donors retain something from them for themselves, as Blessed Father Benedict also taught in his Rule when he laid down how sons of nobles ought to be received. Once this has been established, it must be observed in every respect. For although the Church, with all that belongs to her, is free, nevertheless, following the example of the Lord Christ, she ought not to deny worldly persons what is theirs.

Now the Lord paid the tax which he did not owe, the tax found in the fish’s mouth [Matt. XVII]. That fish signifies the Church. The stater in the fish’s mouth, from which the tax was paid, was found because the Church often possesses something from which she ought justly to render something to worldly persons. But those who, because certain churches justly pay something, wish to subject them to secular persons are shown not to favor justice, but rather to do this so that they may once again openly practice their accustomed simony.

For although it is not so plainly apparent, yet when the eyes are more subtly opened by divine reasoning, this too is proved truly Simoniac. For, according to the testimony of Blessed Augustine, Simon wished to receive God’s grace for a payment so that, appearing more glorious thereby, he might claim for himself the honor of divinity. The princes of our age, who desire to possess God’s churches, why indeed do they seek this but that they may thereby appear more glorious in the sight of men? Strong reason cries out that this must not be granted them, since they ought not to possess churches in order to appear richer or more glorious through them, but ought rather to serve the Church itself for the salvation of souls. A pastor in the Church, moreover, ought to be chosen only for the salvation of souls.

Therefore, one who says, “The churches are mine, and I made them; for they were made from my kingdom, and they ought to serve me; nor can they have rulers unless I give them”—does he not claim as his own right that which belongs to God? [Col. 0674C] Is this not plainly not merely to imitate Simon’s wickedness, but even to surpass it? Or because he does not promise money but threatens the sword, is he therefore not to be regarded as Simoniac?

It is said that Pope Paschal II, compelled by this force, out of compassion, that is, for his brothers and children whom he saw being harshly treated, gave assent so far as to permit by a granted privilege that a bishop should not be consecrated unless invested by kings [manuscript: “regions”] with ring and staff; and that the pope should not elect a pastor without the king’s permission. If he did so, he could not remain in office; instead, a pastor was to be elected according to the king’s will and was not to be consecrated unless first invested by the king. How contrary this is to the grace of the Holy Spirit [Col. 0674D] and how opposed to the sacred canons, we have sufficiently and abundantly taught above.

For if this is granted to kings, the whole Church is subjected to them. And whoever enters sacred order through secular powers is shown to acquire it thus. That this is Simoniac and contrary to the sacred rules is plain to everyone. Therefore the holy pope ought not to observe this, but most diligently to correct it, imitating the faith of his most blessed father, the apostle Peter, whose place he holds by God’s grace in the holy Church. Peter strove to correct with great love of heart what he had timidly denied.

The examples of the holy Fathers, their most sacred words, both those we have already brought forward and those we shall yet bring forward, teach most plainly that these things must be corrected. For the apostle Paul says: “If I build again the things which I destroyed, I make myself a transgressor” [Gal. II]. The most blessed pope must by every means beware of this, he who had previously forbidden this fault of perversity in assembled synods.

Moreover, he ought not to give assent to this matter, not merely lest he appear a transgressor before God, but also lest he incur his own sentence, according to the words of the same blessed apostle Paul:

> There are some who trouble us and wish to overthrow the Gospel of Christ. But though we, or an angel from heaven, should preach to you otherwise, let him be anathema [Gal. I]. As we have said before, so I say again now: if anyone should preach to you otherwise than what you have received, let him be anathema. For do I now persuade men or God? Or do I seek to please men? If I still pleased men, I should not be Christ’s servant. [Ibid.]

His teaching on this matter is that the ecclesiastical order should appoint bishops in the cities, as he himself commanded his disciples. The appointment of bishops pertains not only to spiritual things but also to temporal matters.

### CHAPTER CXVIII.—That the people must be compelled to fulfill God’s will.

The assertion that this was granted so that royal power might bind divided peoples into unity is neither worthy nor just. For one must not act contrary to God’s will in order that the people may be united; rather, God’s justice must be feared so that the people may agree with him. If they do not, they must be restrained by priestly authority and royal power—not by investiture, which was devised in order that by this sign the emperor might show himself to possess God’s sanctuary.

That no assent ought to be given to this, the holy prophet teaches most plainly, with a grave threat, in Psalm LXXXII. Therefore what is said to have been conceded contrary to the authority of the Old and New Testaments must be corrected.

### CHAPTER CXIX.—That a perverse judgment must be corrected.

St Augustine also teaches that a perverse judgment must be corrected, saying:

> It is great wisdom for a man to correct himself.

And again:

> He loves himself far too perversely who wishes others also to err, so that his own error may remain hidden. How much more useful and better it is, when he himself has erred, that he should warn others not to err. But if he does not wish to do this, at least he should not make them companions of his error. For if God grants me what I desire, namely that I may collect and point out, in a work prepared for this purpose, whatever in all my books most rightly displeases me, people will see that I am not partial to myself. [Col. 0675D]

### CHAPTER CXX.—That we must resist the perverse with great zeal, and fear God more than man.

St Gregory shows [manuscript: “that”] with what zeal we ought to resist the perverse, saying:

> We are often left quiet and undisturbed if we do not take care to oppose the wicked for the sake of justice. But if the mind has been kindled with longing for eternal life, if it already beholds the true light within, if it raises within itself the flame of holy ardor, then, so far as place permits and the cause requires, [Col. 0676A] we ought to expose ourselves for the defense of justice and to confront those breaking out into injustice, even when they do not demand it of us. For when they strike justice, which we do not love, in others, they nevertheless pierce us by their blow, even when they seem to be hunting.

### CHAPTER CXXI.—Concerning the same matter.

(POPE INNOCENT.) An error which is not resisted is approved, and truth, when it is not defended, is oppressed. For to neglect, when you can overthrow the wicked, is nothing other than to encourage them; nor is one free from the scruple of secret complicity who fails to oppose an open crime.

### CHAPTER CXXII.—Again concerning the same matter.

(POPE INNOCENT.) What advantage is it to a person not to be stained by his own error if he gives assent to one who errs? Without doubt, both one who sins and one who gives assent to the erring fight against the commandments.

### CHAPTER CXXIII.—Again concerning the same matter.

One who does not come forward to cut things off so that they may be corrected seems, in wandering astray, to consent.

### CHAPTER CXXIV.—Concerning the same matter.

(AUGUSTINE.) Whoever conceals the truth through fear of any authority provokes God’s wrath upon himself, because he fears man more than God.

### CHAPTER CXXV.—On the foregoing.

Both are guilty: the one who conceals the truth and the one who speaks falsehood; for the former does not wish to benefit, and the latter desires to harm.

### CHAPTER CXXVI.—One who fears God must presume nothing against the ordinances of the holy Fathers.

[Col. 0676C]

Whoever fears almighty God does not in any way consent to do anything against him, against the apostles, against the prophets, or against the ordinances of the holy Fathers. We have shown above plainly that this practice now restored again in the Lord’s Church—namely, that worldly powers should dominate the election and investiture of bishops—is contrary to the Gospel, to the apostles, and to the ordinances of the holy Fathers.

It should also be known that it most plainly opposes prophetic teaching. For the Lord says through the prophet Ezekiel:

> Son of man, speak to the children of your people, and say to them: When I bring the sword upon a land, and the people of the land take one man from among their least and set him as their watchman, [Col. 0676D] and he sees the sword coming upon the land, blows the trumpet, and warns the people: whoever hears the sound of the trumpet and does not take heed, and the sword comes and takes him away, his blood shall be upon his own head. He heard the sound of the trumpet and did not take heed; his blood shall be upon himself. But if he takes heed, he has saved his life. But if the watchman sees the sword coming and does not sound the trumpet, and the people do not take heed, and the sword comes and takes away a life from among them, that person is taken in his iniquity; but I shall require his blood from your hand. [Ezek. XXXIII]

Explaining this, St Jerome says (Book X on Ezekiel):

> According to the spiritual interpretation, the Church often chooses a watchman from among the least of her people: namely, the one whom the Apostle, writing to the Corinthians [1 Cor. XV], also presents as judge.

And shortly afterward:

> The watchman of the Church is either a bishop or presbyter, who, elected by the people and knowing from the reading of the Scriptures and foreseeing what is to come, announces it to the people and corrects the offender. Therefore we must greatly fear lest we approach this office unworthy, and, having been chosen by the people, give ourselves to negligence and sloth; and, before this, to pleasures, the belly, and idleness, believing that we have received an honor rather than a ministry. For the Son of Man came not to be served but to serve [Matt. XX]; and he washed his disciples’ feet [John XIII], showing that every stain and fault in disciples ought to be washed away and cleansed by the teacher.
>
> Nor should we immediately answer: “What good is teaching, if the hearer does not wish to do what you teach?” For each person is judged from his own disposition and office—you, if you have spoken; he, if he has despised hearing. Solomon speaks of negligent teachers: “Hidden wisdom and concealed treasure—what profit is there in either?” [Ecclus. XX.] Something of this sort is also signified concerning one who causes one of the least members of the Church to stumble: “It is better that a millstone be tied around his neck and he be cast into the depths” [Mark IX] than that, established on the watchtower, he should harm very many.

### CHAPTER CXXVII.—That nothing ought to be more precious to us than truth.

(POPE FABIAN.) It is altogether certain that neither friendship, kinship, nor royal exaltation ought to be more precious to a person than virtue; for nothing is more precious than God, who is truth.

### CHAPTER CXXVIII.—That others must be recalled from error.

(POPE LEO.) One who does not recall others from error shows himself to be in error. For if anyone has the ability and does not recall one who is going astray from evil, he too is proved a participant in error. For we owe this obligation to charity: that we should permit neither ourselves nor others to perish.

### CHAPTER CXXIX.—Concerning the same matter.

(CASSIODORUS.) In the present matter, therefore, provision must be made not only for ourselves, but also for those who, by sacrilegious presumption, endeavor to take away what belongs to Christ, in such a way that, being unable to accomplish the evil they do, [Col. 0677D] they may cease from evil works.

### CHAPTER CXXX.—Concerning the same matter.

St Augustine likewise says: “It is great wisdom to make a man retract what he has spoken wrongly.”

### CHAPTER CXXXI.—What must be done when we are so hemmed in that we cannot escape without sin.

Blessed Gregory says in the *Moralia*:

> When the mind is constrained between lesser and greater sins, if there is no way at all of escape without sin, the lesser sins must always be chosen. Thus one enclosed by the circuit of walls so that he cannot escape throws himself into flight where he finds the wall lower.

### CHAPTER CXXXII.—Concerning the same matter.

A rash decision is praiseworthily undone; this is not transgression but the correction of rashness.

### CHAPTER CXXXIII.—That one must not do the evil which one has promised by oath.

[Col. 0678A]

The evil which someone had bound himself by oath to do, he must not do at all, because foolish vows must be broken. Yet he should repent because he took the Lord’s name in vain, swearing that he would do what he ought not to do either without an oath or with one.

### CHAPTER CXXXIV.—That for the sake of our own honor we must not inflict a stain upon sacred order.

Therefore, let us, supreme pontiffs fighting courageously for the honor of God and of holy mother Church, deign to imitate the example of holy Father Ambrose, who says (Epistle 20):

> Ambrose is not so important that he should overthrow the priesthood for his own sake; one man’s life is not worth as much as the dignity of priests.

This is truly the dignity of priests: that they rejoice to receive what belongs to God from God alone.

### CHAPTER CXXXV.—What must be done when the Church is disturbed.

In a matter of faith there ought to be a conference of priests, as happened under Constantine Augustus of pious memory, who issued no laws beforehand but gave free judgment to the priests.

### CHAPTER CXXXVI.—That we must not persist in a perverse judgment.

St Ambrose shows that one must not persist in a perverse judgment when it happens, but immediately return to what is good. Speaking of the holy Fathers, he adds:

> The bishops who came to Rimini had first accepted the sincere faith. But, through the action of Emperor Constantius, when certain persons wished to judge matters of faith within the palace, they brought it about that the decisions of the bishops were changed by trickery [Col. 0678C]. Yet they immediately retracted their altered judgment. And certainly the greater number at Rimini approved the faith of the Nicene Council and condemned the Arian decrees.

Thus we must act in this time as well. We must not persist in what has crept in, even for an hour; rather, the good which had been begun must be held all the more firmly.

### CHAPTER CXXXVII.—That we benefit not only ourselves but also the emperor if we do not consent to evil on his behalf.

Blessed Ambrose likewise, when he was compelled to surrender the vessels of the Church, said (*Sermon against Auxentius*):

> If I were compelled or asked to give something of my own—whether an estate, a house, gold, or silver, something belonging to my right—I would freely offer it. But I cannot take anything away from or hand over from God’s temple. I received it to be guarded, not handed over. Further, I take thought even for the emperor’s safety, because it would be neither expedient for me to hand it over nor for him to receive it. Let him accept the voice of a free priest: if he wishes his own welfare to be considered, let him withdraw from injury to Christ.

These words are full of humility, as I think, full of the affection which a priest owes the emperor. Therefore in this place we must consider and ponder with our whole heart how great an evil it is to hand over the whole Church to emperors, when this holy man refused even the Church’s vessels with such constancy. But one hands over the whole Church who permits it to have pastors only through a lay hand.

### CHAPTER CXXXVIII.—That God’s Church, that is, Christ’s inheritance, must not be handed over to the emperor.

[Col. 0679A]

Confirming that the holy Church—that is, Christ’s inheritance—ought not to be handed over to any human being, St Ambrose says (*Sermon against Auxentius*):

> You remember that today the holy man Naboth, the owner of his vineyard, was read of: he was pressed by a royal request to give his vineyard, where the king, having cut down the vines, might plant worthless vegetables. He answered [3 Kings XXI]: “Far be it from me that I should hand over the inheritance of my fathers!” The king was saddened because a right not belonging to him had justly been denied him; but he was also deceived by a woman’s counsel. Naboth defended his vines even with his own blood.

O priests of Christ! O true pastors of the holy Church, to whom God commanded the governance of his faithful people! Attend to what Christ’s priest, the great Ambrose, adds, saying (*ibid.*):

> If he did not hand over his vineyard, shall we hand over Christ’s Church? What answer, then, was given firmly? For I said to the assembled people: “Far be it from me that I should hand over Christ’s inheritance!” If he did not hand over the inheritance of his fathers, shall I hand over Christ’s inheritance? I added also: “Far be it from me that I should hand over the inheritance of the Fathers”: that is, the inheritance of Dionysius, who died in exile for the cause of faith; the inheritance of the confessor Eustorius; the inheritance of Merocles; and of all the faithful bishops of former times. I gave the answer proper to a priest; let the emperor do what is proper to an emperor. He may take my life before he takes my faith.

Now let us consider these things, dearest Fathers, and, following the example of holy Father Ambrose, far be it from us to hand over Christ’s inheritance; far be it from us to hand over the inheritance of the most blessed apostle Peter, to whom Christ deigned to say: “I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven” [Matt. XVI]. At the Savior’s command, Peter himself, and all our most sacred pontiffs and Fathers, handed over this inheritance perpetually to all his successors; and, giving the Holy Spirit to bishops, they gave them staff and ring, so that by a bodily sign they might indeed signify a spiritual reality.

But now, far be it from us to permit lay and secular persons, serving vain glory and greed, to dare to confer what is spiritual. What remains for them except to lay hands upon them? If this is believed wicked not only in deed but even in speech, how much more ought we to abstain from such great depravity?

For we must greatly fear what the same Blessed Ambrose continues and says (*ibid.*):

> Christ enters his temple, takes up a whip, and drives the money-changers out of the temple. For he does not allow in his temple those who sell chairs; he does not allow in his temple slaves of money. What are sacred chairs but offices of honor? What are the doves but the simple minds of the faithful, or souls following faith that is white and pure? Shall I, then, bring into the temple one whom Christ excludes?
