For he commands him to go out who sells dignities and honors; he commands him to go out who wishes to sell the simple minds of the faithful.

### CHAPTER CXXXIX.—Against those who say that we act against the emperor because we preach that pastors ought to possess ecclesiastical things without his investiture.

[Col. 0680A]

Although we preach purely and simply that the election of bishops ought to take place, and command that the elected person, invested and consecrated through the hands of priests, should render to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s, as the Lord himself did—just as Blessed Ambrose and St John Chrysostom also acted, the former carrying out an embassy of peace to Gaul, the latter to Thrace, as many saints are plainly known to have done—some who speak perversely assert that we wish to raise ourselves above the emperor himself.

We must meet them with the words of Ambrose, who speaks of his persecutors, saying (*Sermon against Auxentius*):

> They said: “Ambrose wishes to have more power than the emperor, since he will not surrender even one basilica to the emperor.” When they say this, they seek to seize our words, like the Jews, who tested Christ with crafty speech, saying: “Master, is it lawful to give tribute to Caesar, or not?” [Luke XX.] Will envy against God’s servants always be stirred up concerning Caesar? Impiety even takes this up for its calumny, putting forward the imperial name. And these men cannot say that they do not possess the sacrilege of those whose teaching they imitate. Yet see how much worse the Arians are than the Jews. The Jews asked whether he thought the tax owed to Caesar ought to be paid; these men wish to give the emperor the right of the Church. But as the faithless follow their author, so let us answer what the Lord and our author taught us.

### CHAPTER CXL.—Further confirmation of the same judgment.

Here we must see, here we must store more deeply in the memory of Catholics, what St Ambrose would say concerning Simoniacs who wish to hand over the entire Church, when he said these things against Arians concerning only one basilica. In that place holy Father Ambrose adds (*Sermon against Auxentius*):

> “Jesus, perceiving the deceit of the Jews, said to them: ‘Why do you test me? Show me a denarius.’ And when they gave it to him, he said: ‘Whose image and inscription does it bear?’ They answered: ‘Caesar’s.’ And Jesus said to them: ‘Render the things that are Caesar’s to Caesar, and the things that are God’s to God’” [Luke XX]. [Col. 0680D] “The tax belongs to Caesar; we do not deny it: the Church’s lands pay tax.”

### CHAPTER CXLI.—Against those who say that it lies in the Roman pontiff’s power to hand over God’s churches to emperors.

St Ambrose confirms that no priest can do what is unjust and displeasing to God, saying (Epistle 20):

> At first certain counts of the consistory came to me, demanding that I hand over the basilica and ensure that the people raised no disturbance. I answered what was proper to my order: that God’s temple could not be handed over by a priest.

The people cried out.

### Chapter 142.—Here it is shown to be false what some say: “All earthly things belong to the emperor.”

Again, St. Ambrose, showing that those speak against the truth who say (Epistle 20): “Therefore, what the Church possesses belongs to the emperor, because all earthly things are his,” says: “I myself was approached by counts and tribunes, that through me an exchange of basilicas might be effected, saying that the emperor was using what was his, because all things were in his power, and therefore all ought to be handed over to him. I replied: If he were to ask me for what was mine—that is, my estate, my silver, or any such right of mine—although all that is mine belongs to the poor, nevertheless things that are divine are not subject to imperial power. If he seeks my patrimony, take it; if my body, I will meet you; do you wish to drag me into chains? Do you wish me put to death? It is my desire. I shall be more gladly offered up for the altars.”

### Chapter 143.—That priests ought not to stir up popular sedition; but if it is stirred up on behalf of the justice they preach, it is not to be imputed to them.

[Col. 0618B] And a little later (Epistle 20): “When the people, together with the imperial officials, were disturbed, I was pressed to restrain the people. I replied that it was within my power not to stir them up, but within God’s hand to calm them.” And again, when the people had been calmed by God’s nod, they said: “We beseech you, Augustus; we do not fight. We do not fear, but we beseech.” This befits Christians: that the tranquillity of peace be desired, and that constancy in faith and truth not be recalled even by the danger of death.

### Chapter 144.—Further emphasis of this proposition, and how grave a thing it is to surrender the Church.

And likewise (Epistle 20): “Job was tested by the accumulated reports of disasters; he was tested also through his wife, who said: ‘Speak some word against God, and die’ [Col. 0681C] (Job 2). You see how great disturbances are suddenly set in motion: Goths, weapons, Gentiles. Do you perceive what is commanded when the surrender of a basilica is ordered? It is this: ‘Speak some word against God, and die.’ Nor is it only, ‘Speak against God,’ but also, ‘Act against God.’ The command is given: ‘Hand over the altars of God.’ We are therefore pressed by royal commands, but we are strengthened by the words of Scripture: Job answered his wife, saying: ‘You have spoken as one of the foolish women speaks’ (ibid.).”

### Chapter 145.—That such grave trials are inflicted not upon one man, but upon the whole Church; and that the emperor has no right in divine matters.

And a little later, showing that the Church ought to endure grave trials, he says (Epistle 20): [Col. 0681D] “What reason, then, is there for trials more grievous than this little worm, except that they persecute not me but the Church? Finally, the command is given: ‘Hand over the basilica.’ I reply: It is neither lawful for me to hand it over, nor advantageous for you, Emperor, to receive it. You cannot lawfully violate a private person’s house; did you think that God’s house was to be taken away? It is alleged that the emperor may do all things, that all things are his. I reply: Do not burden yourself, Emperor, by thinking that you possess any imperial right in matters divine. Do not exalt yourself; but if you wish to reign longer, be subject to God. It is written: ‘The things of God to God, the things of Caesar to Caesar’ (Matthew 22). Palaces belong to the emperor; the Church belongs to the priest. You have been entrusted with jurisdiction over public walls, not over sacred things.”

### Chapter 146.—How steadfast blessed Ambrose was in these sacred convictions.

[Col. 0682A]

That blessed Ambrose uttered all these things with firmness of faith and devotion is shown by what he adds (Epistle 20): “For all these reasons I am called a tyrant, and even worse than a tyrant. The emperor, angered, when the officials begged him to lay aside his indignation and go to the church, said: ‘If Ambrose orders you, you will hand me over bound.’ All shuddered at this saying. But Gallicanus, the chamberlain, dared to send me this message: ‘Do you despise Valentinian? I will take off your head.’ I replied: May God permit you to accomplish what you threaten. For I shall suffer what befits a bishop; you will do what befits a eunuch. And would that the Lord turn them away from the Church! Let them turn all [Col. 0682B] their weapons against me; let them satisfy their thirst with my blood!”

The Tripartite History bears witness to this, saying of blessed Ambrose that, when he was ordered to leave the church, he said: “I do not do this willingly, lest I seem to hand over the sheepfolds to wolves, or to those who blaspheme God. Kill me here, if you please; in this place I receive death with ready will.” This Emperor Valentinian, who, at the instigation of his mother Justina Augusta, an Arian, persecuted blessed Ambrose, was the son of that Valentinian under whom blessed Ambrose received the episcopate.

### Chapter 147.—An exhortation to serve the emperor in such a way that God is not offended.

The blessed Father Augustine also, in his books *On the Words of the Lord*, explaining how the words of the holy Apostle commanding us to be subject to higher powers [Col. 0682C] should be understood, says: “‘Whoever resists authority,’ says the Apostle, ‘resists God’s ordinance’ (Romans 13). But what if it commands what ought not to be done? Here certainly despise authority by fearing authority. If a procurator orders something, ought it not to be done? Yet if he orders something contrary to the proconsul, you certainly do not despise authority; rather, you choose to serve the greater authority. Nor ought the lesser to be angry because the greater has been preferred. Again, if the proconsul himself orders one thing and the emperor another, is there any doubt that, disregarding the former, one must serve the latter? Therefore, if the emperor commands one thing and God another, what do you judge? ‘Pay tribute; be obedient to me.’ Rightly so—but not in an idol-temple. In the idol-temple [Col. 0682D] he forbids it. Rightly so. Who forbids it? The greater authority. Forgive me: you threaten prison; he threatens Gehenna. Hence holy martyrs despised earthly authorities in order to serve the true Lord.”

By this exposition all passages of Holy Scripture commanding us to obey earthly powers must be understood. [Thus the manuscript reads: *praecipientes*, “commanding.”] What St. Augustine says concerning an idol-temple is to be understood also of heresy and every iniquity.

### Chapter 148.—That not only the vessels of the altar are sacred, but also everything that is offered.

We have shown above by many examples that all things possessed by the Church are sacred—not merely those which, in common usage, we all call consecrated, namely vessels and basilicas or any other consecrated things, but also lands, vineyards, [Col. 0683A] persons, animals, money, and absolutely all things vowed to the Lord. Here it must be observed that all these things are not holy in themselves, but by reason of the surpassing holiness of him to whom they are offered and the devotion of those who offer them.

That this must be understood thus St. Augustine, speaking on John, declares most clearly when he says of Judas: “Behold, Judas is a thief; and lest you despise the matter, he is a sacrilegious thief—not merely any thief of money-bags, but a thief of the Lord’s money-bags and of sacred things. Thus crimes are distinguished in the law-court between ordinary theft and peculation. Peculation is theft from the state; and the theft of private property is not judged in the same way as theft of public property. How much more severely must a sacrilegious thief be judged? It is one thing to steal from anywhere; it is another to steal from the Church. Whoever steals anything from the Church is compared with the lost Judas.”

The words of the holy doctor must be examined carefully. He calls sacrilegious the thief who stole the Lord’s money. Yet Judas did not steal from the material Church, which did not yet exist, but from the money-bags. That money was not holy, nor were the money-bags holy. Why, then, was he a sacrilegious thief, unless because that money, though not holy in itself, was nevertheless holy because it belonged to holy Christ our Lord and his apostles? So also the Church of the present time: everything it possesses is not holy in itself, but is holy because it belongs to Christ and his Church. Whoever therefore steals those things or seizes them by force is to be judged a sacrilegious thief or sacrilegious [Col. 0683C] plunderer.

Therefore the emperor ought not to have any right in ecclesiastical property, because such things are holy and dedicated to God. Hence blessed Ambrose says (Epistle 20): “Palaces belong to the emperor; the Church belongs to the priest.” We must not understand this childishly, but must recognize that under the name “Church” all things belonging to the Church are designated. The most holy Father Benedict agrees with this sense when, in laying down the Rule for monks, he says of the cellarer of the monastery: “Let him regard all the vessels of the monastery and all its property as consecrated vessels of the altar.”

### Chapter 149.—On the same matter.

The holy Father Gregory also shows in his *Dialogues* that things offered to God are holy even before they are sacrificed, saying: “When a certain priest was bathing in hot waters and was attended by a certain man, he brought with him one day two crowns of offerings. After he had bathed as usual and had used the man’s services in every respect, he offered bread to his attendant as a blessing, asking him kindly to receive what he offered out of charity. The man answered, sorrowful and distressed: ‘Why do you give me this, Father? This bread is holy; I cannot eat it. But if you wish to do something for me, offer this bread for me to almighty God, and then know that you have been heard when, on returning here, you do not find me.’” In these words it should therefore be noted that the holiness of things offered to God is most truly proved not only by the testimony of the living but also by visions of the dead. [Col. 0684A]

### Chapter 150.—True proof that, just as lesser things, so also greater things offered to God belong to the Church by right.

There are some who say: “The church building indeed and the ground surrounding it, consecrated to God, truly belong to no human being except God and his priests; but what the Church now possesses, glorified throughout the world—namely duchies, marquisates, counties, advocacies, public mints, cities and castles, villages and lands, and other things of this kind—belongs to the emperor in such a way that, unless they are repeatedly granted to the pastors of the Church whenever they succeed one another, they ought by no means to possess them.” Hence they contend that a right is owed to the emperor in the Church to such an extent that they say he ought even to invest it.

But if they will peacefully deign to consider what we have set forth above, they will clearly recognize that not only the small possessions formerly held by the Church, but also the great possessions it now holds, are hers. For the small possessions which she held before the Emperor Constantine are hers because they were offered to God; and the great possessions which she possesses after Constantine are hers because they were offered to God. For her Bridegroom, the Lord Christ, who formerly trained her through poverty, has now deigned to enrich her with glory.

But an emperor who preserves piety and justice is not permitted, as we have shown from the words of St. Ambrose, not only to violate the Church’s right, [Col. 0684C] but not even that of any private person. What they observe in the right of a private person, far be it from an emperor to dare to violate in the right of God!

### Chapter 151.—Against those who say: “The Church’s earthly possessions belong to the emperor, and unless pastors receive them from his hand, they ought not to possess them.”

For blessed Ambrose says to the emperor (Epistle 20): “You cannot lawfully violate a private person’s house; did you think that God’s house was to be taken away?” Let those attend to this who have given themselves so thoroughly to a perverse opinion as to say that the emperor cannot subject the Church herself to his own jurisdiction, but that what belongs to the Church belongs to the emperor in such a way that the pastor of the Church cannot possess it unless he receives it from the emperor.

For who would tolerate them if they said: [Col. 0684D] “The emperor cannot indeed violate a private person’s house; nevertheless, his possessions belong to the emperor in such a way that, unless he receives them from the emperor, he cannot by any means succeed in possessing them”? And if this is understood to be so absurd in human affairs that not even the most unjust judge would dare in any way to pronounce such a judgment, how much more must this not be said of the possessions of him who made heaven and earth? For although all things are his, he nevertheless deigns to call specially his own those things given to his bride, namely the holy Church. Hence he says also to his disciples: “Whoever honors you honors me” (Luke 10). But the honor of the holy Church is most truly understood not only in spiritual but also in bodily matters.

### Chapter 152.—That bishops and abbots ought, through their dependents, to render service to emperors from the great possessions they hold.

[Col. 0685A]

It must certainly be understood that, just as a Christian emperor ought not to alter what his Catholic imperial predecessors have done, so also, if something was granted to the Church on the condition that the emperor reserved something from it for himself, it must in every respect be rendered to him, unless he has remitted it, provided it is not contrary to the sacred canons. For just as we ought not assign to worldly persons things already consecrated to God, so we cannot take from them what belongs to them unless they themselves grant it.

Bishops and abbots, observing the precepts of the canons, ought not to involve themselves in secular affairs. But from the income of those great possessions [Col. 0685B] four portions ought to be made in bishoprics according to the decree of the sacred canons; in abbeys, however, all things ought to be held in common according to the rule of the holy Apostles.

### Chapter 153.—Against those who say that emperors invest the Church because they are anointed.

There are also those who say that it properly belongs to the emperor, because he has been anointed with sacred oil, to grant the pastors of the Church. We are surprised if any wise persons say this. For he is not anointed in order that he may govern the Church rightly, but that he may rule the kingdom faithfully. He ought not to order the Church but to obey it as a son.

Was not King Uzziah, like all the kings of Judah, anointed with holy oil? Why then, if sacred functions belong to anointed kings, was he struck with leprosy when he wished to offer incense? [Col. 0685C] (2 Chronicles 18). Is it not greater to confer the prerogative of the episcopate than to offer incense? Let kings and emperors therefore desist from this presumption, lest perhaps the angry Lord strike them with spiritual leprosy and compel them to depart from his Church. Let them love to preserve the rules of the Catholic Church, so that in the eternal Church they may reign with Christ. Amen.

### Chapter 154.—Against those who say: “Spiritual matters belong to bishops; temporal matters do not.”

But lest someone object and say, “Spiritual matters may be subject to the judgments of bishops, but earthly matters by no means,” let him attend to the decree of the religious Emperor Theodosius speaking on this matter.

### Chapter 155.—Constitution of the Emperor Theodosius.

[Col. 0685D] “Therefore, all cases which are handled either under praetorian law or in civil proceedings, when decided by the judgments of bishops, shall remain in perpetual stability; nor shall it be permitted thereafter to reopen a matter which has been determined by the judgments of bishops.”

### Chapter 156.—Various enactments of laws confirming the same things as the sacred canons.

Since we have produced many precepts of the canons and examples of saints in order to prove that pastors are to be introduced into the Church purely and simply; that the Church ought to possess in perpetual right what it holds; and that it is not lawful for the emperor or any great man to invest the Church, subject it to himself in any manner, alienate by any device what it possesses, or grant it to any person—let us now bring forward the imperial enactments of Christian [Col. 0686A] emperors also, and show that they do not depart from the sacred canons. For they decreed thus concerning the ordination of bishops:

### Chapter 157.—What must be observed in the ordination of a bishop.

First, inquiry must be made concerning the bishop’s life: whether it is good or blameworthy, and whether he is supported by good testimony or not. At the time when he is consecrated, the person consecrating him must ask him, if he is able, whether he can perform and observe all that the divine canons command; and if he denies that he can observe them, he is not to be consecrated. But if he promises that he will observe, so far as is possible to a human being, the holy precepts of the canons, then the consecrator [Col. 0686B] ought to admonish and instruct him, and he shall be numbered among religious bishops.

For the canons of the Fathers ought to have the force of laws. But if anyone has given money and by that means has been consecrated bishop, not only he but also the person who consecrated him shall not be among the bishops; and the money or property given for the sake of consecration shall be assigned to the sacred Church—whether the giver is bishop or cleric. The receiver, however, shall lose not only the property but also his clerical rank and honor. Likewise, if the person who received money or property is a layman, he shall lose those things and be compelled to pay to the holy Church, as a penalty, an additional amount equal to what he received. But if he holds public office, [Col. 0686C] he shall cease to hold office and be condemned to irrevocable exile.

### Chapter 158.—That what has been given to holy places ought to remain with them firmly.

Let the rights granted to bishops and all privileges remain. Likewise: let all aids and benefactions given to religious places remain firmly established.

### Chapter 159.—Likewise, on the same matter.

Possessions belonging to religious houses shall acknowledge no assessment.

### Chapter 160.—On an inheritance left in the name of Christ.

If anyone leaves an inheritance in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Church shall receive what has been left.

### Chapter 161.—On an inheritance left to martyrs.

[Col. 0686D]

If anyone leaves an inheritance in the name of the martyrs, the Church shall receive its benefit.

### Chapter 162.—That a bishop’s property should legally pass into the right of the Church.

If, after becoming bishop or before consecration, anyone wishes to offer his own property to the Church of which he will be bishop, this is praiseworthy, because it is not a purchase but an offering.

### Chapter 163.—That Church property is to remain firmly established.

Church rights shall suffer no diminution in respect of property acquired after the episcopate which we have decreed belongs to their Churches.

### Chapter 164.—That bishops are not to be subjected to compulsion for Church property.

[Col. 0687A]

No bishop shall suffer exaction or harassment on account of the property of his Church.

### Chapter 165.—What the emperor ought to do if he wishes to exchange property with the Church.

If the emperor wishes to make an exchange with the Church, he shall have authority only insofar as the Church receives improved property in exchange.

### Chapter 166.—On emperors’ reverence toward clerics.

Behold, from these sacred constitutions it is plainly evident how great reverence sacred emperors ought to have for the Church of God and those who serve it.

### Chapter 167.—Examples of saints by which we are most fully admonished to contend for truth even unto death.

[Col. 0687B] Therefore, after setting forth so many precepts for observing truth, let us now briefly bring forward examples of saints who did not fear to lose this present life for truth, and thus, with God’s help, bring this present little book on the honor of the holy mother Church to an end.

First comes to mind blessed John, the Lord’s forerunner, so great a lover of truth that, in forbidding an unjust deed to the king, he did not fear to die for truth. So too blessed Elijah did not fear to suffer persecution in opposing the king. Blessed Moses also, instructing the people in God’s commandments, endured from them very often not honor but persecution. The blessed Maccabees, martyrs, [Col. 0687C] did not refuse to die for the laws of their fathers. The three youths did not shrink from being cast into the furnace of fire for truth. The holy Apostles likewise, refusing not to draw upon themselves the hatred of the whole world for Christ’s truth, taught us by their death not to fear for Christ and willingly to embrace death.

The examples of blessed Stephen, the first martyr, and of all Christ’s martyrs who followed him must also be imitated. They could not be turned from truth by innumerable and exquisite torments. There are also other most sacred confessors, to whom it was not said that they should worship idols, but that they should alter sacred doctrines: such were blessed Athanasius, bishop of the Church of Alexandria; Hilary of Poitiers; Paulinus of Trier; and Eusebius of Vercelli. Fighting against Arius, they did not hesitate to suffer for the truth of Christ. Indeed, the example of blessed Pope Martin is also greatly to be imitated, for he too did not shrink from suffering exile and chains for faith in the Lord’s Incarnation.

There are so many examples of other saints that time would fail before we could enumerate the Fathers of the Old and New Testaments who, as the Apostle says, “through faith conquered kingdoms, wrought righteousness, and obtained promises” (Hebrews 11). But let us bring forward one more athlete of the holy Church, namely John Chrysostom. He was so perfect, so filled with the Holy Spirit, that in defense of a certain widow, whose vineyard the Empress had taken, he did not hesitate to rebuke her and call her like Jezebel. At last, when hatred had grown strong because [Col. 0688A] he publicly rebuked injustice, and because he again publicly reproved the Empress on account of a certain image which she had dared to set up near the church, he was condemned by a council of pseudo-bishops whom he himself had long before justly condemned; and when the Emperor Arcadius, at his wife’s instigation, persecuted him, he was sent into exile and did not refuse to die for justice.

What would this man have done, what would he have done in these days, when the whole Church is trampled underfoot—he who did not fear, in defense of one widow, to stir the emperor’s mind against himself even unto death? Rightly Pope St. Innocent and all the Western bishops, on hearing of the unjust death of so great a man, were moved and condemned with anathema all supporters of this deed.

Also in recent times Pope Gregory VII, of venerable memory, fighting for the honor of the holy Church, endured many and various storms, but could not be bent because he was founded upon the firm rock. Urban II, his successor, likewise following his example, did not refuse to endure many dangers for the Lord’s bride. For it must be known that in his times the persecution of schismatics increased so greatly that at one time he did not dare remain anywhere in the entire city of Rome. Yet he did not yield; but, enduring patiently, Christ winning the victory for him, all force of the heretics was destroyed, and he himself was restored to the holy Church and rested in blessed death at St. Peter’s in his own see.

Therefore, most holy Fathers, following these examples of the saints, let us preserve, according to the prophetic admonition (Psalm 36), truth and behold equity, because there is a posterity for the peaceful man. But the unjust, [Col. 0688C] although they seem for a time to flourish, shall perish forever. And may the grace of God, which we defend by God’s gift, deign to preserve us both here and for eternity. Amen.

### Chapter 168.—Exhortation that, strengthened by God, we contend even unto death for these sacred doctrines.

Therefore, most holy Fathers, considering the examples of these saints, and recognizing also that these most sacred doctrines of the holy Church were bestowed by the Lord Christ himself, let us strive, strengthened and confirmed by God, to contend for their observance even unto death, certain of the mercy of Christ, who, as the proof of his true love, entrusted his sheep to the first shepherd, the blessed Apostle Peter, to be fed. For if we fall for these things, we shall be delivered to death for justice. But blessed, as the Lord himself says, are those who suffer persecution for justice, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven (Matthew 5).

For it is just to contend even unto death, feeding God’s flock, for the honor of the holy mother Church; and the most blessed John the Evangelist also exhorts us, saying: “As Christ laid down his life for us, so we ought to lay down our lives for our brethren” (1 John 3). May almighty God, who through us, his lowest and least servants, speaks these things in your ears, deign through the grace of his Holy Spirit to speak and confirm the same things in your hearts: he who, for love of his holy Church, deigned to descend from the bosom of the Father [Col. 0689A] and to taste death; who lives and reigns with the Father, God, in the unity of the Holy Spirit [Col. 0690A] through all ages of ages. Amen. Thanks be to God the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. Amen.

Here ends the book *On the Honor of the Church*.

**In the year of the Lord 1119, Peter de Honestis, cleric of Ravenna.**

[Col. 0689]

[Col. 0689]

## Historical Notice

*(Oudin, Writers, II, 1012)*

[Col. 0689B] Peter de Honestis, abbot of St. Mary of the Port near Ravenna, distinguished about the year 1116 for virtue and regular observance, wrote a Rule for the clerics of his institute, commonly called the *Constitutions of Portus*. It has been falsely attributed to Peter Damian, as Gabriel Pennotto proves in Book II of his *History of the Canons Regular*. For the abbey of St. Mary of the Port is still possessed by the canons of the Lateran Congregation.

This Rule is found among the works of St. Peter Damian in the Paris edition published by Charles Chatelain in 1642, Rue Saint-Jacques, under the sign of Constance, and in the final edition of 1663, published by Gilles Tomperé, Rue de la Harpe, near the Puits-Certain. Peter flourished in the time of Pope Paschal II, and is said to have died in 1119, on 29 March. Constantine Cajetan, a Syracusan and abbot of St. Barontus from the Cassinese Congregation, published this Rule.

As the same Abbot Cajetan observes, many have confused this Peter de Honestis with Peter Damian, who was also surnamed de Honestis [Col. 0689C]; and thus they indiscriminately assigned the earlier man, a cardinal of the Holy Roman Church and Benedictine monk, to the order of Canons Regular. But Jerome Rubeus, in Book V of his *History of Ravenna*, correctly distinguishes the two around the year 1116. He speaks thus of this latter Peter de Honestis:

> “At this time Peter, head of the monastery of Portus, was held in high esteem. Born of the noble Ravenna family of the Honesti, and not entirely unlearned, he was a priest. In fulfilment of a vow which, driven by a storm while sailing, he had made to the Blessed Virgin Mary, he built a church and monastery in the harbor of Ravenna. Thereafter, for the reason derived from the place, it was called the monastery of Portus. There he established a community of priests under certain prescribed laws, which Pope Paschal II, at Peter’s own request, confirmed after they had been sent to him at the end of the year 1116. Peter’s letter was as follows: ‘To Paschal, by God’s providence bishop of the supreme and apostolic see, Peter the Sinner,’ etc.”

Then the same Jerome Rubeus learnedly and very aptly distinguishes the two with these words:

> “It can, I think, be sufficiently clear how great is the difference between this Peter of Portus and Peter Damian. Both are indeed named Peter, both are men of Ravenna, both lived holy and innocent lives, and at almost the same time; this caused many not to distinguish them. Both were called ‘Sinners,’ for a custom had grown up that those living religiously then styled themselves sinners through humility of mind; anyone who consults the records of those times will readily recognize this. Yet Peter, head of Portus, was always, as they say, a priest and cleric; Peter Damian, however, was a monk. The former spent almost his whole life in the monastery of Portus; the latter in the wilderness of Fonte Avellana. The former died at Ravenna, the latter at Faenza. The former on the fourth day before the Kalends of April [29 March], the latter on the eighth day before the Kalends of March [22 February]. The former in the year 1119, the latter in the seventy-second year after 1000 [1072]. And Dante, writing of Peter Damian, seems to testify that they differed in this respect: for, when he introduces Peter Damian speaking, he says that he was Peter Damian and had lived in the solitude of Fonte Avellana; but that Peter the Sinner had dwelt with the Blessed Virgin Mary on the Adriatic shore.” [Col. 0690C]

These are the excellent remarks of Jerome Rubeus. The writers *On the Excellence and Prerogatives of the Canons Regular of St. Augustine* argued rather sharply, and wrongly in my judgment, that both these Peters de Honestis belonged to the order of Canons Regular. For it is certain that Peter Damian was a monk and professed the Rule of St. Benedict. Thus Augustine of Pavia wrongly counts him among his Augustinian Canons in Part IV, chapter 22, and Part V, chapter 8, of the *Bulwark of the Canonical Order*; and so also John Trullus, *On the Order of Canons Regular*, Book I, chapter 5.

Conversely, Constantine Cajetan, abbot of St. Barontus of the Cassinese Congregation, in order to return like for like to the Augustinian Canons, vigorously argues that neither of these two Peters de Honestis belonged to the order of Canons Regular: not the first, who is known to have been a monk of Benedictine observance; nor the second, since he never embraced the Augustinian Rule, or the Rule so called, but himself composed his own, having nothing in common with that which is called Augustinian. Those desiring more concerning Peter de Honestis should read the cited Cajetan in the prolegomena to this Rule, Jerome Rubeus in Book V of the *History of Ravenna*, and others who have written on the same subject after him. [Col. 0690D]

## The Rule for Clerics of Peter de Honestis, Cleric of Ravenna

[Col. 0691]

## Preface to His Most Gracious Reader by Dom Constantine Cajetan, Abbot and Benedictine Defender, on the Rule of the Venerable Peter de Honestis, Cleric of Ravenna

[Col. 0691A] At the end of the fourth volume of our most holy doctor Peter Damian, we arranged to add the Rule which Peter, the cleric of Ravenna, wrote for the instruction of clerics and canons, chiefly for two reasons. First, so that all students who until now have generally confused the two may understand that this Peter is different from our own. Second, so that they may recognize that Peter the cleric published this Rule for those clerics and canons who lived regularly in cathedral churches under their bishops, or in other collegiate churches, chiefly according to the norm of the Council of Aachen—not for professed followers of St. Augustine. The observance of the latter’s Rule—if it was a Rule, or rather an epistle—had scarcely been heard of from the death of that holy doctor until almost that period.

As to the first point, although both were called Peter and had Ravenna as their native country, they are known nevertheless to differ as widely as heaven and earth in profession and age. Our Peter, after leaving the surname of his family, took the surname Damian from his elder brother, who had supported him like a father. Yet, as I shall note elsewhere from his writings, he was born of noble, not obscure—as some gratuitously assert—parents. This other Peter was likewise born illustrious in lineage and family, from the stock of the Honesti.

Peter Damian was also, by profession, a monk, hermit, and prior of the monastery of Holy Cross of Avellana in Umbria, not far from Gubbio, of the Order [Col. 0691C] of our holy Father Benedict. This is plainly established not only from weightier contemporary writers but also from his own writings, whatever others may invent in affirming that he was Augustinian rather than Benedictine, or even, as others still falsely claim, that he became Benedictine after having been Augustinian. Before his monastic life he was attached to no Rule; rather, he was a doctor of sacred letters and of both laws, and taught legal learning at Parma, as, God guiding us, we shall show more clearly in our commentary on his Life.

The other Peter, however, was a cleric and prior of clerics. Seeing many abuses among clerics—abuses which Peter Damian especially laments and rebukes in his letters—he founded a monastery on the shore of the Adriatic Sea in honor of the most blessed Virgin Mary, prescribed a Rule compiled from the holy Fathers and, as may be seen, especially from that of our holy Father Benedict, and sent it to Pope Paschal II for confirmation, in order to reform corrupt morals. We do not deny, however, that this same monastery, like many Benedictine ones, was later subjected to the jurisdiction of the Augustinians.

Finally, as regards their dates, all writers of that period have left on record that Peter Damian died in the year of Christ 1072, as the most eminent Cardinal Baronius also proves at length. [Note: [Col. 0691C] Cardinal Baronius, *Annals*, vol. XI, under the year 1072.] Foremost among them, Berthold of Constance, who recorded this in precisely these words in his continuation of Herman the Cripple, writes: [Col. 0692C] “In the year 1072, Peter Damian, of pious memory, [Col. 0693A] passed to the Lord on the eighth day before the Kalends of March [22 February]; and Lord Gerold [Lord Girald], truly a monk distinguished by knowledge of the Scriptures and not unequal in character to his predecessor, succeeded him in the bishopric.”

Moreover, that Peter Damian died in the sixty-sixth year of his life [Note: [Col. 0693D] See the preface of Constantine Cajetan to vol. III of Peter Damian (Patrology, vol. CXLV)], at Faenza, in his monastery of the Congregation of Saint Mary at Avellana, or Columba; and that his sacred relics are preserved there to this day with great veneration, is so clear as to require no proof. On the other hand, Peter the cleric, who lived on into the time of Pope Paschal II, to whom he sent his Rules for confirmation, was contemporary with Paschal II, who reigned from 1099 to 1118. Indeed, there survives a letter of Paschal himself to him, dated from the Lateran, [Col. 0693B] on the third day before the Nones of July, in the seventh indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1115. Writers also add that, being more than eighty years old, he died in the monastery of Saint Mary at Porto, which he himself had built a little outside the city of Ravenna on the shore of the Adriatic Sea, in the year of the Lord 1119, on the fourth day before the Kalends of April. The following verses, which also confirm our opinion, are said to have been inscribed on his tomb:

> Here lies Peter, called by the surname “Sinner,”  
> To whom Christ granted that he should build this house of merits.  
> In the eleven-hundredth year he paid his debt. On the fourth day before the Kalends of April.

Jerome Rubeus writes learnedly on this matter (*History of Ravenna*, book V):

> “It may, I think, be sufficiently evident how great a difference there is between this Peter of Porto and Peter Damian. Each was Peter; [Col. 0693C] each was a native of Ravenna; both lived holily and innocently; both lived at almost the same time; and, what caused many not to distinguish them, both were called ‘Sinners.’ For the custom had become established that those then living religiously styled themselves ‘Sinners’ out of humility of heart; anyone who examines the monuments of those times will readily recognize this. Peter, however, the head of Porto, was always a priest and cleric, as they say; Peter Damian, on the other hand, was a monk. The former spent almost his whole life in the monastery at Porto; the latter in the solitude of Catria. The former died at Ravenna; the latter at Faenza; the former on the fourth day before the Kalends of April, the latter on the eighth day before the Kalends of March; the former in the year 1119 [corrected: 1072], [Col. 0693D] the latter eighty years after the thousandth. And Dante, writing of Peter Damian, seems to testify that they differed in this respect. For, when he introduces Peter Damian as speaking, he says that he was Peter Damian and had lived in the solitude of Catria; but that Peter the Sinner had dwelt in the house of the Blessed Virgin Mary on the Adriatic shore.”

The testimony of Dante Alighieri, the Tuscan poet, is as follows:

> Between two shores of Italy rise crags  
> Not far from thy native land,  
> So high that thunder sounds far lower down;  
>   
> And they form a ridge called Catria,  
> Beneath which is consecrated a hermitage  
> Ordained for worship of God alone.  
>   
> [Col. 0694A] Thus began again the third spirit speaking to me,  
> And then, continuing, said: “There  
> I became so steadfast in God’s service  
>   
> That, living only on food prepared with olive oil,  
> I lightly endured heat and cold,  
> Content in contemplative thoughts.  
>   
> That place was once wont to bear fruit abundantly for Heaven,  
> And to yield its seed with great increase; but now  
> It has become barren, so that its corruption must soon be revealed.  
>   
> In that place I was Peter Damian;  
> And PETER THE SINNER was in the house  
> Of Our Lady upon the Adriatic shore.  
>   
> Little of my mortal life remained,  
> When I was asked and drawn to that cardinal’s hat.”  
> —Dante, *Paradiso*, canto XX

Peter Marianus, a most learned man, distinguished by his extensive knowledge of many subjects and my closest friend, rendered these verses of Dante into Latin as follows:

> [Col. 0694B] With such words he again began to speak to me:  
> Between the two Italian shores rise lofty ridges,  
> Not far from thy city; the swift fire of heaven resounds  
> In the lower region, so high do they touch the clouds with their summit.  
> Here rises a height called Catria, beneath which  
> Stands a house fit for worship of the heavenly Father,  
> Most pleasing to heaven amid deserted cliffs.  
>   
> Here I remained so steadfast in serving the Thunderer  
> That at no season of the year did my table know  
> Foods other than those moistened by Pallas’s tree;  
> But it was my heavenly delight to ponder contemplative cares.  
> That place was once wont to bear fruit abundantly for Heaven,  
> And to yield its seed with great increase; but now  
> (the report will soon pass into the mouths of the people)  
> Unhappy darnel and barren oats grow there instead of grain.  
>   
> There I, Peter Damian, passed my days;  
> And Peter, falsely called by the name “Sinner,”  
> Lived in the Virgin’s house near the Adriatic shore.  
> The end of my mortal life was already pressing upon me,  
> [Col. 0694C] When, unwilling though I was, my temples were encircled with the cardinal’s hat.

Yet although these matters are so clear that they cannot possibly be clearer, writers on Augustinian affairs contend, with sufficient obstinacy even to the present day, that Peter the cleric, surnamed Honesti, was the very same man as Peter Damian, monk and cardinal. I should truly never have believed this, had I not read it repeatedly in Augustine of Ticino, who, discoursing upon the expansion of his order of canons, commented as follows [Note: [Col. 0694D] Augustine of Ticino, *Defence of the Order of Canons*, part IV, chapter 23.]:

> “In Italy, down to the time of Blessed Peter Damian, the order was propagated at Ravenna in the canonical church of Saint Mary at Porto, and afterwards through Italy from that head. For the holy man himself, born at Ravenna from the illustrious family of the Honesti, first led an eremitical life at Avellana; [Col. 0694D] then, having been ordained bishop of Ostia and cardinal, at the time of the schism between Cadalous, bishop of Parma, and Alexander II, he voluntarily renounced the hat and withdrew to the aforesaid canonical church. There, after publishing many notable little works of books and performing magnificent deeds of piety, he rested holily and devoutly in the Lord as prior of that place. There remain even now Constitutions issued by him concerning the common life of regular canons, confirmed by the authority of Paschal II.”

Observe also, reader, what fictions this man of Ticino advances in defending his canons:

> [Col. 0695A] “The same order of canons,” he says, “flourished in regular observance through the holy man Peter Damian in the canonical church at Porto, in the diocese of Ravenna; then throughout all Tuscany, especially in the territory of Lucca at Frigianaria, through the agency of Peter Damian himself, aided by Alexander II and the illustrious Countess Matilda.” [Note: [Col. 0695D] The same author, part V, confirmation, chapter 8.]

John Trullus, likewise an Augustinian regular canon [Note: [Col. 0695D] *On the Order of Canons*, book I, chapter 5.], joins him. After making many assertions contrary to the truth of the matter, he did not shrink from attacking Abbot Trithemius, although Trithemius wrote with complete accuracy:

> “I have related all these things in order to make manifest that Peter Damian was a regular canon, bishop of Ostia, and cardinal; nor should anyone be moved by John Trithemius, who asserts that he was a Benedictine monk, [Col. 0695B] and says that he flourished under Henry IV in the year of the Lord 1050.”

John of Nigra Valle falls into the same error in his work *On the Doctors of the Order of Canons*; Raphael of Volaterra in book XXI of his *Anthropology*; Alphonsus Ciaconius in *Lives of the Supreme Pontiffs*, under Stephen X, called IX; John Baptist Signius in book I, chapter 4, of *On the Order and State of Canons*; Basil Serenius in his book *Privileges of the Canons of Saint Augustine*, p. 10; and many others, all quite recent, who confirm this same utterly false opinion in precisely the same terms.

Nevertheless, other persons have not been lacking who, while asserting that this same cleric Peter of Porto was Peter Damian himself, have numbered him among the Benedictines rather than the Augustinians. Antonius [Col. 0695C] Possevinus has most recently embraced their erroneous opinion, speaking as follows [Note: [Col. 0696D] *Sacred Apparatus*, vol. III.]:

> “Peter, son of Damian—thus he was called by almost everyone, because the surname of his family was Honesti; whence he was also called de Honestis—gave himself another surname when, writing to others, he signed himself ‘the Sinner’: a nobleman of Ravenna, monk of the monastery of Saint Andrew [otherwise, Saint Cross] of Avellana, of the Order of Saint Benedict and the Congregation of Columba, cardinal of the Holy Roman Church and bishop of Ostia, in the year 1058. But in 1072, returning to his monastery out of love for quiet and solitude, he died at Faenza in the monastery of Saint Mary, which he had built together with five others, in the year 1080, on 22 February. Since Volaterranus in book XXI of his *Anthropology*, [Col. 0695D] and certain others, wrote that he belonged to the Order of Saint Augustine, they undoubtedly either did not know what we have said or investigated the matter insufficiently.”

But let us now dismiss fictions of this sort. For just as mists are driven away by the sun’s rays, so those things advanced against the laws of history cannot endure the light of truth, but vanish when weighed according to an exact chronology. Let each religious order therefore retain its own honour; let each preserve and venerate the proper and distinctive images of its forebears; and let neither lay claim to the titles of the other.

[Col. 0696A] Certainly, in the holy Church, which is clothed round with varieties, the merits of all who fear God and keep His commandments are shared through charity; yet the differing distributions of graces are marked and distinguished in the individual religious orders by the diversity of their garments.

But now that the truth has been demonstrated—that the venerable servant of God Peter de Honestis was a cleric of Ravenna and distinct from Saint Peter Damian, the most learned cardinal of the Order of Saint Benedict—we judge it worthwhile to expose another error concerning the profession of this same cleric Peter. For the canons of Saint Augustine, and indeed quite recently, claim him as their own, and make him a canon of Saint Augustine, as they do also Saint Ubald, bishop of Gubbio. [Col. 0696B] This is shown to be altogether false by the documentary records of that age. Since we are inserting here the Rule written by this Blessed Peter the cleric for the instruction of his canons, the subject itself demands, rather than merely affords occasion, that we inquire whether he professed the Rule of the great Augustine. This will cast much light upon the historical question, and many who have hitherto supposed and taught that he was a regular canon of the Order of Saint Augustine will emerge from their inherited error. That this error has no basis in truth will be demonstrated without difficulty.

For, as Jerome Rubeus states:

> “Peter de Honestis, being a priest, in fulfilment of a vow made when he was driven by a storm at sea, built a church [Col. 0696C] and monastery for the Blessed Virgin Mary in the harbour of Ravenna. Thereafter, on account of the cause drawn from its location, it was called the monastery of Porto; there he established a community of priests, of which we have spoken,” etc.

And Baptist Signius says: “Peter, the first rector of Porto, was also the first to establish there the canonical order.”

Therefore no regular institution need be sought in the monastery of Porto except that introduced by its founder and first rector. But this institution was not Augustinian, nor according to the Rule of the great Augustine. Peter prescribed for his own community a Rule which Pope Paschal II afterwards confirmed by apostolic authority. Apart from this Rule, or these Constitutions written by him, which we give here, we read of no norm at that time which shaped the conduct of the priests there. [Col. 0696D] We prove this by a twofold argument: first, from these Constitutions themselves; secondly, because that which is now called the Rule of Saint Augustine—the only Rule which could have entered into the controversy [Note: [Col. 0696D] Signius, book II, near the end.]—had scarcely yet assumed the name and nature of a rule.

As regards the first point, in the preface to these Constitutions Peter is recorded as speaking and affirming thus:

> “After diligent inquiry, [we found] that no one of the holy Fathers, preserving the examples and searching the inner meaning of prophetic and apostolic teaching, had prescribed for clerics living together one certain, fixed, and sufficient rule, containing all the individual matters of the canonical order; wherein, just as monks have in the monastic Rule, clerics might have the most certain manner of living, of doing every necessary thing, and of rendering all things due and fitting to the canonical order.”
>
> Thus he. [Col. 0697A]

What could be clearer for our purpose? For if no one of the holy Fathers prescribed a certain, fixed, and sufficient rule for clerics living together, then the Rule of Saint Augustine was either not known to the world in those times, as we prove elsewhere; or, what is more pertinent here, it was unknown to Blessed Peter de Honestis and the inhabitants of the monastery of Porto. Otherwise Peter would not have asserted so boldly and universally that no holy Father had prescribed a rule for canons, nor would he have assumed for himself the task of prescribing one.

[Col. 0697B] If anyone should reply that Saint Augustine did indeed write a rule, but one not sufficient, not containing the distinct matters of the canonical order, the manner of living, and every necessary practical duty—laugh, reader, at this most unworthy evasion, proceeding as it does from Augustine’s sons or devotees: that that great river of eloquence, treasury of all knowledge, and immeasurable ocean of wisdom and learning, human and heavenly alike, when he applied himself to writing a rule for canons, should nevertheless have written it deficient, incomplete, and lacking. Yet they cannot escape even thus. For if Saint Augustine had drawn up any rule at all, even an insufficient one, and the men of Porto had observed it, they would at least have mentioned it as their foundational rule, containing the essentials of their life.

Produce for me whatever Constitutions, as they are called, of any religious order whatsoever—those which more extensively and explicitly develop what is contained in their rules. Do they not mention the Rule in every chapter and page? And, since such Constitutions are in a sense commentaries on the Rule and glosses on its text, would it not be absurd to imagine that they do not explain the rule upon which they comment, the text upon which they are glosses? Likewise, if these Constitutions of Porto had presupposed the Rule of Saint Augustine as their basis and had explained matters there more briefly set out, they surely ought at least once to have mentioned it and named the Rule which they were themselves more fully elucidating and completing as original and essential. But they did not do this. Indeed, it is clear from the Constitutions themselves [Col. 0697D] and from their arrangement that they have nothing whatever to do with the Rule of Saint Augustine.

We developed this point in our book *On the Antiquity of Regular Canons and the Augustinian Rule* (chapters 1–2), in these words:

> “Further, why should the men of Porto, in the body of their laws, establish—by useless repetition—obedience, poverty, continence, food, clothing, common possessions, and many like matters, without any mention of the Rule they professed or reference to it, if that Rule had previously established these things and had been received by them?”

Let the first chapter of the Constitutions serve as an example. There it was established by a common definition that a cleric ought to renounce his own resources and also his pleasures. They impose this because the Lord in the Old Law forbids the Levites possessions and private property; because Christ counsels it in the Gospel; because the apostles confirmed it by their example; and because the doctors Jerome, Augustine, and Prosper so taught—not because a Rule imposed it upon them.

[Col. 0698A] But tell me, I ask: if they had bound themselves by oath to the Rule of Saint Augustine as a law of life, could they have established more briefly, firmly, and effectively that the clerics, together with the Rule, professed and vowed poverty and the renunciation of private possessions, and therefore were bound to fulfil their vows? For a faithless and foolish promise displeases God. Yet, I say, they make no mention of this promise, of a promised Rule, of a vow, or of Augustine as Father or legislator, but only of Augustine as a common doctor of the Church, just like the others.

Further, in this very first chapter they mention Augustine twice: first, as teaching in his commentaries *On the Words of the Lord*; then, as putting into practice in his sermon *On the Common Life of Clerics* what he had taught. Yet they make not even the shadow of a mention of the Rule—which is precisely what they ought rather to have done. This is to me a most effective argument that Augustine’s Rule, even if it had only then become known and begun to be received, was neither introduced nor observed in the monastery of Porto, and consequently that Peter de Honestis was by no means an Augustinian. So far our own argument.

And this will certainly also be evident to anyone who considers these words of the first chapter of the Constitutions:

> “But lest we seem to be alone in holding this view concerning the life and Rule of Catholic clerics, [Col. 0698C] let other witnesses agree with us in the same judgment—men most religious and most fully endowed with every learning: namely Jerome, Augustine, and Prosper. Let us hear what they have said or understood on this matter.”

And later:

> “Augustine, in the nineteenth chapter *On the Words of the Lord*, writes thus, saying: ‘Tax-collectors came to John to be baptized by him and said to him, “Teacher, what shall we do?” But he said to them, “Exact nothing more than what has been prescribed for you.”’ And shortly afterward: ‘The soldiers also asked him, “And what shall we do?” John said to them, “Extort from no one, make no false accusation, but be content with your pay”’ [Luke 3]. ‘Here every person who serves as a soldier must recognize himself; for Scripture does not speak only of those serving as soldiers,’ [Col. 0698D] etc.”

A little later:

> “For the Catholic cleric is also held bound by this judgment. If he is not content with the pay he receives from the altar at the Lord’s command, but engages in trade, sells intercessions, and gladly accepts the gifts of widows, he seems more a merchant than a cleric,” and so forth. “And so that his deeds might speak more loudly than his tongue, he established in the bishop’s house itself a monastery of clerics, where no one was permitted to possess anything privately, as he himself testifies when he says: ‘I wished to have in this bishop’s house a monastery of clerics. Behold how we live: no one in our community is permitted to possess anything privately. But perhaps some do possess things? No one is permitted to do so; if any do, they do what is not permitted.’”

[Col. 0699A] These are Augustine’s words, and these are the Constitutions of Porto.

Observe with me here that they diligently inquire what Augustine said or thought concerning the life and Rule of Catholic clerics. Could there have presented itself a more suitable occasion for alleging and setting forth the Augustinian Rule, if they themselves observed it? For at the very threshold of the Rule, as they call it, one finds:

> “Call nothing your own, but let all things be common to you; and let food and clothing be distributed to each of you by your superior, not equally to all, because you are not all equally strong, but rather to each according to his need.”

And a little later:

> “Those who possessed something in the world, when they entered the monastery, should willingly desire it to become common property.”

Here you have community of goods, which the men of Porto strive to establish as commanded clearly and expressly by arguments gathered from every quarter. They would therefore have cited these words of their own Rule from Augustine much more aptly for their purpose than the *Commentaries on the Words of the Lord*, which do not serve the purpose as directly as the Rule.

Further, if Augustine’s act, corresponding to his teaching, was to be sought, why do they turn rather to the sermon *On the Life of Clerics* than to the Rule itself? For as the great son Gregory wrote of his great father Benedict [Note: [Col. 0699D] Gregory, *Dialogues* II.26.]:

> “Whoever wishes to know more precisely his character and life can find in the institution of that Rule all the actions of his mastership, because the holy man could in no way have lived otherwise than he taught.”

The same reasoning ought to have been applied to Saint Augustine: his acts and life were to be found better than anywhere else in the Rule itself, for he could not have lived otherwise than he taught.

We must therefore conclude that, since the men of Porto nowhere mention the Augustinian Rule, and indeed have transferred nothing from it but rather from the Benedictine Rule into their Constitutions—for the end of the first chapter and nearly all of the second are taken from chapters 4 and 6 of the Rule of Saint Benedict—since they did not lay it as the foundational stone beneath their own Institutes, from which it is clear that the Rule of Saint Augustine possessed no right or authority in that monastery or over its inhabitants, it must plainly be confessed that it had not yet been brought into the monastery of Porto [Col. 0699D] or imposed on its residents. The legitimate consequence is that Peter de Honestis did not give his name to Saint Augustine, either to his Rule or to his Institute. We establish this by another argument as follows.

For in a substantial volume we prove that Saint Augustine gave or wrote no rule for men. We establish this not by slight conjectures, but by the manifold authority of those who fail to mention this Rule when they most ought to do so; who recognize Benedict alone as legislating patriarch before the year 1000; who mention Augustine’s Rule as later and the canons as more recent; and who expressly assert that Saint Augustine either did not give a rule at all, or at least did not give one to men.

[Col. 0700A] We prove it by reasoning drawn from the nature of a rule: because Possidius nowhere mentions it, and Augustine nowhere mentions it, but instead referred his followers to the Acts of the Apostles from the time at which he would have had to write it; and because throughout that interval, namely between Augustine and Ivo, until some years after the tenth century, regular canons are nowhere ever found. We establish this conclusively from authors and councils of every kind, from the absence of distinguished men, saints, and privileges; we strip them of their fabricated antiquity and deprive them of some saints enrolled in their catalogue before the year 1000.

Since Blessed Peter de Honestis lived in the first century after the year 1000, when Saint Augustine’s 109th letter, written to nuns, first emerged and was adapted into a rule for men, it is certainly to be believed that he barely knew of it. It must altogether be admitted that it was not then introduced into the monastery of Porto. For, just as historians make notable mention of the new Constitutions published by the men of Porto, so the distinguished memory of a new Rule, then first known to the world and introduced into that monastery, would have been transmitted to posterity. [Col. 0700B] Just as it was great praise for Peter to have issued his own forms of life, so he would have deserved the highest encomium had he embraced the illustrious Rule of the great Augustine, newly made public or newly observed by men. This proves that he was in no way subject to the norm or Institute of Saint Augustine.

I pass over other arguments of this kind, which have been developed at greatest length, as I indicated above, in our book *On the Antiquity of Regular Canons*, ready for the press and soon to be made public.

Moreover, I cannot omit to infer with excellent consequence that, if Blessed Peter de Honestis was not a regular canon of Saint Augustine, the monastery of Porto in its earliest years did not observe that same Augustine’s Rule; and neither was Saint Ubald, bishop of Gubbio, a regular canon of Saint Augustine. Apart from the Constitutions of Porto, he observed no Rule in the monastery of Porto, nor did he carry any Rule from there with him to his monastery at Gubbio.

Observe, then, that the church [Col. 0700D] of the holy martyrs Marianus and James was indeed regular, but according not to the Augustinian Rule, but to the Rule of Aachen, which was organized and set down at the Council of Aachen under Emperor Louis the Pious, published by his command, and prevailed in many places throughout Italy, Gaul, and other provinces. Nevertheless, because in the time of Saint Peter Damian observance of it had either declined in most places or fallen into disuse, he complained bitterly concerning these canons and lodged many complaints with Pope Alexander II, especially in Letter 18, where he mentions this Rule.

Blessed Theobald, in his *Life of Ubald*, and Ubald’s successor in the bishopric of Gubbio, describes for us what the discipline of the canons or clerics of the aforementioned church of Gubbio was like:

> [Col. 0701A] “When the servant of God, Ubald, had passed the years of youth with the gravity of old age, and the seriousness of his character commended him to all, he was made prior in the aforementioned church of the holy martyrs Marianus and James and was honourably elevated, by the common vote of all, to the dignity of ecclesiastical pre-eminence. The dignity of the priorate he received was indeed sufficiently honourable; but those who had been appointed to govern the clerics were utterly unworthy of all honour and reverence. For in the aforesaid church at that time no observance of order and absolutely no remembrance of religious life was maintained. A man was hired for an annual wage to ring the bells at the hours of the offices; and because each cleric ate and slept in his own house, nearly the whole observance of monastic worship consisted in the ringing of bells. The cloister stood open to everyone, both men and women; at no time was its gate closed; each had his own concubine; and, abandoning the discipline of ecclesiastical order, they were enslaved to shameful indulgence and feminine lust.” [Col. 0701B]

From this it can easily be inferred that the church of Saints Marianus and James never adopted the Rule of Saint Augustine. For since the Rule only about the year 1000 assumed its name, nature, and force, had it been received in the said church, it surely could never in ten or twenty years have fallen so entirely into oblivion that no trace of it remained; nor could the inhabitants of that church, who had first embraced it, have so turned backward as to withdraw themselves from its yoke in so short a time and become so unlike that most excellent norm.

Conclude, therefore: since Saint Ubald neither found nor professed Augustinian discipline or Rule in that church, and since he brought from the monastery of Porto to his own community the Constitutions of Blessed Peter de Honestis, not the norm of Saint Augustine, conclude, I say, that he was by no means Augustinian, whether by Rule or profession.

[Col. 0702A] You will object to these words in the Roman Breviary for the feast of Saint Ubald:

> “Ubald, having become a priest, distributed his patrimony to the poor and to churches. Embracing the institute of the Order of Regular Canons of Saint Augustine, he brought it into his native country and lived therein most holily for some time.”

I admit that this is authority of great weight, proceeding from so great a quiver. But it must be answered that not everything found in particular histories of saints is a matter of faith. For the compilers of the Roman Breviary followed legends of saints which, prudently judging them to be completely true, they proposed for recitation as such. Nevertheless, because some blemishes had crept into those same histories, correctors were employed by the most holy Pius V and the most prudent Urban VIII, supreme pontiffs, to remove them.

[Col. 0702B] If anything escaped their diligence, this must not be charged against them as a fault, nor should one find in them any deficiency of diligence, prudence, or learning; rather, it must be imputed to those who supplied them with Acts and Lives that were not wholly true. For, just as false matters sometimes enter the narratives of papal bulls, not through the pope’s fault but rather through the fault of those who report incorrectly, so it was through their error that this blemish remained in the Roman Breviary—yet the fault belongs to those who imposed false accounts of Saint Ubald’s deeds upon the Sacred Congregation of Rites.

Thus, just as it is not to be reckoned a fault in the correctors of the Roman pontiffs Pius V or Clement VIII that something escaped their diligence and had to be corrected by our most holy lord Urban VIII, so neither should they be blamed because something escaped the great industry, labour, and learning of those whom His Holiness recently appointed for correction, to be observed by later generations. For day pours forth speech unto day, and night declares knowledge unto night.

These things have been said by me sincerely, not in order to attack anyone, but to undertake the defence of truth. I ask you, candid reader, to receive them in the best sense. Farewell.

[Col. 0701]

# ON PETER THE CLERIC, OR PRIOR OF PORTO, Surnamed “THE SINNER.”

From book five of Jerome Rubeus’s *History of the Deeds of the People of Ravenna*.

[Col. 0701D]

> “At this time Peter, head of the monastery of Porto, was held in high distinction. Born of the noble Ravenna family of the Honesti, and not entirely ignorant of letters, he was a priest. In fulfilment of a vow which, driven by a storm while sailing, he had made to the Blessed Virgin Mary in the harbour of Ravenna, he built a church and monastery. Thereafter, because of the reason drawn from its location, it was called the monastery of Porto. There he established a community of priests, prescribing certain laws, which Pope Paschal II [Col. 0702D] confirmed at the end of this year 1110 after they had been sent to him, at Peter’s own request. Peter’s letter was as follows: ‘To Paschal, by God’s will bishop of the supreme and apostolic see, Peter the Sinner, cleric, with his brethren: greeting in Christ and all obedience. Since divine grace has granted to Your Blessedness to hold Peter’s place in the Church,’ etc. (See under Paschal, above, no. 17, col. 461.)
>
> “But after ordering all things to be read and diligently examined, Pope Paschal replied in this manner: [Col. 0703A] ‘Paschal, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons living canonically at the Church of Saint Mary in the port of the Ravennate exarchate: greeting and apostolic blessing. This Rule of canonical institution,’ etc. (See above, no. 480, col. 414.)
>
> “And not long afterwards: In the year 1119 from the Virgin’s childbirth, Peter the Sinner died in old age on the fourth day before the Kalends of April, at Ravenna in the monastery of Porto which he had built; and he was buried there, on the left hand of those entering the church, beside the Sacred Tower.” [Col. 0704A]

[Col. 0703]

# THE RULE OF CLERICS BEGINS.

## PROLOGUE.

Most beloved brethren, gathered together in one body by love of divine worship, you began diligently to inquire with us whether any of the holy Fathers, preserving the examples and searching the inner meaning of prophetic and apostolic teaching, had prescribed for clerics living together one certain, fixed, and sufficient rule, containing every matter belonging to the distinct functions of the canonical order. In this Rule, just as monks have in the monastic Rule, clerics would have the most certain manner of living, of doing every necessary thing, and of rendering every duty and service fitting to the canonical order.

Because you could not find all these things so arranged as seemed necessary to your sacred community, with divine grace inspiring you, you began with us, according to your capacity and means, to determine each of these matters: partly by the authority of divine Scripture or holy councils, partly from the practice of certain religious men or places, and partly as seemed best to us. You resolved to hand down your statutes to your own congregation alone, and to command that what was handed down should always be observed.

Although Your Holiness was earnestly intent upon observing them, uncertainty began to arise concerning certain of them, through forgetfulness and through the disagreement of those whose memories differed. For this reason, it pleased you to enjoin upon me that I should transcribe in one arranged body all the things which, whether by the authority of divine Scriptures or holy councils, by the custom of regular places or men, by the religious affection of your devotion, or by prudent judgment, you had jointly delivered to be observed by your community; so that, through anyone’s negligence, the statutes might never have occasion either to be altered or abandoned.

Therefore, although I know myself unequal to so great a task and almost without knowledge, I chose nevertheless rather to obey your commands, avoiding pride, than to avoid the biting mockery of the envious. These things, then, which by the favouring grace of the Holy Spirit we have written down for the fuller observance of the divine law, and delivered to your congregation alone for observance as you request—though unpolished, yet because they have been established by us and composed at your petition and command—I ask you kindly to receive; having received them, preserve them, so that through them you may be able to ascend to the summit of higher commandments and finally attain the glory of the heavenly kingdom, with the help of our Lord Jesus Christ, who lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit for ever and ever. Amen.

# BOOK I.

[Col. 0703]

## CHAPTER I. That the order of clerics holds the place of Levites and apostles; and that they ought to imitate their life, renouncing also their own possessions and their own wills.

[Col. 0703B]

The order of clerics in the Church holds the place of the Levitical tribe and preserves the rights and performs the offices of apostolic dignity; no one of sound judgment doubts this. Therefore it is certain that they ought to imitate the rules and lives of the Levites and Apostles, whose place they are known to hold, whose dignity they possess, and whose offices they perform. For whatever law was given to the Levites, and whatever rule was given by the Lord to the Apostles, is without doubt imposed likewise upon Catholic clerics, who supply their offices until the end of the world. [Col. 0704B] Indeed, what is forbidden to the Levites, who still walked in the shadow, how can it be permitted to us, who now abide in the truth, when we read that many things were allowed to them which are undoubtedly forbidden to us?

Thus the Lord says to Aaron and his sons, and to the other Levites: “You shall possess nothing in the land of the children of Israel, nor shall you have a portion among them; for I am your portion and inheritance in the midst of the children of Israel” (Num. XVIII). And a little later it follows: “I have given to the sons of Levi all the tithes of Israel as a possession, in return for the ministry by which they serve me in the tabernacle of the covenant” (ibid.). And shortly afterward, concerning the same persons: “They shall possess nothing else, being content with the offering of tithes, which I have set apart for their use and necessities” (ibid.).

And this is in the Old Testament. But in the New Testament, let us hear what he said to everyone who wishes to adhere to the perfection of his discipleship: “If you wish to be perfect, go, sell all that you have, give to the poor, and come, follow me” (Matt. XIX). And elsewhere: “Whoever does not renounce all that he possesses cannot be my disciple” (Luke XIV). And in another place, when he sent the Apostles to preach, he forbade them, saying: “Do not possess gold or silver” (Matt. X). Peter plainly shows that he fulfilled this, saying: “Silver and gold I have not” (Acts III). The same Peter testifies that the other Apostles did this as well, when he asks the Lord on behalf of himself and his fellow disciples: [Col. 0705B] “Lord, behold, we have left all things and followed you; what then shall be ours?” (Matt. X). To him—and in him to all who do the same—the Lord replies: “Amen, amen, I say to you: you who have left all things and followed me, in the renewal, when the Son of Man shall sit upon the throne of his majesty, you also shall sit upon twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel. And everyone who has left house, or father, or mother, or brothers, or sisters, or fields for my sake, shall receive a hundredfold and shall possess eternal life” (ibid.).

These things were commanded alike to the Levites and to the Apostles: one rule and the same law are prescribed for both; possession is taken away from both, and earthly wealth is forbidden them. [Col. 0705C] Who, then, are bound by this rule and law except clerics, who hold the place of the Lord’s Levites and of Christ’s disciples, fulfill their ministry, maintain their offices, and possess their orders? In order that this command might be kept and fulfilled perpetually, God ordained that the price of sins, the vows and offerings of the faithful, the firstfruits and tithes of goods should be given to their churches; so that those devoted to divine worship and stripped of their own resources might have permanently appointed support, by which they might live, serve the Church, supply the needs of the poor, and more diligently fulfill every ministry of their order, never withdrawing from these on account of anything whatever or of necessity, nor attending to secular affairs.

From these points it is plainly shown that clerics who serve Christ may not both possess earthly resources and receive the goods of the Church; possess an inheritance in the world and receive a share of the churches. The Apostle’s saying is suited to confirm this judgment: “No one serving God entangles himself in secular business, that he may please him to whom he has proved himself” (I Tim. II). And Solomon’s saying: “Woe to the sinner who enters by two ways!” (Ecclus. II). Therefore, whoever wishes to follow Christ’s discipleship must renounce secular affairs; and whoever, once made sacred, has begun to live from sacred things is thereafter commanded to use sacred things for his livelihood.

But lest we seem alone in holding this view concerning the life and rule of Catholic clerics, let other witnesses concur: men most devout and most fully learned in every discipline—namely Jerome, Augustine, and Prosper. Let us hear what they said or understood on this subject.

Jerome, writing among other things to Nepotian concerning the life and conduct of clerics, says:

> “The cleric who serves Christ’s Church should first interpret his own designation and, having set forth the definition of his name, strive to be what he is called. For if *cleros* in Greek is called *sors* [‘lot’ or ‘portion’] in Latin, clerics are so called because they belong to the Lord’s portion; or because the Lord himself is the lot, that is, the portion, of the churches. And because either the cleric himself is the Lord’s portion, or has the Lord as his portion, he ought to show himself such that he himself possesses the Lord and is possessed by the Lord. He who possesses the Lord and says with the Prophet, ‘The Lord is my portion’ (Ps. XV), can possess nothing outside the Lord. But if anyone has anything besides the Lord, the Lord will not be his portion—for example, silver, estates, or various furnishings: with these portions the Lord does not deign to become his portion. But if I am the Lord’s portion and the cord of his inheritance, I receive no portion among the other tribes; rather, like a Levite and priest, I live on tithes, and, serving the altar, I am supported by the altar’s offering. Having food and clothing, I shall be content with these, and naked I shall follow the naked cross.”

And shortly afterward in the same letter he writes to the same person:

> “How can those who are stewards and administrators of other people’s houses and estates be clerics, when they are commanded to despise their own resources?”

Thus far Jerome.

Augustine, in chapter nineteen of his book *On the Words of the Lord*, writes:
