> “Now tax collectors also came to John to be baptized by him, and said to him: ‘Teacher, what shall we do?’ But he said to them: ‘Exact nothing more than what has been appointed for you.’ And shortly afterward soldiers also asked him: ‘And what shall we do?’ John said to them: ‘Do violence to no one, make no false accusation, but be content with your wages’” (Luke III).

Here every person who serves as a soldier ought now to recognize himself. Scripture does not speak only of those soldiers who are occupied in armed service, but whoever wears the belt of his office is enrolled as a soldier of his rank. Therefore this saying may be applied, for example, to soldiers and protectors, to all governors, and to everyone who receives publicly assigned pay: if he seeks more, he is condemned by John’s saying as an extortioner and oppressor.

And shortly afterward Augustine adds:

> “A Catholic cleric is also bound by this saying. For if he is not content with the support which, by the Lord’s command, he receives from the altar, but carries on trade, sells intercessions, gladly accepts the gifts of widows, he appears more a merchant than a cleric,” and so forth. “That he might make his deeds speak more loudly than his tongue, he established in the bishop’s own house a monastery of clerics. Behold how we live. No one is permitted to have anything of his own in our community. But perhaps some do have something? No one is permitted to do so; if any do, they do what is not permitted.”

These are Augustine’s words.

But now let us hear what blessed Prosper thought on this matter:

> “Therefore,” he says, “let him whom the ambition of possessing delights possess God, who possesses all that he has created, with an unencumbered mind; and in him he will possess whatever holy persons desire to possess. But since no one possesses God unless he is possessed by him, let him first become God’s possession, and God will become to him possessor and portion.”

And shortly afterward he adds:

> “What more does one seek when his own creditor is all things to him? Or what is sufficient to one for whom he himself is not sufficient?”

And a little later in the same chapter:

> “Who,” he says, “to whom God deigns to be a possession, seeks anything else? Or who, before love of him, does not despise all things thought great? Therefore, let him who wishes to possess God renounce the world, that God may be a blessed possession to them. Nor should the person renounce the world whom ambition for earthly possession delights; for as long as he does not leave his own things, he serves the world whose goods he retains. And certainly he cannot serve the world and God at once. Thus God wished his worshippers to renounce all things for which the world is loved, so that, once the desire for the world has been excluded, divine charity might grow or be perfected in them. And therefore he ordained that tithes of produce and firstfruits, firstborn animals, sacrifices for sin, and vows which God commanded to be offered to himself, should be distributed to priests and ministers, so that, while a most devout people supplies what is necessary, they might serve their Creator and shepherd with free minds.”

Thus far Prosper.

For the present, then, let these things concerning the renunciation of personal possessions suffice. But that you too, dearest brothers, ought to renounce your own wills, the Lord plainly shows in the Gospel, saying: “If anyone wishes to come after me, let him deny himself and follow me” (Matt. XVI). And: “Whoever wishes to save his life shall lose it; and whoever loses it for my sake shall find it” (John V). And in another place: “I have not come to do my own will, but the will of him who sent me” (Matt. XVI). Elsewhere sacred Scripture teaches us: “Son, turn away from your own wills” (Ecclus. XVIII). For, as is said elsewhere: “Pleasure has punishment; necessity brings forth a crown” (ibid.). And in another place it is commanded: “Do not follow your desires” (ibid.). Let those who follow them hear what is said concerning them through the Prophet: “They became corrupt and abominable in their desires” (Ps. XIII). Therefore the same Prophet, assuming the voice of prelates, writes: “He has subjected peoples to us, and nations beneath our feet” (Ps. XLVI).

Warned by these examples, therefore, brothers, let us not refuse to be subject to others for God’s sake; but, having altogether renounced our own wills, let us in all things carry out Christ’s will according to another’s judgment—yet one that is spiritual and discerning.

## Chapter II. What Canons Ought to Imitate before All Else

Before all else, then, we are taught by prophetic, evangelical, and apostolic admonitions to love the Lord our God with our whole heart, whole soul, and whole strength (Deut. VI), and our neighbors as ourselves (Matt. XXII). On these two commandments depend the whole Law and the Prophets.

Therefore, let them not kill; let them hate no one; let them not commit adultery; let them not steal; let them not covet another’s property; let them not bear false witness. Whatever they wish done to themselves, let them do to another; and what they do not wish done to themselves, let them not do to another. Let them not be puffed up with pride; let them not serve luxury and drunkenness. Let them not speak ill of their brothers (from the Rule of St Benedict, ch. 4); let them wholly resist lust and indecency; let them restrain anger and cast away envy.

Let them not be vain talkers, idle, whisperers, grumblers, sleepy, drunken, excessively gluttonous, or abusive. Let them bless those who curse them; let them grant the aid of prayer in deed to those who persecute and slander them. Let them not return evil for evil, but repay evil with good. Let them not seek vengeance; being injured, let them not injure; let them forgive every wrong and offense. Let them anticipate sunset with the setting of their anger.

Let them neither make oaths nor demand them of others except in unavoidable necessity. Let them beware of frauds and deceits. Let them by no means engage in usury. Let them attribute evil to themselves and good to God alone. Let them flee discord and call the discordant back to harmony. Let them hear the Apostle saying: “Not in reveling and drunkenness, not in beds and indecencies, not in strife and envy; but put on our Lord Jesus Christ” (Rom. XIII). Let them live soberly, justly, and devoutly, turning from every evil and doing good. Let them wholly reject every secular concern, attending to that apostolic saying: “No one serving God entangles himself in secular business, that he may please him to whom he has proved himself” (II Tim. II).

Let them moreover love fasting, refresh the poor, receive guests, clothe the naked, visit the sick, bury the dead, assist the afflicted, console the sorrowful, weep with those who weep, rejoice with those who rejoice, and not abandon charity. If possible, let them have peace with all; let them fear the day of judgment and desire eternal life above all things. Let them entrust their hope to God and place nothing before the love of Christ. Let them obey in all things the commands of their prelates; let them submit to their own bishop in all things according to the institution of the canons. Finally, let them devote themselves to spiritual teaching; let them diligently persist in readings, psalms, hymns, canticles, and the exercises of other good works. Let them recall those who have turned away; let them draw the converted, by life and teaching, toward better things.

Let them by no means stain their religious profession and purpose through unlawful deeds. Let them never seek the company of women. Let them not walk with wandering eyes, an unrestrained tongue, a proud and wanton gait, and loose hips. Let them not attend secular shows and pageants. Let them not engage in gambling or any kind of hunting. Let them not take delight in owning costly clothing. Let them by no means seek occupations of shameful gain. Let them altogether reject secular offices. Let them not accept gifts for the benefits of divine healing. Let them show the modesty and shamefastness of their minds in simple dress and manner of walking. Let them utterly detest obscenity not only in deeds but also in speech. Let them avoid frequent visits to widows and virgins. [Col. 0709A] Let them strive to preserve perpetually the chastity of an inviolate body; and let them not exalt themselves through any desire for boasting.

Finally, let them resist and renounce every vice, cleave to virtues, and always possess them. Let them obey the divine law and the admonitions of the holy Scriptures; let them discipline the body; let them not love comforts; let them not bring anger to completion; let them not reserve a time for anger; let them not offer a feigned peace. Let them strive to speak truth in heart and mouth (Rule of St Benedict, ch. 4). Standing at prayers and divine offices, let them sing in their hearts what they utter with their mouths. Let them guard the actions of their life every hour; dash evil thoughts against Christ and disclose them to their elders. Let them never utter vain, idle, or laughter-provoking words. Let them flee much talking and laughter, especially loud laughter, [Col. 0709B] for the Lord says in the Gospel: “Woe to you who laugh, for you shall weep!” (Luke VI). And the Prophet says: “A fool raises his voice in laughter” (Ecclus. XXI).

Let them give themselves without ceasing to reading and prayer. Let them always confess to God in prayer, with groaning, the evils of the past, and utterly desist from them; let them not fulfill the desires of the flesh. Let them hate their own will and in all things fulfill Christ’s will. Let them not resist the ordinances and commands of their prelates, even if those prelates themselves—God forbid!—act otherwise, remembering the Lord’s command: “Do what they say; do not do what they do” (Matt. XXIII). Let them love the younger spiritually and honor the elder; let them pray for their enemies in God’s love. Let them love one another; let them in turn supply one another’s needs according to the order of charity.

Let them maintain gravity not only in speaking and acting, but also in walking and standing. Let them possess elegance of conduct, holiness, and propriety not only in their actions but also in their speech. Let them season with the salt of wisdom all those with whom they associate, and draw them by their examples toward better things. Finally, let them confess and believe, observe and teach, everything narrated in the sequence of the Old or New Testament.

Therefore, dearest brothers, you have ordained all these things which your charity compelled me to write to be done by you for the observance of these precepts and of similar ones. Although some of them may seem, as it were, different, they were nevertheless devised for the observance of these matters, for the salvation of souls, and for the imitation of honorable manners of life. Therefore, I kindly ask you: receive these things, preserve what you have received, and persist in preserving them, so that through them you may deserve to attain the height of fuller holiness, the supreme perfection of religious life, and, after the labors of the present life, the glory of everlasting blessedness.

## Chapter III. That, Warned by These Examples, the Brothers Have Renounced Their Own Possessions and Wills

Warned, dearest brothers, by these admonitions of the divine Scriptures and by the examples of the holy Fathers, you have left every secular concern and the world with its pageantry; you have renounced your own possessions, wills, and earthly resources; and you have decreed that this rule is to be kept perpetually by your community. Thus, having here resisted the desires of your own will and renounced secular things, [Col. 0710A] you may there attain in fulfillment the fullest desires of your holy will, and possess without end the inestimable and unceasing delights of everlasting life.

## Chapter IV. That One Person Ought to Preside over the Rest

That in every canonical congregation one person ought to be chosen to preside over the rest is required by divinely inspired ecclesiastical practice and plainly shown in both the Old and the New Testament. For the Lord set Moses, and after Moses Joshua, over all the children of Israel; Aaron over the other Levites; and Peter likewise over the other disciples.

## Chapter V. What the Person Chosen to the Priorship Ought to Be Like

What the person set over others ought to be like is plainly shown by the Lord’s threefold question and Peter’s threefold answer. For when the care of feeding the sheep was entrusted to him, the Lord asked Peter three times whether he loved him; Peter answered three times that he loved him; and the Lord three times commanded him to feed them (John XXI). Thus the Lord’s threefold question is followed by Peter’s threefold answer concerning love, and Peter’s threefold answer by the threefold injunction to feed the flock.

But now let us see how this threefold love ought to be present in those chosen. He possesses threefold love who believes and loves God and the things of God in mind; confesses and preaches them in speech; imitates and observes them in deed. The examination is likewise threefold when, as we ought, we inquire, foresee, and investigate whether the person to be chosen possesses this threefold love. If faith and love in the heart are outwardly shown by fitting speech and conduct, a threefold answer now satisfies the threefold question.

The care of feeding the flock is also rightly entrusted to such a person three times, because whoever undertakes to feed sheep must continually provide for them with vigilant heart, admonish and defend them by the office of speech, and always draw them toward Christ by the examples of his conduct. The charge of feeding the flock is therefore rightly entrusted to one who has full inward faith and love in his mind; who possesses outwardly a perfect capacity and knowledge for admonishing, freely reproving, and prudently exhorting; and who observes and follows in deed whatever he says.

Nor should anyone be rejected from this office because of any fault, if he has now made satisfaction; for after Peter’s tearful satisfaction for his threefold denial, because threefold love was manifest in him, the Lord imposed upon him the feeding of the flock. This form of threefold love, therefore, dearest brothers, marked out in the first shepherd by none other than Christ, must be considered in choosing not only priors but all persons to be set over others in the Church.

## Chapter VI. That after the Death of a Prior Another Shall Be Chosen within Three or Four Weeks

I earnestly ask your holiness, dearest brothers, always to endeavor that this congregation of yours should never remain deprived of a prior for more than three or four weeks (Rule of St Benedict, ch. 58). Rather, within this period, let the brothers be assembled together and all matters concerning the election carefully considered. Even if he is the least of all, let that man be chosen unanimously by all who is more eminent in faith and holiness, more prudent in discernment, more fervent in charity, and, if possible, more fully learned; and who knows and is able wisely to guard the souls and bodies of the brothers and govern them according to the rule.

But if, in choosing, disagreement should arise among the brothers from differing preferences, so that the election is delayed beyond the appointed period, then the prelates of the Church shall choose in common, with prayer and fasting, the man whom they recognize as better suited for this, and whose election the greater and better part of the brothers has approved.

## Chapter VII. How the Chosen Person Is to Be Installed

When the prior is installed, after the offices for Mass have been prepared and the praises of the third hour completed, with the brothers standing by, the man to be installed shall prostrate himself in the midst. The superior, or the senior priest, by the command and consent of the brothers, shall say these or similar words:

> “Brother N., your brothers lay upon you in obedience the charge henceforth to minister to their bodies and souls according to God.”

To this he shall then respond in these or similar words:

> “Because I ought to obey the will of God and your command, I do not refuse the burden which you impose, but accept it for charity’s sake and promise to bear it according to God.”

Then let the brothers respond (Rule of St Benedict, ch. 58), “Receive us, O God,” and the rest as customary, with the *Gloria*, the *Kyrie eleison* three times, the Lord’s Prayer, and fitting short lessons. Then follows this or a similar prayer:

### Prayer over the Prior

> “Almighty and everlasting God, we humbly beseech the mercy of your goodness that this your servant may always feel the assistance of your help present with him, so that he may govern and guard your flock in the present life in such a manner that in the life to come he may be able together with it to receive the rewards of eternal blessedness. Through our Lord, etc. Amen.”

Thereupon he shall sit in the prior’s place and perform the office of his priorship.

## Chapter VIII. What the Prior Ought to Do after His Installation

The prior having thus been installed ought canonically to govern both the souls and bodies of the brothers already received into the congregation, and canonically to receive those who are to be admitted. Let us therefore show first how brothers are to be received, and then how those received are to be governed.

## Chapter IX. How, and at What Age, Parents May Offer Their Sons to the Church

If any faithful layman wishes, through devotion, to offer his son to the Church before the age of fourteen years and devote him to divine worship (Rule of St Benedict, ch. 58), he shall present him before the altar in the presence of the prior and brothers, using these or similar words:

> “I, with faithful intent, give this my son N. to almighty God and to these holy relics, associate him in all things with your brotherhood, and entrust him to your holiness for upbringing.”

Let him place upon the altar a written document containing the same words. After this, with the boy prostrate or placed before the altar, let the verse be said: “Receive us, O God,” with the *Gloria*, the *Kyrie eleison*, the Lord’s Prayer, and suitable short lessons. A fitting prayer shall follow, which is found below.

If he is offered so young, then after three or four years of weaning, having become a cleric, let him be loved by all as a son. But after fourteen years, a father cannot offer him unless the son himself wishes it. For persons of this age are permitted, even against their parents’ wishes, to receive whichever religious habit they choose.

Those, therefore, who are their own masters, whether offering themselves or giving what belongs to them, and who repeatedly ask to be received into your clergy, must not be received indiscriminately, because, according to the Apostle, “Not every spirit is to be believed, but it should rather be tested whether it is from God” (I John IV). We establish no fixed procedure or time for this testing, but leave it always to be determined by the prudence and judgment of the prior, or jointly of the brothers. For children must be tested in one way, adults in another; the healthy and strong in one way, the sick and weak in another; those accustomed to wealth and comforts in one way, those accustomed to labor and poverty in another; those whose life is secure or doubtful, whose learning is certain or uncertain, whose will is known or unknown in another.

When the distinctions among all these have been considered, let the prior’s diligence attend vigilantly and, by prudent judgment, appoint the manner and time of testing according to what suits each person. Those who have been tested and appear fit to be received shall first make a lawful disposition of their inheritances and possessions, if they possess any: leaving them either to relatives, distributing them to the poor, or offering them to the Church. When this has been done, and after they have frequently heard the rule which they are to observe, let them be led into choir and made clerics according to usage and order.

After this, in the presence of the brothers, prostrate in the midst, they shall read a written document containing these or similar words:

> “I, N., offer myself to almighty God and promise to these holy relics my service and stability, and likewise obedience according to God to the prelates of this Church and to your order therein.”

Then let the brothers answer, “Thanks be to God,” and add the verse, “Receive us, O God,” according to custom, with the *Gloria*, the *Kyrie eleison* three times, the Lord’s Prayer, and fitting short lessons. Then let this or a similar prayer follow:

### Prayer over the Professed

> “Lord, we beseech you kindly to receive this your servant, who for love of your name renounces the world, and to pour upon him the grace of your Spirit, that strengthened by it and absolved from all sins, he may steadfastly fulfill his promises and attain eternal life.”

Then, joined to the brothers, he shall remain cheerfully beneath all those who entered before him, and shall always strive to fulfill and faithfully maintain the order he has received. If he comes before the age of fourteen having lost his parents, he shall be kept among the boys and brought up. But after this age, once he has disposed of whatever he possesses, he shall be received to clerical status and profession in the manner described above.

## Chapter X. Concerning the Reception of All Unordained Clerics, Both Known and Unknown

If a cleric without orders, who has not been given to any Church either by his own profession or by that of his father (Rule of St Benedict, chs. 60 and 61), asks to join your community and persists in asking, he shall first be tested as we stated above. Then, after the rule has been read or heard and understood, if he promises to observe all things, and after permission has been obtained from his bishop, or also from his archdeacon or archpriest, with the consent of the same persons, he shall not be denied entrance for reception in the diocese of the bishop into whose diocese he asks to be received.

But if he has greater or lesser orders, after he has been tested, frequently heard the rule, and been canonically requested and released, he shall be admitted to profession as we said above. If, however, a cleric who is a stranger or from unknown regions asks to be received, he shall not be heard quickly, nor shall his petition ever be granted unless he has letters of recommendation certainly issued by his bishop, in which his life, vow, rank, and episcopal permission are made known. Such a person, therefore, having been tested with the most diligent care over a long period in all respects, and having frequently heard the rule, shall, with the permission of the bishop of the present Church, be received into the community of brothers by making profession according to the manner stated above.

## Chapter IX. That Moderation Must Be Observed in Adding Brothers According to the Extent of Ecclesiastical Resources

Let the prelates of churches earnestly take care that in the congregation committed to them they neither admit more persons than the Church’s resources can support, nor, through avarice, leave out those whom they are able to support. In the smallest places few should be admitted in number, but they should be great in learning, virtue, and merit, so that what the small number of brothers denies may be supplied by an abundance of learning, virtue, and merit.

## Chapter XII. That Those Newly Received Should Not Be Ashamed to Be Subject to the Others

Brothers who have been received (Rule of St Benedict, ch. 63) should not be ashamed to be subject to those who entered before them, even though these may be of lower rank, age, or learning; nor should they refuse to bear the yoke of obedience under them. For it is far better to be humbled here so that we may be exalted in the future, than to be exalted here and thereby at last be humbled. And the more we are subjected here for Christ’s name, the more, without doubt, we shall be exalted in the future. Therefore no one should ever refuse to show reverence even to humble and lowly persons, in whom we truly recognize that we minister to Christ.

## Chapter XIII. That the Prior Ought to Prefer Even the Least and Most Recently Admitted before Others, If the Brothers’ Welfare Requires It

If the prior recognizes that some persons even among the least and most recently admitted may be of benefit to the congregation as superiors (Rule of St Benedict, ch. 63), we not only do not forbid him to prefer them, but command it. For the rulers of churches are not to be appointed personally or according to the order in which they were received into the community of brothers, but according to the merits of their life and the prerogatives of spiritual gifts. Thus those should always preside who by the word of teaching and the work of holiness encourage the good toward better things and call the wicked back from perversity.

## Chapter XIV. How Subjects Ought to Obey Their Prelates

Whatever prelates command according to God and the holy life of the brothers, all subjects should humbly, willingly, and without delay accept; readily fulfill; and diligently complete without grumbling. “For,” says the Apostle, “God loves a cheerful giver” (II Cor. IX). As he loves the cheerful, so without doubt he hates the sad and grumbling. Therefore we judge that grumbling and disobedience are wholly to be condemned in every place and at every time, as reason requires.

Accordingly, let nothing be done by the brothers with sadness or grumbling; rather, let them gladly receive every command of the elders and fulfill it with readiness. Even if what is commanded seems impossible, let the brothers nevertheless not refuse to accept it, warned by Christ’s example: he, obeying the Father, did not refuse even to accept death. But those who cannot follow the standard of this perfection, when they begin to be weighed down by keeping the command and are brought to what is impossible, should humbly report this to their elders. Let the prelates not despise them, but release them from the bond of an unbearable burden, lest—God forbid—if they do otherwise, the former lay down an unbearable burden with light, as I believe, sin, and the latter become numbered among those of whom it is said: “They lay heavy and unbearable burdens upon others, but are unwilling to move them with their finger” (Matt. XXV).

## Chapter XV. That Canons Ought Not at All to Have or Possess, Give or Receive, Anything

Since the brothers of this congregation of ours have renounced not only their own possessions (Rule of St Benedict, ch. 38), but also their own wills in their very reception into the order, and have through promised obedience entirely subjected themselves in Christ and for Christ to the authority and commands of others, it is certain that they ought to have or possess, give or receive, nothing without permission of their prior. If any relative or friend wishes to offer anything to any brother, it must first be reported to the prior; and then it may be received, if he commands it. Nothing else, however, shall be done with it except what pleases the prior.

## Chapter XVI. How Brothers Ought to Speak with Persons Who Come to Them

If visitors seek to speak with any brother, and the prior permits it out of charity or necessity, a prudent and watchful companion shall be assigned to him, in whom there is no suspicion of evil. In that companion’s presence he shall hear whatever is to be heard and answer whatever is to be answered. Yet if something more private needs to be said, this shall not be denied to persons whose stability is in no way doubted. But it shall by no means be permitted to boys and to persons whose life is doubtful, unless, as stated, a witness is present.

## Chapter XVII. Whether Brothers Ought to Send or Receive Letters

If at any time the prior sees it necessary for any brother to send letters to anyone (Rule of St Benedict, ch. 54), he shall command that they be composed, that when composed they be read, and that when read they be carried by whomever he chooses. But if letters sent by others are delivered to any brother, they shall be received not by the person to whom they are sent, but by one of the prelates, to be given to the prior. When the prior has opened and read them, he shall show them also to the person to whom they were sent, and to others if necessary.

## Chapter XVIII. Whether Those Who Are Learned May Venture to Teach Anything

If any canons, thinking humbly and not holding themselves arrogantly, are so instructed in letters and so full of the knowledge of the divine Scriptures that they can bring some benefit from them, and if the prior judges it right and sees it necessary, then, with every incentive to envy and hatred entirely removed, let him permit or command them to labor in those matters whose knowledge he has recognized as more necessary and useful.

## Chapter XIX. That Prelates Ought to Govern the Souls and Bodies of Their Subjects
The prelates of the churches, therefore, should keep unceasing watch, with constant care, over the brothers entrusted to them; and they should strive so to govern, protect, and feed not only their souls but also their bodies, that through no cause of necessity they may find an occasion for sinning. And just as the prelates do not cease to provide them with all necessities [Col. 0715C], so they should with the most urgent care continually require of them the observance of the whole order. But since nearly all observance of the order is customarily carried out chiefly within the walls of the cloister, where the flock of the Lord is commanded to live in common and obey the injunctions of its elders, let us first set down what a cloister is, and what workshops ought to exist within it, so that afterward we may more freely pursue what is to be done in them.

## CHAPTER XX. On the cloister and its workshops

What a cloister is may be known from the explanation of its very name. For a cloister is called an enclosed court (*clausum atrium*) (Rule of St Benedict, ch. 66), because the court of the church ought to be enclosed on every side by walls or other partitions [Col. 0715D]. Within it all the workshops of the canons and all buildings necessary for their use are to be made: namely, the sacristy, library, chapter-house, vestry, dormitory, dining hall, warming-room, refectory, kitchen, cellar, mill, bakehouse, and chamber; likewise places for the elderly and the sick; likewise, if possible, places for boys and youths still remaining under the strictest discipline, lest, if they stay with the brothers, they hinder those who are reading and meditating. But if this cannot be done in a more remote part of the cloister, the prior should appoint them to be under a master and guardian, so that, remaining under their strict custody, they may learn whatever is necessary and accomplish whatever is commanded.

## CHAPTER XXI. On the buildings for the household

[Col. 0716A]

Outside these, yet within the walls of the same cloister and only slightly separated from them, buildings should be made (Rule of St Benedict, ch. 57), in which all the artisans and workers of the church, and indeed the entire household, may have all their necessities and may carry out their respective offices or keep what pertains to the performance of those offices.

## CHAPTER XXII. On the inner cloister and the restraint of the brothers

The inner cloister, however, should be assigned solely to the canons, so that there, dwelling without any disturbance, they may faithfully serve God, keep the straight path of their profession, fulfil their own order, obey continually the commands of their prelates, serve one another in turn according to order through the office of charity [Col. 0716B], and wholly abstain from all unlawful things and from everything contrary to their order and profession.

Therefore, let each sit in the place assigned to him, obeying the commands of his superior; nor should he be permitted to go from there to another place without that superior’s command. For it is a fault of instability, when necessity does not press, to be now here, now there; now to deal and converse with this person, now with that. And this is undoubtedly done by the instigation of the devil, so that brothers who ought to read and meditate upon what they read, sing psalms and pray, or do some work, may be turned away from these things and led through sin into trifles, lest they accomplish them. Therefore let this vice be cut out by the roots from among the brothers; and whoever practices it in the community should be judged in such a manner that thereafter others may by no means dare to attempt it.

[Col. 0716C]

Let the canons, then, be lovers of seriousness, as the Prophet says: “I will praise you among a weighty people” (Ps. XXXIV). Let them not quickly burst into speech, nor quickly move from place to place, except when the command of a prelate, the order, necessity, or obedience to the divine law requires it. When walking, moreover, let them not proceed at a run, or with an unbecoming or arrogant gait. Let them nowhere, if it can be avoided, utter buffoonish, vain, or idle words, or words provoking laughter; let them not devote themselves to conversations. Let them wholly cut off from themselves unrestrained laughter, not only in the cloister but in every place, remembering that word of the Gospel: “Woe to you who laugh, for you shall weep” (Luke VI); and also Solomon’s saying: “Laughter shall be mingled with sorrow” (Prov. XIV); and: “A fool raises his voice in laughter” (Ecclus. XXI).

Let them devote themselves to holy reading [Col. 0716D], attend the divine offices, and apply themselves to learning sacred teachings at the prior’s command; let them occupy themselves with psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs. Let them also attend to private prayers when they have leisure, though with permission. At times let them perform some work suitable to the cloister, provided that it in no way hinders brothers who are reading, singing psalms, meditating on Holy Scripture, or applying themselves to other sound teaching. Let them by no means leave the cloister without the permission of the prior or of one acting in his place; once gone out, they should not dare, without unavoidable necessity, to remain beyond the time appointed for them. Let them never go alone; and let the prelate assign them good companions, without whom they themselves are not to speak with others, nor others with them.

## CHAPTER XXIII. On brothers sent outside

[Col. 0717A]

For the conducting of any business, or for carrying, receiving, or returning an answer, prelates should strive to send outside such brothers as have no suspicion of evil attached to them and are able prudently to conduct and wisely complete the business entrusted to them—provided that excellent companions are assigned to them (Rule of St Benedict, chs. 50 and 57). Therefore, when going outside, let them say or do nothing unseemly, blameworthy, or in any respect contrary to their order and profession. Rather, let them season with the salt of wisdom all those with whom they associate, and draw them toward better things by examples of holy conduct.

We do not deny confidential consultations of men to those who are sent outside, if necessary—provided they are men whose conduct and steadfastness are beyond doubt. But regarding private conversation with women [Col. 0717B], let them hear not my advice but Jerome’s, who says:

> “If, because of the office of the clergy, some woman is to be visited, never enter her house alone; do not sit alone with a woman alone in private, or without an arbiter or witness. If something must be discussed more familiarly, she has a nurse, a housekeeper, a virgin, a widow, or a married woman. She is not so inhuman as to have no one besides you to whom she ought to entrust herself.”

Therefore private conversation with women is not permitted to clerics, except perhaps to approved priests when they receive women’s confessions. Yet we do not deny to brothers of approved life conversation with mothers, sisters, paternal aunts, and only those persons in whom there is no suspicion of evil.

## CHAPTER XXIV. That clerics should not be sent outside for matters that can be done by laypeople

[Col. 0717C]

If there are in the household laypersons of such character and fidelity that all or some external affairs may prudently be conducted through them, clerics should by no means be sent for matters which can be accomplished through those laypersons.

## CHAPTER XXV. That, at the prior’s command, brothers may work in gardens or perform similar work

If the place is such, and the prior commands some members of the community committed to him to work at times in gardens for the brothers’ use, or to do elsewhere something similar which must be done, the command received is to be fulfilled faithfully, cheerfully, and without delay.

## CHAPTER XXVI. What brothers sent outside should do when leaving and returning

[Col. 0717D]

When any cleric goes out on account of an assigned command, he should bow his head and ask for a blessing. The prior, blessing him, should say: “May the good angel of the Lord accompany you, and may almighty God make your journey prosperous”; or something similar. When he has replied, “Amen,” he should depart, saying: “Show me your ways, O Lord, and teach me your paths” (Ps. II), with *Glory be to the Father*, etc., or similar prayers.

When the purpose of his journey has been completed, on returning he should go to the church; and after praying briefly, he should leave, bow his head, and, having greeted the brothers and, if permitted, requested a blessing, he should immediately proceed to the prior. Having likewise received a blessing from him, he should humbly report what he has done and what has happened to him in connection with the command entrusted to him.

In the morning, or after None, the one who has returned from the road should come into the middle of the chapter-house [Col. 0718A] and declare before the brothers that he has sinned in heart, voice, and action. Bending his knees and prostrating his body, he should say: “Through my fault, I have sinned”; and the brothers should answer: “May God pardon you.” He should continue to say this while bending his knees, and the brothers should continue to make that response, until the prelate commands him to stand and imposes a form of satisfaction according to the character of his offences: in psalms, fasts, or other acts of obedience, if it pleases the prior.

Whatever is imposed on him in satisfaction for his offences, he should fulfil at the hour or time the prior commands. If the number of psalms is very small, he should discharge them immediately upon leaving chapter, before asking for a blessing. When they have been performed, he should go out and request a blessing in the customary manner [Col. 0718B]. Whenever they are sent outside, they must observe this manner in going and returning.

## CHAPTER XXVII. How brothers should be sent to visit the sick, make peace, exhort souls, or arrange some good matter

If brothers must, by reason of their clerical office, visit the sick, make peace between persons at discord, or go somewhere to exhort souls or arrange some matter for good, the prelate should command two or three, or more if necessary, of the wiser and holier brethren to go, so that they may accomplish in a holy and wise manner whatever they see to be necessary [Col. 0718C]. If they must travel far, they should act in going and returning as has been stated above.

## CHAPTER XXVIII. If it is necessary to go to relatives

If the prior permits any brother, whether from charity or necessity, to visit his father, mother, or relatives, he should assign him such a master or companion that he fears that person’s presence and gives him reverence, and may receive from him protection against dangers, consolation in necessities, and assistance in all things. But if the person is such that there is no suspicion concerning him, let the prior allow him to go without a master—yet not alone. For no brother should ever be allowed to go alone, nor in the company of boys or depraved people, to any place, unless he is utterly steadfast and proven in perfection [Col. 0718D]. Rather, if possible, the prior should provide good companions and men of tested reputation, with whom brothers may safely be sent. In asking for blessing and rendering satisfaction as they go and return, they should observe and keep the procedure set out above.

## CHAPTER XXIX. That brothers should not hold private consultations with brothers

If any brothers presume to hold private consultations with certain other brothers, or one with one, except with the prior, the provost, and those priests whom the prior has appointed to receive confessions, and if, having been warned once, twice, and three times, they are not corrected, they should be subject to regular correction as transgressors of the order.

## CHAPTER XXX. On avoiding carnal affection, and on the discipline of those sinning in this or another manner

[Col. 0719A]

If anyone in this your sacred community loves another excessively and carnally, takes more care of his cause than of others’, or presumes, contrary to the order, to defend or praise him above the rest; or if he has pursued some boy or youth as far as indecent touching, and this comes to the brothers’ knowledge, he should be restrained by many harsh and public corrections of word and blow, worn down by prolonged labours of fasting and prayer, and for a time endure such discipline for this offence that others may be afraid even to devise such a thing.

Therefore there should always be such vigilance in the community that boys and youths are not readily entrusted to young men [Col. 0719B], except those whose conduct is found in every respect most exemplary. Yet if—may it not happen—such a thing occurs to anyone and remains hidden from the community, but comes to the knowledge of one person or several, we decree that it should be reported to the prior alone, so that the person who sinned secretly may be healed through the prior’s correction by the secret fomentations of medicine.

But if anyone has sinned in this or another manner, has been detected by no one, and, recognizing his own sin, reveals it to the prior, because he has rebuked and acknowledged himself, he will be healed by the satisfaction of a lighter discipline. If, led by shame or terrified by fear, he is unwilling to reveal it to the prior, let him disclose it to one of the priests whom the prior has commanded to receive the brothers’ confessions, and do penance for his sin according to that priest’s judgment.

Care must be taken that one who, without any accusation, reveals his sin should receive a lighter penance; one who, having been accused, does not deny it, a somewhat heavier one; while one who, having been accused, denies it and is afterward convicted or confesses, ought to be subject to a much sharper punishment [Col. 0719C]. Yet sins that are shameful, obscene, or serious, and whose examples do much harm, should be healed by secret satisfaction unless they have reached so many ears that they can no longer be concealed. If they cannot be concealed, let them be healed, as already stated, by public correction. But those sins which are slight, minor, and open, and which nearly everyone frequently commits through frailty, we judge should be corrected in chapter by public accusation and satisfaction according to the prescribed procedure [Col. 0719D].

## CHAPTER XXXI. On those wishing, under the canonical habit, to lead a stricter or solitary life

If any brothers desire, while retaining the same canonical habit, to lead a stricter or solitary life, they must make their particular devotion known to their prelates. It will belong to the care and diligence of the prelates to consider the condition of the persons, lest those perhaps wish to undertake this who, because of weakness of nature, age, or the long duration of habitual infirmity, cannot bear the unfamiliar burden of vigils and fasts.

Having considered these things, we do not forbid permission being granted to those who desire and seek it, and who, supplied with strength of bodily powers, are able to do so. But if it brings harm to the church [Col. 0720A], or spiritual or bodily injury to their fellow brothers, we advise that it be refused entirely. For those to whom this is to be granted permanently or temporarily, there should be in a more remote place a church fortified and enclosed on every side, around which cells should be made, in which such persons may live according to the prior’s command and follow his judgment in all things.

## CHAPTER XXXII. On the virtue of silence

Having set forth these matters, let us add, by the Lord’s permission, whatever the brothers have resolved concerning silence. For the virtue of silence ought to be observed not only by clerics but also by Christian laypeople, unless their own or another’s necessity, or bodily or spiritual charity, compels them to speak. For when, necessity or charity having ceased, someone utters a word, what he says is idle; and the Lord testifies in the Gospel that one must beware of this, saying: “You will render an account on the day of judgment for every idle word” (Eph. IV) [Col. 0720B]. The Apostle explains what an idle word is by forbidding it: “Let no useless speech proceed from your mouth” (Matt. XXII).

Therefore, in order that we may be able to abstain from unlawful things, we must sometimes refrain even from lawful things. Accordingly, to remove unlawful words from your mouth, it is fitting that we appoint definite places and times in which and when, according to the profession of your holiness, you ought to abstain even from lawful speech.

## CHAPTER XXXIII. That silence should be observed in church, refectory, and dormitory

[Col. 0720C]

In church, therefore, when we enter and stand for the performance of the divine offices, both regular practice and the authority of the elders, as well as reverence for the divine office, teach that silence ought to be maintained. The same regular precaution shows that it must be kept when we enter or stand in the refectory to eat or drink together, and in the dormitory to sleep together.

## CHAPTER XXXIV. That silence should be kept at all times from Vespers until morning, when they come to chapter

At all times, from the evening hours until the next day, when in the morning the brothers leave chapter according to custom, let them keep the strictest silence. In summer, that is, from Easter until the autumnal equinox [Col. 0720D], let them likewise be silent from the sixth hour until they leave chapter after None. In winter, that is, from the autumnal equinox until Easter: if the brothers take two meals, from the sixth hour until they leave chapter after None; if one meal, until after None—not only the brothers, but also the servants, having eaten and left church and afterward chapter, should keep silence. In Lent alone, silence should likewise be maintained from the ninth hour until chapter is dismissed on the following day.

## CHAPTER XXXV. That silence should be kept on certain days beyond the stated rule

Furthermore, it has pleased your holiness to establish that on the highest feasts and throughout the whole day of Preparation Day, silence in the cloister is not to be broken [Col. 0721A]. On principal and popular feasts also, and on every Sunday, all without exception should maintain silence until they leave chapter after None, unless the practice or order of the church, charity, or necessity compels speech.

## CHAPTER XXXVI. That during the time of silence everything in the cloister should be done without sound, except in unavoidable necessity

[Col. 0722A]

Whenever silence is observed in the cloister, reading and psalmody should be performed without sound, unless there is a definite necessity; and everything done there should be done without sound.

[Col. 0721] Here ends the First Book.

# SECOND BOOK

[Col. 0721]

## HERE BEGINS THE PROLOGUE TO THE SECOND BOOK

[Col. 0721]

Having discussed these matters concerning certain observances of the brothers, we have taken care to write, among these other rules of your order, the manner of taking two meals and one meal; abstinence; the use of meat and blood, eggs and cheese, fish and oil, and wine; likewise the quality and number of dishes; and a fixed measure of bread and wine. All these things, dearest brothers, you have resolved, by the inspiration of divine grace, to observe with us.

## CHAPTER I. How one should live between the octaves of the Nativity, Epiphany, and Resurrection

[Col. 0721B]

From the very day of the Lord’s Nativity, Epiphany, and Resurrection until their respective octaves, you have excluded every fast; nor have you forbidden the brothers to eat meat, except on Wednesday and Friday, on which days you have withheld meat but not the use of blood.

## CHAPTER II. How one should live from the octave of the Resurrection until Pentecost, and from the octave of the Nativity until Epiphany

From the octave of the Resurrection and of the Nativity until Pentecost and Epiphany respectively, you have likewise removed every fast, except on those days on which either authority commands fasting or the practice of the Church shows that it is required [Col. 0721C]. Within these Easter and Nativity periods alone, you have renounced the eating of meat on Wednesday, Friday, and Saturday, as at other times; but you have permitted the use of blood on Wednesday and Saturday.

## CHAPTER III. How one should live from the day of Pentecost until the Nativity of St John

From the holy day of Pentecost itself until the Nativity of St John the Baptist, you have omitted the use of meat and blood, and have established fasting on Monday, Wednesday, and Friday.

## CHAPTER IV. How one should live from the Nativity of St John the Baptist until the autumnal equinox

From the Nativity of St John the Baptist until the feast of St Matthew [Col. 0721C], you have prohibited the use of meat and blood on Wednesday, Friday, and Saturday, and have established fasting on Friday.

## CHAPTER V. How one should live from the autumnal equinox until the Kalends of November, and from the octaves of Epiphany until Septuagesima

From the feast of St Matthew until the Kalends of November, and from the octaves of Epiphany until Septuagesima [Col. 0722B], you have prescribed fasting on Monday, Wednesday, and Friday; and on those same weekdays, and on Saturday, you have prohibited the use of meat and blood.

## CHAPTER VI. That one should fast from the Kalends of November until the Nativity of the Lord, and from Septuagesima until holy Easter

From the Kalends of November until the Nativity of the Lord, and from Septuagesima until holy Easter, your devotion has established that, with the use of meat and blood wholly prohibited, only one meal should be taken each day.

## CHAPTER VII. On the fast of the Ember Days and vigils

On Wednesday, Friday, and Saturday of the Ember Days, and on vigils and other fasts instituted universally and in ancient times, fasting is undoubtedly required not only of canons [Col. 0722C] but of all Christians. On the remaining days and at the remaining times, you have permitted yourselves two meals daily.

## CHAPTER VIII. On the use of eggs and cheese

From Quinquagesima until holy Easter, from Advent until the Nativity of the Lord, and during all lawful fasts, you have wholly removed from yourselves, with every exception set aside, the use of eggs and cheese. But from the holy day of Pentecost itself until the Nativity of St John the Baptist; from the Kalends of November until the Advent of the Lord; and from Septuagesima until Lent, you have judged that on Wednesday and Friday eggs and cheese should be abstained from, unless a feast of nine lessons occurs.

## CHAPTER IX. What fast may be relaxed on account of a feast

[Col. 0722D]

I thought it should be added, brothers, which fasts may be relaxed and for what reasons, and which must always be observed inviolate. At every time, on a day on which we celebrate a feast or octave with nine lessons, no authority forbids the practice of two meals, except on the days and seasons of lawful fasting.

## CHAPTER X. Whether, on account of a feast, the use of meat and blood should be restored

[Col. 0723A]

From the first Sunday after the Resurrection until Pentecost; from the octave of the Lord’s Nativity until Epiphany; from the octave of Epiphany until Septuagesima; and from the Nativity of St John until the Kalends of November: if a feast or octave of nine lessons falls on a Friday, you have not withdrawn the use of blood; but if it falls on a Monday, Wednesday, or Saturday, except during lawful fasts, you have permitted the use of meat, as stated above.

## CHAPTER XI. What are lawful fasts

The seasons of lawful fasting are from the Wednesday of Quinquagesima week, called the Chapter of the Fast (*Capitulum jejunii*), until holy Easter; likewise the Ember Days and vigils established by the holy Fathers; and whatever other observances Holy Church has decreed, or may at some time decree, must be perpetually observed [Col. 0723B]. If a feast of nine lessons falls on any of these days, it must indeed be celebrated, but the fast cannot be relaxed.

## CHAPTER XII. On the days on which one should abstain both from wine and from cooked dishes, or only from cooked dishes while retaining the use of wine

Although religious observance would urge that canons abstain from wine and cooked dishes on every day of lawful fasting, the situation of this place and the frailty of our time do not permit this to be observed in the community. Therefore, dearest brothers, we ask and exhort you to use these things sparingly, so that we may destroy in ourselves the vice of desire and yet sustain the strength of the body, in order that we may be able fully to observe our order and gladly and manfully fulfil our ministry and office in the praise of God [Col. 0723C].

Yet on these very few days—namely, the vigils established anciently and universally, Friday from Quinquagesima until Easter, and Ember Friday—you have judged that one should abstain from wine and cooked dishes, although you have permitted raw vegetables and fruit, if available. On Ember Wednesday; on Friday from the Kalends of November until the Nativity of the Lord; and on every Wednesday of Lent and of the preceding week, you have permitted only the use of wine, with additions of fruit and vegetables, cooked dishes having been removed [Col. 0723D].

## CHAPTER XIII. On discretion in restoring wine or a cooked dish, and the reasons for exercising this discretion

Yet you have not forbidden discretion to be exercised in some of these matters, if the prior happens to judge it necessary. If this is done on a day on which wine is forbidden, it is sufficient that only the use of wine be restored. But if it is done on a day on which, though wine is permitted, a cooked dish is prohibited, the concession of one cooked dish is sufficient. On a day on which wine and one cooked dish are permitted, you have not forbidden the addition, if necessary, of another cooked dish.

For there are certain days on which you have judged that only one cooked dish should be given to the brothers: namely, Friday from Pentecost until the Nativity of St John; from Septuagesima until Quinquagesima; Wednesday from the Kalends of November until the Nativity of the Lord; and Ember Saturday [Col. 0724A]. Therefore let the prior exercise this discretion in one matter or several, whether because of great labour, unusually excessive heat or cold, a fast fulfilled on the preceding day or to be fulfilled on the following day, the demanding office of an impending feast which must be celebrated in the best manner, the celebration of Eastertide or another festive season, the excessive weakness of the brothers, or necessary charity toward visiting brothers.

## CHAPTER XIV. If a feast of nine lessons occurs on a lawful fast day

If a popular feast to be celebrated with nine lessons occurs on these days, you have permitted the use of wine and one Lenten dish—or, if the feast is a principal one, two or three Lenten dishes [Col. 0724B].

## CHAPTER XV. That on other days two dishes should be prepared for the brothers

With the above-mentioned fast-days excepted, on all other days, whether days of fasting or of two meals, if resources permit, two dishes should be prepared for the brothers. But on principal feasts and the highest solemnities, you have established that three dishes should be supplied to the brothers, if possible.

## CHAPTER XVI. On the use of fish and oil

The eating of fish and the use of oil are excluded at no time and on no day on which the use of some cooked dish and wine is permitted.

## CHAPTER XVII. On the measure of bread and wine, and the quality of cooked dishes

[Col. 0724C]

Both the custom of regular houses unquestionably requires, and, as I believe, the authority of the elders has established, that an equal measure of bread, wine, and cooked dishes be given to younger and older brothers. Although Luke reports in the Acts of the Apostles: “Distribution was made to each according as each had need” (Acts II), nevertheless an equal and sufficient measure for all should be established. Even those who may not use the full amount are not permitted to use it in excess, but only to the point of sufficiency (Rule of St Benedict, chs. 30 and 40). Whatever remains from those needing less or abstaining more, the brother responsible for hospitality should undertake to distribute daily to the poor.

Accordingly, on fast-days, one weighed pound of bread and three measures of wine for each brother; on days of two meals, one and a half of bread and five of wine: as you yourselves have experienced with us, you have judged these quantities sufficient [Col. 0724D]. The weekly kitchen officers should carefully provide equality in the cooked dishes—or, if otherwise impossible, according to their judgment. Yet if, through carelessness or by command exercised in discretion, something extra or more delicate is set before someone, no one should dare to murmur at all.

## CHAPTER XVIII. On the weekly reader

The brother appointed to read for the entire week (Rule of St Benedict, ch. 28) should, on Sunday after Mass has ended, while the priest is still standing at the altar, come forward into the middle and, bowing his head, say three times: “O Lord, you will open my lips” [Col. 0725A] (Ps. L), and the remainder of that verse. The brothers respond, and after the third repetition follows *Glory be to the Father*. Then the priest, in the presence of the brothers and according to custom, completes the verses and prayer.

This brother, throughout the whole week while the brothers eat and maintain religious silence, all noise and murmuring having been removed, should read through the Holy Scriptures. After the brothers’ meal he should dine together with the servants. The servants should provide everything to everyone in such a manner that no one has to raise his voice because of any necessity. If something must be requested, it should be sought by a sign rather than speech. Yet the prior, or one whom he commands, is not forbidden occasionally to address the brothers briefly and plainly while they are eating, for their edification [Col. 0725B].

When the brothers assemble in chapter in the evening for the collation, the same reader is always to deliver a reading from the Lives of the Saints and the Conferences of the Fathers. On Saturday, when he has completed the reading in the refectory at evening for the charity of the *mandatum*, while the brothers are still seated, he should approach the prior’s table and show reverence, and thus complete the week of his reading.

## CHAPTER XIX. On the weekly kitchen officers, the *mandatum* to be performed on Saturdays, and the charity to be shown

When the brothers have assembled in chapter on Saturday at the sound of the tablet for performing the *mandatum* (Rule of St Benedict, ch. 35), the weekly kitchen officers who are leaving office should come into the middle and bow in reverence to the brothers [Col. 0725C]. Then, while the prior or one acting in his place begins the antiphons, they should wash and dry the brothers’ feet. Those who are entering office should bring the water for washing and, after the washing, pour it away.

Then those leaving office should wash and dry their hands before the chapter-house, using water brought by other brothers and a towel supplied for them. After this, those who washed the feet should bring the water for washing hands, while those who brought the water should bring the towel for drying. When the brothers’ hands have been washed, those about to enter office should come into the middle and, bowing, say three times: “Blessed are you, Lord God, who have helped me and comforted me.” The brothers make the same response, and *Glory be to the Father* follows after the third repetition [Col. 0725D]. Then, once the customary prayer with its verses has been completed, let them sit in their places.

Then those entering office should come into the middle and, bowing, say three times: “O God, attend to my help; O Lord, hasten to help me” (Ps. LXIX), the brothers again responding in the same manner. After the verses and prayer have been completed, the reading should begin there. But first, in the refectory, the customary charity should be completed by the brothers, as we have already said.

On the vigils of the highest feasts, and on the highest and greater feasts if they fall on Saturday, the *mandatum* is to be omitted. Yet you have established that on those occasions the customary charity and the entrance and departure of the weekly officers should still take place. Besides this, at the highest and great solemnities and on their vigils, you have determined that the charity should be performed in the evening at the collation: by the prior at the highest solemnities, but by the provost at the principal ones [Col. 0726A]. Care must be taken that, on feasts and vigils, the reading pertains to those days themselves; and on Saturdays, if available, to the mystery of the *mandatum* and of the Lord’s Day.

## CHAPTER XX. On performing the *mandatum* at the Lord’s Supper

Since, as we have said, the *mandatum* is customarily performed on Saturdays, the Church has nevertheless established that on the Lord’s Supper it should everywhere be celebrated with the utmost devotion and dignity, out of reverence for our Master and Lord, who on that very day gave the command and performed it. Following this practice, dearest brothers, you have judged that throughout this entire day you should devote yourselves especially to washing the feet of poor visitors and giving alms [Col. 0726B]. You have also established that, after your lay brethren who are converts have been led into chapter after supper, you yourselves should perform the same rite and offer the charity in the refectory. After this, on the same day, the *mandatum* of the clerics should be performed by the prior and by the provost. Let the remaining matters be carried out according to the use and order of that day.

## CHAPTER XXI. On the clothing, footwear, and bedding of the brothers
Garments and footwear, as well as bedding, in summer and winter—of whatever number and kind are necessary—should be provided to the brethren with the greatest care by the keeper of the wardrobe. In distributing them, he should take account of the location, the season, and the circumstances of the individual persons. For in cold places more clothing should be supplied, [Col. 0726C] but in hot places less; and it should be such as neither excessive elegance nor unusual cheapness dishonours the canonical habit. In our regions, therefore, you have judged that for each brother one lambskin, one hooded cloak, one doublet, two mantles, two tunics, two pairs of drawers, two pairs of stockings suitable for heat and cold, two pairs of socks, and one under-shoe may suffice. Let them also have in their beds a mattress, pillow, sheet, coverlet, and a woollen or linen blanket. Moreover, let each have one, or, if possible, two linen tunics, and one sheepskin or lambskin fur garment, if resources permit and need requires.

Let the brethren use all these things according to need and the conditions of the season so long as they can [Col. 0726D] be suitably fitted out and repaired in sufficient measure for necessity. But he to whom something beyond the common rule is granted because of need should not rejoice over it, but be grieved that, owing to his infirmity, he is allowed by indulgence what is denied by rule to those who are stronger. Whatever the prior sees to be necessary for anyone, he ought to supply to him; what he sees not to be necessary for another, he shall deny him, even if the latter asks for it. For Luke writes in the Acts of the Apostles: “Distribution was made to each as anyone had need” (Acts II). Therefore, provision must be made for each according to his strength, age, need, and condition.

Accordingly, if the prior, having considered this discretion, commands that certain persons be treated otherwise than has been established, there should be no murmuring in the community on that account, [Col. 0727A] since he plainly opposes the divine law who, either through envy or through the enticements of gluttony, demands for himself the regimen of the sick although he does not feel it necessary for himself. Yet in those who are able to rise from this regimen of the infirm to the strength of sound health, but permit themselves to remain so in order to live more delicately, undoubtedly both here the greatness of sins is increased and there the severity of punishments is prepared.

## CHAPTER XXII. Concerning the sick and the dying

Within the cloister of the canons let a house be established for the support of the sick, where the brethren may suitably minister to their necessities, visit them, and console them by frequent admonition from the divine Scriptures. Yet no one may approach them indiscriminately, except those whom the prior appoints; [Col. 0727B] nor should the prior send others except those who may either minister usefully to them or console and edify them wisely.

If these attendants perceive that a fever persists or an illness grows more serious, then, after the prior or provost and the priests assigned to this office have been summoned, let the sick make a full confession of their sins. Thus, after satisfaction for past faults has first been imposed according to the prior’s command, together with amendment of themselves for the future, and after they have received the blessing of the whole convent and absolution from sins, let them be faithfully cared for by those to whom this charge has been entrusted, so that in all their needs they may have most suitable attendants. At least once daily, when the brethren visit them, they should make confession and always seek from them [Col. 0727C] the blessing of prayer.

But if the sickness increases more and more, after they have been sprinkled by the priests with blessed water, let them be anointed with holy oil and fortified by receiving Christ’s body and blood. Let the brethren also diligently and humbly implore God’s mercy in common for their deliverance and absolution. If they come to their end, holy water should likewise be sprinkled there, and the sign of the cross brought in. When it has been adored by them, if possible, let it be placed there and remain until their passing. Then the brethren present should perform all the offices in due order.

When they have died, after washing, let them be clothed in tunics, with linen tunics laid over them, and let their feet be shod with shoes. Then, wrapped in sheets according to custom, let them be placed in their beds. All else concerning their carrying and burial, [Col. 0727D] and concerning the offices to be performed, should be done as the order prescribes. When these have been completed, the brethren should perform penance for them within the seventh or thirtieth day by Masses, psalms, almsgiving, or fasts. Concerning Masses and psalms to be sung within the hundredth day or the year; vigils to be observed; poor people to be fed from their allotted portions; anniversaries to be celebrated; and offerings to be brought to the tombs: let all be done as the prior has appointed, or as usage or the order teaches.

## CHAPTER XXIII. Concerning the care of sick persons who recover, and concerning medical treatment not to be denied them

But if sick brethren begin to regain strength, let them be cared for, governed, and fed by those whom the prior appoints until their health is restored, [Col. 0728A] so that they may have no cause to murmur through lack of anything or through any occasion of necessity. They themselves, however, must entirely cease to demand things which cannot be had. If they seek things harmful to them, their wishes must by no means be granted.

“For sometimes,” as Blessed Augustine says, “even what gives pleasure is believed to be beneficial, though it harms.” In this matter physicians should also be consulted for the care of the sick, even in such cases. For the aids of medicine, which we believe to have been granted by God, must not be denied to the sick when resources permit, provided that the medicine of souls has come first. Nor should the sick be guarded with less care in the time of recovery than in the time of illness; for then they are guarded lest they grow worse, whereas now they are restored so that, improved, they may return to their former state.

[Col. 0728B] When the time of restoration has come, let them come into chapter in the presence of the brethren; and, stepping into the midst, let them accuse themselves concerning sins, negligences, and breaches of the order which they have incurred on the occasion of illness. Thus, having received the sentence of satisfaction in the manner described above, let them return to their own places, to the society of the brethren, and to observance of the rule.

But if anyone, loving ease or a more luxurious life, delays returning to the observance of the order, and this becomes certainly known to his guardian, let him be subjected to such stern discipline that the others may fear to do the same. Yet we do not say this because we wish them to be joined to the brethren in observance of the order before they are able, but lest they incur the vice [Col. 0728C] of gluttony or pretence. Therefore let the guardian take the greatest care, if possible, neither to permit them to return to the observance of the order before full health, nor to permit them, once they are truly able, to defer it.”

## CHAPTER XXIV. Concerning the use of baths and bloodletting

If any brethren require baths or bloodletting for the preservation or restoration of health, these should be supplied to them even if they do not wish it, so that, strengthened in bodily health, they may prove stronger in every observance of the order. But if any seek this through vice, or more frequently than is fitting, the prudence of their elders should by no means consent to it.

The care of those who have been bled [Col. 0728D] shall be as follows until the third day. Those who are to be bled should undergo bloodletting after terce, or, in Lent, after none. On that day and the following night they should not be compelled to attend the offices; nevertheless, they should be instructed to sing some psalms. From the first hour of the second day until the first hour of the third, they should be required to hear, but not to perform, the offices. But after prime on the third day, let them come to chapter; accusing themselves of their negligences, let them receive the sentence of satisfaction, and then return to their ranks. Until that hour, however, having been fed, according to the means of the house, with more ample and nourishing food, they should remain either in the infirmary or in private quarters under a guardian. Nor should use of baths be denied if any care requires it.

## CHAPTER XXV. Concerning the aged, and likewise the sick

[Col. 0729A]

Let another house also be established where the aged may dwell, since, because of the coldness of nature and excessive weakness, they are no longer permitted to observe the common rule. Therefore let them be governed, fed, and supported by their guardians according to their age, need, and weakness. Like the sick, they should be subject neither to the rule of fasts nor to vigils; nor should they be compelled to attend the offices if unable. Nevertheless, they should be exhorted to sing psalms and pray. If resources permit, let there be a small chapel between the houses of both groups, where they may hear shortened Masses and other offices, if the prior approves.

## CHAPTER XXVI. Concerning boys and youths who are being brought up

[Col. 0729B]

The boys and youths who are brought up and educated in the canonical community should live together in one dormitory, assigned to excellent masters. By these they should be held under such strict restraint that none of them may turn aside in any direction or go anywhere without the supervision of an elder. All of them, both pupils and masters alike, should be entrusted to a most trustworthy elder, who must not permit them to be idle or given to conversation, but should instruct them in good morals, nurture them in holy conduct, and educate them in every ecclesiastical discipline, so that in time they may serve the needs of the Church and be worthily promoted to ecclesiastical ranks.

Let them always attend the divine offices, stand properly in choir beside the older brethren, [Col. 0729C] sit there at the time for sitting in their own stalls, and do everything according to use and order. Let them also assemble with the brethren in chapter; but, as soon as they enter, let them hasten with the elder and their masters to the schools, diligently learning what is necessary. In the refectory likewise, each should eat standing at table in his own section and place before the brethren. They should sleep with the brethren in the dormitory as well, their beds being intermingled with those of the older men.

Therefore let them always be in school when silence is not observed. But while the brethren remain in silence, let them be in the appointed place of the cloister under the care of their elder and masters, observing the whole order as far as they are able, and applying themselves to the disciplines of the divine offices and to holy readings. Yet until the age of sixteen they shall not be subject to the rule of fasts. Let them likewise remain in school until the age of sixteen, [Col. 0730A] or until they have learned most thoroughly to read hymns, psalms, chant, and the Scriptures according to custom. Thereafter, when removed from school, they should remain with the brethren according to the rank in which they were admitted into the community. But if the prior judges it fitting or necessary that schools be kept in some part of the cloister, let him do what he sees to be more expedient, unless it is contrary to the brethren.

## CHAPTER XXVII. Whether some should be instructed in the discipline of grammatical art

[Col. 0730B]

If the prior sees that some of these, or even of the elder brethren, are in truth more fervent in God’s service and true religion; more ready for every obedience and observance of the order; stronger in giving help; more prudent in discernment; and more useful to the souls and bodies of the brethren; and if he truly recognizes in them happier natural ability and wiser judgment, then, if he judges it right, he should command that, setting aside shameful and deceitful books, they be instructed in the discipline of grammar for learning and understanding the divine Scriptures. In this matter no favouritism or respect of persons should be shown, unless the welfare of the Church or [Col. 0730C] of their souls requires otherwise.

## CHAPTER XXVIII. Concerning literate laymen received at a more advanced age

If the brethren receive learned men at a more advanced age, and the prior sees that after the first or second year they labour in vain over training in chant, let them be relieved of useless labour and applied to higher matters better suited to them and more useful to the brethren.

Here ends the second book.

# THIRD BOOK

[Col. 0729]

## THE PROLOGUE OF THE THIRD BOOK BEGINS

[Col. 0729]

Having thus set forth these various matters concerning canons, let us proceed to the number and mystery of the canonical hours, which the holy Fathers, inspired by the Holy Spirit, instituted—as we have learned from our elders and as the practice of the Church maintains—and also to several other necessary observances of the brethren, to the assignment of obediences, and to the reception of places.

## CHAPTER I. Concerning the seven canonical hours established in ancient times, and prime, devised in a later age

[Col. 0729D]

David the psalmist testifies that seven hours were established in ancient times, saying: “Seven times in the day I have uttered praise to thee” (Ps. CXVIII [119]); so that there should be as many offerings of praise in the day as there are days themselves. For antiquity did not deserve to celebrate an eighth hour, since it had not yet deserved to have the everlasting resurrection of the dead.

Therefore the canons ought, following the footsteps of the ancients, to celebrate with the utmost devotion on every day these seven hours: the night watches, matins, terce, sext, none, vespers, and compline. Prime also, although established in a later age, ought nevertheless to be venerated with no less devotion. The Holy Spirit through the ancient and modern Fathers ordained that these eight hours should be duly celebrated in the Church every day; so that, since the day is completed by the course of twenty-four hours, each three hours should have its proper praises, in the offering of which the Holy Trinity might always be worshipped, and our inward person might continually be purified from the sins of thought, speech, and action, [Col. 0731B] in order that he too might deserve more worthily to cleave to the Trinity. They rise to the number eight in order to foreshadow the joy of the universal resurrection, in which, freed from all sins, we shall behold the mystery of the Trinity itself in fullest knowledge and thereafter rejoice with it without end.

## CHAPTER II. Concerning the night watches

These hours, then, were appointed to be celebrated at fixed times of day because of definite mysteries. The watches are observed at night because the destroying angel, passing through by night, struck the firstborn of the Egyptians (Exod. IX), and delivered Israel from their dominion. The Lord Jesus Christ also was delivered up by night to the wickedness of the raging Jews. Likewise the Christian people are chiefly baptized on the night of Easter and delivered from the death of souls.
