Therefore, lest we be joined to the perils of the Egyptians and the wickedness of the Jews; lest we leave without praises the hour of Israel’s deliverance, of our own deliverance through baptism, and of the Lord’s betrayal; and lest we, with Paul and Silas, complete the prayers of nocturnal praise (Acts XV)—and so that, if the Lord comes at that hour, he may find us watching—it is most fitting that, rising at the night hours, we devote ourselves to sacred prayers and divine praises. David testifies that he did this, saying: “In the night I remembered thy name, O Lord” (Ps. CXVIII [119]). And shortly afterward in the same psalm: “At midnight I arose to give praise to thee” (ibid.). And Isaiah: “By night,” he says, “my spirit watches for thee, O God” (Isa. XXVI). And the Lord, exhorting us in the Gospel to nocturnal watches, says: “Blessed are those servants whom the lord, when he comes, shall find watching” (Luke XII). The Evangelist testifies that he confirmed his words by examples: “Jesus was spending the whole night in prayer” (Luke VI).

## CHAPTER III. Concerning matins

Although the office of morning praise was first established in a later age—and, as some report, in the monastery at Bethlehem, where the Lord was born of the Virgin for our salvation—yet the whole Church gladly receives its worshipful observance and solemnly celebrates it. For there is no doubt that this was done by the Holy Spirit, so that the hour which the Lord illumined with the splendour of his Resurrection, and at which the light of our grace and the sun of justice rose for the faithful, might always be cultivated with divine [Col. 0732A] praises and offices.

For this reason also the Lord chose to rise from the dead, as it were, at the end of night and the beginning of day: that he might plainly show us that by his Resurrection the darkness of oldness would come to an end, while the light of newness and grace, and the entrance into eternal blessedness, would find their beginning. At this time, too, as Blessed Isidore testifies, the faithful believe in the hope of the future resurrection, when the righteous, rising from death as from the sleep of slumber, will begin to shine like the sun at the beginning of eternal light and blessedness.

That this time was held in reverence even among the ancients is testified by that ancient psalmist when he says: “At matins I will meditate upon thee, because thou hast been my helper” (Ps. LXII [63]). And: “My eyes have anticipated thee at daybreak, that I might meditate on thy words” (Ps. CXVIII [119]). [Col. 0732B] And elsewhere: “We have been filled in the morning with thy mercy” (Ps. LXXXIX [90]). And: “In the morning my prayer shall come before thee” (ibid.).

## CHAPTER IV. Concerning prime

Although prime was first established and devised in a later age in the East among the monasteries of Palestine, yet because the whole Church has received it, and because there is no doubt that it was added by the Holy Spirit, it too must be celebrated with the highest devotion and offering of praise. It is suitably performed after sunrise, so that the hour in which Christ’s Resurrection was first announced by angels to the women (Matt. XXVIII), and by the women to the apostles (Mark XVI; John XX), may not lack divine praises and worthy offices.

It also seems entirely reasonable that at the first hour of the day we should apply ourselves to divine offices and holy prayers, so that we may give thanks to God because we have come from darkness into light, and ask that throughout the whole day he may direct our hearts and bodies into the way of salvation and justice. And since every virtue, every holiness, every justice ought always to be begun to the praise and honour of God and in the name of Jesus Christ, it was fitting that the beginning of the day, which marks the working of light, should be consecrated by divine praises.

It should also be noted that the Holy Spirit did not will this hour to be established through the apostles, the more ancient Fathers, or even the greater Church, but reserved it by a wonderful and gracious providence to be established in a later age through children subject to the Church. Thus we are made aware that the Spirit of the Lord has reserved for himself [Col. 0732D] this power: whenever and through whomever, by his inspiration, anything right and holy has been established in the Church, no one should dare to reject it because of disregard for persons or because of the newness of the time; rather, he should diligently embrace and hold fast the love of the God who inspires and establishes through a human being.

## CHAPTER V. Concerning terce, sext, and none

Sacred history testifies that Daniel and the three youths also devoted the third, sixth, and ninth hours to supplications to the Lord. Following their example, it is most fitting for us to devote ourselves to divine offices at these hours, especially since in a later age, and for reasons of other mysteries, they have become much more celebrated for us.

For the Holy Spirit, because he is the third person in the Trinity, made the third hour most famous by his descent and rendered it most worthy of divine praise (Acts II). At that descent, they affirm, such grace of the Holy Spirit was present that all the apostles spoke in every language, and the diversity of all languages present understood simultaneously each apostle speaking in whatever single language. Thus it was made known that the Spirit of the Lord joins and unites within the bosom of one Church those whom the pride of the devilish spirit had divided through the building on earth.

The Holy Spirit also suitably descended at the third hour because in the third age Christ renewed the whole world and flooded it with the light of his grace. For these reasons too, the authority of the holy Fathers established this hour of ours as, above all others, the lawful one for celebrating Masses: at it, because we sinned again, we are again redeemed, as it were, by Christ’s death; and, renewed likewise by the Eucharist as by the reception of the Holy Spirit, we are led by a spiritual working to the pure and new life of the third age, as though by another passing-over of Christ.

### Concerning sext

Christ consecrated the sixth hour by the suffering of his crucifixion and made it celebrated by the offering of praise. Christ suitably chose to suffer at the sixth hour in order to show that through his cross and Passion an entrance into life was reserved for us in the sixth age, and that humanity, created on the sixth day but destroyed through the devil’s endeavour, was saved and redeemed by his own blood at the sixth hour and in the sixth age.

### Concerning none

Christ made the ninth hour famous by his death [Col. 0733C] in order to restore us, redeemed from death, to the fellowship of the blessed spirits, who are distinguished in nine orders. He suitably dies as the sun declines toward setting, because the unbelieving Jews lost the rising sun of justice and came into the darkness of sins. Peter and John also sanctified this hour by the healing of the lame man. Moreover, at this hour the way of salvation was first shown to gentile people in Cornelius (Acts XIII). Therefore the faithful of Christ ought to venerate these hours with the greatest devotion and celebrate them with worthy praises because of such great mysteries.

## CHAPTER VI. Concerning the evening hour

The office of evening praise, performed at the end of the day and at the setting of the light, is shown by the rite of ancient sacrifices [Col. 0733D] to be one that must be celebrated. David says: “The lifting up of my hands [is] an evening sacrifice” (Ps. CXL [141]). “At evening, morning, and noon I shall declare thy name.” And at this same hour the Lord Jesus Christ first gave his disciples, as they were dining, communion in his holy body and blood, and commanded that from that time onward it be observed forever. At this same hour also, after his Resurrection, he appeared to the disciples and confirmed them in faith.

Therefore at the same hour we ought to offer God the office of praise, so that, when the end of each day has been celebrated with praises, we may consecrate by mystical observance to God the end of our life and of all our actions, that we may deserve to be fellow-partakers in such great mysteries.

## CHAPTER VII. Concerning compline

[Col. 0734A]

It is called *completorium* [compline] because it completes the actions of the day and, when labour is finished, releases weary limbs into rest. At this hour we are rightly commanded to perform the offices of divine praise, so that whatever we have sinned during the day through the drawing force of fleshly frailty may be cleansed by the offering of those praises; and so that, before our limbs are given to sleep, we may prepare in our breasts a clean dwelling-place for God.

David the psalmist testifies that he did this, saying: “If I ascend into the bed of my couch, if I give sleep to my eyes and slumber to my eyelids, until I find a place for the Lord, a tabernacle for the God of Jacob” (Ps. CXXXII [132]). At this hour too, after supper, the Lord Jesus took three disciples and went out to the Mount of Olives [Col. 0734B] to pray (Matt. XXVI). There he prayed to the Father three times that he might deign to rescue him from the snares laid by the Jews that night. Not because he did not know that he would not be rescued, but so that, strengthened by his example, we might apply ourselves at this hour to divine praises and beseech the Trinity itself with voice and mind in humble prayer to deign to deliver us from the enemy’s nocturnal snares and deceptions.

## CHAPTER VIII. From what materials the offices of these hours are to be composed

For performing the praises of these hours there are principally taken the one hundred and fifty Davidic psalms and six canticles of the Old Testament. [Col. 0734C] There are also the hymn of the three youths; the three Gospel Canticles composed respectively by Zacharias, Mary, and Simeon; the Lord’s Prayer; the Apostles’ Creed; the Greek litanies; the Hebrew praise; the glorification of the Trinity; the ecclesiastical hymn; and the proper openings of the hours.

Besides these, there are the Scriptures of all the canonical books of the New and Old Testaments; homilies and sermons of holy doctors; and also the Lives and authenticated Passions of the saints. To all these are added Ambrosian hymns, invitatories, antiphons, responsories with their verses, short responsories and versicles, petitions for blessings and the blessings themselves, fixed endings of readings, offerings of thanksgiving and praise, confessions of sins, and certain chapters of supplications drawn from the canonical Scriptures; moreover, salutations and prayers with their openings and fixed endings; the Hebrew response; and final absolutions.

How all these are distributed and performed through the individual hours, days, weeks, and seasons is shown by the practice of the Church. The diversity of the offices of the hours is determined by feast-day, hour, and season: they are performed differently on weekdays, differently on Sundays, differently on private feasts, differently on supreme, principal, and popular solemnities, differently in Easter seasons, and differently also on days included within octaves or within the continuations of the greatest feasts. Yet in some of these matters there is found [Col. 0735A] much variety in certain offices according to differing times and places, concerning which the more correct order and practice in each district of the greater churches should give instruction.

## CHAPTER IX. Which feasts are called private, which popular, which principal, and which supreme

We call private feasts those which, since they are not observed by the people, are celebrated only by clerics with three readings. Popular feasts are those which, being observed by the people of many regions, are kept by the clerics of those places with nine readings. Principal feasts are those which are celebrated everywhere with great devotion by all Christian peoples and Catholic churches. Supreme feasts are chiefly the five solemnities of Christ: the Nativity, the Manifestation [Epiphany], the Resurrection, the Ascension, and Pentecost. To these your holiness has been pleased, from a purpose of devotion, to add the feast of All Saints and that of your present and principal dedication, with an almost equal celebration of offices.

## CHAPTER X. Concerning the order of readings throughout the year

At Septuagesima they appoint the Heptateuch until the fifteenth day before Easter. On the fifteenth day before Easter, they appoint Jeremiah until the Lord’s Supper. On the Lord’s Supper they read three readings from the Lamentations of Jeremiah: “How lonely sits the city”; three from the exposition of St Augustine on Psalm sixty-three: “Hear, O God, my prayer when I entreat thee”; and three from the Apostle, where he says to the Corinthians: “When you come together in one”; the second: “Likewise, after he had supped”; the third: “Now concerning spiritual things, brethren, we do not wish you to be ignorant.”

On Preparation Day [Good Friday], [Col. 0735C] three [readings are taken] from the Lamentations of Jeremiah, three from St Augustine’s exposition on Psalm sixty-three, and three from the Apostle, where he says in the Epistle to the Hebrews: “Let us hasten to enter”; the second reading: “For every high priest”; the third: “Concerning whom we have much to say.” On Holy Saturday, three [readings are taken] from the Lamentations, three from St Augustine’s exposition, and three from the Apostle, where he says in the Epistle to the Hebrews: “Christ, having come as high priest.”

At the Lord’s Easter, [they read] homilies appropriate to that day. During the week, [they read] homilies. At the octave of Easter they appoint the Acts of the Apostles, the Catholic Epistles, and the Apocalypse until the octave of Pentecost. At the octave of Pentecost they appoint Kings and Chronicles until the Kalends of August. On the first Sunday of August they appoint Solomon until the Kalends [Col. 0735D] of September. On the first Sunday of September they appoint Job until mid-September; then they appoint Tobit, Judith, Esther, and Ezra until the Kalends of October. On the first Sunday of October they appoint the book of Maccabees until the Kalends of November. Thereafter they appoint Ezekiel, Daniel, and the minor prophets until the Advent of the Lord. On the first Sunday of Advent they appoint Isaiah until the Nativity of the Lord.

At the vigils of the Lord’s Nativity they read three readings from Isaiah: “At the first time,” “Comfort ye,” and “Arise.” Then [they read] sermons and homilies appropriate to that day. On the feasts of St Stephen, St John, the Holy Innocents, and St Silvester, [they read] sermons appropriate to those days. At the octave of the Lord’s Nativity, [they read] homilies concerning that day. On the first Sunday after the Nativity, [they appoint] the epistles of Paul until Septuagesima. At Epiphany, [they read] three readings from Isaiah: “All ye that thirst,” “Arise,” and “Rejoicing.” Then sermons or homilies appropriate to the same day are read.

## CHAPTER XI. Concerning the order of Masses

The lawful hours for Mass are terce and none. At all lawful fasts Mass should be celebrated at none; on all other days, at terce, according to practice and order. But that Mass is sung after the nocturnal vigils of the Lord’s Nativity, on Holy Saturday at the beginning of the Easter night, on Sundays and greater feasts, and on weekdays in the morning for the dead before prime or after prime—and that it is sometimes sung at lawful fasts [Col. 0736B] in the morning or, among some, at terce—there is no doubt that this is done for the sake of a definite necessity or mystery.

At other hours, although no Mass is found appointed in the canons, the practice of the Church nevertheless allows Mass to be celebrated out of necessity from sunrise until terce, and from none until vespers. Therefore on Sundays and supreme feasts the proper Masses, where provided, should be sung. On principal, popular, and private feasts, if proper Masses are available, they should be sung; but if proper Masses are not available, they should be said from the common [of saints] appropriate to the occasion. At lawful fasts also there are proper Masses, which we ought to sing, except for a few vigils on which Masses from the common appropriate to the occasion are sung.

Within the octaves of the greatest feasts, or, as some prefer, of principal feasts, the practice of very many has been to celebrate Masses of the same feasts. During the week of Easter and Pentecost, however, let the proper Masses, where provided, be sung; on the other days let the Mass of the preceding Sunday be said, except that if proper Masses, epistles, or Gospels are provided for Wednesday or Friday, these should be said.

You have also established that a Mass for the dead should always be said in the morning for your convent, except on Sundays, feasts celebrated with nine readings, and days included within the octaves of supreme feasts. In addition, on all supreme feasts, and on those principal feasts for which two Masses are provided, you have established that a Mass should be sung in the convent in the morning before prime. But on other principal feasts, on all popular feasts, on Sundays, and at lawful fasts, you have arranged that Mass be sung for those clerics or laypeople present who, for any reason, cannot attend Mass at terce or none. [Col. 0736D] Therefore, if resources permit, let all the Masses which you have decreed shall be said in convent always be chanted with their offices, according to the use and order of the Church and the appropriateness of the season, with deacon and subdeacon ministering.

## CHAPTER XII. Concerning the hour of collation

When days are long and nights short, around the summer solstice, the hour of collation should be held earlier—that is, while the sun’s ray is still visible. But when the shortening of the days has made the nights longer, it should be held later, [Col. 0737A] that is, when the fading daylight begins to remove the ability to read. It should be increased and decreased in due order only according to the increase or decrease of days and nights. But when the foot-washing is to be performed, or when some eminent solemnity is imminent on which it is necessary to rise earlier than usual, that hour of collation should be held earlier than usual.

## CHAPTER XIII. At what hour of the night we ought to perform the watches

At every season, insofar as this can be observed, on weekdays one should rise for the offices of the watches when two parts of the night have passed and the third still remains. But on Sundays and other solemnities one should rise according to the usage, manner, and extent [Col. 0737B] of the offices, so that on every feast-day and weekday all the divine offices may be duly performed in their proper time.

In summer, however, because the nights are short, the readings in the nocturnal watches should be shortened. In winter, because of their length, we judge that the readings should be extended, unless they are sometimes shortened because of an intolerable severity of cold.

## CHAPTER XIV. In what order or at what times matins and the other hours should be performed

After the watches have been completed, at every season, and after the signal has been sounded if it is permitted, the offices of morning praise should be performed. Prime, terce, sext, none, vespers, and compline should be performed at their suitable hours on every day and in every season according to usage and order. Yet in these offices, and always in all things, consideration should be given to the necessity of the matters at hand, [Col. 0737C] to the days, and to the quantity and character of the offices.

## CHAPTER XV. Concerning what is to be done or said in chapter
When the brethren assemble in chapter in the morning after Prime, the reader, having requested a blessing, shall announce the day of the month, the age of the moon, the feria of the following day, and the feasts, in the customary manner. When these have been announced, the brethren shall rise; and, after the customary versicles of the same Hour have been concluded, they shall sit again and hear a reading concerning the institutions of the canonical life, or concerning the feast of that day, if it be a principal or especially important one. When this is ended, the reader, assigning individually to individual brethren the readings and responsories for the following day, shall announce them.

Then the prior, having requested a blessing from the brethren, shall say whatever he sees to be necessary, [Col. 0737D] whether for exhorting souls, arranging the affairs of the Church itself, or discussing certain canonical matters; and no one there, except the prior and the provost, shall presume to speak unless commanded, questioned, or called upon. And when one speaks there, the rest shall be silent and attend to the speaker’s words until the end. If anyone knows that his brother, in his holy profession, has incurred the fault of a transgression, he shall rise in charity according to the regular custom and, speaking humbly, say: “That brother of ours has acted contrary to the rule.” At this word the accused shall immediately rise and come into the midst; then the accuser, having expressly named his fault, shall sit down; while the accused, prostrate on the ground, shall say: “My fault; I have sinned.” And the brethren [Col. 0738A] shall respond: “May God pardon you.” Then he shall rise, prostrate himself again, and repeat the same words until the prior orders him to stand and imposes the sentence of satisfaction, assigning him a definite hour or day by which he must have fulfilled what was imposed. We do not forbid the same to be done after None, if chapter is held then and the prior approves. This manner of satisfaction ought always to be observed by those accused or those who confess of themselves.

## CHAPTER XVI. Concerning the announcement of principal feasts in chapter, and mutual confession and remission

When principal feasts are approaching, on the fifth or fourth day beforehand, after all that we have already written as to what is to be done in chapter in the morning after Prime has first been completed, [Col. 0738B] one of the brethren, to whom the prior has assigned it, shall come forward and, having requested a blessing, say: “On the fifth or fourth day next to come, most beloved brethren, we shall celebrate that feast of our Lord Jesus Christ. Sanctify yourselves and be ready. But thou, O Lord, etc.” The brethren responding in a moderate voice, “Thanks be to God,” the same reader shall then add, according to the arrangement made by the provost, which brethren ought to say, sing, or read the invitatory, readings, responsories, and whatever else is necessary in the offices.

When these have been announced, let an open confession of all faults be made, followed by the imposition of penance and satisfaction, to be fulfilled before the celebration of that feast, if possible. If, however, [Col. 0738C] anyone wishes to confess something privately, let him confess to the prior or to priests appointed by the prior for this office. The brethren shall also grant remission to one another and to all absent persons whom they have offended, by whatever vow and absolution they can offer. It would be sufficiently praiseworthy and consonant with the rule if this were done also on every Sabbath and on the vigils of the principal feasts. Those who are to sing and read, therefore, on these or any other days, shall look beforehand to what is to be sung and read; and if it is necessary to inquire about anything in these matters, definite persons shall be designated by the prior from whom they ought to seek it at a permitted hour, and who shall provide it humbly and diligently.

## CHAPTER XVII. Concerning the many prayers and observances of the brethren

[Col. 0738D] Concerning the three prayers—at night before Vigils, in the morning before Prime, and in the evening after Compline—and the prayers to be said after Matins and Vespers; concerning the singing of the Songs of Ascents; likewise concerning the Matins and Vespers of saints; concerning the Hours of Saint Mary, if fraternal devotion maintains them; concerning Vigils, Matins, Masses, and Vespers to be offered for the dead; concerning the penitential psalms to be said in the morning; concerning other psalms to be sung after the Hours; furthermore, concerning the manner of entering and leaving church or chapter; concerning the manner of walking, standing, speaking, or keeping silence in the cloister; concerning the manner of sleeping and rising together, eating and drinking together; concerning the preparation of ministers who are to serve at Mass; concerning the washing of hands [Col. 0739A] and combing of heads; concerning the ringing of bells and the tablets; concerning the marking of the divine Hours; likewise the time for conference and the meal; concerning the brethren’s reciprocal service; concerning the order of Sunday or any other processions; finally, concerning all that is to be done within the church and in the brethren’s workshops: usage, order, or the institution of the elders shall indicate whatever is necessary.

## CHAPTER XVIII. That the prior ought to be diligent concerning all these matters

Since it belongs to the prior to inquire continually, personally and through others, into all interior and exterior matters; to examine carefully what has been investigated and ascertained; to handle wisely what has been examined; to establish what is to be established; to command what is to be done; to forbid what is to be avoided; to determine what is suitable for each person; to speak with individuals [Col. 0739B] and provide for each according to need; wisely to correct whatever needs correction; and, according to the measure of the fault, to impose also the measure of satisfaction upon offenders—so that harshness may not draw anyone back from amendment, nor excessive leniency release anyone unwillingly—and, if it is sometimes necessary to show severity outwardly, nevertheless always to preserve humility inwardly in the heart; he ought, when free for it, to devote himself to reading and apply himself to prayers; frequently to irrigate the brethren gathered together with the streams of Holy Scripture; often to instruct them concerning the life and conduct of clerics and the observance of their own order; to set before them for imitation the virtues and examples of the saints; to terrify offenders by enumerating the punishment of penalties; to kindle in those who act well desire for attaining blessedness; and to provide for every person who comes, according to his needs and the rank of persons, if resources suffice. [Col. 0739C] Finally, he must exercise vigilant care for the souls and bodies of all his fellow brethren; preserve, govern, and dispose all the Church’s property, movable and immovable, spiritual and temporal; and supply all persons with all their needs and suitable provisions.

And since one man cannot bear so much, it is necessary that persons be appointed under him, so that the burdens may be divided among them and all necessary things suitably accomplished. Thus Moses, when he could not bear the burden of governing all Israel, even on the counsel of an uncircumcised man chose wise men from all Israel and appointed them over the people as tribunes, [Col. 0739D] centurions, commanders of fifties, and commanders of tens, to settle lawsuits and remove disputes, reserving only the greater matters for his own decision. Moved, therefore, by this example, most beloved brethren, you have ordained that persons should prudently be selected from among the wiser men to assist the prior, so that they might bear, more lightly because divided, the several burdens which pertain inwardly and outwardly to supplying the necessities of souls and bodies and to observing the order.

## CHAPTER XIX. Concerning the provost

You have therefore judged, most beloved brethren, that one man should be chosen from among the fellow brethren: one pure in will, discreet in speech, holy in conduct, outstanding in knowledge and observance of the order, and, if possible, adequately imbued with knowledge of the divine Scriptures; [Col. 0740A] one adorned by the virtue of patience, the love of charity, and the religious devotion of life. Set over the others beneath the prior, he shall exercise vigilant guardianship of his authority in the performance of offices, the governance and custody of the brethren, and the observance of order and rule.

He shall teach the brethren the character, practice, order, and every variation of the offices. He shall command that the customary offices be assigned on the tablets according to usage and order, and afterwards announced in chapter before the brethren. He shall determine, before the weekly servers and the cellarer, the dishes to be prepared for the brethren and all that is to be set before them. He shall take care that clothing and footwear are not delayed when needed, and shall see that the obediences of each person, inwardly and outwardly, are justly governed and regularly fulfilled. [Col. 0740B] He shall therefore have care, under the prior’s counsel and command, of all interior and exterior matters; and in the prior’s absence shall say and do whatever is necessary, greater affairs nevertheless being reserved for the prior’s judgment. Usage and order themselves shall teach all other matters belonging to this office which are not expressly named here. In all these things he shall so exercise the right of his government that he may receive from the Lord the reward of righteous glory.

## CHAPTER XX. Concerning the appointment of subordinate provosts or masters, and the discipline of offenders

Besides this man, the prior shall also appoint beneath him other masters or provosts for the supervision of the brethren, if he sees it necessary. He shall assign each a proper place in the cloister, where they, sitting there, shall nourish in goodness the brethren [Col. 0740C] committed to them and assigned here and there; instruct them in holy conduct; compel them to apply themselves to readings, hymns, canticles, and other ecclesiastical teachings or useful pursuits; compel them to remain in their place and preserve their proper order; and never allow them to leave or depart from their sight except for a definite necessary reason. Finally, they shall preserve them free not only from works of perversity and malice, but also from the practice of idle talk, and shall present them as perfect in every religious observance of holiness and honorable gravity.

If they perceive that anything is necessary for them, they shall make it known to the prior or provost, so that, if resources suffice, every need may be met without delay. If they observe any of those committed to them to be wandering, idle, [Col. 0740D] occupied with useless talk, unwilling to observe their own order, or disobedient to their superiors, and are unable to correct them after warning them once, twice, and three times, then they shall bring them to the provost for correction. If the provost likewise cannot correct them after warning them once, twice, and three times, he shall present them before the brethren in chapter. If they do not correct themselves even through the prior, they shall be put beneath all and insulted by all; finally, deprived of fraternal fellowship and communion, they shall be chastened with fasts, and, if the status of the persons permits, beaten. If they are not amended even thus, they shall be confined in prison to be disciplined by prolonged fasts, or handed over to the judgment of the greater Church or bishop.

Those who have been dismissed, imprisoned, or secretly departed of themselves [Col. 0741A], if at some time moved by repentance they promise satisfaction and obtain pardon by asking for it, shall first be tested outwardly for a long time; and if they truly appear repentant, they may at length be received inwardly, at least in the lowest place. Your charity has judged, most beloved brethren, that this manner of correction should be observed not only among clerics but also among professed laymen.

## CHAPTER XXI. Concerning those holding or receiving obediences

Those who undertake the obediences of the house for the brethren’s benefit and service shall remain under the care and authority of the prior and provost. Whatever they, or other superiors supplying their office in their absence, command them, they shall observe and fulfil without delay. [Col. 0741B] If they commit any fault, they shall make satisfaction in proportion to it, according to the prior’s command and the practice of the order. But if any are found proud, negligent, greedy, prodigal, whisperers, thieves, or in any way squanderers of the Lord’s property; or if they despise the commands of those set over them; or maliciously withhold from anyone what they ought to give; or from love of special favor give anything contrary to usage and order when it was not suitable—the prior shall remove them from their offices and, having imposed penance upon them and a sentence of satisfaction, shall appoint others in their places, who, performing these things more vigilantly and purely, may minister faithfully to Christ and their fellow brethren.

For supplying the necessary things to individual brethren within the house, men shall be selected from among the stronger and wiser brethren: one to undertake the government and custody of the sacristy, [Col. 0741C] another of the chamber, a third of the cellar, a fourth of the refectory, and a fifth of the wardrobe. Whoever comes to undertake any of these or similar obediences shall come into the midst of chapter and, prostrate, begin the psalm: “O God, attend to help me” (Ps. LXV). When the brethren have completed it, with the Lord’s Prayer, the short chapters, and the appropriate prayer, he shall rise; and, kneeling, receive from the prior’s hand the rule or another little book, the prior saying: “With the consent of the brethren, we command you to bear the care and labor of this obedience, for the salvation of your soul, in penance and remission of your sins, out of charity.” Thereafter he shall discharge and complete the care of that obedience [Col. 0741D] with the utmost diligence, prudence, and counsel.

Those from whom such obediences are removed because of some offense, or who are relieved of them by the prior’s will, shall prostrate themselves in the midst and accuse themselves concerning everything they have done amiss in administering them; and they shall begin the fiftieth psalm. When the brethren have completed it, together with the Lord’s Prayer, the short chapters, and the appropriate prayer, they shall rise and receive with cheerful spirit the amount of penance imposed by the prior, completing what they have received within the appointed time.

## CHAPTER XXII. Concerning the sacristan

The oratory, sacristy, library-cupboard, and all that must be done or stored in them, together with all necessary or fitting things, shall belong to the sacristan’s obedience. [Col. 0742A] He shall clean, light, and guard the oratory according to usage and order; close and open it at the proper hour; and shall neither do nor store there anything unbecoming, nor permit anything unbecoming to be done or stored there, for the Lord says: “My house shall be called a house of prayer” (Matt. XXI).

No one doubts that holy oil, the Body of the Lord, and caskets containing saints’ relics should remain in churches. We do not reject other small objects also, provided they are ecclesiastical, present nothing indecorous, and are required daily for divine services. If possible, the sacristan shall guard the choir with such vigilance that no place for leaving or entering it is open to anyone, unless someone humbly seeks admission for prayer or devotion, to offer an oblation, receive the Eucharist, or receive the fellowship of the clergy. [Col. 0742B] At the solemnities of Mass, the priest shall receive the people’s offerings before the choir-door and there administer to them the mystery of the Lord’s Body and Blood. If the people are numerous, however, and wish to approach the altar, they shall not be forbidden. Yet while the clerics remain seated in the choir, women shall not, if possible, be allowed access to the altar.

Whatever is offered in wax, oil, incense, or vestments, necessary for the use of altars or ministers, the sacristan shall receive for storage in the sacristy, to supply the needs of his obedience. The vestments and ornaments of the altar or altar-ministers, and indeed all the church’s utensils, shall be kept locked and stored in the sacristy. [Col. 0742C] Some of these shall be assigned on fixed days, others every day at the appointed hour, as necessity requires and order and usage demand, by the sacristan to the ministers and other brethren who need them. When the offices have been completed, he shall carefully check and receive them all back to be stored again.

Moreover, the sacristan shall keep all books locked in the library-cupboard under his custody; books which he knows to be necessary for the brethren’s offices in church, he himself shall put out and himself put back. Books which he knows to be useful for the brethren in the cloister, he shall place in the appointed place, from which the brethren may take whatever books they wish and to which they must return them after the Hour, for the sacristan likewise to receive and store. Whatever is necessary for writing, fitting, or repairing books [Col. 0742D] the sacristan shall keep with him, so that books not possessed may be made and those possessed may always be fitted or repaired.

Furthermore, the sacristan shall take the greatest care to signal the canonical Hours, both by day and by night, discriminately according to usage, order, and the decision of the superiors, in keeping with the season, the solemnity of the day, and the length of the office, so that all necessary things may fittingly be done. He must also have charge of lighting the dormitory, cleaning the cloister and chapter-house, and consecrating all things necessary for carrying out commands. The sacristan shall therefore provide all these things and wisely accomplish at the proper time, with the utmost diligence, whatever usage, order, or the instructions of the elders show to be necessary concerning or within them. If the sacristan cannot bear all this alone, the prior must give him assistants, through whom his divided burdens may all be borne and fulfilled more lightly.

## CHAPTER XXIII. Concerning the chamberlain

[Col. 0743A] The chamberlain shall have places secured by strong locks, with suitable doors and windows through which necessities may be supplied to those inside and outside. There shall be stored there gold, silver, iron, bronze, every kind of metal, all coinage from whatever source it arrives, and everything needed to make, from these materials, the bodily necessities of interior and exterior offices; likewise, many—and, if possible, duplicate—hand tools and vessels of stone, earthenware, and wood, to be assigned to interior and exterior offices. [Col. 0743B] The chamberlain shall gladly provide, without any delay or murmuring, all such things as the brethren need to perform their duties inside or outside: either leaving them permanently, if they are required for daily use, or receiving them back after the work is finished if this is unnecessary.

Whatever necessities from the goods entrusted to him are distributed for daily use inside or outside shall be distributed in such a way that their custody thereafter belongs to those to whom they are given. When they are worn out by age and new things are again given, the old things, if useful, shall be restored to the chamberlain, whether to be repaired or kept for some use, lest anything that may be useful should perish from the Church’s goods. If any items are lost, broken by accident, and not repaired, others shall be supplied in their place; but those through whose fault they were broken or lost shall do worthy penance, according to the prior’s judgment. If anything is lacking in any obedience, he must supply it, whether by gift or purchase, if he has it or can obtain it. The chamberlain shall therefore endeavor always to possess, whether made at his own expense or bought at a price, everything belonging to him that is necessary for interior and exterior offices, so that at no time may the brethren be able, on account of anyone’s need, to withdraw themselves from observing their order and serving divine worship.

## CHAPTER XXIV. Concerning the cellarer

Let cellars be established within the cloister walls, as near as possible to the refectory, kitchen, and bakehouse, [Col. 0743D] where all provisions necessary for the brethren’s eating or drinking shall remain stored under lock and key, together with all vessels and utensils necessary for storing and preparing them. A cellarer shall therefore be chosen by the superiors who is a prudent man, full of charity, humility, and patience; not greedy, not prodigal, not violent, not excessively fond of eating, not proud, not slow, but honorable in conduct and fearing God, free from vices and cleaving to virtues, neither more lavish nor more miserly than is right. He shall faithfully preserve the brethren’s provisions and dispense them with vigilant care. He shall not distress the brethren in his administration by harshness or delay of speech, by reduction or postponement of what ought to be given, or by the display of a troubled countenance. He shall appear gentle to all, kindly receive everyone coming to him, [Col. 0744A] and supply each according to what he sees is needed. Those whose needs he cannot satisfy, he shall endeavor to comfort with sweet words.

He shall take no small care of the sick, so that whatever is requested for them by their attendants, if he has it or can obtain it, he may provide quickly. If no person has been specifically appointed for this, he shall command the cooks to prepare it swiftly and most suitably, according to the wishes and needs of the sick and the directions of their attendants. The kitchen and bakehouse shall therefore adjoin one another and be near the refectory, assigned with all their vessels and utensils to the cellarer’s custody. The superiors must direct the cooks and bakers to obey the cellarer in every matter and render him account for all goods entrusted to them; from him they shall request and receive whatever they need. [Col. 0744B]

The cellarer shall frequently admonish them and carefully teach them the duties of their craft, laboring abundantly to show them how grave a fault it is to lose the Church’s goods through negligence or, what is worst of all, secretly to plunder them. The cooks shall prepare with sleepless care all that is necessary for the brethren’s food, doing so most cleanly and carefully by command of the cellarer and the weekly-serving brother. The cellarer, to whom all these matters are entrusted, shall endeavor to have the vessels, equipment, and utensils of the bakehouse, kitchen, and cellar restored and renewed through the chamberlain if they are lost, broken, or worn out, and also to repair them himself if he can. The cooks and bakers shall have their own places adjoining the bakehouse and kitchen, [Col. 0744C] where they may help one another in their duties, eat and live together, and perform everything belonging to them.

## CHAPTER XXV. Concerning the refectory and the refectorian

The brethren’s refectory shall also be assigned to someone who receives it gladly and guards what he has received with most diligent care. Let all things be made and kept in and around the refectory which are known to be suitable for brethren who are to eat or drink, according to the practice and regular order of your manner of life. The refectorian must carefully attend to all these matters and diligently provide whatever is necessary at the fitting hour. He shall take the greatest care [Col. 0744D] that nothing unbecoming and nothing harmful to the brethren’s stomachs appears in the refectory; rather, the brethren shall always find it frequently cleaned and suitably prepared. He himself shall open the tables at the fitting hour, set in each person’s place the proper portion of bread and wine received from the cellarer, together with the other necessities for the brethren’s eating, and carefully do everything suitable there according to usage and order. He shall always require the wardrobe-keeper and chamberlain to renew or restore whatever grows old or is lost or broken by some accident, and shall return all old or broken things to them.

## CHAPTER XXVI. Concerning the wardrobe-keeper

Besides these brethren, a wardrobe-keeper shall be appointed, who shall always take the greatest care of the brethren’s clothing, footwear, [Col. 0745A] and bedding. Within the cloister walls he shall have securely protected places where linen and wool, cloth, skins and leather, clothing and footwear, as well as the brethren’s bedding and everything necessary to fit, make, and repair these things, together with other suitable items, may be safely and securely kept and preserved. Their repair, as long as they can be repaired, and their replacement when they must be renewed, shall belong to him.

He shall also keep with him, if resources permit, all that is suitable for washing the brethren’s bodies, bathing, cutting or shaving their hair, and treating them with medicines or remedies, so that the brethren may find all these things prepared when necessary. The prior shall give him one or more assistants, if need be, [Col. 0745B] with whom he shall inspect the brethren’s garments and footwear frequently. They shall see to fitting their beds every day; when the brethren change, they shall collect the changed garments and bring them to the wardrobe for storage; at the appointed hour they shall give them to the washers to be washed, receive them back when washed, and store them again in the wardrobe; and at the time of changing they shall place each person’s things upon his bed. He shall endeavor to inscribe each garment with its owner’s name by actual workmanship, so that each person receives the garments assigned to him and no others.

When these five interior obediences have been established, the prior shall likewise endeavor to arrange external affairs, so that the Church suffers loss in none of its possessions [Col. 0745C] and everything necessary outside may be fittingly done.

## CHAPTER XXVII. Concerning the administrator of external goods

A vigorous man shall be appointed from the faithful household of the Church, who shall carefully and prudently govern and oversee all the Church’s possessions in waters and marshes, if these exist, in woods, meadows, vineyards, and lands. If possible, he shall know by memory how many tenants or possessors there are, what and how much each possesses, and what, how much, and when each must render to the Church; or he shall keep it in writing with him so that it is not surrendered to forgetfulness. He shall know, through himself, bailiffs, and assistants, all things necessary concerning these matters and arrange and carry them out under the prior’s counsel. Leases of immovable property shall be made by the prior, the brethren consenting, with the administrator’s [Col. 0745D] prudent direction, provided their arrangement has been made justly and beneficially.

He shall frequently read or hear read the charters of possessions, preserved in the most secure place by some brother charged with this by the prior, so that he may know from them the leases and revenues of the possessions, lest through negligent forgetfulness the Church suffer loss in its goods.

## CHAPTER XXVIII. Concerning the custody of movable goods

Another most faithful layman shall be appointed, who shall have the greatest care of all beasts necessary for the brethren’s use and all herds, their shepherds, and herdsmen, so that he may command what must be commanded, establish what must be established, demand what must be demanded, and in all things become their prudent guardian and governor. [Col. 0746A] Finally, he shall with sleepless care provide whatever is suitable for each herd and beast, and himself or through others supply whatever is necessary for their keepers. Whatever fruits, valuable goods, or things useful for the brethren may happen to be received or held from this or other obediences shall be given to those whose obediences are known to be entitled to store or expend them. Thus also all necessary things must be sought from those by whom they are to be dispensed.

## CHAPTER XXIX. Concerning the Church’s trader

Besides these, another most faithful man shall be appointed, who himself or through others shall buy what must be bought and sell what must be sold. The chamberlain shall supply the price of things purchased and likewise receive the proceeds of things sold. [Col. 0746B] The Church’s trader shall be such that he can never, or seldom, be deceived, and that he himself diligently deceives no one. Neither to sell more dearly nor to buy more cheaply shall he utter deceit with his mouth, demand an oath from others, or offer one himself.

## CHAPTER XXX. Concerning the obedience of household servants

All servants shall obey their superiors and fulfil joyfully, without delay or murmuring, whatever commands are given. Let no one in the Church household be found useless or idle; rather, let all work, let all serve the Church’s needs, attending to the Apostle’s saying: “Those who do not work shall not eat.” Yet boys, infirm old men, and the weak shall not be compelled to do or perform what they cannot. The prior shall therefore take account of everyone’s age, knowledge, and strength, [Col. 0746C] apportioning to each offices necessary to the house and suited to their strength and skill. Over them he shall appoint more prudent persons as masters, by whom they may be governed and under whose care, command, judgment, and diligence they may fulfil all duties imposed upon them.

Their masters shall provide everything necessary in clothing, footwear, food, and the uses of their duties; they shall procure what is provided and distribute it to them when procured. They shall seek all these things from those to whose obediences they know them to belong. When all these persons are received, prostrate before the altar, they shall promise their faithfulness to those pledges of the saints, and obedience according to God to the superiors of that [Col. 0746D] Church. Thereafter, received by the brethren according to custom, they shall henceforth live under command and serve faithfully.

## CHAPTER XXXI. Concerning the cloister and the guarding of the canons’ gate

The inner cloister shall always be guarded with such strictness that none of those within may ever have leave to go out from it, nor any of those outside to enter it, except according to the established order. If, however, faithful and devout laymen or clerics desire, out of devotion, to enter the interior places to see them and visit the brethren, we do not forbid their admission by the prior or provost outside the hour of silence. Having received the brethren’s blessing and seen the places they wished to see, they shall either depart at once or, if the prior judges it useful, sit for a little while in a more secluded place with the wiser brethren gathered there and with the brethren whom they wished to see. [Col. 0747A] After he, or someone he commands, has briefly addressed them for the edification of souls, they shall again receive the brethren’s blessing, be led outside, and dismissed in peace after necessary charity has been supplied to them in the guesthouse, or, if they are men for whom it is appropriate, in another place appointed for this purpose.

Otherwise, neither they with the brethren nor the brethren with them shall be allowed to join together in the cloister. We utterly condemn women’s entering, much less remaining, in the clerics’ workshops. A house shall therefore be established outside, separated from the brethren’s workshops, where whatever is necessary may be provided to them out of charity. If anything must be said to them by the brethren and the prior permits it, several brethren shall approach them together and shall not presume to speak with them alone unless witnesses are present. The inner cloister shall have an entrance on the more suitable side and, if possible, near the church. Beside it a place shall be made where the canons, with the prior’s permission, may canonically speak with visitors or other necessary persons whom they are commanded to receive.

The prior shall appoint a porter to stand by the outer gate, [Col. 0747B] so that no stranger may have leave to enter unless questioned and commanded. He shall entrust the guard of the inner door to one of the brethren, who shall watch it so diligently that no one finds leave to enter or leave except a person required by the prior or by order. Every day, at the evening hour of conference, he shall lock the door and hand the key, as due, [Col. 0747C] to the prior or provost; at the first Hour of the following day he shall receive it back from him, to keep throughout the day.

## CHAPTER XXXII. Concerning the reception of guests and all visitors

When these things have thus been arranged inwardly and outwardly, the superiors of churches must endeavor to prepare a lodging, somewhat separated outwardly from the servants’ workshops, where guests and all visitors may be received honorably and decently, and each may be most faithfully served by the master and custodians of that guesthouse according to his rank and need. To support, according to the capacity of the place, the needs of all visitors, there shall be entrusted to the master of the guesthouse [Col. 0747D] portions of all revenues of all kinds of Church property, of all tithes belonging to food, and of all offerings and alms, [Col. 0748A] to be spent with the utmost faithfulness for the use of the poor and visitors.

The keeper of the guesthouse shall be a man of good testimony, full of charity, discretion, and the virtue of prudence. He shall consider and provide what is suitable for each person in food, drink, washing feet, preparing beds, and supplying other necessities. The diligence of the superiors must be watchful lest he to whom they have entrusted the guesthouse presume to spend for himself or his own household goods that ought to be distributed to the poor, and make himself a participant in Judas’s condemnation—Judas, who, having the purse, secretly diverted to his own uses what was put into it. He himself, together with others appointed under him to receive the poor, shall receive his own expenses from the common stock according to the measure of the rest, lest, if he supplies his own needs [Col. 0748B] and those of his servants from goods to be distributed, he be unable to assist the needs of the poor and visitors.

If he neglects their care or unlawfully handles the goods to be dispensed, he shall be judged much more severely than other offenders by the prior and removed from this office; another shall be appointed in his place who may discharge it holily, perfectly, according to God, and according to the prior’s command.

## CHAPTER XXXIII. That in the absence of the prior and provost, subordinate provosts ought to take their place

The discipline and observance of these chapters and of the entire order, together with the arrangement of all things within and without, shall be carried out by the chief superiors of the Church. But in their absence, the subordinate provosts must take their place and have care of all interior and exterior matters.

## CHAPTER XXXIV. That by these things one may rise to the observance of greater precepts and receive the joys of everlasting life.

These are the matters, dearest brothers, which, as you requested and ordained, we have set down, with Christ’s help, for your holy community to observe. If you uphold them continually with simplicity, purity, and gladness of heart, you will be able more readily to ascend to the higher works of holiness and to become co-heirs with Christ and sharers in eternal life. Yet in these matters and in all matters whatsoever, the prior shall have authority, according as he perceives before God what is expedient in soul or body, beneficial or harmful, for one or for all, to grant or command, [Col. 0748D] to take away, and to say or establish whatever is necessary.

**IN THE YEAR OF THE LORD 1119: GREGORY, ROMAN PRIEST**

[Col. 0747]

## HISTORICAL AND LITERARY NOTICE

(Ballerini, *On Ancient Canonical Codices*, part IV, chapter 17)

[Col. 0747D] The collection customarily cited under the title of Polycarp became known after the Roman correctors of Gratian praised it in their preface and notes. It is contained in Vatican manuscript 1554. Its author is known from the dedicatory letter to be Gregory, a priest, who entitled it with the name of Polycarp. Oudinus (*On Ecclesiastical Writers*, vol. II, col. 764) thought the author was that celebrated Gregory who later became cardinal-bishop of Sabina of the holy Roman Church. He is mistaken. For that cardinal flourished under Pope Gregory VII and died under Urban II. But the author of the collection, since in book III, title 9, he praises a decree of Calixtus II, who began his pontificate in 1119, is distinct from the aforesaid Gregory of Sabina. That this priest was Roman is inferred not so much from the heading of the Colbert manuscript reported by Oudinus, as from the documents which we sometimes find fuller or more complete in him than in Anselm and Deusdedit; so much so that he derived them from [Col. 0749B] the Roman archives.

The time may be determined from the dedicatory letter. It is addressed “to D., worthily adorned with the pontifical mitre of the Church of Saint James.” We must ask who this bishop of the Church of Saint James—that is, Compostela—was, whose name begins with the letter D. Two bishops of that church are found at the beginning of the eleventh century, Dalmachius and Didacus. The dedication cannot belong to the former, since he had already died in 1103 or 1104, when Didacus, his successor, received a letter from Paschal II, printed in vol. XII of the Venetian edition of the Councils, col. 987. But Gregory’s collection cannot be placed before 1119, because of the decree of Calixtus II mentioned above. Therefore this dedication [Col. 0749C] belongs only to Didacus, successor of Dalmachius.

Cardinal de Aguirre published two documents (vol. XII of the Venetian edition of the Councils, col. 1402) in which this Didacus is mentioned. One is a privilege of Alfonso, king of Spain, attached to the Council of Palencia of 1129. By it, the king granted to Didacus, by God’s grace archbishop of the see of Compostela, all royal rights belonging to the former archiepiscopal Church of Mérida, because Mérida was then occupied by the Saracens and Calixtus II had transferred the archbishopric of Mérida to the Church of Compostela, in consideration of the merits and reverence of the most blessed apostle James. The other document is the synod of Oviedo, to which Didacus, archbishop of Saint James, is recorded as subscribing. This synod is dated 1115 in published editions. But since the archbishopric of Mérida [Col. 0749D] was transferred to Compostela by Calixtus II—if Alfonso’s privilege is genuine—and Calixtus became pope in 1119, the synod in which Didacus is called archbishop of Saint James, or Compostela, must be said to have been held after 1119. Perhaps the year 1115 was written in error by copyists instead of 1125.

Moreover, from a twelfth-century manuscript we have discovered that two Didaci, I and II, governed the Church of Compostela. A copy of this manuscript is preserved by Count Joseph Garampi, canon of the Basilica of Saint Peter and prefect of the Vatican Archive; he communicated to us the following information about these Didaci. The cited copy contains a description of the Church of Saint James at Compostela. In it, the church is said to have been begun [Col. 0750A] under Bishop Didacus I, a most vigorous knight and nobleman, in the era 1116, that is, in the year of Christ 1078. Further, where a silver panel adorned with relief work is described, the following verses inscribed upon it are quoted, in which Didacus II is praised:

> This panel Didacus, the second bishop of Saint James,  
> Made in the fifth year of his episcopate.  
> Alfonso was king, and Duke Raymond was his son-in-law,  
> When the aforesaid bishop completed the work.

Gregory’s collection belongs to this second Didacus. After he had obtained archiepiscopal rank for Saint James’s sake, he was called archbishop of Saint James in the Council of Oviedo, “bishop of Saint James” in these verses, and, in the dedication of this present collection, “adorned with the pontifical mitre of the Church of Saint James.” [Col. 0750B] Perhaps after acquiring this dignity under Calixtus II, Gregory, the Roman priest, composed the collection at Didacus’s own urging and addressed it to him.

The aforesaid Oudinus cites two Colbert manuscripts, numbered 696 and 4047, and mentions only four books. But the Vatican codex presents the collection as divided into eight books. It divides each book into several titles, which in turn contain many decrees and testimonies. Accordingly, the work is not so slight as many have supposed since Antonio Agustín.

Book I treats of the primacy of the Roman Church and its privileges: 27 titles.

Book II treats of the election and ordination of prelates, [Col. 0750C] the pallium, and the orders of other clerics: 38 titles.

Book III treats of churches, monasteries, tithes, offerings, the celebration of offices, the law of churches and monasteries; the body of Christ and its custody; baptism and the laying on of hands; rites, Holy Scriptures, the celebration of Easter, preaching, customs, fasts, and so forth: 30 titles.

Book IV treats of how God’s law is to be read; the duties of bishops; chorepiscopi, abbots, monks, nuns, deaconesses, widows, and offenses of clerics: 40 titles.

Book V treats of judgments: 8 titles.

Book VI treats of emperors, princes, and the remaining [Col. 0750D] laity; marriages and matrimony, and various offenses; penance and penitents; just mercy; the good of obedience; and the prohibition on Christians rashly exposing themselves to dangers: 23 titles.

Book VII treats of excommunication, the power of binding, the unity of the Church, schism, heretics and schismatics, vengeance, and so forth: 16 titles.

Book VIII treats of the sick, death and purgatory, burial and offerings for the dead, the immortality of the soul, the torments of the wicked, and the reception of the souls of the righteous into heaven before the resurrection of bodies: 10 titles.

Below we print the dedicatory letter from the Vatican manuscript.

[Col. 0751]

## SECOND NOTICE

(Theiner, *Critical Disquisitions*, p. 341)

[Col. 0751A] The Ballerini brothers have elucidated this collection quite carefully [Note: [Col. 0751B] Place cited, part IV, chapter 17, pp. 666–669.]; therefore we refer readers to them, and shall note here only those matters which may demonstrate this work’s relationship with other collections.

The entire collection is distributed into eight books, each of which has several rubrics or titles distinguished by their own headings. Book I contains 27 rubrics; Book II, 38; Book III, 30; Book IV, 40; Book V, 8; Book VI, 23; Book VII, 16; and Book VIII, 10. The titles then embrace now more, now fewer chapters; some enumerate a hundred, and sometimes more. The chapters themselves are distinguished neither by numbers nor by customary summaries, and for the most part lack headings.

[Col. 0751B] Where such headings occur, they generally indicate only the source or author of a chapter, for example: Pope Clement, Pope Innocent, Pope Leo, Origen, Ambrose, Augustine, Jerome, Council of Carthage, Council of Orléans, Council of Toledo, etc. Thus it never appears from which decretal letter of the popes, from which book of the holy Fathers or ecclesiastical writers, or finally from which council or [Col. 0752A] canon a given chapter was taken.

The chapters themselves were drawn chiefly from Anselm of Lucca’s compilation and inserted into the collection in the same manner as into that other collection of which we have recently spoken. [Note: [Col. 0751B] To show how our collector used Anselm of Lucca’s collection, we place here the first hundred chapters of our collection together with the corresponding Anselmian ones: *Polyc.* book I, rubric I, chapters 1, 4–17. *Anselm* I, 7, 52, 56, 67; II, 2; I, 23; II, 39; I, 18; II, 30; I, 69, 58, 19, 63, 37, 61. *Polyc.* I, cited chapter, chapters 22–32. *Anselm* VI, 1, 14, 13, 28, 44; V, 12; I, 27, [Col. 0751C] 29, 34; II, 46; I, 40, 69. *Polyc.* I, cited chapter, chapters 34–55. *Anselm* II, 9, 34, 35, 47, 48, 12, 38, 80, 11, 10, 49, 50, 55, 17, 36. *Polyc.* I, cited chapter, chapters 38–62. *Anselm* [Col. 0752B] XII, 10; II, 16; XII, 9; II, 23; I, 64. *Polyc.* I, cited chapter, chapters 69–87. *Anselm* VI, 101–164; V, 24, 25; II, 73; V, 7, 29; II, 53; I, 26; II, 41, 43, 44; I, 50, 62; II, 36; I, 53. *Polyc.* I, cited chapter, chapters 88–100. *Anselm* II, 4, 12, 15; I, 16, 23, 67; II, 14, 27, 28, 29, 56; I, 5 and 6.]

Besides Anselm’s collection, the author also used the aforementioned collection dedicated to Anselm [Note: [Col. 0752B] In such a book, under the same rubric, the following chapters are borrowed from the collection dedicated to Anselm: *Polyc.* I, cited chapter, chapters 26, 21, 63–66. *Anselm, dedicated collection* I, 49 and 30; III, 219, 220; II, 274, 275.], whose author, as is established, was named Gregory. There are also many chapters in his work whose source we have been wholly unable to discover.

As for the usefulness of the collection, we think it can serve only to correct Gratian’s *Decree* in those matters missing in Anselm’s work and added by our author. We have therefore noted, as carefully as possible, in the index which we prepared concerning the sources of Gratian’s *Decree*, the passages which Gratian borrowed from Gregory. [Col. 0752B] [Note: [Col. 0752C] See Dissertation III.]

Yet this collection will be of little use, since it indicates the sources of individual chapters so variously and generally that nothing certain can be obtained from it either for revising Anselm’s text or for correcting the material Gratian took from Anselm. Moreover, the text of the chapters themselves is defective and everywhere full of errors.

[Col. 0751]

## DEDICATORY LETTER OF GREGORY, PRIEST, TO HIS COLLECTION OF CANONS

[Col. 0751C] To D., worthily adorned with the pontifical mitre of the Church of Saint James: GREGORY, the humblest of priests, greeting. [Note: [Col. 0751D] In the passage cited, Oudinus prints from the Colbert manuscripts which he cites the title absent from the Vatican manuscript, and the beginning of the dedication, as follows: “Prologue of Gregory of the Holy Roman Church upon an extract from the authorities of the Roman pontiffs and other saints. To the beloved Lord D. of the Church of Saint James,” etc.]

Long ago, and often since, you have asked me to undertake a difficult task beyond my powers: namely, to compile in order a book of canons, drawing the more useful material from the decrees of Roman pontiffs, the authorities of other holy Fathers, and diverse authentic councils. [Col. 0751D] Yet you did not choose to require this of me, though I was unknowing, because either your wisdom was inadequate to so much weightier a labor, or because you did not have at your disposal many persons better qualified and wiser who would voluntarily comply with your command. Rather, it was so that, long exercised in this great undertaking, I might become better instructed and readier for other greater [lacuna] [Col. 0752D]; or also that, should the smallness of my ability fail in anything, your wisdom, as teacher and helper, might extend a hand to me.

Although this inquiry demanded a keen intellect and was wholly unsuited to my powers, and although I feared that some might judge it rash, nevertheless, lest I offend so great and distinguished a man by refusal, I consented. Finally, chiefly in reliance on the assurance that your authority, being interposed, would defend me from the bites of detractors, I obeyed your command. For just as in the Church formerly, and daily, business succeeds business in diverse ways, and the proceedings of many causes arise according to the course of events, so I joined together under each title many chapters of authors suited to it, having considered the time involved; and I succinctly brought the volume to an end in a division of eight books. By reason of its composition, and upon authority received from you, I appropriately gave it the name [Col. 0754A] *Polycarp*. I earnestly entreat your diligence to examine the composition; and, on examining it, if you discover that anything is lacking or that anything is present beyond what is fitting, to complete what is fitting and remove what is unfitting with careful consideration. I am confirmed as deserving approval, for your praise and for the increase of obedience to your command, with due moderation. Furthermore, lest an undifferentiated subject confuse the reader throughout the course of the book, I thought it proper to set before it the titles of this work, so that he may gather in their proper places what he knows to have been stated under the appropriate number.

[Col. 0753]

**IN THE YEAR OF THE LORD 1119: THEOBALD OF ÉTAMPES**

[Col. 0759]

## NOTICE

(Archery, *Spicilegium*, vol. III, preface, p. 8)

The letters of Theobald of Étampes which I publish readily refute Pitseus, who, in treating of writers of England, wrongly writes that Theobald lived in the thirteenth century and wore the cardinal’s purple at Rome. For from his letter to Roscelin it is absolutely certain that Theobald flourished in the age of Anselm of Canterbury and Ivo of Chartres. Read Anselm’s letters, book II, 41, and Ivo’s, 7, where Roscelin is accused of heresy. Faricius, abbot of Abingdon—having been desired by the king, after Anselm was enrolled among the heavenly citizens—also indicates that Theobald had been his contemporary. [Note: [Col. 0759] Henry of Knighton, among the *Writers of English History*.] Further, Ciaconius speaks thus hesitantly of his cardinalitial dignity under Nicholas IV: “Theobald of Étampes, an Englishman, concerning whose cardinalate I am doubtful, whatever the author, Pitseus, of the *Catalogue of English Writers* may say.”

[Col. 0759]

## LETTERS OF THEOBALD OF ÉTAMPES

### I. [Col. 0759A] To the Bishop of Lincoln — On certain persons who waver concerning Holy Scripture. (About A.D. 1108.)

If anyone preaches, and in preaching rashly determines that a person cannot be saved at whatever hour he gives his hands to repentance, he is mistaken, as Truth testifies, and does not think as a Catholic. For Truth itself says: “On whatever day the sinner turns, his sins shall not be reckoned against him; rather, he shall live and not die” (Ezek. 18:12, 28).

Hence Augustine, against Faustus: “We unquestionably believe that sins are blotted out by repentance of the heart, even in the last breath of life. But whoever thinks otherwise is not a Christian, but a Novatian.”

Hence Gregory, on Ezekiel: “Repentance is never too late for one who repents, as the prophet declares: ‘At whatever hour the sinner groans, he shall be saved’ (Rom. 10:13). Nor would the thief hanging on the cross have received pardon, unless the good will of a single hour had aided him.”

Hence Jerome, against Jovinian: “For one repenting and groaning from a true heart, should he die immediately, good will shall be reckoned to him as though it had performed works.”

Hence, to Damasus: “Lest repentance seem late to anyone, Christ upon the cross made the punishment for homicide into martyrdom.”

Hilary agrees with this, saying: “Repentance changes one’s conduct, and crimes of long duration perish in the blink of an eye, if good compunction of heart has arisen.” Compunction is humility of heart accompanied by remembrance of sins and tears.

Hence Gregory, in the *Moralia*: “Every clamor of a perverse deed is silenced by the force of good compunction. For if the heart truly grieves, vices fall silent against us and vanish like smoke from a mind worn down by the tribulation of sorrow. This is the spirit which shatters the ships of Tarshish: that is, the force of compunction, which beneficially afflicts with the groaning of tribulation minds given over to the sea, that is, the world.”

Hence Ambrose: “True repentance for sin is to cease from that which you have understood must be repented of.”

Hence Pope Calixtus: “In repentance, the length of time or oral confession has only as much force as true [Col. 0760B] compunction of heart. For if anyone confesses with the mouth but does not believe with the heart, he is counted among those of whom it is written: ‘This people honors me with their lips, but their heart is far from me’” (Matt. 15:8).

Hence Pope Alexander: “Nothing so wins God’s mercy as the heart of one who repents.”

Hence the venerable priest [Note: [Col. 0759B] That is, St Jerome.]: “In Christians, the beginning is not sought, but the end; for each person shall be judged by his end.” For whoever has a good end is himself also good.

Let us also hear what God himself answered the woman caught in adultery: “Go; sin no more” (John 8:11). But Peter, having gone out, wept most bitterly over the fault of his threefold denial, and immediately deserved to receive pardon from the Lord himself. Pope Gregory follows him, saying: “Let us baptize our conscience with most bitter tears, because after baptism we have defiled life by the magnitude of our sins.”

Yet let no one despair because of the magnitude of sins, saying: “My sins are many, in which I persevered even into old age, and now I can no longer merit forgiveness—especially because they left me, not I them.” Far be it that such a person should despair of God’s mercy. For God’s great and ineffable compassion does not wish to set bounds for anyone at any time. Whoever is burdened by an excessive weight of sins, if he turns to the Lord while burdened, is immediately relieved of that excessive weight of sins. For God more approves, at life’s end, purity of mind than a long purity of heart in one who falls away from the good at the end.

For example: through his former deeds the thief deserved hell; but, crowned by purity of mind, he entered paradise. Yet a certain hermit, leading an angelic life, deserved paradise, but having fallen once into sin, went down condemned to hell. Further, as the holy Gospel testifies, the householder hires laborers at the eleventh hour and deigns to pay an equal reward of life. It is therefore clear that repentance does not consist in a number of days or in a long period of affliction, but in bitterness of heart.

For whoever believes in Christ, even if he remains in many sins, lives eternally by his faith, as he himself says in the Gospel: “I am the resurrection and the life; whoever believes in me, even if he has died, shall live” (John 11:25). And elsewhere: “I am the way, the truth, and the life” (John 14:6): the way without error for those seeking; the truth without falsehood for those finding; the life without death for those remaining.

What the Apostle says—“With the heart one believes unto righteousness, but with the mouth confession is made unto salvation” (Rom. 10:10)—is true, because confession is necessary for penitents. What we believe concerning Christ, we ought not to be ashamed of, but must confess before all. And if anyone is killed for confession of the faith, although he is hindered by certain faults, he is nevertheless cleansed in that killing so that he is immediately received into eternal glory. This is what is meant by “with the mouth confession is made unto salvation.”

But whereas confession of the mouth is made to one’s neighbor and confession of the heart to God, if oral confession is prevented by some circumstance, confession of the heart is not thereby rejected as fruitless. Augustine, discussing the Sodomites drowned in the lake, says that some of them were saved through good compunction and true groaning of heart, because not only superfluous thoughts but even wicked deeds flee before the force of compunction.

If anyone, however, obstinately asserts that no one can be saved unless he is able to confess with his mouth, he does not rightly distinguish confession, nor has he understood its different forms. One confession is of the heart, another of the mouth, and another is made in both ways. It is indeed good and praiseworthy to confess with heart and [Col. 0762A] mouth, as the Apostle James bears witness when he says: “Confess your sins to one another” (James 5:16), etc. By this authority, as some think, we are not harmed; for it is rightly understood only of those who are able but unwilling to confess. For if anyone, through some infirmity, or even from birth itself, is rendered unable to confess with his mouth, yet has a good and discerning will to make oral confession, then, if he confesses in his heart, he is by the judgment of discerning persons in no way judged excluded from salvation. Hence the Prophet: “The Lord has heard the desire of the poor” (Ps. 10:17), that is, of the humble, who confess not themselves but the grace of God. “Your ear has heard the petition of their heart” (ibid.). And elsewhere: “A contrite spirit is a sacrifice to God; a contrite and humbled heart” (Ps. 50:18). Hence Solomon: “With all vigilance guard your heart, for from it life proceeds” (Prov. 4:23).

That a person can speak or confess in the heart God Himself plainly showed when He answered the silent Moses: “Why do you cry out?” (Exod. 14:15). For he was silent as regards the sound of his voice, but spoke through the devotion of his heart. Therefore, if someone loved God with all his heart, all his soul, and all his mind, but could not express the affection of so great a love with his lips, who would be so presumptuous as to dare judge him excluded from God’s mercy? For when the countenance of the inward person is renewed, cleansed of every vice through true contrition, and, once renewed, obtains purity of heart through genuine groaning, even if he has lost his voice, he is nevertheless not separated from Him who says: “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” [Col. 0762C] (Matt. 5:8): seeing, they will love; loving, they will praise.

For, as Augustine says: “This will be the occupation of those standing before the divine majesty: namely, to see, to love, and to praise. For we shall see and love; we shall love and praise. Yet this praise will not be made with a sounding word, but there the voice itself will be love.” For one who murmurs within himself while reckoning God’s benefits and the evils he himself has returned, and groans in his heart as he reproaches himself for his sins, speaks better without a voice than if he spoke with a voice without these things. For if we ask for eternal life with our mouth but do not desire it in our heart, we cry aloud while remaining silent.
