But if we desire it from the heart, even though we are silent with our mouths, we cry aloud while silent. Hence Jerome: “Whatever you will but cannot do, God counts as done.” For just as deliberation accompanied by the undertaking of vices is condemned, so also good will, when the opportunity to act is lacking, is rewarded; because a person is accused or defended not according to what he could not do or was not permitted to do, but according to what he was and purposed in his conscience, when God judges the hidden things of human beings.

Therefore let no one despair who repents in heart at the end, because there is no place for the devil except through our own desire. Hence Ambrose, in the tenth book on Luke: “Peter was grieved and wept, because he erred as a man. I find that he wept; I do not find what he said. I read his tears; I do not read his satisfaction. For tears confess; tears speak guilt without a voice; tears ask pardon, and merit is found. Peter was silent, and [Col. 0763A] Peter’s good weeping washed away his sin.”

But what Augustine says—“Unless someone confesses a long time before death, he shall not be purified by purgatorial fire, but shall be condemned to eternal punishment”—does no harm to one who understands it rightly. For by “a long time” he means all the time sufficient for amendment. Whoever confesses in time sufficient for amendment confesses a long time before death. Hence Pope Celestine: “The true confession to God of people placed at the extremity of life is to be assessed more by the mind than by time.” Likewise, in the decrees of the pontiffs one reads: “If anyone cannot confess with his mouth, let him make outward signs; and afterwards the most sacred Body is to be entrusted to him, nor is he to be despaired of.” Therefore it does not follow from the decrees [Col. 0763B] of the pontiffs that, if one cannot confess with the mouth, one cannot be saved. For, as authority declares: “God judges not deeds, but the will.” Nothing is happier than a good will, because nothing is more precious to God than a good will.

Hence Cyprian: “Although many things are commanded in the Law which the Apostle testifies cannot be fulfilled, here the good will is sought, which lies within our power, which alone can suffice and take first place.” Hence again authority says: “The hand is never empty of a gift whenever the treasury of the heart has been filled with good will.” Further, as the aforesaid Augustine testifies in the book of the *Confessions*: “No one does good without a good will, even if in human judgment he seems to act well.”

For just as evil will, which is the first [Col. 0763C] death of the soul, is said to condemn—for no evil work exists without evil will, Augustine bearing witness and saying, “Sin is voluntary; where there is no will, sin is not imputed”—so good will saves and crowns the saved forever. In commendation of this good will the angel said to the shepherds: “Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to human beings”—not to others, but “of good will” (Luke 2:14). It is therefore clear that whoever has good will on earth will without doubt obtain peace and glory in heaven. Amen.

But if anyone wishes to disapprove this letter and refuses to accept these aforesaid Catholic doctors, let him be struck with a stone; when struck, let him be shattered; when shattered, let him be reduced to dust.

## II. [Col. 0763D] To Pharitium [or Faricium], Abbot of Abingdon

—Children not regenerated by the sacrament of baptism cannot attain eternal blessedness.

To PHARITIUS, venerable prelate of the Church of Abingdon, his lord and unquestionably his friend, THEOBALD, master of Oxford: may you so exercise care for your subjects that it may not be said, “There is death in the pot.”

I greatly wonder that, while I was proclaiming the uprightness of your character and the unfeigned affection of your sons, you imposed upon me, the day before yesterday, a calumnious charge concerning the salvation of unbaptized children—so abruptly, and indeed with the finger of discernment set aside, as many say. Previously, as a discerning man, you ought to have been an investigator before becoming, if I may say so with reverence to you, an accuser in a fabricated allegation; especially since the whole Church so defines their perdition that it leaves no one who thinks Catholicly in doubt. For all who think Catholicly assert without hesitation—and in asserting do not rashly determine—that at this time no one can become a member of Christ unless regenerated from visible water and invisible Spirit, or, as could occur at another time, purified by some other kind of baptism.

Hence those who, while persecution rages, are baptized in their own blood for Christ’s sake are reckoned by blessed Cyprian among the martyrs. Hence Augustine, writing to Victor in *On the Nature and Origin of the Soul*, says: “Do not say, do not believe, do not teach [Col. 0764B] that the sacrifice of Christians ought to be offered for those who departed the body unbaptized, just as we read that the sacrifice of the Jews was in no way offered for those who departed the body uncircumcised.” Hence Jerome, against Jovinian: “If children die immediately after baptism, they are said to be saved through the sacrament of repentance and faith.” For the sacrament of repentance is indicated where it is said, “I renounce”; but the sacrament of faith is implied where the response is made, “I believe.”

It is therefore plain that the consequence is that children unbaptized at this time are without doubt damned; but baptized children, if they immediately put off the human body, are without doubt saved. If some enemy of truth wished to bark against this Catholic judgment, I would be prepared to refute him in writing and orally as sacrilegious and [Col. 0764C] a wicked dog.

As to the origin of these opinions, I answer you only this: I rejoice far more in imitating the unerring footsteps of earlier watchful doctors than in following the false opinions and dreams of modern sleepers. What the ancient doctors could scarcely reach by watchfulness, younger men now presume to teach while sleeping. Those doctors are called watchful who soundly report what they have heard reasonably from the holy Fathers. But sleeping doctors are called those who continually labour to introduce some novelty of their own. Hence Hilary of Poitiers says in the book he composed on the Trinity: “The best reader is indeed one who reports.” Know, therefore, [Col. 0764D] that I belong not among those who introduce things, but among those who report them; and, so long as life is my companion, I shall persevere diligently in this.

Do not judge this defense to be an attack. It ought not to be judged an attack, but rather a reasonable defense, made with good zeal. For I do not wish to make an enemy of one whom your good moral character lately brought forth as my friend; nor is that proverb applicable to me or to you: “He who wishes to withdraw from a friend seeks occasions” (Prov. 18:1). Farewell. Greet your venerable community in my stead, and especially your good prior, our intimate friend.

## III. [Col. 0765A] To Queen Margaret

—He offers himself and his services to the queen.

To MARGARET, most eminent queen, daughter of a most eminent king, THEOBALD of Étampes, teacher at Caen, wishes that she may, as is customary, frequently recite that song of the faithful soul before the face of the heavenly Bridegroom: “Direct my steps according to your word, that no injustice may have dominion over me.”

First, I wish your affection to know that our inward person rejoices beyond measure with the outward; and in rejoicing does not hesitate to give immense thanks to God, because the fame of your uprightness, munificence, and generosity is spread not only through places near you, but is extended almost [Col. 0765B] throughout the whole world, and in being extended is demonstrably advanced daily, as though from step to step. For munificence in a most generous soul is a precious stone set in purified gold. Just as that beautiful kind of spices which has a fragrance more precious than others draws those present to itself by its scent, so your generosity, breathing forth its good fragrance more widely, sprinkles even those absent and, in sprinkling them, does not cease to draw them to you.

Therefore, if the instability of the sea did not prevent me, and my appearance before you did not generate distaste, I would gladly present myself to your sight—which I have always desired—because I cannot at all restrain my mind, tormented by hunger for the sight of you. Yet even if the sea’s instability became constant, and a languid breeze did not impede my journey by its slowness, [Col. 0765C] I would still rather, shipwrecked, be satisfied by the presence of your sight than return to my own country fasting from it, though free from every adversity.

That in writing I have sampled only very little of your praise should by no means be attributed to dullness or rusticity. For if all my limbs were changed into tongues, all that is worthy of praise in you could still not sufficiently be set forth through them. Therefore, with every manner of supplication, I entreat you to permit me to glory in this: that henceforth I may be counted among the number of your clerics. May the Angel of great counsel and might be with you, so that you may think rightly and never cease to do what is right.

## IV. [Col. 0765D] To Philip, a Friend

—He consoles a friend assailed by injuries.

THEOBALD, master at Caen, to PHILIP, his beloved friend: may you be delivered from the snare of hunters and from the harsh word.

You lament the reproaches and unjust calumnies of those who judge wrongly and do not sufficiently consider, with provident reason, the things that are God’s, which you endure. Against the mad or beastlike barking of such men, let examples come to your aid from prophetic, evangelical, and apostolic writings, by which they may be taught to descend into themselves and not gnaw at the deeds of others with a rash tooth. It will suffice to answer them only with what Tully Cicero testifies: “He who possesses wealth easily despises it; he who does not possess it finds it difficult to regard it as cheap.” [Col. 0766A] Hence Seneca: “The full belly,” he says, “easily disputes about fasts.” For anyone easily disputes about what he does not know.

Likewise, since they are stained with every foulness, they can readily discuss abstinence, though until now they have eagerly laboured to serve the pleasures of the flesh. What they are not, they wish and strive to appear; in this they differ greatly from a certain wise man who among other things says: “I would rather appear infamous in the sight of men, sinning more lightly before them and openly, than appear righteous to men while sinning more grievously before God and in secret.” Hence Jerome, on Isaiah, book six: “It is a lighter evil to sin openly than to counterfeit and feign holiness.”

There are, nevertheless, some who do not dare sin for fear of human beings, though they retain sin within; when an opportunity is found, they do not become evil but reveal what they were. A wolf and a lion desire alike, but they do not harm alike; their desire is equal, but the former fears a dog and the latter does not. There are also some who, soaked day and night in much wine and diligently concerned with the grooming of their skin, reject and detest intercourse with women because they protest that a chaste life pleases them, unaware that a chaste life is called moderation, and failing to heed Jerome’s statement that it is a foul and execrable crime for a he-goat to desire a kid when no she-goat is lacking to him.

For thus Solomon’s page testifies: that evil is good and praiseworthy which drives out what is worst and abominable. Augustine agrees, saying: “It is better to fall upon a bed than upon a sword.” Therefore the world does not judge what is true [Col. 0766C], but looks only to reputation and gives no consideration whatever to a good conscience. Though it ought rather to accuse the fault of its own work than the weakness of an infirm brother, it neglects to examine its own powers and does not call to mind that it is enslaved to vices; and though it lies lower, it despises others as if looking down from on high.

For many, while detesting and censuring lust, cloak avarice under the name of abstinence lest it be seen; they do not consider Solomon’s saying that nothing is more wicked than the miser. Thus they defile themselves more grievously in the pleasure of avarice than in lust. What shall be said of pride, envy, and the other vices? Who is so holy that he is not joined in friendship with one of these? If the lustful person is not bound in their embraces, then the avaricious, envious, abusive person, and very many others are held fast. For “pride is the beginning of every sin” (Ecclus. 10:15), and, like a general pestilential disease, it corrupts the body. Even when it shows itself to be a virtue, it seeks thereby to please not God but vain glory alone.

These and many other vices display in themselves an appearance of uprightness, but arise from the weakness of perversity; and they cloak themselves with such skill that before the eyes of the deceived mind they represent faults as virtues. Thus, from that for which each person expects rewards, he deserves to find punishments. For when he sees a fault as though it were a virtue, he abandons it more slowly in proportion as he is not ashamed of what he commits.

Moreover, God often does not preserve His own people from bodily vices, just as He did not will to preserve David [Col. 0767A]. For many fall into pride through the gift of chastity or some other virtue, and do not recognize that they have fallen. But God allows them openly to fall into lust, which is sometimes less serious than to sin deliberately in silent thought. Since pride is believed less shameful, it is less avoided. But because they are more ashamed of lust, knowing that everyone recognizes it as shameful, they also correct this evil more quickly; they recognize themselves as humble and more worthless among others, and overthrow, by the virtue of humility, the fault of exaltation in which they had previously swelled. Those who had exalted themselves because of virtue return to humility through vice.

Those puffed up by chastity would not be corrected unless they were tempted; nor would they be holy if they were proud of the gift of chastity. Thus, in a wondrous way, while they are tempted they are humbled, and they cease to belong to him whose servants they had been through pride. I do not praise lust, but among vices I rank pride above it. For in lust there is something which we are commanded to bear; in pride there is nothing by which we may be excused. The Apostle permits each person to have his own wife on account of fornication. Blessed Jerome also says that it belongs to an angelic, not a human, nature to live in the flesh beyond the flesh. But “God resists the proud and gives grace to the humble” (James 4:6). We ought therefore to consider that, if we are not equal to others in lust, perhaps we are equal in pride, so that we may look upon them with a heart as humble as that with which we find ourselves among them.

## V. [Col. 0767C] To Roscelin, Cleric of Compiègne

[Note: [Col. 0767D] St Anselm notes Roscelin’s errors, book II, letter 41; and Ivo of Chartres, letter 7.]

—He severely rebukes Roscelin, who maintained that the sons of priests ought not to be admitted to holy orders.

To ROSCELIN, master of Compiègne, THEOBALD of Étampes, master of Oxford: do not think more highly than you ought to think, but think soberly.

Because you calumniate, with reasoning insufficiently provident, the sons of priests and others begotten through a lapse of the flesh, and in calumniating them most shamelessly endeavour to maintain that they are *exleges*, outside the law, we have taken care to recall what we have reasonably heard on these matters from the holy Fathers—not from presumption, but in service of diligence. For, reading in the decrees of Pope Calixtus, we found, and having found, we read: “If anyone teaches that a priest, after a lapse of the flesh, cannot by penance return [Col. 0767D] to sacerdotal dignity, he is mistaken and does not think Catholicly.” But if priests after a lapse of the flesh may return to holy orders, much more may those innocent persons who were born from a lapse of the flesh be distinguished with holy orders.

He errs, he errs, and sharpens and arms an impudent mouth for blasphemy, who calls and judges as *exleges* those whom grace has freed from the slavery of the law into the liberty of the glory of the children of God; for one is not unhappily born who has happily been reborn to eternal life. Hence Paul says concerning the reborn: “We are one body in Christ” (1 Cor. 10:17). And elsewhere: “Heirs indeed of God, and co-heirs of Christ” (Rom. 8:17). Peter likewise says: “In truth I have learned [Col. 0768A] that God is no respecter of persons; but in every nation the one who fears God and does his justice is accepted by him” (Acts 10:34). And elsewhere, concerning the reborn: “An elect race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people for acquisition” (1 Pet. 2:9).

Hence Jerome: “When any baptized person rises from the font, he is anointed on the crown of the head with sacred chrism, that he may know himself to have been advanced to a royal and priestly race: that is, that he may be called Christian from partnership with Christ and be shown to become co-heir of the eternal kingdom. After the sacred anointing his head is also covered with a sacred veil, that he may understand that he is adorned with the diadem of a kingdom and, as has been said, with priestly dignity.” And elsewhere: “All of you who have been baptized have put on Christ” (Gal. 3:27).

Thus, whatever his lineage, this new person is conceived in the womb of the Church; once begotten, he is without doubt joined to the unity of Christ’s body. John too, in the Apocalypse: “He who washed us in his blood and made us a kingdom and priests to God” (Rev. 1:5). With what face, then, do certain petty men, speaking not openly but from hiding places, and polluting the whole of Champagne by their lustful wandering, judge unworthy of the priesthood those whom Peter and John affirm worthy of a royal priesthood? Christ likewise, teaching his disciples to pray in the Gospel, says first: “Our Father.” Hence it is evident that all the reborn are brothers. And elsewhere: “Call no one your Father upon earth, for one is your Father, who is in heaven” (Matt. 23:9).

If, therefore, we all are from the same Father and from the same womb of the holy mother Church [Col. 0768C], there is nothing by which one may bring a calumny against another; therefore one ought not be proud against another. And elsewhere the Lord says: “As I live, this proverb shall no longer remain in Israel: ‘The son shall not bear the iniquity of the father.’ For as the soul of the father, so the soul of the son is mine” (Ezek. 18:4, 19). Therefore God willed to be born from the lineage of a sinful woman, so that human beings might learn that the sins of their parents do not harm them. Hence in Christ’s genealogy no holy women are named, but Tamar and three others whom the divine page censures are added, so that he who came for sinners might deign to be born from sinful women. Hence the lamb to be sacrificed at Passover was commanded to be taken from goats and sheep, because the true Lamb was to be begotten from the righteous and sinners [Col. 0768D]. Thus it benefits more to have lived well than to have drawn one’s origin from righteous parents. For God attends to a person’s life, not to his birth.

But as to what they themselves object—that *exleges* are not lawfully to be placed over the Church—the proposition is indeed good and certain, but inappropriately applied. For they apply it to those reborn persons whom mother Church has received into the court of Christ, nourished with her own milk once received, and strengthened with her own bread once nourished. In this they plainly oppose Jerome, who says: “Far be it, Lord, that in your tabernacle the rich should be preferred to the poor, and the noble to the ignoble.” Hence Basil, against a certain Jew boasting of the law given to him: “True charity in Christ’s body does not prefer the native to the foreigner, the noble to the ignoble, or the poor to the rich; but rather through adoption by the Spirit it makes all children, crying through the same Spirit: ‘Our Father, forgive us our debts.’” Likewise, in Christ’s body he alone is regarded as higher who is stronger in the love of God. Hence a certain wise man speaks against one who presumes upon his nobility, saying: “If you trace far back and turn things over far back, you derive your name from an infamous asylum.”

Again, what do they object? That when a person is baptized, his condition is not changed but his sins are washed away. This is true; but no one doubts that it is said of worldly conditions: if a slave is baptized, that slavery is not changed. Hence the Apostle: “If you are a slave, make use of it rather” (1 Cor. 7:21), because that slavery is not contrary to the crown. Hence elsewhere:

> Be a slave: you will be noble if your mind becomes good;  
> Be free: if your mind is base, you will be a slave.

Further: the prohibition against advancing priests’ sons to orders is to be understood thus according to Augustine: those who hear this prohibition ought to abstain from desires of that kind. For if a priest’s son lives honourably, he ought to be ordained. But if a soldier’s son lives dishonourably, he ought to be rejected; for perfection of life and affliction against sin please God more than proud boasting about legitimate parents. The sons of priests are rejected not because they are *exleges*, as unlearned people suppose, but so that priests may be restrained from the desires of the flesh.

For either divine grace wholly cleanses anyone reborn from the sacred font, or the cleansing of the sacred washing is not sufficient and complete—which contradicts the Catholic faith. Those of whom God Himself is Father, and whom Christ’s grace has begotten—the most loving mother of all the regenerate—must not be judged *exleges*. Nor should we reproach them with their father’s fault or their mother’s bed; instead, we should diligently attend to the perfection of their conduct, since a crime committed by father or mother cannot shut against children [Col. 0769D] the threshold of paradise. Hence a certain wise man: “What have those born from whatever bed deserved to suffer?”

That the sons of priests are rejected from orders [Col. 0770A] has been done out of the rigour of justice, but is in no way just, as Augustine testifies: those who have not committed the fault do not bear punishment justly. Thus those heralds of novelty, laying down new precepts and in some manner nullifying the power of baptism, who bark against the foregoing arguments while disputing fastidiously and contentiously about such matters, beat against a wall as though the door were shut.

But that greater honour and glory may accrue to priests’ sons: John the Baptist, than whom no greater has arisen among those born of women, was the son of Zechariah the priest. Mary also, the mother of the Lord, descended from priestly stock, since she is called the kinswoman of Elizabeth, who drew her origin from Aaron. If I wished to enumerate all who proceeded from a lapse of the flesh and held primacy [Col. 0770B] in the holy Church, life would fail before the examples did.

Jacob likewise made all whom he begot from free women and slave women his sons and heirs with equal honour; nor was the one who appeared nobler according to the flesh preferred by him. Whoever attains the faith of the Lord is obscured by no stains of carnal birth. Jacob is read to have done this in order to show that there is no distinction whether one is Jew or Greek, barbarian or Scythian, slave or free, because Christ is all and in all things. For this reason our Saviour and Lord put on human form and served for free and slave alike, so that he might bestow heavenly rewards with equal honour and glory upon all who believe in him.

Solomon also, who ruled, taught, and prophesied happily, wisely, and subtly, though born through a lapse of the flesh, was nevertheless permitted by God to build His temple—a task which He prohibited David, his father, the legitimate son of Jesse, from undertaking. In this God plainly indicates to us that He approves holiness of life and uprightness of character more than the nobility of legitimate birth. Therefore let not the rich and noble flatter themselves, nor the poor and humble lose confidence, because “the Lord on high regards the lowly, and knows the lofty from afar” (Ps. 137:6): he regards the humble in order to raise them up, and knows the lofty—that is, the proud—from afar in order to cast them down.

For, as the Apostle says: “No one shall be crowned unless he has contended lawfully” (2 Tim. 2:5). When he says “no one,” none is excluded; in this the proud folly of this world is refuted, which calls *exlex* and judges on earth the one whom God places at His right hand and crowns in heaven [Col. 0770D].

**IN THE YEAR OF THE LORD 1119: THEOGERUS, BISHOP OF METZ**

[Col. 0769]

**NOTICE**

(*Gallia Christiana nova*, vol. XIII, col. 738)

[Col. 0769D] Theotger, brother of Count Folcmar of Metz, had been of noble birth in the world. While still a youth, Gerung, a regular canon of Marbach, had once sent him to Abbot William of Hirsau under the pretext that he was to receive penance from him. Having become a monk, he learned both human and divine letters so thoroughly that, together with another monk equally learned, named Herinon, he undertook at his abbot’s command the task of correcting throughout both the New and Old Testaments whatever had been corrupted through scribal error. When promoted to the priesthood, he exercised that office with such reverence that, when he placed the stole around his neck, he almost fainted from excessive fear. Appointed by his abbot William as abbot of the monastery of St George in the Hercynian Forest, and ordained by Gebhard, bishop of Constance, in the year 1090, he set his hand to building a church and cloister.

Accustomed to anticipate the night offices, he scarcely allowed any sleep to his body; so severe was he upon himself that he often burdened the brethren also with very harsh obligations. But at length, after falling from a horse and becoming ill, he learned to sympathize with and show mercy to others. Having suffered much at the hands of the neighboring inhabitants, he eventually bent them by patience and gentleness, so that many submitted themselves in the monastery to his discipline. This most devout abbot took charge not only of men but also of women, to such a degree that seven hundred persons of both sexes entrusted themselves to his instruction; for their benefit he established various monasteries.

For many years the church of Metz had been in a pitiable condition. At that time there was a man of great religious devotion, named Alberius or Albero, who held the office of archdeacon, and later became archbishop of Trier and legate of the Apostolic See. [Col. 0771C] Encouraged by the counsel and letters of religious men, he resolved to bring help to the distressed church of Metz. He therefore went to Rome and laid before Pope Paschal II the wretched state of that church. Moved by this, the pontiff, with the counsel of the cardinals, sent into Gaul Cuno, cardinal bishop of Palestrina, from his own side; and ordered him, after gathering the Catholic bishops together, diligently to arrange how the condition of that church might be restored and, once the pseudo-bishop had been removed, a worthy pastor placed over it.

Cuno convened a synod of bishops at Rheims, and from there sent Alberius to the people of Metz with letters, directing him to see that another should be substituted in the place of the man who had been deposed by judicial sentence both by the pope and by himself. But the people of Metz faced no small difficulty in electing a bishop: first, because according to the decrees of the canons an election could not be held beyond the bounds of the diocese; and second, because within those bounds, owing to fear of the opposing party, the election itself could by no means safely be conducted. At last they assembled at a very deserted place situated almost at the extreme edge of the diocese. There Alberius opened Cuno’s letters, which he had brought from Rheims. By the pope’s authority and command, and at the request of Guy, archbishop of Vienne, these prescribed that an election should be made.

When the votes of the electors were inclining toward different opinions, Alberius proposed Theotger, the most devout abbot of St George in the Hercynian Forest. All agreed to this proposal; but they judged that the affair must be conducted secretly and skillfully, lest either the violence of the king and princes, or of the intruder himself, should render the election void, or the elected man should take flight. It was therefore unanimously decided to send envoys to him with letters—namely, the abbot of St Clement and the prior of Marmoutier—to bring the elect to the presence of Cardinal Cuno.

At that time Theotger was staying in a convent of virgins entrusted to his care. There he received the envoys most graciously, and soon, obedient to their commands, accompanied them to a cell called Hugh’s Court. There, when a certain brother disclosed to him that he had been elected, he firmly declared that he would never consent to it and would proceed no further. He sent one of his most faithful followers, named Erbo, with letters to excuse him before the legate. In these he stated that he was not merely unequal in merit to so great a dignity, but was also marked by the disgrace of his birth: his parents, and all his forebears through a long succession of ancestors, had been either priests or sons of priests.

When Erbo came to the electors of Metz and explained to them the grounds on which his master refused the bishopric, they nevertheless persisted in their decision. They said that, if there had been any defect in Theotger’s origin, it had already been purged by him, since he had lived most devoutly for so many years in a monastery. They therefore asked Erbo to return to Theotger. But he, bound by his abbot’s command, refused and declared that he wished to go to the legate. Since he would not abandon his purpose, Alberius, the principal agent in the entire matter, was given him as companion by the people of Metz. The two arrived at the very famous castle of Compiègne, [Col. 0772C] where the legate was then staying. Erbo presented the legate with his abbot’s letters of excuse and set forth his arguments, which Alberius refuted.

The legate, not at all moved by Theotger’s letters, sternly commanded him by letter to undertake the burden of the bishopric. But since Theotger did not obey even the warnings and orders of the cardinal legate, he sent him further letters through Antony, abbot of the monastery of Sens, compelling him under threat of ecclesiastical penalties to accept the bishopric; and he commanded his brethren, under the same penalties, to give their consent. Yet another ground for refusing the bishopric then arose from bodily illness, which detained him. It could not, however, prevent the cardinal’s letters from being read in the assembly of the brethren. When they had been read, all consented to his election.

In the year 1118, during Rogation Days, Cardinal Cuno held an assembly of bishops at Cologne. Alberius, or Albero, the primicerius, went there to await the arrival of his elect, whom he had heard was coming. When Erbo arrived there, having come to excuse his abbot, he found at the council Conrad, archbishop of Salzburg, recently driven into exile by the emperor; and obtained from him permission to undertake his abbot’s case before the fathers. But when the election to the church of Metz began to be debated in the council, the primicerius defended it with such force of speech that neither Alard nor the archbishop could bend the mind of Cardinal Cuno. [Col. 0773A] Indeed, the primicerius’s outcry prevailed so strongly that Theotger’s election was confirmed by the unanimous judgment of the fathers.

Then at last the cardinal gave Erbo sealed letters. Erbo entrusted them to an illiterate brother to carry to Theotger; in the name of the assembly they commanded him no longer vainly to frustrate the election offered to him. Having received the letters, Theotger was finally compelled to yield to so great an authority. He hastened to present himself before the legate, as he had been commanded. The legate was then staying at Koblenz with Frederick, archbishop of Cologne, and other bishops. There the man of God was received with great honor, especially by the legate, who embraced him and asked how many years he had held the office of abbot.

“Thirty years,” he replied.

At this the legate smiled and, turning to those present, said: “He will be all the more mature for the episcopate, since he has been an abbot for so many years.”

When each then returned to his own affairs, the legate went back to Cologne, taking Theotger with him. From there Theotger turned aside first to the nearby monastery of Deutz, then to Gladbach, where he was detained for some time by a serious illness. After recovering, he returned to Cologne and went with the legate to the castle of Wulckenburg, then to the monastery of St Vitus, or New Corbie, where he was consecrated bishop. It was the octave day of the feast of the apostles Peter and Paul, celebrated on the day before the Nones of July, that is, 6 July. The Sunday assigned for Theotger’s consecration fell that year on the following day. On that day the cardinal legate solemnly ordained Theotger—advanced in age, mature in character, and exceptionally learned—supported on either side by two archbishops: Conrad of Salzburg, metropolitan of all Bavaria, and Aldegot of Magdeburg, metropolitan of Saxony.

Thus ordained, he first consecrated in that same monastery a certain basilica in honor of St George, so that he might dedicate the first fruits of his episcopate to the same saint whom he had had as his special patron in his abbacy. There also he consecrated the crypt and altar of the blessed apostle Andrew. Not long afterwards the new bishop left, intending to go to his own church, and, guided by the aforesaid primicerius, came to a place in the diocese of Toul called Dieulouard. Abbots, clerics, and others of the sounder party gathered there to honor him. But those who adhered to the pseudo-bishop and to Caesar declared that they would never permit him to enter the city. They went so far in insolence as to decree jointly that whoever recognized him as bishop should have his goods confiscated and be expelled from the city. It was therefore decided that, after dismissing all those attending him, he should return to his cell until that sedition had cooled.

On the journey he turned aside to the monastery of regular canons at Marbach in Alsace, where he was received with the greatest honor by the regular canons. Gerung, the venerable old man who had sent him as a youth to the venerable Abbot William of Hirsau under the pretext of penance, happened to be present in that community. Then, having rendered thanks to his hosts, [Col. 0774A] he returned to the monastery of St George, the brethren pouring out to meet him with solemn pomp. While staying there, he dedicated certain churches situated on the monastery’s estate, with the permission of the bishop of Constance. That all these things happened in the same year, 1118, is demonstrated by the fact that after his ordination Pope Gelasius, who died toward the end of January in the following year, wrote letters urging the people of Metz to receive him honorably, as was proper.

Meanwhile the church of Metz, deprived of its lawful pastor, was in great danger, since its seditious citizens, although admonished by Pope Gelasius’s letters, had up to that time refused to receive Theotger, canonically elected and ordained bishop. At length, however, the clergy and people, somewhat swayed by the letters of Bruno, archbishop of Trier—who until then had opposed Theotger’s election because it had been made without consulting him—repeatedly sent messengers inviting the elect to come to the city. Theotger at last, though with difficulty, consented. During Lent he prepared for the journey from the monastery to which he had withdrawn; after crossing the Rhine, he took with him the abbot of Marmoutier and made for the city of Metz.

As he approached, the abbots, the primicerius, and all clerics and citizens of sounder judgment met him and rejoiced at his arrival. Yet the primicerius judged that it was not safe for him to enter the city while the hearts of so many had not yet been reconciled. He therefore advised turning aside to a place called Cappentia, where [Col. 0774C] the bishop celebrated Palm Sunday with certain abbots. As Thursday approached—the day we call the Lord’s Supper and the Day of Indulgence—the episcopal order required that chrism be made. The bishop was uncertain where he might lawfully do this, since sedition among the turbulent people prevented it from being done in the city. At length it was resolved to consecrate the chrism at the monastery of Gorze. When the abbot was informed of his arrival, he made every provision for the day’s solemnity.

On the preceding day, as the bishop approached, the men of that place rushed out against him with swords and clubs as though against a robber. Some of the monks also, either fearing his disciplinary correction or siding with the pseudo-bishop’s party, stirred up the mob to pursue the bishop. Scarcely had the man of God reached the monastery gate when the maddened populace burst from hiding places, took away his horses, and attacked his companions as well, so that even the primicerius barely escaped the hands of his pursuers by flight. Meanwhile the pious bishop entered the basilica and, ignorant of what was happening outside, persisted in prayer. While all were threatening death, he invoked the Author of life.

Then, warned deceitfully by a certain monk to provide for his safety, since it was not in the monk’s power to restrain the madness of the raging crowd, he hurried from the church clothed in his pontifical vestments. Offering himself to the furious throng, he asked in the Lord’s words whom they were seeking. You might have seen all those pursuing him so terrified at his first appearance that they accused themselves of the utmost madness for daring to stretch out their hands against the Lord’s anointed.

When the crowds had thus been somewhat calmed, the bishop decided to proceed to the city. Hearing this, Acelin, abbot of St Clement, invited him to turn aside to his house and received him most kindly. When the citizens learned of this, many, furious and full of madness, poured out a thousand insults against the man of God and threatened not only to drive him from the city but to kill him. Nevertheless, taking with him the abbot of St Clement and clothed in priestly vestments as he had been at Gorze, he went out to meet his enemies, who barely restrained their hands. Meanwhile the city prefect arrived and asked on what business he had come. Theotger replied that he had come to visit with pastoral care the people entrusted to him; [Col. 0775B] moreover, the people of Metz would not act rightly if they barred their bishop from his own right.

These words somewhat softened the prefect and the others, and Theotger prepared to enter the city barefoot. But the prefect implored him not to commit himself to the enraged multitude, but rather to withdraw to some possession of the bishopric until the emperor and the archbishop should decide this matter. He yielded to that advice, returned to the monastery of St Clement, and there celebrated the day of the Lord’s Supper. Leaving there on Good Friday itself, Theotger made for Trier, intending to speak with Archbishop Bruno, who was then staying at Cologne, having been invited to the sacred solemnity by Archbishop Frederick. The man of God soon hastened there. His arrival was troublesome to the archbishop of Trier but very welcome to the archbishop of Cologne, through whose intervention, scarcely two days later—on Thursday, for he had arrived at Cologne on Tuesday—he was admitted to a conference with the archbishop of Trier.

The latter declared that he would address Theotger’s case with the bishops of Toul and Verdun, together with the people of Metz, at the feast of St James. Theotger’s enemies, Arnulf, custos of the church of Metz, and his assistant the primicerius, had arranged this truce with him; in the preceding week they had received chrism from the archbishop. Though the truce was very burdensome to him, Theotger observed it until the archbishop of Cologne, after Bruno had already returned to Trier, sent letters to him and obtained, without Theotger’s knowledge, permission for Theotger to celebrate the solemnities of Mass.

Theotger remained for many days in the company of the archbishop of Cologne. At his request he anointed a great many people in the city with holy chrism and dedicated certain churches. But as the Nativity of the blessed John the Baptist approached, the archbishop of Cologne set out for the imperial court convened on the island of the Rhine, that is, at Trebur, according to the emperor’s edict, taking the venerable bishop with him. There the archbishop of Trier was reconciled with him.

Here the mutilated manuscript of Theotger’s Life ends, greatly to the detriment both of so great a man’s reputation and of historical knowledge; without it we would have almost nothing certain concerning that blessed bishop. A summary of it is reported by Trithemius in his Chronicle of Hirsau.

After various journeys and returns, and various storms, Bishop Theotger at last rested in peace. He was never permitted to enter his own church. Dodechin and the unpublished Saxon Chronographer record his death under the year 1120; they call him Dieggerus. The Saxon Chronographer’s words are these:

> “Dieggerus of good memory, first abbot of St George and afterwards ordained to the church of Metz through the apostolic legate, after suffering many injuries inflicted upon him by the emperor’s faithful supporters, rested in the Lord, buried in the same church over which he had presided; a man exceptionally learned and most steadfast in holy conduct to his last age.”

It may nevertheless be doubted whether he was buried in the church of Metz, which he had not been permitted to enter while alive because of the seditious citizens who supported the emperor and the pseudo-bishop imposed by him. Trithemius, who appears to have read his complete acts, writes in the Chronicle of Hirsau that Theotger attended the council of Rheims in the preceding year, where his election and ordination were confirmed by the supreme pontiff and the other fathers; that when the council had been dissolved Pope Calixtus took him with him to Auxerre, where the pontiff celebrated Easter with his cardinals, and then led him as far as Cluny; and that, after the pope’s departure, Theotger remained there for four months, devoting all the time to contemplation of divine things and prayer. In the fourth month, finally, seized by fever, he received the Lord’s sacraments and passed to Christ on 29 April, the third day before the Kalends of May. He was buried in the church of St Peter on the north side beside the wall of the church, and many miracles afterwards occurred at his tomb.

Nothing, however, is read concerning him in the Bibliotheca Cluniacensis. Trithemius seems rather to have received these and other details from an anonymous author who wrote his Life in two books at the command of his disciple Erbo, the abbot. We received this Life, mutilated at its beginning and end, from Papebroch, from the Villingen manuscript. Trithemius is mistaken in assigning Theotger’s death to the preceding year. It is remarkable that no mention of him is made in the old Chronicle of Metz, which ends in his time, nor in its first appendix, which begins with Bishop Stephen. Stephen was canonically elected in this year and consecrated by Pope Calixtus, but was excluded by the imperial party from entering the city for more than two years.

Moreover, blessed Theotger was a man of extraordinary patience and gentleness, wholly free from ambition, as is clear from what he did to reject the election of the people of Metz. We have already mentioned him in vol. V, col. 1001, among the abbots of St George in the Black Forest.

[Col. 0777]

# MUSIC OF THEOTGER, BISHOP OF METZ

(Dom Gerbert, *Scriptores de musica*, vol. II, p. 182.)

## Notice

The same fate which carried off the book of St William in the fire of our monastery also carried off the following little work of Theotger, monk of Hirsau under the discipline of the same St William. In 1090 he was made abbot of the monastery of St George in the Black Forest, and later bishop of Metz. This musical work of Theotger could, however, also have been restored from the Tegernsee manuscript, with which I had already compared the St Blasien manuscript; likewise from another manuscript recently discovered, which the most reverend Philip Jacob, abbot of the monastery of St Peter in the Black Forest, a most discerning investigator of antiquities, most kindly shared with me. We have also compared this our text with it, and have noted in italic type the variant readings from it, enclosed in brackets marked **P.**

It would only be desirable that more recent writers had not neglected the gravity of the plagal modes, which the author repeatedly commends: “so that,” he says, “we may also in this way be admonished to despise the childish frivolity of chatter and to love the manly dignity of gravity.” And above he says: “The proportional prerogative of gravity has been commended to us: the authority of mature seriousness and the comely integrity of honorable conduct, which must always be preferred to the levity of chatter and wanton exultation.”

# THE MUSIC OF THEOTGER BEGINS

[Col. 0777]

## On the discoverers of the art of music

[Col. 0777A]

Pythagoras the philosopher is said to have been the first discoverer among the Greeks of the art of music (**P.: to have been**). Boethius, most distinguished in lineage and learning, is said to have been its translator into Latin (**P.: of this same science**), and the most profound investigator of that art according to numerical proportion. Guido the monk was a most diligent investigator of pitches, and their most reliable commender and transmitter. The monochord is an especially clear demonstration of this art; its first inventor is also said to have been the aforesaid Greek philosopher.

## On the monochord

A monochord is a musical instrument which in antiquity naturally and sufficiently consisted of [Col. 0777B] eight strings, marked with the first eight letters of the alphabet according to modern practice. For among these strings there are seven distinctions of pitches. As time passed and knowledge of the musical art advanced, skilled persons who understood the art perceived that it would greatly aid the practice of the art if the number of strings were increased. They added eight strings—not different ones, since nature forbade this, but repetitions of the same ones—distinguishing them only by depth and height, as a child’s voice differs from a man’s. Therefore they marked them with the same letters (**P.: with which the former are also marked**), differing only in this (**P.: making this distinction alone**) that the lower strings are marked by larger characters and the higher by smaller characters. Boethius names them by Greek designations appropriate to each sound (**P.: to the strings themselves**), as the reader will find in its place (**P.: in Boethius’s music**). But since these matters [Col. 0778A] are better understood on the monochord (**P.: we have spoken of the monochord**), let us now consider its measurement (**P.: mensuration**).

## On the measurement of the monochord

Let it be divided into nine equal units from bridge to bridge (**P.: Let nine units be divided from bridge to bridge**); for thus we call the hollow pieces of wood which support (**P.: sustain**) the string, at its ends. Let the Greek letter Gamma, Γ, be placed next to the bridge (**P.: bridge**). Then, at the first ninth-unit mark (**P.: at the end of the first unit, or at the first division**), place low A. Again, from A to the end let a division be made into nine units, and behold: at the first ninth-unit mark B is to be placed. Then return to Gamma, and from it make four units to the end. The first unit (**P.: therefore**) contains the *diatessaron* [fourth] and ends at C. The second contains the *diapente* [fifth] and ends at G (**P.: ends at G and contains the diapente**). The third contains the *diapason* [octave] and indicates g (**P.: retains and ends at g**); the fourth ends (**P.: is ended**).

Again, from A to the end make four units. The first, with the *diatessaron*, gives D; the second, with the *diapente*, a. From B to the end, [the text continues in **P.**:] “the third, with the *diapason*, aa; the fourth ends. In the same way make four units from B to the end, and behold: the first unit, with the *diatessaron*, marks E; the second, with the *diapente*, while the remainder are empty.” Again, from C make the same number of units, namely four, to the end: the first with the *diatessaron* shows F; the second with the *diapente*, c; the remainder are empty. Again, from D to the end make four units, and [Col. 0778B] the first with the *diatessaron* represents G, which we already have; the second with the *diapente* gives d; the remainder are empty. Then from E to the end make the same number of units. The first with the *diatessaron* represents a, which we already have; the second, with the *diapente*, e; the remainder are empty. Likewise, from F to the end make the same number of units: the first gives *b synemmenon*—or soft b (*b molle*)—with the *diatessaron*; the second gives high f with the *diapente*; the remainder are empty.

Thus, all the strings having been found except the *B synemmenon* among the low pitches, let us consider low F in order to find it. The same interval by which low *B synemmenon* corresponds to it is that by which high b-flat corresponds more fittingly to high f. The middle position of both strings is unquestionably correct, since it separates the *diapente* on one side and the *diapason* on the other, and is sufficiently rational for each. It is certainly quite reasonable that low F should assume for itself the generation of the upper *synemmenon*, since it is also [Col. 0779B] proportionate and the origin of the lower one. Behold, we have all the strings. The first of them (**P.: that one is first**) is A, as it is always held by all musicians; for Gamma, Γ, has been added in excess (**P.: by superabundance**) for the sake of practice, as I think, rather than for the rule.

## What interval is called a tone, what a semitone, and the rest

With these strings arranged (**P.: thus**) between two strings, one sometimes sees a larger space—for example, between Γ and A, and between A and B—and sometimes a smaller one, as between B and C and elsewhere (**P.: and so with the others**). The larger space is called a tone; the smaller is called a semitone, that is, a half-tone—not a full tone. Again, among three strings there is sometimes a *ditone*, that is, two tones, as from c to e; and sometimes a *semititone* (*semiditonus*), which has only a tone and a semitone, as from D to F and elsewhere (**P.: and likewise in the rest**).

A *diatessaron* occurs when, among four strings, there are two tones and one semitone, as from A to D and from B to E, and elsewhere. A *diapente* is larger by one tone, consists of five strings, and occurs as from A to E and from C to G, and elsewhere. Among six strings there occur a *diapente* with a tone, as from C to a, and a *diapente* with a semitone, as from e to c (**P.: as from C to a, or from E to c**). Finally, the *diapason* occurs in eight strings, as from A to a, from B to b, from C to c, and so forth.

*Diatessaron* means, as it were, “through four,” just as *diapente* means “through five,” because they include that many strings. *Diapason* means, as it were, “through all,” because it encompasses all the modes [Col. 0779D] of pitches.

## On the nine modes of pitches

**P.:** “These are the nine modes of pitches, seven of which Virgil calls the seven distinctions of pitches. For the ancients did not admit the *diapente* with a tone, the *diapason*, or the *diapente* with a semitone. But modern usage has adopted these modes so completely that it cannot lose them without great loss to itself. Moderns also add the unison to these modes, placing it first and improperly calling it a mode, just as grammarians call the nominative a case; yet they still reckon only nine modes of pitches, because they omit the diapason on account of its very rare use in song.”

## On the consideration of numbers

[Col. 0780A]

Let us now digress briefly to the consideration of numbers, to make clear and explain the principle of measurement, so that the proportions and their nature (**P.: natures of proportions**) may satisfy the reader who understands them less well, and so that the discussion may proceed later more plainly and clearly. In arithmetic the double ratio, the sesquialteral, the sesquitertian, and the sesquioctaval are very frequently discussed.

## On the double, sesquialteral, and sesquitertian proportions

A proportion is the relationship in which numbers stand to one another. The double proportion occurs when the greater number contains the lesser twice, as two contains one, four contains two, six contains three, eight contains four, ten contains five, [Col. 0780B] and so on indefinitely. The sesquialteral proportion occurs when the greater number contains the whole lesser number and its half, as three contains two, six contains four, nine contains six, twelve contains eight, and so forth. The sesquitertian proportion occurs when the greater number contains the whole lesser number and its third part, as four contains three, eight contains six, twelve contains nine, and so forth. The sesquioctaval proportion occurs when the greater number contains the whole lesser number and its eighth part, as nine contains eight. Let this suffice concerning numbers.

## On the same proportions considered in measurement

The same proportions are considered in measurement, or continuous quantity. A double [Col. 0780C] proportion occurs when the larger space contains the smaller twice. Thus the double proportion is the model (**P.: a model of that consonance which**) called *diapason*: for all its species are produced in two units. In measurement the sesquialteral proportion occurs when the larger space contains the smaller and its half; and this is the model (**P.: of this consonance, which is**) of the *diapente*, all of whose species are produced in three units.

Likewise, in measurement the sesquitertian proportion occurs when the larger interval contains the whole smaller interval and its third part, as was said earlier (**P.: previously**) concerning four and ten (**P.: three**). This is the form of the *diatessaron*, all of whose species occur at the fourth unit (**P.: by a fourth unit**). Again, the sesquioctaval proportion in measurement occurs when its larger interval contains the whole smaller interval and its eighth part. It occurs, as has been said, between (**P.: in**) eight and nine. This too is the form of the tone, all of whose species, so to speak, occur at the ninth unit. Hence it is more truly and correctly called *epogdous* than “tone”; for this name belongs to it proportionally, because it is “over eight.” “Tone,” however, is derived from *tonando*, that is, “sounding.”

Therefore, by the proportion through which each greater number or greater interval exceeds the lesser, or through which the lesser is exceeded by the greater, the earlier sound of each aforesaid consonance exceeds the later, or the later is exceeded in depth by the greater, earlier sound. Indeed, the proportional prerogative of gravity has been commended to us: the authority of mature seriousness [Col. 0781A] and the comely integrity of honorable conduct, which must always be preferred to the levity of chatter and wanton exultation.

**P.:** “This also should be observed: lower pitches come before higher pitches on the monochord; in this respect the arrangement of the monochord imitates nature and reason. For just as those who are serious and mature are prior and more worthy than the impudent, talkative, and wanton, so in music lower pitches should be held prior and more worthy than high and light ones.”

What we say concerning numbers (**P.: what we have said concerning number**) must be contemplated by the inward eye; but what concerns measurement may also be seen by the outward eye, as is evident on the monochord. We therefore rightly say (**P.: and may say**) that pitches and the modes of pitches are natural, since creative nature, which formed all things, has laid down or impressed such patterns upon them [Col. 0781B] in number, weight, and measure. Now let us return to the matter, though we have not strayed far from it.

## On the division of the monochord

The monochord, before (**P.: after**) it has been measured and completed as prescribed above, is divided into four tetrachords: namely, the tetrachord of low pitches, the tetrachord of finals, the tetrachord of higher pitches, and the tetrachord of the highest pitches.

## On tetrachords

A tetrachord is a space containing four regularly measured (**P.: divided**) strings. It is called the tetrachord of low pitches because low pitches sound there. It is called the tetrachord of finals because every regular chant ends there. It is called the tetrachord of higher pitches because higher pitches sound there. It is called the tetrachord of the highest pitches because the highest pitches sound there.

## How tetrachords are constituted

The first tetrachord consists of a tone, a semitone, and a tone, and extends from low A to low D. The second tetrachord likewise consists of a tone, a semitone, and a tone, and extends from low D to low C (**P.: G**). The third tetrachord likewise consists of a tone, a semitone, and a tone, and extends from high a to high d. The fourth tetrachord, like the preceding ones, consists of a tone, a semitone, and a tone, and extends from high d to high g.

In this division of the four tetrachords, three tones remain: the first [Col. 0781D] between Γ and low A; the second between low G and high a; the third between high g and double aa. Into these four tetrachords, from the outset (**P.: also**), two tetrachords called *synemmena*, that is, “conjoined,” are inserted. One consists of a tone, semitone, and tone, and extends from Γ to low G. The other likewise consists of a tone, semitone, and tone, and extends from low G to high c. Of these two tetrachords, the one among the higher pitches is held and frequently used in common practice; the one among the lower pitches seems less necessary (**P.: to some**) and is contended, apparently, that it should be avoided (**P.: some contend that it should be avoided**). [Col. 0782A] But in our chant, which we call (**P.: boastfully call**) Gregorian, it cannot in any way be avoided, as in the gradual responsory *In sole posuit* [“He placed [his tabernacle] in the sun”], and in other similar pieces sung with such harmony, and in very many other chants. Otherwise, either the chant will be changed to a great extent, or it will not end properly at a determinate final, or it will be omitted altogether.

Since pitches are said to be the same in the species of the *diapason*, we therefore see no reason why, if the tetrachord of the *synemmenon* has a place among the higher pitches between G and c, it may not and ought not also to have a place among the lower pitches between Γ and C. Yet it should be known that these two tetrachords, though they are not very regular, are exceedingly customary. Some musicians, however, do not posit a tetrachord of the *synemmenon*, but only one string, [Col. 0782B] and call it the “soft” one (*mollem*). But pitches are rarely altered at a single string; rather, they run through the whole tetrachord, or even farther.

## On four other tetrachords
[Note: [Col. 0781D] The passages enclosed in brackets are not found in the Petrine codex.] There are, moreover, four tetrachords differing from those mentioned above in name and position: they are called *hypaton*, *meson*, *diezeugmenon*, and *hyperboleon*, and they have the semitone at their end, whereas the former have it between two tones. Their arrangement, when begun from the higher pitches, is very plain. Thus the tetrachord *hyperboleon* extends from double *aa* to *e*; *diezeugmenon*, from *f* to [lacuna] [Note: [Col. 0782D] It should read “from *e* to …”.]; *meson* from *a* to *E*; *hypaton* from *E* to *B*. In the distribution of these tetrachords there remain three tones, from high *a* to high *a*, and from low *B* to low *A*: namely, the *proslambanomenos*, that is, the “added” note, [Col. 0782C] which Ptolemy, king of Egypt, is said to have added to the fourteen notes that the ancients alone are said to have possessed; and also the note which the moderns added. They differ, therefore, in this also from the four regular tetrachords mentioned above: *e* and *E* have conjunction, while *paramese* has disjunction; those others have *d* and *D* as conjunction, while *mese* has disjunction.]

The first of the regular tetrachords is the tetrachord of the low notes, not only in number and position, but also in the prerogative of dignity—or gravity—so that we may be admonished in this way also to despise the childish frivolity of chatter and to cherish the manly dignity of seriousness. It is, moreover, the beginning, fountain, and source of the other three. For it generates the tetrachord of finals by the ratio of sesquitertia [4:3]; the tetrachord [Col. 0782D] of the upper notes by the double ratio [2:1]; and these, once generated, in turn produce the tetrachord of the highest notes: the former indeed—for the tetrachord of finals generates the tetrachord of highest notes—by the double ratio; the latter—indeed, the tetrachord of highest notes is generated from the tetrachord of upper notes—by the epitrite, or sesquitertian, ratio. This generation is so natural that the first produces the first [variant: “second”], the second the second, the third the third, and the fourth [variant: “third”] the fourth, by the measure we have stated. This, I say, is the inviolable pattern of the generated strings according to the principle of the stated ratios; and it is the model for the species of the three symphonies to be described. [Col. 0783A] For among the modes of notes mentioned above there are three called symphonies because of the pleasing conjunctions of notes: namely, *diatessaron*, *diapente*, and *diapason*.

### On the species of the diatessaron

The *diatessaron* has twice four principal species: four among the low notes and four among the high notes—two first, two second, two third, and two fourth species—each, as it were, stamped by its own aforesaid sesquitertian model [variant: “indeed, each is stamped by its own sesquitertian ratio”]. For the first species consists of the first notes, the second of the second, the third of the third, and the fourth of the fourth, in the two tetrachords of low notes and finals; and the first extends from *A* to *d* [variant: *D*], the second from *B* to *E*, the third from *C* to *F*, and the fourth from *D* to *G*. In the same manner, the other first species consists of the first notes, the other second of the second, the other third [Col. 0783B] of the third, and the other fourth of the fourth, in the two tetrachords of upper and highest notes. The first extends from *a* to *d*, the second from *b* to *e*, the third from *c* to *f*, and the fourth from *d* to *g*.

### On the species of the diapente

The *diapente* has only four principal species, which arise no less naturally, each having the pattern of its own sesquialteral ratio [3:2]. For in the same manner the first consists of the first notes, the second of the second, the third of the third, and the fourth of the fourth, in the two tetrachords of finals and upper notes. The first extends from *D* to *a*, the second from *E* to *b*, the third from *F* to *c*, and the fourth from *G* to *d*. (Note that, in these two tetrachords conjoined—rather, those of finals and upper notes—the generation of the species of the *diapente* is properly located rather than in the others, because neither the tetrachords of low notes and finals nor those [Col. 0783C] of upper and highest notes, when conjoined, suffice for this generation owing to their paucity of strings.)

### On the species of the diapason

Further, the *diapason*, like the *diatessaron*, has twice four principal species: two first, two second, two third, and two fourth species, each having the pattern of its own double ratio. The species of the earlier symphonies, however, consist merely of strings or notes; whereas these species of the *diapason* consist of composite species, namely, species of *diatessaron* and *diapente*. The first species of *diapason* consists of the first species of *diatessaron* and the first species of *diapente*, extends from low *A* to high *a*, and has as its middle boundary [Col. 0783D] *D*, which is also the final of the *protus*. The second species of *diapason* consists of the two second species, that is, the second species of *diatessaron* and the second species of *diapente*; it extends from low *B* to high [note omitted in the source], and has as its middle boundary low *E*, which is also the final of the *deuterus*. The third species of *diapason* consists of the two third species, that is, the third species of *diatessaron* and the third species of *diapente*; it extends from low *C* to high *c*, and has as its middle boundary *F*, which is also the final of the *tritus*. The fourth species of *diapason* consists of the two fourth species, that is, the fourth species of *diatessaron* and the fourth species of *diapente*; it extends from low *D* to high *d*, and has as its middle boundary *G*, which is also the final of the *tetrardus*.

The other first species of *diapason* [Col. 0784A] consists of the two first species, that is, the first species of *diapente* and the other first species of *diatessaron*; it extends from low *D* to high *d*, and has high *a* as its middle boundary. The other second species of *diapason* consists of the two second species, namely the second species of *diapente* and the other second species of *diatessaron*; it extends from low *E* to high *e*, and has high [note omitted in the source] as its middle boundary. The other fourth [variant: “third”] species of *diapason* consists of the two third species, that is, the third species of *diapente* and the other third species of *diatessaron*; it extends from low *F* to high *f*, and has high *e* [variant: *c*] as its middle boundary. The other fourth species of *diapason* consists of the two fourth species, that is, the fourth species of *diapente* and the other fourth species of *diatessaron*; it extends from low *G* [Col. 0784B] to high *g*, and has high *d* as its middle boundary. In this distribution [variant: “division”] of the species of the *diapason*, two tones remain: one between Γ and low *A*, the other between high *g* and double *aa*. We have everywhere called these species “principal,” but this must nevertheless be understood with a distinction.

### Why the lower species are more principal

The low species are called principal as the older, and the high species principal as the younger: the former as mothers, the latter as midwives. Finally, just as one says “solemnity of solemnities” and “song of songs,” so the former may be called “the principal species of principal species,” while the latter are the last or final principal species. It should be noted that, in establishing the species, we cannot so properly say “eight [Col. 0784C] species” as “twice four species”; anyone who reads these matters carefully can understand why.

### On the constitution of the four tropes

From these species of the three symphonies the four tropes are constituted. A trope is called from the Greek *tropos*, which is interpreted “turned” or “turning,” because each trope turns itself away from the other tropes toward its own rules and proper figures or modes; or because, however much any trope ascends or descends, it nevertheless finally turns itself toward its own final. Guido, however, calls them modes, and establishes the four of them from the same source from which we establish the species; through them, as through the species, he sets out the four tropes: *protus*, *deuterus*, *tritus*, and *tetrardus*.

### On the protus

[Col. 0784D] The *protus*, that is, the first, is constituted from all the first species; the *deuterus*, that is, the second, from all the second species; the *tritus*, that is, the third, from all the third species; and the *tetrardus*, that is, the fourth, from all the fourth species. We name them by Greek appellations because common usage calls them so, and because the Greeks perhaps adhere more carefully to the natural rules. The *protus*, therefore, consists of the two first species of *diatessaron*, the first species of *diapente*, and the two first species of *diapason*. We have an example in the antiphon *Domine non est alius* (“Lord, there is no other”), which is found written among the litanies. For it begins on low *A* and proceeds [variant: “remains”] as far as high *d*: these two notes include all the first species.

### On the deuterus

[Col. 0785A]

Likewise, the two second species of *diatessaron*, the second *diapente*, and the second [variant: “two”] *diapason* species set forth the *deuterus*, examples of which can readily be found.

### On the tritus

The two third species of *diatessaron*, the third *diapente*, and the two third *diapason* species complete the *tritus*, as the diligent investigator will find in the antiphon *O Christi pietas* (“O mercy of Christ”).

### On the tetrardus

The *tetrardus* likewise consists of the two fourth species of *diatessaron*, the fourth *diapente*, and the two fourth *diapason* species. An example presently before us is the responsory *Audi, fili mi* (“Hear, my son”), which rises and falls through all the fourth species and beyond. This, then, [Col. 0785B] is the constitution of the four tropes, or modes. The following is their division.

### On the division of the protus

When the first species of *diapente* is joined to the first *diatessaron* species, which is among the low notes, and the first *diapason* species is completed, the earlier, so to speak, *protus* is constituted. Likewise, when the same *diapente* species is joined to the other first species of *diatessaron* and the other first species of *diapason* is completed, the other *protus*, so to speak, is constituted. Hence come the names called authentic [variant: *autentus*] *protus* and the plagal *protus*.

### On the division of the deuterus

In the same way, when the second species of *diapente* is joined to the second species of *diatessaron*, which consists among the low notes, and the second species of *diapason* is composed, the earlier *deuterus* is generated [variant: “constituted”]. Likewise, when that same second *diapente* species is joined to the other second *diatessaron* species and the other second *diapason* species is formed, the other *deuterus* is constituted [variant: “generated”]. Hence [variant: “from this”] arise the names by which it is called authentic [variant: *autentus*] *deuterus* and plagal *deuterus*.

### On the division of the tritus

Similarly, when the third figure [variant: “species”] of *diapente* is joined to the third species of *diatessaron*, which is among the low notes, and the third *diapason* species is composed, the earlier [variant: “earlier”] *tritus*, so to speak, is completed. Likewise, when the same third *diapente* species is joined to the other third *diatessaron* species and the other third *diapason* species is completed, the other *tritus*, so to speak, is constituted. Hence one customarily says authentic [variant: *autentus*] *tritus* and plagal *tritus*.

### On the division of the tetrardus

[Col. 0785D]

In like manner, when the fourth species of *diapente* is joined to the fourth species of *diatessaron*, and the fourth species of *diapason* is composed, the earlier *tetrardus*, so to speak, is born [variant: “therefrom”]. Likewise, when that same fourth *diapente* species is joined to the other fourth *diatessaron* species and the other fourth *diapason* species is thence generated, the other *tetrardus*, so to speak, is produced. Hence come the names authentic [variant: *autentus*] *tetrardus* and plagal *tetrardus*. “Authentic” [variant: *autentus*] means, as it were, master and superior, because it takes its name from authority. “Plagal” [variant: *plagalis*], as they say, is Greek, and means [Col. 0786A] pupil, companion, or subordinate.

### That this division is not recent

This division is not recent but ancient: it is old, not new. For in ancient pagan authors we read, for the *protus* and its plagal [variant: “plagal”] form, *Dorian* and *Hypodorian*; for the *deuterus* and its pupil [variant: “plagal”] form, *Phrygian* and *Hypophrygian*; for the *tritus* and its companion, *Lydian* and *Hypolydian*; and for the *tetrardus* and its subordinate, *Mixolydian* and *Hypomixolydian*. Thus far, with divine help, we have proceeded in nearly all things by relying upon natural principles. But now, if in what remains we follow usage without caution, we shall be inconsistent with ourselves.

### That in the division of the tropes the natural rules were not observed

For in dividing the tropes or modes, some did not [Col. 0786B] sufficiently observe the natural rules; indeed, they gave much scope to usage and constructed rules in accordance with usage itself—rules which we can neither avoid nor ought to avoid. Tropes or modes, properly so called, are what we abusively call, as some say, “tones.” Yet, since *tonus* is said to derive from *tonando*, that is, “sounding,” it is as suitably assigned to the epogdoan ratio [9:8] as it is appropriately assigned to a trope or mode. Usage erred more seriously in this: just as it made the first and second from the *protus* and its plagal form, so it made the third and fourth from the *deuterus* and its pupil; the fifth and sixth from the *tritus* and its companion; and confused the seventh and eighth from the *tetrardus* and its subordinate. Since this abuse has become so prevalent, let our own argument also proceed here with its head turned around. Nevertheless, let us now return to what preceded; and, since we can do nothing else, let us endeavor, in support of usage, to find arguments for establishing and confirming it, showing with divine aid why usage transferred the natural constitutions in these very tones.

The low notes, indeed, by the natural ratio of precedence, ought, together with their companions, to hold the principal place according to the reasoning stated above; no one denies this, nor can anyone assert otherwise. The high notes, however, together with their associates, have seized [variant: “hold”] the height of sound and intensity, and in such loftiness have occupied the first place. The farther removed they are, the more eminent they are in this precedence, as their names show: they are called upper and highest [variant: “more excellent”]. That these names are neither recent nor new is proved by the Greek terms which they have, as Boethius testifies: *trite hyperboleon*, *paranete hyperboleon*, and *nete hyperboleon*. Because of the loftiness of such elevation and the relaxation of its opposite disposition [variant: “depression”], custom transferred the [corrupt reading: “intimated”; read “weakening”] [Note: [Col. 0785D] Correct.] to the high notes, but primacy to the low. This, therefore, is the cause and reason why all Latin musicians establish the authentic modes among the high notes and the plagal modes [Col. 0787A] among the low; whether the Greeks do so, we do not know. Let us therefore agree with them, and although it might suffice that we have established them naturally above, let us also establish them here according to usage, as briefly as we can.

### On the first tone

The first tone, trope, or mode normally ranges between *D* and *d*, as is fitting in its species; by licence it takes one note on either side. Its formula is as follows: its *Ejus saeculorum amen* begins on *a*; the chant itself proceeds [variant: “goes”] to *C*, as in the antiphon *Arguebat* (“He was reproving”). More often it begins on *D*, which is its final, as in the antiphons *Ecce nomen Domini* (“Behold the name of the Lord”), *Euge, serve bone* (“Well done, good servant”), *Columna est* (“It is a pillar”), and *Domine Dominus noster* (“O Lord, our Lord”); on *E*, but rarely, as in the responsory *Veniens a Libano* (“Coming from Lebanon”) [and the responsory *Ego te tuli*, “I carried you”]; on *F*, as in *Biduo vivens* (“Living for two days”), *Ave Maria* (“Hail, Mary”), *Apertis thesauris* (“When their treasures had been opened”), and *Domine si hic* (“Lord, if you had been here”) [the antiphon *Beati mundo*, “Blessed are the pure”]; on *G*, as in the antiphon *Secundum magnam* (“According to the great …”) and the responsory *Vidi Jerusalem* (“I saw Jerusalem”); and on *a*, as in the antiphon *Beati mundo*. Sometimes this trope also begins on low *A*, as in the antiphon *Domine non est al[ius]* (“Lord, there is no other”) [*Saulus adhuc*, “Saul, still …”]. This happens very rarely, namely when it is indeterminate, having a *diatessaron* above as well as below.

### On the second

[Col. 0787C]

The second, its subordinate, has the same final as its master, namely low *D*. It ranges between *A* and *a*, that is, within its *diapason*, and takes a note on either side. Its formula is this [as is clear in the figure]: its *saeculorum amen* begins on *F* [variant: *f*]; the chant itself begins on Γ, but rarely, as in the responsory *Educ de carcere* (“Bring [my soul] out of prison”) and *Natus ante saecula* (“Born before the ages”); on *A*, as in the offertory *Ad te, Domine, levavi* (“To you, O Lord, I have lifted up [my soul]”); on *C* [variant: *c*], as in the antiphon *Nonne cor nostrum* (“Was not our heart …?”) [*Sicut lilium*, “Like a lily”]; on *D* [variant: *d*], as in the antiphon *Ecce in nubibus* (“Behold, in the clouds”); on *E*, though rarely, as in the responsory *Ego te* (“I … you”) [the antiphon *Ecce Maria*, “Behold, Mary”]; and on *F*, as in the antiphon *Quem vidistis* (“Whom did you see?”). It is also found to begin on *B* of the lower *synemmenon*, [Col. 0787D] as in the gradual *Salvum fac servum* (“Save your servant”).

### On the third
