The third mode ends on low *E* and normally proceeds to high *e*, passing through its two species and taking one note on either side. Its formula is this [as is clear in the figure]. Its *saeculorum amen* (*euouae*) begins on *C* [variant: high *c*]; the chant itself ends [Col. 0788A] on *E*, as in the antiphon *Quando natus es* (“When you were born”); on *F*, as in the introit *Nunc scio vere* (“Now I know truly”); on *G*, as in the antiphon *Fac benigne* (“Deal graciously”); and on *c*, as in the antiphons *Vivo ego* (“As I live”) and *Unum opus feci* (“I did one work”).

### On the fourth

The fourth, its plagal [variant: “the plagal tone of the third”], has the same final and normally ranges between *B* and [note omitted in the source], taking one note on either side and very frequently touching both forms of *B*, the *synemmenon* [Col. 0788B] *B♭*. Its formula is this. Its *saeculorum amen* (*euouae*) begins on *a*, like that of the first [variant: “first mode”]; the chant itself begins on *C*, as in the antiphon *Hodie natus est* (“Today [Christ] is born”); on *D*, as in *Benedicta tu* (“Blessed are you”); on *e* [variant: *E*], as in *Gaude, Maria* (“Rejoice, Mary”); on *F* [variant: *f*], as in *Ecce merces* (“Behold the reward”); on *G*, as in *O mors* (“O death”); and, though rarely, on *a*, as in *Nisi diligenter* (“Unless diligently”).

### On the fifth

[Col. 0788C]

The final of the fifth is *F*; it ascends [variant: “of one ascending”] from there to *f*, between which its species are contained, while it takes one note on either side. Its formula is this. (Note that the fifth tone does not take a note on the side of the low notes, but only on that of the high notes, as is clear here.) Its *saeculorum amen* [variant: “its *euouae*”] begins on *C* [variant: *c*], like that of the third; the chant itself begins on *F*, as in the antiphons *Adhuc multa* (“Many things still …”) and *Haurietis* (“You shall draw”); on *G*—but rarely—as in the communion chant *Non vos rel[inquam]* (“I shall not leave you”); rarely on *a* [variant: “on *d*”], as in the antiphon *Exsultabunt omnia* (“All things shall rejoice”); and on *c*, as in the antiphons *Elevamini portae aeternales* (“Be lifted up, eternal gates”) and *Ecce jam veniet* (“Behold, now he will come”).

### On the sixth

[Col. 0788D]

The sixth, its pupil, has the same final. It normally goes from *C* to *c* through its species, and here too takes one note on either side; its formula is this [but here it does not take a note on the side of the low notes]. Its *saeculorum amen* [variant: *euouae*] begins on *a*, as in the first and fourth; the chant itself begins on low *C*, as in the antiphon *Vox [Col. 0789A] exsultationis* (“A voice of rejoicing”); on *D*, as in *Si ego verus* (“If I am true”); on *F*, as in *O admirabile* (“O wondrous …”); and rarely on *G*, as in *Nesciens mater* (“The mother not knowing”). More rarely, it begins on the higher *b* of the *synemmenon*, as in the communion chant *Redime me* (“Redeem me”). It is also found to begin on *B* of the lower *synemmenon*, as in the antiphon *Adorna thalamum* (“Adorn the bridal chamber”); this beginning is extremely rare and is avoided by many, especially because many take pains to avoid this *synemmenon*.

### On the seventh

[Col. 0789B]

The seventh mode ends on *G* and proceeds thence to *g*, its *diapason*, taking one note on either side. Its formula is this. Its *saeculorum amen* [variant: *euouae*] begins on *d*; the chant itself begins on *G*, as in the antiphon *Assumpta est* (“She was assumed”); on *a*, as in the antiphon *Ipse praeibit* (“He himself will go before”) and the responsory *Elisabeth*; on [note omitted in the source], as in the antiphon *Cum angelis* (“With the angels”); on *c*, as in *Benedicta filia* (“Blessed daughter”); and on *d*, as in *Agathes laetissima* (“Most joyful Agatha”).

### On the eighth

[Col. 0789C]

The eighth, its companion, ends on the same final and ranges between *D* and *d*, as in its species, taking the whole tone on either side. Its formula follows. Its *saeculorum amen* begins on *c*, like those of the third and fifth; the chant itself begins on *C*, as in the antiphons *Justorum animae* (“The souls of the righteous”) [*Cornelius*] and *Stabunt justi* (“The righteous shall stand”); on *D*, as in *Dixit Dominus mulieri* (“The Lord said to the woman”); on *E*, as in the responsory *Iste [Col. 0789D] est, qui ante Deum* (“This is he who before God …”) and *Hodie Maria* (“Today Mary …”); on *F*, as in *Gloria in excelsis* (“Glory in the highest”); on *G*, as in *Advenerunt nobis* (“They have come to us”); on *a*, as in *Apertum est* (“It has been opened”); on *c*, as in *Aquam quam ego* (“The water which I …”); and on *d*, as in *Tu es qui venturus* (“Are you he who is to come?”) and the antiphon *Undecim discipuli* (“The eleven disciples”). It also sometimes begins on higher *b* of the *synemmenon*, as in the offertory verse *Notas mihi fecisti* (“You have made known to me”).

[Col. 0790A] Since each trope, in its regular course, takes one note beyond its upper range, the first, second, third, and eighth are sometimes found to take two and to form a ten-string system (*decachordum*) consisting of three tetrachords. Written examples of these follow. (Examples of the first tone are the responsories *Haec est Jerusalem*—“This is Jerusalem”—*Plateae tuae*—“Your streets”—and *Filiae Jerusalem*—“Daughters of Jerusalem.”)

### The decachord of the second tone and its examples

[Col. 0790B]

(Examples of the second are these): the responsories *Rorate coeli* (“Drop down, ye heavens”), *Qui vicerit* (“He who conquers”), *Angelus Domini* (“The angel of the Lord”), and *Tentavit Deus* (“God tested [him]”), and the antiphon *In spiritu humilitatis* (“In a spirit of humility”). This decachord of the second, especially frequent among most Germans, is avoided by Italians or Romans, who confine themselves to soft *b*; some Germans imitate them.

### The decachord of the third tone and its examples

[Col. 0790C]

The examples of the decachord of the third are these: the responsories *Virtute magna* (“With great power”) and *Peccavi super* (“I have sinned beyond …”).

### The decachord of the eighth tone and its examples

[Col. 0790D]

(Examples of the eighth are these): the responsories *Ecce radix Jesse* (“Behold the root of Jesse”), *Pretiosus confessor Domini* (“The precious confessor of the Lord”), *Oravit Jacob* (“Jacob prayed”), and *Nuntiaverunt Jacob* (“They informed Jacob”).

[Col. 0791A] Not only these but other examples also can be found by a diligent investigator, especially in the more difficult chant. In the fifth, sixth, and seventh [variant: “we do not find such a chant, perhaps for this reason, because in those tones”], we do not find [variant: “cannot find”] a tetrachord [variant: *decachordum*] consisting of three tetrachords—in the fifth and sixth because of the tritone; in the seventh because of a lack of strings on the monochord. In the fourth tone, however, we can find such a tetrachord, but we do not remember finding such a chant.) Since not only these differences or varieties but also other considerable ones occur in chant, which can lead the singer into error concerning the tropes, so that he does not know which chant is to be assigned to which, we have thought it worthwhile to venture to formulate general [Col. 0791B] rules by which we may clearly distinguish authentic from subordinate or common chants [variant: “authentic from plagal”].

### General rules for authentic chant

Every chant, therefore, which has a *diatessaron* above the *diapente*, even if it descends as far as the twelfth note—namely *D* from *aa*—or stops at any point short of it, is to be assigned without contradiction to the authentic mode, provided only that it proceeds or arrives at its final regularly. The same applies to a chant having two notes above the *diapente*, for example *b* or *c*, and one or no note below it; likewise to one having one note above it and none below the *diapente*. Every chant of this kind is to be assigned without contradiction to the authentic mode, provided only that it ends regularly.

### General rule for plagal chant

A chant having a *diatessaron* below—that is, among the low notes—whether it rises from Γ to the tenth note or descends to the tenth or stops anywhere short of it, is to be assigned to the plagal mode, provided only that it approaches the final according to the rules. The same applies to a chant having two notes below the *diapente* and one or none above it, or stopping anywhere short of that limit [variant: “or if it is short of the *diapente*”]; likewise to one having one note below the *diapente* and none above it, or stopping anywhere short of it. Again, this applies to one having no note below and not ascending fully to the *diapente*. Every such chant must be referred to the subordinate mode, if only it ends regularly.

### General rule for common chant

[Col. 0792B]

A common chant is one which ranges below [variant: “between”] the *diapente*, reaches it fully, and does not wander on either side. Likewise common is a chant which takes one note equally above and below, or two equally on either side. The following is observed in common chant: it is assigned to the trope [variant: “tone customarily assigned”] [Note: [Col. 0791B] Here Tegernsee ends.] with which it agrees more closely, or to which it is customary to assign it. We have stated rules that are plausible and can be demonstrated; but in some matters, as Priscian says, the rule must indeed be known, while usage must be observed.

[Note: [Col. 0791B] In the Saint-Remi codex there are appended here rules concerning *discantus*, which we omit, since they are better explained in their proper place from FRANCO and JOHN OF MURIS. We do not doubt that these rules concerning *discantus* are to be referred to the same period, the thirteenth or fourteenth century [Col. 0792B], and that the verse appended below is to be referred to the scribe of the codex, not to the author: “He who wrote me was named Dieter.”]

## ABOUT THE YEAR OF THE LORD 1119: HUGH OF SAINTE-MARIE, MONK OF FLEURY

[Col. 0791]

## HISTORICAL AND LITERARY NOTICE

(*Histoire littéraire de la France*, X, 285)

Hugh of Sainte-Marie, so called after the name of a village belonging to his father [Note: [Col. 0791B] Note in manuscript no. 4963 of the Royal Library.], where there was a church dedicated to the Blessed Virgin, embraced the monastic life in the abbey of Saint-Benoît-sur-Loire. There, toward the end of the eleventh century, he became celebrated for his learning. This is nearly all that we know of the life and actions of this author, who is known to us only by his name, profession, and writings. The most important of all his works, for solidity and exactness, is his *Treatise on Royal Power and Priestly Dignity*, which Baluze printed in the collection of ancient monuments [Note: [Col. 0792B] *Miscellanea*, vol. IV, p. 65.].

Hugh addressed it to Henry I, king of England, with a prologue or preface placed at its head. The author’s purpose is to calm the disputes dividing the two powers and to combat the error of those who, believing that they know what they do not know, overturn God’s order. What our author rightly calls error, and what he undertakes to combat, is the view of those who maintained that temporal power was not established by God but by human beings, and who consequently placed priestly dignity above royal dignity, although the former ought to be subject to the latter—not in dignity, but by God’s ordering. [Col. 0793] [Note: [Col. 0793A] “They overturn the order established by God, while they think they know what they do not know. For they suppose that the ordering or disposition of an earthly kingdom has been ordained not by God but by men. Therefore they set priestly dignity above royal majesty, though it ought to be subject to it in order, not in dignity.”]

Hugh flatters himself that, after he has dispersed the clouds of this error, men may perhaps yield to the truth and to what he calls divine doctrines [Note: [Col. 0793A] *Miscellanea*, ibid., p. 10: *divinis dogmatibus acquiescent*, “they will assent to divine doctrines.”]. He calls the adherents of the error he undertakes to refute sacrilegious persons and Pharisees. They are madmen who, seeking only to satisfy their madness, overthrow the order established by God himself and maintain divisions between the powers which disturb the Church redeemed by Jesus Christ with his blood.

What name would our author give today, if he were alive, to those who, not content with overturning God’s order by asserting that temporal power comes from men and not from God, also destroy ecclesiastical power, and who, as ignorant as they are impious, attribute to the Vandals [Note: [Col. 0793A] Voltaire, in a pamphlet entitled *The Voice of the Wise Man*.] the distinction between the two powers? The reason that led Hugh to dedicate his treatise to the king of England was to give it greater weight and authority. In this, he says, he followed the example of learned men, who had formerly been accustomed to present their works to kings versed in letters. He asks His Majesty to examine it with wise persons, in order to discover whatever deserves correction.

As for those rash men who overturn the order of things, he foresees that his work will not please them, both because its style will seem crude to them and because it combats their opinion. “For, alas,” he says, “the blind in heart commonly take pleasure in their own blindness and rashness”: *Nam caecis corde plerumque sua, proh dolor! caecitas atque temeritas placet.* He nevertheless exhorts them not to take offence at his style and to prefer truth to eloquence in his discourse: *Malint veros quam disertos audire sermones*—“Let them prefer to hear true rather than eloquent discourses.”

Besides, he knows that there is greater safety in hearing the truth than in proclaiming it oneself: *Tutius veritas auditur quam praedicatur*—“Truth is heard more safely than it is preached.” He therefore asks the bishops and other prelates of the Church who read his book not to believe that he has the presumption and temerity to wish to instruct them, who sit in chairs and have been taught the secrets of divine philosophy.

What we have just related from Hugh of Fleury’s prologue can only give a highly favourable idea of the *Treatise on Royal Power and Priestly Dignity*. It is divided into two books. In the first, after establishing, by the authority of the Apostle, that all power comes from God (chapter 1), that a king is in his kingdom what the head is in the human body (chapter 2), and that he is the image of God the Father (chapter 3), just as a bishop is the image of Jesus Christ, he explains at great length what the duty of a true king consists in (chapter 4). He must employ his office to draw his subjects away from error and bring them back to the paths of equity and justice; in this he can be very useful to the Church.

Our author observes, following a Father of the Church whose words he uses without citing the source, that God often gives peoples kings to govern them according to what they deserve [Note: [Col. 0793A] “Yet the persons of rulers are often granted according to the merits of their subjects; and thus the merits of subjects and rulers are sometimes so joined to one another that, through the fault of the ruler, the life of the [Col. 0794A] subjects becomes worse, and through the merits of the subjects the life of the rulers is changed” (Gregory the Great, *Morals on Job*, book XXV, chapter 20).]; and that there is sometimes so great a connection between the merits of subjects and those who govern them that the life of the subjects becomes more disordered through the fault of the one who leads them, while the prince changes his life through the merit of his subjects.

A good king is a gift of God’s mercy, and a bad king is given as an effect of his wrath, as it is written: “I will give you a king in my fury”; and elsewhere: “He causes the hypocritical man to reign because of the sins of the people.” But whatever kings and princes may be, they must be endured; one must never rashly rise against them by resisting them. In accordance with the Apostle’s precept, if we were under the dominion of a pagan prince, we should have to honour him and patiently endure every treatment he might inflict upon us. We are commanded to pray for them, not to resist them. It is by prayer, not by arms, that evil princes must be resisted. Saint Ambrose opposed to the persecution of the Empress Justina only the continual prayers which he offered to God day and night.

For any prelate to take arms against a king or emperor is rashness and a crime. To resist the powers is to revolt against God himself. Whoever dies bearing arms against his prince dies not as a martyr but as a thief suffering the punishment he deserves. This does not mean, however, that one must obey the authorities if they command evil to be done. If the followers of Jesus Christ owe princes obedience in worldly matters, they owe God their innocence. [Note: [Col. 0794A] “But no one ought to give consent to the authorities for the perpetration of evil; for if earthly service is owed them by worshippers of Christ, innocence is owed to God.”] Therefore, if a Christian should perhaps be compelled either, by obeying them, to violate the rule of justice or innocence, or, by refusing such obedience, to pay any penalty or death, the soul faithful to God should choose rather to lose its fleeting life than to commit guilt. [Note: [Col. 0794A] “Hence, if some Christian should perhaps be compelled either, by obeying them, to break the rule of justice or innocence, or to pay some punishment or death for contempt of this kind, let the soul faithful to God choose rather to lose its fleeting life than to commit guilt.”]

The duty of a good king is to govern his people with fairness and justice (ch. 6), and to defend the Church with all his power. He must be the defender of the orphan, the protector of the widow, and the father of the poor, so that he may say to God with Job: “I was the eye of the blind, the foot of the lame; I carefully investigated cases of which I was not informed.” He must love with all his heart almighty God, who has chosen him to govern thousands of men; and he must love the people entrusted to him as himself. It is also the duty of a great king to adorn and beautify the churches of his kingdom, and to see that religious worship is devoutly maintained in them, after the example of Constantine and many other kings and princes. He must possess the four principal virtues: sobriety, which will make him avoid idleness both of body and mind; justice, which will make him beloved by God and by all sensible people; prudence, which will enable him to distinguish what is just from what is unjust; and temperance, which will prevent him from falling into any excess. It is not enough for him to be adorned with virtues: he must also be educated in letters, so that he may nourish his mind by reading the Holy Books, and may be instructed and strengthened by the examples of great men, ancient and modern. Our author proposes to kings Solomon’s prayer as a model of what they ought to ask from God; and he adds various texts drawn from the books of that king of Jerusalem, [Col. 0795] to instruct them. He requires the prince to reform the morals of his subjects (ch. 7), by exhorting them, instilling fear in them, and himself giving them an example of good; that he show regard for virtuous and wise men; that he receive as oracles of God the counsels given him by holy persons; that he be generous, gracious, calm, cheerful in spirit, truthful in speech, modest in laughter, and so forth; that he possess a learned tongue and a pure faith; that he abhor debauchery, envy, and avarice, the source of all evils; and that his ministers be modest men of sound judgment and good counsel, and so forth.

With regard to kings who depart from the way of God, our author wisely says that the means employed to bring them back must be such that royal majesty is always honoured in them, while sin is nevertheless punished.

> [Note: Col. 0795] “Moreover, in the case of transgressing kings, such remedies must be applied that royal majesty may be honoured in them and guilt punished by the censure of justice. For royal power is placed under the discipline of religion. For although a king is endowed with the summit of power, he is nevertheless held fast by the bond of the Christian faith.” [Col. 0796]

Kings, then, are not, by their dignity and power, exempt from observing the laws of the Church or released from its discipline, to which they are subject through their profession of faith. They must therefore be corrected, not arrogantly, but charitably and with the prudent considerations of wisdom—*charitatis affectu, sapienterque*, “with charitable affection and wisely.” Our author then speaks (ch. 8) of the punishment God inflicts upon kings and princes who disobey his commands. What happened to the first man after his sin happens to them. As soon as he had disobeyed the command of his Creator, he experienced within himself a revolt of his members and the movements of concupiscence rising against his will. The animals, created to be subject to him, shook off the yoke of his dominion and refused obedience. Likewise, it often happens that the subjects of a king rebellious against God rise against him, lay snares for him, and refuse the obedience they owe him. Indeed, as a rule, prevaricating princes perish miserably.

After speaking of royal power, Hugues passes to priestly dignity (ch. 9), whose ministry he extols. The bishop has received from God and Jesus Christ the power to open and shut heaven to men. Kings and powers bow their heads before him, because, although kings and emperors possess supreme authority upon earth, they are bound by the bond of faith: *Quia licet rex vel imperator culmine potestatis sit praeditus, nodo tamen fidei tenetur astrictus*: “For although a king or emperor is endowed with the summit of power, he is nevertheless held fast by the bond of faith.” The bishop must be the salt of the earth by his teaching. He is a king, in order to lead the people; an angel, because he announces good news; a shepherd, because he feeds men with the word of God. Speaking of bad prelates (ch. 11), he complains that this dignity is granted more readily to ambitious and ignorant men than to merit, thereby dishonouring religion and bringing priestly dignity into contempt. Some of them, he says, release persons from the oath of fidelity owed to their lords—an absurdity. He attacks this abuse in the following chapter and censures the indiscreet zeal of pastors who make the severity of discipline serve their hatred and passions in judgments pronounced either against the innocent or in favour of the guilty. Causes must therefore be examined seriously, and only after that examination must the power of binding and loosing be exercised. The bishop must take care not to debase the teaching he preaches by the manner in which he lives: to fail to conform one’s life to it is to debase it and make it contemptible. Nevertheless, whatever his conduct may be, it does not authorize contempt for his person or preaching. That would be contempt for Jesus Christ. The faithful must therefore respect not only bishops, but also priests and clerics; and, even if some of them are blameworthy, that does not make them all contemptible. Besides, all human beings, so long as they are in this corruptible flesh, are liable to make mistakes. But God, to prevent crimes from multiplying through impunity, established kings on earth to punish them with penalties capable of inspiring fear in those who despise his commands. It would be ill-ordered piety to leave crime unpunished, because that would multiply it. Judges, however, must act with great discretion; and for this they must be instructed, so as to distinguish what should be punished from what deserves some indulgence. Thus kings, emperors, and judges do nothing contrary to the command which forbids killing, whether they condemn criminals to death or wage war for just reasons.

Just as kings are established by God upon earth for the punishment of the wicked, so bishops are established in the Church to exercise the power they have received with respect to sinners. There are some whom the bishop must, according to the nature of their offence, separate from the body and blood of Jesus Christ, imposing upon them a penance which they must fulfil in order to be reconciled and restored to the fellowship of the faithful. By the duty of his office, he is obliged to instruct some, correct others, and excommunicate others. Sometimes he delays rebuke, either in order to await a more favourable time or from fear that the person whom he would rebuke might become worse.

These are some of the maxims that our author establishes, on the authority of Scripture and the Fathers, in his first book. There he shows that all power comes from God, and that to resist authorities is to destroy the order established by God himself. Since in this work he exalts temporal power, he seems to have wished to anticipate an objection that might be made to him on this point and to justify himself in the following words: “I do not claim that it is lawful for any king or emperor to do anything contrary to the commandments of God and the holy canons; but I say that, just as a good Christian ought not to obey the laws of kings when they are contrary to the law of God, so one does wrong by failing to obey what they have wisely established. For, as Saint Augustine says, the peace of all things consists in the tranquillity of order.”

Hugues,

> [Note: Col. 0796] Baluze, *Miscellanea*, bk. II, p. 46.

after having solidly proved in the work just discussed that all power comes from God, undertook in a second work to show that God established and placed two powers in his Church, royal and priestly; and that the union and cooperation of these two powers are necessary to secure peace and tranquillity. They are two wings by which the Church rises to heaven; through the pious care of these two powers she has extended from one sea to the other. To prove his point, he goes back to Moses; then he cites Joshua, Samuel, David, Solomon, and others as kings who laboured together with the prophets for the establishment of the Church. He gives the name “Church” to the Synagogue, because what happened then was a figure of what later occurred in the Church established by the blood of Jesus Christ, in which priests hold the place that prophets held in the Synagogue. The Old Testament preceded the New as a figure and shadow, dispelled [Col. 0797] by the light of the Gospel. God, who sent prophets under the old law, sent his Son, who established a new law by shedding his blood to redeem men from eternal death and deliver them from captivity. His disciples, to whom the name apostles was given, preached this new covenant throughout the universe and founded the Church upon Jesus Christ, the cornerstone, in whom the two peoples, Jews and Gentiles, were united to make one people. The Church was established amid the persecutions it endured at the hands of pagan emperors for three hundred years, until Constantine’s conversion; he caused the temples of idols to be closed and churches to be built. On this subject Hugues speaks, in a manner consistent with the prejudices of his age, of the possessions and honours that this emperor granted to the Roman Church. But whatever prerogatives emperors have used to exalt episcopal dignity, bishops have received a far more glorious one from Jesus Christ: the power granted them to open and shut heaven, a power to which princes themselves are subject.

It is the duty of bishops to rebuke kings when they depart from the paths of justice and to bring them back, as is seen in the example of Saint Ambrose, who excluded the great Theodosius from communion and imposed penance upon him, emperor though he was. Such severity toward princes is all the more necessary because their example is more contagious and more capable of carrying the people with it. No Catholic can refuse submission to the laws of the Church, and he must obey the priest who gives him salutary counsel. Our author insists strongly upon the obedience due to bishops, successors and disciples of the apostles; then he returns to what princes have done in favour of the Church and to the services they have rendered her. Among these services he counts the care they have taken to provide her with worthy pastors, and he cites examples. “Therefore,” he says, “the great and holy Pope Gregory, who even today, by the flowers of his eloquence, spreads a sweet fragrance through the holy Church, did not refuse obedience to Emperor Maurice’s command and consented to his ordination.” Before him, Saint Ambrose accepted the prelate’s office of the Church of Milan by order of Valentinian. Saints Ouen and Eligius were likewise raised to the episcopate by King Dagobert and placed, the one in the see of Rouen, the other in that of Noyon. But the Church, wishing to oppose the abuses that soon arose and to set a barrier to the ambition of those who obtained this dignity from irreligious princes by means of money, forbade in a council the ordination of a bishop without the metropolitan’s consent. Popes Gelasius, Celestine, and Leo opposed such an abuse by forbidding recognition as bishop of anyone who had not been elected by the clergy, requested by the people, and ordained by the bishops of the province.

The king must labour to reconcile bishops when division exists among them. In Hugues’s judgment this forms part of the obligations of princes, and he cites several examples to prove it. Valentinian the Younger convened a council to examine the charges brought by Bassus against Pope Sixtus; Sixtus was vindicated and his accuser condemned. Theodoric, king of Italy, took cognizance of the affair occasioned in the Roman Church by the usurpation of the archdeacon Laurence, who wished to seize the see despite the canonical election of Symmachus. To these two examples Hugues adds what Emperor Otto did in the case of Octavian. Hence all the bishops of the kingdom

> [Note: Col. 0797] “All the bishops of his kingdom appear properly to be subject to the king, as a son is found subject to his father—not by nature, but by order—so that the whole kingdom may be reduced to one principle.”

are subject to the king as a son is to his father, by virtue of the order established by God, so that there may be in a state only one governing principle on which everything depends and to which everything is referred. Finally, it belongs to the king to hear all complaints and disputes arising in his realms, prudently examine everything, correct what deserves correction, and establish peace and good order. Therefore, he says, some blame Gregory VII for having been consecrated without first obtaining the emperor’s permission and approval; this caused so many disorders and shed so much blood. Unfortunately, no one is found who discusses this question carefully, examines it prudently, and pronounces an equitable judgment upon it. Our author also censures the decree by which the same Gregory VII forbade anyone to receive from the hand of king or emperor the investiture of a bishopric or abbey. The reason he gives is that holy persons had received investiture from princes; they would not have done so had they believed that they were thereby committing any fault, and God would not have made their holiness known through so many miracles. Yet secular princes, whose greatness inspires pride, often exploit their rank in order to do evil with impunity; and, under the pretext that they are subject to no power, reject the wise counsels of spiritual physicians that might be salutary to them. They would not act thus if they feared God and the fire prepared for the devil and those who imitate him. Here Hugues excuses the liberty he seems to take in criticizing the conduct of persons constituted in dignity, and justifies himself by the example of Saint Paul, who rebuked Saint Peter. Returning to his subject, he cites Pope Nicholas’s decree prescribing what must be observed in the election of a pope, especially the regard that must be shown therein for the emperor, in accordance with Saint Peter’s command: *Subjecti estote omni humanae creaturae, propter Deum, sive regi quasi praecellenti, etc.*: “Be subject, for God’s sake, to every human institution, whether to the king as supreme, etc.” Hugues wishes each power to retain the prerogatives attached to it:

> [Note: Col. 0797] “It is fitting, therefore, that for each power the privilege of its authority always remain safe and unimpaired.” [Col. 0798]

He wishes bishops to imitate the example given them by Jesus Christ their head, and royal power to be honoured. The king, he says, must be the defender of the Church and must therefore be respected not only by prelates but by all those over whom he has authority. This respect is due to the rank God has given him. It is wrong to object that there are few good princes and many bad ones. God places them; he permits them in order to test his elect. We too must therefore endure them, however unjust they may be, not through fear but through charity and love for him who has set them over our heads: *Toleremus malos charitate illius qui eos nobis aequo judicio praetulit atque praeposuit. Legem quippe non implet nisi charitas*: “Let us endure the wicked out of love for him who, by equitable judgment, has preferred and set them over us. For nothing fulfils the law except charity.” Yet the respect due to authorities must not lead us to obey them when they command unjust things. We must then answer that God must be obeyed rather than men, without fearing whatever ill treatment they may threaten us with:

> [Note: Col. 0798] “Finally, if through them—that is, through wicked prelates—the devil incites us by word or presses us by torture to commit evil, let us immediately answer them that we must obey God rather than men.”

In concluding, our author mentions a work he had already composed on the same subject. This work is, as there is reason to believe, none other than the first part of the *Treatise on the Two Powers*. We have dwelt at length upon the extract just given because the importance of the subject appeared to require it. We are persuaded [Col. 0799] that this extract will not displease the reader. He will be pleased to see that, in an age when the unhappy division reigning between the two powers caused so many evils and scandals, and often advanced on both sides so many false and dangerous maxims, there were nevertheless sensible persons who knew how to discern the truth and to walk between the two opposite extremes. Hugues’s treatise is proof of this. In its brevity, this work is especially well suited to give sound ideas of the powers God has established, their rights, their prerogatives, and the obedience due to them. The wise and judicious author of this treatise establishes all that he advances on the authority of Scripture and the Fathers, especially Saint Ambrose, Saint Augustine, and Saint Gregory, in whose writings he was evidently very well versed. Drawing from these pure sources, with which he was very familiar, and following guides so enlightened, he avoided the reefs upon which so many other writers of that time fell: some by attacking ecclesiastical power, others by attacking secular power.

**2.** Another work of Hugues de Sainte-Marie, more substantial in bulk, is his history or chronicle, entitled *Hugonis Floriacensis monachi chronicon*—“Chronicle of Hugh of Fleury, monk.” It is divided into six books. The first contains an abridgment of Jewish history from Abraham to Jesus Christ. In it Hugues treats the ancient monarchies that succeeded one another during that long span, down to the death of Julius Caesar. He identifies the kings who reigned, beginning with Ninus, king of the Assyrians. The great figures of paganism find their place in it; fable is not neglected, though he passes over it lightly, speaking of it only insofar as it serves his purpose: to show God’s governance of humankind during the different ages of the world up to Jesus Christ.

The second book, preceded by a long preface, contains the history of the Scythians, Amazons, and Parthians. In the third, Hugues gives the succession of Roman emperors, from Augustus, under whom Jesus Christ came into the world, to Domitian. Under each emperor he records the popes, apostolic men, persecutions, martyrs, confessors, doctors, heresies, and councils. He follows the same method in the remaining books, all of which are distinguished by particular prefaces. The author carries his history down to Charles the Bald.

It would be wrong to regard this chronology as a tasteless compilation of facts extracted from authors and arranged without art. Since Hugues possessed in his monastery’s library the principal historians and writings necessary for his design, he devoted himself to reading them, comparing them with one another, and extracting what he calls “the marrow of truth,” *medullam veritatis*.

> [Note: Col. 0799] “Rereading ecclesiastical history, published by many historians and comprehended in various ways, I resolved to compress it into this single volume; and, having assembled very many books, to gather their flowers and diligently draw from each the marrow of truth, using the words of those same authors [Col. 0800] in some places, but at other times my own language.”

If he makes extracts, he does so as a skilled historian who knows how to place them aptly and make them his own. It appears that he had before his eyes Eutropius, Justin, Orosius, Gregory of Tours, Einhard, Paul the Deacon, Aimoin, and several other sources that have not come down to us. Thus, as the editor remarks, his history contains many interesting things that had not been written before him, or at least were not commonly available: *Et non pauca aliis intacta, vel saltem non ubivis obvia recenset (praefat.)*: “And he recounts not a few things untouched by others, or at least not everywhere accessible” (*Preface*).

The author’s chief purpose in this history is to instruct readers concerning the principal mysteries of religion, which he accomplishes as a skilled theologian. He mentions no heresy without refuting it, though with great concision. Often the mere account he gives of it is its refutation. This may be observed especially in what he reports concerning Pelagius and his followers.

He does not begin to speak of the French monarchy until his fifth book. For that reason, in the preface at its head he gives a description of Gaul, just as he had given, after Paul the Deacon, a description of Italy in the preface to the third book, which begins with Augustus’s empire. Duchesne inserted this description of Gaul in his first volume of the *Historians of France* (p. 161). Robert Coenal copied it on p. 135 of his history.

We found this chronicle much less extensive in a manuscript in the King’s Library, shelf-mark 4963. This very ancient manuscript may be regarded as original. Its title, in capital letters of the same antiquity, reads: *Incipit liber Historiae ecclesiasticae, gestorumque Romanorum atque Francorum, comprehensus breviter ab Hugone de Sancta Maria*: “Here begins the book of Ecclesiastical History, and of the deeds of the Romans and Franks, briefly comprehended by Hugh of Sainte-Marie.” There follows a dedicatory epistle, hitherto unnoticed, to Adela, countess of Chartres, Blois, and Meaux, a princess who cultivated letters and had the reputation of being a learned woman. “Most serene princess,” the author tells her, “it is altogether right that I should offer this work to you before anyone else: to you, who are most distinguished in our age by birth and virtue, and who enhance the splendour of your rank by your love of learning.” The remainder of the dedicatory epistle confirms what we have already observed: Hugues intended in his history to instruct readers concerning the principal mysteries of religion.

> [Note: Col. 0800] *Praeterea hujus historiae liber nimis profunda latenter continet Ecclesiae sacramenta.* “Moreover, the book of this history secretly contains the Church’s exceedingly profound mysteries.”

He enters into details on this subject that would take too long to report.

In the King’s manuscript, the history is divided into only four books. The first begins with a kind of preamble in which Hugues warns that he carries his work back only to the third age of the world and omits several events reported by Moses. The title of this first book states that Hugh of Sainte-Marie, a Benedictine, composed this history in the year 1109. Yet he carries it only to Louis the Pious, of whom he says nothing. The conclusion, which, although in the same hand, appears to have been added, is like a second dedication. After giving a long recapitulation of the subjects he has treated, Hugues tells the princess that he dedicates his work to her rather than to princes who have no tincture of letters and indeed regard them with contempt: *Non illiteratis principibus, quibus ars litteraria spretui est, sed vobis merito dedicavi*: “I have rightly dedicated it, not to unlettered princes, for whom the literary art is an object of contempt, but to you.” To this epilogue he appends a genealogy of the princess’s ancestors from Rollo, first duke of Normandy, and promises her, in another book, the history both of the Danish and Norman princes, her illustrious ancestors, and of the kings of France from Louis the Pious to his own time.

Although Hugues’s history is less extensive in the manuscript of the King’s Library than in the others we have seen and in the edition published at Münster in 1638, it cannot be called an abridgment. On carefully examining these manuscripts and the printed edition, we observed only additions made in various places that are absent from the King’s manuscript. But everywhere the same historical substance, the same order, and the same expressions remain. From this one may conclude [Col. 0801] that the King’s manuscript contains our author’s history as he first composed it and presented it in that form to the countess of Blois; but that later, after making new discoveries, he revised it and added the material found in other manuscripts and in the printed edition. For example, the comparison he makes at the end of the first book between the learned men of antiquity—the philosophers and the seven sages of Greece—and the patriarchs and prophets inspired by God: this comparison is a substantial addition, of which nothing is found in the King’s manuscript. The third book is preceded in the printed edition by a long preface, likewise absent from the manuscript under discussion. The fifth book corresponds perfectly to the third of the King’s manuscript. Its preface is the same, apart from a few changes that always show the work to have been revised. Finally, the preface to the sixth book, which corresponds to the fourth and last book of the manuscript, is new. We do not speak of the transpositions or the differing division of this history, which is distributed into four books only in the King’s manuscript and into six in those that contain the work as it finally left the author’s hands.

Hugues tells us in his preface to the sixth book that the work of Anastasius the Librarian, of which he had previously had no knowledge, fell into his hands, and that he drew from it many things of which he had formerly been ignorant. The discoveries he made through reading this author, for whom he expresses high regard, undoubtedly led him to revise and enlarge his work. This revised and enlarged work is the History of Hugues de Sainte-Marie found in all the manuscripts. I say “all,” for the King’s manuscript is perhaps the only one containing the history as it first came from the author’s hand, whether because copyists neglected it as less extensive or because Hugues himself contributed to the suppression of his first labour. He spent scarcely more than a year revising and enlarging it and may have offered it to Countess Adela in 1110. But he first sent it to Ivo of Chartres for examination, as we learn from a note at the beginning of the history in a manuscript (Cotton 817) of the Library of Saint-Victor. It states expressly that Hugues, monk of Fleury, or Saint-Benoît-sur-Loire, composed this history for Adela, countess of Blois, Chartres, and Meaux, and sent it to Master Ivo, then bishop of Chartres, in 1110. Until now it has been believed that we possess the letter the author wrote to Ivo when sending him his History; yet the letter does not mention a History. Hugues merely tells Ivo that he is sending him two of his works: *Ecce ego, tibi praecellentissime domine, duo humilitatis meae opuscula transmitto*: “Behold, most eminent lord, I send you two little works of my humility,” without specifying what those two works are. Thus one cannot decide with certainty whether his History was in question, although there can otherwise be no doubt that he sent it to him, given the esteem in which he held the bishop of Chartres and his confidence in his judgment. Moreover, the note already cited says so explicitly: *Eam (historiam) misit magistro Ivoni tunc episcopo Carnotensi*: “He sent it—the history—to Master Ivo, then bishop of Chartres.” The title of the History in certain manuscripts confirms this further: *Historia Hugonis Floriacensis monachi Ivoni*, or *ad Ivonem Carnotensem*: “History of Hugh of Fleury, monk, [addressed] to Ivo,” or “to Ivo of Chartres.” This title has even misled several learned men into believing that the work was dedicated to the bishop of Chartres. But is it plausible that Hugues, having composed his history for Countess Adela—*gratia Adelae comitissae*, “for the sake of Countess Adela”—would have dedicated it to another person? If any doubt remained, Hugues himself removes it and declares most explicitly, in the preface to the sixth book, when addressing the princess:

> [Note: Col. 0801] *Codicem istum tibi merito, o Adela, nobilis comitissa, dicavi; quam non mediocriter eruditam non ambigo, ad deleniendum animum tuum, et acuendam fidem pectoris tui.* “I have rightly dedicated this book to you, O Adela, noble countess, whose learning I do not doubt to be more than moderate, to delight your mind and sharpen the faith of your heart.”

**3.** After Hugues had revised and enlarged his History, he gave serious thought to another work to which he had committed himself by promising the countess to write the deeds both of the Danish and Norman princes, her illustrious ancestors, and of the kings of France from Louis the Pious to his own time. This History has not yet come to light; we possess only the dedicatory epistle published by Dom Martène (*Anecdota*, vol. I, p. 327). It is addressed to Empress Matilda, Adela’s niece, rather than to Adela. This leads us to judge that the pious countess had renounced the world when the work was ready for publication and had already retired to the monastery of Marcigny, where, as is known, she ended her days holily in 1137. Indeed, Hugues appears not to have finished it until the reign of Louis the Fat. For after telling the empress that he had collected the deeds of her ancestors and of the kings of France from Louis the Pious to the prince then reigning—a task, he says, that no one had yet undertaken—he adds that he does not dare join to it that prince’s great deeds, for fear of obscuring them by the lowliness of his style. This presupposes that Louis the Fat had already been on the throne for some time. At the least, it is certain that Matilda bore the title of empress only through her marriage to Emperor Henry V, and that this marriage was celebrated only in 1114. The History under discussion therefore could not have been presented to her in her capacity as empress before that year. Dom Martène did not take this into account when placing the dedicatory epistle in 1110.

We should not pass lightly over our author’s statement that he alone had, until then, undertaken a continuous history from Louis the Pious to his own time. We should conclude that he may be regarded as the original author of this considerable portion of French history. It is highly probable that historians who worked after him drew from this source. Perhaps they did no more than transcribe and insert Hugues’s work into their own writings without naming him, as could readily be shown; and this may be what caused this History to fall into oblivion. It would scarcely be known to us if Dom Martène had not made its dedicatory epistle public.

The two fragments of a chronicle which Duchesne (vol. III, p. 334, and vol. IV, pp. 97–98) inserted in his collection of the Historians of France under the name of Hugh of Sainte-Marie may indeed have been extracted from it. Taken together, these two fragments form a continuous chronology of our kings from the year 997 to 1109. But this chronology does not correspond to the idea one may form of Hugh of Fleury’s work. It contains only dates, dryly marking the beginning and end of reigns, with a few isolated facts and no detail; whereas our author’s work was a collection of the deeds of our kings and of Danish and Norman princes, which he had, with much labour and effort, drawn from several books and different records in which they lay scattered without order or connection. This work was intended to serve as a supplement to the History of which we have spoken [Note: [Col. 0801] “But those matters which we have taken care to cull for you, we did not receive from ourselves, but plucked from many codices by our own labour, as a supplement to that history which we mentioned above and which, as we said before, we recently published.”]. Thus the two fragments reported by Duchesne [Col. 0803A] can be regarded only as a very concise abridgement of this supplement to Hugh of Fleury’s History.

4. Among the works of Ivo of Chartres, in the editions published in 1585 and 1647, as well as in the collection of Historians of France issued by Marquard Freher, there is a short chronicle attributed to the bishop of Chartres. But we subscribe to Duchesne’s judgment, which regards it as a production of Hugh of Fleury. Our author, accustomed to submit his writings to the bishop of Chartres’s criticism and examination, probably sent this work to him; and some inattentive copyist, finding it among the prelate’s writings, attributed it to him. Hugh traces this chronicle back to the origin of the Franks and carries it down to his own time.

All the historical writings of which we have just spoken, although published by the author at different times and dedicated to different persons, nevertheless seem to constitute one and the same work, or one body of history. It would be desirable if some learned person would take the trouble to provide an accurate edition of them, and contrive to discover the part of this history dedicated to the Empress Matilda, of which we possess only the dedicatory epistle. One might perhaps find there matters important for the history of the kings of the third race.

Marquard Freher was the first to bring out Hugh’s History—or rather, a part of it, though in truth the greater part. But when, in 1613, he published in his collection of ancient Historians of France the first four books of this history and the preface to the fifth, he deprived its true author of the credit for the work in order to transfer it to Ivo of Chartres. Yet he cited no manuscript in support of his view and indeed admitted, on the contrary, that no one until then had made any mention of this alleged work by Ivo of Chartres. We shall not conceal, however, that some manuscripts bear the name of the bishop of Chartres. Two may be seen, for example, in the library of Saint-Evroul in Normandy, entitled: *Historia magistri Ivonis* (“History of Master Ivo”). The manuscript in the Emperor’s Library mentioned by Lambecius [Note: [Col. 0803] *Bibl. Caes.*, book II, ch. 8, p. 850.] bears a title still more favourable to Ivo. But these are copyists’ errors. Some ignorant person, copying Hugh’s History, may have read in his exemplar, *Historia Hugonis magistro Ivoni episcopo Carnotensi* (“The History of Hugh [dedicated] to Master Ivo, bishop of Chartres”), or some approximately similar title; and, not knowing Hugh’s name—which may perhaps have been indicated only by its initial—he rashly omitted it. The error subsequently spread into other copies, as ordinarily happens; but no one today doubts that Hugh is the true author of the History which Freher attributes to Ivo of Chartres.

In 1638 Bernard Rottendorf, a learned physician of Münster, had Hugh of Fleury’s History printed in that city under this title: *Hugonis Floriacensis monachi Benedictini chronicon, quingentis abhinc annis, et quod excurrit, conscriptum, Monasterii Westphaliae, typis et impensis Bernardi Raesfeldii*—“Chronicle of Hugh of Fleury, Benedictine monk, written five hundred and more years ago; Münster in Westphalia, printed and published at the expense of Bernard Raesfeld.” It was a quarto volume. Properly speaking, this is the only edition we possess of this history, and it is very rare. The editor appears to have taken every possible care to make it complete; he enriched it with a learned preface and highly interesting notes. Hugh’s letter to Ivo of Chartres, which had not previously been published, is placed immediately after the preface. There follows a prologue in which the plan of the work is set out in nineteen verses. This prologue is addressed to King Louis, whom Dom Mabillon believes to be Louis the Fat; and this is beyond doubt if the prologue is genuinely the author’s. But there is reason to doubt that it is his, since it occurs in none of the manuscripts we have seen. Bernard Rottendorf complains in his preface that the manuscript on which he based his edition was so full of faults of every kind that he could not wholly remedy them. We shall not examine that question here; we observe only that the books are not distinguished in this edition, though they are so distinguished in all the ancient manuscripts, and that we have not found in it the preface to Book VI, beginning with the Emperor Maurice.

We might add various other fragments of chronicle and history printed either in the second part of the contemporary historians published by Pithou and in his collection of the Eleven Ancient Historians of France (p. 83), or in Duchesne’s collection (vol. III, p. 334; vol. IV, p. 97), or finally in Dom Bouquet’s great collection (vol. VIII, pp. 300, 321, 324, 341, 353). Bouquet remarks that several extracts from Hugh’s chronicle were inserted in the chronicles of Saint-Denis, where they are translated into our language.

5. The Life of Saint Sacerdos—or, in abbreviated form, Saint Sardos and Saint Sardot—bishop of Limoges, published by Fr. Labbe (*Bibl. nov.*, vol. II, p. 661) and by the Bollandists under 5 May, is a work of Hugh of Fleury. Our author’s labour consisted solely in correcting and putting into better Latin the Life of this holy prelate, disfigured by copyists and written in the language of the country—that is, in the low Latin still spoken when it was composed. At the request of Arnould, abbot of Sarlat, Hugh undertook this task not about 1130, as Henschenius believed, but at the latest about 1107 or 1108. The proof is plain, since Hugh mentions the Life of Saint Sacerdos, which he had undertaken to correct, in his History, certainly written in 1109 and revised in 1110. In the preface to this Life (*Boll. app. Maii*, p. 593), he warns that, without adhering to the letter, he applied himself especially to expressing its sense, as Abbot Arnould had requested: *Non studeo verbum pro verbo transcribere . . . , sed sensum ex sensu depromere*—“I do not endeavour to transcribe word for word … but to draw forth sense from sense.”

6. The last work of Hugh of Sainte-Marie to have reached us, although it has not yet been printed, is a book on miracles worked in his time through Saint Benedict’s intercession. It continues the collection of Aimoin and Raoul Tortaire, both monks of that abbey and men of distinguished merit. Aimoin had carried it down to 1005 and divided it into three books. We have some extracts from the final book in Duchesne (vol. IV, pp. 142–143). Hugh states in his preface that Raoul had continued this work until his death and had omitted a miracle which occurred in 1059 under Abbot Rainier. It is with this miracle that Hugh begins his work. He then relates nine miracles worked down to 1114; then another performed upon a deaf and mute young man, who was cured of deafness on 4 December 1117 and began to speak on 2 March of the following year. Finally, he concludes his work with the account of three miracles performed in 1119. This work of Hugh of Sainte-Marie is preserved in a manuscript of the Abbey of Saint Benedict.

7. Fr. Lelong, in the *Bibliothèque sacrée* (p. 785), attributes to Hugh, monk of Fleury, a work on the Psalter. Among the manuscripts of Durham Cathedral there is one bearing this title: *Hugo Floriacensis super Psalterium*—“Hugh of Fleury on the Psalter” (*Cat. mss. Angl.*, part IV, no. 299). This is all we can say about this work, which is known to us only through the notices we have reported.

Hugh of Sainte-Marie is an estimable author, deserving particular attention for his [Col. 0805A] *Treatise on the Two Powers*. It is to his credit that he rose above the prejudices of his age and knew how to take the just middle course between two extremes equally defective. Nothing is more exact, wiser, or sounder than what he says concerning royal power and sacerdotal dignity. His writing on this important subject is a precious monument of the Church’s true doctrine, then obscured by the disastrous conflicts between popes and emperors since the pontificate of Gregory VII. The same author’s other works also have merit, especially his history dedicated to Countess Adela. Abbé Lenglet du Fresnoy (*Méthode pour étudier l’histoire*, vol. III, p. 66, ed. 1729) himself admits that it is useful for the later centuries of the Church and Empire. His short chronicle, from 996 to 1109, published by Duchesne (vol. IV, p. 96), is brief but well ordered, in the judgment of Abbé Le Gendre; in few words it contains much matter and is well written. Its style lacks the purity of authors of good Latinity, but it is clear and concise. According to Abbé Lebeuf (*Dissertations sur l’histoire de Paris*, vol. II, p. 174), Hugh has an advantage over the writers of his age which he shares only with Guibert of Nogent: no French writer of the eleventh century, since the death of King Robert, is known to have displayed even the slightest geographical knowledge, except Hugh of Sainte-Marie, monk of Fleury, who perhaps, Lebeuf adds, merely copied some exemplars of Aimoin. We do not see on what basis such a suspicion can rest. It was not by acting as a copyist, but by drawing from sources and reading historians, that our author acquired his learning and made himself capable of composing good works of his own, as we have shown in speaking of his History.

# HISTORICAL WORKS OF HUGH OF FLEURY

(Edited by Georg Waitz in PERTZ, *Monumenta Germaniae Historica*, *Scriptores*, vol. IX, p. 337.)

[Col. 0805]

# PROLEGOMENA

[Col. 0805A] In the first years of the twelfth century, learned men in different parts of Gaul and Germany were devoting themselves to recounting both ancient and more recent history; several, as though guided by a single purpose, undertook the composition of larger chronicles, by which they might transmit to their own age, in a suitably concise form, especially the ancient public and ecclesiastical affairs. At almost the same time we see Ekkehard among the Germans, Sigebert among the Belgians, and Hugh of Fleury among the Franks engaged in this task—men certainly distinguished for learning, who were also by no means remote from the public affairs then being conducted and claimed a part for themselves in that conflict which the Church was waging against royal and imperial power.

This Hugh, whom we now publish, like Ekkehard [Col. 0805B] was not satisfied with undertaking and completing one book, nor with one edition; rather, again and again, he judged that nearly the same matters should be set forth in another form. Moreover, books written by him were soon enlarged and continued by others; as a result, they acquired among the Franks nearly the same authority which the writers mentioned above are well known to have possessed elsewhere. But, as often happens, others also claimed for themselves the fruits of Hugh’s diligence; negligent scribes of manuscripts attributed now others’ works to him, now his own works to others. Since many such errors had already arisen in the Middle Ages, editors in more recent times added new ones and thus [Col. 0806A] entangled the matter so that it became exceedingly difficult to say which works were Hugh’s and which should be ascribed to others. It was therefore necessary to return to the manuscript codices. Catalogues reported that a great number of these existed in public libraries, especially in that very rich Parisian treasure-house of books, from which I rejoice greatly still to have been able to draw for several months. Having carefully examined the codices preserved there and compared them with what learned men have noted concerning the Bern, Brussels, Vienna, and other manuscripts, I think I have achieved this result: Hugh’s chronicles and histories, and those of others, can now be accurately identified and distinguished.

Hugh of Fleury first composed an *Ecclesiastical History*, arranged in four books, down to the death of Charlemagne [Col. 0806B], and dedicated it to Adela, countess of Blois, Meaux, and Chartres. He added a preface and an epilogue in which he explained the work’s plan and use. He wished to comprehend in one small book what was contained in several volumes, and in preparing it repeatedly declared that he had taken especial care to be concise. At times he also altered his plan while writing: at first he thought he should treat heresies more fully, but then, deterred by the abundance of material, he decided to omit them [Note: [Col. 0805] Preface to Books III and IV.]. He proceeds no further than Charlemagne’s reign, but promises that in another book he will set forth the deeds of the Frankish kings from Emperor Louis down to his own time [Col. 0807A] [Note: [Col. 0807D] Epilogue.]. The author himself indicates 1109 as the date of this first work’s composition [Note: [Col. 0807D] Title of the book.].

Not long afterward, Hugh obtained the *Tripartite History*, translated by Anastasius from Greek into Latin, and found there much that had hitherto escaped him [Note: [Col. 0807D] *Ecclesiastical History*, second edition, preface to Book VI.]. This circumstance especially seems to have induced him to prepare a new edition of his work, divided into six books [Note: [Col. 0807D] Cf. *Histoire littéraire*, X, p. 299.]. In the prologue to Book VI he addresses the same Countess Adela: “I have rightly dedicated this codex to you, noble Countess Adela … hoping that, on this occasion also, the memorial of your name may be distinguished to no small degree.” In this edition he arranged much material more suitably, added certain things, especially of theological argument, and discussed disputed questions at greater length in the prologues and elsewhere [Col. 0807B]; yet he cut out other matters or rendered them briefer. He carried the thread of his narrative down to the year 855. Certain manuscripts attest that this was done in 1110, and there is nothing to prevent us from trusting them.

The most excellent manuscript of the earlier edition is the Paris Royal manuscript no. 4963, parchment, early twelfth century, small folio, accurately and carefully written—perhaps the very manuscript which Hugh arranged to have copied from his own exemplar and sent to Adela. Others are Bern no. 208, thirteenth century (*Archiv*, V, p. 489); Vatican, Biblioteca Christiana no. 905, formerly of St Mary of Pontigny, early thirteenth century [Note: [Col. 0807D] In this volume, examined by Bethmann, Hugh is preceded by Dares Phrygius, the *History of Apollonius*, Adémar’s Chronicle, and Paul the Deacon’s *History of the Lombards*; there follow *Names of Regions*.]; and perhaps Oxford, Bodleian no. 599 (*Archiv*, VII, p. 526).

There are more manuscripts of the other edition, both complete [Col. 0807C] and genuine, and enlarged by continuations, or altered and interpolated in individual places. Among them belong the Paris manuscripts of Saint-Victor, no. 311, twelfth century, folio; likewise no. 580, twelfth century, folio; the Royal no. 5013 A, twelfth century, where the beginning of Book I is missing; and no. 4963 B, thirteenth century, folio.—A continuation was added by the manuscript formerly of Saint-Magloire in Paris, now Saint-Germain François Harlay no. 485, parchment, twelfth century, quarto; from it were copied Royal no. 4963 A, thirteenth century, folio, and no. 5009, thirteenth century. In the latter, moreover, the prologue to Book IV is missing. The same manuscripts also contain Hugh’s letter addressed to Ivo of Chartres.—The same letter, though not the continuation [Col. 0808A] just mentioned, is found in Paris, in the library called the Arsenal, manuscript no. 16, twelfth or thirteenth century, folio; there the prefaces to Books IV and VI are omitted [Note: [Col. 0807D] But a genealogy of the Frankish kings is added: “This is the lineage from which King Charles arose. Priam … Eustace, Godfrey, now Duke of Lotharingia, and Duke Baldwin.”].

That Hugh sent this *Ecclesiastical History* to Ivo of Chartres is attested also by another manuscript of Saint-Victor [Note: [Col. 0807D] *Histoire littéraire*, loc. cit., p. 300: “He sent it to Master Ivo, then bishop of Chartres.” I have not seen this manuscript.]; but whether the letter just mentioned belongs to this work or was given on another occasion is uncertain. For it is also read in manuscripts very different from these, of which we shall speak below.

We must now enumerate those manuscripts which contain precisely the same work, save only for the prologue to Book VI, but either leave the author wholly unnamed or call him Ivo of Chartres. Most belong to this class: Paris no. 4890; Vienna, *Historia profana* no. 682; several London and Oxford manuscripts; and a Dublin manuscript, listed in vol. V of the *Annals*—some written in the thirteenth century, others in more recent times [Note: [Col. 0807D] The Monte Cassino manuscript no. 533, fifteenth century, examined by Bethmann, also belongs here.]. They are commonly entitled thus: “Here begin excerpts of Ivo, the venerable bishop of Chartres: first concerning the deeds of certain Assyrian kings, and the deeds of all Roman emperors, and finally concerning Charlemagne, king of the Franks, and his son Louis the Pious.” The Cambridge manuscript, Corpus Christi no. 265, omits both this title and Hugh’s name. Everywhere the prefaces and headings of the books are either confused or wholly absent [Note: [Col. 0807D] In Paris manuscript no. 4890, the preface to Book II is entitled, “Here begins a certain preface”; Book II, “On the situation of Scythia and the diverse peoples of that region and their customs”; the preface to Book III, “Here begin selections from ecclesiastical history”; Book III, “On Octavian Augustus, who after Julius Caesar obtained the monarchy of the Roman Empire.” Then follows, “Here begins the fourth prologue”; when Book IV is completed, again, “Here begins Prologue IV.” Thereafter nothing of the kind is found. In the Cambridge manuscript, apparently only the end of Book I and the beginning of Book II are indicated (*Archiv*, III, p. 526); in the editions of Rottendorf and Freher these are entirely absent.]. Rottendorf seems to have obtained a similar exemplar, which he published at Münster in 1636 under Hugh’s true name. Freher, however, had already made public the first part of the Chronicle down to the beginning of [Col. 0808C] Book V; led by the title just cited, he attributed it to Ivo.

Many long ago perceived that he was wrong. Certainly, the contents of these excerpts of Ivo and of Hugh’s *Ecclesiastical History* are wholly identical, so that scarcely a word appears to have been deliberately changed or added. I would note only that numbers were added to the emperors’ names; the other discrepancies I would attribute to scribal carelessness. Nor should Hugh be thought to have transformed his *Ecclesiastical History* into a Chronicle [Note: [Col. 0808D] I can no longer understand on what basis rested what I myself wrote in *Archiv*, VII, p. 526, concerning a Chronicle of Hugh dedicated to King Louis; certainly I have never read anything on this subject in the manuscripts. What Pertz adduces in *Archiv*, V, p. 489, concerning the difference between the *Ecclesiastical History* and the Chronicle refers to the other Chronicle carried farther forward, to be discussed below.]; rather, some unknown person prefixed his friend’s name to Hugh’s book after it had been deprived of its title and of that preface to Book VI.

[Col. 0809A] Once these works have been restored to Hugh, it is necessary to deny him others.

Duchesne (*Hist. Franc. SS.*, III, pp. 347–349; IV, pp. 142–143) published, as he says, a fragment of the *Chronicle of Brother Hugh, monk of Fleury*, which he asserts was sent to Ivo of Chartres and differs from Hugh’s other books. He used a Paris Royal manuscript, either that now numbered 4963 A or another numbered 5009. I have said above that both were enlarged by a continuation; Duchesne published only this continuation, beginning from the time of Louis, son of Charles the Bald, but wrongly attributed even this to Hugh.

As I noted above [Note: [Col. 0809D] Col. 807.], there survives another Paris manuscript, formerly of Saint-Magloire, written in the early twelfth century, which seems to explain the matter well. In it, Hugh’s *Ecclesiastical History* is first copied exactly as it is read in the genuine manuscripts; afterward, on an inserted leaf, the letter addressed to Ivo is added; and at the end the red words, “Here ends the book of Ecclesiastical History,” have been erased, and in another hand there is added the continuation: “When he was setting out for Rome on his second journey … in the year of the Lord 1034 the city of Paris was consumed by fire.” That this occurred at the monastery of Saint-Magloire is established by the inserted notice of Saint Magloire’s relics having been transferred to Paris. Not a word is found about the monastery of Fleury; virtually everything narrated concerns the city and church of Sens and its neighbouring regions. Most of it agrees so closely with the Annals of Saint-Columba of Sens and with Odorannus’s Chronicle of Sens that it is apparent at first sight that they were drawn from the same sources [Col. 0809C]. This same short History of the Franks of Sens was published in full down to 1015 by Duchesne himself (III, pp. 349–354), from an old manuscript in the library of Alexandre Pétau, which probably later went to Rome, together with that man’s other most excellent books. It begins in 688, but soon passes to the ninth century. From this work, therefore, that monk of Saint-Magloire took up and continued the thread of narrative interrupted by Hugh, adding nothing of his own except the brief mention of his patron and, at the end, the death of King Robert and the Paris fire. I can firmly maintain, after carefully comparing them, that the other Paris manuscripts were copied from the Saint-Magloire manuscript [Note: [Col. 0809D] These manuscripts agree with each other even in particular and erroneous readings. The Saint-Magloire manuscript is older than the others, and its different parts are written by different hands; whereas Royal manuscripts no. 4963 A and 5009, in one hand, present both Hugh’s book and that continuation.]. This being so, everyone will be convinced that this continuation is not Hugh’s. Yet the other Chronicle attributed to Hugh (see below, col. 812), and Hugh himself, incorporated fragments of this book in another Chronicle; Clarius, moreover, copied it more fully in the Chronicle of Saint-Pierre-le-Vif, as did Aimoin’s continuator. The latter’s work, in these sections (edition, book V, chapters 42–47), is composed from the History of Sens and from the accounts which Aimoin himself gave in his book *On the Miracles of Saint Benedict* concerning the kings of the Franks; he inserted only a few matters concerning the monastery of Saint-Germain [Col. 0810A]. As a result, that history acquired no ordinary authority, sometimes under Hugh’s name and sometimes under Aimoin’s, although it is correctly attributed to neither.

There is also a manuscript formerly of Fossat, now Bern no. 324 (*Archiv*, V, p. 491 ff.), which must likewise be derived from the Saint-Magloire manuscript, but which mingles into both Hugh’s work and the History of Sens many matters illustrating the origin and history of the monastery of Fossat. It scarcely needs warning that these must not be foisted upon our Hugh of Fleury.

Having explained these matters, let us return to Hugh, who himself also undertook to narrate the later history of the Franks. For he wrote a book which, to use his own words, “contains the deeds of the modern kings of the Franks,” dedicated to Empress Matilda, daughter of Henry, king of England [Col. 0810B]. In this work he accomplished what he had promised Adela, and believed that he had satisfied others’ wishes as well, since no one seemed to have comprehended recent Frankish history in a single volume [Note: [Col. 0810D] Preface to Matilda.]. This could perhaps rightly be said, since the books of Ralph Glaber, Hugh of Flavigny, and others contained not only the history of the Franks but that of the whole world, while the History of Sens and similar small works were more concise. This book, by far the most useful of all Hugh’s works, long remained hidden from posterity and brought no great fame to its author. Only one complete manuscript survives, so far as I know—formerly of Saint-Trond, now at Liège, written in the early twelfth century. Another, defective manuscript is preserved in the Paris library, no. 6186, thirteenth or fourteenth century, from which Martène first published the preface (*Thesaurus anecdotorum*, I, p. 327). Then the collection of French historical writers established by Bouquet made public some fragments (VIII, pp. 317–321; XII, pp. 9–10), followed by the greater part of the book from the Saint-Trond manuscript (XII, pp. 792–799). The History runs down to King Philip’s death in 1108, but was begun some years later, since Matilda, who is called empress, did not marry Emperor Henry until 1114.

There are also other works which bear Hugh’s name, if not in the manuscripts themselves, at least in titles assigned by modern writers. We must inquire whether they truly belong to him.

[Col. 0810D] In two manuscripts—Bern no. 90, twelfth century (*Archiv*, V, p. 489), and Brussels, thirteenth century (*Archiv*, VII, p. 529)—there is found a large collection of ecclesiastical and secular matters, especially Frankish matters. It is preceded by Hugh’s letter to Ivo, already mentioned several times. Its text is as follows:

“To the glorious and wise Ivo, bishop of Chartres, Brother Hugh, monk of the monastery of Saint Benedict at Fleury.

[Col. 0811A] Behold, most eminent father and lord, I send you two small works of my humility [Note: [Col. 0811D] The remainder, not copied from the manuscript, I reproduce from Rottendorf’s edition, who included this letter from Pétau’s manuscript.], so that, if you see anything in them unseemly or unpolished, you may correct and embellish it with the file of your prudence, and may strengthen and confirm what pleases you. These small works which you now see are [the text reads *suum*; perhaps *sunt*] my weapons against idleness; for I prefer to be occupied with study rather than, like a useless beast, to spend my life in idleness and lethargy. But I desire that all these things be examined by your judgment and seasoned by your wisdom, since what the bond of your authority has once strengthened cannot waver. Yet perhaps someone will say to me: ‘Why did you not blush to send such worthless and useless things to a prudent man seated on the summit of philosophy, when you know it is written: “Prayer and song have little grace unless their eloquence is supreme”?’ To this I reply [Col. 0811B] that I prefer to be approved by the just judgment of a wise man rather than condemned by the opinion of arrogant men. Yet, most honourable father, it is laborious to apply the additions and deletions of your integrity to this volume. But the fruit of labour—charity—is more precious than gold. Farewell.”

I said above, cols. 807–808, that these same letters were prefixed without cause by some scribe to the *Ecclesiastical History*; and I doubt whether they were placed more properly at the beginning of this work. Certainly no Chronicle is mentioned; indeed, two small works are named, which are commended to the criticism and judgment of Ivo, “seated on the summit of philosophy” [Note: [Col. 0811D] In *Archiv*, VII, p. 529, I suspected that the two small works were the *Ecclesiastical History* and the *Deeds of the Modern Franks* joined in this volume; but neither work is actually found there, nor do Hugh’s words seem to indicate them. In the Brussels manuscript the letter is headed: “Here begins the prologue of Hugh, monk of Fleury, to histories of antiquities”; how little this accords with the letter is easily understood.]. And what is added seems to refer rather to some theological or philosophical book—works of which Hugh is known to have written—than to a historical or chronological work [Col. 0811C]. This being so, I should scarcely think that the letter should be referred to that collection of Frankish materials.

The collection in the manuscripts named above contains the following. First is an account of ancient affairs, so similar in arrangement, wording, and even in the prefaces themselves to Hugh’s *Ecclesiastical History* that one seems to be reading almost the same book [Note: [Col. 0811D] Cf. *Archiv*, V, p. 490; VII, p. 530.]. The Brussels manuscript breaks off the thread of the narrative in Book VI before Charlemagne’s time and inserts, apparently in full, Paul the Deacon’s *History of the Lombards*; beneath it are placed Frankish affairs, both ancient and more recent. These begin with the time of Carloman and Charles, preceded by the rubric: “Here begins the book on the deeds of the most glorious Carloman, Roman emperor and king of the Franks” [Note: [Col. 0811D] Thus Bethmann noted.], and continue to 1108. After this begins a new book of Frankish affairs, which, we shall say below [Col. 0812A], belongs to the monastery of Saint-Denis. The Bern manuscript is otherwise arranged. It omits the *History of the Lombards* and in its place presents the familiar *Deeds of the Franks*, with a continuation concerning the mayors of the palace. When these are finished, it continues to narrate Frankish history, so that from Charlemagne’s time onward these passages agree completely with the Brussels manuscript; nor is the final book of Frankish affairs absent.
