Leaving this aside for the moment, if we examine the preceding history more closely and investigate its sources and parts, we shall first discover the latter part of the *Ecclesiastical History*, enlarged with extensive passages taken from Einhard’s *Life of Charles*, the *Life of Louis*, and so forth. To this are added diverse extracts from the chronicles of Ado and Flodoard, from the History of Sens, and from other books. Moreover, the *History* of William of Jumièges, copied almost word for word, fills out its pages; only a few matters concern the monastery of Fleury or elucidate events in its vicinity. Duchesne arranged for only a small portion of this work to be printed (IV, pp. 148–150) from Pétau’s manuscript, omitting the passages copied from William—whether the manuscript or, as I think more likely [Note: [Col. 0812D] Here and there, by placing the sign “. . . . .”, the editor himself appears to indicate that some passages have been omitted. Bouquet’s continuators have already correctly observed that the text published by Duchesne is composed from Hugh’s and William’s works: XI, p. 158, note b.], the editor cut them out. Yet Hugh can scarcely [Note: [Col. 0812D] Hugh did not employ the *Life of King Louis* elsewhere, and perhaps did not even possess William of Jumièges; cf. below, cols. 815–816.] be thought ever to have compiled so vast a collection, since he always took the greatest care for brevity and a fitting arrangement of material. Moreover, the part that appears genuine and indicative of the Fleury author is also transmitted separately.

[Col. 0812C] There are three Parisian manuscripts. One is the Royal manuscript no. 5943 B, formerly P, Pithou’s, later Thuanus’s and Colbert’s, of the twelfth century, folio; there, after other historical works, is read a short history of the Franks, without any title, from Lothair, son of Louis the Pious, down to the year 1108. Another is Notre-Dame no. 135, of the thirteenth century, folio, which, defective at the beginning, starts in the middle of the Frankish history from the time of Pippin, yet everywhere agrees exactly with the preceding manuscript. The third is Saint-Germain no. 1085 (formerly 646), of the thirteenth century, where on fols. 6–12 the same work occurs complete, beginning thus: “Merovech was of the race of Priam,” etc.

Duchesne published its final part (IV, pp. 96–98) from the Thuanus manuscript, that is, the Royal manuscript just mentioned. Bouquet’s continuators used another manuscript (X, p. 215; XI, p. 158; XII, p. 8), and did not hesitate to ascribe these writings to Hugh of Fleury.

[Note: [Col. 0812D] Compare XI, p. 158, note a, although at X, p. 215, note a, they said that these materials were drawn from Hugh. Less correctly, at XII, p. 8, they treat this short history and that modern history of the kings of the Franks as one and the same.]

I too must agree with them. For what is read in this book agrees so closely with that modern history [Col. 0813A] that one readily recognizes the same origin. Yet neither can have been copied from the other, nor should Hugh be thought to have used another man’s book down to his own times. These facts therefore indicate the same author, treating the same events in a similar manner at different times: in one short work he recounts more briefly only the affairs of the kings of the Franks, while in the other, written for the Empress Matilda, he also touches upon the history of other regions.

I would call the Frankish history the later work, since it not only treats individual events more fully and accurately,

[Note: [Col. 0813D] Compare chapter 1, concerning King Odo; chapter 3, concerning the miracle performed at Fleury; chapter 6, concerning Abbot Wulfald; chapter 9, concerning Abbot Gauzlin; chapter 10, concerning the wars of King Henry and the coronation of Philip; chapter 11, concerning Philip’s wife.]

but is also sometimes better arranged and corrects errors made in the earlier book.

[Note: [Col. 0813D] Thus in chapter 8 it corrected Hugh’s eleven years to nine; in chapter 11 it more correctly called Philip’s daughter Constance, while it certainly avoided other errors by passing over them in silence.]

Elsewhere indeed it happened to the writer that he later omitted a true account and accepted a false one.

[Note: [Col. 0813D] Compare what is said in both books, chapter 9, concerning Constance, wife of King Robert; in one he followed Aimoin.]

[Col. 0813B] Duchesne published another fragment of a Frankish history (III, pp. 334–346), omitting its conclusion, which, he said, agreed exactly with the book of Hugh published at IV, p. 96. But in the earlier portion too you will detect traces of Hugh, although entangled with certain additions which Duchesne had taken from the manuscript of Saint-Magloire. Once these are removed, we again have material agreeing with the Modern History; and I scarcely doubt that the Loisel manuscript used here by Duchesne contains either the same work or one very similar, which in the Saint-Magloire manuscript was enlarged by new interpolations. Take care, however, not to confuse this book with the other from the same monastery mentioned above.

Pithou, *Scriptores coaetanei*, vol. I, p. 407 (p. 510 of the Frankfurt edition [Col. 0813C]), vol. II, p. 83, and Duchesne (II, p. 630; IV, p. 85), likewise published from Fleury and Thuanus manuscripts a history of the Franks continued to the year 1110. It too belongs among works connected with Hugh and is linked by a certain resemblance especially with the Modern History of the Franks. But its style is more copious and elegant, and you will find much that is foreign both to Hugh’s works and to his thought.

[Note: [Col. 0813D] Compare what is narrated concerning Pope Gregory and King Henry, excerpted below under chapter 11. In the same way, Flemish affairs are narrated there more accurately. Moreover, this book is fuller in narrating Spanish and other affairs.]

Accordingly, you will judge this work to have been compiled from the books of Hugh and others rather than composed by Hugh himself.

It remains to speak of another short history of the Franks, which we see placed at the end of the volume in Brussels and Berne manuscripts. This has almost nothing in common with Hugh, but in its later part rests upon the continuation of Aimoin.

[Note: [Col. 0813D] Chapters 42–47. Upon examining the Parisian autograph manuscript, Saint-Germain no. 436, I soon recognized that in this chapter the first and old hand of the continuation ends. The final words of this part are: [Col. 0814D] “After him the aforesaid king, together with the queen, appointed Adraldus abbot.” After this, a few lines have been erased. Long afterward, another part of chapter 49 and a further continuation were added.]

Elsewhere, however, it especially concerns the monastery of Saint-Denis near Paris and presents highly fabulous stories,

[Note: [Col. 0814D] Compare chapter 18 concerning Charlemagne; chapters 22 and 23 concerning Charles the Bald.]

such as we know to have arisen and spread there.

[Note: [Col. 0814D] Narratives of this sort are also read in Saint-Germain manuscript no. 1085 (see above, col. 812), fols. 1–6, and likewise on fol. 34, where the beginning of this history bears the title: “Supplements to the History of Gregory of Tours and other fragments of this and other books.”]

It chiefly follows historical notices and books written there—I mean the *Deeds of Dagobert* and the fragment *On the Coronation of King Pippin and His Sons*.

[Note: [Col. 0814D] Published by Bouquet, V, p. 9, from a Saint-Denis manuscript.]

Yet it mentions the monastery of Fleury in only one place.

[Note: [Col. 0814D] Chapter 13.]

Furthermore, it pieced together the earlier part of its book from the *Deeds of the Franks*, the epitomized History of Fredegar, and Paul the Deacon, and appended to it the little book *On the Mayors of the Palace*. These are almost the same works that we see united in that great collection of Frankish materials.

[Col. 0814B] Yet, while the writer retained the little book *On the Mayors of the Palace* and other materials almost word for word, in the first part of the book he used the sources named above more freely. Perhaps he should be judged not to have employed those very sources, but rather to have had some compendium of an older Frankish history,

[Note: [Col. 0814D] You might perhaps call this a Fleury work, for it contains the passage indicated at no. 30. Moreover, remember that the little book *On the Mayors of the Palace* was also published by Pithou from a Fleury manuscript.]

similar to that little book, which he joined to the succeeding materials. Finally, from the letter of the Synod of Quierzy, written to King Louis in 858, he admitted two fragments,

[Note: [Col. 0814D] Chapters 15 and 17.]

while by his own efforts he merely recounted briefly the deeds of the latest kings. If these writings are compared with Hugh’s works, no one would wish to ascribe them to him.

The same history, beginning with the well-known words, “Antenor and the other exiles,” was soon afterward enlarged with certain additions and a brief continuation down to 1137, and was thus copied many times [Col. 0814C]; it was also greatly expanded by new additions as time passed. Manuscripts of this kind are Paris, Royal no. 5999 (*Archiv*, VII, p. 65); Lyons, Latin no. 20 (ibid., p. 133); Paris, Royal nos. 4937 and 4938; and others. *Abbreviation of the Deeds of the Kings of France* is the title under which Bouquet admitted several fragments of it into his collection (VI, p. 238; VII, p. 255; X, p. 236; XI, p. 213; XII, p. 67), using the Parisian manuscripts just mentioned and another, Saint-Victor no. 419. For the continuations, see the same work (XII, p. 285; XVII, p. 432).

Finally, a very short history of the Franks, down to about the year [Col. 0815A] 1108, has often been published under the name of Ivo (*Works of Ivo*, and Freher’s *Corpus historiarum*, pp. 51–54), though some prefer to attribute it to Hugh.

[Note: [Col. 0815D] *Histoire littéraire*, loc. cit., p. 302.]

But it contains nothing indicative of his talent or style.

Having set these matters forth, we have seen that four works should be attributed to Hugh: three bearing his name, and a fourth lacking a title in the manuscripts. They are:

A. *Ecclesiastical History*, arranged in four books;

B. The same work, issued in six books;

C. A brief and concise *History of the Franks*;

D. *Deeds of the Modern Kings of the Franks*.

The former works (A and B) concern only ancient history and aim to collect matters narrated by others and present them more briefly. In compiling them Hugh used the same sources which are known to have been current among most medieval writers [Col. 0815B]: ancient chronographers and ecclesiastical and Roman histories. To these must be added Anastasius’s *Tripartite History*, discovered later than Hugh. In the final pages of the little books Hugh chiefly follows Ado and Einhard. In the second edition he gives certain information concerning the monastery of Fleury which is found in other words in the book of the *Miracles of Saint Benedict*; and he has only a few peculiar items.

Thus in these books he can be praised only for his diligence in collecting and arranging; nor do they excel in that abundance of learning which we admire in Ekkehard, Sigebert, and others. The explanations Hugh added would now please few, though they reveal an upright mind and a sincere spirit.

The *History of the Franks* also, and the *Modern Deeds of the Franks*, rest in large measure upon other authors. Hugh, in his habitual manner, does not always copy them word for word, but follows them in such a way as to shorten their longer narratives and combine them with others. The books particularly at hand were the *Annals of Saint-Bertin* and the short Fleury annals;

[Note: [Col. 0815D] *Monumenta SS.*, II, p. 254 (*Patrologia*, vol. CXXXIX, col. 582). He followed them in chapters 2 and 9.]

Flodoard’s *Chronicle*, the History of Sens, Aimoin of Fleury’s books *On the Miracles of Saint Benedict*,

[Note: [Col. 0815D] Yet he follows this author of the same monastery more rarely. For most of the things he might have furnished here passed into the Chronicle of Saint-Bénigne of Dijon, and from it into the books of Hugh of Flavigny, whom our Hugh valued highly. The Dijon Chronicle, apparently not widely circulated in the Middle Ages, should not be reckoned among Fleury’s resources.]

and Hugh of Flavigny’s *History of Verdun*.

[Note: [Col. 0815D] To this should also be referred matters which agree with the narrative of Rodulfus Glaber; Hugh himself does not seem to have examined Rodulfus’s books.]

Our author describes the Norse expeditions more fully, and there agrees with William of Jumièges in many matters. Yet he never retains William’s actual words, and in not a few places [Col. 0816A] departs further from him even in the events narrated, so that he appears to have used another history of this people, drawn either from William himself or at least from a common source—perhaps the one which I read in Paris, Saint-Germain manuscript no. 1085, fol. 70 verso–82.

[Note: [Col. 0815D] I noted the following about the book: fol. 70 verso: “Here begins the prologue to the book of the deeds of the people of the Northmen. ‘When the Frankish people, having recovered its strength’—and let our pen return to its subject. Here ends the prologue. Here begins Book I. ‘Therefore another column of the Goths,’ etc.” It extends down to the time when England was occupied by William.—In that compilation of the Berne and Brussels manuscripts, these Norse materials are almost everywhere omitted [Col. 0816D], and excerpts from William have been inserted in their place.]

He recounts the First Expedition to Jerusalem in such a way as chiefly to follow the *Deeds of the Franks and Other Pilgrims to Jerusalem* (Bongars, I, p. 1 ff.), though at times he seems to approach more closely the History of Baldric of Dol, drawn from those writings. I would therefore almost determine that Hugh read both books.

[Note: [Col. 0816D] He himself says: “Of this we have offered a slight preliminary taste, because we have already learned that the fullness of this history has been written elsewhere.”]

Hugh added here and there certain matters of his own, especially concerning monasteries founded, events at Fleury, and other matters pertaining to the royal family. The writer’s narrative is everywhere brief [Col. 0816B] and is not free from serious errors, which he either received from others or committed himself.

[Note: [Col. 0816D] Hugh very often errs in indicating years; I have tried to correct this in the margin and notes. Most additions he makes to the words of his sources are false; but sometimes he either misunderstood their plain words or deliberately distorted them. Some things he himself corrected and arranged better in the other History of the Franks.]

Yet it also contains much which you would seek elsewhere in vain; and so, amid so great a scarcity of writers on Gallic affairs, we ought to value these works highly. Hugh employs a simple and rather unpolished style, such as one would scarcely expect from a learned writer approved also by other works.

For Hugh, monk of Fleury, was a man distinguished in his age for learning and adorned with no small praise by many. He himself indicated his native place. In the margin of Paris Royal manuscript no. 4963, the first edition of the *Ecclesiastical History*, one reads at the beginning of the epilogue: “Hugh, who culled this little book from diverse manuscripts, is called Hugh of Sainte-Marie, after a certain small village of his father, in which is situated the church of Saint Mary, Mother of God.” In the same way he is frequently designated in titles of books; there he is called monk or pupil of Saint Benedict of Fleury.

[Note: [Col. 0816D] Entirely different is the other Hugh of Fleury, our author’s contemporary, but monk and afterward abbot of Saint Augustine’s, Canterbury. Concerning him, see W. Thorne, *Chronicle of the Monastery of Saint Augustine*, chapter 9, in Twysden and Selden, *Scriptores rerum Anglicarum*, II, p. 1794. Hugh of Fleury, or of Flori, is called a Norman knight who came to England with William I and “served in military service for a long time” both under him and under his son William II, Rufus. In 1090 he entered the monastery; in the following year he was appointed abbot; and he died in 1124.]

It is not known when he entered this monastery, but he lived there at the opening of the twelfth century and increased the glory of the ancient Church by his writings. He seems to have been connected by some familiarity with the most eminent men and women of his time. He dedicated his histories both to Countess Adela and to the Empress Matilda; he addressed another book, and a most important one, to Matilda’s father Henry, king of the English: *On Royal Power and Priestly Dignity*. In it he endeavored to settle the dispute between kingdom and Church and restore it to a just and equitable [Col. 0817A] peace. From the address of its prologue, it is sufficiently clear that the other Hugh of Fleury cannot at all be thought of as the author of this book.

In the first book Hugh tries to show that royal power was established by God and is therefore in a sense sacred and by no means alien from ecclesiastical matters. In the second, he proves with many arguments and confirms by examples drawn from ancient and more recent history that royal and priestly authority ought to be joined together, “so that both, faithfully adhering to one another, may be mutually associated and bound together.” Throughout he displays sound judgment and a disposition not excessively favorable to the Church; and, since Ivo of Chartres, Hugh’s friend, defended almost the same opinion, it came about that the dispute seemed to others also capable of settlement in the manner indicated by these men.

[Note: [Col. 0817C] On this matter compare Stenzel, *Frankische Kayser*, I, p. 689 ff. See especially Hugh’s passage, I, chapter 5. He said that a bishop might properly be established by both royal and popular election, and continues: “After the election, however, the bishop-elect ought to receive not ring or staff from the royal hand, but investiture with temporal possessions; and, in his orders, he ought to receive from his archbishop through ring or staff the care of souls, so that a matter of this sort may be carried out without dispute and the privilege of its authority may be preserved both for temporal and spiritual powers.”]

This, as is known, first occurred in England and afterward also in the Roman Empire.

It cannot be indicated with certainty in what year he finished this treatise; but beyond doubt he was occupied in writing it between 1100, when King Henry succeeded his brother, and 1106, when the dispute between king and archbishop was settled at the Council of London. Thus that book preceded the histories composed in the following years.

Hugh also wrote the *Life of Saint Sacerdos, Bishop of Limoges*, following an older text that was excessively rough, so that he should be thought to have supplied style rather than narrative.

[Note: [Col. 0817C] Hugh himself, *Ecclesiastical History*, first edition, book III; second edition, book V (compare Rottendorf, p. 127): “Observing,” he says, “that the sequence of the life of this most precious confessor was composed partly in an uncultivated style and partly corrupted through scribal fault, I recently resolved to correct it … and in that same sequence I expressed the truth concerning the virtues of the saint himself in the clearest style.”]

A letter addressed to Arnold, abbot of Sarlat, was prefixed, in which the plan and purpose of the book are briefly [Col. 0817C] disclosed. Henschenius published the *Life* [Col. 0818A] in the *Acta Sanctorum* (May II, p. 14) from a Sarlat manuscript.

Last must be named the book of *Miracles Performed by Saint Benedict at Fleury*, undertaken by Hugh after Adrevald, Adalerius, Aimoin, and Rodulfus, and continued down to the year 1119.

[Note: [Col. 0817D] See *Histoire littéraire*, loc. cit., p. 305.]

The book is unpublished; therefore we do not know what it might contribute to a better understanding of Hugh’s life or of the history of that age. Certainly he seems to have devoted himself to this work after his other books, perhaps continuing it for as long as he remained alive. In recounting, as they appeared to him, the miracles of the saintly patron to whom he had dedicated his life, he laid down the pen with which for many years he had given primary attention to describing both public and ecclesiastical affairs.

[Col. 0818B] Hugh probably died not long after 1119. But no one recorded the year or the day.

Hugh of Fleury can scarcely be counted among writers of German affairs, for he touched only rarely upon matters done beyond the Rhine and had discovered scarcely anything certain concerning them. For this reason his books too were more rarely read among the Germans. Alberic

[Note: [Col. 0817D] Alberic, under the year 1130, says: “The third [Hugh], who wrote the shorter *Ecclesiastical History* for Adela, countess of Champagne, mother of Count Theobald, was a black monk of Fleury, that is, of Saint Benedict upon the Loire in the diocese of Orléans.” He distinguishes him from Hugh of Saint-Victor, of whom he had previously spoken: “Thus far,” he says, “Master Hugh of Saint-Victor arranged his chronicle concerning Roman pontiffs and emperors.” From Hugh of Fleury he presents, for example, certain matters under the years 808, 809, 810, 820, 842, and 844; from Hugh of Saint-Victor, whom he most often adorns with the title “Master,” under 1038, 1073, 1087, 1095, 1099, and 1100. I add another testimony concerning him, excerpted from a Berne manuscript of Sigebert (*SS.*, VI, p. 287 [*Patrologia*, CLX]): “Among these, Master Hugh, canon of Saint-Victor at Paris, flourished almost last, [Col. 0818C] and he arranged the sequence of times from the beginning of the rising age down to the time of Lord Pope Innocent II and the most Christian king of the Franks, Louis, and embraced in a concise narrative the changes of kingdoms.” He died in 1142. Manuscripts of his work are listed at Paris, *Archiv*, VI, pp. 50, 71 (compare VII, p. 304), and at Oxford, *Archiv*, VI, p. 92. Paris Royal manuscript no. 5014, twelfth century, also seems to belong here. At its beginning is read: “CHRONICLE OF HUGH. In the five-thousand-four-hundred-and-seventh year of the world, as blessed Maximus established in his sermon on Easter, Caesar Octavian, the second monarch of the Romans, arose.” It ends in the time of Charlemagne: “For in that same synod inquiry and discussion were made concerning the state of the churches, the order of life of every rank, and what sort of clergy there ought to be.” There follows a catalogue of Roman pontiffs: “Blessed Peter the Apostle first sat at Antioch … Eugenius, also called Bernard, a Pisan by nation, monk of Cîteaux, sat eight years.”]

and others

[Note: [Col. 0818D] For example Henry of Herford, *Archiv*, VI, p. 764; compare Bruns, *Beiträge*, I, p. 8. The materials which Korner reports from Hugh after the time of the Charleses (compare *Archiv*, VI, p. 607) have, unless I am mistaken, all been rashly and without cause attributed to him; they were copied from Henry and correctly referred by him to other sources.]

had the *Ecclesiastical History* at hand. Yet even Alberic seems not to have read the *History of the Franks*, nor do I remember having found any trace of it on this side of the Rhine. It pleased writers of French affairs more, although it is now apparent that most followed not Hugh’s genuine works but books imposed upon him, especially that History of Sens.

[Col. 0818C]

[Note: [Col. 0818D] Neither Clarius in the *Chronicle of Saint-Pierre-le-Vif*, nor Aimoin’s continuator, admitted Hugh’s narrative. The genealogy of the kings of the Franks as well (D’Achery, 2nd edition, II, p. 493; nearly the same in Vatican Library manuscript Christ. no. 637, fols. 80–82) rests upon the History of Sens. Besides the history brought down to 1110, mentioned above, it especially follows another history of the same subject, ending in 1152, which follows a *History of the Franks* composed by Hugh. (Bouquet, continuators, XII, p. 115 ff.).]

I have already said above that Freher, Duchesne, [Col. 0819A] Bouquet, and others who published histories of the Franks treated Hugh badly, attributing false writings to him while generally omitting genuine ones. It has thus happened that only now does Hugh lack false glory yet receive the praise he deserves.

The plan and order of our edition are as follows.

A. We begin with the first edition of the *Ecclesiastical History*. From it we present the dedicatory letter, the prefaces to the individual books, their beginnings and endings, and the epilogue sent to Countess Adela. We have compared the final part of the fourth book with the second edition in such a way as to record variants diligently. We used:

1. Paris Royal manuscript no. 4963, mentioned above, which I myself examined in Paris; about thirty years ago Messrs. Sporlin and Turles transcribed it more fully, though less carefully, for the use of our society;

[Col. 0819B]

2. Berne manuscript no. 208, from which we possess a transcription of the epilogue.

B. There follows the second edition of the *Ecclesiastical History*. From this likewise we extracted, in nearly the same manner, those things which can explain the order of the book and the author’s work, but added the final chapters of Book VI, in which the affairs of Charlemagne and his successors are narrated. Of the great number of manuscripts listed above, the following were at hand:

1. Paris, Saint-Victor no. 311, a manuscript of the highest quality, which from Book VI onward I compared at some places with the printed editions.

2. Vienna, *Historia profana* no. 682, collated by Pertz with Rottendorf’s edition from the beginning of [Col. 0819C] Book IV onward.

3. Berne manuscript no. 324, enlarged by the continuation or interpolation of Sens and of Fossatus. The prefaces and the text itself from Pippin’s time onward have been transcribed for our use.

It seemed sufficient to examine the other manuscripts, especially the Parisian ones, and to note their arrangement.

To this we appended the History of the Franks of Sens, which we read added to Hugh’s book in manuscript 3 and others, supplying the first part of this little work from Duchesne’s edition (III, p. 349). We chiefly followed:

1*. The manuscript formerly of Saint-Magloire (Saint-Germain [Col. 0819D] François Harlay no. 485), which, as I said above, first united these materials with Hugh’s work.

From manuscript 3 we also admitted what was inserted at the monastery of Fossatus and chiefly concerns that monastery.

Moreover, from Aimoin of Fleury’s book *On the Miracles of Saint Benedict*, written at the beginning of the eleventh century (from 1005), we thought it fitting to select those passages concerning the succession of the kings of France. For these passed not only into the continuation of the History begun by Aimoin [Col. 0820A], but were also copied into the Chronicle of Saint-Bénigne of Dijon and from there transferred into the book of Hugh of Flavigny. They are brief, but, as testimonies of an ancient and diligent writer, have acquired great authority not without reason. I followed Mabillon’s edition (*Acta SS. Ordinis S. Benedicti*, IV, 2, p. 356 ff.).

C. We have not wished to publish separately the short History of the Franks, which we think was written by Hugh, because the same events are repeated in nearly the same words, only in a changed order, in the other book (D). Nor could it have suited our plan to insert into this volume that great historical collection in which fragments of this book have been joined to other excerpts. But we have appended the principal variants to the following work [Col. 0820B], using Berne manuscript no. 90, of which we have a copy near at hand, and collating Duchesne’s edition (IV, pp. 96–98).

D. For the book “which contains the Deeds of the Modern Kings of the Franks,” the most useful of the works composed by Hugh, we now present the complete text for the first time. Our Bethmann arranged for a faithful transcription of the Liège manuscript, whose readings we could almost always follow. The book, as the manuscript itself testifies, was not written by a single hand: another hand inserted here and there individual lines and indeed almost whole pages of parchment, usually using darker ink, the same ink with which several lines (preface, chapters 8 and 11) were erased. Yet the narrative always proceeds without interruption, so that the two scribes seem to have received the words of one dictating author. The text is marred by rare and very slight errors. I changed only a few matters in spelling: final *e* for *ae*, excessive use of the letter *c* for *t*, *n* for *m*, and similar features, which must be attributed to scribes rather than to the author.

Lastly, we placed the history of the kings of France from the monastery of Saint-Denis, as it was said above to be found in the Brussels manuscript (1) and the Berne manuscript (2). With these we compared, for the final and genuine part of the work, 3) Bouquet’s edition of the same history continued to 1137; there 3a) denotes Saint-Victor manuscript no. 419.

I trust that in this way not only Hugh’s writings may be properly distinguished and assessed, [Col. 0820D] but that the other histories of the Franks written in the twelfth century may also be brought out of obscurity, and their date, order, and connections so established that easy access may now lie open to everyone seeking genuine information about events. If this opinion has not deceived me, I shall say that the great labor which I devoted to this edition over many years was not in vain, although it has yielded very little fruit for the history of Germany itself. I collected and compared much in order that these few things might be printed.

G. WAITZ.

[Col. 0821]

[EXCERPTS FROM THE ECCLESIASTICAL HISTORY.]

[FIRST EDITION OF THE ECCLESIASTICAL HISTORY, ARRANGED IN FOUR BOOKS.]

HERE BEGINS THE BOOK [Col. 0821A] OF ECCLESIASTICAL HISTORY AND OF THE DEEDS OF THE ROMANS AND FRANKS, BRIEFLY COMPREHENDED BY HUGH OF SAINTE-MARIE.

[Note: [Col. 0821] “in the year one thousand one hundred and nine from the incarnation of the Lord,” added in manuscript 2.]

HUGH, pupil of Saint Benedict of Fleury, the distinction of great felicity, to his lady ADELA, venerable countess.

Most serene lady, I judge it fitting to dedicate the gift of this present work to your graciousness with suppliant affection: both because you are to be preferred to many nobles of our age, distinguished alike by eminent birth and exceptional virtue, and because you are learned in letters, which is a great mark of noble breeding or civic refinement. I call my gift this little book, most subtle in its concise brevity, that it may delight you by its charm [Col. 0821B] and exhort you to good conduct and to the adornment of life with good morals. Not because you are not sufficiently and becomingly endowed with great virtues, but because we exhort you always to advance toward what is better.

For, rereading ecclesiastical history, published in sections by many historians and comprehended in various ways, I resolved to compress it into this single volume. Having assembled as many books as possible, I resolved to cull their flowers and carefully draw out from each the marrow of truth, using the words of those same authors in some passages but at other times my own phrasing. Certainly this is a most laborious undertaking, because brevity is sometimes accompanied by obscurity, while I strive both to be clear and labor to be brief.

Moreover, all the things found there dictated by my rusticity are shown to have been expressed in uncultivated style.

[Note: [Col. 0821] *prebantur* in manuscript 1? Perhaps *prebentur*—“are presented”?]

Yet, however these things have been said, they can still benefit readers and recall to memory a fuller sequence of events: the unlearned, certainly, and the learned occupied in secular affairs, above all those who consider great consolation in life to be found in reading the divine Scriptures. For the person who has read much briefly recalls there the same things, while the ignorant person is instructed by a compendium. But if anyone should not wish to be content with these things, I refer him to the rich and magnificent volumes from which I drew them.

For censorious or biting men, I confess, there lies open in my case an unusually broad field for censure, because I have undertaken with excessive boldness so arduous a work, one which ought to have been reserved for learned men. [Col. 0821D] But to the envious or mocking, who perhaps, from a disposition of pride, will disdain my writings with haughty scorn, I reply that, as I suppose, posterity will not hereafter labor to remember their names; rather, their praises will remain as hidden as their reproaches. But the memorial of your name, my lady, will be left to posterity forever, both through the occasion of this book and through the performance of good works to which you unceasingly devote yourself; nor can it ever be brought to an end by any period of forgetfulness.

Therefore receive gladly this slight gift offered to you by me, and defend it by your favor against the malicious. For the wise men of old did not negligently pass over the deeds of ancient men, but set them down in books for the instruction of the present life. Indeed, through history the sequence of past time is comprehended, and through the successions of kings and emperors many necessary matters are investigated. Therefore I shall begin the account [Col. 0822B] with Octavian Augustus and shall record there, with the greatest care, both the names and deeds of Roman emperors and governors down to Charlemagne and his son Louis.

Behold what you may read in leisure: namely, the deeds of ancient emperors and the equally memorable acts of certain men beloved by God, from the Lord’s incarnation down to the appointed times. If you attend to these, idleness will not dull the splendid and honorable keenness of your intellect. As for praise of your virtues, which the nobility of your descent and the felicity of your nature have bestowed upon us, I am now ashamed to speak, lest I seem to employ the frivolity of a flatterer. I shall speak elsewhere when it is appropriate.

But to those who will take amiss that I have dedicated this [Col. 0822C] work to you, I reply: blessed Jerome the priest often honored holy Paula and her daughter Eustochium in many writings, and the venerable bishop Gregory of Rome sent the four books of his *Dialogues* to Theodelinda, queen of the Italians. Moreover, the woman sitting at the Lord’s feet heard the words of his mouth, and was better not only than the Pharisees and Sadducees but also than Christ’s own ministers, inasmuch as she was more devoted. For the female sex is not deprived of understanding of profound matters; indeed, as we shall clearly show in the following reading, women sometimes possess great industry of mind and the refinement of most excellent morals.

Moreover, this book of history contains, hidden in great depth, the sacraments of the Church. For just as Scripture informs us that the first man was formed by God on the sixth day of the creation of the world, so we shall declare that he was redeemed in the sixth age of the world. And just as we have learned that this same man was made from undefiled earth, so we shall demonstrate, on trustworthy testimony, that our Saviour was born of an untainted virgin. And just as Adam, inspired by God on the sixth day of the week, received from him the power of free choice, by which he might obey his Creator not under slavish necessity but by free will, and so might duly receive either the reward of eternal life for obedience or destruction for disobedience, so it is clear that in the sixth age of the world human beings received from heaven the Holy Spirit, by whom they might fulfil the Lord’s law, or his will, freely—not slavishly, like the other creatures—but as most beloved children.

For the almighty Lord created in the first age rational creatures—namely, angels and human beings—and gave them the power of free choice, so that, enriched with this faculty, they might remain forever in praise of their Creator. But because the former, that is, the angelic nature—though not the whole of it—was corrupted and, through pride, departed from the love of its Creator and became ruinous, it burned with envy against human nature and suggested to it the stumbling-block of sin, in order to defile it with the stain of its own impiety. It believed that it would be a great consolation if they should fall together and alike suffer the penalty of its guilt. Divine majesty did not endure this, but decreed to restore human nature to the nobility of its former dignity. Therefore he took flesh from a woman, so that human nature itself might have, in his incarnation, the means whereby, through his benefit, it could return to that blessedness which it had lost. [Note: “incarnation” perhaps read in the manuscript.]

Thus the Lord displayed the judgment of his justice in the angelic nature which he punished, and the sweetness of his mercies in the human nature which he redeemed. For all his ways are mercy and truth. Therefore, just as through Adam we encountered the sorrow of death in the first age of the world, so through the mystery of the incarnate Word, in that same sixth age of the world, as we have stated above, we recovered the joy of eternal life.

Before these things happened, however, Abraham the patriarch appeared already in the third age of the world. From him the rite and religion of circumcision took their beginning, when all the nations, corrupted by error, were sacrificing to idols. Then the Law was given to the Jewish people, by which the true Lord might be worshipped. And the Lord indeed, who made all things from nothing, could in a single instant have made everything at once and brought the whole human race to reverence and worship of himself. But he did not do so. Rather, by a secret and inscrutable mystery, he ordained to be born of a Virgin, not at the world’s beginning, but at the fitting time. When he shone serenely upon the world through the birth of human flesh, he gathered, in the sixth age of the world, one Church out of Jewish and Gentile people; and he joined the two peoples to one another within the same Church by one Spirit, so that there was no longer any distinction there, but one liberty.

That he chose to be born of a woman showed us a great benefit of his kindness and an immeasurable example of humility. Yet he who came to cleanse flesh could not be defiled by flesh. Nevertheless, according to the flesh, he could be born, crucified, and rise again for our salvation, in a wonderful and ineffable manner, without injury to his impassible and unchangeable majesty. But the faithlessness of the proud cannot scrutinize such holy mysteries, because it does not wish to believe. The holy Church, however, believes, embraces, and pursues all these things in the Lord Jesus Christ with an affection of sincerity and great devotion. [Note: Added in the margin: “It must be known that, just as no one could be saved in the Flood except in the ark, so now no one can be saved except in the Church.”] Therefore you also, daughter of the Lord’s Church, receive these same mysteries with attentive mind; read them joyfully, and believe as you read.

> Live, fare well, rejoice—offspring of kings,  
> Pillar of clergy and people, most worthy of abundant praise;  
> Whom uprightness of character and nobility of forefathers  
> Alike adorn. May every prosperity yield to you!

End of the epistle.

## HERE BEGINS THE PREFACE, OR FIRST BOOK, OF ECCLESIASTICAL HISTORY, BRIEFLY ADAPTED OR EXCERPTED BY HUGH OF SAINTE-MARIE, A MONK OF THE BENEDICTINE MONASTERY OF FLEURY, IN THE YEAR 1109 FROM THE INCARNATION OF THE LORD

Before I undertake to expound the proposed work—namely, to excerpt in a concise abridgment ecclesiastical histories filled with most abundant delight [Note: The manuscript perhaps reads *latissima*, “most extensive,” for *letissima*, “most delightful”]—I think it fitting first to touch briefly in the present volume upon certain matters concerning the condition of the Jewish people, lest I seem wholly to pass over in silence their very celebrated nobility, from whose lineage it is agreed that our Lord Jesus Christ took flesh. Therefore I shall draw a certain line of narrative from Abraham, their patriarch, to the birth of that same Christ, taking my beginning from the Syrian kingdom or its kings, and from the third age of the world, in which Ninus is recorded to have reigned, under whom Abraham was born; omitting many matters contained in the five books of Moses concerning the beginning of the age.

For from the creation of the world to the aforementioned Ninus there are found to be three thousand one hundred and eighty-four years. These have either been omitted or unknown to all Gentile historiographers. Passing them over also for the sake of brevity, I shall endeavour to arrange this ecclesiastical history from the most familiar periods of kings and emperors, and to establish it legitimately by indications of preceding events. I recall that Luke the Evangelist, when weaving the history of the Lord’s incarnation, mentioned King Herod of the Jewish nation at the very beginning of his holy Gospel: “There was, in the days of Herod, king of Judaea, a certain priest named Zechariah, of the course of Abijah.” And again, shortly afterwards: “A decree went out from Caesar Augustus that the whole world should be enrolled,” again making mention of Caesar Octavian.

For, in my opinion, ecclesiastical histories ought to be arranged from the most familiar kings or emperors, and what is related by celebrated report even among the Gentiles ought thereby to be established with complete certainty. Therefore I shall now begin with Ninus, the most familiar of the ancient kings.

Accordingly, Ninus, whom we mentioned above, is recorded to have been the first king who changed the custom long observed by kings—whose practice had been to defend rather than extend their realms—through a novel desire for dominion, and who made war upon neighbouring peoples. When he had subdued all Syria and many other eastern provinces to himself, he reigned for fifty years. During these [lacuna].

This is enough for the present to have said concerning the condition of the Jewish people and the Temple, so that we may turn to the course of ecclesiastical history. [Note: See Rottendorff, p. 24.]

Yet I recognize that it is still fitting to say something about the Parthians, with whom the Roman people are recorded to have divided the empire of the world. We must therefore briefly return to their origin. For it is not right wholly to pass so great a kingdom over in silence. But because the Parthians were Scythian exiles, as is apparent from their very name—for in the Scythian language *Parthi* means “exiles”—I shall first relate a few things about the Scythian kingdom.

The Scythian nation [Note: See Rottendorff, p. 29.]—as in Book II of the second edition, arranged in six parts, below [lacuna]—whom they feared would become the avenger of his father’s blood. At last the often-mentioned Parthians, believing themselves now equal to the Romans in greatness, voluntarily returned to Octavian Augustus the Roman standards which they had seized after Crassus was killed; and, after giving hostages, they made a firm treaty with him. For Augustus achieved more among them by the favour attached to his name than any other emperor could have achieved by the strength of arms.

Having now briefly dealt with the Parthians also, I shall attempt the proposed work and, from the times of the best-known Roman emperors, as I have promised above, establish this whole history in due order. Beginning with Octavian Augustus, I shall set down there in sequence the names of the Roman emperors as far as Charlemagne and his son, the Emperor Louis; and I shall clearly indicate the periods in which they flourished. Thus, following their catalogue, I shall assign accounts of events to their proper times, so that, if you run through the catalogue just mentioned, you may plainly recognize what was done under each emperor.

I shall also insert here the successions of the holy apostles and the names of the Roman bishops, and note what Catholic men undertook the governance of churches in the most celebrated places after the apostles themselves. [Note: Perhaps *praesulum*, “bishops,” rather than *presidum*.] Nor shall I omit the storms of persecutions by which holy martyrs, at various times, were compelled by imperial edicts to be thrown into prison for Christ. Yet, aflame with divine love, they could not be bent by any tortures, though kings, laws, commanders, and peoples raged to put them to death; they always remained unconquered. The early Church brought forth these flowers, and, adorned by them still, flourishes in wondrous variety. It will therefore always be useful to remember them.

Moreover, I shall not pass over the faithless *philocompi*, that is, lovers of vainglory, who, inspired by an evil spirit, wished to corrupt divine doctrines with frivolous inventions. At fitting places, though briefly yet sufficiently, I shall take care, with God’s helping aid, to answer their errors. Nor shall I be silent about the final destruction of the Temple, which took place under Vespasian and Titus, and [Note: The other edition reads, “but I shall relate.”] the overthrow or despoiling of those things called the Holy of Holies—although it was shadow, not truth. Yet the shadow marks the traces of truth and is accustomed, through certain signs, to express future things to attentive observers.

## HERE BEGINS THE SECOND BOOK OF ECCLESIASTICAL HISTORY

The second monarch of the Romans, after Julius Caesar had been killed, was Octavian Augustus, under whom [Note: See Rottendorff, p. 36.] [lacuna] and Arnobius, the very learned African rhetorician. [Note: See Rottendorff, p. 89. This edition lacks the material found in the other edition concerning the popes Miltiades and Sylvester.]

End of the second book, although the first appears to have the character of a preface.

## HERE BEGINS THE PREFACE TO THE THIRD BOOK, CONTAINING A DESCRIPTION OF GAUL

With the assistance of the Holy Spirit, in the preceding book I have treated briefly of certain saints of the early Church who, after the birth of our Saviour and his glorious ascension into heaven, endured countless afflictions for the Catholic faith. In the present volume I shall attempt, if I can, to say something also about those who flourished in days of peace and tranquillity. I shall begin from the time when Roman emperors, renouncing idols for whose sake they had formerly persecuted Christians, began to worship the true God, who created the entire fabric of the world.

For God never ceased at any time to hire worthy labourers into his vineyard, that is, into the holy Church. The Church itself spread its fruitful branches ever more widely in every direction, in proportion as it endured harsher conflicts for the name of its Redeemer. I shall also take care in this book to expose the faithlessness of certain heretics, lest any Christian should ever be caught, ensnared by their traps. For heretics, like bird-catchers, are accustomed to conceal the snare of their fraud and to prepare the poison of their wickedness under certain pretences, in order to deceive the unsuspecting and pierce them with the dart of their faithlessness. And when they have perhaps done this and sprinkled a person with even the slightest stain of their error, they immediately endeavour miserably to entangle him in inextricable bonds and always drag him toward worse things, until whoever does not avoid their deceits and fraudulent lips as deadly poison comes into the abyss of error. [Note: The reading may be *respexerint*, “have looked back,” rather than *resperserint*, “have sprinkled.”]

For iniquity veils the efficacy of the divine gift. After the times of persecution endured by the early Church, the Devil, through the subtle cunning of heretics, made a great effort to overthrow the Catholic faith. But God’s generous mercy armed his holy leaders against the aforementioned wickedness: namely, certain confessors, who by great labour destroyed heretics’ deceits and strengthened the line of the sacred faith with more abundant eloquence. Their merit certainly does not fall short of the dignity of martyrdom. For it is evident that all whom ecclesiastical faith does not enlighten are darkened by the blindness of error; and those whom Christ—who gathered his Church for himself from the whole mass of the world—does not gather, these the Devil indeed carries off with himself to destruction.

I shall also insert in my proposed work certain chapters concerning the deeds of the Franks. For it is not right wholly to pass over the valour of so great a people, which was able to subdue by its arms and hold subject to itself the Gallic nation—fierce, bold, warlike, terrible to all kingdoms, and formidable even to the Romans while they flourished in dominion over the lands. First, however, I shall briefly set out and describe the position of Gaul itself, which the aforesaid nation of the Franks now inhabits.

Accordingly, all Gaul [lacuna] the Cycladic islands, as below, cols. 835–836.

Having said these preliminary things, I shall now unfold the order of history.

Constantine the Great, son of the most moderate and distinguished emperor Constantius, in Britain [Note: See Rottendorff, p. 91.] [lacuna] was the first of Greek race to obtain the Roman Empire. [Note: See Rottendorff, p. 143.]

End of the third book.

## HERE BEGINS THE PREFACE TO THE FOURTH BOOK, CONTAINING A DESCRIPTION OF ITALY ACCORDING TO THE ACCOUNT OF PAUL THE HISTORIAN

Since those occupied with various concerns grow weary of turning over many books, it has pleased me to gather the vast sea of ecclesiastical histories in concise form and to comprise a numerous abundance of books in this one volume, taking the utmost care to avoid prolix discourse in it, since this is accustomed sometimes to produce great weariness in certain people. I therefore seek to please those whom concise and clear speech always delights.

But seeing that even this undertaking of mine is now exceeding the bounds of the proposed brevity, I shall henceforth omit what I have been accustomed to answer, though briefly, concerning individual heresies in certain places. Still, the matters which I answered in the preceding book can bring great benefit to readers, enabling them both to avoid doctrines contrary to the Christian faith and to escape the unguarded inexperience of simplicity. They can be especially useful, I say, to those who do not possess the great volumes of the doctors in which these matters have been answered, or who, entangled in worldly cares, cannot at all read or understand them.

Therefore, content with a historical style, I shall expound what remains of the work. Yet I shall not wholly pass over the heresy of the Acephali, the false prophets. [Notes: *ascephali* perhaps read for *Acephali*; *pseudopropheta* perhaps read for *pseudoprophetarum*.] I shall also briefly set out in the present preface the situation of Italy and make known to those who do not precisely know it the number of its provinces.

Italy, then, the homeland or region of the Romans [Note: See Rottendorff, p. 35.] [lacuna] and is called Cisalpine Gaul, because it lies below the Alps. And this is enough to have said briefly concerning Brennus or the Gauls, whom we mentioned above, so that our discourse may return more quickly to the course of history.

End of the preface.

## HERE BEGINS THE FOURTH BOOK

Maurice, succeeding to the eastern empire upon the death of Tiberius, reigned twenty-one years. [Note: See Rottendorff, p. 143.] [lacuna] [Note: We have compared the end of this book with the other edition; see p. 358 ff.] Finally, Nicephorus, emperor of Constantinople, whom we mentioned above, died after many distinguished victories over the Saracens, and his son-in-law Michael was raised to the imperial throne.

End of the book of Ecclesiastical History and of the Deeds of the Romans and Franks.

## HERE BEGINS THE EPILOGUE OF THE PRECEDING WORK, WRITTEN TO THE VENERABLE COUNTESS OF BLOIS, MEAUX, AND CHARTRES

Moved by the reputation of your generosity, venerable countess, I have gathered these materials from ancient historians, like a bee collecting honey from different flowers. In this one volume [Note: “h. i.,” edition 2.], I say, I have recounted for you the names and deeds of all the Roman emperors and bishops, and indicated what Catholic men undertook the governance of churches in the most celebrated places after the apostles. I have also described the grave storms of persecution which the early Church suffered for its Saviour, and named the most delightful flowers of confessors which it produced in peace.

Moreover, I have sung for you the memorable deeds of the best men—namely the Gauls and other nations—from the third age of the world to the death of the Emperor Charlemagne. [Note: The text perhaps lacks a word before “Charlemagne.”] I have briefly explained also the condemnable blasphemies of the heretics and how they ought to be resisted. I have taken care to write also of the disasters of the Jewish people which they suffered for their impieties, and by whose propagation Christianity has been spread throughout the world. [Note: The text lacks material here.] But I have deservedly dedicated this concise and worthy volume not to unlettered princes, for whom the art of letters is held in contempt, but to you, lest the memorial of your name should ever be corrupted by any antiquity [Note: *nulla*, “no,” is the reading of witness 1.], which is accustomed to be hostile to the memory of posterity.

Moreover, if anyone desires to know the height of your rank [Note: Witness 1 reads *celsitudini*, “to your highness.”], let him know that you are the daughter of William, the most famous duke of the Normans and king of the English, namely the man who subdued that kingdom to himself by his own ability. No king of our times was wiser, more fortunate, or more moderate than he. Yet I believe that no one can adequately praise his royal magnificence and generosity. For he ought not rightly [Note: Omitted in edition 2.] to be compared in magnanimity with his predecessor Rollo; rather, he may be extolled with so much greater praise because he imitated Julius Caesar and the Emperor Claudius, who subdued the aforementioned island—that is, the land of the English—by victorious arms, a thing which no Roman emperor besides them dared to undertake.

Nevertheless, though at his death he left the chief authority of his duchy and kingdom by hereditary right to his sons, your brothers, he bequeathed to you the elegance of his character and the abundance which always accompanied him. [Note: The words from *vobis* (“to you”) to *deseruit* (“he bequeathed”) are absent in edition 2.] For you possess his abundance and refinement of character especially beyond your other brothers, as Gaul testifies: Gaul is now wholly sustained and notably distinguished by your generosity. Therefore you are to be preferred to many nobles, as I said in the first preface of this book, both because of your distinguished lineage and exceptional uprightness, and because you are educated in letters—which is a great mark of noble birth or civilization.

Finally, in this epilogue I shall append the splendid genealogy of your forefathers; and afterwards, in another book, if it pleases you, I shall briefly sing both the deeds of your ancestors—the Danes and Normans—and those of the kings of the Franks from the Emperor Louis, son of the Emperor Charlemagne, down to our own times.

Rollo, whom I mentioned before, the ancestor of the Norman princes, was a most powerful duke of the Danes. But in the time of Charles, king of the Franks, after the death of the Emperor Louis, he entered Gaul by the Seine [Note: Edition 2 reads *secanam*.] and, having entered it, claimed Normandy for himself. His remarkable son succeeded him, named William and surnamed Longsword. As I shall not conceal in the book which I promise you, he recalled Louis, son of Charles king of the Franks, from the exile in which he lay hidden, by his own power, to the kingdom of the Franks. Richard succeeded this William, and another Richard succeeded Richard. Robert succeeded the second Richard, and Robert begot the honourable William [Note: Edition 2 reads *guillermum*.], king of the English, your father.

End of the epilogue.

## SECOND EDITION, ARRANGED IN SIX BOOKS

## HERE BEGINS THE FIRST BOOK OF ECCLESIASTICAL HISTORIES

Ninus was once a most powerful king of the Assyrians. Making war upon neighbouring kings, he subdued to himself all the peoples of Asia except the Indians, and reigned there for fifty years. During these, etc. [lacuna] This is enough for the present to have said about the condition of the Jewish people and the Temple (cf. col. 824). Yet I shall not pass over this: the prophets of that nation preceded the Gentile philosophers both in age and wisdom, lest any nation should vainly boast of the antiquity of its wisdom over the patriarchs and holy prophets, in whom divine wisdom dwelt. [Note: See Rottendorff’s edition, p. 24.] [lacuna] There was much else to be said on these matters; but because this book is becoming too long, the principle of moderation requires that it now end. [Note: See Rottendorff, p. 27.]

End of the first book.

## HERE BEGINS THE PREFACE TO THE SECOND BOOK

Since it is delightful for the wise to know sacred histories, whose very surface is accustomed to drive away the mists of error from human minds and lead them to the image of truth, I shall now endeavour, in accordance with the text of history, to make known to readers how sound instruction in the faith advanced in the world through certain stages and divisions of ages and times; and how the Old Testament ministered to evangelical beginnings by prefiguring divine mysteries, just as childhood is accustomed to precede manhood.

Yet although from the very origin of the world, throughout its whole extent, we find that only two societies of human beings have existed—while so many and such great nations, living throughout the world with different rites and customs [Note: The word *que* is absent in edition 3.], are distinguished by manifold diversity of languages, arms, and clothing—we may rightly call them two cities. One of these cities is predestined to reign with God, and the other to perish with the Devil. Nevertheless, in the third age of the world, when all nations scattered across the earth, forgetful of God’s benefits and of their own creation, senselessly worshipped creatures in place of him, God chose the holy man Abraham, by whose example he might convert the world to knowledge of himself and rescue it from the precipice of error. He also imposed upon him the sign of circumcision, which was a sign of our regeneration, by which, after the common generation of the flesh—because we are born to the world—we are regenerated to God through water and the Holy Spirit. [Note: The manuscript perhaps reads *quam*, “which,” rather than *qua*, “by which.”]

In the fourth age of the world, the same God and Lord first spoke to Moses out of the bush through fire, so that he might lead the Israelite people out of Egypt. At length, after he had again held him in discourse for forty days and nights, Moses was granted to receive the Law written on tablets; by it the same people of God might be guided until Christ should come, who, by the grace of the Holy Spirit having been given, would reveal to his Church the inward meaning of that Law. [Note: The manuscript perhaps reads *quam*, “which,” rather than *qua*, “by which.”]

In that same age, Moses built for the Lord in the wilderness the tabernacle, which signified the universal Church of the present age; and the ark of the covenant, by which Christ was signified, in whom are laid up all the treasures of divine wisdom; and the lampstand, by which is expressed holy preaching, which shows the way of light to those travelling toward life; and the table, by which Holy Scripture is signified; and many other things in which he expressed the exceedingly lofty mysteries of the present Church.

Finally, in the fifth age of the world, Solomon, the peaceful king, built that most noble Temple in Jerusalem, in which too there went before a certain image of the thing to come. In the sixth age of the world, Christ, mediator of God and humankind [Note: Rottendorff reads *hominum*, “of human beings.”], appeared to the world and endured the death of the cross, so that death, which is known to be contrary to life, might by his death become the instrument through which passage might be made to life. Then, rising from the dead, he sent the Holy Spirit from heaven to his apostles assembled in Jerusalem; the Spirit opened to them all the mysteries of the Scriptures and brought them knowledge of various languages. From there they were scattered over the face of the whole earth, baptizing everywhere in the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit.

Then was fulfilled what is written: “From Zion shall go forth the law, and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem” (Isaiah 2:3). For the word of the Lord, proceeding thence, flowed out through the whole world. From that time a tower began to be built on earth, not from stones and mortar but from diverse peoples and languages, whose summit penetrates heaven. This tower is spiritually called Zion, which means “watchtower” or “contemplation”; for it contemplates the great good of the age to come, which God has prepared for those who love him.

It may rightly also be called God’s bride because of the numerous offspring of children whom it bears for him daily through the sacrament of baptism. For, adhering intellectually to Christ its Redeemer in a bodily embrace, if it is permitted to say so, it is filled and made fruitful with true virtues. To it, as to his new bride, the new priest entrusted new sacraments and imposed a light burden and a sweet yoke, so that it might understand how highly he valued it. For in place of circumcision, which burdened the Hebrew people not a little, he gave it the sacrament of holy baptism; and in place of the kinds of various sacrifices, he gave his own body and blood, to be sacrificed and eaten. The ancient sacrifices of the righteous were manifold and varied signs of this true sacrifice.

Thus the first Law was first established as a pedagogue for untrained and carnal people, instructing them, or forbidding them to sin, through fear of present punishment. But the second showed those already instructed a higher way of life without threats of present punishment. Therefore it was not fitting that evangelical perfection should precede the Mosaic Law. For perfect things are accustomed to be later.

These matters having been set forth, it remains now for me also to say something concerning the Parthians, who reigned for a long time in Persia, before I begin the proposed work. For I ought not to pass so great a kingdom over in silence. The Roman people are indeed recorded to have divided the empire of the world with the Parthians. But because the Parthians were Scythian exiles, as is apparent from their name—for in the Scythian language *Parthi* means “exiles”—I shall first relate a few things concerning the kingdom of the Scythians, although the order may seem inverted, since after treating the wars of Pompey and Caesar, which I have already recounted, I shall discuss King Vesones of Egypt, the kingdom of the Amazons, and Cyrus’s entrance into Scythia—events which occurred before Caesar’s birth. [Note: The reading may be *quicquid*, “whatever,” rather than *quod*, “since/that.”]

End of the preface to the second book.

## HERE BEGINS THE SECOND BOOK

The most ancient nation of the Scythians, situated in the north, is bounded on one side by the Pontus, on the other by the Riphaean Mountains, and behind by Asia. But the Scythians had origins no less illustrious than their empire, and they were distinguished no more by the valour of men than of women. For the men founded the kingdoms of the Parthians and Bactrians of whom we speak, while the women founded that of the Amazons. Thus, for those considering the deeds of their men and women, it is uncertain which sex was more illustrious among them. Yet King Vesoges, etc. [lacuna] whom they feared would become the avenger of his father’s blood. Having briefly dealt with the Parthians, I shall set my hand to the proposed work. [Note: See Rottendorff, p. 33.]

End of the second book.

## HERE BEGINS THE PREFACE TO THE THIRD BOOK, CONTAINING A DESCRIPTION OF ITALY

Now, as I am about to excerpt the history I promised, I shall begin with the birth of our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ. Afterwards I shall insert here the successions of the holy apostles and the names of the Roman bishops (cf. cols. 825–826), and then set out what Catholic men undertook the governance of churches in the most celebrated places after the apostles themselves.

Nor shall I omit the storms of persecutions by which holy martyrs, at various times, were compelled by imperial edicts to be thrown into prison for Christ. But, burning with divine love, they could not be bent by any tortures, although kings and laws, commanders and peoples raged for their death; they always remained unconquered. Likewise holy women, bearing faith with a manly spirit, were shut up in prisons, beaten, tortured, burned, torn apart, and crowned. The early Church produced these flowers and, even now adorned by them, flourishes in marvellous variety. It will always be useful, therefore, to remember them.

Furthermore, I shall not pass over the faithless *philocompi*, that is, lovers of vainglory rather than wisdom. Though outwardly covered, by continence, chastity, and fasting, as by a garment of piety, inwardly they possessed a poisoned mind and, through sweet speeches, brought scandal to many in the Church. I shall take care to uncover their faithlessness and, in appropriate places, with God’s helping aid, answer their errors—briefly indeed, but sufficiently (cf. col. 826). I trust that this will especially benefit those who do not possess the great volumes of the doctors in which they have been answered, or who, entangled in worldly concerns, cannot read them at all. From these responses, although brief, they will be able both to avoid the unwary inexperience of simplicity and to reject doctrines opposed to the Christian faith.

Finally, I shall refute the blindness of the Jews, by which they refuse to believe in Christ, whom they know was foretold to them by the prophets (cf. col. 826). Nor shall I be silent about the final destruction of the Temple, which occurred under Vespasian and Titus; rather, I shall recount the overthrow or plundering of those things called the Holy of Holies. Although this was shadow and not truth, the shadow marks the traces of truth and commonly expresses future things through certain signs to those who inspect them attentively.

Moreover, I shall include here memorable deeds of the best men—Romans, Gauls, Goths, and other peoples—and strive to establish this whole work by sound reasoning (cf. col. 825). For, beginning with Octavian Augustus, I shall set down there successively the names of all Roman emperors down to Charlemagne and his son, the Emperor Louis, and clearly mark the times in which they flourished. Thus, according to their catalogue, I shall assign accounts of deeds to their appropriate times, so that, if you run through the catalogue just mentioned, you may plainly recognize what was done under each emperor.

There are, however, some to whom it seems superfluous for ecclesiastical histories to be treated according to the times of kings or emperors. But this is not contrary to ecclesiastical religion or authentic discipline (cf. col. 825). For Luke the Evangelist, when weaving the history of the Lord’s incarnation, made mention at the very beginning of his holy Gospel of Herod, king of the Jewish nation: “There was, in the days of Herod, king of Judaea, a certain priest named Zechariah, of the course of Abijah.” And again, shortly afterwards: “A decree went out from Caesar Augustus that the whole world should be enrolled,” once more mentioning Caesar Octavian, so that matters less known to people might be confirmed and strengthened by those reported almost everywhere in celebrated fame. Many other religious expositors of sacred histories are likewise recorded to have done this. For events that are not commended by any certainty of kings and times are not accepted as history, but are counted among old women’s tales.

Further, Christ delayed coming until the sixth age so that the length of time might not diminish the fullness of the new Law. For if he had come earlier, perhaps the antiquity of time would have abolished all the precepts of the new Law. But now the imminent terror of judgment itself requires their observance, and the nearness of the approaching examination does not permit the perfection of the new faith to be put at risk. Accordingly, it was fitting that he who had made humanity on the sixth weekday and completed it on the sixth day should bring it to the fullness of the Law in the sixth age of the world, renewing it in its old age by his new advent.

Accordingly, in this present preface, since I do not doubt that it is very appropriate to the proposed work, I shall briefly set out the situation of Italy and make known to those who do not precisely know it the number of its provinces (cf. col. 828). Italy, then, the homeland or region of the Romans [lacuna] is called Cisalpine because it lies below the Alps. And this is enough to have said briefly concerning Brennus or the Gauls, whom we mentioned above. Henceforth, supported by God’s help, I shall endeavour to divide the whole work into three books and reduce ecclesiastical history to one body.

End of the preface.

## HERE BEGINS THE THIRD BOOK
The second monarch of the Romans, after Julius Caesar had been slain, was Octavian Augustus, who . . . [lacuna] . . . Therefore, after the final destruction of the Jewish people, I shall briefly refute the unbelief of those Jews who still refuse to believe in Christ. [Note: Col. 0833: See Rottendorff, p. 65.]

End of the Third Book.

BEGINNING OF THE PROLOGUE TO THE FOURTH BOOK.

[Col. 0834C]

A great error is at work in the hearts of the Jews. [Note: Col. 0833: It was thought proper to omit these matters also; see Rottendorff, cited place.] . . . [lacuna] . . . But let it suffice to have said these things against the Jews under the guise of a prologue; and let this be its appointed end.

End of the Prologue.

BEGINNING OF THE FOURTH BOOK.

Domitian, then, the younger brother of Titus, [Note: Col. 0833: See Rottendorff, p. 68.] . . . [lacuna] . . . He also discovered the use of the dalmatic. [Note: Col. 0833: See Rottendorff, p. 89.]

End of the Fourth Book.

BEGINNING OF THE PROLOGUE TO THE FIFTH BOOK, CONTAINING A DESCRIPTION OF GAUL.

In the preceding book (cf. col. 826), by the assistance of the Holy Spirit, I briefly treated of certain saints of the early Church who, after the birth of our Saviour and his glorious ascension into heaven, endured countless afflictions for the Catholic faith. In the present volume, however, I shall attempt, if I can, to say something also about those who flourished in days of peace and tranquillity, beginning from the time when the Roman emperors, renouncing the idols for whose sake they had formerly persecuted Christians, began to worship the true God, who established the whole fabric of the world.

For at no time did God cease to hire suitable labourers into his vineyard—that is, into his Church [Col. 0835A]—nor did that Church cease, through patience, to bear fruits worthy of him. Rather, the harsher the struggles which it endured for the name of its Redeemer, the more gloriously it always triumphed over the Devil. Therefore the impiety of the ancient serpent begrudges the effectiveness of the divine gift, and wickedness arms itself against the justice of piety. For he who long ago, placed in heaven, compared himself with the Godhead and desired to be like God, not through righteousness but through power, and who because of his pride was cast down from heaven [Note: Col. 0835: “is lacking” in witness 3], with his usual cunning, after the times of persecution endured by the early Church, envying its tranquillity, again attempted through certain heretics to overthrow the Catholic faith. He who had earlier stirred up against it the savage storm of persecutions afterward also [Col. 0835B] sowed within it the evil seeds of heretics.

But the bounty of God’s piety armed certain of its champions against this aforesaid wickedness, so that by their great labour they might overthrow the wiles of heretics and strengthen the rule of the sacred faith by richer eloquence. [Note: Col. 0835: “laboured,” witness 3.] Certainly their merit does not fall short of the dignity of martyrdom; for the same labour makes those who contend for the faith equal to martyrs. And because nothing is stronger than truth, so the Catholic faith, by the labour of the aforesaid men, crushed every perversity, just as long ago it shattered the doubtful opinions of ancient philosophers by the authority of the holy patriarchs and prophets.

And just as that blessed host of angels which remained in heaven after the Devil’s fall [Col. 0835C] ministers and serves God according to the order of ranks granted to it, and, obedient to his command, governs the multitude of angels through the archangels, so also now the Church, according to the ranks of order and discipline granted to it, faithfully ministers on earth to God himself, insofar as human ability permits. But those whom it does not gather, the Devil surely snatches away with himself to destruction. And let this suffice for what has been said in the present prologue about the holy Church.

Henceforth I shall insert into the work I have begun certain chapters concerning the deeds of the Franks in suitable places (cf. col. 827). For it is not right to pass over entirely the prowess of so great a people, which was able by its arms to subdue, and by its wisdom to keep subject to itself, the fierce, bold, warlike people of the Gauls—terrible to all kingdoms and formidable even to the Romans when they flourished in dominion over the lands. [Col. 0835D] First, however, I shall briefly set forth and describe the situation of Gaul itself, which the aforesaid people of the Franks now inhabit.

All Gaul, not so extensive as it was renowned, was anciently bounded by three provinces. One of these was called Belgica, another Aquitania, and the third Lugdunensis. The province of Belgica has on the east the boundary of the river Rhine and Germany; on the southeast, the Apennine Alps; on the south, the province of Narbonensis; on the west, the province of Lugdunensis; and on the northwest, the British Ocean. Its celebrated and famous cities are Cologne of Agrippina, Tongeren, Trier, Metz [Col. 0836A]—also called Mediomatricum—Reims, Laon, and the district of the Helvetii, which the Alemanni now inhabit. Through this province flow the Scheldt, the Marne, the Meuse, and the Aisne, which passes beyond the outer limits of Reims. There is also in it a forest called the Ardennes, extending from the banks of the river Rhine to the territory of Trier.

Aquitaine extends from the river Garonne to the Pyrenees, and is almost encircled in a ring by the winding course of the Loire, which bounds it on one side. It contains the distinguished cities of Narbonne, Arvernum—called Clermont—Bourges, Cahors, Toulouse, Rodez, Limoges, Périgueux, Poitiers, Bordeaux, Saintes, and Angoulême. The Dordogne flows through Aquitaine and empties into the Garonne. There is in it the forest of Letenne, [Note: Col. 0835: See Rottendorff, p. 91.] adjoining the Bituriges and Arverni. [Col. 0836B]

The province of Lugdunensis begins at Mount Jura, which lies between the Sequani and the Helvetii, and at Lake Geneva and the river Rhône; it extends to the British Ocean and widens as far as the channel of the Loire, which separates and divides it from Aquitaine. It contains many rich cities: Lyons, Chalon, Autun—also called Augustodunum—Sens, Auxerre, Nevers—also called Nivedunum—Meaux, Troyes, Paris, Chartres, Gennabus, also called Orléans, Rouen, Évreux, Oximus, that is, Sées; Le Mans, Luxovium, Nantes, Andus, also called Andegavis; Avranches, Rennes, and Vannes. Of these, Autun and Sens were of greater importance in ancient times. For Autun became renowned by embracing friendship with the Roman people; the Senones, however, once surrounded Rome with a siege. Through the province of Lugdunensis flow the Rhône, the Arar—also called the Saône—and the Seine, which empties into the British Ocean. Its forests are the Perche and Langularia.

When the Franks had occupied these three provinces of Gaul, they called the region stretching northward between the Meuse and the Rhine Austrasia; and the region extending from the Meuse to the Loire, Neustria. Yet a certain part of Gaul, which the Burgundians occupied within the province of Lugdunensis, is now called Burgundy. Aquitaine, however, still retains its ancestral name. It is called Aquitaine because, beyond the other provinces of Gaul, it abounds in springs and streams. Let this brief account suffice for the present concerning the situation [Col. 0836D] of Gaul. It remains, however, that we should describe the province of Narbonensis also, which is a part of the Gauls.

The province of Narbonensis has the Gothic Alps on the east; Spain on the west; Aquitaine on the northwest; Belgic Gaul on the north; the province of Lugdunensis on the northeast; the Balearic Islands on the south; and, opposite where the Rhône flows into the sea, the Cyclades. Having thus run through these matters, I shall return to the charm of history.

End of the Prologue.

BEGINNING OF THE FIFTH BOOK.

Constantine the Great, son of Constantius, a most moderate [Col. 0837A] and distinguished ruler, in Britain [Note: Col. 0837: See Rottendorff, p. 143.] . . . [lacuna] . . . was the first of the Greek race to obtain the Roman Empire. [Note: Col. 0837: “lecenna,” witness 3.]

End of the Fifth Book.

BEGINNING OF THE PROLOGUE TO THE SIXTH BOOK.

Behold, [Note: Col. 0837: These passages are lacking in Rottendorff; see the preface, p. 339.] while I desire to survey the boundless sea of histories and compress a numerous abundance of books into one volume, I seem to some to have exceeded the measure of my intended brevity. But let those who delight in brief discourse listen, I pray. I confess that brevity ought to be observed in speech, if the subject permits; for a lengthy discourse burdens the minds of some people more than it instructs them. Excessive abundance also lays a crop low, and excessive fertility does not reach maturity.
