[Col. 0837B] Yet what ought to be said must be said, and one who states a matter more narrowly than he should transgresses the standard of perfect discourse no less than one who speaks too diffusely: the latter is said to have exceeded his material, the former not to have fulfilled it. Thus each errs, but one errs through strength and the other through weakness.

Moreover, I answer also those who perhaps despise this book with proud minds because I have compiled it, not from novel inventions, but from the writings of certain illustrious men: Divinity alone has no need of another’s assistance; nor can anything be said by anyone that has not already been said, nor does any hidden knowledge lie in our hearts which the experience of earlier men has not illuminated. [Note: Col. 0837: “is,” reading of witness 1.] Yet I truly affirm that the whole has been drawn from truthful authors. [Col. 0837C]

In truth, I excerpted much of what follows from the book of Anastasius, the Roman librarian, which he translated from Greek into Latin in the time of Charlemagne. The deeds performed under the earlier emperors down to Maurice were clearly contained in Latin books; but from the times of that emperor onward, no series of events rested upon authoritative support. Each historiographer merely set down in his book the opinion of the crowd. This may be observed from the readings which are read in almost all churches on the Feast of the Exaltation of the Holy Cross; every wise person can plainly see that they are filled with falsehood.

But the aforesaid Anastasius, in his own time, set forth in a reasoned account the matters contained in Greek history from Octavian Augustus to Michael, who succeeded Nicephorus, and translated them into Latin speech. In that work he disclosed to us many things hitherto unknown; and there he said little indeed about Muhammad, the false prophet, but clearly indicated in what times he lived. That book, however, lay hidden for many years, but recently, by God’s will, came into my hands. Its authority is neither frivolous nor inept, but authentic, trustworthy, and strong.

Therefore I have deservedly dedicated this book to you, noble Countess Adela, whom I do not doubt to be by no means unlearned [Col. 0838A] in letters, in order to delight your mind and sharpen the faith of your heart. I hope that the memorial of your name may by this means also be made notably illustrious, so that it cannot hereafter be destroyed by any antiquity, which is usually hostile to the memory of posterity. Behold before you the defenders of the Catholic faith; behold the governors of the City of God presiding over Christ’s people in the various churches. Over that royal city presides in power God the Son, true man; and almighty God, who by his wisdom rules, exalts, and defends the whole structure of that city. [Note: Col. 0837: “and God almighty” are lacking in witness 3.] May he join you to the soldiers of the saints for ages of ages. Amen.

End of the Prologue to the Sixth Book.

BEGINNING OF THE SIXTH BOOK.

Maurice, a Cappadocian by race, obtained the Roman Empire in the year 575 of the Lord’s incarnation. [Note: Col. 0837: See Rottendorff, p. 143.] . . . [lacuna] . . .

[ANASTASIUS.] Justinian [Note: Col. 0837: “LXIII. Justinian,” witness 2; and thereafter it adds the numbers in the same fashion.] succeeded his father in the kingdom in the year 678 of the divine incarnation [Note: Col. 0837: “DCLXXXVI,” Rottendorff] and reigned for ten years. . . . [lacuna] . . .

After Ebroin’s death, Pippin, son of Ansegisel, began to exercise rule under the kings in Austrasia. This Ansegisel, moreover, was called Anchises after the name of Anchises, the Trojan prince of old. [Note: Col. 0838C: “was also called A.”] [Paul the Deacon, VI.22.] The aforesaid Pippin had by his wife Plectrude two sons, Drogo and Grimoald; [Note: Col. 0837: “Grimoald,” Rottendorff.] but by a concubine [Note: Col. 0837: “by the concubine Alpaida,” Rottendorff.] [Col. 0838C] he begot Charles Tudites. [Note: Col. 0837: “rudites,” witness 2; omitted in Rottendorff.] . . . [lacuna] . . .

[ANASTASIUS.] Leontius [Note: Col. 0838C: “Leo, who was also called Leontius, reigned as emperor,” A.; there Roman affairs and the imperial chronology are presented differently and more briefly, from Ado.] reigned for three years. . . . [lacuna] . . .

Apsimar, who was also called Tiberius, reigned for about seven years. . . . [lacuna] . . .

Justinian reigned a second time for six years. . . . [lacuna] . . .

[Col. 0838D] [Paul the Deacon, VI.34.] Philippicus, also called Bardanes, was made emperor at Cherson in the year 704 of the divine incarnation [Note: Col. 0837: “DCCXI,” Rottendorff], and reigned for one year and a half. . . . [lacuna] . . .

Anastasius, also called Artemius, reigned for three years and O months. . . . [lacuna] . . .

At about these same times, Childebert died and left the kingdom of the Franks to be held by his younger son Dagobert [cf. Ado]. Pippin also, mayor of the royal household, died; his son Charles succeeded him, [Col. 0839A] and was called Tudites from the large smiths’ hammers by which heavier iron is ordinarily beaten and thinned. Made mayor of the royal court under Dagobert [Note: Col. 0839B: “the younger” added by A.], he fought very vigorously against the Saracens. [Paul the Deacon, VI.46.] For in the preceding period the Saracens, crossing from Africa, had subdued Spain; and in Charles’s time, emerging thence with their wives and little children, they invaded Aquitaine, a province of Gaul, [Ado] and, plundering everything, advanced as far as the borders of Septimania and the Viennese province. [Note: Col. 0839: quaeque (“all things”); quosque (“whomever”), witness 2? R.]

[Einhard, ch. 2.] But Charles Tudites defeated them in two great battles, one in Aquitaine near Poitiers and the other near Narbonne, so that he compelled them to return to Spain. [Paul, cited place.] In [Note: Col. 0839B: “In … killed” is lacking in A., which continues: “This Charles, however, …”] that war he killed 365,000 Saracens. This is the Charles who, because of the [Col. 0839B] constant occurrence of wars, handed over ecclesiastical property to laymen. He also fought against the Saxons and Bavarians, whom he overcame with great difficulty [cf. Ado]. [Paul the Deacon, VI.42.] He frequently fought also with Eudo, duke of the Aquitanians, and drove Ragenfrid, count of the royal palace, from the palace, though he granted him one city, Angers. King Dagobert of the Franks was succeeded by his son Theuderic. . . . [lacuna] . . .

[Paul the Deacon, VI.41.] Theodosius, then, upon Anastasius’s death, reigned for one year. . . . [lacuna] . . .

Leo obtained the Roman Empire in the year 708 of the incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ [Note: Col. 0839: “DCCXVIII,” Rottendorff] and reigned for twenty-three years. [Cf. Anastasius.] . . . [lacuna] . . .

[Col. 0839C] And likewise at about this time Charles Tudites died and was buried at Saint-Denis, not far from the city of Paris, in the year 741 from the Lord’s incarnation, his sons Carloman [Note: Col. 0839: “Charlemagne,” witness 2.] and Pippin jointly holding the mayoralty of the royal household. [Einhard, ch. 2.] Carloman [Note: Col. 0839: “Charlemagne,” witness 2; “Charlemagne,” A.], leaving the administration of the kingdom, went to Rome, where he abandoned secular military life; finally, on Mount Serapti, in the monastery of Saint Sylvester which he had built, he lived there in the monastic habit for some years. But because many nobles from Francia regularly travelled to Rome to fulfil vows, and did not wish to pass by him as though he had once been their lord, they interrupted the leisure in which he took the greatest delight by their frequent visits. [Note: Col. 0840C: “interrupting, they compel him to change his place. For, when he saw that such a throng was incompatible with his purpose, he left Mount Serapti and withdrew into the province of Samnium, to the monastery of Saint Benedict situated in the castle of Cassino, and there …,” as in Einhard, A.]

He therefore resolved to change his abode. For departing thence [Note: Col. 0839: “thence … religiously” is lacking in witness 2, which continues “completing …”] into the province of Samnium, he spent what remained of his temporal life at Castrum Cassinum in religious observance. [Cf. Ado.]

When the aforesaid Dagobert died [Note: Col. 0840C: “having been removed from life,” reading of Theoderic, A.], his son Theuderic reigned in his place; and upon this man’s death [Note: Col. 0840C: “and again upon his death,” A.], [Col. 0840A] Childeric reigned, [Note: Col. 0840C: “Hilderic, a useless man … possessing. Concerning him the oft-mentioned Pippin … asked Zacharias of Rome through his own [lacuna] whether he ought to remain … content. To them [the pope] replied that the man ought to be called king who would govern the commonwealth well. On this occasion the Franks shaved Hilderic and thrust him into a monastery, and Pippin … king. On the Roman see Pope Stephen succeeded Pope Zacharias. Moreover the Emperor Leo at Constantinople … Furthermore, Leo having died, Constantine became emperor,” A., which continues: “Constantine etc.” (note *).] whom they also called Hilderic. [Einhard, cited place; Ado.]

Since he was a useless and negligent man and possessed none of the power of the kingdom except the royal name and a subsistence allowance, which the prefect of the royal household supplied him, Pippin, mayor of the royal household, took care to ask Zacharias, bishop of Rome, through his envoys whether he ought to be king of Francia who, devoted to idleness, was content with the royal name alone. The pontiff replied that he ought to be called king who governed the commonwealth well. [Einhard.] Encouraged by this answer, the Franks thrust Hilderic into a monastery, clothed him in a monk’s tunic, and made Pippin their king. When he had been created king, he subdued all who rebelled against him by great force; he made his brother Grifo king of the Austrasians, [Col. 0840B] and appointed Tassilo, his sister’s son, duke of the Bavarians. Grifo, however, because of the insolence of his mind, declared war upon him. Meanwhile, at Constantinople . . . [lacuna] . . .

[ANASTASIUS.] In the same year the emperor Leo died the death of both soul and body, and his son Constantine became successor alike to his empire and to his impiety, in the year from the creation of the world, according to the Romans, 6,240, but according to the computation of the Egyptians and Alexandrians, 6,232. [Note: Col. 0839: “6,940 from the creation of the world; 741 from the incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ,” Rottendorff.]

Constantine [Note: Col. 0840C: “Constantine then reigned for 27 years,” A., in which the remainder is lacking down to “In his days Pope Stephen” (note **).], persecutor of the laws handed down by the fathers, assumed the empire in the year [Col. 0840C] 734 of the Lord’s incarnation and reigned for thirty-four years, two months, and twenty-six days. [Note: Col. 0839: “he reigned … 734” lacking in Rottendorff.] . . . [lacuna] . . .

[Col. 0840D] [Adrevald, *Miracles of St Benedict*, ch. 15.] Meanwhile the monks of the monastery of Cassino, by the authority of Carloman, [Col. 0841A] of whom we spoke above, came to Rome and asked Pope Zacharias the Great to send letters to Pippin, king of the Franks, directing him to restore to its ancestral place the body of the most blessed Benedict, which the monks of Fleury had secretly claimed for themselves. [Note: Col. 0841: “that he should establish by authority,” witness 2.]

The Roman pontiff assented, and through this same Carloman took care to write to the bishops of Francia, saying: “Zacharias, bishop . . . farewell.” [Note: Col. 0841: As it is read in Adrevald, ch. 15. But for “the excellence of Pippin, mayor of the household,” Hugo wrote: “the excellence of Pippin, king of the Franks.”] Carloman the king presented this letter before his brother Pippin the king, to the peoples of Gaul at a great assembly of the clergy. Then the pious ruler, on hearing this, sent Remigius, bishop of Rouen, together with three bishops, to Fleury with plenary authority, so that they should return to the Cassinese monks the greater part of the body of Saint Benedict, with no small care, while reserving one portion in the place as its reward. [Col. 0841B] By prudent counsel he arranged this in order neither to grieve his brother nor to deprive the kingdom of the Franks of so great an honour.

But since there is no wisdom nor counsel against God, the matter became known to the brothers of Fleury two days before the bishops’ appointed arrival. The brothers therefore observed a three-day fast and prayed to the most blessed Benedict before his holy tomb in these words:

“O our one hope after God, do not leave us orphaned. You came here, not for our merits, but for the salvation of many souls. We certainly know and wholly confess that we are unworthy of your presence, because we are useless workers and have not walked in accordance with our profession in your commandments. But we are ready to amend our negligences, and we willingly submit ourselves to the lashes of your fatherhood, provided only that you do not abandon your dependants, who have gathered here because of your presence. Receive, we pray, our tears, and remain with us in this place, which long ago you graciously chose for yourself. But if, angered by the weight of our sins, you are unwilling to remain with us, let it be known to you that wherever you decide to go, you will have us as most devoted fellow-travellers. The dangers of rivers, the yokes of mountains, or the violence of storms will not terrify us; nor will any creature be able to prevent us from following your fatherhood.”

One would have thought that a great quantity of rain was falling upon the pavement, because of the excessive flood of their tears. [Note: Col. 0841: “is lacking” in witness 2.] And when they had already spent the whole three days in such sobbing and tears, [Col. 0841D] behold, the aforesaid bishops arrived and attempted to carry out the king’s commands; immediately they ordered the doors of the church opened for them.

[Adrevald.] Medo then governed that holy monastery. Having received the royal orders with distress, he replied that he could not return the deposit which he rejoiced to have received for safekeeping, not for restoration. “But if,” he said, “Saint Benedict wishes to be carried back to his former tomb, we cannot retain him; but if he has resolved to remain here, to which he permitted his limbs to be transferred for the salvation of very many souls, know most certainly that you yourselves will return home deprived of the object of your desire.”

Having said this, he summoned to himself the brothers of the whole congregation and shut himself up with them in the nearby church of Blessed Peter. There, prostrate upon the ground and with his face drenched in tears, he devoted himself to prayer. [Note: Col. 0841: “he called,” witness 2.] The bishops, however, entered the church of the holy Mother of God; before they had approached the tomb of Saint Benedict, they were stricken with confusion and terror and with such blindness that they could not recognize even one another. When they realized that they had been blinded by divine vengeance, they began to wander through the church, feeling their way, until they came upon the bell-ropes, which they began to pull with great force. For they could not otherwise [Col. 0842B] make known their misfortune to those who had remained outside.

Awakened by this sound, [Note: Col. 0841: “sleep,” witness 2.] the brothers came out from the aforesaid church of the apostle Peter, thinking that they would see a grievous sight; but they did not know what was causing the delay in the church. Some of them therefore entered to investigate, and immediately, with their own eyes open, found them wandering through the church, and went out saying: “Our pious father Benedict has heard us and received our tears. Come and see the great works of God.” Then, entering the church together, they found them crying “Alas!” and seeing nothing.

When they said to them, “What are you doing, good lords?” [Note: Col. 0841: “lords,” Rottendorff.] they replied: “Alas for us, because we came to violate the repose of holy Father Benedict, and therefore have incurred blindness. But you servants of God, deal more gently with us, and do not repay us in kind according to our presumption. Instead pray to almighty God for us, that he may open our eyes; and we promise you that henceforth we shall never presume to do such things.”

At these words the brothers, prostrate upon the ground, prayed more earnestly that the divine mercy might deign to restore light to them; and while they prayed, their eyes were opened. At length those men returned to the king, recounted what they had suffered, and added that Gaul ought not to be deprived of such holy bones. But while the king delayed the pope’s envoys rather long, Pope Zacharias himself died. Stephen succeeded him in the pontifical see; he too personally came to the same king in Francia. [Col. 0842D] [Note: Cols. 0843C–0844A: A. continues thus (see above, note): “In his days Pope Stephen came to King Pippin in Francia.” Cf. Ado and the *Deeds of the Roman Pontiffs*.]

For a king of Italy named Aistulf was despoiling the Roman Church [Note: Cols. 0843C–0843D: Rottendorff: “was wickedly attacking it and despoiling it of its possessions; and while [Stephen], on his way to seek aid from the king, lay ill in the monastery of Saint Denis, he at last recovered through the prayers of Saint Denis. He therefore consecrated in the same basilica an altar in honour of Saints Peter and Paul, and blessed Pippin and his two sons Charles and Carloman as kings of the Franks. These things took place in the year 754 from the Lord’s incarnation. In the preceding year the monk Carloman had come to his brother Pippin for certain reasons and still remained in Francia. But when the king had raised a great army to give aid to Pope Stephen of Rome, he left him ill at Vienne. The king himself, pursuing the enterprise begun, besieged Aistulf in Pavia and finally received from him forty hostages, that he might restore to Blessed Peter and Pope Stephen all their possessions and rights. All this etc.,” A.] of its possessions.

But while the same venerable pope remained for some time with the king, he fell ill. Confined by this affliction, he lay in bed at the monastery of Saint-Denis, not far from the city of Paris; but at last he recovered through the merits of Saint Denis, and in that same basilica consecrated an altar in honour of the holy apostles Peter and Paul, through whose prayers he had also recovered, in the year 754 from the Lord’s incarnation. After returning to the city of Rome, he began to build within that city a monastery for Saint Denis; but, overtaken by death, he could not complete it. [Note: Col. 0843: “complete,” witness 2.] His successor Paul, however, completed it nobly, gathered there certain servants of God who were Greek by nation, and ordered that the place itself be called “At the Holy Martyrs, in the School of the Greeks.”

King Pippin then raised a large army from Gaul in order to give aid to the aforesaid Stephen, Roman pontiff. [Cf. Ado and the *Deeds of the Pontiffs*.] Entering Italy, he besieged King Aistulf and received forty hostages from him, on condition that he restore all estates to the blessed apostle Peter and holy Pope Stephen and should never again presume to trouble the Roman Church. [Col. 0843B] [Ado.] But when Pippin departed, Aistulf rendered all this void. Yet [Note: Cols. 0843D–0844A: A. continues: “But thereafter divine vengeance was not far from Aistulf. For when …”] after no great interval of time, while he was going hunting one day, he was suddenly struck by God’s judgment and died.

After Aistulf’s death, Desiderius succeeded him. At the same time King Pippin received great gifts from the Emperor Constantine; and, returning from Italy, he proceeded with his son Charles against Waifar, duke of the Aquitanians, and stormed and captured the Aquitanian strongholds of Canteram [Note: Col. 0843: “Cantheram,” witness 2.] and Barbonem; burned Clermont, [Note: Col. 0843: “Clarimontem,” witness 2.] advanced as far as Limoges, and, while returning thence, captured Bourges. Again, not long afterwards, he entered Aquitaine and traversed it as far as Cahors; and, returning from there, he placed garrisons for himself in the fortress of Argentoniacum and in the city of Bourges. [Col. 0843C] Finally, in a third expedition into Aquitaine, he advanced as far as the river Garonne; and on his return he at last killed the aforesaid Duke Waifar in the district of Périgueux. [Note: Col. 0843: “Waiferum,” witness 2.] After this, the same most warlike King Pippin entered Saxony and conquered it. He also claimed all Bavaria for himself. [Note: Col. 0844A: A. continues: “After accomplishing these things, he began to fall ill and, weighed down by disease, died in the city of Paris in the year 768 of the divine incarnation, leaving surviving …”]

[Col. 0844A] [ANASTASIUS.] Meanwhile Constantine, that most impious emperor, marching against the Bulgars, contracted a terrible illness, by which he died, no less filled with the blood of martyrs than Diocletian. His son Leo the Khazar succeeded him. In the Roman see, Paul was appointed in place of Pope Stephen; after Paul another Stephen sat, and Adrian succeeded him. At the same time Saint Boniface, bishop of Mainz, flourished; preaching the word of God in Frisia, he deserved to attain the palm of martyrdom. [Col. 0844B] [Cf. Ado.]

[ANASTASIUS.] Leo the Khazar therefore reigned for five years. In the final year of his reign, after the death of Nicetas, patriarch of Constantinople, Paul, a Cypriot by birth, radiant in word and deed, was consecrated to the same see.

[Cf. ADO., EINH. ch. 3.] In these same days Pippin, who by the authority of Pope Zacharias of Rome had been made king of the Franks from being mayor of the palace, died in the city of Paris in the fifteenth year of his reign and in the year 769 of Christ’s Incarnation, leaving his sons Charles and Carloman surviving, to whom succession to the kingdom belonged.

[ADO.] Of these, Charles [Col. 0846A: Charles was raised to the throne in the city of Noyon in France, and his brother Carloman at Soissons. When this had been done, Carloman, though deprived of his brother’s aid, attacked Duke Hunold, who after Waifar’s death had attempted to retain Aquitaine for himself. At length the most fierce king compelled him to flee and seek Wasconia. Not tolerating his remaining there either, he sent envoys to Lupus, duke of the Wascones, ordering him to surrender the fugitive; if he did not do so quickly, he promised to demand him by war. But Lupus, using sounder counsel, not only surrendered Hunold but also submitted himself and the province under his rule. However, when the two years had passed during which Carloman had reigned, he ended his life, [Col. 0846B] and authority over the whole kingdom of the Franks came under Charles’s power. Meanwhile at Rome Paul succeeded Pope Stephen, and another Stephen succeeded Paul, and after him Adrian. There flourished … to attain it. After Emperor Constantine, Leo the Khazar reigned. — Leo the Khazar therefore reigned for five years. In his time an envoy, etc. A.] received the royal crown in the city of Noyon, and his brother Carloman [Col. 0844C] at Soissons.

[EINH. ch. 3.] But Carloman, when two years had elapsed after he had been raised to the throne, departed this life; and his wife and sons, compelled by no force, fled to Desiderius, king of the Lombards, seeking his protection. Thus, by the consent of the men of the entire Frankish realm, Charles alone obtained the monarchy of the kingdom.

[ADO., EINH. ch. 5.] Accordingly, in the first year of his reign Charles entered Aquitaine and attacked Duke Hunold, who, after Waifar’s death [Col. 0843: the second witness reads *waiferi*], was preparing to retain that province for himself. He also compelled him to seek Wasconia [Col. 0843: the second witness reads *guase*; and thereafter likewise]. But Charles ordered Lupus, duke of the Wascones [Col. 0843: “Lupus, duke of the Wascones,” in the second witness and R.], to surrender the fugitive, threatening that unless he did so promptly he would demand him by war. Lupus, however, adopting the sounder counsel [Col. 0843: the first witness has *usus consilio*; the words *desunt*—“are absent”—in witness 1], not only surrendered Hunold but also submitted himself [Col. 0844D], together with the province over which he presided, to Charles’s authority.

[ADO.] Then, when the kingdom of the Franks had come wholly to Charles, as has been said, Peter, an envoy sent by Pope Adrian in the name of the Roman Church, came to the same glorious King Charles, asking his aid against Desiderius, king of the Lombards, who, following the custom of his father Aistulf, was troubling the Roman Church.

[Col. 0846B: “To the king of the Franks.” Gloss: “Charles came at Pope Adrian’s command against King Desiderius. Then the great King Charles prepared war against Desiderius, who was violently oppressing the Roman Church in an unlawful fashion; and by Mount Cenis, etc.” A.]

[EINH. ch. 6; ADO.] Charles obeyed him, prepared war against Desiderius with a great force, entered Italy by Mount Cenis, and with a strong army besieged Pavia, a city of Italy. There he captured King Desiderius and sent him into exile. Moreover, he drove Desiderius’s son Adalgisus from his paternal kingdom and, after subduing Italy, established his own son Pippin as king.

[EINH. ch. 7.] Once affairs in Italy had been settled, he undertook the Saxon war. The Saxons were so thoroughly subdued and softened by his prowess that he removed ten thousand of their people, with their wives and little children [Col. 0845: the second witness reads “their wives and children”], and distributed them through Gaul and Germany in many separate settlements. The war was finally agreed to have ended on the condition that, abandoning the worship of demons, they should receive the sacraments of the Christian faith and, united with the Franks, become one people.

[EINH. ch. 8.] Yet while this war was still being prolonged [Col. 0845: the second witness reads “while this was still being prolonged”], after stations had been arranged at suitable places, [Col. 0845B] he entered Spain. Having crossed the pass of the Pyrenees and received into submission all the towns and castles which he approached, he returned. But on his way back he experienced the treachery of the Wascones on the very ridge of the Pyrenees [Col. 0845B: “The mountain pass,” A.].

For, as the army marched in a long column, extended as the terrain and narrow places allowed, the Wascones, stationed in ambush in a hollow of the mountain, attacked the rearmost part of the column and threw it down into the valley below. Engaging them in battle, they killed all whom they found. In this battle Eggihard, steward of the royal table, Anselm, count of the palace, and Roland, prefect of the Breton march, were killed with many others. Roland was carried to the castle of Blaye [Col. 0845C] and buried there [Col. 0845: Compare the Book of Turpin, ch. 29].

[Vita Hludovici, ch. 3.] In these same days Charles, the great king of the Franks, returning from Spain, found that his wife Hildegard [Col. 0845: the second witness reads *Hildegardem*] had borne twins at the royal estate called Cassinogilus, situated between the Droth [Col. 0845: the second witness reads *Droh*] and the Warunna [Col. 0845: the first witness reads *Uarunna*]. One of them died before he was born; the other was baptized and named Louis.

[ADO., EINH. ch. 1.] After this King Charles, having subdued the people of Narbonne, returned to Francia. Not long afterwards he travelled through Italy to Capua, a city of Campania; and while returning thence he declared war on the Beneventans. But the duke of that province, named Arigisus, unable to withstand the king’s fierceness, sent his sons Rumald [Col. 0845: the second witness reads *Romald*] and Grimald to him as hostages for the preservation of loyalty.

[Ib. ch. 11.] Again after this Charles [Col. 0845: the second witness reads *Carloman*; A. reads *Charles the Great*] returned to Gaul. Then the Bavarian war arose [Col. 0845: in the second witness, “the war arose” is absent] and was quickly concluded.

[Ib. ch. 12.] War was also made against the Slavs. The Danes and Suebi were allied with the Slavs [Col. 0845: R. reads “Sueones”; the second witness reads “Suebi,” with the word “Slavs”]. But the oft-mentioned king subdued or crushed all of these in a single expedition [Col. 0845: the second witness reads *ac*, “and,” instead of *aut*, “or”], so that thereafter they preferred subjection to rebellion.

[Ib. ch. 13.] This most powerful king also attacked the Huns and Avars. That war was successfully completed within the eighth year from its beginning. Moreover, he subjected all Frisia and Brittany to his dominion. Emperor Leo was succeeded by his son Constantine, a most Christian man.

[ANAST.] Constantine [Col. 0846C: “Emperor Constantine therefore reigned with his mother Irene for eight years. He sent to the king of France and made peace with him. He too was seized and blinded by his own people at Constantinople. His mother nevertheless remained in power. In their times the Balearic Islands were ravaged by Moors and Saracens. And in their sixth year, when at Rome there died, etc. A., with the rest omitted.”] the son of Leo, having received the Roman Empire with his mother Irene, reigned for ten years beginning in the year 791 of the Incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ. Having made peace with the Arabs, [lacuna] [Col. 0846C] [lacuna] so that death immediately followed the torture; and thus Irene ruled a second time for almost five years.

In the same year, when Pope Adrian of blessed memory died at Rome, Leo, a man in every respect worthy of reverence, was consecrated in the same see. In that same year [Col. 0848C: “the same,” A.] the relatives of the aforesaid Pope Adrian stirred up the Roman people against Pope Leo, seized him, and [Col. 0846D] blinded him, though they could not extinguish his sight. But he fled to Charles, king of the Franks, who avenged him [Col. 0845: R. reads “him” rather than “that one”] and restored him to his see.

[ADO.] Leo then crowned him emperor in the church of Saint Peter, clothing him in the imperial robe. Then the whole people of Rome cried out to him [Col. 0845: the second witness reads “Roman”]:

> “To Charles Augustus, crowned by God, the great and peace-giving emperor of the Romans: life and victory!”

[EINH. ch. 15.] The aforementioned wars having thus been successfully concluded, Charles, the great king of the Franks, enlarged and extended with such distinction the kingdom which he had inherited from his father Pippin—already great indeed [Col. 0847: the second witness reads “already so great”; R. reads “great and indeed extensive”; A. reads “great and extensive”]—that he added a second kingdom to it.

Previously, no more than that part of Gaul which lies between the Rhine and the Loire [Col. 0847: the second witness and R. read “and” rather than “or”], the Ocean and the Balearic Sea; that part of Germany which is inhabited between Saxony, the Danube, the Rhine, and the river Saale, which divides the Thuringians and Sorbs, and by the Franks called eastern; and, besides these, the Alamanni and Bavarians, had belonged to the authority of the Frankish kingdom. But by the wars mentioned above he first subdued Aquitaine and Wasconia, and the whole ridge of the Pyrenees as far as the river Ebro, which rises among the Navarrese [Col. 0847B: the second witness reads *Nacarrones*, R. *Navarros*, A. *Nacaros*], cuts through Spain’s most fertile fields, and flows into the Balearic Sea beneath the walls of Tortosa. He also subdued the whole of Italy, extending from Augusta Praetoria to Lower Calabria, where the boundaries of the Greeks and Beneventans meet [Col. 0847: the second witness reads “and”]; all Saxony, a considerable part of Germany; both Pannonias; Dacia adjoining the farther bank of the Danube; and all the barbarian peoples dwelling between the Rhine and Weser, the Ocean, and the Danube. Though almost alike in language, they differed greatly in appearance and customs. He made them tributary to himself.

[Ib. ch. 16.] He increased the glory of his realm also by winning certain kings and peoples to friendship [Col. 0847: this phrase is absent in the second witness]. He bound Andefossus, king of Galicia and Asturias, so closely to him in alliance that whenever he sent him letters or envoys, he ordered that he be called no otherwise than Charles’s own man [Col. 0847C: the second witness reads “his own lord”; the source’s *dominum* means “lord,” whereas the proposed relation is Charles’s own man]. By generosity he so inclined the kings of the Scots [Col. 0847: the second witness reads *Scothorum*] to his will that they never called him otherwise than lord, and themselves his subjects and servants. Letters sent to him survive which attest this disposition toward him [Col. 0847: absent in the second witness].

He also maintained such a concord of friendship with Aaron, king of the Persians, who held nearly the entire East except India, that Aaron placed Charles’s favour before the friendship of every king and prince in the whole world, declaring him alone worthy of honour and generosity from himself.

Accordingly, when Charles’s envoys, whom he had sent with gifts to the most sacred sepulchre of our Lord and Saviour and to the place of the Resurrection, had come to him and made known their lord’s wish, he not only permitted what was asked, but granted that the holy place of Saint Mary of the Latins should be assigned to Charles’s authority. He added his own envoys to those returning, and sent Charles great gifts among garments, spices, and the other riches of eastern lands [Col. 0848A: this phrase is absent in witness 1], although a few years earlier, when Charles had asked him for the only elephant he then possessed [Col. 0847: the second witness reads “friends”], he had sent it to him.

[ADO.] Among the gifts which the imperial envoys brought from Persia, they brought him a clock of brass, mechanically constructed. In it the course of the twelve hours was shown by a water-clock, with as many bronze balls [Col. 0847: the first witness reads *aeneis*, “bronze”], which fell at the completion of the hours and by their fall caused a cymbal beneath them to ring. It also had the same number of horsemen, who emerged through twelve windows as the hours were completed and, by the force of their exit, opened the same number of windows [Col. 0848C: “which had previously been open, they shut. In the same period, A., together with Ado.”].

At about this time the bones of the blessed martyr Cyprian were brought from Carthage, with the relics of the blessed Scillitan martyrs Speratus [Col. 0848B] and his companions, and were placed in the church of Saint John the Baptist in the city of Lyon. The Saracens, driven from Sardinia [Col. 0847: A. adds “moreover”], first engaged the Sardinians in battle; after losing three thousand of their men, they made directly for Corsica. There, fighting the fleet commanded by Count Bulgarius, they were defeated, routed, and killed, having lost fourteen of their ships.

Meanwhile Louis, son of the oft-named Emperor Charles, entered the Spanish lands [compare Vita Hludovici, ch. 10 ff.] and again subjected Barcelona [Col. 0847: the second witness reads *Barcillonam*], which had rebelled against his father.

Charles the Great, while king of the Franks, received at Rome the insignia of Roman emperor on 25 December, in the fourth year in which Irene, mother of Emperor Constantine, after her son’s death received sole power [Col. 0848C: the words from “Charles the Great” through “she died” are absent in A.]. [ANAST.] While the most Christian Augustus Charles ruled at Rome, the patrician Nicephorus rebelled against Empress Irene at Byzantium and [lacuna] where she died.

Charles [Col. 0851C: “Charles the Great therefore, from king of the Franks, emperor of the Romans, reigned forty-seven years. Having undertaken, as stated, and …” A.] the Great, therefore, made Roman emperor from king of the Franks in the year 784 of the Lord’s Incarnation [Col. 0847: R. reads 802], and reigned for about forty-seven years [Col. 0847: “approximately forty-seven,” witness 3].

[EINH. ch. 17.] Having undertaken and ordered the commonwealth, as stated above, he began many works in various places befitting the dignity of the empire and advantageous to the Frankish kingdom [Col. 0847: witness 3 reads “pertaining to the dignity and advantage of the empire and the Frankish kingdom”]. Foremost among them were the basilica of the holy Mother of God at Aachen, built with marvellous workmanship, and a bridge at Mainz over the Rhine, five hundred paces long—for such is the breadth of the river there. Yet it was consumed by fire one year before he died [Col. 0847: absent in witness 3], and could not be rebuilt because of his sudden death, although he planned to replace the wooden structure with one of stone.

He also began splendid palaces: one not far from Mainz [Col. 0849A: the second witness reads *Maguncia*; witness 3 *Magontiaco*], near the estate called Ingelheim [Col. 0849: witness 2 reads *ita*; witness 3 *Ingeleben*; A. *Ingelebem*], and another at Nijmegen, above the river Waal, which flows past the southern part of the island of the Batavians [Col. 0849: the second witness omits the words after “Nijmegen” through “which flows”].

Above all, wherever throughout his whole realm he found sacred buildings fallen into decay through age, he commanded the bishops and fathers responsible for them to restore them, taking care through envoys that his orders were carried out.

[Vita Hludovici, ch. 19.] Therefore many monasteries were repaired during his empire—indeed, built from their foundations [Col. 0849: the second witness reads “indeed, completely from their foundations”; R. likewise]—especially these: the monastery of Saint Philibert; the monastery of Saint Florentius; the monastery of Caroffi; the monastery of Conques [Col. 0849: the second witness reads *Conchas*; R. places Conques before Caroffi and adds Saint Maxentius, Moissac, Menat, and others]; the monastery of Saint Maxentius; the monastery of Menat; the monastery of Magnilocum; the monastery of Moissac; the monastery of Saint Savinus; the monastery of Noviliacum [Col. 0849: witness 3 reads *Noviacum*]; the monastery of Saint Theofridus; the monastery of Saint Pascentius; the monastery of Dorosa [Col. 0849: witness 2 reads “de Rosa”]; the monastery of Solignac; the nunnery of Saint Mary; the nunnery of Saint Radegund; the monastery of Vera; the monastery of Deutera in the district of Toulouse; the monastery of Valida in Septimania [Col. 0849: this is how Hugo separates the words]; the monastery of Saint Anianus; the monastery of Galune; the monastery of Saint Lawrence; the monastery of Saint Mary called “in Rubine”; the monastery of Caunas; and countless others. With these, like so many lamps [Col. 0849: the second witness reads *licnis*; witness 3 *lihnis*], the whole kingdom of Aquitaine is adorned.

The most devout Emperor Charles the Great adorned all these with weights of gold and silver and gifts of precious gems, enriched them with most ample honours, and, what is more precious still, distinguished them with the protection of most holy relics.

[Compare EINH. chs. 26, 33.] These are the names of the metropolitan sees which remained under his rule: Rome, Ravenna [Col. 0849: witness 2 reads *Rauencia*], Milan, Cividale, Grado, Cologne, Mainz, Juvavum [Col. 0849: witness 2 reads *Juvanum*] and Salzburg [Col. 0849: witness 2 reads *Salizbur*; witness 3 *Saltbugk*], Trier, Sens, Besançon [Col. 0849: witness 2 reads *Vesuntium*], Lyon, Rouen [Col. 0849: witness 2 reads *Rothomagum*], Reims, Arles, Vienne, Tarentaise, Embrun, Bourges, Bordeaux, and Tours [Col. 0849: witness 2 abbreviates some names as *Thur.*, *Tur.*, and *Burd.*; R. likewise].

[Ib. ch. 27.] This most powerful emperor honoured all of these with many gifts; but among them he especially defended the Roman Church faithfully and adorned it with his wealth.

[Ib. ch. 25.] Nor was he content with his native tongue, but applied himself to learning foreign languages as well [Col. 0849D: witness 3 reads “he devoted himself”]. He could understand Greek better than he could speak it. In learning grammar he had Peter of Pisa as his teacher, and in the other disciplines Albinus, surnamed Alcuin. He also attempted to write, and carried tablets so that, in his free time, he might accustom his hand to forming letters; but this ill-timed labour, begun late in life, profited little.

[Ib. ch. 26.] He always cultivated the Christian religion with the utmost piety, and diligently attended church morning and evening, at the night offices, and at the time of sacrifice.

[Ib. ch. 27.] He was likewise endowed with the greatest liberality toward the poor, striving not only to relieve them in his own kingdom, but to send large sums of money into overseas regions—to Syria, Egypt, Africa, Jerusalem, Alexandria, and Carthage. For this reason he especially sought the friendships of overseas kings: that some relief might come to the Christians dwelling under them [Col. 0849: witness 2 reads “under those peoples”; witness 3 “some relief”].

[Ib. ch. 22.] Moreover, this most serene emperor was large and robust in body, tall in stature, with a rounded crown of the head, a nose somewhat larger than average, beautiful eyes, venerable grey hair, a cheerful countenance, a clear voice, and sound health.

[Ib. ch. 24.] Finally, he feasted very rarely, and his daily dinner was served with only four dishes, besides roasted meat, which hunters used to bring in on spits and which he ate more willingly than any other food [Col. 0849: absent in witness 2]. During dinner he listened either to some music or to a reader. Histories and the deeds of the ancients were read to him [Col. 0849: witness 2 omits “and of the ancients”; witness 3 includes it]; he also delighted in the books of Saint Augustine, especially those entitled *On the City of God*. He was so sparing in wine and every drink that he rarely drank more than three times at dinner. In summer, after his midday meal, having taken some fruit and drunk once, he removed his clothes and shoes and rested for two or three hours, as he was accustomed to do at night. [Col. 0850C] At night he slept in such a way that he interrupted his sleep four or five times, not only by waking but also by rising.

[Ib. ch. 18.] He had three sons: Charles, Pippin, and Louis. He also had three daughters: Rotrude [Col. 0849: witness 3 reads *Rottrude*], Bertha, and Gisela. He had two other daughters by his wife Fastrada. After Fastrada’s death he took as wife Liutgard, an Alamannian; after her death he again had two concubines, Gersuinda, of Saxon stock, by whom he had a daughter named Adaltrude [Col. 0849: witness 3 reads “a daughter was born to him”], and Regina, who bore him Drogo and Hugh. Moreover, his mother Bertrada grew old in great honour with him [Col. 0849: witness 3 omits “with him”].

[Ib. ch. 19.] He judged that his children should be educated so that both sons and daughters should first be instructed in the liberal studies to which he himself gave attention. Then, as soon as their age permitted, he made his sons ride, after the Frankish fashion, and train in arms and hunting. He ordered his daughters to accustom themselves to wool-working [Col. 0849: witness 3 reads *laneficio*] and to devote themselves to distaff and spindle, so that they should not grow dull through idleness, and to be instructed in every virtue.

Of all these children he lost only two sons and a daughter before his death: Charles, the eldest by birth; Pippin, whom he had made king of Italy; and Rotrude [Col. 0851: witness 2 and A. read *Rhotrude*], his first-born daughter, who had been betrothed to Constantine, emperor of the Greeks [Col. 0851: witness 3 reads “of the Romans”]. Pippin left surviving one son, Bernard, and five daughters: Adelaide [Col. 0851: witness 3 reads *Adelaidem*], Atula [Col. 0851: witness 3 reads *Attulam*], Gundrada, Berthaid, and Theoderada. In these Charles showed a special proof of his affection, by making his grandson succeed his dead father and having his granddaughters reared among his own daughters.

Emperor Nicephorus of Constantinople [Col. 0851: witness 3 reads *Nichephorus*] sent to him, made a most firm treaty with him, and freely granted him all Venice [compare ADO.]. At last, when the magnificent Emperor Charles saw the end of his life drawing near, he left the imperial crown to his son Louis, whom he had long before appointed king of Aquitaine; and he made Bernard, the son of his son Pippin, king of Italy. He died in the seventy-second year of his life [Col. 0851: witness 2 reads “eighty-second”], the forty-seventh year of his reign, and the year 814 of Christ’s Incarnation, in the fourth indiction, on 28 January [Col. 0851C: A. adds “in the year 814 of the Lord’s Incarnation and in the seventy-second year of his age, in the forty-seventh year of his reign, on 28 January”].

[Compare EINH. chs. 30, 31.] He was buried in the church of Saint Mary, Mother of God, at Aachen, and a gilded arch was erected above his tomb. His deeds, which are commonly recounted, have not all been explained here in order to avoid wearying the reader.

Furthermore, at Rome Stephen IV sat after Leo, whom we mentioned above; Paschal succeeded Stephen. In the same period flourished Saint Giles, the distinguished confessor, a Greek by birth, who came to Gaul by God’s guidance and lived as a hermit in the province called Septimania. Paul, the historian of his own people, the Lombards, also flourished in these times. He came from the monastery of Monte Cassino into Gaul, drawn by affection and by the renown of the aforesaid prince Charles, the most eminent emperor.

[ANAST.] Nicephorus [Col. 0851C: “Finally, Nicephorus, emperor of Constantinople, of whom we have spoken above, died after many notable victories over the Saracens, and Michael, his son-in-law, was elevated to the empire.” A. Thus he ended the work, adding the epilogue printed above on p. 353.] therefore, as we have already said above, was made emperor from a patrician and reigned for eight years. He was a cruel and most avaricious man [lacuna] two months and six days after his father’s death. Within these days Michael Curopalates was elevated to the empire.

Michael therefore, invading the imperial power over Stauracius in the year 804 of the divine Incarnation, reigned for two years [Col. 0852A]. From him the reverend patriarch demanded [lacuna]. But Crumnus seized Adrianople. Moreover, in these days the Arabs, contending against one another, lost the stability of their kingdom, and four tyrants arose from one. One of them claimed Egypt and Africa together; two divided Spain between themselves; and the fourth took Palestine.

Louis the Pious, son of Charles the Great [Col. 0851: witness 2 and R. add “emperor”], after his father’s death obtained the Roman Empire in the year 814 of the divine Incarnation and reigned for almost twenty-seven years. He was a man of most gentle nature [compare ADO.]. Yet, because he governed the commonwealth in accordance with the mildness of his character, he met an end full of adversities, cruelly assailed both by his children and by the magnates of the realm. Nevertheless [Col. 0851: witness 3 perhaps reads “again”] he was always a most fervent executor of the Lord’s commands and a most energetic promoter of the holy law.

Gathering bishops and most noble men, he caused a book containing the canonical rule to be compiled and arranged [Col. 0851: witness 3 reads “the canonical rule”]. [Vita Hludovici, ch. 28.] In his time gem-studded belts laden with knives, girdles adorned with gold, elaborate garments [Col. 0851: absent in witness 2], and other secular ornaments began to be laid aside by bishops and clergy.

[Ib. ch. 32.] He also added certain highly necessary chapters [Col. 0851: witness 2 reads “necessary”] to the secular laws.

[ADO.] This most serene emperor had three sons [Col. 0851: witness 2 and R. read “three sons”] by his first wife Ermengard: Lothar, Pippin, and Louis. By his second wife, Judith, he had Charles, king of the Franks [Col. 0852C].

Lothar, the emperor’s eldest son, while he had been established by his most gracious father over Italy, came to Rome. [Vita Hludovici, ch. 36.] On the holy day of Easter, in the church of the blessed Apostle Peter, he received from Pope Paschal a crown together with the title of Augustus. Paschal was succeeded as pope by Eugenius. [Ib. ch. 40.] To him Hilduin, abbot of Saint-Denis and Saint-Médard, sent, asking that the bones of the venerable martyr Sebastian be sent to him. He obtained them and, as was fitting, honourably placed them beside the body of Saint Médard in the city of Soissons [Col. 0851: witness 2 reads “having been placed beside the body of Saint Médard in the city of Soissons”].

[ADO.] In the same period the bodies of the most holy martyrs Hippolytus and Tiburtius were brought from Rome and buried in the church of Saint-Denis, not far from Paris.

[Vita Hludovici, ch. 36.] In these days Drogo, brother of Emperor Louis, succeeded Gundulf as bishop of Metz. [Ib. ch. 41.] In the Roman see Pope Eugenius was succeeded by Valentinus, Valentinus by Gregory IV. [Ib. ch. 48.] With Gregory’s consent Lothar seized his father, Emperor Louis [Col. 0851: absent in witness 2], and ordered him to be guarded at the monastery of Saint Médard. He also exiled Louis’s wife Judith and entrusted Charles, whom Louis had had by her, to the castle of Prüm [Col. 0852D: witness 2 reads *Priugne*, witness 3 *Pruvinne*, instead of *Priumie*]. [Compare ib. ch. 51.]

But not long afterwards the princes of Francia released Emperor Louis from custody and reconciled the son Lothar to his father. Afterwards [Col. 0853: absent in witness 3] the most gracious emperor divided his empire among his four sons: to Lothar he assigned Italy; to Louis, Germany and Saxony; to Pippin, Aquitaine; and to Charles, Francia and Burgundy [compare Hugo of Flavigny]. But Lothar did not bear this division of the empire equably, and attempted to subject the whole empire to himself. When his father learned this, he immediately set out against him; but on the journey itself, seized by a grievous illness, he ended his life.

[Vita Hludovici, ch. 64.] His body was brought by Bishop Drogo to Metz and buried in the church of Saint Arnulf the Confessor. He died in the sixty-fourth year of his life [Col. 0853: add “in the year 840 of the Lord’s Incarnation, on 25 June”]. After his death his four sons fought fiercely at the field of Fontenoy [Col. 0853: witness 3 reads “fought one another”]. In that war almost all the soldiers of Francia, Italy, Aquitaine, Alamannia, Saxony, and Burgundy killed one another with mutual wounds [Col. 0853: witness 2 and R. read “with wounds to one another”]. [Compare ADO.] Nevertheless Charles the Bald won the victory.

In the Roman see Pope Sergius succeeded the aforesaid Gregory; Leo IV succeeded Sergius; Benedict succeeded Leo; and Nicholas succeeded Benedict. In these times Theodulf, abbot of Fleury and bishop of Orléans, flourished. Having been accused before Emperor Louis of many crimes [Col. 0853: witness 3 reads “falsely accused”], he was exiled at Angers [Col. 0853: witness 2 and R. read *Andegaviam*].

While he was held in custody there, it happened that on Palm Sunday the aforesaid most devout emperor came to that place. As the procession passed beside the house in which Bishop Theodulf was held, when silence had been made in the emperor’s presence, he sang through the window the most beautiful verses which he had composed and which are still sung throughout Gaul on that solemnity [Col. 0853: witness 2 reads “are sung”]. Their opening is [Col. 0853: witness 2 reads “is”]:

> Glory, praise, and honour be to you, Christ the King, Redeemer,  
> To whom the tender voice of children offered a devout Hosanna.

Moved by these words, the emperor immediately ordered him released from his chains and restored him to his former favour. But while returning to his own country, he was, it is said, killed by poison. Jonas, a venerable man, succeeded him in the bishopric.

Against Claudius, bishop of Turin, a heresiarch [Col. 0853: witness 2 reads *herisiarcham*], he produced a book *On the Adoration of the Cross*. For that heretic taught that the sign of the Lord’s cross ought not to be adored, although without it nothing is rightly performed when it is applied to our foreheads, to the waters by which we are regenerated, to the chrism with which we are anointed, or to the sacrifice by which we are nourished.

[Col. 0853D: The *History of the Franks* adds: “For he said: ‘If the cross is adored, let girls also be adored, because the Virgin bore Christ; let the manger also be adored, because Christ as a child lay in a manger; let asses be adored too, because the same Lord Christ came to Jerusalem riding on an ass.’”]

But the aforesaid Bishop Jonas [Col. 0853: witness 2 reads “the aforesaid bishop”] responded to him sufficiently clearly and in a Catholic manner in that little book. In the same period there flourished a certain man named Rabanus, who also composed in verse a book on the praise of the cross, decorated with various figures.

Louis the emperor was succeeded by his four sons. Of these, Lothar, not many days after his father’s death, was seized by an adverse illness and, laying aside the governance of his empire, became a monk [Col. 0853: witness 2 reads “and became a monk”], leaving to his son Louis the dignity of the Italian empire. Charles the Pious alone held Francia, Burgundy, and Aquitaine.

[Col. 0853]

# HISTORY OF THE FRANKS OF SENS

[Col. 0853C: This is taken from Duchesne, vol. III, p. 349.]

In the year 688 from Christ’s Incarnation, Pippin of Austrasia, mayor of the royal household, assumed the leadership of the Franks.

In the year of the Lord 711, Childebert, king of the Franks, died.

In the year of the Lord 712, the elder Pippin died, and his son, called Charles Martel, seized the principate.

In the year of the Lord 715, Dagobert the younger, king, died on 19 January. He had reigned in Francia for five years. In the second year after his death Charles Martel, the prince, first fought Ratbod at Cologne, while Theuderic, son of the above-mentioned Dagobert the younger, was reigning [compare the Annals of Saint-Columban].

At that time the impious people of the Vandals began to ravage Gaul. Then churches were destroyed, monasteries overthrown, cities captured, houses laid waste, fortresses demolished, innumerable massacres committed, and much human blood shed everywhere. This calamity thundered most grievously throughout all Gaul, while the Vandals laid everything waste with flame and sword. Reaching the city of Sens, they began to assail it by every means, with missiles and siege-engines. Seeing this, the bishop of that city, named Ebbo, went out from the city with his men and, relying on divine power, drove them from the siege of the city. As they fled, he pursued them until they had departed from his territory.

In the year of the Lord 741, Prince Charles Martel died and was buried in the basilica of Saint-Denis at Paris. [Col. 0855A] Because of the constant wars, he transferred the possessions of churches to laymen. After his death his sons Carloman and Pippin assumed the principate.

In the year of the Lord 750, Pippin was chosen as king, and Childeric, who remained of the stock of King Clovis, was tonsured. Here the offspring of King Clovis came to an end.

In the year of the Lord 768, King Pippin died, and his sons Charles, who is called the Great Emperor [Note: “son,” Ch.], and Carloman were chosen to rule the kingdom.

In the year of the Lord 769, Carloman died [cf. *Annals of St. Columbanus*].

In the year of the Lord 804, Alcuin the philosopher, abbot of Saint Martin at Tours, died.

In the year of the Lord 813, Charles the Great Emperor died, and Louis, his son, who is called the Pious, assumed the kingdom of the Franks and the Roman Empire. In his time, therefore, pagans spread through the province called the county of Ponthieu. In the twentieth year of the reign of the lord Louis, most pious emperor, his son Lothair rebelled against him, taking the kingdom of the Franks away from him. In that same year, having gathered a very large army, Louis the father recovered for himself the kingdom which his son had taken from him.

**[Annals of St. Columbanus.]** In the year of the Lord 840, on 20 June [the twelfth day before the Kalends of July], the Emperor Louis the Pious died. In the same year there was an eclipse of the sun on the fourth weekday before the Ascension of the Lord, at the ninth hour of the day, on 6 May [the second day before the Nones of May].—As the year turned, therefore, on the day of the Ascension of the Lord, the battle of Fontenoy was fought [Col. 0855C] in Burgundy by the four sons of this same Louis—namely Charles, Lothair, Louis, and Pippin—where much human blood was shed. Of these, Charles, who is called the Bald, obtained the kingdom of the Franks and the Roman Empire; Lothair, however, claimed for himself that part of Francia which to this day, from his name, is called Lothair’s kingdom. Louis, moreover, claimed Bavaria for himself and was anointed king.

In the year of the Lord 877, the Emperor Charles, who is called the Bald, son of Louis the most pious Emperor, when he was setting out on his second journey to Rome [Note: “who, when,” manuscripts 2 and 3; “setting out on the journey itself, on the third day before the Kalends,” manuscript 3], died on that journey, on 29 September [the third day before the Kalends of October], in the city of Vercelli; and there he was buried [Note: omitted in Ch.] in the basilica of the blessed martyr Eusebius [Col. 0855D], where [Note: omitted in Ch.] he rested for seven years. Afterwards, however, his body was brought to Francia by means of a vision [Note: C. below, *History of Saint Denis*], and honourably buried in the basilica of the blessed martyr Denis at Paris [Note: the *Annals of Bertin* relate this differently]. His son Louis succeeded to the kingdom [Note: “Ludovicus” in manuscript 1* here and in manuscript 3 throughout].

In the following year Pope John of Rome came to Gaul [Col. 0856A; cf. *Annals of St. Columbanus*] with Formosus, bishop of Porto, carrying with him [Note: “with himself,” Ch.] very precious [Note: “precious,” manuscript 3] relics. First conveyed by ship to Arles, he proceeded through Lyons and other cities as far as the city of Troyes [Note: “Treca-,” manuscript 3] [Note: This was compiled from the *Annals of Bertin* for 878 and the *Annals of St. Columba* for 882]. There, after speaking with King Louis, son of Charles the Bald, he returned to Italy.

After this King Louis of the Franks, son of Charles the Bald, died (879), leaving [Note: The author’s error was already corrected by the monk of Saint-Maur-des-Fossés (manuscript 3)] his little son Charles, called the Simple, together with the kingdom, in the custody of Duke Odo. At that time the unbelieving people of the Northmen spread through Gaul, raging with slaughter, fires, and every kind of cruelty. Then the leading men of the Franks, Burgundians, and Aquitanians assembled [Col. 0856B] together and chose Duke Odo as their king (888).

When King Odo died [Note: omitted in manuscript 3] on the Kalends of January [1 January; omitted in manuscript 3] (898), Charles the Simple, son of Louis, received the kingdom. [Col. 0856C]

**Note:** The Continuation of Aimoin contains what follows.

In his time the Northmen came into Burgundy to Saint-Florentin [cf. *Annals of St. Columba*, year 899]. Richard, duke of Burgundy, met them with his army in the district of Tonnerre; rushing upon them, he struck down a multitude of them by the sword, while the rest fled on 1 June [the fifth day before the Nones of June].

**Note:** “The fifth day before the Nones of June” is omitted in the Continuation of Aimoin.

At that time an earthquake occurred near the monastery of Saint Columba the Virgin, on 9 January [the fifth day before the Ides of January; ibid., year 896].

At that time pagans besieged the city of Chartres (905). Having gathered an army, Richard, duke of Burgundy, and Robert, the prince, attacked them [ibid., year 911], killing 6,800 of the pagans and taking hostages from the few who remained, on 20 July [the thirteenth day before the Kalends of August] [Note: “the twelfth day before the Kalends,” Ch.], on a Saturday [Note: This was a Saturday in the year 905], with heavenly mercy aiding them through the intercession of Mary, the holy Mother of God.

After this, in the middle of March, a star appeared in the northern quarter, emitting great rays [Note: “a great ray,” the Continuation of Aimoin and Ch.] for nearly fourteen days [Note: “days” omitted in manuscripts 1* and 3] [ibid.].

In the following year there was a great famine [Col. 0857A] throughout all Gaul (919). Then, nearly five years later, on the Kalends of February [Note: “December,” manuscript 3], fiery lines of different colours were seen in the sky, a remarkable sight, pursuing one another in alternation [ibid., year 919]. In that same year there was great discord [Note: “dissent,” manuscript 1*] between the king and his princes. For this reason very many massacres of Christian people were perpetrated; but, with God’s favour, all that opposition ceased. In the third year after this persecution Richard, duke of Burgundy, died on the Kalends of September and was buried in the basilica of Saint Columba the Virgin, in the oratory of Saint Symphorian the Martyr [cf. *Annals of St. Columba*, year 921].

In the second year after his death (922), Robert, the prince [Note: “Robert,” manuscript 1* here; Ch. throughout], rebelled against Charles the Simple and was anointed king on 29 June [the third day before the Kalends of July; cf. ibid., year 922]. Before a year had elapsed, on 15 June [the seventeenth day before the Kalends of July], a battle was fought at the city of Soissons [Note: the source manuscripts omit “S.”] between Charles the Simple and that same Robert [Note: “Robert,” Ch. throughout], who had seized the kingdom of the Franks [Note: “Franks,” manuscript 1* frequently]; Robert himself was killed there.—As Charles returned victorious from the slaughter of battle, Herbert, most wicked among the faithless, met him and, under the pretence of a false peace, compelled him to turn aside to lodge in the fortress called Péronne. Thus he captured him by treachery and kept him there. This Robert had Herbert’s sister as his wife; from her Hugh the Great was born. Charles, being confined there, elevated Rudolf, the noble son of Richard, duke of the Burgundians, whom he had received from the sacred font as his godson, to the kingdom [Note: “into kingship,” Ch.], with the counsel of Hugh the Great, son of the aforesaid Robert, and of the Frankish magnates.

This same Charles the Simple, after a long wasting away in prison, died in that confinement and was buried in the basilica of Saint Fursa [Note: “Saint Fursa the Confessor,” Ch.], which is in the fortress of Péronne itself. Rudolf was anointed king at the city of Soissons on 13 July [the third day before the Ides of July] (929) [cf. ibid., year 922].

In those times the pagans again ravaged Burgundy [Note: “Burgundy again,” Ch.], and a battle was fought between Christians and pagans on Mount Chalo. Many thousands of Christians were killed by the pagans on 6 December [the eighth day before the Ides of December].

When King Rudolf died on 15 January [the eighteenth day before the Kalends of February] (936), they buried him in the basilica of Saint Columba the Virgin [cf. ibid.].—After King Rudolf’s death, Hugh the Great, together with the Franks, summoned William, archbishop [Note: archbishop of Sens], and sent him to Ogiva, the wife of the aforesaid Charles the Simple, so that he might bring back her son Louis. For he had fled to his father, the king of the English, out of fear of Herbert and Hugh. When Archbishop William arrived there, and had given hostages to his mother Ogiva under oath, he brought Louis back into Francia. Accordingly, on 19 June [the thirteenth day before the Kalends of July], Louis, son of Charles the Simple, was anointed king at Laon [cf. ibid.].

In the second year after this, on 14 February [the sixteenth day before the Kalends of March], from cockcrow until daylight, blood-red lines appeared over the whole face of the sky [ibid.]. In the following month, on 24 March [the ninth day before the Kalends of April], the Hungarians, still pagans, began to devastate Francia, Burgundy, and Aquitaine with fire and sword.

After this the Frankish magnates rebelled against King Louis, above all Hugh the Great [cf. ibid.]. In that same year a severe and great famine arose throughout the whole kingdom of the Franks, so that a modius of grain was sold for twenty-four solidi. Then, not many days later, King Louis [Note: “son of Charles the Simple,” added by Ch.] was treacherously captured by the Northmen at the city of Bayeux [Note: “Bajogas,” Ch.] (945), many of the Frankish people being killed, with Hugh the Great’s consent [ibid.]. Afterwards, in May, on the sixth weekday, blood rained upon workers [ibid.]. In the same year, in September, King Louis, having passed his whole life in distress and tribulation, ended his last day (954), and was buried at Reims in the basilica of Saint Remigius. In the following month, on 12 November [the second day before the Ides of November], his son Lothair, now a young man, was anointed king at Reims, and Hugh the Great was made duke of the Franks.

In the second year after this, in August, the aforesaid Hugh the Great besieged the city of Poitiers [Col. 0858C] (955), but gained nothing by it [ibid.].—For while he was besieging that city [Note: “was besieged,” manuscript 3], on one day the Lord thundered with great terror, and a whirlwind tore his tent [Note: “beam,” manuscripts 1* and 3] from top to bottom. Great terror seized him and his army, so that they could not remain alive. Immediately they turned to flight and withdrew from the siege of the city. God [Note: “the Lord,” Ch.] did this through the intercession of blessed Hilary, who is always the guardian and defender of that city [Note: “is,” manuscripts 1*, 2, and 3].

In the same year Gilbert, duke of Burgundy, died, leaving the duchy to Otto, son of Hugh the Great [cf. ibid.]. Otto had Gilbert’s daughter as his wife.

In the second year Hugh the Great, duke of the Franks, died [Col. 0858D] at the estate of Drodinga [Note: “Dodringa,” manuscript 3; “Dordinga,” Continuation of Aimoin] on 16 June [the sixteenth day before the Kalends of July] (956), and was buried in the basilica of the blessed martyr Denis [Note: “Saint Denis,” Ch.] at Paris [cf. ibid.]. His sons succeeded him: Hugh, Otto, and Henry [Note: “Henry,” manuscript 1*; “Hainricus,” Ch.], born of the daughter of King Odo [Note: “Otto,” Ch.; Note: she was the daughter of Henry and sister of Otto I]. Hugh became duke of the Franks and Otto duke of the Burgundians. When Duke Otto of Burgundy died, his brother Henry succeeded him [Note: “Duke Henry,” manuscript 3].

At that time (959) a dispute arose between Ansegisus, bishop of Troyes, and Count Robert. Bishop Ansegisus, expelled from the city by Count Robert [Note: omitted in manuscripts 1* and 3], went into Saxony to Emperor Otto [Note: omitted in Ch.] and, having brought Saxons with him, besieged the city of Troyes for a long time in October. When the Saxons came to plunder Sens [Note: the text has *Senones*; manuscript 3 has *Senonis*. Read “Saxons”; see the Continuation of Aimoin, which speaks of the aforesaid people of Sens], Archbishop Archembald and Rainald [Note: “Rainard,” Ch.; “Rainald,” Continuation of Aimoin], Count the Elder, met them with a very large army at the place called Villare. The men of Sens were victorious, having killed the Saxons together with their leader, named Helpo. Helpo had said that he would burn the churches and estates situated along the river Venenas [Note: “Venena,” Ch.] as far as the city and would plant his lance in the gate of Saint Leo [Note: Vannes]. Killed with his people [Note: “with his people,” manuscript 3] by the men of Sens [Note: “by the Senonese,” Ch.], he was carried back to his homeland in Ardenne by his servants. For this had been ordered by Helpo’s mother, named Warna. Count Rainald [Note: “Rainard,” Ch.] and Archbishop Archembald [Note: “Archembold,” manuscript 1*] mourned him with great lamentation, for he was their kinsman. When Duke Bruno [Note: “Bruno,” manuscript 1* and 3; this means the archbishop of Cologne, who was set over the duchy of Lotharingia; who Duke Helpo was is not known to the editor], the companion of Helpo, who had besieged the city of Troyes, saw that his companion Helpo was dead, he returned with his men to his own country.

Then, not many days afterwards [Note: “afterwards, not many days later,” Ch.], King Lothair assembled a very large army (978) and restored [Note: the text has *renovavit*, “restored”; manuscripts 1*, 3, Ch., and the Continuation of Aimoin read this in place of *revocavit*, “recalled”] Lothair’s kingdom to his own dominion [Note: “dictione,” manuscripts 1* and 3; compare Richer III.70 ff.]. Coming to the palace called Aachen, where Emperor Otto lived with his wife, at the hour of dining [Note: “of dining,” Ch.], he entered the palace [Note: “into the palace,” Ch.] without anyone opposing him, and they ate and drank whatever they had prepared for their own use [Note: manuscript 1* reads “against them”]. Emperor Otto, however, fled with his wife and people and abandoned the palace. King Lothair therefore plundered the palace and the whole province and returned to Francia in peace, no one pursuing him.

After this Emperor Otto assembled his army and came to Paris. There his nephew, together with many others, was killed at the city gate, after its suburb had been burned. For he had boasted, saying that he would plant his lance in the gate of the city of Paris. King Lothair therefore summoned Hugh, duke of the Franks, and Henry [Note: “Henry,” manuscript 1*; “Hainricus,” Ch.], duke of Burgundy, and attacked them [Note: “attacking them as they fled,” Ch.]. As they fled, he pursued them as far as the city of Soissons [Note: “the city,” Ch.]. They entered the bed of the river called the Axona [Aisne], not knowing the ford; very many perished there, and the water consumed far more than the sword would have devoured. So many died there that the water itself overflowed with dead bodies [Note: “of corpses,” manuscript 1*], for the water had filled its banks. King Lothair pursued them steadfastly for three days and three nights, as far as the river which flows near Ardenne or Argonne, killing a very great multitude of the enemy. Having ceased to pursue them, King Lothair returned to Francia with a great victory. Emperor Otto, with those who had escaped, returned to his own lands in great confusion. Afterwards King Otto made no further attempt to come into Francia, neither he nor his army.

In that same year (980), King Lothair made peace with King Otto at the city of Reims, against the will of Hugh and his brother Henry [Note: “and against the will of his army,” added by Ch. and the Continuation of Aimoin]. King Lothair granted King Otto Lothair’s kingdom as a benefice; this especially grieved the hearts of the Frankish princes.

**[Manuscripts 1* and 3 add:]** In those days Salvator, bishop of the city of Alet, came to Paris with two abbots, carrying with him the most precious relics—namely, those of the venerable archbishop Magloire; half of Saint Samson the archbishop; the whole body of Maclovius the bishop; of Bishop Sanator [Note: “Senator,” manuscript 3]; of Bishop Leucernus; of Abbot Winguanton [Note: “Wingantonis,” manuscript 3]; and many others. They were received with great honour by the aforesaid king in the basilica of the blessed apostle Bartholomew.

In the year 956 [Note: thus the manuscripts, in place of 986; Ch. has this year], King Lothair died, old and full [Note: “and full,” manuscript 3] of days, and was buried in the basilica of blessed Remigius [Note: “Saint Remigius,” Ch.] at Reims. His son Louis, a young man, succeeded him. In the year 982 [Note: thus the manuscripts, in place of 987; Ch. has this year], King Louis the Young died, having reigned in Francia for nine years. He was buried in the basilica of the blessed martyr Cornelius at Compiègne. His brother Charles (987), son of King Lothair, succeeded him. In the same year Hugh, duke of the Franks, rebelled against Charles because Charles had married the daughter of Count Herbert of Troyes. Hugh therefore gathered a very large army and besieged Laon, where Charles was residing [Note: “living,” Ch.] with his wife. Charles came out of the city and routed Hugh and his army, having burned the lodgings where the enemy were staying [Note: “the guest-houses where the guests were staying,” Ch.]. Seeing, therefore, that he could not defeat Charles at all, Duke Hugh took counsel with the old traitor Ascelin, who was the false bishop of Laon [Note: “of Laon,” Ch.] and Charles’s adviser. Bishop Ascelin therefore betrayed Laon in one night, while everyone was sleeping, to Hugh, duke of the Franks. King Charles was bound with his wife and taken into custody at the city of Orléans (991) [Note: omitted in Ch.]. Charles himself had not yet been anointed king, because Duke Hugh opposed it. While this same Charles remained in custody in a tower at Orléans [Note: “tower,” manuscripts 1* and 3], his wife bore him two sons, Louis and Charles [Note: “him,” Ch.]. In the same year Duke Hugh was anointed king at Reims [Note: omitted in Ch.], and in that year his son Robert was appointed the most pious king [Note: “to the kingdom,” manuscript 1*; “kingdom,” Ch.] (987). Here the kingdom of Charlemagne comes to an end.

[Col. 0861B] In those days there was in the city of Reims an archbishop, a good and modest man, brother of King Lothair by a concubine, named Arnulf. King Hugh envied him, wishing to exterminate the descendants of King Lothair. Having convened a synod in the city of Reims (991), King Hugh invited Archbishop Seguin of the city of Sens [Note: “Seuuinus,” Ch. throughout] with his suffragan bishops [Note: “with,” manuscript 1*; compare Richer IV.51 ff., who recounts these matters more accurately].

At this council, through the treachery of his nephew whom he held in prison, he caused Lord Arnulf, archbishop of Reims, to be deposed, saying that one born of a concubine ought not to be a bishop. In his place he caused Lord Gerbert, a monk and philosopher, to be consecrated [Note: “caused him to be consecrated,” manuscript 3]. Gerbert was the teacher of King Robert, son of this Hugh, and of Lord Leothéric [Note: “Leoteric,” Ch. throughout], archbishop [Note: omitted in manuscript 3], successor of the venerable Seguin. Arnulf, however [Note: “moreover,” Ch.], Hugh caused to be committed to custody in the city of Orléans.

The venerable Archbishop Seguin did not consent to Arnulf’s deposition or Gerbert’s appointment [Note: manuscript 3 reads “does not consent”]. But the king’s command pressed him [Note: omitted in manuscripts 1* and 3]. The other bishops, though unwilling, nevertheless, from fear of the king, deposed Arnulf and appointed Gerbert. Seguin, however, fearing God more than an earthly king, refused to consent to the king’s wickedness; instead, so far as he could, he rebuked the king himself. For this reason the king’s anger blazed against him. With great disgrace the king ordered Arnulf to be expelled from the church of Blessed Mary at Reims [Note: “the king ordered him expelled,” Ch.] and, thus bound, thrust back into prison. Bound [Col. 0861D] in the prison at Orléans, where his nephew Charles was detained, he remained there for three years.

All this was reported to the Roman pontiff [Note: “pope,” manuscript 3; compare Richer IV.89, 95 ff.]. Greatly angered by this act, he placed under interdict all the bishops who had deposed Arnulf and appointed Gerbert. He also sent Abbot Leo from the Apostolic See [Note: “from the Apostolic See to Lord Seguin,” manuscript 3] to Lord Seguin, archbishop of the city of Sens (995), to convene a synod at Reims in his stead; he instructed him without delay to recall Arnulf from prison and depose Gerbert. When the council had again assembled in the city of Reims [Note: omitted in Ch.], Arnulf was recalled from custody by apostolic command and received with great honour [Note: “the greatest honour,” manuscript 3] into his own see [Note: “his first see,” Ch.]. Gerbert, however [Note: “moreover,” manuscript 3], understanding that he had unjustly received pontifical dignity, was moved to repentance.

You will find the highly useful dispute between Bishop Gerbert and Abbot Leo more fully [Col. 0862B] in the *Deeds of the Bishops of Reims* [Note: “in the deeds,” omitted in manuscript 1*; the editor seems to mean Richer’s book, where these matters are related at IV.99 ff.].

After this Lord Gerbert was chosen bishop in the city of Ravenna [Note: “Vienna,” manuscripts 1* and 3] by Emperor Otto and the people of that city. After he had sat as bishop in that city for very many years [Note: “for many years,” manuscript 3], the pope of the city of Rome died. Immediately the whole Roman people clamoured that Lord Gerbert should be given to them [Note: “the Roman people clamoured for Lord Gerbert to be given to them,” manuscript 3]. Taken from the city of Ravenna [Note: “Vienna,” manuscripts 1* and 3], he was appointed supreme pontiff in the city of Rome (999).

In the year of the Incarnation of Christ 998, King Hugh died and was buried in the basilica of the blessed martyr Denis [Note: omitted in manuscript 1*] at Paris. His son Robert succeeded him in the kingdom [Note: “to the kingdom,” Ch. and the Continuation of Aimoin], most pious and modest.

In the year of the Lord 999, the venerable Archbishop Seguin began from the foundations to restore the monastery of Saint Peter at Melun [Col. 0862C]. Sending monks there, he set Abbot Walter [Note: “Gualter,” manuscript 3] over them.

In the same year Walter the knight and his wife surrendered the fortress of Melun to the knight Odo [Note: “Count Odo,” Ch. and the Continuation of Aimoin; compare William of Jumièges VII.14].

King Robert gathered a very large army, and Count Burchard [Note: “Burchard,” and later “Richard,” Ch.; the Continuation of Aimoin adds “to whom the fortress belonged”] did likewise; they summoned the Northmen [Note: “Normans,” manuscript 3 and Ch.] with their duke Richard and besieged the fortress of Melun. Once the fortress had been captured [Note: “When the fortress had therefore been captured,” Ch.], Walter [Note: “Gualter,” manuscript 1*; “Galter,” manuscript 3] and his wife were hanged on the gallows. Count Burchard recovered the fortress of Melun as he had possessed it before.
