Thus Rainald the Elder, count of Sens, after perpetrating many evils [Note: “many evils perpetrated,” Ch.], died (996?) and was buried in the basilica of Saint Columba the Virgin. His son Frotmund [Note: “Fromund,” manuscript 3; “Hugh,” Continuation of Aimoin] succeeded him; he had as wife the daughter of Rainold [Note: “Rainald,” Ch.], count of Reims [Note: The same material is found in Clarius’s *Chronicle of Saint Peter the Living at Sens*, Bouquet X, p. 222].

In the year of the Lord 1000 [Note: the remainder is missing in manuscript 3], in the thirteenth indiction, on 18 October [the fifteenth day before the Kalends of November; Ch. and the Continuation of Aimoin have the sixteenth day before the Kalends], the venerable Seguin, metropolitan bishop, passed to Christ [Note: Ch. reads “passes”]. After his death [Note: “after his passing,” Ch.] the church of Sens remained for one year without sacerdotal blessing [Note: “one year,” Ch. and the Continuation of Aimoin]. All the people clamoured that Lord Leothéric should be ordained for them. He was then archdeacon, of most noble birth [Note: “of most noble birth,” manuscript 1*] and conspicuous in every virtue. Yet very many clerics opposed this, desiring to ascend the episcopal rank. Above all, Count Frotmund, son of Rainald the Elder [Note: “Rainald,” Ch.], sprung from an evil root, would not permit it, because he had a clerical son named Bruno and wished to make him bishop. But, by God’s prompting, the suffragan bishops of the church of Sens assembled, and, with apostolic will and authority, setting aside every human fear, solemnly [Col. 0863B] ordained Lord Leothéric to the episcopal see, to preside over the church of Sens [Note: compare Clarius, cited work].

In the year of the Lord 1001, Henry, duke of Burgundy, died without sons. The Burgundians rebelled against King Robert, unwilling to receive him. Count Landric entered Auxerre and held the city.

In the year of the Lord 1003, King Robert, having taken the Northmen with their duke Richard and a very large army, ravaged Burgundy and besieged Auxerre for many days [Note: “many days,” Ch.]. But the Burgundians, in no way wishing to submit to him, unanimously resisted him. He also besieged the fortress of Avallon for nearly three months and took it by the pressure of famine [Note: “took him,” manuscript 3]; then he returned to Francia [Note: this agrees with William of Jumièges V.15].

[Col. 0864A] When therefore Frotmund, count of Sens, had died [Note: so Ch., the Continuation of Aimoin, Hugh, and Clarius; omitted in manuscript 1*], his son Rainald succeeded him, most wicked among the faithless. He inflicted upon Christ’s churches and faithful such persecution as had not been heard of from the time of the pagans until the present day. Archbishop Leothéric [Note: “Lotherius,” Hugh’s manuscript] was exceedingly distressed by this matter [Note: “exceedingly,” Ch.] and did not know at all where to turn. Committing himself wholly to the Lord, in prayers and vigils he implored Christ that heavenly mercy might grant him aid [Note: Ch. adds “that he might deign to aid him”; compare the Continuation of Aimoin].

Thus, in the year from the Passion of the Lord 1015, in the thirteenth indiction, on 22 April [the tenth day before the Kalends of May], the city of Sens was taken by Archbishop Leothéric through the counsel of Rainald [Note: “Rainold,” Ch.], bishop of Paris [Note: the printed text is uncertain: *pci*; the Paris manuscript 4969 reads “priest,” while Paris manuscript 5009 has a later hand reading “bishop”; the Continuation of Aimoin and Clarius read “bishop”; Ch. reads “bishop of Paris”; Hugh reads “count of Paris”], and handed over to King Robert [Note: “handed over to Robert,” Ch.]. Count Rainald of that city [Note: “Count Rainald, however, fled,” Ch. and the Continuation of Aimoin] escaped naked in flight [Col. 0864B]. Nor without reason. For he had inflicted on Christians such persecution as had not been heard of from the time of the pagans. Therefore the aforesaid archbishop, employing wise counsel, compelled him to leave the city by force [Note: this entire passage is omitted in Ch., Hugh, and the Continuation of Aimoin].

But Frotmund, his brother, and the other knights of the city entered the tower that stood in the city and held it [Note: omitted in Ch.]. The king, attacking it for many days, captured it and took Frotmund, Count Rainald’s brother, into prison in the city of Orléans, where he also died.

[In the year of the Lord 1031 [Note: this is omitted in Ch. and the Continuation of Aimoin], King Robert died, and his son Henry succeeded him. In the third year of his reign, that is, in the year of the Lord 1034, the city of Paris was consumed by fire.]

[Col. 0863]

# Fragments of the History of Saint-Maur-des-Fossés
[Col. 0863C] [Note: These words occur in Hugh’s chronicle after the words “the highly necessary chapters,” above, col. 852, l. 26, in manuscript 3.] Therefore, while, as has been said, the most pious Emperor Louis was reigning, Rorigo, the venerable count of blessed memory, visited Glanfeuil—which he had received from that emperor—and the sacred ashes of Saint Maurus, for the sake of prayer. As he surveyed the sites of ancient ruin, desolated of their former religious observance, he was inwardly moved by grief: the place which had once flourished through Saint Maurus in so many miracles of virtues stood almost reduced to its former wilderness, empty without inhabitant or the due service of religion, irreverently and without honour. He began to consider its restoration; but, hindered again by certain circumstances, he interrupted the work and returned to Brenne, the estate of his possession.

[Col. 0864C] But because Almighty God had care for the place, it was revealed to an abbot of most reverent life, named Jacob, of the monastery of Cormery, how he should explain to the count what he had heard concerning the restoration of the work. The count, however, receiving the message once and twice in a manner insufficiently fitting, was on the third occasion terribly chastened with scourges by Saint Maurus, through whom these things had been shown from heaven, as is related more fully in the book of his translation. [Note: See Odo, *Translation of Saint Maurus*, ch. 2, in Mabillon, *Acta*, IV.2, p. 170 ff., whence these things are taken.] Thus he learned to obey the divine command.

The venerable count, terrified by the blows, dismissed the abbot who had brought this message, rejoicing and enriched with many gifts, to his own home. Encouraged by so great an oracle, he himself set aside all that he had been doing and undertook the work already begun. [Col. 0865A] While he was crossing the Loire in a boat that conveyed him, a fiery sphere, like a shield of exceptional breadth, was seen above his head, so that he feared the force of fire to be present. At the same time he received a heavenly oracle, repeatedly saying: “Build here, build here, build here.”

When all things appropriate to monastic observance had been completed and perfected, according to the traces of the old ruin which he had observed, he summoned from the monastery of Saint Martin two men of religious life, Lantbert and Ebbo, his kinsmen, in order that he might deliberate through their prudence and counsel to what abbot or church he should entrust the place. Now the monastery of Saint-Maur-des-Fossés excelled before the other monasteries of the whole empire of the most pious Emperor Louis in the orderliness of its religious life. For it had neither departed from its first founder [Col. 0865B] nor pursued diverse vanities, as we know certain monasteries of our own time to have done.

When, with his own counsel and the higher counsel of his associates, they had examined many places and weighed with the even balance of judgment the condition and religious observance of the surrounding churches, it pleased them, leaving all the rest, to assign the place to the monastery of Fossés. Therefore the venerable count sent for Ingelbert, abbot of the aforesaid monastery and a man of most holy life; and, with the assent of the most pious Emperor Louis—[Note: See Louis’s diploma, Bouquet VI, p. 591.] from whom he had received it—he assigned in perpetuity to Abbot Ingelbert and to the monastery of Fossés the place of Saint Maurus called Glanfeuil, together with its possessions and all their appurtenances, to govern, improve, and possess. [Col. 0865C]

At the same time, by the gift of that same most pious Emperor Louis, through the intervention of Count Bego of good memory, while Benedict was abbot, God very honourably enlarged the monastery of Fossés with many gifts and possessions. For when the aforesaid count had come to see the commendable zeal of religious life by which such great princes and powerful friends of princes loosened the belts of military service, he praised the remote solitude; yet he marvelled at the scant food and clothing of such great men, and at their spiritual poverty for the Lord’s sake.

Therefore the most pious king, through the intervention of Count Bego of good memory, gave [Note: The charter seems to be lost.] for the increase of food and clothing for the poor of Christ at Fossés, in the district of Paris, the estate called Ferreoles, with all its appurtenances—meadows, woods, and surrounding lands—together with the vicariate-advocacy and the church. Likewise another estate called Oratory or Aratory, with everything that appeared subject to its lordship. Likewise, in the same district, Torcy with vineyards, meadows, woods, all adjacent lands, and its church; also Rentilly with its surrounding lands. In the district of Meaux, he gave the church and estate called [Col. 0866A] Courprotasia, or Pravasia, with its appurtenances.

Moved by the poverty of the place, he also ordered imperial charters to be drawn up and decreed [Note: See Louis’s diploma, Bouquet VI, p. 492.] that nowhere within the dominion of the whole empire should anyone presume to take or exact from them toll, or what is commonly called *ripaticum* (river-bank due), *rotaticum* (wheel or road due), *pontaticum* (bridge due), *portaticum* (harbour due), *travaticum* and *cispitaticum*, nor *salutaticum*, nor any tax, impost, or payment; rather, both they and their people and all their goods should be free to travel in peace and willingly conduct their affairs.

It happened [Note: These passages occur in the *History of Sens* after the words “count of Rheims,” above, col. 862, l. 46.] [Note: These passages do not occur in the *Life of Burchard* by Odo, Bouquet X, p. 349 ff.] that at the same time the people of Le Puy rebelled against the authority of the aforesaid King Robert. When he heard this, he quickly arrived with his forces assembled, surrounded the city, and, encircling it with a manifold siege, [Col. 0866B] sat down before it with a numerous multitude gathered from every side: those favouring the royal majesty came in aid of the king from distant and nearby places. [Note: “came together,” manuscript *c.*] But since the city was difficult because of its position and prepared for this very purpose by the labour of its citizens, the assaults failed, and the whole undertaking was utterly frustrated.

The people and those who, as stated, had assembled from the neighbourhood in support of the king, overcome by weariness from the protracted encampment, gradually returned home. The army grew thinner, and the besieged city rejoiced that, to the king’s grief, it would not be taken. For because he had been less successful by this means, the king, as misfortunes arose, was compelled to devise another course.

Having set down the signs and seals concerning the matters conducted around him, he exhorted and admonished, with entreaty and an attestation of the faith of oaths, his intimate and most beloved count Burchard [Col. 0866C] to meet the danger of this shameful crisis:

> “Come now, my dearest friend, lest in our times something be taken away from the glory of kings through us, or lest the stain of this affair suddenly break out, as a reproach to our rule, from another quarter. Now, now, most loving friend, may the outcome prove the great affection of friendship and devotion which you displayed in prosperous circumstances; and may I not regret having tested you in the danger of supreme necessity—you whom I have always used and found successful in other matters.”

On hearing this, the venerable count, clothed as he was in rough garments and with an even more unkempt beard, delayed neither by dread of danger nor by the labour of the long journey—during which he had exerted himself greatly for the Lord at Jerusalem—recovered his vigour and forgot that he was a pilgrim. Anxious about what to do, he sent envoys through castles and villages wherever he believed hope, resources, and aid might be found; he requested support for himself and his lord. Immediately men came from castles and fortified towns, cities and villages—an incredible thing to say—all promising with devoted hearts whatever aid the count might wish. He himself marvelled that so great a multitude had suddenly gathered, praising and blessing God, who is at hand [Col. 0867A] to those who call upon him in time of need.

Accordingly the venerable Count Burchard set out with an innumerable multitude: foremost in readiness among thousands, first in religious devotion, and most eloquent of all. They were counted at the bridge of Orléans, and thirty thousand armed men were found. Humility returned to the besieged; boldness fled; prosperity turned to its opposite; sudden calamity changed their short-lived fortune.

The king came out to meet him with the magnates. They mingled embraces, lingered in kisses, and, after asking about his welfare, brought him with joy to the camp. The people rush together; they come to the spectacle; the crowd clamours; the young men exult; fierceness returns to their hearts. They threaten war, fit their shields, draw their swords, renew their arms, brandish their javelins, exchange horses, and adorn their trappings. They rush toward death; battle is made over danger; it shames each man to seem the last; they exercise their shoulders; they challenge the enemy; war is waged without an enemy; wars roar, hatreds swell, peace perishes.

Now armed men march in longing for battle; sleep flees their eyes; they press the besieged with watches and drive away a night that seemed longer than all others. The wretched men look down from the walls upon their fate; they plan flight and recoil in horror; leaning on their javelins, they await death; they live only by the gift of night. Feeble old age, once strong yet now bereft of itself, is silent; spirited youth grows cold in counsel. Women rush forth with garments cast aside and hair torn loose; they display their children and beat their breasts.

Meanwhile the desired day returns. Then indeed a cry rises, and, though no one summons it, the crowd rushes forward; they bend the horns [of their battle formations], and test their weapons anew. The king, after ordering silence, spoke privately to the aforesaid Count [Col. 0867C] Burchard and commanded him to take command of the armies and henceforth to follow his counsel.

The venerable old man, therefore, according as he knew this better from the custom of ancient kings, disposed the legions in a circuit, assigned their respective places to the satraps and centurions, ordered the army to advance, showed them the approaches and hidden paths, and thereafter, where the greater danger threatened, himself went forward before all others with his company. At the first signal for the attack, scarcely had the herald’s trumpet sounded when, amid a following shout, missiles flew. Some, rushing headlong into the ditch, filled it up and clung to the ramparts; others raised engines, fitted rams, and fastened ladders to the walls; others threw torches, undermined the walls, and broke down the gates.

What more need be said? In a moment it was as though it had never been. [Col. 0867D] Fire flies upward; the enemy is everywhere; the renowned city falls; wretched citizens are dragged away in chains; the churches are plundered; spoils are seized. And perhaps the hostile sword would have ranged without measure, had it not been recalled by the coming of night. Therefore, on the following day, when all things had been pacified and the surrounding regions subdued, the venerable Count Burchard, having asked leave from the king, departed with his followers.

When he had reached the borders of his county, he ordered a halt; and, addressing those following and standing around him, he said:

> “Thus far, my lords and friends, to whom [Col. 0868A] God has given authority to govern by power, not cruelty, it has been permitted to serve a mortal king who is destined to die. But now, as my years decline, I desire to labour for the immortal King, to whom belong life and death, kingdom and dominion; who abides for ever and ever; whom to serve is to reign; and who gives life after death.”

He spoke; and, taking the sword with which he was girded, he cut off his beard before them all and sent both it and the sword to the church of Fossés. He himself went to Corbeil, which seemed nearest to him, in order to arrange the remaining matters. All marvelled and were astonished, knowing that this was a change wrought by the right hand of the Most High. Some also, pierced in heart, afterwards bestowed very great gifts upon the same monastery.

When the matters had been arranged, he brought with him and carried away many vessels of gold and [Col. 0868B] silver [Note: Thus the manuscript, which lacks its ending, concludes.] [lacuna]

[Note: These passages occur in Hugh’s Chronicle after the words “composed in verse,” above, col. 854, l. 24.]

Here let us briefly retrace the line of kings. The kings of the Franks were customarily produced both by election and succession, from the first Pharamond down to King Hilderic, who, by the command and counsel of Stephen, Roman pontiff, was thrust into a monastery and tonsured. To Pharamond succeeded Clodio; to Clodio, Merovech, from whom the Merovingians were named; to Merovech, Childeric [cf. Aimoin].

He was expelled from the kingdom, but recalled through the wise counsel of Viomadus. When Basina, wife of Bisinus, king of the Thuringians, came to him, and was asked what she sought, she replied: “I know your worth and beauty; therefore I have come here.” [Col. 0868C] By her he begot the great Clovis. Above all others, this man enlarged the kingdom of the Franks, and wherever he went he returned victorious. He took as wife the most Christian Clotild, daughter of King Chilperic and niece of Gundobad; later, through her advice and preaching, he was baptized by Saint Remigius.

When he was preparing for war against Alaric, king of the Goths, he built, at the urging of Queen Clotild, a church for the Prince of the Apostles. There he lies buried; beside him lies Clotild of blessed memory; and there too the most blessed virgin Geneviève now rests. By this same Clotild he begot Clodomir, Childebert, and Clothar. Clodomir begot Saint Clodoald. Childebert and Clothar, in penance for their guilt, built churches: Childebert [Col. 0868D] the church of Saint Vincent, which his stole, brought back from Spain, distinguished; there he himself lies buried, and there now rests the most blessed Germanus, bishop of Paris. Clothar built the church of Saint Medard at Soissons, where he too lies buried.

Clovis also begot his firstborn, Theoderic, by a concubine; Theoderic begot Theodebert. During his reign, Saint Maurus, sent by Saint Benedict his master, the chief and propagator of monastic religion, came into Gaul. [Col. 0869A] When his brothers had died, Clothar alone obtained the empire. He begot Charibert, Guntram, Sigibert, and Chilperic. This Chilperic, after his brothers had died, alone obtained the empire. Clothar succeeded him. He begot the great Dagobert, benefactor of churches, who built the church of Saint Dionysius the Areopagite, in which he himself lies buried. Clovis succeeded him.

During Clovis’s reign Saint Babolinus, through the hand of Audobert, bishop of Paris, and Blidegisil, archdeacon, undertook the construction of the monastery of Fossés. He married Bathild; by her he begot Clothar, who reigned four years after his father and died. At his death his brother Theoderic reigned. Ebroin was mayor of the royal household. He is the man [Col. 0869B] who struck Saint Leodegar, bishop of Autun, with a sword after the piercing of his eyes. But the Franks rose against him, expelled Theoderic from the kingdom, made Ebroin a monk at the monastery of Luxeuil, and sent for Childeric, the third brother, from Austrasia, making him king. But because of his fickleness he was killed by the same men, and Theoderic was restored to the kingdom.

After Theoderic’s death, his son Clovis succeeded and reigned two years. His brother Childebert succeeded him; Dagobert the Younger succeeded Childebert. Under him Charles Tudites was appointed mayor of the royal household, after the death of his father Pippin. On Dagobert’s death, the Franks made a certain cleric Daniel king, calling him Chilperic. But Charles [Col. 0869C] Tudites rose against them, drove Count Ragenfrid, master of the palace, from the palace, and Eudo withdrew beyond the Loire with King Chilperic after taking the royal treasures. In the following year Eudo, for the sake of friendship, handed King Chilperic over to Charles Tudites and died at Noyon.

Then the Franks established as king over themselves Theoderic, son of Dagobert the Younger, who had been raised at the monastery of Chelles. When he had died, Childeric reigned, whom they also call Hilderic. This is the man mentioned above [Note: In Hugh’s history.] who was thrust into a monastery and tonsured.

Pippin, however, mayor of the palace and son of Charles Tudites, was elevated as king at Saint-Denis by the common consent and counsel of the Franks, with Pope Stephen consecrating and blessing him. [Col. 0869D] He reigned fifteen years, died, and was buried in the same monastery face downward, leaving his sons Charles and Carloman alive. But Carloman died after two years, and thus Charles—later called the Great—alone obtained the monarchy of the kingdom. He added an empire to the kingdom.

After he had reigned thirty-three years, he was made emperor, Pope Leo consecrating him; he ruled as emperor fourteen years. The years of kingdom and empire, reckoned together, make forty-seven. He died in the seventy-second year of his life and was buried at [Col. 0870A] Aachen. Louis the Pious, the youngest of his sons, his brothers having died, succeeded as heir of so great a majesty. By Ermengard he begot Lothar, Pippin, and Louis. But Charles, king of the Franks, also called the Bald, he begot by Judith. After many divisions of the empire and countless distresses of war, Pippin and Lothar having died, Charles was established king and emperor. Louis, however, held Germany.

When Charles ruled almost the whole world, he decided to honour Gaul above the other nations. He assigned the nail and crown—relics which his uncle Charlemagne had brought from Constantinople and placed at Aachen—to Saint-Denis; but to Compiègne, which he had decreed should be built in his own time as an image of Constantinople and called Carnopolis after his own name, just as Constantine had called Constantinople after his, he assigned the shroud. To the monastery of Fossés, moreover, he gave the straps by which the Son of God, the salvation of the world, the offering of life, the price of death, was bound before Pilate: he who, having undone enmities in his flesh, came to give release to the bound, remission to captives, and healing of contrition to hearts broken and seeking him. [Col. 0870B]

Therefore, as has been said, the monastery of Fossés has those most precious and venerable straps reverently kept in its possession. In his time it also received and possesses, by the gift of his most gracious liberality, the most holy body of blessed Maurus, disciple of Saint Benedict. When the most serene emperor had come to him for visiting and prayer—indeed, because he had heard of the healings granted, by Maurus’s aid and help, to so many kinds of sick persons—having obtained through his intercession the benefits for which he had come, he sent him two precious cloths. The monastery of Fossés possesses these to this day as an everlasting memorial. [Col. 0870C] He also bestowed very many estates, which are more fittingly recorded in his own sacred charters.

The aforesaid emperor begot Louis by Richildis. [Aimoin, Continuation V.36.] When he died, he sent to his son Louis, by Richildis’s hand, the imperial charter and the sword called Saint Peter’s, together with the royal garment, crown, and sceptre; and thus Louis was made king by all.

He begot two sons, Louis and Carloman. [Note: Hugh, *Deeds of the Modern Kings of the Franks*, ch. 1.] [Note: Ibid., ch. 39.10.] He died on the Preparation Day of holy Easter [Col. 0870D] and ordered his son Louis to be crowned. Charles, son of Louis, king of Germany, went into Lombardy and obtained the kingdom there. He was also raised and consecrated emperor by Pope John. But his brother Louis, living to no benefit of kingdom or church, died. Note the division of kingdom and empire, and that thereafter none of the kings of the Franks ruled as emperor.

Louis, mentioned above, brother of Carloman and son of Louis, son of Charles the Bald, fell ill at Tours; he was carried as far as the monastery of Saint-Denis [Col. 0871A] and buried there. [Chs. 41–44.] After his death the leading men of the kingdom accepted his brother Carloman. When Carloman died, his son Louis, surnamed “Who-Did-Nothing,” succeeded him. At Louis’s death, his son Charles, called the Simple, remained bereft of his father while still an infant in the cradle.

Therefore, compelled by fear of the Northmen, the Franks chose someone to govern them and faithfully guard the child. Odo, son of Robert, count of Anjou, a man of Saxon stock, was accordingly anointed: most faithful guardian of the child and governor of the commonwealth. At his death Charles the Simple recovered the kingdom.

At the same time, when the Northmen came forth, [Col. 0871B] Richard, duke of Burgundy, and Prince Robert, brother of the aforesaid Odo, met them and slaughtered their armies. After Richard’s death Prince Robert openly rebelled against Charles because he was not restored to the share in his brother’s government. By his own violence he was therefore anointed into Charles’s kingdom; but in that same year he was killed, losing both life and kingdom.

When Charles returned from the slaughter, Herbert of Vermandois, whose sister Robert had married and by whom Hugh the Great had been born, met him. Though Charles earnestly resisted, Herbert compelled him to lodge in the fortress of Péronne; but, after the others had departed, this most wicked of evildoers consigned the king to chains. Since the condition of the kingdom was uncertain, although Charles remained in custody, he ordered—on the counsel of Hugh the Great and the nobles of the Franks—that Rudolph, son of the aforesaid Richard, duke of Burgundy, whom he had received from the sacred font, be made king. [Col. 0871C]

Charles himself died under the prolonged wasting of prison confinement, leaving a little son, Louis, by Eadgifu, daughter of the king of the English; he was buried in the basilica of Saint Fursey. After Rudolph’s death Louis recovered the kingdom. Yet certain Franks rebelled against him, above all Hugh the Great. Afterwards he was captured by treachery in the city of Bayeux and died in custody, leaving Charles and Lothar alive. Charles grew old as a private person, but Lothar was anointed king.

Hugh the Great, made duke of the Franks, died and was buried at Saint-Denis. His sons succeeded him: Hugh, who became duke of the Franks, Otto, [Col. 0872A] and Henry. When Lothar died, his son Louis succeeded him, and Charles succeeded Louis. Hugh, duke of France, rebelled against Charles. Since he could not resist, Hugh took Laon by the betrayal of Bishop Ascelin, and consigned the king and his wife to custody at Orléans; yet he had not been anointed king. When these things had been done, the leading men of France chose Duke Hugh as their king. In the same year Hugh had his son Robert consecrated king.

Thus, by succession, Henry succeeded Robert, Philip Henry, and Louis Philip. Louis the Fat [Note: *c.* written above the line.] begot Philip, Louis, and Robert. Philip was anointed king while his father was alive, but was overtaken by sudden death and died, being buried in the basilica of Saint-Denis. Upon his death, [Col. 0872B] his brother Louis the Pious [Note: *c.* written above the line.] was anointed while his father was still alive.

This Louis begot King Philip, most wise, who acquired Normandy, formerly held by the kings of England, and joined many other lands to the kingdom of France. At the bridge of Bouvines he defeated in battle Ferrand, count of Flanders, Renaud, count of Boulogne, and very many others. He reigned for a long time and did many good things. He died in the year from the Lord’s Incarnation 1223 and was buried at Saint-Denis.

His son Louis succeeded him, a man of great spirit and warlike. He reigned only a short time after his father’s death. Marked with the cross against the Albigensians, who at that time erred from the Catholic faith, he died at Montpensier and was buried at Saint-Denis [Col. 0872C] beside his father, in the year of the Lord 1226. [Note: “XXVIII” corrected to “XXVI,” manuscript *c.*] By his wife Blanche, daughter of the king of Spain, he begot four sons: Louis, Robert, Alfonso, and Charles.

After his father’s death Louis, a boy of thirteen, began to reign with his mother and reigned forty-four years. He was tall in stature, most humble and devout, benevolent toward the worshippers of God, and a devoted lover of religious poor people. In his time many monasteries of new orders were built throughout the kingdom of France. He built in Paris, beside his palace, a basilica of wonderful beauty, in which he deposited the Lord’s crown of thorns and the holy cross with many other relics.

Let these statements about the kings suffice for the sake of brevity and order. [Note: With the words, “Now let us return whence we have digressed,” the manuscript returns to Hugh’s text.]

[Col. 0871]

## AIMOIN OF FLEURY, ON THE KINGS OF THE FRANKS

Extracts from the *Miracles of Saint Benedict*.

(See *Patrologia*, vol. CXXXIX, col. 802, under Aimoin of Fleury.)

### DEEDS OF THE KINGS OF THE FRANKS

[Col. 0873]

## HUGH OF SAINTE-MARIE: BOOK CONTAINING THE DEEDS OF THE MODERN KINGS OF THE FRANKS

Compared with the *History of the Franks* by the same writer.

### THE PROLOGUE BEGINS TO THE BOOK CONTAINING THE DEEDS OF THE MODERN KINGS OF THE FRANKS

[Col. 0873A] Hugh, unworthy monk of the monastery of Father Benedict at Fleury, wishes the glorious Empress Matilda joy alike in temporal and eternal happiness. [Note: Thus manuscript 1.] My lady, I have resolved to gather this present little book for you, so that the eminence of your lineage may become known to posterity and the nobility of your ancestors may be made known to coming ages. In this book I shall also endeavour briefly to explain for you the deeds of the modern kings of the Franks, namely those who ruled in France after Emperor Louis, to delight your mind. These matters are nowhere arranged in a continuous history; rather, they remain inserted here and there in certain manuscripts and intermingled with other treatises, because no one until now has taken care to gather them into one body and reduce them to the form of a single book.

[Col. 0873B] In this prologue, moreover, I shall endeavour to recount for you the splendid genealogy of your ancestors; likewise I shall briefly relate their deeds among the deeds of the aforesaid kings, and shall plainly explain to those who do not know what is the nobility of your stock.

Rollo, therefore, from whose blood you descend, was the illustrious duke of the Danes. In the days of Charles the Bald, king of the Franks [Note: Thus manuscript 1.], after the death of Emperor Louis, he entered Gaul by the Seine; having entered it, he claimed the whole of Neustria for himself, which is now called Normandy. Rollo was succeeded by a son named William; William by Richard, a noble and magnificent prince. This Richard begot another Richard, a man dear to God and most holy. This Richard begot Robert, and [Col. 0873C] Robert begot William, the illustrious king of the English, who subdued that kingdom by his own enterprise—a kingdom which no Roman emperor had dared to undertake except Claudius and Julius Caesar.

No king of our times was happier or more moderate than this William. No one can adequately praise his greatness of spirit and magnificence, by which, unto the ends of the earth, he appeared glorious above all kings and princes of our age. Few kings hereafter, I think, will imitate him or enjoy that abundance and elegance of character with which God and fortunate destiny enriched him in this life. His heir and son was [Col. 0874A] Henry, magnificent king of the English, your father. Let this suffice as a passing statement concerning your ancestry and the progeny of your highness.

Long ago, moreover, I undertook to gather for your aunt—the widow, that is, of Count Stephen of Chartres—a book concerning the deeds of the Roman emperors. It contains the coming of the Franks into Gaul and recounts the genealogy of the ancient kings of that people [Note: manuscript *1* reads “recount”] down to Charlemagne and his son Louis. Charlemagne gained the Roman empire for himself by his own enterprise and, on dying, left it to his son Louis. Louis, having begotten four sons, divided it among them. Hence great discord sprang up among them, and the three brothers—Lothar, Louis, and Pippin—fought fiercely against their brother Charles in the second year after Louis’s death, on the field of Fontenoy, seeking to deprive him of the kingdom of France. But they did not prevail, for the army of the Franks prevailed against them.

From that day until now the kingdom of the Franks has remained separated and divided from the Roman empire. Lothar received Germany and Italy, Rome and Ravenna, royal cities, together with the imperial title; his brother Louis received Bavaria and Saxony; Pippin, Aquitaine and Gascony; and Charles, France, Burgundy, Lesser Brittany, and Neustria. Charles later acquired Aquitaine for himself as well. In the following book I shall set out chapter by chapter [Col. 0874C] the genealogy of this King Charles down to Louis, the last king of this line, who died without children. After his death the nobles of France raised over themselves Hugh the Great, son of a certain great Hugh, duke of France. I shall also append his catalogue in due order; and, God permitting, I shall relate in few words the deeds of all of them down to the present King Louis, son of the most clement King Philip, as I have promised.

I do not dare to defile his deeds with my uncultivated style. For what I write I conclude in brief language, [without inserting any embellishment of rhetorical eloquence. Note: In manuscript *1*, “without inserting any embellishment of rhetorical eloquence” has been struck through by a line and was already deleted in antiquity.] Nor have we derived the matters which we endeavour to gather for you from ourselves; [Col. 0875A] rather, by our own labour we have selected them from many manuscripts [Note: manuscript *1* reads *decersimus*] as a supplement to the history mentioned above, which, as promised, we recently published.

I ask you, therefore, to receive favourably the gift offered to you [Col. 0876A] and to see that it is confirmed by the mark of your authority. Farewell. May Almighty God bless you by his grace, make you fruitful in offspring, and always gladden you with prosperity. Amen.

The prologue ends.

### THE BOOK BEGINS

[Col. 0875]

[Col. 0875A] **1.** Charles the Bald, son of Emperor Louis the Pious, obtained the kingdom of the Franks after the battle of Fontenoy in the year of the divine Incarnation 842, and reigned nearly thirty-eight years. [Note: The following also occurs in the *History of the Franks*: “Likewise King Charles of the Franks, Compiègne, etc.”] Since he was a glorious man and very great in spirit, he built in his kingdom the town of Compiègne and ordered it to be called Carnopolis after his own name. He also nobly adorned it with the precious shroud of our Lord Jesus Christ. [Note: The *History of the Franks* reads “precious,” manuscript of Bern.]

The same most serene king also offered Saint Dionysius the martyr one of the nails by which the Lord’s body was fastened to the cross, a small piece of the wood of the holy cross, and a portion of the thorny crown of our Redeemer. [Note: Absent from the *History of the Franks*.]

At this same time William, count of Auvergne and duke of Aquitaine, built the abbey of Cluny. Girard, also, a certain illustrious count of Burgundy, built two churches: Vézelay and Pouthières. [Note: Vézelay and Pouthières.] In one of these Saint Mary Magdalene is now said to lie buried; in the other Girard himself was later entombed. Ebbo, a noble prince of the region of Bourges, likewise built the abbey of Dol, dedicated to Saint Mary, Mother of God. Girald, furthermore, a man of great [Col. 0875C] holiness and distinguished nobility, built the monastery of Aurillac.

[Note: In the *History of the Franks*, at the year 858, this passage reads: “In these days William, illustrious count of Auvergne, founded the monastery of Cluny; and Saint Gerald, a man of distinguished noble birth, established the monastery of Aurillac. At the same time the church of Vézelay was built by the most noble Count Gerard, and in it rests the venerable body of Saint Mary Magdalene.” The manuscript c. of Bern reads *clunacense* for *Cluniacense*.]

[Note: Compare Ademar III.21, where these statements and the foundation of the monastery of Dol are more correctly placed in the tenth century.]

Accordingly, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 858, Emperor Lothar, seized by a debilitating illness, laid aside the governance of his empire; he was tonsured, became a monk, and died at Piacenza, [Note: The author does not distinguish Emperor Lothar I from King Lothar II.] leaving [Col. 0875D] to his son Louis the imperial dignity of Italy.

But Charles, king of the Franks, hearing that his brother Lothar had died [*Annals of Saint-Bertin*, year 869], came to Verdun; there he received many nobles of the Roman kingdom who committed themselves to him. From there he came to Metz on the Nones of September. There he again received into his allegiance Adventius, bishop of that city, Franco, bishop of Tongeren, and Atto, bishop of Verdun, with many other nobles, and deserved to be crowned with the imperial [Col. 0876A] crown on the fifth day before the Ides of that month. [Note: He was crowned king of Lotharingia.]

By chance at that time Louis, son of the deceased Emperor Lothar, and another Louis, king of Germany [Note: Manuscript 1 reads *gemanie*.], were detained by a hostile expedition with all the Saxons, in which they were fighting the Wends, who dwell opposite the Saxons. They defeated them and returned successfully. [Note: This cannot refer to the war waged against the Wends.]

[Same source, year 872.] In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 870, Louis, son of the Emperor Lothair, was crowned at Rome by Adrian, pontiff of that city, and thereafter proceeded into the regions of Benevento. [Same source, year 870.] In the same year Charles besieged and captured Vienne; and, returning thence, celebrated the feast of the Lord’s Nativity at the monastery of Saint Medard. [Same source, year 872.] In that same period Basil, whom Michael, emperor at Constantinople, had chosen as his colleague, killed him and usurped his empire.

[Note: On these passages of the Norman History, compare what I said in the preface, col. 815.]

In those days also the Danes, practising piracy under the leadership of Alstagnus, came forth through the harbour of Flanders and invaded France with great force. They utterly devastated the territories of Vermandois and Noyon, so that they burned the monastery of Saint Quentin the martyr and left nothing outside the gate of the city of Noyon unharmed and undefiled. All churches situated outside fortified places which they could reach were likewise reduced to ashes. For France was bereft of military protection, since its strength had recently perished in the battle of Fontenoy. Therefore King Charles made a treaty with the aforesaid tyrant, and subdued by gold the enemy whom he could not subdue by the sword. Secure under this agreement, Alstagnus crossed the Ocean Sea from the land of the Franks towards Italy, reached the harbour of Luna, and immediately captured the city itself. Having gained possession of it, he remained there for many years and later became a friend of the king—an ally after having been an enemy. Yet this Alstagnus is commonly called Gurmundus.

[Col. 0877A] [Annals of Bertin, years 872, 875, 876, and 877.] In the year of Christ’s Incarnation 873, Adrian, pope at Rome, died, and John, archdeacon of the same city, was installed in his place. In the year of the divine Incarnation 876 Pope John invited King Charles to come to Rome, and graciously crowned him upon his arrival in the church of Saint Peter. He was then crowned a second time with the imperial crown and called Emperor of the Romans. In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 877 Pope John came to Pavia, and Charles went there to meet him and sent through him to Saint Peter a great image of the Crucified One made of pure gold.

[History of Sens.] But when he was returning from there, he ended his life by poison; he was carried to Vercelli and buried in the basilica of Saint Eusebius, where he also lay for six years. At length he was transferred to Saint-Denis and honourably entombed there.

[Annals of Bertin.] When Louis heard that his father Charles had died, he immediately took care to win over the magnates of France, granting them abbeys, counties, and estates according to each man’s request. For he feared, on account of his own incapacity, that he would lose the kingdom of the Franks.

[Note: *ineptiam* is read as *inepciam* in manuscript 1.]

In the preceding year, however—namely, the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 876—while King Charles was attempting to bring under his own power the rights of his nephew, the treacherous people of the Danes entered the Seine from the Ocean Sea and began for the second time to harass the kingdom of the Franks. Their leader was Rollo, a most powerful man and kinsman of the above-mentioned King and arch-pirate Gurmundus. At the first onset of his arrival he immediately subjected Rouen to himself. Then for almost a year he besieged the city of Paris, but could not capture it. Meanwhile, however, he destroyed Bayeux and stormed the city of Meaux. But after one year, during which he had left the sheath of his dwelling-place and polluted the entire seacoast with fire and plunder, he went at the invitation of the king of the English to that island. Remaining there for three years, he bound that people to himself by a firm treaty. This greatly increased his strength and supplied him with an abundance of resources. Charles the Bald was succeeded by his son Louis.

## 2. Louis

Louis, then, after his father’s death obtained the kingdom of the Franks in the year of the divine Incarnation 877 and reigned about three years.

[Annals of Bertin and History of Sens.] In his time, namely in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 878, Pope John came into Gaul with Formosus, bishop of Porto, and held a general synod in the city of Troyes.

[Note: Manuscript 1 reads *ita*, “thus.”]

[Annals of Fleury.] In the following year an eclipse of the moon occurred, when the moon was on the fourteenth day before the Ides of October [2 October]. In the same month there was also an eclipse of the sun, when the moon was twenty-three days old.

[Note: The Bern manuscript of the *History of the Franks*, joining this account to William of Jumièges, reads: “Rollo, emerging for a second time through the Seine, the Loire, and the Varumna—three rivers which flow into the Ocean—with a threefold army, now no longer in a piratical manner but freely ravaging the surrounding lands, began to harass [France]. Thus on the day, etc.; see note **.”]

In that same year Rollo, of whom we have spoken above, relying on English help, came forth for a second time through the Seine, the Loire, and the Varumna—the three greatest rivers of France which flow into the Ocean—with his army divided in three; and, no longer in piratical fashion but openly by land warfare, began to ravage France.

[Note: Similarly Adrevald of Fleury, *Miracles of Saint Benedict*, ch. 33: “no longer,” he says, “practising piracy.”]

Thus the Danes covered the face of the earth like locusts, and it was not easy for any person to restrain them. Leaping from their ships and rushing here and there like rabid wolves, on the feast-day of Saint John the Baptist they attacked and burned the city of Nantes, and slaughtered Bishop Gunhard while he was performing the solemn rites of Mass at the altar of the martyr Ferreolus, which stands to the left of the church of Saint Peter the Apostle, the mother church of that city.

[Note: The following are likewise found in the History of the Franks.]

[Note: This occurred already in 843; compare the Annals of Bertin for that year.]

[Note: Manuscript 1 reads *Gunardum*; the History of the Franks reads *gunardum*.]

[Note: Manuscript 1 reads *obtruncavit*, “he slaughtered”; the reading in the text is plural, “they slaughtered.”]

[Note: The History of the Franks reads: “Finally, after the city …”]

After the city had been burned and laid waste, they began, like a violent storm, to range in every direction and overthrow everything through which they passed. Having also burned the city of Angers, they besieged the city of Tours.

[Note: Compare Adrevald, cited work.]

But it deserved to be delivered from hostile invasion through the merits of the most blessed Martin, whose body had shortly before been brought within the walls of the city. Nevertheless, the monastery of Saint Martin itself, which lay beside the city, was burned; the clerics fled, the monks were scattered, and the venerable body of Saint Martin was carried with honour to Auxerre.

[Note: The History of the Franks reads “through the merits of Martin the martyr.”]

[Note: Manuscript 1 reads *antis*, for *Autissiodorum*, Auxerre.]

[Note: Compare the Annals of Bertin for the year 853.]

[Note: This was in 853.]

While this storm likewise raged, the city of Le Mans was devastated, and the monastery of Saint Scholastica the virgin, situated outside the city wall, was burned.

[Note: Manuscript 1 reads *Cenomannia*, Le Mans.]

[Note: The History of the Franks adds “and.”]

But the body of that holy virgin was placed and preserved within the precincts of the same city.

[Note: Manuscript 1 reads: “her holy body … The rest is lacking.”]

Moreover, many bodies of saints were transferred from Brittany and Neustria into Gaul and placed in fortified cities and castles, where they still remain buried. For almost all the clerics and monks of that land, terrified by so cruel a disaster, sought safer places, carrying with them their relics and church ornaments.

At the same time the palace of Charlemagne, called Cassinogilum, situated between the river Droht and the Varumna, was demolished and destroyed.

[Note: The History of the Franks reads: “But also in Aquitaine the palace of Charlemagne, which was called Cassinogilum, was demolished and overthrown.”]

[Note: Concerning this palace, Annoinus, *Miracles of Saint Benedict* I.1, when recounting the devastations of the Northmen, says: “Among these, the most eminent was the palace of Prince Charlemagne at Cassignol, once the glory and ornament of the childhood of his already-mentioned son Louis the Pious. The nation hostile to God overthrew it so completely that it rendered it uninhabitable, though what it once was remains plainly evident. It is situated where the torrent Codrot flows into the Garonne, and has a brick tower built upon the bank of the said torrent, from which both approaching vessels might be seen in advance and the entry of hostile ships prevented; and likewise so that the royal fleet, built without hindrance from enemies on the smaller river, might be brought down to the waters of the greater stream. It has a church joined to a larger church, vaulted in brick with remarkable workmanship. In it, if I remember correctly, there is a very small sarcophagus, in which the twin brother of Louis the Pious is thought to be buried.” Compare also Aimoin, *Life of Abbo of Fleury*, ch. 20.]

[Col. 0879A] Louis, moreover, accomplished nothing vigorous in the whole course of his life. Having held the kingdom scarcely three years, he died, leaving as his successor his son Charles, not yet grown up.

[Note: The History of the Franks reads: “After this Louis, king of the Franks and son of Charles the Bald, died, leaving a little son named Charles, who is called the Simple, with the kingdom under the guardianship of Odo, duke of Burgundy. He brought up the young man very well and, when he had grown up, willingly restored to him the reins of government. Granted a part of the kingdom by him, he remained faithful to him as long as he lived. Then the magnates of the Franks, Burgundians, and Aquitanians gathered together and elected Duke Odo as their king.”]

[Note: The author adopted and amplified errors partly from the History of Sens (above, cols. 855–856). What he added to the History of the Franks he took from Aimoin of Fleury, ch. 1.]

He appointed as the boy’s guardian and administrator Odo, son of Robert, count of the Angevins.

[Compare History of Sens.]

The magnates of the kingdom later made him king, and his brother Robert duke of Lower Burgundy, in order to restrain the attack of the Danes, who were then harassing France [in 888]. He took care to protect the kingdom entrusted to him from enemies for twelve years, and gently brought up the ward Charles until he came of age. When these years had been completed, he died in the year of the divine Incarnation 891.

[Note: He died in 898.]

Charles, now grown up, succeeded him.

There was also in those days, in the regions of Upper Burgundy, another noble duke named Richard.

[Hugh of Verdun.] Because of his execution of justice he was called the Justiciar; and he had three sons: Rudolf, Boso, and Hugh. Rudolf later became king of France, and Boso [king] of Upper Gaul, which is called Comata.

[Note: This is demonstrably false.]

On the Roman see Pope John was succeeded by Leo; Leo by Benedict; and Benedict by Gregory V.

## 3. Charles

Charles, surnamed the Simple, began to administer his paternal kingdom in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 891 and reigned nearly thirty years.

[Note: He was crowned king in 893.]

In his days Rollo, leader of the Danes, having embarked, proceeded up the Seine and the Sagunna, the greatest rivers of Gaul, entered the territories of Burgundy and the Arverni, and as far as the city of Clermont of the Arverni filled the whole region with various calamities and exhausted every kind of wealth. In these days Paris, Meaux, Beauvais, and the other cities of France were likewise ravaged and depopulated.

[Note: Manuscript 1 reads *maxsima*, “greatest.”]

[Note: Manuscript 1 may read *copia*, “abundance,” rather than *copiam*, “an abundance.”]

Then, in 865, the oft-mentioned Rollo descended through the province of Sens towards the lower country and came to Fleury.

[Note: The History of the Franks continues: “After accomplishing these things, Rollo, of whom we have often spoken, embarked at last and entered by the Seine and the Sagunna, the greatest rivers …, into the territories of Burgundy and the Arverni; he filled the whole region as far as the city of Clermont of the Arverni with various calamities, and returning thence came through the province of Sens to Fleury.”]

[Note: The matter concerns an event which Adelerius recounts more briefly in *Miracles of Saint Benedict*, ch. 41 (Mabillon, *Acta*, II, p. 393), and Diedericus the monk more fully (ibid. IV.2, p. 352). Hugh follows him. Compare also the Annals of Bertin for 865. This must be the same plundering, embellished fabulously.]

[Diedericus.] But two days before he arrived there, news of his coming reached the monks of Fleury.

[Note: The History of the Franks reads *pergeret*, “was proceeding,” for *pertingeret*, “arrived.”]

They at once fled with the greatest speed to Orléans and, in the church of Saint Aignan, bishop, within that city, deposited the precious and venerable body of Saint Benedict until the assault of those evil men had passed.

[Note: “To Orléans” is omitted there.]

[Note: The History of the Franks reads *malignorum*, “evil men,” for *malignancium*.]

For the city of Orléans was then full of warlike citizens and diligently enclosed by very strong walls.

[Note: The words “and carefully …” are lacking in the History of the Franks.]

But when that impious band of Danes came to Fleury, it found there sixty monks of holy desire and certain servants of the church; it immediately slaughtered them with the sword, and in savage fury burned the monastery of Saint Benedict the father, after first laying it waste.

[Note: Manuscript 1 reads *sancti*, “holy,” for *sacri*, “sacred.”]

That same night, however, the holy father Benedict appeared in a dream to a count named Gissilolphus, advocate of that monastery, and said to him:

[Note: The History of the Franks lacks the passage from “There was” through “enclosed.”]

[Note: The History of the Franks reads “in a dream” for “appeared in a dream.”]

[Note: Adelerius calls him Girboldus, a most noble count of Auxerre.]

> “Come, Count! Why have such fear or cowardice overwhelmed you that you left Fleury, the place entrusted to your protection, so undefended that the servants of God lie there unburied, slain by heathens?”

The count replied: “Who are you, father?”

And he said: “I am Brother Benedict, who was brought from the country of Benevento into Gaul. I rejected my own resting-place on Mount Cassino and chose this place, the monastery of Fleury, so that through my bodily presence the lamp of monastic discipline might become known throughout all Gaul. Rise, therefore, as quickly as possible; be a strong and valiant warrior; and pursue the backs of the cruel pagans, who have violated and burned my place, and moreover killed my monks and my fellow-freedmen, and—shame on them!—have escaped unpunished.”

[Note: The History of the Franks reads *Gallias*, “the Gauls,” for *Galliam*, “Gaul.”]

[Note: The History of the Franks reads “on Mount Cassino.”]

[Note: The History of the Franks omits “my monks.”]

[Note: The History of the Franks reads *coliberos*, for *collibertos*, “fellow-freedmen.”]

To this the count replied: “How can I pursue those whom you command, or recover the plunder, when I do not have time to gather my retainers?”

[Note: Manuscript 1 reads “and” for “or.”]

The holy father said to him: “Do not be anxious because of the small number of soldiers. Only hasten: take up the shield with the men who are at hand, and pursue swiftly, fearing nothing, because I shall be with you to encompass your sides; and, unharmed by the missiles of the enemy, you shall return a renowned victor.”

[Note: The History of the Franks omits *inquit*, “he said.”]

After these words the count awoke. Prudently considering with himself what he had seen and heard, he rose quickly, took up arms, and with his men pursued the enemy, encouraged by the promise of so great a father.

[Note: The History of the Franks omits *secumque*, “with himself.”]

[Note: Manuscript 1 reads *patri*, “father,” for *patris*, “of the father.”]

He suddenly rushed upon them with the greatest force, attacked the enemy, freed the captives, recovered the plunder, and returned joyfully as victor without any injury.

[Note: The History of the Franks omits *subito*, “suddenly,” and “and.”]

[Note: The History of the Franks reads “without any injury.”]

After achieving this victory he entered Fleury and, with no small flood of tears, buried the bodies of those who had been killed, recalling the words of the psalmist: “They poured out the blood of the saints, and there was none to bury.”

The deed afterwards came to the notice of Charles, king of the Franks: namely, how Count Gissilolphus, advocate of Saint Benedict, with a few men had overthrown a multitude of enemies, recovered the plunder, brought back the bound men released from their bonds, and returned victorious and unhurt.

[Note: The History of the Franks reads “came to the king’s notice.”]

[Note: The History of the Franks omits *videlicet*, “namely.”]

Immediately the aforesaid count and advocate appeared before the king and recounted to him in order the affair as he had carried it out, calling God to witness that at the moment of the encounter the most blessed Father Benedict, clothed in a monk’s habit, mounted the horse on which he himself was riding. Throughout the whole engagement, as the pious protector had promised, Benedict held the bridle, guided the horse, brandished the shield, and brought him back unharmed with all his men from the battle-line of the enemy.

[Note: Manuscript 1 perhaps reads *Moxqueque* for *Moxque*, “immediately.”]

[Note: The History of the Franks reads *evocatus*, “summoned,” for *advocatus*, “advocate.”]

[Note: Adelerius attributes this victory and miraculous event to Duke Hugh.]

[Col. 0881C] Hearing this, the king glorified the Lord. Coming to Fleury, he gave expression to grief for its desolation; afterwards, with royal generosity, he provided abundant assistance for its restoration. When a most ample supply for the entire restoration had been given, almost the whole monastery was renewed in its former condition within the space of a single year.

There was, moreover, a church built within the fortress of Fleury and dedicated in honour of Saint Peter, chief of the apostles; by divine grace it had remained untouched by the fire. When the year had elapsed, the monks who had fled to Orléans resolved to bring the body of blessed Benedict back by ship from the city of Orléans at the beginning of the Lord’s Advent, and to place it in the aforesaid basilica of Saint Peter, which had remained intact from the fire, until their buildings should be completed according to the regular custom.

[Note: The History of the Franks reads: “But within the year the monks who remained …”]

[Note: The History of the Franks reads *modo*, “fashion,” for *more*, “custom.”]

On the appointed day, a considerable gathering of bishops and abbots came to Orléans, in order that they might bring the Lord’s treasure—that is, the body of Saint Benedict—back to its appointed place. The God-fearing men took the holy body of Saint Benedict and placed it on a ship. When the ship had received this burden of such holiness, in a wondrous manner it began to travel upstream without a helmsman or human oarsman through the entire stretch of the Loire which extends from Orléans to Fleury, without mishap, so that one might have believed Christ to be seated in the ship with the apostles and sovereignly commanding the elements.

[Note: The History of the Franks reads: “as though Christ with the apostles were sitting in the ship and ruling the elements.”]

When the sacred pledges had been placed in the aforesaid basilica of Saint Peter and the divine mystery solemnly celebrated, each returned home with joy. This day is known to have been the day before the Nones of December [4 December], on which, as long as the sphere of this world continues to turn, the honour and memory of so great a glory are celebrated throughout all Gaul.

[Note: The History of the Franks reads: “The same … is solemnly celebrated throughout all Gaul. But when the ship reached the harbour of Fleury, a very great multitude of bishops, abbots, monks, clerics, and crowds of common people came forth to meet it, chanting and saying: ‘Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord.’ And although an intense cold, as is usual at that season, had bound fast all the fields, a wondrous and exceedingly astonishing event occurred. For when the most holy ashes were carried in through the gate now called Paschal, all the trees of the place—fruit-bearing and wild alike—the thorn-bushes too and the shrubs, burst into flower as though it were the middle of April. Thus it became plainly known to all how Saint Benedict the father was exalted in glory and honour with our almighty Lord Jesus Christ. No other cry was heard than: ‘Glory to you, Lord, for now we know what we have received through your gift.’ The sacred pledges having been placed … with joy.” These details are also from Diedericus.]

[Col. 0882C] A few days later the aforesaid Rollo resolved to besiege Chartres.

[Note: William of Jumièges, II.15, tells the same event more briefly.]

At that time a venerable priest named Wantelinus was in charge of the city. Hearing the report of the approaching treacherous enemies, he prayed to Saint Mary, Mother of God, that she would protect the city from the imminent danger. He also awaited the two dukes of Burgundy, Richard and Robert, and Ebles, margrave of Poitou, asking them by their arrival to bring aid to the afflicted citizens. When he had returned from there, Rollo arrived with a large host and began fiercely to attack the city. As he was already preparing to enter it, behold: by God’s will Duke Richard, with Franks and Burgundians, attacked the enemy and suddenly began to crush and scatter them in every direction as they stood off their guard. Wantelinus too, carrying relics of the holy Mother of God, went out through the open gates with armoured soldiers and pressed them vigorously. Thus the aforesaid tyrant, overcome and defeated by God’s power, returned to Rouen with great loss.

When Franco, archbishop of that city, saw him grievously afflicted by the divine scourge, he came to console him. First he soothed his mind with gentle words; then he endeavoured to rebuke him for his evil deeds; finally, he began wisely to invite him to the worship of the Catholic faith and religion. Rollo, softened by his words and simultaneously chastened by the divine scourge, immediately assented. The bishop hastened to report this to King Charles: namely, that the repeatedly mentioned tyrant had been softened by God’s grace and that his heart had in some measure been made receptive to accepting Christianity.

[Note: Manuscript 1 added *intelligens*, “understanding,” but another hand deleted it.]

Robert, duke of Burgundy, happened to be present when the bishop made this report to the king.

[Note: Count of Paris.]

Through that bishop Robert had Rollo informed that, if he wished to become a Christian, Robert himself would receive him from the sacred font and confer his own name upon him. Thus the affair was finally brought to completion. At the appointed place and time Duke Robert came to Rollo with the other magnates of Gaul, lifted him from the sacred font, gave him his own name, and honoured him with magnificent gifts. King Charles then betrothed to him his daughter named Gilla, giving him in benefice Neustria—now called Normandy—from the river Andelle to the Ocean Sea.

In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 912 Franco, archbishop of Rouen, purified the often-mentioned Rollo, carefully instructed in the Catholic faith, with the water of baptism, and Duke Robert received him from the saving font.

[Note: Compare William of Jumièges, II.18. The preceding material is foreign to that work.]

[Note: Manuscript 1 perhaps reads *Rotbertum*, accusative, for *Rotbertus*, nominative.]

From that time the said prince remained a most faithful worshipper of Christ, whose most cruel persecutor he had formerly been. He was baptized at the age of thirty-six, when he had come to devastate France.

In that same year the body of blessed Martin was returned from Auxerre to the city of Tours. The leading men of the city rebuilt his church, recently burned, and enclosed it with a wall lest it should again be easily overwhelmed by enemies.

King Charles also had a bridge of remarkable strength built over the Seine, with skilfully founded castles placed at both ends, in which he stationed garrisons. Having done this, he embraced the means of peace; and, yielding himself to leisure and idleness—

[Note: The History of the Franks reads: “Meanwhile the oft-mentioned King Charles [interlinear addition: the Simple] eagerly [embraced] the means which …”]

[Flodoard, year 920.] Taking as his counsellor a certain knight named Hagano, one of middling rank, he began to despise the counsel of his magnates. Hagano, whom unexpected riches had elevated too highly, stood at his side and administered the affairs of the kingdom. Almost all the magnates of the Franks saw and resented this, and abandoned the king. Count Herbert of Vermandois also took from him the stronghold of Laon [in 920]. The aforementioned Robert, duke of Burgundy, likewise began to rebel against him and, coming from Burgundy with a strong force of soldiers, pitched his camp on the river Aisne.

[Flodoard, year 922.] Charles pitched camp on the little river Saire. But as Duke Robert’s power increased daily and the king’s diminished, Charles secretly departed across the Meuse with his friend Hagano.

[Hugh of Flavigny; Flodoard, cited places.] Afterwards, the aforesaid Robert compelled certain bishops of Gaul, partly by threats and partly by flattery, to crown him with the royal diadem in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 924.

[Note: In 922.]

In the same year Herveus, archbishop of Reims, died, and Seulf, archdeacon of the same church, succeeded him.

[Col. 0884B] In the following year King Charles crossed the Meuse with the Lotharingians of his kingdom and came against the aforesaid King Robert at Attigny. King Robert likewise marched against him and pitched his camp upon the Aisne beneath the city of Soissons. But Charles suddenly fell upon him with his Lotharingians. There Robert, at the very beginning of the battle, was killed [in 923], deprived by no less sudden a blow of fortune than he had formerly been exalted.

[Hugh of Verdun.] But after the battle, when the Lotharingians had returned home, Count Herbert treacherously seized King Charles and sent him to Péronne, where he kept him confined in chains for the whole of five years. At the end of those five years Charles there breathed out his spirit and received burial in the church of Saint Fursey [in 929].

[Compare History of Sens.]

[Hugh of Flavigny.] The said king had a son named Louis by Ægiva, daughter of the king of the English. Fearing that he might be involved in the storm of his father’s calamity, Louis crossed the sea and concealed himself in England. Gaul therefore was unsteady, since the youth of Hugh, son of the recently deceased Duke Robert—who afterwards earned the name “the Great” for his good deeds—prevented him from assuming the royal insignia, while everyone held Herbert in hatred. Therefore certain magnates of the realm assembled and raised Rudolf, son of Richard the Justiciar, summoned from Burgundy, to the royal throne.

[Compare Aimoin of Fleury, ch. 3.]

[Flodoard, same year.] Furthermore, in the time of the aforesaid King Charles, namely in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 922, Berengar, emperor of the Lombards, was driven from his kingdom by his magnates, and Rudolf, king of Cisalpine Gaul, was received by them as king.

At the same time Rollo, also called Robert, prince of the Normans, worn out by old age and exhausted by long warfare, died [in 927], leaving his son William as his successor. Around the same time [in 936] Emperor Henry died and was succeeded by his son Otto.

[Flodoard, 937.] Rudolf, king of the Juras and of Cisalpine Gaul, also died, and his son Conrad succeeded him.

## 4. Rudolf

Rudolf, son of Duke Richard, as stated above, obtained the kingdom of the Franks while King Charles was still alive, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 926, and reigned sixteen years.

[Note: “Rudolf … subjected,” written by a second hand in manuscript 1.]

[Note: In 923.]

Having attained the royal throne, he was severe in restraining evildoers and most shrewd in preserving the kingdom.

[Hugh of Flavigny.] In the first year of his reign he went into Aquitaine [in 924—Flodoard], because Count William of that province disdained to submit to him.

[Flodoard.] At length both came above the Loire, into the district of Autun; and, while noblemen from both sides were moving about, the aforesaid count submitted to the king. Therefore the king granted him the district of Bourges with its city. In the same place he gave Hugh, son of the deceased Duke Rudolf—

[Note: Robert.]

—the city of Le Mans.

In the same year the Huns, led by Berengar, whom the Lombards had long before driven from their kingdom, devastated Italy and set fire to the rich and populous city of Pavia. Having done this, they crossed the mountain ridges and began to harass Gaul.

[Note: Manuscript 1 reads *moncium*, “mountains.”]

[Compare Flodoard, year 926.]

They destroyed many monasteries, and through fear of them the body of Saint Remigius was carried and transferred inside the walls of Reims.

[Flodoard, year 924.] Yet Rudolf, king of Cisalpine Gaul, and Count Hugh of Vienne drove them through mountain byways and compelled them to make for the province of Toulouse.

[Note: Manuscript 1 reads *muntium*, “mountains.”]

There the aforesaid Berengar was killed by his own men, and Gaul was thus freed from their assaults.

In the fifth year of King Rudolf’s reign Count Herbert of Vermandois defected from him.

[Flodoard, year 931.] King Rudolf, having joined Hugh the Great to himself, captured and destroyed one of Herbert’s castles, called Dominicum. In the sixth year of his reign Raymond and Ermengard, most powerful princes of Gothia, and also Lupus, count of the Gascons, became the king’s vassals.

[Flodoard, years 932–933.] The Burgundian city of Vienne was also restored to him. At the same time William, count of the Normans and son of Rollo, voluntarily commended himself to the aforesaid King Rudolf.

In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 931, the Bretons settled in the Horn of Gaul rebelled against the Normans, to whom they were subject, and killed their leader.

[Note: Manuscript 1 reads *interremeruerunt*, apparently for *interemerunt*, “they killed.”]

[Flodoard, year 931.] When William, prince of Normandy, heard this, he entered their land as an enemy and devastated it harshly. He reconciled Berengar, their most powerful leader, to himself; drove Alan, their other leader, from the land; and thus again claimed all Brittany for himself by force.

[Hugh of Flavigny.] King Rudolf died without children in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 936.

[Note: At this point the History of the Franks reads: “In those times Lambert, a simple and just man, flourished as abbot at the monastery of Fleury.”]

When King Athelstan of the English heard this, he sent envoys with gifts to William, prince of the Normans, asking him, with the counsel of the magnates of France, to restore Louis, son of Charles the Simple, to his father’s kingdom [in 936].

[Note: Compare William of Jumièges, III.4.]

[Flodoard.] William gladly accepted and successfully carried this out. With Hugh the Great, Count Herbert, and other magnates of the Franks, he received the aforesaid young man at Boulogne, adjoining the very shore of the sea, and led him as far as Laon.

[Note: Manuscript 1 reads *cuntiguam*, for *contiguam*, “adjoining.”]

On the throne of the Roman Church, Pope John was succeeded by Leo, Leo by Stephen, Stephen by Martin, and Martin by Agapetus. At this time the distinguished bishops Adalbero of Metz and Fulbert of Chartres flourished in Gaul.

[Note: The History of the Franks reads: “Meanwhile, at Rome Pope John was succeeded by the most holy Leo; after him Stephen sat; after Stephen, Martin; and Martin was succeeded by Agapetus. Louis, son of the younger Charles [interlinear addition: the Simple], reigned twenty-nine years.”]

## 5. Louis

Louis, son of Charles the Simple, was crowned, through the favour of the aforesaid princes, by Artald, archbishop of Reims, in the year of the Incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ 936, and reigned nearly eighteen years.

[Flodoard; Hugh of Flavigny.] He betrothed his sister Mathilda to Conrad, king of Burgundy, giving him as a dowry-right the Burgundian city of Lyon.

[Note: Thus Hugh of Flavigny, *Scriptores*, VIII, p. 364, concerning King Lothair.]

He also gave a part of the Lotharingian kingdom to Emperor Otto; Otto in turn gave it to his brother Henry. King Louis married Gerberga, sister of Emperor Otto. Hugh, son of Duke Robert, married Otto’s other sister, daughter of Emperor Henry.

[Flodoard.] In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 937, a part of the sky appeared to burn, and from that direction an invasion of the Hungarians followed through France; villages and fields were devastated, and houses and churches were burned. In the same year Rudolf, king of the Juras and Cisalpine Gaul, died, and his little son Conrad succeeded him in the kingdom.

[Flodoard, year 940.] In the fifth year of Louis’s reign Hugh the Great besieged the city of Reims, expelled Artald, bishop of that city, from his see, and installed Hugh, son of Count Herbert, in his place. In the following year Count Herbert died and was buried at Saint-Quentin [in 943]. Odo, abbot of Cluny and Fleury, also died at Tours in the same year. An eloquent man and powerful in literary learning, among the other little works he composed he also issued that sermon on Saint Benedict which begins: “The festal solemnity of the most blessed Benedict.” After his death Saint Majolus assumed the governance of the church of Cluny.

[FLOD.] Moreover, at this time, namely in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 943, Arnulf, count of Flanders, treacherously murdered William, son of Rollo and ruler of the Normans, who had been invited to a conference, at the castle of Pinquigny beside the waters of the Somme. [Note: Col. 0887D. Cf. William of Jumièges III.11.] William had by a concubine a son named Richard. King Louis [Note: Col. 0887D. Cf. William of Jumièges IV.2 and following], on hearing of the death of the aforesaid ruler, considered how he might bring under his lordship that part of Normandy which lies along the Seine. Then, having summoned Hugh the Great, [Col. 0887B] he gave him the Norman cities of Évreux and Bayeux on condition that he should assist him in the remaining enterprise, so that the king himself might bring the aforesaid part of Normandy under his lordship.

Accordingly, on the appointed day the king went forth to besiege Rouen, and Hugh the Norman city of Bayeux. A certain Norman named Bernard, a very cunning and shrewd man, was at that time keeping the fortress of Rouen. When the king arrived at Rouen, Bernard received him peaceably. Yet, while the king remained in the city, the aforesaid Bernard deceitfully suggested that he should make Duke Hugh withdraw from the siege of Bayeux and should retain all Normandy under his own rule. The king immediately took steps to do this. Hence the seed of discord sprang up between king and duke.

Therefore, when Hugh had departed [Col. 0887C] from the city, the king entered it at once. After restoring his army there for a few days, he returned again to Rouen. [Note: Col. 0887: “Rotdomum,” thus in witness 1.] Taking with him the aforesaid youth Richard, he brought him as far as Laon. But when Richard was eventually treated negligently by the king, one of the king’s knights, named Osmund, secretly carried off the youth Richard, brought him first to the castle of Coucy, and finally restored him to his men and kinsmen.

When the king learned this, he returned to Rouen and was received peaceably. Meanwhile the Normans sent to the king of the Danes, named Aygrold, asking him to hasten to aid his kinsman Count Richard, whom the king wished to disinherit. Aygrold came immediately and sent word to King Louis that he should come to meet him for a conference. Thus the king, deceived by the counsel of Bernard, count of Senlis, and of the other Bernard of Rouen, whom we mentioned above, men who knew of the treachery, came to meet the pagan Aygrold, king of the Danes, suspecting no harm. But the faithless Aygrold suddenly attacked the king as he approached him; finding him unprepared, he killed almost all his soldiers.

At once there was slain on Louis’s side [Col. 0888A] Herluin, [Note: Col. 0887: “herliuinus,” witness 1.] the most noble count of the castle of Montreuil, together with nineteen most valiant counts and no small number of knights. Seeing this, King Louis began to flee alone; but he was seized by the Normans, whom he had hoped would be faithful to him, and was placed under guard at Rouen.

Then Queen Gerberga sought the assistance of Hugh the Great. He received her reverently and then began to negotiate for the king’s release. The Normans, however, demanded that the king’s sons be given them as hostages, declaring that otherwise they would not release him.

[FLOD., year 945.] They sent to the queen for the boys. She [Note: Col. 0887. The words from *Illa* (“she”) through *adolescentem* (“youth”) were added by a second hand in witness 1] sent the king’s younger son, but refused to send the elder. Thus the king’s younger son was given as a hostage; and, in order that the king might be released, Guy, bishop of Soissons, also gave himself as hostage. Then the king [Col. 0888B] reinvested the aforesaid youth Richard with the land of the Normans and so withdrew from Normandy. But Hugh the Great, having received the king from the Normans, did not permit him to depart freely; rather, he entrusted him to his vassal Count Theobald. Theobald kept him enclosed under guard until the king granted Hugh the Great possession of the hill of Laon.

[Ib., year 946.] After these events Theotilo, the venerable bishop of the city of Tours, hastened to the hill of Laon on urgent business. But as he was returning home, he began in the course of the journey to fail from a grave illness. [Ib., year 945.] And when he was already breathing his last, a certain sign of light appeared moving through the air, seeming to be a cubit in length. By its light those conducting his funeral were adequately enabled to dispel [Note: Col. 0888: “depellaendas,” witness 1.] the darkness of the night. [Col. 0888C] Comforted in this way, they carried his body nearly two hundred miles to the city of Tours. Thus he was reverently buried in the monastery of St Julian, which that holy man himself had established with the utmost religious devotion, beside the tomb of Lord Abbot Odo; and from that time the church itself has been made illustrious by divine miracles.

[Ib., year 947.] In the tenth year of Louis’s reign, the king himself celebrated holy Easter in the palace at Aachen with Emperor Otto; richly rewarded by him, he returned to Francia.
