[Ib., year 949.] Accordingly, in the thirteenth year of his reign King Louis unexpectedly attacked Laon; and, in the silence of night, [Col. 0888D] having secretly scaled the wall with engines and broken down the bars of the gates, he entered the town. Yet he could not take the tower which he himself had recently founded beside the gate of the fortress; he therefore cut it off from the city by constructing a wall across the interior. When Hugh learned this, he immediately came there; after placing guards in the fortress with sufficient provisions, he went to meet [Note: Col. 0888D: Flodoard says this concerning the king.] Conrad, duke of the Lotharingians. The duke established a truce between the king and Hugh until August. Thereupon King Louis returned [Col. 0889A] to Reims; there Adalbert, son of Count Herbert, came to him and became his vassal.

[Ib., year 951.] Finally, in the fifteenth year of his reign, King Louis went with an army into Aquitaine. Before he entered it, Charles Constantine, ruler of Vienne, and Stephen, the most renowned bishop of the Arverni, came to him and became his men. William of Poitiers also came to meet him and committed himself to his favour. Thereafter, in the nineteenth year of his reign, King Louis set out from the hill of Laon and was coming to the city of Reims.

[Ib., year 954.] And behold, before he reached the river Aisne, something like a wolf appeared walking before him. As he pursued it, spurring his horse vigorously, he fell and was severely crushed; [Col. 0889B] he was then carried to Reims.

[HUGO FLAV.] There, after lying for a long time in prolonged sickness, he died and was buried at Saint-Remi, leaving two sons alive, namely Lothair and Charles [Note: Col. 0889B: “little Charles,” Hist. Franc.], whom Gerberga, sister of Emperor Otto, had borne him. Lothair succeeded his father; Charles grew old as a private person.

## 6. Lothair

Lothair, son of Louis [FLOD.], was consecrated at Reims by Archbishop Artald and succeeded his father in the year of the divine Incarnation 954; he reigned twenty-three years. In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 956, Richard, [Note: Col. 0889D. Cf. William of Jumièges IV.10.] son of William, ruler of the Normans, married the daughter of Duke Hugh.

[FLOD.; Hist. Sen.] In the same year, however, the aforesaid duke, namely Hugh the Great, died and was buried at Saint-Denis, leaving three sons, whom the daughter of Emperor Otto had borne him: Hugh, Otto, and Henry. Hugh received the duchy of Francia, [Col. 0889C] and Otto [Note: Col. 0889D: “Otto.”] that of Burgundy.

[HUGO FLAV.; FLOD.] Accordingly, in the year of the divine Incarnation 962, Emperor Henry, travelling to Rome, was crowned with the imperial crown by Pope Octavian, who had succeeded Agapitus. But not long afterwards the Romans drove the aforesaid Pope Octavian from his see [cf. HUGO FL.], and substituted for him a certain John. [Note: Col. 0889D: Hugo of Flavigny increased the former errors with new ones.] On hearing this, the emperor returned to Rome and deposed the aforesaid John by synodal judgment.

[FLOD.] In the same year [Col. 0889D] Wulfaud, abbot of the church of St Benedict of Fleury, became bishop of Chartres. [Note: Cols. 0889D–0890A. The Historia Francorum gives this at greater length: “And in the same year Wulfad, abbot of the monastery of St Benedict of Fleury, became bishop of the city of Chartres. For he was an energetic and most wise man. He fortified the monastery of Fleury with rampart and wall. In his time also Malbo, bishop of the Britons, brought with him from the town called Saint-Pol to the monastery of Fleury the body of the same bishop, St Paul, with many ornaments. Oswald, nephew of Odo, bishop of Canterbury, professed himself a monk in that holy monastery. But afterwards he was taken thence and recalled to his native country, and was consecrated bishop at York. In order to show by deeds his heartfelt devotion to Father Benedict, he built in that island a monastery under the name of that most glorious confessor, which he called Ramsey; and he enriched the house of Fleury with many honourable gifts. In the preceding time, under the aforesaid king, a certain bishop came from Britain, named Hedrem, assumed the monastic habit at Fleury, and brought with him the body of the blessed martyr Maurus, who, it is established, suffered at Rome under the prefect Celerinus, in the reigns of the emperors Carinus and Numerian. Likewise another man, named Atto, came to the same monastery and offered to St Benedict the body of a certain holy martyr, Frotgetius. Abbot Richard, [Note within note: Aimoin, Miracles of St Benedict I.7, states that Richard succeeded Wulfald.] who had presided over Fleury before Wulfald, also brought there a substantial portion of the Holy Cross and a part of the sponge with which the most sacred body of our Redeemer, taken down from the cross, was washed.”]

In the time of this man, a certain Mabbo, bishop of the Britons, brought the body of the most blessed confessor and bishop Paul from Britain to the monastery of Fleury, with many ornaments.

[Col. 0890B] In the following year Richard, count of the Normans, [Note: Cols. 0889D, 0890D. Cf. William of Jumièges IV.15, who recounts this in other words.] devastated the lands of Chartres and Châteaudun in an attack upon Count Theobald. Theobald in turn entered Norman territory and captured [Col. 0890C] the city of Évreux. But when he was returning from there, Richard crossed the river [Note: Col. 0889: “anne,” witness 1.] and attacked him at the dwellings of Ermentrude, at the port on the river Seine; having defeated him, he drove him out of his own land. Finally, summoning Danes, Alans, and Deiri to his aid, Richard fought the aforesaid Theobald until Theobald restored the city of Évreux to him. Once this had been done, the barbarians, well rewarded by Richard, left Gaul and returned home.

Moreover, at this time (year 1030), Rodulf, son of King Conrad, died without children. Emperor Henry, having married his sister Gilla, brought Rodulf’s kingdom under his own rule. [Note: Col. 0890D. “Gisela, sister of King Rodulf, married the father of King Henry; Henry’s successor Conrad obtained the kingdom of Burgundy.”]

[HUGO FLAV.] At about the same time there died Odo, [Col. 0890D] count of Tours; Herbert, count of Meaux and Troyes; and William of Poitiers. [Note: Col. 0889: “pictanorum,” witness 1?] King Lothair also ended his life in the twenty-third year of his reign, and his son Louis succeeded him (year 986).

[Hist. Sen.] King Lothair died in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 976 [Note: Col. 0890D: year 986.] and was buried at Reims, at Saint-Remi.

## 7. Louis

[Col. 0891A] Louis, then, son of Lothair, acquired the kingdom of the Franks in the year of the divine Incarnation 986 and reigned two years.

[Hist. Sen.] This Louis [Note: Col. 0891D. Concerning this Louis, MS Bern 90 has the following plainly fabulous marginal note: “In the district of Vimma he fought against a certain cousin of his, Ysenbard, and Guermund, king of the Africans; after destroying their army, which they had brought from overseas regions, he gained a very great triumph.”] died without offspring (year 991) and was buried at Compiègne in the basilica of the blessed martyr Cornelius. After his death, his uncle Charles, desiring to succeed his nephew, was delivered into custody at the city of Senlis [Note: Col. 0892D: “At Orléans,” Hist. Senon.] by the nobles of Francia and above all by Ascelin, bishop of Laon, a most wicked traitor—for he appeared to be the aforesaid Charles’s counsellor—together with his two sons, Charles and Louis (year 991). [Note: Col. 0891: “est—third generation,” added by a second hand in witness 1.] He died not long afterwards while in custody. After his death, the two aforesaid youths fled to the Roman emperor, with whom they too died.

[AIMOIN OF FLEURY II.1.] But the nobles of Francia [Col. 0891B] chose Hugh, duke of Francia and son of Hugh the Great, and raised him to the royal throne at Noyon in the same year in which the aforesaid King Louis died (year 987). Thus, when the second line of the kings of Francia had failed, the kingdom was transferred to a third generation, by the judgment of God who willed it [Note: Col. 0891. The editor asks whether *optante* (“willing”) should be *aptante* (“arranging”)], who raises whom he wills and humbles whom he wills. Those kings who first reigned in Francia were formerly called Merovingians after King Merovech. [Note: Col. 0891. Witness 1 reads *nonc* for *nunc*, “formerly/then.”] That royal line endured down to King Hilderic, who was also called Childeric by another name. Pipin, son of Charles Tudites, was chief of his palace.

Since King Childeric was useless and incompetent, he was, by the judgment of Zacharias, bishop of Rome, thrust into a monastery by the nobles of the Franks and clothed in the monastic habit; [Col. 0891C] Pipin was raised to the royal throne. Pipin was succeeded by his son Charlemagne, who later became emperor of the Romans. Charlemagne too was succeeded by Emperor Louis the Pious. Since he had begotten four sons, he divided his empire among them; great discord consequently arose between them, and they fought the battle of Fontenoy in Burgundy on the day of the Lord’s Ascension. In that battle a great army was destroyed on either side. Yet Charles, their younger brother, whom the other brothers wished to disinherit, obtained the victory. From that day to the present, the kingdom of the Franks has remained divided and separated from the Roman Empire.

From the stock of this King Charles came all those kings whose deeds we have here recorded, down to [Col. 0891D] this Louis, of whom we have just said a few words. Since he died childless, the nobles of Francia, as we have also just mentioned, elevated over themselves Hugh the Great, son of Hugh, duke of Francia.

## 8. Hugh

[Col. 0892A] Hugh, duke of the Franks and son of Hugh the Great, acquired the royal dignity of the Franks in the year of the Incarnate Word 987 and reigned about eleven years.

[Note: Cols. 0892A–B. Historia Francorum adds: “After Hugh had been raised to the kingship, he immediately had his son Robert crowned at Orléans. He reigned with his aforesaid son Robert for about nine years. During that time he caused the venerable Abbo, endowed with both secular and literary learning, to be ordained abbot in the monastery of Fleury. Finally, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1004, Abbo was martyred and died at a certain cell of the aforesaid monastery at the hands of faithless Gascons; to this day great miracles are performed by divine grace at his holy tomb.”]

[The words from “Moreover” through “his son” are deleted by a second hand in witness 1:] Moreover, this Hugh associated with himself in the partnership of the kingdom his son Hugh, [Note: Col. 0892D. This is plainly false. Hugh made Robert his partner in the kingdom, and Robert reigned after his father. The present writer, however, calls his son Hugh king and soon relates his death; see below, chapter 9.] who is usually called Capet by some. After reigning with his father for seven years, he died while his royal father was still alive. [Note: Col. 0891: “con,” witness 1.]

[HUGO FLAV.] In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 983 Emperor Otto II died [and was buried at Aachen; Note: Col. 0891: “and was buried at Aachen” deleted in witness 1], and his son Otto III succeeded him. After he had appointed a pope to the Roman see, John Crescentius, one of the Roman nobles, presumed to deprive that pope of the Apostolic See. When the emperor heard this, he came to Rome, violently and disgracefully deposed that pope from his see as an usurper and destroyer of the holy Roman Church, killed Crescentius, and ordered Gerbert to be ordained there. Because of the learning [Col. 0892C] in which he excelled, Gerbert deserved, as though by certain stages and at intervals of time, to be raised within the holy Church. First he obtained the archbishopric of Reims, then that of Ravenna; finally he was elevated to the Apostolic chair, in which he also sat for many years.

In the year of the divine Incarnation 988, an image of the Crucified placed in the church of the holy apostles Peter and Paul within the city of Orléans was seen to weep. In the following year the aforesaid city was consumed by fire. But Arnulf, the venerable bishop of that city, through his diligence restored the church of the Holy Cross. At that same time Rome was largely burned by fire, and the church of St Peter began to be ravaged by the same conflagration. When [Col. 0892D] human assistance could no longer avail there and beams covered with bronze plates were burning, all the people of the city ran there and began to implore the aid of the apostles. Immediately the fire was checked and extinguished.

In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 994, [Col. 0894A] [Note: The following two columns, 893 and 894, printed in the wrong order in Migne, have been restored to their proper order. The original column numbers are retained.] [Note: Col. 0893D. The Annals of St Martin of Tours, Bouquet X, p. 225, place this in the year 997. On Hervé, see Ralph Glaber III.4.] the church of St Martin at Tours was burned. In its place Hervé, treasurer of that church, a noble and most holy man, built from the foundations the church which we now see, of marvellous beauty.

[Note: Cols. 0894A–B. Historia Francorum reads: “In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 984, the church of the most blessed Martin at Tours was burned by fire. For it Hervé, treasurer of that holy bishop, laid the foundations of the church now seen. Meanwhile the body of St Martin lay for twenty years in the little church within the cloister.”]

King Hugh of the Franks died at Melun in the eleventh year of his reign (year 996) and was buried in the church of Saint-Denis, leaving his son Robert as successor.

## 9. Robert

Robert, son of King Hugh, succeeded his father [Col. 0894B] in the kingdom in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 995 and reigned thirty-four years.

[Note: Cols. 0894B–C. Historia Francorum reads: “This devout king, during his father’s lifetime and at his father’s command, was crowned king at Orléans in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 987 [986, Ch.], and reigned with him nine years. He married Constance, daughter of William, count of Arles, born of Blanche, sister of Geoffrey, count of Anjou; by her he begot four sons: Hugh, surnamed the Great; Henry; Robert; and Odo. While still alive, he had Hugh crowned king at Compiègne. Hugh joined his father in the kingdom rather than succeeded him, because he died young while his father was still living. This gentle king, moderately learned, adorned his kingdom with holy churches and buildings. Among them he built, etc.; see below, note 121.”]

He was a gentle and very learned man, and he had a wise wife named Constance, daughter of William, count of Toulouse. [Note: Cols. 0893D–0894D. Cf. Vaissette, *Histoire de Languedoc*, II, p. 601, who observes correctly that this is accurate. The *Historia Francorum*, and likewise Aimoin, makes Constance the daughter of the count of Arles; but this and its statement concerning her mother Blanche depart from the truth, for Arsindis, daughter of Geoffrey, married William of Toulouse.] She bore him four sons: Hugh, Henry, Odo, and Robert.

Accordingly, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 997, this king entered Burgundy with thirty thousand men; he grievously devastated Count William of Trans-Saône, [Note: Col. 0894D. See Ralph Glaber III.2; “Trans-Saône,” that is, beyond the Arar/Saône.] who had revolted from him, and by great force subjected his land to himself.

[HUGO FLAV.] In the year of Christ’s Incarnation 1002, Emperor Otto III died, and his son Henry succeeded him. [Note: Col. 0894D: Note the writer’s error.] In the seventh year of his reign, and in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1011, [Note: Col. 0894D: Thus for the year 1014, already in Hugo of Flavigny.] this Henry was deemed worthy to be crowned with the imperial crown by Pope Benedict in the city of Rome.

[Col. 0894D] In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1003, the venerable Abbo, [Note: Col. 0894D. Cf. Glaber III.3 and above, col. 893, note ***.] abbot of Fleury, was martyred at an estate of that monastery situated in Gascony, [Col. 0893A] on account of the zeal for regular discipline which he pursued. [Note: Col. 0893: “quem,” thus in witness 1.] Great miracles are now performed by divine grace at his tomb.

He was succeeded by Lord Gaulinus.

[Note: Cols. 0893B–0895A. The *Historia Francorum* reads: “At this time there flourished in the monastery of Fleury the outstanding abbot Gallinus [*Gauslinus*, Ch.], who, because of the excellence of his character and the independence of his spirit [*animi*; *a. sui*, Ch., ‘of his own spirit’], received from King Robert the bishopric of Bourges together with the abbacy of Fleury. In his days the above-named monastery of Fleury was burned in an accidental fire; but through his exertions it was rebuilt and dedicated [*eo insistente i. b. e. r. et e.*, the remaining words abbreviated in print; the English gives their evident sense]. It was burned in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1026, on the third day before the Kalends of August; Ch. adds, ‘on the seventh Sabbath.’ Moreover, Lord Gauslinus, in accordance with his magnificent disposition, began to build [*extruere*; *construere*, Ch., both ‘to build’] a tower of squared stones on the western side of the aforesaid monastery, but death interrupted him and he left it unfinished. The aforesaid abbot [*prefatus abbas*; Ch. omits both words, printed as *p. a. desunt Ch.*] adorned that most sacred church with many ornaments. Among them, he caused an ambo of Spanish metal to be made by casting [*compositum*; *compactum*, Ch., ‘joined together’], above which stands a gilded eagle with outspread wings [*pansis*; *spansis*, Ch., both ‘spread’]. He also furnished a golden censer of most beautiful workmanship and great size, and enclosed the choir of chanters with panels of Spanish copper, made by casting. He separated these by intervening columns decorated with the most renowned carving. He also made eighteen domed ornaments of the same metal, fixed here and there above the same choir. He constructed the wall behind the backs of those seated in front from maple panels, faced on the exterior with porphyry marble. He also decorated the place of his own seat with the same marble. That same Gauslinus [*isdem Gauslinus*; Ch. omits both words, printed as *i. g. desunt Ch.*] also brought into that church [Ch. has the abbreviated alternative *e. sanctae p. n. m.*; its full wording cannot be recovered securely, but it likewise introduces the holy church] a substantial portion of the shroud of our Lord Jesus Christ [*sudarii d. n. I. Chr.*, ‘of the shroud of our Lord Jesus Christ’] and enclosed it in a golden right hand, on whose exterior he caused these verses to be inscribed: ‘This hand bears happy joys, shining, filled with Christ’s shroud’ [the note compresses the verses as *Gaudia . . . refulgens*; the full couplet is printed immediately below]. He further ordained [*etiam*; *denique*, Ch., ‘finally’] that this hand should every year be carried [*deportaretur*; *deporetur*, Ch., a defective spelling of the same verb] around the circuit of the fortress on Thursday, the day of the Lord’s Ascension, so that the faithful people, strengthened by this blessing, might return joyfully [*remearet*; *remeet*, Ch., indicative ‘returned’ versus subjunctive ‘might return’] to their homes. He did many other things which would be far too long for us to enumerate individually.”]

Gaulinus subsequently also obtained the archbishopric of Bourges. [Note: Col. 0894D. In the year 1013; cf. Helgaud, *Life of Robert*, ch. 29.] In his time, namely in the year of Christ’s Incarnation 1026, the monastery of Fleury was burned; but through the exertions of the aforesaid Gaulinus, archbishop of Bourges, it was restored and rededicated within two years. Gaulinus also built there a tower of squared stones on the western side of the aforesaid church; but prevented by death, he could not complete it. He brought into the same church a substantial portion of the shroud of our Lord Jesus Christ and enclosed it in a golden right hand, [Col. 0893B] whose exterior he caused to be decorated with these verses:

> This hand bears happy joys,  
> shining, filled with Christ’s shroud.

He did many other things which it would take far too long to enumerate individually.

[Col. 0895A] King Robert also embellished his kingdom with great buildings and holy churches. He built in the city of Orléans the basilica of St Aignan [Note: Col. 0895D. Cf. Helgaud, *Life of Robert*, chs. 23–24.] and the church of St Mary, Mother of the Lord, between the wall and the ditch. He also built the chapel of St Hilary before his palace. In the forest of Iveline [Note: Col. 0895D: Iveline.] he built a church of St Leodegar, and one of St Medard at the castle of Vitry. He built the basilica of St Regulus in the city of Senlis, and the church of St Cassian near Autun. He also built two churches of St Mary, Mother of God: one at the castle of Étampes and the other at [Col. 0895B] Poissy. Finally, at Paris he built the church of St Nicholas in his palace.

[Note: Cols. 0895B–C. The *Historia Francorum*, continuing from the passage cited above, reads: “Among these he built at Orléans the monastery of St Aignan and the church of St Mary, Mother of God, as well as that of St Hilary before his palace [the source prints this first sentence in abbreviations: *Inter quas edificavit in u. A. monasterium s. A. et ec. s. M. m. D. necnon et sancti confessoris Hyl. a. p. s.*; the English supplies the full sense from the parallel text]. He also built a church for St Leodegar in the forest of Iveline [*Aquilina*; *aquilino*, MS Bern, an inflectional difference] and one for St Medard at the castle of Vitry. He also [*quoque* omitted in Ch.] built the monastery of St Regulus in the city of Senlis and a church of St Mary, Mother of God, at the castle of Étampes; near Autun he built the monastery of St Cassian. At Paris he built the church of St Nicholas in his palace [*e. s. N. in p. s.*, ‘the church of St Nicholas in his palace’], and likewise the church of St Mary at the castle of Poissy. Under the aforesaid ruler, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1014, the aforementioned church of St Martin at Tours was dedicated by Hugh, archbishop of Tours [Ch. reads *s. M. ecclesia*, repeating ‘the church of St Martin’]. At this time Fulk, count of Anjou, built a monastery in his territory in honour of the Holy Sepulchre [*Fulco c. A. ed. c. in t. s. in h. s. Sepulchri*, a printed abbreviation whose full sense is given here].”]

[Note: Cols. 0897B–C. The *Historia Francorum* continues: “King Henry, having gathered very strong forces from every side, first waged war against his mother Constance. Ch. gives the episode more fully: ‘But King Henry, since he was a most valiant knight, quickly defeated his mother when she rebelled against him and by his prudence brought the devices of the treacherous nobles to ruin. Indeed, the first of his engagements he fought with his mother Constance.’ Attacking the castle of Poissy, he soon brought it back under his own lordship; he then besieged and recovered Puteolum. Seeing this, Constance at once sought a pledge of peace from him, and thereafter remained faithful to him as long as she lived [the last sentence is printed as *Q. c. C. mox ab eo d. exp., et deinceps quo advixit tempore sibi fidelis extitit*: *Quod cernens Constantia mox ab eo dextram expetiit...*]. Then King Henry attacked Count Odo, took the castle of Gournay from him, and again brought part of the city of Sens under his authority [*Sen. urbis partem ad s. iterum d. revocavit*: ‘recalled part of the city of Sens to his own lordship again’]. Afterwards, with Baldwin, margrave of Flanders, he destroyed the castle of Hugh Bardulf called Merelis-villa [*Merelis villam*; *merisvillam*, Ch.; its location is unknown], and [*et* omitted in Ch.] brought the castle of Pithiviers, shut up under a two-year siege [*biennali*; *biennalli*, MS Bern, a spelling variant], into his power.”]

In his days Count Fulk of Anjou built a monastery in his territory in honour of the Holy Sepulchre. The same Count Fulk fought Count Odo of Chartres at Pontlevoy, [Note: Col. 0895D: Pont-Levoy. Cf. Fulk’s *History of Anjou*, Bouquet X, p. 204.] where there is now a church dedicated to St Mary, Mother of God. This Odo was the son of Count Theobald, born of the sister of Herbert, count of Troyes. This Odo begot another Odo by Bertha, daughter of King Conrad of Burgundy. Count Fulk likewise begot Geoffrey Tudites. This Geoffrey built in his territory the monastery of the Holy Trinity near the castle of Vendôme.

[Col. 0895C] In the year of the divine Incarnation 1026, Richard, son of the first Richard, setting out for Jerusalem, took with him [Col. 0895D] seven hundred pilgrims, to all of whom he adequately supplied provisions for the journey. [Note: Col. 0895D. This pilgrimage is fictitious; no other writer mentions it. BOUQ. CONT.] He also placed monks in the monastery of Fécamp and bestowed on them many estates for their daily use. When he departed this life [Note: Col. 0895: “descedens,” witness 1.] (year 996), he left his son Robert as [Col. 0896A] his successor.

[HUGO FLAV.] Moreover, at this time the peace called the Truce was established. It was also decreed that people should abstain from meat on Friday and Saturday.

King Robert, as he saw that old age was already weighing him down, made his son Hugh a partner in his kingdom (year 1017; cf. *Annals of Fleury*). But the aforesaid Hugh died in the sixth year of his reign (year 1025). King Robert himself died not long afterwards at Melun (year 1031) and was buried at Saint-Denis, [Note: Col. 0896D. Cf. Ralph Glaber III.9.] leaving his son Henry as successor.

[Note: Cols. 0898B–C. The *Historia Francorum* reads: “In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1037, the aforesaid ruler, count of Champagne, namely Odo [*memoratus*; *m. princeps C. c.*, Ch., ‘the aforesaid ruler, count of Champagne’], led an army against the Alamanni and Lotharingians with excessive pride, and gave them a great triumph over himself. For, when battle was joined with Gozelo, the very powerful [*prepotentissimo*; *pot.* = *potentissimo*, Ch., ‘most powerful’] duke of the Alamanni [Note within note, Col. 0898D: that is, the Germans], he lost a great multitude of his own men, turned his back, and fell pierced through. After his death, his elder son Theobald [Ch. omits *filius ejus*, ‘his son’] claimed for himself the cities of Chartres and Tours, while Theobald’s younger brother Stephen received the cities of Meaux and Troyes. But both began to rebel against King Henry [*Sed hi a. c. r. H. r. c.* = *Sed hi ambo contra regem Henricum rebellare coeperunt*]. The king, however, easily overcame and put to flight the aforementioned counts, Stephen and his brother—the printed initials *Rex autem p. c. St. c. i. facile sup. atque fugavit* are partly uncertain, but clearly name Stephen and the other count. He afterwards also defeated Galeran of Meulan, who was rebelling against the king [*c. R. r. Metlandicum ... Galerannum* = *contra regem rebellantem, Metlandicum ... Galerannum*], disinherited him [*exhereditavit*; *et exh.*, Ch., ‘and disinherited’], and subjected his land to himself. Finally he incited Geoffrey, count of Anjou [*Gaufredum A. c.*], against Count Theobald, and at his command Count Geoffrey surrounded the city of Tours with a siege [*Tur.* = *Turonicam*]. When Count Theobald heard this and hastened there to bring aid [*Quod a. T. c. s. v. eo tetendit* = *Quod audiens Tietbaldus comes, subvenire volens, eo tetendit*], Geoffrey advanced to meet him, fought bravely with him, overcame him, and captured him together with his followers, apparently many of his men [*c. s. et s. m.*; the exact inflection behind the initials is not securely recoverable, so no family members are supplied]; at the same time he wrested the city of Tours from him.”]

[Annals of Fleury, year 1013.] As King Robert’s death approached, rivers overflowed in various regions because of an inundation of rains; above all, the Loire exceeded its bounds, [Col. 0896B] entering villages, overturning houses, carrying off sheepfolds with their sheep, and killing some children of country people. [Note: Col. 0896D. Cf. also Aimoin, *Miracles of St Benedict* II.9.] A comet also appeared on the seventh day before the Ides of March for three days. In the following year hail in July shattered vineyards and trees. [Note: Col. 0895: “cuntrivit,” witness 1.] Consequently, there immediately followed for three years so severe a famine that people ate mice and dogs. [Note: Col. 0896D. Cf. Hugo of Flavigny, *SS.* VIII, p. 399.]

[Col. 0896C] **10. Henry.** [[Note: [Col. 0897A] *History of the Franks*, after the words no. [[ [Col. 0898B] *History of the Franks* thus: “Finally, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1037, the aforesaid [[Col. 0897] *m.* prince C. c. Ch.] count of Champagne, namely Odo, leading an army against the Alamanni and Lotharingians with excessive arrogance, afforded them a great triumph over himself. For, when battle had been joined with Gozelo, the exceedingly powerful [[Col. 0897] powerful Ch.] duke of the Alamanni [[Col. 0898D] That is, the Germans.], he lost a great multitude of his men, turned his back, and fell, pierced through. When he had died, Theobald, his elder son [[Col. 0897] omitted in Ch.], claimed for himself the city of Chartres and Tours; while his younger brother, Stephen by name, obtained the cities of Meaux and Troyes. But these, *a. c. r. H. r. c.* The king, however, *p. c. St. c. i.* easily overcame and put to flight; King Henry afterwards also defeated Galeran of Melun [[Col. 0897] *medandicum* Ch.], whom he disinherited [[Col. 0897] “and disinherited him” Ch.] and whose land he subjected to himself; finally he stirred up Geoffrey, count of Anjou, against Count Theobald; accordingly, at his prompting Count Geoffrey surrounded the city of Tours with a siege. When Theobald, Count of Tours, learned this, he hastened there; but Geoffrey, advancing to meet him, fought him manfully, overcame him, and captured him with seven hundred and sixty knights; and at the same time extorted from him the city of Tours.”]] continues as follows: “Henry therefore, after the death of his father Robert, reigned for nearly twenty-five years [[Col. 0897] thirty, Ch.]. H. m. C. had drawn the greater part of the kingdom into his own power: S., namely, U. and Sen., also the castles of B. and D. M., Puteaux and Melun, as well as P. and C. He had withdrawn many … from their allegiance by evil deceit. Among these he had especially bound to himself Odo, Count of Champagne, to whom he had given half the city of Sens.”]] Therefore, succeeding his father in the kingdom in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1032 [1031], he reigned twenty-seven years.

His mother Constance tried, after her husband’s funeral, to retain under her own lordship a great portion of the kingdom: namely, the cities of Senlis and Sens, and the castles of Béthisy [[Note: [Col. 0896D] *Betisy*.],

[Col. 0896D] Dammartin [[Note: [Col. 0896D] On the river Loiret; Bouquet, X, p. 606.], Puteaux, Melun, Poissy, and Coucy [[Note: [Col. 0896D] Poissy and Coucy.], and Coudicieux. She had also won over many magnates of Francia and Burgundy and detached them from allegiance to her son. This Henry [[Note: [Col. 0897B] *History of the Franks* thus: “King Henry therefore, having gathered very strong forces from every quarter, first undertook war against his mother Constance (yet King Henry, being a most valiant knight, quickly defeated by good fortune his mother, who rebelled against him, and by his prudence crushed the schemes of the treacherous magnates. For he began the first engagements with his mother Constance, Ch.), and, attacking the castle of Poissy, immediately … besieged and recovered it. Queen Constance was at once expelled from it by him, and thereafter, for as long as she lived, remained faithful to him. Then King Henry attacked Count Odo, took from him the castle of Gournay, and restored to his own lordship the part of the city of Sens. Afterwards, together with Baldwin, margrave of the Flemings, he destroyed the castle of Hugh Bardulf, the village of Merelis [[Col. 0897] *merisvillam* Ch.] [[Col. 0897D] Its location is unknown.], and [[Col. 0897] “and” omitted in Ch.] brought under his own power the castle of Pithiviers [[Col. 0897D] Pithiviers.], shut in by a two-year [[Col. 0897] *biennalli*, codex Bernensis.] siege.”]] would not endure; but, attacking Poissy, he immediately restored it to his own

[Col. 0897A] lordship. Finally he besieged and took Puteaux. When Constance saw this, she requested his right hand. After this the king attacked Count Odo and took from him [[Note: [Col. 0897] *abtulit* 1.] the castle of Gournay [[Note: [Col. 0897D] Gournay-sur-Marne.]. He also afterwards restored to his own lordship the part of the city of Sens which Queen Constance had given to Odo.

[Col. 0897C] **[HUGH OF FLAVIGNY.]** In the same period, that is, in the year of Christ’s Incarnation 1037, the aforesaid Count of Champagne, son of Odo, being nephew through a sister of Rudolf, king of Burgundy, and Rudolf having died without children, seized upon his dignity; entering the borders of Burgundy, he took possession of cities and castles as far as the Jura and Mount Joux, and besieged Vienne. The citizens surrendered it to him on the condition that, at an appointed time, he should be proclaimed and crowned king in that city.

Yet before this appointed time he launched an expedition into the kingdom of Lotharingia and took the castle of Bar; leaving five hundred knights there, he turned to other matters. Now King Rudolf of Burgundy had bequeathed his kingdom to the emperor together with the lance of

[Col. 0897D] Saint Maurice, which was the insignia of the Burgundian kingdom. When the emperor heard that Odo had invaded Burgundy, he sent against him Duke Gozelo of all Upper Rhaetia; Gozelo routed Odo’s army and killed Odo himself, torn by many wounds (1037). Nevertheless, his body was carried to Tours and buried. He was succeeded by two sons, Theobald

[Col. 0898A] and Stephen. Theobald received the cities of Chartres and Tours, while Stephen became count of Meaux and Troyes. But afterwards the two of them, having joined to themselves Count Rudolf of Vexin, a very warlike man, began to rebel against King Henry. The king first engaged Stephen, defeated him, and retained Count Rudolf by the fortune of war. Then he incited Geoffrey, Count of Anjou, against Theobald. With the king’s assent Geoffrey besieged the city of Tours. On hearing this, Theobald immediately arrived with his forces. Geoffrey engaged him, promptly defeated him, and captured him together with seven hundred and sixty knights. Geoffrey held him bound in fetters until he extorted from him the aforesaid

[Col. 0898B] city [[Note: [Col. 0897D] Compare Rodulfus Glaber, V.2.].

[Col. 0898C] Meanwhile the king defeated and disinherited Galeran of Melun [[Note: [Col. 0898D] He is called *Mellendensis* in William of Jumièges, V.10; that is, “of Melun.”]. At the same time Hugh Bardulf, a man of considerable courage and noble birth, fortified the castle of Pithiviers [[Note: [Col. 0898D] Pithiviers.] against King Henry. But after besieging it for two years, the king compelled it to surrender [[Note: [Col. 0897] *cunpulit* 1.], deprived the aforesaid Hugh of his honour, and drove him from the land.

**[HUGH OF FLAVIGNY.]** Moreover, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1035, Count Robert, heir and son of Richard, prince of the Normans,

[Col. 0898D] died at the city of Nicea [[Note: [Col. 0897] *miceam* or *nuceam* 1.] while returning from Jerusalem, leaving his son William as his successor. Disinherited by the Normans, William came to King Henry in Francia; he was kindly received by him, and subsequently was fortunate enough to be restored to his inheritance.

In the year [[Note: [Col. 0899A] The *History of the Franks* in Ch. has this: “Finally, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1047, the often-mentioned king … of the Normans, and defeated them, and by force set over them the venerable youth William, son of Robert, the great prince of the Normans, whom they wished to disinherit. This king, having pacified his kingdom, took as wife Anna, daughter of George, king of the Russians. In place of these words the Bern manuscript follows William of Jumièges, but continues no. [[ [Col. 0899B] *History of the Franks* thus: “By her he begot three sons, Philip, Robert, and Hugh, and a daughter Emma; of these Robert died as a boy” (“by her he begot three sons, Philip, Robert, Hugh,” Ch.). “But Hugh [[Col. 0899] ‘indeed,’ Ch.], when he became a young man, took as wife the daughter of Herbert, Count of Vermandois” (“Count of Vermandois, born of the daughter of Count Rudolf,” Ch.). [Col. 0899C] “Through her he obtained two counties, Vermandois and Valois; by her he begot Rudolf, who succeeded him in the kingdom.” (“Valois. Having begotten sons and daughters by her, fired by divine love he set out for Jerusalem with an army of Franks and Germans, and died on this journey,” Ch.)]] below.]] of the Lord’s Incarnation 1047, the aforesaid King Henry, with

[Col. 0899A] only three thousand armed men, fought [[Note: [Col. 0899] *cummisit* 1.] against thirty thousand Normans, defeated them, and by force set the aforementioned youth William over them [[Note: [Col. 0899D] Compare William of Jumièges, VII.17, and the *Historia Northmannorum* in Bouquet, XI, p. 148.].

**[HUGH OF FLAVIGNY.]** In the preceding period, that is, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1045, Emperor Henry married Agnes, daughter of William, Count of Poitou,

[Col. 0899B] at the city of Besançon. In the same period Pope Leo came into Gaul (1050) and consecrated the church of Saint Remigius at Rheims [[Note: [Col. 0899D] Compare William of Jumièges, VII.15.].

The king also took in marriage [[Note: [Col. 0899] *cunjugium* 1.] Anna, daughter of the king of the Russians. She bore him three sons: Philip, Hugh, and Robert. Robert died an untimely death. The same King Henry [[Note: [Col. 0899C] The *History of the Franks* has, after the words cited above in col. 898, note *: “Finally King Henry built a church near the walls of Paris in honour of Saint Martin,” and adds what is read above: “The aforesaid Count Geoffrey also built a monastery of the Holy Trinity at the castle of Vendôme.”]] accordingly built a church outside the walls of the city of Paris in honour of Saint Martin.

[Col. 0899C] At this time a certain Norman knight named Richard, indeed a vigorous and freeborn man, though not of high nobility, went with some knights of his people to Mount Gargano for prayer. But, after travelling through Apulia, he observed that

[Col. 0899D] the people of that land were sluggish and inactive [[Note: [Col. 0899] *animavertisset* 1.]; therefore he remained there and kept his companions with him (1016–1017). Afterwards he sent word to the men of his native country that, if they wished to become rich in wealth and honours, they should gather to him. They began to flock to him, ten and twenty at a time. Among them Robert, nephew of the aforesaid Richard, set out thither. He [[Note: [Col. 0899] “He … proceeded to London,” below in col. 901 (variant [[Col. 0901] *cump.* 1.]), written by a second hand in 1.]—

[Col. 0900A] when they had greatly increased in number and strength—subjugated by their own enterprise a great part of the province. But the aforesaid Robert, being a man of more acute intelligence, afterwards subjected Sicily and Calabria to himself by his ability. At the end of his life (1085), he left two sons, Roger and Bohemond. Of these Roger was a noble duke, while Bohemond filled almost the whole world with the fame of his prowess.

In the Roman see Benedict succeeded Pope Leo [[Note: [Col. 0899D] These events occurred before Leo’s time.], John succeeded Benedict, and Clement succeeded John (1046). The Romans rose against this Clement and drove him from his see. But when Emperor Henry heard this, he came to Rome and restored him to his seat. In that same

[Col. 0900B] year the aforesaid emperor departed this life (1056), and Henry the Third [[Note: [Col. 0899D] Emperor; the fourth as king.] succeeded him. Victor succeeded Pope Clement [[Note: [Col. 0900D] Victor succeeded Leo.], Stephen succeeded Victor, and Nicholas succeeded Stephen.

King [[Note: [Col. 0900C] *History of the Franks* thus: “Philip, still a boy, was raised to the kingship in this manner,” Ch.]] Henry, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1059, seeing that he was burdened by old age, had his son Philip consecrated on Pentecost Day before the altar of Blessed Mary by Gervase, then archbishop of Rheims, in the presence of very many archbishops and bishops of Francia, Burgundy, and Aquitaine, twenty-two in all. Hugh, archbishop of Besançon and legate of Pope Nicholas, was also present. Very many abbots and the leading men of the kingdom were present: Guy, duke of Aquitaine; Hugh, son of Robert, duke of Burgundy; and many others. Not long afterwards, when his father had died, the boy was placed under the guardianship of Baldwin, Count of Flanders, who, etc., no. [[ [Col. 0900D] *History of the Franks* thus: “(He placed his son Philip under the guardianship of Baldwin, Count of Flanders), who nobly and faithfully brought him up and vigorously governed and [[Col. 0899] ‘and,’ Ch.] defended his kingdom.”]] Ch.]] King Henry, however, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1058 [[Note: [Col. 0900D] 1059. See the acts of the coronation, Bouquet, XI, p. 32.], had his twelve-year-old son Philip [[Note: [Col. 0900D] Correct: seven-year-old. BOUQUET, CONTINUATOR.] consecrated at Rheims on Pentecost Day by

[Col. 0900C] Gervase, archbishop [[Note: [Col. 0899] omitted in 1.], in the presence of twenty-two archbishops and bishops of Francia, Burgundy, and Aquitaine, and many abbots. Also present were two legates of Pope Nicholas: Hugh, archbishop of Besançon, and Hermenfrid, bishop of Sion. In the following year (1060) the oft-mentioned King Henry died and was buried at Saint-Denis, leaving his son King Philip, not yet grown up, under the guardianship of Baldwin, Count of Flanders, a man most faithful and honourable to him.

[Col. 0900D] **11. Philip** therefore attained the kingdom of the Franks in the year of the divine Incarnation 1059, and reigned nearly forty years. His mother Anna, Henry’s widow,

[Col. 0901A] married Count Rudolf [[Note: [Col. 0901D] Of Valois and Crépy.], a noble and high-born man.

While King Philip was not yet an adult, certain magnates of Francia entered Spain, stormed and took the city of Barbastro [[Note: [Col. 0901D] On this matter see the *History of the Franks* published by Chesne, IV, p. 88, which, as I said above (col. 813), is connected with Hugh by a certain affinity.]. At this same time, that is, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1065 [1066], a comet appeared for the space of three months; and in the same year William, Count of the Normans, declared war on the English. For Edward, king of the English [[Note: [Col. 0901] *euardus* 1.], having no son, had adopted the aforesaid William and left him his kingdom [[cf. HUGH OF FLAVIGNY.]. Upon Edward’s death a certain English count, Harold, had seized it for himself. Therefore William gathered a large army and sailed thither with seven hundred ships [in

[Col. 0901B] 1066]. When Harold heard that William had entered England, he met him with a great army. Battle was joined, and the fighting was fierce on both sides; but at last Harold was defeated and killed. In that battle William had one hundred and fifty thousand men in his battle-line. Immediately after the war William proceeded to London [[Note: [Col. 0901] *nundoniam* 1.], where he was received and crowned on Christmas Day.

In this same year (1067), the magnates of Tours and Anjou made war upon their lord Geoffrey and, on the Thursday preceding Good Friday [[Note: [Col. 0901D] The *Annals of Anjou*, Bouquet XI, p. 30, give Wednesday, the day before the Nones of April, and say that vengeance followed on the next day. Compare also Fulk’s account, ibid., p. 138.], seized him within the city of Angers and consigned him to imprisonment. The leaders of this wickedness and treachery were Geoffrey’s brother

[Col. 0901C] Fulk; Geoffrey of Preuilly; Robert the Burgundian; Adelard Ticio; also Rainald of the castle of Gontier; and Gerard, son of Belrai [[Note: [Col. 0901D] Gerard of Montreuil is named in the cited passage.]. Divine vengeance fell upon them on that very day. For the people of the same city, in a single conspiracy [[Note: [Col. 0901] *cunsp.* 1.], at about the ninth hour, killed Geoffrey of Preuilly. Rainald of the castle of Gontier and Gerard, son of Belrai, were likewise killed on that same day; Adelard Ticio was burned by fire; and Robert was cut to pieces [[Note: [Col. 0901D] Robert the Burgundian, son of Rainald I, Count of Nevers and Auxerre, survived by more than thirty years the battle in which Count Geoffrey was taken captive; still less was he cut to pieces on that very day. BOUQUET, CONTINUATOR.]. But Count Fulk, who had seized his brother’s dignity for himself, fearing that King Philip would fall upon him for his perpetrated

[Col. 0902A] wickedness and deprive him of his dignity, surrendered to him the county of Gâtinais [[Note: [Col. 0901D] Le Gâtinais.]. Geoffrey and Fulk were nephews of Geoffrey Martel. Their father Aubry, Count of Gâtinais, had been Martel’s son-in-law. Martel himself died without children.

At the same period (1067), Count Baldwin of Flanders died, leaving his son Baldwin as his successor. But the younger Baldwin survived his father only a few years (1070), and was succeeded by his uncle Robert [[Note: [Col. 0901D] Robert, brother of the younger Baldwin, was uncle and successor of Arnulf, whom Hugh omits. BOUQUET, CONTINUATOR. The *History of the Franks* carried down to 1110 [Col. 0902D] (see note 149) relates it thus (Duchesne IV, p. 88): “Baldwin himself died not long afterwards, leaving as his successor a son of the same name, Baldwin, who also survived only a few years. He too left an heir named Arnulf. His uncle Robert, hostile to him, tried to disinherit him, and did so. Arnulf appealed to King Philip and requested his help. The king gathered many thousands of armed men and advanced into Flanders to engage Robert. Robert, mistrusting his strength, at first feared to meet the king. At last, taking courage, he routed the royal army and compelled the king, frustrated of his aim, to return to Francia. In this battle Arnulf, Robert’s nephew, who had invited the king to aid him, fell with many other nobles. Robert obtained the inheritance of his brother Baldwin.”]].

Not long afterwards Count Rudolf of Valois died (1074), and his son Simon succeeded him. Simon himself survived his father only a few days, during which, nevertheless,

[Col. 0902B] he served the world quite vigorously. At last, divinely inspired, he abandoned the pomp of the world in the very flower of youth for the love of God, went into exile, and made his way to Rome (1082). There he passed to God and received honourable burial in the portico of Saint Peter’s. At that same time (1066), a young man named Theobald, distinguished by birth, from the district of Sens, from the castle of Provins, sought the wilderness, where he lived for nearly seven years. When these were completed, he died [“and the Spirit of God rested upon him” [[Note: [Col. 0901] “and the Spirit of God rested upon him” deleted in 1, after two words had been erased after *quem* and one after *locis*.]]]; in certain places God often deigns to glorify him by great miracles.

At this time again, the Saracens, led by a certain king named Juffet [[Note: [Col. 0901] *viffeto* 1?], crossed the sea and occupied the land of King Alfonso of Galicia and Asturias

[Col. 0902C] [[Note: [Col. 0901] *asturciae* 1?]. Alfonso fought a battle against them [[Note: [Col. 0901] *cunmisit* 1.], but was defeated. Knowing that all the Gauls could quickly be summoned to war, he sent into Gaul and told the magnates of the kingdom that unless they brought him aid, he would make an alliance with the Saracens [[Note: [Col. 0901] *cump.* 1.] and abandon Christianity. On hearing this, the Franks eagerly prepared themselves and went there. But when the Saracens heard of their arrival, struck with terror, they returned whence they had come. The Franks, after ranging through Spain, returned to their own country.

[Col. 0903A] Meanwhile William, king of the English, built the monastery of Caen in his territory, endowing it with many possessions (1066). Guy, Count of Poitou, also founded and built in the aforesaid city a monastery in honour of Saint John. At the same time a monk named Gerard built, beside the Loire in the district of Auxerre, a monastery of Saint Mary, Mother of God, called La Charité. Another monk, Gerard by name, a most holy man, built another monastery of Saint Mary, Mother of God, between the Dordogne and the Garonne in the district of Bordeaux, called La Sauve-Majeure. William, abbot of Fleury, also began to build anew, upon a newly laid

[Col. 0903B] foundation, the church over which he presided, devastated by many fires and weighed down by age [[Note: [Col. 0903] *pergrav.* 1?]; but death overtook him before he could complete it.

Accordingly [[Note: [Col. 0903C] *History of the Franks* thus: “Philip, son of Henry, king of the Franks (‘The king,’ Ch.), after reaching young manhood, received his kingdom whole; and, after the death of his guardian Count Baldwin [[Col. 0903] *suo* added in codex Bernensis.], by the counsel of Robert the Frisian took as wife Bertha, daughter of Florent, duke of the Frisians. By her he begot Louis and a daughter named Constance, and [[Col. 0903] *a. H.* omitted in Ch.] Henry.” When she had reached marriageable age, she married Hugh, Count of Troyes; later, [Col. 0905D] separated from him on account of consanguinity, she married Bohemond,

[Col. 0904A] prince of Bari, a high-spirited and vigorous man.]], King Philip, now strong in youth, took as wife the daughter of the duke of Frisia. She bore him Lord Louis, king at the present time, and his sister, named Bertha. Now in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1041 [[Note: [Col. 0903D] Read 1061.], Alexander succeeded Pope Nicholas. Around these days (about 1089), Count Theobald died, and his two sons Stephen and Hugh succeeded him. Stephen became count of Blois, Chartres, and Meaux, and Hugh count of Troyes. King William of the English (d. 1087) was also succeeded by three sons, born of Matilda, sister of Baldwin, Count of Flanders: Robert, William, and Henry; and by their sister Adela. Of these,

[Col. 0903C] Robert, whom he had begotten while still a private man, became Count of the Normans; William, whom he had begotten as king, received his kingdom. Their sister Adela received as husband Stephen, Count of Chartres, Blois, and Meaux.

[Col. 0904A] Finally, in the year of the divine Incarnation 1074 [1073], Pope Alexander [[Note: [Col. 0903D] More correctly these matters are related in the *History of the Franks* carried down to the year 1110 (above, no. 149) (Duchesne IV, p. 89): “When Pope Alexander died, Hildebrand succeeded in his place, and he was also Gregory. Having convened a great synod at Rome, he accused Emperor Henry of certain crimes reported to him. Hearing himself accused, the emperor offered canonical purgation. But the pope said that he would not accept his purgation, and that, since he was unworthy of the empire, he must be struck with anathema unless he laid aside the crown of the empire. When he refused to lay aside the empire, the pope excommunicated him against the will [not a will properly so called, but the desire of the considerably larger party, ED. PATR.] of almost the whole council. This affair threw the whole condition of the Church into confusion. The same pope also demanded that he relinquish control of all the churches of his empire, so that he might grant the pastoral staff to no one, as is contained in the statutes of the ancient Fathers. He refused to do this. This was the more just cause of this anathema. Thus, when the emperor had been deprived of communion with the Church, Pope Gregory appointed a certain Rudolf, a Saxon by birth, to reign in his place. He was killed by the dukes of that same emperor, who had challenged him to war. After this the emperor sent legates to the pope and again and again offered satisfaction concerning the accusations against him. But the pope, persisting in his judgment, advanced upon Rome with a great force of armed men and besieged it for some time. When it had at last been taken, he appointed Guibert, bishop of Ravenna, pope in Gregory’s place; after changing his name, he was called Clement. Gregory fled to Apulia, where he lived as long as he survived. When he died, he was buried at Salerno in the monastery of Saint Matthew. In his place Desiderius, abbot of Monte Cassino, was ordained, and was called Victor by another name. When he died, Odo, also called Urban, of Frankish stock, succeeded him.”]] died, and Hildebrand, archdeacon of the Roman Church, succeeded him; he is also called Gregory VII. He was consecrated without the emperor’s consent and authorization. The emperor took this ill. The newly consecrated pope held a council (1074), in which, among other decrees, he promulgated the following decision (Hugh of Flavigny, VIII, 412): “If any bishop or abbot has received a bishopric or abbey from the hand of any lay person, let him by no means be received among bishops or abbots, nor let any hearing be granted him, unless he has relinquished the dignity which he unlawfully

[Col. 0904B] presumed to assume.”

The emperor regarded this decree as issued against himself. Meanwhile the Saxons, having formed a conspiracy against the emperor (1077), made a certain duke named Rudolf king. He immediately sent to the pope, promising faithfully to observe all submission to him if the pope would grant him his favour. The pope gladly embraced his promise. Subsequently, after holding another council (1080), he excommunicated Emperor Henry and all his supporters, interdicted to him, on God’s behalf and his own, the kingdom of Italy and the Germans, and forbade any Christian to obey him as king. He also prayed that neither Henry himself nor his supporters should obtain any strength or victory in any military engagement.

[Col. 0904C] To Rudolf, however, on God’s behalf and his own, he granted leave to rule the kingdom; he remitted all his sins, both to him and to all who faithfully adhered to him; and bestowed his blessing. Yet the emperor, not long afterwards, met Rudolf in battle and killed him (1080). Finally, raging fiercely, he came to Rome in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1084, took it, overthrew its walls, shut the pope up in the Tower of Crescentius, ordered the archbishop of Ravenna to be consecrated, installed him in the church of Saint Peter, and had him called Clement. Gregory, shut up in the Tower of Crescentius, sent a legate to Robert, duke of Apulia, asking him to come and raise the siege.

[Col. 0904D] [[Note: [Col. 0903] *absidicionem* 1.] When the emperor learned this, he withdrew from

[Col. 0905A] the City with the aforesaid Pope Clement. After his departure Robert arrived and brought Pope Gregory with him as far as Salerno, where Gregory lived until he passed from this life (1085). When he died there at Salerno, the clergy and people adhering to him appointed Desiderius, abbot of Monte Cassino, pope in his place and named him Victor. He died not long afterwards (1088), while Clement was still alive; Odo, bishop of Ostia, succeeded him and was called Urban.

At this same time, namely in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1087, certain men of Bari sailed from Italy to Antioch for trade. As they were proceeding there [[Note: [Col. 0905] *tenderet* 1.], they put in at the city of Myra with three ships. Finding it

[Col. 0905B] deserted by worshippers of Christ—for the Turks had devastated it—they grieved deeply. Then, divinely inspired, they broke open the tomb of Saint Nicholas (1087), took his most holy bones from it, and carried them to their own city. There they afterwards built a new church and deposited that venerable treasure in it.

Moreover, in the year of the divine Incarnation 1100, William, king of the English, son and successor of the great King William, while hunting in the forest adjoining the city of Winchester, was struck by an arrow shot by a certain knight and died. The knight who shot the arrow struck him unknowingly. He had been preparing to shoot a stag; but the arrow, deflected backwards, unexpectedly struck the king and killed him without warning. There can be no doubt that this happened by divine will.

[Col. 0905C] For that king was indeed vigorous in arms and generous, but excessively wanton and wicked. Yet before he died, he ought, if he had been willing, to have reformed himself in response to the great signs shown to him. For when sudden death, demanded by his sins, was threatening him, a foul wave of blood flowed for the space of one day in the very island where he lived, while he was present; this was said to portend his death. Other wondrous signs also appeared in that same island at the time; as has already been said, they ought to have frightened him and led him to reform his life. But, foolish in his youth and proud in his honour, he despised them and remained always incorrigible. Therefore, by God’s just judgment, he fell, overtaken by a sudden and untimely death [[Note: [Col. 0905] *ocubuit* 1.]. His younger brother

[Col. 0905D] Henry, a wise and moderate man, succeeded him.

Nevertheless, in the preceding period, namely in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1098, when the moon was in its twenty-fifth day, stars were seen to fall from heaven on the day before the Nones of April, from midnight until dawn.  
[Note: [Col. 0906D] Cf. Baldric of Dol, *History of Jerusalem*, in Bongars, p. 88 (*Patrologia*, vol. CLXVI).] On that same [Col. 0906A] night Giraldus, abbot of Moutier-la-Celle (*Silva Major*), passed to the Lord.  
[Note: [Col. 0906D] Cf. *Chronicle of Saint-Maxentius of Mallezais*, Bouquet XII, p. 403.]

In the same year (1095), Pope Urban came into Gaul and held a great council at Clermont in the month of November. For the Eastern Empire was grievously harassed by the Turks and the Pechenegs; and Lesser and Greater Cappadocia, Greater and Lesser Phrygia, Bithynia together with Asia, Galatia also and Libya  
[Note: [Col. 0905] Perhaps: Lydia.]  
and Pamphylia, Isauria and Lycia, and the principal islands of those regions, namely Chios and Mytilene, were held by them as captured territory. Every day there occurred various massacres of Christians and insults against Christ the Lord and against our religion.

Therefore at the aforesaid council the pope exhorted the people of Gaul, whom he knew to be most warlike, manfully to aid their oppressed brethren, [Col. 0906B] lest in their time Christianity should utterly perish in the regions of the East. He declared that all who, marked with the Lord’s cross, set out for the Holy Sepulchre in order to carry out this undertaking would attain a glorious and ineffable reward in heaven. He also urged them to hasten there before the barbarians should make Constantinople subject to themselves. There are in that city the statue at which Christ was bound and scourged; the scarlet cloak in which he was dressed; the crown of thorns with which he was crowned; the scourge with which he was scourged; the reed which he held in place of a sceptre; the garments of which he was stripped before being crucified; a portion of the cross upon which he hung fastened; the nails with which he was affixed; and likewise other [Col. 0906C] holy relics. Their loss would bring great harm upon all Christians.

Finally, all the bishops present there testified that all those who defended Christianity from its pressing storm would be joined to the fellowship of the holy martyrs, and would without doubt gain glorious fame forever in this world and an ineffable reward in heaven. They likewise urged all, equipped with arms, to bring aid with all their strength and compassion to their Christian brethren placed in danger.

Thus, not long afterward, one could see an immense multitude of people from every part of the West proceeding thither in companies by voluntary vow: an army, namely, of horsemen and foot-soldiers with various missiles and weapons. Neither childish imprudence, nor [Col. 0906D] the weakness of old age, nor the frailty of their sex kept women at home; rather, all, inspired by God and compelled by the power of no king or prince, eagerly hastened to accomplish so laborious an undertaking. Women went with the men, and even little children.

Among all these, however, the following are known to have been more powerful and more celebrated in renown: [Col. 0907A]  
[Note: [Col. 0907D] Cf. Baldric, cited work, p. 89.]  
Adhemar, bishop of Le Puy; Raymond, count of Saint-Gilles; Hugh, brother of King Philip; Robert, count of the Normans; another Robert, count of the Flemings; his brother Godfrey of Boulogne; Stephen, count of Chartres; Baldwin, brother of Roger, duke of Apulia; Bohemond; and his cousin Tancred; and a certain Peter the Hermit, who led a great army of infantry. But with them were many other nobles from different regions, whose names it is not necessary to list individually now.  
[Note: [Col. 0907] Thus manuscript 1.]

When all these had assembled at Constantinople, the emperor received them and honoured them with great wealth, so that none of them lacked a share in his gifts. Then, having departed from there, [Col. 0907B] after many hardships they reached Antioch (in the year 1098) and besieged it for eight months. When these had elapsed, after many men had been killed on both sides in daily encounters, they entered it with God’s help. For a certain Turk, who appeared to be guarding the city gate, handed it over to them, secretly admitting before daybreak Count Baldwin  
[Note: [Col. 0907D] He was not present at this siege; cf. Sybel, p. 378. In other respects the author seems to follow *Gesta* IV.20; cf. [Col. 0908D] preface.]  
and Bohemond with a numerous force. Seeing this, the citizens, struck by fear, immediately fled to the citadel.

An admiral named Cassianus was in command of the city.  
[Note: [Col. 0908D] Bagi Sian is meant.]  
He at once sent to the sultan of Persia to ask for assistance. The Christians, having gained possession of the city, cut down a great multitude of the profane nation. But those who had entered the citadel constructed a new wall around [Col. 0907C] themselves and defended themselves within it with great strength.

[*Gesta* IV.21. Cf. Baldric.] The sultan of Persia, hearing that the Christians had taken Antioch, gathered a large army under one named Curbaram.  
[Note: [Col. 0908D] Kerbogha.]  
In it were the admiral of Jerusalem, the king of Damascus, Turks, Arabs, Saracens, many Publicani and Agulani. (Chs. 23–33.) And behold, the third day had already dawned since the Christians had entered the city, when that army of the faithless appeared there. Our men went out from the city, arrayed and armed, and took care to meet them. A great battle was therefore joined at the very entrance to the city and continued until evening; many mortals were slain on both sides.

But when night came, our men withdrew within [Col. 0907D] the walls, and the enemies pitched their tents not far away. Yet that night some of our men, terrified by the danger hemming them in within and without, shamefully lowered themselves over the wall and chose flight rather than entrust the hope of their salvation to God. Those who remained were harshly pressed for thirty days, while those stationed in the citadel violently attacked them from above, and those outside prevented them by every means from going forth to forage. [Col. 0908A] Thus provisions began to fail them, and wretched hunger seized them. One egg was sold for fifteen denarii, one hen for fifteen solidi, one cheese for four pounds of denarii, a small quantity of bread for one bezant, and one nut for one denarius. Some ate fig leaves and thistles as the greatest delicacies; some fed upon the flesh of horses, asses, and camels; others boiled and ate animal hides.

And when they had thus suffered for thirty days, one day at the very break of day, fortified by the divine sacraments, all unanimously burst forth and formed six battle-lines against the enemy. In the first line was Hugh the Great with the Franks who were present; in the second Duke Godfrey with the men of his own land; in the third Robert [Col. 0908B] the Norman with the Normans; in the fourth the bishop of Le Puy with the Aquitanians; in the fifth Tancred with the Lombards and men of Italy; and in the sixth Bohemond stood apart with a numerous host, so that, if he should see the Christians being hard pressed by the enemy, he might immediately join them and bring aid.  
[Note: [Col. 0907] *ammiculum* in manuscript 1.]  
For among the other leaders he seemed a man of singular shrewdness.

Raymond, count of Saint-Gilles, a distinguished man, remained inside with some others to guard the Christian tents, lest the Turks should descend from the citadel  
[Note: [Col. 0907] *munione* in manuscript 1.]  
and seize or burn them. Curbaram also divided his entire army into two divisions. Then, when the signal had been raised, the ordered battle-lines fought, and very many were killed on either side; but at last [Col. 0908C] Curbaram, terrified by God’s power, fled. Seeing this, our men pursued them vigorously with a great cry raised to heaven. Then those who were guarding the tents  
[Note: [Col. 0907] “*custodiebant*—there a new page begins, written by a second hand” in manuscript 1.]  
all in emulation gave themselves to flight, leaving their tents behind.

As our men pursued them, they struck down as many enemies as their strength sufficed to pursue that day and as many as their hands could kill. So great was the slaughter of those barbarians that scarcely a few remained from so great an army. Many who were present testified that they saw a great army coming forth from the mountains, preceded by the holy martyrs George, Demetrius, and Mercurius, with white horses and carrying white banners; together with the Christians they pressed hard upon the army of the barbarians. [Col. 0908D]

Thus, when innumerable enemies had unexpectedly been put to flight and slain, the Christian people turned to plundering the tents. There much gold and [Note: [Col. 0907] Omitted in manuscript 1.] silver were found, and great abundance of wine, grain, and flour. There was also found there a vast number of horses, mules, asses, camels, oxen, and sheep. Gathering these things, the whole people, joyful and beloved of God, made eagerly for the city.

Then those who were in the fortress, seeing this, [Col. 0909A] immediately surrendered themselves to the leaders, having obtained life and leave to depart. A few days later, after recovering their strength, the leaders began jointly to deliberate to which of their number they should entrust the city while they completed the journey to the Holy Sepulchre. At length it was entrusted to Bohemond for safekeeping, with the assent of the whole people and the counsel of the wise nobles. Meanwhile the bishop of Le Puy died and was reverently buried there. This battle took place in the year of the divine Incarnation 1098.

On the night before the battle, a great burning light appeared in the northern part of the sky, from the first watch of the night until daylight, foretelling the shedding of human blood which was to occur on the next day. Antioch was therefore taken and retained by the people of God with such ease [Col. 0909B] as no mortal emperor could have taken it, unless the Lord had willed it. For it is spacious  
[Note: [Col. 0909] Thus manuscript 1.]  
and strong, and enclosed by two very strong walls. It is also the head of all Syria and contains sixty monasteries; moreover, the archbishop of that city has precedence over 156 bishops. It is enclosed  
[Note: [Col. 0909] “*Clauditur*—*detruncabant pecudum*, written by a second hand in more than one ink” in manuscript 1.]  
on the east by four great mountains, and on the west is bounded by the Farfar.

But while Christ’s soldiers waited there for a suitable time in which to complete fittingly the journey to the Holy Sepulchre, a certain knight named Raymond Pilet, having gathered companions to himself, severely ravaged the surrounding province. Count Saint-Gilles likewise attacked and captured the very strongly fortified cities of Abaram and Marra. Godfrey of Boulogne also retained for himself [Col. 0909C] Rohes and certain castles lying round about it.

When winter was at last withdrawing  
[Note: [Col. 0909] Corrected thus in manuscript 1; the same scribe had first written “of winter indeed and of spring.”]  
and spring returning (in the year 1099), the whole army beloved of God assembled at Antioch and took counsel to complete the journey it had begun. [*Gesta*, chs. 35–39.] Then they advanced and hastened to accomplish the journey they had undertaken. Having captured many cities on the way, they finally enclosed Jerusalem in a siege.

It was besieged on the eighth day before the Ides of June; Robert, count of Normandy, besieged it on the northern side of the city, beside the church of the blessed protomartyr Stephen. After him the other Robert, count of Flanders, pitched his tents. Duke Godfrey and Tancred besieged it from the west; from the south, where the mountain rises above it, Count Saint-Gilles did so. It was [Col. 0909D] firmly besieged for an interval of six weeks. During these weeks they destroyed the first wall, for it was enclosed by a double wall.

When the six weeks had passed, on Friday of the seventh week (15 July), at the sixth hour, the Christian army, divinely inspired, applied ladders to the inner wall. The first to leap into it were those stationed with Duke Godfrey and his brother Eustace. [Col. 0910A] When the citizens saw this and were unable to resist them, stupefied, they began to flee in every direction. The Christians cut them down like cattle, while others broke down the gates. Thus, once the entrance had been opened, the rest of the multitude of the faithful entered.

Then the citizens, filled and troubled with greater terror, made for Solomon’s Temple. The Christians pursued them, striking and killing. Blood flowed everywhere,  
[Note: [Col. 0909] “*ubique*—*Raimundo*, written by a second hand” in manuscript 1.]  
but especially around the Temple, so that Christ’s soldiers stood in it up to their ankles. Seeing this, the admiral of the city, who was in the Tower of David, surrendered to Count Raymond. The count led both him and those with him unharmed as far as Ascalon. In the very Temple of the Lord, Christ’s soldiers found a great abundance of gold, silver, and precious stones. [Col. 0910B] [Baldric.] A great and inestimable treasure was also found by them in the city’s houses.

Having achieved so splendid a triumph by divine power, they all went away rejoicing and weeping for excessive joy to the sepulchre of Jesus Christ, our Saviour, and offered there the gifts of their devotion. On the following day they gathered together the corpses of the slain. Their heap appeared so great that it seemed equal to the height of the walls. They burned them after setting fire beneath them, lest their stench corrupt the air and cause them trouble.

Thus that army of Christians, beloved of God, enjoyed in all this expedition an inestimable success.  
[Note: [Col. 0909] “*est*—*funditus extirpare*, written by a second hand” in manuscript 1.]  
For it encountered no hostile host which it did not overcome; [Col. 0910C] besieged no city which it did not capture; attacked no nation which it did not trample down.  
[Note: [Col. 0909] Thus manuscript 1; perhaps: “which it did not trample down?”]  
Hence it gained great glory for itself by its merits. For no king or emperor invaded his enemies through so great an expanse of land, or fought so successfully against such numerous peoples. Who could have provided ships, horses, weapons, and supplies for so many thousands of men?

It is therefore evident—plainly evident—that God alone willed to accomplish this triumph through the hand of the Christian people, so that their fame might spread farther and increase.  
[Note: [Col. 0909D] Cf. Baldric: “For they did not ascribe this victory to their own strength, but attributed the whole thing to God, who wrought in them [Col. 0910D] both willing and being able.”]  
Indeed, by his own power he could, if he wished, have overthrown all those nations or plunged them into hell in one moment of time, or utterly extirpated them through his angels. [*Gesta*, ch. 39.]

But Christ’s soldiers, having obtained royal power, [Col. 0910D] left there Godfrey, a valiant and honourable man, adorned with the royal diadem, that he might conquer the neighbouring enemies and assist Christians remaining round about in their necessities. They also consecrated there as patriarch a certain Arnulf, a cleric sufficiently capable and kindly.

Jerusalem is a royal city, [situated among mountains, having the Tower of David to the west, the Temple on the [Col. 0911A] eastern side, and Mount Calvary to the south.  
[Note: [Col. 0911] “Among mountains—Calvary” supplied in the margin in manuscript 1.]] It is, as it were, the navel of the whole world; it abounds sufficiently in inland resources and is not deprived of maritime ones. It also contains within itself the most holy sepulchre of our Lord and Saviour, to be revered by all Christians. In it too the holy Church once sprang up, and our Lord Jesus Christ consecrated it with his own blood. We have touched upon these matters only briefly, since we have learned that the full history of them has already been written elsewhere.

Still in the time of King Philip, namely in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1102,  
[Note: [Col. 0911C] Read: 1100.]  
Godfrey, king of the Jerusalemites, died, and his brother Baldwin succeeded him. Emperor Henry also died in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1106.

[Col. 0911B] In the year [  
[Note: [Col. 0911B] Thus the *History of the Franks* ends: “The aforesaid King Philip died in the year from the Lord’s Incarnation 1108 [ [Col. 0911] 1109, Ch.], on the day before the Kalends of August, at the castle of Melun. In accordance with his father’s directions, Louis had his body carried [Col. 0912A] to the monastery of Fleury and committed to burial in the monastery of Saint Benedict. This having been done, the bishops who had assembled for the king’s funeral gathered at Orléans immediately after the obsequies. Because of the disturbers of the realm, by sound counsel they anointed as king the young Louis, a lover of religion, gentle in character, valiant in arms, and most fierce in war, on the feast of the Finding of the protomartyr Stephen, before the altar of the Holy Cross; and they placed the crown of the kingdom upon his head: Daimbert, archbishop of Sens; Ivo [ [Col. 0911] Hivo, Ch.] bishop of Chartres; John, bishop of Orléans; and Hubert, bishop of Senlis. They were moved by the many examples of other kings who, because of impending disorders, were consecrated in different places by different bishops.”]]  
of the Lord’s Incarnation 1108, King Philip of the Franks, a gentle  
[Note: [Col. 0911] *mittis* in manuscript 1.]  
and wise man, died at Melun,  
[Note: [Col. 0911] *miduni* in manuscript 1.]  
on the third day before the Nones  
[Note: [Col. 0911C] Read: before the Kalends; Bouquet, continuation.]  
of August, in the fifty-third year of his life  
[Note: [Col. 0912C] Correct to fifty-six; Bouquet, continuation.]  
and the forty-first of his reign. He was buried at the abbey of Fleury, in the church of Saint Mary, Mother of God, and likewise Saint Benedict. His son Louis, a king and most valiant knight, succeeded him. In the same year Alfonso, king of Spain, a warlike and wise man, died.

[Col. 0912A] I have written these deeds of recent kings, for those wishing to know them, in bare and simple words, enclosing many memorable matters in a small book. Yet in this history I omit much that I know, and much that is found nowhere among Latin writers. Hence this book seems to contain less than it should. Nevertheless, from it one may learn the sequence of times and many other matters most worthy of knowledge. But I know that all these things will be despised by those among whom the civic discipline of letters is a stranger, whose companion to buffoonery is negligence or idleness, and likewise by those who despise abridgments and whom lengthy works commonly weary.

Nevertheless, all these things may benefit those for whom it is most pleasing to know very much.

Here ends the *New History of the Franks*.  
[Note: [Col. 0911] Another hand added in dark ink: “In the year 1125 the Emperor Henry the Younger died. In the same year Lothar began to reign.” Again another hand: “In 1137 Emperor Lothar died. In the year 1138 Conrad succeeded.”]

[Col. 0911]

# HISTORY OF THE KINGS OF THE FRANKS OF THE MONASTERY OF SAINT-DENIS

[Col. 0911C] **1.**  
[Note: [Col. 0911] Rubric prefixed to 1: “Concerning those who fled from the destruction of Troy and built the city of Sicambria in Pannonia, from whom the Franks are said to derive their name.”]  
[*Gesta Francorum*, ch. 1.] Antenor and other refugees from the destruction of Troy, after wandering through Asia—after a king of the Phrygians had been made and had remained among the Macedonians with his followers—crossed the Maeotian marshes and built a city called Sicambria in the region of Pannonia. [H., epitome, chs. 1–3.] After Antenor’s death they appointed two men, Torgotus and Francio, from whom, as some think, the Franks received their name. When these died, they chose as leaders Sumnon, Genebald, and Marcomir. His son Pharamund was the first among them to reign in royal fashion.

[*Gesta Francorum*, chs. 4–9.] This Pharamund reigned about eleven years and died; his son Clodio reigned in his place for twenty years and died a natural death. Meroveus, of his line, succeeded him in the kingdom. From this useful King Meroveus, [Col. 0912C]  
[Note: [Col. 0911] *itali* in manuscript 2.]  
the Frankish kings were called Merovingians. In his time the nation of the Vandals, laying waste Germany and Gaul, destroyed many cities and shed much Christian blood. Meroveus reigned seventeen years and died.

His son Childeric succeeded him in the kingdom. But later, because of the enormity of his lustfulness, he was expelled from the kingdom by the Franks, and, seeking Thuringia, lived for some time with King Bisinus. Afterwards the Franks, moved by repentance, recalled him and restored him to the kingdom, having expelled the Roman whom they had set over themselves. Bisinus’s queen, named Basina, followed him, leaving her own husband, mentioned above; joined to Childeric in marriage, she bore him a son named Clovis.
