Childeric himself reigned [Col. 0913A] twenty years and died; and his son Clovis reigned after him. He was a king mighty beyond all preceding kings of the Franks. After taking up the government of the Frankish kingdom upon the death of his father Childeric, he defeated and killed Syagrius, son of Aegidius, at Soissons.

**2.**  
[Note: [Col. 0913] Rubric added by manuscript 1: “How King Clovis was baptized by the counsel of his wife, and concerning his death.”]  
[*Gesta Francorum*, chs. 11, 12, 15–19.] After this he took in marriage Chrotild, daughter of Gundobad, king of Burgundy. Though he was an outstanding worshipper of idols, stirred by his wife’s prayers he was baptized by Saint Remigius, archbishop of Rheims. Thereafter he joined battle with Alaric, king of the Goths, near the city of Poitiers, overthrew his army, and gained his kingdom.

He received from Emperor Anastasius documents conferring the consulship; then [Col. 0913B] he proceeded as an Augustus as far as the basilica of Saint Martin at Tours, placed a diadem upon his head, and was called Augustus. After he had slain very many enemies in every direction, he himself came to the end of his days: he died at Paris in the forty-fifth year of his age and the thirtieth of his reign, and was buried in the basilica of Saint Peter, which he himself had built from the foundations. At that time Saint Benedict the abbot flourished in miracles. From the death of Saint Martin to the death of this Clovis are reckoned 112 years.

After his death his four sons—Theoderic,  
[Note: [Col. 0913] Above these names manuscript 2 has letters written: a, d, c, b; perhaps to alter the order.]  
Clothar, Childebert, and Clodomir—divided his kingdom among themselves. Theoderic chose Rheims as his seat, Clodomir Orléans, Childebert Paris, and Clothar Soissons. [H., epitome, ch. 30.] Their [Col. 0913C] sister was sought and received in marriage by Amalaric, son of Alaric.

This Theoderic, born of a concubine, died after taking up the government of the see of Rheims; his son Theudebert succeeded in his place.  
[Note: [Col. 0913] “His” in manuscript 2.]  
In Theudebert’s time the Danes invaded Gaul; but Theudebert defeated them, killed their king, and restored what had been plundered from the land. [*Gesta Francorum*, chs. 19, 26.] He died in the fourteenth year of his reign, and his son Theudobald reigned in his place.

**3.**  
[Note: [Col. 0913] Rubric added by manuscript 1: “How Saint Sigismund and Saint Leodegar the bishop were killed.”]  
[Isidore.] In the same period Justin the Elder held the empire at Constantinople, and Hilderic, king of the Vandals, ordered bishops to return from exile. At that time Theoderic, king of Italy, [Col. 0913D] put Pope John, the patrician Symmachus, and the philosopher Boethius to the sword. [Cf. H., *Historia maior*.]

At the same time Sigismund, king of the Burgundians, married the daughter of this Theoderic,  
[Note: [Col. 0913] *thoder.* in manuscripts 1? and 2.]  
king of Italy, who was born of the sister of Theoderic, son of Clovis. He gave his own sister in marriage to Huneric, king of the Vandals; he likewise joined Malberga to Hermenfred, king [Col. 0914A] of the Thuringians,  
[Note: [Col. 0913] *chorinc.* in manuscripts 1? and 2.]  
and gave a third woman to Huctric, king of the Alemanni.  
[Note: [Col. 0913] I do not know from where the author derived these matters. They contain certain peculiar details, but are undoubtedly false.]

[Paul the Deacon, I.25, 23, 25.] At the same time the senator Cassiodorus, Dionysius the abbot, who composed the nineteen-year cycle, and the poet Arator flourished at Rome. Then Alboin,  
[Note: [Col. 0913] *albonius* in manuscripts 1? and 2.]  
son of Aldoin, king of the Lombards, killed Thurismod, king of the Gepids, in battle. At this same time Priscian of Caesarea, the founder of the art of grammar, flourished at Constantinople. [Cf. *Gesta Francorum*, chs. 27, 20, 21, 24.]

Theudobald, son of Theudebert, died in the seventh year of his reign. At the same time Clodomir, son of Clovis, killed Saint Sigismund, king of the Burgundians, a good and just man, [Col. 0914B] together with his wife and sons. When Clodomir was proceeding with an army against the Burgundians for battle near Vienne, he rashly pursued them as they fled. Riding rapidly among them, he was struck from the opposite side, fell, and died.

His brother Clothar took Clodomir’s wife in marriage. Out of envy for the kingdom, he killed with a knife two of her sons—that is, the sons of his brother Clodomir. One was ten years old, another seven; the third escaped, named Clodoald, and was saved through the aid of brave boys. Later, abandoning the kingdom, he cut his hair with his own hand; having become a cleric, he was endowed with good works. Afterwards he was ordained priest and, full of virtues, passed to the Lord.

[Col. 0914C] **4.**  
[Note: [Col. 0913] Rubric added by manuscript 1: “Concerning the death of King Clothar and how his sons divided the kingdom of the Franks.”]  
[*Gesta Francorum*, chs. 28, 27, 29.] At the same time Childebert, brother of the aforesaid Clothar, died of fever at Paris and was buried in the church of Saint Vincent, which he had built.  
[Note: [Col. 0913] “is” added by manuscript 2.]  
Their mother, Queen Chrotild, also died in the city of Tours  
[Note: [Col. 0913] *defunta* in manuscripts 1? and 2.]  
and, having been carried to Paris, lies buried beside her husband Clovis. Thus the whole monarchy of the Frankish kingdom came under Clothar’s power.

He had many sons by different women. One of them, named Crannus, was appointed prince in Aquitaine by his father. Wishing, but unable, to rebel against his father Clothar, he summoned to his aid a king of the Bretons named Conober. [Col. 0914D] Clothar himself marched against them, fought bravely, killed the Breton king, and captured Crannus. His father Clothar ordered him to be burned with his wife and children. In those days blessed Medard passed to the Lord.

After this, in the second  
[Note: [Col. 0913] “second,” written as *oo 2o.*, in manuscript 1.]  
year of his reign after he had killed Crannus, Clothar was seized by a severe fever and died. [Col. 0915A] His sons honourably buried him in the basilica of Saint Medard at Soissons, which he had built.

Then his four sons, namely Cherebert, Guntrannus, Chilperic, and Sigebert, divided the kingdom among themselves. Cherebert had Paris, Guntrannus Orléans, Chilperic Soissons, and Sigebert the see of Rheims. [Paul the Deacon, II.10.] At this time Pope Benedict presided over the Roman Church. Chilperic obtained primacy over all Gaul, although his brother Sigebert was more vigorous and powerful than he.

[*Gesta Francorum*, chs. 31, 37, 38.] Sigebert took as wife Brunichild, daughter of Athanagild, king of Spain; by her he had a son named Childebert. This Childebert begot two sons, namely Theudebert and Theoderic. Theoderic, by the counsel of the aforesaid Brunichild, [Col. 0915B] his grandmother, killed his brother Theudebert and his sons; and he himself later died by the plots of that same woman, poisoned. She also killed his sons.

**5.**  
[Note: [Col. 0915] Rubric added by manuscript 1: “How King Chilperic left his wife Andovera at the counsel of his servant Fredegund.”]  
[*Gesta Francorum*, chs. 31, 35, 30, 32, 33.] Seeing that his brother Sigebert had taken Brunichild as wife, Chilperic sent to Spain and married Brunichild’s sister, named Galswintha,  
[Note: [Col. 0915] *wasuintam* in manuscript 1.]  
having put aside Queen Andovera, by whom he had already had three sons: Theudebert, Merovech, and Clovis.

Queen Andovera also had in her service a girl named Fredegund. Through Fredegund’s wicked contrivance, the king strangled the aforesaid Galswintha by night in her bed and took Andovera back in marriage. Afterwards Fredegund deceived Andovera in such a way that she made her receive at the sacred font, by wicked counsel, her own daughter [Col. 0915C] whom she had conceived by the king. For this reason Andovera was permanently separated from the king and remained in a monastery, veiled, with her daughter until the end of her life.

Fredegund, at first the queen’s attendant and afterwards herself made queen, was taken in marriage by King Chilperic. By her he had three sons, who died; then he begot a fourth, named Clothar, who was father of the renowned and most famous King Dagobert. The aforesaid Sigebert, after twice overcoming the Huns who had attacked him and putting his brother Chilperic to flight in battle, was killed by two servants through Fredegund’s treachery in the fourteenth year of his reign and the fortieth of his life.

His young son Childebert was secretly carried away and reigned in his place. Chilperic, his paternal uncle, drove Childebert’s mother Brunichild into exile. What Cherebert did or how he conducted himself, however, we do not know with certainty.

[Isidore.] In those days Emperor Justinian ruled at Constantinople. Through the patrician Belisarius he triumphed marvellously over the Persians; then, sent into Africa, Belisarius destroyed the king of the Vandals. At the same time the bones of the monk Anthony, found by divine revelation, were brought to Alexandria and buried in the church [Col. 0916A] of Saint John the Baptist.

After Justinian, Justin the Younger ruled eleven years. Under him Totila, king of the Goths, was defeated by Narses, master of the soldiers of that same Justin. [Cf. Paul the Deacon III.11; Isidore; *Gesta Francorum*.] After Totila, Leovigild, king of the Goths, overcame certain rebels in Spain.

The aforesaid Childebert  
[Note: [Col. 0915] *childertus* in manuscripts 1 and 2.]  
was at peace with his uncle Guntrannus; afterwards he broke that peace, but was later reconciled with him. Then Tiberius  
[Note: [Col. 0915] *tybericus* in manuscripts 1 and 2.]  
Constantine, a most powerful emperor, ruled the empire at Constantinople for seven years. [Paul the Deacon IV.12, 13, 15, 17, 4.] King Chilperic of the Franks sent ambassadors to him and received many golden ornaments from him. After Tiberius, Maurice put on the purple and received the kingdom.

Maurice sent 50,000 [Col. 0916B] solidi to the younger Childebert so that he might drive the Lombards out of Italy. Childebert sent an army and ravaged Italy. The same Childebert also waged war against his cousin Clothar, son of Chilperic, and severely afflicted his army. Afterwards Childebert invaded Spain and inflicted a great slaughter upon that people. [Paul the Deacon III.21, 24; IV.7.] At that time the great Gregory, pontiff of the Roman Church, flourished; Thessalus was made king in Bavaria by the aforesaid king of the Franks.

**6.**  
[Note: [Col. 0915] Rubric added by manuscript 1: “Concerning the death of the most hostile Queen Fredegund, and how Theudebert and Theoderic divided the kingdom.”]  
[*Gesta Francorum*, chs. 35–37.] At that time Queen Fredegund, together with accomplices, killed her husband King Chilperic, against whom she had committed adultery, because she feared discovery of the adultery between herself and Count Landeric. He had reigned twenty-three years; she remained [Col. 0916C] with her son Clothar. Later she grew old over many days and, full of impurities, closed her final day.

[Paul the Deacon IV.12, 14, 18, 27, 29, 30, 31, 35, 37.] At the same time King Guntrannus died. Afterwards Childebert, king of the Franks, son of Sigebert and Brunichild, died young in the twenty-fifth year of his life. After his death the Huns, who are also the Avars, invaded Francia and fought very severe wars with the Franks.

In those days Queen Brunichild governed Gaul with her grandsons Theudebert and Theoderic, who were still little boys; later they divided the Frankish kingdom between themselves. Agilulf, king of the Lombards, confirmed peace with this Theoderic. Around this time the monastery of Saint Benedict was plundered by the Lombards.

Thus Maurice, [Col. 0916D] after ruling the empire for twenty-one years with his sons Theodosius, Tiberius, and Constantine, was killed by Phocas, who had been groom to the patrician Priscus. In this year Kings Theudebert and Theoderic of the Franks fought against Clothar, son of Chilperic. And blessed Pope Gregory passed to the Lord.

7 [Note: [Col. 0915] How Queen Brunhild killed Theudebert and Theuderic. add. 1.]. At that time the son of Agilulf, king of the Lombards, took in marriage the daughter of this King Theudebert. In this period the eunuch Eleutherius, a patrician, when he attempted to seize the rights of imperial rule, was killed by soldiers, and his head was carried to Constantinople [Col. 0917A]. Phocas, after Maurice and his sons had been put to death, held the principate for eight years. At the request of Pope Boniface, he decreed that the see of the Roman and Apostolic Church was the head of all churches, because the Church of Constantinople was claiming for itself precedence over all churches. Against this Phocas, Heraclianus, who governed Africa, rebelled, deprived him of the throne, and Heraclius, his son, undertook the administration of the commonwealth. [G. Fr. chs. 38–40.] At the same time King Theudebert was killed by his brother Theuderic; he too was afterwards destroyed by poison administered by Brunhild. Once they had thus died, the younger Chlothar, namely the son of Chilperic and Fredegund, obtained supremacy over all Gaul and assumed the reins of government [Col. 0917B]. He preferred first to become the avenger of his kinsmen rather than to abandon an occasion for war. Accordingly, at the very beginning of his reign, he summoned Queen Brunhild—who had killed her kinsmen Theudebert and Theuderic, namely the sons of her cousin Childebert, and had destroyed many others of royal stock—as though he intended to join her to himself in marriage. Delighted, she came as she had been ordered, adorned with precious ornaments as if for a wedding. By judgement of the Franks he ordered her placed upon a camel and led around the circuit of the camps, and afterwards bound to unbroken horses and torn apart. Thus, by a shameful death, as she deserved, she descended to hell. Even her bones, consumed in fire, appeared nowhere.

8 [Note: [Col. 0917] How Dagobert, son of Chlothar, fought against the Saxons. add. 1.] [G. Dag. chs. 12, 14, 24]. This Chlothar had a son, Dagobert, a most beloved young man. While he was still alive, his father the king exalted him to the kingdom of the Austrasians. Against him the Saxons, having raised an army, fought vigorously; but, by God’s gift, his father Chlothar assisted him and entered upon war with the Saxons beyond the Rhine. In a single combat he killed their duke Bertoald, because his son Dagobert had been wounded in the earlier battle; and he so subdued their entire country that there did not remain in it a fighting man taller than the length of that sword. So great then was the power of the Franks, and so great the courage of their kings.

In the time of these men, namely Chlothar and his most sweet son Dagobert, the kingdom of the Franks was greatly exalted [Col. 0917D], and the holy Church likewise shone forth in its elevation through priests and ecclesiastical men; so much so that the Roman pontiff, sending into Gaul, requested that men strong in faith and wise in speech be sent to him, able to dispute with him against heretics. At that time Heraclius held the citadel of the Roman Empire. Skilled in the liberal arts, and especially in astronomy, he commanded Dagobert to expel the Jews from his kingdom, which Dagobert did most willingly. For the emperor himself had foreseen in the stars to which he devoted himself [Col. 0918A] that the Roman Empire would be destroyed by the circumcised; but what he understood concerning the Jews is known to have been accomplished by the people of Hagar, whom we call Saracens.

9 [Note: [Col. 0917] How King Dagobert gave Toulouse and all the land as far as the Pyrenees to his brother Charibert. add. 1.]. [P. D. IV, 51; V, 6, 11, 12.] After Heraclius too had died, his son Heraclonas ruled with his mother Martina for two years; afterwards Constantine, also called Constans, his brother, held the Empire for twenty-eight years. He was killed at Syracuse, a city of Sicily, and his head was carried to Constantinople. After him Mezezius ruled from the seventh indiction to the twelfth. [G. Dag. chs. 5, 15, 16, 21.] In the thirty-seventh year of Chlothar’s reign, Bertrude, mother of King Dagobert, died. After her death Chlothar took another wife, named Sichild [Col. 0918B], by whom he had a son named Charibert. Chlothar himself died in the forty-fifth year of his reign and was buried in the church of Saint Vincent in the suburb of Paris.

When his son Dagobert heard this, he ordered all the princes over whom he ruled in Austrasia to advance the army. When he had arrived at Rheims, all the bishops and dukes of Burgundy and Neustria are known to have submitted themselves to him there. But his brother Charibert endeavoured, if he could, to take possession of his father’s kingdom; his wish, however, had little success. Brunulf, brother of Queen Sichild and maternal uncle of Charibert, wishing to establish him in the kingdom, plotted much against Dagobert. Therefore, after many days had passed, he was killed at Ablatona [Col. 0918C] by Dagobert’s dukes on the order of that king.

When Dagobert had occupied the whole kingdom, he employed prudent counsel and granted to his brother Charibert the district of Toulouse, Quercy, Agenais, Périgord, Saintonge, and the territory as far as the Pyrenees, on this condition: that at no time should he presume to make a claim against him concerning their father’s kingdom. Then, returning to Paris, he abandoned Queen Gomatrude, whom he had married on the counsel of his father Chlothar, because she was barren; and, taking in marriage a maiden of most beautiful appearance and noble birth named Nantild, he raised her to be queen.

10 [Note: [Col. 0917] Concerning Sigebert, son of King Dagobert, whom St Amand baptized. add. 1.]. [Gesta Dag. chs. 24, 25, 27, 31, 32.] Finally, while he was travelling about Austrasia in royal state, he was exceedingly sad [Col. 0918D] because he had no son to reign after him. He took into his bed a certain girl named Ragnetrude. By her, in that same year, through many prayers and lavish gifts of alms, by God’s gift he had a son; his brother Charibert received him from the sacred font at Orléans. But while Lord Amand, bishop of Maastricht, was blessing him and making him a catechumen, when the prayer had ended and no one answered “Amen,” the Lord opened the child’s mouth, and, with all hearing, he answered, “Amen.” Regenerated by water and the Holy Spirit, he received the name Sigebert. [Col. 0919A]

After King Charibert’s death, King Dagobert brought his whole kingdom under his own authority. In the same year he sent envoys to Samo, king of the Slavs, requiring him to receive his kingdom from him. Samo replied to them: “Both the land which we possess belongs to Dagobert, and we are his men, if he is disposed to keep friendship with us.” Dagobert’s envoys said to him: “It is not possible for servants of God to join friendship with dogs.” King Samo replied: “If you are servants of God, and we are God’s dogs, then, while you act against him, we have permission to tear you with bites.” Dagobert’s envoys were then driven from Samo’s presence. When he heard this, Dagobert took it grievously and, having assembled an army, devastated their land most cruelly. Returning thence victorious, he stopped in the city of Metz [Col. 0919B]; and by the counsel of his bishops and nobles he exalted his son Sigebert to the kingdom of the Austrasians and permitted him to have his seat at Metz. Since a son named Louis had been born to King Dagobert by Queen Nantild, he confirmed by a bond of agreement with his son Sigebert, king of the Austrasians, on the counsel of his magnates, that Neustria and [Note: [Col. 0919] “that,” add. 1.] Burgundy should belong to the kingdom of that same Louis after the death of King Dagobert.

11 [Note: [Col. 0919] On the death of Dagobert and the benefactions which he conferred upon the church of St Denis. add. 1.]. [Gesta Dagob. chs. 35, 17, 42, 43.] At the same time Sadregisilus, duke of the Aquitanians, was killed by certain persons. Since he had sons raised at court who could very easily have avenged their father’s death but were unwilling to do so, they were reproached by the magnates of the kingdom according to Roman laws and lost all their paternal possessions [Col. 0919C]. Since all these fell to the royal fisc, the glorious King Dagobert most devoutly granted the same possessions to the church of Saint Denis: namely Novingentum in the district of Anjou; Parciacum, Nulliacum, Podenciniacum, Pascellariae, and Anglariae in the district of Poitou; and very many others, with saltworks above the sea. Whoever investigates their names will, I believe, find twenty-seven.

Among the other deeds which he performed praiseworthily, this glorious king, mindful of his vow, adorned the shrines of Saints Dionysius, Rusticus, and Eleutherius with pure gold and precious gems. Although he had constructed the church from its foundations and furnished its interior with marvellous splendour, he also covered outside with pure silver the apse above, beneath which he had buried the bodies of the martyrs [Col. 0919D]. After his glorious administration of the kingdom, in the sixteenth year after he had obtained the kingdom of the Franks, he began to suffer from flux of the belly at the estate of Spinogilo, not far from Paris. A few days later, sensing the danger to his life was at hand, he ordered his counsellor Ega [Note: [Col. 0919] *erga*, add. 1, in an erased place.] to come to him and entrusted Queen Nantild and his son Louis into his hands. Having summoned the leading men of the palace, together with his son and wife, he ordered them to take an oath concerning what he had bestowed upon the church of Saint Denis: that none of his successors nor any power [Col. 0920A] should presume to take it from that church, if he did not wish to incur the wrath of God and the offence of Saint Denis.

All the magnates, overwhelmed by grief, he gently and mildly consoled with such strength as he could. When he had ended speaking after a long exhortation, his son Louis and all the nobles confirmed that decree, according to the king’s command, by their own subscriptions. When these matters had thus been concluded, the most Christian King Dagobert was taken from human affairs. An unbearable grief suddenly filled the whole palace, and the whole kingdom was seized by a most bitter lamentation over his death. Embalmed with spices, he was carried, amid the immense grief and thronging of the people, to the church of Saints Dionysius, Rusticus, and Eleutherius, which he had marvellously adorned, beyond belief, inside and out with gold, precious gems, and ornaments of various kinds [Col. 0920B]. There he had also instituted an order of chanters after the model of the monasteries of Agaune and of Saint Martin at Tours, so that the praise of God might be maintained there continually. He was buried with due honour beside their tomb, on the right side.

12 [Note: [Col. 0919] On the successors of King Clovis, and how Theuderic and Ebroin became monks. add. 1.]. [Gesta Dag. ch. 45; G. Fr. chs. 43, 41, 43, 44, 45.] After his departure, his son Clovis, still under age, took to himself his father’s kingdom. All the dukes of the Franks, of Neustria, and of Burgundy exalted him to the kingdom. He took as wife a woman of Saxon stock named Balthild, very beautiful and intelligent, by whom he had three sons: Chlothar, Childeric, and Theuderic. Sigebert [Col. 0920C], son of the aforesaid Dagobert and king of the Austrasians, died, leaving a son named Dagobert. Grimoald, mayor of the palace of Austrasia, sent this boy, shorn, into custody with Dido, bishop of Poitiers. Therefore Grimoald himself was captured by the Franks, taken to Paris, and committed to chains; he paid the penalties he deserved in prison, where he also miserably ended his life [Note: [Col. 0919] *finiut*, readings 1 and 2.].

Clovis, Dagobert’s son, reigned sixteen years and died. Then the Franks, holding a general assembly, appointed his elder son, Chlothar, king over themselves, and placed his brother Childeric in the kingdom of the Austrasians, while their younger brother Theuderic remained in Francia with King Chlothar, his father [Col. 0920D]. At the same time Archinoald died, and Ebroin, a cruel and proud man, was chosen by the Franks in his place. Afterwards Chlothar died, having ruled four years. His younger brother Theuderic succeeded him in the kingdom. But the Franks, angered because of Ebroin, who was most loyal to him, and knowing his impiety, deposed Theuderic from the kingdom and Ebroin from the dukedom; they cut off their hair and confined them in the monastery of Luxeuil in Burgundy.

They then sent to Austrasia for Childeric, brother of this Theuderic [Col. 0921A], and exalted him to the kingdom when he came with Duke Wulfoald. He was afterwards killed, together with his wife, whose womb was already swelling with conception, by Bodo and other Franks; and Wulfoald escaped in flight to Pippin in Austrasia. Leudesius, son of Archinoald, was chosen mayor of the palace. Bishop Leodegar and his brother Gerinus were involved in this counsel.

13 [Note: [Col. 0921] How the same Theuderic and Ebroin, leaving the monastery, seized the kingdom of the Franks. add. 1.]. Hearing that Childeric had died, Theuderic and Ebroin secretly left the monastery. When their hair had grown, they returned to Francia with a very great display of arms, one for the kingdom and the other for the office of duke. Then Ebroin treacherously killed Leudesius, who had succeeded him in authority, at the fortress of Quierzy. Bishop Leodegar [Col. 0921B] and his brother Gerinus were shamefully tortured and killed by him. Duke Lupus was driven into exile, as is contained in the decree of that same Theuderic: from Lupus’s inheritance the monastery of Saint Benedict was constructed in the territory of Fleury. [Note: [Col. 0921D] Compare the genealogy of the kings of the Franks, Bouquet II, p. 697: “and the most wicked Duke Lupus was driven into exile by King Theuderic; from his inheritance the monastery of Saint Peter was constructed in the estate of Fleury.” This likewise agrees with the present narrative in other places [Col. 0922D].] [G. Dag. ch. 47.] Afterwards Ebroin, having committed many evil deeds, was killed by a Frank named Ermenfred.

—[Book on the Mayors of the Palace.] Finally, from the times of Clovis, son of King Dagobert and father of Theuderic, the declining kingdom of the Franks began to be governed through mayors of the palace. The first of these in Austrasia was Pippin, who left a son named Grimoald; after Grimoald came Archinoald. When he died, Ebroin succeeded [Col. 0921C], while Wulfoald exercised the office of duke in Austrasia. Upon Wulfoald’s death, Martin and the younger Pippin [Note: [Col. 0921] “and younger,” readings 1 and 2.], son of Ansegisel, who was also called Anchises, were mayors of the palace in Austrasia. They also led armed battle-lines against King Theuderic and Duke Ebroin. But Martin, having taken flight, was treacherously killed by Ebroin at Laon-sur-l’Ailette. Pippin returned to Austrasia, and Ermenfred, after killing Ebroin, escaped as a fugitive to him.

The mayors of the palace from whom the royal lineage proceeded were these: first Ansbert the senator, who by Blithild, daughter of the second Chlothar, begot Arnold, father of Saint Arnulf, later bishop of Metz; Arnulf begot Ansegisel, also called Anchises, father of Pippin. In Ebroin’s place the Franks again made Waratto mayor of the palace [Col. 0921D]. His son Giselmar, against the opposition of his father Waratto, waged civil wars with Pippin. Pippin again undertook war against Theuderic and Berchar; he conquered and captured them, and, having received the treasures, appointed one Norbert of his followers mayor of the palace [Col. 0922A]. Afterwards he returned victoriously to Austrasia. His sons were Drogo and Grimoald, of whom Grimoald received the duchy in Champagne.

14 [Note: [Col. 0921] How a certain cleric was anointed king of the Franks, who, once king, was called Chilperic. add. 1.]. When Theuderic died, his son Chlothar obtained the kingdom as a boy. Upon his death, his brother Childebert succeeded. After Charibert too had died, Grimoald, son of Pippin, became mayor of the palace. When King Childebert passed from this life, his son Dagobert, still a boy, succeeded to his kingdom. At that time Grimoald, mayor of the palace, married Theudesinda, daughter of Duke Radbod. He was killed by the Frisian Ragenfrid in the basilica of Saint Lambert; in his place his father Pippin appointed his son Theudoald, whom he had had by another wife, to his father’s rank [Col. 0922B]. Pippin himself died in the same year, that is, in the year 714 of the Lord’s incarnation, in mid-December, after holding the principate under the aforesaid kings for twenty-seven years.

Plectrude, formerly Pippin’s wife, held Charles, Pippin’s son by another wife, captive; but by God’s gift he escaped alive. After the death of the younger Dagobert, who had reigned five years, Charles engaged in many battles against Radbod the Frisian and against Ragenfrid, who had become mayor of the palace on behalf of Theudoald, son of Grimoald the Just and Moderate. Then the Franks established in the kingdom a certain cleric Daniel, after removal of his tonsure, and called him Chilperic. Charles fought against him and victoriously put him to flight [Col. 0922C]. Then, coming to Cologne, Charles recovered his father Pippin’s treasures from his stepmother Plectrude and set up Chlothar as king for himself; Chlothar died in that same year. At length King Chilperic, formerly called Daniel, and Duke Ragenfrid sought Duke Eudo as an ally. Chilperic, also called Daniel, fled with the royal treasures; afterwards Eudo restored him to Charles with many gifts. When he had reigned no more than five years, the Franks made Theuderic, son of the younger Dagobert, king over themselves.

15 [Note: [Col. 0921] How St Eleutherius saw Charles Martel in hell, and how a serpent came out of his tomb. add. 1.]. At that time Charles, mayor of the palace and prince of the Austrasians, undertook many wars with an unequal force against Radbod, Ragenfrid, Eudo, the Bavarians, and the Saracens; and always, through God’s grace, he proved victorious. In the year 741 of the Lord’s incarnation [Col. 0922D], the duke died and was buried by his followers in the monastery of the precious martyr Dionysius. He gave the property of churches to laymen because of the constant wars [Note: [Col. 0922D] Compare Hugh of Flavigny, *Ecclesiastical History*, above, p. 358.], and for this one reason above all he is eternally damned. [Epistle of the Synod of Quierzy.] [Note: [Col. 0922D] A.D. 858, in Baluze, *Capitularies*, ed. Chiniac, II, p. 108.]

For Saint Eleutherius [Col. 0923A], bishop of Orléans, who rests in the monastery of Saint Trudo, was caught up while at prayer into the other world. Among other things which he saw when the Lord revealed them to him, he saw Charles himself tormented in hell. To his question, the guiding angel answered that, by the judgement of the saints who will judge with the Lord at the future judgement, because he had taken and divided their goods, before that judgement he had been consigned, soul and body, to everlasting punishments. Along with his own sins he had received punishments for the sins of all those who, for redemption of their souls, had bestowed their property through reverence and love of God upon holy places, for lights of divine worship and for the sustenance of the poor and servants of Christ.

When he had returned to himself, he summoned Saint Boniface and Fulrad [Note: [Col. 0923] *fultadum*, readings 1 and 2.], abbot of the church of Saint Denis, and, saying such things to them, ordered them to go to the tomb of that Charles; if they did not find his body there, they were to believe that what he said was true. Going to the place where his body had been buried and opening his tomb, they suddenly saw a dragon emerge; and the entire tomb was found blackened inside, as though it had been burned. We ourselves saw men who survived down to our own age, who had been present at this event and told it to us eagerly in their living speech.

—(*Book on the Mayors of the Palace.*) After his death, his sons Carloman and Pippin obtained the chief authority in the kingdom of Francia. One of them, namely Carloman, fought against Duke Hunald of the Aquitanians and afterwards against Duke Odilo of the Bavarians [Col. 0923C]. Finally, becoming a monk on Mount Soracte, he afterwards led a religious life on Monte Cassino. At last he returned to Francia as envoy of Pope Saint Stephen to his brother Pippin, now king; and, on his journey back to Italy, he died after performing his embassy at Vienne, a city of Gaul.

16 [Note: [Col. 0923] How Pippin deposed his brother Childeric from the kingdom of the Franks and was crowned in his place. add. 1.]. At this time Childeric was established in the kingdom of the Franks. While still duke, Pippin sent envoys concerning him to Pope Zacharias, asking whether the kings of the Franks ought to remain so, when they possessed almost no power and were content with the name alone. The Roman pontiff answered the envoys that he who governed the commonwealth ought to be called and to be king. Therefore, after King Childeric had been shorn and confined in a monastery, the Franks made Pippin king over themselves. He subdued those who rebelled against him and appointed his brother Grifo duke of the Austrasians, and his nephew through his sister Tassilo duke of the Bavarians [Note: [Col. 0923D] Compare above.].

After the death of Zacharias, Roman pontiff, blessed Stephen succeeded him. Persecuted by the Lombard Aistulf, he came into Francia, where he fell ill [Col. 0924A] unto death [Note: [Col. 0923D] Compare *Gesta pontificum Romanorum*]. In the church of Saint Denis, before the altar of that martyr, he recovered his former health through the martyr’s visitation and speech. As a pastoral blessing and as testimony of the event for posterity, he left there the keys and pallium of apostolic dignity. He anointed as kings of the Franks the most flourishing King Pippin and his two sons Charles and Carloman. He also marked Bertrada, wife of the illustrious King Pippin, clothed in royal robes, in God’s name with the grace of the sevenfold Spirit. Sanctifying the Frankish nobles with an apostolic blessing, he bound them by the authority of Saint Peter entrusted to him by the Lord, and adjured them never, throughout the course of succeeding ages, either themselves or any descended from their stock to presume in any way to establish a king over themselves from another lineage, but only from their own line [Col. 0924B]. [Gesta pont. Rom.]

Then the glorious King Pippin, assembling the nobles of royal power and instructing them with the exhortation of so great a father, resolved with them to carry out, Christ favouring, what he had decreed together with that pope. Then, by the counsel of the Franks, he sent envoys to Aistulf, most wicked king of the Lombards, demanding that he peacefully restore what had been taken from the churches. But the evil Aistulf refused to do any of these things.

17 [Note: [Col. 0923] How the same Pippin restored to various churches much of what his father had taken from them. add. 1.]. Seeing that he could not soften the stony heart of the most cruel Aistulf, Pippin sent ahead, before his own arrival, some of his nobles to guard the Frankish passes. Hearing this, the insolent Aistulf suddenly fell upon them [Col. 0924C] with his armies. But God’s goodness granted victory to the Franks, so that Aistulf himself took flight and, unarmed through fear of the Franks, shut himself up in the city of Pavia. Pippin besieged and closely pressed it. The most cruel Aistulf begged forgiveness and in every way pledged himself to restore the cities. When the compact had been confirmed, King Pippin sent his counsellor Fulrad, abbot of Saint Denis, to receive those cities; he himself immediately returned happily with his men to Francia.

After this, the pestilential Aistulf, engaged in hunting in a certain place, was struck by lightning through divine judgement and perished by a most cruel death. Then a certain Duke Desiderius, hearing that Aistulf had died, immediately gathered a multitude of armies and, with the assistance of the aforesaid Pope Stephen and Fulrad, abbot of Saint Denis, seized the royal dignity over Ratchis, brother of the aforesaid Aistulf, king of the Lombards [Col. 0924D]. Afterwards the same most blessed Pope Stephen, by God’s assent enlarging the commonwealth and rescuing the Lord’s people like a good shepherd from the snares of enemies, completed his course and, called by God, passed to eternal life.

[Epistle of the Synod of Quierzy.] [Note: [Col. 0924D] In Baluze II, p. 109.] When the glorious King Pippin learned of the condemnation of his father Charles, he caused a synod to be assembled at Liptines. George, legate of the Apostolic See, presided over it with Saint Boniface. For we possess that synod itself; and Pippin took care, insofar as he could, to restore to churches whatever ecclesiastical properties his father had seized. Since, because of the conflict he had with Waifer, duke of the Aquitanians, he could not restore all the church property from which it had been taken, he requested that the bishops make precarial grants from it. He decreed, as is recorded in the book of royal capitularies, that ninths and tithes should be given for the repair of roofs, and that twelve denarii [Note: [Col. 0925] *denariis*, readings 1 and 2.] from each church should be given to the household whose property had been granted as a benefice, until the property itself returned to the church. (Einhard, *Life of Charlemagne*, ch. 3.)

That most glorious King Pippin ruled the kingdom of the Franks nobly for fifteen years and more. He died at Paris, weakened by dropsy [Note: [Col. 0925] *atque*, readings 1 and 2.], and was carried and buried in the monastery of Saint Denis.

18 [Note: [Col. 0925] How Carloman, after his father’s death, became emperor at Rome. add. 1.]. After his departure (cf. Einhard, [p.] 1), the Franks, holding a general assembly, made Charlemagne, his son, king over themselves. Afterwards the holy pontiff Adrian, compelled by injuries and the seizure of the holy Roman Church suffered at the hands of Desiderius, king of the Lombards, came into Francia to lodge his complaint [Note: [Col. 0925D] That these and the following matters are false and full of fables is evident to everyone.]. King Charles, moved by love and honour for Saint Peter and reverence [Note: [Col. 0925] *reverentis*, reading 2.] for the holy bishop Adrian, prepared an expedition, besieged Desiderius in the city of Pavia, and captured him [Col. 0925C] with his wife and one son (A.D. 774). He expelled the other of his sons from the kingdom, sent King Desiderius himself into Francia, and ordered him to be shorn in the church of Saint Denis and become a monk. This was done, and he remained there until the last day of his life, being buried there on the left side of the monastery. [Note: [Col. 0925D] The Greater Annals of St Gall, *SS.* I, p. 75; the Annals of Corbie, the Liège Annals, *SS.* IV, p. 13; and Anselm, ch. 18, *SS.* VII, p. 198, say that Corbie [Col. 0926D] and Liège were places of exile.]

Meanwhile the most renowned King Charles went to Rome, to the thresholds of the Apostles. The aforesaid Pope Adrian, the leading men of the senatorial order, all the sacred clergy, and the whole Roman people received him with honour; moreover, they acclaimed him emperor and consecrated him on holy Easter Day (A.D. 800). When this had been done, he returned prosperously with his men into Francia.

Exalted [Col. 0925D; Note: [Col. 0925] *sublimatur*, readings 1 and 2.] above all the peoples whom, through the aid and labour of the Franks, he had subdued to himself, while he was staying at Aachen he summoned into his chamber Albuin, duke of the Franks, Naimon, chief officer, and the duke of the Gascons [Col. 0926A]. He said to them: “It seems good and right to me that all the Franks should pay tribute to me, just as the other peoples who remain subject to our authority.” Hearing this, the wise men Albuin and Naimon, together with the other nobles present, became sorrowful and said in reply to the king: “Lord king, cease to demand this from the Franks, because by their assistance and labour you have conquered all things for the kingdom.” The king, somewhat moved to anger, said that he in no way wished his purpose to be changed from what he had said. But they asked for a long postponement, and the king granted it. Meanwhile they summoned all the leading men of the kingdom and made known to them the king’s wish. Indignant at this matter, they took it badly.

19 [Note: [Col. 0925] How the Franks wished to fight with King Carloman, and concerning the death of Charles himself. add. 1.]. Nevertheless, they were wisely and pleasantly counselled by Naimon, duke of the Gascons, and Albuin [Col. 0926B]. For they ordered all the Franks to prepare themselves for an expedition of two years and thus, armed, to march against the king. This was done. Unexpectedly envoys were sent to the king to announce that an immense army was advancing against him. When the king heard it, he was dismayed, because he had no time to gather an army.

Why say more? Albuin and the other Frankish nobles [Note: [Col. 0925] *preces* (“prayers”), reading 1.] immediately appeared before Charles, saying: “What are you doing, Charles? Receive the tribute of the Franks; destructive tribute is ready for you.” [Note: [Col. 0925] *extiale*, reading 1.] Hearing this, he said: “I have done wrong; give counsel as to what I should do.” “Send,” they said, “envoys to meet the army, and satisfy everyone by making amends.” This was done. Afterwards the Franks said to the king: “We are your soldiers; armed, we shall go wherever you command.” Thus they were sent with his son King Louis into the regions of Gascony. When the business had been accomplished, they returned with great rejoicing to their own places.

The glorious king, after a long administration of the kingdom (Einhard, *Life of Charlemagne*, ch. 30), exhausted alike by fever and pain in his side, died on the seventh day after he took to his bed, having received Holy Communion, in the seventy-second year of his age and the forty-seventh year from the beginning of his reign, on 28 January [5 Kalends of February], A.D. 814, at the third hour of the day [Col. 0926C]. His followers embalmed and buried him there in the church of the holy Mother of God, which he had built from the foundations.

20 [Note: [Col. 0925] Reading 1 inserts below, before the words “This Lothar”: in red, “On the discord between the most pious King Louis and his son Lothar.”]. His son Louis the Pious, most renowned emperor and inferior to none of the kings of his time [Col. 0926D], succeeded him in the kingdom. This glorious emperor exalted his three sons, Lothar, Louis, and Pippin, and distributed the monarchy of the kingdom among them. For he assigned the Roman Empire to Lothar and divided the remaining portions of the kingdom between the other two.

Then, at the instigation of the enemy of the human race, these three sons, through the faction of certain wicked men, treacherously captured their father, the Emperor Louis (A.D. 833), took from him his wife Judith and Charles, the son of them both, and exiled them; all the people abandoned Emperor Louis and went over to his son Lothar. Ebbo also, archbishop of Rheims, joined them in going over to Lothar. Lothar proceeded through the imperial palaces and brought that same father of his as far as the monastery of Saint Medard at Soissons. There, at the urging and pressure of the other bishops and leading men of the kingdom, Ebbo was compelled to impose public penance upon him, thereby incurring Louis’s severe and perpetual displeasure.

Thereupon [Col. 0927B] a very large part of the nobles and people again turned to the aforesaid Emperor Louis, abandoning his son Lothar, and restored him to the Empire (A.D. 834) at the monastery of Saint Denis. [Note: [Col. 0927D] Compare the Annals of St Bertin, under this year.] At length, long afterwards, father and sons having returned to concord, Emperor Louis himself, with the consent and favour of the above-mentioned sons, admitted Charles to a kingdom: namely, the kingdom of the Franks and Burgundy. While their father Louis lived, they appeared to preserve peace in whatever manner [Note: [Col. 0927] *quoque*, readings 1? 2.]. After a long administration of the kingdom, this glorious emperor entered upon the way of all flesh (A.D. 840), and was buried in the city of Metz by his brother Drogo, bishop of that city [Col. 0927C], in the monastery of Saint Arnulf. [Note: [Col. 0927D] Compare the Annals of Fulda, under this year.]

After his death the Franks, holding a general assembly, made his son Charles the Bald king over themselves. [Note: [Col. 0927D] Once again the author relates fabulous matters.] Against him the aforesaid brothers, stirred by envy of the kingdom, brought forth an expedition from all the forces of their realms, in order to take the kingdom from him by fighting.

21. [Note: [Col. 0927] “How Charles the Bald reigned, and concerning the discord that arose between him and his two brothers.” Added in manuscript 1.] When Charles learned this, he summoned all the leading men of his kingdom and consulted them about the matter. They, unanimously fired with manly resolve, declared that they could not endure allowing the others to enter their territories. Charles thanked them and went with them to meet his brothers. It was the vigil of the Ascension of our Lord [Note: [Col. 0928D] The author here reads 7 Kalends of June, instead of July; that day fell on the Ascension in this year. BOUQUET.] (841). On that day, forces arrived from every side, which had gathered together almost like the sand of the sea, and they encamped [Col. 0927D] in the district of Rheims. On the following day, the devil stirring them up, the army of the three kings—that is, Lothair, Louis, and Pippin—at Fontenoy, hoping that Charles’s army would be weak and inactive because of the holy feast of the Ascension, suddenly attacked him. But, God being favourable, the Franks and the rest of Charles’s army fought bravely, [Col. 0928A] met them, and, after a long engagement, Charles’s side gained the victory.

Afterwards Charles lived peaceably in his kingdom; surviving his other brothers, he joined all their kingdoms to his own rule. Being of incomparable goodness, he surpassed both earlier and later kings of the Franks in generosity toward the Church. For, by exceptional largesse, he enlarged and increased the monasteries throughout his realm. Moreover, he wonderfully enriched the monastery of Saint Denis, where his body rests, with lands and ornaments of diverse kinds. Because of these benefits, in order that he might be delivered from hell, he was led to places of punishment, so that, terrified by them, he might withdraw himself from evil; and again he was shown a flower-bearing field, where the good rest, so that he might advance more and more in good works and at last be able to reach that place. [Col. 0928B] How this happened may be found more fully in his deeds. After his glorious administration of the kingdom, while making his way to the thresholds of the exalted [Note: [Col. 0927] *subimium*, manuscript 2.] apostles, he was seized by illness on the journey itself and died (877). His body was then committed to burial in the district of Lyons, namely in the monastery of Nantua [Note: [Col. 0927] *uantoani*, manuscripts 1 and 2.] [Note: [Col. 0928D] Compare the *Annals of Saint-Bertin*, year 877.].

22. [Note: [Col. 0927] “How Charles the Bald appeared after his death to a certain monk.” Added in manuscript 1.] While he lay buried there for a long time, a vision appeared one night, in the monastery of Saint Denis situated in the district of Paris, to a monk named Erchengar and to a cleric of Saint Quentin of Vermandois named Alfo [Note: [Col. 0927] *aparuit*, manuscripts 1? and 2.]. It said that it was Charles, emperor and called the Bald, and that he had been openly sent to them by God, so that the will of almighty God might be revealed to his son King Louis and to the magnates of the [Col. 0928C] Frankish realm.

23. [Note: [Col. 0927] “The vision related to the monk by Charles the Bald.” Added in manuscript 1.] For he said that God and the holy martyrs Dionysius, Rusticus, and Eleutherius, and all the others, were displeased that his body should be deprived of burial in the basilica of the most holy Dionysius. While he lived, he had eagerly endeavoured, with a willing heart, to bestow there whatever he could: ornaments—still kept in that church to this day—of inestimable value, adorned with gold, gems, and precious stones; and estates and powerful villages. “Let them therefore go as swiftly as possible and transfer my body to the place of Saint Denis.” When his son and the princes of the realm heard this, they summoned archbishops, bishops, and abbots, especially Walter, abbot of Saint Denis; and they honourably conveyed his body from its first burial-place in the monastery of Nantua [Note: [Col. 0927] *uantoani*, manuscripts 1 and 2.] to the place of [Col. 0928D] Saint Denis the martyr, and worthily buried it before the altar of the Holy Trinity.

24. [Note: [Col. 0927] “I myself established this division.”] This glorious king [Note: [Col. 0927] “glorious king,” manuscript 1.] was succeeded by his son King Louis [Note: [Col. 0927] “the Stammerer,” written above the line by a second hand in manuscript 2.], who begot [Note: [Col. 0927] “by a concubine,” added by a second hand in manuscript 2.] Charles the Great and Louis. [Continuation of Aimoin, ch. 42.] Charles the Great begot Louis [Note: [Col. 0927] “who did nothing,” added by a second hand in manuscript 2.]. In his days the Danish people came, about to inflict upon Neustria [Col. 0929A] a third disaster [Note: [Col. 0929] *neustris*, manuscript 1.]. But Hugh, surnamed the Abbot, checked them, destroying their ranks so thoroughly that scarcely a messenger survived. Humbled by this blow, the Danes left Gaul in peace for some time.

After the death of Abbot Hugh and Prince Louis, his son Charles, called the Simple, was an infant in the cradle and remained fatherless. The leading men of Francia judged his age unsuitable for rule; and, as renewed Danish disturbances were already being reported, they deliberated upon the chief affairs of the realm. There survived two sons of Robert, count of Anjou, a man of Saxon stock: namely Odo and Robert. The Franks, Burgundians, and Aquitanians chose Odo, the elder, although unwilling, as guardian of the boy Charles and governor of the kingdom [Col. 0929B]; Walter, archbishop of Sens, anointed him. He was kindly, governed vigorously by repelling the enemies of the commonwealth, and always remained faithful to the boy. When he died, the boy Charles, called the Simple, received the kingdom.

At that time the Northmen came into Burgundy to Saint-Florentin. Richard, duke of Burgundy, met them in the territory of Tonnerre, struck down their multitude by the edge of the sword [Note: [Col. 0929] “by the edge” supplied in manuscript 2; absent in manuscript 1.], and the rest fled. At that time there was an earthquake near the monastery of Saint Columba on 5 Ides of January. Likewise, while the Danes were besieging the city of Chartres [Note: [Col. 0929] *parnotimam*, manuscripts 1 and 2.], the aforesaid Duke Richard and Robert, brother of King Odo, fell upon them. After 6,800 had been killed, they received hostages from the few [Note: [Col. 0929] *paneis*, manuscript 1.] who remained, on 14 Kalends of [Col. 0929C] August, a Saturday, through the help of God and the intercession of the blessed Mary. Likewise, in the middle of March a star appeared in the northwest, emitting a ray for nearly fourteen days.

25. [Note: [Col. 0929] “How Count Herbert confined Charles the Simple in prison at Péronne.” Added in manuscript 1.] In the following year famine grew severe throughout all Gaul. About five years later, on the Kalends of February, fiery battle-lines were seen in the sky, pursuing one another in turn. In that same year dissension arose between the king and his princes; because of it many slaughters were committed. In the third year after this persecution, Richard, duke of Burgundy, died on the Kalends of September and was buried in the basilica of Saint Columba, in the oratory of the martyr Symphorianus.

[The same author, ch. 43.] In the second year after his death, Prince Robert rebelled against Charles the Simple because the portion of his brother Odo’s government [Col. 0929D] was not restored to him. He seized tyrannical power and extorted, partly by flatteries and partly by threats, from certain bishops his coronation with the royal diadem, his investiture with the sceptre of the kingdom [Note: [Col. 0929] *iniri*, manuscript 1.], and his anointing. But he did not obtain a happy outcome from this. For before that year had ended, a battle took place at the city of Soissons between Charles the Simple and Prince Robert. Robert himself was killed there by Charles’s commanders, although his army obtained [Col. 0930A] the victory; yet his allies, undismayed by his fall, did not abandon their stubbornness.

As Charles was returning from the slaughter, Count Herbert of Vermandois, most wicked among the wicked, met him. By a pretended peace [Note: [Col. 0929] *facta* corrected to *ficta*, manuscript 2.] he deceived him, induced him to enter the castle of Péronne [Note: [Col. 0929] *partona*, manuscript 1.] as a guest, and thus shut him up, captured by treachery, in a dark prison. This Robert had a sister of Herbert, by whom Hugh the Great had been born. Since the condition of the kingdom without a ruler was uncertain, Charles, while held in custody, caused Ralph, son of the aforesaid Duke Richard of Burgundy, whom he had received from the sacred font as his godson, to rule, by the counsel of Hugh the Great, son of the aforesaid Robert, and of the magnates of Francia. Ralph was anointed king in the city of Soissons.

Charles, exhausted by prison, died in that custody after reigning twenty-seven years [Col. 0930B] and was buried in the basilica of Saint Fursa, leaving his son named Louis, whom he had had by Heagiva, daughter of the king of the English. Louis, fearing that he too would be caught up in his father’s misfortune, fled with his mother to the English. At the same time pagans devastated Burgundy, and a battle was fought between them and Christians on Mount Kalo; many thousands of our people were killed by the pagans.

26. [Note: [Col. 0929] “How Louis, son of Charles the Simple, obtained the sovereignty of the Frankish kingdom.” Added in manuscript 1.] King Ralph reigned over Francia for thirteen years, stern in restraining plunderers of the Church and in checking Danish attacks. He died and was buried in the basilica of Saint Columba beside his father. After his death, Hugh the Great, together with the Franks, sent Gislebert [Note: [Col. 0929] The *Continuation of Aimoin* and the *History of Sens* more correctly call him William.] archbishop of Sens [Col. 0930C] to Heagiva, wife of the aforementioned Charles the Simple. She had fled with her son Louis to her father, king of the English. Having given hostages under oath, she was brought back into Francia together with her son. Thus, with the consent of Hugh the Great and the leading men of Francia, Louis, son of Charles the Simple, was anointed king at Laon.

In the second year after this, on 15 Kalends of March, from the first cockcrow until daylight, blood-red battle-lines were seen in the sky. In the following month, on 9 Kalends of April, the Hungarians, still pagans, caused Francia, Burgundy, and Aquitaine to be ravaged with fire and sword. After this, the Franks rebelled against King Louis, and Hugh the Great above all.

[The same author, ch. 44.] Then, not many days later [Note: [Col. 0929] “after” supplied in manuscript 1.], this King Louis, son of Charles the Simple, leading a considerable army against the Northmen, was treacherously captured by the Northmen at the city of Bayeux; many Franks were killed, though Hugh the Great consented to it. In that same year famine prevailed throughout Gaul, so that a measure of grain was sold for twenty-four solidi. Afterwards, in May, on a Friday, blood rained upon workmen. In that year, [Col. 0931A] in September, King Louis—having passed his whole life full of hardship and tribulation—died after reigning sixteen years. He was buried at Rheims in the basilica of Saint Remigius, leaving two sons, Lothair and Charles, whom Gerberga, sister of Otto, later emperor of the Romans, had borne to him.

In the following month, on 2 Ides of November, Lothair, his son, already a young man, was anointed king at Rheims, and Hugh the Great was made duke of the Franks. In the second year after this, in August, Hugh himself besieged the city of Poitiers, but it profited him nothing. For while he besieged it, on a certain day the Lord thundered, and a whirlwind tore his tent from top to bottom. Terror seized him and his army, so that they scarcely escaped; turning to flight, they withdrew [Col. 0931B] from the siege, with no one pursuing them.

27. [Note: [Col. 0931] “How Hugh Capet became duke of the Franks.” Added in manuscript 1.] [Continuation of Aimoin, chs. 44–45.] In the same year Gislebert, duke of Burgundy, died, leaving the duchy to Otto, son of Hugh the Great, to whom he had given his daughter in marriage. In the following year Hugh the Great himself died at the estate of Dourdan on 16 Kalends of July and was buried in the basilica of Saint Denis. His sons Hugh, surnamed Capet, Otto, and Henry succeeded him; they had been born of the daughter of Otto, king of the Saxons. Hugh became duke of the Franks, and Otto duke of the Burgundians [Note: [Col. 0931] *burgondionum*, manuscript 2.]. When Otto died, his brother Henry succeeded him.

At the same time a dispute arose between Ansegisus, bishop of Troyes, and Count Robert. Ansegisus was expelled from the city and went to Saxony [Col. 0931C] to King Otto. Having brought Saxons with him, he besieged Troyes for a long time in October. But when the Saxons went out to plunder, Archbishop Archenbald and Count Renald the Old met them with a very large army at the place called Villare. Their leader Helpo was killed there with the Saxons, and the men of Sens were victorious. For Helpo had said that he would burn the churches and villages lying along the river Vanne as far as the city, and would plant his lance in the gate of Saint Leo. Helpo, killed with many of his men, was carried back by his servants to his homeland of Ardennes; for his mother Warna had bound him by oath to this. Count Renald and Archbishop Archenbald mourned him, because he was their kinsman. When [Col. 0931D] Duke Bruno saw that his companion Helpo had been killed, he returned to his own country.

Not many days later, King Lothair of the Franks assembled an immense army and brought Lothair’s kingdom back under his power [Note: [Col. 0931] *indictione*, manuscripts 1 and 2.]. Coming to the palace at Aachen, where Emperor Otto was staying, he entered inside at mealtime without opposition and ate and drank whatever had been prepared for them. Emperor Otto [Col. 0932A] escaped by fleeing with his wife and his people. After plundering the palace and the entire province, King Lothair returned peacefully to Francia, with no one pursuing him.

After this Emperor Otto assembled an army and came as far as Paris. There his nephew and many others were killed before the gate, after the suburb of that city had been burned; for he had boasted that he would plant his lance in the gate of Paris. King Lothair, having summoned Hugh, duke of the Franks, and Henry, duke of Burgundy, suddenly fell upon them and pursued them as they fled as far as the city of Soissons. Entering the channel of the river called the Aisne [Note: [Col. 0931] “they go to the Aronne,” manuscripts 1 and 2.], without knowing the ford, very many perished—far more by water than by the sword. So many were killed there that the river overflowed with dead bodies. Lothair [Col. 0932B] pursued them with the Franks for three days and as many nights, as far as the river flowing beside the forest of Ardennes; he killed many of them and, disdaining to pursue them farther, returned with great victory into Francia. Thus dishonoured, Emperor Otto returned with a few of his men to Lotharingia. After this he never again visited Francia, nor did any of his successors.

In the same year King Lothair and Emperor Otto made peace in the city of Rheims, despite the opposition of Dukes Hugh and Henry and all the leading men of Francia. King Lothair gave Lothair’s kingdom to Emperor Otto as a bond of affection; this especially saddened the hearts of the Franks.

28. [Note: [Col. 0931] A new chapter begins earlier with the words “But Lothair with the Franks,” and manuscript 1 adds the rubric: “How Hugh Capet imprisoned Charles, son of Lothair, at Orléans.”] After this King Lothair died and was buried [Col. 0932C] at Rheims in the basilica of Saint Remigius. His son Louis succeeded him. In the ninth year of his reign Louis died young and without children; he was buried at Compiègne in the church of Saint Cornelius. Charles, his brother—that is, son of the aforesaid Lothair—then obtained the kingdom of the Franks.

In that same year Hugh, duke of the Franks surnamed Capet, rebelled against this Charles, because Charles had married the daughter of Herbert, count of Troyes. Hugh gathered a large army and besieged Laon, where Charles was staying with his wife. Charles came out of the city with his men, put Hugh to flight, and burned the lodgings of the fleeing besiegers. Then Hugh, seeing that he could in no way overcome Charles, took counsel with the traitor Ascelin, bishop of Laon and [Col. 0932D] Charles’s own adviser. Ascelin [Note: [Col. 0931] *astelinus*, manuscript 2.] accordingly handed Laon over to Duke Hugh while all were asleep. Charles and his wife were captured within, and he was shut up in prison at Orléans; for he had not yet been anointed king, Hugh opposing it. While confined at Orléans he begot by the aforementioned wife two sons, Charles and Louis. And here the line and kingdom of Charles fail [Note: [Col. 0931] “and Louis,” added in the margin of manuscript 1.]. [Note: [Col. 0931] Note the pentameter.] In that same year [Col. 0933A] Duke Hugh, surnamed Capet, was anointed king in the city of Rheims; and in that same year he caused his most sweet son Robert to be exalted with the royal diadem.

29. [Note: [Col. 0933] “How the same Hugh, having seized the kingdom of the Franks, wished to exterminate all the descendants of King Lothair.” Added in manuscript 1.] [Continuation of Aimoin, ch. 46.] In those days Lord Arnulf, a good and modest man [Note: [Col. 0933] *donnus*, manuscript 2.], brother of the aforesaid Lothair, though born of a concubine, governed the church of Rheims. King Hugh, having been ordained, laid many snares for him, wishing to exterminate all Lothair’s descendants. He convened a council in the city of Rheims and invited Seguin, archbishop of Sens, with his suffragans. At this council he caused the aforesaid Arnulf, against whom he bore great envy, to be deposed; and he committed him to confinement at Orléans with his nephew Charles, saying that one born [Col. 0933B] of a concubine ought not to be raised to the episcopal mitre. In Arnulf’s place he caused Gerbert the philosopher to be consecrated, because he had been the teacher of his son King Robert and of Lord Leutric, later archbishop of Sens.

Archbishop Seguin in no way consented to Arnulf’s deposition or Gerbert’s consecration, although the king’s command pressed him. Fearing God more than an earthly king, he resisted as far as he could; and for this reason the king’s anger boiled against him. On hearing this, the Roman pontiff suspended from priestly honour the bishops who had consented to Gerbert’s ordination and Arnulf’s deposition. He sent Leo, an abbot, from the apostolic see to Seguin, archbishop of Sens, to assemble a council at Rheims in his stead. Therefore, when the council had been gathered by apostolic command, the aforesaid Arnulf, now entering his third year in bonds, was recalled from custody and honourably restored to his own see. Gerbert, realizing that he had unjustly usurped the honour of the episcopate, was moved to penitence and judged himself unworthy of such honour. Whoever investigates more carefully the disputation between Gerbert and Leo, the apostolic envoy, may find it in the deeds of the bishops of Rheims.

At the same time, through the election of Emperor Otto and the acclamation of the people, Gerbert the philosopher received the bishopric of the city of Ravenna. Having lived there for many years, when the Roman pope died, he was acclaimed by the people of the city of Rome to be made pontiff for them. Taken [Col. 0933D] from Ravenna, he was consecrated bishop in the city of Rome.

30. [Note: [Col. 0933] “On the death of Hugh Capet, and how his son Robert was anointed king.” Added in manuscript 1.] At that same time (996), King Hugh, surnamed Capet, having worn the crown for eleven years, departed from human affairs in the city of Paris and was buried in the basilica of Saint Denis. His successor was his son Robert, the most devout of kings, highly learned [Note: [Col. 0933D] So also Hugh, *Modern History*, ch. 9, above.] and modest. By Queen Constance, daughter of the count of Provence, he begot three sons: King Hugh, [Col. 0934A] who because of the extraordinary beauty of his body and character was called the Flower of Youth; Robert, duke of Burgundy; and Henry, later king of the Franks.

At the same time a certain knight named Walter and his wife handed the castle of Melun over to Count Odo. King Robert and Count Burchard assembled an army and summoned Norman auxiliaries, then besieged Melun. [Continuation of Aimoin, chs. 46–47.] When it had been stormed [Note: [Col. 0933] *expugnanto*, manuscript 1; *repugnante* corrected to *expugnato*, manuscript 2.] and taken, Walter and his wife, because they had betrayed it, were hanged on a gallows before the gate of that castle. King Robert then restored the same castle to Count Burchard [Note: [Col. 0934] *robertus*, manuscript 1.] [Note: [Col. 0933] *burchado*, manuscript 1? and 2.] just as he had formerly possessed it [Note: [Col. 0933] *possederant*, manuscripts 1? and 2.].

Then Renald the Old, count of Sens, full of every evil, died and was buried in the basilica of Saint Columba. His son Frotmund succeeded him, having married the daughter of Renald, count of Rheims. At that time Seguin, archbishop of Sens, marked the final day of his life. After his death, the church of Sens was without a shepherd for one year. All the people of that city asked that Archdeacon Leutric be given to them; but certain clerics seeking ordination resisted, especially Frotmund, son of Count Renald, who wanted his clerical son Bruno [Note: [Col. 0933] *brumonem*, manuscripts 1 and 2.] to be consecrated bishop. But by God’s will and apostolic authority, the suffragan bishops of the church of Sens consecrated Leutric bishop.

In that same year Henry, duke of Burgundy, died without sons, and the Burgundians rebelled, unwilling to receive King Robert, nephew [Col. 0934C] of that same Henry. Count Landric entered and held the city of Auxerre. On hearing this, King Robert gathered an army and summoned Richard, duke of the Normans. He ravaged Burgundy and besieged Auxerre for many days, but the Burgundians unanimously resisted submitting to him. He next besieged the castle of Avallon for almost three months. When it surrendered to him through hunger, he returned to Francia with his army.

31. [Note: [Col. 0933] “How the city of Sens was handed over to King Robert by the counsel of Rainald, bishop of Paris.” Added in manuscript 1; and the chapter begins before the words “When it surrendered through hunger.”] When Frotmund, count of Sens, died, his son Renard succeeded him, the most wicked among the wicked. He inflicted upon the churches and Christ’s faithful a persecution such as had not been heard of from the time of the pagans until the present day. Distressed by this [Col. 0934D] persecution, Leutric, archbishop of Sens, prayed earnestly that Christ might have mercy upon him and his people. Afterwards the city of Sens was captured by Archbishop Leutric, on the counsel of Rainald, bishop of Paris, and swiftly handed over to King Robert. Count Renard fled and hid naked. But his brother Frotmund and the other knights entered the city’s tower and held it for many days.

[Col. 0935A] King Robert attacked it, captured Frotmund there, and committed him to chains at Orléans, where he ended his life miserably. At the same time, in February, on two days—the fourteenth [Note: [Col. 0935] That is, the fourteenth and fifteenth; manuscript 3 omits the words.] and fifteenth—the sun shone marvellously in its strength. Around it was seen an enormous circle of ether-colour, shining like a rainbow in the clouds. Around that circle two suns were seen, like two very long rays: one emitting its brightness toward Aquitaine, the other [Note: [Col. 0935] “and another,” manuscript 3.] toward Francia. These signs were visible the whole day on the fifth weekday; on the following day, the sixth weekday, the same signs [Note: [Col. 0935] Omitted in manuscript 3.] likewise appeared in the sun from the first hour of the day until the [Note: [Col. 0935] “to,” manuscript 3.] full third hour, though not as bright as on the first day. On the first day of this sign the moon was fourteen days old; on the second [Note: [Col. 0935] “first—second,” manuscript 3.] it was fifteen.

32. [Note: [Col. 0935] A new chapter begins below with the words “Among other things which,” manuscript 1; it adds the rubric: “How, after the death of King Robert, his son Henry was crowned king.”] After this, the most Christian King Robert died in the year of the Lord [Note: [Col. 0935] “of the Lord’s Incarnation,” manuscript 3.] 1031 and was laid beside his father in the church of Saint [Note: [Col. 0935] “blessed,” manuscript 3.] Denis. After his death, his son Robert obtained the duchy of Burgundy, and Hugh, Flower of Youth, the elder son, anointed king [Note: [Col. 0935] “was,” added but deleted in manuscript 2.] [Note: [Col. 0935] “while his father was still alive,” added in manuscript 3.], received the crown of the kingdom of Francia. He shone forth, crowned with the splendid distinctions of war and the virtues of great courage [Note: [Col. 0935] *-que* is absent in manuscript 3.]. In the first year of his reign he was removed from human affairs [Note: [Col. 0935] “and honourably buried in the church of blessed Denis, his father still living,” manuscript 3.] [Note: [Col. 0935D] Hugh died before his father Robert, with whom he had been appointed king.]. His brother Henry, a most courageous knight, was raised to the monarchy of the kingdom and anointed king, though his mother Constance opposed him and stirred up many of the leading men of Gaul [Note: [Col. 0935] “Francia,” manuscript 3.] against him. In a short time, however, with a small force, he so overcame them all by arms that [Col. 0935C] they submitted themselves and all that was theirs to his power.

Among his other vigorous deeds, he restored Duke William of the Normans to his honour [Note: [Col. 0935] “honour,” manuscript 3.] after William had been disinherited by certain powerful Normans. William’s enemies having been defeated, some of them were hanged on the gallows, others committed to chains, and others deprived of their offices. By Anne, daughter of the king of Rus’, named Bullesclot [Note: [Col. 0935] *buflesdoc*, manuscript 3.], he begot King Philip and Hugh the Great, later count of Vermandois [Note: [Col. 0935] “afterwards count of Vermandois,” manuscript 3.]. In the third year of his reign [Note: [Col. 0935] “his,” manuscript 3.] the city of Paris [Note: [Col. 0935] “Paris,” manuscript 3.] burned in a fire. During his reign famine also prevailed for five years. Finally, after overcoming many battles and full of days, he died a natural death at the city of Sens [Note: [Col. 0935] “Paris,” manuscript 3.] (1060), and was buried beside his father in the basilica of Saint Denis.

[Col. 0935D] 33 [Note: [Col. 0935] I myself have established this division.]. Philip, however, his son, received the crown of the kingdom after him, anointed king at Rheims by Gervasius, archbishop of that same [Note: [Col. 0935] manuscript 3: “urbis eiusdem” (“of the same city”).] city. During his reign, on the seventh day before the Kalends of May, a comet appeared for nearly five days, sending forth a great radiance [Col. 0936A] toward the west. Not long afterward, namely in that same year (1066), on the feast day of Saint Michael, William, count of the Normans, crossed the sea with a vast fleet of ships and seized and took possession of the kingdom of the English. In those days the bones of blessed Nicholas were translated from the Lycian city of Myra to the Apulian city of Bari beside the sea. After these days the aforesaid William, count of the Normans [Note: [Col. 0935] duke of the Normans. 3.] and king of the English, died (1087), and his sons succeeded him: Robert in Normandy and William Rufus [Note: [Col. 0935] written above the line. 2.] in England. After this there arose a movement of diverse peoples to take Jerusalem (1097), crosses placed upon their shoulders over their garments, with the cry, “God wills it.” At its capture, a brightness was seen in heaven almost throughout the whole world. Afterwards William [Col. 0936B] Rufus, [Note: [Col. 0935] written above the line. 2.] king of the English, while intent upon hunting, was killed by an arrow carelessly discharged (1100). His brother Henry [Note: [Col. 0935] eius (“his”); ipsius (“his own”), manuscript 3.] succeeded him with the greatest speed, lest he be forestalled by his brother Robert, now returned from the [Note: [Col. 0935] “from” is absent in manuscript 3.] Jerusalem expedition [Note: [Col. 0935] At this point manuscript 1 adds in red: “How, after the death of King Robert, Henry his son succeeded to the kingdom of the Franks.”]. In the same year this Henry, crowned with the royal diadem, took as wife Matilda, daughter of the king of the Scots, a woman very learned.

At the same time, in February, a comet appeared; and in the following year, in May, Geoffrey Martel [Note: [Col. 0936D] The younger of this name, son of Fulk Rechin.], count of Anjou, a young man greatly to be lamented, was killed by an arrow during the siege of a certain castle. In that same year Henry, emperor of the Romans and Teutons, ended the last day of his life at Liège, at Saint Lambert’s (1106), while fleeing from his persecuting, perjured, [Col. 0936C] and rebellious son, whom he had honorably exalted as king. In the following year (1107), Lord [Note: [Col. 0935] donnus. 2.] Pope Paschal II came into France, where [Note: [Col. 0935] and. 3.] he was greatly honoured by King Philip and the leading men of Gaul, as befitted the dignity of the Apostolic See [Note: [Col. 0935] “the dignity to the see,” manuscript 1; “the see written above ‘dignity,’” manuscript 3; “the see and dignity,” manuscript 3.]. Having accomplished [Note: [Col. 0935] “which” is absent in manuscript 3.] that for which he had come, he returned in peace to his own see.

King Philip, in whose time these events occurred, at the beginning of his reign (1072) took as wife the sister, namely [Note: [Col. 0935] on the mother’s side, added in manuscript 3.] of Robert [Note: [Col. 0935] King Robert of Jerusalem, count of Flanders, son of Robert the Frisian, manuscript 3.], count of Flanders, whose praise is abundant in military affairs. By her he begot King Louis and one daughter, named Constance, whom her father, the king, joined in marriage to Hugh, count of Troyes. But afterwards, having taken her away from him on account of kinship, [Col. 0936D] he joined her in marriage at Chartres to Bohemond, a warlike man [Note: [Col. 0935] “of Roman descent,” added in manuscript 3 [ [Col. 0937D] “Sirinniorum,” manuscripts 1 and 2].].

Philip himself, while his lawful wife was still living, treacherously carried off at Tours the wife of Fulk Rechin, count of Anjou. [Col. 0937A] By her he begot Philip and Florus [Note: [Col. 0937] “and he begot F. by her,” manuscript 3.] and one daughter, whom Tancred of Antioch [Note: [Col. 0937] “a Norman by descent,” added in manuscript 3.] sought and received in marriage. Philip himself died at Melun, on the fourth day before the Kalends of August, in the forty-eighth year of his reign (1108), and was buried [Note: [Col. 0937] “and was buried,” manuscript 3.] in the church of Saint Benedict upon the Loire, in the district of Orléans. His son Louis succeeded him and was anointed king at Orléans by Lord [Note: [Col. 0937] donnus. 2.] Daigbert [Note: [Col. 0937] “Daimbert,” manuscript 3.], archbishop of Sens. Though harassed in many campaigns, partly through his own simplicity and partly through the disloyalty of his magnates, he nevertheless emerged victorious by God’s gift.

[Note: [Col. 0937A] Manuscript 3 adds: “He took as wife the daughter of Humbert of Maurienne, or, as people commonly say, ‘of the mountains’; by her he begot five sons: Philip, Louis, Robert, Henry—the fifth name does not occur to memory—and he [Col. 0938A] died as a boy [ [Col. 0937] Hugh. To these add Philip, archdeacon of Paris, and Peter of Courtenay.]; and he had one daughter by her. Philip, while his father was living, was anointed king at Rheims; but not long afterwards, falling from his horse in the city of Paris, he died (1129), and was buried in the church of Saint-Denis. In the same year his brother Louis was anointed king in the aforesaid city by Pope Innocent II, while he held a council there (1131). Then, after three years had passed, Henry, king of the English and duke of the Normans, died (1135); and Stephen, his nephew, count of Mortain, succeeded him. In the following year William, duke of the Aquitanians, being brought to his end, commanded his men to join his only daughter in marriage to Louis, the young son of the king of the Franks; for he lacked another heir. For his brother Raymond had shortly before gone to Jerusalem and, after Bohemond the younger, prince of Antioch, died, took his daughter as wife together with the principality of that city.”]

[Note: [Col. 0937B] In manuscripts 1 and 2 there follows a genealogy of the kings of the Franks, before which manuscript 1 places this red heading: “How, after the destruction of Troy, the people who fled were called Franks, and concerning the names of the kings.” The text of the genealogy is as follows:
