“After Troy had been captured and destroyed, Aeneas came into Italy with twenty-two ships—the ships in which Paris Alexander had gone to Greece and carried off Helen, and which bore the remnants of the Trojans. Latinus was then reigning there; Menestheus among the Athenians; Poliphides among the Sicyonians; Aptanes among the Assyrians; and among the Hebrews Lapdon was judge. When Latinus died, Aeneas ruled there for three years, the aforesaid kings remaining the same, except that among the Sicyonians [ [Col. 0937D] ‘Sirinniorum,’ manuscripts 1 and 2.] Pelasgus was now king, and Samson was judge of the Hebrews, who because of his extraordinary strength was thought to be Hercules.

“Also Antenor, the most noble of the Trojans, and many others fleeing from the destruction of the aforesaid city, after traversing Asia—and after making Friga king, while he remained with his followers among the Macedonians—entered [Col. 0937C] the mouths of the river Tanais; and, having passed beyond the Maeotian marshes, built in the borders of Pannonia a city called Sicambria. After Antenor’s death they appointed two men, Torgotus and Francio, from whom, as some think, the Franks received their name. When he died, they chose as leaders Sennon, Genebald, and Marcomer. His son Pharamond begot Clodio the Long-haired, from whom the kings of the Franks were called long-haired. When Clodio departed this life, Merovech, his kinsman, assumed the governance of the kingdom of the Franks; and from the useful King Merovech the kings of France were called Merovingians. Merovech begot Childeric; Childeric, Clovis; Clovis, Chlothar; Chlothar, Chilperic; Chilperic, Chlothar; Chlothar, Dagobert; Dagobert, Louis; Louis, Chlothar and the younger Chilperic and Theuderic; Theuderic, Childebert; Childebert, the younger Dagobert; the younger Dagobert, Theuderic; Theuderic [ [Col. 0937D] ‘Theuderic, Chlothar,’ added in the margin in manuscript 2.] Chlothar.

[Col. 0937D] “And after the migration of the generation, Ansbert begot Arnulf by the daughter of King Chlothar; Arnulf begot Saint Arnulf, later bishop of Metz. Saint Arnulf begot Ansegisel; Ansegisel, Pippin, mayor of the palace; Pippin, Charles Martel; Charles Martel, Pippin, later king; King Pippin, the emperor Charlemagne; [Col. 0938B] the emperor Charlemagne, the emperor Louis the Pious; the emperor Louis the Pious, the emperor Charles the Bald; Charles the Bald, King Louis only [ [Col. 0937D] ‘however,’ manuscript 1.]; Louis, Carloman and Louis; Carloman, Louis ‘Who-Did-Nothing’; Louis, Charles the Simple; Charles the Simple, Louis, who was handed over at Bayeux by Duke Hugh the Great. This Louis begot Lothar and Charles by Gerberga, sister of Emperor Otto; the elder Lothar, Louis and Charles. King Louis died young and without sons; his brother Charles succeeded him. Before he was anointed king, he was handed over with his wife at Laon by Ascelin, bishop of that same city, and delivered up to Hugh surnamed Capet. The names of the kings of France descended from the line of Hugh Capet, added in manuscript 1.]

“This Hugh committed him to custody at Orléans, where he died with his wife and the two sons whom he had begotten there, Louis and Charles. Here the line and kingdom [Col. 0938C] of Charles fail, and [ [Col. 0937D] Continues in another hand in manuscript 2.] pass to the aforesaid Hugh surnamed Capet. He begot King Robert; Robert, Henry; Henry, Philip; Philip, Louis; Louis, Louis the Most Pious, or [ [Col. 0938D] ‘or the Fat,’ added afterwards in manuscript 2.] the Fat. Louis [ [Col. 0938D] These words are written in a later hand, after other words had been erased: ‘Louis the Most Pious begot this Philip …’] begot Philip. Philip begot Louis. Louis begot Louis. Louis begot Philip.”]

Manuscript 1 continues after the words “King Robert” as follows:

“And Henry his son succeeded him. After him Philip his son reigned. When he died, Louis his son received his father’s kingdom. After him Louis his son reigned. After him Philip his son reigned. In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1181, he was anointed king at Rheims by Archbishop William, his maternal uncle, in the presence of his father Louis; and he was attended with martial splendour, while the barons of all France and Flanders stood about him—namely Philip, count of Flanders and Vermandois; Baldwin, count of Namur; Henry, count of Troyes; Stephen, count of Blois; [Col. 0938D] Theobald, count of Chartres, his maternal uncle, and many others. In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1214, the aforesaid King Philip waged war with the Alemanni, Teutons, and Flemings, with their emperor Otto, with the count of Flanders named Ferdinand, with Renaud of Boulogne, and with William Longsword, brother of the king of the English. He fought all of them and defeated them; Otto fled. [Col. 0939A] He brought Emperor Otto and the aforesaid counts, bound in chains, with him into France and committed them to custody. The glorious King Philip died in the sixty-third year of his life and the forty-fourth of his reign. This Philip [Col. 0940A] was the son of the above-mentioned King Louis. After him his son Louis reigned. After him his son Louis reigned, being in the eleventh year of his age.”]

[Col. 0939A] Therefore, when the aforesaid William, count of Poitou, died, Louis, the young king of the Franks, received his daughter together with her duchy. In that same year Louis, the elder [Col. 0940A] king of the Franks, died in the city of Paris on the Kalends of August and was buried in the church of Saint-Denis. His son Louis, king of the Franks and duke of Aquitaine, succeeded him in the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1137.

[Col. 0939]

# Treatise of Hugh of Saint-Mary, Monk of Fleury, on Royal Power and Priestly Dignity

(Baluze, *Miscellanea*, ed. Mansi, vol. III, p. 183.)

## The Prologue Begins

[Col. 0939]

[Col. 0939B] To Henry, most glorious king of the English: Brother Hugh, least of all monks, monk of most holy Benedict at Fleury, the gift of perpetual peace.

Considering, lord king, the peril of discord in which the holy Church is embroiled concerning royal power and priestly dignity—powers which some separate and divide from one another—I have resolved, moved by pious concern and brotherly love, to compose this little book, so that this contention may in some measure be quieted and the error spreading far and wide may likewise be mitigated. I mean the error of those who, rashly separating priestly dignity from royal dignity, overthrow the order established by God, while imagining that they know what they do not know. For they think that the ordering [Col. 0939C] of the earthly kingdom was established or instituted not by God but by men. Therefore they set priestly dignity above royal majesty, although it ought to be subject to it in order, though not in dignity, as this present little book will demonstrate.

Once the dark mist of this error has been driven away, perhaps they will yield to divine teachings and rational arguments. For error must be avoided not only in great matters but also in lesser ones. Error, moreover, is nothing other than to think false what is true, and true what is false; or to take as true what is uncertain; or to depart from the path of reason. But those who, desiring only to satisfy their own fury, strive to overturn the order of things which God has established incur the crime of sacrilege and are deservedly called Pharisees. For our Creator and Saviour, the Lord Jesus Christ, deigned to be called both King and Priest in his most holy ministry, in order to show us by what great bond or affinity king and priest ought to agree with one another. For what is joined in unity cannot be separated. When these powers disagree and conflict with one another, peace is dissolved, and the Church which Christ himself deigned to redeem by his blood is unhappily disturbed.

Therefore, lord king, I have resolved to assign or dedicate this work to you, so that it may be confirmed and strengthened by the privilege of your authority and disseminated in many places; or, if it is useless, torn apart. In this too I follow the footsteps of ancient men, who once presented their studies to kings [Col. 0940C] trained in literary learning. Finally, I pray the excellence of your highness that you reconsider it both privately and with the wise men who are with you, examine it diligently, and strive to expose whatever in it you judge should be refuted. For I know that by those who attempt, in their rashness, to overthrow the order of things, it will not only be condemned but even spat upon—either because it seems to depart from their opinion, or because it seems to explain the subject proposed in rustic speech. For to those blind in heart, alas, their own blindness and rashness often seem pleasing.

Nevertheless, through their magnificence I ask them not to despise my rustic eloquence, but rather to prefer hearing true words to eloquent ones. Besides, I know that truth is heard more safely than it is preached. Therefore I now entreat all venerable bishops and the other prelates and discerning clerics of the holy Church who will read these things not to judge me presumptuous or rash, as though I were arrogantly attempting to instruct those who sit in cathedras and know the mysteries of divine philosophy. No, I beg them not to think so; rather, let them read and receive these things devoutly and with equanimity.

For I desire that they too, [Col. 0942A] all my venerable fathers and lords, may daily advance in Christ Jesus our Lord; that in their times the body of the holy Church, arranged in fitting order, may be strengthened; and that it may continually enjoy the firm bond of peace. But may almighty God deign, lord king, by his grace to preserve you for us sound and unharmed through long courses of time. Amen.

The prologue ends.

## The Book Begins

[Col. 0941]

### Chapter I. That there is no power except from God

[Col. 0941B]

I know that there are some in our times who assert that kings derived their beginning not from God but from those who, ignorant of God, in the beginning of the world—driven by the devil—desired through pride, plunder, treachery, homicide, and finally almost every crime, by blind cupidity and unspeakable presumption or rashness, to dominate men who were their equals. How frivolous their opinion is is evident from the apostolic testimony which says: “There is no authority except from God; and those authorities which exist have been ordained by God” (Rom. 13:1). It is therefore established by this statement that royal power on earth has been established or instituted not by men but by God.

For he, at the very beginning of the world, endowed the first human being with the gift of wisdom and set him over all [Col. 0941C] creatures of the world. In this matter he subtly made known to him that there is one King and Lord of the whole creation of heaven and earth, whom that heavenly court which is above us—distinguished by fixed ranks and powers—rightfully serves and obeys. And so that we may recognize this likewise in the form of our own body, we see that all the limbs of our body are subject to the head. It is evident that all the members of the human body are subject and subordinate to the head both by position and by order.

Thus it is quite clear to us that almighty God not only distinguished the human body by the various forms of its limbs, but also distinguished the whole world by fixed ranks and powers, just as that heavenly court is known to be distinguished, [Col. 0941D] in which God the almighty Father alone holds royal dignity, and in which, after him, angels, archangels, thrones, dominions, and whatever other powers there are are known to preside over one another in a wondrous and orderly variety of powers. Yet the person of the Father is one, that of the Son another, and that of the Holy Spirit another. But Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are one God. The Father alone, however, is not from another; while the Son is born from the Father. Yet, as has already been said, the Father and Son have one divinity and one majesty. There is, I say, one God the Father, from whom are all things, and from whom is the Son, through whom are all things, so that the authority of that first principle may be preserved in all things and the one Godhead may be adored in three persons.

### Chapter II. That, as the head in the body, so the king ought to hold primacy in his kingdom

[Col. 0942B]

God also formed one man in the world, from whom the whole human race afterwards derived its origin. Accordingly, just as God the Son was born of God the Father, so that every creature might be made through him, so woman was formed from man, through whom there might arise the whole progeny of the human race. Woman, I say, was not born from man but made, because she could not be born from a single body. But God the Son was born from God the Father ineffably and incomprehensibly—as spirit from spirit, God from God—so that every creature might be made through him. Woman, however, was made from man, so that birth might arise through her.

[Col. 0942C] Man and woman are nevertheless of one substance; but man is greater in rank, because woman is from man, as the Apostle testifies when he says: “The head of the woman is the man” (1 Cor. 11). The Father and the Son too are of one substance; but the Father is known to be greater in order, not in nature, as Paul testifies when he says: “God is the head of Christ” (ibid.). For, as was already stated, the Father is from no one, while the Son is from the Father, so that the essence of the supreme Trinity may be adored and venerated in the unity of the Godhead.

The principal powers by which this world is governed are likewise two: royal and priestly. The Lord Jesus Christ himself chose to bear these two powers in his own person in a most holy mystery, since he is both King and Priest: King, because he governs us; Priest, because by the sacrifice of his body he cleansed us from the [Col. 0942D] defilements of our sins and reconciled us to his Father.

### Chapter III. That the king bears the image of God the Father, and the bishop that of Christ

Yet the king seems to bear the image of the almighty Father in the body of his kingdom, and the bishop the image of Christ. Therefore all the bishops of that kingdom seem rightly to be subject to the king, just as the Son is found to be subject to the Father—not in nature but in order—so that the whole kingdom may be reduced to one principle. The Lord clearly reveals the sacrament of this mystery in Exodus, where he says to Moses: “Behold, I have made you a god to Pharaoh, and Aaron shall be your prophet” [Col. 0943A] (Exod. 2 [an erroneous citation in the source]). Moses, moreover, seems among the Hebrew people to have borne the image of a king, and Aaron that of a priest, without prejudice to another holy significance of the sacrament. Accordingly Moses himself, in a most holy mystery, builds and sanctifies the tabernacle, consecrates Aaron, sets before the people the ordinances of divine law, and Aaron, with the rod which Moses had handed to him, performs signs and wonders before Pharaoh and his nobles.

### Chapter IV. On the office of the lawful king
The office of a king, therefore, is to correct the people subject to him from error and to recall them to the path of fairness and justice. Hence in the book of Judges you will find that, before the children of Israel had a king, Jonathan, Moses’ grandson, though counted among the Levites, presumed to take the priesthood for himself: “For each man,” it says, “did what pleased himself, because there was no king in Israel” (Judg. XVII). From these words it is plainly evident that where there is no king to govern the people, recall them from rashness, and lead them away from it, the whole body of the kingdom totters.

Accordingly, he is rightly called a king who knows how suitably to govern his own conduct and rightly to regulate those subject to him. For this reason, I say, Almighty God is known to have set a king above other human beings—though he shares with them the same condition of being born and dying—so that he may both restrain by his fear the people subject to him from evil and subject them to laws for right living. Thus through an earthly kingdom the heavenly kingdom often advances: what the priest cannot accomplish through the discourse of teaching, royal power accomplishes or commands through the fear of discipline. For the people are readily corrected through fear of the king. The king himself, however, is scarcely deterred from an unjust path except by fear of God alone and by dread of hell.

Yet he must always recall in his heart the saying of that most wise man: “The greater the fortune, the less the licence.” He must always benefit the people subject to him more than harm them. Nevertheless, the persons of rulers are often bestowed according to the deserts of their subjects; and thus the merits of subjects and rulers are sometimes so mutually bound together that, through the fault of the ruler, the life of the subjects becomes worse, while through the merits of the subjects the life of rulers is changed. Yet Almighty God, the Lord of all creation, so ordered his creation [Col. 0943D] that he should work good from both good and evil persons. God, I say, works good from good and evil persons—he who does and disposes all things justly.

Thus it comes about that both an evil angel and an evil human being serve divine providence, although they do not know what good divine providence or will works through them. His will, moreover, is recognized as just even when it inflicts evils; and because it is just, it is not evil. And what is done well is done justly. Thus, I say, not only all human beings, but every creature according to its kind and order, is subject to the laws of divine providence, so that nothing unjust can happen to creation. This the Evangelist shows where he says: “Are not two sparrows sold for an assarion? Yet not one of them falls to the ground without the will of your Father” (Matt. X).

Therefore it is clear from this testimony [Col. 0944A] that even what human beings consider most worthless on earth is governed by the power of God. But because God himself specially cares for and governs pure and rational souls—whether through the best angels, who are ministering spirits on account of those who are to receive the inheritance, or through human beings who serve him with their entire will—while he disposes and governs the rest through the wicked, the Apostle could most truly say what is written: “Is God concerned with oxen?” (I Cor. IX).

Accordingly, a good king is given to human beings when God is propitious, and a wicked one when God is angry, as he himself testifies through the prophet, saying to the people of Israel: “I will give you a king in my wrath” (Hos. XIII). And elsewhere: “God permits a hypocrite to reign because of the sins of the people” (Job XXXIV). Therefore all kings and princes must be endured by their subjects, and no one should rashly resist them, lest, while their injustice is reproved, humility itself—the teacher of uprightness—be lost.

Thus, I say, subjects must maintain a course of rectitude and humility toward kings and princes: they should disapprove their rulers’ blameworthy deeds in such a way that their minds do not depart from reverence for their superiors. The good sons of Noah are read to have done this when they endeavoured to cover their father’s shameful parts with turned-away faces (Gen. IX). All subjects imitate them whose superiors’ evils displease them, yet who conceal those evils from others. They too carry the covering with turned-away faces when, judging the deed yet revering the master, they do not wish to see what they cover.

Our Lord Jesus Christ, while living on earth, also plainly showed us this model of humility and gentleness when he humbly avoided Herod, that most savage king. For by that very power through which he deigned to summon the Magi from distant lands to worship him, he was able to destroy Herod. He likewise later often withdrew in his gentleness from the princes of the priests raging against him; and he ordered lepers to show themselves to them according to the decrees of the law, although he knew them unworthy of priestly dignity, lest he seem to do them an injury.

All who are placed in authority must likewise be honoured by those over whom they preside, even if not for their own sake, then for the order [Col. 0944D] and rank that they have received from God. For thus the Apostle commands: “Be subject to all higher powers. For there is no authority except from God; and those that exist have been ordained by God” (Rom. XIII). As has already been shown above, God himself sometimes customarily accomplishes his equitable and most just will through the depraved wills of wicked persons: thus Christ was killed for us through the malevolent Jews, according to the good will of the Father.

Knowing and believing this, and likewise observing the Apostle’s command, we honour even pagans who are set in authority and endure patiently the evils they inflict upon us, lest we seem to wrong God, who has raised and exalted them above human beings by the title of office, though they are unworthy of the rank which they enjoy. For we see even reprobate kings honoured by divine revelations. To Pharaoh a dream of the coming famine was divinely revealed. Nebuchadnezzar, with many standing by, is read to have recognized the Son of God in the fiery furnace among the three youths. Caiaphas too, that most wicked high priest, is known from evangelical testimony to have prophesied—not, of course, by his own merit, but by virtue of the priestly office, which he possessed by God’s just and certain judgment.

David also honoured King Saul, whom he knew to have been rejected and deposed by God, so that he did not dare to stretch out his hand against him, although God had delivered him into his hands. For during many years King Saul retained the dignity of royal office, God’s patience sustaining him—God who often declines to impose upon sinners the fitting sentence of his judgment—after he had deserved to be rejected by God for his pride and disobedience.

And when God had already rejected him, as is written, the most holy prophet Samuel went by divine oracle to Bethlehem, to the house of Jesse, not openly but secretly, so that he might appear to fear the king, when he anointed David king. What should I say of the most holy prophet Elijah, who preferred to evade by flight King Ahab and his wife Jezebel, raging against him, rather than inflict any harm upon them? For he was not unaware of the punishment that threatened transgressors of the divine law. Yet he desired rather to await patiently the evil that he knew would someday befall them than to hurt them by any loss of punishment.

The most holy man, therefore, wisely avoided the savage tyranny of the king and the foolish and senseless insolence of his wife. For in God’s hand it lies both to cast down the proud from their lofty seat and to raise every humble person to the summit of dignity. Finally, as the Apostle commands, every soul ought to be subject to higher powers, and all things should be rendered to all persons which, without prejudice to the worship of our Lord God, are rendered to princes. “I urge,” says the same Apostle, “that first of all supplications and prayers be made for kings and all who are placed in high station, that we may lead a secure and tranquil life in all piety and charity” (I Tim. II).

He also commands that all who are under the yoke of slavery should consider their masters worthy of every honour; and that those who have unbelieving masters should not despise them but serve them all the more, because they are believers, on account of him who has subjected them to those masters, knowing that, as the same Apostle says elsewhere, “Every transgression and disobedience receives a fitting recompense” (Heb. II). The Lord Jesus Christ himself seems to have given us an example of this submission and humility in his own person when he did not disdain to pay tribute to Caesar for his own head.

Concerning this most gentle service a certain wise man also declares: “The just person serves freely; the unjust person, in fetters.” Finally, we are commanded to pray for such rulers, not to resist them with abuse, as Samuel is read to have prayed for Saul, though he was not heard. For by the just judgment of God that proud and unrepentant king had already been rejected [Col. 0946A]. Therefore the holy Church customarily prays for kings who transgress the divine law, because the sacred reading of the books makes plain that many holy men have overcome tyrants by pure prayer and have often routed more enemies by blessed prayers than by weapons.

For Moses prayed; he did not fight, when the sea was divided and the people crossed through its midst, while Pharaoh was drowned with his chariots and horsemen in its waves. Moses raised nothing against Pharaoh except the rod alone. Amalek, moreover, was defeated while Moses raised his hands to God. The walls of Jericho likewise fell at the sound of sacred trumpets. King Hezekiah too did not arm himself with weapons, but clothed himself in sackcloth and covered his head with ashes instead of a helmet, when Sennacherib, king of the Assyrians, came against him surrounded by many attendants. But the prayer of the most gentle King Hezekiah ascended to God, and an angel descended into the camp of the most proud Sennacherib, killing eighty-five thousand men from his army.

Who, considering these and similar miracles, would not marvel and understand that wicked kings must be resisted by spiritual prayers rather than carnal weapons? Accordingly, when the Empress Justina, supporter of the Arians, inflicted many injuries upon Saint Ambrose, bishop of Milan, on account of his defence of the Catholic faith, he did not endeavour violently to resist her with arms; rather, he restrained her ferocity with continual—that is, day-and-night—prayers.

For it is impious and rash for any bishop to contend with a king or emperor by arms and to defile holy places consecrated to God with human blood. Our Lord Jesus Christ, our Saviour and Creator, taught this most plainly when the Apostle Peter drew his sword, seized the servant of the high priest, and cut off his ear. For he said to him: “Put your sword back into its sheath. For all who take up the sword shall perish by the sword” (John XVIII). And then: “Do you think that I cannot ask my Father, and he will at once provide me with more than twelve legions of angels?” (ibid.).

Hence those who resist authority not from zeal for God but through their own rashness or arrogance seem to rebel against God, who said: “Through me kings reign and princes rule” [Col. 0946D] (Prov. VIII); his judgments, though they remain hidden, are never unjust. The holy Church is in no way accustomed rashly to resist such persons with arms or to devise their destruction by any deceit, mindful of the Lord’s command in which he says to his faithful: “Vengeance is mine, and I will repay” (Rom. XII).

For a person who remains good is not defiled if joined to an evil person; but the evil person is turned toward good if he follows the examples of the good. The Lord also patiently awaits us daily while we sin, granting us time for repentance, so as to exercise and instruct our patience by his example; thus we may know how greatly we ought to endure evil people, since we do not know what they will become, whereas he who spares them and permits them to live is ignorant of nothing to come. Therefore, if rebels should happen to die because of this obstinacy, they should by no means boast of the name of martyrdom, since they are rightly condemned to punishment as thieves are.

Yet no one ought to give consent to authorities for the perpetration of evil. For if earthly service is owed to them by worshippers of Christ, innocence is owed to God. Hence, should any Christian perhaps be compelled either to violate the rule of justice or innocence by obeying them, or to pay any penalty, even death, for refusing such obedience, let the faithful soul choose rather to lose this fleeting life than to incur guilt, remembering what is written in the Gospel: “Do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul; rather fear him who can destroy both soul and body in hell” (Luke XII).

But Holy Scripture detests flatterers of kings and princes—those, namely, who for earthly profit exalt their rulers’ wickedness with praise—when it says: “Woe to those who call evil good and good evil” (Isa. V). And elsewhere: “No one can serve God and Mammon” (Luke XVI), together with the rest that follows in that chapter. The Lord shows how faithful service is rendered to kings and authorities when he says: “Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s, and to God the things that are God’s” (Matt. XXII): that is, he commands earthly service and honour to be rendered to king or prince, and inviolate purity of mind and body to be preserved for God.

## CHAPTER V. On the election of a bishop

[Col. 0947C]

Therefore, prompted by the Holy Spirit, the king may, as I judge, confer the honour of the episcopate on a devout cleric. But the archbishop ought to entrust to him the care of souls. In promoting ecclesiastical and most holy men, all the most Christian kings and princes of old employed this judicious custom, down to our own times. That cleric appears to be devout whom love of money does not trouble and whom reprobate morals or blameworthy conduct do not render reprehensible or contemptible.

But where a bishop is elected by clergy or people according to ecclesiastical custom, the king ought not tyrannically to inflict any force or disturbance upon those who make the election reasonably, but should give his consent to the lawful ordination. If, however, the man elected is found blameworthy, not only the king but not even the people of the province ought to give their assent or support to his election. Rather, they should publicly expose the crimes by which he is stained with detestable infamy, so that the rashness of those electing him may at least be restrained by this disgrace.

After the election, the elected bishop ought to receive from the royal hand not ring or staff, but investiture with temporal possessions; and, in regard to his orders, he ought to receive from his archbishop the care of souls by ring or staff, so that such business may be conducted without dispute and the prerogative of its authority may be preserved for both temporal and spiritual powers. If this is regularly observed, the saying which our Saviour gave as a command in the Gospel will be fulfilled: “Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s, and to God the things that are God’s” [Col. 0948A] (Matt. XXII). What has been firmly and orderly established will not be shaken, and a great accumulation of tribulations will be far from the holy Church.

For the king, as was stated earlier, appears to hold the image of God the Father, and the bishop that of Christ. Although the Lord Jesus Christ himself appears to say in the Gospel to his disciples and their followers: “You did not choose me, but I chose you and appointed you to go and bear fruit, and that your fruit should remain; and I dispose for you a kingdom as my Father disposed one for me” (John XV)—namely, a kingdom of holy souls, not the kingdom of this world, as he himself testified to Pilate at the time of his Passion, saying: “My kingdom is not of this world” (Matt. XVIII). For, as the Apostle Paul writes to Timothy, “No one serving as a soldier of God entangles himself in secular affairs” (II Tim. II).

## CHAPTER VI. Again, on the office of a lawful king

Moreover, the office of a lawful king is to govern the people in justice and equity and to defend the holy Church with all his strength. He ought also to be guardian of orphans, protector of widows, and helper of the poor, so that with blessed Job he may be able to say to the Lord: “I was an eye to the blind and a foot to the lame, and I diligently investigated the matter which I did not know” (Job XXIX).

Accordingly, he must love Almighty God, who has set him over many thousands of people, with his whole heartfelt affection, and love the people entrusted to him by God as himself. It is also the mark of an eminent king and prince to adorn the churches of his kingdom with most beautiful buildings, enlarge them through his own labours, and preserve in them more devotedly the worship of religion, as Constantine the devout emperor and the other kings and princes of ancient times are known to have done.

He must especially excel in four chief virtues: sobriety, justice, prudence, and temperance. By sobriety he is guarded from all idleness and mental sluggishness; by justice he is found acceptable both to God and to sensible human beings. Through prudence he distinguishes and separates the just from the unjust, and through temperance he avoids every excess. Besides these marks of virtue, it befits him to be learned in letters, so that his mind may be sharpened daily by reading divine books and formed and strengthened by the examples of both ancient and modern men. For knowledge not supported by acquaintance with letters may be judged vain, since it is always known to fluctuate.

“Yet the beginning of wisdom is the fear of the Lord” [Col. 0948D] (Ps. CX). For Solomon testifies: “He who is without fear of the Lord cannot be justified” (Ecclus. XXVIII). For his impetuosity and anger are his own ruin. But one who loves wisdom shall be guided by the Lord. Solomon, not ignorant of this, humbly prayed to the Lord, saying:

> “God of our fathers, who made all things by your Word, and by your wisdom created man, that he might have dominion over your creature which was made by you, and that he might govern the world in equity and judge judgment in justice and uprightness of heart: give me wisdom, the assistant at your throne, and do not reject me from among your children; for I am your servant and the son of your handmaid, a weak man and of short time, and too little for understanding judgment and laws.
>
> But you chose me, Lord, to preside over your people and to judge your sons and daughters. Reveal to me therefore what is pleasing in your sight and what is right in your commandments; for you are the guide of wisdom and the corrector of the wise, and we and our words are in your hand, as are all wisdom, knowledge of works, and discipline.
>
> Send, I pray, Lord, wisdom into my heart from your holy heavens and from the throne of your majesty, that it may be with me [Col. 0949B] and labour with me, and that I may know what is acceptable to you. For it knows and understands all things, and will guide me soberly in my works and guard me by its power; then my works shall be acceptable, and I shall govern my people justly.
>
> Who among human beings, Lord, can know your counsel? Or who can know what you will, unless the spirit of your knowledge from your heights has filled him? For the corruptible body weighs down the soul, and the earthly dwelling oppresses the mind that thinks many thoughts. But through wisdom all who pleased you have been healed.
>
> For you have mercy on all because you can do all things, and you overlook human sins for the sake of repentance. You love all things and hate nothing that you have made; for you would not have established anything while hating it. How then could anything endure unless you willed to preserve it? Yet you spare all things because they are your creatures.
>
> O how good you are, Lord, and gracious toward all: you have mercy on whom you will, and harden whom you will. Some indeed you justify, but others the vengeance of your justice afflicts forever. Others, through the very things by which they sin, you also punish in the present. Yet through all your scourges and mercies you counsel and address many, that, leaving wickedness, they may return to you.
>
> A human being indeed loses his soul through wickedness, for he cannot escape your hand. But woe to all who have not known you, Lord. Yet you, our God, are kind and true, patient and merciful toward all who trust in you, and you order all things mercifully [Col. 0949D]. For even if we have sinned, we are yours, knowing your greatness; and if we have not sinned, we know that we are reckoned as being with you.
>
> To know you, Lord, is perfected justice; and to know your righteousness is the root of immortality. But ungodly persons who deny you shall be crushed by the strength of your arm. For, fearing no one, you will grant pardon for their sins. Who indeed will say to you, ‘Why have you done thus?’ Or who will stand against your judgment? Or what judge of unrighteous people will come into your presence? Or who will charge you if those whom you made perish?
>
> For there is no other God than you, who cares for all and disposes all things by just judgment. Neither king nor tyrant will inquire before you concerning those whom you have destroyed. But you, Lord God of hosts, judge with tranquillity and govern us with great reverence.
>
> You have given judgment over the senseless as an object of derision; and those who were not corrected by mockery experienced due judgment. I look upon the nations of humankind, Lord, and see that no one who hoped in you was put to shame, remained in your commandments, and was abandoned. And who invoked you, and you despised him?
>
> For you are devout and merciful, and in time of tribulation forgive sins to all who seek you in truth. Woe to the double-hearted, to lips of wickedness, and to hands that do evil. Woe to the hypocrite in the sight of human beings. Woe to those weak in heart who do not believe you; therefore they shall not be protected by you.
>
> But those who believe in you shall not be faithless; rather, they shall have patience until they behold you [Col. 0950B], saying: ‘If we have no patience, we shall fall into your hands.’ It is dreadful, Lord, to fall into your hands. The heart that is hard shall fare badly at the last; and he who loves danger shall perish in it.
>
> I know, Lord, that I shall not be hidden among a great people nor concealed in the immeasurable creation, because you hold the throne of heaven, look upon the abysses, and behold the inner parts of the children of humankind. Spare me, Lord, for I speak to you although I am dust and ashes, full of the rottenness of diverse sins; yet I know that, according to your greatness, so is your mercy with you.
>
> Lord, Father and God of my life, do not abandon me to an evil thought; let not my offences appear before you, nor let my enemy rejoice over me. Do not give me haughtiness of eyes, and turn every wicked desire away from me. Turn away from me the desire of the belly and of sexual intercourse; and do not hand me over to an irreverent and unbridled soul, but grant what is necessary for my sustenance.”

This is Solomon’s prayer, which we have collected from his books in scattered portions and included in this book for the instruction of the king, so that he might know what he ought to ask from God.

## CHAPTER VII. Again, on the office of a lawful king

But, setting these matters aside for the present, we again admonish him to endeavour daily to reform the conduct of his subjects by exhorting, threatening, persuading, correcting, and showing examples of good works [Col. 0950D]. He should also strive to honour wise men and, equally, all servants of the Church. Let him receive the admonitions of holy men as though they were oracles of God, and reasonably comply with holy bishops. For by Christ’s servants and wise men, as by certain most firm foundations, the eminence of the kingdom is upheld and strengthened.

For holy Joseph aided Pharaoh far more usefully by the soundness of his counsel than if he had bestowed a great sum of money upon him. Money is easily spent, but the counsels of wise men cannot be exhausted. Hence it is clear that wisdom is better than commerce in silver and gold, and that its fruits are of the first and purest quality. Let him therefore be generous and munificent, affable and calm. Let him also have a cheerful disposition, an instructed tongue, a ready mind, truthful speech, pure faith, outstanding devotion, and restrained laughter. Let his movement be energetic, his bearing and gait honourable, and his fare plentiful, yet not excessive.

Let him cast envy, luxury, and drunkenness from his mind as the vilest filth, and also most evil greed, because “greed is the root of all evils” [Col. 0951A] (I Tim. VI). Let his servants be modest, his counsellors sensible, and his officials faithful and prudent. Let him honour and love his faithful men, and exalt and protect those who serve him.

But toward transgressing kings, remedies of such a kind must be applied that royal majesty may be honoured in them while guilt is punished by the censure of justice. For royal power is placed beneath the discipline of religion. Although the king is endowed with the summit of power, he is nevertheless bound by the bond of Christian faith. Yet he must be corrected wisely, not with the swelling of pride but with the affection of charity. Of the angry or foolish teacher Solomon says: “In the mouth of the fool is the rod of pride” (Prov. XIV). Foolish and proud teachers, therefore, turn the severity of discipline into the frenzy of rage and the monstrosity of cruelty.

Nevertheless, lawful kings are not to be despised on account of reprobate ones. For the sacred principate of the heavenly court was not rejected or despised by God because the devil, their prince, in pride against him seized tyranny and persuaded the ranks subject to him by wicked counsel to sin with him. Rather, the Lord Jesus Christ afterward descended from heaven to suppress that same devil, who had presumptuously claimed for himself the dignity of that name and its throne.

For after God the Father the devil wished to be called God, and rashly desired to sit at the right hand of God the Father—though this did not belong to him, but to the Son of God, who after God the Father, as has already been said, is second not by nature but by order. Therefore the Lord Jesus Christ came into the world as was fitting, and revealed himself not to all human beings but only to his followers, so that, once the person of the devil had been rejected, they might recognize him whose principate and power Satan himself had claimed through his own rashness.

But the devil and the princes of this world were utterly unable to recognize Christ’s divinity hidden in flesh, because, as the Apostle testifies, “Had they known, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory” [Col. 0951D] (I Cor. II). Thus it happened that he who by cunning, not violence, had first subjected the first human being to himself through consent to sin, lost him through God’s cunning, while he inflicted death through his agents upon one whom he dared to kill though free from every sin.

Accordingly, by such an exchange Christ both restored the number of angels and liberated the human race by his blood from the devil’s yoke. Thus it came about that the devil, who through one sinful human being had subjected the whole human race to himself, lost through one human being who did not sin what he possessed. But let what has been said about the devil and his tyranny suffice.

Yet this example plainly shows that a dominion which sedition extorts or ambition seizes is usually destructive. For things begun from an evil principle are with difficulty brought to a good end. Therefore rulers of this kind are rightly called not kings but tyrants; and bishops who presume to ordain them, or give consent to their perverse ordination, must be punished by the dart of anathema.

Likewise, the holy Church customarily condemns a heretical king by divine authority for the defence of the Catholic faith and smothers him beneath a sentence of anathema, lest the fellowship of the holy Catholic community be defiled by association with him. Does not the Apostle Paul separate and divide us from such a man when he says: “Avoid a heretical person after a first and second correction, knowing that one of this sort is perverted and sins, condemned by his own judgment” [Col. 0952B] (Tit. III)?

Solomon also declares a pagan person better than a heretic when he says: “A living dog is better than a dead lion” (Eccl. IX), calling the pagan a living dog and the heretic a dead lion. But many earthly princes persecute truth in holy and just people, because they do not wish their deeds to be condemned by them. Yet one who hates truth is certainly known not to love God, who is truth.

Foreseeing this, the Lord, encouraging the bishop who seems opposed to earthly princes not through his own rashness but through zeal for God to endure the world’s hatred, sets forth his own example and says: “The servant is not greater than his lord. If they persecuted me, they will persecute you also. If they kept my word, they will keep yours also” (John XV). And again: “If the world hates you, know that it hated me before you” (ibid.). Here he calls “the world” those by whom the crimes of this world are loved. Moreover, “he who is of God hears the words of God” (John VIII).

Therefore the king ought willingly to lend his ear to episcopal admonitions and faithfully obey the priest who offers salutary counsel, because the Lord seems to have spoken concerning such men in his own words: “He who hears you hears me; and he who despises you despises me” (Luke X). But if a king begins through his own arrogance or swelling pride to turn his ear away from sound and salutary doctrine, he appears to be obstinate and rebellious not toward the bishop but toward God, whose wrath it is exceedingly dangerous and dreadful to incur. For it is written: “God resists the proud but gives grace to the humble” [Col. 0952D] (Jas. IV).

A king should in no way presume to inflict death or scandal upon such persons. For because of this crime we find that many kings and emperors departed this life miserably and unexpectedly. Concerning these persons—that is, bishops and holy men—the Lord says: “He who touches you is as one who touches the pupil of my eye” (Zech. II). But if this condition should be set before a Catholic man, that he must either favour a heretic or undergo death for the defence of the Catholic faith, let him choose rather to die than to live with the purity of holy faith violated, turning over in his heart what is written in the Gospel book: “What does it profit a man if he gains the whole world but suffers loss to his soul? Or what exchange will a man give for his soul?” [Col. 0953A] (Matt. XVI). And likewise what the Lord promises his faithful, saying: “Whoever confesses me before human beings, I too will confess him before my Father who is in heaven” (Matt. X).

## CHAPTER VIII. On reprobate kings and princes

Moreover, kings, princes, and tyrants themselves, when they refuse to be subject to God and to keep his commandments, commonly lose the force and power of their dominion, just as the first human being is known to have lost the strength of his dominion and the prerogative of his dignity after his transgression. For after he refused to be subject to the divine command, he immediately experienced even the members of his own body rebelling against him and the fiery stings of carnal desire raging against his will in his flesh.

The fishes of the sea, the birds of heaven, and the beasts of the field, which before the commission of the sin had been subject to him as though private animals, began to cast off the yoke of his dominion and no longer wished to serve him as before. Nevertheless, by the force of his reason he eventually began little by little to subject them to himself and to turn them to his own use through ingenious arts.

In the same way, a people subject to a king hostile to God often begins to rise against him, attack him with diverse and manifold plots, and weary him with many adversities. This appears to be the point of God’s decree to punish the Babylonian king not with fierce beasts but with flies and serpents: so that human pride may understand that swollen and proud persons are often subdued and cast down from their height by humble and lowly people [Col. 0953C].

Such people also commonly end their lives by an ignominious death or fail in shameful poverty, as Herod and Pilate did: Herod, crawling with worms, expired miserably; Pilate, condemned to exile, died poor and destitute. Those also who pervert just judgments through love, hatred, fear, pity, negligence, rashness, or the favour of gain commonly suffer dreadful illnesses near the end of life, or disgrace, poverty of possessions, or sickness of their limbs.

## CHAPTER IX. On the dignity of priests
But since, as I think, I have now spoken at sufficient length on these matters according to the capacity of my understanding, it remains for me to add a few remarks concerning those things which pertain to the bishop. Thus to the bishop there has been granted by God and the Lord Jesus Christ the privilege of opening and closing heaven to men. Kings also, and all earthly powers, bow their heads to him for Christ’s sake; for although a king or emperor is endowed with the summit of royal authority, he is nevertheless bound fast by the bond of faith. He too is called the salt of the earth because of the seasoning of doctrine with which he ought to season the minds of the faithful; and king, because of the leadership which he ought to provide for the people; and angel, [Col. 0954A] because he announces good things; and shepherd, because he satisfies men with the fare of the divine word.

The Apostle Paul declares in his epistle what character he ought to possess and with what virtues he ought to shine, saying: “A bishop, he says, must be blameless, sober, chaste, hospitable, prudent, not a novice, not given to wine, not a striker, not contentious, but modest. He must also have a good testimony from those who are outside” (1 Tim. 3). For, as is contained elsewhere, he himself ought to display an example of good works and a better life not only to the people subject to him, but also to unruly persons—that is, Gentiles—so that there may be fulfilled in him what the Lord said in the Gospel when commanding his apostles: “So let your light shine before men, [Col. 0954B] that they may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven” (Matt. 5).

He ought also to command the rich not to think proudly or to hope in the uncertainty of riches, but in the living and true God, who provides all things to all for enjoyment: to do good, to become rich in good works, to give readily, to lay up for themselves a good foundation for the future, that they may be able to attain eternal life (1 Tim. 6). Moreover, he must by no means fight with arms against a Catholic king, although he greatly surpasses him in the dignity of his ministry—by as much, namely, as divine offices are known by their holiness to excel secular affairs.

For by the testimony of Holy Scripture the bishop appears also to possess royal dignity. [Col. 0954C] For the Lord Jesus Christ says to his apostles and their successors: “I appoint for you, as my Father appointed for me, a kingdom” (Luke 22). And the Apostle says: “You are an elect race, a royal priesthood” (1 Pet. 2). Therefore, if it should happen that a bishop is found blameworthy—for there is no person who does not sin—such a matter should be concluded not in a secular court but in a general synod.

Accordingly, the bishop ought to perform between the king and the sheep entrusted to him the office of an excellent shepherd, and readily expose himself to danger for the flock committed to him. He, I say, ought with all exertion to turn the wrath of king and prince away from the people, and to persist night and day before God in devout prayers alike for the safety of king and people. For he appears to hold on earth the place of Christ, the supreme Son of God, [Col. 0954D] who offered himself to be sacrificed for us sinners. Hence he ought to stand as mediator between us and God. He is holy among the holy—namely, among clerics and presbyters—over all of whom he is eminent and pre-eminent. He is the bridegroom of the Church; he is Christ’s vicar, that he may have compassion upon our infirmities. Of him the Apostle Paul says: “Every high priest, taken from among all men, is appointed for men in matters pertaining to God, that he may offer gifts and sacrifices for their sins” (Heb. 5).

All bishops, therefore, are to be honoured as key-bearers of the heavenly kingdom and judges of human faults. For it belongs to their jurisdiction to constrain secular men with judicial severity for those crimes which they commit in places consecrated to God, and to impose fitting penances, with just consideration, for other crimes. They too ought to constrain all presbyters and clerics by judicial sentence, so that the privilege of their authority may be preserved for both earthly and spiritual judges. Finally, they are those who strive, according to the Apostle Paul’s precept (2 Tim. 4), to implant in the minds of those subject to them that good which they have learned through understanding by the grace of the Holy Spirit—by reproving, entreating, and rebuking—watering the hearts of the faithful with divine doctrines as with heavenly rains, so that they may produce the unfading fruit of good works.

## CHAPTER X. Concerning those whom a bishop excommunicates

Therefore let the king take the greatest care not in any way to communicate with those whom bishops have expelled from the Church by a sentence of anathema [Col. 0955B] because of their crimes. For, as Scripture testifies (Rom. 1), equal punishment binds both those who commit acts and those who consent to them. Now he consents to a criminal and supports his guilt who communicates with him after he has been cast out of the Church as his crime demands.

Yet many appear to fear the judgment of the divine gift because their contempt is not immediately followed by punishment. Therefore I shall briefly relate what once happened to a certain king on this account. For it is read in the history of the English people that a certain bishop excommunicated two brothers, men of the royal household, because they had repudiated their wives. It happened that the king of that nation was passing near their house. Softened by many blandishments to turn aside and dine with them, he at length consented. [Col. 0955C] But when the feast was finished and he was returning, he encountered the bishop who had excommunicated those brothers. When he saw him, he trembled; and, leaping down from his horse, he prostrated himself before him in the middle of the road, as he was.

But the bishop touched him with the staff which he carried in his hand, saying: “O king, it is not mine to forgive you, because you despised God when you knowingly associated yourself with the excommunicated. Therefore sentence has been given against you: this year you shall die in the very house in which you associated yourself with the excommunicated.” And so it happened: when the year had passed, the king died there. Behold, the king could not expiate this guilt except by death, nor was the bishop able to forgive him even when he lay prostrate. From this it follows that neither can a bishop whose excommunication is despised forgive such a deed without [Col. 0955D] grave penance.

Therefore, as blessed Pope Gregory commands, the shepherds of the Church should take care, with great restraint, either to loose or to bind. But whether the shepherd binds justly or unjustly, the shepherd’s sentence must nevertheless be feared by the flock, lest one who is subject, even when perhaps bound unjustly, deserve that very sentence of binding because of another fault.

## CHAPTER XI. Concerning wicked prelates

Yet there are some among the number of priests who strive to be called priests through money; and although they are endowed with no learning and supported by no religious devotion, they wish to appear teachers of the divine law. But these are deservedly despised, and deserve to be called not bishops [Col. 0956A] but Simoniacs, after Simon Magus. For they have no share in the word of priesthood, but are held alien from the grace of the Holy Spirit, which is both given freely and received freely. For, as the Gospel testifies, “he who does not enter through the door into the sheepfold is a thief and a robber.” But “he who enters through the door is the shepherd of the sheep; and to him the gatekeeper opens, and the sheep hear his voice” (John 10). And a little later: “They do not follow a stranger, because they do not hear the voice of strangers” (ibid.).

Some bishops also, wishing to exalt themselves contrary to ecclesiastical custom, exercise the impulses of their own will, rather than the merits of cases, in loosing and binding those subject to them. Hence the people, running through byways, now despise the burden of the law more than usual; and while the mighty missile of anathema rages, they feel no reins of reason. For disgrace arises for the Christian religion, and priestly dignity is greatly despised because the priestly mitre is conferred from ambition rather than an estimation of merits, and is bestowed upon every sort of unlearned person.

For some of them absolve from the oath of fidelity those who are held bound by oath to their lords. How absurd this is the Lord shows where he says: “You shall not swear falsely by my name, nor profane the name of the Lord your God” (Lev. 18). And to Zedekiah, king of Judah, who had violated the oath which he had made to the king of Babylon, he says through the prophet: “As I live, the oath which he despised and the covenant which he transgressed I shall lay upon his head” (Ezek. 17).

## CHAPTER XII. Concerning him who breaks an oath against a Christian

[Col. 0956C]

Therefore let every Christian who breaks an oath against his lord or another Christian understand what he deserves, since for this crime Zedekiah, a Jewish man, is known to have been led captive to Babylon by a Gentile king after his eyes were torn out (Jer. 39). For he ought not to consider to whom he swears, but by whom he swears. Otherwise, he also despises him by whom he swears; and an enemy who is deceived by an oath is found more faithful. For he is greatly foolish who deceives the person with whom he had been bound in covenant by an oath in the divine name.

Moreover, an oath uttered carelessly [Col. 0956D] is not to be kept; as when someone promises a perpetually faithful union with an adulteress. For it is more tolerable not to fulfil an oath than to remain in the disgrace of fornication. Yet concerning foolish teachers the Lord says in the Gospel: “If a blind man gives guidance to a blind man, both fall into a pit” (Matt. 15).

Proud and wrathful teachers also sometimes turn the rigor of discipline into the frenzy of rage and the savagery of cruelty. But, as blessed Pope Gregory likewise says, those who follow either their own hatreds or favour in the cases of their subjects cannot judge them worthily. The Prophet too seems to speak of this matter: “They were killing souls which do not die, and giving life to souls which do not live” (Ezek. 13). For he kills one who does not die who condemns the righteous, and he attempts to give life to one who will not live [Col. 0957A] who seeks to absolve the guilty from punishment. Cases, therefore, must be weighed; and only then is the power of binding and loosing to be exercised.

Finally, a bishop must consider and take care lest through his own fault divine teaching become cheapened. For one who does not live as he ought renders contemptible the truth which he preaches. He who has obtained the office of pontiff must also take care to show himself such a person that, while preaching to others, he may not himself be found reprobate. Subjects also ought to consider that, although such a man occupies the place of judging whose life by no means accords with his office, he nevertheless retains the place of the apostles in the office of binding and loosing. Therefore his excommunication and preaching ought not to be despised because of his person, [Col. 0957B] but observed because of the authority of the supreme Judge. For Christ is known to be the shepherd of our souls, and in prelates he is heard and despised. Concerning them the Lord says in the Gospel: “The scribes and Pharisees have sat upon Moses’ seat. Do what they tell you; but do not do what they do” (Matt. 22).

And not only bishops, but all presbyters and clerics, are to be honoured by all God’s faithful as members of God’s household, who appear to serve him night and day. Further, prelates and presbyters appear to be the bases and columns of the holy Church, while clerics and monks appear to be its ministers. For by the hands of these ministers every believer is washed in holy baptism, and by their hands again the most sacred mystery [Col. 0957C] of Christ’s body and blood is performed; through these mysteries we are regenerated and joined to God.

Everyone, I say, who belongs to Christ’s body ought rightly to submit to them, obey their saving admonitions, and show them filial reverence. They, I say, are known to offer the gifts of our prayers and continually to entreat God for us. When they implore God for our sins, God himself becomes propitious to us and turns his wrath from us. They press before God with unwearied prayers always for the living and the dead; they obtain for us abundance of crops; and they repel storms and every danger from Christ’s flock. Our mother, the holy Church, is also adorned, illumined, and preserved by them as by noble [Col. 0957D] attendants.

And if some of them are found to be blameworthy, the rest should not therefore be despised, since wickedness was found even among angels. Men should indeed consider that saying of blessed Job (Job): “Who can make one conceived from impure seed clean, except you who alone are?”—understand: clean. Accordingly, every person, whether layman or cleric, is what he is by God’s gift, if indeed he is anything. Hence it is said in the Gospel: “Do not judge, and you shall not be judged; do not condemn, and you shall not be condemned” (Matt. 31).

Yet although it is written of the children of God, “All who are led by the Spirit of God are children of God” (Rom. 8), nevertheless all mortals, so long as they are held in this corruptible flesh, [Col. 0958A] sin. But lest evil deeds break forth into an immeasurable heap of sins, they ought to be punished by some penalty in this world. Therefore God willed that a king should preside over men for the suppression and correction of those who have resolved to live most wickedly and do not wish to correct their life and morals—that is, fornicators and adulterers, thieves and sacrilegious persons, and other shameful offenders—lest the punishment of eternal torment be reserved for them hereafter. For those crimes which are punished in this world will certainly not harm them in the world to come.

Thus there comes about in them what was said by the Apostle: [Col. 0958B] “If we judged ourselves, we certainly would not be judged. But when we are judged, we are corrected by the Lord, so that we may not be condemned with this world” (1 Cor. 11). Many benefits are bestowed upon unwilling people when their welfare, rather than their will, is considered—for by that will they are found to be enemies to themselves. For it is written: “He who loves iniquity hates his own soul” (Ps. 10). Thus the friends of wicked people are those who correct their iniquities and punish their bodies with some corrective penalty for the crimes they have committed. For sins which might be struck by the fires of Gehenna ought to be corrected by the lash of discipline, so that those who despise God’s commandments may be terrified by temporal punishment. The Psalmist seems to say this when he declares: “Constrain their jaws with bit and bridle, those who do not draw near to you” (Ps. 31).

But just as gold glows under fire and chaff smokes, and just as under the same threshing grain is cleansed and chaff crushed, so [Col. 0958C] a common punishment purifies the good and destroys the wicked. For all good persons are refined in the fire of tribulations, while the wicked murmur and are punished. Yet in some there is grave folly; and iniquity so binds them that not even punishment restrains them from fault. Others, however, seem to suffer evils undeservedly. But the Godhead permits this so that they may be instructed by torments and chastisements. For God “chastises every son whom he receives” (Heb. 12). Yet although not all who are chastised are sons, no son is unchastised.

Moreover, some are left without the lash. Thus, by doing evil, they hasten more freely toward eternal torments. Of them it is written in the book of blessed Job: “I saw a fool firmly rooted” (Job 5). [Col. 0958D] A fool, I say, is seen standing with a firm root when he rejoices in continual prosperity in this life. Nevertheless, in the future the strict Judge will strike with such adversity those whom he rejects as he now corrects with severity those whom he loves. But lest evil deeds break forth into an immeasurable heap of sins, they ought to be punished by some penalty, as has been said above. For disordered pity, when it spares temporarily, draws people toward eternal punishments and permits vices to multiply.

Nevertheless, the measure of discernment must be observed by judges in all things; and, in order that pity may be ordered, one must proceed to knowledge, so that the judge may know what he punishes justly and what he remits through mercy. Thus the prudence of judges ought always to sharpen their hearts toward the good, lest either prudence itself exceed the measure of rectitude or simplicity fall into the deception of ignorance. [Col. 0959A]

Further, kings, emperors, and judges, when by the command of just reason they punish criminals with death or wage wars at the prompting of equity, must not be thought to act against the commandment of the Law which says, “You shall not kill” (Exod. 20). For criminals are put to death under the law so that destructive security may not be granted to deadly sin. And wars are therefore waged not unjustly, that peace may be obtained. For Moses, a meek and most holy man, is read to have killed many men at the command of the divine law, and, with God giving him leadership, to have destroyed many nations by victorious arms. Many other rulers of the New and Old Testament, inflamed by divine zeal, are likewise read to have done this. For fear of God and fear of punishment draw a person back from sin.

Yet that caution of all rulers and prelates is useful and praiseworthy in which reason does everything and rage claims nothing for itself. [Col. 0959B] For penitents, God established the bishop in the Church, although he himself does not despise a contrite and humbled heart. For the bishop ought, according to the measure of the offence, to separate some penitents from Christ’s body and blood during the course of penance, and to impose upon others a definite burden of penance. When this has been completed, they are to be reconciled, joined again to their faithful brethren, and received into the bosom of the holy Church, from whose fellowship they had strayed by sinning. Outside this Church sins are not forgiven, nor can anyone attain everlasting life except through it.

Finally, [Col. 0959C] in accordance with his office he corrects some, instructs others, and excommunicates others at the prompting of the censure of justice. He also sometimes declines to rebuke some, either because he awaits a more suitable time or because he fears that those rebuked may become worse. For one and the same instruction is not to be applied to all people; rather, the exhortation of teachers ought to vary according to the quality of their characters. Harsh rebuke corrects some, but gentle exhortation others. Nor, finally, are all times suited to instruction; but according to Solomon’s saying, there is “a time to be silent, and a time to speak” (Eccl. 3). Hence the oft-mentioned Pope Gregory says in the twentieth book of the *Moralia*: “When holy men see that certain persons despise their words, they understand that such persons are forsaken by God, and therefore they are silent in mourning.”

Nevertheless, we do not say that a bishop should be silent because he is frightened by hatred of evil men, but by the counsel of charity; for the Apostle commands him, saying: “Be urgent in season and out of season; entreat, rebuke, in all patience and teaching” (2 Tim. 4).

Let what we have said concerning the two powers by which the holy Church is governed and guided in this present life suffice. After God, it is known to be illuminated by these powers as the whole fabric of the world is by the two great lights, namely the sun and moon, or as the whole human body is adorned and illuminated by two eyes. No one ought to doubt that these powers are holy. For God and the Lord consecrated, united, and sanctified them in his own person. To them too the Book of Wisdom gives this command: “Love righteousness, you who judge [Col. 0960A] the earth. Think of the Lord with goodness, and seek him in simplicity of heart; for he is found by those who do not test him, but appears to those who have faith in him” (Wis. 1).

By these powers and principalities, I say, the earthly kingdom has been distinguished and ordered. Hence those who strive to overturn this arrangement, distinguished and ordered in fitting fashion by almighty God, appear to belong to the number of those who, ignorant of God’s righteousness and wishing to establish their own, are not subject to his righteousness. Did not God himself make all things in number, measure, and weight? Are not the elements of this world, though one is greatly different from another, known to be mutually harmonious? Does not the Lord say in the Gospel: “Every kingdom divided against itself shall be laid waste, and house shall fall upon house?” (Luke 11). [Col. 0960B] Finally, a certain wise man says: “By concord the smallest things increase, and by discord the greatest things collapse.”

But now it is worthwhile to hear and consider what Gregory, the most holy pope, once wrote to Sabinus, deacon of Constantinople. For he says: “There is one thing which you should briefly suggest to our most serene lord the emperor: I, his servant, if I had wished to involve myself in his death or in the counsels of the Lombards, the nation of the Lombards today would have neither king nor dukes nor counts, but all things would be in utter confusion. But because I fear God, I dread to involve myself in the death of any human being.”

[Col. 0960C] Accordingly, I do not maintain that it is lawful for any king or emperor to do or institute anything contrary to God’s commandments or the enactments of the holy canons. But I say that, just as a good Christian king ought not to obey laws established against God, so one who does not obey laws reasonably established acts wrongly. For, as blessed Augustine testifies: “The peace of all things is the tranquillity of order. Order, moreover, is the arrangement which assigns to each thing its proper place among equal and unequal things.”

But because our discourse may perhaps now have been drawn out too long, it remains that it should end, lest its prolixity produce weariness in the reader. This book, I say, must be closed—a book which I have composed, with the merciful help of God, not from the swelling of pride but moved by brotherly affection—desiring that not only these two powers of which [Col. 0960D] we have thus far treated, but also all worshippers of Christ, may be harmonious and mutually united. This is also commanded by the holy and wise Apostle: “Pursue peace with all, and holiness, without which no one shall see God” (Heb. 12). Christ the Lord likewise gave this pious and most salutary command to his disciples, saying: “I give you a new commandment, that you love one another” (John 13). And, when already near his passion, he again said to them: “Peace I leave with you; my peace I give you” (John 14).

Moreover, I have taken care diligently to support this present little book with examples from Holy Scripture, lest my labour perhaps be found empty and useless. Accordingly, I pray that all who are to receive it with a devout and kindly mind may fare well [Col. 0961A] [Col. 0962A] always in Christ Jesus our Lord. Amen.

Here ends the first book.

# SECOND BOOK

[Col. 0961]

[Col. 0961A] Having finished the preceding little book, I had resolved to be silent—that is, to rest from the present undertaking and turn my mind to other things—when, behold, there came to my mind what is written: “By the mouth of two or three witnesses every word shall stand” (Deut. 19; Matt. 18). And immediately my spirit grew warm again, and I judged it fitting that I should make a second book concerning this same matter, concerning which [Col. 0961B] I had already produced one book, so that one subject might be established and strengthened more firmly by two books.

In the preceding book we have shown sufficiently, as I think, that all power is ordained by God. But now we have resolved to make it plainly known to readers that God himself placed and established two powers especially in his holy Church, namely the royal and the priestly, not without a great and most salutary mystery. The Wisdom of God herself, taking flesh in which she might be seen, assumed these two powers in the unity of her person; and for this reason joined and united them to one another in a kind of kinship: both that there might always be in them one bond of charity, never to be dissolved, and that the two, faithfully adhering to one another, might be mutually associated [Col. 0961C] and joined together. For they always need the assistance or support supplied by one another; and unless they agree with each other, the entire body of the Church is tossed about and the people wander amid uncertainties.

Accordingly, because the Lord himself said in the Gospel that the whole Law and the Prophets hang upon two commandments (Matt. 22), and because charity is known to be twofold—for there are two commandments of charity itself, as we have already said—God and Lord of all fittingly established two powers in the Church, to which he took care to entrust the administration of everything done within it. The Church is supported and sustained by these two powers as by two wings; and endowed with them, it penetrates heaven in free flight. By the industry of these powers it once deserved to be exalted and nobly raised up [Col. 0961D] both in Judaea and among the Gentiles; and their pious care and watchful diligence stretches out its branches from sea to sea.

How this came about—that is, how through these two powers, accompanied by God’s grace, it grew and increased—I shall now relate to my hearers according to the measure of my knowledge. Yet I shall touch briefly upon certain matters, because I cannot comprehensively embrace in general all that pertains to this subject. I shall nevertheless begin with the kings and prophets of the Jewish people.

Moses, then, leader and prophet alike of the Israelite people, to use now the more excellent language of David (Ps. 134), struck Egypt with their firstborn, led Israel out from its midst with mighty hand and uplifted arm, divided the Red [Col. 0962A] Sea into divisions, led Israel through its midst, cast Pharaoh and his power into the Red Sea, led his people through the wilderness, struck many nations, killed mighty kings—Sihon king of the Amorites and Og king of Bashan—and gave their land as an inheritance to his people. In this he signified that most gentle King and Shepherd who transfers those believing in him, through hope and faith, from mortality to immortality.

[Col. 0962B] Hence, as we have already said in the preceding book, he built the tabernacle of God in the wilderness by a most sacred mystery, consecrated Aaron, and set before the people the precepts of the divine Law. But Aaron worked signs and wonders before Pharaoh and his nobles with the rod which Moses himself had given him. After Moses arose Joshua son of Nun; at whose command the sun was stayed in its course until he had overcome the enemies of God’s people. He too was a great and strong man, bearing, in accordance with his name, among kings and prophets the figure of our Saviour, who is King and Priest alike; and who, in the figure and mystery of crossing the Jordan’s channel, divided the land of promise among the people by the measuring-line of distribution.

[Col. 0962C] After him, Samuel the prophet renewed the kingdom by anointing Saul as king. Saul both overcame the enemies of God’s people and faithfully enlarged the boundaries of his kingdom. Yet afterward, raised up by the prosperity of his fortune and becoming proud, he displeased God. Therefore the prophet just mentioned frequently prayed to the Lord for him; but he was not heard, for Saul had already been condemned by God’s just judgment.

After Saul, David reigned, whose name is interpreted “strong king.” He conquered the most monstrous enemy Goliath, signifying that most mighty King who defeated the devil, the enemy of the entire human race. Moreover, David loved with his whole heart him who exalted him; he was the first to bring the ark of God into Jerusalem with great praise and glory; [Col. 0962D] and he composed the outstanding book called the Psalter. Therefore God removed his sin and established his kingdom for many generations. For when, secretly rather than openly, he had defiled the wife of Uriah his soldier with the pollution of adultery, and afterward had wickedly caused Uriah himself to be killed by enemy hands so that the deed committed might be concealed, the prophet Nathan publicly reproved and rebuked him for his deed; and then absolved him when confession had corrected him.

After David reigned his son Solomon. He built a temple for the Lord his God from incorruptible woods and precious stones, in which the holy Church was prefigured. In it he appointed the offices of priests in their ministries and the Levites in their order, that they might minister to the Lord [Col. 0963A] according to the rite of each day, as David his father had commanded him. He too, filled with wisdom, composed the *syrasirim*—that is, the “Song of Songs”—in which through a bridal song he mystically sings the union of Christ and the Church. He was likewise remarkable in proverbs and interpretations, and his name was spread far and wide.

But although he flourished in great wealth and exceedingly great glory, becoming puffed up in heart, he ran without restraint into lust, burned with desire for foreign women, and moreover worshipped their gods. Therefore the Lord was angered and stirred up against him Jeroboam son of Nebat, his servant. He also tore the kingdom from the hand of Solomon’s son. For Rehoboam son of Nebat reigned in Jerusalem. [Col. 0963B] But, lest I linger over each individual matter: when afterward King Hezekiah reigned in Jerusalem and did what was pleasing before the Lord God, according to all that David his father had done, Sennacherib king of the Assyrians rose against him, surrounded by a great army. Then King Hezekiah and the prophet Isaiah arose and prayed to the Lord, and the Lord heard them. In Sennacherib’s camp an angel descended and killed one hundred and eighty-five thousand of his army.
