Thus glorious kings, inspired by God, raised up the holy Church according to their strength; and by their pious care and watchful diligence it first grew in Judaea and at last extended its branches among the Gentiles. Likewise the holy prophets adorned it with the beauty of their virtues and ennobled it with the gold of their wisdom. It is therefore established that the most holy kings and prophets always needed one another’s mutual assistance.

[Col. 0963C] By “Church” I mean the Synagogue, because what was done in it bore the figure of the present Church; and in its sacrifice was prefigured the slaughter of Christ, by whose blood we have been redeemed and restored. Rest also was prefigured through the Sabbath’s cessation from labour. The Law itself likewise preceded the New Testament in figure. Hence, when Gospel light came, the shadow consequently departed.

Now, however, priests hold in the Church of Christ the place of the holy prophets. For thus the Lord speaks to her through the prophet Isaiah: “Behold,” he says, “I shall establish your rulers as at first, and your counsellors as in the beginning” (Isa. 1). And the Psalmist says: “In place of your fathers sons have been born to you; you shall establish them [Col. 0963D] as rulers over all the earth” (Ps. 44).

Therefore God ordered or disposed royal and priestly dignity on earth not without a great and most salutary mystery. It is consequently fitting and altogether appropriate that these two powers should always adhere to one another in brotherly charity and protect one another with mutual solicitude. For unless they agree with one another, the whole body of the Church is tossed about and the people are driven through byways. By these two powers, as by two strong and most firm columns, it is supported and sustained. By these same two powers, as by two wings, its offspring are surrounded and protected from the adversities of this world. But those who refuse to be surrounded by these wings are known to rebel against God.

Let this suffice to have been said concerning the kings [Col. 0964A] and prophets of the Jewish people, so that we may explain gradually and in sequence what we have proposed.

Accordingly, after God and our Lord Jesus Christ by his death redeemed from eternal death the human being whom he had made, and raised from the dead the captivity of our flesh and brought it into heaven, the Old Testament was rendered void, just as childhood is ordinarily superseded when a stronger age succeeds it. For the one God, through his holy prophets and servants, according to the most orderly distribution of times, gave lesser commandments to a people who still had to be bound by fear, and through his Son greater commandments to a people who now ought to be set free by love. The bearers of these commandments of Christ were the disciples called apostles. For they and their successors, [Col. 0964B] proved in faith, long-suffering in hope, mighty in deed and word, patient in tribulation, and instructed in all that the Lord Jesus Christ himself did, went throughout the whole world, breaking up human minds with the ploughshare of God’s word, casting into them the seeds of the new commandments, and laying the foundations of the Church upon Christ Jesus, the cornerstone, in whom the two walls coming from opposite directions—that is, from Jews and Gentiles—might be joined together by a twofold love.

But blessed Peter went down to Antioch and founded the Church there, in which people were first called Christians from the name of Christ. From there he also came to Rome; and there, preaching the word of the Lord, he held the papacy of that city for twenty-five years. To support this shepherd, [Col. 0964C] Paul, Apostle of the Gentiles, was sent by divine appointment, so that each might be a consolation to the other. But Nero, that most savage emperor, condemned both apostles to death. Then, after the Apostle Peter, Clement, a most wise man, consecrated by Peter himself, undertook the governance of the Roman Church; he too, not long afterward, was plunged into the waves of the sea and completed martyrdom for Christ’s name.

And while, still, throughout almost the whole world images were worshipped under the rule of tyrants, Marcellus, the most holy pope of the city just mentioned, having been assigned in the house of the matron Lucina—which he had dedicated to God—to the keeping of public animals, ended his life. And what greater injury could be inflicted on the Christian name than that the supreme pontiff, [Col. 0964D] that is, the prelate of the holy Roman Church, should be a stable-keeper of beasts of burden? I pass over, I say, many other cruel and refined tortures by which many priests of the Lord, both at Rome and elsewhere—to say nothing of other worshippers of Christ—over nearly three hundred and ten years from the incarnation of the Lord attained eternal blessedness through the crown of martyrdom. At that time, whoever presided over the Christian flock by right of priesthood was first dragged away to the torments of martyrdom and suffered the more grievous punishments.

But after the light of truth had been shown to the people sitting in the shadow of death—that is, in the darkness of unbelief—Constantine, the most merciful emperor of the Romans, by his own edict decreed throughout the Roman Empire that the temples of the Gentiles should be closed; and he built several churches in that city itself. [Col. 0965A] Among these he constructed the church of blessed John the Baptist and of the blessed Apostles Peter and Paul; he also enriched them with great possessions and made them wealthy with gold and silver, and enclosed the sacred relics of those same apostles in the purest gold and most precious gems.

He also gave to blessed Pope Sylvester and his successors imperial force and honour, decreeing by his privilege that they should hold primacy both over the four principal sees—namely Antioch, Alexandria, Constantinople, and Jerusalem—and also over all the Churches throughout the world; and that the pontiff of the holy Roman Church should stand higher than all the priests of this world. He also judged it fitting to transfer the power of the Roman Empire and kingdom [Col. 0965B] to the eastern region: so that there the holy law might hold the headship of rule where Peter, prince of the apostles, died while enduring the gibbet of the cross; and that there the nations might bend their necks where their teacher Paul, with his neck stretched forth, was crowned with martyrdom for Christ; and that there they might perform service in the office of our Lord where once they served under the command of an earthly king.

Moreover, he handed over to the Roman pontiff his Lateran palace, the crown of his head, the purple cloak, and all the other imperial ornaments, all the glory of his power, the imperial procession, and the rank of the imperial horsemen presiding over the palace. He also decreed that clerics serving the holy Roman Church should have power and preeminence—that is, should be made consuls and patricians—[Col. 0965C] and should moreover be adorned with the other imperial dignities, so that, as the imperial soldiery was adorned, so too the clergy itself might be adorned and the holy Roman Church embellished, in order that the summit of pontifical dignity might shine forth in the amplest honour.

He offered this privilege over the bodies of the holy Apostles Peter and Paul, choosing for himself the prince of the apostles and his vicars as steadfast intercessors and patrons with God. By this most worthy honour Constantine, the most merciful emperor of the Romans, exalted and honoured the holy Church. Yet episcopal dignity deserved to be exalted by God far more gloriously. For God and our Lord Jesus Christ gave bishops the power to open and close heaven to human beings. [Col. 0965D] Understanding that they possessed this privilege, the aforesaid Emperor Constantine, sitting last of all the bishops at the Council of Nicaea, was unwilling to pronounce any sentence of judgment upon them; rather, calling them all gods, he judged that they ought not to be subject to his judgment, but that he himself ought to depend upon their decision.

For it is the office of those prelates to call royal power back from an unjust path and, if it does not obey them, even to excommunicate it. The holy prophets are known to have done this under the Old Law. Nathan the prophet, as has already been set forth, publicly exposed to King David the sin which he had committed deceitfully and secretly, and afterward absolved him when he had been corrected by confession (II Kings 12). And in the New Testament, blessed Ambrose, bishop of Milan, [Col. 0966A] publicly and openly suspended the great Emperor Theodosius from ecclesiastical communion because of his crime, and brought royal power to repentance.

Saint Germanus, bishop of Paris, also excommunicated Aribert, king of the Franks, because, having abandoned his lawful wife, he had introduced two wives for himself besides her. And because he was not corrected, struck by God’s judgment, he died under that excommunication. It is necessary that the rashness of wicked rulers be restrained by the authority of holy prelates and checked by fitting corrections; for if it is not constrained by deserved chastisement, it will offer the people an easy opportunity to sin.

Moreover, the Apostle Paul separates fornicators and adulterers from the fellowship of the other Christians, saying that with such persons one ought not even [Col. 0966B] to take food (I Corinthians 5). Therefore they are rightly separated from the Church and kept away from the sacraments of the altar. No Catholic ought to cast off from his neck the yoke of ecclesiastical discipline, but should obey a priest who offers him salutary counsel; for, as the prophet Samuel testifies, “Obedience is better than sacrifices, and hearkening more than offering the fat of rams” (I Kings 15).

Obedience, therefore, is rightly preferred to sacrifices, because in sacrifices another’s flesh is slain, whereas by obedience one’s own will is sacrificed. The more quickly, I say, each person makes peace with God, the more he weakens his own pleasures, cutting them off from himself with the sword of the fear of God, with the pride of his own will restrained before God’s eyes. Obedience, indeed, is the virtue that chiefly possesses the merit of faith. Whoever lacks it is proved to be unbelieving, even if he is shown to be faithful; and one who does not render it to priests appears to resist God. For through them—that is, through the holy prelates—the Catholic faith was formerly spread throughout the world, as we have stated above.

For the apostles, whose heirs or disciples they are, cleaving to Christ the supreme Pontiff, were found especially in time of persecution firm in faith, outstanding in religion, and undismayed by fear of death. Hence every Christian now rightly seeks through their aid to be untangled from the bonds of his sins, and honours and reveres them as fathers and teachers.

But since we have now said enough about these matters for the present, it is fitting that we again disclose briefly to those who do not know the magnificence [Col. 0966D] or generosity of the ancient kings, by which they exalted the holy Church. Pippin, king of the Franks, invited by the prayers of Pope Hadrian, came to Rome; he magnificently delivered that Roman prelate from the assaults of Haistulf, king of Italy, and restored the estates taken from him.

Leo succeeded Pope Hadrian; the Romans subjected him to many injuries and likewise drove him from his see. But Charles, the magnificent king of the Franks, coming to Rome, restored him to his place, punished his enemies with death, and bestowed many gifts of gold and silver upon the church of blessed Peter.

Again, in the time of Emperor Henry II, the Romans drove Pope Clement from his chair after subjecting him to many insults. When the aforesaid emperor heard this, he came to Rome [Col. 0967A] and restored him to his own see. But after Pope Clement’s death, the Romans again appointed as pope a certain worthless boy. Henry III, successor and son of the Henry mentioned above, deposed him from the see and put Gregory VI in his place.

Finally, some kings and emperors, out of love for God and for the expiation of those dear to them, showed other fruits of kindness to the needy. Others endured many anxieties on behalf of the people subject to them, and some preferred the peace of their kingdom to their own dangers. Some of them, too, brought great benefits to their people by putting thieves, adulterers, and all equally sacrilegious persons to death through refined punishments. Others gave their peoples laws distinguished by discernment and honourableness. Some were distinguished by kindness; others were wise and endowed with eloquence; others were peaceable; and others conspicuous for every excellence of character.

Some also adorned churches with different buildings; others drove a faithless people from the borders of their kingdom with victorious arms. The Church needs all these things. Some also built churches on their own estates, placed religious men in them, and granted them their lands, so that they might live from their revenues and thereafter serve the Lord there night and day without anxiety. They set over them holy and upright men, whom we call abbots, to instruct them diligently in the divine commandments and likewise provide them with necessities.

From that time they also began, by royal generosity, to confer the honour of the episcopate upon religious men carefully cultivated in divine teachings, and to provide the Church of God with most worthy shepherds. [Col. 0967C] Many kings and princes employed this judicious custom, down to our own times, in promoting the most learned and holy men, as we have already said in the preceding book. Hence even that great Pope Gregory, whose sacred flowers of eloquence today give forth their fragrance in the holy Church, did not refuse consecration at the command of Emperor Maurice. Blessed Ambrose, archbishop of Milan, a most holy man, is likewise recorded to have done so before him: at the command of Emperor Valentinian, he accepted the episcopate of the aforesaid Church.

Many Catholic men also did this, men adorned alike by elegance of character and by a most holy life. Among their number are known to have been Saint Audoin, archbishop of Rouen, and Saint Eligius, bishop of Noyon, men most pleasing to God, as their deeds show, who deserved to hold the episcopal office through the gift of King Dagobert.

Nevertheless, because of those who violently force themselves into the Church and buy the honour of episcopal office with money from irreligious rulers—loving pride and temporal dominion with the vain pomp and arrogance of this world—the holy Council of Nicaea decreed that no one should in any way become bishop apart from the will and consent of his metropolitan. The venerable Roman pontiffs afterward confirmed this: namely Gelasius, Celestine, and the most holy Leo, decreeing that no one should be made bishop for any reason unless he had been elected by the clergy, sought by the people, [Col. 0968A] and consecrated by the bishops of the province at the judgment of the metropolitan.

Therefore we hope it may be salutary and expedient that, if a king or any pious prince wishes to confer the honour of episcopal office in due order upon a holy man, he should not do this by his own judgment alone, but by the counsel and consent of the metropolitan bishop. For in the case of those who promote themselves against religious discipline and seize for themselves the summit of governance rather than attain it, dissension is often wont to spring up, and sometimes grave destruction arises among the people. Therefore it seems prudent to us that, if a matter of this kind cannot be duly accomplished because the schemes of wicked persons obstruct it, it should be deferred until it can be reasonably and lawfully decided in a general synod.

Accordingly, it is also the king’s duty to reconcile bishops who are in disagreement, as we can establish by many examples. In the time of the younger Emperor Valentinian, Sixtus, Roman pontiff, was accused by a certain Bassus. When the aforesaid Augustus heard this, in pious care he ordered a council to be held; in it Pope Sixtus was cleared of the accusation, and Bassus was condemned.

In the time also of Theodoric, king of Italy, Symmachus obtained the apostolic see, and on the same day, through sedition, Laurentius was advanced to the same rank. The Roman senate reported this to King Theodoric and requested that he send them one who might be ordained apostolic. He sent them Peter, bishop of the city of Altinum. But Symmachus summoned a council of one hundred and twenty-five bishops, [Col. 0968C] in which he cleared himself of the charges made against him; and so at last he remained apostolic until the day of his death, while Laurentius was deprived of his see.

Likewise, in the year 962 of the Lord’s incarnation, Pope Octavian, when he was charged with irreligion, was expelled from his see at the command of Otto, emperor of the Romans, and John VII was put in his place. But when the aforementioned emperor had departed from Rome, the Romans received Octavian, drove John from the city, and ordained Benedict pope. When Emperor Otto learned this, he returned to Rome, deposed the aforesaid Pope Benedict by synodal judgment, and restored John to his place.

[Col. 0968D] Thus, as our discourse has clearly shown, all the bishops of a king’s realm appear properly subject to the king, as a son is found subject to his father—not by nature, but by order—so that the whole realm may be reduced to one governing principle. It belongs to him, finally, prudently to hear throughout his kingdom those cases which come before him as complaints, and by the privilege of his authority to correct or settle them.

Accordingly, Gregory VII is commonly reproved by some because he avoided being consecrated with the consent and permission of the emperor. Because of this matter this dissension has arisen; Christians are slaughtered every day; places consecrated to God are defiled and polluted with Roman blood; churches are razed to the ground; worshippers of Christ are driven from their homes; and castles, villages, and estates are consumed by blazing fires. [Col. 0969A] And, alas, no one is found who carefully investigates, prudently examines, and justly decides this case. Clergy and people are left in uncertainty, and the boastful or powerful men are unwilling to extend their arms—that is, their strength—against the onset of tribulation. Instead, all the powerful have become like rams fighting one another.

That decree of his is likewise reproved which provides that none of the bishops may receive investiture of a bishopric or abbey from the hand of king or emperor. This is criticized because holy men of old, as we reported above, did not refuse to receive the honour of episcopal office through the gift of kings or emperors; they would never have done so if they had known that guilt lay hidden in this matter. Nor, as we hope, would God have caused them to shine with such great miracles unless their life had been praiseworthy before him. Therefore it seems superfluous.

Moreover, the pomp of this world is accustomed to instill the swelling of pride and exaltation into rulers; and, while they commit unlawful acts, they are accustomed to say to those who rebuke them: “We ought to be judged by no one, and are placed under no one’s power.” They show themselves untamable toward spiritual physicians—that is, holy teachers—who knew their sins and could heal them with fatherly compassion. Thus they remain in their sickness until they perish, paying no attention to that most wise saying: “All things are lawful to me, but not all things are expedient” (I Corinthians 6).

If they feared God and that fire prepared for the devil and his attendants, they would surely often turn over in their minds [Col. 0969C] what is written in the book of blessed Job: “Can a human being be justified in comparison with God, or one born of a woman appear clean? Behold, even the moon does not shine, and the stars are not clean in his sight. How much more man, rottenness, and the son of man, a worm?” (Job 25). And in the Book of Wisdom: “For the corruptible body weighs down the soul, and the earthly dwelling burdens the mind that thinks many things” (Wisdom 9).

But now I fear lest someone, reproving me, may say: “Brother, it is not your place to rebuke honourable and exalted persons, whose sins God reserves for judgment by his own judgment.” But whoever he may be, let him remember that the most blessed Apostle Peter, who excelled all the other apostles, and to whom God and our Lord Jesus Christ had spoken with his own mouth, saying: “You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church, and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it; and I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven; and whatever you bind upon earth shall be bound also in heaven, and whatever you loose upon earth shall be loosed also in heaven” (Matthew 16)—this Peter Paul, recently converted to the faith, dared to rebuke, and, inflamed with divine zeal, to reprove before everyone.

For the same Apostle Paul, writing to the Galatians, says: “When Cephas came to Antioch, I resisted him to his face, because he was blameworthy. For before certain persons came from James, he ate with the Gentiles. But when they had come, [Col. 0970A] he withdrew and separated himself, fearing those who were of the circumcision. And the other Jews consented to his pretence, so that even Barnabas was led by them into that pretence. But when I saw that they did not walk rightly according to the truth of the Gospel, I said to Cephas before them all: If you, though you are a Jew, live as a Gentile and not as a Jew, how do you compel the Gentiles to live as Jews? We are Jews by nature, and not sinners from among the Gentiles. Yet knowing that a human being is not justified by works except through faith in Jesus Christ, we too have believed in Christ Jesus, that we may be justified by faith in Christ and not by works of the Law” (Galatians 2).

Therefore, if so great an apostle, impeded by bodily weakness, was found blameworthy, how much more blameworthy is one whose heart swells and whose eyes stare as though pondering great things? [Col. 0970B] Yet he who excelled the other apostles, whom the Lord Jesus Christ, the best teacher, had taught by his own mouth and the Holy Spirit had enlightened, did not refuse humbly to hear Paul, recently converted to the faith, offering him salutary counsel; rather, he entirely yielded to him.

But a person endowed with the arrogance of this world’s power, as is read in the book of Job, “is raised up in pride and thinks himself born free like the colt of a wild ass” (Job 11); and therefore he declines to acknowledge his guilt and to give assent to holy people. Yet God is often accustomed to instruct wise people through simple ones. Thus Balaam the prophet, who loved the wages of iniquity, had as the corrector of his madness the dumb animal upon which he was accustomed to ride (Numbers 22).

For the exalted Lord both regards the lowly and knows the exalted from afar. He regards the lowly, I say, to lift them up; and the exalted—that is, the proud—to cast them down. Therefore whoever holds the summit of honour ought diligently to examine himself and let no flattery deceive him, but understand with what danger of eternal death and with what lack of perfect righteousness we live as exiles from the Lord. For although “beautiful are the feet of those who proclaim peace, who proclaim good things” (Romans 10), nevertheless they are accustomed to gather dust from dry ground. And if this is so for the stewards of God’s word and ministers of his sacraments, how much more for some province of the great King? Therefore the Psalmist says to the Lord: “Blessed is the man whom you instruct, O Lord, and teach out of your law” (Psalm 93).

But setting these matters aside for the moment, it is worthwhile to set before our hearers the decree of blessed Pope Nicholas [the text’s “Leonis Nicolai” is uncertain], and to make known to those who do not know what he decreed concerning the ordination of a pope. When, in the year 1058 of the Lord’s incarnation, he had succeeded Pope Leo, he held a council in the Lateran basilica in the second year of his ordination, in the month of April, in the twelfth indiction. Sitting there, with all gathered around him, he said:

“Your modesty knows, dearest brothers and fellow bishops—and neither has it escaped the notice of the lower members—how many adversities this apostolic see, which I serve by God’s authorship, endured after the death of our predecessor, Lord Stephen, of pious memory; and how often it was subjected to the hammers and repeated blows of the money-changers of the Simoniacal heresy, so that the pillar of the living God now seemed almost to totter and the net of the supreme Fisherman, amid swelling storms, to be submerged in the depths of shipwreck.

“Therefore, if it pleases your brotherhood, with God’s help we ought prudently to provide against future contingencies and to take thought for the ecclesiastical condition hereafter, lest revived evils—may this not be!—prevail. Accordingly, instructed by the authority of our predecessors and of other holy Fathers, we decree and establish that, when the pontiff of this universal Roman Church dies, first the cardinal bishops shall deliberate together with the most diligent consideration; then they shall immediately call in the cardinal clerics; and thus [Col. 0971B] the remaining clergy and people shall come to consent to the new election.

“And lest the disease of venality creep in on any occasion, religious men shall lead in the election of the pontiff to be promoted, while the rest shall follow. This is certainly seen to be the right and lawful order of election if, after considering the rules and acts of different Fathers, we also recall that sentence of blessed Leo: ‘No principle permits those to be numbered among bishops who have neither been elected by the clergy, nor sought by the people, nor consecrated by the bishops of the province at the judgment of the metropolitan.’

“Since the apostolic see is set above all Churches throughout the world and therefore cannot have a metropolitan over itself, the cardinal bishops shall without doubt perform the office of metropolitan, advancing the chosen prelate to the summit of apostolic rank. They shall elect from the bosom of this Church itself, if a suitable person is found; but if no one is found from it, he shall be taken from another Church.

“Saving the due honour and reverence of our beloved son Henry, who is at present held to be king and is hoped, God granting, to be future emperor, just as we have already granted this to him and to those of his successors who have personally obtained this right from this apostolic see. But if the perversity of wicked and unjust people should prevail to such an extent that a pure, sincere, and free election cannot take place in the city, the cardinal bishops, with religious clerics and Catholic laymen, even if few, shall retain the right and power to elect the prelate of the apostolic see wherever they judge more suitable.

“Indeed, after an election has been made, if a storm of war or any attempt of human malice should resist, so that the one elected cannot be enthroned in the apostolic see according to custom, nevertheless the elect shall hold, as pope, authority to govern the holy Roman Church and dispose of all its resources. We know that blessed Gregory did this before his election.

“But if anyone, contrary to this decree of ours promulgated by synodal sentence, is elected—or even ordained or enthroned—through sedition, presumption, or any contrivance whatsoever, let him, together with his instigators, agents, and followers, be separated from the thresholds of the holy Church of God by the authority of God and of the holy Apostles Peter and Paul, and subjected to perpetual anathema as Antichrist, invader, and destroyer of all Christendom. Let no hearing concerning this ever be reserved for him, but let him be deposed without reconsideration from every ecclesiastical rank in which he previously stood. Whoever adheres to him, renders him any reverence as though he were pontiff, or presumes in any respect to defend him, shall be bound by the same sentence.

“Whoever proves a violator of this decree or sentence of ours and attempts, against this statute, by his presumption to throw the Roman Church into confusion and disorder, shall be condemned to perpetual anathema and excommunication, and be counted with the wicked when they rise at the judgment. May he feel against himself the wrath of almighty God the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, [Col. 0972B] and encounter in this life and the future the fury of the holy Apostles Peter and Paul, whose Church he presumes to throw into confusion. May his dwelling become desolate, and let there be none to dwell in his tents. May his children become orphans and his wife a widow. Let him and his children be driven away and wander about; let them beg and be cast out from their dwellings. Let the creditor search out all his substance, and strangers plunder the fruits of his labour. Let the whole world fight against him, and let the other elements be hostile to him. Let the merits of all the saints at rest confound him and display open vengeance upon him in this life.

“But may the grace of almighty God protect the observers of this decree of ours, and by the authority of the blessed Peter and Paul absolve them from all bonds of sins.”

Behold, this most holy pope, by sound and most salutary counsel and exceptional discernment, while reserving to the emperor his due honor and reverence in the ordination of the lord pope, observes that command of the apostle Peter which the same apostle wrote in his Epistle, saying: “Be subject to every human creature for God’s sake, whether to the king as supreme, or to governors as sent by him for the punishment of evildoers and the praise of the good; for such is the will of God, that by doing good you should silence the ignorance of foolish people, as free persons, yet not using freedom as a covering for malice, but as servants of God” (1 Pet. II).

For through the earthly kingdom the heavenly kingdom then advances, when what the priest is unable to accomplish by the word of teaching, royal power accomplishes or commands through the terror of discipline. It is therefore fitting that the privilege of its authority should always remain safe and unimpaired to each power in its own sphere. Finally, as the apostle Paul teaches: “No one ought to seize the priesthood for himself, but only one called by God, as Aaron was. For Christ also did not glorify himself so as to become High Priest, but he who said to him: ‘You are my Son; today I have begotten you’” (Ps. II). And elsewhere: “You are a priest for ever according to the order of Melchizedek” (Ps. CIX); he who, in the days of his flesh, offering prayers and supplications with a loud cry and tears to him who could save him from death, was heard because of his reverence. Indeed, although he was the Son of God, he learned obedience from the things which he suffered; and, having been made perfect, he became for all who obey him the cause of eternal salvation, being named by God High Priest according to the order of Melchizedek (Heb. V).

Therefore it is fitting that all bishops follow the pattern which went before in the Head, so that they too may be found worthy to offer spiritual sacrifices acceptable to God through that same Christ our Lord, whose shadow they are known to be. Royal power, moreover, is not to be despised; for it is the king’s office to correct the whole people subject to him from error and to recall them to the path of equity and justice. Hence in the Book of Judges you will find that, before the children of Israel had a king, Jonathan, son of the son of Moses, although assigned among the Levites, presumed to take the priesthood for himself; “because,” it says, “every man did what pleased himself, since there was no king in Israel” (Judg. XVII).

It is also his office to crush the millstones of the wicked and to snatch the prey from his mouth, so that he may rightly be called—and indeed be—the father of the poor, the eye of the blind, and the foot of the lame. He too ought to be the defender of the holy Church. Therefore he must be honored both by all the prelates of his kingdom and by all others over whom he presides, if not for his own sake, then for the honor and rank which he has received from God.

Nor ought we to be disturbed because many bad and few good kings are found. Grain appears very scanty in comparison with chaff. Yet the husbandman knows what to do with the vast heap of chaff, and God knows who are his. Nevertheless, he endures the wicked, in order that, by exercising the faith and prudence of his chosen ones through those men’s perversity, he may strengthen them; and because many from their number are converted and corrected.

Let us therefore endure those whom we see to be unjust, and love those whom we see to be just. Yet I do not say that we should tolerate the wicked through carnal fear, but through love of God. Nor do I say that we should love them while expecting from them a carnal return for our love; or that we should serve them for temporal advantages or temporal glory; nor that we should put our hope in them, for “cursed is the man who puts his hope in man.” Nor do I say that we should offer ourselves to them as instruments for doing evil, so as to please them; for “God shall scatter the bones of those who please men,” as the Psalmist testifies (Ps. LII). Rather, let us love the just because they are just, and endure the wicked through love of him who, by his equitable judgment, has set them before us and over us. For nothing fulfills the law except love.

And if the devil secretly assaults us through them, let us cry out the Psalmist’s words: “My God, deliver me from the hand of the transgressor of the law and of the wicked, for you are my patience from my youth” (Ps. LXX). And let us pray him to instill into us the sweetness of his mercy. For, as the Psalmist testifies: “The Lord preserves all who love him, and he will destroy all sinners” (Ps. CXLIV). And the Book of Wisdom says: “Many mighty men have been violently oppressed, and the glorious have been delivered into the hands of strangers” (Ecclus. IV). And Job says: “Want shall seize the wicked man like water; at night a tempest shall oppress him, and a burning wind shall carry him away” (Job XXVII).

Finally, if the devil incites us through them—that is, through wicked prelates—by word or presses us by torture to commit evil, let us immediately answer them that “we must obey God rather than men” (Acts V). Nor should we be overcome by any tortures, because “the sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the future glory that shall be revealed in us” (Rom. VIII).

Accordingly, many are troubled because the righteous suffer many adversities in this life, whereas the wicked enjoy great prosperity. But the apostle Paul rejoices in his own tribulations, saying: “We glory in tribulations, knowing that tribulation works patience; and patience, testing; and testing, hope. But hope does not disappoint, because the love of God has been poured out in our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us” (Rom. V). Filled—or made drunk—with that Spirit, all perfect men endure every adversity of this world for the sake of him who did not disdain to die for them. For the sake, I say, of him who is loved with burning love, all things are endured.

But the impatient person, while refusing to suffer the evils justly inflicted upon him by God, does not thereby escape evils, but comes to suffer heavier evils. For no one escapes the laws of the Almighty; every creature, willing or unwilling, serves God and lies subject to his power. The good, however, are known to serve God by free will, like good sons, and do what is good. The wicked also serve God, but by necessity; and what is just is done with them. Thus God is accustomed to do good both through the good and through the wicked. Yet whatever is done by him is done justly.

It is therefore more equitable that we should follow his will than that he should follow ours; so that, by following his will itself, we may begin to be rightly ordered. Hence it is appropriate that, if anyone anywhere has severed and separated from one another in discord these two powers of which we speak, he should not neglect to do penance, nor by shame add swelling to a deadly and fatal wound. For nothing is more miserable, nothing more wicked, than not to be ashamed of a wound which cannot be concealed, and to be ashamed of its bandaging.

Let him, I say, who has committed this crime labor to make satisfaction to God by the pain of repentance, the groaning of humility, and the sacrifice of a contrite heart, with alms cooperating. For we are not commanded merely to cease from sins; rather, “pray the Lord,” it says, “concerning your past sins.” Penance, finally, is necessary for all sinners; whoever despises performing it is commonly either struck by God’s scourge or crushed by death. Thus the Book of Wisdom warns the sinner: “My son, do not delay in turning to the Lord, and do not put it off from day to day. For his wrath will come suddenly, and in the time of vengeance he will destroy you” (Ecclus. V).

And concerning the penitent, you will find this written in the Book of Job: “If you return to the Almighty, you shall be restored, and you shall put iniquity far from your tent. He will give you flint in place of earth, and torrents of gold in place of flint; silver shall be heaped up for you, and you shall abound in delights; and you shall pray to him, and he will hear you. The Almighty shall be against your enemies, and, determining the matter, shall come to you” [reading uncertain] (Job XXII). And a little later: “He who has bowed down his eyes shall himself be saved” (ibid.).

I had prepared to say still more. But, lest I cause weariness to my readers, I do not wish to extend the book further or prolong the discourse; especially since I remember having said much on all these matters in another book—things which, once heard, ought to suffice for a wise person.

**Here ends the second book.**

[Col. 0975]

# HUGH’S LETTER TO IVO, BISHOP OF CHARTRES

(See above, among the Prolegomena to Hugh, col. 810.)

[Col. 0975]

# THE LIFE OF SAINT SACERDOS, BISHOP OF LIMOGES, REVISED BY HUGH, MONK OF SAINT MARY OF FLEURY

(*Acta Bollandiana*, May, vol. II, p. 11, from a Sarlat manuscript.)

## PRELIMINARY COMMENTARY

[Col. 0975]

1. The places made famous by the birth, residence, episcopate, death, burial, and translation of the relics of Saint Sacerdos are as follows. Bordeaux, the most celebrated emporium of all Aquitaine, was the place of birth in this life for him, or at least for his father. Next comes the city of Cahors, flourishing in the same Aquitaine through its distinguished bishopric and academy; there, while still a young man, he received his education from the bishop himself.

In the diocese of Cahors, this same Saint Sacerdos made more celebrated the village of Calabre, near the river called by Ausonius and Sidonius Apollinaris *Duranius*, commonly *la Dordogne*. There, having been baptized, he received an estate; there later, by divine prompting, he became a monk and then an abbot; and there he was committed to burial. Near it lies the place now called Calviac; and the old name remains in the pond between Calviac and Carlux, belonging to the rights of the monastery and still called *l’étang de Calabre*, as also *la Tour de Calabre*, an ancient tower with a ruined church. The land formerly attached to its parish [reading uncertain] is called the *Bordarium of Saint Sacerdos*, from the bank of the river beside which it lies.

Called from this place to the episcopal see of Limoges, the foremost city of Aquitaine, he lived nearly the remainder of his life on the river Vienne. But, foreseeing that the end of his life was near, while returning to the monastery of Calabre, he died at Argentat, a place on the Dordogne between Bort and Carennac. He was then carried thence to his monastery of Calabre and received burial there. These places belong to his Life; but besides them he honored another city through the translation of his relics and through miracles wrought there by the power of almighty God, and that city adopted him as its principal patron.

2. That city is Sarlat, in the territory of Périgueux, with its celebrated Benedictine monastery under the title of the Savior of the World. The records of the abbey report that it was founded by King Pepin or by his son Charlemagne. To this monastery, in the time of Louis the Pious, the sacred bodies of Saint Sacerdos and of his mother Mundana, a martyr, are reported below to have been translated; afterward they shone forth through very many miracles. Indeed, in 1663 the dean of Sarlat possessed a manuscript of the year 1542 which asserted that the body of his father Laban too was honored there as that of a blessed man.

Later Pope John XXII raised that monastery to episcopal dignity in 1317, and its church was dedicated as a cathedral to Saint Sacerdos, bishop of Limoges, of whom we are here speaking. To the episcopal mensa, or revenues, was attached the monastery of Calabre or Calviac—perhaps by contraction of the name, as though *Calabriacum*—only two leagues distant from Sarlat. There Saint Sacerdos is commonly called *saint Sardos*, *Sardou*, *Sardot*, or *Serdot*, but not *Saproc*, as some French writers erroneously state.

Under that popular name there are two towns: one in Aquitaine, in the diocese of Montauban, one league from the bank of the Garonne and four from Toulouse; the other Saint-Sardos, called de Granges or de Grangiis, in the diocese of Agen, three leagues from that city and one from the mouth where the Lot flows into the Garonne. Add also the church of Saint Sacerdos of Aurenca, named in a bull of Eugenius III.

3. Who first wrote the Life of Saint Sacerdos, and at what time, is unknown to us. Hugh, monk of Fleury, who flourished under Louis VI, surnamed the Fat, around 1130, wrote the following in his Chronicle—printed at Münster in Westphalia in 1636, p. 127—on the occasion of Ecdicius, son of the emperor Avitus:

> “Ecdicius, son of the former emperor Avitus, is called Altitius, through a corruption of his name, as I suppose, in a book containing the Life of a certain holy confessor, Sacerdos by name and office, of the city of Limoges; and he is believed to have received him from the font of baptism. Seeing that the course of this most precious confessor’s Life had been composed partly in an obscure language and partly corrupted by the fault of copyists, I recently determined to correct it and to identify in the present age, after the lapse of many years, the time in which he flourished. I have set forth the virtues of the saint himself in that same narrative in the clearest language. But concerning this Altitius I did not wish rashly to determine what I cannot prove by manifest testimony, believing it better to leave wholly to God what is unknown to me or about which I am doubtful than to defend doubtful matters presumptuously as certain. Yet that ancient book which contains the deeds of the aforesaid confessor seems to me to suggest that the aforementioned Sacerdos may have been a little child around the time of which we are now speaking.”

4. Thus far Hugh of Fleury, using here nearly the same words with which he began the prologue of the Life itself. When he says that the ancient book of the holy confessor’s deeds had been “composed in an obscure language,” he seems to me to mean the vernacular speech of the people of Périgueux in the ninth century: obscure because it had greatly changed from its earlier form by the twelfth century, in which Hugh flourished; or rather, because it was not common, that is, universally intelligible, as were writings composed in Latin.

Thus Regino of Prüm, two centuries older than Hugh of Fleury, says in his Chronicle under the year 814 that he found matters written “in a certain little book composed in a plebeian and rustic speech, which I partly corrected to Latin rule; I also added certain things,” he says, “which I had heard from the narration of elders”—precisely as Hugh says concerning the Life of Saint Sacerdos. The plebeian and rustic speech called such by Regino was doubtless that used throughout the provinces once subject to the Roman Empire. By the Franks, then possessing those provinces and long accustomed to their native—that is, Teutonic—tongue, it was called Roman, or, as one reads in an ancient capitulary, Rustic Roman; as even now that speech, corrupted from Latin, is called in Spain and other provinces, being the language commonly used by regions formerly under Roman dominion.

5. Hugh may have received a book thus composed from his contemporary and companion in monastic life at Fleury, Aimoin. He was a native of Périgueux, “from the village,” as he himself shows in the Life of Saint Abbo, to be given on 3 November, “which is called *ad Francos*, commonly Villefranche,” only thirteen leagues from Sarlat.

Having received it, Hugh did not merely render and polish it in Latin; he also altered certain things according to his own judgment. At §23 he added matters which he believed useful for explaining the chronological arrangement—an account not foolish for its period, but one which this learned age judges plainly unstable. We now publish for the first time this Life of Saint Sacerdos, thus adorned by Hugh of Fleury, in the form sent to us by Armand Gérard, a man learned in historical antiquity and canon of Sarlat, through whose assistance the Sainte-Marthe brothers published a series of the abbots and bishops of Sarlat.

He himself copied this Life from an old manuscript codex of Lives of Saints in his possession, where it occupied folio-pages 88 verso through 95 verso. He also compared the earlier portion of the Life with that distributed into lessons in an old Sarlat breviary and customarily read throughout the octave. He likewise possessed the same legend in the old Périgord speech, not copied from that ancient text used by Hugh, but translated from Hugh’s Latin—closely adhering to it—into Roman, that is, the vernacular idiom.

6. Bernard Gui of the Order of Preachers, made bishop of Lodève in 1324, somewhat abridged the Life and inserted it in his *Sanctorale*. Johannes Scholtz of the Society of Jesus sent it to us in 1642 from a Prague manuscript; later Étienne Baluze of Tulle published it at Tulle, near Limoges, at the end of his learned *Investigation into the Century in Which This Saint Lived*, from a manuscript codex. Antoine Dadin de Hauteserre, professor at Toulouse, is also said to have discussed it in book VI, chapter 2, of volume II of his *Aquitanian Matters*.

But we know the second volume of that work only from the letter of the aforementioned Armand Gérard, where he also mentions the *Investigation* as written in French. We further find it cited by Philippe Labbe in volume II of the *New Library of Manuscript Books*, where on p. 661 and following he published this Life, collated with the autograph copy of Bernard Gui’s *Sanctorale*, and divided it into small chapters. We omit this second Life, since it is extracted from the earlier one and abbreviated by the omission of miracles, and may be seen in the authors named.

7. A brief compendium of the Life also exists in the Limoges Breviary printed in 1626. In that city and diocese he is venerated with a double rite on this fifth day of May, on which day—that is, the third day before the Nones of May—he is said to have rendered his spirit to God in Hugh of Fleury, Bernard Gui, and the said Limoges Breviary. On the same day his feast is celebrated by the people of Sarlat with a most solemn rite, and Saussaye honors him with a lengthy encomium in the *Gallican Martyrology*.

Meanwhile, through scribal error, he was entered under 4 May in a manuscript Ado which we found at Rome in the distinguished library of Cardinal Sforza, where these words were inserted: “In Périgord, the feast of Saint Sacerdos, confessor and bishop.” The following is read in Bellini’s Martyrology, enlarged at Paris: “In the territory of Périgueux, Saint Sacerdos, bishop of Limoges.” Molanus published this, in his usual way, in his supplement to Usuard; and, citing Molanus alone, Saint Sacerdos was entered in the present Roman Martyrology, as also in Canisius’s German Martyrology.

Ferrarius, in his Catalogue of Saints Not in the Roman Martyrology, presents the same man, as though distinct from the one already listed, under 4 May, in these words: “At Limoges in Gaul, Saint Sacerdos, bishop.” Then in the notes he cites the tables of the church of Limoges, although that church honors him on 5 May. His birthplace is then said to be Bordeaux, “where his body lies”; but it is in the cathedral of Sarlat. Finally, it is added that “in the Lives of the Saints of Gaul by René Benoît he is called a priest”; yet the margin indicates that “*Sacerdos* in Latin, *Sainct Prestre* in French” is said.

But how ridiculous this marginal note of René’s is to those who understand that the bishop Saint Sacerdos is commonly called only *saint Serdot*, and that it is altogether irrelevant to him that the appellative *sacerdos*, insofar as it is assigned to the priestly order, should be rendered in the vernacular as *prêtre*. Away with such explanations, which might confuse this saint of ours with some Saint Priest—if such a person existed—as, we have said, Saint Monica, Augustine’s mother, was confused with Saint Prima, martyr of Ostia, for a similar reason.

As to the day, we prefer, with all the ancient Acts and with the usage of the churches of Limoges, Sarlat, and other neighboring places, to present the Acts themselves on this fifth of May. “Since no one has handed down the day on which the translation to the church of Sarlat took place under Charlemagne, we have not yet ascertained it with certainty,” says the author of the Life. Nevertheless, it is commemorated at Sarlat with a double office on 3 July; and again on 23 August, “the Revelation of Saint Sacerdos.” But neither has proper lessons, so that it is difficult to guess what is meant by “Revelation,” to what time it refers, or what difference there is between it and the Translation. Bernard Gui therefore conflated them.

8. A greater controversy concerns the century and years in which he lived. Hauteserre and Baluze, followed by Labbe and Le Cointe, place Saint Sacerdos in the seventh, or even the eighth, century; indeed Labbe corrects everything in volume II of his *New Library* toward that conclusion. First, among the names and deeds of the bishops of Limoges, on p. 267, he finds these words: “Saint Sacerdos, a native of Bordeaux, who is venerated and rests at Sarlat in the diocese of Périgueux, and who also flourished about the year 517”—and rightly so; but Labbe adds, “read 715, or something of that kind.”

Likewise, on p. 663, because below at §13 he is said to have been ordained bishop of Limoges while King Clovis was reigning, Labbe enclosed this in parentheses: “Perhaps ‘under the equivocal one,’ or something similar, has fallen out; or it was the gloss of a foolish copyist, afterward inserted, as are the statements at the end concerning the time in which he flourished”—that is, our §17.

But we judge that all these chronological markers should be preserved; and that Saint Sacerdos ended his final day in the time of Emperor Justinian, perhaps around the year 530, then having completed about seventy years of life, or at least more than sixty. Thus he was received from the font by Ecdicius, son of Emperor Avitus, who in 467, under Emperor Anthemius, was count and master of soldiers in Gaul, and in 474 was made patrician by Emperor Julius Nepos and commonly called king. Thus, with Hugh of Fleury, we judge that at the beginning of the Life “King Ecdicius” should be read in place of “King Altitius”; otherwise we enter an inextricable labyrinth.

Next, we place Capuanus, otherwise unknown, as bishop of Cahors around the year 480, between Alithus, who lived with Saint Paulinus, and Boethius, who subscribed to the Council of Agde in 506 and the first Council of Orléans in 508 or the following year. Saint Sacerdos became monk and then abbot near the end of the fifth century; after Clovis defeated Alaric, king of the Goths, around 509 he became bishop of Limoges, with Clovis’s approval before the latter’s death. Thus he flourished under the emperors Anastasius, Justin, and Justinian, died around 530, and truly lived with Saints Remigius, Benedict, Vedastus, and Amandus. All these are noted in the ancient Acts, nor can anything be drawn from any council held in those periods which conflicts with this chronology.

9. Bernard Gui in Labbe, although saying that Saint Sacerdos flourished around 517—which we also maintain—nevertheless, after placing two Rusticuses before Exotius, whose episcopate began before 560, as is shown from his epitaph and the age of his successor Ferreolus, and after naming eight others after Exotius, adds to the last of them, Caesarius: “Also the two Roriciuses or Ruriciuses, concerning whose times,” he says, “consult the ancient books of Blessed Stephen’s cathedral church.” Finally, after inserting three more, he names Agericus or Agerius, described in the aforementioned Life as Saint Sacerdos’s predecessor.

Since he does this and, contradicting himself, makes Saint Sacerdos almost a contemporary of Saint Cessator, who flourished in the time of Charles Martel, we rightly suspect that the order of bishops in his work is as distorted with regard to Saint Sacerdos as it is with regard to the two Ruriciuses, one of whom we shall shortly prove flourished in the fifth century and the other in the sixth. The Sainte-Marthe brothers, citing a manuscript catalogue of John Cordes, canon of Limoges, adopt Bernard’s opinion regarding Saint Sacerdos and correct him regarding the Ruriciuses. Yet they themselves still require correction, because they assign to the elder’s episcopate the synods attended by the younger. They acknowledge no Rusticuses, and omit several others named by Bernard, considering them distinct persons introduced only through variations in spelling. I readily agree with them in this; but I judge likewise that no sure chronology can be founded upon catalogues interpolated and altered at the discretion of such recent authors.

10. Further, just as the Sainte-Marthe brothers believe that the Rusticuses should not be considered distinct from the Ruriciuses, so Armand Gérard believes that even Aggericus of Hugh of Flavigny—better written Agerius or Agric(i)us—should not be distinguished from the elder Ruricius, between whom and the younger Saint Sacerdos ought to have sat.

The reason for this conjecture is that, just as in Latin a person from the countryside was called *rusticus* or *ruricius*, so among the people of Périgueux in their vernacular, in which these words were not in use, he should have been called *agre* or *agry*, from *ager*, “field.” When Hugh of Flavigny found the name of the bishop who preceded Sacerdos written thus, and since the Latin and proper names of the bishops of Limoges were less familiar to him, Armand thinks that, wishing to give the Périgord words a Latin form, Hugh called him Aggericus when he ought to have called him Ruricius.

Yet there are those to whom this seems wholly implausible, and who judge that Agericus must certainly be retained as distinct from the Ruriciuses. Nothing, indeed, prevents his being inserted between them. For it is certain that Ruricius I was bishop in 470 and was excused in 506, because of age and illness, from attending the Council of Agde. We find no record of the younger before 535, when he attended the Council of Clermont; he seems to have remained alive until 555 or later. A considerable interval may therefore be set between the two; and room is made not only for Saint Sacerdos but also, before him, for Aggericus, at least for two years, if he was distinct from Ruricius I.

11. The authors who joined the two Ruriciuses had no other basis than that Venantius Fortunatus joined them in his epitaph, singing thus:

> Here the tombs cover the sacred bodies  
> of bishops, shining throughout the world; their spirit inhabits the stars—  
> the two Ruriciuses, bound by name and blood,  
> grandfather and grandson rejoicing alike, one here, the other there.  
> Each in his own time founded the pious churches of the Patron:  
> this one founded that of Augustine, that one of Peter.

Yet the verse no more says that they succeeded one another immediately in the episcopate than that the grandfather founded the church of Saint Augustine and the grandson that of Peter, as Bernard Gui and others after him interpret it. Rather, the syntax of the words, supported by chronological considerations, requires that the grandfather founded the church of Peter and the grandson that of Augustine.

# LIFE OF SAINT SACERDOS

[Col. 0979]

## PROLOGUE

From a manuscript of the Colbert Library at Paris.

[Col. 0979A]

As I reread the ancient account of the life of the glorious bishop Sacerdos, and observed in it some superfluous matters and others corrupted through the fault of copyists, I resolved to correct it for the present age; and to portray more clearly and honorably the text of the same history, transformed and improved by concise brevity. For the polishing and refining of it, I assembled many histories for myself, as though files, so that it might contain nothing but what is splendid and honorable; and, distinguishing the text into eleven chapters, I adorned it from every quarter.

I also noted in the margins, where I judged it appropriate, certain materials from various histories.

> **Note: [Col. 0979A]** No one afterward took the trouble to transcribe these marginal notes attached to Hugh’s first manuscript, not even at Sarlat.

[Col. 0980A]

Thus the reader might learn from them the sequence of times and gather much from little. I added also one chapter concerning the translation of that same most blessed bishop.

> **Note: [Col. 0980A]** This begins below at §21.

But I do not endeavor to transcribe word for word, nor yet wholly to produce new material in place of old; rather, according to the poverty of my small talent, I seek to draw out and improve sense from sense, as the reader’s diligence, by examining both accounts, will readily be able to verify.

In order that I might do this, lord Arnaldus…

> **Note: [Col. 0981A]** The Sainte-Marthe brothers do indeed provide a certain list of the abbots of Sarlat, but it is exceedingly confused and mutilated in more than one place. It is therefore pleasing, on the authority of the much-praised Armand Gérard, to offer another list more accurately set out. According to it, the Arnald named here presided from 1122 until 1134, when Hugh of Fleury could still have been living and flourishing, although he dedicated his Chronicle to Ivo of Chartres, who died about 1115.
>
> The list of abbots is nevertheless preceded by a list of the counts of Périgueux as follows:
>
> “When Count Emenon of Angoulême died in 867, Charles the Bald appointed Wulgrin administrator of the counties of Angoulême and Périgueux. His descendants afterward, like the sons of other counts in the province, under Charles the Simple claimed for themselves, as lords, hereditary right over the counties entrusted to each of them. Therefore we call the said Wulgrin, who died in 884, the first hereditary count of Périgueux.
>
> “He left two sons after him. The county of Angoulême fell to the elder, Hilduin; to the younger, William, called Taillefer—that is, Iron-cutter—fell Périgueux and Agen. Agen had also come to Wulgrin by the dowry of his wife Rogelindis, who was sister of William II, count of Toulouse. William Taillefer died in 920, leaving as his successor in Périgueux his son Bernard, the same man who, after 936, was a benefactor and reformer of the monastery of Sarlat, while the lord Louis was emperor—that is, reigning king—the man whom writers call Louis IV, the Overseas, son of Charles the Simple by Ogiva, from the aforementioned year until 954.
>
> “Bernard had four sons, who after his death and after the year 950 successively bore the title of count of Périgueux; but, dying without children, they left their inheritance to the sons of their aunt Emma, born of Boso the Elder, count of La Marche, and called to the succession in Périgueux about the year 976. The sons of the aforementioned Bernard were Arnald Borsacius—incorrectly called Vortacius by Besly among the counts of Aquitaine—William, Talleyrand, Ranulf Bonus-par, or Bonus-socius, and Richard Simplex.”
>
> All these details are found in the Chronicle of Ademar and the *History of the Bishops of Angoulême*, in Labbe’s *New Library*, vol. II, pp. 165, 167, and 253; and also in fragments of the history of the dukes of Aquitaine and counts of Poitou in Besly. The William Talleyrand just named is the very man who, contrary to apostolic commands, became the seller of the church of Sarlat to benefit Hubert mentioned at §25.
>
> Armand Gérard wishes the series of abbots—which appears in a confused state in volume IV of *Gallia Christiana*, and in which that Simonist Hubert is not found—to be corrected thus: that an abbot should have been appointed at the reform of the monastery of Sarlat about the year 936.

“1. Odo, the same man (as is believed) who, as Abbot of Cluny, reformed the Benedictine Order in Gaul. 2. Adacius, appointed by Odo, about the year 940, after he had previously reformed the abbey of Tulle. 3. Asservarius, or Assonarius, about 950. 4. Bassenus, about 960. 5. Hubert, a simoniac, about 970. 6. Bernard, 975. 7. Gerald, 994. 8. Americus, 1031. 9. Stephen, 1076. 10. Arnald, 1122. He is the very man for whom Hugh of Fleury embellished these Acts of St. Sacerdos. The Sammarthani must in every respect be corrected when they say [Col. 0982B] that the Translation of St. Sacerdos took place under him about the year 1140. For this event is narrated in the Acts as having occurred under Louis the Pious, immediately after the restoration of the church; and in chapter 2 of the Chronicle of Geoffrey of Vigeois it is related how ‘the body of St. Pardulf was brought from the monastery of Guéret to the monastery of Sarlat, and was honourably placed beside the body of St. Sacerdos, bishop of Limoges’—certainly about the year 1000, and thus after the Translation had occurred. 11. Gilbert, 1134, omitted by the Sammarthani. 12. Raymond de Felenon, 1153. 13. Garin de Comarque, 1169. 14. Ralph de Cromiac, not Cormiac, 1195. 15. Arnald, 1202. 16. Bertrand de Limegeoulz, 1208, not Bernard. [Col. 0982C] 17. Guy de Cornil, 1212, passed over by the Sammarthani. 18. Elias de Umion, not Vinion, 1221. 19. Stephen de Rignac, 1229. 20. Elias Petri, 1232. 21. Bernard del Couderc, 1236. 22. Gerald de Vallibus, 1238. 23. Elias de Maignanac, 1249, who was dean of Issigeac. 24. Bernard III, 1250. 25. Gerald d’Albusson, 1255. Between these last three abbots there was a dispute of right as to which of them had precedence, and the case was still pending at Rome in 1260. 26. Arnold de Stapone, 1260, in whose favour it is likely that those three claimants were deposed through a judicial sentence and a new election. 27. Robert of St. Michael, 1274. 28. Bernard de Vallibus, 1283. 29. Armand of St. Leonard, 1312, omitted [Col. 0982D] by the Sammarthani. He was abbot until 1313, when the abbey of Sarlat was raised to a bishopric by Pope John XXII. Since Raymond de Rocacornu, abbot of Gaillac, was created its first bishop, it is credible that the abbey of Gaillac passed in exchange to Armand.”

Thus far that author, whose diligence one might wish were imitated by more people, so that they might make easier use of the sacred catalogues. Although the Sammarthani collected these with industry, we learn from this single example that they nevertheless suffer from serious defects. The Louis during whose rule or reign the charter was drawn up was Louis IV, called “from Overseas” (*Ultramarinus*). For Count Bernard, the author of the reform, succeeded his father William “Iron-Cutter” (*Sector ferri*) in 920 and lived until 950; and Bernard’s second-born son, bearing his grandfather’s name and surnamed Tailerand, sold the abbey to the simoniacal Abbot Hubert about the year 970.] The abbot, the administrator of the very abbey of St. Sacerdos, warned me; and, overcome by his many entreaties, I could not disregard his command. The merit also of so great a confessor compelled me, as did the miracles more frequently wrought at his most sacred [Col. 0982A] bones. When I saw that the histories of ancient tyrants were excellently exalted by the eloquence of orators, while the sequence of the life of this holy and most illustrious star—namely, holy Sacerdos—was diminished by writers’ negligence; and that consequently the account of truth in that sequence was concealed, as it were, by certain windings, just as the sun is sometimes obscured by clouds: it seemed unworthy to me, and I could not possibly endure it without writing something splendid and honourable [Col. 0983A] concerning him. This was especially so because material was not lacking, and the order of ancient histories could sufficiently support this work of ours. Finally, the proof of my faith likewise requires that I devoutly compose some small work in praise of God and his saints, to their praise and glory, so that the saints themselves may obtain for me, from my judge and redeemer, forgiveness of my sins.

As for ability in speech, I have placed my hope in him who said: “Open your mouth, and I will fill it.” Therefore my poor inclination may be enriched by his power, for the praise of this confessor. To add anything to the sequence of his life is not praiseworthy but wicked: true holiness and pure religion do not need human falsehood; indeed, they are rather obscured [Col. 0983B] when wrapped in a fabrication of falsehood. Yet the merit of any person may be commended to humankind by the weight of certain words, and his praise may be made graceful by an orator’s skill. But the quality of each person’s merits is discerned by almighty God without any interpretation of speech.

Having said this beforehand, I now address words to the envious, who disdain old things and pursue novelties. I warn them not perhaps to judge my little work contemptible because it is not new: for no one doubts that all old things were once new. I also ask them to remember that Moses, born in the fourth age, began his history from the origin of the world; that Josephus, the writer of the *Antiquities*, recast the books of Moses in a different verbal form; and that blessed [Col. 0983C] Jerome did not hesitate to translate what had already been translated by the ancients, adding to his translation many things that had been omitted. If I wished, I could here mention more men and provide examples from modern times; but it is enough to have introduced these alone. Thus, as I think, it is permitted to a wise person to weave a truthful history from an ancient subject and to substitute more dignified language for uncultivated expressions. Someone can sometimes discuss one and the same matter in two ways and express the truth in both; indeed, we often see one orator adorn another’s speech with a certain abundance of words and state the same matter differently. Yet I know that I am not permitted what is proved to have been permitted to men most holy and most eloquent, because I lack the eloquence of orators [Col. 0983D] and do not know the art by which such things are done—except that, as I have already said, I have placed the anchor of faith in the power of the Holy Spirit. For even in the present age that same Holy Spirit grants clear and pure effectiveness of speech, for the edification of many, to whomever he wills—the Spirit who formerly gave his holy Church, from a persecutor, a Doctor, and from a tax collector, by his grace, an Evangelist. [Col. 0984A] Relying on that Spirit, though unworthy, I do not fear devoutly to undertake this burden.

## CHAPTER I. Birth, upbringing, monastic life, and abbacy.

[CHAP. I.] 1. The glorious bishop Sacerdos, worthy of imitation by all priests throughout the world, was born in the province of Aquitaine and sprang from an illustrious lineage. Though noble by birth, he shone more nobly through the excellence of his life. Anyone may readily learn what sort of man he was, and how great, from what I have resolved, with the cooperation of the Holy Spirit, to write concerning the character of his life and the abundance of his many miracles. [Note: [Col. 0983D] From this it is clear that the Miracles, omitted by Bernard Gui and related below in chapter 4, were composed by the same ancient author.] His father, therefore, was the most distinguished man Laban, one of the leading citizens of Bordeaux; his mother was called Mundana. At that time the most Christian king Anticius [Note: [Col. 0983D] According to Hugh of Fleury, he is Ecdicius, son of the Emperor Avitus, of whom we have spoken above.] reigned in the province of Aquitaine. It happened that this king came to a certain village named Calabrum [Note: [Col. 0983D] Calabrum, near Calviac, is in the diocese of Cahors, though in the province of Périgord. Thus Armand Gerard in his Notes.], situated between the territories of Cahors and Périgueux, not far from the Dordogne River. While he remained there for some time, Laban, the father of the aforesaid man, standing before him one day, said: “My lord king, if it please your serenity to honour me, I beg that you receive my only son, whom the Lord has lately deigned to grant me, through the regeneration of baptism.” The king gladly replied at once: “If you present him before our eyes, I shall do what you ask.” [Col. 0984C] Then Laban hurriedly brought his son to him, saying: “Behold, my lord king, my son is here, whom you promised to receive from the sacred washing of the font.” Immediately the king, receiving the boy from the sacred water, gave him the aforesaid village of Calabrum, in which these events occurred, to possess by hereditary right; for that village was a royal estate. And by divine disposition it came about that at the reception of baptism the boy was called Sacerdos by name, destined thereafter to be a great priest in office in the Church.

[CHAP. II.] 2. When these things had been done, the venerable boy Sacerdos was entrusted to St. Capuanus, [Note: [Col. 0984D] Prague manuscript: “to Capuanus, bishop of Cahors, a man outstanding among the bishops of Aquitaine.” In Labbe he too is called saint. In the Limoges Breviary, a man of known holiness. He appears to be placed between Alithius and Boethius, and thus would be fifth in the Sammarthani.] bishop of Cahors, so that he might instruct him in letters and Christian discipline. [Note: [Col. 0984D] Sarlat Breviary: “instruct him.”] Capuanus was in those days most eminent [Col. 0984D] among the religious bishops of Aquitaine. This too occurred [Note: [Col. 0984D] The same source: “also happened.”] by the dispensation of almighty God, so that the most holy boy might drink the purest streams of doctrine from a catholic teacher perfected in holiness, and might afterward, once made an outstanding teacher, water the minds of believers; and so that he might not at any time be ensnared by heretical perversity and stray from the straight path of faith, since there was then a very great [Col. 0985A] multitude of such people in that region. [Note: [Col. 0985D] Because of the Visigothic kings, ruling there and infected with the Arian heresy.] Thus in childhood Sacerdos, beloved of the Lord, was adorned by the dignity of his name, the nobility of his parents, a royal gift, and the instruction of a holy bishop, so that mortals might thereby see with what reverence he ought to be honoured, whom divine bounty so exalted beforehand by so many and such great gifts.

3. At length holy Sacerdos, after the years of childhood had passed, while applying himself to salutary teachings and surpassing the years of adolescence by maturity of life, began to excel all his contemporaries in the praise of virtues. Hence he was exceedingly dear to the venerable Capuanus, under whose instruction he lived, and was always [Col. 0985B] at his side. What he eagerly drank from Capuanus’s lips, he stored in the treasury of his heart. His simplicity commended his shrewdness, and modesty tempered his polished speech. He did not glory in bodily beauty or exalt himself because of worldly favour. Yet, when he had already reached the bounds of youth, he immediately became a lover of chastity in that very ardent age and despised the delights of the world. Whenever the tempter came to him seeking an entrance for temptation, he always found the door of his breast shut against him. Why say more? Since inwardly he had already become a pure vessel of the Holy Spirit and daily offered to God upon the altar of his mind a holocaust of pious devotion, the aforesaid Bishop Capuanus, through angelic admonition, ordained [Col. 0985C] him deacon. After this ordination, the same most holy man Sacerdos shone more brightly in the radiance of virtues, and served equally outwardly through ecclesiastical ministry the almighty God whom he had long served inwardly. From that time he began lavishly to distribute alms to the needy and to devote himself more perfectly to the praises of God.

[CHAP. III.] 4. At that same time there was in the already mentioned village of Calabrum a monastery in which forty or more monks lived. To these the beloved of the Lord, Sacerdos, ministered with particular diligence, considering himself undoubtedly to lose all that he did not bestow upon them from his own means. Having first renewed the basilica there, nearly worn away by long age, [Col. 0985D] he also constructed suitable dwellings for the monks. He granted to that monastery likewise the same village of Calabrum, with its appurtenances, which, as was said, he had received from King Anticius to possess by hereditary right. He also prayed frequently, because he had learned that one ought always to pray and not grow weary. One day, when as was his custom he had prostrated himself in prayer, a divine voice was sent to him, saying: “O my beloved Sacerdos, enter the monastery without fear, because I have chosen you for the order of monastic religion; and because you have shown yourself to me as a sanctified vessel from your very cradle, I have assigned angelic protection to you.” At this voice the great deacon [Col. 0986A] Sacerdos immediately began to give double thanks to almighty God because he had deserved to be strengthened from heaven by a voice addressed to him. Taking up the religious habit, he began to observe the rule of his vocation most perfectly. But it is not within the scope of our eloquence to declare how great the purity of his mind and the uprightness of his conduct were; how great the severity of his fasts and, above all, his attention to sacred reading; or what zeal for religious life began, beyond that of the other brethren, to commend him to God and humankind. Thus, endowed with the privilege of these and other virtues, and especially of humility, this most holy man served the Lord under an abbot’s rule for about seven years before he entered the order of priesthood. He never abandoned the practice of right conduct, so as to command others only after he had subjected himself, in the due order of reason, to those greater than himself. [Col. 0986B]

[CHAP. IV.] 5. After these days, the man of God Sacerdos came to preside over the brethren of the aforesaid monastery. Yet he strove to benefit them all more than to rule them. He sought to be worthy of imitation by them and to show good works more by deeds than by words. He devoted himself daily to reading, while also diligently serving everyone. As the servant of all, he served all; but as a most expert judge, he rebuked them for their sins. He appeared least among all; but as a most excellent teacher, he instructed them in salutary doctrines. Like a most kindly father, he loved all; but, like a wise physician, he removed from the body of the Church those whom he foresaw to be incorrigible, as though they were putrid limbs. [Col. 0986C] He tempered strength with gentleness and strengthened self-restraint with prudence. Thus in all his deeds he appeared both just and merciful.

6. Therefore all who lived in that province loved him with their whole strength and extolled him with great expressions of praise. Yet, so far as he could, he concealed the merit of his life, lest perhaps he should swell inwardly with praise and the fruit of humility perish within him. Nevertheless, the reputation attendant upon virtues grew daily concerning him, and no small crowd of people came to him from different regions. Some indeed came in order to become better through the example of so great a man; some merely to visit him; others to receive from him food [Col. 0986D] for the body or other necessities; and others to commend their souls to the Lord through his prayers. To all of these the most holy man offered abundantly the nourishment of divine teachings; and, as each one needed, he laboured zealously, insofar as he could, for their advancement. His concern for the poor and for pilgrims was such that, with great gladness of heart, he spent on their needs whatever he could deny himself. Content with one very cheap garment of his Order, he clothed the naked and loved frugality; sparing toward himself, he was generous toward others.

## CHAPTER II. Miracles during his lifetime; his parents’ conversion to a holy life; the Limoges episcopate; death.

[Col. 0987A]

[CHAP. V.] 7. Meanwhile the man of God Sacerdos desired to ascend to the honour of the priesthood, so that, being higher in rank, he might devote himself more freely to the Lord; and whenever he celebrated the sacred mysteries, he might offer himself in prayer with tears. Yet, so that it might at last be made manifest to humankind how great was his holiness, it pleased divine mercy to adorn his life with the glory of miracles. This happened as follows.

8. In the aforesaid village of Calabrum there was a certain man whose skin leprosy had disfigured. It happened one day that the man of God Sacerdos was warned by an angel to visit him and, after washing his hands, touch every place [Col. 0987B] affected by his illness. After he had done so, offering prayer beforehand, he immediately restored the man to health. When the inhabitants of the place, and indeed all the people of that region, heard of this, they gave thanks to the Lord with joyful hearts, praising the merits of blessed Sacerdos.

9. His mother Mundana also, on hearing that her son had performed so great a miracle, blessed the Lord, by whose wonderful aid all miracles are performed. Stricken in heart, she thereafter despised all worldly delights and desired to imitate the footsteps of her son. At that time her husband Laban was living in the city of Bordeaux.
