She sent for him and informed him through a messenger that the servant of God had performed so remarkable a miracle. On hearing this, Laban [Col. 0987C] likewise glorified the Lord for what had occurred.

[CHAP. VI.] 10. Since Laban, as was said above, was noble by birth, his venerable wife Mundana was like him in character and noble descent. Both were illustrious according to worldly standing and exceedingly rich in abundance of possessions. But one day the venerable Mundana fell at her husband’s feet and tearfully begged that together they might make the blessed exchange of earthly things for heavenly, follow the footsteps of St. Sacerdos by imitation, and live spiritually together as they had lived carnally together. Laban heard her petition, was stricken in heart, and willingly gave his consent. They divided into two portions the whole of their property [Col. 0987D] and possessions: one they gave to Christ’s Church, and the other they distributed to the poor and pilgrims. They also allowed their slaves and household servants to depart free, and devoted the rest of their lives to the Lord. Together, with one mind, according to the command of the Apostle Paul (Romans 12:11), they were fervent in spirit, serving the Lord, rejoicing in hope, patient in tribulation, persistent in prayer, sharing in the needs of the saints, [Col. 0988A] pursuing hospitality, and following in every respect the footsteps of the Lord Jesus Christ. Above all, they loved pilgrims and devoted themselves generously to receiving them.

[CHAP. VII.] 11. One day, when the man of God Sacerdos had assembled with the brethren, as usual, at the second hour for prayer, it happened that his father departed from the world. When messengers came wishing to tell him this, he was engaged most devoutly in prayer, so that he looked at none of them until he had ended the prayer. After the prayer was completed, he went to his father, now lifeless. Finding him laid out dead in the midst, he asked the hour of his departure and discovered that he had died at the very hour when Sacerdos had begun prayer. The venerable Mundana mourned him, as did his relatives and neighbours standing around together. [Col. 0988B] The man of God Sacerdos comforted them, maintaining that one should not mourn a man who, in fulfilling the Gospel’s command, had devoutly distributed the resources of his possessions to pilgrims and the poor.

12. He then asked them again whether they had provided the rites fitting for his funeral. When they answered that he had not partaken of the life-giving mysteries of the Lord’s body and blood, Sacerdos immediately prostrated himself upon the ground in great grief and prayed for a very long time. Then, taking hold of the dead man’s hand, he called him by name once and twice. At once, at the voice of the man of God, he arose as though asleep; and, looking upon the surrounding multitude, uttered these words: “At the second hour of the present [Col. 0988C] day I had departed from the world, but through the merits of my son it has been granted me to return once more to those above.” As he spoke these words, all present marvelled at the miracle of so great a thing; spreading their hands aloft and raising their cry to heaven, they gave thanks to the Lord. When they had become silent, the venerable Sacerdos immediately gave him communion of the Lord’s body, by receiving which he was greatly strengthened. Then the same man of God threw himself before his father’s presence and began, in imitation of the patriarch [Note: [Col. 0987D] Thus Bernard Gui in the Prague manuscript also expressly gives Jacob, as found in Genesis chapter 49. But Labbe gives Job.] Jacob, to request his paternal blessing. When the father immediately blessed him, he again soon rested in peace. O praiseworthy merit of the blessed man, through which the father is restored to those above, refreshed by the viaticum of the Lord’s body, and afterward permitted to rest in peace!

[Col. 0988D] [CHAP. VIII.] 13. Once the things we have described had been accomplished, the fame of the blessed man began to spread far and wide, and the fragrance of his holy conduct to fill neighbouring regions. Thus, when Aggericus, bishop of Limoges, of blessed memory, died, the man of God Sacerdos was raised to the see of the same Church, to the honour of God, by election of the clergy and favour of the people, with the approval also of Clovis, king of the Franks, [Note: [Col. 0987D] Knowledge of both bishops, Aggericus and Sacerdos, as also of Capuanus, bishop of Cahors, is found only in this Life, because the catalogues concerning the earliest bishops are very mutilated.] the elder ruler of that province. [Note: [Col. 0988D] After King Alaric had been defeated by Clovis in 507, Clovis ruled Aquitaine; and before his death, that is, before 27 November 509, St. Sacerdos appears to have been made bishop.] [Col. 0989A] For some years thereafter he governed the same Church by God’s providence. [Note: [Col. 0989D] At least until the reign of Justinian, which began in 527. Armand Gerard observes, however, that this should not be understood as though the saint had entirely banished kites from that place, as some have wished, since they are still seen there as elsewhere; rather, they are not more hostile to hens there than elsewhere.] But lest we weary anyone through verbosity, we avoid prolixity and incline toward brevity; let us now turn to the account of his death.

[CHAP. IX.] 14. Therefore, when the most blessed Sacerdos felt, through revelation of the Holy Spirit, that his last day was at hand, he took leave of the brethren, left the city of Limoges, and endeavoured to return to the land of his birth. For by divine grace preordained he desired his body to be buried where he had begun the religious life. As he travelled, he came to a village called Argentac, where, already long worn down by illness, he was afflicted with severe [Col. 0989B] distress. But after he had recovered his breath a little, he asked for food of eggs. His disciples heard this and hastened diligently to seek throughout the inhabitants of the village the food he had requested; finding none, they at once informed their master. In that village the stock of hens had hitherto been ravaged by the savage voracity of kites and hawks, so that scarcely could any hen ever survive there. When the holy man learned this, he restrained the birds’ nuisance, saying: “Henceforth, within this circuit of the village, let none of the birds of prey dare to harass hens.” The decree of God’s servant remains inviolable forever. [Note: [Col. 0989D] The remainder of this section is untouched in Bernard Gui.] A wondrous thing! Yet this one indication sufficiently shows that the authority of the episcopal office, strong in power, had long been able to bind and loose human beings. [Col. 0989C] For he was truly the disciple of him who, standing in a boat, commanded the winds and sea, and there came to be a great calm. Thus once the most blessed Martin, archbishop of Tours, forbade cormorants to take prey from the river and restrained their ravenous gluttony. Birds obeyed Martin’s commands; hawks still obey the prohibition of Sacerdos, God’s servant. May he, [Note: [Col. 0989D] Sarlat Breviary: “of those who pray.”] we pray, through his prayers release us from sins and defend us who beseech him, as he now protects birds.

[CHAP. X.] 15. Therefore the man of God Sacerdos, the most holy bishop, seeing that his final day had dawned for him, summoned his disciples and ordered that his body be returned to the church in which he had begun the religious life. [Col. 0989D] Finally, having fortified his departure with the divine mysteries, [Col. 0990A] having delivered many words of sacred exhortation to his disciples and to all assembled there, and having commended himself and the spiritual sons whom he was leaving to almighty God, he gave his spirit to heaven on the third day before the Nones of May [5 May]. He now stands, surrounded by angelic choirs, near him whom he had served while on earth. For when our Lord Jesus Christ was on earth, he prayed to the Father: “Father, I desire that where I am, there also may be my servant.”

16. When the disciples who had accompanied him saw their master lifeless, overcome inwardly by excessive grief, they said: “Why, Father, did you come here to die? Why did you choose to live with us for so very brief a term of life? Why, sweetest Father, do you leave us orphans?” As the disciples gave expression to their grief by these and similar laments, they endeavoured to fulfil their master’s commands. They placed his lifeless limbs in a boat and set out along the channel of the Dordogne toward the aforesaid [Note: [Col. 0989D] Therefore St. Sacerdos was not buried at Argentac, where he died, as Saussay wrongly states in his supplement; he makes an even graver error in writing Argentoratum for Argentac, Argentoratum being the German city on the Rhine. Arthur du Monstier in the *Gynaeceum Sacrum* for this day also copied Saussay’s error in part.] monastery. As they were now approaching the dwelling of the mother of Lord Sacerdos, behold, blessed Mundana, deprived of sight, was making her way to her son’s funeral. When, supported by the hands of servants, she reached the riverbank, she immediately deserved to receive her sight by divine power. Now, as in the preceding miracle, let us compare Sacerdos, beloved of the Lord, with the most blessed Martin, archbishop of Tours. Martin [Note: [Col. 0989D] Neither this nor what was stated above concerning [Col. 0990D] cormorants is found in Sulpicius Severus; whence these things were taken we shall investigate on 11 November.] converted his mother from the error of paganism; Sacerdos, the most holy bishop, prompted his mother to reform her life by the example of continence. Martin inwardly enlightened his mother through faith; Sacerdos [Col. 0990C] enlightened her outwardly, to the praise and glory of our Lord Jesus Christ, who lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit through all ages of ages. Amen.

## CHAPTER III. Chronology; burial; translation of the body to Sarlat.

[CHAP. XI.] 17. The reverend bishop St. Sacerdos flourished in the times of the emperors Anastasius [Note: [Col. 0990D] Anastasius ruled from 11 April 491 until 8 July 518.] and Justin the Elder [Note: [Col. 0990D] Justin began to rule on the day after Anastasius’s death; in 527 he declared Justinian his successor on 1 April, and when he died on 1 August, Justinian became sole ruler.] and Justinian, who succeeded one another; while Clovis, [Note: [Col. 0990D] Clovis lived only during Anastasius’s reign.] son of Childeric, held the monarchy of the Franks and Aquitanians. St. Remigius baptized this Clovis. [Note: [Col. 0990D] Baptized in 496, in the seventeenth year of his reign, as we demonstrate elsewhere.] At this same time flourished the outstanding lawgiver of monks, Benedict, [Note: [Col. 0990D] St. Benedict was born about 480 and died in 543, on 21 March, on which day we have given his Acts.] and blessed Amandus [Note: [Col. 0990D] Both are commemorated on 6 February. Of these, Vedastus was made bishop when elderly about 500 and died about 540. But St. Amandus was born about 494 and is believed to have died at about ninety years of age, around 584.] and St. Vedastus, bishops, [Col. 0991A] and many other most holy men. He was also the twenty-ninth [Note: [Col. 0991C] Here some *sphálma* (error) appears, perhaps in the catalogue of the bishops of Limoges known when the ancient Life was written. St. Sacerdos was the ninth after the first among those who, once the episcopate had been firmly established, succeeded one another without interruption; St. Martial and his disciple [Col. 0991D] St. Aurelian are not counted among them.] bishop of the Church of Limoges after blessed Martial, the first bishop of that city and disciple of Peter, prince of the apostles. [Note: [Col. 0991D] Such is the popular opinion. Others, following Gregory of Tours, place him in the time of Decius; this will be examined in his Acts on 30 June. Those who hold the popular opinion must certainly admit a great gap in the succession of bishops; and perhaps for this reason Bernard Gui, in his catalogue, multiplies their names so liberally, as we said above.]

18. When the most glorious bishop of Christ, Sacerdos, as already stated, had been released from the bonds of the body, the monks of the often-mentioned monastery took down his most holy body from the boat, laid it upon their shoulders, and brought it into the church of which, by the Lord’s gift, he had been abbot. What a gathering of men and women then arrived there, and what pomp of ecclesiastical ornaments was borne there, we judge superfluous to say. Yet one could have seen people coming to his funeral both rejoicing and mourning. They rejoiced because they received the patronage of so great [Col. 0991B] a confessor; they mourned because they had lost a sweet consolation. They could not restrain their tears because of tender devotion, yet they were consoled by the arrival of his body. They poured forth hymns and tears together; they exulted and grieved at once.

19. Yet all were refreshed by a most sweet fragrance and at the same time were given an inestimable sweetness to drink. For the entire body of the man of God was fragrant with divine nectar, as though it had been anointed with precious perfume. A choir of angels accompanied him in heaven, whom a choir of virtues had always accompanied on earth. With his most holy soul, rejoicing angels praised the Lord, while those upon the earth honourably performed the funeral rites. Thus, by God’s favour, the relics of the most reverend [Col. 0991C] bishop Sacerdos were happily laid away in the aforementioned basilica.

[CHAP. XII.] 20. A long time afterward, while St. Mundana continually watered her son’s mausoleum with pious tears, she fell slain by the sword in the Vandal [Note: [Col. 0991D] In book II, chapter 17, of *Paulinus Illustratus*, Peter Francis Chifflet shows that writers use the single name “Vandals” for all Gothic or Getic nations and other barbarians. Thus St. Mundana may have been killed in some incursion of the Goths, who still held nearby Narbonensian Gaul. Armand Gerard reported that she is honoured in the Church of Sarlat on 31 May, with a double rite, as a widow and martyr; but Saussay reports her in his supplement on this day, and Arthur follows him in the *Gynaeceum Sacrum*.] persecution and, because of her invincible confession of Christ, underwent the sacrifice of martyrdom. Her body, collected by the faithful, was carefully buried beside the tomb of her most reverend and most holy son, Bishop Sacerdos. [Col. 0992A] There, by the help of divine grace, many miracles take place through the power of our Lord Jesus Christ, who lives and reigns with the Father and Holy Spirit through all ages of ages. Amen. [Note: [Col. 0991D] Here the manuscript Sarlat Breviary ends, where there are [Col. 0992C] as many lessons as the sections numbered by us thus far.]

### Chapter XIII

**21.** While the excellent Emperor Charlemagne held the imperial sceptres, and his son Louis the Pious ruled Aquitaine under his father’s authority, as the little book of their deeds testifies, many monasteries in the kingdom of Aquitaine were restored by that same King Louis, and many were built from their foundations; by these, as by certain lights, all Aquitaine is now adorned. Many bishops, and very many laymen as well, emulated this example, striving to restore what had fallen into ruin and to construct new monasteries. At this same time, in the heart of that province, the church of the Saviour of the world in the village of Sarlat, situated in the district of Périgueux, was restored by religious men.

> **Note [Col. 0992D].** Above all by Bernard, count of Périgueux, with the consent of his wife Garsinda; he had hitherto held the place under his own jurisdiction. See his charter in *Gallia Christiana*, vol. IV, p. 808.

Thus, through God’s merciful working, it came about that Louis, the son of that Emperor, restored the churches which the aforesaid Emperor Charlemagne had damaged in the destructive war which he had at last concluded after many years against the tyrant Waifer, and against Hunald, who had occupied Aquitaine after Waifer’s death.

> **Note [Col. 0992D].** Rather, it was Pippin, Charlemagne’s father, who finished the war against Waifer or Waifar; Waifer was killed in the year 768, before Pippin’s death, which occurred on 24 September. Hunald, Waifer’s father, was put to flight by Charlemagne and then captured. See the *Life* for 28 January, no. 8.

The most pious Emperor Charlemagne himself adorned all these churches with immense quantities of gold and silver, enriched them with the most ample gifts and honours of precious gems, and moreover distinguished them—what is more precious still—with the most holy protection of relics. Among these, that same prince, the beloved lord Charlemagne,

> **Note [Col. 0992D].** Charlemagne is honoured with an ecclesiastical office among the people of Sarlat.

honoured—or rather sanctified—this church of Sarlat of which we speak with no small portion of the wood of the Lord’s Cross. As is read in certain accounts of his deeds,

> **Note [Col. 0992D].** Certain Acts have been published under Turpin’s name and everywhere disapproved.

the Emperor himself

> **Note [Col. 0992D].** Rather, he had received it from Fortunatus or Macarius, bishop of Jerusalem; for he himself had not made a pilgrimage there.

had brought it from Jerusalem together with many other relics.

> **Note [Col. 0992C].** In the Sarlat manuscript the title is given as: “On the revelation of Saint Sacerdos.” In Bernard Gui: “On the Translation of the Body of Saint Sacerdos to the village and monastery of Sarlat in the territory of Périgueux.” Thus the following material is found in André Duchesne, vol. III, p. 385.

### Chapter XIV

**22.** At that time the monks of the same church of Sarlat went to the previously named village of Calabrum,

> **Note [Col. 0993D].** It is strange that Saussaye should say that the name Sarlat was subsequently given to Calabrum, although the two are about two leagues apart.

which had now been reduced almost to wilderness. One night they broke open the tombs of both saints—namely, the most holy Sacerdos and his mother, Saint Mundana the martyr—removed their most holy bodies, carried them away with them, and buried them with the highest honour within the aforesaid church of the Saviour of the world. By careful investigation we have learned that all this happened as we have stated. Yet, since no one has handed down to us the day on which these things were done, we do not yet know it with certainty. Nor is it surprising that knowledge of this matter escapes us, since it is established that throughout those very times all Gaul and all Aquitaine, hindered by wars,

> **Note [Col. 0993D].** He means the Northman wars, waged in the ninth and tenth centuries.

were almost deprived of the cultivation of liberal learning.

**23.** But so that the reader’s discerning intelligence may gain knowledge from matters transmitted by more celebrated report, we have set forth, in a very brief calculation, the time when the most blessed Sacerdos flourished and that in which his body was translated to the village of Sarlat. From the Passion of the Lord until the death of Saint Martin are reckoned four hundred and twelve years.

> **Note [Col. 0993D].** Rather, Saint Martin died in the year of Christ 397.

From Saint Martin’s death to that of Clovis, son of Childeric, in whose time Saint Sacerdos flourished, are one hundred and twelve years. Thus from the Passion of the Lord to the death of this Clovis are five hundred and twenty-four years.

> **Note [Col. 0993D].** According to our calculation, Clovis died on 27 November 509.

Likewise, from Clovis’s death to that of Charlemagne, in whose time the place of Sarlat was restored, are three hundred and one years.

> **Note [Col. 0993D].** According to our calculation, 304 years. Charlemagne died on 28 January 814.

What we have written, however, we have gathered by probable reasoning, reading scattered materials in ancient histories; and, standing before God, we speak only the purest truth. Setting aside what is unknown, we have faithfully explained what we know with greatest certainty, in honour of so great a confessor.

## Chapter IV. Miracles wrought after the Translation; and first, the punishment of those who wronged the saint

> **Note [Col. 0993D].** Here, under the new title “Miracles,” there begins, as it were, a second part of the legend. It is not divided into chapters as the earlier part was; rather, each miracle forms one paragraph, longer or shorter as the matter requires. We follow this arrangement in the consecutive numbering as well.

**24.** Soon after the limbs of the glorious bishop Sacerdos had been deposited in the aforesaid church of Saint Saviour, on the very holy day of Parasceve [Good Friday], the monks’ bakehouse happened to catch fire. Although this fire, now kindled for the third time, was thought to have been extinguished when it had been put out, it regained strength from its prolonged fuel and flared up again, spreading widely through all the neighbouring places. Then suddenly there was an outcry; a crash arose; people ran together in crowds, and the fire was attacked unsuccessfully from every side. For the threatening flame first stretched out sporadically across the roofs of neighbouring houses; then, driven by the wind, its force was carried as far as the very basilica of Saint Saviour.

Nevertheless, people rushed to the ropes of the bells;

> **Note [Col. 0994D].** This should be read *funes signorum*, not *funes lignorum*, as Claude Chastelain rightly observed. By *signa* are meant bells; hence even now in many churches along the Loire, *sonner le seing* means “to ring a bell.” From this comes that ringing which watchmen make in any sudden occurrence or danger: it is called *le tocsin*, as though *tactus signi*, “the striking of the bell”; and the bell assigned to this use is likewise so called.

their sound spread afar. Every ornament in that basilica was hurriedly gathered together; the body of the most precious confessor was brought outside; and all who were present most devoutly cried out for the help of the most holy bishop. Meanwhile a little cloud was seen approaching from the east, preceded, in the sight of all, by a white dove. Then that cloud, driven by a swift blast, spread its covering over the fires and immediately began to pour forth an abundant flood of water. You could have seen the elements in conflict; yet the fire was overcome by divine power.

It is worth considering the sublimity of so great a miracle. Who would not wonder when, at the invocation of God’s beloved Sacerdos, the brightness of the clear sky was darkened, and the violence of the fire was quelled by a sudden inundation of rain? Surely it must be confessed and believed without any doubt that, in order to show the merit of Saint Sacerdos—whose glorious body had so recently, by God’s favour, been translated there—the very Spirit who rested upon Christ in the river Jordan in the likeness of a dove came above his basilica, both to sanctify it and to quell that fire. By so great a sign the Lord acted, sanctifying his own holy church and then delivering it from the threatening fire through the merit of this glorious confessor. And, as we shall unfold in the following work,

> **Note [Col. 0994D].** I do not think something different is indicated; “in the following work” is the same as saying “as this work proceeds,” that is, in the present work.

he afterwards adorned it with the glory of many miracles. May he mercifully do this always, to the praise and glory of his name. Amen.

**25.** The most holy Pope Leo

> **Note [Col. 0994D].** Saint Pope Leo IV appears to be meant; we shall treat of him on 17 June. He held office from 847 to 855.

determined to secure by the privilege of his holiness the church of the Saviour of the world and of the most blessed confessor of Christ, Sacerdos. In that privilege he prohibited under anathema that anyone, puffed up by presumption or arrogance, swollen with nobility of birth, or in any other way, should dare—apart from the lawful election of the monks serving there—to seize lordship over that church, or to plunder, diminish, or alienate in any manner things belonging to it.

Hubert, a cleric in tonsure but in deed a sacrilegious man, disregarded this entirely. Supported by the aid of Count William, he seized control of the aforesaid church and congregation. Stripping the place of every good thing, he emptied and daily made it worse. But one day, when he had laid his limbs down to sleep, behold: Lord Sacerdos appeared to him in a vision, accompanied by two others, and, restraining his rashness, rebuked him thus:

> “Why, most wicked of men, have you presumed, contrary to apostolic decrees, to seize the possessions of this holy church? Why have you assumed the name and tyranny of an abbot? Why have you carried off the furnishings of the monastery?”

As he said this, he raised aloft the staff he held in his hand in order to strike him. But, as Hubert himself later related, recalled by the prayers of those accompanying him, he withheld the staff from the blow. The wretched man rose from bed, at first greatly terrified by the horror of the vision; then, believing himself deceived by a phantom spirit, he gradually relapsed and returned to his former error.

Yet while he raged, and, in the likeness of a serpent and of the deaf asp stopping its ears, rushed headlong into crimes, behold: on another night, while he slept, the saintly bishop stood again before him with greater severity and said:

> “How are you, Hubert? Are you awake or asleep?”

Struck with fear, he at once answered:

> “Who are you, lord?”

The holy man replied:

> “Do you not know me? Have you not seen me already long ago? Why have you insolently despised me?”

With these words he began to beat Hubert’s head and to bruise the other limbs of his body with the staff. Then the wretched man first began to cry out in lamentation:

> “Spare me, lord, spare me, lord!”

At last, though too late, he cried out his guilt, leapt from his bed, and was finally driven mad. To the astonishment of all present, he fled through the monastery cloister and, avoiding human sight, withdrew into a small hut. Some travellers seized him and immediately brought him back to the same church, where they guarded him carefully. Then people throughout that whole province, hearing what had occurred, gave thanks to Christ the Saviour and praised the merits of Saint Sacerdos. As he died, he repeatedly said: “My fault, Saint Sacerdos”; he paid the penalties due. To all who heard this it was plainly made known what punishment he deserves who unjustly usurps tyranny over Christ’s flock, and who, like a thief, wickedly dissipates ecclesiastical property.

Count William of Périgueux,

> **Note [Cols. 0995D–0996D].** In Sammarthani, vol. IV, p. 808, there is a charter in which “Bernard, by God’s grace count of Périgueux, transfers the monastery of Saint Saviour, called Sarlat, which then lived by no means according to rule, with the consent of his wife Garsinda and while Lord Louis was emperor,” to Abbots Odo and Addacius and their successors, to be elected according to the Rule of Saint Benedict, for himself, his wife, sons and daughters, brothers and relatives. Eleven magnates subscribe, probably sons and brothers; in the first place appears the mark of William, whom one might believe to be the eldest son. It follows from this that, although “in the year 860 Charles the Bald arranged Aquitaine through counts,” as is read in the manuscript deeds of the consuls and bishops of Angoulême in Besly, Aquitaine nevertheless had already had its own counts, indeed several simultaneously in different regions. We must therefore recognize not only counts of Bordeaux distinct from the counts of Poitou, but also counts of Périgueux; their titles may at times have coalesced, as is shown by a document of the year 982, “of Ama, countess of the land of Bordeaux or Périgueux,” cited above under 4 January concerning Saint Macarius.

who had become the seller of the church of which we speak contrary to apostolic precepts, lived out an unhappy life to its end, with both hands joined together, his mouth drawn back to his ear, and every part of his body disfigured by deformity.

**26.** Calviniac is a village on the border of the districts of Périgueux and Cahors. Its inhabitants were accustomed to come to the monastery of Blessed Sacerdos. One day, therefore, certain of them were coming as usual. A poor man and his wife had bought wax and wine out of their poverty, and followed those going ahead. But as they took the road more slowly, as we said, and were walking alone, one of the retainers of a certain knight met them and violently snatched away the flask of wine which they were carrying. They nevertheless completed their intended journey more quickly and came to the aforesaid monastery. There, stretching out their hands, they cast themselves upon the ground and sought vengeance from God and from his servant, namely Saint Sacerdos, for the injury done to them.

Meanwhile the man who had seized the flask demanded that a drink be given him from it. Those who were present wished to pour wine from the aforementioned vessel, but could not remove even the small stopper with which it was secured above. Finally, breaking the stopper with a spear, they still could not draw out the liquid wine. While this was happening, the author of the crime was struck by God and seized by a demon; raging against himself, he became the avenger of his own crime. In frenzy he fed upon his own hands and arms with his teeth, and tore with savage bites all whom he could reach. At length he was seized, bound tightly with hard ropes, and immediately breathed out his life. When he had died so terribly, those present carried the flask with its wine to the monastery of the most blessed Sacerdos and hung it in the church in memory of so great a miracle.

**27.** One day it was revealed in a vision to a man burning with the heat of fever that, if he drank of the wine from the flask mentioned in the preceding account, he would immediately recover. Having drunk it, he was at once healed when the illness fled. Nor did that wine benefit him alone: it also served as a remedy for many others who were ill, as long as it lasted. Thus what had been the destruction of one man brought healing to many sick persons.

**28.** In summer, certain persons had come to Saint Sacerdos’s oratory out of devotion and, after completing their prayer, were returning. They carried on their shoulders a wine-vessel, called an *oenophorus*, so that at suitable hours they might drink from it and cool the burning of their thirst. It happened that on the road they were exhausted alike by the heat and by thirst. Compelled by excessive distress, they sat down to drink; then, setting out again, they were more intensely afflicted by the heat and thirst. Anxiously they said: “Let us drink again, for Saint Sacerdos’s gift will not fail.” Having said this, they brought the *oenophorus* to themselves and found it filled to the very top; after drinking, they resumed their journey.

When they had quickly completed the journey, they gathered under the roof of one lodging-place. There again, drinking from the same vessel, they wondered that they found it full again and again. Many came together at this sight, and drank as often as they came, as though no wine were poured from it. The aforesaid pilgrims then returned by the same road, proclaiming everywhere the praise of this miracle. They brought the *oenophorus* with them to the monastery as testimony, hung it in the church, and rejoiced, giving thanks to the Lord.

**29.** At another time, while some people were coming to the church of the holy bishop Sacerdos, a dog happened to accompany them on the road. Attacking a certain peasant’s flock of sheep, it disturbed them across the pastures with barking; but called back by its master, it again walked with the travellers. Thus they came to the monastery and, after accomplishing the purpose for which they had come, returned once more to their homes. Meanwhile the shepherd reported the complaint of the disturbed flock to its owner and maliciously sharpened his mind to fury. That peasant, armed as for war, placed himself in the path of the returning pilgrims and began to assail them with insults, although they offered him lawful compensation for what the dog had done. Yet while he still raged against them and scattered their small baggage here and there, they began to invoke Saint Sacerdos’s help; the peasant mocked their cries.

Leaving there what they had brought with them, they fled to the church of Saint Sacerdos. While they remained there, the peasant was immediately crushed by a severe paralysis of his limbs. His relatives laid him in the hollow of a winnowing basket and hastened to carry him to the shrine of the often-named saint. The feast of that confessor of Christ was being celebrated on that very day; and behold, as the sun was already declining toward sunset, the bearers of the aforesaid peasant burst into the church, presenting him as the witness of so great a miracle and reporting what had happened. But that obstinate peasant, deprived of every use of his limbs, died in the middle of the night.

**30.** A certain knight, returning from Saint Sacerdos’s monastery, met a man who had committed an offence against him and was coming to the same monastery to pray. But that knight, from fear and reverence for Christ’s confessor Sacerdos—whose astonishing miracles he had often seen and more often heard reported—passed him by unharmed and went on. Another mounted man, following the first knight from a distance, encountered the same pilgrim on the road. On account of the offence he had committed against the aforesaid knight, he tried to accuse him and frighten him with threats. But the pilgrim, trusting in Blessed Sacerdos, answered that he feared no mounted man on that road.

Then the horseman, thinking that he was being despised, swelled with pride, spurred his horse, rushed upon him, tore away the tunic which the pilgrim had placed over his head against the heat, and folded it behind him on the saddle. But when the pilgrim implored the help of the holy bishop, the tunic was immediately restored upon his head. The wicked horseman fell down with a broken hip. The horse, driven by frenzied terror, charged at the fallen man and attacked him as he wandered over the field; once seized, it immediately died. The horseman, being carried to the saint’s church, died on the road on the eighth day after these events. Thus, while alive, he had not deserved to have as favourable the one whose merit he had despised.

## Chapter V. Benefits of healing bestowed upon those who invoked Saint Sacerdos; punishment of the malicious

**31.** Thus far we have related how Sacerdos, the Lord’s bishop, crushed tyrants and the proud by pursuing them. We shall now tell how he aided suppliants by strengthening them with the mighty power of signs. Yet whenever saints appear to exercise vengeance upon any of God’s enemies—as we read in the passion of the apostles Peter and Paul that Simon Magus fell from on high at their command—we must understand that it is the Lord who works his justice through the saints, punishing the enemy by righteous judgement for the praise and glory of his name and of his saints. The more they are to be feared, therefore, because it is certain that he is present everywhere—and especially in places consecrated to his own name and to that of his saints—and is not powerless, whenever and however he wills, to exact through their hands vengeance upon evildoers.

Thus each saint, while by his merit he defends those subject to him from the injury of adversaries and punishes the impious by God’s just judgement, opens a way for very many to take refuge with him. And when he sometimes destroys an arrogant man so that he may not dare to violate sacred places, he surely affords a remedy of safety to those who flee to him.

**32.** A general assembly, according to ancient custom, was held in the territory of Cahors, in a place called Pons Rode.

> **Note [Cols. 0997D–1000D].** The vernacular text, as Dom Armand informs us, relates this miracle as follows: “The first miracle which God performed through Saint Sacerdos after his death was this: bishops and prelates of that region and clerics were commanded to assemble at a certain village above the river called Seu, which was named Villa-Pons-Roire; and the bodies of the saints of that region were brought to this council, so that Christianity might be conducted and made illustrious, and the holy body of Saint Sacerdos was kept there.”
>
> From this specimen I understand that the vernacular manuscript was not so simply translated from Hugh that the translator did not grant himself considerable licence, changing not only the phrasing but at times even the order of events. Indeed, I would suspect that it is itself the original, which Hugh rendered into Latin, were it not that at the beginning of the appendix an old legend of the saint is cited as explaining several other miracles which are here only briefly reported.
>
> The river Seu descends from Montfalcon in the region of Périgueux and flows into the Dordogne below Domme. The name of that village is not given on the topographical map; but in the bullarium of the diocese of Cahors it is named *Cura-du-Pont-de-Riou*. I therefore suspect that its name arose from the stream at whose mouth the village lies; nor does the map show any other stream than one rising near Vigan and flowing above Costerauste into the Seuve.

A very great multitude of people had gathered there, and the venerable body of the illustrious Sacerdos had been brought there through the devotion of the faithful. In that region there was a noble matron who supported, for the love of God, a young man blind from birth. When this blind man heard that the bier of so great a confessor had been brought there, he began to ask the matron by whose alms he was supported to buy him a candle, which he himself might place before the saint’s presence, in the hope that the Lord might enlighten him through the saint’s merit. The aforesaid matron answered him:

> “I shall gladly present in your stead the candle which you desire to bring to that saint, for in so great a crowd of people I cannot find anyone to guide you.”

For indeed a vast multitude of people was pouring to the relics of the aforesaid saint. Then the matron did what she had promised, and immediately it happened to her as she wished. In the very same hour in which she placed the candle before the presence of the man of God, the man blind from birth, within her house, was granted through the merit of that saint to see the light of heaven. Those present, astonished, immediately brought the man who had been blind before the presence of the man of God, and rendered countless thanksgivings to God and to the most holy Sacerdos for so great a miracle.

**33.** A certain girl tormented by a demon was brought to Saint Sacerdos’s sanctuary to be healed. After she had remained there for several days and the malignant spirit had uttered many blasphemies through her—which we have thought too long to insert here—she was at last delivered from the demon by divine grace through the merits of that confessor of Christ.

**34.** A boy of ten years from neighbouring parts was brought to the monastery of Saint Sacerdos. From the very time of his birth he had lacked hearing, sight, and the use of speech. But after spending some time there without recovering, he became weary and returned home. Yet though he carried away from that church not even a hope of health, he suddenly received hearing, sight, and the use of speech while still on the road.

**35.** Likewise a boy of seven, denied the use of speech, was brought by his father to this saint’s tomb, that he might there be granted the benefit of healing. But although he had kept vigil there for only one night and had not obtained what he sought, he broke a long silence with abundant speech on his return the next day, before he entered his own country.

**36.** Likewise a woman deprived of the light of her eyes came to the threshold of Saint Sacerdos, seeking his aid. While she remained in his basilica, surrounded by a great throng of people, after many prayers she received clear sight. A great stream of blood flowing from the hollows of her eyes testified that she had been enlightened through the merits of the bishop.

**37.** Another woman, an inhabitant of Limoges, hindered in the use of her limbs by the sinews for twelve years, sought this saint’s aid … bringing faithful votive offerings to the threshold of the saint. Immediately restored to strength, rejoicing in so great a gift, she glorified the Lord in Sacerdos his servant.

**38.** At another time, a young man came to the monastery of this holy bishop. From the beginning of his birth he had lacked the use of speech; but immediately healed, his tongue formed many words, and, offering the tribute of praise, he returned joyfully home.

**39.** Likewise, at another time, the Lord working in the aforesaid basilica performed three miracles together to manifest Saint Sacerdos’s merits. For on a day of the feast of that confessor of Christ, while a very large gathering of people stood there, a mute man gave forth the organs of speech, a blind man was granted to see the dawn of light, and a weak woman received the use of her limbs. She had been laid on a bed before the altar of the Saviour of the world.

**40.** At another time, when the glorious feast of that outstanding confessor was being celebrated again, and a numerous multitude came to his venerable church, two countrymen came together, each bringing his little son, who lacked the use of speech, to be healed. One of these boys had lost the use both of his voice and of all his limbs. Both immediately recovered their health by divine grace through Saint Sacerdos’s merits, and joyfully returned home.

**41.** A nobleman named Eubolus

> **Note [Col. 1000D].** Eubolus or Eubalus was count of Poitou around the year 900, from whom descended the Williams, dukes of Aquitaine and counts of Poitou; but it is scarcely likely that he is meant here.

supported a poor man for the sake of his soul. This poor man, deaf and mute, wandered here and there; oppressed by many miseries, he had come to this nobleman, and knew no father or mother other than him. The Lord, who was at work, had provided him with this man as patron and provider. One day, therefore, that high-born knight, stirred by the most illustrious fame of Blessed Sacerdos—which spread through that whole region on account of the miracles which the Lord performed through his merit at the said monastery—sent this poor man there, that the saint might assist him in his mercy, as he was accustomed to heal others.

The servants of the aforesaid Eubolus came before Saint Sacerdos’s presence, offered the gift of offering which they had brought, and then threw themselves upon the ground to pray for that poor man’s recovery. But as night was already approaching, and they intended to keep the vigil there, as their lord had commanded them, the church’s custodians immediately ordered them to leave.

They resisted only in words, since they did not dare use force, and refused in every way to depart. But when they understood that they could not remain there that night as they intended, they began to invoke Saint Sacerdos’s name. What more need be said? That poor man, deaf and mute from birth, immediately began to speak and hear. Those who could take part in this joy, filled with great gladness, gave praise to almighty God, who through the prayers of his servant Sacerdos had bestowed the gift of health upon that wretched man.

The elders of the place, because they had never heard the healed poor man’s name and did not know by what proper name he ought to be called, named him Salvatus.

> **Note [Col. 1001D].** I think the text should read *audierat et nesciebat*, “had heard and did not know,” so that it may be understood that he who had been mute and deaf from birth, when asked his name, could give no answer, thereby furnishing the occasion for a new name to be assigned to him from the event.

Remaining for a long time thereafter in the same monastery, he repeatedly recounted to many visitors all that we have just related.

**42.** The most holy day of Easter had dawned, and no small multitude of people had gathered at Saint Sacerdos’s church. Among them was a certain Ademarus, noble by birth, who had come from the castle of Montignac.

> **Note [Cols. 1001D–1002D].** Montignac on the Vézère, scarcely four leagues north of Sarlat.

He stood in that church to receive the Easter sacrament as the offices of Mass were being performed. Ademarus had been entrusted by his parents to the discipline of letters, but, having become a robber, he had despised it. He was accustomed repeatedly to harass, with countless acts of violence, travelling merchants, pilgrims, and any other wayfarers passing through that region, as well as neighbouring peasants; in pursuits of this sort he had given free rein to the inclination of his heart.

But while, as has been said, he seemed to be standing unharmed among the people in the church of Blessed Sacerdos, and the Gospel reading was being recited, he suddenly fell to the pavement. For, as he himself later related, Saint Sacerdos appeared before his eyes, adorned with the episcopal mitre, and struck his neck with the staff he held in his hand, compelling him to fall. Those standing around at once lifted him up and carried him inside the cloister enclosure. When the celebration of Mass was complete, the abbot and brothers were immediately summoned and came.

The sick man, miserably reviewing his crimes and greatly fearing imminent death, confessed with tears that by sinning he had provoked almighty God and had deserved Saint Sacerdos’s anger. The abbot and all the brethren of the monastery who were present pitied him, immediately gave him the canonical habit, and at once admitted him to the remedy of penance. With his neck bent sideways, he lay grievously ill throughout the entire week and finally expired on the eighth day. His death terrified many; fearing such an end, they strove to offer the Lord the fruit of repentance.

**43.** A certain monk, Seguinus, was a secular and wandering monk of Saint Sacerdos. Yet he had acquired a reputation for eloquence, was supported by learning, and was well known to the leading men of the country. At one time he was staying with a powerful man not far from the monastery, at the castle called Carlux.

> **Note [Col. 1002D].** The castle of Carlux lies about two leagues above Calviac, on the same bank of the Dordogne river; the monastery of Calabrum was situated between these two places.

He could not bear the yoke of the Rule, but, already full of renown, wandered about from church to church. The day of the Lord’s Nativity, celebrated throughout the whole world, was approaching, and that powerful knight intended to keep the vigil in the church of Blessed Sacerdos. The aforesaid monk, wishing to turn him away from this good intention, promised that he himself would celebrate the entire office of that night there, exactly as if he were present in the said church. The monk prevailed and kept the knight with him.

After he had filled himself with food and wine, he lodged with a certain priest in an adjoining chapel. As he gave himself to sleep, behold, Saint Sacerdos stood before him and said:

> “Why, Seguinus, do you sleep here and become drunk on the cup of forgetfulness? Should you not rather be with the other brethren and render the due office to the Lord on so eminent a feast?”

When he answered, “Who are you, lord?”, Saint Sacerdos looked at him more sternly and said:

> “Do you not know me? Why do you avoid your foster-father Sacerdos by fleeing from him?”

Having said this, he immediately dragged him by the hair from his support, bent his head down to his shoulder, then threw him before the altar and beat him with most violent blows. From a distance one could hear the sound of the strokes and the cry of the sufferer. Why recount many details? He left him half-dead.

The aforesaid priest watched awake as all this happened, but, struck with immense fear, did not know what he ought to do. When the night had passed and the dawn of light was beginning to rise, men throughout the castle got up, all wondering why, on so eminent a feast, the priest delayed to celebrate the night office. Coming even to the chapel door, they mockingly ordered the chaplain to rise. Strengthened by their speech and presence, he rose, opened the door to them, and disclosed what had happened.

Astonished at the sight of so great a miracle, they hurried with the priest to the dwelling of the blessed confessor of Christ. After the brothers of that place had celebrated the solemnities of Mass, the visitors called them all together and reported what had occurred. The monk died miserably, serving as an example to those who saw him, lest wandering and unstable men act against the authority of the Rule, and lest, whether within a church or outside it, they ever omit the divine office.

44. At another time some merchants, travelling with their packs to the city of Toulouse, were passing through the town of Sarlat on their way to the aforesaid city. Moved by the widely celebrated report of the virtues of the glorious bishop Sacerdos, they came to his oratory and, having paid the customary offerings [Col. 1003A], commended themselves and all that was theirs to the Lord and to St Sacerdos. As they departed and pursued their intended journey, certain wicked men seized them, brought them into a certain town, bound their hands behind their backs with very harsh thongs, and fastened their feet in iron shackles. When they had been held for three days and tortured in many ways, they began to call upon the aid of St Sacerdos. The mercy of the compassionate Lord, invoked through prayers to his servant, was present with them; and behold, on the third night their bonds were suddenly loosened, their feet released, and the captives freed from cruel custody. [Col. 1004A] At once they returned by the road they had come and hung the chains of their bondage in the church of the Saviour of the world. At last those who had seized them, moved to repentance, followed them there; and thus all with one accord gave thanks to the Lord, their saviour and deliverer, and to holy Sacerdos. I pass over many things which the Saviour afterwards wrought, to the praise of his most holy bishop Sacerdos, patron of the Church of Sarlat, adorned with the glory of miracles; and which he visibly works daily without ceasing. May he do this, we pray, to the praise and glory of his name, through the endless ages of ages. Amen.

IN THE YEAR OF THE LORD 1130: LAMBERT OF SAINT-OMER, *LIBER FLORIDUS*

[Col. 1003]

[Col. 1003]

NOTICE ON THE *LIBER FLORIDUS* OF LAMBERT THE CANON, A TWELFTH-CENTURY MANUSCRIPT; BY JULES DE SAINT-GENOIS, PROFESSOR-LIBRARIAN AT THE UNIVERSITY OF GHENT.

Extract from the *Messenger of the Historical Sciences of Belgium*.

THE *LIBER FLORIDUS* OF LAMBERT THE CANON, A TWELFTH-CENTURY MANUSCRIPT.

[Col. 1003B] The library of the city and University of Ghent now possesses more than 600 manuscripts, most of them of interest for the study of law, theology, general history, and the history of our country. Among those distinguished by their great antiquity, foremost place must be assigned to the collection known to bibliographers under the [Col. 1004B] title *Liber floridus Lamberti canonici*—“The Flowering Book of Lambert the Canon.” It is one of those unwieldy encyclopaedias so often encountered among the literary monuments of the Middle Ages, which, at a time when books were few, presented within a single volume the chief items of knowledge that might be needed.

[Col. 1005A] An encyclopaedia of this kind, of very great reputation, exists in the Royal Library of Burgundy at Brussels: we mean Brunetto Latini’s *Treasure of Knowledge*, of which M. Fl. Frocheur gave a detailed description in the *Trésor national*, year 1843, second series, vol. II, pp. 157–175.  
[Note: [Col. 1005C] See also, on Brunetto Latini, a notice by M. Marchal, *Bulletin de l’Académie de Bruxelles*, XI, p. 263; Villemain, *Course of Medieval Literature*, vol. I, tenth lecture; and the *Bibliothèque de l’École des chartes*. On the office of the Podestà, see Lenormant, II, p. 313.]

The library of Liège also possesses several compilations of this kind, but they are of a later date.

In the first part of the notice which M. Walwein de Tervliet published concerning the manuscripts of our library in 1815, we find the following description of this curious collection:

> “No. 197. A small chronological and historical book, woven from the flowers of various authors, by Lambert [Col. 1005B] son of Onulf, canon of Saint-Omer, small folio.—This parchment manuscript, containing coloured figures, was written about the year 1125. The collection is fairly valuable.”

In reporting to the Historical Commission, at its meetings of 5 and 6 December 1834,  
[Note: [Col. 1005C] *Bulletin de la Commission royale d’histoire*, I, pp. 59–60.]  
on the Ghent library manuscripts of interest for the study of our annals, M. Warnkönig gives some details concerning the merits of the *Liber floridus*, which is cited with praise in several thirteenth-century manuscripts. Dom Berthod discusses it in his notice on the manuscripts of Belgium. Among the chroniclers who made particular use of the *Liber floridus*, one must mention Jean de [Col. 1005C] Thielrode, writing at the end of the thirteenth century,  
[Note: [Col. 1005D] *Chronicle of St Bavon at Ghent*. Ghent: Vassas, 1835, octavo, p. VI.]  
as well as the Bruges historian Custis.  
[Note: [Col. 1005D] The Ghent Library now possesses almost all the original manuscripts of this prolific writer.]  
And, quite recently, Pertz had recourse to it in the first volume of his *Monumenta Germaniae historica*.

In his introduction to the *History of Flanders and Its Institutions*,  
[Note: [Col. 1005D] I, p. 43, note 1, and p. 64, note 1.]  
M. Warnkönig again speaks of the *Liber Floridus*, and affirms that an older copy exists in the ducal library [Col. 1006A] at Wolfenbüttel.—That learned writer extracted from it a well-known chronicle fragment entitled *Genealogy of the Counts of Flanders*.  
[Note: [Col. 1005D] Ibid., p. 330.]

There is a *Liber floridus* in the library at Douai, numbered 740 among the manuscripts. It is a fifteenth-century copy of the historical portions of the St Bavon manuscript.

Since most of these notices make known only imperfectly one of the most curious compilations in existence, we believed that bibliographers would welcome a detailed notice here of the 192 treatises contained in this volume.

As for its author, Lambert, little is known of his life. It is known that he was the son of Onulf and a canon of Saint-Omer. In the chronological table, [Col. 1006B] to be discussed below under no. 23, the *Liber Floridus* contains this sentence: “1077, the sixth day before the Kalends of February: Onulf, canon, father of Lambert who wrote the book, died.” From these few words we see that Onulf, Lambert’s father, was likewise a canon, and that he died on 26 January 1077 (1078). This fact helps us to determine approximately the time when the volume was written.  
[Note: [Col. 1005D] We had applied to M. E. Taillar, counsellor at the Court of Douai, for information concerning this Lambert. He promptly sent us the following note, the conclusions of which we believe may in every respect be accepted: “Nothing positive is known concerning the person of Canon Lambert of St Bertin at Saint-Omer. Yet everything suggests that he is the same person as an individual of this name who, in the eleventh and twelfth centuries, was successively schoolmaster and abbot of St Bertin. Folquin and Yperius identify the latter [Col. 1006C] as one of the most remarkable men of the period, distinguished alike as a scholar and as a preacher. Elected abbot of St Bertin in 1095, he actively attended to the administration entrusted to him and built the monastery’s watermills. In 1118 he clothed Baldwin of the Axe, twelfth count of Flanders, in the monastic habit; some time afterwards he gave him burial. [Col. 1006D] He had a great part of the church of St Bertin covered with lead; it was consecrated in 1105 by the bishop of Thérouanne. He renewed almost all the bells, built the chapel of Our Lady of the Infirmary, the cloister, the dormitory, and the guest quarters. He also had made a precious cross, still seen in the monastery treasury before 1790. Abbot Lambert died in 1123 and was buried in the chapel of Our Lady of the Infirmary. [See the *Cartulary of St Bertin*, compiled by Folquin and recently published by M. Guérard, quarto collection of *Documents for the History of France*; Johannis Yperii, *Chronicle of St Bertin*, ch. 40, in Dom Martène, *Thesaurus novus Anecdotorum*, vol. III, col. 592 ff.; see also the Benedictines’ *Literary History*, vol. XI, p. 13, and vol. XII, p. 78.]”]

On fol. 154r is found Lambert’s maternal family tree: *Genealogia Ovdvini et Heimerici decani filii sui*, “Genealogy of Ouduin and of his son Heimeric the dean.” It shows that his mother was called Eve; her father, Baduif; his grandfather, Heimeric; and his great-grandfather, Ouduinus. Let us now return to the collection itself.

The volume known in the Ghent Library under [Col. 1006C] the title *Liber Floridus* is a large folio manuscript, on dirty parchment, much handled, damaged, and sometimes illegible in several places. It contains 287 folios, in whose margins notes were written which careless binders have partly cut away. There are several double leaves folded inward. Numerous miniatures, coloured letters, and borders of every kind adorn [Col. 1007A] this volume. The writing, which is in different hands, does not appear later than the year 1125. The binding is modern; on its spine are written: *Floridus Lamberti—Dares Phrygius*.

On the verso of the first flyleaf one reads: *In hoc codice continentur sermones domini Gerrici abbatis,—liber sancti Bavonis Gandensis ecclesie, etc.*, “In this codex are contained the sermons of Lord Abbot Gerric—the book of the church of St Bavon at Ghent, etc.” This inscription tells us that the manuscript belonged to the library of St Bavon. The recto of the first leaf contains grammatical definitions of several Latin words; on the verso is a list of persons to whom useful discoveries and inventions are owed. A brief chronicle ends this leaf; its last four lines read:

> “Lidricus of Harelbeke, first count of Flanders, [Col. 1007B] began to reign in the year of the Lord 792. Baldwin the Iron-Armed, fourth count of Flanders, took Judith, daughter of King Charles the Bald, in the year of the Lord 862. Godfrey, son of Eustace, count of Boulogne, took Jerusalem in the year 1099; Robert the Fourth, [Xus], count of Flanders, established Godfrey as king of the land of Jerusalem.”

The recto and verso of the second leaf contain several chronological notices; at the bottom, under the year 1097, is a brief mention of the taking of Jerusalem.

The recto of folio 3 is divided into seven columns, containing lists: first, of the kings of Assyria, from Belus to Tonos; second, of the kings of Persia, from Arbaces to Denis; third, fourth, and fifth, of the kings of Rome and Roman emperors, [Col. 1007C] from Janus to Henry IV; sixth and seventh, of the kings of France, from Pharamond to Philip II.

The compilation proper begins only on fol. 3v with the words: *Incipiunt capitula Lamberti in Floridum*, “Here begin Lambert’s chapters in the *Floridus*.” In the following prologue, the author, who names himself Lambert, son of Onulf, canon of Saint-Omer, explains the motives of his undertaking and declares that he called the book *Floridus* because he composed its contents *de diversorum auctorum floribus*, “from the flowers of various authors.”

There follows the table of the 190 (192) treatises contained in the manuscript. We shall give here the titles of these treatises as they occur in this table, or as they appear at the head of each work when the latter title is more explicit. [Col. 1008D] When these titles sufficiently explain the subject of a treatise, and the treatise itself presents little interest, we shall refrain from adding elucidations. Whenever we have been able to discover the authors of these different treatises, we have mentioned them. But we acknowledge the inadequacy of our learning for making such investigations complete. Rabanus Maurus, the Venerable Bede, Isidore of Seville, and others are, besides, the customary sources from which the scant scientific knowledge of that period was drawn. It should also [Col. 1008A] be observed that the authors from whom medieval encyclopaedists drew are often cited furtively and mistaken one for another: thus one will find St Jerome for St Chrysostom, Fredegar for Gregory of Tours, and so forth. It is therefore understandable that the research is complicated by further difficulties.

Fol. 5r–13v.—No. 1. *Prologue of Odo, Bishop of Cambrai.* This is a theological dissertation on sin and Christian perfection. On the verso of folio 5 are several verses about St Omer. Below them, within a square medallion, the saint is represented seated upon a hemisphere in the attitude of a blessing prelate; a few words concerning his life are added. The explicit of this treatise occurs on fol. [Col. 1008B] 10r. There another work begins, entitled: *A certain Jew disputing with Gislebert, Abbot of Westminster.*  
[Note: [Col. 1007D] We should point out here that, although the table mentions only 190 treatises, a greater number occurs in this compilation. [Col. 1008D] Under a single rubric given in the table, there are sometimes three or four.]

Folio 13r is filled by a large miniature, supposedly representing the castle of Saint-Omer, with these words: *Sithiu villa, id est Sci Audomari castrum*, “The village of Sithiu, that is, the fortress of St Omer.” Below is a monk, probably Canon Lambert himself, writing in a chair, surrounded by the names of the abbots of Saint-Omer, from St Bertin to Otger.

On fol. 13v is a brief chronology of the Old Testament, beginning from Moses.

Fol. 14r–16v.—No. 2. *Order of the miracles of Christ Jesus according to Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John*: a brief life of our Lord [Col. 1008C] Jesus Christ, drawn from the Evangelists. On fol. 15: *Exposition of Odo, Bishop of Cambrai, on the Gospel canons.* This is a treatise on the harmony of the Evangelists.

Fol. 17–18v.—No. 3. *Bishop Freculf on the judges and kings of the Jews*: a brief chronology of Israel’s judges and kings.

Fol. 19.—No. 4. *The threefold sphere of the peoples of the world: the various peoples of Asia, Europe, and Africa.* In the middle of the text is represented a world map containing the list of peoples of Asia, Europe, and Africa. Among those of Europe are named the Alamanni, Zeelanders,  
[Note: [Col. 1008D] Word added later.]  
Morini, Suebi, Burgundians, Huns, Tungri, and others. The boundaries of the three parts of the world are indicated.

[Col. 1008D] Fol. 19v.—No. 5. *Sphere of rulers through the ages of kingdoms.* A spherical figure divided into six compartments gives a brief chronology of the six ages of the world.

Fol. 20r.—No. 6. *Sphere of the Minotaur, house of Daedalus*: a figure intended to represent the labyrinth, with the Minotaur in the middle.

Fol. 20v.—No. 7. *Sphere of the world, microcosm: ages of the world down to King Godfrey (1099)*: another chronological system, likewise divided into six ages.

[Col. 1009A] Fol. 21.—No. 8. *Bishop Freculf, historiographer: on the beginning of the world, the sons of Adam and Noah, and the rulers of kingdoms down to Christ.*

Fol. 21v.—No. 9. *Hegesippus, historiographer: on the judges of the Jews, their high priests, and their kings.* This is yet another treatise, distinct from that indicated under no. 3.

Fol. 22v.—No. 10. *Caiaphas, also called Josephus, historian of antiquities: on Solomon’s wisdom.*

Fol. 23v.—No. 11. *On Solomon and his glory.*

No. 12. *Sphere of the twelve months and the elements.* No. 13. *On the circle of the upper heaven.* No. 14. *The Apocalypse depicted.*

[Col. 1009B] These four chapters designated in the table are missing from the manuscript; they are replaced by the following: fol. 23r, *What God made in the beginning during six days*; and fol. 23v, *On the age of the world from Adam to Solomon*.

Fol. 24.—No. 15. *The order of Christ’s winds and their nature*: a spherical figure, blue and red, divided into compartments, in which the winds are designated by the German words: *Ost-ost* (“east-east”), *sud-ost* (“south-east”), *sud-sud* (“south-south”), *sud-west* (“south-west”), *west-west* (“west-west”), *nord-west* (“north-west”), *nord-nord* (“north-north”), *nord-ost* (“north-east”). There follows an explanation of thunder according to the Venerable Bede.

Fol. 24v.—No. 16. *Macrobius’s sphere of the five zones*: a sphere divided into compartments painted red, blue, green, and yellow, in which [Col. 1009C] several geographical notions are transcribed, including the words: *Zona australis temperata, habitabilis, sed incognita hominibus nostri generis*, “The temperate southern zone, habitable, but unknown to human beings of our kind.” Clearly, this phrase relates to the idea already held in that period that a fourth part of the world existed.

Fol. 25.—No. 17. *The solstitial and equinoctial course of the sun*: another spherical figure, around whose outer rim the twelve months of the year are designated.  
[Note: [Col. 1009D] This subject is not mentioned in the volume’s table.]

Fol. 25v.—No. 18. *The lunar course and description of the year*: another figure representing the lunar month, with the various phases of the moon’s waxing and waning.  
[Note: [Col. 1009D] The same observation.]

[Col. 1009D] Fol. 26.—No. 19. *Apuleius’s sphere of life and death*: an astronomical calculation based upon lunar movements, for learning the time at which persons afflicted with fever die.

Fol. 26v–32r.—No. 20. *Martyrology.* This is Usuard’s Martyrology.  
[Note: [Col. 1009D] See *Usuardi Martyrologium*, edited by J. Molanus, Louvain, 1568.]  
It is especially interesting because of the historical annotations inserted in it, nearly all concerning Flanders. These notes were published by M. A. van Lokeren as an appendix to the *Chronicle of St Bavon* by [Col. 1010A] Jean de Thielrode, who seems to have made use of these notices.  
[Note: [Col. 1010D] Pages 201–202, and preface, XI.]

Fol. 32v.—No. 21. *Chronicle of Isidore*  
[Note: [Col. 1010D] Isidore of Seville.]  
*on the five ages*: a brief chronicle from Adam to Jesus Christ.

Fol. 33v–36r.—No. 22. *On the Six Generations of the World*: a brief chronicle, but more detailed than the preceding one.

Fol. 36v–45r.—No. 23. *Years of the Lord Jesus Christ.* A chronological table from the year 1 to 1295, containing, down to 1119, the dates of the accession of popes and emperors, of several memorable battles, of the deaths of celebrated persons, and of noteworthy events. It also contains other historical notices, most concerning the monastery [Col. 1010B] of Saint-Omer. From the eleventh century onward these entries become more numerous. It is in this table, as we said above (col. 1006), that we find the day of the death of Onulf, father of the author of the *Liber Floridus*.

After the year 1119 we encounter no further annotations, which allows us to suppose that this manuscript was composed before that date. M. van Lokeren published most of these historical notes as an appendix to Thielrode.  
[Note: [Col. 1010D] Pages 203–208.]  
Not all of them, however, appear to be in the same hand; several were inserted later.

The author also recorded in this table the dominical letters, the Easter term, the indictions, [Col. 1010C] the concurrents, and other observations useful for ecclesiastical computus. On fol. 45v one reads an extract from Jordanes concerning the origin of the Goths.

Fol. 46v–47r.—No. 24. *Names of the Roman emperors.*  
No. 25. *Names of the Roman pontiffs*: a list of emperors down to Henry V and of popes down to Calixtus II, all arranged in eight columns.

Fol. 47v.—No. 26. *On the names of peoples*: names of the peoples descended from Noah’s sons.

Fol. 47v.—No. 27. *On the episcopal sees of the provinces*: a fragment from Gregory of Tours on metropolitan dioceses.  
[Note: [Col. 1010D] It can be seen that there is a lacuna here, for the following leaf is in another hand.]

No. 28. *Map or oresta* [sic] *of the world.*

[Col. 1010D] No. 29. *On the five famous cities.*

These two chapters, indicated in the table, are missing.

Fol. 48r–49r.—No. 30. *On the provinces of the world*: etymological explanations of the principal geographical names of the globe.

Fol. 49r.—No. 31. *On the names of kingdoms: peoples of Asia, Europe, and Africa*: the same explanations for the peoples of the three parts of the world. It is almost a duplication.

[Col. 1011A] Fol. 49v.—No. 32. *On the cities of the world*: a list of the principal cities of the world with the names of their founders.

Fol. 49v–51r.—No. 33. *Martianus Felix Capella: On diverse peoples and monsters*: brief notices concerning little-known or fabulous peoples, extraordinary animals, and so forth.

Fol. 51r.—No. 34. *On changed names of cities: the ancient names of cities of Asia, now changed.*

Fol. 51v.—No. 35. *On paradise and islands.* An enumeration of the principal islands of the earth.

Fol. 51v.—No. 36. *On the rivers of paradise*: a note on the Ganges, Euphrates, Tigris, and Jordan. On fol. 52r is a miniature representing an oddly constructed building, in the middle of which rises the tree of knowledge; above is the word: *Paradysus*, “Paradise.”

[Col. 1011B] Fol. 52v and 53r.—No. 37. *On the rivers of the world*: an enumeration of the principal rivers, springs, and lakes of the earth.

Fol. 53r.—No. 38. *On diverse creatures*: brief notices concerning certain extraordinary races of men.

Fol. 53v.—No. 39. *Greek, Latin, and Hebrew names of Christ.*

Fol. 54r and v.—No. 40. *Eucherius: on interpretations of names*: concise explanations of proper names found in the Old Testament.

Fol. 55r.—No. 41. *On ecclesiastical ranks, ministers, and offices*: explanations of the various [Col. 1011C] terms used in Jewish and Christian liturgy to designate dignities and offices.

Fol. 55v.—No. 42. *On the idols of the peoples*: an enumeration of the false gods of ancient peoples.

Fol. 55v.—No. 43. *On different weights.*

Fol. 55v.—No. 44. *On different measures.*

Designation of ancient weights and measures.

Fol. 56r.—No. 45. *On the names of the Sibyls*: the names of the ten known Sibyls.

Fol. 56r.—No. 46. *Poem of the Sibyl Symmachia on Christ.*

Fol. 57–58v.—No. 47. *Isidore, bishop of Seville: On the natures of beasts*: Isidore of Seville’s treatise on animals. The verso of folio 56, representing [Col. 1011D] a lion and a pig, serves as an illustration to the text of this treatise.

Fol. 58v–60v.—No. 48. *The physiology of birds: On the natures of birds*: a treatise on birds, beginning with a description of the griffin. In the middle of the leaf a griffin devouring a man is represented.

Fol. 60v.—No. 49. *On the dragon, serpents, and snakes*: a description of the reptile class, adorned with a coloured miniature representing a dragon.

[Col. 1012A] Fol. 61v.—No. 50. *On the crocodile of the river Nile*: a figure representing this animal.

Fol. 62r.—No. 51. *On Behemoth, beast of the earth*: a description of the fabulous animal called Behemoth; an odd miniature represents the devil sitting upon this monster, doubtless unknown to our naturalists. Above one reads: *Diabolus sedens super Behemoth Orientis bestiam singularem et solam I Antichristum*, “The Devil sitting upon Behemoth, the singular and solitary beast of the East—I [or: namely] Antichrist.”

Fol. 62v.—No. 52. *On Leviathan the serpent*: a crude miniature representing Antichrist seated, sceptre in hand, upon a dragon painted green, bearing the inscription: *Antechristus sedens super Leviathan serpentem, significantem bestiam crudelem in fine*, “Antichrist seated upon Leviathan the serpent, signifying the cruel beast at the end.”  
[Note: [Col. 1011D] The figure of this dragon, which, like the writing of the text, dates from the beginning of the twelfth century, closely resembles the Dragon that surmounted the tower of the Belfry of Ghent. The latter [Col. 1012D] may well belong to the same period as the miniature in question.]

Fol. 63r.—No. 53. *On the monsters of the Ocean Sea [Col. 1012B] (and fishes).* Among the fish, herring is mentioned, of which the author says: *Allec, pisciculus ad usum salsamentorum idoneus, longo servatur tempore*, “Herring: a little fish suitable for use as salted provisions, preserved for a long time.” Might the practice of barrel-packing herring already have been conceived in that period? On fol. 63v: *On shellfish and shells.*

Fol. 63v–64v.—No. 54. *On the marvels of the island of Britain*: a brief description of the natural curiosities found in England—lakes, hot springs, and caves. Several passages concerning King Arthur, the celebrated paladin of the Round Table and the Charlemagne cycle, occur there. Here are these curious passages:  
[Note: [Col. 1012D] On Arthur, see Henry of Huntingdon, *History*, p. 313. Frankfurt, 1601.]

> “There is a mound of stones in Britain, in the province of Builth, with one stone laid beneath it; and the footprints [Col. 1012C] of the dog called Cabal, belonging to the warrior Arthur, are impressed upon a stone, when he hunted the boar Troynt, in the place called Carn Cabal. Arthur indeed made a mound under that stone. But when the people of that province take a stone from the mound and hide it for two days, on the third day it is found upon the mound.
>
> “There is a tomb in Britain, in the province of Ergyng [?], beside the spring Lycatannir, of the son of the warrior Arthur, called Anir, whom Arthur buried there. When people come to measure the tomb, its length is sometimes five feet, sometimes eight, sometimes eleven, sometimes fifteen; never is it the same on one occasion as on another.”
>
> “There is a palace in Britain, in the land of the Picts, of the warrior Arthur, founded with marvellous art and variety, [Col. 1012D] in which sculpted representations of all his deeds and wars may be seen. He fought twelve battles against the Saxons who had occupied Britain. The first battle was at the mouth of the river called Glein. The second, third, fourth, and fifth were upon the river Dubglas. The seventh was in the forest of Celidon. The eighth was at the fortress of Guinnon; in that battle Arthur carried the image of Holy Mary upon his shoulders, and the pagans were put to flight. On that day there was a great slaughter of pagans through the power of the Lord Jesus [Col. 1013A] Christ and of his holy Virgin Mother. The ninth battle was fought in the City of the Legions; the tenth on the bank of the river called Tribruit. The eleventh was on Mount Agned; the twelfth on Mount Badon, in which battle nine hundred and sixty men fell by one charge of Arthur, with the Lord Jesus Christ helping him.”

Nennius, an English writer of the ninth century, is the author of this passage, which we find in his *Eulogy of Britain*, p. 106, under the title: *On Arthur, the warrior king, and the twelve battles which he fought against the Saxons, and how many adversaries he overthrew in a single charge.*

Moreover, the chapter *On the Marvels of the Island of Britain* may well be wholly by the same author, who, according to G. Camden, *Britannia*, p. 503, wrote a treatise entitled *On Marvels*.

[Col. 1013B] Fol. 65.—No. 55. *On the Temple of the Lord Solomon*: a description of Solomon’s Temple, adorned with a miniature representing a strange building, above which one reads: *Hierusalem celestis*, “Heavenly Jerusalem.”

Fol. 65v.—No. 56. *On the powers of the twelve precious stones.*

Fol. 66.—No. 57. *Isidore, bishop of Seville: on stones and gems; on white pearls; on black pearls; on crystals.*

Fol. 67v.—No. 58. *On the birth of Christ*: a brief life of Jesus Christ.

Fol. 68v.—No. 59. *History of the kings of the English; Bede: here begin the names of the leaders and kings of the Britons.* First comes the list of the kings of England from Storech to Henry, son of William the [Col. 1013C] Conqueror; the fabulous kings and those of the Heptarchy are all named. On fol. 66v: *Here begins the History of the English, composed by the blessed Bede, venerable priest*; then, on fol. 73r: *Here begins Bede’s chronicle: on the kings of the English.*

Fol. 75r: in a kind of table are placed the twenty-eight principal cities of England, each preceded by the word *CAIR*, “which in the British tongue means city.” We again find this passage in Nennius, *Eulogy of Britain*, ch. 56, p. 121. On a strip of parchment attached to this folio is the continuation of the succession of English kings down to Henry, son of William of Normandy.

Fol. 75v.—No. 60. *On weeks of years*: an explanation of the various kinds of weeks known to the ancients.

Fol. 75v.—No. 61. *Sayings of the Seven Sages* (seven lines).

Fol. 76.—No. 62. *Genealogy of the Counts of Normandy.*

Fol. 77.—No. 63. *On the miracles in the Dialogue of St Gregory, Pope*: a philosophical-ascetical treatise, adorned with a miniature on fol. 76v representing a gigantic tree, *Arbor palmarum*, “Tree of Palms,” each branch of which bears the name of a virtue, with that of an opposing vice placed opposite it. Below one reads:

> “Kings of Jerusalem: Expedition of the Christians after the council of Pope Urban, in the year 1097; in the third year thereafter Jerusalem was taken, in the year of the Lord 1098: [Col. 1014A] Godfrey, son of Count Eustace; Baldwin, his brother, a Fleming; Baldwin of Bourcq, a Frank; Fulk, an Angevin; Baldwin, his son.—Urban was then pope at Rome. The council for the expedition to Jerusalem was held by 320 fathers at Clermont, on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of December.—Patriarchs in Jerusalem: Dagobert of Pisa, first bishop; Evermar, a Fleming; Arnulf, a Fleming; Warmund of Amiens; Stephen of Chartres; William, a Fleming; Fulk of Poitiers.”

Fol. 81r.—No. 65. *Gregory, in Book XXXI of the Morals on Job, on the eight principal vices; on the seven principal virtues.*

Fol. 81r.—No. 65. *On the destruction of the Jewish people.*

[Col. 1014B] Fol. 81v.—No. 66. *On a certain servant of the Lord, Drotelm, who was carried away: a vision described by Bede the priest*: an account of a vision experienced by a certain Drotelm in England, in Northumberland.

Fol. 83r.—No. 67. *On the seven virtues of the dove.*

Fol. 83v.—No. 68. *This is the Catholic faith concerning the divine essence.—Likewise on the Trinity*: a series of ascetical maxims, most in verse and each ending with the word *esse*, “to be.”—*The plague of Egypt*: four verses on the plagues of Egypt.
