On fol. 84r: *On the Nativity of the Lord, verses.*—*Verses of Peter: on money*: a charming little poem on the power of money in this world; we believe we shall please our readers by communicating it here.

VERSES ON THE PENNY. (G)*

[Col. 1014C]

> Hail, my pennies: through you I reign;  
> Through you I rule over the princes of lands.  
> That I am approved and revered, loved and sought after—  
> Your favour brings this about; it brings me great things.
>
> Through you Caesar holds empire, and without you  
> No Caesar can possess an empire.  
> Finally, whatever kings do by land or sea,  
> Whether they contend or wage battles, you do it.
>
> Through you that Ilium was reduced to ashes,  
> Which through you also had risen to excessive height;  
> You armed greedy right hands for its destruction,  
> When the greedy soldier sought Phrygian wealth.
>
> [Col. 1014D] Through you tyrants submit to lofty walls,  
> And fierce knights are often subdued without war.  
> Through you mighty Rome was founded with high towers;  
> Through you she found skilled craftsmen.  
> For accomplishing so great a structure in wondrous fashion,  
> Money was of manifold use to ingenuity.
>
> Through you pontiffs, abbots, and provosts  
> Promptly do what they cannot do by themselves.  
> The man who is a defendant in a legal case and fears a harsh judgment—  
> If he has you, he sails with a favourable wind.
>
> If a thief or robber is caught and gives  
> A penny to the judges, once it is given he will straightway be righteous.  
> If anyone is foolish and has not read the sacred arts,  
> Let him continually read coins: he will become an Aristotle.
>
> Let a handsome grown man come to a beautiful lady:  
> [Col. 1015A] if he brings nothing, he is driven from the bedchamber;  
> Let an ugly man enter, attended by blessed money:  
> Without delay he finds everything prepared for him.
>
> The penny reigns, governs, commands, conquers all;  
> With Jupiter the penny holds the empire.  
> Each is made a god and revered by the great world;  
> Yet one does more, though each is a god.  
> For what thunder and lightning cannot make yield,  
> The penny makes yield and makes its own.
>
> Jupiter, when offended, does not avenge every anger;  
> Money avenges countless offences.  
> If a sad poor man knocks at the closed gate of a rich man,  
> It is not opened to him for the love of God;  
> But if a penny knocks, it is opened to it,  
> And, God being shut out, the poor man is shut out of the house.
>
> [Col. 1015B] Every house is happier with such a guest;  
> Whoever lacks this guest will be wretched.  
> Happy the coins to which such great power has been given—  
> Power believed not even to belong to mighty Jupiter.  
> Hear kindly, Jupiter, what I shall yet say, with your leave:  
> Whoever has money can be Jupiter!

The author of these verses, written in very pure Latin for the period, was a canon of Saint-Omer. He wrote other poems as well, as we shall see below under nos. 134 and 135.

Fol. 84v: extract from an ordinance of Robert the Frisian, count of Flanders, intended to maintain peace among his subjects.

Fol. 84v.—No. 69. *The letters of the Greeks, twenty-seven in number.*

[Col. 1015C] Fol. 85.—No. 70. *The Greek letters which serve as numbers among them.*

Fol. 85v.—No. 71. *On the forms of characters*: explanations of the signs adopted for abbreviated designation of weights, such as the ounce, pound, and so forth.

Fol. 85v.—No. 72. *On the kinds of numbers in calculation.—On the four seasons of the year*: the four Ember seasons occurring each year at intervals of ninety-one days from one another, on 1 March, 1 June, 1 September, and 1 December.

Fol. 86v.—No. 73. On years and leap-years; this chapter begins with the division into infinitely small fractions of the different parts composing the year.

[Col. 1015D] Fols. 86v–87r. No. 74. Proverbs of Solomon.

Fol. 87v.—No. 75. On the division of days; etymology of the terms used to indicate the different parts of the day and year.

Fol. 87v.—No. 76. On the nature of the sun; a few notions concerning the nature of the sun, earth, water, and so forth.

Fol. 88r.—No. 77. On the four elements; a miniature representing the spotless Lamb, surrounded by four circles signifying earth, air, water, and fire.

Fol. 88v.—No. 78. BEDE: On Astrology; explanations of the twelve signs of the zodiac, with, at the centre, a miniature representing the sun drawn in a chariot.

[Col. 1016A] Fols. 89r–91v.—No. 79. Further on astrology: On the order and position of the signs; crude miniatures represent the various signs of the zodiac, the more notable constellations, and other astronomical figures connected with occult philosophy and astrology proper, as these were once used in support of accepted planetary systems.—On fol. 92r, a sphere representing the movements of the sun and moon.—A kind of crudely painted world-map occupies fols. 92v and 93v. Upon it one reads: “Globe of the earth,” and then, to the right, this phrase, apparently referring to the assumed existence of the New World: “The temperate southern zone, unknown to the children of Adam: the region of the Antipodes.” On fol. [Col. 1016B] 95v is a figure representing the relation of the chronology of the world to the movement of the planets.

Fol. 94r.—No. 80. On astrology according to Bede; a sphere composed of concentric circles, intersecting in various ways and representing the courses of certain planets.—Fol. 98v: “The seven circles and the courses of the seven planets”; the movements of the seven planets: Saturn, Jupiter, Mars, the sun, Lucifer [Venus], Mercury, and the moon.

Fol. 95r.—No. 81. Extract on astrology; explanations of the respective positions of the signs of the Zodiac in relation to one another.

Fol. 95v.—No. 82. On the twelve signs; further observations [Col. 1016C] on the twelve signs.

No. 83. On astrology. No. 84. On thunder. No. 85. On the natures of the elements.

These three treatises, so entered in the table, are not found in the manuscript; probably the leaves containing them have been torn out.

Fol. 96r.—No. 86. On storms; it indicates the signs by which one may recognize what the weather will be.

No. 87. Jerome: On Samuel and Saul and the Pythoness (15 lines).

Ibid.—No. 88. Solomon’s repentance; another extract from St Jerome.

Fol. 96v.—No. 89. On Alexander, the last king of the Jews, [Col. 1016D] and Herod; a brief history of Alexander and Herod.

Fol. 97r.—No. 90. On Christ and Joseph; a few words concerning Christ’s sepulchre and Joseph of Arimathea.

Ibid.—No. 91. On the falling-asleep of John the Evangelist at Ephesus (7 lines).

Ibid.—No. 92. The names of the twelve Apostles, where they preached, and under whom they suffered.

Fol. 98r.—No. 93. The names of the days according to the Hebrews, Romans, and Gentiles.

Ibid.—No. 94. On the signs of the ten plagues of Egypt, when Moses struck with his rod.

Ibid.—No. 95. On the elect and the reprobate.

[Col. 1017A] Ibid.—No. 96. The ten words of the Law; articles of the Decalogue.

Fol. 98v.—No. 97. On books to be accepted; a list of the sacred books which may be used and read.

Ibid.—No. 98. On the eight prefaces; the nine prefaces customarily used in the Mass by the bishops of France.

Ibid.—No. 99. On books to be read; the lessons or epistles used during the year in the Catholic Church.—At the foot of fol. 99r: a chronological summary from the creation of the world to Jesus Christ.

Fol. 99v.—No. 100. On knowledge of apocryphal books; a list of apocryphal [Col. 1017B] and condemned sacred books or writings.

Fol. 100r.—No. 101. On the two paradises; extracts from St Augustine.

Ibid.—No. 102. On the two hells. Ibid.—No. 103. On the elect and the reprobate. Ibid.—No. 104. On monsters and two-bodied beings.  
[Note: [Col. 1017] These last three subjects are likewise extracted from St Augustine; together they make up only a few lines.]

Ibid.—No. 105. On various prophecies; indications of the means used to make prophetic predictions.

Fol. 100v.—No. 106. In how many ways sins are forgiven.

Ibid.—No. 107. On the Paschal cycle; names of the holy Fathers who concerned themselves with the Paschal cycle.

Ibid.—No. 108. On the four fasts of the four seasons; the dates fixed for the Ember Days.

[Col. 1017C] Ibid.—No. 109. On the twelve vigils throughout the year; the dates of the vigils.

Fol. 101r.—No. 110. On the regimen of the year; an indication of the foods and drinks appropriate to each month of the year for maintaining health, together with recipes for preparing certain medicines.

Fol. 101v.—No. 111. The Lord’s Prayer, in Greek and Latin.

Ibid.—No. 112. The Apostles’ Creed, in Greek and Latin.

The Greek text of the Lord’s Prayer and of the Creed is written in Latin letters.

Fol. 102r.—No. 113. On mountains not covered by the Flood (5 lines).

[Col. 1017D] Ibid.—No. 114. On Jacob and Esau; a few words concerning Abraham and his descendants.

Ibid.—No. 115. On the church of St Omer: On the Danish pirates approaching Flanders (*adeuntes*, as written); relics of the saints of Flanders, deposited at St Omer in order to preserve them from Danish profanations.

Fol. 103r.—No. 116. On degrees of consanguinity; names of the various degrees of kinship; fol. 102v represents a model genealogical tree of ancestors and descendants.

Fol. 103v.—No. 117. Genealogical tree; an enumeration of impediments to marriage between persons [Col. 1018A] of the same family, as established at the Council of Koblenz (*Confluentium*) in 922.

Fols. 104–105.—No. 118. Genealogy of the counts of Flanders. This chronicle of the counts of Flanders, becoming more detailed from Robert the Frisian onward, continues to 1120. On the verso of the leaf sewn into fol. 105, under the title “Genealogy of the kings of France and the counts of Flanders,” is the genealogy of the counts of Flanders combined with that of the kings of France, from Priam to Charles the Good, count of Flanders.

Fols. 105v–108r.—No. 119. The conflict of Henry and Paschal; a detailed account of the disputes that arose between Emperor Henry IV and Pope Paschal at the beginning of the twelfth century concerning [Col. 1018B] the investiture of bishoprics and abbeys. This piece begins with a letter dated February 1111, in which John, bishop of Frascati, informs Richard, bishop of Albano, that Emperor Henry has seized the persons of Pope Paschal and the cardinals.

Fol. 108v.—No. 120. Letter of Methodius: On Antichrist; prophecies concerning the birth, life, and death of Antichrist.

Fol. 110v.—No. 121. Deeds of the Franks who captured Jerusalem, which Fulcher of Chartres, with the Holy Spirit dictating, composed; an account of the First Crusade written by Fulcher of Chartres. It is divided into chapters with the following titles:

Introduction; then:

1. The Pope’s (Urban’s) exhortation to the holy expedition;
2. The first expedition of the army of the Lord, and the names of its leaders;
3. The second expedition of the army of the Lord;
4. The second expedition joins the first at the siege of Nicaea;
5. The assault of a thousand around Jerusalem;
6. The Franks attack the city with engines;
7. How Jerusalem was captured by the Christians;
8. How, etc., the Franks, capturing Jerusalem, render praise and thanks to God;
9. The admiral of Babylon sent Lavendalius, commander of his army, and Arabs to capture Jerusalem;
10. The third battle of the Franks against the Arabs at Ascalon;
11. The battle completed, the Franks joyfully divide the spoils of the Arabs;
12. Bohemond, Baldwin, and Daimbert came to Jerusalem;
13. How Danishmend, the admiral, captured Duke Bohemond;
14. King Godfrey having died, his brother Baldwin makes for Jerusalem;
15. On Duke Baldwin;
16. The fourth war undertaken by Baldwin at Beirut;
17. The war completed, Baldwin was received in Jerusalem with joy;
18. On the coronation of King Baldwin;
19. On the coming of the fire, when it delayed beyond its customary time;
20. King B[aldwin], at Caesarea in Palestine, captured Archadius;
21. The army of the Babylonians came to Ascalon;
22. The fifth battle against the Babylonians near the city of Ramla;
23. On the misfortunes of the Franks who were at the extreme point of battle;
24. The sixth battle between Jaffa and Ashdod;
25. When the Babylonian army sat before Ramla;
26. The seventh battle in Romania, in which Soliman defeated the Frankish leaders wishing to return home;
27. The eighth battle against the aforesaid Babylonians near Ramla, from which the king barely escaped;
28. On the arrival of Hugh [of Tiberias] to the king;
29. The ninth battle against the Babylonians by Jaffa, in which King B[aldwin] barely emerged victorious;
30. On the siege of Ptolemais and the liberation of Duke Bohemond, when he had been captured by Dalimannus in Romania;
31. On the dissension between Patriarch Daimbert and his clergy;
32. On the appointment of Evermar as another patriarch;
33. On Tancred: how he fought with Rodoan, king of Galapye, and put him to flight;
34. On the death of Count Raymond;
35. The king of Babylon sent a very great army to Jerusalem with thirty admirals;
36. The tenth battle between Jaffa [Col. 1019B] and Ramla against the Babylonians;
37. How the Babylonian fleet, upon seeing the severed head of Gimelmuch, turned in flight from the walls of Jaffa;
38. On signs seen in heaven.

—At the foot of fol. 128: “On the lance of Antioch, found in the church of St Peter.”

Fol. 128v.—No. 122. Computation of the moon with a table; calculations arranged in tables concerning the lunar movements of every month: a most complicated astronomical work, whose key would certainly be interesting to possess.—Fol. 132v: “The course of the moon through the twelve signs: Bede the priest composed this page.”—Fols. 133v–134v: further calculations of lunar movements, related to chronological computations known as the Golden Number, Paschal term, regulars, dominical letters, [Col. 1019C] indictions, concurrents, and epacts. Fol. 135r: “Rule for finding Lent.”—“Kindling of the embolismic moons and their extinction.”—On fol. 135: “On the months; a clock according to Bede.”

Fol. 135v.—No. 123. On the moon and the Paschal term; the timing of the Paschal term established according to lunar movements.—Fol. 136r: “On the Kalends of the months.”

Fol. 136r.—No. 124. On the four Marys, the four Marys mentioned in the Gospels.

Fols. 136v–139r.—No. 125. Genealogy of the world; a brief history of the world, divided into six ages, from Adam to Jesus Christ. On fol. 138v, a medallion represents Emperor Augustus seated [Col. 1019D] upon his throne, holding the globe in one hand and a sword in the other, with these words in the exergue: “A decree went out from Caesar Augustus that the whole world should be enrolled.”

Fols. 139v–140r.—No. 126. The order of the eight Beatitudes; eight miniatures representing different trees which allegorically signify the eight Beatitudes.

Fols. 140v–141r.—No. 127. Names of trees and plants. The names of the trees and plants known at that time are transcribed in twelve columns, but without any alphabetical or other order.

Fols. 141v–142r.—No. 128. Josephus: in Book II, and Moses, leader of the Hebrews.

[Col. 1020A] Fol. 143r.—No. 129. Josephus the historian on Christ.

These two fragments are extracted from Flavius Josephus.

Ibid.—No. 130. On Herod and his brother Archelaus.

Fol. 143v.—No. 131. Extract from the homily of blessed Pope Gregory: on the orders of angels and the ranks of the elect.

Fols. 144v–152v.—No. 132. Flowers from the book of Anselm, archbishop of Canterbury: Why was man so called? A philosophical and ascetic treatise on the fall of man, reason, free will, and so forth.

Fols. 152v–153v.—No. 133. Here begins the account of Nectanabus, magician of the Egyptians, who by magical art begot Alexander the Great [Col. 1020B] from Olympias, queen of the Macedonians; a heroic history of Alexander the Great. The verso of fol. 153 represents Alexander on horseback; the framing of this miniature is very curious.—Fol. 154r: “Genealogy of Oduinus and his son Heimericus, the dean.” This is, as we said on p. 493, the genealogy of the mother of Lambert, author of the *Liber floridus*. Below: “Letter of the Flemish clergy sent to Reynald, archbishop of Rheims, on behalf of Robert, count of Flanders, concerning the removal of clerics from his servitude.” This piece is printed in WARNKOENIG, *History of Flanders*, vol. I, p. 330.—On fol. 154v: “On the origin of the world and the offspring of Adam and his sons; likewise on the patriarchs and leaders, prophets, kings and pontiffs governing Judaea, and the Christian bishops of Jerusalem, from Christ to the time [Col. 1020C] of Emperor Theodosius.” This very brief chronicle is scarcely more than a dry list of names.—At the foot of fol. 155v: a method for steeling iron.—Fols. 156r–161r: “Letter of Alexander the Great to Aristotle, his master, concerning his battles and the wonders of India”; curious details concerning Alexander’s Indian expedition.—Fol. 161v: “A comparison in philosophy, made through letters, between Alexander, king of the Macedonians, and Dindymus, king of the Brahmans.” Dindymus writes to Alexander concerning the Brahmans’ manner of life and how it brings them to perfect wisdom. At the foot of fol. 162r, the locations of the twelve cities bearing the name Alexandria are described.

Fols. 162r–163v.—No. 134. Verses on the destruction of the Roman [Col. 1020D] Empire; this poem, by Peter, son of John, canon of St Omer, recounts all the vices to which Rome owed its fall, and bitterly enlarges upon the evils of simony and the corruption of the world (see above, no. 68).

Fols. 164r–166v.—No. 135. Verses on the evil woman; “Here begins the prologue of Peter’s little book on the evil woman”; a poem by the same author concerning the evils due to woman.

Fol. 166v.—No. 136. Chronicle of Orosius, Spanish priest, addressed to blessed Augustine: On the beginning of the world and of the city [Rome]; a year-by-year chronicle of Rome.—On fol. 168r, a large miniature represents a building signifying the Church of Rome, with [Col. 1021A] St Peter seated upon a throne in pontifical vestments.

Fols. 168v–188r.—No. 137. Deeds of the Roman pontiffs; a chronology of the popes from St Peter to Pope Calixtus I, who had been archbishop of Vienne (in Dauphiné) under the name Wido. He was son of William, count of Burgundy, and uncle of Baldwin the Younger, count of Flanders.—Fol. 188v: a note on the ten basilicas built by Constantine at Rome.—Fol. 189r: a privilege granted by Constantine to Pope Sylvester, in gratitude for having been miraculously cured of leprosy.—Fol. 190v: a note on Julius Caesar’s campaigns in Gaul, taken almost word for word from his *Commentaries*, with a few slight changes of phrasing.

[Col. 1021B] Fols. 191r–206v.—No. 138. Deeds of Octavian Caesar and Augustus and of the Roman emperors; an extract from Paulus Orosius, continuing his chronicle [Col. 1022A] to the year 446. Its continuator is, on fol. 202r, Count Marcellinus, under the title: “Chronicle of Count Marcellinus concerning the remaining kings”; his narrative covers the period from Theodosius to Henry IV (the year 1118).—On fol. 207r: “Vision of Charles the Bald, Augustus and king of the Franks, before he lost the Empire.” At the top of this leaf is a miniature representing Charles the Bald seated upon his throne, with the words: “Charles the Bald, son of Louis, grandson of Charlemagne, Augustus and king of the Franks; here he died in Mantua, poisoned by Zedekiah, a Jewish physician” (see the plate below). In this exceedingly curious piece, a spirit appears to the king in the form of a child and foretells the misfortunes of his reign, which will result from his sins. [Col. 1022B]—On fol. 208r, at the foot, a note concerning Norman incursions into Flanders.

Fol. 209r.—No. 139. Hegesippus: On Noah’s ark [Col. 1023A] and the animals; on the verso of fol. 209, a miniature representing Noah’s ark, with a few words of text.

Fol. 209r.—No. 140. On earthquakes and various signs, taken from Marcellinus in the *Deeds of the Franks*; an account of strange signs and extraordinary calamities manifested under the reigns of Theodosius and his successors.

Fol. 210r.—No. 141. On the signs of Jerusalem’s destruction; portents that announced the fall of Jerusalem under Titus.

Fol. 210v.—No. 142. On a certain member of Antichrist; the history of a sectarian from Bourges who passed himself off as Jesus Christ.

Fol. 211r.—No. 143. On signs in the sun and moon.

[Col. 1023B] Ibid.—No. 144. On the removal of a boundary embankment. Ibid.—No. 145. On an earthquake and the fasting of maidens. Ibid.—No. 146. On grain that rained from heaven in the region of Gascony.

Fol. 211v.—No. 147. On famine, wind, and an army.

Ibid.—No. 148. On three persons killed by lightning at Cologne. Ibid.—No. 149. On earth shattered by thunder at Augusta [of the Treveri]. Ibid.—No. 150. On an earthquake at Mainz and a tree. Ibid.—No. 151. On a wolf running about at Sens. Ibid.—No. 152. On signs of the moon and sun. [Col. 1023C] Ibid.—No. 153. On the miracle that occurred at Thérouanne.

The last eleven pieces, each occupying only very few lines, contain accounts of miracles and extraordinary occurrences between the years 811 and 862; all these facts bear witness to the chronicler’s naïve credulity.

Fols. 212r–215v.—No. 154. Deeds of the Danes, Goths, and Huns; in the *Deeds of the Franks*: On the Northmen; a history of the Norman expedition, from 822 to 895.

Fol. 216r.—No. 155. Vision of a certain religious priest from the land of the English, carried away from his body; as a consequence of the evils announced in this vision to a certain English monk, the king of England resolved, [Col. 1023D] in 809, to undertake a pilgrimage to Rome.

Fol. 216v.—No. 156. On the division of the provinces of the Franks: “While Louis Augustus, son of Charlemagne, was reigning, the kingdom of the Franks was divided from the Roman Empire, thus,” etc.; there follows the division of the kingdom of Louis the Pious in 871. Among the places cited, one finds for Belgium: Echternach, Aachen, Alethovia (Aldenhoven?), Frisia, Prüm Abbey, Tongeren, Cambrai, Fosses, Mechelen, Andenne, Taxandria, Veosatum (Visé?), Arlon, Condroz, “from the Ardennes, where the river Ourthe rises,” etc., etc.

Fols. 219–220v.—No. 157. Book of Methodius, bishop of the church of Paterenis [as written] and martyr of Christ, which he translated from Hebrew, and which blessed Jerome praised in his little works; a brief chronicle of the world beginning with Adam and ending with several prophecies concerning the future of the universe.

Fol. 221r.—No. 158. On the five regions of the world: Calcidius on Plato, concerning the five regions of the world; a mystical treatise on angels and demons.—On fol. 221v, a spherical figure containing the five regions discussed in the treatise; around it one reads: “Plato’s sphere.”—On fol. 222r, a triangular figure summarizing Plato’s system concerning God, man, and nature.

Fol. 222v.—No. 159. The Dream of Scipio, extracted from the sixth book of Marcus Tullius Cicero, upon which Ambrosius Macrobius of Milan wrote commentaries; an ascetic-philosophical treatise on life and death.—Fol. 225r, a spherical figure or world-map in which, alongside the three known parts of the world, one again finds the words: “The southern zone, temperate and unknown to the children of Adam: [the land] of the Antipodes.” The plate opposite reproduces this miniature.

Fol. 325v [probably 225v]. Various astronomical figures indicating planetary movements; above: “The seven circles of the seven planets.”—Fol. 226r, a large sphere with the signs of the Zodiac, the movements of the planets, and the revolutions of the sun around the earth, which is represented at the centre by the words Asia, Europe, and Africa within a [Col. 1024C] circle.—On the verso of this leaf, details concerning the dimensions of the planets, their respective degrees of remoteness, the zones, and so forth.—On fol. 227, a square figure bearing the heading: “Course of the seven planets through the Zodiac.”—On fol. 227v, a sphere diagonally divided by a line drawn across the earth, representing the rising sun at one end and the setting sun at the other; above: “The order of the seven planets, and the sphere of heaven and earth according to Macrobius.”—Fol. 228r, another sphere showing the revolutions of the seven planets around the earth: “The seven divided circles of the heavens; the seven planets and the twelve signs.”—Fol. 228v, a sphere whose planetary revolutions are connected with the four [Col. 1024D] seasons and the human body: “Choler, Blood, Melancholy, Phlegm.” These various astronomical works are borrowed from Macrobius.

Fol. 229r.—No. 160 [the source prints “169”]. On the twelve precious stones; a description of the principal precious stones.

Fol. 230r.—No. 161. On the coming of the Lord on the Day of Judgment: Jerome to Marcellus, on those who will meet Christ at his coming.—Fol. 230v, a miniature representing the tree of knowledge.—In a column beside it have been placed the names of the bishops of Thérouanne from the year 600 to 1096.

Fol. 231r.—No. 162. On the seven wonders of the world; description of the seven known wonders of the world.

Fol. 231v.—No. 163. On the good tree and the evil tree; [Col. 1025A] a miniature depicting two trees placed horizontally and joined at the centre by their trunks. At every branch of the left-hand tree is a medallion representing a virtue; each leaf belongs to a different tree. Medallions bearing the names of vices are attached to the tree on the right; all its leaves are fig leaves.—On the verso of fol. 232, a large miniature representing: 1. the Eternal Father in a medallion; 2. Nebuchadnezzar stretched out upon a bed; 3. a king occupied in cutting down a tree with an axe.

No. 164. On the six ages of the world compared with days. No. 165. On simony according to William. No. 166. On the sacrifice of Christ’s body. No. 167. On how alms ought to be given.

[Col. 1026A] No. 168. From what stock Herod was descended.—The leaves containing these five treatises have been lost or torn out.

Fol. 233v.—No. 169. On the Jewish princes and kings reigning after the death of the Maccabees.

Fols. 234r–241v.—No. 170. On the first kings of the Franks: Genealogy of the kings of the Franks who sprang from the stock of Paris, namely Priam and Antenor; a brief biography of the kings of France from Priam to 1116. It enumerates the 1,115 cities and the thirty provinces found in France in the time of Merovech (A.D. 449).—Fol. 238r: “Likewise, genealogy and history of the kings of the Franks and the division of kingdoms among their sons; genealogy of the counts of Blois and of the counts of the Northmen.” The author gives differing opinions concerning the origin of the Franks, whom he derives from Scania; there follows a brief chronology of the kings of France from Priam (!) to Charles the Simple. Here are inserted the descendants of Rollo and the counts of Blois; the series of kings of France then resumes down to Louis the Younger (A.D. 1188).—On fol. 240r, a note concerning the expedition of the Danish pirates (A.D. 846).  
[Note: [Col. 1027] This is the more modern copy of the note found at the foot of fol. 102r. See above, no. 493.]

Ibid., a list, in three columns, of the kings of France from Priam to Philip the Younger; the fourth column is devoted to the genealogy of Lambert, count of Brussels (*Brocsella*).—Fol. 240v, a list of the archbishops of Rheims, Cologne, and Trier, and of the bishops of Noyon (and [Col. 1028] Tournai) and Cambrai.—Fol. 241r, a geographical map of Europe. This curious monument, preceded by several explanations of Europe’s geographical condition, was published by M. MONE in the *Anzeiger für Deutsche Kunde und Vorzeit*, 1836, plate I. As this collection is little distributed in our country, we have provided on the plate below an exact representation of this map.—Fol. 241v, a chronology of the kings of Israel and Persia and of the Roman emperors.—Fol. 242r has been covered with a yellow colour, with a red cross in the middle; it originally contained writing, perhaps the continuation of the chronology above.

[Col. 1029A] Fols. 242v–252 bis v.—No. 171. Isidore against the Jews concerning Christ; proofs advanced by Isidore of Seville against the Jews in favour of Jesus Christ’s divinity and the excellence of his religion.

Fol. 253r.—No. 172. Genealogy of Christ according to Luke; at the head is a miniature representing Christ, with the Synagogue on his left in the form of a woman, whom he repels and whose banner is broken; on the right, the new Church, likewise in the form of a woman, with a baptismal font beside her.

Fol. 254r.—No. 173. Copy of a letter written by King Abgar and sent from Jerusalem to Jesus Christ.

Ibid.—No. 174. Example of the reply from Jesus to Abgar, toparch and king of the city of Edessa.

[Col. 1029B] Fol. 255r.—No. 175. On St Omer the bishop; this title in the table is erroneous; in the body of the manuscript there appears instead: “Various medicines.” These are remedies for eye diseases, canker, gravel, and so forth.—Fol. 256r: “Response and hymn concerning St Omer”; a piece of sacred music notated without lines.

Fol. 256v.—No. 176. On the lots of the Apostles; a kind of table containing a method of predicting the future by numbers.

Fol. 257r.—No. 177. On the diversity of number; names of the various kinds of numbers.

Fol. 257v.—No. 178. On the ages of various times; a brief chronology of the principal events of the world.

[Col. 1029C] No. 179. Rabanus Maurus: On the names of God. No. 180. On Jewish heresies. No. 181. On the Old and New Testament. No. 182. On regions and islands. No. 183. On mountains and places. No. 184. On cities and towns. No. 185. On the heresies of philosophers.

Several leaves have been torn out or removed from this part of the manuscript; the seven chapters just cited are missing. Only on fol. 261v are found the final seventeen lines of no. 185.

Fol. 261r.—No. 186. On true philosophy; a definition of true philosophy according to the Catholic faith.—The leaf ends with a short treatise [Col. 1029D] entitled: “On observing at what time trees should be cut.”

[Col. 1030A] Fol. 261v.—No. 187. On a certain man of Antioch; concerning a just man of Antioch who, after that city’s fall, had the good fortune to see his house and family spared.

Ibid.–263r.—No. 188. On the genealogy of the world; a brief chronology of the world, beginning with Adam and ending in the year 366 with these words: “There were Trojans in the lands of Germany, from whom the kings of Gaul sprang.”

Fol. 263v, 269v, and 258r–259r.  
[Note: [Col. 1029D] Through the binder’s clumsiness, several leaves have been misplaced in this chapter and in the [Col. 1030D] following one.]

—No. 189. The illustrious deeds of the pious King Apollonius; a kind of moral and philosophical romance whose subject is drawn from the history of Antioch.

Fol. 260v.—No. 190.—On St Omer and the provosts of the place; this leaf contains a brief life [Col. 1030B] of St Omer. Fols. 259v and 260r contain two miniatures relating to it. One gives the image of the church of the Abbey of St Omer: “The church of Sithiu,” with an altar upon which rests a saint’s shrine, and below it a brief chronicle of St Omer. The other miniature represents St Omer himself in monastic dress, crozier in hand, with the caption: “Glorious St Audomar, bishop of the Morini.”—Fol. 270 contains: “Miracles after Audomar’s death.” Fols. 270v and 271r contain a list of the abbots and provosts of St Omer and several other particulars concerning the monastery of St Bertin down to the year 1117.  
[Note: [Col. 1030D] All this belongs to chapter no. 190.]

Fols. 271v–278r.—No. 191. Here begins the history [Col. 1030C] of the Trojans, which Dares the Phrygian wrote, who lived at the same time, translated from Greek into Latin by Cornelius Sallust.

Fols. 278v–287v.—No. 192. Freculfus on the kings, consuls, and wars of the Romans; Roman history from Romulus to Julius Caesar. This chapter is not entered in the table.—The final leaves of the manuscript have probably been removed, for this portion is visibly incomplete.

In concluding the analysis of this voluminous manuscript, we admit that it would indeed be rather useless to publish in full this vast and indigestible compilation, entire parts of which have already appeared in print. We nevertheless believe that, for the historical information concerning the Middle Ages, it would be worthwhile to publish all that the *Liber floridus* contains.

## Additions and Corrections

[Col. 1029]

[Col. 1029D] Mr Tideman of Utrecht was kind enough to draw our attention to three manuscripts of the *Liber floridus*, two in the library at The Hague and one in that at Leiden, of which we were unaware when we published our notice of the copy of this manuscript belonging to the library at Ghent. He himself printed, in the collection of the proceedings of the Historical Society known as the *Vereeniging ter bevordering der oude nederlandsche Letterkunde*, year 1844, part 2, p. 88, an unpublished passage from this compilation found only in the manuscripts at The Hague. We were likewise unaware that Messrs J. Zacher and Bethmann had also dealt with this curious encyclopaedic collection in the *Serapeum*, in the years 1842 and 1844.  
[Note: [Col. 1031D] Leipzig, Weigel, octavo, published by Dr R. Nauman.]

In the first of these notices,  
[Note: [Col. 1031D] *Serapeum*, nos. 10 and 17, 1842, pp. 145–154 and 162–172.]

Mr Zacher gives certain details concerning the copies at The Hague and Leiden; the analysis of this compilation which follows is based on those manuscripts. Except for several chapters and subjects whose order has been reversed, we have not observed very notable differences between our manuscript and those examined by Mr Zacher. It is [Col. 1031B] always the same lack of method, the same errors, the same confusion. We should nevertheless observe that one of these manuscripts contains more material than the other. All this is perfectly indicated in Mr Zacher’s work.

It follows from the other notice, published by Dr Bethmann,  
[Note: [Col. 1031D] *Serapeum*, 1845, pp. 59–64 and 79–80.]

that the copy in the Ghent Library, which comes from the former Abbey of St Bavo, is the original, the primitive text of the *Liber floridus*. This scholar believes that it was brought from St Omer to that monastery by Simon, abbot of St Bertin, who came to Ghent in 1136 after the pope had deprived him of his abbatial dignity.

It is our copy that Mr Bethmann analyzes; [Col. 1031C] he does not seem to have known our work, which, indeed, was not published in the *Messager* until last December.

“This work,” he says, speaking of the *Liber floridus*,  
[Note: [Col. 1032D] Ibid., p. 60.]

“is a compilation from Isidore, Bede, Freculfus, Hegesippus, Martianus Capella, Jerome, Josephus, and the Fathers of the Church, without any settled plan.”

We should point out that Mr Bethmann did not follow step by step the different chapters of the Ghent manuscript; he gave neither the numbers of the treatises nor pagination, which makes comparison of the various manuscripts on the basis of this analysis very difficult.

Besides our copy, Mr Bethmann  
[Note: [Col. 1032D] Ibid., pp. 64 and 79–80.]

also gives [Col. 1031D] a description of the seven other known copies of this manuscript.

1. Wolfenbüttel, Gudian I, parchment, large folio, thirteenth century. It begins with Lambert’s prologue and [Col. 1032A] ends with the *Deeds of the Roman Pontiffs*, under Hormisdas; it appears incomplete. The order followed by Lambert is inverted, and several subjects are omitted. To the chapter *Genealogy of the Counts of Flanders* [Note: [Col. 1032D] Probably the same item designated in our notice as no. 118, fols. 104–105 of the Ghent manuscript.] another has been appended: “The Three Counties, Cities, and Abbeys of Flanders.” — “Relics of Saints in the Counties of Flanders.” — “Names of the Counts of Flanders” (down to Charles the Good). — “The Streams of Flanders.”

2. First Hague copy, no. 759, parchment folio, well written. At the end one reads: “This book was begun at Lille and completed in the town of Ninove, in the diocese of Cambrai, for the nobleman of Goux and Wedergrette (Wedergrate), knight, councillor, and chamberlain of the most illustrious prince Lord Philip, Duke of Burgundy and Count of Flanders, A.D. 1460.” It is a very poor copy of the Wolfenbüttel manuscript.

3. Second Hague copy, no. 759a, [Col. 1032B] paper folio. It is a French translation of the preceding manuscript, made “within the town of Enghien for the nobleman and most redoubted prince, my lord Philip of Cleves, lord of Ravenstein, in the year of Our Lord 1512.”

4. Paris, Supplement Latin 10 bis, parchment, large folio, thirteenth century. It is again Lambert’s compilation, but entirely altered; several new subjects, composed after 1120, conclude the volume.

5. Leiden, Vossiani Latini, no. 31, parchment folio, fourteenth century. It belonged to Alexandre Petau. The order of the materials has likewise been arbitrarily inverted, and eight subjects written by another hand have been appended to Lambert’s compilation. [Col. 1032C]

6. Douai, no. 740 (we cited it in our notice).

7. Paris, Supplement Latin 107, from the year 1429.

Baron de Reiffenberg, who kindly said a word about our notice in the *Bulletin du Bibliophile belge*, II, 79, cites several treatises of the *Liber floridus* which were imitated or reproduced elsewhere.

Nor should we forget to say that the learned editor of the *Monumenta Germaniae historica*, Mr. Pertz, discusses this encyclopedia at length in the journal devoted to the historical works under his direction, entitled *Archiv für ältere deutsche* [Col. 1032D] *Geschichtsforschung*, vol. VI, p. 5, and vol. VII, pp. 531–546.

In FABRICIUS, *Bibliotheca mediae latinitatis*, one will find cited most of the authors from whom the *Liber floridus* contains extracts.

## In the Year of the Lord 1130: Hugh of Cleerii, Knight of Anjou; Fulk V, Count, Envoy to King Louis

[Col. 1033]

# Commentary on the Major-Domus Office and the Stewardship of France, Formerly Hereditary to the Counts of Anjou

(*Works of Sirmond*, III, 579)

[Col. 1033A] When God wished to raise Robert, the duke’s son, to the kingship, Geoffrey Grisegonelle, with three thousand armed men, served his lord King Robert. For Otto, king of the Germans, with all his forces of Saxons and Danes, had besieged Mount Morciac and was making many disgraceful assaults upon the city of Paris. In this crisis of battle, King Robert and his father entrusted the command of the first division to the aforesaid Count Geoffrey Grisegonelle and appointed him leader and counsellor for pursuing the German army. Thus King Robert pursued the German king, with Geoffrey Grisegonelle leading the way, as far as the river Aisne. But Count Geoffrey, skilled and experienced in battle, had made so great a slaughter of the enemy upon the river before King Robert’s [Col. 1033B] arrival that you would have thought it a lake, not a river.

When the Germans had fled, King Robert convened a general council and, by the advice of his father, bishops, counts, and barons, granted Count Geoffrey everything that King Lothair had possessed in his bishoprics, namely Anjou and Maine. Whatever else he or his successors might acquire, he committed to him with the same liberty under which he himself held it.

But the wickedness of the Count of Troyes could not endure King Robert’s prosperity. To crush his treachery, the king assembled the largest army he could. He therefore besieged Melun; but after remaining there for a long time, he saw that he was accomplishing nothing. He summoned Geoffrey Grisegonelle with his men of Anjou, who without delay hastened to render their customary service.

[Col. 1033C] On arriving, Geoffrey sent his constables ahead, asking them to show him where he might encamp. They returned and reported to their lord that the army was so great that there was no suitable place for them to lay siege. For the aforesaid town, situated on an island in the Seine, was enclosed on every side by a wall [Col. 1034A] made of lime and sand. Seeing, therefore, that they could find no lodging, the Angevins put on their arms, broke through the middle of the army, crossed the waters of the Seine, assaulted the town, and by their customary courage took the fortress. What the army could not accomplish in three months, they achieved within half a day.

The French, admiring this people’s unprecedented boldness, everywhere extolled them with every praise. Seeing such valor in the prince, and that he prevailed in the realm as much by arms as by counsel, and because he had deserved well in this and other matters, the king then established, amid universal applause and praise, for him and his successors by hereditary right the major-domic office of the kingdom and the stewardship of the royal household.

Count Fulk spoke these words to his chaplain Tescellinus: [Col. 1034B] “Listen, priest, to the services which Count Geoffrey Grisegonelle rendered to his lord King Robert. David, Count of Maine, and Geoffrey, Count of Corbon, refused to receive their fief from the aforesaid king, asserting that they could in no wise be subjected to the Burgundy family. Hearing their pride, and seeing no small diminution of his realm, the king, after taking counsel with Count Geoffrey and the leading men of the realm, fixed a time and day and decreed to besiege the castle of Mortagne.

“But Count Geoffrey, learning of the king’s army’s approach, moved his camp from Vendôme, assaulted the aforesaid castle with his customary courage and the valor of his people, captured Count Geoffrey and his townsmen, who were insufficiently wary, and delivered them to his lord [Col. 1034C] the king. But Count David, refusing to come to a conference with the king, sent word that he would in no way submit to the king and that at no time would King Robert dare to see his Maine. Hearing the arrogance and insolence of the aforesaid count, the king bestowed him and his Maine upon Geoffrey Grisegonelle and granted it to his successors to possess by royal gift.” Thus far are the writings of Fulk of Jerusalem.

But you who hear these writings, know that I, Hugh of Cleerii, saw the writings of Count Fulk of Jerusalem in the church of the Holy Sepulchre at Loches, concerning the major-domic office and the stewardship of the French, conferred upon him and his predecessors by King Robert.

There was great discord between King Louis, son of King Philip, and Fulk, who afterward became king of Jerusalem. For Count Fulk would not serve him. King Louis had given the major-domic office and stewardship of France to Anselm of Garlande, and afterward to William of Garlande, from whom Count Fulk could not obtain his dues and homages. [Col. 1035B]

It happened, moreover, that King Louis was engaged in a very great war with King Henry, son of William the Conqueror of England. King Louis therefore asked Count Fulk to help him in this war. The count replied that he owed him no service whatsoever, since the king was disinheriting him from the major-domic office and stewardship of France.

Then King Louis sent word to the count through Amaury of Montfort, Count Fulk’s uncle, Geoffrey, abbot of Vendôme, and Ralph of Beaugency, that, on their advice, he would make amends to the count concerning all these matters and others of greater importance. Count Fulk therefore consulted his men, namely Robert of Blois, Salmace of Permina, Hugh of Cleerii, Gaudin of Vegea, and many others, and replied to King Louis [Col. 1035C] that, if he did what he had promised, he would gladly provide this and the other assistance requested of him.

On the day on which this counsel was taken, the court of Anjou was filled with good and most wise knighthood. Then Amaury of Montfort and the others who had brought the king’s words advised Count Fulk to reply to the king through someone known to him, and, before the king’s messengers returned, speedily to offer thanks and recompense concerning these matters. The count’s counsellors, hearing Amaury’s advice, approved it. When Countess Aremburga heard this counsel, she approved the proposal that no one should go except Hugh of Cleerii.

I, Hugh of Cleerii, therefore went to Paris, and thence [Col. 1035D] to Genainville, where I found the king and the Count of Beaumont. Having found him at Genainville, between Pontoise, Beaumont, and Chaumont, I spoke with the lord king. First greeting him on the count’s behalf, I offered him thanks and recompense for the message he had sent to Count Fulk. Then I told him that Count Fulk offered him his service, either immediately or, if he wished, after a conference. Delighted, the king said that he preferred a conference first.

A day and place for the conference were accordingly appointed between Marchais and Bricy in the Beauce. Meanwhile the king instructed the count to bring with him to the conference his son Geoffrey, who now lies in the church of Saint Julian of Le Mans. For he greatly desired to see him.

When the day [Col. 1036A] of the conference arrived, Lord King Louis and Count Fulk came to the appointed place with their counsellors. There the count’s rights were acknowledged, namely the major-domic office and the stewardship of France. William of Garlande, then seneschal of France, acknowledged at that conference that he owed homage to Count Fulk for the stewardship of France; and thereafter he was subject to the count’s will. After William, Stephen of Garlande was seneschal, and he rendered homage to the count; after Stephen came Ralph, Count of Peronne, who likewise rendered homage and service.

Whoever is seneschal of France shall render homage and such services to the count. If the count goes to the court of the lord king, the seneschal commands the king’s marshals to prepare and assign lodging to the count. When the count [Col. 1036B] arrives, the seneschal shall meet him and lead him to his lodging. Then the seneschal shall go and tell the king that the Count of Anjou has arrived. If the count wishes to go to the king, the seneschal shall lead him to court and return him from court to his lodging.

If the count wishes to attend the king’s coronation, the seneschal shall have lodging prepared and assigned for him, as is the count’s proper and due right. When, on the day of his coronation, the king takes his place at table, the seneschal shall prepare a most beautiful bench, covered with a cushion, a cloth, or a tapestry; and there the count shall sit until the dishes arrive. When the first dish arrives, the count, unfastening his cloak, shall rise from the bench and, receiving the dish from the seneschal’s hand, shall place it before the king and queen. He shall order the seneschal thereafter to serve at the tables; and the count [Col. 1036C] shall sit back down until the other dishes arrive. As he did with the first, so he shall do with the others.

When the service of the tables has ended, the count shall mount his horse and return to his lodging, accompanied by the seneschal. Thereafter the horse which the count brought to court—namely, the charger—shall be given in feudal right to the king’s cook. The cloak which he wore fastened at court shall be given to the steward, after the meal. Then the pantler shall send the count two loaves and a sextary of wine, and the cook a piece of meat and a draught of wine. This is the seneschal’s allowance on that day. The count’s seneschal shall receive these provisions and give them to lepers.

Further, whenever the count goes with the king’s army, the seneschal of France shall prepare for him a tent able to contain a hundred [Col. 1036D] knights, a packhorse to carry it, cords and pegs, one mounted man to conduct it, and two footmen. When the campaign is ended, the count shall return the tent to the seneschal if he wishes; if he does not return it, he shall nevertheless have a tent on the next campaign. Whenever the count is or goes with the king’s army, he shall provide protection for him; on the return journey, rear-guard protection; and whatever happens to him, whether good or bad, he shall not be reproached for it by the king’s own mouth.

I, Hugh of Cleerii, saw these services rendered to Count Fulk, king of Jerusalem, in two campaigns in Auvergne and at one coronation at Bourges; and I saw them rendered to Count Geoffrey, who is buried at Le Mans, at one coronation at Bourges and another at Orléans.

Likewise Walter of the district of Senlis acknowledged [Col. 1037A] before King Louis, in my presence and hearing, that he held from the Count of Anjou everything that he possessed in the town of Senlis outside the walls; and that the forage-dues of all Arbrie, and every tenement, were held as fiefs of the Count of Anjou. Ralph of Martreuil and his brother Thomas used to render service in Anjou for their fief. And I, Hugh of Cleerii, while speaking with King Louis, heard these words from him: “Ralph of Martreuil, see Hugh of Cleerii, knight of the Count of Anjou, your lord. Go and render the service of your fief of marshalship, and lodge Hugh, because you hold this fief from the count.” Then Ralph lodged me [Col. 1037B] in the name of the marshalship; and the king added: “By the grace of God, I am now on good terms with the Count of Anjou.” [Col. 1038A]

Henceforth the count is called *major* in France because of the rear-guard protection which he provides in the king’s army. Likewise, whenever he is in France, whatever his court judges shall be firm and binding. If, however, any dispute arises and judgment has been rendered in France, the king shall order the count to come and amend it. If the count does not wish to send someone in his stead, the king shall transmit the writings of both parties to the count, and whatever his court judges concerning the matter shall be firm and binding. I, Hugh of Cleerii, saw judgments rendered in France corrected in Anjou many times. Thus it was with the battle fought at Saint-Omer, and with many other [Col. 1038B] pleas and judgments. I saw this, and many others with me.

## In the Year of the Lord 1121: William of Champeaux, Bishop of Châlons

[Col. 1037]

# Historical Notice

(*Gallia Christiana*, new ed., vol. IX, p. 877)

[Col. 1037C] William, also called the Venerable, took his surname from his birthplace, Champeaux, a town of the diocese of Paris in Brie, situated three miles from Melun and distinguished by a church of canons now secular. As a young man he devoted himself to learning under Anselm, then celebrated throughout France and later dean of the Church of Laon. Having made great progress under him, William was made archdeacon of the Church of Paris and was appointed to teach dialectic in the schools of that cathedral. He had many hearers, among whom was the famous Abelard, whose name was in everyone’s mouth; Abelard provoked against himself not only the rivalry and envy of his fellow pupils but also his master’s indignation.

William, however, desirous of a better life, moved in 1108 with several pupils to the Old Cell in the Paris suburb, where there was a small chapel of Saint Victor. Having adopted the habit of the canonical order, he founded the highly renowned abbey of Saint Victor in Paris; we discussed this matter more fully long ago in vol. VII, col. 657. [Col. 1037D] Nevertheless, he continued to teach dialectic, first in that suburb and then in the city itself. But, challenged in both places by his pupil Abelard and finally abandoned by his hearers, he sounded a retreat, renounced philosophical subtleties forever, and devoted himself wholly to monastic life.

This is according to Abelard himself, who seems to have understood by “monastic life” nothing other than the rule of life of canons regular; see Mabillon, *Annales Benedictini*, vol. V, p. 383. Not long afterward, in 1113, William was raised to the bishopric of Châlons, as Alberic testifies in these words: “The bishop of Châlons died; Master William of Champeaux succeeds, he who abridged the *Morals* of Pope Gregory and wrote other works.”

In the following year he attended the Council of Reims and the dedication of the church of Saint Mary at Laon. In 1115 he blessed Saint Bernard as abbot of Clairvaux, with whom he was most closely joined in friendship; and he removed the scruple of Bernard’s monks, who believed that foods temporarily pleasant to the palate should be avoided as indulging the flesh more than the spirit. In the same year he attended the councils of Reims and Châlons. He subscribed [Col. 1038D] the synodal letter of Cono of Palestrina for Saint-Quentin de Monte, and the settlement made by Matilda, lady of Cauniac, to the Church of Paris regarding the advocacy of the land of Viriac.

In 1117 he attended the Council of Rome. In the following year he was present at the Council of Reims; he gave to Odo, abbot of Saint-Remi at Reims, the altar of the estate of Ausson; and with his support the abbey of Trois-Fontaines was founded. In 1119 he subscribed the agreement made between the canons of Saint John at Chartres and the monks of Marmoutier. He went with the abbot of Cluny to Emperor Henry, with whom he negotiated at Strasbourg concerning peace and concord between empire and priesthood. He attended the second Council of [Col. 1039A] Reims.

In the following year he made peace between the canons and monks of Vertus, according to Rapine, p. 260, and attended the Council of Beauvais, which dealt with the canonization of Saint Arnulf, bishop of Soissons. In the acts of that council Lisiard of Soissons praises him as a “pillar of teachers”; indeed, Saint Bernard praises him as a holy and learned bishop. In the Chronicle of Morigny he is also called a great helper of Cono, bishop of Palestrina and legate of the Apostolic See, who had directed the higher schools and then, possessing zeal for God above all bishops of the whole of Gaul, shone in knowledge of the divine Scriptures.

But after granting many altars to the church, he departed this life in 1121—that is, 1122—either on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of February, according to the records of the Church of Châlons and the necrology of the monastery of Molesme, or on the eighth day before the Kalends of February, according to the necrology of Saint Victor at Paris. He was buried at Clairvaux in a chapel which he himself had erected at his own expense. The common opinion is that he assumed the monastic habit at the end of his life; Manrique considers this uncertain.

For what Rupert of Deutz wrote against both William and Anselm of Laon, see Mabillon, *Annales Benedictini*, vol. V, p. 623. A notable fragment of the treatise which William himself wrote on communion under one or both kinds is found in the *Acts of the Benedictine Saints*, vol. III, preface, p. 53. A short treatise *On the Origin of the Soul* is found in Martène, *Anecdota*, vol. V, p. 879. [Col. 1040A]

[Col. 1039]

# On the Sacrament of the Altar: Fragment

(Edited by Dom Mabillon in *Acts of the Saints of the Order of Saint Benedict*, vol. III, preface, p. LIII, from the Cheminion manuscript.)

[Col. 1039B] There are indeed different practices concerning reception of the Eucharist for certain reasons, but the reality is the same. The prohibition against receiving bread dipped in wine arose from a trivial reason—namely, the dipped morsel which the Lord offered Judas as a distinguishing sign; nevertheless, it is good when received in faith.

Likewise, each kind is received separately in order that the remembrance of the body visibly hanging on the cross, and the remembrance of the blood which flowed with water from the side, may be retained more closely and, as it were, presented anew. Yet it must be known that whoever receives one kind receives the whole Christ. Christ is not received piecemeal or gradually, but wholly, whether in both kinds or in one. Hence, newly baptized infants are given the chalice alone, because they cannot use bread; and in the chalice they receive the whole Christ. [Col. 1039C] The chalice must be given them because, just as no one can enter into life without baptism, so no one can do so without this life-giving viaticum.

[Col. 1040B] And after some verses: Therefore, the assertion that both kinds must be received is plainly heresy. For although both sacraments are there according to breaking, smell, warmth, and taste, nevertheless in each kind Christ is whole. After the resurrection he is wholly invisible, impassible, and indivisible: so that neither is blood without flesh, nor flesh without blood, nor either without the human soul, nor the whole human nature without the Word of God personally united to it.

And therefore, although he is wholly received under either kind, for the reason stated above the Church unchangeably retains the sacrament of both kinds. For there are sacraments in the Church which may be altered: for example, the water of baptism, these elements, and the oil of consecration. [Note: [Col. 1039C] I have reported these matters at greater length both because they may not be readily accessible to everyone and because they clearly show that communion under both kinds lasted into the twelfth century. William of [Col. 1040C] Champeaux died in the one hundred and twenty-first year after the thousandth; at that time bread dipped in wine was commonly offered to communicants. MABILLON.]

[Col. 1039]

# Charter of William of Champeaux (1120)

[*Annals of the Diocese of Châlons*, by Fr. RAPINE, p. 260.]

[Col. 1039D] In the name of the holy and indivisible Trinity, WILLIAM, bishop of Châlons.

[Col. 1040D] How great is the power of peace and concord we clearly recognize from the fact that disturbers of peace and sowers [Col. 1041A] of discord are declared, on the authority of Holy Scripture, not only hateful to God but detestable to his soul. Desiring henceforth to preserve, by that zeal of charity with which we persuade every person to seek the good of so great a virtue, an inviolable and firm peace between our brethren—the canons of the church of Saint Martin and the monks of the church of Saint Saviour, who regularly serve God in the town called Vertus—we have taken care, by a common settlement acceptable to both parties, to extinguish the tinder of discord which had until now continually been kindled among them.

For the canons of Saint Martin, claiming tithes from the monks of Saint Saviour for all [Col. 1041B] labours, because that church of the monks was founded within their parish, were trying to turn all their parishioners away from burial by the monks; and in these matters they were stirring up fraternal hatred against their church and embittering their own parishioners. With the brethren on both sides jointly consenting, we have thus decided concerning tithes between them.

From all vineyards which the monks have or shall have within that parish, they shall pay to the church of Saint Martin only one muid of wine yearly. From all grain of every kind which the monks have gathered within the boundaries of the parish through their own labour or through sharecropping, they shall render the canons a tithe according to just custom. But for the rearing of any animals or the cultivation [Col. 1041C] of gardens throughout the canons’ parish, the monks shall pay them no tithe whatever. If, however, anything from the monks’ animals within the parish has been held under sharecropping, then from their own half they shall render a tithe to the canons; the other half shall remain free to the monks from tithing.

And although we know that all parishioners of the church of Saint Martin are subject to the canons throughout their lives by parochial right, nevertheless, to preserve the bond of fraternal peace between monks and canons, we have decreed, with their common consent, that the following be observed regarding knights and their wives. When they come to their end, they may choose a place of burial among either the canons or the monks, provided that they first leave a fitting alms to the parish church and, before the hour of burial, their bodies are carried with due honour to the church of blessed Martin.

If any of the knights or their spouses dies unexpectedly and without having determined a place of burial, he or she shall be buried among the monks or canons according to the choice of the surviving spouse. The same applies to their daughters: their burial shall be provided for at the decision of their parents in either of the two churches. But when they reach the age of legal independence, if a son remains in knighthood without an office, we decree that he and whatever wife he has shall remain subject to the aforementioned rule; if he refuses knighthood, he shall be bound, with whatever wife he has, by the law of commoners. Likewise, a knight’s daughter who has a knight as husband shall be subject to the aforesaid law of knights. If she marries from among the commoners, she shall remain subject to the law we have assigned to commoners. But if she has married a knight and, after her husband’s death, is joined in marriage to anyone [Col. 1042B] from among the commoners, she too shall be compelled to submit to her husband’s law.

If anyone comes from another parish, has no wife and no dwelling of his own in the parish of Vertus, and serves in the monks’ house, eating their bread, then, if he dies, he shall be buried by the monks without objection. Whoever from their entire parish wishes to pass from the secular world to the common life of the monks or to assume the religious habit, we strictly command that no one whatsoever obstruct his vow. But if he is indebted to the parish church in any principal matter for which, while still healthy, he had at some time been summoned into court, his heirs, or the monks themselves, shall answer for him to the canons.

These matters having thus been arranged and confirmed, in a form of concord suitable to both parties, by the presence and testimony of venerable persons of the Church of Châlons, we decree by the authority of our episcopal office that everything above stipulated shall remain unshaken and inviolate for all time. Whoever attempts, by any alteration of these provisions, to disturb the peace shall, by the judgment and power of the Holy Spirit, be punished with the present excommunication until he makes satisfaction, and shall be excluded from the eternal fellowship of the saints. Amen, amen.

Done and confirmed at Châlons, in the presence of Lord William the bishop and the chapter of Saint Stephen, in the year of the Incarnation of the Word 1120, in the third indiction, during the reign in France of King Louis, etc.

Rainaud, chancellor, wrote and subscribed.

## Doubtful Minor Works

[Col. 1043]

# On the Origin of the Soul

(MARTÈNE, *Thesaurus Anecdotorum*, V, 881.)

[Col. 1043A] 1. The question has often been debated: by what justice are the souls of children who die before baptism condemned? That the body, whose seed God made in Adam, contracts the stain of original sin is not especially surprising. But the soul, which was made by the Best Being, does not descend from a corrupted mass, does not choose by its own disposition the body to which it is united, but preserves its obedience where the will of its Creator has placed it. It seems strange why it should be condemned except for those sins which, when the body has grown, it commits by consenting to sensuality. Yet the faith of the Church holds that if a child dies as soon as the soul is united to its body, the soul will be condemned on account of the guilt of origin. In this the Creator seems at fault, since he gave it such lodging [Col. 1043B] that it was necessarily corrupted there.

2. Some are therefore driven to say that the soul, like the body, descends by propagation; and thus the Creator is free of blame, because the soul too descends from the father’s corrupted soul, just as the body descends from the body. They also cite Gregory of Nazianzus, a wise man, who says that as soon as the seeds of father and mother are joined, the soul is immediately present, though it does not exercise its powers—just as a child, when born, does not immediately discern or judge things which it does afterward in mature age. For, as he says, how could that seed be formed into a man unless it contained a seed of soul?

But if he said that the soul is immediately present in the seeds, he did not therefore say that it descends [Col. 1043C] from the parents. God can then also infuse a new soul. Yet the doctors of the Church do not agree even with this; rather, they maintain that a new soul is infused by God either on the sixty-sixth day after conception or in the sixth month. We must therefore consider how the Creator is not blameworthy.

3. At the beginning of creation God made a rational creature, that is, an angel, capable of knowing God and becoming blessed by contemplating him. He also made bodily things, possessing no reason and incapable of blessed contemplation. Thus it appears that brute animals would be superfluous in God’s great commonwealth unless they benefited someone’s blessedness. For the spirit did not feed upon them or need them in any respect.

Accordingly, man was made from rational spirit and [Col. 1044A] body. By his bodily nature he needed these things; by his rational spirit he contemplated God, and thus made blessed both himself and the body joined to him. These two are in a sense so engrafted together that the body is endowed with sensation through the spirit—that is, it has the five senses—and the soul takes on the nature of the body so that it senses, becomes angry, desires, hungers, and does other such things through it.

Man was thus created under this law: he would possess seed, as regards the body, for the successive creation of human beings, while God would infuse new souls. Therefore, if man had persevered in obedience, then, just as he himself was holy and pure, so too would be the seed of offspring proceeding from him. But because the first man himself was corrupted through disobedience, he received as punishment that he should generate in concupiscence. Therefore the particle proceeding to the power of generation is itself also corrupted.

But if man mismanaged that part of generation which belonged to him, should God, who is unchangeable, therefore alter his plan so as not to infuse new souls into seed, whatever its condition when it proceeds from its parents? Inconstancy does not belong to him. God therefore does what he had purposed from eternity: he infuses new souls into unclean bodies, acting not cruelly but fulfilling a just providence; nor has the soul any cause to complain against God. For he made it in order to infuse it into an animating body. If it finds a corrupted vessel, it too is corrupted by it; therefore it must [Col. 1044C] be purified.

Nor has the soul anyone whom it can justly accuse for the evil it suffers except the first parents, through whose sin death entered the world. For, as has been said, God ought not, because of human folly, to alter his plan of animating human beings. But we can affirm with certainty that they will be punished very lightly if the soul is separated from the body before baptism. If, however, the child receives baptism, it is cleansed of every sin; and in this the surpassing kindness of God is especially admirable, since after transgression he found a remedy for humankind. But why God has ordained, concerning those who perish before baptism, that they should not reach baptism, belongs to the hidden judgments of God.

[Col. 1045]

# Dialogue between a Christian and a Jew on the Catholic Faith

(*Bibliotheca Patrum*, twelfth century, Part I, vol. II, p. 1885.) (G)*

[Col. 1045A] To the most reverend Alexander, by God’s grace bishop of Lincoln, a certain defender and servant of the Christian faith wishes right understanding in the Spirit of God and continual joy in his consolation.

Since you are abundantly instructed in letters, trained not only in human but also in divine laws, and endowed with the honour of personal grace, I send you for examination by your judgment a small disputation which I recently composed while disputing with a certain Jew. Having become acquainted with a Jew on account of a certain matter, I repeatedly urged him, under the compulsion of love, finally to become a Christian after abandoning Judaism. I showed him, by the light of truth, the many paths of his error and proved what I said by testimonies from his law and ours. [Col. 1045B] But since he persisted, with hardened heart, in his unbelief and defended his error with foolish questions and arguments, we finally agreed amicably and sat down for the purpose of disputation.

My hearers therefore asked me to commit this to writing for the benefit of the faith. Gladly complying, I have set it down in writing, according to the capacity of my modest talent, under the persons of a disputing Jew and Christian. If anything has been well said, let it be attributed to God’s grace; if your prudence knows that anything is idle and useless and ought to be cut away, whether wholly or partly, I shall most willingly accept whatever you choose to do with it. Thus that Jew, very learned in his own law and not ignorant of our writings either, began as follows.

JEW. If you would patiently hear me and calmly answer my questions, I should very gladly know why you blame and reject the Jews because they are found to observe the Law given them by God through Moses. For if the Law is good and given by God, it must surely be observed; nor, because they observe it, should its observers be cursed. Rather, those who curse them ought more to be despised.

CHRISTIAN. I ask the same of you: hear me patiently and do not reject with an obstinate mind the truth which I shall state. We know that the Law was given to you by God through Moses, and that it is indeed good and to be observed. Nor do we reject you because you observe the Law; but we blame you because you do not keep your own Law as you ought to keep it. Indeed, you destroy it.

[Col. 1045D] **JEW.** How so? Do we not observe circumcision, the sacrifices of the Law as far as we are able, and the other commandments that were given? [Col. 1046A] In what respect, then, do we destroy the precepts of the Law? Rather, you destroy it, since you observe nothing whatever.

**CHRISTIAN.** I shall show you how, by observing the Law in this fashion, you destroy it; how, while holding its precepts, you are proved not to hold them; and how, though circumcised, you are convicted of being uncircumcised. For the carnal Law was given carnally to carnal people, remaining imperfect and enclosed beneath figures signifying things to come, until that Perfect One should come who would bring it perfectly to completion and show that which had long been closed to be opened in himself—he who opens and no one shuts, who shuts and no one opens. Circumcised for us by his own blood, he opened it, so that, abandoning carnal circumcision, we might rather be cleansed in the saving washing of baptism, and, fortified by the keeping of virtues, beware of vices; and so possess spiritual circumcision.

He himself is the paschal and spiritual lamb, whom that paschal and carnal lamb signified. By his death and by feeding upon him, we are delivered from Egyptian slavery—that is, from the devil’s power—and restored by inward sustenance. For what the old Law signified in figure, the new Law has presented in reality. What advantage, then, is there in retaining the signifying Law, when we now hold in our hands the very thing signified by that Law? Therefore, since carnal circumcision and the carnal sacrifices of the Law now avail nothing, they are to be abolished; while spiritual circumcision and the commandments of the new Law, because they avail spiritually, are to be observed in every way. You, therefore, who are circumcised carnally—that is, uselessly—are thereby proved uncircumcised; and, while holding the precepts of the old Law, you are proved not [Col. 1046C] to hold them, indeed rather to destroy them, because in observing them carnally you disdain to hold them spiritually.

**JEW.** What are you saying? You certainly utter grave blasphemy, since you judge that what the Lord established should be abolished. Have you dared to call imperfect the Law which the Lord made and wrote? Did the perfect Lord make anything imperfect? Or is he so changeable that, according to changing circumstances, place, or time, he alters his own sayings and deeds—as you now maintain when you assert that, after the introduction of the new Law, the old must be abolished? Tell me, I ask: how then will that saying remain true: “For ever, O Lord, thy word abides”? If God’s word abides for ever, surely this truth also will remain: “Every [Col. 1046D] flesh that is not circumcised, that soul shall perish from its people.” The Law excepts no one, but commands every flesh to be circumcised and declares that the uncircumcised person is to be cut off from his people. In this it says absolutely nothing concerning the spirit, but speaks only of the circumcision of the flesh. Whence, then, do you draw this spirituality?

**CHRISTIAN.** Hear, Jew, the mysteries of faith; and, with the veil removed from your heart, gaze with lynx-eyed vision upon the horned face of Moses. What the Lord established I do not destroy; rather, with all devotion I uphold it. When I said that the Law was imperfect, I said what is true and said it rightly, because through it there was only the knowledge of sin: the Law was given in order that sins might be recognized and cut away. Yet no one attained eternal life through it. The carnal Law has carnal rewards: it offered abundance of temporal goods, but did not promise anyone entry into paradise. Therefore [Col. 1047B] it was not perfect, since it could not save perfectly. For paradise had long been shut against all through the fault of the first-created man, and a flaming sword had been set before it to forbid entrance to those who wished to enter. Since every human being had sinned originally in the first father, all had fallen into death.

Therefore, for repairing this loss, a Law relying on carnal sacrifices was not sufficient: it could not open paradise, nor could it rescue from hell those who observed it, however righteous they might be. It was consequently necessary for the Son of God to come upon earth, to become for us a sufficient sacrifice, to remove carnal sacrifices, to perfect the imperfect Law, to bear our evils, to destroy our death by his own death, and to open the gates of the heavenly kingdom. Thus he expiated our guilt and, removing the turning sword, made entrance free for all the saints. [Col. 1047C] He therefore accomplished what the old Law could not accomplish, and supplied through the new Law what it lacked for perfection, giving us higher and spiritual commands, through which eternal and spiritual rewards might be given.

For example, the old Law forbids homicide; the new condemns anger and hatred. The former forbids adultery; the latter even the desire of the mind. The former forbids eating pork as unclean; the latter commands it to be eaten as clean, while commanding abstinence from the evil signified by it. Yet old and new precepts are not therefore opposed; rather, they are the same and one, since what the former says carnally the latter fulfils spiritually. Thus the word of God abides for ever. What the old Law established temporally, the new Law fulfilled eternally.

Thus also should this be understood: “Every flesh that is not circumcised, that soul,” it says, “shall be cut off from its people.” Behold the spiritual sense enclosed in the letter concerning the flesh: it asserts not that a soul is to be cut off because its flesh has not been circumcised, but that the soul which has not cut away the vices of the flesh will without doubt perish in eternal condemnation. These two Testaments are therefore ordered into one by Christ, who makes both one, and in him you must believe.

**JEW.** But if these two Laws are inseparably one, as you assert and strive to prove, it is most unjust that our Law—which, even according to your own statement, is the beginning and foundation of your Law—should be utterly abolished. Rather, if the new Law possesses in reality what the old Law signified in figure, let us retain both. But our Law forbids the eating of pork, and [Col. 1048A] your Law forbids the admission of sin: let us abstain alike from pork and from sin. Let us likewise observe circumcision of the flesh and the ceremonies of the Law, while not omitting their spiritual meaning. For even to hear that the unchangeable Lord establishes his own pronouncements changeably is most distressing.

**CHRISTIAN.** If you abandoned the killing letter and received the life-giving Spirit, you would without doubt know what “the change of the right hand of the Most High” means, and that this relation of the two Laws is not an empty change but rather the revelation of a divine mystery. For what was long hidden under figures in the Old Testament has been disclosed in the New by the grace of God and the presence of the realities themselves. No reasoning permits it—indeed, it is impossible—that we should live under that Law, who are not under Law but under [Col. 1048B] grace; otherwise grace would not be grace.

Although we seek new grace, we do not for this reason abandon faith in the Old Testament. Yet in the Law and the Prophets many things are written that differ, indeed conflict, and cannot stand at all according to the letter; therefore they require a spiritual meaning. Of countless examples I shall set one before you, so that, having recognized this, you may be able to perceive the rest similarly. King David, making a certain comparison in the Psalter, says: “Like the dew of Hermon, which descends upon Mount Zion.” You understand well enough how impossible it is, according to the historical sense, for the dew of Mount Hermon to descend upon Mount Zion. Since it cannot stand literally, it is fitting that it be set forth allegorically and said that the dew of Mount Hermon descends upon Mount Zion when the grace of God, which waters parched hearts, descends from Mount Hermon—that is, from the Lord, who is the mountain of our strength—upon Mount Zion, that is, the souls of the saints. Though burdened by bodily mass, these nonetheless, as far as they can, contemplate the Lord through a mirror and in an enigma; for Zion is called “contemplation.” There are likewise innumerable other passages, some of which may be understood allegorically, some morally, and some by the letter alone.

Observe, therefore, from these things that the old Law spoke figuratively when it affirmed so many literal impossibilities. As for what you said—that because the two Testaments agree we should observe both, figure and reality together—I shall prove to you by a clear example how difficult and useless that is.

[Col. 1048D] **JEW.** By what example?

**CHRISTIAN.** Suppose that you are holding a walnut in your hand.

**JEW.** Let it be so: I am holding a walnut.

**CHRISTIAN.** If you ate that walnut unbroken, perhaps you would choke.

**JEW.** That would indeed happen quickly.

**CHRISTIAN.** Therefore a whole walnut is not good to eat.

**JEW.** Certainly.

**CHRISTIAN.** First, then, its shell must be broken, and so one reaches the kernel.

**JEW.** It cannot possibly be otherwise.
