**CHRISTIAN.** Hear, then: you cannot usefully eat a whole walnut, nor reach the kernel unless the shell is first broken, just as you cannot reach the new [Col. 1049A] Law unless the old Law is crushed. For you remember that I have often said that the old Law held the new Law enclosed within itself, set beneath figures and enigmas. Therefore the old thing—that is, the shell—must first be broken, so that the kernel—that is, the new Law, namely God’s grace—may be uncovered and retained. The old shadow must be driven away and the new light of heavenly grace brought forth. It is fitting that the promises of the Prophets—indeed, of God—be fulfilled, promises that long beforehand foretold things to come.

For one was not always to say and promise, “Behold, a virgin shall conceive and bear a son,” because by God’s grace a virgin has now conceived and borne, and after giving birth remained a virgin. Nor was that prophet always to be awaited of whom Moses had said: “The Lord your God will raise up for you a prophet from among [Col. 1049B] your brethren, like me; him you shall hear. Everyone who does not hear that prophet shall be cut off from his people.” For that prophet, and more than a prophet—indeed, the Son of God—has now come; the Lord raised him from the dead after he had been killed by the hands of his own brethren.

**JEW.** It is greatly to be wondered whence you Christians presume to derive such things. Moses says this concerning a prophet, not concerning Christ; he said it concerning Joshua. Why, then, do you twist Scripture to serve your own will?

**CHRISTIAN.** If you attended carefully to Moses’ words, you would undoubtedly not say this. “The Lord,” you say, “will raise up for you a prophet like me.” Joshua was not a lawgiver like Moses, but only brought the people of God into the land of promise. Christ, however, became the lawgiver of the new Law as Moses was of the old, because the Law was given through Moses, but grace and truth came through Jesus. He must be heard and believed; everyone who does not hear him must be cut off from the people of God. For this reason you have been excluded and removed from God’s people: you refuse to hear such a prophet. You vainly await Christ’s coming and observe carnal ceremonies; but there is reason to fear that, because you do not believe that he has come and await another, you will receive not him but another.

**JEW.** It seems to us most grievous to abandon our Law, which the Lord certainly made and gave, and which we have held as handed down and observed by our fathers for thousands of years. But if it is nearly useless, as you maintain, tell me, I ask, if you know, why our holy [Col. 1049D] Fathers observed it so faithfully and pleased the Lord through it. Surely they had foreknowledge of the future and foretold many things to come. Hence it must be believed that they would not have observed it so diligently unless they knew that it contained some usefulness.

**CHRISTIAN.** Open the eyes of your mind and see how I shall now continue the same comparison. Tell me, I beg you: of that whole walnut which you held in your hand, which did you love more, the shell or the kernel? Did you preserve the shell for the kernel that you hoped was inside, or the kernel for the shell?

**JEW.** Certainly I preserved the shell in hope of the kernel that I expected within; for if I had known that there was nothing inside, I would immediately have thrown it away.

**CHRISTIAN.** You have spoken well now. So too did your holy [Col. 1050A] Fathers: they observed the old Law for the sake of the new Law, and with all devotion loved the hope of future salvation which they knew to be enclosed in it. None of them could break this shell until that great prophet came, who shattered it by his great power. Tell me, I ask: once the walnut is broken and the kernel taken out, what will you do with the shell?

**JEW.** Keeping the useful kernel, I shall throw the useless shell into the fire.

**CHRISTIAN.** Come then: do what you say. Throw away the old shell—namely, circumcision together with its practices—and put on the new human being through the grace of saving baptism, which will rescue and cleanse you from old errors and, removing the veil from your heart, will illumine you more brightly than light itself. Christ was sent chiefly to the lost sheep of the house of Israel; he was promised and given to them, but at last, when they rejected him, he was taken away from them and given to us. Yet he whom they rejected will not reject you, for he is the fountain of mercy; rather, he will receive you gladly and joyfully, because he made you—and indeed redeemed what he had made and lost, restoring it by his death to life. Therefore you ought not to be ungrateful for such great benefits; rather, you should give him devout thanks, seek pardon for your blasphemies, believe him to be true God and true human being, and faithfully adore him. He will rejoice in your salvation; we Christians also shall rejoice, and the angels likewise, who rejoice more over one sinner doing penance than over ninety-nine righteous persons who have no need of penance. You will therefore do well, if, abandoning the faithlessness of Judaism, you turn to the faith of the living and to Christian grace.

**JEW.** Put aside as quickly as possible that joy by which you suppose that I have been defeated or converted. You will not persuade me so easily. Many matters still remain by which I shall press you hard, and I shall stand unmoved upon the field of this contest. Answer now why the Lord gave so frail a Law that could not preserve those who observed it. Surely it is a kind of deception to give medicine to a sick person that cannot save him. What benefit was there in keeping the Law if, after death, they were held in eternal fires? But it is altogether incredible that Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, and the other holy ones—the friends of God, to be sure—were in hell; and you will certainly be unable to establish this by any authority.

[Col. 1050D] **CHRISTIAN.** It is no wonder that you despise God’s commands, since you are a stiff-necked people. Therefore my words are burdensome to you, because wisdom shall not enter a malicious soul. Whoever is of God hears God’s words, but the natural person does not perceive them at all. Know truly that Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob were in hell, because they could not escape the common condition. Those also who lived under the Law and observed it with all their strength were there, since the Law was so frail that it could not restrain them from the ways of hell. I shall prove this very thing from the authority of your books: that Israelite who said, “If you do not bring Benjamin back, you will bring down my gray hairs with sorrow to hell”; and Job: “Hell,” he says, “is my house; in darkness I have spread my bed”; and David likewise: “You have delivered my soul from the lower [Col. 1051A] hell.”

Behold, I have produced for you three suitable witnesses from your Law, so that every word may stand in the mouth of two or three witnesses. Although they were not in the lower hell, they testify that they would be in hell, where they would suffer nothing but darkness. For in the lower hell the damned were held, those who were eternally condemned for their crimes.

Further, since, speaking of the frailty of the Law, you gave a fitting example by saying that it is a kind of deception to give medicine to a sick person which cannot heal him: first know that the Lord deceives no one; rather, he mercifully receives everyone who has been deceived. Beware, then, lest your blasphemy fall back upon your own head. Next understand that the written Law was given to restore the natural law. For the natural law had been implanted in the first [Col. 1051B] Fathers, but was afterward wholly erased and transgressed in their children through the wickedness of life and conduct.

> **Note [Col. 1051D].** Note that when he says either that the natural law was wholly erased through sins, or that it entirely fell away, this must be understood with respect to the application of the general principles [Col. 1052D] of natural law to particular actions.

For the ancient Fathers, by natural goodness, knew what ought to be avoided or done: namely, that they should never do to another what they would not wish done to themselves. Since, therefore, this law had entirely fallen from human memory through great length of time and increasing wickedness, it was necessary for the written Law to restore it, recalling the sins to be avoided, so that those who observed it might escape sin and the punishment of sin. For, as Paul—yours and our apostle—says, “Before the Law sin was not imputed, because it was not known”; and: “I did not know sin except through the Law; for I would not have known covetousness unless the Law had said, ‘You shall not covet.’”

Thus the Law was useful in that time to those who observed it, because by recognizing sin they avoided it and likewise escaped sin’s punishment. Finally, the Law’s medicine was in some fashion effective for those who were ill: although it could not heal them perfectly, its caution held them back from imminent evils. But it brought no one to perfection, because it could not obtain a return to paradise.

**JEW.** Blessed be God! For, by your own admission, we Jews ought also to rejoice because we have so strong a Law. Although, in your judgment, it does not save altogether, it is nevertheless not wholly useless but salutary, since it can rescue its observers from the punishments of hell. Certainly one who, though lacking good things, is free from calamities ought greatly to rejoice; and one who, though in hell, does not suffer hell’s evils. Therefore the Law is not to be abandoned but rather retained; though it does not reopen paradise to us, its observance grants temporal goods and will also preserve us unharmed from evils of the soul.

**CHRISTIAN.** You ought not to rejoice but rather to groan and weep, because you will burn miserably in flames while you reject God’s grace with a proud mind. For the Law that benefited your forefathers is now condemnatory for you. It availed them, who awaited the coming of redemption, by avoiding contagion and not incurring punishment; but for you, who await in vain—indeed, reject the offered salvation—it brings contagion, not by removing punishment but by imposing it. For after the Lord sent redemption to his people and established the New Testament for ever, your old delusion profits you nothing, but harms you in every way. Therefore in hell no redemption will be awaited by you; you will perish there eternally, because you do not believe that the redemption already sent has come, but disdain it in grievous obstinacy. Yet you could escape if you were washed in the grace of baptism; unless you do this, you will by no means enter the kingdom of heaven.

**JEW.** Consider what you are saying. If I, or anyone unbaptized, shall not enter the kingdom of heaven because we have not been baptized, then Abraham and the other [Col. 1052B] Fathers will not enter it, since they were not washed with the water of baptism.

**CHRISTIAN.** Certainly Abraham and the other saints are in paradise, because they were baptized in Christ’s death. For he washed them in his own blood and, delivering them from death, restored them to life. By dying he expiated not only original sin but, in forgiving mercy, also wiped away the actual sins of believers.

**JEW.** When you speak of original sin, I take you to mean the sin committed by Adam, the father of all. But what has that to do with us? Hear what the prophet says: “The soul that sins shall itself die; the son shall not bear the iniquity of the father,” and so forth. Let Father Adam, therefore, bear his own iniquity, which does not concern us at all. Though we are his children, we do not bear his iniquity. Why do you impute it to us, who had not yet been created and did not yet exist?

**CHRISTIAN.** Know with certainty that the sin Adam committed, you yourself committed; and the fruit which he bit contrary to God’s command, you bit. For when Adam sinned, no human being existed apart from Adam, but every human being was Adam. Therefore, because Adam sinned, every human being sinned. That stock from which the human race was to proceed was then wholly present together in his body, and nothing had yet flowed from it. If anyone had then been born who did not commit Adam’s sin and did not consent to him as he committed it, that person would certainly be free from the father’s guilt. But because we all were in him and had not yet been separated from him, we sinned inseparably with [Col. 1052D] him; what he committed we likewise committed, and we incurred the same sentence of death. Therefore you bear not your father’s iniquity but your own, and you refuse to be washed in saving baptism from the original guilt which you had committed with him.

**JEW.** Tell me, I ask, by what reasoning baptismal water can cleanse me from original sin. It is also ridiculous to say that material and visible water can in any way abolish spiritual and invisible sin. It is not so subtle that, when the body has been washed, the soul is washed as well. But if Christ expiated that guilt by his death and cleansed us all, [Col. 1053A] why must we afterwards be baptized? Were we not baptized in his death? Was not that redemption so sufficient that we no longer need anything else afterward?

**CHRISTIAN.** The wave of baptism can wash you not only from original sin but also from all actual sins. For the waters are sanctified by the word of God and the ministry of the priest, receiving power to wash not only bodies but minds as well. For the word of God is living and effective, sharper than every two-edged sword, reaching even to the division of soul and spirit, of joints and marrow, and discerning also the thoughts and intentions of the heart. From that word the water receives its cleansing power, provided that you approach with unfeigned faith and preserve inwardly, in perfect faith, what you undergo outwardly.

For if you are baptized without right belief, you will not thereby be saved, but rather condemned. Conversely, if you believe rightly but are not baptized, you cannot at all be saved by your belief without baptism. Faith, therefore, cannot save without baptism, nor baptism likewise without faith. We must therefore believe and be baptized, so that we may demonstrate the faith of the heart by the work of baptism and also utter it through verbal confession. For with the heart one believes unto righteousness, but with the mouth confession is made unto salvation. Nor is it ridiculous, but a great miracle, that material water, endowed with God’s power, can wash away spiritual stains: it removes defilements for believers; for unbelievers, though baptized, it does not remove them but rather [Col. 1053C] brings them.

Since, speaking of Christ’s death, you included yourself as well in the plural, saying, “If Christ cleansed us all, why must we afterward be baptized?” know that Christ’s death benefits believers alone. As it is life for them, so it is death for unbelievers. It avails you nothing as long as you are an unbeliever, because faith without baptismal works is idle; indeed, it is like the faith of demons, who, although they do not love the Lord, nevertheless believe and tremble. But whoever loves the Lord surely hastens to be baptized and proves faith by displaying the work, because the proof of love is the performance of a work. That redemption, therefore, is not sufficient for you without baptism, since you do not demonstrate, either by confession or by baptism, the faith which you ought to have; rather, by contradicting it you deny it. Therefore first believe; then be baptized and cleansed, so that you may receive the pledge of the Holy Spirit, become a temple, and, being buried with Christ through baptism in death, also become a participant in the resurrection.

**JEW.** Since you demonstrate that baptism is necessary, I ask you to say how Christ could have redeemed from original sin when he himself was subject to that sin. For he was born from a woman’s body and was flesh made from Adam’s flesh; he could not be free from that sin, because through his fleshly origin he inherited the stain of sin. Further, it is incredible that one who cannot heal himself should ever heal another.

**CHRISTIAN.** When you say that Christ was subject to original sin, you lie altogether. For he did not have original sin, because he was not conceived in iniquity; indeed, he was free from all others as well, because he committed no sin whatsoever. For he was conceived and born from an immaculate virgin, begotten without male seed; therefore he is not a participant in original guilt. The nature in which the first human being had been created was afterward corrupted when he sinned. If he had not sinned, he would certainly not, in generation, have experienced corrupt and defiling desire; rather, his nature would have remained tranquil and gentle as it had been made. Thus that conception would have been without guilt, because he would not have experienced burning desire. But because he sinned and, drawing sin into himself, corrupted the former goodness of his nature, he immediately experienced, against his will, the lust of the flesh which he had not previously known. The delight of sin seized his captive mind, and he poured that same [Col. 1054B] plague into all posterity.

Accordingly, every person begotten through fleshly desire is born with original sin. Drawing corrupt nature from the first father through depraved lust, and born from the corruption of flesh, such a person lacks the tranquil nature in which the first human being was originally made. But since every lust was absent in Christ’s conception, he contracted no stain from sinful flesh. Rather, through the working of the Holy Spirit, he had a tranquil and pure conception, because he was free from every pleasure of lust; and because he had no father on earth, he was not born from the corruption of flesh. He suffered no sickness at all from original sin, but was able to heal us who were sick, and did heal us, because his mother remained a virgin after giving birth.

[Col. 1054C] **JEW.** Since the order of the argument now requires that we speak of the virgin’s childbirth, tell me how she could give birth contrary to nature, she who, as you yourself say, bore the author of nature. For it is not customary—indeed, it is contrary to nature—that a son was born from Mary without male seed. And if a virgin conceived and gave birth, nevertheless the further assertion you add was not added by the prophet: namely, that she remained a virgin after giving birth. Here, then, your presumption has added what Isaiah did not presume to say, but wholly passed over because he foresaw that it was empty. From this it should be noted that you utter many absurdities and, by interpreting the divine Scriptures, arrange them according to your own will. Unless, therefore, you plausibly prove both that the virgin’s childbirth was not natural and that she remained a virgin after giving birth, I shall not believe it.

**CHRISTIAN.** O Jew, do not be unbelieving but believing, for the righteous lives by faith. Since you marvel that a virgin conceived without male seed, recognize God’s omnipotence, to whom anything whatever is possible because he is almighty. Since he is also the maker of nature, he performs many things contrary to nature, by which he shows himself to be Lord of nature. Was it not contrary to nature when he opened the Red Sea for the Israelites and caused them to pass through its midst on dry footprints? Or when he rained manna in the desert upon your fathers and brought water from a rock? Did Aaron’s rod, which was dry, not act contrary to nature when it flowered, put forth leaves, and bore almonds? And did the bush, which appeared to burn yet did not burn, act naturally?

From these things, therefore, infer God’s power. As Aaron’s dry rod flowered contrary to nature and bore almonds, so the Virgin Mary conceived and bore contrary to nature. And as the bush appeared to burn yet did not burn, so no heat of temptation burned the Virgin Mary, whom the Holy Spirit, coming upon her, overshadowed. Why, then, do you not believe that the virgin gave birth contrary to nature yet by God’s power, when you see that God has done so many things impossible according to nature? Why do you also doubt that she remained a virgin after giving birth? Do you not see that a ray of sunlight shines through glass, yet the glass remains entirely unbroken? Thus also Christ, the sun of righteousness, illumined the virgin by the power of his divinity and, taking flesh, passed through her while preserving his mother’s integrity; and, under the obscurity of humanity, God hidden from the world appeared.

Finally, you yourself must live by and believe in this faith by which we live, without which it is impossible to please God. Trusting in it, we believers dare to say that a virgin conceived and gave birth, and even add what Isaiah does not add: namely, that after giving birth the Virgin Mary remained a virgin. We cannot investigate how this came about, because we are enclosed in mortal flesh and do not know God’s unsearchable counsels. Just as we do not know how Aaron’s rod flowered and bore fruit, and yet do not doubt that it happened by the power of faith, so we do not doubt that blessed Mary the Virgin conceived and bore without male seed, though we are wholly ignorant of the manner in which it happened. Let us therefore attribute all to God’s power, and believe it with sincere faith in the conduct of our lives, so that we may obtain the rewards of that same faith.

Hear, if you wish, what one of our writers says concerning this: “If a divine work is comprehended by reason, it is not wonderful; nor does that faith have merit to which human reason supplies proof.” Therefore you must not disbelieve God’s omnipotence, he who does whatever he wills in heaven and on earth; but rather believe without the proof of human reasoning, because this faith is to be rewarded for ever. This is the catholic faith: that we believe and confess that the Virgin Mary remained a virgin after giving birth. Unless you believe this faithfully and firmly and are baptized, you cannot be saved.

**JEW.** If you proved by clear authority that Christ has already come, you would easily persuade me to be baptized. But while you say that he has already come and do not establish this with persuasive authority, you turn my mind away from your faith.

**CHRISTIAN.** This is easy enough to prove from the authority of your books, for all that was foretold concerning his coming has now been fulfilled in him. I shall set one point before you, by which you may know from the fate of your nation that Christ has come. Jacob, blessing his son, says: “The sceptre shall not be taken away from Judah, nor a leader from his loins, until he comes who is to be sent; and he shall be the expectation of the nations.” If you examine the annals of history, you will clearly find that until the times of the Savior a prince or leader from the Jewish people did not fail. But when Christ was born, King Herod reigned, who was a foreigner to that nation and therefore strove with all his might to kill him. Then the leader from Judah’s thigh and the royal sceptre were removed completely, because afterward Judaea had no king or leader from itself. For at that time the One who was to be sent came: Jesus Christ, Son of God, who is the expectation of the nations.

**JEW.** By your own words you have fallen into my hands. For if your Christ, sprung from our race and born from the tribe of Judah itself, is king and prince, it is plainly established that the Jewish kingdom has not yet ended. Since Judah’s sceptre has not come to an end, you clearly see that the Messiah has not yet come.

**CHRISTIAN.** Rather, you yourself have fallen into the pit which you made, because, willingly or unwillingly, you now confess that [Col. 1056B] our Christ is your king. O blind and wretched people! Why do you not receive him eagerly, and, confessing him true God and true human being, most devoutly adore him? Though he reigns eternally with God the Father as God, governs and orders all things, he declined a temporal kingdom and foretold that his kingdom was not of this world. But he brought your kingdom to its end when the Messiah came, of whom Daniel had long before prophesied: “When the Holy of Holies comes, your anointing shall cease.” Thus your anointing wholly ceased when the Holy of Holies came, because you are without temple and kingdom, scattered throughout the whole world, and accursed, because you refused to receive the Messiah. You may moreover fear that, together with the earthly kingdom, you will also lose the eternal one. But we who received him when he came, and believe by receiving him, shall reign with him, whom we truly adore as Lord and human being. He is your expectation; we await his coming for judgment with fear, in order that we may behold him more securely.

**JEW.** Alas! Woe is me, that you overthrow me with such a whirlwind of words that what I thought would weaken you most instead drives me toward a precipice! Yet you weaken yourself badly when you call Christ God and Son of God. I do not doubt that he was a good man, but I by no means believe that he is God or God’s Son. For the Law says: “Hear, Israel: the Lord your God is one God.” The Law commands that one God be adored and says that he alone is to be served. You know well how erroneous and damnable it is to command me to adore two persons of two gods. Or what authority proves that God ever begot a Son? Unless you prove this, you will be shown to deserve severe punishment for blasphemy, and you will see that you have said everything above in vain.

CHRIST. May I never be able to harm myself more than by calling Christ God or the Son of God; may this “weakness” always hold me fast and never abandon me for eternity. For Christ is undoubtedly a good man, who is also one God with the Father and the Holy Spirit. For we who believe rightly worship one God in a Trinity of persons, and the Trinity in unity of Deity. I shall immediately demonstrate to you from the beginning of your own books the essence of these persons. For when Moses says that God created all things in the beginning [Col. 1057A], nothing is more rightly understood than that He made all things in His Son, who is the beginning, fountain, and source of good things, from whom all things are.

That God the Father begot the Son is testified by David, who relates that the Father, speaking with a father’s voice, said to the Son: “Before the morning star I begot you.” The voice of the Son likewise declares it, saying: “The Lord said to me, ‘You are my Son; today I have begotten you.’” Therefore, when God the Father says that He begot the Son, He openly reveals both His own person and that of the Son; and when the Son declares that He was begotten, He manifests both His own person and that of the Father. For Father and Son are two relative terms: neither can the Father exist without the Son, nor likewise the Son without the Father.

Moreover, concerning the Holy Spirit, who is third of these two in the Trinity but one in Deity, hear what Moses says: “The Spirit of God was borne over the waters” [Col. 1057B]—not wandering about through any sort of movement, but as God, co-operating in the creation and enlivening of all things. The Psalmist also testifies that He is God the Creator, saying: “Send forth your Spirit, and they shall be created; and you shall renew the face of the earth.” He who prayerfully asks that the Spirit be sent forth to create or renew the face of the earth undoubtedly does not doubt that the Spirit is God and Creator. Likewise the prophet Joel says: “I will pour out of my Spirit upon all flesh, and your sons and your daughters shall prophesy.” We now see this grace of God fulfilled, because we are filled with the Holy Spirit, by whom we too prophesy when we announce eternal joys to ourselves and to you.

Moses likewise did not pass over this Trinity in silence when he relates that, intending to create man, God said [Col. 1057C]: “Let us make man in our image and likeness”—that is, rational and intellectual, and possessing a soul that lives eternally. When He says, “Let us make man,” He certainly indicates the Trinity of persons; and when He says, “in the image and likeness” of Deity, He indicates unity. Some ignorant persons misunderstand this, imagining it to be said of bodily limbs rather than rationality or intelligence. They should know that God, being incorporeal and incomprehensible, lacks bodily limbs; consequently, the human body was not made in God’s likeness. Rather, this is said concerning rationality, intelligence, or the immortality of the soul; and God created not only human beings but also angels in His own likeness.

Furthermore, your father Abraham, recognizing the Trinity, did not deny it. Receiving the three angels who came to him as a figure of the Trinity, he saw three indeed, but worshipped them as though one. For, filled with the Spirit of God, he understood in the three the mystery of the Trinity, while nevertheless believing the unity of Deity in the Trinity. Thus, in worship he said: “Lord, if I have found favour in your eyes, pass by and rest in this place.” Here it should be noted that, when he addresses three as though one, he professes his belief in one God in Trinity.

King David likewise believed in the Trinity in unity when he repeatedly said: “May God bless us”—namely, the Father—then, “May our God,” that is, the Son, and again, “May God bless us,” that is, the Holy Spirit. After expressing the Trinity of persons [Col. 1058A], he immediately gathered them under the unity of Deity, saying: “And let all the ends of the earth fear him.” Therefore these two exceedingly exalted witnesses, to whom the promise concerning Christ was specially made, are greatly to be believed. For God, saying to Abraham, “In your seed all nations shall be blessed,” and to David, “Of the fruit of your womb I will set one upon your throne,” fulfilled both promises truly. For in Abraham’s seed, which is Christ, we—all nations—possess by inheritance the blessing through faith in Him; since we do not doubt that He shall sit upon David’s throne and kingdom and reign eternally with the Father and the Holy Spirit.

Indeed, the heavenly angels also proclaim the Trinity, who, Isaiah testifying, continually cry, “Holy, Holy, Holy”; but when they immediately add, “Lord God of Sabaoth,” they enclose their threefold confession within unity [Col. 1058B]. Take heed, therefore, lest you disbelieve what can be proved by such manifold authority. For you too may receive Abraham’s blessing, which you do not yet possess, if, abandoning unbelief, you are reborn in Christ, so that through faith you may become not only a son of Abraham but also a son of God.

JUD. Oh, with what long circling does your unwelcome discourse fly about my ears! Yet, as I listened to you just now, I could scarcely keep from laughing—namely, when you recounted that God said to Himself what He did not say to Himself: “Let us make man in our image and likeness.” For He said this not to Himself but to His angels. Therefore prove your Trinity from elsewhere, if you can; for what you have adduced there gives you no support whatever.

Further, the promise to Abraham which you cite—“In your seed all nations of the earth shall be blessed in you”—was not spoken concerning Christ but Isaac, who was given by God to his father already wearied by old age. And again, “Of the fruit of your womb I will set one upon your throne,” was said not of Christ but of Solomon, who afterward governed that kingdom for a very long time in great peace and glory. Why, then, do you allegorize concerning Christ what you plainly see to have been said not of Him but of Isaac and Solomon?

Again, while you now maintain that incorporeal God made a bodily human being, and therefore one unlike Himself in bodily form, you then maintain that God, born of a virgin, became a bodily human being. You make yourself unbelievable [Col. 1058D], now asserting something and then denying what has been asserted, as one fleeing the truth and seeking corners, perversely twisting the Scriptures by stealth. For your faith turns round and round with the volatility of your words.

CHRIST. Your hardened heart offers more cause for weeping than laughter. When you deny that God spoke those words to Himself and say that He spoke them to angels, your very insolence will refute you—not I alone, but Isaiah, indeed God Himself. For Isaiah, speaking in one place of the Creator’s power, says: “Who has known the Spirit of the Lord, or who has been His counsellor and instructed Him? Or who has first given to Him, and it shall be repaid to him? When did He take counsel with someone, and that person instruct Him and teach Him the path of justice, and show Him the way of prudence?” By these words Isaiah most clearly reveals that God the Creator had no counsellor besides Himself [Col. 1059A]. In the sufficiency of His unsearchable wisdom He never needed the counsel or assistance of angels. What counsel could those give who could not remain standing for a moment without His counsel?

God spoke this to Himself when creating man so that the created human being might recognize his Maker and, recognizing Him, might know that he ought to worship, believing in one God in Trinity. Moreover, the blessing of Abraham’s seed was fulfilled not in Isaac but in Christ, because the abundant blessing of God was poured out upon all nations not through Isaac but through Christ.

The following words show that the Davidic promise was not perfectly fulfilled in Solomon: “If your sons keep my covenant, these things which I shall teach them, then their sons also shall sit upon your throne for ever.” These things were not fulfilled in Solomon or in others, because, not keeping God’s covenant, they were deprived of the royal throne. But Christ, doing the will of His Father who sent Him, shall sit eternally upon David’s throne and kingdom.

You will find David testifying to the same thing in other passages as well. God says: “Once I have sworn by my holy one: if I lie to David, his seed shall remain for ever, and his throne as the sun before me, and as the moon perfect for ever.” And elsewhere: “He shall endure with the sun, and before the moon, through generation after generation.” Thus you clearly see that this is not said of Solomon, because he did not endure with the sun and before the moon, but only for one generation. Christ, however, maker of the sun and moon, born of David’s seed according to the flesh [Col. 1059C], shall reign eternally. His throne shines as the sun before God, and, like the perfect moon for ever, He shall endure before sun and moon unto eternity.

But since you called me one fleeing the truth, you shall shortly hear that you acted unjustly. For I do not flee the truth, nor, seeking corners, do I make myself unbelievable. Nor do I secretly distort the Scriptures, nor does my faith turn with any instability. Rather, I have truly said and say that the Son of God, one God with the Father and the Holy Spirit, created the first human being in His likeness—that is, rational and immortal. Yet there is no bodily form in God; therefore the image or likeness of God is spiritual, in accordance with which the first human being was made intellectual.

But at the end of the ages, at times appointed by God, the person of the Son of God, by rational warrant and just necessity, assumed a human body in order to redeem us from all iniquity. Yet He did not diminish His Deity: He remained God, which He was, and at the same time assumed into one unity humanity, which He had not been. Thus, with the person of God and man united—not through confusion of substance but unity of person—Christ is one true God and true man [Col. 1059D]. For unless humanity had fallen from the heavenly homeland, it could in no way have returned thither.

JUD. You have argued very fully and plainly concerning the Trinity and the other matters, and have confirmed what you said by unanswerable authority. Although I cannot wholly bend my mind to belief, I cannot deny that you have spoken rightly. Yet I should gladly hear, if you can truly demonstrate this: by what necessity did the Son of God, descending from the seat of heaven, deign to become a mortal human being? Since God is omnipotent, He could surely have forcibly rescued humanity, deceived by the devil, by the power of His command alone. Or why did He endure so great a labour? Could He not have done this through an angel, cleansing the world from original sin; or through any righteous human being; or even by creating some new human being and redeeming the old one from destruction? It is wonderful to us by what reasoning the death of one Christ can benefit us all, destroy death itself by dying, and restore humanity to life.

CHRIST. If you were willing to bend your rebellious mind to humility and, attending sincerely, to have ears ready to hear, I would gladly explain to you through what rational love God willed to become human. For with a proud eye and an insatiable heart you cannot enjoy such a benefit, nor understand by what just necessity or ineffable mercy the Author of all things assumed mortality [Col. 1060B].

JUD. I shall indeed listen to you eagerly, but on this condition: if I see anything to be questioned or objected to in your account, I shall by no means remain silent. Yet I shall not disbelieve; rather, I shall gladly obey whatever your reasoning of truth declares.

CHRIST. Therefore the omnipotent God—without beginning or end, abiding eternally in Himself, a Trinity of persons and unity of Deity—created all things. First, out of unformed matter He created heaven and earth; and, that the nature of angels might know and praise the power of His Deity, He made it in His own likeness, intending it to endure eternally [Col. 1060C].

JUD. I ask you not to be troubled if you pause a little. Moses says nothing at the beginning about the creation of angels; nevertheless, I do not doubt that they were made in the beginning, though I confess that I am utterly ignorant at what time they were made.

CHRIST. The angels were surely made with the light, because they are sons of light. For God says: “When the stars were made, all my angels praised me with a loud voice.” From this it is clear that, when the light was made, God had already created the angels.

JUD. Since this is sufficiently credible, continue the argument you have begun [Col. 1060D].

CHRIST. Therefore, after the Lord had created the angels, the first among them in dignity and beauty fell through pride. He disdained to remain under due service to his Maker; indeed, scorning to be subject and humble, he wished to be like God. Therefore, falling from such exaltation, he was cast down; making himself the devil, he came to the depths, so that he who wished to be like God might lose even what he was. Once surpassing others, he became more worthless than all and perished beyond recovery.

JUD. Why, then, did God make him, when divine foreknowledge knew beforehand that he would perish? Or is God so unjust that He freely makes any creature in order that it may perish? And if the devil sinned, nevertheless, lest he perish wholly, God ought to restore him as His creature through repentance [Col. 1061A]. For He is not so implacable that no repentance can appease Him, nor is the devil so obstinate that he cannot be pierced by repentance.

CHRIST. You inquire rightly. But know that God, in making that angel who afterward changed himself into the devil by sinning, certainly made a good and useful work. Although He foreknew that he would fall, He nevertheless ought not for that reason to refrain from creating him, because He knew that many useful consequences would come from his fall. And although he is “a spirit that goes away from God and does not return,” nevertheless his iniquity greatly benefits us. For, with God’s permission, he tempts us; and, by tempting, proves us—God Himself assisting—who makes assaults through evil angels.

Did it not benefit blessed Job that the devil proved him by tempting him [Col. 1061B]? And blessed Paul and others, who were often buffeted by his blows? Therefore God created him usefully; for if he had not been made and fallen, humanity would not have existed at all, from whom as many human beings shall be saved as angels remained in heaven.

Nor ought God to restore him through repentance, since, sinning without cause or anyone’s example—that is, through pride alone—he was wholly without excuse. Therefore, falling into iniquity, he so completely hardened himself in it that he cannot even rise again. God had given those angels free choice—that is, discernment of good and evil. But the devil, with his accomplices, through his own sloth abandoned the good and embraced evil; hardened as an impious being, he fell in such a way that he does not even wish to rise again.

He fell at the very instant in which he was made, because he did not stand in the truth, when he became proud by contemplating himself [Col. 1061C]. For he had not tasted how sweet the Lord is. But if he had tasted how gracious the Lord is, he certainly would not have fallen before being rooted in love. Those, however, who remained with God, corrected by the others’ fall, established themselves so firmly in the love of God that, divine grace rewarding them, they can no longer fall.

JUD. Since God created all things very good, surely, as you say, He also made the angel good. From where, then, did that slothfulness of mind come to him, or how did it happen to him? If God created all things good, I greatly wonder whence sin or evil first came.

CHRIST. God is the supreme good; consequently, whatever He made is good. But evil is nothing [Col. 1061D], because it is not God’s creature; it was invented by the devil, not created. Indeed, it is nothing other than the absence of good, so that, when a substance is absent, nothing remains but emptiness. For example, when light—which is something—departs, darkness remains, which is nothing; for darkness is substantially nothing, but arises from the absence of light. Likewise evil is substantially nothing; it occurs when the good that ought to be present happens to be absent.

It is as if you held a chained bear: while it is held fast by the chain, it is quiet; when the chain is absent, it rages. If it were chained, it would not rage; the absence of the chain makes it rage. Likewise, a ship perishes when its rudder is absent, though it surely would not perish if it were present.

Now all things in the world are threefold [Col. 1062A]: good, evil, and intermediate. The supreme good is love of God; God Himself is love, and whoever possesses this perfectly is perfectly good. The supreme evil is hatred of God; and it is supreme because the one whom God hates, or the one who hates God, is perfectly evil. Intermediate things are riches, beauty, strength, and the like. According to their natural essence these are good, but by the will of those using them they may be turned to good or evil.

When, then, you ask why this slothfulness of mind happened to the devil, you do very rightly. Know, therefore, that in making the angel—that is, the substance or essence of angelic nature—God made him most perfect. To him, made in His likeness, He also gave rational understanding with free choice, so that through the discernment of free choice he might know to reject evil and choose good, and so, through the merit of serving God well, might deserve to ascend to the perfect degree of love which he had not yet attained. For he had not yet perfectly tasted the sweetness of love, nor was he established in that love which “does not envy, is not puffed up, does not act perversely”—that is, wrongly—“is not ambitious, does not seek its own things,” and, finally, never fails [Col. 1062B].

He ought gradually to have ascended to this through the exercise of the intermediate virtues, seeking God’s glory rather than his own from what he had received. But he acted foolishly and perversely in rivalry with his Creator; swollen with pride, he sought his own interests as an ambitious being. Thus the devil, at last taking from himself—from the beauty of his own condition—the material by which he ought to have acquired the love he did not yet possess [Col. 1062C], did not know, blinded by a proud eye, how to attain that love as was fitting. Since he loved himself more than God, he cast himself down by exalting himself.

No one striving toward perfect love ought to love himself more than God; rather, he ought to prefer God’s love and will to his own love and will, and love God with perfect affection. For by loving God, one loves oneself and one’s neighbour as oneself. Since the devil, lacking love, preferred self-love to love and honour of God, and despised his neighbours and equals while exalting himself above them—indeed, wishing to be like his Maker—he fell away from the good into sin. Since he did not exercise as he should the intermediate good which he possessed, he lost the supreme good, the love of God [Col. 1062D], and incurred the supreme evil, hatred of God. Thus, from that by which he ought to have grown, he instead declined all the more; but those who then remained made further progress.

JUD. I understand well your assertion that God made the angel most perfect according to his substantial essence. Why, then, did He not likewise establish him in love for Himself as soon as he had made him, so that He might perfect in love the one whom He had perfected by nature? For if, as you say, he had loved God perfectly, he would not have fallen; but because he did not stand, he fell utterly. Therefore God bears some blame in this: by granting him intermediate goods for serving Himself, He gave him instead an occasion for sin, since He did not establish him in love.

CHRIST. It would not have been fitting for God, in creating humanity, immediately to establish it in love. Rather, the order of reason required that the angel, to whom He had given rational understanding, should recognize his Maker and, recognizing Him, worship Him rationally; and by worshipping attain perfect love, which never fails [Col. 1063A]. Having acquired it by gradual ascent, he would never afterward fall. But because he did not wish to do this, he fell.

God bore no blame because the devil sinned. Granting him rational understanding, He also gave him, together with wisdom, the power to act, by which he could come to perfection. But the devil made evil from the good material God had given him, because he abandoned the good which he ought to have done; seeking his own gain, he did not do the work of his Lord, but as a traitor followed his own will.

Who, then, blames the craftsman if he gives his pupil the very knowledge of the craft and the tools by which he may work, and if that pupil, knowing how to work well yet knowingly working badly—not according to what he learned from his master, but constructing according to his own judgment—destroys what he builds [Col. 1063B]?

JUD. No blame attaches to the craftsman; nor does blame attach to God because the devil sinned.

CHRIST. Therefore, because the devil fell eternally by sinning, it was fitting that this loss should be restored. Accordingly, God created the human being, forming him from the clay of the earth.

JUD. Why, then, did He restore that loss from human beings rather than from angels?

CHRIST. If He repaired that loss from angels rather than from humanity, He would necessarily have created them such as the others had been made at first: perfect in nature indeed, but not yet established in perfect love—just as those who remained with God after their companions fell had formerly been. When these, already firmly established in perfect love, and those others, still weak because that same love was not yet perfected in them, came together as one, what an unsuitable assembly it would be is clear even to anyone blind [Col. 1063C].

Indeed, it was fitting that He should make humanity from the material of nothingness, so that human beings might learn not to be proud, as their predecessor the devil had done when he fell from heaven through pride. Seeing himself made from fragile earth, humanity might display great humility; while the devil, seeing him placed in the position from which he had fallen, might be tortured by grievous envy [Col. 1063D].

JUD. You have spoken so reasonably and well concerning angels that I now see nothing I can object to you about them. Continue what you began concerning humanity.

CHRIST. God therefore made Adam most perfect in wisdom, beauty, and strength, giving him natural perception and sound intelligence, so that by rational understanding he might rule over the other creatures, all of which God had made for his sake. For the propagation of the human race He also gave him Eve, a woman made from the rib of Adam while he slept. Since they needed food for sustenance, He granted them every tree of Paradise, so that, nourished by it, they might be preserved from evils and continually sustained in life. They were not then immortal in such a condition that they could live without food [Col. 1064A]. Unless they ate, they would die; but by the sustaining nourishment of food they would live always, so long as they kept God’s command.

He excepted the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, not because they had previously been ignorant of evil, but because, although they knew evil by knowledge, they had not yet learned it by experience. Thus we commonly say that no one knows what good is unless he has at some time tried what evil is. For if God had made him without knowledge of good and evil, the human being so made would certainly have lacked free choice. But He prohibited him from the tree of knowledge so that, through that commandment, he might know that he had God as his Lord and therefore might not be proud; but, by keeping the command, he might gain by the merit of good obedience the reward by which he would come into the fellowship of angels.

Thus they lived in the earthly Paradise in complete tranquillity and peace. Though naked, they were blessed, since they saw in themselves no defect whatever for which they should blush. Indeed, they would have lived perpetually without death if they had kept the Lord’s command, so that, at God’s appointed time, they might be transferred to the company of angels after generating all those by whom the place of the fallen was to be restored [Col. 1064B].

JUD. Since you have touched briefly on free choice, which is on almost everyone’s lips, I should like to know fully what it is. For, as others say—and I myself think—God gave Adam free choice when He granted him the licence or power to do good or evil.

CHRIST. Whoever asserts this does not know what he says; indeed, he sins, because he accuses God of sin. For if God had given Adam the power to do evil, He Himself would have sinned. But the Lord gave Adam free choice when, through rational understanding, He showed him the distinction between good and evil: forbidding evil lest he do it, and commanding the good which he was to perform. For free choice is nothing other than the knowledge of distinguishing good from evil. This was truly free in Adam when he had not yet sinned. For after he sinned, that choice was not free in him as it had previously been, because he felt in his members the law of sin resisting the law of his mind, a burden which he had not suffered before sin [Col. 1064C].

Indeed, a soldier who has not yet been captured can defend himself better before he is captured than he can free himself after he has been captured and bound [Col. 1064D].

JUD. You have shown most clearly what free choice is and that, after Adam sinned, it was not in him as free as it had been before. But if Adam had remained in Paradise with all his progeny, this world would have come to nothing; and all things which, like Adam himself, were made for humanity would surely have been useless, since the one for whose sake they were made would not use them.

CHRIST. The world and the things in the world were made not uselessly, but for humanity, so that the whole human race might live in this world and exercise dominion, by its ruling reason, over all creatures set beneath it. Yet the world would not be as it is now, but much more beautiful; afterward it was wholly corrupted by the waters of the Flood [Col. 1065A]. That corruption will be cleansed by the fire which, at the end of the world, will burn up the air and, rising as high as the floodwaters rose, will renew heaven and earth by purifying them like gold.

The rainbow in the cloud signifies this same thing: being two-coloured, red and green, it shows the signs of water and fire. The first raged over the world, but could not utterly destroy it; the second will not destroy it, but will renew it by changing it for the better. Thus all would enjoy complete peace, joy, and abundance of things without pain or distress, awaiting the time when, after the number of the elect had been fulfilled, they would obtain heavenly grace.

JUD. If God created all things very good for humanity [Col. 1065B], why are many things harmful to humanity? Human beings do not eat them; rather, they themselves eat human beings—such as serpents, dragons, every kind of creeping thing, birds, flies, and other animals which, though small, are harmful. They not only fail to help human beings, but often assail and injure them. If Adam’s children endured their attacks, they could not enjoy perfect blessedness.

CHRIST. If Adam had not sinned, any bird or beast that he summoned would immediately have come. Fish also, all animals, and every insensible thing—stones, sea, and land—would serve him with peaceful obedience. He even gave them names. But when he sinned, he lost that dominion; because he despised God’s commands, he appeared contemptible to all the things over which he had formerly ruled [Col. 1065C].

God created all things for humanity, and made them all very good, intending them to serve humanity’s welfare. For the worms, snakes, and other things you now abhor are also very frequently eaten by you.

JUD. Far be it from me to eat worms and snakes. Although God may have created them good, law and nature forbid them as food. For if I ate a snake or another venomous creature, I should immediately perish.

CHRIST. Do you eat deer?

JUD. Yes, because the law permits it, since it chews the cud and divides the hoof.

CHRIST. Attend now to how I shall speak with you in natural philosophy [Col. 1065D]. When a deer is sick or weakened by prolonged old age, it goes to the den in which a snake dwells. Then, setting its nostrils to the opening, it forcibly draws out the hidden snake by the power of its breath, which is very strong, tears it entirely apart, and eats it. Then, burning fiercely as the venom spreads through its body, it runs to a clear spring and drinks much and often, fully relieving by this healing draught the burning thirst which it had endured. This drink, cleansing away its former pains, restores the whole deer. Nature teaches it to take this remedy, for not even Hippocrates could provide you a better one.

Thus you see, you who eat deer, that the deer eats the snake; the snake also feeds on frogs and toads; and frog and toad live upon spiders and worms [Col. 1066A]. Likewise, fish and birds eat one another or consume many harmful things which are deadly for humans to eat. For if a person were to eat a serpent or snake tainted with venom, he would immediately die. But it is fitting that, as you live on deer, so deer too may live on snakes, and that the other creatures may be sustained by their own foods.

Yet all things return to the welfare of humanity: even harmful things benefit it most healthfully, while one creature, consuming another, affords delightful pleasure through food. There are also many things which, though unsuitable as food, give human beings assistance: horses, asses, and dogs, for example, commonly relieve human labour usefully. Others are useful in medicine, which wise physicians employ in many ways—such as Hippocrates and Galen, who left absolutely nothing untried, but turned even the lowliest and most despised things to human welfare by the knowledge of their art [Col. 1066B].

JUD. I cannot deny or refute by any reasoning what you say. But when you maintain that God made some animals for human food, others for assistance, and others for medicine, I do not at all see how this can agree with Adam’s original condition. For I cannot believe that he ate flesh in Paradise, when God granted him only the fruit of Paradise for the sustenance of life. Nor would he have needed the help of horses or other things when, with God’s aid, his own strength was sufficient. Why would one who would never be ill require medicines? Since, then, you say that God made all things for him, tell me, I pray, how those things would serve him whose benefit he would in no way enjoy [Col. 1066C].

CHRIST. Adam truly would not eat flesh in Paradise, because he had no need of such food. Nor would one whose own God-given strength was sufficient need the assistance of any creature. Neither would he use medicines, because he was so healthy that even if he drank something deadly it would not harm him. But God made creatures so that humanity, the principal creature apart from angels, might have grounds for glorifying God; and, seeing itself set above all creatures, might give thanks to God for such great honour; and, marvelling at the power of such great might, might magnify the Maker of things. For how would humanity know God to be wonderful unless God made wonderful things?

In this sense holy Church sings: “Bless the Lord, all beasts and cattle” (Ps. CXLVIII)—not because beasts and cattle know how to bless the Lord, but because rational human beings praise God from and for them. God, however, who knows all things before they occur, foreknowing that human frailty would be unable to abstain from flesh, after He had carried out vengeance through the Flood upon those who had presumed to eat flesh without His permission, afterward mercifully allowed it [Col. 1066D].

For before the Flood there were giants, born from the sons of God and the daughters of human beings. Because of their enormous size, fruit and permitted produce did not suffice for their food. Therefore, devoting themselves to robbery and murder, they ate even the half-raw flesh of animals and human beings. Provoked to wrath by them, God brought in the waters of the Flood and utterly wiped them out from the earth [Col. 1067A].

JUD. What you have now brought forward from Genesis appears in our books not as “sons of God” but as angels. It is therefore remarkable how they could have intercourse with women, as the narrative itself says: “Seeing that the daughters of men were beautiful, the angels took wives for themselves from all whom they chose” (Gen. VI). Our elders hand down to us that, after Adam’s fall, these angels of whom we are now speaking fell from heaven and, living among human beings, begot sons. It is therefore marvellous that a spiritual and angelic nature could naturally mingle with human flesh.

CHRIST. The angels fell from heaven only once; strengthened by God’s grace, they could not fall again, either before or after Adam’s fall. Therefore you misunderstand badly if you say that spiritual angels fell and had intercourse with women. Those whom your text calls angels, but ours correctly calls sons of God, were naturally not sons of God or angels, but fleshly human beings. Yet because of the purity of their lives and the excellence of their morals, Holy Scripture chose to call them angels or sons of God. At that time they remained separated from that wicked progeny which, through evil Cain, its ancestor, had degenerated from Adam’s goodness of conduct, holiness, and knowledge. So long as they remained separate, they preserved their natural goodness, until they mingled with the daughters of the wicked. These women, pouring into them the wickedness of their fathers, perverted them from their former goodness [Col. 1067B–C]. From this mingling those great men, the giants, were begotten.

JUD. You demonstrate this so convincingly that I can never contradict it. But let us now return to Adam, and tell me whether the children whom he would have begotten before sin would have been born with such bodily infirmity, weakness of limbs, or ignorance of perception as those who are now born in this world.

CHRIST. They would not be subject to such afflictions; for, since they would be conceived and born without the heat of lust and therefore without sin, they would certainly do so without any pain either to their mothers or to themselves. Once born, they would not be punished by any bodily weakness, debility of age or limbs, [Col. 1067D] or ignorance of understanding; rather, they would immediately be able to speak most eloquently, walk, and naturally enjoy happiness, with no impediment obstructing their perception. And although, as God distributed His gifts among them, one would be wiser than another, all would nevertheless be teachable by God, being filled with great wisdom and instructed by nature, so that they would know nothing imperfectly concerning all things. For even the heavenly angels are not all equally wise, although they think one and the same thing; rather, one excels another, commands, and sends another—not by proud domination, but humbly. Thus one star differs from another in brightness, and one is the brightness of the sun, another that of the moon.

JUD. Why do those who are now born not enjoy the same blessedness, [Col. 1068A] but are instead naked, wretched, and weak, scarcely at last reaching manhood after a long time and much labor? Is the human soul in little children unwise or foolish, increasing in wisdom and strength as it grows with the body? Or is it wise and vigorous in its own nature, but hindered by the frailty of a childish body? Unless indeed even that wise man is shown to be foolish and they suffer many disadvantages of nature.

CHRIST. From this you may observe that they are born from corruption. For those holy persons who would have been begotten before sin would immediately be firm and stable for that very reason, since they would not proceed from corruptible flesh, but would be generated rather from an immortal and incorruptible body. But those now born are impeded by grievous frailty because [Col. 1068B] they are begotten from a mortal and corruptible body. The Wise Man also testifies to this, saying: “The corruptible body weighs down the soul, and the earthly dwelling presses down the mind that thinks many things” (Wis. 9). Since this body is corruptible (1 Cor. 15), it weighs down the soul in many ways, both through the frailty of its limbs and through ignorance of perception: one person, stiff-necked, is foolish; another, by keenness of understanding, beholds and comprehends profound things. And although the soul is always wise according to its nature, it is nevertheless hindered by childhood, old age, or some bodily obstacle, so that it cannot perceive certain things as it ought.

JUD. You speak very well; but if you wish to continue anything further from your account, do so, for I do not see what I can now ask about [Col. 1068C].

CHRIST. Therefore, when the devil saw and envied man blessed with such exaltation and destined for the place from which he himself had fallen through pride, he was inflamed with intense envy and tempted him through the woman, whom he knew by nature to be susceptible to seduction. Thus he deceived her under the appearance of good, promising them that they would not suffer death if they ate from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil. The tree itself was truly good; but this sentence hung upon it: on whatever day a human being ate from it, he would incur the necessity of death. It had received this name on that account: that by eating from it through transgression of the commandment, man might learn by experience how great was the difference between the good which he had possessed through obedience and the evil which he deserved through disobedience [Col. 1068D].

JUD. What is this that God threatened the sinning man with, saying that on whatever day he ate of that fruit he would die the death? For on the day on which he sinned he did not die; therefore that threat is not true.

CHRIST. That threat was true, because on the day he sinned—doing what he had not done before—he incurred the necessity of death; or because sin is death: when he committed it, he perished by the death of the soul.

JUD. Continue what you began, for you have answered briefly and well.

CHRIST. The woman, wholly deceived, believed the devil’s deceits, because she truly thought that there would happen to her [Col. 1069A] what the devil treacherously and wickedly said through the serpent. Having first eaten, she afterward gave to her husband; Adam, however, knowingly consented and believed. For, as the Apostle Paul says, “Eve was deceived in transgression, but Adam was not deceived” (1 Tim. 2). She considered the devil’s promises true, whereas he considered them wholly deceitful. But, as our author Saint Augustine and others say, he loved Eve his wife so greatly that he did not wish to differ from her desire and act. Therefore, consenting to her wishes, he sinned together with her; yet he trusted in God’s mercy, because he did not doubt that he would obtain pardon for his fault. But as soon as they had eaten, they immediately saw themselves naked, because, deprived of inward chastity, they experienced the lust which they had not previously felt; and [Col. 1069B] consequently they were shamefully ashamed. Before, they had known nothing but tranquillity; but as soon as they sinned, abandoned by God, their eyes were opened and they saw their nakedness, because, falling away from good, they immediately incurred evil.

Therefore Adam sinned not from ignorance but deliberately. Although he knew that the devil’s promises were not true, he nevertheless consented to Eve; and, not unwillingly but knowingly and voluntarily abandoning God, he bound himself over to the devil’s service. The devil received him as a slave and lawfully retained as his own one who had been disowned; and he ought justly to do this to one whom he had acquired through his own treachery. For everyone who commits sin is the slave of sin.

JUD. And why did he retain under an unjust condemnation one who, though deceived by his own treachery, had been created by God [Col. 1069C] to restore the number of angels? Does it not seem harsh to you that frail man, sinning not of himself but at the devil’s persuasion, should be handed over to the devil with no ground at all for excuse? Certainly you cannot now say of him what you have already said about the devil, who, sinning for no cause but pride alone, was wholly inexcusable. Man, indeed, sinned not without a cause: he was tempted by the devil and needed food. Therefore he ought to have had some excuse, because, believing his wife out of affection, he took care by no means to separate himself from her wish.

CHRIST. Do you wish to hear why the devil retained him thus? Certainly because he neglected to repent; for had he repented, he would surely have received pardon. Indeed, when God asked why he had done this, he refused to acknowledge his own fault [Col. 1069D] and immediately turned it back upon his own Creator, saying: “The woman whom Thou gavest to be with me gave me of the fruit, and I ate” (Gen. 3). O wretch! If he had immediately cried out that he was guilty, God, appeased by ineffable mercy, would have forgiven him the whole offense. But because he insolently showed contempt and laid his fault upon his Creator on the ground that He had given him that wife, the same Creator rightly passed sentence upon him. Thus, expelling him from paradise, He punished him with the sentence of death; clothing him in dead skins, He signified that at last ashes would return to ashes.

JUD. He perished most justly, because, despising kindness, he neglected to correct what he had wickedly committed. But since God foresaw everything and knew that he would sin, why did He not preserve him from sin?

[Col. 1070A] CHRIST. Because He had created him with such honor that, through the free choice which He had given him, he could, with God’s help, preserve himself so as not to sin eternally. For although tempted, he would not have been overcome by any temptation if he had wished; for he would never have been grievously distressed by temptation. But since he yielded to temptation not under compulsion but willingly, he rightly incurred condemnation, having ruined himself for nothing.

JUD. God made man in order to restore the number of angels who had fallen; therefore He made him for nothing, since by falling through sin he did not repair the angels’ place.

CHRIST. God created him profitably, drawing great benefit from his fault, since from the very point at which he fell he rose more strongly. For if he had not sinned, [Col. 1070B] God would not have become man; through whose incarnation salvation and honor have increased for us, since by assuming our lowliness He joined us to God and even raised it above the choirs of angels. O happy fault, which deserved to have such and so great a Redeemer! Therefore God did not make him for nothing: though he fell through sin, he will nevertheless, redeemed by Christ’s death, someday restore the angels’ place.

JUD. You have given me a very full account of the fall of angels and human beings. But now it is time for you to come to the matter for which our discussion was undertaken. For I asked you to show by reason what necessity caused the Son of God to become man, and why He chose to incarnate Himself rather than another.

CHRIST. You remember rightly. Know, however, that if [Col. 1070C] you carefully consider the discussion we have had concerning angels and human beings, the reason you seek will not be difficult for you to see—indeed, it will be very easy. You asked why almighty God endured so great a labor rather than forcibly snatching from the devil’s power the man whom the devil had deceived. But God, wholly rational—indeed Reason itself—willed to do nothing irrationally, He who ordered all things by reason. If He had forcibly withdrawn man from the devil, He would surely, contrary to holy reason, have committed injustice. For the devil had acquired man by rational cunning, and man himself had willingly given himself to the devil; consequently the devil ought not irrationally but justly to retain him. If, however, an angel to be incarnate had been sent to accomplish this redemption, [Col. 1070D] it would have been most unfitting; for then man would have been beholden to four persons, since while serving the one God in the Trinity, he would also have to worship the angel who redeemed him.

And if some new man had come to redeem the old man, it would never have been fitting, because one whose nature was not related to us—whether man or angel—would in no way have been able to restore us. Rather, it was more fitting that God should become man, taking sinless flesh from that very sinful nature, and that the Maker of man, coming in person, should redeem His own handiwork; and that with the same nature and by the same means by which the enemy had conquered man, He should in turn conquer that enemy. It was especially fitting that He should do this Himself, not through another, so that in one person we might worship God and Redeemer together. Therefore God sent forth one “born of a woman, made under the law,” so that those who were under the law [Col. 1071A] might receive adoption as sons of God (Gal. 4).

Yet this mystery was carefully concealed from the devil, who fearfully awaited His coming, known to him through the Scriptures; for he did not doubt that his power would be destroyed by Him. Therefore, had he known that He was present, he would never have crucified the Lord of glory. But he hesitated: seeing Him shadowed by the weakness of flesh, swollen with pride he disdained to believe that the Most High God would have willed to stoop to so great a humiliation; and yet, beholding the power of His divinity through miracles, he marveled, confidently knowing that no one but God could do such things. Therefore, while anxiously wavering, he assailed Him with the three temptations by which he had overcome the first man. But the Lord moderated His replies, so that the devil withdrew from the very thing by which he wished to become certain, made more doubtful than before. Accordingly, inflaming the hearts of the Jews with fierce envy, he brought Him to the cross through his own members—yet divine grace so ordaining that he who had conquered through a tree should be conquered in turn by a tree [Col. 1071B].

Since the Son of God had come to expiate human sin, He stretched forth upon the cross hands fastened with nails, in order to wash the unclean hands which the first-formed man had extended to take the fruit of perdition. He was given the most bitter drink of gall and vinegar, in order to cleanse by so sharp a remedy the sweetness of taste which the first man had unlawfully experienced. Moreover, just as Eve was formed from the side of the man, so also holy Church was formed from Christ’s side, wounded by the lance upon the cross; its redemption—that is, blood and water—was poured forth from Christ’s body. And by dying He destroyed the death which the first man had brought about, and by rising He restored life.

He was able to do this because He was God, and because the devil, the inventor of death, found nothing of his own in Him. Therefore He could not be held by death, but by overcoming it He destroyed it. And, free not only from original sin but from every fault, He was the spotless lamb who bore the sins of the world and, made an offering for us, offered Himself to God the Father as an odor of sweetness. Isaiah spoke in many ways of His passion, saying: “Truly He Himself bore our infirmities and carried our sorrows; He was wounded for our iniquities, bruised for our crimes; by whose bruise we have been healed, and the Lord laid upon Him the iniquity of us all—He who was offered because He Himself willed it” (Isa. 53). Again: “Because of the crime [Col. 1072A] of my people I struck Him, and He bore the sins of many and prayed for transgressors that they might not perish” (ibid.). What could you seek more clearly than that what Isaiah proclaimed with his voice, Christ fulfilled in deed?

JUD. Certainly nothing could be clearer.

CHRIST. Now, moreover, I ask you to render me a judgment. If some powerful man had a servant, and that servant, while holding possessions from his master, sought by whatever artifice or treachery to bring it about that his master should die, what ought to be done with him?

JUD. Certainly, by a just judgment he would lose whatever he held from his master; and he himself, condemned as a traitor to a most shameful death, ought also to be deprived of life.

CHRIST. You have judged rightly. Therefore infer in like manner [Col. 1072B] that the devil, who had seduced the first man by deceitful fraud and made him subject to himself, and had held him captive for a very long time, afterward unjustly put to death Christ, his God and Lord. He therefore ought justly to lose the man whom he had possessed by God’s permission: thinking him, like other sinners, subject to sin, he did not hesitate to kill Him. But after he had killed Him, he was captured, held, and bound by the One who was free from every sin; and he who had once conquered was in turn conquered and bound by man.

Thus the devil acted like a fish in the water which, while greedily swallowing the iron in order to gulp down the bait, is suddenly caught and held by the hook, dying, mortally pierced. For he mortally pierced himself when, striking the human body of the Son of God, [Col. 1072C] he incurred such great sacrileges by offending against the divinity. And he lost the prey which he had taken from paradise, because Christ, breaking down the gates of hell and shattering the iron bars, powerfully rescued the souls of the saints and, restoring them to paradise now opened, placed them in eternal blessedness.

Moreover, in order to give us hope of resurrection, He rose from death on the third day and, going before us as our head and beginning, ascended into heaven, where by a wondrous ordering He placed our lowliness at the right hand of God the Father, thereby granting all believers hope of ascent. From there also He will come for judgment, when He will repay each according to his merit, sending the wicked into eternal fire but the good into eternal life—which may He who made it grant to us. Amen.

This work was faithfully transcribed from an ancient manuscript of the library of Châlons by Father Robert Desgyves, regular canon of the Gallican Congregation, provost of the Greater House of God at Beauvais.

IN THE YEAR OF THE LORD 1124: CALIXTUS II, ROMAN PONTIFF

[Col. 1073]

HISTORICAL NOTICE

(Mansi, *Councils*, XXI)

[Col. 1073A] Calixtus II of that name, son of William, Count of Burgundy, kinsman of the Emperor Henry, and therefore, as the *Chronicle of Monte Cassino* says, sprung from royal stock, was energetic in secular affairs and exceptionally learned in ecclesiastical matters. On the third day after Gelasius’s death, by the unanimous consent of the entire Roman clergy and people, he was elected, at Cluny in Gaul, from Guido, Archbishop of Vienne, as most worthy pontiff, though unwilling—as he himself testifies in a letter to Adalbert, Archbishop of Mainz, quoted by the chronicler of Ursperg—in the year of the Lord 1119, on the Kalends of February, during the reign of Henry V, King of Germany and emperor, the fourth of that name.

Pandulphus relates this concerning his election in Baronius:

> “He was elected Pope Calixtus by the cardinals who, after Gelasius had been buried at Cluny, had come from the city into France with him, while he was still Archbishop of Vienne. Repeatedly protesting that he was unworthy, he resisted in every possible way, because many still considered it uncertain [Col. 1073B] whether an election of this kind would be ratified at Rome. For that reason he scarcely consented to be clothed in the red mantle until messengers had returned from Rome and confirmed the election canonically and lawfully, orally and by letters, through Lord Peter, then vicar and Bishop of Porto; through all the cardinals; through Lord Peter Leonis—for this man had labored exceedingly in the matter because of his son, the cardinal-deacon Peter Leonis, who had chiefly carried it through in France—through the prefect and consuls, and through the clergy and people.”

Sugerius, in his *Life of Louis*, thus recounts what had been divinely foreshown to him in a vision concerning his election:

> “When, on the preceding night, he had seen in a dream—by an omen apt enough though unknown—a moon, deposited beneath a cloak, entrusted to him by a mighty person, lest the cause of the Church should be endangered by the passing of the Apostolic See, he was elected supreme pontiff by the Roman Church which was present; and he perceived more clearly the truth of the vision.”

Events made this ever more plain.
