For the long war stirred up concerning investitures, which had long and grievously wearied and torn the Church, was at last, when the emperor yielded, most happily suppressed by Pope Calixtus. After the absent cardinals had approved the election by letter, and after he had solemnly dedicated the church of Saint Maurus the Confessor, to which the bodies of Saints Anthony and Constantinian had been transferred from the monastery of Monte Cassino, he returned from Cluny to Rome and was honorably received by the clergy, senate, and Roman people.

“Afterward,” says the historian of Tyre (*Book* XII, ch. 8), “having gained the favor of the divine Emperor Henry, to whom he was related, and relying on his assistance, he departed for Italy with the cardinals and the whole curia. At the city of Sutri, adjoining Rome, he violently seized his rival and heresiarch Burdinus, the schismatic antipope. He also sent him, seated on a camel and clothed in a bearskin, to the monastery of Monte Cassino [Cava], which is known to lie near Salerno, with great disgrace; there he was compelled, until extreme old age, to live a monastic life according to the rule of the place.”

The author of the *Chronicle of Monte Cassino*, in chapter 70 and several following chapters of Book IV, recounts all the benefactions and privileges which he had conferred or adjudicated upon the monastery of Monte Cassino. Among other things, he says that Calixtus gathered an army of Normans and besieged, captured, and banished to the fortress of the monastery of Monte Cassino—which the abbot of that monastery had built—the schismatic antipope whom he calls the heresiarch Maurice, in the city of Sutri, to which the false pontiff had fled. The chronicler of Ursperg adds that the same antipope, intercepted by the Roman army and subjected to many insults and mockeries by the populace, was protected by Pope Calixtus’s authority from further injury and banished to perform penance.

Pandulphus, who witnessed these events, gives the following fuller account:

> “Meanwhile Burdinus, at Sutri near Rome, did not cease to persecute the Church, plunder pilgrims, heap curses upon the pope and others, and do whatever else of that kind he could, both personally and through others. Then the pope, now made fully secure on every side, prepared a great army and sent John of Crema, Cardinal of Saint Chrysogonus, ahead with it against Burdinus at Sutri; he himself followed immediately. At last they assembled at Sutri. The battle was fiercely fought; Burdinus was defeated and captured, brought forth, however, mounted upon a camel.”

A Vatican manuscript asserts that the people of Sutri, when their walls were being shaken, surrendered Burdinus to the soldiers, who exposed him to such ridicule [Col. 1074C]. First of all, they assailed him with blasphemies, crying aloud: “Accursed one, accursed one! Through you such a grievous scandal has come.” Others added: “You are the one who attempted to divide Christ’s tunic and presumed to tear apart Catholic unity.” Then a camel was prepared instead of a tall horse; dressed in the shaggy skin of a wether instead of a red mantle, he was set crosswise upon the camel, and the camel’s tail was put into his hands as a bridle. Thus he was led into the city as an example to others, lest anyone thereafter dare attempt similar things. From there he was first taken to the fortress of Fumone, and then transferred to the monastery of Cava for penance; but heedlessly he persisted in his rebellion [in all things].

Sugerius the abbot, himself an author of this period, affirms the same. He likewise recounts the tyranny of that antipope while he remained at Sutri; and, lest anything necessary to the triumph over the beast exalted by the emperor be omitted, he records matters passed over by other writers as follows:

> “The Romans, favoring both the nobility and generosity of Pope Calixtus, captured the schismatic Burdinus, intruded by the emperor, seated at Sutri and compelling those passing to the thresholds of the apostles to bend the knee. They placed the crooked antipope—indeed, antichrist—crosswise upon the crooked animal, a camel, clothed in raw, indeed bloodstained, goatskins; and, avenging the dishonor of God’s Church, led him through the middle of the city along the royal road, so that the matter might be more publicly proclaimed. At the request of Lord Pope Calixtus, they condemned him to perpetual imprisonment, held captive in the mountains of Campania near Saint Benedict. And to preserve the memory of so great a punishment, they depicted him trampled beneath the feet of the lord pope in the chamber of the palace.”

This is Sugerius in his *Life of Louis*.

The same Pope Calixtus, by the thunderbolt of excommunication, in the councils of Reims, the Lateran, and others convened by his own authority and that of his predecessor, compelled Henry [Col. 1076A] V to restore to the Church every right of investing bishops. Thus, through this pope’s agency, the most desired peace between Church and Empire was at last established, about the fiftieth year after the immense conflict between Gregory VII and Henry IV had arisen over the conferral of benefices. The elections of bishops and abbots, which emperors and kings had usurped, were restored to clergy and monks; and therefore he is depicted holding an image of peace in his hand. Possevino.

After these brilliantly accomplished deeds, the pope, most deserving of the Church, illustrious through many eminent constitutions recounted in Gratian’s *Decree* and through a certain work on the Apostle Saint James which he published, departed to the Lord on the Ides of December, in the year of the Lord 1124, after administering the pontifical office for five years, ten months, and thirteen days. After his death, as Otto of Freising testifies, he was honored with this epitaph:

[Col. 1076B]

> Behold Calixtus, honor of his homeland, glory of the Empire:  
> He condemns wicked Burdinus and restores peace.

Baronius gives further details from Pandulphus.

[Col. 1075]

SECOND NOTICE

(Ciaconius, *Lives and Deeds of the Popes*, p. 382.)

When Gelasius II died at Cluny, the six cardinals immediately considered the election of a new pope who might, by his authority, provide for the Roman Church, then afflicted by a great schism. They feared that if the vacancy of the see were prolonged, the Church might suffer some notable [Col. 1075C] harm. They therefore sought to choose as Roman pontiff someone endowed with nobility of birth, wealth, the favor of princes, authority among all people, virtue, prudence, and skill in affairs—someone who would establish peace in the Roman Church by removing the schism, free it from all the disturbances by which it had been harassed for nearly fifty years, and most steadfastly oppose the Emperor Henry and the false pope.

The arrival of Guido, Archbishop of Vienne, drew them to this view. They fixed their eyes and thoughts upon him as most worthy of so great a priesthood and as one in whom those qualifications that I have enumerated above were found. For besides being of most noble birth—being the son of William and brother of Stephen, princes of Burgundy, and maternal uncle of Baldwin, Count of Flanders—he was also related in the nearest degree of affinity to the kings of France and England, and even to the emperor himself. He was likewise distinguished in all the affairs I have enumerated above; and he conducted himself excellently in the ecclesiastical legation through Gaul entrusted to him by Paschal II. While all the bishops were afraid, he was the first to publish the anathema pronounced by Paschal II against the emperor; and, when a council had been assembled in Gaul, he separated almost all the bishops of Gaul from him.

Consecration and coronation of Pope Calixtus II.

Because of his most distinguished achievements, Guido, on the day after he arrived at Cluny, having been summoned there by Gelasius II, was proclaimed supreme pontiff—though unwilling, wholly reluctant, and resisting—by the votes of all the cardinals, chiefly through the initiative of Peter, son of Peter Leonis, cardinal-deacon, on the Kalends of February in the year of the Lord 1119, at the monastery of Cluny in Gaul. For he feared that the cardinals who were at Rome would not approve the election because it had been made without their knowledge. Therefore he would not allow himself to be clothed in the red mantle or use the remaining pontifical regalia until he learned that his election had been ratified by those cardinals who [Col. 1076] were at Rome.

For this purpose, on the first day of his pontificate, he had sent from Gaul the cardinal-deacon Roscemannus to the City. Roscemannus returned to Cluny with Roman envoys, bringing the cardinals’ consent in writing. [Col. 1076C] On learning this, the pope was consecrated and crowned by Lambert of Ostia and others on the day before the Ides of October of that same year, 1119. He chose to be called Calixtus II because his consecration was celebrated on the feast-day of that holy pontiff. During the reign of Henry V, he sat for five years, ten months, and thirteen days. Before his pontificate Calixtus had been a monk of the monastery of Fuley, as Guido, a Cistercian monk, and Peter Burgianus write in the *Monastic History*.

Because Calixtus II had been chosen with the greatest care at Cluny, he gave Pons and his successors, the heads of that monastery, a ring and ordained that henceforth they should exercise the office of Roman cardinal, as remained written in their chronicle for remembrance. No one had stood more firmly for Paschal II against the emperor; no one had been readier to condemn the instigator’s treachery. At the council held at Vienne on the Rhône, he had hurled upon the emperor a sentence of anathema, as is shown by his letter to Paschal, which still survives. Yet afterward no one was dearer to him: changing his will, he both gave peace to the pope and yielded the tyrannical practice of appointing bishops and abbots.

Awaiting the announcement of this peace and the consent of the Italian people, Calixtus held a synod attended by 450 bishops and abbots. By them ecclesiastical discipline was almost restored. This synod had been summoned at Reims by his predecessor Gelasius; Calixtus II held it on the Kalends of November. At it, the then-rising destructive heresy was condemned—the heresy which denied the Eucharist, infant baptism, holy orders, and lawful marriages, and, through hatred of clerics, took from them temporal goods, tithes, and offerings. At least there was discussion there concerning the establishment of peace between ecclesiastical and secular persons, in the year 1120.

After arranging in Gaul those matters necessary for preserving the condition of the Church, [Col. 1077A] the pope came to Italy. He was received as though some divine being had descended to earth: the blessing of concord deeply entered human hearts, the people came forth to meet him, and he entered the city amid honor, all rejoicing both for the pope and for the Roman city because they saw that he would be the author of tranquillity and peace. He also enrolled among the saints Gerard, a citizen of Piacenza and deceased bishop of Potenza.

When affairs at Rome had been settled to his satisfaction, the pope departed for Benevento, where all the princes immediately assembled, as was customary, to greet the pope—especially William, Duke of Apulia; Jordan, Count of Campania; Arnulf of Ariola; and Robert, Count of Lorotella: distinguished men and, without dispute, readily the leading men of that part of Italy. They also promised, under oath, that they would always remain under the pope’s authority.

Meanwhile, while the Bishop of Palestrina, Gelasius’s legate, [Col. 1077B] held assemblies of German bishops at Cologne and Fritzlar, he declared in both places that Henry had been expelled from the fellowship of the devout. Moved by this, the princes of Germany summoned an assembly at Würzburg and called Henry there to answer, clearly announcing that if he did not come, they would depose him from the kingdom in his absence. Henry hastened to return from Italy to Germany and, moved by the unanimous will of his followers, allowed an assembly to be held at Tribur, declaring that he would there answer all charges brought against him. When papal legates summoned another council at Reims, he also promised that he would meet there in order to be reconciled with the Church.

The pope himself presided at that council in the year 1119, on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of September. Among other matters, he ordered Henry to renounce the conferral of bishoprics. Hearing this, Henry requested time in which he might consult with his princes about the matter. Thus peace was left unmade, and Calixtus confirmed the decrees issued by his predecessors on that question.

After Calixtus’s arrival in Italy, the false pontiff Gregory had kept himself at Sutri, surrounded by the protection of certain counts. Whether blinded by greed or puffed up by insolence, these men made the roads dangerous with robberies and plundered those traveling toward Rome. Therefore Calixtus, inflamed with zeal, gathered an army and sent Cardinal John of Crema to besiege Sutri. But a siege proved unnecessary. Gregory was suddenly surrendered by the people of Sutri and finally confined in the monastery of Cava near Salerno, where he met his death. The emperor’s envoys were graciously received by the pope, and in the following year, 1122, they brought back legates *a latere* of the Apostolic See with unrestricted mandates for establishing peace.

Thus peace and concord were made, in the fiftieth year, more or less, after the great discord between Gregory VII and Henry IV had arisen over the conferral of bishoprics. Elections of bishops and abbots, which emperors and kings had hitherto usurped, were restored to clergy and [Col. 1077D] monks. The legates of Pope Calixtus, whose memory deserves enduring record on account of the settlement, were Lambert of Bologna, Bishop of Ostia and afterward Pope Honorius II; Saxo, a priest of the Counts of Anagni; and Gregory of Papareschi, a Roman and afterward Pope Innocent II, then a cardinal-deacon. A memorial of this event, together with a painting, still exists in the entrance to the popes’ chamber at the Lateran, where this inscription appears:

> Behold Calixtus, honor of his homeland, glory of the Empire:  
> He condemns wicked Burdinus and restores peace.

By their authority an assembly was then summoned at Würzburg for the feast of Saint Peter. Since it could not then be completed, it was transferred to Worms for the sixteenth day before the Kalends of October. There, for seven successive days, conflicting opinions were debated among the princes concerning the settlement of concord; and because the zeal of the opposing parties still remained, the affair scarcely seemed likely to reach a satisfactory conclusion. Then Henry said: “Why,” he said, “do you contend so greatly over a matter that is not necessary, when I am prepared to obey the authority of Holy Church and freely relinquish the right of ecclesiastical appointments, which alone divides the concord? I am also prepared to restore the towns which have been taken from the Church either by me or by my father.” When the papal legates and bishops heard this statement, they immediately received it eagerly with the highest praise and urged him to remain firm in his resolve.

Accordingly, on the ninth day before the Kalends of October, he, together with the entire army which had been infected by the contagion of excommunication, was received into the communion and faith of the Church. With the greatest humility he surrendered into the hands of the Bishop of Ostia the right of appointing bishops and abbots, which he had resolved never to relinquish; and in a written charter he made the following oath:

> “I, Henry, by the grace of God Augustus, Emperor of the Romans, for the love of God and of the holy Roman Church and of Pope Calixtus, and for the salvation of my soul, relinquish to God, to His holy apostles Peter and Paul, and to the holy Catholic Church every investiture by ring and staff, and I grant that election and free consecration may take place in all churches. The possessions and regalian rights of Blessed Peter, taken away from the holy Roman Church from the beginning of this discord to the present day, whether in the time of my father or in my own, which I possess, I restore; those which I do not possess, I will aid in restoring individually. And I grant true peace to Calixtus, to the holy Roman Church, and to all who are or have been on his side; and wherever the holy Roman Church asks for assistance, I will assist in good faith.”

From the other side, the papal legates, on behalf of the pope, granted true peace to him and to all who were or had been on his side during this conflict, and [granted] that the privileges concerning the election, that is, of the bishops and abbots of the German kingdom, should be carried out in his presence without simony or any impropriety. After these documents had been read outside the city, on the plain beside the Rhine, because of the immense multitude of people who had assembled, and after very great cries from all and thanks given to Almighty God, the legate celebrated the divine service with great ceremony; and, offering the kiss of peace and the holy Eucharist, he received Henry into the favor of the Roman Church.

Thereafter, on the feast of St Martin, Henry held another assembly at Bamberg; with the consent of those who had not been present at the Council of Worms, he sent legates to Rome to the pope with exceedingly ample gifts and rendered solemn obedience to the pontiff. Rejoicing at the news that concord had been restored, the pope suddenly convened at the Lateran a numerous and most great council, of nearly a thousand bishops and abbots. The following year, 1123, when the legates had returned to the city with the documents of peace, he summoned 997 bishops and abbots; by their authority he confirmed all that had been done at Worms by his legates. Thus at last an end was imposed upon the long-standing discord, pernicious both in itself and in its example, between pope and emperor. [Col. 1078C–D]

Pope Calixtus II made several ordinations of cardinals, of which only three are found: the first in the second year of his pontificate, in December, in the year 1120, in which nine cardinals were created; the latter in the second year of his pontificate, in which he created one; and thirteen cardinals in the fourth year.

In the year of the Lord’s Nativity 1124, at Rome in the Lateran patriarchal residence, on the Ides of December, in the fifth year, tenth month, and thirteenth day of his pontificate, Pope Calixtus II died, deserving well of God and humankind. His body was buried in the basilica of St Saviour, called the Constantinian [basilica]. The see was vacant for only one day.

[Col. 1079]

# LIFE OF POPE CALIXTUS II, BY PANDULPH OF PISA

(Muratori, *Rerum Italicarum Scriptores*, vol. III, part I, p. 418.)

Calixtus, also called Guy, a Frenchman by nationality, tracing his line of kinship from the kings of Germany, France, and England, presided over the Roman Church for five years and … months. After Pope Gelasius had been buried at Cluny, he was elected pope, under the name Calixtus, by the cardinals who had come from the City into France with Gelasius, while he was archbishop of Vienne. Repeatedly declaring himself unworthy, he resisted by every means, because many considered it uncertain whether such an act would be held valid at Rome. For this reason he scarcely consented even to put on the red cloak, until messengers returned from Rome and, through Lord Peter, then vicar-bishop; through all the cardinals; through Lord Peter Leonis—for he had labored exceedingly in the affair on behalf of his deacon-son Peter, son of Peter Leonis, who had handled France’s cause above all; through the prefect and consuls; and through clergy and people, confirmed by word of mouth and by letters that election itself as canonical and lawful.

When this had been done and very strongly established by the subscriptions of all, the pope was then solemnly consecrated in God’s name by Lambert, bishop of Ostia, and very many others. Together with all his followers he began his journey to Rome. He came into the province in which this same pope dedicated with great solemnity the church of St Julian, a cell of the monastery of Psalmodi. From there, by way of Saint-Gilles, he returned to Rome not long afterward, safe and sound. [Col. 1079A–B]

There he was received by the aforementioned Peter, vicar-bishop of Porto, the cardinals, all the clergy, and the people, with such glory and honor as no bishop in our times had ever received from Rome. Remaining there for some time, he summoned Cardinal Hugh from Benevento, for the same Lord Hugh held Benevento. Together with him and others he proceeded through Campania and the monastery of Cassino to Benevento itself, where he was received gloriously, almost as though he were in Rome.

Immediately there came to him Duke William of Apulia, the prince of the city of Capua, Count Jordan, Ralph of Airola [Note: [Col. 1079D] Papebroch: *Arcola*], Count Jordan of Ariano, Count Robert of Locotello, and innumerable others, who there did homage and swore fidelity to him. When these matters had been arranged, he soon returned to Rome by the coast.

Then, prompted by the Holy Spirit, he delegated to Emperor Henry in Germany Lambert, bishop of Ostia; Lord Saxo, cardinal-priest of St Stephen on the Caelian Hill; and Gregory, deacon of St Angelo, to restore peace to the sons of peace in kingdom and Church. But why say more? Rather, I wish to tell the whole matter in a word: the dispatched legates offered peace in writing, and, as the privilege preserved in the Lateran palace records, peace was both accepted from the emperor according to the pope’s wish and, with the Lord’s approval, established forever. [Col. 1079B–C]

After the legates had returned to the City, he again went down into Apulia. For Count Roger of Sicily—then count, but now king of Italy [Note: [Col. 1079D] Namely from the year 1130, when the antipope Anacletus granted him this title. Papebroch.]—had freely entered Calabria and Apulia, because Duke William of Apulia, intending to receive the daughter of the late Emperor Alexius of Constantinople, who was indeed later given to him in marriage, was staying at Byzantium; and, when he departed, he had entrusted to the lord pope the land which belonged to him.

While the aforementioned count was besieging the fortress in Calabria called Miteforis [Note: [Col. 1079D] Papebroch: perhaps *Nicefori*], the lord pope sent Lord Hugh the cardinal to him, that he might desist from the siege. The cardinal went and returned with the matter unaccomplished. The pope then rose against the count under an omen such as his relatives—“parents” in the text [Note: [Col. 1080D] Papebroch: “the Bari people”]—were afterwards, as we ourselves saw, to rise against him. For he lost nearly all the better cardinals whom he had in those times, as well as the great Cardinal Hugh, noble and energetic, dead along with not a few of his household; and at last Count Roger himself accomplished with the half-dead pope whatever he wished.

He returned to the City on a bed, escaped death, and in that year held the Lateran Council of 997 bishops or abbots, in which this man, sprung from royal stock, restored to the world a peace that had almost perished. [Col. 1079D–1080A]

He made very many ordinations in the City, of cardinals and bishops: first, when he ordained Lord Peter Leonis cardinal of St Mary in Trastevere, oil flowed; Lord Crescentius of Saints Peter and Marcellinus; Master Amicus of Holy Cross; Guy of St Balbina; Theobald of St Anastasia; Robert of St Clement; together with other cardinal-priests: Jonathan of Saints Cosmas and Damian; Matthew of St Adrian; Aymeric of St Mary the New; Angelo of St Mary in Domnica; Gregory [Note: [Col. 1080D] Papebroch: *Georgium*, George.], also called Tarquinius, of St Sergius; John Danferius, a nobleman of Salerno, of St Nicholas in the Tullian Prison; several subdeacons; and he promoted me, Pandulph, as far as the subdiaconate. He ordained countless clerics of lesser office.

No one ever saw him enter St Peter’s basilica without gifts, nor sing Mass there unless he had first assigned a gift. To preserve peace he ordered the towers of Cencius, of the Lady Good [Note: [Col. 1080D] Papebroch: “the House of Tyranny,” etc.], and of Iniquity to be demolished and not rebuilt there. He bought from Count Mortaldo stones of excellent strength above Rome and added them to the honor of St Peter. He gave St Peter many curtains and cloths, silver candlesticks, bells, pavements, landed estates, and hamlets; and he bestowed many benefactions upon other churches. He brought water back to the City, arranged mills with vineyards near the lake, built the church of St Nicholas in the palace, enlarged the chamber, and ordered it painted in a wonderful fashion, as appears today. [Col. 1080B–C]

Meanwhile Burdinus, at Sutri near Rome, did not cease to persecute the Church, rob pilgrims, heap curses upon the pope and others, and commit every other such act that he could, both personally and through others. The pope then, sufficiently strengthened and now secure on every side by the Lord’s will, prepared a great army. He sent John of Cremona, cardinal of St Chrysogonus, ahead to Sutri against Burdinus; he himself immediately followed. At last they met at Sutri; battle was fought intensely; Burdinus was defeated and captured, and was brought in riding on a camel.

With victory, the pope went against Godfrey of Lodi and Counts Rainald of Ceccano, rebels [Note: [Col. 1081A] Papebroch: “Counts Godfrey, Landus, and Rainald,” etc.]. Had not Count Ranulf of Airola intervened, the pope would have exacted from the traitors the justice they deserved. Yet the guardian of peace did not depart without peace: he ordered Burdinus confined in the monastery of Cava, returned to Rome, and dwelt in profound peace, generously providing for the poor. [Col. 1080C–D; 1081A]

The world rejoiced while the pope was prospering. But no power endures long; for the times of the old Octavian were now almost returning. Christ was then continually being born in the minds of the faithful [Note: [Col. 1082A] That is, Advent had begun. Papebroch.], when an unexpected fever arose and suddenly consumed the pope, and in this pope alone the head of us all fell to the ground. Without delay, having confessed and received the rites, amid the wailing of all he fell asleep in the Lord; and thus the father of peace departed together with peace itself. He was buried at the Lateran beside Lord Pope Paschal, on the feast of St Lucy the Virgin.

[Col. 1081]

# SHORT COMMENTARY OF HESSO THE SCHOOLMASTER ON THE NEGOTIATION OF PEACE BETWEEN POPE CALIXTUS II AND EMPEROR HENRY V, IN THE YEAR OF THE REDEEMER 1119; AND ON THE COUNCIL OF RHEIMS

(Gretser, *Opera*, vol. VI, p. 549.)

## TO THE READER

The Abbot of Ursperg, in his *Chronicle* under the year of the Redeemer 1119, where he speaks of the assembly at Tribur, writes as follows:

> Legates were also present, sent both by the Romans and by the Viennese—indeed, by various Churches—confirming the election of Lord Calixtus. When all our bishops had declared obedience to him and had approved the holding of the synod which he had announced for shortly after the feast of St Luke, the king himself promised that he would be present there for the reconciliation of the universal Church. The bishop of Châlons and the abbot of Cluny, meeting him at Strasbourg, obtained this from him by many arguments. Whoever wishes fully to learn the proceedings of that council may find them elegantly explained in the letters of a certain schoolmaster named Hesso: namely, how the king agreed to make concord between kingdom and priesthood; furthermore, how he did not appear in person at that council—at which the aforesaid Pope Calixtus II presided on the third day before the Kalends of November, surrounded by 426 Fathers before an innumerable multitude of clergy and people—yet made himself present nearby; how, after granting the pope’s legates an audience, he ultimately sought another truce because he needed a general conference with the princes concerning ecclesiastical investitures, which he was being so strongly compelled to relinquish; and finally, how the same Apostolic, while leaving concord between himself and the king untouched, confirmed the synodal decrees of his predecessors and vigorously added several others demanded by circumstances. Thus, after about twelve days, when the council had been duly concluded in the power of the Holy Spirit, he permitted all, strengthened by the apostolic blessing, to return home, each with joy.
>
> Not long afterwards, he himself turned toward Italy. It is incredible to recount with what rejoicing and what immense pomp he was received in Christ’s place, not only by all Rome, but also by every province through which he passed. From that time both he, now truly Apostolic, and Christ’s whole flock following him began to advance from day to day, until the party of Burdinus—whom some are accustomed to call “the idol”—was weakened daily and ceased striving against the Church. The disturbance and crime begun by the kingdom, however, did not at all cease.

Thus Ursperg. Consult Baronius under the year 1119.

Although peace and concord between priesthood and kingdom could not be established on this occasion, they were nevertheless established afterwards, in the year 1122, amid the great rejoicing of all good people. On this, see Baronius under the same year, vol. XII.

Moreover, the manuscript did not state Hesso’s name. Nevertheless, following Ursperg’s traces, we did not hesitate to place Hesso’s name at the head, since the things reported by Ursperg concerning Hesso’s composition agree exactly with this short commentary. The author of this account was an eyewitness of the events which he has collected in this narrative, as he himself testifies in its final words.

# SHORT COMMENTARY OF HESSO THE SCHOOLMASTER: HOW THE CAUSE BETWEEN KING HENRY AND LORD POPE CALIXTUS RECENTLY BEGAN AND PROCEEDED

The bishop of Châlons and the abbot of Cluny came to the king at Strasbourg, to negotiate with him concerning peace and concord between kingdom and priesthood. [Col. 1081B–1082B] When the king asked them counsel as to how he could accomplish this without diminishing his kingdom, the bishop answered, taking up his parable:

> “If, lord king, you desire to have true peace, you must utterly relinquish the investiture of bishoprics and abbeys. Yet, that you may know for certain that this involves no diminution of your kingdom, know that I was elected bishop in the kingdom of the Franks and received nothing from the king’s hand either before or after consecration. Nevertheless I render him faithful service in tribute, military service, tolls, and all matters belonging to the commonwealth, which had of old been granted by Christian kings to the Church of God, just as in your kingdom the bishops serve you, although by investing them until now you have incurred this discord—indeed, the sentence of anathema.”

To this the king, raising his hands, replied: “Come then; let it be so. I seek no more.”

The bishop then added: “If, therefore, you are willing to relinquish investitures, restore the possessions of the churches and of those who have labored for the Church, and grant them true peace, we shall labor, with the Lord’s help, to put an end to this contention.”

After consulting his advisers, the king promised to carry out all these things, if he found good faith and justice with the lord pope and if he and his party received true peace and the possessions they had lost because of this *werra* [war]. Having heard this, the bishop requested assurance concerning the stated articles, both that their labor might not be useless and that they might more readily incline the lord pope to carry out the peace. Then the king, with his own hand and under the witness of Christian faith, confirmed in the hand of the bishop and abbot that he would carry out the aforesaid articles without fraud. [Col. 1083A–B]

Afterwards, the bishop of Lausanne, the count palatine, and the other clerics and laymen with him confirmed the same in the same manner. Having received this assurance, the bishop and abbot met the lord pope at Paris and faithfully reported what they had seen and heard. Applauding them, the lord pope replied: “Would that it had already been done, if it could be done without fraud.”

Immediately, after taking counsel with the bishops and cardinals, he sent them back to the king, together with the bishop of Ostia and Cardinal Gregory from his own side, so that they might reconsider the aforesaid articles more carefully, confirm them in writings from each side, and, if he wished to execute them as he had promised, designate before the end of the council the day on which they would be fulfilled.

They met him between Verdun and Metz and reported that the lord pope would gladly receive him if he wished to perform what he had promised. The king, apparently delighted, again confirmed there with his own hand—in the hand of the bishop of Ostia, Cardinal Gregory, the bishop of Châlons, and the abbot—what he had first confirmed at Strasbourg in the hands of those previously named: namely, that on the coming Friday, the ninth day before the Kalends of November, he would faithfully and without any fraud perform before the lord pope at Mouzon the articles contained in the following document. Afterwards Duke Welf, Count Berengar, the count palatine, Count William, and many other bishops, clerics, and laymen swore the same. He also required our party to bind themselves to him in the same fashion: if the matter did not fail through him, the lord pope would on the same day fulfill what was contained in his document. The written agreement was as follows. [Col. 1083C–D]

> “I, Henry, by the grace of God august emperor of the Romans, for love of God, of blessed Peter, and of Lord Pope Calixtus, relinquish every investiture of all churches and grant true peace to all who, since this discord began, have been or are in the *werra* [war] for the Church. I restore such possessions of the churches and of all who have labored for the Church as I possess; and I shall faithfully help them recover those which I do not possess. If any dispute should arise from this, matters ecclesiastical shall be settled by canonical judgment, and matters secular by secular judgment.”

Likewise, the document of the lord pope:

> “I, Calixtus II, by the grace of God Catholic bishop of the Roman Church, grant true peace to Henry, august emperor of the Romans, and to all who have been or are for him against the Church. I restore such of their possessions as they lost because of this *werra* [war] and as I possess; and I shall faithfully help them recover those which I do not possess. If any dispute should arise from this, matters ecclesiastical shall be settled by canonical judgment, and matters secular by secular judgment.” [Col. 1084A]

Having thus received assurance, they hurried back to the lord pope at Rheims. Before the council they reported what they had done and what they had received from the king and his party, while also indicating the day and place for the conference.

The lord pope, sitting at Rheims in the general council on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of November, began among other matters as follows:

> “Lords, Fathers, and brothers, this is the cause for which we have summoned you to council from such remote regions. You know how long the Church has struggled against various heresies; and just as Simon Magus, by the judgment of the Holy Spirit, was removed from the Church of God and perished through blessed Peter, to whom the Lord especially said: ‘I have prayed for you, Peter, that your faith may not fail; and when you have turned again, strengthen your brothers’ [Luke 22], so even to our own times he does not cease, through his vicars, the followers of Simon, to attack and root out from the Church of God that same [heresy].
>
> “I too, whatever I may be, although unworthy, am his vicar. With God’s help I desire, by our counsel and aid, to remove by every means from the Church of God the simoniacal heresy, which has been revived against the Church of God especially through investitures. Therefore, if it please you, hear more carefully from our brothers who carried words of concord between us and the aforementioned German king the course of the affair; and let each of you, according to his capacity, consider with wiser counsel what we must do in these matters, since the cause is a common one.” [Col. 1084A–B]

The lord pope then instructed the bishop of Ostia to explain the course of the affair in Latin to the whole council. When the bishop of Ostia had set it forth wisely, the bishop of Châlons, again by the lord pope’s command, explained the same matter in the native language to clergy and laypeople. When this had been completed, he proposed many articles on that day and the following day, and postponed their complete execution until the end of the council.

On the following day, when he had sat in the council of bishops to determine whether the lord pope should proceed on the appointed day to the conference for arranging peace and test in person whether that man acted sincerely, the lord pope continued near the end of the council that day:

> “Lords, Fathers, and brothers, you know how long our mother, holy Church, struggled in our fathers against the simoniacal heresy, especially that which occurs through investitures. Since it has pleased Almighty God in our days to offer peace to his Church, and since the approaching day of conference compels us tomorrow to go to that place, we earnestly ask you patiently to await our return and, if God gives us peace, to announce the common joy to the whole world.
>
> “But if—God avert it!—the adversary should attempt to deal deceitfully with us, we shall return to you quickly. And just as we desire to confirm with you and through you the agreement of peace, if it is made, so, if he proves faithless, we shall attempt, by the judgment of the Holy Spirit and yours, to wield the sword of blessed Peter against the contriver of fraud.”

Having imposed this under the obligation of obedience upon archbishops, bishops, and abbots, he also ordered them meanwhile, and especially on the day of the conference, to offer psalms, prayers, and spiritual sacrifices to God, and to proceed barefoot in procession from the greater church of Rheims to the church of Blessed Remigius. [Col. 1084C–D]

Thus, the council being dismissed in the meantime, on Wednesday the lord pope went out to the place of conference; on Thursday he arrived with many people, only with the greatest difficulty. On Friday, summoning into his chamber archbishops, bishops, abbots, and the other wise men, many of whom he had brought with him, he had both written agreements read before them all. When the king’s document had been read, the bishops began to examine it more carefully, especially the clause that said, “I relinquish every investiture of all churches,” saying:

> “If the king is acting straightforwardly, these words suffice. But if he attempts to quibble under this clause, they seem to us to require definition, lest perhaps he seek to claim for himself the ancient possessions of the churches, or again invest bishops from those same possessions.”

Likewise, in the lord pope’s document they examined more carefully the clause that said, “I grant true peace to the king and to all who were or are with him in this land,” lest they understand in the granting of peace something more than restoration to communion with the Church, and lest, under this phrase, the Church be compelled to receive people whom it could not endure without grave offense, whether they had been imposed upon lawful pastors or canonically deposed.

Therefore, after all matters had been carefully examined, the bishop of Ostia, Cardinal John, the bishop of Viviers, the bishop of Châlons, the abbot of Cluny, and many others with them were sent to the king’s camp, carrying the documents in their hands. When they reached the camp, they displayed the writings and defined the articles as had been determined by the common counsel of all. [Col. 1085A–B]

When the king heard this, at first he utterly denied that he had promised any of these things. Then the bishop of Châlons, inflamed with zeal for God and girded with the sword of God’s word, replied for them all:

> “If, lord, you wish to deny the written document which we hold in our hands and the definition which you have heard, I am prepared, under the testimony of the religious men who were between you and me, to swear upon the relics of the saints or upon Christ’s Gospel that you confirmed all these things in my hand and that I received them under this definition.”

When the testimony of all convicted him, he was at last compelled to confess what he had previously denied. Yet he complained bitterly against them that, although he had promised it on their advice, he could not carry it out without diminishing his kingdom.

The bishop answered him:

> “In our promises, lord king, you will find us faithful in every respect. The lord pope does not seek in any way to diminish the condition of the empire or the crown of the kingdom, as certain sowers of discord falsely allege. Indeed, he publicly declares that in the rendering of military service and in every other matter in which they had been accustomed to serve you and your predecessors, they should serve you by every means.
>
> “But if you think the imperial condition diminished because you will no longer be permitted to sell bishoprics, you ought rather to have hoped for the increase and advancement of your kingdom, if you cast aside, for love of God, those things which are contrary to the Lord God.” [Col. 1085B–C]

As he could not answer these points, he began to speak more mildly and sought a truce until morning, saying that he wished during that night to confer with the princes concerning the affair, bend their hearts, if possible, toward carrying out the promise, and report one way or the other at first light.

After this, his party began to confer with ours regarding the manner of absolution and reception. It seemed harsh to them—indeed intolerable—that their lord should come barefoot for absolution, according to the custom imposed on others. Accommodating them, our party replied that they would work by every means to have the lord pope receive him shod, as privately as possible.

The conference ended that day with these words, and our party returned to the lord pope, reporting what they had found. The lord pope, as though now despairing of peace, was making energetic arrangements to return in the morning to the brothers whom he had left at Rheims. But, by the counsel of the count of Troyes and many others, he was compelled to remain in the same place on Saturday until about the sixth hour, in order to stop every mouth of his adversaries and remove from everyone grounds for reproach. [Col. 1085D]

At first light the bishop of Châlons and the abbot of Cluny were again sent to the king’s camp to hear his answer concerning the truce granted. When they arrived, the bishop, as he had done the previous day, presented the truth of the document with the attestation of an oath, saying:

> “Yesterday, lord king, we could rightly have departed from you, because on the appointed day we were prepared both to receive your promise and to fulfill ours. But since, in seeking a truce, you postponed matters until this day, we do not wish so great a good to fail through us because of the interval of a single night. If today you are willing to fulfill your promise, the lord pope is still prepared to carry out by every means what he promised you through us.”

Then the angry king again began to seek a truce until he could hold a general conference with the princes of the kingdom, without whose counsel he did not dare to relinquish investitures.

The bishop replied: “Since, by repeatedly seeking a truce, you evade fulfilling what you promised, there is no further business between us and you. I shall return to the lord pope.”

Thus he returned without taking leave and reported what he had found. The lord pope immediately moved with his followers in great haste to another castle of the count of Troyes. The king sent a messenger to the count, earnestly asking him to detain the lord pope there on Sunday, promising that he would by every means do on Monday what he had so often denied. When this was reported to the lord pope, he gave this brief reply:

> “Brothers, for the desire of peace I have done what I have never heard to have been done by our predecessors. I left a general synod assembled and many brothers almost forsaken; coming with great labor to this man, I found in him none of the things of peace. Therefore I shall by no means wait longer for him, but shall return as quickly as I can to our brothers and to the council. If, however, God gives us true peace in the council or after the council, I shall be prepared to receive and embrace it.” [Col. 1086A–B]

Accordingly, on Sunday he departed from that place before daybreak and hurried with such speed to Rheims that, after completing twenty leagues, he celebrated Mass at Rheims that same day; at this Mass he consecrated the bishop-elect of Liège as bishop. On Monday, weakened by excessive exertion, he could scarcely attend the council. He had his departure and return and the course of the affair explained to the council, and remained silent that day. On Tuesday, still held by illness, he could not sit in the council. But on Wednesday, about the third hour, he came to the council. That day until the ninth hour he received the complaints of many persons and dealt with many articles. From the ninth hour onward, wishing to finish the council that day, he had the synodal decrees brought forward and read. [Col. 1086B–C]

# DECREES OF THE SYNOD

What has been established by the enactments of the holy Fathers concerning the depravity of simony, we likewise confirm by the judgment of the Holy Spirit and the authority of the apostolic see. Therefore, if anyone sells or buys, either personally or through any subordinate person, a bishopric, abbey, deanery, priesthood, archdeaconry, provostship, prebend, or any ecclesiastical benefice, promotion, ordination, consecration, dedication of churches, clerical tonsure, seat in choir, or any ecclesiastical office, both seller and buyer shall incur the penalty of forfeiting his rank, office, or benefice; and unless he repents, pierced by the sword of anathema, he shall be cast out by every means from the Church of God which he has injured. [Col. 1086C–D]

We utterly forbid the investiture of bishoprics and abbeys by a lay hand. Therefore, whoever among laypersons shall henceforth presume to invest [another] shall be subject to the punishment of anathema. Moreover, whoever has been invested shall utterly lose the rank in which he was invested, without any hope of recovery.

We decree that all possessions of churches, granted to them through the liberality of kings, the gifts of princes, or the offerings of any faithful persons, shall remain forever secure and inviolable. If anyone removes, seizes, or holds them by tyrannical power, he shall, according to that decree of blessed Symmachus, be struck with perpetual anathema.

No bishop, priest, or anyone at all of the clergy shall leave ecclesiastical ranks or benefices to anyone as though by hereditary right. We also add this command: that absolutely no payment be demanded for receiving baptism, chrism, holy oil, burial, or the visitation or anointing of the sick. We wholly forbid priests, deacons, and subdeacons cohabitation with concubines and wives. If any are found in such relationships, they shall be deprived of ecclesiastical offices and benefices; and if they do not even then correct their impurity, they shall be deprived of Christian communion. [Col. 1086D–1087A]

After many decrees against the simoniacal heresy had been read and unanimously approved and confirmed, they came to the decree by which the investiture of churches was forbidden to laymen. It contained the following:

> “We forbid by every means the investiture of all churches and ecclesiastical possessions by a lay hand.”

When this was read, such a murmur from certain clerics and many laypersons sounded through the council that they dragged the day on until evening in grave contention. For it seemed to them that, under this clause, the lord pope was seeking to curtail or take away tithes and other ecclesiastical benefices which laypersons had held from ancient times. The lord pope, therefore, satisfying all parties, postponed ending the council that day, so that on the following day he might modify the decree by common counsel and confirm it, together with the provisions that followed, by the unanimous approval and authority of all. [Col. 1087A–B]

On Thursday he came to the council to carry out what he had proposed. He devoutly began the hymn of the Holy Spirit. When it had been sung with deep feeling by all, he, kindled like the flame of an invisible fire, began to speak in a fiery tongue concerning the Holy Spirit and spoke wonderfully, teaching that he is the highest good, the fountain of wisdom and understanding and of all learning, the bond of charity, unity, and concord. After ranging at length over each of these points, to the admiration of all, he finally came to the issue, saying:

> “Dearest brothers, we know that your labor, by which you took care to come to meet us from such distant regions for the common liberty of our mother holy Church, has pleased God and the Holy Spirit, in whose power and sanctification we are one in Christ. And because it has pleased the Holy Spirit and us, it has displeased the hostile spirit, who has sought and found fellow-workers for his malice, by every means to disturb the concord of your brotherhood.
>
> “For what shall we say, brothers? If you came, summoned to a council, with such labor and expense, and on returning to your regions can take nothing back because you refuse to listen to us. For, according to the Truth who says, ‘Whoever sins against the Holy Spirit, if he persists in that sin, shall not be forgiven either in this age or in the age to come’ [Matthew 12; Luke 12], and, ‘Whoever hears you hears me, and whoever rejects you rejects me’ [Luke 10]—
>
> “We know also that when the Lord Jesus set before his disciples: ‘Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you have no life in yourselves’ [John 6], many were scandalized and turned back [ibid.], and no longer followed him. So too, when yesterday we proposed certain measures for the liberty of the Church, certain unbelievers were scandalized. Therefore we too say with apostolic authority: ‘If the unbeliever departs, let him depart’ [1 Corinthians 7], and let him give place to the faithful to deliberate on what belongs to the Church and is necessary for the Church’s liberty.
>
> “But to you, who hold in the Church of God the place and office of the apostles, we say what the Lord said to the Twelve: ‘Do you also wish to go away?’ [John 6].” [Col. 1087B–1088B]

When he had spoken with such force, he so moved the hearts of all and silenced the voices of those who objected that not one person thereafter dared open his mouth against the synodal decrees that were read. Nevertheless, the lord pope moderated, by sounder counsel, the decree from which the murmur had arisen, and had it read to the council in this form:

> “We forbid by every means the investiture of bishoprics and abbeys by a lay hand.”

When this pleased all, they confirmed it, along with everything else that had been read, by the judgment of the Holy Spirit and ecclesiastical authority.

At last 427 candles were brought in, lit, and distributed one to each person; the bishops and abbots holding staffs were instructed to rise, all holding their candles. When they had risen, the names of many persons whom the lord pope had particularly proposed to excommunicate were read aloud. First among those named were King Henry and Burdinus, invader of the Roman Church; and these, before all others and together with many others, were solemnly excommunicated [Col. 1088C]. The lord pope also, by apostolic authority, released from their oath of fealty to the king all who had sworn it to him, unless perhaps he should repent and make satisfaction to the Church of God. Finally, when these matters had been duly completed, he absolved them all and made the sign over them by the authority of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit; and thus allowed each to return home, and so brought the council to an end. What I saw and heard, I have faithfully described in plain language, as briefly as I could.

[Col. 1087]

## Confirmation of the Election of Calixtus II, Strengthened by the Subscriptions of the Cardinals Present in Rome

(Martène, *Amplissima Collectio*, I, 647, from the manuscript of Laurence of Liège.)

[Col. 1087D] To the venerable bishops, cardinals, clerics, and laymen who were with Lord Gelasius: the bishops and cardinals and the other clerics and lay faithful of Blessed Peter send greeting in the Lord.

We grieve all the more deeply at the death of our lord Pope Gelasius, of blessed memory, because we had hoped for greater assistance through him. Yet because it so pleased Him who by His will governs and orders all things, blessed be His name for ever. After his death, moreover, we do not doubt that you were under the necessity both of providing for yourselves and for your safety, and of deliberating concerning the state of the Church and the election of a pontiff. Therefore, what you did under the pressure of supreme necessity—as we ourselves know—we too hold to be ratified and firm; and we direct our brethren who are elsewhere to hold the same opinion with us.

For, having received the letters which you sent, we assembled on the following day at the church of St. John on the Island: bishops, cardinals, priests, deacons, and subdeacons, with the other clerics, judges and scriniaries, the other ranks of the palace, and many Roman nobles. The prefect also, through his messengers; and, with a great gathering of clergy and people, we praised and confirmed the election made by you according to Roman custom [Col. 1088D]. After the confirmation, indeed, the clergy sang *Te Deum laudamus*—“We praise thee, O God.” The laypeople, as is customary, acclaimed in loud voices: “St. Peter has chosen Calixtus as pope.” Many also who were then able to be present with us, when they heard what had been confirmed by us, gave their approval.

That you may be more fully assured of the harmonious unanimity of our agreement, we have sent you in writing the names of those—though not of all—who took part in this confirmation.

I, Crescentius, bishop of Sabina, approve and confirm the election, made by the grace of God by our brethren the bishops and cardinals, of Lord Guy, bishop of Vienne.

I, Peter, bishop of Porto, approve and confirm.  
[Col. 1089B] I, Vitalis, bishop of Albano, approve and confirm.  
I, Boniface, of the title of St. Mark, approve and confirm.  
I, Manfred, bishop of Tivoli, approve and confirm.

I, Paul, reader, approve and confirm.

I, John, archpriest of St. Peter the Apostle, together with all the Catholics of that church, approve and confirm.  
I, Alexis, porter, approve and confirm.

## [Letters and Privileges]

[Col. 1093]

# Letters and Privileges of Calixtus II, Roman Pontiff

## I. To Adalbert, Archbishop of Mainz—Concerning His Own Election  
(Year 1119, February)

(Mansi, *Concilia*, XXI, 190.)

[Col. 1093A]

Our lord Gelasius, of happy memory, when departing from Vienne, directed me to hasten to his presence after he himself had arrived at Cluny. When, after some days, I was making efforts to fulfill this command, news of his death was brought to me on the journey. In order that I might offer such consolation as reason required to the brethren who had come with that lord, I proceeded to Cluny in great sorrow. But while I was considering more carefully how to console them, they imposed upon me a most grievous burden, altogether beyond my strength. For, on the day after my arrival, bishops, cardinals, clerics, and Roman laymen assembled together and unanimously chose me—wholly unwilling and resisting—as pontiff of the Roman Church, under the name of Calixtus [Col. 1093B].

## II. To D[idacus], Bishop of Compostela—He Commends to Him Robert Francis, His Brother-in-Law  
(Year 1119, 2 March)

(Flórez, *España sagrada*, XX, 273.)

Calixtus, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother D., bishop of Compostela: greeting and apostolic blessing.

We have sent this nobleman and member of our household to you on certain business, and we ask that you receive him honourably and confidently comply with what he tells you on our behalf [Col. 1093C]. Through him also, if you need the counsel or assistance of the Roman Church, take care to inform us; for we are ready, insofar as the Lord permits, both to help and to support you as a son most dear in Christ.

Given at the town of Crista, on the sixth day before the Nones of March [2 March].

## III. Consecration of the Church of St. Anthony  
(Year 1119, 20 March)

(*Acta Sanctorum* of the Bollandists, vol. II for January, p. 155.)

Calixtus, bishop, servant of the servants of God.

Our Lord Jesus Christ, existing before the ages, one God with the Father and the Holy Spirit, at the end of the ages became true man from a true mother; and, through human nature as mediator, deigned to open the entrance to heavenly life for all who believe in true faith and worthy conduct [Col. 1093D–1094A]. As a further token of His great mercy, He granted to His apostles—created, like ourselves, from earthly material and supported by no excellence of carnal wisdom or rank—the power of binding and loosing sins, saying thus to the blessed Apostle Peter, in the person of the universal Church: “I give to thee the keys of the kingdom of heaven; and whatsoever thou shalt bind shall be bound, and whatsoever thou shalt loose shall be loosed.”

Though unworthy, we act in his stead; and we have consecrated, on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of April [20 March], the church made venerable by the body of the blessed confessor Anthony, to the praise and name of the holy and undivided Trinity and to the honour of Blessed Mary ever Virgin, under the protection of so great a patron. Therefore, to all who flee to him in hope of obtaining mercy, we wish and grant health, apostolic blessing, and remission of sins, provided that they repent from the heart, by the authority of the blessed Apostles Peter and Paul [Col. 1094B].

But invaders and violators of the cemetery, or of the property of the monks and clerics serving God there, and of the other people belonging to it, we place under the excommunication of anathema, separated from all Christian fellowship, until they make satisfaction and restore what they have wickedly seized. Present at this decree as its approver and confirmer was Guigo, son of Desiderius, with his sons; with his hand placed in ours, he confirmed under oath that he would henceforth exercise no invasion or violence against the property of the monks or clerics of the church; and that, if he should do so, he would, when admonished, make amends within thirteen days, and would keep inviolate the established boundaries of the cemetery for himself and his people [Col. 1094C].

The bishop of Ostia, John of Crema, and our cardinals were present. G., prior; B., chaplain; D., canon of Romans; and others. Soferde, priest of B.; Nantelmus, Gago, P. of Provence, G. Rascas, with the other clerics and laymen. In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1119.

## IV. To Bernard, Archbishop of Auch—He Grants That Bodies of the Dead May Henceforth Be Freely Buried at the Church of St. Mary of Auch  
(Year 1119, 15 April)

(Dom Bouquet, *Recueil*, XIV, 322.)

[Col. 1094D] Calixtus, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother Bernard, archbishop of Auch: greeting and apostolic blessing [Col. 1095A].

The administration of the Apostolic See, in which, though unworthy, we serve by the Lord’s gift, makes us debtors to all churches. Therefore, dearest brother in Christ, we have judged that your request ought to be granted, so that we may grant free burial henceforth to the mother church of Blessed Mary at Auch, over which by God’s providence you preside. Accordingly, by the authority of this decree, we establish that henceforth the bodies of the dead may be freely buried at the same mother church of Blessed Mary.

Indeed, our most blessed father and master Pope Gregory undertook to correct John, bishop of the old city of Orvieto, because he forbade the burial of the dead in a monastery, by issuing the following words [Col. 1095B]:

> “If this is so, I exhort you to withdraw from such inhumanity and to permit the dead to be buried there and Masses to be celebrated, with no further objection whatsoever; lest the venerable man Agapitus be compelled again to lodge before me a complaint concerning the matters which have been mentioned.”

Therefore, let no one henceforth have authority to harass your church on this account; rather, let it have free burial hereafter, so that none may oppose the devotion and last will of those who decide to be buried there, unless they are excommunicated. If, therefore—which may it never happen—anyone, having learned the tenor of this decree, attempts to oppose it, let him suffer the loss of his honour and office, or be punished by the penalty of excommunication, unless he corrects his presumption by fitting satisfaction.

[Col. 1095C] Given at Le Puy, through the hand of Chrysogonus, cardinal deacon and librarian of the Holy Roman Church, on the seventh day before the Kalends of May [25 April], in the twelfth indiction, in the year 1120 of the Lord’s Incarnation.  
[Note: [Col. 1095D] According to the Pisan reckoning.]  
In the first year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Calixtus II.

## V. To Frederick, Archbishop of Cologne—He Announces a Council to Be Held at Rheims in Autumn for the Prosperous Condition of the Church  
(Year 1119, 16 April)

(Martène, *Amplissima Collectio*, I, 631, from a Colbert manuscript.)

Calixtus, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother F[rederick], archbishop of Cologne: greeting and apostolic blessing.

So long as we sail upon the sea of this world, we must endure storms and the collisions of the waves [Col. 1095D]. Therefore we must exercise great vigilance, that, by the Lord’s help, we may direct the course of the vessel entrusted to us in such a manner that we may be able to reach the harbour of rest with the ship and [lacuna] intact. Be therefore provident, dearest brother; and, as you have begun, look about you diligently, because the Lord our God is at hand—He who powerfully commands winds and sea and suddenly brings calm.

We know indeed that the enemies of the Lord and of the Church can bark out attacks against the Church. But it is found neither in divine nor in human law that the Apostolic See may be judged by anyone, much less by those who have been condemned by the judgment of the Church [Col. 1096A]. Nevertheless, lest the people of God be led astray by anyone’s flatteries, persuasions, or deceptions, let anyone who believes that he has a case against the Church of God come to the council which, by God’s grace, we intend to celebrate near Rheims in the coming autumn.  
[Note: [Col. 1095D] That council was held on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of November [20 October] in the year 1119, at which Henry renounced the investitures of churches.]

For there religious and wise men, masters of the Church, will be present; there deliberation will be held concerning the condition of the Church; there, with the Lord’s cooperation, the Church’s condition will rise again and hostile assault will be destroyed; and there, by the Lord’s help, a sufficient answer supported by the authority of the Fathers will be given. Act therefore steadfastly, valiant soldier of Christ, and do not cease to run in the contest of the course you have undertaken until you attain the prize. Take particular care also [Col. 1096B] that your purity is not touched by the most foul corruption of those invested by that tyrant. For the Lord is a mighty fighter with you; nor shall our counsel and assistance, which divine mercy has bestowed upon us, fail you.

Given at Le Puy, on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of May [16 April].

## VI. To the Clergy and People of Lucca—He Commands Them Not to Permit the Brethren of St. Frigidianus To Be Harassed  
(Year 1119, 1 May)

(Baluze, *Miscellanea*, ed. Mansi, IV, 587.)

Calixtus, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the clergy and people of Lucca: greeting and apostolic blessing.

We have heard that some among you have most rashly stirred up a disturbance against the brethren of St. Frigidianus [Col. 1096C]. Therefore, visiting your beloved community by this letter, we ask and command you—as we remember having directed also our brother B., your bishop—that you in no way permit the aforesaid brethren to be harassed by anyone until, with the Lord’s help, we come to your region. For then, if any have a case against them, they may come into our presence, and we shall administer justice to them according to what is right.

Given at Brioude, on the Kalends of May [1 May].

## VII. To Franco, Abbot of Tournus—Privilege for Tournus  
(Year 1119, 10 May)

(Mansi, *Concilia*, XX, 203.)

[Col. 1096D]

Calixtus, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son in Christ Franco, abbot of Tournus, and to his successors regularly appointed for ever.

It is fitting for us to give assent to just wishes and lend our ears to just petitions, since, although unworthy heralds of justice, we are seen, by the Lord’s ordering, to be set in the lofty watchtower of the Apostles Peter and Paul. Therefore, graciously assenting to your petitions, we extend to the monastery of Tournus, over which by God’s providence you preside, the protection of apostolic guardianship; and, after the example of our predecessor Pope Paschal, of holy memory, we confirm by the text of this decree to you and your successors those places which either the industry of your predecessors or your own diligence has reasonably acquired or lawfully recovered, or which have been granted to that monastery by the generosity of ancient princes or bishops [Col. 1097A].

Namely, in the diocese of Clermont, the monastery, etc.

It enumerates the possessions of that church. Then:

Whatever else, moreover, by God’s gift, you may hereafter be able to acquire justly, shall remain firm and unimpaired for you and your successors. We decree, therefore, that it shall be lawful for no person whatsoever rashly to disturb that monastery, to take away its possessions, retain those taken away, diminish them, or harass them by reckless vexations; but that all things be preserved intact, to be of every benefit to the uses of those for whose support and governance they were granted [Col. 1097B].

Furthermore, we add that the same place, in which rest the bodies of Blessed Valerian the martyr and St. Philibert the confessor, shall remain free for ever from every yoke of secular power. Nor may the bishop of any diocese disturb that place under pretext of excommunication, absolution, or any other administrative act; nor impose crosses or any new exactions upon the borough or the other possessions of the monastery. We also forbid public Masses to be celebrated in that monastery, or a station to be held there by the bishop, without the consent of the abbot and brethren [Col. 1097C].

We confirm also all the other provisions which were confirmed to the monastery of Tournus by the privileges of the pontiffs John, of venerable memory, and the aforesaid Lord Paschal II. Moreover, out of reverence for Blessed Mary ever Virgin, by whose name your place is distinguished, we grant that the angelic hymn may be pronounced by the abbot or the brethren during the solemn celebration of Mass on the Annunciation of our Lord and Saviour.

When you, now abbot of that place, or any of your successors, dies, let no one be set over it by any cunning of fraud or by violence, except one whom the brethren by common consent, or the sounder part of the brethren, shall elect according to the fear of God and the Rule of St. Benedict, to be consecrated by the bishop of the Apostolic See or by his legate, because of the difficulty of the journey [Col. 1097D].

If, therefore, any ecclesiastical or secular person in the future, knowing the text of this our constitution, rashly attempts to act against it, and, having been admonished a second and a third time, does not amend by suitable satisfaction, let that person be deprived of the dignity of power and honour, and know himself or herself guilty before the divine judgment of the iniquity committed; let that person be cut off from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Redeemer, and be subject at the final judgment to stern vengeance. But let all who preserve what is right for that place have the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that here they may receive the fruit of good action and, before the strict Judge, find the rewards of eternal peace [Col. 1098A]. Amen, amen, amen.

I, Calixtus, bishop of the Catholic Church, have subscribed.

Given at Celsiniania, through the hand of Chrysogonus, cardinal deacon and librarian of the Holy Roman Church, on the sixth day before the Ides of May [10 May], in the twelfth indiction, in the year 1120 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the first year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Calixtus II.

## VIII. Privilege for the Monastery of the Valley, in the Diocese of Besançon  
(Year 1119, 24 May)

(Chevalier, *Mémoires historiques de Poligny*, Lons-le-Saunier, 1767, quarto, vol. I, p. 320.)

[Col. 1098B] Calixtus, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons, the monks of the monastery of St. Mary of the Valley, situated in the diocese of Besançon near Poligny, both present and future, for ever.

The authority of our office exhorts us to labour for the welfare of churches and, with the Lord’s help, to provide for their peace. Therefore, graciously assenting to your petition, we confirm to you and your successors for ever whatever has been bestowed upon your monastery by Otto, count of noble memory, surnamed William, our great-grandfather, and by his son Renaud: namely, four iron cauldrons and their sites in the saltworks; the vineyards which belonged to Beatrice; the village of Glenon, with the tithes of the church and all appurtenances [Col. 1098C]; the village of Milan, and its church with tithes and all its appurtenances, and the customary rights in the forest of Maidun; the village of Besan, with its church and tithes and all that belongs to it; the place called Mutua and all its appurtenances; the gift made from Gunther and the land which he held; the fishery of Givry, with all the land belonging to it; and whatever has been acquired in the borough of Groson.

We also confirm to you the church of Merriac with its tithes; the church of Frontenay with its tithes; the church of Mintrio (Mentri) with its tithes; the church of Sancey with its tithes; and the churches of Mornay, Mount St. Benignus (Saint-Barain), and Tormont, with their tithes; together with whatever has been lawfully acquired by your monastery through you or offered from their own right by any faithful persons, and whatever may hereafter, by the Lord’s gift, be justly and canonically acquired or offered [Col. 1098D].

We decree, therefore, that it shall be lawful for no person whatsoever rashly to disturb that monastery, take away its possessions, retain those taken away, diminish them, or harass them by reckless vexations; but let all things be preserved intact, to be of every benefit to the uses of those for whose support and governance they were granted. If, therefore, any ecclesiastical or secular person in the future, knowing the text of this our constitution, rashly attempts to act against it, let that person be deprived of the dignity of power and honour, and know himself or herself guilty before the divine judgment of the iniquity committed [Col. 1099A]; let that person be cut off from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Redeemer, and be subject at the final judgment to stern vengeance. But let all who preserve what is right for that place have the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that here they may receive the fruit of good action and, before the strict Judge, find the rewards of eternal peace.

I, Calixtus, bishop of the Catholic Church.

Given at Mancy, through the hand of Grisogonus, cardinal deacon and librarian of the Holy Roman Church, on the ninth day before the Kalends of June [24 May], in the twelfth indiction, in the year 1120 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the first year of the pontificate of the most holy father Lord Calixtus II.

## IX. Apostolic Bull Declaring the Chapter of Brioude To Be Immediately Subject to the Roman Church, and Granting It the Right To Receive Chrism, Holy Oil, the Consecration of Churches or Altars, and Clerical Ordinations from Whatever Bishop It Chooses  
(Year 1119, 1 June)

(*Gallia Christiana nova*, vol. II, documents, p. 132.)

[Col. 1099B]

Calixtus, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons in Christ, the canons of the church of St. Julian at Brioude, both present and future, for ever.

Although we are debtors to all the children of the Church by the authority and benevolence of the Apostolic See, it is especially fitting that we devote a more earnest zeal of charity to those places and persons which adhere more specially and closely to the Roman Church [Col. 1099C]. Therefore, we have judged that your petitions ought to be granted, so that we might fortify the church of Blessed Julian at Brioude with the protection of the Apostolic See. By the text of this present privilege, we establish by apostolic authority that whatever goods and possessions that church presently holds by grants of pontiffs, generosity of princes, offerings of the faithful, or other just means, and whatever it may hereafter, by God’s help, be able justly and canonically to acquire, shall remain firm and unimpaired for you and your successors.

Among these, we have thought it right to record by their proper names: the abbey of St. German of Embrun; the abbey of St. Marcellinus of Cantogila; the abbey of St. Mary of Pebrac; the abbey of St. Julian of Tours; the church of St. Ferreolus; the church of Brassac [Col. 1099D]; the church of the Valley with its tithe; the church of Solignac with its tithe; the church of Despaleneus with its tithe; the village of Tarraza; the church of Faveirolas with its tithe; the church of Surlange with its tithe; the church of Bellomont with its tithe; and the church of Fontibus.

We decree, therefore, that it shall be lawful for no person whatsoever rashly to disturb that church, take away its possessions, retain those taken away, diminish them, or harass them by reckless vexations; but that all things be preserved intact, to be of every benefit to the uses of those for whose support and governance they were granted. Moreover, let the church and estates which have been alienated through the rashness of provosts or other ecclesiastical persons, or through the violence of laymen, be restored to the use of the church and henceforth be preserved unimpaired, without contradiction from any person [Col. 1100A].

And, since your church is established under the protection and jurisdiction of our holy Roman Church, in which, by God’s providence, we serve, let it always remain free and undisturbed. We forbid any priest of any church to exercise any jurisdiction whatever over it, except the rector of this Apostolic See. You shall receive chrism, holy oil, the consecrations of altars and churches, and the orders of clerics who are to be advanced to sacred orders, from whatever Catholic bishop you prefer.

When the abbot or provost of that place dies, let no one be placed over it by any cunning of fraud or by violence, except one whom the brethren by common consent, or the sounder part of the brethren, according to God, shall determine ought to be elected [Col. 1100B]. As a token of the right and ownership of the Roman Church, and of your liberty, you shall pay one gold piece annually to the Lateran palace.

If, therefore, any ecclesiastical or secular person in the future, knowing the text of this our constitution, rashly attempts to act against it, and, having been admonished a second and third time, does not amend by suitable satisfaction, let that person be deprived of the dignity of power and honour, and know himself or herself guilty before the divine judgment of the iniquity committed; let that person be cut off from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Redeemer, and be subject at the final judgment to stern vengeance [Col. 1100C]. But let all who preserve the rights of that church have the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that here they may receive the fruit of good action and, before the strict Judge, find the rewards of eternal peace.

I, Calixtus, bishop of the Catholic Church.

Given at Brioude, through the hand of Grisogonus, cardinal deacon and librarian of the Holy Roman Church, on the Kalends of June [1 June], in the twelfth indiction, in the year 1120 of the Lord’s Incarnation.  
[Note: [Col. 1099D] The year 1119 according to the new style.]  
In the first year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Calixtus II.

## X. Bull for the Monastery of St. Blaise  
(Year 1119, 18 June)

(Neugart, *Codex diplomaticus Alemannicus*, II, 47. From the original of the same monastery, no. 232, 1, 3.)

[Col. 1100D]

Calixtus, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son Rustinus, abbot of the monastery of St. Blaise, situated in the diocese of Constance, namely in the place called the Black Forest, and to his successors regularly appointed for ever.

It is fitting to grant ready assent to religious desires, so that faithful devotion may swiftly attain its effect. Therefore we mercifully accede to your petition, and receive under the protection of the Apostolic See the monastery of Saint Blaise, over which, by God’s authorisation, you preside, together with all that belongs to it. Therefore, by the authority of the Apostolic See, through the present document of privilege, we decree [Col. 1101A] that whatever the same monastery now possesses, or may hereafter be able justly and canonically to acquire through the grant of pontiffs, the generosity of princes, or the offerings of the faithful, shall remain secure and unimpaired for you and your successors.

Let no person whatsoever therefore presume rashly to disturb that monastery, to take away its possessions, retain what has been taken away, diminish them, or harass them by reckless vexations; but let all things be preserved intact, to be wholly beneficial for the uses of those for whose support and governance they were granted.
