You shall receive consecrations of altars or churches, ordinations of monks, chrism, holy oil, and the other things pertaining to the episcopal office from the bishop of Constance, in whose diocese you are, [Col. 1101B] provided that he is Catholic, is in grace and communion, and is willing to furnish these things freely and without impropriety. Otherwise, you may approach whatever Catholic bishop you prefer and receive from him the sacraments of consecration, he being supported by the authority of the Apostolic See and granting what is requested.

We likewise decree that burial in that place shall be entirely free, and that no one shall oppose the devotion and final wishes of those who have resolved to be buried there, unless they are perhaps excommunicated. Moreover, let no opposition by any bishop or provost prevent you from receiving clerics or laypersons living in the secular estate for conversion. Upon the death of you, now abbot of that place, or of any one of your successors, no one [Col. 1101C] shall be set over it by any device of fraud or by force, except one whom the brothers by common consent, or the sounder part of the brothers’ counsel, shall provide to be elected according to the fear of God and the Rule of Saint Benedict.

If, therefore, any ecclesiastical or secular person in future, knowing this document of our constitution, rashly attempts to act against it, and, having been warned a second or third time, does not make due amendment by suitable satisfaction, let that person be deprived of the dignity of power and honour; let him know that he stands guilty before divine judgment for the iniquity committed; let him be separated from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, our Redeemer; and let him be subject, at the final judgment and examination, to strict vengeance. But upon all who observe what is just toward the same place may there be the peace [Col. 1101D] of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that they may receive here the fruit of good action and find, before the strict Judge, the rewards of eternal peace. Amen, amen, amen.

I, Calixtus, bishop of the Catholic Church, have subscribed.  
I, Cono, bishop of Palestrina, have subscribed.  
I, Lambert, bishop of Ostia, have subscribed.  
I, Peter, cardinal deacon of Saints Cosmas and Damian, have subscribed.  
I, Boso, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Anastasia, have subscribed.  
I, Gregory, cardinal deacon of Saint Angelo, have subscribed.  
[Col. 1102A] I, Deusdedit, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Lawrence in Damaso, have subscribed.  
I, John, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Chrysogonus, have subscribed.

Given at Saint-Gilles, through the hand of Chrysogonus, cardinal deacon and librarian of the Holy Roman Church, on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of July [18 June], in the twelfth indiction, in the year 1120 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the first year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Calixtus II.

[Note: [Col. 1101D] Calixtus II, formerly called Guy, was elected on 1 February 1119 and crowned on 9 February of the same year at Vienne in Gaul, whose archiepiscopal see he had held. [Col. 1102D] The notary therefore did not count the months elapsed from February.]

## XI. He confirms the privileges and possessions of the Hospital of Jerusalem. (Year 1119, 19 June.)

*[Codice diplomatico del sacro militare ordine Gerosolimitano, I, 269.]*

## XII. Bull for the monastery of Blessed Mary of Alet. (Year 1119, 19 June.)

*[Hist. de Languedoc, II, proofs, p. 408.]*

[Col. 1102B]

CALIXTUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son RAYMOND, abbot of the monastery of Blessed Mary of Alet, and to his successors canonically appointed in perpetuity.

The authority of our office exhorts us to be solicitous for the condition of churches and to establish securely what has been rightly ordained. Therefore we judge that your petitions, most beloved son in Christ, Abbot Raymond, ought not without reason to be granted, so that we might fortify by the privilege of the Apostolic See the monastery of Blessed Mary of Alet, over which, by God’s authorisation, you preside. It was offered by its founder, Count Bera of noble memory, to blessed Peter under a payment of one pound of silver every two years, [Col. 1102C] following the example of our predecessor Pope Leo.

Therefore, by the authority of the Apostolic See, through the present document of privilege, we decree that whatever goods and possessions that monastery lawfully possesses in the present twelfth indiction, or may hereafter, God granting, be able justly and canonically to acquire, shall remain firm for . . . successors and unimpaired. Among these we have considered the following worthy of being recorded by their proper names: namely, the monastery of Saint Paul called Valolas, on the banks of the Aude, with its appurtenances; the church of Saint Polycarp on the bank of the Rivigrand, with its dependencies, as it was confirmed to your monastery by the judgment of our lord predecessor Pope Paschal of holy memory; [Col. 1102D] the church of Saint Mary of Urbion; the church of Saint Columba of Chercobes on the bank of the Aude; the church of Pairan; the monastery of Saint Papoul; the church in the land of Copelata at Villeneuve; the village of Flacian; the village of Cornelian; the church of Saint Martin of the cell, with its appurtenances; the church in the castle of Rasindo; the church of Saint Mary of Esperazan; the castle of Puncian and its church; the castle of Verzola with two churches; the castle of Cornelian; and the castle of Blancafort.

We decree, therefore, that no person whatsoever [Col. 1103A] may rashly disturb that monastery, take away its possessions, retain what has been taken away, diminish them, or harass them by reckless vexations; but that all things shall be preserved intact, wholly beneficial for the uses of those for whose governance and support they were granted. Upon the death of you, now abbot of that place, or of any of your successors, no one shall be set over it by fraud, cunning, or force, except one whom the brothers by common consent, or the sounder part of the brothers’ counsel, shall provide to be elected according to the fear of God and the Rule of Saint Benedict. The elected person shall be consecrated by the diocesan bishop, if he is willing to provide consecration freely and without impropriety; otherwise, he shall receive consecration from whatever Catholic bishop he prefers.

We also add the following chapter to this present privilege: because your place is an offering to blessed Peter and belongs by right to his Roman Church, no archbishop or bishop whatsoever shall have authority to pronounce against it, against you, or against any of yours a sentence of excommunication or interdict. Rather, you shall remain always free and undisturbed under the right and protection of the Apostolic See, and you shall pay to the Lateran Palace one pound of silver every three years, as was established by the aforesaid count. [Col. 1103B] If, therefore, any ecclesiastical or secular person in future, knowing this document of our constitution, rashly attempts to act against it, and, having been warned a second or third time, does not make due amendment by suitable satisfaction, let that person be deprived of the dignity of power and honour, separated from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, and subject, at the final examination, to strict vengeance, etc.

Given at Saint-Gilles, through the hand of Grisogonus, cardinal deacon and librarian of the Holy Roman Church, on the third day before the Kalends of July [29 June], in the twelfth indiction, in the year 1120 of the Lord’s Incarnation.

[Note: [Col. 1103D] Read: “the thirteenth day before the Kalends of July” [19 June], Jaffé.]

## XIII. He confirms the rights and goods of the monastery of Saint-Gilles. (Year 1119, 28 June.)

*[MÉNARD, History of Nîmes. Paris, 1750, quarto, vol. I, proofs, p. 28.]*

CALIXTUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved [Col. 1103D] son in Christ, HUGH, abbot of the venerable monastery of Blessed Giles, and to his successors canonically appointed in perpetuity.

Among the other churches located throughout the province of Gothia, the monastery of Blessed Giles is known to belong more especially and intimately to the Apostolic See. For the venerable Father Giles himself offered that place to blessed Peter and his Roman Church, and assigned it by right of ownership to the Apostolic See, as the records of ancient writings more clearly demonstrate. Therefore, we have determined to love that monastery with fuller affection and to foster it with more earnest charity.

Accordingly, we confirm by the document of this privilege every liberty and immunity granted to you and your monastery by the privileges of our predecessors, decreeing that no archbishop or bishop whatsoever may extend a hand of excommunication or interdict over that monastery, its abbot, or the monks there serving the Lord; but that both you and the monastery, together with the town, shall always remain undisturbed and free, through the grace of almighty God, from every episcopal exaction or burden. [Col. 1104A] We entirely forbid that monks, priests, or clerics dwelling in your obediences be seized, beaten, or compelled to ransom payments by any laypersons for their offences.

Moreover, all that your monastery presently possesses in this twelfth indiction through grants of pontiffs, princely generosity, offerings of the faithful, or other just means, and all that it may hereafter, God granting, be able to acquire, shall remain always undisturbed and unimpaired. Among these the following seemed fit to be recorded by their proper names: namely, the abbeys of Saint Giles in Hungary and Saint Eusebius in Provence; and the churches of Saint Giles of Aceio, Saint Giles of Duno, Saint Giles of Limantio, Saint Giles of Supervia, Saint Eusebius of Lombardy, Saint Baudilus of Spain, Saint Eulalia of Barbasta; the church of Ruminas, with the town itself; the church of Boccona, with its town; the church of Saint Andrew of Lucopello; the church of Saint Giles of Tholmone; the church of Saint Giles of Cressiac, with its town; Saint Hippolytus of Melreo, with its town; Saint Lupus; Saint Mary of Fraxinet; Saint John of Gardonenca, with its town; Holy Cross [Col. 1104C] of Molerano; Saint Martin of Cervario; Saint Stephen of Corconna; Saint Amantius, with its town; Saint Martin of Orianiches; Saint Martin of Sinthiano; Saint Andrew of Berniz; Saint Saturninus of Seura, with its town; the town of Bion; the church of Saint Cecilia of Stagello, with its town; Saint Felix of Aspirano, with its town; Saint Columba, with half the town; Saint Andrew of Campo Mariniano; Saint Mary of Saturanigues; Saint Giles of Missiniac; Saint Stephen of Calesues; Saint Peter of Provencheriis, with its town; Saint Andeolus of Robiac, with its town; Saint Victorinus of Villaforte; Saint Peter of Vannis, with its town; Saint Mary of Mont Alto, with its town; Saint Baudilus of Somerio; Saint Servus beyond the Rhône, with its town; Saints Peter and Michael beside the castle of Roussillon; Saint Privatus, with its town; Saint Stephen of Minerba, with its town; Saint [Col. 1104D] Christopher of Vacheriis, with its town; Saint John of Albennatis, with its town; Saint Mary of Rodose, with its town; Saint Columba of Wapinco; Saint Giles of Padernas; Saint Maximus of Medenas; Saint Peter of Intermontes, with its town; Saint Peter of Trancatellas; Saint John of Negano; Saint Sebastian of Alsatis; Saint Peter of Launiac; Saint Saviour of Caisanigues; and Saint Eugenius of Obresat, with the chapels and other possessions belonging to them.

We decree, therefore, that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the aforesaid monastery, take away its possessions, retain what has been taken away, diminish them, or recklessly harass them; but that all things be preserved intact, wholly beneficial for the uses of those for whose support and governance they were granted. [Col. 1105A] We confirm by the authority of the Apostolic See the renunciation of Count Raymond of Toulouse, of noble memory. For the count himself, at the Council of Nîmes, swearing an oath, left to Abbot Odilo and his brothers, for the honour of God and reverence for Blessed Giles, all honours pertaining to Saint-Gilles—both in the valley of Flavian and outside it—whatever he seemed to hold justly or unjustly; all lawful or unlawful customary dues which his predecessors or he himself had possessed. He bound himself and all his successors with condemnation and a curse, should they ever attempt, so far as lay in their power, to render this gift void; and he caused a sentence of excommunication concerning this matter to be pronounced in the council by our aforesaid lord, Pope Urban of holy memory.

Furthermore, for greater veneration of Blessed Giles, we decree that within the boundaries established by our predecessors and also confirmed by us, no one whatsoever shall dare either to plunder or assault the town of Saint-Gilles itself, or to inflict a more serious injury upon any person. If, therefore, any ecclesiastical or secular person in future, knowing this document of our constitution, rashly attempts to act against it, and, having been warned a second or third time, does not make due amendment by suitable satisfaction, let that person be deprived of the dignity of power and honour; let him know that he stands guilty before divine judgment for the iniquity committed; let him be separated from the most sacred [Col. 1105C] body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, our Redeemer; and let him be subject at the final examination to strict vengeance. But upon all who observe what is just toward the same place may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that they may receive here the fruit of good action and find, before the strict Judge, the rewards of eternal peace. Amen, amen, amen.

I, Calixtus, bishop of the Catholic Church, have subscribed.

Given at Maguelone, through the hand of Grisogonus, cardinal deacon and librarian of the Holy Roman Church, on the fourth day before the Kalends of July [28 June], in the twelfth indiction, in the year 1120 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the first year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Calixtus II.

## XIV. For the same monastery. (Year 1119, 28 June.)

*[History of Languedoc, vol. II, proofs, p. 408.]*

[Col. 1105D]

CALIXTUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons Abbot HUGH and the monks of the monastery of Saint-Gilles: greeting and Apostolic blessing.

Because of the dissensions and scandals that have frequently arisen between your house and the count, and between the abbot and the monks, your monastery has suffered very serious loss in its temporal goods. Indeed, matters have come to such a point that, among other things, the greater part of its treasury has been sold off and dispersed, as we have learned from your report. You should know that this grieves us all the more because [Col. 1106A] your place, by the offering of Blessed Giles himself, is known to belong especially and intimately to the Roman Church.

Therefore, lest this evil gain any further force, we decree by a regulation to remain perpetually in force, and prohibit in every manner by the authority of the Apostolic See, that no abbot or monk shall dare alienate, sell, or pledge the treasury or the rights and properties of the Church, whether now held or hereafter acquired by the Lord’s gift, except perhaps for these three reasons: namely, for the redemption of captives, for the common and grave need of the community, and for purchase or redemption. If this should occur, moreover, it shall be done by the common deliberation of the entire chapter, so that nothing may be undertaken through fraud or any deception, but only under the pressure of the aforesaid necessities.

If any abbot or monk, knowing the tenor of this decree, attempts to act contrary to it, the abbot shall be deprived of the governance of the abbey and subject to a sentence of excommunication; the monk, however, shall be wholly excluded from the monastery and its rights and properties, and bound by the same sentence of excommunication, unless either abbot or monk corrects his presumption by worthy satisfaction according to the common judgment of the chapter. [Col. 1106B] Finally, we promulgate a sentence of excommunication against those who receive the monastery’s treasury or rights and properties otherwise than as defined above.

I, Calixtus, bishop of the Catholic Church, confirm, etc.

Given at Maguelone, through the hand of Grisogonus, [Col. 1106C] cardinal deacon and librarian of the Holy Roman Church, on the fourth day before the Kalends of July [28 June], in the twelfth indiction, in the year 1120 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the first year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Calixtus II.

## XV. To the canons of the church of Saint John at Besançon.—He releases the contending canons of Saint John and Saint Stephen from their oaths. (Year 1119, 30 June.)

*[MANSI, Councils, XXI, 197.]*

CALIXTUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons, the canons of the church of Saint John the Evangelist at Besançon: greeting and Apostolic blessing.

A certain union of possessions between your church and that of Blessed Stephen was effected by our fellow-brother Humbert, Archbishop of Lyon. It seemed likely to inflict very serious harm upon both churches, and the oaths made in consequence could not be maintained at all without danger to souls. Our aforesaid brother, having carefully considered this together with your Archbishop Anseric, and also upon our admonition, entirely released the oaths of both parties by the permission and authority reserved to himself and to your archbishop. [Col. 1106D]

Accordingly, judging that this release was necessary for both churches, we confirm it by this document of decree and decree that it shall remain ratified in perpetuity. By the authority of the Apostolic See we establish and strictly command that neither you shall henceforth presume to molest the canons of Saint Stephen concerning that oath, nor they you, nor any other person. Nor may any person whatsoever claim for himself your rights, estates, possessions, or whatever belongs by right to your church, on account of the bond of that union, or further intermingle them. Rather, all shall always be preserved for you and your successors undisturbed and entire, just as they are known to have been preserved from the time of Hugh of Salins, Archbishop of Besançon, of good memory, until the time of Archbishop Hugh, our brother, who passed to the Lord on the pilgrimage to Jerusalem.

If, therefore, any ecclesiastical or secular person in future, knowing this document of our constitution, rashly attempts to act against it, and, having been warned a second or third time, does not make due amendment [Col. 1107B] by suitable satisfaction, let that person be deprived of the dignity of power and honour; let him know that he stands guilty before divine judgment for the iniquity committed; let him be separated from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, our Redeemer; and let him be subject at the final examination to strict vengeance.

I, Calixtus, bishop of the Catholic Church, confirm and subscribe.

Given at Maguelone, through the hand of Chrysogonus, cardinal deacon and librarian of the Holy Roman Church, on the second day before the Kalends of July [30 June], in the twelfth indiction, in the year 1120 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the first year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Calixtus II.

## XVI. To R., abbot of Marseilles.—He permits him and his brothers to celebrate the divine office in the church of Saint Nicholas at Tarascon and to have it consecrated. (Year 1119, 1 July.)

*[Drawn from the archives of Saint Victor of Marseilles by D. Furnerius.—Published by D. Martène, Amplissima Collectio, I, 663.]*

[Col. 1107C]

CALIXTUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons R., [Note: [Col. 1107D] Rodulf, abbot-elect of Saint Victor in the year 1117.] abbot of Marseilles, and his brothers: greeting and Apostolic blessing.

Our predecessor, Pope Urban of holy memory, as we have learned from his letters and those of Pope Gelasius, granted the favour of his authority to Richard, Archbishop of Narbonne, then abbot of Marseilles, so that at Tarascon, namely at the place donated by Countess Stephanie, [Col. 1107D] he might build a church in honour of God. That pope himself also planted a cross in the same place and sprinkled holy water.

Accordingly, wishing that the just right of your monastery be preserved for it, we grant you permission for your brothers to celebrate the divine offices in that place; and, once the church has been completed, if the bishop of Avignon either refuses to consecrate it or is unable to do so because of opposition from clerics, you may have it consecrated by whatever Catholic bishop you prefer.

Given at Béziers, on the Kalends of July [1 July].

[Note: [Col. 1107D] From this you may infer that this bull was issued while Calixtus, after holding the Council of Reims, was directing his journey toward [Col. 1108D] Italy and was about to leave Gaul; this occurred in the year 1120.]

## XVII. Extract from a bull issued in favour of the monastery of Saint Mary of Sorèze. (Year 1119, 6 July.)

*[Gallia Christiana, XIII, documents, 266.]*

[Col. 1108A]

Pope Calixtus II, acceding to the petitions of Amelius, bishop of Toulouse, and Peter, abbot of Sorèze, receives the monastery of Blessed Mary of Sorèze, with all belonging to it, under the protection of the Apostolic See and strengthens it against the wickedness of evil men by the safeguard of his protection. He decrees that whatever goods and possessions that monastery lawfully possesses, or may hereafter, God granting, be able justly and canonically to acquire, shall remain secure and unimpaired for Peter himself and his successors. “Among these,” he says, “we have considered the following worthy to be stated by their proper names: the town of Sorèze itself with the churches of Saint Martin and Saint Michael, together with the tithes, offerings, and other things belonging to it; [Col. 1108B] the church of Saint Vincent of Gandels, Saint Mary of Blan, Saint Martin of Puy-Laurens, Saint Peter of Poditio, Saint Anatolius, Saint Salvius, Saint Saturninus of Cadicio, Saint Martin of Maderio, Saint Pardulf, and Saint Stephen of Cocoringo, with their dependencies; the town of Palajac with the churches of Saint Martin and Saint John; the church of Saint Martin of Superio, Saint Mary du Cauce, and Saint Genesius of Peirenhx; the town of Picta with the church of Saint John and all belonging to it; the town of Maur in the district of Auch; and the monastery of Saint Peter of Cellamedulf with its appurtenances.”

“Upon the death of you,” says the pontiff, “abbot of that place, or of any one of your successors, no one shall be set over it by any device of fraud or by force, except one whom the brothers by common consent, or the sounder part of the brothers’ counsel, shall provide to be elected according to the fear of God and the Rule of Saint Benedict.”

Given at the castle of Avignon, through the hand of Grisogonus, cardinal deacon and librarian of the Holy Roman Church, on the second day before the Nones of July [6 July], in the thirteenth indiction, in the year 1120 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the second year of our pontificate.

## XVIII. The church of Saint Polycarp is confirmed to the monastery of Alet. (Year 1119, 14 July.)

*[MANSI, Councils, XXI, 231.]*

[Col. 1108D]

CALIXTUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son RAYMOND, abbot of Alet: greeting and Apostolic blessing.

Concerning the church of Saint Polycarp, a decision was made long ago by our predecessor Pope Paschal of holy memory between your monastery and the monastery of Crassus. Recently, however, at the council which by God’s grace we celebrated at Toulouse, Berengarius, abbot of Crassus, brought a complaint that the monastery of Crassus [Col. 1109A] had been burdened in that decision, because the judgment had been pronounced in the presence of only one brother of Crassus. Therefore, lest any ground for complaint remain to him, we heard his complaint more fully than was necessary. Yet, after a more careful investigation of the case, we were able to find nothing in it other than what the judgment of our aforesaid lord had determined.

Therefore, with God as author, we confirm by the authority of the Apostolic See what has been established by that same Apostolic See concerning the church of Blessed Polycarp, and decree that it shall remain ratified in perpetuity. We command that no person whatsoever may withdraw that place from subjection to the monastery of Alet or harass you on that account by reckless vexations. If anyone, knowing the tenor of this decree, should rashly attempt—God forbid!—to act contrary to it, let him suffer loss of his honour and office or be punished by the penalty of excommunication, unless he corrects his presumption by worthy satisfaction.

The brothers who were present at this reconsideration and decision of ours are these: Cono, bishop of Palestrina, and Lambert, bishop of Ostia; Boso and Deusdedit, cardinal priests; Peter and Gregory, cardinal deacons; Richard, Archbishop of Narbonne; Ato, Archbishop of Arles; Bernard, Archbishop of Auch; Raymond, bishop of Barbastro; Walter, bishop of Maguelone; Arnald, bishop of Carcassonne; Amelius, bishop of Toulouse; Berengarius, bishop of Girona; Gregory, bishop of Bigorre; Bernard Aton, viscount of Béziers; and Centule, count of Bigorre.

I, Calixtus, bishop of the Catholic Church.

[Col. 1109C] Given at Toulouse, through the hand of Grisogonus, cardinal deacon and librarian of the Holy Roman Church, on the second day before the Ides of July [14 July], in the twelfth indiction, in the year 1120 [1119] of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the preceding [read: first] year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Calixtus II.

## XIX. To Didacus, bishop of Compostela.—He wishes him to attend the council to be held at Reims “on the feast of Blessed Luke.” (Year 1119, 14 July.)

*[FLÓREZ, España Sagrada, XX, 278.]*

CALIXTUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother DIDACUS, bishop of Compostela: greeting and Apostolic blessing.

Before undertaking the ministry of the Apostolic See, we loved you with brotherly charity. Now that by divine disposition we have been placed in the governance of that same see, we desire to love you all the more, insofar as the administration committed to us more fully persuades us to do so. Therefore, visiting your brotherhood by these present letters, we ask and exhort you to strive to assist your mother, the Roman Church, according to the ability granted you by the Lord. For we desire to honour both you and your Church with due honour, insofar as the Lord permits.

We also ask you, for the sake of our nephew the king, to assist and support him for love of us so manfully and steadfastly that we may the more willingly grant you a hearing in your petitions. Matters less suited to letters we have entrusted to be related more fully [Col. 1110A] to you by his and our faithful men Peter, Girard, and A. We command your brotherhood to attend the council which, God granting, we have decided to celebrate at Reims on the feast of Blessed Luke, if this can in any way be done. But if you are hindered by a canonical impediment, present yourself before us before we cross the mountains.

Given at Toulouse, on the second day before the Ides of July [14 July].

## XX. Bull concerning the gift of the church of Saint Liberata, made to Stephen, abbot of Casa Dei, by Hildebert, bishop of Agen. (Year 1119, 15 July.)

*[Gallia Christiana, II, documents, 428.]*

CALIXTUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son STEPHEN, abbot of the monastery of Casa Dei: greeting [Col. 1110B] and Apostolic blessing.

In the church of Blessed Liberata, situated in the diocese of Agen, clerics formerly lived in an excessively secular manner. Recently, however, inspired by divine grace, they entrusted both themselves and their place to your monastery for the amendment of their life, so that henceforth almighty God might be served there under the rule of the monastic order. But lest our brother Hildebert, bishop of Agen, should seem to be burdened by this, we asked him in person to grant the aforesaid church, for the honour of God and the discipline of monastic religion thereafter to be maintained there, to your monastery; otherwise your brothers refused to receive it.

He, however, moved by our prayers, out of desire and, as we believe, pure will, granted by full donation through our hands the same church of Blessed [Col. 1110C] Liberata, with its appurtenances, to Blessed Robert and to your monks present and future, while preserving the episcopal right which he had hitherto appeared to possess in that church. Therefore we confirm by the authority of the Apostolic See this concession of the aforesaid bishop as though made through us, and decree that the often-mentioned church of Blessed Liberata shall remain with perpetual stability in every respect under the protection and disposition of you and your successors.

Indeed, if anyone—God forbid!—attempts to act contrary to this decree of ours, let him suffer loss of his honour and office or be punished by the penalty of excommunication, unless he corrects his presumption by worthy satisfaction.

[Col. 1110D] Given at Toulouse, on the Ides of July [15 July], in the twelfth indiction, in the year 1120 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the first year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Calixtus II.

## XXI. Synodal letter of Calixtus, presiding at the Council of Toulouse, by which the cell of Saint Mary of Gordian is adjudged to the monastery of Aniane, against the Archbishop of Arles and the monks of Casa Dei. (Year 1119, May.)

*[MANSI, Councils, XXI, 227.]*

CALIXTUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son PONCE, abbot of the monastery of Aniane: greeting and Apostolic blessing.

A dispute concerning the cell of Saint Mary of Gordian has long been before the Apostolic See. During the time of our lord Pope Paschal of holy memory, both you for your monastery and the monks of Casa Dei for theirs repeatedly attempted to claim it. But after many complaints, when the aforesaid lord had heard your allegations carefully at an appointed time, he at last, after a diligent investigation of the truth, adjudged that cell to your monastery and imposed perpetual silence upon the monks of Casa Dei in that dispute, as is more fully contained in the document of his decision.

Nevertheless, although those brothers appeared from that time to have remained quiet throughout the whole pontificate of that same lord, they renewed the same complaint before us at Clermont, asserting that they had been prejudiced in the judgment because their claim had not [Col. 1111B] been fully investigated. So that no opportunity might remain for them to complain against the Apostolic See, we examined their documents and arguments and, finding in them nothing of strength or consequence, commanded the brothers henceforth to desist from this disturbance.

When our brother Ato, Archbishop of Arles, heard this, he too began to complain, saying that the Church of Arles had been unjustly despoiled of its possessions, since the aforesaid cell of Gordanicis with its property belonged to the right of the Church of Arles, and through that church the monks of Casa Dei had held the place under an annual rent. When he repeatedly pressed this point, lest we should seem to inflict any injury upon him, we set a day for hearing the case at Montpellier, [Col. 1111C] where both parties appeared and presented their arguments. After these had been sufficiently examined, it was adjudged by the judgment of our brethren that the archbishop ought to be reinvested with the same church, if he could prove by competent witnesses that the Church of Arles had possessed that place before the judgment of our lord.

The judgment having been carried out, possession was immediately restored to him, while of course preserving whatever right the monastery of Aniane might have. A date was then fixed at which the right of ownership should be debated at Toulouse in the presence of both parties. Thus the question was raised in that council. The monks of Aniane claimed the cell through the written instruments and grants of Emperor Louis, son of Emperor Charlemagne, and of his son King Charles, as belonging to the monastery of Aniane. [Col. 1111D] The archbishop, however, relied upon a charter of Louis, son of Boso, king of Vienne.

The case having therefore been debated for some time before all, we instructed our brethren Cono of Palestrina and Lambert of Ostia, bishops and cardinals; Boso of Saint Anastasia, Deusdedit of Saint Lawrence in Damaso, and John of Saint Chrysogonus, priests; Peter of Saints Cosmas and Damian, Gregory of Saint Angelo, and Chrysogonus of Saint Nicholas in Carcere, deacons; the archbishops Oldegarius of Tarragona and Bernard of Auch; likewise the bishops Raymond of Barbastro, Guido of Lescar, Walter of Maguelone, and Golo of León; and the abbots Arduin of Saint-Savin and Amicus of Saint Lawrence Outside the Walls, [Col. 1112A] to withdraw apart and determine the controversy by canonical judgment.

Having left the council, the brethren deliberated among themselves at length. Finally, after arguments had been examined on both sides and the documentary evidence repeatedly reviewed, they delivered the following judgment before the hearing of the council: that the instruments of donation granted to the Church of Arles by the aforesaid King Louis, son of Boso, concerning the cell of Gordanicis, after the confirmations of Emperor Louis, son of Charlemagne, and of his son King Charles, possessed no force. For what had once been offered to God by some persons could not thereafter be bestowed upon others.

It was further added, in order to remove all doubt, that the monks of Aniane should prove by the testimony of three competent witnesses that the monastery of Aniane had possessed the cell of Gordanicis without lawful interruption for a period of thirty years before it was obtained by the monks of Casa Dei, through whom the Church of Arles had entered into possession. [Col. 1112B] Thus the same place was thereafter to remain in the right and possession of the monastery of Aniane.

The brothers—our archbishops, bishops, and abbots—acclaimed that this judgment was indeed pleasing to the whole council. At once the monks of Aniane brought forward three aged monks, who, having touched the most sacred Gospels, affirmed that the monks of Aniane had possessed the cell of Gordanicis for a period of thirty years without lawful interruption, before the monks of Casa Dei obtained it.

Therefore, the judgment issued by the brothers named above concerning the often-mentioned cell [Col. 1112C], and approved by the assent of the whole council, we, by God’s authority, confirm by the protection of our decree; and by the authority of the Apostolic See we utterly forbid any accusation or challenge concerning it to be brought against the monastery of Aniane in future.

Moreover, whatever the monastery of Aniane possesses through the authentic privileges of our predecessors John, Nicholas, Alexander, Urban, and Paschal, Roman pontiffs, we confirm to you and your successors forever. For that place stands in a special manner under the jurisdiction and protection of Blessed Peter.

The archbishop of Arles renounced the aforesaid cell of Gordanicis into our hand, by the staff which he carried, in the sight of the whole council [Col. 1112D]. Restoring it at once by that same staff to you, Pontius, most beloved son in Christ, and through you to the monastery of Aniane, we imposed perpetual silence, under obligation of anathema, upon both the Church of Arles and the monastery of Casa Dei regarding that cell. We also command that the documentary charters be returned to you by the archbishop and the monks of Casa Dei, lest any new ground for dispute arise through their occasion. If, therefore, in the future any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowingly opposing this page of our confirmation, should rashly attempt to act against it, then, having been warned a second and a third time, unless he makes due amends by suitable satisfaction, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and office; let him know that he stands guilty before the divine [Col. 1113A] judgment for the iniquity committed; let him be excluded from the sacrament of the body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, our Redeemer; and at the final judgment let him be subject to severe vengeance. But upon all who preserve what is due to that place may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that they may receive here the fruit of good action and find, before the strict Judge, the rewards of eternal peace. Amen, amen, amen.

I, Calixtus, bishop of the Catholic Church. I, Cono, bishop of Palestrina. Oldegarius, administrator of the Church of Tarragona. The sign of Raymond, bishop of Barbastro. I, Bernard, archbishop of Auch, have subscribed. [Col. 1113B] I, Lambert, bishop of Ostia. Richard, archbishop of Narbonne. I, Peter, cardinal of Saints Cosmas and Damian. I, Boso, cardinal-priest of the title of Saint Anastasia. I, Ato, bishop of Arles. I, Gregory, cardinal-deacon of Saint Angelo. I, Deusdedit, cardinal-priest of the title of Saint Lawrence in Damaso. I, Fulco, archbishop of Aix, have subscribed. I, Walter, bishop of Maguelonne. I, John, cardinal-priest of the title of Saint Chrysogonus, was present at and subscribed this judgment. I, Amicus, abbot of Saint Lawrence Outside the Walls. [Col. 1113C] I, Arduinus, abbot of Saint-Savin.

Given at Toulouse, through the hand of Chrysogonus, cardinal and librarian of the Holy Roman Church, on the Ides of July, in the twelfth indiction, in the year 1119 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the first year of the pontificate of Pope Lord Calixtus II.

## XXII. To B., provost, clergy, and people of Hildesheim  
*(1119, 15 July.)*

[Edited by Jaffé from a fifteenth-century Hildesheim manuscript preserved in the Royal Hanover archive: *Regesta pontificum Romanorum*, p. 529, with this notice: “Sent by H. Sudendorf, V.D.”]

[Col. 1113D]

To B., provost, clergy, and people of Hildesheim: greetings and the Apostolic blessing.

On the octave of the Apostles (6 July), we held at Toulouse a council with our brother archbishops, bishops, and abbots of the province of Goczie (Gaul?)—Gascony. There, by God’s grace, investiture was utterly condemned. Therefore, in visiting your whole community by a visitation of the Apostolic See, we request and command that you reject from among you the man who, through secular power, has seized your Church, and that within twenty days after receiving this letter you hasten to make a canonical election.

Given at Toulouse, on the Nones of June [read, apparently: the Ides of July].

## XXIII. To Berengar, abbot of the monastery of Crassus in Septimania, and his successors: he grants the church of Saint Peter of Valeries “at an annual rent of two gold pieces”  
*(1119, 20 July.)*

[Baluze, *Miscellanea*, Lucchesi edition, III, 13.]

[Col. 1114A]

Calixtus, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son Berengar, abbot of the monastery of Crassus: greetings and the Apostolic blessing.

Both the claim of justice and the order of reason admonish and compel us to provide, with fatherly care, for the destitution of churches—especially those which appear to belong in a special manner to the Apostolic See. Indeed, the church of Blessed Peter of Valeries, which belongs by right to the Holy Roman Church, has been worn down inwardly and outwardly and greatly diminished both in spiritual and temporal matters [Col. 1114B]. Therefore, providing for that place with due concern, we entrust it to you, beloved son in Christ, Abbot Berengar, and to your successors, to govern and administer at an annual rent of two gold pieces, together with all that belongs to it and with all the freedom and immunity which our predecessor, Pope Paschal of holy memory, is known to have granted it by the text of his privilege. This grant shall endure so long as you retain communion and favor with the Apostolic See and, by the Lord’s help, the discipline of monastic order flourishes in your monastery. For we trust in the mercy of almighty God and in your religious devotion that, through your diligence [Col. 1114C], that place ought, by God’s grace, to be restored to a state of religious observance and also increased in temporal resources. It is therefore your concern henceforth to remain more devotedly and earnestly in obedience and service to the Roman Church, and to take such care for the advancement of the place that, by God’s bounty, you may always be found more worthy of this favor. If any person should rashly—God forbid!—attempt to oppose this our commission, let him suffer the loss of his rank and office, or be punished by the penalty of excommunication, unless he corrects his presumption by worthy satisfaction.

I, Calixtus, bishop of the Catholic Church. I, John, cardinal-priest of the title of Saint Chrysogonus. I, Peter, cardinal-deacon of Saints Cosmas [Col. 1114D] and Damian.

Given at Saint-Théodard, through the hand of Chrysogonus, cardinal-deacon and librarian of the Holy Roman Church, on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of August, in the twelfth indiction, in the year 1119 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the first year of the pontificate of Pope Lord Calixtus II.

## XXIV. To the noblewoman Jussolina and her sons, of the same tenor as the preceding  
*(1119, 20 July.)*

[Baluze, *ibid.*]

Calixtus, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved daughter Jussolina, noblewoman, and her sons Peter [Col. 1115A] Sicardi and Rainard of Pérignan: greetings and the Apostolic blessing.

We give thanks to almighty God and to your nobility because, as good patrons, you have hitherto aided and supported the church of Blessed Peter of Valeries, which belongs by right to the Roman Church. We ask, however, that henceforth, by God’s grace, you do the same still better. For, grieving with due concern over the destruction of that place, we have entrusted it to our beloved son Berengar, abbot of Crassus, and his successors, to govern and administer, together with all its rights and possessions and with every freedom and immunity, as is contained in the privilege of Pope Paschal, our predecessor of holy memory. For we trust in the mercy of almighty God [Col. 1115B] that through his diligence that place may be restored both in spiritual and temporal matters. Therefore we again ask your affection, and enjoin it upon you for the remission of your sins, that according to the ability divinely granted you, you take care to aid and support the aforesaid church more fully. But if anyone should attempt to act against this our commission, defend that same place with the assistance of your protection. May almighty God, through the prayers of the blessed Apostles Peter and Paul, absolve you, as you perform deeds pleasing to Him, from all sins and bring you to eternal life. Amen.

Given at Saint-Théodard, on the thirteenth day before the Kalends [Col. 1115C] of August, in the twelfth indiction.

## XXV. Bull for Gerald, prior of the church of the blessed protomartyr Stephen at Cahors  
*(1119, 30 July.)*

[William de la Croix, *Series and Acts of the Bishops of Cahors*, p. 68.]

Calixtus, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons Gerald, prior, and his brethren professing the regular life in the church of the blessed protomartyr Stephen at Cahors, both present and future: greetings and the Apostolic blessing forever.

We have the Lord’s command: “Enter through the narrow gate, for narrow is the way that leads to life.” Therefore, since you, most beloved sons in Christ, inspired by divine grace, have resolved to restrain your conduct under the discipline of the regular life and, that you may be able to enter through the narrow gate, to serve almighty God together according to the institution of the holy Fathers [Col. 1115D], we rejoice in your vows with fatherly affection. Accordingly, already granting due assent to your petition with fitting kindness, we strengthen your purpose of religious life by the authority of this present privilege. For we decree that no person whatsoever may alter in your church the order of canonical life which you have professed. Nor may anyone of your profession, prompted by any impulse of levity or under the pretext of a stricter religious observance, leave his state without permission of the prior or congregation. If he leaves, no bishop, abbot, or monk [Col. 1116A] may receive him without the safeguard of letters issued jointly, so long as, by God’s help, the tenor of canonical order flourishes in your church. Furthermore, no one may be set over you as bishop, prior, archdeacon, or minister of any ecclesiastical dignity by any deceitful contrivance, cunning, or violence, unless he is regularly chosen, with the common consent of the brethren or the counsel of the sounder part of the brethren, in the fear of God. The election of archdeacons, made with the counsel of the prior and the sounder part of the chapter, shall be presented to the bishop, who shall give his assent to it when regularly made, for the honor of God and the support of the Church. But if any archdeacon should rashly—God forbid!—presume to oppose the canonical life or stubbornly to injure the common welfare of the house [Col. 1116B], and, having been canonically admonished, should disdain to make satisfaction, another shall be substituted in his place, and he shall remain quietly in the cloister with the other brethren.

Moreover, to you, beloved son in Christ, Prior Gerald, by the page of this present decree we confirm whatever right, honor, or reverence your predecessor Gosbert of blessed memory—founder in your church of the canonical order—is known, by reasonable provision, to have possessed in the discipline and ordering of the Church of Cahors. Further, by the privilege of Apostolic protection we safeguard all the brethren living the common life, with all the goods of those who now are or formerly were members; and we confirm to you and your successors the church of Saint Agapitus of Pairinihac, all the common property of the Church of Cahors, peacefully held and possessed hitherto down to these times [Col. 1116C], and all other things which our predecessors Popes Urban and Paschal II, of holy memory, are known to have confirmed in common to your church. Therefore no person whatsoever may rashly disturb that church, remove its possessions, retain what has been removed, diminish them, or harass them with reckless vexations; rather, all things shall remain intact for the benefit and use in every way of those for whose support they were granted, saving in all things the reverence due to the bishop of Cahors.

We also add this clause to the present chapter: the guarantee established in the Church of Cahors by Gerald, bishop of blessed memory, and confirmed by his successors, shall hereafter remain firm and inviolate—namely, that wherever they may be [Col. 1116D], unless perhaps they have been excommunicated for their own fault, they shall hear Mass on the second feria, and burial shall not be denied them when they die. If, therefore, any ecclesiastical or secular person in the future, knowing this page of our constitution, should attempt to act against it, then, having been warned a second or third time, unless he makes amends by suitable satisfaction, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and office; let him know that he is guilty before divine judgment for the iniquity committed; let him be excluded from the precious body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, our Redeemer; and at the final judgment let him be subject to severe vengeance. But upon all who preserve what is just for that place may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that they may receive here the fruit of good action [Col. 1117A] and find before the strict Judge the pledge of eternal peace. Amen.

I, Calixtus, bishop of the Catholic Church.

Given at Saint-Léonce, through the hand of Chrysogonus, cardinal-deacon and librarian of the Holy Roman Church, on the third day before the Kalends of August, in the twelfth indiction, in the year 1120 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the second year of the pontificate of Pope Lord Calixtus II.

## XXVI. To Henry, king of the English, concerning the settlement of the controversy over the primacy of the Church of York  
*(1119.)*

[*Monasticon Anglicanum*, III, 143.]

Calixtus, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his most beloved son in Christ Henry, illustrious king of the English [Col. 1117B]: greetings and the Apostolic blessing.

The question which has so long been debated concerning that profession between the archbishop of Canterbury and the elect of York is burdensome to the Apostolic See and brings no small injury upon the Church of York. Therefore we ask your nobility to permit these our brothers to come to the council to which we have summoned them, as we have already requested of the others, so that, by God’s authority, in our presence and that of our brethren, that long-standing question may receive its proper conclusion. If either of them should previously wish to visit us, grant him the same permission.

## XXVII. To Hervey, abbot of the monastery of Redon.—Let him restore to Quimperlé [Col. 1117C] the money taken from Belle-Île, or come to the Council of Reims to render an account  
*(1119, 3 August.)*

[Dom Bouquet, *Recueil*, XV, 231.]

Calixtus, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son Hervey, abbot of Redon: greetings and the Apostolic blessing.

We have received the complaint of Abbot Gurhand and the brethren of the monastery of Holy Cross at Quimperlé against you: that you have by no means restored to them the money from Belle-Île which you seized by violence. Judgment concerning this matter was rendered by our fellow brother Gerard of Angoulême, then legate of the Apostolic See. We therefore command your affection either to restore the money without delay [Col. 1117D], or, if you are confident that you have some right in the matter, to come to the Council of Reims, there to render a full account of it, the Lord granting.

Given at Périgueux, on the third day before the Nones of August.

## XXVIII. Bull for Guy, abbot of Turturiac  
*(1119, 5 August.)*

[*Gallia Christiana*, new edition, II, instruments, 491.]

Calixtus, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son Guy, abbot of Turturiac, and to his successors to be regularly appointed forever.

The monastery of Turturiac, built in his own allod for the honor of God and of the blessed Apostles Peter and Paul by Guy, viscount of blessed memory [Col. 1118A], is known to belong specially to the Roman Church by the offering of that viscount himself. Therefore we have decreed to protect it under the guardianship of Blessed Peter and to sustain it by the protection of the Apostolic See. Accordingly, to you and your successors, beloved son in Christ, Abbot Guy, and through you to that monastery, we confirm forever what you presently possess lawfully, whether by the gift of the aforesaid viscount or by any other acquisition: namely, the church of Saint Martin of Granges, with its tithes and other appurtenances; the church of Saint Stephen of Naillac; [lacuna] of Castris, in which the church of Saint John is contained; the church of Saint Trojan, with its tithes and appurtenances; the chapel of Château-Félix; the church of Saint Raphael the Archangel [Col. 1118B], with its appurtenances, and the gift which Peter Bertram, archpriest, made concerning the cemetery of that church into the hand of Bishop Rainald; the church of Saint John of Valentino, with their appurtenances; the church of Saint Raphael situated within the walls of the castle of Gelosium, as Bertram, bishop of Bazas, and his clerics delivered it to our [perhaps: your] monastery, together with its cemeteries situated within or outside the walls; the chapel of Saints Magnus and Medard, situated within the walls of the castle of Excidolium; the church of Saint Saturninus of Majac; the church of Saint Christopher of Saviniac; the church of Saint Michael of La Pendula; the church of Saint Eulalia; the church of Saint Martin of Boseira with its dependencies; the church [Col. 1118C] of Saint Pantaleon; the church of Saint Bartholomew of Bausens; the church of Saint Peter of Bars, with its tithes and dependencies; and the church of Saint Peter of Sarlhac. Moreover, whatever you may hereafter be able to acquire justly and canonically, by the Lord’s favor, through the grants of pontiffs, the liberality of princes, or the offerings of the faithful, shall remain firm and unimpaired for you and your successors.

We decree, therefore, that no person may rashly disturb the said monastery, take away its possessions, retain gifts already offered, diminish them, or harass them by reckless vexations; but all shall be preserved intact, for the benefit and use in every way of those for whose support and governance they were granted. Upon the death of the present abbot of this place [Col. 1118D], or of any of your successors, no one shall be placed there through any contrivance of deception or violence, except one whom the brethren by common consent, or the sounder part of the brethren by counsel, shall provide to be elected according to the fear of God and the Rule of Blessed Benedict. We also decree that the burial-ground of your monastery shall remain free according to ancient custom. As a token of this protection which you obtain from the Apostolic See, you shall pay one gold piece each year to the Lateran palace. If, therefore, in the future any archbishop, bishop, count, viscount, or any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowingly opposing this page of our constitution, should rashly attempt to act against it, then, having been warned a second and a third time, unless he makes amends by suitable satisfaction [Col. 1119A], let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and office; let him know that he is guilty before divine judgment for the iniquity committed; let him be excluded from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, our Redeemer; and let him be subject to the judgment of severe vengeance. But upon all who preserve what is just for that place may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that they may receive here the fruit of good action and find before the strict Judge the rewards of eternal peace. Amen [lacuna].

Below may be seen the pope’s seal, on which is written—and on the reverse side—“Pope Calixtus II.” Around the circumference of the seal [Col. 1119B]: “The Lord is the support of those who fear him.” Near the seal the supreme pontiff subscribed thus: “I, Calixtus, bishop of the Catholic Church.” The papal bull closes with these words: “Given at Périgueux, through the hand of Chrysogonus, cardinal-deacon of the Holy Roman Church and librarian and archivist, on the Nones of August, in the twelfth indiction, in the year one thousand one hundred and twenty of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the first year of the pontificate of Pope Lord Calixtus II.”

## XXIX. Extract from a bull of Pope Calixtus II for the Most Holy Trinity of Poitiers  
*(1119, August–September.)*

[*Gallia Christiana*, new edition, II, instruments, 362.]

Pope Calixtus confirms to Abbess Elizabeth of the Poitiers monastery of the Most Holy Trinity [Col. 1119C] the goods of the monastery: namely, the church of Saint Peter of Camberria, with its tithe; the church of Saint Martin of Pailet, with its tithe; the church of Saint Julian, with its court; the church of Saint Nicholas of the Cursed Meadow, with its court; the church of Saint Peter of Secondignec, with its court; the church of Saint Maximus of Contre, with its court; the church of Saint Hilary of Villafolet, with its court; the church of Saints Gervasius and Protasius, with its court; the church of Saint Mary of La Forest, in its entirety; the church of Saint Mary of Murnai, in its entirety; the church of Saint Gregory in the suburb of Poitiers, in its entirety; the church of Saint Pelagius in the suburb, in its entirety; and, within the city of Poitiers itself [Col. 1119D], the girls’ monastery of Saint Peter, in its entirety. Thus too the cellarer shall receive his office, and the canons their prebends, from the hand of the abbess in chapter; and they shall render in full to the monastery and abbess the service due and obedience, as they are known to have done hitherto.

Given at Poitiers, through the hand of Chrysogonus, cardinal-deacon and librarian of the Holy Roman Church, on the fifth day before the Kalends of September, in the twelfth indiction, in the year 1119 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the first year of Calixtus II.

## XXX. Bull for the abbey of Saint Vincent of Senlis  
*(1119, 3 September.)*

[*Gallia Christiana*, X, instruments, 210.]

Calixtus, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son Baldwin, abbot of the church of Saint Vincent [Col. 1120A]: greetings and the Apostolic blessing.

We have learned that the church of Saint Vincent in the suburb of Senlis, on royal land, was founded by Philip, king of the Franks, and his mother Anne, endowed with many possessions, and granted every freedom after the model of the royal churches of Saint Geneviève of Paris and Saint Frambald of Senlis. Seeing with the eye of pity and mercy, in the time of our apostolate, that this church had been reduced through the negligence of its inhabitants to utter misery, we received it under the protection of Blessed Peter and, by the authority of the Apostolic dignity, confirm the liberties which it lawfully holds, so that it may always hold them. Thus that church shall remain in complete freedom, together with its precinct, all its guests [Col. 1120B], and its servants; and, recovering from them offerings, tithes, and all revenues belonging to it by right, its clerics shall endeavor honorably and solemnly to fulfill the offices of Christian ministry. We command, moreover, that regular clerics under the profession of Saint Augustine serve God perpetually in that church. Forbidding under anathema anyone to presume to alter or disturb that order, we enjoin upon all faithful persons who desire to bestow good gifts upon them for devotion’s sake that they do so for the remission of their sins. But to you, son Baldwin, to whom the care and responsibility of the aforesaid church has been entrusted, we grant by the authority and dignity of the Apostolic See that, in whatever bishopric they may be, you may freely reclaim and by every means recover the possessions of the church which wrongdoers or secular powers have seized from you during the time of your predecessors [Col. 1120C]. Their presumption in invasion shall not prevail against you, because the authority of a just and royal gift prevails for you and your church. In the churches of Blessed Mary, Saint Regulus, Saint Frambald, and Saint Evremund of Credulio, we command that the clerics of the same church receive without distinction the canonical share of all revenues. We forbid under anathema anyone to presume to injure the aforesaid church, and we bestow the grace of the Apostolic blessing on all who preserve what is just for that place.

Given at Saint-Florentin (in the diocese of Sens), on the third day before the Nones of September.

## XXXI. To [Turgid], bishop of Avranches, and [Hildebert], bishop of Le Mans, etc.—He commends to them the monastery of Savigny  
*(1119, 9 September.)*

[Martène, *Amplissima Collectio*, I, 659.]

[Col. 1120D]

Calixtus, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the venerable brethren the bishops of Avranches and Le Mans, to the count of Mortain, and to the lords of the castles of Fougères, Mayenne, and Saint-Hilaire: greetings and the Apostolic blessing.

We inform your affection that we have received our beloved son Vitalis, a wise and religious man, abbot of Holy Trinity at Savigny, and his monastery [Col. 1121A], under the guardianship and patronage of Blessed Peter. That place also, as we have learned, is venerable, and the observance of monastic religious life is maintained there by God’s grace. We therefore ask, admonish, and command your charity that, for reverence toward Blessed Peter and love for us, you henceforth take greater care to love and aid that monastery with all that belongs to it, and the brethren serving the Lord there, and vigorously defend them according to the ability granted you by the Lord. But if any person should perhaps—God forbid!—presume to diminish, remove, or disturb the goods of the aforesaid monastery, let him be struck by a sentence of excommunication until he has made satisfaction. But whoever takes care to help that place and honor it with his goods shall obtain the blessing and grace of almighty God [Col. 1121B] and His Apostles, and forgiveness of his sins.

Given at Angers, on the fifth day before the Ides of September.

## XXXII. He confirms the possessions and privileges of the nunnery of Saint Mary of Fontevraud  
*(1119, 15 September.)*

[*Gallia Christiana*, new edition, II, 1314, in the text.]

Calixtus, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved daughter Petronilla, abbess of the monastery of Saint Mary of Fontevraud, and to those who shall regularly succeed her in the same office forever.

As we were passing through the diocese of Poitiers in the service of the Church, at the suggestion of our venerable brother William, bishop of Poitiers [Col. 1121C], we turned aside to the monastery of Blessed Mary of Fontevraud. There, having learned that the discipline of monastic order flourished through the mercy of almighty God, we decreed to sustain that place, together with all belonging to it, under the patronage of Blessed Peter. Accordingly, with our own hands—as though they were the hands of Blessed Peter—we dedicated, in honor of the most blessed and most glorious Mother of God and ever-virgin Mary, the oratory; consecrating its altar with relics of the blessed martyrs Felix and Adauctus, Saturninus and Sisinnius, and of Blessed Cecilia, virgin, which were kept in our archives. When all had been solemnly celebrated, with God’s assistance, we addressed in the customary manner the people, whose multitude had poured thither from every direction [Col. 1121D]. Taking more careful notice of their devotion, by the authority of almighty God and of Blessed Peter—whose office, though unworthy, we exercise in the Church—we remitted one year of their penances to all who had come to the dedication and had been under penance for four years or more; but to those under penance for three years or less, forty days. We decree the same also concerning those who, from the beginning of the fast until the octave of Easter in subsequent years, so long as the order of monastic religious life flourishes in that place, take care to visit the monastery with due devotion and to assist it from their resources.

Moreover, through the kindness of the Apostolic See, we endowed the aforesaid abbey with this immunity: that all [Col. 1122A] the space enclosed around it by crosses set up at our command shall hereafter remain externally undisturbed and inviolate. Thus anyone who within it kills or wounds a person, makes plunder, or commits any grave offence, shall be regarded as guilty of sacrilege until he makes satisfaction. On the following day, entering the chapter house in the fuller assembly of both brothers and sisters, we judged ratified and ordered to be observed inviolate the precepts of Robert, priest of Arbrissel, of venerable memory, founder both of the place and of its religious observance. We decree in every respect that all faithful persons who, for the salvation of their souls, have vowed—or shall in future vow—to persevere in the service of God and of your church, either at your monastery or in places belonging to it, shall persevere in that good purpose; and that, according to the direction and obedience of the abbess of that place, or of the prioresses appointed in places belonging to the monastery of Fontevraud, they shall faithfully and religiously serve the sisters in honor of God [Col. 1122B], as is known to have been instituted by the aforesaid Robert, priest of Arbrissel, of blessed memory.

To enable you to render to almighty God the services due to Him more peacefully and more devoutly, we have judged that the possessions and places of your monastery should be protected by the privilege of the Apostolic See against the malice of wicked men. Therefore, we confirm in perpetuity to your monastery all that you now lawfully possess in the thirteenth indiction, or may in future be able to acquire by grants of pontiffs, the liberality of princes, offerings of the faithful, [Col. 1122C] or other just means.

Namely, the place of Agreria, by the gift of Berlay of Montreuil, Rainald son of Hugh, and Fulk Fexard; the place of Raalai, by the gift of Rainaud of Salmuntiachaico; the place of Cavanaici, by the gift of Aimery of Bernezaico and Gironius son of Gainer; the place of Gaina, by the gift of Ralph of Saint-Jean, Stephen of Maixime (Messemé) [Note: [Col. 1121D] From this Stephen the noble lords of Messemé derive their origin.], and his son Parcend [Aimery]; the place of Mongoguier, by the gift of Aimery Flocel; the place of Varentis, by the gift of Pagan of Nozilliac; the place of Cantaloup, by the gift of Fulk the Younger, count of Anjou; the place of Sovolie, by the gift of Peter of Brissac; the place of Gironde, by the gift of Rainaud of Piollant, Solomon, man of the viscountess [Col. 1122D] of Château-Ayrald, and Hugh of Vivonne; the place of Bois-Rotard, by the gift of Fulk, count of Anjou, and Lisiard of Sabrol; the place of Mauthaici, by the gift of Auberet of Mont-Jean; the places of Lajaria and Chevrerii, by the gift of William of Mirembel; the place of Astrici, by the gift of Reemffreia and her sons Peter Achard and Airaud; the place of Podiae, by the gift of Peter Senebaut; the place of Villesalem, by the gift of Geoffrey Gastinel; the place of Preth, by the gift of Cothard and his son; the place of Flathaici, by the gift of Geoffrey of Emglis; and the place of Landa of Belloveerio, by the gift of Peter of Gasnachia, his brother Gothelin, and their nephew Peter of Thoucia.

The place of Lagrola, by the gift of [Col. 1123A] Brientius of Comiquers and his brothers; the place of Landa d’Apremonte, by the gift of William and his brother of Asperomonte; the place of Landa of Machecol, by the gift of Garsius of Raes; the place of Jafras, by the gift of Ralph Maliclavi and Isdercius; the place of Dentis, by the gift of Giraud of Sostei, his son Arbert, and William of Roccafort; the place of Tucio, by the gift of Fulcaud Frenicard and his brother Aimery, Bernard Cantagrel and his brother Aimery Aimarivillanus, Dalmatius of Mont-Borulf, and Aimery of Rancon, from whose fief it was held—free and undisturbed in the same manner as is contained in the ruling of our venerable brother Gerald, bishop of Angoulême, then legate of the Apostolic See, and in the privilege of our lord predecessor Pope Paschal II, of holy memory.

The place of La Gasconeria, [Col. 1123B] by the gift of Arbert of Burno, William of Cella, and William of Borno; the place of Arblenth, by the gift of William Aimery; the place of Montazesum, by the gift of Aimery Bernard; the place of Aufoillos; the place of Conoul; the place of Lobilleri, by the gift of Peter of Vars and his brother; the place of Calumme, or the Count’s Wood, by the gift of Simon Avisant, with the consent of Fulk, count of Anjou; the place of Saint Boniface, by the gift of Peter, bishop of Poitiers, and the chapter of the monks of Saint-Cyprian; the place of Ajars, or Adarci, at Mont-Saint-Jean, by the gift of Stephen of Magnac; the place of Bobun, by the gift of Peter of Montifreebo, Iterius Bernard, and Aimery Brun; the place of Argenteria, by the gift of Milesendis of the New Monastery. These three places last named are in the diocese of Limoges.

In the diocese [Col. 1123C] of Bourges: the place of Ursani, and the places of Parthaici and Villulae, by the gift of Aalard Guillebaud; the place of Jarzaici, by the gift of Hubert of Barsella and his mother Saturnina; the place of Villebratae, by the gift of Rainaud of Scurels and Roger Senescau; the place of Letardi, by the gift of Erchembaud of Borbum; the place of Montaudun, by the gift of Giraud of Corb. and Giraud Coraus; the place of Villa Osmeri, by the gift of Arveus the priest and his brother Achaud; the place of the villa of Corb., by the gift of Geoffrey of Blanqueffort, Guimonsbed, and Supplicius of Concartau; the place of Dry Plum-grove, by the gift of Supplicius of Concartau, Agnes, countess of Assis, and Guimunsbeth; the place of Marthauges, by the gift of Ralph Becuns, his wife Elisabeth, and their children; the place of Funuernum, by the gift of Agnes, countess [Col. 1123D] Dosassis; the place of Funtarcherii, by the gift of Patrick of Brulleio; the place of Saugosa, by the gift of John of Lineriis and Hugh of the monastery; the place of Taes, by the gift of John of Lineriis; and the place of Molins, by the gift of Odo of Duis.

In the diocese of Tours: the place of Raleii, by the gift of Pagan of Mirambel, his wife Belutia, and their sons; the place of Calfurneii, by the gift of Leo, his wife, and son; the place of Laruncia, by the gift of Oger the Smith, William of Tisthai, and all their brothers; the place of Columberols, by the gift of Rainaud Rufus and Gautherius-Jesu; the place of Barba Nova, by the gift of Fulk the Younger, count of Anjou; the place of Beffos, by the gift of Bartholomew son of Rahard and Gili of Mota; the place of Vallissicard, by the gift of Audeburgis of [Col. 1124A] Montreuil; and the place of Pissabo, by the gift of William of Rullei. These two places last named are in the land of Le Mans.

The place of Choseaci, by the gift of Aubert of Liger and many others, with the consent of Fulk, count of Anjou; the mills, weir of Chinon, meadows of Verrom, land of Doe, and its meadows and rents, by the gift of Fulk the Younger, count of Anjou; the port of Challeii, by the gift of the young man Alon and his brother, in Anjou; the port of Rest, its rent, tithe, and wine-tax, by the gift of Geoffrey Fulcrei; the place of Logias, by the gift of Sanita and Robert’s son; the place of Curleo, by the gift of Hersendis and her son Stephen of Montsoreau; the place of Chanzellas, by the gift of Girorius of Chinziac, Galeth and Hugh, two brothers, and their mothers and sisters; [Col. 1124B] the place of Borennas, by the gift of Fulk the Younger, count of Anjou; the place of Pignoneria, the land of Arcalors, and the land of Peter of Mont-Seibert; the land and rents of Fulk which the church of Fontevraud bought, with the count’s consent; the land which Adam held at Pignoneria from Achaia as far as Anjou, by the gift of Adam himself, through the hand of Bishop Rainaud, with the consent of the count and countess, together with the charitable gift made by Abbess Petronilla, his kinswoman; the place of Saint-Calais, by the gift of Chalon of Blazon; the place of Perillera, by the gift of Philip of Blazon and his wife; also the wood and meadows which he held from Roho Wood as far as Alodia; the place of Segnes, by the gift of Griscia of Doe and her son; the place of Escoblant, by the gift of Oger, Martrerius, and his son Deri; the place [Col. 1124C] of Saint Mary of the Hospice near Orléans, by the gift of the bishop of Orléans, the chapter of the canons of Holy Cross, and Louis, king of France; Clos Auberi, by the gift of Louis, king of France; the place of Haute-Bruyère, by the gift of the aforesaid king and of his stepmother Bertrea, from whose dower it was, and those things which King Philip had given her at Tours as dower, with the consent of King Louis and his wife.

Therefore we decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the same monastery, take away its possessions, retain what has been taken, diminish them, or harass it with reckless vexations; but that all things be preserved whole, for the benefit in every way of those for whose support and governance they were granted. If, therefore, in the future any ecclesiastical or secular person, etc.

[Col. 1124D] Given at Tours, at Marmoutier, through the hand of Grisogonus, cardinal-deacon and librarian of the holy Roman Church, on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of October, in the thirteenth indiction, in the year 1119 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the first year of the pontificate of Pope Calixtus II.

### XXXIII. He confirms the possessions of the monastery of Saints Peter, Paul, and Ghislain at Celles. (3 October 1119.)

[REIFFENBERG, *Monuments pour servir à l'histoire des provinces de Namur, de Hainaut et de Luxembourg*. Brussels, 1844, vol. VIII, p. 345.]

### XXXIV. He confirms the privileges of the monastery of Vendôme. (8 October 1119.)

[MANSI, *Concilia*, XXI, 195.]

[Col. 1125A]

**CALIXTUS**, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son **GOFFREY**, abbot of the monastery of Vendôme, and to his successors regularly appointed in perpetuity.

Although by the authority and benevolence of the Apostolic See we acknowledge ourselves indebted to all the children of holy Church [addition: “we”; perhaps read: “we acknowledge ourselves”], yet toward those places and persons which adhere more especially and intimately to the Roman Church, we ought to show a more earnest devotion of charity. Therefore, dearest son in Christ, Abbot Geoffrey, we have rightly judged that your petitions [Col. 1125B] should be granted: namely, that we should protect with a privilege of the Apostolic See the monastery of Vendôme over which, by God’s authority, you preside, and which was offered to the Apostolic See by its founders themselves, Geoffrey, count of Anjou, and Agnes, countess of Poitou, following the example of our predecessors of holy memory, Alexander, Urban, and Paschal, Roman pontiffs.

Accordingly, as the same founders vowed and as is contained in their charter, we decree that the same monastery shall always remain, under the defense of the Apostolic See and Roman freedom, released and free from every jurisdiction of other persons. That is, [Col. 1125C] no person whatsoever, of whatever dignity or order, shall be considered an intermediary between the Roman pontiff and you and your successors. Nor shall the abbot of Vendôme ever be compelled to attend a council at which the pope is not personally present.

Moreover, we confirm to you and your successors, with all the dignity pertaining to it, the church of Blessed Prisca on the Aventine Hill, which your predecessors are known to have possessed for a long time, together with all its appurtenances, by the grant of our aforesaid lord Pope Alexander. By the judgment of the Holy Spirit we decree that henceforth no ecclesiastical or secular person may presume, by any craft or pretext, to take from you or your successors the aforesaid church of Blessed Prisca or its dignity.

Should it happen that a legate of the Roman Church visits the aforesaid monastery [Col. 1125D] of Vendôme, he shall be received there charitably and shall carefully be supplied, according to the means of the place, with the necessities of the body. But that legate shall not presume to order or correct anything there on his own authority, nor, under pretext of his legation, to trouble the superior of the place or the brethren. If he discovers anything that requires correction, he may report it to the pope. If anyone wishes to bring a case against that place concerning any matter, neither the abbot nor the brethren shall answer him in any way before consulting the Roman pontiff, because whatever is alienated or decided without our judgment or that of our successors shall be void.

Further, as a sign of this liberty received from the Roman Church, you shall pay annually to the Lateran palace twelve solidi in the currency of your country.

[Col. 1126A] If, therefore, in the future any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowingly violating this page of our constitution, rashly attempts to act against it, and, having been warned a second and third time, does not make amends by suitable satisfaction, let that person be deprived of the dignity of power and honour, know himself or herself guilty before the divine judgment of the iniquity committed, be cut off from the most sacred body and blood of God and Lord, our Redeemer Jesus Christ, and be subject to strict vengeance at the last judgment. But upon all who preserve what is right for that place, may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that they may receive here the fruit of good action and find before the strict Judge the rewards of eternal peace. Amen.

I, Calixtus, bishop of the Catholic Church, have subscribed.

[Col. 1126B] Given at Paris, through the hand of Chrysogonus, cardinal-deacon and librarian of the holy Roman Church, on the eighth day before the Ides of October, in the thirteenth indiction, in the year 1119 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the first year of the pontificate of Pope Calixtus II.

### XXXV. Privilege for the abbey of Saint-Denis, near Paris. (13 October 1119.)

[DOUBLET, *Histoire de l'abbaye de Saint-Denis*, p. 477.]

**CALIXTUS**, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son Adam, abbot of the venerable monastery situated near Paris in honour of the blessed martyr Dionysius, [Col. 1126C] and to his successors regularly appointed in perpetuity.

A pious request should be pursued and fulfilled with willing affection, so that the sincerity of devotion may shine forth laudably and the benefit sought may assuredly obtain its force. Therefore, since your belovedness has fled to the haven of the Apostolic See and has sought its protection with due devotion, we mercifully grant your petition and receive under the protection of the Apostolic See the venerable monastery of the blessed martyr Dionysius, over which, by God’s authority, you preside, together with all that belongs to it.

By the page of this present privilege, we decree by apostolic authority that whatever liberty and whatever dignity has been granted by the authentic privileges of our predecessors Zacharias, Stephen, [Col. 1126D] Leo, and Alexander II; whatever goods are known to belong to that monastery through the lawful offerings of Catholic kings or other faithful persons; and whatever it may in future be able to acquire justly and canonically by grants of pontiffs, the liberality of princes, or offerings of the faithful, shall remain firm and unimpaired to you and your successors.

Therefore we decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the same monastery, take away its possessions, retain what has been taken, diminish them, or harass it with reckless vexations; but that all things be preserved whole, for the benefit in every way of those for whose support and governance they were granted.
