Upon the death of you, the present abbot of that place, or of any of your successors, no one shall be set over it [Col. 1127A] by any intrigue, craft, or violence, except one whom the brethren by common consent, or the sounder part of the brethren’s counsel, shall elect according to the fear of God and the Rule of Blessed Benedict. The person elected shall be consecrated by the Roman pontiff, or by whatever Catholic bishop he prefers.

You shall receive chrism, holy oil, consecrations of altars and churches, and the ordinations of monks or clerics belonging to the same monastery, from Catholic bishops, as has been established by privileges of canonical equity issued by our predecessors. We forbid public masses to be celebrated or a station to be held in that monastery without the abbot’s consent; nor do we permit bishops or their officials to interdict, excommunicate, summon to synod, either the abbot or the monks [Col. 1127B] of that place.

Furthermore, we grant both you and your successors leave to appeal to the Apostolic See in more serious matters; nor shall any injury befall those who appeal before the conclusion of the case, so that, by God’s help, you may remain peaceful and diligent in the pursuits of holy religion.

If, moreover, any ecclesiastical or secular person knowingly attempts to violate this page of our constitution, and, having been warned a second and third time, does not make amends by suitable satisfaction, let that person be deprived of the dignity of power and honour, know himself or herself guilty before the divine judgment of the iniquity committed, be cut off from the most sacred body and blood of God and our Lord Jesus Christ, and be subject to strict vengeance at the last judgment. [Col. 1127C] But upon all who preserve what is right for that place, may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that they may receive here the fruit of good action and find before the strict Judge the rewards of eternal peace. Amen.

Written through the hand of Peter, notary of the region and registrar of the sacred palace.

I, Calixtus, bishop of the Catholic Church, have subscribed.

Given at Senlis, through the hand of Grisogonus, cardinal-deacon and librarian of the holy Roman Church, on the third day before the Ides of October, in the thirteenth indiction, in the year 1119 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the first year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Calixtus II.

### XXXVI. He enumerates and confirms the possessions of the abbey of Bourbourg, a convent of noble Benedictine nuns newly founded by his sister Clementia, duchess of Burgundy. (22 October 1119.)

[MIRAEUS, *Opera diplomatica*, IV, 8.]

[Col. 1127D]

**CALIXTUS**, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved daughter **GODILDIS**, abbess of the monastery of Saint Mary at Bourbourg, and to those who shall regularly succeed her in the same office, in perpetuity.

Just as no effect should be granted to those seeking what is unjust, so the petition of those desiring what is lawful should not be delayed. Therefore, beloved daughter in Christ, Abbess Godildis, granting the petitions both of you and of our dearest sister Clementia, countess of Flanders, founder of that [Col. 1128A] place, we receive under the protection of the Apostolic See the monastery of Blessed Mary at Bourbourg, over which, by God’s authority, you preside, and fortify it with the patronage of Blessed Peter.

We decree that the same monastery shall always remain, by God’s grace, free from every episcopal exaction and every secular burden, peaceful and undisturbed.

Moreover, all things granted to that place from their own right by the aforesaid countess, her husband Robert and her son Baldwin, counts, or by any other faithful persons; all things acquired through your diligence; and all things which, God granting, may in future be offered or acquired by other means, shall be preserved firm and unimpaired in perpetuity. Among these we have thought fit to record the following by their proper names:

One sheep-farm, called Bonhem, in the parish of Saint Folquin, with all land that may thereafter be added there.

One sheep-farm in the village of Lon. One sheep-farm in the village of Slipi, on the river Satha. New land on the river Yser, between the land of Saint Walburga and Lamine Chinescuot, and whatever land may thereafter be added there. A sheep-farm.

The altar-right of Fersnara [otherwise Varssenaere near Bruges]; one mill on the Lodic. At Diksmuide, half the revenues from all the mills which are there now or may later be there. Crumadicuet and Paleendic, with their revenues. In the parish called Saint Peter’s Brug, five *ren.*; at Clarambaldibruc [Col. 1128C] land with twelve cows. The land of Folquin son of Walger. The land of Robert son of Hugh of Paris, with twenty-one cows.

In the parish of Erembald’s Chapel, land with twenty-one cows. New land, now made from marsh, between the church of Watten and Bourbourg, with its tithe, and the whole tithe of land that may later arise from that same marsh. Tithes of the new land of Castellan Tinard. The land of Baldwin Taxard in the parish of Bulingosela. Sixty-six jugera of land at Stapla.

Five holdings of Ruhault land in the parish of Ferlingehem. The land of Petrihout, with its tithe. The land of Godin, with its tithe. Tithes of new land at Pevile, both cultivated and to be cultivated; likewise, twenty jugera of land in the parish of Chilhem. Land rendering [Col. 1128D] forty *hod.* of oats. The land of Dodo and his wife Gisla.

In the parish of Loberga, fifty-five jugera of land. At Winningosele, thirty jugera of land. At Greveninga, one *lasallecum*. At Bourbourg, one measure of eels. At Lon, one measure of butter. Old land adjoining the church of Saint Mary itself, with its tithe. Also the benefices granted to your church by nuns of your religious profession: namely, at Rubrus, one fourth of the tithe; at Bulingasela, Berwald’s land; in the neighbouring village of Crumbecca, ninety jugera of land; at Popringahem, twenty jugera; likewise, at Bulingasela, the land of Alumi, Blitingari, and Tidinari.

At Siger’s chapel, the land of King Alfer; in the parish [Col. 1129A] of Saint Folquin, forty jugera of land, by the gift of Geoffrey of Cassel. Likewise, in the parish of Saint Folquin, eighteen jugera by the gift of Emma. In the parish of Bourbourg, three jugera and the holding of Godinarius the provost.

At Schalcleta, one holding of land. At Affinga, twenty jugera. At Bourbourg and Craiawic, twenty jugera. In Orphans’ Land, twenty-eight jugera. At Piticham, Robert’s land and twenty *hod.* of oats. At the chapel of Aeggefrid, fourteen and a half jugera. All the land and property of Hildegard, wife of Baldwin.

At Druicham, twenty-six jugera and the land of Proiastra.

Therefore we decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the same monastery, take away its possessions, retain what has been taken, diminish [Col. 1129B] them, or harass it with reckless vexations; but that all things be preserved whole, for the benefit in every way of those for whose support and governance they were granted, saving the canonical reverence due to the bishop of Thérouanne.

Upon the death of the abbess of this place, no one shall be set over it by any intrigue, craft, or violence, except one whom the sisters, by common consent or by the sounder part of their counsel, shall provide to be regularly elected according to the fear of God.

In addition, we decree that, whenever the episcopal parish has been interdicted from divine offices, you may celebrate divine offices behind closed doors, provided that those under interdict or excommunication are in no way admitted.

[Col. 1129C] Moreover, clerics or laypersons living in the secular condition, who are bound within the enclosure of the cloister to the diligent service of your church, shall answer only to the abbess concerning their transgressions.

We further add that anyone wishing, for the sake of religion, to devote himself or herself, or his or her possessions, to your church shall not be forcibly or unjustly prevented by anyone.

If, therefore, in the future any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowingly attempting rashly to violate this page of our constitution, and, having been warned a second and third time, does not make amends by suitable satisfaction, let that person be deprived of the dignity of power and honour, know himself or herself guilty before the divine judgment of the iniquity committed, be cut off from the most sacred body and [Col. 1129D] blood of God and of our Lord and Redeemer Jesus Christ, and be subject to strict vengeance at the last judgment. But upon all who preserve what is right for that place, may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that they may receive here the fruit of good action and find before the strict Judge the rewards of eternal peace. Amen.

+ I, Calixtus, bishop of the Catholic Church.

Given at Rheims, through the hand of Grisogonus, cardinal-deacon and librarian of the holy Roman Church, on the eleventh day before the Kalends of November, in the thirteenth indiction, in the year 1119 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the first year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Calixtus II.

### XXXVII. To Codebald, bishop of Utrecht.—He grants him the episcopal mitre. (30 October 1119.)

[HEDA, *Historia episcoporum Ultrajectensium*, p. 148.]

[Col. 1130A]

**CALIXTUS**, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother **GODEBALD**, bishop of Utrecht, greeting and apostolic blessing.

We had hoped that you yourself would be present at the council. Yet, as we learned from the statement of your brethren whom you sent to us, you were prevented by God on the journey, so that you could by no means reach us without grave danger. For this reason, out of paternal affection, we excuse your absence, trusting that henceforth you ought faithfully to persevere, according to your ability, in the service of God and of your Church. As for those provosts who, though invited by you in your place, did not appear at the council, we commit them to your judgment, so that you may execute canonical justice upon them; for whatever you do in this matter, with the Lord’s aid, we shall hold ratified.

Furthermore, for reverence toward the Church entrusted to you, and because of the affection of our long-standing mutual love, we grant that the episcopal mitre shall be conferred upon you and your successors.

Given at Rheims, on the third day before the Kalends of November, in the thirteenth indiction, in the year 1120.

### XXXVIII. He receives the monastery of Murbach under protection and confirms its privileges. (30 October 1119.)

[WURTWEIN, *Nova Subsidia diplomatica*, Heidelberg, 1781, 8vo, vol. VII, p. 33.]

[Col. 1130C]

**CALIXTUS**, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons in Christ, those professing the canonical life in the Church of Murbach, and to their successors who, by the grace of almighty God, shall remain in the same religious observance in perpetuity.

The authority of our office urges us to be solicitous for the condition of churches and to strengthen what has been rightly established. Therefore we readily grant the petitions of our venerable son Gerung, your provost. Following in the footsteps of our predecessors, namely Urban II and Paschal [Col. 1130D] II, of holy memory, we receive both you and all your possessions under the protection of the Apostolic See and fortify you by the authority of this present privilege.

Whatever they granted you for the liberty of your place and the protection of your religious observance, we likewise grant and confirm: namely, that whatever your church now lawfully possesses, or may in future lawfully and canonically acquire, shall remain firm and unimpaired to you and your successors. Furthermore, whatever freedom was granted to your church by the canonical equity of those our aforesaid predecessors—whether in the election of your superior, the stability of those professing under him, the reception of all sacraments, or other matters suitable to the canonical religious profession and its stability—we establish also by the page of this present writing.

In addition, we forbid any assault, under whatever pretext, within the precinct of your monastery. If, however—God forbid!—violence should happen to be inflicted in your courtyard, whether by the shedding of blood, by violent speech, or in some similar manner, your church shall by no means on that account be prohibited from the divine offices. We further decree that the tithes of your labours and of animals which are cultivated or reared near that place itself at your own expense and labour shall remain free and unimpaired to you; nor do we permit you to be troubled concerning this by the bishop of that diocese, his officials, or parish priests.

For those who live the common life, as blessed Gregory writes [Col. 1131B] to Augustine, bishop of Canterbury, there is now no need for us to speak concerning portions to be made, hospitality to be shown, or mercy to be fulfilled, since all that remains over must be expended upon pious and religious causes.

We also decree that the burial-place of that monastery shall be entirely free, so that no one may oppose the devotion and last will of those who have decided to be buried there, unless they are excommunicated. Moreover, no opposition by any bishop or provost shall prevent you from receiving clerics or laypersons living secularly for conversion. If anyone knowingly attempts rashly to contravene the tenor of this decree, let him be punished by the judgment of Peter, prince of the apostles, and by ours. But upon those who preserve these provisions may peace and mercy from God be preserved for everlasting ages. Amen, amen, amen.

I, Calixtus, bishop of the Catholic Church.

Given at Rheims, through the hand of Grisogonus, cardinal-deacon and librarian of the holy Roman Church, on the third day before the Kalends of November, in the thirteenth indiction, in the year 1119 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the first year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Calixtus II.

### XXXIX. He confirms the privileges of the Church of Saint Martin of Tours. (30 October 1119.)

[*Défense de l’insigne église de Saint-Martin de Tours*, folio edition, documentary proofs, p. 14.]

**CALIXTUS**, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved [Col. 1131D] sons in Christ, the canons of the Church of Blessed Martin of Tours, present and future, apostolic blessing.

Although by the authority and benevolence of the Apostolic See we acknowledge ourselves indebted to all the children of the Church, yet toward those places and persons which adhere more especially to the Roman Church we ought to show a more earnest devotion of affection. Therefore, dearest sons in Christ, granting your petitions all the more willingly, we fortify with the protection of the Apostolic See the Church of Blessed Martin in which you serve almighty God, because that place is especially renowned for the body of the most blessed confessor of Christ [Col. 1132A] and is known to belong by right to the Roman Church.

Whatever liberty, immunity, benefice, or honour has been bestowed upon that church, whether through the privileges of our predecessors, the Roman pontiffs Adeodatus, Leo, Adrian, Sergius, Gregory, and Paschal; through the writings of the archbishops of Tours, Crotbert, Ivo, and Airard; or through royal charters, we confirm, by the page of this present privilege, to you and your successors and through us to the aforesaid Church of Blessed Martin. We decree that your cloister shall remain free and undisturbed as far as the buttresses of the wall, as it is known hitherto to have remained.

The priests dwelling within the precinct of the church in their cells, in your oratories, in the church of Saint Venant, and in the chapel of Saint Peter called de Cardonet, shall likewise remain in the liberty in which they are known to have remained in former times. Furthermore, the borough, and all other things contained in King Louis’s charter—the church of Saint Paul of Cormery, the church of Saint Mary of Bellomont, the church of Saint Cosmas with their dependencies—and all other things which you now lawfully possess or may in future, by the Lord’s gift, lawfully acquire, shall be preserved firm and unimpaired to you and your successors.

No person whatsoever may therefore rashly disturb that church, take away its possessions, retain what has been taken, diminish them, or harass it with reckless vexations; but all things shall be preserved whole, for the benefit in every way of those for whose support and governance they were granted. [Col. 1132C] You shall receive chrism, holy oil, and the ordinations of canons who are to be advanced to holy orders from the archbishop of Tours, provided that he possesses the favour and communion of the Apostolic See and is willing to provide these things freely and without wickedness; otherwise you may approach whatever Catholic bishop you choose and receive the same sacraments from him.

If one of your canons is also a canon of the Church of the archbishop, then, once he has renounced his benefice, the archbishop shall have no power to excommunicate him.

If, therefore, in the future any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowingly violating this page of our constitution, rashly attempts to act against it, and, having been warned a second and third time, does not make amends by suitable satisfaction, let that person be deprived of the dignity of power and honour, know himself or herself guilty before the divine judgment of the iniquity committed, be cut off from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord and Redeemer Jesus Christ, and be subject to strict vengeance at the last judgment. [Col. 1132D] But upon all who preserve what is right for that church, may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that they may receive here the fruits of good action and find before the strict Judge the rewards of eternal peace. Amen.

I, Calixtus, bishop of the Catholic Church.

[Note: The dating clause is erroneous; I think that *Rheims* should be read in place of *Rome*, and that after “III Kal.” “November” should be added. JAFFÉ.]

Given at Rome, through the hand of Grisogonus, cardinal-deacon and librarian of the holy Roman Church, [Col. 1133A] on the third day before the Kalends, in the year 1119 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the first year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Calixtus II.

### XL. He confirms the liberty and privileges of the monastery of Saint-Bertin at Saint-Omer. 31 October 1119.

[*Collection des Cartulaires*, vol. III, p. 260, Paris, 1841, 4to.]

**CALIXTUS**, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son **LAMBERT**, abbot of the monastery of Saint-Bertin at Saint-Omer, and to his successors regularly appointed in perpetuity.

It befits us to give assent to just requests and to lend an ear to rightful petitions, since, though unworthy, we are, by God’s authority, seen to be set as guardians and heralds of justice in the lofty watchtower of the Apostles Peter and Paul. [Col. 1133B] Therefore, beloved son in Christ, Abbot Lambert, granting your petitions, we receive under the guardianship and protection of the Apostolic See the monastery of Saint Bertin at Sithiu, situated in the diocese of Thérouanne, over which, by God’s authority, you preside; and we fortify it against the malice of wicked men by the privilege of this authority.

For we decree that everything lawfully belonging to that monastery shall always be preserved undisturbed and inviolate for you and your successors: namely, the comital rights over all the lands which Saint Bertin possesses in the castellany of Broekburg, as Count Baldwin granted them to you through the hand of Bishop John; and over all lands which arise through the recession of the sea or from marshy places, that is, in all the parishes which Saint [Col. 1133C] Bertin possesses in the aforesaid castellany; two sheaves of the tithe, and the tithe from all sheepfolds and cattle-farms, as Baldwin, Count of Lille, granted you; and everything which that same man confirmed by his written instrument; the mills built in the courtyard of your monastery; and the lands of Culhem, Flechmel, and Helescolke, which you established as your right through the bishop.

Moreover, we judge entirely valid that agreement made before the aforesaid venerable Bishop John between you and Everard, clerk, namely concerning the altar of Helcin and its chapels.

Likewise, in the diocese of Thérouanne: the churches called Oxelare, Warnestim, and Haveskerke; the altar of Merchem; and the church of Eggafridi Chapel. In the diocese of Tournai: the churches of Coclara, Ruslethe, and Runbecca, [Col. 1133D] with their chapels; and the churches of Lisgnege, Snelgerkeke, Hermingehem, and Bovenkerke. In the diocese of Arras: the altar of Anesin. In that of Cologne: the churches of Fresquena and Wildestorp. In that of Beauvais: the land called Hubertuisin, with all its rights and appurtenances; likewise the land of Clarembald of Lustingehem; the land which Count Robert gave you for the remedy of his soul and that of his son William; likewise, the sheepfold which Count Baldwin—who was buried in your monastery—gave you while still alive, and which Charles, succeeding him in the county, granted by lawful donation; also the sheepfold given in exchange for the estate of Ostresele; [Col. 1134A] and two portions of the tithe of Brucsele.

Furthermore, we decree that all tithes shall be gathered annually by the brothers’ own efforts, lest, under the pretext of rendering a payment, your property be disturbed or hindered by being made subject to rent. We likewise decree that the monastic estates shall remain so freely at the brothers’ disposal that no one shall have any hereditary right in return for guarding them.

Furthermore, in accordance with the enactments and privileges granted to that place by our predecessors Popes Victor, Urban, and Paschal, the monastery itself shall be preserved forever in its full liberty and immunity, so that it shall answer to no one in any matter except the Roman pontiff—while nevertheless preserving the canonical reverence due to the bishop of Thérouanne—so long as the vigor and discipline of the regular order remain there.

Moreover, we decree that no one other than the man whom the brothers, by common consent or by the sounder-minded part of the brothers, have elected according to the fear of God and the Rule of Saint Benedict, shall preside as abbot in that monastery. We also grant your religious community the right, during a general interdict upon the diocese, to celebrate divine offices behind closed doors.

We therefore decree that absolutely no person may rashly disturb the said monastery, and all the rest to the end, as set forth above in the privilege of Pope Paschal (no. 344).

I, Calixtus, bishop of the Catholic Church, have subscribed.

Given at Reims, through the hand of Grisogonus, cardinal-deacon and librarian of the Holy Roman Church, on the second day before the Kalends of November [31 October], in the thirteenth indiction.  
[Note: [Col. 1133D] More correctly, the twelfth.]  
In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1119, in the first year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Calixtus II.

### XLI. He confirms the privileges of the Church of Cambrai. (1119, 31 October.)

[Memoir of M. de Choiseul against the magistracy of Cambrai, document VIII, cited by LEGLAN, *Glossary of Old Cambrésis*, p. 131.]

[lacuna]

Given at Reims through the hand of Grisogonus, cardinal-deacon and librarian of the Holy Roman Church, on the second day before the Kalends of November [31 October], thirteenth indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1119, in the first year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Calixtus II.

### XLII. To the clergy and people of Hildesheim. (1119, 31 October.)

[Published by JAFFÉ, *Regesta Pontificum Romanorum*, with this notice: “In the archives, register of Hanover.—Sent by H. Sudendorff.”]

[Col. 1134D]

To the clergy and people of the Church of Hildesheim [printed: *Hildenensis*; read: *Hildesheimensis*], greeting and apostolic blessing.

Having heard and learned of the constancy of your obedience, which you displayed in the canonical election of your bishop, we rejoiced exceedingly. Therefore we have thought fit to visit your beloved community by this letter, warning and commanding you always to persevere in obedience to the Roman Church and to your bishop. For at the council held at Reims we approved and confirmed by apostolic authority, together with archbishops, bishops, abbots, and all the clergy, the canonical election and free consecration of our brother B[erthold], your bishop. [Col. 1135A] Therefore, if any among either clergy or people have not yet consented to your canonical election, having been admonished by us they must not delay in holding the same view as you, lest, continuing in their obstinacy, they become subject to ecclesiastical punishment.

Given at Reims, on the second day before the Kalends of November [31 October].

### XLIII. He commands G[ilbert], Archbishop of Tours, to convey the following letter to [Henry], King of the English, and, with the assistance of G[odfrey], Archbishop of Rouen, diligently to commend Thomas [read: Thurstan], Archbishop of York, to the king. (1119, October–November.)

[*Monasticon Anglicanum*, III, 144.]

[Col. 1135B]

CALIXTUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother GILBERT, Archbishop of Tours, greeting and apostolic blessing.

Because we have recognized the affection of your devotion and the constancy of your fidelity, often proved in the service of Saint Peter, we have thought it especially fitting to entrust his business to you. Accordingly, by the counsel of our brethren, we wish you to discharge our legation on behalf of our venerable brother Thomas, Archbishop of York; and you yourself, as we believe, do not fail to know how great an injury is thereby inflicted upon us and the Roman Church.

Therefore, dearest brother, we entreat and command your diligence [Col. 1135C] to convey into Normandy, to the King of the English, those letters which we are sending concerning the same brother, Thomas; and, before delivering them, you and your fellow-brother G., Archbishop of Rouen—whom we assign to you as a companion in carrying out this mission—must make every effort to meet the king himself on our behalf. And you must urge him most earnestly to heed in the restoration of our aforesaid brother the prayers of his mother, the Roman Church, so that he may prove himself her true son. [lacuna]

### XLIV. To Henry, King of the English. (1119, October–November.)

[*Monasticon Anglicanum*, III, 144.]

[Note: [Col. 1135D] Through the copyist’s error this letter is joined to the preceding one so as to appear a single document. It begins at line 15 with the words “servant of the servants of God,” before which must be added: “Calixtus [Col. 1136D] bishop, servant.”]

[lacuna] servant of the servants of God, to his dearest son in [Col. 1135D] Christ, HENRY, illustrious and glorious King of the English, greeting and apostolic blessing.

We remember that we have already often admonished your beloved person, by word and letter, on behalf of our venerable brother Thomas, [Note: [Col. 1136D] Read: Thurstan.] Archbishop of York; yet we have so far been able to obtain nothing from you in his affair for the honor of God and of the Church. You were certainly deserving, therefore, of a more severe correction; but because we embrace you with a twofold love, we have thought fit for the present to show indulgence to your person in the execution of justice.

Nevertheless, we can no longer tolerate the contempt of our fellow-brother R., Archbishop of Canterbury. Although admonished both by our predecessors of blessed memory, Lords Paschal and Gelasius, and by ourselves, he has been unwilling either to lay hands upon the elect of the Church of York without exacting a profession, or to present himself to our hearing concerning this affair. [Col. 1136A] We therefore prohibit him from exercising episcopal and priestly office; and we prohibit every celebration of divine offices and the burial of the dead, except the baptism of infants and penances for the dying, both in the mother Church of Canterbury and throughout the entire proper diocese of York, until our aforesaid brother Thomas is restored to the Church of York and is allowed to remain there in greater peace.

For if our aforesaid lord Pope Paschal did not in any way permit him, while still only elected, to be driven from the Church of York, [Col. 1136B] neither can nor ought we to permit one now consecrated, by God’s grace, through our hands as it were those of Saint Peter, to suffer complete exile.

### XLV. Bull concerning the privileges of the monastery of Saint Mary of Josaphat in the diocese of Chartres. (1119, 1 November.)

[BALUZE, *Miscellanea*, Luc. ed., III, 13.]

CALIXTUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son GIRARD, abbot of the monastery of Saint Mary of Josaphat near Leuges, situated in the diocese of Chartres, and to his successors canonically appointed in perpetuity.

It is fitting readily to give assent to religious desires, so that faithful devotion may obtain a swift [Col. 1136C] effect. Therefore, beloved son in Christ, Abbot Girald, granting both your petitions and those of our venerable brother Geoffrey, Bishop of Chartres, we receive under the protection of the Apostolic See the monastery of Blessed Mary, over which, by God’s authority, you preside; and we strengthen it against the malice of wicked men by the privilege of our authority.

For we decree that whatever goods and possessions the same monastery now lawfully possesses, or may in the future, by God’s favor, justly and canonically acquire, shall remain secure and inviolate for you and your successors: namely, the church of Saint Martin of Operatorium, and the church of Saint Arnulf, with the tithes and the land given by Goslenus of Leuges.

Therefore no person whatsoever may rashly disturb that monastery, take away its possessions, retain what has been taken, or harass it by reckless vexations; rather, all things shall be preserved intact for the use and benefit in every respect of those for whose support and governance they were granted—while, certainly, preserving the canonical reverence due to the Bishop of Chartres. [Col. 1136D]

If, then, in the future any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowing this page of our constitution, should rashly attempt to act against it, and, having been warned a second or third time, should fail to make suitable satisfaction, let that person be deprived of the dignity of office and honor; let that person know that he or she stands guilty before divine judgment for the wrong committed; let that person be cut off from the most sacred Body and Blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Redeemer; and let that person be subject to severe vengeance at the final judgment. But upon all who preserve justice for that place, may the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ rest, so that here they may receive the fruit of good action and, before the strict Judge, find the rewards of eternal peace. Amen.

I, Calixtus, bishop of the Catholic Church.

Given at Reims, through the hand of Grisogonus, cardinal-deacon and librarian of the Holy Roman Church, on the Kalends of November [1 November], in the twelfth indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1119, in the first year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Calixtus II.

### XLVI. He confirms the decree issued by Geoffrey, Bishop of Chartres, against simony. (1119, 2 November.)

[*Gallia Christiana*, VIII, instruments, 318.]

[Col. 1137B]

CALIXTUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother Geoffrey, Bishop of Chartres, greeting and apostolic blessing.

Those measures established in God’s Church with due regard for the honor of religion ought to be preserved with unshaken firmness. Indeed, dearest brother in Christ, desiring to expel every simoniacal evil from the Church entrusted to you, with the consent of the dean, precentor, subdean, succentor, and the other prelates [Col. 1137C] of the Church—and with the community of brethren approving and unanimously requesting the same—you enacted that neither dean, nor precentor, nor subdean, nor succentor, nor any other ecclesiastical person, nor any canon, should demand or receive anything in connection with ecclesiastical offices or prebends, either personally or through an intermediary.

Likewise, none who becomes a canon shall give or promise anything for a prebend, either personally or through an intermediary. Further, after the death of the prelates now living in your church, no dean, precentor, subdean, or succentor shall be installed in such office until he has plainly sworn in the common chapter that he has given or promised nothing for his office; and until he has also sworn that he will demand or receive nothing for prebends, [Col. 1137D] either personally or through an intermediary.

Similarly, after the death of the ordinary canons now living in the Church of Chartres, no one shall be appointed canon in their place unless first, in the common chapter, he—or, if he is under age, his guardian on his behalf—swears that he has given or promised nothing for the prebend, either personally or through an intermediary.

We therefore, by God’s grace, confirm by the authority of the Apostolic See this constitution, devised by your brotherhood for the honor of God and the salvation of souls, and decree that it shall remain valid in the future, etc.

Given at Reims through the hand of Crisogonus, cardinal and librarian of the Holy Roman Church, on the fourth day before the Nones of November [2 November], in the thirteenth indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation [Col. 1138A] 1119, in the first year of the pontificate of Lord Calixtus II, etc.

### XLVII. He confirms the monastery of Springiersbach and its discipline. (1119, 4 November.)

[Only a notice of this privilege survives in JAFFÉ, *Regesta Pontificum Romanorum*, p. 531, with this statement: “In the archives of Coblenz. From Pertz’s papers.”]

### XLVIII. To Morvan, Bishop of Vannes, and Brictius, Bishop of Nantes.—That they compel the Abbot of Redon by canonical coercion to repay money owed to the Abbot of Quimperlé. (1119, 9 November.)

[Dom BOUQUET, *Recueil*, XV, 231.]

[Col. 1138B]

CALIXTUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the venerable MORVAN, Bishop of Vannes, and BRICTIUS, Bishop of Nantes, greeting and apostolic blessing.

We recently commanded Hervey, Abbot of Redon, to restore without delay the money which he had unjustly taken from the monastery of Holy Cross at Quimperlé, in accordance with the judgment rendered by our fellow-brother Gerard, Bishop of Angoulême and then legate of the Apostolic See; or else to present himself before us at Reims to answer concerning this matter. But when he had come to the Council of Reims, he returned with the matter unresolved and, what is more serious, as we have learned, he strives to defend his fault by the power of the count.

We therefore command your brotherhood to admonish him on our behalf [Col. 1138C] to repay that entire sum to the Abbot of Holy Cross by the octave of the coming Epiphany. Otherwise, impose canonical coercion upon that abbot, his abbey, and its dependent houses situated within your dioceses, until he makes satisfaction in our presence both to us for his contempt and to the abbot for the injuries inflicted.

Given at Reims, on the fifth day before the Ides of November [9 November].

### XLIX. He confirms the privileges of the monastery of Saint Remigius at Reims. (1119, 10 November.)

[MARLOT, *Metropolis Remensis*, II, 271.]

CALIXTUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son in Christ ODON, abbot of the venerable monastery [Col. 1138D] of Saint Remigius, situated near the city, and to his successors canonically appointed in perpetuity.

By the authority of the Apostolic See we are compelled to labor for the condition of all Churches, etc. We decree that whatever goods you may acquire by God’s favor shall remain secure and inviolate for you; among them we have thought fit to specify the following: the church of Saint Mary, situated outside the walls of the castle and called Regitestis, with everything belonging to it, as our venerable brother Rodulf, Archbishop of Reims, granted it to your monastery after it had been surrendered by Count Hugh; the church of Saint Timothy, with the parish of Bourg and the appurtenances of Bourg; [lacuna] the annual payment of sixty solidi from the castle of Codiciac; and the dwellings of Pont Vidulari, situated in the freehold estate of Saint Remigius, which Frederick, founder of the same place, granted to your monastery. [Col. 1139A] We therefore decree that absolutely no person may rashly disturb that monastery, etc.

Given at Reims through the hand of Chrisogonus, cardinal-deacon and librarian of the Holy Roman Church, on the fourth day before the Ides of November [10 November], thirteenth indiction, Incarnation 1119, in the second year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Calixtus II.

### L. He grants privileges of liberty and immunity to the abbey of Saint Amand, or Elnone, of the Order of Saint Benedict. (1119, 20 November.)

[MIRAEUS, *Opera diplomatica*, II, 1155.]

[Col. 1139B]

CALIXTUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son in Christ BOVO, abbot of the venerable monastery of Saint Amand, called Elnone, and to his successors canonically appointed in Christ.

Both divine precepts instruct us and apostolic admonitions direct us to watch with tireless zeal over the condition of churches.

Therefore, beloved son in Christ, Abbot Bovo, we grant assent to your petitions; and by the privilege of the Apostolic See we fortify the monastery of Elnone, over which by God’s authority you preside, where the body of Saint Amand himself is believed to rest.

We decree that whatever goods and possessions that place now possesses through the grant of pontiffs, the generosity of princes, the offerings of the faithful, or other just means, and whatever it may in the future, by God’s favor, justly and canonically acquire, shall remain secure and inviolate under the protection of Saint Peter for you and your successors.

Among these, we have thought fit to record by their proper names the following: namely, the estate of Elnone with its appurtenances, free from every lordship of secular persons, as it is known to have been emancipated by the religious kings Dagobert, Pippin, Charles, and Louis, and by Count Baldwin.

In the district of Laon, the cell of Barisiacum, with its dependents and appurtenances.

In the district of Cambrai, Braccolum, Neuville, and Haltiacum, with their appurtenances.

In the district of Hainaut, Guariniacum, Moncelz, and Scalpouz, [Col. 1139D] with their appurtenances.

In the district of Ostrevent, Diptiacum, Ferinium, Scaldinium, Lurcium, and Ruoth, with their household and appurtenances.

In the district of Tournai, Guillelmel, Frigidum Montem, Hertinium, Bovinias, Rumam, and Spiere Holtein, with their appurtenances.

In the district of Brabant, Herinias, Sein, Allenium, Varcinium, Anuinium, Securiacum, Vilare, Novas Domus, the lands of Germinium, Milam, Rodam, and Baceroth, with their appurtenances.

In Flanders, the lands of Bonarda, Roslare, Ledda, Hardoia, Guinguiniis, Marchengen, Lapiscura, Holscherca, Berneiam, and Lecca, with their household and appurtenances.

[Col. 1140A] In Testerep, a freehold paying twenty-three pounds annually.

At Bruges, the chapel of Saint Amand.

On the river Meuse, the estate of Haringas, with its household, church, and appurtenances.

On the river Rhine, the lands of Sulla and Bogarda.

Moreover, we decree that the altars which you lawfully possess in various dioceses shall be preserved forever for you and your successors, free from every personal charge, while nevertheless reserving the customary provisions due to bishops or episcopal officials.

In the bishopric of Noyon: the altar of Saint Martin; the altars of the cell, Rongi, Ruma, Guillelmel, Frigidum Montem, Hertinium, Marchengen, [Col. 1140B] Guinguiniis, Bernean, Sedelegien, Bichengen, and Ledda.

In the bishopric of Laon: the cell of Barisiacum with the altar of Saint Remigius.

In the bishopric of Cambrai: the altar of Neuville with its appurtenances; the altars of Gariniacum, Scalpous, Guariniacum with its appurtenances, Villari, Anuinium, and Lombisiacum.

In that of Arras: the altars of Bulcinio, Masten, Helenuna, Lurcio, Scaldinium with its appurtenances, Ruoth, Ditiacum with its appurtenances, and Bulciniolo; the tithe of eels at Bulcem; and one fisherman in the fishpond.

Furthermore, whatever liberty, protection, and immunity has been granted to your monastery by the authentic privileges of our predecessors of holy memory, the Roman pontiffs Martin and Paschal II; and whatever was granted by the fatherly provision of our venerable brother Rodulf, Archbishop of Reims, in a written instrument—at the request of our nephew, Count Baldwin of illustrious memory—concerning the unjust customary exactions renounced by the provost of the town, the remission of two days from the three general judicial assemblies, the obstruction at Tuns, and the division of the wood of Saint Amand and that of the aforesaid Count Baldwin: [Col. 1140C] all this we confirm to you and your successors.

We therefore decree that absolutely no person may rashly disturb that monastery, take away its possessions, retain what has been taken, diminish them, or harass it with reckless vexations; but all things shall be preserved intact for the use and benefit in every respect of those for whose support and governance they were granted.

Upon the death of you, the present abbot of this place, or of any of your successors, no one shall be appointed there by any device of deceit or by force, except the person whom the brothers, by common consent or by the sounder-minded part of the brothers, from their own community or, if necessary, from another, elect according to the fear of God and the Rule of Saint Benedict, to be consecrated by God’s grace by the diocesan bishop without any exaction or improper dealing by him or his clergy.

We absolutely forbid public Masses to be celebrated in the same monastery by the bishop, or stations or any ordinations [Col. 1141A] to be held, apart from the will of the abbot and brothers, lest any occasion be given for popular gatherings in the retreats of the servants of God.

To this we add that no person shall have the power to invade that monastery or bring upon it the violence of invasion, so long as the brothers of that monastery take care to live according to the Rule and to obey the regularly elected abbot according to the sound customs of the Church.

If, then, in the future any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowing this page of our constitution, should rashly attempt to act against it, and, having been warned a second or third time, should fail to make suitable satisfaction, let that person be deprived of the dignity of office and honor; let that person know that he or she stands guilty before divine judgment for the wrong committed; [Col. 1141B] let that person be cut off from the most sacred Body and Blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ; and let that person be subject to severe vengeance at the final judgment. But upon all who preserve justice for that place, may the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ rest, so that here they may receive the fruit of good action and, before the strict Judge, find the rewards of eternal peace. Amen.

Place of the + seal.

I, Calixtus, bishop of the Catholic Church.

Given at Beauvais through the hand of Grisogonus, cardinal-deacon and librarian of the Holy Roman Church, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of December [20 November], thirteenth indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1119, in the first year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Calixtus II.

### LI. He urges Ralph of Durham, R[alph] of Orkney, John of Glasgow, and all the bishops throughout Scotland, suffragans of the Church of York, to obey T[hurstan], Archbishop of York, consecrated by him. (1119, 20 November.)

[*Monasticon Anglicanum*, III, 146.]

[Col. 1141C]

CALIXTUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the venerable brethren RADULF, Bishop of Durham, R., Bishop of Orkney, JOHN of Glasgow, and all bishops throughout Scotland subject to the Church of York, greeting and apostolic blessing.

By God’s ordering, the care of the Apostolic See has been entrusted to us so that we ought to bear concern for all Churches. Therefore, in accordance with our divinely appointed charge, we have shown fatherly compassion to the metropolitan Church of York; and we have graciously received our venerable brother Thomas, its elect, when he came to us. [Col. 1141D] With the Lord’s help we consecrated him archbishop and granted him the distinction of the pallium, that is, the fullness of pontifical office, according to the custom of the Apostolic See.

For it did not seem reasonable to your brethren that, because of that complaint of your fellow-brother R., Archbishop of Canterbury, the Church of York should remain vacant any longer—especially since that brother, though frequently admonished by the Apostolic See, has been unwilling on any ground to show him this reverence. Therefore, by the authority of this present letter, we command your brotherhood [Col. 1142A] to take diligent care to love and honor our aforesaid brother Thomas as your metropolitan and henceforth, setting aside every pretext, to render him the obedience and reverence due.

Given at Beauvais, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of December [20 November].

### LII. Letter addressed to the Kings of Norway concerning the admission of Ralph, Bishop of the Orkneys. (1119.)

[*Monasticon Anglicanum*, III, p. 145.]

CALIXTUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons in Christ AISTAN and SIWARD, Kings of Norway, greeting and apostolic blessing.

From the very beginning of the Christian faith, the Churches of God [Col. 1142B] have increased in temporal goods through the munificence of princes; and indeed the Lord will honor those who honor him and will enlarge their power more abundantly. Therefore, dearest sons in Christ, visiting your beloved persons by apostolic letters, we ask and exhort you in the Lord graciously to receive our son, the Bishop of the Orkneys, canonically elected as we have learned and consecrated in his metropolitan church of York; to defend him from injury; and to permit him to remain in peace in his bishopric.

### LIII. He confirms the possessions and privileges of the Parisian monastery of Saint Martin of the Fields. (1119, 27 November.)

[*Bullarium Cluniacense*, p. 39.]

[Col. 1142C]

CALIXTUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son in Christ MATTHEW, prior of the monastery of Saint Martin called “of the Fields,” greeting and apostolic blessing.

No effect is to be granted to those who ask for unjust things; so neither is the petition of those who desire what is lawful to be delayed. Therefore, beloved son in Christ, Prior Matthew, assenting to your requests, we fortify by the authority of this present decree the monastery of Saint Martin, over which, by God’s appointment and through the institution of our venerable brother Pontius, abbot of Cluny, you preside; decreeing that, like the other members of Cluny, it shall always remain under the protection of the Apostolic See [Col. 1142D].

We likewise decree that all things which appear to belong to that place in the present twelfth indiction shall always remain peacefully and unimpaired in your possession: namely, in the district of Paris, the tithe of the aforesaid monastery of Saint Martin itself, and the altar and tithe of Callevium. In the suburb of the city of Paris, the church of Saint James with its parish. Near the monastery of Saint Martin, the chapel of Saint Nicholas. Within the city, in the street called that of the Jews, a certain oven, and two mills at the Great Bridge. The church of Saint Denis of Montmartre, with the chapel called Saint-Martyr. The estate of Nusiellum, with its church and atrium, and all its appurtenances. The estate of Rusiacum, which Anselm the seneschal gave. At Taverniacum, Turnum, and Moncellum: tenants [hospites] [Col. 1143A], vineyards, rents, and the Chestnut Wood, by gift of Count Odo of Corbeil; another Chestnut Wood adjoining it; and the church of Erigniacum. At the castle of Pontoise, by royal gift and by gift of Ralph Delicatus and Warner of Senlis: tenants, rents, and lands. In the valley of Jouy: land, rents, and tenants, by gift of a certain monk Berengar, with the consent of Osmund of Beaumont; the estate of Châtenay, with its church and tithe; the land of Puteaux; and the altar of Fontenay. The altar, church, atrium, and tithe of Esven. The altar, atrium, and tithe of Champigniacum. The church of Doctmont with its appurtenances. The altar of Ermenonville. The church of Duniacum and the mills, and the other possessions of Saint Martin there. At the bridge of Ebali: the manor and [Col. 1143B] lands.

The estate of Ceurentium, with its appurtenances, and the church of that estate, with the chapel and tithe of Luriacum. Bonseias, with its church and appurtenances. At Nuseium Siccum: land and rents. And at Clerici: land and rents; Penthinum, with its church and appurtenances; and Roveredum, with the surrounding lands. At Luuram in the Paris district: the church with its atrium. At the castle of Gornacum: the monastery of Saint Mary with all its appurtenances. The estate of Nuseium with all its appurtenances. Maiatlas, with its church and appurtenances. The tithe of Atiliacum. The estate of Confluentia, with its church and appurtenances. At Saint-Marcel: the land given by the monk Cleophas. At the estate of Vitriacum: a house, winepress, vineyards, and rents, and the mill of Arcueil [Col. 1143C].

At Clamart: church, land, vineyards, and rents. At Saint-Cloud: the land called Alnetus, with its appurtenances. At Mont Savias and Montmartre: winepresses and vineyards. In the district of Chartres: the church of Bonnella, with its court, tenants, and all its appurtenances; the estate of Visanis, with its church and appurtenances; Bolovilla, with its appurtenances; Escun and Mount Olan; and the estate of Goucolum, with its church and tithe. At Meudonville: tenants and lands. At La Chapelle: tenants and lands; Rodenisvilla, with its church and appurtenances. At Chartres, in the borough of Saint Caralnus: tenants and rents. At the estate called Tabula: a money rent and the tithe of Beveriis. At Crisperiae: church, tithe, and tenants. The estate of Bault [Col. 1143D].

Saint Hilary, with its church and appurtenances. The pond of Pissyacum. At Medenda: from each vessel passing across the water, three obols, by gift of Gervase the seneschal and with the consent of King Philip. At the castle of Miliacum and at Contiacum: the said Gervase’s share, namely one tenth, of the toll revenue. In the district of Orléans: Hyenvilla, with its church and the whole parish of Puteacium, and the tenth market with all its appurtenances, and the altar of Novavilla. In the district of Sens: the estate and court of Pringi and Novas. At Conam: church and court with their appurtenances. In the district of Soissons: the estate called Sainte-Gemme, with its church and appurtenances, and the land of Mont Aldon. In the district of Meaux [Col. 1144A]: the estate of Anet, with church, court, and appurtenances. In the district of Laon: the estate of Disiacum, and the freehold of Branna with its appurtenances. In the district of Noyon: the church of the castle called Capii, with its appurtenances; the altar of Heldicurte; and the altar of Bevelone. In the district of Amiens: the church of Signiacum with its appurtenances. At the castle of Arenas: the church of Blessed Mary with its appurtenances. At Rue, Verton, and Waben: revenues of salt and fish-weirs. In the district of Thérouanne: the altar of Feurentiacum with its appurtenances. In the district of Beauvais, at Beaumont: the church of Saint Leonorius with its appurtenances, and the tithe of Mediana Curia. At Nusiacum: land and rents. At Mervacum: estate, altar, court, and tithe with their appurtenances [Col. 1144B], and the altar of Saint Omer with its appurtenances. At Beauvais: the church of Saint Pantaleon. At Montiacum of Saint Opportuna: the church of that saint with its appurtenances. In the district of Senlis: the monastery of Saint Nicholas of Aciacum with its appurtenances. At Lorvillare: church, court, tithe, and tenants. In England, at London: rent-paying land and tenants, by gift of Ralph of Juin, with the consent of King Henry. At Barnstaple Castle: the church with its appurtenances. And all other things contained in the privileges of our predecessors of holy memory, Pope Urban and Paschal II.

Whatever, besides these, has been bestowed from their own right upon the same place by anyone, or may hereafter be bestowed upon it, shall remain forever firm and unimpaired, to be possessed, administered, and possessed in perpetuity by you and by others who shall be set over that place through the abbots of Cluny [Col. 1144C].

Therefore we decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb this monastery, take away its possessions, retain what has been taken away, diminish them, or harass it with reckless vexations; but let all things be preserved whole for the use and benefit in every way of those for whose support and governance they were granted. If, therefore, any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowing this document of our enactment, shall rashly attempt to act against it, and, having been warned a second or third time, does not make proper amends by satisfactory reparation, let that person be deprived of the dignity of his power and honour; let him know himself guilty before the divine judgment for the iniquity committed; let him be separated from the most sacred Body and Blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, our Redeemer; and let him be subject to severe vengeance at the last judgment [Col. 1144D]. But upon all who preserve what is right for that place may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that they may receive here the fruit of good works and find with the strict Judge the rewards of eternal peace. Amen.

I, Calixtus, bishop of the Catholic Church.

Given at Saint-Denis, through the hand of Grisogonus, cardinal-deacon and librarian of the holy Roman Church, on the fifth day before the Kalends of December [27 November], in the thirteenth indiction, in the year 1119 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the first year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Calixtus II.

LIV. Bull for Abbot Pacanus and the canons of Blessed Mary’s, Étampes. (Year 1119, 4 December.)

[FLEUREAU, *Les Antiquitez de la ville et du duchez d’Estampes*. Paris, 1683, quarto, p. 491.]

[Col. 1145A]

CALIxtus, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons Pacanus, abbot, and the canons of the church of Blessed Mary at Étampes, present and future, for ever.

The authority of our office exhorts us to make more careful provision for the peace of churches and, so far as the Lord permits, to preserve intact each one’s right. For we have received your complaints [Col. 1145B] against those who stubbornly presumed to bury your parishioners without your consent. Therefore, moved by your prayers and by those of our most beloved son Louis, glorious king of the Franks, we decree, and by apostolic authority forbid, that anyone may bury your parishioners, knights or others, only with your consent, in order that the peace and liberty of your church may by God’s grace be preserved.

Moreover, we confirm to you and to your successors forever the church of Saint Basil and the mill situated in the borough, and all other things which your church now possesses, or may hereafter, by the Lord’s bounty, lawfully and canonically acquire through the grant of pontiffs, the generosity of kings, the offerings of the faithful, or other just means [Col. 1145C]. Let no person therefore have licence, by rash presumption, to disturb your church, alter your good customs, take away its possessions, retain those taken away, diminish them, or harass them with reckless vexations. Rather, let all things be kept whole for the use and benefit in every way of those for whose support and governance they were granted, saving the due reverence of the archbishop of Sens.

If any ecclesiastical or secular person hereafter, knowing this document of our enactment, shall rashly attempt to act against it and, having been warned a second or third time, does not make proper amends by satisfactory reparation, let that person be deprived of the dignity of power and honour; let him know himself guilty before the divine judgment for the iniquity committed [Col. 1145D]; let him be separated from the most sacred Body and Blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, our Redeemer; and let him be subject to severe vengeance at the last judgment. But upon all who preserve what is right for that place may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that they may receive here the fruit of good works and find with the strict Judge the rewards of eternal peace.

Given at Sens, through the hand of Grisogonus, cardinal-deacon and librarian of the holy Roman Church, on the second day before the Nones of December [4 December], in the twelfth indiction, in the year 1119 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the first year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Calixtus II.

LV. To Josceran, bishop of Langres.—He appoints him judge in the dispute between the abbot of Saint-Pierre-le-Vif at Sens and the abbot of Molesme. (Year 1119, 5 December.)

[MANSI, *Concilia*, XXI, 196.]

[Col. 1146A]

CALIxtus, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Josceran, bishop of the people of Langres, greeting and apostolic blessing.

We have received the complaint of Abbot Arnald and the brethren of the monastery of Saint Peter the Living, that the abbots of Molesme and Reims have unjustly taken from them certain possessions long held by the monastery of Saint Peter. We therefore command your brotherhood to set aside prolonged delay and render them canonical justice [Col. 1146B]; nor are you to allow it to prejudice that monastery that documents drawn up without the impression of a seal are recognized according to the ancient custom of the land.

Given at Sens, on the Nones of December [5 December].

LVI. To the monks of Saint Viventius of Vergy.—He commands them, under penalties of interdict, to receive a prior from the monastery of Cluny. (Year 1119, 7 December.)

[Dom BOUQUET, *Recueil*, XV, 252.]

CALIxtus, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the monks and household of the monastery of Vergy: greeting, if they obey, and apostolic blessing.

We have received the complaint of our most beloved sons Peter [Note: [Col. 1145] Correct to “Pontius,” as is certainly established from the date given below], abbot of Cluny, and his brethren, that you refuse to receive [Col. 1146C] a prior from the monastery of Cluny, although your house has had a prior only from that same house for almost thirty years. In this you are plainly causing great injury to yourselves and to your church. For whereas you ought to devote yourselves to peace and religious observance, you remain in dissension and scandal.

Therefore, by these present letters, we command you under obedience to receive, by the coming feast of Blessed Thomas, a prior from the monastery of Cluny and to render him the obedience due to him, as has hitherto been done. Otherwise, from that time we forbid you entry into churches, and prohibit the celebration of divine offices in your monastery.

Given at Auxerre, on the seventh day before the Ides of December [7 December].

LVII. He asks Bishop B[enedict] of Lucca to furnish secure protection to persons coming to him or returning from him. He commends Prior A. and the church of Saint Frigdianus. (Year 1119, 11 December.)

[BALUZE, *Miscellanea*, ed. Luc., IV, 588.]

[Col. 1146D]

CALIxtus, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother B., bishop of Lucca, greeting and apostolic blessing.

As we have already instructed your affection in other letters, we desire to love you as a most beloved brother in Christ and, so far as the Lord permits, to honour you [Col. 1147A]. We ask your brotherhood, therefore, according to the prudence granted you by God, to take particular care at this time to assist His Church, and to ensure that persons coming to us or returning from us are safely conducted through that country. Moreover, we ask your affection to take greater care to love and assist your son A., prior of Saint Frigdianus, and his church, out of reverence for Blessed Peter and affection for yourselves. For that place stands especially under the guardianship and protection of Blessed Peter, and we can neither fail nor ought to fail it.

Given at Auxerre, on the third day before the Ides of December [11 December].

LVIII. To Stephen, abbot of Cîteaux.—He confirms the chapters of the Cistercian monastery. (Year 1119, 23 December.)

[MANSI, *Concilia*, XXI, 190.]

[Col. 1147B]

CALIxtus, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his most beloved sons in Christ Stephen, venerable abbot of the monastery of Cîteaux, and his brethren, greeting and apostolic blessing.

By the Lord’s ordering, we are seen to have been raised to the governance of the Apostolic See so that, by His gift, we may increase religious observance and establish by the authority of our office those ordinances which are right and conducive to the salvation of souls. Therefore, most beloved sons in Christ, we grant your petition the assent owed by charity; rejoicing with paternal affection in your religious life, we place the hand of our confirmation upon the work of God which you have begun [Col. 1147C].

For by the common consent and deliberation of the abbots and brethren of your monasteries and of the bishops in whose parishes those monasteries are situated, you have enacted certain chapters concerning observance of the Rule of Blessed Benedict and certain other matters which seemed necessary to your order and place. You ask that these be confirmed by the authority of the Apostolic See for the greater peace of the monastery and observance of religious life. Rejoicing, therefore, in your progress in the Lord, we confirm those chapters and constitutions by apostolic authority, and decree that all of them remain valid forever. We expressly and altogether forbid any abbot to receive your monks without a regular letter of commendation.

If any ecclesiastical [Col. 1147D] or secular person shall presume with any rashness to oppose our confirmation and your constitution, let that person, as a disturber of religion and monastic peace, be struck by the sword of excommunication through the authority of the blessed Peter and Paul and our own, until satisfaction has been made [Col. 1148A]. But whoever proves a protector shall obtain the blessing and grace of almighty God and His apostles. We further forbid anyone to receive your professed lay converts for residence.

I, Calixtus, bishop of the Catholic Church, have confirmed and subscribed.

Given at Souvigny, through the hand of Chrysogonus, cardinal-deacon and librarian of the holy Roman Church, on the tenth day before the Kalends of January [23 December], in the twelfth indiction, in the year 1119 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the first year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Calixtus II.

LIX. He declares Bruno, archbishop of Trier, free from all authority of a legate, unless the legate is sent from the pope’s side. (Year 1120, 3 January.)

[HONTHEIM, *Historia Trevirensis*, I, 504.]

[Col. 1148B]

CALIxtus, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother Bruno, archbishop of Trier, greeting and apostolic blessing.

The custom of the Apostolic See, and the very order of reason, requires that we should especially honour and love wise and religious persons devoted to the obedience of the Roman Church. Therefore, sweetest brother, we graciously assent to your request, embrace your person in the arms of affection, and exempt it from the authority of any legate, unless he be sent from our side. For we trust [Col. 1148C] in the Lord that great honour and benefit will result for God and the Church from your wisdom and religious devotion.

Given at Cluny, on the third day before the Nones of January [3 January].

[Note: [Col. 1147D] The *Deeds of Trier*, in Martène, vol. IV, p. 192, relate as follows the reason and occasion on which this papal decree was obtained: “In the tenth year of his ordination he [Bruno] decided to go to Rome, in order to renew the privileges of his see. He was indignant at the insolence of Adalbert, bishop of Mainz, who, arrogantly exalting himself because the legateship of the Roman See had been granted to him, especially since by concessions of earlier popes the bishop of Trier ought to obey no one save the Apostolic See alone or one sent from its side. As Hincmar, archbishop of Reims, recalls in his letter addressed to Pope Nicholas, saying: [Col. 1148D] ‘The Church of Reims never had a primate, except the Roman pontiff, save for the time when, its bishop having been driven from it by the violence of the tyrant Milo without any fault of his own, and being without a shepherd in the time of Prince Charles, it was entrusted for a while to Boniface, legate of the Apostolic See, just as the Church of Trier was also entrusted …’ When the festival days had passed, they proceeded together to Cluny, where Bruno explained the reasons for his coming; and, having produced before him the privileges of his see, he asked that these be established for himself and his church by the confirming guarantee of an apostolic subscription—which he obtained.”]

LX. He confirms to Archbishop Bruno metropolitan jurisdiction and other ancient honours. (Year 1120, 3 January.)

[HONTHEIM, *ibid.*]

CALIxtus, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother Bruno, archbishop of Trier, greeting and apostolic blessing.

We too desire, by God’s help, that the dignity conferred upon churches or persons by the authentic privileges of our predecessors should be preserved unimpaired [Col. 1148D]. Therefore, that dignity and honour which have been bestowed by the Apostolic See upon the Church of Trier and your predecessors, we establish by the authority of the same See, with the Lord’s aid, and decree to remain lawful and perpetual: namely, that the Church of Trier shall be metropolitan over the three cities of Metz, Toul, and Verdun, and that the bishops of those cities shall acknowledge it as their mother and mistress, the authority and reverence of the Roman Church being preserved in all things [Col. 1149A].

Moreover, most beloved brother in Christ, we confirm to you and your lawful successors the use of the pallium; and, by the liberality of the Apostolic See, we grant you the right to ride upon a beast furnished with a purple saddlecloth during the appointed stations of the church, and to have the cross carried before you, as it is established that our predecessors granted to your predecessors.

I, Calixtus, bishop of the Catholic Church.

I, Lambert, bishop of Ostia.

Given at Cluny, through the hand of Chrysogonus, cardinal-deacon and librarian of the Holy Roman Church, on the third day before the Nones of January [3 January], [Col. 1149B] in the thirteenth indiction, in the year 1120 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the first year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Calixtus II.

[Note: [Col. 1149D] What moved Bruno to seek this decree from the Roman pontiff is related in the cited *Deeds of Trier*, p. 192, as follows: “At that time a certain Stephen, nephew of Pope Calixtus through his sister, presided over the Church of Metz. His aforesaid uncle had already granted him leave to proceed wearing the pallium in the celebration of Masses, while the authority of the metropolitan see of Trier remained wholly intact. Elated by the honour of the pallium, and as though relying upon the favour of the aforesaid kinship, he raised himself above what was fitting, striving by every means, if somehow he could, to depress the Church of Trier, advance his own, and make it metropolitan, hoping that Calixtus would approve whatever he undertook. This is evident from the fact that whenever he was summoned by the metropolitan to come and subscribe obedience and subjection to the metropolitan see, as is customary for suffragan bishops, he disdained to come, saying that his predecessors had once been archbishops—something no authority of writings affirms or declares. Only five bishops of Metz are reported to have used the pallium, and he is counted as the sixth; yet in all things they maintained subjection to the metropolitan. For not all who use the pallium are archbishops, unless their see is a metropolitan see presiding over other cities and bishops subject to it.”]

LXI. *He orders the preservation of the hospital house founded by Bruno, archbishop of Trier, at Koblenz before the church of Saint Florinus. (Year 1119, 3 January.)

[GUNTHER, *Codex diplomaticus Rheno-Mosellanus*, I, 169.]

LXII. To Vol[ricus], bishop of Constance.—That he restore to the men of Schaffhausen an estate taken by force. (Year 1120, 3 January.)

[NEUGART, *Codex diplomaticus Alemannicus*, II, 46.]

[Col. 1149C] CALIxtus, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother Bishop Vo. and the canons of the Church of Constance, greeting and apostolic blessing.

The brethren of Schaffhausen do not cease to renew their long-standing complaint. They complain that you are violently taking away an estate offered to them by that Tuoto [Note: [Col. 1150D] Cf. the Chronicle of Petershausen in P. Ussermann, *Prodromus Germaniae sacrae*, vol. I, p. 370 (*Patrologia*, vol. CXLIII).]. We therefore command your affection either to restore the estate itself to them in peace and quiet, or, if you believe that you have any right in it, to come at a suitable place and time for the administration of justice. Yet it would seem to us more honourable and advantageous if each person possessed what is his own without scandal and as befits brethren. For although that Tuoto has fallen into apostasy and turned backward, against the honour of God and the salvation of his own soul [Col. 1150A], no reason permits him to have taken away what he had freely and willingly offered.

Given at Cluny, on the third day before the Nones of January [3 January].

[Note: [Col. 1150D] In February of this year, Calixtus II departed from Cluny and came to Valence in the Dauphiné; in March, having crossed the Alps, he came to the village of Saint Ambrose near Susa. D. DE SAINT-MARC, *Abrégé chronologique*, vol. IV, p. 1074, under the year 1120.]

LXIII. Privilege for the monastery of Saint Saviour of Schaffnaburg. (Year 1120, 3 January.)

[Udalric of Bamberg, *Codex*, no. 300, in ECCARD, *Corpus historicum*, II, 299.]

CALIxtus, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son in Christ N., abbot of Schaffhausen, and to his successors to be regularly appointed, forever.

The authority of the office committed to us exhorts us to labour for [Col. 1150B] the condition of churches and to establish what has rightly been ordained. First, therefore, most beloved son, Abbot N., we judged that your petitions, made through our most beloved brother N., archbishop of Trier, should be granted: that we should fortify with the privilege of the Apostolic See, following the example of our predecessors of holy memory, the Roman pontiffs Gregory VII and Urban II, the venerable monastery of Saint Saviour over which, by God’s appointment, you preside. It was built by N., once a count, at the estate of N., in honour of All Saints, and offered to Blessed Peter in perpetual right.

Accordingly, by this document of the present privilege, we decree by apostolic authority that whatever possessions and goods have been offered to the same monastery from their own right by the aforesaid Counts N. and N. or by other faithful persons, or may hereafter by the Lord’s bounty be offered or acquired through any just means, shall remain firm and unimpaired for you and your successors [Col. 1150C]. Therefore let no person whatsoever be permitted rashly to disturb the aforesaid monastery, take away its possessions or other property, retain things bestowed upon it, diminish them, or harass it with reckless vexations. Rather, let all things be preserved whole for the use and benefit in every way of those for whose support and governance they were granted.

Upon the death of you, now abbot of that place, or of any of your successors, no one shall be set over it by any artifice of deception or force, except one whom the brethren by common consent, or the sounder part of the brethren, have chosen according to the Rule of Blessed Benedict [Col. 1151A]. You shall receive the preparation of the holy oil, the consecrations of altars or churches, the ordinations of clerics, and other things pertaining to the episcopal office from the bishop of Constance, in whose diocese you are, provided that he is Catholic, enjoys the favour and communion of the Apostolic See, and is willing to supply these things freely and without improper exaction. Otherwise, you may approach whatever Catholic bishop you prefer and receive from him the sacraments of consecration.

We likewise decree that the burial-ground of the monastery itself shall be entirely free, so that no one may oppose the devotion and last will of those who determine to be buried there, unless they are excommunicated. Further, we altogether forbid the cells of Blessed Agnes and Blessed Mary, by any pretext, to be withdrawn or alienated from the ownership of your monastery by you, your successors, or anyone else [Col. 1151B]; and we forbid their goods to be rashly or forcibly taken away or diminished. If anything has perhaps been taken away, we command that it be restored under solemn warning of divine judgment.

Moreover, by a decree to remain in force forever, we establish that no living person may claim in your monastery any condition of proprietary right—neither hereditary right, advocacy, investiture, nor any kind of authority injurious to the brethren’s liberty and peace. Rather, the abbot with the brethren shall appoint for themselves the advocate whom he judges more useful; and, if need be, after removing him, he shall provide another or a third. No injunction of any bishop or provost shall prevent you from receiving for conversion laypeople or clerics living in the secular manner. Moreover, tithes held by laymen [Col. 1151C] which belong to churches that you possess or shall possess, if, with God’s consent, you are able to recover them, we decree shall be assigned perpetually to your use without any opposition from bishops, saving episcopal reverence.

We further add to this present chapter that no bishop may, without the permission of the Roman pontiff, subject your places or monks to interdict or excommunication. As a token of the liberty received from the Roman Church, you shall pay one ounce of gold yearly to the Lateran palace. If any ecclesiastical or secular person henceforth, knowing this document of the privilege, shall rashly attempt to act against it and, after a second or third warning, does not make proper amends by satisfactory reparation, let that person be deprived of the dignity of power and honour [Col. 1151D], let him know himself guilty before the divine judgment for the iniquity committed, let him be separated from the most sacred Body and Blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, our Redeemer, and let him be subject to severe vengeance at the last judgment. But upon all who preserve what is right for that place may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that they may receive here the fruit of good works and find with the strict Judge the rewards of eternal peace. Amen.

Given at Cluny, through the hand of Grisogonus, cardinal-deacon and librarian of the holy Roman Church, on the third day before the Nones of January [3 January], in the sixteenth indiction, in the year 1120 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the first year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Calixtus II.

LXIV. To Hugh, bishop of Auxerre.—He grants him authority to assign to churches of canons and monks churches held by laymen. (Year 1120, 3 January.)

[BOUQUET, *Recueil*, XV, 232.]

[Col. 1152A]

CALIxtus, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother Hugh, bishop of Auxerre, greeting and apostolic blessing.

We ought not only to favour the religious desires of our brethren, but to encourage their minds toward them. For you desire, most beloved brother, that certain churches of your bishopric may by God’s grace be regularly ordered for the honour of God. Therefore, rejoicing with paternal affection in your good will, we grant you licence [Col. 1152B] to establish regular canons or religious monks in the churches entrusted to you within your diocese in which secular clerics are present.

Moreover, having great confidence in your religious devotion, we grant you, as justice dictates, free authority to confer upon churches of communities of regular brethren—canons or monks—within your parish certain churches which laymen have customarily held unjustly. In addition, by authority of the Apostolic See we confirm to your brotherhood the canonical ordering and administration of the cathedral church, as well as of the other churches of your bishopric, so that both churches and monasteries may in every respect show you the reverence due to you as father and master, just as they are known to have shown it to your Catholic predecessors [Col. 1152C]. But if anyone should break out against these provisions with audacious rashness, let him undergo ecclesiastical punishment until he has made satisfaction.

Given at Cluny, on the third day before the Nones of January [3 January], in the thirteenth indiction.

LXV. Privilege of Pope Calixtus confirming the decree of the Council of Beauvais concerning the dispute between William, bishop of Châlons, and the canons of Cheminon, to whom Richard, bishop of Albano, had granted excessive immunity. (Year 1120, 5 January.)

[*Gallia Christiana*, X, documents, 162.]

CALIxtus, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Abbot Alard and his brethren, professing the regular life in the church of Blessed Nicholas [Col. 1152D], present and future, forever.

Our brother Richard, bishop of Albano, of good memory, then vicar of the Apostolic See in those regions, received your place and the church of Blessed Nicholas in the wood of Luviz, from the beginning of its construction, into the possession and jurisdiction of the Apostolic See, as we have learned from his written document. He blessed the church and its court and emancipated it from the jurisdiction of all bishops; and our predecessor of holy memory, Lord Pope Paschal, confirmed this by the authority of his decree.

But when we were staying in the regions of Gaul in the service of the Church, you made a complaint before us and our brethren at Beauvais because our brother William, bishop of Châlons, was severely harassing that place, situated in his parish [Col. 1153A].
