Therefore our brethren who were present with us approached the same bishop with due charity, asking him either to desist from that harassment or, if he believed himself aggrieved in this matter, to set forth his grievance quietly and peacefully, since he would receive complete justice from us.

Then he, as a religious and wise man, having taken counsel with his brethren who were with him, answered that, for the honour of God and reverence for the Apostolic See, he would make up with episcopal generosity whatever had been lacking in the endowment of the aforesaid place and church. Therefore, in the presence of ourselves and our brethren: Cono, bishop of Palestrina; Lambert, bishop of Ostia; Leodegarius, bishop of Viviers; Clarembald, bishop of Senlis; and Peter, bishop of Beauvais [Col. 1153B]; and of the cardinal-priests Boso of Saint Anastasia and John of Saint Chrysogonus; and of the cardinal-deacons Peter of Saints Cosmas and Damian, Gregory of Saint Angelo, Chrysogonus of Saint Nicholas, and Romanus of Saint Mary in Portico—the same venerable brother William, bishop of Châlons, granted the oft-mentioned place and church of Saint Nicholas in the wood of Luviz, in its own right and complete liberty, to Blessed Peter and his Roman Church; and into our hand he renounced henceforth every claim concerning it.

Taking account of his gentleness and good will, we granted to him and to his Catholic successors the promotion of clerics to holy orders and the provision of chrism and oil, provided that they are willing to supply them freely and without improper exaction. Otherwise [Col. 1153C], you may approach whatever Catholic bishop you prefer and receive from him the same sacraments. Concerning the priest who must govern the people, however, we decree that he shall be elected by the canons, presented to the bishop, receive from him the cure of souls, render him account concerning it, and attend his synod when summoned.

Accordingly, we confirm by the authority of the Apostolic See all the matters set out above, and decree that they shall remain confirmed, unimpaired, for all future time. Moreover, following in the footsteps of our aforesaid lord Pope Paschal, we strengthen, with the Lord’s aid, the order of canonical life which you have professed according to the Rule of blessed Augustine; and we forbid anyone, after making that profession, to possess anything as private property, or to leave residence in the cloister without the permission of the abbot or the community. When you, the present abbot of that place, or any of your successors, die, no one shall be set over it through any trickery of usurpation or violence, except one whom the brethren, by common consent, or the sounder part of the brethren, shall in the fear of God have regularly judged fit to elect; and the person elected shall be confirmed by the Roman pontiff. We also decree that the burial-place of that house shall be free, so that no one may obstruct the devotion and final will of those who choose to be buried there, unless they are excommunicated. Further, the land situated around the precinct of your church, as is contained in the charter of Count Hugh—entirely as far as Cotem, the Lime-Kiln, Rainald’s valley, the field of Durfosson, the road of Saint Veran [Col. 1154A] above the water of Chimenon, Fulcrad’s stock, the furthest brook of Braydis, Francvadum, which lies on the water of Brosson, and beyond Hilduin’s seat to the distance of a crossbow-shot, together with all the land of Culmont, with its water and woods and other uses—shall always be preserved peacefully and freely in your right and that of your successors, so that no person may carry on any work there without your consent; nor may bishops or any ministers of churches have authority to exact tithes or *terragium* [land-dues] from the produce of that land, which is cultivated by the labour of your house, or to inflict annoyances. We likewise decree that the adjacent village shall remain in the freedom granted and confirmed in writing by the aforesaid count. Furthermore, we decree that all estates and goods which you now lawfully possess, [Col. 1154B] or may in future be able justly and canonically to acquire through the grant of pontiffs, the generosity of princes, or the offering of the faithful, shall remain firm and inviolate for you and your successors; among these we have thought fit expressly to name the church of Saint Oeildis, with all that belongs to it.

Therefore let no person whatsoever presume rashly to disturb the aforesaid church, remove its possessions, retain what has been removed, diminish them, or harass it by reckless attacks; but let all things be preserved intact, to serve in every way the benefit of those for whose support and governance they were granted. As a token of the right and possession of the Roman Church, and likewise of your freedom, you shall annually pay ten solidi of Châlons currency to the Lateran palace. [Col. 1154C] If, therefore, in the future, any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowing this page of our constitution, should rashly attempt to act against it, then, after a second or third warning, unless he makes amends by suitable satisfaction, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and honour; let him know himself guilty before divine judgment for the iniquity committed; let him be cut off from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, our Redeemer; and let him be subject to severe vengeance at the last judgment. But upon all who preserve what is just for that church may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that they may receive here the fruit of good action and find before the strict Judge the rewards of eternal peace. Amen, amen, [Col. 1154D] amen.

I, Calixtus, bishop of the Catholic Church, have signed.  
I, Lambert, bishop of Ostia, was present and have signed.  
I, Peter, cardinal-deacon of Saints Cosmas and Damian, was present and have signed.  
I, Gregory, cardinal-deacon of Saint Angelo, was present and have signed.  
I, Romanus, cardinal-deacon of Saint Mary in Portico, was present and have signed.

Given at Cluny through the hand of Chrysogonus, cardinal and librarian of the Holy Roman Church, on the Nones of January [5 January], in the thirteenth indiction, in the year 1120 from the Incarnation of the Lord [Col. 1155A], in the first year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Calixtus II.

LXVI. He confirms the immunity and possessions of the monastery of Vézelay. (1120, 12 January.)

[Only a mention of this privilege survives in Mabillon, *Annals of the Benedictine Order*, vol. VI, p. 46.]

LXVII. To B[erard], bishop of Mâcon, and G[ualter], bishop of Chalon.—He reports that he consecrated the altars of the monastery of Tournus and blessed its cemetery. (1120, 14 January.)

[MANSI, *Councils*, XXI, 205.]

[Col. 1155B] CALIXTUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the venerable B., bishop of Mâcon, and G., bishop of Chalon: greeting and apostolic blessing.

We wish your belovedness to know that, when we recently came to Tournus, at the request of the abbot and brethren of that place we consecrated the altars and blessed the cemetery; and, sprinkling holy water there, we ordered boundaries to be set around it. Within these boundaries—as they are marked by crosses according to the custom of the land—we both forbade and utterly forbid seizures, plundering, assaults, or any such acts. If anyone, therefore, should presume with audacious rashness to oppose this our constitution, let him be suspended from divine offices [Col. 1155C] until he has made satisfaction. But whoever observes it shall obtain the blessing and grace of almighty God and His apostles.

Given at Mâcon, the nineteenth day before the Kalends of February [14 January], thirteenth indiction.

LXVIII. To the canons of Mâcon.—Against the devastators of the village of Mont-Godin. (1120, 14 January.)

[MANSI, *Councils*, XXI, 214.]

CALIXTUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons, the canons of the Church of Mâcon: greeting and apostolic blessing.

We have heard that the village of Mont-Godin belongs to your church [Col. 1155D] and is administered through your ministry. Certain knights, however, are plundering that place under a pretext. By the authority of these present letters we warn them to desist from that devastation and disturbance. If they prove contemptuous, let both they and their supporters be excluded from the thresholds of the churches, and let divine offices be forbidden in their lands, except for the baptism of infants and penance for the dying, until they make satisfaction either by the judgment of the archbishop of Lyons, in whose [Col. 1156A] parish the place lies, or by that of your bishop.

Given the nineteenth day before the Kalends of February [14 January].

LXIX. To A[delbert], abbot of Schaffhausen: he informs him that he has undertaken protection of the monastery. (1120, 14 January.)

[NEUGART, *Codex Diplomaticus Alemannicus*, II, 46.]

CALIXTUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons A., abbot of Schaffhausen, and his brethren: greeting and apostolic blessing.

At the representation of our venerable brother B. [Note: [Col. 1155D] Bruno, archbishop, founder of the monastery of Saint Florin of the Order of Saint Benedict at Confluence, flourished at this time.] archbishop of Trier, and Hu. [Note: [Col. 1155D] Read: Hugh.] the scholastic, we have received your church and its goods into the guardianship and protection of blessed Peter, and have fortified them by the safeguard of our writings. We have also sent letters to our venerable brother Vo., bishop of Constance, concerning the complaint [Col. 1156B] at issue between him and you. [Note: [Col. 1156D] Namely the letters reported above under no. 62, 3 January.] Therefore it appeared less appropriate to us to send another privilege to your church through your brother M., or to repeat other letters concerning the same complaint. Yet we earnestly ask and request that you pour out continual prayers to God for us and for the unity of the Catholic Church, and that you remain more diligently in that unity which is Christ. We also ask, as we have already asked in other letters, that you send us one of your brethren who knows both the German and the Latin language.

Given at Mâcon. [Note: [Col. 1156D] Calixtus II therefore withdrew in January from Cluny to Mâcon, in the same province of Burgundy, and again to Cluny. Compare the note on letter 62.] The eighteenth day before the Kalends of February [15 January].

LXX. He confirms the privileges of the nunnery of Beau-lieu. (1120, 23 January.)

[DE LA MURE, *Ecclesiastical History of Lyons*, p. 300.]

CALIXTUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved daughter PETRONILLA, abbess of the monastery of Saint Mary of Fontevraud, and her sisters: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Things offered from their own right to the churches of God by any of the faithful, in consideration of divine love, ought to be kept unimpaired and inviolate.

Accordingly, our son Theotard, archdeacon of the Church of Lyons, the chamberlain Chotard, Pontius the canon, and also the noblemen Bonus Par, with his wife Tubelle and their children, and Dalmaticus [Col. 1156D] with his sons Dalmatius and Pontius, inspired by divine grace, gave to your monastery their estate, formerly called Mount Chotard but now called Beau-lieu.

Moreover, we will and command that the gifts made by Gandemarus Carpinellus, with the consent of his wife and his brother John, for the salvation of their souls, in the province called Forez, shall remain whole and undisturbed hereafter.

Our venerable brother [Col. 1157A] Humbald, archbishop of Lyons, together with the aforesaid archdeacon, requested that this gift be confirmed by our authority.

Accordingly, assenting to their requests, by the present charter we confirm to your monastery the donation of the aforesaid estate, with the church built upon it and all else placed there from their own right by the persons named above or by any others, or which may hereafter, through God’s generosity, happen to be granted.

Therefore no person whatsoever shall have authority to withdraw the aforesaid place and its appurtenances from the unity and subjection of your monastery, to remove its possessions, retain what has been removed, or diminish them; but let all things be preserved intact, for the benefit of the handmaids [Col. 1157B] of God and the poor.

I, Calixtus, bishop of the Catholic Church, have confirmed.

Given at Lyons through the hand of Chrysogonus, cardinal-deacon and librarian of the Holy Roman Church, on the tenth day before the Kalends of February [23 January], in the year 1120 from the Incarnation of the Lord, in the first year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Calixtus II.

LXXI. To Marbod, bishop of Rennes.—Concerning the sentence of excommunication pronounced against the abbot and monks of Saint Melaine. (1120, 5 February.)

[BALUZE, *Miscellanea*, III, 14.]

CALIXTUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother MARBOD, bishop of Rennes: greeting and apostolic blessing.

We thank your prudence for having hitherto firmly observed the sentence of excommunication pronounced against the abbot of Saint Melaine and the monks because of their contumacy. We ask and command that you continue to do the same, until, after the canons have been fully reinstated in accordance with our command, the abbot himself, with the monks and with testimony from the canons, comes to us and makes satisfaction before the judgment of the Church for his contempt of us.

Given at Vienne, on the Nones of February [5 February].

LXXII. Privilege for the monastery of Saint Mary of Bonneval. (1120, 7 February.)

[MANRIQUE, *Cistercian Annals*, I, 94.]

[Col. 1157D]

CALIXTUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons JOHN, abbot of the monastery of Saint Mary of Bonneval, and his brethren, present and future, for ever.

Although, by the benevolence of the Apostolic See, we consider ourselves debtors to all the children of the Church, it is especially fitting that we provide for you with a more earnest devotion of charity. For while we were still governing the Church of Vienne, acting upon the counsel of wise and religious men, we chose your place; and, with the assent of our most dear son Stephen, abbot of Cîteaux, we took you from that venerable and religious monastery of Cîteaux and established you there, so that henceforth the discipline of monastic religion might be preserved there under the Lord’s protection. Therefore, dearest sons in Christ, granting your petitions, we receive you and your aforesaid place under the guardianship of the Apostolic See and fortify all that is yours by the patronage of blessed Peter. We further confirm to you all the land called Bonus Fons [Good Spring]; the holding of Asueni; together with the lands and woods of Sinco, knight of Bellovisu; Garin of Pineto; William of Castellio [lacuna]; the holding of Ribato, by grant of William, abbot of Saint Theodore, and his brethren; etc., etc. We decree that no one may dare rashly to disturb you or your monastery, remove its possessions, retain what has been removed, diminish them, or harass it with reckless vexations; but that all things be preserved whole and inviolate, to be of benefit in every way to those for whose [Col. 1158B] support and governance they were granted. If, therefore, any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowing this page of our constitution, shall rashly attempt to act against it, then, after a second or third warning, unless he makes amends by suitable satisfaction, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and honour; let him know himself guilty before divine judgment for the iniquity committed; let him be cut off from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, our Redeemer; and let him be subject to severe vengeance at the last judgment. But upon all who preserve what is just for that place may there be the peace of the Lord Jesus Christ, so that they may receive here the fruit of good action and find before the strict Judge the rewards of eternal peace. Amen.

[Col. 1158C] I, Calixtus, bishop of the Catholic Church.

Given at Vienne through the hand of Grisogonus, cardinal-deacon and librarian of the Holy Roman Church, on the seventh day before the Ides of February [7 February], in the third indiction, in the year 1120 from the Incarnation of the Lord.

LXXIII. To Umbald, archbishop of Lyons.—Against the devastators of the village of Mont-Godin. (1120, 10 February.)

[MANSI, *Councils*, XXI, 214.]

CALIXTUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his dearest and venerable brother UMBALD, archbishop of Lyons: greeting and apostolic blessing.

[Col. 1158D] The complaint of our venerable brother B., bishop of the Church of Mâcon, has reached us: your parishioners, namely Wicard of Anton. and Guido “the chained one,” do not cease to inflict injury and grievance upon the Church of Mâcon in the village of Mont-Godin, oppressing that place by unjust exactions. Therefore we enjoin upon your brotherhood that you diligently admonish them either to leave the property and churches free or to render justice concerning this matter in your court or that of the bishop of Mâcon himself. If they scorn this, you shall execute full justice upon them as sacrilegious persons, as required by your office.

Given at Vienne, the fourth day before the Ides of February [10 February].

LXXIV. Bull for the monastery of Saint Cucuphas in the region of Vallès. (1120, 13 February.)

[MARCA, *Marca Hispanica*, Appendix, p. 1253.]

[Col. 1159A]

CALIXTUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son ROLAND, abbot of the venerable monastery of Saint Cucuphas, martyr, of Octavianum, and to his successors to be regularly appointed for ever.

It is fitting that apostolic protection be present for those who choose the religious life, lest perhaps an assault of rashness by anyone should either turn them from their purpose or—God forbid—break the strength of holy religion. Therefore, beloved son in the Lord Roland, we graciously grant your pious petitions and receive, under the protection of blessed Peter and of ourselves, following the example of our predecessors Sylvester, John, Benedict, and Urban II, Roman pontiffs, the aforesaid monastery [Col. 1159B] of Saint Cucuphas, martyr, which is known to belong directly, without any intermediary, to the right and ownership of blessed Peter, and in which you are devoted to divine service; and we fortify it by the privilege of this present charter. We decree, therefore, that the aforesaid monastery, both in its head and members, and all possessions and goods which it now possesses or shall acquire, shall be preserved firm and entire forever under the right and lordship of blessed Peter, with full right. First we establish that the monastic order according to God and the Rule of blessed Benedict shall be continually observed in the same monastery; among which possessions and goods we have thought fit to specify the following by their proper names:

The place itself in which the aforesaid monastery is situated, in the village belonging to that monastery; the castle of Octavianum, of Fruneto or Aqualonga; likewise the castle of Ricarli, of Cirtulo, and of Saint Emeterius; the valley of Gausach and Campiniano, with all tithes and first-fruits, waters, boundaries, and mountains; the freeholds and possessions of Budigiis and Aculione, as Abbot Oto bought them; the house of Rivosicco with its possessions; the freeholds and possessions, with waters and mills, situated in the castle of Rivorubeo; the monastery of Saint Cecilia of Monte Ferrato, with the churches of Saint Felix and Saint John of Vocarisses; the monastery of Saint Paul [Col. 1159D] outside the walls of Barcelona, with the freehold which Giribertus and his wife offered there; the monastery of Saint Saviour of Breda, with the hill of Monte Sirtille; the monastery of Saint Lawrence, with the church of Saint Stephen on its mount and the church of Saint Stephen of Castella, with the possessions of the said monasteries; the churches of Saint Peter and Saint Severus, entire, at Octavianum; the church of Saint Vincent of Aqua Alba, with its demesne; the churches of Saint Stephen and Saint Mary of the Palace within the walls, together with the whole hamlet of Caberictibus and of the village of Tort; and the village of Saint Stephen and Blessed Mary, with its buildings and the tithes and first-fruits belonging thereto; the chapels of Saint Genesius and Saint Eulalia of Tapiolas, with tithes [Col. 1160A] and first-fruits; the entire demesne of the valley of Gregoria; the chapels of Saint Cucuphas of Rifano, Saint Atisclus of Vilanzir, Saint Martin and Saint Roman of Monte Cathano, and Saint Margaret of Buada, with their demesnes; the churches of Saint Stephen of the palace of Auzito, Saint Felix of Castella, Saint Sebastian of Monte Maiori, with that same mount, Saint Mary of Toldello, and Saint Felix of the village of Mylanis, with their demesnes and with tithes and first-fruits; the chapels of Saint Mary of Fontisrubei, with the freehold which Geraldus Mironis offered there; Saint Emeterius; Saint Mary of Gausach; and Saint Lawrence of Fonte Calciato, with their possessions; the churches of Saint Mary with the castle of Feles; Saint Mary of Monasteriolo; Saint Peter of Masquefa [Col. 1160B] with the castle of Holy Cross of the Palace; Saint Mary of Capellatiis; Saint Mary of Aqualata; and Saint Mary of Clariana, with its castle and demesnes, and the tithes and first-fruits belonging to the said churches; the chapels of Saint Sylvester of Valzano, Saint Cucuphas of Moja, Saint Cucuphas of Garrigiis, Saint Benedict of Spicellis, Saint Stephen of Castelleto, and Saint Peter of Vim, with their demesnes, possessions, and tithes and first-fruits; the churches of Saint Julian and Saint Mary of Santa Oliva, with that castle, and Saint Saviour; Saint Mary of Calderio, with that castle, ponds and waters; and Saints Vincent and Bartholomew of Albipryana, with that castle and its boundaries and possessions, tithes and first-fruits; [Col. 1160C] the churches of the Holy Sepulchre and Saint Mary of Amposta; the castle of Ripa de Cascayo with its church, ponds, waters, villages, all possessions, tithes and first-fruits; with Algena of Tortosa, from the water of Uticona to the extremity of the village of Alcozer, as is contained in the instruments of the general grants; the chapels of Saint Martin, Saint Felix, and Saint Genesius situated at the manor of Fagio, and Saint Felix of the Castle of the Faithful, with their demesnes; the church of Saint Quiricus and Saint Peter of Cortentibus, with all tithes, first-fruits, possessions, freeholds, and appurtenances.

Finally: gardens, vineyards, and water in the city of Barcelona; and in the demesnes of Provinciana, Saint Baudilius, Lupricato in many places, Saint John of Pinu de Sanctis, Sarriano, Galiffa, Duodecimo, and Cervilione; the comital gardens, as the lord count left them to the aforesaid monastery; those of Orta, Palomar, and Bitulona; together with the abbatial holding and its *pariliatae* [uncertain tenure or dues]; the demesnes of Massanis, Gerunda, Corniliano, Molletum, Ficana, and Pedrenchs, with the chapel of the palace of Auzito; the castle of Malleato, of Pulchrovicino; the demesnes of Plegamans, Calidis, Laura, Castellar, Minorisa, Ausona, and Garnisas, with the chapel situated there; the freeholds and possessions situated in the castle of Tarracia, Upper and Lower Lizano, Upper and Lower Corrono, Samalus, Laroxa in many places, [Col. 1161A] Monte Cathano, and at the foot of Monte Cathano toward the east beside the river Bisancius, and on the other side toward the south and around, between the mountain and the village of Rafiam or Calciatam; the freeholds and possessions of the towers of Bisibus, of the castle of Fontisrubei, of Carol, Priniana, Monte Acuto, Castro Viti, Messana of Monte Superbo, and of the castle of Olerdula; and all freeholds, possessions, and appurtenances situated in the bishoprics of Barcelona, Girona, Vic, Minorica, and Tortosa, together with everything above granted to the aforesaid monastery and belonging to it.

We also confirm the tithes and first-fruits, offerings, funeral dues, and revenues belonging to your monastery in the above-mentioned churches or elsewhere, in parishes, castles, lordships, and other places, which your monastery has possessed for thirty years or more by the grant, liberality, donation, purchase, or sale of our predecessors, kings, counts, bishops, clerics, or other persons. [Col. 1161B] We decree that these, together with all your above-mentioned property, shall be preserved for ever wholly untroubled, entire, and immune. We further decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb or invade your aforesaid monastery, remove its possessions, retain what has been removed, claim for his own use things unjustly given or alienated, diminish, sell, improperly alienate, or harass it with reckless vexations; and if anything has been done otherwise than stated, we decree it entirely void. We establish [Col. 1161C] that no king, bishop, or person established in any rank or office shall ever dare to press vexatiously upon the affairs of the same monastery or to constrain its people for any cause; but, as is read above, it is to be held by you and your successors and governed in the fear of God. We decree that the cemetery of that place shall be wholly free, so that no one may obstruct the devotion and final will of those who choose to be buried there, unless they have been excommunicated. When you, the present abbot of this place, or any of your successors, die, no one shall be set over it through any trickery of usurpation, except one whom the brethren by common consent, or the sounder part of the brethren, shall elect in the fear of God and according to the Rule of blessed Benedict. The person elected [Col. 1161D] shall be consecrated by the diocesan bishop, provided that he enjoys the favour and communion of the Apostolic See and is willing to administer it freely, without any wickedness, fraud, or reservation. Otherwise, he shall have recourse to his mother, the Roman Church, or to the Roman pontiff, or shall be consecrated without any disturbance by another Catholic bishop whom he may prefer, acting under our special command. By the same authority we decree concerning the ordinations of the brethren who are its clerics, concerning chrism, oil, and the consecration of altars or basilicas. We establish that the abbot may forbid, correct, and excommunicate his clerics if an evident cause exists, keeping God nevertheless before his eyes. We confirm the baptism customarily belonging to the monastery and its churches. And if the abbot, monk, or any cleric or layman of that monastery and its churches is justly or unjustly placed under interdict or excommunicated by an archbishop, diocesan bishop, or any prelate or ecclesiastical person, he shall remain absolved therefrom by our apostolic authority. Therefore we decree that, since the same monastery with its walls is specially of the right and property of blessed Peter, and this has hitherto been observed there, no one except the Roman pontiff may subject it to an interdict or bind it with the bond of excommunication. As a token of the protection conferred by the Apostolic See and of the freedom due to it, for the church of Saint Paul [Col. 1162B] you shall pay one Byzantine annually to the Lateran palace. If, therefore, any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowing this page of our constitution, should rashly attempt to act against it, then, after a second or third warning, unless he makes amends by suitable satisfaction, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and honour; let him know himself guilty before divine judgment for the iniquity committed; let him be cut off from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ; and let him be subject to severe vengeance at the last judgment. But upon all who preserve what is just for that place may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that they may receive here the fruit of good action and find before the strict Judge the rewards of eternal peace. Amen, amen, amen.

[Col. 1162C] I, Calixtus, bishop of the Catholic Church, have subscribed.

Given at Rome [Note: [Col. 1161D] Read: Rome. JAFFÉ.] through the hand of Grisogonus, cardinal-deacon and librarian of the Holy Roman Church, the seventeenth day before the Kalends of March [13 February], in the thirteenth indiction, in the year 1120 from the Incarnation of the Lord, in the second year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Calixtus II.

LXXV. He confirms the goods and privileges of the canons of the church of Saint John the Evangelist at Besançon. (1120, 15 February.)

[MANSI, *Councils*, XXI, 197.]

CALIXTUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons, the canons of the church of Saint John the Evangelist at Besançon, [Col. 1162D] present and future, for ever.

Just as no effect is to be given to those who ask for what is unjust, so the petition of those who desire what is lawful must not be deferred. Therefore, dearest sons in Christ, we graciously assent to your petition; and, strengthening both you and all that is yours by the protection of the Apostolic See, we confirm for ever to you and your successors what you are seen lawfully to possess at present—namely, your houses, etc. It enumerates the possessions of that church. Then:

We decree, therefore, that no person may rashly disturb that church, remove its possessions, retain what has been removed, diminish them, or harass it with reckless [Col. 1163A] vexations; but that all things shall be preserved whole, to be of benefit in every way to those for whose support and governance they were granted. Further, we forbid the treasure of your church to be alienated except perhaps for the ransom of captives, necessity caused by famine, or the purchase of lands. We forbid your archpriests and archdeacons to presume to subject your churches and their priests or clerics to a sentence of interdict without the common counsel of the archbishop and your whole chapter. Moreover, giving more earnest attention to the peace of your church and desiring to preserve its rights, we confirm the customs which the church of Saint Stephen is known from ancient times to owe it, and which are contained in the book called the [Col. 1163B] *Rule*: namely, that on the Purification of Blessed Mary the canons of Saint Stephen shall come to the procession and provide seventy-two candles; on Maundy Thursday, they shall come with candlesticks and the greater cross for the preparation of the holy chrism; on Holy Saturday, they shall supply six pounds of wax for making the great candle, four canons to read the four lessons, and, in addition to them, a canon-priest for the collect; on Easter Day, they shall solemnly bring the arm of Saint Stephen in procession; on the Saturday of Pentecost, they shall send two canons to read two lessons and, in addition to them, a canon-priest for the collect; at the harvest and vintage of Poligny, wax sufficient for the purpose; on the feast of Saint Stephen in August, a cow or four solidi, and a measure [Col. 1163C] of wine; at the vintage of Ultrajurensis, wax sufficient for the purpose. Throughout the year, while there is wine in Saint John’s cellar, they shall provide one cubit of candle every evening. If the canons dine together, they shall provide as much candle at dinner as is needed; otherwise, to every canon residing from the Black Gate as far as the old wall, half a foot of candle; to the provost one ell, and likewise to the dean. At the Nativity of the Lord, as at Easter, they shall solemnly bring the arm of Saint Stephen in procession. From the whole mountain, clerics and laypersons shall render the tithe to your parish; nevertheless, laypersons shall pay all parochial dues to the church of Saint John the Baptist. Whenever a plea is held, God’s offering shall be divided between the canons of Saint John and Saint Stephen. The cemetery of Saint Stephen, with the alms of the householders, shall remain common to both churches. At the reception of kings and bishops alike, the clerics of Saint Stephen shall come to your church in silk copes. At the election of the archbishop of Besançon, the clergy and people of the city shall assemble in your chapter according to the ancient custom of your church. We also establish by perpetual confirmation that all the customs and tenures which your church held and possessed from the time of Hugh, your archbishop of Salins, to the time of the aforesaid our brother Hugh, likewise your archbishop, who died on the Jerusalem pilgrimage, shall henceforth be held and possessed by it wholly and peacefully. If, therefore, in the future any ecclesiastical [Col. 1164A] or secular person, knowing this page of our confirmation or grant, shall rashly attempt to act against it, then, after a second or third warning, unless he makes amends by suitable satisfaction, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and honour; let him know himself guilty before divine judgment for the iniquity committed; let him be cut off from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, our Redeemer; and let him be subject to severe vengeance at the last judgment. But upon all who preserve what is just for that church may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that they may experience here the fruit of good action and find before the strict Judge the rewards of eternal peace. Amen, amen.

I, Calixtus, bishop of the Catholic Church, have subscribed.

[Col. 1164B] Given at Rome, the fifteenth day before the Kalends of March [15 February], in the thirteenth indiction, in the year 1120 from the Incarnation of the Lord, in the second year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Calixtus II.

LXXVI. To the archbishops of Arles, Aix, and Embrun, and the other bishops throughout the province. (1120, 18 February.)

[DE BELZUNCE, *Antiquities of the Church of Marseille*, vol. I, p. 422.]

CALIXTUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brothers ATTO, archbishop of Arles; FULCO, archbishop of Aix; and [WILLIAM], archbishop of Embrun; and to the other bishops throughout the province: greeting and apostolic blessing.

[Col. 1164C] Your belovedness, we believe, does not fail to know that the monastery of Marseille belongs in a special manner to the Roman Church. Therefore we ask and command your brotherhood to leave undisturbed henceforth all possessions which that place is known to have held for thirty years and more. If anyone believes that he has any right in them, let him approach the Apostolic See, and we shall render him justice with full authority.

Given at Valence, the twelfth day before the Kalends of March [18 February].

LXXVII. Privilege for the monastery of Cluny. (1120, 22 February.)

[MANSI, *Councils*, XXI, 208.]

[Col. 1164D]

CALIXTUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his dearest son in Christ, PONTIUS, abbot of Cluny, and to his successors regularly appointed for ever.

The monastery of Cluny, a mirror of monastic religion in modern times and an example in the regions of Gaul, was, from the very beginning of its foundation, offered into the proper jurisdiction of the Apostolic See. Accordingly, our fathers of holy memory—John XI, likewise John XII, Agapetus II, Benedict VI, likewise Benedict VII, Leo VII, likewise Leo IX, Gregory VI, likewise Gregory VII, Alexander II, Stephen, Victor III, Urban II, Paschal II, and Gelasius II, pontiffs of the Roman Church—endowed that place [Col. 1165A] with the prerogative of singular affection and liberty, and fortified all that pertains to it by the enactments of their privileges.

For it was established that all churches, cemeteries, monks, and all laypeople dwelling within the boundaries extending from the stream of Salnai and from the church of Rusiac and the cross of Lornant; likewise from the boundary of the mill of Tornasach, through the village called Varentia, together with the wood of Burseius; and also from the boundary called Perois, as far as the bank at Salnai: should remain under the jurisdiction and protection of the Apostolic See alone. Nor are the priests or parishioners of the place of Cluny to be compelled to attend any synod or assembly except that of the Roman pontiff and the abbot of Cluny.

Indeed, for the ordination of the abbot, monks, or clerics dwelling within [Col. 1165B] the aforesaid boundaries; for the preparation of chrism; and for the consecration of holy oil, churches, altars, and cemeteries, the monastery of Cluny may summon whichever bishop it prefers. No person whatsoever, apart from the Roman pontiff and a legate sent for this purpose, may excommunicate or place under interdict Cluniac monks dwelling anywhere.

Moreover, if a monk, cleric, layman, or person of any order or profession—unless perhaps he has been excommunicated for a definite cause—chooses a dwelling in a Cluniac cloister, he shall be received without anyone’s objection, and whatever he has brought from his own right shall be freely held by the monastery. No one may take away or diminish the altars, cemeteries, tithes, [Col. 1165C] or anything else belonging by right to the Cluniac monks.

No bishop may judge concerning Cluniac monks or monasteries, saving any canonical right that he may have in them; rather, justice shall be sought from the abbot of Cluny. If it cannot be found with him, recourse shall be had to the Apostolic See.

In the abbeys which, together with their abbots, have been given to the governance of the monastery of Cluny—namely, Saint Martial of Limoges, Saint Eparchius of Angoulême, the New Monastery at Poitiers, Saint John of Angély, the monastery of Lezat, Moissac, Figeac, and Saint Giles of Nîmes; in Auvergne, Mozac, Thiers, and Menat; in the diocese of Autun, Vézelay; in that of Auxerre, Saint Germanus; in that of Cambrai, Hunolcourt; in that of Rouen, [Col. 1165D] the abbey at Pontoise; in that of Thérouanne, Saint Bertin and Saint Wulmar; and in Italy, Saint Benedict above the Po—no election shall be made in any way without the command of the abbot of Cluny.

With regard to your altars, churches, and tithes, no bishop may have power to impose any burden or annoyance upon you. Rather, as you have possessed them, in some cases in part and in others in full, by their promise, so you shall possess them in the future. If reverence for your religious life can, according to God, withdraw from lay control the tithes of your churches which are held by laymen, you may possess them for the maintenance of yourselves and the poor.

You shall henceforth hold more peacefully, without any opposition from bishops or episcopal officials, the tithes from your labours—those, namely, [Col. 1166A] which they call *dominicaturae*, cultivated at your expense by the dependents of your monasteries and cells—for which bishops have been accustomed to trouble both you and other men of the monastic profession; and these tithes you distribute to your own brothers who are strangers and to the poor.

All your churches, wherever situated, together with your chapels and cemeteries, shall be free and immune from every exaction, except for the customary episcopal *parata* and the bishop’s jurisdiction over priests if they offend against the dignity of their order. You or your brethren may choose priests for your churches, provided that they receive the care of souls from bishops or bishops’ vicars without payment. But if those bishops should, God forbid, perversely refuse to confer it, then, by the kindness of the Apostolic See, the priests shall obtain permission to celebrate the offices.

If diocesan bishops refuse to perform the consecrations of your churches without charge, you may receive them from any Catholic bishop. Nor shall the brethren of your cells wherever situated suffer suspension of the divine offices because of any interdict or excommunication; rather, the monks themselves, their servants, and those who have dedicated themselves to monastic profession shall, with the doors of the churches shut and diocesan officials not admitted, celebrate the offices of divine service and perform burial rites. You shall also have the striking of your own coinage or money, whenever and for as long as you please.

Therefore, all these things, as they were established by our predecessors, we also establish by apostolic authority [Col. 1166C] and confirm by the decree of this present privilege.

Furthermore, beloved son in Christ Pontius, whom, while we held the governance of the church of Vienne, we consecrated abbot with our own hands by the grace of God: embracing both your person and the place over which, by God’s authority, you preside with the whole fullness of our affection, and providing more carefully for your peace, we have judged the following to be added: no bishop shall lay hands of consecration or ordination upon persons elected to your abbeys without letters of recommendation from the abbot of Cluny. Otherwise both the consecrator, as a violator of the apostolic constitution, shall be subject to a more severe penalty, and the election or ordination of the consecrated person shall be held invalid until satisfaction is made to the Apostolic See and to its monastery of Cluny [Col. 1166D].

Moreover, we grant to the priests of the Cluniac parish churches of Saint Mary and Saint Odo permission, according to ancient custom, to admit and dismiss penitents from the church and to draw up nuptial charters. We forbid both the bishop of Mâcon and all others to impose annoyances upon you concerning this matter or any other matters established for you. Therefore, if anyone with rash presumption, etc.

I, Calixtus, bishop of the Catholic Church, have subscribed.

Given at Valence through the hand of Chrysogonus, cardinal-deacon and librarian of the Holy Roman Church, on the eighth day before the Kalends of March, in the thirteenth indiction, in the year 1120 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the second year of the pontificate of lord Pope Calixtus II.

## LXXVIII. To the Canons of Vienne.—He confirms the ancient privileges of the Church of Vienne.  
*(A.D. 1120, February 25.)*

[MANSI, *Councils*, XXI, 191.]

[Col. 1167A]

Calixtus, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons PETER, dean, and the canons and clerics of the Church of Vienne, present and future, for ever.

Although, by reason of the administration of the Apostolic See, the care of all churches rests upon us, it is nevertheless especially fitting that we provide for Vienne with particular solicitude. For it was the first church committed, by God’s disposition, to our care, and it was for its governance that we received the grace of episcopal consecration. Moved therefore by the duty of common and special affection, we have determined, dearest sons in Christ, to love and honour your mother, the holy Church of Vienne, [Col. 1167B] and to foster it under the patronage of Saint Peter.

Accordingly, every dignity, protection, and grant which it possesses, whether granted through the authentic privileges of our predecessors Sylvester, Nicholas, Leo, Gregory, and the other Roman pontiffs, or through the benefactions of emperors, kings, princes, and other faithful persons, we too, by God’s authority, grant and confirm by the text of this present privilege: namely, that it shall hold the primacy over seven provinces—over Vienne itself, Bourges, Bordeaux, Auch, which is called Novempopulana, Narbonne, Aix, [Col. 1167C] and Embrun—and that in them the archbishop of Vienne shall act in the place of the Roman pontiff, convene synodal assemblies, and decide ecclesiastical matters justly and canonically.

Moreover, the following six towns or cities—Grenoble, Valence, Die, Alba, Viviers, Geneva, and Maurienne—shall remain in obedience and subjection to him as to their own metropolitan. The archbishop of Tarentaise, although by a grant of the Apostolic See he is held by some to be preeminent, shall obey the archbishop of Vienne as his primate and be subject to him.

Further, in the archdeaconry of Salmorac, the Church of Vienne shall, without anyone’s disturbance or diminution, possess consecrations, ordinations, and everything belonging to the pontifical office. Likewise, the abbey [Col. 1167D] of Saint Peter situated outside the gate of Vienne; within the same city the abbey of Saint Andrew, one for monks and the other for nuns; the abbey of Saint Theuderus; and the abbey of Saint Mary of Bonnevaux, which, God granting, was founded at our expense and through our labours, shall remain under the jurisdiction and subjection of the aforesaid Church of Vienne.

In the church of Romans itself, although it asserts Roman liberty, nevertheless, after examination of the privileges of our predecessors and the imperial decrees, we decree that the bishops of Vienne shall possess full power over secular and regular clerics and canons there ordained or to be ordained. Likewise in the church of Saint Donatus and Saint Valerius, and the church of Saint Peter of Campania and Blessed Mary of Annonay.

Furthermore, we confirm in perpetuity to the Church of Vienne the castles recovered or acquired by us: namely, Pompeiacum, Sasserlum, and the castle of Malavalle [Col. 1168A]. We decree that the cemetery consecrated around the church of Saint Maurice by our predecessor of holy memory, Pope Paschal, shall be free, so that no one may hinder the devotion or last will of those who decide to be buried there, unless they are excommunicated; the right of their own parish being, of course, preserved.

Furthermore, in greater affection for the Church of Vienne, we grant that the cross may be carried before the archbishop of Vienne throughout his province; and we forbid the Church of Vienne to be subject to any legate other than a cardinal or another person from the Roman province sent from the side of the Roman pontiff. Moreover, in the churches which [Col. 1168B] we consecrated in the diocese of Vienne after undertaking the ministry of the Apostolic See, the archbishop of Vienne shall have the same power of interdicting and ordaining which he had before.

Within the precinct of the cloister, where the residences of the clerics are situated, no layperson whatsoever shall henceforth have a residence, make an assault or robbery, or dare inflict bodily injury upon anyone.

If, therefore, any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowing this text of our confirmation or grant, should rashly attempt to act against it, and, having been warned a second or third time, does not make proper amends through suitable satisfaction, let that person be deprived of the dignity of power and honour; let him know himself liable before divine judgment for the iniquity committed; let him be cut off from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord, Redeemer Jesus Christ; and let him be subject to severe vengeance at the final judgment [Col. 1168C]. But upon all who preserve the rights of that same Church may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that they may receive here the fruit of good action and find, before the strict Judge, the rewards of eternal peace. Amen, amen.

I, Calixtus, bishop of the Catholic Church.

Given at Valence, five days before the Kalends of March, in the thirteenth indiction, in the year 1120 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the second year of the pontificate of lord Pope Calixtus II.

## LXXIX. He transfers to the Church of Compostela the metropolitan dignity of the Church of Mérida.  
*(A.D. 1120, February 26.)*

[FLOREZ, *Sacred Spain*, XX, 292.]

Calixtus, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother DIDACUS, archbishop of Compostela: greeting and apostolic blessing.

By the disposition of the Almighty, times are changed and kingdoms transferred. Hence we read that nations once of great renown have been worn down and humbled, while insignificant peoples are sometimes exalted. Hence, in some regions the dignity of Christian power is trampled down by the tyranny of pagans; in others, the ferocity of pagans has occupied the dominion of the Christian name—as is known to have happened, because of sins, to the city of Mérida.

For when it appeared noble among the noble cities of Spain, it was so delivered, by the divine ordering of changed times, to the power of the Moabites or Moors that both the glory of its episcopal rank and the dignity of the Christian faith perished there [Col. 1169A]. Its suffragan cities too, except only three—namely Coimbra, Salamanca, and Ávila, in which by God’s grace an episcopal see still endures—having been occupied by the same tyranny, likewise fell from their former glory.

In this change, however, following the customary dispensation of the Apostolic See and the counsel of our brethren, we judged that provision should be made both for God’s honour and for the salvation of souls, lest the unity of a proper head should be lacking to those remaining Christians, or the pontifical authority of so noble a church should perish altogether.

Therefore, out of greater reverence for the blessed Apostle James, whose glorious body adorns your Church, [Col. 1169B] and out of special affection for his person, at the petition of our nephew Alfonso, king of Spain, and of our brethren H., bishop of Portugal, and P., abbot of Cluny, as well as Laurence, canon of your Church, we grant, by God’s authority, the dignity of the aforesaid metropolis to the see of Compostela, honourable and abounding in a multitude of clergy and people. Its suffragans, whether they now possess their own sees or shall, through the Lord’s mercy, possess them in the future, we subject to you, dearest brother and fellow bishop Didacus, and to your successors, to be ordained and governed by metropolitan right. In those cities which formerly had their own bishops, should the multitude and wishes of clergy and people warrant it, we grant you free authority [Col. 1169C] to ordain bishops.

It is therefore your duty henceforth so to love the Roman Church and so to persist in its obedience and fidelity that, established as archbishops through its goodwill and generosity, you may be found worthier through the favour of this dignity.

If, therefore, any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowing this text of our constitution, should rashly attempt to act against it and, having been warned a second or third time, does not make proper amends through suitable satisfaction, let that person be deprived of the dignity of his power and honour; let him acknowledge himself liable before divine judgment for the iniquity committed; let him be cut off from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, our Redeemer; and let him be subject to severe vengeance at the final judgment [Col. 1169D]. But upon those who obey and observe it may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that they may receive here the fruit of good action and find, before the strict Judge, the rewards of eternal peace. Amen.

Fare well.

Given at Valence through the hand of Grisogonus, cardinal-deacon and librarian of the Holy Roman Church, four days before the Kalends of March, in the thirteenth indiction, in the year 1120 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the second year of the pontificate of lord Calixtus II.

## LXXX. To bishops, abbots, clerics, etc., established throughout the provinces of Mérida and Braga: he announces that he has entrusted his authority in their regions to Didacus, archbishop of Compostela.  
*(A.D. 1120, February 27.)*

[FLOREZ, *same work*, p. 295.]

[Col. 1170A]

Calixtus, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved brethren and fellow bishops, abbots, clerics, princes, and all the faithful established throughout the provinces of Mérida and Braga: greeting and apostolic blessing.

The ancient institution of the Apostolic See requires, and the obligation of charity compels us, to visit those who are near and those who are far away, and diligently to provide for the salvation of all. Therefore, dearest sons in Christ, we have judged it necessary to entrust our authority in your regions to our venerable brother D., archbishop of Compostela, so that together with you he may carefully hear the ecclesiastical matters arising among you and diligently provide for your needs and for the support of your churches [Col. 1170B].

We therefore ask and command all of you to take him reverently as our vicar and obey him with due humility, as sons of Saint Peter ought to do. Moreover, when the need of ecclesiastical utility requires it, assemble at his summons and celebrate synodal meetings with him in honour of the Lord, so that, with your cooperation, he may by God’s grace correct what requires correction and confirm what requires confirmation [Col. 1170C].

Given at Valence, three days before the Kalends of March.

## LXXXI. Special letter to the archbishop of Compostela.  
*(A.D. 1120, February 27.)*

[FLOREZ, *same work*]

Calixtus, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother DIDACUS, archbishop of Compostela: greeting and apostolic blessing.

The works performed make manifest the abundance of affection with which we embrace both your person and the Church entrusted to you. For we have entrusted to you our authority over the provinces of Mérida and Braga, and have adorned the church of Saint James with the glory of metropolitan dignity [Col. 1170D]. We therefore exhort and admonish your brotherhood in the Lord to acknowledge the benefaction of the Roman Church and, God cooperating, to strive to fulfil the obedience imposed upon you, so that you may both provide beneficially for those whose care has been entrusted to you and always merit the favour of Saint Peter.

Given at Valence, three days before the Kalends of March.

## LXXXII. He orders G[undisalvus], bishop of Coimbra, and I[eronymus], bishop of Salamanca, to obey Didacus their metropolitan.  
*(A.D. 1120, March 2.)*

[FLOREZ, *same work*, p. 294.]

Calixtus, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable [Col. 1171A] brethren and fellow bishops G. of Coimbra and J. of Salamanca: greeting and apostolic blessing.

The authority of the office entrusted to us compels us, by God’s grace, to be solicitous for the condition of all churches. Therefore, dearest brethren, we have judged that provision should be made both for you and for your churches, so that, according to the custom of suffragan bishops, you may have a head to whom you ought to have recourse.

We have accordingly provided to entrust this charge to our venerable brother and fellow bishop Didacus of Compostela. We command your brotherhood henceforth to render full obedience and reverence to him, established as archbishop over you and the remaining bishops and parishes of your province by the generosity of the Apostolic See, [Col. 1171B] and to recognize the Church of Saint James of Compostela as your mother from this time forward.

Given at the Castle of Crista, six days before the Nones of March.

## LXXXIII. *He receives the Portuguese Church under protection and confirms its possessions.*  
*(A.D. 1120, March 2.)*

[Mention of this privilege occurs in RIBEIRO, *Chronological and Critical Dissertations on the History of Portugal*. Lisbon, 1810, octavo, vol. V, p. 5.]

## LXXXIV. To the bishops, princes, counts, knights, and other faithful throughout Spain.  
*(A.D. 1120, March 4.)*

[FLOREZ, *Sacred Spain*, XX, 316.]

[Col. 1171C]

Calixtus, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved brethren and sons, bishops, princes, counts, knights, and all other faithful throughout Spain: greeting and apostolic blessing.

After his son-in-law Raymond, count of noble memory and our brother, had died, Alfonso, king of illustrious memory, made Raymond’s son king and secured the kingdom for him by the oaths of the magnates, as you yourselves know more certainly. Afterwards, however, the mother of this boy king, daughter of the aforesaid king, after having had him crowned, forcibly extorted other oaths contrary to the former ones and, forgetting maternal affection, directed the whole force of her design toward the destruction of her son.

How impious [Col. 1171D] and contrary to every principle this is, anyone who uses reason can readily perceive. For the boy ought not so irrationally to have been deprived of his grandfather’s benefaction, nor ought the mother to have been stirred by such wickedness against her son that, through her, persons who had sworn one thing to the son should be compelled to do another.

We therefore command by apostolic authority that no one whatsoever, because of the extortion of the subsequent oath made by the aforesaid queen, shall fail to observe inviolably the first oath made to her son. Since, after an oath has been lawfully made, no other oath ought to be made which is subsequently extorted against it, it is by no means to be observed.

Given at Veneriis, four days before the Nones of March.

## LXXXV. To Pelagius, bishop of Braga.  
*(A.D. 1120, March 5.)*

[D. Rodrigue DA CUNHA, *Catalogues of the Bishops of Porto*. Porto, 1742, folio, part II, p. 10.]

[Col. 1172A]

Calixtus, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother PELAGIUS, bishop of Braga: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Our predecessor of holy memory, Pope Paschal, by the authority of his letters ordered the churches of the Portuguese bishopric, which the Church of Braga had usurped, to be restored to our fellow brother Hugh, bishop of Portugal, according to the ancient definition of the boundaries. Since this was not at all carried out, he obtained canonical justice both concerning these churches [Col. 1172B] and against those who had defied the command.

When similar rash audacity was afterwards discovered, our son B., cardinal-priest and legate of the Apostolic See in those regions, promulgated against it, as we have learned, a more severe sentence in the council of Burgos. We therefore, following the steps of our aforesaid lord, command by a renewed injunction of the Apostolic See that within forty days after these letters reach you, you cause those same churches to be restored to our aforesaid brother Hugh, bishop of Portugal, together with the full integrity of their property. Otherwise, from that time onward, confirming by the authority of the Apostolic See the sentence of our aforesaid lord and of his legate, promulgated according to canonical equity, we forbid you the exercise of the episcopal office until you make satisfaction to him.

[Col. 1172C]

Given at Beveris, three days before the Nones of March.

## LXXXVI. Privilege for the Church of Saint Mary Magdalene of Besançon.  
*(A.D. 1120, March 11.)*

[*Memoirs and Unpublished Documents of Franche-Comté*, vol. II, p. 317.]

Calixtus, bishop, servant of the servants of God.

We confirm the liberty and safe-conduct within the city granted by Hugh of Salins, archbishop of Besançon of good memory, to your cloister and the houses adjoining it, as is contained in that archbishop’s chirograph. We also confirm the possessions granted by the same brother: namely, the holding of the armarius’ chaplain [Col. 1172D], with its oven and appurtenances; the street at the eastern end of your church between the holding of Sibo and that of Varnerius, and the holding of Odo on the western side; the road from the gate of that same city to your refectory from the southern gate; the land extending from the Gate of the Arenas to the dormitory of the canons, whether occupied by houses or vineyards or vacant; the wood which lies near the city [lacuna] of Besançon; the church of Saint James within the Arenas, with its appurtenances; the holding of Remigius above the Doubs; the holding of Constantine near the mill in the street of Baptent; part of the street of Baptent; the revenues called *Manaydae* in the press of Naal; your forage-right which you won in judicial combat against Hubald of Abbans; [Col. 1173A] the land of your church, whether occupied by vineyards or houses or vacant; three solidi of annual rent at the general plea, granted by Stephen the viscount; the tithes of your parish, as you have hitherto possessed them canonically; and we decree that the ancient and reasonable customs of that Church shall remain valid.

Given at Vapnuci [Note: [Col. 1173D] Read: Vapinci, i.e. Gap], on the fifth day before the Ides of March, in the thirteenth indiction, in the year 1120 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the second year of the pontificate of lord Pope Calixtus II.

## LXXXVII. He confirms the discipline, possessions, and privileges of the canonry at the *People of the Martyrs* (*Plebem martyrum*; Ulciensis).  
*(Giofredo testifies in* Historical Monuments of the Fatherland, *Turin, 1836, Writers, p. 376, that this bull was given at Asti on 28 March 1120.)*

[See the Cartulary of the Church of Ulciensis, Turin, [Col. 1173B] 1753, folio, p. 2.]

## LXXXVIII. *To Amadeus, bishop of Maurienne.—He commands him to restore the Church of Saint Mary at Susa to Arbert, provost of Ulciensis, within forty days.*  
*(A.D. 1120, March 28.)*

[See above.]

## LXXXIX. He confirms the possessions of the Church of Saint John of Monza.  
*(A.D. 1120, April 11.)*

[GIULINI, *Memoirs of Milan*. Milan, 1760, quarto, V, 555.]

Calixtus, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son GUILLELMUS, archpriest of Monza, and his successors canonically appointed in perpetuity.

[Col. 1173C] Just as no effect ought to be granted to those who make unjust requests, so the petition of those who make lawful requests ought not to be delayed. Therefore, beloved son William, archpriest, we receive under the protection of the Apostolic See the church of blessed John the Baptist, over which, by God’s authority, you are known to preside, and strengthen it with the patronage of Saint Peter together with all that pertains to it.

That place, built by Queen Theodelinda of noble memory and richly endowed with honours, possessions, and treasure by her generosity, is held worthy of veneration and renowned. Therefore, by the text of this present privilege, we establish by apostolic authority that all goods and all possessions which it now possesses by grants of pontiffs, liberality of princes, offerings of the faithful, or other just means, or which, by the Lord’s bounty, it may justly and canonically acquire in the future, shall remain firm and inviolate for you and your successors [Col. 1173D].

Among these, the following appeared proper to name expressly: namely, the monastery of Saint Peter of Cremella, with the church of Saint Sisinnius; the church of Saint John of Blutiaco; Saint George of Coltiaco; and Saint John of Castromartis. At Vellate, the church of Saint Mary and Saint Fidelis; the church of Saint Julian of the parish of Colonia, with its chapels; and the church of Saint Eusebius. At Sesto, the church of Saint Alexander, Saint Michael, and Saint Saviour; the churches of Saint Martin, Saint Peter, Saint Michael, Saint Saviour, Saint Agatha, Saint Donatus, Saint [Col. 1174A] Maurice, Saint George, and Saint Alexander; and Saint Eugenius of Concorezzo.

No person, therefore, shall have power rashly to disturb your church, take away its possessions, retain what has been taken, diminish them, or harass it by reckless vexations; rather, all things shall be preserved whole and inviolate, to be of every benefit for the uses of those for whose maintenance and governance they were granted.

We confirm by apostolic authority for you and your successors those sound fief-benefices which our venerable brother Jordan, archbishop of Milan, granted to your church in the aforementioned churches for the common maintenance of the brethren. We establish that no one whatsoever may henceforth take or withdraw them from the common benefit of the brethren, or alter them in any manner [Col. 1174B].

Furthermore, for the peace of you and your church, we confirm the statutes and customs which are known to have been maintained hitherto in tranquillity through reasonable deliberation in your church and in the chapels belonging to it.

If any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowing this text of our constitution, should rashly attempt to act against it and, having been warned a second or third time, does not make proper amends through suitable satisfaction, let that person lose the dignity of power and honour; let him know himself liable before divine judgment for the iniquity committed; let him be cut off from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, our Redeemer; and let him be subject to severe vengeance at the final judgment. But upon all who preserve the rights of that same place may there be the peace of our Lord [Col. 1174C] Jesus Christ, so that they may receive here the rewards of good action and find, before the strict Judge, those of eternal peace. Amen.

I, Calixtus, bishop of the Catholic Church.

Given at Tortona, through the hand of Chrysogonus, cardinal-deacon and librarian of the Holy Roman Church, on the third day before the Ides of April, in the thirteenth indiction, in the year 1121 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the second year of the pontificate of lord Pope Calixtus II.

## XC. He confirms all the goods and rights of the Monastery of the Holy Saviour at Pavia.  
*(A.D. 1120, April 17.)*

[MARGARINI, *Cassinese Bullarium*, vol. II, p. 135.]

Calixtus, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son in Christ JOHN, abbot of the venerable monastery called that of the Lord Saviour near Pavia, and to his successors regularly appointed in perpetuity.

[Col. 1174D] The authority of our office exhorts us to labour for the welfare of churches and to make firm those things that have been rightly established. Therefore, beloved son in Christ John, abbot, we graciously grant your petition and receive under the protection of the Apostolic See the monastery of the Lord Saviour, over which, by God’s authority, you preside, together with all that pertains to it, following the example of our predecessors of holy memory, the Roman pontiffs John, Benedict, and Paschal.

That monastery is known to have been restored at her own expense and also endowed by the generosity of the Empress Adelaide. Therefore, by the authority of this present privilege, we establish that whatever goods, urban or rural estates, cultivated or uncultivated lands, possessions, utensils, or ornaments were granted to that monastery from their own right either by the aforesaid empress or by other faithful persons, or whatever it may justly and canonically acquire in the future through concessions of pontiffs, liberality of princes, or offerings of the faithful, shall remain firm and inviolate for you and your successors [Col. 1175A].

We decree, therefore, that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the same monastery, take away its possessions, goods, utensils, or ornaments, retain what has been taken, diminish them, or harass it by reckless vexations. [Col. 1175B] Rather, all things shall be preserved whole for the complete benefit of those for whose maintenance and governance they were granted.

Nor shall tithes of the revenues of the aforesaid monastery of the Lord Saviour be demanded by the prelate or ministers of any church. Upon your death, who are now abbot of that place, or upon that of any of your successors, no one shall be placed there through any craft of intrigue or by force, except one whom the brethren by common agreement, or the sounder part of the brethren, shall elect according to the fear of God and the Rule of Saint Benedict.

The person elected shall go to the Roman pontiff to be consecrated. You shall receive chrism, holy oil, the consecration of altars and churches, and the ordination of your monks or clerics who are to be promoted to holy orders, from whichever Catholic bishops you prefer [Col. 1175C]. Moreover, we permit baptism to be celebrated in those churches of that monastery where it is known to have been celebrated in former times.

We forbid any bishop to celebrate public Masses in that monastery, or to hold a station or perform any ordination without the abbot’s consent. Furthermore, in accordance with the enactments of our predecessors, we grant to you and your successors the use of the dalmatic, sandals, and gloves. We decree that the monastery shall remain free, without any yoke or jurisdiction of any person whatever, so that it shall be held subject to the Roman See and the Apostolic Church alone.

If, therefore, any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowing this text of our constitution, should rashly attempt to act against it and, having been warned a second or third time, does not make proper amends through suitable satisfaction, let that person lose the dignity of power and honour; let him know himself liable before divine judgment for the iniquity committed; let him be cut off from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, our Redeemer; and let him be subject to severe vengeance at the final judgment [Col. 1175D]. But upon all who preserve the rights of that same place may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that they may receive here the fruit of good action and find, before the strict Judge, the rewards of eternal peace. Amen.

I, Calixtus, bishop of the Catholic Church.

Given at Piacenza, through the hand of Chrysogonus, cardinal-deacon and librarian of the Holy [Col. 1176A] Roman Church, on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of May, in the thirteenth indiction, in the year 1121 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the second year of the pontificate of lord Pope Calixtus II.

## XCI. *He receives the monastery of Saint Paul of Argon under protection and confirms its goods and privileges.*  
*(A.D. 1120, April 17.)*

[See LUPI (M.), *Diplomatic Codex of Bergamo*. Bergamo, 1784, folio, II, 907.]

## XCII. He confirms the privileges and possessions of the Church of Saint Evasius at Casale.  
*(A.D. 1120, April 23.)*

[DE CONTI, *Historical Notices of the City of Casale*, vol. I, p. 334.]

[Col. 1176B]

Calixtus, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son GERARD, provost, and to his brethren living according to the rule in the Church of Saint Evasius, present and future, for ever.

The desire shown to pertain to religious governance and the salvation of souls ought, with God as its author, to be fulfilled without any delay. Therefore we graciously grant due assent to your petition; we confirm by the authority of this present privilege the order of canonical life which you have professed; and we forbid anyone, after making his profession, to possess anything as his own or to leave the cloister without permission of the provost or of the community. We place both you and all that is yours under the protection of the apostolic see [Col. 1176C].

Accordingly, we decree that you and your successors who, by God’s grace, shall remain in the same religious life, shall hold in perpetuity all that you are now seen lawfully to possess for the support of the common life. Whatever you may in future be able to acquire by grants of pontiffs, the generosity of princes, the offerings of the faithful, or other just means, shall remain secure and unimpaired to you and your successors. Nor shall any provost have authority to grant the estates of the church in fief to secular persons, or to alienate them by any contrivance whatever.

We therefore decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the aforesaid church of Blessed Evasius, invade the houses of your cloister [Col. 1176D], take away its possessions, retain things taken away, diminish them, or harass it with rash vexations; but let all things be preserved intact, to be wholly beneficial for the use of those for whose support and governance they were granted.

Moreover, let no opposition of any bishop or provost prevent you from receiving clerics living in the secular manner for conversion under your provost. We further strictly forbid any knight or any secular person whatsoever to presume to take tithes from the property of that church or from the peasants belonging to the parishes of that church. Rather, in accordance with canonical enactments, they are to be assigned to your uses or to those of your church.

We also grant to you and to your successors who remain in Catholic unity the authority that, should the Church of Vercelli at any time lack a Catholic bishop, you may receive chrism, holy oil, and the ordination of clerics from whichever Catholic bishop you prefer, while preserving for the future the due reverence owed to a Catholic bishop. In addition, we grant you permission that, at two feasts of your church, an appropriate remission of sins may be made each year to the faithful who assemble there [Col. 1177A].

If, therefore, in the future any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowing the contents of this charter of our constitution, should rashly attempt to act against it, and, having been warned a second or third time, should not make amendment by suitable satisfaction, let that person be deprived of the dignity of power and honour; let him know himself guilty before the divine judgment for the iniquity committed; let him be cut off from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, our Redeemer [Col. 1177B]; and let him be subject at the last judgment to severe vengeance. But upon all who uphold what is right in that church, may the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ rest, so that they may receive here the fruit of good works and find, before the strict Judge, the rewards of eternal peace. Amen.

I, Calixtus, bishop of the Catholic Church.

Given at Piacenza, through the hand of Grisogonus, cardinal deacon and librarian of the holy Roman Church, on the ninth day before the Kalends of May, in the thirteenth indiction, in the year 1121 of the Lord’s Incarnation.  
[Note: [Col. 1177] In this bull the Pisan era of the Incarnation is used; consequently, for us the ordinary year is 1120.]  
In the second year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Calixtus II.

XCIII. He grants to Oberto, bishop of Cremona, and to his successors the right to consecrate the abbots of the monastery of St. Peter. (A.D. 1120, 23 April.)

[UGHELLI, *Italia sacra*, IV, 600.]

[Col. 1177C]

CALIXTUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother OBERTO, bishop of Cremona: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Recognizing, dearest brother, both your fidelity and devotion, and those of your Church and city, we have resolved to honour you especially with the customary kindness of the apostolic see. Therefore, acceding to the petitions of your belovedness, we grant, by the liberality of the apostolic see, to you and your successors the consecration of the abbot of the monastery of St. Peter, situated in your city, with the right, payment, and reverence due in all things to the holy Roman Church, which, by God’s will, we serve, remaining unimpaired [Col. 1177D].

It is therefore your concern, dearest brother, so to recognize in this grant the kindness of the Roman Church that hereafter you may, by God’s grace, be able to obtain from it still greater things. If anyone, knowing the contents of this charter of our grant, should rashly attempt to act against it, unless he correct his presumption by worthy satisfaction, let him incur loss of his honour and office, or be punished by the penalty of excommunication.

Given at Ronco Vecchio, on the ninth day before the Kalends of May.

XCIV. *He confirms the possessions of the monastery of St. Saturninus at Cagliari.* (A.D. 1120, 12 May.)

[Col. 1178A]

[Mention of this privilege occurs in MARTENE, *Amplissima Collectio*, I, 657.—Given at Pisa, through the hand of Grisogonus, cardinal and librarian of the Holy Roman Church, on the fourth Ides of May, in the thirteenth indiction, in the year 1121 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the second year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Calixtus II.]

XCV. He dedicates the cathedral church of Volterra. (A.D. 1120, 20 May.)

[UGHELLI, *Italia sacra*, I, 1439.]

ROGER, bishop of Volterra, in the year 1120 received as his guest at Volterra Calixtus, who was travelling from Gaul to Rome, and obtained from him the consecration of the cathedral [Col. 1178B], as plainly appears from this inscription restored by Luca Alemanni, bishop of Volterra.

Lord Calixtus II, Supreme Pontiff, while travelling from Gaul to Rome to receive the crown of the pontificate, arrived at Volterra and solemnly dedicated this church, consecrated to the Virgin Assumed into Heaven, with twelve cardinals, the archbishop of Pisa, and five bishops present together with Roger, bishop of the Volterrans, amid solemn and celebrated ceremony. He honoured it with the gift of the holy head of Victor the Moor, covered with gold; and he granted to all who devoutly visited it each year a remission of twenty days from the penances imposed, during eight days, on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of June, 1120. Luca Alemanni, bishop of Volterra, snatched its memory, now on the point of perishing, from the jaws of time, having drawn it from most ancient monuments [Col. 1178C], and made it everlasting in this marble stone, on the sixth Ides of March, 1610.

XCVI. To John, prior of Camaldoli.—Privilege for the monastery of Sexten. (A.D. 1120, 21 May.)

[MITARELLI, *Annales Camaldulenses*, vol. III, p. 285.]

CALIXTUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son in Christ, JOHN, prior of the brethren of Camaldoli: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Things established with a view to religion ought to be preserved with enduring permanence. For our lord and predecessor, Pope Paschal of holy memory, entrusted to you, dearest John, prior in Christ, and to your successors, the governance and administration of the monastery of Sexten, which belongs to Blessed Peter [Col. 1178D] and exists under the sole protection and disposition of the apostolic see, so that, through your care and zeal, the discipline of monastic order might there be maintained with the Lord’s help. For that place, much diminished both spiritually and temporally, seemed especially able through you to be reformed to a state of religious observance.

We therefore, graciously acceding both to your petitions and to those of your brethren, and directing more earnest attention to the improvement of the said place before God and men, confirm, with the Lord as author, what was done by our aforesaid lord [Col. 1179A]; and we decree that the aforesaid monastery of St. Saviour at Sexten shall remain in future times under your rule, administration, and authority and that of your successors. Hence we grant you free authority, according to the custom of your congregation, by God’s grace to appoint an abbot in that place and to administer the monastery in spiritual and temporal matters. We confirm, with the Lord’s aid, every liberty granted to that monastery by our predecessors, while preserving in all things the right and reverence of the apostolic see.

For we trust in the Lord that, through your diligence and care, the often-mentioned place will be reformed to the discipline of monastic religion and will receive an increase of temporal goods [Col. 1179B].
