If anyone, having learned the tenor of this charter, should rashly—God forbid!—attempt to oppose it, let him incur loss of honour and office, or be punished by the penalty of excommunication, unless he correct his presumption by worthy satisfaction.

I, Calixtus, bishop of the Catholic Church, have signed.  
I, Lambert, bishop of Ostia, have signed.  
I, Deusdedit, cardinal priest of St. Susanna, have signed.  
I, John, cardinal priest of the title of St. Chrysogonus, have signed.  
I, Peter, cardinal deacon of Saints Cosmas and Damian, have signed.  
I, Gregory, cardinal deacon of St. Angelo, have signed.  
[Col. 1179C] I, Peter, cardinal deacon of St. Adrian, have signed.

Given at Volterra, through the hand of Grisogonus, cardinal deacon and librarian of the holy Roman Church, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of June, in the thirteenth indiction, in the year 1121 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the second year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Calixtus II.

XCVII. Bull for the monastery of St. Mary of Morrona and its abbot Girard. (A.D. 1120, 21 May.)

[MURATORI, *Antiquitates Italicae*, III, 1131.]

CALIXTUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son, the abbot [name lost] of the monastery of St. Mary of Morrona … [and to those] regularly appointed in perpetuity.

We are instructed by divine precepts and informed by apostolic admonitions that we should watch with untiring zeal over the condition of churches [Col. 1179D]. Therefore, beloved son in Christ, Abbot Girard, we graciously accede to your petitions and, receiving under the protection of the apostolic see the monastery of Blessed Mary over which, by God’s will, you preside, together with all things belonging to it, strengthen it by the patronage of Blessed Peter, to whose jurisdiction it is known to belong.

By the authority of this present privilege, therefore, we confirm in perpetuity to that monastery all things which have been lawfully conferred or granted to it by us … by Count Uguccione and his sons Ugolino, Rainerio, Lotherio, and Bolgarino, or by any other faithful persons … [lacuna] the castle of Vivario with Pantano [Col. 1180A] and its other appurtenances; the possessions of Morrona, of the castle of Sojana, of Negotiana, of …alto, of Massa, and of Monte Gemmule. Whatever else, moreover, that monastery may hereafter, through the Lord’s bounty, be able justly and canonically to acquire shall remain secure and unimpaired to you and your successors … [lacuna]

Therefore let no person whatsoever be permitted rashly to disturb the oft-mentioned monastery, take away its possessions, retain things taken away, diminish them, or harass it with rash vexations; but let all things be preserved intact, wholly beneficial for the uses of those for whose support [lacuna] and governance they were granted. If, therefore, in the future any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowing the contents of this charter of our constitution, should rashly attempt to act against it, and, having been warned a second or third time [Col. 1180B], should not make amendment by fitting satisfaction, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and honour [lacuna]; let him know himself guilty before the divine judgment for the iniquity committed; let him be cut off from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, our Redeemer; and let him be subject at the last judgment to severe vengeance. But upon all who observe what is right in that place may the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ rest, so that they may receive here the fruit of good works and find before the strict Judge the rewards of eternal peace.

I, Calixtus, bishop of the Catholic Church, have subscribed.  
I, Lambert, bishop of Ostia, have subscribed.  
I, Peter, cardinal priest of the title of St. Susanna, have subscribed.  
[Col. 1180C] I, John, cardinal priest of the title of St. Chrysogonus, have subscribed.

Given at Volterra, through the hand of Grisogonus, cardinal deacon and librarian of the holy Roman Church, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of June, in the thirteenth indiction, in the year 1121 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the second year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Calixtus II.

XCVIII. To Stephen, chamberlain and his legate, staying at Trier.—Concerning his arrival in the City. (A.D. 1120, 3 June.)

[HONTHEIM, *Historia Trevirensis diplomatica*, I, 506.]

We cannot conceal from you, son, that we travelled through the regions of Lombardy and Tuscany without any disturbance, indeed with great good fortune; and on the third day before the Nones of June, with the Lord’s favour, we drew nearer to the City [Rome; Col. 1180D]. Moreover, our brethren the bishops and cardinals, together with the entire clergy, nobility, and people, came out beyond the City to meet us and received us with the highest honours. And when a crown of the Frigii [Note: [Col. 1179D] A Roman family.] had been placed upon our head, they joyfully and exultantly escorted us in solemn procession along the Sacred Way as far as the Lateran palace. There, after we were, by God’s will, safe and well established, Peter, son of Leo, in a great assembly of persons of every rank, bound himself to the Church and to us by oaths of fealty. The same was done by the prefect and his brothers, as also by Leo Frangipani, his whole family, Stephen, and the Norman. Nor did Peter Colonna and the other nobles of the Romans withdraw themselves [Col. 1181A] from their exertions and their eager willingness to obey. Therefore, for these affairs so prosperously and happily accomplished, I desire that you give the fullest praises and thanks to God our Lord; and that, in the regions where you now remain, you strive with all the strength you can to uphold and enlarge the cause of the Church.

XCIX–C. He confirms all donations made to the monastery of Monte Cassino by Gunnari and his wife, adding an annual payment to be rendered by the monks to the Lateran palace. (A.D. 1120, 9 August.)

[COCQUELINES, *Bullarum Collectio*, vol. II, p. 169.]

CALIXTUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his dearest sons in Christ, GIRARD, abbot of the monastery of Monte Cassino [Col. 1181B], and his brethren, present and future, in perpetuity.

Both the concern of the office committed to us requires and the kindness of paternal love compels us to provide for the needs of all churches. Yet it is fitting that we devote more earnest affection to those places and persons which adhere more especially and familiarly to the Roman Church and which excel by reason of greater religious distinction and dignity. Therefore, dearest sons in Christ, we judge that your petition should not without reason be granted, so that we may bestow some aid for the support of your station.

By the authority of this present writing, with perpetual stability, we grant to you and your successors those churches which the noble lord Gunnari, together with his wife Helena, is known to have bestowed upon Blessed Peter: namely, the churches of St. Peter of Nugulbi [Col. 1181C], St. Nicholas of Nugulbi, St. Elijah of Sitin, and St. Peter of Nurci, with their appurtenances. From their revenues, according to the available means, clothing shall always be provided for the community of Monte Cassino, with the annual payment of four solidi in Pavia denarii reserved to the Lateran palace.

We likewise confirm under the protection of the apostolic see all possessions and gifts which the aforesaid Gunnari has bestowed, or shall bestow, upon Blessed Benedict, decreeing that all these likewise shall be preserved in perpetuity for the provision of your clothing. If, therefore, in the future any judge, lord, or ecclesiastical or secular person [Col. 1181D], knowing the tenor of this decree, should presume to take away or diminish the aforesaid churches and the other offerings of the aforesaid Gunnari, or to withdraw or divert them from the established provision of clothing for the community of Monte Cassino, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and honour; let him know himself guilty before divine judgment for the iniquity committed; let him be cut off from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, our Redeemer; and let him be subject at the last judgment to severe vengeance. But upon all who prove to be its observers, through the prayers of our most blessed father Benedict, may the grace and blessing of almighty God and of his apostles Peter and Paul [Col. 1182A], and remission of sins, be bestowed. Amen.

I, Calixtus, bishop of the Catholic Church, have signed.

Given at Benevento, through the hand of Chrysogonus, cardinal deacon and librarian of the holy Roman Church, on the fifth Ides of August, in the twelfth indiction, in the year 1121 of the Lord’s Incarnation.  
[Note: [Col. 1181D] For the other chronological notes to agree with the year, it must certainly be read as the year 1120, in which the thirteenth indiction was current [Col. 1182D], and in August indeed the second year of Calixtus’s pontificate.]  
In the second year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Calixtus II.

CI. To the nobleman Gunnari. (A.D. 1120, 10 August.)

[GATTULA, *Historia Casinensis*, vol. I, p. 426.]

CALIXTUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the illustrious man GUNNARI, to his wife HELENA, and to their daughters VERA and SUSANNA: greeting and apostolic blessing.

[Col. 1182B] We have heard concerning you that, inspired by divine grace, you have bestowed certain possessions from your resources upon Blessed Benedict and his monastery of Monte Cassino. For this we give you thanks and pray the mercy of almighty God that, through the prayers of Blessed Benedict, he may repay you with a worthy reward for this in the present life and in the life to come.

We ask you, moreover, and enjoin it upon you for the remission of your sins, that you remain more steadfastly in what you have begun. For it is not beginning but completing that is virtue; and “he who perseveres to the end shall be saved” (Matthew XXIV). Accordingly, we confirm by the authority of the apostolic see both the churches and the gift which you have made to that monastery, forbidding anyone to remove or diminish it, or in future to dare to exchange it without the consent of the brethren of Monte Cassino [Col. 1182C]; rather, let it always remain peaceably and unimpaired for the clothing of those brethren.

Given at Benevento, on the fourth Ides of August.

CII. He commands Roger, bishop of Volterra, to protect the possessions donated to the monastery of Monte Cassino by Gunnari. (A.D. 1120, 10 August.)

[GATTULA, *Historia Casinensis*, vol. I, p. 426.]

CALIXTUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother ROGER, bishop of Volterra, legate of the apostolic see: greeting and apostolic blessing.

We do not believe it escapes your knowledge how especially and pre-eminently the monastery of Monte Cassino belongs to the protection of the Roman Church [Col. 1182D]. Therefore we ask and command your brotherhood to ensure that the gift made to Blessed Benedict and his monastery by the illustrious lord Gunnari and his wife Helena, out of reverence for Blessed Benedict, remains undisturbed and free from every attack.

For we have confirmed that gift by the authority of our writing, and, by the liberality of the apostolic see, we have granted to the aforesaid monastery of Monte Cassino certain churches belonging to Blessed Peter through the offering of Gunnari himself and his wife Helena. We therefore do not wish them to be taken away or harassed by the violence of anyone; rather, let all things be preserved peacefully and freely for the clothing of the brethren of Monte Cassino [Col. 1183A]. We also earnestly commend to your care the other churches and possessions which Blessed Benedict holds in the regions of Sardinia.

Given at Benevento, on the fourth Ides of August.

CIII. At Bishop Robert’s request, he orders the Church of Aversa to remain a suffragan of the Roman Church. (A.D. 1120, 24 September.)

[UGHELLI, *Italia sacra*, I, 486.]

CALIXTUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother ROBERT, bishop of Aversa, and to his successors canonically appointed, in perpetuity.

We have learned from the report of brethren who investigated the matter more fully that, almost from the very beginning of its existence, the Church of Aversa has faithfully adhered to the Roman Church. Therefore the Roman Church has especially claimed it as her special daughter and has ordained bishops there as in her other special churches [Col. 1183B]. Thus our lord and predecessor, Pope Leo IX of holy memory, consecrated Azolinus as its first bishop; afterwards Urban consecrated Guimundus, and Gelasius consecrated Robert, as bishops. Following their authority and example, we have decreed that the aforesaid Church of Aversa shall remain under the sole subjection of the Roman Church.

Accordingly, by apostolic authority we establish and decree with perpetual stability that the same Church of Aversa shall persevere in the unity and obedience of the Roman Church and, as a suffragan, be subject to that Church alone as to its metropolitan, so that a bishop may always be consecrated there by the hand of the Roman pontiff [Col. 1183C]. Let no person whatsoever be permitted to violate this charter of our exemption, etc.

I, Calixtus, bishop of the Catholic Church.

I, Peter, bishop of Porto, have consented and subscribed.

I, Robert, cardinal priest of the title of St. Sabina, have consented.

I, Benedict, cardinal priest … have consented and subscribed.

I, Anastasius, cardinal priest of the title of St. Clement, have subscribed.

I, Desiderius, cardinal priest of St. Praxedes, have consented and subscribed.

I, John, cardinal priest of the title of St. Chrysogonus, have subscribed.

[Col. 1183D] I, John, cardinal priest of the title of St. Eusebius, have subscribed.

I, Peter, cardinal priest of St. Marcellus, have subscribed.

I, Peter, cardinal priest of St. Mary in Aracoeli.

I, Peter, cardinal priest.

I, Romuald, cardinal deacon of St. Mary in Via Lata.

I, Stephen, cardinal deacon of St. Mary of the Schola Graeca.

Given at Benevento, through the hand of Grisogonus, cardinal deacon and librarian of the Holy Roman Church, on the eighth day before the Kalends of October, in the fourteenth indiction, in the year 1121 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the second year of the pontificate of Calixtus II.

CIV. *He consecrates Gerald, archbishop of Ragusa, grants him the pallium, and confirms the possessions and rights of his Church.* (A.D. 1120, 28 September.)

[See FARLATI, *Illyricum sacrum*, vol. VI, p. 60.]

[Col. 1184A]

CV. *He commands the bishops of Upper Dalmatia, or Dioclea, to obey their metropolitan, Gerald, bishop and archbishop of Ragusa.* (A.D. 1120, 28 September.)

[See ibid., p. 62.]

CVI. Bull for the monastery of Vulturnum. (A.D. 1120, 10 October.)

[MABILLON, *Annales Benedictini*, VI, 641, from a parchment autograph in the possession of the distinguished Roman Francesco Valesio.]

[Col. 1184B]

CALIXTUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son MANSON, abbot of the venerable monastery of St. Peter, situated on Mount Vulturnus near the crypt of Blessed Michael the Archangel, and to his successors regularly appointed, in perpetuity.

Although, by reason of the office entrusted to us, we are debtors to all churches throughout the world, it is nevertheless fitting that we devote more earnest attention to the protection of those places known especially to belong by proper right to the holy Roman Church, which, by God’s will, we serve. Therefore, beloved son in Christ, Abbot Manso, we graciously grant your petition and, following the example of our predecessors, cherish under the protection of the apostolic see the monastery of Blessed Peter at Vulturnum [Col. 1184C], over which, by God’s will, you preside.

For we establish that the monastery itself, its abbots, and its monks shall be subject to no one except the Roman and apostolic see, to which it belongs by right and ownership. Nor may any bishop establish or ordain in that place or its dependent cells anything which seems contrary to the sacred canons or to this our decree. Nor, if, being oppressed, you appeal to the Roman see, may they under any pretext of judicial process inflict violence upon you or your successors, except before the Roman pontiff or his legate.

By the charter of this present privilege we also confirm to you and your lawful successors, and through you to that monastery: the church of St. Andrew of Octavianus [Col. 1184D], with its castle; the castle of Monticulo with its churches; the village called Aquatecta; the cell of St. Mary of Luco; the churches of St. Nicholas of Vitealba, St. Christina, St. Lawrence in Rapulla, St. Nicholas, St. Mary of the Mount, St. George, St. Barbara, and St. Apollinaris on that same Mount.

In Melfi: the churches of St. Antoninus, St. Nicholas, St. Eustace, St. Martin, St. Peter of Berula, St. Felix of Fuciano, St. Fabian beyond the Ofanto, St. James, St. Lawrence, and St. Stephen below the Cistern. Likewise St. Marcian beyond the Ofanto. In Lavello: the churches of St. Barbara, St. Mark, Saints John and Paul, and All Saints. In the territory [Col. 1185A] of Spinazzola: the church of the Holy Trinity at Catuna, St. Mary of Ulmeto, St. Mary in Edera, and St. Giles. At Andro: the churches of St. Saviour and St. Nicholas. At Gurgo: the church of St. Saviour. At Paciano: the church of St. Angelo, with olive groves and presses. At Baro: the church of St. Matthew and Leucius. At Arbore Longa: the church of St. Angelo. In the territory of Salpi: the churches of St. Nicholas of Varisento, St. Theodore, St. Martin, St. Stephen at Plancaro, and St. Mary of Calavio, with all their appurtenances. On Mount Melone: the church of St. Andrew.

Furthermore, whatever the aforesaid monastery possesses at present, in this fourteenth indiction, through grants of pontiffs, the generosity of princes, offerings of the faithful, or other just means, or may hereafter be able to acquire, shall remain secure and unimpaired to you and your successors [Col. 1185B].

We therefore decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb that monastery, take away possessions subject to it, retain things taken away, diminish them, or harass it with rash vexations; but let all things be preserved intact, to be wholly beneficial for the uses of those for whose support and governance they were granted. Upon the death of you, the present abbot of that place, or of any of your successors, no one may be placed over it through any deceptive contrivance or violence, except one whom the brethren, by common consent or by the sounder part of the brethren’s counsel, have elected according to the fear of God and the Rule of Blessed Benedict, to be consecrated by the Roman pontiff.

You shall receive holy oil, the consecration of altars and churches, and the ordination of clerics of whatever profession or order from the bishops in whose dioceses you are [Col. 1185C], provided they are willing to confer these freely and without misconduct, and possess the favour and communion of the apostolic see. Otherwise, you may receive the sacraments of consecration from whichever Catholic bishop you prefer. In addition, we decree that you may receive, without any molestation or opposition from bishops, alms freely offered to the monastery for the living or the dead. As a sign of the aforesaid ownership and of the freedom received from the Roman Church, you shall pay one ounce of gold annually to the Lateran palace.

If, therefore, in the future any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowing the contents of this charter of our constitution, should rashly attempt to act against it, and, having been warned a second or third time [Col. 1185D], should not make amendment by fitting satisfaction, let that person be deprived of the dignity of power and honour; let him know himself guilty before divine judgment for the iniquity committed; let him be cut off from the most sacred body and blood of God and our Lord Jesus Christ, our Redeemer; and let him be subject at the last judgment to severe vengeance. But upon all who uphold what is right in that place may the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ rest, so that they may receive here the fruits of good works and find before the strict Judge the rewards of eternal peace. Amen.

I, Calixtus, bishop of the Catholic Church.

[Col. 1186A] I, Peter, bishop of Porto.

I, John, cardinal priest of the title of St. Chrysogonus.

Given at Benevento, through the hand of Grisogonus, cardinal deacon and librarian of the holy Roman Church, on the sixth Ides of October, in the fourteenth indiction, in the year 1120 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the second year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Calixtus II.

CVII. To the bishops and other faithful of the provinces of Bourges, Bordeaux, Auch, Tours, and Brittany.—He appoints Gerard, bishop of Angoulême, apostolic legate. (A.D. 1120, 16 October.)

[MANSI, *Concilia*, XXI, 212.]

[Col. 1186B] CALIXTUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved brethren and sons, the archbishops, bishops, abbots, princes, and all others, clerical and lay, established throughout the provinces of Bourges, Bordeaux, Auch, Tours, and Brittany: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Both the ordinance of the preceding Fathers requires and the obligation of brotherly love compels us, with the Lord’s help, to make provision beneficially for all the children of the Church. But since we cannot be present everywhere or personally transact everything, we call our brethren, whom we judge suitable, to share in our responsibility. Therefore we have thought fit to commit our office in your regions to our venerable brother Gerard, bishop of Angoulême [Col. 1186C], just as our lord and predecessor, Pope Paschal of holy memory, is known to have entrusted it to him.

For we trust in the Lord that he will faithfully exercise this ministry, with the cooperation of the Holy Spirit, for the honour of God and your salvation. Therefore we ask, exhort, and command all of you humbly to obey him as our vicar; and, whenever the advantage of the Church requires it, to take care to gather unanimously at his summons and solemnly celebrate synodal assemblies with him, so that, by common deliberation, he may, with the Lord as author, correct what requires correction and confirm what requires confirmation.

[Col. 1186D] Given at Benevento, on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of November.

CVIII. He receives under protection the monastery of St. Sophia at Benevento and confirms its goods and rights. (A.D. 1120, 29 November.)

[UGHELLI, *Italia sacra*, VIII, 104.]

In the name of the Lord Almighty, our Saviour Jesus Christ, and in the name of the most holy and undivided Trinity. CALIXTUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son in Christ, JOHN, abbot of the venerable monastery of St. Sophia, situated within Benevento, and to his successors regularly appointed, in perpetuity.

Set, by divine mercy’s ordering, in the administration of the apostolic see, we have the necessary duty [Col. 1187A] to cherish all churches under the patronage of Blessed Peter and to provide for their peace with paternal care. Yet it is fitting that we render more earnest assistance to those places and persons which adhere more devotedly to the Roman Church and excel by reason of greater religious distinction. Therefore, son John in Christ, we graciously accede to your request and decree by the authority of this present charter that the monastery of St. Sophia, to whose governance we consecrated you, with the Lord as author, by our own hands as though by those of Blessed Peter, shall remain perpetually under protection and jurisdiction as it has remained hitherto: namely, subject to the Roman Church alone and held free from every yoke of churches and persons.

Furthermore, following the footsteps of our predecessors, we grant to you and to your successors regularly appointed by this present privilege everything assigned to your predecessors, by their privileges, for the immunity or possession of that monastery [Col. 1187B]. We also confirm for perpetual possession the dependent cells, churches, and villages which your predecessors appear to have justly and reasonably acquired for the aforementioned monastery. These are: the church of St. Benedict called the Hospice of St. John; St. Euphemia; St. Peter, called Trasanii; St. Raymond; St. Mary Rotunda within the same city of Benevento; and, outside before that same city in Pantano, the churches of St. Mary, St. Peter, St. Nicholas, St. Erasmus, St. Marcian, St. Mary, and St. Angelo; the churches of St. Benedict, St. Vitalis, St. Mercurius, by the olive tree [of] St. Angelo [Col. 1187C], and St. Mary of Scolcaturi, together with all appurtenances; at Vado Azara, St. Benedict; at Faffone, St. Valentinian; by the votive place of St. Felix, with lands; at Cornito, St. Sylvester, with two streams; St. Mary at Parituli; St. Marcian at Ventecano; St. Martin at Cuano; St. Peter at Pazano; St. Nicholas.

Likewise at Benevento: St. Stephen at Paloaria; St. Mary at Lucornara; and two estates of St. Mary at Sabbeta and St. Mary at Templana. In the city of Triana: St. Angelo with its cells, and St. Stephen. At Fromarii: St. Gregory. At Escle: St. Angelo at Peloso. At Aliperao: the churches of St. Mary, St. Angelo, St. Peter, St. Mark, St. John, St. Lawrence, St. Lucy at Casale, St. Mary, St. Apollonia, St. Anne at Calisti, and St. Mary [Col. 1187D]. In the territory of St. Marcellus: at Carfiano, St. Maurus, St. John, St. Constantine, and St. Anastasius; at Asculo, St. Peter and St. Desiderius; at Illiceto, St. Ephrem; at Morteto, St. Peter; at Tuscano, St. Adolph, St. Jerome, St. Gerard, St. Severinus, and St. Anastasius. By Arola: St. Mercurius; by Bivinum: St. Martin.

In Biferno: the monastery of St. Angelo, with the cells of St. Peter, St. Vincent, and the Holy Trinity; in Valle Luparia, Holy Cross. By Rederium: St. Martin; at Alirino, St. Michael and St. Mary; on Monte Malo, St. Felix; at Sertore, St. Vitus. By Montes: St. Mark; beside the ditch, St. Stephen; in the territory of Campi Laeti, St. Lucy; beside the city of Florentia, the monastery of St. Saviour; at Clusano, St. Christopher; the castle of Forneto [Col. 1188A] with all its appurtenances; the old castle with all its appurtenances; and the church of St. Donatus with all their appurtenances, movable and immovable.

Accordingly, by the text of this present privilege we establish by apostolic authority that whatever the aforesaid monastery now justly possesses, and whatever it may in future be able justly and canonically to acquire through grants of pontiffs, the generosity of princes, or the offerings of the faithful, shall remain firm and unimpaired to you and to your successors. Therefore we decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the same monastery, remove its possessions, demand its offerings, diminish them, or harass it by reckless vexations; but that all things shall be preserved intact [Col. 1188B], wholly advantageous to the uses for the support and governance of those for whom they were granted. Moreover, upon the death of the abbot of that place, or of any one of your successors, no one shall be set over it by any intrigue, cunning, or violence, except one whom the brothers, by common consent, or the sounder part of the brothers, have elected in the fear of the Lord and according to the Rule of blessed Benedict, to be anointed and consecrated by the supreme Roman pontiff. You shall receive chrism, holy oil, consecrations of altars or churches, and the ordination of monks to be advanced to holy orders, from the bishops in whose dioceses you are, provided that they possess the grace and communion of the Apostolic See and confer these things freely and without corruption. But if anyone should obstruct this, you may receive the aforesaid sacraments from whichever Catholic bishop you wish [Col. 1188C].

If, therefore, any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowing the text of this our constitution, should rashly attempt to act against it, after a second or third admonition, unless he makes amends by suitable satisfaction, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and office; let him know that he stands guilty before the divine judgment for the iniquity he has committed; let him be made alien to the most holy blood and body of our Almighty Lord Jesus; let him be cut off; and at the final judgment let him be subject to strict vengeance. But upon all who, on the contrary, observe these provisions justly, may there be the peace and tranquillity of our Almighty Lord Jesus Christ, so that here they may receive the fruit of good [Col. 1188D] action and before the strict Judge may find the rewards of eternal peace. Amen, amen.

I, Calixtus, bishop of the Catholic See and Church. **THE LORD IS THE SUPPORT OF THOSE WHO FEAR HIM.**

Given at Benevento through the hand of Sico, cardinal-deacon and librarian of the Holy Roman Church, on the third day before the Kalends of December [29 November], in the fourteenth indiction, in the second year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Calixtus II; and in the year 1120 from the Incarnation of our Almighty Saviour Jesus Christ.

CIX. He orders Alpherada, abbess of the nunnery of St Mary at Capua, to come before him “on the Thursday after the octave of Pentecost (9 June 1121), to render an account [Col. 1189A] of by what right she took the church of St Mary of Cingla from the monastery of Cassino.” (Year 1120.)

[See Peter, *Chronicle of Cassino*, book IV, chapter 70.]

CX. *He confirms the privileges of the hermitage of Turrita.* (Year 1120, 1 December.)

[*Life of St Bruno, First Founder of the Carthusians*. Brussels, 1639, octavo, p. 414.]

CXI. To Wulgrin, Archbishop of Bourges.—On the expulsion of the nuns from the nunnery of Carenton. (Year 1120, 3 December.)

[Martène, *Amplissima Collectio*, I, 664, from the cartulary of the Archbishop of Bourges.]

[Col. 1189B]

CALIXTUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother W., Archbishop of Bourges, and to the canons of St Stephen: health and apostolic blessing.

A privilege of our lord predecessor of holy memory, Paschal, makes clear that your predecessor Archbishop Leodegarius established regular canons at the church of St Mary of Carenton, after expelling the nuns who had been there because of the insufficiently honorable character of their way of life, and placing them in other religious monasteries. But after his death, certain of your brothers, the canons of St Stephen, with lay support, expelled those regular canons and introduced those nuns into the same church. In this matter [Col. 1189C], both the religious enactment of your predecessor and the venerable confirmation of our predecessor have indeed been annulled. We therefore command and direct your charity that, having removed those nuns, you restore the aforesaid canons to the church and ensure that they remain quietly and peaceably in the discipline of the canonical order. But if either the nuns should refuse to leave or you should refuse to restore the canons, we forbid both them and their supporters entrance into churches, and command that the place itself be deprived of divine services until the requirement of our mandate is fulfilled.

Given at Saint-Germain, on the third day before the Nones of December [3 December].

CXII. *He commands the clergy of St Mary of Susa, under threat of excommunication, to restore that church within forty days to Arbert, provost of Oulx.* (Year 1120, 15 December.)

[See the *Cartulary of the Church of Oulx*, Augustae Taurinorum [Turin], 1753, folio, p. 111.]

CXIII. To Pons, Abbot of Cluny.—He assigns the church of St Theodore to Cluny. (Year 1120, 28 December.)

[Mansi, *Councils*, XXI, 207.]

CALIXTUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his dearest son in Christ PONS, Abbot of Cluny, and to his successors regularly appointed in perpetuity.

The monastery of Cluny, a model of monastic religion in the present age [Col. 1190A] and an example in the regions of Gaul, was from the beginning of its foundation offered to the Apostolic See as its own rightful possession. Accordingly, our fathers of holy memory, Pope John XI and the other pontiffs of the Roman Church down to our own time, endowed that place with the prerogative of singular affection and freedom, and fortified all that belonged to it by the enactments of their privileges. Therefore, most blessed son in Christ, Pons, whom, when we were placed in charge of the church of Vienne, we consecrated abbot with our own hands through God’s grace: embracing both your person and the place over which, by God’s authoring, you preside with the full affection of our heart, and taking attentive care for your peace and that of your churches, we confirm by apostolic authority, both to you and to your successors for all time, and secure by the text of the present privilege, the church [Col. 1190B] of St Theodore of Rocha Bovecorit, with all its appurtenances. It was humbly and devoutly given to you and to the church of Cluny, with the approval of the clergy of that church, by our venerable brother William, Bishop of Périgueux. If anyone, therefore, by rash audacity and impious presumption against God, his holy apostles, and his own soul, should attempt in any respect to infringe this privilege of our apostolic authority, let him know without delay that he has been pierced by the sting of our apostolic curse, transfixed by the weapon of our apostolic excommunication, and run through by the sword of our apostolic anathema [Col. 1190C], and that he cannot be restored to his former salvation except through worthy satisfaction. But upon one who proves a protector, may there be the peace of the Lord Jesus Christ, so that here he may receive the fruit of good action and before the strict Judge may find the rewards of eternal peace. Amen.

I, Calixtus, bishop of the Catholic Church, have subscribed.

Given at the Lateran through the hand of Chrysogonus, cardinal-deacon and librarian of the Holy Roman Church, on the fifth day before the Kalends of January [28 December], in the fifteenth indiction, in the second year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Calixtus II.

CXIV. To Didacus, Archbishop of Compostela, legate of the Roman Church. (Year 1120, 31 December.)

[Flórez, *España Sagrada*, XX, 309.]

[Col. 1190D]

CALIXTUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother D., Archbishop of Compostela and legate of the Holy Roman Church: health and apostolic blessing.

Out of affection we have resolved especially to communicate to your special brotherhood our situation and the matters concerning us. After we were received with the greatest honor in the City, we went down into the region of Benevento and thence into Apulia as far as Bari. We received the Duke of Apulia, the Prince of Capua, and the other counts and barons into homage and fealty. Thereafter, returning prosperously to the City, we visited the church of Blessed Peter, which our faithful had liberated from the hands of enemies [Col. 1191A]. We celebrated the solemnities of Mass upon the altar of Blessed Peter, and in that same church, with the Lord’s favor, performed ordinations of priests, deacons, and subdeacons. Now, through God’s grace, we remain safely and peacefully in the Lateran palace. I therefore ask you, dearest brother, to love, assist, and sustain your mother, the Roman Church, as a good son. We particularly commend to your affection our most beloved nephew, King Alfonso, asking you to endeavor to counsel and aid him according to the wisdom given you by the Lord; for by this we shall love your person especially and shall more readily hear you in your petitions. Furthermore, hold the bearer of this letter, Abbot D., in still greater favor for our sake [Col. 1191B].

Given at the Lateran, on the second day before the Kalends of January [31 December].

CXV. Bull for the monastery of the holy Apostles Peter and Paul at Canterbury. (Year 1120.)

[*Chronicle of W. Thorn*, in Twysden, *Rerum Anglicarum Scriptores*, II, 1797.]

CALIXTUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, etc.

Just as the monastery of the Apostles Peter and Paul at Canterbury was the first, at the beginning of Christianity’s growth in the kingdom of England, in observing monastic religion, so in future, with all that belongs to it, it shall remain free from every service; undisturbed by every worldly tumult [Col. 1191C]; and it shall in no way be subject to ecclesiastical conditions or compulsory services, nor to any secular duties whatever, nor be bound by any canonical rights, etc. And a little later follows:

Adding this, that for the celebration of divine worship you may, whenever it pleases you, ring the bells of your church. Moreover, we entirely remove from the same monastery that shameful exaction of rams, bread, and drink, which the monks of Holy Trinity endeavor to claim there for themselves under a certain purported custom.

CXVI. To [Radulf], Archbishop of Canterbury. (Year 1120.)

[Ibid.]

[Col. 1191D] CALIXTUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved brother in Christ, the Archbishop of Canterbury: health and apostolic blessing.

Of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul, etc. And below: Moreover, as we have learned, you burden them by the delayed ringing of their bells and by an unseemly exaction of rams, bread, and drink—something wholly contrary both to the ordinances of the holy Fathers and to the privileges of our predecessors. Therefore, by these present letters, permit the brothers serving in the same church to ring the bells at the feasts of those saints whose relics they possess, as they wish; for it is unworthy that a church endowed with so great a liberty by the Roman pontiffs should be subject to exactions of this kind.

CXVII. At the request of Pons, Abbot of Cluny, he receives the nunnery of Marcigny under protection. (Year 1120.)

[*Bullarium Cluniacense*, 41.]

[Col. 1192A]

CXVIII. He removes from the archbishops of Pisa the right of consecrating Corsican bishops. (Year 1121, 3 January.)

[Mansi, *Councils*, XXI, 269.]

CALIXTUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved brothers and fellow bishops established throughout the island of Corsica and to their successors in perpetuity.

It is not to be ascribed either to inconstancy or to injustice if, owing to the necessity of circumstances, certain arrangements are at times made in a different way [Col. 1192B]. For the Roman Church, mother and head of all Churches, established by our own Head, the Lord Jesus Christ, must, through the governance of her dispensation, provide for the peace and salvation of all Churches and peoples. Accordingly, we, who, though unworthy, by the Lord’s ordering bear the care of the apostolic administration, have resolved, through God’s grace, to reform to a better condition those things done either by us or by our predecessors with less caution and deliberation, lest we perhaps obstinately furnish an example to others.

Our lord predecessor of happy memory, Pope Urban, constrained by many and grave necessities, in return for the affection and service abundantly and repeatedly rendered to the Roman Church and city by the Church and city of Pisa [Col. 1192C], determined to honor that Church from the generosity of the Apostolic See. Accordingly, he granted to the Bishop of Pisa, together with the dignity of the pallium, the consecration of the bishops of the island of Corsica. Yet concerning that grant a grave disagreement arose between the Pisans and the Genoese. The Corsican bishops themselves altogether refused to come for consecration to the Bishop of Pisa. Pope Urban, deeply fearing this discord and compassionately responding with due kindness to the lamentation of your people, who had long lacked the administration of episcopal office, recalled the consecration of those bishops to the Roman pontiff and retained it in his own authority. From that time, throughout the whole period both of his own pontificate and that of his successor, Pope Paschal II of holy memory [Col. 1192D], Corsican bishops were consecrated only by the Roman pontiff, although the Bishop of Pisa repeatedly pressed the ears of that same Lord Pope Paschal concerning this matter.

Later, Pope Gelasius of pious memory, compelled by an equal, indeed even greater, necessity and petitioned by those same Pisans, renewed by the privilege of his grant the ordinances of the aforesaid Pope Urban’s concession.

Following in his footsteps, when we came to the Church of Pisa, observing the devotion of its people and clergy and more mercifully granting their petition, we confirmed the same by an assertion of our favor. Consequently such discord grew between the Pisans and Genoese [Col. 1193A] that plunderings, wars, and much shedding of blood occurred. This discord also gave the Saracens such boldness that, invading the borders of all Italy, they devastated certain coastal places with sword and fire and carried off many men, women, and children as captives. In the city of Rome itself there was likewise such a disturbance among clergy and people that, before the very body of Blessed Peter, in the full assembly which we held, nearly all the clergy and people demanded revocation of this arrangement, because the Roman Church suffered loss through the loss of the aforesaid bishoprics and seemed to be the cause and seedbed of the whole scandal and war. In that same assembly clerics and laymen of the island itself were present with letters, humbly requesting the same of us [Col. 1193B].

Therefore, after the case had been debated for many days among the brethren and carefully examined, it was decreed—with the common deliberation of bishops, cardinals, clerics, and Roman nobles, and with no small approval of the people—that this concession should not in future have force, because it had been made outside the City with only a few persons, to the detriment of the Roman Church, and because, as stated, many scandals and dangers resulted from it. Therefore, for the honor of Almighty God and of the holy Apostles Peter and Paul, with the assembly of bishops, cardinals, and clerics, we establish by apostolic authority that in future the consecration of the bishops of the island of Corsica shall be performed by the Roman pontiff alone. We forbid [Col. 1193C] you and your successors to be subject to the Pisans, or to any other bishop or archbishop; rather, you shall remain forever in obedience and subjection to, and consecration by, the Roman pontiff alone.

If, therefore, in future any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowing the text of this our constitution, should rashly attempt to act against it, after a second or third admonition, unless he makes amends by satisfaction, let him lose the dignity of his power and office; let him know that he stands guilty before the divine judgment for the iniquity committed; let him be alienated from the most holy body and blood of God and of our Lord and Redeemer Jesus Christ; and at the final judgment let him be subject to the strict vengeance of anathema. But upon all who observe the same constitution may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ [Col. 1193D], so that here they may receive the fruit of good action and before the strict Judge may find the rewards of eternal peace. Amen, amen, amen.

Written through the hand of Gervasius, *regionarius* and notary of the sacred palace.

I, Calixtus, bishop of the Catholic Church.

Given at the Lateran through the hand of Chrysogonus, cardinal-deacon and librarian of the Holy [Col. 1194C] Roman Church, on the third day before the Nones of January [3 January], in the fourteenth indiction, in the year 1121 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the second year of the pontificate of Lord Calixtus II.

CXIX. He confirms the possessions of the canons of St Lawrence of Genoa. (Year 1121, 5 January.)

[Ughelli, *Italia Sacra*, IV, 853.]

CALIXTUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons VILLANUS, provost, and the canons of the mother church of Blessed Lawrence at Genoa, both present and future, in perpetuity.

We ought not merely to favor worthy secular undertakings, but also to encourage towards them the minds of those who are compelled, by the obligation of our office, to provide for the salvation of all. Thus Marianus, judge of Cagliari, for the remedy of his soul and for the restoration of his honor, offered to your mother church of Blessed Lawrence six estates belonging to him by right: namely Quartum, Arsemina, Caput Terrae, Sepullum, Acquafrigida, and Fontana de Eugas, with all their appurtenances. Later, having taken back three of them with your consent, he restored to your church, in exchange for those three—namely Quartum, Caput Terrae, and Acquafrigida—six others: Sebathus, Paudus, Baral, Tracasali, Fercella, and St Victoria of Villa Pupulci, where the place is called Tereste, with all their appurtenances. This was done on the condition that your church should suffer no loss in that exchange, but should receive the three estates first granted to it [Col. 1195A], with their appurtenances, free from claim and contradiction. At the request of your affection, we confirm this offering and grant by authority of the Apostolic See and decree that it shall remain valid forever.

We also confirm to you the church of St John of Arsemina, with its churches and other appurtenances. It was handed over to us and confirmed by the guarantee of his written instrument by our venerable brother William, Archbishop of Cagliari, with the said judge, his wife Pretiosa, and their kinsmen approving and earnestly petitioning. Furthermore, whatever your church now lawfully possesses, or may hereafter be able, through God’s bounty, justly and canonically to acquire, we decree shall always be preserved firm and unimpaired to you and your successors [Col. 1195B]. Therefore no person whatsoever may rashly disturb your church, remove its possessions or retain what has been removed, diminish them, or harass it by reckless vexations; rather, all things shall be preserved intact, wholly beneficial for the uses of those for whose support they were granted. If anyone, having learned the tenor of this our confirmation, should rashly attempt—God forbid!—to oppose it, let him suffer loss of his honor and office and be punished by the penalty of excommunication, unless he corrects his presumption by worthy satisfaction.

I, Calixtus, bishop of the Catholic Church.

Given at the Lateran through the hand of Chrysogonus, cardinal-deacon and librarian of the Holy Roman Church, [Col. 1195C] on the Nones of January [5 January], in the fourteenth indiction, in the year 1121 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the second year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Calixtus II.

CXX. *He confirms the primacy of Archbishop Umebald of Lyons.* (Year 1121, 5 January.)

[*Primacy of Lyons*, preface, p. 5, on the testimony of Bréquigny, *Chronological Table*, II, 500.]

CXXI. *He confirms the rights of the Church of Ravenna.* (Year 1121, 7 January.)

[Rubei, *History of Ravenna*, 323.]

CXXII. Bull concerning the establishment or restoration of the bishopric at Tres Tabernae (in Calabria). (Year 1121, 14 January.)

[Martène, *Amplissima Collectio*, I, 669.]

[Col. 1195D]

CALIXTUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the venerable man, Brother JOHN, Bishop of Tres Tabernae, consecrated by our hands through God’s grace, and to his successors canonically appointed in perpetuity.

Both the authority of synodal decrees and the sequence of pontifical acts show that the Apostolic See has often been permitted to unite what was divided and, according to the requirements of the times, to alter sees and churches. In former times the church and see of Tres Tabernae is known to have had its own bishop [Note: [Col. 1195D] On the title and antiquity of this bishopric of Tres Tabernae, see the author of the *Life of St Vitalian* and Brother Jerome of Pulistina, in the *Description of Calabria*, book II, chapter 21, fol. 347. See also the book of *Chronicles* written in a very ancient hand by Roger, canon of Catanzaro, master William’s son, which contains the entire history.] But because it could not preserve its episcopal see owing to Saracen violence, it had recourse to the Roman Church to obtain a bishop. Therefore the Roman Church, mother of all Churches throughout the world, joined it to the church of Squillace. Yet in our times the divine majesty has been pleased mercifully to visit that place and, since its multitude of clergy and people has been restored, to restore it to its former condition. Therefore, wishing to be co-workers of divine grace, after taking counsel with our brethren, through our dearest brother [Col. 1196B], Cardinal-Priest Desiderius, whom we sent into those regions, after the suitability of the whole matter had been carefully examined, and with the petition of the people, the election of the clergy, and the consent of the count and the other leading men, we consecrated the cardinal as bishop there by our own hands through God’s grace.

Accordingly, by apostolic authority we command that the aforesaid church of Tres Tabernae shall henceforth have its own bishop and, under his direction and care, shall be governed through Almighty God’s grace according to the institutions of the holy Fathers. Moreover, dearest brother and fellow bishop John, we confirm to you and your successors the same diocese with its towns, villages, and appurtenances: namely Taberna, Catanzaro, Rocca, Tiriolo, and Sellia. We also confirm to you the estate of the glorious Count Geoffrey: namely, one hundred villeins with lands and vineyards at Cantarazium, one mill, and all the possessions, villeins, and the mill which William Carbonellus restored to the church into the hand of the aforesaid cardinal. Likewise, from the gift of John Capriolus, thirty villeins with two hundred *modii* of land and five thousand feet of vineyard. Whatever else your church presently possesses through the generosity of princes, the offerings of the faithful, or other lawful means, or may in future acquire through the Lord’s bounty, shall remain firm and unimpaired to you and to your successors. We therefore decree that no person may alter this restoration of episcopal dignity, rashly disturb the oft-mentioned church, remove its possessions [Col. 1196D], retain what has been removed, diminish them, or harass it with reckless vexations. Rather, all shall be preserved intact, beneficial both for your uses and for those of the clergy and the poor. If anyone in future, whether in ecclesiastical or secular pre-eminence, knowing the text of this our constitution, should attempt to act against it and should not make amends by suitable satisfaction, let him lose the dignity of his power and office and know himself guilty before the divine judgment for the iniquity committed. But whoever obeys the foregoing shall receive here the fruit of good action and before the strict Judge shall be found a participant in eternal peace [Col. 1197A]. Amen.

Given at the Lateran through the hand of Grisogonus, cardinal-deacon and librarian of the Holy Roman Church, on the nineteenth day before the Kalends of February [14 January], in the fourteenth indiction, in the year 1121 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the second year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Calixtus II.

CXXIII. He receives under protection the monastery of Saints Philip and James and St Walburga in the Sacred Forest, and confirms its goods. (Year 1121, 22 January.)

[Würdtwein, *Nova Subsidia Diplomatica*, VII, 43.]

[Col. 1197D]

CALIXTUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son BERTHOLF, abbot of the monastery built in honor of the holy Apostles Philip and James and of the virgin St Walburga, in the diocese of Strasbourg, namely in the place called Sacred Forest, and to his successors regularly appointed hereafter.

It is fitting to give ready and willing assent to religious desires, so that faithful devotion may obtain a speedy result. Therefore, beloved son in Christ, Abbot Bertholf, we graciously grant your petition and, following the example of our lord predecessor Pope Paschal of holy memory, fortify with the protection of the Apostolic See the monastery over which, by God’s authoring, you preside. It was offered to Blessed Peter and his holy Roman Church under an annual payment of one gold coin and dedicated to the honor of Almighty God, the holy Apostles Philip and James, and the virgin St Walburga [Col. 1198A]. We establish that everything granted to that monastery from their own right by the religious princes Duke Frederick and Peter, founders of that place, or by other faithful persons, or that may hereafter be given, offered, or acquired by other lawful means through God’s bounty, shall remain quiet and unimpaired to you and to your successors. No person whatsoever may rashly disturb the same place, remove or diminish its possessions, or harass it with reckless vexations; but all things shall be preserved intact, wholly beneficial for the uses of those for whose support and governance they were granted [Col. 1198B].

If any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowing the text of this our constitution, should rashly attempt to act against it, after a second or third admonition, unless he makes amends by suitable satisfaction, let him lose the dignity of his power and office; let him know that he stands guilty before the divine judgment for the iniquity committed; let him be alienated from the most holy body and blood of God and our Lord Jesus Christ; and at the final judgment let him be subject to strict vengeance. But upon all who uphold what is just for the same place may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that here they may receive the fruit of good action and before the strict Judge may find the rewards of eternal peace [Col. 1198C]. Amen.

I, Calixtus, bishop of the Catholic Church.

Given at the Lateran through the hand of Chrysogonus, cardinal-deacon and librarian of the Holy Roman Church, on the eleventh day before the Kalends of February [22 January], in the thirteenth indiction, in the year 1121 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the second year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Calixtus.

CXXIV. To Wido, Bishop of Chur. (Year 1121, 4 February.)

[Borgia, *Brief History of the Temporal Dominion of the Apostolic [Col. 1198D] See in the Two Sicilies*. Rome, 1789, quarto, appendix, p. 47.]

[lacuna] After we were received with the greatest honor in the City and liberated the church of Blessed Peter and the other churches of the City from the hands of enemies, invited by our faithful we proceeded to Benevento. There we received the Duke of Apulia, the Prince of Capua, and the other barons and captains of the land into our homage and fealty. Thence, descending into Apulia as far as Bari, we established the peace and truce of God throughout that land. After these things, returning to the City, we visited the church of Blessed Peter, performed ordinations of priests and deacons in it, and, returning honorably to the Lateran palace, celebrated the feast of the Lord’s Nativity (25 December 1120) [Col. 1199A]; in that palace we now remain safely.

CXXV. He assigns the church of Bornhem to the monastery of Affligem. (Year 1121, 11 February.)

[Cocquelines, *Bullarium*, II, 173.]

CALIXTUS II, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son FULGENTIUS, abbot of the monastery of Affligem, situated in the diocese of Cambrai in honor of Blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, and to his successors regularly appointed in perpetuity.

What is established for the sake of religion ought to be preserved with unshaken stability. Thus our venerable brother Burgundus, Bishop of Cambrai, by the counsel and assent of the archdeacons and other clerics of his Church, likewise by the counsel and exhortation of our venerable brother Ralph, Archbishop of Reims (as is contained in the letters sent to us by them), and also at the request and supplication of Sifrid, Abbot of Bornhem, and his brethren, entrusted the church of Bornhem to the monastery of Affligem, so that henceforth, through God’s grace, the discipline of the monastic order might be maintained there. Formerly a canonical order had indeed been established in that place; but when wars arose, it was so reduced by lack of resources that it could neither preserve the canonical order nor continue independently in ecclesiastical respectability.

Therefore, acceding to the petitions both of the aforesaid brothers and [Col. 1199C] of our sister Clemence, Countess of Flanders, who is the administrator of that place, and having the fullest confidence in your religious observance, we confirm by the text of the present privilege the assignment of the aforesaid church of Bernhom.

We establish that, by God’s authoring, it shall persevere forever in union with and subjection to the monastery of Affligem, under the discipline of the monastic Rule; namely, free and undisturbed just as it had formerly been under the canonical order, together with the altars of Havesdunc, Hingem, Kereberga, Rimenham, and Merchecloa, and with everything that it lawfully possesses at present or may in future, through God’s bounty, justly and canonically acquire.

Therefore no person whatsoever may remove the aforesaid church of Bernhom from the direction of your monastery [Col. 1199D], withdraw it on any pretext, remove its possessions, or harass it with reckless vexations. Rather, it shall remain under your monastery as was established by our aforesaid brother Burgard, the diocesan bishop, and confirmed by his own charter.

If, therefore, in future any person of whatever rank or dignity, knowing the text of this our confirmation, should rashly attempt to act against it, let him suffer loss of his honor and office and be punished by the penalty of excommunication, unless he corrects his presumption by worthy satisfaction.

But whoever proves a protector shall obtain the blessing and grace of Almighty God [Col. 1200A] and of the Apostles Peter and Paul. Amen.

I, Calixtus, bishop of the Catholic Church, have approved this.

Given at St Peter’s through the hand of Chrysogonus, cardinal-deacon and librarian of the Holy Roman Church, on the third [add: “Kalends”; Note: [Col. 1199D] “Ides” should be read. Jaffé] of February, in the fourteenth indiction, in the year 1121 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the second year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Calixtus II.

CXXVI. At the request of Bishop Dodo, he confirms the boundaries of the bishopric of Modena and the goods of its church. (Year 1121, 4 March.)

[Ughelli, *Italia Sacra*, II, 117.]

CALIXTUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable [Col. 1200B] brother DODO, bishop of Modena, and to his successors canonically appointed in perpetuity.

Just as no effect ought to be granted to those who request unjust things, so the petition of those who lawfully desire something ought not to be delayed. Therefore, dearest brother in Christ, Bishop Dodo, acceding to your prayers, we decree by the authority of this present act, for the perpetual peace and stability of the holy Church of Modena over which, by God’s grace, you preside, that all the boundaries of the bishopric shall henceforth be preserved wholly undisturbed and intact for you and your successors. These boundaries extend according to the following divisions: namely, from those boundaries which separate the bishoprics of Lucca and Pistoia from that of Modena, as far as the river called Burana; and as far as the boundary called [Col. 1200C] Mutia; and thence as far as that boundary which separates the bishopric of Bologna and that of Modena from Reggio.

We grant and confirm to you and your successors, in accordance with the enactments of the holy canons, the consecration of the churches situated within these boundaries, the promotion of clerics, tithes, and offerings—especially in the parish church of St. Mary of Bodriuntio, which is in the estate of Sici, and in its chapels; in all the churches in the castle and estate of Solaria, and in the parish church of Roncaglia and its chapels; in all the churches of Ponte del Duca; in the church of Camurana; in the churches of the estate of Curtiola; in the church of Scoplano; in the church of St. Peter in Siculo; and in the churches situated in the castle and estate of Paciano, in the abbey of Leonense, and in all [Col. 1200D] the churches in the parish church of Rubiano.

Moreover, whatever goods and possessions you now lawfully possess, or may hereafter, by God’s bounty, be able justly and canonically to acquire, shall remain secure and unimpaired for you and your successors. We therefore decree that no bishop whatsoever shall have authority, within the aforesaid boundaries and without the consent of you or your successors, to consecrate a church, prepare chrism, or ordain clerics—excepting the churches and clerics of the castle and borough of Nonantola. Nor may anyone disturb the aforesaid church, take away its possessions, retain possessions taken away, diminish them, or harass it through rash vexations; rather, let all things be preserved intact for the benefit both of yourselves and of the clergy and poor. [Col. 1201A]

With regard to priests installed in churches throughout parishes belonging to monasteries, we confirm the ruling of our predecessor Pope Urban II of holy memory, decreeing that abbots shall not, without the counsel of the bishops, install priests in the parish churches which they hold; rather, with the abbots’ consent, bishops shall entrust the care of the parish to a priest. Such priests shall render account to the bishop for the care of the people, but shall show the abbot the due subjection in temporal matters belonging to the monastery, so that the rights of each may thus be preserved.

If, therefore, in future any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowing this text of our enactment, [Col. 1201B] should rashly presume to act against it, and, having been warned a second or third time, should fail to make amends through fitting satisfaction, let that person be deprived of the dignity of office or rank, know himself or herself guilty before the divine judgment for the iniquity committed, be separated from the most sacred Body and Blood of God and of our Lord and Redeemer Jesus Christ, and be subject to strict vengeance at the final judgment. But upon all who preserve the just rights of your church may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that they may receive here the fruit of good action and find, before the strict Judge, the rewards of eternal peace. Amen.

I, Calixtus, bishop of the Catholic Church.

### CXXVII. To A., prior of St. Fridianus at Lucca. (1121, March 14.)

[BALUZ, *Miscellanea*, ed. Luc., IV, 387.]

[Col. 1201C]

CALIXTUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son A., prior of St. Fridianus, greeting and apostolic blessing.

It has pleased our brother bishops and cardinals that the regular canons who had been established by our lord and predecessor Pope Paschal, of blessed memory, in the Lateran church, and who afterward, compelled by persecution, withdrew, should now, peace having been restored, be brought back by God’s grace to that very place. Therefore, sending them our letters, we have commanded them to return to that church, with every excuse set aside. Let your diligence therefore help them and strive to assist them in this matter for the love of God and out of affection for us, so that [Col. 1201D] you may deserve grace from God in God’s grace, and that we may more willingly grant your petitions when the occasion arises.

Given at the Lateran, on the second Ides of March.

### CXXVIII. He confirms the possessions and privileges of the monastery of St. Clement at Pescara. (1121, March 29.)

[*Chronicon Casauriense*, in MURATORI, *Scriptores Italici*, II, II, 881.]

CALIXTUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son in Christ GISO, abbot of the venerable monastery of St. Clement, situated on the island of Pescara, and to his successors regularly appointed in perpetuity.

[Col. 1202A]

We are bound by the authority and duty of the Apostolic See to concern ourselves with the condition of all churches, and, with the Lord’s help, especially to provide for the peace of those which adhere more particularly to that See and are subject to it as by proper right. Therefore, dearest son in Christ Giso, we have rightly judged that your petitions should be granted, so that we might strengthen by the authority of the Apostolic See the monastery of Blessed Clement, over which, by God’s grace, you are known to preside, where, indeed, we believe the most glorious body of that martyr rests, as is contained in the privilege of our lord and predecessor Pope Leo.

Accordingly, by a decree to endure forever, we establish that whatever possessions and goods that monastery now lawfully possesses shall remain secure and unimpaired for you and your [Col. 1202B] successors. Among them we have thought fit to name expressly the following: in the county of Chieti, the castle of Insula; the monastery of St. Nicholas at Caramanico, with its cells and other appurtenances belonging to the same monastery; the church of Holy Cross; the church of St. Martin at Gutta; the church of St. John; the church of St. Cesidius; the monastery of the Holy Trinity of Lapidaria; the churches of St. Mary in Pesile, St. Angel, St. Cesidius, and St. Bartholomew of Orta; and the castle of Fara.

In the county of Valva, the monastery of the Holy Trinity with its appurtenances. In the county of Penne, the castles of Alanne, Bectorrita, Castellione, Olibula, Corvaria, Pesclu, Rocca de’ Soti, and Pietra Iniqua, with their churches and appurtenances. In the same county, the monastery of St. Desiderius and the church [Col. 1202C] of St. Quiricus, with their appurtenances. In the county of Abruzzo, the monastery of St. Clement with the castles—namely, Castro Vetere, Santo Vetere, and Guardia—and with the churches and villages belonging to the aforesaid monastery.

Moreover, whatever you may hereafter acquire through the grants of pontiffs, the generosity of princes, the offerings of the faithful, or other just means, shall remain secure and intact for you and your successors. We therefore decree that no bishop, count, or any person whatsoever shall have authority rashly to disturb the aforesaid monastery, take away its possessions, retain or diminish possessions taken away, harass it through rash vexations, or impose any exactions upon it; rather, let all things be preserved intact for the benefit of those for whose support and governance they were granted. [Col. 1202D]

If, therefore, in future any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowing this text of our enactment, should rashly presume to act against it, and, having been warned a second and third time, should fail to make amends through fitting satisfaction, let that person be deprived of the dignity of office and rank, know himself or herself guilty before the divine judgment for the iniquity committed, be separated from the most sacred Body and Blood of God and of our Lord and Redeemer Jesus Christ, and be subject to strict vengeance at the final judgment. But upon all who preserve what is just for that place may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that they may receive here the fruit of good action [Col. 1203A] and find before the strict Judge the rewards of eternal peace. Amen.

Written through the hand of Gervasius, regional scriniary and notary of the sacred palace.

I, Calixtus, bishop of the Catholic Church, have subscribed.

Given at the Lateran through the hand of Grisogonus, cardinal deacon and librarian of the Holy Roman Church, on the fourth day before the Kalends of April, in the fourteenth indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1121, in the fourth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Calixtus II.

### CXXIX. To Otto of the castle of Iringi.—He grants authority to build a church and monastery under specified conditions. (1121, March 30.)

[MANSI, *Concilia*, XXI, 211.]

[Col. 1203B]

CALIXTUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the noble and illustrious man OTTO of the castle of Iringi, greeting and apostolic blessing.

We have observed your devotion, because you have offered to Blessed Peter and to his Roman Church your estate of Puribergk, where you desire to build a church in honour of the Apostles Peter and Paul, in which regular brethren may, indeed, be consecrated together in the service of almighty God. Receiving this offering for the honour of God and the salvation of your soul, we fortify that place by the protection of Blessed Peter. For we establish that no one may occupy it, [Col. 1203C] launch attacks there, or dare rashly to inflict disturbances; rather, all things which have already been bestowed by you or may in future be conferred from their own right by any faithful persons shall be preserved peacefully and intact under the protection of the Apostolic See.

On this condition, however: that from it, as a payment, an alb with its amices shall be rendered every four years to the Lateran basilica of St. Lawrence. We also establish that henceforth neither you nor any of your heirs may assume the advocacy of the aforesaid place; rather, an advocate shall be appointed there, by God’s grace, according to the election and free will of the brethren. We decree that the same is to be observed with respect to the superior of the place.

But if anyone—may it never be!—should rashly attempt to contravene this our enactment, let him incur the loss of his rank and office [Col. 1203D] or be punished by the penalty of excommunication, unless he corrects his presumption through fitting satisfaction. But whoever takes care to assist the place itself and the brethren serving the Lord in it, and to honour them with his goods, may receive the blessing and grace of almighty God and of his Apostles Peter and Paul, and forgiveness of his sins. Amen.

I, Calixtus, bishop of the Catholic Church, approving, confirmed this letter through the hand of Chrysogonus, cardinal deacon and librarian of the Holy Roman Church, on the third day before the Kalends of April, in the fourteenth indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1121, in the third year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Calixtus II.

### CXXX. He takes the church of St. Mary and St. Walburga of Furnes under his protection and confirms its goods and privileges. (1121, March 30.)

[MIRAEUS, *Opera diplomatica*, III, 33.]

[Col. 1204A]

CALIXTUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons FROMOLD, provost of Furnes, and his brethren serving God in the church of the holy Mother of God Mary and St. Walburga, greeting and apostolic blessing.

It befits us to grant assent to just wishes and to give ear to just petitions. Since, therefore, your charity has fled to the harbour of apostolic security and has devoutly sought its protection, we mercifully grant your supplication [Col. 1204B] and receive under the protection of the Apostolic See the church of St. Mary and Blessed Walburga of Furnes, with everything belonging to it; and through it may we, by the Lord’s favour, renew all secular matters. [The final clause is textually uncertain.]

By the text of this present privilege, therefore, we establish by apostolic authority that all estates and goods donated to that church by the Catholic princes of Flanders, or gathered through the lawful donations of other faithful persons, together with whatever it now justly possesses, shall be preserved for it peaceful and intact. We have set down part of them by their proper names.

Namely: one hundred measures of land at Polinchova; seventy-six from the *berquaria* of Menger and twenty-four from the *berquaria* of Reinger; thirty-six measures [Col. 1204C] of land from the *berquaria* of Siger; measures of land at Sandeshove from the *berquaria* of [lacuna]. All these lands Countess Gertrude, of noble memory, with the affirmation of her nephew Count Baldwin, son of Robert the Younger, offered as prebends for four of your brethren: twelve measures of land from the *berquaria* of Reinger for the lighting of the church; thirty-six measures of land from the *berquaria* of Hagaben at Sandeshove, from the gift of the aforesaid countess and with the consent of her nephew Count Baldwin, for the use of the brethren and for the church’s lighting; forty measures of land from the viscountcy, from the *berquaria* of Gerard, as the prebend of one brother.

Also, the tithe of seven parishes—namely Binanburgh, Butanburgh, Wulpen, Duncapella, Romescapella, Ingeri Chapel, and Parevis—whether as it is now or if it should increase through newly reclaimed land; one pound from the count’s larder; likewise, in the viscountcy, one *berquaria*, namely Nabasce [lacuna], for restoring the aforesaid church; and at Sandeshove, one *berquaria* in flour [lacuna]. From all these, fifty pounds are paid every year. Of this, five pounds yearly are for administering the schools; and, for the provostship at Dunkirk, a cattle-farm with twenty-five cows and nine measures of land. [Col. 1204D]

Moreover, whatever your church may hereafter acquire through the grants of pontiffs, offerings of the faithful, or other just means, shall always remain secure and unimpaired for the common use of the brethren.

We therefore decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb [Col. 1205A] the same church, take away its possessions, retain or diminish possessions taken away, or harass it through rash vexations; rather, let all things be preserved intact and wholly beneficial for the use of those for whose support and governance they were granted.

We likewise decree that the burial-place of the same house shall be wholly free, so that no one may obstruct the final devotional wishes of those who have resolved to be buried there, unless they are excommunicated.

Furthermore, no one shall be placed over your community as provost except one chosen for this office, in the fear of God, by the common consent of your church.

We grant you, therefore, this prerogative of apostolic favour: that your church shall remain free from every obligation of episcopal exaction; and that, whenever the episcopal parish has been interdicted from divine offices, you may celebrate the divine offices behind closed doors. Moreover, your authority has also provided, in accordance with justice, that clerics who are engaged in the constant service of your church within the precinct of the cloister shall receive the discipline due for their offences within that same cloister. [Col. 1205B]

If, therefore, in future any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowing this text of our enactment, should attempt to act against it, and, having been warned a second or third time, should fail to make amends through fitting satisfaction, let that person be deprived of the dignity of office and rank, know himself or herself guilty before divine judgment for the iniquity committed, be separated from the most sacred Body and Blood [Col. 1205C] of God and of our Redeemer Jesus Christ, and be subject to strict vengeance at the final judgment.

But upon all who preserve what is just for that church may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that they may receive here the fruit of good action and find before the strict Judge the rewards of eternal peace. Amen, amen, amen.

I, Calixtus, bishop of the Catholic See.

Given at the Lateran through the hand of Chrysologus, cardinal deacon and librarian of the Holy Roman Church, on the third day before the Kalends of April, in the fourteenth indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1120, in the second year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Calixtus II.

### CXXXI. To all the faithful.—He announces that he besieged Sutri until the antipope Burdinus and the city itself were surrendered to him. (1121, April 27.)

[MANSI, *Concilia*, XXI, 280.]

[Col. 1205D]

CALIXTUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved brothers and sons, the archbishops, bishops, abbots, priors, and all other faithful of Blessed Peter, clerical and lay alike, established throughout Gaul, greeting and apostolic blessing.

Because the people abandoned the law of the Lord and did not walk in his judgments, the Lord visited their iniquities with a rod and their sins with scourges. [Col. 1206A] Yet, preserving the tender mercy of a father, he does not abandon those who trust in his mercy. For a long time, indeed, as sins demanded, the faithful of the Church were troubled through that idol of the king of the Germans, namely Burdinus; some were captured, while others were afflicted even unto death by the wasting ordeal of prison.

But recently, after the Easter feasts had been celebrated, since we could no longer bear at all the cries of pilgrims and the poor, we departed from the City with the faithful of the Church and besieged Sutri until divine power delivered into our authority both the aforesaid enemy of the Church, Burdinus, who had made there a nest for the devil, and the place itself in its entirety. We therefore ask your charity to give thanks with us to the King of kings for such great benefits, [Col. 1206B] and to remain most steadfastly in obedience and service to the Catholic Church, being destined to receive through his grace due recompense from almighty God both in the present and in the future. We also ask that, with all negligence set aside, you cause these letters to be presented from one person to another.

Given at Sutri, on the fifth day before the Kalends of May.

### CXXXII. To the regular canons of Berchtesgaden.—He approves their rule. (1121, May 9.)

[MANSI, *Concilia*, XXI, 212]

CALIXTUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons EBERQUIN, provost, and his brethren professing the regular life in the church of Saints John and Martin, situated in the district of Salzburg, [Col. 1206C] namely in the place called Berchtesgaden, present and future, in perpetuity.

We have the Lord’s command: “Enter through the narrow gate, for narrow is the way that leads to life” (Luke 13; Matthew 7). Since therefore you, most beloved sons in Christ, inspired by divine grace, have resolved to restrain your conduct under the discipline of the regular life and, so that you may be able to enter through the narrow gate, to serve almighty God together in accordance with the rule of the holy Fathers, we rejoice in your desires with paternal affection. Accordingly, granting your petition the assent due from our kindness, we establish your purpose of religion by the authority of this present privilege.

We decree that no person whatsoever may alter in your church the canonical manner of life which you have professed. Nor may any member of your profession, prompted by instability or under pretext of a stricter religious life, leave the cloister without the permission of the provost or community. If he does leave, no bishop, abbot, or monk shall receive him without an assurance contained in letters from the community, so long as, by the Lord’s gift, the observance of canonical order flourishes in your church. [Col. 1206D]

You shall receive the sacraments of ecclesiastical jurisdiction from the diocesan bishop, provided that he possesses the favour and communion of the Apostolic See and is willing to provide them freely and without impropriety.
