Upon the death of you, the present abbot of that place, or of any of your successors, let no one be set over it by any crafty fraud or violence, except one whom the brethren by common consent, or the sounder part of the brethren, have elected, in the fear of God and according to the Rule of blessed Benedict, to be consecrated by the Roman pontiff. Furthermore, you shall not be compelled to submit to the judgment of the surrounding abbots, except perhaps of those who belong to the proper jurisdiction of the Apostolic See, when the necessity of ecclesiastical affairs requires it.

You shall receive chrism, holy oil, consecrations of altars and churches, and the ordinations of monks who are to be promoted to sacred orders, from the bishop of Passau, [Col. 1234B] provided that he enjoys the favor and communion of the Apostolic See and is willing to confer these things freely and without improper exaction. Otherwise, you may approach whichever Catholic bishop you prefer and receive from him the sacraments of consecration, provided that, supported by the authority of the Apostolic See, he grants what is requested.

Let no opposition of any bishop or provost prevent you from receiving laypersons or secular clergy for conversion. We likewise decree that the burial-place of that monastery shall be entirely free, so that no one may oppose the devotion and final wish of those who have decided to be buried there, unless they are excommunicated. Let Margrave Liupold, or his heir who holds the march, remain advocate of the same place.

Yet neither they nor [Col. 1234C] any person whatsoever may presume rashly to claim anything in that monastery or among its goods for themselves, or to take away its possessions, retain what has been taken, diminish them, or harass them by reckless vexations. Rather, let all things be preserved intact for the benefit in every respect of those for whose maintenance and governance they were granted.

As a token of the exemption received from the Roman Church, you shall pay one gold piece annually to the Lateran palace. If, therefore, any ecclesiastical or secular person in the future, knowing the contents of this page of our constitution, should rashly attempt to act against it, then, after a second or third warning, unless he makes suitable amends by satisfaction, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and honor. Let him know that he stands guilty before the divine judgment for the iniquity he has committed; let him be separated from the most holy body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Redeemer; and at the final judgment let him be subject to severe vengeance. [Col. 1234D] But upon all who preserve the rights of that place may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that they may receive here the fruit of good action and find before the strict Judge the rewards of eternal peace. Amen, amen, amen.

Given at the Lateran through the hand of Chrysogonus, cardinal-deacon and librarian of the holy Roman Church, on the sixth day before the Ides of March, in the fifteenth indiction, in the year 1122 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the fourth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Calixtus II.

## CLXX. To Archbishop Anseric and the Canons of Besançon.—Privilege concerning the mother-church status of the Church of Saint John in relation to the Church of Saint Stephen. (1122, 19 March.)

[Mansi, *Concilia*, XXI, 199.]

[Col. 1235A]

Calixtus, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother Anseric; to Manasses, dean; Stephen, archdeacon; Stephen, treasurer; Hugh, archdeacon; and the other canons of the Church of Saint John the Apostle and Evangelist at Besançon: greeting and apostolic blessing.

As it befits a successor to preserve the enactments of his predecessors insofar as they are lawful and just, so he ought also, by salutary provision, to correct what was wrongly done. Therefore we have taken care to restore to the order of truth and justice that deception committed against our lord and predecessor of holy memory, Pope Paschal, by the clerics of Saint Stephen concerning the judgment on mother-church status.

For a long time a dispute had been conducted between you and the canons of Saint Stephen over the episcopal throne and ecclesiastical mother-church status. The canons of Saint Stephen alleged, as best they could, that their church had formerly been the mother church, but that, because of its destruction, the bishops had withdrawn to the Church of Saint John. You, on the contrary, established by documentary record and the testimony of old men that your church had possessed the episcopal see lawfully and without interruption throughout long periods of time. [Col. 1235B]

When this dispute came to the hearing of our aforesaid lord, he entrusted its settlement to our examination, because we exercised his office in those regions. Specifically, if the canons of Saint Stephen could prove through five suitable witnesses that, after the rebuilding of their church, within thirty years they had raised legal proceedings concerning this complaint—by which their possession might appear to have been interrupted—before either their bishop or a legate of the Roman Church, then, after that proof had been completed in a public hearing, their privileges would retain their proper force and the episcopal see would be held at the Church of Saint Stephen. Otherwise, you would remain free from this complaint and would retain the episcopal see as you had held it before.

The same lord further commanded us to complete and bring to conclusion the determination of this matter by the next ensuing feast of the Assumption of Blessed Mary. [Col. 1235C] Obeying his commands, we assembled at Trénorcin both parties, together with our brethren and fellow-bishops Gauceran of Lyons, Hugh of Grenoble, Leodegar of Viviers, Berard of Mâcon, Stephen of Autun, Walter of Chalon, Gauceran of Langres, Pons of Belley, Guy of Geneva, Gulinus of Sion, Pons, abbot of Cluny, seventeen abbots, and other religious men.

There, when your party presented the grounds of its justice, we required from the canons of Saint Stephen the performance of the proof laid down by the aforesaid lord. At last they produced a few witnesses, but not suitable ones. One was rejected because he had committed perjury or because of base birth; another for sacrilege; another because he had been hired for a price; another because he had long been bound by excommunication. Thus the aforesaid canons of Saint Stephen, no longer able to defend their party’s cause, failed in the proposed proof in the sight of all. [Col. 1236A]

Then, by the common judgment of the brethren, it was decided that your Church of Saint John ought forever to retain the prerogative of mother-church status. Accordingly, together with them, we decreed that your church should henceforth be free from that complaint, firmly establishing that the episcopal see should remain in it. Moreover, by apostolic authority, whose share of pastoral responsibility we had been called to exercise, we commanded under obligation of anathema that no cleric or layperson should thereafter disturb it on this account or presume to give support to one who disturbed it.

After this sentence had been promulgated by common deliberation, the canons of Saint Stephen approached us privately, humbly asking us to appoint a day for establishing peace between you and them. Suspecting no deceit or trickery whatever in their words, we granted their request and appointed them a day, as they had asked. Immediately afterward, however, having devised a plan of fraud, they withdrew from us and secretly sent one of their brethren, namely Peter de Moneta, to our aforesaid predecessor, while we suspected nothing of the sort. [Col. 1236B]

After he had appeared before the curia, bringing forward many lies and inventing others, he dared, among other things, to suggest to our lord that we had done nothing concerning the aforesaid affair and had not wished to obey the command of the Apostolic See in carrying it out. Leaving after these fabrications and returning again to the curia, he brought with him the rest of his fellow-deceivers, and, after they had assembled, an inquiry was conducted as if from the beginning.

At last, certain persons who, as stated above, had been rejected in so celebrated a judgment—and indeed others who were not at all suitable—were admitted to the aforesaid proof. Two of our clerics, whom we had sent to confirm the already mentioned judgment, arrived; but though they carefully set forth all that had been done, they could accomplish nothing. For the canons of Saint Stephen had by then so filled the entire curia with the deceits of their fabrications and the blandishments of flattery [Col. 1236C] that, since no room was left there for others, they themselves received the document concerning mother-church status.

After some time, the same lord is said both to have recognized their fraud and to have grieved intensely over it. He therefore also granted you, dearest brother Archbishop Anseric, by the authority of his written instrument, free power to perform episcopal functions in whichever church you wished.

But after we were placed, by divine grace, in the administration of the Apostolic See, you repeatedly brought this complaint to our attention. Since we knew fully both the aforesaid deception and the whole case—for from the time of our childhood we had been brought up in those regions and had seen the truth of the entire matter with our own eyes—we summoned both parties a second time into our presence. You attended as commanded, but they withdrew without submitting any excuse. Finally, we fixed for both them and you a third date, on the feast of Saint Luke; but on the other side we were again treated with contempt. [Col. 1236D] For although you were present and remained at the curia for fifteen days beyond the appointed date, they neither came nor sent any representatives. Therefore it seemed to our brother bishops and cardinals, and also to the archbishops, bishops, and abbots who were with us, that the canons of Saint Stephen had sought flight so that the affair might not be heard before us, since we knew with complete certainty both their deceitfulness and the purity of your claim.

Accordingly, by the common counsel of those same our brethren, we annul by apostolic authority that document concerning mother-church status which was fraudulently procured from our aforesaid lord through so great a deception. We establish that it shall possess absolutely no force in the future. Rather, throughout the parish of the city of Besançon, the Church of Saint John alone shall possess for future times all the dignity of the episcopal see and of the mother church which it is known to have possessed in ancient times. [Col. 1237A]

Furthermore, let all the customary payments which the Church of Saint Stephen made to your church, both spiritual and temporal, from the time of Hugh of Salins, archbishop of Besançon of blessed memory, until the time of our brother Hugh, who died on the Jerusalem pilgrimage, henceforth be peacefully rendered to you and to your same church.

Moreover, we strengthen by the present page of decree and decree to remain perpetually valid the absolution from that oath, made to the clerics of both churches by you, dearest brother and Bishop Anseric in Christ, and by Humbert, archbishop of Lyon, and confirmed by us while we were still in the regions beyond the mountains. By authority of the Apostolic See we establish and command in every way that neither you shall presume any longer to prosecute the canons of Saint Stephen over that oath, nor they, nor any other person, to prosecute you.

If the canons of Saint Stephen should attempt to oppose our present enactment by audacious presumption, [Col. 1237B] we grant you, beloved brother Anseric, archbishop of Besançon, and your successors, leave, with God’s help, to enforce justice against their persons and even against the church itself until they make satisfaction.

If in the future any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowing this page of our constitution, should rashly attempt to act against it, then, after a second or third warning, unless he makes suitable amends by satisfaction, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and honor. Let him know himself guilty before divine judgment for the iniquity committed, let him be separated from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Redeemer, and at the final judgment let him be subject to severe vengeance. But upon all who preserve the rights of that same Church of Saint John [Col. 1237C] may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that they may receive here the fruit of good action and find before the strict Judge the rewards of eternal peace. Amen, amen.

Written by the hands of Gervasius, regional scrivener and notary of the sacred palace.

Given at the Lateran, on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of April, in the fifteenth indiction, in the year 1122 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the fourth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Calixtus II.

I, Calixtus, bishop of the Catholic Church, have subscribed.

## CLXXI. Papal protection (*mundiburdium*) granted to the monastery of Reichenbach. (1122, 24 March.)

[Ried, *Codex diplomaticus Ratisbonensis*, from a contemporary codex of the Reichenbach *Traditions*.]

[Col. 1238B]

Calixtus, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son Erchenger, abbot of the monastery of Saint Mary, situated at Reichenbach in the bishopric of Regensburg, and to his successors canonically appointed in perpetuity.

A pious request ought to be fulfilled with an effect corresponding to the desire expressed. Therefore, beloved son in Christ, Abbot Erchenger, we have judged that your petition should be granted, and we place under the protection of the Apostolic See the monastery of blessed Mary over which, by God’s ordinance, you preside. It was founded by the worthy man Margrave Diepold and his wife Adelheid, and offered to blessed Peter and his holy Roman Church. [Col. 1238C]

By the present page of decree, therefore, we establish by apostolic authority that all possessions and goods which that monastery now lawfully possesses, or may hereafter, by the grant of pontiffs, the generosity of princes, the offerings of the faithful, or other just means, obtain through the Lord’s bounty, shall be preserved secure and entire for you and your successors.

We decree, therefore, that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the aforesaid monastery, take away its possessions, retain what has been taken, diminish them, or harass them by reckless vexations. Rather, as stated, let all things be preserved intact and serve in every respect the benefit of those for whose maintenance and governance they were granted.

Upon the death of you, the present abbot of that place, or of any of your successors, let no one be set over it by any crafty fraud or violence, except one whom the brethren by common consent, or the sounder part of the brethren, have elected according to the fear of God and the Rule of blessed Benedict. [Col. 1238D] We command the same concerning the appointment of the advocate; if that advocate proves burdensome to the brethren and useless to the monastery, he shall be removed and another substituted.

You shall receive the abbatial blessing, consecration of altars, and ordinations of monks from the bishop in whose diocese you are, provided that he enjoys the favor and communion of the Apostolic See and is willing to confer these things freely and without improper exaction. Otherwise, you may approach whichever Catholic bishop you prefer and receive the same sacraments from him.

We likewise judge the burial-place of that monastery to be entirely free, so that no one may oppose the devotion and final will of those who have resolved to be buried there, unless they are excommunicated, while preserving in all things the right and reverence due to the diocesan bishop. [Col. 1239A] As a token of this freedom received from the Roman Church, you shall pay annually one gold piece to the Lateran palace, as had also been established by the aforesaid Margrave Diepold.

If, therefore, any ecclesiastical or secular person in the future, knowing this page of our constitution, should rashly attempt to act against it, then, after a second or third warning, unless he makes suitable amends by satisfaction, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and honor. Let him know himself guilty before divine judgment for the iniquity committed, separated from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Redeemer, and subject at the final judgment to severe vengeance. But upon all who preserve the rights of that place may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that they may receive here the fruit of good action and find before the strict Judge the rewards of eternal peace. Amen.

Given at the Lateran, on the ninth day before the Kalends of April, in the fifteenth indiction, in the year 1122 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the fourth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Calixtus II.

## CLXXII. Privilege for the monastery of Zwiefalten. (1122, 24 March.)

[Petrus, *Suevia ecclesiastica*, 916.]

Calixtus, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Udalric, [Col. 1239C] abbot of the monastery situated in the place called Zwiwulda, and to his successors canonically appointed in perpetuity.

It is fitting readily to grant pious desires, so that faithful devotion may attain a swift result. For Liutold and Cuono, counts and most devoted sons of the Apostolic See, under the Lord’s inspiration built from their own resources a monastery in the place called Zwifulda. Consecrated in honor and in the name of the blessed Mother of God, ever-Virgin Mary, they offered it to blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, and to his holy Roman and Apostolic Church.

Confirming this offering by the authority of the Apostolic See, following the example of our predecessor of holy memory, Pope Urban, we receive the aforesaid place to be fostered under the protection of blessed Peter, and protect it against the attacks of all living persons by the firm force of the present decree. [Col. 1239D] We establish that whatever the aforesaid counts, moved by the inspiration of God, have bestowed upon the monastery, and whatever has hitherto been bestowed, or may hereafter, with the Lord’s consent, be bestowed by any faithful persons from their own right, shall always remain secure and inviolate for you, dearest brother in Christ Udalric, whom by divine disposition we know now to preside over that place as abbot, and for your successors.

Therefore no person may disturb that monastery, take away its possessions, retain what has been taken, or harass it by reckless vexations. Rather, let all things be preserved intact, to serve in every respect the benefit of those for whose maintenance and governance they were granted.

Upon the death of you, the present abbot of that place, or of any of your successors, let no one be set over it by any crafty fraud or violence, except one whom the brethren by common consent, or the sounder part of the brethren, have judged should be elected according to the fear of God. [Col. 1240A] We command the same concerning the appointment of the advocate. If that advocate is found useless to the monastery, he shall be removed and another substituted.

You shall receive chrism, holy oil, and consecrations of altars and churches from the bishop in whose diocese you are, unless he is shown to be simoniacal or not to possess communion with the Apostolic See. If that proves to be the case, you may receive both the ordinations of clerics and the other sacraments from whichever Catholic bishop you prefer. If any secular person wishes a place of burial to be prepared for himself in that monastery, you may grant what is piously desired.

As a token of this freedom received from the Roman Church, you shall pay annually one gold piece to the Lateran palace. If in the future any archbishop, bishop, emperor, king, prince, duke, count, viscount, judge, powerful or powerless person, knowing this page of our constitution, should rashly attempt to act against it, then, after a second or third warning, unless he makes suitable amends by satisfaction, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and honor. Let him know himself guilty of the iniquity committed and separated from the most sacred [Col. 1240B] body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, and at the final judgment let him be subject to severe vengeance. But upon all who preserve the rights of that place may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that they may receive here the fruit of good action and find before the strict Judge the rewards of eternal peace. Amen, amen, amen.

I, Calixtus, bishop of the Catholic Church, approving.

Given at the Lateran through the hand of Chrysogonus, cardinal-deacon and librarian of the holy Roman Church, on the ninth day before the Kalends of October, in the fifteenth indiction, in the year 1122 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the fourth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Calixtus II.

## CLXXIII. He confirms the monastery of Saints Peter and Paul at Echenbrunn. (1122, 24 March.)

[Col. 1240D]

[Lang, *Regesta sive Rerum Boicarum autographa e regni scriniis*, Munich, 1822, quarto, vol. I, p. 119.]

## CLXXIV. Privilege for the monastery of Saint Mary at Godesberg. (1122, 25 March.)

[Wenck, *Hessische Landesgeschichte*, I, 287.]

Calixtus, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son Burchard, abbot of the monastery of Saint Mary, situated in the parish of Speyer at the place called Godesova, [Col. 1241A] and to his successors canonically appointed as provosts.

The authority of our office urges us to concern ourselves with the condition of the Church and to confirm what has been rightly established. For the illustrious Count Berthold of Hohenburg, at his own expense, built the monastery of Blessed Mary over which, beloved son in Christ, you preside by God’s ordinance, on his own estate in the place called Godesova, and offered it to blessed Peter and his Roman Church under an annual payment of one denarius of Speyer currency.

We, therefore, considering his praiseworthy devotion and granting your prayers, place that offering, with everything belonging to it, under the protection of the Apostolic See, in honor of God and blessed Peter, prince of the apostles. We establish that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb that monastery, take away its possessions, retain what has been taken, diminish them, or harass them by reckless vexations. Rather, all that it now lawfully possesses, or may hereafter lawfully obtain through the Lord’s bounty, shall be preserved peaceful and free under Roman protection. [Col. 1241B]

Upon the death of you or of any of your successors, let no one be set over it by any crafty fraud or violence, except one whom the brethren by common consent, or the sounder part of the brethren, have elected according to the fear of God and the Rule of blessed Benedict. We command the same concerning the appointment of the advocate; if that advocate is found useless to the monastery, he shall be removed and another substituted.

You shall receive the consecrations of churches and the ordination of the abbot and brethren from the bishop in whose diocese you are, unless he is shown to be simoniacal or not to possess communion and favor with the Apostolic See. If that is the case, you may approach a Catholic bishop and receive the same sacraments from him.

We likewise judge that the burial-place of that monastery shall be entirely free, so that no one may oppose the devotion and final will of those who have resolved to be buried there, unless they are excommunicated, while preserving in all things reverence due to the diocesan bishop. [Col. 1241C]

If, therefore, any ecclesiastical or secular person in the future, knowing this page of our constitution, should rashly attempt to act against it, then, after a second or third warning, unless he makes suitable amends by satisfaction, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and honor. Let him know himself guilty before divine judgment for the iniquity committed, separated from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Redeemer, and subject at the final judgment to severe vengeance. But upon all who preserve the rights of that place may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that they may receive here the fruit of good action and find before the strict Judge the rewards of eternal peace. Amen, amen.

I, Calixtus, bishop of the Catholic Church, approving.

Given at the Lateran through the hand of Chrysogonus, cardinal-deacon and librarian of the holy Roman Church, on the ninth day before the Kalends of April, in the fifteenth indiction, in the year 1122 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the fourth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Calixtus II.

## CLXXV. He receives under protection the monastery of the Savior at Millstatt and confirms its rights. (1122, 27 March.)

[Col. 1242A]

[See Hormayr, *Archiv für Geographie, Historie, Staats- und Kriegskunst*, Vienna, 1810, quarto, p. 329.]

## CLXXVI. At the request of Bishop Benedict, he confirms certain privileges of the Church of Lucca. (1122, 4 April.)

[Baluze, *Miscellanea*, Lucca edition, IV, 187.]

Calixtus, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother Benedict, bishop of Lucca: greeting and apostolic blessing.

We give thanks to Almighty God, whose mercy is better than life, who in these days has inclined the people of Lucca to full obedience to their pastor. [Col. 1242B] Although prudent and religious men governed the Church of Lucca in former times, the people, seeking temporal things rather than providing for their salvation, were very unwilling to obey them as they ought. Hence it came about that certain goods of the Church of Lucca, both ecclesiastical and secular, were plundered by many persons and retained for private use.

Since, therefore, dearest brother, divine mercy has granted this favor to you and to the people of Lucca, so that they desire humbly to bind themselves to you as their father and bishop of souls, we earnestly command your brotherhood to labor to recover what has been wickedly alienated, both among parish churches and chapels and in other possessions. For the Lord has granted you the ability you possess so that, with his help, through your diligence those things may be restored which, through the negligence of your predecessors, have passed into the possession, as it were, of strangers. [Col. 1242C]

So that you may be continually vigilant in these matters and in the other concerns belonging to episcopal administration, we have judged it fitting to grant your petition with due kindness. By apostolic authority, therefore, we prohibit the construction of any monastery or church in the bishopric of Lucca without the bishop’s knowledge, in accordance with the chapter of the Council of Chalcedon on this point.

We also forbid monks to presume to administer anointings of catechumens or the sick among the people, or to impose public penances. If the people of a parish should gather at a monastery for participation in divine worship, those same sacraments shall be administered through a chaplain-priest to whom the bishop has entrusted the governance of the people and care of souls, while the customs of the other churches remain intact.

Concerning parish churches held by monks in the bishopric of Lucca, we confirm the synodal decree of our predecessor of holy memory, Pope Urban II: namely, that monks shall not place priests in them without the bishop’s counsel. Rather, with the consent of abbots or priors, the bishop shall entrust pastoral care to a priest, so that such priests shall render account to the bishop concerning the care of the people, while rendering due subjection to the abbot in temporal matters belonging to the monastery. Thus the rights of each shall be preserved. [Col. 1242D]

Furthermore, if monasteries or churches of the diocese of Lucca have disputes among themselves and a complaint reaches the bishop from one party, the controversy shall be settled by his judgment, without prejudice to the authority of the Roman Church and excepting monasteries and churches belonging to the Roman Church.

We also wholly forbid anyone to receive persons excommunicated or placed under interdict by the bishop of Lucca, who thereby participates in forbidden communion. Furthermore, by a decree to endure forever, we establish that the bishop of Lucca shall be elected by the canons of the Church according to the constitutions of the holy Fathers, and not through the violence of any laypersons.

Moreover, we confirm for you and your successors the privileges of our predecessors, the pontiffs of sacred memory Alexander II and Paschal II, and strengthen them with perpetual stability. [Col. 1243A]

If in the future any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowing this page of our constitution, should rashly attempt to act against it, then, after a second or third warning, unless he makes suitable amends by satisfaction, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and honor. Let him know himself guilty before divine judgment for the iniquity committed, separated from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Redeemer, and subject at the final judgment to severe vengeance. But upon all who preserve the rights of that Church may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that they may receive here the fruit of good action and find before the strict Judge the rewards of eternal peace. Amen.

Given at the Lateran through the hand of Cridovonus, cardinal-deacon and librarian of the holy Roman Church, [Col. 1243C] on the second day before the Nones of April, in the fifteenth indiction, in the year 1123 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the fourth year of the pontificate of the divine Pope Calixtus II.

## CLXXVII. Privilege for the monastery of Saint Mary at Praglia. (1122, 1 May.)

[Orsato, *Historia di Padova*, Padua, 1678, folio, p. 295.]

Calixtus, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son Iselbert, abbot of Saint Mary, situated in the bishopric of Padua in the place called Pratalia: greeting and apostolic blessing.

From the report of our venerable brother Bernard, bishop of Parma, we have learned that your monastery [Col. 1243D] was founded at their own expense upon an estate of their hereditary property by Maltraverso of Montebello, his brothers, and other kinsmen who were counts; and that it was offered to blessed Peter and his Roman Church under an annual payment of two gold pieces. Receiving that offering at the request both of you, beloved son in Christ Abbot Iselbert, and of our same brother, we place that monastery with all its appurtenances under the protection of the Apostolic See.

We establish, however, that whatever goods and possessions it lawfully possesses at present, in this fifteenth indiction, or may hereafter, by God’s gift, justly and canonically obtain, shall remain secure and inviolate for you and your successors. We decree, therefore, [Col. 1244A] that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb that monastery, take away its possessions, retain what has been taken, diminish them, or harass them by reckless vexations. Rather, let all things be wholly preserved intact, to serve in every respect the benefit of those for whose maintenance and governance they were granted, so that, in accordance with Gregory’s decrees, they may always be able to serve God in peace.

As a token of our present protection and confirmation, you shall pay annually two gold pieces to the Lateran palace. If anyone, knowing the tenor of this decree, should rashly—God forbid!—attempt to oppose it, he shall incur the peril of losing his honor and office and shall be punished by the penalty of excommunication, unless he corrects his presumption by satisfaction proportionate to it.

Written by the hand of Gervasius, regional scrivener [Col. 1244B] and notary of the sacred palace.

I, Calixtus, bishop of the Catholic Church.

Given at the Lateran, on the Kalends of May, in the fifteenth indiction, in the year 1123 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the fourth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Calixtus II.

## CLXXVIII. He confirms the possessions and privileges of the monastery of the Savior and Saint Boniface at Fulda. (1122, 9 May.)

[Dronke, *Codex diplomaticus Fuldensis*, 378.]

Calixtus, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son Erlolf, abbot of the venerable monastery of the Savior, our Lord Jesus Christ, and Saint Boniface, situated in the place called Buchonia, beside [Col. 1244C] the bank of the river called Fulda, and to his successors canonically appointed in perpetuity.

Source/review notes: The supplied source ends with only the headings and bibliography for CLXXXVII–CLXXXVIII; the draft supplies no text beyond the material provided.

When, by the authority and benevolence of the Apostolic See, we recognize ourselves as debtors to all Churches throughout the world, it is nevertheless fitting that we provide with more zealous care for those places known to belong more particularly to the Roman Church. Therefore, beloved son in Christ, Abbot Erlolf, graciously receiving your petitions, we place under the protection of blessed Peter the monastery of the Saviour, our Lord Jesus Christ, and of Saint Boniface, entrusted to your rule, following the example of our predecessor Pope Alexander of holy memory. For we decree that whatever goods and possessions the same monastery possesses at present in this fifteenth indiction, whether by grant of pontiffs, liberality of kings or emperors, offering of the faithful [Col. 1244D], or other just means, and whatever it may hereafter, by God’s bounty, be able to acquire, shall remain secure and unimpaired to you and to your successors.

Indeed, we forbid every priest of any Church, and especially the bishop in whose diocese that place is built, to exercise any jurisdiction or authority there apart from our Apostolic See; so strictly that, unless invited by the abbot, he may not presume even to celebrate there the solemnities of Mass. We likewise forbid any great or small person whatsoever to have power to inflict violence or raise a dispute against that monastery in respect of its property or dependants. Nor may anyone ever hold a court there or in its other places; nor [Col. 1245A] compel its servants or tenants to render any service, except one to whom the abbot has given consent for the benefit required by necessity. Nor may any woman presume, through any rashness, to enter there.

Furthermore, whatever has been granted and confirmed to your aforesaid monastery in gifts, offerings, and tithes of the faithful by the privileges of our predecessors, we too grant and confirm by the text of this present privilege. We also grant, from the liberality of the Apostolic See, to you, dearest son, and to your successors, the use of the dalmatic and sandals, as established by our predecessors. Upon the death of you, the present abbot of that place, or of any of your successors, no one may be set over it through any deceitful stratagem or violence, except one whom the brethren by common consent, or the sounder part of their counsel [Col. 1245B], in the fear of God and according to the Rule of blessed Benedict, shall elect for consecration by the Roman pontiff. He shall hold precedence, in every place and assembly, before the other abbots of Gaul and Germany; and if he should perhaps be accused of any crime, he shall await judgment from the Apostolic See alone.

At suitable times let the religious condition of your monastery be made known to the Apostolic See, lest—God forbid—the disposition and course of your uprightness be withdrawn from the standard of justice through the freedom granted by our privilege. Moreover, following in the footsteps of our fathers, we grant and confer upon you and your successors, with inviolable permanence, the monastery of Saint Andrew the Apostle, called Exaiulum, situated at Rome beside the church of Saint Mary, Mother of God and ever-Virgin, called *ad Praesepe*, with all its dwellings with fireplaces and cells, with court, well, and entrance through the principal gate from the public road, and with everything rightfully belonging to it within or outside the city [Col. 1245C].

If, therefore, any archbishop or bishop, emperor, king, duke, margrave, count, or any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowing the terms of this our enactment, should rashly attempt to act against it, then, after a second or third warning, unless he makes due satisfaction and amendment, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and office; let him know himself guilty before the divine judgment of the iniquity committed; let him be cut off from the most sacred Body and Blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Redeemer; and at the Last Judgment let him be subject to severe vengeance [Col. 1245D]. But upon all who preserve what is just for that place may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that they may receive here the fruit of good action and find with the strict Judge the rewards of eternal peace. Amen.

Written through the hand of Gervasius, regional notary and notary of the sacred palace.

*(Seal.)* I, Calixtus, bishop of the Catholic Church. *(Bene valete.)*

Given through the hand of Grisogonus, cardinal-deacon and librarian of the holy Church, on the seventh Ides of May, in the fifteenth indiction, in the year 1122 of the Incarnation of the Lord, and in the fourth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Calixtus II.

## CLXXIX. He assigns to the monastery of Saint Remigius at Rheims the mother church of Saint Martin, with half the estate of Saint Remigius; and to the monastery of Montmajour the other half of the estate, with the chapel of Saint Mary. (1122, 16 May)

[MABILLON, *Annales Benedictini*, VI, 644.]

[Col. 1246A]

Calixtus, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons in Christ Odo, abbot of the monastery of Saint Remigius, and his brethren: greeting and Apostolic blessing.

Matters examined by the truth of judgment ought to be maintained with unshaken firmness. For a dispute concerning the church of Saint Martin in the estate of Saint Remigius has long been conducted between you and the monastery of Montmajour [Col. 1246B]. Concerning it our predecessors of holy memory, Paschal and Gelasius, pontiffs of the Apostolic See, issued a definitive judgment in accordance with the grants of Arbert, bishop of Avignon, of good memory. But since the monks of Montmajour resisted and wholly refused obedience, after many evasions by delay we too sent letters concerning restitution.

Finally, regarding with a fatherly eye the labours and losses of both monasteries, after some time we again sent letters, fixing a term for both parties to plead their cause. You appeared at the appointed term, prepared and furnished with the necessary documents; but the abbot of Montmajour was absent and delegated no one for himself or for the whole affair except a certain cleric Rodulf [Col. 1246C]. Therefore, after the case had been diligently discussed and more carefully investigated in the presence of ourselves and our brethren, it was settled by common counsel that the decision of the aforesaid Fathers and the bishop’s grant must be preserved unshaken and inviolate: namely, that the mother church of Saint Martin in the estate of Saint Remigius, together with half of that estate, shall remain forever under the jurisdiction and ownership of the monastery of blessed Remigius; while the monastery of Montmajour shall hold peacefully and unimpaired the ownership of the remaining half, together with the chapel of Saint Mary. Yet all parochial rights throughout the entire estate shall be assigned to that mother church.

But if women rising after childbirth should come to the same chapel out of devotion to blessed Mary, Mother of God and ever-Virgin [Col. 1246D], we permit them to discharge their vows there. We therefore confirm by Apostolic authority this judgment of definition and decree that it shall be preserved wholly unshaken and inviolable, imposing perpetual silence upon the abbot and brethren of Montmajour in this matter. If anyone, knowing the terms of this decision, should rashly attempt—God forbid—to oppose it, then, unless after a second or third warning he makes satisfaction, let him be liable to the peril of his office and to the punishment of ecclesiastical severity.

I, Calixtus, bishop of the Catholic Church, approving, have subscribed. I, Cono, bishop of Palestrina, was present at the judgment and have subscribed. [Col. 1247A] I, Lambert, bishop of Ostia, have subscribed. I, Vitalis, bishop of Albano, have subscribed. I, Clunzo, bishop of Tusculum, was present at the judgment and have subscribed. I, Gregory, bishop of Terracina, was present and have subscribed. I, Rainer, bishop of Rimini, was present and have subscribed. I, Gregory, cardinal-deacon of Saint Angelo, have subscribed. I, Hyacinth, prior subdeacon, have subscribed. I, Romanus, subdeacon of the Holy Roman Church, have subscribed. I, Hugh, subdeacon of the sacred basilica, have subscribed. I, GG., cardinal-priest of the title of Lucina, appointed judge, was present and have subscribed. [Col. 1247B] I, Peter, cardinal-priest of the title of Calixtus, appointed judge, was present and have subscribed. I, Saxo, cardinal-priest of the title of Saint Stephen, have subscribed. I, John, cardinal-priest of the title of Saint Chrysogonus, have subscribed. I, Odaldus, cardinal-priest of the title of Saint Balbina, was present and have subscribed.

Given at the Lateran through the hand of Grisogonus, cardinal-deacon and librarian of the Holy Roman Church, on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of June, in the fifteenth indiction, in the year 1123 of the Incarnation of the Lord, and in the fourth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Calixtus II.

## CLXXX. To R[odulf], Archbishop of Rheims—Concerning the avoidance of simony in the prebends of Saint Timothy; the recall of Robert, prior of Saint Oriculus; and the preservation of monks in the church of Reistest. (1122, 16 May)

[MABILLON, *De re diplomatica*, 618, from the autograph of Saint Remigius.]

[Col. 1247C]

Calixtus, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother R., archbishop of Rheims: greeting and Apostolic blessing.

We rejoice in you, dearest brother, and give thanks to almighty God and to your love because you labour with all your strength to govern diligently the churches established throughout your bishopric and restore them to a fitting condition. It has, however, been reported to us that secular canons reside in the church of the holy martyrs Timothy and Apollinaris, belonging to the monastery of Saint Remigius [Col. 1247D]. When one of them dies, the abbot of Saint Remigius has customarily granted or sold his prebend; and your prudence does not fail to know that this is contrary to God and to the institutions of the holy Fathers.

We therefore command your brotherhood to endeavour, by God’s grace, to change that evil custom for the better: namely, that the abbot of Saint Remigius shall not henceforth presume to grant or sell a prebend; but, as the canons presently residing in that church die out, monks shall be established in their place [Col. 1248A], who under the obedience and direction of the abbot of Saint Remigius must observe the Rule of blessed Benedict and the discipline of monastic life.

We also command you to remove completely from that place Robert, prior of the church of Saint Oriculus, who was formerly abbot of Saint Remigius and through whose negligence the goods of that church are now being wasted; so that, after he has been placed in the cloister of blessed Remigius, another may be appointed by the abbot in that church, with your counsel, who by God’s help may preside beneficially over that place and be able to provide soundly both in spiritual and temporal matters.

[Note: [Col. 1247D] Robert, prior of Saint Oriculus at Senuc, near Grandpré, is the author of the *History of the Jerusalem Expedition*. On account of bad administration he was removed from the abbacy of Saint Remigius [Col. 1248D] and relegated to Senuc, where he composed his history; but, as you see here, change of place did not change his character.]

Moreover, see that the ordinance which you issued concerning the church of Saint Mary of Registet, belonging to the monastery of blessed Remigius, and which was confirmed by the text of our document, is inviolably preserved in future [Col. 1248B]. Do not permit monks who have been placed, or are to be placed, in that location in accordance with that ordinance to be expelled from choir or processions through the violence of any canons or laymen. If anything is done contrary to our command, execute full justice, by the Lord’s aid, upon those who presume to do it.

Given at the Lateran, on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of June.

## CLXXXI. He commends Otto, Count Palatine, because he repents of having served in the king’s army when Paschal II was captured. He urges him to build a church to remain under the authority of Saint Peter. He commends A[zzone], bishop of Acqui, sent into Germany. (1122, 25 June)

[*Monumenta Boica*, X, 233.]

[Col. 1248C]

Calixtus, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the illustrious Otto, Count Palatine: greeting and Apostolic blessing.

We have heard that you grieve and are greatly saddened because you were in that expedition of the king in which our lord Pope Paschal, of holy memory, was captured with excessive cruelty; yet you gave neither counsel nor assistance for his capture or detention. We therefore rejoice greatly and give thanks to almighty God because the visitation of the Holy Spirit has inclined your heart to repentance.

That you may advance from good to better, and may always persevere in the unity and obedience of the Church, we impose upon you, for the remission of your sins, the obligation to construct a church of regular brethren which, in honour of God and for the salvation of your soul, must remain forever under the right and jurisdiction of blessed Peter and his Roman Church [Col. 1248D]. For by this means you will be able to obtain the grace of almighty God and our counsel and aid. We commend to your nobility our dearest brother and kinsman A., bishop of Acqui, whom we have sent into your regions, asking you, for reverence toward blessed Peter, to provide him with guidance and whatever else may be necessary.

Given at the Lateran, on the seventh day before the Kalends of July.

## CLXXXII. He notifies the Archbishop of Dol, his suffragans, and other prelates of Churches established throughout that province, of a general council to be held in the City. (1122, 25 June)

[MANSI, *Concilia*, XXI, 255.]

[Col. 1249A]

To the venerable brethren, the archbishop of Dol and his suffragans, and the abbots and other prelates of churches established throughout the same province: greeting and Apostolic blessing.

Because of the great and diverse affairs of the Church, we have resolved to celebrate a general council in the City during the coming Lent. We therefore command that, setting aside every excuse, you be with us in the City on the Sunday in that Lent on which “My eyes” (*Oculi mei*) is sung [Col. 1249B], so that we may celebrate, by God’s grace, a general council with you and with the other brethren—archbishops, bishops, abbots, and religious men—and, through common assistance, deliberate upon those matters which, with the Holy Spirit working with us, may lead to the honour of God and to the peace and welfare of his Church.

Given at the Lateran, on the seventh day before the Kalends of July.

## CLXXXIII. He commands Count *Raynulf*, under penalty of excommunication, to restore the church of Cingla to the monastery of Cassino within twenty days. (1122)

[See PETER, *Chronicle of Cassino*, IV, ch. 70.]

## CLXXXIV. He notifies Otto, archbishop, and the clergy and people of Capua, of the interdict imposed upon the church of Cingla and the monastery of Saint Mary, and of the deposition and excommunication of Abbess Alpherada. (1122)

[GATTULA, *History of Cassino*, 49.]

[Col. 1249C]

Calixtus, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother Otto, archbishop, and to the clergy and people of Capua: greeting and Apostolic blessing.

Let your love know that we have warned Alpherada, abbess of the monastery of Saint Mary of Capua, four times and more by our letters and messengers to reinstate the brethren of Cassino in the church of Blessed Mary at Cingla, of which they had unjustly been despoiled. Yet she did not at all obey our admonitions; rather, adding obstinacy to contempt, she replied that in this affair [Col. 1249D] she would never comply with us.

For this reason, judging that her contumacy should be restrained by the reins of ecclesiastical severity and that the right of the monastery of blessed Benedict should be preserved, we prohibit all divine offices in the aforesaid church of Cingla and also in the Capuan monastery of Blessed Mary itself. We remove the said abbess from the governance of the monastery and subject both her and her supporters in this matter to excommunication. Therefore, dearest brother archbishop, we command you under obedience not to permit any divine office to be celebrated in that monastery of Blessed Mary. Cause this judgment of interdict and excommunication, given by us, to be announced and observed throughout your diocese. And we absolutely forbid you clergy and laity [Col. 1250A] to presume in any way to enter that church contrary to our interdict, or to communicate with the excommunicated.

## CLXXXV. Privilege for the monastery of Cassino. (1122, 16 September)

[GATTULA, *History of Cassino*, II, 335.]

Calixtus, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his most reverend and dearest brother Girard, abbot of the monastery of blessed Benedict at Cassino, and to his successors canonically appointed forever.

We give thanks to almighty God, whose mercy is better than lives, who is glorious and wondrous in his saints and in ineffable goodness displays his powers wherever he wills. By the power of his gracious favour he established the most blessed Benedict as father of all monks; he ordained him to be both giver and practitioner of the monastic law. By that saint’s merits he set the monastery of Cassino, in which Benedict both lived most holy and died most gloriously, above all monasteries throughout the West, in merciful goodness [Col. 1250B].

The authority of the Apostolic See and your ardent devotion toward the Roman Church, always and especially in our own time, urge us to become cooperators in this divine goodness. Therefore, pursuing the purpose of the divine ordinance, we embrace that place with special affection and decree that all belonging to it shall remain forever peaceful and free from the yoke of all mortals, under the right and perpetual protection of the holy Roman Church alone [Col. 1250C]. Among these we have thought fit to record the following by their proper names:

First, the monastery of the Lord Saviour at the foot of Mount Cassino; the monastery of Saint Mary, Mother of God and Virgin, called Plumbarola; the monastery of Saint Mary at Cingla; the cell of Saint Benedict at Capua with its cells and appurtenances; Saint Angelo ad Formam; Saint John of the Maidens; Saint Rufus; Saint Benedict of Pizuli; Saint Angelo ad Odaldiscos; Saint Agatha at Aversa; Saint Cecilia; Saint Demetrius at Naples; Saint Sophia at Benevento; Saint Benedict at the gate of Rufinus; Saint Nicholas in the New City; Saint Benedict in Pantano; Saint Nicholas at Petra Pulecina; Saint George at Fenacleo; Saint John at Turlecoso; Saint Peter at Rossano [Col. 1250D]; Saint Angelo at Capraria; Saint Januarius near Benevento; Saint Martin there; Saint Dionysius at Ponte; Saint Anastasius; Saint Mary at Canneto beside the River Trigno; Saint Benedict; Saint Lawrence at Salerno; Saint Mary at Tremiti with the islands themselves; Saint Liberator in the March with all its appurtenances; Saint Benedict in the Marsi; Saint Mary at Luco; Saint Connatis at Civitella; Saint Angelo at Rarrejo with all its appurtenances; Saint Mary of the handmaids of God in the city of Cosenza; Saint Mary at Banza; Saint Peter of the Lake; Saint Peter of Ovellano; Saint Erasmus; Saint Benedict and Saint Scholastica at Gaeta; Saint Magnus in the estates; Saint Stephen; Saint Benedict and Saint Agatha at Terracina; Saint Peter in Foresta; Saint Paul there; Saint Mary at Ponte Curvo; Saint Angelo; Saint Nicander and Saint Thomas [Col. 1251A] at Troia; Saint Eustasius at Paulatia; Saint Benedict at Altarino; Saint Benedict at Pectinari; Saint Mary at Casale Piano; Saint Illuminata in the castle of Lemusano; the Holy Trinity and Saint George at Termoli; Saint Focas at Lesina with the inlet and fishery; Saint Benedict at Ascoli; Saint Eustace at Petra Abundans; Saint Eustace at Vipera; Saint Mary at Baretano; Saint Scholastica at Pinnis; Saint Saviour at Tave; Saint Nicholas beside the River Tronto in Abruzzo with its appurtenances; Saint John at Scurson; Saint Benedict at Frunto; Saint Benedict on the River Tesino; Saint Apollinaris at Fermo, called *ad Opplaniis*; Saint Mary at Arboscla; Saint Martin at Saline; Saint Angelo at Marano; the Holy Seven Brothers; Saint Lawrence; Saint Benedict at Ripaursa.

In the county of Aquino: the cell of Saint Gregory [Col. 1251B]; Saint Mauritius; Saint Paul; Saint Constantius; Saint Christopher; Saint Nicholas; Saint Mary at Albaneta; Saint Nicholas at Ciconia; Saint Benedict at Clia; Saint Nazarius at Comino; Saint Valentine; Saint Martin; Saint Urban; Saint Angelo; Saint Paul; Saint Felix; Saint Saviour; Saint Angelo at Valleluci; Saint Michael at Oliveto; Saint Nicholas at Pica; Saint Angelo at Cannucio; Saint Mary at Berulis; Saint Peter at Escleto; Saint Lucy and Saint Peter at Coruli; Saint Silvester; Saint Martin and Saint Lucy at Arpino; Saint Mary of the castle of Zopponis; Saint Martin at the foot of Arx; Saint Benedict on the hill of Insula; Saint Mary at Baruco; Saint Nicholas at Turrice; Saint Germanus at Sora; Saint Benedict at Paskesano; Saint Peter at Morinis; Saint Angelo at Pescolo Canale; Saint Pater at Formis; Saint Angelo at Albe; Saint Erasmus at Pomperano; Saint Mary [Col. 1251C] in Cellis; Saint Pastor in the city of Tivoli.

At Venafro: Saint Benedict; Saint Nazarius; Saint Martin in Furta itself; the estate of Saint Mary at Sala; Saint Benedict of Pizuli there; Saint Benedict at Cesima; Saint Benedict at Sessa; Saint Leo; the estate called Lauriana; Saint Benedict at Tiana with its appurtenances; Saint Mary at Calvo; Saint Nazarius at Anglena; Saint Adjutor and Saint Benedict at Alife; Saint Dominic at Telese; Saint Martin on the Volturno. At Amalfi: Holy Cross and Saint Nicholas; Holy Cross at Isernia; Saint Mark at Carpinone; Saint Valentine at Ferentino; Saint Angelo at Algido; Saint Mark at Ceccano; Saint Agatha in Tusculanum; Saint Jerusalem; Saint Benedict at Albano. At Rome: the monastery of Saint Sebastian at Palladio; at Lucca: the cell [Col. 1251D] of Saint George; in the territory of Pisa: Saint Silvester and Saint Saviour at Civitella. In the duchy of Spoleto: Saint Mary at Calena; Saint Benedict at Trani; Saint Benedict at Baro; Saint Peter Imperial at Taranto. In Calabria: the cell of Saint Anastasia; Saint Mary at Tropea; Saint Nicholas at Salectano; Saint Euphemia in the March. In the county of Arezzo: the monastery of Saint Benedict and Saint Benedict at Crema. On the island of Sardinia: the churches of Saint Mary at Thirgo, Saint Elias on the holy mountain, and Saint Heliseus with all their appurtenances; Saint Mary of Sabucco; Saint Mary of Soralbo; Saint Mary of Tanecle; Saint Peter of Trecingle; Saint Nicholas and Saint Mary at Solio with their appurtenances; Saint Nicholas of Talasa; Saint Michael of Ferrucisi; Saint George at Ticillo; Saint Peter of Simbrano; Saint Peter at Nurchi; Saint Nicholas [Col. 1252A] of Nugulli and Saint John; Saint Elias of Sitin.

Likewise, the city called Saint Germain at the foot of Mount Cassino; the castle of Saint Peter, called of old the castle of Cassino; the castle of Saint Angelo; Plumbarola; Pignatario; Piedimonte; Junctura; the castle of Saint Ambrose; Saint Apollinaris; Saint George; Vallefredda; Saint Andrew; monastic Venafro; comital Venafro; Saint Stephen; Teramum; Fractae; Castrum Novum; Mortula with the estate called Casa Fortini; Cucurutium; Camino; Suio, with all its appurtenances on both sides of the river; the tower by the sea beside the River Garigliano; the castle of Ponte Curvo; Saint Peter at Flia; Saint Victor; Torrochim; Cervaria; Saint Elias; Valle Rotonda; Sarracinesco; Cardeto; Acquafondata [Col. 1252B]; Vitecosum; the castle of Cetraro with its appurtenances and churches; in the March of Chieti, the castle of Latinianum, Mount Albrici, Mucclam, Saint Quiricus with its harbour, Frisa, and Saint Justa; in the county of Ascoli, the castle called Octavum, and Postmontem Civianum, Trivilianum, and Cavinum; in the principality, the castle of Ripa Ursa, Montembello, and Petra Fracida; at Comino, Vico Alvo; in the territory of Carsoli, the castle of Auriculum, Piretum, Rocca in Camerata, and Fossa Caeca; at Annolfi, Fundicum; in the territory of Troia, Castiglione of Baroncello, Saint Justa, and the estate of Saint Nicholas called of Galliciano; on Mount Saint Angelo, the hospice; in the territory of Capua, the former property of Liburia; in the county of Teano, the estate of Saint Felix with the church of Saint Hippolytus.

By the text of this present privilege we likewise decree by Apostolic authority that whatever your monastery now rightfully possesses, and whatever it may hereafter be able rightly and canonically to acquire by grant of pontiffs, liberality of princes, or offerings of the faithful, shall remain secure and unimpaired to you and your successors [Col. 1252C]. We decree, therefore, that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the same monastery, take away its possessions, retain what has been taken, claim for his own use things unjustly given, diminish them, or harass it by reckless vexations; but that all shall be kept whole for the use of those for whose support and governance they were granted, so as to benefit them in every way.

Moreover, following in the footsteps of our fathers, we declare that your monastery is to take precedence over the other monasteries throughout the West. We decree that both you and your successors shall sit above all abbots in every assembly of bishops or princes, and shall pronounce judgment before the other men of your order. We grant to you and your successors, on principal feasts and Sundays at Mass or in a council session, the use of fastenings, gloves, dalmatic, and mitre [Col. 1252D].

Indeed, in the venerable monastery itself and in its cells, we forbid any bishop or priest of any Church, except the Roman pontiff, to presume to exercise any jurisdiction of excommunication, interdict, or summons to synod; so that, unless invited by the abbot or prior of the place, he may not dare to celebrate there the solemnities of Mass. The brethren of the monastery itself and its cells may receive, without objection by bishops or any person, clerics of any rank or laymen from any bishopric who come for conversion, whether in health or sickness and together with their possessions—unless those clerics or laymen have then been excommunicated by their diocesan bishops for specified crimes. You may judge the subjects of your monastery, monks and religious women alike, without prohibition by any secular or ecclesiastical authority. Brethren in cells located in cities may, whenever they wish, ring bells [Col. 1253A] for celebrating divine offices; and no bishop may forbid the people of God, except under a general interdict of the whole city or parish, from entering either the monastery itself or its cells to hear God’s word.

You may receive chrism, holy oil, consecration of altars or churches, and ordination of clerics from whichever Catholic bishop you prefer; but you shall conduct baptisms and visits to the sick through your own clerics in your towns and villages. We also grant to you and your successors, as a perpetual hospice, the cell of Palladio, so that you may appoint there whomsoever you wish from your congregation. If the Roman pontiff should perhaps wish to promote him as abbot, we nevertheless decree that he shall remain entirely under your direction as a monk of your congregation.

We remit to your vessel, if it comes there, the duty customarily exacted by our officials at Ostia or Porto from ships [Col. 1253C]. Upon the death of you, now abbot of that place, or of any of your successors, no one may be set over it through any deceitful stratagem or violence, except one elected by common consent of the brethren, or by the sounder part of the brethren’s counsel, in the fear of God and according to the Rule of blessed Benedict, for consecration by the Roman pontiff, as is contained in the privilege of our predecessor Lord Pope Leo of holy memory.

Furthermore, resisting the avarice and wickedness both of present and future persons, we forbid by Apostolic authority every sedition called *levas*, or act of plunder, occurring at the death or election of any abbot [Col. 1253D]. Moreover, because of the fuller favour which, beyond the affection of our predecessors, we bear toward your monastery, we grant to you and to your lawful successors permission, if anyone violently takes the possessions or goods of your monastery or its cells, to pronounce against such plunderers the canonical sentence of excommunication, after they have been warned a second or third time, provided that their bishops, invited by you three times, have altogether refused to do justice concerning them.

We decree that the burial-ground of your place and monasteries is wholly free, so that no one may hinder the devotion and last will of those who have decided to be buried there, unless they are excommunicated.

[Col. 1254A] If, therefore, any ecclesiastical or secular person in future, knowing the terms of this our enactment, should rashly attempt to act against it, then, after a second or third warning, unless he makes due satisfaction and amendment, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and office; let him know himself guilty before the divine judgment of the iniquity committed; let him be cut off from the most sacred Body and Blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Redeemer; and at the Last Judgment let him be subject to severe vengeance. But upon all who preserve what is just for the aforesaid monastery may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that they may receive here the fruit of good action and find with the strict Judge the rewards of eternal peace. Amen, amen, amen.

I, Calixtus, bishop of the Catholic Church, have subscribed.

[Col. 1254B] Given at Berulis through the hand of Hugh, subdeacon of the holy Roman Church, on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of October, in the first indiction, in the year 1123 of the Incarnation of the Lord and in the fifth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Calixtus II.

## CLXXXVI. Bull for the monastery of Saint Saviour at Lodève. (1122, 18 September)

[*Gallia Christiana*, VI, instruments 277.]

Calixtus, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son Augerius, abbot of the monastery of Saint Saviour situated within the city of Lodève, and to his successors canonically appointed forever.

[Col. 1254C] It is fitting readily to grant assent to religious desires, so that faithful devotion may obtain a prompt effect. Therefore, acceding to your prayers, beloved son in Christ, Abbot Augerius, we receive under the protection of blessed Peter the monastery of Saint Saviour over which, by God’s appointment, you preside, founded by Fulcrand, bishop of Lodève, of good memory; and we fortify it, with all belonging to it, by the protection of the Apostolic See.

We decree that whatever the same monastery rightfully possesses at present through the grant of Bishop Fulcrand himself or his successors, by the offering of other persons, or by other lawful acquisition, and whatever it may hereafter, by God’s bounty, rightly and canonically be able to acquire, shall remain secure and unimpaired to you and your successors. Among these we have thought fit to record by their proper names [Col. 1254D]: namely, whatever your place possesses within the city of Lodève itself or outside it, in people and other goods; the church of Saint Martin of Combis, with its whole parish and appurtenances; the church of Saint Genesius of Furnis, with Mount Vinacoso and its appurtenances; the chapel of Saint Michael and the estate of Conchis in the same parish; the church of Saint Vincent of Gutta; the church of Saint Peter of Crozo; and the church of Saint Pontius at the Two Dwellings.

In the bishopric of Béziers: the church of Saint Felix of Solaco, with chapels, tithes, and all its other appurtenances; the church of Saint George of Busiaco; one third of the castle of Nefiano; and the church of Saint Alban with its appurtenances. We decree, therefore, that no person whatsoever may inflict injury upon that monastery [Col. 1255A], exact new exactions from it, rashly disturb it, take away its possessions, retain what has been taken, or harass it by reckless vexations; but that all shall be kept whole, wholly beneficial for the uses of those for whose support and governance they were granted.

Upon the death of you, abbot of that place, or of any of your successors, no one may be set over it through any deceitful stratagem or violence, except one whom the brethren by common consent, or the sounder part of the brethren’s counsel, in the fear of God and according to the Rule of blessed Benedict, shall elect. The diocesan bishop shall provide the blessing of abbots, consecration of altars, and other episcopal acts to your monastery freely and without any exaction. We likewise decree that the burial-ground of your place is free [Col. 1255B], so that no one may hinder the devotion and last will of those who have decided to be buried there, unless they are excommunicated.

If, therefore, any ecclesiastical or secular person in future, knowing the terms of this our enactment, should rashly attempt to act against it, then, after a second or third warning, unless he makes suitable amendment by canonical satisfaction, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and office; let him know himself guilty before the divine judgment of the iniquity committed; let him be cut off from the most sacred Body and Blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Redeemer; and at the Last Judgment let him be subject to severe vengeance. But upon all who preserve what is just for that place may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that they may receive here the fruit of good action and find with the strict [Col. 1255C] Judge the rewards of eternal peace. Amen.

I, Calixtus, bishop of the Catholic Church.

Given at Anagni through the hand of Hugh, subdeacon of the Holy Roman Church, on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of October, in the first indiction, in the year 1123 of the Incarnation of the Lord, and in the fourth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Calixtus II.

## CLXXXVII. He commands *T[arasia]*, Queen of Portugal, whom he has captured Pelagius, Archbishop of Braga, to release him under penalty of excommunication; otherwise he pronounces from that time a sentence of excommunication against her and her supporters.

(See the following letter.)

## CLXXXVIII. He commands D[idacus], Archbishop of Compostela, to exhort T[arasia], Queen of Portugal, to release P[elagius], Archbishop of Braga, from custody in accordance with his letters. Unless she does so within the appointed time, he orders the queen’s excommunication and an interdict upon her land to be proclaimed. (1122, 24 September)

[FLOREZ, *España sagrada*, XX, 380.]

Calixtus, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to D., Archbishop of Compostela, greeting and apostolic blessing.

It has come to us that T., queen of Portugal, has seized our brother P., Archbishop of Braga, and still holds him captive. Therefore, sending her our letters, we ordered that, by the coming feast of blessed James the Apostle and Thomas, she should release him freely, together with his men and possessions, and leave him unmolested; [Col. 1256A] otherwise, from that time forth, we have pronounced a sentence of excommunication against her and her supporters, and have interdicted divine offices throughout all her land, except the baptism of infants and the penance of the dying, until she releases that brother and makes satisfaction to the Roman Church for this injury. We therefore command your brotherhood, brother, to admonish that same T. by your letters and messengers; and, unless she releases that our brother within the appointed term in accordance with the command of our letters, you shall assemble the brethren and fellow bishops of those regions and cause this our sentence to be announced and firmly observed throughout your parishes and theirs.

Given at Anagni, the eighth day before the Kalends of October.

## CLXXXIX. He congratulates Peter, created abbot of Cluny. (1122, October 21.)

[MABILLON, *Annals of the Benedictine Order*, VI, 79.]

[Col. 1256B]

Calixtus, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son in Christ, PETER, Abbot of Cluny, greeting and apostolic blessing.

From the report of our sons, the brethren of Cluny, we have learned that by common vote, assent, and desire you have, through the grace of God, been established in the government of the abbacy. We therefore give thanks to almighty God, and by the authority of the apostolic see confirm what has been done concerning you by those brethren. We accordingly admonish and exhort your belovedness in the Lord that you may govern both the house and the congregation entrusted to you with such diligence, and strive, with divine assistance, so to direct them [Col. 1256C] that, through the effectiveness of your care, the monastery of Cluny may increase both in spiritual and temporal matters, and that the integrity of religious observance in that place may never be violated by any occasion, for the salvation of souls. For we wish to love both your person and the place itself with that affection, and to foster it with that honor and assistance, with which we know that your predecessors were alike loved and assisted by our predecessors.

Given at the Lateran, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of November. [Note: [Col. 1255] The first indiction, which corresponds to this year if, as is customary, the indiction is reckoned from the month of September, must be supplied from the following letter.]

## CXC. To the Cluniacs.—He approves Peter, elected abbot. (1122, October 21.)

[Ibid.]

Calixtus, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons [Col. 1256D] in Christ, the monks of the monastery of Cluny, greeting and apostolic blessing.

Because at this time the almighty Lord has visited us through the loss of our shepherds, we have heard that your monastery has incurred great hardship in many respects, and that your brotherhood has suffered certain losses and labors. Know that we are grieved by this all the more deeply, in proportion as that place appears to belong more particularly to the Roman Church. Yet you, most beloved sons in the Lord, should not be amazed at disturbances of this kind, knowing that all who desire to live devoutly in Christ will suffer persecution. [Col. 1257A] For one does not attain the crown except through tribulations and struggles, as the Apostle says and testifies: “No one will be crowned unless he has competed lawfully.” Therefore, do not fear or be dismayed in these struggles, for the Lord, your strengthener and helper, will be with you. He never abandons those who hope in him, but grants victory from heaven and bestows the unfading crown of glory upon his faithful who persevere manfully to the end. We also shall always love you as our dearest sons, always assist you insofar as we can, and always, with the Lord’s help, endeavor to protect you. Moreover, your abbot Peter, whom you recently elected by common vote and consent, for the honor of God and blessed Peter and for the benefit of your monastery, [Col. 1257B] we establish, with the cooperation of the Holy Spirit, in that office of government. We wish to love him, as a special son of blessed Peter, with special affection; and we confirm to him, and through him to your monastery, the possessions, all goods, and dignities which our predecessors confirmed to you, and which your house is known to have held peaceably until now.

We also command and strictly decree that no one among your brethren, nor any person whatsoever, may dare, on account of Pons, formerly abbot, to stir up scandal in your congregation. For, just as we had entrusted that monastery to him on behalf of blessed Peter and the Roman Church, so he himself surrendered it, by means of a certain staff, into our hand to blessed Peter and the Roman Church forever, without any hope of recovery. [Col. 1257C] If, therefore—God forbid—anyone should presume to stir up such scandal in your congregation against this our prohibition, he shall incur the indignation of God, blessed Peter, and the apostolic see. But whoever preserves the peace and renders due reverence and obedience to the aforesaid Abbot Peter shall obtain the favor of almighty God, of the apostles Peter and Paul, and of ourselves, and also, by the Lord’s generosity, forgiveness of his sins.

Given at the Lateran, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of November, in the first indiction. [Note: [Col. 1257D] What the pope says concerning the hardships and burdens endured by the Cluniacs is to be understood of the dissipation of their property and of the injuries inflicted upon the monastery of Cluny by Abbot Pons, and later renewed by him anew. [Col. 1258D]]

## CXCI. To the regular canons of Bernried.—He approves their institution. (1122, November 12.)

[MANSI, *Councils*, XXI, 211.]

[Col. 1257D]

Calixtus, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons in Christ, OTHO the provost and his brethren professing the regular life in the church of Blessed Martin, both present and future, forever.

It is fitting readily to grant assent to religious desires, so that faithful devotion may readily obtain its effect. Therefore, moved both by your prayers and those of the nobleman Otto, we receive into the guardianship and protection of blessed Peter and the Roman Church, and strengthen by the patronage of the apostolic see, your church, built [Col. 1258A] in honor of the Lord and Savior and of blessed Martin, within the diocese of Augsburg, in the place called Bernried, where you have resolved to serve almighty God under the observance of the regular life and the discipline of the canonical order.

We decree that everything which has already been bestowed upon it from the property of that Otto and his wife Adelheid, or by other faithful persons, or which may hereafter, by the Lord’s generosity, be conferred, shall remain secure and unimpaired to you and your successors who remain in the same religious life. We also decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb that church, take away its possessions, retain what has been taken away, diminish them, or harass it by reckless molestations; but that all things be preserved entire and be wholly devoted to the use of those for whose support and direction they were granted, saving the reverence due to the bishop of Augsburg.

Let the election of provosts be free and canonical, especially from that community or from any spiritual congregation whatsoever. After profession has been duly made, let none of you be permitted to possess private property or to leave the cloister without permission of the provost or the congregation, so that, by the Lord’s generosity, you may remain steadfast forever in the purpose you have undertaken. Advocates and defenders useful to that cell shall be provided and freely elected by the brethren of that place. As a sign of this liberty received from the Roman Church, [Col. 1258C] every third year you shall pay to blessed Peter, in the chapel of the Lateran palace, an alb with girdle and amice. If, therefore, any ecclesiastical or secular person in the future, knowing this charter of our constitution, should presume rashly to act against it, etc.

I, Calixtus, bishop of the Catholic Church.

Given at the Lateran through the hand of Hugh, subdeacon of the holy Roman Church, on the second Ides of November, in the first indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1122, and in the fourth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Calixtus II.

## CXCII. He confirms all the rights and privileges of the monastery of Saint Eustace of Nerresta. (1122, November 22.)

[MURATORI, *Italian Antiquities*, V, 815.]

[Col. 1258D]

Calixtus, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son GERBERT, Abbot of Saint Eustace, and to his successors regularly [Col. 1259A] appointed forever.

By the authority and duty of our office we are compelled to labor for the condition of churches and to establish what has been rightly established. Therefore, assenting to your prayers, beloved son Gerbert in Christ, we resolve to foster under the patronage of the Roman Church, and to strengthen by the privilege of the apostolic see, the monastery of blessed Eustace, over which, by God’s will, you preside. It was offered to the apostle blessed Peter by the gift of Count Rambald and his mother Gisela, and we regard it as a place belonging to our jurisdiction.

Accordingly, by the Lord’s authority, we confirm all that this place rightly possesses by the donation of that count and his mother or by the benefaction of other men: all appurtenances in churches, holdings, estates, hamlets, houses, and households; serfs by birth; goods and possessions; produce and legal claims; waters, mills, olive groves; and whatever it appears to possess or hold in whatsoever places. Whatever else the aforesaid monastery may hereafter acquire through the grant of popes, the liberality of princes, or the offerings of the faithful, shall remain secure and unimpaired to you and your successors.

We therefore decree that no person whatsoever [Col. 1259B] may rashly disturb that monastery, remove any of its goods, retain what has been removed, diminish them, or attack it with reckless violence; but that all things be preserved entire, wholly benefiting the use of those for whose direction and government they were granted. [lacuna] You shall receive episcopal ministrations from the bishop of Treviso, provided that he has the favor and communion of the apostolic see and is willing to provide them freely and without improper exaction. Otherwise, you may receive them from whichever Catholic bishop you prefer.
