When you, the abbot of that place, or any of your successors, die, no one shall be placed over it through any artifice of deception or violence, except one whom the brethren, by common agreement—or the sounder part of the brethren’s counsel—have elected in the fear of God and according to the Rule of blessed Benedict [Col. 1259C], to be consecrated by the Roman pontiff. You shall have permission to receive laymen as well as clerics for conversion, in accordance with the ordinance of blessed Benedict. We decree that you may retain, without objection from any bishop, the tithes of your produce which you gather at your own expense or by your own labor. As an acknowledgment of the Roman Church’s right of ownership, you shall pay six Venetian solidi each year to the Lateran palace. If, therefore, in the future any archbishop, bishop, emperor, king, prince, duke, count, viscount, margrave, castaldus, or any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowing this charter of our constitution, should rashly presume to act against it, etc.

[Col. 1259D] Written by the hand of Gervasius, regional scriniary and notary of the sacred palace.

I, Calixtus, bishop of the Catholic Church.

Given at the Lateran through the hand of Hugh, subdeacon of the Roman Church, on the tenth day before the Kalends of December, in the first indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1123, and in the fourth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Calixtus II.

## CXCIII. He congratulates Emperor Henry that he has at last returned to the bosom of the Church. He commends to him his legates staying with the emperor. He wishes imperial legates to be sent to himself. (1122, December 13.)

[MANSI, *Councils*, XXI, 280.]

[Col. 1260A]

Calixtus, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his dearest son in Christ, HENRY, glorious August Emperor of the Romans, greeting and apostolic blessing.

We render praise and thanks to almighty Lord our God, the author of all good things, who through the immeasurable mercy of his goodness has enlightened your heart by the inspiration of his Spirit and has now at last recalled you to the bosom of the Church, though for a long time you had resisted too greatly. [Col. 1260B] For, as we have learned from the report of our beloved son, the cardinal deacon, and of your faithful messengers, and from the reading of your letters, you have followed sound counsel and humbly obeyed our salutary admonitions and those of the Catholic Church. We therefore receive you as a son of blessed Peter in the arms of paternal affection; and we desire henceforth to love your person and the empire all the more abundantly and kindly, and, with divine grace leading the way, to honor them, in proportion as you have obeyed the Roman Church with greater devotion than your present predecessors, and as you are more particularly joined to us by blood relationship.

Act then, dearest son, that you may enjoy us and we you in the Lord. Let your imperial excellence consider how much harm the long discord between Church and empire has brought upon the faithful of Europe, [Col. 1260C] and how great an increase of good fruit our peace may bring, with the Lord’s cooperation. Let your belovedness know concerning our condition that, although at times we have been seriously ill, we are now, through God’s grace, well; and we desire your health of soul and body in every respect.

Concerning the matters which you entrusted to your aforesaid faithful messengers for oral communication, through those same men we reply what seems right to us and our brethren. We earnestly commend to your goodwill our legates who are with you, and ask that, because the council summoned by us is approaching, you may, by the Lord’s gift, send them back to us quickly. [Col. 1260D] Send your own legates, however, instructed in such a way that, in accordance with your promise, they may restore in full to the Roman Church the regalian rights. Further, we offer thanks to your kindness on behalf of our nephew, the bishop of Metz, and his brethren, because in them we have recognized the first fruits of your goodness. For that peace is shown to be one of good will from which works of good will are displayed. The brethren—the bishops, cardinals, and the whole Roman clergy—together with us greet you and your princes and barons, praying the mercy of the divine majesty to preserve you long for his honor and that of his Church.

Given on the Ides of December.

## CXCIV. *He confirms certain possessions of the monastery of Saint Mary of Pinerolo. (1122, December 28.)

[Col. 1261A]

*Monuments of the History of the Fatherland*. Turin, 1836. Charters, I, 754.

## CXCV. *Privilege for the same monastery. (1122, December 28.)

[Ibid., p. 756.]

## CXCVI. *He orders [Otto], Archbishop of Capua, and forbids penalties against clerics who have injured the Capuan monastery subject to the monks of Monte Cassino. [Col. 1261B] (About 1122.)

[See PETER, *Chronicle of Monte Cassino*, book IV, ch. 72.]

## CXCVII. To Berengar, Bishop of Fréjus.—Against those devastating a certain village belonging to the monastery of Lérins. (Between 1120–1123, December 24.)

[Dom BOUQUET, *Collection*, XV, 247.]

Calixtus, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the venerable BERENGAR, Bishop of Fréjus, greeting and apostolic blessing.

Our son Peter, Abbot of Lérins, coming to us with his brethren, laid before us the complaint that Troand, a knight and your parishioner, has devastated one of their villages and oppressed the inhabitants of that village, monks and laymen, with many burdensome exactions. He also complained that Adalbert and his brother Raymond, likewise your parishioners, set that village on fire; and it is known that the monastery of Lérins has suffered very great loss through the destruction of that village. We therefore command and order your brotherhood to admonish Troand himself to leave the aforesaid village, together with its inhabitants and appurtenances, wholly free and undisturbed to the brethren of Lérins, and not henceforth to harass it with any vexations. If he refuses, you, dearest brother and fellow bishop, shall render to the monastery of Lérins, which is ours, such justice as you wish us to render to you in your own affairs.

Moreover, against those who committed the burning, pronounce the sentence issued by our lords and predecessors Urban and Paschal against those who set fires, and confirmed by ourselves; except insofar as, through the prudent judgment of your discretion and with the counsel of the Abbot of Lérins or its community, mercy may be granted on account of the satisfaction which they have made.

Given at the Lateran, on the ninth day before the Kalends of January.

## CXCVIII. *He confirms the possessions and privileges of the hospice of Saint John of Jerusalem. (1123, January 8.)

[BOSIO, *History of the Sacred Order of St. John of Jerusalem*, Rome, 1621, folio, I, 48.]

## CXCIX. *He exhorts the monks of Monte Cassino to obey Oderisius, abbot-elect. (1123.)

[Col. 1262A]

[See PETER, *Chronicle of the Monastery of Monte Cassino*, book IV, ch. 78.]

## CC. He enumerates the goods and rights of the monastery of Saint Euphemia of Brescia and confirms them under the protection of the holy Roman Church. (1123, February 10.)

[MARGARINI, *Bullar of Monte Cassino*, II, p. 136.]

Calixtus, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son PETER, Abbot of the monastery of Saint Euphemia, situated in the diocese of Brescia on the side of the mountain called Dignus, and to his successors regularly [Col. 1262B] appointed forever.

We are instructed by divine precepts and guided by apostolic admonitions to watch diligently for the welfare of churches. Therefore, beloved son Peter, abbot in Christ, we have deemed it fitting graciously to assent to your petition, that we might strengthen by the protection and patronage of the apostolic see the monastery of blessed Euphemia, over which, by the Lord’s will, you preside, and which Landulf, bishop of Brescia of pious memory, built from its very foundation.

By this charter of the present privilege, therefore, we decree by apostolic authority that the possessions, estates, and all goods which that monastery now rightfully possesses, or may hereafter, by the Lord’s generosity, acquire by lawful means, shall be preserved to it secure and unimpaired in perpetual right. Among these [Col. 1262C] we record by their proper names: the castle of Saint Euphemia, with the chapel of Saint Mary; the court of Bazano; Zoco; Raina; Siluole; the court of Rezati, with its castle and chapel of Saint Peter; two farm holdings situated at Virle; Bistone; the Alps of Letina; half the court of Mazzano, with its castle, towers, and chapel of Saint Bartholomew and Saint Margaret; half the castle of Gurzago; whatever you hold in the parish of Gavardo and in the parishes of Salò, Maderno, Toscolano, and Gargnano; in Brescia, one ground-floor house; in Francia, six *goba* [an uncertain local land-unit] of vineyards; in Cobiade, six allotments; in the place called Villo, the chapel of Saint Euphemia; at Fontasio, four farm holdings; at Burne, one allotment with households; in the parish of Civitas, four plots of vineyards; at Lauze, two allotments with households; [Col. 1262D] at Pascardo, one; at Niardo, one; and at Aune, one; beside the river Mella, the court of Leole with its castle and chapel of Saint Martin; at Cassivico, three allotments; at Calino, two allotments; at Miliano and Mistriano, one small court; the castle of Rodengo, with the chapels of Saint Mary and Saint Andrew; at Corsano, one small court with a household; at Dunello, eight allotments with the chapel of Saint John; and at Carso, the chapel of Saint Lawrence with three allotments.

Let no archbishop, bishop, abbot, or person whatsoever have authority rashly to disturb that monastery, remove its possessions, retain what has been removed, diminish them, or harass it with reckless vexations. Rather, let all things be preserved whole, wholly benefiting the use of those for [Col. 1263A] whose support and governance they were granted, saving the canonical reverence due to the bishop of Brescia. When you, now abbot of that place, or any of your successors die, no one shall be set over it through any artifice of deception or violence, except one whom the brethren, by common consent or the sounder part of their counsel, whether from their own body or, if necessary, from another community, elect in the fear of God and according to the Rule of blessed Benedict, to be consecrated by the bishop of Brescia; as was established by the aforesaid Bishop Landulf of good memory. Moreover, we decree that the same monastery shall remain in that liberty in which the aforesaid bishop and founder of the place is known to have established it.

If, therefore, any ecclesiastical or secular person in the future, knowing this charter of our constitution [Col. 1263B], should presume rashly to act against it, after a second or third admonition, unless he makes proper satisfaction, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and honor; let him know that he stands guilty before divine judgment for the iniquity he has committed; let him be excluded from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, our Redeemer; and let him be subject at the last judgment to severe vengeance. But upon all who preserve the rights of that place, may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that here they may receive the fruit of good action and before the strict Judge may find the rewards of eternal peace. Amen.

Written by the hand of Gervasius, regional scriniary and notary of the sacred palace.

I, Calixtus, bishop of the Catholic Church.

[Col. 1263C] Given at the Lateran through the hand of Hugh, subdeacon of the holy Roman Church, on the fourth Ides of February, in indiction I, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1123, and in the fifth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Calixtus II.

## CCI. He confirms all rights and privileges of Frederick, archpriest, and of the canons of Carpi. (1123, February 10.)

[MURATORI, *Italian Antiquities*, V, 821.]

Calixtus, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son FREDERICK, archpriest, and the other canons of the parish church of the holy Mother of God, the Virgin Mary, situated in the district of Carpi, and to their successors forever.

Entrusted to us by the authority and duty [Col. 1263D] of the apostolic see, we are compelled to labor for the welfare of all churches, and especially, with the Lord’s help, to provide for the peace of those which adhere more particularly to that see and are subject to it as by a proper right. Astulf, king of the Lombards, is known to have built, in a district of his kingdom called Carpi, a church of the blessed ever-virgin Mary. In order to make it wholly free from the disputes and molestations of neighboring bishops, within whose borders that district lay, he gave to each of them certain possessions from the aforesaid estate in suitable locations: to the bishop of Modena, near the church of Saint Thomas, and to the bishop of Reggio, near the church of Saint Apollinaris. In addition, he decreed that that church should remain forever under the jurisdiction of the apostolic see [Col. 1264A] and obtained its liberty through the privilege of Pope Stephen. Our predecessors preserved this liberty for the aforesaid church of Carpi down to our own time.

We, therefore, decree that this same liberty shall, by the grace of God, be preserved for the aforesaid church: namely, that it shall be subject to no bishop and to no ecclesiastical or secular person whatsoever, but only to the apostolic see, to which, as stated above, it is known especially to belong by right of ownership and of protective guardianship. We further decree that the tithes of the territory of Carpi shall remain forever secure to you and your successors, without any division or diminution, as you have held them until now through the grant of our predecessors of apostolic memory, Gregory VII, Urban, Paschal II, and [Col. 1264B] others; so that no one may possess or receive any of the aforesaid tithes from anyone except by the consent and permission of the parish church.

We grant you free permission to receive chrism, holy oil, your ordination, and the consecrations of churches from whatever Catholic bishop you wish, as is known to have been granted by the aforesaid pontiffs. We further decree that the chapels known to belong by right to your church—namely, Saint Martin, Saint Lawrence, and Saint Nicholas—shall remain established in every respect forever to you and your successors without molestation. Within the boundaries of your parish, we command that no church be built except by your permission and subject to you. Within those same [Col. 1264C] boundaries we permit the provost of the parish church to ordain clerics; to his care and disposition shall belong both the ordinations and promotions of clerics to be ordained or promoted within that parish and the appointments of those who are to advance in the subordinate churches. We also grant you authority to impose penances for crimes committed within the aforesaid boundaries and to effect reconciliation.

Furthermore, by the charter of this decree, we establish by apostolic authority that whatever estates or possessions that church rightly possesses, or may hereafter rightfully and canonically acquire through the grant of popes, the liberality of princes, or offerings of the faithful, shall remain secure to you and your successors. We decree, therefore, that no person whatsoever [Col. 1264D] may rashly disturb that church, exact legal claims or any gift from your congregation, grant any of your goods as a benefice to anyone, remove or diminish the possessions of that church, or harass them with reckless vexations. Rather, let all things be preserved whole, wholly benefiting the use of you and your successors.

If hereafter any archbishop, bishop, provost, abbot, emperor, king, margrave, duke, count, viscount, judge, castaldus, or any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowing this charter of our constitution, should presume rashly to act against it, after a second or third warning, unless he makes proper satisfaction, let him be deprived [Col. 1265A] of the dignity of his power and honor; let him know himself guilty before divine judgment of the iniquity he has committed; let him be excluded from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, our Redeemer; and let him be subject at the last judgment to severe vengeance. But upon all who preserve the rights of that church may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that here they may receive the fruit of good action and before the strict Judge may find the rewards of eternal peace. Amen, amen, amen.

I, Calixtus, bishop of the Catholic Church, have subscribed.

Given at the Lateran through the hand of Hugh, subdeacon of the holy Roman Church, on the fourth Ides of February, in the first indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1123, [Col. 1265B] and in the fifth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Calixtus II.

## CCII. Confirmation of the privileges of the church of Saint Rupert of Salzburg. (1123, February 19.)

[HANSIZIUS, *Sacred Germany*, vol. II, p. 941.]

Calixtus, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons HERMANN, provost, and the canons professing the regular life in the episcopal church of Saint Rupert at Salzburg, both present and future, forever.

Through the prophet, the Lord commands those who inhabit the earth justly to meet the fugitive with bread. Therefore, dearest sons, fleeing from the world [Col. 1265C], we gladly receive you and foster you by the protection of the apostolic see through the grace of the Holy Spirit. By this charter of the present privilege, we confirm the order of canonical life established in your church by our most beloved brother Conrad, Archbishop of Salzburg. We decree that no person whatsoever may change that order in your church. We forbid any of you, after making profession, to possess private property or to abandon life together in the cloister without the permission of the provost or congregation; and we strengthen both you and all your possessions by the protection of the apostolic see.

We decree that you and your successors who remain in the same religious life shall possess forever all that you now appear lawfully [Col. 1265D] to possess for the support of your common sustenance and whatever you may hereafter acquire. We further decree that no one may rashly disturb your church, remove its possessions, retain what has been removed, diminish them, or harass them with reckless vexations; but that all things be preserved whole, wholly benefiting the use of those for whose support and direction they were granted, saving the reverence due to your own metropolitan. Further, we decree, having heard the matter, that, upon the death of the provost of that place, no one shall be set over you as provost through any artifice of deception or violence, except one whom the brethren by common agreement, or the sounder part of the brethren’s counsel, shall decide ought to be elected according to the fear of God. [Col. 1266A]

If, therefore, any ecclesiastical or secular person in the future, knowing this charter of our constitution, should attempt to act against it, after a second or third warning, unless he makes proper satisfaction, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and honor; let him know that he stands guilty before divine judgment for the iniquity he has committed; let him be excluded from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, our Redeemer; and let him be subject at the last judgment to severe vengeance. But upon all who preserve the rights of that place may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that here they may receive the fruit of good action and before the strict Judge may find the rewards of eternal peace. Amen, amen, amen.

I, Calixtus, bishop of the Catholic Church.

[Col. 1266B] Given at the Lateran through the hand of Hugh, subdeacon of the holy Roman Church, on the eleventh day before the Kalends of March, in indiction I, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1123, and in the fourth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Calixtus II.

## CCIII. He decrees that the estate of Wilzacara, with the church of Saint Caesarius in the territory of Modena, belongs to the regular canons, against the claim of the monks of Nonantola. (1123, February 26.)

[MURATORI, *Italian Antiquities*, V, 257.]

Calixtus, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the canons of the church of Saint Caesarius, situated in the estate called Wilzacara, both present and future, who shall remain under regular observance forever.

[Col. 1266C] The authority of our office exhorts us to labor for the welfare of churches and, with the Lord’s help, to establish what has been rightly established. Countess Matilda, the singular daughter of blessed Peter, long ago resolved to gather regular brethren on the estate of her paternal right called Wilzacara. When the monks of Nonantola raised a claim concerning that estate, the same illustrious lady carefully ensured that no ground for litigation remained against the brethren living there. For, when judgment had been prepared according to the command of our lord and predecessor Pope Paschal of holy memory, lawful witnesses established by oath that the aforesaid estate had been possessed [Col. 1266D] for forty years by Margrave Boniface and his daughter Matilda. They also established that the church of blessed Caesarius, situated on that estate, with its possessions, had remained free from the monks for forty years, without any exercise of monastic lordship or the initiation of a lawful lawsuit against it.

We therefore, following the example of our aforesaid lord and predecessor, receive that place and your congregation into the jurisdiction and protection of the holy apostolic see, and decree that it shall remain free henceforth from the exactions of all persons. We decree that all goods granted by the aforesaid countess for the use of the brethren serving God there, or which may hereafter, by God’s generosity, lawfully be given or offered by other faithful persons, shall always be preserved peaceably and intact. Let no one whatsoever [Col. 1267A] rashly disturb that church, remove its possessions, retain what has been removed, diminish them, or harass them with reckless exactions. Rather, let all things be preserved whole, wholly benefiting the use of those for whose support and direction they were granted.

You shall receive chrism, holy oil, consecrations of altars and churches, and the ordinations of clerics to be promoted to holy orders, from whichever Catholic bishop you prefer. As a sign of liberty received from the Roman Church, you shall pay one gold bezant each year to the Lateran palace. If any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowing this charter of our constitution, should rashly presume to act against it, after a second or third warning, unless he makes proper satisfaction [Col. 1267B], let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and honor and know himself guilty before divine judgment, etc.

Written by the hand of Gervasius, regional scriniary and notary of the sacred palace.

I, Calixtus, bishop of the Catholic Church, have subscribed.

Given at the Lateran through the hand of Hugh, subdeacon of the holy Roman Church, on the fourth day before the Kalends of March, in the first indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1123, and in the fifth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Calixtus II.

## CCIV. Privilege for the abbey of Saint Mary of Vangadizza. (1123, March 6.)

[MITTARELLI, *Camaldolese Annals*, III, appendix, 292.]

[Col. 1267C]

CALIXTUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son Litald, abbot of the monastery of Saint Mary of Vangadice, situated in the county of Mount Silicanus above the old Athesis, and to his successors regularly appointed in perpetuity.

The care of our office admonishes us, with God’s saving assistance, to attend to the welfare and peace of all churches, especially those belonging to the right of blessed Peter and of the holy Roman Church. Therefore, granting your petitions, beloved son in the Lord, Abbot Litald, we place under the protection of the Apostolic See the monastery of the Blessed Virgin Mary, Mother of God, at Vangadice, over which, by God’s appointment, you preside. It was built by Hugh, marquis of noble memory, and from its very foundation was endowed with liberty by our predecessor, Pope Sylvester of holy memory. We decree that its possessions and all goods which that same marquis, or any other persons, have brought to that place from their own right, or which may hereafter rightly be offered to it by anyone, shall remain secure and unimpaired to you and to your successors. Among these we have thought fit to record by their proper names the following: namely, the abbey village, in which the monastery stands, with the parish church of Saint John; the village of Vangadice, with the church of Saint Michael; the village called Salvaterra, with the church of Saint Antoninus; and the village of Cavazzana, with the church of Saint Lawrence.

In the diocese of Verona, the church of Saint Saviour built within the city, with its appurtenances; those possessions both in Bardolino and in other places of the same diocese. In the diocese of Vicenza, the land of Albaretto. In the diocese of Padua, the church of Saint Peter situated on Mount Silicanus, with its appurtenances; the estate of Valle Almerico, with the church of Saint Andrew. In Este, the church of Saints Firmus and Peter, with its appurtenances. In Palso, the church of Saint Michael; possessions in the court or estate of Villa, and in other places of the same diocese. In the diocese of Adria, the church of Saint Peter in the village of Conceda; the church of Saint Bartholomew of Gorgnano; Borseto, with the church of Saint Zeno; in Contina, the church of Saint Sixtus; Venice, with the church of Saint Martin; and other possessions in the same diocese or county; possessions in the diocese of Ferrara; and, in the diocese of Bologna, the church of Saints Simon and Jude of Urbizano, with its appurtenances.

We therefore decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb or harass that monastery with reckless vexations; but that all things be preserved whole, to be of every benefit for the uses of those for whose support they were granted. Further, wishing to observe the ordinances of the aforesaid predecessor of ours, we enact by apostolic authority that this monastery, remaining safe under the protection of the Apostolic See and at peace in all things, shall remain free from the power or lordship of bishops, together with all churches which it now possesses or may hereafter justly acquire, and wholly exempt from synodal exactions.

It shall therefore be lawful for you and all your successors freely to possess each of your churches, with cemeteries, baptisteries, chapters, and synods, and to appoint their priests yourselves without opposition from any bishop. Moreover, we likewise decree firmly that the promotion of your clerics, the consecration of churches, the baptism of infants living in your villages, and episcopal confirmations shall be performed by such bishops as you consider worthy to invite to these ministries. Furthermore, by the favor of this present privilege we grant priests residing at any time in the parish churches of the monastery permission to impose both public and private penances upon their parishioners. Questions arising before them concerning marriages are also to be referred, through their diligence, to you and to your successors, in order that they may be decided in accordance with the ordinances of the holy Fathers.

Each year the abbot of the monastery shall receive the most holy chrism through his delegates from whatever bishop he chooses, and shall take care to distribute it, once received, according to custom to the baptismal churches. We grant you, moreover, out of compassion, the tithes in their entirety from the estates of the abbey, Vangadice, Salvaterra, and Cavazzana. In other places, concerning lands which you cultivate at your own expense and concerning your revenues, it shall be lawful for you, by our authority, to claim their tithes.

Upon the death of you, now abbot of that place, or of any of your successors, no one shall be set over it by any artifice of intrusion or by force, except one whom the brothers, by their common consent or by the sounder part of the brethren, shall provide to be elected from among themselves—or, if necessary, from another community of religious brethren—according to the fear of God and the Rule of blessed Benedict. The person elected shall come to the Roman pontiff to be consecrated.

If, therefore, in the future any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowing the text of this our constitution, should rashly presume to act against it, and, having been admonished a second or third time, should not make due amendment by suitable satisfaction, let that person be deprived of the dignity of office and honor, and know himself or herself guilty before divine judgment of the iniquity committed; let such a person be excluded from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, our Redeemer, and be subject at the last judgment to severe retribution. But upon all who observe what is just toward this place may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that here they may receive the fruit of good action and before the strict Judge may find the rewards of eternal peace. Amen.

I, Calixtus, bishop of the Catholic Church. **The Lord is the strength of those who fear him.**

Given at the Lateran through the hand of Hugh, subdeacon of the holy Roman Church, on the second day before the Nones of March, in the first indiction, in the year 1123 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the fifth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Calixtus II.

## CCV. To D[idacus], Archbishop of Compostela

*(A.D. 1123, March 6.)*

[FLOREZ, *Sacred Spain*, XX, 385.]

[Col. 1269C]

CALIXTUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the venerable brother D., archbishop of Saint James and legate of the Roman Church, greeting and apostolic blessing.

Having examined the messengers of the Church of Lucca and of its bishop, we learned that your belovedness is by no means exercising the legation once worthily entrusted to you by us, owing to the obstruction of certain perverse persons, I know not whom. We were therefore greatly grieved and wonder that our authority in your regions should have fallen into such tribulation. Accordingly, we confirm to you the same legation as before; and we admonish you, as a most beloved son, to carry out our business in your regions, and, by the permission and authority of this holy see, to correct and amend what requires correction. Farewell.

[Col. 1269D]

I, Cardinal Deusdedit of Saint Lawrence, have confirmed. John, cardinal. Peter, cardinal, . . . . . has confirmed.

Given at the Lateran on the second day before the Nones of March. Written by the hand of Hugh, subdeacon.

## CCVI. He confirms the privileges and goods of the canons of the Church of Cremona

*(A.D. 1123, March 6.)*

[MURATORI, *Italian Antiquities*, V, 247.]

CALIXTUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the beloved sons, the canons of the Church of Cremona, and to their successors in perpetuity.

The authority of our office urges us to exercise paternal solicitude for the condition of churches and to establish what has been instituted for their peace and tranquility. Therefore, dearest sons in Christ, graciously granting your petitions, after the example of our predecessor of holy memory, Pope Urban, we defend your church of the Blessed Mary, Mother of God, with all its property, under the protection and patronage of the Apostolic See.

For we decree that whatever goods and possessions the unity of your congregation is known by authentic and lawful documents to have possessed hitherto—whether by gift of bishops, kings, or the offerings of other faithful persons—shall remain forever firm and unimpaired to you and to your successors. Among these we designate by their proper names: Butaningum, Castrum Vetus, Insula, Radaldiscum, Casa Nova, Butalianum, Atunellum, and Fontanella; the chapel of Saint Saviour; the churches of Saint Peter of Curticella beyond the Po, Saint Mary of Mareulingo, Saint Michael of Marasse, and Saint Michael in the suburb of the city, with their appurtenances; and likewise the oratory of Saint Maurice, with its appurtenances.

We decree also that the offerings of the altar of Saint Imerius and of the other altars of your church shall forever be applied to the uses of your community. Whatever may in future be justly and lawfully conferred for the governance of your congregation shall always be kept firm and entire in perpetual stability, to be of every benefit for the uses of those for whose support and governance it was granted.

In addition, we command that no bishop, count, viscount, or procurator may harass you in respect of this canonry, or, against your will, take from its lands fodrum [a feudal levy] or any payment, or ever trouble or dispossess you or your successors of those lands without lawful judgment. Furthermore, that by God’s grace you may attend more peacefully to the service of almighty God, removing you and the aforesaid church from the burden of bishops, we decree that they may not reside in your canonry against the will of the brethren.

But you, most beloved sons in the Lord, ought to correct your conduct from every evil and preserve your manner of life according to the rule of canonical observance, so that you may be what you are called, not only in name but also in reality before the eyes of the divine majesty.

If in future any archbishop, bishop, emperor, king, prince, duke, marquis, count, viscount, judge, or any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowing the text of this our constitution, should rashly attempt to act against it, and, having been admonished a second or third time, should not make due amendment by suitable satisfaction, let that person be deprived of the dignity of office and honor, and know himself or herself guilty before divine judgment of the iniquity committed; let such a person be excluded from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, our Redeemer, and be subject at the last judgment to severe retribution. But upon all who observe what is just toward this place may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that here they may receive the fruit of good action and before the strict Judge may find the rewards of eternal peace. Amen, amen, amen.

I, Calixtus, bishop of the Catholic Church.

Given at the Lateran through the hand of Hugh, subdeacon of the holy Roman Church, on the second day before the Nones of March, in the first indiction, in the year 1123 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the fifth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Calixtus II.

## CCVII. *He receives the monastery of Leno under protection and confirms its goods and privileges*

*(A.D. 1123, March 16.)*

[ZACCARIA, *Three Books on the Most Ancient Abbey of Leno*. Venice, 1767, quarto, p. 111.]

## CCVIII. Privilege for the Church of Blessed Mary of Blois

*(A.D. 1123, March 19.)*

[*Gallia Christiana*, VIII, documents, 421.]

[Col. 1271B]

CALIXTUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Stephen, abbot, and to the canons in the Church of Blessed Mary at Blois who profess the regular life, both present and future, in perpetuity.

We ought not merely to favor the good desires of religious brethren and holy men, but also to encourage their minds toward them. For the nobleman Theobald, count of Blois, at the warning and exhortation of our venerable brother Geoffrey, bishop of Chartres, restored and wholly relinquished to God and to you, through the hand of that same bishop—as we have learned from his testimony—your church of the blessed and glorious Virgin Mary, Mother of God, which he retained under the secular power of his lordship, together with all its goods and possessions. This was done on the following condition: when the secular clerics of that church die, their benefices and ecclesiastical possessions shall be assigned to the use of yourselves and of the brethren who, by God’s appointment, shall succeed you in the regular life; but so long as those clerics live, they shall not be compelled to surrender the revenues of the prebends which they have held hitherto.

Moreover, the same count, devoutly attentive to your common benefit, committed to your use, through the hand of the aforementioned bishop, the chapel of Saint Carilefus, which his father and he himself had first possessed. This was done so that, whenever the persons belonging to it die, the revenues of the prebends shall be transferred to the Church of Blessed Mary, and, at a suitable time and according to the abbot’s judgment, some regular clergy may be appointed in that chapel.

Therefore, judging praiseworthy the desire of the aforesaid vigorous and illustrious count, and granting his requests, we confirm what he has done concerning the aforesaid churches through the hand of our brother and fellow bishop Geoffrey, and command that it remain ratified and inviolable in future times. If anyone, knowing the tenor of this decree, should rashly—God forbid!—attempt to oppose it, let that person incur the loss of honor and office, or be punished by the penalty of excommunication, unless he correct his presumption by worthy satisfaction.

I, Calixtus, bishop of the Catholic Church.

[Col. 1272A]

Given at the Lateran through the hand of Hugh, subdeacon of the holy Roman Church, on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of April, in the first indiction, in the year 1123 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the fifth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Calixtus II.

## CCIX. Privilege for the monastery of Usinhoven

*(A.D. 1123, March 26.)*

[*Monumenta Boica*, vol. X, p. 449.]

CALIXTUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son BRUNO, abbot of the monastery of Saint Mary, situated in the diocese of Freising in the place called Schira, and to his successors regularly appointed in perpetuity.

Apostolic teaching declares that we are debtors to all; nevertheless, the authority of the administration entrusted to us urges us to give more attentive aid to religious men. For you, dearest son, as we have learned by the testimony of truthful men, were living with your brethren in the monastery in the place called Usinhoven, but because of the excessive inconvenience of that place and scarcity of water, you could make no provision either for your own welfare or for theirs. Therefore, having taken counsel with our venerable brethren Archbishop Adalbert of Mainz, legate of the Apostolic See, and Archbishop Conrad of Salzburg, you jointly resolved to transfer your dwelling to Schirrum.

That place was offered to God and blessed Peter through our hands by Otto, Count Palatine, with the consent of the distinguished lady Countess Petrissa and of five other counts, by the investiture of a certain glove (*scirotheca*). It is suited to monastic life and seems well adapted to the needs of the brethren. Accordingly, out of true love and charity, granting assent to your most humble petitions, we confirm this change or transfer for the honor of God and the increase of religion, provided that you in no way lose the care of the former place, which belongs to blessed Peter. Moreover, we cherish this place of your new dwelling under the protection of blessed Peter, and uphold you as sons beloved by the Lord with the arms of our defense.

By the text of this present decree, therefore, we establish by apostolic authority that whatever estates and goods Hazocha of noble memory, with his sons the counts Ekkahard, Bernhard, and Otto; likewise Count Berthold of illustrious memory; Count Conrad and his brother Otto; and the brothers Otto, Bernhard, and Ekkahard, and other faithful of Christ are known to have offered from their own right to your congregation for the salvation of their souls; and whatever you may hereafter be able justly and canonically to acquire through the grant of pontiffs, the generosity of princes, or the offerings of the faithful, shall remain secure and unimpaired to you and to your successors.

We therefore decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb or harass your monastery with reckless vexations; but that all things be preserved whole, to be of every benefit for the uses of those for whose support and governance they were granted. You shall receive chrism, holy oil, the consecration of altars or churches, and the ordination of monks who are to be promoted to sacred orders from the bishop in whose diocese you are, provided that he enjoys the favor and communion of the Apostolic See and is willing to provide these things freely and without improper dealing. Otherwise, it shall be lawful for you to approach whichever Catholic bishop you prefer, who, supported by the authority of the Apostolic See, shall grant what is requested.

Upon the death of you, now abbot of that place, or of any of your successors, no one shall be set over it by any artifice of intrusion or by force, except one whom the brethren by common consent, or the sounder part of the brethren, may elect, whether from their own community or, if necessary, from another, according to the fear of God and the Rule of blessed Benedict. Furthermore, we decree that the burial-place of your house shall be wholly free, so that no one may obstruct the devotion and last will of those desiring to be buried there, unless they are excommunicated.

We also grant you an advocate, chosen according to your judgment and that of other religious and prudent men—whomever you consider most suitable—who, out of regard for the fear and love of God, shall make proper provision for your welfare. Yet if he should prove troublesome to you, it shall be lawful for you by our authority to appoint another suitable person. Neither he nor anyone else shall have power to claim the advocacy of your house as if hereditary, or to possess it against your will.

If in future any archbishop or bishop, emperor or king, prince or duke, count, viscount, judge, or any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowing the text of this our constitution, should rashly attempt to act against it, and, having been admonished a second or third time, should not make due amendment by suitable satisfaction, let that person be deprived of the dignity of office and honor, and know himself or herself guilty before divine judgment of the iniquity committed; let such a person be excluded from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, our Redeemer, and be subject at the last judgment to severe retribution. But upon all who observe what is just toward this place may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that they may receive the fruit of good action and before the strict Judge may find the rewards of eternal peace. Amen.

[Col. 1273D]

I, Calixtus, bishop of the Catholic Church.

Given at the Lateran through the hand of Hugh, subdeacon of the holy Roman Church, on the seventh day before the Kalends of April, in the first indiction, in the year 1123 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the fifth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Calixtus II.

## CCX. In a general council he enrolls Conrad, formerly bishop of Constance, among the saints

*(A.D. 1123, March 28.)*

[MANSI, *Councils*, XXI, 289.]

CALIXTUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the venerable brother Udelric, bishop, clergy, and people of Constance, greeting and apostolic blessing.

The brethren whom you sent to the Apostolic See related to us and to our brethren many miracles concerning the deeds of that holy deceased man, Conrad, your bishop, and sought to establish by written records and verbal testimony the things which almighty God had done through him. It seemed good, therefore, to our brethren the bishops and cardinals, and to the other archbishops, bishops, abbots, and religious men who were present, that, as he is honorable before God by his merits, so we should make his memory honorable among men, insofar as it is lawful for us.

Accordingly, in the general council which we are holding, we announce his veneration to all the brethren. Therefore, for the honor of God and reverence for Saint Conrad himself, by the Lord’s gift we establish that his commemoration shall henceforth be kept among the saints; and that the miracles said to have been performed by God through him, if they are true, shall thereafter be retained in writing and in readings, committed to memory.

But you, dearest brethren and sons, refreshed by the fragrance of the flowers appearing in your land, strive henceforth, with the Lord’s cooperation, so to conduct yourselves and so to live devoutly that you too may be able, through the grace of the Holy Spirit, to emit to others the fragrance of virtues. May almighty God, through the prayers of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul and of the aforesaid holy man, preserve us in his mercy and bring us to eternal life.

Given at the Lateran, on the fifth day before the Kalends of April.

## CCXI. To Girbert, Bishop of Paris—That all clerics and abbots of his diocese shall obey him; likewise, that a canon of Paris who becomes bishop of another church shall lose his prebend

*(A.D. 1123, March 28.)*

[MANSI, *Councils*, XXI, 210, from the lesser *Pastoral* of the Church of Paris.]

[Col. 1274C]

CALIXTUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the venerable brother Girbert, bishop, and to the canons of the Church of Paris, greeting and apostolic blessing.

By the obligation of apostolic administration we are called to preserve for churches their dignity and justice. Therefore, by God’s grace, we desire that your mother church of Blessed Mary remain in the state of its dignity. For the stability of this present writing we decree that all clerics and abbots belonging to the see of Paris shall always render due obedience and reverence to you, dearest brother Bishop Girbert, and to your successors, as to their shepherd and as members joined to their head.

We further decree, in accordance with the judgment of the saints, that if any canon of the Church of Paris is promoted to the dignity of the episcopate and receives the governance and benefices of another church, he shall be deprived of his canonry in the church from which he was taken.

Given at the Lateran, on the fifth day before the Kalends of April, in the first indiction.

## CCXII. He receives the monastery of Saint Bertin at Saint-Omer under protection and confirms its privileges

*(A.D. 1123, March 30.)*

[*Collection of Cartularies*, III, 262.]

[Col. 1275A]

CALIXTUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son Lambert, abbot of the monastery of Saint Bertin at Saint-Omer, and to his successors regularly appointed in perpetuity.

Just as no effect should be granted to those who seek what is unjust, so the petition of those desiring what is lawful ought not to be delayed. Therefore, granting your just petitions, beloved son in the Lord, Abbot Lambert, we receive the monastery of blessed Bertin at Saint-Omer, over which by God’s appointment you preside, to be cherished under the guardianship and protection of the Apostolic See.

We decree that no abbot shall be set over that monastery except one whom the brethren, by common consent or the sounder part of the brethren, shall provide to be elected from their own community according to the fear of God and the Rule of blessed Benedict. Furthermore, in accordance with the decree of our predecessor of holy memory, Pope Paschal, we decree by apostolic authority that the appointment of an abbot at Alciacum shall be made from no source other than your monastery.

Likewise, in accordance with the confirmation of Count Robert, we decree that no other mills whatsoever shall stand from the village of Arkas and the mills situated within the bounds of your monastery as far as Broburg and Lodic, just as none stood in former times. We decree that you shall henceforth possess freely and without all opposition the millers and all milling dues which you have hitherto peacefully possessed from the office of the advocate of Saint Bertin or from any other source.

Further, we confirm to your church by the present decree the whole expanse of the enclosure which lies on every side of your basilica as far as the middle course of the River Agnion, as is established to have been consecrated by our brother John, bishop of the Morini; together with its fisheries and adjoining lands, cultivated or uncultivated—namely, from the aforesaid village of Arkas as far as the old monastery—as you possessed it in ancient times.

We also confirm by the authority of this document one half of those tithes which accrue to you and to the canons of Saint Audomar by common right: namely, those of Saint Michael, Saint Quentin in Lokenes, Saint Martin outside the borough, Saint James of Tatinghuem, and Cormettes; and also those four denarii of the common toll which your fraternity, together with the aforesaid canons, lawfully claimed for itself against the burgesses before the bishop of Thérouanne.

Moreover, we decree that the provision for refreshment which you have established to be given to the monastic brethren and the poor on your anniversary shall remain inviolate. If, therefore, in the future any ecclesiastical or secular person, etc.

Given at the Lateran, through the hand of Hugh, subdeacon of the holy Roman Church, on the third day before the Kalends of April, in the first indiction, in the year 1123 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the fifth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Calixtus II.

## CCXIII. To John, bishop of the Morini

*(A.D. 1123, March 30.)*

[Ibid., p. 294.]

CALIXTUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the venerable brother John, bishop of the Morini, greeting and apostolic blessing.

We believe it is well known to your brotherhood that the monastery of Saint Bertin, with all its goods and possessions, belongs to the right of the Roman Church. In this respect we have confirmed by the text of our decree those of its goods which it is known to have possessed from ancient times. Therefore, with entreaty, we command your belovedness to endeavor to maintain and defend all its goods, and especially those confirmed by the privileges of our predecessors. Endeavor also to ensure and firmly maintain in future that the appointment of the abbot at Alciacum shall be made from the aforesaid monastery; and, without any pretext, impose the hand of blessing upon the man elected from it, so that we may know that the sons of blessed Peter are more fully loved by you for our sake, and that you may deserve to receive from us expressions of gratitude.

Given at the Lateran, on the third day before the Kalends of April.

## CCXIV. He vindicates the Church of Saint Macarius for the monastery of Holy Cross at Bordeaux

*(A.D. 1123, March 30.)*

[MABILLON, *Benedictine Annals*, VI, 98.]

[Col. 1276C]

CALIXTUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons Andro, abbot, and the monks of Holy Cross, greeting and apostolic blessing.

A dispute has arisen between you and the monks of Saint Macarius concerning subjection and obedience. You wished, according to your custom, to retain those brethren in religious observance and in subjection to your monastery; but they, having become rebellious and disobedient to you, strove to withdraw themselves from your subjection. Accordingly, summoned by the archbishop of Bordeaux, they appeared before him, but despised obedience to his judgment and to that of the religious abbots and monks who were present. For this reason they were excommunicated by him.

Then, rising still more fiercely against you, they went to our legate Gerard, bishop of Angoulême, and by certain deceptions obtained from him a certain pastoral staff. On the strength of that staff they wished the Church of Saint Macarius to be a free abbey in its own right, just as the monastery of Holy Cross was. Thereupon the archbishop, summoned to our council, summoned them by his commands and admonitions to answer before us concerning this transgression. When both parties had come into our presence and they had requested a delay from us, we set a day for both parties upon which the dispute might be settled before us and our brethren. On the appointed day you were present, but the other party withdrew from our sight.

Therefore it seemed just and reasonable to us and to our brethren that neither you should be defrauded of your right nor they profit from their absence. Accordingly, in the general council of our brethren—the cardinals and bishops, and other archbishops, bishops, abbots, and religious men—we approved that the aforesaid Church of Saint Macarius, as it was in ancient times, shall henceforth remain subject to the obedience and direction of your monastery. That staff, or rod obtained by deception, shall be placed under your authority, and shall be completely broken so that it may cause no further scandal. If anyone should rashly violate this constitution and approval of ours and of the general council, that person shall be subject to the judgment of the Holy Spirit and to the indignation of the Apostolic See. The monks of Saint Macarius, moreover, shall remain under the excommunication with which they were struck both by us and by the archbishop, until they return to obedience to the abbot of Holy Cross.

I, Calixtus, bishop of the Catholic Church.

Given at the Lateran through the hand of Hugh, subdeacon of the holy Roman Church, on the third day before the Kalends of April, in the second indiction, in the year 1123 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the fifth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Calixtus II.

## CCXV. To the people and clergy of Augsburg

*(A.D. 1123, March 31.)*

[KHAMM, *Hierarchy of Augsburg*, part I, p. 198.]

CALIXTUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the clergy and people of Augsburg, greeting and apostolic blessing.

Our beloved brother Hermann, your bishop, came to the Apostolic See with much labor and hardship, and acknowledged the holy Roman Church, his mother, with due humility and obedience. We received him with paternal affection and carefully retained him with us as an obedient son. Therefore, sending him back to you with our favor and with the full integrity of his episcopal office, we ask, admonish, and command your entire community to receive him kindly, to love him with special affection, and humbly to render him reverence and obedience as to your father and teacher, and also as bishop of your souls.

Given at the Lateran, on the second day before the Kalends of April.

## CCXVI. At the request of Bishop Nicholas, he confirms the liberty and possessions of the Church of Monopoli

*(A.D. 1123, March 31.)*

[UGHELLI, *Sacred Italy*, I, 963.]

CALIXTUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved brother Nicholas, bishop of Monopoli, and to his successors canonically appointed in perpetuity.

Just as no effect should be granted to those who seek what is unjust, so the petition of those desiring what is lawful ought not to be delayed. Since, therefore, your belovedness, taking refuge in the haven of the Apostolic See, has with due devotion sought its renewed protection, we graciously grant your petition and fortify by the authority of this present decree the aforesaid Church of Monopoli, over which by God’s appointment you preside.

We decree that the same church shall owe the reverence of subjection to no one other than the Apostolic See, as was determined by our predecessor of apostolic memory, Urban II, in the synod of Benevento and confirmed by the testimony of a privilege, and likewise strengthened by the protection of a privilege from Pope Paschal of holy memory. We therefore decree that you and your successors, enjoying the favor of this liberty, shall remain forever under the obedience of the Apostolic See alone. We establish that whatever the Church of Monopoli has hitherto possessed justly, now possesses, or may hereafter justly and canonically acquire—in castles, villages, woods, churches, monasteries, and other possessions—shall always be preserved for your episcopal governance and direction, and for that of your successors, saving in all things the reverence due to the Roman and Apostolic Church.

Upon the death of you or of any of your successors, the clergy and people of Monopoli shall have the right, with all improper influence excluded, canonically to elect a bishop; and the person elected shall be consecrated by the Roman pontiff.

If in future any archbishop, bishop, emperor, king, prince, duke, count, viscount, judge, or any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowing the text of this our constitution, should rashly attempt to act against it, and, having been admonished a second or third time, should not make due amendment by suitable satisfaction, let that person be deprived of the dignity of office and honor, and know himself or herself guilty before divine judgment of the iniquity committed; let such a person be excluded from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, our Redeemer, and be subject at the last judgment to severe retribution. But upon all who observe what is just toward this place may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that here they may receive the fruit of good action and before the strict Judge may find the rewards of eternal peace. Amen, amen, amen.

I, Calixtus, bishop of the Catholic Church.

Given at the Lateran through the hand of Hugh, subdeacon of the holy Roman Church, on the second day before the Kalends of April, in the first indiction, in the year 1123 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the fifth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Calixtus II.

## CCXVII. He commends to the people of Hamburg Archbishop Adalberon, consecrated by him and granted the pallium

*(A.D. 1123.)*

[LAPPENBERG, *Hamburg Documents*, I, 126.]

[Col. 1278D]

CALIXTUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the clergy and people of Hamburg, greeting and apostolic blessing.

Desires of your charity being in accord with our judgment, we kindly received at the thresholds of the Apostles and in our presence our beloved brother Athelberon, who came to us and whose election had met with your approval—one whom we trust conforms to the canonical rules of the Fathers and is not ignorant of ecclesiastical order. Embracing him, dearer from one dear, in the arms of affection and the depths of charity, we consecrated him as your archbishop by our hands, as it were by those of blessed Peter. [Col. 1279A] Upon him thus consecrated we also bestowed, with the abundance of our grace, the pontifical pallium—that is, the fullness of office—through the benevolence of the Apostolic See. He is to use it within the church at the solemn celebrations of Mass on those days distinguished in the privileges of your church. Therefore, sending him under the authority of our letters to govern your church, we exhort you with full affection to love him and with full humility to reverence him. For we confidently trust that, through his teaching and prudence, God being the author, a great fruit of benefit will accrue to you all.

CCXVIII. Confirmation of all the rights of the Church of Squillace. (1123, April 2.)

[COQUELINES, *Amplified Collection of Bulls*, vol. XI, p. 184.]

[Col. 1279B] CALIXTUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother PETER, archbishop, transferred by us from the Church of Squillace to that of Palermo, and to his successors canonically instituted, forever.

It is fitting for us to grant assent to just wishes and to lend our ears to just petitions, since, although unworthy, we are seen, by the Lord’s ordering, to have been set as guardians and heralds of justice upon the lofty watchtower of the princes of the Apostles, Peter and Paul. Therefore, acceding to your just petitions, dearest brother in Christ Peter, archbishop, we strengthen by the authority of the Apostolic See the holy Church of Palermo, over which, with the Lord as author, you preside by our appointment. We decree that Palermo, Misilminum, Cornelianum, Bicaris, and Thermae with their appurtenances, and [Col. 1279C] the possessions, tenants, tithes, and episcopal rights of that parish, as well as everything which the rulers of the land and other faithful persons have bestowed upon that Church from their own right, and whatever appears to belong to the Church by ancient right, shall remain secure and free under your authority and that of your successors, by the protection of our authority. We likewise grant to you by Apostolic authority, and through your diligence concede to that Church, every liberty which is known to have been granted by our predecessors of holy memory—Alexander II, Gregory VII, and Paschal II, pontiffs of the Roman Church—to your predecessors Nicodemus and Alcherius, archbishops of Palermo, and through them to the Church of Palermo; and we confirm it by the page of this decree. [Col. 1279D]

We also grant to your beloved person the use of the pallium which was granted to your predecessors by our predecessors; you are to use it on those days distinguished in the privileges of your Church. Since the honor of this garment must be maintained by the restrained vigor of one’s conduct, we exhort you to make it accord with the adornments of your character, so that, God being the author, you may rightly be conspicuous in both respects.

Accordingly, dearest brother, since the duty of pastoral care binds you: love the brethren; let even adversaries be joined to you in affection toward you, because of the Lord’s command; pursue peace with all, and holiness, without which no one shall see God; devote yourself to pious works; abound in virtues. Let the breastplate of judgment shine upon your breast, joined to the action of the ephod [*superhumerale*]; [Col. 1280A] thus go forth before God and all Israel. Offer such examples to the flock entrusted to you that they may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven. Let speech be upon your tongue and heavenly ardor in your mind. Cultivate the Lord’s field entrusted to you while it is permitted; sow in fear; while there is time, do not cease from doing good, for in its own time you shall reap if you do not fail, keeping watch. Therefore, leaving earthly concerns, pant after heavenly things; forgetting what lies behind, stretch yourself toward what lies before. Let not your mind be dispersed amid secular realities, but let it run and flow wholly into the one end which David beheld with wondrous sweetness when he said: “One thing have I asked of the Lord; this will I seek: that I may dwell in the house of the Lord all the days of my life.” May the Holy Trinity [Col. 1280B] surround your brotherhood with the protection of its glory and grant that you may attain the end which does not end.

But if in the future any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowing the page of this our constitution, should rashly attempt to act against it, after a second or third admonition, unless he makes suitable amends by satisfaction, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and honor; let him know himself guilty before the divine judgment for the iniquity perpetrated; let him be cut off from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Redeemer Jesus Christ; and at the last judgment let him be subject to severe vengeance. But upon all who preserve what is right for the same Church, may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that they may here receive the fruit of good action and, before the strict Judge, find the rewards of eternal peace. [Col. 1280C] Amen, amen, amen.

I, Calixtus, bishop of the Catholic Church.

Given at the Lateran, through the hand of Hugh, cardinal-subdeacon of the Holy Roman Church, on the fourth day before the Nones of April, in the first indiction, in the year 1123 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the fifth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Calixtus II.

CCXIX. To Anthony, abbot of Senones. (1123, April 2.)

[*Gallia Christiana*, XIII, documents, 488.]

CALIXTUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son in Christ ANTHONY, abbot of the monastery of Senones, situated in the diocese of Toul.

[Col. 1280D] Therefore, acceding to your just petitions, dearest son in Christ Anthony, abbot, we decree, etc., that the following shall remain inviolate, which seemed proper to express in their own names: the church of Vipodicella, etc.; the church of Plania; the church of St John; the church of St Maurice of Senones, etc.; the church of Stopax; the church of the bishop’s estate; the church of Danuebrium, etc. Moreover, we order that whoever shall be appointed advocate of your place by the bishop of Metz, etc., shall be content with the benefit assigned to the advocates, etc. But upon all who preserve what is right for the same place, may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, and may they find, before the strict Judge, the rewards of eternal peace. Amen, amen, amen.

Given at the Lateran, through the hand of Hugh, cardinal-subdeacon of the Holy Roman Church, on the fourth day before the Nones of April, in the first indiction, [Col. 1281A] in the year 1123 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the fifth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Calixtus II.

CCXX. To Otto, bishop of Bamberg, apostle of the Pomeranians.—Concerning privileges granted to the Church of Bamberg. (1123, April 3.)

[MANSI, *Councils*, XXI, 193.]

CALIXTUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother OTTO, bishop of Bamberg: greeting and Apostolic blessing.

We ought not only to favor the good endeavors of our brethren, but also to encourage their minds toward them. Therefore, inclined by your supplications, dearest and venerable brother Otto, bishop of Bamberg, we receive into the protection of blessed Peter and of his Roman Church, to be defended against the wickedness of evil men, the monasteries which you have built at your own expense and, having conferred them upon the Church of Bamberg, have requested to be fortified by the protection of the Apostolic See. [Col. 1281B] We decree that the possessions, estates, and all goods which your brotherhood has bestowed upon those monasteries out of love for God, and which have been granted by the just offerings of other faithful persons—or shall hereafter be lawfully and legally acquired or offered—shall, God being the author, remain firm and inviolate to them. Let them receive the ordinations of their abbots or monks from Catholic diocesan bishops. But we decree that the care and administration of the goods of those monasteries shall remain at the discretion and under the power of you and your successors. [Col. 1281C]

Therefore let no person have the power to disturb those monasteries, remove their possessions, retain what has been taken, diminish them, or harass them with rash vexations; rather, let all things be kept intact for the benefit in every way of those uses for whose support and governance they were granted. If, therefore, any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowing the page of this our constitution, should rashly attempt to act against it, after a second or third admonition, unless he makes suitable amends by satisfaction, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and honor; let him know himself guilty before the divine judgment for the iniquity perpetrated; let him be cut off from the most sacred body and blood of God and of the Lord Redeemer Jesus Christ; and at the last judgment [Col. 1281D] let him be subject to severe vengeance. But upon all who preserve what is right for the same monasteries, may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that they may here receive the fruit of good action and, before the strict Judge, find the rewards of eternal peace.

Written by the hand of Gervasius, regional scrivener and notary of the Sacred Palace.

CCXXI. Privilege for the monastery of St Benedict of Crema. (1123, April 3.)

[GATTULA, *History of Monte Cassino*, I, 285.]

CALIXTUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son VIVIAN, provost of the church of Blessed Benedict near [Col. 1282A] Rome: greeting and Apostolic blessing.

It is fitting readily to grant assent to religious desires, so that faithful devotion may obtain a swift result. Count Henry of Bergamo, with the support and assent of the entire people of Crema, for the salvation of their souls, offered with devotion and reverence a cell dedicated in honor of blessed Benedict upon an estate of his own possession. The venerable brother Roger, then bishop of Volterra, son of the same Count Henry, had formerly requested that this cell, at the desire and request of his father and the people of Crema, be received under the protection of the Apostolic See, like the other dependencies of the monastery of Cassino.

Therefore, acceding both to their petitions and to yours, beloved son Vivian, provost of the same place, [Col. 1282B] out of reverence for our most holy Father Benedict and love for our son Abbot Oderisius, to whose care that place belongs by right from the abbey of Cassino, we receive the said cell under the guardianship and protection of the Apostolic See by the page of this present decree. We decree that the same cell shall always remain quiet and free in the possession and unity of the monastery of Cassino, and that no person whatsoever may withdraw or separate it from the right and lordship of the monastery of Cassino. Whatever estates and possessions have been bestowed upon the same place for the support of the brethren by the aforesaid Count Henry, by the people of Crema, or by other faithful persons, or shall hereafter be bestowed by the Lord’s favor, shall be preserved for you forever secure, undisturbed, and entire. These [Col. 1282C] possessions are held in the territory of Cremona: in the village of Heire, at Rivi Zinga, at Veilate, at Mozanica, at Vauri, at Josano, and at Boteliano.

We therefore decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the same monastery, remove its possessions, retain what has been taken, diminish them, or harass them with rash vexations; rather, let all things be preserved intact for the benefit in every way of those uses for whose support and governance they were granted. You shall receive the ordinations of monks who are to be advanced to sacred orders, and of clerics belonging to the monastery, from whichever Catholic bishop you prefer, who, when requested and supported by the authority of the Apostolic See, shall grant them. If in the future any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowing the page of this [Col. 1282D] constitution, should rashly attempt to act against it, let him incur the penalty of his honor and office, or be punished by the vengeance of excommunication, unless he corrects his presumption by worthy satisfaction. But whoever takes care to cherish that house and those serving the Lord in it, and to honor them with his goods, shall obtain the grace of almighty God and His Apostles. Amen, amen, amen.

I, Calixtus, bishop of the Catholic Church.

Given at the Lateran, through the hand of Hugh, subdeacon of the Holy Roman Church, on the third day before the Nones of April, in the first indiction, in the year 1123 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the fifth year of Pope Calixtus II’s pontificate.

CCXXII. He receives under protection the convent of St Saviour and St Julia at Brescia, and confirms its possessions and privileges. (1123, April 3.)

[MARGARINI, *Bulls of Monte Cassino*, II, 137.]

[Col. 1283A]

CALIXTUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved daughter in Christ ERMINGARD, abbess of the monastery of our Lord and Saviour and of St Julia, virgin and martyr, called the New [Monastery], situated in the city of Brescia, and to her sisters both present and future, forever.

What has been established by our predecessors with a view to the welfare of the Church ought to be preserved with enduring permanence. Therefore we have judged it right to grant your petitions, dearest [Col. 1283B] daughter in Christ, so that we might fortify by the privilege of the Apostolic See the monastery of Blessed Julia, over which, God being the author, you preside, and which Queen Ansa built within the city of Brescia. By the page of this present writing, therefore, we decree that the same monastery, placed under the protection of the Apostolic See and royal defense, shall never be subjected to the jurisdiction of any other person; so that no priest, unless invited by the abbess of that place herself, may presume to celebrate the solemnities of Mass there. We confirm to you, your sisters, and those who shall succeed you in the same religious life the possessions of that place, lawfully granted by the same Queen Ansa, by her successors the emperors, or by other faithful persons: [Col. 1283C] namely, the estates of Sirmione, Cervanica, Nuvelaria, Berciagum, Barbada, Alfianum, Calvatone, Ciconiaria, Miliarina, Sermida, together with Cosenagum Novum and Monticellum, with all the churches belonging to the same monastery—namely one at Sirmione, one at Nuvelaria, two at Berciagum, one at Barbada, one at Alfianum, two at Calvatone, one at Ciconaria, and one at Meliarina—as well as estates, villages, castles, churches, and everything belonging to the same monastery. Moreover, whatever you may hereafter be able justly and canonically to acquire, through God’s favor, shall remain firm and inviolate to you and to the same monastery.

We decree, therefore, that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the same monastery, remove its possessions, retain what has been taken, diminish them, [Col. 1283D] or harass them with rash vexations; rather, let all things be preserved intact for the benefit in every way of those for whose support and governance they were granted. Upon your death, or that of any abbess of the monastery, let no one be placed over it by any cunning stratagem; rather, let the sisters, by common consent—or the sounder part of the sisters’ counsel—choose, in accordance with the fear of God and the Rule of blessed Benedict, the one to be appointed. The abbess of that place shall have authority, for the honor of God, to build churches and, for the monastery’s advantage, to establish markets and castles wherever she wishes on lands belonging to the aforesaid monastery. No bishop, duke, margrave, count, viscount, or any great or small [Col. 1284A] person may presume to exercise any jurisdiction in any places of that monastery, or hold any court without the abbess’s permission; nor may they alienate the monastery’s goods in any way, inflict molestation there, or exact *fodrum* [provisioning levy], lodging-duty, river-toll, compulsory supplies, or any imposts. We further confirm to your convent the tithes and first-fruits of your labors, and jurisdiction over the serfs and free persons belonging to it. We freely grant, and decree to be given without objection, chrism, holy oil, consecrations of altars or churches, ordinations of the abbess, nuns, or other clerics who are to be advanced to sacred orders, and whatever pertains to the sacred mystery, whenever requested from any Catholic prelates—as Anselperga, the first abbess of that monastery, obtained from Paul, pontiff of the Apostolic See of blessed memory, on account of the frailty of the female sex. [Col. 1284B]

But if in the future any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowing the page of this our constitution, should rashly attempt to act against it, after a second or third admonition, unless he makes suitable amends by satisfaction, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and honor; let him know himself guilty before the divine judgment for the iniquity perpetrated; let him be cut off from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord Redeemer Jesus Christ; and at the last judgment let him be subject to severe vengeance. But upon all who preserve what is right for the same place, may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that they may here receive the fruit of good [Col. 1284C] action and, before the strict Judge, find the rewards of eternal peace. Amen, amen, amen.

I, Calixtus, bishop of the Catholic Church, have signed.

Given at the Lateran, through the hand of Hugh, subdeacon of the Holy Roman Church, on the third day before the Nones of April, in the first indiction, in the year 1123 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the fifth year of Lord Pope Calixtus II.

CCXXIII. Privilege for the church of St Deodatus. (1123, April 3.)

[*History of the Church of Saint-Dié*, p. 377.]

CALIXTUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to ALBERT, venerable provost of St Deodatus, and to the other brethren: greeting and Apostolic blessing.

[Col. 1284D] The canons of your church, our beloved sons Hunald and your scholasticus Hugh, came to us and asked that we should likewise establish by our authority the possessions, rights, and dignities of your church as contained in your privileges—both those which you obtained from our predecessors, the bishops of the Roman See, and those which you received from other pontiffs, emperors, or dukes. Mercifully acceding to their petition, which appeared just, we confirm to you and to your Church forever whatever was established in the privilege of Pope Leo, our predecessor of blessed memory. We further specifically confirm the church of St Remigius on the hill, as the venerable brother Riquin, [Col. 1285A] bishop of Toul, confirmed it to you by his writing and seal. We also confirm the tenor of your churches which you possess in the diocese of Basel, as you have held them down to our time and as you received them confirmed by the writing and seal of Rudolf, bishop of Basel of blessed memory: namely, that in the fourth year the church of Ungersheim shall pay forty solidi of Basel currency for tithes, the chapel of Mittegvibre five solidi, and that of Vuegvibre likewise five. When the aforesaid churches become vacant, priests are to be appointed in them at the will of the provost and brethren of your church. Whatever may also hereafter accrue canonically to your church through the grant of princes, the generosity of pontiffs, or the offerings of the faithful, we decree by the authority of the Apostolic See to remain firm and unshaken for you. [Col. 1285B] If anyone, therefore, knowing the tenor of this decree, should rashly—God forbid!—attempt to oppose it, let him incur the penalty of his honor and office, or be punished by the vengeance of excommunication, unless he corrects his presumption by worthy satisfaction.

I, Calixtus, bishop of the Catholic Church.

Given at the Lateran, through the hand of Hugh, subdeacon of the Holy Roman Church, on the third day before the Nones of April, in the first indiction, in the year 1123 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the fifth year of Lord Pope Calixtus II.

CCXXIV. *For the monastery of St Ghislain, he affirms that certain altars were granted by Burcard, bishop of Cambrai.* (1123, April 4.)

[Col. 1285C] [See REIFFENBERG, *Monuments*, vol. VIII, p. 348.]

CCXXV. Bull for Albero, archdeacon and treasurer of the church of St Stephen at Metz. (1123, April 5.)

[MEURISSE, *History of Metz*, p. 414.]
