CALIXTUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son ALBERO, archdeacon and treasurer of the church of St Stephen at Metz: greeting and Apostolic blessing.

What benefits have been conferred upon churches by our brethren, we ought, God being the author, to preserve intact. Therefore we confirm the endowments bestowed upon the altar of our church of St Stephen by devout bishops as part of its dower. Among these we expressly name [Col. 1285D] the church of Guapeio, together with its entire estate and all the appurtenances of that estate: namely, holdings, lands cultivated and uncultivated, meadows, pastures, groves, woods, rents, springs, streams and their courses, *mundiliones* [term uncertain], fields, and also those vineyards situated in the territory of the village called Lauriacum, together with the full *ban* [jurisdictional right], just as they have been granted freely and absolutely, without any opposition, for the use of the principal treasurer and the other sub-custodians, and possessed by your predecessors. We decree that whatever further goods and possessions belong to that altar, whether churches, cultivated or uncultivated lands, vineyards, meadows, woods, serfs, rents, or revenues within or outside the city of Metz, for the use of you and your successors as treasurers, shall be preserved secure [Col. 1286A] and free, so that no ecclesiastical or secular person may have power to take them from you or, by rash boldness, inflict injury upon you. But if anyone, knowing the tenor of this our decree, should rashly—God forbid!—attempt to oppose it, let him incur the penalty of his honor and office, or be punished by the vengeance of excommunication, unless he corrects his presumption by worthy satisfaction.

I, Calixtus, bishop of the Catholic Church.

Given at the Lateran, through the hand of Hugh, subdeacon of the Holy Roman Church, on the Nones of April, in the first indiction, in the year 1123 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the fifth year of Lord Pope Calixtus II.

CCXXVI. To the canons of St John at Besançon.—He settles controversies between the churches of St John and St Stephen. He orders the return of the privilege granted by Pope Paschal to the church of St Stephen. (1123, April 6.)

[MANSI, *Councils*, XXI, 202.]

[Col. 1286B]

CALIXTUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons, the canons of Blessed John the Evangelist: greeting and Apostolic blessing.

You are to know that the discord which has persisted for a long time between you and the canons of St Stephen has been concluded by us, in the presence of our brethren the bishops and cardinals, with the following settlement. Namely, on the vigil of the feast of the Finding of the body of St Stephen, at Vespers, the canons of St John shall go in procession to the church [Col. 1286C] of Blessed Stephen; and on the morrow of that Finding, they shall receive from the canons of the church there one measure of wine and the meat of one cow, or four solidi in Besançon currency. Likewise, on the vigil of St John Before the Latin Gate, at Vespers, the clerics of St Stephen shall come to St John. The dean of St Stephen shall always perform homage to the archbishop and shall hold in perpetual right, from his hand, the archdeaconry of Dole and Amos. The candles that were anciently supplied to the canons of St John by the canons of St Stephen in the outer houses of the cloister shall not be paid at any time except during the forty continuous days after the Finding and the other forty days after the dedication of Blessed Stephen’s altar. The wax that was sent to the vintage of the district of Lausanne shall no longer be paid. [Col. 1286D] Six *brae* of wax shall be paid to St John’s treasurer on Holy Saturday of Easter; and on the Purification of St Mary, one candle shall be given to each canon of St John who has come to the procession. Candles shall likewise, according to the customary practice, be paid nightly to the cellarer while the canons’ wine remains common. All other customs, both spiritual and temporal, shall be observed without dispute by the clerics of St John as well as by those of St Stephen.

Moreover, the canons of St Stephen shall return, to Anseric, archbishop of Besançon, or to the bishop of Lausanne, by the next octave of the Apostles Peter and Paul, the privilege concerning maternity (*maternitas*) which was issued by our lord Pope Paschal of blessed memory. [Col. 1287A] If anyone should attempt either to retain that privilege contrary to this our command or to violate this peace, let him, as one guilty of sacrilege and a disturber of ecclesiastical peace, be subject to excommunication; and in places where he may be, for as long as he remains there, the divine offices shall not be celebrated, until he returns to the unity of that peace. But whoever proves a guardian of it shall obtain the blessing and grace of almighty God and of His Apostles Peter and Paul. Amen.

I, Calixtus, bishop of the Catholic Church, have subscribed.

Given at the Lateran, through the hand of Hugh, subdeacon of the Holy Roman Church, on the eighth day before the Ides of April, in the first indiction, [Col. 1287B] in the year 1123 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the fifth year of Lord Calixtus II.

CCXXVII. He declares that the privilege of the Church of Pisa concerning the consecration of Corsican bishops was condemned on the final day of the Lateran Council. (1123, April 6.)

[MANSI, *Councils*, XXI, 290.]

CALIXTUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved brethren and fellow bishops established throughout the island of Corsica and to their successors forever.

How many changes, how many mutually conflicting writings, have been made concerning your consecrations is now known to almost all Europe. From this, because of sins, there have arisen many scandals, many slayings and robberies, and also many homicides and perjuries. Therefore the Roman Church was accused by many of fickleness and inconsistency, since it appeared itself to be the seedbed and occasion of this discord. Accordingly, at the council which we recently held at the Lateran, we set forth before all the brethren who were present with us the whole course of this affair: namely, that our predecessor Pope Urban of happy memory, compelled by a certain necessity, granted by his privilege to the archbishop of Pisa the consecration of Corsican bishops; yet later, fearing scandal to the Roman Church and seeing grave discord arising between the Pisans and Genoese, he altered that concession and consecrated your predecessors with his own hands, as had been customary. [Col. 1287D]

After him, our lord Pope Paschal of pious memory, although he fell into many and most grave necessities, could nevertheless be induced by no prayers or promises to confirm those aforesaid concessions to the Pisans; instead, he preserved the consecrations of your predecessors to the Roman Church.

His successor, Pope Gelasius, compelled by greater and more serious necessity to leave Rome and to make his way by ship to regions beyond the mountains, renewed, when he came to Pisa, that same privilege which Pope Urban had granted the Pisans concerning your consecration. [Col. 1288A] Yet later, foreseeing the same disturbance between Pisans and Genoese, he annulled it.

We also, who have succeeded in their place—indeed, in the place of blessed Peter, although unworthy—hastening to the City from regions beyond the mountains, came to Pisa. There, following in the footsteps of those same predecessors of ours, Urban and Gelasius, overcome by the prayers and devotion of that people, we renewed the same concession. But when by God’s grace we had come to the City, we found, concerning the matter, no [lacuna] disturbance among clergy and people; for in that concession, made outside the City and with few persons present, the Roman Church suffered diminution and appeared, as stated, to provide fuel for the entire discord. [Col. 1288B]

Therefore, after much and prolonged deliberation, having taken counsel with our brethren the bishops and cardinals, and with the nobles of the Romans, as well as with a great multitude of clergy and people, we annulled those same concessions and restored to you and your successors the liberty of the Apostolic See by privilege; and we consecrated our brother Sago, bishop, with our hands, as it were those of blessed Peter. Finally, we caused all the writings issued by the Apostolic See to either party concerning this matter to be read in the presence of the Pisans and Genoese, whom we had summoned to the council for determination of the matter, before all the archbishops, bishops, abbots, and the remaining multitude of clergy and people; and we committed our act, concerning which no mortal is permitted to judge, to be settled by the counsel and judgment of our brethren. [Col. 1288C]

Judges were selected from among them who appeared free from every suspicion. Their names are these: the Patriarch of Venice; the archbishops of Vienne, Ravenna, Capua, Salerno, Narbonne, Siponto, Palermo, Bari, Naples, Tarragona, Sens, and Bordeaux; the bishops of Viviers, Troyes, Maguelonne, and Asti; and several others. Having withdrawn to a part of the Lateran palace, and having more diligently investigated the entire case on both sides, after much deliberation and consultation they stated with common assent that the privileges granted concerning this matter to the Church of Pisa ought to be annulled, and that the latest act, made by us through a Corsican bishop for the correction of others and for recovery of the patrimony of blessed Peter, ought to retain its own force. [Col. 1288D]

Our venerable brother Walter, archbishop of Ravenna, on behalf of the appointed judges, recited that counsel to us and to the remaining brethren, declaring that the same council had the force of a judgment. Moreover, we ordered that what had been decided by our aforesaid brethren should be read aloud on the final day of the council before the entire synod. When all the archbishops, bishops, abbots, and the remaining multitude of clergy and people had repeatedly acclaimed their approval, we, having learned their judgment and perceived the will of the Roman clergy and people, by the judgment of the Holy Spirit and Apostolic authority, condemned the writings granted to the Church of Pisa concerning your consecration, and by the same authority confirmed what we had established concerning your liberty, imposing perpetual silence upon the Pisans concerning this matter under the bond of anathema. [Col. 1289A]

But if in the future any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowing the page of this our constitution, should rashly attempt to act against it, after a second or third admonition, unless he makes suitable amends by satisfaction, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and honor; let him know himself guilty before the divine judgment for the iniquity perpetrated; let him be cut off from the most sacred body of God and of our Lord Redeemer Jesus Christ; and at the last judgment let him be subject to severe vengeance. But upon all who observe it, may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that they may here receive the fruit of good action and, before the strict Judge, find the rewards of eternal peace. Amen. [Col. 1289B]

I, Calixtus, bishop of the Catholic Church. I, Robert, cardinal of the title of St Eusebius, have subscribed. I, G. G., cardinal of the Holy Apostles, have subscribed. I, Benedict, cardinal of the title of St Eudoxia, have signed. I, Anastasius, priest of the title of Blessed Clement, have signed. I, John, cardinal-priest of the title of St Cecilia, have signed. I, Theobald, cardinal of the title of Pammachius, have signed. I, Desiderius, cardinal-priest of the title of St Praxedes, have signed. [Col. 1289C] I, G. G., cardinal-priest of the title of St Lucy, have signed. I, Theobald, cardinal-priest of the title of St Anastasia, have signed. I, John, cardinal of St Chrysogonus, was present and have signed. I, Peter, cardinal-priest of the title of St Marcellus, have signed. I, Crescentius, bishop of Sabina. I, Peter, bishop of Porto, have subscribed. I, Vitalis, bishop of Albano, have subscribed. I, the bishop of Palestrina, have subscribed. I, Aegidius, bishop of Tusculum, have signed. I, Peter, cardinal-priest of the title of St Calixtus, have signed. I, Crescentius, cardinal-priest of the title of the Holy Martyrs Marcellinus and Peter, have subscribed. I, Gherard, cardinal-priest of St Prisca and St Aquila, have subscribed. [Col. 1289D] I, Sigizo, cardinal-priest of St Sixtus, have signed. I, Deusdedit, cardinal-priest of the title of St Lawrence in Damaso, have subscribed. I, Rossemannas, cardinal-deacon of St George at the Golden Veil, have subscribed. I, Comes, cardinal-deacon of St Mary in Aquiro, have subscribed. I, G. G., cardinal-deacon of St Angelo, have subscribed. I, Romanus, cardinal-deacon of St Mary in Portico, have subscribed. I, Stephen, cardinal-deacon of St Mary of the Greek School, have subscribed. I, Jonathan, cardinal-deacon of Saints Cosmas and Damian, have subscribed. [Col. 1290A] I, G. G., deacon and cardinal of Saints Sergius and Bacchus, have signed. I, John, deacon of St Nicholas at the Prisons, have subscribed. I, Ubert, cardinal-deacon of St Mary in Via Lata, have subscribed. I, Gregory, cardinal-deacon of St Lucy at the Seven Steps, have subscribed. I, Angelus, cardinal-deacon of St Mary in Domnica, have subscribed. I, Gregory, cardinal-deacon of St Vitus, have signed. I, Matthew, cardinal-deacon of St Adrian, have subscribed.

Given at the Lateran, through the hand of Guy, chamberlain of the Roman curia, on the eighth day before the Ides of April, in the first indiction, in the year 1123 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the fifth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Calixtus II.

CCXXVIII. To Peter, bishop of Segovia.—At the request of “his nephew King Ildefonsus,” he restores the former rights of that Church, recovered from the Saracens. (1123, April 9.)

[COLMENARES, *History of Segovia*, p. 110.]

[Col. 1290B]

CALIXTUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son PETER, bishop of Segovia, and to his successors canonically instituted, forever.

It is clear to all who know the decretal decisions of the saints that the Church of Segovia was once of great nobility and power in the regions of Spain. But when the multitude of the people’s sins brought this about, that city was captured by the Saracens, and the freedom of the Christian religion there was reduced to nothing, so that for three hundred years and more [Col. 1290C] no dignity of a Christian bishop flourished there. In our own times, however, when divine mercy looked upon its people again, through the exertions of Alfonso of glorious memory the city of Segovia was rebuilt and restored to the Christian religion. Therefore, by the unanimous will and consent of the clergy and people of that city, it pleased the scrutiny of the divine Majesty that none of the bishops of the province should be elected, as the letters requested, as the first prelate of that city after so long a time. And so, responding to the compassion of heavenly grace—both through the customary goodwill of the Roman Church and through the reverence due to the Church of Segovia, and moved by the prayers of our most illustrious nephew, King Alfonso—we wish by the authority of this privilege to restore the former rights of your Church, and we confirm its goods and possessions [Col. 1290D]. We therefore decree that the possessions, boundaries, and all goods which that bishopric now holds, or may hereafter, by the Lord’s gift, justly and canonically acquire, shall remain secure and unimpaired for you and your successors.

Among these we have thought fit to record the following by their proper names: namely, the estate from Petrone as far as the path of Collad Formoso; from Balbatome as far as Manblela; from Monteillo as far as the ford of Soto. And within these boundaries: Coca, Íscar, Collar, Portellium, Peña Fiel, Castrellum de Lacer, Covas, Sacramenia, Bebigure, Bernoie, Maderol, Fraxinum, Alchite, Setempublica, and Pedraca.

We therefore decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb that bishopric [Col. 1291A], take away its possessions, retain those taken away, diminish them, or harass it with reckless vexations. Furthermore, from all the villages as well as castles now named, the church of St. Mary shall have and possess the tithes and offerings of the living and the dead from the whole bishopric; and no bishop may perform ordinations of clergy of that bishopric, or consecrations of churches, without the authority of its own bishop. If, therefore, in future any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowing this page of our constitution, should rashly attempt to act against it, then, having been warned a second and third time, unless he makes suitable amends by satisfaction, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and honor; let him know himself guilty before divine judgment of the iniquity committed; and let him be excluded from the most sacred [Col. 1291B] body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, our Redeemer, and be subject to severe vengeance at the last judgment. But upon all who preserve the rights of that Church may the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ rest, so that they may receive the fruit of good action and find, before the strict Judge, the rewards of eternal peace. Amen.

**The Lord is the strength of those who fear him.**

**St. Peter. St. Paul.**

**Pope Calixtus II.**

I, Calixtus, bishop of the Catholic Church. Given at the Lateran through the hand of Hugh, subdeacon of the holy Roman Church, on the fifth Ides of April, indiction 1, in the year 1123 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and the fifth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Calixtus II.

## CCXXIX. Privilege for the monastery of Saint Victor of Marseilles.  
*(A.D. 1123, April 11.)*

*[History of Languedoc, II, preface, p. 424.]*

[Col. 1291C]

Calixtus, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son Radulf, abbot of the venerable monastery of Saint Victor of Marseilles, and to his successors regularly appointed in perpetuity.

The authority of our office urges us to be solicitous for the condition of churches and to make secure what has been rightly established. Therefore, beloved son in Christ, Abbot Radulf, graciously granting your petition, we decree that the monastery of St. [Col. 1291D] Savior, situated in the place called Quiriacus, which, at the request of your predecessor Richard, then abbot of Marseilles, and by command of our lord predecessor Pope Urban of blessed memory, who was present there, was dedicated on his behalf by very many archbishops and bishops, shall remain, with all its churches, lands, and possessions, as free and undisturbed for you and your successors, and through you for the monastery of Marseilles, as Richard himself and the brethren of Marseilles are known to have held it on the day of its consecration. To that monastery of Quiriacus, indeed, we confirm by the page of this present privilege all the dignities and liberties which it has possessed from the beginning of its foundation [Col. 1292A], etc. Nor may any bishop remove from the service of the monks those dwelling in that monastery or throughout the adjacent village, or compel them to go forth on any military expedition or communal service, etc.

Given at the Lateran through the hand of Hugh, subdeacon of the holy Roman Church, on the third Ides of April, indiction 1, in the year 1123 of the Lord’s Incarnation.

## CCXXX. Privilege for the Church of Pavia.  
*(A.D. 1123, April 15.)*

*[Spelta, History of Pavia, 1597, quarto, p. 287.]*

Calixtus, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to brother [Col. 1292B] Bernard, bishop of Pavia, and to his successors in perpetuity.

It is fitting that we grant assent to just wishes and lend an ear to just petitions, since, though unworthy, by the Lord’s ordering we are seen to be placed as guardians and heralds of justice upon the lofty watchtower of the princes of the apostles, Peter and Paul. Therefore, reverend brother and fellow bishop in Christ, Bernard, graciously assenting to your prayers, we too make secure by the authority of this present privilege every dignity granted to your Church by the privileges or authentic documents of our predecessors. Thus we grant that your brotherhood may use the pallium during the sacred solemnities of Mass; and, both to you and your successors, that in the Palm procession and on the Monday after Easter you may ride a white horse covered with a *udone* [uncertain term], and may likewise bear the cross before you while walking.

We decree that the monastery of Saint Donatus of Ticinum—formerly founded at Scovilla by Bishop B. Liutphred [as the reading states]—although it appears to lie outside your diocese, shall always remain under your jurisdiction and disposal, together with everything belonging to it, as it has hitherto been held. The canonical ordering of the other monasteries also within the boundaries of your diocese, and the examination, election, and consecration of their abbots or abbesses, shall always be reserved to your judgment, saving in all things the privilege of the apostolic see. We prohibit, indeed, that general baptism be performed in monasteries or in any chapels [Col. 1292D] apart from the mother church, to which those persons, or their priests, ought suitably to come for your council. If any provisions issued contrary to the sacred canons should perhaps be found in them, they shall not prejudice our canonical enactments. No one may presume, without your knowledge, to summon before judgment the clerics, nuns, or widows of your city, or to inflict violence upon their property. No person may presume to withdraw from you either the care or authority of cemeteries within or outside the city; nor may any person, of whatever rank or power, under pretext of hospitality, presume without the consent of you and your successors to lodge in your venerable bishopric or in the houses of your priests and all your clerics. Nor do we permit, without legal cause and against your will, any invasion or violence to be inflicted upon moveable or immoveable goods, or persons [Col. 1293A] of whatever condition, belonging to your Church.

We therefore decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb that Church, take away its possessions, retain what has been taken away, diminish them, or harass it with reckless vexations; rather, let all things be preserved whole, to be of every benefit for the uses for which they were granted—the maintenance and governance of those concerned. Moreover, confirming this for the greater dignity of the Church of Pavia itself, we decree that, in synodal assemblies, both you and your successors shall perpetually hold the first place of seating at the left hand of the Roman pontiff.

If, therefore, in future any ecclesiastical or secular person knowingly attempts [Col. 1293B] to contravene this page of our constitution, then, after canonical warning a second and third time, unless he corrects the matter by suitable satisfaction, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and honor; let him know himself guilty before divine judgment of the iniquity he has committed; let him be excluded from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, our Redeemer; and let him be subject to severe vengeance at the last judgment. But upon all who preserve what is right for that Church may the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ rest, so that here also they may receive the fruit of good action and find, before the strict Judge, the rewards of eternal peace. Amen, amen, amen.

Written by the hand of Gervasius, *scriniarius regionarius* and notary of the sacred palace. [Col. 1293C] I, Calixtus, bishop of the Catholic Church, have subscribed. I, Peter, bishop of Porto, have consented and subscribed. I, Gregory, cardinal deacon of St. Angelo, etc. I, Roazanus, cardinal deacon of St. Mary in Portico, etc. I, Matthew, cardinal deacon of St. Adrian. I, G. G., cardinal priest of the title of St. Lucy, was present and subscribed. I, Jo., cardinal priest of the title of St. Chrysogonus, was present and subscribed. I, Peter, cardinal priest of the title of Calixtus, subscribed. [Col. 1293D] I, Comes, cardinal priest of the title of St. Sabina, subscribed.

Given at the Lateran through the hand of Hugh, subdeacon of the holy Roman Church, on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of May, indiction 1, in the year 1123 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and the fifth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Calixtus II.

## CCXXXI. To Amadeus, bishop of Maurienne: he grants the provostship of the church of St. Mary of Susa, together with parochial jurisdiction over the city of Susa itself.  
*(A.D. 1123, April 26.)*

*[See Monuments of the History of the Homeland, Charters I, p. 751, Turin, 1836.]*

## CCXXXII. He confirms the liberty, privileges, and possessions of the monastery of St. George of Venice, imposing upon the monks an annual payment of two gold pieces.  
*(A.D. 1123, May 8.)*

*[Ughelli, Sacred Italy, V, 1204.]*

[Col. 1294A]

Calixtus, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son Tribunus, abbot of the monastery of St. George, situated in the Venetian region, and to his successors regularly appointed in perpetuity.

A pious petition ought to be fulfilled by a corresponding effect, so that the sincerity of devotion may shine forth commendably and the benefit sought may unquestionably receive force. Since, therefore, your belovedness, most reverend son in Christ, Abbot Tribunus, fleeing to the haven of the apostolic see [Col. 1294B], has with due humility sought its protection, we graciously grant assent to your supplications and strengthen the monastery of Blessed George, over which, by God’s authority, you preside, by the patronage of the Roman Church. For by this page of the present privilege we decree by apostolic authority that this place shall be preserved free for ever under the guardianship and protection of Blessed Peter.

No patriarch, bishop, or any ecclesiastical or secular person may presume to compel you or your successors to attend a council; pronounce a sentence of excommunication or even interdict against you or your monks; establish anything in the monastery itself contrary to your will; absolve or receive your monks when excommunicated, expelled, or fugitive; or promote them to orders without the consent of you and your successors. Further, whatever you now lawfully possess, or may hereafter, by God’s gift, justly and canonically acquire, shall remain secure and unimpaired for you and your successors. Therefore, no person whatsoever may rashly disturb that monastery, take away its possessions, retain what has been taken away, diminish them, or harass it with reckless vexations; rather, let all things be kept entire, to be of every benefit for the uses for which they were granted, namely the support and governance of those concerned.

You shall receive chrism, holy oil, consecrations of altars or churches, and the ordinations of monks to be promoted to sacred orders [Col. 1294D] from the diocesan bishop, provided that he enjoys the favor and communion of the apostolic see and is willing to confer them freely and without improper exaction. Otherwise, for receiving these sacraments, you may approach whichever Catholic bishop you prefer; supported by the authority of the apostolic see, he shall grant what is requested.

Upon the death of you, the present abbot of that place, or of any of your successors, no one shall be set over you by any stratagem of deceit or by force, except the person whom the brethren, by common consent or by the decision of the sounder part of the brethren, shall judge fit to elect in the fear of God and according to the Rule of St. Benedict. As a token of this liberty received from the Roman Church, you shall pay two gold pieces each year to the Lateran palace.

If in future any patriarch [Col. 1295A], archbishop, bishop, ecclesiastical or secular person, knowingly attempts rashly to contravene this page of our constitution, then, having been warned a second or third time, unless he makes suitable satisfaction, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power or honor; let him know himself guilty before divine judgment of the iniquity committed; let him be excluded from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, our Redeemer; and let him be subject to severe vengeance at the last judgment. But upon all who preserve what is right for that place may the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ rest, so that here also they may receive the fruit of good action and find, before the strict Judge, the rewards of eternal peace. Amen, amen, amen.

I, Calixtus, bishop of the Catholic Church.

[Col. 1295B] Given at the Lateran through the hand of Aimeric, cardinal deacon and chancellor of the holy Roman Church, on the eighth Ides of May, indiction 1, in the year 1123 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and the fifth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Calixtus II.

## CCXXXIII. The monastery of St. Mary of Glastonbury is received under the protection of the apostolic see; all its goods and donations are confirmed.  
*(A.D. 1123, May 15.)*

*[Cocquelines, Collection of Bulls, II, 187.]*

Calixtus, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his most beloved son Sigeferd Pelochin, greeting and apostolic blessing.

It is proper readily to grant assent to religious desires, so that faithful devotion may obtain a swift result. [Col. 1295C] Therefore, dearest son in Christ, graciously assenting to the desires of your petition, we receive into the protection and guardianship of the Roman Church the monastery of the blessed Mother of God and glorious ever-virgin Mary, over which, by God’s favor, you preside; and by its privilege we protect it against the molestations of perverse men. For by the page and authority of this present decree we establish that whatever has been conferred upon your monastery by lawful gift from apostolic archbishops, kings and princes, and other faithful persons shall be preserved to it undisturbed and whole. Whatever further things you may, by the Lord’s gift, justly and canonically acquire in future shall remain secure and unimpaired for you and your successors.

We therefore decree that no person whatsoever [Col. 1295D] may entirely disturb that monastery, take away its possessions, retain what has been taken away, diminish them, or harass it with reckless vexations; rather, let all things remain whole, to be of every benefit for the uses for which they were granted, namely the maintenance and governance of those concerned. If in future any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowingly attempting to act against this page of our constitution, should do so, then, having been warned a second or third time, unless he makes suitable satisfaction, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and honor; let him know himself guilty before divine judgment of the iniquity committed; let him be excluded from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, our Redeemer; and let him be subject to severe [Col. 1296A] vengeance at the last judgment. But upon all who preserve what is right for that place may the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ rest, so that here also they may receive the fruit of good action and find, before the strict Judge, the rewards of eternal peace. Amen.

Given at the Lateran through the hand of Aimeric, cardinal and chancellor of the holy Roman Church, on the Ides of May, indiction 1, in the year 1123 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the fifth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Calixtus II.

## CCXXXIV. He confirms the possessions, liberty, and privileges of the monastery of All Saints at Bari.  
*(A.D. 1123, September 12.)*

*[Ughelli, Sacred Italy, VII, 618.]*

Calixtus, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved [Col. 1296B] son Melo, abbot of the venerable monastery called All Saints, in the place of Cuti in the suburb of Bari, and to his successors regularly appointed in perpetuity.

Just as no effect should be granted to those who make unjust demands, so the petition of those who desire what is lawful ought not to be delayed. Therefore, beloved son in Christ, Abbot Melo, we strengthen by the authority of the apostolic see the monastery of All Saints, over which, by God’s authority, you preside. We also confirm by the page of this present document every provision for its peace and liberty which Ursus and Elias, bishops of the Church of Bari of good memory, had bestowed upon that monastery, and which our lord predecessor Pope Paschal of holy memory confirmed, so that the place itself, with all goods rightfully belonging to it [Col. 1296C], shall remain free from the lordship or oppression of any person.

No bishop of the Church of Bari, nor any other person—God forbid—acting rashly, may dare to impose excommunication on that monastery, or inflict upon its persons or goods, in any manner contrary to justice, molestation or litigation. Let him grant the ordinations of clerics and churches freely, laying aside abuse and every exaction. We absolutely prohibit public Masses from being celebrated there by the bishop without the consent of the abbot and brethren, lest any occasion be offered for popular gatherings in the retreats of God’s servants.

Upon the death of you, then abbot of that place, or of any of your successors, no one may be placed there by any stratagem of deceit or force, except the person whom the brethren, by common consent or by the decision of the sounder part of the brethren, shall deem fit to elect according to the fear of God and the Rule of Blessed Benedict. If any graver matter should arise, he may freely appeal to the hearing of the apostolic see. In addition, we decree that whatever goods have been obtained for that place through your diligence or by the offerings of faithful persons, or may hereafter, by God’s favor, justly and canonically be obtained [Col. 1296D], shall remain secure and unimpaired for you and your successors. Nor may any person whatsoever rashly disturb that monastery, take away its possessions, retain what has been taken away, diminish them, or harass it with reckless vexations; rather, let all things remain whole, to be of every benefit for the uses for which they were granted, namely the support and governance of those concerned.

If in future any ecclesiastical or secular person knowingly attempts rashly to act against this page of our constitution, then, having been warned a second or third time, unless he makes suitable satisfaction, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and honor; let him know himself answerable before divine judgment for the iniquity committed; let him be excluded from the most sacred body of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, our Redeemer; and let him be subject to severe vengeance at the last judgment [Col. 1297A]. But upon all who preserve what is right for that place may the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ rest, so that here also they may receive the fruit of good action and find, before the strict Judge, the rewards of eternal peace. Amen, amen, amen.

I, Calixtus, bishop of the Catholic Church.

[Col. 1297B] Given at Benevento through the hand of Aimeric, cardinal deacon and chancellor of the holy Roman Church, on the second Ides of September, indiction 2, in the year 1123 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and the fifth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Calixtus II.

## CCXXXV. To Louis, King of the Franks.—He commends Cardinal P[eter], apostolic legate.  
*(A.D. 1123, September 30.)*

*[Mansi, Councils, XXI, 210.]*

Calixtus, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his dearest son in Christ, Louis, illustrious and glorious king of the Franks, greeting and apostolic blessing.

We know, and rejoice, that you acknowledge the grace granted you by the Lord and your royal power [Col. 1297C]. For you love God, venerate the churches, and show ecclesiastical persons the reverence and honor due to them. Therefore, dearest son, we have thought fit to visit you with apostolic blessing, exhorting and admonishing you to persevere by his grace in this glorious purpose of God as a religious and Catholic king, so that the King of kings, who has conferred on you an earthly kingdom, may also grant you the crown and glory of the eternal kingdom.

Moreover, we earnestly commend to your nobility our dearest son P., priest cardinal of our see. In accordance with the ancient custom of the apostolic see, we are sending him from our side into the territory of your authority, to correct and confirm what must be corrected and confirmed [Col. 1297D]. We therefore ask and exhort your excellency in the Lord to receive him reverently as our vicar, treat him honorably, and furnish him with such counsel and aid from your resources that he may fulfill the ministry entrusted to him.

Through you we greet and bless your wife, the lady queen, and your son Philip, whom we love as our own bowels; beseeching the mercy of almighty God that he may preserve you and them unharmed for a long time under the protection of his right hand. We also greet and bless Stephen the chancellor and all your faithful men.

Given at Benevento, on the day before the Kalends of October.

## CCXXXVI. To Richard, provost of Springiersbach, and his brethren, he grants certain privileges.  
*(A.D. 1123, October 12.)*

*[Jaffé supplied the title of this privilege, Registers of the Roman Pontiffs, p. 545, with this notice: “In the archive at Koblenz, from Pertz’s slips.”]*

[Col. 1298A]

## CCXXXVII. To the suffragan bishops and abbots of the province of Besançon.—He announces to them the judgment he has rendered concerning the mother-church of St. John.  
*(A.D. 1123, November 10.)*

*[Mansi, Councils, XXI, 202.]*

[Col. 1298B] Calixtus, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved brothers and sons, the suffragan bishops and abbots established throughout the province of Besançon, greeting and apostolic blessing.

After, by the Lord’s ordering, we were promoted to the ministry of the apostolic see, the canons of the Church of Blessed John the Evangelist at Besançon repeatedly laid before us their complaint concerning the controversy long conducted between themselves and the canons of Blessed Stephen—namely, concerning the episcopal throne and the dignity of the mother church. Accordingly, we summoned both parties a second time to appear before us. But although the canons of Blessed John came to us according to our command, the canons of Blessed Stephen withdrew without offering any excuse [Col. 1298C]. At length, for the third time, we appointed a date for both parties on the feast of Blessed Luke. The aforesaid canons of Blessed John presented themselves before us, prepared to render and receive justice; but the canons of St. Stephen neither came to us nor advanced any excuse on their behalf.

Therefore, by the common counsel of our brethren, the bishops and abbots who were with us, we decree by apostolic authority that the aforesaid Church of Blessed John shall henceforth possess every dignity of the episcopal see and mother church which it is known to have possessed in ancient times. Consequently, by our letters we commanded the canons of Blessed Stephen to return to us that privilege of maternity which they had obtained from our lord predecessor Pope Paschal of holy memory through lies and deceitful craftiness. We therefore ask, exhort, and command your belovedness to recognize in every respect the aforesaid Church of Blessed John as your mother [Col. 1298D], and to render it obedience and reverence with due humility. For we did this because we knew more fully, having seen with our own eyes, the truth of the entire matter; because reason demanded it; and because the canons of Blessed Stephen, summoned three times, scorned to come to judgment.

Given at Taranto, on the fourth Ides of November.

## CCXXXVIII. To the Spanish bishops, abbots, and provosts established throughout the provinces of Mérida and Braga.—That they obey Diego, archbishop of Compostela, his vicar.  
*(A.D. 1123, November 29.)*

*[Flórez, Sacred Spain, XX, 394.]*

[Col. 1299A]

Calixtus, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the venerable brothers and fellow bishops: the archbishop of Braga; the bishops of Coimbra, Porto, Tui, Ourense, Valibre, Lugo, Astorga, Ávila, Salamanca; and to abbots and provosts established throughout the provinces of Mérida and Braga: greeting and apostolic blessing.

The ancient institution of the apostolic see requires, etc., as above in letter 80.

[Col. 1299B] Given in the borough of St. Fabian, on the third day before the Kalends of December.

## CCXXXIX. To all bishops, etc., dispersed throughout Europe.  
*(Between 1119 and 1124.)*

*[Eccard, Corpus of Medieval History, p. 363.]*

Lord Pope Calixtus, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved brothers—the bishops, abbots, parish priests, canons, chaplains, and other faithful throughout Europe—greeting and apostolic blessing.

The principle of justice and the order of reason require that we preserve, by the Lord’s authority, what our predecessor Pope Paschal of holy memory established out of charity. We earnestly commend to your charity the bearer of these letters, sent to you by Raymond, provost of the hospice of Jerusalem [Col. 1299C]. For Raymond is commended by the testimony of all returning from Jerusalem, because he sincerely, devoutly, and continually cares for pilgrims and the poor. He now implores the assistance of your charity for the relief of their needs.

Therefore do not forget beneficence and sharing, for God is won by such sacrifices. Take care, then, to relieve poor Christ in his poor, so that he too may make you sharers in his riches. For he is not without the reward of the pilgrimage to Jerusalem who supplies assistance from his goods to pilgrims of Jerusalem. Whoever gives to the poor lends to the Lord. May the Lord himself both accomplish in you what he promises and make every grace abound in you [Col. 1299D], so that, by refreshing him in his least ones, you may deserve to receive in the joys of the eternal Jerusalem the reward of eternal refreshment.

## CCXL. To Pelagius, bishop of Braga.—Concerning the privileges of that Church.  
*(Between 1119 and 1124.)*

*[Mansi, Councils, XXI, 193.]*

That the metropolitan see of Braga was once illustrious and shone among the kingdoms of Spain with many titles of dignity and glory is shown both by the evidences of its ancient nobility and by the testimonies of old writings. But because it pleased the divine ordering to correct the sins of the people dwelling in it, when the Moors or Moabites invaded [Col. 1300A], both the dignity of the metropolitan see was diminished and the boundaries of its parishes were thrown into confusion. Yet, after long intervals of time, divine mercy again deigned to restore the metropolitan see and to free its parishes in great part from the tyranny of unbelievers. Hence our lord predecessor Pope Paschal of holy memory, restoring its former dignity, united to it its several members by a privilege of the apostolic see.

Following in his footsteps, therefore, dearest brother and fellow bishop Pelagius, we confirm by the page of this present privilege to the Church of Braga, over which, by God’s authority, you preside, the entire city of Braga, together with that whole *cauto* [probably a territorial unit] which Count Henry and his wife Teresa granted to that Church, and with the boundaries of the bishopric of Braga as contained in the description of the aforesaid lord. We also restore to the metropolitan see of Braga the province of Galicia and, within it, the cities of episcopal sees; likewise Astorga, Lugo, Tui, Mondoñedo, Ourense, Porto, Coimbra, and the towns now bearing episcopal rank—Viseu, Lamego, Idanha, and Britonia—with their parishes [Col. 1300B].

## CCXLI. Bull for the Church of Barbastro.  
*(Between 1119 and 1124.)*

*[Aynsa, Foundation of Huesca, p. 318.]*

Calixtus, bishop, servant of the servants of God, etc., to the venerable brother, greeting and apostolic blessing.

[Col. 1300C] You yourself, brother, know that we have loved you for a long time and wish to continue loving you. But that report greatly disturbs your brethren: that you have horribly expelled the bishop of Barbastro from his see without judgment or reason; and, although requested and even placed under interdict by our predecessor Pope of good memory, you do not desist from that same violence. We therefore ask and command your brotherhood fully to restore that brother to the episcopal throne of his see, etc.

## CCXLII. To the bishop of Pamplona.  
*(Between 1119 and 1124.)*

*[Aynsa, Foundation, Excellences, Grandeurs, and Memorable Things of Huesca. Huesca, 1619, folio, p. 318.]*

Calixtus, bishop, servant of the servants of God, etc.

[Col. 1300D] We had pronounced a sentence of excommunication against the bishop of Huesca because he expelled our venerable brother Raymond, bishop of Barbastro, from his own see without hearing or judgment and, having been warned to come to us, treated the summons with contempt. But afterward, moved by the prayers of the king of Aragon, when we absolved him, etc.

## CCXLIII. To Benedict, bishop of Lucca, he grants the use of the pallium.  
*(Between 1119 and 1124.)*

*[Ughelli, Sacred Italy, I, 819.]*

Calixtus, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the venerable brother Benedict, bishop of Lucca, greeting and apostolic blessing.

[Col. 1301A] We are prompted both by the obligation of charity and by the benevolence of the apostolic see to confer honor upon our brethren and to impart the dignity of the holy Roman Church also to other churches, especially those which persevere more closely and devoutly in obedience and service to Blessed Peter. Therefore, dearest brother and fellow bishop in Christ, Benedict, we have thought fit to grant the petitions of your brethren and the nobles of the city, in order that we may honor more particularly, from the generosity of the apostolic see, the Church of Lucca, over which, by God’s authority, you preside. For, together with its clergy and people, it has in our days so devoted itself to the Roman Church and subjected itself to the obedience and service of Blessed Peter that, by the customary generosity of the apostolic see, it rightly ought both to be honored and to rejoice.

Remembering, then, what has passed and trusting for the future in the constancy of our mutual love and service, we grant from the kindness of the Roman Church to you and your successors the use of the pallium within the church only, at the solemnities of Mass, on the following specified days: namely, on the Nativity of the Lord; the feast of Blessed John the Evangelist; Epiphany; the Lord’s Supper, within the city and outside it if a graver reason intervenes; the Resurrection; the following Monday; Ascension; Pentecost; the Nativity of St. John the Baptist; the feast of the apostles Peter and Paul; the Assumption of Blessed Mary; the commemoration of St. Michael; the feasts of St. Martin and St. Frigidian; the dedication of the major church; the ordinations of priests and deacons; and the dedications of churches in the city of Lucca [Col. 1301B].

We wish you to uphold in every respect the character of this pallium; for the honor of this garment is humility and justice. Let your brotherhood, therefore, hasten to show itself with all its heart humble in prosperity, and, in adversity—if any comes—erect in justice; a friend to the good and opposed to the perverse. Accepting no person’s face against truth; compassionate toward the weak; rejoicing with those of goodwill; reckoning others’ losses as its own; exulting in others’ joys as in its own; mercifully severe in correcting vices; soothing the souls of hearers in fostering virtues; retaining judgment without anger in anger; and, in tranquility, not abandoning the censure of just severity. This, dearest brother, is the dignity of the pallium you have received. If you guard it diligently, you will possess inwardly what you show yourself to have received outwardly [Col. 1301D]. May the Holy Trinity preserve your brotherhood unharmed through long ages. Amen.

Given, etc.

## CCXLIV. Privilege for the monastery of Andres.  
*(Between 1119 and 1124.)*

*[D’Achery, Spicilegium, II, 797.]*

Calixtus, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son Rainald, abbot of Andres, and to his successors regularly appointed in perpetuity.

It is fitting that we should give assent to just requests and lend an ear to rightful petitions, we who, although unworthy, are seen—by the Lord’s ordering—to be set as guardians and heralds of justice in the Church of the chief apostles Peter and Paul. [Col. 1302A] Therefore, beloved son in Christ, Abbot Rainald, we graciously grant your petition and take under the protection of the Apostolic See the monastery of Saint Saviour and Blessed Rotrude at Andres, over which, by God’s authority, you preside. By this present decree we confirm its appurtenant possessions, whether granted by pontiffs, bestowed by counts and barons, offered by other faithful persons, acquired by other lawful means, or to be acquired in future times:

Namely, all pasture around the church of Andres; the fertility of the turf, marsh, and water; the chapel of St Mary of the castle of Guînes; the altar revenues of Bredenarde, Andres, Lullinghem, Ferques, and Eilinghem; and one third of the altar revenues [Col. 1302B] of Terdeghem, with their tithes; two parts of the tithe of Spetleca; the land at Antingehem, with its tenants, jurisdiction, and woodland; the mill in the village of Odingehem; land with tenants in the village of Terdeghem; land with tenants in the village of Ravantum and Elbedingehem; land in the village of Buxin; land with tenants in the village of Wadingatun, and at Seiles, Bessingahem, and Hetberga; the tithe of Destrones; land with three tenants and vavassors in the village of Fraitun; land with tenants near Nieles; land with tenants in the village of Marcknes; Hammes and Curtalo; land at Elingatun; land of two ploughlands in the village of Bochardes, with tenants and tithe; lands and tenants in the village of Guînes, and a fishpond and mill-site; land of two tenants beside the abbey; [Col. 1302C] Odin’s land, with tenants, tithe, woodland, and jurisdiction in the village of Campagne, together with the tithe of Adunard’s land; Roger’s land, with tenants and tithe at Borcharcbuse; Hermar’s land, with tenants and tithe; the land of Baldwin Portevin, with a tenant and tithe; all the land of Stephen and of his daughters Adelaide and Hermingard; the land of Gautho Hugh; all the land of Eustace and his sister Adele; that of Ralph Penard, with tenants, woodland, and tithe; the lands of Guinemar Crassa Vacca, Guisfrid, Galant, and Heremar Buce, with tenants, woodland, and tithe; the entire tithe of the land of Baldwin Botzard and of his sister Domelina, of old Heremar, of Hugh, and of Baldwin Dedisacra; the land of Mascelina, with a tenant, woodland, and tithe; the land of Hadwida of Pernes; [Col. 1302D] land and tenants in the village of Bucolt; the land of Eustace and a share of his mill, with tenants, waters, and woodland in the village of Baveiingahem, and a tenant in the village of Ruham; the land of Suanaildis in the village of Herchem; the land of Dunrupit; the land of Ermingard, with tenants in the village of Calvastert; Walter’s land, with tenants in the village of Oya; land and two tenants in the village of Morlingehem; in the village of Landringatun, a ploughland and the land of Alulf and Reiner; land in the village of Altinges; land of one ploughland near Wesvich; one third of a mill, and land, meadow, and woodland in the village of Cossebronne; land in the parish of Haldinehem and of Boninges; land of three ploughlands in the village of Suanacas, with villagers and jurisdiction; [Col. 1303A] other lands in the parish of St Martin; the land of Guisfrid of Bredenarde, with court, house, tenants, and jurisdiction, given by Count Manasses, his vavassor Manasses, and the latter’s son Florentius; lands, tenants, and jurisdictions in the parish of St Martin of Northguerca, Suthguerca, Adroic, and Polingona; land of one hundred and fifty measures in the wilderness near Pitheem, with jurisdiction; the land of Orbert of Fornes and of his brother Lambert at Suanacas, with jurisdiction; the meadow of Stochbrigga; the entire freehold of Adelaide of Fielnes and her son Guarin, and everything which they held in the jurisdiction of Guînes—lands, woods, vavassors, male and female serfs, tenants, water, and one mill; in the village of Bocardes, the lands of Jorni with tenants; the land of Surches, with jurisdiction; [Col. 1303B] the exchange of lands which Gilbert, abbot of your monastery, concluded with his neighbour Hugh Malo; and all other things known to belong by right to the monastery.

We therefore decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb that monastery, take away its possessions, retain things taken away, diminish them, or harass it with wanton vexations. Rather, let all be preserved entire and serve in every way the uses for whose support and governance they were granted, saving in all things the canonical reverence due to the bishop of Thérouanne. We further decree that burial in that place shall be free, so that no one may hinder the devotion and final wishes of those who have resolved to be buried there, unless they are excommunicated. [Col. 1303C] Therefore, if in future any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowing this decree of our constitution, rashly attempts to contravene it, and—after a second or third warning—does not make fitting amends, let that person be deprived of the dignity of office and honour; let him know that he stands guilty before divine judgment of the iniquity perpetrated; let him be cut off from the most sacred Body and Blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Redeemer; and let him be subject to strict vengeance at the final judgment. But upon all who preserve the rights of that place may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that they may receive here the fruit of good action and find, before the strict Judge, the rewards of eternal peace. Amen.

## CCXLV. To A., prior, and the brethren of St Frigdianus of Lucca. (Between 1120 and 1124, 6 July.)

[Baluze, *Miscellanea*, Lucca edition, IV, 587.]

[Col. 1303D]

CALIXTUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons A., prior of St Frigdianus, and his brethren: greeting and apostolic blessing.

We have sent back to you your brother Blasius, who desired to live in the Lateran church according to your rule, because this was by no means possible at present, owing to the exigencies of the time. We therefore command your beloved community to receive him with affection and love as your brother, and to retain him among you.

Given at Rome, 2 July.

## CCXLVI. He forbids B[erard], bishop of Mâcon, to exercise episcopal office until he ceases his injuries against the monastery of Cluny. (Between 1121 and 1124, 9 January.)

[Mabillon, *Annales Benedictini*, VI, 38.]

[Col. 1304A]

The things which you have inflicted upon the monastery of Blessed Peter at Cluny grievously trouble both us and our brethren. After our warnings, after letters repeatedly sent, you have extended your hand over that parish—something hitherto unheard of—you have excommunicated clergy and laity, and in the church of Blessed Odo have entirely forbidden the celebration of the divine offices. You have also, as they affirm, inflicted grave injuries on the monks and taken away certain things belonging to them. Yet in all these matters [Col. 1304B] we spared you in paternal kindness, awaiting your correction, as our venerable brother Hugh, archbishop of Lyons, when he came to us, had promised. But you persisted obstinately, both before and afterwards. Therefore, no longer able to endure this presumption and so great a contempt for the Apostolic See, though unwillingly, out of regard for former affection and friendship, we forbid you, by the authority of the Apostolic See and on the reasoned judgment of our brethren, to exercise episcopal office until you desist from harassing the monastery of Cluny, its clergy and laity, and its chapel, and make satisfaction to us for your contempt.

Given at the Lateran, 9 January.

## CCXLVII. To E. [read C., that is, Conrad], archbishop of Salzburg: he commends A., a priest ordained by the bishop of Augsburg. (Between 1121 and 1124, 25 January.)

[Mansi, *Concilia*, XX, 1228.]

[Col. 1304C]

CALIXTUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother E., archbishop of Salzburg: greeting and apostolic blessing.

This brother, A., a priest and bearer of the present letter, having approached the clemency of the Apostolic See, stated that he was ordained by the bishop of Augsburg, at the time when that bishop had obtained the favour of the Roman Church from our predecessor of holy memory, Pope Paschal, at the council held at Piacenza. Since it is not fitting to deny mercy and indulgence [Col. 1304D] to those who rightfully ask for them, if his petition rests upon grounds of truth, receive him in his order and permit him to exercise the ministry of priestly office without disturbance.

Given at the Lateran, 25 January.

## CCXLVIII. He grants remission of sins to all who are to be buried in the church of Conza. (Between 1119 and 1124, 30 March.)

[Ughelli, *Italia sacra*, VI, 810.]

CALIXTUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to all the faithful of the Church: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Since we have heard of, and in part know, the desolation inflicted upon the church of Conza in former times, [Col. 1305A] and since we have been asked to consecrate it by our beloved son H., the venerable archbishop of that church, and also by . . . . Countess B., lady of that land, and . . . . . . have been unable to be [there]: therefore, for the dignity of that church, by the authority of the apostles Peter and Paul and by our own authority, we decree remission of all sins for all Christians who have confessed and have caused themselves to be buried there.

Given at the Lateran, 30 March.

## CCXLIX. To all kings, counts, and princes.—He urges them to aid the afflicted Church in Spain, granting indulgences to those who assist, and commends to them Olegarius, archbishop of Tarragona. (Between 1121 and 1124, 2 April.)

[Mansi, *Concilia*, XXI, 217.]

CALIXTUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to all bishops, kings, counts, princes, and the other faithful of God: greeting and apostolic blessing.

The concern of the pastoral office entrusted to us by God requires that with every vigilance and circumspection we both guard and feed the Lord’s flock. We believe that none of you can be unaware by how many calamities, by how many deaths of God’s children, the Church in Spain is continually crushed through pagan oppression. Therefore, we admonish your love as though God—whose embassy we perform—were exhorting you through us, and we urge you, as dearest sons, with such prayers as [Col. 1305C] we can, never to cease labouring for the defence of your brethren and the liberation of the churches. To all who steadfastly serve in this expedition, we graciously grant, by apostolic authority and by the power divinely granted to us, the same remission of sins which we have granted to the defenders of the Eastern Church. But those who have placed the sign of the cross upon their garments for this cause, if from this Easter until the next they do not strive to fulfil their vow, we exclude from the bosom of Holy Church until they make satisfaction. Since we cannot, as we should wish, visit your army in person, we have taken care to appoint our dearest brother Olegarius, archbishop of Tarragona, as our legate among you, [Col. 1305D] specially entrusting to him our office in this matter: that, by his counsel and direction, what needs correction may be corrected, and what needs confirmation may, with the Lord’s assistance, be confirmed. Should any doubts arise in that army, let them be resolved by his experience. We therefore earnestly commend him to your love, asking that he may find in you that charity which compels us to commend him to you. May almighty God, through the merits of his blessed apostles Peter and Paul, preserve us in his mercy and grant that we may attain a glorious victory over the enemies of Christians and a happy consummation.

Given at the Lateran, 2 April.

## CCL. To Geoffrey, abbot of Vendôme.—He confirms as valid all privileges of the monks of Vendôme. (Between 1121 and 1124, 6 April.)

[Mansi, *Concilia*, XXI, 195.]

[Col. 1306A]

CALIXTUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his most beloved son in Christ, GEOFFREY, abbot of Vendôme: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Both the sincerity of your devotion toward the Roman Church and our continual mutual friendship urge us to visit you more frequently with letters of apostolic blessing. We therefore visit you, embrace you as a dearest brother in Christ in the arms of a fuller love, and desire henceforth to hold you as more intimate than an intimate friend and dearer than dear. We desire to honour your person and assist and support your Church. We greet your brethren in the Lord through you and bestow upon them the blessing of almighty God and of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul. Whatever dignity or immunity has been granted by the Apostolic See to you and your monastery, we likewise decree shall remain valid and entire for ever.

Given at Rome, 6 April.

## CCLI. To Atto, archbishop of Arles, Raymond, count of Barcelona, and Gaufred Porcelet.—That they should assist the monks of St Giles against Count Ildefonsus of Toulouse and his supporters, whom he declares excommunicated. (Between 1122 and 1124, 22 April.)

[Vaissette, *Histoire de Languedoc*, vol. II, documentary proofs, col. 421.]

[Col. 1306C]

CALIXTUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother ATTO, archbishop of Arles, and his dearest son RAYMOND, count of the Barcelonans, and to GAUFRED PORCELET: greeting and apostolic blessing.

The monastery of Blessed Giles, with all its possessions, belongs by right to the Roman Church and pertains to the Apostolic See. Thus whoever wrongs that place and the brethren serving the Lord in it undoubtedly wrongs us. Since Count Ildefonsus has expelled our son Abbot Hugh and his brethren from that monastery and, by secular force, occupied the monastery together with its town and other appurtenances, [Col. 1306D] we have pronounced a sentence of excommunication against him, Raymond of Baux, William of Sabran, Elzéar of Castries, William Rainald of Médenas, the viscounts of Mesoaga, and Rainon of Castlar, as well as their supporters and helpers in this wickedness; and a sentence of interdict upon their lands. Moreover, by letters sent from us, we have released the count’s men from his homage and fealty until the count restores the monastery of Blessed Giles, with its town and appurtenances, to the aforesaid abbot and his brethren, leaves it free and wholly undisturbed, destroys the castle newly built against it, and makes satisfaction to us for the injuries inflicted. We therefore ask and admonish your love that, for the love of God and the reverence of the Roman [Col. 1307A] Church, you take care to aid, uphold, and support that abbot and his brethren in such a manner that you may receive recompense from God, Blessed Peter, and St Giles, and full favour from us.

Given at the Lateran, 22 April.

## CCLII. To Walter, bishop of Maguelone, and others.—That they should assist the monks of St Giles against Count Ildefonsus of Toulouse and his supporters, whom he declares excommunicated. (Year 1122, 22 April.)

[D. Bouquet, vol. XV, p. 244.]

CALIXTUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother WALTER, [Note: [Col. 1307D] It was chiefly through Walter’s efforts, as he exercised apostolic authority in this region, that peace was established in 1125 among the contending princes of Occitania, as he himself testifies in a letter to Robert, provost of Lille, among Mabillon’s *Analecta*, p. 461, adding the following words at its close: “By God’s grace going before us, through our unremitting labour and insistence, peace has been restored among our princes; hence our whole country rejoices.” For the terms of the peace, see [Col. 1308D] the instrument published by Catel, *On the Counts of Toulouse*, p. 188, and Bouche, vol. II of *History of Provence*, p. 105.] bishop of Maguelone, and to his beloved sons BERNARD, viscount of Béziers, BERNARD of Anduze, and RAYMOND, dean of Posquières: greeting and apostolic blessing.

The monastery of Blessed Giles, with all its possessions, belongs by right to the Roman Church and pertains to the Apostolic See. Thus whoever wrongs that place and the brethren serving the Lord in it undoubtedly wrongs us. Since Count Ildefonsus has expelled our son Abbot Hugh and his brethren from that monastery and, by secular force, occupied the monastery together with its town and other appurtenances, we have pronounced a sentence of excommunication against him, Raymond of Baux, William of Sabran, Elzéar of Castries, William Rainoard of Médenas, the viscounts of Meesoaga, and Rainon of Castlar, and against their supporters and helpers in this wickedness; [Col. 1307C] and a sentence of interdict upon their lands. Moreover, by letters sent from us, we have released the count’s men from his homage and fealty until the count restores the monastery of Blessed Giles, with its town and appurtenances, to the aforesaid abbot and his brethren, leaves it restored, free, and wholly undisturbed, destroys the castle newly built against it, and makes satisfaction to us for the injuries inflicted. We therefore ask and admonish your love that, for the love of God and the reverence of the Roman Church, you take care to aid, uphold, and support that abbot and his brethren in such a manner that you may receive recompense from God, Blessed Peter, and St Giles, and full favour from us.

Given at the Lateran, 22 April.

## CCLIII. He commands the bishop of Roussillon to cease harassing the monastery of Albare. (Between 1122 and 1124, 22 April.)

[Ughelli, *Italia sacra*, III, 663.]

[Col. 1307D]

CALIXTUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the venerable bishop of ROUSSILLON: greeting and apostolic blessing.

In our presence you promised us that you would lay aside all hostility toward our son, the abbot of Albare, and would restore peace and good will to him. Yet after you departed from us and returned home, you inflicted injury upon him and his monastery, with insults also [probably: many insults]. You should therefore take care lest that proverb commonly spoken of poor wine come upon you: “Before it enters the vessel, it turns sour.” We admonish your brotherhood altogether to desist from harassing the aforesaid abbot and his brethren, and wholly to absolve from the interdict which you pronounced against them the clergy of the Church of Monte Calvo belonging to the monastery of Albare. [Col. 1308B] If, moreover, you have any case against the abbot or the monastery, we, to whom the ownership of that place belongs, shall render due justice in the matter at a suitable time. But if you scorn to heed us, you should fear lest, while you unjustly persecute God’s servants, you experience the righteous displeasure of the Apostolic See in such a manner that others, warned by your example, may not thereafter presume to do such things.

Given at the Lateran, 22 April.

## CCLIV. He confirms the goods, rights, and privileges of the monastery of Hugeshoven, founded by Count Wernher of Ortenberg. (Between 1122 and 1124, 14 May.)

[Würdtwein, *Nova Subsidia diplomatica*, vol. VII, p. 36. From the parchment Salic book of Andlau Abbey, fol. 13.]

[Col. 1308C]

CALIXTUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons, the brethren of the monastery of St Michael the Archangel, called Hugh’s Court, both present and future, for ever.

To apply the counsel and assistance of pastoral vigilance to the strengthening and protection of God’s holy Church is required by the office of stewardship entrusted to us and by the hoped-for reward from God, the happier reward of eternity: so that ecclesiastical benefit, receiving strength through the favour of the Apostolic See, may increase, and sincerity of devotion may shine forth. Count Wernher, a most devoted son of the Apostolic See, [Note: [Col. 1308D] Wernher, who in a diploma of Emperor Frederick of 1162 is called count of Ortenberg, is said to have founded Hugeshoven Abbey in the year 1000.] by God’s inspiration built, from his own resources, the monastery called [Col. 1308D] Hugeshoven. Consecrated in honour and in the name of the most blessed Archangel Michael, he offered it to Blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, and subjected it to the holy Roman and Apostolic Church itself, for the sake of protection and in a spirit of piety.

We therefore, at the pious request of the beloved Countess Adelaide, [Note: [Col. 1308D] Countess Adelaide was the granddaughter (*petite-fille*) of Count Wernher of Ortenberg, and thus the daughter of Volmar and Heilicha, who in 1061 transferred Hegshoven Abbey to the Church of Strasbourg. Adelaide married Count Ludolf, who had already died before 1120.] niece of the same count, and granting the assent of paternal kindness to your religious desires, most beloved sons in the Lord, receive, in the place of Blessed Peter, under the special fostering protection of the Apostolic See, the aforesaid monastery in which you are devoted to divine service, with all things now bestowed there or to be bestowed in future. We establish for it by apostolic authority perpetual liberty and fortify it against the assaults of all wicked persons by the decree of this privilege. We decree that all things which appear lawfully to belong to that place—whether bestowed upon that monastery by the said Count Wernher, his heirs and successors, at the prompting of divine inspiration, or otherwise hitherto granted through the devotion of other faithful persons, [Col. 1309B] or hereafter granted with God’s assent—shall be preserved inviolate for you and, through you, for that Church. Among them, the following have seemed proper to be expressly named: the monastery itself, with male and female dependants and its other appurtenances; [Note: [Col. 1309D] Hugh’s Court Abbey now lies in ruins; only certain traces of the buildings and the church of St Michael remain. Its revenues have belonged to Andlau Abbey since 1616.] the parish church situated there, together with the chapel of Rognesbach; [Note: [Col. 1309D] Today Roschbach, or Renrupt, belonging to the Duke of Choiseul-Meuse. Andlau Abbey holds one half of the tithes there; the other half belongs to the parish priest at Colroy, the patronage of whose parish also belongs to that abbey.] the freehold at Scherwilre; [Note: [Col. 1309D] Scherweiler belongs to the Lord of Choiseul-Meuse. The tithes and the right of patronage are divided between the greater chapter of Strasbourg and Andlau Abbey.] the estate near Mackenheim; [Note: [Col. 1309D] Mackenheim belongs to the Lord of Flachslanden.] the estate near Fruolsheim; [Note: [Col. 1309D] Fridolsheim belongs to the bishop and city of Strasbourg.] another at Egenesheim; [Note: [Col. 1309D] Today Egisheim in Upper Mundat.] and another at Reinenkeim. [Note: [Col. 1310D] Reningen, a village situated in the lordship of Thann.]

Possessions at Marcolvisheim, [Note: [Col. 1310D] Marckolsheim belongs to the bishop of Strasbourg.] at Breitenheim, [Note: [Col. 1310D] A village formerly called Brestenheim, a quarter of a league from the village called Musig; the chapel and the name of the district of St Michael remain, and the district belongs to the Duke of Zweibrücken.] at Heiolvesheim, [Note: [Col. 1310D] Today Heidelsheim, belonging to the same Duke of Zweibrücken.] and at Northus. [Note: [Col. 1310D] Northausen or Nartz, a village belonging to the bishop of Strasbourg.] Also, the estate in Lorraine, given to the aforesaid monastery of St Michael the Archangel by Count Ludolf of blessed memory and his wife Countess Adelaide, situated namely at Geberesdhorf, [Col. 1309C] [Note: [Col. 1310D] Geberesdhorff, so called also in the bull of Innocent II of 1135 and in a charter of 1144, is the present Lorraine village of Glonville on the Meurthe, in the bailiwick of Lunéville, four leagues from Lunéville.] with everything lawfully appurtenant to it; and the church at Wibre, [Note: [Col. 1310D] Weiler or Viler belongs to the Lords of Choiseul-Meuse; Andlau Abbey enjoys there the tithes and right of patronage.] with its appurtenances, given to you by the same countess: these we confirm for you to hold and possess.

We establish for you the fishing in that valley [Note: [Col. 1310D] The Valley of Valerian, now called the Val de Viler.] as far as Lutenbach; timber from the demesne forest necessary for every use; one half of the forest fruits; and swarms of bees found in that forest. We also decree as firm and ratified by apostolic authority what the aforementioned Count Wernher, in the generosity of his pious devotion, granted for the benefit of that place: that it be lawful for any of his ministerials or members of his household, whether he be present or absent, to give his own property to that place. [Col. 1310A] Yet because it is said to be customary in the province of Alsace that no member of the household of the Church of Strasbourg may grant any of his own estates to another church not under its jurisdiction, we will that the aforesaid monastery of St Michael the Archangel, situated in that district, shall always enjoy this special privilege granted by the favour of the Roman and Apostolic See: namely, that anyone belonging to the household either of the Church of Strasbourg or of any other church anywhere in the world may, without obstruction from anyone’s opposition, sell, lend, or freely give estates or other property of his own to that monastery, strengthened by apostolic authority.

Let the community of the monastery have free authority, without any opposition, to appoint an abbot by election in accordance with the decree of St Benedict: that it may rest in the brethren’s judgment whom they wish to elect from among themselves and set over themselves according to God, if a suitable person can be found among them; otherwise, let them seek from another regular monastery whomsoever they can find better, and, supported by authority, obtain him after election. [Col. 1310B] The aforesaid brethren shall also receive freely from the bishop in whose diocese they are located chrism, holy oil, consecrations of altars and churches, and the ordination of brethren to be promoted, unless he is shown to be simoniacal or not in communion with the Apostolic See. If that is shown, they may request and receive the ordination of an abbot and monks and the other sacraments from whatever Catholic bishop they choose.

We grant no authority to the bishop of Strasbourg in that place to transact or order even the smallest matter except in accordance with the common will of the brethren and abbot. Nor do we permit a sentence of excommunication, for any cause, to be pronounced against the abbot himself or his monastery by any bishop or archbishop other than the pontiff of the Apostolic See alone. We further specifically ordain that the same monastery, with its precinct and all its appurtenances, shall be free from every incursion by any persons; and that it shall be exempt in every respect from all services and burdens imposed by the bishop of Strasbourg or any bishops, [Col. 1311A] episcopal officials, kings, emperors, dukes, counts, and all persons whatsoever.

If any layperson desires to prepare burial for himself there, it shall be lawful for the monks living there to grant the piously desired permission, nor may any priest forbid it. Concerning the appointment of an advocate, we decree that no one shall obtain this office as though it were due to him by hereditary right, unless he is appointed by the common or sounder election of the brethren. Such an advocate, however, shall never unjustly or violently lay hands upon that place or the possessions of those serving God there. Without the abbot’s consent, he may not burden the monastery itself, the peasants of the monastery, or its household with frequent hospitality, nor extort any exactions from them. Nor may he exercise any judicial pleas unless invited by the abbot; and from the many judicial pleas which they call *justitiae*, he may not take more than the third part customarily due to him—and that only from those pleas to which he has been invited by the abbot. [Col. 1311B] If he is found to be a transgressor of this at the monastery and, after a second or third warning, does not correct his fault, he shall be removed; another whom they approve—or none, if they approve none—shall be substituted.

We also add, or determine on the authority of the blessed Pope Gregory, that the brethren of that place shall never be required to pay tithes or first fruits to the parish church in the monastery’s valley from their ploughlands, labours of any kind, or their own produce. We decree, therefore, that that place, endowed with complete liberty, shall for ever be safe and free, both from every right claimed by mortals and from every wanton disturbance of troubles; that an abbey shall perpetually be maintained there and specially protected under the guardianship of the Apostolic See; and that one gold bezant shall be paid annually to the Apostolic Palace, and, beyond the obligation of that payment, that no further service to the Roman Church may in any manner be demanded from it. [Col. 1311C] Let this be a memorial at Rome concerning the liberty of this monastery of the Blessed Archangel Michael, so that it may not be forgotten there, where all religious life claims its head. If the payment should perhaps sometimes be omitted, nothing shall ever be exacted as satisfaction except that the same tribute be restored in full.

But if in future any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowing this decree of our constitution, rashly attempts to contravene it, and—after a second or third warning—does not make fitting amends, let that person be deprived of the dignity of office and honour; let him know that he stands guilty before divine judgment of the iniquity perpetrated; let him be cut off from the most sacred Body and Blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Redeemer; and let him be subject to strict vengeance at the final judgment. But upon all who preserve the rights of that place may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that they may receive here the fruit of good action and find, before the strict Judge, the rewards of eternal peace. Amen.

[Col. 1312A] Given at the Lateran, 14 May, in the year 1120 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the second year of Lord Pope Calixtus. [Note: [Col. 1311D] The chronological indicators are corrupt.]

## CC LV. To John, bishop of Glasgow. (Between 1122 and 1124, 26 August.)

[*Monasticon Anglicanum*, III, 145.]

CALIXTUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to JOHN, bishop of Glasgow: greeting and apostolic blessing.
