Moved by the many entreaties of our beloved son Alexander, king of the Scots, we granted you a respite for some time, so that within the period fixed you might return with due humility to obedience to our venerable brother Thomas, archbishop of York. Yet, as we learn from the tenor of his letter, [Col. 1312B] you have presumed to withdraw yourself from his obedience and subjection. We therefore command you to return, within thirty days after receiving this letter, to the subjection and obedience of the aforesaid archbishop; otherwise, we confirm the sentence which he has pronounced against you.

Given at the Lateran, 26 August.

## CCLVI. To A., prior of St Frigdianus, and his brethren. (Between 1122 and 1124, 11 October.)

[Baluze, *Miscellanea*, Lucca edition, IV, 588.]

CALIXTUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons A., prior of St Frigdianus, and his brethren: greeting and apostolic blessing.

[Col. 1312C] Brother Ursus, formerly prior of the Lateran Church, burdened by illness and wearied by the government of the brethren, and henceforth wishing to devote himself solely to prayer, returns to your church with our favour and permission. Receive him honourably for our sake and treat him with honour. Moreover, we command the prudent humility of your brotherhood diligently to provide for the Lateran Church, as we hope well of you in the Lord, and to hasten to send to us at least four of your prudent and religious brethren. One of them, with the Holy Spirit’s assistance, should learn to preside over the others; while the others should strive to form the remaining brethren through gracious discipline and religious life.

Given at the Lateran, 11 October.

## CCLVII. He informs Louis, king of the Franks, that Bishop Robert of Arras, summoned to court by Burchard, bishop of Cambrai, in a general council, has come to him with his letter. (Year 1123–1124, 19 February.)

[Mansi, *Concilia*, XXI, 217.]

[Col. 1312D]

CALIXTUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his dearest son in Christ, LOUIS, illustrious and glorious king of the Franks: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Coming to us with your letters, we received our venerable brother Robert, bishop of Arras, with the affection of paternal charity, out of regard for your love and for reverence toward his rank. We had summoned him to our presence on an appointed day, to answer concerning the right of the diocese of Arras to our fellow-brother Burchard, bishop of Cambrai, who had lodged a complaint against him in the general council. But, before the fixed date on which he was to appear before us, we were informed by certain letters that the bishop of Cambrai, coming to us to pursue his case, had been detained by the emperor until the conference which we are to hold with him. Therefore, owing to the absence of one party, we could not for sound reasons examine the same case. Accordingly, we sent him back to his church with our favor. At that conference, moreover, we shall take care to inform you, as our most beloved son and a son of the Church, of whatever good, the Lord working through us, we shall have accomplished.

[Col. 1313B] Through you we greet your wife Adelaide, our beloved niece and queen, and your most dear sons, our nephews Philip, Louis, and Henry; and we desire that they may share in the blessing of blessed Peter and in ours.

Given at the Lateran, 19 February.

CCLVIII. He reproves the bishop of Rosselló because, contrary to his command, he persists in inflicting injuries upon the monastery of Albore. (Year 1123–1124, 25 February.)

[UGHELLI, *Italia sacra*, III, 662.]

CALIXTUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his brother the bishop of ROSSELLÓ, greeting and apostolic blessing.

[Col. 1313C] We are greatly astonished at you, because, although you are still new in episcopal administration, you have so quickly presumed to do anything contrary to our command. For we commanded you to make peace and concord with our son, the lord abbot of Albore, and not to molest either him or the monastery of Albore, which belongs by right to blessed Peter. You indeed made peace and concord with him; but not long afterward, as has been reported to us, you prohibited that monastery from receiving the burials, offerings, and other things of your parishioners which it had hitherto possessed in peace. Such conduct is certainly altogether inconsistent with episcopal dignity.

We therefore command and enjoin your brotherhood publicly to restore to the aforesaid monastery what you have prohibited it from having, [Col. 1313D] just as the prohibition was publicly imposed. Allow that place to remain quiet and free, together with all those things which it is known to have held peacefully in the time of its predecessors and yours. But if you believe that you have any just claim against the abbot or the monastery, come into our presence, and, concerning that place as concerning our own, we shall by God’s grace do you justice. If, however—God forbid!—you should scorn to obey our command, we shall, the Lord granting it, correct your rashness so that henceforth it will not seem easy to you to despise the commands of the Apostolic See.

Given at the Lateran, 25 February.

CCLIX. *He commands the monks of Cluny no longer to concern themselves with Pons.—He commands Pons not to harass the abbey of Cluny.* (Year 1123–1124.)

[See the bull of Honorius II addressed to Peter, abbot of Cluny, in volume CLXVI of the *Patrology*.]

[Col. 1314A]

CCLX. He forbids the customary dues remitted by Raynald, count of Burgundy, in the village of Tussiac—commonly called *marascalcia* and *canaria*—to be reimposed upon the church of St. John [at Besançon]. (Year 1124, 8 January.)

[D’ACHERY, *Spicilegium*, III, 479.]

CALIXTUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the beloved sons, the canons of the church of St. John the Evangelist, [Col. 1314B] greeting and apostolic blessing.

Placed by God’s providence in the governance of the Apostolic See, we have the duty of providing for churches and ecclesiastical interests. Thus Raynald, count of Burgundy, of illustrious and distinguished memory, had enjoyed, during the lifetime of his father William and during his own, a certain customary exaction in an estate belonging to your jurisdiction, called Cussiac: namely, one concerning his horses or his dogs, commonly called *marascalcia* [farriery or horse-service] and *canaria* [dog-service]. Considering this custom to be exceedingly harmful and injurious to your church, he renounced it forever for the remedy of his own soul and those of his parents and heirs. Moreover, he relinquished and abandoned all other exactions which his men had unjustly levied in that [Col. 1314C] estate and in the lands belonging to it.

This was done on the condition that their names should be written individually in the Canon, and that the psalm “Incline, O Lord” should be sung after the reading of the chapter on every day on which this may lawfully be done, for the salvation of their souls. We therefore confirm by the authority of this present writing the aforesaid renunciation and relinquishment, together with the arrangement established in consequence of it; and we decree that it shall be preserved unimpaired and inviolably for all future times.

Given at the Lateran, 3 January, in the second indiction.

CCLXI. Bull confirming the possessions belonging to the church of St. Mary. (Year 1124, 6 February.)

[DE LA CANAL, *España sagrada*, XLV, 300.]

[Col. 1314D]

CALIXTUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the beloved sons in Christ Gerald, prior, and the canons professing the regular life in the church of St. Mary of Leton, both present and future, forever.

Paternal charity and the kindness of the Apostolic See persuade us to grant the devout petitions of religious brethren. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously admit your requests and sustain with the support of the Apostolic See the church of Blessed Mary, in which you serve almighty God under the rule of the canonical order. We confirm by the text of this present decree that the order of canonical life which you have professed shall be observed there forever. We also confirm to you and to your successors who shall remain in the same religious profession the possession of all that you are seen lawfully to possess at present for the support of the common livelihood, and whatever you may hereafter acquire by lawful acquisition. Among these, we record by their proper names:

[Col. 1315A] The church of St. Felix with all its rights, and all the freehold estates which the aforesaid church of Blessed Mary appears to possess within the boundaries of the same parish; the estates which it possesses, or ought to possess, in the parish of St. Andrew of Borracian; likewise the churches of St. Mary of the Hermitages, with all the freehold estates which you possess there; also the cell of St. Thomas, situated in the diocese of Ausona, with all its appurtenances; the church of St. Mary of Villar Elenen, and St. Michael of Cold Spring, and St. Christopher of Stella; likewise the possessions which you hold in the parish of St. Peter of Navata, and all the estates which the lords of Navata bestowed upon the aforesaid church of Blessed Mary; also the mills which you possess in Fluviano; all the donations and relinquishments which the lords of Creissello made to the said church; and likewise the estates which belonged to Berengar William of Clusa, and to Peter Amblard and his heirs.

Upon the death of yourself, the prior of that place, or of any of your successors, no one shall be set over it through any contrivance of usurpation, except one whom the brethren by common consent, or the sounder part of the brethren’s counsel, shall duly provide to be elected, whether from their own community or, if necessary, from another. [Col. 1315C] We likewise decree that the burial-ground of that place shall be entirely free, so that no one may oppose the devotion and last will of those who resolve to be buried there, unless they are excommunicated.

Therefore no person whatsoever may rashly disturb that church, take away its possessions, retain what has been taken away, diminish them, or harass it with reckless vexations; rather, let all things be preserved whole for the use and benefit of the regular brethren and the poor. Moreover, we decree that the immunity established in that place by Berengar, bishop of Girona, of good memory, shall remain inviolate: namely, that within the circuit marked by crosses no one shall presume to seize, injure, or plunder anyone. If anyone, having learned the tenor of this our constitution and confirmation, should rashly attempt—God forbid!—to act against it, let him incur the loss of his rank and office, or be struck by the sword of excommunication, unless he correct his offense by worthy satisfaction. But may those who endeavor to assist that place and its brethren, and to honor them from their goods, obtain the grace of almighty God, remission of their sins, and indulgence.

It is formally authenticated by a rubric. Calixtus, Pope II.

I, Calixtus, bishop of the Catholic Church.

Given at the Lateran through the hand of Stimeric [Aimeric], deacon cardinal and chancellor of the Holy Roman Church, on 6 February, in the second indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation [Col. 1316A] 1123, and in the sixth year of the pontificate of Lord Calixtus II, pope.

CCLXII. He settles the dispute between Obert, bishop of Cremona, and his canons. (Year 1124, 22 March.)

[MURATORI, *Antiquities of Italy*, V, 225.]

CALIXTUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother Obert, bishop of Cremona, greeting and apostolic blessing.

It is not fitting for the head to be at variance with the members, nor for the members to dissent from submission and service to the head. For the structure of the human body cannot long remain sound if the head does not exercise harmonious and reasonable governance and the members do not perform their own duties. In like proportion, therefore, it is proper for a bishop to govern the clergy and people entrusted to him with the discernment of paternal charity, and for them, as to their own head, harmoniously to obey him with the humility of devotion. For no service can otherwise be rendered acceptably to God, the author and lover of peace, unless human minds are rooted in charity.

Accordingly, having heard that disagreement had arisen between you and the canons of the greater church of Cremona, and having taken counsel with our brother bishops and cardinals, we have established this concord between you: that no one shall be installed in the greater church without the assent and will of the bishop, who, as he is the head of the Church, so his will and judgment ought to take precedence. [Col. 1316C] The canons shall promise and maintain obedience to the bishop by placing their hands in his. When he eats at the canons’ table with the canons, he shall come with one cleric and one servant, or with two clerics, and shall be honored as bishop. He shall receive every offering from the altar of St. Imerius, except food offerings placed at the foot of the altar, which shall be reserved for the use of the canons, and except half of the wax and incense offered there, which shall be reserved for the service of the church. With the consent of the canons, the bishop shall appoint the archdeacon, the cantor, and the other officials. He shall hold peacefully and quietly the church of St. Michael and the estates and possessions which he can prove by suitable witnesses properly belong to the episcopate.

And because the canons granted the house in which they had formerly lived for the enlargement of the church, they shall retain henceforth, for the sake of concord and charity, the house in which they now live—although it belonged by right to the bishop—for communal life together; and they may receive guests there whenever they wish.

I, Calixtus, bishop of the Catholic Church, approving.

Given at the Lateran through the hand of Aimeric, deacon cardinal and chancellor of the Holy Roman Church, 22 March, in the eleventh indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1124, and in the sixth year of the pontificate of Lord Calixtus II, pope.

[Note: Observe what is said in the present bull concerning the bishop: [Col. 1316D] “When he eats at the canons’ table [Col. 1317D] with the canons, he shall come with one cleric and one servant, or with two clerics.” These words reveal that the canons still had a common table. Yet clearer are the words concerning the canons at the end: “They shall retain henceforth, for the sake of concord and charity, the house in which they now live—although it [Col. 1318D] belonged by right to the bishop—for communal life together.” Here, in explicit words, the still continuing communal life of the canons in the monastery or cloister is indicated.]

CCLXIII. Privilege for the monastery of Mount of the Angels. (Year 1124, 5 April.)

[*Gallia Christiana*, V, documents, 515.]

[Col. 1317A]

CALIXTUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the beloved sons Adelhelm and the brethren of the monastery of St. Mary, which we wish to be called Mount of the Angels (*Engelberg*), greeting and apostolic blessing.

The nobleman Conrad of Sellenburon came to us and handed over to blessed Peter and to the Holy Roman Church, through the hands of the nobleman Egelolf of Gamelinchoben, your church, built at his expense upon an estate of his own jurisdiction, together with all that belongs to it, [Col. 1317B] subject to an annual payment of one gold piece of Zurich currency, to be paid each year at the altar of blessed Peter by the father of the aforesaid monastery. Attending to his devout intention, we have received your place and all that belongs to it into the right and protection of blessed Peter.

Therefore, by the authority of this present writing, we decree that whenever they are deprived of a spiritual father, they shall have free authority, according to the Rule of St. Benedict, to elect and appoint one from among themselves, or, if necessary, from elsewhere. We further decree that this monastery, with all its appurtenances now conferred and to be conferred after this day, shall not henceforth be subject to the yoke of any earthly power or person, except to the lordship, authority, and governance of the father of the monastery alone.

[Col. 1317C] With the counsel of his senior brethren, he himself shall choose an advocate wherever he pleases, and entrust the office to him for the remedy of his soul; it shall never pass to anyone by hereditary right. The advocate must be willing, solicitous, and zealous to defend the goods, established liberty, and rights of the monastery, not for earthly advantage but for eternal reward; nevertheless, at the request of the father of the monastery, he shall receive lawful *bannum* [ban or jurisdictional authority] from the king. But if he proves not an advocate but rather a vexatious claimant and invader of the monastery, the abbot, with the counsel of the senior brethren, shall have full authority entirely to reject him and, aided by royal power if it cannot otherwise be done, to select elsewhere another more useful to them.

If, however—God forbid!—anyone, wickedly induced by rashness [Col. 1317D] or obstinacy, should dare to disturb, harass, or despoil the aforesaid monastery, let him know that, unless he comes to his senses, he shall perish by eternal damnation under our judgment, for contempt of the Holy Roman Church and for the destruction of this testamentary writing of ours.

Given at the Lateran in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1124, 5 April, in the second indiction, on Holy Saturday, the seventeenth day of the moon.

CCLXIV. Privilege for the monastery of Bifurco. (Year 1124, 11 April.)

[MITTARELLI, *Camaldolese Annals*, vol. III, p. 301.]

[Col. 1318A]

CALIXTUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the beloved son in Christ Theoderic, abbot of the monastery of St. Benedict at Bifurco, and to his successors to be regularly instituted, forever.

We are instructed by divine commands and formed by apostolic admonitions to keep vigilant watch with untiring attention over the condition of churches; hence we must care for churches and religious servants of God in a special manner. [lacuna] Beloved son in Christ, Abbot Theoderic, graciously receiving your prayers, we receive into the right and protection of blessed Peter the church over which, by God’s authorship, [Col. 1318B] you preside; and, by his authority, against the wickedness of evil men, [lacuna] we decree that the estates, possessions, and all goods which your church now possesses either by royal grant, by donation of other faithful persons, or by another acquisition, shall remain secure to you and your successors. [lacuna]

Namely: the boundaries of your church, with its vineyards, demesne lands, and Alpine pastures—from the east at the stream issuing from the lake, from the west at the ridge of the Alps, from the north at Lake Ceresio, from the south at the hill of Gimellis—with tithes and [lacuna], together with all their complete appurtenances; the parish church of St. Martin in Alpe, with its vineyards and demesne lands, and two chapels, one in the castle on the plain of Mercury, [Col. 1318C] the other on Monte Alto; the church of St. Mary at Granario, with all [lacuna] its appurtenances; the parish church of St. Cassian at Pennino, with lands, vineyards, and demesne lands, together with all its appurtenances, and the chapel of St. Sabinus belonging to the same church, with all that belongs to it; the parish church of St. Peter at Octontuta, with vineyard and demesne land [lacuna], tenants, tithes, and first-fruits; the church of St. Mary at Flumicello, with the chapel of St. Helena and all its appurtenances; the chapel of St. Mary of Sirena, with all its appurtenances; the chapel of the Castle of Mesauri, with all [lacuna] its appurtenances; the church of St. Peter at Castagneto, with its vineyards, woods, mills, and all its appurtenances; the church of St. Clement, with one *mansus* [landholding] and [Col. 1318D] all its appurtenances; at Galiano, one chapel with all [lacuna]; St. Peter’s at the stream, with tithes, first-fruits, and offerings of the living and the dead; the church of St. Andrew at Pisseto, with offerings of the living and the dead and all its appurtenances; the church of St. Valerian, with all [lacuna]; the church of St. James at Mincajello, with a hospice and all its appurtenances.

Outside the walls of the city of Florence, beside [Col. 1319A] the church of St. Lawrence, one hospice with lands, vineyards, and all its appurtenances; the church of St. M . . . at Astole, with all its appurtenances. Finally, whatever it shall hereafter justly and canonically acquire by the Lord’s grant, let it possess inviolably and without disturbance. Therefore no mortal may rashly disturb your church, take away its possessions, retain those taken away, diminish them, or trouble it by reckless vexations; rather, let all things be preserved whole for the benefit in every respect of those for whose support and governance they were granted.

For the judgment, right, and protection of the Holy Roman Church, you shall pay two gold pieces yearly to the Lateran palace. You shall receive chrism, holy oil, consecration of churches, and ordinations of your monks from the diocesan bishop, if he is willing to provide them freely, without payment or exactions; otherwise, you shall receive these same sacraments from whatever Catholic bishop you prefer.

[Col. 1319B] If any ecclesiastical or secular person in the future, knowing this text of our constitution, should rashly attempt to act against it, and, after a second or third warning, should not make amends by suitable satisfaction, let that person be deprived of the dignity of authority and office; let him know himself guilty before the divine judgment for the iniquity committed; let him be excluded from the most sacred body and blood of God and our Lord, Redeemer Jesus Christ; and at the last judgment let him be subject to strict vengeance. But upon all who preserve what is just for that place may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, [Col. 1319C] so that they may receive here the fruit of good action and find, before the strict Judge, the rewards of eternal peace. Amen, amen, amen.

I, Calixtus, bishop of the Catholic Church. “The Lord is a stronghold for those who fear him.”

Given at the Lateran through the hand of Aimeric, deacon cardinal and chancellor of the Holy Roman Church, 11 April, in the year from the Incarnation 1123, in the second indiction, and in the sixth year of the pontificate of Lord Calixtus II, pope.

CCLXV. To Otto, bishop of Bamberg.—Concerning privileges granted to the church of Bamberg. (Year 1124, 13 April.)

[MANSI, *Councils*, XXI, 194.]

[Col. 1319D]

CALIXTUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother Otto, bishop of Bamberg, greeting and apostolic blessing.

The precepts of the holy Fathers and canonical ordinances show that the estates and possessions of churches—which are called the offerings of the faithful, the price of sins, and the patrimony of the poor—ought not to be sold or alienated. For what is dedicated to the service of the divine majesty and to the use of heavenly mysteries ought not to be transferred to another’s ownership or changed into a form of another’s service. Indeed, to use the words of blessed Pope Symmachus, [Col. 1320A] “We do not permit possessions which anyone has given or bequeathed to his own church at discretion to be alienated under any titles or dispositions, or upon any pretext whatever.”

Therefore, assenting to your just petitions, we decree by the confirmation of this present writing that the *mansi* [landholdings] devoted to the service of your episcopal table shall remain in future times in the condition in which they are known to have been well arranged by you. We establish that none of your successors, nor any person, may sell them, grant them as a lay benefice, or convert them to other uses. Rather, as you have arranged, one denarius each year from each of the aforesaid *mansi* shall be contributed to the church of Bamberg to maintain the lights, for the soul of Emperor Henry, its founder. No one may hereafter alter the abbeys and regular canonries [variant: canonical communities] which you have established in religious order by your diligence, or the other arrangements rightly made by you. If anyone should rashly presume to act against this confirmation, he shall be subject to the bond of excommunication.

Given at the Lateran, 13 April, in the second indiction.

CCLXVI. *He confirms the privileges of the monastery of Derve.* (Year 1124, 13 April.)

[BOUQUET, *Recueil*, XV, 250, in the notes to the following letter.]

CCLXVII. To Jocerannus, bishop of Langres, etc.—He commends the monastery of Derve as subject to the Roman Church. (Year 1124, 14 April.)

[D. BOUQUET, *Recueil*, vol. XVI, p. 250.]

[Col. 1320C]

CALIXTUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the venerable brethren Jocerannus, bishop of Langres; Hato, bishop of Troyes; Ebalo, bishop of Châlons; and Ricuinus, bishop of Toul, greeting and apostolic blessing.

Venerable places and religious persons who have fixed their purpose in the service of God ought not to be shaken by any burdens or troubled by any molestations. We therefore command your brotherhood to honor, for reverence toward blessed Peter and ourselves, the brethren of the monastery of Derve, constructed in honor of the holy apostles Peter and Paul. It belongs by right to the Roman Church, and it is clear that it relies upon its protection and is subject to its lordship. [Col. 1320D] Accordingly, do not permit the monastery itself, its churches, chapels, dependent houses, estates, possessions, and movable, immovable, or self-moving goods to be troubled, taken away, or burdened by any molestations.

But if anyone, under the pretext of advocacy or any other claim, should presume to usurp by wicked exactions anything beyond the customs established by Count Theobald in the time of Henry, king of the Franks, or should violently take their goods either in life or at death, restrain him, as a violator of an apostolic decree, by the duty of your office.

Given at the Lateran, 14 April.

[Note: We learn the year in which this commendation was made [Col. 1320D] from the sealed diploma of Calixtus himself, communicated to us, likewise for the monastery of Derve: “Given at the Lateran through the hand of Aimeric, deacon cardinal and chancellor of the Holy Roman Church, 13 April, second indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation [Col. 1322D] 1124, and in the sixth year of the pontificate of Lord Calixtus II, pope.”]

CCLXVIII. *He confirms the privileges of the church of St. Frigdianus at Lucca.* (Year 1124, 26 May.)

[See the *Lateran Bullarium*, published at Rome in 1727, folio, p. 7.]

[Col. 1321A]

CCLXIX. To B[enedict], bishop, and the canons of the church of Lucca. (Year 1124, 26 May.)

[BALUZE, *Miscellanea*, Lucchese edition, IV, 589.]

CALIXTUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother B., bishop of Lucca, and to the canons of that church, greeting and apostolic blessing.

[Col. 1321B] It is the duty of good men to love religious life and to cleave to religious persons by the closest bond of fellowship. Therefore, we command you all by way of request that, out of regard for us, you honor and love our beloved son A., prior of St. Frigdianus, and the canons there devoted to service, and do not permit them to be harassed by any troubles. We give thanks to your affection because, as that prior states, you treat the church of St. Frigdianus kindly, and we have in part been heard by you concerning the request which we made for it last year.

Nevertheless, we do not cease to ask that, more fully accepting our request, you allow the aforesaid brethren of St. Frigdianus to celebrate Mass solemnly on the second day of Easter. Receive the prior, moreover, on that day and on two other principal [Col. 1321C] feasts, together with one or two brethren of St. Frigdianus, for the solemn celebration of the divine office with you, in a kindly and gracious spirit. Before a complaint between the canons of St. Frigdianus and those of St. Angelus begins to come before us, we have heard that it arose over a certain deceased woman. Therefore we command you, brother bishop, to strive to settle this dispute with such diligence that the canons of St. Frigdianus may be able, to the honor of God and without scandal or disturbance, to offer grateful service before the presence of the most high Lord.

Given at the Lateran, 25 May.

CCLXX. He grants Diego, archbishop of Compostela, that the city of Mérida shall remain subject to the city of Compostela forever. (Year 1124, 23 June.)

[FLOREZ, *España sagrada*, XX, 402.]

[Col. 1321D]

CALIXTUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother Diego, archbishop of Compostela, and to his successors canonically promoted, forever.

The Church recognizes that the power of binding and loosing in heaven and on earth was principally entrusted by God to blessed Peter and his successors in the words by which the Lord addressed Peter: “Whatever [Col. 1322A] you bind upon earth shall be bound in heaven, and whatever you loose upon earth shall be loosed also in heaven.” By the same divine author, both the strengthening of his own faith and the confirmation of another’s faith were likewise granted to him when it was said: “I have prayed for you, Peter, that your faith may not fail; and you, once converted, strengthen your brethren.”

It is therefore incumbent upon us, who, though unworthy, appear to sit in the place of blessed Peter, to correct what is wrong, confirm what is right, and arrange all matters to be arranged throughout the Church according to the judgment of the inner tribunal, so that our judgment may proceed from the countenance of God and our eyes may behold equity. Accordingly, assenting to the petitions of your brotherhood, we confirm by the authority of this present document that the church of blessed James at Compostela—in which his most venerable body is laid—shall hold forever, out of reverence for that apostle beloved by God, the dignity of an archiepiscopal see [Col. 1322B] which we had granted it temporarily, until the city of Mérida should be restored to Christian rule. Thus that city of Mérida, once exceedingly wealthy and renowned, which now, because of sins, is possessed by the impious tyranny of the Saracens, shall remain subject forever to the city of Compostela as to its metropolitan see.

Furthermore, the prelate of the church of Compostela shall henceforth hold wholly and peacefully the entire fullness of pontifical office which the bishops of the church of Mérida formerly possessed. The suffragan bishops of the metropolitan see of Mérida—those of Salamanca, Ávila, Coimbra, and the rest who are known once to have been subject to that same Mérida—shall wholly render obedience and reverence to the archbishop of Compostela, [Col. 1322C] whose consecration belongs solely to the Roman Church, as to their own metropolitan. By the authority of the Apostolic See, he shall have entirely free power to consecrate them, order their churches, summon them to his councils, and settle ecclesiastical affairs with them.

If, therefore, any ecclesiastical or secular person in the future should violate this our constitution and, after a second or third warning, should not repent and humbly make satisfaction, let that person be excluded from communion in the most sacred body and blood of the Lord and from the thresholds of the Church.

Given at the Lateran through the hand of Aimeric, deacon cardinal and chancellor of the Holy Roman Church, 23 June, in the second indiction, [Col. 1322D] in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1124, and in the sixth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Calixtus.

I, Calixtus, bishop of the Catholic Church, confirm. “The Lord is a stronghold for those who fear him.”

Fare well.

CCLXXI. To the bishop of Salamanca, concerning obedience to be rendered to the lord of Compostela. (Year 1124, 24 June.)

[FLOREZ, *ibid.*, p. 409.]

CALIXTUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable [Col. 1323A] brother M[unio], bishop of Salamanca, greeting and apostolic blessing.

Because in the regions of Spain the church of Compostela is held glorious and distinguished on account of the venerable body of blessed James the apostle, we have decreed, by the favor of the Apostolic See, to foster it and enlarge it with the prerogative of a better status. We have therefore granted to that church of Compostela the dignity of the metropolitan see of Mérida, to be possessed forever. Accordingly, beloved brother, since you are known to be subject to the church of Mérida, we command you to strive to render submission and obedience to our venerable brother D., archbishop of Compostela, as to your own metropolitan.

Given in the territory of Orte, 24 June.

CCLXXII. To the bishop of Coimbra, concerning obedience to be rendered to the lord of Compostela as legate and his metropolitan. (Year 1124, 24 June.)

[FLOREZ, *España sagrada*, p. 410.]

[Col. 1323B]

CALIXTUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother G[undisalvus], bishop of Coimbra, greeting, etc., as above.

CCLXXIII. To the archbishops and the other ecclesiastical orders throughout Gaul, Germany, and Francia. (Year 1124.)

*Deeds of Godfrey, archbishop of Trier*, in PERTZ, *Monumenta Germaniae historica, Scriptores*, VIII, 201.

[Col. 1323C]

CALIXTUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to our most beloved brethren in Christ, the archbishops and the other ecclesiastical orders established throughout Gaul, Germany, and Francia, greeting and apostolic blessing.

We send to you our brother William, bishop of Palestrina, granting him authority, with your charity, to consecrate any bishops among you who have not been consecrated, and to bring to completion, with the brotherhood of all remaining unoffended, whatever other ecclesiastical matters of this kind are incomplete. Peace be with you.

CCLXXIV. To Geoffrey, bishop of Chartres; John, bishop of Orléans; and Stephen, bishop of Paris.—That the interdict imposed because of an unlawful marriage be observed. (Year 1124, 26 August.)

[MANSI, *Councils*, XXI, 214.]

[Col. 1323D]

Just as the Catholic Church defends everything that is blameless, [Col. 1324A] so it strives, according to the principle of equity and justice, to undo things undertaken contrary to the decrees of the canons. We entrusted for settlement the case of the marriage contracted between William, son of Count Robert, and the daughter of the count of Anjou—against which the impediment of kinship is alleged—to our beloved son, I . . . ., cardinal priest. After receiving the proof of kinship from suitable witnesses, he prohibited the celebration of divine offices wherever William, son of Count Robert, might be, unless William should dissolve the marriage by the deadline which the cardinal had set. We therefore command your brotherhood to ensure that this sentence, confirmed by us, is observed throughout your dioceses.

Given at the Lateran, 7 September.

CCLXXV. He receives the monastery of Rastede under his protection and confirms its goods and privileges. (Year 1124, 27 September.)

[LAPPENBERG, *Hamburg Documents*, I, 127.]

[Col. 1324B]

[Note: From the Rastede Codex, fol. 83. There are also found there a second confirming bull of Pope Adrian IV from the year 1158 and a third of Pope Clement III from the year 1190. I have marked the differences in place-names contained in them with 2 and 3.]

CALIXTUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son Svidero, abbot of the monastery of St. Mary, situated in the regions of Ambria, in the village called Rastede, and to his successors regularly appointed, forever.

Since the desire of pious intention and the purpose of praiseworthy devotion must always be aided by the endeavors of priests, care must be taken with solicitude that what has been ordained for the peace of religious life may be neither neglected by indifference nor disturbed by any presumptuous act. [Col. 1324C] Therefore we have received into the right of the Roman Church and under our protection the monastery entrusted to you, which Count Huno, his wife Countess Willa, and Count Frederick built in honor of the holy Mother of God and Virgin Mary, so that it might become a community of monks, and offered to the common father of all Christians, namely St. Peter; and we confirm to it all the possessions which it lawfully holds.

That is, in Ambria: two parts of the village of Radestad, with the whole tithe; a part of the village of Henninchusin, with its tithe; Borbeke, with its tithe; the tithe of the village of Lynsvidon; Barchornun; Lage; Genlide; Wadinbechi; Radehornen.

[Note: [Col. 1323] Hankhausen, Berghorn, Loy, Rehorn, parish of Rastede.]

[Note: [Col. 1323] Borbek, parish of Wiefelstede.]

[Note: [Col. 1323] Linswege, parish of Westerstede.]

[Note: [Col. 1323] Berchorn. 2.]

[Note: [Col. 1323] Hankhausen, Berghorn, Loy, Rehorn, parish of Rastede.]

[Note: [Col. 1323] Hankhausen, Berghorn, Loy, Rehorn, parish of Rastede.]

[Note: [Col. 1323] Loge, Merhusen [ [Col. 1323] Wahnbeck, Moorhausen, parish of Oldenburg.], Lynebrok, Ghelinde (*Ghenlinde* in 3), with the tithe from Goltwertae to the boundary of Omestede on the northern side. (Hunte added in 3.) 2, 3.]

[Note: [Col. 1323] Gellen, parish of Alten Huntorf.]

[Note: [Col. 1323] Wahnbeck, Moorhausen, parish of Oldenburg.]

[Note: [Col. 1323] Hankhausen, Berghorn, Loy, Rehorn, parish of Rastede.]

[Col. 1324D] In Frisia: the estates of Varlas, Echwardi, Bonwardi, Tvislon, and Nertin, with their appurtenances; thirty marks of canons in the village of Anaclingun; Ebeswerdi, Withlike, Fronohusin, Wellin, Haroldessem, Berle, Scohorst.

[Note: [Col. 1323] Varel.]

[Note: [Col. 1323] Eckwarden, in the land of Butjadingen.]

[Note: [Col. 1323] Perhaps Boitwardi: Boitwarden, parish of Golzwarden.]

[Note: [Col. 1323] Perhaps to be sought on the Ahne.]

[Note: [Col. 1323] “with meadows and marshes and” in 2.]

[Note: [Col. 1323] “in the village of Enelinghe, fifty.”]

[Note: [Col. 1323] Eueswerden. 2. Eueswarden, Wideke, Wischusen. 3.]

[Note: [Col. 1323] Barle; Godinge, two rods; Scrotinh; Geuere. 2.]

[Note: [Col. 1323] Barle, Utmore, Scohurst, Scrotinghe, Geuere. 3.]

[Col. 1325A] In Steringeng (*Steringe* in 2; *Steringen* in 3): the estates of Reminchuson, Brunin, Engilin, Gatisdorf, Enschinin, Magelissin, and Habenhuson, with their woods, pastures, and appurtenances.

[Note: [Col. 1325] The district of Stuhr, whose name survives in the Oldenburg diocese and bailiwick of Stuhr, was bounded on the northeast by the Weser. Ganderkese marks its western boundary. See the *Life of St Willehad*. To the south it touches the diocese of Minden.]

[Note: [Col. 1325] Reninchusen. 2.]

[Note: [Col. 1325] Brüne and Engeln, parish of Vilsen, in the district of Alt-Bruchhausen.]

[Note: [Col. 1325] Gödestorf, parish of Heiligenfeld, district of Syke.]

[Note: [Col. 1325] Inscinnen. 2, 3. Gatisdorf is absent in 2, 3. The latter inserts: Papehusen.]

[Note: [Col. 1325] Päpsen, parish of Mellinghausen, district of Nienburg, appears too far south for this district.]

[Note: [Col. 1325] Intschen, parish in the district of Thedinghausen.]

[Note: [Col. 1325] Magelsen, parish on the Weser, in the district of Hoya.]

[Note: [Col. 1325] Habenhausen, parish of Twistringen, in the district of Ehrenburg.]

[Note: [Col. 1325] “with … their appurtenances” is absent in 2.]

In Westphalia: the villages of Betenchuson, Benchinhusen, Swirlichin, Asschinberghen, with their appurtenances; Leffrinchusin, Gedinchtorp, Smerlachen, Mardie, Yslo, Haperne, Wisteren, Widinchusen, Brochusen, Harinctorp, and Berder, with their appurtenances.

[Note: [Col. 1325] *Benchinhusen … earum* is absent in 2.]

[Note: [Col. 1325] Mardinge. 2. Mardige. 3.]

[Note: [Col. 1325] Yserlo. 3.]

[Note: [Col. 1325] Winstrin. 2. Winsteren. 3.]

[Note: [Col. 1325] Windenchusen. 3.]

[Note: [Col. 1325] “Berder, Asscheberghen, Benechinchusen, Holthof, with churches and appurtenances.” 2.]

[Note: [Col. 1325] These places are probably all to be sought near the city of Soest, where Bettinghausen, Benninghausen, Lyringsen, Schmerlicke, Mardey, Iserlohn, Brockhausen, and Herringen are also found on Le Coq’s map. As Wolters reports in *Chronic. Rasted.*, p. 91, the emperor had given Count Huno many estates belonging to the Empire and situated beside the city of Soest.]

Near the Wümme: the estates of Willinstede and Bocholt; Brochlo, with its appurtenances; Quilechorne; Widagheshude.

[Note: [Col. 1325] The Wümme, a river.]

[Note: [Col. 1325] Wilstedt, a parish in the district of Ottersberg, to which Buchholz and Quelckhorn belong ecclesiastically. The patronage of the church at Wilstedt, together with other possessions of Rastede monastery, passed to the counts of Oldenburg and is still held by the present grand dukes.]

[Note: [Col. 1325] Brockel, a parish village in the district of Rothenburg. The right of patronage of the church passed from the abbot of Rastede to the Grand Duke of Oldenburg.]

[Note: [Col. 1325] “pastures, woods, and” in 2.]

In Bardinge: the estates of Totimesborch and Reynestorp, with their churches and appurtenances; the village of Melinchuden, with its appurtenances. In Bardewich, thirty plots, the toll from the bridge and from the pastures; the church of Rode, with its appurtenances; Reindale, Dalsche, Hoygerstorp. In Luneborch, six *panstalia*.

[Note: [Col. 1325] Thomasburg and Reinstorf, parish villages in the district of Lüne.]

[Note: [Col. 1325] Melichuden. 2. Melechuden. 3.]

[Note: [Col. 1325] Rode, parish village in the district of Fallersleben.]

[Note: [Col. 1325] Hogerstorf, in the parish and district of Bodenteich.]

Moreover, whatever possessions and whatever goods that same monastery now justly and canonically possesses, or may in the future be able to acquire, by the grant of popes, the generosity of emperors or princes, the offering of the faithful, or other just means, God being favourable, shall remain secure and unimpaired to you and your successors.

But upon the death of you, Swidero—“upon the death of you, Donatus” in 2—now abbot of the same place, or of any of your successors, no one shall be placed over it by any cunning of surreptitious acquisition or by force, except one whom the brethren, by common counsel and consent, or the sounder part of the brethren’s counsel, according to the fear of God and the Rule of Blessed Benedict, shall have judged fit. But if they cannot find in their own community anyone sufficiently suitable for this government, they may choose a man from whatever place they prefer, provided that he is of their order and profession.

You shall receive the ordinations of your monks who are to be promoted to sacred orders from the archbishop of Bremen, provided that he is willing to confer them freely and without exaction. Otherwise, you may approach whichever Catholic bishop you prefer, who, acting under our authority, shall grant what is requested.

[Note: [Col. 1325] From “We also appoint an advocate …” to “But as a token …” there is an erasure in the manuscript. The words which follow are, however, found on an attached parchment leaf. They seem to me to agree with what can still be discerned in the erased passage.]

We also appoint Count Egilmar as advocate of the aforesaid place and its goods; Count Huno had provided that Egilmar’s father should succeed him in the advocacy. Therefore, in succeeding generations, the eldest by birth in the same kinship shall possess the same advocacy by perpetual right. Yet that advocate shall hold no court with the household of the same church unless he is requested by the abbot. Nevertheless, we assign no service of advocacy to the advocate or his descendants, because none was ever rendered to his father, and because a benefice from the goods of the same church was granted and assigned to him for his labour, [Col. 1326B] on the condition that he shall appoint no deputy in that advocacy.

As a token of the right and protection of the Roman Church, you shall pay two ounces of gold yearly to us and our successors. We therefore decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the aforesaid monastery, take away its possessions, retain things taken away, or afflict it with any vexations; rather, all things shall be preserved intact for the use and advantage, in every respect, of those for whose governance and support they were granted, saving the authority of the Apostolic See.

If, therefore, in the future any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowing this page of our constitution, should rashly attempt to act against it, let that person lose the dignity of his power and honour; let him know himself guilty before divine judgment of the iniquity committed and cut off from the most holy body and blood of God and of the Lord, our Redeemer Jesus Christ; and, unless he makes amendment by suitable satisfaction, let him be subject at the last judgment to severe vengeance. But may the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ be upon all who observe what is right toward that place, so that here they may receive the fruit of good action and before the strict Judge find the rewards of eternal peace. Amen.

Given at the Lateran, through the hand of Aimeric, deacon-cardinal and chancellor of the holy Roman Church, on the fifth day before the Kalends of October, in the third indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1124, in the sixth year of the pontificate of Pope Calixtus II.

## CCLXXVI. Privilege for the monastery of Saint-Bertin at Sithiu.  
*(1124, 11 October.)*

[Collection of Cartularies, III, 292.]

Calixtus, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son John, abbot of the monastery of Saint-Bertin, and to his successors canonically appointed in perpetuity.

The principle of equity and justice persuades us to confer upon churches lasting security for their possessions and safeguards of unshaken strength. For it is not fitting that the servants of Christ, devoted to divine service, should be harassed by the perverse annoyances of wicked people or wearied by the reckless vexations of anyone whatsoever. Likewise, estates dedicated to the uses of heavenly mysteries ought not to endure any forced services imposed by the powerful, nor anything extraordinary.

Since the care of all churches has been entrusted to us, we receive into the guardianship and protection of blessed Peter and ourselves, following the example of our predecessors, the monastery of Saint-Bertin entrusted to you, beloved son in the Lord, Abbot John, with all that belongs to it. We decree that everything lawfully belonging to the same monastery shall always remain peaceful and unimpaired to you and your successors.

Moreover, in accordance with the enactments and privileges bestowed upon that place by our predecessors Victor, Urban, and Paschal, we decree that the monastery itself shall forever be preserved more fully in its liberty and immunity, so that it shall answer to no one concerning its status except the Roman pontiff, while preserving the canonical reverence due to the bishop of Thérouanne.

Likewise, we confirm all things belonging to the same monastery: both those hitherto bestowed there by the devotion of Christ’s faithful and those which may hereafter be lawfully bestowed—arable lands, fields, meadows, pastures, woods, waters and watercourses, mills, fisheries, villages, churches, counties, households, vineyards, orchards, and all movable and immovable property, cultivated and uncultivated.

[Col. 1327D] We also confirm that the altars which your monastery is known to possess in the diocese of Arras shall henceforth be possessed peacefully and without any molestation by you and your successors: namely, the church of Werkin, the church of Salomes, and the church of Hautay; likewise the altars of Lisvegne, Snelgnekerke, Erninghem, and Bovenkerke, which were conferred upon your church through the hand of Lambert, bishop of Tournai; also the sheep-rent of forty pounds in the territory of Furnes, which Charles gave for the soul of Count Baldwin; and likewise the land of Buri which your church is known to possess in the district of Beauvais.

We decree that no one may presume to build a mill from the village of Arkas to Lodic without the consent of you and your successors; and that in all your parishes no one may build a church or monastery contrary to your will. Nor may any priest or cleric, in your churches or chapels, whether by himself or through another’s force, have permission to remain or assume any office without your consent and free will.

If, by command of the bishop, the land has been placed under interdict, your monks and clerics shall nevertheless continue to celebrate the divine mysteries in your churches and chapels, with the doors shut and laypeople excluded. If any of your parishioners have been excommunicated for a particular offence, divine offices shall not be denied to others merely because those persons have been excluded from the Church.

We further establish that no abbot shall be placed over the same monastery except one whom the brethren, by common consent, or the sounder part of the brethren’s counsel, according to the fear of God and the Rule of Blessed Benedict, shall have provided to be elected from their own congregation.

We therefore decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the oft-mentioned monastery, take away its possessions, retain things taken away, diminish them, or afflict it with reckless vexations. Rather, all things shall be kept entire for the benefit, in every respect, of those for whose support and governance they were granted. If, therefore, any ecclesiastical or secular person in the future, knowing this page of our constitution, rashly attempts to act against it, then, after a second or third warning, unless that person makes amendment by suitable satisfaction, let him lose the dignity of his power and honour; let him know himself guilty before divine judgment of the iniquity committed, and cut off from the most sacred body and blood of God and of the Lord, our Redeemer Jesus Christ; and let him be subject at the last judgment to severe vengeance.

But may the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ be upon all who observe what is right toward that place, so that here they may receive the fruit of good action and before the strict Judge find the rewards of eternal peace. Amen.

Given at the Lateran, through the hand of Haimeric, deacon-cardinal and chancellor of the holy Roman Church, on the fifth day before the Ides of October, in the third indiction, in the year 1124 of the Incarnation, in the sixth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Calixtus II.

## CCLXXVII. He takes the monastery of Saint Mary of Pomposa under protection and confirms its goods and privileges.  
*(1124, 16 October.)*

[Muratori, *Antiquitates Italicae*, V, 823.]

[Col. 1328D]

Calixtus, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son Aurelius, abbot of the monastery of Saint Mary situated on the island of Pomposa, and to his successors canonically appointed in perpetuity.

The principle of equity and justice persuades us to confer upon churches lasting security for their possessions and safeguards of unshaken strength. For it is not fitting that the servants of Christ, devoted to divine service, should be harassed by the perverse annoyances of wicked people or wearied by the reckless vexations of anyone whatsoever. Likewise, estates dedicated to the uses of heavenly mysteries ought to endure no forced services imposed by the powerful, nor anything extraordinary.

Since the care of all churches has been entrusted to us, acceding to your requests, beloved Abbot Aurelius in Christ, and strengthening by the protection of the Apostolic See the monastery of Pomposa, over which, by God’s authority, you preside, dedicated to the blessed and glorious ever-virgin Mary, Mother of God, we confirm the possessions and goods which it lawfully holds either from the holy Roman Church or from elsewhere.

Namely, the whole *massa* called Materaria; the whole *massa* called Maseuli; the whole estate called Casale Publicum; the *massa* called Nepoti; and, in the *massa* called Caputbovis, the land and vineyards which you now have and hold by the right of blessed Peter the Apostle. Also the bank of the river Alemon on both sides beside the *massa* called Prata, that bank extending from Agaziolo to the field of Bedulli.

Land and vineyard beside the walls of the city of Ravenna, together with the whole Torre Umbratica, from the Posterula of Augustus to the Taurensian Gate. One whole garden at the place of Ponte Calciato in the district of Saint Andrew: on two sides by right of that saint, on the other two by the public road.

The lake called Saint, with all its property and appurtenances, its parish church, chapels, and dependent churches—namely, Saint Mary, Saint Martin, Saint Peter, and Saint Venantius—with tithes and first-fruits; with the fishery called Tidini, the archpriest’s ditch, and the fishery called Falci; with the place called Monticellus Lacisicus; with the banks of the rivers Po and Gaurus on both sides as far as the sea; and from the place called Conca Agathae on one side as far as the sea, together with the whole place called Masinzatica, within the boundaries of the entire place and territory of the *massa* called Lake Saint:

on one side, the mill-ditch of Volta Latercli descending into Aquiliolo, and from the river Triba to Elia, then through the marsh to the middle of Curba, beyond Curba to the Po, beyond the Po to Gazium belonging to the bishop of the holy church of Comacchio, and thence to the river called Cesi;

on the other side, Curlus descending into Conca Agatula and through it into Gaurus;

on the third side, the marsh extending between the stream of Angeli and Masinzatica as far as Monticellum and Vedetosa, flowing into the Po;

on the fourth side, Vaculinus, Ager Malus, and the road of Vincareto extending to Laterclum.

Further, we grant you the whole fishery called Volana, with the stream Badereno and Greater Gavelana belonging to that fishery, together with the Porticelli on both sides, as they formerly entered the sea and likewise belong to it.

All these things, then, we grant to you, your lawful successors, and the brethren living religiously, to possess in perpetuity, provided that every year you pay to the officers of our holy Roman Church, without delay, three silver solidi as an annual pension. Whatever else you may justly and canonically acquire by the grant of Roman pontiffs or other bishops, the generosity of princes, or the offerings of the faithful, shall remain secure and unimpaired to you and your successors.

Furthermore, we decree that no archbishop and no bishop may impose a burden upon your monastery or exercise authority in it or over its property. No person may, apart from the will of the abbot and brethren of the monastery, extort fodrum or impose other exactions upon the peasants or villagers, male or female servants belonging to the monastery, whether from its dependent houses, villages, castles, or parish churches. Rather, may you always be sustained by the protection of the Apostolic See and, if necessary, preserved through a hearing, saving in all things the authority of that Apostolic See.

You shall receive chrism and holy oil from the bishop of Comacchio, if he is Catholic and willing to give them freely to you without a wrongful exaction. Otherwise, for receiving these sacraments, you may have recourse to whichever Catholic bishop you prefer. You may likewise receive the blessing of the abbot, the ordinations of your monks, and the consecrations of the altars of your monastery and of those within the *massa* of Lake Saint, from whichever Catholic bishop you prefer, who, supported by the authority of the Apostolic See, shall grant what is requested.

We also establish by a perpetual decree that neither you nor any of your successors shall be compelled to attend the synod of any bishop unless invited by the Roman pontiff or his legate.

If, therefore, any ecclesiastical or secular person in the future, knowing this page of our constitution, rashly attempts to act against it, then, after a second or third warning, unless that person makes amendment by suitable satisfaction, let him lose the dignity of his power and honour; let him know himself guilty before divine judgment of the iniquity committed, cut off from the most sacred body and blood of God and of the Lord, our Redeemer Jesus Christ, and subject at the last judgment to severe vengeance.

But may the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ be upon all who observe what is right toward that place, so that here they may receive the fruit of good action and before the strict Judge find the rewards of eternal peace. Amen, amen, amen.

I, Calixtus, bishop of the Catholic Church.

Fare well.

Given at the Lateran through the hand of Aimeric, deacon-cardinal and chancellor of the holy Roman Church, on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of November, in the third indiction, in the year 1124 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the sixth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Calixtus II.

## CCLXXVIII. Privilege for the church of Saint-Bénigne of Dijon.  
*(1124, 29 October.)*

[Pérard, *Recueil de pièces*, etc., p. 216.]

Calixtus, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son Hugh, abbot of Dijon, and to his successors canonically appointed in perpetuity.

Just as, in the structure of the human body, natural reason, providing for the health of every member, teaches each its particular and proper functions while preserving to the nobler members their dignity, so in the body of the Church apostolic providence governs all churches according to the institutions of the sacred canons. It preserves the worthier and more renowned in the prerogative of their status. For it is equitable and reasonable that the honour proper to every church should be confirmed by the protection of the Apostolic See.

Therefore, beloved son in the Lord Hugh, abbot of Dijon, consenting to your just requests, we have judged that, by the Lord’s authority, provision should be made for the liberty and peace of your monastery. We establish that, upon the death of you, now abbot of that place, or of any of your successors, no one shall be placed over it by any cunning of surreptitious acquisition or by force, except one whom the brethren, by common consent, or the sounder part of the brethren’s counsel, shall elect, whether from their own community or, if necessary, from another, according to the fear of God and the Rule of Blessed Benedict. The consecration of the person elected shall be performed as was established by our predecessor Gregory VII, of blessed memory.

We forbid anyone, after having made profession, to leave the monastery without the abbot’s permission. We also establish that the divine offices shall not be interdicted to your monastery by the bishop or ministers of the church of Langres, but shall be celebrated continually, unless the brethren must cease for the same causes specified in the decree of Benedict, bishop of the Apostolic See.

We confirm in perpetuity to your monastery the liberty which the venerable Robert, bishop of Langres, is known to have conferred upon the churches situated in the borough of your monastery—namely those of Saint John the Baptist and Saint Philibert—and upon the priests serving the Lord in them. We also confirm, by the assent of this present decree, the remission and immunity which the same bishop or his predecessors are known to have granted your monastery from *paratae* and synods.

We also confirm to you and your successors, in the diocese of Langres: the dependent house of Saint-Amator, with the church of Saint-Ferreolus, courtyards, churches, and other things belonging to them; likewise the dependent house of Montignac; that of Noyant, with the chapel of the same castle; that of Clermont; Saint Mary’s dependent house by Saxon’s Spring; and Saint Stephen’s dependent house by the stream of Vuangion, with all things belonging to them.

[Col. 1331D] In the diocese of Toul: the dependent house of Bertiniaca Curtis and that of Mont Solini, with the churches, villages, lands, and all things belonging to them. In the diocese of Autun: the dependent house of Belne, with the churches of Vuilliac and Cosletot, the meadow of Forgeolo, and all their appurtenances; the dependent houses of Sarmatia, Curbeltat, and Arneto, with all things belonging to those dependent houses. In the archdiocese of Besançon: the dependent houses of Saint-Marcel, Offonis Villa, Sarcophagis, and Logia Novella; the church of Torpa; and, at Salins, the dependent houses of Saint Peter and Saint Michael, with everything belonging to them.

In the diocese of Chalon: the dependent house of Saint Mary and that of Palluel, with all appurtenances. In the diocese of Valence: the dependent house of Saint Genesius on Mount Madrian, with its appurtenances; and the churches of Vulpilleniis, Tornoz, and Glun. In the diocese of Die: the church of Boventia. In the diocese of Bayeux: the dependent house of Saint Vigor, with its appurtenances. In the diocese of Sens: the dependent house of Saint-Bénigne at Vunon, with all its appurtenances; the dependent house of Eschino with all its appurtenances; the church of Granciac and all that belongs to it; the dependent house of Rulth with its appurtenances; the chapel of Hex, with the tithes and lands granted there; and the chapel of Vuangion’s Stream with all that belongs to it.

The charter of King Robert of the Franks concerning the dependent house of Belne; the chapel of Saint Mary Magdalene at Salins and all that belongs to it. Likewise, the possessions: the village of Dinatum with its appurtenances; the village of Casnedum; again Casnedum Hispaniacum; Marcennac, Norgias, Vareias, Sariac, Longovic, and the tithe of the aforesaid Sariac; the village of Atiniac; Plombières; Prunedum; Erchiriac; Flariac; Mont Magny; Viverias; Salciac in the wood, with their tithes; and whatever other things in any places now belong to the rights of your monastery or shall hereafter belong to them through the Lord’s generosity.

We therefore decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the same monastery, take away its possessions, retain things taken away, diminish them, or afflict it with reckless vexations. Rather, all things shall be entirely preserved for the benefit, in every respect, of those for whose support and governance they were granted, saving the canonical reverence due to bishops. Yet neither they nor their ministers may harass the churches of your monastery with unjust interdictions so long as the vigour of monastic order remains, by the Lord’s grant.

If any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowing this page of our constitution, rashly attempts to act against it, then, after a second or third warning, unless that person makes amendment by suitable satisfaction, let him lose the dignity of his power and honour; let him know himself guilty before divine judgment of the iniquity committed, cut off from the most sacred body and blood of God and of the Lord, our Redeemer Jesus Christ, and subject at the last judgment to severe vengeance.

But may the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ be upon all who observe what is right toward that place, so that here they may receive the fruit of good action and before the strict Judge find the rewards of eternal peace. Further, we establish that whatever has been granted to the monastery of Dijon by authentic privileges of our predecessors, the Roman pontiffs, shall remain secure. Amen, amen, amen.

Given at the Lateran through the hand of Imeric, deacon-cardinal and chancellor of the holy Roman Church, on the fourth day before the Kalends of November, in the third indiction, in the year 1124 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the sixth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Calixtus.

## CCLXXIX. Privilege for the church of Saint Stephen of Dijon.  
*(1124, 10 November.)*

[Pérard, *ibid.*, p. 100.]

[Col. 1333A]

Calixtus, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons Galon, prior, and the brethren professing the regular life in the church of Saint Stephen in the castle of Dijon, both present and future, in perpetuity.

The care of the universal Church has been entrusted to us by God, the provider of all good things, so that we may love religious persons and strive by every means to advance the religious life pleasing to God. For no service is ever pleasing to God unless, proceeding from the root of charity, it is preserved in the purity of religion. Therefore, lovers of the Christian faith ought to cherish religious life and carefully foster venerable places, together with the persons therein devoted to divine service.

Accordingly, most beloved sons in the Lord, assenting to your requests, we confirm by the authority of the Apostolic See the order of canonical life which you have professed in our Church according to the Rule of Blessed Augustine. We establish that, after the deaths of Abbot Garnerius and Provost Garnerius, no secular abbot or provost shall be appointed there; instead, he whom the regular brethren, or the sounder part of their counsel, according to the fear of God and the Rule of Blessed Augustine, shall provide to be elected as a regular shall be set over all.

We further command that, as the secular clerics who remain die, no one except a regular canon shall be substituted in their place in your church. We confirm by the page of this privilege the churches, chapels, and other things which your church lawfully possesses or may hereafter acquire by just means, through the Lord’s generosity: namely, the church of Saint Stephen, with its churches, villages, male and female servants, and lands; the church of Saint Medard; the church of Saint Michael, with cemetery and tithes; the church of Saint Anian of the Aqueduct, with cemetery, tithes, and lands; the church of Saint Martin of Quintiniac, with cemetery, tithes, and lands; the church of Saint Maurice of Siliciac, with cemetery, tithes, and lands; the church of Saint Germanus of Copiac, with cemetery, tithes, and lands; the church of Saint Mary of Marceniac, with lands; the church of Saint Andrew of Parriniac, with tithes and lands; the church of Saint Florentius, with the chapel of Saint Mary, cemetery, tithes, lands, and their other appurtenances; the church of Saint Peter of Mirebel, with cemetery, tithes, lands, and its appurtenances; the tithe of Geyac; the tithe of Cucciac; the church of Saint Martin of Prato, with cemetery, the chapel of Fontanis, and their appurtenances; the church of Saint Mary of Gemellis, with the chapel of Pygangis, tithes, and lands; the church of Saint Andrew of Ormentiac, with chapels, cemeteries, and tithes; the church of Columnerio, with chapels and their appurtenances; the chapel between Langlerium and Saint Fidol, with its appurtenances; the place of Putcolo; the place of Agnino Fonte; the place of Goldo Altrei, with its appurtenances—while in all things preserving the right of the bishop of Langres.

Further, the church of Saint Martin of Arco, with its appurtenances; the place of Mount Ciconiac, with its appurtenances; and the place of Franceis, with its appurtenances.

If, therefore, any ecclesiastical or secular person in the future, knowing this page of our constitution, rashly attempts to act against it, then, after a second or third warning, unless that person makes amendment by suitable satisfaction, let him lose the dignity of his power and honour; let him know himself guilty before divine judgment of the iniquity committed and cut off from the most sacred body and blood of God and of the Lord, our Redeemer Jesus Christ; and let him be subject at the last judgment to severe vengeance.

But may the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ be upon all who observe what is right toward that place, so that here they may receive the fruit of good action and before the strict Judge find the rewards of eternal peace.

I, Calixtus, bishop of the Catholic Church, have subscribed.

Given at the Lateran through the hand of Aimeric, deacon-cardinal and chancellor of the holy Roman Church, on the fourth day before the Ides of November, in the third indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation one thousand one hundred and twenty-four, in the sixth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Calixtus II.

## CCLXXX. He takes the monastery of Saint Nicholas of Buttenburg under protection and confirms its goods and privileges, at the request of John, bishop of Thérouanne.  
*(1124, 24 November.)*

[Mir., *Opera diplomatica*, I, 524.]

Calixtus, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons Nicholas, abbot, and the brethren of the church of Saint Nicholas of Buttemburch, both present and future, in perpetuity.

The care of the universal Church has been entrusted to us by God, the provider of all good things, so that we may love religious persons and strive by every means to advance the religious life pleasing to God.

Accordingly, beloved sons in Christ, at the intercession also of the prayers of our venerable brother John, bishop of Thérouanne, we graciously receive your requests. Confirming by the authority of the Apostolic See the order of canonical life which you have professed in your church according to the Rule of Blessed Augustine, we receive your monastery, with all its appurtenances, into the patronage of blessed Peter and our protection.

We establish that whatever goods and whatever possessions it now lawfully possesses, or may in the future justly acquire through God’s generosity, shall remain secure and unimpaired.

Among these we have judged that the following should be specified by their proper names: two chapels, the first consecrated in honour of Saint Denis and the other in honour of Blessed Nicholas; sixty measures of land which Theoderic Rufus, son of Folpoldus, had held by feudal right, and which, after he had publicly restored them to Count Charles before the leading men and princes of Flanders, the count himself gave by his own hand to the aforesaid church, free and exempt from every exaction whatsoever, to be possessed by perpetual right; twenty-five measures which Hadologa and her son Eustachius gave to the aforesaid monastery; and likewise ten measures which Rodulphus Hecra gave.

…when you now die as abbot of that place, no one shall be set over it by any cunning device of usurpation, except one whom the brothers, by common consent—or the sounder part of the brethren—shall, in the fear of God and according to the Rule of Blessed Augustine, determine ought to be elected from their own community or from another. No canon of the same church shall presume to possess anything as his own, or, prompted by any impulse of fickleness [Col. 1335B] or under the pretext of a stricter life, to depart from the same cloister without the common permission of the abbot and brethren. Moreover, if any one of the faithful wishes to have burial there, it shall be granted him freely and without any objection. If, therefore, any ecclesiastical or secular person in the future, knowing this document of our constitution, shall attempt to act against it, then, having been warned a second or third time, unless he makes amends by suitable satisfaction, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and office; let him know himself to be answerable before the divine judgment for the iniquity perpetrated; let him be cut off from the most sacred Body and Blood of the Lord God, our Redeemer Jesus Christ; and at the last judgment let him be subject to strict vengeance.

But upon all who preserve what is right for that same place may there be [Col. 1335C] the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that they may receive here the fruit of good works and find, before the strict Judge, the rewards of eternal peace. Amen.

Given at the Lateran, through the hand of Aimeric, cardinal-deacon and chancellor of the holy Roman Church, on the eighth day before the Kalends of December [24 November], in the third indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1124, and in the fifth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Calixtus II.

CCLXXXI. He exhorts J[ordan], prince of Capua, not to lay waste the land of the monastery of Cassino. (1124.)

[See PETER, *Chronicle of the Monastery of Cassino*, book IV, chapter 82.]

CCLXXXII. [Note: [Col. 1335D] Doubtful.] To Rustinus, abbot of the monastery of St Blaise in the Black Forest. (1120, 19 March.)

[D. GERBERT, *History of the Black Forest*, vol. III, p. 48.]

[Col. 1336A]

CALIXTUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son RUSTINUS, abbot of the monastery of St Blaise, situated in the diocese of Constance, in the place called the Black Forest, and to his successors canonically appointed in perpetuity.

We acknowledge that, by the Lord’s ordering, we have been advanced to the service of the Apostolic See for this purpose: that we ought effectively to assist, defend, and protect, as the Lord grants, his children when they implore help. Therefore it is fitting that we extend the hand of protection to venerable places [Col. 1336B] and provide more attentively for the peace of God’s servants. Accordingly, graciously assenting to your petitions, beloved son in Christ Ruostinus, [Note: [Col. 1335D] Rustenus, fifth abbot of the monastery of St Blaise and successor in 1108 to Utto, was especially intent on preserving its property by the charters of pontiffs and emperors, and on freeing himself from the advocacy of the bishops of Basel, or rather of those whom they had appointed as sub-advocates. Accordingly, through his action at Basel in 1112, by the mediation of Cardinal Gregory, legate of Calixtus II, an amicable settlement was reached. (See vol. I of the *History of the Black Forest*, p. 380.)] we confirm to the monastery of Blessed Blaise entrusted to your governance, with the reverence due to the bishop of Constance preserved, the cell in the forest of Schwarzwald, built by St Reginbert, with all possessions, churches, estates, and lands belonging to it. [Note: [Col. 1335D] Here the reason for the confirmation is evident: namely, the possessions, churches, estates, and lands belonging to the cell of St Reginbert by the donation of Emperor Otto II in 983, which were afterwards confirmed to the monastery of St Blaise.]

Further, we specifically confirm to you the church of Nollingen, [Note: [Col. 1335D] The church of Nallingen in the duchy of Württemberg remained subject, together with its possessions, to the monastery of St Blaise under the designation of a provostship until the time of the change of religion [Col. 1336D].] recently given to your monastery by the nobleman Anselm together with one half of its tithes. We also confirm the church of Sneisane, [Note: [Col. 1336D] Schneisnigon, a parish church in Aargau and in the rural chapter of Regensperg, remains dependent upon St Blaise to this day.] bestowed by Count Ellewin; the church of Batemaringin, [Note: [Col. 1336D] Batemaringen, or Bettmaringen, in the chapter of Stühlingen.] granted by a certain Arnulf; likewise the churches of Berowa, [Note: [Col. 1336D] Shortly before this, Abbot Rustenus had transferred nuns from the valley of St Blaise to Mount Berowe.] Nunchilcha, and Omingin, lawfully handed over to you by their founders, with their shares [Col. 1336C] of the tithes, and to your successors, by apostolic authority.

Therefore, concerning these churches and the others which you possess, we decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the aforesaid monastery or harass it with any vexations, while preserving episcopal right and reverence. We also confirm the arrangement which our dearest son Emperor Henry established concerning the advocacy of your monastery, [Note: [Col. 1336D] These are the very words of the diploma in which Emperor Henry V describes the boundaries of the properties belonging to the cell of St Blaise and confirms to the abbot the free power of choosing an advocate; see P. Herrgott, *Codex of Proofs*, vol. II, part I, p. 136. But that diploma, first given on the Kalends of January 1123, could not already have been confirmed by Calixtus II in 1120. Therefore one of two conclusions follows: either that some earlier enactment of Emperor Henry concerning this matter existed, or that this arrangement [Col. 1337D] had already been made by the emperor at that time but was only issued at Speyer in 1123; in it the given fourth indiction is erroneous, for in 1123 the first indiction was current.] namely, that in choosing an advocate the abbot shall have free authority, with the counsel of his brethren, to choose one whom he recognizes as good and useful for defending the liberty of the monastery. Such a man should desire to hold and administer that advocacy properly, not for earthly profit but for the love of God, forgiveness of sins, and the reward of eternal blessedness [Col. 1336D] [Col. 1337A]. But if, proving a vexatious claimant rather than an advocate, he seizes the monastery’s goods and, having been warned once, twice, or three times, does not make amends, the abbot shall have the power to appoint another advocate more useful to himself.

As a token of our protection and of the liberty granted to your monastery, you shall pay one gold coin each year to the Lateran palace. If anyone, knowing the tenor of this decree, should rashly—God forbid!—attempt to oppose it, let him suffer loss of his rank and office, or be punished by the penalty of excommunication, unless he corrects his presumption by worthy satisfaction. Amen, amen, amen.

[Col. 1338A] I, Calixtus, bishop of the catholic Church. I, Cono, bishop of Palestrina. I, Lambert, bishop of Ostia. I, Boso, cardinal-priest of the title of St Anastasia. I, John, cardinal-priest of the title of St Chrysogonus.

Given at the Lateran through the hand of Chrysogonus, cardinal-deacon and librarian of the holy Roman Church, on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of April [19 March], in the twelfth indiction, [Note: [Col. 1338D] These chronological data agree with the year 1120 and the day of 19 March, on which the twelfth indiction was still running, until the twenty-fifth day of the same month, according to the pontiffs’ method of reckoning.] in the year 1120 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the first year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Calixtus II. Amen, amen.

[Col. 1337]

LETTERS OF VARIOUS PERSONS TO CALIXTUS.

I. Letter of heretics to Pope Calixtus II.—They declare their assent to his election. (1119.)

[MANSI, *Councils*, XXI, 224.]

[Col. 1337B]

To CALIXTUS, by God’s grace universal pontiff: R., cardinal of St Eusebius, G., of the Holy Apostles, and M., abbot of St Pancras, obedience in the Lord.

Although the letter concerning your election has not reached us, yet when it was made known to us we rejoiced, praying God that, if anything be lacking in it, his gracious favor may supply it for you and for us. We, having now for seven years been greatly wearied in confessing catholic truth and scarcely able any longer to endure, ask through God’s mercy for relief.
