But [Col. 1337C] because we believe that God can grant this through you, we have embraced your election as one given by God—an election which neither Simon’s leprosy nor the swelling of ambition has infected.

For we understood that, in your case, the chapter on election had been fulfilled which the Apostle set forth in the Epistle to the Hebrews: “No one,” he says, “takes this honor upon himself, but he who is called by God, as Aaron was.” Therefore, since you have been called by God to your pontificate, we embrace and approve your election, finding no stain in it according to our conscience and approving it in accordance with the wish which we have always maintained, trusting that every stain of heresy may be driven from the Roman Church by your holy zeal. Accordingly, with diligence awakened in us, we subscribe to your election, confirming it, all the more [Col. 1337D] devotedly because we trust, by God’s grace, that it is the purer.

Likewise Priest Bonushomo; Priest Berard; Priest Angelus of St Andrew; Priest Angelus; [Col. 1338B] John, archpriest of St Mary Rotunda; Dodo, priest of St Mary in Aquiro; Desiderius, archpriest of the Holy Apostles, with all the clergy of that church; Priest Benedict of St Stephen; Priest John of St Nicholas; Angelus of St Mary in Via; Beraldus of St Basil; Astaldus and John, abbot of St Apollinaris; Priest Mannus of St Peter in Chains; Priest Leo; and Nicholas of St Lawrence in Lucina, with many others.

II. Petition of Urban, bishop of Llandaff, to Pope Calixtus II at Rheims. (1119.)

[WARTHON, *Sacred England*, II, 673.]

[Col. 1338C] To the venerable apostolic CALIXTUS, supreme protector of all Christendom, URBAN, bishop of the Church of Llandaff, faithful service and the prayers due.

The Church of God—and ours, which under God and under you belongs to your mercy and compassion—sends this letter to you and humbly begs you, for Christ the highest King’s sake, to command that it be carefully read to you and mercifully heard by you. From the time of the ancient Fathers, most beloved Father and lord, as the charter of our holy patron Teilo attests, this aforesaid Church, first founded in honor of St Peter the Apostle, always stood as mistress of all the churches of Wales in dignity and every privilege; until at length, through dissensions and the disasters of so many wars [Col. 1338D], and through the long-standing tenure of my predecessor Herwald, the Church, weakened thereby, began to decline; and was almost bereft of a pastor and brought to nothing by the cruelty of the natives and the invasion of the invading Norman people. [Col. 1339A]

Nevertheless, religious men always remained attached to serving in it: partly because of the proximity of the English, from whom they differed in no respect in ecclesiastical ministry, since among them they had both been brought up and educated; and partly because from ancient times—that is, from the time of Pope Eleutherius of the Roman See—the bishop of that place, and after Augustine’s coming to the island of Britain the metropolitan of the Church of Canterbury, had always been devoted and altogether obedient both to its archbishop and to the king of the English. More recently, during the reign of King William, though the greater part of the clergy had already perished, the Church was still furnished with twenty-four canons, of whom at present none except two remain in it; and the Church’s domain consists of four ploughlands and four pounds. Nor is the Church now desolate and stripped only in its bestowed territories, [Col. 1339B] but also in the tithes taken from it and from all the clergy of the whole bishopric, both by lay power and by monastic encroachment, and also by our brother bishops—namely, those of Hereford and St David’s—through their great invasion alike of territory and parish.

Now I entreat you, as a father: like one unarmed addressing one armed, and one weak addressing one strong, come to the aid of our Church committed to you, so that he who made you may himself hold you by the hand and, when your labor is ended, lead you to everlasting consolation. Amen.

III. Louis VI, king of the French, to Calixtus.—He writes that he will never tolerate the subjection which the primate of Lyons demanded from the archbishop of Sens. (1121.)

[MANSI, *Councils*, vol. XXI.]

[Col. 1339C]

Your sublimity wrote to us concerning the capture of that apostate Burdin, and concerning the security of your position. Therefore, sweetest Father, we love you greatly and above all others, and we understand that your honor is in every respect our concern. By relaxing, for our honor, the sentence imposed upon the metropolitan of Sens, you have partly calmed our mind; but since it has been relaxed only for a time, you have left us gravely anxious and doubtful. For the archbishop of Lyons appears still to entertain some hope concerning the subjection which he seeks; but, to speak the truth, I would rather endure the burning of our entire kingdom, even danger to our own life, than the disgrace of subjection and abasement. For this seems to touch upon our contempt: that something should be done against us in this fashion which has never been done before.

Your experience knows that the kingdom of France has been ready in service and your friend in necessities, and that neither the prayers nor promises of the emperor have ever been able to draw us away from fidelity to the Roman Church. And with what fervor of spirit, with what humility of mind, we have obeyed you—if your voice be silent, let our deeds cry out, let my services testify. For, to pass over other matters, your fatherhood will remember among others that, though I was suffering, as you know, from a severe illness, with bodily distress [Col. 1340A] pressing heavily upon me, I nevertheless strove to attend the Council of Rheims, at cost to myself but to your honor; and I had more regard for your will than for my own ability, and more for your honor than for my own dominion. Sweetest Father, we have written this to remind you, not because we regret having done it, but because we wish it not to have departed from your memory.

Therefore, if our love and service have any value or power with you, we ask and beseech that the Church of Sens, which up to now has been separate and free from the subjection now claimed against it, may not through you become a slave; rather, may its ancient liberty be strengthened by apostolic authority and protected by the firmness of a privilege. Yet in this nothing contrary to justice is required of you. For [Col. 1340B] if it is objected that an ancient institution conferred the primacy upon the Church of Lyons, the contrary answer is that possession of ancient liberty protects the Church of Sens from its subjection. For what is acquired by ancient possession is, as it is said, taken away by no law, even though it be known to have belonged by right to the Roman Church.

For this reason, then, the liberty of the Church of Sens ought to remain unshaken and untouched; it ought not to be assailed or violated for the sake of a subjection newly and imprudently made. For this subjection, it is said, was imposed secretly and almost furtively: that is, without the knowledge of the clergy of Sens, without consultation with the bishops of that diocese, and without the king’s knowledge. Upon all these things the dignity of the Church depends; and a subjection imposed in such a manner seems to tend rather to the disgrace of the person who improperly accepts it than to the advantage of the Church that knows nothing of it. A common matter must be dealt with by common counsel, not settled by a secret and private conference.

Since the dignity belongs to the Church, not to an individual, if this archbishop of Sens alone has done, concerning what was not his own, what he ought not to have done, or has promised what he ought not to have promised, the Church of Sens has nevertheless not lost what belongs to it, nor the personal liberty it has possessed from antiquity; nor should it be compelled to a subjection which it has never rendered. Since matters stand thus, let your discernment, sweetest Father, take care lest the city of Lyons, which belongs to another kingdom, flourish at the cost of our loss; and lest friend be subjected to friend. For if a friend is deceived on account of a friend, a friend will justly become [Col. 1340D] an enemy from a friend.

Therefore the king of France, who is a special son of the Roman Church, if he is despised in an easy matter and a slight petition, is left without hope in a greater one, and will no longer endure refusal in other matters if he suffers the affront of rejection in these. For it is better for royal honor to desist from requests than to incur, through rejection, the stain of shame. Whatever is insufficiently contained in this letter, the bearer of the present letter, Algrinus, will supply orally; receive and keep his words as though from our own mouth.

IV. Ralph, archbishop of Canterbury, to Calixtus.—He complains of an injury done to himself and the Church of Canterbury in the consecration of the archbishop of York. (1122.)

[WILKINS, *Councils of Great Britain and Ireland*, vol. II, p. 396, from Cotton manuscript Domitian A. V, fol. 2 and following.]

[Col. 1341A]

To the most reverend lord and uniquely honored Father, the supreme pontiff CALIXTUS, and to the entire holy and apostolic Roman Church, RALPH, archbishop of Canterbury, and the whole Church of Canterbury, greeting in the Lord and due submission.

Because, through our sins, an adversity new indeed in these times to the Church of Canterbury, and unheard of since the beginning [Col. 1341B] of English Christianity, has arisen, we presume now to address your majesty in a manner other than formerly customary, most blessed lord and uniquely honored Father. For we are compelled to complaints—may God, who changes and orders all things as he knows best, regard the cause of his Church.

Indeed, from the time when blessed Father Gregory sent the holy and venerable man Augustine to preach to the English people, it became an established religious custom that the Apostolic See should confer upon the Church of Canterbury whatever dignity of primacy and privilege was fitting according to catholic and canonical practice; and that the Church of Canterbury should render to the Apostolic See, with perpetual constancy, whatever humility, submission, and faith were fitting according to Christian and ecclesiastical law. [Col. 1341C] This was preserved firm and inviolate, except that a certain Stigand seized the prelacy of this holy Church of Canterbury against canonical and proper custom. In the time of Pope Alexander II, before cardinals sent from the Apostolic See, he was accused, convicted, and deposed in the city of Winchester, and ceased from his proud presumption. Apart from him, neither history nor memory has taught us that any bishop of Canterbury has seized or presumed anything against the Apostolic See.

Accordingly, it was rightly and fittingly done that, for five hundred years and more, whatever the first and highest authority of the Apostolic See handed down to posterity for confirming the truth of catholic faith, maintaining the peace [Col. 1341D] of the holy and universal Church, or advancing the honor of good morals, the holy Church of Canterbury should preserve inviolate and preach among its subjects throughout all parts of Britain. Who, then—even the greatest adversary of our side—would dare confess that within the space of so many years he has learned anything else concerning our Church? Indeed, to speak with your leave, whoever claims to know the sequence of our Church’s ancient histories finds such enduring and perpetual goodwill between the Apostolic See and the Church of Canterbury that he would judge them no longer as though two churches—the greater one and the lesser one—but, so far as the common will of authority and obedience is concerned, would consider them one and the same [Col. 1342A]. For among Christians, just authority and the willing service of obedience readily make many minds into one. Moreover, what Rome supplied to Canterbury, Canterbury willingly and beneficently supplied to all Britain.

Why, then, has the gold grown dim and the finest color changed? By the craft and accusations of a few men your eminence has been disturbed; and through rumors of novelties the harmony of so great duration has begun, weakened for a while, to fail. And unless, by God’s permission, the wickedness of these present days had become so great, it would have been unworthy that the novelty of accusers should so easily proceed to our injury and throw into confusion the unity of Christian peace.

Moreover, since it is written: “Do not transgress the boundaries [Col. 1342B] which your fathers set,” it is irreligious for the bishop of York to extend one step beyond the measure of his Church and the rule of ancient custom by a new presumption. On the other hand, it will be a debt and a disgrace of eternal ignominy to the bishop of Canterbury if he diminishes anything of the privileges of his Church and, by consenting through his own negligence, permits it to be stripped in his days of what he finds it rightly invested with from ancient times. “I would rather,” says blessed Gregory, “suffer any adversities than that the Church of Peter should decline in my time.”

Since Paul says, “Let every soul be subject to the higher powers,” the bishop of Canterbury asks nothing undue from the bishop of York, except that he owe him the canonical humility of submission which it is faithfully established that his predecessors owed to the predecessors [Col. 1342C] of the former. Hence blessed Gregory says: “Let all things which antiquity established be preserved unviolated.” Surely it is unknown to no wise person of whose head he is a member, who, through the vanity of his own encroachment, wears down the right of another Church; and to whom he is subject by the ordinance of Christian institution, against whom he strives to set himself contrary to the law of righteousness. For it is indeed the Apostle’s pronouncement: “He who resists authority resists God’s ordinance.”

This, therefore—this, most serene Father—is what the whole Church of Canterbury laments: as has been said, the unprecedented insolence of a few men proceeds to our injury. And a place which has hitherto possessed some degree of religious standing through the favor of our Church will, at the end of days, by the audacity of its own invention, detract from our right. Certainly we are not moved without cause, because the remotest corner, so to speak, of our country has brought the burden of dissension into the Church of God and would abolish the eminence, so enduring, of the Church of Canterbury. If York hitherto does not know what benefits Canterbury has conferred upon it during more than four hundred years, or what Canterbury itself was owed, let them read the public and ancient histories of the English people, investigate the privileges of both the Churches of York and Canterbury, and not introduce into truth corners which it does not possess. If they do not believe the ordinances and writings of the ancient Fathers, neither will they believe our words.

“We wonder,” they say, [Col. 1343A] “in what institutions of the ancients they glory; especially since blessed Gregory, who first provided the office of Christianity for the English people and established the laws and customs of our Churches, seems to have appointed in England two pallia, two metropolitan sees—namely London and York—and two archbishops. After Augustine’s death he laid upon them this distinction: that the one first ordained should be held first. Thus he seems indeed to have intended that London, rather than Canterbury, should be called and should be the metropolis.”

From this the truth is clear to the wise: the transfer of a metropolitan see to another place was not, nor ought it to have been, the removal of ancient dignity from the other see to which it had not been transferred. But the metropolitan see was found to have been transferred to Canterbury neither before that decree nor after it [Col. 1343B]. Therefore it does not concern us at all what distinction is made between London and York, provided that canonical reverence toward Canterbury is maintained by each of them.

For in the Ecclesiastical History of the English people, which the venerable priest Bede recounts in a brilliant and most truthful style, it is clearer than light that, while Augustine and his companions preached the word of God to the people of Canterbury, both their king and that people, abandoning the rite of paganism, joined themselves by faith to the unity of the holy Church of Christ. Nor did the king delay in giving to his teachers a site in his metropolitan city of Canterbury appropriate to the rank of their see, while also bestowing upon them necessary possessions of various kinds.

Meanwhile the man of God Augustine came to Arles, and there, in accordance with the commands he had received from holy Father Gregory, was ordained archbishop for the English people. Returning thence to Britain, now archbishop not of London but of Canterbury, he immediately sent to Rome the priest Laurence and the monk Peter, to report to blessed Pope Gregory that the English people had received the faith of Christ and that he had been made bishop not of London but of Canterbury; and at the same time he sought the Pope’s advice concerning questions which seemed necessary. Without delay he received answers appropriate to his inquiry, which Bede also judged it useful to insert in his History.

It should further be known that at that time in London and its neighboring people, not yet converted to the faith, as the same historian records, authority was held not by the king himself but by a certain [Col. 1343D] nephew of Æthelberht, king of the people of Canterbury, although he was subject to the power of that same Æthelberht. But Augustine, Bede testifies, when he had received the episcopal see in the royal city, as we have said, restored there, supported by royal aid, a church which he had learned had been built there in ancient times by Roman believers; he consecrated it in the name of the Holy Savior, and there established a dwelling for himself and all his successors.

After this, those who, as stated, had been sent to Rome returned and brought back to Augustine that most famous letter of blessed Father Gregory, in which he seems to have made a distinction concerning the often-mentioned see of London. To ensure that no uncertainty might remain concerning the sense of this distinction, John the Roman deacon, writing in the *Life of Blessed Gregory* to Pope John, says as follows: “Blessed Gregory,” he says, “sent Augustine the pallium, commanding him to ordain twelve bishops under his metropolitan see of Kent, and to send one bishop each to London and York. These men, likewise consecrating twelve bishops under themselves, should receive the pallium from the Apostolic See; and after Augustine’s death, he among them who should first have merited to consecrate [a bishop] was to be held first.”

In accordance with this judgment of a prudent man, blessed Gregory by no means indicated that anything of the primacy or dignity which he had granted Augustine, as apostle of that people, by the authority of the Apostolic See, ought to be withdrawn from Augustine’s successors. Indeed, from his own time down to the present, the investiture of the bishops of Canterbury has held this without interruption [Col. 1344B].

Finally, in the same passage blessed Gregory says: “We desire you to send to the city of York a man whom you shall judge fit to ordain, so that, if that city together with the neighboring districts receives the word of God, he too may ordain twelve bishops and enjoy metropolitan honor.” Yet neither Augustine, nor Laurence, nor Mellitus—the third archbishop of Canterbury after Augustine—sent anyone to York to be ordained bishop. But Justus, the fourth after him, consecrated Bishop Paulinus and sent him as a preacher to the province of York.

Concerning that Justus, I should like to know whether they assert that the bishop of York was of lesser dignity in relation to him than Augustine decreed he would be in relation to himself, or of the same dignity: for Justus did what Augustine ought to have done, though perhaps could not [Col. 1344C] do. “Of precisely the same dignity,” they will say, “because the difference of persons is no impediment where the same will and authority accomplish the same act”—yet in such a way that Paulinus’s successors should likewise be reckoned in relation to Justus’s successors as they were decreed to be in relation to Augustine’s successors.

Augustine therefore had at least one successor whom the Church of York both had and ought to have as primate. But Paulinus converted the people to whom he was sent from the error of paganism, received the pallium from the Apostolic See, and established an episcopal chair at York; yet at that time he created no bishop in the province. Afterwards, when Justus died, Honorius succeeded him as bishop of Canterbury. Then, when the affairs of the Northumbrians were thrown into confusion and Paulinus saw that nowhere was there any protection except in flight, he returned to his mother Church of Canterbury and was received with great honor by Archbishop Honorius.

At that time the Church of Rochester, which until then had been subject not only to Canterbury’s spiritual authority but also to its temporal lordship, had no pastor. Therefore the aforesaid Paulinus, at the invitation and command of Archbishop Honorius, undertook and held its care until, in his own time, he too ascended to the heavenly kingdom with the glorious fruit of his labour. Dying in that Church, he also left there the pallium which he had received from the Roman pope. Hence it is plain even to simple hearers that Augustine had no other successor equal to himself in all his primacy [Col. 1345A]—unless perhaps the men of York say that their Paulinus was not subject while he was theirs, but was subject because he afterwards became bishop of Rochester. Certainly, whatever he did bore the character of subjection, and what he received was a distinguished benefit of the Church of Canterbury. Finally, throughout that entire history of the venerable priest Bede, it is certain that York possessed no stability either in faith or religion except by the benefit and grace of the Church of Canterbury. Indeed, until these times of the Northmen, it scarcely ever established clerics or monks, produced no bishop in its province, and did not even provide burial for its own pontiffs.

Meanwhile, after the departure of Paulinus, the province of the Northumbrians wavered in religion [Col. 1345B] and faith. Accordingly, at the request of Oswald, the king beloved by God, the Scots sent into England Aidan, of blessed memory, consecrated bishop; he first received an episcopal see on the island of Lindisfarne, and, circumstances having later changed, he who was then called bishop of Lindisfarne is now called, and is, bishop of Durham. After him the Scots likewise sent, one by one, as many as four bishops to the same island. These Scots must not be passed over, because, according to the decree of the blessed Father Gregory, they were suffragans of the Archbishop of Canterbury.

For in that often-mentioned letter, after sufficient treatment of the distinction between the bishops of London and York, from which so great a controversy is stirred, blessed Gregory adds to Augustine as follows [Col. 1345C]:

> “But let your Fraternity have subject to it—not only those bishops whom it shall ordain, nor only those ordained through the bishop of York—but also all the priests of Britain, through the authority of God our Lord Jesus Christ.”

And in his answers to the same man he says:

> “Over the bishops of Gaul we grant you no authority; but we commit to your Fraternity all the bishops of the Britains, so that the unlearned may be taught, the weak strengthened by persuasion, and the perverse corrected by authority.”

He uses “Britains” in the plural because of the different provinces of the same island and the divisions of languages. For when Bede described the character of Britain, he said:

> “This island at present, according to the number of books in which the divine law was written, searches out and confesses one and the same knowledge of the highest truth and true sublimity in the languages of five peoples: namely, of the English, Britons, Scots, Picts, and Latins; the last being made common to all the rest through the study of the Scriptures.” [Col. 1345D]

Again, in the third book of the same History:

> “Finally, Oswald received under his dominion all the nations and provinces of Britain which are divided among four languages: those of the Britons, Picts, Scots, and English.”

And repeatedly in the same volume Bede distinguishes between the Scots who inhabit Britain and those who inhabit Ireland. Therefore blessed Gregory declared the bishops of Scotland to be suffragans of the Church of Canterbury—namely those whom, by that authority of the apostolic see, he decreed to be bishops established before blessed Augustine’s arrival in England by Britons and Scots converted long ago. Of them, as is there read:

> “Augustine, at the beginning of his episcopate, summoned very many to a conference with him, fraternally exhorting them to undertake, in Catholic peace with him, the common labour of evangelising the nations for the Lord. But after a long dispute they refused to give assent to Augustine and his companions. At last, a blind man was brought into the midst by agreement of both parties; and by his enlightenment it was inferred that whatever Augustine asserted was true. Yet they replied that they would do none of those things asserted, nor would they acknowledge him as archbishop.” [Col. 1346A]

Thus it came about, as Augustine warned and foretold, that they afterwards suffered, with their own people, the most severe punishment for their perversity, because they refused usefully to obey the arguments of truth.

And Bede continues concerning Laurence, Augustine’s successor:

> “Finally, he took care not only of the new Church gathered from the English, but also sought to bestow pastoral concern upon the peoples of the old inhabitants of Britain, and likewise upon the Scots who inhabit the island of Ireland, near Britain.”

The Church of Canterbury never afterwards ceased to exercise that pastoral concern, with both benefit and primacy, for all Britain and Ireland—unless now, when everything is being corrected into something different and better by the new and most subtle doctors of the Church of York [Col. 1346B].

After Honorius’s death, Deusdedit was received as sixth bishop of the Church of Dorobernia [Canterbury]. In his time a certain man named Ceadda, of great and devout simplicity, was chosen to the episcopate of the Church of York. When he came to Dorobernia to be consecrated, he found that Archbishop Deusdedit had already departed this life. Therefore he turned aside to one of Deusdedit’s suffragans, the only orthodox bishop remaining in all Britain, and, consecrated by him, returned to York.

Meanwhile, while Dorobernia was vacant, a certain Wilfrid, chosen by the king of the Northumbrians, was sent to Gaul; having been consecrated, he returned to England. Thus both the king of Kent [Col. 1346C] and the king of the Northumbrians, although the latter had already obtained the consecration of two bishops in his province, feared that all Britain, newly converted to the Christian religion, was wavering because Canterbury lacked an archbishop. By common agreement they sent to the apostolic see, to be consecrated, an elected priest named Wighard. He was excellently received by Pope Vitalian, but, when a pestilence arose there, he died abroad.

After his death, a monk of great virtue named Theodore, born at Tarsus in Cilicia, endowed with both Greek and Latin, and richly furnished with both secular philosophy and ecclesiastical wisdom, was chosen and consecrated by the pope himself. Accompanied by Abbot Adrian, a man of the greatest wisdom, he was sent as archbishop not only of Dorobernia, but, as Bede repeatedly recalls, of all Britain [Col. 1346D].

The aforesaid historian elegantly describes the renown of his praiseworthy life and supreme dignity:

> “For, to say it briefly, so great a spiritual advance began in the Churches of the English during his episcopate as they had never before been able to attain. Nor since the English came to Britain were there ever happier times: they had kings most valiant and Christian, a terror to all barbarian nations; the desires of all were fixed upon the joys of the heavenly kingdom newly heard of; and whoever wished to be instructed in sacred reading had teachers readily available to teach them.”

Theodore therefore came to his Church, sent from no other source but the apostolic see, accompanied by Adrian, as Bede relates. Adrian, acting as his fellow-worker, carefully watched lest Theodore, after the Greek manner, introduce anything contrary to truth, faith, or the Church into the Church over which he presided [Col. 1347A]. Immediately, after traversing the whole island wherever English peoples dwelt—for he was most gladly received and heard by all—he spread a right rule of life among clergy and people alike; he changed what needed changing and corrected what needed correction. Through his primacy and teaching, both the state of the Churches and the number of bishops increased. He was the first among the archbishops of Dorobernia, as Bede testifies in these same words, to whom the whole Church of the English agreed to render submission.

[Col. 1347C] Where then was this new and wondrous enterprise of the men of York, which in these latest days wickedly strives to seize what the Church of Canterbury has deserved to possess inviolate for more than four hundred years? Neither history teaches, nor memory preserves, any time throughout so long a period when the Church of Canterbury is said to have been stripped of its primacy—unless it is now, when York’s novelty is raised vigorously and successfully to our injury. By the authority either of blessed Gregory or of the sacred canons we have learned that whatever one Church has deserved to hold unharmed even for thirty or forty years ought not afterwards to be lost through another Church’s wrongdoing. Yet for us, most miserable of all men [Col. 1347D], not even the duration of four hundred years will be able to help.

It must plainly be confessed that, according to the prophet, many have passed through, and the knowledge of the new men of York is manifold. If they wish, let them confess and proclaim that we belong to them, that the Church of Canterbury is enslaved to their service; let both their will and presumption stand to them as reason. Or let them say at what time, and by whose authority, the Church of York shook off this submission. For after blessed Theodore until now, the Church of Canterbury has deservedly merited to retain both benefit and primacy.

But meanwhile let us see, as Bede reports, what blessed Theodore did regarding York and its province: what he accomplished there for Christian religion, for faith, and for ecclesiastical and canonical order [Col. 1348A]—unless perhaps they wish to annul everything he ordained because, in their absence, indeed before they yet existed, he presumed to ordain anything.

Thus Theodore, hearing that Ceadda, bishop of York, had been ordained with non-Catholic bishops assisting, deposed him. But because Ceadda was a man of venerable life and remarkable religion, Theodore later reconciled him canonically and appointed him for a time to a Church in the province of Dorobernia, now called Chester. The aforesaid venerable man Wilfrid administered the episcopal see of the city of York; he was bishop not only of York but also of all the Northumbrians.

When this same Wilfrid, owing to causes which had arisen, had been driven from his bishopric through Theodore’s authority at the insistence of King Ecgfrith [Col. 1348B], Theodore, unwilling that the province of the Northumbrians should lack the consolation of bishops, ordained two bishops and placed one over the Church of York and the other over that of Lindisfarne. At a fitting time he later added three others in suitable places within the same province; and when some of them died, he substituted others of his choosing. How many good things Theodore did there, how often he convened councils, and how many monasteries he established through his disciples, is clearer than daylight to see in the ecclesiastical history of the English.

After King Ecgfrith had been killed, Theodore himself restored the aforesaid Wilfrid, who had been removed from the bishopric of Chester—which Wilfrid himself had first founded at Selsey after converting the entire province of the South Saxons to faith in Christ—to be bishop of York and of the whole province of the Northumbrians [Col. 1348C]. He removed those whom he himself, as we have said, had long ago appointed to the same province when Wilfrid was expelled. After Theodore’s translation to heaven, his successor Berhtwald, Archbishop of Canterbury, convened a general council in the diocese of York and removed the often-mentioned Wilfrid from his place and bishopric on account of an act of disobedience committed against the Church of Canterbury. Later, admonished by Pope John of Rome, he restored him to all his possessions. Wilfrid then survived four years in peace and in the fifth went to the Lord, as Saint Michael the Archangel promised him when he was returning from Rome and fell ill at Meaux, a city of Gaul.

Therefore no wise person can doubt that both Theodore and his successor possessed primacy in York and its province, since they repeatedly appointed and restored bishops in those same places, and since all, as Bede testifies, agreed to render them submission [Col. 1348D].

Thus far the venerable Bede recounts the faith of our people, the first beginnings of its Church, and its ancient succession. But the men of York seem to claim for themselves no little on the basis of a kind of equality, since Pope Honorius judged that the bishop of Canterbury and the bishop of York should agree thus: when one of them departed this life, the survivor ought to ordain another in the deceased man’s place. Indeed, it is established that this has hitherto been observed: whenever the bishop of York was to be consecrated by the bishop of Canterbury [Col. 1349A], he came for consecration wherever the bishop of Canterbury commanded; or whenever the bishop of Canterbury was to be consecrated by the bishop of York, the consecrator came to the place where the bishop of Canterbury commanded.

Therefore no equality of parity is to be proclaimed where, by time, primacy, care, benefit, authority, and the uninterrupted duration of investiture, one party rightfully claims the whole. And, unless I am mistaken, neither history nor memory provides the men of York with anything by which they can contradict all these points. Christian ears therefore perceive clearly what rash audacity it is for a daughter to wish to rebel against her mother, from whose ministry she has always received the milk and grace of her religion. York thus proudly attempts to take away from Canterbury what is owed to it by so great a claim of ancient subjection [Col. 1349B].

Blessed Gregory says:

> “It is exceedingly grave for priests to usurp anything for themselves contrary to ancient custom. The religion of Christian truth is to prefer humble subjection where it is fitting over proud equality with superiors where it is unfitting.”

“They say, ‘That subjection lasted while the Church of York lacked a pallium.’” Indeed, I reply, as is found in the ancient chronicles of the English, it continued for one hundred and twenty-five years without a pallium. What could be maintained for so long a time ought not lightly to be disregarded. And if the Church of York deserved to be nourished by Canterbury, it should not then be ungrateful for the benefit; rather, it should be all the more humble and beholden to its mother’s support. The cruelty of fledglings is commonly remarked upon when, after they have grown, they aim at their mother’s throat. And the Lord says through the prophet: “I have nourished and exalted sons, but they have despised me” [Col. 1349C].

Moreover, even if, after the restoration of the pallium, it deserved in some degree to grow, it did not grow so much that it could stand on its own. For how can he rightly be called a metropolitan or archbishop to whom no province of bishops is suffragan? “It has,” they say, “Lindisfarne, which is also Durham; it has Glasgow.” Apart from this present time of the Northmen, I plainly confess that in earlier times the Archbishop of York never had either Lindisfarne or Glasgow as a suffragan.

But let the men of York say: what Archbishop of York ever appointed a bishop? Whom did he ever consecrate in his province? Rather, if it may be said without offence to them [Col. 1349D], the Churches of Ripon and Hexham, which the Church of Canterbury established, the Church of York deprived by the usurpation of temporal power. As for Glasgow, it need only be briefly stated that it is the bishopric of the ancient Britons, whom blessed Father Gregory decreed individually to be subject to the bishop of Canterbury. The bishop of that Church, as their elders relate, was accustomed, until these times of the Northmen, to be consecrated either by the bishop of the Scots or by that of the Welsh Britons. Moreover, it has already been shown clearer than daylight by whom the bishop of Lindisfarne used to be appointed or consecrated. But what concern is it of the men of York meanwhile to provide for the institutions of the ancients?

Let them boldly invade and say: “Others have laboured, and we enter into their labours. Naboth has been stoned; let us possess his vineyard, with no one hindering.” But let it be so: let York have two suffragan bishops [Col. 1350A]. If either or both die, it is not clear how York, left alone, could canonically replace others—unless perhaps, whenever it pleases, it orders either the Archbishop of Canterbury or his provincials to be summoned, and, as they arrive more swiftly than a word spoken, York appoints its own bishops.

“They say, ‘Blessed Gregory decrees that the bishop of York ought to ordain twelve bishops, who are afterwards to be subject to his jurisdiction.’” Let the lord of York have twelve, or thirteen, or however many bishops he himself has appointed and consecrated. At least let him graciously leave to Canterbury those whom Canterbury established and long possessed without the revival of accusations. “But after the pallium was restored,” they say, “did the Archbishop of York have no suffragan?” If he had, let them show, by the history of truth or the record of testimony, the investiture of any bishop under him before these times of the Northmen.

Finally Alcuin, also called Albinus, the most holy and ancient teacher of Emperor Charles, writing to Æthelhard, Archbishop of Canterbury, says among other things [Col. 1350B]:

> “Let ecclesiastical dignity everywhere be exalted, and let the holy see which was first in faith be first in holiness and honour. It has indeed been partly torn apart, not, as it seems, by reasonable consideration, but by a certain desire for power. If it could be peacefully reunited and the division repaired, this seems good to be done with the counsel of all Christ’s priests; so that then he may not be deprived of the pallium during his lifetime, although the ordination of bishops should revert to the holy and first see.”

Alcuin also testifies in the same letter that this division of the Church and the aforesaid restoration of the pallium resulted from invaders of the kingdom. For Pope Leo too, in the course of that usurpation, makes this clear in writing to Coenwulf, king of the Mercians, concerning the peoples of the English:

> “Concerning the letter which the most reverend and holy Æthelhard sent us, as your Excellency requested, we gave his Holiness a fuller answer, as was fitting. For we judged that apostate cleric who had ascended the throne to be like Julian; we rejected and anathematised him as corrupted, in order to expel him from the most wicked kingdom and to provide for the salvation of his soul. For this reason we greatly praised our brother, the aforesaid archbishop, because he laid down his life for the orthodox faith.” [Col. 1350C]

Behold: by ancient and hitherto unbroken custom, Rome blesses Canterbury for defending the orthodox faith and marks the invader of the kingdom as an apostate—the man by whose agency another, who ought not to have been invested with a pallium, was so invested against the due honour of the Church of Canterbury. Behold: the teacher of another and far-off empire calls it the first see by a name long current in the world, and judges that, while the pallium remains, the ordination of bishops ought to revert to the first see. Yet at the end of the ages the Church of York hastens, by new rashness against an ancient and unbroken custom, to disinherit that see [Col. 1351A].

O marvellous and unheard-of perversity—if the audacity of usurped rashness prevails more than the faithful memory of enduring and unshaken truth! It was never the custom, nor a newly introduced practice, of our Church to presume new or customary things against ancient ordinances. As we have learned from the authority of ancient histories, so we believe and therefore speak. This was the primary excellence of the Church of Canterbury throughout the whole age of the English, O most blessed and uniquely venerable Father!

But whatever agreement has existed between the men of Canterbury and York throughout this entire time of the Northmen, present and living memory will declare. For when England had been conquered by the Northmen and, as was said above, Stigand deposed, the Church of Canterbury was vacant. Lanfranc, abbot of Caen, was chosen archbishop: a most reverend man, supremely skilled in both divine and secular philosophy, and a most learned master of all Latin learning [Col. 1351B]. Consecrated in his own see by his clergy, he invited Thomas, the bishop-elect of York—a man of honourable chastity and sound learning—to come to the first see of Canterbury for consecration. Thomas came, but, when called upon, delayed to make the profession. At length he made it and was consecrated.

Meanwhile both came to Rome and presented themselves before Pope Alexander regarding their pallia. It might seem arrogant to say how great was the reverence then shown to Lanfranc at the apostolic see, or with what submission Lanfranc, throughout all his days, followed the command of apostolic majesty. Having received their pallia, Thomas brought before the pope a complaint concerning the profession which he had sought and made. Lanfranc, for his part, produced the privileges of his Church appropriate to the place and time. The lord pope, after mature deliberation, ordered each to return home and the division to be settled by gathering the elders—both bishops and nobles—of Britain together, through their recollection and the testimony of ancient histories. When this had been done, nothing else could be determined but what the ancient custom of the Churches, as we have stated, both maintained and established. Therefore Thomas, taught the truth of the matter hitherto unknown to him [Col. 1351C], humbly sought pardon and was reconciled to Lanfranc and the first see.

At the time of that reconciliation every possible future occasion of dispute was removed. Then for the first time the bishop of the Church of Lindisfarne became a suffragan of the metropolitan of York, with Lanfranc’s consent. This was so only in order that no scruple concerning the making of the profession should remain in future, and that Canterbury’s first faith might endure in the ancient honour of its primacy. Accordingly Pope Alexander wrote, among other things sent to Lanfranc:

> “We have received from certain persons coming from your regions to the thresholds of the holy apostles Peter and Paul that certain clerics, having joined to themselves the counsel of temporal power—that is, of laymen—and filled with a diabolical spirit, are attempting to expel the monks from the Church of the Holy Saviour at Dorobernia, which is the metropolis of all Britain, and to establish clerics there.” [Col. 1352A]

Thomas of York consecrated three bishops, succeeding one another in turn, in the Church of Lindisfarne, one of whom survives even today. Yet he did not consecrate them in his own city, for he could not do so alone, but where the Church of Canterbury allowed within its own province and supplied the assistance of its bishops.

After this Lanfranc died in a good old age, and Anselm, abbot of Bec, of blessed memory, was chosen in his place. A divine radiance of spiritual and incomparable wisdom illuminated Anselm’s life, glorious in miracles [Col. 1352B]. Thomas of York came to ordain him in his metropolitan city of Dorobernia and consecrated him primate of all Britain. His obedience, humility, and faith towards the apostolic see are attested by the persecutions, exiles, and dangers which he endured for the liberty of the Roman Church, as nearly the whole world knew.

When William Rufus, the most cruel king of the English, compelled Anselm to renounce Pope Urban, Anselm almost alone with his Church in all England did not stain the splendour of the Roman name. Therefore, among other things he endured, this lord Thomas of York, fearing neither God nor respecting fidelity to Roman majesty, at the command of the aforesaid king, with sacrilegious speech renounced fraternity with the Christian and holy man [Col. 1352C].

After Thomas’s death, a certain Gerard succeeded him. It is better to be silent concerning his learning, life, morals, and most wretched death than to recount anything offensive to Christian ears. Meanwhile the apostolic see was steadfastly negotiating with the king of England concerning the investitures of churches. Pope Paschal of good memory, writing to Archbishop Anselm, had prudently decreed that the investitures of Churches should not be given through the hands of laymen, and then added:

> “Teach these things as you know to be expedient for your primacy, which indeed we confirm to your Fraternity as full and entire as it is known to have been possessed by your predecessors.”

Again Paschal spoke to Anselm concerning confirmation of that primacy:

> “Formerly, in letters sent to you from the apostolic see, we granted you the primacy of the Church of Canterbury as full as it is known to have been possessed by your predecessors. But now, granting your petitions, we confirm by this present letter to you and to your lawful successors that same primacy, and whatever dignity or power is known to pertain to that holy Church of Canterbury or Dorobernia.” [Col. 1352D]

But Gerard, having received the pallium from Rome and returned to Britain, lied grievously against the decree of the lord pope in accordance with the king’s will. In the faith by which a bishop ought to live, he swore that the lord pope had, contrary to his own decree, granted to the king of the English the investitures of churches. Letters both of Anselm to Paschal and of Paschal to Anselm survive on this matter.

Gerard of York presumed to attempt these things and others like them against the Roman Church, while Anselm of Canterbury did not fear gladly to suffer persecutions and exile for it. Woe to my sins, through which whatever my predecessors most deservedly won is reckoned against me as evil, while Lord Thurstan of York redeems solely by injury to our side whatever his predecessors did wickedly. Or, if his predecessors’ guilt ought not to be imputed to him, the virtue and justice of my predecessors ought not to profit me. For even if Ralph’s sins are so great that he ought to suffer such things, Augustine, Theodore [Col. 1353A], Lanfranc, and Anselm committed no sins such that they deserve to suffer these things in these last times.

Gerard had sworn to Anselm that he would make the required profession, but, deceptive in heart as he was, delayed to do so. He saw himself meanwhile prospering with the king in his own course, while Lord Anselm was afflicted by injuries and human hatred in the way of God and faith in the apostolic see. Pope Paschal of blessed memory then wrote to Gerard:

> “Although we know that you have acted perversely against us—indeed, against your mother, the holy Roman Church—nevertheless by this letter we command you not to neglect to make your profession to our venerable brother Anselm, bishop of Canterbury. For we have heard that a predecessor of yours once stirred up contention on this very matter, and that, when it had been discussed in the presence of Pope Alexander II, a determination was reached by his command. After various disputes, he made the same profession to Lanfranc, his predecessor, and to Lanfranc’s successors. Therefore we wish, by God’s authority, that what was determined at that time be kept firm and inviolate.” [Col. 1353B]

Meanwhile Gerard of York died a wretched and sudden death, and a very chaste and well-educated man, Thomas the younger, was appointed in his place. Not long afterwards, when Anselm, the most Christian archbishop, had died in peace, Thomas made the profession and was consecrated for the holy and first Church of Canterbury in London by the bishop of that city.

Thomas then ordained a certain Briton as bishop for the Church of Glasgow, which had for almost beyond memory lacked the consolation of a bishop [Col. 1353C]. Concerning that bishop it must be understood that, as stated above, if he is bishop of the ancient Britons, then by the decrees of blessed Father Gregory he is a suffragan of the Church of Canterbury. But if, perhaps because of the proximity of provinces, he ought to be regarded as the same bishop of the Picts, although both place and people have changed, he is nonetheless suffragan to the Church of Canterbury, since, as Bede testifies, he was appointed and established by Archbishop Theodore.

Yet, as is found in the Acts of the holy men Columba—the priest and abbot who, according to Bede, first preached Christ in Britain to the peoples of the Scots and Picts before the coming of blessed Augustine—and the venerable Bishop Kentigern, who first presided over the Church of Glasgow [Col. 1353D], this is not the bishop of Whithorn whom Theodore appointed. Rather, he was one of those ancient bishops of the Britains whom, as has often been said, blessed Gregory individually subjected to the Church of Canterbury.

This, therefore, is the order of the ancient custom of the Churches of Canterbury and York, which not by a momentary and novel rite but by an unbroken practice of more than four hundred years, by the authority and prudent dispensation of holy fathers in Christian simplicity, has accepted and maintained, O most blessed pope and uniquely venerable father. This is what the Church of Canterbury seeks: not something extorted by the violence of pride, but what is owed by the obligation of Christianity and obedience [Col. 1354A].

Indeed, it is a demand of justice, not a fault of violence, for priests not to neglect to vindicate whatever the use of liberty and the privilege of grace require for their Church. Accordingly Augustine says in the first book addressed to Simplicianus:

> “Who does not see that no one can be charged with injustice who exacts what is owed to him, nor certainly one who refuses to give away what is owed to him?”

And who, I ask, with sober speech could rebuke the lord of York as though he had accepted a calamity and insult, if he wished to pay to the first see and holy Church of Canterbury whatever is found formerly to have been due by both the long duration of custom and the merit of justice? Thus the eleventh Council of Toledo, chapter [Col. 1354B], says:

> “Everyone who is about to enter ecclesiastical ranks shall not receive consecration to his office until he promises the binding obligation of his undertaking.”

And certainly Ralph the sinner is not rightly to be charged with any disgrace, since he is bound by the bond of Christian faith not to overthrow the pre-eminence of liberty of his Church, whose governance he has received, though unworthily—an eminence which so many of his most holy and wise predecessors wished and were able to maintain for so long. For Roman pontiffs are accustomed, before their own consecration, to profess that they will observe without deviation the decrees of their predecessors; and yet someone dares impose upon me the obligation to destroy the privileges of my Church.

If, perhaps upon some occasion, I presume even to touch so great an outrage [Col. 1354C], it is certain that I shall be guilty of spiritual adultery, because I have made the first faith void. Hence blessed Gregory writes:

> “It is exceedingly grave, and plainly contrary to priestly purpose, to wish to confound the privileges granted long ago to any Church.”

And Pope Zosimus testifies that not even the supreme pontiff may act contrary to the traditions of the holy Fathers:

> “The authority even of this see cannot grant or alter anything contrary to the ordinances of the Fathers.” [Col. 1354D]

Let the supreme prudence of the apostolic see judge how worthy of the goodwill of truth are those by whose cunning and denunciation your ingratitude against us has gained strength, so that it has deigned to begin, concerning the consecration of my lord the bishop of York, what none throughout the time of your predecessors was accustomed even to begin. And may God prevent the envy of those who maliciously say that Canterbury transgresses against us from creeping into your Majesty: for Canterbury justly demands the lawful subjection of the bishop of York according to the limits of paternal ordinances.

They are mistaken, I say, because this is what Canterbury has deserved; this, with all due regard for the benevolence of the exalted Roman see, it has held not against Peter but with Peter and under Peter for many thousands of days; this was established by the investiture of ancient custom and the venerable majesty of antiquity. And, to use meanwhile the words of blessed Gregory:

> “Since it is clear to all whence the holy faith came forth into the regions of the Britains, when the humility of the Church of Canterbury reclaims the ancient custom of the apostolic see [Col. 1355A], what else does the good offspring do but return to the bosom of its mother?”

In the time of blessed Gregory, a bishop of Ravenna established an ancient custom of his Church concerning the use of the pallium in solemn litanies solely by the sworn testimony of witnesses. Yet neither the history of truth, nor privileges granted by the apostolic see, nor investiture over so long a duration will suffice to help us.

“They say, ‘Though summoned, you were unwilling to come to the lord pope when he was near.’” I was unwilling to come, I reply, because I was unable. God, who chastened me by his will, knows that the distress of my suffering could not endure the commotion and terror of so great a majesty. For illness knows no law.

Therefore, however greatly the violence of my lord the bishop of York and his men may wish to stone me, certainly I shall not give up [Col. 1355C] my vineyard or sell the inheritance of my fathers [Col. 1355B].

“They say, ‘Let us have an indication of truth and expediency: it is easy to show that we owe Canterbury nothing except what every Church owes every Church.’”

All their alleged facility, I say, of which they boast, we have set forth above, most serene lord and most reverend Father! Yet, whatever the extent of their competence, it ought rightly to be examined here, where the records of antiquity and the chronicles of old are held, where the individual regions and places within the provinces can be identified, and where the present recollection of witnesses can be brought forward. Indeed, in secular courts lesser authorities customarily deal in their own court with whatever disputes seem to arise between themselves and their inferiors, nor are they brought before the court of a greater authority before they are found to have violated the truth of justice in their own sphere. Nor is anyone judged obliged to undergo trial until he is restored to that of which he has suffered deprivation without trial. Nor do the sacred canons seem to differ in this respect: they attest that, even for establishing the truth, possession for thirty or forty years is sufficient in ecclesiastical matters. And why do we attempt to make assertions about human beings, when between God and the authorities of the churches there is such a relation that whatever is loosed by their judgment in the court of ecclesiastical religion is believed loosed in heaven, and whatever is bound here is held bound there also?

Therefore it is in no way unworthy of Your Excellency if the Church of Canterbury, which, as is known, received the beginnings of faith from the piety of the Apostolic See, reaped the fruits of virtue, and received increase in religion, deserves within the court of its own province to retain in the Christian faith that which, by the lawful will of your predecessors, it was able to possess for so long a time. Nor should the lord of York, with your permission, resent rendering to the holy Church of Canterbury what his predecessors rendered, humbly attending to this and turning over in his mind with the prophet: “Nor am I better than my fathers.” And let him wisely remember that Christ “scattered kings over the dove,” and that “cursed is he who performs the work of God deceitfully.” Let him understand whose head he follows—the one who said in his heart: “I will ascend above the height of the clouds, and I will be like the Most High.” We covet or invade no one’s possession; we justly claim the boundaries which our fathers established. The Church of Canterbury has always held the giving of the hand (*manus datio*), subjection, and profession of the Church of York; we demand the same because we find it thus possessed. Therefore let the supreme justice of the Holy Apostolic See consider whether that which could be held through so great a span of time ought to be stripped away through the deceitful maneuver of one man.

Remember, with your leave that I say so, what the Apostle says: “Fathers, do not provoke your children to anger.” And, for God’s sake, take care lest what Truth itself cries out should come upon you: “Children shall be betrayed by their parents.” Nor indeed will any wise and well-disposed person acknowledge it to be just that, whenever we are challenged by a suffragan of our jurisdiction, we should go each time to the court of Roman Majesty. Finally, we appeal to the loftiness of your holiness and justice, that you may preserve firm and intact the boundaries of our Church which your fathers established, so that, in its accustomed way, the Church of Canterbury may follow the command and most excellent primacy of all your good will. If this appears useful and not burdensome to you, you can and ought to send here such of your cardinals and of the bishops of Gaul as you choose, in whose presence it may always be established whether the primacy of our Church was as we have stated or not, or whether the men of York possess anything by which they can prove with certainty anything contrary to all these things. Again and again we appeal to Your Majesty: do not, in these latter days, despise the good faith of the holy Church of Canterbury and its excellent obedience toward the supreme and first see of blessed Peter.

May Your Holiness flourish in Christ, most blessed pope and uniquely venerable Father.

## V. Letter of Adalbert, Archbishop of Mainz, to Calixtus

He informs him of what Cono, bishop of Strasbourg, suffered from the emperor after being reconciled to the Church. (1122.)

[MARTÈNE, *Amplissima Collectio*, I, 676.]

To CALIXTUS, his most blessed lord and father of the universal Church, [ADALBERT], by the grace of God and of himself, whatever he is, due obedience with every devotion.

In the obedience owed by humility and devotion, we judged that all matters occurring around us should be reported to the hearing of Your Majesty, so that we may both remove from ourselves the fault of negligence and, so far as our littleness permits, forewarn your serenity concerning matters better known to us. Our brother Cono, bishop of Strasbourg, immediately after the Council of Rheims sought mercy and received absolution from a cardinal of the holy Roman Church.

> [Note: The Council of Rheims was held in 1119, on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of November [20 October]. Fifteen archbishops and more than two hundred bishops attended with the pope, while abbots and others formed an innumerable multitude. Cols. 1357D, 1358D.]

Since he had previously been constantly in the king’s service, we often admonished him to obey the Church of God and thus to advance more profitably. We wrote many times to the canons, urging them to withdraw from his error and return to the unity of Christ’s peace. They, however, not only remained disobedient, but also scorned even to open and read the letters of your authority which we had most recently sent them for that very purpose. But after the bishop was absolved, he withdrew himself from the emperor in heart and body, and, though unjust and sinful in some respect, nevertheless remained a faithful and useful defender of truth in the Church’s service and fidelity. They persecute him in every way and, having lost canonical voice and standing before the judgment of our brethren, surround him with every snare in their power. Seizing this opportunity, the emperor pursued him with such bitter hatred that he stripped him of all his possessions and expelled him from the city.

The emperor accomplished all this because of the settlement of this peace, since previously he had been unable to prevail against the bishop, after the bishop withdrew from him and returned to the Church. For before he returned to the Church, he was reckoned among the emperor’s foremost friends. We say this not because we seek to defend or approve the bishop’s injustice, but because we speak before God: if such unrestricted power to rage against this bishop, whatever kind of man he may be, is granted to the emperor, scandal and intolerable persecution will arise for the other faithful who have remained with the Church of God. Therefore, if it pleased your discernment, the counsel—or rather the most devout supplication—of your humility would be this: that for the present you should refrain from enforcing a sterner discipline for his correction, because in this way your dispensation may restrain the assault of this violent man against the other faithful, while in its proper place and time the Church of God will obtain full justice concerning the aforesaid bishop.

## VI. Second Letter of Adalbert, Archbishop of Mainz, to Calixtus

(1122.)

[MANSI, *Concilia*, XXI, 275.]

To CALIXTUS, his most blessed lord and Father, pontiff of the universal Church, A., by the grace of God and his mercy, whatever he is, due obedience with every devotion.

[Col. 1358A] Hitherto placed amid many great persecutions and distresses, whenever we have written to Your Majesty concerning the person of the lord emperor—what pleased you, what our princes thought, and finally upon what decision they had agreed—we do not doubt that the blessedness of your discerning judgment remembers it. In all these matters we have learned through your letters and envoys that the desire of your piety has always been directed especially toward this: that, through apostolic dispensation, peace and concord might descend upon the whole world particularly in your days, provided that the emperor both gave and received such a peace without obscuring the honor of God and Mother Church, and provided it was acceptable to our lords and fathers the cardinals, who were sent to us from your side for this purpose. We have devoted the strength of all our counsel and judgment to ensuring that so general a good should not be further delayed, to the common benefit of Church and realm.

But because both the Empire and the emperor wished to possess the staff and ring as though by a kind of hereditary right—and because the whole multitude of laypeople of the Empire denounced us as destroyers—we could in no way strip the emperor of these things until, by the common counsel of all, with the brethren present and the lord cardinals who sympathized with our peril, yet feared the Church’s censure and therefore scarcely assented to us, we all together accepted that the Church should make the election in his presence. In doing this we enacted nothing and, far from it, prejudged in no respect the apostolic ordinances and canonical traditions; rather, we reserved everything for your presence and deliberation. For we do not doubt that the commands established by eternal law for protecting and strengthening the liberty … of the Church are in every respect unalterable and fixed. Yet the emperor, paying little heed to the greatness of the danger from which he has escaped through your mercy, and to the fact that the power granted to him, however qualified, still causes obstruction—thus, in the presence of your legates, you will be able to learn from your examination how he has abused the concessions by which he was released.

Accordingly, if through this [lacuna] the Church of God must endure the same [lacuna], whether more grievous, or only the force [lacuna], this alone remains: that, instead of the palm of victory, she should henceforth be subjected to [lacuna] contempt and disgrace. [Col. 1358D] We have not said these things because your circumspect Excellency can be fully forearmed in every respect through us. But because without [lacuna] we desire the liberty of the Church under your authority. Therefore, prostrate at the knees of Your Majesty, we ask, as humbly as justly, that in brother [lacuna], Bishop Rokker, you may deign to recognize the work of the Church, and that your mercy may confirm him whom the Church herself freely and canonically promoted to this height, and may forbid [lacuna]. By expulsion the liberty of the Church is so stifled that a certain layman still occupies his see and, by ravaging the bishopric, persecutes and destroys it; he [lacuna] the faithful [lacuna], who, last of all, did not shrink from investing with ring and staff at the very point of an excommunication that was to bring destruction.

For this reason your clemency ought to remember [lacuna] that, in the service and fidelity of the holy Roman Church, they are still proscribed from their patrimonies and benefices. We have entrusted all this to be conveyed by letter; and many other matters are needed in this holy council, which we ourselves would have brought to you had we not been hindered by illness, as the cardinals know, and had the harshness of the Alps and the difficulties of so many places not beforehand brought danger upon us, especially in these evil days. For we long with longing to see your face before one or the other of us enters upon the way of all flesh.

## Concordat of Worms

(23 September 1122.)

[PERTZ, *Monumenta Germaniae Historica*, *Legum* II, 75.]

### Introduction

We have prepared a new edition of this agreement, by which the dispute that had arisen between Church and Empire was at last settled, with the aid of seven manuscripts of the best standing:

1. Vatican manuscript no. 1984, parchment, folio, of the beginning of the twelfth century, which I used as the basis; then

2. The Imperial Vienna manuscript, among the books of canon law, no. 91, parchment, folio, twelfth century;

3. London, British Museum, Cotton Domitian A. VIII, parchment, twelfth century;

4. London, British Museum, Cotton Claudius A. I, parchment, twelfth century;

5. Saint-Trond, now in the Library of the University of Liège, beginning of the twelfth century;

6. Salzburg manuscript no. 404, parchment, large quarto, beginning of the twelfth century, now preserved in the Imperial Library at Vienna;

7. Bamberg manuscript, beginning of the twelfth or thirteenth century.

Also used were:

**Bbg.** The Paris and Leipzig twelfth-century manuscripts of the *Bamberg Annals*, commonly circulated under the name of Conrad of Ursberg, which agree very closely with manuscripts 5, 6, and 7, together with the editions.

**G.** Goldast’s edition in the *Imperial Constitutions*, superior to the others; and **L.**, Leibniz’s edition in the *Corpus Juris Diplomatici*. I have not recorded, however, readings of lesser importance from these. The Saxon Annalist and Baronius did not seem worthy of being copied again, except from the Bamberg Annals. I was unable to inspect Vatican manuscript II, used by Baronius, but I have added its readings. Moreover, Henry’s diploma, preserved without seal in the Vatican archive (*Armar.* I, case 6, no. 11), is said to bear the date of the ninth day before the Kalends of October [23 September].

## Privilege of Pope Calixtus II

[Col. 1359B] I, Calixtus—

> [Note: At Col. 1359: “Calistus” in 2, 6, Bbg.; “Calixtus” in L.]

bishop, servant of the servants of God, grant to you, my beloved son H., by God’s grace august emperor of the Romans—

> [Note: At Col. 1359: 1 reads “emperor august”; 2, “august emperor”; “you” is absent in 6, 7.]

the elections of bishops and abbots of the German kingdom—

> [Note: At Col. 1359: “theutonici” in 5, 6.]

which belong to your kingdom—

> [Note: At Col. 1359: “your kingdom” in 3.]

to be held in your presence, without simony or any violence; so that, if any disagreement should arise between the parties, you shall give assent and assistance to the sounder party by the counsel or judgment of the metropolitan and the suffragan bishops.

> [Notes: At Col. 1359: “consecrations” in 2; “helections” in 1. “And” for “so that” in 2. “And” for “or” in 2, 6. “Have” for “give” in 6; 2 reads “give assent and assistance.”]

The elected person, moreover, shall receive the regalian rights from you by the sceptre, without any exaction, and shall perform what he owes you by right on their account.

> [Notes: At Col. 1359: 6 reads “the regalia from you by the sceptre without exaction.” “Without all exaction” is absent in 2, 3, 4, 5, 7, Bbg., L, G. “By the sceptre” is absent in 3, 4. Manuscripts 5, 6, 7, Bbg., and L place the clause “excepting all things known to belong to the Roman Church” immediately after “receive,” rather than after “shall perform what he owes.”]

But in the other parts of the Empire, one who has been consecrated shall receive the regalian rights from you within six months, by the sceptre and without any exaction, and shall perform what he owes you by right on their account.

> [Notes: At Col. 1359: “From [the other parts] … shall perform” is absent in 2. “Without all exaction” is absent in 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, Bbg., L, G. “And shall perform what he owes you by right on their account” is absent in 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, Bbg., L.]

Excepting all things known to belong to the Roman Church. Concerning these, if you make complaint to me and ask for assistance, I shall give you assistance according to the obligation of my office. I grant you true peace, and to all who are or have been on your side during the time of this discord.

> [Notes: At Col. 1359: 2 has the variant phrase “complaint to me—if you do so” (*q. m. q. si feceris*). “And ask” is absent in 5, 7, Bbg., L. “My” for “your” in 7, Bbg., L. Bbg., G, and L add: “Given in the year 1122, on the ninth day before the Kalends of October.”]

## Decree of Emperor Henry IV

[Col. 1359C] In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity—

> [Note: At Col. 1359: “In the name of holy and undivided Trinity” is absent in 5, 6, 7, Bbg. Manuscript 7 prefixes: “Given in the year 1122, on the ninth day before the Kalends of October, at the Council of Worms.”]

I, Henry, august emperor of the Romans, for the love of God and of the holy Roman Church and of lord Pope Calixtus, and for the remedy of my soul, relinquish to God and to God’s holy apostles Peter and Paul, and to the holy catholic Church, every investiture by ring and staff; and I grant that canonical election and free consecration shall take place in all churches within my kingdom or Empire.

> [Notes: At Col. 1359: “Calisti” in 2, 6; “Callisti” in L; “of the pope” in 2. At Col. 1361: “of God” is absent in 1. “And the holy catholic Church” in 2. “In” is absent in 2. The clause “which are in my kingdom or Empire” is absent in Bbg. “Canonical election” is absent in 6; “helection” in 1.]

The possessions and regalian rights of blessed Peter which, from the beginning of this discord until the present day, whether in my father’s time or in my own, have been taken away, and which I possess, I restore to that same holy Roman Church; and those which I do not possess I shall faithfully assist in restoring.

> [Notes: At Col. 1361: 6 reads “which I possess, I restore.” “Eydem” in 1. “I restore” is absent in 6. “Abeo” for “I possess” in 1. “Be restored” for “be given back” in 5, 6. “I shall assist” for “I shall help” in 6 and L.]

I shall likewise restore, by the counsel of the princes or by justice, such possessions of all other churches, princes, and other persons, clerical as well as lay, as I possess and which were lost in this war; and for those which I do not possess I shall faithfully assist in their restoration.

> [Notes: At Col. 1361: “Possession” singular in 1; “holy” in 5. The clause “which were lost in this war” is absent in 5, 6, 7, Bbg., L. “War” appears as *querra* in 2 and *werra* in 3, 4. “Lost” appears as *amissa* in 2 and *amissae* in 3, 4. “And” for “or” in 5, 6, 7, Bbg., L. In Bbg., “I shall restore what I possess; what I do not possess, I shall help to restore” is absent. The whole clause “which I do not possess … faithfully assist in restoring” is absent in 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, Bbg.; L has “I shall assist.”]

And I grant true peace to lord Pope Calixtus, to the holy Roman Church, and to all who are or have been on its side. In matters in which the holy Roman Church asks my assistance, I shall faithfully assist; and concerning matters of which it makes complaint to me, I shall render it due justice.

> [Notes: At Col. 1361: “I grant” is absent in 7; “pope” absent in Bbg.; “Calisto” in 2, “Callisto” in L, and omitted in 6 and Bbg.; “and the holy” in 2, 3, 4. The clause “in which the holy Roman Church asks my assistance” is absent in 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, Bbg., L. “I shall assist” appears as *adiuvabo* in 6; the remainder is absent in 5, 6, 7, Bbg. “Makes complaint to me” in 3, 4; L has “concerning which it makes complaint to me.” L reads “I shall render justice,” and its text ends there; so too Vatican II.]

All these things were done by the consent and counsel of the princes whose names are subscribed: Adalbert, archbishop of Mainz; Frederick, archbishop of Cologne; Bruno, archbishop of Trier; H., bishop of Regensburg; O., bishop of Bamberg; Bruno, bishop of Speyer; H., bishop of Augsburg; G., bishop of Utrecht; Ou., bishop of Constance; Herdolf, abbot of Fulda; H., duke; Frederick, duke; S., duke; Bertolf, duke; Margrave Diepold; Margrave Engelbert; Godfrey, count palatine; O., count palatine; Count Berlingarius.

Frederick is “Fredericus” in 3 and F. in 2. Bruno of Trier is absent in 1, 2, G, and 7. H. of Regensburg is “Ardwinus” in 3; “H., bishop of Regensburg” is absent in 7. II, and H. in G; “abbot of Fulda” is *vulnensis* in 1, *fuldensis* in G and Vatican II; Vatican II adds “and other archbishops, bishops, and abbots whose names are not subscribed here. ## First Lateran Council

(27 March 1123.)

[PERTZ, *Monumenta Germaniae Historica*, *Legum* II, 182.]

### Chapter I

Following the examples of the holy fathers and renewing the obligation of our office, we absolutely forbid, in accordance with apostolic authority, anyone to be ordained or promoted in the Church of God for money. If anyone acquires an ordination or promotion in the Church, let him be utterly deprived of the dignity acquired.

> [Note: At Col. 1361: “Acquired” is absent in the manuscript.]

### II

We absolutely forbid persons excommunicated by their own bishops to be received into communion by other bishops, abbots, or clerics.

### III

Let no one be consecrated bishop unless he has been canonically elected. If this is presumed, the consecrated person and the consecrator are condemned without hope of restoration.

### IV

No archdeacon, archpriest, provost, or dean whatsoever shall confer the care of souls or ecclesiastical prebends upon anyone without the bishop’s judgment or consent. Rather, as the holy canons establish, the care of souls and administration of ecclesiastical property shall remain under the bishop’s judgment and authority. If anyone presumes to act contrary to this, or to claim for himself authority belonging to a bishop, let him be excluded from the thresholds of the Church.

### V

We judge invalid the ordinations made by Bordino, the heresiarch, after he was condemned by the Roman Church, and likewise those made afterward by pseudo-bishops ordained through him.

> [Note: At Col. 1363: The manuscript reads “by ordino.”]

### VI

No one shall be appointed provost, archdeacon, or dean unless he is ordained priest or deacon.

### VII

We absolutely forbid priests, deacons, and subdeacons to keep concubines or wives, and to live with other women except those whom the Council of Nicaea permitted to reside with them solely because of kinship: namely, mother, sister, paternal aunt, maternal aunt, or others of this kind concerning whom no just suspicion can arise.

### VIII

Moreover, in accordance with the decree of the most blessed Pope Stephen, we establish that laypersons, however religious they may be, shall have no power whatsoever to dispose of any ecclesiastical property. Rather, according to the canons of the apostles, the bishop shall have care of all ecclesiastical affairs and shall administer them as before God’s gaze.

### IX

If, therefore, any prince or other layperson claims for himself the disposal, dominion, or possession of ecclesiastical property, let him be judged sacrilegious.

> [Note: At Col. 1363: The manuscript reads “ecclesiastical [persons/things]” (*ecclesiasticorum*).]

### X

We forbid unions of blood relatives, since both divine and secular laws prohibit them. Divine laws dealing with this matter not only cast out those born from such unions but call them accursed; secular laws call such persons infamous and exclude them from inheritance. Therefore, following our fathers, we brand them with infamy and judge them to be infamous.

### XI

Furthermore, desiring by God’s grace to preserve undisturbed the possessions of the holy Roman Church, we command and, under the strictness of anathema, forbid any military person to presume to invade or hold by force Benevento, the city of blessed Peter. Whoever presumes otherwise shall be bound by the bond of anathema.

> [Note: At Col. 1363: The manuscript reads “Beneventa.”]

### XII
