To those who set out for Jerusalem and effectively lend their aid to defending the Christian people and defeating the tyranny of unbelievers, we grant remission of their sins; and, as was established by our lord Pope Urban, we have received their houses, households, and all their goods under the protection of blessed Peter and the Roman Church. Whoever presumes, while they remain on that journey, to alienate or take away these things shall be punished by the penalty of excommunication.

> [Note: At Col. 1363: Thus the manuscript.]

### XIII

Those known to have put crosses upon their garments for the Jerusalemite or Spanish expedition and subsequently to have laid them aside, we command by apostolic authority to take up the crosses again and undertake the journey from the approaching Easter until the next Easter. Otherwise, from that time we exclude them from entry into the Church and prohibit the divine offices throughout all their lands, except for the baptism of infants and penance for the dying.

### XIV

We judge that the wicked custom of the Porticans which has hitherto prevailed there must be abolished, by the counsel of our brethren and of the whole curia, and also by the will and consent of the prefect: namely, that the goods of inhabitants of the Portico who die without heirs shall by no means be seized contrary to the deceased person’s disposition. Yet this shall be on the condition that the Porticans henceforth remain faithfully obedient to the Roman Church and to us and our successors.

> [Notes: At Col. 1363: The manuscript reads “or” (*sive*) for “without” (*sine*). “In the future” is absent in the manuscript.]

### XV

In agreement with the canons of the holy fathers, we absolutely forbid and, under the strictness of anathema, prohibit offerings from being taken by laypeople from the most holy and most venerable altar of blessed Peter, of the Savior, and of the round church of Saint Mary, from the church of Saint Nicholas of Bari, Saint Giles, or from the altars or crosses of any other churches. By apostolic authority we also forbid churches to be made into castles or reduced to servitude.

### XVI

Whoever knowingly makes counterfeit coin or deliberately spends it shall, as one accursed, an oppressor of poor people, and a disturber of the city, be separated from the fellowship of the faithful.

### XVII

If anyone presumes to seize Roman pilgrims and other pilgrims visiting the thresholds of the apostles and the shrines of other saints, to despoil them of the goods they carry, or to harass merchants with novel exactions of tolls and transit-dues, let him be deprived of Christian communion until he makes satisfaction.

### XVIII

We absolutely forbid monks to administer anointings, visit the sick, or celebrate public masses.

Examples from Leo to Dioscorus: that Levitical and priestly ordination should be held on the day of the Resurrection, chapter 19.

That ordination may be held on Sunday morning after the Sabbath fast has been continued, chapter 20.

## Works Falsely Attributed to Calixtus

### Notice

(*Literary History of France*, vol. X, p. 532.)

Several writers, even ancient ones—that is, from the thirteenth century onward—have attributed to Calixtus a book of the *Miracles of Saint James*, at the head of which stands a letter bearing that pope’s name. Vincent of Beauvais inserted nearly the whole of it into his *Historical Mirror* (book XXVI, chapter 30); most manuscripts found of it are of the same antiquity. Alberic discusses it at some length in his *Chronicle* (under the year 1118). In succeeding centuries people continued to make Calixtus the author of the book of the *Miracles of Saint James*. Saint Antoninus gave several extracts from it (*Summa historialis*, part II, title 17). Trithemius speaks of it with praise (*On Ecclesiastical Writers*, under the year 1120), saying that Calixtus composed this work carefully and in an elegant style: *Scripsit expolito sermone et maxima diligentia*—“He wrote in polished language and with the greatest care.” He adds that the author, then still a student (*scholaris*), had seen, read, or heard related the miracles that he reports.

The Centuriators of Magdeburg (century XII, pp. 1397–1398) did not fail to seize this occasion to slander this pope and accuse him of having invented false miracles in order to authorize idolatry—thus they characterize the veneration which the Church renders to saints’ relics—in favor of the church of Compostela, which he had just raised to metropolitan rank: *Compostellanam Ecclesiam in archiepiscopatum sublimavit, et pro confirmanda illa idololatria de confictis sancti Jacobi miraculis librum consarcinavit*—“He elevated the Church of Compostela to an archbishopric and, to confirm that idolatry, stitched together a book from fabricated miracles of Saint James.” In speaking this way, these writers failed to notice that their desire to slander led them into contradiction. They assert that Calixtus composed this work after raising Compostela to metropolitan dignity. If that is so, how could he have composed it while still a student, *cum esset adhuc scholaris*—“when he was still a scholar”?

It is unnecessary to pause and enumerate all ancient and modern writers who have attributed the book of the *Miracles of Saint James* to Calixtus. We admit that their number is great; but however great it may be, it remains no less certain that this work was never produced by Calixtus’s pen. What created the illusion was the letter placed at the head of the book. Yet the entire learned world now agrees that this letter was fabricated by an ignorant impostor, who also interpolated the book of the *Miracles of Saint James* in several places. This is the judgment pronounced by the continuators of Bollandus themselves (25 July, p. 43 ff.). But if the letter is supposititious and falsely attributed to Calixtus, as cannot be doubted, the same judgment must necessarily be made concerning the book, which was attributed to him only as a consequence of the letter, whose author he was believed to be.

Originally the work bore no author’s name, as can readily be demonstrated from the copy of the book which Guibert, abbot of Gembloux, found in the abbey of Marmoutier during the time of Abbot Hervé, who resigned in 1187. In Dom Martène’s great collection (vol. I, p. 923), we possess a letter written by this Guibert to Hervé and his religious, thanking them for allowing him to make a copy of the book of the *Miracles of Saint James*. He names no author there and does not attribute it to Calixtus (Mabillon, *Analecta*, vol. II, p. 347). Is it believable that he would have failed to do so if the letter in question had stood at the head of the work? Would he not have expressed to them the satisfaction he felt at discovering in their library a work by that great pope, of whom he had previously had no knowledge? Guibert adds that from the same manuscript he transcribed Turpin’s *History of Charlemagne* and the martyrdom of the celebrated Roland.

This, undoubtedly, is what gave occasion for attributing the book of the *Miracles of Saint James* to Calixtus. It was known that this pope had elevated the archbishopric of Compostela to metropolitan rank; his relations with the new archbishop were known. It was also known that he had made a journey to Saint James. All this supplied the foundation for the fiction and material for the impostor who fabricated the letter. It is even what still persuades many today that Calixtus had a singular devotion to the apostle Saint James. This prejudice, founded solely upon the spurious letter, prevented the continuators of Bollandus from considering the book in question a work falsely attributed to Calixtus; it led them to believe that, while occupying the see of Vienne, or even in his youth, and having a particular devotion to Saint James, he could have compiled some of that holy apostle’s miracles. “I do not deny,” says one of these critics, “that Calixtus, perhaps while he held the Viennese see, or even when he was younger, owing to his singular affection for Saint James, may have collected some of his miracles”: *Non inficior … a Calixto, cum forte Viennensem cathedram obtineret, aut etiam junior esset, pro singulari suo erga sanctum Jacobum affectu, aliqua ipsius miracula collecta fuisse.*

We have seen that the establishment of his brother in Spain was the reason for the journey that Calixtus made there before his elevation to the pontificate. If he later raised the bishopric of Compostela to an archbishopric, this was not from any particular devotion to Saint James; he did so at the request of the king of León, Pons, abbot of Cluny, the cardinal legates in Spain, and the lords of Galicia. Furthermore, no trace of this singular devotion of Calixtus appears either in his *Life* written by Pandulf or in any contemporary author. There would be more basis for attributing to him a singular devotion toward the saints in whose honor he consecrated churches and subsequently endowed those churches with privileges.

The authors of the history of Compostela, whose manuscript the Bollandists cite, wrote only a few years after Calixtus’s death. They maintain profound silence about the collection of the *Miracles of Saint James*, although otherwise they are very exact in relating everything this pope did in favor of the Church of Compostela. That silence, noted by Ambrose Morales (*General Chronicle of Spain*, vol. I, book IX, chapter 1, p. 241), is, according to that Spanish historian, decisive proof that Calixtus did not compile a collection of the *Miracles of Saint James*.

[Col. 1367] We shall not speak of the Compostela manuscript, which is filled with so many errors, anachronisms, and absurdities that, in the judgment of the Bollandists, it would be an insult to Calixtus to attribute to him what it contains. With regard to the collection which Guibert, abbot of Gembloux, had seen and copied at the abbey of Marmoutier, there is ample reason to doubt that it was compiled before Calixtus’s death; for Guibert, abbot of Nogent, who lived in this pope’s time and died in the same year, appears to have had no knowledge of it in the account he gives of a miracle of Saint James (*Monodies*, book III, ch. 8).

We are rather inclined to believe that Blessed John, first abbot of Bonneval and subsequently bishop of Valence (*Ann. Cist.*, year 1114, ch. 1, p. 73; year 1118, p. 96), was the author of the collection. He had made a pilgrimage to Saint James and throughout his life had a particular veneration for that holy apostle; these are established facts. The author of this work directs that it be read not only in churches but also in the refectories of religious houses, which creates a presumption that he himself was a religious (*Bolland.*, ibid., p. 47). Besides, we offer this only as a conjecture. It is enough to have shown that Calixtus was not the author of the collection of the Miracles of Saint James, which was attributed to him only in the thirteenth century.

Following this collection (*Boll.*, ibid.), several other works occur in the manuscripts: namely, the history of the holy apostle’s martyrdom, the *Passion of Saint James*; the account of his translation; and the Life of Charlemagne by the false Turpin (Baronius, note on the Roman Martyrology, 25 July). This is what led Cardinal Baronius into a rather serious blunder. This writer, failing to examine these various works closely and attending only to the title of the collection, *On the Miracles of Saint James*, believed and asserted that there were five books of miracles. The continuators of Bollandus did not deign to insert these writings in their great collection, judging them unworthy of publication; they contented themselves with reporting a fragment of the history of Saint James’s translation in order to point out the absurdities scattered through it. Yet these authors do not intend thereby to undermine the Spanish tradition on this subject. They are far from doing so, and make every effort to dispel M. de Tillemont’s doubts (vol. I, note 7, pp. 627–628, etc.) concerning the validity of the proofs advanced in support of that tradition. They indicate the bull of Leo III, which that learned critic had found nowhere, and which exists in the Breviary of Évora, printed at Lisbon in 1548, divided into four lessons for the office of the day. We shall not enter here into discussions that would exceed the limits we have set for ourselves. To return to the writings following the book of the Miracles of Saint James: we subscribe to the Bollandists’ judgment concerning them and agree with them that Calixtus neither composed nor approved them. Indeed, no one today possessing even a little critical discernment thinks otherwise.

Besides the writings of which we have just spoken, four sermons on Saint James have also been attributed to this pope, allegedly preached at Compostela or Rome on the days of the translation or other feasts of that apostle (*Lipenius, Bibl. theol.*, vol. II, p. 53); but they bear the same marks of fabrication. Baronius mentions them in his Martyrology (25 July, p. 309). They were printed at Cologne in 1618 and were afterward included in the *Bibliotheca Patrum* printed at Lyons (vol. XX, pp. 1278–1293).

Among the works for which bibliographers and other writers name Pope Calixtus as author (Possevino, *App.*, vol. I, p. 288), there are two further works that require a word. The first, entitled *On the Death and Life of the Saints*, is the same work, as Fabricius observes after Oudin (Fabricius, *Med. et inf. lat.*, book III, p. 891; Oudin, vol. II, p. 1006), which was so long attributed to Saint Isidore of Seville, under the title *On the Life and Death of the Saints*. This work is the production of an impostor, who sought to authorize by two venerable names the ridiculous fables he had heaped together. Wion had some fragments of it in his hands. One may consult Father Alexandre’s fifteenth dissertation (p. 158) on the ecclesiastical history of the first century.

The second work is a treatise on remedies, known under the title *Treasury of the Poor*. We do not see upon what pretext it could have been assigned to Calixtus, since its true author was John XIX, or John XXI, called Peter Julian, or otherwise Peter of Spain, *Petrus Hispanus*. It is under this name that it is identified in a manuscript of the public library of Cambridge: “*Treasury of the Poor, edited by Peter of Spain*” (*Cat. mss Angl.*, vol. III, no. 1329). His entry occurs in the *Library of the Popes* by Father Louis-Jacob de Saint-Charles (book I, p. 138), who reports the different editions of this work (ibid., pp. 36–37). It is surprising that this same author inserted it in the list of Calixtus’s writings as a work by that pope. In this list is found a book on the discovery of the body of Turpin, archbishop and martyr, which need not hesitate to be placed among spurious writings.

The same bibliographer (ibid.), on Molanus’s authority, also mentions another work entitled *On Unlawful Contracts*. It is otherwise unknown to us.

Bollandus (16 January, pp. 26–28) has given us an imperfect Life of Saint James, first bishop of the Church of Tarentaise, and believes that this Life may be Calixtus’s, though offering no proof. M. de Tillemont (*Hist. eccl.*, vol. XII, notes 5 and 9, p. 483), who knew how to assess things at their true value, despises this production, which does little credit to its author, whoever he may be.

[Col. 1369]

# LITTLE BOOK OF THE MIRACLES OF SAINT JAMES THE APOSTLE

(Vincent of Beauvais, *Speculum historiale*, vol. IV, book XXVII, ch. 30.)

“In the year of the Lord 1124,” says Vincent of Beauvais, “Pope Calixtus, of blessed memory, died. This was Calixtus II, who, as is read, wrote the little book *On the Miracles of Saint James*, compiling into one volume what he had read scattered about; from it I have taken care to insert here certain things for the edification of readers.”

## HERE BEGINS THE LITTLE BOOK OF THE MIRACLES OF SAINT JAMES THE APOSTLE, COMPILED BY POPE CALIXTUS

(Pope Calixtus.)—When I was a scholar, loving Blessed James from childhood, during a period of fourteen years, as I travelled through barbarian lands and provinces, I diligently wrote down on a few cheap little slips whatever I found written about him, so that I might comprise it in one volume. O wondrous fortune! I fell among robbers, and although all my possessions were plundered, the codex nevertheless remained to me. I was cast into prison, and though I lost all my property, the codex alone remained to me. I often fell into the depths of many waters, close to death, yet the codex escaped wholly unharmed. The house in which I was was burned, and though my possessions were consumed, the codex escaped the fire with me.

While I was earnestly considering how that codex—for which I had suffered countless anxieties, and which I had laboured to complete with my own hands—might be acceptable to God, I was caught away by night in an ecstasy. In a certain splendid royal palace I saw a most beautiful and splendid young man, crowned with laurel and seated royally upon a throne. He said to me, as I sat at his feet: “Hand over the gloves which you have in your hand.” When I gladly offered them to him, and he entered the chamber, one of his companions said to me: “This is the Son of the Most High King. As he has received the gloves from your hands, so he will graciously receive the apostolic codex after you have completed it.”

Again, as on the venerable day of the apostle’s translation I was meditating upon the sermon and holding its text in my hands, he himself appeared in an ecstasy together with Blessed James, saying: “Write what you have begun; correct the crimes of wicked innkeepers dwelling on the road of my apostle.” Therefore let no one despise this book: whatever is written in it is authentic and set forth with great authority. Accordingly, let the miracles contained in this codex be read in refectories on his feast days.

In the time of King Aldetonsus [reading uncertain], twenty Christian men in parts of Spain, one of whom was a priest, were captured by Saracens and bound in a dark prison in the city of Saragossa with chains of various kinds. When, inspired by God and prompted by the priest, they invoked Blessed James, he shone forth in the darkness of the prison and addressed them thus: “Behold, I am here, whom you called.” Then, lifting their faces, which in grief had been fixed upon their knees, they fell at his feet. With the ointment of his power he broke their bonds; and, their hands freed from the shackles, they were divinely delivered from prison by his power. With him as their guide they came to the gates of the city, which, when he made the sign of the cross, willingly supplied an exit in reverence for the apostle. As dawn was almost breaking, he led them to a certain castle held under Christian protection; there, bidding them call upon him, he visibly ascended into heaven. Then, calling out with a great cry, they were received within when the gates were opened.

(Bede the Priest.) In the time of Blessed Theodore, bishop of Compostela, a certain man committed a grave sin which he scarcely dared confess to his priest and bishop. On hearing it, the bishop was astonished and, not daring to impose penance upon him, sent the man to Saint James with a written slip on which that sin had been recorded. When he arrived there on the saint’s feast day, he placed the slip upon the altar, weeping and asking Saint James to blot out that sin by his merits. Meanwhile the bishop approached to celebrate Mass and, seeing the slip, asked why and by whom it had been placed there. The man immediately came forward and, weeping, recounted the course of the matter for all to hear. Opening the writing and finding nothing written there, he understood, as all related, that the sin had been forgiven.

(Hubert of Besançon.) In the year of the Lord 1080, thirty men from Lorraine, travelling to Saint James, mutually promised one another to keep faith in preserving their common strength. Yet there was one among them who did not make this promise. When they had safely arrived at the city called Porta Clusa, they carried one companion who had fallen ill there, with great labour, for fifteen days as far as the Cifrean passes, because of the pact they had made, although the fifteen stages might have been completed by unencumbered travellers in five days. At last, being burdened, they left the sick man behind. Only the one who had not pledged his word remained with him at the foot of Mount Saint Michael.

The sick man then asked him, if possible, to carry him up that mountain. He gladly carried him, and as the day declined toward evening the sick man died. Seeing this, the living man was greatly afraid because of the gathering darkness of night, the duty owed to the dead man, and the savagery of the barbarous people. Thus utterly abandoned, he gave himself to prayer; and immediately Saint James appeared to him in the form of a knight and asked the reason for his weeping. “Lord,” he said, “it is night, and this dead man cannot be buried.” Then the saint said: “Give me this dead man, and mount the horse behind me.” When this was done, before sunrise that night, having completed twelve stages, they arrived at Mount Joy, which lies half a league short of Saint James. There Saint James set the living and the dead man down from the horse, commanding the living man to invite the canons of Saint James to bury the dead pilgrim. Having completed his pilgrimage, when he found his companions in the city called León, he was to rebuke them for breaking their agreement and tell them on Saint James’s behalf that, because of this, their pilgrimage was invalid. Having said this, the saint disappeared. When the man returned and reported this to his companions upon finding them, they were greatly astonished and, as he had done, undertook penance concerning it from the bishop of León.

[Col. 1371] (Pope Calixtus.) In the year of the Lord 1090, certain Germans visited Saint James and were received at lodging in the city of Toulouse by a certain townsman. At night he made them drunk, placed a silver cup in their pack, and in the morning, as they departed, called them back as though they were thieves. They said that he should punish the one in whose possession he found his money. Searching them, he found his cup in the pack of a father and son; and so, seizing their goods, he brought them before judgment. When the judge mercifully ordered that only one of them be hanged, and the father wished to die for the son and the son for the father, the son was finally hanged, while the father, sad and distressed, went on to Saint James.

After thirty-six days, returning, he turned aside in lamentation to the body of his son, still hanging. As he called upon him with tearful groans, behold, the hanged son began gently to comfort him, saying: “Do not weep, dearest father, but rejoice, for it has never been so well with me. For until now Saint James’s hand has sustained me and refreshed me with heavenly sweetness.” Hearing this, the father ran to the city. The people, having been assembled, took the living and healthy man down, and immediately hanged their host.

In the year of the Lord 1090, a certain Frenchman, wishing to escape the mortality among men in France, resolved to visit Saint James with his wife and children. When he came to the city of Pamplona, his wife died there, and his host retained all his money together with the donkey upon which the children rode. Yet, though utterly desolate, carrying his children on his shoulders and leading them by the hand, he did not abandon his journey. As he was leaving the city and recounting the sorrows of so great a misfortune, a man with a donkey met him on the road and, after hearing his plight, lent him his donkey to carry the children.

Thus, having reached Saint James with this assistance, while he kept vigil and prayed in the church, Saint James appeared and asked whether he knew him. When he denied it, the saint said: “I am James the apostle, who lent you my donkey at Pamplona; and now I lend it you again for your return. I announce to you that your host, who unjustly retained what was yours, will die by falling from the upper story of his house; and likewise all innkeepers like him, who keep travellers’ goods which should be given for the relief of the dead.” Having said this, he disappeared. Returning with the donkey and the children, the pilgrim found his host dead just as the apostle had foretold. When he arrived joyfully in his homeland and had set the children down from the donkey, that donkey immediately disappeared.

In the year of the Lord 1091, when a sailor named Frison, a Frisian, was steering a ship of pilgrims across the sea, a Saracen named Auctus came against him to fight, intending to take all the pilgrims captive with him to the land of the Moabites. When the two vessels, Saracen and Christian, came together and fought fiercely, Frison fell between the two ships into the depths of the sea, clad in iron mail, helmet, and shield. But when, strengthened by God’s mercy, he invoked Saint James, Saint James immediately appeared to him in the depths of the sea and, taking him by the hand, restored him safe to the ship. Then, in the hearing of all, he said to the Saracen: “Unless you leave this little Christian vessel, I shall deliver you and your helmet into their power.” The latter replied: “O renowned hero, why do you endeavour to take away my prey? Are you the god of the sea, that you resist our people upon the sea?” The apostle said to him: “I am not the god of the sea, but the servant of the God of the sea, coming to the aid of those in danger who cry to me, both on sea and land.” Immediately, by God’s power, the Saracens’ ship began to be endangered by a violent storm, while the Christians’ vessel, led by Blessed James, arrived at its desired destination.

In the year of the Lord 1092, a certain bishop from Jerusalem was sitting near the edge of a ship and chanting from a suitable psalter, when a powerful wave of the sea came and swept him away into the sea with several others. When they were now floating upon the waves almost sixty cubits from the ship and invoked Blessed James, he immediately stood upon the waves with dry feet and said to those in peril: “Do not fear, my children.” At once Thetis, at his command, restored soundly to the ship all whom she had violently seized; even the open book from which the bishop had been reading remained entirely unharmed. The apostle immediately disappeared. That bishop afterward composed in his honour a certain responsory with its verse.

In the year of the Lord 1104, a certain pilgrim returning from Jerusalem, seated upon the side of a ship, fell overboard. As he loudly implored Blessed James, one of his companions threw his shield into the sea for him, saying: “May most glorious James, whose help you invoke, help you.” Taking the shield, that man, guided by Blessed James, swam for three days and nights in the ship’s wake; he arrived safely at the desired harbour with the others and related to all how Blessed James, from the hour when he invoked him, had continually gone before him holding him by the crown of the head with his hand.

In the year of the Lord 1105, a certain Bernard was captured in Italy, bound in chains, and thrown by enemies into the depths of a tower. As he implored Blessed James continually day and night, the saint appeared to him and said: “Come, follow me as far as Gaul.” His chains were broken, and the saint disappeared. Immediately the pilgrim, supported by the aid of Blessed James and without human help, rose hanging from the neck of an ox to the summit of the tower; and, making a single leap from the outer height of the eleven-cubit tower to the ground, he escaped completely unharmed.

In the year of the Lord 1106, a certain merchant, wishing to travel with his merchandise to a fair, approached the lord of the land to which he intended to go, who happened then to be in that town, and asked him to conduct him safely with him to that fair. The lord promised to do so and gave his pledge. But once they had departed, he was moved by the devil’s prompting, seized the merchant and his goods, cast him into prison, and bound him tightly. When the merchant invoked Blessed James, the saint appeared to him one night in prison, while the guards were still awake, commanded him to rise, and led him to the summit of the tower. The tower bent down so far that it seemed to set its top upon the ground; descending from it without a leap or injury, he left, freed from his bonds. The guards pursued him and came near him; but, not finding him, they went back blinded.

As the year of the Lord 1110 approached, soldiers from two hostile Italian cities met in battle. One party, defeated by the other, began to flee. In this rout, a knight accustomed to seek the shrine of Blessed James fled and, despairing now of his life, invoked Blessed James, saying: “O Blessed James, if you deign to deliver me from the imminent danger, I shall present myself and my horse—for I have nothing more precious—to your province.” Then the apostle appeared between him and his enemies, who thirsted to capture him in fierce pursuit, and protected him with his shield while the enemies pursued for six leagues. That he might not become liable for failing his vow, he offered himself and his horse to the apostle, though the horse was not worth twenty solidi of the lesser currency.

In the year of the Lord 1108, in the regions of Gaul, a man whose wife was barren and who had no son visited Saint James on this account. Returning, he had a son, whom he named James. When the child was fifteen years old, he proposed to visit Saint James with him and the mother, and to offer him there. But in the middle of the journey the boy fell ill and died. In great grief over his death, the parents, almost mad, filled the whole wood with cries. The mother thus appealed to Saint James: unless he restored her son to her, she would have herself buried alive with him. Meanwhile, while the boy was being carried to the tomb, he came to life, as if awakened from sleep. Before all those standing by, he recounted how Saint James had held him in his bosom and ordered him to complete the journey begun with his parents.

[Col. 1373] (Hubert of Besançon.) Three knights of the diocese of Lyons were journeying to Saint James. A little old woman, meeting them, asked them in pity to carry her wallet for the love of Saint James. One of them did so and carried the woman’s bag until they were twelve stages from Galicia. He found a sick man on the road, who asked him to lend his horse. Taking the sick man’s staff and the woman’s bag, he followed his horse, which carried the sick man. But he fell ill from the heat of the sun and the labour of the journey. Remembering that he had offended in many things, for the love of Blessed James the apostle he bore his illness with equanimity as far as Galicia.

There he lay sick, and his companions urged him to confess and receive communion, as a good Christian should. He heard well, but was unable to answer, and remained mute for three days. Thus his companions were greatly troubled for the salvation of his body and soul. On the fourth day, as they watched around him and awaited his death, he sighed deeply and said: “I give thanks to God and Saint James because I have been delivered.” When they asked what he had said, he replied: “Since I lay down, I wished to do what you advised; but while I was considering it, demons suddenly came to me and bound me so tightly that I could say nothing pertaining to salvation. I heard you, indeed, but could not answer. But Saint James immediately entered here, carrying the woman’s bag in his left hand and the poor man’s staff in his right—the things by which I aided them on the road. He had the staff as a spear and the bag as a *parma*, that is, a shield; and, coming as though angry, he raised the staff and compelled the fleeing demons to depart. And behold, the grace of Blessed James has delivered me and restored speech to me. Therefore have a priest come, for I cannot remain longer in this life.”

When he delayed, he warned one of his companions: “Friend, do not serve your lord henceforth, for know that he is truly damned and will shortly die an evil death.” The outcome later proved this true. When they had buried their companion and returned, they told this to that lord. But he did not amend his ways and treated their words as a dream. Soon afterward he was run through by the lance of a knight in battle and died.

Near the city of Lyons, a young furrier, whose father had died, supported his mother by his own labour and was accustomed every year to visit Saint James. Though he had long lived chastely, at last one night he fornicated with a woman. In the morning, because he had previously intended to go to Saint James, he set out with two neighbours, taking a donkey with him, to visit Saint James. Finding a certain beggar on the road, they took him along for companionship and the apostle’s love, giving him what he needed.

Then the devil appeared by night to the young man in the likeness of Saint James and said: “Do you know who I am?” When he denied it, the devil said: “I am James the apostle, whom you have been accustomed to visit every year. Know that I greatly rejoiced over you, because I hoped for very great good in you. But lately, before leaving your house, you fornicated with a woman; yet, neither confessed nor repentant, you dared come here and set out as a pilgrim with your sin, as though your pilgrimage pleased God and me. It ought not to be so. Whoever wishes to make pilgrimage for my sake must first declare his sins in confession and afterward repent through pilgrimage of the offenses he has committed.” With these words the demon vanished.

The distressed young man then resolved to return home, confess his sins, and thus begin the journey anew. But the demon immediately appeared to him as before and reproved this intention, saying that he could by no means blot out that sin unless he cut off his genitals, and that he would be much more blessed and a martyr if he dared kill himself. Having heard this, the simple young man, while his companions slept at night, drew a knife, cut off his genitals, and pierced himself through the belly with the same knife. As blood flowed and he throbbed in death, his companions awoke, lit a fire, and found him dying. Fearing the charge of homicide, they fled in the morning, leaving him with the beggar.

A little later, as they prepared his grave, behold, the man who had died from loss of blood and had been laid outside the church came to life and sat up in the bier. Immediately those standing around fled, and at their cry all the others gathered. He then began to speak and recounted everything that had happened to him. After relating the foregoing, he added: “When I had killed myself, demons seized me. As they were taking me toward Rome, Saint James swiftly flew after us. After they had disputed at length with one another, for me and against me, at his urging we came to a certain meadow where Blessed Mary sat in conference with all the saints. Blessed James therefore pleaded before her for me against the demons. When she rebuked the demons, she commanded that I should live again. Thus Saint James received me and restored me here at once.”

When those present heard this, they carried him joyfully into a house. He was immediately healed, and only scars remained in place of the wounds. After spending three days, he, with the donkey and the beggar, met his returning companions. They scarcely recognized him, and he told the astonished men what had occurred. When all returned to their homeland after the pilgrimage had been completed, he confirmed in fact what his companions had earlier reported. Saint Hugh, abbot of Cluny, with many others, saw this man and all the signs of death; and, because of the wonder, declared that, as had often been revealed, he had been accustomed to see this himself.

In the year of the Lord 1100, a citizen of Barcelona, having arrived at Saint James, asked only this of him: that thereafter he might be held captive by no enemies. Returning to his own country through Sicily, he was captured at sea by Saracens and sold and bought at markets and fairs in thirteen pagan cities; and the chains with which he had been bound were always loosed. At the thirteenth sale, while bound round the legs with double chains, he called upon Saint James. The apostle appeared to him and said: “Because when you were in my church you asked me for the liberation of your body, not for the salvation of your soul, you immediately fell into these dangers. But because the Lord has had mercy on you, he has sent me to deliver you even now.” Immediately the apostle disappeared, the chains broke, and the man was freed. Carrying a portion of the chain in his hands as testimony to so great a miracle, he returned openly to his homeland through the cities and castles of the Saracens, before the Saracens’ eyes. Whenever a pagan who met him tried to seize him, he fled in terror as soon as he saw the chain.

Many bears and lions, leopards and dragons likewise wished to devour him as he travelled through deserts; but as soon as they saw the chain which the apostle had touched, they withdrew. I myself saw this very man carrying the chain in his hands and relating this account.

In the year of the Lord 1119, a man named Bruno of Mimeliacum, returning from Saint James, began to lack money and had not enough even to buy a pennyworth of bread. One day, fasting until the ninth hour and ashamed to beg, he was very sad and anxious. Invoking Saint James, he rested alone under a tree. Sleeping there for a little while, he dreamed that Saint James was feeding him. On awaking, he immediately found a loaf baked under ashes at his head. From it he ate sufficiently twice a day for fifteen days, and on the next day found the same loaf whole in his bag.

(Pope Calixtus.) Recently the Count of Saint-Gilles, named Pons, went with his brother to Saint James. When they arrived, they asked the custodian to allow them to keep vigil before the apostle’s body. The custom was that the doors of this oratory were shut after sunset until morning. He refused. They withdrew sadly to their lodgings, gathered all the pilgrims of their company, prepared lights to hold in their hands, and strengthened in faith came to the closed doors, nearly two hundred pilgrims. Praying, they said in a loud voice: “Saint James, if our pilgrimage pleases you, open your oratory to us.”

[Col. 1375] They had not yet finished speaking when, behold, the doors opened with such a crash that they thought them broken into fragments. The bars, bolts, and chains with which they had been secured were broken.

A certain bishop from Greece, named Stephen, left his bishopric and came to Saint James in poor garb. A cell of reeds was made for him there, in which he devoted himself day and night to fasts, vigils, and prayers. One day, while he prayed, a crowd of peasants beside his cell began thus to beseech the apostle: “Blessed James, good knight, deliver us from our pressing evils.” Hearing this, he rebuked them, saying: “O foolish peasants, call Blessed James not a knight but a fisherman.”

That night Blessed James appeared to him in a dazzling white garment, holding two keys in his hand and bearing weapons that shone like the rays of the sun. Calling him three times, he said: “Stephen, servant of God, since you directed that I be called not a knight but a fisherman, I appear to you in this manner, that you may know that I wage war for God. And so that you may believe this more firmly: tomorrow, at the third hour, I shall open with these keys which I hold in my hand the gates of the city of Coimbra, which King Fernando of the Christians has oppressed with siege for seven years, admit the Christians, and give the city into their power.” And so it happened.

A very fierce war once arose between the Count of Fontis Calcariae and his knight, named William. The count captured William and had him brought before him. When the count ordered him beheaded, the knight cried: “James, apostle of God, whom Herod killed with the sword at Jerusalem, help me and deliver me from the executioner’s sword.” With his hands raised to heaven, he received three enormous blows upon his bare neck and was not harmed. Then the executioner thrust his sword into his belly, but Blessed James so blunted it that he did not even feel its blow. The count then ordered him confined in his castle.

When he invoked Blessed James, the apostle appeared in the morning, standing and saying: “Behold, I am here, whom you invoked.” Then the house was filled with such sweet fragrance that all who were there thought they were in paradise because of the fragrance and the immense light which appeared there. In that very radiance Blessed James led him out before all, holding him by the hand, and brought him to the outermost gate of the castle. The guards were as though blinded, and the gates opened; they proceeded along the road for a mile outside the walls. The knight, inflamed with love for the apostle, then went to Galicia to visit the apostle’s body.

## On Heavenly Punishment upon Those Who Do Not Keep the Feast of Saint James

These are the miracles which in former times occurred, through divine vengeance, to those who did not observe the feasts of Blessed James.

Among the Spaniards, at Tudela, on Saint James’s feast day, a peasant threshed wheat all day in the threshing-floor. As evening fell, he entered a bath near that same castle, wonderfully constructed in ancient Saracen workmanship. As he sat in it, the skin of his back immediately adhered to the walls of the bath from his shoulders to his legs, and, before all who saw it, he gave up the ghost for violating so great a feast.

Among the Basques, at Albinetum, the people refused to observe Saint James’s day and worked all day. But by divine vengeance their entire castle was consumed by fire on the following night, and no one knew from what direction the fire advanced; it was said, however, to have come from heaven.

In the diocese of Besançon, Bernard of Majora, on this day of Saint James, spent the whole day carrying sheaves of wheat in a cart, despite his neighbours’ objections. As he worked at evening, a sudden and violent fire came from heaven and reduced the cart, the sheaves, and the oxen to ashes. Some women who were with him were carried by others who came up to a nearby spring in order to escape the heat of the fire, and barely escaped.

Likewise Harduin, a knight of the same town, spent that same day hauling his cart loaded with sheaves of wheat; but divine vengeance blinded the oxen’s eyes.

Among the Goths of the province of Montpellier, at the order of a certain knight of Mircoriensis, a peasant woman in the village of Saint Damian made and baked ash-bread on Saint James’s day. When it was brought to table and broken before all who were reclining there, it appeared bloody. And the more it was broken, the more and more it poured forth blood. “This is the Lord’s doing,” etc.

Let these things said from the little book of Pope Calixtus suffice.

[Col. 1375]

# FOUR SERMONS ON SAINT JAMES THE APOSTLE, DELIVERED IN GALICIA

(First published by Fr. Juan de Mariana, S.J.; afterward reprinted in the Lyons *Bibliotheca Patrum*, vol. XX, p. 1278.)

## FIRST SERMON: ON THE VIGIL OF SAINT JAMES, SON OF ZEBEDEE, THE APOSTLE

[Col. 1375A]

A reading according to Mark, chapter III, verse 13: “At that time the Lord Jesus went up upon the mountain, called to himself those whom he himself wished, and they came to him; and he appointed twelve to be with him, and to send them out to preach,” etc.

The vigil of the most holy solemnity of blessed James, son of Zebedee, apostle of Galicia, has come upon us, dearest brethren. During it we must cease from evils, persist in good deeds, and rejoice with the inmost affection of divine charity. It is fitting that we strive to precede this solemnity with fasting and [Col. 1376A] vigil; that, insofar as we can, we wipe away the stains of our sins with groans, tears, and almsgiving; that we cherish concord and charity; despise the passing delights of the world; love, with all the eagerness of our mind, the true joys of the heavenly homeland; and, so that our debts may be remitted by the just Judge, may be found worthy for love of him. Hence ecclesiastical observance ordained abstinence from unlawful things, fasting, and watching before the solemnities of the greater saints, so that on this day the flesh, somewhat afflicted through self-restraint, may be cleansed of the filth of sins. Although it is appropriate to pray and abstain every day, on this day one ought to devote oneself more abundantly to fasts, almsgiving, and prayers.

And lest you, beloved, grow sluggish in the matters to which we exhort you, take an example from secular persons. If any of you had to receive the servant of some earthly ruler, you would take pains to make the house of your lodging clean with diligent care. If a bodily house is cleansed for the entry of human beings, why is the house of the soul not prepared with the utmost diligence of purity, especially for God who is coming? Know indeed that whoever worthily and cleanly receives in solemn service a soldier of the eternal King also receives the eternal King himself in that soldier, as he himself testifies in the Gospel, saying: “What you did to one of these least ones of mine, you did to me” (Matt. 25:40). If, therefore, what is done to one of Christ’s least ones is done to Christ himself, it follows that what is done to one of his saints is done to him.

Let us also be stirred by the apostolic utterance: “It is now the hour for us to rise from sleep” (Rom. 13:11). For we are asleep while we grow dull in the pleasure of the flesh and remain in the habit of sinning. Just as the body is weighed down by sleep, so the mind is depressed by fleshly pleasure and the habit of sinning. Therefore it is written: “Awake, you righteous, and do not sin” (1 Cor. 15:34). We rise from this kind of sleep when, setting aside fleshly pleasure and abandoning the habit of sinning, we become prompt for the love and service of God. Yet it is especially now time to rise from this sleep, since tomorrow we shall celebrate the venerable solemnity of the great James, whose vigil we are undoubtedly now observing.

Therefore the Lord also exhorts us through Isaiah, saying: “Wash yourselves; be clean” (Isa. 1:16). We must wash ourselves by confession, repentance, weeping, and affliction for the evils we have committed, and persevere in that cleanliness, lest we again be defiled by unlawful acts. For just as one who has washed after contact with a corpse becomes unclean if he touches it again, so he who repeats a sin is reckoned defiled. Hence the Psalmist says: “Turn away from evil and do good” (Ps. 36:27); and from this it is also clear that it is not enough for a person to abstain from evil unless he does what is good. This is shown when it is again said through Isaiah: “Cease to act perversely; learn to do good” (Isa. 1:16). For as we are separated from God by acting perversely, so we are joined to him by doing good.

Know, dearest brethren, that just as it is unbecoming for a man about to dine at an earthly king’s table to approach in defiled garments, so it is shameful for a Christian soul to come, at the celebration of so great an apostle, with certain vices. Moreover, just as it is offensive to an earthly king if he sees anything filthy or blameworthy in someone seated at his table, so it is unseemly before the divine gaze of God if perhaps anything horrible or vicious should be found in a Christian at the festival celebration of blessed James. Therefore we must take care not only to avoid a vicious lapse on his days, but also to abstain long beforehand, so that, not disfigured by grave crime but rather adorned with the flowers of good works, we may approach the feast of so great an apostle. Otherwise there may be said to us what the Lord says to the reprobate man who entered the wedding naked of good works: “Friend, how did you enter here without a wedding garment?” But he was speechless. Then the king said: “Bind his hands and feet and cast him into the outer darkness; there shall be weeping and gnashing of teeth” (Matt. 22:12).

You observe, dearest brethren, that just as this man, because he was naked of the wedding garment, is cast out from the fellowship of the banqueters, so I fear that he who approaches the celebration of the saints’ solemnities naked of good works may become estranged from the fellowship of the saints. And if he who comes without a good work to celebrate the feasts of saints is excluded from their fellowship, what then will become of one who comes with evil works and without repentance? I fear that he will be punished with an equal penalty. But know that whoever celebrates the feasts of blessed James justly and worthily will, without doubt, share in the everlasting age in the solemnity of the holy angels together with him whose victorious day he observes. For if we celebrate his feasts in the world, the angels celebrate them far more sublimely in heaven. O how worthy and glorious it is, dearest brethren, to celebrate the feasts of saints with the angels, whose kingdoms we shall receive with them in heaven.

[Col. 1378A] Therefore whoever has fallen into fornication, homicide, adultery, or other vices, let him have recourse to the remedies of repentance, so that he may become fit to celebrate the solemnities of so great an apostle of Christ; thus, having worthily celebrated his solemnity, he may deserve to have a share in the eternal festivity of the saints. For if anyone, having fallen perhaps into some crime, is present at these sacred solemnities of blessed James; or comes to his feast without repentance for a sin previously committed; or refrains from a good work during them; or is preoccupied with worldly matters—unless he repents, he has celebrated the feast in vain, because he has made his praises empty before God.

Accordingly, through the prophet the Lord commands us to abstain not only from wicked deeds but also from evil thoughts, saying: “Remove the evil of your thoughts from before my eyes” (Isa. 1:16). For to celebrate the feasts of saints is to signify the perpetual rest of the peoples. When on these days we rest from earthly activities, we then show that, just as he whose feast [Col. 1378B] we celebrate is in eternal rest, so we too shall be in the everlasting rest of paradise with him, God granting it, if we cease from evil deeds and engage in good ones. And when we fast during their vigils, we show that, as we abstain from bodily foods, so we ought to abstain from harmful deeds. For as long as Adam abstained from forbidden and vicious foods, he remained in paradise; as soon as he ate, he was immediately expelled. From this it may be understood that he who sanctifies the vigils of the saints in the present life with fasting, prayers, and almsgiving will share in their glory in the future. But he who does not fast during them, or ceases from good works, as we have said, or does unlawful things, will surely be alienated from the fellowship of the saints. He who fasts and abstains from evil in other matters, and does good, shall have a crown. But he who does not fast on this day, does not do good, and does not cease from evils, shall suffer punishment.

But what is worse: the envious devil, the minister of vices, who tempted Adam in paradise and who never ceases to turn saints away from good works, is himself more intent, during saints’ solemnities than on other days, upon deceitfully tempting them with his goads. There are even some, worse still, who are accustomed to become more depraved through vices on feast days than on other days, rather than becoming better. Certainly the person found on feast days in envy, detraction, drunkenness, excessive feasting, fornication, worldly preoccupation, homicide, hunting birds or cattle, games of dice or chess (*schacci*), siege, vengeance, battle with enemies, oppression of brethren, or any grave crime, does not celebrate the feasts of saints. Rather, he celebrates them who is found and occupied in distribution to the needy, hospitality, chastity, visiting the sick, sacred reading and prayer, speaking peace between those at discord, or some other good work.

This is shown in holy Moses and the Israelite people [Col. 1378D], when Moses remained with the Lord on Mount Sinai while the faithless people made a molten calf (Exod. 32). What does it mean that Moses stands with the Lord in divine contemplation while the people worship the calf, except that all religious persons who desire rightly to celebrate the feasts of saints and to persevere in contemplation abstain from vices long beforehand; while, conversely, the perverse, who previously abstained for many days, now commit sins by ceasing from good works? Therefore Scripture says: “He celebrates the Sabbath badly who refrains from good works” (Mark 3:4; Luke 6:9); and the Psalmist says: “They exchanged their glory for the likeness of a calf that eats grass” (Ps. 105:20). The perverse exchange their glory for the likeness of a calf when they celebrate apostolic solemnities in a beastly fashion, devote themselves to vices during them, and approach their celebration with their crimes unrepented of. And it rightly says: “They forgot the Lord who saved them” (Ps. 105:21), because those who desire to celebrate the sacred solemnities of his saints not with good deeds but with drunkenness, unchaste excesses, and idle words do not know the Lord.

The Hebrew people, who committed not many sins in Egypt but later fell in the wilderness through the worshiped calf, are said to have offended God by the calf. What does this mean? It means that there are some who abstain from vices before the feast of this blessed apostle of the Lord, James, but are now caught in the devil’s snares by acting wickedly. May God avert this from you, brethren, lest it happen. Behold, beloved, how we may worthily celebrate the apostolic solemnity. Behold how we ought to honour his great and venerable festival and prepare ourselves with the greatest purity. For we must consider how to make ourselves clean again, as far as possible, through abstinence, and how to attend fittingly at his offices on the most celebrated day of his solemnity, so that, when he comes on the last day with the twelvefold company of apostles to judge the twelvefold Israelite multitude, we may deserve to escape the judgment of his vengeance by his protection and reign with him endlessly in the heavenly kingdoms [Col. 1379B].

The ecclesiastical custom which celebrates the vigils of the greater saints at night in churches with confessions, lamps, and candles took its origin from the ancient fathers of the Old Law. [Note: [Col. 1379D] See Baronius, *Roman Martyrology*.] Therefore, on the day before the vigil, the basilica should be cleaned of dust and swept with brooms, and adorned with carpets, hangings, curtains, and rushes, so that clergy and people may more fittingly devote themselves there to prayer.

That the faithful people ought to receive penance from priests preaching in the Church before the vigil is shown by the book of Exodus, which says: “When the people had washed their garments, Moses said to them: ‘Abstain from your wives; be ready until the third day; and do not approach your wives’” (Exod. 19:14). Therefore, just as the Hebrew people, about to receive the Law, washed their garments and abstained from their own wives, so the Christian people, about to celebrate apostolic solemnities, ought on the day before the vigils to wash not only their clothing but also their hearts and bodies through penance received from priests [Col. 1379C], and to abstain from their own wives until the eighth day. And indeed, if one must abstain from lawful wives, how much more from unlawful pollutions?

That the people ought throughout the whole night to pray in church before the altar, hold burning candles in their hands, stand rather than sit, keep watch rather than sleep, is attested by the Lord, who says: “Let your loins be girded, and lamps burning in your hands” (Luke 12:35). He commands the loins to be girded in order to show that lust, which is in the loins, must be restrained. He commands a lamp to be held in the hands in order to signify that good works must be done. That those who keep vigil ought to stand on their feet in church, and not sit except temporarily, is attested by Paul, who says: “Stand therefore, having girded your loins with truth” (Eph. 6:14). And the Lord says to the prophet: “Stand upon your feet” (Dan. 10:11).

Many formerly had their faces burned by burning candles during sleep so that they would not fall asleep; for they preferred their beard and hair [Col. 1379D] to burn rather than defile their mind with shameful thoughts before the altar of God. That each person’s candle should burn from evening until the first Mass has ended is attested by the Israelite people, who, journeying through the desert, deserved to be illuminated by the pillar of fire which appeared over them at night in the cloud. For it endured from the beginning of night until the dawn-star, that is, the morning star.

But among other things, it should be known that the candle held in the hands by the watcher signifies faith in the Trinity. In the wax is signified God the Father; in its wick, his Only-begotten Son; in its light, the Paraclete Spirit proceeding from both. Whoever holds the candle in hand through the night must hold this faith firmly in heart. The cloths, silks, carpets, and other ornaments hung in church on these days signify faith, hope, charity, and the other virtues with which we ought to adorn the bridal chamber of our heart, so that we may deserve to receive the supreme guest, namely the everlasting King Jesus [Col. 1380A] Christ. The rush which, together with other herbs, is spread beneath the feet signifies pride, which, together with the other vices that follow it, we ought to trample beneath our feet by acting well.

The people of the Passover in Egypt prefigured such vigils: desiring to escape Egypt’s sorrow and enter the promised land, they kept awake at night, girded their loins, put on shoes, supported themselves with staffs, and consecrated the doorway of their house with a lamb’s blood (Exod. 12:11). If, therefore, that people celebrated at night its Passover—that is, its passage from Egypt to the promised land, from temporal things, that is, to temporal things [as printed]—how much more ought we to celebrate by watching the feast-day of blessed James, on which he passed from temporal things to the paradisal dwelling-places? For by his favour we believe that we shall pass from the exile of this flesh into paradise.

And if those people ate their earthly lamb, though figurative, by families and households at night, how much more ought we, on the feast-day of our James, in churches at earliest dawn, after the darkness of sins has been driven out, to sacrifice and receive in communion the true immaculate Lamb who takes away the sins of the world? If they kept watch at night, desiring to be delivered from enemies by Moses’ hand, how much more ought we to keep watch on the night of the blessed apostle, since we desire by his protection to be delivered from vices and demonic enemies? If they put on shoes, how much more ought we to direct our steps by the preaching and examples of dead animals—that is, of the first Fathers—and recount their deeds? If they were supported by staffs because they hastened to set out on a journey, how much more ought we to implore the saints to help us on the journey to the kingdom of heaven? If they marked the doorposts of their houses with lamb’s blood, how much more ought we to fortify the house of our heart with the banner of the Lord’s cross and watchful eye against demonic temptations? And if the Hebrew people, desiring to enter the promised land, girded their loins, then rightly also the Christian people, desiring to enter the heavenly homeland promised them by God [Col. 1380C], ought, while keeping vigil, to gird their loins and restrain lust, so that they may keep vigil more purely before blessed James.

For in the manner of those who keep watch over a dead body, we keep vigil for saints when in their churches we perform their funeral rites with prayers. Some, beloved, mourn the death; others rejoice because of the honours and spoils received. Some devote themselves to the prayers of chanting the Psalter. Therefore, just as a body to be watched is placed among the watchers, so blessed James truly remains among his watchers, carrying their prayers before God. Many testify that while they were keeping vigil on the eve of his feast, they saw him in apostolic form.

Therefore on his vigil we ought, through contrition of heart and confession of mouth, to mourn our sins; and further to rejoice, because, if we keep it well, we shall receive the honours and spoils of eternal life. The Galicians especially, who received the spoils—that is, the venerable body—ought daily both to rejoice and to mourn: to mourn when they dispose of these things badly, but to rejoice when, like Lawrence, they distribute them well. For it is sung of him thus: “He scattered; he gave to the poor, not to the rich.” Likewise, just as it is customary for clerics to chant at a dead person’s funeral rites, so all who keep vigil on the eve of blessed James ought to chant with heart and voice. “Let us come before the face of the Lord in confession,” says the Psalmist, “and rejoice in psalms to him” (Ps. 94:2). And the Apostle says: “I will sing psalms with the spirit, and I will sing psalms with the mind” (1 Cor. 14:15). For there were formerly many who did not know the psalms but gave great rewards to persons reading psalters on this night.

That the solemnities either of blessed James or of the greater saints ought to be observed for eight days is attested by Chronicles, which says concerning Solomon’s temple: “Thus Solomon held the solemnity at that time for seven days, and all Israel with him, a very great assembly” (2 Chron. 7:8); “and on the eighth day he held an assembly,” namely in the temple. Therefore on this [Col. 1381A] night we must keep watch and pray, lest we succumb in perverse temptations. For it is written: “Watch and pray, lest you enter into temptation” (Matt. 26:41); and again: “Watch, because you do not know at what hour your Lord will come” (Matt. 25:13); and elsewhere: “Watch [and pray]; labour in all things” (2 Tim. 4:5); and again: “Blessed is he who watches daily at my gates” (Prov. 8:34). The gates of wisdom figuratively are the apostles, through whom the faithful enter the kingdom of heaven. Therefore, whoever watches during the vigils of the apostles watches at the gates of the kingdom of heaven.

Yet if anyone keeps watch well on this night, he is said to prepare himself to hope that he will obtain that reward [Note: [Col. 1381D] Perhaps: “he is said to hope that he will come to that reward,” etc. Editor.] which the prudent virgins received: they held lamps in their hands and persevered in good works until the coming of their true Bridegroom. For when at midnight the cry of the Bridegroom’s coming arose, the prudent entered with him into the everlasting marriage-feast of the heavenly palace; but while the foolish slept in sins, the door of the heavenly hall was closed, and this answer was given: “Amen, I say to you, I do not know you” (Matt. [Col. 1381B] 25:12). For one who does not know God in sins shall be unrecognized at the door of the kingdom of heaven.

Gideon instructed his warriors to conceal burning lamps in jars, carry them in their hands, and, when the enemies approached, smash the jars (Judg. 7:19). So it was done: the jars were broken, and the enemies, stunned by the wonder of the lamps’ brightness, fled. By the jars our bodies are figuratively represented; by the lamps, the hidden good desires of our hearts; by the enemies, demons and vices. We hide lamps in jars when we think in our hearts about heavenly goods. We smash the jars when we afflict our bodies by abstinence on these days. We display burning lamps when we give all people the example of good works. The enemies flee before the lamps, because when demons see us always intent upon good works, they and the vices withdraw far from us.

And indeed, just as the Lord, looking upon the camp of the Egyptians during the morning watch through the pillar of fire and cloud, destroyed their army and delivered his people, so, if we diligently celebrate the vigils and solemnities of blessed James with the lights of heart and body, we believe that in the morning, when Mass has been celebrated, we shall be delivered by apostolic merits from vices and demonic enemies [Col. 1381C].

Therefore this night is in many respects like the night of the Paschal solemnity. For just as that night brings salvation to many, namely believers, and condemnation to many, namely unbelievers, so this night brings salvation to some and harm to others. Those who commit shameful, vain, or idle words; quarrels; fornication; adulteries; thefts; drunkenness; unlawful banquets; perform or watch various entertainers’ games; or sing deceptive songs—[Note: [Col. 1382D] That is, lying songs.] unless they come to their senses, shall surely be condemned. But those who repent of what they have committed, hold candles in their hands as we have said, and persevere until daylight in prayers and divine words, shall without doubt be eternally rewarded by the Lord through the merits of the apostle.

This night loves the chaste, hates the lustful, drives away the unjust [Col. 1381D], loves the devout, rebukes the sleepy, rewards the watchful, glorifies those who praise together, hates sinners, loves the sober, repels drunkards, multiplies the generous, condemns the avaricious, builds up the hospitable, disregards the cruel, makes blessed those who bring joy, restrains the wrathful, condemns the malicious, preserves lovers, reconciles the peaceful, restrains the quarrelsome, bestows favour on the poor, strengthens the infirm, saves penitents, and cherishes true mourners. The sanctification of this night therefore drives away crimes, washes away faults, and restores innocence to those who have fallen, joy to the sorrowful; it drives away hatreds, brings concord, and bends down powers.

This is the night which throughout the whole world restores to grace those who believe in Christ—namely, those separated from worldly vices in this solemnity—and joins them to holiness, drawing them away from the darkness of sins. This is the night of which it may rightly be said: “The night is my illumination in my delights” (Ps. [Col. 1382A] 138:11). It shall not be darkened by darkness, but shall be illuminated like day by the true light, namely in the hearts of those who truly celebrate it. O truly blessed night, which strips the Egyptians—that is, those doing penance—of sins, and enriches the Hebrews—that is, believers passing from earthly things to heavenly—with wealth! O truly blessed night, whose day was worthy to know the time and hour in which the first apostle was stripped of this frail life,

> And for his merits the first crown is given to him!

Therefore let us cease from works of the flesh and do good in these sacred solemnities. For whoever, as we have said, ceases from unlawful acts and perseveres in good works to the end ought to hope that he will ascend to that true mountain of which Mark says in today’s reading: “Jesus the Lord, ascending the mountain, called to himself those whom he himself wished; and they came to him, and he made twelve to be with him, and sent them out to preach.” In sacred discourse, a mountain sometimes signifies the Church, sometimes the heavenly kingdom, sometimes the humble, sometimes higher commandments, sometimes virtues, sometimes saints, sometimes Jews.

It signifies the Church, as Truth says: “A city set upon a mountain cannot be hidden” (Matt. 5:14). It signifies the heavenly kingdom, as the Psalmist says: “Lord, who shall dwell in your tabernacle, or who shall rest in your holy mountain?” (Ps. 14:1); and the Holy Spirit answers him: “He who walks without stain and works righteousness; who speaks truth in his heart; who has not practiced deceit with his tongue nor done evil to his neighbour” (ibid., vv. 2–3). It shows the humble, as the same Psalmist says: “Let the mountains receive peace for the people, and the hills righteousness” (Ps. 71:3). It signifies higher commandments, as it is written in the Gospel: “Jesus, seeing the crowds, went up the mountain” (Matt. 5:1). It signifies virtues, as the Psalmist says: “Why do you look with envy upon the curdled mountains?” (Ps. 67:17). It expresses the Jews, as David says: “Mountains of Gilboa, let neither dew nor rain come upon you” (2 Sam. 1:21).

But above all mountains there is one mountain of God: the Only-begotten, who is exalted above all angels. This mountain is higher than all heavens, deeper than every abyss, broader than all lands, loftier than every height. Concerning this mountain Job said to one speaking with him: “It is higher than heaven—what can you do? deeper than hell—how can you know him? Its measure is longer than the earth and broader than the sea” (Job 11:8). For just as speech fails to recount the height of heaven, the breadth of the earth, the depth of the abyss, the days of the age, and the drops of rain, so the human mind fails to conceive the sublimity of divine majesty; yet it is enlarged for believing. What a human being cannot grasp concerning God by human reason may be grasped by faith. God, who cannot be comprehended by human reason, may be comprehended by whole faith. Therefore his immeasurable sublimity and depth must be believed, as he was in the beginning, is now, and ever shall be.

He is therefore the mountain of which the prophet says: “Come, let us go up to the mountain of the Lord” (Isa. 2:3). This mountain called to himself those whom he himself wished, he who “wills all people to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth” (1 Tim. 2:4).

“And he made twelve to be with him, and sent them out to preach; and gave them power to heal infirmities and cast out demons.” To the apostles whom the Lord sent to preach, he granted power to perform miracles so that they might confirm their preaching by accompanying signs. For it was fitting that those who preached new things should do new things. “And he gave Simon the name Peter.” Mark calls Simon Peter to distinguish him from the other Simon, who is called the Canaanean. But it should be known that long before this, as is read in another Gospel, the name Cephas was given to Simon by the Lord: namely, when he had been brought to him by his brother Andrew, Jesus looked at him and said, “You are the son of John; you shall be called Cephas,” which is interpreted Peter [Col. 1383A] (John 1:42). There he is called Cephas; here, Peter, so that his name might be known among Chaldeans, Greeks, and Latins. For *Cephas* in Syriac or Chaldaic is called *Petrus*, “Peter,” in Greek as well as in Latin; in both languages this name derives from *petra*, “rock,” namely that rock of which Paul says: “And the rock was Christ” (1 Cor. 10:4). It should be noted that, in representation of this naming, a priest gives names to children in baptism; and furthermore the bishop, when he reconciles a penitent, most fittingly confirms him.

“And he called James, son of Zebedee, and John, James’s brother; and gave them the names Boanerges, that is, sons of thunder.” Mark calls him James, son of Zebedee, to distinguish him from the other James, called Alphaeus. The Lord called these two brothers, James and John, sons of thunder because, just as a good father instructs his son in his own occupation, so he taught them to thunder when the Father thundered in their hearing upon Mount Tabor at the Transfiguration, saying: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matt. [Col. 1383B] 17:5). Nor is it surprising if those who had learned from his thunder afterward thundered themselves.

John thundered wonderfully to the seven churches which are in Asia, saying: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God” (John 1:1). James, however, thundered—by the Lord’s command—in all Judaea and Samaria and as far as the furthest boundary of the earth, that is, Galicia: he makes fearful thunder-sounds, waters the earth with rains, and sends forth lightning. Likewise these two brothers gave forth fearful sounds, when “their sound went out into all the earth, and their words reached the ends of the world” (Ps. 18:5). They watered the earth with rains when through their preaching they conveyed the shower of divine grace into the minds of believers; they sent forth lightning when they shone through signs and miracles.

And he called Andrew and Philip, Bartholomew and Matthew, Thomas and James of Alphaeus, Thaddaeus and Simon the Cananaean, and Judas Iscariot, who also betrayed him [Col. 1383C]. The twelve apostles are named individually by the Lord and recorded by the Evangelists, lest false apostles presume to boast that they belong to the number of the elect. The number of the apostles is not devoid of a great mystery. Twelve, composed of three and four, signifies those through whom the faith of the Holy Trinity was to be preached among the elements [Note: [Col. 1383D] Perhaps: through the four regions.] of the world.

It should be known that these heroes, as Paul relates, were predestined, chosen, and sanctified before the foundation of the world for the salvation of humankind. These barons [Note: [Col. 1384D] A Hispanism; *varones*, “strong men.”] are God’s fishermen, drawing sinners’ souls out of the perilous sea of the world. For thus had the Lord formerly promised the world. The Lord says through the prophet: “Behold, I shall send to them many fishermen, and they shall fish them; my hunters, and they shall hunt them” (Jer. 16:16). Again, concerning them the Lord says through Isaiah: “Who are these that fly like clouds, and like doves to their windows, whiter than snow, more gleaming than milk, redder than old ivory?” (Isa. 60:8).

The apostles are called clouds because, just as clouds bearing rain travel from place to place and water the earth, so they too, going from city to city, water with the life-giving rains of God’s word the earthly, blinded hearts of human beings. As water descends to the earth through clouds, so through those preachers the Son of God is revealed to the world. “Drop down, heavens, from above, and let the clouds rain the Just One; let the earth be opened and bring forth the Saviour” (Isa. 45:8). The heavens above drop dew when the prophets foretold Christ to the world from their heavenly seats, and likewise the angels announced that he would come from the Father on high. The clouds rained the Just One when the apostles preached him to the world. The earth opened when the Virgin Mary received him. The earth brought forth the Saviour when the Virgin Mother of God gave Christ to the world, for the salvation of the world from Adam’s sin [Col. 1384A].

That blessed Mary is typologically the earth is testified by the Psalmist: “Truth has sprung up from the earth” (Ps. 84:12). That the Lord is typologically water is testified by the same Psalmist, who speaks in his person: “I have been poured out like water, and my bones have been scattered” (Ps. 21:5). The only-begotten Son of God was water poured out, because, as water washes away filth and irrigates the earth, so he washed away our sins with his blood and watered human hearts with his Spirit and faith. The bones typologically are the apostles, because, as bones are firm in the body, so the apostles are strengthened and joined together in the Son of God by faith and works.

These men descend like doves from lofty windows to the lowest lands when, either from Christ’s divinity to his humanity or from contemplation to action, they condescend through preaching. They return from the lowest places to the lofty windows when, either from Christ’s humanity to his divinity or from action to contemplation, they ascend in speech. Snow is white and by nature cold; it cooks vegetables and waters the earth when the sun warms it [Col. 1384B]. Therefore the apostles were whiter than snow, because those whom they made white through preaching by the confession of faith they rendered cold, that is, having expelled the heats of vices. Snow cooks the earth’s vegetables because the apostles, by preaching, struck down worldly tyrants and utterly destroyed the vices of the world. The sun warms snow because Christ filled the apostles with the Holy Spirit. Snow waters the earth because the apostles gave the Holy Spirit, which they received from the Lord, to believers through preaching.

Milk gleams by its whiteness and is sweet by its richness. Therefore the apostles were more gleaming than milk because they shone upon the world through miracles. They were sweeter than wine and milk because they nourished the childish world with their most sweet exhortations. Ivory belongs to the elephant. Since it is a chaste animal, it does not mate except once; it cannot bend its knees to the earth; it bears white skin and bones, and its hair becomes reddish in old age. Therefore the apostles were redder than old ivory through the shedding of blood [Col. 1384C], when they gave up their bodies in faith for Christ through various kinds of martyrdom. For John says: “They washed their robes and their bodies through the shedding of blood, and made them white in the blood of the most true innocent Lamb through the whiteness of faith” (Apoc. 7:14 and 22:14).

The elephant is said to be a chaste animal and unable to bend its knees to the ground because the apostles are said to have been chaste through continence and are reported, after their conversion, in no way to have bent toward earthly affairs. The elephant bears white skin and bones because the apostles at the end were made white through good works. Again the Lord says of them through the prophet: “How beautiful are the feet of those who proclaim peace, who proclaim good things” (Isa. 52:7). Before the Lord’s coming there was discord and war between the world and God; but these barons, bearing peace, established eternal friendship between them.

These are the salt of the earth, the light of the world, the towers of God’s strength, witnesses of truth, rays of the true sun, soldiers of heaven, messengers of the highest King, bright windows of the true light, gates of heaven [Col. 1384D], keys of the kingdom, lofty mountains, trumpets of Olympus, heralds of Christ, prudent as serpents, simple as doves, new lambs, rams of the true Naboth, proclaiming the glory of heaven, true fathers, judges of the ages, the laver for the washing of souls, divine gold and silver, treasuries of divine Scripture; they are held to be the baskets of the Old and New Testament, the hands of the Lord, Christ’s feet, God’s eyes, and the Church’s breasts. Of them the Psalmist truly says: “The heavens declare the glory of God” (Ps. 18:1). They are the heavens in whom Christ dwells and abides, in whose words he thunders exceedingly [possibly *minis*, “threats”], flashes in miracles, and distils dew in grace.
