They are the twelve hours of the worldly night and the twelve rays of the sun.

Before they were even born into the world, these men were prefigured by great mysteries, many figures, and arguments: by the twelve sons of Jacob; by the twelve princes of the twelve tribes of Israel [Col. 1385A]; by the twelve living springs at Elim, that is, in the desert; by the twelve stones engraved on Aaron’s breastpiece; by the twelve loaves of presentation; by the twelve stones from which the altar was made; by the twelve stones taken up from the Jordan; by the twelve oxen supporting the bronze sea; by the twelve stars placed in the crown of a certain bride; by the twelve signs of heaven; by the twelve months of the year; by the twelve senators of Rome; and by the twelve wise men. In the New Testament also they are indicated by the twelve baskets of fragments, by the twelve names which John saw written over the gates of Jerusalem in the Apocalypse (Apoc. 21:12), and by the twelve foundations of the same city.

It should further be noted that the Lord chose the apostles according to the number of the twelve patriarchs, that is, the sons of Israel, and according to the number of the twelve prophets. And just as he appointed three patriarchs—Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob—over the twelve sons of Israel, so from the twelve apostles [Col. 1385B] he chose above all others three barons and masters: Peter, James, and John. In one manner he chose these three heroes by the Sea of Galilee; when he raised the daughter of the ruler of the synagogue in the house, he brought them with him to see the miracle while the other disciples were absent; to them he disclosed his secrets more fully than to the others; to them he showed his Transfiguration on Mount Tabor; and in his Passion he grieved as it were with his beloved friends, showing them the sorrow of his flesh and saying: “My soul is sorrowful unto death” (Matt. 26:38). In likeness of these heroes, the bishop now distributes the Holy Spirit in the Church over the presbyters.

It should also be considered that the twelve apostles whom the Lord sent out to preach, and to whom he gave power to heal the sick and cast out demons, signify priests. To these he entrusted the word of preaching, the power to heal infirmities of souls through the office of absolution, and to cast out demons through the mystery of baptism [Col. 1385C]. And it must be believed that what he then did bodily in bodies through the hands of the apostles, he now does spiritually in souls, including sick souls, through the hands of priests, with the Holy Spirit at work. For just as the Lord gave the apostles power to heal infirmities of bodies and souls, so he divinely gave priests power to heal infirmities of souls and bodies.

What the apostles’ names signify in interpretation, priests ought to practise in action. For it is fitting that those who make use of their offices should imitate their names by their deeds. Simon means “obedient”; Peter, “acknowledging”; Bar-Jonah, “son of a dove”; Cephas, “head.” Peter was obedient by God’s grace, because he obeyed the Lord unto death through the mystery of the cross which he undertook; he was acknowledging, because more than the others he confessed Christ as God and man, saying: “You are Christ, the Son of the living God” (Matt. 16:16; John 6:70); he was the son of a dove because he was filled with the Holy Spirit [Col. 1385D]. He is fittingly called “head,” because his Church is held to be the head of all churches. He is called God’s grace because heavenly grace is given to the faithful through his preaching, merits, and prayers.

Thus priests ought to obey God in all things and undergo death on the cross for him if it is inflicted, or perhaps if they are persecuted for righteousness’ sake. They ought also to know the hidden things of the Scriptures, so that through preaching they may more effectively make God’s will known to human minds. They ought likewise to be sons of the Holy Spirit in faith and works. Moreover, they are held to be heads of all those who are saved and sanctified through their most holy mysteries.

James means “supplanter,” because through his preaching he supplanted idolatry and unbelief in the hearts of Jews and Gentiles and cut off vices. Thus priests ought to supplant human vices by examples of good works and by the preaching of Scripture. John means “God’s grace,” because by preserving virginity he deserved to possess Christ’s privilege of love [Col. 1386A], since he gave priests an example that they should live chastely in mind and body in the churches.

Andrew means “manly” or “beautiful”: manly through endurance of the cross, beautiful through the confession of the heart. For the people confessed concerning him thus, saying to Aegeas: “Grant us the righteous man; restore to us the holy man; do not kill the man dear to God, righteous, gentle, and devout.” [Note: [Col. 1385D] In the Life of St Andrew.] Thus priests ought to be manly by enduring adversity, and beautiful by the confession of mind and mouth, in confessing sins. “For with the heart one believes unto righteousness, but with the mouth confession is made unto salvation” (Rom. 10:10).

Philip means “mouth of a lamp,” because what he understood concerning God with a faithful heart, he confessed to all by preaching with an open mouth. A lamp in its narrow body has oil, in the oil a wick, in the wick fire; and it always has a great open mouth through which it sends its brightness to those standing around and drives away darkness. By the oil [Col. 1386B], wick, and fire is expressed the faith of the Holy Trinity; by the mouth, its preachers. Priests ought to have this faith in their hearts, confess it to all with their mouths through preaching, and illumine the dark minds of their hearers.

Bartholomew means “son of him who suspends the waters,” which plainly denotes the Son of God, who raises and suspends the minds of his preachers for the contemplation of heavenly things, so that, the more gladly they fly through lofty places, the more truly they may intoxicate earthly hearts with the drops of their words. That water signifies peoples is testified by Scripture, which says: “The waters are many peoples.” Therefore, as Bartholomew was a son of God by adoption and suspended the waters, that is, peoples, toward heaven by preaching, so priests ought to be sons of God by obedience and, through preaching, raise to heaven’s summit the watery peoples—that is, those baptized in water.

Matthew means “given” or “taken up.” He was taken from the mass of the lost when the Lord took him to himself from the customs-house. Thus priests ought, through continence, to be strangers to those who work evil [Col. 1386C], and through good works to be given to God’s grace. Thomas means Didymus, “twin,” or “abyss.” He was a twin because he was double in faith: before he saw the Lord’s wounds in the Resurrection, he would not believe; but then he both saw and believed. He was an abyss because he faithfully knew and retained the depth of Christ’s mysteries, for which reason he received the martyrdom of the sword in India. Thomas is also called Didymus, that is, “like Christ,” because he was of royal stature and like the Lord. In the same way preachers ought to be an abyss: that is, they should know the height of God’s mysteries and the depth of the divine Scriptures, so that they may be able to comprehend with all the saints what is the breadth, length, height, and depth.

Mark names James of Alphaeus (3:18) to distinguish him from James of Zebedee. This James, like the other, is interpreted “supplanter,” because by a worthy life and admonition he supplanted people’s vices. This suitably teaches that preachers ought to supplant their own vices through diverse afflictions and those of their subjects through frequent admonitions [Col. 1386D]. Of this lesser James it is written that he drank neither wine nor *sicera* [strong drink], rode no animal, ate no meat, had no iron come upon his head, was not anointed with oil, and did not use baths; to him alone was it permitted to enter the Holy of Holies.

Some hold that this James was the Lord’s brother and kinsman, because James the Lord’s brother is also read of in the Gospels and in the Epistle to the Galatians (Gal. 1:19). Some refer this to one James, others to another, and still others to both together. Some indeed assert that there were three sisters: Mary, the Lord’s mother; Mary, mother of James of Alphaeus; and Mary, mother of the sons of Zebedee. For in the time of the apostles a nephew and kinsman was called a brother. But because opinions differ, the sound conclusion is this: whichever of them was the Lord’s brother by bodily kinship, he was nevertheless his brother through doing God’s will [Col. 1387A], as the Lord himself affirms when he says: “Whoever does the will of my Father who is in heaven, he is my brother” (Matt. 12:50). It is greater to be the Lord’s brother spiritually than bodily. Therefore whoever calls either James of Zebedee or James of Alphaeus the Lord’s brother speaks truly.

Alphaeus, James’s father, means “learned,” which suits the same preachers, who ought to be firmly learned not only in both Testaments but also in God’s divinity. Thaddaeus is the one whom Luke in his Gospel (6:16) and in the Acts of the Apostles named Judas of James. For he was the brother of James, the Lord’s brother, as he himself writes in his Epistle; hence he too was called the Lord’s brother. This is attested by his fellow townsmen, who, astonished at his powers, said: “Is this not the carpenter, Mary’s son, brother of James and Joseph and Judas and Simon?” (Mark 6:3; Matt. 13:55). This man, that is Thaddaeus, was called Letheus by some.

Thaddaeus means “little heart,” as though “cultivating the heart” [Col. 1387B], because he cultivated by preaching with his mouth the good desires of his heart, namely those inspired by God, and fulfilled them by the work of his hand. In the same way preachers ought to cultivate such desires by oral admonition and fulfil them in action. Mark gives Simon the Cananaean in order to distinguish him from Simon Peter; Luke gives him, according to interpretation, as Simon the Zealot. Simon means “obedient”; Cananaean means Zealot, that is, “emulator.” He was Simon because he obeyed God in all things unto death; he was Cananaean because he received this surname from Cana, a village of Galilee, and through a spiritual zeal for God was set over peoples by preaching. When used in a good sense, zeal in Scripture expresses holiness, as the Apostle says: “For I am zealous over you with God’s zeal” (2 Cor. 12:2). In the same way, preachers ought to obey the Lord’s commands and inflame their hearers with special zeal, together with the Apostle who says: “For I am zealous over you with God’s zeal.”

Judas, who betrayed the Lord, is given by Mark to distinguish him from Judas of James [Col. 1387C]. He took the name Iscariot, a foretoken of his damnation, either from the town in which he was born or from the tribe of Issachar. For Issachar, which means “reward,” suggests the price of damnation. Scarioth, however, meaning “memory of death,” proves that he committed the crime of betraying the Lord not suddenly persuaded, but after long meditation. But why did the Lord choose this evildoer when he knew that he would betray him? For he himself testified of him to the apostles, saying: “One of you is a devil.” Why then did he choose a devil beforehand into the apostolic order? So that he might have an enemy within his household; and he who is perfect does not fear even a wicked intimate; so that he might teach us to endure evil persons among us and cast no one out of our company; and so that he might show that the apostolate and ecclesiastical ranks are not a merit but a ministry, since divine miracles and sacraments are performed through this ungodly man as effectively as through Peter.

In his place is set blessed Matthias [Col. 1387D], who was one of the seventy disciples and was chosen by lot (Acts 1:16). Matthias in Hebrew means in Latin “given.” Given by God to the apostolic order in place of Judas, he signifies priests, whom the Lord chose by the lot of the Holy Spirit in apostolic succession and gave to his Church for the governance of the faithful peoples. Judas, meaning “confessor,” when used in a good sense signifies priests, who ought to confess to all with their mouths the confession of faith which they possess in their hearts and continually commemorate in preaching the death of the Lord’s Passion.

But when Judas is used in a bad sense, he signifies evil bishops, presbyters, abbots, monks, and wicked prelates of the holy Church, who sell the Lord as Judas did when they take payment for sacred orders; for the ordination of bishops; for ecclesiastical prebends; for the nuptial blessing; for burials of the dead; for dedications of basilicas; for priests to be placed justly in churches [Col. 1388A], or for priests unjustly placed; for the obsequies of the dead; for the baptism of children; for penances given to sinners before they are excommunicated in church; or for masses and matins. As a merchant or butcher in a market makes three, six, twelve, or thirty coins from meat set out for sale, so wicked priests and monks pursuing the Simoniac heresy, selling ecclesiastical offices, make from the Lord three, seven, thirteen, or thirty coins when, even for masses, vigils, and services for the dead which should be sung freely, they demand one, seven, fifteen, or thirty coins. Let them know, therefore, that they are to be condemned for ever by that punishment by which the lost Judas is condemned eternally. As Judas, who betrayed Christ’s body and received the price of thirty coins, is condemned, so one who sings thirty masses, more or fewer, and seeks for them the price of thirty coins, more or fewer, is punished.

Some of these merchants are called Judases [Col. 1388B], others Simoniacs, others Gehazians. For as Judas, who first received money and then gave the body for it, is condemned, so bishops, priests, archpresbyters, deans, and archdeacons who first receive money and then give ecclesiastical gifts for it are condemned. And as Simon Magus, who offered money to blessed Peter the apostle in order to receive the Holy Spirit from him, to work miracles through it and seek profit from them, and who deserved to hear: “May your money perish with you” (Acts 8:20), is condemned, so bishops, priests, clerics, and monks who offer money to their superiors in order to receive ecclesiastical ranks are condemned. And as Gehazi, the servant of Elisha the prophet, asked Naaman the Syrian for money after the cleansing of his leprosy and, by his master’s judgment, received the leprosy which the prince had lost, and is condemned (4 Kings 5), so those who seek profit after spiritual gifts and ecclesiastical blessings have been given will be filled with the leprosy of all the sinners [Col. 1388C] whose money they receive and will be condemned by divine vengeance.

Therefore, brothers, let us flee their deeds, lest we endure damnation with them in eternal punishment. Let us learn to give freely what we have freely received from God: “Freely you have received, freely give” (Matt. 10:8); bestow it on all. The Lord did not seek payment from us when he gave the spiritual gift; let us not seek earthly profit from those to whom we give it. It should be understood that there is no sin in receiving, but in asking. If we ask for money in return for an ecclesiastical office given, we sin; if the giver freely gives of his own accord, without being compelled by any pressure and without our asking, and we receive it, we do not sin. Again, clerics and monks who sell land to a dead person for burial are condemned. He is an alien merchant who conducts such a market with a corpse; he who sells earth to the dead holds a barbarous market. It is true that someone said concerning the canons on Simoniacs:

> All justice has departed;  
> goodness appears nowhere;  
> iniquity fills everything,  
> and vanity of vanities.
>
> Through the desire for coins,  
> the celebration of masses  
> and every consecration  
> are governed by a price;
>
> but all this destruction  
> and this defilement  
> have proceeded from the beginning  
> from the vice of priests.
>
> By now very many clerics  
> are lovers of the world;  
> no longer Christ’s disciples,  
> they have become servants of Mammon.

Nor will evil prelates be less condemned who fraudulently take money from those who break the *treba* [an uncertain legal term], or commit graver sins—namely twenty or twenty-six solidi, or a mark of silver [Col. 1389A], more or less. Thus the prelate does not say to the accused man standing before him: “Alas, you who have broken the *treba*, or done so many evils, make right with me; repair the *treba*; give me sureties for certainty.” He does not say this in order that the sinner may make satisfaction to God, but in order that he may make right with himself, whom he has not offended. But the accused person, having supplied sureties, will give the prelate either money on loan, as he demands, or the prelate will condemn him by the sentence of strict judgment or excommunication.

Alas, alas—an utterly deceitful affair! He does not wish to impose penance for sin on the sinner, nor does he care for the salvation of his soul; instead he puts deceitful money—indeed money cursed beyond what it is lawful to believe—into his purse, and shuts the soul up in hell. Woe, woe to such men, brothers. This prelate is among those of whom the Lord, complaining through the prophet, says: “They eat the sins of my people, and they raise their hands to their iniquities” [Vulgate: “they shall lift up their souls to their iniquities”] (Hos. 4:8). They are said to eat the sins of the people [Col. 1389B] who, as we have said, receive money in this manner from their subjects. Evil judges eat the sins of God’s people when they overturn just judgments by money, or when, sparing those whom they ought not acquit, they take money from them. Evil prelates and evil judges raise their hands to the iniquities of God’s people when they rejoice upon finding one of their subjects guilty, someone whom they can accuse and from whom they can extort money.

Likewise, any prelate who, on a slight pretext, takes a cure from any priest or from anyone holding any benefice, and grants it to another after receiving money, is condemned. Just as such a prelate does not wish to be deposed from his own rank, so he ought not depose another on a slight pretext, as the Lord says in the Gospel: “What you do not wish done to yourself, do not do to another” (Tob. 4:16; Matt. 7:12; Luke 6:3).

A wicked custom has arisen from Gaul; it was established neither by the ancient holy Fathers nor by those of the present time, and therefore must be eradicated and abolished by all Catholics [Col. 1389C]. Certain false, hypocritical, demoniacal persons have arisen, whether clerics or laymen, clothed in religious garb. In remote places they impose false penances upon pilgrims travelling on the road to Vézelay, to St James, to St Giles, or to Rome, or upon any other unwary persons whom they find. For as they travel at times with these people, they first utter very fine words, setting out in order all vices before everyone; then, speaking separately with each individual, they secretly question them one by one about their consciences and sins committed. As soon as they have confessed, they impose on one thirty masses and on another thirteen for each sin.

“Have thirty masses,” they say, “celebrated for thirty coins by such priests as have never committed fornication, eaten meat, or possessed private property.” But one who does not know how he may find such men gives thirty coins, or their price, to the person who says that he will find them. The receiver does not care for the sinner’s salvation, but puts the money into his purse [Col. 1389D], spends it luxuriously, and consigns his own accursed soul to hell.

Many priests of the Church do this same thing: in the figure of the twelve apostles or of the thirty coins for which Christ was sold, they greedily demand thirty coins—or even merely ten—for thirty masses and vigils, whether for a dead person or a living one. As Judas sold the Lord for thirty coins, so they sell Christ’s body for thirty coins. Oh, what an evil market, what a most shameful profit! These are destroyers of truth: imposing false penances, selling to sinners Christ’s body which should be given freely, sending souls into hell as false witnesses, restoring the whole Simoniac heresy, blind men leading the blind. Such people should not only be removed by ecclesiastical prelates, but also despoiled by secular authorities [Col. 1390A].

Likewise, a lustful presbyter who entices to sin with him a woman who comes to him for penance, by his lustful suggestions or mocking words, is condemned. That woman resembles someone who seeks water at a well, slips into it, and dies. She also resembles one who seeks the right path in the desert and finds a bear hidden away that devours him. That priest resembles one who spreads nets in the harvest to catch a bird: while he sings sweetly, the most gentle bird comes and, falling into the net, is deceived. [Note: [Col. 1389D] “The fowler sings sweetly on his pipe while he deceives the bird.”]

On the road of St James I saw a certain man hanged who, before he was hanged, had been accustomed to urge pilgrims to depart before dawn at the entrance to every town. In the pilgrims’ manner he cried in a loud voice: “God, help! Saint James!” Whenever some pilgrim went out to travel with him, he would go with him a little way, until he reached a secluded place where his companions were waiting; with them he immediately killed and robbed him [Col. 1390B]. Clearly like him is the priest who deceives with lustful words a woman coming to him for penance. He is the well into which one falls while drinking from it; the bear devouring the lamb; the lion swallowing the sheep; the thief killing the traveller; the blind man leading the blind.

For this reason bishops should take careful thought to entrust the power of assigning penances to such most chaste priests as impose upon sinners the lawful burdens of penance not from greed, hatred, favour, ignorance, or impurity, but according to the authority of the canons and the penitent’s capacity. A different penance must be assigned for one and the same sin to a sick person and to a healthy one, to a cleric and to a layperson, to a soldier and to a religious, to a traveller and to one remaining in place, to a youth and to a grown man, to a woman and to a man.

Therefore, brothers, let us put aside the deeds of the wicked, lest we perish with them in everlasting punishment. Let each person take care not to assign deceitful penances for the sake of greed, nor seek the price of his own damnation for masses that should be sung freely [Col. 1390C]. A sinner should not be exhorted by a priest to have a mass sung; rather, the presbyter should be humbly entreated by the sinner to sing it. A priest ought to celebrate the Eucharist whether willing or unwilling; but the sinner ought willingly to offer at Mass, for the sins of the living and the dead, offerings from his goods.

Let us therefore hasten, by living and preaching well, to ascend to the fellowship of the holy apostles whose commemoration we have observed, so that, aided by the merits and intercessions of those in whose place we serve on earth, we may deserve to rejoice with them in heaven.

## SERMON II. ON THE PASSION OF ST JAMES THE APOSTLE.

On this day, brethren, the venerable feast of the most holy celebration of the blessed apostle James has shone forth for us, because it is fitting that we offer to God with prayers and hymns a sacrifice of praise, so that the merciful giver of pardon may grant us forgiveness—he who bestowed upon his apostle the palm of life. For this James was, as the Gospel history bears witness, the son of Zebedee, the brother of John the Evangelist, the glory of the Spaniards, the advocate of the Galicians, blessed in life, great in power, ardent in charity, beautiful in deed, eloquent in speech. Divine providence not only consecrated him in his mother’s womb, but also chose him beforehand before the foundation of the world, that through him it might show to this world the light of truth and give the Spanish people a shepherd of piety.

This James is greatly to be venerated: holding primacy in the illustrious court of the apostles, he deserved to be the first of them crowned by martyrdom, the first to ascend to heaven, and the first to possess the sceptre of victory, the crown of glory, and a seat in the sky. Luke, in the Acts of the Apostles (ch. 12), says that none of them died before blessed James; and, after narrating his passion, other apostles are recorded as still living. Therefore it is clear that he sits in the apostolic choir as the first adorned with the martyr’s laurel. Christ is the Lord, who distributes his gifts to each as he wills: he gave blessed Stephen, the protomartyr, primacy among the martyrs’ choir in heaven; he established blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, upon earth because of the merit of his faith; and he granted to blessed James, his beloved, primacy among the apostles in heaven through the first triumph of martyrdom. Accordingly, he is honored in glory nearer to Christ than all the rest, inasmuch as before the other apostles he was Christ’s imitator in suffering.

We command all Churches—not only those of Galicia, but throughout the whole world far and wide—to celebrate the solemnities of his passion, on the sacred day of the eighth day before the Kalends of August [25 July], with vigil, fasting, and an octave. We also command that his election and translation be proclaimed aloud by all bishops in their synods and by priests in their churches on the third day before the Kalends of January [30 December]: how he was chosen by the Lord beside the Sea of Galilee and translated from Jerusalem to Galicia; and likewise that the feast of his miracles be announced on the fifth day before the Nones of October [3 October], concerning how he raised the man who killed himself, and performed his other miracles. We further command that all the people, together with the whole clergy, assemble at church, cease from earthly work, and spend those days in the praises of Christ, with bells ringing, continuous hangings and cloths spread in the basilica, and manifold festive chants. If any basilica anywhere should perhaps have been placed under interdict, it is absolved by us, on the part of the Lord and the apostle, for these days; and the feast is to be celebrated there solemnly with great joy among those who hear it. Rewards follow for those who keep these solemnities in this manner and seek his benefits; torments await those who refuse. Rightly, therefore, should they celebrate his solemnities as they celebrate the renowned feasts of the apostles Peter and Paul.

Let the court of heaven therefore exult to the Lord in boundless praises; let earth rejoice with heavenly joys at these sacred solemnities of the most exalted apostle of Christ, James; let the Church of the faithful rejoice, adorned by his powers; let the human mind, illumined by his patronage, resound with pleasing praise to God. It is surely fitting that we return praise to him on earth with all devotion, since angels render him honor in heaven. Though all the members of my body were turned into tongues and sounded with a human voice, they would not suffice to praise the great James in Christ.

What praises, then, shall I speak of him? As soon as he heard the Lord’s voice beside the Sea of Galilee, he left all things and followed the Redeemer. Who is more blessed than he, who for Christ’s sake, having overcome Herod by steadfastness in faith, delivered his body to the sufferings of martyrdom? Who can worthily accomplish the praises due to him, who deserved to see the Son of God transfigured in the Father’s glory? “Blessed,” says the Lord, “are the eyes which see the things that you see” (Luke 10:23). Or what praises may the company of the faithful bestow upon earth on him to whom the Lord granted primacy among the apostles in heaven?

For as one entering a field abounding in various flowers, seeing the great variety of flowers, turns his gaze now here, now there, and does not know which he ought to gather or which wholly to leave behind, so I, entering the meadow of the virtues and miracles of great James, hesitate what I should say first. I desire indeed to pluck every flower of his deeds; but because they are like an immeasurable sea, they cannot be comprehended by us briefly. When I behold the sublime deeds which, before the Lord’s Ascension, he performed with the other followers while the Lord was present, I stand astonished at the special love which the Lord bore him. When I consider the mighty things which, after the coming of the Holy Spirit the Paraclete, he worked through divine grace before he suffered, I tremble. But when the inmost parts of my heart recall the loftier, unspeakable, and incomprehensible miracles which, from the day on which he suffered until the present day, God working through him has performed—not only in Galicia, but among all peoples who invoke his name, indeed miracles which I have seen with my own eyes—I am utterly astounded. But since the authority of the Evangelists compels me first to speak of those things recorded concerning him in the Gospels, I shall explain them by relating them.

Let us all venerate in the Lord James, son of Zebedee, patron of Galicia, who deserved to be honored by our Savior Jesus Christ before all the apostles, holding third place in calling and election. According to Matthew (10:3), he holds third place by election: for when our Savior was passing beside the Sea of Galilee, he first called Peter and Andrew; then, going on a little farther, he saw two other brothers, James the son of Zebedee and John, with their father Zebedee, mending their nets, and called them, saying: “Come, follow me, and I will make you fishers of men” (Matt. 4:19).

O marvelous mercy of the Redeemer! From unlearned men he made learned men; from perverse men, good men; from fools, skilled men; from fishermen, renowned preachers. O great mystery of the Savior, O wonderful reward, by which fishermen of fish deserved to become fishers of souls! When blessed James and John were caught by Jesus, they in turn catch us in the net of faith by their preaching. The apostles who were caught by the Savior themselves caught us, drawing us from the salt waters where the dragon’s heads are. For before the Incarnation of his Son, the Restorer of humankind promised these fishers to peoples endangered upon the sea of this world, speaking through Jeremiah the prophet: “Behold, I will send many fishers to you” (Jer. 16:16). Rightly did the Son both call to himself and send forth to preach the souls whom the Father had chosen beforehand.

Happy, then, were the apostles who followed so great a master while he was present; happy those who could shine while the sun was present; happy those to whom it was said, “Follow me” (Matt. 4:19). And immediately, having left father, net, and little boat, they followed the Savior. They follow the Lord not merely with the steps of their feet, but by imitation of good works. Rightly, therefore, do those follow the Lord who follow him both with their bodily steps and by imitation of good deeds. True faith knows no attachment to temporal things, knows no tie of blood, disregards the claims of father and mother, and rejects every ground for refusal. For it is written in the old Law: “They said to their father and mother, ‘We do not know you’; and to their brothers, ‘I do not know you.’ They kept my word and preserved my covenant, says the Lord” (Deut. 33).

These brothers, whom we serve through Christ’s favor, say to father, mother, brothers, sisters, children, friends, and every affection: “We do not know you. Do you wish us to know you? Believe in our Father, and we shall begin to have you as brothers from the Father. We do not know father; we do not know mother; for there is one Father who begot us. We acknowledge the Father. If you wish us to acknowledge you, then acknowledge the true Father also, that we may all be brothers.”

Happy therefore were the apostles—happy even in worldly terms. For if James and John had not disregarded their parents, churches throughout the world would not today resound with their names. If James and John had not disregarded their father, I should not know them as masters. Yet they left small things and found great ones; they left an earthly father and found a heavenly Father, in whom they became fathers of all believers. They disregarded their father’s earthly authority, but received the power of binding and loosing. They disregarded earthly inheritance, but became heirs of heaven. They left their house in one little village, but became chiefs of churches throughout the whole world. They disregarded acquaintances and relatives, but begot brothers and acquaintances throughout all the world. They left all earthly things and found all heavenly things.

If, then, they left everything and retained nothing for themselves, what will become of us, who have left little and possess everything? Indeed, in our minds we possess the things we do not have, as though we had them. If James and John had not disregarded fleshly things, they would not possess spiritual things; likewise, we shall by no means possess heavenly things unless we abandon fleshly things. [Col. 1393A] They left all things and found every good thing. Nothing was lacking to them even temporally, because they had with them the giver of all good things. So nothing will be lacking to those who have left all things if they have God with them, as he himself testifies when he asked his disciples: “When I sent you without purse, bag, and sandals, did anything fail you?” And they said: “Nothing” (Luke 22:33). Elsewhere he said: “Seek first the kingdom of God, and all these things shall be added to you” (Matt. 6:33). For the Lord himself made all things; the world is his; he created everything. Whoever has him has what is his. Whoever possesses so great a treasure lacks nothing.

“Hope in the Lord,” as the Psalmist says, “and do goodness; dwell in the land, and you shall be fed upon its riches” (Ps. 36[37]:3)—“riches,” that is, its feasts. And elsewhere: “Cast your thought [Vulgate: your care] upon the Lord, and he shall nourish you” (Ps. 54[55]:23). Therefore let nothing trouble the Christian; let him not think about tomorrow. For its own evil is sufficient for the day.

Let us therefore praise the Lord our Savior, who chose the brothers James and John out of the world and makes them rejoice in his kingdom. This is true brotherhood: amid worldly changes it could not be violated, but, leaving all things, swiftly follows the blessed footsteps of the Redeemer. By despising earthly things they reached the heavenly kingdoms. They were brothers upon earth, and they are found brothers in heaven; brothers by an earthly father, and brothers found in the heavenly Father. These are truly brothers, whom the Lord chose in unfeigned charity and to whom he granted heavenly kingdoms. By their teachings the Church shines as the sun and moon: it shines as the sun among the contemplative, as the moon among the active. They are also the two luminaries of the heavenly court, and two radiant lamps before God, whose light never fails through the ages: one made purple by martyrdom, the other made white by confession.

For “those whom the Lord called, he also justified; and those whom he justified, he also magnified” [Vulgate: “glorified”] (Rom. 8:30). Truly he magnified them in heaven, because “your friends, O God, have been exceedingly honored” (Ps. 138[139]:7). While on the mountain, the Redeemer gave this James and his brother John most fitting names, calling them, as Mark relates, Boanerges, that is, “sons of thunder” (Mark 3:17). For as the voices of thunder resound upon the earth and make it tremble, so the whole world resounded and trembled at their voices while they preached everywhere, the Lord working with them and confirming the word through the signs that followed (Mark 16:20).

To this James the Lord granted such grace that upon Mount Tabor he displayed his venerable body transfigured in the glory of the Father (Matt. 17; Mark 9; Luke 9). For James, beloved of the Lord, saw the Lord’s face shining like the sun, with Peter and John standing there as witnesses; he saw his garment gleaming like snow; and he heard the Father speaking with him and saying: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased; hear him” (Matt. 17:5). He also saw two prophets speaking with him, Moses and Elijah: one had died long before, while the other had been taken up to heaven. O marvelous thing! Those who were already reckoned among the dead appeared alive.

The transfiguration of our Savior figuratively manifests the form of the future resurrection and the appearance of everlasting life. The Lord’s face, which shone like Titan, signifies the incomparable glory and ineffable joy which the saints will receive on the last day. Hence Scripture says: “The righteous shall shine as the sun in the kingdom of their Father” (Matt. 13:43). His garment, gleaming as snow, shows the immortality of the body which we shall receive in the resurrection. Thus Paul says: “This corruptible must put on incorruption, and this mortal must put on immortality” (1 Cor. 15:43). The old Law is signified through Moses, prophecy is displayed through Elijah, and the new grace held through faith in the Trinity is signified through the three disciples.

Therefore, amid two prophets and three disciples, our most merciful Redeemer chose to appear transfigured, shining like the sun, so that the old Law, prophecy, and the Gospel might truly bear witness in the world to his divinity and assumed humanity: “that every word may stand in the mouth of two or three witnesses” (Matt. 18:16)—namely, that Word “which was made flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1:14), to whom all the prophets also bear witness (Acts 10:43).

Tabor, interpreted “coming light,” to which the Lord led his disciples up from the valley of the hills, signifies the only-begotten Son of God, the eternal light, who will come at the time of judgment. He will lead his elect from corruption to incorruption, from mortality to immortality, and from the depths to the heights of heaven; and by the light of his countenance he will make them rejoice in the future resurrection, which blessed James saw figuratively upon that mountain. O how blessed were the eyes which saw the Redeemer of all the saints transfigured in the Father’s splendor! O sublime merit of the three to whom it befell to see in the world what the world has not believed! O prophecy of Isaiah: “The eyes of those who see the Lord shall not be darkened” (Isa. 32:3).

Moreover, it should be known that on that mountain, at the place where the Lord was transfigured, when the Christian religion increased, the faithful people built a basilica of wonderful workmanship in the name of the Holy Savior, in memory of that transfiguration, and established there practitioners of the monastic rule. The inhabitants of that mountain also relate that such splendor shone upon it on the day of the Transfiguration that a stone, formerly black, has appeared there even to the present day white like alabaster. The inhabitants of that place make small crosses from this stone with iron files. Pilgrims visiting those most holy places receive them, and, returning home, carefully carry them suspended from their necks as testimony to the Lord’s Transfiguration. And the more the material is cut, the more, they relate, it increases until the turning of the year. Many who are anointed with wine in which a cross of this stone has been boiled are healed.

Exceedingly happy, pleasing to God, and worthy of every praise was James, to whom the Father from heaven wished to show the Savior of the world, still mortal, transfigured in his Father’s glory—a sight which no prophet or patriarch of old was able to behold.

> Happy is he who deserved to behold the promised Christ.

For this reason he deserved to be greatly honored by the Lord with the grace of special love. When the eternal lover, the most merciful Redeemer and our Savior, raised the daughter of the ruler of the synagogue, he allowed no one, according to Mark (5:37), to follow him into the house to see the miracle except this James together with two other followers. He who knows how to bring the good with himself into eternal rest and to exclude the ungrateful from himself, deigned also to show this miracle to his beloved.

O ineffable grace of the Savior! O his venerable working, by which the Maker of the world showed blessed James a vessel formerly shattered by a double death restored! Next, together with his brother John, James remarkably sought from the Lord that most excellent gift which no other disciple or prophet, before or after, dared to ask, as Matthew says: the mother of the sons of Zebedee came to Jesus with her sons James and John, worshipping and asking that one might sit at his right hand and the other at his left in his glory (Matt. 20:20).

It should be understood that the sons of Zebedee received the dignity of Christ’s seats, but not in the sense in which their mother asked, that one might sit at his left in his kingdom and the other at his right. For no one is said to sit at the left in the heavenly kingdom, since at the final judgment all the elect are recorded as being at Christ’s right hand (Matt. 25:33). It seems impossible that anyone should sit between the Father and the Son, since the Son sits at the Father’s right hand and the Father at the Son’s left. Thus blessed Luke also testifies in the book of the Acts of the Apostles (Acts 1:4): “The Lord Jesus,” says Mark (16:19), “after he had spoken to his disciples, was taken up into heaven and sits at the right hand of God.”

But if Christ’s left and right are to be understood in a mystical sense, it is plain that they sat at his left and right. By Christ’s left-hand seat in this place is understood the present life; by his right-hand seat, mystically, eternal life. For it is written: “Length of days is in his right hand, and riches and glory in his left” (Prov. 3:16). Whoever endeavors worthily to govern the faithful people in the present life sits in the seat at Christ’s left; whoever holds a place of rest in eternal life sits in the seat at his right. Thus the sons of Zebedee, James and John, both sat temporally at Christ’s left when, in this present life, they presided with apostolic authority over the governance of faithful peoples—in that kingdom of holy Church of which Truth itself said: “The kingdom of God is within you” (Luke 17:21). For by the kingdom of God the Church is understood: “The Son of Man shall send his angels, and they shall gather out of his kingdom all scandals” (Matt. 13:41).

At Christ’s right hand, therefore—that is, in eternal blessedness—our James and John, with the other apostles, are said to sit, beholding the desired face of the Lord. Hence they are called the judges of all ages who will come with him on the last day. But since we have said how they sit at Christ’s left and right, let us see what their mother, the sons themselves, and Zebedee signify.

Mystically, this venerable mother signifies the present Church, which became mother of two sons, that is, two peoples—the Jews and the Gentiles—through the washing of holy regeneration. For them she came to the Lord and prayed in the Psalm, saying: “From the ends of the earth I cried to you; when my heart was distressed, you lifted me up upon a rock” (Ps. 60[61]:2). The Church became mother of the Jewish people because many of them formerly came to Christ’s faith, including Paul, who holds Christ’s left-hand seat by governing the faithful people of past, present, and future through the teaching of his letters. The Church is likewise mother of the Gentile peoples, for many of them formerly were converted to the Lord’s faith through baptism, among whom were these two and many others.

For these sons the holy mother Church obtained from Christ the left-hand seat of the Lord, when from among them she established bishops and priests to govern the faithful people in this present life. She obtained for them the Lord’s right-hand seat because the children whom she regenerates through the grace of baptism she enables, through the good conscience of faith and works, to ascend into heavenly blessedness. Her spouse is Zebedee, interpreted “sacrifice of the Lord,” or “leaving the fleeing devil.” In this passage he signifies the spouse of the Church, who offered himself as a living sacrifice to God the Father upon the altar of the cross for our crimes; who also left the fleeing and proud devil when he separated him from the fellowship of the good angels and, appearing in the flesh, cast him out of the world, saying: “Now the prince of this world shall be cast out” (John 12:31).

When Zebedee is used in an evil sense, it is interpreted “the fleeing devil leaving”; but when used in a good sense, as here, the interpretation is changed: Zebedee means “leaving the fleeing devil.” A son of this spouse is John, interpreted “grace of God,” typifying those who preserve by good works, to the end of their lives, the grace of baptism which they have received. In them God’s grace so abounds that they not only raise themselves to heavenly things but also inflame others by admonition and good works.

A son of this spouse is also James the Great, interpreted “supplanter” and “comforter.” For Jacob is called “supplanter”; *hus*, with the aspiration added, as is written in Job, is interpreted “comforter.” Thus James is fittingly called “supplanter and comforter,” because those whom he formerly overthrew from vices by his preaching he confirmed in Christ’s faith by the consolation of the Holy Spirit through the laying on of his hands. Now too he seems to overthrow from evils before God, by his prayers and assistance, those who invoke him with their whole heart. Those whom he overthrows from vices he strengthens, through the same consolation of the Holy Spirit, in holy virtues.

And as a farmer or gardener roots out superfluous weeds from his garden while planting good ones, so blessed James, worshipper of Christ, formerly cut away from the field of holy Church the thorns and briars of vices by his preaching, planting roses and lilies of virtues. He thereby figuratively signifies those who overthrow the sins of the flesh through repentance and good works. But it should be noted that all who desire the kingdom of God must have these two sons of Zebedee: unless each of us has these two brothers with him, he shall by no means possess the kingdom of heaven. For unless we have God’s grace and have overthrown our vices, we shall not have everlasting life. We have John when God’s grace remains in us; we have James when we overthrow the vices of the flesh.

In these two brothers are signified all saints from the beginning of the world until the present day. All had God’s grace; all overthrew the sins of their flesh. But we must observe that it is better for us first to have James and then John, because unless we first overthrow our vices, we shall by no means have God’s grace. Solomon says: “For the Holy Spirit of discipline will flee the feigned” (Wis. 1:5). We must first overthrow the crimes of the flesh, that we may deserve to possess God’s grace. First James, by his supplanting, cleanses the shrines of our hearts; then John adorns them with divine grace. Let James therefore cleanse the temple of our heart, so that God’s grace may dwell in it.

That John is described as more beloved by the Lord than the others, and is known to have been untouched by fleshly defilement and persecution by the sword, signifies that the contemplative life is beloved by the Lord, free from the corruption of the flesh, and tranquil amid adversities. That blessed James, the supplanter of vices, is read to have been crowned with martyrdom signifies that the active life must overthrow vices by keeping them from itself and bear the adversities of the present life, so that, joined to contemplation, it may be crowned. The active life sometimes enjoys tranquility and sometimes adversity, but the contemplative life is found more in tranquility than the active. This is what the Lord testifies when, speaking to Martha as she ministers, he signifies the active life: “Martha, Martha, you are anxious and troubled about many things” (Luke 10:41); and immediately he signifies the contemplative life, saying: “Mary has chosen for herself the best part, which shall not be taken away from her” (ibid.).

May we deserve to enjoy that chosen and desired part, so that, together with blessed James, whose votive solemnities we celebrate, we may be able to rejoice in the heavenly kingdoms, by the grant of the Lord Jesus Christ, who lives and reigns as God with the Father and the Holy Spirit through infinite ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON III. ON THE SAME SOLEMNITY

Therefore, most beloved brethren, with spiritual joy, let us greet in the Lord on this sacred day the most excellent apostle James, son of Zebedee, patron of Galicia, with whom Christ shared grief in his Passion, as one beloved shows to his beloved the sorrow of his flesh, saying: “My soul is sorrowful even unto death” (Matt. 26:38). Yet the Lord was not sorrowful in death, but unto death; for he did not say, “My soul is sorrowful in death,” but “unto death.” He was sorrowful unto death because he who took on a human body had to undergo all things belonging to the body: hunger, thirst, anguish, and sorrow. His divinity did not know alteration through these affections of the soul. He was not sorrowful in death, for he who willingly came forth from the Father’s bosom, clothed in flesh so as to redeem humankind, willingly underwent death for us upon the wood of the cross. Thus Isaiah says: “He was offered because he himself willed it” (Isa. 53:7); and: “He himself bore our sorrows” (ibid., 4).

It should also be noted that the Lord is described as having his final meal with blessed James beside the Sea of Tiberias after his resurrection, because of the exceeding love with which he loved him; Peter, Thomas, Nathanael, John, and two others stood with him. O truly happy and God-beloved man, to whom the venerable Savior deigned to grant such grace that he ate and conversed with him last of all! Why, then, does the Lord celebrate his final meal with seven attendants? Because he declares that only those who are filled with the sevenfold grace of the Spirit shall be with him at the eternal banquet. Let each of us therefore cease from evil and do good, so that he may be able to possess the grace of the Holy Spirit and thus be refreshed with the Lord at the eternal banquet. “For if anyone does not have the Spirit of God, he is not his” (Rom. 8:9).

Finally, after the coming of the Holy Spirit, when the apostle of Christ, James, preached the word of God in Judaea, bore witness to the resurrection of our Lord Jesus Christ, and performed many signs and miracles, he converted innumerable multitudes of peoples to the faith. As he went on and preached the word of salvation to all nations, no one can learn how many thousands of Gentiles were converted to Christ at that time. He restored sight to the blind, movement to the lame, hearing to the deaf, speech to the mute, life to the dead; and he healed peoples of every kind of illness, to Christ’s praise and glory. He inwardly kindled all the dry hearts of the Gentiles with the fervor of the divine word, following the commands of his Master: “Heal the sick, raise the dead, cleanse lepers, cast out demons” (Matt. 10:8; cited here as Matt. 3:15). And elsewhere: “He who believes in me shall himself also do the works that I do” (John 14:12).

Not by medicines, electuaries, compounds, syrups, various plasters, potions, purgatives, emetics, or other antidotes of physicians, but by God’s grace alone, obtained from God, did the most merciful apostle restore many sick persons to complete health: lepers, the frenetic, maniacs, those afflicted with scabies, paralytics, the possessed, phlegmatics, sufferers from fever, headache, demonic possession, gout, strangury, stones, liver disease, fistulas, consumption, dysentery, snakebite, jaundice, lunacy, diseases of the mouth, rheum, madness, *epistrosi* [uncertain disease-name], albugo or corneal opacity, and persons suffering from many diseases. He did not administer to them *geram fortissimam*, “Alexandrian triferum,” Saracenic medicine, “great triferum,” *geram pigram*, *geram rufinam*, *geram paulinam*, *apostolicon*, *geralogodion*, *adrianum*, or any potion; rather, he poured out the divine grace given from above. Melancholy, red or black bile, phlegm, and blood could in no way prevail to cause harm where his most powerful virtue was present.

He aided humankind more beneficially by the saving practices of divine medicine than Hippocrates, Dioscorides, Galen, Macer, Vindicianus, Serenus, or the other physicians through the practices of the medical art. For Hippocrates and his followers benefited only the human body, whereas James prevailed divinely for body and soul alike. No pen can describe the great powers, signs, and wonders which Christ showed to the nations through him. He lived only a short time after Christ’s passion, but gained a great people.

He was most beautiful in form, handsome in appearance, tall in stature, chaste in body, devout in mind, lovely in countenance, endowed with prudence, distinguished for temperance, firm in inward strength, constant in long-suffering, strong in patience, gentle in humility, zealous in charity, enduring in hope, sober in vigils, constant in prayer, gracious in teaching, wholly truthful in speech, cautious in utterance, most prudent in counsel; bound by no chain of the world; generous in liberality toward the needy; ready in service to God’s servants; strongest in adversities, like mustard; safest in moderation; most joyful in hospitality; secure amid reproaches; beneficent amid hatred. The enemy of humankind could find in him nothing to deceive by fraud or darken by pretence. Why linger with further words? In all his conduct, shining like the morning star among the stars, he gleamed like a great lamp.

For Christ, the King of kings, had chosen this soldier, whom he sent as a most gentle lamb against the most savage legions of beasts. “Behold,” he says, “I send you as lambs among wolves” (Matt. 10:16). Thus the man of God, vigorous in the Holy Spirit, strongest warrior, lawful soldier, excellent standard-bearer, protected by the shield of faith, clothed with the breastplate of righteousness, boldly girded with the sword of God’s word, covered by the helmet of salvation, and shod with preparation for the Gospel of peace (Eph. 6:16), advanced into open battle against the ancient enemy. He shattered all that enemy’s most wicked weapons, defeated the powers of the air, rescued people from the hand of death through Christ’s power, and, after conquering the enemy, brought many spoils into Christ’s Church. He was as formidable to the enemy of humankind as he was necessary to humankind: the redeemer through Christ not merely of his own soul, but of many souls. It is not so much possible to recount the miracles done by him as to acknowledge the power of the miracles by which he gained a great people for the heavenly King in his days.

O venerable apostle of Christ! O marvelous man, abounding in piety, rich in mercy, mighty in charity! He is the true worshipper of God, who planted Christ’s Church with his blood, adorned it with great humility, cultivated it with true charity, planted it with the preaching of the word, and watered it with the heavenly dew of everlasting salvation. Thus divine mercy, through his watering, gave great increases of faith among many peoples. He shone gloriously not only in the regions of Jerusalem through the lights of preaching and works of piety; rather, as the morning star leaps across the watery plains of Ocean and, rising in the east before the daylight, scatters the shadows of night, so his fame illumined foreign nations and regions as the grace of miracles ran everywhere, so that his glory has been active throughout the world to the present day.

Concerning his powers and exhortations, blessed Fortunatus, distinguished composer of verse, confessor of Christ, and bishop, sang:

> The fame of the Lord’s worshipper has gone forth throughout the world;  
> There is no place where his lofty glory fails.  
>
> Noble in descent from the ancient stock of his fathers,  
> Yet more nobly so through merit in Christ.  
>
> An honored summit, kindly glory, abundant light,  
> Whose every distinction is enlisted in his praises.  
>
> Source of his race, guardian of his country, rebuke of the people,  
> River of eloquence, fountain of salt, speaking wave.  
>
> Preserving limbs unstained for God through modesty,  
> Faith bore him to the stars because of his merits.  
>
> [Col. 1398D] In his breast victorious patience reigned;  
> Amid such waves, it was the anchor of his mind.  
>
> Free from gall, gentle in spirit, nourished by sweetness,  
> When offended, anger did not know how to return injury.  
>
> Sweet in speech, gentle in holy self-restraint:  
> In his understanding anger lost its place.  
>
> In a patient heart he overcame another’s agitation;  
> What fickleness injured, he endured with steadfastness.  
>
> A worshipper of churches, restoring citizens by song,  
> He was a faithful remedy for his country’s wounds.  
>
> Desiring to dissolve the bonds of the bodily prison,  
> That the human being might be joined more fully to the Lord.  
>
> He who grants many miracles to earthly peoples,  
> And thereby stands forth as their singular love.  
>
> Showing by words and adding miracles to deeds,  
> So that the work might accomplish what speech bestowed.  
>
> Here he teaches Gentiles and likewise rebukes Jews,  
> And, bearing fruit for God, sows faith throughout the world.

[Col. 1399A] In the branches of heresy [Note: [Col. 1399D] Perhaps, “Heresy in the branches,” from Fortunatus, *Poems*, I, in the following poem; but the preceding verses have not been published, not even in the latest Mainz edition of Christopher Brower, S.J.; yet he attributes them to Blessed Martin of Dume. The earlier couplet is found in Book I, Poem 9.], he fixed the devout shoots of faith.

And what was a wild olive now flourishes as a rich olive.

The tree which stood scantily clad, its foliage bereft,

Now blossoms in new splendour, about to bear food.

The mournful fig-tree, destined for the hearth without hope,

When cultivated with dung, prepares its bosom for fruit.

The trembling grape of the vine-shoot, liable to be torn by the plundering birds,

Lies hidden under this good guardian, not destined to perish [Note: [Col. 1399D] Christopher Brower emends: *non perit uva lacu*, “the grape does not perish in the hollow.”].

The vinedresser set the vine-posts upright in apostolic service [Note: [Col. 1400D] He has in view Virgil, *Georgics* II: “Now the vinedresser sings of the final effects of the vine-posts.” There Servius says: “*Antes*: the outermost rows of vines, or the walls by which vineyards are enclosed.”],

Turning the ground with the hoe and pressing down the shoots with the pruning-hook.

From the Lord’s field he cut out the unproductive wild vine,

And there is a cluster where formerly there was only a shrub.

From God’s sowing he uprooted the bitter tares,

And a joyful crop rises, even in height.

In a shepherd’s care he returns continually around his own folds;

Lest the wolf enter among the sheep, he guards the flock in love.

With supporting hand he himself draws the wavering sheep to Christ’s pastures,

Lest error devour it among the mountains.

His voice, flowing back to the people from a health-giving fountain,

[Col. 1399B] Offers salt through his mouth, that they may drink faith through the ear.

You know [Note: [Col. 1400D] Another reading: *Hosti*, “to the enemy.”] the losses indeed; he prepared devout vows for the Lord,

And returns the talents entrusted to him doubled.

The gracious labourer, looking for the divine voice [Note: [Col. 1400D] Another reading: “Awaiting the evangelical voice.”],

That it may be said to him: “Good little servant, go on:

For since you have been faithful to me over a few things,

You shall be appointed over very many.

Behold, now enter more joyfully into your Lord’s joys;

Great rewards are prepared for you in return for brief labour.”

Describing, among other things, his remarkable integrity, the Wise Man said: “He shall minister in the midst of great men, and shall appear in the sight of a ruler, and shall pass through the land of foreign nations” [Note: [Col. 1400D] In the Vulgate: “he shall pass over into the land of foreign-born nations.”]. “For he shall test good and evil in all things” (Ecclus. 39:4).

Blessed James ministers in the midst of great men, because by his preaching he supplied life-giving food of eternal life to the hearts of kings and princes. He appeared in the sight of a ruler, because before King Herod he fearlessly preached the word of God. He passed through the land of foreign nations [Col. 1399C], because from Jerusalem as far as Galicia he spread abroad the Lord’s name. He tested good and evil in all things, because among both Jewish and Gentile peoples he implanted evangelical teaching and cut away heretical perversity. For thus the Lord commanded him through the prophet Isaiah, saying: “I have set thee as a light to the Gentiles, that thou mayest be salvation unto the end of the earth” (Isa. 49:6).

Blessed James is set by the Lord as a light to the Gentiles, because, having driven out the darkness of sins, he brought the nation by his preaching to the light of true faith. He was salvation even to the end of the earth, because by his word he made known even to the furthest islands of the sea him who is the salvation of the whole people. Thus the Lord long ago promised through the prophet Joel to the Gentiles, saying: “Exult, daughters of Zion, and rejoice in the Lord your God, because he has given you a teacher of righteousness, and will cause the early and the latter rain to descend upon you as in the beginning” (Joel 2:23).

Then the daughters of Zion exult in the Lord; that is, [Col. 1399D] the holy Churches rejoice in Christ through good works and divine contemplation. Blessed James was given as a teacher of righteousness to the daughters of Zion, because by the divine word he opened to the children of the Church the way of righteous faith through which they might go to the kingdom of heaven. He caused the gracious early rain to descend upon them, because the grace of God’s Spirit descended at the sound of his preaching, so as to inflame his hearers. The prophet calls the Holy Spirit the early rain, because, just as early rain makes the earth moist so that the excessive heat of the sun may not destroy the seeds, so the word of God and the gracious Spirit strengthen the minds of hearers, lest demonic temptation, sinful instability, and cunning [Col. 1400A] scatter the seeds of the divine word.

The prophet calls the Spirit of the Lord the latter rain, because, as the evening dew moistens both cultivated and uncultivated ground, but makes only the cultivated ground germinate, so the gracious Spirit, although he breathes upon all, nevertheless abides and bears fruit in the good. For the Lord himself says elsewhere through the prophet: “Upon whom does my Spirit rest, except upon the humble and quiet man, who trembles at my words?” (Isa. 66, according to the Septuagint). The prophet calls God the Father “the beginning,” because all things took their beginning in him and will finally receive their end. “I am the beginning,” he himself says, “I who also speak to you” (John 8:25). Blessed James, therefore, caused rain to descend in the beginning upon the daughters of Zion, because by preaching he showed to the children of the Church that the Holy Spirit is in the Father and the Son.

Thus he fulfilled Isaiah’s saying: “The Lord made [Col. 1400B] my mouth like a sharp sword” (Isa. 49:2). A sharp sword cuts quickly to right and left; so he judged that the good who are to be saved would come to the right hand of the coming Judge, and the evil, condemned, to the left. Again Isaiah says in the same place: “And he made me like a chosen,” or “hidden,” arrow. Certainly that arrow is hidden which, when released, more swiftly kills the enemy. Since an arrow has three penetrating elements—namely iron, straight wood, and a guiding feather—the arrow signifies the Trinity and unity of the Lord. Blessed James, therefore, was a chosen arrow, because, as the swift arrow of the archer kills an adversary, so by preaching the Trinity and unity of the Lord he destroyed in men the enemy of the human race and overthrew the ramparts of vices.

Again the prophet says: “He hid me in his quiver” (Isa. 69:2). The quiver, in a typological sense, is the womb of the undefiled Virgin, Blessed Mary, in which the chosen arrow—that is, the Son of God, one God with the Father and the Holy Spirit—lay hidden. The arrow is hidden in the quiver because divinity [Col. 1400C] dwelt in humanity. “For in him dwelt bodily the fullness of the whole Godhead” (Col. 2:9). Therefore the Lord hid Blessed James in his quiver, because in the manner of his humanity he imbued him with kindly teachings.

And again he said to him through the prophet: “Make thy cords long and strengthen thy pegs; for thou shalt penetrate to the right and to the left, and thy seed shall inherit the Gentiles” (Isa. 54:2). By the cords, with which craftsmen are accustomed to bind together any two things that are at variance, are signified the Lord’s commandments, by which God and humanity are bound together through the performance of good works.

Between God and humankind discord was once brought about through the transgression of the first-created man; but by the exercise of the Lord’s commandments concord was made. Therefore the apostle made his cords long, because he extended evangelical teaching from Judaea to the Mediterranean, or western, sea. He strengthened his pegs, because he fixed the counsels of Catholic faith in human hearts. He penetrated to the right and left, because he proclaimed to the elect the heavenly reward of their good works and to the reprobate the terror of the final judgment. And his seed inherited the Gentiles, because by his preaching he made believing peoples heirs with him of the kingdom of heaven.

As the sun illumines the obscurities of day and the moon the darkness of night, so the holy Church shone forth in his teachings. Like a bow gleaming with various colours amid the clouds of heaven, so amid the adversities of savage Gentiles and Jews he shone, burning with various [Col. 1401A] virtues; like a springing rose among thorns and a lily flowering beside waters, so he blossomed among the Gentiles by divine examples; like incense and frankincense fragrant in fire, so he became for all nations the odour of eternal life unto salvation, in order to call all back to the kingdom of eternal blessedness.

For divine power shone in him—in his life, his conduct, his preaching of the word, his gentleness and meekness of spirit, his signs and wonders, and also in every mortification of the flesh, vigils, fasts, and divine prayers. He went about villages, castles, and hamlets, preaching the word of God in the synagogues of the Jews, pressing on in season and out of season, so that one law and light of everlasting life might shine upon all nations ignorant of the Lord, and that all who had together descended to death might together rise to life. Indeed, fortified by zeal for faith, he did not cease, even because of the threats of rulers or the words of the wicked, to preach Christ’s name before the eyes and ears of savage Jewish and Gentile men, until [Col. 1401B] the hour of his death.

For, like a client sent by a great emperor, he did not fear to bring the light of truth to very great crowds of people, so that where many gathered, many might be instructed by his example or teaching. For just as a fisherman spreads his nets where he knows that a multitude of fish, birds, or beasts gathers, so that when many gather a great part of them may be caught, so too blessed James, fisher of men and hunter of beasts, did not cease to spread the nets of his preaching among crowds of Gentiles, so that, since many assembled under the pretext of this matter, many might be caught by the arrow of his preaching. And, like a faithful steward appointed by the Lord over his household to give them food at the necessary time, he hastened by every means to restore barbarian peoples with spiritual foods: teaching gently, instructing most excellently, and striving with all his soul’s strength to draw them back from the errors of idols.

O rich vessel of the Holy Spirit, who abundantly [Col. 1401C] ministered to the people the fatness of Christ’s wheat, the gladness of oil, and the sober intoxication of wine! For he was an eye to the blind and a foot to the lame, a father of the poor and wretched, a comforter of orphans and widows. Like a sailor, he guided the ship of the Church, full of the riches of the Gentiles, across the sea of this turbulent age, casting the anchor of faith, to the harbour of salvation.

Like the superintendent of the Church’s vineyards, he planted the vineyard with great labour: uprooting the thistles of vices, cutting away the thorns of perverse deeds, planting good vine-shoots, building around it the hedge of evangelical doctrines against savage beasts, and driving far away heretical foxes, whose custom is to destroy vineyards. He built the winepress of the new altar and the tower of faith. Like a modern ploughman, he first knowingly furrowed the untilled earth with the blade of his new preaching and the plough of faith, so that those who came after might more readily plough by preaching, and the ground, cleansed of the brambles of vices, might receive seed and bear more abundant fruit, some a hundredfold and some sixtyfold.

And just as one who directs a path in wooded places toward any city, making ways of knowledge [perhaps: “casting out the knots of the path”], so blessed [Col. 1401D] apostle James, the most straight-going traveller of the new law, raised up faith so that it might convey people to heaven. He levelled the rough way, removed hard stones, straightened the winding path, and made clearings among the thickets beside it for the knots of the divine commandments, so that those who came after might be worthy to travel more fittingly. For the narrow path, made wide by the passage of those following him, became a broad road. The path of the Old Testament was narrow and winding, by which few ascended to heaven at that time; now the way of the New Testament is broad and straight, by which many walk.

Therefore, when the fame of great James had spread far and wide throughout the world, Jews came to him, and then many Gentiles and worshippers of idols; they were baptized, and the idols which they had made were destroyed. Hence the ancient enemy, grieving that the nations whom Christ was acquiring through his servant were failing him, turned all the devices [Col. 1402A] of his craft against the Church of God. He so inflamed Herod, king of the Jerusalemites, and stirred him to such a frenzy of indignation that he seized the apostle and killed him.

And thus Herod, the Lord’s enemy, driven by the dart of envy, laid hands upon certain members of the Church to afflict them, and killed James, the brother of John, with the sword. Alas, alas—what a very treacherous deed! He killed him whom the angel of the Lord had once drawn from prison in Jerusalem. He slew him whom the Lord had chosen and consecrated from the world, making him worthy and dear to himself.

But after great James, apostle of Christ and invincible athlete of martyrdom, had willingly endured Herod’s sword out of love for Christ, his gracious soul, freed from bodily chains and earthly sufferings, joyfully returned to its maker and at last ascended to meet him amid the applause of angels. He gave his body back to the earth and his spirit to the dwellings of paradise, where, joined to the companies of angels, he reigns and exults in the dignity of his merits.

Blessed, therefore, was the punishment of his wound, through which he gained for himself the palm of everlasting life. [Col. 1402B] He who by death crushed death, holding the golden crown possesses the kingdoms of paradise; by shedding his blood, he himself became a sacrifice to God. Thus, when Herod killed James, the host of angels rejoiced because it had received a companion; on earth the company of believers grieved because it had lost its shepherd. The assembly of idolaters rejoiced because it saw its accuser dead.

Concerning the glorious death of blessed James, the same blessed Fortunatus, bishop of Poitiers and confessor of Christ, sang as follows in brilliant elegiac verses:

> James sent his soul from earth to Olympus:  
> O blessed man, by whose death death itself is crushed.  
>
> Before the Father’s tombs gifts of salvation are now bestowed,  
> And the mangled body cherishes many bodies.  
>
> Tell me, hostile death, where do you lie? Where, life, do you recline,  
> When you see vows granted through a saint’s death?  
>
> Him whose salvation you wickedly believed you would end in death,  
> [Col. 1402C] He gives life to many and keeps his own.  
>
> Here you lie captive, where you thought you would wage war;  
> In attacking you perish, and in raging you kill yourself.  
>
> Your own punishment presses you; your own chains likewise torment you:  
> The groans you wish to inflict, you yourself groan while bearing.  
>
> The triumphant martyr possesses heaven; you, hostile death,  
> A bright witness against yourself, inhabit black Tartarus.  
>
> Blessed one, you now remain without end in a flower-bearing seat,  
> Among fragrant choirs where incense burns warmly.  
>
> With the Judge appeased, he fears no accusations;  
> Rather, as a victorious soldier, he seeks the rewards he must receive.  
>
> Thus James, borne heavenward for his merits,  
> Is not confined by the urn of the pyre, but is held in God’s urn.  
>
> If you ask his merit, miracles disclose the truth;  
> Through them friendly salvation is brought to the weak.

But it must be considered that Herod, the beheader of blessed James, typologically signifies the devil reigning in the world. For, persecuting the Lord in his members, [Col. 1402D] he said: “Skin for skin, and all that a man hath will he give for his life” (Job 2:4); and elsewhere: “The enemy said: I will pursue and overtake; I will divide the spoils; my soul shall be filled” (Exod. 25:9). For just as our adversary the devil sought to overthrow Christ’s passion—that is, our salvation—through Pilate’s dreaming wife, saying, “Have thou nothing to do with that just man” (Matt. 27:29), so Herod, at the devil’s prompting, wished to overthrow by killing James the apostolic preaching appointed by God for the Gentiles.

Herod is interpreted as “made of skin,” or “the glory of skin.” This interpretation fittingly applies to him, because he thought not of heavenly glory but of the glory of skin and flesh. Such are those “whose god is their belly, whose end is destruction, and whose glory is in their shame, who mind earthly things” (Phil. 3:19).

Thus Herod killed the Lord’s apostle. For through him he thought he would lose his kingdom, and he feared losing his earthly kingdom more than the eternal one. [Col. 1403A] But because the Lord wished to avenge the death of his apostle, he allowed Herod to undergo such a death as is recounted in the book of the Acts of the Apostles (Acts 12:23). When Herod saw that the death of blessed James pleased the Jews, he seized the apostle Peter and cast him into prison; led by the angel of the Lord, Peter escaped unharmed by night. But when day came and Peter was not found, Herod, grieved, went down from Judaea to Caesarea and remained there.

Now he was angry with the Tyrians and Sidonians. They came to him unanimously and, having persuaded Blastus, who was over the king’s bedchamber, requested peace, because their regions were supplied with food from his territory. On the appointed day Herod, dressed in royal apparel, sat upon the tribunal and addressed them. The people cried out: “The voices of God, and not of a man!” Immediately an angel of the Lord struck him, and, consumed by worms, he expired, because he had not given glory to God and had unjustly shed the blood of blessed James.

Thus Herod killed James, and the angel of the Lord struck him: [Col. 1403B] the innocent man is killed by him, and he himself is killed by the angel of the Lord. I have not read that any of the persecutors of the apostles was slain by the Lord through an angel except this Herod, the beheader of blessed James. From this it is understood that this James was greatly loved by the Lord above others because of the honour of his pre-eminence; therefore he is greatly loved by the Lord both on earth and in heaven.

O Herod, impious king, cruel enemy of the Lord, why did you kill so great and such a man? Did you not know that you were to be slain by the Lord? You killed the armour-bearer and were killed by the soldier; you killed the servant and were slain by the Lord. O gracious apostle of God, why did you endure such things? You endured such things precisely because you were worthy to suffer reproaches for the name of Jesus. For you knew that “the sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the future glory” (Rom. 8:18).

O merciful God, why did you allow the apostle to be killed, only afterwards to kill the king? Surely in order to prepare a crown for the apostle and punishment for the wicked king. [Col. 1403C] Both, therefore, received the recompense of their merits; you gave to each according to his own merit, because you granted the apostle the crown of the kingdom and the king the hell of fire.

Thus is fulfilled in this event what is read in the Book of Wisdom: “But the righteous man who has died condemns the living ungodly; and youth swiftly brought to completion condemns the long life of the unrighteous. For they shall see the end of the wise man, and shall not understand what God purposed concerning him, and why the Lord fortified him. For they shall see him and despise him; but the Lord shall mock them. And hereafter they shall be dishonoured corpses, and an object of reproach among the dead for ever” (Wis. 4:16–19).

Therefore Christ’s apostle rejoices in that everlasting blessedness where there is joy without pain, life without death, and joy beyond telling. He fought lawfully on earth for God’s faith; therefore he is crowned in glory. He is venerated by angels, honoured by all the saints, whiter than snow, ruddier than ancient ivory. Now he sees face to face him whom he saw in likeness on Mount Tabor: [Col. 1403D] now eternally, then temporarily; now with love, then with trembling. Now he is eternally refreshed with divine feasts together with the Lord, with whom he celebrated a final, temporal meal after the resurrection at the Sea of Tiberias.
