Now he possesses in heaven that most excellent gift which he sought from the Lord while on earth. He knowingly possesses, with the elect, the seat at the Lord’s right hand which he had sought from him unknowingly.

His festivals are called not funeral observances but birthdays, because he began to live when he departed from this world. Thus it is written of a certain perfect man: “He was translated living from among sinners, because his soul was pleasing to God” (Wis. 4:14). Of such persons Solomon says: “The righteous is delivered from distress” (Prov. 11:8); of men of this kind the Lord says through Malachi: “He walked with me in peace and equity, and turned many away from iniquity” (Mal. 2:6).

Hence the Lord speaks through Isaiah, saying: “I called him and blessed him; his way is straight” [Col. 1404A]. Hence also it is said in Ecclesiasticus: “It shall be well with him that fears God at the last, and in the day of his death he shall be blessed” (Ecclus. 1:13, 19). The Book of Wisdom says: “The fruit of his good labours is glorious, and he triumphs crowned for ever” (Wis. 3:15). Then the Psalmist says: “The righteous shall be in everlasting remembrance; he shall not fear evil tidings” (Ps. 111:6).

Truly and worthily is he held in the remembrance of angels and human beings, whom the Lord made wonderful by the grace of preaching and miracles. He shall not fear the evil announcement when the Lord says: “Depart from me, ye cursed” (Matt. 25:41).

This James is read not only in the New Testament, but is also designated in the Old Testament: he is figured in Jacob and shown in Israel. For James takes his name from Jacob the prophet, and is interpreted, like him, as “supplanter”; he is rightly said to have been of his stock and is likened to him in many respects. It should be noted, indeed, that Jacob son of Isaac signifies the Gentile people, Esau the Jewish people, Isaac the Father of the Lord, and Rebecca the Holy Spirit.

[Col. 1404B] The Jewish people were formerly entitled to the grace of blessing; but because they delayed, as though coming from hunting, to the faith, the Gentile people received faith in Christ as their inheritance. Thus the disciples said to the Jews: “It was necessary that the word of God should first be spoken to you; but because you rejected it and judged yourselves unworthy of eternal life, behold, we turn to the Gentiles” (Acts 13:47).

So Jacob obeyed the counsels of his mother Rebecca, and thereby deserved his father’s blessing. Jacob bought his brother’s birthright by giving lentils; and our James, by abandoning earthly things, purchases heavenly things. Jacob saw a host of angels on Mount Bethel; but our James saw not angels, but the very Son of God transfigured in the glory of the Father on Mount Tabor. The patriarch Jacob deserved to be blessed by his father by supplanting his brother; James deserved to be joined to the Lord by supplanting the vices of the flesh. Jacob fathered twelve sons; James begot many sons in faith.

This man is [Col. 1404C] typologically one of the twelve sons of Israel, from whom he created the faithful peoples of the Church. Figuratively, he is one of the twelve fountains of Elim, which the Israelite people found while travelling through the wilderness with forty palm trees, and from which the whole Church is watered to this day. Typologically, he is one of the twelve leaders appointed by Moses to govern the Israelite people, and by whom the gracious Church is governed even now. Figuratively, he is one of the twelve precious stones represented on Aaron’s garment, from whom the Church stood at God’s right hand in gilded raiment, surrounded by the variety of its merits (Ps. 44:10). He is one of the twelve loaves of presentation, always warm and offered upon the Lord’s table, by which the whole world is fed.

Typologically, he is one of the twelve scouts sent by Moses into the promised land. Returning, they bore between two men a vine-shoot with a grape-cluster hanging from a pole, and also brought pomegranates and figs. By the grape-cluster between two men, understand Christ between the two [Col. 1404D] Testaments; by the pomegranates, the martyrs; by the figs, the Church’s teaching; and by the scouts, the twelve apostles, who do not cease even to this day to announce to the Church of God the delights of the kingdom of heaven.

He is one of the twelve stones of the Jordan, carried by chosen men from the twelve tribes to the places of encampment as a testimony to God’s miracles, upon which the whole structure of the Church is built (Eph. 2:21). Typologically, he is one of the twelve stones which Joshua set in the midst of the Jordan (Josh. 4:5), at the place where the feet of the priests carrying the ark of the covenant stood. They remain unmoved to this day, showing believers the way in Christ’s baptism. Through his prayers may we deserve to be aided by Christ our God, who lives and reigns with the Father and Holy Spirit through the endless ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON IV. ON THE TRANSLATION OF BLESSED JAMES THE APOSTLE

[Note: [Col. 1405D] On the third day before the Kalends of January the feast of the election and translation of St James Zebedee is celebrated.]

[Col. 1405A]

A reading from the Book of Wisdom (44:16 ff.): “James pleased God and was translated into paradise in order to give repentance to the Gentiles,” etc.

Beloved brethren, as today we celebrate the present sacred solemnities—the election [perhaps: elevation] and translation into Galicia of blessed James Zebedee, apostle and brother of St John the Evangelist—we ought to receive the words of this most beautiful reading with the graceful, fitting, and fragrant flower of exposition, to the honour of our Lord Jesus Christ.

For the divine reading says: “James pleased God and was translated into paradise” (Ecclus. 44:16). He was translated into the land of the living because he pleased God in the land of the dying. But where the first part of this verse—namely, “James”—is written, Enoch stands in the sequence of the Book of Wisdom. For what is written concerning Enoch himself, though it is understood typologically of Christ or of any righteous person, nevertheless the subject demands that it be taken as signifying St James.

But first it must be asked why Enoch was translated into paradise. Enoch was translated alive in his own body into paradise because, with the prophet Elijah, whom the Lord likewise formerly bore into heaven in a whirlwind, he will come at the end to overthrow Antichrist. But by what means do Elijah and Enoch live and receive clothing, since they have been placed outside the world and are bodily? Because the same most merciful Lord who fed the children of Israel with manna in the wilderness nourishes them as he wills.

And why will the Lord send men, rather than angels or archangels, to defeat Antichrist? Because, just as God formerly sent not an angel but his Son, a man of this world, to defeat the devil and free humanity, so he established that men, not angels, should be sent to conquer Antichrist. [Col. 1405B] But why will he send them rather than apostles, who are closer to Christ and members of God’s household? Because, if apostles or certain saints [Col. 1405C] of the new law were sent, then the people of the old law would have no witnesses. For there are three periods: one before the law, another under the law, and another under the grace of baptism. From these the Son of God willed to have witnesses against Antichrist: Enoch from among those who were before the law, Elijah under the law, and the apostles under grace. He formerly had the apostles as witnesses at his first coming; he will have Elijah and Enoch at his second.

And why did he preserve men still destined to die in human flesh for this work? Could he not, at the end of this present age, have raised up certain disciples of his, apostles, or men holier than they? Yet if he then recalled people already dead to this life, they would not fight with proper confidence, knowing that they would have to die again, because they would fear death. For the shadow of death is of such bitterness that one who has tasted it once is greatly afraid to taste it again.

Therefore Enoch, whose name means “dedication,” denotes Christ, who dedicated his Church by his blood. That Enoch pleased God by words, examples, and good works points to the Only-Begotten himself, who pleased God the Father in all things and through all things, as the Father himself bears witness concerning him on Mount Tabor, in the hearing of blessed James, and over the Jordan, saying: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased; hear him” (Matt. 3:17; 17:5).

That Enoch was translated alive in body into paradise signifies the Son of God, raised bodily from the dead, whom God the Father, after the prince of hell had been overcome, exalted not merely into paradise but above all the hosts of heaven. That Enoch will come at the end, give repentance to the Gentiles, and overcome Antichrist manifests Christ, who as conqueror finally cast out the devil, the prince of this world, as he himself says: “Now shall the prince of this world be cast out” (John 12:31). He gave repentance to all who come to him, as the Gospel says: “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven has drawn near” (Matt. 3:2).

And as Enoch pleased God and was translated into paradise, so blessed James pleased God in faith and works—God whose favour rests upon those who fear him and hope in his mercy—and was translated into the promised dwelling of paradise. Moreover, he preached repentance to all: “Repent,” he says, “and turn, that your sins may be blotted out” (Acts 3:19).

“[Col. 1406A] He was found perfect and righteous, and in the time of wrath he became reconciliation. Everlasting covenants were placed with him, lest all flesh should be destroyed.” These two verses are headed under Noah. Noah, whose name means “rest,” and who is found perfect and righteous, signifies the Son of God, who is more righteous than all righteous persons and more perfect than all who are perfect. In him are eternal rest, continual peace, and abiding tranquillity; in him the souls of the saints rest, as he himself says to the disciples: “You shall find rest for your souls” (Matt. 11:9).

[Col. 1406B] Just as Noah, at the time of wrath—that is, of the flood—saved the world through the wooden ark which he made and the water upon which it floated, so Christ through his cross and the water of his baptism reconciled the ruined world to God the Father. Thus blessed Paul says: “Christ reconciled the world to God through the blood of his passion” (2 Cor. 5:19); and the Church sings: “The Lamb redeemed the sheep; innocent Christ reconciled sinners to the Father.”

And as Noah was a witness to the world in the time of the flood, lest all flesh should be destroyed, so the Son of God is given as a witness to the world before God the Father, lest all flesh be destroyed in the time of perdition. For the Father says thus concerning his Son through the prophet: “Behold, I have given him as a witness to the peoples, a leader and teacher to the Gentiles” (Isa. 55:4). And blessed Job says: “My witness is in heaven, and he who knows me is on high” (Job 16:20).

By Noah, as we have said, Christ is signified; by the ark, the Church; by the water, Christ’s baptism; by those drowned in the water, our sins extinguished in baptism; and by those saved in the ark, the salvation of believers in the Church. [Col. 1406C] For those outside the Church—namely heretics, Jews, Gentiles, and the anathematized—fall into the destruction of the flood.

And just as Noah made a window in the side of the ark, so our most gentle and merciful Redeemer, pitying us most wretched people, offered his side while hanging on the cross to be opened by the soldier, so that from it might flow most abundant streams: namely, the blood of the Redeemer and the water of baptism, by which our sins are washed away.

That Noah built the ark in order to save the remnant of the world may rightly be understood of St James, because through his preaching and the shedding of his own blood he built the Church in order to call the world back to saving faith. Thus, to Christ’s praise, the Church rejoicing in his merits and teaching sings concerning him together with the other apostles: “These are they who, living in the flesh, planted the Church by their blood.”

The great father of a multitude of nations; and none like him has been found in glory, who kept the law of the Most High. [Col. 1406D] This verse, together with the four following verses, is headed “On Abraham.” By Abraham—whose name is interpreted “exalted father,” and who is called “father of a multitude of nations”—is understood the Son of God, who is regarded as the loving Father of all who believe in him, and is shown to be loftier not only than other nations but even than all the heavens and angels. Of him the Psalmist testifies, saying: “The Lord is exalted above all nations, and his glory above the heavens” (Ps. 112:4). For he is above all things, beneath all things, and whatever exists is in him. Of him blessed Job says to one speaking with him: “He is higher than heaven—what can you do? Deeper than hell—how can you know him? His measure is longer than the earth and broader than the sea” (Job 11:8).

This great and such a maker of all things, holding the world in his fist, enclosed in the womb of the blessed Virgin Mary, formerly existed beneath the ark for the salvation of the world; he kept in all things and through all things the law of the commandments of the exalted Father. [Col. 1407A] Therefore none has been found like him in the glory of angels and men, as the Psalmist says: “There is none like you among the gods, O Lord, and none according to your works” (Ps. 85:8); and elsewhere: “O God, who shall be like you?” (Ps. 82:2). And as Abraham was father of many nations, so blessed James stands forth as the most loving father and helper of the many pilgrims coming to him in Galicia; and while he still lived, he diligently kept in all things the law of the exalted God. But among the apostles none was found like him in glory, who deserved before the other apostles to follow Christ first through Herod’s sword; and he deserved to sit in heaven nearer to Christ than all the apostles upon a most exalted throne.

And the Lord was in covenant with him: as the Lord was in covenant with Abraham in the covenant of circumcision and the promise of offspring, so indeed God the Father and the Holy Spirit were with Christ in the glory of baptism and in the new offspring of Catholics; and they were present with blessed James [Col. 1407B] through the grace of divine preaching. He established the covenant in his flesh, and he was found faithful in interpretation. As the Lord established in Abraham’s flesh the covenant of circumcision, so in James and Christ’s other apostles he caused the covenant of baptismal new grace to endure. Abraham was witness and discoverer of circumcision; the witnesses and apostles are those of baptismal new grace. And as Abraham was found faithful in the Lord’s trial, when it was said to him, “Take your son Isaac, whom you love, and offer him as a burnt offering” (Gen. 22:2), so our Lord Jesus Christ is held to be most faithful when, in his temptation, the devil says to him: “All these things I will give you if you fall down and worship me” (Matt. 4:9).

Likewise blessed James proved faithful throughout his life amid diabolical temptations, in prosperity and adversity. In the same manner, whether we are tried by the Lord or by the devil, we must act faithfully and patiently. Of the Lord’s trial it is written through the Apostle: “God tests you, that he may know whether you love [Col. 1407C] him.” Of diabolical temptation the Lord says in the Lord’s Prayer: “And lead us not into temptation, but deliver us from evil” (Matt. 6:13). Therefore let the Spaniard, or any Christian, take care that, if perhaps he is captured among the Moors, he may remain faithful in all things unto the debt of death, so that he may receive the reward which God promised, saying to the faithful: “He who perseveres to the end shall be saved” (Matt. 10:22).

Therefore by oath he gave him offspring among his people, to increase him like a heap of earth, and to exalt his offspring like the stars of heaven. The offspring which the Lord gave by oath among Abraham’s people is properly the flesh of our Savior, which descended from Abraham’s stock. It is most fittingly likened to seed, since, just as many grains arise from one grain of seed, so by the blood of that same flesh thousands upon thousands of peoples and nations are regenerated through the grace of baptism. This seed grew like a heap of earth, because the Lord, the heaper-up of all good things, piled prophets and patriarchs, [Col. 1407D] apostles, martyrs, confessors, and all the elect above the heights of Olympus. Abraham’s seed is exalted like the stars because the Redeemer’s flesh is raised above the choirs of angels, and his inheritance extends “from sea to sea, and from the river unto the ends of the earth” (Ps. 71:8). Heirs inherit from sea to sea of Abraham, because Christ’s faithful are multiplied everywhere by the ordering grace of God. And as Abraham is regarded as father of a multitude of nations, so blessed James is shown to be the loving father of diverse peoples and nations who come to his venerable tomb in Galicia. And as Abraham’s seed increases like a heap of earth and is exalted like the stars, so the pilgrim people of blessed James increases daily upon earth and is exalted with him above the stars of heaven in the heavenly homeland.

He acknowledged him in his blessings, and gave him an inheritance; and he divided for him a portion among the twelve tribes. [Col. 1408A] This verse, with the following one, is headed “On Jacob.” Since Jacob greatly loved blessings, the Lord acknowledged and loved him, as he himself says through the prophet: “Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated” (Rom. 9:13). Jacob covered his hands and bare neck with goatskins; he denied that he was himself, changed name and speech, fashioned himself in his brother’s likeness, asserted falsehood as truth, supplanted his brother, and deceived his father, so that he might deserve to be blessed by him (Gen. 27). On Mount Bethel, wrestling all night with the angel, he was made lame, that he might deserve to receive a blessing from the Lord (Gen. 32). Therefore he saw the Lord at the summit of the ladder, and the Lord acknowledged him (Gen. 28:12–13).

Accordingly, we too must cover our souls—which the malignant enemy has stripped of holy virtues and the blessedness of paradise by the falls of vices—with repentance of mind and mortifications of the flesh, so that we may deserve to be blessed by God our Father. Again, we must wrestle with the Angel [Col. 1408B] who is the Angel of Great Counsel (Isa. 9:6, according to the Septuagint), namely the Lord Jesus Christ: not with the weapons of vain power, but with constant prayers, frequent fasts, almsgiving, and divine preachings, so that we may deserve to be blessed by the Lord, not on Mount Bethel but in heaven.

The inheritance which the Lord bestowed is typologically the Christian people, which God the Father granted to his Only-Begotten Son. Concerning this, Truth itself testifies thus, saying: “A praiseworthy people, whom the Lord of hosts has blessed, saying: You are the work of my hands, Israel is my inheritance.” Of this inheritance the Psalmist says: “My inheritance is glorious to me” (Ps. 15:6). The heir of this inheritance is the Son of God, whom the Lord, according to the Apostle, “appointed heir of all things, through whom also he made the ages” (Heb. 1:2). This inheritance is called the Christian portion, which the Lord divided to his Son among the twelve tribes, because, having sent his twelve apostles to preach, he separated it for himself [Col. 1408C] from heretics, Jews, and unbelieving Gentiles. For when someone divides something, he takes one part and leaves another; so the Lord, on the day of the final judgment, rejects the evil portion of the wicked and receives that of the good. Hence it is written in the Old Book: “I have separated you from other peoples, that you may be mine.” And elsewhere: “If you separate the precious from the vile, you shall be as my mouth” (Jer. 9:10).

And he preserved for him men of mercy, finding favor in the eyes of all flesh. Jacob, for whom the Lord preserved men of mercy—that is, his twelve sons, namely the twelve patriarchs of the world—signifies God’s Only-Begotten Son, for whom God the Father faithfully preserved men of mercy, that is, the twelve apostles, both here and in the world to come, as the same Son asked the Father for them, saying: “Holy Father, keep those whom you have given me in your name” (John 1:4). And elsewhere he says to them: “Not a hair of your head shall perish” (Luke 2:5). And as the twelve patriarchs found favor in the eyes of all flesh, so [Col. 1408D] much more did the twelve apostles find unfailing favor in the eyes of the true divinity, Christ the Son of God.

Jacob, who beheld the Lord on Mount Bethel, signifies blessed James, who saw the Lord transfigured in the divinity of the Father on Mount Tabor. Jacob is interpreted “supplanter”; our James too is similarly called a supplanter, because the one who supplanted his brother by fraudulently obtaining his father’s blessing foreshadowed our James, who continually supplanted human vices both in himself through mortification of the flesh and in others through preaching the divine word.

Beloved by God and by men, whose memory is in blessing. This verse is set forth in the person of Moses. Moses, whose name is interpreted “watery,” because he was found in water, and who is loved by God and men, signifies Christ the Son of God. Christ was watery when, through the water of baptism and the blood of his passion, he gave the kingdom of heaven to the faithful; and he is found [Col. 1409A] in water when he bestows his grace upon penitents through the sweet streams of tears. Thus he himself says through the prophet: “Seek the Lord while he may be found” (Isa. 55:6). In him is found the love of God the Father and of men. If Christ is loved by God and men, then through love in him humanity is united to God, and human things are joined to heavenly things.

O brothers, how precious and glorious it is to love our Redeemer, whom God the Father loves! As a bridegroom is united to his bride in love in the bridal chamber, so our love is joined in Christ to the Father’s love. For when we love Christ with worthy love, we are united to God. Through the sin of the first man we were estranged from God, but through love in Christ we have been united to him. So long as our love is in Christ, God the Father is with us and we with him. Therefore, according to the Apostle, we must provide [Col. 1410A] “things good not only before God but also before all men” (Rom. 12:17), so that through love of God and neighbor we may deserve to be loved by God and men.

Blessed James is loved by God, because him whom the Lord chose on this day beside the Sea of Galilee, he worthily crowned in the heavenly seats according to his merits. He too is loved by men in this world, because throughout the four regions of the world he is loved, invoked, venerated, and honored by all the faithful, and moreover is sought in Galicia. Therefore may that most loving apostle of Christ, James—whose feasts of election and translation we celebrate—deign to help us in all our needs and bring us to the heavenly kingdom, through the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, who lives and reigns as God with the Father and the Holy Spirit through infinite ages of ages. Amen.

[Col. 1409]

[Col. 1409]

## LIFE OF SAINT JAMES, BISHOP OF TARENTAISE

(*Acta Sanctorum* of the Bollandists, January, vol. II, 16 January, p. 26.—Drawn from an old manuscript by Petrus Franciscus Chiffletius of the Society of Jesus.)

### NOTICE

Forum Claudii, in the Graian Alps, was a city of the Centrones, situated on the bank of the river Isère. It was afterwards called Arantasia, Tarantasia, and Tarentasia, and is now an archiepiscopal see. Its first bishop was Saint James, a disciple of Saint Honoratus of Arles. Ferrarius records his feast on 16 January from the registers of the Church of Tarentaise in these words: “At Tarentaise, Saint James, bishop of the same city.” He reports that James is also venerated at Augusta Praetoria, since that city is subject to the metropolitan see of Tarentaise. Saussay, in the supplement to the Gallican Martyrology, writes of him as follows:

> “At Tarentaise, in Gaul Narbonensis itself, Saint James, bishop and confessor of that metropolitan see. Filled with apostolic spirit, he illuminated this region with the torches of the Gospel and filled it with faith and religion. Having established there a permanent episcopal see, organized its hierarchy, and appointed Marcellinus—a man of proven virtue and grace—as heir to the sacred office, he had most holily presided over the flock which he had gathered; then he received from the Lord, whom he had served zealously, the reward of faithful stewardship. He also founded the episcopal church of the Salassi at Augusta Praetoria, and established Saint Eustachius as its first shepherd.”

Petrus Franciscus Chiffletius, one of our own, copied and communicated to us the Life of Saint James, though mutilated, from an ancient codex. He conjectures that its author was Guy, of the counts of Burgundy, first archbishop of Vienne and then Roman pontiff Callixtus II. “For,” he says, “we read that he wrote several Lives of saints; Tarentaise lies in old Burgundy and in the province of Vienne; and in our manuscript codex this Life appeared after the book of that same Callixtus on the translation and miracles of Saint James, apostle of the Spains.”

## THE LIFE BEGINS

[Col. 1411]

### PREFACE

[Col. 1411A]

1. Since, through the changeability of times and the departure of mortals, good deeds are sometimes handed over to oblivion, we transmit for later generations to read, as we believe to their great profit, the Life of the most blessed James, archbishop of Tarentaise. As we are about to speak of his virtues and miracles, we humbly warn our hearers that, when they have learned the mighty deeds which almighty God deigned to work through him, they should strive also to imitate his life and character. Let them know that those who wish devoutly to follow and diligently to cling to his footsteps shall themselves attain the joy into which he entered, through the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, who is God above all, blessed for ever. Amen.

## CHAPTER I. Saint James’s monastic life

2. Therefore, when the trumpet of the holy Gospel was sounding through almost the whole [Col. 1411B] world, saying, “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven draws near,” blessed James, a soldier who in worldly rank was held illustrious among the Assyrians, [Note: [Col. 1411D] Saint Hilary therefore says truly in his *Life of Saint Honoratus*, ch. 3, no. 17: “For what land still exists, what nation, that does not have its own citizens in his monastery? What barbarism did he not soften?” etc.] being anticipated by divine gift, strove to enter by the narrow gate that leads to life, as became clear at the end. Accordingly, rejecting the military dress in which he shone, he resolved diligently, as one poor, to follow the footsteps of Christ who was poor; and, converted to the Lord, he strove with all his strength to fulfill in deed what he held in his heart.

Above all things he had an immense desire to be able to find somewhere a teacher who would instruct him more fully in faith and love of God. Thus, within no long time, receiving the sacrament of baptism and attaching himself to a certain servant of God, the monk Honoratus, who at that time flourished in Gaul, he wholly gave himself over to the service of God. Thereafter utterly abhorring the service of the crafty enemy, he chose the better part when he joined himself to the holy master.

[Col. 1411C]

3. When he had remained for some time in that place, where the devoted disciple was joined to his venerable master, a report spread widely that a pestilential dragon had besieged the island of Lérins and, as was its habit, overwhelmed those sailing about that island with a most foul odor. Then the man of God Honoratus, having summoned only his disciple James, left behind his own sheep which he had won for the Lord in that place [Note: [Col. 1411D] A word such as *leaving behind* appears to be missing.], and travelled through parts of the province. Then, approaching the said island by ship, he constantly implored the Lord’s mercy together with his disciple in the faith, and utterly drove the pestilential dragon [Note: [Col. 1411D] The composer of the apocryphal Life of Saint Honoratus tells many fables about this dragon. Pliny, *Natural History*, book VIII, ch. 14, and Solinus, ch. 2, write astonishing things concerning the size of serpents, especially boas.] from that island, so that it never afterwards appeared anywhere there.

4. The servants of the Lord, seeing that the said island had been cleansed of the ancient enemy and was suitable for the uses of monks, [Note: [Col. 1412D] That is, a sacred building. Thus Pliny, book XII, ch. 23: “also from the oracle of Hammon, beside which the tree grows.”] built an oratory and erected a cell. There they lived together for several years, strong in virtues and radiant with miracles; and, having gathered disciples, that place, founded from the same community, is governed to this present [Col. 1412A] day in religious observance by monks.

## CHAPTER II. His episcopate; the building of a church; miracles

5. Meanwhile the fame of the man of God Honoratus grew as far as Arles. He was sought by the clergy, nobles, and common people of that city, because their bishop had already passed to the Lord, that they might be worthy to have as bishop the same servant of God, the monk Honoratus. Thus the clergy of the aforesaid city took him unwillingly, brought him with them, and, with great rejoicing and common counsel, all chose him as their bishop.

6. While he was illustrious upon the episcopal throne and his disciple James was constantly with him, he saw him to be a man of extraordinary holiness. He addressed him and begged him with all the affection of his heart [Note: [Col. 1412D] Papirius Massonus, in his book *On the Rivers of Gaul*, reports that Centron was a village from which those peoples took their name, “now almost insignificant; and, if it did not still retain its name today, entirely obscure.”] to go to the town of Cendron and convert to Christ’s faith the people living there under the rite of paganism. [Col. 1412B] When he heard this, the obedient disciple gladly and with ready humility gave his consent, and promised that, with the Lord’s help, he would do so according to his ability.

Therefore the venerable Father, having summoned other priests, ordained James bishop and sent him to the aforesaid town and the valley of Tarentaise to preach the word of the Lord. When he arrived, as though secretly, God’s providence caused his fame to spread through the people, so that they openly said that the beloved servant of Christ, Bishop James, had now come to them. On learning this, God’s priest James rejoiced at such great benefits from Christ. At first dawn, when he began to preach, an innumerable crowd was converted to the faith of Christ; and without delay, almost all the people of the aforesaid town came together, with ready heart and one will, to the grace of baptism.

7. But a few unbelievers remained in the valley of Tarentaise, who did not joyfully submit their necks to the preaching of Bishop James. Seeing this, the venerable bishop rejoiced and exulted over the great flock won for Christ, [Col. 1412C] and founded a basilica. Then he ordered his servants to cut in the woods beams and other timbers, as well as materials for the roof of that building. As the Christians, inflamed with more fervent faith, were bringing them with their oxen, a huge bear sprang from its cave. With utmost ferocity, seizing in its claws one of the oxen yoked to haul a beam, it tore and gnawed it with savage and shameless mouth. When the servants saw this, struck by fear, they ran with greatest speed and reported it to the bishop.

Hearing this, the holy man hurried there and found the bear devouring the ox’s corpse. It is said that he told it: “I, James, servant of Christ, command you, most savage and bloody beast, in the name of the Lord, to bend your stiff neck to the work which you have hindered, and submit your proud neck to the yoke of the ox which you killed.” Immediately at the voice of God’s servant, though roaring, it placed its neck beneath the yoke. [Col. 1413A] The servant of the Lord bound it with the straps which had belonged to the ox and caused the beam to be drawn to the work that had been begun.

At this sight the older inhabitants of the town were amazed at so great a miracle; but the younger men, whom sluggishness still held, took up swords and tried to kill the bear. When the man of God perceived this, he restrained the young men with gentle speech and said: “My little sons, allow the beast, which you have caught with no snare, to leave your borders alive.” When they obeyed, blessed James commanded the bear never thereafter to inflict any harm in that valley. It withdrew unharmed into a deep wilderness and was never again seen anywhere in the said territory.

8. Then the Lord, wishing to show the splendid merits of his most faithful servant, displayed a second great miracle. The beam which the bear, yoked with the ox, had brought from the wood was found to be five feet shorter than the other beams. The servant of God sprinkled that beam with consecrated water [Col. 1413B] and, praying in the sight of all, made it equal to the others. When this miracle had been performed by God’s gift, all the inhabitants of that valley, inflamed with divine love, utterly cast away the darkness of their former error, clung unwaveringly to the true light, which is Christ, and established their foundation upon that cornerstone, Christ Jesus our Lord.

## CHAPTER III. His journey to the prince, made illustrious by various miracles

9. When the basilica had been fittingly completed and dedicated in honor of Saint Stephen the first martyr, it seemed good to God’s servant Bishop James to visit the prince of the Gauls and bring him certain small gifts, so that they might merit to gain his acquaintance. Accordingly, he took snow gathered in summertime; and, loading an ass with it, set out with his disciple James and other servants. A marvelous and most worthy thing to report! Although the heat of the burning sun, which at that season [Col. 1413C] dried the fields, completely melted all other snows by the excessive heat of its blaze, neither summer’s mildness nor any heat melted the snow he had taken from the town of Cendron; rather, hardened with icy cold, it remained whole.

10. As he was making the journey he had begun, weary from excessive heat, [Note: [Col. 1413D] Greek *kauma*: heat, the sun’s burning.] he turned aside into some shade, and the little ass that bore the snow rested a while. A most hideous bird flew up—at the instigation, it seemed, of the ancient enemy, who always opposes God’s servants insofar as he is permitted—and settled upon the resting ass, tearing out its eye. When the servants saw blood dripping from the ass’s cheek, they told their master. He immediately arose and, invoking Christ’s name, ordered the bloody raven to return, saying: “I command you, most hideous bird, in the name of the Lord, immediately to bring back what you stealthily took from our ass.”

It was marvelous to see the raven bring back, croaking, what it had taken. [Col. 1413D] Having vomited out the eye at the very place from which it had violently torn it, it restored the snow-bearer to its master sound and whole. They immediately placed the load of snow upon it and continued the journey they had undertaken.

11. After these events, before the labor of the long journey was completed, one of his disciples—his kinsman according to the flesh and still nearer according to the spirit—named James, was seized by a fever. This occurred, as later became evident, by divine ordinance, so that the merit of the most holy bishop might be revealed both among distant lands and nearby regions. At length, having entrusted the sick man to the faithfulness of Christians, he proceeded on his way [Col. 1414A] and came to the prince of the Gauls. Presented before him, he first offered a greeting and then the snow. But the prince, filled with an evil spirit, repeatedly cried out in a loud voice, calling God’s servant a deceiver, a great sorcerer, and an evildoer; with swelling and angry heart he contemptuously ordered that the snow be received.

12. Immediately he was tortured by most severe pains of fever. Languishing and dying, already at death’s extremity, he at once sought a remedy for health. Then one of the nobles present wisely addressed him: “Why do you now eagerly seek the medicine of health, when you presumed to grieve the man of God, who is full of the Holy Spirit, illustrious and powerful in miracles, and performs great wonders everywhere through the Lord’s power?” On hearing his nobleman’s rebuke, the prince was seized with great fear. He ordered the servants attending him to go after the bishop with the greatest speed; and instructed them, falling at his feet and kissing his footprints, to strive to obtain his consent to visit in person and help the sick man with a kindly countenance.

13. When the matter became known to the man of God, moved by his customary mercy he promptly returned, entered the prince’s court, and poured out prayers before the Lord; he cured the sick man of his violent fevers. On account of this miracle, so suddenly and evidently wrought by God through the holy man, the whole household of the prince rejoiced exceedingly. Extolling the holy man’s power, they unanimously returned boundless praises to the Lord. The prince, wonderfully rejoicing at the desired recovery of health obtained through the holy bishop’s prayers, gave many thanks to God and to God’s servant. He asked him to request confidently [Col. 1414C] whatever he wished to obtain, for he would by no means suffer him to be refused.

To this the holy man replied: “O glorious ruler of all Gaul and Burgundy, I have undertaken the difficulty of so long a journey from the desire to see you. I ask from you neither gold nor silver. But because the place of my diocese is enclosed amid steep and narrow Alpine mountains and is not suitably spacious for habitation, it is expedient for us that your dignity should take care to enlarge its boundaries somewhat. I therefore mercifully entreat your magnificence that, for God’s sake and in love of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, and for the perpetual remembrance of your name, you may deign to grant us, for the honor of God and blessed Peter the apostle, some increase from the lands of your kingdom lying around our humble church—an increase profitable for our use and that of our successors, and to be possessed in perpetuity by the tenor of your most firm decree.”

The prince answered him: “Whatever you wish to ask shall be done for you.” [Col. 1414D] The holy man replied: “What I ask of you is indeed most fitting and necessary for me, but may be light and very easy for you to give: namely, a certain rock of projecting stone, which the inhabitants of that place in their ancient language call Pupim . . . . . [Note: [Col. 1414D] Here the torn parchment fails me. Saint James, apostle of the people of Tarentaise, is venerated in his own diocese and in other neighboring places on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of February [16 January], the day on which his master Saint Honoratus, bishop of Arles, is also commemorated.]”

# IN THE YEAR OF THE LORD 1124: RADULF, ARCHBISHOP OF RHEIMS

[Col. 1415]

## NOTICE

(*Gallia Christiana*, new edition, vol. IX, col. 80)

[Col. 1415A] After Manasses’s death, while Richard, archdeacon of Verdun, and Lambert, abbot of Saint-Bertin, refused the archbishopric, the canons of Rheims and all those who by right ordinarily cast votes in the election [Note: [Col. 1415C] *Acta Sanctorum Ordinis Sancti Benedicti*, vol. IX, p. 507.] divided into two factions. Some named Radulf the Green, provost and treasurer of the greater church, a man of outstanding learning and integrity. Paschal immediately confirmed him without waiting for the king’s consent. Others, however, strongly favoring the royal party [Note: [Col. 1415C] *Annales Benedictini*, vol. V, p. 674.], elected Gervasius, son of Count Hugh of Rethel and Milesendis, archdeacon of the Church of Rheims. Relying upon royal authority, Gervasius stoutly opposed Radulf’s enthronement, although the pope vainly threatened an interdict.

The pontiff nevertheless stood by Radulf, whom [Col. 1415B] the clergy received as legitimate; the king stood by Gervasius. Thus there were two archbishops in the city and two factions, each group supporting whichever party it pleased. Meanwhile Louis VI, king of the Franks, assumed the reins of the kingdom and was consecrated at Orléans on 2 August 1108 by Daimbert, archbishop of Sens—not by either of the disputants—while the canons of Rheims protested in vain.

At last peace was restored to the Church of Rheims. At Christmas 1108, chiefly through the agency of Ivo, bishop of Chartres, and Lambert, bishop of Arras, Radulf rendered to the king, by hand and oath, that fealty which, as Ivo himself says, all archbishops of Rheims had previously rendered to their predecessors, the kings of the Franks, [Col. 1415C] as had all other bishops of the kingdom of the Franks, however religious and holy. Gervasius, however, not yet initiated into holy orders and deprived of the bishopric, resumed, according to Alberic, the dignity of archdeacon which he still held in 1112; later he abandoned the clerical state, seized the hereditary county of Rethel, and married Elizabeth, daughter of Geoffrey, count of Namur, born of Sibylla, daughter of Count Roger of Porcien.

In 1109, the third year of his archiepiscopate, Radulf gave three altars to the monks of Saint-Nicaise. In 1110 he attended the Council of Fleury. In 1112, after the funeral rites of Gaudry, bishop of Laon, had been celebrated, he consecrated Hugh as his successor. In the same year he approved the foundation of the priory of Rumigny, dependent on the abbey of Saint-Nicaise. [Note: [Col. 1416C] Baluze, *Miscellanea*, vol. V, p. 357.] At about the same time Herbert, archdeacon of Thérouanne, was elected bishop of Tournai; but we have already observed that Radulf refused to lay hands on him because he favored Lambert, whom the people of Noyon had taken as bishop, and thus the efforts of the people of Tournai were frustrated. [Note: [Col. 1416C] *Gallia Christiana*, vol. III, p. 211.]

In 1113 he subscribed the charter of foundation of Saint-Victor [Col. 1416B] of Paris, and consecrated Bartholomew bishop of Laon. In 1114, in September and December, he attended the synods of Rheims and Beauvais; then in the following year, in March, another synod of Rheims held by Cono of Palestrina, legate of the Apostolic See. At about the same time he received letters from Pope Paschal II, warning him that, after the death of Lambert, bishop of Arras, he should take care to have another bishop set over that church. In 1116 he gave two altars to the canons of Saint-Denis at Rheims for his anniversary. In 1117, at the request of Abbot Bovo, he confirmed the privileges of the monastery of Saint-Amand. In 1118 he approved the restoration of the church of Blessed Mary at Rethel, made by Count Hugh in favor of the monks of Saint-Remi. [Col. 1416C]

In 1119 he gave the altar of Sorbon to Boso, abbot of Fleury. In the same year, in October, Pope Callixtus II convened a most celebrated council in the metropolitan church of Rheims. At about the same time, together with the legate Cono, Radulf held a council at Soissons against [Col. 1417A] Peter Abelard; and he confirmed the privileges of the collegiate church of Saint-Symphorien at Rheims. In the following year, at the synod of Beauvais, he approved with the same Cono the decree of the Fathers concerning the raising from the earth of the body of Saint Arnulf, bishop of Soissons. In the same year he confirmed the foundation of Saint-Martin of Ypres. At about the same time the canons of Beauvais appealed to him as judge concerning the cloistral houses of canons, which were not to be possessed by laymen. In 1122 he confirmed the foundation of Francheval in favor of the Premonstratensians. In 1123 he settled a certain controversy between the Cluniac monks and Saint-Prix. In 1124, a few days before his death, he granted to the monks of Saint-Remi the altar of Saint Julian adjoining the church of Blessed Remigius, to be held without a personal incumbent. [Col. 1217B]

Anschérus, abbot of Centula, and Lisiard, bishop of Soissons, dedicated to him books which they had written or revised: the latter a work on the life of Saint Arnulf, the former one on the miracles of Saint Angilbert. John, formerly scholasticus of Rheims and later a monk of Saint-Evroul, likewise dedicated to him the poem he composed in praise of Saint Ebrulf. The necrology of the metropolitan church says of him:

> “On the tenth day before the Kalends of August [23 July], Lord Rodulf, archbishop of great holiness, died. He acquired Attigny for this church and governed both the whole church and province with great honor for the glory of God.”

Orderic Vitalis writes in this manner:

> “Radulf, surnamed the Green, archbishop of the people of Rheims, was eminent among the Fathers for learning and eloquence. In our time he was laudably devoted to worthy pursuits; a father and instructor of monks and clerics, and the patron and defender of the poor and all subject to him. After many praiseworthy works, he died in a good old age. After him Rainald, bishop of Angers, in many respects unlike his predecessor, obtained the see.”

His body was carried not to the church of Saint-Denis, as the Sammarthani say, but to the church of Blessed Remigius, which he had loved intensely in life. It was committed to burial [Col. 1418B] beside the entrance to the choir on the north side. There survives a letter of Saint Bruno to Radulf the Green, complaining that he had not fulfilled his vow to embrace the monastic life. Yet our Martène said that he found, in the register of monks who lived under Azenarius, abbot of Saint-Remi, the name of Archbishop Radulf. From this it must be inferred that perhaps, while ill and near death, the prelate took vows and became a monk of Saint-Remi.

[Col. 1417]

# LETTERS OF RADULF, ARCHBISHOP OF RHEIMS
I. Of the Chapter of Reims to Radulf.—That he should no longer seek the archiepiscopal see.  
[Note: [Col. 1417C] After the death of Manasses II, the clergy of Reims, divided into two factions, could not agree upon the choice of an archbishop. Some elected Raoul the Green, provost of the chapter; the others, Gervais, archdeacon and son of the count of Rethel. The pope approved Raoul’s election; the king declared for Gervais. [Col. 1418C] Hence arose clashes so serious that the pope placed the city under an interdict. This schism finally ceased in 1108 through the efforts of Ivo of Chartres and Lambert of Arras. Gervais, compelled to withdraw, left Raoul in possession of the episcopal see.] (Year 1107.)

[Acts of the Ecclesiastical Province of Reims, II, 166.]

[Col. 1417C]

To RADULF, provost of the church of Reims: the brethren, all the priests who are at Reims, RICHERIUS the cantor, and those with them, who shun the ways of discord and strive toward the vision of peace.

The brethren of the church of Reims, worn down by prolonged and unceasing affliction, throw themselves at the knees of your judgment, begging and imploring that, while there is still time, while every opportunity has not yet wholly slipped away, you may have pity upon the church of Reims, may grieve with her in her daily tears [Col. 1418C], may provide a remedy for her wretched and violent dismemberment, and may show indulgence toward the intolerable want of the brethren. Finally, do not—if the expression may be pardoned—be so negligent and cruel toward your reputation, hitherto unblemished. For what cruelty is harsher or less heard of than to reject the tears of that mother who raised you needy from the dust; who, when you were small in your own eyes, set you as a head over her tribes?

Remember, as one learned in letters, that although all vices belong to Satan’s household and family, these two are more especially domestic to him and continually dwell in Satan’s inner chambers: ambition and envy. To force oneself by any means into the title of bishop, when neither people desire one, nor clergy elect him, the princes reject him, and the king’s displeasure has disowned him [Col. 1419A]—what does this appear to be but ambition? For no one ought to take honour to himself, but he who is called by God, as Aaron was (Heb. 5). We understand him to be called by God whom election calls; but he takes honour to himself whom ambition seizes through swords, through fire and blood, through the oppression of the poor and the tearing apart of churches. Yet he whose charioteers are ambition and envy must needs rush headlong.

And envy indeed: for, though you may conceal and deny it with your lips, your conscience nevertheless cries within you that the schism of the church of Reims did not proceed from zeal for religion but, as is clearer than daylight, from envy. Do not be disturbed if our letter has exceeded somewhat in sharpness, since it is difficult to keep [Col. 1419B] moderation in words concerning matters in which daily sighs, the dispersal of their goods, the violent and continual oppression of the poor, the silencing of divine worship, and the whirlwinds and assaults of almost every adversity can find no end. Yet harsh correction, sparing least, when uttered lovingly from the mouth of a neighbour, is better and more useful than flattering persuasion on the tongue of an adulator, who has no concern for a man’s reputation.

Let your prudence therefore see how every sex, every age, every condition reproaches you in words. For whereas their former judgment concerning you was that you laboured for the liberty of the church of Reims, behold, all now cast it in your teeth that this is not the liberation of the church, but the sole cause is fierce and shameless ambition, vainly alleging that it comes from the lord pope—whom, on reasonable grounds, you may readily excuse [Col. 1419C] from driving you into the chair of the man whom you accused; it will be easy and consonant with reason to restrain yourself.

But if—God forbid!—you are moved neither by the tears of your mother the Church, recalled neither by the intolerable poverty of the brethren, touched by no pity for the oppression of the poor, nor restrained by reverence for bloodshed, and contend to be advanced amid schism, then we, as brethren, stand opposed to a brother: for we consent neither to the election nor rejoice in the advancement. May the God of peace and love remove far from your mind and deed whatsoever may belong to schism and hatred.

II. Of Radulf to Lambert, bishop of Arras. (Year 1112.)

[See Patrology, vol. CLXII, col. 692, among the letters of Lambert and various persons to him.]

[Col. 1419D]

III. Of Bruno, archbishop of Trier, to Radulf, concerning the injuries inflicted by certain nobles upon the nuns of the Blessed Virgin Mary at Trier. (Year 1115.)

[HONTHEIM, Diplomatic History of Trier, III, 499.]

To RADULF, venerable archbishop of the church of Reims, BRUNO, servant of the church of Trier: the service of devout devotion.

[Col. 1420A] The goodness of Your Blessedness, often experienced, compels me to love you; and I stand ready at all times to demonstrate the affection of that love. Therefore, not at all distrustful of your charity in this reciprocal matter, I presume to ask what I desire to obtain through the gift of your kindness and in expectation of fitting recompense: namely, that you receive and hear our sister, the bearer of this letter, in the place of myself and of all her sisters who serve our Lady [Note: [Col. 1419D] In the royal monastery at Horreum.] Saint Mary, Mother of God, at Trier; and that, after taking counsel with your fellow bishops, religious brethren [Note: [Col. 1419D] Gathered at the synod of Reims held in this year. On this synod, see Marlot, *History of Reims*, vol. II, book II, chap. 26.], and with the princes of your land, you do not delay to render justice against Nicholas and Guy [Note: [Col. 1420D] Nicholas of Rumigny and Guy of Guise. See the following charter.] who have for so many years despoiled our Lady Mary at Condé and in her dependencies.

May it avail us that the brethren of Saint Remigius [Col. 1420B], and other men of your parts, as you may learn from them, have seldom departed without consolation according to our means after appealing to my lowliness in your name concerning their possessions situated in our land. May it also avail us that your church and ours are found to have been united from ancient times, and no one acquainted with the privileges of our churches has denied that they are sisters. May Your Holiness ever fare well in Christ.

IV. Another letter of the same to the same, of similar subject matter. (The same year. Ibid.)

To RADULF, venerable archbishop of the holy church of Reims, BRUNO, by the mercy of God archbishop of Trier: such devout offices [Col. 1420C] of prayers and service as are his due.

The report of your equity and piety toward God invites us, who have long suffered a most unworthy and intolerable injury in your archbishopric, to implore your aid, which you ought neither to deny nor delay us. For although all churches participate in a certain kinship of social unity and, according to what befalls them in turn, should rejoice and grieve by apostolic authority, nevertheless our church and yours are found to have been joined from ancient times by a more particular bond of charity; nor are they denied to be sisters by anyone who knows well the privileges of our churches. Accordingly, from this sisterly fellowship and confidence [Note: [Col. 1420D] On this sisterly bond between the churches of Trier and Reims elsewhere more frequently.], we lay before your charity the injury of your sister [Col. 1420D].

Nicholas of Rumigny and Guy of Guise and of Hirson, and other men of theirs, have long usurped for themselves, contrary alike to divine and human laws, these villages of Ludousa, Aneia, Balbeneis, and Guartheneis, with their dependencies, which are the property of our Lady Saint Mary and of the nuns serving her at Trier. They abuse the revenues of these possessions by plunder and boldly withhold the maintenance of the aforesaid handmaids of God and His Mother. We therefore beseech the charity of Your Dignity to admonish them to desist from such presumption; and, if they persist obstinately in perpetrating [Col. 1421A] this sacrilege, to restrain them with the due severity of the episcopal office.

My predecessor delivered their predecessors to Satan, since they claimed those same aforementioned villages for themselves by the same violence as these men do; they were buried under that sentence of delivery and sent into hell. But I have not wished to bind these men with the bond of this anathema until I heard your response on the matter. May the blessing of the Lord be upon you and upon all entrusted to you.

[Note: [Col. 1421C] Marlot reports, *History of Reims*, vol. II, p. 259, that there is also a letter from the chapter and clergy of Trier to Radulf, archbishop of Reims, on the same subject, indicating that it was sent at the same time as the others during the synod; its words are these: “When this letter has been read by Your Holiness, command that it be read or made known first to our brethren in the chapter of Saint Mary Mother of God, and then to the synod of the holy council, so that, by their counsel and especially by the help of your brother Bartholomew, bishop of Laon, you may bring our petition to effect.” Marlot adds in the cited place that these repeated complaints of the people of Trier, together with what Abbot Suger relates in various places, clearly [Col. 1422C] show with what fury the nobles of that time preyed upon ecclesiastical property: here Thomas of Marle throughout the dioceses of Laon and Amiens; there the lords of Rumigny and Guise in the territories of Trier adjoining Reims; elsewhere the counts of Champagne, Rethel, and Roucy, and others. Yet none of these measures appears to have succeeded in procuring peace and safety for the nuns from the invasions of these nobles, since our Adalbero later wrote again, in nearly the same tenor, to Reinald, archbishop of Reims. The letter was published by Martène and Durand, *Amplissima Collectio*, vol. II, p. 626.]

V. Of Goscelin, dean of Beauvais, to Radulf, archbishop of Reims.—Concerning houses of canons not to be held by laymen. (About the year 1120.) [MARTÈNE, *Amplissima Collectio*, I, 349, from the cartulary of the church of Beauvais.]

[Col. 1421B]

To Father and Lord RADULF, by God’s grace archbishop of Reims, and to the assembly of the holy church of Reims: GOSCELIN, dean, and the congregation of the church of Beauvais, greeting and due submission.

First, we entreat your gentleness not to be wearied by a lengthy letter, because this matter cannot be explained briefly. We have a cloister in which no lay possessor has a dwelling, but only clerics reside there, rendering from it no rent and no customary due, but offering service only to God and the church of blessed Peter. The houses within the cloister may pass from cleric to cleric, either by gift or by sale, as has happened in our time [Col. 1421C].

For in our time it happened that a certain canon of ours, named Roger, had a house in the cloister from his maternal uncle Walter, a canon and dean. The same Walter possessed it freely and without challenge for many days and years during Roger’s lifetime and for more than fourteen years after Roger’s death, while Lord Adam, knight, brother of the aforesaid Roger, remained alive from that time until now and lived [Col. 1422A] in our city. But Peter, son of this Adam, having this year been girded with the belt of knighthood, brought a complaint against Walter the canon, who held a house which, by hereditary right through his uncle Roger, Peter claimed ought to be his; Roger had received it from his maternal uncle Walter, canon and dean.

Walter replied that he knew nothing of the inheritance asserted by Peter, but that he had bought the house itself from Roger the canon, and had possessed it freely and without challenge, as a canon, for many days and years, both during Roger’s life and after Roger’s death. This house owes no rent and no customary due except its service to God and the church of blessed Peter; and upon this he submitted himself to judgment and justice through competent judges.

We therefore ask that, according to the custom of our cloister which [Col. 1422B] we have described, you write back to us what ought to be pronounced in judgment concerning the complaint of Peter the knight. His father Adam the knight is still alive and makes no claim concerning it, nor has he made any claim hitherto; and concerning the reply of our canon Walter, who bought the house from Roger the canon and possessed it freely and without challenge for so long a time, as a canon, during Roger’s life and after his death. Farewell.

VI. Radulf’s reply to the preceding letter. (The same year.—MARTÈNE, ibid.)

RADULF, by God’s grace archbishop of Reims, to his dearest sons GOSCELIN, dean, and the entire congregation of the church of Beauvais: greeting.

[Col. 1422C] Concerning those matters about which your charity has consulted us, we write this to you by the counsel of our church. If the house concerning which you wrote to us is in the cloister, and no layman ought there to hold possession, competent judges—namely clerics, since the possession is ecclesiastical—ought to judge that Peter, son of Adam, must by no means recover it through his complaint. Farewell.

[Col. 1423]

DIPLOMAS OF RADULF, ARCHBISHOP OF REIMS.

I. [Col. 1423A] For the foundation of the priory of Saint Peter of Rumigny. (Year 1112.)

[Acts of the Ecclesiastical Province of Reims, II, 175.]

I, RADULF, the slight minister of the church of Reims by divine mercy alone, wish all worshippers of the orthodox faith happily to aspire to the joys of the heavenly homeland.

Since the church of Saint Peter of Rumigny had until modern times been subject to the violent dominion of laymen, we have taken care to commit to the memory of posterity by the present record how it was emancipated from their hands and passed into ecclesiastical right, to be governed under the monastic order—from the time of Odo, called the Strong, until that of Nicholas son of Nicholas. That church [Col. 1423B] had customarily passed by succession to the posterity of heirs; and through this detestable abuse, not only were its outward estates, the earthly patrimonies bestowed upon it, diminished, but its inward resources, which concerned the worship of God, had perished through being annulled. For the small number of clerics assigned there for service, oppressed by the unjust dominion of a secular hand, was rendered less able to perform divine offices or even to preserve the slight ecclesiastical resources which remained to them.

At last the aforesaid Nicholas, prompted by the grace of the Holy Spirit and judging it a monstrous crime to possess the sanctuary of God by hereditary law, surrendered the said church of Saint Peter, namely that of the castle called Rumigny, into our hands at the request of Lord Jorann, abbot. He asked and obtained that we devoutly grant it, with all that belonged to it, to the monastery of blessed Nicasius the martyr, over which Jorann presided. He further wished a religious agreement to be added to this petition: that monks should be installed in that church; and that when the Lord should finally call him from this prison of the flesh, the anniversary of his death, and also those of his father and mother, should be celebrated yearly both there and in the monastery of Saint Nicasius.

Assenting that this be done, we received the aforesaid church from his hand and granted it to the monastery of Saint Nicasius to possess perpetually under this condition. Moreover, lest in the course of time disputes should arise from the claims [Col. 1423D] of any presumptuous person against this ordinance, both ours and Nicholas’s, we decreed that a testamentary charter of this gift should be made, and, in order that it might remain unshaken forever, confirmed it by the authority of our seal [Col. 1424A] and by the testimony of lawful persons.

Sign of Azenar, abbot of Saint Remigius. Sign of Hugh, abbot of Hautvillers. Sign of Harderic, abbot of Mouzon. Sign of Hugh, abbot of Saint Basolus. Sign of Jorann, abbot of Saint Nicasius. Sign of Bernard, abbot of Saint Calocerus. Sign of Gervais, archdeacon. Sign of Fulk, archdeacon. Sign of Ebal, provost. Sign of Joffrid, dean. Sign of Lambert, cantor. Sign of Cyricus, vicedominus. Sign of Bartholomew, treasurer.

II. [Col. 1424B] He assigns to the abbey of Saint Remigius of Reims the church of Blessed Mary outside the walls of the castle of Rigestes. (Year 1118.) [D. MARLOT, *Metropolis of Reims*, II, 261.]

Radulf, by God’s grace, though unworthy priest of Reims, to all who are called and glory in being sons of the church of Reims.

It is well known from ancient times that the church of Blessed Mary, situated outside the walls of the castle named Rigestes, had fallen under lay dominion and was subject by hereditary succession to their violent control. But Count Hugh of the said castle, who had long usurped it for himself, considering that it was no small peril for an outsider [Col. 1424C] to approach the sanctuaries of God and possess them by inheritance, chose to provide for his soul and took care to correct what he had done wrongly. Accordingly, through the intervention of Azenar the abbot, he came before us; repenting that he had erred, the said count renounced the aforementioned church into our hands under this religious agreement: namely, that we should grant it to blessed Remigius.

He further wished that the three prebends which he had already granted to certain clerics of his should be permitted to remain theirs in that church; but after their deaths, and the deaths of the others assigned there, it should be at the abbot’s discretion either to install monks or to leave canons there, as they still are. When these terms had been granted by us and by the abbot, we received the aforesaid church from the count’s hand and, by this testamentary charter, granted it with all that belonged to it to blessed Remigius to hold forever. And lest [Col. 1424D] this gift should be annulled through the passage of time, we ordered it to be confirmed by suitable witnesses and by the authority of our seal [Col. 1425A].

Sign of Archbishop Radulf. Sign of Azenar, abbot of Saint Remigius. Sign of Odo (afterward abbot of Saint Remigius). Sign of Hugh, abbot of Hautvillers. Sign of Joffrid, abbot of Saint Theoderic. Sign of Haideric, abbot of Mouzon. Sign of Hugh, abbot of Saint Basolus. Sign of Jorann, abbot of Saint Nicasius. Of the canons of Saint Mary: sign of Nicholas, archdeacon; sign of Cyricus, archdeacon; sign of Ebal, provost; sign of Joffrid, dean; [Col. 1425B] sign of Lambert, cantor; sign of Gerard, Elbert, and Adam, priests; sign of Fulk, Richard, and Albert, deacons; sign of Simon, Albric, and Leo, subdeacons. Of the monks of Saint Remigius: Lambert, prior; Richer; Peter. Of the laymen: Count Hugh, and on his behalf Haimo the castellan, Rainald of Bourg, John of Hautmont, Adam and Albric of Rigestes. Of the men of Saint Remigius: Thomas the mayor, Ernald, Hugh the chamberlain. Of the clerics of Rigestes: Otbert the provost, Dodo, Roiric, Heribert.

[Col. 1425C] Done at Reims in the year of the Incarnation 1118, the eleventh indiction, the tenth year of the reign of King Louis, and the twelfth year of the archiepiscopate of Lord Radulf.

III. Confirmation of the privileges of the collegiate church of Saint Symphorian at Reims. (Year 1119.) [*Gallia Christiana*, vol. X, col. 36, Documents.]

RADULF, though unworthy, by the disposing mercy of heaven archbishop of Reims, to the congregation of the church of the Holy Apostles and Saint Symphorian—to those whom the present existence of our times reaches, and to those whose succeeding posterity is awaited—in perpetuity.

A devout petition of the will ought to be fulfilled when its effect follows it [Col. 1425D]. Therefore, graciously receiving the petition of your charity, we grant you the requested result. Assenting to the requests of your desire, we strengthen by the authority of the present privilege the aforesaid church, in which you have been assigned to serve God, and which is known to have possessed the dignity of an episcopal see during the times of the first nine bishops of Reims.

We confirm to you and your successors, to hold forever, your entire church and all its appurtenances: namely, the demesne holding of Wisterey with the entire village, its viscountcy, ban, and all other appurtenances of that village; the altar of Wisterey with the entire church and its chapels at Matrey, Burigny [Col. 1426A], and Marconicourt; the altar of Fraxina with the whole church and its chapels formerly at Bausey and Ausilerias; likewise the altar of Beruc; the altar of Saint Genevieve with its chapels at Bisannes and Lut; likewise the altar of Mearc with its chapels at Bourg and Corvey; the altar of Coulommes; the altar of Marcheney; the altar of Frasney; the altar of Maure; the altar of Saint Hilary; your houses; and the suburbs situated before the prison gate. Let all these be wholly free from every exaction and right of our officials and those of our successors, as they have hitherto been held.

Moreover, let the treasurer of your church hold in perpetuity, for providing whatever is necessary in the same church, one hundred *journals* of arable land from the endowment of the altar of Saint Symphorian, lying in the territory of Courtemontreuil, with its rent and tithe; and the tithe [Col. 1426B] of the land likewise belonging to the endowment of the altar, which lies in the territory of Nantolio. If anyone bring a complaint against any of you, no person shall be permitted to summon you to suit outside your chapter; rather, in your chapter, through your dean or your abbot, you shall administer justice by the judgment of your canons.

Furthermore, whatever the same church now justly possesses, and whatever it may lawfully acquire in the future through grants of bishops, the generosity of princes, or offerings of the faithful, shall remain firm and unimpaired to you and your successors. To this end we decree [Col. 1426C] that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the same church, take away its possessions, retain or diminish offerings, or harass it with rash exactions; but that all things be preserved whole, to benefit in every way the use of those for whose support and governance they have been granted. And that the text of this our privilege may remain valid and unshaken, we command that it be secured and confirmed by the impression of our seal and the testimony of trustworthy persons.

Sign of Odo, abbot of Blessed Remigius; Hugh, abbot of Hautvillers; Haideric, abbot of Mouzon; Josfrid, abbot of Saint Theoderic; Odo, abbot of Saint Peter of Orbais; [Col. 1426D] Jorann, abbot of Saint Nicasius; Hugh, abbot of Saint Basolus; Durann, abbot of Mourmont; Ursio, abbot of Saint Denis. Of the canons: Nicholas, archdeacon; Ebal, provost; Josfrid, dean; Lambert, cantor.

Gerard, Elbert, Adam, and Odo, priests; Fulcran, Ermonic, Fulchrad, and Richard, deacons; Simon, Gerard, Thomas, and Rodulf, subdeacons.

Done at Reims in the year of the Incarnate Word 1119, the eleventh indiction, in the twelfth year of the reign of Louis, most glorious king of the Franks [Col. 1427A], and the thirteenth year of Radulf’s archiepiscopate.

Fulcrad the chancellor reviewed, wrote, and subscribed it.

IV. The altar of Sorbonne is granted to the monks of Fleury. (Year 1119.) [*Gallia Christiana*, vol. X, col. 37, Documents.]

RADULF, by God’s grace, though unworthy minister and servant of the church of Reims, to his beloved in Christ, the venerable BOSO, abbot of the monastery of Fleury, and to his successors in perpetuity.

The care due to the government entrusted to us compels us, whom gracious divinity has appointed ministers of His Church, to provide with diligent concern for the welfare of churches and monasteries and to give assent to devout desires for good things. Therefore, assenting to the just petitions of your charity, we grant to your monastery the altar of Sorbonne, without succession of incumbents, to hold perpetually. And that the text of this our grant may remain valid and unshaken, we have commanded it to be secured and confirmed by the impression of our seal and the testimony of trustworthy persons.

Sign of Odo, abbot of Blessed Remigius of Reims. Sign of Hugh, abbot of Hautvillers. Sign of Joffrid, abbot of Saint Theoderic. Sign of Hugh, abbot of Saint Basolus. Sign of Haideric, abbot of Mouzon. [Col. 1427C] Sign of Odo, abbot of Orbais. Sign of Jorann, abbot of Blessed Nicasius. Sign of Durann, abbot of Mourmont. Sign of Nicholas, archdeacon. Sign of Ebal, provost, and of others.

Done at Reims in the year of the Incarnate Word 1119, the eleventh indiction, the twelfth year of Louis, king of the Franks, and the thirteenth year of the archiepiscopate of Lord Rodulf.

Fulcard the chancellor reviewed, wrote, and subscribed it.

V. He confirms the possessions of the monastery of Saint Denis at Reims. (Year 1123.) [VARIN, *Administrative Archives of Reims*, I, p. 274. Paris, 1839. Quarto.]

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity . . . . Amen. RADULF, by the most mighty dispensation, though unworthy priest of the church of Reims, to the brethren [Col. 1428A] dwelling in the church of Saint Denis the martyr, in the suburb of our city, in perpetuity.

While, aided by heavenly grace, we administered the archbishopric of Reims, our brother Ursio, abbot of Saint Denis, came before us, humbly imploring that we should cause the altars and other benefices which the vows of the faithful had bestowed upon Saint Denis, and which were contained in various written records, to be brought together into one body; and that by the authority of our seal we should confirm them to Saint Denis to hold perpetually. Inclining a willing ear to his just petition, we assented and granted that it should be done as requested.

The said church held the altars of . . . . [Note: [Col. 1427D] We omit the altars previously mentioned in the charter granted by Archbishop Rainald in 1100.] Saint-Pierre-Mont, Saint-Jovin, Brucigny, Condé, Neuville, [Col. 1428B] Essia, Bocio (thus; perhaps Boeio?), and Brecey. In the diocese of Noyon, the altar of Montcourt. In the diocese of Arras, the altar of Assia. In the diocese of Thérouanne, the altar of Stambere.

Moreover, the same church of Saint Denis held the archbishop’s benefice: the tithe of bread, wine, and all his revenues. It also held certain properties which Gervais, archbishop of good memory, had purchased for it: namely, land and mills at Aulnay. The same archbishop gave that church land situated in the suburb of the city [Note: [Col. 1427D] A bull of Innocent II issued in 1139 (*Cartulary of Saint-Denis*, p. 30) states: “The borough itself from the Vidule gate to the Basilica gate, with its immunity and customary liberty and accustomed parochial right.”], from the Vidule gate to the postern. He further granted it the tithe of the ditches surrounding the city, excepting the land of the saints. From the said postern as far as [Col. 1428C] the Basilica gate, Manasses, his successor, who was later deposed, gave land to the same church.

At the village called Ventiliac, the aforesaid church has the whole tithe of the fields and meadows which had belonged to the archbishops, but half in the holdings. In the village of Tassy and in the village called Seilles, it likewise has the tithe as the eleven female offerers held it. Lord Rainald, archbishop, gave the same church the field of Toirey, between Culmissy and the free town of Saint Mary.

In the village called Attigny [Note: [Col. 1427D] Rainald’s charter containing this gift is found on page 14 of the cartulary and states: “. . . . In the estate of Attigny, once royal, and its dependencies, which divine mercy, through the gift of Lord Hugh, venerable count of Champagne, with the consent and approval of Louis, most glorious king of the Franks, bestowed upon the church of Reims for the table of ourselves and our successors, we granted to that church the tithe of grain, hay, and all lawful revenues, on this condition: that on the first Sunday of Septuagesima a meal be prepared from it for the brethren, that the anniversary of our death be celebrated yearly in the same church, and that, if the revenues exceed the need, the brethren shall have a meal from them on that day.” See Marlot on Attigny, vol. II, p. 327.] Radulf himself gave blessed Denis the tithe of rents, tolls, and *capitulacia*; and, with our counsel and assistance, the chapel of Charleville, with all that belonged to it, yielded to the lordship of the same church, without prejudice to the right of the monastery of Hautvillers [Col. 1428D], in whose parish the chapel is situated. Likewise, with our counsel, Fulk of the village of Bétheny and his wife gave all their possessions to blessed Denis after their deaths.

Adam the canon, surnamed the Great, gave himself to the aforesaid church and [Col. 1429A] a portion of his freehold estates at Boeium and Seleriacum, and at Seven Saltworks, in lands, mills, male and female serfs. Likewise Guy, canon of Saint Mary, gave Saint Denis a parcel of land situated by the stone in the middle of the market-place of Reims, paying yearly ten shillings and nine denarii. Hescelin, count of Grandpré, likewise gave that church his freehold estate at Amblé, in lands, meadows, and woods, with mills and the whole fishery. At Berny the church itself has land, mills, water, male and female serfs, which Count Hugh of Rigestes gave it. At Pont-Fabricé, the same church has the land and freehold of Odo and Rener of Quarnac, for which the church paid twenty-two pounds in the money of Châlons.

Givellus [Note: [Col. 1429D] Givellus’s gift is recorded in these terms in a charter of Archbishop Radulf: “Richerus Balderannus held for some time from Givellus a parcel of land in the Fiscal Field, for which he paid him two shillings in rent for many years. Later he gave Givellus a certain horse worth sixty shillings or more, on the condition that Givellus should give him as a freehold that land which he had held at rent. Givellus received the horse and gave the land to Richerus as a freehold; Richerus possessed it quietly [Col. 1430D] and without any challenge for a long time. Finally, moved by the spirit of repentance, he granted the same land to the church of Blessed Denis as a freehold to possess forever, with the consent and approval of his wife Porcia, his daughters, and their sons. Moreover, the same Richerus, renouncing the world and becoming a canon in that church, ended his life there . . . . Done at Reims in the year . . . . 1119, the eleventh indiction, the twelfth year of the reign of the king of the Franks, and the thirteenth year of our archiepiscopate . . . .” (*Cartulary of Saint-Denis*, p. 18).] [Col. 1429B] of the village of Marmery made himself a canon of Saint Denis, to which he gave nine *journals* of freehold land in the Fiscal Field. Hermenric, canon of the cloister of Saint Mary, gave blessed Denis, for his soul, an oven situated in his freehold at the prison gate.

In the fishery at Amblé the canons of Épernay hold one half; the church of Saint Denis also holds that half from them at an annual rent of five shillings in Provins money. Of all lands belonging to the administrative offices attached to the archbishop’s household, the church of Saint Denis ought to have the tithes, wherever they lie: the whole if its own parishioners cultivate them; but, if they are cultivated by parishioners of others, one half. At Little Mormory the aforesaid [Col. 1429C] church of Saint Denis holds in freehold one mill, one meadow, arable land, and four shillings less one denarius in Châlons money, which Arnulf, surnamed “the Scattered,” of Neufchâteau gave the church for his soul. At Greater Mormory Saint Denis has a fourth part of one mill, which Haimo, priest and inhabitant of that village, gave it.

We grant all the foregoing to the church of Saint Denis to hold in perpetuity; and, in order that it may remain unshaken, we confirm it by the seal of our pontificate and approve it by suitable witnesses.

Sign of Lord Radulf, archbishop. Sign of Lord Odo, abbot of Saint Remigius. Sign of Lord Jorann, abbot of Saint Nicasius. Sign of Ursio, abbot of Saint Denis.
