[Col. 1429D] Sign of Lord Nicholas, archdeacon. Sign of Lord Hugh, archdeacon. Sign of Frearlic, provost. Sign of Joffrin, dean. Sign of Leo, cantor. Sign of Hugh, treasurer. [Col. 1430A] Sign of Adam, Odo, and Albert, priests. Sign of Guy, Ermenric, and Rainer, deacons. Sign of Gervais, Peter, and Gerard, subdeacons. Sign of William, Herbert, and Stephen, readers.

Done at Reims in the year of the Incarnate Word 1124, the first indiction, in the sixteenth year of the reign of Louis, most devout king of the Franks, and likewise the sixteenth year of the archiepiscopate of Lord Radulf.

I, Fulcrad the chancellor, wrote and subscribed it.

VI. He settles a dispute over a certain tithe arising between the church of Saint Timothy and that of Blessed Sixtus. (Year 1123.) [D. MARLOT, *Metropolis of Reims*, II, 281.]

[Col. 1430B]

I, RADULF, by God’s grace, though unworthy minister of the church of Reims, wishing to decide a dispute concerning a certain tithe between the church of Saint Timothy and that of Blessed Sixtus, have settled the doubtful case by the testimony of this present document.

At the time when Master Alberic held the tithe of Saint Sixtus as a benefice from Hugh, treasurer of the Church of Reims, a dispute arose concerning the tithe of a certain cultivated field of Saint Timothy, lying between Viriliacum and Tassieium. The canons of Saint Timothy maintained that half of the tithe from that field belonged to them, because it was land of Saint Timothy; but the abbot of Saint Nicaise, to whose monastery the altar of Saint Sixtus belongs, was prepared to prove by lawful persons and suitable witnesses that the tithe belonged to the Church of Saint Sixtus. Yet, for the sake of peace, we made this settlement between them: from the things produced on that same land, outside the houses of Saint Remigius, the manor, and the gardens, and also outside other buildings to be constructed for agricultural purposes, the aforesaid canons shall receive only half the tithe; while the aforesaid resident clergy, together with their tithe, shall belong to the church of Saint Sixtus. Witnesses of this settlement are Odo, abbot of Saint Remigius, in whose presence it was made; William, abbot of Saint Theodoric; Nicholas, archdeacon; Frederick, provost; Joffrid, dean; Hugh, treasurer; Adam, Odo, and Albert, priests.

VII. [Col. 1430D] He confirms the altar of Saint Julian to the monastery of Saint Remigius at Reims. (A.D. 1124.) [Ibid., p. 282.]

In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit. RADULPH, [Col. 1431A] raised solely by divine mercy to the summit of the Church of Reims, to ODO, venerable abbot of Saint Remigius, and to the brethren of the same place: may you advance for ever from good to better.

Those who abound in temporal goods and are exalted by perishable things ought to exchange transitory possessions for enduring ones, and perishable goods for eternal ones. Considering this, and desiring to provide for our endangered soul, we grant and concede to you and to your church, without attachment to any person and to be held in perpetuity, the altar of Blessed Julian, adjoining the church of Blessed Remigius, because that same church had hitherto held it under the protection of its person, out of love for this same our patron. We ask that [Col. 1431B] the anniversary day of our death be celebrated yearly in common in the aforesaid church. Desiring this charter to remain valid, we confirm it by the testimony of our image [Col. 1432A] and the attestation of suitable persons.

Sign of Nicholas, archdeacon; sign of Hugh, archdeacon; sign of Frederick, provost; sign of Joffrid, dean; sign of Leo, cantor; sign of Odo, sub-treasurer; sign of Adam and Albert, priests; sign of Rainer and John, deacons; sign of Gervase and Stephen, subdeacons.

Done at Reims in the year 1124 from the Incarnation of the Word, in the tenth indiction, in the sixteenth year of the reign of Louis, king of the Franks, [Col. 1432B] and in the seventeenth year of the archiepiscopate of Lord Radulph.

Fulchrad, chancellor, wrote and subscribed.

IN THE YEAR OF THE LORD 1124: CONON, CARDINAL BISHOP OF PRAENESTE

[Col. 1431]

HISTORICAL NOTICE ON CONON

(Ughelli, *Italia sacra*, vol. I, col. 197, among the bishops of Praeneste.)

[Col. 1431C] Conus, or Conon, a German, formerly a regular canon of the Church of Saint Nicholas of Arvasia, a man most distinguished for holiness of life, was made cardinal bishop of Praeneste by Paschal II while the latter was staying in Gaul. In 1111 the same pope sent him as legate to the East. There, when he learned that the impious Emperor Henry had broken faith with the pope and had violently seized Paschal and thrown him into prison, he was kindled with most righteous anger. In a council of bishops convened by himself, he struck the oath-breaking Henry with the weapon of religion, to his everlasting disgrace. Returning to the West, he steadfastly pursued the same censure against the sacrilegious emperor through five councils held in Greece, Pannonia, Saxony, Lorraine, and Gaul; and afterward he secured the confirmation, in 1116, by the fathers of the Roman council of the sentence which he had repeatedly pronounced. [Col. 1431D] He not only achieved this easily, but through this ardent zeal of piety for the pope and head of the Church acquired such a celebrated name that thereafter mortals revered Conon as though he had descended from heaven.

Meanwhile the Germans began to waver in the faith. Therefore Gelasius II, lest the evil spread further, sent Conon, invested with legatine authority, into Germany, since as a German by birth he seemed capable of administering a more effective remedy to his wavering native province. Accordingly, at councils which he himself held both at Cologne and at Fritzlar, he again bound Henry—the head of the disturbance and firebrand of sedition—with the censure of excommunication.

This is that cardinal bishop of Praeneste whom Gelasius II, struggling almost with death at Cluny, proposed to the senate of cardinals as a man most holy and equal to the pontificate, to be chosen. Indeed, the result would have answered the dying pope’s wish, had not Conon, wholly removed from every ambition, diverted the almost rushing enthusiasm of the cardinals away from himself and turned it [Col. 1432D] toward Guy, archbishop of Vienne. In 1119 they accordingly made Guy pope, at Conon’s urging, under the name of Calixtus II.

Baronius calls this bishop of Praeneste—who is said to have refused the pontificate offered to him—Oddo, plainly reversing the name when he ought [Col. 1433A] to have said Conon. For Conon was alive in that same year; in the preceding year he had exercised a legation in Germany; and he is recorded as having subscribed for Calixtus II in 1122. He is mentioned by the abbot of Ursperg and by Sigebert in their chronicles, and by Geoffrey of Clairvaux in a letter to the bishop of Albano. Geoffrey relates that Conon, while holding a council at Soissons in Gaul, condemned the writings of Peter Abelard together with their author, and burned them as contaminated with the poison of heresy.

The following marble inscription, affixed there, reports that Conon dedicated the crypt and altar of Saint Agapitus in the cathedral church of Praeneste. We give it in a text more correct than that of Suarez:

In the year 1116 of the Lord’s Incarnation, on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of February, in the tenth indiction, the altar [Col. 1433B] and crypt of Saint Agapitus the Martyr were dedicated by Lord Conon, bishop of Praeneste. In that altar rest the bodies of the holy martyrs Agapitus, [Col. 1434A] Gordian, and Abundius; and relics of the holy martyrs Milianus and Nympha are deposited.

In 1117 he dedicated the upper part of the same church together with the altar of Saint Agapitus, as another inscription there records. We likewise give it in a text more correct than that of the same Suarez.

RC. In the year 1117 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the month of December, on the sixteenth sacred day, in the eleventh indiction, the upper church and the altar of Saint Agapitus the Martyr were dedicated by Lord Paschal II, pope, in the nineteenth year of his pontificate. In that altar are deposited relics of the Apostles and of the holy martyrs Calixtus, Martin the Pope, Agapitus, Valentinus, Tiburtius, and Sondus; of Blessed Agatha the Virgin; and of Saint Sylvester the Confessor. Present at this dedication were Maifredus, bishop of Tivoli; Berardus, bishop of the Marsi; and [Col. 1434B] the cardinal priests and deacons of the Roman Church. G. G. AURIFEX.

[Col. 1433]

LETTERS OF CONON

I. Synodal letter of Cardinal Conon for the monastery of Saint Quentin of the Mount near Péronne. (A.D. 1115.)

[Mabillon, *Annales Benedictini*, V, 694.]

[Col. 1433C]

CONON, by divine grace bishop of Praeneste and legate of the Apostolic See, to all the faithful, present and future.

While we were exercising our legation in Francia, a complaint arose against Henry, abbot of Saint Quentin of the Mount, from certain monks of Saint Vaast, concerning a piece of land at Botencourt which he defended for himself by a chirograph. Yet the abbot of Saint Vaast and several of his brethren bore witness to that chirograph and did not deny their assent. When this case had thus been brought before us, we sent our letters to those monks, directing them either to cease from their unjust complaint or, if they trusted that they had anything against [Col. 1433D] the chirograph, to present their complaint for determination at the council which we had appointed to be held at Châlons. Therefore, when we held the council at the appointed time, we found that none of those who had anything to say against the abbot of Saint Quentin or his chirograph was present. Thus, by the judgment of the council, we declared that chirograph valid; and, in order that it may henceforth remain firm and inviolate, we confirm it under the protection of this charter by the authority of the Apostolic See.

Done at Châlons in the year 1115 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the eighth indiction.

Witnesses present at this confirmation: the sign of Radulph, archbishop; the sign of Godfrey, bishop of Amiens; [Col. 1434B] the sign of Gualo, bishop of Paris; the sign of William, bishop of Châlons; the sign of John, bishop of Thérouanne; the sign of John, bishop of Orléans; the sign of Philip, bishop of Troyes; the sign of Robert, bishop of Arras.

II. [Col. 1434C] Judgment of Conon, legate of the Apostolic See, for the Church of Hanache, settling the dispute between the abbess of the monastery of Saint Mary and the canons of Miliac. (A.D. 1115.) [P. Louvet, *Antiquités de Beauvais*, vol. I, p. 620, Rouen, 1614, octavo.]

A judgment rendered through Lord Conon, bishop of Praeneste and legate of the Apostolic See, concerning the Church of Hanache, between the abbess of the monastery of Saint Mary, called Saint Paul’s, and the canons of Miliac. The altar of that church belonged to the monastery of Saint Mary, as was maintained without any contradiction by the spokesmen of the abbess herself. Therefore the aforesaid abbess said that she ought to appoint the priest to that church, and that for thirty years up to the day of this hearing she had administered that church by appointing its priest. The canons of Miliac did not refute any part of the abbess’s assertions. But they said only this: since they possessed the greater tithes and a share of the lesser tithes, the priest, after being appointed concerning this matter by the abbess of the same monastery, ought to come to them and remain in that church by their permission. They asserted that this had been their practice for thirty years up to the day of this hearing. These are the arguments of both sides.

It was therefore adjudged that, since the altar was said without contradiction to belong by right to the monastery of Blessed Mary, [Col. 1435A] and since it could not be denied that for thirty years the abbesses of that monastery had sent a priest to the church of Hanache, henceforth, by appointment of the abbess herself and without any recourse to the canons of Miliac, a priest shall be sent to the church of Hanache.

These are the names of the judges: Rainald, abbot of Vézelay, who pronounced the judgment; Goscelin; Halegred, dean of Beauvais; Roger, archdeacon; Gerald, abbot of Saint Lucian; Odo, abbot of Saint Symphorian; Seranus, canon; Drago, canon of Saint Quentin; Eustace, clerk.

This was done at Beauvais in the presence of Lord Conon, bishop of Praeneste, who approved this judgment and confirmed it by the impression of his seal, with Peter, [Col. 1435B] bishop of the Church of Beauvais, presiding.

III. Letter of Conon, legate of the Holy Roman Church, to Theoger, abbot of Saint George. (A.D. 1118.) [D. Bouquet, vol. XIV, p. 210.]

CONON, by God’s grace bishop of Praeneste and legate of the Holy Roman Church, to his beloved brother THEOGER, abbot: in all the labours of this life, the consolation of the Holy Spirit.

The renown of your religious devotion and integrity, and the steadfastness you display in defending truth, have made you known and acceptable to the Roman Church. Therefore, since we have come into Gaul in the exercise of our legation to meet the archbishop of Mainz [Col. 1435C]—Adalbert [Note: [Col. 1435D] The Saxon annalist, under the year 1116, reports that Adalbert was ordained in 1115, on the feast-day of Saint Stephen, 26 December; see Eccard, vol. I of the *Corpus historicum*, col. 634.]—concerning the pallium which we are bringing him, and to discuss certain important matters with him and others, we have judged it necessary to summon you also, so that we may have the counsel and testimony of your paternity. We have sent the abbot of Saint Clement to conduct you to the place of our conference; and we request and command you to come with him without any delay.

IV. Letter of Conon, legate of the Holy Roman See, concerning the election of a bishop for the Church of Metz. (A.D. 1118.) [D. Bouquet, vol. XIV, p. 209.]

CONON, by God’s grace bishop of Praeneste and legate of the Holy Roman Church, to his beloved sons [Col. 1435D] and brethren in Christ—the abbots and clerics assembled in Christ’s name to elect for the Church of Metz—the presence and consolation of the Holy Spirit.

Since I know that you are not ignorant of the sacred canons, and know how the election of a bishop ought to be made, by the authority and command of the lord pope, and moreover at the request of the lord archbishop of Vienne, I have thought it right to write only a few words to you. Let none of you then complain of your small number. I admonish you in the voice of the Lord himself, who says, “Do not fear, little flock,” etc. (Luke 12:32); and elsewhere, “Where two or three are gathered in my name, I am [Col. 1436A] in their midst” (Matthew 18:20). He did not say, “I, Wisdom, dwell among many,” but “I, Wisdom, dwell in counsels” (Proverbs 8:12). Nor should the disagreement of the many trouble you: it is neither new nor unheard of for the clergy and people to be of differing opinion in the election of a bishop. Sacred Scripture therefore judges that one should yield not to the larger party but to the sounder party.

Accordingly, by the same authority, we command you, laying aside partisan hostility, to elect a worthy shepherd for the Church of God. Once he has been elected, whoever he may be, we command that every honour be accorded to him on behalf of God and the Church. If anyone should reject him, we subject that person to excommunication; we decree that his house be called in Israel “the house of the unshod,” that he be held guilty for as many souls as he might have benefited, and we add that on the Day of Judgment he be pelted with hail. Moreover, whatever the bearer of this letter tells or enjoins you on our behalf, receive as though from our own mouth; and do not delay to carry out what you have heard.

V. (A.D. 1118.) [D. Bouquet, ibid., p. 212.]

CONON, by God’s grace bishop of Praeneste and legate of the Apostolic See, to his beloved brother THEOGER: greeting and affection.

We have received, through Brother Alard’s report, the letter of your brotherly affection in which you exhorted the Church of Metz to act steadfastly and confidently. Now, however, with God’s assent, all the children of that church, obedient both to your admonitions and to those of others, and all meeting in a canonical election, have chosen you by unanimous vote and consent as the shepherd provided for them by God. They therefore unanimously and earnestly ask us to give assent to their election and to take measures that they may have you as their shepherd, since they know you to be residing within the bounds of our legation.

For our part, having investigated the testimony concerning your life and conduct, we have found, by God’s grace, nothing that could offend against the sacred canons. Therefore, most beloved brother, by this letter we admonish you and, in admonishing you, command by apostolic authority that you not evade the burden and care imposed upon you—the care of the holy Church of Metz, deprived of the comfort of its own shepherd. Rather, set yourself up as a wall [Col. 1436D] for the house of Israel, and do not neglect in any way to sustain and aid the wavering Church of Christ amid the pressing storms and the most savage fury of persecutors by resisting them, after the example of those saints who, accepting pastoral responsibility in the primitive Church, did not hesitate, when necessity required, to expose themselves to the perils of death in defence of the Church.

But if—may it never be so—you despise the admonitions of the Church and ours, know that you are without doubt liable to the peril of your order, and that no entrance into churches will be open to you unless you consent through obedience. Therefore, again and again admonishing [Col. 1437A] your belovedness, we command you, all excuse set aside, to accept the obedience imposed upon you; and, after accepting it, do not neglect to render obedience to the lord archbishop of Vienne and legate of the Holy Roman Church, so that, having received the blessing of episcopal ordination, you may worthily serve in the Church of Christ.

VI. Letter of Conon, legate of the Apostolic See, to Theoger, bishop-elect of Metz. (A.D. 1118.)

[D. Bouquet, ibid., p. 212.]

CONON, by God’s grace bishop of Praeneste and legate of the Apostolic See, to his beloved brother THEOGER, bishop-elect of Metz: the spirit of obedience together with the spirit of fortitude.

[Col. 1437B] Since the Son of God was obedient to God the Father, you, by evading obedience, have denied that you are his member. See to it, therefore, most reverend brother, that by disobeying you do not become an idolater and are not consigned to eternal fires. You see that the Church of God is suffering, yet you refuse to contend; rather, you have chosen repose in order to labour for eternity. Therefore, by apostolic authority, we admonish you and, in admonishing you, command you humbly to accept the election of the Church of Metz and to present yourself before the Roman legate, the archbishop of Vienne, by Low Sunday, the Sunday of the Lord’s Mercy. Unless you do so, we exclude you from every divine office. And we command your brethren, under the strictest obedience, to assent; unless [Col. 1437C] they do so, we subject them to the same sentence.

By our mercy, we grant you the governance of the monastery of Saint George until, at a suitable time, you are able to elect a worthy shepherd for that church. May the Holy Godhead, most reverend brother, teach you obedience.

VII. Letter of Conon, bishop of Praeneste, to the bishop of Langres on behalf of Arnald, abbot of Saint Peter the Living. (A.D. 1119.)

[*Spicilegium* of D. Luc d’Achery, vol. II, p. 768.]

CONON, bishop of Praeneste and legate of the Roman Church, to JOSCERANNUS, bishop of Langres: greeting.

[Col. 1437D] We have heard the complaint of the venerable Arnald, abbot of the monastery of Saint Peter the Living, against the abbot of Molesme and the abbot of the monastery of Saint John of the Meadow: one of them is taking a church from him, the other a village with its appurtenances. You have already twice fixed a day of hearing for him, but neither you nor the abbots have been willing to attend either of them. Since we understand that the injustice in this matter lies with you, we command—and in commanding beseech—you to do him full justice in this affair. If you are unwilling to do so, know that, since his case falls within our legation, I shall bring his complaint before the lord pope and pursue his cause as far as I can.

VIII. [Col. 1438A] Letter of Conon to Frederick, archbishop of Cologne.—He writes that the king may be excommunicated by him. (A.D. 1120.)

[Martène, *Amplissima collectio*, I, 664, from a manuscript of Saint-Germain-des-Prés.]

CONON, by God’s grace bishop of Praeneste and vicar of the Apostolic See, to his venerable brother FREDERICK, archbishop of Cologne, the half of his own soul: joy and gladness in the Holy Spirit.

We declare to you in the name of the Lord that you must not quickly be moved from your judgment either by the words of our pseudo-brethren or by others who say that it does not belong to you to excommunicate the king, because [Col. 1438B] the king has not been entrusted to us and does not appear to belong to our diocese. To these persons we reply forcefully from the mouth of the lord pope: although he may not have been entrusted to us by diocesan right, nevertheless by the authority of the Holy Spirit and the holy Fathers we ought justly to have excommunicated him for so great a crime. Consider that Blessed Ambrose excommunicated the Roman emperor Theodosius, though Theodosius was not entrusted to him; Ambrose was neither pope, patriarch, nor legate of the Roman Church; and the crime had been committed not in his diocese but at Thessalonica. Certain false brethren have informed us that there is peace between you and the king, but neither the lord pope nor we have been willing to believe it until we see you.

IX. [Col. 1438C] Letter of Conon, legate of the Apostolic See, to the bishop of Nevers.—It treats of the inauguration of Pope Calixtus II. Then it declares the count and his followers excommunicated for sacrileges committed against the church of Vézelay.

CONON, by God’s grace bishop of Praeneste and legate of the Apostolic See, to the venerable and beloved brother, the bishop of Nevers: greeting and fraternal affection in Christ.

We wish to make known to your belovedness what has taken place among us since you departed from us. On the very day on which we separated from one another, by God’s mercy we hastened with our elected leader toward the region of Lyons. Before we reached Lyons, [Col. 1438D] the lord archbishop of Lyons assented to our election and subscribed at Lyons. There, after a solemn procession had been made, he honourably received the lord pope Calixtus and us. The bishop of Angoulême had also subscribed before leaving us and had humbly submitted himself to the lord pope. From there we came to Vienne, where on Quinquagesima Sunday the lord pope was crowned.

When, after leaving him, we came to Vézelay, we discovered to be true the report which, spread abroad by rumour, we had received with sorrow. We were sorrowful, I say, both for the church of Vézelay—for in its injury the mother Church of Rome was injured, since Vézelay is her special daughter—and for the count of Nevers himself, whom we have greatly loved. The count’s retainers broke and burst open the gates of Vézelay and its cloister; they dishonoured with thrown stones the bodies of the holy martyrs Lazarus and Martha his sister, and of the holy martyrs Andeolus and Pontianus; they also dishonoured the cross in which a portion of the wood of the Lord is kept; they beat and stoned the monks; and they seized one of them and, laying hands on him, disgraced him beneath his monastic habit.

For all these things we admonish you and command you by apostolic authority to summon the count on our behalf and admonish him to make reparation for so great a sacrilege. If he says that he did not take part in this crime, accuse him of consenting to it: for, although he himself came to Vézelay on that very day and found all the sacrilegious men who had committed the crime there, he refused—neither voluntarily nor after being warned by the abbot, in the presence of many witnesses—to exact justice or honour, or to make satisfaction to the church of Vézelay, from his men. [Col. 1439B]

Therefore let him fear the sentence of the most holy Pope Lucius, which occurs among other provisions in his first decretal addressed to the bishops of Gaul and Spain:

> “That the property of your churches and the offerings of the faithful, which you have reported to be harassed by certain assailants and taken from you and your churches, is beyond doubt a most grave sin. Scripture testifies when it says: ‘Whoever takes anything from father or mother and says that it is not a sin is a partner of a murderer.’ Our Father, without doubt, is God, who created us; and our mother is the Church, which bore us spiritually in baptism. The prophets, the apostles, their successors, and the decrees of all Catholic Fathers forbid these acts, and such presumptions are judged sacrileges. Following their examples, together with you we drive from the thresholds of Holy Mother Church by apostolic authority and condemn all such presumptuous persons, plunderers of the Church, and alienators of its resources; we judge them to be sacrilegious, and not only them but all who consent to them. For not only those who commit the acts are judged guilty, but also those who consent to those acting. The same punishment embraces perpetrators and those who consent.”

Likewise Pope Symmachus, against invaders of churches:

> “In general, whoever presumes, by dangerous or violent attack, to confiscate, claim, or invade ecclesiastical property, unless he very quickly correct himself by making satisfaction to the church concerned, shall be struck with perpetual anathema. Likewise, those who retain the right of the Church either through grants of princes or certain powerful persons, through some invasion, or by tyrannical power, and leave it as though hereditary to their sons or heirs—as we have heard has already been done by some—unless, warned by a bishop and recognizing the truth, they swiftly restore the property of God, shall be struck with perpetual anathema. For we judge it unjust that we should be deemed keepers of charters rather than defenders of entrusted things, as has been commanded.” [Col. 1440A]

If the count himself despises the privileges of the church of Vézelay, let him hear Pope Anacletus, third from Blessed Peter:

> “The holy Apostles decreed, at the command of their Saviour, that the privileges of churches and priests should remain in force for all time.”

And the secular laws provide:

> “If the privileges of a venerable church have been violated through anyone’s rashness or neglected through simulation, the offence shall, according to the sanction of the laws, be compensated to the church against which it was committed threefold, [Col. 1440B] and our ban shall be paid to us threefold.”

Likewise elsewhere:

> “Sacred, religious, and holy things are no one’s property; for what is of divine law belongs to no one’s estate.”

Likewise Justinian says against those who broke down the gates:

> “Holy things also, such as walls and gates, are in a certain sense under divine law and therefore belong to no one’s estate. We call walls holy because capital punishment has been established for those who commit any offence against walls.”

Yet, dearest brother, we do not wish to exaggerate what occurred, lest we be forced to judge what it deserves. Rather, we wish you to notify the count that he must cause satisfaction for the sacrileges perpetrated by his men—whose names will be subscribed—to be made to us into our own hand by the middle of Lent, and that he must cease thereafter from troubling the Church. If he does not obey, we, following the judgments of the saints quoted above, shall, though unwillingly, strike both him and his land with the sword of anathema after the deadline we have fixed has passed.

These are the names of those who appear to have taken part in that sacrilege: Rainald, provost of Moncellis, and his brother Nicholas; William the marshal; Pagan the butler; Peter the pantler; Odo Camarlancus; Petiz of Moncellis; Theobald the cook; William, provost of Cerciacum; Groslebos; Renald, nephew of Mainfred of the Gate; Berald of Moncellis; the two sons of Aimbert of Moncellis; John Deli; Tardet of Moncellis; [Col. 1440D] Seguin of Moncellis; Guichard, brother of Walter Baticularius; Burgensis of Moncellis, so called by surname; Gaudric of Clamecy with seven companions; and many others, whom, until we name them individually, we leave to be punished by their own consciences if they do not make worthy satisfaction.

IN THE YEAR OF THE LORD 1124: ERNULF, BISHOP OF ROCHESTER

[Col. 1441]

HISTORICAL AND LITERARY NOTICE

(Warthon, *Anglia sacra*, vol. II, preface, p. XXX.)

Ernulf, bishop of Rochester, who held the see from 1114 to 1124, compiled a book concerning the foundation, endowment, charters, legal proceedings, and other matters relating to the Church of Rochester. The dean and chapter of Rochester, with the greatest kindness, sent me the manuscript preserved in the archives of the Church of Rochester. It has become known to many antiquaries of our nation under the title *Textus Roffensis*. At the beginning of the book a very ancient hand placed this title: “Text concerning the church of Rochester, by Bishop Ernulf.”

It contains many records written both in Latin and Saxon: namely, in Saxon, the laws of Kings Æthelberht, Alfred, Guthrum, Edward, Edmund, and Æthelred; in Latin, the ordeal exorcism, the laws of King Cnut, the constitutions of King William I, extracts from papal decrees, the ordinances of King Henry I issued in 1101, the succession of Roman popes and emperors, of the bishops of Jerusalem, and of the four patriarchal sees, and the names of the archbishops and bishops of England, arranged by individual sees from Saint Augustine onward. It also contains, in Saxon, the judgments of the city of London, the genealogy of King Edward from Adam, and the genealogies of all the heptarchs of England from Adam; and, in Latin and Saxon, the privileges, charters, ordinances, and other documents of the Church of Rochester.

There are no items in the manuscript later than Ernulf’s own time, except thirteen names in the catalogue of archbishops of Canterbury and fifteen names in the catalogue of bishops of Rochester, which were added by another hand in different centuries, as is evident from the handwriting and ink. One hand added the names of the six bishops following Ernulf; another, later hand added those of nine further succeeding bishops. To these must be added a few matters concerning events in the time of Bishops John and Ascelin, collected after folio 203. Everything else was written by a hand contemporary with Ernulf.

These matters might perhaps seem trivial, if one had not examined the material concerning the history of Rochester drawn from this manuscript. Then it will readily become clear why we considered it necessary to say these things in advance. Ernulf, moreover, became renowned through other works of learning. Among them is his excellent letter to Walkelin, bishop of Winchester, *On Uncertain Marriages*, published by the Reverend Father Luc d’Achery in his *Spicilegium*, vol. III, p. 410 (folio edition, vol. III, p. 464). The same letter, ascribed to Ernulf, exists in a very ancient manuscript of the Lambeth Library, differing from d’Achery’s text by scarcely a single letter.

Bale, however, erred most disgracefully (*Centuries*, II, ch. 70), by attributing to Arnulf, bishop of Rochester, certain works of Arnulf, bishop of Lisieux, and of Arnold, abbot of Bonneval; he also confused him with Arnulf the priest, whom Platina relates, in his *Life of Honorius II*, to have been removed through the plots of Roman clerics in the time of Pope Honorius II, because he inveighed too sharply against the vices of the Roman curia. In fact, that preacher Arnulf was utterly different from our bishop of Rochester, who died before the pontificate of Honorius began. Truth, however, mattered little to Bale, provided that he could increase the number of enemies of the Roman Church. We, moreover, have selected and transcribed the more notable records of the Church of Rochester from Ernulf’s miscellany, and have now published them for the first time.

[Col. 1443]

COLLECTIONS OF ERNULF, BISHOP OF ROCHESTER, CONCERNING THE AFFAIRS OF THE CHURCH OF ROCHESTER, FROM THE FIRST FOUNDATION OF THE SEE TO HIS OWN TIME, from the *Textus Roffensis*, compiled by Ernulf.

(Henry Warthon, *Anglia sacra*, vol. II, p. 329, London, 1691, small folio.)

Names of the bishops of Rochester.

[Col. 1443A] I. Justus. [Note: [Col. 1443A] Justus, a Roman by birth, was sent to Britain by Pope St Gregory in 601, to assist St Augustine of Canterbury in spreading the faith; and he did so diligently and not unsuccessfully. As the faith spread more widely through the neighbouring districts, Augustine judged it expedient to appoint bishops in nearby cities, and in 604 ordained Mellitus bishop of London and Justus bishop of Rochester. At Augustine’s request King Æthelberht of Kent had built and richly endowed cathedral churches in both cities, dedicated in the former to St Paul and in the latter to St Andrew. After Æthelberht’s death, which occurred on 24 February 616, Justus, compelled by the pagan king Eadbald, Æthelberht’s successor, to leave the country, withdrew to Gaul with Mellitus. When Eadbald shortly afterwards converted to the faith, Justus was recalled and governed the see of Rochester until 624, [Col. 1443B] when, after Mellitus’s death, he was transferred to Canterbury. Bede, *Ecclesiastical History*, I.29; II.3, 5, 6, 7, 8.]. He died on 10 November.

II. Romanus. [Note: [Col. 1443B] When Justus was transferred to the archbishopric of Canterbury, he ordained Romanus bishop of Rochester in his place. Before the end of 627, the year in which Justus himself died, he sent Romanus as envoy to Pope Honorius, who began his pontificate on 28 September 626. Romanus, crossing the sea on this embassy, perished in a shipwreck. Bede, II.8, 20.].

III. Paulinus. [Note: [Col. 1443B] Paulinus, sent to Britain by Pope Gregory together with Justus in 601, was ordained archbishop of York in 625. Driven from York by Cadwallon, king of the Britons, in 633, he returned to Canterbury; and he accepted from King Eadbald and Archbishop Honorius the care of the bishopric of Rochester, which had been vacant for six years, retaining it until his death. He died on 10 October 644 and was buried in Rochester Church, after presiding over the see for eleven years [Col. 1443C] (for I think Bede’s passage must thus be corrected), two months, and twenty-one days. Bede, I.29; II.20; III.14.]. He died on 10 October.

[Col. 1444A] IV. Ithamar. [Note: [Col. 1443C] Ithamar, the first Englishman to attain episcopal rank, was appointed by Archbishop Honorius in succession to Paulinus in the see of Rochester in 644. He was a native of Canterbury, but, in Bede’s judgment, inferior to none of his predecessors in character and learning. The manuscript annals circulated under the name of Asser of St Davids place his accession in 647. Incorrectly, I think; for Bede indicates that he was substituted for Paulinus immediately. In 655 he consecrated Deusdedit archbishop of Canterbury; and, while that archbishop was still in office, and apparently soon afterwards, Ithamar died. Bede, III.14, 20.].

V. Damianus. [Note: [Col. 1444A] Damianus, of the race of the South Saxons, succeeded him, having been consecrated by Archbishop Deusdedit. After his death the see of Rochester, according to Bede, remained vacant for a long time. He seems to have died shortly before Deusdedit, who died on 4 July 664. For when Ceadda came to Canterbury to be ordained archbishop of York, he learned of the death of Archbishop Deusdedit and departed without receiving consecration; and the priest Wighard, designated as Deusdedit’s successor, was sent to Rome to be consecrated. Yet if Damianus had survived Archbishop Deusdedit, both would have received consecration from him. Nor could Damianus have died long before Deusdedit; otherwise the archbishop would have provided him with a successor before his own death. Bede, III.20; IV.1, 2.].

VI. Putta. [Note: [Col. 1444A] Archbishop Theodore, arriving at Canterbury [Col. 1444B] in the middle of 669, ordained Putta bishop of the Church of Rochester: a man learned in ecclesiastical disciplines and especially skilled in chanting according to Roman practice. He attended the synod convened by Theodore at Hertford in 673. In 676 Kent was grievously ravaged by Æthelred, king of the Mercians, and the city of Rochester suffered in the general disaster. The bishop, then absent and lacking practical ability in secular matters, resolved never to return, but withdrew to Sexwulf, bishop of the Mercians. Receiving from him a small church and a modest plot of land, he grew old there, instructing neighbouring districts in the Roman rules of ecclesiastical chant; nor could any arguments persuade him to resume the bishopric he had abandoned. He nevertheless attended the Synod of Hatfield in 680. Bede, IV.2, 5, 12; *English Councils*, I, p. 680.].

VII. Guichelmus. [Note: [Col. 1444B] More correctly, Quichelmus, for this is how Bede calls him. He was consecrated by Archbishop Theodore in Putta’s place about 676; after no long time, compelled by want of resources, he abandoned the bishopric. Bede, IV.12.].

VIII. Gybmundus. [Note: [Col. 1444C] Upon Quichelmus’s departure, Theodore appointed Gebmund in his place. He is said to have attended the Council of Berghamsted in 697, in the first indiction, and to have subscribed King Wihtred’s privilege in 700. Bede, IV.12; *English Councils*, I, pp. 194, 199. Godwin assigned his death to 692; by what authority he did so I do not know. I nevertheless infer that he died before the middle of 693, in which year Archbishop Berhtwald was consecrated by the metropolitan of Gaul. For the consecration of an archbishop seems at that time to have belonged to the bishops of Rochester. The assertion that he was present at the Council of Berghamsted in [Col. 1445A] 697 is shown erroneous by the number of the indiction; and the charters and privileges—if there are any other arguments, we do not dwell much on them—confirm the conjecture. The Rochester Annals confirm it. I eventually discovered in the Peterborough manuscript of the Saxon Annals that he died in 693.].

IX. Tobias. [Col. 1445A] [Note: [Col. 1445A] At Gebmund’s death, Tobias—a man furnished with knowledge of both Greek and Latin, and with extensive learning, and a disciple of Archbishop Theodore and Abbot Hadrian—was ordained in his place by Berhtwald, archbishop of Canterbury. He died in 726 and was buried in the portico of St Paul the Apostle, which he had made for himself inside Rochester Church as a burial place. These matters concerning him are stated by Bede, V.9, 24. He appears to have been consecrated in 693, as Florilegus also suggests. [Col. 1445B] For in the following year he attended the Council of Baccanceld. *English Councils*, I, p. 180. Pseudo-Asser has calculated very badly in the manuscript annals by placing his accession in 715.].

X. Alduulfus. [Note: [Col. 1445B] Aldwulf, ordained by Archbishop Berhtwald in Tobias’s place, was alive in 731. Bede says no more of him than this, V.24. The Saxon manuscript annals place his consecration in 727; Domitian A.8, in 731. He consecrated Tatwine archbishop of Canterbury. In 732 he obtained from Æthelbald, king of the Mercians, a grant to himself and his successors of the annual revenue of one ship, by a charter given in September, in the seventeenth year of King Æthelbald’s reign. He likewise received as a gift from Eadberht, king of Kent, land for ten ploughs at the place called Andscohesham, and secured confirmation of the gift from Archbishop Nothhelm in 738. Rochester Text, fols. 121, 119, 120. Florence says that he died in 741; Symeon of Durham, the Chronicle of Melrose, and pseudo-Asser, in 739.].

XI. Dunno. [Note: [Col. 1445C] Dunno, in English Dun, succeeded Aldwulf in 740 according to Melrose, and was consecrated in 741 according to the Saxon Chronicle. He attended the Synod of Clovesho in 747. *English Councils*, I, p. 242.].

XII. Eardulfus. [Note: [Col. 1445C] The year in which Eardulf succeeded Dunno is uncertain. The Rochester Text first mentions him in 761, when, in the fifteenth indiction, he obtained from Sigered, king of Kent, one and a half acres of land in the city of Rochester for the enlargement of the Church. In the following year King Eardwulf of Kent gave him pasture for twelve herds of swine. In 764 Offa, king of the Mercians, gave him land for twenty ploughs in Aeslingahain; in 765 Ecgberht, king of Kent, gave him certain land within the castle walls. Rochester Text, fols. 122, 123, 124, 126. The Rochester Annals bear still more directly upon the matter, recording that Woldham was granted to him by King Æthelberht in 750.].

XIII. Diora. [Note: [Col. 1445C] Diora, called Dyorannus by others, succeeded before 778, in which year King Ecgberht of Kent gave him and [Col. 1445D] the Church of Rochester land at Bromley and the marsh of Scaga, and confirmed the gift in 779. In 781 the same king gave him land within the city walls and land for ten ploughs at Halling. Rochester Text, fols. 129, 130, 131, 128.].

XIV. Weormundus. [Note: [Col. 1445D] Weremund, in English Worre, succeeded. In 788 Offa, king of the Mercians, gave him land for six ploughs at Trottesclib; and in 789, at the Synod of Celchyth, land for one plough at Broomgeheg. In 790 Æthelberht, king of Kent, gave twenty acres. Rochester Text, fols. 132, 133, 135. The last donation, however, is rendered deservedly suspect by the added subscription of Archbishop Ceolnoth. In an extremely ancient copy among the archives of Worcester Church, only slightly later in date than the council itself, he is indeed found subscribing to Offa’s charter to Worcester Church at the Council of Calcuth held in 789. He attended the council of Baccanceld in 798—or rather that of Clovesho in 803, for there was only one council, and it was held at Clovesho—and appears to have died in the same year. [Col. 1446A] Florence places his death, and the Saxon Chronology the accession of his successor, in 802. But either the council must be said to have been held in 802, or Weremund to have died in 803. *English Councils*, I, pp. 318, 325.].

XV. Beornmodus. [Note: [Col. 1446A] Beornmod succeeded Weremund. According to the Saxon Chronology and Florence, he was consecrated in 802—or rather in 803, if the council at Clovesho is held to have convened that year. In the register of Canterbury Church survives his profession made to Archbishop Æthelhard of Canterbury, by whom he had been consecrated. Æthelhard, however, died in May 803. In 804, in the eleventh indiction, King Cenwulf gave him and his Church of Rochester three ploughlands south of the city; in 838, in the first indiction, King Egbert gave several lands; and in 841, in the fourth indiction, King Æthelwulf gave land at Holanbeorges. Rochester Text, [Col. 1446B] fols. 137, 138, 139. He is recorded as attending the Synod of Celchyth in 816 in *English Councils*, I, p. 328. I pass over his many other subscriptions found in royal charters of about this period in the *Monasticon Anglicanum* and elsewhere. But Florence and the Rochester Annals plainly err in reporting that he died in 804 and yielded his place to Puthric. That Puthric, more correctly called Burthric, did not obtain the bishopric before the very end of the century; and an ancient list of Rochester bishops at the end of the Saxon Chronology confirms that Tadnoth succeeded Beornmod.]

XVI. Tadnothus. [Note: [Col. 1446B] I have nothing else to say of Tadnoth except that the Rochester Text, fol. 122, establishes that he presided over the see of Rochester in the time of Archbishop Ceolnoth and Berhtwulf, king of the Mercians—that is, between 841 and 852.].

[Col. 1446A] XVII. Badenothus. [Note: [Col. 1446B] Nothing survives concerning Badenoth except the name preserved by Ernulf. From Beornmod to Burhric William of Malmesbury and Florence omitted every bishop in their lists of Rochester bishops. In his *On Bishops*, p. 567, Godwin rashly inserted a certain Godwin after Badenoth, for no other reason than that Godwin, bishop of Rochester, is found subscribing, in Ingulf, pp. 488, 490, to a charter of King Wiglaf of Mercia granted to Crowland monastery in 833 and to another of King Berhtwulf in 851—as though any credit should be given, against the evidence of other records, to monastic charters fabricated at pleasure.].

XVIII. Cuthuulfus. [Note: [Col. 1446C] The Rochester Text, fol. 141, says that King Æthelred gave several lands to Bishop Cuthwulf in 868.].

XIX. Suithufius. [Note: [Col. 1446C] The Rochester Text, fol. 142, reports that King Æthelred granted land at Cucolanstan to Bishop Swithwulf in 880, in the thirteenth indiction. The same man, appointed by King Alfred in 897 guardian of western Kent against Danish incursions, died shortly thereafter [Col. 1446D] of plague. Florilegus and the Saxon Chronology.].

XX. Burhricus. [Note: [Col. 1446D] Burhric, called by others Burthric, Burgrice, and Puthric, succeeded. Edmund gave him three ploughlands at Malling, the gift being confirmed by Archbishop Odo; Rochester Text, fol. 143. Edmund began to reign in 941 and ceased in 946. A booklet of the monks of Rochester reports that the manor of Frekingham was granted to him by King Alfred, who died in 901. In 938 he subscribed the charter of King Æthelstan granted to Malmesbury monastery, in William’s *Life of Aldhelm*, p. 32. The claims made by Florilegus and the Rochester Annals concerning his succession in 804, and his subscription of King Berhtwulf’s charter to Worcester monastery in 841 (*Monasticon*, I, p. 122), as well as Godwin’s placing him between Chineferth and Alfstan, are worthless.].

XXI. Ceolmundus. [Note: [Col. 1446D] Nothing else is recorded of him anywhere. He succeeded Burhric after 941.].

XXII. Cynefertus. [Note: [Col. 1446D] Only the name survives. He died before 955.].

XXIII. [Col. 1447A] Aelfstanus. [Note: [Col. 1447A] Alfstan, called Athelstan by others, obtained from King Edgar confirmation of the manor of Bromleage in 955; Rochester Text, fol. 151. He subscribed charters of Edgar granted to Ramsey and Malmesbury monasteries in 974. *Monasticon*, I, p. 236; *Life of Aldhelm*, p. 33. Osbern, in his *Life of Dunstan*, p. 114, teaches that a certain bishop of Rochester died about 984. The brief and very ancient manuscript Rochester Annals, Vespasian A.22, written by the monk Benedict, confirm that this was Alfstan in the following words: “In the year 984 Elfstan, bishop of Rochester, died; Godwin succeeded.” On the dispute between him and King Æthelred, and the siege inflicted upon Rochester on his account in 983, see Florilegus under 983 and Osbern, *Life of Dunstan*, p. 114. Godwin consistently attributes these matters to his successor, but against the truth, [Col. 1447B] as will readily appear from what has been said.].

XXIV. Goduuinus I. [Note: [Col. 1447B] Godwin, called Godric by some, succeeded in 984. In 995, in the eighth indiction, Æthelred gave him six hides at Woldham; in 998, in the eleventh indiction, he restored Bromley, which had been granted in the first years of his reign; and in 1012, in the tenth indiction, he gave him fifteen hides at Stantun and Hiltune. Rochester Text, fols. 155, 154, 158, 160. I omit his subscriptions, by which he validated very many of Æthelred’s charters. More noteworthy is the report of Florence, Hoveden, and others that he was captured by the Danes, together with Archbishop Ælfheah, in the capture of Canterbury in 1011.].

XXV. Goduuinus II. [Note: [Col. 1447B] Malmesbury omits him, but Florence recognizes him with Ernulf. The year in which he entered the bishopric is wholly unknown. Only this is certain: he was alive in 1038. Godwin’s statements about a vacancy following his death are uncertain and supported by no authority. Indeed, nowhere is it found that episcopal sees remained vacant for any length of time under the peaceful rule of King Edward; [Col. 1447C] and there is precedent for two bishops jointly governing a see for seventy-four years. In the Canterbury obituary one Godwin is said to have died on 9 March, the other on 12 April.].

XXVI. Sywardus. [Note: [Col. 1447C] Siward, abbot of Chertsey, quite distinct from Siward, abbot of Abingdon and vicar of Archbishop Eadsige, however much Godwin, following Malmesbury, may dispute it—as shown above, p. 107—was consecrated at Canterbury by Archbishop Stigand in 1058, according to the manuscript Saxon Annals, Domitian A.8 and Peterborough, and Florence. In 1070 he attended the consecration of Archbishop Lanfranc; and in 1072 he subscribed the agreement made between Lanfranc, archbishop of Canterbury, and Thomas, archbishop of York, in Ingulf, p. 92, Oxford edition. He died in 1075 according to the ancient Rochester Annals, Vespasian A.22. Florence incorrectly assigned this to 1067.].

XXVII. [Col. 1448A] Ernostus. [Note: [Col. 1448A] Ernost, a monk of Bec, was consecrated by Lanfranc in the church of St Paul, London, at the beginning of 1076. Surviving scarcely half a year, he died on 15 July. Saxon Chronology and Canterbury Obituary.].

XXVIII. Gundulfus. [Note: [Col. 1448A] His *Life*, p. 291, reports that he was consecrated by Lanfranc in 1077, [Col. 1448B] on the third Sunday in Lent. In that year the day fell on 19 March; consequently both the author of the *Life* and the brief ancient Annals, which say he was consecrated on 21 March, are mistaken. He died on 8 March 1108, the third Sunday in Lent. This is attested by the author of the *Life*, p. 291, and the Canterbury Obituary. The historian of Durham incorrectly gives 7 March.].

XXIX. Radulfus. [Note: [Col. 1448B] Ralph, formerly abbot of Sées in Normandy, was designated as successor by Anselm on 29 June 1108 and consecrated on the following 9 August. Elected archbishop of Canterbury on 26 April 1114, he was enthroned on 17 May, as Eadmer, *Historia Novorum*, pp. 96, 110, states. Godwin incorrectly writes, on Florence’s authority, that Ralph was consecrated on 2 August.].

XXX. Ernulfus. [Note: [Col. 1448B] Ernulf, a Frenchman and disciple of Lanfranc, was first a monk in the monastery of St Lucian at Beauvais, then at Canterbury Church, shortly thereafter prior of Canterbury, and afterwards abbot of Peterborough. He was elected bishop [Col. 1448C] of Rochester on 28 September 1114, enthroned on the following 10 October, and consecrated at Canterbury by Archbishop Ralph on 26 December 1115, according to Eadmer and Florence. He ruled nine years and some days, and died on 15 March 1124, aged eighty-four.].

## Donations made to the Church of Rochester

[Col. 1447C]

In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 600, King Æthelberht founded the church of St Andrew the Apostle at Rochester and gave it Prestefeld, and all the land lying along the Medway as far as the eastern gate of the city on the south side, and other lands outside the city wall towards the north.

[Col. 1447D]

In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 738, Eadberht, king of Kent, gave the church of St Andrew the Apostle at Rochester Stokes and land for ten ploughs in Hoo, called Andscohesham, and entrusted them to Bishop Ealdulf.

In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 764, Offa, king of the Mercians, and Sigered, king of Kent, gave the church of St Andrew Aeslingeham with all its appurtenances, namely Freondesberia and Wicham, that is, twenty ploughlands; and entrusted them to Bishop Eardwulf. Likewise, King Offa and Ecbert, king of Kent, gave the church of St Andrew Bromgeheg and entrusted it to Bishop Diora, and afterwards to Bishop Waermund.

Ecgberht, king of Kent, gave the church of St Andrew [Col. 1448C] Halling—that is, land for ten ploughs—and entrusted it to Bishop Diora.

In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 788, Offa, king of the Mercians, gave the church of St Andrew Trottesclib and entrusted it to Bishop Waermund. Offa, king of the English, died on 12 August.

Cenwulf, king of the Mercians, gave the church of St Andrew [Col. 1448D] Borcstealle and entrusted it to Bishop Beornmod.

In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 838, Ecbert, king of the West Saxons and of Kent, gave the church of St Andrew extensive liberties, and the following manors, Halling and Snodigland; and entrusted them to Bishop Beornmod.

In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 841, Æthelwulf, king of the West Saxons, gave the church of St Andrew Holanbeorgestun and entrusted it to Bishop Beornmod.

In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 870, Æthelwulf, king of the Saxons, gave the church of St Andrew Cucolanstan and entrusted it to Bishop Swithwulf.

Edmund, king of the English, gave the church of St Andrew [Col. 1449A] Malling and entrusted it to Bishop Burhric.

A certain very powerful and honourable man named Brihtric, with his wife Ælfswith, gave the church of St Andrew Damtun, Langafeld, Darent, and Falcheham; and entrusted them to Bishop Ælfstan.

In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 945, Edgar, king of the English, gave the church of St Andrew Bromleage and entrusted it to Bishop Ælfstan.

In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 995, Æthelred, king of the English, gave the church of St Andrew Woldham and Littlebrook and entrusted them to Bishop Godwin. The same king gave the church of St Andrew Stantun and Hiltun, namely fifteen hides of land, and entrusted them to Bishop [Col. 1449B] Godwin.

William I, king of the English, restored Fracenham, land of St Andrew, to Archbishop Lanfranc, which wicked men had unjustly taken away; and Lanfranc rightly restored it to Bishop Gundulf. Lanfranc himself likewise recovered Stokes, land of St Andrew, from the seizure of tyrants and restored it to the aforesaid Bishop Gundulf and his monks. The same King William restored to Rochester Church Denintun and Falcheham, formerly unjustly taken away. Moreover, among the many great benefits that he bestowed upon that church during his life, as the hour of his death approached he gave it one hundred pounds, his own royal tunic, an ivory horn, and many other ornaments. He died on 9 September.

William, son of King William, gave the church [Col. 1449C] of St Andrew his manor of Lamhyth and entrusted it to Bishop Gundulf. The same king granted the liberties which Rochester Church has possessed to this day, and by his charter confirmed the gifts of all the persons named above. He died on 2 August.

Archbishop Lanfranc gave the church of St Andrew the manor of Hedenham for the monks’ maintenance; the aforesaid William, son of King William, granted this. Lanfranc died on 28 May.

The same King William, son of King William, gave the manor of Estun to the church of St Andrew and entrusted it to Bishop Gundulf.

The most noble King Henry bestowed many benefits: namely, the churches of Boxley, Aylesford, Dartford, [Col. 1449D] and Sutton, with the chapels of Wilmington and Kingsdown; likewise the churches of Chislehurst and Woolwich; likewise the tithes of Strood and Chalk; and many other things.

## Concerning the plea at Penenden Heath between Archbishop Lanfranc and Bishop Odo of Bayeux

In the time of the great King William, who conquered the English kingdom by arms and brought it under his dominion, it happened that Odo, bishop of Bayeux and brother of that king, came to England much earlier than Archbishop Lanfranc. He established himself with great power in the county of Kent and exercised there no small authority. Since in those days no one in that county was able to resist a man of such power, Odo, because of the great authority he possessed, seized several lands belonging to the archbishopric of Canterbury and certain customary rights, appropriating them and entering them under his own lordship.

Not long afterwards, however, Lanfranc, abbot of the church of Caen, also came to England at the king’s command; and, by God’s ordering, was raised to the archbishopric of Canterbury and to the primacy of the whole kingdom of England. After he had resided there for some time, he found that many of his Church’s ancient lands were lacking, and discovered that they had been assigned and alienated through the negligence of his predecessors. Having carefully investigated and fully learned the truth, he promptly and energetically petitioned the king concerning the matter. The king therefore ordered the whole county [Col. 1450B] to assemble without delay, together with all the men of the county—Frenchmen and especially Englishmen—skilled in the ancient laws and customs. When they had assembled, they all sat together at Penenden Heath.

Because many pleas concerning the legal recovery of lands, and arguments concerning legal customs, arose there between the archbishop and the aforesaid bishop of Bayeux, as well as between the royal and archiepiscopal customs, and could not be settled on the first day, the whole county was detained there for three days. During those three days Archbishop Lanfranc legally recovered from the bishop of Bayeux, and from the bishop’s aforesaid men and others, many lands then held by the bishop’s men—namely Herbert son of Ivo, Turold of Rochester, Ralph of Curvaspina, [Col. 1450C] and many others—with all the customs and property belonging to those lands: namely Detling, Estoces, Prestetuna, Damtuna, and many other small estates. From Hugh of Montfort he legally recovered Hrocinges and Broc; and from Ralph of Curvaspina, pasture worth sixty shillings on the Isle of Grain.

He recovered all these lands and others so free and quit that, on the day when the plea was concluded, there remained no person in all the kingdom of England who challenged any part of them or made even the slightest claim upon those lands. In that plea he renewed and, having renewed them, legally established not only the named lands and other lands, but all the liberties and all the customs of his Church: *soke*, *sake*, toll, *team*, *flymena-fyrmthe* (“refuge for fugitives”), *grithbrece* (“breach of the peace”), *foresteal* (“obstruction before another”), *heimfare* (“home-entry”), *infangenetheof* (“the right to judge a thief caught within one’s jurisdiction”), with every other custom equal or inferior to these, on land and water, in woods, roads, and meadows, and in all other matters, within and outside the city, within and outside the borough, and in every other place.

It was legally established there by all the worthy and wise men present, and agreed and adjudged by the whole county, that just as the king holds his lands free and quit in his own demesne, so the archbishop of Canterbury holds his lands wholly free and quit [Col. 1451A] in his own demesne. Present at this plea were Geoffrey, bishop of Coutances, who acted in the king’s place and held that court; Archbishop Lanfranc, who, as stated, pleaded and legally established the whole matter; the earl of Kent, namely the aforesaid Odo, bishop of Bayeux; Ernost, bishop of Rochester; Æthelric, bishop of Chichester, a very aged man and most learned in the laws of the land, who was brought by the king’s command in a four-horse wagon in order to examine and expound the ancient customs of the laws; Richard of Tonbridge; Hugh of Montfort; William de Arques; Hamo the sheriff; many other barons of the king and of the archbishop; many retainers of those bishops; and also men from other counties together with the whole county of Kent—men of great number and authority, Frenchmen and Englishmen alike.

In the presence of all these, it was demonstrated by many and most evident arguments that the king of the English possesses only three customary rights in all the lands of Canterbury Church. These are the three rights he possesses. The first is this: if any man of the archbishop digs up the royal road that runs from city to city. The second: if anyone cuts down a tree beside the royal road and throws it upon the road. In these two offences, persons found guilty and arrested while doing such things, whether security has been taken from them or not, shall make such redress as is justly due, upon the prosecution of the king’s officer and by surety.

The third custom is as follows: [Col. 1451C] if anyone sheds blood, commits homicide, or does anything else which may by no means lawfully be done upon the royal road itself, and is caught and arrested while doing so, he shall make redress to the king. But if he is not apprehended there and departs from it once without giving a pledge, the king can justly exact nothing from him.

It was likewise shown in the same plea that the archbishop of Canterbury Church ought justly to possess many customs throughout all the lands of the king and the earl. From the day on which the Alleluia is closed until the Octave of Easter, anyone who sheds blood shall make redress to the archbishop. At every season, both outside and during Lent, whoever commits the offence called *Cilduuite* (‘child-fine’) shall owe the archbishop either the whole or half of the compensation: during Lent the whole, and outside it either the whole or half. He also possesses in all these lands everything that appears to concern the pastoral care and salvation of souls.

After the king heard the settlement of this plea, established by many witnesses and many arguments, he approved it; approving it, he confirmed it with the consent of all his princes; and he firmly commanded that it should thereafter remain unimpaired. This has therefore been written here so that it may serve eternal memory in future, and that the future successors of the same Church of Christ at Canterbury may know what and how great things, among the dignities of that Church, they ought by God’s grant to hold and by perpetual right to demand from the kings and princes of this realm.

## Concerning Fracenham

[Col. 1452A]

WILLIAM, by the grace of God king of the English, to Bishop ERFAST, to Abbot BALDWIN, to PICOT and ROBERT MALET, sheriffs, and to all my other faithful men, greeting.

Know that I have granted Archbishop Lanfranc the manor called Fracenham, just as Harold held it on the day when I crossed the sea, and just as Turbert and Gotin held it from Harold, with all its lands, meadows, pastures, woods, villeins, sokemen, and everything else.

## How Lanfranc restored to the monks the lands taken from the Church of St Andrew and other lands acquired; and concerning Bishop Gundulf

Moreover, it should be noted—and especially made known to all faithful persons in future times—how great was the benefit and honour which this Lanfranc, archbishop of blessed memory, conferred during his life upon the Church of Christ at Canterbury and likewise upon the church of St Andrew at Rochester. For he acquired for his Rochester church, through his prudence and wisdom, not only the lands of Christ Church named above, but also lands under the lordship of various tyrants. He restored to that church the lands which had been taken away and scattered through the negligence of former times: namely Denitun, Stoches, Falcenham, and Fracenham. By something like the force of legal proceedings, he wrested them from the hands of the aforesaid bishop of Bayeux, his men, and other men. And not only these, but other goods as well, he bestowed during his life for the use of the monks whom he first established in that Church.

For those established in the service of God and of the holy apostle Andrew, he took care to provide by definite arrangement everything that seemed necessary for their food and clothing. In this work he was aided and supported in every way by Bishop Gundulf of blessed memory. While Lanfranc too was prior of the church of St Mary at Bec, he had loved Gundulf above all others—then a monk and sacristan of that church—for the merit of his holiness and blessed religious life. Having loved him, Lanfranc caused him to come to England as soon as possible, and set him above everyone else, second only to himself, over his whole household—indeed, over all the property which he possessed in the archbishopric.

Having thus appointed him, and long tested him in every sense of wisdom and prudence, Lanfranc was at last moved by divine prompting to consecrate him devoutly and set him as bishop over the aforesaid Church. Gundulf survived there for thirty-one years. He built anew from the foundations, as it appears today, the church of St Andrew, which was almost ruined by age. He also constructed every building necessary for the monks, insofar as the limitations of the site allowed. He received twenty-two monks, clothed those he had received in the habit of holy religion, and himself blessed and ordained those thus clothed who were fit for sacred orders or worthy of the blessing of holy religion. With all the diligence in his power, both personally and through others, he continually instructed them in the fear and love of God. Having instructed them, he loved and honoured them, after God, above all things; [Col. 1453A] and throughout his life he never ceased, so far as he could, to increase their endowments in many ways.

When he entered upon the bishopric he found no more than five canons in the church of St Andrew. On the day when he departed from this present world, he left more than sixty monks, well read and excellent singers, serving God and His apostle, fearing God and loving Him above all things. Yet among the benefits which he conferred upon them, he performed one worthy of remembrance. Fracenham, which, as has been said, Archbishop Lanfranc had wrested by his prudent management from the unjust power of outsiders and assigned in perpetuity for the monks’ maintenance, Bishop Gundulf retained in the hands of himself and all his successors because the manor was too far distant from Rochester in remote regions. With the licence and advice of the oft-mentioned Archbishop Lanfranc, he gave Woldham to the monks in perpetuity in exchange for it, preferring that he and his successors should make the annual labour of journeying on horseback to seek their maintenance so far away, rather than burden the monks or the poor inhabitants of that village by transporting provisions each year.

## Concerning Falchenham

Among that archbishop’s other benefits, he likewise recovered Falchenham, as we have said above, from the unjust power of the bishop of Bayeux. This was done partly with the assistance of the great King William, for which assistance Ralph, a monk of Caen and then Lanfranc’s chaplain, was sent to the king himself in Normandy; and partly by an agreement concerning money, namely sixty pounds, which the archbishop promised to give that king. Of this sum the king received thirty pounds and remitted thirty. At length, by means of the king’s letters, which Ralph brought back with him to the bishop, and the promised payment, the archbishop obtained the manor and immediately assigned it for the monks’ maintenance, yielding an annual farm of fifteen days.

## How King William, son of King William, at the request of Archbishop Lanfranc, granted and confirmed to the church of St Andrew at Rochester the manor called Hedenham for the support of the monks; and why Bishop Gundulf built the whole stone castle of Rochester for the king at his own expense

The bishop Gundulf, of blessed memory, also bestowed upon them another benefit, no less memorable [Col. 1453D], but rather worthy of veneration throughout all ages to come. For the castle, which is situated in the more beautiful part of Rochester, Gundulf built, in return for the royal grant of that gift which the often-mentioned archbishop had arranged for the aforesaid church for the maintenance of the monks—namely, the giving of the manor called Hedenham, situated in the county of Buckingham. The archbishop could not otherwise give that manor to the church with permanent validity without the king’s grant, because the king’s father had given it to the archbishop only for his lifetime, when he was raised to the archbishopric.

Accordingly, when William, his son, succeeded his father in the kingdom and was asked by the archbishop and bishop to grant that manor, he replied that he wished to receive one hundred pounds in money [Col. 1454A] for the grant. When the archbishop and bishop heard this, they answered together, greatly distressed, that they had no such large sum then available, nor did they know how they could obtain it.

But two friends, favourable to both parties—Robert son of Haimon and Henry, Earl of Warwick—on the one hand respecting the king’s honour and fully observing his will, and on the other promoting friendship and, for the love of God, a great and beneficial honour to the aforesaid church, advised the king that, instead of the money he demanded for granting the manor, Bishop Gundulf, since he was highly skilled and effective in masonry, should build for him, at his own expense, a stone castle at Rochester.

When this was made known to the archbishop [Col. 1454B] and bishop, they said, now beyond doubt even more distressed, that they wholly refused the royal grant; indeed, they would rather the manor itself were sunk in the depths of the sea than that the aforesaid church of St Andrew should be subjected in future times to royal exactions. For whenever anything should happen in that castle through some mishap—whether a breach in its wall or a crack in its masonry—it would immediately be demanded of the bishop or church that it be repaired at regular expense. Thus the bishop and church would be subjected, for all future ages, to the most stringent royal demands.

Terrified by this prospect, each said: “Far be this from me,” said the archbishop. “Far be it from me as well,” said the bishop.

When Earl Henry heard this reply, stirred as it were by the pricks of restrained anger, and giving a sudden murmur of indignation, he said: “Until now I have thought, in my own estimation, that Archbishop Lanfranc was one of the wisest men in the whole world. But now I do not say that he is devoid of understanding—far be it!—nor do I dare to affirm that the wisdom in which he formerly excelled has in any respect continued in force at present.

“For what burden is there,” he said, “in building a castle, even a larger one, for forty pounds, according to the king’s wishes; then, after it is built, showing it to the earl or sheriff of the county, or to any others whom the king may please; once it has been inspected, handing it over complete in every respect; and, once it has been handed over, being entirely quit of it, never thereafter interfering in it [Col. 1454D], nor even looking toward it? The king, moreover, should in no way seek against the bishop or church an occasion for future servitude, but should rather free them from every service; and, as became a king, should wish, for the fear of God and the honour of the age, to preserve them in the fullest liberty.”

At last, persuaded by these and several other arguments of this kind, the archbishop consented. Therefore, when this agreement had been made before the king, Bishop Gundulf built the whole castle completely at his own expense, at a cost, I think, of sixty pounds. As long as it can endure in this world, it will stand as a speaking and manifest testimony to Bishop Gundulf, bearing eternal witness for him: that the manor of Hedenham shall remain for the church and monks of St Andrew entirely free and undisturbed, for ever and ever, from every exaction and claim of the king and of all men [Col. 1455A].

## Grant of King William the Great

**WILLIAM**, by the grace of God king of the English, to **HAIMON** the steward and to all his thegns in the bishopric of Rochester, greetings.

I command and order that the church of St Andrew in the city of Rochester shall have the customs which it had in your lands, whether in grain-rent, pigs, or other things, in the time of King Edward; and that you shall render them.

## On the dispute between Gundulf and Pichot

In the time of William, great king of the English and father of William, king of the same people, a dispute arose between Gundulf, bishop of Rochester, and Pichot, sheriff of Cambridge, concerning a certain [Col. 1455B] piece of land which belonged to Freckenham and lay in Giselham. A servant of the king named Olchete had presumed to occupy it, with the sheriff’s approval. The sheriff said that it was the king’s land; but the bishop maintained that it belonged rather to St Andrew. Therefore they came before the king.

The king ordered all the men of that county to be assembled, so that it might be proved by their judgement to whom the land more rightly belonged. But, when assembled, they declared, out of fear of the sheriff, that the land belonged to the king rather than to St Andrew. Since the bishop of Bayeux, who presided over that plea, did not believe them readily, he ordered that, if they knew what they said to be true, they should choose twelve from among themselves to confirm by oath [Col. 1455C] what they had all stated.

When they had withdrawn for consultation and there been intimidated by the sheriff through a messenger, they returned and swore that what they had said was true. These were Edward of Chippenham, Herold and Leofwine, *saca* of Exning, Eadric of Giselham, Wulfwine of Landwade, Ordiner of Berlingham, and six others among the leading men of the county. When this had been done, the land remained in the king’s hand.

In the same year a monk named Grim came to the bishop, as though sent by the Lord. On hearing what they had sworn, he was greatly astonished and denounced them all as perjurers. For the monk had long been reeve of Freckenham; from that same land he had received services and customary dues as from the other lands of Freckenham [Col. 1455D]; and he had had under him, in that same manor, one of those who had sworn.

When the bishop of Rochester heard this, he came to the bishop of Bayeux and recounted the monk’s words in order. Upon hearing them, the bishop summoned the monk and learned these same things from him. Afterwards he caused one of those who had sworn to come before him. The man immediately fell at his feet and confessed that he was a perjurer. [Col. 1456A] Then, after he had summoned the one who had sworn first, that man too, when questioned, likewise confessed that he was a perjurer.

Finally he ordered the sheriff to send the rest to meet him in London, together with another twelve of the leading men of that county, who had confirmed that what those men had sworn was true. He also caused many of the leading barons from all England to come there. When all had assembled in London, it was judged by both French and English that they were all perjurers, since the man after whom the others had sworn confessed himself a perjurer. Once they had been condemned by this judgement, the bishop of Rochester held his land, as was just.

The other twelve wished to affirm that they had not consented to those who had sworn. But the bishop of Bayeux said that they must prove this too by judicial ordeal [Col. 1456B]. Since they promised to do so but could not accomplish it, they paid the king three hundred pounds, as judged by the other men of their county.

## Donations

Ælfric, priest of Cuxton, formerly a canon of the church of St Andrew, gave the monks one *mensa*—an estate or revenue-unit—rendering twelve pence yearly, for the soul of his wife Godgyfa, and because the monks had honourably buried her.

Ælfwine, son of a priest, together with his wife, gave to the church of St Andrew and to the monks serving God there a marsh within the Isle of Grain, for their souls in perpetuity. In return for this gift [Col. 1456C], the monks promised to perform service to the end, as for a brother and sister.

Goldwine, priest of Rochester, gave the church of St Andrew half a haga in Rochester belonging to Frindsbury. In return for this gift, the monks of St Andrew, at his request, made his son a monk there.

This agreement was made between the monks of Rochester and the wife of Robert the Latinist. This woman held certain land of Frindsbury, which after her death was to pass to the monks of Rochester. Long before her death, therefore, she chose to restore that land to St Andrew and the monks. To make the arrangement more secure, the monks gave her sixty shillings; these were later cunningly extorted by Brodo the priest, who had her daughter [Col. 1456D], and so forth. Witnesses to this agreement are Robert the priest, son of Goldwine the priest, and so forth.

Gilbert, clerk of Hedenham, granted to the church of St Andrew at Rochester three hides of land which he held in demesne at Hedenham, on the condition that, whenever he wished, he should become a monk there. His son Ralph likewise granted and confirmed this in full. Osmund, Gilbert’s son-in-law, is mentioned later.

[Col. 1457]

# Here begins the booklet, or letter, of Ernulf, bishop of Rochester, concerning incestuous marriages. (A.D. 1115)

(Dom Luc d’Achery, *Spicilegium*, La Barre edition, vol. III, p. 464.)

[Col. 1457A] Ernulf, least among those who live under the religious habit, to Walchelin, a man of lofty counsel and most unimpaired integrity, worthy bishop of the church of Winchester: may you live happily while life is here lived, and in the life which has no end may you enjoy true and blessed happiness.

Blessed be God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who has enriched your blessed soul with an abundant ardour of love and longing for Himself, filled it with both worldly and divine counsel and prudence, and, having filled it, adorned it with honourable conduct. That this is so escapes no discerning person: for it is known that your blessedness patiently bears the daily cares of worldly business in defence of the poor; that, in safeguarding the liberty of the Church, you devote your efforts to the necessities of royal majesty [Col. 1457B] and the welfare of the whole kingdom.

Nor is it hidden that, in matters belonging to the episcopal office, you labour without interruption by hand, word, and every other form of care: cultivating both your own life and that of your subjects, and never ceasing carefully and diligently to seek out whatever may promote the formation of both. I learned the truth of this through personal experience when, at Canterbury, you wished me, being there, to share your conversation. For at the time when royal officials had assembled at Canterbury, it happened that your eminence came to the same city. There, rendering to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s and to God the things that are God’s (Matt. 22:21), and briefly setting aside your business, you proposed to me a question concerning the divorce of a certain adulterous wife [Col. 1457C] and preferred to discuss it with me—not so much seeking to know my opinion as, I think, the opinion that ought to be mine, lest perhaps the opinion that ought to be mine might agree with that which you had made your own.

> **Note [Col. 1457C]:** “Agreeing” (*consonantes*). Read *consonaret*: “might agree.”
