The question, then, was whether a wife who had suffered adultery with the son of her husband—not with her own son—ought, on account of that act, to be removed from her husband’s bed by episcopal judgement.

It happened that, holding contrary views on the question proposed, each [Col. 1458A] of us undertook to defend the position he preferred. I therefore attempted by every means to establish that spouses ought to be separated in the manner stated and for the stated reason. I maintained that this should be done both on the counsels of the Fathers, the penitential books, and the custom of the Church—a custom which it is believed is not merely unlawful, but impious, to oppose.

Your holiness steadfastly declared that this must by no means be thought or done, seeking to prove that position by adducing supports from both evangelical and apostolic authority—authority which everyone knows, and already knows, must be opposed to and preferred above every Scripture, every body of learning, and finally every argument. Thus there was a modest and courteous contest on both sides; but, owing to your preoccupations, both of us gently ceased without an examined resolution of the truth [Col. 1458B].

Seeing, therefore, the care which your reverence gave to the aforesaid question, and seeing also that the cares pressing upon your highness, both royal and episcopal, denied you leisure to investigate it, I thought it fitting and useful to set forth and disclose in the compass of a little book what I think concerning the matter before your majesty. The task is indeed difficult, because anyone who does not handle its links and knots incautiously knows that the question of marriage is involved. The great doctor, blessed Augustine, bears witness to this in his book *On Adulterous Marriages*, in these words:

> **Note [Col. 1458C]:** Book I, chapter 25, near the end.

> “I am not unaware that the question of marriages is most obscure and complicated. Nor do I dare to profess that I have yet explained, either in this work or another, all its recesses, or that I could now explain them if compelled.” [Col. 1458C]

Therefore, as I began to say, I wish in a brief writing to reveal to your excellency what I hold concerning the question proposed, so that what could be done less fully by speech may be done more clearly in writing; and that, the more plainly and fully it is expressed, the more attentively it may be heard, the more easily understood when heard, the more firmly remembered when understood, and the more subtly judged [Col. 1459A].

Nor does it seem irrelevant to bring forward the decrees of the Fathers and the custom of the Church, not as offering any opposition to evangelical or apostolic authority, but as joining it in familiar reverence and reverent familiarity.

That all that is to be said may shine with clear light, let the question which I undertake to examine first be arranged in two parts, that is, yours and ours. Thus, with every ambiguity removed, the reader may recognize what our side affirms and what yours denies; and, when the supporting arguments have been set before him, may see without doubt from what source the affirming side affirms and the denying side denies.

First, in due order, let that position with its supports be presented which you judge should be preferred because the excellence of evangelical law defends and strengthens it, while the protection of apostolic persuasion confirms it [Col. 1459B]. I say that it confirms it—I say so on behalf of your position—yet I do not promise that the conclusion can be so established; this will become evident below.

What you maintain, and strive to establish, support, and strengthen by divine law, is this: a wife who has suffered adultery with her husband’s son is not to be separated from her husband by the hand of a bishop on account of that crime. It follows that the testimonies drawn from the Gospel and the Apostle, by which you attempt to prove this, should now be set out in sequence.

Matthew: “Everyone who puts away his wife, except on account of fornication, makes her commit adultery; and whoever marries her when put away commits adultery” (Matt. 5:32). Again, after much intervening matter: “A man shall leave father and mother and shall cleave to [Col. 1459C] his wife, and the two shall be one flesh. Therefore they are no longer two, but one flesh. What God has joined together, let no human being separate” (Matt. 19:5). And shortly afterward: “Whoever puts away his wife, except for fornication, and marries another, commits adultery” (ibid., 19:9).

Mark: “A man shall leave his father and mother and shall cleave to his wife, and the two shall be one flesh. Therefore they are no longer two, but one flesh. What God has joined together, let no human being separate” (Mark 10:7). And again: “Whoever puts away his wife and marries another commits adultery against her; and if a wife puts away her husband and marries another, she commits adultery” (ibid., 10:11–12; printed “14”).

Luke: “Everyone who puts away his wife and marries another commits adultery” (Luke 16:18).

If any reader turns over and runs through all the Scriptures of the Gospels [Col. 1459D], he will find that I have omitted nothing and evaded nothing which might be thought relevant to defending and strengthening your proposition. You seek to summon these things in defence of your position, and you are confident that in them lies the supreme strength of your case. I too approve them and judge them worthy to be approved with reverence. Yet I am not so confident that what is at issue can be proved from them; indeed, I greatly doubt it. This will become clear in the explanation which follows in its proper place. But let us return to the matters proposed.

From the Apostle also, as we have done from the Gospel, collecting aids for your proof, apostolic wisdom, wisely understanding this previously ordained teaching of the supreme Teacher, providently wrote to the Romans: “A woman who is under a husband [Col. 1460A] is bound by the law while her husband lives. But if her husband has died, she is released from the law of her husband. Therefore, while her husband lives, she will be called an adulteress if she is with another man. But if her husband has died, she is freed from the law of her husband, so that she is not an adulteress if she is with another man” (Rom. 7:2–3).

Again, instructing the Corinthians regarding the same law, he says: “Because of fornication, let every man have his own wife and every woman her own husband. Let the husband render the debt to his wife, and likewise the wife to her husband. A woman does not have authority over her own body, but her husband does; and likewise a husband does not have authority over his own body, but his wife does. Do not deprive one another, except perhaps by agreement for a time, that you may be free for prayer; and return again to the same” (1 Cor. 7:2–5). And after a few intervening words: “I command—not I, but the Lord—that a wife not depart from her husband; but if she departs, she should remain unmarried or be reconciled to her husband” (ibid., 7:10–11) [Col. 1460B].

I say that the Teacher of the Gentiles understood wisely and wrote providently those things in which he did not presume to dissent from his own—indeed, the universal and supreme—Teacher: allowing neither spouse, of either sex, to leave what was his or hers or seize what was not; mercifully counselling each to have his or her own; just in one respect, merciful in another, and in both doing the will of his Lord.

This law, granted by so great a teacher and strengthened by so great a testimony, we declare must be violated by no innovation, defiled by no intrusion, and rashly attacked by no opposition whatever.

You enlist this law in defence of your cause, but, with your leave, you ought to consider more sharply what follows from it [Col. 1460C]. For one thing is asked and another is proved. The question is whether a wife made adulterous by her husband’s son ought to be separated from her own husband by episcopal authority. What is proved is that a spouse should not separate himself or herself from a spouse—an innocent person from an innocent person—by personal will and personal authority.

For what else do the aforesaid commandments of the Lord concerning spouses say—commandments which it is clear that the Lord uttered, gave, and made known either in answer to questioners or in teaching his hearers—except the law and covenant by which persons joined to one another are bound to one another, and by which one cannot be dismissed by the other except on account of fornication? What else do the words of the Apostle themselves prescribe, whether they say that one must not depart from marriage [Col. 1460D], or urge that reciprocal marital obligations be fulfilled, or bid people return from discord to harmony? What else, I ask, do they say or cry out, except that those bound by the marriage covenant ought not abandon their mutual covenant?

I mean the covenant commanded from heaven and given to married persons, which they ought to keep as an obligation of right. In the command to observe it, the exception for fornication was made precisely so that it might be understood that the innocent party may dismiss the guilty party on account of fornication.

Having thus presented your part of the question as promised, I think it neither unsuitable nor to be rejected next to set out what we place on our side, what we oppose to yours, and what supporting arguments we bring to bear.

The rulers of the churches, observing the weakness of certain spouses in preserving the laws mentioned above—some falling more readily in the very matter in which they ought to have striven with greater constancy (for they sinned reciprocally among the relatives of spouses, falling the more easily because they conversed more familiarly)—the rulers, I say [Col. 1461A], held councils and decreed laws of such severity as would punish transgressors of this sort and deter others from such wickedness.

They decreed that those who would not maintain conjugal chastity but committed incestuous fornication should, after penance had been imposed, be compelled by episcopal judgement to abstain for ever from lawful intercourse. And not without reason is such presumption to be punished with such loss and penalty: it is not to be tolerated by righteous men but sharply struck down. Those known to have committed unlawful acts are rightly ordered to abstain from what is lawful and permitted.

How much more, then, ought those be punished with strict severity and severe strictness who, prompted by licentiousness, commit acts which the wicked consider criminal and adulterers call unclean and unspeakable? Such shameless people are deservedly compelled to bring forth fruits of repentance, abstain from carnal desires, and avoid embraces, both that they may appease God’s wrath and that they may not commit like acts again [Col. 1461B].

If any bishop, contrary to the rule, ordered this to be done according to his own judgement, he would without doubt command a wicked thing; he would not proceed according to the truth of the Gospel, but would depart from the path of preaching. If, perhaps, any higher authority attempted to presume the same, it would itself, as one separated from God, be terribly struck by canonical punishment.

Hence some have explained the evangelical saying, “What God has joined together, let no human being separate” (Matt. 19:6), as directed specifically against the presumption of human power. For, by the provident ordering of truth, they believe that the word *homo*, “human being,” was added so that human power might be understood to be indicated. By this distinction, power to separate is reserved for divine power, while the possibility of doing so is removed from human power.

That separation plainly is not to be attributed to human power but to God’s judgement, where no one forcibly contrives divorce, but rather the counsel of God does so. For that is shown to have been arranged by divine providence which is known to have been established by decrees of the Fathers, by the force of ecclesiastical discipline [Col. 1461D], and by long-standing custom. Nor should anyone be disturbed if those joined through God are said to be separated by God, as though God were thinking against Himself and changeably altering the unchangeableness of His counsel.

There is no change in the divine counsel where, according to the nature of cases and the diversity of times, different dispositions of heavenly commands are granted. The Gospel shows this when, at one time, a purse is commanded to be carried and, at another, not to be carried. Of this blessed Augustine says in his work against the heretic Faustus:

> “They do not yet understand how commands, counsels, or permissions are changed according to the diversity of times, not through any inconsistency in the one commanding, but by the reasoned ordering of the one dispensing.” [Col. 1462A]

Therefore, instructed by the commands, teachings, and rules of holy bishops, we say that a wife sinning incestuously with her spouse’s offspring ought canonically to be compelled to do penance and, as both councils and the custom and authority of the Church testify, ought by pastoral judgement to be removed permanently from marital intercourse.

> **From the Council of Mainz**
>
> **Note [Col. 1461D]:** First Council of Mainz, A.D. 847, canon 19. The text here varies in some particulars.
>
> “If anyone marries a widow and afterwards commits fornication with his stepdaughter, or with two sisters; or if a woman does so with two brothers, or with a father and son; if anyone violates his brother’s widow, his niece, stepmother, daughter-in-law, cousin, maternal uncle’s daughter, or her widow, or his stepdaughter [Col. 1462B], we order them to be separated and never again joined in marriage.”

The same command is found in the council held at Verneuil (chapters 10, 11, 12), at Mâcon (II, chapter 18), and at Tribur (chapters 41, 44). Since these are numerous and say the same thing, I have thought it unnecessary to include them in epistolary abridgements, lest I become burdensome to ears that are impatient or weary.

A similar ruling applies to those said to have lifted their own children from the sacred font—that is, to have served as their baptismal sponsors. This is well guarded in the sequence of sacred canons and fully and clearly defined in the decrees of the Fathers and councils. Deusdedit, bishop of the Roman and Apostolic Church, says among other things:

> **Note [Col. 1462D]:** Letter to Gordius, bishop of Seville. The reading varies in the editions.
>
> “We have found in the archive of this apostolic see [Col. 1462C] that such cases had already occurred in the Church of the Isaurian Ephesians, and likewise at Jerusalem. The bishops of other cities asked this apostolic see whether men and women who had lifted their own children from the sacred font should return to their own marriage-bed. The most holy Fathers of blessed memory, Julius, Innocent, and Celestine, together with an assembly of many bishops and priests in the church of the prince of the blessed apostles, prescribed and confirmed a prohibition: that women and men who, for whatever reason, received newborn children from the sacred font should by no means take one another back in marriage, but should be separated, lest, at the devil’s instigation, such a sinful vice grow throughout the world and their error increase among all.”

By these and similar rulings is declared the position which, in the question set out, we established above [Col. 1462D].

Moreover, all who have concerned themselves with this matter know that this is and has been the custom and practice of the Church: those who, in their own places, have consulted foreign experts, or, when abroad, local experts in such matters. I myself once saw and heard this while staying at Venice, and learned both to whom and concerning whom it had been done.

I know that this ecclesiastical custom has been preserved by holy Fathers; and I judge it inviolable because it accords with the truth of the Scriptures. Hence the Teacher of the Gentiles says: “If anyone seems contentious, we have no such custom” [Col. 1463A] (1 Cor. 11:16), making known that the Church’s custom must not be rashly violated, since he seeks to support his argument by the authority of commands.

Blessed Augustine well shows, in the book he wrote against Faustus, how great a sin it is to violate the Church’s custom. He says (book XXII, chapter 47): “When it was customary to have several wives, it was not a crime. But now it is a crime precisely because it is not customary.” Again, in his replies to Januarius (*Epistle* 54, chapters 5–6): “Whatever the authority of divine Scripture has foreseen should be done, we must without doubt do as we read. The same is true of what the Church throughout the whole world observes.”

By these statements, whoever confesses its faith and acknowledges its teaching to be his own and holy may freely prove that ecclesiastical custom is firm, valid, and not to be altered by any hostility [Col. 1463B]. Moreover, were not those who established these matters Catholics? Did they not live as Catholics, read the Gospels and the Apostle, preach what they read, and teach through preaching? Why, then, did they command such things if they understood that they ought not be done? Or how did they govern the Church of God and illuminate it by word and example, if, contrary to God, to God’s Apostle, and finally to the welfare of almost the whole Christian religion, they were emissaries of falsehood and heralds of error?

Yet we read, remember, and cite them as men who worthily worshipped God and taught the things of God among the saints. Accordingly, holy Church prudently and reverently received their certainly recognized wisdom, faithfully retained it, strengthened it by custom and antiquity, and rejected no one. It is therefore clear that the commands imposed on such criminals to correct unlawful presumption and chastise wicked depravity were beneficially devised, divinely given, and speak for truth rather than against truth [Col. 1463C].

Furthermore, if they were not established by the universal Church, are they therefore to be rejected? Did all confessors or defenders of the Christian faith decree all statutes and canons with one spirit and the same understanding? Many things were defined by one person and some by several; yet all were gladly received by everyone and scorned by no one.

There is also this. If every divorce of spouses were forbidden by the Lord, except for the cause of adulterous fornication which you cite from the Gospel, no other cause of separation could be admitted [Col. 1463D]. By what right, then, or with what audacity was a new exception introduced by the very preachers of the divine word? For, as mentioned above, they say that spouses ought to be divorced because they have received their own children from the saving font. With what facility and what effrontery, then, was the Lord’s command—clear in meaning and ambiguous to no one—impaired by human beings and another rule put in its place? Or why did the Church accept the exception just mentioned, which the Lord did not except?

Why, I ask, except because they properly understood the commands of God, devoutly received them, and recognized that they could lawfully exercise this authority, while preserving reverence for the canonical Scriptures? Further, who distributed the degrees and kinds of penances according to the quality and quantity of sins, if not the Church of God, instructed by God’s word and taught and governed by God’s Spirit [Col. 1464A]?

For modes of penance are not read in the whole sequence of the Old and New Testaments, although repentance itself is taught by both examples and commands. Who, then, I ask, can, dare, or presume by what right or what novelty to overthrow penitential books strengthened by the Church’s decree and confirmed by custom and antiquity? Surely no one; let no one seize for himself the height of such presumption.

If, then, the other distributions of penance are accepted and administered once accepted, why are those beneficially given in this matter—and contrary to no canonical ruling—rejected or condemned? Finally, it is clearer than light that the Lord governs and directs His Church everywhere and in all things, and through it determines and distinguishes His judgements. On this matter the Church herself cries out joyfully in the Psalm: “The Lord rules me” (Ps. 22:1). And the Evangelist says: “Behold, I am with you” (Matt. 18:20); and elsewhere: “Where two or three are gathered in my name, I am in their midst” (Matt. 18:20). And: “You are not the ones speaking, but the Spirit of your Father speaking in you” (Matt. 10:20).

If, therefore, the Lord dwells in His own, speaks through them and in them, what human being, what believer—who, I ask, being sound-minded and in possession of himself—would deny, reject, or contradict that the decrees of so great men are decrees of God, mercifully provided for human salvation at the prompting of God’s Spirit [Col. 1464B]? Therefore, since clear reasoning shows that these are enactments of the Lord Himself—for though uttered by His heralds, they are issued with Him presiding—they ought to be ranked very high, placed in great honour, and observed with sublime reverence. Certainly they are not without reason kept with such reverence: the Author of all established them through His servants, and the usage and authority of the holy Church strengthened them.

Some, considering human frailty, say that persons fallen into this sin in marriage ought on no account to be separated, lest a greater and worse downfall result from what is intended as their remedy. For when they are thought able to be healed by the rigour of this discipline, their burning incontinence prepares for them a snare and an abyss of fornication.

They prove the impossibility of continence for some from the Gospel passage in which the Lord says: “Not all receive this saying” (Matt. 19:11); and from the Apostle, who, arranging marital beds, says: “Each person has his own gift from God” (1 Cor. 7:7). Hence, among his evangelical words, he also inserted: “Or be reconciled to her husband” (ibid., 7:11), thereby indicating that it is especially preferable to be reconciled to one’s own spouse rather than be joined to another’s [Col. 1464D].

From these sayings they infer: “Therefore, whoever wishes to separate spouses should know that he preaches against the Gospel, thinks against the Apostle, and works against the salvation of many—indeed, labours toward their most miserable destruction.”

I think that objections of this kind must be answered in the manner in which we read that blessed Augustine answered people disobedient in this way:

> **Note [Col. 1465D]:** Augustine, *On Adulterous Marriages*, book II, chapter 10, middle.

> “Do you think that God’s law ought to be changed on account of their incontinence? What if intercourse is prevented by captivity, violence, or illness? Shall the incontinence of any married person, after abandonment of marital chastity and contempt for God’s law, find a remedy for itself in Christian judgement? But if, in mercy toward others because of incontinence, each is permitted to possess what is his or her own, it is judged a fitting punishment that such shameless persons should be separated from what is their own. Incontinence assists the former, lest, without possessing their own, they be unable to remain continent; it assails the latter, because, though they had their own and could have remained continent, they refused to do so, falling more miserably because, neglecting what was their own, they presumed to rush upon what belonged to another.”

Someone says that a man who has not sinned is unjustly condemned, [Col. 1465B]—namely, that he should be separated from a wife with whom he has not sinned. For it is not equitable that a penalty be imposed upon one whose guilt was not equal. To this we answer in the Apostle’s words: “O man, who are you to answer back to God?” (Rom. 9:20). To whom, I ask, has almighty God revealed his counsels? What sin has a man committed whose newly married wife falls ill, or is taken away, or is otherwise so completely alienated from him that, while she lives, he is compelled to remain continent without her? God’s judgments are hidden, but just. How do you know whether God permitted one destined to perish to fall into this condition, in order that, because of humble patience and observance of obedience, he might crown one whom he had predestined to live without end? Perhaps for this reason he willed the innocent man to suffer in this life, so that, proved by such patience, he might place him in eternal life. Or how do you know whether [Col. 1465C] the man whom you pronounce just thereby deserved punishment, and ought not to obtain pardon, because, through negligence or ill will, he did not show his wife that kind and degree of love, correction, and guardianship which, if he were just or prudent, he ought to have shown? Moreover, even if an innocent spouse is not stained by any defilement from the guilt of the other spouse, does it not seem sufficient for a common penalty that they are one body and one flesh, so that, because of the unity of their union, they may justly be afflicted together in the matter for which they were made one flesh?

Having set out both parts of the proposed question, together with the supporting argument for each part, it seems appropriate here briefly to recall the evangelical command [Col. 1465D] which you bring forward and emphasize in support of your case: what it commands to whom, and what bearing it has upon the question, so that it may plainly and beyond doubt appear that one thing is maintained by you and another alleged from the Gospel. Then it will not be inappropriate, nor out of place, to say how the later enactments neither oppose nor contradict the earlier ordinances, and in what way they agree with them and in some measure lend them support.

In the sermon which our Redeemer delivered on the mountain, as recorded by Matthew, after some preliminary statements he said: “Whoever puts away his wife, except on account of fornication, commits adultery” (Matt. 5:32). Elsewhere in the same Gospel we read that he was questioned on the same matter by his tempters in these words: “Is it lawful for a man [Col. 1466A] to put away his wife?” (Matt. 19:3). Mark, removing the ambiguity, expressed it thus: “Is it lawful for a husband to put away his wife?” (Mark 10:2). Here it is plainly shown that what one Evangelist calls “a man,” the other calls “a husband.” Therefore the Saviour, replying to this question and giving the reason in his reply, according to both Evangelists drew the same conclusion: “What therefore God has joined together, let not man separate” (Matt. 19:6; Mark 10:9). In this conclusion, then, what else can or ought we to understand by “man” but “husband,” and by “separate” but “put away”? For he had to answer the same thing concerning the same matter about which he had been questioned. Truth had not come in order to deceive, but rather to remove deceit and teach truth. “The words of the Lord are pure words” (Ps. 11:7). Therefore, “What God has joined together, let not man separate” means the same as if it were said: “What God has joined together, let not the husband put away.” [Col. 1466B]

By this explanation we find that the evangelical teaching simply maintains that no husband may put away his wife—that is, a chaste husband his chaste wife. Since, therefore, he added, “except on account of fornication,” by this qualification he indicated that a chaste husband may put away an incestuous wife. The Apostle too is shown by the words cited above to hold and teach the same view. Since, therefore, this is understood and firmly held on the authority of both Scriptures—that no husband ought to put away his wife, that is, a chaste husband a chaste wife, except as there provided on account of fornication—it might reasonably be inferred that the husband of whom the discussion began, namely, the one whose son defiled her marriage-bed, ought not to reject or put away his own wife, except on account of fornication, [Col. 1466C] if indeed both were just. But since he is chaste and she incestuous, it may rather be proved from the Scriptures that he may lawfully put her away; for this is the force of the words, “except on account of fornication.” What I have said—that the Gospel speaks of chaste spouses—could be proved by reasoning which teaches and leads to that conclusion; but what was proposed by you cannot, as it ought and should, be proved from that sentence.

For your proposition, stated and defended by you as best you could, was that a spouse with whom her son had sinned should by no means be separated from her husband by episcopal authority on account of such wickedness. The question, therefore, concerned a chaste and an incestuous spouse. As I said, the aforesaid sentence of the Gospel, [Col. 1466D] which speaks of two chaste persons, neither approves nor confirms this proposition. For if anyone should attempt to conclude from the general evangelical proposition which says, “Let no husband put away his wife”—that is, a chaste husband a chaste wife—except on account of fornication, that the husband of whom the discussion began ought not to be separated by episcopal authority from his wife on account of incestuous fornication, does the argument proceed correctly and run regularly to its conclusion? I say confidently: not at all. For that evangelical proposition, which declares that the separation of a chaste spouse from a chaste spouse is not to be made, is so distinct and separate from your proposition, which forbids the separation of a chaste spouse from an incestuous spouse, that [Col. 1467A] they have no mutual relation through any force of reason or affinity of proof. For as there is a very great difference between the chaste and the unchaste, so there is no slight difference whether the discourse is directed to the former or the latter, or whether an argument is constructed about these or about those.

Yet there is something drawn by your holiness from the Apostle which seems to supply you with no little confidence. The Apostle says: “Do not defraud one another, except perhaps by agreement” (1 Cor. 7:5). When you hear “by agreement,” you understand that, by equal reasoning, no spouses should be withdrawn from the marital obligation except by mutual consent. But let your holiness observe that the Apostle in that place was not speaking to spouses who had withheld what was due, or seized what was not due. Such are reported to have been those concerning whom [Col. 1467B] the question was proposed by you and long debated by us. Rather, he wrote to those who had kept mutual faith with one another, and who needed more discerningly to understand the extent and character of the agreement by which that faith was to be kept. For this reason, speaking to such persons and devoutly admonishing them concerning the preservation of marital chastity, he prudently taught them the rights of marriage; and, becoming weak with the weak and sympathizing with the frail, he advised them to render the marital due lest they break out into adulteries. Hence it is clear that that apostolic admonition has no bearing on the doubt which caused us to inquire concerning a chaste and an incestuous spouse.

But the statement that spouses may be reconciled seems alone to bear upon the matter and more closely approach the question. For this alone, spoken concerning a chaste and an incestuous spouse, implies that the incestuous person is to be reconciled to the chaste person. This is the principal argument by whose force your side is considered superior and victorious, ours inferior and defeated. For the Apostle says that a woman can be reconciled to her husband. You therefore propose: if reconciliation is lawful according to the Apostle, who can forbid reconciliation against the Apostle? This is cleverly said, indeed, but must be considered more keenly and examined more subtly. For even here the mercy of God will not fail, which can enlighten the blindness of the ignorant and wishes to explain the difficulties of this little question.

The Apostle, recalling the law laid down by the Lord, says: “I command—not I, but the Lord—that a woman not depart from her husband; but if she departs, let her remain unmarried [Col. 1467D] or be reconciled to her husband” (1 Cor. 7:2). Either this or that must indeed happen. Yet it is not necessary that this alone or that alone happen. For it is not necessary to remain unmarried, nor is it necessary to be reconciled. But a woman who remains separated must remain unmarried; for the Lord commands that this be done. Reconciliation, however, is not the Lord’s command but the Apostle’s permission or counsel. Therefore it is lawful to be reconciled, and lawful not to be reconciled. Yet not all women may be reconciled. Those who vow continence by mutual consent ought, after the vow, by no means to expect marriage, once renounced, again.

Accordingly blessed Augustine says:

> [Note: [Col. 1467D] Augustine, *On Adulterous Marriages*, book I, ch. 24.] “What is most rightly vowed, [Col. 1468A] when people have vowed it, must not be broken under any condition if they vowed it without any condition.”

To weaken the force of your opposing argument, it is enough to show that some persons cannot be reconciled. Therefore not all women separated from their husbands are to be reconciled to those husbands by apostolic permission. Since reconciliation is permitted to some but is evidently unlawful for others, the proposed enthymeme is rightly judged frail and weak. Those women may be reconciled for whom the Lord’s law does not forbid it. But those women are not to be reconciled who, through reconciliation and agreement with their husbands, fall into offence against and hatred of their God. Hence it is clear that neither from this further saying of the Apostle can you uphold your side, nor weaken ours [Col. 1468B]—a fact not unknown to anyone who knows how to recognize the truth of things, investigate the meaning of Scripture, distinguish the proper force of words, and understand to what each thing ought to be referred.

Behold: as we proposed, clear reasoning shows that the sacred authorities of Holy Scripture which you enlist as proofs avail and accomplish nothing for the proposition which you undertook to prove. Just as, as has been shown, they provide no support for your side, so neither do they oppose ours nor are they in any way assailed by it. For the later enactments were not devised so that the commands of earlier teachers should perish or be weakened. Rather, they are known to have been imposed upon the lustful and negligent in order that the words of God might be kept inviolate with greater care. [Col. 1468C] For when transgressors of the Lord’s command, despisers of marital chastity, and violators of the kinship of spouses are ordered to be punished by the severity described above, are not sinners of this kind made more careful in observing the commandments—becoming the more cautious as they are frightened by the harshness of the precepts? In these matters there is no doubt that ecclesiastical custom, or the councils of the Fathers, not only does not oppose evangelical or apostolic institution, but serves it, as it were, with a certain reverent obedience. From this one may also infer with evident probability that the measures given for so great a salvation of humankind are pleasing to him who came to minister salvation to humankind.

These points having been arranged, the appropriateness of the place now seems to urge us to set forth at last, in the next place, the judgment on the question which your [Col. 1468D] highness had requested and which has been so long deferred. As has often been said, the Lord commanded that a husband should not put away his wife except on account of fornication. Blessed Augustine, in the book which he composed in expounding the Lord’s Sermon on the Mount, says that this fornication is general: he affirms that fornication is every transgression which makes the soul, when it uses its body wrongly, alien to its Creator. Therefore fornication is not to be understood only of sexual intercourse, but also of theft, sacrilege, homicide, idolatry, and other capital sins which deprive a person of eternal life. According to the explanation of this same doctor, it is lawful for a husband to depart [Col. 1469A] not only on account of his wife’s fornication but also on account of his own: that is, either because she commits fornication or lest he himself commit fornication. For one who departs for either kind of reason is taught to depart on account of fornication.

If, then, a chaste man can live in holiness with an unchaste wife deceived by some form of fornication, so that he neither incurs nor fears that he will incur danger to his soul through her companionship, and if he hopes to provide for her offenses, he finds sound counsel for himself if he does not hastily wish to leave her, but, forgiving her offense, wishes to show and teach her a better way. This is understood to be the point of the Apostle’s counsel: “If any brother has an unbelieving wife, and she consents to live with him, let him not put her away” (1 Cor. [Col. 1469B] 7:12). A few verses later he made plain that this was said not to impose necessity but through mercy seeking the salvation of both, saying: “How do you know, husband, whether you will save your wife?” (ibid., 16).

But the man who sees himself so easily prone to a fall and so exposed to danger that he cannot turn aside in another direction from the utterly evil will of a wicked woman, in this case prudently puts her away because danger presses upon him. Without her he can make his life pleasing to God; with her, amid her defilements, he can redeem his soul at no price, as the Apostle says: “For if we sin willfully, there no longer remains a sacrifice for sins” (Heb. 10:26). Thus, if some woman is held by such a desire for theft, evil deeds, or bodily impurity that she is not merely uncorrected by her husband, [Col. 1469C] but rather compels him by a certain violence, whether pleasant or painful, to commit these things or consent to them, it is better to leave such a woman than to perish with her under a just judgment.

The Council of Elvira well accords with this judgment (ch. 70):

> “If a wife has committed adultery with her husband’s knowledge, it has been decreed that communion is not to be given to him, not even at the end. But if he leaves her, let him receive communion after ten years, if he knowingly kept her, though adulterous, in his house for some time.”

This canon shows how great is the sin in which the man is entangled, and by what judgment of God he is condemned, who wished to consent to his wife’s sin and who did not wish to exclude her when she sinned, but preferred to retain her. How wisely would wise Solomon [Col. 1469D] have utterly expelled his wife rather than allow himself through her to be expelled from God and worship idols. It would have been better to cling to God eternally than to cling wantonly for an hour to such a woman’s embraces.

If any pastor of the Church knew with certainty that spouses under his governance were engaging in sexual intercourse in some such foulness, ought he not most rightly to correct, rebuke, reprove, and finally, if the matter required it, separate them? Since, therefore, there is no doubt that a clean spouse ought to put away an unclean spouse lest he become unclean, no one has doubted that a just husband must not be reconciled to an incestuous wife when it is certain that reconciliation itself exposes him to capital sin. [Col. 1470A] For just as it benefits her to leave him so that she may save her soul, so it benefits him not to be reconciled lest he lose his soul.

Moreover, the Old Testament contains: “Whoever lies with his stepmother, or whoever sleeps with his daughter-in-law, shall surely be put to death” (Lev. 20:11, 12). These precepts were not more deservedly received by the predecessors of the Saviour who came into the world than by his successors. For great Augustine reports that the precepts for the conduct of life given to the ancients have likewise been bestowed upon us, upon whom the end of the ages has come. This does not mean that sinners of this kind are to be punished by bodily death in the New Testament, since by the death of one the whole world has been redeemed from death and a single sacrifice has been offered for the sins of all. Rather, this sin is shown [Col. 1470B] to be unto death for those to whom satisfaction through penitence has not been granted. For in that time they were punished with such death because they had not yet been redeemed from such sin by any sacrifices.

Since, therefore, those who commit this kind of intercourse are believed to reach eternal death—because they do not fear to violate what was threateningly forbidden by the mouth of God speaking face to face with Moses, and refuse to observe the immovability of the commandments, terrifyingly attested by the severity of thunder, fire, clouds, and lightning—it is declared a horrible wickedness, and counted among the greatest crimes, for a son to lie with her with whom his father lay, or for a father to offend against the woman whom his son had had.

Further, the Apostle says: “He who joins himself to a prostitute becomes one body with her” [Col. 1470C] (1 Cor. 6:16). Since, therefore, the son of whom we spoke above became one body with his stepmother through sexual union, he whose son he is has become her son, and she his daughter. If the father should then resume lying with her, he will lie at once with his wife and with his daughter. How great a wickedness this is is known to all, even if I say nothing.

This can also be clearly demonstrated from the ancient deeds of holy David. When Absalom had deprived him of the kingdom, he entered, on counsel, to his father’s concubines, as Scripture testifies: “They spread a tent for Absalom upon the roof, and he went in to his father’s concubines in the sight of all Israel” (2 Kings 16:21). After Absalom’s death and the king’s restoration to the royal house by common consent, the king recoiled [Col. 1470D] from going in to them again, knowing that it was unlawful for him after so great a crime to return thereafter to the same women. Hence it is written: “When the king came to his house in Jerusalem, he took the ten women, his concubines, whom he had left to guard the house, and placed them in custody, providing them with food; and he did not go in to them, but they were shut up until the day of their death, remaining in widowhood” (3 Kings 20:3).

Moreover, it is read to have been determined both by decrees and by councils that no one may lie, up to the seventh degree of kinship, with a woman with whom any person of his own kin has lain; whoever presumes to violate this is judged worthy either to be punished by the laws or struck with perpetual anathema. We too follow this; all acclaim it; we know no one who dissents. [Col. 1471A] If anyone should urge or compel that it be done otherwise, he would surely dissolve binding ordinances and condemn the aforesaid authorities.

After their decree, to restrain this same plague, spouses in later times were also commanded that anyone who had committed similar incest should never return to marital intercourse. This was imposed not only upon incestuous spouses but also, as has been said, upon those who spiritually regenerate their carnal children. This injunction, as is read in the *Penitential Book*, was imposed upon some merely by disciplinary rigor; but upon those of whom we have spoken above it was added out of fear of fornication, so that they should be the more cautious as both the fear of fornication repels them and the severity of obedience restrains them.

[Col. 1471B] Therefore, if any despiser, disobedient person, or presumptuous person transgresses these commandments of God, he is most rightly understood to commit fornication away from God and against God—that is, to alienate his own soul. He deserves condemnation even for one single transgression; but for contempt of all these commands he deserves especially to be rejected by God and utterly cast out. If, therefore, such great precepts, reverently observed by Christians and diligently imposed to preserve Christian fellowship, are nullified by reconciliation between a chaste and an incestuous person, who could judge that such a person may lawfully be reconciled to such a person in such a sin? Especially when the soul which ought to have repented begins, through that very agreement, to be in worse danger, and after bodily fornication commits fornication in mind, which is worse.

What reasoning, counsel, or permission [Col. 1471C] leads a person to a reconciliation which brings him into deadly fornication? Who would advise that anyone ought to be reconciled in a fashion in which he sees that person cannot avoid being separated from God? Which bishop, which sound-minded person, would urge him to return to an agreement which, because of rightly demanding guilt, he should have struck with a severe anathema when formed by another?

Jerome [Note: [Col. 1471D] Jerome, vol. III, epistle 148, below the middle.] in his letter to the presbyter Amandus, who asked whether a woman who had left an adulterous and sodomitical husband and had been forcibly taken by another could communicate with the Church without penance while the man whom she first left was still alive, gave this decision on the question:

> [Note: [Col. 1471D] Ibid., shortly before the end.] I speak of a new matter—or rather, not a new but an old one, confirmed by the authority of the Old Testament [Col. 1471D]. If she leaves her second husband and wishes to be reconciled to the first, she cannot. It is written in Deuteronomy: “If a man takes a wife and has her, and she does not find favor in his sight because of some uncleanness, he shall write her a bill of divorce and give it to her and send her out of his house. When she has gone out and taken another husband, and he too hates her, gives her a bill of divorce, and sends her out of his house—or if he has died—the first husband may not take her again as wife, because she has become defiled and abominable before the Lord” (Deut. 24:1).

If, therefore, adulteresses of this sort, after adultery has been committed, are not permitted [Col. 1472A] to return to their husband’s bed, by what right or law will she be permitted to be reconciled who has committed so great an incest? Once reconciled, she will double the incest and violate the commandment. What has been commanded may not lawfully be left undone; what has been permitted may lawfully be left undone. For one may without sin either be reconciled or not reconciled, provided that no commandment of God is offended. But where a commandment intervenes, permission must cease. For commandment is greater than permission. A commandment is wholly holy; permission, however, is sometimes not free from sin.

It is commanded that a wife not depart from her husband; but if she departs, that she remain unmarried (1 Cor. 7:10). It is permitted: “Let each have his own wife because of fornication; but this I say by way of concession, not command” (ibid. 7:2, 6). Where there was concession, there was room for sin. Therefore, since commandment is greater and permission lesser, where the commandment is present, let permission be at rest.

Great Augustine, whose name is to be uttered with reverence, thus discusses God’s commandments and apostolic permissions in his book *On Adulterous Marriages* [Note: [Col. 1471D] Augustine, book I, ch. 21, below the middle.]:

> “Let this be held first and especially: that unlawful acts are not committed. But where something is so lawful that doing otherwise is not at all unlawful, let what is expedient, or more expedient, be done. Those things, then, which the Lord says as Lord—that is, not by the counsel of one advising but by the command of one ruling—may not be left undone, and therefore are expedient.”

And shortly afterward [Note: [Col. 1472D] Ibid., ch. 22, beginning.]:

> “These ordinances of the Lord must be observed without any reconsideration. For they possess that justice [Col. 1472C] which is before him, whether people approve or disapprove; and therefore one ought not to say that, because of offenses of human beings, or lest people be hindered from the salvation which is in Christ, they are not to be observed.”

And again, after several intervening remarks [Note: [Col. 1472D] Ibid., end of ch. 24 and beginning of ch. 25.]:

> “Nothing unlawful is expedient, and nothing which the Lord forbids is lawful. But in matters left to our power by no binding command of the Lord, let the Apostle be heard, exhorting and counseling in the Holy Spirit, so that either better things may be chosen or things that are not expedient may be avoided. There let him be heard saying: ‘I have no commandment of the Lord, but I give counsel’” (1 Cor. 7:25).

Recognizing the limits of my own measure, I approve these things not from my own judgment or the force of my own understanding, but infer them from the teaching and authority of the sacred Scriptures. I judge that nothing in the Christian religion should be rashly determined; that nothing, if it can be avoided, should be settled without examination by the divine word; yet that something should also be supplied by us, insofar as possible and as reason requires, through rational argument. But if anyone thinks otherwise and chooses to assert and prefer what he thinks with unyielding spirit, this is not to the prejudice of the better judgment—provided only that Scripture’s testimony supports it and the authority of the Lord’s command does not overshadow it. [Col. 1472D]

Observing this judgment of the holy man and, as has often been said, resolving through the fear of discipline [Col. 1473A] to restrain the enormity of the crime, they decreed that spouses to whom, through the devil’s deception, so grave an offense had befallen should not be reconciled. They knew it was safer for a reasonable cause to alter a permission given by an advising servant than irreverently to offend against the venerable and reverend commandment of almighty God. Nevertheless, their marital bond may by no means be dissolved, since, according to the Apostle, it can be loosed only by the death of one party. For he will always be called the husband of his wife, and she the wife of her husband. Let them hear only this: released from the marital obligation, they must neither demand nor render it; henceforth each must remain continent—the chaste spouse during the lifetime of the incestuous spouse, and the incestuous spouse during his or her own lifetime.

For the same kind of fornication, spouses were likewise commanded together to remain continent—namely, those who together received their own children from the water of baptism. For those who despise obedience and transgress God’s commandments are said to commit fornication away from God and against God. God’s commandment is: “Let not a godfather lie with his spiritual co-mother.” Hence it is found written in the decrees of Gregory the Younger [Note: [Col. 1473B] Gregory, Fourth Roman Council, ch. 4.]:

> “If anyone takes his spiritual co-mother in marriage, let him be anathema.”

From this the Church’s custom has prevailed: anyone who has not recoiled from lying with such a woman is to be barred from the thresholds of the Church as the author of an unspeakable crime and, with the agreement of all, commanded to be deprived of Christian communion. Therefore, if the father and mother of a child whom they begot carnally became, by professing on that child’s behalf, spiritual parents, it is not lawful for them—by God’s command, Catholic custom, and the decree of the Fathers—to return to their own bed. For if they are reconciled, they will be drawn into the destruction of the aforementioned fornication.

[Col. 1474A] To strengthen your proofs against our position, you also add the lord Lanfranc, archbishop of glorious memory, who, you say, held and declared concerning the separation of a chaste spouse from an incestuous one what you yourselves hold. For it is widely remembered that a similar dispute arose before that prelate, with several bishops in attendance, between a mother and daughter contending against one another over the daughter’s husband: by the bishops’ judgment the husband whom the mother had usurped for herself was taken from the mother and restored to the daughter. Indeed, venerable Father, that venerable archbishop did what he ought, but did not complete what he should have done. Since the daughter complained of the mother’s robbery and the husband’s deceit, justice dictated that the female robber should rightly be deprived of her plunder and that what was hers—namely, the deceitful husband—should be restored to her who had suffered deceit. In restoring her due by legal right, he did what he ought.

But because he neither prescribed the measure of penance appropriate to the crime committed nor set forth by teaching the nature of future precautions, he did not complete what he should have done. Owing to his outstanding learning, he ought to have settled these matters so as not to leave uncertainty to posterity; but, after resolving the complaint, he preferred to leave them unresolved, lest he seem to usurp the rights of the bishop to whom the matter belonged. Let your glorious blessedness know that we have sometimes discussed this judgment with the lord archbishop; and, because of the loveliness of his humility and the venerability of his patience, since we attended him as intimates, we discussed it familiarly with him. What you object to us—that we understood it in that way at that time—we objected to him; and what we answer you, he answered us.

ANNO DOMINI 1124 . . . . ARNALDUS, ABBOT OF SAINT PETER VIVUS OF SENS

[Col. 1473]

## NOTICE

(*Gallia Christiana nova*, vol. XII, p. 138)

Arnaldus, also Ernaldus, whose election Clarius, an eyewitness, narrates thus:

> “Before Archbishop Richerius died, on the sixth day before the Kalends of January, 1096, he commanded the brothers of the monastery of Saint Peter to elect and provide themselves, during his lifetime, with an abbot. This they did, choosing Arnaldus, the least of all, a monk, and presenting him to the archbishop. In the presence of many persons, he told them who Arnaldus was: namely, one born of humble family and stock, whom he desired to live in such a way as to be worthy to govern those entrusted to him, among whom he himself wished to be one.”

In 1103 he won over Count Hugh of Troyes and his wife Constance. At about the same time he had a dispute with Archbishop Daimbert [Note: [Col. 1473] Baluze, *Miscellanea*, vol. VI, p. 429 ff.], who, contrary to the custom of his predecessors, subjected the churches of the monastery to an interdict. On this matter Arnaldus lodged complaints not only with the supreme pontiff but also with Hugh, archbishop of Lyons, who deferred the affair to a council to be held at Troyes on the Monday after the octave of Pentecost.

For in 1103 Arnaldus went to Rome, and there obtained from Paschal II a very ample privilege on 10 November, in the fifth year of that pope’s pontificate. At the subsequent Council of Troyes he obtained from the Fathers confirmation of Saint Peter’s privilege; he caused Gausbert, dean of the cell of Mauriac and a monk of La Chaise-Dieu, who was disobedient and rebellious against his commands, to be deposed, and substituted in his place Peter of Saint-Balderic, one of his own monks.

These events were the signal of misfortunes. For after the abbot returned, he was seized by soldiers of the Robertines at the instigation of Peter Armarius, who imposed unjust customs on the cell of Mauriac; he was thrown into prison in the castle of Ventadour in the district of Limoges, and was at last freed by Peter, bishop of Clermont. In 1108 he attended the election of William, abbot of Saint-Remigius. In the same year he obtained an ordinance from King Louis VI, as Louis’s grandfather Henry and his father Philip had previously granted.

In 1109 Arnaldus, having learned of the cruel crime of the dean of Mauriac, went again into Auvergne. There, intending to bring an accusation against the offender, he suffered a harsh rebuff, since the bishop of Auvergne secretly favored the criminals. The apostolic legate and the archbishop of Bourges were invoked in vain and could not persuade the man to prevent the obstinate men of Auvergne from pursuing the abbot and his companions with arms and drawn swords. Finally, no remedy remained to curb them except royal authority. Relying therefore on royal power, he compelled the rebels into order in 1110.

Two years later, when war broke out, Arnaldus fortified the borough of Saint Peter with a ditch, hedge, and other defenses suited to protection. In succeeding years, though exhausted by old age, illnesses, and troubles, he carried on a long and vexatious lawsuit with the abbots of Molesme and Saint-Jean of Réome concerning certain estates of his monastery which they had claimed for themselves contrary to right and equity. Nevertheless, in 1120 he conveyed the estate of Pauliac to Guy, abbot of Molesme.

In the same year, while he was traveling to the Council of Beauvais, he was overcome by illness and stayed at Naud; he sent the monk Clarius in his name to the legate Conon. While he remained there, he received sacred relics from Alexander, chaplain of Count Stephen, which Alexander had received from Arnulf, chancellor of King Baldwin. In 1123 he ordered books assigned to divine offices and sacred reading to be copied and put into excellent order. Finally, after twenty-eight years and four months of rule, he resigned the abbacy in 1124.

[Col. 1475]

# LETTERS OF ABBOT ARNALDUS

## I. [Col. 1475A] To Joscerannus, Bishop of Langres.—Concerning the dispute between the abbots of Saint Peter Vivus, Molesme, and Saint-Jean of Réome.

(*Chronicle of Saint Peter Vivus*, in Achery, *Spicilegium*, vol. II, p. 482.)

To his lord Joscerannus, venerable bishop of the people of Langres, brother Arnaldus, abbot of the monastery of Saint Peter Vivus: may you bear the cross of the Lord in such a way as to be able to cross the sea by its oarage.

It is known to your dignity that the lord archbishop sent you his letters at the last synod and appealed to your justice concerning injuries inflicted upon our monastery by the lord abbot of Molesme and Rainard of Montbar. But you postponed the day of the hearing until you should come to Sens. [Col. 1475B] When I appeared before you there, you set a date only concerning Rainard at Retiacum. Although I was overcome by bodily weakness, I nevertheless had myself carried there as if in a litter; but, since neither judge nor respondent was found there, I considered myself badly treated.

Accordingly, we again have recourse to you, asking that you do not allow us to be deprived of justice. Moreover, concerning the church of Retiacum, which we had hoped Rainard still held from us and had not lost, we appeal to your mercy and to that of this holy synod, that whatever right we can demonstrate in it may be awarded to us judicially. Farewell.

## II. To Bernard, Abbot of Saint-Jean of Réome.—On the same subject (ibid.)

To Lord Bernard, his friend, venerable abbot of the monastery of Saint-Jean of Réome, brother Arnaldus, [Col. 1476A] abbot of the monastery of Saint Peter Vivus, greeting in the Lord.

If you and all that is yours are well, we rejoice at it. For although the Lord’s chief commandment is that we love one another, we have nevertheless received you and yours among our especial friends and brethren. Yet when, at the recently held synod of Langres, from which you were absent, we renewed the complaints that we had made at the preceding synod—among other matters concerning the church of Retiacum, which Rainard held from us—we invoked the justice of the lord bishop, from whom we learned that you had occupied it. Therefore, by his counsel, and that of the Cassidenses, we address you concerning this matter and admonish you kindly and charitably to relinquish what is ours. For if—God forbid!—after the fellowship between us and you had been confirmed [Col. 1476B], you deliberately occupied what belonged to us, this is what has turned us to excessive astonishment. And because your monks at Troyes said quite insultingly to our monks that we had, at the synod, made a complaint against your person without mutual hearing of the case, we utterly deny this; and, that you may find us truthful, we send you a copy of the letters which we sent to Langres and now send to you. Farewell, and reply to us appropriately by letter concerning this matter.

III. To King Louis.—He asks permission to transfer the lepers elsewhere. (D. Bouquet, *Recueil*, vol. XV, p. 339.)

To LOUIS, magnificent king of the Franks, his dearest lord, ARNALD, humble abbot of Saint-Pierre-le-Vif, with the whole flock committed to him: greeting and faithful prayers.

[Col. 1477A] At the entreaties of our father, the archbishop of Sens [Daimbert], and of clerics acting on your behalf, we have been pressed to provide our leprous brethren with a place to live, where at first, out of compassion alone, we permitted one person to dwell. But let your Highness know that their number has grown so great that it is altogether intolerable to us and to our townsmen. For that place lies in the midst of our fields and vineyards [Col. 1478A]; consequently, their comings and goings, their frequenting of the place, and their walking about are wholly unbearable. Therefore our archbishop caused another spacious place to be given them and, with their consent, commanded that they should dwell there. Now then, lord, do not take it amiss if we wish to remove our provisions somewhat farther from them, because, by holy truth, we fear that we may be endangered with them by their disease.

ANNO DOMINI 1124. PONTIUS, ABBOT OF SAINT-RUF

[Col. 1477]

LETTER TO THE ABBOT OF CHAUMOUSEY

He answers the questions submitted concerning daily fasting, continuous silence, abstinence from wine, and the woollen garments of the canons of the monastery of Chaumousey.

(Martène, *Anecdota*, vol. I, col. 359, from the manuscript of Stamedium.)

[Col. 1477B] To the most beloved brethren: the abbot, by God’s grace, of the church of Chaumousey, and the whole convent; P., humble minister of the church of Saint-Ruf, together with the assembly of the entire congregation: may you walk upon the royal way, turning neither to the right nor to the left.

Having read the letter of your affection, reverend brethren, we learned that you have put to us certain questions concerning our Rule. Although the authority of your prudence could have answered them more surely, we have perceived, in your consulting us, how great reverence you show to our littleness [apparently to be added: “you show”]. Thus, since you desire an answer to your scrupulous contention, there comes before us the fact that those who try to impose upon your necks a yoke which neither we nor our fathers were able to bear say nothing other than what is answered by this: “We believe that through the grace of God we shall be saved, just as they also.” Therefore, having examined more closely the rationale of the four requirements—namely, daily fasting, continual silence, abstinence from wine, and woollen clothing—we shall undertake, if we can, to meet their objection, supported by the utterance of both Testaments.

We greatly wonder by what authority they so insist that that writing, long known to us, establishes the Rule of blessed Augustine, when in some respects it appears greatly contrary to his life and to his institution, and to that of the other fathers who were founders of this profession; in very many respects it is so obstructed and obscure that it can scarcely, or never, be understood; and in still more respects it is so different that it would become wholly unheard-of throughout the world. When, therefore, it asserts that daily fasting must be observed, it seems to conflict with the sacred canons, which forbid fasting during the Paschal solemnity and on Sundays; moreover, as is read in the life of blessed Augustine, his table sometimes included meat for guests or for certain weaker persons. It seems quite absurd and Jewish not to eat meat and to fast every day. If anyone should insist contentiously that he had meat only for guests and weaker persons, and not for himself, let him read Augustine’s life, and he will plainly find that the holy man could never teach otherwise than he lived.

But when they say that continual silence must be maintained, understand that all things have their season: “a time to keep silence, and a time to speak.” If, therefore, there is a time for speaking and a time for silence, it follows that, according to the prophet, the door of circumstance should be opened at the fitting time. Silence, then, is to be maintained, but not continually. For blessed Augustine says in the Rule: “If a brother commits a fault, admonish him at once.” And elsewhere: “For you are the more harmful, if by keeping silence you allow your brethren to perish whom you can correct by judging them.” We too most strongly approve the continual observance of silence from idle tales.

But their requirement of abstinence from wine, except on Saturdays and Sundays, wholly opposes the life and institution of blessed Augustine, since it is read in his life that his table always had wine; and we have learned also from Solomon that wine drunk in moderation is health to soul and body. In the Rule of blessed Augustine likewise it is commanded: “Subdue your flesh by fasts and by abstinence from food and drink, insofar as health permits.” Observe the words: not abstinence from drinking water, but fitting abstinence from wine is commanded, although longing for bread and craving for water are prohibited in like manner. It is also read in his Life that clerics were always fed and clothed with him, in the same house, at the same table, and from common expenses. He had also established for them that no one should swear, not even at table; if anyone lapsed, he lost one . . . portion. For the number of drinking-cups allotted to the clerics living and dining with him was fixed.

What they assert concerning woollen garments—saying that it is the proper work of fullers to wash not linen but woollen clothing—seems ridiculous, since everywhere, and especially in our regions, fullers wash clothing both linen and woollen. Yet when blessed Augustine ordered in the Rule that garments should be washed at the discretion of the superior, whether by fullers, lest excessive desire for a clean garment should contract inward stains of the soul, it is plainly evident that he meant linen, not wool. For what desire can arise in washing a woollen garment, which seems the more soiled the more it is washed, and is never changed from its appearance except by becoming worse? Thus no desire is shown in the frequent washing of a woollen garment in order that it may appear whiter.

But we, who, though unworthy, desire to live the apostolic life, can prove by clearer testimonies that linen garments are to be used. For James, the brother of the Lord, always wore linen garments. In the Old Testament also our dress is prefigured in many ways. Aaron the priest, at the Lord’s command, is clothed with two linen tunics, namely an outer and an inner one. From the breeches even to the tiara he shines with linen whiteness.

We do not say this because we avoid fasting, silence, or the harshness of garments; rather, according to the measure of our weakness, we observe, desire, and approve them in accordance with the ordinances of our Rule and of the holy Fathers, and we urge you to observe and desire them. But each has his own gift from God. If those brethren intend to climb to the higher summits of the mountain, we do not dissuade them—provided only that he who stands take heed lest he fall. Let little Zoar suffice for us, provided only that we may be saved in it.

Now what could be said more absurd or more monstrous than that division of the daily and nightly office which follows neither Roman, monastic, nor ecclesiastical usage? For, according to the Apostle, our worship must be reasonable. Therefore, if excessive length did not exceed the limits of a letter [Col. 1480B], it should be explained why, in the ecclesiastical office, nineteen psalms, nine lessons, and nine responsories are said on Sunday, and why in the week of Easter and Pentecost three psalms and three lessons are said.

Therefore, brethren, persevere unanimously, with the Lord’s help, in the calling in which you have been called, and cling without hesitation to the footsteps of the fathers who have gone before. Do not be moved from your conviction, either by discourse or by letter; nor be tossed about by every wind of doctrine. Rather, hold firmly what you have heard, seen, and learned; and may the God of peace and love remain always with you all. Amen.

ANNO DOMINI 1137. JOHN OF CONSTANCE

[Col. 1479]

LETTER TO GEOFFREY, ABBOT, RICHARD, PRIOR, AND THE MONKS OF THE MONASTERY OF SAVIGNY; OR PREFACE TO THE BOOK ON ECCLESIASTICAL COMPUTATION

(Martène, *Anecdota*, vol. I, col. 362, from a Savigny manuscript.)

[Col. 1479C] To the most reverend lord and servant of God, GEOFFREY, abbot of Savigny, and likewise to RICHARD, venerable prior of the same monastery, and to the entire convent: JOHN of Constance wishes that they may advance from virtue to virtue, so as to deserve to see the God of gods in Zion.

I render thanks and praise to the divine mercy, because the fruitful olive trees of the house of the Lord, the lofty cedars of Lebanon, indeed the cypresses of Mount Zion, deign by their grace to invite and set me—an idle servant, a tree nearly useless and, like an elm, unfruitful—to support at least the Lord’s vineyard. For you request, my lords, that from the great and wide sea of computistical writings I should select briefly and compile for you in one work those things most necessary for the support and governance of the holy Church of God [Col. 1481A], and that, by writing in plainer and more common speech, as is usually done for children being introduced to a subject, I should make all things clear, interpreting even the names of things and words, and explaining their etymologies.

Although I knowingly stir up against myself the teeth and laughter of many who think differently from me in many matters, nevertheless, trusting gladly in the Lord’s mercy and aided by your merits and prayers, I undertake the requested burden and work, and shall complete it as God grants. If, therefore, I delay its completion somewhat longer than you expect, I humbly ask that my lords not be wearied; for I am seriously hindered by the cold and harshness of midwinter and by ecclesiastical service.

But you, my blessed lords and true philosophers, whose true philosophy is now spread far and wide in human and divine matters—if you find anything useless in this little work, correct it, or inform me that it needs correction. For I know that your holy and venerable community contains many honourable and learned men, who, had it pleased you [Col. 1482A], could have completed this little work more sufficiently and who, where necessary, will be able to amend it.

I wish, however, to warn you beforehand that you may know that in this work I pass over many things from the rules, tables, and calendars of the ancients, because they sometimes err and cannot preserve the path of truth. Since the subject will be those matters that assist ecclesiastical computation, the title of this work shall be *Ecclesiastical Computation*. Its purpose is to treat of that computation according to the courses of the sun and moon, and of what is derived from them. Its usefulness is that a reader instructed by this computation may know how to announce and observe at their proper times and on their proper days the holy Paschal feast, the feast of feasts, the other principal festivals of the year, and the feast-days of saints established by ecclesiastical ordinance [Col. 1482B]; may also calculate the course and condition of times; and may constrain heretics and all who go astray to the path of Catholic truth by authority and reason. May the merciful Lord deign to hear your charity as it prays for us.

ORDER OF MATTERS CONTAINED IN THIS VOLUME.

PASCHAL II, ROMAN PONTIFF.

Notice from the *Bullarium*. 9. Notice from the Councils. 9. Life of Pope Paschal II, by Peter of Pisa. 13. Metrical praise of Pope Paschal II, by Milo the Cardinal. 27. Diplomatic notice. 27.

I.---To Hugh, Abbot of Cluny.---He announces Urban’s death and his own election. 31

XIII.---To Hermann, Bishop of Augsburg. 37

He further decrees that no lay or ecclesiastical person shall summon the abbot or his successors before a secular court; nor shall any bishop compel them to attend a synod, “except in a matter of faith,” or, finally, compel them to abandon the solemnities of their monastery and attend urban affairs. 37

He promises that Daibert, their archbishop, “now patriarch of the city of Jerusalem,” will be defended by him against Arnulf, invader of that see, and commended to “the noble and vigorous man Godfrey, and the other Christian princes still residing in Syria and the regions beyond the sea.” He commends their envoys, “who are to proceed first to Genoa and then to Sardinia.” 44
